## Volume front matter

### Series title page

**The Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, and Economical Library of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have survived from the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, carefully collated with one another and with certain manuscript codices, and corrected with the greatest diligence; continually illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the extensive editions produced during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indices following each individual volume and each author of importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject treated; augmented with works both doubtful and apocryphal, and with others possessing some authority and influence in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indices: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever any one of the Fathers has written on any topic may be seen at a glance, and the other of Sacred Scripture, from which the reader may readily discover which Fathers have commented on the several books of Scripture and in what places in their works they have done so. An exceptionally accurate edition, easily preferable to all others when one considers the clarity of its type, the quality of its paper, the integrity of its text, the perfection of its correction, the variety and number of the works reprinted, the exceedingly convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, and the low price; above all, this collection is a single, methodical, and chronological gathering—first in our library—of six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, drawn from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.**

**Second series**, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of complete courses in the several branches of ecclesiastical learning. Patrology was printed in two editions, one Latin and the other Greek-Latin. The Latin edition is sold for 1,200 French francs; the Greek-Latin edition for 1,300. The purely Latin edition includes all authors, both Western and Eastern; the Eastern authors, however, are presented in it only in Latin translation.

## Ratherius, Bishop of Verona

**Prolegomena**, col. 9.

**First part of the works.**—Six books of the *Praeloquia*, which explain the duties of people of every age, sex, and condition, elsewhere entitled *Meditations of the Heart* and *Agonisticus*, composed between February 935 and August 937, col. 145.—*Life of Saint Ursmar*, abbot and bishop, written around 938, col. 345.—*Deliberative Conclusion* enacted at Liège, when Ratherius, expelled from the see of Liège, urged that it yield to the intruder; # In the year of the Lord 974

## Ratherius, Bishop of Verona

According to the edition published at Verona in the year of the Lord 1765, prepared by Peter and Jerome Ballerini, brothers and Veronese priests.

# Prolegomena

[Col. 0009]

## Dedicatory Letter

[Col. 0009]

Peter and Jerome Ballerini, priests of Verona, respectfully greet Thomas Quirino, Knight and Procurator of the Church of Saint Mark.

There is more than one reason why we present to you, most distinguished Knight and Procurator of Saint Mark, the works of Ratherius, Bishop of Verona, a writer highly celebrated among those of his age—works which we have now collected for the first time, enlarged with unpublished material, and illuminated with great care, and which learned men have long desired.

First of all, you are adorned by many distinctions: the nobility of a most ancient family, a considerable number of illustrious ancestors, and above all your own qualities and prerogatives, which show you to be not an unworthy descendant of your most renowned forebears but their most glorious imitator. Thus, if you draw from those men, abounding in every distinction, anything with which to adorn yourself, there is also much in you that flows back to their honor.

For in the gravest and most difficult public offices entrusted to you, not only Verona, Brescia, and Palma, over which you presided for many years, have admired your diligence, prudence, fairness, justice, humanity, steadfastness, generosity, and piety, your zeal for preserving religion intact, and especially your tireless devotion in carrying out official business and your remarkable endurance of labor and, when necessary, your contempt for danger; England also has admired you, where very recently you discharged an exceptionally honorable extraordinary embassy for the republic.

Accordingly, that same republic, which has reserved certain highly distinguished honors for its most deserving citizens, has given a double testimony to your splendid achievements. After you had borne the labors of Verona, Brescia, and Palma, it elected you, with the great agreement and applause of all, Procurator of the Church of Saint Mark—a dignity for which, apart from the highest principality, there is none greater. Moreover, when it learned that, after completing your extraordinary embassy with the highest praise, you had been admitted by the King of Great Britain into the most distinguished order of knighthood and commended by a most honorable diploma, it approvingly and congratulatorily acknowledged this second degree of honor by a decree through which it wished to proclaim a new testimony to your merits.

All these titles are so great, splendid, and radiant so far and wide—not merely titles of honor but also of authority—that this edition of Ratherius, dedicated and commended to you as it comes to light, could rightly and deservedly promise itself from you not only great splendor but also protection, unless something else more immediately at hand were available.

Yet there are other considerations belonging both to us and to the edition itself. From the time when, as governor and propraetor, you undertook the administration of our Veronese city, you have bound us to yourself by so many acts of kindness that we have judged it necessary, when a suitable occasion arose, to offer you some public testimony of our gratitude and obedience.

No occasion could have been more suitable or opportune than this edition. Just as you, delighted by the finest studies—for whose sake you have built, and continue daily to enlarge, a select library of distinguished books intended not merely for ornament but for your own scholarly pursuits—have shown outstanding love both for those studies and for their cultivators, so we have repeatedly experienced your goodwill and favor toward us and toward our literary labors.

Since, among your other studies, the one that most interests you is the study of the Middle Ages, especially of books that contribute to illuminating the history of the cities under Venetian rule, when you first set out for England, and soon afterward when you returned from there on your way back to your homeland, you passed through this place and asked us when the edition of Ratherius would appear, understanding that it would contain much concerning Verona and other exceedingly obscure events of his age.

We therefore trust that this edition, for which you showed such kindness and a certain eagerness, will not be unwelcome to you. We also judged that, if it were offered to you, nothing could be more suitable for providing and preserving for future ages a public and perpetual memorial not only of your services toward us but also of our gratitude toward you.

Accept, then, this small gift of ours, whatever its worth. If it seems less worthy of your greatness, we nevertheless hope that the very modesty of the gift will be raised up by the greatness of your kindness toward us.

Finally, we ask you not to cease extending to us that favor and protection with which you have long encouraged us, if you perceive in the dedication of this edition the respect that we owe and are able to show you.

[Col. 0011]

# Preface to the Edition of the Works of Ratherius

[Col. 0011A]

## I

After the edition of the works of two Veronese bishops—Saint Zeno, who flourished in the fourth century, and John Matthew Giberti, who flourished in the sixteenth century—our attention and thoughts were seized by the collection and edition of the works of our own Ratherius, likewise Bishop of Verona. Although he lived in the tenth century, the most corrupt and obscure of all centuries, he nevertheless distinguished himself by uprightness of conduct, zeal for discipline, devotion to letters, and every branch of learning, so that he is among the most celebrated and highly praised writers of that century.

How widespread vice was at that time, and how greatly ignorance occupied the minds of men, is well known. Hence not a few heterodox writers took occasion to attack the Church, as though, amid the darkness covering that century, ecclesiastical discipline had been especially corrupted and the ancient purity of the faith had failed. “No one,” they say, “came forward to confront the evils raging everywhere—namely, ignorance and unrestrained license.”

To refute this injurious prejudice against the Church, although it cannot be denied that in this century, amid the thickest darkness of ignorance, morals were exceedingly corrupt, it can nevertheless be demonstrated that everything was not then so depraved that the Church lacked men distinguished both by holiness of conduct and by learning, men who opposed the vices raging around them and preserved and handed down intact the pure doctrine of the faith received from antiquity.

For this reason it is especially advantageous to the public interest to bring the ecclesiastical authors of this century to light and to illuminate their deeds and works accurately. Since Ratherius was especially eminent among them, we owe a great debt of praise to those who extracted and published certain of his minor works from the libraries in which they lay hidden.

Now, however, to gather into a single body those works printed separately and scattered here and there, to add whatever else can be found that has not yet been published, and to illuminate everything with the author’s life and annotations, as we have undertaken to do, will be of much greater benefit. We trust that learned men will approve it.

### § I. On the author’s renown and on the usefulness and excellence of his works

## II

A discussion of Ratherius’s character and stricter manner of life—which contributes greatly to recommending the name and authority of an ecclesiastical writer—will be given in the *Life* to be placed after this preface. At present we must speak of his renown on account of the distinguished learning by which he was especially ennobled.

We shall bring forward writers of his own age, who attest the common opinion and reputation of the man, so that there will be no need to rely on the testimony of later writers, who merely repeat what they drew from them.

First we should hear Everaclus, Bishop of Liège, who addresses our Ratherius in a letter in these words:

> “Who is more distinguished than you in wisdom, integrity, devotion to the liberal arts, innocence, or any other kind of excellence?”

Similarly, two contemporary authors, Rotgerus in the *Life of Saint Bruno, Archbishop of Cologne*, no. 34, and Fulcuinus in *The Deeds of the Abbots of Lobbes*, chap. 23, use exactly the same words, one having borrowed them from the other:

> “Because of the abundant learning and copious eloquence by which he appeared to flourish among the wisest men, he was thought likely to be of great benefit not only to that Church over which he presided but also to many others throughout the surrounding regions.”

Liutprand, deacon of Pavia and later Bishop of Cremona, likewise a contemporary of Ratherius, writes in *History*, book III, chap. 11:

> “A certain monk named Ratherius had come into Italy with the aforementioned Hildwin. Because of his religious life and his knowledge of the seven liberal arts, he was appointed Bishop of Verona.”

Hence he came to be commonly called “learned” (*Itinerary*, no. 2), or, as is recorded elsewhere (*Discord*, no. 7, and *The Madness*, no. 11), his wisdom was praised throughout the entire century—that is, everywhere.

## III

Lest these statements be thought more glorious than true, it must be observed that from childhood he devoted himself entirely to the study of letters. He applied himself not only to sacred authors but also to secular historians, orators, poets, and philosophers.

For this reason certain questions were proposed to him, first by the Milanese and afterward by Robert, Archbishop of Trier, which had to be resolved from secular authors, as we learn with certainty from his letter to that Robert.

The works that survive sufficiently demonstrate his knowledge of the ancient secular writers. He not only cites them repeatedly but also often inserts verses and sayings from them without mentioning their names, and uses, as it were, their language and formulas.

He devoted himself to this study before becoming a bishop. “After I had received the episcopal insignia,” he says in the letter to Robert mentioned above, “I immediately ceased doing that, reflecting that, once this office had been imposed upon me, I ought rather to meditate day and night on the law of God.”

Thus he turned himself entirely to the study of Sacred Scripture, the holy Fathers, and the canons. His secular learning, with which he had been enriched, proved all the more useful to him because he converted it to a better purpose, just as the Israelites benefited from the spoils of the Egyptians.

## IV

It is astonishing to relate how great his devotion was to reading, so that it may most truly be said of him that he handled the ancient writers by night and handled them by day.

For this reason his critical reviewers reproached him with it in *The Conjecture of Character*, no. 2:

> “He always keeps his nose in a book”;

and in no. 5:

> “As soon as he can, he returns to his lodging and takes up his book. … If he were allowed, he would sit all day alone, turning and re-turning books.”

Whatever he read he retained so firmly in his memory that he repeatedly inserted very long passages, in the same words, into his own works without the assistance of the books themselves.

This became manifest to us especially from the books of the *Praeloquia*. Although he composed this exceptional and very extensive work while confined in the prison at Pavia and deprived of books, he nevertheless wished to explain in it nothing except what was drawn chiefly from the statements and teaching of Scripture and the holy Fathers; and sometimes he wrote out entire chapters excerpted from them by memory.

When we compared these passages with the books of the Fathers themselves, we were repeatedly and profoundly astonished that the words generally corresponded word for word, as though he had transcribed them from a codex.

We admit that at times, though more rarely, he varies certain expressions slightly while retaining the meaning. This nevertheless confirms that he drew the text not from a book but from memory.

In the confinement of that prison, and especially in the deprivation of books which he twice testifies to in the passage cited, it might perhaps have been possible for him to receive one or another book on loan from someone. But the same cannot possibly be supposed of the very many volumes by so many authors whose words he recites.

## V

Because he devoted himself so diligently to reading not only in his early years but even into old age, whatever he had read so assiduously was, through the felicity of his memory, always at hand whenever needed.

There is no need to speak of his use of the sacred books and the holy Fathers, since the exceedingly frequent testimonies from them with which his works are filled make this perfectly clear. Indeed, one may doubt whether any other writer of this age surpassed Ratherius in this respect or could be compared with him.

He is recognized as no less well versed in the study of the canons. The more he saw them neglected in his own age, and people contradicting their precepts without fear or scruple, the more he delighted in meditating upon them and strove to restore their observance and honor.

Several of his works are deliberately directed toward this end. If, at times, he praises apocryphal canons or spurious constitutions of the Roman pontiffs, as others commonly did at that time, this must be attributed and pardoned to the conditions of his age, which lacked the art of more penetrating criticism.

## VI

A bishop so steeped in the study and use of Sacred Scripture, the Fathers, and the canons professed a doctrine and discipline that was exceedingly pure and in harmony with those same sources.

Catholic doctrines repeatedly occur in his works, and they furnish highly distinguished testimonies to the tradition of the tenth century. Especially notable are his extensive statements, chiefly in two minor works—*Letter 1* and the *Confession*—concerning the real presence of the Lord’s body and blood in the sacrament of the Eucharist.

Thus the transmission of this doctrine is especially confirmed by that very writer whom certain heterodox persons, ignorant of these works, had turned into a defense of their own error.

In many passages he inserted numerous statements on free will, the necessity and efficacy of divine grace, and original sin that are plainly in accordance with Augustine’s position.

There are also passages concerning the veneration and invocation of the saints; the necessity and use of tradition; the indissoluble bond of marriage; the distinction between mortal and venial sins; confession; the celibacy of sacred ministers; purgatory; suffrages for the souls of the dead; the eternity of punishments in hell; and other Catholic doctrines.

In the books of the *Praeloquia*, whatever he teaches concerning the mysteries of religion—especially at the end of book III—is consonant with the Creed attributed to Saint Athanasius and with the teaching of Saint Augustine.

He prefers the sound doctrine of the Church so strongly that he sharply attacks those who have attempted to stain or assail it with various errors.

Two such errors, arising or reviving in the tenth century and vigorously censured by Ratherius, should be mentioned. One was held by a certain person who admitted that the saints rejoice in heaven but maintained that they neither reign nor will reign with Christ. The other was held by certain people in these regions who, more from ignorance than malice, defended the ancient heresy of the Anthropomorphites.

See the fourth book of the *Praeloquia*, no. 15, and the second sermon on Lent, no. 29 and following.

Because he desired pure worship of God, he did not cease inveighing against certain superstitions that were spreading.

Much more could be added concerning matters that contribute to our knowledge of the morals and discipline of this period. Among other works, the books of the *Praeloquia* mentioned above are particularly important in this respect. In them he instructs people of every age, sex, and condition in such a way that he exposes the vices of each and prescribes their duties.

Several other books concern the reform of the clergy, so that the discipline of the tenth century can be recovered from no other writer more fully than from ours.

It should also be added that the history of Veronese affairs in the same tenth century cannot be derived from any other source, as the Marquis Scipione Maffei rightly observed.

### § II. On the works of Ratherius previously published and the editions in which they are scattered; on the unpublished works to be added in this edition; on works still missing and on other works attributed to Ratherius

## VII

Quite a few works of our writer had indeed been published previously, but they had been inserted separately into and dispersed among various collections—a state of affairs whose inconvenience everyone can see.

The *Life of Saint Ursmar*, which Ratherius rendered more detailed after it had been written in a less explicit manner by Abbot Anso, first appeared through the work of Laurentius Surius in the April volume of the *Lives of the Saints*.

## VIII

In the first volume of the *Deeds of the Bishops of Tongeren*, published in 1613, Jean Chapeauville published from a manuscript of the monastery of Lobbes in Belgium three letters of Ratherius: one to John, the supreme pontiff; a second to all the bishops of Italy, Germany, and Gaul; and a third to Bruno, later Archbishop of Cologne. He also added a letter of Everaclus, Bishop of Liège, to Ratherius himself.

## IX

Next, Father Lucas d’Achery, who most diligently excerpted several unpublished works from various manuscript copies and published them in the *Spicilegium*, obtained in Gaul a Laudunensis codex containing several minor works of Ratherius that had not yet been printed. From this codex he brought the following works to light in the second volume of the first edition of the *Spicilegium*, under these titles:

*Two Parts on Contempt for the Canons.*  
*The Deliberative Conclusion Enacted at Liège.*  
*The Conjecture of Character.*  
*The Discord between Ratherius and the Clerics.*  
*The Apologetic Book.*  
*On Rebellious Clerics.*  
*Clerics Substituted after the Monks Were Removed from the Small Abbey of Magonziano.*  
*On an Unlawful Marriage.*  
*Letter to Martin.*  
*Another Letter to the Roman Church.*  
*Synodical Letter to the Priests, etc.*  
*Itinerary of Ratherius Traveling to Rome.*  
*A Very Long Sermon on Lent.*  
*Against the Critics of the Same Sermon.*  
*The Second Sermon on Lent.*  
*Sermons on Easter I and II.*  
*Another Sermon on the Octave of Easter.*  
*Another Sermon after Easter.*  
*Two Sermons on the Ascension.*

These works were available to Father Lucas d’Achery from a single Laudunensis codex.

In the same volume, however, he inserted three other letters previously published by Chapeauville. We discovered that he had taken them not from the Laudunensis codex but from Chapeauville’s edition itself, since they display the same readings, the same errors, and the same lacunae.

In the second volume, already printed but not yet published, Acherius received other minor works of Ratherius transcribed at Charles Boesman’s expense from manuscripts at Lobbes. In the preface to that second volume he promised to publish them in the third volume.

What these works are he explains in the catalogue of the second volume in the following words:

> “There are other unpublished minor works of Ratherius, namely two sermons, one on Pentecost, one on Mary and Martha; *On His Own Fall*—it should be determined whether this differs from the work we published among the sermons on Easter; *On Idle Speech*. In addition, the *Meditations of the Heart* of a certain Ratherius, indeed Bishop of the Church of Verona but a monk of Lobbes, while in exile. He judged that these, arranged in six little books, should be called a volume of *Praeloquia*, because they preface a certain minor work called *Agonisticus*; two letters; and a book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, consisting of ninety-nine chapters.”

When he wrote this in the catalogue, he evidently had either not yet received these minor works or had not examined them. Had he read them, he would clearly have recognized that *On His Own Fall* is different from the sermons *On Easter*.

We shall demonstrate shortly that the book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord* was wrongly attributed to Ratherius.

Moreover, Acherius published in the third volume none of the works that he had promised to print there. He published only one letter of Ratherius, to Patricus, in the twelfth volume.

In the newest and corrected Paris edition of the same Acherian *Spicilegium*, published in 1723, Louis-François-Joseph de la Barre reproduced what Acherius had published in volumes two and twelve, undertaking to correct some passages and illuminate others. These reprinted materials are read in volume one, pp. 345 and following.

## X

In 1728, when Bartholomew Campagnola, archpriest of Saint Cecilia, printed at Verona a book entitled *Civil Law of the City of Verona*, he added at the end a minor work—or rather a fragment of a minor work—by Ratherius, *On the Life and Translation of Saint Metronis*, as well as a letter by Ratherius with a fragment of another letter to Manasses, as he thought; it should be read “to Milo,” the bishop.

He found these texts written in the author’s own hand in two codices of our cathedral-library collection.

## XI

Father Bernard Pez had mentioned in the introductory dissertation prefixed to volume I of the *Thesaurus Anecdotorum* an ancient book belonging to the cathedral chapter of Freising in Bavaria, which contains several works and letters of our writer.

He himself excerpted only some items from it and published them in 1729 in volume VI of the *Thesaurus*. To this volume, which was also published separately, he gave the title *Diplomatic-Historical-Epistolary Codex*.

The works he published are the following:

*To the Clerics of His Church, Concerning Those Ordained by the Intruder into His See.*

Letters to Ambrose, to Adelaide Augusta, and to Nanno.

[Col. 0016D]

*The Testament*, together with *the Foundation and Endowment of the Clerics of the Church of Verona*, which in our edition we shall present under the title *Judgment*.

## XII

The copy of the Lobbes manuscripts that, as we indicated in no. 9, had been sent to Acherius and left by him in the library of Saint-Germain-en-Laye, was useful to Fathers Edmund Martène and Ursin Durand.

From it they published in volume IX of the *Amplissima Collectio of Ancient Writers and Monuments*, in 1733, the six books of Ratherius’s *Praeloquia* and three letters: one to the archbishops Wido and Sobbo, etc.; another likewise to the archbishop Robert; and a third addressed to all the faithful.

Furthermore, in the same volume, at the end of Paschasius Radbertus’s work *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, they printed a certain supplement from a Lobbes manuscript. Since it appears to us to have been composed by our author, we have judged that it ought not to be omitted from the edition of his works.

Thus the works of Ratherius, hitherto printed separately, have appeared through the diligence of six—or rather seven—editors. Consequently, those who study so great a man must acquire and consult six different kinds of editions.

From this the usefulness, not to say the necessity, of collecting all such works is readily apparent, especially since it commonly happens that one work depends for its interpretation on another, and that the author’s importance can be assessed only by comparing them all.

## XIII

Since, in collecting and editing the works of any author, works previously published and scattered through various volumes are less urgently sought than those that have never been printed, we judged that other works of Ratherius should be investigated, if any had escaped the diligence of others.

Accordingly, concerned to locate manuscripts of the author, we learned that manuscripts containing some minor works of Ratherius were to be found in only four libraries.

One is preserved among the codices of the Church of Laon. Concerning it Acherius reported the following in his preface:

> “Moreover, concerning the codex of Ratherian works, elegantly written in the time of Anselm the dean but disfigured by very many errors, which had formerly been stolen from the library of Blessed Mary of Laon and eventually restored, I give thanks to the distinguished gentleman Antonio Bellotte.”

Since Ratherius was at Laon after relinquishing the Bishopric of Verona, and remained there for some time, delivering a sermon on Saint Stephen’s Day in the chapter of the nuns (*Praeloquia*, book V, final chapter), perhaps it was at this time that the same codex was copied from the author’s autograph by a less skilled scribe, not without errors.

We discovered that all the works contained in this manuscript copy were composed after Ratherius’s third restoration to his Veronese see.

Nothing is found in this copy that was not published by Acherius.

XIV. All the material transcribed in the manuscript from Frisingen likewise belongs to this period. Father Pez testifies that this manuscript is seven hundred years old. Joseph Frisingellus, a Roboretan priest and a most devoted student of the best literature, had it copied rapidly, insofar as the short time allowed, while he was staying with his friend at Frisingen, with the latter’s assistance. From the copy that was available to us, we learned that most of the material contained in the Frisingen manuscript had already been published, partly by Acherius, who had found the same works in the Laudunensis manuscript, and partly by the aforementioned Father Pez. But there we also found five short works that had not yet appeared in print: namely, the *Decree concerning Clerics Ordained by an Usurper*; two treatises, *On His Own Fall* and *On Idle Speech*; and two sermons, one *On Pentecost* and the other *On Mary and Martha*.

Since we had learned from Father Bernard Pez that the said codex also contained a work *On the Translation of the Body of Saint Metron*, of which, as we noted, Bartholomaeus Campagnola had published only a fragment from the copy belonging to the Veronese chapter, while Frisingellus, for reasons unknown to us [XI], had by no means found it in the Frisingen manuscript and had displayed only its title in his copy, we hoped that the complete work might nevertheless be found there. We therefore approached our most noble fellow-citizen, Count Giovanni Battista de Verità, who, having departed for Verona from the court of the most serene Bavarian family, was due to return to that same court. We asked him to arrange for some experienced person to examine the codex more carefully and, if the desired work were found, to copy it.

We found a man most devoted to literary studies who, while greatly approving this edition of Ratherius’s works and being ready to offer it every assistance, entrusted the task to his close friend Francis de Werdenstein, bishop of Ténare and suffragan of the most eminent bishop of Frisingen, a man devoted to the best studies. After he had applied every diligence to the matter, we received the complete work, accurately transcribed.

Something else in the same codex deserves notice. After Ratherius’s works, a blank page was left, bearing only this title: “Sermons on Certain Feasts.” Several sermons follow, however, compiled here and there from the words of Saint Gregory; they are utterly foreign to Ratherius’s style and practice. Among them is one on Saints Firmus and Rusticus, similarly composed from Saint Gregory, which we shall publish by way of example in the Appendix. See the *Admonition* prefixed to that sermon.

XV. In the manuscript codices of the chapter of the Veronese Church, in which Ratherius wrote most of his short works, it is astonishing to say that, apart from the few works published by Bartholomaeus Campagnola, we were able to find nothing. But when he departed from Verona for the third time, apparently never to return here, he seems to have taken his works with him.

XVI. Since he had at some point withdrawn to his monastery of Lobbes, in which he had professed the monastic life, we hoped that most of his works would be found in the codices of that monastery. Fulcuinus, abbot of Lobbes; Anselm, canon of Liège; Sigebert of Gembloux; and Giles of Liège [XII] make particular mention of those works.

Enticed by this hope, the Marquis Scipione Maffei, who was especially eager for this collection of Ratherius’s works, was undertaking an erudite journey through Belgium. He repeatedly asked the most reverend Abbot Theodulf, whom he had unsuccessfully sought at Lobbes but found at Brussels, to send Verona an accurate account of the Ratherian codices in his monastery. After Maffei had returned to Verona, and while we were particularly eager for a copy of the unpublished works, as well as of those works that we possessed from the Frisingen manuscript but that had not yet been published, we sent the same abbot a catalogue. We asked him, once he knew what was already available to us, to distinguish easily what was lacking and to have those items carefully transcribed.

But an ancient fire had devastated this celebrated monastery, and many codices had been destroyed. Consequently, as Antonius Sanderus reports (*Bibliotheca Belgica*, p. 293), only a very few survive, rescued from the flames through the diligence of a certain Minorite. He sent us several transcriptions, among which he supplied only two of Ratherius’s works that had not yet been published: a sermon *On the Supper of the Lord* and Ratherius’s *Book of Confession*. The other materials that we received, although previously published, nevertheless proved useful for correcting several passages.

XVII. Not satisfied with this diligence, we arranged with the aforementioned Count Giovanni Battista de Verità that he should write to the most reverend Abbot Paul du Bois, who had succeeded the aforementioned Theodulf, urging him to undertake a new and more careful examination of the Lobbes codices.

The abbot agreed. After a more exact investigation, he replied that three manuscript copies were then to be found in that library containing some of Ratherius’s works. One was a folio manuscript from which, under Abbot Theodulf, the aforementioned sermon *On the Supper of the Lord* had been copied. This codex, however, contains many acts of holy martyrs and several other items relating to Verona. Since it was believed to have been written in Ratherius’s own hand, some people even suspected Ratherius of being the author of certain of the acts.

Although we were unable to inspect the codex itself or compare its script with Ratherius’s hand—which is certainly Ratherius’s in some of the copies belonging to the Veronese chapter—we nevertheless do not at all think that it was written by the bishop himself. Certainly the acts of Saints Firmus and Rusticus, as well as several other materials relating to Verona, have different authors, not Ratherius. For those acts are also found in other codices older than Ratherius.

The *Life of Saint Zeno, Bishop of Verona*, was written by Coronatus the notary, who preceded Ratherius by at least two centuries. The same must be said of the poem that praises Verona: it was composed by an anonymous author who lived during the reign of Pippin, king of Italy. The ground plan of the same city, appended to that poem and most recently published by Giovanni Battista Biancolini from the same codex (*On the Bishops and Governors of Verona*, p. 55), likewise seems to belong to the same genre and period.

Similarly, other short works and acts of this kind, foreign to Ratherius even in style, found in other ancient copies and also printed, point to a copyist who was Ratherius’s contemporary. It happened that this copyist found, together with Ratherius’s sermon *On the Supper of the Lord*, certain Veronese documents perhaps brought by Ratherius from Verona to Lobbes; he then chose to copy these, along with the other short works and saints’ lives by other authors, into the codex.

The second codex, smaller in quarto format, contains six more extensive books by Ratherius entitled *Meditations of the Heart*, and so forth, or *Prefaces*, together with two letters, one to Wido and Sobbo and the other to Rotbert. We observed that all these works had been made public by Fathers Martene and Durand from a copy sent to Acherius.

Finally, we discovered the *Book of Confession* received from the most reverend Abbot Theodulf preserved in a third codex. This codex also contains letters of Ratherius published by Chapeauvillius, as well as the letter to Patricus edited by Acherius and another letter to all the faithful, which Fathers Martene and Durand printed from this same codex.

Besides the unpublished *Book of Confession*, this codex, through the diligence of the most reverend Father Abbot Paul du Bois, supplied another unpublished work, namely the *Phrenesis*, which had formerly been praised by Fulcuinus and later by Antonius Sanderus (*Bibliotheca Belgica*, p. 303), but had remained desired. From what has been said so far, it is established that nine short works of Ratherius will first see the light in this collection [XIV].

XVIII. Other works, of which we find some mention in writers, we were unable to locate anywhere, despite every diligence. Their catalogue must not be omitted from this preface.

Ratherius himself, in Letter 3 to Archbishop Rotbert, no. 1, mentions a short work that he had written before becoming bishop, in which he answered the little questions of the Milanese—questions plainly similar to those proposed by Rotbert. From the same letter, especially Notes 4 and 5, it may be gathered that these questions concerned secular studies, which he had renounced after becoming bishop.

He mentions another volume in the sixth book of the *Prefaces*, chapter 7, into which he had inserted the opinion of a certain philosopher. Whether this is the same work as the preceding one, or a distinct work that was likewise lost, is unclear.

As for the twelve volumes mentioned by the author in the preface to the *Phrenesis*, see what we shall discuss more fully in his *Life*, § 10, no. 61.

XIX. Fulcuinus, in *On the Deeds of the Abbots of Lobbes*, chapter 20, also mentions a lost work of Ratherius entitled *Sparadorsum*, *On the Art of Grammar*. He describes where and why it was written in these words:

> “While he was staying in that part of Burgundy called Provence, he was asked to take in a certain very rich man’s son, named Roestang, to teach him letters. For him he wrote a book on the art of grammar, which he called *Sparadorsum* in the vernacular manner of speaking, because a little boy who became accustomed to the schools might thereby preserve his back from the blows.”

Acherius has *Sperardorsum*. Valerius Andreas, however, in *The Manuscript Library of Belgium*, vol. 1, p. 303, and Aubertus Miraeus, in his scholia on chapter 127 of Sigebert in Fulcuinus’s codex, read *Sparadorsum* [Col. 0020D], more correctly, deriving it from the ancient Germanic word *sparen*, meaning “to spare,” Italian *risparmiare*, as Muratorius noted (*Italian Antiquities*, vol. II, col. 1281).

That this work was written somewhat after the year 940, when the author, released from exile at Como, withdrew to Provence, will become clear from what will be said in his *Life*, § 6.

XX. Ratherius himself cites his *Chronography*, in which he attacks both himself and others and leaves no one untouched [XV], in two works: *Conjecture concerning Quality*, no. 2, and *Itinerary*, no. 8.

Aubertus Miraeus states in his scholia on chapter 127 of Sigebert’s *On Illustrious Men* that he had seen a copy of this *Chronography* in the codices of the library of Gembloux. But that library too was destroyed by fire, leaving us without this copy.

In the scholarly journey undertaken by two monks of Saint-Maur and published at Paris in 1717, after mention of the fire that had consumed that library thirty years earlier, several of Ratherius’s works are said to have been rescued from it (part II, p. 202). Therefore, so that we might spare no diligence, we arranged to ask the steward of the monastery of Gembloux whether this *Chronography* might perhaps be found among the codices rescued from the flames.

He replied on 20 March 1761 that nothing of the kind had been found.

Some have suspected that Ratherius’s *Chronography* might be the *Invective*, whose opening period names a chronicler. But they had seen only the title of the *Invective* and the first words of its opening period in Father Bernard Pez. Whoever reads the *Invective* itself, which will now be published in full, will understand that it concerns Saint Metron and his body, allegedly stolen by the people of Verona. Its subject and method differ greatly from those of the Ratherian *Chronography* just mentioned. Compare what we shall add about this work in the notes to *Conjecture concerning Quality*.

XXI. At the end of his Veronese episcopate, that is, in the year 968, Ratherius, harassed by many troubles and feeling himself increasingly driven to resign the episcopate and return to the monastic life, sent a book to Fulcuinus, abbot of Lobbes. He entitled it *The Conflict of Two*, “because, while arguing in it whether or not he should return, he fluctuated anxiously” (Fulcuinus, *On the Deeds of the Abbots of Lobbes*, ch. 28). We were unable to find this book anywhere.

XXII. Of Ratherius’s letters that are mentioned somewhere, two are missing: one to Frodoard of Reims, with which he sent him the books of the *Prefaces*, as the aforementioned Fulcuinus reports in chapter 20; and another to Everaclus [XVI], bishop of Liège, which Ratherius mentions at the very end of his reply among the letters to be included.

Among the unpublished short works of Ratherius that Father Lucas Acherius listed in the catalogue of the second volume, only one was missing to us: one of the two sermons *On Pentecost*. We searched for it in vain in the manuscripts at Lobbes, from which he appears to have obtained all those short works.

XXIII. Fulcuinus likewise testifies, in chapter 25, that Ratherius wrote “many other works.” Since, however, in listing individually the works of Ratherius he passed over in silence twelve of those now available to us, as well as several letters that we have found, he may have meant by “many” not only these works but also quite a few others whose memory perished through the changes of time.

It seems beyond doubt that a man as devoted to study as anyone of his age, who spent almost his entire life among books, composed many other works.

XXIV. Sigebert, in chapter 127 of *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, from whom others took the same information, attributes to Ratherius a book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, as well as another *On the Predestination of God*. But, Mabillonius says, “I fear that he has attributed Ratramnus’s books to Ratherius” (*Acts of the Saints of the Benedictine Order*, fifth century, under Ratherius, no. 20).

And rightly so. For not only are these two works on the same subject certainly by Ratramnus, but there is also no indication from the contemporary writer Fulcuinus that Ratherius wrote them. Fulcuinus, in his catalogue of Ratherius’s works, mentions other short works of lesser importance. Even if he omitted some shorter items, he nevertheless covered enough of Ratherius’s writings either in his letters—one of which, to Patricus, deliberately discusses the Eucharist—or in the words “and many other works.” Would he have failed to mention even one of those two longer and more distinguished works if he had known Ratherius to be their author?

Moreover, Ratherius delighted in certain unusual and obscure titles, whereas these two titles are simple and familiar. We have no doubt that Sigebert was led into error in this matter.

Since in chapter 95 he attributed the same two works to Bertramnus—for that is how Ratramnus began to be corruptly written—he was perhaps deceived by the varied and abbreviated writing of the codices [XVII]. Those two certainly Ratramnian works are found copied together in the codices, as in the Lobbes manuscript praised by Mabillonius in the second preface to the fourth century of the Benedictine Order, no. 83.

When the codex that Sigebert saw bore the name Bertramnus in its title, he attributed the works to Bertramnus. In another codex containing the same works, however, *Rat.* may perhaps have been written instead of *Ratramnus*, as sometimes happened. Without suspecting a scribal error in the name Bertramnus, and without considering or comparing the works themselves in the two codices, he carelessly took the difference in the writing of the author’s name to indicate different authors and different works on the same subject. Not recognizing Ratramnus, he seems to have interpreted the letters *Rat.* as referring to Ratherius, whom he knew from elsewhere and who had worked on both subjects just as Bertramnus had.

XXV. Some may perhaps think that Sigebert is supported by the codex from which Acherius, in the aforementioned catalogue of the second volume, listed among Ratherius’s unpublished works a book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord* consisting of ninety-nine chapters.

The Lobbes manuscript, whose catalogue Acherius had received when he printed that catalogue, certainly presents this book under Ratherius’s name. For the copy of this codex sent to us, likewise bearing the name of Ratherius in its title, divides the work into the same number of chapters.

There is also a Vatican manuscript belonging to Queen Christina of Sweden, numbered 498, in which the work is copied under the title *Ratherius’s Account of a Certain Servant of God*. This account might have appeared to be an unpublished work of his, but we discovered that it is a fragment of the aforementioned work attributed to Ratherius, *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*. In the Lobbes copy mentioned above, it appears as chapter 60.

There can therefore be no doubt that some manuscript copies have attributed, and continue to attribute, the book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord* to Ratherius. But no other copy known to us attributes to him the other work *On the Predestination of God* mentioned by Sigebert. For this reason, we think that Sigebert used other manuscripts containing both works [XVIII], and we consider it more probable that, through some error, he attributed to Ratherius works that belong to Ratramnus.

If Sigebert is thought to have used, at least in part, those codices that name Ratherius as the author of only one work, *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, this would not help his case but would harm it still further and reveal his mistake more clearly. For the error of such codices in the name Ratherius became most manifest to us from the reading of the aforementioned Lobbes copy.

We discovered that this was the celebrated work on the same subject, written not by Ratramnus but by Paschasius Ratbertus. Ratherius himself attributes it to him at the end of his *Book of Confession*, when, intending to append it to his *Confession*—and in the same Lobbes copy it is indeed found appended—he wrote these words:

> “I ask you to allow certain excerpts, arranged by chapter, from the writings of a certain Paschasius Ratbertus on this subject to be brought to your attention without envy.”

The work appended there is Ratbertus’s own *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*.

This will become even clearer to anyone who reads the extremely accurate edition of Paschasius’s work published by Fathers Martene and Durand (*Collection of Ancient Writers*, vol. IX, col. 374). In preparing and annotating that edition, they used the same Lobbes manuscript among other codices.

When Father Acherius attributed the work to Ratherius, he had received only the catalogue of that codex’s works, in which the book was erroneously ascribed to Ratherius. But when Fathers Martene and Durand were preparing the work for publication, they clearly discovered that the work of Ratbertus had been wrongly assigned to Ratherius in the title. The preliminary letter and the concluding section in the same codex name Paschasius Ratbertus and demonstrate that the title was corrupt. They had no doubt that Ratbertus was the author, to whom all the other codices attribute it and to whom it had formerly also been assigned by the so-called Cellotian Anonymous, first published by Louis Cellotius at the end of his *History of Gottschalk*.

Although the Cellotian Anonymous may have had the Lobbes copy or another similar manuscript before his eyes, he testifies that the work published by Cellotius extended to nearly one hundred chapters. This division into chapters has so far been found only in the Lobbes manuscript [XIX].

That this Lobbes manuscript, or another similar one, was inspected by the same Anonymous is confirmed by the fact that the true author of the work published by Cellotius was Heriger, abbot of Lobbes and a contemporary of Ratherius. Mabillonius demonstrated this not merely by conjecture (*Second Preface to the Fourth Century of the Benedictine Order*, no. 47), but also by the evidence of the Gembloux codex.

The same is confirmed by another codex cited by Oudinus, who reports in volume II of *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, p. 486, that he had seen the same book of the Cellotian Anonymous “under the name of Herigerus in manuscript in the library of Signy, of the Cistercian order, in the diocese of Reims.”

The authority of these two codices seems preferable to that of the Gottwic codex, from which Father Bernard Pez published the same work, printed by Cellotius, under the name Gerbertus in volume I, part II of the *Anecdota*, p. 132.

XXVI. On this occasion another passage of Sigebert must be examined. He writes there about this Heriger and the work in question:

> “He also gathered together against Ratbertus a number of writings by Catholic Fathers concerning the body and blood of the Lord.”

All Sigebert’s codices read this way except one, that of Saint Martin, or Saint Martin of Leuven, which Possevinus cites (*Sacred Apparatus*, vol. I), where *against Ratbertus* is replaced by *against Ratherius*.

Possevinus considers this reading more correct. For that reason Oudinus, in the passage cited shortly before, and Albert Fabricius, volume III of *Library of Medieval and Later Writers*, p. 564, think that Heriger wrote against Ratherius, whom they suppose, on the basis of the same Sigebert, to have composed a book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*.

But one manuscript of Sigebert should not be preferred to all the others, which, as Possevinus himself testifies, read not *against Ratherius* but *against Ratbertus*. This reading is strongly confirmed by the continuator of Fulcuinus (Acherius, vol. II of the *Spicilegium*, p. 774), who likewise reports that, toward the end of the eleventh century, Heriger wrote against Ratbertus.

Moreover, their opinion rests upon the hypothesis that we have shown to be utterly groundless—namely, that Ratherius wrote the book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*. If Heriger praises and follows Ratbertus in that work, he does so with respect to the Catholic doctrine that Ratbertus taught. But in several places he rejects Ratbertus’s peculiar formulations, which, because they appeared novel, gave rise to the controversy, and excuses them in the name of simplicity, as may be seen in Mabillonius, in the passage cited, no. 61.

XXVII. Father Le Long praises an *Exposition of the Apocalypse* by Ratherius, volume II of the *Sacred Library*, p. 920. He cites the *Reibach Ordinary*. Since no ancient writer lists such a work among Ratherius’s writings, and since Ratherius did not devote himself to similar short works on Sacred Scripture, we have no doubt that it was attributed to Ratherius through some error.

XXVIII. In his catalogue of our author’s works, Trithemius lists a book written by him in exile. Since he sometimes mentions the *Agonisticon*, or six books of the *Prefaces*, as though it were a distinct work, some have thought that the book previously indicated in the singular as having been written in exile should be distinguished from the books of the *Agonisticon* and counted among the lost works.

But it is certain that the six books of the *Agonisticon* were written in exile at Pavia. Fulcuinus and Liutprandus called them a book in the singular. Following them, Sigebert likewise calls it a book in his *Chronicle* under the year 932:

> “He was exiled at Pavia, where he also published a book about his sufferings.”

In his work *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 127, however, Sigebert praises the six books of the *Agonisticon*. Hence Trithemius, who followed Sigebert, listed as two distinct works the book composed in exile and the six books of the *Agonisticon*, although they are one and the same work.

XXIX. We believe that Sigebert fell into a similar error when, in the aforementioned passage of *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, he lists as two distinct works:

> “He wrote a book which he entitled: ‘Idle Chatter, Ineffectual, as It Seemed to Him.’”

And shortly afterward:

> “He wrote against the heresy of the Anthropomorphites,” and so forth.

The title *Idle Chatter, Ineffectual, as It Seemed to Him* was attached by Ratherius to a short work—or rather, a longer sermon—which in our collection is the second sermon *On Lent*. Sigebert had this title before his eyes, copied directly from it.

In this sermon the heresy of the Anthropomorphites is attacked at greater length, and we do not think that Ratherius wrote anything else against it [XXI]. Fulcuinus, who mentions neither the long sermon *On Lent* nor *Idle Chatter, Ineffectual*, apparently counted the work, because of its length, among the treatises rather than among the sermons; he refers to it as a short work in chapter 24, saying:

> “There is also a short work by the same author against the Anthropomorphites.”

Sigebert, who had also read Fulcuinus, seems to have thought that Fulcuinus’s words referred to a work distinct from *Idle Chatter, Ineffectual*. If Giles of Liège, Trithemius, and others likewise distinguished the works, this should not trouble us: they all drank from Sigebert’s source.

§ III. What has been accomplished in this collection and edition

XXX. The works of Ratherius that we have collected from those previously printed, together with the unpublished works that will be added, are evident from the preceding section.

We devoted much care and labor to correcting the text. We wished that several copies of each work were available, so that corrupt passages in one could be corrected from others and the lacunae that occasionally occur could be supplied. But since for only a few short works are as many as two codices available, we corrected the text from a manuscript whenever we could; elsewhere we relied on conjecture. We nevertheless observed this precaution: no emendation was inserted into the text unless a certain or almost demonstrably correct reading was available, with the earlier reading supplied in the notes. Where the emendation was not entirely certain, it was placed in the notes or enclosed in brackets in the text.

XXXI. Once the text had been corrected as far as possible, we encountered in it two further difficulties: one concerned matters that are sometimes obscure and resemble riddles; the other concerned the defective punctuation transmitted in the printed editions and the extremely difficult and tangled syntax of the author.

Two factors make the subject matter obscure. First, some events of that period are repeatedly hinted at so sparingly that they are scarcely indicated before the author breaks off. At the time they were sufficiently apparent and well known to everyone; now, however, unless it is possible to explain them from other writers or documents, what is being suggested so briefly remains hidden.

Writers on the events of the tenth century are extremely rare, and documents are likewise very scarce. Whatever writings or documents of that period have survived to our own time, we carefully examined. Whenever we found anything relevant, we tried to illuminate in the appended notes the passages to which it appropriately belonged.

Second, although Ratherius attacked the greatly corrupted morals of men and spared no one, he nevertheless exercised such caution and restraint that he did not express the names of men, especially distinguished men, whose vices he was exposing. He often omitted proper names and sometimes substituted other names for the real ones. At times, when writing about his own affairs, he concealed his identity, so that when he speaks about himself he appears to be speaking about someone else. See the *Admonition* to the books of the *Prefaces*, no. 5.

To explain in the notes matters resembling riddles, sometimes by conjecture and sometimes by more certain evidence, required no small labor.

XXXII. These difficulties of subject matter were compounded by the punctuation transmitted in the printed editions, which was often misplaced and corrupt. At one moment it perverted the sense; at another it left the text so gaping that something appeared to be missing. Sometimes the defect in punctuation could be detected only through repeated reading and prolonged examination.

Many passages that seemed hopeless were restored in this way.

The author’s syntax is also usually extremely difficult and very intricate, especially when he chose to employ a kind of rhetorical eloquence. Longer periods, unusual transpositions of words, and other inconveniences of this sort occur frequently. To understand them, it was necessary to read the same period two or three times, or even more, and to reflect upon it attentively.

What we had achieved through such study and labor, we considered it our duty to construct and explain in the notes, so that readers might be spared the same difficulty.

XXXIII. The chronology [XXIII] of Ratherius’s works seemed so difficult to Muratorius, because of the many changes in his life, that he wrote in dissertation 43 of volume III of the *Italian Antiquities of the Middle Ages*, p. 831:

> “Ratherius was subject to so many sufferings, exiles, and changes . . . . . . that it would not be easy for you to establish the chronology of his [book] correctly.”

He is speaking of the book entitled *On Contempt for the Canons*, but the same applies equally to the others. Indeed, unless one first has a precisely ordered account of the author’s life, which is entangled in many difficulties, nothing can be accomplished.

Much study therefore had to be devoted to arranging the chronology of Ratherius’s actions and changes of fortune, so that his works and letters could be placed in chronological order. The date of each work and letter will be established in the *Admonitions* or in the first note attached to each one. We have also attempted to do this for the sermons, with one exception.

XXXIV. Concerning the division and distribution of the works into three parts, only this needs to be noted: three letters were not listed among the letters presented in the second part because they had been incorporated or prefixed by the author himself into works of the first part and therefore ought not to be repeated uselessly in the second.

The first is Ratherius’s letter to a certain Urso or Ursus, written in the prison at Pavia. It is inserted in full in the third book of the *Prefaces*, no. 25 and following.

The second is a letter—or rather, a very brief admonition in the form of a letter—written by Ratherius, while he was in exile at Como, to the archbishops Wido and Sobbo and the other fellow bishops assembled in council. It will be found in the fourth book of the *Prefaces*, no. 12.

Finally, the third is a letter to the monks of Lobbes, likewise composed at Como. Ratherius prefixed it as a prologue before the *Life of Saint Ursinarius*.

XXXV. Finally, the author’s *Life*, in arranging which we chiefly labored, had to be excerpted and assembled here and there from the author’s own works and from contemporary or nearly contemporary writers and documents [XXIV].

To accomplish this fairly, several highly obscure and complicated matters—not so much of sacred as of secular history—had to be investigated, explained, and established in greater detail. Some concerned the history of Verona; others concerned the affairs of Italian kings, emperors, dukes, and counts.

These are the principal matters that we thought should be prefaced and announced in advance.

[Col. 0027]

# THE LIFE OF RATHERIUS, BISHOP OF VERONA

[Col. 0027B] [XXV] The deeds of Ratherius, bishop of Verona, were first set forth by the distinguished John Mabillonius in the tenth-century volume of the *Acts of the Saints of the Benedictine Order*. Albert Fabricius, however, wisely observed in volume VI of the *Library of Medieval and Later Writers* that:

> “His life deserves to be carefully written by a learned man, after his works have been read through and the historians of those times have likewise been consulted, since many matters most worthy of notice will certainly be found in it. For the life that Mabillonius supplied in the fifth Benedictine century is good for its purpose, but it is not yet sufficient for a complete knowledge of matters concerning him.”

Others subsequently devoted attention to the same subject. But since the deeds of the author themselves, as indicated in his works, are entangled in many difficulties, and the chronology of the periods is obscure—something that could not be established without close attention to and comparison of all the works, both published and unpublished—a considerable degree of confusion is found in the accounts of several otherwise distinguished men.

Most recently, Count Francesco Florio, primicerius of the archiepiscopal church of Udine, devoted more careful work to this matter. Two dissertations of his, written in Italian, were printed at Rome in 1754. In one of them he set out Ratherius’s life at greater length and arranged it in chronological order; he therefore prefixed the title *Essay on the Life of Raterio, Bishop of Verona*.

Everywhere it displays the author’s extensive learning, sharpness of intellect [XXVI], sound critical judgment, and perspicacity in understanding and disentangling the most obscure matters.

Although this specimen of a life, excerpted from Ratherius’s works and from other contemporary writers more accurately and more fully than before, reports most of his deeds, it became clear to us, as we examined each work more closely and compared various other documents, that much still remains to be noticed by anyone who undertakes to write not merely a specimen but a full life of him. There are also matters that become clear only from the entire body of evidence and that must be explained and established differently from the way they appeared to the aforementioned writer.

Let us therefore begin at the beginning.

## § I. Ratherius’s Homeland and Nobility. His Year of Birth Conjectured

2. Ratherius, celebrated less for his knowledge of letters and his zeal for ecclesiastical discipline than for the changes of his sufferings, was Belgian by nationality and was born in the diocese of Liège [or Leodiense]. Everaclus, bishop of Liège, calls Liège his native homeland in a letter to Ratherius (Marten, *Collection of Ancient Writers*, vol. IV, p. 859).

Hence the author who wrote the *Deeds of the Bishops of Tongeren*, or of Liège, testifies that Ratherius was a countryman of ours by birth (vol. I of the *Deeds of the Bishops of Tongeren*, pp. 173 and 176).

Anselm, canon of Liège, and Giles, likewise of Liège, state in Chapeauvillius that he was born in our region [XXVII].

For this reason Ratherius himself, in the *Deliberative Conclusion*, no. 8, calls the people of Liège “the people of my native homeland, joined to me by the affinity of neighborhood,” and declares himself a son of that same Church of Liège through baptism.

The words “joined to me by the affinity of neighborhood” deserve notice. They seem to indicate that he was born not in the city of Liège itself but in a place near the city, that is, somewhere in the diocese.

Some more recent writers report that his father was one of the counts of the duchy of Luxembourg, which belonged to the diocese of Liège. On what foundation this rests, however, we do not know.

### 3

The following passages in the preface to the *Phrenesis*, no. 4, seem to establish the nobility of his lineage. They attribute to Ratherius not merely *ingenuitas* [Col. 0028D]—which designates a freeborn man—but also a kind of free birth that antiquity commended. This means, of course, the antiquity of a family that would adorn free birth: it suggests a long line of ancestors who were not merely freeborn but distinguished, and who added nobility to that free status.

He openly declares that he had illustrious relatives in his letter to Urso, which is reproduced in its entirety in the third book of the *Praeloquia*. There, in no. 27, speaking of the barbarian Italian people who had come from Burgundy and were serving in the army of Hugh, king of Italy, he relates that, during the general slaughter inflicted by that people upon the Veronese, he was spared and carried away “because of the kinship which I had with their leading men.” Since he was related to the leading men of King Hugh’s army, he is clearly shown to have had noble and distinguished relatives; and this contributes greatly to establishing his nobility.

This nobility is confirmed by the first book of the same *Praeloquia*. There Ratherius, recalling that someone had passed over the distinction of his nobility in silence, speaks of himself—although suppressing his name—as will become clear from the notes appended there. [Col. 0029B] All doubt is removed by the epitaph of his tomb, which will be given at the end of his *Life*, where he is explicitly called noble.

Nor should one object to the statements according to which some people said that Ratherius had “perhaps been a beadle in his homeland, or the son of a carpenter” (*Qualitatis conjectura*, no. 2). They said this in mockery, because he had no concern for honor, like a beadle, and because, as though he were a carpenter’s son, he devoted himself to building or rebuilding basilicas. In any case, the mocker himself testifies in the same passage that something quite different was more commonly said among us—that is, among the Veronese: the Veronese had more often heard that he was born of a noble family. [XXVIII]

Perhaps the statements in the preface to the *Phrenesis*, no. 5, will seem more difficult: “The most thoroughly deceived man shudders if someone asserts that he is learned, or NOBLE, or—which is much more unjust—not being so, just . . . . .”; by these words he seems to imply that he was neither learned, nor noble, nor just. But these words were spoken by a man who had resolved to disparage himself excessively, and they should not disturb us. Who, on this basis, would deny him learning, when other documents establish that he was the most learned man of his age? The same must be thought of his nobility, which is evident from other evidence.

### 4

Since we are here discussing Ratherius’s lineage, the passage in the *Qualitatis conjectura*, no. 12, which mentions his relatives must not be omitted:

> “He is troubled by no concern for his relatives, either because he thinks that none of them needs anything so much that he knows only himself and a brother among them to be poor—for he frequently uses *fore* [‘to be going to be’] for *esse* [‘to be’]—or because he knows that canon law forbids him to give them anything, or because, being decrepit, he thinks that he has no relatives, since those who do exist are already, in relation to him, in the sixth generation, and a succession of great-grandchildren has taken the place of brothers.”

So that the earlier words, which imply that a poor brother survived him, may not seem to conflict with the concluding statement, where he affirms that a succession of great-great-grandchildren (*abnepotes*) remained in place of brothers, one may conjecture that the surviving brother was a monk. He calls him poor because, like himself, he was bound by a vow of poverty. The great-great-grandchildren, meanwhile, were those born from other brothers who had already died, and who, Ratherius says, were six generations—or degrees—removed from him, now that he himself was decrepit.

That he may have marked so many generations hyperbolically is perhaps indicated by what his mocker, or censor, adds immediately afterward in the same place: “Yet, being as he is a chatterbox, he says this in a chattering and most mendacious manner.” [Col. 0030A]

### 5

Since the year in which he was born cannot be established by any certain indication, it must be inferred with some probability from several testimonies.

While writing the second book of the *Praeloquia* in 936, he reveals that he had reached approximately the middle of life. “For,” he says in no. 1, “from the twilight of childhood I have been brought almost to this MIDDAY OF LIFE.” In the same book, no. 36, he extends the final period of old age to approximately eighty years. In instructing an aged and decrepit man who was awaiting the hour of death, he says: “You should reckon eighty years, or years near them, whether already past or now approaching.” He therefore assigns approximately forty years to the middle of life.

If, in 936, when he composed the book just mentioned, he was about forty years old, he must have been born around 896. Certain passages in the *Book of Confession*, written in 960 or 961, seem to place his birth somewhat earlier, since in no. 21 he calls himself seventy years old, and in no. 31 almost seventy. But the particle *almost*, indicating that he was short of seventy by several years, can easily be reconciled with a birth around 896. On the other hand, an approximately middle age—namely, approximately forty years—falling in 936 cannot equally well be reconciled with a birth in 890 or 891.

## § II.—He embraces the monastic life. His studies. He writes a letter to Patricus. The opinion of some that the abbacy of Saint-Amand was offered to Ratherius before his episcopate is disproved.

[Col. 0030C]

### 6

Since it was customary, according to the prescription of the Rule of Saint Benedict, for boys to be offered to monasteries, Ratherius was offered to God in the first years of his life at the monastery of Lobbes, situated on the River Sambre at the boundary of Hainaut, Toxandria, and the territory of Liège.

He himself describes this rite of offering in the *Book of Confession*, no. 12:

> “For when I was still a little boy, a certain freeborn man came and, holding me at an altar of Saints Peter and Paul—the church of the aforesaid monastery was dedicated under their name—with bread and wine . . . offered me to God and Saint Peter as a holocaust . . . as though by the law of a Nazarite . . . to serve immutably . . . in order to confirm the covenant perpetually.”

Since Ratherius is said to have been offered not by his father but by a freeborn man, unless the designation “freeborn man” refers to his father, one of his relatives must be understood. Mabillon observes in the *Benedictine Annals*, book XXXVI, no. 88, that the Rule of Saint Benedict granted the ability to offer boys to monasteries not only to parents but also to other relatives. [Col. 0030D]

This offering was not bare and solitary but was made together with bread and wine and with other provisions for life, some indication of which may perhaps be missing in the lacuna. Likewise, when the boy Megenfridus was offered by his father Ruodwald to the monastery of Sithiu, Mabillon testifies from a charter of donation cited by Iperius that “a certain estate of twelve *bannaria* in the county of Boulogne was granted for his food and clothing” [XXX] (*Benedictine Annals*, book XXXVI, no. 38). [Col. 0031A]

The words “to serve immutably” are added because the offering of such boys was regarded as irrevocable under chapter 59 of the Rule of Saint Benedict. This may be seen in Mabillon’s second preface to the fourth century of the Benedictine Order, no. 199, and in his first preface to the fourth century, no. 36. Several ancient formulas of these offerings, expressing the same perpetuity, are available and are indicated by Mabillon in his first preface to the fourth century, no. 53. Fathers Martène and Durand published two from the tenth century; one was taken from a very ancient codex of the monastery of Elnon-Saint-Amand (vol. IX of the *Collectio*, p. 159).

The words “to confirm the covenant perpetually” imply that it had become customary for boys who had been offered in this way—although bound by the irrevocable vow of their parents—to confirm their offering by their own profession when they reached lawful age. Unless one should perhaps prefer to believe that, in this century, the ancient discipline governing offerings of this kind had been relaxed, so that these boys were not obliged to remain in the monastery until they had ratified their offering upon reaching legal age.

Ratherius did confirm his offering by the following profession, which he records in the same book:

> “But having myself taken up the pen when I had reached mature and lawful age, I wrote as follows and placed the writing upon the altar—not upon any other altar, but upon that very one, namely, of Saints Peter and Paul: I, Ratherius, promise my stability, the conversion of my ways, and obedience according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, before God and his saints.” [Col. 0031C]

### 7

Mabillon rightly observes that “the Benedictine Order, almost by itself, sustained the studies and sciences over the course of many centuries throughout the whole of Europe” (*On Monastic Studies*, part I, chapter 16). Hence the celebrated schools of the monks in the monasteries.

Among these, the monastery of Lobbes was especially renowned in the tenth century. It was there that Ratherius, the most perceptive of all his contemporaries, was educated, as Fulcuinus, abbot of that monastery, records (*On the Deeds of the Abbots of Lobbes*, chapter 19):

> “At that time the study of letters flourished among us. Those who devoted themselves to learning them were Scaminus, Theoduinus, and, the most perceptive of them, Ratherius.”

For this reason, in the letter prefixed to the *Life of Saint Ursmar*, he attributes the whole fruit of letters and disciplines to the monks of Lobbes.

Trithemius relates that Ratherius had Hilduin as his teacher. But one who confesses that he owes everything to the instruction of monks had monks, not clerics, as teachers; Fulcuinus testifies that Hilduin was among the latter when he was promoted to the see of Liège.

The following statement in the *Phrenesis*, no. 3, must not be omitted:

> “He learned little from his teachers and more by himself—things which others would scarcely have acquired from eminent instructors even with the greatest labor.”

Moreover, since he possessed a keen intellect and an exceptionally happy memory, not only contemporary authors but also his works themselves show how much he advanced through this education in both secular and sacred studies. Compare what we have observed more fully in the general preface, nos. 3 and 4.

We will add one point here. That there were teachers who taught the Greek language even at this period is testified by Rotger, author of the *Life of Saint Bruno, Archbishop of Cologne* (*Patrologia*, vol. CXXXIV), who employed Greek teachers.

Several indications show that Ratherius also applied himself to Greek. He repeatedly uses certain Greek words constructed according to Latin usage, which it has not been possible to find in any Latin writer—for example, *bromius*, *eumorpha*, and similar forms. He also explains the force of certain Greek words from the Greek itself.

In the fourth book of the *Praeloquia*, no. 23, addressing the king, he says:

> “Recognize even in the name, in Greek, your office, by interpreting it according to both Greek and Latin usage: you must understand that you are to carry the people, not oppress them.”

He has very plainly explained the Greek name βασιλεύς (*basileus*, “king”). See the note there, no. 56.

In the *Confession*, no. 15, he writes more explicitly from the Greek:

> “Give us today our consubstantiated bread,” is said to God.

Add that, in the sermon *On Mary and Martha*, no. 2, he expresses two Greek words in Greek letters. In no. 3, when he is about to offer a particular interpretation of the word *angelus* (“angel”), one that suits the sense of its context, he seems to derive it from the Greek ἄγχι (“near”), a root that only someone highly skilled in the Greek language could have investigated and discovered.

Finally, a significant indication of the same proficiency seems to be found in the words in which the malicious censor, in the *Qualitatis conjectura*, no. 2, recalls Ratherius’s lost work entitled *Chronographia* and attributes to his vanity the practice of giving the titles of Latin books a Greek appearance. “By making it Greek,” he says, “the vain man calls it *Chronographia* . . . .” Of the same kind is the other title, *Climax Syrmatis*, given as the heading of the *Conclusio deliberativa*. [Col. 0032C]

### 8

No works of Ratherius from the period during which he lived among the monks of Lobbes have come down to us, except for one letter to Patricus, which we shall infer from the notes to have been written by him before his episcopate.

This letter, dealing with the body and blood of the Lord, is famous because it contains a notable testimony concerning the real presence of Christ in the Eucharist. The occasion was a question that Patricus had posed at Horna—a place still within the diocese of Liège—to someone: whether Ratherius had sung Mass.

It is clear from this that the discipline governing the celebration of Mass was not uniform in this century. Some, like Ratherius, celebrated rarely or very rarely; others, like Patricus, celebrated daily.

The passages in which Patricus is said to have been scandalized by the bath in which Ratherius cleansed himself on the vigil of the Feast of the Circumcision also establish that some approved the use of baths before the more solemn feasts, out of reverence for Holy Communion, while others rejected it.

The formula used for administering the Eucharist is also noteworthy:

> “May the body of our Lord Jesus Christ be propitious to you unto eternal life.”

Because Ratherius feared that Patricus might understand these words figuratively rather than literally, he clearly affirmed the real presence of Christ in the Eucharist and the transubstantiation of bread and wine into the body and blood of Christ. [Col. 0033A]

As for the other more subtle and curious questions that can be raised on this matter, he says:

> “Do not trouble yourself, since you hear that it is a mystery, and that it belongs to faith. For if it is a mystery, it cannot be comprehended; if it belongs to faith, it must be believed, not investigated.”

This is an excellent principle, and one that ought especially to be observed in the questions about the other mysteries of faith that are introduced with excessive curiosity.

### 9

At the end of the fifth book of the *Praeloquia*, which he wrote in a little tower at Pavia, Ratherius relates that the abbacy of Saint-Amand was offered to him and rejected by him. Some think that this occurred while he was still a young monk, before he was promoted to the episcopate of Verona.

But two considerations exclude that period.

First, the abbacy of Saint-Amand was not vacant during the years preceding Ratherius’s episcopate. Laymen held it: first Rotbert, a royal official, whose document from the year 921 survives; then Count Rotger, who succeeded Rotbert and, according to documents, presided over the same abbey from 925 and the following years down to 937.
