See Mabillon’s *Annals*. The abbacy therefore could not have been offered to Ratherius while he was still a monk.

What if the event itself did not occur before Ratherius composed the aforementioned book of the *Praeloquia*, but much later, so that he described it much later and inserted the account into that book afterward? The second consideration makes this clear.

Indeed, it is evident from his words that the event occurred not long before, but in the very year in which the author described it:

> “I think it quite appropriate to have related what happened this year to my anxiety. For when I was at Laudun . . .,”

and so forth.

If he had written these words while composing the aforementioned book of the *Praeloquia* in the Pavia tower, he would have written them between February 935 and August 937, during which time, as we shall see, he was detained there in prison.

But Ratherius was neither at Laudun in those years, when he was in prison, nor in the preceding years, when he was already bishop at Verona. The event is said to have occurred at Laudun; consequently, the words “what happened this year to my anxiety, when I was at Laudun” cannot apply to this period.

If they indicated a year before his Veronese episcopate, he would have written “several years ago,” not “this year.” Since the words fit none of the years in which he was at Verona or in the prison at Pavia, rather than at Laudun, it plainly follows that they belong to a later period, after he had left the episcopate of Verona. Fulcuinus assigns the event to that period, as we shall explain more fully in its place.

In the books of the *Praeloquia* written at Pavia, this passage is therefore an addition. Since Ratherius inserted it into the fifth book in the same year in which the event occurred, he used the expression “this year” with complete accuracy.

## § III.—Ratherius follows the party of Hilduin, bishop of Liège; after Hilduin is expelled from the see of Liège, Ratherius adheres to him as bishop of Verona. He answers questions proposed by certain Milanese. When Hilduin is elected to the see of Milan, Ratherius travels to Rome; returning from there, he succeeds Hilduin in the Veronese see. The year of Hilduin’s election and Ratherius’s consecration is established.

[Col. 0034A]

### 10

Ratherius would have spent his life peacefully in the monastic institution which he had professed, had not the plans of Hilduin, bishop of Liège and abbot of Lobbes, whose party he had supported, drawn him away from it.

The matter must briefly be retraced from an earlier point. At this time, and throughout almost the preceding century, the monastery of Lobbes belonged so completely to the jurisdiction of the bishop of Liège that whoever was bishop of Liège was also abbot of Lobbes.

After Bishop and Abbot Stephen died, a major dispute over the bishopric of Liège arose in 920 and the following year between Hilduin and Richarius (*Frodoard, Chronicle*; and Hugo of Flavigny in the *Chronicle of Verdun*). [Col. 0034B]

Some demanded that Hilduin, a cleric of that church, be made bishop. With the support of Gislebert, duke of Lorraine, who had usurped for himself the supreme authority of the Lotharingian kingdom against Charles, king of France, Hilduin was consecrated in the church of Liège by Hermann, metropolitan of Cologne, in a new and unprecedented manner—that is, without the consent of the king and nobles.

Others, on the contrary, with the assent of King Charles, sought Richarius, abbot of Prüm. When the case was brought before the Apostolic See, Hilduin and Hermann, his consecrator, as well as Richarius, designated by the king, were summoned there. When Hilduin avoided judgment, Pope John XI ordained Richarius in 922, and he obtained the church of Liège peacefully. [Col. 0034C]

### 11

Not long afterward, in 926, around the month of June, Hugh, count of Arles and margrave of Provence, who was related to Hilduin by marriage, obtained the kingdom of Italy. Hilduin soon withdrew to Italy, hoping that Hugh would place him over some Italian church (*Liutprand*, book III of the *History*, chapter 11).

He also attempted to bring with him Ratherius, who had supported his party against Richarius. To this situation we refer the passage in the first book of the *Praeloquia*, no. 25:

> “You will find some nobleman almost deprived of all things, stripped of whatever power and dignity he may perhaps have acquired, and utterly cast down as far as concerns what avarice dictates and nobility demands”—he means Hilduin, who had been expelled from the see of Liège—“who, attempting to raise an arm against so harsh a calamity of misfortune, and being unable by himself . . . to accomplish anything, does not hesitate, through the sweet allurements of flattering words, to entangle and summon to follow him someone”—namely, Ratherius—“who, while quiet and favored by abundance, could either subsist on his own”—that is, in the monastery—“or, for a great profit, serve another”—namely, Bishop Richarius.

Ratherius indicates that he yielded to these allurements because of his love for Hilduin, when he adds shortly afterward:

> “Because of that love alone, which is strong as death, he preferred to neglect himself entirely and to come to the aid of that man, even amid countless dangers to his life, so that he might recover either the glory he had lost or one greater, rather than care for himself and seek what he needed, when it might have been available, according to his wishes.”

Thus Ratherius, supporting Hilduin’s party, adhered inseparably to him, as Fulcuinus records (*Deeds of the Abbot of Lobbes*, chapter 19).

### 12

Meanwhile, after Notherius, bishop of Verona, died on the fourth day before the Ides of August in 928, King Hugh placed Hilduin over the see of Verona—or rather, according to the abuse of that age, granted him that church by a stipendary right, so that he would have the means of living until a more distinguished see became vacant (*Ratherius*, letter 5 to Pope John, no. 3; and *Liutprand*, book III, chapter 11).

We have assigned Notherius’s death to the year 928, not 929, as some have thought. That year is clearly derived from his funerary epitaph, which still exists in the cathedral and was published by Ughelli in volume V of *Sacred Italy*, among the bishops of Verona, column 733. It explicitly reads:

> “He died on the fourth day before the Ides of August, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 928, indiction 1.”

If the recently published Notherian charters by the cathedral canon Marquis Dionysius contain the following statement (*On Two Bishops*, p. 103):

> “In the reign of Lord Hugh, king here in Italy, in his second year, on the fifteenth day of the month of November, indiction 1,”

and if those charters, in which Notherius is presented as alive in November under the first indiction, seem to conflict with the epitaph, it must be observed that the first indiction is to be reckoned from September 927 to September 928. The cited charters must therefore be assigned not to 928 but to 927, when the first indiction was running in November and the second year of King Hugh was current; otherwise Hugh’s third year would have had to be recorded. [Col. 0035C]

A document from the archive of the nuns of Saint Zacharias in Venice, published by Giovanni Battista Biancolini (*On the Bishops of Verona*, p. 120), agrees with this. It records Hilduin, Notherius’s successor, as bishop of Verona:

> “In the reign of Lord Hugh, king here in Italy, in his fourth year, on the eleventh day of the month of July, indiction 2.”

These are certain chronological indications of the year 929: Hugh’s fourth regnal year had scarcely begun in July, and it coincided with the second indiction. If Hilduin held the bishopric of Verona in July 929, Notherius’s death, which occurred on the fourth day before the Ides of August, cannot possibly be assigned to August 929; it is correctly assigned in the epitaph to August 928.

### 13

On this occasion, when Hilduin was promoted to the see of Verona, Ratherius was filled with considerable hope of succeeding Hilduin, “the king’s promise remaining that, when the time came to promote him to a higher position, Ratherius would be given to the Veronese as bishop” (Fulcuinus, chapter 19).

Hence, in the *Qualitatis conjectura*, no. 13, the same Ratherius says:

> “It has now been almost forty years since I began to seek power.”

Here he understands “power” to mean the episcopate; consequently, shortly afterward, when he speaks of a long administration of power conducted wickedly, he uses *potentatus* in the same sense.

Since the *Qualitatis conjectura* was written in 966, almost forty years, understood broadly, correspond reasonably well to 928. If the expression is thought to have to be taken more strictly, so that its beginning must be assigned to 926, when Ratherius came to Italy with Hilduin, then it must be said that Hilduin promised to act with King Hugh so that Ratherius too might be promoted to some episcopal office. [Col. 0036A]

Certainly, in the *Confession*, where he laments having abandoned the monastery and monastic way of life, he seems to indicate quite clearly that he thrust his foot into the net—that is, into the episcopate—and sought it, when he writes in no. 19:

> “He thrust it in especially, thrust it in, if he also sought it.”

### 14

Before proceeding further, mention must be made here of a work that has otherwise been lost, in which Ratherius answered several questions of the Milanese before his episcopate.

Evidence of this work is found in letter 3 to Rotbert, no. 1:

> “At the very beginning,” he says, “when I was not lightly challenged by the little questions of certain Milanese, I seemed to have offered a preliminary answer to some of the matters which I do not doubt that you are asking about.”

When he says “at the very beginning,” he indicates the period when he first followed Hilduin to Italy and had not yet been consecrated bishop, as can be gathered from what follows.

What these questions were remains unknown. We know only that they concerned secular studies, in which it was widely known how capable he was. Later, when Rotbert proposed precisely similar questions to him as bishop, he excused himself on the grounds that, although before his episcopate he had not refused to resolve corresponding questions of the Milanese, it was not fitting for a bishop to engage in such matters: he ought to be occupied not with secular but with divine and sacred studies. [Col. 0036C]

The following saying of a certain philosopher may perhaps have been inserted into this work. Ratherius mentions it in the sixth book of the *Praeloquia*, no. 7:

> “As in the example of a certain philosopher who, when he was provoked to anger—as I have already related in another volume—is said to have said to the one who was provoking him: ‘I would strike you now, unless I were angry.’”

If this saying was not inserted into the book in which he answered the questions of the Milanese, then one must posit another unknown volume written by Ratherius before the *Praeloquia*. We certainly do not doubt that this exceptionally learned man of his age composed many other works before those books of the *Praeloquia*, the memory of which has perished.

### 15

After Hilduin had presided over the church of Verona for nearly two years, the metropolitan Lambert died, and the archiepiscopal see of Milan became vacant. Since it appeared more suitable for Hilduin, he was transferred from the see of Verona to that of Milan. Thus the moment arrived when, according to King Hugh’s promises, Ratherius was to be promoted to the Veronese see.

But “as worldly instability often restrains itself through its own fickleness,” Ratherius writes in this letter 5, no. 3, “the king decided otherwise than he had promised. For, as was reported, he preferred to give the Veronese a bishop from among three men: either some Aquitanian, or Garafridus, or Manasses, archbishop of Arles, contrary, indeed, to the law of the canons.”

Ratherius had already gone to Rome on behalf of his lord Hilduin, in order to bring back for him the papal diploma together with the archiepiscopal pallium. While there, he was acting not so much for Hilduin as for himself—perhaps he had foreseen Hugh’s fickleness—and at the same time brought back a letter from Pope John XI:

> “It contained,” he says in the same passage, no. 4, “the requests of that lord and of the whole Roman Church that I should be given as bishop to the Veronese. This displeased the king greatly, since he was working toward the opposite; but the Apostolic petition prevailed, with my aforementioned lord Hilduin, foremost among the nobles of the kingdom, pressing his request and entreaty.”

Another and more compelling consideration perhaps moved Hugh to consent. Ratherius continues:

> “I was lying almost half-dead, sick”—after the Roman journey, that is. “The king was persuaded, I think, by those who loved me, that I would not survive. Led on by this hope, he consented, eager to satisfy both the lord pope and the others whom it seemed improper to offend, since they were making the request.”

He hoped, evidently, that Ratherius would die under the pressure of his illness and that the election would thereby become ineffective. But after medical treatment had been administered, Ratherius recovered and was consecrated bishop.

### 16

The year of this consecration, which will be useful in establishing several subsequent matters, can be determined more reliably from Hilduin’s translation to the see of Milan than from any other evidence.

Papeprochius assigns the beginning of Hilduin’s archiepiscopate at Milan to 932. Joseph Antonius Saxius, however, in his *Historical and Chronological Series of the Archbishops of Milan*, volume II, pages 340–341, more accurately places his promotion to that see at the end of June 931.

He establishes this partly from the succession of Hilduin’s predecessors and partly from ancient catalogues, which record the years and days during which each archbishop held office and the dates of their deaths.

Saxius rejects Papeprochius’s proposed date of 932 because Papeprochius made a one-year error in the succession of Hilduin’s predecessors after Anselm II, whom he thought had died in 897. A parchment decree preserved in the archive of the monks of Saint Ambrose proves this error decisively. The decree, dated 896, mentions Archbishop Landulf, who was appointed in place of Anselm II.

If Anselm’s year of death is moved to 896, and the beginnings of the succeeding archbishops—whose years and days are established by valid documents—are likewise moved one year earlier, it will be clear that Hilduin’s tenure began in 931, not in 932. [Col. 0037D]

According to the ancient catalogues of the bishops of Milan edited by Muratori (*Italian Historical Records*, vol. I, part II), Hilduin held the see of Milan for five years and fifteen days—or, as one catalogue gives it, twenty-five days—and died on the fourth day before the Kalends, or alternatively the ninth day before the Kalends, of August.

His episcopate at Milan therefore began most appropriately at the end of June 931, while his death occurred on either the fourth or ninth day before the Kalends of August 936.

One objection is provided by a privilege of Kings Hugh and Lothair, dated 937, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July, published by Muratori (*Italian Antiquities*, vol. II, p. 57), in which Hilduin is mentioned as archbishop of Milan.

But Muratori correctly observed that some defect must exist in the chronological indications of this privilege, just as he had noted in two other charters drawn up under the same rulers, since the Christian years given in them do not agree with the remaining chronological indications.

Indeed, another document from Como, dated 937 and printed by Ughelli and Father Tatti, gives all the chronological indications corresponding to that year:

> “The seventeenth day before the Kalends of July, in Hugh’s eleventh year and Lothair’s seventh, indiction 10.”

Our privilege, which is dated only one day later, incorrectly reads:

> “In Hugh’s tenth year and Lothair’s fifth, indiction 10.”

Who does not see the obvious error? A document whose chronological indications are so plainly corrupt cannot prejudice the chronology which Saxius established with such precision.

### 16 bis

For this reason, however, we do not think that Ratherius’s episcopate at Verona should be assigned to the same year, 931.

After Hilduin’s election, Ratherius went to Rome; on his return he suffered a serious illness, and it was thought that he would die. Hugh, moreover, abandoned his earlier decision and wished to entrust the bishopric to someone else. Only after yielding to the papal letters and to the requests of Hilduin and the leading men of the kingdom did he designate Ratherius as bishop while he was still ill and in danger of his life.

Once this decision had been made, it is quite probable that Hugh ensured that the election of the Veronese clergy and people should take place according to custom. For it could be demonstrated by many examples from the tenth century that the method of choosing bishops at this time was for the clergy and people to elect the person desired by the prince and then to seek the prince’s assent.

Moreover, after his election Ratherius had to recover from illness and danger before he could be consecrated. [Col. 0038C]

Nor can he be said to have been ordained by Hilduin of Milan, since Verona did not belong to the metropolitan jurisdiction of Milan. For this reason Ratherius, in letter 5 to Pope John, no. 6, reproves Manasses, archbishop of Arles, because, beyond the boundaries of his own province, he “consecrated a certain bishop of his own diocese to the title of the church of Verona.”

Therefore, he who observed ecclesiastical canons and discipline with the greatest care must be said to have been ordained by the patriarch of Aquileia, under whose jurisdiction Verona lay.

To allow sufficient time for all these events to take place after Hilduin’s election, a period of one or two months is not enough.

We infer from two passages that Ratherius entered upon the see of Verona in August. In the second book of the *Praeloquia*, no. 1, he assigns his first captivity to the month of February. In the aforementioned letter 5, no. 5, he clearly states that he was captured two and a half years after beginning his episcopate at Verona.

The beginning of his episcopate therefore falls approximately in August. Since, from the considerations already set out, this beginning cannot be assigned to August 931, it plainly follows that it must be placed in August 932.

The year of the captivity mentioned above, which we shall see was 935, confirms the same conclusion. If one counts backward two and a half years from February 935, when Ratherius was captured, one arrives at August 932.

From this it is clear that Sigebert erred in assigning Ratherius’s episcopate to 928, as did many more recent writers who assign it to 931.

## § IV.—The disastrous beginnings of Ratherius’s episcopate. He adheres to Count Milo and receives Arnold, duke of Bavaria, at Verona against King Hugh. Captured by Hugh’s soldiers, he is thrust into the prison at Pavia.

### 17

Since King Hugh had chosen Ratherius as bishop not willingly but because he had been overcome by the requests of others, hoping that Ratherius—who was suffering from a serious illness—would die, when he saw him rescued from death and consecrated bishop, “he became extremely angry,” as Ratherius himself says in letter 5, no. 4, and “he swore by God—and he did not lie—that throughout his life I would not rejoice in that ordination.”

He describes what Hugh did first in these words:

> “He sent in a written memorandum a fixed amount of the stipend which I was to retain from the property of the church, demanding an oath concerning the remainder, so that during his lifetime and that of his son I would not seek anything further. Understanding what great absurdity would result from this, I did not consent.”

He noted this as the first cause of the king’s hostility toward him in book IV of the *Praeloquia*, no. 20:

> “This, I think, was the cause of the disagreement; this was the charge of which you accuse me: namely, that you”—he is addressing Hugh—“wanted to retain all the property of the church, while he”—that is, Ratherius—“was to be your hireling, not the shepherd of Christ’s flock.”

When this first attempt had failed, the king adopted another means of harassing the bishop:

> “He brought persecutors and adversaries against me from every side, who would either frighten me so that I might flee”—these are the words of the author in the aforementioned letter 5—“or provoke me, so that they might find an opportunity to expel me.”

The bishop endured this persecution for two and a half years.

18. Meanwhile, Ugo found the opportunity he was seeking to expel the bishop and thrust him into prison. Several men in Italy were ill-disposed toward Ugo. For this reason they thought that Rodulf II, king of Burgundy, who had been deprived of the Italian kingdom somewhat earlier, ought to be recalled (LIUTPRAND, book III, chapter 13). When Ugo perceived this, he sent envoys to Rodulf and, by relinquishing to him certain territories that he held in Provence, secured sufficient guarantees from him concerning the Italian kingdom. Shortly afterward the Veronese, hostile to Ugo, summoned Arnold—or, as others call him, Arnolf—duke of Bavaria and Carinthia. That this rebellion was organized by the faction of the archdeacon and clergy of Verona, together with certain leading citizens, is clear from Ratherius’s letter to the deacon Urso, inserted in the third book of the *Praeloquia*, section 27.

Liutprand, however, identifies Count Milo and Bishop Ratherius as the leaders of the rebellion. He writes that Arnold, duke of Bavaria, who had crossed the march of Trent with an army, reached Verona (LIUTPRAND, same book, chapter 14), “where he was gladly received by Count Milo and Bishop Ratherius, who had invited him.” Milo, a distinguished man of Frankish origin under Emperor Berengar (same author, book II, chapter 20), had been raised by that emperor from youth in intimacy and luxury. After the emperor was killed at Verona in 924, Milo exercised some considerable authority. He ordered Flambert—who is called a *sculdascius* in Notherius’s testament of 922 [Note: “He is called a *sculdascius* in Notherius’s testament of the year 922, in Ughelli, volume V, column 729.”]—his murderer (same source), “and those who had connived with him in that abominable crime, to be seized by force and to end their lives on the gallows.”

At this time Milo appears to have been count of Verona (DIONYSIUS, *On Two Bishops*, p. 107). In the codicil of Bishop Notherius of 927, however, he subscribed without any title of count, though before the *scavinus* and the judge. Moreover, among the witnesses is recorded Sigibald, Milo’s vassal, just as in Notherius’s testament of 922, after Ingelfred—then count of Verona—Ingelfred’s vassal is named among the witnesses. In a document of 929 Milo likewise lacks the title of count, but is nevertheless called a royal vassal (BIANCOLO, *On the Bishops and Government of Verona*, p. 120); this indicates his exceptional nobility. When, therefore, he summoned Arnold against Ugo, he certainly already held the dignity of count of Verona. By that title he ranked among the foremost men of the Italian kingdom and administered the city with supreme authority.

What subsequently happened to him in the rebellion against Ugo has been recorded by Liutprand. When the same king, who had his seat at Pavia, heard that Arnold had been received at Verona, “he gathered an army,” Liutprand says, “and marched to meet him. When he had arrived there and was sending cavalry detachments all around, as they commonly say, a considerable part of the Bavarians, coming out of a fortress called Gauseningo, began to fight with the Italians.”

Perhaps *Gauselingo* should be read in place of the name of the site called *Gusilingus* in a charter of 825 and now called Gussolengo (DIONYSIUS, *Apologetic Reflections*, p. 33). From there it would have been easy to advance against Ugo’s army arriving from Pavia and the other Italian cities, but not from the fortress called Ossenigo. In the aforementioned codicils of Notherius of 927 the name is not written *Gauseningo* but *Ursanico*. Since that fortress lies beyond the Adige and faces toward Trent, no one would believe that troops were sent from there by the man governing Verona against an army advancing from the Italian cities toward Verona on this side of the Adige.

When the Bavarians’ battle went badly, “Duke Arnold was filled with no small confusion. Consequently, after taking counsel, he wanted to capture Count Milo and lead him into Bavaria, Italy having been abandoned, so that, once his army had been restored, he could return with him again. Milo was not unaware of this. Torn by conflicting thoughts, he had no idea at all what he should do. He was plainly afraid to approach King Ugo, as he deserved; but to be led into Bavaria with Arnold he regarded as not merely death but hell. In this uncertainty, because he knew that King Ugo was quickly inclined to mercy, he decided to flee from Arnold and deliberately make his way to him” (Liutprand, same passage).

Perhaps in order to appease Ugo and make him favorable, Milo arranged for his brother to defend against Arnold a fortification that stood at Verona. But after it was conquered, Arnold “led Milo’s brother and his soldiers, who had tried to defend it, with him into Bavaria.” Count Milo himself, after reconciling with Ugo, retained his former dignity.

19. The fate of Bishop Ratherius was altogether different. “After Arnold’s departure,” Liutprand adds, “the city was soon restored to King Ugo, and Ratherius, bishop of that city, was captured by him and banished to Pavia.” Hence, in letter 5 to Pope John, section 4, Ratherius admits that some fault of his own had contributed to this calamity, but he seems to deny that he had possessed a rebellious spirit hostile to Ugo, on account of which he might have been reduced to such misery:

> “Ugo began [to act against] me and thrust me into custody in a little tower at Pavia. I do not say that this happened without fault on my part—for who, amid such events, has not offended at least in word? He is a perfect man—but he acted against the law in this matter, and without a hearing. Let everyone say what he wishes: everything is full of rash judgments, as Augustine says. Yet I confess that from the time I first saw him until he laid aside his human form, I always wished for him the happiness of the Emperor Theodosius, and even now the memory of him weighs upon me with deep grief.”

These words, written not while Ugo was alive but after his death, deserve serious consideration. Ratherius attributes to rash judgments the charge of genuine rebellion against Ugo, whom he had always loved and for whom he had always desired every prosperity. He complains that he was given no hearing at which he might explain his conduct. The fault from which he acknowledges that he was not entirely free he counts among the lighter faults of which James says: “Whoever does not offend in word is a perfect man” (James 3:2).

Discussing the same matter more extensively in book IV of the *Praeloquia* (sections 5 and 7), which he wrote in the Pavia prison, he suggests that the rebellion of which he himself was said to be the author had been spread through the mere quibbling of envious men and rested on the following basis, as they said in section 7: “Because he associated with evildoers”—that is, with the Veronese who had instigated the rebellion—“and was found when he was captured.” This was as though the bishop, in order to remove every suspicion, ought to have left the city and gone to the king, bringing forward the treasonous sons.

He justifies his stay with the rebels by appealing to the example of Jeremiah: “who, as blessed Gregory says, because he could not restrain the citizens from entering Egypt, out of charity took pains to descend there with them himself.” And after a number of other points:

> “Are you therefore to judge that all those should be deposed who, knowing that their citizens and sons were rebels against kings, did not betray them so that they might be punished, but instead celebrated Masses for them, baptized their sons, preached to them, confirmed them, granted them penance, and reconciled them?”

Finally, in replying to those who objected that he had openly received Arnold, he tries, by examples of the saints, to show that it is sometimes permissible to admit enemies and invaders into a city. Yet in the book of his *Confession*, section 2, when he writes that he is suffering much because he had abjured his allegiance to Ugo, he again admits some fault of his own in the rebellion.

These statements can be reconciled with the preceding ones only by saying that Ratherius was not in fact the author of the rebellion, but that, once the rebellion had already broken out, he descended into the rebels’ party through connivance, compliance, and a certain necessity. Nor should Liutprand’s testimony disturb us. In identifying Ratherius, just as much as Count Milo, as a leader of the rebellion, he followed the common report spread by envious men. If this fault had been certain, Ratherius would have been captured immediately after Ugo’s victory and led into prison. At that time, however, the whole fault, as it existed, was assigned not to the bishop but to the clergy and the leading citizens (the *Praeloquia*, book III, section 27); nor did the entire ruin fall upon Ratherius’s head until after a certain letter had been written, of which he himself was represented as the author and the instigator of the whole undertaking.

20. We shall now attempt to extract from Ratherius’s own works this notable event, from which his calamity followed, although he touched upon it in several places, often somewhat obscurely, and to arrange the material in historical sequence. First, we must establish the time, as historical matters especially require.

The chronographer of Salzburg, cited by Father Ansizius, leaves no room for doubt that Ugo’s victory over Arnold should be assigned to the year 935. He assigns to that year the death of Udalbert, archbishop of Salzburg, who had followed Arnold, duke of Bavaria, on his Italian expedition against Ugo, writing: “He died while returning from the invasion of Italy.” If Udalbert died in 935, and, as was his custom, followed Arnold’s campaign and returned with him from the invasion of Italy, Ugo’s victory must certainly be assigned to that same year.

That Ratherius was captured by Ugo in February is clear from the second book of the *Praeloquia*, section 24. There he calls the seventh month—the month of September—the eighth month “from the onset of this calamity which overwhelms me, indeed instructs me.” He means the captivity under which he was suffering; if September was the eighth month, the captivity had begun in the preceding February. See the notes at that passage.

We can also determine the third day of that month from book V of the *Praeloquia*, section 12. In that treatise he testifies that he had been deceived in the matter for which he was led into captivity on the day after the feast of blessed Mary at which he had been given the kiss of peace during the solemn celebration of Mass. The feast of the Purification of blessed Mary is indicated, since it is the only Marian feast that falls in February. The matter was therefore conducted on the day after that feast—that is, on the third day of February, in the year 935, as we have established—and through it he was deceived and fell into captivity.

[Col. 0042D]

21. How this happened must now be explained. Two texts in particular will shed light on the matter: one from the letter to Urso, inserted in book III of the *Praeloquia*, section 27; the other from book V, section 12.

After Verona had been recovered by Ugo, a solemn service was celebrated on the feast of the Purification. During it, certain men, apparently bishops, gave Ratherius the kiss of peace, “thinking that he had been condemned not because he was a sinner, but because he had been deceived.” Others, perhaps eager to please the king, who was presumably present, severely reproached those who had given the kiss of peace, as though Ratherius were plainly guilty and unworthy of that kiss.

This is the account in book V, section 12, where it is added that a consultation and deliberation were held on the following day, bringing ruin upon Ratherius. This deliberation, conducted at daybreak, is explained more fully in the letter to Urso, a cleric of the church of Verona.

The cause of the deliberation was what had happened on the preceding day, the very day of the Purification, somewhat after the solemn celebration of Mass. A fierce people—“barbarian” to us, or rather to you, that is, not of Italian stock—which was serving in Ugo’s army, returned to Verona after Arnold’s forces had been defeated and driven into Bavaria. It attributed all the blame for the rebellion, as it stood, to the archdeacon of the church of Verona and to certain more distinguished Veronese, but especially to the entire clergy. It was attempting “to plunder the whole house of God, to dismember or carry away captive all the leading citizens, and to hang on the gallows the man already identified as the archdeacon, together with those who later became the principal authors of the treason” against Ratherius.

Hence, in the book of his *Confession*, section 2, he mourns “the murders, blinding, dismemberments, plundering, burnings, devastation, and depopulation that occurred because of the faith sworn away from Ugo.”

That same people spared one bishop, although he had been found with the rebels, “because of the kinship which I had,” he says, “with their leading men, and with their supposed leader Ugo himself.” Kinship with the leading men of that people is asserted without qualification, because Ratherius was actually related to them by blood. His kinship with the king, however, is presented as resting only on that people’s opinion, in the phrase “as it said.” This opinion may have arisen because, knowing that he was intimate with Hilduin, the people also believed him to be a blood relative; Hilduin, however, was related to Ugo by marriage.

Although Ratherius was spared for this reason, and thus withdrawn from the calamity suffered by the others, he was nevertheless carried away to some secure place. There, deeply anxious about the danger threatening the archdeacon, the clerics, and the other captives, he spent the entire following night without sleep, striving to rescue them “by prayers, humiliations, tears, promises, and the intervention of friends.” Among the others, he secured the life and freedom of Urso.

To ensure the safety of the rest as well, “on the following day”—that is, on February 3—a certain foremost and most powerful man, “on whom all confidence in a favorable outcome rested,” sent messengers repeatedly to Ratherius and instructed him “not to deviate in anything from his counsel, promising that he would arrange everything with the best possible outcome, provided only that he remained steadfast in the promised agreement” (the *Praeloquia*, book V, section 12).

From the context it is clear that this foremost and most powerful man, although all confidence in a favorable outcome rested upon him, was a bishop whose counsel ultimately brought about Ratherius’s ruin. In the same passage the author complains about bishops who involved themselves not only in affairs of state but also in other, worse matters, and he introduces his own misfortune as an example. He therefore also indicates, though not obscurely, that those who caused his calamity were not only sons of his own Church but that one of them held the same office as he did, namely, the episcopate, when he introduces another man speaking to him in these words:

> “If this is so, it is fitting that you should mourn yourself and your own people no less than the traitors themselves, especially if they were sons of your church—or, God forbid, of the same office as yourself.”

This foremost man, who held the same office, was Hilduin, archbishop of Milan. This can be gathered from the first book of the *Praeloquia*. Ratherius’s entire confidence in Hilduin was certainly justified. Writing about him, as we believe, while suppressing his name, he says that he had followed Hilduin from Belgium into Italy and presents him as the author both of his former promotion to the episcopate and now of the evils “into which, deceived, he has already fallen for his own sake”:

> “Remembering what he bestowed, he forgets what he took away; recounting the heights to which he raised him, he is silent about those from which he cast him down; while concealing the distinction of his own nobility, he reports the mark of poverty which he himself inflicted.”

See the notes at that passage.

Therefore, intending to follow the counsel of this bishop in whom he had placed his greatest confidence, Ratherius asked him to send the leading citizens to him. Accordingly, a council was held with these men and with certain outsiders “at daybreak.” It was decided that a certain letter should be written, so that if the archdeacon “dared to send it, he would be dismissed from the charge as though ignorant of it; but if not, he would immediately suffer the death penalty” (the *Praeloquia*, book III, section 27). Likewise, the other men involved in writing the letter would escape all danger.

To whom this letter was addressed, or what it contained by which the archdeacon and the others conscious of the rebellion were to be withdrawn from mortal danger, is unknown. We know only that it was full of insults, and that Ratherius agreed to its composition in order to rescue his flock from the evils threatening them. By giving this assent, however, “he cast over himself, as it were, a noose by which he would be held” (same source, book V, section 12).

After the letter had been circulated, apparently without its author’s name, someone to whom it had been sent by the archdeacon asked who had written it. Urso, by whose hand it had been written, admitted that he had composed it; but, passing over in silence the others who had taken part in the work, he presented Ratherius alone as its author and the instigator of the entire undertaking (same source, book III, section 27).

Thus, after the letter had rescued the others from all danger, it was turned against Ratherius alone. For this reason he wrote in the aforementioned letter to Urso:

> “While I advised you”—by consenting to that letter—“I neglected myself, as it seems; while I spared you, although partly aware of your undertaking, I betrayed myself.”

By “undertaking,” we believe, he means the rebellion. When he calls it “your undertaking,” not “ours,” he indicates that its authors were the Veronese, to whom, as we have seen, Ugo’s soldiers attributed all the blame. At the same time, he signifies that he himself was exempt from it.

When he testifies that, although conscious of the rebellion, he spared the rebels themselves, he may be referring to what we explained above from book IV of the *Praeloquia*, section 7: namely, that although he knew the rebels to be citizens and sons of the king, he had nevertheless not betrayed them so that they might be punished.

The letter in question may have dealt with this undertaking against Ugo, but in such a way as to spare the names of its authors. When Ratherius consented to the letter, he likewise spared the naming of the actual guilty parties. But when Urso was questioned and declared that the bishop himself was the author of the letter and the instigator of the entire undertaking, and when no hearing was granted him before judgment was pronounced, he alone was placed in danger.

Thus, while King Ugo was reigning, Ratherius was taken captive to Pavia. In book V of the *Praeloquia*, section 27, he attributes this calamity to fraud, deceit, and faction, complaining that he was “betrayed by fraud, abandoned through negligence, captured by deceit, and brought down to these misfortunes by faction.”

§ V. — What he suffered in the prison at Pavia. He writes to Urso, a cleric of the Church of Verona. After the bishop was taken away, many infants died at Verona without baptism. In the leisure of prison he writes six books of the *Praeloquia*.

22. Ratherius calls his prison the little tower of Walbert (letter 5 to John, section 6), perhaps deriving the name from the powerful judge Walbert, who, after conspiring against Ugo, was beheaded in prison at Pavia (LIUTPRAND, book III, chapters 10–11). The prison was closed by three locks or doors, as indicated by the author’s words in book II of the *Praeloquia*, section 1: “And I am confined in a prison closed in three ways.”

He spent two and a half years detained there. The extent of his suffering is suggested in book III of the *Praeloquia*, section 13, where, speaking in the person of the bishop “groaning in prison under chains,” he represents himself as “despised, insulted, scorned, imprisoned, bound, naked, hungry, thirsty, and filled to overflowing with every kind of misery.” He repeats similar statements in book IV, section 7.

To these miseries were added the slanders spread against him by the Veronese. He complains of them in book III, section 24:

> “Meanwhile there are also in the episcopal residence certain gnawers who . . . . . . . now compose certain slanders against this man; and this is done not by outsiders but by private persons—that is, by intimate associates and familiar friends—who ought to have been witnesses to the goodness of his purpose. I say that this is done not by enemies but by deceitful friends, men once united with him, formerly dear and familiar, who together with him used to eat sweet food in the house of God—namely, the ecclesiastics of Verona—as though walking together in agreement, raising him to heaven itself, and proclaiming him blessed, just, and holy with praises no less deceptive than flattering.”

One of these slanderers was a man whose name, Urso or Ursus, is indicated in the following words of a letter that the bishop sent to him from prison:

> “Let them not be called Ursini or Ursani from your derived name.”

His father-in-law was archdeacon of the cathedral church, and Urso himself was also counted among the canons of that church. Both men, together with the rest of the clergy, had conspired against the king. Both had been brought into mortal danger, and Ratherius had protected both of them at the cost of his own danger, as we explained in the preceding section. Yet after so great a benefaction, Urso proved ungrateful and did not cease slandering Ratherius even though he was a captive.

Ratherius therefore sent him the aforementioned letter from prison to restrain him from his abuse. He also grieves that he had been abandoned by everyone, especially by the bishops, who, like mute animals, said nothing on his behalf in so great a calamity. The words of book IV of the *Praeloquia*, section 22, suggest that some powerful bishop was responsible for this silence: “Most wretched man, your mouth has been closed by someone of the same order”—that is, of the episcopal order—“through silence of the worst and most unheard-of kind.”

23. Such numerous and great calamities and slanders did not break Ratherius’s spirit at all. He bore with equanimity the traitors who spoke against him. Raising the vision of his mind to God and referring the cause of all his afflictions to his own sins, he says:

> “Alas for the grief! Through my sins, which caused and deserved much greater things, I have been brought down to these sufferings” (the *Praeloquia*, book VI, section 25).

He gave thanks to divine mercy, which dealt with him in such a way “that, consuming and erasing me in this furnace of necessity, it might so cleanse me in this world that it would find nothing for that devouring, unquenchable future fire to burn; rather, by its grace it might find something to reward, and by its justice something to crown” (same source, book V, section 26).

For this reason he treated his traitors and slanderers, who had provided the occasion for what he calls his great benefit, as though they had deserved exceedingly well of him, showing them every kindness. Let us hear what he wrote to the deacon Urso, who had harmed him most of all:

> “It is read, my son, in the *Tripartite History*, that a certain man, occupied in tending livestock, killed someone and, driven by fear, fled into the desert. Having been trained in goodness by the examples of the holy Fathers, he became a perfect hermit and always blessed the crime that had been the cause of such great progress for him. I have related this so that you may gather from it how much you served my progress when you accused me so gravely, intending that I should utterly perish. For if you were present and permitted it, I would caress with the sweetest kisses the hands that wrote that letter, because this was the cause, the material, and, as I think, the whole sum of my salvation. Through it I was, as I believe, rescued from eternal death and restored to life . . . .

> “I consider that I have progressed so much through this occasion that I see no one whom I ought to embrace more than you, who were the material cause of so many blessings for me. O how fortunate I am—fortunate, I say, through my very misfortune—even if the only benefit I had received from it were that I came to know you and men like you! Therefore, sparing you in everything and also returning you the fullest thanks for these things, I admonish you, my son: since you have now benefited me beyond expression, beware lest, through hatred of me, you harm yourself completely” (same source, book III, section 28).

24. Meanwhile Ratherius was distressed by the losses suffered by his flock and by the souls entrusted to his care, which were enduring the greatest damage after the bishop had been taken away. This is the point of the passage in which he introduces another person speaking with and consoling him:

> “Although you ought to mourn greatly the abandonment of your people, you should nevertheless not do so inconsolably . . . . If the length of time torments you and the loss of those who are dying without the help of baptism grieves you, and if you perceive that your torturers do not care about your people, but seek only to complete their own purposes through your torment; submitting yourself wholly to God’s will and disposition, use the voice of the one who said: ‘If this storm is because of me, take me up and cast me into the sea’ (Jonah 1:12). Be ready to give your very life, not to mention to undergo every loss of honor, for the sake of the flock—only let the ship of the Church no longer be endangered because of me, sending so many, alas for the grief, sons into eternal death.”

The misfortune briefly indicated here is explained more fully in book IV of the *Praeloquia*, section 21:

> “To whom, let us ask, will it be attributed that such a multitude, piously freed by the grace of Christ and destined to enter the kingdom of heaven, impiously abandoned, filled hell? For . . . we learned from the report of certain people, alas for the grief, that during the very period in which he was absent—the bishop—and at Easter, since the baptismal rite had not been celebrated in that church, because chrism was lacking and there was no one to provide it, such a great disaster occurred in the city among infants, and solely among those who had not been baptized, as no one remembers among earlier generations. Thus, scattered throughout the houses, although not intentionally suffocated by their mothers, they could all together have produced one lament throughout the entire city—if only the fear of God still existed in that place—some mourning as divine judgment demanded, and others lamenting both the temporal and eternal death of their children and of the mothers who had given them birth.”

We believe that this event occurred in the year 935. Since the bishop was taken captive from Verona to Pavia at the beginning of February of that year, amid the resulting disorder no provision was made for the sacred chrism, which had to be consecrated by a bishop and was needed for the preparation of the baptismal font at Easter. Thus the blessing of the font was lacking that year, and many infants consequently died without baptism.

When Ratherius speaks of “innumerable sons sent into eternal death,” he calls this the “disaster of the infants.” In doing so, he is evidently following the teaching of Saint Augustine and other Fathers.

25. In the prison at Pavia, free from external cares, he composed the notable work of the *Praeloquia*, divided into six books. In it he explains the duties of people of every age, sex, condition, and rank, and touches upon the vices and abuses that were becoming prevalent at that time. He also gave it the titles *Meditations of the Heart* and *Agonisticon*, because these books provide material for extensive meditation and train the Christian as though for an athletic contest. This was the fruit of his Pavia imprisonment.

The first two books contain instruction for the private life of every person. The third and fourth instruct a ruler. After explaining matters pertaining to the ruler’s life and what he owes to his subjects and to himself, they discuss at greater length what he owes to the Church and its ministers. This appears to be the principal aim of these books.

The author says much about the two powers. When he commends episcopal dignity and authority, he also intersperses many references to his own sufferings and to the events that had occurred because of them. He inserts the letter written in prison that we mentioned earlier. And lest anyone suspect that some error concerning the faith had brought him into such misery, he presents his teaching as consonant with the teaching of Saint Augustine and appends at the end of the third book a profession of faith conforming to the creed of Saint Athanasius.

The fifth book deals at greater length with bishops, and more briefly with the other ranks of the Church and with monks. While attacking abuses among bishops, he again brings forward certain matters concerning his own calamities. Finally, the sixth book discusses the common duties of Christians, the capital vices, penance, charity, the relation of works to God, and many other matters of the same kind. Throughout these books, much illuminates the discipline of his age, some passages illuminate its history, and many others illuminate Catholic doctrine.

26. In this last respect, it should be noted that in book IV, section 15, he clearly refutes the unsound opinion of a certain man who, in the presence of several bishops who were not at all unlearned, dared to criticize what is sung in the Church—namely, that all the saints will reign eternally with Christ. He claimed that it should neither be said nor believed that anyone besides God reigns eternally, but that it should be acknowledged that the saints merely rejoice with him. In this matter he unfortunately became so confident that he removed from the Church’s song the melody, sweet with the sound of such great blessedness, for which he is now laboring so greatly—or perhaps, “only so greatly”—in the present life.

The words of the hymn sung at Lauds on the feast of All Saints are indicated:

> “All you who reign in the high court of the stars, princes,” etc.

The man who, because of these lines, or even because of a single line, removed the entire hymn from the Church’s song was apparently a bishop of great authority. The words that follow indicate that, when his error had been openly proposed, the others who connived at it offered no opposition:

> “O blindness of the blind—of the one who speaks and of those who connive with him in this one matter, and in the most foolish way, if indeed such folly is defended!”

And in section 16:

> “Tell me, I ask: you who either say this, or consent to it by keeping silent, or—which is much worse—confirm it by supporting it,” etc.

§ VI. — After the prison at Pavia, he is banished to Como. He corrects and rewrites in clearer style the life of Saint Ursmar, which he found there. Released from his exile at Como, he goes to Gaul. He writes to Robert, archbishop of Trier. In Provence he teaches Roestang by letter and writes a book on the art of grammar. He refuses the episcopate there and returns to Lobbes, his monastery.

[Col. 0048D]

27. After spending two and a half years in the prison at Ticinum—that is, from February 935 until August 937—Ratherius was sent into exile (letter 5 to John, section 5). We learn both from Fulcuin and from Ratherius’s letter to the monks of Lobbes, which he prefixed to the life of Saint Ursmar, that this exile was at Como (FULCUIN, chapter 20).

He testifies that he was an exile in that city with its bishop when he writes in the aforementioned letter, section 1: “Recently, as exiles under the venerable bishop of the holy Church of Como, by the just judgment of God,” etc. The bishop of Como with whom he was an exile was named Azo, as is clear from a document of 937 published by Ughelli.

While he was staying in the episcopal residence, he found there the life of Saint Ursmar, first abbot of Lobbes, written by Abbot Anso. But its style was so barbarous and corrupted by errors that, offended by its obscurity, he decided that it should be not so much corrected as rewritten in a clearer style. It will therefore appropriately be published among his works. The author sent this revised and elaborated version to the monks of Lobbes, who venerated Saint Ursmar as the patron of their monastery.

28. Meanwhile, a synod of bishops was to be convened in that part of Gaul then called the kingdom of Burgundy. The archbishop Wido of Lyon, Sobbo of Vienne, and the bishops Godescalcus and Aurelius also invited Ratherius. Because of the fame of his name, they held him in the highest regard and greatly desired to acknowledge him publicly and deliberate with him at the council.

They may have known that he had been released from prison, but they did not know that he was still being detained in exile at Como. He therefore sent them a letter. In its address he presents himself as an exile, and he declares that his exile prevented him from attending the synod to which he had been invited:

> “Lords, this above all is the reason why I have not appeared before your lordships in accordance with your command: I am not my own master.”

He modestly diminishes the reputation that had circulated about him. He touches only lightly upon the misery that oppressed him even outside prison, in exile, and offers as evidence that he lacked the paper on which to write a longer and more worthy letter.

He asks for some assistance. Since he could not travel to them himself, he sent them, in his place, the six books of the *Praeloquia* that he had composed in the little tower at Ticinum (see the notes to book V of the *Praeloquia*; FULCUIN, chapter 20), as Fulcuin also records.

He also gave them another very brief letter—or rather, a note cast in the form of a letter—which he inserted into book V of the *Praeloquia*, section 13. Its heading presents them as assembled in council:

> “Ratherius, an exile, to Wido and Sobbo, archbishops, and the other fellow bishops sitting in council.”

This note was inserted into the aforementioned book at the point where he complains that no one can be found “to intervene for the needy or to plead for the condemned.” He urges them to reread and consider the matters that might move them to pity him, to offer him help, and to interpose their patronage on his behalf, especially since he was confident that they possessed great influence with their fellow-regional king, Ugo.

29. He spent as many years in exile at Como as in the prison at Pavia, namely two and a half years (Letter 5 to John, no. 5). He was therefore in exile at Como from August 937 until approximately the beginning of 940. Since he asserts that he was freed from this exile against Hugh’s will, either he secretly escaped from Como, or he said that the king was unwilling in the sense that permission to depart was not granted voluntarily, but was perhaps forced from the king through the intervention of the bishops mentioned above. From Como he withdrew into Gaul, perhaps to Widon or Sobbo, who desired to see him. At this time he seems to have traveled through the three provinces of Gaul—Burgundy, Provence [LV], and Septimania—which he mentions in the *Conjecture on Quality* [Col. 0050A], no. 3.

While he was staying in one of these provinces, he received a letter from Rotbert, archbishop of Trier, who proposed several small questions for him to solve. In the reply that Ratherius gave him, Letter 3, he calls him “the noblest of archbishops,” since Rotbert was descended from Theodoric, duke of Saxony, and had as his sister Saint Matilda, the mother of Otto, king of Germany and later emperor. Since the questions proposed concerned secular studies and were of the same kind as those which he had earlier received from the Milanese to solve before his episcopate, he excuses himself from solving them on the ground that he had renounced such studies after entering the episcopal order:

“Once invested with the mitre”—he says—“and bearing this burden, which by God’s mercy I discharge, I immediately ceased to pursue such matters, considering that in this office entrusted to me I ought rather to meditate day and night upon God’s law” [Col. 0050B].

He does not deny that these studies might provide some assistance to a bishop, if he turned them to sacred use:

“But that wicked servant,” he adds, “is condemned to eternal punishment in the Gospel because he preferred to bury the talent of his understanding in the earth rather than dedicate it wholly to heaven. This likeness, as I believe, warns me the sinner, among other things, that the very small measure of talent which I have acquired by God’s gift ought rather to be sharpened where Christ is seated at the right hand of God than entrusted to earthly vanity, from which I might gain nothing but empty wind, and that not without the greatest injury to my soul.”

Since Rotbert had promised him some assistance, Ratherius gives thanks and begs that it be provided as soon as possible in his present necessity [Col. 0050C]. The same archbishop also seems to have requested some book of Ratherius. Ratherius sent him the one volume of the *Praeloquia* that he had at hand, on the condition that Rotbert return it to him promptly. He wrote this letter after the beginning of 940, once he had been released from his exile at Como and before he devoted himself to Roestang’s instruction in Provence. Since he was consequently under obligation to no one, he presented himself as ready for Rotbert’s service, as we established more fully in the first note to that same letter.

30. Meanwhile, in want of everything, he undertook the occupation of teaching in Provence in order to obtain a livelihood. “While he was staying in that part of Burgundy,” says Fulcuinus, chapter 20, “which is called Provence, he accepted, at the request of a certain very wealthy man, his son named Roestang, in order to instruct him in letters” [Col. 0050D].

In this occupation he composed a book “on the art of grammar, which, in the customary language of the pagans, he called *Sparadorsum*, because a boy who became accustomed to the schools could thereby save his back from the blows.” See the general preface, no. 19.

He spent a considerable period instructing Roestang. Because of this, “there” (that is, in Provence), as the aforementioned Fulcuinus reports, “a bishopric was given to him; and, leaving it, he returned to Laubias.” In the book of the *Confession*, written later, he implies that only two bishoprics were conferred upon him, namely Verona and Liège. Since he had been expelled from both equally, in the same book, written after his expulsion even from the see of Liège, no. 2, he reports that his confessor said to him: “Two bishoprics have ruined you” [Col. 0051A].

If he lost only two bishoprics, he had undertaken only two. Thus this third bishopric in Provence, which was given—or, rather, offered—to him may be said to have been offered, but not actually conferred.

31. Accordingly, after educating Roestang, he refused the bishopric offered to him in Provence and returned to Laubias, to his fellow monks. Fulcuinus indicates the time:

“Richarius,” he says, “was still alive. He received him favorably and allowed him to live at Laubias. Not long afterward Richarius died, after having spent twenty-two years in the episcopate” [Col. 0051B].

Richarius, bishop of Liège and at the same time abbot of Laubias, had been promoted in 922, as we saw in no. 10. If he “spent twenty-two years in the episcopate,” he died toward the end of 944, or rather at the beginning of 945, the year in which two chronicles, the Liège and Lobbes chronicles, together with Frodoard, recorded his death and the election of Ogo, or Hugh, his successor.

Ratherius, therefore, was received into the monastery of Lobbes by Richarius, both bishop and abbot, shortly before Richarius’s death. In 944 he left Provence for Laubias. He remained there only a short time, however; for in 946 he returned to Italy in order to recover the bishopric of Verona, as will become clear from what follows.

[LVII] § VII. Ratherius returns to Italy to meet King Hugh. He is captured by Berengar. He is recalled to the bishopric of Verona by Count Milo. King Hugh left Italy in 947, not in 946; but he died in Provence not in 947, but in 948.

[Col. 0051C]

32. Berengar, margrave of Ivrea, grandson through Gisla of the emperor Berengar, had taken refuge with Eticho, duke of Swabia, in 940 in order to escape Hugh’s plots. In 945, advancing into Italy with a small troop through the Venosta Valley, he pitched his camp at a fortification in the Tridentine territory called Formicaria.

Manasses, archbishop of Arles and a kinsman of King Hugh, to whom the king had entrusted three churches of his kingdom—or, “more truthfully,” says Liutprand, “had given them over as prey” (*Liutprand*, book IV, chapter 3)—namely Verona, Trent, and Mantua, and who also administered the margraviate of Trent, had entrusted the aforementioned fortification to his cleric Adelard (*ibid.*, book V, chapter 12).

After conferring with him, Berengar swore that he would give Manasses the Church of Milan if Manasses assisted his party [Col. 0051D]. Lured by this hope, Manasses not only surrendered that fortification to Berengar, but also attempted to win all Italy over to him. When news of this spread rapidly, some soon began, abandoning Hugh, to join Berengar. Among these was Milo, the extremely powerful count of Verona, who, having been summoned to Pavia because Hugh suspected him and being watched there by guards secretly stationed around him, prolonged dinner until midnight. When the guards had been lulled to sleep by wine and fatigue, he escaped and reached Verona with only one companion. There he immediately summoned and received Berengar.

As more and more people subsequently joined Berengar’s side, especially the Milanese, King Hugh, toward whom the Italians were ill-disposed, sent his son Lothair to Milan. He asked Berengar and the other leading men of Italy that, if they no longer wished Hugh to reign in Italy, they should at least recognize his young son as king—a son who had done them no wrong and could be educated according to their wishes. [LVIII] Moved by pity, they raised Lothair, who had been prostrate before the cross in the church, and proclaimed him king.

That this occurred in 945 is made certain by Frodoard, a contemporary author. For in that year he writes in his *Chronicle*: “Hugh, king of Italy, was driven from the kingdom by his own people, and his son was received into the kingdom.”

Meanwhile Hugh, fearing for his life, had departed from Pavia with a large quantity of gold and silver and had begun his journey toward the Alps, intending to leave Italy. On the way, a messenger reported that the Italians did not object to his also being king of Italy. Hence the aforementioned Frodoard reports under the year 946: “Hugh, king of Italy, is received into the kingdom by his own people” [Col. 0052B].

This was brought about by Berengar’s stratagem, so that Hugh would not carry beyond the mountains the treasures with which he could gather an army of Burgundians and other Gauls and recover the Italian kingdom. Since Frodoard assigns this event to 946, while Liutprand describes the reception first of the son and then of the father in such a way that the two events were not far apart, we believe that the former occurred toward the end of 945 and the latter toward the beginning of 946.

In any event, the Italians in reality left Hugh and his son Lothair only the bare title of king [Col. 0052C], while supreme authority and power over the entire kingdom were transferred to Berengar.

33. In these straitened circumstances Hugh regretted what he had done against Ratherius and perhaps also regretted having placed Manasses in Ratherius’s see, since Manasses had defected so openly. He repeatedly expressed his desire to see Ratherius and, if possible, restore him (Letter 5 to John, no. 5).

When Ratherius learned of this—in 946, namely—“I resolved,” he says in Letter 5, “to visit him and console his misfortune through service on every day; for there had been no lack of someone to tell me—late, as I fear, and may God avert it from him—that he had often wished in repentance that God would grant him the opportunity for me to come to him, so that, if he were able, he might obtain my restoration; or, failing that, that he would give me enough money so that I would no longer be in want” [Col. 0052D].

Accordingly, Ratherius left Laubias to meet Hugh. But Berengar captured him on the way. This was done at Manasses’s instigation, since Manasses feared that Ratherius would take the Church of Verona away from him. Ratherius was held in custody for three and a half months. He was then released and restored to the Church of Verona through the efforts of Count Milo, so that he might expel Manasses [LIX]. Milo feared that Manasses, who possessed very great power, might, moved by repentance, defect from Berengar and be reconciled with his uncle Hugh, thereby once again bringing ruin upon Milo as a rebel.

That these events occurred in 946 is made clear by a document in which Ratherius is shown in possession of the bishopric of Verona in January 947 [Col. 0053A]. This document, recently published by the marquis and canon of our cathedral church, de Dionysiis, is the original instrument of an exchange carried out “in the city of Verona between the lord Ratherius, venerable bishop of the holy Church of Verona, and Leo, son of the late Theudelavus of Aregasta.” Ratherius himself subscribed it in his own hand together with the other clergy of the cathedral church:

“While our lord Hugh reigns here in Italy, in the twenty-first year, and his son Lothair reigns, in the sixteenth year, on the day of the month of January, in the fifth indiction.”

These are the chronological indicators of the year 947.

If in January 947 Ratherius was peacefully enjoying his episcopate, while three and a half months previously he had been held captive, his captivity clearly fell in the year 946; and it is even more probable that his restoration to the episcopate should be placed before January 947.

34. No one will dispute that the year 946 is the year to which we assigned Ratherius’s captivity and restoration to his episcopate. The only question concerns the place where he was captured by Berengar. A recent, otherwise very learned author, believing that Hugh finally left Italy in 946 and withdrew to Provence, where he died (Florius, *On Privileges*, dissertation 2, p. 77), thinks that Ratherius set out from Laubias for Provence to meet Hugh and was captured on this journey.

But it is certain that he was captured by Berengar in Italy while traveling to Hugh, who was still living in Italy, because Berengar exercised royal authority only in Italy. Moreover, Hugh did not leave Italy until 947, after Ratherius had been restored to his see.

In the brief *Chronicle of the Kings of Italy* published by Muratori, two entries occur which establish this beyond doubt (*Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, vol. IV, p. 149). One concerns King Hugh:

“He reigned for twenty-one full years, nine months, and three days.”

The other concerns Lothair:

“After the death of Hugh, Lothair himself reigned for three full years, seven months, and two days. He died on Friday, the tenth day before the Kalends of December, in the year 950.”

Taking the words of this second entry, “after the death of Hugh,” to refer to Hugh’s death, Muratori, calculating the years during which Lothair reigned after him, assigned Hugh’s death to 24 April 947 (*Annals*, under 947) [Col. 0053D]. But he overlooked the earlier entry. Since, as Muratori himself demonstrates, Hugh began to reign around June 926, his death, when the years, months, and days given in that entry are calculated, falls in February or March 948. Both Sigebert and the Saxon annalist edited by Eckhard confirm 948 as the year of Hugh’s death.

Since the same Hugh, after going to Provence, “entered the way of all flesh shortly thereafter,” according to Liutprand (book I, chapter 14), it must be said that he left Italy in the preceding year, 947 [Col. 0054A]. The words of the other entry, “after the death of Hugh,” indicate only “after Hugh left Italy.” That he left in April 947 is recognized from the chronological notices recorded there. Accordingly, Sigebert and the Saxon annalist rightly report in that same year that “Hugh returned to Arles, from which he had come.”

Indeed, the instrument of exchange mentioned above, which records “King Hugh here in Italy” in January 947, demonstrates that he was still in Italy at that time; for after he had left Italy he could not have been called “king here in Italy.”

Muratori objects with a diploma of Lothair issued for the Church of Reggio on 19 May 946, in the seventeenth year of Lord Lothair and in the fourth indiction (*Annals*, under 946). Since King Hugh is not mentioned in it, Muratori concludes that Hugh had already left Italy before 19 May 946 [Col. 0054B].

This argument deserves little consideration, since the chronological notices of that diploma contain an obvious error. The seventeenth year of Lothair neither agrees with the fourth indiction nor with the year 946. Since Lothair began his reign toward the end of May 931, the seventeenth year of his reign began toward the end of May 947 and ended toward the end of May 948.

Thus, if the diploma is genuine, 19 May of the seventeenth year of King Lothair belongs to the year 948. The chronological entry should accordingly be corrected to read: “14 Kalends of June, in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 948, in the seventeenth year of Lord Lothair, in the sixth indiction” [Col. 0054C].

At that time only Lothair is named as king, because Hugh had left Italy long before and was already dead; Lothair alone therefore enjoyed the royal title in Italy.

This correction is also confirmed by another original document preserved in the archive of the Veronese monastery of Saint Mary in Organis, where the following chronological notices are found:

“While our lord Lothair reigns here in Italy, in the seventeenth year of his reign, on the day of the month of February, in the sixth indiction.”

Nor does a diploma of the same Lothair, published by Muratori in volume V of the *Antiquities of Italy*, p. 357, contradict our position. In it only King Lothair is mentioned, with these chronological notices appended:

“On the fourteenth day before the Kalends of February, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 947, but in the seventeenth year of King Lothair, in the sixth indiction” [Col. 0054D].

For January, when joined with the seventeenth year of Lothair and the sixth indiction, corresponds to the year 948 of the common era. It cannot be reconciled with the year 947 unless the year of the Lord’s Incarnation in this diploma is thought to have been calculated according to the Florentine and Venetian custom, so that it began on the Kalends of March. By that reckoning, January of the year 947 coincides with January of the common year 948.

At this time Lothair alone was king, Italy having been abandoned by Hugh in April 947.

All the documents, whether corrected or reconciled, must therefore be accepted as showing that Hugh remained in Italy throughout 946 and until April 947, and that Ratherius, while traveling to Hugh, who was still living in Italy, was captured by Berengar in 946 and restored to his see through Milo’s agency.

[LXII] § VIII. What hardships Ratherius endured from the clergy after his restoration to his see, while Count Milo supported them. What it means to hold a synod, attend the chapter of the clergy, and perform ecclesiastical offices. Manasses, archbishop of Arles, ordains a bishop of his own diocese to the title of the Church of Verona. After two years Ratherius is expelled once again from the see of Verona to make way for Manasses.

35. After being restored to Verona, Ratherius held the bishopric for two years (Letter 5 to John, no. 6), that is, from the year 946, to which we assigned his restoration, until 948. Three ancient documents from this period also establish the fact.

The first is the instrument from January 947 that we mentioned in no. 33. The second, from the same year and the month of June, was seen by Alexander Canobius in the archive of Saint Stephen. He mentions it in an Italian manuscript work preserved by Giovanni Battista Biancolini, entitled *Annals of Verona*, book VI, in these words:

“In this same year (947), Bishop Racherio, in the month of June, made an exchange with Garimberto, a deacon of the cathedral church, who at that time was also custodian and rector of the church of Saint Stephen. The bishop gave him two ancient tombs, which were in an old cemetery near the body of Saint Maurus, bishop of Verona; and Garimberto gave the bishop a piece of land outside the gate of Saint Stephen at Fontanelle. The instrument is subscribed by the bishop and by Garimberto, as seen in the records of Saint Stephen” (*On Two Bishops*, p. 115) [Col. 0055C].

The third document, published by the marquis and canon de Dionysiis, is Ratherius’s exchange with Ursemarius, carried out “while our lord Lothair reigns here in Italy, in the seventeenth year … in the sixth indiction.”

The seventeenth year of King Lothair began toward the end of May 947 and ended before the end of May 948. Since the sixth indiction began in September 947, this document, in which the month is not given, was written between September 947 and the end of May 948 (Letter 5 to John, no. 6).

During these two years of his episcopate Ratherius was afflicted by so many and such serious troubles [LXIII] that he became weary of life and considered the calamity he had endured in the prison at Pavia lighter [Col. 0055D]. Count Milo was the instigator and author of these evils. He had arranged for Ratherius to be recalled solely in order to exclude Manasses, the usurper of the see of Verona, whom he feared. Although he treated Ratherius with every outward courtesy and appeared to be his closest friend, in reality he harbored a hostile disposition toward him and encouraged and supported the rebellion of Ratherius’s clergy.

36. The bishop, who was exceptionally devoted to the sacred canons and ecclesiastical discipline, ardently desired to eradicate the many abuses of that age. He began with the clergy, among whom serious abuses were flourishing; these will be discussed elsewhere. On this occasion he began collecting the sacred canons that restrained those abuses, which he later inserted into a book entitled *On Contempt for the Canons* (part I, no. 1, note 6).

The clergy stirred up great disturbances against the bishop on this account. With Count Milo supporting them, the bishop found that all his efforts were fruitless and every avenue of action closed to him. He was driven into such straits that nothing was left to him of the authority called jurisdiction, and only the authority called order was permitted to him.

This is implied by the opening words of the first part of *On Contempt for the Canons*, no. 1:

“When the madness of rebellious clerics once rose up against me, leaving me nothing of that office concerning which it was said to one man, ‘Feed my sheep,’ except the making of chrism and the power to chrismate …” [Col. 0056B].

The latter is the power of order.

Let us hear what he later wrote at greater length on this subject to the supreme pontiff, Letter 5, no. 6:

“If I attempt to recount the martyrdom that I endured for two years through the tricks of that same Milo, you will think it a history—that is, a fable. To summarize it as briefly as possible: with him supporting all the clergy, soldiers, tenants, and servants against me, I did not dare to hold a synod, attend the chapter of the clergy, mention anything that needed correction, or establish or abolish anything. Nowhere could I say anything that he might wish to know without his learning it immediately. For I believe that he had extorted an oath concerning this from everyone. And when all his people insulted me in his presence, he alone, as though on my side against them all, acted for me, so that, provoked, they might report still greater accusations [LXIV]. Even what I did at his command—for I did not dare to oppose his orders—he turned into a fault, secretly fabricating a charge against me among the clergy, while deceitfully promising me vengeance upon them.

“This went so far that one day, while I was performing ecclesiastical offices, the archdeacon went out with the entire clergy, leaving me alone in the church, and claimed for himself another church against me.”

And after some further remarks:

“Although Milo was the instigator and author of all these things, he nevertheless sought to be seen and called my advocate and protector. Thus he afflicted me most bitterly, so that scarcely anyone in the kingdom failed to consider him my very close friend. But I was so worn down and anxious, day and night, that I became weary of my life. I would rather have sat, as once before, in Walbert’s little tower than in the cathedral of Verona; I would rather have been hungry under Hugh than feasted with Milo.”

Several matters in this lengthy testimony deserve attention.

37. When he says, “I did not dare to hold a synod or attend the chapter of the clergy,” this must be understood of those synods and chapters held during visitations of the parishes of the diocese.

For in these circumstances they said that a “synod was held” when the bishop addressed the assembled people during a visitation and required certain leading members of the congregation, bound by oath, to answer questions concerning matters that had to be investigated during the visitation regarding the condition of the parishioners.

This meaning is clearly gathered from the canon of the Council of Rouen preserved by Regino, book II, chapter 1, and by Burchard, book I, chapter 90, where we read:
