“When the bishop travels around his diocese, the archdeacon or archpriest must precede him by one or two days through the parishes that he is going to visit. After the people have been summoned, he must announce the arrival of their own pastor and require everyone, except the sick, to appear without fail at his SYNOD on the appointed day.”

An oath is then prescribed, which “the bishop, seated in the SYNOD after an appropriate address,” required from the more mature and respectable men; finally, the questions to be put to them are set out.

This is also confirmed by Gerard in the life of Saint Ulrich, bishop of Augsburg, both of whom were contemporaries of Ratherius. In chapter 6, speaking of diocesan visitations and calling the gathering which the preceding testimony calls a “synod” a “council,” he uses these words (Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints of the Benedictine Order*, vol. VII, p. 428):

“When he had arrived at those places where his councils had been announced … sitting in the COUNCIL, he ordered the people to be summoned before him and commanded that the more prudent and truthful be questioned under oath,” and so forth.

Later he adds:

“After the COUNCIL had been completed, he returned to his lodging.”

Ratherius’s words in the *Itinerary*, no. 5, refer to this synod held on the occasion of visitations:

“For whom among the laity would I have dared to confront concerning adultery in the synod?” and so forth, as we shall explain in the note there.

38. “Chapters of the clergy,” however, were the gatherings at which, after the synod of the entire congregation had been held, all the clergy of that congregation were summoned together whenever necessary and questioned before the bishop. This is evident from the same Gerard, who, after describing the councils mentioned above held by Saint Ulrich among the parishes, adds:

“On certain days, however, he decided to hold CHAPTERS with the clergy in those places where the archpriests thought that this could most suitably be done and where they believed him to be freer from other worldly councils”—that is, the gatherings previously mentioned, which concerned the laity. “After the clergy had been assembled before him, he carefully questioned the archpriests, deans, and the best men whom he could find among them,” and so forth, namely, about matters pertaining to the clergy.

Concerning the ancient formula of these interrogations, some of which concerned the clergy and others the laity, see what we said in the admonition to Ratherius’s synodical letter [Col. 0057D].

Since, therefore, Count Milo encouraged and supported “all the clergy, soldiers, tenants, and servants” against Ratherius, Ratherius did not dare to “hold a synod,” at which soldiers, tenants, and servants—that is, all the lay inhabitants of the parishes—were to be summoned during visitations, nor to hold chapters, which the clergy were required to attend. He could neither mention anything that needed correction nor establish or abolish anything.

We do not deny that clerical matters were also dealt with in diocesan synods, as is evident from the *Itinerary* mentioned above, no. 6. But when, in the aforementioned letter to the supreme pontiff, Ratherius distinguishes the synod from the chapters of the clergy and mentions not so much the clergy as “soldiers, tenants, and servants”—that is, laymen—and since their cases were not heard in diocesan synods but in those convened on the occasion of visitations, we have therefore believed that the word “synod” must here be understood of such visitation synods.

39. We formerly thought, together with others, that the words “while I was performing ecclesiastical orders” referred to the conferral of sacred orders [LXVI]. Now, however, after more mature consideration, we believe that these words signify some solemn ecclesiastical function.

For Ratherius uses a similar formula in Letter 1: “Conrad performed ecclesiastical orders.” As we observed in the third note to that letter, he expressed by this phrase the performance by Conrad of some sacred function, not a sacred ordination.

Indeed, if Ratherius had been occupied with conferring sacred orders, how could all the clerics who were also candidates for ordination—men who are ordinarily concerned about their advancement—have abandoned him and left him alone in the church? If the matter concerned only the conferral of orders, there would have been no reason for the archdeacon, leaving the bishop alone in the church, to claim another church for himself against the bishop.

These circumstances clearly indicate that the bishop was celebrating some solemn function in the cathedral, with the entire clergy present; but after abandoning the bishop, the clergy, led by the archdeacon, transferred the same function to another church near the cathedral, such as the church of Saint George or Saint John at the Fountain.

The archdeacon Adelard is listed as a subscriber to the instrument of exchange confirmed by Ratherius after his restoration in January 947, which we mentioned in the preceding paragraph, no. 33 [Col. 0058C]. If this archdeacon did not die soon afterward, he was the leader of this rebellion.

40. Manasses, archbishop of Arles, inflicted another and no less serious injury upon Ratherius. He feared neither the prohibitions nor the penalties imposed by the sacred canons upon metropolitans who transgressed the boundaries of their provinces. “Laying an ambush for the bishop of Verona, he consecrated a certain bishop of his own diocese to the title of the Church of Verona” (Letter 5 to John, no. 6).

Ratherius also accuses Milo of instigating this trouble. Milo had subsequently abandoned the suspicions that he had earlier conceived against Manasses—perhaps after Hugh’s departure from Italy—and had become his friend [Col. 0058D].

Since Manasses presented himself as bishop of Verona and arranged that, after Ratherius had been expelled, the same Church should be handed over not to the cleric whom he himself had ordained bishop, but to Manasses himself by royal command, as we shall soon see, let others judge in what sense he consecrated him “to the title of the Church of Verona.”

41. “After I had endured this for two years,” Ratherius adds, “and this was the most grievous prison of all the miseries that I had suffered before and afterward [LXVII], while I was going to celebrate the evening synaxis, a messenger of Lord King Lothair arrived, ordering me to leave the city and give way to Manasses’s invasion of my see. He added a sufficiently friendly piece of advice: namely, that it would be better for me to withdraw than to be dismembered or killed through Milo’s treachery, or—or this would be much less severe than those alternatives, but would be most grievous to me—to be captured and taken away to a place where I least wished to go” [Col. 0059A].

This was accomplished partly through Milo’s efforts and partly through those of Manasses. There can be no doubt that this command was issued in the name of King Lothair by Berengar, with whom Milo and Manasses possessed very great influence. For, as we noted earlier in no. 32, Berengar conducted everything in Lothair’s court, leaving Lothair only the royal title and honor.

Ratherius willingly yielded to this command. He would previously have withdrawn from so many plots and calamities, had he not feared incurring the reproach of the hireling who, fleeing out of fear, abandons the flock entrusted to him to the wolves.

“I did, when ordered,” he says, “what I would previously have done most willingly without being ordered, had the Lord’s saying in the Gospel concerning the hireling not forbidden it. But I could not do so with impunity. Those wolves were not seeking to attack the flock, but the shepherd; and when persecuted in one city, I could have fled lawfully to another.”

Since the two-year period during which Ratherius endured this persecution at Verona ended in 948, it is clear that his second expulsion from the bishopric of Verona occurred in that year.

[LXVIII] § IX. Ratherius goes to Germany. He writes to Bruno, the brother of Otto I. The beginning of Otto’s reign in Italy. The chronological notices of several documents are corrected. In 951 Ratherius returns to Italy with Otto and his son Liutolf, hoping to recover his bishopric. He finds Milo’s nephew established as bishop, to whom Manasses had sold the bishopric. He appeals to the supreme pontiff and to a synod of bishops. He writes three letters on this matter.

[Col. 0059C]

42. After being expelled a second time from the see of Verona, Ratherius withdrew to Germany. There, settling nowhere permanently and seeking the means of sustaining his life, he wandered from place to place, so that he was called a *gyrovagus*, or wanderer (Letter 5, no. 3).

On this occasion he seems to have traveled through Noricum—that is, Bavaria—Swabia, and Saxony, which he mentions as witnesses of his life in the *Conjecture on Quality*, no. 3. He testifies in letters that he received assistance from the Germans, namely, the bishops of these provinces; he wrote those letters to the Roman pontiff in the year 951, as we shall see in its proper place.

43. At this time Bruno, the brother of Otto I, was renowned not so much for moral discipline as for his devotion to letters. He later became archbishop of Cologne [Col. 0059D]. He kept at his household the more learned men of the age and cultivated under their instruction Latin, Greek, secular, and sacred literature. As a result, his house seemed to be a dwelling place of letters and of learned men.

In the poverty that we have described, Ratherius sent him the books of the *Praeloquia* together with a letter, so that, once he had learned their author from the books, Bruno might summon him if he judged him useful to his service and support him among the others:

“If, therefore, the work pleases you,” he says, “may the little servant who produced the work also please you, and do not disdain to suggest what he is worth. Perhaps, among thousands more distinguished, this man too may obtain his place. If you wish, you can also acquire him for your service; for I have heard that you are very far from stinginess. … Once this difficulty has been removed, use your power, knowing that I eagerly desire this. For my prophetic mind seems almost to foresee that through your distinction my destitution will be relieved, provided that I can render a service worthy and suitable to your lordship” [Col. 0060A].

He wrote this when he was in need. He remained in need until 951 or 952, when, in two other letters, the sixth and seventh, he asked for alms so that he might undertake the journey to Rome.

He therefore wrote to Bruno sometime between 948, after he had left Verona, and 951 or 952. He was indeed received into Bruno’s household, but not immediately after his expulsion from his see; for under so great a prince, to whom he was most welcome, he would not have needed the alms of the pious.

Indeed, in the sixth letter, written in 951 or 952, no. 1, he says: “Nowhere do I have rest in any lodging, nowhere any refuge, except a place of mercy,” thereby implying that until this time he had not been received into any fixed lodging [Col. 0060B]. We shall see in the following paragraph that he was summoned by Bruno in 952.

44. After King Lothair died on 22 November 950, and after twenty-four days during which the kingdom of Italy was vacant, “on Sunday, 15 December, in the basilica of Saint Michael, which is called the Greater, Berengar and his son Adalbert were elected and crowned as kings” (T. IV *Rer. Ital.*, p. 149). So reports the brief Chronicle published by Muratori (S. Odilo, *Life of Saint Adelaide*, in Canisius).

Not long afterward, Berengar treated Adelaide, Lothair’s widow, who had been harshly persecuted despite her innocence, with great cruelty and threw her into a foul prison. Donizo reports that the prison was the extremely well-fortified fortress of Garda, in the territory of Verona, on the shores of Lake Benacus (*Life of Matilda*, book I, vol. I of *Rer. Ital.*). Because of this, the Italians, alienated from Berengar, summoned Otto, king of Germany, so that he might rescue Adelaide from her many dangers—she had fled from Garda and been received by Azo in the fortress of Canossa—and restrain Berengar, who was abusing the kingdom.

Otto immediately sent his son Liudolf to Italy. Finding the Italians prepared and obedient, Liudolf soon returned, as Roswitha, the historian of this period, says, “bringing back a glorious triumph without battle.” Otto then entered Italy with that same son before October 951. It is established from two diplomas cited by Muratori, and from records at Pavia, that in the same month he was called king of Italy: “at Pavia, on 10 October, in the year 951 from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the tenth indiction, in the sixteenth year of the reign of Otto, king in Francia”—that is, eastern Francia, by which name Germany was called—“and in the first year in Italy” (*Italian Annals*, year 951).

An earlier diploma of Otto, signed at Pavia on 9 October, was published by the canon Dionysius. In it the year 952 was mistakenly written instead of 951 (*On Two Bishops*, p. 121): “Given on 9 October, in the year 952 from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, indiction 10, in the sixteenth year of the reign of Otto, king in Francia, and the first in Italy.” All the other chronological indicators agree exactly with the two preceding privileges and demonstrate that the year is erroneous. For in October 952 the eleventh, not the tenth, indiction was in progress; and the year of Otto’s reign in eastern Francia, or Germany, was not the sixteenth but the seventeenth, since Otto had been made king of Germany after the death of his father Henry, which occurred in July 936. Moreover, in October 952 Otto was neither at Pavia nor in Italy: he had returned from Italy to Germany immediately after Easter of that year.

The same canon also printed another document, drawn up “in the village of Runco” in the territory of Verona, which is dated: “with our lord Otto reigning here in Italy in his first year, on the day of the month of May, in the ninth indiction” (ibid., p. 71). The ninth indiction agrees with May of 951. If one should not suspect an error in the indiction, it would have to be said that Otto had entered Italy as early as May of that year, before being hailed as king at Pavia in October 951, and had been called king of Italy at Verona.

But it is established from two diplomas cited by Muratori (*Italian Annals*, year 951) that Berengar and Adalbert remained kings of Italy until September 951. One of those diplomas was issued at Pavia on 22 September, the other at the parish church of Saint Marinus on 26 September. In the single charter that places Otto’s first year of rule in Italy five months earlier—while all the other charters continue to assign the Italian kingdom to Berengar and Adalbert through September—we believe that an error entered the indiction, especially since this one charter was copied not from the original but from an ancient transcript. Thus, instead of the ninth indiction, the tenth should probably be read, which agrees with the year 952.

This becomes still more probable because another document written at Verona and published by the aforementioned canon is dated: “with our lord Otto king reigning here in Italy in his first year, on the day of the month of June, in the tenth indiction” (*On Two Bishops*, p. 118). If the people of Verona had dated Otto’s first year by the ninth indiction in May of the preceding year, 951, then in June 952 they ought to have recorded not the first but the second year. It is not credible that they used one calculation for the beginning of Otto’s reign in 951, before October, and another after October, in conformity with the other Italian cities.

45. Let us now hear from Ratherius himself what he did amid these changes in the Italian kingdom. “When our most glorious and most devout king, celebrated throughout the whole world” (Otto), “had entered Italy, I was present with his most illustrious son, trying, if the opportunity were granted, to be restored to my position” (letter 5, no. 8)—that is, to the see of the Church of Verona.

Otto’s entry into Italy with his son belongs to the year 951, when he entered Italy with his son Liudolf. For when Otto came to Italy again in 961, he brought no son with him. Liudolf had died in 958; and, when Otto was about to set out for Italy in 961, he left his other, still-young son in Germany, entrusting him to the care of his son William, archbishop of Mainz (the Continuator of Regino and the Saxon Annalist). See the note on the fifth letter.

Thus Ratherius came to Italy with Otto and his son Liudolf in 951. He hoped to be restored to his see once Berengar, who had been hostile to him, had been suppressed. Perhaps he also believed that authority would be taken away from Milo, count of Verona, who supported Berengar.

That something unfortunate had happened to Milo seems to be indicated by a passage in the seventh section of the fifth letter. There, after recounting his second expulsion and apparently referring to Milo as his opponent, Ratherius says: “Although I could accuse this unfortunate man, I refrain, lest I add to his wounds some further pain, which the prophet forbids by his lament.” Certainly, when Otto entered Italy a second time, he placed Germans whom he trusted in charge of Verona. It is quite believable that he did the same on his first arrival, so that Milo did not recover the county of Verona until after Berengar had regained the whole kingdom of Italy.

46. Ratherius himself explains what prevented him from being restored to his see on this occasion:

“But what prevented it was that the king found another person installed there” [in the see of Verona], “namely Milo’s little nephew; and it is not difficult to conjecture why Milo inflicted such great evils upon me. Manasses had sold the see to him” (letter 5, no. 8).

Liudprand likewise reports, in book four, chapter 3, that Manasses sold the bishopric of Verona into which he had been intruded. From this passage of Ratherius we learn that the person to whom Manasses sold it was Milo’s nephew—whether through his brother or his sister is unknown. Ratherius conjectures that the count inflicted such great evils upon him for this reason: by excluding Ratherius and restoring Manasses, Milo hoped eventually to install his nephew in the see of Verona.

The nephew’s name was also Milo. A document from that same year, cited by Giovanni Battista Perettus, attests that in 951 he was bishop of Verona (*Catalogue of the Bishops of Verona*, p. 61).

Manasses had been promoted in 949 to the archbishopric of Milan, which Berengar had promised him. Since he had simultaneously presided over five bishoprics—Arles, Verona, Trent, Mantua, and finally Milan (letter 5, no. 6)—he must be judged to have sold the see of Verona to Milo’s nephew not before that archbishopric, but not long afterward, probably around the year 950.

When this nephew was ordained bishop, he was about eighteen years old. He had been born after Ratherius had assumed the chair of Verona (letter 8 to Milo, note 5). Hence he is called a “little nephew,” or “young man” (letter 5, no. 8). Perhaps for this reason it was reported that “permission for such an ordination” had been sought and obtained from the apostolic see, so that the young man might be permitted to be ordained.

47. Milo’s supporters proclaimed this permission of the supreme pontiff as the approval and legitimate confirmation of his bishopric. Otto, who earnestly desired to obtain the imperial dignity from the supreme pontiff, dared do nothing against Bishop Milo and thereby frustrated all Ratherius’ hopes. Thus Ratherius, yielding both to apostolic authority and to royal majesty, was compelled to leave Italy.

At this point two testimonies of Ratherius should be noted. In one, in the *Itinerary*, no. 4, he affirms that he had been exiled three times; in the other, in the short work “Against the Clerics Who Rebelled Against Him,” no. 2, he says: “You have already driven me out for the fourth time.”

In both passages he counts that expulsion from the see of Verona as his third exile and third expulsion. He had come to Italy in 951 intending to recover the same see; but, because of Milo, whom he found there as bishop, and because of Milo’s supporters—in whom the clerics mentioned in the latter testimony are clearly included—he departed without accomplishing his purpose. See the note on the *Itinerary*.

48. At first, when he saw that the restoration he had hoped for had vainly come to nothing, he said:

“I had resolved, after being freed by God’s mercy from prisons and exiles and led out into the spacious freedom of free choice, to seek the solitude of a monastery and there await God, who would save me from faintheartedness of spirit and from the storm of my persecutors; and, by repenting, to exact from myself the causes of my expulsion, judging myself so that I might not be judged” (letter 5, no. 8).

But while he was turning these matters over in his mind, he heard that his rivals were bringing certain charges against him. They claimed that he had been deprived not by force but by a lawful sacerdotal proceeding. He also feared that, if he yielded completely without any defense, he might appear to have evaded judgment, as though he were unable justly to defend his case.

Therefore he decided that the matter should be referred to the apostolic see. For this reason he wrote to that very pontiff who was said to have approved Milo’s ordination. After clearly setting out his previous hardships and reversals up to the year 951, he presented his petition in these words (ibid., no. 10):

“Therefore, lest I appear to be a criminal accused of crime, or a fugitive challenged to trial, I ask for a hearing; I demand a hearing. Boldly calling the invader of my Church a thief and robber together with the shepherd of all shepherds, I call him so because he climbed up from elsewhere and did not enter through the door. For a legitimate wife is not permitted to marry another man while her husband lives. Before the apostolate of your see I challenge him to a canonical contest, on this further condition, if it pleases your lordship: whether the law prevails for me or for him, grant the bishopric to whichever of us seems right to us [both]—only in the Lord. I do not desire to preside any longer if I am able to benefit no one, as I did before.”

And a little later:

“That one of the two of us is not a bishop is something that even the reasoning of children, if they possess it, can grasp clearly enough. Which of us it is, your pastoral care must decide. You cannot leave the matter arising from this dispute entirely unexamined without the greatest danger to yourself, if I may dare say so” (ibid., no. 11).

49. It can be sufficiently inferred from the context that this letter was addressed to Agapetus II, who was said to have granted permission for Milo’s ordination, and that it was written by Ratherius in 951 or at the beginning of 952. This is confirmed more fully by what we discussed in the note prefixed to the same fifth letter.

The present heading gives the name of Pope John, Agapetus’ successor, because the original heading was soon suppressed for unknown reasons and the work was reissued under John XII with only the inscription altered, as we observed in the same note.

50. Since Ratherius wished to appeal to the judgment of the apostolic see, he wrote another letter to all the faithful (letter 6), in which he requested alms from devout people for a journey to Rome. In this letter the words in section 3 should be noted, where he says that he was “more widely separated from the Roman Church”—that is, very far distant from it.

It may therefore rightly be questioned whether this letter, together with the preceding and following letters, which were written on the same matter and at the same time, was composed in Italy in 951, before the author departed from there, or rather in Germany toward the end of that year, or in 952. Perhaps, as soon as he saw that every hope of recovering his bishopric had been cut off, he withdrew there, before Otto returned to it.

51. The seventh letter, addressed to all the bishops “throughout Italy, Gaul, and Germany,” must be joined with these two letters. It expresses similar statements on the same matter and also appeals to a council of bishops. Miserable Ratherius, wishing to leave nothing untried, thought that the supreme pontiff and all the bishops should be summoned to canonical judgment.

It now seems certain that Ratherius himself suppressed these three letters at this time. He perhaps abandoned the plan of publishing them because, while he was considering the matter, Bruno, Otto’s brother, received him into his court, as Ratherius had once requested.

§ X.—Ratherius, having returned to Germany, is received among the household of Bruno, brother of King Otto. Through Bruno’s efforts he becomes bishop of Liège. The solemn rites of his promotion. He is subsequently expelled from the see of Liège as well. For this reason he writes two short works. Which of his former bishoprics were assigned to him again for his support.

52. Bruno had come to Italy with his brother, King Otto. Accordingly, in several diplomas issued at Pavia in 951, he is found subscribed as “Bruno, chancellor”; and in the text of some documents he is expressly named “our beloved brother Bruno,” or “through the intervention of our brother Bruno” (Puricelli, *Monumenta Ecclesiae Ambrosianae*, no. 172). A document that had been written to Bruno while absent likewise acknowledges him as present in Italy (Dionysius, *On Two Bishops*, p. 120).

When King Otto had gained possession of the kingdom of Italy, married Adelaide, Lothair’s widow, at Pavia, and then returned to Saxony in 952 because of disturbances that had broken out in Germany, celebrating Holy Easter there, Bruno also went there. Bruno had entered the clerical service. He was exceedingly fond of learning and learned men, becoming daily more accomplished through their use and companionship. Among the other teachers whom he maintained in his household, he summoned Ratherius to himself. Ratherius so surpassed the others that he was regarded as first among them and especially useful for Bruno’s instruction.

“Otto,” says Fulcuinus (*Deeds of the Abbot of Lobbes*, chapter 22), “then the most powerful king, ruled over the Austrasian territories and conquered Italy. His brother Bruno, destined to become the one unique and singular ornament of Christ’s Church, was polished like a most precious stone by the many arguments of the philosophers. Ratherius was summoned and held first among the philosophers of the palace. Why say more? He did not stop until he had made that royal and wondrous nature, so perceptive in every discipline, discerning and perfect in all things.”

The words stating that King Otto “then ruled over conquered Italy,” or reigned in Italy, indicate the period when he had not yet restored the Italian kingdom to Berengar and Adalbert under fixed conditions. That restoration took place in 952 (see below, no. 68). Therefore Ratherius must be said to have been summoned by Bruno and received among the palace teachers before that restoration, though still in the same year. This point must be carefully noted, lest someone, misunderstanding the word “ruled,” accuse Fulcuinus of error, as though he had referred it to the later period when, in 961, Otto completely excluded Berengar and Adalbert from the kingdom of Italy and obtained the title of emperor from the Roman see in 962.

53. Ratherius remained in Bruno’s court for approximately one year. In 953, when two churches—the churches of Cologne and Liège—became vacant, Bruno was promoted to Cologne and Ratherius to Liège.

Ratherius was promoted to the see of Liège not merely in that same year but on the very day on which Bruno was consecrated archbishop. Ratherius himself testifies to this in the *Deliberative Conclusion*, no. 26. For this reason Rotgerus says that Bruno promoted Ratherius “at the very beginning of his priesthood” (*Life of Saint Bruno*, no. 34).

It is certain from the contemporary writer Frodoard, in his *Chronicle*, followed by all the others, that Bruno was ordained archbishop of Cologne in 953. Accordingly, the *Chronicle of Liège* in Labbe (vol. I, *Bibliotheca manuscriptorum*, p. 338), another Chronicle of Lobbes in Martène and Durand (vol. III, *Thesaurus anecdotorum*, p. 145), and the *Deeds of the Bishops of Liège* by Giles of Liège, chapter 45 (vol. I of Chapeauville, p. 176), correctly assign Ratherius’ promotion to the year 953. By contrast, Sigebert and those who followed him incorrectly assign it to 954.

54. Both Rotgerus and Fulcuinus report that Ratherius reached the see of Liège through Bruno’s efforts, or, as it is stated in the *Phrenesis*, no. 1, “through his intervention” (Rotgerus, *Life of Saint Bruno*, no. 34; Fulcuinus, chapter 23).

The kingdom of Lothair, or Lotharingia, which in the time of Hilduin and Richarius had been counted as part of the kingdom of Gaul, had not long afterward passed to the German kingdom. Thus, after Conrad—whom Otto, king of Germany, had appointed duke of Lotharingia—was deposed for rebellion in 953, the same king appointed his brother Bruno, although still a cleric, as duke in his place and placed him over the Church of Cologne, which had become vacant in that same year.

Bruno also arranged for Ratherius to be placed over the vacant see of Liège after the death of Farabert. The most holy Bruno did this not for human reasons, but because he judged that placing Ratherius over that Church, “on account of his abundant learning and rich eloquence, by which he appeared to flourish among the wisest men, would be greatly beneficial not only to that Church over which he presided but also to many others throughout the surrounding region.” So writes the aforementioned Rotgerus in the *Life of Saint Bruno*, no. 34.

He adds another and more distinguished reason for this election, which demonstrates most clearly that Bruno had come to know Ratherius’ uprightness through intimate familiarity:

“At the same time, because in those regions, through zeal and rivalry . . . certain priests of the Lord also, for the most part, were scandalizing the ignorant people—what is disgraceful to say—by relying more than was right on earthly power, the aforementioned lord Bruno, archbishop of Cologne, who already bore responsibility for administering the whole kingdom [of Lotharingia], judged—and this was true—that by bringing this man, previously expelled and neglected, into that great office, he could lead the people to a bond of faith and truth from which no one could draw them away. He therefore believed that he could finally silence the mouths of those who spoke wickedly if no occasion for scandal could be found in their bishop.”

Bruno had evidently found Ratherius so outstanding in his devotion to ecclesiastical discipline and integrity of life that he firmly believed no occasion for scandal could be found in him. Fulcuinus repeats these same reasons for choosing Ratherius from Rotgerus.

The reason that Fulcuinus adds from himself—writing that Ratherius was attached to the Church of Liège through Bruno’s diligence “for the benefit of teaching”—seems unworthy of Bruno’s holiness unless it is explained more charitably.

55. We learn from the *Phrenesis* and partly from the *Deliberative Conclusion* how Ratherius’ promotion was carried out through Bruno’s agency.

It was customary in this period to elect bishops with the king’s consent. Unless force or fraud had intervened, however, the election of the clergy and people was required according to the canons. Saint Bruno considered that nothing should be done except according to law. Hence Rotgerus says of Ratherius: “He was attached to the vacant see of Liège through Bruno’s great diligence, according to the provisions of the canons.”

Fulcuinus, who transcribed this passage from Rotgerus, omitted the words “according to the provisions of the canons” and substituted “for the benefit of teaching.”

In the preface to the *Phrenesis*, no. 1, two elections of Ratherius are distinguished. One took place at the palace of Aachen “on the fourth weekday of the solemn fast of the seventh month.” In 953 this fell on 21 September, the feast of Saint Matthew. The other took place at Cologne “on the following Sunday,” namely 25 September.

The author states that the earlier election was carried out there “by those who had the more particular interest in the matter.” Since he says that the second election was made “by the same people, that is, by the people of the Church of Liège,” it is clear that those who had the relevant interest were the people of Liège.

That the consent of the Liège clergy was not absent is indicated by the words of the *Deliberative Conclusion*, no. 21, where Ratherius declares that his promotion was carried out by the legitimate archbishop Bruno “in the presence of the whole Church and with the consent—which the laws indeed require—of the clergy.”

In the *Phrenesis* he adds that at Aachen he was not only elected by the people of Liège, who had the relevant interest, but also “requested by the bishops, abbots, counts, and all the leading men of the kingdom.” These men were evidently in Bruno’s retinue and had gathered in very large numbers for the ordination of Saint Bruno, archbishop of Cologne.

Ratherius’ election, established or approved by Bruno, is said to have taken place “on the same day” after Bruno’s ordination and “after Ratherius had made his profession, as is customary, that he would always be obedient to the canons,” in the cited *Conclusion*, no. 26. Thus Bruno was consecrated first, on 21 September, and Ratherius was elected afterward.

Not only Bruno, already consecrated archbishop, but also the other bishops approved this election as legitimate and judged that nothing contrary to the canons had been done in it. Hence, in the *Conclusion*, no. 21, the author mentions “the judgment of the prelates, the testimony of the decrees, and the sanction of the canons.” He adds in no. 22 “the king’s concession,” that is, his consent; and in no. 25 he implies that some diploma had been signed by the king’s hand.

Similarly, in the election of Saint Ulrich, bishop of Augsburg, Gerard the priest praises “the king’s edict” in his *Life*, chapter 2, no. 7 (vol. VII of the *Acts of the Saints of the Benedictines*, p. 420).

Since Bruno’s ordination was carried out at Aachen on 21 September by Robert, archbishop of Trier, his public installation in the Church of Cologne appears to have been postponed until the following Sunday, 25 September. On that occasion, on the same day, 25 September, a new and more solemn election and attachment of Ratherius was celebrated there, as we learn from the aforementioned preface to the *Phrenesis*, where these words are found:

“Again, on the following Sunday, he was elected by the same people—that is, by the people of the Church of Liège—and, with the assent of seven fellow bishops, two of whom were archbishops and the others bishops, namely the aforementioned Bruno, Robert, Baldric, Hildebold, Drogo, Berengar, and Folbert; with the agreement of the decrees, the consent and examples of certain ancients to whom the same thing had happened; with the highest favor of the entire assembly that was present, he was assigned to that Church and solemnly enthroned there.”

The two archbishops were Bruno, archbishop of Cologne, and Robert, archbishop of Trier. Baldric was bishop of Utrecht on the Rhine; Hildebold was bishop across the Rhine, that is, of Minden; Drogo was bishop of Osnabrück; Berengar of Verdun; and Folbert of Cambrai.

The statements in the first part of *On Contempt for the Canons*, no. 9, may refer either to this second election or to the first. There Ratherius testifies that, concerning his promotion to the Church of Liège, “the glorious council of prelates was consulted; they mercifully elected me, and, with the united assent of the people, fraternally enthroned me.”

In both cases several bishops had assembled. In both cases the issue at stake was examined: whether a man who was bishop of Verona, expelled from that see, could be promoted to another. After the relevant canons, papal decrees, and examples of the ancients had been considered, the council’s judgment determined that nothing stood in the way; indeed, in accordance with both the decrees and the examples of the ancients “to whom the same thing had happened,” such a transfer was approved as lawful. See the *Deliberative Conclusion*, no. 40.

56. This solemn enthronement of Ratherius took place in the cathedral of Cologne. Saint Bruno, metropolitan, handed him the pastoral staff of the Church of Liège before the altar of Saint Peter (*Conclusion*, no. 30). This rite deserves notice.

Soon afterward Archbishop Robert delivered a sermon from the pulpit before a very large crowd, in which he praised Ratherius with particular emphasis “above the ambo of the Church of Cologne, while the entire assembled people looked on” (*Phrenesis*, no. 1).

The people and nobles then acclaimed him; the clergy sang; and there was the sound of the signals which we call bells.

A synodical letter was also written to the clergy and people of Liège concerning Ratherius’ promotion. It was signed by the seven prelates whom we mentioned shortly before. Some of them had been sent by the council as delegates with Bruno to escort Ratherius to Liège. After reporting what had been done, including the king’s consent, they installed him in the episcopal seat and actually placed him over the clergy and people of Liège.

The author indicates in no. 39 of the aforementioned *Conclusion* how great was the joy with which all the people of Liège received him. There he declares that he did not wish to leave that Church, “lest I be falsely accused of having received ungratefully so spontaneous, so joyful, so devout, and so populous a reception, filled with the praises of Christ”—so many praises, because he had been given to that Church—“and of the most devoted people toward me.”

57. These joyful beginnings, however, soon turned into open and sorrowful rebellion.

The new bishop labored greatly for the welfare of the people entrusted to him, and an allegory inserted in the *Book of Confession*, no. 38, seems to indicate that for some time his efforts succeeded. See note 79.

Not long afterward, however, a more powerful faction, hostile to him, “prevailed to its own destruction,” as Fulcuinus says. “Whatever was done for their salvation, they regarded as harmful to themselves. What more is there to say? A mistake was made, violence was done, and they did not stop until, by expelling him, they had satisfied their own cruelty and wickedness.”

A recent author believes that “a mistake was made” should be read “there was fighting,” and suspects that Ratherius fought with weapons in order to defend himself against the rebels.

The same Ratherius, however, completely excludes this suspicion in the short work *Phrenesis*, which that author, because it was unpublished before the present edition, was unable to see. In the preface to that work, no. 2, Ratherius does not deny that, according to the view of his opponents, he was “frenetic,” since “in a manner unusual at that time, in such a crisis he fled not to money, NOT TO ARMS, as some did, nor to an abundance of friends, but to books, to bookcases [libraries], and to the examples of the ancients.” Repeating this afterward, he makes clear that he fought not with arms but with books and written works.

Moreover, not only does Fulcuinus’ edition read “a mistake was made,” but so does Rotgerus in the *Life of Saint Bruno*, from which Fulcuinus transcribed this passage. Both printed editions of Rotgerus—Surius’ and Leibniz’s, taken from two manuscripts—preserve the same reading, as does the contemporary manuscript of Rotgerus that Fulcuinus had before his eyes.

Therefore, in such agreement among the manuscripts, nothing should be emended.

The expression “a mistake was made” refers to what precedes. Rotgerus had narrated that Saint Bruno, when he promoted Ratherius to the see of Liège, had hoped that “no occasion for scandal could be found in their bishop.” When the opposing party subsequently prevailed and a great scandal was stirred up, Bruno discovered that he had been mistaken.

Even if Fulcuinus had read “there was fighting,” however, since this cannot refer to Ratherius, whom we have seen to have abstained from arms, it would unquestionably have to refer to the rebels. The following words—“violence was done, and they did not stop until, by expelling him, they had satisfied their own cruelty and wickedness”—also concern them.

In the same preface Ratherius himself testifies that he was expelled by public force and that Baldric was intruded into the see.

58. The ancient author of the *Deeds of the Bishops of Tongeren*, published by Martène and Durand, attributes the cause of this rebellion to the harsher criticism with which Ratherius attacked the corrupted morals even of powerful men:

“For while he inveighed against human conduct both in writing and in speech with more biting severity than was proper, the insolence of the powerful could not endure this, and he was nevertheless cast down from our see” (vol. IV of *Collectio veterum scriptorum*, p. 859, no. 20).

Anselm, a canon of Liège, chapter 33, and Giles, likewise of Liège, chapter 45, whose works were published by Chapeauville, report similar things.

Our author states in the aforementioned preface to the *Phrenesis*, no. 1, that the expulsion itself was accomplished “by the contrivance of Baldric,” bishop of Utrecht, “by the execution of Robert,” archbishop of Trier, “and by the public force of the counts Regener and Ruodvolt.”

Baldric, bishop of Utrecht, whom the same author calls Robert of Trier’s “standard-bearer in [Ratherius’] overthrow” (*Phrenesis*, preface, no. 2), sought to elevate to the see of Liège another, younger Baldric, the son of his brother, although he was very young—indeed, he is called a child.

The two aforementioned counts, Regener and Ruodvolt, who were extremely powerful in those regions, joined in the effort. The younger Baldric was their nephew; “so that it is not difficult to conjecture why such things happened” (*Phrenesis*, preface, no. 1).

Bruno, who valued Ratherius highly, would have wished to support him in his see. But he found no helper either among the bishop’s friends or among the soldiers and nobles. Moreover, he feared that the aforementioned counts, who at that time were acting against Conrad, might, if he opposed the promotion of the younger Baldric, pass over to Conrad’s side and undertake some action against the king, causing every effort on Ratherius’ behalf to fail. He was therefore compelled to abandon his plan.

In this matter, Ratherius’ enemies, wishing to put forward some apparently legitimate reason for excluding him, attacked his attachment to the see by which he had been transferred from Verona to Liège and invoked the sacred canons that prohibited the transfer of bishops (*On Contempt for the Canons*, part 1, no. 9).

Ratherius defended himself both by the decree of Pope Antherus, which at that time everyone regarded as genuine, and especially by the examples of the ancient saints who had transferred from one see to another (*Conclusion*, no. 40).

He added that, since he had been deprived of the episcopate after being expelled from the see of Verona, he could not truly be said to have been transferred from one see to another. He warned that no one could condemn transfers themselves when they were made not for some human reason but from necessity or for the benefit of the Church. He further stated that he had not been enthroned “out of greed or pride, but, driven by necessity after being expelled from my own see, I approached at that time the most devout king—now that most glorious Caesar—consulted the council of prelates, and they mercifully elected me and, with the united assent of the people, fraternally enthroned me.”

So Ratherius writes in the first part of *On Contempt for the Canons*, no. 9, where he reports having held a discussion on this matter with some ecclesiastical person at Liège.

These arguments, however, could accomplish nothing where force, not reason, prevailed.

Bruno yielded to such violence. As we have said, responsibility for the entire administration of the kingdom of Lotharingia had been entrusted to him.

“Therefore he yielded,” says Rotgerus, and after him Fulcuinus, “so that he might not be overcome by evil but overcome evil with good; he yielded to the will of his opponents so that he might cut them down with their own sword” (Rotgerus, *Life of Bruno*, no. 34; Fulcuinus, chapter 23).

The younger Baldric was therefore consecrated bishop and installed in the see of Liège by public force.

For this reason Ratherius calls him “a thief and a robber” in the *Deliberative Conclusion*, no. 2:

“A thief,” he says, “because by theft he took my see from me; a robber, because he took it by force and public authority”—that very “public force” by which Ratherius himself was expelled by the counts Regener and Ruodvolt, “so that their nephew Baldric might be installed” (*Phrenesis*, no. 1).

59. Fulcuin relates that this rebellion against Ratherius began on Christmas Day, while the same bishop was staying at Lobbes. “While he was celebrating the Nativity of the Lord festively and lavishly among us,” he says (ch. 23), “a most serious conspiracy was formed against him at Liège.” The beginning of this rebellion must therefore be assigned to Christmas Day of the year 954, so that the expulsion of Ratherius, [Col. 0070D] which we shall see followed somewhat later, falls in the year 955. This is indeed the year to which the two ancient Chronicles of Lobbes and Liège assign it, together with Aegidius of Liège; and in a matter concerning the Church of Liège they deserve greater credence than Sigebert and the other chroniclers who followed Sigebert. For just as those writers erred when they assigned Ratherius’s promotion to that same see to the year 954 instead of 953, so they also erred when they placed his expulsion in the year 956.

The year 956 is certainly incompatible with what Ratherius himself reports about his expulsion in *Phrenesis*, no. 1. He indicates that he was expelled while Duke Conrad was still alive, “who was then acting against King Otto.” This duke had died before the year 956, after having meanwhile been reconciled with the king and having fought against the Hungarians in August 955 (Necrology of Fulda, in Leibniz, vol. V, *Rerum Brunsvicensium*). Hence, when the aforementioned Aegidius writes that Ratherius’s episcopate at Liège lasted “nearly three years,” it should more correctly be read “nearly two years,” just as Fulcuin reads “almost a biennium.” This will become clear from the text that we shall explain at the beginning of the thirteenth paragraph.

This “almost a biennium” of Ratherius’s episcopate, which began with his promotion on 21 September 953, requires us to say that he was expelled not immediately after the rebellion broke out on 25 December 954, but several months later. For many events occurred after the beginning of the rebellion before his expulsion and Baldric’s ordination took place. Nothing could be accomplished without Bruno’s consent. He was not only Archbishop of Cologne, to whom the ordination of the new bishop of Liège belonged, but also Duke of Lotharingia, administering the whole region.

This great patron of Ratherius did not readily yield to the rebels. Fulcuin’s words, “What more shall I say? There was error, there was violence, and there was NO RELENTING until, by his expulsion, they had satisfied their cruelty and wickedness,” indicate that a considerable period of time was spent in this sedition before Bruno was induced to yield. The two counts Regenerus and Ruodvoltus, powerful men in that region and Baldric’s uncles, had stood for King Otto, Bruno’s brother, against Duke Conrad. In the conspiracy against Ratherius they were especially violent, and they “did not relent” until they had extorted Bruno’s consent.

“Countless storms converged from every side,” Fulcuin says in the same place. “The ship of the Church, with its rower struggling, was tossed by the waves; the helmsman himself could not withstand the force of the storm. Therefore he yielded . . . . . . he yielded to the will of his opponents, so that he might cut their throats with their own sword. They voluntarily bound themselves to him by the pledge of oaths, so that, if they should be worthy to receive the bishop whom they sought, they would thereafter defend the authority of the Church and the imperial right with unshakable firmness.”

Bruno evidently feared that, if he resisted longer and more forcefully, the two counts would defect from the king and pass over to Conrad, “who was then acting against the king” (*Phrenesis*, no. 1). After they had bound themselves by oath to him, Bruno judged that Ratherius must finally be dismissed and the younger Baldric consecrated.

To these matters must be added the production of the canons forbidding the translation of bishops; the dispute held on this subject by Ratherius, perhaps at some assembly of bishops; the election of the new bishop at the request of the clergy and people; the king’s consent; the convocation of the bishops; and other requirements of this kind. All these circumstances extend Ratherius’s expulsion into the year 955 by several months, so that nearly two years must be understood to have elapsed between his election and his expulsion. There is no other reasonable way to understand it.

If the rather broadly understood excommunication which our bishop arranged to have imposed on the Archbishop of Trier, the principal supporter of his expulsion, on Maundy Thursday of the year 955, and which is mentioned very obscurely [Col. 0072A] in *Phrenesis*, no. 16 (we attempted to explain it there in notes 50 and 51), was imposed before his expulsion, as seems more probable, then this expulsion of Ratherius, as well as Baldric’s election and ordination, must be placed after Easter, which fell that year on 15 April.

Some may object that Duke Conrad, during whose opposition to Otto Ratherius was expelled, had already been reconciled with the king long before this time. Most writers connect his reconciliation with the reconciliation by which Liutulf, the king’s son—who had been incited and angered against his father by Conrad—returned to the king’s favor on 17 December 954. They rely on the testimony of Widukind, who in the third book, in a single continuous passage, states that Otto received his son Liutulf and his son-in-law Conrad back into favor.

But we are certain that Conrad’s reconciliation occurred after that of Liutulf. The peace made with the son on 17 December 954 is clear from a notice inserted by Archbishop William of Mainz into the Chronicle of Marianus Scotus. How, however, could Conrad have made peace with the king on that same day, if, according to Fulcuin, the rebellion against Ratherius arose later, on Christmas Day of the same year, and if Ratherius was expelled from the see of Liège somewhat later, while Duke Conrad, as Ratherius himself testifies, was still acting against the king?

It is therefore evident that, after Liutulf had made peace with his father on 17 December 954, Conrad continued for some time to stand against the king, and was reconciled with him only later in 955, shortly before the battle in which he fought for the king against the Hungarians. Hence Fulcuin, chapter 25, after recounting the Hungarian events of 954 and preparing to describe the battle of 955, which that people undertook “I suppose, encouraged by the success of the preceding year,” and in which they were defeated while Conrad, or Cono, fought bravely, says:

“Cono was present there—not now as duke, but as a soldier—wholly, as was thought, converted to peace, which shortly before”—note the words “shortly before”—“he had fiercely opposed.”

Only the peace of Liutulf, made on 17 December 954, is mentioned both by William of Mainz in the notice cited above and by Gerard in the *Life of Saint Ulrich, Bishop of Augsburg*, who was the mediator of that peace. But if Conrad’s reconciliation must be assigned to the year 955, nothing prevents Conrad from having acted against Otto in that same year somewhat before his reconciliation, so that Ratherius was expelled while he was acting against the king in 955, as we have concluded from the documents previously considered.

60. After our bishop had been expelled from the see of Liège following the intrusion of the younger Baldric, and while he was staying at Liège, many people pressed him insistently either to surrender the bishopric to the intruder himself or to leave it to him. He resisted resolutely and wrote a *Deliberative Conclusion*, in which he explained in forty [LXXXV] arguments why he ought not to resign or yield.

In this work he presents himself as especially opposed to requesting any portion of the ecclesiastical revenues for his support in life as a condition for consenting to such a resignation. Thus, in no. 14, he says that he could not consent to such a concession for this reason as well:

“Lest I be defamed as having first said, ‘Leave me one priestly portion, so that I may eat a morsel of bread . . .’”

He nevertheless indicates that some agreement or offer had been proposed to him in this matter and rejected by him, when he writes at the end:

“I would rather suffer violence from anyone, however needy, than be judged to have made a compact with death and a peace with hell. To anyone offering some assistance in alms—except that most notorious robber”—that is, except the usurper of the see, from whom he does not even wish to accept alms—“I do not withdraw my hand ungratefully.”

This little work, which contains much concerning the rite of electing bishops, was written at Liège, as is clear from its title itself: *The Deliberative Conclusion Enacted at Liège*. It was also written after Baldric’s intrusion, as is evident from no. 2, column 203.

61. When Ratherius left Liège, he withdrew to Mainz, where he was received with the greatest kindness and generosity by Archbishop William, the son of King Otto. In that city, “when leisure was granted him, he took care to arrange in books the events that had occurred around him, laboring so that the character of his own age would not remain hidden even from the curious. When the two men who were especially his enemies, namely Robert and Baldric, heard this, they said that he was insane” (*Phrenesis*, no. 1).

For this reason he called the book that he wrote against them *Phrenesis*. Another explanation of the title is given in the heading of the preface, expressed in these words:

“Here begins the preface of Bishop Ratherius to the book which he called *Phrenesis*, because in it he attacked certain persons with excessive severity.”

He deals at length with Robert, Archbishop of Trier, whom he addresses in the work itself as the principal author of his expulsion; and to some extent also with the younger Baldric, the intruder into the see of Liège. He inserts a few brief remarks concerning other men hostile to him.

In the aforementioned preface, no. 6, he sets out the subjects of the twelve volumes that he composed on this matter. He did not, however, arrange all of them at Mainz. Certainly he had written the *Deliberative Conclusion*, to which he assigns the place of the eleventh volume, while he was still living at Liège. Perhaps he also composed before his expulsion several other short works or letters indicated among those subjects—some such volumes consist of letters—in order to defend himself in his own see. Later, at Mainz, he distributed these together with the other works composed there into twelve books.

If all these books survived, we have no doubt that they would provide much additional material for illuminating this event. But apart from the *Deliberative Conclusion*, which the author later reissued, during the period of his episcopate at Verona, with a few additions because of circumstances not unlike those involved here, and which is preserved in the Laon manuscript, of the other eleven books mentioned only the first book, entitled *Phrenesis*, has been found in the manuscript of Lobbes. At its end that manuscript also adds a profession of faith, which, judging from the list of subjects, belongs to the second book.

To this profession of faith the author had added two letters in the same second book. “Of these,” he says in the preface cited several times above, no. 6, “one does not cease to weary the Roman See with complaints, the other the flock of fellow bishops”—that is, one was addressed to the Roman pontiff, the other to all the bishops.

In the Lobbes manuscript, however, three letters follow the profession of faith: one to Pope John, a second to all the faithful, and a third to all the bishops of Italy, Gaul, and Germany. But since these refer to his expulsion from Verona, not from Liège, they cannot belong to the volumes of *Phrenesis*, which, as is clear from the subjects of the third and following volumes, dealt with the affair of Liège. For:

The Third, as the aforementioned preface says, contains a complaint brought before the king, together with certain letters. [Col. 0074B]

The Fourth contains only two letters to prelates: a very brief one to Bruno and a fairly lengthy one to Robert.

The Fifth is a complaint addressed more particularly to Bruno, although it contains a general element, and is dedicated to the archbishop.

The Sixth, Seventh, and Eighth, although addressed to the intruder himself—namely, the younger Baldric—attack Robert in many ways and sharply and briefly criticize the conduct of the elder Baldric.

The Ninth answers with an invective beneath a cloak of humility; its writer, formerly quite favorably disposed toward Bruno, laments in mournful speech.

The Tenth addresses the most grievously deceived flock and prescribes the relief of repentance.

The Eleventh is a deliberative conclusion, great in its judgments and brief in its speeches. [Col. 0074C]

The Twelfth is a dialogue composed for a certain affair, yet not wholly unrelated to him himself. [LXXXVII]

It is enough to have indicated these matters, so that what is missing may be recognized from these subjects. One further point must not be omitted here: in *Phrenesis*, no. 16, the author cites a fifteenth volume concerning this affair of Liège. Yet in no. 18 he testifies that at first he arranged twenty volumes on this matter, but later reduced them to twelve. Compare the *Admonition to Phrenesis*, no. 2, column 213.

62. An ancient author of the *Deeds of the Bishops of Tongeren*, no. 2, relates that when Ratherius was expelled from the see of Liège, provision was made sufficiently for his livelihood “by granting him some small fields belonging to the bishopric for the use of life” (Marten and Durand, vol. IV, *Collectio Veterum Scriptorum*, p. 859, col. 33). Anselm of Liège says similarly: “by granting him whatever small revenues of the bishopric there were” (in Chapeauville, vol. I, p. 178).

It is established from the book of the *Confession*, which Ratherius wrote after his expulsion, that he had been placed in charge of a certain abbey in the diocese of Liège, as we shall demonstrate more fully in the following paragraph. Hence the revenues of the Liège bishopric said to have been assigned to him for his livelihood seem to have been the revenues of the abbey over which he presided. Since that abbey was subject to the rights of the bishops of Liège, as will likewise become clear in the following paragraph, its revenues were counted among the revenues of the Liège bishopric.

§ XI.—After his expulsion from the see of Liège, Ratherius is placed in charge of a monastery. Which monastery it was. He writes the book of the *Confession*. To what extent, while living there with monks, he did not return to the monastic way of life, and why. He addresses to John XII a letter written and suppressed under Agapetus II.

[Col. 0075A]

63. It is certain that Ratherius, after being expelled from the see of Liège and spending some time with the Archbishop of Mainz, assumed the administration of a certain monastery. He wrote the book of the *Confession* in the retreat of some monastery. There he presents himself as placed in charge of monks. Addressing the monks in no. 22, he says [LXXXVIII]:

“Caring for myself and neglecting others, especially you who have been entrusted to me,” etc.

The same thing is confirmed in no. 24, where, concerning the monk Oderadus, who had abandoned his monastery after purchasing the prelacy of another monastery, he says:

“Know that this was done without my permission.”

It is also confirmed in no. 34, when he complains that another monk “had dispensed wool without my order”; and when, in no. 24, he accuses himself because, concerning Oderadus’s purchase, “although I neither commanded nor wished that it be done, I nevertheless, through my fault, gave occasion for it to happen by not preventing it, insofar as I was able.”

Hence in no. 21 he counts himself among abbots, when he indicates that the names both of bishop and abbot had been assigned to him. In no. 34, recalling a certain decree of the Rule, he says:

“Indeed, we little abbots embrace this so earnestly, out of that special love of ourselves, not of God: ‘Let him do nothing without the abbot’s command.’”

And, to omit many other passages, he indicates more openly that he was an abbot when, in no. 35, turning his speech toward himself, he says:

“You rejoice because nothing is done without your command: consider what you command. You demand obedience: establish what you demand; for they are bound to obey you, while you are bound to the Rule. They sin if they do anything outside your will and arrangement; you sin if you arrange or command anything contrary to the established Rule.”

64. It may be inferred that the monastery over which he presided belonged in some way to the Church of Liège, because in no. 34 he records that, from Liège, a distinguished ecclesiastical man, as it seems, came to that monastery with a large retinue, and that the monks and clerics went out to meet him, singing sweetly in his honor. See note 62 to the book of the *Confession*.

Since Bishop Baldric of Liège had likewise visited the monastery of Lobbes with his maternal uncle, Count Raginero, to whom Baldric had entrusted the abbey of Lobbes in commendatory form (Fulcuin, ch. 26), we initially suspected that Ratherius had been placed in charge of that monastery—especially since its church was dedicated under the name of Saint Peter, just as was the church of the monastery administered by Ratherius (see note 34 to Ratherius’s *Confession*).

But that the administration entrusted to him belonged to a monastery distinct from Lobbes is plainly demonstrated by the fact that Ratherius himself, in no. 23, comparing himself with Oderadus, a monk of his monastery, describes himself as “a stranger and newcomer” to that monastery; whereas he calls Oderadus “a legitimate servant of that same Church”—or monastery—“because he had been legally handed over and, by his own hand and profession, permanently enslaved to its service.”

If the subject had been the monastery of Lobbes, he could not have called himself “a stranger or newcomer,” since he had been “legally handed over to it and, by his own hand and profession, permanently enslaved to its service” (see above, no. 6). Indeed, in many passages of the same work he acknowledges that he was continually urged and encouraged to return to that service, which he had there promised to God.

Moreover, at that time Count Reginerus held the abbacy of the monastery of Lobbes, while Erluinus presided in his place under the title of provost (Fulcuin, ch. 26). Therefore Ratherius, who was virtually an abbot, must have presided over another monastery.

There were also other monasteries in the diocese of Liège consecrated in honor of Saint Peter. One of these was Alne, as we learn from Mabillon (vol. I of the *Annales*, year 653, no. 28). At its foundation it was assigned by Saint Ursmarus to the abbey of Lobbes (Fulcuin, ch. 4). But since afterward the bishop of Liège was also abbot of Lobbes, the monastery of Alne, together with the other monasteries subject to that renowned abbey, belonged to the Bishop of Liège.

The distinctive feature of this monastery was that, when the other monasteries were later restored by Bishop Everaclus to their former arrangement, Alne remained under the jurisdiction of the Liège bishopric. Consequently, when Ratherius returned to his own people in 968 after completely abandoning the see of Verona, the abbot of Lobbes gave him two monasteries from those belonging to him, Waslar and Saint Ursmarus, while Everaclus, from the rights of the bishopric, gave him Alne.

Thus Ratherius seems to have been abbot of this monastery at the time when he was expelled from the see of Liège, so that he might have something from which to live. Since the revenues of that monastery, apart from the portion set aside for feeding the monks, passed to the Bishop of Liège and were therefore reckoned among the revenues of the bishopric, Anselm reported that, when this monastery was granted to Ratherius after his expulsion, some small revenues of the Liège bishopric were granted to him for his support. That this must be assigned to the year 955 is clear from the arrangements described above (see no. 62).

Sammarthanus, on the basis of the more recent *Annals of the Province of Hainaut*, reports Ratherius as abbot in this year 955 of the monastery of Hautmont, dedicated to Saint Peter. But since, in the latest edition of *Gallia Christiana*, they write on the basis of the same *Annals* that not only the abbey of Hautmont but also two others, Saint-Amand and Saint-Denis, were given to Ratherius for his necessities in life in the year 955, it is evident that the names of these abbeys were transferred from Fulcuin into those *Annals*. Fulcuin, however, reports that they were given to Ratherius not after his expulsion from the see of Liège, but after he finally abandoned Verona, namely in the year 968.

We believe that the abbey of Alne, rather than that of Hautmont, was granted to him in 955 for the following reason: Hautmont, being situated in the diocese of Cambrai, did not belong to the jurisdiction of the Bishop of Liège in the way that Alne certainly did. Perhaps Alne remained under the rights of the Bishop of Liège even after the abbot of Lobbes recovered the other monasteries because the abbey had been separated from the monastery of Lobbes and united to the Liège bishopric before the abbey of Lobbes passed under the jurisdiction of that bishopric. Or perhaps, when that restoration was made to the abbot of Lobbes in 960, Ratherius, while he was still enjoying his profession in that abbey, could not be deprived of it; but after he subsequently departed for Italy, the same abbey returned to the jurisdiction of the Bishop of Liège, who therefore granted it again to Ratherius when he returned in 968.

65. In the solitude of whatever monastery it was, the author, by then nearly seventy years old, wrote the book of the *Confession* around the year 960 or 961. We have sufficiently explained its singular and very obscure character in the admonition prefixed to it and have established its date. Here we shall indicate several noteworthy matters.

He attended not only the services of the day but also those of the night, and sometimes preached from the ambo. He indicates that he was repeatedly tormented by severe pains that produced increasingly intense groans. In no. 34 he says that on another occasion he groaned so loudly “that, if someone happened to be standing outside the door, he could have supposed that I was being tortured by that affliction so familiar to me.”

He exposes certain abuses by which the license of some monks had corrupted monastic discipline and caused him great sorrow and anxiety. He likewise touches upon certain particular actions, both his own and those of others, which increased his grief; but these are generally so entangled and obscure that, unless we unravel and explain them conjecturally in the notes appended below, we can extract almost nothing certain that seems appropriate to insert into this life. We therefore prefer to refer readers to the book itself and its notes. [XCI]

One matter, however, which caused Ratherius the greatest anxiety and fear, deserves special attention. He indicates that he was in danger concerning his salvation because, although he was living among monks and in a monastery, he had not returned to the monastic way of life to which he had bound himself by profession.

For, apart from the fact that the monastery over which he now presided was not the monastery of Lobbes, where he had promised to serve God perpetually, he had not withdrawn to Alne, over which he presided, with the intention of serving God there until death, as he had vowed in his profession. Evidently he had not yet abandoned the hope and desire of recovering the bishopric of Verona, as will appear from note 32 to the book of the *Confession* and will also be confirmed by what follows shortly.

66. In many passages he declares that he was anxious about this matter and struck by no slight fear. In no. 19 he indicates the sole excuse, or reason, why he did not return fully to his former way of life:

“For just as no one can promote himself by his own power to any rank in the Church, so no one can, even if he wishes, depose himself, however he may have been instituted or may have lived.”

From this Ratherius seems to have understood that anyone who had been taken from any institution or profession into the episcopate could not abandon that rank at his own discretion, unless he were either deposed by canonical judgment or released by legitimate authority from the bond of the Church to which he had been canonically assigned as bishop.

He explained this reasoning in another, more probable sense in the *Conjecture of His Condition*, no. 6, after he had been restored to the Church of Verona. He introduces the same perplexity and disturbance of mind by which he was still afflicted, when his critics charged him with desperation, in these words:

“And alas, miserable and unhappy man! Why does he not at least turn back within that course of life in which he now stands”—that is, by returning to his monastery?—“But it seems to us that he is therefore desperate because he has thrust his foot into such a net”—that is, into the episcopate—“that, walking amid its meshes, he can in no way extricate himself.

“For while he was a monk and is now a bishop, if he abandons the sheep and returns to the monastery, he fears hearing: ‘O shepherd, abandoning the flock and the idol!’ But if he remains, he fears that the Apostle said of him: ‘Having condemnation, because they have made their first faith void,’” etc.

From the book of the *Confession*, however, it is established that Ratherius earnestly desired to return to his former way of life and poured out prayers to God that this might be granted to him. “But I am greatly hindered,” he says in no. 28. When asked by what he was hindered, he replies:

“By myself. For I do not wish to accuse another, lest I seem to imitate Eve. The snares by which I myself bound myself hold me fast, and the meshes of the net into which I rashly thrust my foot”—when, intending to follow Hilduin, he abandoned the monastery and rose from the monastic life to the episcopate.

Nor should we omit what is written in the *Conjecture of His Condition*, no. 6. When, amid the disturbances that arose at Verona after his third restoration, Ratherius “thought that he was then to be expelled altogether, he rejoiced that he himself had not abandoned the bishopric, but that the bishopric had abandoned him, and by this means, as he said, wished to return to the monastery. When this had made no progress”—for he was not then expelled—“he thought that the following words had been spoken concerning him in utter desperation: ‘If God has shut a man in, who can say to him, Why have you done this?’”

Now, although, when he was expelled from the see of Liège, the episcopate had abandoned him, he nevertheless still believed himself hindered by the episcopal rank as if by a kind of net, so that he could not return, as he desired, to the monastic way of life (see note 31 to the *Conjecture of His Condition*, column 380).

67. Since Ratherius had not entirely abandoned hope of recovering the bishopric of Verona after his expulsion from the Liège episcopal chair, when an opportunity arose to procure that restoration, he subsequently inscribed to John XII the fifth letter which he had written to Agapetus II and suppressed in 951—John having succeeded Agapetus in 956 (see the *Admonition to Letter 5*, nos. 6 and 8).

Two opportunities might have seemed suitable: one when Liutulf descended into Italy with an army in 956 to defeat Berengar; the other when King Otto returned to Italy in 961 for the same purpose and, after defeating Berengar, proceeded to Rome in 962. Which of these opportunities led Ratherius to place John XII’s name before the letter formerly addressed to Agapetus II is uncertain.

Since he added nothing in the text of the letter concerning events that had occurred after the year 951, inserted nothing proper to John, and changed nothing except the heading, it is sufficiently credible that he did not actually send it to John XII. The reason, apparently, was that, after circumstances had changed, he understood that his cause had to be pursued by different means.

Liutulf’s unexpected death in Italy, which cut short his victories and left Berengar, hostile to Ratherius, as king, completely destroyed whatever confidence Ratherius may have acquired of recovering the bishopric of Verona at that time. But when Otto returned to Italy in 961, Ratherius was restored so promptly, as we shall see (§ 13), that, although a Roman judgment followed afterward, those letters presenting him as a bishop expelled from his see and living in exile were no longer appropriate.

§ XII.—King Otto, while leaving the Italian kingdom to Berengar, retained the Veronese March for himself. The March and its dukes, as well as the Friulian March, are discussed more fully, and many matters hitherto obscured are explained, including several testimonies of Ratherius that mention a duke and a duchess. Some additional remarks are made concerning the Trevisan March.

68. Before explaining Ratherius’s restoration to his own see, which must be assigned to the year 961, when King Otto again set out for Italy, together with the events that followed that restoration, we must first touch upon certain events preceding Otto’s second journey and discuss especially the origins of the Veronese March and its dukes. All these matters are useful not only for the events to be related later but also necessary for properly understanding certain passages of Ratherius.

When that same king hastened back from Italy in 952 because of disturbances that had arisen in Germany, Berengar and his son Adalbert, whom he had deprived of the Italian kingdom, came to him together with many Italian bishops. At the assembly of Augsburg in that same year they were reconciled with him and, after promising him fidelity, obtained the restoration of his kingdom under certain conditions, which may be read in Widukind and in the nun Hrotsvit.

The continuator of Regino, followed by the Saxon Annalist and Otto of Freising, notes the change introduced into the Italian kingdom on this occasion. Berengar, he says, together with his son Adalbert, “gave himself in every respect into vassalage to the royal dominion, and again received Italy to govern by the king’s favor and gift. Only the Veronese and Aquileian March was excepted, and it was entrusted to Henry, the king’s brother.”

Thus, when King Otto granted the Italian kingdom to Berengar and Adalbert, he reserved for himself Verona with Trent, Vicenza, Padua, and Aquileia—that is, Friuli—separated from the Italian kingdom, so that he might have easy access into Italy if Berengar should abuse the kingdom granted to him and withdraw from the conditions established and accepted. This is the first mention of the Veronese March.

69. *Marchia*, or *marca*, is a Germanic word signifying a borderland. It denoted a region or city situated at the boundary of a kingdom and especially requiring defense against enemies who might burst in from neighboring places, so that access into the kingdom itself could be blocked.

Earlier, when the kingdom of Italy was still intact, there were two cities this side of the Adige that bordered the German kingdom: Trent on one side and Friuli on the other. Hence Liutprand mentions the Tridentine March and Manasses, Margrave of Trent (Liutprand, book III, ch. 14; book IV, ch. 3). The designation Friulian March occurs in Einhard under the year 788 and more frequently in other writers.

But under Otto I, when Verona and the other cities as far as Friuli had been added to the German kingdom, and its boundary with the Italian kingdom was no longer Trent or Friuli but Verona, the name Veronese March began to be introduced. The entire region extending broadly from Verona as far as Friuli was included under the name of the Veronese March and was entrusted for administration to Henry, Otto’s brother, who was Duke of Bavaria.

Although the continuator of Regino calls this March not so much Veronese as Aquileian, insofar as it extended to Friuli, or Aquileia, you will find the name Aquileian March nowhere else used during this period. The designation Veronese March alone continued to prevail for a longer time.

[Col. 0080C]

70. Many will oppose this opinion, by which we have assigned the origin of the Veronese March to the age of Otto I, and will carry it back to an earlier period. They believe that the March extending from Friuli as far as Verona, whose duke or margrave presided over the entire region and over the counts of its individual cities, had already been established under the Franks from the eighth century onward. At first, they think, it was called the Friulian March; later, under Berengar I, the name Veronese March was substituted, because during his reign the man placed in charge of the entire March transferred his seat to Verona. For the same reason, they say, the designation Friulian March fell into disuse, and the county of Friuli began to be named instead, since no longer a margrave or duke but a count subject to the duke or margrave resided at Friuli.

Although this opinion is widespread among scholars, we consider it supported by no sufficiently firm foundation. That, in the later period under the German kings, the Veronese March extended as far as Friuli, so that the duke or margrave placed over it presided by special right over all the counts of the cities, is clear from those documents that testify to the judgments and other acts of jurisdiction performed by these dukes or margraves, now here and now there, within the territory of the March.

But no similar evidence has so far been produced under the Frankish kings for any such right exercised by the dukes or margraves of Friuli.
