It is now generally agreed that under the Lombards the dukes of Friuli did not exercise their authority outside Friuli at all. It has been established from numerous published documents that at that time each city in these regions had its own duke, who was not dependent upon another duke.

When the Lombards surrendered Friuli to Charlemagne, he confirmed Rotgaud as Duke of Friuli, but did not extend the limits of his jurisdiction. Moreover, when Rotgaud and his other confederates, who governed other Italian cities, defected from Charlemagne in 776, Charlemagne “having captured the city of Friuli, Tarvisium together with the remaining cities, arranged all of them under the Franks” (*Annals of the Franks*, in Canisius, for the year 776, vol. II, part II). These words indicate a change of rulers introduced by him, not a change in jurisdiction.

71. The advocates of the contrary opinion commonly bring forward the testimony of Hermann the Lame, who, in his *Chronicle* under the year 895, writes of Arnulf, king of Germany, descended from the Frankish line of Charlemagne: “He distributed Italy on this side of the Po among the counts Waltfred and Maginfred.” Waltfred is called margrave of Friuli in the *Annals of Fulda* under the year 896; Maginfred, who was later killed at Milan, is believed to have been margrave of Milan. Since, however, that division of Cisalpine Italy between Waltfred and Maginfred was accidental, it cannot be referred to in order to establish the proper territory and boundaries of either march. [XCVI] Hence, although Waltfred defended Verona against Berengar the Elder, as the cited *Annals* reported, [Col. 0081C] it cannot therefore be inferred that the Friulian march had been extended as far as this point. He defended Verona chiefly for this reason: in that part of his assigned charge the city of Verona was the most strongly fortified of all, and it left Arnulf’s German route open through the territory of Trent.

But if that part of the Italian kingdom entrusted to him extended “as far as the river Adda,” as some think—for from this, they say, when Arnulf had died, Berengar “recovered the Italian kingdom as far as the Adda,” as the aforementioned *Annals* testify—it would be much clearer that the Friulian march could not extend over the entire region placed under his authority by Arnulf. For no one extends the proper boundaries of that same march as far as the Adda.

Some believe that this Waltfred, margrave of Friuli, was the same as Waltfred who is identified as count of Verona in a document of the year 880 (MURATORI, vol. I, *Antiquitates Italicae*, p. 435). It is more probable, however, that this count was a different man. For a poem to Bishop Adelard, published from a Vatican manuscript (BIANCOLINI, *De’ vescovi e governatori di Verona*, p. 35), mourns the death of that same count after the deaths of the emperors Louis II and Charles, and of John VIII, Roman pontiff. This suggests that he died shortly after the year 882, when John VIII died, or somewhat later, shortly after the year 888, if the poem is thought to refer to Charles the Fat, who died in that year, rather than to Charles the Bald. Add that the aforementioned Berengar, already emperor, twice praises Waltfred in a diploma of the year 920 as the former “glorious count” of Verona (DIONYSIUS, *Diplomatic Collection*, pp. 101, 102)—something he would certainly not have said of the margrave Waltfred, who was hostile to him. But this is by the way.

72. They oppose this with a diploma of Berengar preserved by Muratori and dated to the year 905, in which “the illustrious man Grimoald” approached him to request a benefice for Teudibert “in the county of Verona” (vol. I, *Antiquitates Italicae*, p. 1017). Since, however, Grimoald, called “glorious margrave” in two privileges of the year 921, obtained other benefices from the same Berengar for Patriarch Frederick and for Peter, priest of Aquileia, they conclude that at this time both Friuli and Verona were included in his march (DE RUBEIS, *Monumenta Ecclesiae Aquileiensis*). But the first diploma, from the year 905, does not call Grimoald a margrave, but only an “illustrious man.” In other documents of the year 913 he is called “most glorious” or “distinguished count” (BIANCOLINI, *Cronica di Verona*, part I, p. 317; DIONYSIUS, *Diplomatic Collection*, p. 98), no less than in another document of the year 920 preserved by Campi (CAMPI, *History of Piacenza*, vol. I, appendix). Only in the privileges of the year 921 is he called “margrave.”

But if in 905, although he was an “illustrious man,” he was not yet either count or margrave, what can the cited diploma of 905 contribute toward indicating the territory of the march? Even if he had been a margrave, nothing would compel this conclusion, since bishops and others endowed with rank or with the favor of the prince often obtained privileges for churches and persons situated outside their own jurisdiction. [Col. 0082C]

73. Berengar eventually preferred to reside at Verona because it pleased him more and was more strongly fortified; this has no bearing whatsoever on establishing the name or extent of the march. That the march under him was indeed called Veronese, although formerly it had been called Friulian, because he preferred to reside at Verona, is disproved by a diploma of his given at Verona in the year 923, in which the name “Friulian march” is still used (UGHELLI, vol. V). That this march was not extended beyond Friuli is likewise proved by the same document.

The same emperor reports that he and his wife Anna II requested for the Church of Belluno “a certain estate belonging to our royal domain, called Docale . . . which belongs to the county of Ceneda, etc., and also Clusae of Abintione, which belongs to the march of Friuli.” You see that the “march of Friuli” is distinguished from the county of Ceneda. If the latter had been included in that march, Clusae of Abintione would have belonged to the same march no less than the estate of Docale, which belonged to the county of Ceneda.

Nor should it cause difficulty that, in another of the aforementioned privileges of Berengar from the year 921, the county of Friuli is named, whereas in the preceding privilege of 923 it is called the march of Friuli (DE RUBEIS, *Monumenta Ecclesiae Aquileiensis*, p. 455). From this we learn that the terms “march” and “county” were sometimes used interchangeably. Thus, in the third placitum of the year 845, the county of Trent is mentioned (MURATORI, vol. II, *Antiquitates Italicae*, p. 972), although at that time, under Louis II, king of Italy, Trent was a march of the Italian kingdom governed by Duke Liutfred.

The designation “Veronese march” was therefore introduced under Otto I in the year 952, and it was introduced for this reason: Verona, together with the other cities of that march extending as far as Friuli, had been assigned to the German kingdom and entrusted to a German duke; it thus began to be a portion and frontier of that kingdom.

74. This march, scarcely established, easily passed into Berengar’s power in the year 953, when Otto I and Duke Henry were embroiled in a very serious war. At that time, once Verona had ceased to be a march of the German kingdom, Trent and Friuli returned to their former status as frontiers of the Italian kingdom, so long as Berengar retained those places and the kingdom.

Hence, when in Milo’s testament, drawn up at “Runco” in the Veronese territory, “our lords Berengar and Adalbert, his son, kings here in Italy in the fifth year, on the tenth day entering the month of July, indiction 13,” that is, in the year 955 (UGHELLI, vol. V), are said to be reigning, and Milo himself is called “margrave,” this seems to refer either to Friuli or, more probably, to Trent, which was likewise a frontier city of the Italian kingdom and is called a “march” by Liutprand.

Berengar perhaps entrusted this march—through which German forces were accustomed to enter Italy—to his supporter Milo, formerly count of Verona, to govern and defend. From this it is also clear that these places had been subdued by Berengar before the year 955, that is, shortly after the German war against Otto and Henry broke out in the year 953.

75. Once the war in Germany had subsided, King Otto sent his son Liudolf with troops into Italy in the year 956 in order to restrain Berengar. After defeating him within a short time, Liudolf gained possession of almost the entire Italian kingdom. But his death on the sixth of September in the following year, which removed the victor from the world, opened the way for Berengar to recover the whole kingdom.

[Note: These two documents were published by the margrave and canon Dionysius in the *Diplomatic Collection*, pp. 121 and 124. The year 957 of the first document is clearly established by the seventh year of the kings’ reign and by the first indiction. Since the seventh year of the reign of Berengar and Adalbert began on 15 December 956 and ended on 15 December of the year 957, while the first indiction also began in September of the year 957, the month of October in the seventh year of the reign and the first indiction, recorded in that document, does not correspond to October of the year 958 but to October of the year 957.]

Accordingly, two documents are extant: one, “drawn up in the city of Verona” in October of the year 957; the other, “in the castle of Roveclaria” in the Veronese territory, in the year 959. Both record the reign of Berengar and his son Adalbert “here in Italy.” They possessed Verona itself to such an extent that they issued a diploma there in person [XCIX] [Note: The common year 958 is indicated by the eighth year of the kings’ reign and the first indiction, which do not correspond to the month of January except in the common year 958, for the same reason indicated in the preceding note. If, however, the copy we have seen gives the year of the Lord’s Incarnation as 957, then, unless a scribal error has occurred through omission of the unit, it must undoubtedly be said that in this diploma the years of Christ were reckoned according to the Roman and Venetian practice, which begins the year in March, as can also be observed in quite a few other documents.] on the Ides of January in the year 958, for the monastery of Leno in the diocese of Brescia. We saw a copy of it in the possession of Father Abbot John Louis Luchius. They likewise issued another diploma at Verona in the year 961, on the third day before the Kalends of June. It was first published by Muratori, vol. V of the *Antiquitates Italicae*, col. 403, and again by the editors of the *Camaldolese Annals* in the appendix to volume I, p. 66.

Since, moreover, Berengar attributed the entire cause of his former misfortune to “the bishops and counts and all the other leaders of Italy,” pursuing them all with hatred and enmity and making them his bitterest enemies, as the continuator of Regino has recorded, King Otto was invited by them and entered Italy again in the same year, 961. He completely deprived Berengar of the Italian kingdom.

Although Otto himself possessed the whole kingdom, he nevertheless wished that this part of Italy, extending from Verona to Friuli, should be regarded as a frontier of the German kingdom and, as before, be called the “Veronese march.” He therefore placed over it a duke of German origin, who would defend it against the other Italians, should any of them perhaps attempt rebellion. [Col. 0084B] The other successors of Otto did the same; for this reason, the dukes of either Bavaria or Carinthia are recorded as having been placed over that same march. Hence the name “Veronese march” continued for a longer time under the kings of Germany, namely until the twelfth century, and Friuli consequently began to have its own count, as did the other cities of that same march.

76. The dukes of this march were attached to no fixed seat. They stayed now here, now there, wherever they wished or circumstances required. Their authority over the counts themselves and over the entire march is clear from their decrees, as we have indicated.

The same is confirmed by a privilege of the year 998, in which Otto III granted to Berinfred, a Veronese deacon, and to his brothers and sisters “that they should serve no one’s placitum, nor present themselves before anyone in order to undergo judgment, except before us or before our duke” (DIONYSIUS, *Diplomatic Collection*, p. 185). He thus granted them a form of protection (*mundeburdium*), by which they were exempted from the counts and all other judges and could be summoned only before the emperor or before the duke of the march. This displays the remarkable authority of the dukes and margraves.

The same is also evident from Ratherius’s works. In Letter 8, addressed to Milo, the usurper of the see of Verona, he asserts that he had been seized by him and led into exile “to the disgrace of the emperor and, although they conceal it, as he says, of our dukes.” And later, near the end: “If you never intend to come to your senses, if you attempt other things, I suggest that you try what you have begun by this route: obtain, if you can, from the emperor and our dukes the authority by which I may depart.” These words indicate that not merely the emperor but the dukes themselves, as governors of the Veronese march, possessed authority at Verona.

Two other passages may also be referred to this matter, occurring in the *Conjecture on Qualities*, where he mentions a duke or duchess of Verona endowed with special authority. The first is in section 5: “Ratherius does not serve the emperor, and certainly not the duke.” Again, in section 14: “The illustrious duchess, fearing,” he says, “that something worse might happen to me than what had already occurred, commended me to the protection of the count.” Finally, in the *Itinerary*, section 4, he states that he was “rescued and restored by the mercy of the emperor and the assistance of the most excellent duchess.” It is clear from the circumstances already established that “our dukes” and “this illustrious duchess” were those who governed the Veronese march.

77. To understand who these persons were under Ratherius, it will be useful at this point to compile and explain the succession of the dukes who administered that same march in the tenth century—a succession not yet sufficiently understood, but useful for clarifying many matters.

The first duke of this march, appointed by Otto I in the year 952, when we have seen the march established, was Henry, Otto’s brother, who had already held the duchy of Bavaria since the year 945. Thus, when Rotger calls him “duke of the Bavarians and illustrious margrave,” he must not be understood as referring to the eastern march, now Austria, as some do, but to the Veronese march.

This Duke Henry had married Judith, daughter of Arnulf, or Arnold, duke of the Bavarians—that is, of the Arnulf who, when invited by the Veronese to come into Italy against King Hugh, gave occasion for the many misfortunes of Ratherius that we have described. This wife of Henry is praised by many [Note: Continuator of Regino, year 953; Thietmar, book II, pp. 332 and 339, vol. I of *Brunswick Historical Sources*; *Life of Saint Queen Mathilda*, chapter 4, no. 19, vol. I of *Brunswick Historical Sources*, p. 201; and the Saxon Annalist in Eckhard, under the years 945, 953, and 955.] and bore him Henry II [Note: *Quedlinburg Chronicle*, vol. II of *Brunswick Historical Sources*, p. 279] in the year 951.

When Henry the father died in the year 955, King Otto “gave the duchy and the march to Henry II, his son,” as the continuator of Regino and the Saxon Annalist write—namely, the duchy of Bavaria and the Veronese march, which his father had received from that same Otto.

Since, however, in this year 955 and for some time afterward Berengar and Adalbert still held our regions, Henry II could not in reality possess the Veronese march, except perhaps during those months in which Liudolf, after defeating Berengar, remained alive. Certainly, he possessed it in the year 961, when King Otto returned to Italy in order to expel Berengar.

At this time Henry was scarcely ten years old, and therefore his mother Judith administered everything in her son’s name. Thus “our dukes,” whom Ratherius mentions in Letter 8, written to Milo in the year 965, were Henry II and Judith. In two other works composed in the year 966, he calls her more explicitly “the illustrious and most excellent duchess”—that is, his mother Judith—rather than her son, because, while the son was still a minor, the mother enjoyed greater authority.

It might appear that this Henry held the march until the year 995, when he died, as may be inferred from a document of the year 993, which will be mentioned below. But this is not so. Others obtained the same march during the intervening period.

78. In order to provide information about the margraves who governed our march during this interval, it is necessary to search out the history of events—which, because of the scarcity of monuments, lies in obscurity—and present it as briefly as possible.

The Veronese march appears to have been given to Henry I and his son, the dukes of Bavaria, for this reason: at that time the duchy of Bavaria included all of Carinthia and the entire region adjoining that march, just as it had under Arnulf and Bertolf, the predecessors of Henry I. The former is called by Liutprand “duke of the Bavarians and Carantanians,” and in a document from Freising is called “duke of the Bavarians and also of the neighboring regions” (MEICHELBECK, *History of Freising*, vol. I, part II, p. 429).

Hence, in a diploma of Otto II from the year 974 granted to the Church of Freising, certain lands are said to have been granted “through the intervention of Henry,” second duke of Bavaria, “situated in the duchy of the aforesaid duke and in the county of Poppo, which is called Carniola.” If Carniola was part of Carantania in a county subject to the duchy of Duke Henry of Bavaria, Carantania necessarily belonged to the same duchy.

In the following year, 975, war broke out between Henry II and Otto, duke of the Alemanni or Swabians. Emperor Otto II, who favored Duke Otto, captured Henry and deprived him of the duchy in the year 976 (Saxon Annalist, in the *Chronicle*).

At that time the duchies of Carinthia and Bavaria were divided. The aforementioned Otto, duke of the Alemanni and son of Liudolf, was made duke of Bavaria. For this reason, in section 80 of the *Life of Saint Udalric*, bishop of Augsburg, the same Otto is called “duke of the Alemanni and Bavarians, after Henry had been deposed.”

The duchy of Carinthia was given to Henry, son of Bertolf—or Berthold—the former duke of Bavaria. For this reason, in a diploma of Otto II from the year 977, preserved in the Ughellian additions, volume V, p. 46, this Henry is called “duke of the Carantanians.”

As long as this division lasted, the Veronese march, which bordered Carinthia on every side but not Bavaria, was subject to the man who held the neighboring duchy of Carinthia, not to the man who held the more distant duchy of Bavaria. For it will never be found assigned to the duke of the Bavarians unless the same man was simultaneously duke of both the Bavarians and the Carantanians.

Thus there can be no doubt that the aforementioned Henry, son of Berthold, received the government of the Veronese march together with the duchy of Carinthia. Toward the end of the year 977, Henry II, who had escaped from the place where he was being held (Saxon Annalist), conspired with Henry, duke of the Carantanians, against Otto, duke of Bavaria. He invaded the city of Passau and was soon besieged there by Emperor Otto II. He was sent into exile together with that same Henry, duke of Carantania.

Hence Carantania, together with the Veronese march, appears to have been assigned to Otto, duke of Bavaria. [CIII] After Duke Otto’s death, which occurred in the year 982, Emperor Otto, reconciled with the younger Henry, son of Berthold, granted him the duchies of Bavaria and Carinthia at the assembly held at Verona in the year 983.

Writing about this Henry in book III, Thietmar mentions only the duchy of Bavaria: “Henry the younger, released from exile, was made duke of the Bavarians” (vol. I of *Brunswick Historical Sources*, p. 343). But that Carinthia was also granted to him and annexed to the duchy of the Bavarians, as had occurred under his predecessor Otto, the same author shows in book IV under the year 984, when he demonstrates that Henry was not so much duke of Bavaria as of Carinthia, saying: “Because of Duke Henry, who at that time ruled the Bavarians and the Carentanians” (ibid., p. 348).

The Veronese march therefore returned to him as duke of Carinthia: “At that time,” says Thietmar—that is, in the year 984—“he ruled the Bavarians and the Carentanians.”

When, in the following year 985, after Otto II’s death, Henry II “returned to himself and, seeing that he had been cast down by vain exaltation, when the king [Otto III] came to Frankfurt, he himself went there and, with folded hands, humble in appearance and conduct, moved by true repentance, restored himself to royal power” (Saxon Annalist), he earned the duchy from the same king.

The reconciliation with the younger Henry was arranged in such a way that he, content with the duchy of Carinthia alone, ceded the duchy of Bavaria to the other. For this reason, a document of King Otto III from the year 986, preserved by Hansiz, presents both Henrys as “dukes,” one of Bavaria and the other of Carinthia, “through the intervention . . . of our two nephews, Henrys, namely the dukes of the Bavarian and Carinthian regions” (vol. I of *Germania Sacra*, p. 226).

In another document of the year 988, preserved by Ughelli, Henry the younger is called “duke of the Carantanians” (vol. V of *Italia Sacra*), as also in another document dated 1 October of the year 989, as can be seen in Meichelbeck, vol. I of the *History of Freising*, p. 185.

When the younger Henry died toward the end of the year 989, Henry II, duke of Bavaria, received the duchy of Carinthia and the attached Veronese march. This is made clear by a placitum of the same Henry held at Verona in the year 993, in which he is called “Henry, duke of the Bavarians and Carantanians, and of this Veronese march” (DIONYSIUS, *Diplomatic Collection*, p. 176).

This Henry II finally died in the year 995, on the sixth day before the Kalends of September. Again, the duchies of Bavaria and Carinthia were separated. The duchy of Bavaria passed to his son Saint Henry, who later became emperor (*Quedlinburg Chronicle*, vol. II of *Brunswick Historical Sources*; *Fulda Necrology*, vol. III of *Brunswick Historical Sources). Carinthia, together with the Veronese march, was obtained by Otto, whom Conrad, duke of Lorraine, had fathered by Luitgarde, daughter of Otto I.

For this reason, the same Otto is called “duke of the Carentanians and count of the Veronese” by Thietmar and by Adelbold in the *Life of Saint Henry the Emperor*. “Count” is used in place of “margrave,” for he governed not merely Verona but the entire Veronese march. In other documents he is called “duke of this Veronese march” (DE RUBEIS, *Monumenta Ecclesiae Aquileiensis*, p. 497).

The Saxon Annalist, speaking of his son Bruno, who was promoted to the supreme pontificate under the name Gregory V in the year 996, says: “Bruno, son of Otto, who guarded the Veronese march,” and so forth. If this Otto governed the Veronese “march” in the year 996, it is clear that he succeeded Duke Henry II in the year 995.

Some suspect that this Otto was duke of the same march in the year 983, when Emperor Otto II, at the assembly at Verona, granted a privilege to Patriarch Rodoald of Aquileia “through the intervention and petition of Duke Otto” (ibid., p. 479). But at that same assembly the duchies of Bavaria and Carinthia, together with the attached Veronese march, were granted by the same emperor to the younger Henry, as we saw above.

Moreover, all the nobles of Germany had been summoned to that general assembly. Therefore, the Duke Otto who requested the privilege for Patriarch Rodoald cannot immediately be said to have been duke of Carinthia and of the Veronese march at that time. Before he obtained Carinthia and our march from Otto III, he was duke of Worms, or of East Francia, now Franconia. When that duchy was subsequently transferred to his sons, he himself obtained the duchy of Carinthia together with the Veronese march.

79. Since the succession of the later dukes of this march is known, we shall stop here. One point remains to be noted: some incorrectly confuse the Veronese march with the Trevisan march, as though it were the same march that was called at one time Veronese and at another Trevisan.

In fact, the Trevisan march began to be heard of only in the thirteenth century, when the Veronese march had already disappeared, as the cities of Italy conspired to secure their freedom. Treviso alone seems to have been given the name of a march, perhaps because among the Italian cities that had won their freedom it was a frontier city.

But let us now return to Ratherius.

[CV] § XIII.—Ratherius returns to Italy with Otto I in the year 961. A difficult passage in Fulcuin is examined. Through Otto’s agency he is restored to the see of Verona. The decree of the supreme pontiff and of the Council of Pavia is added. The proceedings and date of the Synod of Pavia. Bishop Peter of Ravenna, deposed from his see, obtains in the same synod, like Ratherius, a favorable decree. Otto’s edict on behalf of Ratherius. The theft of the body of Saint Metrone, and Ratherius’s short work on the same matter, written in the year 962. The emperor urges the bishop to send soldiers for the siege of Garda.

80. Otto I, after holding the assembly at Worms in the year 961, at which his son Otto was made king of Germany on Pentecost, returned to Saxony. After settling affairs there, he entered Italy with an army through Bavaria and the valley of Trent. There he “found almost all the counts and bishops along his route, and, honorably received by them as was fitting, entered Pavia with authority and without any resistance” (Continuator of Regino and Saxon Annalist).

In that city he celebrated the Christmas feast of the same year, and then set out for Rome so that he might be crowned emperor by John XII, the supreme pontiff. At Rome he obtained the imperial crown on 2 February 962.

Considering these circumstances highly favorable to his restoration, Ratherius came to Italy. Through the intervention of Bruno of Cologne, his great patron, acting with Otto, his brother, he recovered the see of Verona.

In order to establish the date of this restoration—which we believe must be assigned to the year 961—a difficult passage in Fulcuin, which has misled some, must first be examined. After recounting in the words of Rotger the intrusion of Baldric into the see of Liège and the expulsion of Ratherius, Fulcuin adds in his own words:

“Thus, after Ratherius had spent almost two years in this deposition, when military support had failed him, he returned to Italy” (*On the Deeds of the Abbots of Lobbes*, chapter 24).

He immediately continues in Rotger’s words:

“And lest anything in such a matter should remain incomplete and cause scruple to those inquisitive investigators of other people’s affairs, Bruno, together with his brother the emperor [Otto I], arranged that the ancient see of the Church of Verona should be restored to the same man, who had already been deposed twice.”

Most have understood this testimony as though Ratherius, “after almost two years,” had returned to Italy following his expulsion from the see of Liège and had, through Bruno’s efforts, been restored by Otto to the see of Verona. They therefore think that this restoration occurred “after almost two years,” namely in the year 957.

But we shall demonstrate shortly, from certain documents, that Ratherius was not restored until the year 961, when Otto returned to Italy. For there is a document from March of the year 959 from which it is known that not Ratherius but Milo was still presiding over the Church of Verona in that year (DIONYSIUS, *Diplomatic Collection*, p. 124).

Since Rotger’s testimony lacks the words mentioning “almost two years,” it signifies only that Saint Bruno, although he had yielded to the violence of the rebels by appointing Baldric after Ratherius had been expelled, later acted with Otto so that Ratherius might be restored to his former see of Verona. These words, which designate no year, agree perfectly with the events and with the restoration in the year 961 that will shortly be demonstrated.

The entire difficulty therefore lies in the words that Fulcuin inserted on his own authority: “After Ratherius had spent almost two years in this deposition, when military support had failed him, he returned to Italy.”

There can be no doubt that something is corrupt or incomplete in this text. We believe that the words “when military support had failed him” indicate nothing other than the soldiers or magnates who had defected from Ratherius, so that Bruno could find none of them to assist in his defense. See the *Phrenesis*, preface, section 1.

They did not defect from Ratherius “after almost two years had elapsed” from his deposition or expulsion from the episcopal chair of Liège, but near the end of the nearly two-year period during which he held that chair. Before he returned to Italy after his deposition and recovered the bishopric of Verona through Bruno’s agency, he did not spend almost two years in his deposition, but six years and more.

For this reason, instead of “deposition,” one should perhaps read “appointment,” or something similar, by which it would be indicated that Ratherius had spent almost two years in the episcopate of Liège, to which he had been legitimately appointed—from the year 953 to the year 955.

When nearly two years had elapsed and the soldiers or magnates had defected from him, he “was driven from that see” (these words must be understood or rather supplied) and sought Italy—not immediately, however, but when Otto came down there, as Fulcuin explains in the following words taken from Rotger.

The words Fulcuin places immediately afterward demonstrate that, when he wrote “he returns to Italy,” he was writing of the return to Italy of Ratherius about which Rotger speaks. To imagine another journey, earlier than this and later than the year 955, is simply fanciful.

Just as Fulcuin customarily indicates, in the case of other bishops, the years during which they presided over the see of Liège, so, when Rotger had omitted the duration of Ratherius’s episcopate, Fulcuin inserted these words to signify that he had been bishop of Liège for “almost two years,” as indeed he was.

81. Whatever may be considered the more probable interpretation of this passage of Fulcuin, it is certain that Ratherius did not recover the bishopric of Verona before the year 961. Two testimonies of Ratherius himself will establish the matter. Both attribute his restoration to Otto when Otto returned to Italy, and Otto did not return before the year 961.

One testimony requires the year 961; the other is consistent with the year 962. We shall explain how the two can be reconciled.

In the *Invective on the Theft of the Body of Saint Metrone*, which the Veronese believed had been stolen “with January ending at the sixth Kalends,” that is, on 27 January, the author assigns the theft to the time when “Otto, the emperor Augustus, had happily entered Italy to triumph,” in section 3.

This fits the month of January in the year 962, which was the first January after Otto’s entry into Italy. Although he was not yet emperor Augustus in that same month, Ratherius uses this title in the *Invective* itself, since he wrote it later, after Otto had already received the imperial crown.

Moreover, the theft was said to have occurred while Ratherius held the bishopric of Verona, as will be clear from the admonition in section 3 of the *Invective* itself. He had therefore been restored to the see of Verona some time before 27 January 962. More probably, this occurred before the end of the year 961, when Otto entered Italy and was first received by the Italians at Verona. For it is most probable that Ratherius returned to Italy together with Otto in order to be restored.

82. This conclusion appears to be contradicted by the words of section 4 of the *Itinerary*, where he testifies that he was “restored synodically by the mercy of the most pious Caesar, at the command of the apostolic pontiff who then presided over the Roman see, and by the judgment of the bishops.”

The synod by whose judgment he was restored, as we shall shortly see, was the Synod of Pavia, held after the middle of the year 962. These statements, which seem to conflict with what was said above, can easily be reconciled if we say that Ratherius was in fact restored to his own see by Otto immediately upon Otto’s arrival at Verona in the year 961, after the usurper Milo had been brought back into order.

Since Milo nevertheless continued to resist and defend his own claim, the prince referred the matter to Pope John XII, in order that, when Otto went to Rome, Ratherius’s episcopate might also be confirmed by ecclesiastical judgment. After the matter had been investigated and determined there, and subsequently at the Council of Pavia, the case was adjudicated to Ratherius by both authorities.

83. That the synod which restored Ratherius was the Synod of Pavia is indicated in section 7 of the *Apologeticus* in these words: “Certainly, as was once proclaimed in the Synod of Pavia, if I am bishop of the Veronese,” and so forth.

The obscure and largely unknown history of this synod must be drawn out from certain indications. We find that three major episcopal cases were brought before and decided by its fathers.

The Council of Reims of the year 992, chapter 43 (Wechelius’s edition, Frankfurt, 1600, p. 99), presents two cases as having been judged together in an earlier council: one concerning Ratherius, bishop of Verona, against the usurper Milo; the other concerning Peter, archbishop of Ravenna, against Honesto.

“Likewise, whatever occurred concerning Ratherius, bishop of Verona, or concerning Peter, archbishop of Ravenna, by usage or custom, has been abolished by all. For neither had accepted a successor after presenting a letter of resignation or laying aside the insignia of the priesthood: Ratherius [had accepted] Milo, and Peter [had accepted] Honesto, abbot of Saint Apollinaris.”

Although these words make no mention of the Synod of Pavia, it is nevertheless clear that both the case of Ratherius of Verona and that of Peter of Ravenna were judged by the same “universal” decision. Since the words quoted from Ratherius make clear that his case had been decided in the Synod of Pavia, the same must be said of the case of Peter of Ravenna.

84. Fathers Giovanni Benedetto Mittarelli and Anselmo Costadoni, who compiled the *Camaldulian Annals* with great diligence and learning, when speaking of Honestus, who succeeded Peter, suspected nothing [Col. 0091C] about a synod at Pavia or any other synod that had judged Peter’s case. They immediately append these words from the acts of the Synod of Reims to the preceding discussion:

> “Peter had received Honestus, abbot of the monastery of blessed Apollinaris [supply: as his successor], whom Pope John, surnamed ‘the Good,’ saw presented to him for consecration before he had learned of Peter’s deposition, or even of it through report.”

They distinguish two men named Honestus, and understand these words as referring to Honestus II, whom Pope John consecrated. They believe that this John, surnamed “the Good,” was not John XII, whose conduct incurred reproach, but John XIII, who ascended the apostolic see in 965. If this John consecrated Honestus, however, the synod at Pavia [Col. 0091D] in 962 certainly could not have judged Peter’s case against Honestus. They therefore hold that the cited words of the Synod of Reims indicate what occurred in 971, when Peter is said to have relinquished the archbishopric of Ravenna to Honestus. At the same time, however, they warn that “the commonly held opinion that Peter voluntarily relinquished the administration of the Church of Ravenna to Honestus II is not entirely grounded in truth, since the Fathers of the Gallican synod” of Reims “assert that he had been deposed from his see.”

We do not agree. Those who report that Peter relinquished the see of Ravenna to Honestus are not recent authors but ancient ones; unless something clearly compels us to do so, we cannot assert that they were mistaken. Among them is Saint Peter Damian, who writes in book 1, letter 9:

> “Peter, too, the archbishop, relinquished the Church of Ravenna; while he was still alive, Honestus succeeded him—under Otto I, that is, when Otto was first governing the reins of the empire.”

Alberic likewise indicates the same event and the same year, certainly from another source, in the *Chronicle* of Leibniz’s edition under the year 971:

> “Peter relinquished the bishopric of Ravenna, after which Honestus was appointed in his place” (*Historical Additions*, vol. II, p. 19).

All the others report the same thing, so much so that the authors of the *Camaldulian Annals* themselves acknowledge this opinion to be “common.” Yet the acts of the Council of Reims not only do not compel us to brand all these writers as erroneous—as though Peter had not relinquished the bishopric in 971 but had been deposed from it—but rather seem [Col. 0092B] to require us to place his deposition, and subsequently his restoration, before 971. For this reason, we must distinguish his deposition from the relinquishment that must be assigned to the year 971.

In the same acts of Reims, it is plainly suggested not only that Peter was deposed—which is the sole point considered by the authors just mentioned—but also that he was restored, since they state that the acts against him, by which he had been expelled from the episcopate, were “abolished by all”—that is, by all the Fathers of the synod [CX]. On the view that he was deposed in 971 and that Honestus was substituted for him, there is not even a word about Peter’s restoration and Honestus’s exclusion. Nor do documents from that period, which show Honestus continuing in his see in 972 and the following years, even after Peter’s death, allow us to place Peter’s restoration and Honestus’s removal at that time [Col. 0092C].

Moreover, in the cited acts of Reims, Peter’s case and restoration are joined with Ratherius’s case and restoration in such a way that both were decided by the same judgment. Once the acts against both men had been abolished—acts by which Honestus had been substituted for the deposed Peter and Milo for Ratherius—both were restored to their own sees. Therefore, just as the acts against Ratherius were abolished at the Council of Pavia in 962, so too the proceedings against Peter of Ravenna were annulled there and in the same year. His restoration, then, cannot be assigned in the synod at Pavia to the year 971. Rather, that year must be assigned the relinquishment of the bishopric which Saint Peter Damian and all the others unanimously reported.

Thus, two events must be distinguished, and everything is thereby reconciled without any need to posit two Honestuses or to interpret the words of the Synod of Reims otherwise. Peter was first removed from the archbishopric of Ravenna under John XII, who, unaware of his deposition, consecrated Honestus. Nor should the surname “the Good” cause difficulty. Unless an error has entered this expression, John XII may have been called “the Good” ironically, or on account of some title other than his character. Certainly, although John XIII was endowed with the best character, we are told that he received not the surname “the Good” but “the White Hen.”

Then, in 962, when the proceedings against Peter, just as those against Ratherius, had been abolished by the judgment of the Synod of Pavia, both men were restored to their sees. From this period there survive monuments of Peter, already archbishop, from the years 963, 965, 967, and 970. The Fathers of the Council of Reims speak of this first event [Col. 0093A]. The second event was transmitted to memory by Saint Peter Damian and the ancient chroniclers. In 971, that is, after reaching an agreement with Honestus, Peter voluntarily relinquished the bishopric to him. Consequently, the documents that follow mention Honestus as bishop; grateful toward his predecessor, after Peter’s death in 974 he established annual rites for his soul, as can be seen in a document reported by the aforementioned Camaldulian annalists in volume I of the appendix, p. 93 [CXI].

85. Let us now present the third case of the Synod of Pavia. Frodoard, under the year 962, supplies the case of Hugh of Reims, which he testifies was first judged in a Roman synod and later in the Synod of Pavia. After Attaldus, bishop of Reims, died on the day before the Kalends of October [Col. 0093B] 961, there was a major dispute over the choice of his successor, and it continued into the following year. Hugh’s relatives sought to restore Hugh, who had previously been excommunicated and expelled, with the support of Hugh, duke of the Franks.

“King Lothair,” Frodoard says in his *Chronicle* under 962, “having spoken with his cousin Hugh, was asked by him to restore the bishopric of Reims to the aforesaid Hugh; and from there they arranged a truce until the middle of April. A synod of thirteen bishops was held in the district of Meaux, over the river Marne, from the dioceses of Reims and Sens, with the bishop of Sens presiding. Certain bishops were working to restore the bishopric of Reims to the frequently mentioned Hugh; but Rorico, bishop of Laon, and Gibuinus, bishop of Châlons, resisted especially, asserting that one who had been excommunicated by so many bishops could not be absolved by a smaller number. Thus the matter was left pending until the Roman pope’s examination.”

Later, in the same year, he writes:

> “An embassy arriving from Pope John announced that the aforesaid Hugh, formerly a bishop, had been excommunicated both by the pope himself and by the entire Roman synod, but had been absolved by another synod held at Pavia. Once informed of this embassy through Bruno, archbishop of Cologne, we chose for the bishopric of Reims Odalric, an illustrious cleric … and he was ordained at Reims by the bishops Wido of Soissons and Rorico of Laon,” and so forth.

The truce arranged by King Lothair and Duke Hugh “until the middle of April” of the year 962 seems to have been made because, around that time, they hoped the dispute would be resolved in the Synod of Meaux. Since the bishops, divided into factions, had referred the same case to the judgment of the Roman pontiff, a Roman synod held after April is recognized, and somewhat later still a Synod of Pavia.

To avoid positing without necessity two synods held at Pavia in this year 962—one issuing judgment concerning Ratherius of Verona and Peter of Ravenna, and the other concerning Hugh of Reims—we judge it more probable that three such cases were heard and decided in the same Synod of Pavia around the middle of 962 [CXII].

The argument that Ratherius presented in letter 5 to Pope John, in order to prove himself the legitimate bishop against Milo, comes down to this: he had been deposed by no canonical judgment and had not voluntarily resigned; he had been excluded by force alone, and had yielded his place to Milo. This argument agrees with the one approved by the Council of Pavia and indicated in the acts of the Synod of Reims of 991 in these words:

> “He had received no successor after presenting a document of resignation or laying aside the insignia of the priesthood.”

86. In letter 8 to Milo, §3, Ratherius recalls an imperial edict and an oath which Milo, no less than Ratherius, had sworn to Otto:

> “I advise you,” he says, “to consider how, after swearing faithfulness to the emperor with the utmost solemnity, as I did, you are acting against yourself when you strive to destroy his edict and compel those who took the same oath to him as you did to commit perjury by drawing them into your support in this matter.”

Otto’s edict, which Milo later attempted to destroy when he did not cease attacking Ratherius and incited the Veronese clergy, his supporters, against him, appears to have been the edict by which the aforementioned king, after entering Verona and restoring Ratherius to his see, wished him to be accepted by everyone as the legitimate bishop and ordered that no attempt be made against him. Hence the words in the same letter to Milo:

> “Against the emperor’s command, which forbids every evil.”

The oath by which Milo, Ratherius, and all the others pledged loyalty to the same prince likewise required obedience to that edict. Consequently, when Milo stirred up disturbances against Ratherius, he is said to have attempted to destroy the edict and, together with his supporters, to have incurred the crime of perjury [Col. 0094C].

Perhaps, to induce Milo more readily to yield the bishopric to Ratherius, a promise—or at least a strong hope—of succeeding him had been offered, since one was nearly seventy while the other was still quite young. Hence Ratherius, asking in the aforementioned letter why Milo was attacking him, says:

> “This is the more recent—or rather the most immediate—cause: that I am neither dying nor, as you urge, taking flight.”

For in either event Milo would have succeeded him in the bishopric of Verona, as indeed he did when Ratherius finally relinquished the bishopric in 968.

87. The body of Saint Metro, which was kept in the basilica of Saint Vitalis the Martyr and was renowned for innumerable miracles, was secretly stolen and carried elsewhere on 27 January 962, as we indicated shortly before, no. [Col. 0094D] 81. Ratherius casts doubt on this theft in the title of his *Invective*, in these words:

> “The removal is lamented on the sixth day before the Kalends at the end of January, although perhaps vainly. For whether it happened or not, it may not have been properly known to anyone among temporal people.”

By adding, “although it is believed as something plausible, certainly at the time when it occurred,” he indicates the popular opinion concerning such a theft; and in the *Invective* itself he presupposes that the theft took place. Certainly, however, either that holy body was not stolen, or it was recovered not long afterward, since it has been preserved in the church of Saint Vitalis from time immemorial. No other city ever claimed it, nor does any now claim it.

Compare what Father Giovanni Francesco Manzoni, a priest of the Oratory, observed on this subject in his booklet published at Verona in 1756, entitled *Information Concerning Saint Metro*.

The theft of sacred relics or bodies was frequent in those times. This theft occurred all the more easily because, owing to an abuse that had already existed for sixty years, the revenues of the aforesaid basilica had been granted to laymen as a military benefice, and no priest lived there to guard the sacred body and the church.

As soon as news of the theft became public—perhaps on 8 May, when the deposition of Saint Metro is celebrated—many began to place the blame on the bishop and to speak against him more harshly, as though the theft had been committed through his negligence or even with his consent. Since the bishop who was being attacked was Ratherius himself, he composed the *Invective*, in which, while assigning the blame to others, he defended himself [Col. 0095B].

That this little work was composed after Ratherius’s third restoration is sufficiently indicated by the Freising manuscript, in which it is copied in full. The manuscript contains only works written by him after his third restoration. This is confirmed even more clearly by the title “Augustus Emperor,” applied to Otto in §3; Otto had assumed this title in February 962.

Although the theft itself occurred on 27 January of that year, as we conjectured more fully in the admonition, the fact that this work was written afterward, and that it should be assigned to that same year or, at the latest, to the beginning of the following year, is suggested by the aforementioned Freising manuscript. In it, not only do all Ratherius’s works seem to be arranged in chronological order, but this work is copied first [Col. 0095C], before Ratherius’s judgment concerning the clergy ordained by the usurper, which, as we shall see, was issued on the Ides of February of the following year.

The same conclusion is supported by the word “recently,” inserted in §3, by which the author indicates that he wrote this *Invective* not long after the emperor’s entry into Italy.

This work must be regarded as extremely important, for it is the oldest document through which the acts of Saint Metro, although reported more briefly, have come down to us. Ratherius first praises the ancients who wrote the acts of the early saints, but then adds in §2:

> “But now, shame upon us! In our own times and those of our grandfathers … such a poverty of writers has invaded the world that, if any distinction of merit has shone forth in our times or in those of the men whom they produced, the common people rather than any educated writer has raised it up.”

He thereby indicates that no life of Saint Metro and no miracles had been written down; only popular tradition survived, and from that alone was he able to draw.

The words “in the times of our grandfathers” suggest that the same saint belonged to the age of the “grandfathers,” or at least was not much earlier; he therefore seems to belong to the ninth or eighth century.

The form of penance to which Metro devoted himself—standing for so long before the church of Saint Vitalis the Martyr, bound by an iron chain to a stone until God should show by some sign that his sins had been forgiven—is shown by examples cited by Mabillon to have been frequently practiced (*Preface to the Second Century of the Benedictine Order*, no. 4).

Others, bound by the command of a bishop on account of public crimes and imploring pardon for those crimes, traveled as pilgrims through sacred places. Saint Metro, however, fastening a chain to his foot and securing it with lead to a large stone before the door of the aforesaid church, remained there in penance for seven years, until the key with which he had locked the chain was thrown by him into the nearby Athesis and, by God’s providence, was found.

88. The events narrated by Ratherius in part I of *On Contempt for the Canons*, §8, should be assigned approximately to this period:

> “For I myself once, when we were being compelled by an imperial command to besiege the fortress of Garda, and the bishops and clergy of this province, motivated not indeed by love of religion but by hatred of the labor, maintained that this did not properly belong to their order, answered them, as I often do, with a bold saying: ‘Just as the canons do not allow a cleric to fight, so neither do they allow him to commit fornication.’”

The event mentioned occurred around the year 962. When Otto entered Italy toward the end of 961 in order to subdue Berengar II, Berengar withdrew into the town of Saint Leo, while his wife Willa withdrew to an island called Saint Julius. Three other fortifications—Garda, Travallium, and the island in Lake Como—were held by his supporters.

In 962, after Otto had been proclaimed emperor at Rome, he began the siege of the island of Saint Julius. When he was also considering an attack on the other fortifications, he compelled the bishops and clergy of that province to take part in the siege of Garda. Garda, however, came under his control only at the end of 963, as the continuator of Regino [Col. 0096C] and the Saxon Annalist report.

This was a very strongly fortified castle in the Veronese diocese, on the shore of Lake Benacus. Shortly before, Adelaide, the widow of King Lothair, had been held captive there by Berengar II (Donizo, *Life of Matilda*, book I).

The bishops and clergy of that province whom Otto urged to besiege Garda were those who lived in the part of Italy nearer to Garda, not all the bishops and clergy of the Italian kingdom or of Lombardy, as some have thought. For Bishop Waldo of Como, occupied in another military expedition, conquered the island in Lake Como in 964, as the continuator of Regino relates.

From the time of Charlemagne, bishops and clergy had been compelled by the kings themselves to take up arms and go on campaign, on the grounds that they enjoyed many royal possessions and were believed to be bound to bear the burdens of their vassals.

“For this reason,” says Ratherius, “it is nowadays considered a very slight matter for a priest, as though out of loyalty to his lord—that is, to his prince—to prefer to fight in armor rather than be called perjured, although perjury is said to be expiated by the most severe penance, whereas this other offense is expiated by none” (*Part I, On Contempt for the Canons*, §12, col. 351b).

89. Muratori gives many more examples of this corruption (vol. II, *Italian Antiquities*, dissertation 26). Although the privilege of immunity exempted its holder from this service, it did not exempt him entirely. Thus, in the privilege of immunity granted by Otto I to the bishop of Worms in 966, which Muratori records, we read:

> “Nor shall a hostile expedition be required of the men of that church, except when necessity shall demand it for the advantage of the kings; then they shall go together with their bishop.”

Although some holy bishops also performed this service, as Gerard reports concerning Saint Ulrich, bishop of Augsburg, in his *Life*, §§13 and 36, others recoiled from this corruption. Thus, concerning Saint Radbod, bishop of Utrecht, his *Life* reports in §11:

> “When the king invited him to render him some service, he would courteously reply: ‘It is right to obey higher authorities; but who can doubt that it does not belong to bishops to become entangled in secular affairs, since the soldiers of Christ serve in their camps? They ought, spiritually clothed in ecclesiastical armor, to implore the Lord with their people for the safety, peace, and stability of the king and the people, seeking the gain of souls through continual prayers, not pursuing earthly things. It is proper that soldiers, girded with the belt of royal service and enriched with benefices, should perform that task.’” (*Acts of the Saints of the Benedictine Order*, vol. VII, p. 31).

Ratherius likewise was wholly opposed to this military service, which, in the passage cited, he acknowledges to be forbidden to clerics by canon law. Thus, in the *Conjecture of Quality*, §5, it is written of him:

> “He does not serve the emperor … he never goes on campaign.”

He states in the *Itinerary*, §1, and also in the sermon *On Mary and Martha*, §4, that he was ordered only to send his soldiers when necessary—not to go himself.

It is therefore evident how wrongly some have believed that Ratherius performed military service for the emperor at the siege of Garda and was for that reason granted a military benefice by him. Ratherius mentions such a benefice in the same *Itinerary*, §4, addressing his clergy:

> “Since I am not so inhuman toward you, despite my little poverty, as to keep a military benefice for myself—and this without payment—ten of you have been enriched.”

Military benefices were estates granted to laymen by right of usufruct, carrying the obligation of military service or of sending soldiers whenever necessary. Some of these, although granted to ecclesiastics, retained the character of military benefices because the same obligation of serving or directing soldiers was imposed upon them.

Not only emperors conferred such benefices; bishops did so as well when they entrusted church estates to someone with the same obligation. Thus those who received benefices of this kind from them became vassals of the churches, or vassals generally, and were called “soldiers.”

Therefore, when Ratherius wrote that “from his little poverty” he had given a military benefice to ten clerics of his Church, he was not referring to a benefice once granted to him by the emperor because he had served him “in the army,” to which he “never” went. Rather, he was referring to some estate belonging to the Church’s possessions and pertaining to the bishopric and the bishop, with which he had endowed those clerics not in the form of ecclesiastical benefices but in that of military benefices.

§ XIV. — Two decrees of Ratherius in 963 concerning clerics ordained by the usurper Milo. He writes to the Roman Church, in the name of his clergy, a booklet on the same matter. Sermons from the same year and a little work on his own lapse. During Lent in 964 he refutes the heresy of the Anthropomorphites, which had revived in these regions, in a lengthy sermon that also touches upon the error of certain people concerning Saint Michael. An apology for the same sermon, explaining several passages that had been misunderstood.

90. After Ratherius had been restored to the see of Verona before the end of 961, and had subsequently been confirmed in that same see both by the command of John XII and by the judgment of the bishops at the Synod of Pavia held after the middle of 962, he began to concern himself with those ordained by Milo, the usurper of his see.

For, ever since the proceedings concerning those ordained by Constantine, the usurper of the Roman Church, had been undertaken (see P. Chardon, *History of the Sacraments*, vol. V, part II, chapter 6), an opinion had begun to spread among some that ordinations performed by intruders were invalid. Ratherius too therefore doubted whether those whom Milo had promoted to the diaconate or priesthood were truly deacons or priests, or whether they needed a new ordination.

Accordingly, on the second Sunday of February 963—which that year fell on the eighth day of the month—he issued a decree ordering those ordained by Milo “to abstain until the day of a lawful ordination from the office in which Milo himself had illegally instituted them.”

When the same ordinands caused great disturbances over this matter, the bishop arranged on the following day for the decree to be withdrawn, but without success. He therefore issued another decree addressed to the same clerics, abandoning the severity of the earlier one and compelled to leave them to their own consciences, although he once again called their ordinations into question [Col. 0098C].

From this second decree it is clear that, among other arguments, those ordained by the usurper had opposed to their own defense the fact that some priests ordained by him had been promoted to the episcopate, while no one nevertheless doubted their episcopal consecration.

Although Ratherius does not wish to decide the matter, he nevertheless introduces sufficient doubt and raises another abuse: certain deacons had been consecrated bishops without the order of the priesthood [CXVIII]. Although he does not approve this consecration, as it is called, “by jumping over” an order, he nevertheless does not declare it invalid, because those who had consecrated them said that the priesthood was contained within the episcopate.

This appears to be the meaning of these words from his decree:

> “The authors of the act assert that whoever is a bishop is consequently also a presbyter, or certainly a priest.”

He merely wishes those “who by an ordination of this kind have obtained the episcopate” to have “received the diaconate from a legitimate pontiff”—that is, not from the usurper.

91. The year 963 is especially confirmed by a third document written on this subject, which certainly belongs to that same year. It is a booklet written in Ratherius’s style and hand but issued in the name of the clergy of Verona to the pontiff and clergy of Rome and to all the bishops of the Christian world. In it, the clerics ordained by Milo are presented as setting forth the canons and apostolic decrees that the bishop had brought against them, as though submitting the case for decision to the judgment of the Roman pontiff and the bishops [Col. 0099A].

Among the canons, the fragment of a Lateran council under Stephen III concerning those ordained by Constantine, the usurper of the Roman see, deserves particular attention. It has come to light only through this booklet.

Ratherius appears to have used this booklet as a means of presenting the authorities that led him to believe that the aforementioned ordinations ought to be questioned. Most of the texts tend toward declaring those ordinations invalid, while, solely as an act of mercy, allowing clerics ordained in this manner to retain the rank they had held in their own Church before such an ordination.

Such a booklet could do little to help them, since it defends the bishop’s case more than that of the clerics. Still less helpful were those passages in which, after reciting the canons that the bishop had cited against them, they are presented as foreseeing that the judgment would be directed against them if the matter were decided according to the canons. They therefore take refuge in the mercy of the judges and, to move them more effectively, make them an unmistakable promise of reward and payment if they deliver a favorable judgment:

> “But if you deign to come to our aid in such great peril to our souls, you need no instruction concerning the one from whom you ought to expect your reward. Since we are numerous, we promise that there will be someone who will return to your holiness, giving God glory in you and a reward worthy of your fatherly dignity. Venerable knights, we especially entreat you from this point onward for your reward.”

These words may indicate that Ratherius feared his clerics might use such a method to extort victory—a method which, as will become clear, they later employed on another occasion (§19).

We have no doubt that this booklet, dated “on the Kalends of August,” must be assigned to the year 963. This follows both from its inscription and from the reference to the Kalends of August.

The inscription reads:

> “To whoever is lord and apostolic of the holy Roman see, and to the entire senate and all the legislators of holy and canonical law, and finally to the holy assembly of all who live under the Catholic faith: the entire clergy of the holy Church of Verona offers the service of its dutiful devotion.”

The words “to whoever is lord and apostolic of the holy Roman see” indicate a period when, as the deposition of John XII was being considered, Ratherius did not know whether John himself still occupied the Roman chair when he was writing these words, or whether someone else did.

Rumor of John XII’s deposition began to spread “before Cancer”—that is, before 21 June, when the sun enters Cancer—in the year 963, according to the continuator of Liutprand. John was deposed, however, in a pseudo-synod at Rome in November of that same year.

This same year is confirmed by the Kalends of August. They do not fit the pontificate of John XII after he recovered the see from which he had been deposed, since, after recovering it in February 964, he lost it again only a few days later, being overtaken by death. Nor do they fit the pontificate of Benedict V, his successor, who was expelled before August of the same year.

The Kalends therefore belong to the single year 963. At that time, while Ratherius was staying at Verona, it was especially uncertain who presided over the Roman see. On the Kalends of August of that year, therefore, the bishop composed the aforesaid booklet in the name of his clergy. The two preceding decrees, written in February and providing the occasion for the booklet, must likewise be assigned to that year.

92. That Ratherius did not neglect the principal duty of bishops, namely the ministry of the word, can be gathered from the sermons that survive. We have been fortunate to find four sermons delivered in the year 963.

The first, on Lent, although brief, explains a highly useful and practical manner of fasting. The first sermon on Easter reveals what true paschal joy is and derives instruction from Saint Paul and from the ceremonies prescribed to the Israelites in connection with the eating of the paschal lamb. It also shows that the discipline concerning the reception of Christ’s body and blood was still in force at that time [CXX].

The first sermon on the Ascension, apparently delivered on the Sunday before the feast, deals chiefly with the three days of Rogation. In discussing these Rogations—which we call the lesser litanies—our author also includes the greater litanies, which likewise are celebrated within the fifty days of Easter. Through a chronological error, however, he states that litanies were first introduced generally by Saint Gregory and then by Saint Mamertus of Vienne, whereas Saint Mamertus, who was earlier than Saint Gregory, first instituted the lesser litanies, and Saint Gregory later prescribed them in response to the need caused by a pestilence. They were subsequently assigned to 25 May and called the greater litanies.

Ratherius implies that the fast to be observed on these Rogation days, as Saint Mamertus had instituted it—and as he also states in the *Synodica*, §10—was required no less during the lesser than during the greater litanies. In this sermon he seems to append an apology for this fast, which was especially foreign to the Roman Church’s practice during the fifty days of Easter.

He attempts to guard against the error of certain people who, through a mistaken understanding of a Gospel testimony, believed that the baptized would attain salvation through faith alone. He also seeks to uproot another error: some thought that hail and lightning were sent by the devil, or by evil people with the devil’s assistance.

Finally, the first sermon on Pentecost explains the solemnity of the feast and the manner in which it should be celebrated. The other sermons that the ravages of time have not destroyed will have to be assigned to other years.

93. See note 1 to the first sermon on Lent for why we think the little work *On His Own Lapse* should be assigned to the year 963 or to the beginning of 964.

This “own lapse” was a lapse of the tongue; another work also survives under the title *On Idle Speech*. The same lapse is mentioned in the *Conjecture of Quality*, §7, where Ratherius’s critics seem to imply that, overcome by grief, he repeatedly condemned the lapse and perhaps exaggerated it excessively:

> “He also admits that he said one idle word—and, as he forces us to believe, a most shameful one—in such a place.”

94. Around this time the heresy of the Anthropomorphites became known to have revived in the diocese of Vicenza, neighboring that of Verona. Ratherius refuted it in a very lengthy second sermon on Lent.

“Three days ago,” he says in §29, “one of our people reported to us that the priests of the diocese of Vicenza, our immediate neighbors, believe God to be corporeal. They have been led to this belief because Scripture says: ‘The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are toward their prayers’ (Psalm 33:16); and: ‘Your hands made me’ (Psalm 118:73); and: ‘Let us make man in our image and likeness’ (Genesis 1:26).”

This moved the bishop to deliver a sermon before the people, in order to ward off the danger of so great an error from the flock entrusted to him. He discovered that the error had taken such hold among certain people that it had also seized some Veronese priests, who, after hearing the bishop’s address, muttered:

> “What shall we do? Until now we thought we knew something about God. Now it seems to us that God is absolutely nothing if he has no head, no eyes, no hands, and no feet.”

He therefore considered it part of his duty to refute so great an error more extensively in the aforementioned second sermon on Lent, which bears this title:

> “A very lengthy sermon on Lent by Ratherius of Verona, or, as it seemed to him while he was alive, an ineffective babbling.”

That this sermon belongs to the Lent of 964 will be established from note 1. This sermon—or rather treatise—divided into forty-one paragraphs, is one of the more notable and useful works written by Ratherius. For, while it displays a sufficiently polished style, it also contains, in addition to the refutation of the Anthropomorphite heresy, many other excellent instructions.

At the beginning he touches upon certain abuses by which the observance of Lent was being corrupted. He criticizes those who fasted every other day and indulged in gluttony and drunkenness on the alternate days, believing that they were observing Lent, although twenty days of fasting made a twentieth, not a fortieth.

Since the ancient discipline of fasting had already been relaxed, it was permitted to break the fast at the ninth hour. Some, however, taking nothing at that permitted hour, fasted every day until nightfall for the purpose of being able “to stuff their bellies at night, as though with permission.”

He reproves others who anticipated the hour for breaking the fast on Holy Saturday to such an extent that, by the third hour, they staggered on their feet from gluttony and drunkenness. He also reproves those who celebrated Masses before the ninth hour on the day of the Lord’s Supper and thereafter broke their fast [CXXII].

He suggests that there were some who thought the violation of the fast on these two days—Holy Thursday and Holy Saturday—could be excused on the grounds that the two days were compensated for by adding two other days of fasting to Lent, namely the Wednesday and Thursday before the first Sunday of Lent, since formerly “the beginning of the fast” started with the first Sunday.

He notes various other vices that had crept into the practice of those who fast—vices that are also common in our own times—and explains the true manner of fasting, by which one abstains not so much from food as from sins, joining prayer, almsgiving [Col. 0102A], and penance to the fast.

95. In addition to refuting the Anthropomorphite heresy more fully and energetically, he touches upon another, cruder error in the same sermon. Certain people believed that Saint Michael sang Mass on Monday and therefore considered it a religious duty to visit his church on that day rather than on others.

Although Ratherius’s teaching on these matters was correct and sound, he nevertheless could not avoid the criticism of certain people who had misunderstood several statements directed against the Anthropomorphites and against superstitious devotion to Saint Michael. He therefore had to explain himself more clearly, and this gave rise to the apologetic appendix to the same sermon.
gave.

§ XV.—Ratherius’s Book *On Contempt for the Canons*: The reasons for writing it. The vices and abuses rife among the clergy. On the illicit marriages of clerics. On the inequitable distribution of ecclesiastical revenues and the evils arising from it. Ratherius’s effort to introduce a fairer distribution and to vindicate the authority of bishops asserted by the canons. How greatly the clergy resisted, and why.

[Col. 0102B]

**96.** Around the time of Lent in the year 964 (see the note on the book *On Contempt for the Canons*), Ratherius published another important work, bearing the twofold title *Perpendiculum*, or *On Contempt for the Canons*. In order that the reasons for this work may become clear—by which he strove to confront the vices rife among the clergy and to restore observance of the sacred canons [CXXIII]—the matter must be traced from an earlier point.

From the very beginning of his episcopate there had always been dissension between Ratherius and the Veronese clergy (*Discordia*, nos. 1, 5), arising from a disagreement in principles [Col. 0102C]. For the bishop, learned in the sacred canons, seeing that they had been abandoned and neglected, wished to introduce their observance through zeal for discipline. The clergy, on the other hand, abhorring the discipline of the canons and regarding as lawful, in the name of custom, abuses that had become widespread, did not cease resisting the bishop, lest they be drawn away from what they called their customs.

Thus, in the book *Discordia*, no. 1, he says that he had never been able to achieve remarkable concord with those same clerics, “since they have always preferred the custom of their predecessors—who were incessantly rebellious toward their own pontiffs—to the canons that are holy and decreed by God; whereas I have thought that the holy canons decreed by God ought to be preferred to practices invented by the devil.” The greatest abuse, and the one most strongly condemned by the sacred canons [Col. 0102D], was the clerics’ “womanizing” (*mulierositas*), which he explains as having spread widely and publicly in these words in *Discordia*, no. 1:

“For to keep women forbidden by the Council of Nicaea with such habitual regularity and such publicity, with such little regard for the reverence owed to God and human beings, and with the fear of hell so entirely set aside that they think it not merely permissible but even necessary to do so—so that no one who avoids doing this appears, in their eyes, capable of being free from that most wicked crime which the Apostle mentions in his Epistle to the Romans—does it not seem to you that the devil invented this?”

The clerics, then, kept women so universally that they believed whatever had been accepted by common practice to be lawful; indeed, they considered it not only lawful but also necessary, lest anyone without women [Col. 0103A] should serve the unspeakable and most wicked crime condemned by the Apostle.

**97.** This vice prevailed so widely that not only the senior and wealthier clerics but also the junior and poorer ones were afflicted by it. The senior and wealthier clerics are noted in part 1 of *On Contempt for the Canons*, no. 4, where he says that, enriched with the Church’s more substantial and ample revenues, they were, among other reasons, so endowed “that they might also have the means to procure wives for their sons and husbands for their daughters.”

The junior and poorer clerics are indicated in *Discordia*, no. 6. After reporting that they had been compelled by an imperial order to dismiss their women, he adds this excuse of theirs:

“Almost everyone’s excuse was that this could in no way be done because of poverty; but it could have been done somehow, if [Col. 0103B] they had received the stipend due to them from the Church’s possessions” [CXXIV].

The words “everyone” and “because of poverty” deserve notice, since they indicate that the matter was very common among the poorer clerics. How they provided for themselves in their “poverty” through women can be explained from a letter of Atto, bishop of Vercelli and a contemporary, to his clergy against incontinent clerics (vol. I of Acher’s *Spicilegium*, p. 440):

“There are those who seek to excuse themselves for keeping company with women while setting forth what they call their necessity. For they say that, unless we were supported by their hands, we would already be wasting away from hunger or nakedness.”

**98.** It may be questioned whether this womanizing of the clerics, so common and public and regarded as lawful [Col. 0103C], should be understood as referring to concubines, whom no one could have failed to know were forbidden by divine law itself. Ratherius indeed indicates that “marriage” was involved. In *Qualitatis conjectura*, no. 2, accusing clerics joined to such women of adultery, he calls “an illicit marriage adultery”; and in the *Apologeticus*, no. 7, he says of monogamous clerics: “Public adultery, since it is certainly an illicit marriage”; and in *Discordia*, no. 1: “For us, an adulterer is one who, contrary to the canons, is a husband.”

The word “husband” (*uxorius*) presupposes a marriage contracted with a woman. Hence, in *Discordia*, no. 6, Ratherius expressed the decree of the synod of Ravenna against clerical womanizing, fortified both by the authority of the Roman pontiff and by an imperial order, in these words [Col. 0103D]:

“When the Augustal will thundered against them concerning the dismissal of womanizing,” and so forth.

In his letter to Nanno, no. 2, he called this “the legation of that pope concerning the dismissal of wives,” so that “concerning the dismissal of womanizing” means the same as “concerning the dismissal of wives.”

Women who lived with clerics were therefore regarded as wives, even though the canons prohibited this and “no law grants marriages to ministers of the altar” (*Itinerarium*, no. 15). Nevertheless, every such prohibition was considered annulled by custom, and these marriages were consequently believed to be lawful; indeed, they were believed lawful to such an extent that clerics entered into them publicly and without any fear. Accordingly, in the sermon *On Mary and Martha*, no. 4, our author describes the clerics as “opposed to the canonical law even to the point of public marriage.”

The following words of the author in book V of the *Praeloquia*, no. 18, col. 155c, do not contradict this. There, among other distinctions between ecclesiastics and laymen, he lists “that wives are not taken by us as they are by them.” For he wrote this long before, and from the entire context it is clear that he was not referring to clerics but to bishops, whose morals he is expressly discussing there. Elsewhere, however, in part 2 of *On Contempt for the Canons*, no. 2, col. 367c, where he is discussing the morals of clerics, he repeats almost the same words of the *Praeloquia* among the distinctions between these men and laymen, including matters clerics share with bishops, but appears to have omitted “that wives are not taken by them as by laymen” [Col. 0104B] because marriage was not as foreign to clerics as it was to bishops.

Thus, in this century, the beginnings of that corruption are already clearly visible in our regions—a corruption that became much more widespread in the following century and was defended with much greater effort by many advocates of the lawfulness of clerical marriage. At this same period, “the clerics themselves openly took wives,” as is recorded in the *Life of Saint Adalbert, Bishop of Prague*, tenth century, no. 11 (Mabillon, ch. 7, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Benedictini*, p. 841). The same is seen in England, as may be observed in Orderic Vitalis, book V of the *Ecclesiastical History*, p. 574; and evidence of the matter also appears in the *Life of Saint Æthelwold, Bishop of Winchester*, no. 16 (Mabillon, ibid., p. 602).

It should nevertheless be observed that these marriages were entered into by at least most of the clerics before sacred orders, yet in such a way that those who had taken wives did not leave the clergy but remained within it; nor were they separated from their wives in any way, and they were even promoted to sacred orders. The chief indications of this seem to be found in Ratherius’s little work *On Illicit Marriage*. The illicit marriage that occasioned the work was the marriage of a certain cleric whom his father—himself also a cleric—had joined in matrimony to the daughter of another cleric. He also mentions there another marriage of a different cleric, contracted through the agency of his father.
