That these and other similar clerics did not become laymen on account of marriage but remained in the clergy is suggested by the words in no. 4 with which our bishop addresses incontinent clerics:

“Therefore, brothers, you must be admonished and entreated: since, alas, you are in no way able to be restrained from women, at least let the sons born from you remain laymen, and join your daughters to laymen, so that your adultery may at least be brought to an end at your death and may nowhere last to the end of the age.”

Here too he calls the clerics’ marriages adultery. Yet this adultery could nowhere “last to the end of the age” on account of the marriages mentioned if the clerics’ sons, after marriage, had fallen out of the clergy and passed into the rank of laymen. It is said to last forever because, since those men remained in the clergy after marriage and were even promoted to higher orders, they assigned the sons born from such marriages to the clergy and joined them in marriage; similarly, marriages contracted by clerics would continue to the end of the age and make the adultery perpetual.

The following passage from the same number is relevant:

“When a priest or deacon, who cannot have a legitimate wife, makes a son born from that fornication—or, worse, from adultery—into a priest” [understand: and one joined in marriage by his father], “that man makes another priest from one similarly born of himself; that one in turn makes his own; another again makes his own; that adultery, spreading in this fashion to the end of the age—whose is it, if not his who first sowed it?”

The distinction between “a son born from fornication” and “one, worse still, born from adultery” must be noted. The author calls “a son born from fornication” one whom a cleric had fathered by a free woman, or concubine [CXXVI] [Col. 0105B]; but “born from adultery” one whom he had fathered from an illicit marriage, which in Ratherius’s language is called “adultery.”

There were therefore clerics who maintained concubines, and others who had wives. Almost all the sons of these men had been enrolled in the clergy, to such an extent that in the *Itinerarium*, no. 5, he declares that scarcely any little boy would be found in the clergy who was not a “bastard” (*manzeres*), that is, born from fornication or adultery:

“If I were to expel the bastards, whom among those same little boys would I permit to stand in the choir?”

He likewise implies that all except the little boys were entangled in this illicit marriage when he writes:

“If I were to drive the men with many marriages from the clergy, whom but little boys would I leave in the church?”

Even if he wrote hyperbolically and with exaggeration, it nevertheless cannot be denied from all this that such a vice had seized many, indeed most, of the clerics [Col. 0105C].

**99.** We have already indicated above the excuse of the junior clerics, “because of poverty.” Another abuse had evidently grown up: since the senior clerics had claimed almost all the Church’s revenues for themselves, the junior clerics were oppressed by extreme want.

“The property”—that is, the possessions and goods—“of those” clerics of the cathedral church “is, thanks be to God, by no means insignificant; yet it is so divided among farms and other things of this sort that some of them grow rich from it, while the multitude languishes in poverty; and—shame upon the wickedness!—those who render the greater service to God in the church receive either nothing or very little, while those who scarcely ever perform any service for the Lord become wealthy from ecclesiastical possessions.”

So he writes in *Discordia*, no. 6. To divide “among farms” (*per massaritias*) is the same as dividing among fields and vineyards, which easily produced inequality (see note 7 on *Discordia*). For the more powerful and senior clerics had claimed for themselves more numerous and better fields, from which the origin of the richer prebends may be discerned.

Similarly, in the same work, no. 2, he complains:

“What has generally been assigned to all the clerics is divided so unequally and among farms that some of them thereby become, from being among the poorest, the richest; some moderately wealthy; and some receive nothing at all from it, according to the practice and custom” by which that division was defended.

And in part 1 of *On Contempt for the Canons*, no. 4:

“The clerics themselves divide among themselves, according as each is more powerful, the things bestowed upon the Veronese church—not according to the custom of other churches, by which they ought to accrue to all the clerics of the church, but according to their own will, to deacons and priests alone,” and so forth [Col. 0106A].

See also the *Apologeticus* [CXXVII], no. 7. When he says “only to deacons and priests,” this should not be understood of all deacons and priests, but of the senior ones, whom we call canons; for there were other junior priests who are described as poor in the *Judicatum* and called “chaplain priests.” There is no doubt, however, that these had previously spent some time in the diaconate before the order of priesthood.

**100.** This inequitable distribution of ecclesiastical revenues is said to have provided the cause for other vices as well, which infected both senior and junior clerics (*On Contempt for the Canons*, part 1, no. 4) [Col. 0106B].

The senior clerics, being wealthy, could rebel more easily against the bishop and dominate their inferiors to such a degree that, whenever they wished, they could compel them even through secular power to join their party, force them to swear an oath of loyalty to another bishop whom they had drawn over to their side, and, if they did not obey, even expel them from the church.

The junior clerics, on the other hand, since they had no means of living suitably and devoting themselves to ecclesiastical studies and duties, did not hesitate to abandon or neglect these activities. From this the beginnings and causes may be detected of the decline and gradual disappearance of the offices of the minor orders.

To provide a remedy for such great evils, the bishop believed that a fairer distribution of revenues ought to be introduced. He maintained that this belonged to his authority [Col. 0106C] on the basis of the sacred canons, which he had collected before his second expulsion to refresh his memory on this matter.

His intention was not to take anything away from the goods of the cathedral church and claim it for others. He was concerned only that what had been bestowed generally upon the clergy of that church should, through a fairer division, suffice for the suitable support of clerics of every order, so that divine worship and sacred offices would not suffer harm; so that some would not become insolent through excessive abundance of possessions and power, while others, under the pretext of poverty, would devote themselves to womanizing; and so that all would not fall into vices of various kinds.

Nothing could be more just or more consonant with the sacred canons. Yet the Veronese clerics, wholly unwilling to submit to this authority and equity, opposed to it the sole support on which they relied: the custom of their predecessors. They considered that custom preferable to every standard of equity and to every canon.

Not only the wealthy senior clerics but also—and this may seem surprising—the poor junior clerics strongly resisted that more suitable division of revenues, which would have benefited them, for two reasons (*ibid.*, no. 4, and *Discordia*, no. 6). First, so that by pleading poverty they might more easily withdraw from divine service; second, because each hoped to live long enough eventually to rise into the rank of the senior clerics who were dying.

Thus, since everyone opposed the bishop, he complains that no episcopal authority had been left to him “apart from the making of chrism and some power to chrismate” [Col. 0107A] (*On Contempt for the Canons*, part XIX): that is, only the power of order was permitted him, while the power of jurisdiction, distribution, and punishment was wholly obstructed.

**101.** The canons that he had collected against these abuses before his second expulsion he arranged and published in the aforementioned book *On Contempt for the Canons* during Lent of the year 964.

This book is divided into two parts. In the first, after a brief prologue in which he indicates the occasion for writing, he produces canons and decrees that entrust to the bishop not only the care and administration of spiritual matters but also of the Church’s temporal goods. If he lacks this authority, he will be able to accomplish little or nothing even in spiritual matters. For, as he says in no. 4:

“Since you very rarely see anyone acting from generosity, but rather from fear or from an alliance of affection, how will one fear you when you can take nothing away? How will one love you when you can confer nothing?” [Col. 0107B]

He adds many other things. Although, because of the abuse of the Veronese clerics—which he was striving to eradicate—he attacks them sharply and in a bitter style (see *Discordia*, no. 5), he nevertheless relies not on force and command but on reason and persuasion.

He then turns to contempt for the canons, which he says has spread so widely, in no. 6, “that I am unable to find anyone among them who cares for them, from the very lowest member of the church to the most distinguished,” and so forth. He discusses at greater length the causes of such contempt, the chief of which was that those who ought to promote observance of the canons and restrain their violators were themselves sinning against the canons.

He inserts several examples that demonstrate the extreme corruption of the clergy and contempt for the canons. In the second part, which is much shorter, he places the incontinence of the clerics as another particular cause of contempt for the canons; because of it, those same clerics were held in the greatest contempt by laymen. He relies chiefly upon the authority and threats of the sacred books.

Ubertus, to whom he addressed this work in the form of a letter, was the bishop of Parma and an intimate of the emperor Otto, from whom he had obtained the county of that city; later, he rose to the dignity of archchancellor. [CXXIX] He had once asked Ratherius to send him some prayer that was familiar to him. Now, to satisfy him, Ratherius appends at the end of the second part a “collect,” excerpted from a liturgical book belonging to another Ubertus, who was the bishop of Parma’s friend, “and,” he says, “my companion in pursuing me.”

Hence there is suspicion that Ubertus of Parma favored Ratherius’s enemies [Col. 0107D]. The “collect” itself, to be recited in the sacrifice of the Mass, appears to have been composed against violators of the canons and against persecutors.

§ XVI.—At the beginning of the year 965, Ratherius is captured through the agency of Milo the invader. Shortly afterward he is restored through the intervention of the duchess Judith. Judgment and settlement against the rebels. How great the danger in which he still found himself, and with what care he protected himself. Pressured to yield the episcopate to Milo, he refused. Two letters to Milo written around the Christmas feast. He reproduces, with an addition, the *Deliberative Conclusion*. A very obscure passage concerning Sikerus explained.

**102.** When Milo, Ratherius’s rival, saw that the Veronese clergy had been aroused against the same bishop for the reasons already mentioned [Col. 0108A], he thought the time opportune to attempt something more violent against him, having brought the leaders of that clergy over to his side.

Signs of this conspiracy came to the notice of “that illustrious duchess,” who for that reason commended Ratherius to the protection of a count, as is reported in the *Qualitatis conjectura*, no. 14:

“When that illustrious duchess learned of such conduct toward me, and, consequently, learned that I had many enemies and was deprived of the protection of friends, since I was a newcomer, she feared that something worse might happen to me than what had already occurred, and commended me to the protection of a not-unknown count.”

This “illustrious duchess” was Judith, mother of Henry II, duke of Bavaria. Since, while her son was still a minor, she administered both the duchy of Bavaria and the March of Verona in his name, she was living at this time in Verona together with her son [Col. 0108B]. See § 12, nos. 76 and 77.

The “not-unknown count” was called Bucco, under whom this conspiracy occurred. See letter 12 to Ambrosius, no. 3. At first Bucco had been hostile to Ratherius, so much so that Ratherius urgently desired to be freed from him. But through the intervention of the aforementioned duchess [CXXX] he began to favor him, and for this reason our bishop adapted to the count these lines of Ovid (*Epistle II to Nanno*):

“He who had earlier spoken insults against the Theraphnean wife,

Soon sang her praises with a more fortunate lyre.”

He adds the explanation:

“For after I had said of him”—that is, of Bucco, who was certainly hostile to me—“‘He who delivered Israel from the hand of Pharaoh, may he deliver Ratherius from the hand of Bucco,’ when he, as he was about to depart, began to grow better, I too began to address him in this fashion.”

Let us now see to what extent he supported Ratherius [Col. 0108C] in the difficulties just mentioned.

**103.** In the lower part of the mountain on which the castle of St. Peter now stands, there was at that time a sufficiently secure stronghold called the “Palatium” (see *Qualitatis conjectura*, no. 14, and the note). Bucco had ordered Ratherius to withdraw there. The bishop, however, refused to leave the episcopal residence.

An armed incursion was therefore made into it, and the bishop was captured and carried away. That Milo was the principal author is clear from letter 8, written to that same assailant:

“You seized me, brought me away, despoiled me, drove me into exile: all these things, however, were to the disgrace of the emperor and, although they conceal it, of our dukes”—namely, Judith and Henry II.

In the *Itinerarium*, no. 4, he writes that almost all the clerics agreed to the same conspiracy, and even contrived it through united efforts:

“From that same invader” [Milo], “you were not wholly ignorant, nor were you so opposed to him that there were not a thousand who believed that almost all of you had not merely consented but had contrived this: afterward they seized, expelled, injured, stripped, and imprisoned me,” and so forth [Col. 0108D].

He testifies in the *Qualitatis conjectura*, no. 16, that one man above all was “the principal instigator of all those who seized me.” To the other calamities inflicted upon him on this occasion he adds the plundering of the church and the destruction of the episcopal residence.

Ratherius’s capture occurred around January 21 or 28 of the year 965 [Col. 0109A]. The date is established by the following words in the *Qualitatis conjectura*, no. 6:

“When he had been captured, the most foolish man began to sing: ‘Now I see what I desired.’ For he thought, he admits, that he was then to be expelled entirely; and he rejoiced that he himself had not abandoned the episcopate, but that the episcopate had abandoned him. By this device, he says, he wished to recover his monastery.”

The words “Now I see what I desired” occur in the antiphon at the *Benedictus* for the two feasts of Saint Agnes, first on January 21 and then on January 28. He therefore appears to have sung it because he was captured on one of those two days. Similarly, he was accustomed to use other verses and antiphons of the days that were passing while he wrote, as we shall see elsewhere. The year 965 will be confirmed by the context of the history that follows.

[Col. 0109B]

**104.** Not long afterward, Ratherius was rescued and brought back “by the clemency of the emperor and through the assistance of the most excellent duchess” Judith (*Itinerarium*, no. 4).

The rebellion nevertheless did not subside; indeed, it broke out more openly, since it attacked not only Ratherius but also Count Bucco himself, who was protecting Ratherius. Hence the author says in letter 12 to Ambrosius, no. 3:

“In Bucco’s presence they formed a conspiracy against him and against me.”

This count had warned Ratherius not to entrust himself again to the episcopal residence, in which he had suffered so much, but to inhabit “the high court” (*Qualitatis conjectura*, no. 14), not far from the episcopal residence and more strongly fortified. Ratherius obeyed and made it still stronger than it had been.

As the disturbance increased, the same count judged that it would be safer if the bishop ascended to the aforementioned “Palatium,” built on the mountain.

“I obeyed,” he says; “it was extremely dilapidated, and I had it recovered”—that is, repaired—“as quickly as possible” (*ibid.*).

But when the rebels also conspired against Bucco, he ordered his wife and sons to live together with Ratherius in the “Palatium.” The count himself withdrew to the circus, or amphitheater, which even then was commonly called the “Arena,” and which stood on the opposite side of the city as a defensive position.

It seemed quite absurd for the bishop to live in that “palatium” together with the count’s wife and sons. He therefore left the “palatium” and returned to the episcopal residence, though it was alarming. Since he did not dare to remain there longer, he was considering departing for Garda, a very strongly fortified town. But, because the paschal feast was approaching—and in the year 965 it fell on March 26—he did not wish to be absent from the episcopal offices during so solemn a celebration. He selected a place in a corner of the city that appears to have been public property, and sought the count’s permission to construct a building there [Col. 0109D].

Whatever had been built with not only the count’s consent but also his assistance was immediately burned down. When Ratherius wished to rebuild the structure, the count at first prohibited him, then permitted it again. He rebuilt it better than before. But when the count’s wavering will aroused suspicion in Ratherius, once the paschal feasts had ended he again contemplated fleeing to Garda [CXXXII].

Meanwhile, the deacon John came and began lamenting that the portico of Saint Peter was threatening to collapse unless the bishop, to whom the restoration of churches belonged in those days, came quickly to its aid [Col. 0110A]. The portico meant that of the church of Saint Peter on the mountain (*ibid.*).

Ratherius therefore immediately ascended there and set his hand to the restoration. The portico, whose remains still survive in that place, is believed to be the one repaired by Ratherius. He judged that the site of Saint Peter’s, reached by steps, was suitable for his protection and should not be abandoned, since it was not too far from the city and the cathedral.

His enemies, however, criticized him for not returning to the episcopal residence. Exposing their malicious purpose, he says in *Qualitatis conjectura*, no. 15:

“I know very well, so that your malicious intention may not remain unmentioned, that you preferred me to remain in such a place that I would be accessible to my enemies, and that you were not troubled because I had left the suspicious house, but because I had placed myself in a safer one” [Col. 0110B].

Thus we shall see that he remained there until the year 968, when he wrote a letter to Ambrosius, and subsequently abandoned Verona altogether.

**105.** After many such changes of fortune, judgment was at last instituted against the rebels. Although many crimes and injuries were involved in the case, however, all of them were disregarded and proceedings were brought on only one oath-breaking offense, by which the oath sworn to the emperor during the conspiracy raised against Ratherius had been violated.

“When my capture,” he says in the same work, no. 16, “my expulsion, despoiling, abduction, imprisonment, the plundering of the church, the destruction of the episcopal residence, the destruction of the emperor’s alms, the undoing of that act”—namely, the act by which Ratherius had been restored by the emperor himself—“the incursion into the city, contempt for imperial reverence, and many other things connected with these were still in the case, as they still are; leaving improvement aside, the case was conducted solely on the murderous oath-breaking” [perhaps: “the case was completed”].

“Improvement” is understood as examination and correction. Hence, in the *Itinerarium*, no. 4, he similarly asks whether all the things committed against him had been left unexamined, as though nothing could be found in them that could even lightly be condemned by the laws.

The oath-breaking, which alone was dealt with, refers to the loyalty that Ratherius, Milo, and all the Veronese had sworn to Otto when he entered Verona. Ratherius’s enemies certainly violated it when, stirring up persecution against him, they made an incursion into the city [Col. 0110D] [CXXXIII] and, inflicting so many other evils upon him and the Church, attempted to destroy the imperial edict by which Otto, restoring Ratherius, had ordered that no harm be done to him. See what we wrote in § 13, no. 86.

Nothing, however, was brought to judgment concerning the many and serious crimes perpetrated against Ratherius. Only the oath-breaking was punished.

**106.** The settlement established in this judgment for such oath-breaking, or the penalty imposed upon the rebels for it, is explained in letter 12 to Ambrosius:

“They were brought to settlement and compelled to pay one hundred pounds of silver.”

But since they were unable to pay so large a sum, he adds:

“When they came to me, they borrowed almost thirty pounds from the Church’s treasury, under this condition nevertheless: that if they had not repaid this sum by the appointed time, they would make double restitution as a penalty. Three years have now passed, and they pay back absolutely nothing” [Col. 0111A].

From these final words the date of the aforementioned judgment and of Ratherius’s capture can plainly be deduced. For letter 12 to Ambrosius was written on the Kalends of July in the year 968. The three-year period, therefore, which elapsed from the fine decreed in that judgment and from the lending of the thirty pounds, begins approximately in the middle of the year 965; consequently, the judgment and settlement fall in that period.

To allow a suitable amount of time for the changes of fortune that befell Ratherius from the day of his capture until this judgment, it appears that he was captured around the feast of Saint Agnes in that same year [Col. 0111B]. The same year is confirmed by a sermon delivered on the Octave of Easter in 968. In it he says that he had spent almost forty pounds during “these three years” on restoring the episcopal residence, which had been destroyed in the rebellion mentioned above. If one counts back three years from the Octave of Easter in 968, from the time when Ratherius began devoting himself to restoring the episcopal residence, one arrives at the year 965.

**107.** After that judgment, in which nothing concerning the wrongs inflicted upon the bishop was examined or punished, the rebels did not enter upon plans for peace. Indeed, when no hope of reconciliation appeared, Ratherius seemed to have only one option remaining: to yield the episcopate to Milo “after receiving the price of souls” (*Qualitatis conjectura*, no. 16) [Col. 0111C].

The originator of this plan was Milo himself, who found bishops willing to support it. One of these, and the principal one, was Ubertus, bishop of Parma [CXXXIV], whom we have mentioned elsewhere (*Qualitatis conjectura*, no. 16).

Even among Ratherius’s closest friends there were some who approved the same counsel. One of them, won over by money or gifts, approached the duchess Judith, who was residing in Verona and favoring Ratherius, and assured her that the emperor likewise wished this; perhaps he even added that the emperor had ordered Ratherius to surrender the episcopate to Milo.

This effort became especially heated toward the end of the year 965. Accordingly, as the Christmas feast approached, Ratherius sent a letter to Milo in which he called him “Vicentine” by origin, not by episcopate (*Epistle* 8). For Milo had been ordained bishop of Verona against Ratherius [Col. 0111D], and Ratherius therefore calls him “the most vehement assailant.”

He proposes two reasons why Milo had inflicted so many evils upon him: one older, because Ratherius had been promoted to the Veronese see before Milo was born; the other more recent, because he would yield the episcopate to Milo neither through death nor through flight. He indicates Milo’s efforts to compel him to flee.

Emphasizing his own steadfastness in enduring every hardship, so that he might not consent to surrender the episcopate, he signifies that he would yield only to the command of the emperor and the dukes, provided that it were certain and explicit:

“If you never intend to recover your senses,” he says, “but to contrive other things, try what you have begun. I suggest the way: obtain, if you can, the command of the emperor and our dukes that I depart—and not through some indirect indication,” as had been done in the presence of the illustrious duchess, “but simply and openly, so that it may be understood; for everything else you contrive is in vain” [Col. 0112A].

He mentions the “pontiffs,” that is, bishops, as Milo’s “supporters.”

In a fragment of another letter to the same man (*Epistle* 9), written at the same time and for the same reason, two classes of men are distinguished: some consented to Milo, while others offered Ratherius no assistance at all.

On this occasion he reproduced the *Deliberative Conclusion*, written at Liège in the year 955, when he was being pressured by several persons to surrender the episcopate of Liège to Bishop Balderic. He added only a few words at the end, in which he declares that the sixteen arguments set out earlier in that little work, which he had brought forward in the Liège case, apply equally to the Veronese case [Col. 0112B]. He now reproduces them in order “to answer the wicked instigators.”

He declares that he will never yield unless he is expelled either by canonical judgment or by imperial power.

108. That such great difficulties existed, by which Rather was being driven to surrender his see to Milo—partly by the money offered, partly by the importunate persuasions of certain bishops, and partly by threats—is clear from the fact that Milo himself at this time confidently expected to win the bishopric. This becomes evident from what happened to Siker, which occurred four years after Rather’s third restoration. These four years, counted from the end of 961, when Rather was restored for the third time by Otto, likewise end at the close of 965, when he was being pressed most urgently to surrender the bishopric.

That event, obscurely set forth in *Qualitatis conjectura* no. 9 in a passage requiring considerable thought for its explanation, seems to be understood as follows. Before he was expelled for the second time, Rather had given Siker a castle belonging by right to the church of Verona, from which, besides the service of his vassals, he could receive six pounds of Venetian denarii each year. When, in 961, Otto entered Verona and restored the same bishop, Siker obtained from Otto a privilege by which the same castle was confirmed to him. He had offended the bishop three times; and perhaps, fearing that the restored bishop might take the castle away from him, he secured such a document—one which the bishop would not dare, or perhaps would not wish, to resist.

But when Siker subsequently made himself a very close friend of Rather, the latter not only left him in peaceful possession of the castle for four years after his restoration, but also granted him land belonging to the church of Verona, situated across Lake Garda and perhaps near the aforementioned castle. When four years had elapsed, toward the end of 965, “on the day when Milo had thought that he would win the bishopric over him” (Rather), Siker sent Rather a written memorandum listing whatever he himself had bestowed upon Rather in the form of a gift. At the same time he declared that he had given these things “not for any settlement, but for the acquisition of land.” It therefore followed that the land was his as though he had bought it and did not belong by right to the church.

Perhaps by this means he wished to secure himself regarding that land, just as he had secured himself regarding the castle by an imperial diploma, lest, if Milo should win the bishopric—as he expected—Milo should reclaim the land and restore it to the church’s jurisdiction. Since Rather had accepted whatever Siker had given as gifts bestowed out of friendship, once this audacious effort by Siker had been exposed, he regretted having given him the land. Yet, respecting the emperor’s diploma, and raising no question about the castle, he replied: “It should be enough for him that he himself had given the castle.” But when Siker affirmed that he wished to retain both the land by his own right and the castle, which he claimed had come to him through the emperor’s “gift,” the indignant bishop took the land away from him.

## § XVII.—Rather’s acts in the year 966

He writes *Qualitatis conjectura*. In the abbey of Magonzano, now Maguzano, after removing its ill-behaved abbot, he establishes clerics. During Lent he holds a synod and issues a *Synodica*. His work *On Illicit Marriage*. He plans a journey to Rome, and for what purpose. He publishes an *Itinerary*.

109. When Rather’s enemies understood that he was unwilling to surrender the bishopric to Milo unless compelled by an imperial order, they began to attack his character and life with numerous censures—or rather, with quibbles. By reporting these to the emperor, they hoped to elicit the imperial order they desired. To frustrate this maneuver, the bishop decided to set forth publicly, in the name and words of those same adversaries, the very quibbles they had used, in a work entitled *A Certain Person’s Conjecture Regarding Character*.

Explaining the malignity of his censors in the *Apologeticus*, no. 4, he says: “Some people—I do not know whether you think this, or whether they have rather invented it themselves—hurl accusations at me. Some do not cease to darken whatever good deeds I seem to perform with sinister interpretations.” Since he himself was not afraid to criticize himself, and was also accustomed to enlarge and exaggerate his lesser offenses, as we observed in the little book *Confession*, it is not surprising that in *Qualitatis conjectura*, following the character of such accusers and providing them with material for their censures, he mixed “truths with falsehoods, and matters that may be believed with certainties,” expressed in their own name, as he indicates in the first section.

This rare—or rather unique—method of writing and accusing himself was, as he himself says, “like something which, I believe, no one before me has ever done about himself.” He was especially negligent in defending himself, even allowing everyone to think still worse of him, adding: “Let whoever wishes read, and, if he can, bring forward something worse about me.” It will therefore be difficult to distinguish which of the censures directed against Rather in this work are “true,” which “false,” which “certain,” and which merely matters of opinion.

Nevertheless, from the zeal with which he burned and from his stricter manner of life, it is highly credible that at least the more serious accusations brought against him were either wholly false or greatly exaggerated. See the *Admonition* to the excerpt from the confessional dialogue, no. 3. In any event, to those who judge correctly and do not distort even his good and praiseworthy qualities into evil through perverse interpretation, this entire censure by the quibblers will appear as a notable encomium of the author, sufficiently exposing the malignity of his accusers.

For it portrays the bishop as a man alien to pride, luxury, and gifts; a despiser of wealth; humble, poor, and penitent; one who wore unkempt and very inexpensive clothing and used other modest furnishings; who occupied himself with servile tasks and slept on a bench, or more willingly on the ground; who prepared a frugal table and admitted the poor to it; who often abstained from meat and almost entirely from wine, on which account he was called a teetotaler; who fasted and performed penance for others; who did not seek glory—indeed, detested it—and did not care if anyone spoke against him; who sometimes even rewarded those who spoke against and reviled him.

[Note: How bravely and calmly our bishop endured not only detractors but even persecutors, regarding with lofty mind as a great good of his own whatever more bitter evils proceeded from them, you will see from what was said above at no. 23. Hence too it may be understood in what sense Everaclus, bishop of Liège, writing to Rather in Letter 14, col. 570 b, extolled his patience in adversity in these words: “If patience is mentioned—if it is permissible to say so without impairing the faith, lest I offend God—you are patience itself.”]

He was carried away by zeal for discipline into sharper criticism of everyone, nor did he spare himself: he openly confessed his own offenses and sometimes, as we have indicated, enlarged and exaggerated them as well. He did not wish to have a servant or chaplain; he did not visit the king or the powerful, nor ask anything from them. He was eager to build or rebuild sacred basilicas; he wished to convey none of the church’s property to his relatives; he was wholly devoted to books; he hated crowds and loved solitude; he recoiled from games, hunting, and similar pleasures.

These and many other qualities of the same kind, although highly commendable, are nevertheless presented by the censor in the celebrated work as grounds and apparent instances of reproach. An episode is inserted against the Jews, who are known to have been very powerful at Verona, and also against those who offered friendship and favor to the Jews.

The abuses are noted by which many church properties had been unjustly alienated under one name or another. For certain church lands, occupied by powerful men or initially granted by bishops for a time under the title of usufruct, were later bestowed and confirmed by a princely diploma, so that, as though brought under royal jurisdiction, they ceased to belong to the church. Compare what we reported about Siker toward the end of the preceding paragraph.

Three kinds of contracts by which church property was alienated are criticized, namely “exchanges, *libelli*, and precarious grants”; and all these are said to have occurred partly through the necessity of bishops and partly through fraudulent surreptitious appropriation.

Rather concludes with a eulogy of the emperor Otto. In order to make him well disposed toward himself, he briefly explains his own difficulties and danger. But so that the emperor may not lend an easy ear and credence to his enemies when they press false accusations upon him, he points out their habit of shifting onto the bishop the blame for certain wrongs of which they themselves are guilty.

He gives the recent example of a certain cleric promoted to the diaconate by an usurper. While this man was holding and plundering land belonging to the bishop by secular authority, he “fled to the feet of the Lord Emperor, with no one pursuing him, and lied that” Rather “had taken away his benefice.” The reason for assigning this little work to the beginning of 966 will become clear from the first note appended to it.

110. At this same time, when Rather was being fiercely attacked by “the quibbles of malicious men,” he published a little work on the abbey of Magonzano, now Maguzano, in which he explains the reason for the change introduced there.

This little abbey, situated on the boundary of the diocese of Verona, near that of Brescia, together with its estate, was so subject to the disposition of the bishops that, either when its abbot died or when he was ill-behaved and incorrigible, another man from the diocese of Verona was to be substituted by the bishop, so that he might ensure that those serving there observed the monastic life. But this had not turned out well in accordance with the founder’s intention.

The Hungarians, who in this century invaded Italy and devastated it with fires and plundering, had burned the monastery of this abbey. The affairs of the abbey and the corruption of the times had consequently reached such a state that only one abbot remained there, and he was of depraved morals, publicly supporting a wife and children with general scandal.

Rather tried to bring him back to reform, but in vain. For the man escaped by flight three times and attempted, through intermediaries and by offering money to the bishop, to settle the matter with him. Rather recoiled from such a great crime and for some time hesitated about what he should do.

“For if I,” he says, “were to retain for myself, as though I would administer it better, or give to one of my own people, the little possession granted to the Mother of God, I truly feared that one of my successors, acting similarly after my example, might destroy the almsgiving represented by those goods.”

Since at that time it was exceedingly rare and difficult to find monks who exactly observed the proposed rule, he installed in the same abbey three priests together with a deacon, a subdeacon, and several clerics, who were to devote themselves to the sacred offices. He assigned each his portion and specified their duties. He placed over them another priest, more senior than all the rest, to preside over discipline and the distribution of revenues. Several other matters are missing, for the work has no ending.

111. Since the sacred canons require bishops to hold a synod twice a year, Rather would not have failed to carry this out if he had believed that he could accomplish anything useful in synods. But, he says in the *Itinerary* to his clerics:

“You know, you know that I have always postponed doing this for the reason that I said I did not know at all what I ought to synodize about. For in synods, if anything has been done contrary to the canons, it is usually corrected. But if I had attempted to do this, after searching through everything written in the canons, I would have seen that you cared nothing at all about any of it.”

He adds several examples that reveal the depravity and perversity of the age. To make some attempt at testing the matter, in this year 966, during Lent, he convened a diocesan synod.

He reports the outcome of this synod in the aforementioned work, no. 6. Before the synod he had ordered that two days beforehand the archpriest and archdeacon, together with the ordinary clergy—that is, the canons—of the cathedral, should examine those who were required to attend the synod, both from the urban titles and from the rural parish churches, and should diligently investigate whatever needed correction, so that on the third day, when the bishop was to preside over the synod, they could report what required amendment.

Because of the multitude of people assembling for the synod, all the canons—not merely the archpriest or the archdeacon alone—had undertaken the duty of inquiry, so that the examination might be completed within the two days. When the synod had been convened on the third day, the bishop, seated, asked what had been done. One man, whose responsibility it especially was, replied that they had inquired about the psalms and other matters of that kind, “and, thanks be to God, had found nothing very bad.”

To this the bishop, who was aware of many evils, added ironically: “What would I have had left to do with so many saints, then, except give thanks to God?” Shortly afterward he continued:

“If the only inquiry in this council is to concern the psalms and nothing else, bring me first for examination; for I can be convicted of not knowing them as I ought. How, then, could a synod be held, when nothing more requiring correction was found? Accordingly, when I questioned them about the faith, I discovered that many did not even know the creed believed to have been that of the apostles. For this reason I was compelled to write a *Synodica* for all the priests.”

He indicates that this synod was held “in the middle of Lent” and that a *Synodica* was issued at it. In the *Admonition* to the *Synodica* itself, we have shown that this means the middle of Lent in the year 966.

112. This *Synodica* is a particularly important document of the tenth century, from which we learn especially about the discipline of that period. It is addressed to all priests and the other orders established throughout the diocese. He had summoned them to examination at the synod three times; and, since on account of the abundance of matters and their ignorance of the more important points he had been able to accomplish almost nothing by words, he thought it necessary to provide for the matter by publishing it in writing in this synodal letter.

To remedy their ignorance concerning the creed, he ordered three creeds to be written down and committed to memory: the creed, or “collation,” of the apostles, “as it is found in corrected psalters”; the creed sung at Mass; and the one circulated under the name of St. Athanasius. He warned that no one should be promoted to the priesthood or remain in the priesthood unless he knew these creeds by heart, when he would next be summoned for examination (*Itinerary*, no. 7).

He summoned them again several months later, while in this same year he was planning his journey to Rome. Consequently, those found disobedient were struck with such fear of the penalties that they not only promised thereafter to carry out everything he had ordered, but also, apparently in the form of a fine, promised assistance toward undertaking that journey.

The entire *Synodica* is filled with highly useful instructions. It deals at length with the sanctification of Sundays and feast days, as well as with the matters clerics ought to know and the practices in which they ought to be trained. While insisting on the necessity of study, he declares that candidates for ordination will in no way be promoted to orders “unless,” he says, “they have spent some time either in our city”—that is, in his cathedral school—“or in some monastery, or with any learned man, and have acquired some education in letters, so that they may appear suited to ecclesiastical dignity.”

A distinctive provision is the abstinence from meat prescribed for the four weeks before Christmas, except on feast days. Likewise, continence is prescribed for married people both during Advent and for the twenty days after Christmas, during the octaves of Easter and Pentecost, on the days of the litanies, on the vigils of all feasts, and also on Fridays, but especially on every Sunday.

The prescribed time for breaking the fast during Lent reveals a milder ecclesiastical discipline. For whereas according to the ancient institution the same fast had to be prolonged until evening, in the *Synodica* its termination is permitted after the ninth hour. On this matter, see more in the notes to the same *Synodica*, note 48.

He requires that no feasts of the saints—except the feasts of the Blessed Mary, the apostles, and the patron of the church—be celebrated during Lent or on the fasting days of the four seasons. He gives this reason: on those days “the fast should rather be maintained than a feast celebrated.” Since, according to the discipline of the Church, the fast was not observed on feast days, as is clear from the Sundays of Lent themselves, he thought that feasts falling on fast days should be transferred.

Finally, it must not be overlooked that inserted in this *Synodica*, from no. 6 through no. 12, is a certain solemn ecclesiastical formula, to be read or recited in the synod. In better manuscripts it is entitled *Admonition*, or *Synodal Sermon*; some mistakenly attribute it, under the title *Sermon*, to Leo IV. See more on this matter in the *Admonition* to the *Synodica* itself, no. 2.

113. Since in this *Synodica*, as we have indicated, the bishop especially urges the sanctification of Sunday, we think that an event relating to this same sanctification should be recalled, from which it will become clearer how important this observance was to him.

“When I prohibited under threat of excommunication,” he says in Letter 12 to Ambrose, “that they should engage in servile work on Sunday, and when I was entirely unable to enforce this, I ordered the gates”—understand, the gates of the city—“to be closed against approaching wagons.”

Whether this occurred at the time of the *Synodica* and in the same year, 966, or at some earlier or later time, is uncertain. Certainly, however, this action was later seized upon by malicious people when they attacked the bishop with many accusations in open rebellion. Hence he adds: “They judge that this deed ought to be expiated either by my death or by my expulsion.”

114. After Lent in the year 966, Rather wrote a little work *On Illicit Marriage* (see note 1). The occasion was provided by John, a cleric of the church of Verona, who during the preceding Lent had given a wife to his son, himself also a cleric.

Although the bishop had always detested clerical marriages, he attacks this one especially because it had been contracted under a double illegality: during Lent and consummated on a Sunday night. Pedrevert had done something similar earlier, but he had taken the precaution of having the marriage contracted secretly by his son. John, however, “did this so openly that no one in this city could remain unaware of it.”

The bishop considered such a great scandal intolerable: “For if it is left unreproved, it will certainly appear to have been lawfully done; for no one will fail to think that he may take as an example what he has discovered no one censured.”

He thinks that the parents’ intention in arranging these marriages for their sons had been that, by comparison with the evil, it would be better for them to be joined to one wife than to wander more destructively among several women. But, apart from the forbidden time for marriage, he places before their eyes as the principal evil this: in such clerical marriages, which he regards as equivalent to adultery because they are forbidden by the sacred canons, when clerical fathers join clerical sons in marriage and the sons behave similarly with their own sons, the adultery of the parents passes to the children and thus becomes perpetual.

“Therefore,” he says, “brothers, you must be admonished and entreated: since, alas, you are in no way able to refrain from women, at least leave the sons born from you as laymen, and join your daughters to laymen, so that your adultery may at least end with your end and not last until the end of the world.”

He similarly warns laymen not to join their daughters to clerics. Accordingly, he addresses, in no. 5, a certain noble woman, honored with the title “lady,” who had given the daughter of her clerical brother in marriage to John’s clerical son, in these words:

“O that you, lady, to whom so good a brother left such great goods, had thought of this beforehand and had given his daughter, blessed by those goods, to some good layman, and had put an end to his sin”—namely, the sin he called adultery.

He imposed forty days of penance upon those who had violated the forbidden time by the marriages mentioned above. And, in a measure that contributes greatly to edification, he prescribed the same penance for himself, since, he says, “up to this point, because I did not resist, I was certainly consenting.”

This penance consisted chiefly in fasting, “namely, that if the other faithful are refreshed at the third hour, we should be so at the sixth; if they at the sixth, we at the ninth; and if they at the ninth, we should fast until evening.”

115. In the year 966 the emperor Otto I returned to Italy to suppress the rebellion that had been raised against John XIII, the supreme pontiff. Perhaps for this reason he ordered the bishops to send their soldiers to war as vassals of the empire. Thus he also ordered Rather to send his soldiers.

Two testimonies bearing on this matter are found in two works by our author written in the same year, 966. He indicates the imperial order concerning the dispatch of soldiers in the sermon on Mary and Martha, composed after the middle of August of that year, no. 4: “Even when I compel my own soldiers because of the emperor’s command.”

He indicates that the order itself to undertake the Roman expedition had already been announced to him in the *Itinerary*, which he wrote around the feast of St. Andrew, when in no. 1 he writes that he would depart for Rome “not by imperial command—for it was not commanded that I go—but because I was ordered by him [Otto I] only to send my soldiers, since this had been commanded me.”

Since he is discussing a journey to Rome which he affirms he would undertake neither by imperial command nor for the purpose of war, there can be no doubt that he is alluding, not obscurely, to a military expedition ordered by the emperor and directed toward the Roman region against the enemies of the Roman pontiff. The emperor ordered only the soldiers or vassals of the church of Verona to be sent; he did not wish Rather himself to go to war, for he rejected military service, which canonical law forbade to clerics and even more strictly to bishops.

116. The reason Rather wrote the aforementioned work, called the *Itinerary* (see note 1), toward the end of this year must be explained. He had no doubt that the emperor would be in Rome together with many bishops from both Italy and Germany.

“For I know,” he says in no. 3, “that the wisest men, both from this kingdom”—that is, the Italian kingdom—“and from those who came with our lord, the ever-August”—clearly from Germany—“will be present there,” namely at Rome.

Since a plenary council could be summoned from among these men, he hoped that one would in fact be convened through the efforts of the pontiff and the emperor: “whom,” he says, “I believe will summon a universal synod, if God grants the holy Church one that is, as it should be, useful.”

It was therefore in the hope of this council that he testified he would travel to Rome, so that, after the causes of the disagreement between himself and his clerics had been presented there, the supreme pontiff and so many bishops might determine what ought to be done by him and by his clerics.

In no. 2 he inserts an outstanding testimony concerning the authority and learning of the Roman see:

“For what concerning ecclesiastical doctrines is known anywhere that is unknown at Rome? There the supreme teachers of the whole world are found; there the foremost leaders of the universal Church have shone forth. There are the decretal letters of the pontiffs, the assembly of all, the examination of the canons, the approval of what is to be received, and the rejection of what is to be despised. Finally, nowhere is valid what there has been declared invalid; nowhere is invalid what there has been judged valid. Where, then, is my ignorance better cared for than where the fountain of wisdom is seen to be?”

He also praises John, the supreme pontiff, whom some mistakenly believed to have been John XII, although in reality he was John XIII. He praises the emperor Otto himself in several respects, but especially because he had arranged for this same John XIII to be promoted to the supreme pontificate.

As was his custom, he explains and censures the vices of the clerics by which the canons were attacked; he renews his account of the actions of Milo the usurper and of the rebels against him; and he recalls the diocesan synod that had been uselessly convened during Lent.

He hoped for a remedy for so many and such great evils from the authority of the Roman council, aided also by the favor of imperial power. This work is of the same character as the one *On Contempt for the Canons*. Whether Rather actually undertook the journey to Rome and presented his case at the Roman synod held at the beginning of the following year is unknown, owing to the lack of documents.

Some indeed believe that he composed this work in order by this device to bring the clerics to their senses. It is certain, however, that he took part in the synod at Ravenna, which was, as it were, an appendix to the Roman council, as will become clear from what follows in the next paragraph.

## § XVIII.—Events of the year 967

On the Roman and Ravennate councils. Decree against clerical cohabitation with women. Rather returns to Verona from the council at Ravenna and convenes a diocesan synod. Proceedings of this synod. He provides for poorer clerics in a *Judicatum*, subscribed by the patriarch of Aquileia and the neighboring bishops assembled in synod. An imperial privilege granted to Rather. Tumult among the clerics of Verona and Rather’s work *On Rebellious Clerics*. His letter to Martin, bishop of Ferrara.

117. The emperor Otto, who in the preceding year had held an assembly in Germany after the middle of August, soon descended into Italy. For when Rather wrote the *Itinerary* in the same year, around the feast of St. Andrew, Otto had already “come” there with many German bishops, intending to proceed to Rome, as is stated in the same work, no. 3.

He was indeed at Rome toward the end of December, where he celebrated the Christmas festivities. Several Italian bishops also went there with the same Augustus. That the council which Rather hoped would be assembled there from German and Italian bishops was in fact held at the beginning of 967 is established by an imperial privilege of that same emperor, issued at Rome in favor of the monastery of Subiaco, which mentions the Roman synod.

This privilege was first published by Muratori in volume 5 of *Antichità Italiane*, dissertation 65; it was later reprinted by the canon Garampi in his work *On the Silver Coin of Benedict III*, p. 169. From it we append these words:

“Otto, by the favor of divine clemency, emperor Augustus. At the petition of Gregory, a venerable man, formerly *secundicerius* of the apostolic see and religious abbot of the monastery of the most blessed Benedict and his sister Saint Scholastica, which is called Subiaco, who came into the bosom of the basilica of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, where, together with Lord Pope John XIII, we were attending the holy synod for the benefit of that same Church and of venerable places, while very many bishops from the Roman territory, Italy, and the transalpine kingdom were seated around us with the archbishop of Ravenna,” and so forth.

The chronological notes are: “Given on the third day before the Ides of January, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 967, in the fifth year of the reign of Lord Otto, most pious Caesar, indiction 10.”

You see that the Roman synod, attended by the Roman pontiff John XIII and the emperor Otto himself, together with very many Italian and German bishops, was held before January 11 of the year 967. What was established at the Roman synod is unknown. We know only that after the Roman synod the emperor went to Ravenna and there celebrated Holy Easter together with John XIII, as the Continuator of Regino reports.

118. A well-attended synod was also convened at Ravenna, which may be regarded as an appendix to the Roman synod. Among the fathers of this synod was Rather as well, as is established by the sole surviving judgment of that council against Herold, archbishop of Salzburg, on which our bishop is recorded as a subscriber (vol. XI of the Venetian edition of the Councils).

Rather states that this synod was held “in the middle of April” (Letter 12, no. 1). The aforementioned judgment against Herold agrees with this, being dated “the seventh day before the Kalends of May.” The chronicler Saxo indicates the place under the year 969, namely “at Ravenna, in the suburb, in the church of the blessed confessor and bishop Severus.”

The Continuator of Regino testifies that many matters were established at the same synod “for the benefit of the holy Church.” Its principal purpose was the restoration of ecclesiastical discipline. This is inferred from the decree against clerical cohabitation with women and clerical marriages, which Rather mentions.

For after returning to Verona from the council at Ravenna, he immediately convened a diocesan synod in order to present the decrees of that same council and ensure their execution.

“After the universal synod had been celebrated at Ravenna in the middle of April,” he says in Letter 12 to Ambrose, no. 1, “I returned and summoned priests and deacons from all the parish churches of our diocese, in order to report, by command of the most serene emperor, what had been established there.”

Since this diocesan synod was assembled immediately after the Ravennate synod held “in the middle of April” of the year 967, it seems that it should be assigned to June or July, so that sufficient time might be allowed for the bishop’s return and for the people summoned to the synod.

Among the matters Rather enacted at the synod, he mentions one command concerning the dismissal of women. This, therefore, was among the principal enactments of the Ravennate council. In order to eradicate this vice, which was spreading so widely and publicly among the clerics, both ecclesiastical and imperial authority acted together. Consequently, Rather now calls the celebrated decree of the Ravennate council concerning clerical cohabitation with women, or the dismissal of wives, the command of the emperor and now that of the supreme pontiff.

He calls it “the command of the most serene emperor” in the aforementioned Letter 12 to Ambrose, “the Augustal will” in *Discordia* no. 6, and “the legation”—that is, the command—“of the pope” in Letter 11 to Nanno, no. 2.

119. Although the bishop had summoned everyone to the synod, not everyone assembled. For, he says in Letter 12, no. 1:

“Because of the rebellious men’s habitual cunning toward me, certain elders of our mother Church”—that is, the canons—“who lay snares for my life, deigned not to come.”

When he had repeatedly tried to summon “those who did not come,” “a messenger named Giselpert appeared and, on behalf of his master, forbade them under ban to come in any way to our council.”

In Letter 11 to Nanno, no. 2, he attributes this prohibition to Nanno himself, count of Verona, who had been substituted for Buccho:

“You so completely forbid the priests to come to the synod, hear the pope’s command concerning the dismissal of wives, and obey the bishops in every respect, that you receive them into your hands as soldiers and do not fail to offer them protection in all the abominations they commit against God; and, as though it had been said to you, ‘Whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven,’ you make them disregard our prohibition as nothing.”

Nanno must therefore be understood by the name “master,” and Giselpert was his “messenger.”

But what of those who did assemble at the synod? “Some of them,” he says in the passage cited to Ambrose, “deliberated with the greatest arrogance that they would neither abandon their cohabitation with women nor cease from office.”

From this it may be inferred that the decree of the Ravennate council against incontinent clerics had two parts: they were either to dismiss the women, or, if they refused to dismiss them, to cease from office as though deposed.

There were some who refused to obey this decree. Rather ordered that they be arrested and committed to custody until satisfaction had been made. By “satisfaction” he means a monetary penalty or fine, as the words he immediately adds indicate:

“I devoted the amount of the satisfaction to restoring—or, more accurately, adorning—the church of the blessed Mother of God”—that is, the cathedral—“in the hope that, since they were utterly ineffective in performing penance, being exceedingly drunken men, the intercession of the Mother might at least obtain for them from the Lord the forgiveness which they would otherwise make no effort to secure through amendment.”

It is uncertain whether this arrest and fine of the disobedient occurred at the diocesan synod, or after they had demonstrated by their actions that they were unwilling either to abandon their cohabitation with women or to cease from office.

It is likewise uncertain whether three other events which he immediately adds should be assigned to the time of the synod:

“Certain men accused of various crimes in the city, when they disdained to come to make satisfaction, I caused to be arrested, as is customary, by men sent from my side”—supply, *with beadles*—“together with the church doorkeepers, and I spent the satisfaction that had been made on the same work.

“A certain priest called me ‘mouth of the vulva’; I likewise had him arrested. When he escaped by flight, I took from him whatever I could, but did not contribute it to the church, because I was scarcely bold enough to offer God vengeance for my insult, since I ought rather to have been its pardoner than its avenger.

“A certain deacon, whom in the previous year I had made a canon, contrary even to expectation, and who held, together with one of my own party, one of the better parish churches with its estate, called me a felon, a deceiver [the printed word *bausiatorem* is uncertain], and a perjurer. I took it away from him and, because it was necessary, retained it for myself.”

120. While Ratherius was pressing in the diocesan synod the command that clerical relationships with women should be abandoned, “nearly all [especially the lower clergy of the cathedral church] offered the excuse that this could in no way be done because of poverty; yet it could have been done somehow if they had received the stipend owed to them from the church’s resources (Discordia, no. 6).” We explained this passage more fully above, § 15, no. 97. Since he understood that a more equitable distribution of ecclesiastical revenues had to be introduced in order to remedy the poverty of the lower clergy, he again addressed the matter with the canons after the diocesan synod—something he had previously attempted in vain. The principal complaints concerned the clergy of the cathedral church.

“For this reason,” he says, “I wished to ascertain everything that had either been granted by my predecessors or bestowed upon them by God-fearing men.” From the very instruments of donation he believed it could be demonstrated that the goods and revenues of the cathedral church had generally been granted not so that the senior clergy, or canons, might receive almost everything and grow rich while the others, receiving nothing or little, suffered poverty [CXLIX], but so that the offerings might be distributed according to the norm of Acts 4:35, to each according to his need.

The canons resisted this more equitable distribution of revenues, which the bishop intended to establish on the basis of the donation instruments themselves, so vehemently “that they declared they would rather die than see it carried out.” The bishop then showed them the sacred canons; they, on the other hand, brought forward only the custom of their predecessors (ibid., no. 7).

The bishop was dealing with this matter while hoping that a synod of the bishops of the province would be convened at Verona, of which we shall speak shortly. He intended to bring the question before that synod. Meanwhile he sent several leading citizens to the canons, instructing them to adjure the canons by the fidelity which they had more than once sworn to him, and to ask them not to conceal any authentic account or documentary evidence by which their custom might be supported. Otherwise, when both parties came to the synod, the bishop might be put to shame if, while demanding a different distribution of revenues, he were proved to be demanding something unjust.

This too accomplished nothing. “For,” he says, “as though they were showing that I could never have placed any confidence in their oaths, they said—shamefully!—that they knew well enough that they had sworn many things to many people which they could in no way fulfill (among others, they had sworn no less to Ratherius than to Milo the usurper), adding that it was foolish for me to try to teach them. I again instructed some of them that they would be at fault in either case, whether they knowingly allowed me to contend against them or themselves to contend against me. The one whose interest was greatest replied that he would be acting most foolishly if he presumed either to teach me, who had been proclaimed throughout the whole world, or to teach his own masters.”

Let us continue the rest of this dispute in his own words (ibid., b):

“When this did nothing to help, I tried another way to compel them to peace—not indeed the peace of the world, but that of Christ. Since some of them held benefices from my property, I threatened them that, if they prevented me from doing what belonged to me—namely, introducing a more equitable distribution—I would take back what I had granted them. They replied that they cared so little about this that, even if I took away whatever I had given to any of them, they would not therefore be less faithful to me; only, they said, I must not disturb them at all with regard to those things which had been assigned to the canons by custom.”

And after several further remarks, in no. 8 [CL]:

“What I had brought forward as a threat, I did not delay to turn into action. Using the command that says, ‘Give to the good, and do not receive the sinner’ (Ecclus. 12:5), I took these things away from them and gave, or rather restored, them to two good recipients: the blessed Mother of God and Saint Stephen the protomartyr. In addition, I drew up a document concerning certain properties, which they call a *Judicatum*, that is, a decree, for the poorer clergy of that same church—those for whose sake alone I had endured such labor: the chaplain-priests, seven subdeacons of the *secretarium*, seven cantor-subdeacons, seven acolytes of the *secretarium*, five cantor-acolytes, and six doorkeepers. I did this not so that they would be more faithful to me, but so that they might become more ready in the service of the Lord and, once the excuse of poverty had been removed, might be more diligent in serving the Lord by day and by night” [Col. 0124B].

121. This confrontation of Ratherius with the canons, undertaken to relieve the poverty of the poorer clergy, took place after the diocesan synod held in June or July of the year 967 and before the provincial council convened at Verona, which we shall see took place in the same year, at the beginning of November. It therefore occurred approximately in August or September.

In this confrontation, in order to persuade the same canons to accept a more equitable division of revenues, he employed reason, not force. Against their will he neither touched nor removed anything from the revenues which they had received by custom. He merely threatened to withdraw certain benefices which he himself had granted to some of the canons, so that he might provide in some measure for the lower clergy.

Yet he did not carry this out unconditionally. He did so only after they had given their consent, provided that he spared the goods which by custom belonged to the canons. Nor did he carry it out in the confrontation itself, immediately after they had given their consent. Rather, after the confrontation, he took away the goods which he had granted them and converted them to other pious uses, providing for the poorer clergy by means of the *Judicatum*.

He had enriched ten canons with military benefices drawn from goods which were subject to the bishop’s jurisdiction and had been assigned for the purpose of military benefices. As he states in the *Itinerarium*, no. 4:

“For, despite my little poverty, I am not so inhuman toward you as to have ten of you maintained on a military benefice—and that without payment.”

Compare *Discordia*, note 25.

He therefore stripped these ten canons of the benefices he had granted them and converted such benefices to three kinds of use [Col. 0124D]. Some he gave to the cathedral church, which bears the title of the holy Mother of God; others to the church of Saint Stephen the protomartyr, or “rather [CLI] restored” them. The word “restored,” which Ratherius uses, seems to indicate that, before they were assigned to the canons as military benefices, these benefices had been goods belonging to those same churches.

At that time all the goods of the churches, except for the portion assigned to their clergy, were subject to the bishop’s jurisdiction and disposition; they could therefore be granted by him to whomever he considered appropriate. Thus the goods which Ratherius had granted to certain canons he now took away and restored to the churches, apparently for their repair or adornment, matters that belonged to the bishop’s care [Col. 0125A]. Finally, he assigned a third—and perhaps more important—portion to the support of the poorer clergy, by means of that foundation document which he called the *Judicatum*.

122. In this little work he laments an intolerable abuse and scandal: the lower clergy, who bore nearly the greater part of the labor in the church and were oppressed by more severe poverty, not only “murmured without ceasing,” but also “in their poverty hastened to approach the sacred orders unlawfully,” so that by this means some assistance might come to them. They approached those orders even though “their age plainly did not admit them, their knowledge did not recommend them, and the uprightness of their conduct did not distinguish them.”

He decrees that the revenues of this foundation should be divided equally, “not by fields and vineyards, however, but by bushels and sextaries, so that no opportunity for quarrels or envy might be given” [Col. 0125B]. He plainly did not want particular fields and vineyards divided among the clergy. By that method nearly everything had come to the senior and more powerful clergy, while the other, lower and weaker clergy were left in poverty. Distribution by bushels and measures, however, more easily preserves equality and guards against the fraud of the powerful.

For a similar reason he ordered that the revenues of the abbey of Maguzzano be divided among the clergy established there not by fields and vineyards but by measures.

He wished this benefice to be common to all the lower clergy of the cathedral church who were then living, including the chaplain-priests. When these men died, he ordered that everything should be divided equally among only the three lower orders: the subdeacons, acolytes, and doorkeepers—namely, among seven subdeacons of the *secretarium* and seven other cantor-subdeacons; seven acolytes of the *secretarium* and five other cantor-acolytes; and six doorkeepers.

The mention of “chaplain-priests” [CLII] is noteworthy. They were distinguished from the senior priests, or canons, just as in our cathedral church today those priests who are not canons are called “chaplains.” The distinction is likewise noteworthy between the subdeacons and acolytes “of the *secretarium*,” who served the celebrating bishop in the sacred rites, and the other subdeacons and acolytes, the “cantors,” who sang in the choir.

In addition to a portion of specified revenues, to be divided equally with the cantor-subdeacons, cantor-acolytes, and doorkeepers, he assigned to the chaplain-priests, subdeacons, and acolytes of the *secretarium* certain other goods which were to benefit them alone and were not to be divided with the cantors and doorkeepers.

He further gives a particular reason why he thought provision should be made for these three orders of subdeacons, acolytes, and doorkeepers:

“For I considered,” he says in no. 4, “that since, besides what they perform in ecclesiastical ministry, these three orders labor more particularly than all the others in the pontifical service, they ought to receive something more special from the bishop in return for the service specially rendered to him. Yet I gave them little because I did not have an abundance to distribute—since, while others were in control, I alone sat mourning and sang—and because I thought I had to avoid giving them grounds for envy against those others” [Col. 0126A].

If anything else was bequeathed by pious people to this same college of lower clergy, he orders that everything too should be divided equally among them.

He takes care that neither the bishop nor, especially, the other senior clergy of the cathedral church should afterwards subtract anything from what had previously been customarily assigned to them, “as though they could say: ‘You have your stipend [from what Ratherius has granted]; let that suffice. Or, if you want to share our possessions with us, put what has been given to you into our common fund.’”

He makes various other suitable arrangements and carries them out. Finally, he concludes with praise of the emperor:

“Relying on whose aid,” he says, “I undertook these things; and therefore the work is more his than mine” [Col. 0126B].

123. To understand the words “relying on whose aid, I undertook these things,” we must explain the passages in which he mentions his “confidence in the imperial presence” in *Discordia*, no. 5, and calls that “confidence in the imperial presence of one who decides nothing other than what is just” in the sermon *De Octavis Paschae*, no. 4.

Since the bishop, taught by many experiences, had no confidence in the canons after they appeared unwilling to surrender the benefices he had granted them, and since he greatly feared that they might stir the secular powers against him so as to invalidate the foundation, or *Judicatum*, he did not wish that foundation to become public unless it had first been secured by the emperor’s favor and protection.

He knew that the emperor would soon come to Verona to meet his son Otto II, who was coming from Germany into Italy. The emperor did in fact arrive at Verona toward the end of October 967, and there he celebrated the feast of All Saints with his son on the first of November (*Annalista Saxo*, year 967).

On this occasion, therefore, Ratherius seems to have informed the emperor of the *Judicatum* he had previously prepared and to have hoped that Caesar would protect it by his authority. It was under this “confidence,” in turn, that he published it.

Certainly, to impose a check upon the other powers which the canons might rouse against him and against this foundation, he obtained from that same emperor an important diploma issued “at Balsameta” —a place in the diocese of Verona near the Mincio—“on the Nones of November [5 November], in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 967, and in the sixth year of the empire of Lord Otto, most pious Caesar, in the eleventh indiction” [Col. 0126D].

In *Qualitatis conjectura*, no. 13, he had written that he would ask the emperor for certain things, and these were granted in this diploma. It not only confirmed the privileges granted to the church of Verona by his predecessors, but also exempted the castles and persons of the bishopric from the jurisdiction of the counts and other inferior powers.

A special privilege was also granted to Ratherius, called *mundeburdium*. By its force he was so protected “that if anyone should henceforth, as until now, presume to disturb him, or become rebellious, or refuse to render to God what belongs to his ministry, then, if he is a cleric, he shall be expelled from the church until lawful and fitting satisfaction has been made, with everything he possesses reduced into the power of the bishop; and if he is a servant, he shall suffer what servants suffer and shall remain in the bishop’s power as a matter of due obligation,” and so forth.

The authority of all counts and other powers was also restrained, so that they could not in any way intrude against the bishop’s will into matters belonging to him, receive his cleric or servant into their protection without his permission, or offer assistance or favor against anything the bishop might decree—as in the case of what he established in the *Judicatum*.

Finally, the lease-contracts, exchanges, and precarious grants by which the goods of the church had been deceitfully alienated were annulled. We learned from the cited passage of *Qualitatis conjectura* that this was among the bishop’s wishes (see above, no. 109).

These things, which Ratherius obtained from the emperor, show that his confidence in the imperial presence was not unfounded [Col. 0127B].

Along with the imperial presence, he also associates the synod to be convened, in the two passages previously indicated, and he shows that he placed confidence in it as well:

“Although now,” he says in *Discordia*, no. 5, “confidence in the imperial presence and in the synod to be assembled has plainly been indicated”; and similarly in the sermon *De Octavis Paschae*, no. 4: “Confidence in the imperial presence of one who decides nothing other than what is just, and in the synod to be convened,” and so forth.

What that justice was which the imperial presence decreed is clear from the diploma just mentioned. From this it appeared that what the bishop had established in the *Judicatum* was sufficiently secure.

124. What, then, was the “synod to be convened,” and did it do anything concerning Ratherius’s *Judicatum*? This must now be examined [Col. 0127C].

The author calls the *Judicatum* a charter in Letter 12 to Ambrose, no. 4, and states that it was “confirmed and delivered with the signatures of the patriarch, myself, and all the co-bishops of our province.” He therefore took care that the foundation should be ratified and secured not merely by imperial authority but also by ecclesiastical power, having it confirmed by the subscriptions of the patriarch of Aquileia, his metropolitan, and the other bishops of this province.

There can be no doubt that these bishops assembled at Verona when the emperor Otto arrived there. It was customary for bishops to meet the emperor when he came into a province and to offer him their service. This was even more necessary at Verona on this occasion, when the emperor received there his son, who was entering Italy from Germany for the first time [Col. 0127D].

The gathering of the patriarch and the provincial bishops who flocked to Verona was therefore the “synod to be convened” which Ratherius had anticipated and which he associated with the imperial presence in the two passages. It appears actually to have been convened when the patriarch and the other bishops of the province subscribed the *Judicatum*.

Since in both texts Ratherius subordinates the synod to be convened to the imperial presence, this synod may have been held immediately after the emperor’s departure, before the bishops returned to their own sees.
