Thus the *Judicatum*, which Ratherius had previously prepared, was not published until the emperor’s approval—or, through the diploma mentioned above, imperial protection—had been secured, together with the subscriptions of the patriarch and bishops [Col. 0128A].

Unless the copyist who transcribed this work from Ratherius’s papers omitted the chronological notices and subscriptions, as sometimes happened with other documents, the date would be clearer (Letter 12, no. 4). The work was sent to Ambrose, the emperor’s chancellor, so that he too might defend the matter by his advocacy before Caesar.

125. Who would not have considered the *Judicatum*, fortified by such great and twofold authority, sufficiently secure? This too was Ratherius’s “confidence.” Yet all his hopes came to nothing.

Indeed, the discord which had always existed between the clergy and the bishop, though previously it had crept along in secret, burst openly forth with the publication of the *Judicatum*, and began to attack the bishop openly.

“Those who had said,” he writes in *Discordia*, no. 8, “that they did not care if I took away whatever they possessed from my property, and that they would not therefore be less faithful to me, provided only that I ceased troubling them about those things over which I had challenged them [namely, the revenues formerly divided among them], now, confident that I have ceased [with regard to the revenues mentioned], are striving, through the patronage of certain powerful men, to trouble me concerning what I have recovered from them on account of their ingratitude” [Col. 0128B].

They had plainly declared, in order to prevent Ratherius from introducing a new distribution of their goods and revenues, that they did not care if they were deprived of the benefices they had received from him. But when they had clearly recognized from the *Judicatum* that they were sufficiently secure in their own goods and revenues, they attempted, through powerful influence, to reclaim as their own the benefices previously granted and most recently taken away.

For this purpose they sought the patronage of powerful men, and someone was secretly sent to the emperor to accuse Ratherius and move Caesar, by whatever means possible, to rescind the bishop’s *Judicatum* [Col. 0128C].

It is clear from the work *De Clericis rebellibus* that this open rebellion broke out immediately after the *Judicatum* was published. That work (see note 1) was written in Advent of the year 967.

The bishop’s exceptional moderation is revealed there. Although he could have excommunicated such manifest rebels by both canonical and imperial authority and expelled them from the church, he nevertheless imitated divine mercy and refused to do so.

“For this reason,” he says in no. 2, in accordance with the Apostle’s words [CLVI], “ ‘Be imitators of God, as beloved children’ (Eph. 5:17), he mercifully awaits them, I think. I did not dare to pursue them cruelly, perhaps promising myself—though vainly—their conversion, when I had resolved to expel you as rebels from the Church, both legally and imperially, as has been sanctioned; my spirit spared itself the clothing of a double shame” (ibid.).

Moreover, he knew that the canons had sent a messenger to the emperor to act against him. Yet he himself thought that no one should be sent on his behalf and entrusted the entire matter to divine providence.

The canons’ messenger, supported by the patronage of powerful men, was believed to have obtained from the emperor the dispatch of a special “legate” to Verona, who would investigate the circumstances of both parties and report back to the emperor. If no special “legate” was sent to Verona for this purpose, nevertheless, as we shall see, two prominent persons at Verona performed the same function around Easter of the following year, 968 [Col. 0129A].

Meanwhile, although Ratherius did not wish to expel the rebels from the church, he did ask them not to perform sacred offices in the cathedral, but to choose some other church. He says that he made this request not because he despised their brotherhood, but because, “as the rustic example teaches, in which it is said: ‘What the eye does not see, the heart does not grieve over,’ it seems,” he says, “that some very necessary lessening of grief would result if, while those who have inflicted such evils upon me and do not cease to inflict them were not seen by me, remembrance of their evils were for a little while removed, while a small degree of forgetfulness obscured the authors of those evils.”

[Col. 0129B] 126. It will suffice to indicate briefly a few things concerning the letter to Martin, bishop of Ferrara, which was likewise written in Advent of the year 967 (see note 1, on Letter 10).

Ratherius had recognized him, at least at the Council of Ravenna. Martin had incurred criticism for two reasons: he ordained boys who had not reached the canonical age, and he carried this out in return for payment. This letter demonstrates Ratherius’s zeal, for he sought to correct the faults even of a senior bishop.

[CLVII] § XIX.—Events of the Year 968. Ratherius delivers sermons on peace during Lent. He writes a little book entitled *Discordia*. The canons send a messenger to Rome, who brings back a rescript in their favor. The bishop publishes an *Apologeticus*. An inquiry is initiated against him. Other sermons of Ratherius, and his *Testament*. Nanno, as the emperor’s legate, holds a judicial hearing against him, and Ratherius complains about this hearing in three letters. Everaclus, bishop of Liège, invites him. Finally, he resigns the episcopate and returns to Belgium.

[Col. 0129C]

127. As the rebellion against the bishop publicly grew more heated from day to day, in all the sermons which he delivered to the people during Lent of the year 968 (*Discordia*, no. 7), he attempted to call the rebels back to peace. He promised that he would enter into peace with them most willingly, “provided only that they wished to bring this about in true peace.”

But in vain. This rather increased their pride and inflamed their malice, so that they spread accusations against the bishop worse than those which had most recently been reported to Ambrose in *Qualitatis conjectura*.

Referring to these accusations in the *Apologeticus*, no. 4, he says: “Some people—whether you think so, or whether they have invented them more from their own minds—hurl accusations at me” [Col. 0129D]. In no. 8 he calls them “so great, so outrageous, so foul, so disgraceful, so unbelievable, and even contrary to my age.”

Since, therefore, he could not bring the rebels to peace, during that same Lent he composed a little work entitled *Discordia inter ipsum et clericos* [Discord between himself and the clergy], which reveals the beginnings and causes of the disagreement.

He recalls four causes of this discord:

1. The difference between the character of the bishop and that of the clergy.

2. The bishop’s concern to promote observance of the ecclesiastical laws.

3. His effort to abolish the clergy’s relationships with women, in accordance with the decree of the Council of Ravenna and of the Roman pontiff, as well as the emperor’s command.

4. The fact that the bishop could not tolerate the less equitable division of ecclesiastical revenues, from which many evils and scandals resulted [Col. 0130A].

He reports the proceedings of the diocesan synod convened after the Council of Ravenna; he describes the meeting held with the canons after that synod in order to provide for the poorer clergy [CLVIII]; and he indicates their efforts before the emperor.

Finally, expressing his confidence in his cause and repeating the words of Job, “I diligently investigated the cause that I did not know” (Job 29:16), he says that he fears only that, through the patronage of the powerful and the accusations of ill-wishers, the emperor may be misled, and that what happened to the wretched men of whom we read may happen to him, wretched as he is—men who, even if they had pleaded their case among the Scythians, would undoubtedly have been released without blame.

[Col. 0130B] 128. While he was writing these things, he had perceived that the clergy had approached the emperor; but he did not know that they had likewise fled to the Roman pontiff.

They thought that the emperor should be entreated to institute an inquiry against Ratherius, by which his *Judicatum* might be rescinded and the goods taken from them restored. To ensure that in the future the goods belonging to them would be secure and exempt from the jurisdiction of the bishops, they also judged that the authority of the Apostolic See should be invoked.

They therefore secretly sent a legate to Rome. Perhaps the same man who had been sent to the imperial court was instructed, after completing the business before the emperor, to approach the Roman pontiff as well (*Apologeticus*, no. 7).

He returned with what were “as it were apostolic letters,” by which, under penalty of anathema, Ratherius and his successors were forbidden to interfere in any way in the property of the canons [Col. 0130C].

The bishop describes this action in harsher terms. Although he asserts that payment was involved in the matter, we do not believe that Pope John XIII himself was corrupted by money, since his integrity is commended by many testimonies, including Ratherius himself (*Itinerarium*, no. 2).

The wealthy canons, just as they had secured the patronage of powerful men with money and had thereby turned the emperor’s previously favorable disposition toward Ratherius—as will become clear later—seem by the same method to have found certain Roman patrons and obtained from them that the matter should be settled in Ratherius’s absence and without consulting him, and that apostolic letters should be written against him.

When the bishop sought to intervene in the goods and revenues of the clergy of the cathedral church, his intention was not to take anything belonging to them and transfer it to other uses. Rather, he wished that the very resources which had generally been bequeathed to the clergy of the cathedral church should be distributed among them in such a way that the lower clergy would not be crushed by poverty and divine worship would not suffer detriment.

Since the bishop’s intention and these circumstances were not known [CLIX], it could easily appear unjust that the same bishop, who had acquired a bad reputation because of numerous accusations brought before the emperor, should wish to introduce a new distribution of the goods and revenues in question, contrary to ancient custom—a distribution which was opposed even by those very lower clergy on whose behalf the matter was being conducted.

Thus the rescript exempting these revenues from the bishop’s authority could easily have been secretly obtained on the assumption that it was equitable [Col. 0131A].

News of this rescript was brought to Verona before Easter of the year 968, since Ratherius testifies in the *Apologeticus*, composed as that Easter approached, that the event had occurred “very recently” (no. 7).

The opinion of Rodoald, patriarch of Aquileia, on this same matter was subsequently issued in that year. It is said that the other bishops and Ratherius himself assented to it; it will be presented as spurious in the Appendix.

129. When the emperor Otto was at Verona in the preceding year, he gave Bishop Ratherius some silver to repair the basilica of Saint Zeno. The emperor’s presence caused the bishop much difficulty and expense, as is clearly shown by the statements in *Apologeticus*, no. 2:

“After everything on which I had depended for my livelihood had been swallowed up by his [Otto’s] power—I do not say by force, I deny that—but certainly by his presence” [Col. 0131B].

Perhaps, as a tacit compensation for some of these expenses, Augustus gave the bishop whatever quantity of silver it was, expressly for the repair of the basilica mentioned.

When the bishop had promptly carried out everything according to the emperor’s wishes, a malicious caviler—a canon, though not from Verona (see note 13), and a principal supporter and defender of Ratherius’s adversaries—attempted to turn or interpret this entirely upright and just deed into an evil one.

Imitating the example of Judas, he kept insisting that the money ought to have been spent on the poor (Matt. 26:9) [Col. 0131C]. This criticism is refuted in the *Apologeticus*.

First, Ratherius denies that he could have converted the money to any use other than that for which the emperor had given it. He adds that there were no poor people at Verona in such need that the rebuilding of churches should have been abandoned on their account.

He praises the generosity of the Veronese, who were so lavish toward the poor that, without making any distinction, they gave generously even to those who devoted themselves to gluttony and drunkenness; indeed, they compelled people to give to them even before the appointed hour, including during the Lenten fast [CLX].

He demonstrates how much more necessary the rebuilding of the churches was than the needs of the other poor. “For,” he says in no. 5, “the churches of this region are everywhere either completely ruined or largely destroyed, either by the fires of the pagans” —that is, the Hungarians, who in this century, as heathens in religion, repeatedly invaded Italy—“or by the negligence of pseudo-bishops,” who had been intruded into Ratherius’s place [Col. 0131D].

At that time the restoration and care of the churches belonged entirely to the bishop. Moreover, he was so burdened by many responsibilities, especially by guests, that he had no means to support himself and his household adequately. Therefore, in no. 2, he says:

“Thanks be to God, I find no poor people here, except—strange to say, unbelievable to hear—myself and those whom I myself ought to have supported as members of my household.”

Since, then, the need of the churches was greater than that of the other poor, why should he himself, the poorest of all and unable to rebuild the churches from his own resources, give to the poor that imperial gift which had been entrusted to him for the repair of the basilica of Saint Zeno?

On this occasion he also inserts a considerable discussion of the clergy’s rebellion. He speaks at length about the rescript recently brought from Rome, which forbade him to interfere in any way in the affairs of the clergy.

Interpreting the rescript that particularly distressed him more broadly than is warranted, he concludes that by the word “things” it removed from the bishop’s authority not only the clergy’s external goods but also their souls. He then develops at greater length how many absurd and unreasonable consequences would follow from this.

Everyone can see how excessive this inference is. Yet it must be forgiven in a man from whom the force of very recent pain had drawn this inference, since he found that the clergy who refused to obey him and had been emboldened by that rescript were plotting one thing after another against the bishop [Col. 0132B].

130. He gives a not obscure indication that these men were plotting something more serious against him on the very day of the Lord’s Supper, when he gave them Communion, in his second sermon on Easter, which he delivered on Easter Day of the present year, 968.

After showing from the words of the Gospel that every hostility must be set aside and that peace must be made even with those who have injured us, he adds in no. 3:

“Yet I have seen certain people despise this counsel—alas!—to such an extent, and I wish it were not especially those who ought to offer others a good example [CLXI] [Col. 0132C], that even they, while he who was sending the holy bread into their mouths said, ‘May the Body of our Lord Jesus Christ profit you unto eternal life,’ did not cease to spread snares of destruction and, as though before Pilate in those same days, to cry, ‘Crucify, crucify!’—not remembering the words: ‘Woe to the wicked traitor, woe to his accomplices, even today in his Church.’”

He foretells that, unless they repent, they will become imitators of Judas, into whom Satan entered after the morsel, “certainly through the effect of an evil deed, which had already been present in him through the disposition of a malicious will.”

### 131

What they were plotting, however, became clear immediately after Easter. Ratherius discusses this matter in his sermon on the Octave of Easter, no. 1:

“After Satan had entered into them after the morsel [John XIII, 27], through the working of evil—he who had already long before been present in them through their most wicked intention—as though they had heard from him who had handed them that same morsel: ‘What you are doing, do quickly’ [ibid.], from that time onward they did not cease to carry out as quickly as possible what they had previously plotted, especially throughout that entire Lent . . . against that same man—would that no one knew that I was he—sending out openly against him, by every means they could, every contrivance of ambush and every utterly false fabrication, and inventing such things about him as no one could believe unless he had done the same or many similar things himself.”

He then adds what took place during that very Easter week, from which the rebels’ hostility and their wicked scheme against him became publicly evident. The episcopal residence had partly fallen into ruin because of guests and partly through the malice of the neighbors:

“Those staying there,” he says, “do not cease to destroy it by force and authority, while I am, of course, unable to resist any one of them . . . although it is clear that they are returning especially from the imperial army, or going to it.”

And shortly afterward:

“They destroy it with such force, those staying in it, that if anyone concerned with the matter comes there to inspect the servants, they immediately seize him, scourge him most severely, and bind him with straps.”

From a letter to Ambrosius, letter 12, we learn that these guests were chiefly Bavarians. There he also explains who the “neighbors” were who were destroying the same house:

“The Bavarians,” he says in no. 4, “and the clerics living nearby, and especially the servants, are destroying it.”

In the same place he mentions that the doors were “partly taken away by theft,” that is, secretly, and “partly removed by force.” He testifies that he spent nearly forty pounds on restoring the same house and restored its doors six times; but nothing helped. The enemies’ malice was such that the bishop who suffered these losses was represented as the author of them.

This was one of the principal accusations. To have it brought before the emperor as sufficiently proved, two influential persons in the city, corrupted by money, were led around during Easter week to inspect the episcopal residence. One was Nanno, count of Verona, Ratherius’ bitterest enemy [see note 5 on the sermon on the Octave of Easter]; the other was perhaps the viscount.

The rebels, however, shifting all the blame onto the bishop, say:

“They accuse me,” he says in no. 1 of the sermon on the Octave, “with inspectors whom they have hired, of destroying the same house, as though it could be believed that I would either destroy myself, or willingly allow to be destroyed, what I had built at such great expense of my own.”

Some attributed these troubles to the fact that the bishop did not live in the episcopal residence. He answers this in letter 12 to Ambrosius, no. 4:

“It was most inappropriate for him to remain in that house, lest he either be seized as formerly, or, if he tried to defend himself, the basilicas surrounding it on his account should be burned with fire—for what would the Veronese populace not dare? If neither event occurred, what would he do when, as one of your countrymen”—that is, one of the Germans departing for the emperor’s army or returning from it—“left it, and another prince succeeded him, and another succeeded that one, and yet another the latter? Could the bishop live with such men in one house?”

He touches on the same matter in other words in the sermon on the Octave of Easter, no. 2. Meanwhile, he did not cease urging the rebels still to make peace. See his sermon on the Octave of Easter, another sermon after Easter, and the second sermon on the Ascension of the Lord, all of which were delivered in this same year, 968.

### 132

In the same year Ratherius wrote his Testament, whose opening breathes piety; its bequests, however, declare him poor rather than wealthy. In the appendix that he later added to it, when he says that he hopes for “the promised departure,” this “departure” seems to be the one of which he says in letter 13 to the empress Adelaide:

“I desire rather to withdraw safely and dwell in the solitude of my monastery.”

Since, harassed by so many and such great plots of the Veronese, he could no longer hope for peace in the episcopate, he began at last to think about relinquishing it. Yet, since he believed that it was unlawful for him to resign it voluntarily [see above, no. 66], he appears to have desired an imperial order compelling him to leave Verona so that he could return to his monastery [CLXIII]. He seems indeed to have received an indication of such an order when, in this appendix, he mentioned “the promised departure.”

### 133

The matter was not long delayed. For on June 30, the feast commemorating Saint Paul, Nanno, count of Verona, as though sent by the emperor’s party, held a hearing against Ratherius.

“On the very solemnity of blessed Paul the apostle,” as we read in letter 12, no. 4, “almost the entire city was present, and Nanno, seated on the tribunal, began to speak as follows.”

Nanno presented four charges to the people.

The first concerned a meadow beside the river Athesis. Since people continually cut it down as they came and went and devastated the vineyards adjoining it, the bishop had ordered it to be plowed and millet sown in it. When Nanno asked, “What do you think of this meadow, which you see plowed?” they all answered unanimously: “Very badly.”

The second charge concerned the episcopal residence. When Nanno asked, “What is your judgment concerning this house, which you see destroyed in this way?” everyone answered: “It is the bishop’s fault.”

The third charge concerned Ratherius’ judgment by which certain benefices had been taken away from ungrateful senior clerics, or canons, and assigned to the support of poor clerics.

“What,” said Nanno, “do you think of those clerics”—that is, the senior ones—“who have thus lost their benefices?” They all shouted: “Nothing could be worse.”

The fourth charge was this:

“What do you say about the fact that, if one of his clerics or servants does not come to the bishop when summoned, at his own wish, he sends his staff-bearers, who seize the man by force and bring him to the bishop?”

Here, although they might all most justly have answered with Terence’s words, “Well done indeed!”, they all responded instead with a more than swinish squealing.

Finally, Nanno pronounced judgment by imperial authority in these words:

“I have been sent to you by the emperor and by my lady”—namely, the empress Adelaide—“so that, if from now on any one of them should dare to do this, everyone is to resist him with all his strength.”

Thus he sharpened and inflamed the rebels’ hostility against the bishop. Soon afterward he declared the same bishop’s judgment wholly invalid.

“When he had said this,” Ratherius adds, “whatever I had taken away from all my adversaries and had assigned to the poor clerics by the document sent to you”—that is, to Ambrosius—“he restored entirely to them, saying that the emperor had sworn never to allow this to stand.”

Everyone can easily see how tumultuous and illegitimate this hearing was, in which the judge followed the rebels’ sentence and condemned Ratherius unheard, although he could have refuted the charges brought against him on many points.

### 134

Understanding from these events that great danger was threatening him, the bishop immediately wrote three letters. One was addressed to Nanno, the count, and in the annotations we have shown that it was written on July 1, the eighth day after the feast of Saint John the Baptist. The second was addressed to Ambrosius, the emperor’s chancellor; the third to the empress Adelaide [see note 1 on letter 2].

Nanno the count had succeeded Buccho. But since the latter had initially been hostile to the bishop, although he later favored him, Ratherius seems to have offered the new count Nanno certain gifts in order to win his favor. These, however, were useless, because afterward he did not show him the same generosity.

“For it is arranged in such a way,” he says in letter 2, no. 1, “that you destroy old benefits unless you support them with later ones.”

Ratherius’ enemies won him over against the bishop with richer gifts. In the letter, however, he complains that his opponents’ lies had prevailed and that the count was, at the peril of souls, lending his support to their crimes and rebellion:

“You yourselves are taking their souls away from them, by forbidding them so completely to come to the synod, to hear the pope’s legation concerning the dismissal of wives, and in every respect to obey bishops, that you receive them into your hands like soldiers and never cease to support them in all the abominations they commit against God; and thus you make them despise our prohibition.”

Since Nanno had praised in the hearing the command not so much of the emperor as of the empress, Ratherius suggests that she had been deceived and more strongly prejudiced against him. At the same time, he still expresses some confidence in the emperor, whom he does not believe to be forgetful of the words of blessed Job (Job XXIX, 16):

“I diligently investigated a cause that I did not know.”

He therefore adds:

“I earnestly beg you to stop frightening me by invoking the authority of the ever most pious Caesar, since you cannot do so; for I fear you a thousand times more than I fear him.”

He had no doubt, then, that if the emperor investigated the matter carefully, he would expose the calumnies and malice.

### 135

In the other letter to Ambrosius, letter 12, he first reports what he had done after the council of Ravenna to reform the corrupt morals of the clerics, and how strongly they had resisted with Nanno’s support. He describes Nanno’s hearing and exposes the injustice of each charge on which the judgment was based. Finally, he shows that matters had reached the point where, unless a prompt remedy were provided, his life was at stake. He therefore asks Ambrosius to inform the emperor about the whole affair and obtain an imperial rescript by which the entire conspiracy might be suppressed.

### 136

In his letter to the empress Adelaide, letter 13, Ratherius assumes that she had been especially maliciously prejudiced against him. The principal reason that seems to have influenced her was that she had been persuaded that the affairs of the bishopric of Verona were daily falling into such ruin under Bishop Ratherius that, unless he were removed, everything would soon suffer total destruction. The following words refer to this:

“If you are acting for the sake of the bishopric.”

He asks her at least to allow him to remain safely in Verona until he completed the cathedral church. Otherwise, he presents himself as ready to relinquish the bishopric and return to his monastery.

He suggests that the empress had been misled by false reports and that his case should be examined more carefully in these final words:

“Oh, how greatly it would benefit all who hold positions of authority—as I have more than once urged upon Your Majesty—if they did not deliver judgments so precipitately, but had considered the words of blessed Job: ‘I diligently investigated a cause that I did not know.’”

Fearing that he might anger the empress by this letter, he tries to excuse himself in a very brief addition, as though written afterward, on the grounds that, with his stomach swollen with bitter aloe, he cannot belch forth the sweetness of honey.

### 137

From this letter Ratherius is recognized as having been cast into great straits. Since no hope appeared of calming the rebels or eventually settling affairs, he became wholly despondent and began to turn over in his mind the plan of voluntarily relinquishing the bishopric before he was expelled by force.

Yet, struggling with contrary emotions, he wrote to Everaclus, bishop of Liège, and to Fulcuinus, abbot of Lobbes. After Baldrich, bishop of Liège, died in 959, Everaclus, dean of the Church of Bonn—whom others call Evracrus or Eraclius—had succeeded him. He was exceedingly devoted to restoring the monastic rule. Since during this period the abbots of the monastery of Lobbes were the bishops of Liège themselves, in 960 he restored a proper abbot to the monastery and appointed Aletranus over it. When Aletranus died in 965, the monk Fulcuinus was substituted in his place.

Accordingly, Ratherius sent Everaclus, whom he had known previously, a small gift with a letter in which he indicated that he was considering returning to his homeland and monastery, although the plan was held up by certain difficulties. Everaclus replied with a letter in which he both offered distinguished testimony to Ratherius’ virtues and earnestly urged and invited him to return to his homeland (letter 14):

“Your native homeland stretches out imploring hands to you and invites you to return. All who belong to either order, clerical or military, cry out with mind, will, zeal, and voice that you should come; they desire to see you. In rendering you service, we set no limit either to number or measure. Everything we possess will be in your hands, according to what has taken root in your heart, beloved Ratherius.”

### 138

To Fulcuinus, however, our bishop sent not so much a letter as a book, which is lost. Let Fulcuinus himself be heard (On the Deeds of the Abbots of Lobbes, chapter 28):

“Ratherius was still at Verona. Disgusted with the insolence of the citizens and at the same time suspicious of the innate and peculiar treachery that characterized them, he was thinking about returning, proposing the saying that one can often live well in another’s homeland but die badly. He therefore sent the abbot”—Fulcuinus himself—“a book which he entitled The Conflict of Two, because in it he anxiously wavered while debating whether he should return or not.”

That he finally inclined toward returning is shown by what follows:

“Also asking”—perhaps in the letter with which he sent the mentioned book—“that horses and companions be sent to him, so that he might hasten his journey to us more easily.”

Fulcuinus promptly agreed:

“It was done,” he says; “they were sent, and he came.”

What he adds—that Ratherius “took with him not, I will not say weights of gold and silver, but, to use his own words, masses and heaps”—seems utterly unbelievable.

Many things show how alien Ratherius was throughout his life from accumulating riches, especially the reports found in several places concerning his contempt for wealth and his generosity. But this is especially clearly attested by the words written by Everaclus, bishop of Liège, in a letter to Ratherius when he was about to leave Verona for the last time:

“You not only did not seize what belonged to others, but did not even desire it; you gave away what was yours, grieving over the miseries of others and not envying their prosperity.”

He was so inclined toward poverty that he “used to say that he wanted to die a beggar, so that his corpse might be covered by another’s alms.”

How great his poverty and want were toward the end of his Veronese episcopate, we learned from the Apologeticus that he wrote shortly before Easter of this year, 968. How narrow his household resources were is also shown by the Testament written in the same year, in which we read the following about money:

“If I have any denarii, I wish them to be divided as follows. If there is one pound, let it be given to those responsible for my funeral; if there is another, unless it is lacking, to the clerics possessing the church of Saint Mary the Consoler, together with the others listed in the same Judgment. Whatever remains—whether much, which I do not believe, or little, or certainly nothing, which I do not disbelieve—let Martin have it, who now keeps my little chests, or whoever, when I die, then holds the same office.”

How could a man suffering such a shortage of money in 968, shortly before leaving Verona, take with him, on departing, “not, I will not say weights of gold and silver, but masses and heaps”?

If Ratherius said this, he undoubtedly said it ironically, as was his custom. If he did bring some gold and silver with him, and it did not appear insignificant, it should be attributed chiefly to the clerics—especially the rebellious ones, whom we have seen to be very wealthy and lavish—and to the generosity of the Veronese. To rid themselves at last of a bishop so burdensome and detested by them, they may have sent him away with many great gifts and abundant provisions for the journey.

Perhaps Milo, who succeeded him in the episcopate, also contributed something toward the same end, so that he might hold the see peacefully.

Ratherius departed not long after Nanno’s hearing, in July or, at the latest, August of the year 968. For a document of Milo, already bishop, was published from the archive of the church of Saint Proculus by Biancolino (On the Bishops and Governors of Verona, p. 123), bearing these chronological notices:

“In the seventh year of the reign of our lord Otto the Great, in the first year of his son, in the eleventh indiction.”

These are the dates of the year 968. Since the eleventh indiction ended in August of that year, it is clear that the document was written before September, when the twelfth indiction began.

Moreover, another document from May of the same year (Dionysius, Diplomatic Collection, p. 128) still presents Ratherius as bishop of Verona. He was likewise still at Verona on June 30, when Nanno held his hearing, and on July 1, when he wrote to Nanno, Ambrosius, and Adelaide. Since he remained there for some time afterward, until he received replies and horses for the journey after writing to Everaclus and Fulcuinus, it is evident that he departed toward the end of July or the beginning of August, and that at approximately the same time Milo—who had had a prolonged dispute with him over the episcopate—succeeded him before September.

## § XX. — Received by Everaclus, bishop of Liège, and Fulcuinus, abbot of Lobbes, he is placed over several small abbeys. The passage in the *Praeloquia* in which the true facts concerning the abbey of Saint-Amand are explained, and by which he is cleared of the purchase of that abbey through simony, must be cited here. He is placed over the abbey of Lobbes by Everaclus after Fulcuinus has been removed, but is restored by Notker, Everaclus’ successor. The death of Ratherius and the year of his death.

### 139

As he had promised, Everaclus, bishop of Liège, received Ratherius with the greatest kindness and, according to Fulcuinus, gave him the village of Alna with its revenues (chapter 28). We have conjectured with sufficient probability in § 11 that this was the same village and abbey that he had received in 955 from Baldrich, Everaclus’ predecessor, as an appropriate means of support after his expulsion from the bishopric of Liège.

Fulcuinus, abbot of Lobbes, also, with the consent of the brothers, gave him the villages of Strata and Gosniacas, the small abbey of Saint Ursmarus, and another monastery they called Waslare.

Two other monasteries, Saint-Amand and Altimont, Ratherius is said by Fulcuinus to have subsequently bought for money, but in such a way that he soon abandoned both through fickleness and returned to Alna.

“He purchased from King Lothar,” Fulcuinus says, “the abbey of Saint-Amand. Having scarcely possessed it for one night, he abandoned it—as he was a man of extraordinary fickleness—and returned to the village of Alna, which he had obtained through the munificence of the lord bishop.

“From there, in the same way, he bought the monastery called Altimont, paying a great price. There he gathered, after making a donation, whatever was especially valuable to him in church ornaments and vestments, as well as everything he had previously given to our church”—that is, Lobbes—“but had later taken back. After abandoning this one too, he returned once again to Alna.”

### 140

Since various disagreements subsequently arose between Ratherius and Fulcuinus, which we shall explain later, Mabillon suspected that Fulcuinus’ account of these two alleged purchases through simony deserved little credence (vol. VII of the *Acta Sanctorum* of the Benedictine Order, p. 479):

“From his other deeds,” he says, “we understand how greatly our bishop hated simony. Let the following among other examples serve as evidence. When he had expelled from a certain small abbey subject to the Veronese church, called Magonzianus, an abbot of bad morals who alone lived there after the little monastery had been burned by the Hungarians, that man tried through intermediaries to infect Ratherius with the leprosy of Gehazi—that is, he attempted to have Ratherius accept money in exchange for allowing him to remain there . . . . Ratherius rejected the pseudo-abbot’s simoniacal offering so as not to be infected by Gehazi’s disease.

“Would he himself, then, have attempted to obtain abbeys by paying a price? Certainly this seems in no way credible. Perhaps Fulcuinus learned this from the report of flatterers; offended by Ratherius, he readily believed it and committed it to writing. Fulcuinus was likewise unfair toward Erluinus, abbot of Gembloux, for a similar reason in chapter 25, as we shall show in its proper place.”

So far Mabillon. Another example may be added from the book of the *Confession*, where Ratherius most vehemently condemns Oderadus’ simoniacal purchase. Moreover, it is unbelievable that Ratherius would have abandoned both abbeys so quickly if he had bought them at a high price, or that he had acquired them through so great a crime when he was under no pressure of poverty and had been adequately provided for both by Everaclus and by Fulcuinus himself.

### 141

Certainly, what Fulcuinus reports about the simoniacal purchase of the abbey of Saint-Amand is proved false by what Ratherius narrates in book 5 of the *Praeloquia*, no. 33:

“When I was at Laon,” he says, “on the day of the Nativity of the Lord, the abbot asked me to come on the feast of Saint Stephen into the chapter of the sisters and”—to use his own words—“say something good to them. I agreed, and after the customary reading, having requested and received the blessing, I said:

“‘Since I have been asked to say something good to your charity, I find nothing else—whatever it may be—except to tell Your Ladyship what happened to me this night.

“‘Yesterday I was excessively pressed to accept the administration of the abbey of Saint-Amand. While keeping vigil at the nocturnal office, so that—shamefully!—I seemed to be standing there often asleep, when the reader came to a passage from the treatise of blessed Jerome in which the Lord, continuing his words to certain persons in the Gospel, says, “All these things will come upon this generation” (Matthew XXIII, 36), I understood this through the explanation of the same aforementioned teacher as meaning that anyone who unjustly kills his brother—that is, any Christian—draws upon himself a greater guilt than those who killed various people from righteous Abel to Zachariah son of Barachiah (Luke XI, 51), insofar as he bears all that guilt through his association with that generation, as well as his own guilt, which he committed by imitating them.

“‘When this terrified me greatly, as often happens, I began to gather one thing from another and to conclude that what had been understood concerning homicide ought, by evident reasoning, to apply also to the other crimes. I began to say within myself: “Are you, then, to become an abbot with such a conscience? First become a monk,” since at that time the matter of the episcopate had fallen away from me, except that many had also undertaken it unworthily.’”

Since book 5 of the *Praeloquia*, at whose end this event is described, was composed at the beginning of the year 936, some have thought that the event belonged to Ratherius’ earlier years, before he had been promoted to the bishopric of Verona.

We have clearly shown, however, in § 2, no. 9, that at that time the abbey of Elnon-Saint-Amand was entrusted to noble laymen who held the place of abbot. We therefore proved there that such an event did not occur before Ratherius wrote that book of the *Praeloquia*.

The event must consequently be assigned to a later period. Fulcuinus, in fact, reported it after Ratherius’ resignation from the Veronese episcopate. That period also agrees with Ratherius’ words:

“For at that time the episcopate had fallen away from me.”

The event did not occur in that youthful period when he had not yet attained the episcopate, but at the time when, after resigning the Veronese episcopate, he no longer thought about the episcopate.

The anonymous poet who continued the series of the abbots of Elnon also agrees with this chronology. He narrates the same event after the death of Abbot Genulfus, who is known from the chronicle of Elnon to have died in 969 (Marten and Durand, *Anecdota*, vol. III). Hence it is clear that this event, which must be assigned to the year 969, was added by Ratherius to the books of the *Praeloquia* at a later date.

It is plainly evident that Ratherius and Fulcuinus are referring to the same event from their mention of one night on which the matter of the same abbey of Saint-Amand was discussed. The entire difference lies in certain circumstances, which Fulcuinus presents in one way and Ratherius in another.

Greater credence, however, must be given to Ratherius, who was accustomed to accuse openly, indeed even to aggravate, his own faults, not to diminish them. The very description of the event in Ratherius wholly removes the stain of simony:

“For he is said to have been ‘pressed to accept the administration of the abbey of Saint-Amand,’ but while reciting the nocturnal office he was deterred and drawn away by a certain meditation from accepting the abbey that was being offered.”

He had therefore not yet received the abbey, nor had he purchased it for a price. He had not sought it himself, but had been unsuccessfully pressed by others at Laon to accept it.

Fulcuinus was therefore deceived when he believed those who reported a simoniacal purchase. The celebrated anonymous poet, much later than Fulcuinus, was likewise deceived. He not only branded Ratherius with the same vice of simony, but also represented the abbey as not voluntarily rejected by Ratherius, but as handed over to him after the brothers expelled him, in these verses (in Mabillon, *Benedictine Annals*, vol. III, p. 557):

> But scarcely had he entered when the stirred crowd of brothers  
> drove him from the buildings and removed him from the house.

Once the purchase of this abbey of Saint-Amand has been excluded, the alleged purchase of the other abbey, Altimont, which seems to have been attached to Ratherius by a similar embellishment and carelessly swallowed by Fulcuinus, is also sufficiently cleared away.

Fulcuinus also reports in chapter 28 another purchase, that of the church of Saint Dionysius, which Ratherius “had bought from Count Rotbert at the assessed price of twenty pounds.”

Because of the abuse of that age, churches possessing revenues were commonly handed over to laymen in the form of military benefices. It may be conjectured that Ratherius redeemed the church of Saint Dionysius, which had passed into the benefice of Count Rotbert, for twenty pounds and wished to restore it to ecclesiastical jurisdiction.

### 142

The reason for the disagreement that arose between Fulcuinus and Ratherius must now be explained. Fulcuinus himself presents the matter as follows:

“He”—Ratherius—“always execrating our place, was plotting against the abbot”—Fulcuinus—“with some people urging him on to this. Why delay over many details? Matters reached the point that the abbot withdrew from the place, knowing that the bishop”—Everaclus—“also wished this, for we have nothing else to say about him.

“To show the causes of his earlier hostility, Ratherius invaded the place. Fearing the abbot’s courage, and at the same time his kinship, which was not insignificant, he surrounded the cloister like a fortress, using, as he said, the remaining money he possessed to purchase the support of certain princes.

“He also willingly gave up the church of Saint Dionysius, which he had bought from Count Rotbert at the assessed price of twenty pounds, for this purpose, and paid no attention to what, how much, or to whom he should give anything on that account.

“What more is there to say? That year passed in this way until Bishop Evracrus died and Notker succeeded him in the see . . . . He, not wishing his beginnings to be regarded as weak or precipitous, summoned the abbots—namely, Werinfrid of Stavelot and Heribert of Andage, with some brothers—and first investigated the origins of the conspiracy. He weighed and examined what he found, and then used what had been examined as the basis of a judgment. When he saw that everything was frivolous, he reconciled the brothers to the abbot and restored him.”

Two conclusions clearly follow from this.

First, there was a considerable disagreement between the monks of Lobbes and Fulcuinus their abbot. Because of it, they had become alienated from Fulcuinus and demanded Ratherius as their abbot. The disagreement is sufficiently indicated by the statement that Fulcuinus was not restored until the brothers had been reconciled to the abbot:

“He reconciled the brothers to the abbot and restored him.”

That they sought Ratherius as abbot, and even urged him to favor their party and arrange Fulcuinus’ exclusion, is suggested by the words “with some people urging him on to this.”

Second, Ratherius did nothing in this matter without the authority of the bishop under whom the monastery of Lobbes stood. Certainly no force was used in Ratherius’ appointment. For this reason Fulcuinus is said not to have been expelled by force, but to have “withdrawn from the place,” knowing that the bishop also wished this.

Ratherius therefore believed that he had been lawfully appointed. The expression “invaded,” used by his rival Fulcuinus, must be excused: because he regarded as “frivolous” all the grounds that had led to Ratherius’ appointment, as was recognized in the later judgment, he considered Ratherius an invader.

Only after Ratherius had been appointed abbot by the bishop’s legitimate authority, fearing that Fulcuinus, because of his courage and the power of his relatives, might retake by force the place from which he had withdrawn, did he surround the cloister like a fortress and seek the support of powerful men through gifts. For the same reason he gave up the church of Saint Dionysius, which he had redeemed for twenty pounds.

He possessed the monastery of Lobbes for scarcely a year, namely, only as long as Everaclus the bishop who had appointed him lived. Everaclus died in November 971, and Notker succeeded him at the beginning of 972.

Thus Ratherius was placed over the abbey of Lobbes at the beginning of 971, while Fulcuinus was restored by Notker’s judgment in 972. Ratherius then returned to Alna and, after becoming reconciled with Fulcuinus, spent the remainder of his life there without complaint.

### 143

He did not long survive this. After subsequently departing for Namur, “while he happened to be staying there with the count, he died,” as Fulcuinus recorded for posterity (chapter 28).

Some assign his death to the year 973. Sigebertus, and especially the Chronicle of Lobbes, are to be preferred, however; they report that he died in 974 (Marten and Durand, *Anecdota*, vol. III). Chapeauvillius designates April 25 as the day of his death (*Deeds of the Bishops of Tongeren*, vol. I, chapter 45).

According to the testimony of the aforementioned Fulcuinus, his body was brought to the monks of Lobbes and, “after a solemn celebration of the pontifical funeral rites, was honorably buried in the church of Saint Ursmarus on the northern side.”

As Mabillon noted (*Acta Sanctorum* of the Benedictine Order, vol. VII, p. 479), this church is the site of the Lobbes cemetery, now parochial, where all the distinguished men of that monastery were buried. It is situated on a hill, at whose foot stands the monastery beside the Sambre.

The following epitaph was carved on his tomb; it is presented by a Lobbes codex at the end of Ratherius’ *Praeloquia*:

**VERSES OVER HIS TOMB**

> Bishop of Verona, but three times Ratherius an exile,  
> Once a monk, and afterward yours, Lobbes.  
> Noble, courteous, well-mannered in his time,  
> He asked that this be inscribed upon his own tomb.  
> Trample him, feet of men, the salt that has lost its savor;  
> May the gracious reader aid him with prayers.

# THE FIRST PART OF THE WORKS OF RATHERIUS, BISHOP OF VERONA, CONTAINING THE BOOKS AND OPUSCULA OF THE *PRAELOQUIA*

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING BOOKS OF THE *PRAELOQUIA*

Father Lucas Acherius mentions the books of the *Praeloquia*, or *Agonisticus*, together with several other short works of Ratherius, transcribed from the Lobbes codex, in the note appended to the list of the second volume of the first edition of the *Spicilegium*. In his notice concerning Ratherius’ works, he had promised that he would publish the same books in the third volume.

Since he did not fulfill that promise, the books were published from a copy that the aforementioned Acherius had left with the Benedictine Fathers of Saint-Germain-des-Prés in Paris, under the care of Fathers Edmond Martène and Ursin Durand (*Collectio Veterum Scriptorum et Monumentorum*, vol. IX, cols. 787 ff.), in Paris in 1733.

These are the first books from Ratherius’ works to have come down to us.

## II

Fulcuinus, in chapter 20 of *The Deeds of the Abbots of Lobbes*, testifies that these books were written by Ratherius in exile:

> “During that exile, in which Ratherius said that he had been placed, while relieved of episcopal duties, he published a book which he called the *Agonisticon*. Liutprand, then a deacon of the Church of Pavia—called Ticinum at that time—mentions this same work in Book III, chapter 14, of his *History*: ‘Ratherius . . . . . bishop, having been captured by him [Hugh, king of Italy], was banished into exile at Pavia. There he began, with sufficiently witty elegance, to compose a book about the hardship of his exile. If anyone reads it, he will find there, on this occasion, certain matters set forth which can please readers no less than they can benefit them.’”

These statements, copied from Liutprand by Sigebert and several others, agree perfectly with the books that follow. In them Ratherius inserted many details concerning his hardships, which were known to Liutprand, and discussed many other matters deliberately; we shall soon speak of their usefulness. The exile to which he was banished at Pavia was his first exile. Since he remained for a long time imprisoned at Pavia—or, as he says in Letter 5 to John XII, no. 4, “in a certain little tower at Pavia”—there can be no doubt that this work was composed by him in such a prison.

Accordingly, not only does he repeatedly introduce, in the earlier books, the hardships he endured in that same prison; in the sixth and final book, no. 9, while discussing an event that had occurred “the day before yesterday,” he also states that he was still “confined in prison.” If two passages in the books themselves do not fit imprisonment, they must be said to have been added and inserted by Ratherius at a later time.

One is a certain admonition of his, taking the form of a letter to the bishops Wido and Sobbo, which is read in Book V, no. 12. We shall show, in note 38 to that same fifth book, that this was added at Como. The other is an event that happened to Ratherius at Laon, which will be found described in the same book, no. 32. We demonstrated in §20 of the author’s *Life* that this belongs to a later period of his life, after he had completely renounced the bishopric of Verona.

## III

Since Ratherius was brought to the prison at Pavia after King Hugh’s victory—see §§4 and 6 of the author’s *Life*—in February 935, and remained confined there for two and a half years, that is, until approximately August 937, this work is now recognized as having been written between February 935 and August 937.

He was writing Book II in September 935, as will become clear from note 23 to that book; Book IV, in which he commemorates the feast of the Holy Innocents, was being composed toward the end of that same year, as will be evident from note 70. Finally, from note 30 you will infer that Ratherius worked on Book V at the beginning of 936.

## IV

He called this work chiefly useful, the *Agonisticus*, because it instructs the Christian athlete for combat. Its scope is very broad, for it instructs people of every rank, condition, sex, and age. Thus the author considered this work exceptionally rich and filled with the finest teachings, to such an extent that he sent copies of it to the most distinguished and “most learned” men he knew: namely, the archbishops Sobbo and Wido; the bishops Godescalc and Aurelius; and also Bruno and Rotbert, the most noble and learned archbishops of Gaul in philosophical studies; finally, Frodoard of Rheims, as Fulcuinus testifies (*Deeds of the Abbots of Lobbes*, chapter 20).

Letters still survive by which this same work was sent to the men mentioned above, except for the letter to Frodoard of Rheims, which is missing.

## V

In the preface he asserts that he composed these books chiefly for his own sake, namely, to arm himself against the hardships with which he was struggling in the prison at Pavia. He notes two other reasons for writing in Book VI, no. 26. The first was that, by reviewing what he had learned through extensive reading, he might recall it, lest it perhaps slip from a memory weakened by grief.

He gives the second reason in his own words:

> “The second [reason is] that, since, as I said, there are no books, no companions with whom to converse, while there is consuming sadness and grief itself incessantly gnawing at the mind, I might have some consolation in this [work], might use it as a kind of conversing friend, and might be refreshed by it as by a sort of companion.”

## VI

Finally, it must be observed that our author declares in the same work that he described himself and his vicissitudes there, but with such caution that he might be thought to be recounting not his own circumstances but those of others:

> “In the prefaces [he means these books of the *Praeloquia*],” he says, “I have almost entirely portrayed myself: my condition, lineage, name, assigned office, fortune—if I dare call it so—and even the torturer himself, writing about my own [circumstances] through certain indications . . . . . Although all these things seem to have been brought forward as though under the personas of others, so that they could not easily be discovered, they have nevertheless been so fitted to me that they immediately become clear when they are presented to the eyes.”

Since he censures not only the faults of his opponents but also those of other people—of many people, indeed, including men of the highest secular and ecclesiastical rank—he nevertheless spared them by not using their proper names:

> “Proceeding cautiously,” he says in the preface to Book III, “let us touch the string of rank in such a way that, like harpists, we remain silent about the person; let us address the order in such a way that, while addressing those ordained, we omit the name.”

For this reason he merely hints at certain events and breaks off others after scarcely indicating them. Referring to this, he says in Book V, no. 12:

> “We could easily weave a long discourse from this, but here we judge that it ought much more to be swallowed up because of that danger which we remember mentioning in the preface to the preceding little book—namely, lest the truth itself bring us hatred. Let the utterly shameful deeds of such people therefore be suppressed here, lest, if by chance they were forced to be brought forward and reported with an insolent recital, the names of those who committed them should produce the greatest turmoil of discord.”

Consequently, many matters are exceedingly obscure and difficult to explain. Since very few documents from this period survive that might shed light on them, even after great effort it was sometimes impossible to establish anything certain, and we had to rely solely on conjecture.

The text also caused no little labor. Since it was extremely corrupt in places—through numerous, and not minor, errors in the words, as well as defective punctuation—it often yielded no intelligible meaning at all. We did not hesitate to insert into the text better punctuation and readings that could safely be emended. We relegated other, less certain emendations, together with certain words that seemed to require supplementation, either to the margin or to the notes.

# The Six Books of Ratherius, Bishop of Verona, of the *Praeloquia*

[Note: Ratherius himself prefixed this title. Fulcuinus, in chapter 20 of *The Deeds of the Abbots of Lobbes*, volume II of Acherius’s *Spicilegium*, column 736 of the latest Paris edition, quotes it somewhat differently, as follows: “Meditations of the heart of a certain Ratherius, indeed bishop of Verona, but monk of Lobbes.” Although, from the arranged sheets, he judged the volume should be called the *Praeloquia*, it is called the *Agonisticon*.]

Meditations of the heart, in exile, of a certain Ratherius, indeed bishop of the Church of Verona but monk of Lobbes, which, arranged in six books, he judged should be called a volume of *Praeloquia*, because they speak beforehand of a certain work of his called the *Agonisticus*.

## The Preface Begins

Since I was free from my episcopal duties, and since both the time and the place and circumstances were equally favorable—

[Note: “Free,” that is, free from the cares of the episcopate. Hence Fulcuinus says in the passage cited above: “During that exile, in which Ratherius said that he had been placed, while relieved of episcopal duties, he published a book which he called the *Agonisticon*.”]

[Note: “And since both the time and the place and circumstances were equally favorable,” that is, because the circumstances of my confinement also smiled upon me—namely, because the prison at Pavia, where I was free from every care and anxiety concerning earthly matters, was likewise favorable.]

—it seemed appropriate to gather in this little book, in the name of the Lord, a few remedies from the innumerable medicines of divine authority. Through them, may the athlete of God, about to wrestle with his adversary in this passing form of the world, daily be anointed with his powers already exerted and his muscles strained, so that, competing lawfully, he may deserve the crown of victory.

[Note: Ratherius seems to have taken this expression metaphorically from Paul, 1 Corinthians 7:31: *παράγει γὰρ τὸ σχῆμα κόσμου τούτου*, “for the form of this world is passing away.” There *schema* signifies an outward form or appearance. Thus “in this form of the world” means “in this world,” whose form or appearance soon becomes visible and passes away.]

So that I may perhaps make this clearer to anyone less inclined to desire these things in this way, I shall try, I say, as much as God grants, to gather from every quarter words of devout supplication, by which our athlete, addressing the wrestling emperor, the elevated spectators, and the supporters of his side, may beseech them to favor him and terrify his enemy alike with fear, blows, and shouting.

[Note: He continues the allegory of wrestling, in which one person tried to throw down and overcome another. By “the wrestling emperor” he means God, who assists Christians wrestling with the devil and wrestles together with them. “The elevated spectators” signifies the angels and saints. This agrees with Book VI, no. 23, where he says: “If, through efforts of devout intention, you first exercise yourself in the field of action, you will, I confess, present yourself as an undefeated athlete to the wrestling emperor and to all the elevated spectators.”]

Let the reader, or anyone who proceeds through this work—understand, “this little book”—know that it applies especially to the person who, stripped of every concern of the present world and entirely freed from all cares of passing things that cloud the watchtower of the mind, is confined somewhere either voluntarily or by another’s command, whether in order to pursue true philosophy or in defense of justice and truth, which properly belongs to the blessed, as the Lord himself testifies (Matthew 5:10), or, as often happens, for the correction of some fault.

[Note: He distinguishes two kinds of people who were confined somewhere for the correction of a fault. Some were confined voluntarily, others at another’s command. The first were those who withdrew into monasteries for the sake of penance or out of love of solitude; they were called *inclusi* or *reclusi*, “enclosed” or “recluses.” Concerning these terms, see Du Cange. Others were those who, for some reason, were thrust into prison. Ratherius himself belonged to the latter group. He testifies in Letter 5 to Pope John, no. 4, that he had been confined by King Hugh in a little tower at Pavia, not without some fault of his own, since he might have appeared to have favored Arnulf, duke of Bavaria, against Hugh. We discuss this more fully in §4 of the author’s *Life*.]

This little book, composed chiefly for my own sake, but necessary for many if they should deem it so, may anyone who finds it useful in any respect, I ask, call with me the *Agonisticus*, or the medicinal work. For he will find it both highly persuasive for battle and exceedingly useful as medicine, if he is willing to judge its contents as they stand. On one side it summons you to battle; on the other, it soothes and heals the wounds inflicted by the adversary through the marvelous care of its art. Here it urges the strong and robust to combat; there it reforms and restores the broken, the enervated, and the defeated. Now it raises up the humble and timid so that he may dare; now, by reproving the elevated person who presumes upon his own strength, it humbles him and shows him in whose strength he ought to place his confidence. At one moment it removes the security of those who idly remain at leisure; at another it reveals the reward of those who fight bravely. Now it foretells the battle of temptations; now it promises the palm of victory.

Come, then, proceed now on your course under sound guidance, and investigate for yourself whether all these things are so. You will find almost nothing of mine that ought to produce distaste; you will find everything culled from the sayings of the holy Fathers. First, if you wish, read this admonition of the preface, divided into six brief *Praeloquia*—quite brief with respect to its subject, though somewhat more verbose in estimation.

Perhaps you will derive some benefit from it that will kindle your desire for what follows—or rather, that will make entirely clear why we wished to publish it.

Moreover, I entreat and implore you, reader or transcriber of this work, by him who lives forever and by his terrible judgment, and by that charity through which “God loved us and gave himself for us as an offering and sacrifice to God, for a fragrant odor” (Ephesians 5:2), not to omit what I place here at the beginning as a precaution whenever you undertake either to read or to copy this work.

Certain things are found in these little works that the author himself does not entirely approve—for example, what he recounts in Books III and IV concerning the deeds or sufferings of a certain Origen.

[Note: By the name “a certain Origen,” Ratherius seems to refer to himself. He is the person whose deeds or sufferings he recounts in Books III and IV. See Book III, no. 13 and following, and note 10 to that book; also Book IV, almost throughout.]

But since, on account of these matters, the work is supported all the more by testimonies of divine authority, forgive, I ask you, reader, one who narrates matters partly seen, partly heard, partly uncertain, and partly discovered, without concerning yourself whether the substance of the deeds contained in these books of the *Praeloquia* is true, false, or doubtful—provided that you receive the truth and the sound teaching of the words with all the greater willingness, the less you observe them to deviate from the path of uprightness.

It is true that this *Praeloquium* contains:

1. Any Private Person—that is, the following *Praeloquium*;
2. The Soldier;
3. The Artisan;
4. The Physician;
5. The Merchant;
6. The Advocate;
7. The Judge;
8. The Witness;
9. The Procurator;
10. The Patron;
11. The Hired Worker;
12. The Counselor;
13. The Master;
14. The Servant;
15. The Teacher;
16. The Student;
17. The Rich Person;
18. The Person of Moderate Means;
19. The Beggar.

# The First Book Begins

### 1

Although all the Lord’s commandments generally apply to the entire Church, certain commandments are specially suited to individuals according to the diversity of times, ranks, conditions, ages, habits, dispositions, sexes, and circumstances.

In peacetime, for example, one is commanded to give up one’s tunic (Matthew 5:40), whereas in persecution one is commanded to lay down even one’s life for a brother (1 John 3:16). When the Lord says, “Sell everything you have, give to the poor, and come, follow me” (Matthew 19:21), if everyone immediately fulfilled this command, who would cultivate the earth? Again, if everyone abandoned their wives, from where would offspring continue? When he says, “Give alms” (Luke 12:33), what will the person give who has retained nothing for himself?

When he says, “Give to everyone who asks of you,” as Matthew seems to say,

[Note: Here Ratherius, who lacked books, mistakenly cited Matthew instead of Luke. The quoted testimony is found in Luke 7:30.]

he addresses everyone, exhorts everyone, and leaves no one out. If you have something to give, give it; do not delay. If you have nothing, give yourself: offer the benevolent disposition of a generous mind.

“For glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14). And the Psalmist says: “In me are your vows, O God” (Psalm 55:12).

Again, when he says, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your mind, and with all your strength, and your neighbor as yourself; you shall not steal, you shall not kill, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not bear false witness, you shall not covet your neighbor’s property or wife” (Luke 10:17), he addresses everyone: young and old, male and female, slave and free, rich and poor, clergy and laity. He spares no one, excludes no one, and embraces everyone. No one who transgresses these commandments is innocent; no one can commit them without guilt.

Thus, in matters of this kind, there appears to be no distinction.

[Note: The passage is corrupt or incomplete, but its meaning seems to be this: in matters of this kind there appears to be no difference or distinction among people. The sense is similar below, no. 17, where, from Deuteronomy 1:16, he says: “Let there be no distinction of persons.”]

## Title I — The Duties of Christians

### 2

Do you wish to be a Christian—a good Christian among the many Christians, from the people, the assembly, the congregation, the common crowd, the outlanders, or the country folk?

Be a laborer who is not merely just but also diligent; content with what is yours; defrauding no one, harming no one, insulting no one, and slandering no one. Fear God, pray to the saints, attend church, honor the priests, offer to God the tithes and first fruits of your labors, and give alms according to your means.

Love your wife; know no woman besides her. Even with her, on certain days—that is, feast days and days of fasting—abstain by mutual agreement out of fear of God. Raise your children in the fear of God. Visit the sick; bury the dead. Give others what you want for yourself, but do not do to another what you do not want done to you.

## Title II — On Soldiers

### 3

Are you a soldier? In addition to these things, hear what John the Baptist says:

> “Do not extort anything from anyone, do not accuse anyone falsely, and be content with your pay” (Luke 3:14).

If you cannot earn your pay by soldiering, pursue your livelihood by working with your hands. Flee plunder; beware of murder; avoid sacrilege.

“What sacrilege?” you ask. That sacrilege, namely, which the Psalmist recalls so terrifyingly. Hear him:

> “They said, ‘Let us take possession of the sanctuary of God as an inheritance.’ My God, make them like a wheel, and like straw before the face of the wind; like fire that burns a forest, and like a flame that consumes the mountains. So you will pursue them with your power, and in your anger you will trouble them, and so forth” (Psalm 82:13).

The sanctuary of the Lord is whatever has been offered to the Lord and belongs to his house.

[Note: Here he seems to be attacking the abuse by which offerings made to God and given to churches were handed over as benefices to soldiers or noble laymen. Thus, in the work on Saint Metrone, no. 3, speaking of the church of Saint Vitalis at Verona, he complains that its revenues had been given to soldiers. See also note 16 there.]

For Moses says:

> “Everything that is offered to the Lord is holy, the holy things of the Lord, and belongs by right to the priests” (Leviticus 18:23).

But hear how displeasing plunder is to God:

> “Because of the misery of the needy and the groaning of the poor, now I will rise, says the Lord” (Psalm 2:6).

By “rising,” that is, preparing himself for vengeance, he shows what he will do when he says:

> “Will the Lord not avenge his elect who cry out to him? Will he have patience with them? I tell you that he will quickly avenge them” (Luke 18:8).

Hear what this vengeance will be:

> “The vengeance of the impious flesh is fire and worms” (Sirach 7:19).

“But then,” you say, “there will be fire, yet extinguishable, and worms, yet mortal.” The Prophet, on the contrary, says:

> “Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be extinguished” (Isaiah 66:24).

Understand “flesh” as expressing the whole human being through the lesser part, just as Scripture often understands the whole person by “soul,” through the greater part.

Likewise:

> “The Lord will not show partiality to the poor, and he will hear the prayer of the injured. He will not despise the prayers of the orphan, nor the widow when she pours out her complaint. Do not the widow’s tears rise up [or, perhaps, descend] to his cheek, and her cry against the one who causes them? For they rise from her cheek to heaven, and the Lord, who hears, will not be pleased with them” (Sirach 35:16).

Finally:

> “The bread of the needy is the life of the poor; whoever defrauds him is a man of blood; whoever takes away bread earned by sweat is like one who kills his neighbor” (Sirach 34:25–26).

The holy apostle John says:

> “Every murderer has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God” (1 John 3:15).

### 4

But perhaps, when the Lord says, “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity” (Luke 16:9), you think that you can redeem yourself through the same plunder. Hear that same writer cited above:

> “The offering of one who sacrifices from unjust gain is defiled, and the mockeries of the unjust are not pleasing. The Most High does not approve the gifts of the wicked, nor does he look upon the offerings of the unjust; nor will he be reconciled to their sins by the multitude of their sacrifices. Whoever offers a sacrifice from the substance of the poor is like one who sacrifices a son before his father” (Sirach 34:21–24).

Hence Maximus, speaking about fasting, says:

> “What good does it do not to eat one’s own bread while seizing the food of the wretched?”

And again:

> “You will rightly give a coin to the poor if you have not taken it away from someone else.”

Again, the writer cited above says:

> “Do not offer a corrupt gift, for God will not accept it, since the Lord is judge, and with him there is no partiality toward persons” (Sirach 35:14).

The Prophet also says:

> “Woe to you who plunder; will you not yourself be plundered?” (Isaiah 33:1).

Job likewise says:

> “The soul of the wounded will cry out, and the Lord does not permit it to go unavenged” (Job 14:12).

And truly:

> “To you,” says the Psalmist, “the poor person is abandoned; you will be the helper of the orphan” (Psalm 9:34).

Comparing these few passages with the innumerable testimonies of divine law, therefore, practice temporal soldiery in such a way that you do not lose your soul, which lives eternally.

## Title III — On Artisans

### 5

Are you an artisan? Hear:

> “The prayer of artisans is in the work of their craft, applying their mind and seeking the law of the Most High” (Sirach 38:39).

Understand from this that, through your very work, you can offer God acceptable praise—namely, the praise of prayers—if you strive to apply your mind to God and seek the law of the Most High by keeping the words of his commandment.

This happens if, while your craft is available to support the body, you strive to make it also some assistance to the soul. From it, finally, give alms; give tithes to the Lord. Remember that from everything he has bestowed, he always demands what belongs to him. Take care lest, if you withhold his portion from him, you rather deprive yourself of your own portion, both in the present and in the future.

## Title IV — On Physicians

### 6

And, moving from the general category to a particular kind of artisan by addressing one of them, are you a physician? Hear the Lord commanding you literally as well:

> “Physician, heal yourself” (Luke 4:23).

That is, while you treat bodily illnesses in others, strive to heal the health of your own morals.

This happens if you strive to serve your Creator through the very skill of healing: toward the poor, using the command that the Lord gives in the Gospel,

> “You received without payment; give without payment” (Matthew 10:8);

toward the rich, using the Apostle’s command,

[Note: The text read *illius apostoli*, “of that apostle,” incorrectly. The context requires the correction. Just as in the preceding passage he said that he should use the command of the Gospel, so here the phrase “using the command of the Apostle” is understood before the quoted words.]

> “Let no one defraud his brother in business, for the Lord is the avenger of all these things” (1 Thessalonians 4:6), and so forth.

Thus, you should mercifully assist the poor without payment for the love of God, but faithfully provide treatment to the rich for the remuneration you receive, lest, by defrauding them, you experience God as their avenger.

“But,” you say, “I did not receive without payment, as you claim, because I purchased instruction from teachers for a fee and medical substances at a price; moreover, I am very often burdened by vigils and many labors for the sake of medicine and the sick.”

The Lord replies:

> “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:4).

The Apostle also says:

> “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Corinthians 4:7).

And again:

> “Who has first given to him, so that he might be repaid?” (Romans 11:35).

James likewise says:

> “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above” (James 1:17).

For it is as though God were now confronting you, saying: “Who gave you the payment that you have bestowed? Was it not I? Who gave your teacher the knowledge to teach, and you the understanding to learn? Was it not I? Does this saying escape you: ‘All wisdom is from the Lord God’?” (Sirach 1:1).

Who could have given you the will by which your teacher would at least teach you for payment, if I had entirely turned it away? Who granted you the price with which you paid for the medicines? Through whose help did you enjoy ability, inclination, and comfort in your labors? Finally, while you were working, who granted effectiveness to your work? Was it not often your experience that your labor was worth nothing unless I decided to grant health?

When, in two people suffering from a similar illness, one medicine restored one person to life and sent the other to burial, from where did all these things come to you? By what merits of yours? By what privilege? By what reward? By what services?

Recognizing me—me, the giver of gifts, me, the one who apportions the results of works—carry out this art with such humility, charity, prudence, and utmost caution that you consider me present with both parties, so that both here you may obtain the beneficial result of your work and there you may deserve to be rewarded for your own labor.

### 7

Recognizing also that there is a considerable distinction between light and darkness, truth and falsehood, the works of the devil and the kindness of God, consider what belongs to medicine and what belongs to the deception of sorcerers.

To carry out, in God’s name, through pigments, herbs, and various substances of creation, what the most skilled intelligence inspired by him has discovered belongs to physicians.

[Note: *Pigmentum* is here understood as a medicinal drink compounded from various ingredients.]

But to use auguries, incantations, or other superstitious practices of sacrilege belongs to astrologers or Marsi.

[Note: The printed editions had *Marsorum*, “of the Marsi,” corruptly. The Marsi were not in Africa but, as the author himself adds shortly afterward, in Italy. Since he has just named astrologers before the Marsi, we have corrected the text to *mathematicorum*, “of astrologers,” whose particular class or species is here described in Africa. Shortly afterward he calls these people not Marsi but Psylli, in their proper name. Pliny assigns similar practices to them in Book VII, chapter 2. He says that the Psylli, peoples of Africa named after King Psyllus, customarily exposed newborn children to snakes in order to test the chastity of their mothers.]

There is a class of astrologers in Africa to whom snakes do no harm. When they wish to test whether their children are truly theirs, they send them among snakes; and if they are of foreign stock, the snakes devour them.

The Psylli, on the other hand, were in Africa, while the Marsi were in Italy, as enchanters of snakes; they either killed them or prevented them from causing harm.

[Note: Pliny, in the passage cited above, mentions the Psylli of Africa and the Marsi of Italy, who were famous for enchanting snakes. A poison was said to be innate in their bodies, and its odor put snakes to sleep. The Marsi, however, healed snakebites with their saliva. Thus the Psylli and the Marsi are said to have been different kinds of snake enchanters: the Psylli killed snakes by their odor, whereas the Marsi prevented them from causing harm through their saliva.]
