For a carbuncle, or malignant pustules—the ailment commonly called *malampnum*—the remedy, they say, is this: a herb called *radix* in the Frankish tongue is to be thoroughly crushed and squeezed out, and placed upon it.

[Note: In the Benedictine history of the translation of Saint Augustine and his companions, inserted by Mabillon in Part II, p. 738, we read: “A carbuncle, a disease which the Franks, by antiphrasis, call *bonum malamnum*, ‘the good evil.’” Accordingly, Ratherius seems to require correction here from *quem malum* to *quod malum*, unless one takes *quem* as referring to the carbuncle, and *malum* not as a noun but as an adjective joined to the noun *malampnum*.]

It should remain upon the wound until the same hour at which it was applied. Care must be taken also to give the sick person the juice of the root to drink at the same time, lest the poison return inwardly to the heart. The root should then continually be taken as food, little by little until the hour at which it was applied, as much as possible so that it does not perhaps cause nausea.

[Note: *Radix* is Italian *radicchio*, Latin *cichorium*, chicory.]

But something unspeakable, which ought not even to be mentioned here, written on a slip of paper in the shape of a crown and placed upon the wound, although it may seem to produce the same effect, provides no remedy, because it is sorcery; rather, it brings extremely deadly danger to the soul.

But what of the fact that such things very often seem to bring genuine bodily health? I say, on the contrary, that reason itself gives the answer.

What of the fact that the devil, although—according to the Lord’s testimony—he never stood in the truth, often seems to speak the truth? Will the word of Truth therefore be nullified when he says:

> “He was a murderer from the beginning, and he never stood in the truth, because there is no truth in him” (John 8:44)?

### 8.

But lest I leave you wholly ignorant through this, and lest you either falsely declare these things accursed to any Christian in order to deceive him, or suppose them so in order to be deceived, I offer—not from my own words but from theirs—certain passages from which you may derive complete satisfaction and have no grounds for doubt. [Col. 0153B] For Aurelius Augustine of blessed memory says in Book Four of *On the Trinity* (chapter 17):

> “The aerial powers, proud and deceitful—even if they are found to have uttered through their prophets certain things that they had heard from the fellowship and city of the saints and from the true Mediator, through holy prophets or angels—did this so that, through these foreign truths, they might also lead the faithful from God over to their own falsehoods. God, however, did this through those who were unaware, so that truth might resound everywhere: for the faithful, as assistance; for the impious, as testimony.” [Col. 0153C]

This, then, explains why the devil [editorially supplied: *diabolus*] often appears to speak the truth. But why does the devil sometimes appear to provide bodily health? Hear it from the words of Mark the martyr, as it is read in the passion of Saint Sebastian:

> “This,” he says, “is the whole cunning of the battle; this is the devil’s fraudulent design: to rescue the body from punishments and subject the soul to vices. Let us, on the contrary, strive not to yield to the enemy, to despise the body, and to assist the soul.” [Col. 0153C]

That this is so is also clear from the confession of the devil himself—the most mendacious of beings—when he was compelled by divine power through the Apostle Bartholomew, as it is read in the passion of that same saint. [Col. 0153D]

And these things concern the devil’s ever-iniquitous will: the will, I mean, to deceive by words and to mislead by benefits, through which he often, by God’s just permission, draws people through false goods to genuine evils.

[Note: Construe as follows: “And these things concern the devil’s ever-iniquitous will to deceive by words and mislead by benefits, through which he often, by God’s just permission, draws people through false goods to genuine evils.” Now certain matters must be said concerning the devil’s just power, which often, although unwillingly, he exercises by God’s mercy: through it he educates the faithful toward good and leads the impious to their deserved punishments—the former, when they are corrected after being scourged by this power; the latter, when they are punished after being subjected to it, especially since those deceived by this power attribute it to the deceiver himself. If you seek something more persuasive than what Augustine says, you desire to surpass humanity, and so forth.] [Col. 0154D]

Now something must be said concerning that just power by which the devil often, although unwillingly, educates the faithful toward good and leads the impious to their deserved punishments: the faithful, while they are corrected by being scourged through it; the impious, while they are punished after being subjected to it—especially since, having been deceived through it, they attribute it to the deceiver himself. I shall relate certain passages set forth by Augustine in Book Three of the work mentioned above; if you seek anything more persuasive than these, you desire to surpass humanity, although you know that it is written: “Do not seek what is too high for you” (Ecclesiasticus 3:22).

[Augustine, *On the Trinity*, Book III, chapter 7.]

> “I see,” he says, “what may occur to a weak understanding when certain matters have been placed before it: namely, why these miracles are also performed by magical arts. For the magicians of Pharaoh likewise made serpents, and other similar things (Exodus 7:12). But this is more worthy of wonder: how the power of the magicians, which could make serpents, failed entirely when it came to the tiniest flies. For *cinifes* are very small gnats, by which the proud people of Egypt were struck in the third plague. There, when the magicians failed, they said: ‘This is the finger of God’ (ibid. 8:19). [Col. 0154A]

> “From this it is understood that not even the transgressing angels and aerial powers—cast down from the dwelling of that lofty ethereal purity into this deepest darkness, as into a prison belonging to their own kind—can make magical arts effective in whatever way they are effective, unless power has been granted from above. Power is granted either to deceive the deceitful, as it was granted against the Egyptians and even against the magicians themselves, so that they might appear wonderful through the seduction of those spirits by whom they were being condemned by God’s truth; or to admonish the faithful, so that they might not greatly desire to perform such things, for which reason these matters have also been handed down to us by the authority of Scripture; or to teach, test, and manifest the patience of the righteous.

> “For it was not by a small power of visible miracles that Job lost everything he had, including his children and even his bodily health. Yet one must not therefore suppose that the material of visible things obeys these transgressing angels at their command; rather, it obeys God, by whom this power is granted to the extent that He judges unchangeably from His sublime and spiritual seat. Even for condemned and wicked men, water, fire, and earth serve in metal, so that they may make from it whatever they wish—but only insofar as they are permitted. [Col. 0154B]

> “Nor should those wicked angels be called creators because, through them, the magicians resisting God’s servant made frogs and serpents. They did not themselves create them. For hidden seeds of all things that are born bodily and visibly lie concealed in the corporeal elements of this world. Some of these are already visible to our eyes in fruits and living creatures; others are the hidden seeds of those seeds, from which, at the Creator’s command, water first produced swimming and flying creatures, while earth produced the first plants and the first animals of its kind.

> “For these offspring were not then produced in such a way that the whole power of generation was completed in the things produced. Rather, suitable opportunities of combination are often lacking, through which they may burst forth and complete their forms. Consider: a tiny shoot is a seed, since, when suitably planted in the earth, it produces a tree. The subtler seed of this shoot is some grain of the same kind; and this, in turn, is visible to us up to this point. [Col. 0154C]

> “The seed of this grain, however, although we cannot see it with our eyes, we can nevertheless infer by reason, because unless some such power existed in these elements, things that had not been sown there would not often spring from the earth. Nor would so many animals be born, without any preceding union of males and females, whether on land or in water—animals that nevertheless grow and, by mating, produce others, although they themselves arose without parents having mated. Bees, certainly, do not conceive the seeds of their offspring by mating; rather, they gather them with their mouths as though scattered throughout the earth.

> “The Creator of invisible seeds is Himself the Creator of all things, since whatever comes forth by being born into our sight receives from hidden seeds the beginnings of its development, the increases appropriate to its size, and the distinctions of its forms from their original patterns, as from rules. Therefore, just as we do not call parents the creators of human beings, nor farmers the creators of crops, although through the external movements they apply God’s creating power works inwardly; so it is not permissible to regard either wicked or good angels as creators. Rather, according to the subtlety of their perception and body, they know more hidden seeds of these things than we do; they secretly scatter them through suitable combinations of the elements and thus provide opportunities for things to be generated and for their growth to be accelerated. [Col. 0154D]

[Note: This reading seems better than that in the common editions of Augustine: *si pro subtilitate* (“if according to subtlety”).]

[Note: Many manuscripts of Augustine read more appropriately: “And this up to us.”]

> “Yet the good do not do these things except insofar as God commands, nor do the wicked do them unjustly except insofar as He Himself justly permits it. For the wicked person’s malice has his own unjust will; but he receives power only justly, whether for his own punishment, or for the punishment of other wicked people, or for the praise of the good.” [Col. 0155A]

### 9.

And again, shortly afterward (chapter 9):

> “One thing,” he says, “is to establish and govern creation from the innermost and highest pivot of causes. He who does this is God alone, the Creator. Another thing is to apply some operation externally through the powers and capacities distributed by Him, so that what is being created may emerge at one time or another, in one way or another. For all things have already been created originally and primordially in a certain structure of the elements, but they emerge when suitable opportunities are provided. [Col. 0155B]

> “For just as mothers are pregnant with offspring, so the world itself is pregnant with the causes of things being born. These causes are not created within it except by that highest Essence in whom nothing dies or is born, nothing begins to be or ceases to be. Not only wicked angels but also wicked human beings can apply externally additional causes which, although they are not natural, are nevertheless applied according to nature, so that the things hidden in the secret womb of nature may somehow burst forth and be created outwardly, unfolding their measures, numbers, and weights—the things they received secretly from Him who arranged all things in measure, number, and weight (chapter II, 21). I have already taught this above by the example of agriculture.

> “Nor should the matter of animals disturb anyone as though it involved a different principle because they possess the breath of life, together with the sense of desiring what is according to nature and avoiding what is contrary to it. It is evident how many people know from which herbs or meats, or from the juices and fluids of any kinds of things, whether placed in one way, buried in another, crushed in another, or mixed in another, animals are ordinarily born. [Variant: Augustine reads *quae* (“which”) for *quod* (“that”).] Yet who would be so mad as to dare call himself their creator? [Col. 0155D]

> “What wonder is it, then, if, just as any utterly wicked human being can know from what source particular worms and flies are born, wicked angels, according to the sublimity of their perception, know from the more hidden seeds of the elements from what source frogs and serpents are born, and, applying these through hidden movements at definite and known opportunities of combination, cause them to be created—but do not create them?

> “Human beings do not marvel at the things that human beings themselves commonly do. If anyone happens to marvel at the speed of the elements—at the fact that those animals were made so quickly—let him consider how even these things are produced by human beings, according to the limited measure of human ability. [Note: Augustine reads more appropriately, “the speed of their growths” (*incrementorum*).] Why do bodies become worm-infested more quickly in summer than in winter, and more quickly in warmer places than in colder ones? [Note: Augustine has “the same bodies” (*eadem corpora*).] [Col. 0156A] Human beings apply these conditions with greater difficulty because the subtlety of their senses and the mobility of their bodies are lacking in earthly and sluggish limbs.

> “Thus, the nearer causes of the elements are more easily gathered by angels of whatever kind; and, correspondingly, their speed in such works appears more marvelous. Yet no one is a creator except the one who forms these things in their primary fashion. No one can do this except the one with whom the measures, numbers, and weights of all things first reside. He is the one God, the Creator, from whose ineffable power it also comes about that, although these angels could do certain things if they were permitted, they cannot do them because they are not permitted. [Col. 0156B]

> “For there is no other apparent reason why they could not make the tiniest flies, although they made frogs and serpents, except that the domination of God, who was prohibiting them through His Spirit, was greater. The magicians themselves also confessed this when they said: ‘This is the finger of God’ (Exodus 8:19). [Col. 0156C]

[Note: Augustine’s text has “through the Holy Spirit.”]

> “What they can do by nature but cannot do because of prohibition, and what they cannot do because of the condition of their very nature, is difficult for a human being to investigate—or rather, impossible—except through that gift of God which the Apostle mentions when he says: ‘To another, the discerning of spirits’ (1 Corinthians 12:10). [Col. 0156D]

> “For we know that a human being can walk, yet cannot even do this unless permitted; but cannot fly, even if permitted. So those angels can do certain things if they are permitted by more powerful angels acting under God’s command; but they cannot do other things, even if they are permitted by those angels, because He does not permit them—the One from whom they have received such a limit of nature, and who, through His angels, often does not permit even those things which He has granted them the ability to do.

> “Apart, therefore, from those things that occur bodily in the order of nature through the customary passage of time—such as the risings and settings of the heavenly bodies, the generations and deaths of animals, the countless varieties of seeds and sprouts, mists and clouds, snow and rain, lightning and thunder, thunderbolts and hail, winds and fire, cold and heat, and all such things—and apart also from those things which, in that same order of nature, are rare, such as eclipses of the heavenly lights, unusual appearances of the stars, prodigies, earthquakes, and similar phenomena—all of which have no first and highest cause other than the will of God: hence, when certain things of this kind had been mentioned in the Psalm—‘Fire, hail, snow, ice, and storm-wind’ (Psalm 148:8)—lest anyone believe that they occur either by chance, or merely through bodily causes, or even through spiritual causes existing apart from God’s will, it immediately adds: ‘Which do His word.’ But apart from these, as I began to say, there are other things which, although they arise from the same bodily material, are nevertheless brought divinely before our senses to announce something; these are properly called miracles and signs.” [Col. 0157A]

### 10.

Here you have the authority of so great a teacher: demons can do many things through that angelic nature of theirs, and yet cannot do certain things because of divine prohibition. They can do nothing, however, unless power has been granted from above—either to deceive the deceitful, such as the Egyptians, whose kind are those who either venerate the devil’s deceptions as divine or desire them as beneficial, although they are much more detestable than those who practice them, or through whom they are practiced, as though they were powers; or to admonish and test the faithful. [Col. 0157B]

They admonish them so that, by desiring to do similar things, they may not become like the demons; they test them so that, instructed, exercised, and exposed by these trials, they may show how far they are raised up by the devil [printed *erecti*; perhaps *erepti*, “snatched away”] and are subject to God.

For who among those who are deceived today by such matters to the destruction of their souls—so thoroughly that they even propose as queen, indeed as a goddess, that Herodias whom, as Gen. says, they call the slayer of Christ’s Baptist—would, on seeing someone scourged with such great miraculous power, and this through demons, as that extraordinary man Job was, encourage him to say, or even believe that it was justly said: “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; as it has pleased the Lord, so has it happened” (Job 1:21)? [Col. 0157C]

[Note: Jerome Tartarottus considers this passage corrupt in *Del congresso notturno delle Lamie*, Book I, chapter 5. After the relative *quas*, which he thinks is missing several words indicating the nocturnal assembly of the Lamiae, it has not been possible to discover which “Gen.” is being cited here. Several writers made Herodias the presiding figure of such nocturnal assemblies; Tartarottus carefully collected them. What if, instead of *quas*, one reads *de quibus*? The woman to whom Herod promised that he would give a third of his kingdom was not Herodias but Herodias’s daughter. Since the daughter’s name is not given in the Gospel, the unknown author “Gen.” from whom Ratherius took this passage believed that mother and daughter had the same name.] [Col. 0157D]

Would he not instead attribute it not only to wicked angels but also to certain wretched human beings, believing that any sender or, as they say, repeller of storms is to be summoned and appeased with gifts so that he might deign to remedy the matter, just as Mercury once healed the companions of Ulysses by touching them with his herald’s staff? [Col. 0158A]

[Note: Here he attacks the error of those who, persuaded that certain people possessed the power to send and dispel storms, gave them gifts so that they would avert them. This error had become so prevalent in the preceding century that Agobard, bishop of Lyons, wrote a tract against it, entitled *Against the Foolish Popular Opinion concerning Hail and Thunder*. These people were called *Tempestarii* by Agobard and by other authors of the same age whom Baluze cites in his notes on Agobard. Ratherius refutes the same error again in Sermon I, on the Ascension, no. 4.] [Col. 0158C]

[Note: Supply “he believes,” or something similar. The passage should be construed and explained as follows: “Rather, attributing this”—that is, someone’s being scourged as Job was—“not only to wicked angels but also to certain wretched human beings, he believes that anyone who casts off or drives away storms, as they say, is summoned with gifts so that he might deign to remedy the matter,” just as Mercury once healed Ulysses’ companions by touching them with his herald’s staff. For—not to mention so great a loss to such great glory as Job’s—people would not do this even over some worthless little object, such as a knife or a strap, if the preceding words mean that they would not encourage anyone to say, or believe that it was justly said, “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away,” and so forth. Yet we have often seen this done—namely, recourse to superstitions in order to recover lost things—by those in whose hearts the words of our frequently mentioned Augustine have not sounded: “You rejoice because you found your possessions,” and so forth.] [Col. 0158C–D]

For I shall not even speak of the loss of so great a glory as belonged to blessed Job: people would not do this for a most worthless little object, whether a knife or a strap. Yet we have often seen it done by those in whose hearts the words of our frequently mentioned Augustine have not resounded:

> “You rejoice because you have found your possessions; you are not sad because you have perished. Your tunic would have perished much more readily than your soul.” [Col. 0158B]

And also the Psalmist’s words:

> “Let all who practice vanity be put to shame” (Psalm 24:3).

The Apostle likewise says concerning a much lesser fault:

> “You observe days and months and seasons and years; I fear that I may have labored over you in vain” (Galatians 4:10).

And in the Fourth Book of Kings:

> “Is there no God in Israel, that you go to consult Beelzebub, the god of Ekron?”

Therefore the Lord says this concerning King Ahaziah:

> “You shall not come down from the bed to which you have gone up, but you shall surely die” (4 Kings 1:16).

### 11.

And behold, through this example, although certain people often appear to be healed by such practices—whether they are spared by God’s mercy in expectation of repentance or abandoned to themselves by His justice—know what they deserve when seized by God’s judgment. For if the just Judge were to avenge everything in this age, there would be no need for that final judgment; but if He cared for no human affairs, scarcely anyone would believe it. [Col. 0158C]

Know, therefore, according to the judgment of a certain supremely wise man, that it is not fitting for you to seek the protection of the most contemptible spirits, when that Wisdom wishes to shape you toward such excellence that, insofar as His concession allows, He can make you like God. Consider also, as that same teacher instructs, that such is the nature of minds that whenever they cast aside true opinions, they are clothed in false ones. [Col. 0159A]

Exercise yourself especially in this: as I suggested at the beginning of my address, prefer the genuine skill of physicians inspired by God, because experience has shown it to be sound, to the madness of wretched prostitutes, driven by the devil, which they have invented. Thus no darkness of unbelief will confuse that true judgment by which something appears to be appropriate to do. For the sake of wisdom and of the assistance of healing granted by God, you will receive from kings—or rather, as Scripture says, from the King of all kings—both a temporal and an eternal gift (Ecclesiasticus 38:2–8). Discipline, too, will exalt your head, and you will be praised in the presence of the great. Your virtue will be recognized among human beings, and the Most High will grant you knowledge to be honored in His wonders. In these matters you will soothe pains while caring for the sick, prepare fragrant medicines, and compound healing ointments; your works will not be consumed, but the peace of God will always rest upon the face of your land. [Col. 0159B]

## Title V—On Merchants

### 12.

Are you a merchant? Listen:

> “Because of poverty many have sinned, and he who seeks to become rich will turn away his eye. As a stake is driven into the middle of a joint of stones, so sin becomes wedged between buying and selling. Sin will be crushed together with the sinner. If you do not constantly restrain yourself in the fear of the Lord, your house will quickly be overturned” (Ecclesiasticus 27:1). [Col. 0159C]

And again:

> “Nothing is more wicked than the miser. Nothing is more unjust than loving money; for such a person has sold his own soul” (Ecclesiasticus 10:9).

But the Lord says in the Gospel:

> “See and beware of all greed, because a person’s life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions on earth” (Luke 12:15).

And again, the one cited above says:

> “Gold and silver have destroyed many” (Ecclesiasticus 8:3);

and:

> “For a man who is greedy and grasping, wealth is without reason; and he who gathers unjustly gathers for others, and another will squander his goods” (Ecclesiasticus 14:3).

Again:

> “The merchant is scarcely freed from negligence, and the innkeeper will not be justified from the sins of his lips” (Ecclesiasticus 26:28). [Col. 0159D]

Since these things are so, consider, I beg you, how dangerous a calling you have undertaken for your soul. Know that, although with somewhat greater excuse, you are called a publican together with robbers. The word by which you hear many people calling you *cupidenarius* shows that you serve vice—not a minor one. [Col. 0160D]

[Note: The reading was *cupedinarius*. But this word conflicts with the sense of the passage. For, according to Donatus’s interpretation of Terence, *cupedinarii* are sellers of food and drink—people who sell delicacies, that is, more luxurious foods and rarer wines. We have introduced the correction *cupidenarius*, which agrees with Ratherius’s meaning. The manuscripts of Uguccio cited by Du Cange have: “A *cupidenarius* is a merchant greedy for money.”]

For, as the Apostle testifies, “the root of all evils is greed” (1 Timothy 6:10).

### 13.

Nevertheless, do not despair, because it is written:

> “The blessing of the Lord is upon the head of those who sell” (Proverbs 2:26).

But consider whose heads. Therefore, while it is still day, do what I urge you:

> “Lend to your neighbor in the time of his need; for he shows mercy who lends to his neighbor, and he who prevails by his hand keeps the commandments” (Ecclesiasticus 20:2). [Col. 0160A]

Invite Christ into your house. Prepare a banquet and supper for Him. Wash His feet, bathe them with tears, dry them with your hair, feed Him, clothe Him, warm Him, give Him drink, receive Him as a guest. He will not disdain to turn aside to your house; indeed, He thrusts Himself forward openly. Every day He asks to be received, although you ought to compel Him. He is concerned not with His own need but with your greed.

Then hasten to His house. Address His disciples; offer gifts and entreat them to provide and obtain from God for you forgiveness, counsel, and indulgence.

Consider, while you heap up profit at home, how great a loss you are acquiring for your soul. For the Lord says:

> “What does it profit a person if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul?” (Matthew 16:26). [Col. 0160B]

And the Apostle says:

> “The world is passing away, and its desire” (1 John 2:17).

Fear, therefore, lest, while you greedily yearn for transitory things, you be deprived of those that endure. Be a good physician to yourself. From the instrument of greed, bring assistance to your soul:

> “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity,”

the Lord says (Luke 16:9).

In saying this He does not encourage fraud, but, after you have committed fraud, He invites you to correction. For example, you certainly ought not to have robbed anything, gathered anything by wicked cleverness, or deceived anyone in any transaction. You ought to have been certain—since the Apostle predicts and testifies that the omnipotent Lord is the avenger of such things (1 Thessalonians 4:6)—and remained content with the food of the day, hoping for everything from God, who feeds even the birds every day (Matthew 6:26). Whatever He had given, you ought yourself to have received with thanksgiving and shared with others; what He did not wish to give, you ought neither to desire but to glorify His justice.

### 14.

But why, having transgressed these commands, did you seize things violently, gather them fraudulently, love usury and excess, surrender yourself to your own cleverness, prove ungrateful to God, who gives everything although you are unworthy, fail to share with another according to the Lord’s command, seek repeatedly what He did not wish to give, and, when you did not obtain it, murmur many times?

After all these things—which ought never to have occurred—He does not yet wish to destroy you. He shows you the riches of His goodness and prepares an antidote of forgiveness for you from the very poison of greed:

> “When you fail, they may receive you into the eternal dwellings” (Luke 16:9). [Col. 0160D]

Therefore distribute what was badly acquired, more badly found, and most wickedly gathered to those who, when life fails, will be able to repay you in heaven, recompense what you have given, gather it together, or rather multiply a hundredfold what you have scattered.

Take care, however, that, if it can be done—that is, if those from whom you took something are present and circumstances permit—you first restore, according to Zacchaeus (ibid. 19:8), fourfold if you are able or willing; but if not, at least restore the principal. [Col. 0161A]

Remember also how many perjuries you uttered in the very assessment of prices, how many lies in the very act of selling. Take counsel concerning these matters, knowing with complete certainty—on the testimony of the Lord Himself—that the devil is the father of lies (John 8:44). The Lord is also known to have cried out through the Law:

> “You shall not swear falsely by the name of the Lord your God” (Leviticus 19:12),

and through Himself:

> “But I say to you, do not swear at all” (Matthew 5:34).

Hence the same wise man cited above says:

> “Better a thief than the continual company of a lying man; yet both will inherit destruction” (Ecclesiasticus 20:17).

And again:

> “Do not accustom your mouth to swearing, for many are the falls that come through it. Let the naming of God not be continual in your mouth, and do not mix yourself with the names of the saints, for you will not be free from guilt because of them” (Ecclesiasticus 23:9). [Col. 0161B]

Elsewhere he also says:

> “Speech that greatly benefits will set shuddering upon the head” (Ecclesiasticus 17:25).

If you wish to know where that shuddering—namely, the horror of the hair that commonly occurs through sudden fear or excessive shame—takes place, listen especially to the Apostle:

> “It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God” (Hebrews 10:31).

And Job says concerning places of punishment:

> “Where there is no order, but everlasting horror dwells” (Job 10:31). [Col. 0161B]

But lest you perhaps, moved by my authority—which is none—be unwilling to accept advice from me, hear certain words of the Holy Spirit Himself, as they are also found in the sacred writings and are appropriate to your salvation:

> “Fear God with all your soul, and sanctify His priests. Love Him with all your strength, who made you, and do not abandon His ministers. Honor God with all your soul, and honor the priests, and purify yourself with arms. Give them portions of the first fruits, as it has been commanded you, and cleanse yourself from negligence with a few offerings” (Ecclesiasticus 7:31). [Col. 0161C]

> “Stretch out your hand to the poor, so that your propitiation and your blessing may be perfected” (Ecclesiasticus 8:1).

> “Do not quarrel with a powerful man, lest you fall into his hands; do not contend with a wealthy man, lest he turn the lawsuit against you. Do not withhold kindness from the dead, nor fail to comfort those who mourn, and walk with those who grieve” (Ecclesiasticus 7:37–40).

Do not be reluctant to visit the sick; through such acts you will be strengthened in love. What more is there to say? In all your works remember your last things, and you will never sin.

## Title VI—On Lawyers

### 15.

Are you a legal advocate or lawyer? Consider what sort of designation you have received, and show yourself a faithful minister of so good a cause. For it is said of the Lord that we have Him as an advocate with the Father. Sometimes also overlook a legal dispute in order to preserve charity. [Col. 0161D]

## Title VII—On Judges

### 16.

Are you a *locotheta*—whom we call a count of the palace—or a prefect or judge? [Col. 0161]

[Note: Ratherius took the word *locotheta* from the Greeks, among whom *λογοθέτης* means one who determines matters by judging. In Lombard law he is called the person appointed in a place, or the guardian of a place.] [Col. 0162A]

Consider whom you too will have as your examiner or judge. Reflect on how heavy a yoke you have taken upon yourself, and suppose that no yoke is heavier. For it belongs only to one who has nothing in himself for which he may be judged to judge freely concerning another’s sin.

Finally, hear Him Himself:

> “Do not judge, and you will not be judged; do not condemn, and you will not be condemned” (Matthew 7:1).

Hear also another, though taught by His Spirit:

> “Do not seek to become a judge, unless you are able to break through iniquity, lest you fear the face of the powerful and place a stumbling block in your justice” (Ecclesiasticus 7:6).

“But,” you say, “your words seem to mean that God does not want judges at all. Where, then, is the law? Where is justice? Where is the very distinction between good and evil? Will everyone be permitted to do anything with impunity? Will theft be praised as equally as generosity? Will vices rejoice with virtues under an equal crown? Who will divide an inheritance among brothers? Who will defend a widow from her accuser, a virgin from her abductor? Who will protect the needy?” [Col. 0162B]

God does not say that He prohibits there being some judgment among human beings in the present age; but He declares the danger, so that you may avoid sin. What is dangerous for one person ought not to be rashly undertaken by many.

### 17.

Finally, when I considered the matter, I could scarcely ever see a judge without greed. Greed itself does not distinguish what is just; rather, it blinds the hearts of judges.

I want judges, therefore, not robbers; judges, not plunderers; judges, not slanderers; judges, but truthful ones; judges, but not men greedily longing for wealth.

For when someone was about to advise his friend concerning the distribution of the burden of authority, he said:

> “Appoint as judges those who hate greed” (Exodus 18:21).

The Book of Wisdom likewise begins:

> “Love justice, you who judge the earth” (Wisdom 1:1). [Col. 0162C]

Jesus son of Sirach also says:

> “In judging, be merciful to orphans as a father, and be as a husband to their mother; then you will be like an obedient son of the Most High, and He will have mercy on you more than a mother” (Ecclesiasticus 4:10).

The Lord also says in Deuteronomy:

> “Cursed is he who perverts the judgment of the stranger, the orphan, and the widow” (Deuteronomy 27:19).

And again, the one cited above:

> “Do not leave anyone behind you to curse you, for the prayer of the one who curses you in the bitterness of his soul will be heard; and God, who made him, will hear him” (Ecclesiasticus 4:5);

and again:

> “Do not love falsehood against your brother, nor bind double sins upon yourself; for you will not be innocent in one matter” (Ecclesiasticus 7:13).

The Psalmist also says:

> “How long will you judge unjustly and show favor to sinners? Judge for the needy and the orphan; justify the humble and the poor. Rescue the poor and free the needy from the hand of the sinner” (Psalm 81:2).

Another passage says:

> “Do not show partiality to the poor in judgment” (Ecclesiasticus 35:16).

Know that this is to be observed when, as often happens, the rich person has a just case and the poor person an unjust one.

And again:

> “Hear, and judge what is just, whether he is a citizen or a foreigner; let there be no distinction between persons. Hear the small as the great, and do not accept anyone’s person in judgment, because judgment belongs to God” (Deuteronomy 1:16).

A judge is so called as though he were “one who speaks the law”; to speak the law is to judge justly.

Finally, hear someone whose authority you cannot doubt:

> “A good judge ought to decide nothing according to his own discretion, nor judge anything according to the purpose of private inclination; he ought to bring forward nothing prepared or premeditated at home, but pronounce on everything according to the laws and legal rights, obey the decrees, and indulge no personal will.” [Col. 0163A]

[Note: The common editions wrongly read *dona proferre*; the intended reading is *domi proferre*, “bring forward at home.”] [Col. 0163D]

How well this voice, speaking these words, agrees with the voice of the supreme and only Judge without falsehood, who says:

> “I judge as I hear” (John 5:30).

So you too should judge as you hear, and decide according to the actual nature of things.

Take care, however, not to catch anyone in his words. Reject the example of the Pharisees, who watched in ambush to see how they might catch the Lord in His speech (Matthew 22:13). Remember that you yourself offend not only in speech but also in many other ways every day, while the supremely just Judge looks on. [Col. 0163B]

Even when you judge justly, beware of demanding a reward or any service, lest the Lord appear to complain about you, saying:

> “My people have been despoiled by their exactors” (Isaiah 3:12).

Listen rather to His command:

> “You shall pursue what is just, justly” (Deuteronomy 16:20).

For the person who, while doing what is just, seeks a reward acts unjustly and does not hesitate to sell justice itself.

Let this brief treatment suffice. But if you wish to be instructed more fully, read the little book of Isidore appropriate to you.

## Title VIII—On Witnesses

### 18.

Are you a witness? Beware of the saying:

> “A false witness will not go unpunished” (Proverbs 19:5).

[Col. 0163C] For, as someone has written:

> “He who is silent about the truth and he who speaks falsehood both wander wickedly:
>
> the former because he does not help, the latter because he desires to harm.”

I consider nothing a greater disgrace than false testimony, because the witness is held guilty before the Lord, against whom he swears falsely; before the judge, whom he deceives; and before his neighbor, whom he harms. He heaps the other person’s whole guilt upon himself and inflicts all his neighbor’s calamity upon his own soul.

As someone has said, it is easier to avoid a quarrelsome person than to evade a deceiver.

## Title IX—On Public Officials
19. Are you a procurator, tax collector—called *gastaldus* by many in ordinary usage [Note: The Vulgate has *gestaldus*, erroneously. Among the Lombards, *gastaldi* were called the superintendents of places, villages, and estates, and administrators of the lord’s property; among the Franks, however, they were called *majores*, that is, mayors of the palace. Those who collected taxes were called *thelonearii*. They possessed some jurisdiction, as is clear from what follows. Hence Hincmarus also, in *Opusc.* 85, names as secular judges Helmigarius, the tax collector of the palace market, and Flotharius and Ursio, mayors of the royal estates.]—or, in Frankish usage, a *major*, or a tax collector, or a minister of any other public office? Consider what sort of office you exercise, knowing that it has been said with complete truth: “From the one to whom more is entrusted, more is required” (Luke 12:48), even with the interest of punishments. I warned at the beginning that the office should be considered because I know that there are various kinds of offices: some lighter, others more serious. Among these I know none more serious than that which Italians call *curatura* [Note: *Curatura* was a tax collected from markets. [Col. 0164D] For this reason, in the privilege of the emperor Frederick I granted to Theobald, bishop of Verona, in the year 1154, one must read from the original: “Half of the toll of the public market of Brescia, which they call *curatura*”; whereas Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, vol. V, col. 795, erroneously reads: “which is called *curaturae*.”]. For while, in accordance with its very name, it continually presses to have earthly matters administered, it compels the wretched soul to be neglected most miserably. All kinds of vices flow toward it as though toward a certain refuge; and although it is the duty of that office to punish every vice, none is found of which he is not clearly guilty.

For it is the procurator’s duty to hand thieves over to prison, although he himself appears daily to pursue almost nothing but robbery and fraud. In my opinion, it is a lesser evil to steal anything without violence than to extract something from another by torture; it is less evil to commit any robbery out of the necessity of poverty than to perpetrate fraud against one’s lord [Note: “Lord” (*senior*) is understood here. See below, note 28. The printed editions shortly afterward wrongly read “A thief is preferable”; the correction is supplied by the Vulgate version.]—or anyone else, or indeed oneself—in the ardor of greed, thereby also falling into perjury and seeming not to avoid theft. The Wise Man confirms this when he says: “A thief is better than the constant presence of a lying man; yet both will inherit destruction” (Ecclesiasticus 20:27). Likewise, concerning the evil of perjury: “The man who swears much,” he says, “will be filled with iniquity, and the scourge will not depart from his house; and if he deceives, his sin will be upon him; and if he swears falsely, he will not be justified, for his house will be filled with tribulation; and if he conceals it, he sins doubly” (Ecclesiasticus 23:12–13). To conceal perjury is to swear deceitfully. He who does this sins doubly because he is held guilty both before God, whose presence he does not shrink from, and before his neighbor, whom he is not afraid to deceive. He sins doubly because he incurs the mark both of deceit and of perjury.

20. The procurator assigns adulterers and prostitutes to punishment, although his whole life, serving most shamefully drunkenness and the other luxuries [Col. 0164C] that commonly foster adultery and fornication, plainly shows that he himself practices the very things he condemns in others. To complete his destruction, if one of such people happens to find something to offer him, he immediately acquires even the avenger of his crime as its protector. Thus what is read in the Psalm is fulfilled in him: “When you saw a thief, you ran with him, and you placed your portion with adulterers” (Psalm 49:18).

What more is there to say? In brief, let us indicate that this business is of such a kind that it seems as though one man out of many thousands is selected and handed over to eternal destruction for the correction or advantage of others. But what am I doing, when I see some people seeking this very kind of office by payment? What, I ask, follows from that? Have you never seen someone pull out little cords from which a rope was to be made for hanging him? Therefore attribute the device of such madness—and of this most wretched man [Note: Construe and explain it thus: “Therefore attribute also the device, or deceit, of this most wretched man”—that is, the man who failed in his office because of payment—“attribute it, I say, to the madness,” that is, the insanity, “of this kind,” by which an office destined to bring ruin to the soul is purchased for money.].

21. But lest, in the Pharisaic manner, while vehemently reproving the crime, we should seem to instill despair of correction, let us display the riches of God’s goodness and show also how you may be saved. Above all, we give you this counsel: if you are in any way able, shake yourself free from this deadly snare; then, having recourse to the remedies of repentance, seek a cure of satisfaction proportionate to the measure of your crime.

But if you are entirely unable to do so, then, carrying out what has been commanded with great trembling, beware above all of cruelty; then of fraud, greed, and rapacity; and no less of drunkenness. Finally, beware of the Psalm verse we cited: do not, seduced by any payment or deceived by a kind of false mercy, conceal any theft or defend any crime that ought to be prosecuted.

In punishing crimes, carry out what suits your office in such a way that you never lose from memory what the Lord set before all people in a parable—and especially before you, whose end is expressed in these words: “Wicked servant, ought you not also to have had mercy on your fellow servant, just as I had mercy on you?” Then, in anger, he handed him over to the torturers (Matthew 18:32).

But I also ask you often to remember this: “Let him who is without sin among you be the first to cast a stone at her” (John 8:7). And, while carrying out your office, never cease to enlist the aid of almsgiving. Perhaps, if with humility of heart you knock at the merciful ears of the Almighty, you will at some time deserve that he himself come to you and, as he visited and healed Zacchaeus and Matthew, visit and heal you; and that he graciously reply to those who once despaired that you could be saved: “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” (Matthew 9:13).

TITLE X—Concerning the Nobles

[Col. 0165C]

22. Are you a *patronus* [Note: *Patronus*, whence the Italian *padrone*, here signifies a nobleman who had servants and hired laborers. [Col. 0166D] The title *senior*, Italian *signore*, was properly bestowed upon kings and princes. Gradually, however, it was usurped by patrons, who for that reason are said to have sought the name *senior* more commonly.]—or, as many customarily prefer to call it, a *senior*? Hear this: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do also to them” (Matthew 7:12). Moses likewise says: “The work of your hired laborer shall not remain with you until morning” (Leviticus 19:13). Understand “work” as standing for the payment for work, just as you very often read that anything is signified by the agent that produces it and by the container that contains it.

Another says: “He who sheds innocent blood and he who defrauds a hired laborer are brothers: one destroys, and the other builds. What profit is there for them except labor? One prays, and the other curses; whose voice will God hear?” (Ecclesiasticus 34:17). And through Malachi the Lord says: “I will be a swift witness against sorcerers, adulterers, and perjurers, and against those who oppress the wages of the hired laborer” (Malachi 3:5). In explaining this passage, Jerome calls attention to what he said: “Let us by no means consider perjury, failure to pay the laborer, and the other matters joined to these as trivial sins; they are compared with witchcraft, sorcery, and adultery.”

The Apostle also says: “Whoever does not care for his own, and especially for the members of his household, has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (1 Timothy 5:8). Consider that at the beginning of the creation of humanity God said: “Increase and multiply, fill the earth, subdue it, and rule over the fish of the sea, the birds of the heavens, and the beasts of the earth” (Genesis 1:28). Understand from this that human beings were appointed not over human beings but over birds, beasts, and fish; and that all were created by God equal in nature, but that inequality of character has caused some to be subjected to others to such an extent that some even rule over those who are better.

For this reason the ancients preferred to call those who ruled the rest “fathers of their country,” dictators, and consuls rather than kings, judging it hateful to say that human beings, like cattle, were ruled by anyone. You ought also to remember—as Gregory tells you—that our holy Fathers were not kings of men but shepherds of flocks.

Augustine, likewise, concerning equality of nature and the social bond of friendship (no. 1), says: “Since each human being is a part of the human race, and human nature is something social and possesses a great and natural good, namely, the power of friendship, God therefore willed all human beings to be created from one ancestor, so that they might be bound together in fellowship not only by the likeness of their race but also by the bond of kinship.”

Blessed Pope Leo, expounding the same point most brilliantly, says: “Together with servants we possess this: that we were created in the image of God. They are separated from us neither by bodily nor by spiritual birth. We are sanctified by the same Spirit, live by the same faith, and hasten to the same sacraments.”

Severinus Boethius, discussing the same matter at length and presenting much that could be clear even to the blind, concludes as follows: “If you consider your beginnings and God the author of them, no one is found degenerate, unwillingly cherishing what is worse and abandoning his proper origin.”

A saying of another person, Benedict by speech, conduct, and name, agrees with this. He says somewhere: “Whether slave or free, we are all one in Christ, so that under one Lord we bear the equal service of military duty, because with God there is no acceptance of persons. We are distinguished before him in this respect alone: if we are found better than others in good works and humble.”

23. But take note, whoever you are who glory arrogantly in the pride of an abusively exalted lineage: since the whole human race rises on earth from a similar origin, you too were formed from no other substance but the same mass, created from one father and from the same mother as any servant.

For if we are all one in Christ also (Romans 12:5), redeemed at one price and reborn in the same baptism, whoever attempts to divide this unity of brotherhood by placing himself above others is plainly shown, as far as lies in him, to cancel and, so to speak, deny the fatherhood, redemption, and regeneration by which we become his children [Note: The Vulgate has *efficiuntur*, “they become,” less suitably.].

But if we are distinguished by God in this respect alone—if we are found better than others in good works and humble—then the one who serves you humbly is proved better than you, who despise him arrogantly; the one who faithfully provides what he promised you is nobler than you, who deceitfully cheat him; and the one who safeguards the laws of nature and does not abandon his proper origin is more honorable than you, who, nourishing vice upon vice, violate the great and natural good that is the power of friendship.

Thus, supported by authorities so entirely truthful and so very reliable, and by propositions conceded without any internal contradiction, we arrive at the firmest conclusion: human beings differ from one another not by nature but by will.

To instruct the ignorance of fools and refute the insolence of the arrogant, he who says in the Gospel, “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John 5:17), daily humbles one before our eyes and exalts another, for “he raises the needy from the dust and lifts the poor from the dung heap, to set him with princes” (Psalm 112:6). Thus, whenever anyone boasts of the nobility of his lineage, let him consider that people from poor and humble origins can rise to the highest honors, and recognize that this could also have happened to his ancestors, so that he may strive to restrain his pride.

“For every good gift and every perfect gift is from above” (James 1:17), and “there is no authority except from God” (Romans 13:1). This is shown most clearly by the sons of nobles reduced to the disgrace of poverty, and by the offspring of servants obtaining the distinguished inheritances of the powerful [Note: The *summates* are named as a class of the Alexandrian fleet in Book 32 of the Theodosian Code, *On Shipowners*. Here, however, *summatum* means “of the nobles and powerful.” Construe it as follows: “And the offspring of servants, having obtained the distinguished inheritances of the nobles, acquired them in whatever manner.”].

Let us place before our eyes any son of a prefect whose grandfather is known to have been a judge, his great-grandfather a tribune, or a *scoldascius* [Note: More frequently written *sculdascius* or *sculdais*. This name, used in Italy, derives from the Lombards. A county, such as the Veronese county, was divided into *sculdasciae* (see Muratori, *Antiquitates Italicae*, vol. I, p. 513),, whose judge was called a *sculdascius*. Rather distinguishes the *scoldascius* from the judge: he assigns the name *scoldascius* to the judges of villages or castles, while he gives the title “judge” to those who administered justice in a city and stood above the *scoldascii*. The author is evidently noting degrees of nobility, beginning with the highest and proceeding downward. The prefect, with whom he begins, belonged to a nobler rank than the judge; for the word “prefect” includes the count of the palace, the duke, and the marquis. The judges of a city were the count and vice-count, who presided over the *scoldascii* of villages and castles. The lowest rank mentioned by Rather is that of the ordinary soldier, a term by which he includes anyone who lived from his own patrimony and was distinguished from the common people. Thus, in Book IV, no. 13, distinguishing the soldier from the commoner, he says: “Have you ever seen a soldier or a commoner?” A soldier was called one who was supported by his own patrimony, because generally, enjoying some benefice or fief either from a prince or from the Church, he was obliged to serve militarily when necessary.], while his great-great-grandfather was a soldier. Who was the father of that soldier? Was he a diviner or a painter; a bath attendant or a fowler; a fishmonger or a potter; a tailor or a maker of sausages; a muleteer or a pack-horse driver [Note: The Vulgate has *sagnio*, corruptly. It should be read *sagmio*, that is, one who drives a *sagmarium*, or packhorse.]; finally, a horseman or a farmer; a slave or a free man? Who remembers after all this? For:

“Kingdoms they will give to slaves, triumphs fate to captives,”

as was once sung by a certain satirical poet; although this must be attributed not to fate but to the ordered law of the Almighty.

What, moreover, if one of them should experience what Varro testifies happened to a certain flute player—namely, that someone was at times raised to the highest honor from an ignoble occupation, just as that man, by the same art, so delighted the people that he deserved to become king? [Note: These words are also found in Augustine, *On the Quantity of the Soul*, chapter 19: “A certain flute player, as Varro relates, so delighted the people that he became king.”] Could the flute player’s elevation ennoble him, when the flute produced what nature had not been able to produce? But let us leave this doubtful matter aside, and perhaps not regard it as worthy of belief.

24. Why should we not demonstrate the matter clearly, not by the clever arguments of the pagans but by the certain assertions of Sacred Scripture? David, after his brothers had been rejected, was chosen by God as king. Since by God’s gift he preceded them in kingship, did he therefore surpass them in birth? Or was his offspring, because of his kingship [Note: *Regnatus* means kingship, or the administration of a kingdom. Construe the sentence: “Or was his offspring, because of kingship, other than the same offspring that nature produced without kingship?”], other than the same offspring whom nature had produced without kingship?

Was he noble because he was king, and his brothers ignoble because they were soldiers? Or rather—and this is the truth—did he acquire this nobility for himself by virtue together with God’s grace, so that one unknown by family became illustrious by character?

For this reason Cicero, arguing beautifully against Sallust, says: “I should like him to answer me: Were those whom the Scipios and Metelli produced already held in reputation and glory before their achievements and their blameless life commended them? And if this was the beginning of their name and dignity, why should we not be judged in the same way?”

And again: “Therefore do not throw ancient men in my face. It is better for me to flourish through my own achievements than to rely upon the reputation of my ancestors, and to live in such a way that I may be the beginning of nobility and an example of virtue to my descendants.”

Today the opposite is done. A man prefers that his grandfather be praised rather than himself. “If you do not possess your own distinction,” says Boethius, “the glory of another does not make you splendid.”

But, to return to what we commonly see happening every day, do you not see many people, through service or some other ability, not merely earning their freedom but even obtaining the inheritance of their masters, and—though an unequal marriage with a noble person intervenes—the offspring of servants often being preferred even to the offspring of their lords? Whether it happened or did not happen, I have related what was reported.

The son of a certain rich man suffered from a convulsive seizure, which they call the falling sickness [Note: *Gutta cadiva* is epilepsy, as Cangius demonstrates from the Biblical Glosses, where it is written: “Those who have the falling sickness are called epileptics.”]. The skill of all the most highly approved physicians proved ineffective against it and had brought the father’s and mother’s minds to despair of his recovery. Then one of the servants suggested that flowers of a peach tree, carefully cleansed, should be gathered in a glass vessel on the first Monday of April [Note: Manuscripts often have *die Lunis* instead of *die Lunae*, that is, Monday].

The vessel was to be buried by anyone they wished, without anyone’s knowledge, beneath the root of that same tree; the person who had buried it was to return on the same day of the following year, if possible at the same hour, and, after digging up the vessel, find the flowers changed into oil and the tree dried up. The vessel was then to be placed beneath an altar and, without the priest’s knowledge, sanctified by nine Masses celebrated over it. Immediately after the onset of the same illness, the oil was to be given to the sick man nine times as a drink, one dose each day, with the Lord’s Prayer—except that after “deliver us from evil,” the person administering it was to say: “Deliver, O God, this man, N., from the falling sickness.”

For those nine days he was also to hear Mass daily, and after fasting to take unleavened bread and Lenten food; thus, by God’s mercy, he was to recover.

It happened—if indeed it happened—that he recovered. The servant was emancipated and even enrolled as heir. The remedy, approved by countless people, also brought remedies for health to many others.

I have wished to relate this so that readers might themselves try it [Col. 0170A] [Note: Rather had previously condemned superstitious remedies in this very book, when discussing physicians in no. 7. Why, then, does he here recommend experimenting with a remedy that is plainly most superstitious?], so that through my efforts some assistance might also be prepared for certain people against such an affliction, and so that I might admonish you, the person with whom I am speaking, by such examples: “Do not seek yourself outside yourself,” nor foolishly wish to place some person highly commended to you [Note: “Those commended” were free people who entrusted themselves to patrons and lords, binding themselves to provide them with their labor or some service. In the following title, *Concerning the hired laborer, client, or commended person*, he treats them as the counterparts of patrons. See the notes there. Two diplomas of Louis the Pious, published by Pierre Pithou in *Annals of the Franks*, vol. II, pp. 291 and 294, speak of Spaniards who, fleeing from Spain after its occupation by the Saracens into the neighboring regions of Gaul, commended themselves to counts or royal vassals and received from them deserted places to inhabit and cultivate. These were the lesser vassals of those who had granted them the benefice; and their obligation is described in the first diploma in these words: “If any of them should obtain a benefice from the person to whom he has commended himself, let him know that he must render to his lord from that benefice such service as our countrymen customarily render to their lords from a similar benefice.” In the second diploma, it decrees that they and their descendants cannot be deprived of the lands they received.] before yourself as though he were nobler than you. Be certain that you are of the same condition, the same mortality, and the same dust; and that, if the dignity of this world is examined minutely, it consists not in the class of people but in possession itself—that is, in the fact that we seem to weigh not the people themselves but the things surrounding them.

His future offspring will be more glorious if fortune, passing, so to speak, from you to him, should make his offspring rich and yours poor [Note: Explain it as follows: “And his offspring”—namely, the offspring of the person most highly commended to you, as he said above—“will be more glorious if passing fortune should make his offspring rich and yours poor.”]. Indeed, to state the truth without hesitation, the Almighty may have ordained that he be exalted and that you be humbled.

If you do not advise yourself of all these things, let sight advise you—or that wise man who says of such matters: “I have seen a servant sitting in the place of lords” [Note: These words agree with Ecclesiastes 10:7: “I have seen servants on horses, and princes walking upon the earth like servants.”]; and, although the comparison is far from equal, another says: “The son of a free man closes the side of the rich man’s servant.”

25. I have seen in certain people a most serious vice, which I am all the less able to leave untouched because I can read it, as it were, in a certain book within myself, having experienced it myself [Note: The adversity described here, which Rather affirms that he experienced in himself, was certainly some misfortune in which he was involved. He speaks of a nobleman almost entirely deprived of his possessions and stripped of power and dignity, who, while trying to raise his arm against such calamity, did not hesitate to entice another person—living quietly, with fortune smiling upon him, able either to support himself or to serve another with substantial profit—to follow him, and to lead him from great prosperity into terrible ruin. Unless we are mistaken, this seems to point to Hilduin. Deposed from the see of Liège and intending to travel to Italy to his kinsman King Hugh, hoping that Hugh would place him in some church of the Italian kingdom, Hilduin persuaded Rather, who was living quietly and prosperously and could either remain in the monastery of Lobbes for himself or serve another with great advantage—for example, the bishop who had replaced Hilduin in the see of Liège—to follow him to Italy. There, after appearing to have made considerable progress with Hilduin’s assistance, Rather was promoted to the bishopric of Verona but was then brought into terrible ruin when, captured by Hugh, he was delivered to the prison at Pavia, where he wrote these words. No other interpretation, so far as we know, allows what he says he experienced in himself to be applied to Rather. If this interpretation is correct, the other matters that follow concerning Hilduin and Rather must also be understood and explained in this way. It is unknown to what extent Hilduin’s glory rose together with Rather’s punishment, namely his imprisonment, or how much Hilduin’s advantages increased through Rather’s losses. Perhaps, favoring Hugh during the revolt of the Veronese and increasingly winning the king’s favor against Rather himself, Hilduin obtained something further from the king, beyond the archbishopric of Milan, which he had already acquired, and this brought him greater glory and profit. Meanwhile, he showed no gratitude to Rather, who had followed him and was now in prison. If he had granted Rather any compensation when he arranged his promotion to the see of Verona, then, after the disagreement that later arose between Hilduin and Rather over the reception of Arnold at Verona, Hilduin, forgetting their former friendship and Rather’s good will—by which Rather had preferred to assist him even at the risk of his life so that he might recover glory either lost or greater glory in Italy—reproached Rather with the very things to which, deceived on his own account, he had now fallen: namely, the hardships of the prison at Pavia. Since Rather indicates that he had been deceived on Hilduin’s account, the things he relates in Book V, no. 27, seem to concern Hilduin. There, among the betrayers by whom he was deceived, he names one of the same office—that is, a bishop—and in no. 18 calls this chief deceiver of his “the supreme one,” in whom all hope of a good outcome had rested, and indicates the manner of the deception. See the notes there.] You will find any nobleman almost entirely deprived of his possessions, stripped of power and dignity—if he has happened to acquire any—and utterly cast down, insofar as greed dictates and nobility demands. While striving to raise his arm against so harsh a calamity of fortune, and unable to accomplish anything by himself—for the nature of such efforts is such—he does not hesitate to entangle with the allurements of honeyed flattery someone who, living quietly with fortune smiling upon him, could either support himself or serve another with substantial profit, and to lead him from great prosperity into terrible ruin.

But while the punishment of the one has raised the glory of the other, and the other’s advantages have grown through the one’s losses, either you see no gratitude for a fitting repayment at all, or, if some compensation has been granted, whether great or small, and even the slightest separation through discord has crept in, you will find him forgetting their former friendship; forgetting such good will that, persuaded not by any gift that commonly attracts the eyes through deception but solely by that love which is “strong as death” (Song of Songs 8:6), the other preferred to neglect himself entirely and to assist him even amid countless dangers to his life, so that he might recover glory either lost or greater than before, rather than care for himself and seek what he needed when it was available.

You will find him forgetting what both men then possessed, and what could have become more abundant day by day; forgetting what he possessed when he was deceived [Note: The received editions read *qui tunc*, “which then,” incorrectly. The following phrase means “the things with which Rather was powerful in the bishopric of Verona when he was deceived.” The kind of deception involved has been explained in the *Life*.]; and reproaching him with those very things into which the one who records this has now fallen, deceived because of him [Note: “The one who records this” means “the one who writes this.” Thus he indicates that he himself, who wrote these words, was the person who had been deceived and had fallen into these hardships. Hilduin, whom he had followed, was the one who had first bestowed good things upon Rather by raising him to the episcopate and later took those good things away by leading the deceived man into imprisonment.]; forgetting what he saw that man possess, he recounts what has happened to himself not to possess.

34. For, remembering what he bestowed, he forgets what he took away; recounting the heights to which he raised him, he is silent about the depths from which he cast him down; and, suppressing the splendor of his nobility [Note: This most clearly confirms Rather’s nobility. The subject here is Rather, upon whom the praised Hilduin inflicted the mark of poverty in which Rather was suffering in the prison at Pavia. Hilduin reported this poverty while remaining silent about the splendor of the nobility with which Rather was adorned.], he reports the mark of poverty that he himself inflicted.

Since this single crime, in order to describe the matter as it is, demands another volume of its own [Note: Just as the matter here is said to demand its own volume, so the subject mentioned in Book V, no. 12, is said to require “a sufficiently long discourse.” This confirms that both passages refer to the same person, namely Rather himself.], let it suffice here to mention even a small part of it, so that you may [perhaps: raise] your spirit to vigilance, if you wish to have the Lord favorable toward you.

TITLE XI—Concerning the Hired Laborer and the Client

26. Are you a hired laborer, a client, or a person commended to anyone? [Note: In this passage, “client” and “commended person,” like “hired laborer,” refer to those who, in whatever manner, bound their labor or service to patrons in return for payment or an acquired benefice, as you will easily understand from the duties of such people described in this title. By origin they were free, and by their obligation to provide labor they entered servitude only in the broad sense. When they had been commended to the patron’s clientship or protection, they acquired the names “client” and “commended person.”] Hear the Lord commanding: “What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another” (Tobit 4:16). To show how this concerns you, I urge you: just as you do not wish to be defrauded by your patron of the gift owed for your service, so beware lest you ever defraud him of the service owed to him, lest he seem to complain about you.

The Wise Man says: “Many have regarded usury as a means of gain and have caused trouble to those who helped them. Until they receive, they kiss the hands of the giver; in their promises they humble their voice; but at the time of repayment they ask for time, speak words of annoyance and murmuring, and make excuses about the time” (Ecclesiasticus 29:4, 6). Understand “the time of repayment,” which you promised, as the time of service, when you joined hand to hand with your lord [Note: Observe the manner in which clients and commended persons bound themselves to patrons or lords. Hence, when vassals performed homage or pledged loyalty, they also placed or joined their hands in the hands of their lord. See Cangius, additions under “Homagium.”].

Beware, therefore, lest, while carrying out what you promised sluggishly, arrogantly, or faithlessly, you seem to apply to yourself the words of blessed Job: “A vain man is lifted up in pride and thinks himself born free like a wild ass’s colt” (Job 11:12). You can recognize from the judgment of the same authority that you were by no means born free, since he plainly says that a human being is born for labor. But labor seems to belong more to servitude than to freedom. Hence another wise man says: “Food and a burden are for the ass, and bread, discipline, and work for the servant” (Ecclesiasticus 33:25).

Thus Seneca says: “To receive a benefice is to sell one’s freedom.” Therefore, do not claim for yourself the freedom that you sold for the sake of profit. Rather do what Solomon urges, recognizing that no one ought to be a closer friend to you than yourself: “My son, if you have stood surety for your friend, you have given your hand to a stranger. Do therefore what I say, my son, and free yourself, because you have fallen into the hands of your neighbor. Run, hasten, stir up your friend; do not give sleep to your eyes, nor let your eyelids slumber” (Proverbs 6:1–4).

All this, since—as I said—even according to the literal sense, without prejudice to the spiritual interpretation appropriate to the rulers of the Church, you ought to do for any friend, is much more fitting for you to do for yourself, for two reasons: first, so that your patron may not rightly complain that you have failed to repay with service what you owe him for his benefices; and second, so that the Lord, who sees all things from heaven, may not stand forth as avenger, according to the Apostle (1 Thessalonians 4:6), when he sees you deceiving your brother in the matter of what was given and received.

Remember very often the one who says: “Understand your neighbor from yourself” (Ecclesiasticus 31:18). Likewise: “Many did not lend at interest because of wickedness, but because they feared being defrauded without compensation” (Ecclesiasticus 29:10). From this, infer from your own case that it is not always the fault of patrons when they delay for a time the wages of hired laborers or of any persons commended to them; often their wickedness, idleness, or arrogance causes this.

Hence the same author mentioned above, Seneca, says: “They teach that the ungrateful become especially malicious.” Thinking about this wisely and carefully, prepare your mind manfully for service, so that you may be able to serve more faithfully and diligently, certain that the father of the household, whose servants both of you are, will look down from heaven upon your affliction and labor.

If he sees you being deceived by your patron, he will also reprove your patron, setting the fraud before his face on the fearful day of that just judgment. But if you have not worked for the same wage worthily, you will be required to pay it in punishment [Note: *Componere* meant to settle and expiate some offense through an agreement involving payment, or to pay a sum as the penalty due for an offense; if it was not paid at once, sureties were given. Here, however, the offense is said to be paid not with money but in the punishment of hell, where there will be neither sureties nor any possibility of redemption by payment.], where, of course, the help of a surety and the price of redemption will be lacking.

TITLE XII—Concerning Counselors
27. Are you a counselor? Beware that prophetic saying: “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil” (Isa. V, 20). For, as the old proverb has it: “If you have entered the service of a fortunate and powerful man, either truth or friendship must be sacrificed.” Consider this: we say that the Jews crucified Christ, although it was not they but the Roman soldiers who crucified him, so that you may understand that the entire weight of the crime rests upon the one who did not hesitate to give advice concerning it. Hence we curse Caiaphas more than Pilate: Caiaphas said, “It is expedient that one man should die for the people” (John XVIII, 14), whereas Pilate said, “Take him yourselves and judge him according to your law” (ibid. 31). Hence the Apostle also says: “Not only those who do these things, but also those who consent to those who do them, are worthy of death” (Rom. I, 32). And observe that he does not say “those who command” or “those who give counsel,” but—something far less—“those who consent,” so that you may understand how deadly is counsel leading to destruction, since even consent itself is so harmful. For, as Seneca says, “He who can rescue a man on the point of perishing, but does not rescue him, kills him.”

Today, however, the opposite is done: people prefer to find someone compliant rather than a friend. A friend [36], as Gregory says, is called the guardian of the soul. Yet today a greater number is found of those who say to the seers, “Do not see,” and to those who look, “Do not look at what is right for us; speak to us pleasing things, see errors for us” (Isa. XXX, 10). This is not friendship—not at all, I say—but the greatest enmity. For whoever kills another in that part by which he is to live forever is the worst kind of murderer.

The law of friendship, with Laelius as witness, is that we should ask honorable things of our friends and do honorable things for our friends’ sake. Every counsel, moreover, ought to contain three things: what is honorable, what is useful, and what is possible. If one of these is lacking, the counsel will not be acceptable. But a companion, as it is written in the Book of Wisdom, “rejoices with his friend in his enjoyment, and in a time of tribulation becomes an adversary” (Ecclus. XXXVII, 4).

Recognizing this, Pope Gregory, already mentioned and of blessed memory, writes to someone: “Choose such counselors for yourself,” he says, “as love you, not what belongs to you.” Therefore, whoever you are—one among a thousand—whom someone has chosen as his counselor, consider whose favor you enjoy; and, loving your friend not for what he possesses but for himself, give him honorable counsel and do honorable things for his sake. For we read that the Lord himself is called “the Angel of Great Counsel” (Isa. IX, 6, according to the Septuagint). If we wish to imitate him, let us give no one counsel except what is sound, just, and honorable, lest, by acting against them, we be judged not counselors but betrayers of friends; be called not cooperators in goodness but inventors of evil; and thereby become supporters of the devil.

## TITLE XIII—Concerning masters

28. Are you a master? Do not become arrogant. Remember that you are a servant, that you have one Master, and that therefore you are a fellow servant. Although a certain wise man, most wisely considering the arrogance of wicked servants, says, “Bread, discipline, and work for a servant” (Ecclus. XXXIII, 25), and so forth, nevertheless take care not to impose upon him something he cannot bear, or at least a service he can undertake only with difficulty.

Know that discretion is the mother of all virtues. Indeed, according to the admonition of blessed Pope Leo, the fact that you share his subjection ought to make you gentler in every respect, since you are subject with him to the one God by the same servitude. Hence someone says most beautifully: “He who is cruel to servants shows that he lacks not the will to command others, but the power.”

Let the punishment of Pharaoh therefore terrify you. Consider that God looks down from heaven upon the affliction of the wretched. Give him some time each day—not so that he may devote himself to idleness, but so that he may be able to serve his Creator. If discipline is necessary—and indeed it is—let it be moderate.

If he has perhaps injured you, stolen something, committed fraud, fled, or done anything else improperly, strive to correct everything in such a way that you seem not to be satisfying your anger but caring for the negligent; not to be carrying out vengeance but pursuing the fault; and to be saving the soul of the offender. In all these matters, do not let that terrible sentence slip from your mind, in which it is said:

“Wicked servant, I forgave you all that debt because you entreated me. Ought you not therefore to have had mercy on your fellow servant, as I had mercy on you?” Then his lord, being angry, handed him over to the torturers (Matt. XVIII, 32–34), and so forth.
