But if he is well-behaved and faithful, hear this: “If you have a faithful servant, let him be to you as your own soul” (Ecclus. XXXIII, 31). Do not defraud him of his freedom, nor leave him destitute.

## TITLE XIV—Concerning servants

29. Are you a servant? Do not grieve. If you serve your master faithfully, you will be the freedman of the Lord of all; for we are all brothers in Christ.

Hear, then, the Apostle saying: “Servants, be subject to your masters with all fear” (1 Pet. II, 18). What fear does he mean, and what is meant by the word “all”? It means, first, the fear of God, and then that of earthly masters; or first servile fear, which charity casts out (1 John IV, 18)—namely, fear lest you be flogged, beaten, or bound, and finally lest, because of contempt, you be led into eternal fire. For “whoever resists authority resists the ordinance of God,” and “there is no authority except from God” (Rom. XIII, 2).

“You have placed men over our heads,” the Psalmist also says (Ps. LXXXII, 33). And according to the saying of someone: “He who attempts to resist God must necessarily lose a great good and incur a great evil, because he has opposed the supreme good and clung to a worse evil.”

Finally, submit through chaste fear—understand, “be subject”—which endures forever and ever; that is, lest, if you are lazy or sluggish, you lose in the future the glory promised to those who labor courageously. Therefore, if you steal any hours from your master, restore them to your Creator.

And do not suppose that you were subjected to servitude by chance or without God’s providence, whatever the order of events by which it occurred. Hear Isidore:

“Because of the sin of the first man, the punishment of servitude was divinely imposed upon the human race, so that, for those whom he sees to be unsuited to freedom, he mercifully assigns servitude. And although this came about through original sin, nevertheless the just God has so ordered human life that he has made some servants and others masters, so that the servants’ license to do wrong may be restrained by the masters’ power. For if all were without fear, who would restrain anyone from evil? Hence kings and princes were also chosen among the nations, so that by their terror they might restrain peoples from evil and subject them to laws for right living.

“As far as reason is concerned, there is no partiality with God (Rom. II, 11), who chooses the base and despised things of the world, and things that are not, to destroy the things that are, so that no flesh—that is, no carnal power—may glory before him (1 Cor. I, 28). For there is one Lord, who gives counsel equally to masters and servants. Subjection in servitude is better than exalted freedom. Many are found freely serving God while placed under disgraceful masters; although they are subject to them in body, they are nevertheless superior to them in mind.”

Consoled, then, by the testimony of so great a man—not so much because it is eloquent as because it is true—be a faithful and good servant, always keeping in your heart the counsel that the angel gave Hagar, Sarai’s maidservant: “Return to your mistress and humble yourself under her hand” (Gen. XVI, 9).

## TITLE XV—Concerning teachers

30. Are you a teacher? Remember that you owe discipline joined with affection to your pupils, following the example of him who is the Master of all above, who chastises and rebukes those whom he loves (Prov. III, 12), and who was accustomed to call his disciples not servants but his friends (John XV, 15). Thus, by correcting their faults with both words and blows, you too ought to nourish the persons of the offenders with affection.

## TITLE XVI—Concerning pupils

31. Are you a pupil? Know that you owe obedience to your teachers, and that this is a moral principle: one should require from subordinates what one remembers having shown to superiors.

And, to weave together a mixed and, as it were, popular discourse: are you a pupil? Hear also, I ask, the Lord commanding: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do also to them” (Matt. VII, 12).

Likewise, are you a teacher? Hear this: “Do not be called Rabbi” (Matt. XXIII, 8).

Are you a pupil? Hear this: “Do what they say, but do not do what they do” (ibid. 3).

Are you a teacher? Hear this: “Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him that an ass’s millstone be hung around his neck and that he be drowned in the depths of the sea” (Matt. XVIII, 6).

Are you a pupil? Take care. “There will be a time,” the Apostle says, “when they will not endure sound doctrine, but according to their own desires they will heap up teachers for themselves,” and so forth (2 Tim. IV, 3).

Are you a teacher? Take heed: “Desiring to be teachers of the law, understanding neither what they say nor concerning what they make assertions” (1 Tim. I, 7).

Are you a pupil? “In honor,” he says, “anticipating one another” (Rom. XII, 10).

A teacher? “Not lording it over the clergy, but becoming examples to the flock” (1 Pet. V, 3). [Note: [Col. 0175D] He applies to teachers the text “not lording it over the clergy,” because the pupils were generally clerics, so much so that those of noble birth who were sent to school were enrolled in the clerical militia. This, Ratherius says in part I of *On Contempt for the Canons*, no. 22 [Col. 0176D], seems nowadays to be done more from ambition for the episcopate than from desire to serve the Lord.]

Finally, are you a teacher, or are you called one, or do you wish to be called one? Take care to preserve the rights of the teaching office, lest you be called one improperly. Desire to be useful more than to preside.

Are you a pupil? Strive to submit humbly, so that you may eventually be able to benefit both yourself and many others.

Are you a teacher? Teach humbly what you know.

A pupil? Learn eagerly what you still do not know at all.

A teacher? Desire rather to be loved than feared; for, as Augustine says, gloomy and excessively severe cruelty turns many people away from itself.

Hence Gregory also says: “If anyone has the manners of a wild beast, he must live alone like a beast.”

A pupil? Strive, by obedience, to win the love of your teacher. For the poet sings to you:

“Fortune is the conqueror of wisdom; and we also call those happy who have learned, with life as their teacher, to endure the troubles of life and not to cast off the yoke.”

Are you a teacher? Take care to govern your teaching office by this art, so that you may seem to preside over pupils in order to form them rather than to blunt them.

For some are so slow and forgetful in understanding that they can scarcely grasp the very first elements of letters, much less anything from the deeper kinds of instruction. Some, to quote Aurelius Augustine’s words, are so foolish that they differ little from cattle.

Others, however, have such an agile intellect and such zeal for study that, often through their own understanding and application, they grasp even greater things than they have learned from their teachers.

There are also those who grasp with difficulty and lose easily. Some grasp with difficulty but retain firmly what they have grasped. Some grasp easily and lose more easily. Some grasp most easily and lose most difficultly.

To these last nothing need be suggested except that they nourish the swift agility of their understanding through the exercise of study, lest, by failing to learn what they are capable of learning, they offend their author through ingratitude and, emptied of wisdom, eventually pay the penalty for contempt.

For the others, you should know that the precepts of instruction must be moderated according to each person’s capacity and the variety of their understanding, lest, if you try to force doctrines upon them that they cannot grasp, they fall more deeply into the pit of blindness.

Read Augustine’s book *Soliloquies*, and there you will find clear counsel on this matter, though it does not conflict with our own. But perhaps the book is lacking—namely, Augustine’s book—and cannot be found despite being sought? We tell you what we read in it: reaching wisdom in a certain order is the work of good discipline; without order, happiness is scarcely credible [f. “happiness”].

Accordingly, I advise that those mentioned above [that is, the pupils] be handled with such skill in teaching that, like physicians who wish to make the sun visible to those suffering from inflamed eyes, one should first offer them instruction suited to the very slightest capacity; then something somewhat stronger, though not much; then at last something which, in some small part, is removed from this and, by certain conjectures, may open their sight a little to it; afterward whatever is near its light; now a little of wisdom, now somewhat more, and finally the radiance of wisdom itself, if it can in any way be grasped.

Otherwise, it is preferable for someone with inflamed eyes to go around the shops early in the morning, with his sight still intact, and bring something useful home, than, having been completely blinded by the splendor of the midday sun, to grasp after darkness itself with a kind of appetite and without any benefit.

32. Just as different degrees of understanding are found among hearers, so different mixtures of disposition are found among teachers.

Some have a will so obstinate that, although they seek to be called teachers, they do not wish anyone to be instructed by them through any art of teaching. They desire to be called teachers, yet, blocked by envy, they altogether refuse to be taught.

These are surely the ones who, having dug beneath the treasure of the wisdom of the heart and hidden it in a cave, are pierced in judgment by the dart of condemnation, according to the saying: “He who hides grain will be cursed among the peoples” (Prov. XI, 26).

Others, by contrast, appear so lavish that they seem to pour out doctrine rather than distribute it. Of them, as Gregory bears witness, it is said in the Law: “A man who suffers an emission of semen is to be excluded from the priesthood.”

For he suffers an emission of semen who, uselessly pouring out what ought to have generated offspring of good virtues in the hearts of his hearers, is seen by his very excess to render those same hearers sterile.

Their division is fivefold, and only one part seems to serve virtue [Note: [Col. 0177] The vulgate text incorrectly reads: *qui nefaria cum sit divisio una, virtuti*, etc. (“since the division is wicked, one [part serves] virtue,” etc.). The following context, which sets out five divisions, confirms the emendation.]—that is, when someone possesses such ardent charity that, if it were possible, he would pour himself entirely into the heart of the listener, according to the Apostle’s saying: “I wish that all were as I myself am” (1 Cor. VII, 7); and: “Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians; our heart is enlarged. You are not restricted by us, though you are restricted in your own hearts” (2 Cor. VI, 11–12). It is as though he had said: although the vessel of your heart is narrow and able to contain little, the hand of charity that pours out is not narrow.

The second division appears to serve flattery: someone, under the guise of teaching and wishing to please some powerful person, introduces satire and violates doctrine.

The third is found to serve avarice. Many, in their eagerness for profit, sell by speaking what ought to be concealed in silence.

The fourth serves boasting more particularly. In order to appear to know a great deal, someone very often reveals what he ought to have concealed, contrary to the Psalmist’s words: “I have hidden your sayings in my heart, that I may not sin against you” (Ps. CXVIII, 11). Hence Augustine, explaining the same verse, says: “He who divulges secrets diminishes Christ’s beauty.” To this the poet Persius’ saying neatly corresponds:

“Is your knowledge really worth nothing unless another knows that you know it?”

The fifth part of these teachers is produced solely by heedless loquacity. Many, while they relax their tongues by speaking too carelessly and without restraint, thoughtlessly utter what, although they may desire it, they cannot recall.

Of these five divisions, the first should be praised and retained; the second together with the fifth should be pitied and corrected; the third together with the fourth should be wholly avoided.

After these there are those who dare, with excessive presumption, to teach others what they themselves have scarcely learned. Of them the Apostle says: “Desiring to become teachers of the law, understanding neither what they say nor concerning what they make assertions” (1 Tim. I, 7). Very often, while they disdain to become pupils of truth, they become teachers of error.

There are also some who, according to the Apostle, are “always learning and never arriving at a knowledge of the truth” (2 Tim. III, 7). There are likewise those who speak at length about what they do not understand. Conversely, there are those whose understanding is abundant but whose eloquence is lacking.

The person in whom both eloquence and understanding make him distinguished should be praised. The first kind I mentioned should be blamed for presumption; the other should not be reproved but embraced—unless, perhaps, he is full of envy or avarice and, as usually happens, empty of kindness or charity. I urge you most earnestly to beware of such a person.

## TITLE XVII—Concerning the rich

33. Are you rich? Beware that proud rich man who despised Lazarus. Fear lest, if you deny a crumb to the poor, you should desire but not receive even a drop of water (Luke XVI).

You appear to possess certain things? Scatter them, so that you may truly possess them.

“How,” you ask, “shall I possess them truly? Do I not even now truly possess them when I enjoy them?”

You do not need to ask this of me. Ask yourself; confront yourself; argue your case with yourself.

Tell me, I ask, of what things do your riches consist?

“Of estates,” you say, “of servants, maidservants, horses, oxen, and other cattle; of the obedience of those who serve; of the pleasure of dogs and hawks; of an abundance of clothing, utensils, grain, wine and oil, weapons, silver, gold, and gems.”

Very well. Now I wish to confront you. Tell me, I ask: has a storm never struck these estates of yours?

“How could it have happened otherwise?” you ask.

“How,” I say, “can you say that you ever truly possessed what a storm was able to take away? For what can become another’s through someone else’s invasion is in no sense truly yours.” Hence the saying of the wise man: “Do not call your own what can be changed.”

But let us examine the rest. Perhaps you possess those things more securely. Can servants, maidservants, horses, and oxen be seized by robbers or overwhelmed by disaster? Finally, is not the lot of dying theirs as much as yours? [Note: The Vulgate has *aequa tibi* (“equal to you”), less appropriately.]

“Clothing cannot be destroyed by moths?”

“I know a remedy for that,” you say.

“Do you know some remedy by which it cannot be consumed by fire?”

“No,” you say, “but I send it there where the gold is kept as well.”

“I grant that there is a vaulted place to which fire cannot gain access. Will it always remain there? Will it never come out?”

“It certainly will.”

“What then?”

“If it is safe, it is safe; if it is lost, it is lost.”

Where, then, is such great diligence, such great guarding? What benefit came from guarding it for so long, only to lose it eventually?

Let none of these things happen. When you depart from here, who carries your riches with you? Do I not see you, with your thumbs tied and almost naked, being carried to the grave? And if this happens to you, I might perhaps call you blessed, for I have often heard of a rich man being eaten by wolves.

34. “What, then,” you ask, “should be done? Should we devote ourselves to laziness, do no work, and beg from everyone? Who will give if everyone begs?”

“No,” says the Lord; “I do not command that. Indeed, I forbid it in every way. For I foretold to you that you would eat your bread in the sweat of your face” (Gen. III, 19). When I foretold that, I imposed labor. You, on the contrary, wish to do no work but to take from those who work; while you are idle in sins and pleasures, you impose labor upon others. Yet you read that I said in the Psalm: “You shall eat the labors of your hands; blessed are you, and it shall be well with you” (Ps. CXXVII, 2).

And through the Apostle: “If anyone is unwilling to work, neither let him eat” (2 Thess. III, 10).

Therefore work, I say; enjoy, distribute, scatter. Just as I do not cease to give—or rather, to entrust—so you must not cease to distribute. And always, because I have commanded it, persist in work, so that you may have something to distribute and there may be no need to store it up.

Idleness, unless it is for my sake on appointed days, is an enemy of the soul. Indeed, I do not want you to be idle at any time. For although I said through the Prophet, “Be still,” I added, “and know that I am God” (Ps. XLV, 11), so that you may understand that you must devote yourself to me and serve me.

Why do you need to store up, when by my gift you receive enough each day? Why is it appropriate for you to store up when you do not know whom you serve?

“I serve my children,” you say.

“Perhaps they will die before you.”

“I will give for their souls,” you say.

“When? After hell has swallowed them up? Have you not heard the Psalm saying, ‘Who will confess you in hell?’ (Ps. VI, 6.) Have you not read, ‘A brother does not redeem; a man will redeem’?” (Ps. XLVIII, 8.) Finally, have you not heard me say, “These will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life”? (Matt. XXV, 46.)

How, moreover, can something be eternal if, once acquired through someone’s gift, it can be made nothing? Have you not heard: “The tree, wherever it falls, there it will remain”? (Ecclus. II, 3.)

35. Therefore, if you wish to give for your own soul or for anyone else’s, give while you possess it; while it is within your right, your judgment, and your power; while you can be redeemed and while you can be liberated. For your riches can go before you; they absolutely cannot follow you.

Begin giving while you are healthy. If illness comes, distribute even more diligently. And if death intervenes, do not be afraid. What is distributed here will be of benefit there—provided only that God does not judge the beginning too late, does not take necessity into account, approves the will, and does not condemn the intention. Let him consider that here, while healthy, you wished to give; let him see that here you began and here wished to complete it. For he judges the will and the intention.

“But perhaps,” you say, “my parents left these things to me. May I not leave them to my children, grandchildren, or some heirs?”

Woe to those who left everything to you and took nothing for themselves—or rather, took a great deal. What they took will never fail: they took perpetual condemnation for themselves; they took eternal fire for themselves. It is as though God could not feed both us and you by their generosity, he who feeds the whole world every day.

“My father,” you say, “left it to me.”

“Who gave it to your father?”

“My grandfather,” you say.

“And who gave it to your grandfather?”

“My great-grandfather.”

“And your great-grandfather—from whom?”

“So-and-so.”

“And from whom did they receive it?”

“Why do you weary me by asking?” you say. “From Adam, unless from someone else.”

“And Adam—from whom?”

“From God.”

Then it belonged to God—or rather, whether you wish it or not, everything belongs to God; even if he does not receive it from you, he possesses it through you. “The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness” (Ps. XXV, 1).

But woe to those whose heirs have inherited so much that the Lord has never been worthy to be their heir. Break, my son, break, I beg you, this cord, lest you be bound with them in destruction. Take the Lord as your heir, so that he may receive you as a sharer in his kingdom. Share with him the inheritance of your children and make him their brother. If you do not wish this, neither will you seize his inheritance.

Nevertheless, whether you wish it or not, I shall prove by your own testimony that you do not possess your riches.

“Do so,” you say.

“Distribute,” I say.

“I will not,” you say.

“Why?”

“I fear,” you say.

“What do you fear?”

“Poverty.”

Then your riches belong to poverty, not to you. For the master is the one who forbids the subject, and whatever is forbidden belongs to the one who forbids it.

Behold: by your own confession I have discovered not only that you do not possess your riches, but also that you are possessed by poverty, to which your riches are enslaved.

But I see what you have evaded. Since you are a servant of avarice, and do not dare even to name it, you have chosen to take refuge under the cover of poverty, although it is clear that you do not fear poverty but recoil from it. You ought rather to curse the one whose love makes you recoil from poverty.

For why should you fear poverty? Do you not see that there are more poor people whom God feeds every day than there are rich? Do you not know that those same poor are raised to such a height that, in that judgment where your sole and singular consolation will be to deserve placement on the right because of the service you have rendered them, they are called brothers by the Lord himself? Do you therefore despise—or is perhaps the brotherhood of God of little value to you?

36. “I am ashamed,” you say.

“Why?”

“Those who honor me now will later hold me in contempt. Yet it is a beautiful thing to be pointed out with a finger and to hear it said, ‘This is he.’”

Reason answers you: O the cares of men! O how much emptiness there is in human affairs! Why do you desire this so eagerly, as I see you do?

The Psalm can teach you how futile it is: “I saw the wicked exalted and raised up like the cedars of Lebanon; I passed by, and behold, he was not; I sought him, and his place was not found” (Ps. XXXVI, 35–36).

“Behold another mistress,” I say.

“Which one?”

“Pride.”

For what harm can anyone’s contempt do to you if you possess yourself and remain firmly rooted in humility? Throw a dart at a marble column and see what will happen.

“Now,” you say, “I rejoice, I delight, I rest.”

Behold luxury, the third mistress. But erase that third claim, for you do not rest. Nor is it without reason that God joins anxiety to riches in the Gospel (Luke VIII, 14), since, penetrating the hearts of all, he knows very well what anxiety torments wretched rich people.

The wise man who says, “Everything that rises above others is more afflicted by sorrows than it rejoices in honors,” would certainly not have said this unless he knew very well what evils the rich endure inwardly.

Finally, considering yourself and placing yourself before yourself as the judge of your own condition, question your soul: what is it that constricts it so greatly? What increases your vigils and takes away your sleep? What makes you run about and forbids you to lie down? What is that confusion between love and fear, what that anxiety, and what those frequent sighs?

You will see as clearly as daylight how fiercely you labor under the plague of restlessness, by what tumult of thoughts you are driven, and by what storms of sorrow you are battered—although you say that you rest, delight, and rejoice. You know very well how earthly riches, though they sometimes delight for a time, also prick the heart.

You rejoice while acquiring; you grieve while losing. You pant while demanding; you fear while being demanded of. You appear, as a *myrmicoleo* [Note: *Myrmicoleo*, a compound word formed from the Greek μύρμηξ (*myrmēx*), “ant,” and the Latin *leo*, “lion,” denotes a small animal very hostile to ants. It hides in the dust and kills ants carrying grain. It is called both ant and lion because toward other animals it is like an ant, but toward ants it is like a lion. See Du Cange, s.v. *Formicaleo*.], to be neither unlike an ant to some nor unlike a lion to others.

To complete your misery, you very often fear those to whom you seem incomparably superior in power. Hence someone says most eloquently: “How can a rich man be at peace when the very things he possesses, lest he lose them, continually make him restless? Therefore desire has preferred a rich man to be restless and fearful rather than secure.”

Hence Seneca says that things are much worse for kings than for servants, because servants fear individuals, whereas kings fear many.

Placed, then, in such great disturbance of mind and, so to speak, completely deceived concerning yourself, what can you say is yours when you yourself have been subjected to another’s right? Hence the Lord says beautifully: “You cannot serve God and mammon” (Matt. VI, 24), having first declared that no one can serve two masters.

37. But lest anyone think that I am saying this about all rich people, let him know that there are two kinds of rich: one good, the other bad; one proud, the other humble.

Who does not know that King David was exceedingly rich? Who would call Abraham and Job poor? Yet David says: “But I am needy and poor” (Ps. LXIX, 6). Abraham likewise says: “I shall speak to my Lord, although I am dust and ashes” (Gen. XVIII, 27). Job says: “If I have despised judgment with my servant and maidservant when they contended against me” (Job XXXI, 13).

See how great is the humility among this kind of rich.

Of this kind of rich is the one of whom it is said: “Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and the poor” (Ps. XL, 2). And elsewhere: “The cedars of Lebanon, which the Lord planted, will there the sparrows make their nests” (Ps. CIII, 17)—that is, whatever powerful people there are in the world, in whose estates, as Augustine also approves, monks build cells and oratories, and in them guests, pilgrims, strangers, captives, and the poor are gathered.

Of this kind of rich is also the one whose praise the Psalmist celebrates in these words: “Glory and riches are in his house, and his righteousness endures forever” (Ps. CXI, 3).

This is the kind of rich who seek nothing else in their riches except the redemption of souls, the food necessary for themselves and their households, and a generous use of their possessions.

Although these people are exceedingly wealthy, they are not money-grubbers. According to the saying of a certain wise man, they do not desire riches, but, if riches are present, they arrange them with the greatest wisdom and care (Wis. VIII, 5).

Of them Isidore also says: “There are certain humble rich people whom the pride of possessions does not inflate, as were often the saints of the Old Testament, who abounded in riches and yet excelled in humility.”

And concerning both kinds he says: “Some perish through human possessions, which they loved too eagerly; others are saved while, admiring the beauty of the Creator’s most beautiful providence in those possessions, they praise it, or while through the work of mercy they purchase heavenly goods from them.”

38. Let us now consider and beware of the other kind of rich. “Woe to you rich,” says the Lord, “for you have your consolation” (Luke VI, 24).

And in the Psalm: “They will leave their riches, and their tombs will be their houses forever” (Ps. XLVIII, 11–12).

Likewise: “Do not be afraid when a man becomes rich, and when the glory of his house is multiplied” (ibid. 17).

And shortly afterward: “He will enter into the generation of his fathers; forever he will not see light” (Ps. XLVIII, 20).

Job says something more explicit: “They spend their days in good things, and in a moment they descend to hell” (Job XXI, 13).

Another says:

“Come now, rich people,” he says, “weep and howl over the miseries that will come upon you. Your riches have rotted, and your garments have been eaten by moths. Your gold and silver have rusted, and their rust will be a testimony against you and will eat your flesh like fire. You have stored up treasure on earth and have nourished your hearts in luxury on the day of slaughter. You have brought wrath upon yourselves in the last days. Behold, the pay of your laborers who harvested your lands, which was defrauded by you, cries out, and their cry has entered the ears of the Lord of Hosts. You have killed the righteous, and he did not resist you” (James V, 1–6).

Just as true humility is no greater cause of salvation for good rich people, so there is no surer cause of ruin for these people than their pride. Pride not only destroys them but also oppresses, burns, and torments others, while devaluing those who are better than themselves [Note: *Depretio* is used by Tertullian, Cyprian, and others in the sense of “to depress” or “to value more cheaply.”]

Hence the Psalmist says: “When the wicked becomes proud, the poor man is set on fire” (Ps. IX, 23).

Likewise, in prayer: “Have mercy on us, Lord, have mercy on us, for we have been filled exceedingly with contempt; our soul has been filled exceedingly with the reproach of the prosperous and the contempt of the proud” (Ps. CXXII, 4).

The Apostle therefore applies a kind of medicine to them: “Command the rich of this world,” he says, “not to be proud or to hope in the uncertainty of riches” (1 Tim. VI, 17).

And, more generally, to all of them: “Let them do good, let them be rich in good works, let them give readily, let them share, storing up for themselves a good foundation, so that they may take hold of the true life” (ibid. 18–19).

Behold how the camel, having laid aside the burden of its hump, is able to pass through the eye of a needle (Matt. XIX, 24); how the crooked animal, having laid aside its burden, can take up the wings of a dove (Ps. LIV, 7) and rest in the branches of the tree grown from mustard seed (Luke XIII, 19). And not only this: it can also be enriched with so great a prerogative that Midian, Ephah, and Sheba may carry gold and frankincense to the temple of the Lord upon its *taspharus* (Isa. LX, 6) [Note: [Col. 0183D] *Tasphorus* means “back,” upon which burdens for transport are placed; it derives from the barbarous word *tassus*, “heap” or “pile,” and the Greek *φορός*, “bearing.” Hence shortly afterward it is written that the riches of merchants—that is, of those who work well—are carried on the back.].

The Ishmaelite merchants, too, may carry stacte, *thymiama* (incense), and resin growing in Gilead (Gen. XXXVII, 25)—that is, holy preachers may carry the words of Scripture like a collection of spices and a desirable treasure of wisdom. Through these they may enrich others, kindle them to the love of God with the fragrance of a good reputation, and offer the healing of a good example to weak minds, so that all may steadfastly recognize that what is impossible with human beings is altogether possible with God (Mark X, 27).

How this may happen, Truth itself did not conceal when it said in the Gospel: “Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward” (Matt. X, 41), and so forth.

And the Apostle says: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Gal. VI, 2).

Therefore, O rich man, receive someone who prophesies in Christ’s name, in his name, and you will receive the prophet’s reward together with him. Support the righteous with your resources, and you will receive the merit of righteousness. For this is what it means to carry the riches of merchants—that is, of those who do good—on one’s back: to offer them assistance in good work.

The assistance given to them obtains a share in them; and their fellowship will acquire an eternal kingdom, by the gift of him who lives and reigns forever.

## TITLE XVIII—Concerning people of moderate fortune
29. Are you of moderate means? Hear the Apostle: “Not that there should be relief for others and tribulation for you, but that, by equality, your abundance may supply their need, so that their abundance may also be a supply for your need” (II Cor. VIII, 13–14); and that passage from Tobit: “If you have much, give abundantly; if little, strive to share even that willingly” (Tob. IV, 9). But if you are altogether poor, consider the widow’s two small coins (Luke XXI, 2). Perhaps you lack even these? You have a cup of cold water (Matt. X, 42). “There is no well,” you say; “there is no spring or river; the stream itself is absent; there is no drawing-vessel at all.”

[Note: A *hauritorium* is an instrument for drawing water.]

And here too the Lord’s counsel is not lacking. Hear, then, the angels’ song in the Gospel: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke II, 14). But, according to Jerome, the miser lacks what he has just as much as what he does not have.

But alas! How senseless I am—what have I accomplished? For, while I hasten more quickly than is appropriate, I have entirely omitted the greatest fault of certain people, both of the rich and of those of moderate means. Yet I shall retrace the path of my discourse; I shall say it again, repeat it again, cry it out, say it, and not let it go. Still, I shall not speak from myself: I shall thunder with another’s voice. It is so great and of such a kind that I dare not suppress it, even if I cannot explain it in my own words. I could perhaps manage it somehow, but reason [or: discourse] opposes me, since it has already been expressed most eloquently by another.

It may happen, however, that this labor of ours falls into the hands of someone entirely unacquainted with that author’s statements.

[Note: The Vulgate has *penitus*, “entirely.” A slight alteration of the sense suggested the correction; for this reason we printed *cujuslibet* above, where *quorumlibet* stood. If *quorumlibet* were retained, then *expertes sint* would have to be corrected.]

For I certainly know that countless people will not be lacking who are so abundantly furnished with these and many other things far removed from our own knowledge that they would disdain to have their sight obstructed even for a moment by looking at our writings, much less desire to enjoy them by reading. Therefore I more willingly use here the discourse both of this author

[Note: “This author” refers to the one whom he had previously mentioned with the words “I shall thunder with another’s voice,” namely Saint John Chrysostom, whom he shortly afterward calls the golden mouth and from whom he quotes a lengthy testimony.]

and of others like him than my own, so that those who cannot find their statements elsewhere may be able to find them here, and through their association may gain some strength for our own work.

30. Say, then, I ask you; speak, cry out, you who are admirable in speech, learning, and intellect—and therefore rightly called “the golden mouth”—you most powerful executor of God’s grace, which you appear to bear in your own name.

“He cannot,” he says, “show mercy who, with possessions spread far and wide, does not permit another to possess even the land adjoining his own. While he joins boundaries, he extends his limits; he brings charges against the poor, oppresses the person of moderate means, excludes his neighbor, and drives away by harassment and persecution everyone placed around him. For him alone, what is a public evil is good: he either hoards the harvest, or seeks to corner the grain supply, or inflates prices, or increases interest; he seeks the arts of acquiring profit and of doing harm.

“Can such a person fulfill the duties of mercy, whose delight is the sweet groaning of orphans and whose pleasure is the weeping of widows, while he delights in such plunder and feeds upon spoils—one who is rich by his chest, not by merit; by possession, not by birth; by name, not by dignity? Can mercy touch or humanity move one whose greed neither finds his own property sufficient nor sets a limit to what belongs to others? Even if he gives something to a poor person, he is worse if he takes it from one person in order to give it to another; if he feeds a hungry person with the bread of another hungry person; if he clothes the naked with another’s spoils—for it is written: ‘He who offers a sacrifice from the substance of the poor is like one who sacrifices a son in the presence of his father’ (Ecclus. XXXIV, 24).”

See, prudent reader, that you can discern three distinctions within one class of rich people, if you wish: first, those who seize and do not give; third, those who seize much and give little; and the middle group, those who are said neither to seize nor to give, but who devote themselves to increasing their profits and hoard in two ways—that is, here for another person, although they do not know for whom, and in the future for themselves, the wrath of God.

Now let us learn from the same honey-flowing mouth what other kind—the kind opposed to these—is found among good people.

“He,” he says, “is truly rich who is wealthy in mercy rather than in riches, who shares his resources with the poor; who shows himself rich by giving rather than by possessing; who remembers that he has riches for this purpose: to lend to God, to feed Christ, to clothe the Lord; who does not seek to leave his patrimony to an ungrateful heir, but desires to entrust it to Christ in the poor; who entrusts his riches to heaven rather than to the world; who desires to be superior in works rather than in the resources of his substance; who sends his treasures to the things above; who lives in order to work; who works in order to deserve to live forever; who is moved by the misfortunes of widows, stirred by the misery of orphans, takes up the cause of those who suffer, and condemns the arrogance of the proud.””

31. Since, then, you have expressed so wittily and so comprehensively—on what might be called the ten-finger scale, with the two-handed operation of your discourse—how the humility of good rich people, disemboweling the three-forked breast of the proud, reveals its hidden places to those who wish to know and avoid what is opposed to them, I now ask you to bring forth the crosses which they also endure in this world, and thus, loosening the reins, let us hurry on to other matters.

[Note: This intricate period should be constructed and explained so that it does not delay readers. He addresses Saint John Chrysostom: “Since, then, you have expressed”—that is, explained—“so wittily and so comprehensively, on what might be called the ten-finger scale and with the two-handed operation” (that is, most clearly and with the greatest lucidity), “how the humility of good rich people, disemboweling the three-forked breast of the proud” (he calls it three-forked because he previously distinguished three kinds of proud rich people), “reveals its hidden places”—that is, those of the breast of the proud—“to those who wish to know and avoid what is opposed to them, I ask you now to bring forth what crosses these same rich people endure in this world,” and so forth.]

“To possess,” he says, “and not to act; to be able to show mercy, and not to wish to do so . . . . He considers it entrusted to him that which, through his own torment, he transmits to his heir; and the wretched man is not permitted to touch what belongs to him, because he is compelled to reserve it for someone who will come after him. He guards more anxiously than he acquires, keeps more painfully than he seized; for he sighs while awake as he acquires, and sighs while asleep as he preserves. For him there are neither joyful vigils nor secure sleep, neither happy day nor safe night. He rushes about, is tormented, groans, and, as though what he acquires benefited him, desires to increase what he will also leave—together with his own torment—to another, even to an ungrateful person, so that the burden of his patrimony may be matched by a corresponding accumulation of anxiety.”

32. Having shown this briefly and most eloquently, let the person of moderate means also hear, I ask, what is most clearly suited to him in your words, even if he places before himself every sort of cloud of excuse.

[Note: “Your words,” he says, because he is addressing Saint John Chrysostom here; hence he soon says, “you wrote.”]

“No one is wretched,” you say, “except one who has refused to show mercy, because no one who desires to show mercy can fail to have something to give. No one can leave a petitioner empty-handed except one who has refused to lend to him. For the prices of mercy have not been fixed; nor, unless someone gives much, can what is given be acceptable. Nor do the needy ask anyone for as much as those who are asked are unable to give; rather, someone is compelled to give much from little, or very much from something small, since divine kindness gladly accepts a little given from little.”

Behold the rich person, in addition to pride and cruelty, also exceedingly greedy; behold the person of moderate means, exceedingly tight-fisted. And if I seemed to you to spare you by hurrying, certainly this eloquent teacher did not spare you; nor does the all-encompassing voice of Holy Scripture spare you. Therefore I ask and admonish you: do not flatter yourselves in anything, lest you suddenly be seized and rescued by no one.

## TITLE XIX.—On the Beggar

33. Are you a beggar? Hear the Apostle: “If anyone does not wish to work, neither should he eat” (II Thess. III, 10). Hear also the proverb of Wisdom: “Every sluggard is always in want” (Prov. XXI, 5); and again: “Because of the cold the sluggard would not plow; therefore he will beg in summer, and nothing will be given him” (Prov. XX, 4); and again: “Poverty and disgrace belong to the one who abandons discipline” (Prov. XIII, 18); and again: “A slack hand produces poverty” (Prov. X, 4); “There is one who seems rich when he has nothing, and one who seems poor when he has many riches” (Prov. XIII, 7).

The same author again says: “He who works his land will be satisfied with bread, but he who pursues idleness is most foolish” (Prov. XII, 11; Ecclus. XX, 30). And: “Go to the ant, O sluggard; consider its ways and learn wisdom. Although it has no guide or overseer, it prepares its food in summer and gathers in the harvest what it may eat. How long will you sleep, O sluggard? When will you rise from your sleep? You will sleep a little, doze a little, fold your hands a little to sleep, and a greater want will come upon you, as it were, and poverty like an armed man” (Prov. VI, 6–11).

I have set this out in order so that I might urge you to consider what cause makes you beg, lest perhaps, like many people, you wish under this pretext to gather riches or to serve idleness. There are also many poor people, as you heard above, whose pride exceeds the arrogance of the rich; while, conversely, there are rich people whose humility surpasses the meekness of many poor people. Hence Truth beautifully says: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V, 3). You should understand that some people, in the most wretched condition of poverty, deprived here of the joys of this world because of lack of possessions and in the future of the kingdom of God because of the wickedness of their merits, are excluded from this blessedness and wholly alien to it.

Hence comes that saying of the Wise Man: “Good is the substance that has no sin in the conscience, and most wicked is poverty in the mouth of the ungodly” (Ecclus. XIII, 30). Therefore Jerome also says most clearly:

“Riches,” he says, “do not harm the rich person if he uses them well; nor does poverty make the poor person more commendable if, amid filth and want, he does not avoid sins.”

Abraham and [lacuna]

[Note: The passage has a gap. Supply “wicked poor people,” or “thieves,” or something similar.]

furnish daily examples in testimony to both matters: the one was God’s friend amid the greatest riches; the others, caught daily in crimes, pay the penalties prescribed by the laws.

Here too is Isidore:

“There is an arrogance among poor people whom not even riches elevate, and whose sole will is pride. Although they lack wealth, because of the swelling of their minds they are condemned more than proud rich people.”

Augustine also, speaking of disabled people, says:

“Oh, what great evils the blind commit—evils from which an evil mind abstains!”

34. Since these things are so, strive, I ask you, to serve God humbly according to your ability, so that at that supreme judgment you may be placed with the sheep on his right and may deserve to be called brother and blessed by the highest and just Judge—not placed with the goats on the left because of pride, marked also by greed, and deservedly separated from the presence of God and the saints as accursed.

Know also that you must not be free from works of mercy, since the Lord most certainly testifies that offering a cup of cold water to one’s neighbor is not without reward (Matt. X, 41). You also find the angels’ song in the Gospel: “Glory to God in the highest,” they say, “and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke II, 14).

Hence John Chrysostom, in his customary eloquence, says:

“Lest anyone be able to clear himself by the excuse that he possesses nothing, the duties of mercy are imposed without payment, so that it may be shown that the Lord has laid upon the poor themselves the obligation of performing them. To offer a cup of cold water to a prophet is promised as the prophet’s reward. To visit a sick person or one confined in prison is to visit God, so that the person who cannot show mercy from his substance may nevertheless be rewarded for good will. Thus it is already clear that, according to the circumstances of human beings, the duties of mercy ought not to cease, so that heavenly rewards may be repaid to those who labor; so that, when the merciful begin to be examined, the barren may be condemned, and the merciful person, because he has shown mercy, may rejoice, while the barren person may discover punishments he did not expect.”

[Note: Here *expungere* means “to scrutinize” or “to examine,” as in Suetonius, *Claudius* 15: “When he was examining the lists of offices, so that he might dismiss some judges and retain others.” There *expungeret* has the same meaning as “he examined.”]

Reflecting on this with yourself, and setting aside every excuse—even if you are maimed

[Note: The Vulgate has *intrinsecus* in the text and *altruncus* in the margin. We preferred the marginal reading, which we believe to be that of the manuscript, because it better suits the sense: people are called *trunci* when they are disabled or mutilated in some limb.]

and wholly deprived of the function of every limb—provided that your inner sense, deliberating, remains sound, offer to God whatever you can, diligently knowing that you too will be a debtor to all those whose resources support you.

But woe to you if you are able to live by your own labor and yet, sluggish with idleness, enjoy the work of another. “But infirmity compels me,” you say. Then give thanks to God, take care that you do not murmur, and pray for those by whose resources you are sustained.

[Note: *Continere* is frequently used by Saint Gregory in the sense “to nourish” or “to sustain.” See Book I, Letters 44 and 45; Book V, Letter 30; Homily 20 on the Gospels; and elsewhere.]

“I am healthy,” you say, “but a multitude of children weighs me down.” If you can, I say, with your wife’s consent practice continence, and work with your hands, so that you may be able to sustain both yourself and others. “I cannot,” you say. Then lament the fault, for this too is a serious disadvantage; beg for what is sufficient, and beware of excess. Take care that you do not thereby feed mice and worms.

You who are healthy, support the rest; visit the sick; bury the dead; share with everyone the blessing bestowed upon you by the Lord. Be eyes to the blind, ears to the deaf, a tongue to the mute, and feet to the lame. Never be anxious for tomorrow on your own account. If your way lies near a church, take care not to pass by until there too you have begged forgiveness for your offenses and eternal life for your benefactors.

# HERE BEGINS BOOK TWO

This book likewise contains the following Preface:

I. The Man; II. The Woman; III. The Husband; IV. The Wife; V. The Celibate; VI. Father and Mother; VII. Son and Daughter; VIII. The Widow; IX. The Virgin; X. The Little Child; XI. The Boy; XII. The Adolescent; XIII. The Old Man.

[Col. 0189]

With you, God, as my guide, having briefly completed the first book, I confidently undertake this second little work, still relying upon you; speaking sorrowfully through no one’s loquacity

[Note: “Through no one’s loquacity,” he says, because, while writing these things in prison, he had no one with whom he could converse.]

and about to relate matters for the most part read, but in small part learned by experience. For, although from the twilight of infancy I have been led almost to the midday of this age, I still suffer the blind night of various misfortunes; and, shut away in a triple prison,

[Note: He indicates the tower at Pavia, in which he was confined behind three locks or doors.]

I am bound in a workhouse. Once I seemed to have been appointed to free the people from darkness and to call them to the wondrous light of your vision; but I have been deprived of the fellowship of my flock because I was unwilling to entrust it to the wolf who was lying in wait for it—as is reported, and would that it were truthfully said.

[Note: The man who invaded the see of Verona after expelling Ratherius was Manasses. Accordingly, he appears to indicate him here by the name of “wolf,” just as in other later works he calls Milo a wolf, since Milo afterward occupied the same see after Ratherius had again been expelled. It was commonly reported that Manasses was one of the three whom Hugh wished to appoint to the Church of Verona. The king alone consented to the election of Ratherius, because he hoped that Ratherius, being ill, would soon die. But when he discovered after the election that Ratherius had recovered from his illness, he regretted the election and employed certain men either to drive him into flight or to compel him to leave the Church, or to treat him so excessively that he would have an opportunity to expel him. For he wished to give the bishopric to others, especially to Manasses, and indeed later gave it to him. Here Ratherius appears to imply that he was unwilling to entrust the bishopric to Manasses as to a wolf.]

I have been exposed to punishment because I feared to expose it alone to danger; I have been subjected to the domination of the world because I believed that I ought to submit myself to you alone, O Lord.

Yet, knowing that nothing occurs in the world created by you while you are wholly opposed to it, I calmly endure this storm, supported by your consolation.

[Note: Construe the passage as follows: “Yet, knowing that nothing occurs in the world created by you, with you wholly opposed to it, I endure this storm, supported by your consolation,” and so forth.]

I believe that you can easily calm this sea whenever and if ever you wish, you who first set sand as a boundary for the sea: “Thus far you shall come, and you shall go no farther; here your waves shall be broken against yourself” (Job XXXVIII, 11).

Thunder, then, again from heaven, O Christ, if it pleases you, with your command; and even now forbid what you have most frequently forbidden by threatening through many and through yourself, mercifully taking pity on this most wretched man. Speak mercifully to the one crying from the depths: “Come out”; say to the one surrounded by dreadful darkness: “Rise from the prison-house.” Say: “Do not forbid.”

[Note: The printed editions wrongly have *interdicet*, “he will forbid,” here. The construction immediately following is: “Speak mercifully to the one crying from the depths: ‘Come out’; say to the one surrounded by dreadful darkness: ‘Rise from the prison-house’; do not forbid.”]

But since what seems long to the person who desires it, and almost difficult, is brief and entirely easy to the one who arranges it, I shall strive meanwhile to set down here whatever you suggest to my mind—whatever may complete this little work also with your help—committing the rest to your mercy, at whose nod I know that all things are favorable [or: come to pass].

## TITLE I.—On Men

2. Are you a man, bearing a name derived from *virtus*, “virtue,” or from *vireo*, “to be vigorous,” or from *vires*, “strength,” or from *vis*, “force,” together with the verb *rego*, “to rule,” as I once heard someone argue—not inappropriately, as it seemed to me? Avoiding feminine softness, strengthen your mind in virtue. For the Apostle says: “The soft will not possess the kingdom of God” (I Cor. VI, 9). You can do this if, relying on your strength, you raise the force of your spirit to the stars, subdue the flesh to the soul and the soul to God, and, always firm and unbending, advance with God’s help against the pleasures of the world and the allurements of the flesh, keeping ever before your eyes the Psalmist’s words: “Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened, all you who hope in the Lord” (Ps. XXVI, 14).

And also the Lord’s words to Job: “Gird your loins like a man” (Job XXXVIII, 3). Considering that you have been directed to wage the Lord’s battles against the aerial powers, which are signified by the kings of the Canaanites, so that you may deserve to enter the promised land—for, having already been led out of Egypt through the Red Sea, that is, through baptism consecrated by Christ’s blood, you are walking through the wilderness of this world—apply to yourself the command: “Be strong and courageous” (Deut. VII, 23).

For how greatly the lax and dissolute guardianship of the mind harms even the pursuits of the perfect is demonstrated by the falls of that most just Lot, that most powerful Samson, and that wisest Solomon. The death of Ish-bosheth also shows whether the entrance to the heart should be entrusted to feminine or masculine guardianship (II Kings IV, 5).

## TITLE II.—On Women

3. Are you a woman? Strive to direct the softness which you bear in your name toward the virtue of obedience, not toward the vice of dissolution. In the beginning, woman was called *virago*, that is, “strong woman” (Gen. II, 23), so that you may remember that you must be strong against vices and flexible in submission to the Lord’s commands.

Therefore, a man in mind and a woman in flesh, strive also to overcome the raging assaults of vices and pleasures rising against the spirit, with the strong vigor of your mind. Consider that the divine Scriptures provide you with very many examples for this work: in the Old Testament, although all the men had been consumed by fear, as though by the sleep of death, before an enemy terrifying to the whole world, you read that by God’s grace a wondrous victory was won; and in the New Testament, innumerable women who had forgotten feminine weakness, having completed a manly combat and conquered their enemies, earned with the triumph of glory the palm of victory and a distinguished crown.

## TITLE III.—On Spouses

4. Are you a wife or a husband? Consider what fidelity you owe your spouse, and who is regarded as the exactor and witness of that fidelity. You can perceive from the testimonies of Holy Scripture that marriage is good—under this condition, of course, of being born and dying in which we were created—and that violating this good is a grave crime. This is especially clear since, at the beginning, the Lord wished to make the bond of this covenant so indissoluble that he did not wish to fashion two separate individuals separately, but one from the other, with the command that followed and showed why he had done so:

“For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” (Gen. II, 24).

“The two,” he says, “shall be one flesh.” If, therefore, such is the power—or rather, since such is the power—of this union, let those who, through a most perverse misuse, sever this bond of such great fidelity and such indissoluble love, whether by committing adultery or by entirely abandoning their wives or husbands, consider what a grave and harmful crime they acquire for themselves. This is especially so since they have an evident command against it both in the Gospel and in the Apostle of the Lord.

And if violated charity, when hatred overturns it, is marked as the crime of murder in two brothers regenerated spiritually, what happens when not only the spirit but also one flesh is dragged apart into different directions by an abominable divorce?

5. It must be known, however, that there are two kinds of marriage: one without fault, the other venial with fault. Anything added beyond these is already adultery, even if the perpetrator violates no one else’s marriage bed, because in himself—within whom he ought to have lain—he violates the temple of God.

The Creator himself deigned to ennoble the first kind so greatly that he not only commanded it but also deigned to be present at the wedding, and, performing his first miracle, distinguished it with his own gift (John II, 1–11). It is clear that this kind exists solely for the love of children, so that the multitude of human beings might be propagated to fill the world, might exercise legitimate dominion over the creatures granted to it, and might render due service to the Creator; and so that the city of God might be completed from the number of the predestined.

The other kind, venial and permitted, is conceded by the Apostle solely because of fornication, namely so that no one, impatient under lust, may fall into adultery or any illicit desire, or—what is incomparably worse—be compelled to transgress in any way against nature. Because of such things it is said: “It is better to marry than to burn” (I Cor. VII, 9), that is, to be inflamed even to dissolution or an illicit or most filthy emission, and not to be restrained by any love of God or fear of hell.

See how much even a marriage involving fault is worth, since it is conceded by necessity because of something worse. Hence Augustine writes beautifully in his book *On the Good of Marriage*, against the heretic Jovinian (nos. 11–12):

“Intercourse necessary for the sake of procreation is without fault, and it alone is nuptial intercourse. But intercourse that proceeds beyond this necessity already obeys not reason but lust. Nevertheless, not to demand this from one’s spouse but to render it, lest the spouse sin damnably through fornication, belongs to the marital person. If both are subjected to such desire, they do something that is not wholly a matter of marriage. Yet if, in their union, they love what is honorable more than what is dishonorable—that is, what belongs to marriage more than what does not belong to marriage—then, by the authority of the Apostle, this is conceded to them as a pardon. Their marriages do not encourage this fault, but plead for pardon, provided that they do not turn away God’s mercy from themselves, whether by abstaining on certain days so that they may devote themselves to prayer and, through this abstinence, commend their prayers, as also through fasting, or by changing natural use into that which is against nature, which is more damnable in a spouse.

“For while natural use, when it slips beyond the agreements of marriage—that is, beyond the necessity of procreation—is venial in a wife, it is damnable with a prostitute; that which is against nature is performed execrably with a prostitute, but more execrably with a wife.”

6. Again, in the little book addressed to Valerius, Book I of *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, against the recent heretics, he explains the Apostle’s words, “I want you to be without anxiety” (I Cor. VII, 31):

“I say this, brothers: the time is short; that is, the people of God are no longer to be propagated carnally [the printed text has *carlianter*, probably for *carnaliter*, ‘carnally’], by temporal generation, but are now to be gathered spiritually.”

[Note: Augustine has *regeneratione*, “by regeneration,” which is preferable.]

“Therefore what remains is that those who have wives should not be subjected to carnal desire; that those who weep over the sadness of present evil should rejoice in hope of future good; that those who rejoice because of temporal advantage should fear eternal judgment; that those who buy should possess as though they possessed nothing, so that they may not cling through love to what they have acquired; and that those who use this world should consider that they are passing through it, not remaining in it. For the form of this world is passing away.

“But I want you to be without anxiety: that is, I want you to have your heart above, in the things that do not pass away, rather than in passing times.”

[Note: Augustine has: “I want you to have your heart in the things that do not pass away.”]

Then he adds:

“He who is without a wife thinks about the things of the Lord, how he may please God; but he who is joined in marriage thinks about the things of the world” (I Cor. VII, 32).

And in a certain way he explains what he had said above: “Those who have wives should be as though they did not have them.” For those who have wives in such a way that they think about the things of the Lord—how they may please the Lord—and do not think about pleasing their wives in the things of the world, are as though they did not have wives. This happens when the wives too are such that their husbands do not please them because they are rich, eminent, noble by birth, or attractive in body, but because they are faithful, religious, chaste, and good men.

But in married people, just as these things are to be embraced and praised, so other things must be tolerated, lest they fall into damnable crimes, that is, fornications or adulteries. To avoid this evil, even the intercourse of spouses that is not for the sake of procreation but serves victorious desire—wherein they are commanded not to defraud one another, lest Satan tempt them because of their lack of self-control—is not commanded according to an order, but conceded according to pardon.

For it is written:

“Let the husband render the debt to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband. The woman has no power over her own body, but the husband; likewise, the husband has no power over his own body, but the wife. Do not defraud one another, unless perhaps by mutual consent for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer; and return again to the same, lest Satan tempt you because of your lack of self-control. But I say this according to indulgence, not according to command” (I Cor. VII, 3–5).

Where pardon is given, therefore, it can by no means be denied that there is some fault. Since intercourse undertaken with the intention of procreation is not culpable, and is properly attributed to marriage, what does the Apostle concede according to pardon except that spouses, when they do not abstain, seek from one another the debt of the flesh—not from the desire for procreation, but from the pleasure of lust?

This pleasure, however, falls into fault not because of marriage, but receives pardon because of marriage. Hence marriage is also praiseworthy in this respect: it causes even what does not belong to it to be forgiven on account of it. For the intercourse by which lust is served is not conducted in such a way as to hinder the offspring sought by marriage.

Yet it is one thing not to have intercourse except from the sole desire to procreate, which has no fault;

[Note: We supplied *non*, “not,” from Augustine. A little later, where the editions of Ratherius have *propter*, “because of,” we corrected it to *praeter*, “beyond.” Shortly afterward we printed *concumbitur*, “intercourse is had,” following Augustine and the sense, where the same editions incorrectly read *obsistitur*, “is resisted.”]

it is another thing to desire the pleasure of the flesh through intercourse, but not with anyone other than one’s spouse, which has venial fault. For although intercourse is not undertaken for the sake of propagating offspring, nevertheless propagation is not obstructed because of this lust, whether by an evil intention or by an evil deed.

For those who do this—that is, those who by intention or by some action bring it about that children are not born to them—although they are called spouses, are not spouses and retain none of the truth of marriage; instead, they place an honorable name over their shame as a covering. They are exposed when they go so far as to abandon the children born against their will. For they hate to nourish or possess those whom they had feared to beget.

Thus, when dark iniquity rages against its own children, whom it has begotten unwillingly,

[Note: Augustine adds “unwillingly.”]

it is brought into the light by manifest iniquity, and hidden shame is convicted by evident cruelty. At times this lustful cruelty—or cruel lust—goes so far as to procure even poisons of sterility; and, if these have no effect, to destroy and expel conceived fetuses from the womb, wishing its offspring to perish before living, or, if it was already alive in the womb, to be killed before being born.

Absolutely, if both are such, they are not spouses; and if they were such from the beginning, they came together not through marriage but rather through fornication. But if both are not such, I dare to say that either she is, in a certain sense, her husband’s prostitute, or he is his wife’s adulterer.

Again, shortly afterward:

“In marriage,” he says, “let these goods of marriage be loved: offspring, fidelity, and the sacrament. But offspring not merely so that it may be born, but also so that it may be reborn; for it is born to punishment unless it is reborn to life.

“Fidelity—not the kind that unbelievers have among themselves, jealously guarding the flesh. For what man, however impious, wants an adulterous wife? Or what woman, however impious, wants an adulterous husband? This is indeed a natural good in marriage, but it is nevertheless carnal. A spouse who is a member of Christ ought to fear adultery for the sake of the spouse, not for his or her own sake, and to hope from Christ for the reward of the fidelity shown to the spouse.

“As for the sacrament, spouses should preserve it harmoniously and chastely; neither separation nor adultery causes them to lose it.

“For this alone is what even a sterile marriage retains by the law of devotion, after the hope of fertility has been abandoned, for the sake of which the marriage had been joined. Let the person who wishes to praise marriage praise these goods of marriage; but the desire of the flesh is not to be attributed to marriage, but tolerated. For it is not a good that comes from natural marriage, but an evil that comes from ancient sin.”

By the testimony of so holy and learned a man, I have shown why I said at the beginning that marriage is good, and why the adulterer or one who entirely abandons it incurs such a harmful crime: namely, because it is both useful and without fault when it is undertaken solely for the purpose of procreation according to the Lord’s command; and it is both useful and venial when it is entered into to avoid the evil of fornication, according to the concession made by the Apostle.

### 7.

As for the fact that some rich men take wives because of poverty—wives who, being taken because of want, are plainly meant to drive away various necessities—I leave it to others to decide whether this should be referred to that permissible kind of marriage or not. I follow Augustine in this one respect and affirm that marriage is praiseworthy even in this matter, because it causes what does not belong to it to be forgiven for its sake. [Col. 0195A] Although I know that some refer this to a third kind of marriage, proposing that the Creator of all things himself said at the beginning: “It is not good for man to be alone; let us make him a helper like himself” (Gen. II, 12).

Whatever the order—whether they are entered into for the sake of offspring, out of disdain for fornication, or because of a rejection of poverty—faith and the sacrament proper to marriage have such force that a woman abandoned by one man cannot be another man’s wife, except as the wife of a deserter; while the woman brought in upon her, however holy, chaste, noble, and modest she may be, is, in truth, regarded as a prostitute. The man who has taken a woman from the opposite side is himself an adulterer, as the Lord’s own voice bears witness and says: “Whoever dismisses his wife, except for the cause of fornication, commits adultery; and whoever takes the dismissed woman commits adultery” (Matt. XIX, 9).

Observe, however, that although dismissal is elsewhere altogether forbidden, dismissal for the cause of fornication is permitted, because, plainly, when she has fornicated, she has already broken the bond and has ceased to be one flesh. From this, let adulterers and adulteresses understand what detestable crime they incur if, contrary to the prohibition of the Creator—“What God has joined together”—they separate by committing adultery or by utterly rejecting one another, since they cannot be one flesh except by preserving faith with each other and keeping the sacrament. [Note: [Col. 0195D] We have supplied the particle “not,” as required by the sense.] [Col. 0195B] The clearest reason teaches that whatever is not permitted to women is likewise not permitted to men, insofar as the agreement of the compact is concerned. It is exceedingly shameful if, although by right of sex the stronger demands something from the weaker, he does not, conquered and subdued by lust, render the same to the weaker.

By “compact” and “sacrament” I mean the betrothal documents, or tablets, [Note: [Col. 0195D] These are the tablets by which marriage was contracted. Augustine calls them marriage tablets in Sermon 52, no. 22: “The tablets are recited, and they are recited in the presence of all who bear witness . . .”; [Col. 0196D] and they are called marriage tablets. The conditions and agreements of the marriage were recorded in these tablets; for, as the same teacher says in Sermon 9, no. 18: “The tablets also indicate that, where it is written, it is for the procreation of children.”] or charters, by which they are mutually bound together inseparably in the presence, sight, and testimony of God, the just Judge.

May all that we have said therefore serve this purpose: since you have already fled from burning Sodom—that is, the illicit fires of the flesh—by a sounder counsel, and since you have not decided to climb the mountain—that is, the height of celibacy—at least in Segor (Gen. XIX, 23), that is, in the midst of these things, which is understood to be carnal marriage, may you contain yourself as continuously and chastely as you can. Love your wife according to the Apostle’s command, as Christ loved the Church (Eph. V, 25), and know no woman apart from her. Abstain from her also on the days legally forbidden by the Church, with her consent, while preserving continence and perpetual fidelity toward her. Know with absolute certainty that if you deceive or circumvent her in any matter, the Lord will be present from heaven as the swiftest avenger, the most just judge, and the truest witness, observing all things—the Lord whose command you have become a transgressor of. [Col. 0195D]

### 8.

They think childishly—I scarcely dare pass over this—who understand the statement “The two shall be one flesh” (Gen. II, 24) as referring to a son, so that, because of the male seed and the female flower from which physicians discuss the formation of offspring in the womb, the two, namely father and mother, are one flesh, that is, one in their son. For if this were so, a harlot would be worth as much as marriage, provided only that offspring were born from her. Yet the Apostle plainly said that such people too become one body, not because of the generation of children but because of the intercourse itself. Thus he says: “Do you not know that the one who clings to a prostitute becomes one body? But the one who clings to the Lord is one spirit” (I Cor. VI, 16).

If the matter were also as they claim, a son would be quite entitled to say what only the only-begotten Son of God, co-essential and co-eternal God, abiding with God, could truthfully say: “The Father is in me, and I am in him” (John X, 38); and, “The Father who remains in me performs the works” (John XIV, 10); and, “I and the Father are one” (John X, 30). He says “one” in the singular but “we are” in the plural, so that you may understand that two exist inseparably in one substance, deity, eternity, majesty, operation, will, and power. To repeat the point, such a son could say: “I and my father and mother are one”; and, “My father and mother are in me, and I am in them”; and, more madly still: “I am my own father and mother, because both are in me as one, though they had previously been two”—which could not happen unless they had ceased to be in themselves and had been transformed into me.

What, moreover, would be the case when not one son but two, or even twenty or more, were born? In that case it ought to have been said of such children; they ought not to have been passed over, but, I say, it ought to have been said: “The two shall be twenty fleshes.” Rather, this must be understood: “The two shall be one flesh”—one flesh in law, love, and faith; in one bond of flesh and one compact of flesh—so that the two fleshly persons are bound together with such union that what is not permitted to one is not permitted to the other. Neither, for example, may approach the flesh of another woman, nor the other that of another man, while his or her own spouse remains. Just as flesh cannot be divided from flesh without great pain, so a wife cannot be separated from her husband without great crime.

Otherwise, those who have remained in perpetual virginity, just as we read that many saints did even after being joined in marriage, or those who were sterile, including old people already reduced to corpse-like bodies, would seem to be excluded from this law of charity—and indeed from this good of marriage—which is good for no other reason than this bond’s complete inseparability. God willed to make two from one, so that those who were divided in bodies might be one in effect and faith toward each other. From these two a third was to be made, who would no longer be one with them but, leaving them, would cling to another; and in this way, following their example, the two would be one flesh, and the human race would be propagated.

This is a good that distinguishes human beings from beasts and the other animals: those irrational creatures, unable to be one through the affection of love, dissolve into promiscuous intercourse; but rational beings are bound by a most tenacious compact and, joined also in the flesh, by one affection of charity. [Col. 0196D]

### 9.

If someone should object to me that Jacob had two wives, and David and Solomon even more, I invite you to investigate the mystery, because all these things happened as figures (I Cor. X, 11). I boldly affirm that here too the city of our God and his holy mountain were prophetically represented: in that city it is not permitted for a man to have more than one wife, nor for a wife to have more than one husband. Living chastely with that spouse, she is to be a cause of offspring, or, through fear of fornication, she is to preserve unbroken fidelity toward him forever, together with the sacrament—especially since this too pertains to something greater, namely, the Church and Christ.

For the Apostle says of the same matter: “This sacrament, that is, mystery, is great; but I speak of Christ and the Church” (Eph. V, 32). To venture to draw a little from this: just as those two are one flesh, so Christ, although he is true God and true man in his body, which is the Church (Col. I, 24), remains one from two natures and cannot be separated from her forever, for whom he poured out his own blood in the marriage covenant—just as a husband may not leave his wife, nor a wife her own husband.

And just as a lawful divorce may occur between either spouse on account of fornication, so each soul is rejected by Christ after committing fornication with alien lovers—that is, various sins—or with the suggestions of unclean spirits, unless perhaps it is reconciled to him again through repentance (I Cor. VII, 11), just as the Apostle teaches that a wife may be restored to her husband.

### 10.

The statement also made by the Apostle, “The two are one flesh” (Eph. V, 31), is not to be understood casually. It must be said that at the beginning there were two, because one was taken from the other; and they were one flesh, because they were mutually, as it were, one body. He was in the rib that had been taken from him, while she had in herself the whole body from which the rib had been taken and from which she was created for him.

Similarly, Christ is one with the Church insofar as he is her head, as he himself also testifies in the Gospel, saying: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven” (John III, 13). It is as though he had said: No one will enter the kingdom of heaven more fittingly except one who is united and, as it were, incorporated into him who descended from heaven as man, yet through the power of his divinity is in heaven, filling both earth and heaven.

Christ and the Church, however, are two insofar as she consists of human beings, and indeed of pure human beings, whereas he is true man and also true God. Let this suffice for now; let us hasten to what remains.

## TITLE IV.—Concerning Wives

### 11.

Are you a wife? Consider that everything we have already set forth applies to you, together with those things that God the Creator himself, both through himself and through his servants, by examples as well as by words—and especially through the Apostle—has specifically commanded you: “You shall be under your husband’s power, and he shall rule over you” (Gen. III, 16).

For this reason the Apostle Peter holds Sarah up as an example, wishing to instruct you about what you ought to do, saying: “As Sarah obeyed Abraham, calling him lord, whose daughters you are when you do what is good” (I Pet. III, 6). Therefore, if you wish to deserve to become a daughter of the patriarchs by doing good, strive to obey your husband even in the very language of humility, displaying submission and dignity of conduct, so that the praise of the Wise Man may apply to him who says: “Blessed is the husband of a good woman; the number of her years is doubled” (Ecclus. XXVI, 1)—that is, blessed with the joy both of the present age and of the age to come.

Likewise: “A brave woman delights her husband, and she will complete the years of his life in peace. A good woman is a good portion; she will be given to a man for his good deeds” (ibid., 2). And truly, as the Apostle testifies, “the unbelieving husband will be saved through the believing wife” (I Cor. VII, 14).

But conversely, according to the same author cited above: “A jealous woman is sorrow of heart and mourning” (Ecclus. XXVI, 8); and, “In a jealous woman there is a scourge of the tongue” (ibid., 9). A jealous woman is one who is quarrelsome or who makes her husband jealous. A jealous husband is one who, with care and anguish of heart, guards his wife’s chastity.
