Hence the Lord is also called jealous through Moses (Exod. XXXIV, 14), because, just as a husband carefully guards his wife’s chastity, so he restrains us from fornicating against him, sometimes by fear of punishment and sometimes by the promise of the kingdom.

Likewise: “A quarrelsome woman is great anger; her insult and disgrace will not be concealed, but a holy and modest woman is grace upon grace” (Ecclus. XXVI, 11).

The Apostle, while instructing Titus about ecclesiastical matters, teaches how he should admonish you as well, saying among other things: “Speak what befits sound doctrine: that older men be sober, modest, prudent, sound in faith, in love, and in patience. Older women likewise must have a holy bearing, not slanderers, not enslaved to much wine, teachers of what is good, so that they may teach the young women prudence: to love their husbands, to be prudent, chaste, sober, keeping house, kind, subject to their husbands, so that the word of God may not be blasphemed” (Tit. II, 1).

To the Ephesians also he says: “Let women be subject to their husbands as to the Lord, because the husband is the head of the woman, just as Christ is the head of the Church, he himself the savior of his body. But just as the Church is subject to Christ, so also wives to their husbands in everything” (Eph. V, 22).

And when he commands husbands, he says: “Love your wives, as Christ also loved the Church and gave himself for her, to sanctify her.” Thus husbands too ought to love their wives as their own bodies; for no one has ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the Church, because we are members of his body, of his flesh and of his bones. “For this reason,” he says, “a man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh. This sacrament is great, but I speak of Christ and the Church” (ibid., 25).

That is: although in human and carnal union it also happens that two who cling to one another become one flesh, the sacrament nevertheless pertains to Christ and the Church. For just as Eve was fashioned from the man’s rib, so the Church, redeemed from Christ’s side, grew; and just as the husband is the head of the wife, so Christ is the head of the Church. Hence he adds: “Nevertheless, let each one of you love his wife as himself” (Eph. V, 33), because Christ likewise acted for the Church by giving himself for her; and he adds: “Let the wife fear her husband.”

### 12.

You have heard from the apostolic commands what sort of person you ought to be toward your husband. Now gather from the words of the blessed Cyprian, bishop and martyr, what sort of person you ought to be toward yourself:

“Chastity of the body,” he says, “is not to desire what belongs to others, to avoid every impurity, not to wish to taste before the proper hour, not to provoke laughter, not to speak vain and false words, to have in every respect an orderly appearance suited to one’s purpose, both in hair and in clothing, as is fitting, not to enter into companionship with the unworthy, not to look at anyone with a haughty gaze, not to permit the eyes to wander, not to walk with a pompous and seductive step, to appear inferior to no one in a good work once begun, to inflict insult or shame on no one, to blaspheme no one, not to mock the elderly, not to quarrel with one who is better, not to discuss what you do not know, and not to reveal everything even of what you do know. These things make a person lovable to his neighbors and acceptable to God.”

To return, then, to our subject: if you have a good husband, imitate Sarah, Rebecca, Rachel, and Elizabeth. But if you have an unjust and cruel one, you also have women to imitate: in the New Testament, Anastasia and Theodora; in the Old Testament, Abigail, the wife of Nabal of Carmel, and Esther, the wife of Ahasuerus.

Finally, hear the Apostle saying: “The unbelieving husband will be saved through the believing wife” (I Cor. VII, 14); and likewise: “She will be saved through the bearing of children” (I Tim. II, 15). Here understand not children of the flesh but children of the mind—those whom you are nevertheless commanded to seize and dash against the rock (Ps. CXXXVI, 9), that is, to raise all your works and thoughts toward Christ, so that whatever good you do, you may strive to attribute it not to yourself but to him, without whom you can accomplish no good.

## TITLE V.—Concerning Celibates

### 13.

Are you celibate? Consider what an exceedingly high summit of holiness you have climbed, and be all the more watchful to avoid a precipitous fall the higher you stand. Consider, then, what cause made an angel into a devil; and, remembering the Lord’s saying, “Without me you can do nothing” (John XV, 5), know that in this matter you especially need his mercy and grace. For, as Jerome truthfully says, to live in the flesh beyond the flesh is not a human achievement but a divine gift.

Hence, as Gregory testifies, celibacy itself is not commanded but praised. For it is foolish—indeed, extremely proud—for dust and ashes to presume that by its own power it can accomplish what nature has granted not to itself but to angels together with God’s gift. Thus Truth itself says: “The children of this age marry and are given in marriage; but in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in heaven” (Luke XX, 34). And elsewhere, concerning the same matter: “Let the one who can receive it receive it” (Matt. XVII, 12). He shows that it is not everyone who wishes to climb the citadel of so great a height, but only the one to whom God grants the ability.

Therefore, presuming nothing about yourself but about him without whom you can do nothing, come down, according to the Prophet, “you who are more beautiful,” and dwell with the uncircumcised (Ezek. XXXII, 19)—that is, humbly condescend to all, not only those joined in marriage but also those who care for the flesh in concupiscence. Do not, in your own estimation, prefer yourself to anyone, as though the rest were sinners while you, because of the gift of chastity, were uniquely holy.

Know that God often permits certain vices to dominate certain people for a time, so that, after their conversion, they may learn through whose mercy they were redeemed from captivity and through whose power they were rescued from the authority of a cruel tyrant, and may render greater thanks to their liberator in proportion to the greater danger from which they were delivered. Conversely, certain gifts of sublime virtues sometimes come to certain reprobates, so that, puffed up by them, they may fall more grievously; thus the elect, terrified by their fall, may not presume upon themselves but may plant the step of their mind more firmly in God’s mercy.

Hence the Apostle says beautifully: “Let the one who stands take heed lest he fall” (I Cor. X, 12).

### 14.

The Psalmist demonstrates in prayer the particular cause of this fall: “Let not the foot of pride come to me, and let not the hand of the sinner move me. There have fallen those who work iniquity” (Ps. XXXV, 12). Nor is this unjustly said, because, as Scripture testifies, “Before ruin the heart is exalted” (Prov. XVI, 18). We must understand that no one slips from virtue into any vice unless, by a leap of vanity and instability, he first happens to be changed from the rock of humility into the sand of pride. For unless hidden pride had preceded, the manifest fall into lust would not have followed.

Hence Prosper also says:

“Addicted to the desire of the flesh,” he says, “he seems to have nothing of pride, especially since the passion itself appears to humble him through lust. Yet unless he had first become rebellious against God, despising through the presumption of a proud spirit his salutary command concerning the preservation of chastity, no desire for wantonness would have provoked him. [Note: [Col. 0199D] The received text wrongly reads *enim* (“for”).] In his mind, contempt and fear of God contend for a long time. Either contempt of God prevails, and the proud mind, having received desire, loses chastity; or fear prevails, and the mind subject to God resists both desire and pride.”

This concerns the particular cause of the fall. Now hear the same author’s teaching about the material through which that same fall very often occurs:

“Many,” he says, “are shamefully released into wantonness by gluttony and the desire for wine; others are inflamed against chastity by filthy thoughts; offered occasions cast some down from their resolve of chastity; examples of those who live dissolutely place others beneath the yoke of immodesty. There are others whose life is inflamed by an obscene tongue and whose impure conscience is revealed: at first they either utter shameless words or listen to them willingly, and afterward, as the disease gradually grows, they fall away from uprightness. For thought is what pollutes the mind when it is obscene, just as it purifies it when it is honorable.

Hence that bodily discharge which occurs without guilt in those who are asleep sometimes occurs through guilt in those who are awake. But one thing is what happens in a sleeping person, another what an awake person does: there, the fullness of moisture is naturally expelled; here, shameful desire is made public.”

Therefore, celibate, do not despise the gift of chastity lest you lose it. Recall the prophet’s command: “How you have fallen from heaven, Lucifer, who rose at dawn!” (Isa. XIV, 12)—that is, you who appeared beautiful and admirable to all through the splendor of virginity.

For this exclamation is not prompted by ignorance, but is a mark of reproach. As we have already said, such a miserable fall occurs through the fault of pride, because the devil overturns the entire race of the perishing—especially, indeed entirely, through these two vices, lust and pride. Yet one hangs upon the other. Just as through pride one goes into the prostitution of lust, so through lust one arrives at hardness of mind, and—alas!—falls even to contempt of the Creator. Thus the heart which ought through humility and purity to be a temple of God becomes through pride and impurity a shrine of demons—or, to put it more aptly, a monument of the devil.

For this reason, as we cannot deny, the Lord himself says to blessed Job: “He sleeps under the shade, in the secret place of the reed and in moist places” (Job XL, 16).

Beware, therefore, whoever still enjoys so great a prerogative of chastity, lest, attributing it to your own merits, you fall into elation while avoiding lust; and lest, while guarding against elation, you fall negligently into lust. To enable you to do this, set the fear of Gehenna before the eyes of your mind, and, just as one nail drives out another, let fear of this fire drive out the burning heat of that vice. Consideration of earthly frailty should also restrain the fear of elation.

Thus, defended by Christ’s help both from the poison of elation and from the fire of lust, you will rejoice forever with the companionship of angels, since you have imitated an angelic life on earth.

## TITLE VI.—Concerning Fathers and Mothers

### 15.

Are you a father or a mother? Remember that you owe discipline to your children, and obey the apostolic admonitions in such a way that you may also avoid the destruction of Eli the priest (I Sam. II, 4). “Fathers,” the Apostle says, “do not provoke your children to anger, so that they may not become fainthearted” (Eph. VI, 4).

## TITLE VII.—Concerning Children

### 16.

Are you a son or a daughter? Remember that you owe reverence to your parents. The Only-Begotten himself, who was conceived not from sin as you were but from the Holy Spirit and born of a Virgin, after he had been found in the temple and had instructed his parents—that is, his virgin mother and his most chaste foster-father, who was therefore called his father—about the power of his divinity, by which he possesses and inhabits all things with the Father, and they had not understood, “went down with them,” says the evangelist, “and came to Nazareth, and was subject to them” (Luke II, 51).

Why, then, should you disdain to be subject to your parents, when the Lord, who created and nourishes all things, did not disdain to be subject to his foster-father?

It often happens that, while the father is poor, the son is rich. What, I ask, is more disgraceful in the order of nature? While others commonly take pride in the nobility of their paternal ancestry, you, to your own disgrace, leave your father, marked by poverty’s brand, to walk through the streets begging.

For what does the beggar cry out except that he shows you to be a newcomer, an adopted person, that thing recently invented by those who boast that they make men—that is, manufactured [Note: [Col. 0201D] The Vulgate has *faticium*, incorrectly. *Factitius* is understood here as one who has recently been made rich. In the same sense, *novitius* means “very new”; *assumptus*, “taken up”; *allevatitius*, that is, “taken and lifted up from poverty.” [Col. 0202D]]—an upstart, a bastard, and illegitimate? If someone were to reproach him with any of these things, even falsely, would this not have been a great cause for anger?

So much for worldly considerations. But according to God, since he says in the Psalm, “Blessed is the one who understands concerning the needy and the poor” (Ps. XL, 2), concerning whom, I ask, will you show understanding, if you do not even recognize your own begging father by taking pity on him? To whom, I ask, do you extend alms, if you do not recognize nature itself in your father?

Although mercy is to be shown to everyone, even to those outside the faith, especially, as the Apostle says, “to those who are of the household of faith” (Gal. VI, 10), what is owed to those who are not only of the household of faith but also of the household of blood—whether they are the origin of your lineage, or, as someone beautifully says in the “Ten-Stringed” Psalm, “he who does not render honor to his own parents, whom will he be able to obey?”

Something, therefore, must be given to everyone, but everything must be entrusted to the father and wholly subjected to his authority. Whether you are a father, a son, or any blood relation, hear the Apostle: “If anyone does not care for his own, and especially for those of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (I Tim. V, 8).

## TITLE VIII.—Concerning Widows

### 17.

Are you a widow? You have Anna as your rule, so to speak (Luke II, 37). But if you wish to live otherwise, hear the Apostle: “The widow who lives in pleasure is dead while she lives” (I Tim. V, 6).

## TITLE IX.—Concerning Virgins

### 18.

Are you a virgin? Rejoice humbly in the Lord, and take care not to lose what you are. You have Mary as a mirror of chastity, a title of virginity, a mark of humility, and an ornament of innocence. Examine her song; it can suffice for the ordering of your conduct.

Consider with what supreme virtue she strove, so that she might deserve to be enriched with the prerogative of this gift, so lofty and exalted that it was granted to no one after her and to no one before her. Strive as far as you can to imitate her. To make this easy for you when you seek it, let her answer wisely when humbly questioned: “Because he has regarded the humility of his handmaid” (Luke I, 48).

There is the reason. For long ago he had made the same promise through the prophet: “Upon whom shall I look,” he says, “except upon the humble and quiet one who trembles at my words?” (Isa. LXVI, 2).

The whole cause of our destruction is pride; the whole cause of our restoration is humility. Humility is the mother of virtues and the ornament of all conduct. Without it there is no virtue; apart from it, all virtues are not virtues but vices.

Finally, I present to you three men, in one order, about whom you cannot doubt: all three were marvelous teachers, all three supreme bishops, all three wondrous to the whole world. One presided at Rome, another at Milan, and the third at Hippo.

“There is no virginity of the flesh,” says the first (Gregory), “which the sweetness of the mind does not commend.”

“It is fitting,” says the second (Ambrose), “that the more chaste the virgin, the more humble she should be.”

“An humble marriage,” says the third (Augustine), “is better than a proud virginity.”

## TITLE X.—Concerning Little Children

### 19.

Are you a little child? May he nourish you in this world who nourished Samuel in the temple. Listen, then, as you can; strive, as you can; attempt, as you can; exert yourself, as you can; follow, as you can—you who hear Wisdom saying: “How long, little ones, will you love infancy?” (Prov. I, 22).

Know that the master of the household is present and calls you yourself every day at the dawn of your age. For as you advance, as you desire to read, to understand, and certainly to ask questions, you will find some who, at five years of age—and, what is even more astonishing, at three years—rushed of their own accord to martyrdom, resisted the powers of the world with the greatest wisdom and strength, displayed miracles in the Lord’s name, endured torments bravely, mocked their torturers with the utmost steadfastness, willingly accepted death for the Lord—not so much premature as precious—and clearly demonstrated that they had received the crown of immortality with the palm of victory, while signs and miracles shone around their extinguished bodies. [Note: [Col. 0203D] Construe: “and most clearly demonstrated that they had received the crown, with signs and miracles shining around their extinguished bodies.”]

And, what will be an even more incredible marvel, you will find many exceedingly brave virgins of the same age who, victorious over the devil in the struggle, advanced for love of Christ’s name. You will also find wretched people of the same age who, after original sin had been remitted, purchased hell through their own merits and made this known to human beings by certain clear indications, through the merciful permission of him who wished this example to be written for your caution.

## TITLE XI.—Concerning Boys

### 20.

Are you a boy? Hear the Apostle: “Do not become children in understanding; be little ones in malice, but be mature in understanding” (I Cor. XIV, 20). Imitate him of whom it is written that “he advanced in age and wisdom and grace before God and men” (Luke II, 52).

According to his divinity he remained wholly perfect, having nothing in which he could advance, since he exists without beginning in such a way that no end can come through decline. Yet according to the humanity that he accepted for your sake, he wished to advance, in order to show you the way in which you ought to advance—or rather, in order that he himself might provide you with the means to advance.

Know, then, that the master of the household is present and calls you to cultivate the vineyard all the more diligently as the members of your body for labor and the faculties of your mind for understanding already seem to be growing. With the addition of the conjunction, he invites you and those who follow, saying: “Go also into my vineyard” (Matt. XX, 7). Elsewhere it will become clear why he does this.

Remember also that death, although premature, can unexpectedly come upon infants, boys, and young men, just as it comes upon the old in due course.

## TITLE XII.—Concerning Adolescents

### 21.

Are you an adolescent? Hear the Lord: “To you I say, arise” (Luke VII, 14). Hear also the Apostle: “Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you” (Eph. V, 14).

Do not be angry that I seem to awaken you so terribly at the very beginning. Know that I do this both because an age of this kind is inclined to many kinds of falls and because [understand: on account of] a two-branched path at the very entrance into life [Note: [Col. 0203D] The Vulgate incorrectly has *iniquus*. Construe: “Know that I do this both because this age is inclined to many kinds of falls and because of the two-branched path at the very entrance into life.” The letter of Pythagoras is the letter Y—not because Pythagoras invented it, but because, since it presents a trunk divided into two branches, Pythagoras used it to represent the two-branched path of human life, extending on one side toward virtues and on the other toward vices. Hence in Virgil’s poems:

“Pythagoras’ letter, divided by its forked branching,

seems to present the form of human life,” and so forth.]—which the letter of Pythagoras of Samos can serve to recall to you, if ever you should wish to forget it [perhaps *nolueris*, “if ever you should not wish to forget it”; the printed reading is *volueris*, “should wish”].

But let that blessed Augustine also come to our aid—the one who has already helped, increased, adorned, and strengthened in many respects the work that we are laboring on—so that nothing may seem to be lacking and so that he may explain this matter. May he, I ask, come as quickly as possible. “Youth,” he says, “is freer for love, more heedless of falling, more fragile in weakness, and harder to correct.” [Note: [Col. 0204D] The common editions incorrectly have *vivit*. Construe: “But let that blessed Augustine also come—the one who has already helped, increased, adorned, and strengthened in many respects our work, which we are laboring on—so that nothing may seem to be lacking in its explanation. May he, I ask, come as quickly as possible: ‘Youth,’ he says, etc.”]

It would take too long to state what Ecclesiastes, the books of Proverbs and Wisdom, and also the authors [perhaps *auctores*, “authors,” for printed *auctorum*, “of authors”] of both the New and Old Testaments, moved by the forewarnings of both the shadow of truth and of truth itself [variant: *praesagus*, “prescient,” for *praesagiis*, “forewarnings”], express about the particular character of your age and with what teachings they instruct and fortify you, lest this obstruct our purpose of proceeding to other matters.

But lest, while you need many things, we seem to defraud you of some as well, we urge you, if you are willing, to lend the ear of your heart to the words of the Psalmist, who, by asking, immediately received counsel suitable for himself: “How,” he says, “does a younger man correct his way? By keeping your words” (Ps. CXVIII, 9).

Note, then, to use Augustine’s words once more, that this is not a remedy discovered by human presumption but received through divine inspiration, and that it suddenly offers you a cup of healing. For your mind, which degenerates in its shoots, begins to produce better fruits if it has been sprinkled with the seeds of heavenly words, which the heavenly farmer nevertheless customarily sows only in a certain furrow. [Note: [Col. 0204D] *Versus* is used for “furrow” by reputable authors. Thus Pliny, Book XVIII, chapter 19, wrote that in plowing a *versus* is completed.]

Finally, hear the minister of this most fruitful sowing: “Let everything of yours be done honorably and in order” (I Cor. XIV, 40).

Direct, therefore, the gaze of your heart toward his commands, and do not follow the winding coils of the crooked serpent. “Prepare the way of the Lord who comes to you; make straight the paths of your God” (Luke III, 4). For he deigns to walk only upon a straight way, as Scripture says of him: “The ways of the Lord are straight” (Dan. III, 27); but “the paths of the wicked are crooked” (Prov. II, 15). If, then, you wish to follow Christ, walk along the way on which he walks, lest it be said of you: “O you who have abandoned the straight paths!” (II Pet. II, 15).

22. Consider what better counsel the prophet decides you should follow in the Lamentations: “It is good for a man when he has borne the yoke from his youth” (Lam. III, 27). And as though you were to ask, “Why his own?” he added: “He shall sit alone and keep silent” (ibid., 28). “You mean,” you say, “there is no other benefit?” For this [Note: Here *enim* should be understood ironically, as *enimvero* (“indeed”).] is what people chiefly count as advantageous. Indeed, to walk surrounded by throngs clinging to one’s side, to be pressed by the wedges of many attendants, is said to be a mark of great happiness.

[64] You advise taking up the yoke [that is, assuming it] so that I may sit alone, whereas I see many people taking it up for this very reason: that they may be accompanied by many. He continues and joins to this what the solitary man deserves: “For he shall lift it upon himself” (Lam. III, 28). “Where,” you ask, “shall I be lifted? Why shall I be lifted? Is it so that it may be said of me, ‘Whoever exalts himself will be humbled’ (Luke XIV, 11), or so that I may say, ‘You have lifted me up and dashed me down’ (Ps. CI, 11)?” No; rather, so that it may be said of you: “Whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke XIV, 11). And: “Whoever dwells in the help of the Most High will abide under the protection of the God of heaven” (Ps. XC, 1). Then, rejoicing, you will be able to sing: “You have held my right hand, and by your will you have led me, and with glory you have received me” (Ps. LXXII, 24). And many, to your praise—or rather, to God’s—will be able to say: “Blessed is he whom you have chosen and taken to yourself; he will dwell in your courts” (Ps. LXIV, 5).

But ask Paul where he will exalt you: “He raised us up together,” he says, “and made us sit together in the heavenly places” (Eph. II, 6). And the Lord himself says: “Where I am, there also will my minister be” (John XII, 6). Serve Christ, therefore, and you will be with Christ. Where? “While they watched,” he says, “he was lifted up, and a cloud received him from their eyes” (Acts I, 9), while the angels said: “This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven” (ibid., 11), etc.

If, then, you wish to belong to him, strive [Col. 0205D] to cleanse the earth from your heart, so that, unencumbered and free, you may ascend to heaven, where he is, on the wings of the virtues, impeded by none of those things with whose glue I showed above that you were entangled.

### 23

As for what you said—that you did not wish to complain by saying, “You have lifted me up and dashed me down”—lest you think that I have taken this superficially, I shall say as best I can, though not as I ought, that it may be understood in a good rather than an evil sense: namely, that when you have been lifted to the summit of the virtues, you may be dashed down gratuitously into humility. Indeed, let him dash you down—not in the whirlwind and hailstone (Isa. XXX, 30), but in the spirit of gentleness (I Cor. IV, 21), which is fully able to raise up the one who has been cast down (Ps. CXLV, 8); which touches the mountains, and they smoke (Ps. CIII, 32); and which, while putting to death, gives life (I Sam. II, 6); taking away the spirit of the lofty-minded, so that they fail and return to their dust (Ps. CIII, 29)—that is, so that they recognize themselves to be dust.

He commands this [Note: The Vulgate mistakenly reads *percipiens* (“perceiving”).] when he says: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things” (Ecclus. III, 20). In this way you will be able to recognize that he alone places the humble in exalted positions and raises the sorrowful to health [Col. 0206B], and that you must attribute nothing to your own merits, but everything to him alone, who is known to be the author, giver, and rewarder of good things. For, as has been said before, through the evil of empty glory you may be brought down from the heights to the depths; but through the good of humility you may be raised from the depths to the heights.

But if you still ask, and do not believe that you have been satisfied as to how you can be lifted above yourself, know—through the teaching of the Apostle [that is, Wisdom]—“that the corruptible body weighs down the soul” (Wis. IX, 15). No one can raise himself by his own strength to the heights unless he is lifted by the grace of him who descended to the depths for our sake.

Yet because, in the testimony that I have cited for your sake, it is said not only, “He shall lift it upon himself,” but also—and this is what you seemed somewhat inclined to reject—“He shall sit alone and keep silent” (Lam. III, 28), I do not think this should be understood casually. Rather, we must inquire carefully what this sitting and silence are, and what they signify. Perhaps the meaning will become clear in due course: through gravity, purity of heart, and silence of mouth, the virtue of divine contemplation is generated. Through contemplation, the very fellowship is acquired which imitates [understand: the fellowship of] the heavenly kingdom, once the mind’s thought has been restrained and purified from every desire and impurity of mortal things.

### 24

So that I may not begin to wander through many matters, there is still fresh in our ears what has just sounded in the Gospel: Mary. For on the sixth [day] of the seventh month from the turning of the year [Note: He is speaking of the reading in which, on the day when this was written, the Gospel was read about the converted sinful woman: “A certain Pharisee asked Jesus,” etc. Hence he calls it “today’s reading” and “the present reading,” which has just sounded. This Gospel was read, as it is still read, on the Friday of the September Ember Days, that month being called the seventh month. Thus “the sixth of the seventh month from the turning of the year” means the sixth day, that is, Friday, of the seventh month. Later, near the end of no. 30, which he wrote on the following day, he praises another Gospel reading, saying “today,” namely the Gospel about the fig tree, which is read on the Saturday of the Ember Days of the same month. September, the seventh month, was for Ratherius the eighth month from the beginning of his calamity, since he had been captured in February and taken to the tower at Pavia, where he composed this work by night.]—but the eighth from the beginning of this calamity which weighs me down, or rather instructs me—this serious reading [f.: Friday] properly came before us, contributing, as I believe, not a little, and by God’s agency, to the matter I have undertaken to investigate.

Let us therefore see, so that we may believe; let us believe, so that we may see. What do I mean? Let us see that God alone is the one who reveals hidden things from darkness; let us believe that he is always present to us, especially when he speaks about himself. Let us believe what we do not yet understand about him, so that by believing we may be able to see and understand. For he said: “If you believe, you will see” (John XI, 40).

Let us ask how this most holy sinner, this most chaste harlot, bore the yoke, how she sat alone, and how, keeping silent, she lifted herself above herself. And if today’s reading does not assist us, we have in another reading concerning her—provided, that is, that she is to be believed to be the same woman—very clear and appropriate evidence for all these matters. Let us begin.

“A certain Pharisee asked Jesus to dine with him” (Luke VII, 36), and he did so. While this was taking place, “a certain woman who had been a sinner in the city” (ibid., 37) entered. Pause here for a moment and note that he says “had been”; why does he not say “was”? Had she not yet heard: “I tell you, her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much” (ibid., 48)?

[Col. 0207B] But the evangelist knew that the woman’s coming was caused by the Lord’s mercy, which drew her. The one who inwardly drew her by mercy was the same one who, through gentleness, was about to receive her outwardly. And therefore, when he looked upon her and chose to draw her, she ceased to be what she had been and became what she was destined to be through the mercy of the one who received her. For thus he promises through the prophet: “At whatever hour the sinner turns and groans, he shall be saved” (Ezek. XXXIII, 12).

Let us now attempt what follows: “She brought an alabaster jar of ointment, and standing behind him at his feet, she began to bathe his feet with her tears; and she wiped them with the hairs of her head, and kissed his feet, and anointed them with the ointment” (Luke VII, 37–38).

Behold the yoke that she bore. As many pleasures as she had previously possessed within herself, so many holocausts did she bring forth from herself. She subjected every kind of delight, while, leaving nothing of herself for herself, she poured herself entirely into tears of heavenly longing. She burned with the fire of divine love, though previously she had burned with the fire of sensual pleasure. She washed away with tears the stains of sin that she had acquired through the delight of guilty pleasure. She subjected her hair, her eyes, and indeed her entire body to this yoke, though she had once armed all these things in contempt of the Creator. She transformed the multitude of her vices into a corresponding number of virtues, so that everything which had served the world—or rather, the devil—in guilt might serve entirely in penitence.

Behold, from the present reading you recognize, as I think, the yoke that this Mary bore.

### 25

Now, as I promised, let another passage demonstrate how she sat alone and silent, and how by sitting she lifted herself above herself; and may God’s action accomplish everything we have proposed.

“Jesus entered,” he says, “into a certain village, and a woman named Martha welcomed him into her house. And she had a sister named Mary, who also, sitting at the feet of the Lord, listened to his words” (Luke X, 38–39).

Understand her sitting and listening in silence. But was she alone? Pay attention. “Martha stood and said: ‘Lord, is it no concern to you that my sister has left me alone to serve?’” (ibid., 40).

Here too you have one alone, if you wish. For two had previously been named, Martha and her sister Mary; Martha served alone, while Mary sat, kept silent, and listened alone. And rightly she kept silent, since she had such an advocate speaking on her behalf.

Behold, as I believe, nothing remains ambiguous either about the one sitting or about the one keeping silent. Let us now likewise consider her exaltation; as we see it, let us embrace it, and by embracing it let us desire it for ourselves.

“Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things” (ibid., 41). For this reason, I think, she was called twice: either because of love, or because she did not yet sit beside the One as Mary did, but served two things—seeking heavenly realities while attending to earthly ones. She too had once done this, as the reading already discussed above shows; but now, freed from these things, having cast off the yoke and become free, she willingly subjected all her members to the divine feet.

Thus Martha was alone, but not alone; Mary was alone. Martha was alone because she was occupied with many things; Mary, because she attended to the One. “One thing is necessary” (ibid., 42). For those many things bear no fruit if they do not arrive at this one thing; and therefore the many need the One, while the One does not need the many.

“Mary chose the better part, which shall not be taken away from her” (ibid.). Behold to what height she rose when exalted: after bearing the yoke, she longed to sit alone in silence. For by clinging alone to the One, she merited God himself, the One, the only portion.

### 26

“But why,” you ask, “do you so hastily say that this portion is God, when you have not yet produced any testimony to establish that it must be held?” I produced none for this reason: the clearest testimony is already present above: “Whoever ministers to me, let him follow me; and where I am, there also will my minister be” (John XII, 26).

“Then,” you say, “Martha, who ministered, will be there, not Mary, who sat.” You would be right if she had sat out of laziness; you would be right if she herself had not already ministered. Many things are ministered to, although one thing is sufficient; but one is reached through the ministry of many.

What, then, is the One? God, certainly. And what are the many? Works of mercy. Through works of mercy one reaches God; when one has reached him, everything that is being done ceases, because there is no longer any necessity for action. The fruit for whose sake the work was undertaken remains; the love by which it was undertaken remains—alone for the One, the only one for the Only One; and this singular love clings forever to the Singular One.

That very sitting by which you strive to accuse Mary is so far from being unproductive that nothing is more laborious; although it may seem most like inactivity, it can rightly be called “active rest” even in this age.

But lest you think that I have failed to offer an example through poverty of speech, you have that blessed young man, that holy adolescent—indeed, Mary herself, who bore the yoke—speaking in the same Lamentations (III, 24): “God is my portion, my soul has said; therefore I will wait for him.” And the Psalmist says: “My portion is in the land of the living” (Ps. CXLI, 6, 25).

As for the fact that it will never be taken away from her, listen: “You are the same, and your years will not fail; the children of your servants will dwell there, and their descendants will be established forever” (Ps. CI, 28). And: “The Lord is my portion forever” (Ps. LXXII, 26).

[Note: The Vulgate mistakenly reads *nunquam auferatur auditu, inquit: Idem ipse*, “it shall never be taken away by hearing, he says: The same himself,” etc. The correction was suggested by the sense and confirmed by the reading of the Psalm: “You are the same.”]

Thanks be to God, for by reasoning we have been led to this point, so that through your very hesitation I may persuade you to take up the yoke with Mary and minister with Martha, so that afterward you may be able to sit well with that same Mary. By sitting most excellently with her—that is, by devoting yourself contemplatively to freedom from worldly affairs and listening silently to the word of God—you may be able to choose, happily obtain, and possess the better portion.

### 27

This yoke, then, is easy; this burden is so light. It can lift and raise you so greatly that you may merit having God himself as your portion. It does not crush the neck but adorns it; it dignifies the throat and does not torment it. Do not hesitate or delay, I beg you, to take it up in your youth, lest, if you wish to take it up late, there be no place left for you, and it be said to you: “What you did not gather in your youth, how will you find in your old age?” (Ecclus. XXV, 5).

Therefore anticipate the years of old age through fitting action and correction, knowing that it is more desirable for you to be able truthfully to say, “God, who has fed me from my youth” (Gen. XLVIII, 15), and “God, you have taught me from my youth” (Ps. LXX, 17), than to pray distrustfully from the recollection of your falls and lament, saying: “Remember not, O Lord, the sins of my youth and my ignorances” (Ps. XXIV, 7).

The former is the strength of salvation; the latter, the medicine of illness. In the one case, a remedy for the wound is sought; in the other, thanks are returned to the healing grace.

Since “the life of man upon earth is warfare” (Job VII, 1), is it not better to stand bravely on guard in the youth of this same warfare, so that in old age you may be able to obtain a place of higher rank among the veterans, than to devote your adolescence to sloth and then try to enlist in the army when old age impedes your labor, weakens your limbs as your strength fails, and your looser muscles are disabled from hoping to win the victory of the contest? [Note: The same Vulgate editions read *enerves* (“enervated”), without sense. Construe: “and, as strength fails, [old age] weakens the limbs, with the looser muscles barred from the hope of attaining victory in the contest.”]

This is especially so since life itself does not promise you so many years that, after your labor is completed, you will be able to exchange military service and be invested with the honors of a higher rank. Rather, with your limbs exhausted and with no herald of praise preceding you, you will be glad if at least you are counted among those who seek a donative for the very fact of their enlistment, or among the provincials who provide the soldiers with their rations as a tax [Note: Augustine likewise says in Sermon I on Psalm XC, no. 10, that the devoted provincial supplies provisions to the soldiers]. For this reason, he says above that it is good to take up the yoke in youth.

For the one who takes up that yoke after the time of youth has passed encounters many kinds of opposition. Habitual vices goad him; evil custom weighs him down; conscience itself harasses him. Familiarity with error makes him unstable; he struggles with himself and falls beneath himself. He wishes to wipe away old things, but effectiveness does not follow his will. Like birds caught in a net, when he wishes to free his foot for action, he is held fast by the meshes of accustomed behavior.

Thus everything is in danger for the latter, while everything is secure for the former. The solitary man will sit; finding few or perhaps none worthy of his companionship, he will quietly and freely devote himself to divine duties, enriched with angelic revelations and rewards, disturbed by the enticements of pleasures neither past nor present, nor by the tickling touches of the flesh that provoke him. Alone, quiet, free, he will rejoice in security.

### 28

Whoever you are, then, who strive for this most singular height: first exercise yourself communally in the field of the living. Sit attentively and diligently beside those of greater weight. Learn to show honor to your elders, love to your equals, and an example to your juniors. Follow the authority and instructions of the wise, and believe that through these God himself speaks to you.

When you sit in the council of elders, bring your hand to your mouth; listen attentively and learn diligently, so that, receiving the judgments of old men, you may carefully gather what you will preserve for a later age. I also want you to restrain yourself from the talk of your contemporaries, so that through practice itself you may be trained to become sparing of speech, and, still inexperienced because of your youth, may not easily slip into illicit speech.

But, withdrawn from others, may you be able to attend to the instructions of elders, the sayings of the ancients, the oracles of the prophets, and the teachings of the apostles. For the one is to be praised who wishes [perhaps *mavult*, “prefers”] to learn by silence what ought to be said, rather than to utter what he thinks before he has learned how to speak.

If God’s grace should grant you these natural gifts, you should add what was wittily counseled by the man mentioned above to a certain exceedingly insolent but eloquent young man: do not become vain by attributing more to yourself than is fitting, nor, again, grow cold through casting yourself down and despairing.

In the midst of these matters, observe that the householder calls you, an idle man, to cultivate the vineyard—not simply as he called those others early in the morning, but with an added conjunction [“you also”], by which you should understand a note of reproach: “Go, you also, into the vineyard” (Matt. XX, 7). That is: you too, who ought to have been present in the morning and at the third hour, hurry at least at the sixth hour and profit from the middle portion of the day that remains.

## Title XIII — On the Old

### 29

Are you old? Rejoice in the Lord, who has brought you this far—not only because you have escaped so many shoals of the Syrtes and shipwrecks, but also because the harbor toward which you seem to be heading is now near, provided that you are serious, upright, dignified, adorned with good morals, decked with virtues, venerable in the grayness of your mind, and honey-sweet in the beauty of your speech—provided you can say with the Psalmist: “My old age is in abundant mercy” (Ps. XCI, 11).

If the opposite is true—which God forbid—please do not be angry if I, though younger, dare to admonish you, knowing that I presume upon this very duty, insofar as I see that it concerns you. No age should be too late to learn what is necessary. And although, as someone before us seems to have said quite properly, old men are more suited to teaching than to learning, it is nevertheless more fitting for them to learn than to remain ignorant of what they should teach—or rather, of what they should do, which we can add without excess.

Listen, then, to what Ecclesiastes says: “If a man lives many years, he must remember the dark time and the many days; when they come, the things of the past are judged vanity” (Eccles. XI, 8). And: “The child of a hundred years shall be accursed” (Isa. LXV, 20). Likewise: “Old age is venerable not because of long duration, nor is it reckoned by the number of years” (Wis. IV, 8).

Hear also the guardian who speaks generally to all, but specifically to you: “Morning has come, and also night; if you seek, seek; turn back and come” (Isa. XXI, 12). Hear the Apostle too: “Whatever grows old and ages is near destruction” (Heb. VIII, 13).

As I look upon the snow-white hairs that you carry upon your head, I confess that I am in no small doubt where I should begin my speech. For I would gladly, if I could, bring both reverence for your age and instruction to your folly. But may he graciously be present, I beg, who once turned the braying of a she-ass into human speech for the instruction of senseless men (Num. XXII, 28).

I shall retrace the sequence of the Gospel reading recited today (Num. XXII, 28). And if you perhaps find something of your own in it, please do not blame me, who am reciting it; rather, receive what is yours as yours, and turn to your benefit what has been spoken, even if you think it has been spoken as an insult.

### 30

[Note: This indicates the Saturday of the September Ember Days, on which the Gospel of the fig tree is read. These words were therefore written on that day, just as the preceding material had been composed on the preceding Friday. Compare note 210 above.]

“A certain man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard” (Luke XIII, 6), etc. If this reading still does not persuade you that trees signify human beings, read something clearer in Daniel, where the dream of a great and lofty tree is reported (Dan. IV, 7). After many praises of its dignity had been described, it was finally ordered to be cut down; and when this was interpreted concerning the king’s exalted position, the loss demonstrated the very one whom the excellence had marked out.

For he, raised up by innumerable honors of advancement, as though by a blending of the elements, and lifted like a tree almost to heaven, was cut down from his height and fell from his honor. [Note: The same verb, *inalto* for *exalto* or *extollo* (“I raise up”), occurs in Apuleius’ *Asclepius*: “The roundness of the world is raised up in the manner of a sphere.” Hence the Italian *inalzato*.] Abandoned by those who had served him, like a tree abandoned by fleeing birds, after seven periods had been changed over him, he returned again to his former state of elevation.

There are many things in Scripture that signify one thing according to nature and another according to understanding; but they require the reader’s diligence. Let us therefore see what happened to this tree—whether it is you, or I, or both of us, or anyone to whom the things reported about it apply.

“He came,” it says, “seeking fruit on it, and found none” (Luke XIII, 6). Who came? The one whose vineyard it was, and whose fig tree it was. If you are the fig tree, then the one who planted you is the Lord; for he himself says: “I planted you as a choice vine” (Jer. II, 21).

If you do not believe this, there is a parable from another reading to confirm it. The vineyard in which he planted you is the Church. He came seeking fruit in you and found none. How many times he has come [supply: “has come”], let him say himself. For I do not wish to force or invent anything here from my own resources, lest you judge me not a reliable disputant but an inept storyteller.

“He said to the vinedresser: ‘Behold, it is three years since I have come seeking fruit on this fig tree, and I find none’” (Luke XIII, 7). Hold on to the words, “It is three years.” Let us examine something else.

I have called you the tree, the vineyard the Church, and that certain one—or rather, the lord of the vineyard—God. Whom shall I call the vinedresser? If the text had said “the cultivator of the fig tree,” perhaps your mind might have understood an angel, to whom, as some suppose, or rather as you may rightly suppose, you have been entrusted. But by saying not “the cultivator of the tree” but “the cultivator of the vineyard,” it requires someone else who has undertaken to cultivate not you alone, but other fig trees as well—indeed, to guard the whole extent of the vineyard.

Why, then, are we troubled? Not because we find something good—for what is found with greater difficulty is held more sweetly, as Ambrose testifies, and the slower the attainment, the more welcome the enjoyment.

[Note: The text seems to require: “Not because we are troubled if we find something good. For what …”]

I could already point out to you the vinedresser, insofar as the Master of all above deigns to water the valley of my smallness through those very mountains that have already treated this subject sufficiently. But I wish to draw you through an example of more eminent authority, so that you may become more ready to seek and, when you see that I have not discovered these things from myself but have demonstrated them from Scripture, may be made all the more receptive because you are all the more eager.

[Note: Construe it as follows: “For I could already show you the vinedresser, insofar as the Master of all above deigns to water the valley of my smallness through those very mountains that have already treated this matter sufficiently; but I wish …” By “mountains” he understands the holy Fathers, who are designated by this name in certain places in the sacred Scriptures.]

### 31

“Another reading” [Note: “As this [reading],” namely, the Gospel parable of the fig tree previously set forth.], though also a reading of the Gospel, says: “There was a certain man who was rich, who planted a vineyard, surrounded it with a hedge, leased it to farmers, and …” until, when he returned, “he will destroy those wicked men wickedly and lease his vineyard to other farmers” (Matt. XXI, 33, 41).

Because this has been fulfilled, and has already been disclosed by the account itself to many people, that fact can more perceptively assist in revealing what is now being sought.

Those wicked cultivators of the vineyard, who not only refused to return the fruit but also killed the servants after inflicting various injuries upon them, and who moreover did not refrain from laying hands upon the son himself, have already been destroyed wickedly. The vineyard has already been leased to the apostles and to their successors—the bishops, priests, and the other sacred orders. Each of these, according to his capacity or ministry, laboring in the vineyard, awaits the lord of the vineyard, not so that he may destroy wicked men wickedly, but so that, receiving the fruit he desires, he may reward the good laborers with generous kindness.

Which of these men he may be—whether the bishop or the priest who has undertaken to cultivate you—does not concern me. He himself addresses you and complains that you have not produced fruit, declaring, by showing him your conduct, that you are unconverted and have long been fruitless—not only by his own mouth, that is, by the voice of Scripture, but also by your actions.

“Behold,” he says, “it is three years since I have come seeking fruit on this fig tree, and I find none” (Luke XIII, 7). These words are spoken when the cultivator of your heart sees in you those things which, under the Lord’s instruction, he recognizes as blameworthy. Then he hears the one to whom you refuse to offer the fruit of your works complaining about you.

If you deny that years signify periods of life, just as hours do elsewhere in the Gospel (Matt. XX, 3–12), there are many testimonies that may confront you. But lest, while we labor to surround with testimonies a matter about which there is no need for scruple, we arrive too slowly at the place toward which we are hurrying, know that the Lord’s coming to you has already taken place in three periods of life.

He came to you first in infancy and childhood, so that you might receive the One through his nearness: giving baptism, supplying understanding, providing teachers, and seeking the fruits that had been bestowed. What you returned, you yourself know better.

He came a second time in adolescence and youth, increasing understanding, multiplying gifts, and requiring merits. What you repaid then, I believe you remember.

Now he is present [Note: “Now” means in old age; here he is addressing old men]. See what you are doing. For he wants to cut you down.

And do not flatter yourself that, if you are cut down, you will again be raised up, as that tree above was after seven years [Note: “That tree” means the tree he had earlier said was cut down in Daniel and restored to its former height after seven periods had changed]. That tree was one thing and you another. It was not a fig tree but a cedar—not one of the cedars of Lebanon, which the Lord planted (Ps. CIII, 16), but one of those of which it is said: “The Lord will break the cedars of Lebanon” (Ps. XXVIII, 5).

For although “Lebanon” is interpreted as “whitening,” there are nevertheless some who are like whitened tombs, to whom Truth himself says, “Woe!” (Matt. XXIII, 27). This cedar did not stand in the vineyard but in the open field.

Believe me: if you are cut down uncorrected, you will immediately be cast into the fire. For the householder has already threatened, saying: “Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matt. III, 10).

Then grace was awaited; now judgment is expected. The pagan, because he nevertheless possessed some good, was rewarded in the present so that he might be tormented eternally. You, because you are a Christian, although negligent, are being required to correct yourself willingly here, so that you may live forever.

All this, however, is in excess of what is needed, since that cutting down meant nothing other than the loss of kingdom and understanding, whereas your cutting down, of which the present passage speaks, means the loss of the soul and the onset [*subitio*, that is, “incursion”] of death. If that death is good, it is not death but a birthday [Note: That the death of the righteous, especially of martyrs, is called a “birthday” is clear from ancient liturgical books and ecclesiastical writers]. But if it is evil, it will be immortal death, unending decline, enduring destruction, unchanging corruption, mourning without consolation, groaning without cessation, and calamity without end.

### 32

Remember, then, as I continue to speak to you from the Gospel that remains, what your cultivator—whether he is a bishop or someone praying to God on your behalf as your advocate—says: “Lord, let it alone this year also, until I dig around it and put manure on it; and if indeed it bears fruit—but if not, afterward you shall cut it down” (Luke XIII, 8–9).

O how brief the interval! O how sufficient, if you turn back! O how sudden, if you turn away—or rather, if you persist in this hardness of heart in which he found you!

But do not say that I am arbitrarily taking “year” for “year,” since above I took “year” to mean an age. Consider your own age here as well, I beg you. Think how long you have lived, and see whether your age still promises so many spans of time—especially since even in infants the outcome is uncertain, because death often comes prematurely.

Consider that you are not called a *silicernius* at this age without a definite reason [Note: *Silicernium* was the name of the funeral banquet held during the rites of burial, as Festus records. Old men were called *silicernii* because, on account of their decrepit age, a *silicernium* would soon have to be held for them], but so that you may be warned to attend to your appointed end, and attend all the more carefully the nearer it is.

Place before your eyes the *taphus* [Note: *Taphus* comes from the Greek τάφος (*taphos*), “a mound” or “tomb.” Gerhard uses it in this sense in *The Life of Saint Ulrich, Bishop of Augsburg*, chapter 13. Here, however, it seems to indicate a bier or coffin, since mention of the tomb follows distinctly. Shortly afterward we wrote *potes*, where the text mistakenly had *potest*]. in which you must be received when you depart from here. Let the tomb never recede from your sight. Let the memory of sins, the enormity of punishments, the dread of penalties, the contemplation of the Judge, and that final sentence of eternal destruction never flee from your meditation.

This is the manure by which you can be restored to a state of richness; this is the trench of humility by which you may produce the fruit of pious action. In other words, let the awareness of your depravity touch the memory of your thoughts, and let the root of your heart return to fruitfulness through the digging of confession and contemplation of your foul deeds, while you grieve over what you remember having done.

### 33

And lest, by reckoning the time already spent to have been excessively long and what remains for repentance to be very brief, you should despair, I beg you: consider David, look upon Zacchaeus [Col. 0214C], and, if you have the means—understand, “by which you may redeem yourself”—imitate him. But if you are so poor that you possess nothing with which to redeem yourself, and death suddenly overtakes you, imitate that blessed thief: a thief for a long time—understand, “for a long period”—but suddenly a confessor, suddenly a martyr; long a murderer, at once an inhabitant of paradise. Imitate the Ninevites, who wiped away ancient guilt by three days of repentance (Jon. III, 4–10).

For ineffable, inconceivable, and incomprehensible is the goodness of the heavenly physician, who saves some by long satisfaction, others by moderate satisfaction, others by the briefest satisfaction, but all solely by the benevolence of his grace, saving no one by any action of his own, as you heard in the psalm: “For your mercy is better than lives” (Ps. LXII, 4). For if time is available, he wishes you to chastise prolonged errors by prolonged mortification [Col. 0214D], just as he says to the soul: “For I will show him how much he must suffer for my name” (Acts IX, 16). This is as though he said: “The one who fought against me for a long time, I want him to contend for me for a longer time.”

Indeed, David had already been forgiven his sin, and yet, killing his son against his own wish, allowing another to rise up against him, and laying the people low, God still threatened punishment for the sin [Col. 0215A]. But if the moderate course of life intervenes, God does not reject a moderate course of repentance—understand, “God does not reject it”—provided that the will is not moderate but immense. Hence the holy Fathers wisely established [Note: [Col. 0215D] In Burchard, book XIX, chapter 31, this canon, attributed to Jerome, is expressed as follows: “The canons therefore do not prescribe with sufficient clarity a measure of time for performing penance for each crime, so as to say of each one how each ought to be amended; rather, they determine that the matter should be left to the judgment of an understanding bishop, because before God the measure of time does not have as much value as the measure of grief.” The substance of these words, which are found in the ancient penitentials, was taken from the holy Fathers. Augustine, for example, says in the Enchiridion, chapter 65: “In the performance of penance, when the offense committed is such that the offender is separated even from the body of Christ, the measure of time should not be considered so much as the measure of grief.”] that, in the cases of penitents, the measure of time ought to be considered less than the measure of grief.

But if the final hour itself suddenly overtakes you, while you still breathe, while your pulse still flutters, however little you are able, send forth the voice of confession; let it grieve you that you have come there unprepared. Yet do not despair, do not doubt: cry out confidently, entreat with your whole heart. He sees what is in the heart; he considers with what feeling you cry out. Believe me truly—I promise you—for if he sees that you repent and confess at the very moment of death with not a divided but a simple [Col. 0215B] heart, he will bestow the medicine of salvation.

Let so great a clemency of the Creator give courage to the hesitancy produced by guilty fear; let that saying of the apostle James, though universal, be especially particular to you and terrify the hardness of an obstinate heart: “Behold, the judge stands before the door” (Jas. V, 9). For that unforeseen departure is the door for each person, and that irrevocable lot sits there like a thief, watching for the hour in which it may unexpectedly snatch away the soul and lead it there where it will receive what belongs to it according to its merits. You ought to have been wary of this thief from the beginning of your birth, lest he break in, as he is accustomed to do, before the proper time; how much more now, when he is present with a certain judicial authority, as is fitting?

### 34

Do not therefore act sluggishly; do not fall asleep, lest he catch you sleeping—that is, unoccupied with pious works. Hear the Apostle rousing you from this lethargy of deadly torpor with a saving voice: “It is already the hour,” he says, “for us to rise from sleep” (Rom. XIII, 11). Do not henceforth grant any holidays; enough. By now you have sabbatized sufficiently with the Jews. Put an end now to idleness and devote yourself to pious labor. See that your flight does not occur in winter or on the Sabbath (Matt. XXIV, 20)—that is, lest he find you cold toward charity or unoccupied with good works.

Know that your final hour is already at hand; the one sent to summon you is already at hand. Seize whatever you can carry with you. But know that you will carry with you whatever you have striven to send ahead here. “The axe is already at the root of the tree” (Luke III, 9): the tree is dry through ripeness, barren and fruitless through torpor; nothing remains except that it should be cut down. You will be cut down immediately, I tell you; you will be cut down. But see that you are not thrown into the fire. It cannot happen that you are not cut down, because the lord of the vineyard complains that you occupy the ground uselessly.

Many trees are cut down, but they are not immediately thrown into the fire [Col. 0216A]. From the others, however, different works, different utensils, and different vessels are made; some are even excellent, and some, though very rare, are more precious than gold. I suggest this to you because I know with complete truth that in this hour, in this age, in the period of life you now possess, you ought to be cut down. I do not want you to be fuel for the fire, but a most precious cup in the hand of the heavenly King.

Therefore may that Solomon, truly peace-bringing, who makes peace between us and God and has joined earth with heavenly things, graciously pour out for his participants a drink of joy—that is, the joys of your conversion and salvation—for “his intoxicating cup is exceedingly excellent” (Ps. XXII, 5). May these words, modest indeed in relation to your benefit, but sufficient in relation to our respite, suffice.

### 35

Now, since the occasion has presented itself on your account, we judge it fitting and appropriate to append from the same Gospel certain general matters for ourselves and for you [Note: [Col. 0216D] The Vulgate has *subvertere* (“to overturn”) incorrectly; the reading here is *subnectere* (“to append”).], which God may grant to benefit both parties. But because they have been expressed with incomparable eloquence by someone before whose authority ours yields not a little, we fear to defile them by any admixture of our own speech. Therefore, just as he set them forth at the end of his discourse, we shall place them here unaltered. He says [Note: [Col. 0216D] The verb *ait* (“he says”) is governed by the nominative *Gregorius* (“Gregory”), which the author has postponed to the end of the sentence. Moreover, when he adds that he has recited certain points from Gregory’s discourse, though not with a meaning so very different, he indicates that earlier he took certain things from the same homily of Gregory, *Homilies on the Gospels*, book II, homily 31, using different words but the same meaning; from that homily he is now about to recite the same words.]—after certain matters that had already been set forth with sufficient clarity by others, but from which we have recited certain points in a discourse for your particular benefit and, generally, for the benefit of ourselves and many others, not indeed as was fitting, but as the dryness of our intellect permitted, and without so great a difference in meaning—Gregory (*Homilies on the Gospels*, book II, homily 31, no. 5):

> “There are many,” he says, “who hear reproofs and yet disdain to return to repentance, and, fruitless before God, remain green in this world. Let us therefore hear what the cultivator of the vineyard says: ‘If indeed it bears fruit; but if not, in the future you will cut it down’ (Luke XIII, 9). For surely the one who here does not wish to grow rich in fruitfulness through reproof falls there from which he will no longer be able to rise through repentance, and in the future he will be cut down, although here he may appear to stand green without fruit.
>
> “He was teaching in their synagogue on the Sabbaths (Luke XIII, 11). And a certain woman had a spirit of infirmity for eighteen years (ibid., 11). We said a little earlier that this was the Lord’s threefold coming to the fruitless tree [Note: With Gregory we have supplied *erat* (“was”).], and that the number eighteen years signifies the bent woman. For on the sixth day man was made, and on that same sixth day all the works of the Lord were completed; and the number six, multiplied into a triangle, produces eighteen. Since, therefore, the human being, who was made on the sixth day, did not wish to possess perfect works, but was infirm before the law, under the law, and at the beginning of dawning grace, the bent woman remained so for eighteen years.”

And shortly afterward (in the same place, no. 7):

> “Very often we see what ought to be done, but do not accomplish it in deed; we strive and grow weak. The mind perceives the judgment of uprightness, but the strength for action yields to it; for it is surely already a punishment for sin that one can indeed see what is good, but is driven away by merit from what one sees [Note: In Gregory, the reading is *ut ex dono quidem* (“that indeed by gift”). Then *quo pretio redemptus* (“at what price he was redeemed”) is better than the vulgate text of Gregory, *quo praemio sit redemptus* (“by what reward he has been redeemed”).]. For habitual guilt binds the mind, so that it can in no way rise to uprightness. It struggles and falls, because where it has long persisted voluntarily, there also, when it does not wish to, it falls under compulsion.”

Likewise:

> “If the soul itself does not cast itself down to desire what is low, the perversity of demons cannot prevail against it in any way; nor can they pass through one whom they fear as rigid against them. We therefore, brothers, give a road to evil spirits when we desire earthly things, when we bend ourselves toward the desire for temporal things. Let us therefore be ashamed to desire earthly things and to offer the backs of our minds to adversaries as they climb upon them. The bent person always looks at the ground; and the one who seeks what is low does not remember at what price he was redeemed.”

Likewise:

> “The one who bears a hump always looks at what is low. He is therefore excluded from the priesthood, because whoever is intent only on earthly things is himself a witness that he is not a member of the High Priest.”

Likewise:

> “If we cannot perform the summit of virtues, God himself rejoices in our lament. We shall please him by the very beginning of righteousness, when we punish the wrongs we have committed.”

Let it suffice that I have proceeded this far beyond the path of my subject, delighted by the charm of so flower-filled and verdant a meadow.

### 36

Now, returning to you, lest I seem to have interrupted the work in any respect, I admonish you by suggesting—since I know that, on account of your gray hair, you are owed reverence—that you compare these things with what precedes and acquire from them the task of obtaining salvation. And lest you rightly be called “aged in days of evil,” I now beg you to strive, while you are able, to halve your days and to contend to be renewed in the spirit of your mind.

And because up to now you have poured yourself out more than was right into bodily concerns, gather yourself back to yourself; and, now at least, having stripped off the old human being, become young again before God as a new man. Look upon your eighty years, whether nearly completed, already passed, or now approaching; do not despise the gentleness of God that is coming upon you, lest, bearing correction too harshly, you observe the almond blossom of your head [Note: [Col. 0217C] “The almond blossom” is understood as the gray hair of the head, an indication of old age [Col. 0218C], for almond blossoms are white.]

And if even now the locust—that is, the former agility of your steps—has been made heavy by swelling of the feet or, at any rate, of the legs; or, as the poet says,

> “Stony gout  
> already makes the joints  
> like the old branches of a beech,”

await with suspicion and fear that hour in which you must go to the house of eternity, whether for good or for evil (Eccl. XII, 5). For afterward, whatever may happen in the streets as the cause of your lamentation will not help you when you have been placed in torments—though, while you were still alive here, you neglected to take thought for yourself and to devise counsel for yourself against the distress of so great a calamity that was about to come, even though you knew very well that it would be unchangeable.

Meanwhile, while there is an opportunity to weep fruitfully, while it is an acceptable time, while the day of salvation still lasts, while you live, while you are still spared by the Judge [Note: [Col. 0218C] The Vulgate read *a vidice*, incorrectly; by the slightest alteration of letters we have corrected it to *a judice*, “by the Judge.”], I urge you to strive toward what is better. While he delays the stroke of the axe, take counsel for yourself; while he suspends vengeance, correct your life. Conversion is not difficult or slow before God, for he is pleased by the very beginning of righteousness.

But woe to the one who is not permitted to be corrected before he dies. For, as the one mentioned above says, a greater anger of vengeance usually follows the great obstinacy of despised gentleness and grace; and the longer the unconverted person has been awaited, the more harshly he is struck. As generously as mercy is extended in the present, so severely judgment is threatened against the ungrateful in the future.

# THE THIRD BOOK BEGINS

Its contents are prefaced as follows:

I. You are a king? Let royal delight instruct you.  
II. Discern with what intention each person does what he does.  
III. Do not cloak virtues under the pretext of other things that are discordant with them.  
IV. Rule what has been entrusted to you by fearing God.  
V. The Church is catholic, and its grace is catholic.  
VI. A king should not disdain to submit to God’s judges.  
VII. That we have become an object of reproach and mockery.  
VIII. Just as bishops are the lot of the saints by the ministry of their order, so also should they be so by the privilege of honor.  
IX. That the Holy Spirit is often present even with a negligent bishop.  
X. That a bishop can be judged by no one except God alone.  
XI. Prayer for those placed beneath the altar.  
XII. The threefold division of the children of the Church.

[Col. 0217]

### 1

Having traversed in the preceding two books, in prefaces concerning periods of life, persons, offices, sexes, and ages, with as much brevity as we could, though not with as much elegance as was fitting, by God’s gift, we now confront the vast seas of dignities, orders, and dispositions—seas often shipwreck-producing because they are filled with the most abundant reefs of promontories. Entrusting ourselves to adverse winds, we set Christ himself before us as a barrier, eager to plow through the same waters in the three-prowed skiff of these volumes—that is, in the three other books, the third, fourth, and fifth—provided that his oarage [Note: [Col. 0217D] The construction is: “now attempting to pass through the vast seas, and therefore often shipwrecked because they are filled with the abundant reefs of promontories; through the seas, I say, of dignities, orders, and dispositions, entrusting ourselves to adverse winds, we set Christ himself before us as a barrier, eager to plow through those same waters in the three-prowed skiff of the volumes,” that is, in the three other books, the third, fourth, and fifth, “provided that his help is not lacking,” and so forth.] is not lacking.

Indeed, the more insistently we demand that his help, necessary for us, be present in this work, because he knows that we undertake it with all the more hesitation in proportion as it is more dangerous. For on one side we fear the storm of the heavenly spectator, and on the other that of this excessively boiling sea. We fear in every way for our ship, whose helmsman, his oar already broken and his rudder lost, weary and battered against many rocks, his strength spent, borne not in a little boat but tossed by the waves, biting his very tongue with trembling teeth, lies in one of the shoals [Note: [Col. 0219D] Shoals are shallow places in the sea, dangerous to sailors. Hence Virgil, *Aeneid* I:

> “[lacuna] Eurus from the deep  
> drives him onto shoals and sandbanks.”

], and we fear in every way the loss of the ship, knowing that this pitiable collision has befallen it because of its headlong course, since, while it did not know how to avoid a perilous deviation [Note: [Col. 0219D] The construction is: “And we fear in every way the loss of our ship, whose helmsman, with his oar already broken and his rudder lost, weary and battered against many rocks, his strength subdued, borne not in a skiff but tossed by the waves, biting his very tongue with trembling teeth, lies in one of the shoals. We fear, I say, the loss of the ship, knowing that this pitiable collision occurred because of its headlong course, while he did not know how to avoid a perilous deviation.”].

For although, as Scripture says, “The tongues of the wise are like goads, and like nails driven deeply” (Eccl. XII, 11), and although we know the steadfast constancy of divine authority to be such that it knows neither to spare anyone nor to flatter anyone, nevertheless we know that even today the men of worldly learning observe with the greatest care what they may say more cautiously rather than what they may say more truthfully. They judge what the comic poet teaches more useful than what the Lord threatens; they value the saying,

> “Compliance produces friends; truth produces hatred.”

(Terence, *Andria* I, 1)

more highly than the saying, “Whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, the Son of Man will be ashamed of him when he comes” (Luke IX, 26). Perhaps that saying is considered more useful because it is more eloquent; because it is grandiloquent, it is judged most salutary. But this saying, because it has been stripped of the beauty of leaves—or rather of the thickest shade of vanity—is therefore regarded by the prudent of the world as simple, and, so to speak, rustic, and worthy of little esteem, although it seems to them to bring no less caution to a more suspect matter [Note: [Col. 0220D] “A more suspect matter,” namely, one that produces greater suspicion.] when those who say:

> “To those who see, ‘Do not see’; and to those who behold, ‘Do not behold for us the things that seem right; speak to us pleasing things; behold errors for us’” (Isa. XXX, 10).

But with Truth as the same teacher who is also the way, and with that same Truth speaking of itself through another: “This is the way; walk in it” [understand, “and do not turn aside”], “neither to the right nor to the left” (Isa. XXX, 21), let us strive to moderate our speech by this method, so that we do not presumptuously attempt higher things on the right and then turn aside to the left by timidly yielding to falsehood. Thus, although it may be spoken absurdly, we may speak in such a way that Terence does not, through insufficient prudence, sharpen anyone’s hatred against us, nor Christ indicate that anyone has less freely preferred anyone’s friendship to truth.

To prevent this from happening, let us walk carefully between these two with measured steps. Let us touch the chord of dignity in such a way that we remain silent about the person of the cithara-player [Note: [Col. 0220D] By “cithara-player” he designates the king whom he is about to attack in what follows without naming him. It will become clear later that this was Hugh, king of Italy, by whom the author was captured and thrown into a tower at Pavia. By “order” he means the episcopate; for he will repeatedly criticize, likewise concealing their names, certain bishops of the same order in which he himself excelled.]; let us address the order in such a way that we omit the name of the person ordained; let us address the disposition in such a way that we do not permit the lack of charity to hinder us, whose benefit we ought here especially to seek. This is particularly necessary since we believe that the envy of those who hate us will not be absent—men who will not hesitate to criticize our boldness in this matter also, although, apart from authority and without violating the reverence due to our office, they know that we possess no particular knowledge at all with which they might form a sufficiently excessive conjecture about this matter too.

## TITLE I — On Kings

### 2

Are you a king? I beg you, let the dignity itself, while it delights you, instruct you. There are certain insignia of the royal order, without which, although the name may somehow remain, such dignity certainly cannot truly subsist. Use these; exercise yourself in these; adorn yourself with these. Be prudent, just, brave, and temperate.

Mounted as though upon this four-horse chariot, survey the boundaries of the kingdom. Finally, use this chariot on the road, so that with the most holy Elijah you may even deserve to be called a charioteer (2 Kings II, 12). Armed with this fourfold breastplate, do not hesitate to meet your enemies without fear. For you will not be able to be overcome by any adversity if you have deserved to be fortified by such protection.
