## TITLE II — That one must discern with what intention each person does what he does

### 3

First, therefore, before we attempt other matters appropriate to your serenity, I wish to instruct both you and all who are placed in high position concerning these individual points. I add this: each person should diligently strive to discern what he does and with what intention he does it.

For, as we have learned both by experience from ourselves and by reading the statements of the ancients, vices very often pretend to be virtues. Hence Seneca says quite aptly in his *Proverbs*: “The timid calls himself cautious; the miserly, thrifty.” For cunning, as one of our own writers also says, often wishes to appear prudence—namely, so that, while we capture someone by deceit, we may congratulate ourselves on having acted prudently.

Against this the Psalmist says—and Peter also says it of Christ (1 Pet. II, 22): “He who speaks truth in his heart, who has not acted deceitfully with his tongue” (Ps. XIV, 3). One of our writers says: “Deceit in the heart, the more prudently it excels among human beings, the more foolishly it deceives before God.”

Likewise the Psalmist says: “His enemies shall lick the earth” (Ps. LXXI, 9). To lick the earth means to take away something earthly from someone by the sweetness of speech. Although some among worldly people count this vice as refinement, it must be avoided by pious minds with all the greater care, since by this testimony we learn that the person who deceives his neighbor by persuasive speech through falsehood is specially called God’s enemy—either stripping him of possessions through this pretense or, what is worse, mocking the same person in the manner of a treacherous betrayer, according to the saying: “He speaks peace with his friend with his mouth, but in secret he sets an ambush for him” (Jer. IX, 8).

And again: “They say, ‘Peace, peace,’ when there is no peace” (Jer. VI, 14); and: “Under his tongue are labor and sorrow; he sits in ambush with the rich in secret places, to kill the innocent” (Ps. X, 7–8). And shortly afterward: “He lies in wait,” he says, “to seize the poor; to seize the poor while he draws him away” (ibid., 9). Elsewhere: “His words have been softened beyond oil, yet they are arrows” (Ps. LIV, 22). Then, transferring the image to the kind in the customary manner and bringing forth the punishment that is due, he says: “But you, O God, will lead them down into the pit of destruction” (ibid., 24).

Job, however, speaks all the more terribly because he speaks more explicitly: “Hypocrites and the crafty provoke the anger of God” (Job XXXVI, 13). Here it should be noted that he says they do not merit but provoke it, so that you may understand something even more fearful [Note: [Col. 0221] Perhaps *et formidolosius* should be read, from *formidolosus*, “more fearful.”]. It must be feared lest he be provoked so far that no one can resist him, lest it be said: “I live, says the Lord, because this iniquity shall not be expiated by sacrifices and offerings forever” (1 Sam. III, 14).

### 4

How disgraceful it is for any Christian to pursue this vice is also shown by the example of the ancients, who, not through divine fear but through a natural love of honesty, determined that every victory obtained by deceit would be shameful. The madness of impatience also often wishes to give birth to strength [that is, “to appear as strength”]. For each person seeks to seem brave when he strikes with his fist, having been defeated by insult.

But it is foolish, as one of the most skilled writers says, to call a defeated man brave. It must also be understood that the frenzied often possess greater strength than the sane. According to Augustine, virtue should be valued more highly in proportion to the more things it despises.

Cruelty also, as a form of impiety, and ambition itself, as the most ardent desire, sometimes strive to seize the trophy of justice: namely, when someone satisfies his anger and thinks he is serving justice; or even when what he does is just, he does it for the sake of gain, contrary to the command of the one who orders: “You shall carry out what is just, and only what is just” (Deut. XVI, 20).

Sloth also sometimes wishes to appear temperance—namely, when we avoid doing something rashly but do not know how to moderate it through discernment. Even the things that ought to have been done, because we are insufficiently provident, we leave undone through sloth; and while we fear one vice, we fall into another. For often, when someone strives to restrain anger, he falls into negligence; and frequently failing to restrain vices is a greater crime than avenging them, while neglecting the delinquent is no less serious than hating him.

At times, while avoiding the Scylla of deceit, we fall into the shoals of folly. Very often, while avoiding things that ought bravely to be carried out, we serve the vice of sluggishness in our torpor.

### 5

But what benefit is there in recognizing their rivalries if it should happen that we do not know by definite signs what the virtues themselves are? Let us therefore define what they are, and it will appear more brightly than lightning what they are not.

Justice is, as the ancients have already defined it, a disposition of the soul maintained for the common benefit, assigning to each person his dignity. Hence justice is properly so called, as though it were *juris satus*, “the sowing of law.” Law is a proper rule; and the just person is one who guards the law—that is, the proper rule—or one who bestows upon each person what is proper to him, as in the Lord’s saying: “Give back to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s” (Matt. XXII, 21).

Prudence is truthful knowledge of good and evil things. Temperance is firm and measured mastery over desires and other improper impulses of the soul. It is also called moderation, because it does everything with measure or proportion. Fortitude is the considered undertaking of dangers and the firm endurance of hardships.

These four are recognized as properly royal virtues, so that with them even a rustic may appropriately be called a king; without them, not even one who possesses almost the entire monarchy of the world can justly be called king, even abusively. For, as the one mentioned above says, by ruling badly one loses supreme authority.

How beneficial it is not only for kings but for all human beings to ally themselves with these virtues is attested by the one who says in praise of wisdom: “For it teaches sobriety and wisdom, justice and virtue, than which nothing is more useful to human beings on earth” (Wis. VIII, 7). Let the attentive reader note that sobriety means temperance, wisdom means what we have called prudence, and virtue means fortitude. Blessed is the one to whom it is said: “You shall clothe yourself with all these as with garments.”

## TITLE III — Vices must not be cloaked

### 6

Having set these things forth, as I believe, not without consideration, now, if there are matters that must be said, may your greatness receive them in such a way that, when things long perhaps unknown have been revealed, what has been neglected may be corrected.

First, therefore, I beg you not to wish to debase the virtues themselves in any way, or to cloak them under the pretext of other things that may be discordant with them. I say: be prudent, not cunning; although prudence is often understood by the name of cunning, as in the saying: “It belongs to the cunning to understand his way” (Prov. XIV, 8). Be brave, not proud; temperate, not idle or lax; just, not cruel.

Honor God; rule yourself first; indeed, commend yourself to the ruler himself. See which trees are shaken by the stronger blast of winds; consider which buildings fall more heavily, and do not incur what is written: “The judgment will be most severe upon those who rule” (Wis. VI, 6); and “the powerful will suffer powerful torments” (ibid., 7); and “a harsher punishment awaits the more powerful” (ibid., 9).

Embrace with care the saying, “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. V, 7), so that you may at the same time escape this: “Judgment without mercy will be for the one who has not shown mercy” (Jas. II, 13); and understand that no one is wretched except the one who has been unwilling to show mercy.

Do not think yourself brave when you strike with a sword, defeated by vice, nor rejoice greatly when you subject very many people to yourself. Hear what was said long before us: “The one who wishes to have others subject to him is first himself subjected.” To whom he is subjected, I leave you to investigate, since the Lord can teach you quite suitably about this by saying: “No one can serve two masters” (Matt. VI, 24); and, “You cannot serve God and Mammon” (ibid.).

The Apostle likewise says: “Let not sin reign in your mortal body” (Rom. VI, 12); and, “Whoever commits sin is the slave of sin” (John VIII, 34); and, “By whatever a person is overcome, to that he is also enslaved” (2 Pet. II, 19). And in Daniel: “The prince of the kingdom of the Persians resisted me” (Dan. X, 13).

For it is not without reason that demons are called the spirits of fornication, pride, and the other vices: it is because they have subjects over whom they dominate, namely, those who serve those same vices.

### 7

When you have learned this most clearly, consider what the Lord says through the prophet:

> “Woe to you who join house to house and unite field to field, even to the boundary of the place. Will you alone dwell upon the earth? All these things are in my ears, says the Lord of hosts” (Isa. V, 8–9).

And shortly afterward:

> “Therefore hell has enlarged its soul and opened its mouth without any limit, and its mighty ones, its people, and its lofty and glorious ones shall descend to it” (ibid., 14).

Likewise:

> “Woe to you who justify the wicked for gifts and take away the justice of the just from him. Therefore, just as fire devours straw and wood and the heat of the flame consumes them, so their root shall be like ash and their shoot shall ascend like dust” (ibid., 23).

Consider, I beg you, how grave the crime of greed is, since it can consume both you and your people and the whole of your offspring. But if everything yields according to your wish, if the necks of all who oppose you suddenly bow before you, let no useless boastfulness strike you on account of it.

Remember that the Psalmist promised such things to the one whom divine justice had despised: “His judgments are removed from his sight; he shall rule over all his enemies” (Ps. X, 5). Know also from physicians that the desperate are not prevented from consuming whatever they desire.

## TITLE IV — How bishops are to be honored

### 8

Rather, fear God; rule—or rather, nourish—the people entrusted to you; entreat the saints; venerate the bishops. Know that they have been set over you, not you over them; and, to say more, that they have been given to you as gods by the supreme, one, and singular God, and as angels by the Angel of Great Counsel himself.

If you think I am lying, question your predecessor Constantine; question the psalm itself; question the Lord. “You,” says that aforesaid Constantine, “have been given to us by God as gods, and it is not fitting for a human being to judge gods” (Rufinus, book I, chapter 2).

The Psalmist, moreover, says: “God stood in the assembly of gods” (Ps. LXXXI, 1), and a little later: “I said, ‘You are gods’” (ibid., 6); and, “The God of gods, the Lord, has spoken” (Ps. XLIX, 1). The Lord himself said to Moses: “Behold, I have appointed you god of Pharaoh” (Exod. VII, 1); and, “You shall not revile the gods” (Exod. XXII, 28); likewise, “Bring him before the gods” (ibid., 8).

Again, in the Psalm: “He makes his angels spirits and his ministers a flame of fire” (Ps. CIII, 4)—that is, he makes his preachers spiritual and burning with charity. And through the prophet: “The lips of the priest shall guard justice, and they shall seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. II, 7).

When in the Apocalypse of John you hear of the angels of the seven churches, understand no others than their bishops. In the Gospel also, observe what he says and what authority he grants them: “Whatever you bind upon earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose upon earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. XVI, 19).

The same thing, though scattered in different places, had already been proclaimed by the Psalmist and the Prophet: “Your friends, O God, have been greatly honored; their rule has been greatly strengthened” (Ps. CXXXVIII, 17). Whose? The apostles, evangelists, bishops, clerics, and monks who renounce the world. Because they do not wish to possess anything in the world, they rightly rule with God and judge the world, preferring to rule those who possess gold rather than to possess gold themselves.

“Princes of the peoples,” he says, “have gathered together with the God of Abraham, because the strong gods of the earth have been greatly exalted” (Ps. XLVI, 6). Behold, you have it stated most clearly: the princes of the peoples are themselves the gods of the earth.

But what is this rule? What is this rule for? “To bind their kings with fetters, and their nobles with iron shackles, to execute upon them the judgment that has been written” (Ps. CXLIX, 8). Behold what rule they have received, for what purpose they have received it, and how that rule has been strengthened. Where? Here and in the future. By what means? Throughout the whole world.

Wherever Christ is worshiped, the priest is honored after him; indeed, in the priest Christ is honored.

9. Therefore, let no one take Jerusalem, Rome, Alexandria, or any other church in this prerogative and exclude the rest: the Church is catholic, and its grace is catholic. There are not several churches; there is one, and the rock that contains it is one; the Church is unique. For thus it is said of her: “She is one to her mother” (Song 6:8), that is, there is one law for the whole world, which regenerates by grace. Although customs are differentiated according to the rites and particularities of peoples, all are consecrated by one Spirit, just as all are washed by one baptism. And although there are divisions of graces—for some excel others in the Church, as there are also orders in heaven—the givers are not divided; for there is one giver, one who effects all things, and he alone is God essentially. Indeed, that which cannot be comprehended, and which we express better by wonder and faith than by thought, reasoning, or speech—that is, that he exists substantially, lives, is able, knows, and understands, always remaining the same—he distributes to each as he wills, how he wills, and through whom he wills. Therefore it is said: “There is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been ordained by God.” Hence, by his ordering, it has been established which authority should receive the privilege appropriate to it, which should be placed above or beneath another, so that the highest authority is the one that, because all things were created by it, distributes, orders, governs, and contains the universe. Next follows that authority which, having been placed above the others by him, says—as one proceeds from the heavenly powers passed over in silence to the celestial things that we call ecclesiastical—“Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven” (Matthew 16:19).

For he did not say, “Whatever things you may bind will be bound,” as though he were leaving you the option of understanding that some things might remain exempt from this law; rather, he said “whatever”—that is, everything that you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven.

[Note: This passage should be construed as follows: “Even now we have been unable to find, whether by thinking, reasoning, or reading, anything that could be placed above this authority—that is, the authority in question—since nothing seems to remain beneath its subordination, nor does anything appear capable of being properly or Christianly established through it that could order the other subordinate things.”]

But even now we have been unable to find, whether by thinking, reasoning, or reading, anything that could be placed above this authority, since nothing seems to remain beneath its subordination, nor does anything appear capable of being properly or Christianly established through it that could order the other subordinate things.

10. Yet if we should perhaps find someone who contradicts this authority, let him produce evidence from the divine Scriptures, and we shall believe him—provided only that we do not hear that the Holy Spirit, proceeding from the Father and the Son and breathing where he wills, can be given by a human being; for we do not assent even to an angel who says this, but rather, together with the Apostle, we anathematize the one who says it (Galatians 1:8).

And as for what is brought forward here as an apparently invincible proof—namely the statement of that same Apostle, “Submit yourselves to every human creature, whether to the king as preeminent” (1 Peter 2:13)—it would have some force for establishing the point if it said “to God as preeminent,” or “to bishops as preeminent.” But since this qualification is omitted, it is to be understood only that the king is preeminent over earthly things; and therefore, in order that justice may be maintained, the honor due to him—that is, greater honor than to the other earthly creatures, though not greater than to the heavenly ones—is to be rendered. Even this is not on his own account, but with reverence preserved for the exalted powers, to which both human authority itself and every human soul are commanded to be subject. These are none other than those who, through the Holy Spirit, received from the highest authority itself, in the Apostles and their successors, the power to judge, bind, and absolve all things.

## TITLE VI

11. Therefore, O king, do not disdain to be subject to such men, since, whether you wish it or not, you will have them as gods, as angels, as princes, and as judges. They have the power to release you; they have the power to bind you. For you have authority over some, whereas they have authority over you and over all. Honor them, therefore, with as much veneration as you can, so that they too may honor you with a fitting recompense.

Take care that you do not happen to inflict any injury upon them; rather, if another has inflicted one, strive to avenge it as far as you are able and reason dictates. Do not grieve the Holy Spirit, who is in them, in any matter (Ephesians 4:30), lest it prove disadvantageous to you.

Take heed and recall—if you have read it; or, if not, read in the book of Genesis what threats the Lord issued on their behalf under the persons of Abraham and Sarah (Genesis 20:3), and again of Isaac and Rebecca (Genesis 26:11), and likewise of Jacob while fleeing from Laban (Genesis 31:29). Also take as a warning for your conduct the ark of the Testament, which mystically signifies them: it was captured by the Foreigners and placed in the temple of Dagon (1 Samuel 5:2). Look, provide for yourself, and consider without disguising from yourself what happened to them.

Consider also what Oza—whose name means “the strong one of the Lord”—deserved when he wished to raise the ark itself after it had tilted because of the oxen’s kicking (2 Samuel 6). And if you should perhaps see in them some decline—that is, deviation—of negligent life, beware lest you wish to correct and raise them by your own agency; lest, while you strive to appear strong for the Lord, you become the throat of the striking angel (1 Chronicles 21).

Look also at the prophet sent to Bethel and devoured by a lion because of his disobedience (1 Kings 13:24). And, besides the withered hand of the king (ibid., 4), consider in that irrational beast how great the reverence ought to be with which you, a rational being, should honor the living, since even the beast did not dare to appropriate the dead donkey on account of its fault (ibid., 24).

Look at the two captains of fifty who cursed Elijah, and fear the fire of heavenly wrath (2 Kings 1:10, 12). Consider also the forty boys at Bethel who mocked Elisha (2 Kings 2:24), and restrain your tongue, your power, and your hands from slander and injury against the prophets—for such men they themselves are.

But if perhaps you have aspired to this, if you have presumed or usurped it, so that the examples already proposed should suffice; or if, provoked by them, you have been lifted up by your own power and therefore thought yourself superior to them when you were not—for neither a human being can be placed above God, nor an earthly being above a heavenly one, nor a worm rule an angel, nor a king rule another king, but only one of greater excellence can rule—then let it suffice for you that you have been brought to this by their sin and by your own misfortune.

Take care lest, driven from bad to worse by a very wicked charioteer, you attempt to hand over any of them to punishments in the manner of slaves, even if they are infants throughout the whole world, provided only that they are steadfast in the Catholic faith, when by right they themselves ought rather to exercise the office of masters.

Know that this practice belonged not to Catholics, but to tyrants, whose portion is far removed from yours. If the negligence of some evil custom of theirs requires that they be driven forward by blows, so that in the Church they may be the Lord’s drawn-out trumpet, beware of becoming the hammer; for while the trumpet is lengthened, the hammer is blunted.

For although the merciful Lord avenges all their offenses, and visits their iniquities with the rod and their sins with blows (Psalm 88:33), do not become the rod yourself. Hear what has been said: “Whoever spares the rod hates his son” (Proverbs 13:24).

[Col. 0226D] Fear, therefore, lest, while through you one of them is spared punishment because he is beloved, you yourself should not be spared when broken because you are despised; and while he, because beloved, advances through correction toward the inheritance, you, because despised, should through impiety decline toward destruction. Palaces are swept with brooms, but the brooms themselves, worn down and brought to the hearth, provide fuel. Gold too is purified by fire, not consumed; but wood, by which the fire is fed, is reduced to ashes.

12. “But,” you say, “sons who are highly pleasing are scourged” (Hebrews 12:6); “what wonder, then, if negligent servants are scourged?”

“But,” I reply, although they may be negligent, they do not belong to that servile condition in which they ought indiscriminately to be scourged by anyone.

I boldly—and almost insolently, by enumerating them—declare to you what they are, lest you fail to know and thereby offend; yet I declare it all the more freely because I bring it forward not from myself but from divine authorities.

[Note: In the common editions the text is corruptly printed as *ostendas*. Construe and explain it thus: “I boldly, and almost insolently, declare to you by enumeration what those bishops are, lest you fail to know and offend; yet I declare it all the more willingly because what I bring forward comes not from myself but from divine authorities. But it is a marvel if such great and ineffable things—and things incomprehensible even to the one who enjoys them—can be conferred by a human being, for example by a king, by whom bishops were said to be made. What difference is there between God and a human being, or why should God himself be asked to act in the election or consecration of a bishop, if dust can bestow such great things? To think this—wrongly printed in the common editions as *quid cogitare*, and shortly afterward as *quid dicere*—what is it other than to wish to climb into heaven? To say this, what is it other than to exalt one’s throne above the stars of heaven—which, if they are truly what they are called, the bishops are? What is it other than to attempt to climb above the heights of the clouds, which the prophet testifies that they are, when God says: ‘I have commanded,’ and so to consider oneself their equal? They are gods, they are the Lord’s, and so forth. All these are the great prerogatives that he affirms he will bring forward from divine authorities concerning bishops.”]

What a marvel it is if such great and ineffable things, incomprehensible even to the one who enjoys them, can be conferred by a human being! What difference is there between God and a human being, or why should God himself be asked to act, if dust can bestow such great things? To think this, what is it other than to wish to climb into heaven? (Isaiah 14:13.) To say this, what is it other than to exalt one’s throne above the stars of heaven (ibid.)—which, if they are truly what they are called, are the bishops? What is it other than to attempt to climb above the heights of the clouds (ibid., 14), which, as the prophet reports, God testifies that they are, saying: “I will command my clouds not to rain upon them” (Isaiah 5:6), and therefore to consider oneself their equal?

They are gods, they are lords, they are Christs, they are heavens, they are angels, they are patriarchs, they are prophets, they are apostles, they are evangelists, they are martyrs, [Note: In the printed editions, *vincti* (“bound”) is erroneous.] they are anointed, they are kings, they are princes, they are judges—not only of human beings but also of angels. They are the rams of the Lord’s flock; they are shepherds of the sheep, not just any sheep but those washed in Christ’s blood. They are teachers, heralds of the coming Judge, watchmen, the apple of the Lord’s eye, friends of the living God, sons of God, fathers, lights of the world, stars of heaven, pillars of the Church, physicians of souls, gatekeepers of paradise. They carry the keys of heaven; they have power to open and close heaven. They are clouds [supply: “they are”] upon which the Lord placed his ascent; they are the foundations upon which the entire structure of God’s temple rests.

If, then, someone moves any one of these by a single impulse—for the sake of brevity, let us reason at least about this one—what, I ask, does he do to the building erected above him? (Psalm 103:3.)

13. The Lord cries out on their behalf, threatens on their behalf, and fights on their behalf, even if you do not know it. He cries out, I say; he cries out, he does not dissemble, he is not silent, lest you perhaps be able to say, “I did not know.” He cries out and says: “Do not touch my anointed ones” (Psalm 104:15).

And this he says to you so that you may know, beware, and come to your senses; indeed, so that you may not attempt to act, presume, dare, or touch them—nor even slander them. For he cries aloud, thunders this, and proclaims this: “You shall not slander the gods” (Exodus 22:28).

Do not, therefore, excuse yourself by saying that you did not know. Strengthening and encouraging those very men, and giving them courage so that they would not fear, he says: “Do not fear, but take confidence, because I have conquered the world” (John 16:33).

“I,” he says, “I: I your God, I your Father, I your Brother, I your Head, I who by nature am what you are by office, I who share in you, I Christ, I the Anointed, I the Shepherd, I the Priest, I the Bishop, I the High Pontiff, I the King of kings—I have conquered the world.”

Whom do you fear? He has been conquered. Whom do you dread? He lies beneath your feet.

And to prove this, rise up, whoever you are who fear—and perhaps you are groaning in prison beneath chains. Raise your hand, lift up the sign, display the trophy, show the standard, extend the labarum.

You will see what that arrogance, that height, that pride, that thick neck, that erect neck of the daughters of Babylon, that tower of Shinar, the walls of Jericho, and the strongest walls of Kiriath-sepher will do and attempt: how they will yield, plead, totter, fall, and be put to shame; and, leaning down and humble in mind, they will worship one who was despised, injured, held in contempt, imprisoned, bound, naked, hungry, thirsty, and filled to overflowing with every kind of misery.

“For you are my witnesses” (Luke 24:48); “whoever despises you despises me, and whoever troubles you troubles me” (Luke 10:16); “whoever does an injury receives what he has done unjustly” (Colossians 3:25); and “whoever touches you is like one who touches the apple of my eye” (Zechariah 2:8).

## TITLE VII

14. “But we have been touched, crushed, despised, driven away, abused; the structure that seemed to stand over us has fallen. They have ruled over us, O Lord, without you” (Isaiah 26:13). We have become “a reproach to our neighbors, a mockery and derision to those around us” (Psalm 78:4), “their example, spectacle, tale, and song all day long” (Lamentations 3:14).

“Understand, you senseless among the people; and you fools, become wise at last. He who planted the ear, will he not hear? He who formed the eye, will he not see?” (Psalm 94:8.)

Why do you marvel, then, if the world hates you, when it hated me before you? (John 15:18.) For, “if you were of the world, the world would love what was its own” (ibid., 19). Why do you seek the friendship of the enemy, when neither do I wish to tear you away from fellowship with the Head, nor does the world itself judge you worthy of its own friendships?

Take care lest you seem unwilling to be in the body if you do not wish to endure the world’s hatred together with the Head. For what are they doing to you that they have not already done to me and to my greater members? “If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you” (John 15:20).

Just as “I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28:20), so there will not be lacking those who hate me in you, persecute you, and despise your word—not because it is yours, but because it is mine. For if it were yours—that is, worldly, carnal, and favorable to vices—it would certainly be loved.

Why do you wish to gather the weeds before the harvest (Matthew 13:20), without taking care lest you uproot the wheat along with them, when even in such an act you have often seen the godly perish together with the ungodly? “Vengeance is mine; I will repay,” says the Lord (Hebrews 10:30).

## TITLE VIII

15. But if you slander what has been written about the saints, saying that I ought not to turn to us, who lie far beneath their feet, I answer that in this age, just as we share with them in the ministry of the order, so we also share in the dignity of the name and the privilege of honor. If we strive to conform our life to theirs, we shall share in eternal glory. If otherwise—which God forbid—we shall be separated there, although here we appear to perform the common duty of honor and ministry.

For if this were otherwise, what value would that Christianity which we have undertaken to govern possess? And if our pontificate were not sanctified by the same Spirit by which theirs was sanctified, what benefit would it be that the people are baptized through our ministry with consecrated chrism?

[Note: Construe: “And if our pontificate were not sanctified by the same Spirit by which their pontificate was sanctified, what benefit would it be,” and so forth.] What, finally, would be the benefit of the celebration of Mass, of blessing, of the consecration of various things, or of the performance of any divine worship?

Either, then, declare that Christianity has failed and deny the truth of what Truth itself, which knows no falsehood, says: “Behold, I am with you all days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28:20); and confirm that it did not obtain what it requested when praying to the Father: “I pray not only for these, but also for those who will believe in me through their word” (Job XI, 45). The following too would consequently be absurd: when announcing that he would be born, the angel says, “He will reign over the house of Jacob forever” (Luke 1:33).

If you cannot establish this, then, whether you wish it or not, allow our priesthood to be of the same honor and dignity as theirs, because there is not one priesthood before the Law, another under the Law, and another under grace, but the very same one—first foretold in figures and riddles, and afterward exhibited in the truth itself—with the same classes of names and the same things signified.

For as long as the people are a flock, the bishop will be called and will be a shepherd; as long as the word of God is announced, the announcer will be called and will be an angel; as long as chrism is prepared, the preparer will be called Christ; as long as prophecy is recited, the reciter will be called a prophet—unless you perhaps wish to think false the saying in Proverbs: “When prophecy has failed, the people will be scattered” (Proverbs 29:18), and also: “Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward” (Matthew 10:41), taking these words as referring to the past rather than to the future or the present.

As long as these insignia endure, so long the same crimes as in ancient times will attach to those who despise, injure, and persecute them, and their punishment will be no different in any respect—except that insolence is punished more severely than ignorance, and contempt more severely than transgression. The Lord says: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin” (John 15:22); and, “The last state of that person becomes worse than the first” (Matthew 12:45).

Likewise: “Behold, you have become well; go, and do not sin any more, lest something worse happen to you” (John 5:14); and: “It will be more tolerable for the land of Sodom and Gomorrah on the day of judgment than for that city” (Matthew 10:15), which heard the word of God but scorned believing it; and: “Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida!”—and, concluding, “It will be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon on the day of judgment than for you” (Matthew 11:21–22).

And the Apostle says: “It would have been better for them not to know the way of truth than, after knowing it, to turn back” (2 Peter 2:21).

Through Moses also the Lord himself says: “The person who sins through ignorance before the Lord—the priest shall make expiation for him; because he sinned unknowingly, he shall obtain pardon for him, and it shall be forgiven him. But the person who commits anything presumptuously shall perish from his people, because he was rebellious against the Lord; therefore he shall be erased and shall bear his iniquity” (Numbers 15:28).

Countless testimonies also establish that those who sin knowingly are judged more severely than those who sin unknowingly. Hence also the saying in the Psalm: “Let them descend alive into hell” (Psalm 55:15). For the living are reckoned to be those who know what ought to be done; the dead are those who enjoy no use of knowledge.

16. Moses himself also demonstrates how much reverence is owed even to negligent priests. When Aaron had fashioned a calf for the children of Israel to worship, and twenty-three thousand of the people had been killed, Moses rebuked the very man who had been the author of the crime with only the mildest reprimand, saying: “What did this people do to you, that you should bring upon them so great a sin?” (Exodus 32:21.)

Consider, therefore, how presumptuous it is, for any fault whatsoever, for any layman even to rebuke any priest, if so great and so eminent a prophet, in such an unspeakable crime, after the others had been slaughtered, did not presume even to rebuke the leader of the crime harshly, thinking that this belonged by the dignity of the office to God alone.

For whoever persecutes a bishop does not persecute a bishop in him, but Christ himself—the supreme and spotless pontiff—insofar as the office of bishops is concerned. Nor is it the culpable bishop who is insulted, but the Holy Spirit himself, who dwells in him through the grace of blessing. When the person of a priest is touched, the very apple of the Lord’s eye is touched, because through him the Church is governed by divine providence.

Therefore, let every persecutor of such men fear, since to do this is also to sin against the Holy Spirit, lest perhaps no one be found who can forgive you that sin. For besides the principal sentence in which this is contained, it is said elsewhere: “If a man sins against a man, God may be appeased for him; but if he sins against God, who will pray for him?” (1 Samuel 2:25). In this passage you are rightly warned to understand not every sin, but a particular kind.

For David too is read, in the same history, to have seriously transgressed against a soldier who was utterly faithful to him, and yet to have obtained pardon (2 Samuel 11–12); whereas the sons of Eli, who slandered the Lord’s sacrifice, are reported to have been slain by the avenging sword (1 Samuel 2:34).

Consider here also, I ask, how severe God’s justice is when, after a pontiff has been taken away, this true sacrifice is taken away from him for a long period.

[Note: Here he indicates that he was removed from his see at Verona, shut up in prison, and for a long time prevented from celebrating the holy sacrifice of the Mass.] If God showed that he regarded this as so serious a blow, what must he have thought of that shadowy sacrifice?

[Note: He calls the sacrifice of the Old Testament “shadowy.” When the sons of Eli withdrew the people from it, they were punished so severely. He contrasts the Eucharistic sacrifice with that shadowy one and calls it “true,” because in it the very flesh of the Redeemer is offered. Ratherius was prevented by imprisonment from celebrating it.]

Unless perhaps you still do not know that there is a great difference between shadow and truth, between the flesh of an animal and the flesh of the Redeemer, and between the ashes of a heifer and the consecration of the Eucharist.

## TITLE IX

17. That the Holy Spirit is often present even with a sinful bishop is also demonstrated by the example of Caiaphas (John 11:49), who, as the Gospel testifies, was able to prophesy so truthfully about the Lord precisely because he appeared to be high priest that year. We can prove that this is not incredible by several similar examples, though they are far from equal.

For example, when the sun enters a sewer, it illuminates the sewer just as it does the most beautiful dining room. Whatever mud is inside the sewer contributes to the sunbeam neither darkness nor defilement, but contributes just as much increase or diminution of light as it would if a wall of the purest gold stood there. Moreover, if you throw something into the sewer, you cannot touch the mud before you strike the sun itself.

So it is with the honor and insult of any bishops, even those liable to certain faults. The light of grace itself, the blessing itself, the Holy Spirit himself, the sun of justice—Christ—dwelling in them is honored or insulted; and before the crime that anyone attempts to strike is reached, he who also illumines the criminal is himself struck.

For he who can do all things did not say without reason that salt, once it has lost its savor, is not even to be put on the dunghill (Luke 14:35). Among other things, he wanted you to recognize this also: a bishop is called by the name of salt because he ought to season the minds of the faithful with the flavor of heavenly speech, so that they may be capable of being God’s food; and if they have sinned, no one at all except the Almighty himself can or ought to correct them by any penance.

For who would dare to judge a judge, correct an angel, or—much less—bind him, except one who is above the angels?

In one and the same person there is often both healthy blood and poor health. When someone ignorant of medicine tries to restore good health, he commonly disturbs the healthy blood. Take the spirit of blessing as healthy blood, and negligence—or, as you prefer to say, the bishop’s criminal action—as poor health. Beware lest, although it is not your office, since you do not exercise the ministry of a physician, you appear, while attempting to attack the disease of the crime, instead to injure the Holy Spirit.

A well also supplies water that is perfectly clear both for drinking and for washing. Often something unsuitable lies near its opening, yet it neither prevents drinking nor pollutes washing. But when we insert a hook and try to remove it, the condition of the water is necessarily disturbed.

This third comparison can no less serve to admonish you, since in the speech of a certain author you have the priest appropriately represented by a well, and in the Gospel you have the Holy Spirit represented by the name of water (John 7:38).

## TITLE X

18. That they can be judged or rebuked by no one except God himself, the Apostle testifies when answering certain slanderers: “It is now required among stewards that one be found faithful” (1 Corinthians 4:2). And, taking our part while defending his own, he says: “The one who judges me is the Lord” (ibid., 4).

The Lord himself also says concerning the Pharisees: “Do what they say, but do not do what they do” (Matthew 23:3). He did not say, “Correct them,” as someone is known recently to have done—an action sufficiently absurd and therefore unworthy of being reported.

[Note: Recently, at the command of King Hugh, Ratherius had been captured and taken to the prison at Pavia.]

Yet, so that I may say something about it, however briefly, and excuse myself for neither concealing it through fear nor approving it through favor: would that God had cried out from heaven to him as he did to Saul; or at least that he himself had learned that God had already cried out, as is found in the truthful Scripture: “They have taken away my judgment from me” (Acts 9:4). Certainly he would not have raised his tribunal or throne against him so rashly.

But, to make a brief allusion to an act concerning which a general lament by all is more appropriate, I say that in this matter he furnished priests, or physicians of souls, with the greatest example—if only they wish to follow it—so that they may know with what severity they ought themselves to restrain those who must be bound, if those who bind study with such care to restrain them by binding.

With what diligence ought shepherds to recall wandering sheep from their errors, if the errant sheep with such vigilance seek to lead their shepherds away from transgressions by scourges—or, to speak more precisely, by bites—in an order not merely savage but inverted.

19. “But,” you may perhaps object, “I have heard from my predecessors that many of them were sent into exile.”

I immediately reply: Were they not also handed over to prison? Indeed, if you wish to regard as your predecessors those who are reported or read to have done this, you will also find that many were dismembered, blinded, flayed, handed over to the flames, hung on crosses, and beheaded by them.

But ask who those predecessors were, and see whether it benefits you to become their successor.

Certainly I have heard the Lord himself—the supreme pontiff himself, our companion, the head of all without exception insofar as the office of bishops is concerned—I have heard him, I say, speaking in the Gospel of God: “Behold, I send to you prophets and wise men and scribes; some of them you will kill and crucify, and some of them you will scourge in your synagogues and persecute from city to city, so that upon you may come all the righteous blood that has been shed upon the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah, son of Barachiah, whom you killed between the temple and the altar. Amen, I say to you, all these things will come upon this generation” (Matthew 23:34–36).

Likewise: “Fill up the measure of your fathers” (ibid., 32); and again: “Their fathers did the same things to the prophets” (Luke 6:26); and: “Gather the weeds first and bind them into bundles” (Matthew 13:30)—that is, associate like with like.

By these examples you have one generation; provide another: “The generation of the upright will be blessed” (Psalm 112:2). Provide a third, if you can.

“I cannot,” you say.

If, then, you cannot, determine in which of these two generations you will find those who are read to have done what you stated above. Measure your own conduct by theirs, your reward by theirs, and choose what you wish: either pay the penalties with that most wicked generation—not only for what you do, but also for what they did from Abel to the final “rememberer of the Lord” and “son of blessing.” For these two names signify this:

[Note: The two names are those of Zechariah and Barachiah, contained in the preceding testimony of Matthew: “to the blood of Zechariah, son of Barachiah.” For *Zacharias* is rendered in Latin as “memory of the Lord,” and *Barachias* as “blessing the Lord.” Therefore, using this interpretation, he says here: “to the final rememberer of the Lord and son of blessing.” He says “final” in order to signify all those who will exist until the end of the world.]

—or restrain your tongue, your power, and your hands from persecuting any ecclesiastics, even those of the lowest order, because they are called prophets, wise men, and scribes. Then you will be able to bless with the generation of the upright and reign without end with it.

For if you despise a criminal bishop, or even subject a priest to punishments, beware, I ask, lest you make light of the many whom the Gospel reading has just shown you to have been killed from the beginning and will be killed until the end of the age. If you do not fear to injure one, consider whether you can endure torments on behalf of all.

And truly, if I were attempting to establish this from my own words, you could say that I had invented it for my own sake. But now that you hear this statement from the Word of Truth, which threatens nothing rashly and makes no promise that can be gainsaid, what escape, I ask, do you find?

## TITLE XI

20. Consider also the continual prayer beneath God’s altar of those who were killed because of the Lord’s testament; and understand no less that the altar itself is the same one who is both pontiff and victim.

Fearfully observe, I ask, whose vengeance they seek: “How long, O holy and true Lord, will you refrain from judging and avenging our blood upon those who dwell on the earth?” (Revelation 6:10.)

O what a terrible thunderclap, showing that the one who does not awaken to this is not merely asleep but completely dead!

They do not speak of those who killed us, for they already know that such men are being tortured without end in hell. Even if they did speak of them, they would in no way lessen the divine sentence stated above. But they speak of “those who dwell on the earth,” who still persecute others—not indeed people like us, but nevertheless members of our body, members of our community, though still weak as we too once were—who persecute them, thrust them into prisons, torture them with hunger, torment them with cold, condemn them to exile, drive them from their own sees, and injure them with various forms of affliction.

This too the universal Church throughout the world cries out every day. It cries out here—where, seeing the image of its Head through a mirror and in a riddle (1 Corinthians 13:12), mixed with weeds and often suffering worse things from its own members than from strangers. It cries out also there—where, already exalted in a great part of certain members, it sees its Head, its very Creator, face to face—and it cries out all the more attentively because it can do so more freely:

“Let the groaning of the prisoners come before you; repay our neighbors sevenfold into their bosom” (Psalm 79:11).

Therefore, whoever hears these things, O neighbor—that is, one of the same house, family, faith, and redemption—fear, O Catholic and most Christian good king. And while you rejoice when you hear the Church say daily, “Lord, save the king,” I fear what follows: “And hear us on the day when we call upon you” (Psalm 20:10).

For, since the matter is sufficiently clear, what benefit do you think it brings you when prayer is offered for you, if the very people who pray are not permitted to live peacefully for your sake? The Apostle says and commands: “Pray for kings, for rulers, and for all who are in high positions” (1 Timothy 2:2). See what follows: “so that we may lead a quiet and tranquil life.”

Take care, therefore, lest, while what you have just heard is sung, God is invoked against you—while the prisoners cry out, cry out on their own behalf, and their companions cry out with one voice, just as they are united in charity.

### 21

“But, you say, those who pray evil prayers are not heard, since God commands that they pray for their persecutors (Matt. 5:44). Very well. What of the fact that prayer very often returns into the bosom of the one who prays? Therefore, lest you flatter yourself childishly, hear the Lord saying:

> ‘But will not God avenge his elect, who cry to him day and night, and will he be patient with them? I tell you, he will quickly avenge them’ (Luke 18:7).

And Job says:

> ‘The soul of the wounded cries out, and God does not permit it to go unavenged’ (Job 24:12).

Another says:

> ‘Do not leave behind you a curse; for the prayer of one who curses you in the affliction of his soul will be heard; and God, who made him, will hear him’ (Ecclus. 4:5).

And:

> ‘Whoever turns his ear away from the cry of the poor will himself cry out and not be heard’ (Prov. 21:13).

And:

> ‘I have indeed seen the affliction of my people, and I have heard their groaning’ (Exod. 3:7).

And:

> ‘The blood of Abel cries out to me from the earth’ (Gen. 4:10).

And:

> ‘The Lord has heard the desire of the poor; the righteous cried out, and the Lord heard them’ (Ps. 10:16).

And:

> ‘The Lord is near to those who are troubled in heart, and he will save the humble in spirit’ (Ps. 33:19).

But who knows whether they will be saved when you have been converted—that is, while those very people are interceding for you—or when you have been lost, since devout prayer returns not to you but into the bosom of those by whom it was uttered? In this matter, it is fitting that you fear no more the voice of the afflicted than those of the whole Church—that is, of all the faithful—who cry out, among whom you too cry out against yourself on behalf of the afflicted, saying:

[Note: The construction is: ‘In this matter it is fitting that you fear no more the voice of the afflicted than those of the whole Church, namely all the faithful, who cry out, among whom you too cry out against yourself on behalf of the afflicted, and say: “Help us, O God,” etc.’]

> ‘Help us, O God, our savior’ (Ps. 78:9);

and:

> ‘O God, attend to my help’ (Ps. 69:2);

and:

> ‘Lord, deliver my soul from lips of iniquity and from a deceitful tongue’ (Ps. 119:2);

and:

> ‘Let all who show evil to your servants be put to shame’ (Dan. 3:44);

and:

> ‘Deliver us, O God, by your wonders, and give glory to your name’ (ibid., 43:4).

For when those who have been delivered cry out these things and others like them—things too numerous to count—they undoubtedly cry out for those who are to be delivered; and this is no less established by experience than it is true.

Do you not hear this every day, and see that it is customary in the world for a king to speak on behalf of a king, even when they are bitter enemies, since each plainly looks after himself; for a bishop to speak on behalf of a bishop, a cleric for a cleric, a monk for a monk, a layman for a layman, a judge for a judge, a cupbearer for a cupbearer, and, to come down to things most humble though necessary, a baker for a baker and a cook for a cook?

If, then, we help one another because we share an order in which charity is greatly imperfect, what do you suppose those do for their companions who, striving not only to climb the citadel of that charity than which there is none greater (1 Cor. 13:13), but even, if it were possible, to rise above it, while they laid down their lives for their friends, even prayed for their enemies?

[Note: The construction is: ‘Those striving not only to climb, but even, if it were possible, to rise above, that citadel of charity than which there is none greater, while they laid down their lives for their friends, even prayed for their enemies.’]

Should we not suppose that those who feared to neglect their very enemies will not abandon us when we pay them their due honor—though much more negligently than is fitting—and invoke them daily for help and defense?

[Note: The construction is: ‘Should we not suppose that those who feared to neglect their very enemies will abandon us, who pay them their due honor, though much more negligently than is fitting, and invoke them daily for help and defense?’]

[Note: The construction is: ‘Should we not suppose that those who feared to neglect their very enemies will not abandon us when we pay them due honor, though much more negligently than is fitting, and invoke them daily for help and defense?’]

But perhaps you say: ‘They indeed wish to help us, but because our sins deserve it, they are unable to do so.’ What, I ask, is that blessedness which some ineffective desire torments? What happiness is that which any poverty of impossibility makes subject to itself? What could be more childish to think this? What could be found more perverse to say it?

While we speak these things to you without interruption, you perhaps turn the matter over inwardly: ‘What is to be done if one of them rises up against my rule?’

[Note: Here the question of King Hugh is proposed: namely, what should be done if someone rises against his rule. Ratherius complained that this had happened when Hugh received Arnold, duke of Bavaria, at Verona.]

I cannot imagine how that could happen. For how can one who holds the higher honor aspire to yours? And who, in your judgment, is considered greater: the one who appoints, or the one through whom someone is appointed?

When you read that the Lord commanded Samuel, saying, ‘Take the horn of oil and go, anoint him’ (1 Sam. 16:1), or ‘anoint him king’; and when you read that Nathan and Zadok anointed Solomon (1 Kings 1:45), inquire whether you have found anywhere that any king anointed anyone, although a king is said to have appointed some priest or prophet. Then you will see which of them, after God, holds the higher place.”

### Title XII

### 22

“All the sons of the Church, among whom you too are numbered—if indeed you do not disdain this, and if, like Absalom, who was to be punished by the tree as his avenger, you do not pursue your father with a sword (2 Sam. 18:9); if you do not gnaw your mother’s womb with a viper’s mouth—still, do it, do it: you are numbered among them. But beware lest you defraud yourself of their inheritance and co-inheritance.

All the sons of the Church, I say, are either of the Lord’s portion and are called clerics and monks; or they are servants of the Church, while bishops are fellow-servants; or they are laborers, slaves and free; or they are the kingdom’s soldiers.

[Note: ‘Laborers,’ some of whom were slaves and others free, means the common people; ‘soldiers of the kingdom’ means noblemen. Thus, in the following book, the common people are distinguished from the soldiers. They are called soldiers of the kingdom because almost all feudal tenants were obliged to serve militarily for the kingdom.]

The earth belongs to the Lord (Ps. 3:1), and it has been entrusted to your defense. Its revenues are either the Holy of Holies, belonging to the Lord and pertaining to the rights of priests, and they cannot be taken away by anyone except one who does not fear committing public sacrilege; or they are yours by imperial right—and I think, indeed I judge, that no one can take them away without prejudicing his own life; or they belong to the inhabitants of the district. Whoever attempts to invade that right is restrained by legal sanction.

But although priesthood, like kingship, is conferred by God alone—indeed, it is much more exalted than kingship, as thousands of testimonies prove—the matters that now strike the mind demand their place here.

It was said to Moses:

> ‘Behold, I have appointed you a god to Pharaoh’ (Exod. 7:1).

And certainly it was not an earthly king, nor any earthly power, but that very divine voice speaking from the bush which gives authority to his king and exalts the horn of his Christ (1 Sam. 2:10), and certainly of his own Christ. In the Psalm it says:

> ‘I said: You are gods’ (Ps. 81:6).

‘I,’ it says; ‘I, not any other human being. I said; I appointed—the one who also created you human beings. I said; I did not grant this to just anyone so that he might say it, be able to do it, or dare to do it. Human beings were created by me; you were called gods by me. This only God could do; only the Lord of all could grant it.’

And the same power, not another—the same force, the same authority, the same command, the same majesty—says:

> ‘I have appointed you as a watchman for the house of Israel’ (Ezek. 3:17);

and elsewhere:

> ‘You shall go wherever I send you’ (Ezek. 3:17);

and:

> ‘Behold, today I have appointed you over nations and over kingdoms, to uproot, destroy, ruin, and overthrow, to build and to plant’ (Jer. 1:10).

Beautifully, and in harmony with the New Testament, it says:

> ‘Whatever you bind on earth will have been bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven’ (Matt. 18:18).

One of them also says:

> ‘To some we are the odor of death unto death, but to others the odor of life unto life’ (2 Cor. 2:16).

Wisdom itself says:

> ‘By me kings reign, and lawgivers decree what is just’ (Prov. 8:15).

Whom does it understand as the ‘lawgivers’? Surely not those who produce laws, but those who unlock the Scriptures. They seem to make God’s laws when they strive to explain them; for to one who does not know them they are as though they did not exist, just as to the defiled nothing is clean (Titus 1:15).

But if this wording perhaps displeases you, another edition expresses it more clearly:

> ‘By me kings reign, and the powerful write justice.’

To this agrees Wisdom herself, now clothed in flesh:

> ‘Therefore every learned scribe in the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings forth from his treasury things new and old’ (Matt. 13:52).

And elsewhere, though still in the Gospel, she says to one person, and through him more particularly to all of the same order:

> ‘I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven’ (Matt. 16:19).

And—if one may say it—with an authority so much greater because mortality had now been conquered, death triumphed over, immortality put on, the ascension approaching, and the resurrection completed:

> ‘Feed my sheep’ (John 21:17).

‘My,’ he says; ‘my, my: mine by creation, mine by redemption, mine by right; not yours, not Tiberius’s, not Claudius’s, not Constantine’s, not Theodosius’s, not Maurice’s, not Charles’s.’

And to all alike he says:

> ‘Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive or retain are forgiven or retained’ (John 20:13);

and:

> ‘Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature’ (Mark 16:15).

Remembering this, he [namely, St. Peter], to whom the command was first given and in whom it was given to the entire succession of preachers, says:

> ‘The Lord commanded us to preach to the people’ (Acts 10:42).

And, established before rulers and magistrates, he says:

> ‘We must obey God rather than human beings’ (Acts 5:29).

His companion in suffering, Paul, says in his Epistle:

> ‘We act as ambassadors for Christ’ (2 Cor. 5:20);

and elsewhere:

> ‘How will they preach unless they are sent?’ (Rom. 10:15).

And by whom are they sent, I ask, except by him who said:

> ‘I sent you to reap what you did not sow’?” (John 4:38).

### 23

“You have, briefly but sufficiently, the rights of the priesthood, conferred by God himself through the Holy Spirit. Let no one, therefore, continue to call human what is especially the gift of God. Let anyone cease, overcome by this authority, even if unknowingly blaspheming God, to say to God: ‘I made this one and that one’ (Isa. 14:13), lest, while wishing in some respect to make himself equal to God, he be cast down with him who wished to raise his throne against God in heaven.

For we hold with complete certainty that no created substance is creative, so that if anyone thinks otherwise, he could undoubtedly find nothing more insane. But if a bishop has been made specifically by a human being, although the whole world was created generally by God, this is ridiculous.

If images still seem not to be worshiped but nevertheless revered—for it is said in the Psalm, ‘The images of the nations are the work of human hands’ (Ps. 113:4)—then this is far more perverse still: ‘God,’ he says, ‘gave him bones and flesh; everything else I supplied.’

Here God is placed immeasurably beneath a human being. I believe that no rational person is unaware how greatly the marks of grace by which a human being is called an angel, indeed a god, differ from the condition in which he is called dust and ashes.

Consider, then, how greatly that one is preferred—if indeed the two expressions are understood in this sense, or rather in this madness—who could make an angel from dust and a god from ashes, to the one who was able to create only dust and ashes.

[Note: If dust and ashes are indeed two different things. The passage should be construed as follows: ‘Consider how greatly that one—that is, the king—who could make an angel, that is, a bishop, from dust, namely a human being, and could make a god from ashes, as this man says he has done, is preferred to him—that is, to God himself—who was able to create only so much dust and ashes, which he seems to concede to God alone.’ The king attributes to himself the power to make bishops, and seems to concede to God alone the ability to create dust and ashes, or human beings. To hear this is intolerably obscene.]

This is intolerably obscene to hear and utterly detestable, although never, except in our own age—alas for the crime!—has it been said or heard. Nevertheless, I think that the prophet’s words may be directed at such a person:

> ‘O shepherd and idol who abandons the flock!’ (Zech. 11:17.)

He calls him ‘shepherd’ in the customary manner appropriate to his office, but ‘idol’ because he thinks this gift [that is, the episcopate] was bestowed on him by a human being. And for this reason he abandons the flock in its necessity: he does not know from whom, or by whom, he will receive his reward for its defense, being overcome by the judgment of his conscience.

Indeed, he may be thought to believe on this basis that something can be done without God. Alas, what intolerable misery of the soul: to be utterly without knowledge of its own Creator!”

### 24

“Meanwhile, to return to what I began: even in the episcopate there are gnawers who, following the example of those who, in the second year after the preceding one, devised Thyestean banquets against a certain bishop, are now composing certain slanders against this man as well.

[Note: Ratherius appears to have written this about the second year after his captivity, that is, in 936. Thus ‘the second year after the preceding one’ indicates 935, to which the following accords. It points to the conspiracy of many Veronese against Hugh, king of Italy, in which many churchmen were also implicated. When this conspiracy failed early in 935, after some had been killed and others had escaped, they imputed the entire blame to Ratherius, who had been thrown into the prison at Pavia; and now too, while he was writing this, in 936, they were speaking against him.]

[Note: The story of the Thyestean banquet is well known: Atreus, Thyestes’ brother, killed Thyestes’ sons and served them to him as food. This allegory seems to allude to some of Ratherius’s spiritual sons, that is, ecclesiastics, who were killed in the conspiracy mentioned above. In the second book of the *Confession*, no. 2, he laments the murders, blinding, and mutilations perpetrated on that occasion.]

And this is done not by outsiders, but by intimates, who ought to have been witnesses to the goodness of his purpose.

[Note: Here *privati* means intimate and familiar persons; examples of this sense can be found in Du Cange. These good witnesses of Ratherius’s purpose ought to have been his intimates and familiars. They knew that his advice in agreeing to a letter written by Urso—the source of the entire calamity—had been well intentioned. But after he was captured and taken to prison, they became his adversaries and spread many things against him.]

They do this, I say, not as enemies but as deceitful friends: men once united with him, formerly dear and familiar, who once ate sweet food with him in the house of God (Ps. 54:15), walking together as though in agreement and raising him to the heavens.

[Note: These were undoubtedly ecclesiastics who, at the beginning of Ratherius’s episcopate, were raising him to the heavens.]

They declared him blessed, just, and holy with praises no less deceitful than flattering. May God spare them, turning away from them lest death come upon them and they descend alive into hell (Ps. 54:16)—that is, lest, knowingly committing deeds worthy of hell, they fail to guard against a sudden death.

This is done by the remnants of the traitors,

[Note: He calls those ‘traitors’ who were once his friends and later became hostile to him. One of these is the man to whom, at the beginning of his exile and captivity, Ratherius wrote the following letter.]

without any heavenly repayment of vengeance having yet been exacted for this, so far as some people seem to think. To one of them he wrote the following from exile.”

### 25

“Alas for me, my son!

[Note: The printed editions incorrectly read *filium quid*. Here *fili mi* is correct. This man appears to be one of those who once ate sweet food with Ratherius in the house of God, as he had just said. He was evidently a member of the Veronese clergy, whose archdeacon, as we shall shortly see, was his father-in-law. His name was Ursus or Urso; for at the end of the letter Ratherius asks that his accomplices not thereafter be called Ursini or Ursani after his name. Ursus, or Urso, deacon of the Church of Verona, is mentioned in three documents. One, from the year 947, and another, from 959, were published by Canon de Dionysiis in his collection of diplomas and documents, pp. 113, 115, and 126. The third, from 968, was printed by Giovanni Battista Biancolini in Dissertation 2, entitled in Italian *Dei vescovi e governatori di Verona*, p. 121. It cannot be affirmed whether this Ursus was alive in 935, or whether he is the same person to whom Ratherius gave this letter. The entire letter is intended to restrain Urso, who was speaking against the bishop imprisoned in jail.]

What shall I do? Whom shall I mourn first: myself, dead, or you, insulting one who is dead? As though the same condition of dying did not also await you—or rather, which is much more miserable, as though you were not drawing the stench of the dead through your nostrils, breathing it in through your mouth, and sending it, far worse, into your lungs, and, what is more serious, offering this drink to others so that they too may die with you.

[Note: That is: ‘and sending the stench into your lungs, where you will die far more grievously, and, what is more serious, offering this same stench to others so that they may die with you.’ He says that Ursus will die far more grievously because, by insulting the dead man and speaking against him, he was committing a more serious sin.]

Do you not know, my son, that a certain castle near you, beside the sea, is called Commacchio [Italian *Comacchio*], where, as they say, the dead kill the living?

As for how much, beyond countless things known not only to you but also to me and to everyone except God alone, and no less worthy of mourning, I judge that I ought rightly to mourn in the very things you report—and would that they were false!—I would tell you lovingly, my son, as I have often done, in conversation, if I had an opportunity to speak with you.

[Note: The sense is: ‘How much, beyond countless things known not only to you but also to me and to everyone except God alone, and no less worthy of mourning—how much, I say, I judge that I ought rightly to mourn even in those things reported by you, and would that they were false!—I would tell you lovingly, my son, as I have often done, in conversation, if I had an opportunity to speak with you.’]

But since every opportunity is entirely lacking, I shall say something briefly for the present.

First, I mourn myself, because I have been found to be such a person that you could call me such.

Second, because by my example I have instructed you for this very purpose, just as you now instruct others; for, in your presence, I too often disparaged many people—alas, forgetting my own grief—and even people better than myself.

Third, the genuine terror of the listeners, who are endangered by your stench as well as by mine.

[Note: The passage is interrupted or corrupt, but its meaning is nevertheless sufficiently clear. He gives as the third cause of his mourning the terror of the listeners—those who, having heard both his own and Urso’s slanders, were in danger of their souls. The word ‘stench’ refers to the parable of Lazarus, who had been dead four days and stank, as will become clear from what follows. Here he designates himself and Urso, because of their habitual vice of slander, by the name of stench, presenting them as though they were the stinking Lazarus. For this reason he feared that those who heard such slanders would also suffer danger to their souls. Elsewhere he calls any vice by which others may be infected ‘stench’; see Sermon 2 on Lent, no. 24, where he says that the third class of sinners consists of those who are said to stink—that is, those who infect their neighbors with despair of recovery.]

But stop, my son, in this respect imitating me no less than accusing me. If I have been greatly harmful to you, as you assert, I have been especially so to you.

You have sound advice here to follow, since divine mercy, foreseeing that such ill-smelling tombs of corpses would not be lacking—that is, the tombs of people who indulge in slander—gave thought to the living, lest they be killed by their stench through following their example, and said:

> ‘Do what they say, but do not do what they do’ (Matt. 23:3).

For even if I am the cause of your death, because I was the material or occasion of it, nevertheless know that, whatever the manner or whatever crime by which you die, you will be counted among the dead as one who is dead. For thus God says:

> ‘He himself will die in his iniquity, but I will require his blood at your hand’ (Ezek. 3:20).

And truly, what did it profit Eve to have said:

> ‘The serpent deceived me’?” (Gen. 3:13.)

And while I write these things to you, concerned for you, in order to restrain you, I am striving most earnestly both to free you from death and to prevent myself from being held guilty of your blood.

This can happen; for I do not despair that it can happen through him for whom the ability to do something is the same as the willingness to do it. Nor should you despair on this account, since you have read that he raised a man who had been dead four days.

Nor do I remember having taught you otherwise in the work on parricide that you wrote with your own hands.

[Note: The sermon on parricide that Urso wrote with his own hands is the fatal letter from Ratherius, which will be discussed later. ‘Parricide’ is introduced here because the word does not signify merely death, but every grave evil inflicted on a father or fatherland. That letter was the cause of the evils that befell Ratherius, Urso’s spiritual father. That the subject here is parricide committed against Ratherius is confirmed by the fact that shortly afterward Ratherius asks Urso to cultivate toward him a brother-in-law’s affection rather than a parricidal one.]

Thus I now cry out to life with a groan of divine compassion, although you still say that I stink—as he knows better than you, since he calls me a man four days dead. For there are also pious sisters weeping over me; among them I ask that you too may be numbered. That is, may there be in you a brother-in-law’s affection, not a parricidal one. If you can confess that I stink, I do not truly take offense; indeed, I ask for this in every way, provided that I may deserve to hear that Lord’s honey-sweet voice promising me resurrection and you a miracle.

I ask only that you consider the danger of those who hear, and do not disregard your own. For, as I believe, it was spoken by divine authority, and even if you do not remember it, you do not fail to know it:

> ‘Whoever curses father or mother shall be put to death’” (Lev. 20:9).

### 26

“When, on rereading this here, you have brought it back to mind, after you have considered the twofold death lying beneath it separately and recognized that each division has its own substance—one merely mortal in a mortal manner, the other immortally mortal and mortally immortal—then, I ask, do not forget with what grievous stains you besmirch the mother herself.

Lest you perhaps take ‘mother’ superficially, I repeat that she is the Church, if indeed you are a son. If not, then a father or some blood relation is speaking about you:

> ‘They went out from us, but they were not of us.’

Be a son, then—understand ‘son’ here—be one, I beg; be one, I ask. Nevertheless, as I said, I insist that you not forget how grievously you stain your mother while you burn your father with so foul a mark of crime.

[Note: He calls himself ‘father’ because Urso had represented him as the author of a certain letter and undertaking.]

For marital love is as indissoluble as it is compassionate, since the same relationship also shares the same honor. You would certainly never dare to do all this, my son, if you wished to recall the command:

> ‘Honor your father and your mother’ (Exod. 20:12);

or if you valued regeneration more highly than generation,

[Note: By ‘regeneration’ he indicates that he was Ursus’s spiritual father, since he regarded him, as a Veronese and still more as one of the clergy, as among his spiritual sons.]

and remembered the prohibition:

> ‘Do not touch my anointed ones’ (Ps. 104:15);

and:

> ‘Whoever touches you touches the apple of my eye’ (Zech. 2:8);

and:

> ‘Whoever despises you despises me’ (Luke 10:16);

and:

> ‘You shall not revile the gods’ (Exod. 22:28);

and:

> ‘Whoever slanders the king slanders the law’ (James 4:11).

To persuade you to believe that the priesthood of the Church is royal, Peter’s testimony alone, among countless others, should have been sufficient:

> ‘But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood’ (1 Pet. 2:9).

You should also have kept before your eyes the judgment of someone in the decrees of a most holy pope:

> ‘I judge that no crime is worse than for Christians to slander their own priests.’

You should have remembered the sacrilege of Ham’s curse (Gen. 9:25), and feared, following his example, to expose the more shameful parts of your father. Nor should you have set aside the canons and councils of the holy Fathers, in which you could have observed many condemned for this reason, if you had read them.

You should also have feared being handed over to the curia and serving it, infamous—or perhaps ‘an infamous person,’ according to the uncertain reading—without any hope of restoration, for all the days of your life.

You should also have remembered the vengeance inflicted on behalf of the most blessed Narcissus (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book 6, chapter 9).

[Note: The archdeacon of the Church of Verona was a principal participant in the conspiracy against King Hugh. Although he was initially rescued from the death to which the barbarous people destined him after recovering Verona, he was later struck, as this passage shows, either by death or by some grave misfortune, while Ratherius was writing. Whatever it was, Urso attributed it to chance, because although Urso himself was privy to the same rebellion and had likewise spoken against Ratherius, he had so far suffered no harm.]

You should not have thought that our archdeacon was struck by chance merely because you still suffer nothing. For the longer the unconverted person is spared, the more harshly he is struck. May almighty God turn this away from you and from your accomplices.”

### 27

“And perhaps your observers, though they were my enemies, wished to be obedient and accommodating to you, and so deceived you.

Just as those men once attempted to deceive the assembly of the saints when, in the council against Athanasius, they presented the severed arm of someone as though it were Arsenius’s,

[Note: The printed editions incorrectly read *facere* and later *fecisti*. The context requires *fallere* (‘to deceive’) and *fefellisti* (‘you deceived’).]

so you too—may God forgive you—deceived someone out of hatred for me. That man produced a letter full of insults, once addressed to him by that master of yours already mentioned, and, trying to discover the author of the deed, found you openly confessing that you were the writer. You, leaving aside the others, who were not so closely connected with you as I was, presented me as the author and as the instigator of the entire undertaking.

[Note: The master already mentioned appears to be the archdeacon mentioned shortly before, for whose safety this letter, as will presently be said, was chiefly intended. The construction is: ‘He who produced the letter full of insults, formerly sent to him by that master of yours already mentioned, and strove to discover the author of the deed, when he found you openly confessing yourself the writer, you—leaving aside the others, who were not as suitable for you as I was—presented me as the author and instigator of the entire undertaking, namely the writing of that letter, which seems to have touched upon the rebellion.’]

[Note: This is the letter written by Urso’s hand, which freed others from danger but brought ruin upon Ratherius. We have explained this entire complicated history, which Ratherius chose not to set out more distinctly, as fully as circumstances permitted in the author’s *Life*, section 4.]

And certainly, when you chose to tell this as you pleased,

[The reading may be *dixisti*, ‘you said.’]

you could, if you had wished, have told the truth without sufficiently accusing me and while excusing yourself. You would have done so if you had shown me as much love as I showed concern for you and for my entire flock, and especially for that father-in-law of yours already mentioned,

[Note: The archdeacon was exposed to the greatest danger to his life, since he would immediately have suffered capital punishment unless, after the letter had been praised, he was released as though unaware of the crime. Ratherius therefore chiefly looked after him when he agreed to the letter. Hence this same archdeacon, already mentioned, seems to be understood as Urso’s father-in-law. *Praetaxatus* may be understood as ‘aforementioned’; several examples in Du Cange confirm this.]

when I agreed to that letter—God knows with what intention.
