For, as you know very well, when the other side arrived, and that fierce and barbarous people, foreign to us [perhaps ‘to you’], having examined the matter and being rightly suspicious of its own life, since in many similar affairs among you it had often come to grief, had turned all the blame, as it stood, upon that same archdeacon and upon certain more honored men of our side—especially upon the entire clergy—while sparing me, though carrying me away because of the kinship I had with their leaders, and, as they claimed, with Prince Hugh himself,

[Note: Perhaps this belief occurred to that barbarous people because they knew that Ratherius had been a familiar associate of Hilduin, had come to Verona with him, and had later succeeded him in the see of Verona. From his association with Hilduin they believed Ratherius to be related to him, and therefore connected with Prince Hugh, to whom Hilduin was related.]

they intended to plunder the entire house of God, to mutilate or imprison all the leading citizens, and to hang from the gallows the man already mentioned [that is, the archdeacon] and those who, after me, had been leaders in the betrayal involving him.

[Note: These are evidently the men who later turned the fabricated letter to my ruin.]

God knows what a night I passed. You too, who admit that you know nothing good about me, know very well—as I said—by what prayers, humiliations, tears, gifts, promises, and interventions of friends I obtained life and liberty for you.

Yet, keeping all these things silent, you preferred to produce the one thing that would kill me.

[Note: Namely, the letter that Urso wrote and produced, which furnished the cause of Ratherius’s exile and imprisonment.]

At daybreak it was decreed—not by me alone, as you said, but by everyone, both our own people and foreigners; although I do not fully recognize anyone other than the devil as the author of this counsel—that a letter such as the one that was produced should be made. If the archdeacon dared to send it, he would be released as though unaware of the crime; otherwise, he would immediately suffer capital punishment.

What I have said was done both against me and against the others.

[Note: This letter was used against both Ratherius and the others, but with different outcomes. The others were rescued from danger, whereas Ratherius, by order of King Hugh, was thrown into prison at Pavia. Thus, as is stated immediately afterward, by agreeing to the letter and looking after others, he neglected himself; by sparing others, although partly aware of their plotting, he betrayed himself.]

But thanks be to God: while I looked after you, I seem to have neglected myself; while I spared you, although partly aware of your plotting,

[Note: He says ‘aware’ because he had foreseen in part that the advice concerning the writing of the letter—which he accepted for the benefit of others—would harm him. He says ‘in part’ because, although he anticipated that it would bring him some danger, he did not suppose that the danger would be as great as that which he actually suffered.]

I betrayed myself.”

28. “It is read, son, in the *Tripartite History* (Book VIII, chapter 1) that a certain man, occupied in pasturing livestock, killed someone and, driven by fear, fled into the wilderness; there, becoming accustomed to the good through the examples of the holy Fathers, he became a perfect hermit. He always blessed the crime that had been the cause of such great progress for him. I have related this so that from it you may gather how much you have served my progress, when you accused me so severely that I might utterly perish. For if you were present and permitted it, I would soothe with exceedingly sweet kisses the hands that wrote that letter, because this was, as I think, the cause, material, and whole sum of my salvation; through it, I believe, I was snatched from eternal death and restored to life. Through it, I believe, it came about that I could now largely guard against both those by whose stench [Note: Here, too, “stench” is understood as the fault of slander against the bishop, whom Urso was sparing. Compare note 154.] you are still endangered and the almost entire Church entrusted to me, which you corrupt with the deadly decay of pestilence—although it may also be that everything is not as you say, and that it can now be believed that I have largely guarded against the many others, innumerable and far removed from your knowledge; though from this I have begun to acquire no security, since that would not be appropriate, inasmuch as I lack certainty.

“Yet I consider myself to have advanced on this occasion so greatly that I see no one whom I ought to embrace more than you, who have been the material of so many benefits for me. O how fortunate I am—even in this very misfortune of mine, if I may say so—and even if the sole benefit I had received from it were that I came to know you and those like you! Therefore, sparing you in everything, and not only sparing you but returning the fullest thanks to you for these things, I admonish you, son: since you have now benefited me beyond words, take care lest, through hatred of me, you become wholly harmful to yourself.

“But, to use a kind of abbreviation, since the messenger is hurrying and the little sheet is quite exhausted, I beg that the just mercy of the Almighty spare you as you repent; rather, I ask that He kindly grant that you repent. For, as far as your injury is concerned, He Himself knows that I suffer this from you without cause—if one can properly be said to suffer progress in this manner of speaking—inasmuch as through you also your fellow conspirators may be corrected, and may deserve to be called not Ursinians or Ursanians, after your derivative name, but Christians or lambs, after Him who said, ‘Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart’ (Matt. 11:29); and after one of His own, ‘Obey your leaders and submit to them’ (Heb. 13:17): that is, may they deserve to be called the meek rather than the savage, lovers rather than mockers of shepherds.

“If this comes to me through my prayer, I can scarcely conceal, much less suppress, the joy itself; if it does not, I attribute it to my sins. At least, however, I ask that divine mercy grant this: while you pronounce my sins against me—or rather against yourself—may it forgive them; while you record them, may it erase them; and may it make you recognize in this present age that, although you have striven irreparably to harm me, you have harmed yourself beyond estimation [or: have contended with yourself], and have benefited me beyond words. May you be well in the Lord, I pray, corrected, amen.”

29. In the midst of these things, if I may dare to say so, images stand fixed everywhere [Note: By the name “images” he seems to designate those bishops who, in this calamity of theirs, spoke nothing on their own behalf, like mute images.], giving no sound even for their own sake, as though by that very silence they seemed to cry out that they were altogether devoid of reason. But I ask that they be angry not with me, but rather with themselves. I neither know nor say that they are this; yet I greatly fear that they may rightly be called so, while I hear them patiently endure being said to have been made bishops by a human being—or even return abundant thanks to the one who says it [Note: He attacks those bishops who said that they had been made bishops by a man and who thanked those who said so. Elsewhere he repeatedly insists that bishops, although elected or appointed by human beings, are instituted by God through the sacred ordination itself, not by human beings. See the beginning of the following book, section 2. Soon below, *audio* is corruptly printed as *audeo* in the common editions.]. For they will neither be, if I say it, nor not be, if I remain silent; but they will be [understand: “they will be so”] if they say or wholly consent to it.

“And how much more beautiful it is to be called ‘perfect’ than ‘made!’ Every person will be perfect if he is like his teacher (Luke 6:40). Woe, however, to the one who does not have as teacher Him who says this, the Lord, whom we cannot become like by comparison, but whom we ought to imitate—not in every respect, but in those things commanded us by Him. Although He paid tribute to the world, rendering to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s and to God the things that are God’s (Matt. 22:21), nevertheless, by that very humility of His He trampled upon the world itself and showed that it had been subjected to Him and must also be subjected to you, after He had said, ‘All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me’ (Matt. 28:18). Whom would you rather fear as lord or as servant, as the one subjecting or the one subjected, as the giver [or: the one giving] or the possessor? Through one of His disciples, He gave this reminder concerning Himself as a master and, insofar as you are concerned, concerning masters: ‘It is necessary to obey God rather than human beings’ (Acts 5:29) [Note: Construe it as follows: Through one of His disciples, insofar as it concerns Him, and through one of the masters, insofar as it concerns you—namely, through one who, insofar as it concerns Him, is a disciple, but insofar as it concerns you, is a master—He gives this reminder: whom you should rather fear, the Lord or the servant; the one subjecting or the one subjected; the one giving or the possessor. He says, ‘It is necessary to obey,’ and so forth.].

“And certainly He was not crying this to you in a lecture hall, at a reading stand, or on a pulpit, but before the rulers of the world, amid threats, amid scourges, amid the very men who were beating you; yet you do not dare either to say or, much less, to do this, when the emperors themselves are already subject to you.”

30. “But, to return now to what I began: the priest and the Levite pass by, plainly not understanding that they are descending by the same road, and they offer no remedy to their wounded brother. And, if God avert it, this seems especially suited to our times, because ‘when iniquity has abounded, the charity of many will grow cold’ (Matt. 24:12). No one is found who, at least out of regard, fear, or love of God, dares—or rather, wishes—to refresh the hungry, give drink to the thirsty, clothe the naked, visit the sick or imprisoned, console the grieving, or support the distressed [or: the one distressed], especially since no one is forbidden to do so. Indeed, it is not even read that such a thing was forbidden to anyone by that generation of the ancients, as the letters of Paul written in prison clearly show; in them he seems also to remember those who ministered to him, and he does not fear that they will be discovered [Note: If *deprehensae* is to be retained, the word refers to the letters, so that the sense is: he does not fear that the letters will be discovered and that those who ministered to him will be exposed. Alternatively, *deprehensi* should be read, so that the noun refers to those who ministered. Soon below, *terrorem* may perhaps need to be read as *terrae regem*, “the king of the earth.”], since he knew that both he and they feared God more than terror.”

31. “Having first stated [Note: Either understand *hoc*—namely, ‘having stated this’—or read *Praemitto* or *Praemittens*.] that I share with blessed Augustine the belief of the catholic faith, although he was far unlike me in the liveliness of his acuity for investigation, the capacity of his understanding for retention, the power of his eloquence for expression, and the quality of his life for meriting this with God’s grace; and renouncing with my mouth or rejecting in my heart every heresy against God—even if I perhaps cannot detect it—I confess that I believe in the equality, coessentiality, or, to put it that way, consubstantiality of the Trinity eternally, and in the Trinity of unity: that is, in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, creator and governor of all things that exist either in heaven or on earth—and, if it is necessary to add, in the sea and in all the abysses. The substance of the Godhead remains one and the same, while the properties of the persons are distinct: the Father is the one who created all things, the Son the one through whom all things were created, and the Holy Spirit the one by whom all things were created. I declare the Father to be the authority of the Son, the Son the wisdom of the Father [Note: We have supplied the word *wisdom*, which was absent from the common editions, from a similar profession of faith that the author appended to the little book *Phrenesis*.], and the Holy Spirit the communion of the Father and the Son.

“Believing that in these three there is one and the same equality of Godhead, understanding that there is in them nothing earlier or later, nothing greater or less, I believe that the Father is from Himself, not from another; the Son from the Father alone; and the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son. I believe that the Father eternally and ineffably begot the Son; that the Son was eternally and ineffably begotten from the Father alone, not made—like light from light, the word in the heart, or, to speak more explicitly, something expressible. I believe that the Holy Spirit, that is, the consubstantial love of both, was never absent from them, and that He proceeds from the one to the other and from the other to the one, without local movement, without change, eternally, and therefore ineffably; that He is sent by the Father and the Son to inspire the minds of the elect, while He comes temporally from Himself. I believe that the Son alone was born eternally from the Father without a mother, and temporally from a mother without a father.

“When I hear that He was conceived by the Holy Spirit, I do not understand the Holy Spirit to be another father; rather, I believe that the Word, remaining eternally in the heart of the Father, when He willed, by His own and His Father’s will, went forth from the Father and came into the world in such a way that He did not leave either the Father or heaven. Through the body that the entire Trinity together formed in the womb of the Virgin Mother from the substance of that same ever-virgin mother, He was made visible to human beings.

“And when I hear, ‘The Word became flesh’ (John 1:14), I do not understand God to have been changed into a human being. Rather, while the substance of the unchangeable Godhead remained, I confess that the Word united a human being to Himself, so that, just as from body and rational soul there is one human being, so from human being and God there is one Jesus Christ—not composite, but ineffably existing and born.

“When I hear that He suffered, died, was buried, rose on the third day, and ascended into heaven, I attribute neither division to Christ nor passibility to God. Rather, just as a human being—who is certainly flesh and soul—is said to have been killed by someone, although the rational soul does not undergo death, so I confess that God, in the human being whom He assumed, endured all these things without suffering in His Godhead.

“And when I say, ‘I believe in the Holy Spirit,’ and immediately add, ‘the holy Church,’ I do not conceive a quaternity there; I confess only that I believe in the holy catholic Church. Through one baptism, namely the catholic baptism, and through the grace and faith of God that works through love (Gal. 5:6), I trust that we shall also receive the communion of the saints and the remission of sins, if we so will.

“As I know and confess that the resurrection of the flesh was real and not imaginary in the Lord Jesus Christ, so I confess that it will also occur for all, both elect and reprobate: for the elect, so that they may go with body and soul into eternal life; for the reprobate, so that they may likewise go with soul and body into eternal punishment; but the former without fear, through the justice of rejection, and the latter without hope of any merciful restoration.”

32. “Forgive me, reader, I beg you, forgive me, for what I have said about the ineffability of so great an incomprehensibility—perhaps too boldly because I have considered it too simply, without examining it fully. For I am blind in those eyes by which such things ought to be contemplated—that is, the blessed eyes of the pure in heart; miserable because I cannot see them, I have nevertheless touched upon them by feeling my way. Just as a blind person wishing to report things not seen can do so only by applying some likeness drawn from what he has seen, so I, lacking things proper [Note: The common editions wrongly read *propriisque*. Here *propriis* indicates those things that belong properly to God or are appropriate to God.] to God—which, in the filth of this mortal condition, do not present themselves to us—conducing certain matters easy for my understanding, though not wholly foreign to the authority of holy Scripture, questioned my mind by reasoning about what it thought concerning God and His creation. I was eager to discover whether I might—otherwise blameworthy in the judgment of many and condemnable in my own judgment—be found culpable even in the affirmation of the catholic faith, and therefore rightly expelled from the episcopate entrusted to me, that is, from the Church of Verona, if the authority of a universal council should so decide.

“Moved by the ineffability of the matter and the novelty of the proof [Note: The subject understood is the mind, which he had said he questioned about what it thought concerning God and His creation. This mind, therefore, moved by the ineffability of the matter and the novelty of the proof, nevertheless did not delay answering, with God giving—or perhaps assisting—the power to do so. For *valere* understood as ‘to assist’ is supported by other examples in Cange. It may, however, be better to read *volente*, ‘with God willing,’ as in a similar profession of faith appended to the little book *Phrenesis*.], my mind nevertheless did not delay answering, with God enabling it through His wisdom, by which all things were created.

“When I had compared that answer with the faith that we call Athanasius’s and also with that of the Council of Nicaea, despite the dryness of my little intellect, begrimed with the dust of faults, and had been able to perceive that it disagreed in nothing from them [Note: The common editions wrongly read *dissentirem*, ‘I disagreed.’ ‘From them’ means from the Nicene faith and from the faith called that of St. Athanasius.], I dared, not with the obstinacy of one defending himself, but with the confidence of one who believes that he had found what he sought, to believe in my heart for justification and confess with my mouth for salvation (Rom. 10:10) the creative and governing unity of the Trinity and the Trinity of unity. Therefore I rejoice if I am not in error; but if I am, I earnestly desire in every respect to be corrected with charity.”

## HERE BEGINS BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0249]

### 1

A weary traveler often postpones to another day a journey that could even be completed in a single day, lest, by arriving too late, he deprive the exhausted man of the opportunity to rest. An industrious sailor, too, whenever a contrary wind prevents him from reaching his intended destination, is accustomed to seek the shore adjoining some island, so that, having obtained small boats, he may use them as aids, like Paul once did, lest the ship fall into a sandbank (Acts 27:17).

This example, which is not inappropriate, compelled us also to transfer a discourse intended for one day to another, lest its length bring weariness to the reader, and lest the very importunity of our loquacity, as often happens, expose us to some danger because of things we might say contrary to certain persons [Note: Construe it as follows: “lest the very importunity of our loquacity bring some danger upon us for saying things contrary to certain distinguished men whom he has attacked and will also attack in the following book.”]. For at the third hour of the day, filled with the Holy Spirit and thoroughly drenched with new wine (Acts 2:13), they themselves were called theologians [that is, the apostles]; how much less should we be judged to have spoken anything soberly at sunset.

### 2

“After we had satisfied the matter that it had itself offered for treatment—namely, the matter of the images, or of the shepherd and the idol [Note: In the preceding book, section 29, he had attacked the fixed images, that is, the bishops who did nothing to support themselves; and in section 23 he had charged the same men under the names of shepherd and idol. He indicates that he had strayed beyond the proper path, or beyond the purpose of this book, which is to deal with the king.], we have, as it seems, wandered somewhat idly from the path, since we have related some things that were not altogether relevant and fear that we may perhaps have injured someone. Now let us hasten, as we began, to investigate what a bishop ought or can contrive or think against you. But because we have poured ourselves out somewhat too verbosely, let us put back into order the matters just as they were completed.

“I said, unless I am mistaken, that bishops are instituted by God alone, like kings—and much more pre-eminently than kings, since kings are instituted by bishops, whereas bishops, although they can be elected or appointed by kings, cannot be ordained by them [Note: Construe: “bishops instituted by God alone, like kings,” and so forth.]. I do not regret having said this, since He Himself also bears witness, the only one who can bear witness for Himself: for He Himself says, ‘I sent you to reap’ (John 4:38). There are many testimonies to this—many, I say, and infinite.

“Woe to those who usurp [understand: the episcopate] without being commanded; who are permitted but not sent. Woe to those of whom it is said: ‘They have reigned as kings, but not from me; princes have arisen, and I did not know them’ (Hos. 8:4). Woe to those who climb up by another way and do not enter through the door (John 10:1) [Note: The following sentence is a prayer. He asks that God, the Good Shepherd, who alone and all-powerfully can turn woe into ‘well done,’ free those who have usurped the episcopate by climbing up another way and not entering through the door—those who were neither commanded nor sent, that is, without divine calling and mission—from the source of that woe. He asks that He not punish them strictly in the next life, but kindly permit them to be changed or converted here, that is, in this life. The common editions corruptly read *vel in euge*.]. May the Good Shepherd, who alone can do all things, free them from that woe and turn it into ‘well done,’ not punishing strictly there those whom here He kindly permits to be changed.

“I said that the sons of the Church are either clerics and monks, or servants, or laborers—slaves and free persons—or soldiers of the kingdom [Note: Through an inept repetition, the common editions read *aut liberos*, ‘or free persons.’ We have corrected it from the preceding book, section 22, whose summary is given here: ‘or soldiers of the kingdom,’ that is, nobles. Compare note 144 there]. The land of the Lord has been entrusted to your royal protection; its revenues, however, are either [understand: ‘are’] the Holy of Holies of the Lord and belong by right to the priests, or are your property, or belong to the inhabitants of the district.”

### 3

“I mentioned these things earlier and have now repeated them so that, if I can, I may determine what disagreement or division can exist between you and the bishop, since you ought to be his defender and he your shepherd. He ought to sow spiritual things for you, and you ought to supply him with temporal things—not from his own resources, but from yours. Thus one of them states more explicitly: ‘If we have sown spiritual things for you, is it a great matter if we reap your temporal things?’ (1 Cor. 9:11). He ought to bless you, and you ought to honor him. Finally, your temporal possessions have also been divided by God with such complete balance that neither you ought to seize his, since they are not his but the Lord’s [Note: That is: you ought not to seize the bishop’s temporal possessions, because they are not his but the Lord’s], nor he desire yours, except only for the salvation of your soul. For he is told, ‘Not seeking the gift, but the fruit’ (Phil. 4:17).

“To you, however, when God is entreated, this is said—and I wish it were not fruitlessly cried out: ‘Those who said, “Let us possess the sanctuary of God as an inheritance,” my God, make them like a wheel,’ and so forth (Ps. 82:13). And: ‘You shall not muzzle the ox while it is treading out the grain’ (1 Cor. 9:9).”

### 4

“The voice of a good bishop ought often to be: ‘Let every soul be subject to higher authorities’ (Rom. 13:1); and: ‘Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s’ (Matt. 22:21); and: ‘Render to all what is owed: tribute to whom tribute, tax to whom tax’ (Rom. 13:7); and: ‘There is no authority except from God’ (ibid., 13:1); and: ‘Obey your leaders and submit to them’ (Heb. 13:17). And, as someone most beautifully said, ‘The obedience offered to superiors is offered to God,’ along with other statements of this kind.

“If the bishop thinks, preaches, and commands nothing else against you, he ought not merely to avoid offending you in this matter [or: this man], but much more, as one who feels through you [or: on your behalf], he ought to appease you. But if the contrary is the case—God forbid—and he is pleased not to show patience but to carry out vengeance, there is a way for you to do him an injury without contracting so grave a fault yourself.

“The bishops have general assemblies among themselves, universal synods, ancient canons, written councils, decrees of the holy Fathers, and enactments of various pontiffs. There is nothing that can happen among them for which they cannot find a proper judgment among themselves. Finally, there is the universal, principal, chief see—so called because it is distinguished by the very heads of the Church—the nurse, mother, judge, and teacher of all. If anything has been done contrary to right by anyone, or against any one of these persons, it can be judged, examined, or punished there by lawful sanction [Note: He repeats this very point several times in later works. See Letter 5 to John XII. The same is also read in Atto, bishop of Vercelli and a contemporary of Rather, Book II of *On the Distresses of the Church*.].

“Consult these authorities, bring the matter before them, and entrust the case to them. If anything is found to have been done improperly against you, believe me, it will be strictly punished by the judgment of the canons. You cannot find anyone else who could lay hands upon any of these with impunity, while leaving God Himself untouched—even if you could fly with wings.”

### 5

“You, on the contrary, perhaps say—for today I also heard this said by someone yesterday, with no less madness than stupidity—‘What need is there of a judge, when we are already using him as censor? For he has been so thoroughly discredited that everyone knows he is rightly to be condemned.’

“You could have said all this correctly if you had learned it from his own confession, canonically examined in a council. But, O seat of pestilence (Ps. 1:1), upon which that blessed man and gentle king of Zion, who became human for our sake, disdains to sit! O abominable judgment, which must be crushed at its very root! O unjust sentence, peculiar only to that age when, for our sake, thousands of saints were seized and prisons stuffed with innocent people solely through the acclamations of a seditious mob! O sentence worthy of being met by the Lord’s own declaration: ‘Do not judge according to appearance, but judge a just judgment’ (John 7:24).

“And of Himself, He says, ‘As I hear, I judge’ (ibid., 7:30): ‘as I hear,’ He says, not ‘as I heard.’ After the accusations of the slanderers have been presented, and the accused person’s reply has followed, a just and nonviolent judge can discern justly, so that he may truthfully say, ‘I judge as I hear’: that is, as the law itself determines, not as the gossip of raging people chatters; as the person himself confesses while present, not as those absent lay snares.

“Thus someone said quite wittily: ‘He who judges hastens to punish; he hastens,’ he says, ‘to punish, not to discern.’ For it is said: ‘By your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be judged’ (Matt. 12:37)—that is, both in a worldly and in a divine manner, mercifully and justly. Mercifully, as it is said: ‘You first declare your iniquities, that you may be justified’ (Job 40:3); justly, as in the statement: ‘Out of your own mouth I judge you, wicked servant’ (Luke 19:22).

“Here, too, you should consider a kind of security placed between you and God. Each person is judged justly out of his own mouth; but he is justified mercifully when he first declares his iniquities. Hence, in schools, children who confess voluntarily the offenses they have committed obtain pardon more quickly, whereas the obstinate are beaten with rods for a long time [Note: That is, children who are to be nourished or educated in schools.].

“The Truth, serving as the guardian of this security, says: ‘In the measure with which you measure, it will be measured back to you’ (Matt. 7:2)—that is, if justly, justly; if mercifully, mercifully. There, too, that sentence must carefully be weighed: ‘Let the one among you who is without sin cast the first stone at her’ (John 8:7).

“The imitation of the Pharisees must also be avoided. They watched in order to catch the Lord in His words (Mark 12:13); and for this reason human laws, with considerable foresight, took care to provide for unwitting defendants [Note: The common editions wrongly read *considerantur*; the correct reading is *consideranter*.]. If, therefore, a layperson can be condemned only after being convicted by his own mouth [Note: The same common editions read *conjunctus*, ‘joined,’ incorrectly], how much less should one whose judgment is in the hand of God alone be driven at will by the quibbles of certain envious people [or: be subjected to them] [Note: The same editions corruptly read *dolet*.]!

“For how do you know with what intention this same disgrace arose; and, if you know the occasion or cause from which it arose, with what disposition it was publicized—out of zeal for charity or out of zeal for spite [Note: Construe it as follows: ‘How do you know with what intention this same disgrace arose; and, if you know from what occasion or cause it arose, with what disposition it was publicized—out of zeal for charity or out of zeal for spite?’ This comes closer here to the objection proposed shortly before: ‘He has been so thoroughly discredited that everyone knows he is rightly to be condemned.’ It concerns Rather, who had been discredited as the author of a conspiracy against Hugh when he received Arnold, duke of the Bavarians. He replies that one must consider with what intention this disgrace arose, from what occasion or cause, and with what disposition it was publicized.”

### 6

“And, to reach the matter by reasoning, stop for a little while, I ask you, and let us consider it. The old Law also prohibits a priest from taking a widow or a divorced woman (Lev. 21:14). Consecrated virgins, however, ought to be kept much farther removed from the use, conversation, or sight of anyone, insofar as possible, the more they strive to preserve themselves chaste for that most chaste bridegroom, the most beautiful among the sons of men (Ps. 45:3), and to keep themselves undefiled before Him—not yet in deed, word, hearing, or even thought, insofar as this is possible for a human being striving most earnestly with God’s help.

“The holy canons also entirely forbid bishops to live with women, except those specifically exempted in them [Note: That is, except the cohabitation of those women who are excepted or permitted by the canons.]. You see one of these women often conversing with a bishop; you see it sometimes happening in private; and you see it being publicized by the common people. Do you wish him, as you think, since he has been discredited, immediately to be deposed on this ground alone, as you said, and made his own censor?

“For how or by what means do you know whether he may be compelled to do something that is secret to you but manifest to himself and to God, yet nevertheless pious—that is, for the purpose of winning a soul? Thus, it is read, a certain hermit, no less renowned than the most famous of the anchorites, converted a very notorious prostitute. Another, no less strong in his purpose, used to lure women who had been won over by payment—as was customary—and bring certain prostitutes into lodging in a city. When he was so thoroughly discredited that the people shouted that he ought to be cast into the flames, he shone forth, leaving the world with so great a multitude of converted women, that in that densely populated Alexandria, which had abounded in three thousand of them when he entered it, not even one prostitute could be found when he departed.”

### 7

“‘What,’ you say, ‘if the sons also approve the crime?’ [Note: That is: ‘If the sons also approve the crime,’ namely, if they are involved in the same crime for which the father has been discredited. He replies that the sons’ fault can originate elsewhere than from the father: while the father sows words of instruction, another may creep in and plant the seed of lust. The common text formerly read *nisi ipsa*, which made no sense. We have corrected it to *nisi ipse*, that is, ‘unless the father himself.’ We have likewise corrected *subripere* to *subrepere*, where the printed text was wrong.]

“I answer conversely: who knows this, I ask, except the person himself and God? Have you not read: ‘While the people slept, the enemy came and sowed weeds among the wheat and went away’ (Matt. 13:25)? This should make you understand that, while one person sows words of instruction, another can creep in and plant the seed of lust.

“Let us say something else. The canons state: ‘Let a bishop who is a drunkard either cease or be deposed’ (Apostolic Canon 42). Yet we often see many of the same order almost serving this vice, while we are entirely ignorant of the intention with which they do so. It may happen that someone acts as a drunkard among drunkards, according to the Apostle, eating and drinking with them in order to win them, or that he does this for some other reason—although hidden, nevertheless with a good disposition.

“Do you therefore think that he ought to be deposed on account of such a reputation, without his own confession, at the shout of the crowd? How grave seditions, plunder, and wars are is demonstrated, among other things, by the murders they themselves approve. Now, when the Lord says, ‘It is necessary that scandals come’ (Matt. 18:7), and, ‘Nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom’ (Luke 21:10), and Job says, ‘Nothing on earth happens without cause’ (Job 5:6), suppose that, when some occasion arises, a certain disagreement occurs in a city, or a separation from the kingdom, and some murders take place [or: there are not a few murders]. Everyone says that the bishop contrived the whole thing.

“Do you think he should be deposed without a canonical examination or his own confession? Or, much more improperly, that he should be insulted because of the outcry, with everyone accusing him while he alone denies it? For what if he is free from such a crime? How do you infer that he is not? ‘Because,’ you say, ‘while the affair was being conducted, he associated with evildoers and was captured with them.’ You judge that one must consider not what he intended but where he was, whereas we know that the Lord judges not the deed but the intention.

“What if he did this with a good intention, because it was a just one? For example, consider the prophet Jeremiah, who, as blessed Gregory says, out of charity, when he could not restrain the citizens from entering Egypt, made a point of descending there with them himself. And indeed, which bishop do we read of who, when Italy was invaded by the Lombards, abandoned his flock and went over to Maurice? [Note: The author has fallen into a chronological error. When Italy was invaded by the Lombards, it was not Maurice but Justin II who was emperor. He seems to have fallen into this error because, when he was about to give the example of St. Gregory, he knew that Maurice was emperor in Gregory’s time.]

“Was it perhaps this man just mentioned [namely, St. Gregory], since Maurice was likewise suspect to him, even though the saint himself had taken Maurice’s son from the sacred font, and Maurice daily reproached him for having obtained the apostolate of the chief see through his assistance, deed, and decree? When Gregory had fled unwillingly and had received that office—though Maurice consented and later repented—did he decide to act in such a way that he would leave the flock entrusted to him by traveling to Constantinople because of the wickedness of the citizens and the invasion of the enemy? [Note: The Lombards never occupied Rome, nor did any invasion of enemies into Rome occur during St. Gregory’s time.]

“Did the father Augustine, of most excellent memory (Letter 228), when a similar circumstance pressed upon him, decide to act in this way, or show by his example how one should act in such matters? And the man who, when questioned by the enemies about his name, is reported to have replied that he was a servant of Christ, while the enemy correspondingly replied that he was the scourge of Christ—was he rightly to be condemned because he immediately opened the city to the entering enemies?

“Do you therefore judge all those bishops worthy of deposition who knew that citizens were rebels against kings and were their sons, yet did not betray them to be punished? On the contrary, they celebrated Masses for them, baptized their sons, preached to them, confirmed them, granted them penance, and reconciled them?”

## 8

But perhaps you think that you rightly say this for the reason that you recall the Lord’s saying: “If you offer your gift at the altar,” etc. (Matthew 5:23); and because, just as a remedy does no good in a wound if the iron is still in it, so repentance does no good for one whose mind is discordant with his neighbor—how much more with the Lord—since the Lord’s chief pronouncement stands: “Unless you forgive people their sins, neither will your Father forgive you your sins” (Matthew 18:35). [Note: [Col. 0254D] Construe: “Repentance does no good for one who has a discordant mind”; the context and what follows suggest that this final word must be supplied.] But who is fit to discern these things except God alone, who knows everything?

For how do you know whether someone, although acting discordantly, may nevertheless have a harmonious disposition toward someone? Have you not read: “If it is possible, insofar as it depends on you, live at peace with all people” (Romans 12:18)? Have you not heard: “Whoever wishes to be a friend of this world is constituted an enemy of God” (James 4:4)? Do you not know that it is said: “Those who said to father or mother, ‘We do not know you,’ kept your covenant” (Deuteronomy 33:9)? Do you not recall what Jehoshaphat said when he was giving assistance to Ahab: “You give help to the impious, and you join in friendship with those who hate God?” (2 Chronicles 19:2).

And does the Psalmist not come to mind, saying: “Do I not hate those who hate you, Lord, and did I not waste away over your enemies?” (Psalm 138:21); and: “I hated those who act treacherously” (Psalm 100:3), and that whole psalm; and: “The righteous man will rejoice when he sees vengeance” (Psalm 57:11); and: “I have hated the wicked” (Psalm 118:113)? Finally, do you not recall the Lord saying: “I did not come to bring peace, but a sword” (Matthew 10:34); and, in Job, concerning the concord of the wicked: “The members of his flesh cling to one another” (Job 41:14), “one adheres to another, and no breath passes between them” (ibid., 7)?

In such great diversity, then, who but God alone can know—unless from words or from certain conjectures based on actions—who does what, and with what intention, when, even if we know that intention to be wholly evil, it remains our ministry to labor watchfully so that it may be improved? Surely Job must be condemned when he says: “I have become a brother to dragons and a companion to ostriches” (Job 30:29). Must Lot be condemned because of the crime of the Sodomites? Must those be condemned to whom the Apostle says: “In the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, among whom you shine like lights in the world, holding fast the word of life” (Philippians 2:15–16)? Must that angel—or rather, that bishop—to whom it is said in the Apocalypse be condemned: “I know where you dwell, where Satan’s throne is; you hold fast my name, and you have not denied my faith” (Apocalypse 2:13)? Must Noah and his sons be condemned because they were in the ark with serpents? Must the whole Church be condemned, to whom it is said: “As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among daughters” (Song of Songs 2:2)?

## 9

If the ship of the Church must by no means be abandoned in calm weather, how much less in a storm? And if the flock must never be abandoned when the wolf is concealing himself, how much less when he is threatening openly? Are the healthy to be guarded, but the sick wholly neglected? And where then is the saying: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (Matthew 9:12)?

Who has ever abandoned a beloved son driven into madness, when, even if he could not be bound, he could at least somehow be guarded? For since we see this very often done even with the persons of the most worthless servants, when provision is made lest they come to harm while sane, how much more fitting is it, when necessary, to act in this way toward beloved sons?

Indeed, when divine mercy, taking counsel for its shepherds—whom it knew would be especially harassed by the wolf’s attack—had granted them this instruction, saying: “If they persecute you in one city, flee into another” (Matthew 10:23), it showed by the example both of the shepherd and of the hired servant what must be done in a general emergency, saying: “The good shepherd gives his life for the sheep, but the hired servant flees” (John 10:11–12). And elsewhere: “When these things begin to happen, look up and raise your heads, because your redemption is drawing near” (Luke 21:28); likewise: “Watch at all times, praying that you may be considered worthy to escape all these things that are about to happen, and to stand before the Son of Man” (Luke 21:36).

Thus we are commanded in a general emergency to give our life for the sheep, to refresh the heart [reading uncertain: *exhalare* may be intended instead of *exhilarare*], to watch, and to pray—not to flee—although in a particular emergency we are by no means forbidden to flee.

## 10

Stop, then, saying only these things, whoever you are; and if by going beyond the mark you have already said them, do not increase your offense by defending them, lest you rightly appear to deserve deposition both from temporal and from eternal honor. For, although you remain in that same honor, you do not understand; and therefore you appear more comparable to beasts than to bishops, more to cattle than to shepherds, since you so despise yourself and strive so impiously to oppose the laws—laws that, if you were truly what you are called, were promulgated with the greatest piety for your own sake as well.

And by opposing me with that gigantomachy, theomachy, or rather idolomachy of yours in this matter, you have not allowed this vice to remain concealed [reading uncertain: *promisisti*; perhaps *permisisti*, “allowed”]. For while you pursue the manner of one more a lover of battle than a true philosopher, although you parade the philosopher’s appearance, repeatedly rereading and recalling gigantomachy rather than psychomachy, you show yourself to be more a worshiper of idols than a pontiff of Christ. Indeed, you suggest that you yourself are an idol, since you try so anxiously to protect yourself—lest you be pursued, overtaken, seized, and cast down by giants, or rather by him “who rejoiced like a giant to run his course” (Psalm 18:6)—with the frivolous circumlocutions of empty talk, as though you might hide “behind the tree from his heat” (ibid., 7), although, unable to remain concealed, you will be found in need of correction by him, covered with the leaves of the wild fig tree [reading uncertain: *foliorum*, perhaps *foliis*] (Genesis 3:7), not clothed with the innocence of the true lamb; painted with colors dyed in Indian pigments (Job 28:16), not whitened with snow on Zalmon (Psalm 68:16).

[Note: Construe and explain the passage as follows: “Since you are so fearful lest, pursued by giants—or rather by him who rejoiced like a giant to run his course—you should be overtaken, seized, and cast down, as though you might be found concealed behind the tree from his heat, although you cannot be hidden, you will be found in need of correction by him. You try to protect yourself with the frivolous circumlocutions of empty talk, covered with the leaves of the wild fig tree, not clothed with the innocence of the true lamb, painted with colors dyed in Indian pigments, not whitened with snow on Zalmon. Nor do you wish to assume wings, etc.” He rebukes the bishop, who has appeared until now to defend and protect himself through worldly empty talk rather than through true wisdom. In explaining this through allegories, he indulges in several and excessively long periods, so that the meaning becomes more difficult.]

Nor do you wish to assume the wings of a dove (ibid., 15)—that is, the virtue of simplicity—with which you might fly away and find rest, but rather the wings of a kite (Zechariah 5:9), with which you may be lifted up and vanish. Nor do you seek wings covered with silver, so that “the hindparts of your body may be like the appearance of gold” (Psalm 68:14), but rather silver changed into dross (Isaiah 1:22), and you pursue the gold of Ethiopia (Genesis 2:12), which does not equal wisdom, instead of that finest gold of Ophir (1 Kings 10:11). Our true peacemaker, who “made both one” (Ephesians 2:14), ordered that gold to be brought to him in ships, so that he might adorn the coffered ceilings or vessels of his temple—namely, the hearts in which he deigns to dwell and to store his precious treasure.

You embrace more readily the foolish wisdom of the world, which the weak and despised one confounds (1 Corinthians 1:27), our Lord, “beautiful beyond the sons of men” (Psalm 45:3), than that eternal and true wisdom which your teachers—whom you praise, exalt, and magnify—have judged foolishness. You pile up vessels borrowed from the Egyptians (Exodus 12:35), not among the Lord’s tabernacle furnishings, but among the ornaments of that same Egypt, forcing the Lord’s wool and linen—understand, along with those vessels—to serve the queen of heaven (Jeremiah 44:17), that is, earthly exaltation.

You introduce Marius’s Jugurtha, conquered by deceit, rather than the world’s pomp subdued by Christ through the wood; captured Syphax, rather than the dragon cast down by Michael (Apocalypse 12:7); and a triumphant figure into our battle, in which you ought not to have mounted a horse but to have ascended from the opposite side—Scipio, Pompey, and Deiotarus, and the most eloquent Cato—rather than recalling Peter, Paul, and John, the Lord’s most beloved disciple.

You repeatedly reread “Wars through the Emathian fields” (Lucan, Book 1, line 1), rather than the councils celebrated by Christian teachers—or rather by invincible warriors—through the most delightful fields depicted in Holy Scripture; and “right granted to crime,” rather than the rule established for pious living:

> “The victor struggled in a little body.”  
> —Statius

rather than: “Power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9), as the Apostle says.

And therefore fear that you may be struck by the mountain “cut without hands” [Note: The printed editions have *vere*, “truly,” incorrectly; the sense requires the correction *verere*, “fear”], while you do not fear offending against that mountain, suspecting—or rather teaching—that the mountains gathered together are the fertile mountain of God (Psalm 68:17), that is, the mountain that makes fruitful, by divisions of graces, those whom he wishes and as he wishes. You dare to say that this is done by a human being, although sometimes and in part it is done through a human being [understand: “although it may be done through a human being”].

And because you are from the earth, since you speak only of earthly things while wholly rejecting heavenly things, beware lest that ancient dragon devour you while you strive to become his food. For he promised him who cannot lie: “Earth”—that is, earthly people—“you shall eat all the days of your life” (Genesis 3:14).

But when you were putting these things forward cunningly, as it seemed to you, you ought to have remembered that Cariath-Sepher (Joshua 15:16; Judges 1:12)—that is, the city of letters—had already been destroyed by Joshua [Note: Since Rather, especially in the prison at Pavia, where he lacked books, recited everything from memory, he attributes to Joshua what is indeed read in the Book of Joshua; yet both here and in the Book of Judges it is attributed not to Joshua but to Othniel.], who gives life in the Spirit to those whom the letter kills (2 Corinthians 3:6); and that the kingdom of God already consists not in speech but in power (1 Corinthians 4:20).

Already our strong-handed one—namely, another David, to whom the Lord swore, “You are a priest forever,” and will not repent of it (Psalm 110:4)—has struck the Valley of Salt (2 Samuel 8:13), that is, the proud talkativeness of the supposedly wise. It is called a valley because “everyone who exalts himself will be humbled” (Luke 14:11), not because “the valleys will abound in grain” (Psalm 65:14)—that is, because “whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 14:11)—by him who sends springs into the valleys, so that the waters may run between the mountains (Psalm 104:10), not those waters that once stood above the mountains (ibid., 6) of the Churches—that is, waters which temporarily covered them with the swelling of persecutions.

Now, thanks be to God, they have fled from the Lord’s rebuke, although you insist on calling them back, to your own detriment; they have ascended and descended to the place that he founded for them (Psalm 104:8)—that is, the place where the Lord has permanently established them—so that they may not again be joined together, even if they wish to cover the earth. For although the kingdom of God still struggles in certain places and its adversaries are many, nevertheless throughout the greater part of the world a great and evident door has now been opened to apostolic preaching (1 Corinthians 16:9; 2 Corinthians 2:12).

Nor, let me add this as well, does the Lord send his springs between those mountains of the cataclysm—those among which the Church is watered, washed, and cleansed, as you, in your profound wisdom, desire to teach—but among those mountains which he waters from above (ibid., 13), namely those upon whose summit he himself has been established (Isaiah 2:2), and who is also the stone cut from the mountain without hands (Daniel 2:34)—that is, Christ, born from David’s seed according to the flesh without human agency (Romans 1:3).

The Church is not cleansed by the waters of Egypt, which rush headlong, but by the waters of Siloam, which flow quietly (Isaiah 8:6). For although Naaman the Syrian judged the rivers Abana and Pharpar of Damascus better than all the waters of Israel (2 Kings 5:12), nevertheless he could be cleansed of leprosy only in our Jordan, after washing there seven times, not without mystery (ibid., 14).

That Church, moreover, which [a word is missing here, perhaps “assails” or “rages”] … against physicians—that is, false theologians, whom you still follow, while introducing the propositions and assumptions of Cicero in the Church’s cause—could not be cured by any of them, although it could suffer much from them.

In this matter, therefore, we shall cut short your *cataphasis* and *apophasis* [affirmative and negative modes of assertion] only to the extent that we shall show it healthier and wiser to answer in accordance with the Apostle: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8). In the other matter, we shall not only carefully avoid joining the number of those “who have strengthened themselves in words, wicked words” (Psalm 64:6), but also, while preserving the Catholic faith and stepping around the pit—that is, without abandoning our office—we shall prefer humbly to yield to the words of others rather than obstinately to devote ourselves to disputes.

## 11

All these things have been proposed in order to establish that, if some such bishop as you describe—God forbid—should be found, he cannot be judged except by himself, by no human being, with the sole exception of the authority of the canons.

By himself he is judged through a pure confession before God and before a faithful advocate whom he has chosen, so that he may not be judged strictly by God; rather, confessing his iniquities against himself beforehand and snatching the voice from his accuser, he may be justified.

By canonical authority he is judged if, after a legitimate examination, he has publicly declared his crime in his own council.

By the Lord he is judged in many ways: according to the Psalmist, through illness, losses, the attacks of enemies, or any other kinds of affliction. God does not indeed command these things, but permits them, and through his affliction the bishop is punished—either so that he may be corrected in the present age, lest he be condemned with the world in the future, or so that the iron of his mind may reach the sharpness of a fine edge, its alien perversity rubbed away by the file, enabling him also to cut away what sprouts wickedly in the hearts of others.

## 12

Let us approve that all this is indeed so, not by Cato’s utterances but by the Lord’s. The Apostle also bears witness that bishops are to be judged by no human being, saying of them, while speaking of himself: “It is the Lord who judges me” (1 Corinthians 4:4); and: “The spiritual person judges all things, but is himself judged by no one” (1 Corinthians 2:15). The Lord likewise asserts that salt which has lost its savor is not even fit to be placed on the dunghill (Luke 14:35).

They are judged by themselves, as the same Apostle says: “If we judged ourselves, we would not be judged” (1 Corinthians 11:31). The same is shown by the passage concerning Moses: “He also made a bronze basin in which Aaron and his sons would wash when they entered the sanctuary; he made it from the mirrors of the women who kept watch at the door of the tabernacle” (Exodus 38:8).

They are judged by the Lord, as in the saying: “I will visit their iniquities with a rod, and their sins with blows” (Psalm 89:33). This is not said of the one who is recorded in the Gospel as having washed the disciples’ feet (John 13:5).

How a bishop is judged by canonical authority is shown clearly enough by the one who says: “I judge as I hear” (John 5:30), and: “Out of your own mouth I judge you” (Luke 19:22).

The Apostle also teaches that this must be observed in the present, insofar as you consider the Lord to be present: when he reveals by some evident sign of his presence either a person who, although unwilling and compelled, nevertheless brings forth and freely confesses the manifest truth, or someone who has been exposed publicly through a just and legal judgment. “Do not judge before the time,” he says, “until the Lord comes, who will also bring to light the hidden things of darkness” (1 Corinthians 4:5).

In common usage, *mundeburdium* is the name for a certain kind of royal protection. Whoever possesses it is generally protected by royal authority through a special privilege, so that no one may inflict anything upon him, whether by force or by judgment—even if he has been caught in guilt—before he has been heard in the presence of that same majesty.

If mortal power is feared in this way, and if a judgment pronounced in writing is preserved today but tomorrow, once erased by fire, water, or age, has no strength because its letters no longer remain [Note: This refers to the privilege of the *mundeburdium*, which was written down], with what reverence and fear ought the edicts of the one whose words do not pass away, although heaven and earth pass away, to be preserved? (Mark 13:31.)

What clearer *mundeburdium* could you seek to defend especially the princes or ministers whom that most powerful King of kings [understand: “has placed”] in the Church than: “Do not touch my anointed ones” (Psalm 105:15)?

They also call a *wiffa* a certain sign: whoever has received it as a royal gift, and has suffered harm through someone’s attack, is defended by the avenging sword.

But what sign could be found more terrifying than the pontifical *pedalum* [Note: *Pedalum*, that is, *pedum*, the episcopal staff. Sigebert calls it the pontifical *petalum* in *The Life of Theodoric, Bishop of Metz*, chapter 3; it is also so called by the author of the *Life of Sulpicius the Pious, Bishop of Bourges*, no. 37]?

What more conspicuous *wiffa* could you desire than the crown they wear upon their heads? The stole, chasuble, dalmatic, girdle, stockings, and sandals likewise tell you—if you were capable of understanding nothing else within them—that they are unmistakable insignia of divine protection and veneration, since you see them using these things contrary to the custom of others. I am also somewhat afraid that these have come to you by your own judgment, when I see you treating them with such contempt that you would prefer them to be plundered and killed rather than defended by these insignia.

## 13

Having briefly read these points against such a perverse and wholly inappropriate judgment, even among laymen, I ask you to consider the person whom I mentioned above, since bishops too have their own judgments among themselves if they commit some offense.

Have you ever seen a soldier or a commoner dare to rebuke, much less judge, a palatine judge [Note: The following is read above, Book 1, no. 16: “Are you a *locotheta*, whom we call a count of the palace, a prefect, or a judge?”]?

In any case, it ought already to have satisfied you that bishops are judges of everyone—not only of human beings but also of angels, namely apostate angels (1 Corinthians 6:3). But, to impress this upon you lest the shifting of various concerns carry it out of your mind, I think it should be repeated, with something added that perhaps you either still do not know or pretend not to know.

Know, then, that there will be four orders at the judgment: one that judges with God; another that is delivered by God through judgment; a third that is condemned through judgment; and a fourth that, having already been judged, will be present, as we believe, for no other reason than to be tormented still further by the happiness of the pious, as it is written in the Psalm: “The sinner will see and be angry” (Psalm 112:10), and by the words they will utter in the anguish of their spirit.

To make this clear through the most evident examples, hear the Lord promising: “You will sit upon twelve thrones” (Matthew 19:28)—that is, upon the seats of the apostles—not merely the twelve of them, but all the righteous who hold the same office.

And lest you think this new or perhaps conjectured by us, hear one of their number, but already the thirteenth, since he was called from heaven after Matthias: “Do you not know,” he says, “that we will judge angels?” (1 Corinthians 6:3.)

You doubt in vain about the seat belonging to this order, since you know that they are apostles insofar as they perform this work—if, indeed, the term itself does not deceive you, since it is Greek—and the Psalmist sings: “The princes of the peoples have gathered together with the God of Abraham” (Psalm 47:10).

What these gathered princes do—rejoicing in glory and delighting in their beds—the same Psalm says elsewhere: “Two-edged swords are in their hands, to execute vengeance among the nations, rebukes among the peoples; to bind their kings with fetters and their nobles with iron shackles, to execute upon them the judgment written” (Psalm 149:6–9).

If you do not understand what the sword is, when you see that their hands have performed the works by which those destined to live are freed through judgment and vengeance and rebuke, while those destined to die are condemned, you may take notice, as one of their number—already holding the sword, even if not openly brandishing it—says: “To some we are the odor of death leading to death, to others the odor of life leading to life” (2 Corinthians 2:16).

Simeon likewise says of the Lord, in addition to the other meaning: “Behold, this one is set for the fall and resurrection of many” (Luke 2:34). The Lord himself says: “There is one who accuses you: Moses” (John 5:45). And concerning the apostles he says: “They will therefore be your judges” (Matthew 12:27). Again: “The men of Nineveh will rise in judgment with this generation and condemn it, because they repented at the preaching of Jonah” (ibid., 41). And: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin” (John 15:22).

But if, as I said, you do not understand what this sword is, let Paul himself identify it: “The sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Ephesians 6:17); and concerning the final and chief form of pride: “The Lord Jesus will kill him with the breath of his mouth” (2 Thessalonians 2:8); and: “The word of God is living and effective, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit” (Hebrews 4:12).

Why are the swords two-edged—that is, sharpened twice? In addition to what has just been said, consider that Gehenna—that is, twofold punishment—is called the written judgment: “Bind their hands and feet” (Matthew 22:13) sufficiently explains the fetters and iron shackles (Psalm 149:9), which are compared with the harshness of cruelty.

The unjust are therefore judged by the just, who avenge and rebuke, with hands and two-edged swords, because here the unjust not only refused to attend to the works of the righteous by imitating them, but also strove to attack their word through many persecutions and deaths. And because here they willingly kept their hands and feet bound against good work, there they will rightly be bound unwillingly in eternal condemnation.

“If they are few,” you say, “who will ever reach this state,” I will number them, he says (Psalm 139:18). Perhaps there will be twelve on account of Matthias, or eleven on account of Judas, or thirteen on account of Paul. “They will multiply beyond the sand,” he says (ibid.). Consider how many judges there are, and see whether it is a small matter to rebuke even one person among so many.

## 14

You have the order of the judges [Note: At no. 13 he had said: “There will be four orders at the judgment: one that judges with God; another that is delivered by God through judgment; a third that is condemned through judgment; and a fourth that, having already been judged, will be present, as we believe, for no other reason than to be tormented still further by the happiness of the pious.” He has so far explained the first order, those who will judge with God. He now undertakes to explain the other three orders: the order of those saved through judgment, the order of those condemned, and the fourth order of those already judged], and let us set forth the order of those saved through judgment: “Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and the poor; on the evil day the Lord will deliver him” (Psalm 41:2).

Give also the order of those condemned through judgment. “When it grows hot,” blessed Job says, “they will be dissolved from their place” (Job 6:17)—namely, from that left-hand place, destined for everlasting punishment.

The Gospel discourse divides these two according to the merits of each, saying: “These will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matthew 25:46).

As for the fourth order, the Psalmist proclaims it by saying [Note: Supply here: “the order of those who have already been judged”; or read: “let us set forth the order, the Psalmist proclaiming…”]: “Therefore the wicked will not rise in judgment” (Psalm 1:5). The same discourse also explains this: “Whoever does not believe has already been judged, because he has not believed in the name of the only-begotten Son of God” (John 3:18).

## 15

It seems worthwhile here to oppose the unhealthy opinion of a certain person who, in the presence of several bishops who were, alas, not at all uneducated, dared to condemn what is sung in the Church [Note: It is sung in the hymn that is even today recited at Lauds on the feast of All Saints:

> “Whoever, as princes, reign  
> In the high hall of the stars.”]

namely, the belief that all the saints will reign eternally with Christ. He asserted that one must neither say nor believe that anyone besides God reigns eternally, but must confess that the saints merely rejoice with him—as though rejoicing with God were not the same as reigning, reigning the same as living, and living the same as always existing.

In this matter he became so disastrously hardened that he removed himself from the singing of the Church while it was present, and from the sweet-sounding melody of that great happiness for which he now labors so intensely—or so greatly [reading uncertain: *totum*, perhaps *tantum*].

He would indeed be right to do this if he understood God’s unique divinity, his reign—that is, his principality—and his power, by which all things created are governed and ruled by his own singular will and by his own singular authority and direction, with such devout reverence that he would fear impiously to oppose the gratuitous mercy which, from vessels of wrath, makes vessels of mercy (Romans 9:22–23), enriching them with so great a gift that, by ineffable kindness, it grants them not only to be and be called kings, but even to be and be called gods.

But, O blind one among the blind—and most foolish foolishness, if it is defended—blind both the one who speaks and those who connive with him in this matter alone! For while human beings try to measure God by themselves, they think that he too, like them, begrudges another’s advancement—as though he were constrained by such narrowness of possession and power, while being expanded by such greatness of desire and ambition, that what another acquires is thought to diminish him.

Yet he alone possesses everything, and he holds his treasure with such even moderation that it can neither be exhausted nor increased. His power cannot fail in anything, nor can it increase at all, although he himself, according to his will and in harmony with the natures and causes of things, both increases and diminishes everything: granting growth to some and applying decline to others, containing mutable things while remaining immutable himself; illuminating from himself those who must be illuminated beneath him, without taking any light away from himself, so that he rightly and most kindly permits them also to be called light [reading uncertain: *luce*, perhaps *lux*].

He could have understood this well enough from the kings already mentioned: he should have known and confessed that God is essentially the King of kings, but of those who have been established—as he is the Light of lights, but of those who have been illuminated.

## 16

But now, to turn our discourse to the very author of the error [page 117], tell me, I ask: by saying this, consenting to it by silence, or—what is much worse—confirming it by agreement, are you contradicting the apostolic testimonies?

“Not at all,” you say. What hidden meaning, then, do you think is contained in that very clear statement of the Apostle, where he says: “If we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him” (2 Timothy 2:12)?

What do you make of the passage in the Apocalypse of John, where, taking a finite number for an infinite one, you read: “They will reign with him for a thousand years” (Apocalypse 20:6)?

What will he give those to whom, at the judgment, he will say: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom” (Matthew 25:34), except the kingdom itself, so that they may reign with him?

Which earthly king, when distributing among his subjects prefectures, estates, or other such things belonging to the share of the kingdom, do you ever hear saying “Receive the kingdom” except when he distributes it to a son who will reign with him or certainly succeed him?

Or, because of the twelvefold session of those who will judge, can you not understand that the number twelve previously mentioned also concerns those who will reign [Note: Construe: “Which earthly king, when distributing among his subjects prefectures, estates, or other such things belonging to the share of the kingdom, do you hear saying ‘Receive the kingdom,’ except when he is distributing it to a son who will reign with him or certainly succeed him? Or, because of the twelvefold session of those who will judge—referring to ‘You will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel’—can you not understand that the twelvefold number mentioned above also concerns those who will reign?”]?

When in the Psalm you hear: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Psalm 45:8), whom do you understand by “companions” except those who reign with him?

And when you read that the angel said to Mary: “He will reign over the house of Jacob forever” (Luke 1:33), what, I ask, do you understand?

Do you think that some kingdom, previously unknown and existing somewhere beyond his universal presence, was promised to his divinity, by which he reigns everywhere without beginning or end, being coeternal and consubstantial with the Father? Or was it not rather attributed to his humanity, which he assumed for us in time, by the divinity that he shares with the Father, so that he might reign over the house of Jacob (Luke 1:32)—that is, in the kingdom of the Church—which began from the time he himself was born, or from the time he deigned, for our sake, to ascend the tribunal of the cross?

The Psalmist bears witness to this when he cries out to Christ’s faithful: “Say among the nations” (Psalm 96:10), “The Lord has reigned from the wood” [Note: The words “from the wood,” which among the Greeks are preferred by Saint Justin in his *Dialogue with Trypho*, and among the Latins by Tertullian, the ancient author of the commentary attributed to Ambrose on the First Epistle to the Corinthians, Prudentius, Saint Augustine, Saint Leo, and others, are also read in both Greek and Latin in the very ancient manuscript Psalter of the Church of Verona, edited by Father Joseph Blanchini], that is, from his ascent upon the cross. This kingdom, clearly, is to be without end, with the same Jacob forever—that is, with the head together with the body.

Do you think otherwise? Do you suppose that the head can reign even temporarily when something cannot live without its members?

Or perhaps you do not recall that this was said of him: “With his body, which is the Church” (Romans 8:17)? Likewise: “If children, then heirs—heirs indeed of God, and fellow heirs with Christ.” Heirs of what, I ask, except the kingdom?

Finally, when in the prayer he himself handed down to you, you say: “Your kingdom come” (Matthew 6:10), what, I ask, are you requesting? That he should now hasten to reign, when he is never believed not to have reigned? Or, what is more true, that you may deserve to reign with him by adoption, not by nature; by gift, not by inherent right; by donation, not by what is owed; by concession, not by equality; by grace, not by essence; through the piety of the giver, not through a comparison of equality?

Indeed, from certain distinctions made by him concerning dwelling places (John 14:2) and by the Apostle concerning stars (1 Corinthians 15:41), we can truthfully gather from their words—not only that Jesus Christ himself, for whom reigning is essentially the same as living, reigns forever and is incomparably superior to adopted kings, but also that among those who reign there will be a considerable difference in the manner of their reign [Note: Understand: “We can truthfully gather certain distinctions from the statements of Christ concerning dwelling places and from the Apostle’s statements concerning stars: not only that Jesus Christ himself, for whom reigning is essentially the same as living, etc.”].

Stop, then, my son, defending this of yours—not indeed an opinion, but the greatest ignorance—lest you someday be found among those who, while trying to defend God, offend against him.

Rather, vindicate your dignity by your conduct as well, lest you lose so great a prerogative. For you ask for this in prayer to no purpose if, while despairing of attaining it, you do not desire to attain it; just as you also call him your Father only in vain, unless you do so in the same way.

### 17

But returning to you, having left aside the man with whom I have already been engaged for a long time in a discussion concerning no small matter, I ask you to consider this: if the supreme pontiff is to be reproved by no one, how much less should any one of them be scourged, [Col. 0264C] handed over to prison, and tormented by hunger and thirst, cold and nakedness, and every other kind of affliction?

I ask you also to attend to one point and judge it from your own experience. Suppose you had a negligent servant whom you nevertheless cherished with such great love that, in one of your domains, you placed him immediately after yourself in rank, authority, and power: whatever you had to do or decide, you entrusted to him; whatever he determined, you confirmed; whatever he revoked, you revoked; whoever he blessed would be blessed by you, and whoever he cursed would be cursed; and you granted him your rights, your insignia, your throne, scepter, purple robe, and even the crown itself. You decreed that he should be called by your own name. Finally, you retained for yourself nothing except the very essence, rule, and governance [Col. 0264D] by which you would rule and govern him together with those entrusted to him—and whatever he did, decided, established, or defined, he would do by your power, not his own.

Suppose, amid all these honors, he were caught by one of his fellow servants who surpassed him in some respect [Note: In the common editions the text was wholly unintelligible: “aliquid cum in aliquo.” The sentence demands a correction. It should be construed and explained as follows: if this man, whom you, O king, had adorned with so great an honor, were, amid these marks of honor, seized by one of his fellow servants who surpassed him in some respect, and were wronged by that man without your knowledge, although you were present, etc. “Excedente eum aliquid” means “by one who surpassed him in some respect.”], and, without your knowledge, though you were present, were wronged by him, handed over to prison, killed by hunger, thirst, and frost, and disgraced in respect of what he wore, his name being subjected to insults, mockery, and contempt—what, then, good king and pious prince, would you decide ought to be done in such a case?

“I know,” you say, “what I would do. But he is not as dear to God as you claim.”

“What do you know?” I ask. Do you not see him adorned with a throne, scepter, crown, purple robe, and even the name itself, in a manner sufficiently splendid? [Note: *Praeclueo* was used by Prudentius in the hymn after meals, verse 37, in the sense of “I shine exceedingly.” *Clueo* occurs in Plautus, *Trinummus* 2.4.95: “so that his name may be renowned,” that is, “I am celebrated, I become famous.” Thus the adverb *praeclue* means “very splendidly.” When he says, “I, you say, marked him out with insignia,” he is speaking of the king, who repeatedly claimed that he made bishops. See Book Three, no. 23.]

“You marked him out with insignia,” you say.

“You? In what way? Were you able to give what you do not even dare to touch? Were you able to grant what you are yourself compelled to adore? Was anything ever in your power that is now so far above you? It is astonishing, then, that you have taken so much credit to yourself and attributed it to another. But stop even thinking this. For if you had been able to give it, you would certainly also have been able to take it away.”

Yet although you are able to strip him of his possessions, drive him from his homeland, exile him, hand him over to prison, deprive him of his sight, flay him, dismember him, and finally kill him—even at the cost of your own condemnation—you cannot by your own force, judgment, authority, or power take away that name, that scepter, that crown together with the purple robe, that blessing, that power of binding you yourself—even from the one by whom you are held bound—and of loosing [Note: That is, the power of loosing.] you, that judgment, that primacy, that angelic dignity, that apostolic dignity, that pontificate, that royal office, that pastoral office, and finally—what surpasses all these—that anointing and that divinity: recognize that what you see approaching God Himself so closely is far above you. It can be taken away only by Him, granted only by Him, and by Him alone can it be so indissolubly admitted into fellowship with Him that no untouched person can lay hands upon it.

For all those things can indeed be inflicted by human beings upon bishops, even against the bishop’s will, while God, although He most dreadfully forbids them, nevertheless permits it [Note: The common editions incorrectly read *te tamen*. The correction is confirmed by what follows: “although God permits it, even though He does not will it.”]: this is a supreme injury to God and a supreme misery for the one who inflicts it, yet it is nevertheless an immeasurable glory of that same order. This is attested by those who went away rejoicing from the presence of the council because they had been deemed worthy to suffer disgrace for the name of Jesus (Acts 5:41).

### 18

… having risen up gravely against the one who was giving [Note: Some material is missing here. The objection was that the bishop had been subjected to these evils because he had risen up against the king from whom he had received his episcopate. Rather replies: “If he had risen up gravely against the one who was giving …” These or similar words must be supplied. Shortly afterward we have corrected *inquis* (“you say”), where the reading was *inquit* (“he says”).] while offending him so outrageously—what is that to you?

“Because,” you say, “he disturbed my kingdom and stirred up wars and carried out countless raids.”

“I do not think so,” I reply. “But let us say that he did; let us say it merely to accommodate your will.”
