But, O if only, after you had captured him and held him in your power—God permitting it, although not willing it—for it is neither right nor permissible to say or believe that He supports what He has forbidden to happen—you had recalled that he said to everyone, and especially to you: “Whoever honors me, I will honor; but those who despise me will be of no account” (1 Samuel 2:30). And also: “God has given him a place, but he abuses it for pride” (Job 24:23). And concerning certain people: “They turned away their eyes so as not to see heaven, nor did they remember the judgments of the righteous” (Daniel 13:9).

The Wise Man might also have whispered to you that saying which has become a proverb: “He twice conquers who conquers himself in victory, and whoever conquers an angry enemy overcomes the greatest enemy.” Likewise: “In taking revenge, the inheritance is criminal.” And another saying of the same sort, from Cicero’s speech *For Marcellus*:

> “To conquer one’s spirit, restrain one’s anger, moderate one’s victory, and not merely raise up an adversary who has fallen but even magnify his former dignity: whoever does these things, I do not compare with the greatest men, but judge him most like God.”

On the contrary, it would be ridiculous, in the case of the man mentioned above, to destroy an innocent man out of hatred for the guilty. You should also have brought to mind what David did: how, when he found Saul, who was pursuing him, delivered into his hands by God, and when his men urged him to strike him, he refused, saying instead: “May God be gracious to me, that I should not stretch out my hand against the Lord’s anointed” (1 Samuel 26:11).

In this you should first have noticed that he asked God to be gracious to him so that he would not do what, since God had given Saul into his power, he could justly have done. For woe to the one who, according to the Psalmist, is “left to his own will” (Psalm 80:13). Scripture elsewhere, identifying some people as having become corrupt and abominable in their pursuits (Psalm 14:1), says: “Do not follow your desires, and turn away from your own will” (Sirach 18:30); and: “There are ways that seem right to human beings, but their end plunges down to the depths of hell” (Proverbs 16:25).

Yet many people often desire things which, when granted to their own harm, they are accustomed to receive. Hence someone said quite cleverly: “Nothing is so insane as to desire that by which you may perish.” Another likewise, with as much wit as the Wisdom itself teaches, said: “If it is miserable to have wished for evil, it is more miserable to have been able to do it.”

Job says: “The tents of robbers abound, and they boldly provoke God, although He has placed everything in their hands” (Job 12:6). How are they robbers if God has given them everything? Because, although God justly permits it, they have unjustly rushed upon plunder. And why do they boldly provoke Him? Because God has given them room either for correction or for the punishment of sinners—or, certainly, for their own harm: left to themselves and not restrained by the physician, they consume what will destroy them; they drink the cup of the Lord’s fury, from which, once intoxicated, they fall more grievously and perish eternally; they heap up crimes, by which hell is kindled more fiercely for them, “adding iniquity upon iniquity” (Psalm 69:28). Their evil will thus reaches its most wicked fulfillment, so that they do not enter into the righteousness of God, but are blotted out of the book of the living and are not written among the righteous (ibid., 29). The poor and afflicted person, having been received into the salvation of God, magnifies Him in praise and praises His name in song (ibid., 31).

Why, then, as I said, do they provoke God’s anger? Is it not because, although God permits them to act according to the hidden arrangement of His counsel, they receive from Him the opportunity to do everything dictated by their anger, greed, or pride? They neither fear the justice of the One who permits it, nor consider His mercy, nor dread the two-edged sword of God, nor take account of His regard for the affliction of the wretched. Finally, they do not even, out of consideration for themselves, pity the sufferings of others, nor remember that prophetic reproach in which the Lord, speaking against such people under the figure of wicked Babylon, says:

> “I was angry with my people; I defiled my inheritance and gave them into your hand. You showed them no mercies, and you remembered your last end” (Isaiah 47:6).

And after a little while He concludes terribly:

> “Evil will come upon you, and you will not know its origin; calamity will fall upon you, which you will not be able to expiate. Misery will come upon you, of which you know nothing” (Isaiah 47:6).

And the rest—though I do not know whether anything more terrifying could be found.

### 19

But, to return to David, if you answer in the customary manner … [Note: The source is lacunose here.] that it was indeed an example of great patience, but that such conduct is not appropriate today, I reply that such conduct is more appropriate today than it was then. For then it was permitted to take vengeance justly; now one may not even become angry (Matthew 5:22).

“You say that David acted in this way because Saul had been his lord” [Note: Construe and explain: “You say that David acted in this way because Saul had been his lord.”], you say.

“You,” I reply, “because he had been your shepherd, your prophet, your angel, your judge, and your God, should have acted more appropriately.”

But if you wish to examine more deeply what this deed signifies, know that David represented your injury in this disturbed kingdom, as you call it, while Saul represented the order of those set over the Church, anointed indeed but persecuting the righteous and negligent in their duties.

Saul therefore relieves his bowels (1 Samuel 24:4) when any one of them draws from himself the stench of a bad reputation. David grieves that he cut off the edge of Saul’s cloak (ibid., 6), because anyone must greatly fear … [Note: A lacuna occurs here.] even if he too is anointed like David, or, in the final act, rebukes any one of the Hebrews.

That our priesthood is royal is confirmed by Peter’s testimony (1 Peter 2:9) and by thousands of testimonies. I had not intended to introduce this testimony while hastening to set down another, but since it presented itself of its own accord, it could in no way be cast aside. Perhaps it will prove no less useful elsewhere, at the appropriate time.

### 20

But if we examine the matter more carefully [Note: That is, “more exactly,” or “with a more diligent examination,”], we may find that throughout the matter is not as you say. For I seem to understand perfectly what you desired. Since you yourself are a wolf, you wanted to find a timid shepherd and a mute dog. And since you are a public robber of the Church, you wanted no one to be found who would contradict you.

But, O unbearable burden! Where then is this: “Not only those who do such things, but also those who consent to those who do them, are worthy of death” (Romans 1:32)? Where is what the same author says elsewhere: “Whoever wishes to be a friend of this world is made an enemy of God” (James 4:4)? Where is the Psalmist’s saying: “When you saw a thief, you ran with him” (Psalm 50:19)—that is, you consented to him?

This, as I think, was the cause of the dispute; this was the mark of the crime you allege: namely, that you wanted to keep all the possessions of the Church, while you wanted him [Note: The common editions give the passage in a confused and erroneous form, *cum vero tu*. “Him,” that is, the bishop, the king wanted to be not a shepherd of Christ’s flock but a hireling. The reference is to an action of King Hugh, expressed in Letter 5 to John XII, no. 4, as follows: “King Hugh sent, in a little document, a fixed amount as a stipend that I was to retain from the goods of the Church, demanding an oath from me concerning the rest, so that during his days and those of his son I would exact no more. Realizing what great absurdity would follow from this, I did not consent.”] to be your hireling, not the shepherd of Christ’s flock. He showed his displeasure at this by some form of resistance, judging from the very etymology of the word that you were a king when you acted rightly, but a thief when you committed sacrilege [Note: This is said of the bishop, who in this matter did not consent but resisted the king. Construe *pensus* as “having judged”: he had judged from the etymology itself that you were a king when you acted rightly, but a thief when you committed sacrilege. Shortly afterward we have written *caeterum*, where the reading was incorrectly *certum*.].

But whatever was done, whatever happened wrongly—for the speech must be framed as though it had been done and had happened—our present effort insists that it must not be done or happen. Should not the author of the deed first have been lawfully examined according to the judgment of the canons? And if he had been legally convicted, should he not himself, having become the witness, judge, and censor of his own condemnation, have been condemned no longer as bishop, but, once deposed if the law so required and another substituted in the Church’s place, have justly paid the penalty for his offense, if you wished, without the most sacred ministry being violated in any respect and without the mother Church suffering, through so long a period of time, such serious injury from the excessive loss of her children?

For where are the children whom that same Church ought to have borne in even a single Easter season, while the mother herself was, so to speak, a widow, existing without the companionship of a husband—that is, without a bishop, whose duty it was to baptize at Easter? [Note: To make the passage yield a coherent sense, it seems to be construed as follows: “Where, then, are the children” (supply *they will be*) “whom that same Church ought to have borne in at least one Easter season, while the mother herself existed as a widow, so to speak, without the companionship of a husband—that is, of the bishop, whose duty it was to baptize at Easter?” We have written *tanquam* (“as though”), where the text had *quan­quam* (“although”).]

The saying, “What God has joined together, let no human being separate” (Matthew 19:6), exceeds the bounds of ordinary speech, since the Apostle, in commending primordial virginity and explaining the prophecy of the first human being, says: “This is a great mystery; but I speak of Christ and the Church” (Ephesians 5:32). [Note: He calls “primordial virginity” the state referred to in the account of the condition of innocence before the use of marriage: “A man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” (Genesis 2:24). Repeating this text, Saint Paul adds: “This is a great mystery,” and so forth.]

### 21

To whom, let us ask, will it be charged that so great a multitude—piously liberated by the grace of Christ and destined to enter the kingdoms of heaven—was impiously abandoned and thereby increased hell? [Note: Saint Odo, abbot of Cluny, held in this same century this same Augustinian view, according to which the souls of children dying without baptism are said to descend to hell. He was deeply troubled for the soul of a child captured by the Normans, fearing that by some mischance the child and his soul might be consigned to Gehenna without the washing of the font, as John, his disciple, relates in his Life, Book II, no. 6. See *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Benedictini*, vol. VII, p. 170. Rather, again expressing the same view in the following book, no. 28, while speaking of the same infants who died without baptism, wrote: “Sending so innumerable—alas for the sorrow!—children to eternal death.”]

For, returning briefly to the subject from which we have digressed, after the lengthy discussion already devoted to the man himself, we learned from the report of certain people that, during the same Easter season in which he was absent [Note: “The bishop” is understood.], when there was no baptistery—for there was no one to administer the chrism—a disaster befell the infants in that same city, and especially those who had not been baptized, so great that no one remembered anything like it among former generations. Thus, throughout the houses, the mothers, though they had not suffocated the children willingly, could have formed one lamentation throughout the whole city—if there were any fear of God in that place—with some mourning the divine vengeance and others lamenting both the temporal and eternal death of their children and of the mothers themselves.

What, then, let us ask, will that judge say about this when he comes in terror—he who first came gently to seek and save what had been lost (Luke 19:10)? What will he say, except that, as far as those children are concerned, he came in vain and sought them in vain, as though, I do not know by what means, he himself had been hiding [Note: Join the adjective *mitis* with the preceding verb *venit*: “What, then, will that judge say about this when he comes in terror—he who first came gently to seek and save what had been lost? What, I ask, will he say except that, as far as those children are concerned, he came in vain and sought them in vain,” as though he himself had hidden, if this can properly be said metaphorically, so that they could not be found and saved.].

In vain will he complain that he appointed ministers [Note: *Actionarii* are those who conduct the affairs of others.] to gather them from wherever they might be found; in vain will he cry out that he gave his blood for them. Suppose the bishop sinned: what did any one of those children [Note: That is, “of the infants.”] sin? What harm did Christ do to any one of them that he should suffer this? What did the Church commit?

And if you think that this must be attributed to the sin of the guilty man’s exile, let us agree that this is so. Nevertheless, you too—I am addressing the author of the deed—will not escape God’s judgment. Indeed, the pain you will feel will be all the greater because you seem to have avenged your own injury through an injury to Him, while He, by His own example, warns you [Note: Construe as follows: “Since He, who patiently continues to await your repentance because of the many similar evils you have committed—if anything similar can even be found—also awaits you in this matter which you commit daily …” Shortly afterward the common editions read *in illam*; we have corrected it to *in illum*, that is, “against the bishop.”]—He who patiently continues to await you, so that you may repent, despite the many similar evils you commit daily—not only not to refer the case against him, but not to return evil for evil to your brother (Matthew 5:44), and rather to repay evil with good, so that you might deserve to be the son of so great a Father.

Since you rejected this, see whose son you deserve to be called, since there are only two fathers, just as there are only two generations.

Perhaps, if this too may provide an opening [Note: Or, “if this too should be added.”], the prophet Elisha could have answered you when consulted about the matter: “You shall not strike him; for you did not capture him with your sword or bow in order to strike him” (2 Kings 6:22).

But whatever God may have forgiven in that punishment which, according to your own account, you inflicted on him justly, but in fact unjustly, utterly detestable to God, and wholly contrary to justice in the Christian world inasmuch as it concerned the episcopal office—just as we read happened to the thief on the cross (Luke 23:43) and to certain others who, subjected to punishment for their crimes, obtained Christ’s grace in the midst of their torments—do you really think that God will leave so great a loss to His kingdom unpunished?

Even if this man committed an offense, did you correct it by injuries? To whose judgment do you commit what you are doing? Surely to God’s, who, as is stated in Job, permits nothing to go unavenged (Job 24:12).

Even if you wish to err and, as though by pretending not to notice it, hide the matter, God is not mocked (Galatians 6:7), as the Apostle says. The proverb of the Wise Man testifies that a crime must never be avenged by a crime. For it is exceedingly shameful when the accusation is recognized in the accuser, and when a criminal condemns a criminal.

With such great and terrible thunderclaps of judgment going before the very storm of judgment, which will come in a whirlwind, I ask you not only to awaken but also to be terrified. Restrain your force, tongue, and hands from afflicting any member of the clergy, however insignificant or negligent.

Otherwise, perhaps, when God corrects them through you—as He now corrects others through others—they and the others will stand with great confidence against you, the one who afflicted them (Wisdom 5:1). And you, groaning with your companions in anguish of spirit and repenting too late, may begin to say to those who judge you sternly: “These are the ones whom we once held up to ridicule and made an object of reproach” (Wisdom 5:3).

I have wished to point these matters out to you briefly, although I could have done so at infinite length. And if, ignorant of these things, you had carelessly fallen into this most wicked and singular crime of rebellion against God, I would suffer punishment for your destruction, since, while exposing other crimes of far less danger, I would seem to have spread them by refusing to forbid this one through silence.

### 22

But to return to one of those whom we have now divided among the North [Note: The passage is corrupt and obscure. If there is no error in *Boreae*, *dimisimus* (“we dismissed”) seems preferable to *divisimus* (“we divided”), with the conjunction *et* or *vel ubi* (“and,” or “where”) supplied. Thus: “whom we have now dismissed to the North, and whom I know to govern a tetrarchy quite vigorously.” Rather, in order to soothe King Hugh, suggests by a certain rhetorical device that what he has said thus far concerning the calamities inflicted on him should not be understood as referring to that king himself, but to one of those whom, he says, “we have now dismissed to the North,” that is, to the region of the North, and whom he knows to govern a tetrarchy quite vigorously.], and whom I know to govern a tetrarchy with considerable vigor, I shall refer all these matters. I think I have introduced these points at leisure because I see that you are most Christian and have exchanged neither rule for tyranny nor power for madness.

I know that the Church still possesses teachers so numerous, so capable, and of such great stature that, if—God forbid—you were driven to conduct of this sort [Note: The common editions incorrectly read *impelleris* (“you are driven”). “Tyranny” and “madness” should be supplied, giving the sense: “There are still so many and such great teachers in the Church that, if—God forbid—you were driven by tyranny and madness of this kind, they would be able to restrain you sufficiently.”], you could be adequately restrained by them.

Woe to them, then, if either they fear you so greatly, placing you before God, although you are of the same condition as they and made of the same dust, and can do nothing except what is permitted, while for a long time you greatly surpass them in the authority of your power; or if they hate you so intensely, although you are their sheep, son, defender, advocate, and patron, and perhaps—what is still worse and more burdensome, since it is an excess arising from evil [Note: Since he is speaking of an oath, he alludes to Matthew 5. After Christ says that one should not swear at all, He adds in verse 37: “Let your speech be ‘Yes, yes,’ ‘No, no.’ Whatever is more than these comes from evil.”]—are bound to them by some kind of oath [Note: When kings were elected, they took an oath by which, among other things, they promised to preserve the goods of the Church. See the act of King Guido in Muratori, *Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, vol. II, part I.].

For most true is the judgment of Pope Clement: “To neglect one person is no less than to hate him.” And equally true is this: “Whoever,” as one of the wise men says, “can come to the aid of a person in danger but does not, kills him.”

A still worse woe threatens them if, although the Lord appointed them as dogs over the sheep (Isaiah 56:10) so that they might always defend them by barking against the attacks of wolves, they have become so mute that they not only neglect to defend those sheep [Note: Supply *neglectant*, or something similar.], but also, with their mouths most unhappily stopped by a certain man of the same order through a silence of the worst and most unheard-of kind, allow any one of their own—however weak and useless, exhausted by every kind of illness and wholly unfit for any purpose, yet still their companion, called both a dog and a shepherd—to be strangled by anyone before his own people [Col. 0271C] [Note: He indicates that he himself was afflicted in prison, while none of the bishops intervened on his behalf.].

For it has been said with complete truth in connection with this very affair [Note: He alludes to some powerful bishop who imposed silence on the other bishops so that they would not intervene for Rather. The passage should be construed thus: “So that they not only neglect to defend those sheep, but also, with their mouths most unhappily stopped by a certain man of the same order—that is, by a bishop—through a silence of the worst and most unheard-of kind, allow any one of their own … to be strangled by anyone before his own people; for it has most truly been said …”]: “He inflicted death upon the sick man who, when he could, did not prevent it.”

For if the rage that has now boiled up, as it already did, were to boil up again on this occasion, ought they not voluntarily to have offered their necks to the sword for their brother—indeed, for Christ?

Yet everyone among us is of such merciful gentleness, such obedient devotion to God, and such gracious kindness toward human beings that he does not hesitate to grant a generous and firm assent to the requests of anyone who asks, and is more likely to fall into error through ignorance than through malice.

What veil of excuse, I ask, can they possibly put forward, except that they seem wholly to neglect themselves by failing to look after their own interests? And while they perhaps allow you to be betrayed—since they permit it and desire it—they kill themselves.

I dare to say this without hesitation, and I do not think that I am mistaken in it: no one can, wishes to, or dares to offer you counsel, consent, or assistance in a crime of this kind of falling, except one who either does not know God or has denied Him; or who wishes to be a traitor to your life, kingdom, and honor—both present and future; or who, even if ignorant, either does not understand or does not remember the oath he swore to you, while he neglects it so perversely.

“Understand these things, you who forget God, lest He suddenly seize you, and there be no one to rescue you” (Psalm 50:22).

[Col. 0272B] **23.** But you, good king, most Christian prince, while you prudently guard yourself against such men and their like out of regard for him by whom you are daily raised up through prosperous successes answering your desires, henceforth conquer your enemies and preserve your citizens. Receive from foreigners, if you receive anything; give to your own. Consider carefully both that in which you stand out [*minaris*, that is, *emines*] and whose services you employ most often. Also recognize, by interpreting it between its Greek and Latin forms, your official title [variant: *officium*, “office”]: that you ought to carry the people, not oppress them.

[Note: [Col. 0272D] **King**, in Greek βασιλεύς, as though from βᾰ́σις λαοῦ, “the base” or “foundation of the people,” since he carries and supports the people like a base or foundation. You may see this same interpretation from the Greek in Saint Gregory, *Commentary on Job*, book IX, chapter XVI, no. 25.]

Be upright toward the proud, but submissive toward the humble; gentle toward all, approachable to everyone; discerning, generous, moderate; thinking about power for the sake of usefulness, but concealing it for the sake of fear. Hear Wisdom saying: “Mercy and truth preserve the king.” And again: “Take impiety from the heart of the king, and his throne will be strengthened by clemency” (Prov. XX, 28).

A common saying also seems to agree with this: he ought not to have power who does not have patience. Therefore, according to the saying of a certain wise man, love the good with justice, and pity the wicked. For, according to another proverb, the best policy is not to eradicate criminals, but crimes.

Give alms not only continually, as others do, but without interruption. I would also say something to you, but I fear that you will be angry; nevertheless, whether you do it or not, I dare not remain silent. For I fear what I heard in the Gospel yesterday: “Whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, of him the Son of Man will be ashamed when he comes in his glory and that of the Father and of the holy angels” (Luke IX, 26).

“What is it,” you ask, “that you wish to say?”

“See,” I reply, “from where you give alms, to whom, why, and how.”

From where? That is, do not take them from another:

> “For whoever offers sacrifice from the substance of the poor is like one who slaughters a son in the sight of his father” (Eccli. XXXIV, 24).

For although you are commanded to make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity (Luke XVI, 9), this does not mean that you should unjustly take from one person what you kindly give to another; rather, you should recognize that riches, however they may have been gathered [variant: may be], proceed from iniquity. For, as Jerome says, every rich person is either unjust or the heir of an unjust person. It is unjust that what God has bestowed on all in general should be gathered by some in particular. Therefore, either the gatherer is unjust, or the successor of the gatherer is the heir of an unjust person.

Both an old proverb and daily experience show that profit cannot be made without another’s loss. Thus riches are called “mammon of iniquity,” because those who gather them at the prompting of the spirit of avarice unjustly make what belongs to everyone in general their own in particular; these riches, or this profit, are called *mammon* in Punic—

[Note: [Col. 0273D] He took this from Augustine, who says in Sermon 113, chapter 2: “What is mammon? It is a word that is not Latin. It is a Hebrew word related to the Punic language . . . What the Punic people call *mammon* is called *lucrum* in Latin. What the Hebrews call *mammona* is called ‘riches’ in Latin.” Likewise, in book II of *On the Sermon on the Mount*, chapter 14: “Among the Hebrews, *mammon* is said to mean riches. The Punic name agrees with this, for profit is called *mammon* in Punic.” Hence this passage of Ratherius, which in the printed editions was given as *qui Punice illo vocatur nomine*, as though the spirit of avarice were called *mammon* in Punic, had to be corrected to *quae . . . vocatur*; for the Punic name refers to those riches, or to that profit.]

unjustly make what belongs to everyone in general their own in particular. Conversely, of one who scatters and gives to the poor it is said: “His righteousness remains forever and ever” (Ps. CX, 3).

To whom should you give? That is, first to your own people, then to everyone. For what does it accomplish [variant: *refert*, “matter”] if you leave your own herdsman naked while clothing another?

Why should you give? First, because it is your duty. You are the steward of what God has bestowed—or rather entrusted—to you; and for that reason he entrusted much to you, so that you might distribute much. Next, give for the condition and peace of your kingdom; and finally, for the past and daily crimes of both yourself and your people. For many things are done against the public interest by your people through their audacity, your authority, or their reliance upon you—things that you do not even know about.

“For,” as someone says, “the burden of a household is dangerous and exceedingly burdensome to the Lord himself if the family is morally corrupt.”

Therefore that most powerful, strongest, most just, most temperate, most prudent, and most holy king whom you too ought to imitate cried out:

> “Who understands his offenses? Cleanse me, Lord, from my hidden faults, and spare your servant from those belonging to others. If they do not rule over me, then I shall be blameless, and I shall be cleansed from the greatest offense” (Ps. XVIII, 13–14).

See how greatly he feared that offense, which he called the greatest. For, as was said before us, whatever proceeds from you returns upon you; and whatever is committed by disciples concerns the teacher.

Finally, do not wish, by relying on almsgiving, to commit future and daily crimes as well, but to erase past ones. Erase the past and beware of the future. By “future,” I mean not things I wish to come, but things that may occur unless they are guarded against.

I prefer to suggest this to you on another’s authority rather than my own, which possesses no authority beyond my office; for even if I were able to set it forth worthily, I know that you would not willingly receive it from me. For I know, as Gregory teaches, that although a person may preach what is right, one who is not loved is rarely heard willingly.

Let that Aurelius of august memory therefore be present here, soothing the ears of your heart with his ten-stringed melodies (Augustine, Sermon IX, chapter 11):

> “Exercise yourselves in mercy, in almsgiving, in fasting, and in prayers; for by these the daily sins are cleansed which, because of human frailty, can scarcely fail to creep into the soul. Do not despise them because they are small, but fear them because they are many. Pay attention, my brothers: they are small, not great. It is not a beast like a lion, which breaks the throat with one bite; yet often many small beasts kill. If someone were thrown into a place full of fleas, would he not die there? They are not larger creatures, but human nature is weak and can be destroyed even by the smallest beasts. So it is with small sins: you notice that they are small, but beware because they are many. How tiny are grains of sand! If more sand is poured into a ship, it sinks it and is destroyed. How small are raindrops! Do they not fill rivers and bring down houses? Therefore do not despise these things.

> “But you will say: ‘Who can be without them?’ Do not say this [because truly no one can be].

> [Note: In Augustine the reading is: “Do not say this (because truly no one can be). Merciful God,” etc. Since Ratherius, deprived of books in prison, copied from memory testimonies he had formerly read, he here, as sometimes elsewhere, gave some things differently through a lapse of memory. Thus he gives some expressions in the plural which Augustine gives in the singular; likewise below, “These things must be changed, so that, if you were an adulterer, you are so no longer,” whereas Augustine has, “This thing must be changed: if you were an adulterer, do not be an adulterer”; and similarly other instances, which we omit for brevity. We note this so that Ratherius’s distinctive memory may be especially demonstrated by the fact that, when he produced longer testimonies, he departed from the authentic text even in such slight and infrequent places.]

> God, in his mercy, seeing our frailty, has appointed remedies. What are the remedies? Almsgiving, fasting, and prayer. These are the three. But, if you wish to speak truthfully in prayer, almsgiving must be carried out perfectly.

> “What is perfect almsgiving? That from what you have in abundance you give to the one who has nothing, and that, even when someone injures you, you forgive him.

> “But do not suppose, brothers, that adulteries should be committed daily and cleansed by daily almsgiving. Daily almsgiving is not enough to cleanse greater crimes. It is one thing where you change your life, another where you endure life. The former must be changed: if you were an adulterer, be one no longer; if you were a fornicator, do not fornicate; if you were a murderer, do not be a murderer; if you went to a diviner or to other sacrilegious plagues, stop doing so now. Would you suppose that these things, unless they cease, can be cleansed by daily almsgiving?

> “I am speaking of those daily sins that are easily committed by the tongue, such as a harsh word, or when someone slips into immoderate laughter, or into similar daily trifles. There are sins even in things that are permitted. If, with one’s own wife, the proper measure of intercourse for begetting children is exceeded, it is a sin. For this reason a wife is taken, as the marriage contract itself indicates, where it is written: ‘for the purpose of begetting children.’ When you wish to use your wife more than the necessity of begetting children requires, it is already a sin; and daily almsgiving cleanses such sins.

> “There are sins even in food, which is certainly permitted, if perhaps you exceed the proper measure and take more than is necessary. These things I mention are daily; yet they are sins and are not insignificant. Because they are daily and very numerous, the collapse caused by their multitude must be feared.

> [Note: In the same Augustine there is added: “because they are many.” Perhaps it was not Ratherius, but Ratherius’s copyist, who passed over these words because of the repetition of *quia* (“because”). Likewise, after *multitudinis* Augustine adds: “though not in magnitude.”] Such sins, brothers, we say are cleansed by daily almsgiving.”

Again, after a little:

> “How much do you give to actors, how much to hunters, how much to disgraceful persons who kill you? Through these entertainments they kill your souls, and you rage to see who will give more. If you were raging to see who would save more, you would be intolerable. To rage over who will save more is avarice; to rage over who will give more is extravagance. God wants you to be neither avaricious nor extravagant. He wants you to invest what you have, not throw it away.

> “You compete to see who will prevail in what is worse; you do not take pains to see who is better. Would that you did not give away your possessions and say: ‘We are Christians.’

> [Note: Augustine reads: “Would that you did not give [them away], [competing] to be worse. And you say: ‘We are Christians.’] You throw away your possessions for the favor of the crowd, while against the commands you hold on to your possessions. Behold: Christ does not command; Christ asks; Christ is in need. ‘I was hungry,’ Christ says, ‘and you did not give me food’ (Matt. XXV, 42). He wished to be in need for your sake, so that you would have somewhere to sow the earthly things he gave you and reap eternal life.”

You see, my brothers, Christ’s mercy. Thanks be to God, because while alive you have heard about deadly dangers. Let no one deceive you: God hates these things; God punishes these things.

**24.** Come now, excellent prince: who would dare say these things to you today? Indeed, if I had said them, you would either call me degenerate or a *bacularius* [an official carrying a staff], or say that I was insane; I would not be able to endure your own *bromii*, and their abuse of me would know no bounds.

[Note: [Col. 0275D] *Baculares* were called attendants or apparitors, as will become clear from the notes on the conjecture concerning *Qualitas*.]

[Note: [Col. 0275D] *Bromius*, βρόμιος, is a surname of Bacchus, from the Greek βρέμω, “I roar” or “I rage.” Here it indicates men whose insults Ratherius feared. Later, in book V, no. 6, he contrasts the *bromii* with philosophers: “Those who embrace the *bromii* more dearly than philosophers.”]

Yet this was the unwavering severity of the ancients, accompanied by remarkable holiness, while the purest truth breathed through them and the most fervent charity set them aflame. They dealt with men of such a kind that there was no fear whatever that those men would become angry; rather, the men themselves were entirely glad to be advised in such matters. In the same period the emperor Theodosius of most merciful memory acted in this way . . . . .

(*Tripartite History*, book IX, chapter 30)

Thus may be fulfilled what was spoken through the prophet:

> “The Lord will destroy the head and the tail, the one who bends and the one who restrains, in one day” (Isa. IX, 14).

No one is found—as there is no one even among teachers of falsehood, nor in the assembly of the aged—who dares show you your danger, at least by some device like Nathan’s with David (II Sam. XII, 15). You are not, God forbid, a son of Belial, so that no one could speak to you; nor, thanks be to God, do I know that you wish to be numbered among those of whom it is said, as though of one person:

> “Consider the works of God, for no one can correct the one whom he has rejected” (Eccl. VII, 14).

Therefore it must be feared that, in order to obtain a perpetual “well done” at that judgment, scarcely anyone of this age will address the Lord, saying:

> [Note: The printed editions wrongly read *Domini* (“of the Lord”). Construe: “The action of scarcely anyone of this age”—that is, scarcely anyone—“will address the Lord, saying,” etc.]

> “I spoke of your testimonies before kings, and I was not ashamed” (Ps. CXVIII, 46),

after their sin has been made manifest. May God separate you from the company of those who said to the Lord God: “Depart from us” (Gen. XXVI, 16), because they did not obey his preachers, although he desired to draw them near to himself, to walk among them, dwell among them, and live with them, so that he himself might be their God and they might be his people.

[Note: [Col. 0276D] Construe as follows: “While they did not obey his preachers”—that is, the preachers of God—“who desired to draw them near to himself, to walk among them, dwell among them, and live with them, so that he might be their God and they might be the people of him who desired this,” namely, of the one who desired it.]

From these two alternatives—so that you may escape one and obtain the other—let us bring to completion what we began concerning almsgiving, so that we may then instruct you most fully about the other matters pertaining to it.

**25.** See how you should give: humbly, not proudly, lest it happen to you as it did to the Pharisees, who heard:

> “Truly I tell you, they have received their reward” (Matt. VI, 2).

For what should anyone take pride in almsgiving, since even if it were possible—for James and John testify that it is not possible, one saying, “For in many things we all offend,” and the other . . . . . (James III, 2)—the money he gives is nevertheless not his own?

[Note: [Col. 0276D] John’s text is missing here; perhaps it is the passage from the First Epistle, III, 7: “The one who does righteousness is righteous.” For the word “righteousness” is soon interpreted in connection with almsgiving. After a little, construe as follows: “Because the money that is given belongs to the one who commands that almsgiving be performed.”]

For this reason it is called righteousness, and not mercy: the money that is given belongs to the one who commands almsgiving to be performed. If you distribute it faithfully, you are crowned for righteousness; if you retain it greedily, you are condemned for righteousness; if you give it arrogantly, you are judged for fraud.

Fraud is to reduce or disperse what has been entrusted—not according to the will of the one who entrusted it, but according to one’s own will and for one’s own favor. And if [understand: if almsgiving] is performed for sins, and one then takes pride in it, it is as though a sick person were to squander his substance on physicians and, driven into delirium, were to rejoice that illness had brought him to this necessity, . . . . . and count as good what is necessity—or rather madness—when it would be better for him to possess his wealth while healthy than to lose it while sick.

**26.** Do not think that I say this because I wish in any way to diminish good works, as though I were asserting that giving alms for sins has no merit. I do not assert this; rather, as far as I can, I argue against it. For what greater merit can a sinner have than the blessedness obtained through the forgiveness of sins?

> “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven and whose sins have been covered” (Ps. XXXI, 1).

Therefore the person who gives alms for sins does not lose his substance, since, as is rightly apparent, he received it for this purpose [the reference is to the substance], provided that he acquired it not through some evil but through labor or skill; and provided that he gives alms. Yet even in this the mercy of the one who seeks and came to save what had perished (Luke XIX, 10) is not absent.

For that great model of such persons is present: Zacchaeus, great in grace though small in stature. He is present, I say, crying out, but inspired:

> “Behold, Lord, I give half of my goods to the poor; and if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold” (Luke XIX, 8).

“But who knows,” you ask, “whether this action pleased him?”

[Note: The printed editions incorrectly read *novum* (“new”) for *novit* (“knows”).]

The evangelist added:

> “Jesus said to him: ‘Today salvation has come to this house, because he too is a son of Abraham’” (Luke XIX, 9),

a son by imitation, certainly, not by descent. For just as Abraham left Chaldea at God’s command (Gen. XII), so this beloved servant of God renounced avarice.

I repeat: the person who gives alms for sins does not lose his substance; rather, from it he obtains forgiveness, through God’s grace extinguishes hell for himself, and prepares eternal life.

But the person who gives for the sake of empty glory loses his substance; rather, he acquires punishment and God’s anger for himself: punishment because of fraud, anger because of pride.

What fraud? The fraud already described: appropriating as one’s own what was entrusted, and dispersing it according to the desire of one’s own exaltation, when in doing this, after reckoning the entire sum, he will gain nothing from it except empty wind—that is, the favor of flatterers—and perhaps he will not even find that, although he sought it with all his striving.

But he does find the anger of God that he provokes, and he makes an enemy of the one whom by that act he ought to have reconciled to himself. For:

> “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James IV, 6).

**27.** Besides these, there is a fifth form of almsgiving, to which a sixth—much superior to the others—is added: the forgiveness of a brother’s offense. A seventh follows, when with pious exhortation we offer nourishment in the word to one who is ignorant.

I prefer, after briefly touching on the following points, to present them not in my own words but in those of the person whom I introduced earlier, lest you say that I fabricated them for my own sake.

[Note: “For my own sake,” he says, because what follows is suited to the wretched condition in which Ratherius was distressed.]

He says in this sense and in these words:

> “Mercy is rightly owed to all who are in need; but a greater movement of compassion is stirred when suffering casts some person from wealth and nobility into the lowest condition and the necessity of poverty.”

You have here brief but sufficiently prudent instructions on giving alms. Let us pass to the remaining matters.

**28.** Yet a saying presses upon my mind, one that I learned from a child, although I think it was not first invented in a childish way; for besides being exceedingly wise, it is also exceedingly true.

In my hearing, a certain little boy was jokingly asked by someone, “Whose man is the king?” Without any hesitation he immediately replied: “The man whose works he does.”

Although this caused me no small astonishment at the time, I learned from someone else that the proverb was celebrated in sermons. I turned to God and prayed that you too might hear it in the same way that I had, so that, comparing it with the Lord’s word—“No one can serve two masters” (Matt. VI, 34)—and also remembering that it is written, “Whoever commits sin is the slave of sin” (John VIII, 34), and that “by whatever a person is overcome, by that he is also enslaved” (II Pet. II, 19), you might flee not only the worst master but also vindicate your nobility by your conduct, resist him with an upright neck, disdain to be subject to him, and strive to belong entirely to the best Master.

You should strive to be the man of no other than the one who made you a human being—or rather, who made you excel other human beings—by doing his works.

For we know that you must be more carefully on your guard than others, lest, when the king of Babylon has killed your sons—which we fear—namely, when he has destroyed the offspring of good thoughts and works whom you have begotten for God, or when those entrusted to you have been lost through your fault or example at Riblah, interpreted as “this road leading many to destruction,” the broad and spacious road of this age, as it is also called by the Lord (Matt. VII, 13)—lest, while you do not raise your arm against that king of Babylon on behalf of your slain offspring, repenting, that is, of your offenses, changing your conduct for the better, and taking up the weapons of righteousness, you should, deprived by the advance of impious domination even of your eyesight, be thrust by him into prison, so that, like Samson—

[Note: [Col. 0277D] Unless this text is considered mutilated, *ne quando rex* should be corrected to *ne quando a rege*. This is an involved and syntactically very difficult passage, in which the allegory of King Zedekiah is pursued. His sons were killed by the king of Babylon, while he himself was blinded and led away captive. The passage should be construed as follows: “You must beware lest, when the king of Babylon has killed your sons”—that is, when he has scattered the offspring of good thoughts and works, if you have begotten any for God, or when those entrusted to you have been lost through your fault or example at Riblah, which is interpreted as “this many-leading-to-destruction road,” also called by the Lord the broad and spacious road of this age—“you should, while not raising your arm against him,” namely, against the king of Babylon, “on behalf of your slain offspring,” that is, repenting of your offenses, changing your conduct for the better, and taking up the weapons of righteousness—“be thrust by him into prison, deprived even of your eyes,” and so on.]

that man, although exceedingly strong, weakened by the seductions of women, you may be assigned to the mill (Judg. XVI, 19–21), whose wheel the wicked go around (Ps. XI, 9). With the sight of reason taken from you—the sight by which you ought to have foreseen the needs of yourself and those entrusted to you—you may enter, without foresight, the prison of eternal perdition.

For it often happens to the most wretched soul that, while its virtues gradually fail day by day, it does not raise the shoulders of its mind to restore itself to its former or at least a better condition. As misery increases, it reaches the point where, with sin reigning in its mortal body (Rom. VI, 12), it becomes so subject to its desires that, deprived even of the light of reason, it neither recalls what has been done nor sees what must be done.

Lest this happen to you, drive the demon [not: the Lord] from your heart by resisting those desires with the greatest strength. Take upon yourself Christ’s easy yoke and his light burden. Make those subject to you serve under him by prudent governance, not only through commands but through examples, so that you may merit to reign without end with them.

[Note: [Col. 0279D] The printed editions incorrectly read “the Lord.”]

And do not, I beg you, disregard that wholesome, though very small, instruction uttered above by a child, since, as today’s solemnity reminds us—

[Note: [Col. 0279D] The solemnity does not indicate the feast of the saints generally, but the feast of the Holy Innocents, on which this was written. That the feast celebrated in the year 935 is indicated is clear because the author certainly composed this book after book II had been completed in September of that same year and before the following book was written at the beginning of 936. Compare notes 102 and 189 of this volume.]

—you should know that even the testimony of those who cannot speak has pleased God himself.

**29.** Nor, as we now resume the journey we have undertaken, should you think that you are permitted to carry out everything that your will suggests to your heart.

When you hear that “the heart of the king is in the hand of God” (Prov. XXI, 1), know that this can be understood in three ways, as far as we have been able to investigate: the first applies to you, the second to your subjects, and the following one generally to everyone. The last is the one that must be held more firmly and observed more carefully.

To speak of the first, know that your heart is in God’s hand. You should then understand that he directs it when you strive to receive in your heart what he commands and to fulfill it in action.

By “heart” we do not mean that bodily part lying beneath the ribs, which is so called and from which the streams of the veins are known to proceed. We mean that power by which thoughts are formed. As the ancients understood, and as the great Father Augustine also said, it is called by this name because, just as the motion by which the pulse is diffused everywhere through the veins does not cease in the heart, so we do not cease to turn something over in thought.

With this whole heart, therefore—that is, with this power of the soul—we are commanded to love God. From this too come the terms *excordes* (“heartless”), *concordes* (“of one heart”), *discordes* (“of divided heart”), *vecordes* (“mad”), and *socordes* (“foolish” or “dull-hearted”).

Hence it is said to some:

> “Return to your heart, transgressors” (Isa. XLVI, 8),

so that they may understand that they are driven by madness, not ruled by the heart, since, wishing to establish their own will, they disdain to submit themselves to the will of God, who loves nothing except what is just and good (Rom. X, 3). They do not turn their heart to God for this purpose; rather, they fill their heart with madness opposed to God.

[Note: [Col. 0280D] Construe as follows: “So that they may understand that they are driven by madness, not ruled by the heart . . . and that they do not turn their heart to God for this purpose”—this refers to what follows, “The heart of the king is in the hand of God; he will turn it wherever he wishes”—“but fill their heart with madness opposed to God.”]

Recognize that this is also said for a second reason: so that no one may fear your anger more than is proper or court your favor more than is proper:

> “It is better to hope in the Lord than to hope in princes” (Ps. CXVII, 9);

and, as another prophet says, the person who places his hope in a human being is accursed (Jer. XVII, 5).

Likewise:

> “I am the Lord, forming light and creating darkness, making peace and creating evil” (Isa. XLV, 7).

By saying, “The heart of the king is in the hand of God; he will turn it wherever he wishes” (Prov. XXI, 1), he wishes to warn everyone that you can accomplish nothing in anger except what God himself permits, nor grant anything when appeased except what he himself wishes.

Therefore he wishes only himself to be feared, only himself to be loved, and nothing at all to be attributed—or still less preferred—to himself. This has been beautifully and briefly expressed by the apostle:

> “Fear God; honor the king” (I Pet. II, 17).

As though he were saying: Fear the Lord; honor his servant.

But why do I weaken the statement by changing the verb? He said, “Fear God; honor the king,” and, I suppose, not casually. You are made honored by the services of others, although in your own nature you are of the same condition as they are.

To be powerful, you must know with complete truth that it depends not on you but on the hands of those who serve. Hence you fear more the people whom you terrify.

Avienus says that one should measure oneself [printed: *quemquam dicit, ut*; emended: *quisquam debet, ut*] and be helped by one’s own praises, not bear the good things of another, that is, not count them as one’s own.

See, then, that he by whose commands you are honored is also honored by your services. While using the goods of others, do not prove ungrateful to the giver.

For after saying elsewhere, “Be subject to every human creature” (I Pet. II, 13), he immediately added, “for God’s sake.” That is: honor the creature for the sake of the Creator; submit to the created thing, not out of love for the thing made, but out of love for its maker. “Whether to the king,” he says, “as to one who is pre-eminent” (ibid.), meaning, for God’s sake.

The point is that he should recognize with what reverence he himself ought to be subject to the Creator, since such reverence is shown to him by a creature of the same nature.

What may the Lord of all rightly demand for himself [printed *exigit*; emended *exigat*], when a servant of the same nature appears to demand so much from his fellow servants?

Fear God; honor the king. Fear the Lord who chastises; honor the king through whom [emended reading: *quem*, “whom”] you are corrected by him. Fear the patron; honor the staff by which you are sustained. Revere the father, and do not despise the teacher who instructs you. Tremble at the father’s voice, and do not scorn the guardian’s person.

**30.** Thus it is said:

> “The heart of the king is in the hand of God; he will turn it wherever he wishes” (Prov. XXI, 1),

just as it is said:

> “The Lord has done all that he wished in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the abysses” (Ps. CXXXIV, 6);

and:

> “In his hand are all the ends of the earth” (Ps. XCXIV, 4).

The whole substance of these citations, unless I am mistaken, comes to this conclusion: whatever happens, whatever has happened, whatever will happen—whether it is a thing, a body, an action, or a passion—is done, ordered, and accomplished by him as he disposes, wills, commands, helps, completes, assents, grants, or permits. Nothing can happen to a human being, an angel, any beast, any breeze, any element, a serpent, a worm, or even a fly without his nod, will, and power making it possible.

From this also follows what the wise have already defined and hold most firmly: as the person mentioned above says with considerable wit, only a thoroughly purified soul can perceive it—namely, that everything is governed by such great providence and justice of God that nothing, not even death itself, can happen unjustly to anyone, even if an unjust person appears to inflict it.

Among natures, there is none that is not from him. Among wills, there is no good will that does not benefit from him, and no evil will that he cannot use well.

For, as that same blessed and most eloquent teacher Augustine says most clearly, it is certainly believed that divine providence rules over all creatures in two ways: granting existence to natures, but granting wills the condition that they can do nothing without his command or permission.

Both points are most clearly evident in Job’s sufferings. He is said to have received the blows both undeservedly and not undeservedly, both by the Lord’s own assertion and, though the expression is fitting, by another’s utterance. The devil had taken everything from him, yet he said:

> “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has happened” (Job I, 21).

It is certain that nothing except what is just pleases the Lord. The adversary himself, who uniquely exalts himself against God, attributes no power to his own wickedness but to the Lord’s power, when he says:

> “Stretch out your hand and touch all that he possesses” (ibid., 11).

We have heard what the Lord says about the smallest living creatures:

> “Are not two sparrows sold for an assarion? And not one of them will fall to the ground without your Father” (Matt. X, 29).

What wonder, then, if the heart of a king—or of any other human being—is in God’s hand, when even the feather of the smallest flying creature is in his hand? Or what is not held in his hand, who measures heaven with a span and contains the earth in his fist (Isa. XL, 12)?

Therefore do not arrogantly wish to claim for yourself alone what all creatures are known to have received in general: that your heart is solely in God’s hand. Outside his hand, if anything exists, it is undoubtedly lost; indeed, I boldly say that it does not exist.

For it was said to him:

> “You hate none of the things that you have made” (Wis. XI, 25);

and the apostle says:

> “From him are all things, through him are all things” (I Cor. VIII, 6).

To believe that his hand—that is, his power—is something other than himself is not merely foolish; it is madness beyond comparison. For in him, to know, to be able, to will, to live, and to understand are the same as to be.

31. But lest, while you are undertaking something, you unjustly say that God turns your heart toward it, know with complete certainty that he wills nothing evil and impels no one’s heart toward any crime, but that it is the devil and one’s own will that do so. The same man who shortly before made this point, and no one more wittily, continued in Letter 166, no. 5, to Jerome, saying:

> I am certain that the soul has fallen into sin through no fault of God, no necessity imposed by God or by itself, but through its own will.

Yet I do not deny—indeed, I affirm—that God, by his hidden but never unjust judgment, sometimes permits even what he does not will, as we have already said in many ways. Why this happens at times, beyond what I said above on the matter, the Apostle explains in his Letter to the Romans:

> Because, although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God (Rom. 1:21);

and:

> Therefore God gave them over to a debased mind, to do what is unfitting [or: what is not fitting] (ibid., 28).

Here I earnestly warn you not to understand this as meaning that God hands anyone over to evil. When he says “he gave them over,” supply “that is, he permitted them to be handed over,” just as he says, “I hardened Pharaoh’s heart” (Exod. 4:21), that is, “I permitted it to be hardened.” And David says, “If God stirs you up”—that is, “allows you to be stirred up.” Concerning Shimei: “Leave him, that he may curse; for the Lord has commanded him to curse David” (2 Sam. 16:10): “commanded” means “permitted.” And in prayer we say every day, “Do not lead us into temptation” (Matt. 6:13), that is, “Do not allow us to be led into it,” and similarly in the other passages of this kind.

Therefore, when you do something good, ascribe it to God; when you do something evil, blame yourself. For he habitually does many good things—not because of any merit of ours, but through his own goodness—not only through us but even from our evil deeds, just as we, conversely, do many evil things from his gifts.

This being so, no one’s favor should be courted with God abandoned, nor should any power be feared, even if there is some power that exalts itself above a king. Only that power is to be embraced above all, and only that power is to be feared, which compels whatever it wishes to serve whatever purposes it wishes, even those things it does not love. Under its governance, all things have not been left in their own possession [Note: That is, they have not been left to possess themselves, namely, in their own control; for God knows how to turn those very evils toward good.]. In its praise a certain wise orator speaks most wisely:

> For you know, Lord, that you can do good even through the wicked, since, when you have turned toward aid what had been prepared to cause harm, you judge it better to turn injuries [Vulgate: evil, the injury] to usefulness than to cut away the causes of evils at the root.

But if I wished to gather together everything that arises here, or could arise if it were investigated in detail, I confess that a week would run out, let alone that a single day would suffice.

32. As we approach the third mode of understanding this sentence, let us bring forward the very method that we used above in order to explain it. Thus, when he explains in two ways that verse of the Psalm in which some say, “My soul is continually in my hands” (Ps. 118:109), while others read, “in your hands”—rejecting neither the former interpretation but choosing the latter for himself—the first seeming to belong to those who speak with confidence, the second to those who rely solely on God’s mercy—he says:

> The prophet knows where to place the protection of his soul and from where to hope for help. He wishes to place his soul in God’s hands, because the king’s heart is in God’s hand. Whoever has subdued his own body and, with fitting vigor in governing himself, has not permitted his soul to be disturbed by its passions, restraining himself well by royal power, is called a king because he knows how to rule himself, so that he is not dragged captive into guilt nor carried headlong into vice.

Another, more elegant in proportion as he is more concise, says:

> If you are ruled by your mind, you are a king; if by your body, a slave.

Another man likewise says:

> “Have [perhaps: ‘Have, O king’] honor; I shall give you great authority, and rule yourself.”

This is also why, in common usage, a road that is ancient and straight is called royal; and the gate through which one enters the palace is called royal, signifying that whatever proceeds rightly and by its own example shows others the road of an upright journey and a blessed dwelling is royal.

For, as the etymology of the name itself suggests, the word *king* (*rex*), derived from *straight* (*rectus*), shows that he must do nothing except what is straight, lest his conduct disagree with his name. What wonder, then, if any good soul that rightly governs its own body is properly called royal, since a road that leads rightly is called royal, and a gate through which one does not ascend by some other route but enters lawfully is also called royal?

Moreover, another translation shows that what often gives considerable arrogance to those who misunderstand it, from the Book of Proverbs—“Divination is in the king’s heart; his mouth shall not err in judgment” (Prov. 16:10)—is to be understood rather of the king [that is, God, the King of kings], saying:

> Nothing false will be said to the King, and nothing false will come from his mouth;

for, as Bede also explains, he can neither be deceived by anyone who lies nor ever lie himself.

In the joy of that king there is also life, because all who at that supreme judgment are deemed worthy to see his joyful face will be granted to live with him forever. Concerning them, in his exposition of the preceding sentence, he also says:

> Why does he say that the king’s heart is in God’s hand, and not rather the hearts of all human beings, since it is written, “In his hand are all the ends of the earth” (Ps. 94:4), unless he calls anyone a king who knows how to conquer within himself the battles of vices and to be surrounded by the warfare of virtues? For just as the Lord, by the many divisions of the waters, fills the ends of the earth and the air far and wide at once, and also covers the upper regions of the heavens with waters (Ps. 103:3), so he inclines the king’s heart wherever he wishes. For just as he distributes the divisions of grace to angels and human beings according to his will, so he renders the hearts of the saints worthy through whatever gifts he wills; nor does he leave any place for the Pelagianist claim that anyone can be saved without God’s grace (1 Cor. 12:4).

33. But, so that these matters may now suffice, although they are slight and supported by the great authority of those who have spoken, I shall still offer you a few principles for living, and then, leaving you, shall proceed to other matters. Above all I say this: it is right that you ought to obey the laws. Know that your rights must be preserved for you by human beings if you also show them reverence. For, as Isidore says, you are bound by your own laws; and you yourself must not condemn your own laws by acting against the ordinances that you establish for your subjects. The authority of your word is just if you do not allow yourself to do what you forbid the people.

As the truthful proverb says, the one whom many fear ought to fear many. And, to address you in the words already spoken, I warn you to know that secular princes sometimes hold within the Church the heights of authority they have acquired, so that through that same authority they may strengthen ecclesiastical discipline. Indeed, powers within the Church would not be necessary unless the power were to command through the terror of discipline what the priest is unable to accomplish through the word of instruction. Behold what power has been granted to you in the affairs of the Church, and why.

34. Therefore, lest you fall away from your ministry, restore the churches of God after the example of your predecessors; raise up the monasteries and enrich them with resources. For perhaps a time will come when those resources themselves will be expended for your salvation.

Ask which of the earlier kings proceeded justly or wisely; which sought to do the will of God more fully; which ruled the people rightly; which built churches, founded monasteries, or established hospices. Embrace that king, follow him, imitate him. Take care that no one should ever persuade you to remove anything from these institutions for the use of yourself or your people. Know with complete certainty that, if they will have a reward for what they gave, you will have punishment for what you took away; if they purchased eternal life by giving, you acquire hell by taking away.

For the Church’s possessions are fiery. You can neither give alms from them nor eat or drink from them unless it is either by the Church’s gift or through your sacrilege. You do not need to be taught what he deserves according to the laws, since you have been appointed by God and by the people as the avenger of such matters.

Know, however, that you have been appointed the advocate of God’s Church, not its master—for no one can rule over his mother except absurdly; its guardian, not its steward, though you should know that, according to the Lord’s teaching (Luke 12:42), the steward is a bishop; its patron, not its minister. If you read the Gospel, you can find the Lord himself saying that he too is the same [Note: “Whom”—namely, the steward—you should know, according to the Lord’s teaching, to be the bishop, the patron and not the minister; and you can find, if you read, that the Lord himself also said that he was this same bishop.].

[Note: The Vulgate has *Domini*—“of the Lord”—incorrectly.]

Beware lest, if you wish to usurp more than has been entrusted to you, you be compelled to pay the penalty for your seizure at the judgment. Hear the Lord, so that you may also understand this literally, saying in the Gospel:

> Do not give what is holy to dogs (Matt. 7:6).

Hear that same Lord proclaiming through the Law:

> Whatever is offered to the Lord is most holy and belongs to the right of the priests (Num. 18:9).

Therefore see to it, whether you or anyone else [that is, the priests], that you do not give to dogs what has been contributed for feeding the poor or sustaining the priests.

35. Amid these matters, love your wife and flee the company of concubines. That practice belonged to an earlier age because of the scarcity of human beings; but when the necessity has ceased, what was done because of necessity ought also to cease, especially since we know that the new man gave new commandments (John 13:34).

Choose for yourself ministers and counselors who are found to love not what belongs to you but you yourself. Choose them not merely as well-mannered men but as friends—that is, guardians of your soul—who will correct you in mercy and rebuke you, and will not caress your head, that is, your mind, with the oil of harmful or deadly flattery.

Beware also the deceitfulness of informers. Remember that through their fraud the innocence of many has already been proscribed. To mention even one of them as a warning, know that Joseph was imprisoned while innocent (Gen. 39:20). You will recognize, on the testimony of Hegesippus, that such men will never be lacking if you wish to be credulous toward them.

Take care lest, while you seek to be called pious in edicts, letters, or decrees, you appear impious in your deeds. And, to venture still to touch on some secular matters:

> Blush, Sidon—for the sea itself has spoken (Isa. 23:4).

Pay attention also, I beg you, to what the poet says to you in a satire:

> When at last the long-awaited province  
> Received you as its governor, put a bridle on anger,  
> Put a limit also on greed, and pity the poor and your allies.

He says “allies,” not slaves, not subjects. For, according to the Apostle, “we are all one in Christ” (Rom. 12:5).

But I shall now try to leave you, lest I appear to wish to criticize someone’s character. At the same time, even if late, I must remember that I ought not to swim against the current.

35. Are you a queen? Besides countless other examples, you also have many models that suit you and were set before you above: Helena, Constantine’s mother, after Mary the mother of Christ; Queen Radegund, who was also a virgin; Clotild, the wife of Clovis; and Placilla, the wife of Theodosius. If you wish to imitate these women, you will be able to obtain both the scepters of the present kingdom here happily and, there—where they have already gone before you—if you do not disdain to follow them, the rewards of the heavenly kingdom most happily.

# HERE BEGINS THE FIFTH BOOK

[Col. 0285]

It may happen that someone wonders why, after proposing to test the neighboring waves in the three-prowed boat of our volumes, we have [Note: On this matter he says *qua de re* instead of *quare* or *cur*. The construction is: “Since I had proposed to test the neighboring waves in the three-prowed boat of the volumes”—that is, in the three preceding books—“perhaps someone may wonder why, or for what reason, amid this sea of such enormous breadth which, with God’s gift, we have swum across”—namely, in Book Four—“we have entered a small boat, or have allowed unequal ships to depart from the remaining shores.”] entered a small boat amid such an enormous expanse, which, by God’s favor, we have crossed, allowing unequal ships to depart from the remaining shores.

But let him know that, apart from the inappropriateness of the time, the discordance of the winds above all demanded this. The matter required not merely one or two but many helmsmen who could guide our ship cautiously and directly across the waters, with the reefs broken. For while the ship of our discourse rejoiced that it had now escaped the sea, nearby Charybdis warned it to give its arms once more to the oars that break the waves.

The work was so timely for all these misfortunes that it seems remarkable not that our helmsman suffered shipwreck, but rather that he escaped alive—if indeed he escaped. But, with Christ as our guide, let us now undertake this bay of the sea, unequal though it is, yet by no means small.

Perhaps even here he has suffered [or perhaps will suffer] some danger, from which the all-powerful Pilot may free our little boat. Therefore, while the sea is still calm and somewhat gentle, let us call many companions and pray that they take up the oars and drive them across the waters, so that the desired vessel may more quickly touch the shores, returning our nautical friend, rescued from death, to our watching eyes.

Come, then! Give new aid, O God, and enter into our minds [that is, grant that our distinguished course of discourse may not deviate from you in anything].

2. Are you a bishop? The very name, I beg you, should admonish you and teach you your office. Let so great a dignity correspond to you; consider ancient things and set present things in order. Consider how lofty, how holy, how ancient is the name that you bear.

See your sacrifice accepted in Abel (Gen. 4:4), your purity transferred in Enoch (Gen. 5:24), and yourself preserved in Noah on account of righteousness (Gen. 6:8). Understand the ark as the Church (ibid., 14), the living creatures as the various kinds of human beings distinguished by their dispositions [Note: Understand “living creatures” as kinds of human beings distinguished by their different dispositions.], and the Flood as the world (Gen. 7:7); keep watch against shipwreck.

Whenever tranquility is granted, beware lest drunkenness creep in. Consider that Melchizedek offered bread and wine (Gen. 14:18) and prefigured your royal priesthood. Abraham pleased God by faith (Gen. 15:6), by which you live—if indeed you live justly—and he was a priest, as you also are, if indeed you are what you are called.

What are Isaac and Rebekah except the Lord and the Church? (Gen. 24:67.) Finally, after he had been offered because he willed it, he often offered sacrifices, fed the flock, and dug wells. When foreigners filled them, he did not delay digging others again, laboring for himself and instructing you, so that through continual sacrifices—that is, through the mortification of the flesh and contrition of the heart—you may offer yourself daily to the Lord God on the altar of your mind.

Commend your priesthood to the one from whom you received it. Dig wells—that is, draw out the hidden things of Scripture from the depths of its mysteries and offer them to your rational sheep, lest the thirst of ignorance kill them.

When Jacob placed his head on a stone and raised that same stone as a monument after pouring oil over it (Gen. 28:18), does he not reveal to you most clearly [Note: This period is very long and obscure. The construction is: “Does he not reveal to you most clearly that, when you sleep free from secular cares or activities, you ought through contemplation to place the head of your mind upon Christ, so that you may deserve to behold the ascent and descent of the angels—that is, where the divine utterances rise above the heavens? But where, by descending to us so that they can in some manner be grasped, they accommodate themselves to our understanding, you ought to understand them in their humility; and finally you ought to pour upon that stone the oil of mercy and fraternal compassion. This means that you should always exalt mercy above judgment, so that you too may deserve to obtain the same mercy from the Lord. Christ himself ought to be the head of your actions—that is, their beginning and end, the hope, crown, title, and emblem of all your glory—as though upon the ramparts of a noble citadel: that is, while remaining sober, and so forth.”], that, when you are free from secular cares or activities and sleep in contemplation, you ought to place the head of your mind upon Christ, so that you may deserve to behold the ascent and descent of the angels—that is, where the divine utterances rise above the heavens. But where, by descending to us so that they can be grasped in some fashion, they accommodate themselves to our understanding, you ought to understand them in their humility. Finally, you ought to pour upon that stone the oil of mercy and fraternal compassion, which means that you should always exalt mercy above judgment (James 2:13), so that you too may deserve to obtain it from the Lord.

Christ himself ought to be the head of your actions—that is, their beginning and end—and the hope, crown, title, and emblem of all your glory, as though upon the ramparts of a noble [the text reads *sibilis*, perhaps *nobilis*, “noble”] citadel. This means that, remaining sober with your brothers but rapt in mind toward God, if you boast of anything, you should boast in the Lord (1 Cor. 1:31).

Finally, Jacob supplanted his brother, fed flocks, and took two wives—of whom the elder was bleary-eyed but fertile, while the younger was beautiful in appearance but infertile in conception. Whom did he teach in all these things more than you? He taught you to outwit the devil’s cunning through prudent foresight; through the exercises of active life and pastoral care to produce abundant fruits of works; and, through the intention of heavenly contemplation, always to cling to God by seeking, understanding, and loving the things that belong to contemplation.

For these two things are suited to no order so equally as to pontifical excellence.

What else does Joseph’s long, many-colored tunic signify except the insignia of your priesthood? Whom does Job, offering sacrifice for his sons on the eighth day and sanctifying them by blessing them in word and deed, instruct more fittingly than you? Moses himself is known to be almost wholly yours. You will find nothing in his words or deeds which, if you understand it correctly, you will not be compelled to imitate either literally or spiritually.

What need is there to go through Aaron and his sons, Joshua, Samson, and all the judges of Israel, as well as Samuel, obtained through prayers, nurtured in the temple, and adorned with all the insignia of ecclesiastical office, when the deeds of their persons and the very names of their offices proclaim, instruct, and reveal your character, your rights, and the insignia of your priesthood?

Let us come to that most holy prophet David, most powerful king, strongest warrior, most warlike [the text has *pugnatissimum*, perhaps *pugnacissimum*, “most combative”] soldier, and priest most acceptable to God. What among all that is read about him fails to teach you what you should do, either spiritually or morally, even in those matters that appear reprehensible according to the letter?

Finally, he fed the flock, killed a bear and a lion, and struck down the giant with a slingstone (1 Sam. 17:49); he calmed the demon by the sound of the psaltery (1 Sam. 16:23); he spared his enemy (1 Sam. 24:7; 26:9); he fled from his son (2 Sam. 15:14); and he danced before the ark of the Lord (2 Sam. 6:14). What do you understand morally and spiritually in all these actions except the strength of an ecclesiastical shepherd, courage, the benefits of prayers, patience, the practices of divine worship, and finally the patterns of right preaching and priestly life?

What have Solomon and all the kings of Judah and Israel taught, through all their good deeds and through the anointing itself, more especially than you? Why should we run through the prophets, when you ought to imitate the prophets, expound the prophets, and yourself also be a prophet? For, as the Lord testifies, you ought to bring forth new and old things from the treasure of your heart (Matt. 13:52).
