What does that exceptionally strong wing of the Maccabees, in all its battles and successes of victory, proclaim except your daily struggle against visible and invisible enemies through prayer, preaching, and pious action, promising you the palm of triumph and the prize after victory?

These examples are from the Old Testament, so that you may recognize and embrace the antiquity of your ministry.

3. But in the New Testament, what language could say, or what understanding grasp, how many guides to living are available to you? Here, as I think, I address you more appropriately and entrust everything to your diligence. Search the Scriptures; turn over the books of divine speech; look to the apostles; see the martyrs; attend to the confessors; contemplate even the virgins who conquered both the world and their sex.

Consider the many witnesses of God renewed against you, according to Job (Job 10:17). While they walk with you along this road of the present journey, make peace with them for the good of both yourself and them, and teach others to do likewise. Otherwise you will not deserve to be what you are called.

4. Finally, look at the weight that presses upon you; weigh the burden that you seem to carry. And even if you are already good, holy, just, and entirely blameless, nevertheless consider your people and carefully attend to those entrusted to you, to see whether they too are such.

For you will not be presented to the Lord alone, as others are, but together with the whole flock. Nor will you have to render an account only of the deeds of your own body, according to what you have done (2 Cor. 5:10), but also of the entire people entrusted to you.

But if you happen to be presented alone—speaking mildly, so as to say nothing more severe—where will your “Well done” be [Note: “Your ‘Well done’” is the same as your blessing and reward. It refers to Christ’s words to the faithful servant: “Well done, good and faithful servant; enter into the joy of your Lord” (Luke 19:23)]?

Lest you lack it, listen carefully to the Book of Wisdom, crying out and giving counsel:

> My son, if you have become surety for your friend, you have pledged your hand to a stranger. Do therefore what is useful for you, and free yourself, because you have fallen into the hands of your neighbor. Run, hasten, rouse your friend; do not give sleep to your eyes, nor slumber to your eyelids (Prov. 6:1–4).

Hear the Lord crying out to you through Ezekiel:

> I have appointed you as a watchman for the house of Israel (Ezek. 3:17),

and so forth. In the same book, hear Jeremiah also lamenting you in the Lamentations—words against which nothing is more threatening:

> The children asked for bread, and there was no one to break it for them (Lam. 4:4).

Let at least this thunder of judgment awaken you:

> Wicked and lazy servant, why did you not put my money on the table, so that when I came I might at least have demanded it with interest? (Luke 19:23).

These words are for the sluggish and negligent.

5. But what reproach do we think awaits those who, although they have received no money of instruction, boast shamelessly and with a brazen face of a talent not granted to them as though it had been granted; who burst forth everywhere to be called shepherds, although they know nothing of the pastures of life, and wish to appear stewards of the Lord’s substance, although they plainly suffer from the plague of famine?

What, I ask, does one distribute who receives nothing? What does one give who has nothing? What does one administer who lacks everything?

When the master of the household says, “Feed my sheep” (John 21:17), from where, I ask, does the man feed them who has not yet found the pasture himself?

Since the one whom the Lord placed over his household ought to be a faithful and prudent steward, so that he may give it its measure of wheat at the proper time (Luke 12:42), what does the man administer who, hungry and foolish, struggles with the very thing that ought to be administered? What wheat does he distribute who utterly does not know what wheat is?

Here I greatly fear with you lest you should hear:

> Friend, for what purpose have you come, or how did you enter here? (Matt. 22:12)

Through what door? By what gate? By what merits? By what privilege? By virtue, wisdom, or learning? Or perhaps, although the grace of preaching was lacking, did the innocence of your life commend you?

Did I not foretell to you what you could also see with your bodily eyes, saying:

> Can a blind man lead a blind man? Will they not both fall into a pit? (Luke 6:39)

What did you attempt that suited you? Why did you undertake so heavy a yoke when you could not even carry yourself? And since you did not know how to hold the reins of your own life, why did you seek to become judge of another’s?

How could that wise man not persuade you, the one who said:

> Do not concern yourself with a matter that does not belong to you.

Where, I ask, were your ears when it was said:

> Do not seek what is above you (Ecclus. 3:22)?

Where had you read that the task was beyond your strength—not merely for you, but for all who are under heaven, immeasurably superior to you in wisdom, speech, and virtue, as those accustomed to converse with God [Note: It seems that the text should read *utpote Dei colloquiis assueti*, so that the sense is sufficiently clear: “as those accustomed to the conversations of God, who are immeasurably superior in wisdom, speech, and virtue to all who are under heaven.”]?

How did that Gospel saying sound to you, and how did it fail to move you, frighten you, and turn you back from what you had begun?

> Cut it down; why does it even occupy the ground? (Luke 13:7)

What were you thinking about yourself when you heard me complain:

> Those who held the law did not know me (Jer. 2:8)?

What did the Psalm persuade you, saying:

> They have neither known nor understood; they walk in darkness; all the foundations of the earth will be shaken (Ps. 81:5)?

And when, because of ignorance, you did not know how to bear not only others but even yourself with steadfastness of character, how did you suppose that it could happen that, with the burden of the whole house of God placed upon you, what had been built above it would not certainly fall when the foundation was shaken? [The text is uncertain here: perhaps *quid tibi, et subaudi irretito*, “what did it [or what did you suppose], with the implication ‘for you, entangled as you were…’?”]

6. These matters, although extremely serious in themselves, appear light in comparison with more serious ones. Touching upon those graver matters in part, and not presenting them altogether as they are—for they surpass not only our eloquence but even the judgment of the most talkative people—what torment do we think awaits those who not only neglect the flock entrusted to them, even if they appear suited to feed it, but also never cease, in the madness of so great a name that they bear, to drive themselves over the precipices of vice?

They are continually occupied with secular games, hunting, and seductive bird-catching;

> Accustomed in Teutonic fashion to hurl *cateiae* [printed *catcias*].  
> (Virgil, *Aeneid* 7.141.)

they become completely unaccustomed to the sacred Scriptures;

they strip themselves of God, clothe themselves in the world, and do not fear to be wrapped in the garments of laymen themselves.

What, however, should I complain about laymen, when I have often seen certain men dressed in foreign styles and, so to speak, barbarian ribbons [Note: A *redimiculum* is a woman’s head ornament.] so inappropriate and disgraceful to the priesthood—far beneath the dignity of such an office—that they were not so much clothed as disfigured, preferring to be distinguished by

> … by the Quirinal robe and Gabine girdle.  
> (Virgil, *Aeneid* 7.141.)

than by ecclesiastical dress?

They prefer to be called hunters rather than teachers, bold rather than gentle, crafty rather than simple, Maccabees [that is, strong men] rather than bishops.

Would that they used this name of life in that contest in which Christ set them in the world to triumph over it and over its ruler!

They play with the hoop, but by no means avoid dice;

they exercise themselves more with the gaming board than with Scripture, with the discus than with the book;

they know better how much the ruinous *canicula* throw can gnaw away [Note: This comes from Persius, *Satires* 3.49: “how much the ruinous little die might gnaw away.” We have corrected *radat* to *rodat*, where the text had *radat*. The *canicula* is a particular throw of the dice that indicated a single point; whoever made it was defeated. The *senio* is another kind of die and game, discussed by John of Salisbury, *Policraticus* 1.5, and by Faber in the *Thesaurus*, under *Sex*.] than they know how much saving Truth commands, forbids, or promises, and what it has said; they prefer *senio* to considering what they themselves must render to God;

they prefer actors to priests, *thymelici* to clerics, *bromii* [Note: Compare note 243 of this volume.] to philosophers, rogues to truthful men, the shameless to the modest, and mimes to monks;

they pursue Greek splendors, Babylonian pomp, and foreign adornments;

they busy themselves making golden goblets, silver dishes, cups of greater value, and mixing bowls—or rather shells—of heavier weight and of a size unknown to any age;

their wine vessel is painted, while the basilica beside them appears covered in soot [Note: The Vulgate has *sessiliis*, incorrectly. The correction is supported by Persius, who in *Satires* 5.118 mentions a *sessilis obba*:

> And let the Veientine red wine  
> Breathe forth, damaged by stale pitch, from the seated *obba*.

An *obba* is a wine vessel; *sessilis* means “low,” as though it sits or lies down. These bishops are censured because, although the very cheap vessels are painted, the basilica itself is covered with soot.].

[Col. 0291C] **7.** Amid these banquets, laden with every delicacy, the feast itself is marvelous beyond its multiplicity because of its very variety; and in all these things, whoever is greedier is more lavish, whoever is keener is better, whoever is wealthier is wiser, whoever is more landholding (*massutior*) [Note: *Massus*, and *massa*, have the same meaning as *mansus*, that is, a definite quantity of fields or estates. [Col. 0292C] Hence *massutior ille* means one who possesses more fields or estates. Perhaps, however, one should read *massucior*, from *massucus*, that is, “gluttonous,” concerning which see the ancient glosses in Du Cange.] [f., *massucior*], is the more celebrated; that one is a man, well known, famous, praised by everyone’s mouth. To be called frugal is now so detested that it is censured even among monks themselves—although we not only do not at all condemn the charitable generosity of the most liberal men when exercised with the greatest munificence, but it is rightly extolled with the highest praises [Col. 0292A]. For a bishop seems to live without purpose if he is not wealthy. Besides [Note: The Vulgate reads *tu praeter*. We deleted the pronoun *tu*, since it was manifestly intrusive. Construe: “Besides those things, laughter is with you, immoderate, usually heaped up from the simplicity of those who renounce these things through fear of God; the cithara and lyre are with you at banquets; but the work of the Lord, and the woe promised to those who do such things, is in no one’s memory,” as the prophet also says.] those things, laughter is with you [understand: “there is”], immoderate, usually heaped up from the simplicity of those who renounce these things through fear of God; cithara and lyre are at the banquets, as the prophet also says (Isa. V, 12); but the work of the Lord is in no one’s memory, nor the woe promised to those who do such things.

With you are the symphony and every kind of music, the allurements of singers, the plague of dancing girls, and all conversation that perhaps concerns human beings rather than God, the creature rather than the Creator, present things rather than future ones, the earthly elder [Note: *Senior* here signifies a king or prince.] rather than the heavenly Lord. Then that man is celebrated, while no one remembers this one; his name is sworn by, while this one is not even remembered; people drink to his health, while this one, though thirsty, is not given drink; the belly is distended through drunkenness for love of him, while this poor man, perhaps needing even crumbs in prison, is not refreshed; he is placed first, this one beneath; his memory is held in the foremost place, while this one is not held even in the second.

Moreover, dogs themselves run about on the table; horses fly more than they run in swift chariots; the falcon [Note: *Cappo*, elsewhere *capus*, from *capere* (“to seize”), was so called by the Italians, meaning a falcon, as Papias noted. A little later we have written *nec aliqui*, where the manuscripts erroneously had *nec aliquis*.] balances its rapid flight; the hawk overtakes the hoarsely crying crane. Amid all this there is no prophet, no apostle, no doctor, scarcely any canons, nowhere the decrees of the fathers, far away the enactments of pontiffs; far from everyone’s memory are the sufferings, frugality, humility, poverty, and deeds of the saints.

That proud rich man is not brought before their eyes; at least he is not licked by the tongues of dogs, but rather Lazarus is gnawed by them (Luke XVI, 21). Belshazzar’s destruction for such conduct is not remembered (Dan. V, 1–4). That jar with the talent of lead, carried by the prophet on the wings of a kite from the land of Shinar, is not recalled (Zech. V, 8–9); nor does anyone notice the camel’s hump and the eye of the needle (Matt. XIX, 24); nor does anyone remember the coming day of the Lord.

No one, with his mouth full of food, his eyes shedding tears, and his tongue loosened for tasteless jokes, takes care to notice that someone has recently died [*nemo abundat*: “no one gives it sufficient attention”]; nor that God therefore commanded us to watch, praying at all times (Luke XXI, 36). On the day of the banquet of Job’s first-born son, the destruction of his children escapes everyone’s eyes. No one remembers Lot leaving Sodom, nor Noah entering the ark.

Finally, the canons are given over to oblivion, although they command that all the revenues of the Church, because they are the Holy of Holies of the Lord, be divided into four parts. If these revenues were administered faithfully, there would be no lack—not merely of what would make a crater, a basin, or a vessel, or, to say something even more astonishing (and would that I were lying), a cauldron, but certainly of what would make a cup. The daily food itself—or the evening meal—would often be compelled, after the example of that man shut in the pit, to be restored by God (Dan. XIV, 30) [Note: In the printed editions the words are separated without any intelligible sense. The correction is also approved by the history of Daniel, for whom food was prepared by God. The meaning is: If the revenues of the Church are faithfully divided into four parts, as the canons command, not only will there be no lack of material for making craters and so forth, but even the daily or evening food will have to be restored by God, as he did for Daniel shut in the lions’ den.].

I am lying if so many ruined basilicas throughout the world do not bear witness to this: widows, orphans, strangers, innumerable poor, captives, prisoners, those bound, those confined in jail, the blind, the lame, the weak, the sick [Col. 0293B], monks, virgins, those constrained by debts, those crushed beneath another’s financial burden, and, finally, all those assigned to whatever fate. If one is able to provide some assistance for each person’s need and does not wish to grant it [Note: The printed editions erroneously read *alicujus suffragii*. Unless one prefers to supply *opem* (“aid”), one should judge the correction necessary. A little later the same editions had *si valet, et non valet prorogare* (“if he is able, and is unable to postpone”), which we have emended as the sense requires.], he will seem to incur the condemnation of a fraudulent steward. For it was said, with complete truth, by a man of no contemptible authority: Every Christian who does not help some people as far as he can will be judged; a bishop who neglects anyone will be condemned.

**8.** Suppose, however, that all these things were justly and fully expended, and that this did not impede luxury. Should a teacher pursue what he teaches others must avoid in every way? What if he is struck by that apostolic sentence: “You who preach that one must not steal, do you steal?” (Rom. II, 21); and by the Lord’s word: “First remove the beam from your own eye” (Matt. VII, 5); and: “Physician, first heal yourself” (Luke IV, 23)? Where then will be that saying of the same apostle: “I chastise my body and bring it into subjection, lest, after preaching to others, I myself should become disqualified” (I Cor. IX, 27)?

For, as a most experienced and holy teacher already said before us: “When a man’s life is despised, it remains that his preaching too will be held in contempt” (Gregory, Book I, *Homilies on the Gospels*, homily 12). But what does one of such men say to himself in his inmost heart when outwardly he says to others: “Not in revelry and drunkenness” (Rom. XIII, 13); and: “Humble yourselves beneath the powerful hand of God” (I Pet. V, 6); and: “Do not love the world or the things that are in the world” (I John II, 15); and: “Whoever wishes to be a friend of this world is constituted an enemy of God” (James IV, 4)? Even if he wishes neither to do these things nor to teach them, what then when he is compelled to cry, “Lift up your hearts”?

**9.** But, leaving aside the particular form and once again turning, with our steps somewhat straying, to the general category: after this, bishops drenched and overcome by draughts of wine [Note: The Vulgate reads *vini potest haec*, corruptly. It should be written *vini post haec*, as a little later we find *lectus post haec*. This exceedingly obscure passage must be construed and explained as follows: “But, leaving aside the particular form and turning aside or deviating somewhat in our steps—for *varico* is found in ancient glosses in the sense of *diverto* (“I turn aside”)—let us return to the general category: after this the bishops under discussion, soaked and overcome by wine-drinking, lest they appear wholly unlike those of whom it was said, ‘The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play,’ lest, I say, they appear entirely unlike them in anything except idolatry—for this too is not absent in the other, namely avarice itself, which Paul calls the service of idols (Eph. V, 5)—leave their high and lofty platform, mount chariots, and so forth.”], lest they appear entirely unlike those of whom it was said, “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play” (Exod. XXXII, 6), leave their high and lofty platform, mount, so to speak, chariots and carriages, and climb upon foaming horses adorned with golden reins, silver cheekpieces, German bridles, and Saxon saddles; and they hasten to whatever games their drunkenness dictates.

Then that man sitting upon an ass (John XII, 15), strong and mighty in battle (Ps. XXIII, 8), does not come to anyone’s mind. With you, the very kings of the world are sought to be surpassed in worldly glory rather than the poverty of the apostles imitated; the pleasure of the rich is sought to be surpassed rather than the holiness of fishermen followed [Note: The sense of this sentence must be explained. *Tecum* means that one strives to surpass the kings themselves in worldly glory rather than imitate the apostles’ poverty; and to surpass the pleasures of the rich rather than follow the holiness of fishermen.].

**10.** After this, a bed is adorned, exquisitely inlaid with golden panels; silk-covered supports are brought forth to be made; the mattress itself is covered with the finest cloth; a footstool is covered with a Gothic tapestry. Amid these things [Note: Construe: “Amid these things, the manger of our infant is not present to the mind, nor his rags, nor the lodging itself”; far from memory is the one who had nowhere to lay his head.], the manger of our infant, his rags, and the lodging itself are not present to the mind (Luke II, 7); far from memory is the one who had nowhere to lay his head (Luke IX, 58).

At last, when sleep has been shaken off by biting cares, as they roll about upon the pleasure of the bed and cannot rest, they utter certain murmurs in place of the morning hymns [Note: “Certain murmurs” indicates prayers uttered more rapidly, with a kind of murmuring.], more suited to insult than to grace, to contempt than to reception, to cursing than to being heard.

**11.** When it comes to clothing, they are dressed, as I have said, in foreign rather than native ornaments [Col. 0294D]. Their legs are cylindrical in appearance, fashioned, so to speak, more by a lathe than by hand, so that any one of them might more properly be called a column than a shin [Note: The Vulgate reads *curribus* (“chariots”), incorrectly. That the subject is legs is shown both by the adjective *teretibus*, which signifies something elongated and rounded, and especially by what follows: *quaevis earum*—more properly *quolibet eorum*—“any one of them”; *volumen* is more aptly said of a column than of a shin.].

The whole body, however, is adorned with such care that the very garment, which ought to have been prepared solely for protection against the cold, is made so much better the thicker it is, since it is made from the finest cloth [Note: *Haeresium*—unless there is an error in the text—was a kind of *lacerna*, or cloak, made from the finest cloth, which protected the whole body against cold. Here *pallium* means the cloth itself, whether silk or a more valuable material. Hence in Italian *correr al pallio* is said of a horse race, because a cloak or more precious cloth was offered as the prize to the winners. Du Cange shows that the word *pallium* is used in this sense in other documents. He also notes the cloths made in the province of Venetia, as does Rather in Letter 2 to Nanno, no. 1.], and has a border of another, which, if it could be found, would be better than the finest. Its width exceeds the measure of a cubit, unless it is somewhat reduced. If any kind of garment is placed over it, it is fitted above with such an elaborate display that, either through its fineness or even through some tearing at the cost of the garment, it reveals the marvelous object that ought to have been covered beneath it.

The very loincloth, extending down to the feet of the seated man, fastened with a golden clasp, displays at its top to onlookers a golden belt [Note: Here *lumbare* means the undergarment, or longer breeches, which had a golden clasp and a golden belt or girdle.], thrust before the eyes of many, not without severe torment to their ambition, so that in this alone it might seem fulfilled: “While the impious man grows proud, the poor man is set on fire” (Ps. IX, 2).

Then you may see some using a *mastruga* instead of a cloak, a Hungarian cap instead of a priestly headdress, and a scepter instead of a staff; nor do they consider the Apostle’s words, “Not in costly clothing” (I Tim. II, 9); nor remember him who says, “Give alms from what remains” (Luke XI, 41); nor, “What is exalted among human beings is an abomination before God” (Luke XVI, 15); nor the words, “I was naked and you did not clothe me” (Matt. XXV, 36), although he himself commanded the possessor of even two tunics to give one to the needy (Luke III, 11).

**12.** Thereafter, when Mass has been hurried through rather than chanted—or, what is more serious, sometimes entirely neglected—the bread having been received, together with the drink [Note: *Bibere* (“to drink”) is an ancient noun meaning “drink,” used as *biber* by some ancient writers, as may be seen in Charisius, Book I, where he cites examples from Gaius Fannius and Titinius.], which could certainly suffice for a royal meal, there being no one who wishes to remember, either literally or in meaning, the saying, “Woe to the land whose princes eat in the morning, and whose king is a servant” (Eccles. X, 16), they again mount Faliscian horses—not, indeed, the ones of the preceding day, lest frequent sight make them cheap [Col. 0296A]—adorned with golden collars and silver bridles, of such weight that merely carrying them would be enough even for the strongest horses.

On these horses they practice, to express it poetically:

> Golden necklaces hang down from their breasts,  
> and, covered in gold, they chew tawny gold beneath their teeth;

and again:

> They exercise their limbs in grassy wrestling grounds;  
> they compete in play and wrestle upon the tawny sand;

or:

> They exercise themselves on horseback and tame chariots in the dust,

or they stretch taut bows, or with their arms hurl flexible arrows (Virgil, *Aeneid* VII, VI, VI); or they practice things similar to these, to return to our subject. Or, certainly, abandoning heavenly things, they handle and care only for earthly affairs; those who ought to decide ecclesiastical matters determine how the commonwealth should conduct itself.

Would that nothing else were being handled there! If God were offended there only by this, it might perhaps be pardonable, though not commendable. Yet what happened recently—that is, at this very time [understand: “happened”]—would certainly not have occurred.

Nearly a year earlier [Note: Since Rather wrote these things in the prison at Pavia, while the event described here preceded his captivity, it is clear that “the preceding year” must refer to the year 935, before his capture. The event must be explained more clearly. He complains about certain bishops who, in the preceding year, after King Hugh’s victory over Arnold, duke of Bavaria, sought to please that king and conspired to bring about Rather’s destruction. For, as misfortune followed and the trouble increased—when Arnold had been driven from Verona and Rather, one of his supporters, was being denounced—they not only thought but said that he had been abandoned by the Lord. On the very feast of the holy Mother of God, some were severely rebuked because they had permitted him the kiss of peace in church during the solemn celebration of Mass, supposing that this was customary, and so forth.

Since he indicates an event that occurred shortly before his captivity, while in what follows “the next day having been completed” suggests another event that immediately preceded that captivity, which took place in February of 935, as we have seen elsewhere (*Life of the Author*, § 4), the feast of the holy Mother of God mentioned here is the Feast of the Purification in that same year. After Hugh’s victory, a solemn Mass was celebrated on that feast with Rather and the other bishops present. This fifth book, however, which attributes such an event to “nearly the preceding year,” is recognized as having been written at the beginning of 936.], certain bishops sought to please him, lest they too should fall into the same circumstance which they habitually sang next in the same verse:

> “He will bow down and fall when he has gained dominion over the poor;  
> for he has said in his heart: ‘God has forgotten; he has turned away his face, so as not to see to the end’” (Ps. IX, 10–11).

For, as misfortune followed and the trouble increased, they not only thought but said that he had been abandoned by the Lord, to such an extent that on the very feast of the holy Mother of God some were severely rebuked because they had granted him the kiss of peace in the church—as is customary during the solemnities of Mass—thinking themselves fortunate and most prudent because he had been condemned, not because he was a sinner [Note: The Vulgate reads *a Deo non qui a peccatore*, apparently corruptly. The context favored the emendation. Construe and explain: Those who gave Rather the kiss of peace during the solemnities of Mass did so, thinking themselves fortunate and most prudent, because he had been condemned on account of deception [namely, rebellion], not because he was a sinner; for punishment does not make guilt, but the cause does. Rather, amid the difficulties caused by the favor he had shown Arnold after Hugh’s victory, was thought to have been condemned because he had been led into Arnold’s cause by deception, not because of hostility toward Hugh. In his letter to John XII he testifies that he had always loved Hugh and always wished him prosperity, but had received Arnold at Verona after being deceived.], but because he had been deceived; for punishment does not make guilt, but the cause does, and, as Aurelius of venerable memory bears witness, the punishment of the guilty is in a certain sense their absolution.

When the following day had been completed [Note: We believe this refers to the proceedings held at daybreak on the day described in Book III, no. 27, when Rather was induced to consent to the writing of that letter whose author he himself was, and whose entire undertaking’s instigator he was accused of being; then he was captured and thrown into the tower at Pavia. This proceeding was therefore held on the third of February, the day after the Feast of the Purification mentioned above. On the Feast of the Purification itself occurred the invasion of the barbarian people that preceded the following day and the proceedings just mentioned. Compare the author’s life, § 4, where we explain this passage more fully.], none of the promised things was carried out in deed. Nevertheless, through intermediaries, that eminent man in whom lay all confidence of a favorable outcome repeatedly ordered him not to depart in any respect from his counsel [Note: Since he touches his misfortune here more obscurely, as we noted in note 289, and does not wish to name the actors, as he will soon indicate, *Rather* is understood as the nominative: “that Rather should not depart from his counsel.”], promising that he himself would arrange everything with the best outcome, provided only that Rather persevered in the promised agreement.

And he did so [Note: Rather, that is, did so: he did not depart from the counsel of that eminent man, who, from what is said elsewhere, seems to have been a bishop of the highest authority.]—as can be seen and may be supposed, to his own detriment, but in reality, as we ought to believe, and as is evident, to his own advantage. He also requested that certain leading citizens be sent to him at once by that same man. When he had done this, he cast upon himself, so to speak, a kind of noose by which he might be held.

With those leading citizens, then, it was arranged that something which the ever-present eye [Note: Construe: “which in no way escaped that eye present everywhere,” that is, God—was not hidden from him. He hints at the manner of his betrayal, discussed more fully in Book III, no. 27, and in the *Life*, § 4.] nowhere failed to see, and which the Almighty either mercifully avenges or releases in the present age so that he may not punish it strictly in the future, should be carried out.

What more is there? We could weave a sufficiently long account from this point, but we judge it much more appropriate here to swallow it, because of the danger which, as we remember saying in the preface to the preceding little book, the truth itself may bring upon us—namely, hatred. Let the utterly abominable deeds of such men therefore be suppressed here, lest, if by chance they are compelled to be brought forth and reported in an insolent account, and the names of those who committed them [Note: He means the names of those whose deeds he censures. He indicates that they cannot be mentioned without danger of disturbance.], should be spoken, they become the cause of the greatest discord [understand: “should become”].

Yet although present circumstances are such, no one is found, even out of regard for God, who intervenes for the needy, intercedes for the condemned, or makes the cause of orphans, widows, or any afflicted persons his own. This is demonstrated by the fact that Rather’s own affliction was relieved by no one [Note: “And this one” means Rather himself: his affliction, relieved by no one, proves that there is no one who intervenes for the needy or intercedes for the condemned.].

**LETTER OF THE SAME [Note: You will find the complete letters to Widon and Sobbo, by which he sent these six books of the *Praeloquia* to them, among the author’s other letters, no. 2. The letter inserted here, however, addressed to the same archbishops and to the other bishops sitting in council, may or may not be complete; it may instead be a fragment of a letter. Perhaps Rather copied only these words here under the title “letter,” in order to warn them that they should especially read what follows, where he complains that no one helps him although he was condemned without any hearing having preceded it. He calls himself an exile in the heading because, when he inserted these words, he was no longer detained in the prison at Pavia but was living in exile at Como. Further, the words “I beg you to receive this, the volume of the Lord, in place of my presence” are understood from the second letter. He had evidently been invited to the council. Since he was detained in exile at Como, he could not go there. Having sent the volume of the *Praeloquia*, he asks that it be received and read in his place.].**

Rather, an exile, to Widon and Sobbo, archbishops, and to his fellow bishops sitting in council.

Receive this, my lords, in place of my presence, and I beg you to deign to read it. For perhaps it will not be irrelevant to the present matter.

**13.** There are thereafter no councils of the Church anywhere, no synodical assemblies in any place; nothing is approved or disapproved by ecclesiastical law, accused or excused, defended or opposed. Rather, everything is commanded, carried out, and endured by force, secular power, and secular judgment, justly or unjustly. This man too stands as a witness to the matter [Note: “This man” is Rather himself, as in the preceding section and in the phrase *istius*. See note 37. He is the man who, without any judgment of the bishops and with no hearing preceding it, was carried into exile by laymen.], having not been judged by his fellow bishops [understand: “not judged,” or something similar], but transported into exile by laymen without any preceding hearing, with absolutely no one to set up a barrier of defense (Ezek. XXII, 30), rise up against the opposing side, setting himself as a wall before the house of Israel, and stand in battle on the day of the Lord (Ezek. XIII, 5).

That is, while the world rejoices and the Lord is dishonored, so far as those men are concerned [Note: These words refer to what precedes: “transported into exile, while no one at all remained who might set up …”—that is, this happened while the world rejoiced, and so forth.], although the same matter—as [Note: The manuscripts read the corrupt and senseless *et sine sensu in aures, sicut*. We restored *in aures* from the sense. The phrase refers back to the preceding words, “This man too stands as a witness to the matter.” What follows adds that the same thing happened not on only one occasion or merely on the evidence of one person, but to many. The same misfortune befell not only Rather but many other bishops, as the contemporary author Atto, bishop of Vercelli, also noted in Book I *On the Pressures of the Church*, in the first volume of Acher’s *Spicilegium*, p. 418, col. 2. What death in this present age could be more cruel than for pastors of the Church to be separated from their sheep, shut up in prison, or driven into exile, their bodies worn down by deprivation and their minds afflicted by grief? They sigh for themselves, lament over those entrusted to them, suffer present punishments, and are threatened with future ones by their executioners; they fear their superiors, while their comforters are taken away; accusers or intimidators stand constantly beside them. Compare also what the same author relates on p. 405, where he complains that bishops were condemned without defense. He appears to be pleading Rather’s cause.] occurs not merely on one occasion—so it does not happen merely on the proof of one person, but usually on that of many.

For Lazarus did not lie before the rich man’s gate without reason, but so that the one might be tested by what happened and the other condemned: the one because he was in need, the other because he did not give. For when the Lord says in the psalm, “I tested you at the waters of contradiction” (Ps. LXXX, 8), where, I ask, can or ought the vigor of zeal and the intention of pastoral courage be displayed, except where there is not merely some contradiction but the greatest contradiction?

And since no one is crowned unless he has competed lawfully (II Tim. II, 5), from where, I ask, does he hope for or seek a crown who, fleeing when battle threatened, never fought? What then? Even if victory cannot be obtained, should one therefore always turn one’s back on the enemy? Have we not often seen the child of a slain soldier rewarded for the father’s boldness, steadfastness, or devotion?

Since our battle is altogether different, our dangers too are more serious. The one who flees dies eternally; but the one who falls, provided that devotion does not fail [Note: Since he is speaking of the bishops’ battle, he distinguishes three classes: those who flee, those who fall, and those who obtain victory. The first are condemned. Those who fall—namely, those who suffer some adverse downfall in that battle or persecution—are not only raised up again if devotion, that is, episcopal fervor, does not fail in them, but are also crowned eternally for the injury they suffered. Those who are victorious receive God himself as their reward and crown.], is not only raised up again, but is also crowned eternally for the injury. For the one who obtains victory [understand: “the victory”], has the same crown as shield, weapon, and victory—that is, God himself is all things: he protects those whom he inspires, crowns those whom he protects, raises up those whom he permits to fall, and rewards those whom he allows to be victorious.

For in this battle no one but he himself fights against the adversary. He fights; he is besieged; he is confined; he stands by; he defends the circuit of the walls. Yet the victory falls to us, is ascribed to us, and is reckoned to us.

What kind of sluggish spirit is it fitting for anyone to have, when his contest is from God—not his but God’s—so that he does not even need to consider how or what he should speak (Matt. X, 19), provided only that the devotion with which he wishes to speak does not fail, as I have said? Why should anyone tremble, when the very one who is the rewarder is also the protector and, finally, the fighter? For, to such an extent is he present when you fight, present when you battle, that even when you think you are being struck, it is he, not you, who is struck. Thus today you have heard, just as yesterday you had read: “Whoever touches you is like one who touches the pupil of my eye” (Zech. II, 8); and: “Whoever despises you despises me” (Luke X, 16).

**14.** Therefore, if you wish to please the commander, do not flatter the enemy; for you cannot win his favor if you refuse to conquer him [The text reads *separari*; the sense requires *superari*, “to be overcome.”]. Without exception the Apostle says: “All who wish to live piously in Christ Jesus will suffer persecution” (II Tim. III, 12). Therefore he seems unwilling to live piously in Christ Jesus who does not suffer persecution for Christ Jesus. As was said before us, he also refuses to be in the body who does not wish to endure the world’s hatred together with the head.

“I dare not,” you say; “it is dangerous today . . . .” And the Lord says: “Out of your own mouth I judge you, wicked servant” (Luke XIX, 22). You have renounced military service if you have lost your courage. Why then did you take up arms? Why did you enlist? Why did you seek to be called a shepherd, when you had decided to flee at the wolf’s coming? Why did you take up the staff if you feared to meet danger? If you did not dare to defend the flock, why did you accept its payment? With what face do you eat the milk of the flock, when you fear either to raise your voice against the thief, awaken the master of the household, or urge on the dogs? Why have you clothed yourself in the sheep’s wool when you fear even a kid mixed among the lambs, let alone scorn a roaring lion or bear? Why did you take my money if, although you knew that you ought to distribute it, you were afraid to do so? And you who raise yourself so boldly against me—how do you subject yourself so fearfully to him whom I hold beneath my feet?

“It is dangerous,” you say. Then there is a storm at sea if the ship is in danger? What do you intend to do? Show why you took up the oar: was it so that, as a doomed man, you might thrust your head into the bilge? Exert your strength instead, fight bravely, sail steadfastly. The harbor is at hand; he lies in the ship, though he sleeps for you—he to whom the sea and winds obey (Matt. VIII, 27).

**15.** “I fear the displeasure of the elder”—that is, the king. The Apostle answers: “If I were still pleasing human beings, I would not be a servant of Christ” (Gal. I, 10). What will the elder’s displeasure do to you? It may change things; perhaps he will take away what he granted. You might perhaps rightly fear all this if you did not have the promise of the one who says: “Rejoice and exult, for behold, your reward is great in heaven” (Matt. V, 12); and if you did not know what the Apostle said: “Who is there who can harm you, if you are zealous for what is good? But even if you suffer anything for righteousness’ sake, you are blessed; and do not fear their fear” (I Pet. III, 13).

“I fear something more,” you say.

“What?”

“To die,” you answer—which is to say: “There is a lion in the road; I will be killed in the midst of the streets” (Prov. XXII, 13).

But hear the Lord: “Not a hair of your head will perish” (Luke XXI, 10). Hear also that servant of the same order to which you belong, Augustine, so often cited here: “Fear death,” he says, “if you are able not to die.” Hear another: “He who is born from a human being will also die.” Hear the Apostle: “I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die for Christ Jesus” (Acts XXI, 13). Hear also a certain pagan, to your shame: “He who orders one to die is more tolerable than he who orders one to live wickedly.”

The king’s anger can kill you; can his favor ensure that you will not die? But, I beg you, do not err. It is not just any king who kills; it is the one who said: “I kill and I make alive” (Deut. XXXII, 39). For if anyone besides him could kill someone, the furnace of fire would not have spared the three young men, nor would the hungry lions have spared Daniel. Susanna, though condemned according to the laws, as it was thought, would not have been liberated so swiftly. Nor would Jonah, swallowed by the whale, have been vomited forth at God’s command.

What is more ready to kill than a lion’s rage? What is more difficult to release than one condemned by a law that knew how to spare no one? What is more voracious for swallowing than the depths of the sea—or rather, than the appetite of a beast? And yet none of these things, though they possessed the power, availed anything against divine protection when God willed it. Hence, concerning one of those examples—that is, the three young men named first—we customarily sing in the Church:

> “The fire forgot the force of its power,  
> so that your children might be delivered unharmed”  
> (*Antiphon 4, Third Sunday of Lent*).

## 16.

Whether these things are indeed as we have said or not, you can also judge from the words of Cassiodorus, if you wish, who says:

> “Moreover, it seems astonishing that an incorporeal thing should be bound together with the most solid limbs, and that natures so different should have been brought into such unity that the soul can neither separate itself when it wishes nor retain itself when it has recognized the Creator’s command. Everything is closed to it when it is ordered to remain within; everything is opened when it is commanded to depart. For although the bitter pain of a wound may be inflicted, life is not surrendered without the Author’s command, just as it is not preserved without his gift.” [Col. 0301C]

Although these things are so, we can also gather them with unshakable certainty from reason itself, on the basis of our own condition: having entirely laid aside manly steadfastness and assumed womanly cowardice; erect against God [Note: “Erect against God,” that is, raised up against God, just as later “exalted toward the brothers,” that is, toward the brothers; and in section 17 “erect against the world,” that is, against the world]; subject to the world; idle and effeminate; insatiably desirous of empty glory; provoking one another and envying one another; negligent and utterly wretched; swollen with pride and devoid of goodness; enslaved to the pleasures of the flesh; exalted over our brothers; inflamed by the torches of greed in acquiring possessions, yet ineffectual and sluggish in gathering the riches of virtues; while we pursue worldly honor, losing the glory that comes from God—alas, miserable creatures!—and while we strive to be set above our brothers, through pride we are placed beneath the world, in a manner worthy of lamentation [Col. 0301D] [Note: “In a manner worthy of lamentation,” that is, in a manner deserving tears].

While we despise the Lord who rules, we suffer the servant; and although, by the power granted to us, we ought to tread upon serpents and scorpions and every power of the enemy (Luke 10:19), in reversed order we ourselves are daily trodden underfoot, so that we may eventually fear that what is written in Job will also be fulfilled in us [Note: That is, so that we may fear that what is written in Job will eventually be fulfilled in us]:

> “He will flee from iron weapons and fall upon a bronze bow” (Job 20:21);

and:

> “Those who fear the frost—snow will fall upon them” (Job 6:16).

This happens when temporal anger is feared but eternal anger is incurred; earthly danger is dreaded, while the heavenly and unavoidable judgment of wrath rushes upon us.

## 17.

But if we had wished to vindicate our honor by our conduct—our honor by which we were not only created in the image of God but also, through our office, placed above all creatures beneath heaven [understand: “we are placed above them”]—if, that is, we had been subject to Christ, as our predecessors were, raised up against the world, bearing one another’s burdens according to the Apostle (Galatians 6:2), helping one another, anticipating one another in honor, all having the same mind in the Lord, fervent in spirit, zealously burning with the zeal of charity for the house of Israel after the example of Elijah, teaching through instruction, mutually exhorting one another through encouragement, giving one another what was useful according to need [that is, what was useful to each other] in simplicity, administering authority with diligence, showing mercy to one another with cheerfulness, possessing love of God and brotherly love without pretence, hating evil and clinging to what is good, preserving brotherly charity toward one another, not setting our minds on high things but associating with the lowly (Romans 12:8–17). I confess that we would not only fear no one, but would also be feared by everyone.

Nor would this prophetic saying be fulfilled in us—God forbid!—which says:

> “Each one shall devour the flesh of his own arm: Manasseh, Ephraim, and Ephraim, Manasseh; together they are against Judah” (Isaiah 11:20),

that is, against the Church distinguished by its confession of God [Note: The words “against Judah” are interpreted as meaning “against the Church distinguished by its confession of God”]. Biting one another, we are consumed by one another, and, divided from each other, we are left desolate. [Col. 0302A]

For Truth itself, which is always truthful, does not lie when it says:

> “Every kingdom divided against itself will be laid waste” (Matthew 12:25).

Nor should we reject the saying of someone who, although he did not know God, declared that through harmony small things grow, while through discord the greatest things fall apart.

We should also always keep in mind the Apostle’s exhortation:

> “Let us pursue the things that make for peace, and the things that make for edification let us preserve toward one another” (Romans 14:19).

For:

> “Whoever serves Christ in this is pleasing to God and approved by human beings” (Romans 14:18).

Likewise:

> “Do you not wish to fear authority? Do what is good, and you will receive praise from it” (Romans 13:3).

And:

> “This is the will of God: that by doing good you should silence the ignorance of foolish people” (1 Peter 2:15).

Another says:

> “When a person’s ways are pleasing to the Lord, he turns even that person’s enemies toward peace” (Proverbs 16:7).

And through the Lord’s Psalmist:

> “If my people had listened to me, if Israel had walked in my ways, I would perhaps have humbled their enemies for nothing” (Psalm 80:14–15). [Col. 0302D]

Likewise, through Jeremiah [Baruch]:

> “If you had walked in the way of God, you would surely have dwelt in peace upon the earth” (Baruch 3:13).

And through Moses:

> “Behold, I send my angel before you, to go ahead of you and always guard you. Only be attentive and listen to my voice; and I will be an enemy to your enemies, and I will afflict those who afflict you” (Exodus 23:20–22). [Col. 0303A]

## 18.

We, however, act in the opposite way. Although all these things are wholly unsuitable for the perfect and should not be sought, and although good things should be done for God’s glory while adversities should be endured out of love for him rather than vengeance being desired, we are more accustomed to avenge ourselves than to be avenged; to defend ourselves by our own efforts than to be defended by God.

And when we are not capable of this, we hasten to enter into a kind of pact with our enemies, agreeing with them in evil [Note: The common text has *consentiens*, “agreeing,” incorrectly; the subject requires the plural *consentientes*], rather than invoking God as our protector with our hands and hearts raised to him. Against the inner robber—who is never overcome more effectively than when the exterior is loved—we hasten to seize our weapons.

Like those who, seeking the salvation that is given by God alone, make sacrilegious vows at springs or trees for the sake of earthly advantages, we strive to pray to the earth itself rather than to him who made heaven and earth. [Col. 0303B]

And so that they may not be deprived of the result of their prayers [Note: The same printed books have *fraudentur*, “may be deprived,” incorrectly; shortly afterward they also have *proposuit* instead of *praeposuit*, likewise incorrectly. He is speaking of bishops], having entirely abandoned him who appointed you over the world, and having abandoned every duty except its name, we serve the world itself more especially than others [Note: That is, we serve the world more especially than others, so that, while others strive to render to God the things of God and to the world the things of the world, we do the opposite].

While others strive to render to God the things of God and to the world the things of the world, we, conversely, render to the world the things of God—that is, every kind of love and worship—and to God the things that ought to have been rendered to the world—that is, every kind of disdain and contempt.

And so that we may be bound more tightly to the world itself, lest, when it does not recognize us, we should be despised by it, we have abandoned our manner of life, our worship, and even our dress, and we use the customs and pursuits of the world, including its garments, to such an extent that, apart from the shaving of the beard and the tonsure, and the fact that we do not take wives as they do, and whatever praise we seem to render to the Lord with our mouths alone, and even that very rarely, we appear in no respect different from secular people [Note: That is, we appear different from secular people only in what I may call “barbirasio”—the shaving of the beard—and the tonsure, in the fact that we do not take wives as they do, and in whatever praise we seem to render to the Lord with our mouths alone, and that very rarely. Apart from these things, I say, we appear in no respect different from secular people. Compare Part II, *On Contempt for the Canons*, section 2]. [Col. 0303C]

Thus the prophetic saying that concerns the present age can rightly be believed to have been spoken about us:

> “And it shall be as with the people, so with the priest” (Isaiah 24:2).

And we can lament with the words of another in the Lamentations:

> “How the gold has grown dim, how the finest color has changed, how the stones of the sanctuary have been scattered at the head of every street” (Lamentations 4:1).

We can also lament that a great part of the stars has already been drawn down from heaven to earth (Revelation 6:13)—that is, that a multitude of priests, cast down from the heights to the depths, now follows only earthly things [Note: That is, we may lament a multitude of priests who merely follow those cast down from the heights to the depths, namely, demons who were cast down from heaven into hell]—although their works ought to shine before human beings so that God might be glorified (Matthew 5:16). [Col. 0304A]

## 19.

It does not seem irrelevant to insert here, for the sake of such men, a brief but very useful saying of a certain priest who lived almost in our own time.

When he saw his bishop—horrible to relate!—playing at tables, he mocked him and shook his head with a mutter [Note: Fulgentius, in *On Ancient Speech*: *Frigutire* is said of muttering subtly].

When the bishop saw this, he became angry—and quite justly, if only his anger had been directed toward the person to whom it ought to have been directed [Note: That is, he was right to be angry, but only if he had been angry with the person with whom he ought to have been angry]—and immediately threatened him with prison unless he at once said where the canonical law had forbidden him to do this.

Pretending to be afraid, although he had at hand the means by which to fasten a noose around the fugitive’s neck, he fell at the bishop’s feet and said:

> “Forgive me, my lord. I have been so shaken by fear that I cannot remember even the first verse of the first psalm, much less bring forward anything from the decrees of the canons. But, most holy father, I beg you to help me recall its meaning, since I have lost it through fear” [Note: The meaning, namely, of the first verse of the first psalm].

Then the bishop, dissolved in laughter and amusement together with all those standing by, finally yielding to the priest’s insistence, recited the first verse together with the next, saying:

> “Blessed is the man,” and so forth (Psalm 1:2). “But his will is in the law of the Lord, and in his law he will meditate day and night.” [Col. 0304B]

The priest, answering in the bishop’s own words, instructed him in this way:

> “Excellent, most holy father. As for what time remains, play at tables.”

[Note: That is, if any time remains for one who ought to meditate on the law of the Lord day and night, let him play at tables.]

I have wished to place this story here so that, in this very brief saying, you may clearly infer both what you ought to avoid and what you ought to do.

But I shall now try to leave you, lest I seem foolishly to be sending water from a river to thirsty gardens, especially since I fear that one of those who, in the poet’s phrase, turn black into white—calling evil good and good evil, thinking darkness light and light darkness, judging truth to be falsehood and falsehood truth—might say to me:

> “You shall surely die, because you have spoken a lie in the name of the Lord” (Zechariah 13:3). [Col. 0304C]

I shall proceed instead to matters that are closer to my profession [Note: “To my profession,” he says, that is, to the monastic profession, because Ratherius had been taken from the monastery and elevated to the episcopate], and therefore, in equal measure, more frightening.

## 20.

Were you unexpectedly taken from the monastery? Consider from where and to where you have come: from the greatest place to a great one; from the greatest quiet of the monastery to the great labor of the world; from the bosom of the safest shore to the storms of the most frequent tempest.

Therefore sail with caution, since you refused to enjoy security while in harbor. Strive, labor, make an effort to accomplish something greater than others—or rather, something more humble and more perfect—knowing that you are subject to two burdens. [Col. 0304D]

For you are compelled, as a monk, to render what belongs to a monk, and, as a bishop, what belongs to a bishop. See that no one persuades you ever to change your habit, even if he wishes to approve this by the examples of the ancient Fathers, except when you approach that divine ministry which requires its own proper ornament. Even then, when it is not worn on the body, let it not depart from the heart.

Hear the Apostle saying:

> “They incur condemnation because they have rejected their first faith” (1 Timothy 5:12).

Therefore temper food with fasts, bodily pleasures with prayers, and the delights of the world with tears.

But if perhaps you were taken from the position of abbot, or, as commonly happens, had already presided over two or even more monasteries, consider what caused such a change. [Col. 0305B]

I beg you, do not spare yourself; do not deceive yourself; do not flatter yourself; do not wish to conceal from yourself what you know very well. For, as Augustine says, there is no hiding place from God, even if the deceitfulness of the one hiding is complete. Nor does he fail to know it because you pretend to be ignorant of it. Rather, acknowledge it humbly, if you wish him to forgive you.

As one of the pagans says, the first form of vengeance is that no guilty person acquits himself when he is his own judge.

Consider, therefore, whether you properly presided over those monasteries. If you discover that you did, grieve that you did not persevere; but if not, then for that very reason let daily groans never cease throughout your life.

Remember that you are subject to as many burdens as there were offices over which you were placed and in which, having been unworthily adorned with the insignia bestowed by the Giver, you proved ungrateful through your misuse of them. While you ought to have benefited many, you were the cause of progress for few, or perhaps for none. Indeed, having abandoned these and then moving on to others, bringing no fruit from either them or those others—not even from yourself—to the granary of the Lord’s threshing floor, you will be required at judgment to make up as many sheaves as you ought to have carried. [Col. 0305C]

## 21.

Therefore, while it is still day, do what I advise. While the time of sowing is still available; while the steward is still watching [that is, waiting]; while the keeper of the threshing floor is threshing, has not yet driven out the chaff, has not yet taken up the winnowing shovel, and has not yet begun to winnow—work, sow, gather. Grant yourself no holiday, no dalliance, no rest, and no time for idleness. [Col. 0305D]

Apply yourself wholly to sowing, so that there may be something to bring to the threshing. Keep the threshing floor itself constantly before the eyes of your mind; attend to it. Consider daily lest the chaff remain, lest the weeds multiply. Remember that the wheat must be stored in the granary (Matthew 13:30), while the chaff must be burned in unquenchable fire.

Therefore kindle those who are near with frequent exhortations, and those who are far away with very frequent letters, so that they may return to the worship of God. Accuse and rebuke both your own former sluggishness and theirs. Invite and entreat them—and know that you must carry this out not only in words but much more through deeds—so that they may be stirred up with you, revive, lift up their spirits, recover their diligence, exert their strength, regain their steadfastness, and grow warm again in faith, hope, and love of God. [Col. 0306A]

For Pope Leo’s saying is true: examples are stronger than words, and teaching through action is greater than teaching by voice.

Be diligent also in attending to their temporal needs. If, as a superior, you defrauded anyone, restore what was taken when you are a bishop. If, when you were an abbot, you remember having given anyone less than was due from you, do not hesitate, as pontiff, to make amends.

## 22.

Nor, when doing this, should you fear that someone may say that you were once a sinner or that you proved fraudulent. Take care only that you do not become a reproach to Christ, a horror to God, or accursed in the sight of the Holy Spirit.

This happens if you neither wipe away the past nor repair the present through amendment. Rather, when these things are said about you, rejoice humbly in God if it is truly said of you, together with the others:

> “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord; and such were some of you, but you were washed, you were sanctified” (1 Corinthians 6:11). [Col. 0306B]

If someone slanders, speaks against you, curses you, or reproaches what you have done, let your firm hope and solid refuge be in the help of him to whom the Prophet said:

> “They will curse, but you will bless” (Psalm 108:28).

And, raising the gaze of your mind, cry out without ceasing:

> “Take away from me reproach and contempt” (Psalm 118:22),

not indeed the reproach of human beings, which passes away, but your own reproach—which, if it does not cease here, will find no end there.

For I fear that, while you judge past deeds worthy of reproach, you may also consider present deeds worthy of contempt. This happens if past faults are corrected sluggishly and present duties are carried out negligently. [Col. 0306C]

Bring forward also, for your own benefit, Sarah’s prayer:

> “I beg you, Lord, to release me from this bond of reproach, or at least to take me away from the earth” (Tobit 3:15),

not by taking away my substance before the appointed time of destiny, but by raising my mind wholly to you.

“They will say: ‘Here is a new prophet, a recently appointed apostle, suddenly made an angel. This is Saint Martin; this is Saint Zeno, just sent down from heaven.’ They will say: ‘These are signs of vanity, hypocrisy, pretence, or frivolity; this is a change of affections, not any true religion.’

Oh, what a harsh saying! But take care lest it be true. [Col. 0306D]

## 23.

Beware also of the snare of the hunters, which lies hidden nearby.

Many, terrified, embittered, and ashamed by that harsh saying [Note: Namely, the saying mentioned shortly before—“Oh, what a harsh saying!”—by which zeal was branded as hypocrisy, vanity, and pretence], have abandoned the good work they had begun and have been caught in the hunters’ trap.

You, on the contrary, should answer them in your heart, not with your mouth; and while thinking about these things, beware of them yourself. For there are also certain inner caverns within you where the enemy’s robbing ambushes may be present.

Say, then, in your heart—think it with fear, but say it with caution—what someone far superior to you said, though certainly unlike you; and you will not be lying:

> “To change one’s purpose for the better is not frivolity but virtue, and not guilt but grace” [Note: The passage is corrupt in the common editions; we seem to have restored it by adding the particle “but” here and below].

There will also be people who, while considering nothing—or rather, refusing to acknowledge any good of their own—if they see any good in you will immediately begin to praise it and marvel at it as something extraordinary [Note: Construe: “while they consider no good of their own, or rather refuse to acknowledge any good of their own; if they see any good in you, they immediately begin to praise it,” and so forth]. [Col. 0307A]

If you believe them, abandoning the testimony of your own conscience, I confess—and I do not lie—you will immediately be lost.

You, on the contrary, while displaying what is present, should always strive to remember the past and at the same time consider God’s strict and incomprehensible judgments. For often an offense is incurred where grace is thought to be deserved, and grace is acquired where an offense is feared to be incurred.

Restrain your tongue not only from criminal speech but also from idle speech, knowing that it is written through James:

> “If anyone thinks himself religious and does not bridle his tongue but deceives his own heart, his religion is worthless” (James 1:26). [Col. 0307B]

## 24.

But, having begun, let me address you briefly once more. I advise you carefully to reconsider anything you did in your youth, and anything you did while you were still in the monastery—that is, before you were appointed to any position of authority. Perhaps there too you will find something that you ought greatly to fear.

It will also be discovered in what manner you were appointed and by what necessity you were chosen. For human ambition’s pride, always inclined toward worse things and now occupying every age, does not even today abandon the monasteries. It sees to it that those chosen are assessed not by the merits of their virtues but by the praises of that rotten thing which they call earthly nobility, though in reality it is corruption.

It is not asked who surpasses others in obedience, excels in humility, or stands out in prudence; [supply: “but”] whose chest is fuller, whose storeroom stronger, whose gifts more abundant; whose stables are more amply filled; whose estates and benefices are more widely extended; whose father is richer, whose brother wealthier, whose lineage nobler, whose descendants more powerful. [Col. 0307C]

In all this, even old age itself is not honored. Youth invades the place of age; what is wholly divine is offered as a reward; and earthly profits are sought, although only the earnings of souls ought to have been gathered.

If you should discover that you were caught by these and other falls of the worst ambition that commonly accompany them, I beg you not to give joy any place in your heart.

Perhaps, raised up under such auspices, you were brought to the point that you happened to ascend to the height of honor in which you now serve through some assistance from secular support [Note: The common text has *et illud*, “and that,” incorrectly]. [Col. 0307D]

If this is so, I cannot sufficiently describe how greatly you ought to grieve, even if every limb of the body were to resound in every possible tongue.

But do not think that I say this because I wish either to cast you down or to make you despair. I do not neglect to give you whatever counsel I can; the rest I entrust to your diligence. [Col. 0308A]

## 25.

Many sayings of the holy Fathers have already been inserted in various short works. Read these again and obtain from them the business of your salvation.

Yet it seems to me that, while you are meanwhile seeking these things, slowness in finding and carrying out what they say may perhaps hinder you. Therefore, without despairing in any way, placing firm hope in him who made everything from nothing, give yourself wholly to tears and to pious works—not as one who began practicing them from childhood, but as one who, having spent and consumed the whole time of life in wicked pleasures, remembers that, if any remaining space of time is granted, he must devote himself exclusively to God [Note: That is, practicing pious works not as one who began them from infancy, but as one who, considering the whole time of life given over and consumed by evil pleasures, remembers that he must devote whatever span remains, if any is granted, to God alone]. [Col. 0308D]

And although I know that you did not enter through the door in this order, but rather climbed up by another route, I nevertheless do not dare to despair of you completely, because I know the power of this householder to be so great that, if he wishes, he can make a shepherd even from a thief, just as he is often said to have made a sheep from a wolf.

For what can the Almighty not do? What can he not do except what he does not wish to be able to do? Can he not make a pious bishop from an ungodly usurper, who was able to raise up children for Abraham from stones? (Matthew 3:9.) [Col. 0308B]

Could he not restore one who had been killed, when he was able to create one who did not exist? “These things,” you say, “are exceedingly difficult.” But difficult for whom? Surely not for God. What is difficult for him who was able to make all things from nothing?

Have you not heard his saying today:

> “If you can believe, all things are possible for the one who believes” (Mark 9:22)? [Col. 0308C]

Do you not know that even in human affairs there is a custom of praising a physician all the more highly the more hopeless the sick person was considered, since, the more hopeless the soul’s occasion of death, the more people are often corrected by the same example?

For this reason one of our own says, in the same sense expressed above:

> “Look at David; consider Peter. The higher their position, the more serious their fall; but the more serious the fall, the more pleasing is the mercy of the one who raises them.”

Thus the same man was accustomed to pray very beautifully:

> “O God, who chiefly manifests your omnipotence by sparing and showing mercy, multiply your mercy upon us.”

What if he permitted all these things to happen precisely so that you might have greater cause to praise him—allowing you to be endangered in many things so that you might cry out without failing? [Col. 0308D]

What if he wished you to be an example to such men—who, alas, are innumerably being established throughout the world today—so that they might take some counsel even for themselves when they see you restored whom they knew to have been destroyed, and thereby, if possible, escape the death of anathema promulgated by the canons and drive away from themselves the curse of the chief of the apostles through the mercy of God and the Lord of the apostles? [Col. 0309A]

For he also deigned to become a curse for us (Galatians 3:13), so that he might redeem us from the curse not only of the Law but also of original and actual sins.

Only do not despair; do not act sluggishly; do not turn to the right through exaltation or to the left through despair; do not be deceived by the quality of good or, as commonly happens, by the quantity of evil; do not, looking at the conduct of others, raise yourself arrogantly or humble yourself despairingly; and do not continue to give the adversary a place within yourself.

Do not ever permit what you grieve has happened to you to happen to anyone else, insofar as you are able to resist it; nor allow yourself to fall again into such things or even similar ones, considering how difficult it may be for one who has been struck down to rise again. [Col. 0309B]

## 26.

A certain person gives you and others like you a very useful admonition, beautifully enough, although somewhat more mildly than the authority of the canons requires:

> “Whoever such people are, if they do not wish to be removed from the Church when the Lord comes, let them also remove these things [that is, the things which, when the Lord saw them being done in the temple, he punished with a whip made from cords or small ropes] from their hearts, and let them not make the house of God a house of commerce.” [Col. 0309D]

Of all these things . . . [lacuna] by that *sacratic* example, in which he says:

> “I am indeed lustful; it is my task to overcome lust itself. Commit nothing to your own virtue, your own caution, or your own strength” [Note: The passage is defective: something is missing and it may also be corrupt. In the common editions, perhaps *Socratico* is written in the margin instead of *sacratico*. We would prefer to supply and correct it thus: “Remembering—or carrying out—all these things, abominate the example of him who says, ‘I am indeed lustful; it is my task to overcome lust itself.’ Commit nothing to your own virtue, your own caution, or your own strength,” etc.]. [Col. 0310D]

Strive wholly to belong to him, and commit your whole self to his keeping, striving with heart and hands to entrust yourself to the keeping of him who was pleased to create, redeem, and call you [Note: Construe: “and, striving with heart and hands, entrust your whole self to the keeping of him who was pleased to create, redeem, and call you”].

He himself can guard you when you are somewhat raised up, who wished to raise you up completely when you had been cast down. He himself can keep you sound, who wished to heal you when you had been crushed. He himself can make you continually *spudius* [Note: *Spudius*, that is, industrious or zealous, from the Greek σπουδαῖος], who wished, contrary to nature and beyond all hope, to gather even one who had become foolish.

Although you can do nothing good without him—indeed, you cannot even will it, much less accomplish it—nevertheless do not believe that you will be saved entirely without some effort of your own, since you can know with complete certainty that God created you as a rational being, granting you freedom of choice.

Therefore strive to cling to him continually, not hurriedly or as if merely passing by: with him you can exist only happily, and without him you can exist only unhappily.

If, amid these things, some adversity should befall you through the merciful arrangement of a just—indeed, most merciful—judge, whether illness, loss of household possessions, or any other kind of punishment, do not grieve as though you had been despised; rejoice as one who has been mercifully regarded.

Know and confess that this has happened to you because of your sins, and declare that it is far less than your wickedness deserved [Note: The common text has *profiteri*, “to declare,” incorrectly; the required form is *profitere*]. [Col. 0310A]

For the rust of such great crimes could not be consumed except by the fire of various punishments.

Therefore exult, rejoicing humbly in the Lord, that in this world you have partly received an exchange of evils which in the other world you had great reason to fear you would have to endure all at once, since it is certain that God leaves nothing unpunished. By this means those mentioned above—namely, those who humbly receive tribulations in this world—are accustomed to be freed from their sin through his mercy [Note: Explain: “Those mentioned above, who humbly receive tribulations in this world, are accustomed by this means to be freed from their sin through his mercy”].

Therefore accuse yourself continually before him, and cry out with the Prophet:

> “You are righteous, O Lord, and your judgment is upright” (Psalm 118:137);

and with another:

> “You are righteous, O Lord, in all the things that you have done to us” (Daniel 3:27);

and:

> “All that you have done to us, O Lord, you have done in true judgment, because we have sinned against you” (Daniel 3:31); [Col. 0310B]

and:

> “I will bear the wrath of the Lord, because I have sinned against him, until he pleads my cause” (Micah 7:9).

### 27

In the tribulation itself, do not give yourself over to sluggishness, as though you were certain—although for this reason you must not despair entirely—that all your sins have been forgiven because of this punishment, or at least that a portion of your more serious sins has been remitted to you. In addition to those things which necessity compels you to do, devote yourself more frequently and more earnestly to vigils, prayers, and fasts, being uncertain, of course, by what kind of scourge you have been struck: whether by that with which sons are corrected, or by that with which slaves are scourged or criminals punished. For, as Scripture testifies, “Every son whom he receives he chastises” (Heb. XII, 6); yet also, “Many are the scourges of the sinner” [Col. 0310C] (Ps. XXXI, 10), as well as “the snare, fire, sulphur, and the spirit of storms” (Ps. X, 7). Although these things appear altogether intolerable, they are nevertheless “not even a part of their cup” (ibid., 8); and again: “I have struck you with an incurable wound, with cruel chastisement” (Jer. XXX, 10); likewise: “Why do you cry to me over your brokenness? Your pain is incurable” (ibid., 15). And, describing the punishment of those condemned forever, he says: “Let them be clothed with their confusion as with a double cloak” (Ps. CVIII, 92). Hence in the psalm he twice prays the same thing: “Lord, rebuke me not in your fury” (Ps. VI, 37).

Another says: “Correct me, Lord, yet in mercy and not in your fury, lest perhaps you reduce me to nothing” (Jer. X, 34). When you have considered that all these things belong to that kind of scourging by which, following the examples of Pharaoh and Herod, the impious are scourged both in the present and in the future, know—on Gregory’s testimony—that only those are freed from eternal scourges by temporal scourges whom it happens to be transformed here from their iniquities.

Know also that you stand in combat with an adversary who rages all the more fiercely because he grieves over the power he has lost over you; and, in addition, that he is afflicted more grievously by the fact that you, who were accustomed to serve him, challenge him in battle [Note: [Col. 0311C] It would be better to read *afficere* (“to afflict”) rather than *affici* (“to be afflicted”). Immediately afterward, the printed editions mistakenly had *ante* instead of *a te* (“by you”).].

Do not hesitate to show mercy even to those through whose treachery you were betrayed, through whose negligence you were abandoned, through whose deceit you were captured, and through whose faction you were brought into these misfortunes [Note: [Col. 0311C] These words seem to allude to what happened to Ratherius himself: he was betrayed through treachery, abandoned through negligence—namely, that of the bishops who ought to have assisted him but neglected to do so—captured by deceit, and through faction driven into the misfortunes which he was suffering in prison while writing this.]. Be certain that if you retain their offenses in your heart, you too will lack forgiveness for your own, as Truth itself teaches (Matt. V, 45). If you forgive, you will one day rejoice in the remission of your own sins and will rejoice eternally in the sonship of God.

But as for yourself, attribute everything that you suffer to yourself: impute everything to your fault, everything to your sins. For perhaps this disturbance of yours also had some purpose, on account of which you were given over to this kind of punishment [Note: [Col. 0311C] He continues here to speak of himself.
