The passage should be explained as follows: “Perhaps this disturbance also—the disturbance stirred up against Hugh—was yours,” since it was indeed attributed to him among other things, as we explained in *Life*, § 4; “and on account of this you were given over to this imprisonment. If that is not so, you have more reason to rejoice; but if it is so, you have more reason to grieve, though not despairingly,” and so forth.]. If this is not so, you have more reason to rejoice; but if it is so, you have more to grieve over—yet not despairingly, because no one can weigh, much less estimate, the riches of God’s goodness.

If this is so, it is no less fitting for you to mourn yourself than to mourn your own betrayers, especially if they were sons of your Church, or perhaps—God forbid—of the same office as you. For you recognize that you were not merely the occasion but also the material cause of the death of your sons, and you can grieve that so many lights of heaven, enveloped in your darkness, should be extinguished through your downfall [Note: [Col. 0311D] Understand: “If this is so, it is no less fitting for you to mourn yourself than your own betrayers, especially if they were…” He indicates, among other things, that his betrayers included the sons of his Church at Verona, and perhaps also some of those who held the same office as he did, namely, certain bishops. He adds that you should recognize yourself as having been the occasion of the death of your sons, because you recognize yourself as having been the material cause of their death. He seems to mean spiritual death, which he did not doubt that those same sons incurred because of their betrayal. Ratherius himself can be seen to have been not only the occasion but also the material cause of this death: the occasion, because he consented to that agreement or letter which was turned into his own ruin; the material cause, because that betrayal, which brought spiritual death upon them, was undertaken for the sake of his downfall. The “lights of heaven” are the bishops who fell silent in his downfall and offered no assistance, or those whom he suspected of having shared in his betrayal.].

But because here the merciful Just One is accustomed to strike certain people severely, so that he may not find anything there that he ought eternally to punish, let the memory of his mercy refresh you amid your very lamentations. Through that mercy it came about that you can sing with the Psalmist:

> “But I will rejoice in the Lord; I will exult and be glad in your mercy, because you have regarded my humility, you have saved my soul from distress, and you have not confined me into the hands of the enemy; you have set my feet in a spacious place” [Col. 0311C] (Ps. XXX, 8).

You will rightly be able to say all this if you have not neglected the time granted for repentance, if you have patiently endured the punishment inflicted, knowing that this punishment proceeded from the cause of your former sin: the punishment of your present sin, by which, having been seized by iniquities, you could be seen not to sin while sinning, so that you might not sin [Note: [Col. 0312C] This exceedingly obscure sentence seems to require correction and explanation as follows: “by which you, seized by iniquities”—namely, former iniquities, of which he has spoken by saying “the sin of the past”—“could be seen not to sin while sinning, so that you might not sin.” Ratherius could evidently have appeared to sin when, compelled by necessity and with a good purpose, he joined the party of the rebels against Hugh, although he did not sin in doing so—as we discuss more fully in *Life*, § 4—and was consequently captured and confined in prison so that, as a penitent, he might not sin, or might thereafter guard against other sins. We would gladly hear anyone who could explain it better.].

Therefore pray assiduously that divine mercy may most graciously forgive you this as well, and that, consuming in this furnace of necessity those things on account of which you were brought into it—or rather into them (by “them” I mean both the sin and the scourge of sin, referring the entire burden to you) [Note: [Col. 0312C] Construe: “And that divine mercy, consuming in this furnace those things on account of which you were brought into this—or rather into these things—may erase them.” By “these things” he refers to the whole sum of your sin, so as to remember both the sin and the scourge of sin.], it may erase them, and purify you in this world so thoroughly that the devouring, unquenchable fire of the future may find nothing to burn; or rather, that by his grace it may find something to reward and by his justice something to crown.

### 28

Although you ought to lament greatly the abandonment of your people [Note: [Col. 0312D] “The abandonment of your people,” he says, because, with their shepherd carried away, the sheep had been left deserted.], you ought not to do so without consolation. For you know that the supreme Shepherd said through the prophet:

> “Behold, I myself will seek my sheep and will visit them, as a shepherd visits his flock on the day when he is in the midst of his scattered sheep” (Ezek. XXXIV, 11).

And you recognize the saying of a certain wise man: where human help is absent, divine help must be present.

But if the length of time torments you, and the loss of those who die without the help of baptism saddens you, and you perceive that your torturers do not care about this [Note: [Col. 0312D] That is: “You perceive that your torturers”—namely, the authors of your misfortune—“do not care about this,” that is, about the destruction of those who die without baptism, provided only that they fulfill their own wishes through your suffering.], being concerned only to fulfill their wishes through your anguish, submit your whole self to the will and disposition of God [that is, to his arrangement], and be prepared to give up life itself—not to mention every loss of honor—for the sake of the flock. Use the words of him who said:

> “If this storm is because of me, take me up and cast me into the sea” (Jon. I, 12),

lest, for my sake, the ship of the Church continue any longer in danger, sending so many—alas for the grief!—sons to eternal death [that is, those dying without baptism].

But let these things suffice for now. May God grant that they benefit you [Note: [Col. 0313D] The printed editions give a disordered reading: “But these things we now wish. Are you a cleric? I ask that the word itself, *suffice*, should agree with the mind.” We have restored the true reading, which agrees with the sense. Shortly afterward, the printed editions also read *propter ipsum* (“because of him”) incorrectly.]. Amen.

### 29

Are you a cleric? May the very name, I ask, suit you: recognizing from your lot that you ought to belong to the Lord, fear somewhat that, by seeking anything besides him, you may lose fellowship in so great a good; rather, show yourself worthy of such a companion.

If you are called a canon [Note: [Col. 0313D] He does not say, as usual, “Are you a canon?” but “If you are called a canon,” because this name was being eagerly adopted in Ratherius’s age, having been introduced not long before. Hence the same bishop wrote in his book *Concerning Clerics Rebelling against Him*: “They eagerly desire to be called canons.”], take care not to depart from the holy canons. But if perhaps you reject them, consider before what kind of judgment you must be presented: you have renounced the order of the laity [understand “order”], yet have not kept the ecclesiastical order.

Are you a presbyter? Preserve in your conduct the dignity which you appear to bear in your title.

Are you a deacon? Recognizing that you are a minister of the heavenly sacraments, conduct yourself in every way as a chaste man, according to the Apostle (I Tim. III, 8), worthy of such offices; preserve before God the celibacy of heart and body, knowing that the most sacred sacrifice, instituted to cleanse the sins of all, ought not to be handled by unclean hands.

Are you a subdeacon? Know that you ought to be subject not only to God but also to all the prelates of the Church, so that you may deserve to be exalted by the Lord here and rewarded in the future.

Are you an exorcist? Do not permit the one whom, by adjuring him, you expel from the bodies of others to rule your own senses.

Are you a candle-bearer? Since you minister light to others, do not allow yourself to be darkened by the shadows of sins and ignorance. Rather, I ask you to strive to be illuminated within yourself and to offer others the light of a good example.

Are you a lector? By persistently doing that from which you derive your title, take care not to deviate from your office.

Are you a doorkeeper? Open your heart to God; close it to the devil when he lies in wait.

### 30

Are you a monk? You need no admonition—unless it is to persevere most excellently in what you have begun well, provided that you truly are what you are called, what you are thought to be, and what you profess in your habit [f. *nisi*, “unless”]. But if you are otherwise—God forbid—woe to you, who conceal a wolf beneath a sheep’s skin.

Nevertheless, take care not to despair [Note: [Col. 0313D] The Vulgate has the corrupt reading “lest you despair of expelling [him].” The context requires the correction.]. Rather, expel the wolf from your heart and restore the sheep to its own skin. Remember that the Lord, as we have already said elsewhere, changed a sheep from a wolf—or rather, by God’s grace, changed not only a sheep but also a shepherd [Note: [Col. 0314D] He means Saint Paul, who by God’s grace emerged from being a wolf not merely as a sheep but also as a shepherd.].

But in excusing him I will accuse you more strongly: it is one thing for someone ignorant of goodness to rage openly; it is another to deceive others under the pretext of religion and, by pretending, to provoke God’s anger against oneself for what one is not [Note: [Col. 0314D] These words offer an excuse for Saint Paul, who says in the First Epistle to Timothy (I, 13): “I was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor, and insolent; but I obtained God’s mercy, because I acted ignorantly in unbelief.”].

But even if you are not doing this through pretense, you are drowsily sluggish because you have been lulled to sleep by a certain negligence. Therefore recover your strength, resume your steadfastness, put on courage, so that, like a giant, you may fight bravely against the powers of the air. For otherwise you will neither be able to conquer them nor ascend so arduous a height by any other means.

Meditate on the Rule; reread frequently the lives of the holy Fathers; behold yourself in them as in a mirror, and conform your life to theirs. First impose obedience upon yourself. Avoid public gatherings; flee the companionship of worldly people. Know that someone very truthfully said—and, alas for the grief, we too know by experience that it has been proved—that a sheep which leaves the sheepfold is exposed to the bites of wolves [Note: [Col. 0314D] “We know,” he says, “that this has also been proved by our own experience: when a sheep leaves the monastery’s fold and becomes a bishop, it is exposed to the bites of wolves,” that is, to the persecutions of adversaries.].

But if obedience or some just necessity ever requires you to appear in public, let your very habit, speech—or rather, your solitude itself—your walk, your expression, and your complexion be an object of wonder, fear, and example to everyone.

Make “mine” and “yours” a kind of sacrilege in your life, without which the universal community of all could exist in the greatest peace.

And after you have fulfilled everything that befits a monk, remember that you are still navigating this dangerous sea, in which almost everything is uncertain, everything doubtful: both the favorable and the adverse, both the shipwrecked and the tranquil. Therefore, until you reach the harbor, do not make yourself secure.

Hear Ambrose:

> “The helmsman cannot be praised before he has brought the ship into harbor.”

### 31

Are you an abbot? Remember what you are called and how difficult and arduous a task you have undertaken. And, to bring this discourse to its conclusion in you, attend, I ask, to the dignity of so great a name and mentally perceive whose place you occupy.

A monk is one who, seeing himself so hemmed in by difficulties that he is almost driven to despair, yet held back by the anchor of the all-powerful mercy of God lest he fall utterly into its Charybdis, supposes that his fear has arisen from God’s mercy and returns to himself. He avoids placing upon himself the noose with which Judas was strangled; abandoning everything he possessed in the world—worldly ambition itself together with its understanding—he seeks the monastery and gives himself wholly to the Lord, reserving nothing for himself from all that he has, since he knows and has determined that not even his own body is to be retained under his personal authority. He counts it forbidden even to think, much less to say, “What shall we eat?” or “What shall we drink?” or “With what shall we be clothed?” He is confident that all necessities will come to him from the father of the monastery. Of the monk, I say, I declare that enough has been said.

### 32

But what shall we say about the abbot? We have said a little, but let us continue somewhat further concerning him.

An abbot is, if authority allowed us to speak in this way, the most monk-like of all monks. He is able to fast more, pray more, read more, and sing more psalms; to endure with greater patience fasting, nakedness, poverty, insults, contempt, hunger, thirst, cold, wind, rain, snow, hail, abuse, mockery, and derision—in short, every hardship. Where benevolence is not supported by beneficence, he should show more benevolence than all others, even toward those who pursue him with hatred. He should be more teachable and more obedient than the rest; if it can be so—that is, if his other virtues agree—wiser; fuller of charity; more willing to enforce discipline; gentler through an abundance of kindness; superior in generosity; more ready to sympathize with the afflicted; humbler and more submissive than everyone else.

And here too, just as in the case of the monk, I declare that enough has been said about the abbot.

### 33

As for those whom I have repeatedly found—shamefully!—to aspire merely to preside over monks, rather than to be monks, I declare that they ought rather to be fled than followed. Their example could hardly provide a sound way of life, since it is clear that they have brought forth from themselves things so harmful, so countless, so grave, and so monstrous.

I think it appropriate to relate what happened to my anxiety this year [Note: [Col. 0315C] *Horno* is an adverb meaning “this year.” Since the event described below occurred at Laon after the year 968, as we established in *Life*, § 20, this narrative is known to have been added later to Book Five.].

When I was at Laon on the day of the Nativity of the Lord, the abbot asked me to come on the feast of Saint Stephen into the chapter-house of the sisters and, to use his own words, say something good to them. I agreed. After the customary reading, having asked for and received the blessing, I said:

> “Having been asked to say something good to your charity, I find nothing else except that, whatever it may be, I shall report to your lordship what happened to me this night.
>
> “Yesterday I was exceedingly troubled about receiving provision for the abbacy of Saint-Amand. While I was standing watchfully at the nocturnal office—though, alas, often dreaming—as the reader reached a passage from the treatise of blessed Jerome where the Lord in the Gospel continues speaking to certain people, saying, ‘All these things will come upon this generation’ (Matt. XXIII, 36), I understood this, following the explanation of that same famous teacher, to mean that whoever unjustly kills his brother—that is, any Christian—contracts a greater offense against himself than those who killed various people from righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah, since he possesses the whole of that offense by reason of sharing in the same generation, and in addition his own offense, which he committed by imitating them.
>
> “When this had greatly terrified me—as often happens, when one thing is gathered from another—I began to reason within myself that what had been understood concerning homicide ought, by evident reason, to apply to the other crimes as well. I began to say to myself: ‘Then ought you to become an abbot with such a conscience? First make yourself a monk.’”

At that time he had abandoned all thought of the episcopate, since Ratherius had already renounced the bishopric of Verona [Note: [Col. 0315C] At the time when the event just related occurred, Ratherius was no longer thinking about the episcopate, having renounced the bishopric of Verona. He reports, however, that many had undertaken that dignity unworthily. The same was also noted by Atto, bishop of Vercelli, in his work *On the Pressures of the Church*, part II of the *Spicilegium*, latest edition, p. 421.], except that many had also undertaken that office unworthily.

Therefore, since we have wandered far from the place where the conclusion of this book ought to have been made, let us now cast our anchor here, so that the helmsman, refreshed for a little while, may more quickly and easily recover his strength.

Let the conclusion of this discourse of our text end, then, in praise of the Holy Trinity:

> “To you praise, to you glory, to you thanksgiving, O blessed Trinity. Have mercy, have mercy, have mercy on me, though most unworthy and trembling to speak improperly of you, whose name does not escape your knowledge in me.”

## HERE BEGINS BOOK SIX

[Col. 0315]

### 1

It is customary for sailors to fear pirates no less than storms, and sometimes to fear the proximity of the harbor itself more than the open sea, when a dromon, often loaded beyond its capacity, is unexpectedly dashed upon the sandbanks by its excessive weight, and all hope of the labor perishes together with those who labor, while friends watch from nearby [Note: [Col. 0315D] A *dromon* is a long and swift ship, from the Greek δρόμος (*drómos*), “course” or “running,” since it races over the waters with great speed. See Du Cange, under *Dromones*. It would be preferable, on account of the gravity of the matter, to write *propter gravitatem*, so that the construction would be: “while the heavily loaded dromon is often unexpectedly dashed upon the sandbanks because of its weight,” by which it is driven lower and strikes the sandbanks. The author may also be suggesting that it was loaded beyond what the size of the dromon could bear.].

Lest this happen to us as well, rising, let us pray: “Save us, lest we perish” (Matt. VIII, 25). For without you the mind begins nothing lofty, much less completes it, while this sixth gulf—that is, this sixth book—strives to be plowed by us, who presume upon you, O supreme Godhead, our helmswoman, and who already behold the harbor toward which we are heading [Note: [Col. 0316D] Construe: “Rising and already looking toward the harbor to which we are heading, we pray: Save us, lest we perish.” The author has written *exsurgens* and *respiciens* in the singular instead of *exsurgentes* and *respicientes* in the plural. Without you the mind begins nothing lofty, much less completes it, while this sixth gulf—that is, this sixth book—strives to be plowed by us who presume upon you, supreme Godhead, our helmswoman.].

Now, having briefly touched upon the sacred orders, let us come to the varied conduct of human beings, addressing them also as briefly as we can.

Are you just? I suggest that you dissemble—or rather, think that you are not just—so that you may truly be just.

Are you a sinner? Strive with all your strength not to be a sinner, recognizing that you truly are one. In this way, with God’s help, you may eventually cease to be one.

Are you just? Take care lest you fall.

Are you a sinner? Try to rise.

Are you just? Let the fall of the angel hold you back as a warning.

Are you a sinner? Let the ascent of the human being toward repentance encourage you.

Therefore let neither the former trust first in his own conduct, nor the latter despair of God’s mercy, because although it may be known what sort of people you are today, neither of you knows at all what you will be tomorrow.

The fall and rising of those who fall daily show that both the darkness and the light of the heart are changeable [Note: [Col. 0317D] There is some error in the word *tantum* (“only”). From the sense one should read *sanctorum* (“of the saints”), or *justorum* (“of the just”), or something similar.]. Hence, after saying elsewhere, “Let him who stands take heed lest he fall” (I Cor. X, 12), the Apostle says: “You were once darkness, but now light in the Lord” (Eph. V, 8).

Are you a sinner? Hear what may make you rejoice:

> “There is joy in heaven over one sinner who repents, more than over ninety-nine righteous people who have no need of repentance” (Luke XV, 10).

Are you just? Hear what you must beware of:

> “I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven” (Luke X, 18).

### 2

But are you neither so very just nor so very sinful? Does a certain middle position between these two please you? I beg you, fear that very lukewarmness, lest from it you fall back into coldness. For just as one often passes from lukewarmness to warmth, so, as Gregory testifies, one often declines from the same lukewarmness into coldness [Col. 0317B].

Finally, hear what is said to the angel of Laodicea:

> “Would that you were hot or cold! But because you are lukewarm, I am beginning to vomit you from my mouth” (Rev. III, 16).

Woe to the one who is irretrievably vomited from the mouth of God.

In contrast, the Psalmist says of the saints:

> “They will go from strength to strength” (Ps. LXXXIII, 88),

because, as blessed Leo says, knowing that they are trees planted by the Lord in the garden of the Church, they not only take care that they do not decline for the worse, but also apply themselves earnestly to advance toward what is better.

Although a very beautiful saying of one of our own—beautiful because most gentle—is held to be that no one who has attained even a portion of good works is outside mercy, nevertheless we must retain no less firmly the definition of another, because it is most true:

> “Whoever does not advance, falls back; and whoever acquires nothing, loses something.”

Another, agreeing with him, though not inferior, says:

> “Every decline tends toward nothingness.”

With these things connected as they are, we must fear lest, while you do not strive for progress, you succumb to decline and become nothing.

There are some, Gregory testifies, whose company you should strive to escape: those who serve God strategically so that they may enjoy the world. On the contrary, seek to be found among those who serve the world only in passing so that they may enjoy God.

I consider this the middle position of justice. But if you cannot at all raise yourself—as indeed you cannot—to that highest order of pleasing God, at least I ask you to hold humbly and most firmly to this middle position, lest one day you fall through a deviation from the path into that lowest condition [Note: [Col. 0318D] The printed editions have *infirmum* (“weak”), incorrectly.].

For you ought not to become lost because you cannot be perfect, nor ought you to become the worst because you cannot be the best. Finally, that very humility by which you regard yourself as lowly, if it is genuine and not rather sluggishness, will eventually be able to raise you to sublime things, as the Lord’s own word testifies (Matt. XXIII, 12).

### 3

But lest, while I deal with you more gently in these matters, you suppose that I am advising—or perhaps even permitting—you to abstain from certain sins while serving some vice as though with permission, know that I understand, as the Apostle teaches, that “a little leaven corrupts the whole lump” (I Cor. V, 6).

Hear what James says:

> “Whoever observes the whole law but offends in one point is guilty of all” (Jas. II, 10).

Whether by “the whole law” he means the Gospel, the Old Testament, or both together, we leave to diligent students to investigate, since Truth itself, when asked, said that the whole law and the prophets depend upon two commandments (Matt. XXII, 40), and the Apostle said that the fullness of the law is love (Rom. XIII, 10).

We know that Augustine said:

> “If someone keeps one commandment but transgresses another, it does him no good. Does someone guard himself from greed but not from adultery? Certainly, convicted in one matter, he is condemned even by the laws of the world; nor does abstinence from one crime benefit him who has been found guilty of another.”

Although what he said in this sense is exceedingly terrifying, Jerome has nevertheless already been consulted concerning this same saying of the Apostle. Nor is it unknown to us that the whole law is understood as those ten general commandments, from which every particular commandment flows as though from a certain stream, distinguished by the strings of a ten-stringed instrument.

These ten commandments, derived inseparably from those two greatest and first commandments, form ten streams: seven pertaining to love of neighbor and three pertaining to love of God. Yet they preserve the nature of the source from which they emerged, so that one cannot truly embrace or reject one without the other, just as the members cannot do so without the head.

For just as the one who does not love his neighbor is shown not to love God, as John says:

> “If anyone says, ‘I love God,’ and hates his brother, he is a liar” (I John III, 9),

and not merely one’s neighbor but even one’s enemy, as the Lord says:

> “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V, 44),

and since there is no more evident return of love than that of a father toward a son and a son toward a father, one is convicted of not loving the father whose command one scorns: so also no one who truly observes that first commandment can transgress those three which derive from it.

For no one who loves God worships another besides him, takes his name in vain, or does any good except for the sake of the true Sabbath, that is, eternal rest.

And just as the one who does not love God is shown not to love his neighbor—for he does not even love himself, as the Psalmist says, “Whoever loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Ps. X, 5)—so the one who truly loves God does not neglect the other commandments derived from this love.

He honors his parents; he does not commit adultery; he does not kill; he does not steal; he does not bear false witness; he does not desire his neighbor’s wife or any of his possessions.

But whoever transgresses any one of these is held guilty of all, because he appears to have violated the very fountain from which they all proceed, since one who truly loves his neighbor cannot do any of the things that are forbidden [Note: [Col. 0319D] The printed editions have *dum et proximum*. We have deleted the words *dum* and *et*, which disturb both the sense and the construction, unless one prefers to read *dum est*. Construe: “Since one who truly loves his neighbor cannot do any of the things that are forbidden; for love of neighbor works no evil.”], for “love of neighbor works no evil” (Rom. XIII, 10).

We have said all this so that, if you wish at least to hold the middle position of goodness, you may strive to be free from every capital vice.

### 4

Know that the capital sins are those which the Decachord, written on tablets of stone, forbids [Note: [Col. 0319D] The “Decachord written on tablets of stone” is the Decalogue, or the ten commandments of the Decalogue.].

And, following the same sense, let us enumerate them as blessed Augustine has already arranged them.

First, there is the unbelief of idolatry, from which he forbids you when he says:

> “Your God is one God” (Mark XII, 29).

Next comes the error of heresy and of various superstitions: incantations, what are commonly called *facturae* [Note: [Col. 0319D] *Factura* means the same as sorcery or witchcraft; from it we recognize the origin and antiquity of the Italian word *fattura*.], and those things which the Psalmist calls vanities and false insanities (Ps. XXXIX, 5); as well as the practices which the Apostle solemnly enumerates:

> “You observe days and months and seasons and years; I fear that I may have labored over you in vain” (Gal. IV, 10).

You are restrained from all such things when you hear:

> “You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain” (Exod. XX, 7).

Perjury also seems to me to be forbidden under this commandment.

Next come pride, arrogance, empty glory, and love of the world, for which those who do not love God labor above all in all their dealings. You are drawn away from these when you are commanded to keep the Sabbath: that is, by turning away from evil and doing good (Ps. XXXVI, 27), to rest from sin and serve God; and to do everything humbly, not proudly, for the sake of eternal reward, not for the empty glory of the world.

These are the three divisions of the commandments and prohibitions of evils.

The following pertain to love of neighbor:

> “Honor your father and your mother” (Exod. XX, 12),

where, in addition to your natural parent, you are especially commanded to honor God the Father, Mother Church, and the prelates of the Church.

> “You shall not commit adultery” (ibid., 14),

by which you are restrained from every form of lust.

> “You shall not kill” (ibid., 13),

by which you are forbidden every kind of cruelty.

> “You shall not steal” (ibid., 15),

by which you are restrained from greed and rapacity.

> “You shall not bear false witness” (ibid., 16),

by which you are forbidden falsehood, perjury, and disparagement [f. *detraction*, “slander”].

> “You shall not desire your neighbor’s wife” (ibid., 17),

by which you are recalled even from adulterous thought.

If you keep these things unstained, I can admonish you, following the example of the Lord responding to the young man who said that he had observed them, so that you may be raised to greater things (Mark X, 20) [Note: [Col. 0319D] Here something is missing, such as “of the respondent” or “of the one giving the command.” Construe: “Following the example of the Lord who responded to the young man saying that he had observed these things, I can admonish you so that you may be raised to greater things.”].

But if I discover that you have transgressed any of these, I do not urge you toward better things—rather, I advise you to correct what is wrong; I do not tell you to climb from virtue to virtue, but to turn from wickedness to goodness.

For this is not, as you thought, the middle position of goodness; rather, it is no position at all. Whoever, by transgressing any one of these ten commandments, is shown neither to love God nor neighbor, even if he appears to have fulfilled some of them, what goodness do you think he possesses before correcting those things which he recognizes he has done less well? [Note: [Col. 0320D] That is: “Whoever is shown, by transgressing any one of these commandments, neither to love God nor neighbor—even if he appears to have fulfilled some of them—what goodness do you think he possesses?”].

When I recognize that you have been cleansed, either through the practice of goodness or through the satisfaction of correction, from the vices forbidden by these ten commandments, and adorned with the virtues which they commend—that is, love of God and neighbor, faith, and hope [Note: [Col. 0320D] The printed editions have *quae* (“which”) incorrectly; afterward they have *aut ad superiora* (“or to higher things”), where *ut* or *aut ut* should be read.], I believe that you have entered the middle position. And, so that you may rise to higher things, namely by selling everything and giving it to the poor and following Christ, I admonish you; or at least I urge you to hold firmly to these things, because I know that through these alone you will not merely be saved but also rewarded.

The Psalmist says:

> “Your eyes saw my imperfect state, and in your book all shall be written” (Ps. CXXXVIII, 16),

that is, both the perfect and the imperfect.

The perfect are those which, as we have already said, the Lord offered to the young man:

> “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come and follow me” (Matt. XIX, 21).

The imperfect are those which we have already set forth while describing the middle position of justice. Through these, we believe that even worldly people can greatly please God, and that through the worthy fruits of repentance we may hope to obtain the grace of the most merciful Judge even after having held him in contempt in many ways. We believe that, reconciled, we shall receive again the wedding garment which we lost through earthly injury, if not with a crown, at least with forgiveness.

All these things have been said to restrain presumption and to arouse devotion, not to cast anyone into despair [Note: [Col. 0320D] Understand: “All these things have been said,” namely, to restrain presumption and arouse devotion, since they were not spoken to induce despair.].

### 5.

It must also be understood that even the smallest things very often have great value, since by the mere generosity of almsgiving the greatest sins are forgiven those who have been converted. This is accomplished solely by the free grace of God, which, in its mercy, inspires what it inspires and, in its mercy, helps it to be brought to completion; in its mercy, receiving what is made perfect, it crowns it. [Note: “Receiving what is made perfect,” namely, receiving that which is perfect.] [Col. 0320D]

Charity also accomplishes this, extinguishing all sins—for no one truly has compassion on another unless, for the love of God and of the person on whom he has compassion, he has compassion [understood]—and so great is the prerogative of this virtue [Col. 0321A] that even its imperfect acts are greatly accepted. For a virtue lacking this charity, even if it appears to be some virtue, is nothing, as the apostolic voice bears witness (I Cor. XIII).

Now, to speak of the faith by which we believe in God: if, by believing in him, we worship him for any reason other than love of him and of our own soul, we acquire no benefit. [Note: Construe: If, by believing in him, we worship him for any reason other than love of him and of our soul, we acquire no benefit.] And what else are we chiefly commanded to hope for from him except that, through loving and being loved by him, through vision and knowledge, we shall enjoy him eternally?

What good do we suppose it does us not to commit adultery, not to kill, not to steal, not to bear false witness, not to covet our neighbor’s property, nor to desire his wife, or anything else, unless [understand: unless one abstains from these things] for the love of God and of one’s brother?

Therefore, whatever good you do, however small, if you do it for the sake of charity, be confident: you do it with fruit. If you do it for some other reason, do not be mistaken: you do it in vain. If the love of charity restrains you from any evil, you will not lack a reward. If you act for some other reason, you are considered worthy neither of forgiveness, much less of grace.

Therefore, whoever wishes to attain the middle station of righteousness, observe these Ten Commandments, and observe them for the sake of those two things—namely, love of God and of neighbor. But if it should happen that you perhaps slip away from these, return as quickly as you can to the compassion of the physician whom you love; confessing that love itself has been slighted, though somewhat less, and lamenting it deeply, strive to be restored to your proper place.

For he loves those by whom he is not loved; much less will he despise you, by whom he is loved in some manner, however negligently. Therefore hasten to be reconciled with so great a friend, and to be restored from the place where you fell, since you see that some who were restored have even been advanced to better things.

True restoration, however, exists where there is true confession; true confession, where there is true conversion; and where there is true conversion, there is true healing. For what does it accomplish to show a wound to a physician if you do not wish to be cured by him? [Note: The Vulgate reads *carere*, “to lack.” We have emended it on the basis of the preceding and following context, which concerns healing.] Yet wounds that are shown repeatedly and not healed swell further, so that by their stench they infect even those who see them; through frequent handling they become worse.

### 6.

Are you penitent, or do you wish to be? Consider the rule of repentance expressed in the words of the Lord’s Baptist. “Produce,” he says, “fruits worthy of repentance” (Matt. III, 8); and shortly afterward: “Whoever has two tunics, let him give to one who has none” (Luke III, 11); and, expounding the other works of mercy [that is, continuing his exposition], he teaches most clearly that the one who wishes, by pursuing his faults, to present a fruit worthy of repentance, ought mercifully to devote care to the needs of others, so that he may obtain mercy from the Lord.

Therefore the naked person must be clothed by one who wishes to recover the ornament of innocence that he has lost. Let him feed the hungry who desires to escape the soul’s deadly hunger. Let him give drink to the thirsty who wishes to escape the sickness of his conduct. Let him console one confined in prison who does not wish to enter the dungeon of hell. Let him strengthen the sorrowful who does not desire to see eternal grief. Let him receive the stranger into his lodging who wishes to be received by the Lord into that eternal tabernacle of paradise.

Let him ransom the captive who longs to be freed from the devil’s snares. Through Christ, let him comfort one who is placed in some necessity, if he wishes to be freed from the necessities of various afflictions. Let him bury the dead who longs to escape the death of eternal destruction. Let him free one imprisoned for debts who longs to be freed from his own sins. Let him rescue those who are being led to death who wishes to escape hell’s prison. Let him overcome the impatient spirit who wishes to conquer the raging devil. Let him correct the negligent person with mercy who wishes to appease God the Father, who corrects him.

[Col. 0322B] ### 7.

Besides these, there is another and more particular means of obtaining mercy, proportionately greater because it was instituted by the Lord’s own mouth and added to the others—or rather, superior to them in order, nature, and usefulness:

“Forgive,” he says, “and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you” (Luke VI, 37); and: “Unless you forgive people their sins, neither will your Father who is in heaven forgive you your sins” (Matt. VI, 15).

Third, repeating the same point in the same sense, he says: “When you stand to pray, forgive, if you have anything against anyone, so that your Father who is in heaven may also forgive you your sins” (Mark XI, 25).

Fourth, after setting forth the parable that likewise demonstrated this: “So also my heavenly Father will do to you, if each of you does not forgive his brother from your hearts” (Matt. XVIII, 35). [Note: The Vulgate reads *promissa*, “promised,” incorrectly; *praemissa*, “set forth beforehand,” is correct.] This is so that no one may imagine that he can deceive God with his lips, since God sees what is in the heart.

Fifth, he says: “If you offer your gift at the altar and remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go first to be reconciled with your brother; then come and offer your gift” (Matt. V, 23).

But perhaps you say: “The one whom I injured is far away, and I cannot approach him.” The angel says to you: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke II, 14). The psalm also says to you: “In me are your vows, O God, which I shall repay to you as praises” (Ps. LV, 13). The Apostle also says: “If it is possible, and in whatever way you can, retain peace in your will”; and so the Lord says: “If a son of peace is there, your peace will rest upon him; but if not, it will return to you” (Luke X, 6)—that is, it will not be lacking from your will and reward, even if it is not received by that person.

Gregory also says: “Therefore we must go in mind to our neighbor, although he is far away and greatly separated from us, submit our spirit to him, and appease him by humility and goodwill.”

Sixth, finally, the Lord says: “With whatever measure you measure, it will be measured back to you” (Matt. VII, 2).

Seventh, speaking about the adulterous woman, he says: “Let the one among you who is without sin be the first to throw a stone at her” (John VIII, 7)—that is, let the one who has no sin in himself by which he could be struck strike another’s offense without mercy. Hence Seneca says: “See whether you are still wicked, and spare those like yourself; but if you have ceased to be so, why do you cut off from others the benefit of amendment, provided that the person involved here is not inconsistent with this?”

Eighth: “First remove the beam from your own eye, and then you will see clearly to remove the speck from your brother’s eye” (Matt. VII, 3). He calls the speck sudden and slight anger; the beam, pride, hatred, and the retention of enmity.

Ninth: “Physician, heal yourself” (Luke IV, 23)—that is, first correct anger or hatred in yourself, and only then, by pursuing it, heal another’s sin. This is illustrated by a certain philosopher who, when he was becoming inflamed with anger, as we have already related in another volume, is said to have said to the person who was provoking him: “I would strike you already, if I were not angry.” [Note: This shows that Rather had previously written another work in which this saying of a certain philosopher was included. That work, however, is now lost. Whether it was the work in which he answered certain questions of the Milanese before becoming bishop of Verona, or a different work, is unknown. Atto, bishop of Vercelli, also quotes the same saying of the same philosopher in *On the Troubles of the Church*, part I, in these words: “For the philosopher Terentianus says to his steward: ‘Wretched man, whom I would afflict if I were not angry.’”]

If it happened that one of the faithful had said this, what else would he do? Would he not, by guarding the health of his own mind, cure the other’s frenzy by an infusion of patience? But what would that same pagan cry out—shame upon it!—to us who carry a beam in our own eye and try to pull a speck from another’s eye? What else, I ask, would he cry out to us in such a situation except what the prophet cried out long ago: “Be ashamed, Sidon, says the sea” (Isa. XXIII, 54)?

It would be as though by that very example he were saying: With what face would any Christian, carrying the beam of pride, attempt to remove from another’s eye the speck of some vice, when the philosopher sees that I do not even wish to carry the speck of anger in the eye of my heart, while I strive to pull the beam of arrogance from another’s eye? [Note: The text formerly read *clamavit*, “he cried out,” instead of *clamaret*, “he would cry out,” and *non quod*, “not that,” incorrectly. The sense requires the correction. Construe: “What would that same pagan—shame upon it!—cry out to us who carry a beam in our own eye and strive to remove a speck from another’s eye? What, I say, would he cry out to us in such a situation, except what the prophet cried out long ago when he said: ‘Be ashamed, Sidon, says the sea’?”]

Tenth, likewise, the Lord says: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and sends rain upon the just and the unjust” (Luke VI, 27).

Therefore let all the deceitfulness of those who repent unworthily—indeed, of those who by this pretense provoke God to anger—be gone, struck at least twice by the thunderbolts of the divine mouth, in addition to countless others. Let every deceitfulness of those, I say, who repent unworthily, indeed who by this pretense provoke God to anger, now judge that they can in no way deserve forgiveness of sins so long as they retain in their hearts any frenzied hatred. [Note: The Vulgate reads *aestimantium*, “of those who think,” incorrectly. The sense supplies the correction. Construe: “Let every deceitfulness of those who repent unworthily, indeed of those who by this pretense provoke God to anger, be gone, struck at least twice by the thunderbolts of the divine mouth, beyond the countless others; let them now judge that they can in no way deserve forgiveness of sins so long as they retain,” etc.]

### 8.

This too belongs especially to the worthy fruit of repentance: that one who considers himself to have committed unlawful acts should carefully restrain himself even from lawful acts, and should thereafter beware of accustoming his body to the enticements of those very things that he recognizes to have been the cause of some crime for him.

He knows that someone spoke most truly of this—would that it had not been made most clearly known to us and, alas, recently proved by experience—that one thing is an exhausted plague, another a plague merely lulled to sleep. For the raging adversary, knowing himself to have been driven from someone’s heart and seeking to avenge the injury of his expulsion, watches above all for that entrance through which he was accustomed to be admitted, besides a thousand other arts of doing harm. Unless a manly guard is applied with God’s help—as in the death of Ish-bosheth, who, while his doorkeeper slept, unexpectedly met his end (II Reg. IV, 5), having been struck in the groin by robbers after the ears of wheat being cleaned had also been removed [Note: That is, ears of wheat which were being cleaned.]—he generally bursts in with all the greater violence the more unexpectedly, in accordance with what the Lord says:

“When the unclean spirit has gone out from a person, it travels through waterless places seeking rest; and not finding it, it says, ‘I shall return to my house from which I came.’ And, coming to the house, etc., then it goes and takes with it seven other spirits more wicked than itself; and entering, they dwell there, and the last state of that person becomes worse than the first” (Luke XI, 24).

Behold what evil is generated by negligence, sloth, or torpor. Hence the Psalmist, while describing the people’s bodily needs, was morally displaying our falls when he said: “Their soul abhorred every kind of food, and they drew near to the gates of death” (Ps. CVI, 18).

The food of souls is prayer, psalmody, fasting, almsgiving, and continual reading. Whoever abhors these things, unless what follows happens to him—namely, that he cries to the Lord when he is afflicted (ibid., 19), so that he may be freed from his needs [or: from his necessities]—is undoubtedly believed, on Gregory’s testimony, to incur the danger of eternal death. For the temporal life of one who rejects bodily nourishment is also considered hopeless.

### 9.

But, to draw myself into the example of what I have begun to discuss: when three days ago I was behaving somewhat more loosely than was fitting, I sensed—shame upon it!—that on a very small occasion, as it seemed to me though it was not in fact so, that bitter sweetness of pleasures had pricked and tormented me, even while I was in prison and worn out with grief. It was much milder than it had been accustomed to be, yet again quite different from what I had expected.

Thus I was at least able to recognize that I ought to have placed at the gates of my heart not a soft but an altogether strong guard, not a womanly but a manly one.

This, O good Jesus, pious, heavenly, and most wise physician, ought to be set down here—not to reveal it to you, who know all things before they happen, but so that I may provide for those who will also read this work [Note: The words “but so that” are to be joined with “also for those who will read this work.”]—in addition to what must above all be begged: that while I write this down so that you may erase it, while I confess it against myself, you may erase it, together with innumerable and more serious sins.

I wish those who read this to consider justly the cause of your punishment that I am suffering, so that they may glorify your justice in this matter. Let them consider how guilty I appeared in your sight when I judged myself to be altogether blind even to that fact. [Note: “Me neither to be that” has the same meaning as “me not to be guilty either.”]

For even now, struck down and prostrate, with my eyes opened for a little while, and knowing you, as it seems to me, to some extent—whether I truly know you is known by you—and wishing, with your help, not so much to amend myself as to be corrected, so that I may deserve to see you; and having resolved, by fleeing back to you, to turn my back on those most cruel masters who received me while I was fleeing from you; yet still held by the bond of an ingrained habit and by the stains of harmful repetition, pierced most miserably by the devil’s blow and struck through by the arrows of sin, I am being transfixed. [Note: Construe: “And knowing you to some extent, as it seems to me—whether I truly know you is known by you—and wishing, with your help, not so much to amend myself as to be corrected, so that I may deserve to see you; having also resolved, by fleeing back to you, to turn my back on those most cruel masters who received me while I was fleeing from you; still held by the bond of an ingrained habit and by the stains of harmful repetition, pierced most miserably by the devil’s blow and struck through by the arrows of sin, I am being transfixed.”]

Let them consider again how wretched I was: completely turned away from you, yet still appearing to you as though I were converted, so uselessly; how impious I was when I cruelly killed myself, yet how unjust I am when I mercifully ask to be restored by you; what proud flesh did in prosperity, since it still grows proud in such great adversity; what the wanton mind was attempting when certain things smiled upon it according to its desire, since it now grows faint when everything resists it.

Let them at the same time derive from my loss the benefits of caution for themselves. For blessed is the one whose instruction is another’s scourging. [Note: That is: blessed, therefore, is the one for whom another’s scourges serve as instruction.]

And on behalf of me, most wretched as I am, let them plead your mercy all the more earnestly the more numerous they recognize my guilt and the more abundantly they understand my need of intercession.

### 10.

But, to return to you, with whom I was speaking: I suggest that, while you are doing penance, you restrain your tongue not only from evil but also from good, as the Psalmist teaches when he says of himself: “When the sinner stood against me, I was silent, humbled, and kept silence from good things” (Ps. XXXVIII, 2). Yet he had previously said: “I set a guard over my mouth.”

For it is one thing to be guarded so that one may speak reasonably when usefulness requires it; another thing to be completely stopped, so that one may not speak at all. Hence in another psalm he prays, saying: “Set, O Lord, a guard over my mouth, and a door around my lips” (Ps. CXL, 3). A door, however, is both opened and closed.

Here understand the devil to be indicated by the name “sinner”; at the time of temptation or repentance, as has already been said, he is proved to stand especially against us. For the Apostle commands that the man who had violated his father’s wife be handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord (I Cor. V, 5).

To be handed over to Satan means for conflict, not for domination; for battle, not for slavery; for the destruction of the flesh, not for the harm of the soul. That is, while the flesh fights against the adversary through fasting, vigils, and other bodily afflictions and perishes, the spirit, once the enemy has been conquered, may be saved on the day of the Lord.

Hence elsewhere, likewise offering certain secular examples, he says: “Everyone who competes in the contest abstains from everything” (I Cor. IX, 25). And most truly. For in the *scamma*—the area of sand assigned to wrestlers, beyond which they were not permitted to advance—abstinence from certain things was prescribed for those who were to wrestle. [Note: A *scamma* is a space of sand marked out for wrestlers, beyond which it is not permitted to proceed. Caelius Aurelianus, book II, chapter 1: “In the area of sand, which they call the *scamma*.” Shortly afterward, *quorumdam*, “of certain things,” means *quarundam rerum*, “of certain things.”]

They were even given athletic food, that is, lighter food, which strengthened the body by restoring it rather than weakening it by burdening it. And because luxury also weakens the body excessively, they placed sheets of lead around their loins because of nocturnal pollution.

They did all these things carnally for the sake of obtaining a perishable prize. We, however, ought to act spiritually in this very different struggle, so that we may subject the flesh to the spirit, overthrow the devil, and receive an everlasting prize for victory.

The statement “to hand such a one over to Satan” (I Cor. V, 5) may also be understood in another, more appropriate way. For “Satan” is interpreted as “adversary” or “opponent”; by this name of opposition, the sinner handed over to the contrary habits of his former life is signified. For example, one who previously indulged in pleasures should now make use of bitterness, and should practice during the days of repentance whatever is opposed or contrary to pleasures, so that, while this opposition perishes through the affliction of the flesh [Note: The common text reads *carnei*, “of the flesh,” incorrectly; *carne*, “in the flesh,” is required.], the spirit may deserve to be saved on the day of the Lord.

### 11.

It must be understood that there is one kind of repentance by which a person does penance for a definite period according to the judgment of the whole Church, and another by which we repent voluntarily at all times.

The former is bound by no law except insofar as each person wishes to impose it upon himself, to the extent that he knows he ought to apply the medicine of salvation according to the measure of his sickness. The latter, however, is bound by this condition: he may do nothing more lenient for himself than what has been commanded unless he is relieved by the authority of the one by whom he was bound, or unless that person happened to impose the obligation with such prudence that, if he himself were absent, the penitent might lawfully request absolution from another. [Note: He is not speaking of sacramental absolution, but of the relaxation of an imposed penance, which the sacred canons teach may be granted according to the fervor of the penitent and other just reasons. This was to be done only by the person who had imposed the penance, unless he had imposed it with such moderation that, in his absence, it was permitted to request from another an absolution, or mitigation, of this kind.]

Neither the one nor the other is judged to perform penance worthily if, while pursuing one particular vice by mortifying himself, he does not hesitate to commit another similar vice, or perhaps a more serious one, or certainly several others.

There are some who, repenting of homicide, meditate another homicide. There are also those who, while repenting of homicide, do not shrink from committing adultery. What happens to such people except what is said: “Woe to the sinner who enters the earth by two paths!” (Sir. II, 19).

He tries to enter the earth by two paths who, while pursuing one vice, appears to seek the way of salvation, but, by pursuing the remaining vices, is shown to walk the way of death. For the Apostle James says most plainly: “Whoever offends in one thing will be guilty of all” (James II, 10). What I have said by way of example about homicide and adultery, each person should understand to apply to the other sins as well.

### 12.

Meanwhile, it must be noted what kind of wicked people the Lord receives when they are converted. He says:

“If the wicked person turns away from his wickedness and practices repentance from all his sins that he has committed, keeps all my commandments, and does judgment and righteousness, he shall surely live and shall not die” (Ezek. XVIII, 27).

“If,” he says, “he practices repentance from all his sins and keeps all my commandments”—so that you may not think that by repenting you can erase some sin if you are a despiser of the Lord’s commandments.

Therefore the one who desires to obtain pardon must abandon all crimes and keep all the commandments of God. Beware, then, whoever you are who desire to do penance, lest you wish to enter that struggle with a divided heart; lest, while you think that you can deceive God, you appear not indeed to deceive him but rather to provoke him—the one whom you ought to appease by the most humble and purest satisfaction.

### 13.

But who is equal to this, since no one can accomplish anything by his own strength? Therefore cry out daily—indeed, incessantly—and, even while remaining silent and doing anything else, ask with desire: “Create a clean heart in me, O God” (Ps. L, 12).

And if, while you strive, the result proves difficult because of the very bad habit that must be stripped away, do not, I beg you, therefore give up. This is the natural condition of every effort. A great stone is raised with difficulty to the heights, but quickly falls to the depths; nor can anyone be perfect from the beginning. For Augustine bears witness that it is difficult for a person to be changed in such a way that he has nothing for which he may be reproved.

Then hold fast to Christ and cry out: “Draw me after you” (Song I, 4); and: “Bring my soul out of prison” (Ps. CXLI, 8).

And do not rely on your own strength. Hear Augustine himself: “Fight against your desires, if God ceases to help you—if you can. You can labor; you cannot conquer.”

Hence the Psalmist says: “If I take my wings at dawn and dwell at the ends of the sea, even there your hand will lead me, and your right hand will hold me” (Ps. CXXXVIII, 9). It is as though he were saying: However much I strive, however much I labor, however far I fly on the sharpness of my mind, however high I climb by making progress, I know that I shall fall with those very wings unless your right hand provides its accustomed help.

He shows elsewhere how greatly he trusts in that help: “I promise you, little children, and I am certain that if anyone repents from the heart and does not return to the vomit of sin, he will be saved; only let him not doubt in faith, lest he return to his pleasures.”

### 14.

Therefore, if, when a sudden temptation strikes you, you unexpectedly happen to slip either in thought, in word, or finally in deed, do not despair; do not abandon what you have begun; do not interrupt the course of good action in any respect. Repair the renewed contest, resume the struggle, rekindle your courage, and avenge the injury.

A commander usually loves more the soldier who, pierced by frequent blows, attacks the enemy again after renewing the battle than the one who either never attacks [understand: never attacks him] or has turned his back and shown no courage in defeating the enemy.

Hear also the counsel of Holy Scripture on this matter: “If the spirit of one who has power rises against you, do not leave your place, because healing will cause great sins to cease” (Eccles. X, 4). [Note: Because the words “great sins” had been transferred in the manuscript to a position after the following words, “Praise the one who guards you,” so that they would produce some sense there, the editors placed two additional words in brackets as follows: “Praise the one who guards you, great sins (life through) the mercy of God.” Once those words have been returned here, where they are truly found in Ecclesiastes, no addition is necessary, and the text is understood to have been restored perfectly.]

### 15.

Are you healthy? Praise the mercy of God that guards you. Are you sick? Praise the justice of the good Father who scourges you.

“It is good,” says the Psalm, “to confess to the Lord and sing psalms to your name, O Most High.” How? “To proclaim your mercy in the morning and your truth through the night” (Ps. IX, 5)—the morning signifying prosperity, the night adversity. It is as though he had said: In prosperity it is good to proclaim your mercy; in adversity, by praising you, to proclaim your justice.

Are you healthy? Hear from whom you are preserved: “The Lord guards all their bones” (Ps. XXXIII, 21). Are you sick? Hear from what you may be consoled: “Many are the tribulations of the righteous” (ibid., 20), and so forth; and: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Rom. VIII, 18).

Are you sick? Hear this, lest you grieve impatiently: “For whom the Lord loves, he corrects” (Prov. III, 12). Are you healthy? Hear this, lest you exult insolently: “If you are without discipline, in which all have shared, then you are adulterers and not sons” (Heb. XII, 8).

Are you healthy? Fear lest it be said to you: “Son, remember that you received good things during your life” (Luke XVI, 25). Are you sick? Desire that it be said of you: “And Lazarus likewise evil things.” Take them to yourself: “but now he is comforted here.” Fear them yourself: “but you are tormented.”

Nevertheless, lest sickness itself make you careless, or health make that other person ungrateful, know that for some people sickness, or any kind of scourging, is given either for progress, for testing, or for the sole glory of God; but for others it is given either for correction or as the beginning of evils—namely, so that, while they are scourged here without being corrected, they may begin here to be tormented, in order to be tortured eternally.

“For there are many scourges of the sinner” (Ps. XXXI, 10). Consider Pharaoh; consider Herod.

For some people, health or other temporal goods are given either for testing, for the benefit of others, or for judgment. Sometimes, however, they are given so that, when one has an abundance of provisions in the present life, one may proceed more freely toward lasting goods; or so that, while one purely administers what belongs to another, one may eventually arrive at what belongs to oneself; and while temporary things are administered for the glory of God, one may arrive gloriously, with the fruit of good works, at eternal things.

For it is written: “He gave them the regions of the nations” (Ps. CIV, 44), and so forth.

Therefore a person ought to be affected or exalted by neither of these two things to an even greater degree than he can discern in this difficult world why they have been granted.

[Col. 0329B] ### 16.

Are you wise, do you wish to be wise, or are you perhaps called wise? According to the Apostle, become foolish in this world so that you may be wise (I Cor. III, 18).

Are you foolish? According to Solomon, incline your ear to the prudent (Prov. V, 1), lest you be foolish. Are you wise? Hear this: “Do not know more than it is fitting to know” (Rom. XII, 13).

Are you foolish? Hear this: “But whoever is ignorant will be ignored” (I Cor. XIV, 38). Are you wise? Hear this: “Set a limit to your prudence” (Prov. XXXIII, 4).

Are you foolish? Hear this: “How long, little ones, will you love infancy, and fools desire the things that are harmful to them, and the imprudent hate knowledge?” (Prov. I, 22.) Are you wise? Hear this: “Good understanding belongs to all who practice it” (Ps. CX, 10).

Are you foolish? Understand this: “Whoever turns his ear away so as not to hear the law, his prayer will be accursed” (Prov. XXVIII, 9). Are you wise? Beware of what the Apostle says: “It would have been better for them not to know the way of truth than, after knowing it, to turn back” (Heb. X, 26).

Are you foolish? See what the Lord says: “The one who is from God hears the words of God; for this reason you do not hear, because you are not from God” (John VII, 47).

Are you wise? Avoid carnal wisdom. Foolish? Pursue spiritual wisdom. Wise? Hear this: “Do not be wise in your own sight.” Foolish? “Fear God and depart from evil” (Prov. III, 7).

Wise? Acknowledge your own ignorance. Foolish? Dare to be wise, lest temptation subdue you before fear.

Wise? Hear this: “You will be wise if you do not believe yourself to be so” (Augustine, *On the Soul and Its Origin*, book III, chapter 1). Foolish? Wisdom is denied not by nature but by negligence.

Are you wise? Hear this: “Do not seek what is too high for you.” Foolish? “Always consider what God has commanded” (Sir. III, 22).

Hear the same person speaking to both together: Neither is excused, neither the one who read nor the one who refused to read; the one who denied what he read is more guilty.

But the one who, when he could have known what he ought to do, refused to know it, will by no means escape. For it is said in Job, in a certain description of a curse—whether of the Jews who crucified the Lord, or of Judas who betrayed the Lord [repeat: “it is said”], or of that original pride, or of the whole generation of the wicked—for the sense applies to both:

“The heavens will reveal his iniquity, and the earth will rise up against him, and his sin will be made manifest on the day of the Lord’s wrath” (Job XX, 27), together with those [that is, together with their sin] who say to the Lord God: “Depart from us; we do not want to know your ways” (Job XXI, 14).

Likewise: “They spend their days in prosperity, and in a moment they descend to the underworld.” And Wisdom says the same thing with sufficient terror: “I called, and you did not come,” and so forth; “I too will laugh at your destruction” (Prov. I, 26), and so forth.

The prophet also, lamenting in the Lamentations, says: “Therefore my people have been led captive, because they had no knowledge” (Isa. V, 13).

Another says: “Every iniquity descends from ignorance.” And this: “He refused to understand so that he might act well” (Ps. XXXV, 4).

Again: “They did not know and did not understand; they walk in darkness; all the foundations of the earth will be shaken” (Ps. LXXXI, 5).

But the Lord says in the Gospel: “The one who is from God hears the words of God” (John VIII, 47).

But lest you—or anyone else—think that I am inviting you to any kind of wisdom except that which is from God, or that, when I urge caution, I am restraining you from some other wisdom, since there is no other, I shall try to explain as quickly as I can that there are three kinds of growth in the soul just as in the body, following the very words of the one who earlier contributed much in support of this work—namely, Augustine. [Note: Construe: “I shall try, as quickly as I can, to explain—that is, to expound—that there are three kinds of growth in the soul just as in the body. I shall do so by following word for word the one who spoke here, namely, the one who earlier contributed much in support of this work, Augustine.” In brief: “I shall try to explain and show, in Augustine’s words, that there are three kinds of growth in the body and likewise in the soul.”]

“For,” says Augustine, “one kind in the body is necessary, by which natural proportion is fulfilled in the limbs; another is superfluous, as when people are sometimes born with six fingers; the third is harmful, which, when it occurs, is called a swelling. For although the limbs are said to grow, in reality they occupy a larger space, having overcome good health.

“In the soul likewise there are certain growths that are, as it were, natural, when the soul is said to be enlarged by disciplines suited to honorable and good, blessed living. But when we learn things that are more marvelous than useful, although they are often advantageous for certain purposes, they are nevertheless superfluous and must be counted among the second kind. The harmful kind, however, consists of those arts by which the soul is wounded.”

Therefore, to supply how these three things ought to be understood: the worst kind of knowledge must be rejected in every way; the second must be avoided; the first must be embraced. For this is true wisdom—indeed, there is no other wisdom—which recommends nothing except what is honorable, teaches nothing except what is useful, and commands nothing except what is acceptable to God.

### 17

Are you prudent? Be simple as well. Are you simple? Be prudent as well. For neither one without the other has any value sufficient to make it a virtue. Prudence without simplicity is cunning; simplicity without prudence is foolishness. Hear the Lord saying: “Be prudent as serpents and simple as doves” (Matthew 10:15).

I therefore want you to be, as Gregory wittily says of a certain man [Note: That is, Saint Benedict, of whom Saint Gregory wrote at the beginning of Book II of the *Dialogues*: “Thus he withdrew, knowingly ignorant and wisely unlearned.”], knowingly ignorant and wisely unlearned.

Are you joyful? Would that your joy were in God. Are you sad? Would that you were sad on account of your exile. Are you joyful? Hear in what you ought to rejoice: “Rejoice in the Lord always” (Ephesians 4:4). Are you sad? Hear how you ought to be affected: “The sorrow that is according to God,” says the Apostle, “produces repentance leading to lasting salvation” (2 Corinthians 7:10).

The Psalm says to you: “Rejoice in the Lord” (Psalm 31:11). The Apostle also says to you: “Consider it all joy, my brothers, when you fall into various trials” (James 1:2). [Note: The Vulgate reads, “Hear,” it says, “and do not grow insolent.” No one will disapprove the correction from context and sense.] Let the joyful hear, lest he become insolent: “Woe to you who laugh, for you shall mourn and weep” (Luke 6:21). Let the sad hear, lest he grow bitter: “Blessed are you who weep now, for you shall laugh.”

The joyful should hear: “Rejoice that your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10:20). The sad: “Again I shall see you, and your heart shall rejoice, and no one shall take your joy from you” (John 16:22). The joyful: “Rejoicing in hope” (Romans 12:12). The sad: “As sorrowful, yet always rejoicing” (2 Corinthians 6:10). Let the sad hear: “Rejoice in the Lord, you righteous” (Psalm 62:1).

The joyful: “Mourn like a virgin” (Joel 1:8). The sad: “Rejoice and be glad, daughter of Zion” (Lamentations 4:21). The joyful: “To the extent that she exalted herself and lived in luxury and joy, give her an equal measure of mourning and lamentation” (Revelation 18:7). Let the sad hear: “Is any one of you sad? Let him pray with an even spirit and sing psalms” (James 5:13). Let the joyful hear: “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).

I have therefore joined these two together in such a way that the sad person strives to moderate his sorrow by equanimity, prayer, and frequent psalmody, if he is suited to it, lest he fall into bitterness; while the joyful person humbly strives to show his gladness to God in good works, in no other way [that is, otherwise] than with God’s grace, lest he incur offense on account of his joy and prepare merit in return for a benefit.

For someone said, as I believe, most truthfully—and by the purity of his life he acquired such authority in speaking that no one ought to doubt his testimony: “He who gives bread to the needy sadly loses both the bread and the merit.” Hence that man mentioned above, Augustine, says very frequently: “If you do good with gladness, you do it yourself; but if with sadness, it is done through you, not by you.”

When temporal joy steals too insistently into the heart, let the restrained strength of the soul, grieving over the blindness of the present age, answer inwardly: “What joy shall I have, who sit in darkness and do not see the light of heaven?” (Tobit 5:12.) Again, when sadness intrudes unbearably, let steadfastness, raised into the citadel of the mind, say: “Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation? Or distress?” (Romans 8:35.)

### 18

Since it is, in a certain sense, natural for everyone to weep more than to laugh—for we all seem to begin life by weeping—the one who is excessively given to laughter is shown to transgress the law of nature if he can rarely, or perhaps never, bring forth any weeping from his heart or draw it from his eyes: neither out of desire for heavenly things, nor on account of the loss of earthly things, nor in contemplation of mortality itself, which, because of its unavoidable decline, is daily subject to as many misfortunes as it serves necessities.

That sadness is sometimes more useful than joy is attested by the one who says: “The heart of fools is where there is joy, and the heart of the wise where there is sadness” (Ecclesiastes 7:5). The man mentioned above agrees with this quite elegantly: “Sadness,” he says, “is often more useful, for it is accustomed to have gravity as its companion.”

Another says: “God rejoices in our very lamentation”; hence it is said: “Before ruin the heart is exalted” (Proverbs 16:18). And this statement, although chiefly concerning future destruction [Note: The Vulgate reads *tamen si* (“yet if”), less well.], can also be understood of what comes to pass through the vicissitudes of the present: “Laughter shall be mingled with sorrow, and mourning shall seize the end of joy” (Proverbs 14:13).

How, then, the mind ought to maintain its balance between these two, he wisely teaches who says: “In the day of evils do not be forgetful of good things, and in the day of good things do not be forgetful of evils” (Sirach 11:27). For this will make one neither dissolved by joy nor despairing through sadness. The incomparable master of eloquence, mentioned shortly above, expresses this most eloquently in golden words [Note: That is, the one who expressed it a little above, whose testimony was cited shortly before.]: “If there is any joy of the present time, it ought to be experienced in such a way that the bitterness of the punishment to come never departs from memory.”

When these matters have been set forth, each person must consider why he ought to rejoice in the present, lest he grieve in the future; or why he ought to be sad, lest he incur the mark of bitterness. For people both laugh and weep in the present; and what they laugh at often ought to be wept over, while what they grieve over ought to be rejoiced in.

Someone laughs at what ought to be wept over, as is said of certain people: “They rejoice when they have done evil, and exult in the worst things” (Proverbs 2:14). Again, someone weeps when adversity has befallen him, although he ought rather to rejoice, because “the Lord chastises the one he loves, and scourges every son whom he receives” (Hebrews 12:6 [printed: 16]).

Over what, then, is one to rejoice, if not over the progress of the godly? Over what is one to grieve, if not over their decline? Over what is one to rejoice, if not over the happiness that has been promised? Over what is one to grieve, if not over this long exile? Desire for one’s homeland is slight if tears are entirely absent during exile; and love lies exceedingly cold and numb in the heart if one does not know how to rejoice over a brother’s progress and grieve utterly over his decline. Hence Augustine says: “He hates his homeland and greatly dishonors it who thinks himself well off while he is in exile.”

### 19

There is also another cause of rejoicing, not indeed customary for many, but nevertheless commanded by the Lord’s precepts. After listing certain signs that would precede his coming, he says to his disciples: “When these things begin to happen, look up and raise your heads, because your redemption is drawing near” (Luke 21:18)—as though he had said: “When you see the things you do not love passing away, know that what you have eagerly sought is near.”

A Christian must greatly fear grieving over the world’s being struck down, lest, while he is discovered to love the world by sharing its suffering, he appear to incur God’s enmity, while the Apostle thunders terribly: “Whoever wishes to be a friend of this world is constituted an enemy of God” (James 4:4).

Nor should one mourn in prayers for an earthly thing, since, as Gregory says, lamentations have no fruit when, with tears, they strive to seek things destined to perish. Esau’s empty dismay confirms this. Nevertheless, even concerning small matters one ought to pray to God moderately—or, as Plato says in the *Timaeus*, to implore God’s protection.

What ought to be done in such matters is shown by the oracle of the prophet Habakkuk. After he had enumerated certain disasters of the world, he concluded by adding: “But I shall rejoice in the Lord” (Habakkuk 3:18). And the Psalmist says: “The righteous shall rejoice when he sees vengeance” (Psalm 57:11), knowing that the reward of the good is near when he sees vengeance increasing against the wicked. Likewise: “My soul refused to be comforted” (Psalm 56:3).

This, then, is the joy especially belonging to the good; none of the wicked shares in it. In this world the wicked appear to rejoice and to suffer just as the righteous do. They rejoice when they acquire and groan when they lose. The saints do likewise, but not in the same way, because their objects differ: the former grieve over earthly losses, whereas the latter grieve over heavenly longings. Yet the saints rejoice when they acquire the fruit of their labors, and they mourn when they lose—that is, when they see some people fall away from their fellowship.

The wicked mock those who piously weep; the saints lament those who laugh vainly and those who mourn vainly as well. For they proceed from sight to mourning, and from weeping even to weeping: from weeping with laughter to weeping without laughter. Each of them mourns a neighbor going to the kingdom, when he ought rather to mourn himself hastening toward destruction.

Therefore, do not rejoice insolently or mourn vainly. Rejoice in the Lord; exult in God your Savior. Mourn in the world; groan for the heavenly desire. Weep for your own sin and that of your neighbor; sigh and grieve over this long exile. He will give you joy in place of mourning, exultation in place of groaning, and jubilation in place of lamentation—he who is the consolation of the sorrowful, the hope of those who labor, and the help of those who perish; he who speaks through the Gospel: “Again I shall see you, and your heart shall rejoice, and no one shall take your joy from you” (John 16:33 [printed]).

Long ago the prophet had also promised this: “The Lord shall give you a crown in place of ashes, a garment of praise in place of a spirit of sorrow” (Isaiah 61:3).
