Therefore, carry your ashes confidently, since a crown is promised you; bear the spirit of sorrow only temporarily, since a garment of praise remains for you without end. Obey diligently the one who commands—indeed, embrace with gratitude the one who most graciously refreshes you.

“He who weeps,” he says, “as though not weeping, and he who rejoices as though not rejoicing” (1 Corinthians 7:3): that is, if you weep over the sadness of present evil, rejoice in hope of future good; and if you rejoice over temporal advantage, fear eternal judgment. For, as Gregory says, a counselor inhabits the soul that, grieving over present things, hastens toward eternal ones.

### 20

But since, with God’s assent, we seem to be drawing near the end of our preface, we must beware lest, by hastening more quickly than is fitting, we leave or neglect anyone, since we have once begun to admonish everyone. To prevent this, I exhort and admonish all Christians, all the baptized, every order, condition, sex, age, and profession; the rich, the middling, and the poor; the healthy and the sick; the young and the old; infants themselves; sinners and righteous; clergy and laity—in short, everyone, leaving no one behind and excluding no one who wishes to have a share in Christ’s kingdom.

Let all rouse themselves and admonish themselves; let all lend the ears of their hearts to that parable which the Lord himself told concerning a king and his servants, the good and the wicked (Matthew 25:15), one of whom received five talents to distribute, another two, and a third one. For what he is said to have done, he himself does not cease to do every day; and what he narrates as having happened to them will happen to all on the day of judgment, according to the diversity of their works. Let the one who has ears to hear hear (Matthew 11:15), understand, and acknowledge this without hesitation.

No one can excuse himself by saying that he received no talent, even if he seems altogether feeble, since infirmity itself is often given as a gift. Does someone possess wisdom? This is the greatest talent, for none is greater. Does someone possess wealth? It is indeed a lesser talent, but most suitable for distribution. Does someone practice any craft? He can multiply through it a very useful talent. Does someone have influence with a ruler or a friend? What he cannot accomplish from his own resources, he can accomplish through that person’s talent. Everything is lacking. Yet life remains; let good will also be present, and it gathers no lesser profits.

### 21

Having thus passed briefly and systematically over these matters—as it were, superfluously, since they had not been proposed to my mind, yet, I think, not uselessly—and having first shown in a few words how divine remedies apply to everyone in their entirety and to each person individually in an appropriate way, it remains for us now, addressing the one to whom we are offering this athletic contest, finally to insert certain passages of blessed Augustine concerning the usefulness of vigils [Note: The text of Augustine which he promises here is found transferred to the end of the book.], and then to begin the work itself in the name of the Lord.

Be present here in your entirety, then, and receive what is said with the open [that is, unbarred] senses of your mind. First, I want to ask you in every way whether you wish of your own accord to undertake this singular contest. “I do,” you say.

If this is so, then consider carefully [Note: The text was wrongly read *ego* (“I”) for *ergo* (“therefore”), and *vide* (“see” or “consider”) was absent. To make the sense of what follows cohere, *vide*, or something similar, had to be supplied.] at the very beginning—before you begin to enter upon this exceedingly difficult journey, undertaken by few, begun sluggishly by some and more sluggishly abandoned; seized upon vigorously by others but completed in a very different manner; begun well by some and brought to completion excellently—whether, having first cautiously tested the ground with the foot of diligent discernment, you will be able to carry this journey, once well begun, to the end of the best perfection.

For the highest good is begun in vain if it is abandoned before the end; nor is a victim acceptable in the Lord’s sacrifice if its tail is missing (Leviticus 3:9). Not to mention the garments of the brothers, Joseph’s tunic is reported as both variegated and reaching to the ankles (Genesis 37:23): variegated because of diversity, reaching to the ankles because of completion.

Against such people the Prophet invokes a curse upon the wicked: “Let them become like grass upon the housetops” (Psalm 128:6). And he who is accustomed to give a denarius to those who labor until evening says: “He who perseveres to the end shall be saved” (Matthew 10:22 [printed: 21]). A thousand testimonies occur here showing that beginnings have no power for anything good if holy perfection is absent.

Let that likeness of the Lord which he presented, as it is read in the words of the Gospel, remind the soul striving toward the heights: “For which of you,” he says, “wishing to build a tower, does not first sit down and calculate the necessary expense, whether he has enough to complete it? Otherwise, after he has laid the foundation and has not been able to finish, all who see him may begin to mock him, saying: ‘This man began to build and was not able to complete it’” (Luke 14:28).

All this was clearly spoken so that you might know that it is more advantageous for anyone humbly to restrain himself in the lowest places than rashly to attempt the highest and, failing to attain them, shamefully to fall short and provide spectators with an occasion for mockery.

One must take the greatest care that, while someone imprudently strives to move from common good works to matters exceeding the strength of many, and does not reach through perseverance what he attempts in beginning, what is read in Job may befall him: “For all who see him shall say, ‘Where is he?’” (Job 36:25.) That is, he is found neither here, where he might prosper honorably with the others, nor there, where he seemed to hasten forward uniquely after surpassing the rest.

Amid these things it is fitting to consider the devil’s many and exceedingly subtle snares, especially his envy, and how he seems to direct it particularly against those whom he sees hastening toward higher things. Seeing himself cast down to the depths, he suffers unspeakably whenever he observes someone being lifted to the heights. Accordingly, he never ceases daily to surround each of these people with three kinds of siege: at the beginning of intention, along the road of action, and at the end of completion.

### 22

If you wish to be taught more fully about these three matters one by one, you have them treated most sufficiently in Gregory’s *Moralia*. But if, with the resolute spirit we desire, remembering the saying, “He who observes the winds does not sow, and he who considers the clouds does not reap” (Ecclesiastes 11:4), you desire fearlessly to enter such a struggle, beware above all that nothing earthly, nothing worldly, nothing bestial remains in your heart: “If a beast touches the mountain, it shall be stoned” (Exodus 19:12).

Therefore, considering that your ship is still on this great and spacious sea, in which there are innumerable creeping things (Psalm 103:25), I warn you: watch carefully for the dragon. Mock him before he mocks you. Observe the basilisk [that is, the king-serpent] at the very sight of your intention. Know that its nature is such that, when it kills a person by seeing him first, it too is killed when the sight of a person anticipates it.

Carefully anticipate the tongue of the viper’s suggestion; and, rising up, you will be able to kill the asp-like beginning of the evil work. When, at the beginning of the work, you have shown the first face of a human being, strive not to end as a beast, marked by the monster of irrational execution—the monocentaur.

Beware the barren assembly of the hypocrite (Job 15:24). Avoid the reed which is moistened before the sun but dries up at its rising (Job 8:16 [printed: “before the sun”]). [Note: The Vulgate had, through faulty punctuation and a corrupt reading, “Beware the reed written before the sun.” We have restored the punctuation and, as we believe, the true reading, confirmed by the passage in Job to which this alludes: “Can the reed flourish without moisture? … It appears moistened before the sun comes, and at its rising its shoot will spring forth.” A moistened reed is a wet, water-filled reed.] Avoid it when it has dried up.

Observe the fertile vines, neglected and willingly trampled by beasts and birds, rather than the barren ones. “Do not wish to enter the land by two roads” (Sirach 3:28), while you do good out of love for God and, as a result, desire to please human beings.

Do not carry a treasure openly along the road, lest you lose it to the robbers who lie in wait along the way and plunder it. Do not catch at empty wind, when you ought to receive an eternal reward.

Among all the innumerable kinds of cunning belonging to the serpent, with its thousand forms and tortuous coils, know that none must be watched more cautiously than the exceedingly wicked vice of vainglory. It uses this so subtly in overcoming the saints that, unless they guard themselves most vigilantly and take care to detect the robber’s deceptions—not merely in their intention but in the entire body of their actions—it usually strikes them unexpectedly and casts them down from virtue itself more grievously than it is accustomed to overthrow them through vices.

Only then restrain your tongue with the greatest prudence. For, as Augustine testifies, it is so easy and slippery, and so inclined and effective at casting the soul down from its citadel, that it often happens that, through the facility of speech, it incurs what the mind does not think.

And lest you consider it a small matter often to slip in speech, hear especially what the Apostle James says to you: “If anyone thinks he is religious but does not bridle his tongue, deceiving his heart, his religion is worthless” (James 1:26). And elsewhere: “The tongue is a restless evil, full of deadly poison” (James 3:8). Likewise: “Death and life are in the power of the tongue” (Proverbs 18:21). Again: “In much speaking sin shall not be absent” (Proverbs 10:19).

One of our own people has beautifully added two matters: “No one,” he says, “should be thought capable of being saved so long as he is not afraid to remain attached to disordered conduct, to delight in superfluous words, and to be ravaged by turbulent thoughts.” [Note: He says “joined to three” because the following sentence concerns not only sins of the tongue but also two other vices, namely disordered conduct and turbulent thoughts.]

Thanks be to God. For suddenly and, as it were, unexpectedly, while I sought to summon this testimony in order to warn against loquacity, I have almost completed the entire task which, through many circumlocutions of words, I had thought could scarcely be brought to an end.

Do you wish to be saved, rewarded, and crowned? While you guard against disordered works, also abstain from superfluous words; restrain yourself from unclean thoughts; follow with an unhindered step the voice of the Lord calling: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Luke 9:23).

To follow—that is, to imitate Christ [supply: means] to go after him by the same road along which he himself proceeds. This means not seeking earthly things, not pursuing fleeting profits, avoiding the lowest honors; willingly embracing adversity and the world’s contempt for love of him; wishing to benefit everyone, even beyond one’s strength; inflicting injury on no one, but patiently bearing injuries inflicted by anyone; granting benefits even to those who inflict them, if one has the means, and, if not, diligently seeking forgiveness for them by prayer; raising with oneself as many people as one can toward love of the heavenly homeland.

### 23

If you first exercise yourself in these efforts of pious will on the field of action, I confess that you will present yourself as an undefeated athlete to the Emperor, the wrestling-master [Note: See Note 11 on the preface to Book I], displaying yourself to all the more elevated spectators—provided that, unlike those to whom this has most miserably happened, you do not grow weary in these things and always strive toward better ones, until, having fought the good fight excellently, completed the course successfully, and preserved the faith without faltering, you are gloriously enriched with the everlasting prize.

For this reason, I think, under the direction of him in whose hand both we and our words are, the discourse has been extended at such length: so that, after the qualities and properties of lesser actions had been shown, it might finally arrive at the highest summit of deeds which you are attempting to undertake. Thus, having cautiously and step by step climbed, as it were up a ladder, from the lowest commandments of the Lord toward higher things, nothing more would remain for you to seek below, since, through a way of life inaccessible to many, you would already deserve to cling to the heights themselves.

Or else, if—whatever your order, condition, dignity, affection, sex, or age—you wish to lend your hand to this much-praiseworthy work of struggle, you may find here how you ought first to exercise yourself in your own circumstances, so that at last you may ascend with fortunate progress to things beyond you. Otherwise, once you have put your hand to the plow, you may be forced, under the pretext of some domestic concern, to turn the eyes of your intention backward from what you have begun, and either make the furrow crooked and useless or injure the tracks of the ploughing oxen.

If someone is found—as we have already taught in another epilogue—not of his own will but compelled by another’s coercion to imitate this way of life, either for a fixed period or for the whole of his life, I believe that I have already satisfied him in what follows.

Here, I believe, nothing remains except to add this: if, by God’s grace, it should happen that he is freed from this necessity, let him never at any time entirely abandon the way of life to which he has become accustomed in penance, but throughout all his remaining days let him obey in his deeds the merciful Lord, who long ago restrained him with his reins from the winding paths of wanton vanity.

By doing this he will appear to acquire merit for himself, gratitude toward his teacher, satisfaction toward the Lord, and praise for God, who chastised him in the present so that he would not perish eternally, educating him temporally so as to make him a worthy heir of the everlasting kingdom.

But if he prefers to turn aside from this path of our counsel, let him see what he does. We nevertheless greatly fear that this divine reproach may apply to him: “There was no one found who returned and gave glory to God” (Luke 17:18). Worse still, he may be subject to the sentence which that same Lord demonstrated concerning the unclean spirit that goes out and returns with seven other spirits (Luke 11:24–26).

Hence he says to a certain person who had been healed: “Go, and sin no more, lest something worse happen to you” (John 8:11). And there is the statement over which the prophet laments: “You struck them, and they did not grieve; you consumed them, and they did not return” (Jeremiah 5:3).

I also see that this must be considered by him: a prolonged illness often reforms certain people to life, but afterward the slightest occasion of any matter completely destroys them from life, when, relaxed by a kind of security, they guard themselves too carelessly.

Let him therefore fear that this may also happen to him, and let anyone in such a condition take counsel for his salvation while there is opportunity, lest, when he wishes to do so again, he may no longer be able.

### 24

But if someone is perhaps troubled that in this preface I have used examples of modern teachers [Note: He calls the modern examples of teachers testimonies of the holy Fathers, while he calls the ancient ones authorities of the holy Books. In a similar sense he later calls them “modern” and “ancient.”] no less than those of the ancients, and wishes on this account to call me a patcher, or, in the more usual term, a compiler—as though I wanted to construct something of my own with another’s resources—I shall not delay to give the reason.

The Psalmist says: “Lord, watering the mountains from his upper waters” (Psalm 103:13). Insofar as, while he himself waters through them the aridity of my little intellect [Note: Construe and explain it thus: “insofar as I was able to understand, while the Lord himself watered through them—that is, the modern teachers, as he calls them, or the holy Fathers—the aridity of my little intellect; he who also of himself watered their superiors—that is, the writers of the sacred Books—and through these latter—that is, through the sacred writers—watered those men—that is, the holy Fathers—and through them watered us, who are still exceedingly dry; not because rain was lacking, but because we preferred to be soaked by the dusty squalor of vices rather than by the willing rain which God himself set apart for his inheritance, and covered ourselves with a kind of garment of iniquities”: insofar, I say, as I was able to understand this, it seemed fitting that we should use their examples—that is, those of the modern teachers—as freely as those of the ancients; for, and so on.], who also of himself watered their superiors and through these watered those men [Note: The Vulgate reads “through those men, these.” The sense of the context requires “through these, those”: “these” are the superiors whom God watered of himself, namely the sacred writers; “those” are understood to be the holy teachers, who were watered through the sacred writers. Shortly afterward the printed text had *nisi quia*; we have corrected it to *non quia*, as the sense requires.], and through those men us, who are still exceedingly dry—not because rain was lacking [supply: but because] we preferred to be soaked by the dusty squalor of vices rather than by the willing rain which he himself set apart for his inheritance (Psalm 67:10), and therefore covered ourselves with a kind of garment of iniquities—I was able to understand this.

It seemed appropriate that we should use their examples indiscriminately, just as those of the ancients, since what they received from their superiors they rained down upon us, their inferiors, in such a way that, whatever the particular meaning of each passage ought to be, it becomes clearer through their discernment. Nor is anyone required to wander through byways and attribute what belongs to one place to another, when in their very extensive treatises you find what meaning each passage especially possesses and what place it properly occupies.

Therefore, whenever usefulness requires you to cite something from the testimonies of Scripture, it is not a useless or perhaps dangerous labor that you must undertake, but you should present it as they have brought it forth.

Since, then, I have been led to rely more upon the examples of the holy teachers than upon those of the ancients [Note: By the name “those men” we have observed that the holy teachers are understood; by “the ancients,” the ancient sacred writers. Shortly afterward the printed text has *est labyrinthus*. We have restored *est*, since the sense is that two things persuaded Ratherius to use the examples of the holy Fathers rather than those of the sacred writers: both the labyrinth of the sacred Scriptures, still exceedingly difficult for him to enter, and the practice of two celebrated Fathers, who derived their understanding of the sacred Letters not from their own presumption but from the writings and authority of their predecessors.], both the labyrinth of the Scriptures, still exceedingly difficult for me to enter, and the example of two men persuaded me.

These two, whom ecclesiastical history calls “sons of fatness” and “lights standing to the right and left of the lampstand of the law” (Exodus 35:14), were produced, nourished, and taught by Cappadocia, which at that time was more fruitful than the neighboring regions to the extent that it was more filled with clouds; indeed, through them Cappadocia itself, imbued, nourished, and instructed, shone more luminously than all others. [Note: These two Fathers, celebrated in Cappadocia, are Saint Basil and Gregory of Nazianzus. Shortly afterward we have corrected “your time” to “that time,” where the printed text had *tuum temporis*.]

For thirteen years they devoted themselves to all the books of the secular Greeks, excluding only the volumes of divine Scripture, yet they followed the understanding of those Scriptures not from their own presumption but from the writings and authority of their predecessors; and it was clear that those predecessors themselves had received the rule of understanding through apostolic succession.

And because no one knows except what he learns—although some people even say what they do not know—I could not, compelled by reason, say anything except what I knew to recount, even though I may seem to have inserted certain ambiguities, very few indeed, and themselves necessary to sorrow. [Note: He calls “ambiguities” those matters he inserted concerning his own misfortune; he wrote something similar in the preface to Book I.]

25. There is also another reason, already given above and no less weighty than the reason for this delay: namely, that if someone, guided by our authority—which is none—even if he had something of his own to offer, should refuse to give credence to what has been said or was to be said, he might at least not refuse to believe those who wished to gather these things from Scripture and bring them to us in sound sense, with our agreement. For since I can find nothing in myself by which I might please anyone, I know how displeasing I am to all, and I approve as most true that saying: “When a man’s life is despised, it remains for his preaching also to be scorned” (St. Gregory, book I, Homily 12 on the Gospels). Therefore I fear to put forward anything on my own authority, even if I possessed any, without their accompaniment, lest I myself receive from the Lord the mark of rebuke [understand: “lest I myself receive it”], and lest those who read acquire from me, the speaker, an occasion for criticizing what I say.

For what sort of purpose I might dare to compose a little book, although I have resolved to state this at the end of the work, I think it more fitting to say here, since no suitable occasion presents itself even now. Thus, through my sins (alas, the grief!), which have brought me to this condition and deserve much greater punishments, while I wish to contemplate what I once was, what I now am, what I was not, what I am not, what I ought to be, and what I ought to have been, I cannot discern where, or in what place, or in what manner I contracted this blindness. Nor do I find anything for which to complain or grow angry against either the giver of light or the guides themselves; rather, I see that it must be attributed to the sluggish torpor and indolence of my own negligence.

This concerns what I have not perceived [Note: “What I have not perceived,” that is, things which I did not perceive]. But when I come to what I did indeed perceive, yet afterward forgot when I reviewed it in my mind, I count it as the greatest cruelty toward myself, the greatest tyranny directed toward my own destruction, and the greatest crime: that by my own action I wounded, buried, and blinded myself so completely that, whenever I desire to raise my eyes toward that light which I have lost, the great night of guilty habit so covers me with a self-produced film [Col. 0340C] that, struck by the very light, I am unable not only to see what I desire and restore to my mind what flies toward it like a dream, but also quickly return to those very darknesses with a certain pleasure [Note: Construe: “so that, struck by the very light, I am unable not only to see what I desire and restore to my mind what flies toward it like a dream” [but also—understand this—“quickly to return to those very darknesses with a certain pleasure”].].

Having already been greatly wearied by this long-lasting blindness, my mind lingered for a little while on the author of the light that had been given and then lost. As it now seems to me, it is no longer permitted even late to seek that one who in the beginning bestowed upon me eyes sound and capable of light, and who is able to anoint the eyes of my mind with the salve of his mercy, so that he himself may illuminate the sense of my heart [Note: That is, “so that he himself may also illuminate the sense of my heart,” namely, he who …], who is able to do all that he wishes.

And because, as I said, a little love has now lingered in my mind, by that love itself—granted by the one who gave it—I understand that I have also earned this: that I should know I must not suddenly and presumptuously thrust myself into that radiance with the very sight by which I am still in darkness, lest, when my eyes are struck back by the brilliance itself, I return disgracefully to darknesses worse than those in which I now remain.

Therefore I think I must seek certain approaches to that same light [Note: The “approaches to the light” are certain beginnings of light, which the Italians call *barlume*], by gradually becoming accustomed to them. When, through their use, the dust has been driven from my eyes, however little, I may at some time be able to direct my gaze toward the very ray of light when it is reflected, to desire it eagerly, and, whenever it deigns to present itself, to behold it with an unimpeded sight and to love it forever with steadfast affection.

To deserve to attain all this, I thought it best to accustom myself to the vigils of certain physicians who, although more recent, have nevertheless discussed this subject more openly and composed little books on their art in such a way that they both imitated their teachers in everything and instructed their pupils: namely, how that light itself is to be sought, found, held, seen, and loved; with what salve the eyes are to be anointed; with what beneficial or harmful powder they are to be dusted; with what observance they are to be nourished; and with what care they are to be preserved.

Seeing that I am the most unlearned in all these matters, yet having become long ago a lover of this same light, I wished to compose this little book from their statements for my own benefit. In it I would gather together from their medical writings as much medicinal remedy as possible, supplied by their discoveries, and would not cease to explore for myself the byways of the earlier books [Note: It seems that we should read: “nor would I cease to explore for myself all the byways of the earlier books,” that is, of the ancient books—a name by which he designated the sacred books and writers above. The following is especially appropriate to those books: “In them, although entry into something is easy, exit through many things is difficult.” Hence he adds: “But I would follow those holy Fathers in everything and undertake the well-trodden path by their footsteps; for, after traversing those same [ancient, or Scriptural] byways through long and continual practice, they were able to proceed in a free course without any guide’s assistance, with only the light of the spring that flowed around them, flowed into them, and flowed beyond them going before, accompanying, and following them. He continues the allegory of the labyrinth, by which name he had earlier called the sacred Scriptures: ‘The labyrinth of the Scriptures is still almost inaccessible to me.’ He proposed to have the byways of this labyrinth, or its winding paths—whose entrance is easy and exit difficult—explored for him by the holy Fathers as guides.], in which, although entry into some things is easy, exit through many things is difficult. But I would follow those Fathers in everything and undertake the path worn smooth by their footsteps; for, after traversing those same paths through prolonged and varied investigations and continual practice, they were now able to proceed in a free course without anyone’s guidance—only the light of the spring that had flowed around them, into them, and beyond them going before, accompanying, and following them.

26. I have done this not because I presume by this method to impart instruction to anyone, but lest these same reflections, having already eluded me as they did before, should again escape me [Note: That is, “lest they should escape me,” as they had already escaped me.]. Nor is it surprising if I have been able to gather only a few things, and to remember only a few; nor if I have been able to set down even what I remembered without much eloquence and orderly arrangement. For these few things are abundantly sufficient for so small a work; books are lacking to provide assistance, and friends with whom to converse are absent. The labor of misfortune is also present, clouding the very edge of the mind, while grief has blunted my memory. Indeed, eloquence itself usually falls silent when a sick person remains conscious, and a badly shaken string does not sound well on the lyre [Note: The received texts incorrectly read *ergo*. The sense is: “Eloquence usually falls silent when a man is master of himself while sick.” Ratherius, however, presents himself as though sick because of the calamities he was suffering.].

Notice, then, reader, what anguish drove me to this, what calamity and what necessity showed me these paths of writing. The first cause, to summarize and state it more plainly [Note: The first cause for writing this work was fear of forgetfulness, as will become clear from what follows], was fear of forgetfulness. In order to disgorge all the venom of the spreading poison, I feared that, already overwhelmed—as I am—by the debris of every kind of vice, surrounded by the darknesses of evils, and interrupted by the harmful clamors of many worldly cares, I might completely forget these matters, while, by recalling something from them, I have instead been glad in many ways to recollect them.

The second cause was that, since, as I said, books are lacking and companions with whom to converse are lacking, while an excruciating sadness is present and grief itself incessantly gnaws at my mind, I might have some consolation in this work, use it as a kind of conversing friend, and be refreshed by it as by a companion. In accordance with the comic poet, I did not complain, saying to myself: “Who will read these things?” [Rather,] seeing myself as the reader and the sole—though not the only—lover of this work, I saw that, since I was in need of other [understand: books], the love of reading that was within me could at least be consoled by this [Note: That is: “I did not complain … seeing myself as the reader and the sole (though not the only) lover of this work; since I was in need of other [books], I saw that the love of reading which was in me could at least be consoled by this work.” After some intervening material, the received texts have *vocantius* incorrectly instead of *vacantius*.].

Let whoever wishes read it; let whoever wishes neglect it. Let no one call me its instigator. And because I found this time somewhat more available than I wished, in these prefaces [Note: He calls these books of introductory material “prefaces” both here and elsewhere] I have almost entirely depicted myself: my condition, my origin, my name, the office entrusted to me, my fortune—if one dares call it that—my punishments, and my torturer himself, writing of him through certain indications, as well as the punishment awaiting him unless he repents; from this punishment, I beg God to deliver him.

Here again, what should be done and what has not been done, what has been done and what should not be done: although all these things seem to have been brought forward as though under the characters of others, so that they cannot easily be ferreted out, they have nevertheless been fitted to me in such a way that they will at once become clear when they are placed before the eyes. Anyone who wishes to search them out diligently will be able to find them all so carefully worked out that, in revealing these things, our intellectual ingenuity might be thought to have labored throughout this lengthy series of prefaces.

I have assembled the entire body of the work in such a way that, turning from “discourse” to “reading,” and from “reading” to “discourse” [Note: The received texts incorrectly have *conversum*. Moreover, he uses the words “discourse” and “reading” in a particular and unusual sense. By both words he seems to indicate these books of introductory material, using “discourse” for those passages which he himself composed from excerpts gathered here and there from the statements of others, and “reading” for the longer testimonies of the Fathers which he inserted word for word. James Gothofredus proves by several examples in his commentary on the single law of the Theodosian Code, *On the Responses of the Jurists*, that *lectio* was used for a *περικοπή* (*perikopē*), that is, a text, citation, authority, testimony, or section excerpted from somewhere and brought forward and recited in legal proceedings, writings, and also in the Church. He confirms the same meaning in his commentary on the ninth law, *On Invalidating Those Things Which Were Done under Tyrants*. We are encouraged to apply the same meaning to this passage of Ratherius by what follows: “You will find nothing there [that is, in this work of the *Praeloquia*] except the connection itself and, so to speak, the knots of my limbs; but the discourses are composed by many, although I have also inserted some at the very beginnings which I judged appropriate to the present undertaking; the readings, however, are excerpted from the books of the saints.” Certainly, since he had just testified that he lacked books in prison, he could not possibly understand “readings” here in the ordinary and familiar sense of things to be read.], I have allowed no collusion between athlete and opponent, nor granted any pause: while the one fights by praying, the other is defeated; while the one is animated by reading, the other is rebuked; in one, virtues increase, while in the other, strength fails; in the one, counsel is given, while in the other, fear is introduced.

These matters being so, the prologue seems to be almost entirely mine. In it I have dared to set down many things from myself, although they had been investigated by others [Note: “Investigated,” that is, “explained.” Ratherius uses *exploro* in the sense of “explain” in the second letter, as will be evident from the notes.]. The contest itself, however, belongs to the common struggle of all who lend their hands to the wrestling. Thus you will find nothing there except the connection itself and, so to speak, the knots of my limbs. The discourses are composed by many, although I have also inserted some at the very beginnings which I judged appropriate to the present undertaking; the readings, however, are excerpted from the books of the saints.

How the preface, although I wished to dispatch it as concisely as possible, came to occupy so long a stretch of words remains partly unknown even to me. Whatever has been understood concerns another place of discussion [possibly: “another place of speech”]. For it is still uncertain toward what outcome God wishes the case to tend [Note: By saying that it is uncertain what outcome God wishes, he seems to indicate by “the case” his own distress and imprisonment, since when he wrote these things he did not know the outcome of his case. We think this is the sense. As for what has been understood concerning why these books became so lengthy, that concerns—or rather awaits—another place: namely, when Ratherius, released from prison, will be able to explain his thought more freely.].

Meanwhile, gracious Jesus, I ask your pardon, while, without your being unaware, I continually contract guilt. Why I have prefaced these things, I seem partly to know; but whether I have prefaced them properly, since I can scarcely comprehend this in many cases, I confess that in some I do not know at all. Everything that is humbly spoken and does not disagree with the whole truth—which you are—is proper. If anything, then, has been rightly said, Lord, I ask that it may benefit me; but if anything is truly discordant, I ask that your mercy forgive it, and that your majesty grant that someone who understands these things better than I do may correct them, but that no one corrupt or delete them.

Your majesty, before whose nod all things are available, can bring it about—for with you willing is the same as acting, and being able the same as being—that these same things may happen to benefit someone who wishes to entreat you on behalf of me, most wretched as I am, and whom you may most piously deign to hear, returning to him a recompense for his service. Amen.

Here is to be placed what we promised: blessed Augustine’s [work] on the usefulness of vigils [Note: It has not been possible to find this text in Augustine’s printed works. Nevertheless, its reading of Psalm 146:7, “Begin to the Lord with confession,” which occurs three times in the same doctor—namely, *Tractate 4 on the First Epistle of John*, no. 3; *Sermon 1 on Psalm 103*, no. 4; and *Exposition of Psalm 146*, no. 14—suggests that it comes from one of his sermons that has been lost. The word *defensaculum* (“defense” or “protection”) is also used by him in his *Exposition of Psalm 67*, no. 21.].

Accordingly, since we are taught how great is the usefulness of vigils by these testimonies and by many testimonies of other teachers, and moreover by numerous testimonies of Holy Scripture, we admonish our aspiring Olympic victor [Note: The received texts incorrectly have *olymphionicam*. An *olympionices* is one who has emerged victorious in the Olympic contest. Here it refers to one who is about to fight in the hope of victory] that, since he has resolved to enter into a solitary contest with the ever-watchful enemy, he must know that he ought to undertake solitary vigils, by which he may guard with the utmost vigilance the camp of his virtues against the enemy’s manifold ambushes.

Let him anticipate the vigils of others through his eagerness to enter the contest, lest the enemy, while he sleeps, burst in unexpectedly—more savage in proportion as he is more ashamed of having previously been defeated. Therefore, as soon as he has opened his eyes, remembering the command: “Begin to the Lord with confession” (Psalm 146:7), and also recalling his innumerable benefits, let him immediately hurl this weapon against the enemy, a weapon which will be a protection for him safer than any shield.

The sixth book of the *Praeloquia* of Ratherius, formerly bishop of the Church of Verona but monk of Lobbes, ends here.

You who granted that the book should be begun  
Have granted that it should be ended, Almighty,  
By granting what was asked to your servant.

I, Ratherius, undertook this labor for you;  
Wash away my offenses, O Christ.

[Col. 0345]

# Ratherius, Bishop of Verona: The Life of Saint Ursmar, Bishop and Abbot of Lobbes in Belgium

[Note: The Life of Saint Ursmar, bishop and abbot of Lobbes, had been left on sheets by his disciples. Anso, then a monk of the same monastery, arranged it into an orderly work in the eighth century at the command of Theodulf, bishop and likewise abbot of Lobbes, whom he succeeded in the administration of the monastery in the year 776, as Fulcuin reports in *Deeds of the Abbots of Lobbes*, chapters 8 and 9. This Life, discovered and published by Mabillon in volume III of the *Acts of the Saints of the Benedictine Order*, p. 242, seemed so obscure and difficult to Ratherius that the reader could repeatedly fail to grasp its meaning. Thus, while he was an exile at Como from the year 937 until the year 939, having obtained a copy of the same Life from Azo, bishop of that city, he undertook not so much to correct it as to expound it in a clearer style.

We, who compared this work with Anso’s composition and noticed a great difference—not in subject matter, but in words and expression—as well as not insignificant additions to the sense in some places, judged it worthy of publication among Ratherius’s works. He dedicated it to the monks of Lobbes. For this reason Fulcuin, abbot of the same monastery, says in the work mentioned, chapter 20: “He also found at Como, while he was in exile there, a little book on the life of Saint Ursmar, which he corrected, having found it full of solecisms, and sent to us.”

Laurentius Surius first published this Life in the month of April. Mabillon subsequently reprinted it in the aforementioned volume, based on Surius’s edition and checked against the Lobbes manuscript, p. 245. We now reproduce it from that edition.]


## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0345A]

To the most reverend lords, most beloved Fathers, most learned teachers, and also to the entire flock of worshipers of Christ dwelling in the monastery of Lobbes:

Ratherius, formerly a monk of the same monastery but now bishop of the people of Verona, though utterly unworthy of God the Lord in both conditions, [sends] those things in the Lord which he himself prepared for his faithful from the beginning.

### 1.

Recently, while in exile at the venerable bishop of the holy Church of Como, by the just judgment of God, we found a little book containing a few things about the virtues of our lord and special patron, namely Saint Ursmar, bishop. Its content was preferable to refined gold and topaz; but in its expression it was so filled, within the limits of its ability, with solecisms [Col. 0345B] that it was difficult to determine whether this had happened through the negligence of the writer or through the ignorance of the composer.

Since this had offended us considerably in the circumstances of the time, we took care only to correct those faults of the same work through which either the reader’s understanding could be shipwrecked in the meaning, or which, by their excessive deformity, could cause disgust in those listening. But although the entire text of the discourse could appear elevated to the wise, it was simple and, so to speak, almost rustic; we therefore judged that it should not be completely changed, because we know that the authors of the sacred Scriptures also despised the rods of the grammarians, and everywhere we see that the simple teaching of fishermen pleased God more, for the salvation of converted nations, than the sophistries of philosophers.

The preface to a certain epistle of Anso—a holy man, as may be believed, though not especially eloquent—which he had placed before that same work, likewise seemed to be omitted altogether, because it contained such confusion that even the author’s intention is wholly concealed in it.

Therefore let the most holy charity of your fatherhood receive from one who was your—if we do not dare say “son,” then your servant, and indeed (shame upon it!) your fugitive—whatever small fruit of your instruction this may be, and let it compare it charitably with what is read among you. If the two agree, excellent; if not, let your most discerning and urbane palate distinguish which of them contains something better and more pleasing in taste, and retain that one for use as the better and more savory.

Let it thoughtfully consider with us, for the benefit of the less learned, that according to the judgment of a certain wise man: “Good is speech which plainly, pleasantly, and appropriately moves the listener”; still less ought a history to contain anything obscure [that is, doubtful], since it is published for no other reason than to convey the causes of present or past events to the knowledge of those yet to come.

Meanwhile, I pray that amid the most wretched shipwrecks of this world the anchor of your prayers may hold me fast, while I await the same from my smallness: may the piety of God not disdain to attend to the sighs of so great a sinner.

Now may God, the Father of peace, who brought back from the dead the great Shepherd of the sheep through the blood of the eternal covenant, our Lord Jesus Christ, make you fit in every good work, so that you may do his will, accomplishing in you what is pleasing in his sight through the same Jesus Christ our Lord. Through whose mercy may we deserve always to find in the most holy Ursmar a most pious intercessor, whose Life we have undertaken here to elucidate for the praise and glory of the all-powerful Trinity and for the edification of the assembled people.

## THE LIFE BEGINS

[Col. 0347A]

### 2.

Blessed Ursmar, bishop, worthy of every commendation of goodness, was born in the Teoracian district, in a village called Fleon. He was chosen by the Lord through predestination before he was given to the world through birth.

When his mother was pregnant with him, a venerable old man appeared to her in a vision. He held a little boy in his hand and said: “Take this little boy and nourish him.” For at that time a great famine was oppressing that region. The woman replied to the old man: “How shall I do this, lord, when I have no bread because of the great famine we are suffering?” But he gave her a very white loaf of bread and said to her: “With this bread you shall nourish him.” When she had taken it, it grew very large in her hands [Note: Anso reads: “His hand grew very large in the earth.”].

Then the same woman said: “What does this thing that I see signify, lord?” He replied: “You are going to bear a son who will win for Christ some portion of the kingdom.” He later showed by his actions that this had been true. For he obtained such great grace from the Lord that he refreshed with the nourishment of the divine word all who came to him for the sake of conversation.

Again, his mother, overcome by sleep, immediately saw another vision. She saw a ladder standing before her, whose top touched the heavens, and by which the same boy climbed and entered heaven. She followed him as far as the top of the ladder, but, as she declared, she was able to follow him but could not at all reach him. Returning to herself, she immediately understood that all these things truly prefigured her own son, whom she was holding enclosed in her womb.

His mother learned many other things of this kind from her own son, both before his birth and afterward; to recount them individually would be lengthy. Thus, rejoicing in the Lord, his mother said: “I know with complete certainty that, through the working of God’s mercy, the son I carry will be great, and I declare myself blessed to have received such a child.”

### 3.

When the child was born, he was called Ursmar. As he grew, he was handed over to teachers of the sacred Scriptures. They instructed him in sacred letters and divine law, not moderately but perfectly; not in a worldly manner, but monastically and according to the Rule.

From childhood onward, while performing works worthy of old age, he walked not according to his own will but according to the divine will. As his age advanced, he also grew strong in uprightness of conduct. He was chaste in body and incorrupt in mind; lovable to all and affable toward everyone; kind in spirit and most handsome in body; skilled in prudence and vigorous in courage; calm in temperance and severe in justice; perfect in long-suffering and generous in almsgiving; sparing in abstinence and endowed with patience and humility; refreshed by gentleness and piety, and filled with sincere charity; stable in robust faith and patient in unshaken hope.

His wisdom, arranging everything in his mind, increased the value of all these virtues. His speech, too, was seasoned with salt, according to the Apostle (Colossians 4:6). Whenever he saw that the time was opportune, he never allowed an hour to pass without the edification of his neighbors. Despising all earthly things and desiring heavenly things, he wished to devote himself solely to the one to whom, in devotedness, he had surrendered himself entirely from childhood.

### 4.

Frequently devoting himself to prayer, he entreated the Lord with tears and contrition of heart that whatever he contemplated or did might be acceptable in his sight. The Lord himself, who had powerfully inspired those prayers, mercifully deigned to hear his pious requests.

Afterward, having obtained the pastoral chair [Note: Concerning this matter, which indicates Ursmar’s episcopate, one should note what Fulcuin relates in the place cited, chapter 3:

“Why we say that he was a bishop has often been asked of us. For the text describing the Life itself teaches that he was a bishop, but it is entirely silent about the place and time of his ordination, or by whom he was ordained. Yet in charters drawn up in his time, and in very ancient scraps of parchment preserved in the archives of our Church, we find him inscribed under the name of bishop and pontiff.

Our elders give differing accounts of this. Some say that he was ordained bishop for the sake of preaching—as was appropriate at that time, in the beginnings of the new faith—in order to suppress the excessive rites of the barbarian people; we also read that this was done in the case of Saint Amandus. Others assign this dignity to the place and defend their opinion by a certain argument: namely, that a royal place constructed with royal generosity and adjoining the royal palace—Liptines, specifically—would not have been entrusted to anyone unless he had first been ordained bishop. We shall say in what follows that this dignity also continued in many of his successors.

We leave which of these accounts is truer to the judgment of the reader, nor do we detract from the holy man in either direction, since, whichever may be the case, we do not deny that he was a bishop.”

Mabillon adds in his preliminary observations on the same Life:

“Saint Ansgar, in the Life of Saint Willehad, bishop of Bremen, reports that Willehad was called bishop seven years before he was consecrated bishop, evidently because of his preaching of the Gospel. Could Ursmar and his successors likewise have been called bishops for this reason? Although Balderic, in the *Chronicle of Cambrai*, book II, chapter 37, thinks that Ursmar was consecrated bishop only through preaching without ordination. At that time, moreover, there were bishops and abbots in some monasteries, as was noted in the preface.”]

he was so exalted by the grace of the Lord that he surpassed almost all mortals and, while living in the world, possessed nothing of the world within himself.

He was, in short, a teacher of the Scriptures, builder of monasteries, provider for churches, guardian of souls, nourisher of orphans, defender of widows, and redeemer of captives. He loved the flock entrusted to him as the Truth itself had taught that it should be loved (John 10:11). For if the madness of tyrants had raged as it did in ancient times, he would not have feared to die for the Lord’s sheep. What more?

### 5.

This man was very unlike those whom we now see everywhere in our own times; nor have we heard of anyone who, without the executioner’s sword, suffered martyrdom under such cruel torments. We are not capable of recounting or writing all the sufferings he endured in the world, especially since, because of bodily illness, he lived for nine years and ten weeks without the nourishment of bread.

The food he did take was so thin and scant that no human being could have been sustained by it, except by a divine miracle, as he himself was. Everyone who saw him or heard him speak marveled that, living without the nourishment of bread, he was so vigorous and eloquent. His drink was water, and occasionally *sicera*—a fermented drink—which he used only a little and rarely. His nourishment was whatever he was able to take without the use of his teeth.

His patience in these and other tribulations was so great that it could be compared with the patience of the most blessed Job, who did not sin with his lips nor speak anything foolish against God (Job 1:22). On the contrary, he continually sang the Lord’s praise and, according to the Prophet, blessed the Lord at all times; his praise always resounded in his mouth (Psalm 33:2).

We may most truly conjecture that this man lived on that bread which descended from heaven for our salvation. For, as we have already said, he was so eloquent through a spiritual gift that he seemed like a flowing spring or an overflowing river. Whatever he preached with his mouth, he established by his actions, knowing that examples are stronger than words and that one teaches more by deeds than by speech.

### 6

I judge it worthwhile now to pursue in writing how effective was the holy man’s power for driving away the attacks of the ancient enemy.

There was a certain monastery called Melbodium [Note: Melbodium, or Malbodium, a famous nunnery, commonly called Maubeuge in Hainaut; concerning it, see Mabillon, *Life of Saint Aldegund*, second century of the Benedictine Order, under the year 684.], situated nearly twelve miles from his monastery of Laubach, which was under his care. There was a considerable company of nuns there. One of them was seized by an evil spirit, and it began to torment her violently, tearing her apart, while through her mouth it spoke filthy and shameful words. The inhabitants of the place were overcome by great horror, and excessive fear terrified even the hearts of the neighbors.

[Note: These matters, and those that follow down to the words “The following day,” which we have marked with an asterisk, are absent from the published Life of Anso. Ratherius either derived them from a fuller copy of Anso or, more probably, added them from his own store.]

The sisters who were holding her said to the demon by way of rebuke: “How did you dare to enter the handmaid of God?” And they added: “Most impure demon, come out of her.” He replied to them: “I will not come out before Bishop Ursmar comes and himself compels me to leave.”

We certainly do not attribute this confession to the one who was a liar from the beginning and did not stand in the truth (John 8:44); rather, because divine command forced him, we acknowledge that he spoke the truth, though not willingly, just as the demons say in the Gospel: “We know that you are the Son of God” (Mark 3:12). This statement was entirely true, and, among countless other testimonies, the blessed Peter confirms it by offering the Lord’s glorious confession in the same words when the Lord questioned him (Matthew 10:10). Yet the Lord’s Passion bears witness that, in another respect, that malice lied most deceitfully, since it was prompted by the devil to bring about the Passion through wicked men.

For although he knew that Christ had come for the salvation of the human race, he did not know the order of our liberation; and so he was deceived by the Lord’s death, like a bird by a snare. When the mortality of the flesh—which he desired to destroy—was displayed, he was caught by the hidden hook of divinity. Moreover, if he had known without doubt that this was Christ, the Son of the living God, he would have recognized that Christ could in no way be held by the laws of death. If he had recognized that Christ could not die, he would not have urged that he be crucified.

The most audacious butcher of human destruction did not understand that, by raging against the world’s Savior, he would be frustrated in the exercise of his power. The ancient malice did not know that it would have no right over the destruction of humankind if it had restrained itself from the blood of the Redeemer. Hence the Apostle says: “If they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2:8).

We can infer from another statement of his whom he calls “the rulers of this age.” He says: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against rulers and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 6:12). The Lord himself also says: “The prince of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (John 14:30).

This may also appropriately be understood of Herod and Pilate, according to what is said in the Psalmist’s voice: “The kings of the earth stood by, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ” (Psalm 2:2). But those rulers were specifically rulers of one people; they were not called, in general, “rulers of this age.”

Therefore, since the statement “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16:16) is most truthful when spoken by the testimony of blessed Peter, the statement “We know that you are the Son of God” is most false when spoken by the testimony of the devil. And just as Peter says: “Flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (ibid., 17) [Note: He means, of course, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God”; for Christ replied to Peter: “Flesh and blood has not revealed this to you,” and so forth.], so the devil was not led to confess this by the cleverness of his cunning or the subtlety of his nature, but by the force and power of the one who came from heaven to destroy him.

Just as the divine presence hidden within the man tormented the demon, so that, while lying, it spoke the truth involuntarily and uncertainly, so here the power of the Lord working in blessed Ursmar compelled it to speak the truth against its will. In both cases it acted not according to its own desire but under compulsion from the command of the one giving orders.

The following day, by the arrangement of divine providence, blessed Bishop Ursmar arrived. When he was informed about the girl who was being tormented by the devil, he immediately ordered her to be brought before him. When this had been done, he—relying not on his own power but on the Lord’s—took a book and began to read an exorcism over her head. Then, after blessing oil, he anointed her nostrils, eyes, and mouth, and at once drove the unclean spirit from her.

Although the girl had been freed, a certain fear, which had been planted by the devil’s presence, still remained in the sinful hearts of the neighbors. But the man of God ordered water mixed with salt to be brought to him. After blessing it, he commanded that it be sprinkled throughout all the places of the monastery, and so all the fear departed along with its author, Satan.

### 7

At another time a certain secular girl, full of a demon, was brought to him, and he ordered that she be carried into the oratory. When this had been done, he commanded that she be released from the bonds with which she was held. Afterward he began to invoke God’s power over her head and to rebuke the demon himself, ordering him to depart from God’s living creation.

In a wondrous manner that ancient enemy immediately began to be distressed and to roar, emitting various terrible and dreadful voices. Saint Ursmar ordered her to be dragged outside the oratory, and, following after her, struck her three times with the staff he carried in his hands. Then the evil spirit came out of her as quickly as though he himself had been struck.

The blessed bishop immediately restored her to the oratory in perfect health, and, anointing her with blessed oil, allowed her to depart free.

### 8

The holy bishop had a niece in the aforesaid monastery of Melbodium, whom he himself, when she was still a little girl, had entrusted to Saint Aldegund. After she had grown up, a very severe illness arose in her neck, called *gutteria* [Note: *Gutteria*, or, as others write with Anso, *grutteria*, a disease of the throat; see Du Cange, *Glossary*, s.v. *Gutteria* 2.], in the Gallic language.

The physicians maintained that it could not be cured in any other way than by cutting the flesh with an iron hook and drawing the disease outward. While they were considering doing this, it happened that the holy bishop of the Lord arrived. He summoned a physician and asked him: “Tell me whether you are able to cure her.” The physician replied: “I cannot, unless I cut the flesh with an iron hook and draw the disease out.”

When the man of God heard this, he absolutely forbade it, because he loved the girl exceedingly and clearly saw that the procedure was very dangerous. Instead, repeatedly placing his hand that day upon the place of the wound, he said: “See, daughter, that you do not allow iron to be put into you. For I believe in the Lord’s mercy that he himself will free you from this illness.”

That same night the holy man poured out abundant prayers to the Lord for her recovery. At dawn the next day the girl rose from her bed healthy, so completely that not even a trace of the illness remained in her.

### 9

At the same time another sick woman lay within the enclosure of the same monastery, afflicted by so severe an illness that all who saw her entirely despaired of her recovery. When she heard of the arrival of so great a man, she began, as best she could, to say: “I beg you to ask him to come to me, for I trust in God that I shall quickly recover if I am found worthy to see him.”

When this had been reported to the holy man, he approached her without delay. After looking at her, he raised his hand and made the sign of the cross over the sick woman; immediately the fever was driven away and the woman recovered. She herself very often recounted to many that God had restored her life through the intervention of the holy man.

### 10

After this, therefore, the venerable bishop, seeing that his bodily strength was gradually failing and that the day of his calling was approaching, began to take considerable care lest the flock entrusted to him be left without a shepherd.

Then, with God’s approval, and with everyone’s desire, Saint Erminus was chosen—a man filled with every virtue, equal to his teacher in character [Col. 0352B], and tacitly preferable to all the men of that age. The kindly Father lovingly admonished him, as his dearest son, to tend the flock entrusted to him diligently and to strive to carry it with him to heaven through both conduct and words.

Erminus accepted the task, indeed, with reluctance; but, with God cooperating, he performed it energetically. He began humbly, but persevered faithfully.

Thus the good shepherd of Christ’s flock, Ursmar, mature in character and years, was summoned to the heavenly kingdom to receive the worthy rewards of his merits. Commending his spirit to the faithful Creator through the prayers of his dearest sons whom he had nurtured in Christ, and rejoicing in the Lord in their presence, he was released from the prison of the flesh on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May in the year 713, to live forever with Christ.

Carried into heaven by the ministry of angels, he was brought into the heavenly paradise, where without end he enjoys the faith of the patriarchs, the hope of the prophets, the company of the apostles, the fellowship of the martyrs, and the companionship of confessors and virgins; and he delights in the perpetual rejoicing of all the citizens of heaven.

His body was reverently prepared by the disciples and buried with honorable observance. On the summit of the mountain, at whose foot the monastery already stands, an oratory has been built in honor of the holy Mother of God. There they deposited the treasure of the blessed body. There divine mercy daily demonstrates the merits of the relics kept in that place, to the praise and glory of his majesty, whose honor, glory, and power remain without end. Amen.

[Col. 0353]

## RATHERIUS, BISHOP OF VERONA

[Note: Fulcuin mentions this little work under the name *Syrma* in *Deeds of the Abbots of Lobbes*, chapter 24. It was written at Liège—as is clear from the inscription itself—in the year 955, when Ratherius, although expelled from the see of Liège, was still residing at Liège and was being pressed to surrender the bishopric to Balderic, who had been substituted in his place. He explains the reasons why he cannot yield.

Hence the work is entitled *A Deliberative Conclusion*, which he establishes by forty arguments. Ratherius reproduced this same work, composed at Liège against Balderic, at Verona in 965, after adding a few things at the end, against Milo, when some people were trying to persuade him to relinquish the see of Verona. Thus the same work was published by d’Achery from a manuscript of Laon, in which Ratherius’s works circulated after his third restoration to the bishopric of Verona.

Finally, it should be noted that Ratherius inserted this same work among the twelve volumes that he had placed after the *Phrenesis*, as is clear from the summaries of those volumes given in the preface to the same *Phrenesis*. See there the summary of the eleventh work, which, however, we were unable to find among the other volumes in the Lobbes manuscript from which we received the transcription of the *Phrenesis*.]

## THE CLIMAX OF THE SAME *SYRMA*, OR THE DELIBERATIVE CONCLUSION COMPOSED AT LIÈGE; THE REST IS OF NO VERY SMALL [VALUE]

[Note: *Climax* comes from the Greek and means “ladder” in Latin. The author gave this name to the work because he ascends to the establishment of a deliberative conclusion by forty arguments, like the steps of a ladder.

As for the word *syrma*, its meaning is not entirely certain. *Syrma* was a kind of elongated garment that swept the ground. *Syrmata* are so called because they are dragged, says Donatus—or whoever the author of the prologue to Terence may be. Does Ratherius call this same conclusion a *syrma* because he draws it out by so many arguments and reasons?

In the chronicle of Mouzon, published by d’Achery in volume II of the new edition of the *Spicilegium*, p. 566, the privilege of John XIII is called a *syrma*. The text that follows describes how Bishop Adalbero himself established, through the *syrmata* of the Roman pope and his council, the decree of the pope. Similarly, in the *Life of Saint Gerard, Abbot of Brogne*, no. 29, another, more extensive papal privilege granted to the monastery of Brogne is called a *syrma* by Mabillon, volume VII of the *Acts of the Saints of the Benedictine Order*, p. 274.

In the remaining words of this title, which yield no suitable meaning, there is evidently some error or a defect in certain expressions.]

### I

Since it is clear that satisfying everyone by the convenience of a reply would be an immeasurable labor, setting aside every circumlocution, I openly reveal, as plainly as I can, the irrevocable decision I have made to those who are willing to know it.

Let everyone know that I have always asked, do ask, and shall ask God of the universe that, by the deserts of my sins, it may never happen that, lured by some advantage to myself or frightened by some disadvantage, I expose to the wolf, with my own mouth and while the whole Church concerned looks on and applauds, the flock publicly entrusted to me.

### II

Lest, by my resignation and by yielding through silence to iniquity, I conceal within that same flock, to the destruction of the sheep entrusted to me, the thief and robber condemned by the mouth of God himself: a thief because he stole my see, a robber because by force and public authority he extorted from the hands of those ordaining him—perhaps, “the ordainers”—the curse and leprosy by which he fatally deceives those who think him a bishop and defiles those who communicate with him.

[Note: Construe: “Lest, by my resignation and by yielding through silence to iniquity, I conceal within the same flock, to the destruction of the sheep entrusted to me, the thief and robber condemned by the mouth of God himself: the thief because he stole my see; the robber because he extorted it by force and public authority; [lacuna] the curse and leprosy by which he fatally deceives those who think that he is a bishop and defiles those who communicate with him.”]

### III

Lest, while fleeing from the same man, I bring upon myself the name of a hireling.

### IV

Lest, while taking care to avoid the thief, I myself justly claim the name of thief.

### V

Lest I cease to summon fellow shepherds and fellow servants [Note: Supply: “I should cease to summon fellow shepherds and fellow servants against that thief.”].

### VI

Lest I cease to incite the household dogs, so that by canonical barking they may disturb him.

### VII

Lest I be convicted of having joined my portion with the adulterer of so clear and sacrilegious an invasion: “You have shared your portion with an adulterer” (Psalm 49:18), having prostituted the Church entrusted to me to him.

### VIII

Lest, sitting and speaking against my brother (ibid., 20) [Note: Construe: “Lest I sit and speak against my brother,” that is, against the people of my native country—such as Liège—which is joined to me by the kinship of nearness, since Ratherius was born in a place near the city, or in the diocese of Liège, and which has been abandoned [rather than “delegated”] to the pastoral office—lest, I say, I speak against this people by persuading it to become perverse with the perverse man, that is, with the invader.

The word “nearness” is used for the city. The people joined to Ratherius by the kinship of nearness was the people of Liège, since both acknowledged Liège as their common homeland.

In the preceding number he regards a civic origin, calling the Liège people his “brother”; here, however, he regards a spiritual origin, explaining the following words of the psalm: “And against the son of your mother you placed a stumbling block.”], that is, the people of my native country, joined to me by the kinship of nearness, assigned [read: abandoned] to the pastoral office, I speak by persuading it to become perverse with the perverse man (Psalm 2:27).

### IX

Lest I place against the son of my mother (ibid., 20)—that is, against the people of that Church, of which I too am a son through baptism—a stumbling block so monstrous that even infants are well aware of it.

For if I forget myself—that is, if I yield to the invader—although God may be silent, as he is now, alas, silent to many, yet I fear that he will not remain silent to me when he comes openly; then indeed fire will burn before him, and a violent storm will rage in his presence (ibid., 3).

[Note: Construe: “Lest I place so enormous a stumbling block against the son of my mother, that is, against the people of that Church of which I too am a son through baptism, that even infants are well aware of it.

If I forget myself—that is, if I yield to the invader—even if God remains silent, as he is now, alas, silent to many, I fear that he will not remain silent to me when he comes openly, when fire will burn before him and a violent storm will rage in his presence.

In the preceding number, when he explains for his own purposes the words of Psalm 49:20, “Sitting, you spoke against your brother,” he interprets “brother” as the people of Liège, joined to him by the civic kinship of the same city. Here, explaining the following words, “And against the son of your mother you placed a stumbling block,” he understands “son” as that same people, or commonalty, which received baptism in the same Church. Observe the differing perspectives: in the preceding number he considers civic origin, here spiritual origin.]

### X

Lest I fall into the sect of the Nicolaitans, which God himself declares that he hates (Revelation 2:6).

### XI

Lest, after the example of the *strudocamelon* [Note: *Strudocamelon*, that is, the ostrich mentioned by Pliny and others. He refers to Job 39, where it is written concerning the ostrich: “She abandons her eggs on the ground … she forgets that a foot may trample them … She is harsh toward her young, as though they were not hers.”], I be judged to have exposed those whom I myself ought to have nurtured to those who trample them.

### XII

Lest I immediately be accused of having deceived those who are not canonically permitted to be absent from their sees even for a three-month period [Note: The Council of Trent, session 23, *On Reform*, chapter 1, decreed that bishops’ absence from their Churches, except for just causes, should in no way exceed two months, or at most three. Saint Gregory indicates the absence of a certain priest from his Church for two months, though because of illness, in letter 13 of book IX, to Clementinus. From this passage of Ratherius we learn that a three-month absence was canonically permitted to bishops.].

### XIII

Lest I deservedly receive spittle in my face from that same Church if I first give it a letter of repudiation, as a legitimate rejection [Note: Construe: “Lest I deservedly receive from that same Church the spittle of legitimate rejection in my face if I first give it a letter of repudiation.”].

### XIV

Lest I myself first be defamed for having said—something once prophesied—“Release me to one of the priestly portions, so that I may eat a morsel of bread” (1 Samuel 2:36) [Note: Construe: “Lest I myself first be defamed as having said, ‘Release me to one of the priestly portions,’ and so forth,” as was formerly prophesied.

In the *Deeds of the Bishops of Tongeren*, in Martène and Durand, volume IV of the *Collection of Ancient Writers*, p. 859, no. 20, Ratherius is said to have been driven from the see of Liège but to have been granted certain small fields from the bishopric for his lifetime. On this matter, see what we have discussed in the author’s *Life*, §10, no. 62.]

### XV

Lest, being mad, I regard as nothing the fall of a thousand perjurers [Note: Explain: “Lest, being mad, I regard as worthless the fall of a thousand perjurers,” namely those perjurers who abandoned the faith given to Ratherius and submitted themselves to the invader.].

### XVI

Lest, if the deadly plague of excommunication should seize the whole country as well, I be convicted of taking the name of God in vain (Exodus 20:7), on the grounds that defending it is no danger at all, or perhaps only a very slight one—or, worse, of bringing it about that many should take God’s name in vain.

### XVII

Lest I destroy by my example what has been canonically granted—not merely as permissible but as necessary—to be done mercifully, fraternally, and charitably, for the common utility or necessity, which will certainly increase day by day as the world, lying in wickedness (John 5:13), draws nearer to its end.

This has been granted by those in whose hearts God was present and on whose lips the pure truth of Christ had always been [lacuna]. If I, unhappy man, yield, I shall destroy it by my example.

[Note: The reading was *propinquitate*. The sense required the correction. Shortly afterward, where we have placed dots, the edition read *quia*, which the latest editor of the *Spicilegium*, rightly seeing that it should be removed, advised should be read *pura*, or something similar.

The whole complicated sentence is therefore to be construed as follows: “Lest, if I, unhappy man, yield, I destroy by my example what has been canonically granted—not merely to be permissible but also necessary—to be done mercifully, fraternally, and charitably, for the common utility or necessity. This necessity will daily increase as the world, lying in wickedness, grows worse with the approach of the end. This, I say, was granted by those in whose hearts God was present and on whose lips the pure truth of Christ had always been. To resist the invader and stand firm is what, in these circumstances, he affirmed to be not merely permissible but necessary.”]

### XVIII

Lest I, miserable man, first shut off, to my own peril, this one divinely opened refuge for the wretched, who likewise will be deprived of and driven out from their sees as the heralds of Antichrist grow strong.

“If they persecute you in one city, flee to another” (Matthew 10:23).

Although I do not fail to understand that, by this command, “If they persecute you,” and so forth, the heavenly Jerusalem is principally to be sought as a refuge by those whom the Babylon of worldly confusion pursues.

[Note: The Vulgate reads *et Babylon*. But *eis* (“for those”) should be corrected in place of *et*, as the context requires; the same reading is also found in the following number.]

### XIX

Lest I cruelly block the entrance granted to them by the same command, by which they may canonically recover a bishopric in other Churches that are vacant, when they are entirely unable to recover their own Churches [Note: That is: “Lest I cruelly block access to those other vacant sees which the same command has canonically granted them as a means of recovering a bishopric, since they are entirely unable to recover their own sees,” namely those from which they were expelled.

In this number he suggests from the canons that a bishop who has been expelled by force from his bishopric and cannot recover it may go to another bishopric if it is vacant, that is, if it lacks a legitimate bishop.

Thus Ratherius rather clearly indicates that, after being driven from Verona, he was canonically promoted to the see of Liège, which was vacant through the death of Bishop Farabert.].

### XX

Lest I, miserable man, become a contradictor of the principle that God prefers mercy to sacrifice (Matthew 12:7) [Note: Construe: “Lest I, miserable man, become one who contradicts the fact that God prefers mercy to sacrifice.”

Christ used this text, taken from Hosea 6:6, in Matthew 12:7 to refute the Pharisees, who criticized his disciples for plucking ears of grain when they were hungry, something not permitted on the Sabbath. Christ replied that necessity made this permissible, although otherwise it would not have been, because God had already declared that he desired mercy and not sacrifice.

Ratherius thought that this principle applied to his own case, suggesting that someone expelled from his own bishopric may transfer to another vacant bishopric, although this is otherwise forbidden by the canons.].

### XXI

Lest I decide that what was done publicly, in the presence of the whole Church, by the judgment of the bishops, by the testimony of decrees [Note: By “decrees” he means the constitutions of the popes, which in the Dionysio-Hadriana collection used by Ratherius are called *Decrees*. Thus, in part I, *On Contempt for the Canons*, he also cites those constitutions in this way: “In the decrees of Pope Siricius”; “in the decrees of Pope Innocent,” and so forth.

For which decrees he is referring here, see no. 40.], by the sanction of the canons, and by the legitimate archbishop, with the consent of the clergy—which is also required by the laws—can in any way be invalidated.

[Note: The acts carried out publicly when he was promoted to the see of Liège at the first election at Aachen are indicated here. The legitimate archbishop was Bruno, Archbishop of Cologne. See below, note 434, and the author’s *Life*, §10.]

### XXII

Lest I assert—or at least appear to believe—that the most merciful and truthful concession of the most pious king [Note: “King” means Otto, who, when he granted his consent to Ratherius’s promotion to the see of Liège, was still only king. Here, and in no. 38, “consent” means will or approval.
