It was the custom of that age for the king or emperor to be informed of a bishop’s death; he would then propose to the clergy and others concerned the person to be chosen. See, among many other examples, the *Life of Saint Wolfgang, Bishop of Regensburg*, chapter 14, and the *Life of Saint Ulrich, Bishop of Augsburg*, chapters 1 and 28.

After Farabert’s death, King Otto proposed that Ratherius be chosen bishop of Liège and, as the following number relates, succeeded. See part I, *On Contempt for the Canons*, no. 9.] was either fickle or—or what is more disgraceful—fraudulent.

### XXIII

Lest I obscure with the darkness of ingratitude the dignity of the benevolence that obtained [supply: “that I should be promoted to the see of Liège”] it.

### XXIV

Lest I myself mark it with the branding iron of instability.

### XXV

Lest I condemn the hand of so great an authority, which accomplished this [Note: Construe: “Lest I condemn the hand of so great an authority, which accomplished this”—namely, so that I might be promoted to the see of Liège. We infer that Otto wrote something for this purpose or gave some letter.].

### XXVI

Lest I assert that my ordainer was himself ordained under so ill-omened an auspice, to speak improperly, that I accuse him of having established something contrary to the canonical laws on that very day on which he was ordained, after making the profession customary for him to make, that he would always be obedient to canonical precepts; lest, I say, I favor the madness of those who, foolishly criticize my incardination carried out on that same day and by the hand of the same man, do not know whom they ought rather to attack.

[Note: Construe: “Lest I assert that the ordainer of my ordination was himself ordained under so ill-fated an auspice, improperly speaking, that I accuse him of having established something contrary to the canonical laws on the very day on which he was ordained, after making, as was customary, his profession that he would always obey canonical precepts. I would thereby favor the madness of those who, foolishly criticizing my incardination, carried out on that same day and by the hand of the same man, do not know whom they ought rather to attack.”

He calls Saint Bruno his “ordainer,” since on the very day on which Bruno was ordained Archbishop of Cologne—namely, 21 September 953—he confirmed Ratherius’s election to the see of Liège and in a certain sense transferred him from the see of Verona, as we explained in the *Life*, §10.

An ordainer is not called only the one who consecrates a bishop, but also the one who promotes and appoints someone already ordained to a particular bishopric. Likewise, priests placed in charge of a Church are said in several documents to be “ordained,” that is, appointed.].

### XXVII

Lest, by failing to praise it, I appear to diminish a privilege worthy of praise throughout all ages, granted in our days to him and to his nephew by divine providence alone and not by chance: namely, the privilege by which either of them deserved to ordain the other on the day of his own ordination. In the case of our man [that is, Bruno, who ordained or appointed me], this privilege is all the more worthy of praise because it was more merciful. He acknowledges that he was promoted through mercy. Hence, in part I, *On Contempt for the Canons*, no. 9, he says that, driven from his own see, he was compelled by necessity to approach the most pious Caesar; that he consulted that most glorious council of bishops about the matter; and that they mercifully chose him.

We have observed in the preceding note that this most worthy nephew, the primate, was Saint Bruno, who, on the same day on which he was ordained Archbishop of Cologne, as metropolitan of the Church of Liège, also ordained Ratherius—that is, transferred him—to the same Church.

The man who ordained Bruno, his nephew, can be none other than Robert, Archbishop of Trier, the brother of Saint Queen Matilda, who was the mother of Otto and Bruno. If one ordained the other—that is, if Robert ordained Bruno, and Bruno ordained Ratherius as bishop on the day of his own ordination—then Robert must also be said to have ordained Bruno on the same day on which Robert himself had formerly been consecrated Bishop of Trier.

Robert is said to have been consecrated bishop in 928. Yet in that year the Sunday generally assigned for episcopal ordinations did not coincide with the Sundays of the year 953, when Bruno and Ratherius were ordained. Since episcopal ordinations were not always performed on Sundays but sometimes on other feast days—for example, Saint Ulrich, Bishop of Augsburg, was consecrated in 924 on the feast of the Holy Innocents, which that year fell on a Tuesday, as is related in his *Life* in Mabillon, volume VII of the *Acts of the Saints of the Benedictine Order*, p. 420—a feast day must be posited on which Robert was ordained Bishop of Trier in 928, Bruno was consecrated Bishop of Cologne in 953, and Ratherius, already a bishop, was appointed to the see of Liège in that same year.

In the preface to the *Phrenesis*, no. 1, Ratherius assigns his election to the bishopric of Liège to the Wednesday of the solemn fast of the seventh month. In 953, according to Solar Cycle X and Dominical Letter B, this was 21 September, the feast of Saint Matthew. On this day, therefore, not only was Bruno consecrated in the year 953, but Robert too was consecrated in the year 928, although in that year the feast of Saint Matthew coincided with a Sunday.

Nor does it present an obstacle that Ratherius says in the aforementioned preface that he was elected again and solemnly enthroned on the following Sunday, namely 25 September. Since on 25 September 928 there was no feast on which Robert could have been consecrated bishop, it is evident that the day which Ratherius here assigns to Robert’s ordination, Bruno’s ordination, and his own promotion can refer only to the feast of Saint Matthew.

When he calls his promotion to the see of Liège in no. 26 an incardination carried out by Bruno’s hand, by “incardination” he means Bruno’s act by which, confirming the first election on 23 September, Saint Bruno, as metropolitan, in a certain sense transferred the former Bishop of Verona to the see of Liège and incardinated him there, although the second election and the more solemn incardination were postponed to the following Sunday, 25 September.]

Lest I, by failing to praise it, appear to diminish the privilege worthy of praise throughout all ages, granted in our days to him and to his nephew, the most worthy primate, by divine providence alone and not by chance: namely, the privilege by which either of them deserved to ordain the other on the day of his own ordination. In the case of our man, this privilege is all the more worthy of praise because it was more merciful.

### XXVIII

Lest I accuse him—he means Bruno, as also in what follows—of having subjected God himself to the persons of men, and of men far inferior to him, by confessing that Bruno had irrevocably yielded to their wickedness; of having utterly destroyed what Bruno himself had done after consultation with canonical law; and of strengthening or confirming what had been wrongly accomplished.

[Note: Construe and explain: “Lest I accuse him”—Bruno—“of having subjected God himself to the persons of men, and of men far inferior to him, by confessing that he had irrevocably yielded to their wickedness, and of having utterly destroyed what he himself had done after consultation with canonical law, while strengthening or confirming what had been wrongly accomplished.”

To understand this, Rotger, in the *Life of Saint Bruno*, relates that Bruno, who was then the king Otto’s brother and administered the whole province not so much as Archbishop of Cologne as Duke of Lotharingia, yielded to the madness of those who, through a very serious conspiracy, wished to expel Ratherius from the see of Liège and substitute Balderic in his place.

In this number Ratherius declares that he does not wish to yield the bishopric, lest, by confessing that Bruno had yielded to the wickedness of men far inferior to him, he accuse Bruno of having subjected God himself to such men and of having destroyed what God himself had done after consultation with canonical law when he placed Ratherius over the see of Liège, while strengthening or confirming what had been wrongly accomplished.]

### XXIX

Lest I make the dignity of so great a see, in which these things occurred, worthless to anyone [Note: The see of Cologne is meant. After Ratherius’s second election, carried out on Sunday, 25 September, Bruno more solemnly placed him over the Church of Liège, as is related in the preface to the *Phrenesis*. See the author’s *Life*, §10.

Shortly afterward, *nulli* is used for *pro nihilo*, “as worthless,” as also above in no. 15.].

### XXX

Lest I, most unhappy, disdain the reverence due to holy Peter, unquestionably chief of the apostles, before whose most sacred altar I was deemed worthy to receive the pastoral staff—a reverence despised by the world but to be venerated by the whole universe.

[Note: [Col. 0360C] The cathedral church of Cologne is indicated, dedicated under the name of Saint Peter, as Sigebert attests in his *Chronicle* under the year 871. There, on Sunday, 25 September, Ratherius’s more solemn promotion and enthronement were celebrated. Note also the rite of instituting a bishop by the presentation of the pastoral staff, which Ratherius received from Bruno before the altar of Saint Peter.]

### XXXI

Lest I despise the venerable pulpit ("cujus eodem die edito," uncertain), especially assigned to the people looking on, as though ignorant of the honour it ought to possess [the intervening words are corrupt; Col. 0360A].

[Note: [Col. 0360C] Construe: “Lest I despise the venerable pulpit of the Church of Cologne, especially assigned to the people looking on, as though ignorant of the honour it ought to possess.” The remainder is defective and corrupt, and its meaning cannot be understood; we have enclosed it in brackets. From what follows, however, it is clear that a sermon was delivered by the archbishop on that same day. From the preface to the *Phrenesis* we learn that this archbishop, who praised Ratherius above the ambo of the Church of Cologne, was Rotbert, archbishop of Trier.]

### XXXII

Lest I despise the dignity of the preacher, who was also an archbishop [understand: “despise”].

### XXXIII

Lest I despise the cry of so noble a people.

[Note: [Col. 0360C–D] “The cry,” that is, the acclamations, of so noble a people as the people of Cologne, when Ratherius’s more solemn promotion was celebrated at Cologne.]

### XXXIV

Lest I despise the hymn-singing praise of the most distinguished clergy, amid the ringing of bells.

[Note: [Col. 0360D] The signals refer to bells. See Du Cange, under *Signum* 8. That episcopal elections were celebrated by the sound of bells is evident from the *Life of Saint Udalric*, no. 79, vol. VII of the *Acta Sanctorum* of the Benedictine order, p. 453, where, concerning the election of Henry, his successor, it says: “When this election had been made known to the church’s soldiers and household, it was confirmed by all while the bells were ringing.”]

### XXXV

Lest I lightly pass over the most sacred and sweetest melody of that hymn which resounded.

### XXXVI

Lest I be proved to have yielded by condemning the subscription of seven such venerable prelates, two of whom had also been archbishops.

[Note: [Col. 0360D] These subscriptions were appended to the letters sent by the bishops to the clergy and people of Liège concerning Ratherius’s promotion. Two of those bishops, who were archbishops, were Rotbert of Trier and Bruno of Cologne. For the names of the others, see the preface to the *Phrenesis*.]

### XXXVII

Lest I seem to disparage the persons of the legates, since they too were bishops who appointed me over the people entrusted to me, one of whom was also a metropolitan.

[Note: [Col. 0360D–0361C] Construe: “Lest I seem to disparage the persons of the legates”—that is, those delegated by the council held at Cologne for Ratherius’s promotion—“since they too were bishops who appointed me over the people entrusted to me, one of whom was a metropolitan,” namely Bruno of Cologne, whose suffragan was the bishop of Liège. Hence Bruno, leading Ratherius to Liège with certain other bishops, installed him in possession of the bishopric.]

### XXXVIII

Lest, when the judgment commonly accepted by all is that the bishop’s words must be either true or sacrilegious, I dare to call or believe their report false, which set forth the grant of the most pious king in my affair.

[Note: [Col. 0361C] Acherius published *concessumque*. The most recent editor conjectured that it should be corrected to *consensumque*. He correctly emended *quae*, but *concessum* should be retained, since at no. 22 there is likewise mention of the grant of the most pious king. Construe as follows: “Lest, when the judgment commonly accepted by all is that the bishop’s words are either true or sacrilegious, I dare to call or believe false the report of those men”—that is, the legates mentioned in the preceding section—“which reported the grant of the most pious king in my case.”]

### XXXIX

Lest I ungratefully slander the reception so spontaneous, so joyful, so devout, so populous, and so clamorous—filled with so many praises of Christ because I had been given to that people—which I received from a people most devoted toward me.

[Note: [Col. 0361C–D] The “praises” were public acclamations, whose formulas in sacred ceremonies included: “Praises to Christ,” “Christ conquers, Christ reigns, Christ commands,” “Hear us, O Christ,” and similar expressions.]

### XL

Lest I dare admit so profane a sacrilege of impiety—one which every wise person will judge to outweigh all the matters set forth above by as much as heaven appears to be distant from earth, and sunrise from sunset—so that, by yielding illegally, if resistance is possible, I might be proved, together with those who accuse me of being unlawfully attached to this church, to condemn those whom, although unequal in merit, it is nevertheless established were transferred in ancient times, for definite reasons, from their own sees to others by the same authority by which it is established that I was transferred.

[Note: [Col. 0361D–0362C] Construe: “Lest I dare admit a sacrilege of so profane an impiety, which every wise person will judge to surpass all the foregoing matters by as much as heaven seems distant from earth and east from west; a sacrilege, I say, of so profane an impiety that, by yielding unlawfully, if resistance is permitted, I might be proved, together with those who accuse my incardination, to condemn those whom, though unequal in merit, it is established were transferred long ago, for definite reasons, by the same authority by which I was transferred, from their own sees to others. So many are known from the testimony of books to be worthy examples—our countrymen excepted, since no mention of them has survived where this occurred—even though Dionysius, the most illustrious standard-bearer among the martyrs, and Cassian, the holiest of the Aedui, shine forth, together with countless others whom ignorance has concealed from us or forgetfulness has removed.”]

These men are known, on the testimony of books, to have been so many worthy examples—apart from those of our own country, since no mention of them appeared where the events occurred—although Dionysius, that most renowned leader among the martyrs, and Cassian, the most holy bishop of the Aedui, shine among them, together with countless others whom either ignorance has concealed from us or forgetfulness has taken away.

[Note: [Col. 0362C] Here and in what follows Ratherius recalls bishops who were transferred from one see to another. First, among those of his own country, as he calls them—that is, among the Gauls—he mentions Dionysius, bishop of Paris, since he supposed that Dionysius had previously presided over the Church of Athens.]

Saint Peter—not just any Peter, but the one to whom God himself is known to have said with his own mouth, “Feed my sheep” (John 21:15)—had gone before this unconquerable company.

[Note: [Col. 0362C–D] Thus the most recent editor of the *Spicilegium* of Acherius printed the reading *non qualiscunque*, whereas previously it had been read *non quascunque*. Among bishops transferred from one see to another, Ratherius also lists Saint Peter the apostle, Felix, and Eusebius; we have discovered that he took these names from a pseudo-letter of Pope Antherus. Thereafter Perigenes and others down to Silvanus are listed by Socrates, together with the proper names of the sees from which and to which they were transferred; their names are known to have been excerpted by Ratherius from book 12, chapter 8, of the *Tripartite History*, in the same order. The final three were taken from Saint Gregory: Martin of Corsica from book I, letter 79, and John of Squillace from book II, letter 37. One of them is called by Agnellus “the man of Terracina”; see book III, letter 13.]

There follow immediately Felix, Eusebius, Perigenes, Gregory of Nazianzus, Meletius, Dositheus, Alexander, Reverentius, John, Palladius, another Alexander, Theosebius, Polycarp, Hierophilus, Optimus, Silvanus, Martin of Corsica, John of Squillace, and a certain man of Terracina.

Their supporters are Pope Callixtus, Pope Antherus, and Gregory, the theologian and our highly esteemed authority—if, indeed, the testimony of so great an authority is not doubted. I consider myself most fortunate to be condemned, if they are condemned, together with those men.

[Note: [Col. 0362D] That is, Saint Gregory the Great, in the letters indicated in the preceding note, in which he approved the transfers just mentioned. Construe what follows: “with whom, if they are condemned, I consider myself most fortunate to be condemned.” Also, where the manuscript had *cuilibet*, we have written *a quolibet*; and with the editor of the *Spicilegium* we have retained *vim*, where Acherius had read *ubi*.]

But if, disregarding the authority of so many and such men, I am expelled by public force, let the responsibility lie with the one who inflicts it. I would rather suffer violence from any person, however needy, than be judged to have made a pact with death (Isaiah 28:15) and to have made peace with hell.

I do not withdraw my hand ungratefully from someone extending it to offer some support of alms—even from that exceptional robber. And, O utterly blinded hearts of the sons of the old Adam! O darkness still so dense in Egypt that it can be felt!

For among a thousand who seem, as it were, to recognize the crime, saying, “How grave is the sin that that deprived bishop appears to be treated so unjustly,” scarcely one is found who would speak more correctly: “How grave is the crime that so great a multitude bearing the Christian name has been deceived in this way!”

Certainly my deprivation can be alleviated by enough daily bread; but no one can perceive how irrecoverable his ruin is.

This might perhaps have been perceived, if someone—someone whose concern it was—had deigned to consider whether anyone could be made a shepherd of the Church by the incantation, or, so to speak, the blessing—that is, the consecration—of some mortal, when the prince and author of shepherds, God himself, the shepherd and Creator, calls him a thief and a robber, condemning and rejecting him.

Or whom can the one who has himself been rightly condemned by the curse of an anathema bless?

Let anyone who wishes to smooth over these matters, if he can, take care: to me they are of the utmost gravity.

[Note: [Col. 0362D–0363A] Construe: “If anyone whose concern this is would deign to consider whether anyone can become a shepherd of the Church through the incantation—or, so to speak, the blessing—of a mortal, when the prince and author of shepherds, God himself, condemns and rejects him as a thief and robber.”]

Accordingly, these forty adverbial arguments—if my reckoning does not deceive me—which I, Ratherius, once brought forward when I resisted the most persistent advisers in the matter of yielding the bishopric of Liège, let the reader know that I have been compelled to reply more mildly to those sixteen earlier perverse persuaders concerning Verona.

[Note: [Col. 0363A–0364A] He calls the forty reasons previously set forth “adverbial” because he used them to oppose those who pressed him most insistently to give up the bishopric of Liège. He reproduced the same arguments when, having been restored for the third time to the bishopric of Verona, he found some persuaders who urged him to yield to Milo the invader; one of them was Hubert, bishop of Parma. See the work entitled *Conjecture of Character*, no. 16. Next, we have printed *sit* where the text had *sic*.]

Moreover, let him who has wearied me further, apart from the censure of a canonical judgment or the authority of the most pious emperor, be condemned with that Judas Iscariot—unless repentance comes to his aid.

[Note: [Col. 0364A–B] He excepts two things, to which alone he promises that he will yield: canonical judgment and an imperial command. On the latter, see letter 8 to Milo, at the end.]

## [PHRENESIS]

### Editorial Notice concerning the *Phrenesis*

#### I

In the affair in which Ratherius was expelled from the see of Liège, Fulcuinus, in chapter 24 of *The Deeds of the Abbots of Lobbes*, mentions another little book written by Ratherius, in addition to the *Deliberative Conclusion* that we placed first, entitled *Phrenesis*.

This book, which had been sought in vain, was found among the manuscript codices of the monastery of Lobbes. The most reverend Paulus du Bois, abbot of that monastery, most kindly complying with our wishes, arranged for it to be transcribed and sent to us. We place it after the *Deliberative Conclusion*, because it was written later, while Ratherius, expelled from the see of Liège, was living at Mainz, as is clear from the preface (no. 1).

Since he was expelled shortly after Easter in the year 955, it must be said that he wrote the *Phrenesis* at Mainz later in that same year, while Duke Conrad—who at the time of Ratherius’s expulsion was acting against King Otto—had subsequently returned to the king’s favour and had not yet died. For this book contains no indication of his death such as the author gives in the *Book of Confession*, composed after Conrad’s death, where at no. 3 he calls Conrad, under the name of Cono, a former duke. Conrad died while fighting for Otto in August of that same year, 955 (*Necrologium Fuldense*, vol. III of Leibniz’s *Rerum Brunsvicensium*).

#### II

In this affair at Liège Ratherius had written twenty little books (*Phrenesis*, nos. 7 and 18), which he later reduced to twelve. In the preface to the *Phrenesis* he presents the subjects of these twelve volumes, as he calls them; the eleventh among them is the *Deliberative Conclusion*, which we mentioned earlier.

Although he states in the preface (no. 7) that the *Phrenesis* was placed before all these little books, he nevertheless affirms that it was written last, and likewise brought to completion more quickly (no. 10), because Rotbert, archbishop of Trier, against whom it had chiefly been written, was reported to have died.

We hoped that the other little works, from which much useful material for history would come to light, would also be found in the same Lobbes manuscript after the *Phrenesis*. We wrote requesting that the codex be examined more carefully; but after the *Phrenesis* only Ratherius’s *Faith* was found, which belongs to the beginning of the second little work. See what we have noted more fully about this matter in the *Life of the Author*, § 10, no. 61.

Since Fulcuinus mentions only two little works in the Liège affair—the *Phrenesis* and the *Syrma*, that is, the *Deliberative Conclusion*—it appears that he too found only these two in the Lobbes manuscripts of his own time.

Since none of the other such works is mentioned in the very full catalogue of the manuscript works of the library of Lobbes, which was carefully compiled at the beginning of the eleventh century, it is clear that they were already absent from that library at that time.

#### III

It is surprising, however, that Fulcuinus should write that Ratherius called the earlier book *Phrenesis* because, like a madman, he attacked Baldricus too harshly and beyond measure. It is clear from what he immediately says about the *Syrma* that by Baldricus he understood the invader of the see of Liège; in the *Syrma*, he says, Ratherius attacks that same Baldricus, whom he calls “the usurper of his see.”

The title of the preface to the *Phrenesis* indicates that the name was prefixed because Ratherius attacked certain men too harshly. In the work itself there is much against Rotbert, archbishop of Trier, and some against another Bishop Baldricus, the Baldricus of Liège’s uncle, namely Baldricus of Utrecht; there is very little against Baldricus of Liège.

The author himself gives a more truthful reason for assigning the title *Phrenesis* in the preface. While enjoying leisure at Mainz after being expelled from Liège, he undertook to arrange in books the events that had happened to him. When Rotbert of Trier and Baldricus of Utrecht heard of this—those two having been chiefly responsible for expelling him—they said that he was mad.

Embracing this insult, he called the little book that he immediately hastened to compose against them *Phrenesis*, in accordance with their judgment, and called himself mad because, in a practice certainly unusual at that time, he fled in such a crisis not to money, not to weapons as some did, and not to a multitude of friends, but to books, to bookcases—that is, to a library—and to the judgments of the ancients.

He says that he “fled” and “hastened,” because in the preface, down to no. 7, he assumes another person and writes about himself as though about someone else. He also writes in such a way—and this deserves notice—that, following his own disposition, by which he was accustomed to lash not others so much as himself, he touches upon and brings forward for criticism certain deeds of his own in much the same kind of judgment that he later used more extensively in the *Conjecture of Character*. See the *Life of the Author*, § 17, no. 109.

#### IV

One final point in this notice requires particular attention. Although Ratherius’s style and syntax repeatedly present some difficulty and obscurity, nothing more difficult or obscure is found in this work.

The author openly professes that he deliberately cultivated obscurity in the work itself. Thus, in the preface, no. 3, [Col. 0365] he says:

> “This also produces difficulty for those who must deal with the little books he composed: a parenthesis is very frequently found inserted there; and, in order to make his speech clear, he often gives the words a remarkable arrangement, producing the most difficult material for a construction which, although difficult, is nevertheless excellent for those who understand it.”

And near the end of the same preface, no. 9:

> “Let him recognize that I have deliberately placed certain things obscurely in my little books; nevertheless, he will soon be able to clarify them if he has an industrious and diligent constructor.”

Hence quite a few passages that cannot easily be understood at first reading, and that we could grasp only through careful examination, had to be explained by means of the constructions supplied in the notes.

Many other things, however, cause difficulty apart from the complexity of the syntax. As the author himself observed in the same place, ignorance of the subject matter, as in his other books, often makes understanding difficult here as well. For he repeatedly indicates certain events that are not otherwise known with such brevity that it is not at all clear what is meant by a few words of indication.

The difficulty is increased by faulty writing. This defect occurs so frequently in the work that in some periods two, three, or even more errors have now been detected. We have removed many of them from the context or from a sense known elsewhere. But in some places, when the matter itself or the author’s meaning was completely hidden, we thought it better to venture nothing in the corrupt text than to guess uncertainly.

For these reasons, since many passages still remain tangled and obscure, whose meaning we were unable to extract even with the construction supplied, we hesitated for some time over whether the little work should be published at all. Since it contains some material useful for arranging the life of Ratherius, however, and material that must be cited there but would be sought in vain elsewhere, we judged that it should not be omitted.

#### V

After we had written these remarks, the learned and most devoted student of antiquity, Count Joseph Garampi, having departed for Germany from the honour of the papal household in order to contribute some assistance to this edition, informed us that, while he was at Cologne, he had found in the library of the monastery of Saint Pantaleon a thirteenth-century parchment codex containing an unpublished *Life of Saint Bruno, Archbishop of Cologne*, written by an anonymous author. It included an entire chapter concerning our Ratherius.

We subsequently received the chapter itself, whose title is *Concerning the Bishop Who Was Expelled and Restored to His See by the Lord Himself [Bruno]*, accurately transcribed by Joseph Antonio Pinzi, to whom Garampi, as he was about to move elsewhere, had entrusted the matter because Pinzi had rendered distinguished service to letters.

The chapter begins with these words, which present an encomium of Ratherius that ought not to be omitted:

> “The Church of Verona in Italy was governed by a vigorous man named Ratherius, a monk in habit, an outstanding practitioner of the whole religious life, and a most distinguished interpreter of the divine Scriptures.”

What the same anonymous author immediately relates about him is known to have been taken for the most part from the first section of the *Phrenesis*, to such an extent that not only the same ideas but repeatedly the same words are inserted.

Yet, through a remarkable hallucination, he attributes to Ratherius’s episcopate at Verona events that in the *Phrenesis* belong to his episcopate at Liège. We thought this should be noted here, lest, if this *Life of Saint Bruno* is ever brought to light, what it says about Ratherius as bishop of Verona should create difficulty and confusion for the less cautious.

[Col. 0365]

# THE *PHRENESIS* OF RATHERIUS, BISHOP OF VERONA

The preface of Ratherius, bishop, begins, in the book he called *Phrenesis*, because in it he attacked certain men too harshly.

[Col. 0365A]

### 1

The investigation of any writing is especially hindered when its investigators do not know the subject matter—that is, the first author, the intention of the author, and the matter under discussion.

The reason for the term *Phrenesis* is revealed in what follows: because, after he had been expelled, etc.]

Two elections are distinguished: one at Aachen and the other at Cologne, as we explained more fully in the *Life*, § 10.]

—he had been requested; then on the following Sunday he had been elected again by the same people—that is, by the people of the Church of Liège—and, with the greatest favour of the entire assembly present, had been appointed to that Church and solemnly enthroned by seven fellow bishops, namely Bruno, Rodbert, Baldricus, Hildibaldus, Druogo, Berengarius, and Folbertus, two of whom had been archbishops and the others bishops, with the concurrence of decrees, the consent, and the examples of certain ancients to whom the same thing had happened.

so that it would not be difficult to conjecture how such things happened, and so that the basis of this acceptance of persons [the manuscript reads *acceptione*] might be clear in every respect, he had been expelled through disregard of the timidity of the aforementioned brother of the king—namely, lest the aforementioned counts should desert the king for Conrad, who was then acting against the king himself, and should become his enemies together with Conrad—or, as the defenders of the archbishop assert more truly, because the same archbishop, although he had desired it, could not obtain any helper from among the friends or soldiers of Bishop Ratherius to resist or assist in resisting.

[Note: [Col. 0368C–D] Regenerus was a very powerful count of Hainaut. Fulcuinus also reports that Regenerus, Baldricus’s uncle, greatly assisted him in obtaining the episcopate. [Note: [Col. 0368C–D] The particle *then* clearly designates Conrad as being an enemy of King Otto at the time when Ratherius was expelled from the see of Liège, on the day of the Lord’s Supper—that is, 12 April 955—as is stated below at no. 16. ### 2

Embracing the insult, which rekindled the writing-fervour that had already been lulled, he immediately hastened to compose against them a little book that he would present publicly to all. He calls its substance, in accordance with their judgment, *Phrenesis*, and calls himself mad because, in a practice certainly unusual at that time, he had fled in such a crisis not to money, not to weapons as some did, and not to a multitude of friends, but to books, to bookcases, and to the judgments of the ancients.

In the preface he attacks Rodbert more extensively and Baldricus more sharply. Hence, at the very beginning, as though treating him with contempt, he declares that Baldricus is free from the vice of *phrenesis*, by which he wishes madness to be understood—a madness cleansed by the ancient poetic hemlock (*HORAT.*, book II, epistle 2, verse 53).

[Note: [Col. 0368D] He means Baldricus, bishop of Utrecht on the Rhine. Hence below, at no. 9, he similarly says: “But also against Baldricus, his standard-bearer, although in a very different battle-line.”]

He also calls Rodbert, in his own defeat, his “standard-bearer,” though in a different battle-line: that is, not with the skill of speaking which Rodbert claimed, but with greater cunning in deception.

[Note: [Col. 0368D–0369A] The skill of speech is attributed to Rodbert of Trier, who, as you will learn from no. 14, disputed eloquence with Ratherius. See note 497.]

Let no one think that he spares anyone except the one whom integrity protects, although he often spares no one less than himself, like another Lucilius.

[Note: [Col. 0369C] Construe: “Let no one seem to be spared except the person whom integrity has protected; although he often spares no one less than himself, like another Lucilius.” This must be understood of Ratherius himself, whose habit included lashing himself, as is related in the *Conjecture of Character*, no. 2. Whom does he praise who always criticizes himself?]

Those who investigate his works can see how far he is from leaving the archbishop untouched.

[Note: [Col. 0369C] That is, Rodbert of Trier.]

### 3

This also creates difficulty in understanding the little books he composed: a parenthesis is very frequently found inserted there; and, in order to make his speech clear, he often gives the words a remarkable arrangement, producing the most difficult material for a construction which, although difficult, is nevertheless excellent for those who understand it.

His loquacity, if not considered with due care, must certainly have deceived many, as must also the character of his conduct. I confess that he was stronger in understanding than in technique, and in a certain practice of writing each thing than in the abundant expression of speech, and more in knowing many things than through any special privilege of knowledge. He was taught to compose not so much by the precepts of the art itself as by his curious investigation of the ancients.

He learned little from teachers and acquired more for himself through reckless presumption—*temperando* in the manuscript, perhaps for *comparando*—than others could scarcely have learned from the foremost teachers with the greatest labour.

[Note: [Col. 0369C–D] Construe: “His loquacity, if not carefully considered, as well as the character of his conduct, must certainly have deceived many. I confess that he was stronger in understanding than in technique, stronger through a certain practice of writing than through the ability to speak abundantly, and stronger in knowing many things than through any special privilege of knowledge. His curious investigation of the ancients taught him to compose more than the precepts of the art itself. He learned little from teachers and acquired more for himself through reckless presumption—[the manuscript has *temperando*, perhaps for *comparando*]—than others could scarcely have learned from the foremost teachers with the greatest labour.” Hence a certain wise and equally religious man, lest knowledge puffed up and unsupported by charity—as the Apostle warned—should overthrow him, after rereading some of his little works, said that grace was stronger in him than wisdom and that he seemed more worthy of wonder than praise. Rather, merciful grace is to be wondered at and proclaimed: grace which, while not abandoning one who had abandoned himself, bestowed such things on such a man by abandoning him. At the point marked by dots, the manuscript adds *non deserendo deserens* (“forsaking while not forsaking”); since this appears to conflict with what precedes, we judged it to have been inserted erroneously.]

Hence a certain wise and equally religious man, lest knowledge not supported by charity should overthrow him, as the Apostle had warned—“knowledge puffs up” (1 Corinthians 8:1)—after rereading some of his little works, said that grace was stronger in him than wisdom, and that he seemed more worthy of wonder than of praise.

Rather, merciful grace is to be wondered at and proclaimed: grace which, while not abandoning one who forsook himself, bestowed such things on such a man by abandoning him [lacuna].

[Col. 0369C] 221

### 4

For—and, in touching upon something concerning his character, I would not be attacking him, or rather praising him—who would have been more competent to say what was good than to do it, when in both activities (that is, both in speaking and in doing) there served him a pretence of intention that entirely deprived those observing him of a more certain judgment about him?

[Note: This is a very intricate passage, and perhaps corrupt, unless it is explained as follows: “For, even if to have touched upon something concerning his character should not be to tear him apart but rather to praise him, who would have been more competent to speak of good than to do it, when in both activities a pretence of intention served him—one that entirely removed from those observing him a more certain judgment of him?”]

For since impatient weakness drove him more often to avoid things than the attraction of those things’ pleasures drew him toward them, and since ineffectual sluggishness rather than probity—or, if one may call it so, obedience—turned him away from doing things, he often seemed happiest when angry, while, though apparently cheerful, he frequently concealed the greatest grief within. He gave without being asked, impatient to be asked, as though, when injured, he were often holding back an unknown hatred; and he had acted in many ways of this kind, extremely difficult to detect.

[Note: That is, he had acted in many ways like this, which were exceedingly difficult to detect; hence he himself was exceedingly difficult to understand.]

Perhaps he would have been blessed if the habit had made him a monk, as it shows that it would; nor would he ever have been absent from the monastery of Lobbes, if he had remained steadfast in his vow.

He possessed that nobility which, as is reported, antiquity had commended more than kinship displayed.

[Note: Construe: “He possessed that nobility which antiquity, as is reported, had commended more than kinship could display.” That is, he possessed a nobility joined to the antiquity of his family and illustrious ancestors, and commended more on account of that antiquity of lineage than on account of living relatives—perhaps because, when he wrote this, he lacked relatives of great name and power. “As is reported,” he says, just as in the conjecture concerning his character in no. 2 he rather clearly indicates that he had frequently been called noble by the people of Verona. See what we noted in the Life, § 1, no. 3.]

Gray hairs had begun to come upon him, while he was composing these things—not through an untimely onset, but through the maturity of advancing age.

[Note: *Cujus* seems to require correction to *cui*. Construe: “While he was composing these things, the maturity of age, not untimely onset but advancing years, had begun to bring him gray hairs.”]

To sum it up: he had almost become liable to condemnation before his detractors, if an innocent man had not been harmed by someone else’s example, or if not to have done good were not equivalent to having done harm. Yet in which direction he was ambiguous, as I have said, so that his state of estimation can scarcely be judged fairly.

[Note: Construe: “To sum it up: he would almost have been guilty before his detractors, if some innocent person had not been harmed by example, or if failing to do good had not been equivalent to doing harm. In which direction he was thus ambiguous, as I have said, so that his condition could scarcely be fairly assessed.”]

Although he was spirited in the opinion of many, he had nevertheless become accustomed—strange to say!—to being moved by the slightest things, so that he was wonderfully calm in enduring the greatest.

[Note: Construe: “Although he was thought spirited by many, he was accustomed to being moved by the slightest things—strange to say!—so that he was extraordinarily calm in bearing the greatest burdens. Let no one therefore compare him with those whom he seemed to imitate, lest he justly hear the prophet crying out to him: ‘Woe to those who call evil good and good evil.’ Again, I praise what he did well, lest someone should bite him with a tooth, lest blessed Job seem to say to him: ‘Envy kills the little one.’”]

Let no one, therefore, compare him with those whom he seemed to imitate, lest he deservedly hear the prophet crying out to him: “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil” (Isaiah 5:20). Again, I praise what he did well, lest someone should bite him with a tooth, lest blessed Job seem to say to him: “Envy kills the little one” (Job 5:2).

[Col. 0371A] 5

In any case, the quality of this little book would perhaps have been greater, had it not been cut short, just as a woven web already completed is cut off (Job 7:6), as soon as he learned of the death of the aforesaid Rodbert—although a false rumor had previously announced that death.

[Note: Construe: “The quality of this little book would perhaps have been greater, had it not been cut short, just as a web already completed is cut off—cut short, I say, immediately after he learned of the death of the aforesaid Rodbert, whose death a false rumor had nevertheless announced beforehand.”]

He touches upon this sufficiently sharply at the beginning of the preface and reveals it more openly at the end.

The examples from Tullius, Maro, Horace, and other poets were forced upon him by the necessity of his work, because all people of the present age—shame upon it!—including himself, delight more in the husks that are the pasture of swine than in the banquets that are the life of blessed souls.

[Note: He is evidently saying that he inserted such material in order to gain readers for these books, because he knew that none of his like had even touched such a cup with the tips of their lips; or because things easily discovered quickly cheapen the nectarous taste of the heavenly gift, unless this poison—namely, secular examples—has poisoned the liquid. For writings, however heavenly, do not taste good unless sprinkled with profane examples. The manuscript read *terrenum hoc invenenasset liquorem*, doubtless erroneously; we have corrected it to *venenum hoc ni venenasset liquorem*. The following should be construed thus: “These contrived examples—or examples of profane writers sought with excessive zeal—prove how displeasing true simplicity and pure wisdom are, when someone works to appear wiser than others rather than to be wiser, inserting foreign material into his own, as this man does, merely to persuade more people that he has read much. This is rather to tear away scraps from the arts than to possess the arts themselves; to seek the glory of the great rather than to follow them.”]

To gain them readers, therefore, he is shown to have inserted such things, because he knew that no one like himself had touched such a cup even with the tips of his lips. Either because things easily discovered quickly cheapen the nectarous taste of the heavenly gift, unless this poison has poisoned the liquid.

Such contrived material proves how displeasing true simplicity and pure wisdom are, when someone works to appear wiser than others rather than to be wiser, inserting foreign things into his own—as this man does—in order merely to persuade more people that he has read much. Yet this is rather to strip away scraps from the arts than to possess the arts themselves, to seek the glory of the great rather than to follow them.

“O imitators, slavish herd,” said someone, and truthfully, “and cattle” (Horace, Book 1, Epistle 19, verse 19)—those whom our Bœotian did not fail to criticize.

### 223

Therefore, in my judgment, those who are useless and pernicious in this matter to everyone—those who, if they have deceived any people, make them deceivers of others—are people who, considering some small portions of my knowledge insufficiently, suppose that the whole, or the greater part of the sum of that knowledge, has fallen to them, and by praising it cause others to think so as well.

[Note: Construe: “Therefore those who are useless to themselves and pernicious to all in this matter are those who, if they have made anyone deceived, make them deceivers of others—namely, those who, considering certain portions of my knowledge too little, suppose that the whole or the greater part of that knowledge has come to them, and by praising it make others think so. Our prohibitor seems to imply the same to me when he forbids anyone to place a stumbling-block before the blind. For I do not know whether someone can be thought not to be blind who is incapable of seeing whatever is placed before his eyes. Since it is clear that the Apostle carefully guarded against this, desiring no one to estimate himself as more than what he saw in him and heard from him, our writer shudders if some utterly deluded person asserts himself to be learned, noble, or—what is much more unjust—just, when he is not such. He asserts this especially in writings, which, after his death, speak while he is silent, and thereby make others lie as well. If through ignorance he makes himself an obscure stumbling-block to the blind, it would have been much happier for him to have remained hidden both in life and in death than to have enjoyed the praise of a false rumor. Hence even the dead do not cease to sin when, after death, they cause themselves to be falsely praised. Let this suffice: it has neither maliciously detracted from this writer’s knowledge nor falsely added to it, but serves as an indication of the whole character and endeavor of the man.”]

The one who forbids this seems also to imply it to me when he forbids anyone to place a stumbling-block before the blind (Leviticus 19:14). For, when something is placed before the eyes, incapacity to see it—I do not know whether this can be regarded as not being blindness.

It is clear that the Apostle carefully guarded against this, desiring no one to estimate himself as more than what he saw in him and heard from him (2 Corinthians 12:6). He shudders if some utterly deluded person asserts himself to be learned, noble, or—what is much more unjust—just, when he is not such, especially in writings which, after death, speak while he is silent, making others lie as well. He makes himself, through ignorance, an obscure stumbling-block to the blind, although it would have been much happier for him to have remained hidden in death as he had been in life than to have enjoyed the praise of a false rumor.

Thus even the dead do not cease to sin when they cause themselves to be falsely praised after death. Let this suffice concerning the knowledge of this writer: it has neither been maliciously diminished nor falsely augmented, and it is an indication of his entire character and endeavor.

## Summary of His Books

### 6

Let us therefore retain, in outline, the order of the little works. Although this one is the preface to the others, its size nevertheless compels it to be considered a little book.

One volume.

The next contains the faith of the writer, together with two letters: one never ceases to weary the Roman See with complaints, while the other addresses the flock of fellow bishops.

One volume.

The third contains a complaint brought against the king, together with certain letters.

One volume.

[Col. 0372C] The fourth contains only two letters to bishops: a very brief one to Bruno and a sufficiently long one to Rodbert.

One volume.

The fifth is devoted to a complaint more specifically against Bruno, although it contains a general account, and is addressed to the archbishop.

One volume.

The sixth, seventh, and eighth, although they are letters sent to the invader himself, criticize in many ways, sharply and briefly, the conduct of the elder Baldric.

One volume.

[Note: He calls the younger Baldric the “invader,” because he had been substituted in the see of Liège after Ratherius had been expelled. He calls his uncle, the bishop of Utrecht, who bore the same name, the elder Baldric.]

The ninth book answers an attack under the cloak of humility. The writer, who had been quite favorably disposed toward Bruno, complains in mournful language.

One volume.

[Note: It seems that *Nono* should be read, and construed as follows: “In the ninth little book the writer, who had been sufficiently favorably disposed toward Bruno, complains in mournful language and answers the attack under the cloak of humility.”]

The tenth addresses a thoroughly deceived flock and prescribes the relief of repentance.

One volume.

The eleventh is a deliberative conclusion, large in its judgments but brief in its discourses.

One volume.

[Note: Although the Lobbes manuscript, among the twelve volumes indicated in this preface, presents only the first and, from the second, only the writer’s profession of faith, we previously published this eleventh volume, entitled *Deliberative Conclusion*, from another manuscript at Laon. It was copied and found separately from the others in the Laon manuscript because it contains Ratherius’s works published by him toward the end of his episcopate at Verona. At that time, thinking this little work also suitable for the Veronese sedition, he repeated it separately, adding a few things at the end.]

The twelfth is a dialogue composed for a certain affair, though not wholly unrelated to him.

One volume.

### 7

This arrangement of the books has not been made because, as with historians, expositors, poets, and other composers of works, these writings form a continuous sequence in their execution, so that the meaning of the preceding discourse answers to that of the following. Rather, each little book exists independently and was composed without preserving an order of composition. Since they are all composed about one subject but contain different material, each has received its own place.

[Note: Construe: “Each little book exists independently, without an observed order of composition. They were all composed about one subject but contain different things, and each received its own place.”]

It is not continuity of speech but continuity of reasoning that has joined them; and the result would be the same if whichever is first were last, or whichever is fourth were eighth.

Their great dissimilarity confirms this as well. Some of them are nothing other than collections of letters; some possess a continuous form, like the little works of certain authors; some seem to have a divided structure, though their meaning and subject matter continue throughout; while one of them is separated into sections of six lines according to its statements because its author arranged it in verses, as can be seen in Martianus, Fulgentius, and Boethius.

[Lacuna.] To compose statements drawn from the same subject matter.

To anyone who thinks it improper to call a collection of letters itself a little book, or to say that any one of them has acquired the same designation through its length, let him observe in this work the book of the Maccabees which is called the Second, and among us the epistolary books of the apostles, Augustine, Jerome, Gregory, and many others. Among secular writers, let him consider Tullius, Seneca, and Pliny himself, who composed and titled epistolary books; and, to oppose the barking of detractors, let us set against all satirists Horace Flaccus, who deserves preference, and among the books entitled *From Pontus*, Ovid Naso.

[Note: In this little book, which contains only one letter, one may observe the Second Book of Maccabees, which likewise is composed of only one letter. As for the others, which contain several letters, examples among Catholic writers are the letters of the apostles, Augustine, and other Fathers distributed into books; among secular writers, the letters of Tullius, Seneca, and Pliny; and, to silence the mouths of detractors, Horace’s satires and Ovid’s books from Pontus, which present letters.]

They could, moreover, have been said to number twenty, as had originally been determined; but, shortened somewhat out of consideration for a certain matter and compressed into twelve, they must be called and regarded as twelve in number according to the evaluation of the subject, though twelve according to the variety of their expression.

This preface, however, deserved to be called and made the first by its function, although it is last in composition. It is itself the answer to the reproach provoked by others, demonstrating in the other works how greatly the madness of their author shines forth.

### 8

It is reported that when the entire Senate had conspired against Nero, he sent to one man whom he thought his friend, seeking advice for his safety. When that man refused to come, he sent again to someone who was his bitterest enemy among the conspirators, so that, when he came, he might kill him—unwilling, of course, to die ignominiously while the whole city looked on, as the Senate had decreed. When even this man delayed, he is said to have remarked: “Now I have neither friend nor enemy” (Suetonius, *Nero*, 47).

The example fits either me or my little books well enough. For since Scripture testifies: “The envy of a man is toward his friend and neighbor” (indeed, an Indian does not envy a Briton, nor a Frank a Parthian)—

[Note: We find the following text nowhere in sacred Scripture. Sometimes, however, a saying of a wise writer is cited under the name of Scripture, as is clear, among other examples, from the Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 7, second degree of humility: “Scripture says: The will has punishment, and necessity brings a crown”; and from Saint Valerius’s sayings on the kinds of monks, quoted by Benedict of Aniane in the *Concordia Regularum*, chapter 3, where we read: “Scripture testifies that every sin which a lax and undisciplined brother commits immediately returns upon the negligent elder.”]

—and since, once all the things for which these writings had been composed, goods almost contrary to the judgment of God, had been removed, only misery remained, which is without envy—you often see the man who grieves over the misfortunes of others endure their good fortune less well.

[Note: Unless there is a corruption in the word *contrariis*, “goods contrary to misery” must be supplied, so that the sense agrees with what follows. When Ratherius was expelled from the see of Liège, the goods contrary to misery—his dignity, revenues, the favor of princes, and so forth—are said to have been removed. He had written such books to recover them. These goods had brought him envy and enemies. Once deprived of them, only misery remained; from it he feared neither envy nor enemies. Thus one may partly explain how Nero’s saying, which he has introduced, fits him or his books. His books will find no enemies among those who read them, since their author, oppressed by misery, had no envious persons or enemies. He next speaks of friends, and the passage should be construed thus: “Although you, O dirges”—he means his little books—“seek the favor of all, not even our very intimate A. L. D. will deign, offended by the unworthiness of the title *Phrenesis*, even to touch or see what precious things you contain within, saying, ‘They are far too obscure’; judging otherwise that it is arrogant to criticize our writings, as though any writer, Augustine testifies, could ever be found able to speak so as to be equally understood by all.” Augustine further says that the Holy Spirit magnificently and beneficially ordered his Scriptures so as to meet hunger in clearer passages and dispel weariness in more obscure ones.]

“You, O dirges”—although you seek the favor of all, I believe that not even our very intimate A. L. D. will deign even to touch or see what precious things you contain within, offended by the unworthiness of the title and saying, “They are far too obscure,” judging otherwise that it is arrogant to criticize our writings—as though, as Augustine testifies, any writer had ever been found able to speak in such a way that he could be understood equally by everyone.

[Note: The following should be construed thus: “Although you, my little books, seek the favor of everyone, nevertheless not even A. L. D., however intimate with us, will deign to touch or see what precious things you contain within, offended by the unworthy title and saying, ‘They are far too obscure’; and by judging our work otherwise he will condemn it as arrogant, as though, according to Augustine, any writer could ever be found who was able to speak in such a way that he could be equally understood by all.”]

Augustine adds that the Holy Spirit wisely and beneficially shaped his Scriptures so that in their clearer passages he might satisfy hunger, while in their more obscure passages he might remove disgust.

Such obscurities are less hostile to those who have discerning eyes precisely because, as Boethius testifies, the more they are guardians of a secret and converse only with those worthy of it.

It can also happen—and Augustine does not fail to say that it always happens in some cases—in the book entitled *On the Morals of the Church* (Book 1, chapter 1), that many things seem absurd to the unlearned; but when they are expounded by the more learned, they appear all the more worthy of praise the more contemptible they had seemed to be, and they are received the more sweetly as open things the more difficultly they were opened when closed.

Therefore, to leave aside innumerable examples, I should like the person who judges everything else rejectable because certain things are less clear to teach me at least one reason why someone in the Gospel is said to have been loved by the Lord although he was not chosen to follow him (Mark 10:21–22), or what moved the Evangelist to record this so carefully.

[Note: Construe: “Therefore, whoever judges the rest rejectable on account of certain less-clear passages, I should like him to teach me at least one reason—leaving aside countless others—why someone in the Gospel is said to have been loved by the Lord although he was not chosen to follow him, or why the Evangelist thought it relevant to note this so carefully.”]

What, moreover, from among our own authors can be thought to contribute, besides other things, to the obscurity of this work that lies before us? It is the preface of our aforesaid Boethius to his work on arithmetic.

[Col. 0376A]

### 9

O rivalry, always eager to disparage, and, when ability is lacking, always ready to bring forward reasons at least for not attending to what is displayed, or for attending to it less effectively!

[Note: “O rivalry, always eager to disparage, and, if ability is lacking, always ready to bring forward reasons for not attending at all, or for attending less effectively, to what is shown!”]

“He burns,” he says, “by his brilliance the one who weighs down the arts placed beneath him; once extinguished, that same man will be loved.”

(Horace, Book 2, Epistle 1, verse 13.)

Let both the one who disapproves of these books and the one who produced them, both the neglecter and the reader, know that, in the matter we have undertaken, he cannot find books more useful to the unfortunate bishops of the present age. Nor are they so lacking in other arts and advantages that, if the will is present, instruction could not readily be found in them concerning matters that would be exceedingly difficult to discover elsewhere.

To which bishop would these writings not abundantly offer assistance in undertaking victory in any canonical contest against adversaries? I concede that nowhere in the world will anyone be able to say, if such books are certainly at hand, that what is needed has not been supplied—though I put this obscurely.

Let envy, which is always pretending ignorance, stop looking for a knot in a rush. Let it recognize that I have deliberately placed certain obscure things in my writings, which it will nevertheless be able to clarify immediately if it has an industrious and studious interpreter.

For, apart from the fact that ignorance of the subject matter, as in other books, often makes understanding difficult here, it is certain that the man who declares that he does not understand my dictated work proves himself wholly ignorant of construction.

[Lacuna.]

He also admits that he does not know what *climax*, *syrma*, and *parenthesis* are.

[Note: Here *climax* figuratively indicates a gradation; *syrma*, a term sometimes taken from tragic discourse, seems to signify the grandiloquent speech customary among tragedians.]

He who does not know how to observe these things in our books arrogates Latin to himself in vain, while complaining that he lacks the ability to grasp such matters.

**THE PREFACE ENDS.**

**THE BOOK CALLED *PHRENESIS* BEGINS.**

[Col. 0376C]

### 10

You, Lord, together with the revered Baldric—who is entirely free from that vice and who was not merely a supporter of your party against me but also its standard-bearer, although in a different battle-line—have been pleased to call this work *Phrenesis* and to suggest to others that it should be so called.

To you, Lord, I direct a little stream of a certain *Phrenesis*, that is, a rivulet drawn from something like the great sea of his complaints, so that it might appear to you, if you were granted to perceive it.

[Note: He addresses Rodbert, archbishop of Trier, whom he calls the standard-bearer of his own defeat, while calling Baldric the Elder, bishop of Utrecht, his fellow-standard-bearer. This is clear from no. 2 of the preface. They had called Ratherius mad, as he relates there; for this reason he gave the title *Phrenesis* to this book. Construe: “I direct to you, Lord, a little stream of a certain madness, that is, a rivulet drawn from something like the great sea of his complaints, so that it might appear to you to have grown, if you were granted to see it grow: a *Phrenesis*, I say, which it pleased you to call by that name and to suggest to others that it should be called so, together with the revered Baldric, entirely free from that vice, who was not only a supporter of your party against me but also its standard-bearer, though in a different battle-line.”]

The haste with which I had this little book sent out caused it to be unpublished, to contain some things in an incomplete form and others more crudely than the same book, once corrected, contains in its proper place.

[Note: He seems to call the book unpublished because it was not yet complete in a form deserving public circulation. Construe and explain: “That haste caused this book to be sent out unpublished, incomplete in some respects and containing certain things more crudely than the corrected book that I recommend in this preface would contain in its proper place.”]

It was sent out unfinished because, besides the fact that I myself had thought by a swift absence to escape the pursuit of my enemies—he withdrew to Mainz in order to distance himself from the rebels—a frequent rumor, although false, had recently not ceased announcing, perhaps with an omen not wholly vain, that those oppressed by your burden, or power, had been released by your death.

[Note: It had been reported that Rodbert had died, as is related in the preface, no. 5. “With an omen,” he says, “perhaps not entirely groundless,” if the omen attributed to a divining populace is true.]

The matter concerning them, however, let others more successfully correct or interpret in greater detail.

[Note: “Let others more successfully correct or interpret the matter concerning them in greater detail.”]

I have deliberately omitted the names of the persons, leaving it to your judgment to decide whether the malignity of certain people has accumulated its slander with just cause or through some envy.

For the mind conscious of the deed could not fail to perceive what kind of name you had bestowed upon him. For, in such a great and serious danger, while it is customary for some people to hurry to a heap of money, your madman chose to take refuge in books: while they rushed to arms, he rushed to bookcases; while they rushed to an abundance of friends, he rushed headlong to the judgment of the ancients.

[Note: He refers to the name “madman,” which Rodbert gave Ratherius because he seemed to be suffering from madness when, during the revolt in which his episcopate was endangered, he did not flee—as others customarily did—to money, friends, or arms, but to books and the study of the ancients. He gives the same reason for the name in nearly the same words in the preface, no. 2.]

Nor is it unjust that this should be *Phrenesis*, as you assert: it replies with words spoken by someone whom you do not wholly fail to recognize, “We cannot all do everything.”

[Note: That is: “It is not unjust that *Phrenesis* should be what you assert, since it answers with words spoken by someone whom you do not entirely fail to recognize: ‘We cannot all do everything.’”]

For he had noticed that he himself did not lack an abundance of predecessors, whose negligence he preferred to imitate—so that I may almost affirm this in the words of the comic poet Terence—rather than their clever diligence.

[Col. 0377C]

The Lord himself declares that the children of this age are wiser in their generation than the children of light. It is therefore not surprising if anyone at all ranks this as madness with you (Luke 16:8).

### 11

By the king’s clemency, through the intervention of the archbishop, who was chiefly concerned in the matter; by the election of clergy and people; by the concord of the decrees; by the examples of men of no ordinary excellence; by the agreement of the canons; by the judgment and counsel of the neighboring bishops; by the proclamation of a preacher of such great eloquence as you were, preaching so persuasively from the lofty pulpit of so splendid a church that what had been done could not be concealed from anyone; by the favor of such distinguished clergy and so great a multitude; praised by the pealing of bells accompanied by the melody of hymns; appointed, installed, and ordained bishop of the vacant church—he was utterly unable to discover why, after all these things, he had been expelled, as he himself asserted in his madness.

[Note: Construe: “The proclamation of a preacher of such great eloquence as you were,” and of one preaching so persuasively from the lofty pulpit of so splendid a church that what had been done could not be concealed from anyone. It indicates the sermon of Archbishop Rodbert, delivered in the cathedral church of Cologne on his promotion to the bishopric of Liège; in the preface, section 1, he reports similar details. While enumerating the circumstances of the common agreement, which he explains more fully in the *Deliberative Conclusion*, he declares that after all these things he cannot discover why he was expelled.]

Persuaded by his friends—indeed, by that very ordainer of his, a fact that ought then to have remained silent—trusting in justice and, as he supposed, in the authority of those who had appointed him, what would he say while imploring assistance, especially to you, whose wisdom is proclaimed throughout the whole world, as appears through a certain Gnathonic flattery, rather than through a true report? What, I say, would he say, and what would the steadfastness of the firmest charity and the charity of the strongest steadfastness have supplied, unless perhaps something had been done by word or deed against your will by the very man who am I, recounting all these things?

[Note: The construction is difficult. It may be understood as follows: “Persuaded by his friends, indeed by that same ordainer of his, Bruno—something that ought then to have remained unspoken—he trusted in the justice and authority of those who had appointed him. What would he say while demanding assistance, especially from you, whose wisdom is proclaimed throughout the world, as though by Gnathonic flattery rather than by a true account? What, I say, would he say, and what would the stability of the firmest charity and the charity of the strongest stability supply, unless perhaps something had been done by word or deed against your will by the one who am I, recounting all this? For, with a negligent yet simple mind, as often happens, he confessed that he had sinned in some offense arising from a wrongful intention. That sin could in every way be excused, so that, burned away by your cautery, your judgment of more severe vengeance might entirely erase it; thereafter he might honor you as his unique patronage and, by honoring you, never cease perpetually to enjoy the same patronage. Yet he would not mix in gratuitous matters those greater expenses which he knew you incurred in turn, especially in this affair, which entirely had to be conducted with regard to God alone.”]

He confessed that, through a negligent but nevertheless simple disposition, he had sinned in some offense of wrongful intention—an offense that your judgment could entirely excuse and, having burned it away with the cautery of harsher punishment, erase completely. Thereafter he could rightly honor you as his singular patron, and by honoring you never cease to enjoy your patronage; yet he would not mix with it gratuitous matters which he knew involved greater expense on your part, especially in this affair, which had to be conducted wholly for the sake of God alone.

For the examples of the holy Fathers submitted below and brought before your most eloquent fatherhood—not for purposes of gaining knowledge, but of recalling what is already known—plainly acknowledge that it would be superfluous to weary the ears of anyone like you, or of anyone who recognizes and preserves equity.

[Note: Construe: “The examples of the holy Fathers submitted below and presented to your most eloquent fatherhood, not for purposes of knowledge but of recognition, plainly acknowledge that it would be useless to weary the ears of anyone like you, or of anyone who recognizes and preserves what is equitable.” These examples make clear that if someone has been lawfully placed in office—having come not of himself but sent by one possessing the authority to send—and has once received, wherever and in whatever manner, the office of presiding pontifically over a church, then, although unworthy, once lawfully appointed he cannot lawfully be moved from that place, provided the protection of ecclesiastical order remains intact and the status of the one who sent him and of those who agreed to his appointment is preserved, even if ill-wishers rage as far as death; unless perhaps, and so forth.]

They make clear that anyone lawfully appointed from wherever, lawfully placed, coming not of himself but sent by one who possesses the authority to send, and having once received the office of presiding pontifically over some church in whatever manner, cannot thereafter be lawfully removed from his position, even if he was unworthy, provided the status of the sender and likewise of those who agreed to the appointment remains intact—although ill-wishers may rage even to the point of death—unless perhaps the laws of the forum prevail more strongly than the examples of the saints, or a mill has greater authority than a pontifical office.

For the administrator of a mill cannot be expelled from the provision once granted to him without a prior hearing and without the neighbors’ consent. In the case of degrading a bishop, this example requires no force. Reason, praise and blame, the consent of the people, and the prohibition of the law all apply to the parties with equal justice and advance the matter in equal measure.

### 12

In this matter, trusting that all who fear God and revere human infamy—all, I say, while setting aside every hostility, confident that everyone will perceive the same thing when a person acts for his own interest and takes counsel for his own welfare—I trusted especially that you would perceive it, since you have been granted both greater capacity for understanding the truth and a superior capacity for taking care that you attempt nothing against what everyone will perceive, taking care, as is most customary, with mouth, hand, and heart:

“The zeal of your house has consumed me” (Psalm 68:10).

I would not fail to say, “The zeal of your house has consumed me” (Psalm 68:10), and that you would ascend in opposition and set yourselves as a wall of defense for the house of Israel, so that you might stand in battle on the day of the Lord (Ezekiel 13:5), and this indeed at the waters of contradiction (Deuteronomy 33:8; Psalm 80:8), where the firmness of your devotion might be tested.

Animated beyond measure by the confidence of this hope, I judge it wholly inappropriate to weary any of you with exhortations, since I know that you are well acquainted with the most biting judgment of Pope Alexander:

“For if anyone withdraws himself from the assistance of such men, he will be judged not a priest but a schismatic.”

The following, then, are the supports for my appointment despite my unworthiness—not that I thrust myself forward voluntarily, but that I obeyed the one commanding me. I entrust these supports to be assessed by your most sacred hands, adjuring you before the Lord not to deprive any bishop who is present at the case of knowledge of these supports, but to display and proclaim them to everyone, lest any opportunity to defend me be lacking.

[Note: Construe: “These are the supports for my appointment despite my unworthiness—not that I thrust myself forward voluntarily, but that I obeyed the one commanding me. I entrust these supports to be assessed by your most sacred hands, adjuring you before the Lord not to deprive any bishop present at the case of knowledge of them, but to display them openly to all, lest any opportunity for defending me be lacking.” Here this madman—called “the frantic one,” as his opponents styled him—strives to prove that he was lawfully enthroned in a vacant church on the basis of decrees of the holy Fathers, namely Antherus, Calixtus, and Gregory, and of the examples of many saints. After inserting these decrees and examples below, he adds: “Suppose that someone, entirely unable to deny that the act was lawfully done, should wish it nevertheless to be undone by a true or false accusation. These are the patronages on which, thanks be to God, I again rely; but I do not know whether they will be of any use, for these are times,” and so forth.]

This madman, striving to prove from the decrees of the holy Fathers—namely Antherus, Calixtus, and Gregory—and from the examples of many saints that he had been lawfully enthroned in a vacant church, inserted these materials below and then added:

“Suppose that someone, entirely unable to deny that the act was lawfully done, should nevertheless wish it to be undone by the charge of some crime, whether true or false. These are the patronages on which, thanks be to God, I again rely; but I do not know whether they will be of any use. For these are times—alas for the wickedness!—that do not admit the law.”

When he had indisputably proved himself, through the sanctions of the holy Fathers, to have been installed, especially by the proclamation of your own mouth—

[Note: Rodbert, archbishop of Trier, whom he addresses in this work, had praised Ratherius at his ordination, or promotion, to the see of Liège from the pulpit of the church of Cologne, as can be understood from section 1 of the preface.]

—and when, as Pope Telesphorus says, he had surrounded himself with a wall constructed by those same Fathers, he continues:

“Your own proclamation likewise beginning—these things are, as the sacred prudence of your episcopate needs no instruction, scattered in great number throughout the fields of divine doctrine and, if necessary, can be found with the greatest ease. But we believe these things sufficient, and I would not even mention them except to one whose eyes the king of Babylon removed from King Zedekiah of Jerusalem at Riblah (Jeremiah 39:6), a place interpreted as ‘many things.’ We know from Gregory’s teaching [*On Job*, book 6, section 37] that these signify the immoderate care of this age, which, like the Stygian Phlegethon, draws those entangled in it down to the abyss—not fictitiously, but in reality. Hence it has happened to some that, though seeing, they do not see, and though hearing, they do not understand; so that what was said of those who turned their eyes away so as not to see heaven or remember the judgments of the just may rightly be applied to them (Daniel 13:9).

“We desire that such people be summoned through your diligence, so that they may not need to be warned by the psalmist’s voice in words so terrifying:

‘Understand this, you who forget God, lest he suddenly seize you, and there be no one to rescue you’ (Psalm 49:22).”

### 13

O mad frenzy! O frenzy of a prudent man, according to your judgment! It was not enough for you to lament your own miseries; you were not ashamed, in your dullness, to bewail the justly inflicted hardships of King Zedekiah, inflicted more than a thousand years ago.

But perhaps your wantonness seemed to you not entirely frenzied even in this: that, together with Gregory, you lamented many Zedekiahs of the present age, not this one alone. Hence, following his example, you continued, saying that it had miserably happened to certain people that, though seeing, they did not see, and though hearing, they did not understand.
