At the summit of these people, it seemed to you that the following could have occurred: that a man solemnly enthroned was expelled so wickedly, in defiance of the divine law, from the episcopate lawfully entrusted to him, and that he was expelled not by others but by those very men who had installed him—the man whom you had begun to lament so deeply.

[Note: Construe: “That the man who had been solemnly enthroned was expelled so wickedly, in such clear defiance of the divine law, from the episcopate lawfully entrusted to him; and that he was expelled not by others but by those same men who had installed him—the man whom you had begun to lament so deeply.”]

Yet remarkable was the hardness of the man to whom you were speaking, if indeed he possessed any quality of goodness, since he could not be softened by such words.

Rather, it is you who are astonishing, madman, for saying such things to such a man, plainly unaware that you were telling a story to that deaf man who—as our mythographer relates in the tale of the covetous and the envious—had chosen not merely to neglect his own soul where he was, but, as it seemed to you, to ruin it utterly, rather than endure, much less labor for, your restoration, according to his own judgment, most insanely.

Unless perhaps, eagerly wishing to bait a miser with proclamations of praise, you had been led by this sufficiently witty saying of Aurelius of blessed memory:

“Anyone is often called good, not because he is good, but so that he may be admonished to become good,”

following the practice of those who deliberately commend fraudulent men, so that, while they consider that trust is placed in them, they may fear being themselves branded with the infamy of fraud.

[Note: Construe: “While you were sending him as an envoy to those who had forgotten the Lord, he himself might diligently fear forgetting God’s commandments, and might realize that he, like them, could suddenly be seized and, unless he took care, could in no way be rescued by anyone.”]

While you were sending him as an envoy to those who had forgotten the Lord, he himself might diligently fear forgetting God’s commandments and realize that he, like them, could suddenly be seized, from which no one could rescue him unless he had taken care.

### 14

But it is altogether too easy to see from where he conceived such hatred against you.

[Note: Construe: “It is exceedingly easy to see from where Rodbert of Trier conceived such hatred against you” (a corruption seems to lie in the phrase concerning the “clever men”). “For it is the mark of a less capable—or inept—man to investigate hidden things. Just as they suppose that you hate the insolent loquacity of that man, so they suppose that he hated in you your loquacity rather than you yourself. And just as someone asserted that Cicero had snatched eloquence from Demosthenes lest Cicero himself be the first or the only orator, so they suppose that you contended with one another in a sufficiently windy contest, not without envy—the most just avenger of arrogance and the truest accuser of folly. For quarrels are always found among the proud. If you had truly been what one of you was said to aspire to be—eloquent—you could not in any way have disagreed with one another, because nature does not allow separation among like things. In this contest, however, he appeared to have won in every respect: after he had thrown you, vested with the mitre, from the episcopal throne you had long desired, and over which you swelled with pride, he also tried to strip you of the reverence due to that office, revered by all. For when rumor had reported that you had excommunicated someone who even disdained repentance for public sacrilege—reported it, I say, in his presence—he boldly cried out that no attention should be paid to your excommunication of an outsider [perhaps one pronounced against someone else, or against one not subject to you]. It would indeed have been astonishing that he said this if he had been aware of your character as you are aware of it yourself. Let others correct what follows, if they can, and explain it.”]

For investigating hidden matters is the work of one less competent. They suppose that, just as you hated his insolent loquacity, so he hated in you your loquacity rather than you yourself.

And just as someone asserted that Cicero had taken eloquence away from Demosthenes lest he himself be the first or the only orator, so they suppose that you contended with one another in a sufficiently windy contest, not without envy—the most just avenger of arrogance and the truest accuser of folly.

For quarrels are always found among the proud. If you had truly been what one of you was eager to be called, you could not possibly have disagreed with one another, since nature denies separation to things that are alike.

In this contest, however, he appeared to have won in every respect. After he had thrown you, vested with the mitre, from the episcopal throne you had long desired—so long desired that it could not escape his notice, and over which you swelled with pride—he also tried to strip you of the reverence due to that office, revered by all.

For when rumor had reported, in his presence, that you had excommunicated someone who even disdained repentance for public sacrilege, he boldly cried out that no attention should be paid to your excommunication of an outsider.

It would indeed have been astonishing that he said this if he had been aware of your character, just as you are aware of yourself.

But he was whitewashed on the outside, as those who looked upon him were accustomed to be deceived; inwardly he was, as I have said, a muddy tomb. His character and quality were handsome only in an attractive skin, as a certain satire has it.

For it is truly astonishing that you, so abruptly hostile to what he had seen nowhere within, dared to deliver a judgment against the one who, speaking inwardly, cited the Apostle [or, perhaps, the Psalmist] by Christ’s authority:

“You sit and speak against your brother, and against the son of your mother”—that is, the people standing around—“you place such a stumbling block” (Psalm 49:20).

And for that reason you said that he was not a bishop because he had been expelled from the episcopate, whereas, according to Aurelius, guilt is not created by punishment but by the cause, and punishment is in some sense the acquittal of the things themselves. For, as Isidore says with considerable wit, “It is not the one who is accused but the one who is justly and lawfully convicted who is guilty.”

### 15

“If your sons abandon my law,” the Lord promises David—and indeed with a strong hand—“I will visit their iniquities with a rod and their sins with blows; but I will not take away my mercy from him” (Psalm 88:31–34).

The same passage in *Malachim*, but with the singular number, says:

“If his offspring acts wickedly, I will chastise him with the rod of men and with the blows of the sons of men; but I will not take my mercy away from him, as I took it away from Saul, whom I removed from before my face” (2 Samuel 7:14).

So that you may understand how great is the difference between the ordinary institutions of the state and the sacred institutions of the Church, and how God, who himself grants honors, differs from those honors which miserable men are often able to confer—that is, where he himself permits it—or, to express this more beautifully in Augustine’s words, how the height not seized through human arrogance but bestowed by divine grace surpasses all earthly summits, which tremble with temporal instability.

[Note: Explain: “So that you may understand how great is the difference between the ordinary institutions of the state and the sacred institutions of the Church, and how God, who himself grants honors, differs from the honors which miserable men can often bestow, that is, where God himself permits it; or, to state this more elegantly in Augustine’s words, how the height not usurped through human pride but granted by divine grace surpasses all earthly summits wavering in temporal instability.”]

Let anyone judge as he wishes whether the episcopate ought to be an empty shadow and a name without honor, or whether some authority follows it, and strength follows that authority—a strength which lack of worldly substance may elevate rather than oppress.

“Sing to the Lord,” he says elsewhere, “with stretched-out trumpets”—that is, trumpets extended through the crushing of blows. “Praise the Lord, souls—or, having been corrected by blows, bless the name of the Lord together with the elect.”

[Note: That is: “Let those who have themselves been corrected by blows bless the Lord’s name together with the souls of the elect.”]

Yet it must not be passed over that, while the trumpet is being extended, the hammer is blunted, so that we may believe that the injury inflicted harms the one who inflicts it more than the one who bears it.

What did the little altars of the sons of Levi, preserved by God’s command for those who had themselves been condemned, teach?

“And I will move your lampstand from its place” (Revelation 1:20)—not utterly tear it out.

[Note: Construe: “Not to repeat innumerable matters: it was also proper to a wise man to consider what the altars of the sons of Levi, preserved by God’s command for those who had themselves been condemned, taught, and for what purpose it was said, ‘I will move your lampstand from its place; I will not utterly tear it out.’”]

It would have been the part of a wise man to consider what this meant, so that I need not repeat countless things.

But it is worthwhile to consider how witty—and, besides being witty, how entirely truthful and how fitting for you—is this saying of a certain urbane man, not altogether unknown:

[Note: It is worthwhile to consider how witty, as well as entirely truthful and especially appropriate to you, is the following saying of a certain urbane man who is not altogether unknown.]

“Here too,” he says, “an additional burden is added to our troubles: that the judgment of most people looks not to the merits of things but to the outcome of fortune, and judges only those things to be rewards which prosperity has commended. Hence it comes about that a favorable opinion is the first of all things to desert the unfortunate. I would also say that the final burden of adverse fortune is this: when some crime is attached to the wretched, they are believed to have deserved the things they endure.”

### 16

But, so that the loquacity of our little book may now hasten to return to your madman, who would not judge it to exceed every form of insanity that, although he was a bishop and had no lack of cause, he dared to excommunicate an archbishop—even though he excommunicated him by taking in advance, or seizing beforehand, words of the Lord from the Gospel?

[Note: Construe and explain: “But so that the loquacity of our little book may now hasten to return to your madman, who would not judge it to exceed every form of insanity that, although he was a bishop and had no lack of cause, he dared to excommunicate an archbishop, although he had seized beforehand—even from the Gospel—the Lord’s words by which he did so?” The extent to which these words can be said to contain excommunication, not strictly but in a broader sense, will be explained in the following note, where it will also become clear who that archbishop was.]

In the fifteenth book of this *Frenzy*, according to you—for it is called *Frenzy* according to your judgment—it is recorded that, when on the feast of the Lord’s Supper, a feast than which, in my judgment, nothing more festive can be found, you were receiving, as is customary, the offerings of women, his equally frenzied audacity caused this to be brought before you:

[Note: Although at present the preface of this *Frenzy* mentions only twelve books, it is stated below, in section 18, that there had originally been twenty, which were later reduced to twelve. Thus the fifteenth book belongs to the earlier division. Since, apart from this first book and the eleventh, the other books in which this event was described more fully have been lost, the particular circumstances that would have made the matter clearer are unknown.

The time and manner of the excommunication mentioned here are indicated. When, on the day of the Lord’s Supper, the archbishop was receiving women’s offerings, that madman—namely Ratherius—caused this Gospel passage to be brought or suggested to him, perhaps through someone else. For Ratherius, who lived at Liège, does not appear to have been present there on the day of the Lord’s Supper, when the archbishop was celebrating in his own church.

These words in some way prevented the offerer from continuing the Mass unless he had first been reconciled with his brother; the author presents this here as a kind of excommunication. Such an excommunication could be imposed by a bishop upon an archbishop. The archbishop appears to have been Rodbert of Trier, who supported Ratherius’s expulsion. Since the present book was directed to him and the author addresses him throughout, the words “you were receiving the offerings” and “caused this to be brought before you” refer to him.

The passage should be construed as follows: “For, as is recorded in the fifteenth book of this *Frenzy* according to you—that is, according to your judgment it is called *Frenzy*—when on the feast of the Lord’s Supper, than which, in my judgment, nothing more festive is found, you were receiving, as is customary, the offerings of women, that equally frenzied audacity caused this to be brought before you: ‘If you offer your gift at the altar,’ and so forth.”

The words enclosed in parentheses are extremely obscure because of our ignorance of the events, and may also be corrupt, with uncertain punctuation. In place of *nacta*, if that participle is referred to the ablative *pulsione*, perhaps *pacta* should be read, referring to an arrangement or decision concerning that expulsion on such a solemn day. *Acta* does not seem possible, for if the expulsion of Ratherius had been carried out on that day—that is, if it had actually happened—then it would not have been known merely through rumor. Moreover, Ratherius was expelled with the public force and authority by which Baldricus was elected or ordained and installed in the see; neither of these actions is appropriate to a day on which bishops conduct sacred rites in their own churches and do not assemble for elections or ordinations.

What if *nacta* is thought to refer to *fama*, as though rumor had discovered or revealed the deed? What if the words “on such a solemn day” are to be referred to “to lament”? But in a matter so thoroughly tangled and obscure, we have believed that nothing should be emended in the words beyond the authority of the manuscript, nor do we wish to assert anything certain about the meaning of this parenthesis.]

“‘If you offer your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar and go first to be reconciled with your brother; then come and offer your gift’” (Matthew 5:23–24).

Here, Lord, I am uncertain which of the two insanities I ought to marvel at more. Suppose that he was driven mad by grief: where, I ask, was your sanity? And where was the one who was present, since you were so present there, Lord, yet absent?

The estimation of the one who sent him had rightly become worthless; but the command of the one who ruled ought to have been weighed. Unworthiness prevented the petitioner from obtaining what he sought; yet the majesty, dreadful to all, compelled obedience. But perhaps the ability to do what was being requested was lacking.

“Consider me excused in replying … why, I ask, could humility not do it?”

Moreover, as though you were accustomed to the habits of a raging man, chattering so often in this manner, as though you had deliberately cultivated many forms of madness over the course of many years, the favor of your loquacity—[possibly *our* loquacity]—became so senseless that you could not perceive with intellectual hearing that terrible Gospel thunder: that the man who had been injured by you had something against you, and that because you were rightly obliged to be reconciled to him by the Lord’s command, you were able to understand this only when he explained it to you. Therefore he immediately hastened to present it to you.

[Note: The manuscript had *securi alterius queat*, which makes no sense. The correction has been introduced conjecturally on the basis of the sense. Construe: “So that another may be secure concerning his salvation, my once dearly beloved Father, the former beneficence of your rule forbids me to conceal from anyone the danger of a hidden illness, though the following maleficence continues to compel me not to offer the remedy of advice.” If anyone supplies a better emendation or construction, we shall gladly accept it.]

So that another may be secure concerning his salvation, my once most dearly beloved Father, the former beneficence of your rule forbids it to be mine to conceal from anyone the danger of a hidden illness, and yet not to offer the remedy of advice.

The Gospel embassy now brought before you teaches that I, whom you have injured—however gravely you have injured me—ought rather to be reconciled, since I am the injured party.

[Note: Construe: “The Gospel embassy now brought before you—that is, the words of the Gospel recited shortly before, ‘If you offer your gift at the altar,’ and so forth—teaches that you ought to be reconciled to me, whom you have injured, however gravely you may have injured me.”]

As you are of the most discerning mind, you can easily perceive that, if Scripture says, “Understand your neighbor from yourself” (Ecclesiasticus 31:18), the strength of the soul which rightly governs yours was not lacking—although perhaps it was lacking when I considered it true episcopacy to suggest to certain people:

“Understand this, you who forget God” (Psalm 49:22),

namely, to those who had turned their eyes away so as not to see heaven or remember the judgments of the just (Daniel 13:9).

Therefore, far be it—far be it from us—that that ancient serpent, who does not cease even now to attempt to tear from human hearts what he tore away at the beginning by his word, should continually do this, striving to make light of what he threatens.

[Note: Construe: “Far be it, far be it from us that that ancient serpent, who is still striving and does not cease to tear from human hearts what he tore away at the beginning by his word, should continually do this, attempting to make light of what he threatens.”]

### 17

On the other hand, let the fitting apostolic utterance which is read today be a persuader.

Climb, I beg you, to the tribunal of an equitable judgment against yourselves . . . Let conscience stand before the truth and deny nothing; and permit my mind to be assessed by yours.

When you find that I have been injured, and injured not lightly, but that the one who forbids—namely God—has been injured most gravely; and when, among the two with whom you can be reconciled, you find one absent, namely me, while the majesty of the other, God, is most present—then have recourse to Gregory, who gives this most salutary warning:

“We ought in mind to go to the one whom we have injured, even though he is far away, and appease him with kindness and submission.”

If you do this, and just as you have harmed me so you intend to help me, you may lawfully offer a gift to God, at least in this respect. If you neglect it, I believe that you will one day discover how difficult it is to break a threefold cord (Ecclesiastes 4:12), and what that cord was, by which the traffic in doves was once driven in confusion from God’s temple (John 2:15)—though you may discover it too late.

To prevent this from happening, I adjure and admonish you through the ministry of today’s feast. If you disdain reconciliation with me, be reconciled to God, seeking by whatever means to restore the special breach made by you—and, if it is permitted to speak truth in peace, the complete breach made by you.

Observe carefully, if you please—you are entirely able to do so—how openly the decree of Pope Antherus disturbs the judgment of your rash loquacity against me, as well as every more extended judgment of the same authority.

[Note: Construe: “Observe carefully, if you please—you can do so very well—how openly Pope Antherus’s decree overturns the judgment of your loquacity, as well as every further judgment of the same authority rashly pronounced against me. For it had been judged that Ratherius should be expelled from the see of Liège because he was the bishop of Verona, even though, having been driven from the chair of Verona, he no longer possessed it. But the decree of Antherus, which was then considered authentic, demonstrated that such a judgment against Ratherius was inequitable.”]

For, after first speaking kindly enough of my case, he said:

“To both parties—that is, both to those suffering from hunger for the word and to bishops when they are enthroned in other cities—no small mercy is shown. Those who deny this, although they may appear to possess the appearance of piety, deny its power.”

As though he were directing his attack especially against you, and as though you were standing before him, he suddenly added, with the finger of his intention almost extended toward you:

“For in such a matter I do not recognize ancestry.”

[Note: “You” refers to Rodbert, whose lineage was distinguished. He was the son of Count Theodoric and Reinildis, descended from the Frisians and Danes, and brother of Queen Mathilda, who married Henry I, king of Germany, and gave birth to King Otto.]

Yet if any of the wise men whom the storm of this age has joined to others is stained by participation in crimes, the splendor of the wise man is stained; and although he incurs communion in crimes, he nevertheless does not know how to present himself as a leader to sinners.

18. Moreover, you will find me most obedient in everything which you may wish to command, if you do not disdain to carry out fully whatever you know to be just; I say this with regard to a just matter. For when no check from any reply had restrained the license of such insolent men—for, as Chremes says, “we are all the worse”—their frenzied freedom burst into such audacity that, with the most loquacious babbling of twenty volumes, which nevertheless, with sufficiently unstable frivolity, it now attempts once more to compress into twelve, eagerly striving to fit things of equal size together, it does not cease to assail everyone, especially those whom you will be able to detect here, if you do not dislike reading. It spares no one’s dignity, no one’s standing, [Col. 0387C] so that it may rightly appear to you to be madness, a power that has no integrity as its patron, although recently there has been a report that he obliterated a very large part of those same volumes, compelled by the gentleness of a certain merciful king out of love for him; yet the madman does not cease to admit that he did this.

Whatever he had not hoped for has now indeed happened, and, suffering monstrous grief [read: “grieving”], he seems moreover to have added this: that you should be judged as though you were a spur voluntarily running onward; he seems to have exhausted the most insolent arrogance and, in order to attack anyone whatever, especially you, to have provoked his pride in some way to this extreme. For, just as Festus once thought that the Apostle had gone mad through his writings (Acts 26:24)—when you said that he was mad through his writings—you seem to have judged that same man quite differently, since it is more credible that

19. Ah! Be silent, be silent, I beg you, be silent! Now the opposite is announced, for the person is said to be absent. Stop squandering your little coins on buying skins and hiring notaries. Truly insane is your shamelessness; and when at last the frenzied tablet has been dismissed, say, like blessed Job, with a lamenting howl: “For I feared the very thing that happened” (Job 3:25). For he whom you were attacking has gone away and, alas, has departed never to return; he has also been allotted an eternal absence. [Note: The manuscript wrongly reads que. This refers to Robert, archbishop of Trier, who was reported dead when the author wrote this; for this book was composed against him.]

The clamor, alas, remains as the sound of these signs. He has died, rather than merely gone away; he has gone before, rather than merely departed. You yourself, pouring out foolish nonsense as a purveyor of trifles, were prophesying like a madman together with the people; beware, I say, lest you insult the dead. Do not weary us any longer by dictating your foolish babbling, which no one should heed. Who will read these things? Rather, coming to your senses in your hunger, say with the satirist: “For he has learned”—since the rich man supports it, as the miser complains—“only to admire, only to praise eloquent commoners”; you have pursued rumors in vain. In the end, not everyone admires and loves the same things. Please stop seeking everyone’s favor pointlessly. Do not curse the deaf, nor rail against one who is absent—otherwise commendable conduct, yet not so inhuman, considering the time and place, toward one who is hostile to you. But shout rather; cry out from the depths of your being.

Here begin verses composed by the same author.

[Note: We do not know whether the following verses were written so inaccurately and confusedly in hexameters that they might seem to have been poured forth by a madman. The sense is certainly very obscure and difficult, so that scarcely anything can be extracted from it at the end.]

20. If the diligent reader wishes to learn what our little books contain within, take them.

The author gives zeal by which, with a true champion, he may shake, overthrow, raise up, strengthen, unite,

console, revive, encourage, fashion, and adorn his companions;

you, friend, who more heavily endure the burden of Aetna.

For just as gout seizes and torments everyone,

and a hump oppressively rests upon the back, incongruously imposed by the stars,

and, like a savage beast, tears apart its mother’s ribs,

and tries to be the avenger of its dead parent,

so the people who have abjured God struggle to assail themselves

with inward civil war, with a canine tooth,

by biting one another and inflicting impious laws

upon their own head, while some madman labors, concerned to will

that what God has brought forth straight as a gift

and once fastened with firm bonds

in the times which each person established for himself and in beautiful order,

[Col. 0388D] the teacher, intoxicated with divine nectar, has placed—

they should fear the hearts enslaved to that evil god.

The fool teaches great things as small, while each person

joins the left to the right and declares the distorted straight,

the white black, the square round, the savage kind.

It pleases him to say that he has changed these things and to attack what is just;

to bless the contrary for these men, so that a Tartarean woe may carry them away,

confounding the straight thing born through the Lord’s gift,

which He once produced and joined with firm bonds

in the times in which each person, in his own place and beautiful order,

established it.

Thus honor and reverence, bestowed upon the sacred orders from heaven,

rush headlong into ruin, and thus

240 Ephraim and Manasseh, Manasseh assails Ephraim,

and together they prepare to wage war against Judah,

in a closely joined battle-line, with no triumphs dwelling among them,

forgetting the Lord, waging civil wars

against themselves, knowingly turning the scourge against themselves.

If, while my hand does not leave them untouched here,

it is thought that I have rendered great assistance to the afflicted,

by marking them as unjust with a hostile mind,

while he recites himself and proves himself more than our cause,

he will rightly be laughed at by everyone, since he himself

is more strongly inclined to madness, and madness supplies his frenzy and his care.

Therefore, may the Powerful One be present at my right hand and, in pity,

grant me willing help, so that I may be said to have avoided the brief Syrtes,

fierce Scylla, and Charybdis;

and may I quickly be able to find within the sacred, venerable treasuries of doctrine

what may benefit many equally:

may it raise these by helping them, restrain those by curbing them,

lest those who have been held back be able to complete what they wished.

But long oppressed by perverse laws,

and wearied by this great burden, may the company of priests

receive strength; may the firm wall of the Lord’s doctrine

remain unbroken, and may Telesphorus himself,

the pious pope whom he once said had built it for us,

lament that the whole company had driven away no one except one

whom it was able to break, and for whose help it is seen to have been constructed.

Therefore, let no one disdain what is ours,

for he will certainly be able to endure many things suitable to himself

and to help himself, provided that one who may care for such matters

does not fail these people.

For it is clear that this kind of people is increasing in these suns;

I beg that the merciful Lord may turn them away

and grant that those now more heavily oppressed may be relieved of their grievous burden.

[Col. 0389C] Since I now seem to be publishing especially for you,

O holy part of the men, the Lord’s portion and minister,

I prepare to give you weapons by which each of you may defend his own rights

and, with Christ as leader, be able to show himself victorious over evils,

while a treacherous band attacks him. For God Himself will soon conquer;

and steadfastness itself, victorious through what is right,

will always conquer, accompanied by its own supporters,

and will crush all hostile, harmful, and inimical enemies;

may it conquer, disturb, and mutilate them—I beg, demand, and insist.

Amen; so may it be. And may all things resound accordingly, I demand.

21. Spare Your servant [Note: That is, Robert the archbishop, who, as we have noted, was reported to have died.], God; in pity, have compassion on the redeemed,

mercifully granting this man a pious pardon with rest.

Nothing belongs to me, nothing, because I am yours; yet it is proved that I have sinned,

as one who wishes to slaughter another person’s sheep.

For he is held guilty not before the sheep but before the Lord;

the law is one and the same throughout all the earth.

You alone can grant pardon; you alone can bring healing,

if, by sparing, you wish soon to be able to do so more piously [read: “more gently”].

Therefore I earnestly ask You, God, being entreated,

that he may go free along the star-bearing ways.

May fortunate Porthmea disregard him, and may no care of one who fears

[Col. 0390A] his fate torment this man with anything worthy of it.

241 May no Lamia of Erebus touch him, nor the black marshes;

may Cerberus stand aside, and may he look down upon the Gorgon;

may he not have to swim across the Stygian lakes or see the foul

Tartarus, whom the right-hand road assists.

Nor may he encounter Chaos or Phlegethon, the dwelling places of black monsters.

Let those things be present which he might undergo or mourn as having to undergo.

Order that he not see the rocky wastelands of Cocytus,

for whom heaven was hoped to be his homeland.

Deny that the chambers of the Eumenides have grown,

and let him see the hosts of the righteous at the same time as he sees himself.

May this man not know the road descending toward the waters of Tartarean Acheron;

may heaven know him and wish to possess him.

May my misfortunes do you no harm, You who are said to have built

[Col. 0390B] prosperity for many and who bring only good things.

Many conform themselves to great things and speak of good deeds;

let them be silent about their opposites, lest harmful things prevail.

I ask only that You favor whom You will; let nothing, however great it may be,

hinder God.

All-powerful, You make it possible for the one who wishes to favor to do so,

for Your right hand makes right hands shine.

Although they may know little, surely the left hand vanishes,

as the fire-devouring north wind scatters chaff.

Then the trumpet, producing a terrible sound for those who do not expect it,

will give each person his rewards according to his merits.

“If he denies that they have escaped, say: ‘Well done; depart!’”

For this is the fate that holds many noble persons.

“Do not fear in terror,” He says, “O flock; for it pleased Me

to ennoble you on the throne of the Father’s kingdom.”

Yet blessed is that man, blessed by the lot granted to him.

“Come”: he receives; he is, he will be, and he was.

For, as his number of saints who behold all things increases,

so too his merit has always increased.

Hear this, O immense God; by this pious gift

do not wish to frustrate our hope, and count us among the righteous.

May Your mother, O kindly Christ, obtain this for us, Mary;

may the heavenly assembly ask pardon for this man;

may Peter the blessed open the heavenly gates,

and then may the saints come to meet him and bring assistance.

Thus my madness troubles you; thus, O Robert,

thus, I say, it asks that you be happy and enjoy yourself.

Again Ratherius against the envious Baldric.

[Note: He means Baldric, bishop of Utrecht, whom he called “the greater Baldric” in the title of the sixth, seventh, and eighth volumes. See the preface, no. 6.]

22. I have often considered how, with him absent and left behind, I might deal with you, Baldric, still present, in publishing the little works which I had composed against him, or especially on his behalf. For you had escaped it, because you were wholly free from that defect with which either of us was said to have labored: literary madness—relying, of course, more on money than on books, more on weapons than on armories, and more on an abundance of friends than on the judgment of the ancients.

[Note: Likewise, in the preface, no. 2, he calls this Baldric free from the defect of madness.]

[Note: In what follows, repeatedly down to the end, so many readings are corrupt that they can neither be properly understood nor safely emended. Yet the principal sense seems to be this. The author would have wished to publish these little books sooner, while Robert was alive. Some of them he had already read before many persons while Robert still lived, and had given others to read; indeed, he had almost published those which he had begun. Now, although on hearing of Robert’s death they seemed to require suppression lest he act too harshly against a dead man, he nevertheless considered prompt publication necessary when he saw that many of Robert’s followers and his own rivals survived. He wrote this when he believed Robert truly dead. Later, when he composed the preface, he discovered that the report of Robert’s death was false.]

Your misfortune appears to have been an example of God, so that you might avoid, through diligent reflection, the repentance that accompanies sudden generosity and provide for restraint through a longer discussion—for, as Flaccus writes, “a word once sent forth does not return.” Indeed, meanwhile I was gaining practice and a more certain recognition of myself. Some things which I myself would have been capable of, and which I could either attempt pointlessly or, once attempted, scarcely or not at all accomplish, I would now wish had been released by me sooner than by another, especially amid these services, by someone who understood me and by whom I might seem to have been approved—particularly after his [that is, Robert’s] death had been reported.

Although I had often read those same little books before many people, and had given them to others to read while he was still alive, so that the reputation of an adversary’s steadfast hostility, as they say, might be preserved as that of a friend—for I would not wish anyone ever to think this of me—nevertheless, after his death, I also almost published those works which I had begun while he was alive, although I had not yet completed them—I speak more boldly.

But since he survives—so, at least, I seem to have prophesied to myself—and since great phalanxes of rivals still remain, of whose reconciliation, or even cessation of hostility, I think I had no further hope, he would be unequal to himself in his reasoning unless he were equally sound. Therefore, with an exceptionally hurried effort at publication, I shall strive to make it known to the fair-minded and the unjust alike that, just as I once took care not to attack him, so now I have considered it the greatest crime to refrain from proclaiming the truth, and merely to assail any one of you after death, even in writing, with only a light curse. For, as Pliny the Younger says quite wittily, “the gratitude of evil men is as faithless as the men themselves.”

Therefore above.

[Note: This is the profession of faith which is called Ratherius’s faith in the preface, no. 6, and is assigned to the second book, whose subject is given there as follows: “There follows the little book which contains the faith of the one dictating, together with two letters.” Therefore this faith is wrongly joined to the first book of the Madness, since it belongs to the beginning of the second. Hence the closing formula which we have attached to the faith from the following manuscript—“The book called Madness is finished,” etc.—ought more properly to be placed here, where the first book of the Madness ends; and in place of “Therefore above” this title, or another similar title of the second volume indicated in the preface, ought to have been prefixed to the faith: “The faith of Ratherius, with two letters, one of which does not cease to weary the Roman See with complaints, the other the flock of fellow bishops.” But apart from the evidence of the manuscript, we wished to alter nothing, especially since the two letters indicated in the preface, one to the Roman See and the other to all the bishops, which from the entire context ought to concern the affair of the See of Liège and Ratherius’s expulsion from that see, are missing from that manuscript, as are likewise ten other volumes praised there on the same subject, as we noted in the Admonition.]

23. Having made this preliminary statement, I firmly maintain the truth of the faith, although I am equally unable to establish it. I profess that I confess and believe, together with Aurelius Augustine, the blessed and most steadfast defender and promulgator of that same faith, and with the other confessors and propagators of the same religion, the eternally inseparable and consubstantial unity of the Trinity, the Trinity of unity—that is, one God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—and the other matters which are read as inserted word for word in the profession of faith in the third book of the Praeloquia, no. 31, through the end of that book. After its final words, the following closing formula is added in the manuscript:

THE BOOK CALLED MADNESS, COMPOSED BY RATHERIUS, BISHOP, IS FINISHED.

[DIALOGUE OF CONFESSION.]

[Col. 0391]

ADMONITION ON THE EXCERPT FROM THE DIALOGUE OF CONFESSION.

1. This work now first comes to light from a manuscript of Lobbes. Ratherius mentions it twice in the Qualitatis conjectura. First, in no. 3, where the following words are read: “If what is written in the book of my Confession is not enough,” etc. And again in no. 8, from which we shall shortly quote the actual words. Sigebert also praises it among Ratherius’s works in On Illustrious Men, where he calls it the Book of Confessions.

P. Mabillon, in the second preface to the fourth century of the Benedictine order, no. 48, describes a manuscript from Gembloux in which various works, partly little books and partly fragments, concerning the sacrament of the Eucharist and the presence of Christ’s body and blood had been collected. Among these were read certain excerpts from the book of the lord Ratherius’s Confession concerning the body and blood of the Lord; these are in fact found in this work.

II. To establish its date, we observe first that Ratherius wrote this Book of Confession while he was presiding over some monastery which was not far from Liège and was subject to the bishop of Liège, as we explained more fully in the Life, § 2. Moreover, he reports that he had lost two bishoprics, namely Verona and Liège, from his possession, in no. 2.

He was excluded from the bishopric of Liège in the year 955. Therefore this Book of Confessions cannot be placed before that year. He lost the bishopric of Verona three times: twice before the year just mentioned, and the third time in the year 968. Since, however, in the Qualitatis conjectura, which was composed at Verona before he abandoned that bishopric for the third time, this Confession is cited twice, it is clear that it cannot be assigned to the period when, after abandoning the See of Verona for the third time, he withdrew to a monastery. It must therefore be placed between the year 955, when, in addition to having already lost the bishopric of Verona for the second time, he also lost that of Liège, and the year 961, at whose end he recovered the See of Verona for the third time. 245–246

Since he wrote this while he was in charge of some small abbey, a not insignificant span of time is evidently required for the events which he records as having happened to him while he was in charge of that abbey. Thus this work was written not in the earlier but in the later years during which he presided over the abbey in question, that is, in the year 960 or 961.

This later date is confirmed much more strongly by nos. 21 and 31, in which he admits that he is almost seventy years old. Since he was born around the year 896, the beginning of his seventieth year falls approximately in the year 965. But since he wrote this work before he was restored to the See of Verona for the third time—that is, before the end of the year 961—his nearly seventy years correspond more suitably to the year 960 or 961 than to earlier years.

He wrote this work partly near the end of Lent, according to no. 37, and partly during the Easter season; and he completed it shortly after the feast of Saints Philip and James, which is mentioned in no. 34.

III. In this work, which presents Ratherius’s own Confession, the principal matter to be observed is what he reports as having been said about himself by one of his own censors in the Qualitatis conjectura, no. 8:

“What more? Whoever wishes to know him [Ratherius] should make an effort to read his entire Book of Confession. For if he is such as he describes himself there, no one in the world is worse than he. But if he lies about being such, he is proved to be the greatest liar.”

These words raise the question whether everything reported in this Confession about Ratherius himself is true. Certainly, from the course and sequence of his life—he was offered to God from childhood, educated in a monastery, later professed the monastic rule at the proper age, devoted himself for a long time and very diligently to both secular and sacred studies, and finally was raised to the episcopate, where he followed a stricter discipline and endured many misfortunes—at least most of what is described in this work seems incredible.

In his epitaph, among other praises, he is credited with having been well-conducted according to the circumstances of his time. But if everything which he attributes to himself in this Confession were true, he would not have been well-conducted according to the circumstances of his time; he would have been the most ill-behaved and wicked of all times and almost all men. For there is scarcely any crime of which he does not accuse himself.

Moreover, Everaclus, bishop of Liège, who knew Ratherius intimately at the very time when this Confession was written, later testified in a letter which he sent to him at Verona that he had recognized not only his wisdom but especially his outstanding integrity and innocence. “For who among you,” he says, “is superior in wisdom, integrity, devotion to the best arts, innocence, or any other kind of praise?”

Furthermore, his contemporaries Rotgerus, himself the author of the Life of Saint Bruno, no. 34, and Fulcuinus, in Deeds of the Abbots of Lobbes, chapter 23, report that Ratherius, expelled from Verona, was promoted to the See of Liège by that same Saint Bruno, archbishop of Cologne, who had known him for a long time among his intimates, because he possessed such virtue that no one could seduce him; and because Bruno hoped that the mouths of those who spoke against bishops could be stopped if no occasion for scandal could be found in their bishop—namely, Ratherius. These praises are wholly inconsistent with the offenses listed in the Confession.

IV. What, then? This does not seem to be a true and proper Confession, but, under the name of Confession, a certain unusual form of censure, to which Ratherius’s fervent and rather bitter character gave itself so freely that he repeatedly attacked not so much others as himself.

Hence, while describing his own crimes, he attacks those of others, as is clear from the very beginning, where he touches upon the crime of the confessor, who therefore says in no. 37: “When you proposed to recount your crimes, as you claimed, you began with mine.” Similarly, after Ratherius had previously rebuked other faults of the monks, the same confessor added in no. 22: “While you spare not even yourself, you sharply gnaw at me—or rather, at all of us.”

Do not the apostrophes and invectives inserted into the dialogue, by which he sometimes attacks certain people more bitterly, even by name, show an intention foreign to the nature of confession? He is accustomed to exaggerate and magnify his own sins so that they appear most serious, although sometimes, once they are explained, they will be found either to be nothing or very slight.

Thus, when he says in no. 5 that he committed adultery “through the movements of those whom, while wandering, I had driven into adultery,” he portrayed Manasses and Milo, the invaders of the See of Verona, as adulterers. He indicates that he drove them into adultery by wandering because, exiled and wandering from that see, he had given them an opportunity. But what crime was it for him if, not voluntarily but by force, expelled from the see, he was compelled to wander?

In no. 2 he represents himself as guilty of the blinding, mutilations, murders, arsons, and other calamities of this kind which the Veronese suffered after abjuring their allegiance to King Hugh, because he seemed in some way to have shared in the revolt from Hugh.

247–248 He inserts in no. 4 a general formula of confession, of the sort that occurs elsewhere in penitential books. When penitents read these formulas, they could not thereby be said to have sinned in everything contained in them. Many examples of exaggerated crimes will be found, some of which we shall expose in the notes.

Among the many things that are plainly incredible, the most incredible is that the man who did not hesitate to exaggerate his own crimes and even to publish them in writing had, until that time, confessed them to no one except God alone, as he reports of himself in no. 10. For the present, reader, it is enough to have touched upon these matters. You will note more in the Confession itself.

[Col. 0393]

[Note: Although this work is twice called the Book of Confession in the Qualitatis conjectura, here it is called the Excerpt from the Dialogue of Confession; these titles seem to indicate that it was taken from a larger work, as do the references in nos. 19 and 22, and also the words prefixed to no. 33, “After certain things,” and likewise “After certain things.” Nevertheless, we have no doubt that the very lengthy work preserved in the monastery of Lobbes is the whole work which Ratherius actually composed, and that he gave it the title and form of an Excerpt in order to indicate that certain other matters had been omitted.]

EXCERPT FROM THE DIALOGUE OF CONFESSION OF A CERTAIN MOST WICKED MAN—WONDERFUL TO SAY, RATHERIUS, INDEED BISHOP OF VERONA, BUT A MONK OF LOBBES.

[Col. 0393A] 249 I beg and adjure you by Him who lives forever and ever: if you have begun to read this, read it all, if He Himself has granted that you do so. Since, with deadly curiosity, neglecting your own affairs, you desired so greatly to know my crimes that recently, after being persuaded to swear falsely by someone, you extorted from him one—[Note: One crime, namely, one act of perjury; hence, shortly afterward, “the perjury which you induced.”] although it is in itself sufficiently harmful, yet is clearly the least insignificant in comparison with the others, I wish to satisfy this desire of yours and report to you such deeds—so great and so unheard-of, if indeed it had been granted you to consider also their inventions [read: intentions]—and their madness concerning myself, so that I may make you burdened with my crimes, even if you had none of your own, so that in this Lent you may have something to mourn, while for nearly all the time you are free from such things.

But lest you think that even the perjury which you induced is not yours, consider Eve, I advise you, and in the serpent the devil. The serpent persuaded; Eve sinned; but the one who persuaded in no way sinned, while the one who sinned somehow earned pardon. The Jews cried, “Crucify!”; the crucifiers drank the blood of the Crucified One unto salvation.

2. But, to accomplish what I have promised, you need not seek anyone worse than I and more entangled in the vices of that same age from infancy itself. When, at the proper time, I had reached youth, I began so early and so extensively to indulge in wantonness in very different ways, and to devote myself to gentleness, jokes, and buffoonery, that, even if it would have been altogether useless for you to hear an enumeration, it would nevertheless have been utterly impossible for me to list each item.

[Note: This is a very difficult and corrupt passage, in which some words also seem to have been wrongly displaced. In order to produce a suitable sense, they must be restored to a more appropriate position; the entire period may be constructed or explained as follows: “I, most wretched in the consciousness of ambition and hostility, indeed of forgetfulness of those things which I now deservedly suffer for the faith abjured to Hugh—for he who said, ‘He who repays evil for good shall not depart from his house’ does not know how to lie, and this has plainly been fulfilled in you [read: in me]—I, I say, most wretched, declare that you ought not to wonder at what I now say, namely, how many murders, blinding, mutilations, plunderings, arsons, devastation, and depopulation occurred because of that crime, namely, the abjured allegiance, and because of the construction or reconstruction of fortifications against that same Hugh.” Here the calamities resulting from the rebellion against Hugh are indicated. As for the extent to which these crimes committed by others can be charged to Ratherius’s guilt, he explains this himself in no. 24: “For I did none of these things, nor did I order them, nor did I wish them to be done; but I committed something on account of which these things were perpetrated.” The occasion was that, when he received Arnold, duke of Bavaria, at Verona, he appeared to favor rebellion. See what we have discussed more fully in the Life, § 4.]

After I had abjured my allegiance to Hugh because of ambition and hostility, indeed because of forgetfulness of those things which I now deservedly suffer—for he who said, “He who repays evil for good shall not depart from his house” (Proverbs 17:13) does not know how to lie; and this has plainly been fulfilled in you [read: in me]—you ought not, I say, in my most wretched state of conscience, to wonder at what I now relate: how many murders, blinding, mutilations, plunderings, arsons, devastation, and depopulation occurred because of that crime, and because of the construction or reconstruction of fortifications.

Norica, Italy, Germany, and France can testify better than I can that I was, and again that I was most wretched, such as I was or could be said to have been. 251

Through my fault I separated two lawful marriages: one, as it were, by right [read: “as it were, with property”], the other merely through pitiable vanity. Let anyone who can consider how weighty this alone is; let him measure the crime and contemplate its enormity. Alas, what things were the wretched women saying! What groans, what sighs were they uttering, when one of them saw a rival sitting in a prominent place, mingling kisses owed to herself, ruling the household, arranging what was to be done, while she herself had become worthless, rejected, and clinging to ashes? The other, although farther away, heard of a wealthy rival and saw herself as poor.

“But what,” you ask, “did they say?” You ask? Perhaps what has rightly happened to you, wretched man. For you brought husbands upon two women; two bishoprics lost their man—[Note: Ratherius means that he was first deprived of the bishopric of Verona and then of that of Liège.] and may nothing more disastrous happen to you on that account!

3. As for the crime involving Warnerius, once brother of the duke Cuno [Note: Cuno, or Cono, also called Conrad, married Luitgard, the daughter of Otto, and died in the year 955. He was duke of Lotharingia. The Continuator of Regino, under the year 943, likewise calls him the son of Werinber. His brother Warnerius may perhaps be the man who is called a nobleman in the Life of Saint John of Gorze, no. 13, and who held power in Lotharingia at this time; for the same saint, before putting on the monastic habit, joined himself to him in the matter of the church of Saint Lawrence on the border of Toul—Toul being a city of Lotharingia—and devoted himself very familiarly to its affairs in the name of the Lord. Ratherius calls Cuno a former duke because, when he wrote this, Cuno had already died.] which also, in my most unhappy state, befell me, it is stated in the Psalm: “You assigned your portion with adulterers” (Psalm 49:18).

Do not ask me about the places entrusted to my care, their resources squandered and their souls neglected; no, do not ask me. Look only at this and draw an inference from it. But since memory fails while the miserable abundance of things to be said is overwhelming, let this summary suffice for you, I beg: it will report nothing except what is proper to me, although it is a collection of another’s matters and only partly my own.

CONFESSION OF THE SAME MAN

[Note: Compare what we observed in the preceding Admonition concerning the crimes listed in this Confession.]

[Col. 0397A]

4. For I confess to the Lord God Almighty, to all His saints, and to you, whoever you may be, priest of God, who will read this, all my sins, whatever I have committed from the beginning of my life up to this most wretched hour, knowingly or unknowingly, willingly or under compulsion, awake or asleep, in thought, word, and deed, in sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch; especially in pride, the mother of all vices; likewise in hatred and murder, 252 in detraction, in tripping up some brother, in perjury, in false testimony, in theft, in various fornications, in adultery, in robbery, in fraud, in various impurities and most shameful pollutions, in drunkenness and gluttony, in every kind of lust, in vainglory, [Col. 0397B] in sloth, in sadness, in avarice, in quarrelling, in strife, in hostility, in envy, in discord, in desire, in ambition, in hypocrisy, in cowardice, in idleness, in laziness, in drowsiness, in talkativeness, in laughter, and in mockery of others.

5. Furthermore, I, a sinner, sinned because I did not observe the Lents and other prescribed fasts, nor fast as I ought. I violated, alas for the crime, the feasts of the saints and the Lord’s days, and did not celebrate them with the honor due, as I ought. I also repeatedly and most seriously sinned by violating their Parasceve in person, as a most wretched violator.

It must also be added that, if by persuading you to commit the perjury already mentioned you became a perjurer, then, just as Saul guarded the garments of all those whose hands stoned Stephen, so I, while sleeping or eating, while performing Mass or Matins or carrying out anything else whatever, [Col. 0397C] committed adultery through the movements of those whom, while wandering, I had driven into adultery.

[Note: Perhaps one should read “I perpetrated.” He commonly calls the invasion of another’s see “adultery,” just as he calls the invaders “adulterers.” Here he seems to be noting first Manasses and then Milo, invaders of the See of Verona, to whom, having been expelled from that see and wandering in a certain sense, he gave an opportunity by wandering. He turns this into a crime against himself with great exaggeration, as though he too had committed adultery by wandering—that is, by traveling elsewhere—through the movements of those whom, while wandering, he had driven into adultery; just as the man who persuaded another to commit the perjury already mentioned above, in no. 1, became a perjurer, and just as Saul stoned Stephen with the hands of all those whose garments he guarded.

Just as here, by dwelling on the allegory of adultery, he indicates not adultery in its proper sense but the invasion of a bishopric, so, when he soon says that he was born from a prostitute and became the godfather of a certain man who had abandoned his most noble wife for a prostitute, perhaps he is likewise indicating something allegorically: that someone, abandoning a most noble bishopric, transferred to another church, and regarded that transfer as prostitution because it was contrary to the canons. Hence, when he calls himself an “exmanzer” and a godfather, no one should suppose that a true exmanzer, or one truly born from a prostitute, or a true godfather is being indicated.]

I also became, wretched man that I am, an exmanzer—that is, one born from a prostitute (Deuteronomy 23:2)—and the godfather of a certain man who had abandoned his most noble and highly distinguished wife for a prostitute.

6. I confess also to the Lord God Almighty that, defiled by these and by all the more numerous crimes of pleasure, darkened by every kind of pollution, always without any compunction in my stony heart, always without any sincerity of mind, I received—I confess—the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood unworthily, always without unleavened bread, always without wild lettuces, with the leaven of malice and wickedness; ungirt, without sandals and staff, sluggish and not hastening toward the homeland of the eternal promise; most wretchedly receiving in judgment—I grieve to say, my own judgment—the Paschal Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world, guilty of that same body and blood of the Lord, eating it and rashly presuming to do what was forbidden; and, when many had many offerings before the altar, and you, Lord, especially, had them, offering them most shamelessly against the Lord’s prohibition [the verb “I sinned” is understood]; in exhortations and malicious flatteries, in ignorance, negligence, underhanded dealings, in giving and receiving gifts; in practicing usury I do not recognize myself as equally culpable, yet I do not deny it. For I confess and regret that I was more prodigal—a trait less appropriate to a usurer.

[Note: That is, also offering them most shamelessly against the Lord’s prohibition, when many—and especially you, Lord (he means the priest to whom he directs this confession)—had many gifts, or offerings, before the altar.]

7. I sinned in withholding the alms of the poor; in the reproachfulness and harshness of my answers; in unworthy hospitality and reception of the poor; and because I did not love or honor my parents and relatives as I ought, and often loved them irrationally, indeed more than I ought; and in afflicting my household or those entrusted to me as subjects. I did not visit or serve the sick and those in distress. I neither buried the dead nor had them buried as I should have done; and I did not clothe the poor, nor refresh the hungry and thirsty as I ought. I did not honor or love my elders and teachers, or my rulers, friends, and benefactors, with the love due to them; nor did I observe their possessions, interests, counsels, and commands as I ought.

8. I, a sinner, sinned in kisses and seductive embraces, touching and caressing wickedly; and, standing or sitting in church, where the sacred readings or divine offices are performed, I occupied myself with idle stories or wicked thoughts. I did not think about what I ought, but rather about what I ought not, and I did not lend my ears to holy things. I also sinned by looking unjustly and wantonly, and by recalling—what is worse even for men—the sexual intercourse of animals and beasts, and certain other obscene things.

9. In addition to these things I sinned while playing, riding, walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, and in all the other vices by which human frailty can sin against God. I confess myself guilty before the Lord God Almighty, before all his saints, and before you, whoever and wherever you may be, priest of God.

10. Having seen the endless number of these things, you perhaps say: “You demand the impossible. Have you ever confessed these things to anyone?” “No,” I reply, “except to him who, even if I did not confess, could not fail to know them. For I served the lust of my simulation with such art—and, wretched man that I am, still do so—that before you I have found no one who could detect me so thoroughly, that is, so plausibly. Only those who favored me in these matters knew them with me; and although I was most filthy—and I do not deny, sorrowfully, that I am still so—I was thought, said, and, what is worse, gladly said to be most chaste by many, deceived in my misery by that hypocritical saying which many habitually use deceitfully: ‘Though not chastely, yet cautiously.’”

[Col. 0399B] But the reason why I confessed to no one was not uniform. One reason was that others might not become worse through my example; another, that others might not grow proud by comparing themselves with me and with themselves, and that both parties might not perish, as it were, from the stench of my corpse. The chief reason, however, was that my criminality should not make me contemptible. A third reason, more serious—indeed the most serious of all—was my fear that my patron might say to me what the law orders to be said to fugitives: “Return and be reconciled to your lord.” For just as a physician’s treatment does not benefit a wounded man if the iron is still in him, so your confession and repentance do not benefit you.

11. For when I was still a little boy, a certain freeborn man came and, holding me at a certain altar of Saint Peter and Paul with bread and wine, [supply: “offered me to God”] and to Saint Peter as a holocaust, [lacuna] by the law, as it were, of a Nazirite, [lacuna] to serve immutably [lacuna] in order to confirm the covenant forever. But when I myself had taken up the pen, at a mature and legally appropriate age, I wrote in this manner and placed the written document upon the altar, not upon any other altar but that very one:

“I, Rather, promise my stability, the conversion of my morals, and obedience according to the rule of Saint Benedict, before God and his saints.”

[Note: Parents, when they offered their children to a monastery in childhood, swore that they were handing their son over to God in such a way that from that day onward it would not be lawful for him to shake his neck free from beneath the yoke of the rule, as is found in the already published forms for such offerings.]

[Note: The sons themselves voluntarily confirmed the offering made by their parents when they reached a suitable age, as may be gathered from the Council of Aachen, canon 36. Hence, below, in section 23, another monk is said to have been lawfully handed over and permanently bound to service by his own hand and profession.]

Thus my innumerable offenses—ineffably grievous, though those that have been written down are already grievous enough—could not be set down in this confession. Nor should the condemnable crime of a certain little prostitute have been left unmentioned, since it concerns you greatly: she killed her own son in two ways, out of fear of you and of the death of the man who, because of your old-womanish arrogance, suffered a fatal fall beneath the mill wheel. Remember also the spectacle you witnessed concerning those who were falling and those who compelled others to fall. And do not forget the reason why those three lost their eyes; yet, in comparison with this single matter—provided this one thing is not omitted—it was exceedingly light.

[Note: The parents, when offering their children to the monastery in childhood, swore that they were handing over their son to God in such a way that from that day onward it would not be lawful for him to withdraw his neck from beneath the yoke of the rule, as is related in the published forms for such offerings.]

[Note: On the offering of children in monasteries, see Mabillon’s first preface to the fourth century of the Order of Saint Benedict, no. 53. The freeborn man who offered Rather to God is to be understood as his father, or another person exercising paternal authority over him; for parents, or others to whom their authority had passed, offered children to God in monasteries. *Ingenuus* means “freeborn”; the designation also applies to nobles. Thus, in the Lombard laws, book I, title 9, law 4, concerning a freeborn or free woman, it is written: “Let her be appraised as a free woman according to her nobility.” Similar words are found in title 16, law 3. We have proved Rather’s lineage to have been noble in the *Life*, § I, no. 3.]

[Note: The title “of Saints Peter and Paul” indicates the church of the Lobbes monastery, which Fulcard, its abbot, records in his letter to Emperor Henry as dedicated under the title of the apostles, Blessed Peter and Paul (Acher’s *Spicilegium*, vol. II, p. 747), and before him Fulcuin in *The Deeds of the Abbots of Lobbes*, chapter IV. Observe, however, that although Rather first mentions Saints Peter and Paul together, he later introduces only Peter’s name, when he says that he was offered to God and Saint Peter. That the mention of Saint Peter alone was more customary is also clear from the cited letter of Fulcard: at its beginning he indeed asserts that the Lobbes church was dedicated under the title of the apostles Blessed Peter and Paul, but afterward he writes only “the village of Saint Peter” and “the altar of Saint Peter.”]

“What one thing?” you ask.

“Unconvertibility concerning this matter,” I reply. For if, reconciled, I could escape from this one thing alone—which is apostasy, that is, denial of God—as a fugitive from my lord, and could fruitfully confess [lacuna] repentance and hope to obtain pardon for myself from others [lacuna]. But if, concerning this one matter alone, I should seek counsel [lacuna], hoping for pardon for myself [lacuna], it seems entirely to be given [lacuna] by ingenuity. [lacuna] But what counsel?” you ask. [lacuna] of those things, that is, what concerns everything [lacuna] rather that Scripture: “He who conceals his crimes will not prosper” (Prov. 28:13).

[Note: This work, entitled *The Confessional Dialogue*, here presents the priest—or another person speaking with Rather—as speaking in dialogue form. Likewise, afterward, sometimes Rather speaks and sometimes the priest.]

12. “And you,” you say, “do not conceal them, since you confess them even to me, indeed to friends and enemies, and even in writing.”

“I do confess them,” I reply, “I do; but I beg you, do not deceive me. Let us rather hear Scripture together: ‘But he who confesses’—you hear that?—”

“Do not hurry,” I say; “wait and see what follows: ‘and abandons them.’ Let us do this both with many things and with one thing, but especially with this one, and let us hear joyfully: ‘will obtain mercy.’ This was always, this had always been, the reason why I confessed none of those crimes: because I had not yet at all resolved to abandon this one. To abandon the others was readily possible, as I have already done with a few—if only not uselessly, if only perseveringly. But in this one, the vanity of the world had hardened me; now, however, a kind of necessity arising from impossibility has intervened.

May God’s compassion break these chains; otherwise I shall not offer him the sacrifice of praise (Ps. 115:17). Hear in the Book of Psalms what the sacrifice of praise is: ‘Let us anticipate his face in confession’ (Ps. 94:2). But what does confession profit unless abandonment of the things you confess follows? What does a fugitive’s satisfaction, or his desire to return, profit if the possibility of returning to the Lord does not follow—if he does not deny the return that is nevertheless not hidden from God?

Let whoever wishes go; let him console me—or rather deceive me—with empty words, by which the wrath of God comes upon the children of unbelief (Eph. 5:6), that is, of the devil, who is therefore called ‘unbelief’ because by making the wretched trust in vanity now, he causes them utterly to despair of salvation at their final hour. Let whoever wishes now persuade me not to abandon what I have confessed, and yet to hope for pardon by confessing throughout every Lent, or whenever fear of death presses. He may advise this, but he will never persuade me—believe me.

“But why, then, have you confessed?” you ask.

“For two reasons,” I reply. “For although I have already abandoned certain many things out of necessity and a few others by choice, I now seem to be beginning to compel myself in some way; for I feel disgust at a small portion of my former way of life. And may God grant that I now wish to abandon this one thing, without which I abandoned the others uselessly; for I find myself wretched and bound, unable to do so.

Since these matters are so numerous, so countless, and so far from negligible, I would forget them under the accumulating mass of similar things, and, with the devil supplying the meal, I would not happen to remember that I had once written these things down, nor would I recall and be ashamed that I had wished to abandon them to God but had not fulfilled that wish. For you could have learned how prone the human race is to all these things, if you too had not most wretchedly forgotten yourself.

Since I cannot at least see with my eyes the sins that I ought constantly to consider in my mind, it seems to me exceedingly useful either that another person, seeing me, may look back upon himself in me and recognize and correct his own actions from mine.”

13. “And when you felt yourself to be such a person,” you ask, “how did you dare, in his presence, to celebrate Masses or perform such acts, when he said to the sinner: ‘Why do you recount my statutes?’” (Ps. 49:16.)

“I confess it, I confess it. Some do this with greater confidence the more strongly they feel themselves to be sinners. For a part of not being a sinner is humbly to recognize oneself as a sinner. The judgments of God are indeed a great abyss (Ps. 35:7), and within his foreknowledge—or, more safely, his knowledge—it is already what will undoubtedly come to pass.

“Does that have any force?” you ask.

“Very much, I think,” I reply. “But would that it harmed only me, and that it might truly be said of no others at all. The sacraments of God belong neither to this person nor to that, neither to the righteous nor to the sinner, but to him of whom it is said: ‘He upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining upon him is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit’ (John 1:33).

“The only requirement is that, if you are righteous, you should be as though you did not know yourself to be what you are; and, if you are a sinner, that you should grieve to be what you are. Let each hear the Psalmist admonishing: ‘Sing praises wisely’ (Ps. 46:8).

“Why?” you ask.

“Because it is not just anyone to whom you sing, but God, the King of all the earth. And elsewhere he says to the Lord: ‘You will destroy all who speak falsehood’ (Ps. 5:7). Another passage says: ‘Cursed is he who does the work of the Lord negligently’ (Jer. 48:10). If he who acts negligently is cursed, what of one who acts falsely?”

14. Concerning receiving or not receiving the Eucharist, if you perhaps raise a scruple or, as I think, an accusation against me, because what was read yesterday in the Gospel must be compared with what will likewise be read in the Apostle on the fifth day of the week, know this warning:

“Unless,” he says, “you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood” (John 6:54)—that is, bread and wine—“receiving the true blood by nature, and not figuratively, through the incomprehensible operation of the Holy Spirit and the indwelling of divinity, you will have life in yourselves” (ibid.), so that, if [lacuna], but the death of the soul, which certainly [lacuna] Gehenna [lacuna].

“Eat, then,” I tell you, “so that you may not lose life.”

[Note: Do not infer from this corrupt passage that Rather believed bread and wine to be received in the sacrament of the Eucharist according to their natural substance, rather than Christ’s body and blood. Rather defends Catholic teaching on Christ’s real presence in the same sacrament so openly in Letter I to Patricius that he teaches that only the color and taste of bread and wine remain, while the true body and blood of Christ are to be believed to be present in the Eucharist really, not figuratively. The following statements confirm the same doctrine: he declares that Christ enters the person to whom “The body of the Lord” is said in the same flesh which he assumed, in which he suffered much, was crucified, died, was buried, and rose again; and later he writes, “It is God who is received, God indeed, but as then hidden in flesh, so now, most truly, in bread changed into flesh,” thereby plainly indicating transubstantiation. To make the present severely corrupt text accord with this doctrine, it seems that it should be read: “receiving the true blood according to nature, and not figuratively.” A little later the copy transmitted to us read *Sacrificamini*; we have restored *Sanctificamini*. For Rather likewise cites this same precept of the Law in the Letter to Patricius: “Sanctify yourselves,” he says repeatedly.]

“What life?” you ask.

“God, of course; for he himself says: ‘I am life’ (John 14:6), namely, of souls.”

“I do so,” you say, “and he himself does so.”

“Very well,” I reply. “But hear him through the Law: ‘You shall pursue what is just, what is just’ (Deut. 16:20).”

“How?” you ask.

“I shall tell you. You shall eat him—that is, the lamb—in this manner. You shall gird your loins—that is, if you wish to eat, you shall live chastely. You shall have sandals on your feet—that is, you shall surround the steps of your works with the examples of those who mortified their bodies in order to give life to their souls. You shall hold staffs of governance and reason in your hands of action. And you shall eat hastily (Exod. 12:11) toward the glory of the heavenly solemnity—that is, you shall not seek the reward of a good work here, but run with the desire of your heart to where it is eternal. Eat in this way, and you will have life in yourself.

“Otherwise hear the Apostle: ‘He who eats the Lord’s body and drinks his blood unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself’ (1 Cor. 11:29).”

“How is it judgment,” you ask, “if it is flesh and blood?”

“Flesh and blood,” I reply, “for the worthy; judgment for the unworthy.”

“Who is worthy?” you ask.

“You have heard it from the Apostle. I answer: he who eats as he himself commands. For he speaks of the present [lacuna], not of one who once was barefoot [lacuna], who carried no staff [lacuna], who preferred to hasten into the mire of crimes [lacuna] and had eaten judgment upon himself [lacuna].

“If these things have been corrected, or if one remains in the effort to correct them, yet does not eat, he will not, I think, have life. This, I believe, is what the Apostle next commands: ‘Let a person examine himself’ (1 Cor. 11:28), that is, let him investigate what disposition he is in. If it is a disposition to sin, let him abandon it; if to amend, let him eat with trembling.

“Let no one, however, put second the passage in Kings: ‘If the young men are clean from yesterday and the day before, especially from women’ (1 Sam. 21:4), when the matter concerned the bread of the Presence; and what is heard so frequently in the Law: ‘Sanctify yourselves,’ that is, abstain from intercourse.

“The examination which the Apostle commands consists, I think, chiefly in cleansing the conscience from criminal acts, in expelling envy, and in correcting hatred and injury toward one’s brother, lust, or any incestuous conduct [‘to be corrected’ is understood]. And what you ought most urgently to have remembered, most wretched man, is that the Apostle—who knew how to distinguish the most sacred food from other foods—granted the others only for the body’s use, but this one for the salvation of body and soul; and that it must not even be handled with the haste or wantonness with which the other food is handled, much less consumed.”

15. [Note: More recent heterodox writers who attacked the Catholic dogma of Christ’s real presence in the Eucharist represented Paschasius Radbertus as an innovator. In his book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord* he expounded the same dogma more fully; and, because certain expressions of his seemed novel to some contemporaries who otherwise agreed with Catholic doctrine—expressions by which, in chapter I, no. 2, he taught that Christ’s flesh in the Eucharist is altogether no other than that born of Mary, which suffered on the cross and rose from the tomb—these same heretics advanced them as patrons of their error. Eminent writers have abundantly refuted this effort, showing that the disagreement between Paschasius and other Catholic men of his own or a later age lay not in doctrine but in what they mistakenly regarded as novelty of expression. See, among others, Mabillon, second preface to the fourth century of the Benedictine Order, chapter I, § 4. It is especially remarkable that the same heretics who attacked Paschasius also counted Rather among his opponents, although this passage makes clear that he used the same expressions.]

Nor should the words “the Lord’s body” be heard casually; rather, one must consider what is said, concerning whom, and to whom.

“What?”

“The same body of the Lord.”

“Of which Lord?”

“If you say ‘of that Lord,’ then certainly of the one who assumed flesh for you, suffered many things in it for you, was crucified, died, and was buried, rose again, and carried it up into heaven; and now he enters you, to whom this is said.

“See how you have cleansed and adorned the dwelling of so great a guest. If it pleases him, he approves and blesses it; if it displeases him, because he rejects it, what follows is something greatly to be feared: he may even curse it, unless the swiftest confession and repentance avert this through his mercy, which may he mercifully grant you.

“To whom?” you ask.

“That you may see for yourself.
