For if you are the one who fulfills this—or rather, the things that have been commanded, namely, ‘You shall gird your loins, you shall have sandals on your feet, holding staffs in your hands, and you shall eat hastily’ (Exod. 12:11), that is, not saying ‘tomorrow, tomorrow’—then you may rejoice in the great art of the Master, that is, not in yourself but in the Lord. Otherwise it is greatly to be feared that the Gospel saying may apply: ‘And when he had dipped the morsel, he gave it to Judas Iscariot, the son of Simon’ (John 13:26). See, then, lest by imitating him you yourself become he.

“Therefore, lest we be deceived, or deceive ourselves, it is God who is received—God indeed, but just as then hidden in the flesh, so now truly changed into flesh in the bread. Hence, more explicitly in Greek, it is said to God: ‘Give us today our consubstantiated bread’; that is, through the invocation of yourself and through the entry of yourself, this is brought about ineffably, yet not unbelievably. For this is to discern the Lord’s body: to distinguish it from all other bodily foods, and to recognize that in dignity and divinity it surpasses everything that can be seen or exist.

“Yet, with God’s help, one must take the greatest care lest a person who is entirely dead dare profane such mysteries—that is, one who clearly possesses no love. ‘He who does not love remains in death’ (1 John 3:14). Therefore, if you perceive that you possess no love at all either toward God or toward your neighbor, fear to profane such holy mysteries; and the less love you perceive in yourself, the more fearfully, I say, should you approach.

“Nor should the return be considered less carefully than the approach, since receiving the Lord is no less a grace than having him with oneself. ‘After the morsel,’ he says, ‘Satan entered into him’ (John 13:27). And concerning the manna and the foods given from heaven, which signify the same thing: ‘While the food was still in their mouths,’ he says, ‘the wrath of God rose against them’ (Ps. 77:30).

“Therefore the dwelling of the heart must be cleansed before reception and guarded after reception. Notice also that the Spirit is not merely said to descend upon the Lord, but to remain (John 1:33), so that you may understand that with others it is not so: it comes into some through grace and departs through offense.

“What follows from that?” you ask.

“Fear and consolation,” I reply. “Fear, if by our wicked ways we grieve the Holy Spirit and drive him from us; for we must fear that he may depart irrevocably. Consolation, because through our satisfaction he can be recalled.

“We may also infer the following: if, in examination [or, according to another reading, ‘confirmation’] and consecration, the Holy Spirit is given to someone through a true invocation not corrupted by scribal faults, and is afterward driven out again by his evil acts, he has not so entirely abandoned his dwelling that, once appeased, he cannot revisit it. Therefore, having laid aside despairing fear, one ought confidently to hope for his return and recall him with continual prayers, especially since he himself has promised: ‘Turn to me, and I will turn to you’ (Mal. 3:7). ‘Do not kill us,’ it says, ‘for we have hidden treasures in the field’; and he did not kill them (Jer. 41:8). The hidden treasure in the field is hope in repentance. As for the rest, inquire where I took this.”

16. “Why do you recount my statutes?” he says (Ps. 49:16).

“I answer,” if the reply may be fitting: “Because your mercy is better than lives; my lips shall praise you” (Ps. 62:4). For after the severity of justice, consolation from piety follows, most piously proclaimed in the same psalm: “He who sacrifices a sacrifice of praise honors me, and there is the way by which I shall show him the salvation of God” (Ps. 49:23). Yet this sacrifice is more a matter of deed than of voice, though it is also a matter of voice.

“To know why, or to whom, he forbids the recounting of his statutes, if what follows is not sufficient, hear what was said earlier: ‘Sacrifice to God a sacrifice of praise’ (ibid., 14).”

“Am I forbidden?” you ask.

“You are forbidden,” I reply, “you are forbidden if you neglect to do what follows: ‘And fulfill your vows to the Most High’ (ibid.).”

“If you happen to have forgotten what your vows are, Christian, and ask, remember what you promised God in baptism. And if you ask, monk, what you later also vowed, I remind you to recall it and fulfill it. The promise of the Creator says: ‘Call upon me in the day of tribulation, and I will deliver you, and you will glorify me’ (ibid., 15).”

17. “Why are you sad, my soul?”

“Hear from where you may be consoled: ‘Hope in God.’”

“Why?”

“Because ‘I will still confess him’ (Ps. 41:6): I still live, breathe, and carry myself on my own feet; it is still the day of salvation; it is still the acceptable time (2 Cor. 6:2).

“Again you say: ‘You flatter yourself too much.’

[Note: We have supplied the particle “not,” required by the sense of the context.]

“Let us not ignore, as Jerome says, repentance, lest we sin easily.”

“Let us not sin,” I say. “What more is there to sin? Sin has been committed beyond measure. This is a plank after shipwreck, not a solid ship. If we cease sinning, we can indeed be brought back to the harbor of salvation from which, through negligence, we have drifted.

“But, if I dare presume something, earthly things often teach us what we ought to hope for from heavenly things. For, as the Apostle says, ‘His invisible attributes are understood through the things that have been made’ (Rom. 1:20).

“If a fugitive is captured by his lord against his own will, what can he hope for? There is no doubt that he must receive the punishment he deserves. But if he returns of his own accord, what then? Mercy, certainly; otherwise the fault of cruelty could be inferred against the lord, since he would not have been able to endure the fugitive’s flight.

“Yet this mercy is justly and firmly strengthened if, secure in his return and pardon, he does not begin to grow proud or become sluggish in his service, but, always reflecting upon the crime of his flight, strives with the greatest humility to continue day and night, so that he may both make compensation for the service neglected during his flight and add something by which he may receive the merit of a just reward.”

18. “Do you think,” you say, “that you have yet reached that servant’s degree?”

“I would think so,” I reply, “if I had returned to the purpose of my profession. What, then, now?”

“It seems to me,” I reply, “but as though through darkness with a doubtful light, that I may correspond to the servant who, having fallen into flight and remained absent from his lord for a long time, is at last compelled by fear of his threatening lord to send envoys in the hope of obtaining some remedy of mercy—lest he be suddenly captured while unaware and handed over either to the gallows or to punishments.”

“Who are your envoys?” you ask.

“If I make any effort,” I reply—“if only I were making an effort in God’s service. And, if nothing else, at least a spoken desire, speaking with the Lord, and, would that it might be that desire—or the desire of the others who must be supplicatively invoked for this purpose. For it is written in the psalm: ‘The Lord has heard the desire of the poor’ (Ps. 9:17), as though he were saying: ‘The Lord knows very well the desire of his fugitive.’

“Hear also something resembling the preparation for a journey: ‘Your ear has heard the preparations of their heart’ (ibid.). Does it not seem to you that it is a kind of embassy of a fugitive seeking to escape from a foreign lord, when you hear him crying from the depths: ‘Deliver me from the hand of the sinner’ (Ps. 70:4)? For this man wishes to escape, but cannot unless his legitimate lord helps him—or rather, rescues him.

“Can the one who cries, ‘My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready’ (Ps. 56:8), also be understood to be preparing his flight, provided that he cries this truthfully? For just as every tyrannical and unjust possessor prevents a fugitive from returning to his lord and ensnares him so that he cannot obtain the opportunity to escape, so the devil also—as I have now experienced—introduces various obstacles, so that the fugitive either does not wish to return, cannot return, despairs of returning, or is even ashamed to return; or, what is much worse, makes him so detestable to his own lord that the lord prefers to snatch him away suddenly and hand him over to eternal punishments rather than reconcile him to his grace through repentance.

“This happens especially when, through pride, he instills in him security concerning the same embassy of prayers, desire, or some great or small thing; or an exaltation over good works; or, certainly, sluggishness or laziness without any security. For there are some, such as I still am, who, relaxed through a certain sloth, neglect themselves entirely by neglecting their free will—which God certainly both requires and leaves free—and, as though committing themselves to God’s mercy, choose to loosen the reins of idleness: yawning even in church, standing drowsily, wandering about everywhere not only in body but also in mind, sitting or lying down, rather than sending some embassy to God’s mercy through a good work, reading, prayer, or at least meditation on some good thing, so that he may at some time deign to rescue them more fully from the devil’s snares.”

19. Again, after some things:

“This seems to me the case; you may think what pleases you. Just as no one can promote himself by his own power to any rank in the Church, so no one can wholly depose himself, even if he wishes, whatever manner or order of life he has entered or followed (see the *Conjecture*, section 6). It seems that, by the same necessity by which he is compelled to maintain his order, he is also compelled—although unworthy—to perform the duties belonging to that order, unless you think otherwise.”

“I would judge nothing to be more certain,” you say, “unless I happened to read in the Council of Neocaesarea, canon 9, that if a bishop, priest, or deacon confesses that he has sinned bodily, he should not consecrate the offerings, but should remain in the other offices for the sake of good zeal. I do not dare oppose a holy council, especially since I also hear the Lord judging the same matter through the Law: ‘The priest who has a blemish shall not offer the breads to the Lord, nor approach his ministry’ (Lev. 21:17–18).

“But why does no one accuse himself of such things in a council? If he fears exercising the duties appropriate to his order, let him also be deposed.”

“Because that is exceedingly harsh,” I reply. “For that reason you find no one who does it.”

“Suppose someone did it—not being conscious today of what he was doing—because he would fear that the same objection once brought against the Pharisees concerning a woman caught in adultery might be raised against him. Yet the incomparable Gregory is read to have spared such men so greatly that he received into favor Maximus, who, contrary to his prohibition, had invaded the episcopate of the city of Salona with military force over Honoratus, whom the people had elected, and through the heresy of simony as well, and who for seven years had remained a despiser and rebel against Gregory’s excommunication; Gregory allowed him to remain a bishop because, just as it is fitting to be strict toward those who persist in guilt, so it is fitting for us to be gracious toward those who repent and grant them pardon.”

[Note: The copy read *non decet* (“it is not fitting”). The correction was persuaded less by the sense than by the reading of Saint Gregory’s own letter, book 9, letter 81, from which Rather extracted this passage.]

“That is a grave condition.”

“As far as the soul is concerned,” you say, “could not this be said of such a person: ‘He has cast his foot into a net, and walks in its meshes’ (Job 18:8)? Yet is there any remedy?”

“None,” I reply; “none except God’s mercy alone. For he has cast it in—he has cast it in especially if he has also walked in it.

“But what shall we do? Shall we despair of one crying from the depths? Where then is the merciful omnipotence of the one who swears, ‘I do not desire the death of the sinner’ (Ezek. 33:11), and who makes human beings from stones? (Matt. 3:9.) Will he not similarly be able to make a guardian from a thief, a guardian from a robber, a shepherd from a hireling, a sheep from a wolf, a living man from a dead one, one who gives off the sweetest fragrance from one who stinks, one who is loosed from one who is bound, one who departs from one who is immobile? It would take too long to recount how many times he has accomplished this. Make him willing, and you will immediately see that he is able.

“Did I not tell you,” he says, “that if you believe, you will see the glory of God? (John 11:40.) But what glory? The resurrection, certainly, of one who had been dead four days.

“Let the intercessors come, those importunate sisterly sisters—that is, those who do not deny the weakness of humility and the death of a brother. Let them pour out prayers to the Lord: one first, a witness of devout action; the other, a teacher of theoretical contemplation and purest prayer—not without significance, however, in their number or order.

“For they teach that there are two orders in the Church that care for the salvation of those who are perishing: one through preaching and works; the other through persistent prayer, imploring the Lord, interceding for the dead, and knocking so that they may be able to be raised.”

[Note: The copy read *peccando, mortuis* (“sinning, for the dead”), incorrectly.]

“Let them confess that such a death occurred through the absence of divine protection, as the result of negligence. It is remarkable that both should have said: ‘Lord, if you had been here, our brother would never have died’ (ibid., 12).

“Let despair be banished far away; let constant confidence in hope be present: that a dead man of four days, stinking, buried beneath the heaviest mass of habitual crime, bound and immobile, may still be awakened and raised after a long sleep; that he may overcome the burden laid upon him, be loosed, and be able to depart.”

[Note: The copy incorrectly read *abisse* (“to have departed”).]

“You will immediately see Christ stir with the spirit of mercy and prayer and trouble himself. You will hear him cry: ‘Come out!’ (ibid., 43). You will see the one of whom you despaired immediately emerge, show himself alive though bound, conceal nothing, confess, and go forth freed—that is, set his conduct in order according to reason. He will hear the command, so that others, who are even more grievously dead, may return to life through his resurrection and believe in Christ, that is, the Savior of all.”

### 20

“But what,” you say, “if none of these things happens—what ought we to do? Are we to venerate as alive one whom we know to be dead?”

“Not yet,” I reply. “As I infer from this, you do not yet know what you ought to venerate in anyone: either what God has made, or what the man himself has devised for himself. But because I see that you are blind in matters of this kind, I consider that you must be drawn on more by examples than by reasoning. ‘The scribes and Pharisees,’ he says, ‘have sat on Moses’ seat; therefore, whatever they tell you, observe and do; but do not act according to their works’ (Matthew 23:2–3), and so forth.”

This is as though he had said something different: “Venerate what God has conferred; tolerate what they do, not on their own account—for they are evil—but on account of the honor which they have received; and that honor is good precisely because it has been granted by the good Giver.”

Give the vilest little donkey the task of carrying the finest wine: the donkey becomes worthless, but you embrace the wine. A most precious ring is often worn by a misshapen finger: desire burns for the ring, while the contempt of the observer recoils from the finger.

“But,” you say, “you declare that honor is good because it has been granted by the good God. What of the honor which God did not confer?”

“Who,” I reply, “could that be, when the Apostle testifies: ‘There is no authority except from God’ (Romans 13:1)? Or do you wish authority to be one thing and honor another? But authority without honor is weak, and therefore is not authority either. ‘They have made kings,’ you say”—and understand, “God says”—“but not from me; they have appointed princes, and I did not acknowledge them.” ‘Not from me,’ I say, means: they did not reign according to me; they did not act rightly, as I commanded; “I did not acknowledge them” means, “I did not praise or approve them.” Nevertheless, they reigned while I looked on.

But if you cannot be persuaded to desire bishops of another kind—such as God’s mercy would wish—except the sort whom the Apostle portrays when he says, “It is necessary that a bishop be blameless” (Titus 1:7), which, alas, is today a rare bird upon the earth, consider Caiaphas, whom Peter appeared to obey. Yet when Caiaphas said this, he did not depart from Moses’ seat. Consider, I say, that the matter is not far removed from what was read yesterday: “He did not say this of himself” (John 11:51).

What does “of himself” mean? It means: from his own malice, by which he wished Christ to be killed. For he did not desire Christ’s death so that the whole nation might be saved—for according to his malignity this was altogether impossible—but so that Christ might be removed from the kingdom in his presence.

Although such was his conscience, what the seat of Moses uttered through him was true, just as what echoes from a string belongs to the one who sets it vibrating. For thus it is written: “Since he was high priest of that year, he prophesied” (ibid.).

Here too observe the words “of that year.” Had God commanded this through Moses? Certainly not. Behold the monstrous indignity: this was not a lawful authority, and yet it was permitted by God—indeed, authority granted by the wicked Herod. If even one who was merely permitted to hold authority could prophesy, what could authority given by God accomplish? Certainly more: it could both will and speak what is good, whereas this authority could only speak.

For the nation was not liberated because Caiaphas willed it; rather, he spoke because the dignity of the seat caused him to say what had to be said. Whom, then, do you seek who is more unworthy? Yet you hear that he prophesied, so that you may note how great is the force of authority, whatever the life of its holder may be, and how great the dignity of such an order. Do not therefore hesitate over my assertion that honor is good because it has been granted by the good God, since even permitted authority could reach the effectiveness of prophecy.

Yet, to accommodate you in some degree, I see that it must be noted that when the Apostle says, “There is no authority except from God” (Romans 13:1), this wording leaves room for understanding both what is permitted and what is granted, especially since he adds: “Those that exist have been ordained by God” (ibid.).

This does not mean that Caiaphas’s authority was orderly—it was most disorderly—but it is to be venerated in the sense which we demonstrated above. Let us nevertheless strive and take care that we do not do so in vain. For this entire argument is an indication of my unworthiness and misery: while I labor to draw Scripture to my aid against its resistance, I am explaining, perhaps, not whether it can be done, but what it is or what is happening.

### 21

Therefore, lest I deceive myself any further, I confess that although the all-powerful mercy of God can accomplish this—just as it was able to create the world from nothing—if it does not do so, it is certain that I, together with those like me, am utterly lost. I bear the false name of bishop or abbot, not without the danger of eternal condemnation, even if it should be granted to me, as formerly to Caiaphas, to prophesy. I can be freed from this only by entirely abandoning the vanity of the world, if Christ’s mercy grants it.

For I am amazed that I can endure this, while I hear Scripture crying out against me and those like me. I grieve to consider figuratively that none of these things is unsuited to me:

“Whoever has a blemish shall not offer the bread of his God, nor approach his ministry: if he is blind, if lame, if he has a small, large, or crooked nose, if he has a broken foot or hand, if he is hunchbacked, if bleary-eyed, if he has a white spot in his eye, if a persistent scab, if an impetigo on his body, if he is overweight” (Leviticus 21:17–20).

Yet amid all this I find no confidence, not even the confidence of familiarity, by which I might intercede with God at least on my own behalf.

“You despair,” you say. “I see it. Why do you labor in vain?”

“I neither despair nor hope,” I reply. “I hope in God; I despair of myself—and I consider that I ought to hope in him all the more, the less I ought to hope in myself.”

I despair because I know what I must do, yet do not even begin it. I do not despair that it will be done, if God should in every respect be pleased to do it. Whether I labor in vain, however, I do not know, because I do not yet see what I am laboring to obtain for this purpose. If there is something, it is not what is suitable; it is what I said above about myself, rebellious, evil, and fugitive, that you could have remembered: I am a servant.

For I act, if ever I do act, not from love of the Lord, nor from devotion to the religion which I denied, nor from longing for the place from which I miserably fled, and finally not from desire for eternal life, but from fear of Gehenna. If I dared to abandon it, I certainly would not do it. For this reason I cannot imagine what God might care about such a servant.

I see that I ought to become contemptible even to myself, since I read words spoken by a pagan, most truly, in contempt of me and my companions:

“The good hate sin from love of virtue.”

But I see that I and those men fear sinning more than we love not to sin.

The matter stands thus. If I had been a layman and sought penance for all those things, and if two hundred and sixty-five years were imposed upon me, from whom would they be granted? What would a man already seventy years old do?

I know what my advocate would say, if he were nevertheless worth anything: “You cannot do these things, because time is lacking. Give yourself wholly to God and abandon the world. Behold, everything is remitted, because it has been entrusted to the merciful God.”

I am a monk only in habit and, barely, in law; but I am a deserter from the law I promised. Suppose I complete all those years in penance, and everything is remitted, but this one thing remains: that I have irrevocably fled from my own law. Does it not seem to you that I would be condemnable for this alone?

For this alone, then. All those other things I can heal; this one thing I cannot heal.

### 22

After certain further considerations, I reached, as it were, by stages of the mind, the point at which it seemed to me that I had abstained from this and from all the other things in vain, if God had not granted me to remain a monk, as I had promised, until the end of my life.[^c0042-1] For even if I had possessed no other faults, I had been destined to eternal punishments for this alone.

What had it profited me to abstain from those things—and from the pleasures with which the world so sweetly entices—when I had also been deprived of the profit of eternal punishments?

I wished, after many other shipwrecks of the same kind, as I supposed, to impress this certainty upon you, who boast of a continence acquired more through old age than through virtue, and to bring you back from this security to necessary lamentation and fasting, especially to the resolve of a monk, whose name and habit alone you share with me. I preferred to speak of everything that concerns me rather than now recall even some of the things that concern you.

For to someone ignorant of your condition, seeing the cheerful security of all of you even in this Lent, it might appear that none of you had any sin.[^c0042-2] Thus—shame upon it!—some pest of false hope, deadly despair, or wicked hardness of heart has taken possession of you through my sin, because I neglected to warn you, so that it has also made you insensible; and this is known to be the more dangerous in every kind of sickness.[^c0042-3]

“You do not spare yourself,” you say, “but you sharply attack me—or rather, all of us.”

“How else,” I reply? For if I cared for myself while neglecting others, especially you who were entrusted to me, what greater crime could I either possess or confess?

Yet I am, I am—I do not deny it—such a sinner by my own fault that in prayer I must say more intensely, “Have mercy on me,” than, “Have mercy on us.” And when I say “on us” as well, I am compelled by the enormity of my crimes to remember myself more than anyone else. By this I show that charity has grown cold in me, and I doubt even more that my sins can be extinguished.

Would that at least your sins were sometimes made as clear to you as mine are to me while I write these things! I believe that this would restrain our—or perhaps your—cheerfulness somewhat and would produce a desire to escape from these things as quickly as possible. It would also check the idleness of those who grow sluggish through indolence, especially those to whom it applies more greatly: the older men, or the elderly, whom you know to face the greatest danger, as I do also—God forbid that this should happen.

For these men, together with me, have done what is written in the prophet: “They broke the yoke; they burst the bonds” (Jeremiah 5:5). See how recently one of them served the devil with such cheerfulness.

When he was accustomed to complain of the poverty of the common life,[^c0042-4] and to neglect the others and the precepts of the Rule, he suddenly brought forward the money which he had long accumulated from that common life, so that it might not unreasonably be shown that he had served mammon so faithfully and for so long, and had devoted himself to the service of idols with no little diligence. He did what you knew before I did.

Even at such an age he was not ashamed to imitate Simon, especially since I suppose he had heard that his predecessor, a man of the same age, was a kind of bandit. After money had been contributed for the same transaction, the man died a miserable death—as he deserved—before he had been permitted to enjoy it even for a single day.

[^c0042-1]: “To remain until the end,” that is, to persevere until the end of life.  
[^c0042-2]: Understand: To someone ignorant of your condition, observing the cheerful security of all of you even in this Lent, it might seem that none of you had any sin.  
[^c0042-3]: Understand: I do not know what plague of false hope, deadly despair, or wicked hardness of heart has taken possession of you through my sin, because I neglected to warn you; it has made you insensitive as well, something known to be especially harmful in every kind of sickness.  
[^c0042-4]: The same thing also occurred in the monastery of Gembloux: under the pretext of poverty, ordinary discipline was undermined, as the author of the little work *On the Deeds of the Abbots of Gembloux* testifies (volume 2 of Acher’s *Spicilegium*, p. 763): “When ecclesiastical property had been dissipated everywhere, and revenues and stipends had been reduced, their household resources—the monks’ resources—were greatly diminished. Thus, under the pretext of poverty, while each person looked to his own interests and, neglecting the dignity of common life, sought privately to increase his own possessions, they lived with excessive license, which is wholly harmful to the souls of monks.”

The same witness states on page 762 that in the monastery of Lobbes, after perfect common ownership had been abolished, this abuse arose: those who held the abbacy treated everything as merchandise; selling the doves in the Church of God—that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit—they made the house of God a den of thieves. He adds shortly afterward: “Since none of these men wished to lack the great revenues of the abbey, they annually sold and withdrew the provostships which, in the name and by the merit of obedience, they ought to have entrusted to religious and God-fearing men, treating them as though they were rustic stewardships.”

Fulcuin, a contemporary of Ratherius, gives the same testimony in *On the Deeds of the Abbots of Lobbes*, chapters 19 and 21.

Two monks guilty of this simoniacal stain are indicated here: they bought an abbacy with money they had collected. One of them, before he had even been permitted to enjoy it for a day, was extinguished by a miserable judgment—as was fitting. The other, who succeeded him in the same abbacy after likewise contributing money, is the man whom Ratherius now accuses of the same crime, while later accusing himself as well because he did not resist or contradict him.

This monk, named Oderadus, is said to have been very old and later to have become the uncle of a certain abbot. He is also said to have bought an abbacy for eighty pounds. See notes 36, 40, and 61.

Ratherius blames himself for not reproving this man or prohibiting such a purchase. Since he charges him with having made the purchase without his permission, Ratherius shows that he was the superior of the monastery to which this monk belonged. Hence, addressing the monks of that place shortly before, he had said: “If I cared for myself while neglecting others, especially you who were entrusted to me,” and so forth.

### 23

From this point it is absolutely necessary to consider—consider, alas!—how backward a path we are pursuing, we who ought, like our predecessors, to go before secular men on the path of righteousness.

For if any secular priest acquires a church (see Apostolic Canons 39 and 40 and Book 2 of the *Capitularies*, chapter 150), he may sell, give, or assign in any manner he wishes to anyone whatever he possessed previously. Whatever he acquires afterward, however, belongs to the right of the Church.

But a monk, who ought not even to have his own will under his own control, for whom may he gather anything? To whom may he give or leave what he has gathered—especially if what he appears to possess has come from the provision of a stipend, from which he ought to have been clothed and fed, or perhaps from the administration of some obedience?[1]

And where will this wretched man be, if such a thing has happened to him? What, I ask, will he say in his heart when he hears this read in chapter:

“Let Ananias and Sapphira always be remembered, lest those who have kept something back for themselves—or all who have committed any fraud concerning the monastery’s property—suffer in their souls the death which they suffered in their bodies.”

How many ornaments and books could have been made in that same church for so many pounds of silver, from which this money was acquired and collected?

I heard someone murmuring in the sacristy:

“They say that we ought to possess nothing privately. Who, then, contributed these ornaments and books here, unless the monks of this place?”

To this I myself confess and say: It would have been better not to have possessed them than to have contributed them to that place. Nevertheless, in lessening the evil, it was better to have left them here than to have dissipated them elsewhere.

“Good,” you say. “Good; that is enough. Return to yourself. Look at yourself, lest it truly be said to you:

‘Hypocrite, first remove the beam from your own eye; for why do you see the speck in your brother’s eye but do not consider the beam that is in your own eye?’ (Luke 6:41; Matthew 12:3).”

“I do consider it,” I reply; “I do consider it, and I add this also to that same beam. As though what I miserably did by myself were not enough, I gave this man an opportunity to act while I knew it and yet did not prohibit it.”

Not only those who do such things, but also those who consent to those who do them, are worthy of death (Romans 1:32).

But if you are acting humanely, do you think it was more tolerable and more natural that this man should have acted in such a way out of the necessity of poverty—an outsider, poor, exiled, a beggar, and a most deluded newcomer—than that he should have acted from the most arrogant ambition while a citizen, resident, entirely self-sufficient, and, to speak truthfully, the legitimate servant of that church, since he had been lawfully delivered into its service by his own hand and profession, after breaking the yoke and bursting the bonds of the Rule without the permission of the superior?[2]

But, to accommodate you once again, so to rebuke him that I do not spare myself, I confess that we both acted most thoughtlessly. For if, now almost decrepit with age, as he is, I am overtaken by death or depart before I have restored to the holy place the value of the twenty-two pounds by which I despoiled it, I fear a hellish reckoning. He too, no less a debtor to this place and, as I said, my contemporary, if he has neither made satisfaction here nor faithfully preserved what he bought, will without doubt—unless it be he who has sometimes lost his sight—be subject to eternal punishment with Ananias, Sapphira, and Simon.

I beg you, recognize that it is Peter who both struck those men by command for their fraud and ordered this man to perish in everlasting condemnation for his arrogant ambition: Peter, whose money this was; Peter, whose abbey was most unjustly alienated. But let us consider both beams, mine and his; for here I see no speck. Perhaps today, with your eyes better opened, you will see both hanging over my neck, or rather two becoming for me one monstrous beam. “If you do not announce to the wicked man his iniquity,” he says, “I will require his blood at your hand” (Ezekiel 3:18). He who said, “What is done amiss by disciples reflects upon their master,” showed this to be most just. And he—whose edict we are both proved, in this one matter, to have transgressed and rebelled against, he because he acted and I because I did not oppose him—says: “Let the Abbot know that whatever less profit the father of the household may find in the sheep is charged to the fault of the shepherd.”

To excuse that nephew whom I mentioned shortly before, together with myself, for neglecting to restrain him as we ought, I can perhaps seem to have followed the example of a physician who forbids a person despairing of life anything which he wishes to take.

Thus Jerome says in a similar case: “Physicians say that serious illnesses should not be treated, but left to nature, lest the remedy intensify the pain.” For if he saw that the man had become irrecoverably hardened in deadly obstinacy against his own purpose, what would it have profited to forbid him some worldly advantage? Would it have been so that he might suffer loss here and punishment there, especially since he knew well that he himself was not less able to distinguish the pit of his own destruction?

Was this what the Lord’s servant used to sing, even while contemplating such things:

“We ought to despise the world,”

and then add that we should be able to follow Christ the Lord—as though we could not follow the Lord together with the world?

And while exaggerating the warning that we must not lose eternal life for the sake of the empty glory of this world, was he not unafraid that someone might answer him indirectly:

“Out of your own mouth I judge you, wicked servant” (Luke 19:22)?

[1]: “Obediences” were the monastic offices assigned for a year. Hence Fulcuin says in *On the Deeds of the Abbots of Lobbes*, chapter 19: “Annual obediences,” which is the customary exchange of ministries. The monks criticized here are those who reserved something for themselves from the provision attached to such offices.

[2]: The superior whose permission he did not obtain, and who had left the monastery’s service, was Ratherius himself. Thus, in section 24, speaking of the same elderly monk who abandoned the monastery after purchasing a small abbacy, he says: “You should know that I rejoice because it was done without my permission.” Likewise, in section 34, he writes of another monk: “It had been reported that your Bonito had distributed wool to the brothers at the command of someone without my permission.” The term “provider” was used for the superior or abbot of a monastery.

The preceding description suits Ratherius, who, driven from the see of Liège, received an abbey to administer and govern as a means of support. He is called an outsider and newcomer both because the monastery over which he presided was not Lobbes, where he had made his profession, and because he came there not as a monk of that place, to serve God there permanently, but as a poor, exiled, beggarly bishop and newcomer who had not wholly abandoned hope of returning to the bishopric of Verona.

“Departure” means before he left the monastery over which he presided when writing this; he still hoped to return to the episcopate of Verona, to which he was restored not long afterward. We believe that he spent the twenty-two pounds by which he says he despoiled the monastery to meet some pressing necessity; this necessity seems to have arisen when a great multitude of guests flocked to the monastery.

*Componere* is a term used in ancient charters for paying a penalty in money. Here the “hellish reckoning” signifies the punishment of hell.

The words “Peter, whose money this was”—namely, the eighty pounds which the monk paid for the purchased abbey—refer to the monastery over which Ratherius presided. We have inferred that this monastery, distinct from Lobbes and situated in the territory of the bishop of Liège, was Alnes, whose church was consecrated in honour of St Peter; thus the money alienated by the monk was St Peter’s. The other phrase, “Peter, whose abbey was most unjustly alienated,” appears to refer to the abbey that the monk acquired for eighty pounds and unjustly detached through such a purchase from another abbey bearing St Peter’s name—such as Lobbes, to which several monasteries, including Waslare and St Ursmar’s, were subject. Perhaps he detached one of these from Lobbes and St Peter when he bought for himself an abbatial prelation there. So long as a monastery adhered to its principal house, officials removable at the will of the principal abbot were set over it and called provosts, priors, or by similar titles; when abbots were established, they became permanent superiors, and the formerly united monastery was in a sense separated from its principal house and no longer depended on the principal abbot’s will.

The words from “But I was ashamed” to the end of the section are spoken by the priest who assumes the role of confessor. He first states Ratherius’s excuse—“But I was ashamed,” you answer, “out of reverence for his old age”—and immediately refutes it: “You certainly lie,” and so on.

The abbot addressed in the following apostrophe, presented as religious, was the nephew of the monk criticized above for buying an abbey for eighty pounds and abandoning the monastery’s service without Ratherius’s permission. This monk, described as very old, was the abbot’s uncle; Ratherius says that he went mad when he concluded the purchase of the abbey.

The archaic Italian word *barba*, meaning “uncle,” is noteworthy.

A sacred place is indicated, to which they went as though to pray, where the simoniacal purchase in question was arranged and its price of eighty pounds paid.

The phrase about frequent journeys and returns is taken from Terence, *Phormio*, act 5, scene 8, verse 24: “Were these the frequent journeys and long stays at Lemnos?” The journeys and returns criticized here perhaps indicate trips made to the place just mentioned until that purchase was concluded.

### 24

Consider carefully, I beg you, consider carefully. You tried yesterday to remove a speck from the beam, and I warn you not to dare to equate denial of God and worship of the devil with any crime.

Of all the things which you remember me confessing above (see section 2)—homicides, gougings-out of eyes, mutilations, burnings, plunderings, and many others—you should know that I am not more guilty of any of them than of this. I did not commit, command, or wish any of those things to be done. I did commit something from which such deeds were occasioned.

Here, however, there is something more. Although I neither commanded nor wished it to happen, I nevertheless gave it the opportunity to happen through my fault, by failing to prohibit what at least I was able to prevent.

You should know only this about me: I rejoice that it was done without my permission, since this seems to offer some alleviation.

“Who understands his sins?” says the Psalmist, necessarily adding: “Cleanse me, Lord, from my hidden faults, and spare your servant from those of others.” Then he continues: “If they do not rule over me”—that is, other people’s sins—“then I shall be blameless and cleansed from the greatest fault” (Psalm 18:13–14). The greatest fault—yes, the greatest.

For does it not seem to you a great fault that one who is indebted for twenty-two pounds through his own wickedness has added eighty pounds, through another’s crime, to the accumulation of his debt?[1]

And what a miserable condition is that of ruling! Who, unless he felt secure about himself, would not rightly flee such danger? Another sins without your knowledge, and you are compelled to pay the penalty.

But in order to excuse the nephew mentioned shortly above, together with myself, for neglecting to restrain him as we ought, I may seem to have followed the example of a physician who forbids a person despairing of life anything that he wishes to take.

Therefore Jerome says in a similar case:

“Physicians say that serious illnesses should not be treated, but left to nature, lest the remedy intensify the pain.”

If he saw that the man had become irrecoverably hardened in deadly obstinacy against his own purpose, what would it have profited to forbid him some worldly advantage? Would it have been so that he might suffer loss here and punishment there, especially when he knew very well that the man himself was no less able to discern the pit of his destruction?

Was this what the Lord’s servant used to sing, even while contemplating such things:

“We ought to despise the world,”

adding that we must be able to follow Christ the Lord—as though we could not follow the Lord while possessing the world?

And while insisting that we must not lose eternal life for the sake of this world’s vain glory, was he not unafraid that someone might answer indirectly:

“Out of your own mouth I judge you, wicked servant” (Luke 19:22)?

[1]: The monk had paid eighty pounds for the purchase of a certain abbacy, as will become clear from section 550; see note 577. The twenty-two pounds attributed to Ratherius, for which he was indebted through his own crime, were explained above in note 548.

### 25

But in order to show that it is now time for us to return, I want you to know, I say, that this saying from the prophet brings me great consolation—would that it were not empty:

“Coming to Babylon, there you shall be delivered” (Micah 4:10).

For in the house of God, while no one knew except my supporters, I committed many crimes under the pretext of holiness, as many others do, through shameless deception. You alone detected and exposed me in this one matter. I was brought down into such great confusion that, once this crime had been exposed, I no longer cared whether any of my crimes remained hidden.

I judged that what I could have suffered fruitlessly for that one matter would be better suffered together with the fruit gained from all of them. Thus, having been brought by you, so to speak, into Babylon, I may be believed—and would that through the mercy of God I might truly have been delivered.

Nor is an iron frying-pan lacking, in which even my bones—perhaps once making some very vain claim about themselves—are being roasted.[1]

“So I have benefited you greatly,” you say, “by doing great harm, though I had benefited you little when I was favorable.”

“But what of me?” I reply. “How much the salvation of the world benefited Judas!”

Through Jesus, and through the common hope, I beg you: remove from yourself the stench of my crimes, lest, by joining it to the stench of your own, you increase the unbearable grief of me, who believe that you have perished because of me. And I beg you as I warn you: do not, overwhelmed by my darkness and unable to consider yourself, fall worse than you have fallen because you do not know where to place your foot in action.[2]

Let us direct the gaze of the mind, rather, toward the most splendid light of the saints, as toward the shining stars of the upper air, after anointing it with the collyrium of the Rule. There each of you—or perhaps each of us—will see what he ought to judge about himself and about another.

“You bring up the Rule again,” you say.

“What else,” I reply, “can be done if it is set aside? Even if you return through all the Scriptures, together with the Gospel itself, you must return to it, whether you wish it or not, if you wish to care for your soul.”

Tell me, I beg you: have you ever heard “son of Belial” used in a good sense?

“Never,” you say.

“But who,” I reply, “is worse than a pagan?”

For “Belial” is interpreted as “without a yoke.” Yet no human condition can be governed without some yoke. The yoke for each person is the discipline of the law by which he lives: for the Lombard layman, the Italian law; for clerics, canon law; for monks, monastic law.

Once that law has been rejected, what yoke restrains you from turning aside to anything, or loosens you to do anything? If none does, you are not merely the son of Belial—that is, of the devil—but you yourself are Belial.

If, then, you have ever heard of either the son of Belial or Belial himself obtaining forgiveness through penance without conversion, persuade me of it, if you can. If not, persuade yourself that the labor of penance without the yoke of your own law can benefit anyone in anything.

“I mean the very yoke which is penance,” you say.

“Who imposed it?” I reply.

“I see what you are attempting, impostor,” you say. “As usual, you are bringing me back again to the abbot and the Rule.”

“Precisely,” I reply. “Precisely. For whatever a monk does without that man’s permission will be attributed to presumption and empty glory, not to reward.”

“While I listen to your arguments,” you say, “I cannot stop being scandalized. In some matters you are extremely severe, in others very lax. You seem to be cooking a kid in its mother’s milk, which is forbidden” (Exodus 23:19).

For when you recount your own very grave and numerous crimes, you yourself close the door against the penance that was necessary, and open it at your own pleasure. What, then, do you want to do? You complain that you are without a yoke; thus you admit that you too are the son of Belial.

“What,” I ask, “are you asking?”

“What is said in the psalm, if God’s mercy nevertheless grants it? For I find no other counsel.”

“What is this?”

“Listen,” he says, “O daughter, and see; incline your ear, forget your people and your father’s house” (Psalm 44:11).

Pay attention: the one who calls indicates that he is the father, so that he may draw you away from your father.

Let us therefore leave this father with his harsh yoke, and follow him whose yoke is easy and whose burden is light (Matthew 11:30).

“Why do you not do this?” you ask.

“What we say,” I reply, “I suppose comes from there.”

But it is written: “If you offer rightly and do not divide rightly, you have sinned.”

And elsewhere: “You shall pursue what is just, and only what is just” (Deuteronomy 16:20).

And the Apostle says: “Let all your things be done honorably and in order” (1 Corinthians 14:40).

And the theologian of the Roman See says: “Care must be taken that our good works be neither nothing, nor small, nor unexamined.”

[1]: The Latin is difficult: *ossa ... mea* (“my bones”) are perhaps described as once making some very vain claim about themselves.

[2]: Understand: “I beg you through Jesus, our common hope, to remove the stench of my crimes from yourself, lest, by joining it to the stench of your own, you increase the unbearable grief of me, who believe that you have perished because of me. And I beg you, while warning you, not to fall worse than you have fallen because, overwhelmed by my darkness and unable to consider yourself, you do not know where you ought to place your foot in action.”

### 26.

As I considered what should be done with my misery, the advice of the fugitive came to me—advice to which all other kinds of counsel yield, if not in every respect, at least in this one: “Love extinguishes every offense” (Prov. X, 12). And: “Her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much” (Luke VII, 47). For although I may have committed countless offenses, I have not committed every kind; there are also many other matters in which human frailty stumbles, but from which my criminality is innocent. Even if I had done all these things, it would be very easy for love to extinguish them. Therefore, you say, acquire such love toward God that, having abandoned everything else, you desire to enjoy him alone; and toward your neighbor, such love that, as far as—and even beyond—as you are able, you wish to contribute to his welfare; then, secure against all the ranks of your crimes, mock them.

“This,” I said, “this is absolutely necessary for me; but you should know that it is exceedingly difficult, unless I hasten, after the example of the fugitive, to restore myself to my profession while it is still day.”

[Note: Construe and explain as follows: “Unless, following the example of the fugitive slave who voluntarily returns, I hasten to restore myself to my profession while it is day; and until that happens—if indeed, by God’s mercy, it ever happens—climb into heaven and return from there”; that is, even if you climbed into heaven and returned from there, you would not be able to persuade me that I could hope for the salvation of my soul from anywhere else. “Strive,” you say, “strive.” “I shall strive,” I reply, “if God helps me, but not as the ill will of those who grow weary of my presence desires”—so that I may speak calmly, and would that I were truly calm!—“nevertheless, I shall strive,” and so forth. From this passage we understand that, in the little monastery over which Rather presided, his presence had been burdensome to some.]

—restore myself to my profession, I mean, while it is day: 273 until this happens (if indeed, by God’s mercy, it ever happens), climb into heaven and return from there: you will not be able to persuade me that I can hope for the salvation of my soul from anywhere else. “Strive, strive,” you say. “I shall strive,” I reply, “if God helps me, but not as the ill will of those who are weary of my presence desires”—so that I may speak calmly, and would that I might speak truthfully and calmly!—“nevertheless, I shall strive.”

One does not withdraw from God or draw near to him by bodily steps, but by those of the mind; although, since I am going to leave what I fear, I may first have attempted this by the steps of the mind.

“It would have been enough,” you say, “if the rash profanation of sacred things did not still move me so greatly.”

“But in the matter that you twice set against me,” I reply—that is, “The judgments of God are a great deep” (Ps. XXXV, 7)—“I think that something is concealed which must be denied to me.”

“Certainly, certainly,” I say; “for I did not promise to tell you everything I knew how to say, but to burden you with my crimes. If these are not enough, add your own, and, believe me, your burden will not depart empty.”

I shall say one thing, however; and if you cannot obtain from it what you seek, I do not wish to labor with you any longer: “A person does not know whether he is worthy of love or hatred, but everything remains uncertain for the future” (Eccl. IX, 1).

But if, for no other reason—so that I may resume what I left off much earlier—I ought at least to refrain from such things, it would be so that, rewarded only with temporal goods, they might not expect anything else in that world except to hear the sufficiently disastrous reproach: “Remember that you received good things during your life” (Luke XVI, 25). What good are those very goods to me without permission to enjoy them?

[Note: That is, unless they hear there, in that world, the very ill-omened reproach: “Remember that you received good things during your life.” What benefit are those good things to me without permission to enjoy them?]

But if there were to be at least so much greater refreshment there as less evil had been committed here, even this would be a most wretched benefit of relief. For, matters being as they are, it would have been better to have been there long ago—speaking in the voice of the despairing—than daily here to pile up the causes of torment.

But if, once these matters had either never been committed or had been removed through repentance, only that one remained, and if the punishments of hell were ready to be awaited because of that one alone, while, if that one had either never been committed or had been erased by returning, we ought not to fear any punishment in that world, regardless of the enormity or multiplicity of all these offenses, reason advises that this return must by no means be abandoned but, once the opportunity is granted, must be undertaken without any delay.

[Note: This return to the monastery must not be abandoned or postponed; once the opportunity is granted, it must be undertaken without any delay. Hence the following concerns the return to one’s purpose, or monastery. Construe what follows thus: “God’s mercy must be hoped for, and, so that it may not be lacking, it must be implored by every kind of embassy of good intentions, as it were, and by the intervention of continual prayers, so that the longing soul may be able to obtain the desired result.”]

“But what if the efficacy of the opportunity is lacking?” you ask.

God’s mercy must be hoped for; and, so that it may not be lacking, it must be implored through every kind of embassy, as it were, of good intentions and through the intervention of continual prayers, so that the longing soul may at last obtain the desired result. [lacuna] may be able, through entreaty, to obtain it.

[Col. 0420A]

### 27.

“But what of the fact that you say you are doing this unwillingly, compelled by fear, like the worst kind of slave?”

“Please do not call me the worst,” I reply; “it is enough, I say, to have called me evil. For that person is worse who returns neither led by love nor compelled by fear. Many who had long remained rebellious returned through fear of torments; afterward they loved their masters most fully, and were even loved by their masters to the point of freedom.

“But hear briefly what our Lord said about himself to those coming to him: ‘You did not choose me, but I chose you’ (John XV, 16). And concerning them: ‘Because you have loved me’ (John XVI, 27)—which they certainly merited through the prior action of his love.

“From where, then, do you think that there is at least a fear of hell extending even to the desire to return to God?”

[Note: That is, the fear of Gehenna extending even to the desire to return to God.]

“From the prior gift of his mercy,” I reply. “For even when he first threatens so that you may fear, he inspires the counsel that you should carry out in fear, and promises gifts if you return.”

“But how,” you ask, “do you persuade yourself that, while such an enormity of crimes remains, you can merit escape from eternal torments merely by returning to the monastic way of life?”

“Because,” I reply, “he promises this through the Gospel, unable to lie: ‘Everyone who has left everything for my name’s sake will possess eternal life’ (Matt. XIX, 29).”

“You say that you are not leaving anything for his name’s sake, but for the sake of hell.”

“And what authority,” I reply, “does hell have to punish me without the power of his name? Unless God casts me there, hell does not receive me. He, therefore, is to be feared rather than hell, because he alone can consign one to hell; indeed, he is rather to be loved, since by threatening he delays giving hell, so that to those who fear, take precautions, and return to him, he may grant the kingdom of heaven.

“But consider his name as well. He is called Jesus on our account—that is, Savior. And the one who is converted so that he may not be cast into hell—does he not desire to be saved? And by whom is he saved except by the Savior? Therefore, the one who is converted in order to be saved is converted for the sake of the name of Jesus; and the one who is rescued from hell is saved. Therefore, he is converted for the sake of the name of Jesus.”

### 28.

“What then?” you ask. “Why do you keep creating delays? Why do you not draw near to return to the Lord?”

“I seem to be doing so,” I reply. “Is that not so?”

“But what is it, I ask?”

“What I told you earlier about the fugitive slave,” I reply. “If I am striving, my prayers are a kind of embassy of return—unless here too, as in many other matters, I am deceiving myself. For I perceive that I am doing this sluggishly, and therefore not doing it; for this is not itself a return. And even if I dare to presume that I am already beginning to return in mind, I am greatly impeded.”

“By whom?” you ask.

“By myself,” I reply. “For I do not wish to accuse another, lest I seem to imitate Eve. The snares by which I bound myself hold me fast, and the meshes of the net” (Job XVIII, 8) into which, heedless, I thrust my foot.

“The tyrant also—whose citizenship I preferred to the service of my master—is the more hostile in impeding me the more precipitously he hears me wanting to abandon him. He sees me not merely confessing this, but describing him as well.

“But I fear that, in one respect, he has great hopes of me.”

“In what respect?” you ask.

“In what you yourself have said more than once.”

[Note: The confessor had said more than once, in the preceding passages, that although Rather desired to return to the monastic way of life, he did not yet will it effectively. This ineffective will is the one thing because of which Rather had earlier said: “I fear that, in one respect, the tyrant—that is, the devil—has great hopes of me.” The following repeats this: “I fear that one thing, that one thing,” and so forth.]

“That very thing,” I reply; “I fear that very thing. Know that I fear nothing so much as that very thing. For if that one thing remains, the return will be imperfect—and I fear that it will be no return at all.”

And terrified by that same thing—understand, “I fear that very thing”—which I still perceive myself to be in prison because of, I should have cried out from there, from the depths, without yawning.

“An obligation,” you say, “an obligation—if you use *opus* to mean what is necessary.”

“For I think that antiquity used *opus* more often to mean use or advantage.”

[Note: The ancient use of *opus* in the sense of “utility” is clear from Cicero, Book I, Letter 9, at the end: “It is useful for the curiate law to be brought to the consul, though it is not necessary,” where *opus* is distinguished from *necesse* and signifies what is useful.]

“I agree that it is necessary for you, in the depth in which I see you lying, to cry out—not yawning, as you think.”

“But I see you continually yawning, and gradually interrupting even this embassy of yours, and I fear that it may happen to you to return to Egypt in this manner; to return, I say, to return. Would that at least you had been granted the opportunity to leave!

“Do you not see me sitting beside the flesh-pots? Do you not see me still occupied with bricks and clay? Do you not see me, beneath the burden of labor, sometimes even groaning and sighing as I yawn, bound with the straps of my own self-imposed bondage, restrained by the barriers of ingrained habit, tied by the meshes of a tightly connected net, and miserably moving my foot from one exercise to another?

“Do you not consider that dreadful things pass over me and come upon me? Do you not see me bend down at the signals that break forth, so that we may cross? Do you not often hear my soul, see me observing my enemies—that is, my habits—and mocking my Sabbaths?”

### 29.

“But perhaps, when you were standing on high ground and heard me singing our Passover with you, you thought that I had made some passage from the depths to something worse.”

“I did,” I confess; “I did. I do not deny that I made a passage—alas, a wrongful one, and one I ought never to have made. For I passed from fasting to gluttony, from weeping to laughter, from the depths to lower depths, not to things above; from harmful things to worse things; from nightly vigils to sleep even during the day; from indiscriminate silence to excessive speech and, what is worse, corrupt and disgraceful speech; from psalmody to idleness; from reading to laziness and torpor; from salutary sadness to the world’s empty and harmful joy.

“But surely,” you say, “in view of the joy of so great a solemnity, one should at least refrain from these things? Surely one should exult and rejoice?”

“One should refrain,” I reply, “one should refrain, but not cease entirely; one should exult and rejoice, but one must by no means yield to vices; rather, one must devote oneself more earnestly to the Lord.

“For the Psalmist says, ‘Let my heart rejoice,’ not merely so that it may be secure and play, but ‘so that it may fear your name’ (Ps. LXXXV, 11). And elsewhere the same writer says: ‘Serve the Lord in fear, and exult—not for yourselves, but in him—with trembling’ (Ps. II, 11), not with security, which certainly prepares the soul for a fall.

“If you do not understand this, I shall put it briefly: in eating, since I cared more for the flesh in desire than in necessity, I confess that I touched what was unlawful, pursued more luxurious foods, exceeded the measure of sufficiency, and thereby made what was lawful unlawful.

“In Lent one must abstain from foods and vices; at Easter, from vices alone. I confess that I did none of this at all. In Lent one must weep and mourn; at Easter one must give thanks and rejoice in the Lord.

“While intending to speak useful things, I mixed in useless things and, worse still, highly harmful ones; I compensated serious matters with amusements. I did not heed the promise, ‘Woe to you who laugh’ (Luke VI, 25), and even raised my voice in laughter, which is characteristic of fools.

“Although heaven and earth were watching, I most wretchedly raised my voice without keeping before my eyes that I shall have to render an account to God not only of my actions but also of my thoughts.”

A sluggish torpor of this kind also seized me, so that I could scarcely complete, much less add anything to, the prescribed and legitimate offices of the synaxis during these unhappy days. Hence I grieve that they were entirely interrupted, though not sufficiently the necessary efforts of my embassy. For, as I—most deceived—perceive, the difficulty of attaining a return arises from this, and it is no small difficulty.

### 30.

“Since you perceive this difficulty,” you say, “I advise you, at least as a matter of necessity, to discharge the unceasing duties of thanksgiving to the one who inspires it.”

[Note: If you read *suadeo* (“I advise”), the sense is quite coherent. “Since you perceive,” you say—that is, since you perceive that the difficulty of returning arises from this—I advise you at least necessarily to discharge the uninterrupted duties of thanksgiving to the one who inspires you, namely God, who inspires this awareness in you. But it seems to me that, if you were able, you ought to investigate more deeply the causes of such ineffectiveness.]

“It seems to me,” you continue, “that, if you are able, you ought to investigate more deeply the causes of this ineffectiveness. For it may be that the prohibition of the Law—which, astonishingly, you said you could bear by touching on it only briefly—generates this kind of difficulty.”

[Note: This is the prohibition in Leviticus XXI, verse 17, which he had previously mentioned in section 21: “For it is astonishing that I can endure this, while I hear him crying out against me and those like me: ‘Whoever has a blemish…’”]

“It certainly does,” I reply, “it certainly does, as you infer. Indeed, so that you may know it—and so that the whole company of readers may know it—I have, as far as I can, carefully examined how I perceive that everything noted there applies to me.”

[Col. 0422D]

[Note: “There,” that is, in the prohibition of the Law of Leviticus mentioned earlier and repeated shortly afterward, where the person is barred from the altar not only if he has a blemish but also if he is blind, lame, and so forth.]

“For in the single blemish noted there, my unworthiness—especially in receiving the Eucharist—can be recognized. Come now: ‘The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to Aaron your brother, and say to him: Any man who is a priest from the seed of Aaron, throughout his families, who has a blemish shall not offer bread to his God, nor approach his ministry’” (Lev. XXI, 17).

As for the blemish of which I spoke, let this suffice—would that it were the only one! Yet among those that follow, not one is absent. 277

“If he is blind” (Lev. XXI, 18): I cannot deny that I am so, when the gait of those who see is taken into consideration.

“If he is lame”: I cannot deny this either, since, through weakness of mind, I cannot follow even the good that I see.

“If he has a small nose”: I confess that I am such, since I cannot maintain a certain kind of breath—or discernment—in my actions or plans, being far too headlong.

“If he has a small, large, or crooked nose”: because I often confuse the rectitude of action [or: the rectitude of action itself] under the appearance of discernment.

“If he has a broken foot or hand”: who would not notice this in me? For, being unable to proceed along the Lord’s way, as you heard a little earlier, I idly and sluggishly remain inactive in good works, as though I had a broken hand.

“If he is humpbacked”: would that, Lord, I were not so burdened either by the yoke of iniquity or by the earthly weight of anxiety!

“If he is bleary-eyed”: who does not see that, although some light of knowledge flashes forth in me through divine grace, carnal works miserably obscure it [or: obscure it]?

“If he has a white spot in his eye”: and how great the blindness of my arrogance is, partly known to God alone and partly to me, I am able to tell no one. I usually call its invasion the assault of the spirit of vainglory, reckoning it the cause of all evils.

“If he has a continual itch”: when what I have considered above is weighed—namely, from when I began to indulge in wantonness and how long I have continued—if you understand that the itch signifies lust, you will recognize that it applies to me especially, and I do not deny this. Clearly, it is generated by the assault of lust itself.

“Where there is pride, there will also be insult,” since I am said to know this most certainly, while I see that even the weakness of age itself cannot contradict it.

“If he has an eruption on his body”: I do not deny that this applies to me especially.

Would that I had been free from avarice—or at least from as much of it as I seem to possess!

“If he is heavy”: woe to me, most wretched, who, even when I have not practiced shameful conduct bodily, have felt myself weighed down by the same thing in spirit almost all the time, right up to this old age—and, miserable man that I am, I do not cease to feel it.

Sullied by these blemishes, along with many others, I confess that until now I have offered bread to the Lord despite the prohibition; and that what is a remedy of salvation for those who offer worthily I have made for myself a judgment of eternal condemnation.

[Note: Construe this as follows: “This can certainly be regarded, as you said it could be, as an indication of the difficulty I suffer in returning to the Lord.”]

This can certainly be regarded, as you said it could, as an indication of the difficulty I suffer in returning to the Lord.

### 31.

But what I can do, I see not at all. For a long time I have been accustomed almost always to ask the Lord that, once forgiveness of my sins had been granted, he remove from me the desire for the world and the desires of the flesh—desires with which I have labored throughout the night no less than any thirty-year-old sleeper or wakeful person; and even now, as I write, I feel that I, nearly seventy years old, am being titillated by them.

I also pray that he remove the appetite for human praise. You can observe how deeply it exists in me even in these amusements, which I seem to seek despite my resistance, and which I feel are thrust upon me by the impulse of the spirit of vainglory.

[Note: The reading was *facetus* (“witty” or “clever”). The context supports the correction. The sentence should be construed thus: “I also pray that he remove the appetite for human praise, which you can observe to exist deeply within me even in these amusements, which I seem to seek despite my resistance, and which I feel are thrust upon me by the impulse of the spirit of vainglory; and I pray that he remove also the vice of laziness and torpor, which makes me run about everywhere not so much bodily as mentally; likewise, that he remove inconstancy and fickleness of mind, hardness and duplicity of heart, corrupt speech of heart and mouth. In justly reproving all these things in me, I infer with you that they arise because, although I have implored God’s mercy and grace as I ought in order to be delivered from them, I, foolish man, do not compel myself to cooperate as I should, so that my free choice may be restored; and this harms me more than it helps me.”]

I pray also that he remove the vice which makes me run about everywhere not so much bodily as mentally—the vice of laziness and torpor—as well as inconstancy and fickleness of mind, hardness and duplicity of heart, corrupt speech of heart and mouth.

In justly reproving all these things in me together with you, I infer that they arise because, although God’s mercy and grace have been invoked as they ought, so that I may be delivered from these things, I, foolish man, do not compel myself to cooperate as I should, so that free choice may be restored; and this harms me more than it helps me.

While I neglect to contribute what depends on me, I prove that I deceitfully ask for what depends on God. For example, I ask for the shore of continence after the shipwreck of chastity; but I absolutely do not wish to impose upon myself either mortification of the flesh or flight from fornication.

### 32.

I confess that there is also another thing that considerably obstructs the paths of my embassy. For everything that is necessary for anyone, nothing is as suitable as that unique sacrifice which represents our Passover to us every day—namely, Christ, truly sacrificed for us.

If I were to offer this gift worthily—though I do not attain that worthiness—even if not daily, at least often, I think that no embassy could compare with it in obtaining what is sought, as many say.

But I am hindered by what I hear: “Go first and be reconciled to your brother” (Matt. V, 24).

But if we are all brothers in Christ, our head, who is less likely to be offended by him, so that he may not have something against us of which we must be still more afraid? Yet he does have two things against me, I confess: both that I have wounded his members, and that I do not cease to wound him himself.

And since days and nights are not enough merely for reconciliation, I ask: when will an opportunity be given to offer the gift?

But I presume that an opportunity would be given to him if the gift were reconciliation, if satisfaction had been made to one’s neighbors. I confess that I have nowhere wounded them more than in the matter concerning which the Savior gives this grave warning—consider how seriously he declares it:

“Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble,” he says, “it would be better for him that a millstone be hung around his neck and that he be drowned in the depths of the sea” (Matt. XVIII, 6).

### After some intervening material

### 33.

“You seem to me,” you say, “to be evading the issue excessively, and, like the neck of Ennius’s bird, to change color along with movement. For now I marvel at excessive severity in you, now at the greatest softness; now at something like fervor, then at tepidity; now at steadfastness, now I observe dissolution; now you seem to me sincere—and would that this were so even occasionally!—now feigned, so that, alas, you always seem to report everything, while also concealing certain things by confessing them in a pitiable manner. This is like that first matter, which, although I recognized it no less than you did, remains hidden from me as I read, as though it had not been said at all.”

“So it is,” I reply; “I confess that it is so, and I demonstrate it equally by my actions.

“Nevertheless, regarding what you say, because I realized that it would be worse if it were open to everyone, I thought it enough if, by whatever means, you alone could thereby become better informed.

“While I address you, I see before me anyone with eyes—such as the rule transgressed by us prescribes—who knows how to care for his own affairs and not expose or publicize the wounds of others.

“For you must not forget what you heard earlier concerning the confession that had been neglected for so long.”

“Why, then,” you ask, “and to whom do you confess, if you want to remain hidden?”

“To God,” I reply, “and to me.”

“Why to God?”

“Not so that he may know,” I reply—for nothing can remain unknown to one who cannot be ignorant—but so that he may deign to forgive.

“For I hear the Prophet also presuming to say this, so that I may be able to say with somewhat greater truth and security: ‘My sin is always before me’ (Ps. L, 5)—which certainly would not have been the case if it had not happened that I wrote it down; and I rejoice at the saying: ‘Blessed is the one who is always fearful’ (Prov. XXVIII, 14). And: ‘A heart that knows the bitterness of its own soul will not admit a stranger into its joy’ (Prov. XIV, 10).”

“But it would have been better,” you say, “to have written it on the tablets of your heart.”

“Better,” I reply, “better indeed; yet I think it is more excellent both there and here.”

“We have the Apostle confessing on parchment made from sheep,” following Augustine’s example: “I was formerly a blasphemer, persecutor, and insolent man” (I Tim. I, 13).

“From this,” you say, “some temptation of pride, empty glory, or at least vain security may steal upon you.”

“Almost to the point,” I reply, “of deadly despair.

“For when I hear that ‘the righteous person is first an accuser of himself’ (Prov. XVIII, 17), the most miserable folly—or the most foolish misery—murmurs to me in my wretchedness that, in this respect, I am an unhappy imitator of some righteous people. And I see that, if matters proceed in this way, I am being treated as though no more conspicuous monster had ever been given to the earth—though I am the most wretched and ruined of men.

“For since pride—that is, ambition—has always been the cause of ruin, it seems to me that the ruin within me is worse than I had thought, because humility itself is an exaltation.”

[Note: Construe this as follows: “It seems to me that the ruin within me is worse than I had thought, because humility itself is an exaltation.”]

“For I grow proud precisely because I regard myself as utterly despised and certainly beneath everyone, whereas others usually glory in what makes them see themselves superior to others.

“Unless I at least avoided disgraceful speech in this matter, I could unfold it in an apostolic example worthy of it. But since eloquence fails me, and I cannot express what I suffer from myself, although outwardly I see myself to be well known to you, so that inwardly I may not remain hidden from you as well, I direct you to Gregory the God-speaking. Ask him what he thinks about the rejected hypocrites and the arrogant; draw it from him. There you will be able to see me whole.”

“In avoiding solecisms,” you say—“that is, errors of construction—you seem to be more perceptive about language than about reasoning, and about words than about actions. For you are plainly more eager, if it should succeed, to seem eloquent than to carry out yourself what you speak well.”

[Note: Construe this as follows: “But in avoiding solecisms—that is, errors—you seem more perceptive about construction than about reasoning, and about words than about actions, since you are plainly more eager, if it should succeed, to seem eloquent than to carry out yourself what you speak well.”]

“I gladly see you planting a grove, contrary to the prohibition, in the house of the Lord, since you are so devoted to arranging little trees.”

“Wait,” I reply, “wait. You will see more clearly who I am, I promise; yet the swelling once conceived will not, for that reason, be restrained.”

### 34

The Psalmist says: “If I have regarded iniquity in my heart, the Lord will not hear” (Ps. 65:18). Although this may be understood in one way or another according to one’s discretion, the Lord says: “If you do not forgive people their sins, neither will your heavenly Father forgive you” (Mark 11:25). And elsewhere: “Whoever turns his ear away from the cry of the poor will himself cry out and not be heard” (Prov. 21:13). Like the hypocrite Herod, because they seek God deceitfully, they never deserve to find him.

Yet no one more frequently and continuously devotes himself to psalmody, celebrates the solemn rites of Mass more often, gives the necessities of life to the poor, or applies himself more earnestly to preaching. In all these matters, I confess—especially by my own experience—that I see with the greatest clarity that the iniquity of which he speaks is precisely the duplicity that I recognize in myself. For, as though with two tongues, I recite two different things: psalms or something else to those who hear, but other things, innumerable and altogether dissimilar, to the Searcher of hearts.

**Note:** That is, I recite psalms orally to those listening, but in my heart I recite other, innumerable things utterly unlike them to God, the Searcher of hearts.

Thus, on this very night, the one whose morning this is—the vigil, that is, of the apostles Philip and James—when, as often happens, I was kept awake by the adversary, although it would certainly have been more useful for me to sleep, I lay down while still swollen with anger over what had happened to me contrary to my wish. For it had been reported that your Bonito had distributed wool to the brothers by your order, without my authorization. As I exaggerated to myself the fact that this and other things were taking place here unlawfully, and, while awake, brought their phantoms before my mind, I came in thought to the place where the following is contained in the rule that we wretches renounced:

> “Let him do nothing without the abbot’s command.”
