**Note:** That is, I came to the place where this is found in the rule—the monastic rule, naturally—which we wretches abandoned. It contains, as I say, the principle that we former little abbots embrace so passionately, with that particular love of ourselves rather than of God: “Without the abbot’s command, let him do nothing.” The author calls himself a “little abbot” out of humility, or perhaps because he presided not over a more distinguished and principal monastery, such as Lobbes was, but over some lesser monastery, which we have conjectured in the previously mentioned passage of his Life to have been Alne.

As I brooded over this and gathered reasons for punishment, I began to consider whether there might be some other reason why we should gape so eagerly after a dignity of this kind. I could find absolutely none.

When the time for Matins came, I recited the psalm with my mouth, but cried out in my heart:

> “O most foolish Oderad, was this what you did not hesitate to buy for eighty pounds, although you were thought to be extremely stingy?—for in this way, wretched men that we are, we often err in court concerning our own affairs.”

**Note:** Oderad is the monk whom Ratherius proved guilty of simoniacal purchase in section 22; compare the note there, n. 544. Here we learn what he bought: evidently some ecclesiastical office, or perhaps a small abbey among those monasteries dependent upon the principal monastery of Lobbes. After proving Oderad’s purchase, Ratherius immediately turns the accusation against himself when he says, “Be silent, be silent, I warn you; I warn you, I say,” and so forth, making himself guilty of a much greater crime. We shall explain by conjecture what sort of crime this was at the end of note 65. Ratherius’ practice, however, is to attack the faults of others while exaggerating his own, even when his own are much lighter.

“Be silent, be silent, I warn you! I warn you, hypocrite, be silent!” I began at once to cry. “Look at yourself; leave him alone. Cast the beam out of your own eye, and then, if you wish or are able, remove the speck from your brother’s eye. For, to confess the truth most fully, in comparison with the stupidity you marvel at, your own is a most massive beam, while his is a very slender speck.”

**Note:** He denotes a wandering of the mind which, while he was attending Matins, rushed upon him amid the chanting of the psalms, stirred by a recent event: someone had come from the city of Liège to the monastery with a great retinue. He does not say who this was. Though he speaks somewhat obscurely and enigmatically, Fulcuin, in *The Deeds of the Abbots of Lobbes*, ch. 26, relates that Baldric, bishop of Liège, came to the monastery of Lobbes with his uncle Count Raginer, to whom that bishop had given the abbey of Lobbes, and that they were splendidly entertained there to the great detriment of the common resources. We believe that something similar happened to the monastery over which Ratherius presided, as this passage indicates when he complains of money spent by him on that occasion. The clerics and monks who received the arrival with sacred song suggest that some distinguished ecclesiastic, on whom Ratherius’ monastery depended, arrived with a retinue. This may perhaps have been the aforesaid Baldric, bishop of Liège, to whose see the monastery of Alne belonged; after Ratherius had been expelled from that see, Alne was, as we have plausibly conjectured in §11 of the author’s *Life*, granted him from the same see as a means of support. On this interpretation, *nuper* (“recently”) is used more broadly, meaning “not long before,” and should be referred to the year 958 or the beginning of 959, since Baldric died in that year.

And behold, amid those honey-sweet songs of the hymns, there suddenly burst upon my mind the great army recently received from Liège: an immeasurable multitude of servants—and of what sort! The neighing of the most noble horses, differing in a thousand ways; the equipment of mastrucae and other garments, table furnishings, benches, curtains, and the most various possible array of other conveniences; the sound of the most noble clerics and hooded monks, sweeter than the song of swans; a noble, countless, beautiful, and beloved crowd of kinsmen; and also, if I am to remember the poorer people, a weeping and wailing crowd, seeing that it was being left behind.

**Note:** That is, a noble, countless, beautiful, and beloved crowd of kinsmen rushed in—those who had flocked to the monastery on the occasion mentioned. A crowd also rushed in, weeping and wailing because it saw itself being left behind.

**Note:** These most noble clerics and monks, singing sweetly, had gone out to meet the arriving visitor. Among others, the author of the *Life of Lietbert, Bishop of Cambrai*, ch. 21, attests this ecclesiastical custom: when he came to Laon, he says, all went out to meet him according to ecclesiastical custom.

The forebodings of their abandonment rushed in upon me; innumerable and dangerous labors of journeys, expenses, and illnesses endured for this one principle; money, in my case a very large amount, dissipated on that account through a payment; and when I had turned my thoughts solely toward it, recalling and considering that most precious garment of his, which I had brought here and which had also been acquired through the clearest sacrilege, I could have breathed out my life in the most dreadful grief, if nature had allowed me to die of sorrow.

**Note:** Construct and explain the passage as follows: “The forebodings of their abandonment rushed into my mind”—that is, of the clerics and monks. But what is meant by *desertitudo*, “abandonment”? Could it mean desertion in the sense of dissipation? For *deserto*, “I abandon,” was used in the Middle Ages for “I dissipate”; several examples are confirmed by Du Cange. In this sense the dissipation of the monastery’s goods through the splendid reception of so many and such important guests may be indicated. In a similar case concerning the monastery of Lobbes, Fulcuin, in the passage cited, says: “They lament in common that the brothers are being diminished so that others may gorge themselves.” The author of the *Gesta abbatum Gemblacensium* likewise reports that the monks cried out and complained that their goods were being lavishly squandered and that the substance of the monastery was being excessively consumed by the banquets of secular persons.

When Ratherius says that they had endured the labors of journeys, expenses, and illnesses “for this one principle,” he means the principle that he had shortly before said the abbots embraced so passionately: “Without the abbot’s command, let him do nothing.” Since it was for this reason that the title and authority of abbot were sought, some endured innumerable and dangerous journeys, expenses, and illnesses in order to obtain this office. Thus, for example, Oderad’s journeys and returns undertaken for the same purpose were touched upon in section 24, and the expense of eighty pounds, by which he bought the title of abbot, had been mentioned shortly before.

Finally, do the words “money, in my case a very large amount, dissipated through a payment on that account” indicate the twenty-two pounds that Ratherius confessed in section 23 to have spent from the monastery’s goods? If this is considered probable, these twenty-two pounds, like the precious garment that he says he brought here, ought to be described as having been dissipated on that account—that is, for the same principle, or for the sake of the office that he seems later to imply he acquired by some purchase.

Since he had set aside those twenty-two pounds from the monastery’s revenues after he had become abbot and was administering them—for before such administration he could not have taken anything from those revenues to contribute toward acquiring the abbey itself—it cannot be said that he initially bought and acquired the rank of abbot with those same pounds. We have seen that Ratherius was initially placed in charge of the monastery not by any price or purchase, but by a certain arrangement, so that, having been excluded from the see of Liège, he might live from the revenues of that monastery.

Everything mentioned here, as the context makes clear, occurred on the occasion when, not long before, a distinguished ecclesiastic from Liège—apparently Baldric, bishop of Liège—arrived at the monastery with a large retinue. On this occasion Ratherius seems to have given him the precious garment and to have spent, in receiving this guest and his company, the twenty-two pounds that, as he had said earlier, necessity had forced him to take from the monastery’s revenues. Unless someone prefers to understand from the word “payment” that he also gave those same pounds to Baldric—either because money was customarily offered on such visits, or because Ratherius feared that Baldric, who had expelled him from the see of Liège, would also expel him from the little abbey that he had received permanently as a means of support under the terms of their arrangement, unless he conciliated him by some gift.

What others might perhaps have called the redemption of an obligation, Ratherius portrays as a kind of simoniacal purchase; for it is his habit not only to criticize his own deeds but also to exaggerate them. Indeed, he exaggerated this act so much that for this reason he presents himself as guilty of a much greater offense than Oderad, who had acquired another abbey through open simony for eighty pounds.

The confessor, judging the matter more mildly in section 36, says: “Whatever way it was granted to you”—he means the rank of abbot—“you ought not to have valued it so cheaply. For whatever I see you grieving over as lost because of what you spent or gave for such a thing, even if it had been Arabian gold, would in every way have been safe if heavenly grace had given you the resolve to live thereafter as you described in the few words of the rule itself.”

What is meant by the precious garment that he had brought with him when he came to the monastery, and in what sense it is said to have been acquired through “the clearest sacrilege”—whether through the exaggeration apparently characteristic of Ratherius—is entirely unknown.

Thus the forebodings of those men rushed upon me. They had endured innumerable and dangerous labors of journeys, expenses, and illnesses for this one principle; and money, in my case a very large amount, had on that account been dissipated through a payment. When I had turned my thoughts solely toward it, recalling the precious garment of his which I had brought here and considering that it too had been acquired through the clearest sacrilege, I could have expired in the most terrible grief, if nature had granted me death.

This matter, brought before the eyes of my mind, made me groan and sigh so deeply that, if someone had happened to be standing outside the door, he could have thought that I was being tortured by that affliction so familiar to me. At last, when these thoughts had been removed for a little while, I began to consider what benefit you might expect in the future world from something purchased in this world at so great a cost, as you see.

**Note:** Construct the sentence as follows: “I desire to know what benefit you will have begun to possess in the future world from something purchased—or because of something purchased—in this world at so great a cost, as you consider.” What is meant by the purchased object seems to be explained by what follows, when he says of the title of abbot: “Behold what you acquired most unhappily at so great a price—not only of money but also of innumerable labors.” This suits Oderad rather than Ratherius. As for the way Ratherius, by exaggeration, attributes to himself a kind of purchase, see the preceding note.

And behold, once again before the gaze of my heart came that dove sold from the Temple; behold, in the hand of Jesus, the whip made from cords; behold, that terrible expulsion from the Temple; behold, the curse of Simon; behold, the dreadful leprosy of Gehazi, together with the condemnation and anathema of Ananias and Sapphira, who received what ought to have been given and received freely.

“Without the abbot’s command,” the rule says, “let him do nothing.”

Behold what you acquired most unhappily at so great a price—not only of money but also of innumerable labors. But do not take the following superficially when you hear it, I warn you:

> “The abbot himself, however, must do everything with fear of God and in accordance with the ordering of the rule.”

And again:

> “Let the abbot know that whatever useful thing the master of the household finds lacking in the sheep is laid to the shepherd’s account. Therefore he must neither teach, establish, nor command anything contrary to the Lord’s precept—God forbid—always mindful that, in the dread judgment of God, an account will have to be rendered both of his teaching and of the obedience of his disciples.”

### 35

So you rejoice because nothing is done without your command? See what you command. You demand obedience; establish the principle on which you demand it. They are obliged to obey you, while you are obliged to obey the rule. They sin if they act outside your will and ordering; you sin if you arrange or command anything contrary to the rule’s constitution.

“Let him indicate in his own deeds,” the rule says, “that all the things he teaches his disciples to be contrary are not to be done. Let him know that he who has undertaken the governance of souls must necessarily prepare himself to render an account; and in proportion as he knows that he has under his care a certain number of brothers, let him recognize with certainty that on the day of judgment he will have to render an account to God for all their souls, doubtless with his own soul included in the reckoning.”

O most foolish vanity! With so many labors, so many hardships, tribulations, pains, and anxieties; with so great a price in this world and so many punishments in hell, to have bought the mere title of “Rabbi” from human beings—

**Note:** “To have bought being called Rabbi by human beings,” that is, to have bought an office because of which you are called abbot.

—when the Judge himself, who will come, has instructed us, saying: “Do not be called Rabbi” (Matt. 23:8). It is as though he said: “Do not desire in this world that honor for which, once deprived of the honor that the Apostle, eagerly attempting to describe it, was unable to express—‘What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart’ (1 Cor. 2:9)—you will suffer such great and likewise indescribable torments in hell.”

As I consider the very hot heaps of curses rushing upon me like the most violent billows of the Euxine Sea, I confess that, most wretched as I am, I can find no breath of confidence in my salvation. These curses alone, not to mention those joined to them, compel me not to breathe in any hope. Among them the first, though directed later, presents itself. I want you to hear what it is in the words of Gregory himself, who uttered it:

> “Just as one who, when invited, refuses, and when sought, withdraws, ought to be promoted to the sacred altars, so one who voluntarily seeks office or thrusts himself forward too insistently must unquestionably be rejected. For what does he do who strives to climb to higher things, except that by rising he declines? Why does he not consider that the blessing is turned into a curse for the one who is promoted in order to become a heretic?”

**Note:** Attend to what a curse this is, and how deadly. The following curses of this kind come after it, although they ought to have preceded it: “Cursed are those who turn away from your commandments” (Ps. 118:21); “Cursed is the one who announces to my father, saying, ‘A male child has been born to you’” (Jer. 20:15; 48:10); “Cursed is the one who keeps his sword from blood” (Jer. 17:5); “Cursed is the one who, so that his heart may depart from the Lord, places his hope in a human being” (Jer. 48:10); “Cursed is the one who performs the work of the Lord negligently” (ibid.). There are now other curses that cannot be recalled. Nothing in me is more astonishing than the fact that I am able to remember them, much less write or recount them, with dry eyes. In this, I confess, you can see more clearly than daylight the hardness of my heart.

### 36

“As you say, so it is,” you reply. Although I never cease to marvel at the instability of your fickleness, I am no longer surprised that something of this kind could happen to you bodily at this stage of your life—as that other event did, which I know—since I still see you behaving so wantonly in spiritual matters.

From your own writing and words I infer what you are pretending: that you do not meditate on these matters with a sufficiently sincere heart. For if you had truly deliberated about returning to the Lord—that is, about conversion from evil to good—you ought not, in whatever way it was granted to you, to have valued this so cheaply. Whatever I see you grieving over as lost because of what you spent or gave for such a thing, even if it had been Arabian gold, would have been entirely safe if it had been divinely granted you, whatever sort of person you had formerly been, to live thereafter as you described in the few words of the rule itself.

But, since Scripture says, “Whoever watches the wind will not sow, and whoever considers the clouds will not reap” (Eccles. 11:4), I see you as so weak, fainthearted, timid, fickle, double-minded, and excessively enervated by sloth that I would have been forced utterly to despair of your rescue, unless I were considering the immeasurable riches of the almighty mercy, goodness, and freely given compassion of God, bestowed innumerably against hope from the beginning of the world.

So that you may understand that I am addressing you in prophetic words, I ask you to consider how worthless you have become, “repeating your ways” (Jer. 2:36). And while you most truthfully write yourself down as a grievous sinner, I ask you to heed the warning: “Do not repeat the word in your prayer” (Ecclus. 7:15). Consider what a washed sow gains by returning to the mud (2 Pet. 2:22), and remember how much the dog, returning to its vomit, offends the eyes of the one who sees it.

You should recall with proper shame that you have already made cycles and revolutions of turning toward and turning away from the Lord through those vices over which I grieve that you still labor. Even now, while you stand in what is surely your final hour, fix your mind upon stability. “A foolish person changes like the moon” (Ecclus. 27:12); whether what was dreamed about you, as you were accustomed to act, was true or not, it can nevertheless, beyond doubt, be seen to fit you exceedingly well.

How many times you have shone, then again been darkened, through the vicissitudes of fortune and misfortune, conversion and aversion! Once more, as I might say, the transmarine earth is already singing of your being darkened again. “We treated Babylon on your account,” says the Lord, “but she was not healed” (Jer. 51:9): your wretched confusion still sprouts anew.

“You have acquired the forehead of a prostitute; you refused to be ashamed” (Jer. 3:3). Unless you had been blind in mind, you could have recognized that this was spoken of you, when you were able to recount such things—so many, so great, and so countless—without shame or groaning, and even to narrate things that, as the Apostle commands, ought not to be named (Eph. 5:3) as though they were honorable, and, if you had been able, pompously as well.

But I see what you are most shamelessly attempting. Since you see that everyone embraces the statement, “The righteous man is the first to accuse himself” (Prov. 18:17), and since many of your accomplices do the same, you prefer to adorn yourself with a confession of sins that ought to be mourned beyond words rather than to humble yourself. Therefore, although you speak most truthfully when you call yourself a sinner, you would cunningly persuade your hearers, if you could, that you say this more from humility than from truth. For if you wished to appear and be called a sinner to the extent that you write, you would not have grieved so greatly that I had made you known.

If you cannot persuade them that you are righteous—for no one fails to see that you are not clear-sighted—then persuade at least some of them that you are learned. Thus I am certain that you do not examine your life by the examples of better people, nor consider your own foulness or the duplicity of your fickleness. Nor do you consider yourself reproved when you hear: “A double-minded man is unstable in all his ways.” And what Sallustius [is understood to have] said to Cicero—that one should trust neither this man nor that, neither Caesar nor Pompey—certainly applies to you. For you are shown to preserve no constancy of faith, so to speak, either toward the Lord or toward the adversary whom you obey.

### 37

To repay you in kind—for since you proposed to recount your crimes, as you claimed, you began with mine—I shall end with yours. I will reveal the craft with which you handled the matter.

Although you pretended that the matter was completely unclear to you, and although you feared that I would expose you, you opposed my affairs to the matters I was to attend to, sufficiently cunningly in your own view but in reality with excessive deceitfulness, so that I would leave your matters alone. And what you pursued at such length concerning the violation of the rule, as I believe I see, you did not seem to do for any other reason than that, by the magnitude of that offense, you might somehow lessen the gravity of the deed that I knew you had committed—whether through the vanity of arrogance or through restlessness.

I, I say, like a thief caught in this matter also, do not know at all what I should answer. Yet, if I do what is appropriate, I do it in bewilderment, unable sufficiently to understand why God either permitted or wished me to do this.

“As I see it,” you say, “what you read in the dialogue already mentioned about a certain exceedingly wealthy Chrysarius has slipped from your mind” (Gregory, *Dialogues* IV.38). When he was dying, Chrysarius saw the adversaries of the human race pressing upon him. He asked for a postponement until morning, but did not receive it, nor could he conceal from those standing around him what he was suffering.

From the authority of the same holy Gregory it is therefore clear that, while alive, he saw such things for our sake, not for his own, without the benefit of usefulness to himself. Thus, I think, you may judge the same about this remarkable act of yours: if it does not benefit you, perhaps it may benefit readers, when they recognize in themselves things such as they may think you confessed about yourself with good intention, since Scripture says, “A friend comes, and he will investigate him” (Prov. 18:17).

Although the Scripture speaks of a friend, one better than you, rather than of future things, you may nevertheless know truthfully that they will discover you to have heaped up such material rather from a desire for display and applause, and from that innate restlessness of mind—already demonstrated so very often—and from the exceptionally strong love you bear for your own inventions, which is known to be closely allied to arrogance.

Therefore, you ought not to have been surprised when, a little earlier, you said confidently—or perhaps, “with confidence”—that you were able to utter such things with dry eyes. For what fire of charity could melt the ice of coldness that is in you into streams of tears?

Since you are wholly wax, it is certainly not surprising if a little tear is sometimes drawn from you. That it proceeds from instability, as from that Balaam—or rather from Balaam’s example—rather than from wholesome contrition is clearly proved by the fact that you cannot shed any tears unless someone sees you, or unless you see another weeping before you. The excessive hilarity that immediately follows so often also shows that this is true.

But consider how much the inward Judge values such weeping:

> “Daughters of Jerusalem,” he says, “do not weep over me, but over yourselves” (Luke 23:28).

The person who weeps over another and not over himself is one who, moved by another’s goodness, neglects to imitate the good by which he himself is moved. Tears that arise from a place where the weeping spirit has no concern may rightly be counted as wasted.

You plainly lack the necessary counselor who formerly cried out inwardly—your very dear counselor, as I see it—urging you:

> “Pour out tears like a torrent by day and by night, and let not the pupil of your eye be silent” (Lam. 3:18).

Then you could, as would be fitting, bring forth in your final hour, at least against the accusers pressing upon you, the words:

> “Let my eye pour down streams of water” (Lam. 3:48),

since those accusers will certainly calumniate you by saying that you have not properly wept, amended, repented, or ever inwardly desired to amend any of your crimes, despite having written about them:

> “Who will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes, that I may weep over my contrition, not to mention that of my people”—that is, of the flock entrusted to me? (Jer. 9:1).

For, while you sang concerning your neighbor:

> “Howl, shepherds, and cry out; sprinkle yourselves with ashes”;  
> “Mourn like a virgin, my people” (Jer. 25:34; Joel 1:8),

who ever saw in your face anything not merely of sadness but even of gravity? Who saw tears in your eyes, as would have been fitting, according to what you had written, for a criminal?

Who, I say, ever heard a fitting sigh for your own sins—so grave, so numerous, and so foul—not to mention the sins of those entrusted to you, when, most wretchedly and to your own detriment, you were doubly numbered among the shepherds?

**Note:** The manuscript copy read *impastorum*, incorrectly. But the sense requires *in pastorum*. The sentence should be understood as follows: “Who, I say, ever heard a fitting sigh for your own sins, so grave, so numerous, and so foul, not to mention the sins of those entrusted to you, when, most wretchedly and to your own detriment, you were doubly numbered among the shepherds?” This is because he was both bishop and abbot.

At that time, certainly, like many others, out of reverence for those three days you were abstinent, silent, and writing down your crimes, preparing, as it were, an unleavened Passover. But, as it turned out, rustic lettuces escaped the notice of the careless cook; without them you ought not to have believed that you were permitted to eat the Paschal Lamb, slain for you.

**Note:** The “three days” are Maundy Thursday, Good Friday, and Holy Saturday, during which much of this confession was written by Ratherius.

Even then, I confess, you were already foreshadowing that one day you would forget what is now done. You were already indicating by certain signs that, after Easter, you would not even think of, much less say, what you had exclaimed to me:

> “Let us not sin, I say. What more is there to sin? Sin has been committed in abundance.”

It was as though you had already resolved not to sin further. But, following Balaam’s example, you now begin to offer counsel for scandal through the very virtues that you had blessed. You are already returning like a dog to its vomit; already wallowing in the same mud in which you were previously immersed; already disregarding what you said from the pulpit at Easter ought to be avoided—namely, that after Lent had passed we, foolishly, should not destroy the house built during Lent, or burn it by introducing fire, and thus bring back the unclean spirit expelled from us through penitence, returning with seven others (Matt. 12:45).

For now you are growing fat again; it seems that you may choose how and on what you are fed. You are scarcely restrained from wantonness; you run idly here and there. You who had been silent quarrel and slander. You begin skillfully to reconcile yourself with the security most familiar to you, as I may put it, because you had left it for a short time; and, taking care that it should not lose its strength, you mix obscene speech with deceits.

Although you had made no effort to avoid *racha*, you feared to say “fool.”

**Note:** The copy read “Yvi racha.” We did not hesitate to insert *Cui* instead of *Yvi*, since it fits the sense better. There is also some difficulty in what follows. The passage seems to be constructed as follows: “You feared to speak foolishly, although you had made no effort at all to avoid *racha*; now that you have found even thousands of insults, you are not afraid to cross the boundaries of Lent, nor do you fear exceeding them even with your hands.”

Now that you have found even thousands of insults, you are not afraid to transgress Lent, nor do you fear exceeding its limits even with your hands.

By stages such as these you move backward, although you pretended that you wished to return to the Lord, who is set on high. You clearly fall, although you lied to me that you wished to rise. By asserting that you have escaped from your former way of life, you reveal how highly you still value it.

38. But what is more? Let others see what they think of you; to me you seem to have become worse than the worst, on the evidence of this kind of confession, if there is lacking that inward and continual groaning which must be given to you through God’s mercy and therefore sought from him without interruption [or: which must be sought], and which you both confess is not in you and I see is not in you. For if a sleeping man sees nothing, that is natural; but just as it is evident that a man who is awake sees, so it is also evident that he is responsible for himself if he neglects to avoid the one who is set before him to destroy him.

[Note: Construe: “But just as it is evident that a man who is awake sees, so it is also evident that he is responsible for himself if he neglects to avoid the one who is set before him to destroy him.”]

How many destroyers of your soul you see placed before you, and yet you neglect to avoid destruction by groaning at least, if you cannot do so by worthy repentance; and you compel me not to despair of you.

[Note: That is, “it compels me also not to despair of you.”]

For what good, miserable man, do you suppose it does to have recognized what is impending, if it happens that you have not escaped?

You see that, though you are a priest, you are barred from offering loaves to God, and you do not grieve at all? You see that the Lord’s curses are hurled against you, and you cannot weep? Truth calls you a thief and a robber, yet you neither wish to return what you stole nor abandon what you seized by force; nor do you at least mingle tears or some sighs, your spirit struck with terror, not only for the theft and robbery, but even for the very stubbornness of refusing to amend?

You see that you lack the wedding garment of the flesh; and at the marriage feast of Christ and the Church, with your feet and hands bound, you do not fear lest you be shamefully thrust out to be cast into the fiery furnace, but dare at least to recline there without tears? You hear the anathema pronounced against the recipient, and is it impossible for you to weep?

“You and your money be with you for destruction” (Acts 8:20), you hear the Apostle Peter saying to Simon Magus, and, so that destruction may be turned away from you, you do not ask for prayer [that is, you do not pray]?

You see Ananias and Sapphira expire for a sacrilege also committed by you, and is it utterly impossible for you to weep? You see Gehazi’s leprosy, and do you not wash your leprous soul clean with tears?

You have violated God’s temple in yourself and in others; you have carried away your Father’s offering from the Lord; and while acting boldly in the house of God’s Church, you confidently place the offerings of the faithful upon his altar without tears?

You see that you lack wild lettuce, and dare to eat the Lamb of God? You do not have unleavened bread, and presume upon the Passover? You feel within yourself the leaven of malice and wickedness, and dare to feast in the Lord—or at least to think that you do?

You do not fail to know that many have many charges against you, and yet you bring gifts before the altar? You hear that what you are doing is rashly prohibited, and do not desist from doing it at all?

But what if you desist? You are judged for disobedience; for since, somehow or other, you have been assigned the ministry, necessity lies upon you to fulfill it, lest you appear to have been assigned it for judgment rather than for ministry. Consider, I beg you, anxiously, how desperate and pitiable you are, caught in this twofold dilemma.

But if you had not anticipated this confession yourself, I would nevertheless fear that I might be presenting as absolutely applicable to you, and not craftily, whatever Gregory says in the *Moralia* against the reprobate, hypocrites, and arrogant men.

For, considering the loquacity of your arrogance, I seem almost to hear Elihu say:

> “I am full of words, and the spirit of my inward parts constrains me. Behold, my belly is like wine without a vent, which bursts new wineskins; I will speak, and I will breathe a little” (Job 32:18).

But you ought to have feared greatly, as should your companions in this sort of conduct, who, while you strive to rival eloquent men, imitating empty talkers, imitate philosophers more and follow *philopompoi*—lovers of labor—without noticing that you are branded by the saying:

> “A fool gives vent to all his spirit” (Prov. 29:11),

and, to add another:

> “As a city open and without the protection of walls, so is one who cannot restrain his spirit in speaking” (Prov. 25:28).

As I said, you ought to have feared lest you hear this said about yourself together with the one whom you strive to imitate; [supply: “you ought to have feared”] and lest you should also hear that saying about the whirlwind, from which you cannot be reconciled even by any sacrifice:

> “Who is this who wraps up arguments in words without knowledge?” (Job 38:2).

You can understand how far beneath that same man whom you follow you certainly are, since you do not see at all that you possess the spirit of prophecy, as he possessed it. But if such a reproach is made against a prophet, what can be said of a compiler and sycophant who, as it is written, “considers what he does not know in the likeness of a diviner and soothsayer” (Prov. 23:7)—what can be said of one so utterly vain and, worse, so mendacious?

39. But so that you may recognize how this vanity of yours is despised by the wise, consider that Saul was rejected along with them, that Caiaphas prophesied; recall the words of reason: that the ass received speech from the vision of an angel; that demons said, “We know who you are: Christ, the Son of God” (Luke 4:34); and from this you will be able to infer that, even if you are more talkative than others, you are of no importance.

For the man who suffered from a discharge of semen (Lev. 15:2), unclean according to the law, will not be conspicuous—as you strive to appear. Likewise, concerning the labors of your most restless restlessness, by which, with your neck held high and your eyebrows raised, you used to say inwardly, as your Nabuchodonosor:

> “Is this not Babylon, which I built by the strength of my dignity and power?” (Dan. 4:27),

you used to say that the Church, enlarged by you, was reduced in extent, enlarged in merits, and—though enormous in size—of construction most paltry in comparison with thousands, with no improvement whatever in religion (may the Almighty grant that there was no worsening).

[Note: This passage is greatly disordered, and perhaps also corrupt, since it seems to indicate a church enlarged by Ratherius and afterward demolished by factional men at the king’s command. We are very uncertain whether it is to be understood of a genuine material church. For it is not probable that a faction of men opposed to Ratherius raged so fiercely that they thought a temple enlarged by him should be demolished; still less is it likely that King Otto supplied authority and soldiers for so great a sacrilege. It is therefore more plausibly understood allegorically of the mystical or living Church of Liège. While he was laboring to build or enlarge it, and matters were proceeding so well that considerable glory would have come to him after his death, suddenly factional men, gathered together from the greatest to the least, arranged for the whole such edifice to be demolished by military force and royal authority, when the bishop himself was expelled from that see by public force.]

See, therefore, how worthless to everyone was what had pleased you monstrously, when those whom you had supposed would become your praisers after your death, gathered together while you were still alive, from the greatest to the least, became such revilers of those things that by royal authority and military force they demanded that the sacrilegious structures you desired to be celebrated by everyone with the highest praise should be demolished.

They did well by you; it turned out well for you, you ash-covered and blackened one, who, though you are not even a man, being in many respects without reason, and who do not understand your own honor, have been compared with foolish beasts and become no different from them (Ps. 48:13), and, if it had been granted, sought by adulterous fraud to be exalted with praises due to God alone.

[Note: The manuscript had the erroneous reading *cinerente*. We corrected it to *cinerate*, since this same word, joined with the following *cacábate*, is used by Palladius. In the *Apophthegmata of the Fathers* edited by Cotelier, chapter 4, where the demon expelled by the monk Moses is discussed, the Greek reads: “Having gone out, he said to himself, ‘They have treated you well, ash-covered black one.’” These last two words are translated in the Corbie manuscript by Palladius as *cinerate, cacabate*, as Cotelier also notes. See Du Cange’s *Glossary*, s.v. *Cacabatus*, *Cineratus*: *cineratus*, “stained with ash”; *cacabatus*, “blackened,” as a cooking pot is blackened.]

This, surely, was why you could not weep: because you thought yourself to be something through such deception. But, thanks be to God, they exposed you as you deserved to be exposed. Of you, who use the sight of a mole and of goats within yourself, we, learned and unlearned alike, write poems everywhere:

> “We write poems everywhere, learned and unlearned” (Horace, Book 2, *Epistle* 1, line 117).

See, then, what complaint you would bring even against the wise men of the world, when you presume to compose books without knowledge of doctrine—and, O how many beasts you observe while you think so highly of yourself!

If you had paid attention to human beings, you would certainly have said, “I have sinned”; if you saw the light, you would not value darkness so highly. But while you think yourself superior to beasts, while you consider yourself more clearly seeing than the blind, what swelling of heart, I ask, can you, most stupid man, conceive from that? What great thing is it if a fool surpasses an animal, or a seeing man surpasses a blind one?

But since you cannot at all compare yourself either with some wise man or with a just man, why, I ask, are you proud? Is it because you are not even equal to the most foolish and most depraved? Take care lest, in these matters, you be judged by the inner Judge to be still more foolish and depraved.

For with the same sharp judgments by which you seem to strike down an enemy, you kill yourself after the example of Eleazar, when, in what you perhaps rightly think about God, you seek your own glory, not God’s—rejoicing as though your hand had found something, rather than grieving, as you ought, because you had not done those things—and when you insolently kiss your own hand with your own mouth.

[Note: The sense is: “You kiss your own hand with your own mouth, and do not even fear to attribute to yourself, by the testimony of your own speech, the virtue of the one who acts.”]

But remember, I say, that this is the greatest crime and, in the assertion of the most holy Job, a denial of the Most High (Job 31:28); and do not deny that you are one of the more outstanding among the arrogant, while, after the stronger matters already mentioned, you always relapse into superfluous words.

> “Consider,” he says, “the works of God, that no one can correct the one whom he has despised” (Eccl. 7:14).

For if you had considered what would have suited you better, you would have ceased writing so much. Rather, with an inward groaning, and with the mind gathered back from the things into which it is scattered—something which I see you are nevertheless unable to do—you ought to have persisted in prayer and tears, washing away such things as you continually write, rather than devoting yourself to this kind of vanity.

For while you very often imagine that you are praised in such matters, believe me, with your wish turned in the opposite direction, you are more severely blamed and mocked.

It is once reported that someone most unhappy, when he was dying, saw the demons offer him a great book written inside and out. But, to make a play on this in your case, they will not need to offer you any other book than the one you yourself wrote; and you should know that they will interpret what you desired in it and also what you did.

I judge you from your book, lest you happen to hear this; but I warn you: take care.

[Note: Construe: “But I warn you: take care lest you happen to hear, ‘I judge you from your book.’”]

For when, rising very often from the proper course, and even now from the Mass, through the fault of restlessness, you go to write what you had also conceived in your mind while singing, where, I ask, is what you had written above? Namely:

> “But whatever things he teaches the disciples to be contrary, let him show by his own deeds are not to be done.”

For it must be said to the disciples: “No one of the same religion which he often pursued should place anything before the work of God.” If nothing should be placed before it, where is the pomp of vainglory?

40. But why do I labor, when I see that I accomplish nothing? I see that only one thing remains; nevertheless, I do not cease at all to despair of you, and I presume to attempt this at the urging of the Law, although you claimed that you had grieved over having transgressed it, while you do not cease altogether to transgress it.

“If he has provided remedies, if he has provided medicines from the divine Scriptures, if he has seen that this or that, and his own diligence, have accomplished nothing, let him apply what is greater—namely, his own prayer and that of everyone for him—so that God, who can do all things, may work salvation for the sick brother.”

Let the woman of Canaan, therefore, once come—I beg it—who, unless I am mistaken, was changed from the curse of Ham to the blessing of Christ, to whom it may rightly be said, “Great is your faith” (Matt. 15:28), and for whom the Lord’s disciples also appealed to him.

Let the holy congregation of all the saints cry out:

> “Have mercy on me, Jesus, Son of David; my daughter is grievously tormented by a demon” (Matt. 15:22),

that is, the soul of this sinner—of you, I mean—begotten from me through baptism and nourished by the milk of my teaching. It is grievously tormented by a demon when, even worse, it is hardened. “Have mercy on me,” even if you disdain her; for her destruction is, as it were, the defect of any baptized person who is mine, just as her salvation is her progress.

Let the same woman repeat this even to importunity at the prayers of Christ’s familiar friends, and let her obtain from him, for whom nothing is impossible, what seems impossible to me—at least by her own merit or by her cry, since she cannot obtain it through my and your appeal.

Certainly, pure confession frees from death—an ancient saying—which you embrace, as I do not doubt, and in which you rejoice that you have acted.

Remember, I beg you, the saying, “He who curses father or mother shall die the death” (Exod. 21:17); and recall that you frequently called your father yesterday a “traitor”—which is certainly more than foolish—and your mother a *puta*, a word that exceeds *racha* monstrously, thus adding to the accumulation of your other crimes.

[Note: The word *puta*, which greatly surpasses *racha*, is understood in an evil and insulting sense and signifies a prostitute; it is still used in Italian as *puta*. Thus the ancient origin of this Italian word should be noted, as also that of *fellonem*, which in Latin signifies “treacherous.”]

I mean Adam and Eve, whom, as reason certainly teaches, I think you should recognize as established in and restored to the heavenly homeland which they had lost by sin, now recovered through Christ’s redemption [or: through Christ’s purchase], and reconciled to God—although they cannot be your homeland.

As a young man, you offered to a certain king, in commendation of yourself and as though they were your own, verses on the purification of holy Mary, Mother of God, most brilliantly composed by someone unknown, thereby making them lost as well. In these you can discern that many things remain which you have left behind against yourself as accusations for the accuser concerning your past deeds; for I can promise that it would be enough for him if he observed the things you will do hereafter—if only you continue to be such as you now are.

[Note: That is, “if you persist in being such as you now are,” and so forth.]

And I consider it very much to be feared that you will persist in this way, although may God grant that it be otherwise, since you have not even confessed that what you have often heard sung has been fulfilled in you:

> “A fire is kindled in my anger, and it shall burn to the lowest depths of hell” (Deut. 32:22), and so forth.

I see that you are monstrously deceived in one matter, because, when the Lord truly says through the book of Wisdom—he who is himself unable to lie—“Whom God loves, he reproves” (Prov. 3:12), you suppose yourself to be described there on account of the countless punishments you have suffered in this world because of your guilt.

[Note: Construe: “You suppose yourself—though I warn you not to regard this falsely—to be described there on account of the countless things you have suffered in this world through your own guilt.”]

But I warn you not to see this falsely. You make yourself secure, as though punishment had been exacted, without recalling that there are four kinds of blows; if you do not remember them, I refer you to Gregory. But, to summarize his assertion, temporal scourges free from eternal ones only those whom they change.

For although you have been called from the end of the roads—that is, from the failures of your efforts—nevertheless, because you are without a wedding garment, you have reason to fear lest it be said to you, “Friend, how did you come in here?” (Matt. 22:12).

Carefully, I beg you, observe whether what follows here does not fit you, since scourges do not restrain you from iniquity. I have first stated that, unless you correct the insolence of your precipitate tongue, your vanity—even if it possessed some religious character—is this religion of confession, as the Apostle James attests (Jas. 1:26).

What is vain, moreover, naturally lacks the weight of reward. As I said, I suggest that you also see yourself gravely marked out and blush in such matters.

> “Though you pound the fool in a mortar, with a pestle, like grain, his folly will not depart from him” (Prov. 27:22).

And so that you may not read hastily what the prophet says against you and concerning you, complaining about you and those like you, I warn you also to heed this:

> “You struck them, but they refused to accept correction” (Jer. 5:3).

Likewise, hear the same inspirer and Lord of the prophets:

> “I killed and destroyed this people, and yet they did not return from their ways” (Jer. 15:7).

> “The house of Israel has become dross to me; all of them are bronze, tin, iron, and lead in the midst of the furnace” (Ezek. 22:18).

That is, no one is silver or gold purified, as you suppose, by the fire of tribulation.

Again, against you and concerning you in particular:

> “It was heated with much labor, but its rust did not go out of it, not even through the fire” (Jer. 24:12).

And likewise:

> “The refiner has refined in vain; their wickedness”—certainly yours and that of your companions—“has not been consumed” (Jer. 6:29).

41. Had you not earlier refuted yourself with that verse of Flaccus, how would the conversion you claim from sins—if indeed there is any conversion—be shown to be worthless, since it arises not from love of virtues but from fear of punishments?

But because I see you so devoted, even in this description of your crimes, to external senses that you remember what you know perfectly only when you see it, I warn you that you do not possess the Spirit of the Lord. You will recognize this if you lack freedom.

> “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Cor. 3:17).

Know, therefore, that you are a wicked servant, not a son; an enemy, not a friend, if you are compelled by punishments either to do anything or to avoid it. For if you did not fear punishment, as I have learned from your own assertion, you would perpetrate things worse even than those you do.

You could have learned that good things ought to be loved, even if not from divine writings, at least from the sayings of Cicero and others of this kind, and from the same author whom you recently cited; they ought to be performed for their own sake, not under compulsion from punishments.

“Be ashamed, Sidon,” he says; “the sea has spoken” (Isa. 23:4). It is certain, however, that innocence of the body is lost before God, in whose sight offenses are committed by the movements of the heart.

> “Hand in hand”—if you also supply “even when nothing is being done”—“the wicked shall not be innocent” (Prov. 11:21).

He also resists God to the best of his ability who would wish that the torments created by God had never existed, so that he might be permitted to sin with impunity.

But in the matter of your inability to weep for your sins, which I have perceived both from your words and from my observation, I see clearly that you do not consider why, as the prophet reasons, the drops of tears have been withheld from you.

[Note: The text of the prophet Jeremiah 3:3 is: “Therefore the drops of rain have been withheld, and the late rain has not come.” Construe it thus: “Why the drops of tears have been withheld from you,” as the prophet reasons—tears which, even if late, would at least now wash away your sins and, when the dryness that seems to be in you had been soaked and the hardness of your heart had been moistened, would make the seed of the word grow in you, to be made fruitful by the Lord and stored in the barn of heaven, unless, most miserably, your criminality and incapacity for conversion prevented it.]

The drops of tears have been withheld from you (Jer. 3:3), tears which, even now, at least belatedly, would wash away your sins and, once the dryness that seems to be in you had been soaked and the hardness of your heart moistened, would make the seed of the word grow in you, to be made fruitful by the Lord and stored in the barn of heaven—unless, most miserably, your criminality and incapacity for conversion prevented it.

For what do you think of the guilt you contracted from this one insult alone? Hearing that, as is customary, vigils were being held by the brothers for his soul, you said precipitately, in your customary manner, that you would not pray for him because you knew that he was in hell.

[Note: *Tuatim*, that is, “in your manner,” as in Plautus, *Amphitryon* 2.1.4: “Look, you are already doing the matter in your own way.”]

You said this concerning a man who, after promising for so long that he wished to become a monk that he even obtained entry into the monastery by paying the required fee, from which you also received one pound, died most wretchedly, after a crow-like delay, unhappily in clerical dress, as it seems to you.

[Note: The manuscript read: “after the monastery’s stipend had been given at its entrance, he acquired it.” The sense required correction. For the man who had promised that he would put on the monastic habit did not acquire the stipend by paying for entry; rather, he acquired entry into the monastery by paying the stipend, from which one pound came to Ratherius the abbot. The syntax *coenobii introitum stipendio dato acquisierit* is more suitable. Since Ratherius has a peculiar syntax, however, we have not altered the arrangement of the words. *Stipendium* signifies a kind of dowry which those entering monasteries offered. Thus, when boys were handed over to monasteries to serve God perpetually, ancient formulas express that something was given in the name of an offering. See Martène and Durand, *Collectio veterum scriptorum*, vol. 9, p. 159.]

For whose guilt is his destruction after his death more attributable—if indeed he is lost—to him than to you and all the brothers, who, after receiving what belonged to him, did not care about him but abandoned him to the devil?

You ought continually to have warned him to hasten to render to God what he had vowed, before what has now happened to him [supply: “was to happen”]. And because you did not do this, ask the prophet—since he died in his sin—from whose hand God should require his blood (Ezek. 3:18), especially since, even if he had been given the opportunity to act, the Lord’s sentence would bind you in this matter:

> “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you traverse sea and land to make one proselyte, and when he has been made, you make him twice as much a son of Gehenna as yourselves” (Matt. 23:15).

Therefore I pity the most pitiable man, because you cannot weep for your own sins, though you ought to have wept even when compelled to weep for the sins of another.

And the less you are able to weep, the more you should know that you are to be wept over by all good people, considering also the slap you gave today to the peasant who was crying out against you. You thereby show how far you are from those about whom the Apostle James says:

> “If anyone thinks himself religious, not restraining his tongue but deceiving his own heart—that is, thinking himself religious—his religion is vain” (Jas. 1:26).

For you, most wretched man, are unable to restrain not only your tongue but even your hands.

[Note: The words “you are to be wept over” are governed by the verb *know*, which you will find supplied later.]

42. I also see that you are deceived by false hope in such words of the Lord as these:

> “You have sinned; cease. I do not desire the death of the sinner” (Ecclus. 21:1).

And:

> “At whatever hour the sinner is converted, he will be saved” (Ezek. 33:12).

And:

> “Turn to me, and I will return to you” (Zech. 1:3).

And that Gospel saying:

> “There is joy in heaven over one sinner more than over ninety-nine righteous persons” (Luke 15:7),

along with many similar sayings scattered throughout the fields of the divine books. All these sayings, although uttered both most mercifully and most truthfully, are corrupted by the negligence of the person who misunderstands them, weighing either what precedes or what follows less fairly than he should.

To encompass the rest by one example: it promises that there is joy in heaven over one sinner more than over ninety-nine righteous persons. But if you rejoice because you consider yourself a sinner, hear over what kind of sinner it says that the joy itself exists in heaven; and strive to be such a sinner, at least because you are unable to be righteous. It says of that sinner, “when he does penance” (Luke 15:7).

How long? I do not tell you, because I do not hear that stated here.

But when I hear it said in the Law concerning those cleansed from guilt through various sacrifices, “He shall be unclean until evening” (Lev. 15:11), I confess that every sin, even when forgiven, seems to me to be mourned until the final hour.

“You have sinned,” he says; “cease” (Ecclus. 21:1). You have ceased from one sin; cease from committing the same, or a similar, or perhaps a worse one.

It is worse if you do not mourn what you have done; for you do not cease sinning if you do not repent. You have not erased what you wrote, even if you have stopped writing; nor have you therefore amended the insults inflicted on someone because you have kept silent about them.

[Note: Namely: “You have not amended the insults inflicted on someone merely because you kept silent about them.”]

Perhaps you mourned some crime for a time and crushed your heart. But if you did not abandon the crime or repent of it, because you did not also humble your heart, you may reasonably and authoritatively fear that you have been rejected by God.

With what face, moreover, do you dare to enroll yourself among the ninety-nine righteous—even if they could be found—so that you would not, of course, think that greater things were necessary for you than for them, who ought to have remained righteous as they did?

Because you did not do this, you ought to do penance, and at least cause some joy in heaven among the angels—that is, joy proportionate to your repentance.

You can nevertheless understand that this is possible in you, when you consider the freedom of the will granted by God’s grace.

With what mind do you neglect to mourn the sins committed after baptism, when the supreme Shepherd, eager to admonish some who were terrified by consideration of their evil deeds to be baptized, first said:

> “Repent” (Acts 2:38),

although he did not doubt that all sins could be cleansed by the sacrament of baptism, even if no repentance had preceded it?

As I keep pressing such things upon you—things by which, I may say, even iron could be softened, so that you might be moved to tears, since I do not see that you are—I continue to suspect that this saying is addressed to you:

> “I have struck you with the wound of an enemy” (Jer. 30:14).

Nevertheless, lest I seem to add poison to a cruel sword—that is, lest I inject despair into the hardness of your heart—I take care to leave you to God’s care, now that an end has been placed upon refuting you, for God to tend you in a manner perhaps ineffable and incredible.

May his all-powerful mercy and freely given clemency, I beg, accomplish what no effort or persistence, as I see, is able to accomplish.

Concerning the Eucharist, which you must certainly not receive rashly: because you observed that I was moved, you also chattered beyond what was possible, eagerly wishing to vomit out what you had not yet most foolishly swallowed.

[Note: Construe: “Concerning the Eucharist, which you must certainly not receive rashly: because you observed that I was moved, you chattered beyond what was possible, eagerly wishing to vomit out what you had not yet most foolishly swallowed.” This indicates what Ratherius had earlier said about not receiving the Eucharist unworthily: he represents it as slight and garrulous, and as unworthy of so great a matter. These words, by which Ratherius prefers Paschasius Radbertus’s work to what he himself had earlier said about the Eucharist as though despising the latter, show how highly he valued that work.]

You did not at all consider that this would be the greatest crime, after the wretched example of Jeremiah and the Psalmist, because, contrary to my intention, I am compelled by a kind of unavoidable necessity to tell you what I learned afterward and to demonstrate how much less you have thought of it than certain others.

Permit me, I beg you, without envy, to set before you in brief sections certain excerpts from the works of a certain Paschasius Radbertus on this subject. In this matter I owe you a return of service also; perhaps you will perceive how much my importunity has benefited you here as well.

[Note: The “certain excerpts from the works of Paschasius Ratbertus” which are said to be appended to this *Confession* do not seem to indicate excerpts taken from one of his works, but rather the whole work of Paschasius himself, entitled *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*. In this same Lobbes manuscript it is found complete, but incorrectly prefaced under the name of Ratherius. Compare what we noted in the general preface, §2, no. 24.]

[EXHORTATION AND PRAYERS.]

[Col. 0443]

297. EDITORIAL NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING EXHORTATION AND PRAYERS.

At the end of the preceding work the author stated that he would append to it certain excerpts from the works of a certain Paschasius Ratbertus on this subject—that is, on the sacred Eucharist—namely, from his work *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*. In the Lobbes manuscript this same work of Ratbertus immediately follows Ratherius’s *Confession*, which we have placed above. Although it is complete, Ratherius nevertheless seems to have called it an excerpt, just as he also gave his own *Confession* the name of an excerpt, although it contains not part but the whole of the work, as we conjectured in the first note.

Moreover, in the same Lobbes copy, some items are appended to Paschasius’s work which, since they are absent from all the other manuscript copies of that work, cannot be attributed to Paschasius Ratbertus.

Since Ratherius himself appended this work to his *Confession* in brief sections, as he says—that is, perhaps distinguished by him into ninety-nine chapters, for in this one manuscript so many chapters are found with their titles—and since the material added after the final chapter displays Ratherius’s style, certain opinions familiar to him, and his peculiarly intricate and difficult syntax in some places, it may be regarded as written by Ratherius himself. For this reason we have thought it should be appended here.

We believe it was written at approximately the same time as the *Confession*, when the author appended Paschasius’s work to the *Confession*. Here too, as in the dialogue of the *Confession*, he mentions his old age and indicates that he was set over others; these are likewise significant indications of the same author.

We have taken this addition from the Fathers Martène and Durand, who appended it to the Paschasian work from the Lobbes manuscript. A copy of that same manuscript supplied several corrections.

[Col. 0443]

298. EXHORTATION AND PRAYERS, APPARENTLY COMPOSED AND APPENDED BY RATHERIUS TO THE WORK OF PASCHASIUS RATBERTUS ON THE BODY AND BLOOD OF THE LORD.

[Note: We prefixed this title for clarity; the manuscript does not contain it.]

[Col. 0443B] What law you must observe, dearest one, you have still read and read through. What, I ask, you have resolved to do, now disclose. [Col. 0444B] Show whether you have become deaf or whether you have become mute. I see both. When I consider how greatly you are astonished, I am somewhat afraid of what is read in the prophet concerning such persons (Micah VII, 16). Yet I advise you that, if you find nothing else to do, when every other confidence has utterly failed you, surrender yourself wholly to God’s clemency, and not, as before [Note: We have added *ut* (“as”) from our copy.], to sheer sluggish idleness; but continue your labor, having at least renounced inwardly those things which, on the authority of the Apostle, you do not doubt to be mortal sins. And since this is not enough—“Turn aside from evil,” he says, “and do good” (I Cor. VI, 9)—if you cannot (for I know that you cannot) perform penance in proportion to your faults—for time, age, bodily health, liveliness of mind, and the ability to complete it are lacking—if you cannot [Note: The same copy likewise attests the repetition of the words “if you cannot.”], then do at least a little, and let it be continual. Lawful things present themselves from time to time; remember that you have more often practiced unlawful things. [Col. 0445B] Beg a supply from somewhere [Note: Thus, better, from the same manuscript than the edition’s *aliunde* (“from elsewhere”).], or wrest from the earth a quantity of wild lettuces, and cook the unleavened bread; cast away the leaven of malice; gird your loins; take in your hand the staff of governance, reason; hasten through desire toward what you cannot attain by merit. Reconcile yourself to some by satisfaction, to all by affection, offering yourself; thereafter act with all the greater fear, the more wantonly you have acted. [Note: Construe: Since you cannot, as would have been more advisable, wrest from your mind a cessation—namely, from offering sacrifice—promise this cessation with tears, if that is granted; if not, with inward sobbing. The cited copy supplied the words “promise this,” since the edition lacked *hanc* and had *praemitte* (“send before”) instead.] Wrest from your mind, since you cannot, as would have been more advisable, a cessation; promise this: if it is granted, with tears; if not, with inward sobbing. Give something of your own according to necessity, inserting into the hearing [Note: The same copy reads: “inserting into the prayer the embassy of the most devout Redeemer into the hearing.” The construction seems to be: “inserting the embassy of the prayer of the most devout Redeemer into the hearing”; for Ratherius frequently applies the term “embassy” to prayers. See the passages indicated in the index under “Prayer.”] the embassy of the prayer of the most devout Redeemer. For who knows whether he may turn, forgive, and turn away from the anger of his wrath, so that you may not perish eternally? You have indeed perished criminally.

[Note: Since, at the end of the Confessional Dialogue, the confessor, addressing Ratherius, had added that the work of Paschasius Ratbertus *On the Body and Blood of the Lord* should be read, after this work had been copied—which in the Lobbes manuscript is indeed appended to the same dialogue—the same confessor, continuing his address to Ratherius in the same manner, added this exhortation. From it it is confirmed that Ratherius himself was the author both of the Confessional Dialogue and of this exhortation. We subsequently corrected the text further from a copy of the Lobbes manuscript. In the edition of Martène and Durand the passage is defective. That edition places in brackets what you have just read; yet this does not seem sufficient to restore the passage. If, however, *Quid* at the beginning is corrected to *Quae*, the sense becomes coherent enough. Since in the final chapters of the preceding Paschasian work the law concerning the eating of the paschal lamb had been explained, so that the manner of receiving the body and blood of the Lord might be indicated, these first words of the exhortation seem to be constructed and explained as follows: “You have still read and read through, dearest one, in the work of Paschasius just presented, what law you must observe in order to receive the sacred Eucharist correctly.”]

## PRAYERS

[Col. 0445C]

Behold me, Lord; behold me, who was not worthy, miserable and wretched as I was, to enter the courts of your church, nor to pass through the holy thresholds into your house. I approach to minister at your holy altars, and I stand guilty and sinful before the sight of your divine majesty, without any adornment of good works, without any worthy fruit of repentance, and without even a single pure thought. For I am exceedingly unworthy and criminal; yet, trusting in your ineffable piety and [Col. 0446A] mercy, and in the merits of your saints, although trembling and fearful I presume to approach to offer sacrifices to your holy name.

And therefore, most merciful Lord and creator, most clement Redeemer, who desire to amend rather than destroy every soul that confesses and repents, and who willed to become incarnate not for the righteous but for sinners, and who not only spared the thief hanging on the cross and confessing your majesty, but also promised that he would enter paradise with you: do not, in your piety and mercy, reject me, wretched and sinful, confessing my sins and repenting of them, though sluggishly; nor receive in vain the faith, hope, and confidence that I place in your inestimable clemency. But just as you spared all criminals and sinners who believe in you and trust in your mercy, so deign to spare and forgive me, wretched as I flee to you [*f.*, “take refuge in you”], renouncing the devil after my many sins and crimes and returning to you; and deign, in fatherly kindness, to make me worthy and to receive me for celebrating the office entrusted to me.

And although I thrust myself forward more boldly than was fitting—for I cannot fail to know that the judgment of both the Old and the New Law forbids me to do so, since I know without disbelief from your sacred oracles that the destroyers of the wicked and guardians of your holy altars, angels carrying vessels of slaughter in their hands, are wholly present (Ezek. IX, 1)—yet, having seized [Note: Construe: “Having seized a certain confidence arising from an earlier presumption concerning your true mercy, because those avengers of your injuries, Lord, did not kill me, as I deserved, until this old age to which I have come, aged amid evil days and always provoking you; they did not kill me, perhaps knowing that your kindness would most patiently await me, though I was storing up wrath for the day of wrath and the revelation of your just judgment, while many brothers also held grievances against me. For, Lord, I stand here truly suspect and trembling, lest I should suddenly be struck, as is just, when you are present in your body and blood, though you are nowhere absent in your divinity. Yet spare me,” and so forth. This very long and difficult syntax displays Ratherius’ style.] a certain confidence based long ago on trust in your true mercy, because those avengers of your injuries, Lord, namely the angels, did not kill me, as I deserved, until this old age to which I have come, aged amid evil days while continually provoking you; perhaps they knew that your kindness would most patiently await my repentance, though I was storing up wrath for the day of wrath and the revelation of your just judgment, while many brothers also held grievances against me. For, Lord, I stand here truly suspect and trembling, lest I should suddenly be struck, as is just, when you are present in your body and blood, though you are nowhere absent in your divinity. Yet spare me, I beg, still presuming upon your mercy, most merciful one; spare me. Delay the blow; suspend vengeance; and, not looking upon the iniquities, crimes, and sins of my youth—and, what is worse, I confess, also of my old age—but upon your many mercies and acts of compassion, by which you have always been accustomed to pity the human race, receive the prayers and offerings that I presume to offer to your majesty for my sins and for the sins of your faithful, both living and dead.

Remember that we are flesh, formed from fragile material (Job XV, 15). Even the heavens are not pure in your sight (Job IV, 18), and your angels were found blameworthy before you; how much more earthly, unworthy, and [Col. 0447B] impure human beings? For we cannot be pure unless, through your piety and mercy, we daily deserve to be cleansed in heart and body.

Therefore you, Lord—you who wished to rouse my sluggish, miserable, and polluted intention and devotion to receive the sacred mystery of your altar [Note: We supplied *accipiendum*, “to receive,” which was absent from the edition.] and permitted me, though unworthy and sinful, to approach shamelessly to minister to you—mercifully restrain the anger I deserve; display your gratuitous clemency; and graciously grant that the celebration of this sacred mystery, to which I approach lukewarm and fearful, may result for me not in judgment and condemnation but in the forgiveness of sins and everlasting salvation.

## ALSO

[Col. 0447C]

Thus, Lord, with the consciousness of immense guilt bearing witness, we are confounded that we can approach your office neither confidently nor freely. For who, weighing his sin, would not wish to hide himself from your face, if it were possible to avert the eyes of such majesty, if he could escape by hiding or escape once concealed? Or who would not desire more greatly to see you, if he did not fear more because you behold him while he sins? Therefore, since you find us everywhere, we flee to you, from whom we can never flee. Nothing remains for the wretched but to find—not hiding places, but tears. Let indulgence cherish those whom offense terrifies. Power threatens, but let mercy console. From you comes one who frees [Note: Thus from our Lobbes copy; the common text wrongly has *libet* (“it pleases”).]; through you comes one who excuses. Spare us, almighty Father, and deign to reward unto recompense those whom you see humbled by guilt and raised up [Note: Thus, better, in the same copy than the edition’s *numerare* (“to count”)]; and do not make those whom you understand to be wretched through confession confused at the examination.

## ALSO ANOTHER

Forgive, God, whatever the rebuke of our incautious mouth [*al.*, “incautiously”], through the intemperance of a biting tongue, has wounded among our subjects. Whatever we have said that fell short of the perfection of goodness, spare us; whatever we have uttered incongruously or with insufficient restraint, forgive. Let presumption not punish me, unwary as I was; but let your merciful piety absolve me, who acknowledge my iniquities.

[Note: In these words Ratherius seems to be referring to the fault of sharper reproof, by which he used to attack and censure the crimes of his subordinates with greater fervor.]

And since I have no confidence anywhere except in your mercy, arm my mouth also with the proclamation of truth, and sanctify my work with fuller abundance, so that you may save me as one worthy and, in your piety, justify the flock entrusted to me. [Note: When Ratherius wrote this after the *Confessional Dialogue*, he was head of a certain abbey belonging to the monastery of Lobbes, as we have shown from the same dialogue in the *Life*.] Whatever you see corrupted in them, heal; whatever you discern to be faulty in me, cure. If they have contracted or are contracting any stain through the fault of my lukewarmness or negligence, overlook it [read: “forgive it”]. If, whether without my knowledge or knowingly, they have fallen into sin, and if they have incurred guilt through the offense caused by my example, forgive me, and for such faults do not repay wretched me with vengeance.

Yet for those to whom I seemed to have applied the judgment of rebuke, may the rebuke itself profit them unto salvation, and may this prayer, interceding for them, recall them from the error entrusted to them, so that they may not endure Tartarean torments. For them we, being mortal [*al.*, “mortal”], have imposed laws of repentance, so that, sparing the disadvantages of both parties, you may grant forgiveness to their iniquities and wash away my offense, contracted through the hardship of governing [Note: The common edition reads “the offense of the hardship of governing that is to be contracted.” We have preferred the reading of the copy.].

Grant, God, an ear to our sacrifices; inscribe me and those entrusted to me in your pages, so that, together with the flock committed to me, I may be cleansed from every crime and deserve to reach you in peace. Make the dwelling place of our hearts peaceful, by expelling carnal vices; and since I now strive to exercise the height of virtues in my subjects [*f.*, “to display” them], may I, with the troubles of mind and body pacified, deserve, when you judge, to be crowned peacefully with the angels.

Therefore, we ask you, merciful God, make us look upon you [Note: The same copy reads thus. The edition reads less well: “so that we, God, looking upon you”; and in the same place it omits *ut ante zelus*, “so that zeal may previously.”] with minds aflame in your sight through the gift of your grace, so that zeal for your house may consume us. Let us govern our subjects through the vigor of the Holy Spirit with such restraint that they may gain profit from the disciplines of our governance, that their hardness may be broken, and that their life may be sanctified [Note: The editions wrongly read “may bear fruit.”].

Receive, Lord, the libations of our vows, so that through them we may rejoice that whatever correction we bestow upon our subjects by word or merit has profited both them and us—not toward our discord, but toward everlasting joy and sweetness. Absolve us from both another’s offense and our own, so that, receiving in both cases the efficacy of spiritual grace [Note: The edition reads “desiring to receive.”], we may supplicate your name with greater confidence. Through the Lord.

## ITEM

The office of ministering urges me to offer the people’s saving sacrifice for their offense. The conscience of an unworthy priesthood terrifies me because of my guilt. If I, the refuse of all priests, offer the sacrifice, the crime of a polluted conscience is increased. If it is not offered to such great majesty, the judge of all flesh, the guilt of negligence is imputed.

Amid these things I implore the balance of your mercy, Almighty One, whose day of vengeance I fear, with my conscience accusing me, so that in your mercy you may not judge unworthy the one whom you do not exclude from the time of repentance. Suspend the axe until the cultivator of the vineyard brings a basket of manure to the root of the fruitless tree.

Spare me, most clement Lord, a penitent, you who mercifully recalled David to forgiveness after his fall; who mercifully regarded the tears of Peter, weeping bitterly; who illumined the thief, guilty of so great a crime on the cross, by divine grace. His confession immediately obtained for him the clear vision of the Son of God; faith obtained its reward, punishment forgiveness, lamentation everlasting joy—while, after the cross, the confessor became possessor of paradise.

But since my words need the pardon of your mercy, and the works of an unworthy priesthood do not commend me, at least receive the vows of those standing here, so that through their prayers before you you may grant forgiveness to me, and through their merits the sacrifices offered for our wounds may beneficially bring us healing. Since, Almighty One, you became a sacrifice for all on account of sins, be our sanctification [Note: Thus the Lobbes copy; the common text reads “sacrifice.”] in the sacrifice for offenses, Christ, Savior of the world, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God through all ages of ages. Amen.

May the one who wrote this live in peace, and may the one who reads it rejoice forever. [Note: This closing formula—which I do not dare affirm to be Ratherius’—is found in the Lobbes copy.]

[ON THE TRANSLATION OF SAINT METRON]

[Col. 0449]

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING INVECTIVE

I. P.
