Bernard Pez, in the introductory dissertation prefixed to volume I of the *Anecdota*, while speaking of a certain manuscript of the chapter of Freising, containing several little works by Ratherius, mentions the following *Invective* and account of the translation or removal of the body of Saint Metron in such a way as to divide it into two works. To the first he assigns the title: “A sufficiently severe invective against certain persons, and a mournful account of a certain Ratherius of Laubia, a Veronese, from monk an exile, from exile a bishop, made, unmade, remade, and again unmade in the manner of the most unfortunate Attalus, whose maker, unmaker, remaker, and destroyer alone knows the omen of what was made, unmade, and remade.” To the second he gives, as though it were another title: “On the translation of the body of a certain holy Metron, whose deposition is celebrated on the eighth Ides of the month of May,” and so forth.

Of the first work alone, as he calls it, he quotes the opening in these words: “As the most sacred, most ancient, and most truthful chronicler of an earlier age relates…” Bartholomeus Campagnola, archpriest of Saint Cecilia, printed this work—or rather a fragment of it—from manuscript 65 of the chapter of Verona at the end of an old book of the civil law of the city of Verona, p. 231. He made the work entitled *Invective* include the passages also dealing with the translation of the body of Saint Metron, without inserting any distinction or indication between the two works. It is therefore clear that it is one work, though it appeared to P. Bernard Pez to be two.

Since the parchment from which Campagnola extracted this fragment was corroded and mutilated in places, its ending is missing, in addition to certain lacunae occurring throughout and marked by dots in the edition. The Marquis Giovanni Giacomo de Dionysius, a canon of the cathedral church of Verona and highly skilled in examining ancient documents, reread the same manuscript with greater care and very courteously communicated to us several corrected readings and supplied some lacunae. He also showed us the manuscript itself. When we saw in it several words altered by Ratherius’ own hand, with the earlier readings deleted and new ones written above them, we judged that this was the first draft of the work, mutilated through the loss of leaves, and had no doubt about it.

II. We hoped to obtain something more certain and complete from the Freising manuscript seen by P. Pez. Nor was our hope disappointed, through the assistance of Count Giovanni Battista de Verità, a most distinguished Veronese patrician, who holds many honors at the court of the Most Serene Bavarian house. Together with the most illustrious Francesco Werdenstein, bishop of Tenas [or Tenaria] and suffragan of the bishopric of Freising, he arranged for the complete work to be copied from the manuscript exemplar of the cathedral chapter of Freising.

We found very great diligence in the copy sent to us, for which we confess that we owe much to both men. Once the work had been given a single title—one that P. Pez had divided into two—it was more fully confirmed that there are one, not two, works, since the *Invective* is directed against those who were complaining about the removal of Saint Metron’s body.

The work is complete, containing nothing broken off and nothing mutilated. When we compared it with the fragment previously published, we discovered something distinctive and not insignificant: some passages had been substantially altered, while others had been added here and there. Thus the Veronese manuscript presents Ratherius’ first efforts, whereas the Freising manuscript presents his final hand, revealing the author’s care first in composing his works and afterward in correcting and enlarging them.

To make this distinction between the first and second drafts clearly discernible, we shall first publish the entire work as it appears in the Freising exemplar; afterward we shall append the fragment of the same work as it was edited from the Veronese manuscript, supplying and correcting in it those passages that must be credited to the diligence of the aforementioned canon.

III. For establishing the date, the statements in section 3 are relevant, where it is related that the theft of Saint Metron’s body had recently occurred, namely at the time when “the emperor Otto Augustus had entered Italy successfully, to triumph.” Otto entered Italy twice in triumph: first in the year 951, when he so subdued Berengar II that, although he restored the kingdom to him in the following year, he nevertheless compelled him to remain subject to himself, as though a vassal, under certain defined conditions; and secondly in the year 961, when he attacked the same Berengar more fiercely after he had crossed the prescribed boundaries, and finally defeated him completely.

It may be doubted whether the theft of Saint Metron’s body should be assigned to the earlier or the later entrance. The title “Augustus,” by which Ratherius designates Otto, suits only the second entrance, since he was called Emperor Augustus on 2 February 962. Although Ratherius might have used this title because Otto was emperor when he wrote the work, even though he did not yet bear that title at the time of the theft, we nevertheless believe it more probable that the theft occurred after Ratherius had already been restored to the see of Verona. Since, as we have shown in the *Life*, he was restored not after Otto’s first entrance into Italy but after the second, we have no doubt that the theft must be assigned not to Otto’s first entrance but to his second.

The words in section 3, “through the fault of the one who was then presiding there most disgracefully,” may seem to refer to Milo, whom Ratherius would have declared to be presiding most disgracefully as an invader of his see. Milo, however, had held the Veronese see from the year 951, when Otto first entered Italy. But since Ratherius elsewhere also calls himself “most unworthy,” we believe that those words refer to Ratherius after his restoration to that see, and that the entire event must be referred to the period when he was presiding at Verona.

For since this *Invective* aims to defend or excuse a bishop against whom certain persons were speaking abusively because the theft had been committed in his presence, he seems to be pleading his own case rather than Milo’s. Ratherius was accustomed not to defend Milo, whom he regarded as his invader and rival, but to accuse him. Certainly he never wished to call this man a bishop. Thus, in the second decree concerning clergy ordained by the same invader, he says: “I did not dare to call the invader of my office a bishop, lest I condemn myself by my own voice.”

In this work, however, he calls the man whom he defends both “prelate” and “bishop.” “He would surely have agreed,” he says in section 4, “as you contend in your accusation, under some higher counsel . . . your bishop.” A little later, in section 5: “When someone had asked your prelate . . .” Finally, in section 13, where he attributes this theft in part to his own fault, he clearly indicates that it occurred while he was holding the bishopric: “Whether this happened to you through our fault—which it would not be right for us to deny—and through neglect . . .”

Therefore the theft must be said to belong to Ratherius’ period, namely when, after Otto’s second entrance into Italy, Milo had been expelled and Ratherius had been restored to his see. After Otto’s first entrance, although Ratherius tried to be restored, he was unable to achieve it.

This removal occurred “as January was ending, on the sixth [day] before the Kalends”; from the words “as January was ending,” it must be assigned to 27 January. Since this theft is said to have been recently carried out at the time when Otto had entered Italy successfully to triumph, it must undoubtedly be assigned to the first January after Otto’s second entrance, that is, January of the year 962; for Otto entered Italy for the second time before the end of the preceding year.

When the theft was discovered by the Veronese, many railed against the bishop, as though the sacred body had been taken away through his negligence or complicity. Thus these defenses of the bishop were entitled *Invective*, because they rebuke his detractors. They seem to have been written by Ratherius in the same year, 962, when Otto, having been raised to the imperial dignity at the beginning of February, could in this work be called Augustus and emperor.

IV. One historical point must be noted. The words in the title concerning the theft of the sacred body—“Whether the deed happened or not may well be known to no mortal person, although at the time when it was done it was certainly believed to be probable”—seem to cast doubt on whether the sacred body was truly stolen.

Although the author in the work itself assumes that it was taken away, in section 14 he shows that this assumption rests solely on common report and opinion. Speaking of the sacred body as having been brought elsewhere while only the ashes were left at Verona, he uses the expressions “you are said” and “you are believed”: “In the worship and veneration of your members, holy one, where you are said to have been carried, and of your ashes, where you are believed to have been left.” These words indicate nothing certain, but only the opinion and report of others, which are uncertain.

It was not known whether the sacred body had been sold by someone for a price, nor whether any Veronese had been party to the theft. Whatever the truth may be, if it was stolen in Ratherius’ time, it was certainly recovered afterward. For, according to an immemorial tradition confirmed by ancient witnesses and even by a solemn recognition and translation of the same body, it is kept in the church of Saint Vitalis, and everyone agrees with us in this matter; you will find no one who has claimed or claims it for himself. See the fuller discussion of this matter by P. Giovanni Francesco Manzoni, a priest of the Veronese Oratory, in the booklet *Information Concerning Saint Metron*.

[Col. 0451]

## A SUFFICIENTLY SEVERE INVECTIVE AGAINST CERTAIN PERSONS, AND A MOURNFUL ACCOUNT OF A CERTAIN RATHERIUS OF LAUBIA, A VERONESE

From a monk [Note: In the Freising manuscript, from which alone we have taken this title, the text reads incorrectly *exsul* (“exile”), followed shortly afterward by *praesul* (“bishop”). The wordplay “made, unmade, remade, and so forth, in the manner of the most unfortunate Attalus” is taken from Orosius, who wrote of Priscus Attalus: “in this emperor, made, unmade, remade, and unmade,” and so forth.] an exile, from an exile a bishop, made, unmade, remade, and again unmade [Note: *Defecti iterum*, “again unmade,” as we publish it from the manuscript, that is, “again driven out.” Since Ratherius wrote this work at Verona after being restored to his see, it is clear that he wrote it after being restored from his second expulsion, when Otto had been raised to the imperial dignity; Otto is mentioned in section 3.] in the manner of the most unfortunate Attalus—of whose making, unmaking, remaking, and again unmaking only the maker, unmaker, remaker, and destroyer knows the omen of what was made, unmade, and remade.

## ON THE TRANSLATION OF A CERTAIN SAINT METRON

Whose deposition is celebrated on the eighth Ides of the month of May [Note: “On the eighth Ides of May” is written for “the eighth day before the Ides of May,” that is, 8 May, on which day the feast of Saint Metron was celebrated both in the ancient calendars of the Veronese Church and still in our own time]; whose removal is lamented on the sixth day before the Kalends as January ends [Note: “On the sixth day before the Kalends as January ends,” the day on which the theft was said to have occurred, is the same as 27 January, that is, the sixth day before the Kalends of February]; though vainly: for whether the deed happened or not may well be known to no mortal person, although at the time when it was done it was certainly believed to be probable.

[Col. 0451A] 301–302

### 1.

As the most sacred, most ancient, and most truthful chronicler of an earlier age relates, when the mercy of God determined to free, after a very long period of affliction, his people from the hands of the Memphis tyrant—or rather, so to speak, from the jaws of the Nile monster (Exod. XII, 35), among the other commands appropriate to that work he ordered that, as each man was departing, every member of that people should borrow from his friend vessels of gold and silver (Exod. XI, 2). Thus, as one may reasonably infer, the impious nation would be stripped of the riches it had long possessed unjustly, being about to be swallowed in the depths of the Red Sea through the peculiar guilt of its own most just leader, while the God-worshiping offspring of Abraham would be enriched by a heavenly gift.

But the cause of this mystery was perhaps somewhat like that deception [Note: The very intricate syntax seems to be constructed as follows: “But the cause of this kind of mystery was perhaps somewhat like that deception which is everywhere condemned by the law of nations. Yet, if the impenetrable obscurity of human wisdom, which God confounds, is considered, there appears here the greatest incomprehensibility of the wisdom and knowledge of God. With the Apostle who speaks of God, it is sound for the wise to marvel at its height, but with the most insane catalogue of heretics to scrutinize and criticize it. There also appears the incomprehensibility of the divine dispensation, which has nevertheless been discussed and shown to us through those to whom authority is said to have been given to fill twelve baskets with the remains of the fragments.”] which is everywhere condemned by the law of nations. Yet, if the impenetrable obscurity of human wisdom, which God confounds, is considered, there appears here the greatest incomprehensibility of the wisdom and knowledge of God—whose height it is fitting for the wise to marvel at with the Apostle who speaks of God (Rom. XI, 33), but to scrutinize and criticize with the most insane catalogue of heretics—and of the divine dispensation, which has nevertheless been discussed and shown to us through those to whom authority is said to have been given to fill twelve baskets with the remains of the fragments (Matt. XIV, 20).

When we carefully consider the manifold mysteries of this incomprehensibility, and how much that most merciful Distributor of graces deigns to add to the effort of our own investigation despite our sluggishness [Note: Construe: “When we therefore carefully consider the manifold mysteries of this incomprehensibility, to the extent that that most merciful Distributor of graces deigns to add them to the investigation undertaken by our sluggishness, it very often happens that the incomparable Sage of that age was not ashamed to confess to everyone, saying: ‘I sought wisdom, and it was far from me’”], we very often find what the incomparable Sage of that age was not ashamed to confess to all, saying: “I sought wisdom, and it was far from me” (Eccles. VII, 24). Nor was this without reason.

For these twelve baskets were filled with fragments from the two fish obtained, not without laborious ingenuity, from the waves of the shore of Zebulun [Col. 0453C] and Naphtali, where perhaps the venerable patriarchs of apostolic offspring were commanded to dwell; and all these things undoubtedly signify something. Again, these baskets were filled with fragments from the number five of the loaves, not without mystery [Note: Construe: “For these twelve baskets were filled with fragments from the two fish obtained, not without laborious ingenuity, from the waves of the shore of Zebulun and Naphtali, where perhaps the venerable patriarchs of apostolic offspring were commanded to dwell—and all these things undoubtedly signify something—and likewise from the number five of the loaves, not without mystery. If you are willing to store these things in the belly of memory, and to bring them forth through the cud of recollection, so that they may be more subtly ground by the millstones, we shall experience,” and so forth.]. If you are willing to store them in the belly of memory and to bring them forth through the cud of recollection, so that they may be more subtly ground by the millstones, we shall experience the truth of the saying: “He who adds knowledge adds labor” (Eccles. I, 18).

For they are not made of wheat, so that they can be stripped easily, but of barley (John VI, 9), to whose marrow even the most devoted labor can scarcely reach. Therefore, with the upper millstone set turning, and the lower one lying as though idle, though not without mystical meaning, this barley mass [Note: “Mass,” that is, quantity. The construction is: “Therefore, with the upper millstone set turning, and the lower millstone lying as though idle, though not without mystical meaning, this barley mass—which we have undertaken to sift before us—having necessarily been ground by this millstone and likewise offered to the taste, gives flavor to the palate of our mind—that is, teaches us—that Egypt signifies the world placed in evil, that Pharaoh signifies the devil, prince of that same world, that the people oppressed by mud and bricks signifies the human race, whom the Lord, sent forth, descended to free, that the Red Sea signifies baptism dyed with the blood of Christ, that those submerged signify sins, and so forth.”] which we have undertaken to sift before us, having necessarily been ground by the lower millstone and likewise offered to the taste, gives this meaning to the palate of our mind: Egypt signifies the world placed in evil; Pharaoh, the prince of that same world, signifies the devil; the people oppressed by mud and bricks signifies the human race, whom the Lord, having been sent, descended to free; the Red Sea signifies baptism dyed with the blood of Christ; those submerged signify sins; and those freed, washed in baptism and redeemed from the death of the soul by the blood of Christ our Savior.

If the question arises concerning the vessels of gold and silver stolen through the liberator’s advice by deceptive borrowing, we say that they are the ornaments and trappings of secular books. As we see, these were wholly taken from the pagans and, through Christ’s grant, long ago passed into the possession and adornment of the Church.

“But to what end is all this?” the keen questioner asks. Certainly so that we may confess that this saying of the Apostle does not fail to suit our own time: “Where is the wise man? Where is the scribe? Where is the one who weighs the words of the law? Has not God made the wisdom of the world foolish?” (I Cor. I, 20).

By now, indeed,

> Already Joshua had destroyed Kiriath-sepher,  
> and had utterly cast down Jericho’s walls upon the earth,  
> while all the crossroads of the world resounded with the rejoicing of the saints.

## 2. 304

Our historiographers eagerly strove to describe, with no less zeal, ornament, and charm, the contests of the martyrs who had preceded them, the merits of confessors, the celibacy and continence of virgins and widows, and the repentance of converts, than those men—conspicuous for eloquence and renowned throughout the world—whom lying Greece especially produced as inventors or propagators of the liberal arts, and whom poetic garrulity, always inflating falsehood with ornament, had once never ceased to extol as its heroes. But now, shamefully, in our own days and those of our ancestors, we are compelled to suppose that the coming of the one about whom it was prophesied is not far off, “because want shall go before his face” (Job XLI, 13). Such poverty of writers has invaded the world that, if any distinction of merit has shone forth either in our times or in those I have mentioned, the common crowd has praised these men more than any learned person has done.

Let them tell me, then, I demand, for what purposes they borrowed from the Egyptians those vessels, whether golden or silver, which they possess, if they display none of them as adornment of the Lord’s tabernacle or temple. There is considerable reason to fear that, unless the piety of God spares them contrary to their deserts, the statement about Achan may not be unfitting for them, together with the example: namely, the theft of the golden rod, which was not shown to Joshua.

[Note: The sense is: “There is considerable reason to fear that the statement, together with Achan’s example, may not be unfitting for them—unless God’s piety spares them contrary to their deserts—because of the stolen golden rod, which was not shown to Joshua.” “The statement together with Achan’s example” refers to the sentence pronounced by Joshua against Achan, who had taken away the golden rod and had not shown it to Joshua.]

“The Lord Jesus was casting out a demon, and it was mute; and when he had cast out the demon, the mute man spoke” (Luke XI, 14). May God repeat this miracle, we pray, so that our mouth may speak the praise of the Lord.

## 3.

How rightly, then, should I be angry with the scholars of our own time and that of our uncles—let me now draw it out sufficiently in a mournful account! I confess that this first happened recently, that is, at the time when Otto, the most glorious, most just, and most devout emperor Augustus, praised throughout the whole world, had entered Italy successfully to triumph.

[Note: This must refer to Otto I’s second entry into Italy, as we show in the *Admonition*, no. 3.]

For the people of Verona there resulted a very serious loss, caused not only by the guilt of the bishop who then most unworthily presided there,

[Note: By the pronoun “his,” Ratherius himself is indicated, as will be clear from the same *Admonition*.]

but also by the guilt of the sixty-year period of the bishops who had preceded him.

[Note: That is, by the guilt of those bishops who preceded him, over the course of sixty years. For, as he explains shortly afterward, the revenues of the church of Saint Vitalis, where the body of Saint Metro lay buried, had already for sixty years been assigned to soldiers in such a way that no priest or anyone else guarded that church and holy body.]

The common, unlearned people used to say that the body of a certain holy Metro—I hesitate whether to call him a confessor or a martyr—had been carried away from the suburb of that city, where the basilica of blessed Vitalis the martyr contained it, by a praiseworthy theft but a blameworthy loss.

[Note: “Amisso” means “by the loss,” just as above and below *disposito* is used for “disposition.” The Verona manuscript indeed reads *amissione*.] Since the crowd, moved by religious love, frequently visited the shrine of this saint because of the innumerable miracles of the same blessed man displayed there,

[Note: Monuments in which the bodies of saints lay were called *Memoriae*, “shrines” or “memorials.”]

the place had become so worthless to those same people—shame on the deed!—that, once the revenue belonging to that church had been given to soldiers, no priest was there to care for the place containing so precious a treasure. It had become cheap only to the most wretched bishops and to those who, in the utterly vain labor of eating the husks of swine rather than the bread of wheaten sweetness—in which the prodigal son of the Gospel, about to return to his father, lamented that the multitude of hired servants abounded while he himself was perishing from hunger—were occupied.

[Note: This abuse had become established: ecclesiastical revenues were given even to soldiers, or noblemen, who had either deserved well of the prince or were required to serve militarily for the Church when need arose. The bishops themselves gave revenues and estates to the latter; hence in the *Life of Saint John of Gorze*, volume V of the *Acta Sanctorum* of the Benedictine order, published by Mabillon, p. 377, we read: “Whatever of the possessions lay outside [the monastery of Gorze], Count Adelbert held as a benefice from the bishop whom he served—a favor truly unwelcome.” The preceding words indicate that this happened to the church of Saint Vitalis sixty years before the theft of the holy body: “over the course of sixty years”; see above, note 637. Construe: “so that, once the revenue belonging to that church had been given to the soldiers,” and so forth.]

Alas, sorrow! O grieving little circles [the expression is uncertain], I beg you, weep. Since, as the whole world degenerates, we could suppose that everything was groaning and daily rushing headlong to ruin—unless, when these things began to happen, we rather commanded our heads to be lifted up (Luke XXI, 28), that is, our hearts to be cheered, lest divine justice judge us to be more attached to the present world, which passes away with its misery and desire (I John II, 17), than to the world whose coming draws near with its happiness and glory—and since we would judge that, by differing in anything from the will and ordinance of the Creator, we had erased his image in ourselves and found fault with his work: who could sufficiently attack you, or rather—what is safer and more reasonable—lament you alone, wretched Italy?

You abuse the princes of the apostles most shamefully; you walk over the martyrs; you trample confessors beneath your feet; with your filthy feet you wear down the venerable tombs of virgins. Like a dog jealously preventing others from reaching the hay by its barking, you pursue with curses those whom you had refused to venerate while they were present—indeed, more truthfully, those who were fleeing from you and visiting others.

Were you not in this most envious and most avaricious? You ought rather to rejoice with those whose honor had become cheap to you because of their number, and not envy the desire, devotion, and salvation of those who, having no saints,

[Note: That is, those who possessed no saints, or no bodies of saints, and deserved to receive a few from the Lord.]

deserved to receive a few from the Lord.

Why, at least in this matter, does it not please you to remember that apostolic saying: “Whoever has the substance of this world and sees his brother in need, yet closes his heart against him, how does the love of God remain in him?” (I John III, 17). And: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matthew XIX, 19). Why do you grieve over what was lost, when, while you possessed it, you did not love it very much? But in truth you do not grieve; you deceitfully pretend to grieve in order to taunt certain people. For if you truly grieved over those who were lost, you would visit those who remained with more devoted worship and service.

## 4.

Yet although, in your envy, you are able—as you attempt—to criticize those placed before you by your reproaches, I advise you to consider that you have by no means deserved better men. For it is most truthfully written of God that he makes the hypocrite reign because of the sins of the people (Job XXXIV, 30). And he himself says concerning them: “I shall give them kings in my fury, and in my anger” (Hosea XIII, 11). By “kings,” understand not only those who are customarily called kings in this world, but also all those placed over others in any rank for the purpose of governing.

If you loved your martyr so greatly, why had you guarded him so badly? Perhaps your bishop consented, as you insist on accusing him, to this through a higher counsel and an ordinance more in keeping with God. But you, who had recoiled from so great a crime, I want you to know why you recoiled.

“Because it is a very bad thing,” you say, “that we lose our saints in this way.” Most true. But you would speak more appropriately if you said that our saints flee from us in this way.

Although no saint is greedy for shameful profit, no one among the saints is found to have rejected honorable gain. Honorable gain, however, is that which enriches heaven and strips hell.

But if it pleased some saint, while fleeing from you, to go by whatever effort to that place where, in return for the reverence that he had not received from you, paradise would be filled with devout souls through the love shown to him in Christ, and the infernal prison emptied; and if, throughout so many years, none of your own had deserved this on account of similar devotion, take care lest you appear to be distressed by heaven’s advancement and to rejoice in its losses. For the example you display is one that you neither want to see among yourselves nor want the saints to possess anywhere.

## 5.

But, great Verona, once that Platonic city, Athens, or judged to be another Athens because of its multitude of wise men, why did you not exalt your saint in lofty strains? Why, if you did not publish the miracles God had worked through him in metrical style, did you not at least publish them in prose?

What the unlearned populace sang—you may be sure—you would have read with greater honor, and you would have adorned this tabernacle of God with Taphnite bronze and embellished it with silver or gold, with what the cultivator of the land of Gessen had borrowed.

[Note: Construe: “and you would have embellished it with silver or gold, with what the cultivator of the land of Gessen—that is, the Hebrew people who cultivated the land of Gessen, or Egypt (Exodus VIII, 22)—had borrowed.”]

For, to your disgrace, when someone—let me say, a man acquainted with the bishop—had asked your bishop, who had sought the episcopate of Verona, what sort of sanctity that blessed man had possessed,

[Note: Ratherius suspects that he was aware of the theft because he had sought the bishopric of Verona, over which that blessed man, Metro, had presided. Those who sought to carry the relics or bodies of saints elsewhere were accustomed carefully to investigate any written acts, or, when such acts were lacking, whatever information they could obtain. Many examples of this practice from that period can be read in the *Discovery of the Saints Found by Lord Deoderic, Bishop of Metz*, volume II of Acher’s *Spicilegium*, p. 133 onward.]

he did not turn to a book of that man’s deeds composed through the diligence of one of your people. Instead, he turned to the truthful report of those who, with the Psalmist, could sing: “We have heard, O God, with our ears; our fathers have declared it to us” (Psalm XLIII, 1).

From their account he learned that this same saint, in his youth, had been entangled in such worldly activities as the divine book describes: “Those who desire to become rich in this world fall into the snare and trap of the devil” (I Timothy VI, 9).

When this had happened to him—as it has often happened to many others—by the merciful permission of the just God, he was moved by consideration of his guilt and did not delay in rising up against himself and abandoning everything in this world, so that, unencumbered and free, he might devote himself to the Lord alone.

Thus he climbed a sycamore for the sake of the cross, as Zacchaeus did so that he might see Jesus in order to be delivered (Luke XIX, 4). And so that he would not carry the same cross under compulsion with Simon (Matthew XXVII, 32), but, being put to death with Christ, would carry it together with his vices and desires—not for a time only, but daily, indeed continually—he is said to have chosen for himself a punishment which, even if he wished to escape when overcome by the wantonness of the flesh, he could not possibly evade.

Judging himself a publican and sinner beyond all other men, he barred himself from the thresholds of the church. Standing at a distance, he arranged that he could cry out with the other man who was mercifully justified: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner” (Luke XVIII, 13).

[Note: Construe: “He arranged that, standing at a distance, he could cry out with that other man who was mercifully justified: ‘God, be merciful to me,’” and so forth.]

## 6.

But why make much of something that does not at all fit the posture of standing—as though I had heard that anyone among our people, before or after him, had inflicted such a martyrdom upon himself? More appropriately, I should say “rolling about,” for it does not accord with “standing.”

To pass over those torments that concern the belly or stomach—for I leave it to the thoughtful reader to assess the rest—I shall speak of the punishment he inflicted upon himself externally, and of one unheard of.

As though the most impious and cruel torturer were saying to him in his own voice: “Because, when you were in honor, you did not understand; you were compared with senseless beasts and made like them” (Psalm XLVIII, 13), “I want to restrain you with the leather of beasts, so that you may no longer wander about in a wanton manner,” he placed a chain on his foot.

[Note: This was once a customary form of public penance, by which public sinners, bound with a chain and iron fetters at the bishop’s command, traveled about among sacred places. Unless the bonds were loosed by a miracle, they could be removed only by the bishop after a suitable period, as may be seen in Mabillon’s preface to the second century of the Benedictine order, no. 41, and in Muratori, *Italian Antiquities*, dissertation 23. What was peculiar to our Metro was that he voluntarily imposed this penance upon himself. Instead of making a pilgrimage to holy places, he stood for seven years chained before the door of the church of Saint Vitalis, until, by God’s providence, the key was found in the belly of a fish.]

He fastened it with lead to the great stone that still lies before the basilica’s door, secured the foot-ring surrounding his foot with a door-lock, and threw the key into the depths of the nearby Adige, a well-known river on whose bank the basilica mentioned above stands. I speak more plainly, so that the meaning may be understood. Perhaps he prayed for God’s mercy, asking that he might never see it until the clemency of the Almighty had forgiven the sins he had resolved to mourn.

I have used the adverb “perhaps” because, although I did not learn this by report, it is nevertheless established by the miracle that this is what happened to him, God granting it by the outcome of events.

Thus he is said to have remained chained to the stone beneath the open sky for seven years.

[Note: It is usually written *sub dio*, that is, “under the sky”; but some consider *sub divo* the more correct form.]

This continued until, by the merciful will of God—who was now bringing an end to the sufferings that attended such a punishment and crowning his martyr with heavenly honors—fishermen brought to the bishop a fish in whose belly that holy key was found, announcing that all his crimes had been forgiven. When the key was recognized and the fetter of the chain unlocked by the city’s bishop, that blessed man was washed, clothed, restored to the Church, and refreshed by participation in the most holy body and blood of the Lord.

Immediately afterward, when that most welcome offering of the Lord had been carried up to heaven by an angelic oar through the release of his spirit, no one endowed even with childish reason was permitted to doubt that the saint had won the palm of victory in heaven, together with the crown of martyrdom, for conquering the one who, having contended with him, had foolishly rejoiced for a moment that he had overcome him.

The relics of his body, buried in the earth, likewise did not cease to testify to this through the efficacy of their miracles.

But, as I said, the negligence of those men concealed this. If they had obtained any talent of knowledge from God, they preferred to bury it in the shroud of earthly vanity and surrender it to worldly pageantry for the sake of pleasing the world,

[Note: Construe: “They preferred to surrender this talent, buried in the shroud of earthly vanity—I mean, to surrender it more to worldly pageantry for the sake of pleasing the world—than, in the manner of the money-changers, to entrust it to peoples who desired the praise and glory of God, as an example to those who would hear.” The reference is to the evangelical parable of the talents, Matthew XXV.]

rather than, in the manner of the money-changers, entrust it to peoples who desired the praise and glory of God, as an example to those who would hear.

Behold what honor, what a protector, what a treasure you have lost—at least in this respect, unfortunate Verona! If you had learned of him by reading, or at least had come to know him through the eloquent account of someone, I think you would not so lightly have lost such a necessary protector.

Would that those to whom he may perhaps have been given from heaven might hear this, and not neglect so precious a jewel granted to them by God!

Therefore, I say, be angry—be angry—with those poets and writers who filled your walls with verses, greedy for empty glory, and did not commit his deeds or miracles to their pages.

[Note: From this it may be inferred that, both in this period and in the preceding century after Saint Metro’s death, it was common at Verona to insert monuments expressed in verse into the walls.]

For if you had known him, you would not have guarded him so wickedly.

## 7.

But I turn my gaze to you others, who are weighed down by the gravest crimes and, together with me, think little of what the Apostle most truthfully confesses—a saying which this saint, the subject of our discussion, did not hear without understanding: “If we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged” (I Corinthians XI, 31).

Not remembering this saint and many others like him, and not considering why they suffered such great and such terrible things, I confess that, having suffered, you go to ruin.

[Note: Construe: “Not remembering this saint and many others like him, and not considering why they suffered such great and such terrible things, I confess that you go on ruined.”]

Without doubt they suffered such things because they had not merely swallowed with their ears the Psalmist’s words: “You commanded that your commandments be kept exceedingly” (Psalm CXVIII, 4).

“Why exceedingly?” you ask. Clearly because, as was most truthfully said before our time, “great rewards cannot be reached except through great labors” (Saint Gregory, *Homily 37 on the Gospels*, no. 1).

For, as the Apostle says, “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that shall be revealed in us” (Romans VIII, 18).

Without doubt all the apostles, martyrs, and saints pondered this. Whoever did not ponder it utterly neglected himself.

Let us place before our eyes anyone who has incurred the same offense that this saint deserved to wash away through such great torments—an offense all the more criminal because it was committed knowingly. This blessed man, however, had fallen into it unknowingly.

He who lies before his tomb, beating his breast and crying out, “Saint Metro, intercede for me, a miserable sinner”—does it not seem possible that the holy martyr might answer him obliquely: “Do what I did, and you will obtain what I obtained”?

What shall we do, entangled in worse crimes and, more gravely still, in crimes committed habitually, sweating upon a feather bed, and murmuring the verses of the Psalms—when even this is a rare bird—and vainly promising ourselves forgiveness through such penance?

“When it is cold, before the fire; when harvest comes, in the shade,” groaning and hoping for indulgence, deceived by mere presumption?

This saint, naked or nearly naked, rolled about day and night for seven years on the most uneven ground.

We criminals, when we are about to ask forgiveness, put on over our hair a woolen cap, though we ought to have torn out those hairs in mourning, so that we might not grow cold.

His *cuphía*—a kind of small cap, Italian *cuffia*—was snow, hail, and rain-bearing wind: winter’s harsh cold, sufficiently grievous, to wash away the crime he had committed.

[Note: Construe: “His *cuphía* was snow, hail, and rain-bearing wind, the sufficiently grievous winter cold.”]

[Note: The meaning is: “His head was covered with winter down in place of the cap that mourners customarily stuff inside with exotic furs”—that is, the cap which those mourning obscene acts, acts contrary to the whole community, or innumerable acts of the same kind customarily stuff with fur.]

That straw cap of Saxon custom, which they place upon the head to ward off the sun’s heat, was for him blazing Phoebus himself. His tent was this airy sky, so that the ethereal sky might not be shut off from him.

The sun served him for shade; the heat (*cauma*, from the Greek word meaning “burning” or “scorching”) served him for refreshment. The waxing and waning of the moon reproached him for what had failed to advance and had rushed toward decline.

Whenever the arranger of the stars had made the starry sky shine with golden lights, the innumerability of the stars continually reminded him to count his innumerable faults and ceaselessly impressed upon him complaints of ingratitude.

What were the crash of thunder, the violence of storms, the stones of hail, and the darts of lightning except the terrifying judgment of divine punishment thundering into his heart?

His star-bearing roof—often rainy, sometimes stormy, and generally clear when God willed—was that varied heavenly sphere. Its alternation compelled mortals to devise dwellings. That roof, I say, was continually for him the entire changing vault of heaven, not warding off the rain but pouring it down, giving snow like wool, scattering mist like ashes, and sending crystal morsels to his unresisting mouth.

Before the cold of these he patiently remained alone until the power of God, sending forth his word, melted them; his spirit breathed, and the waters flowed (Psalm CXLVII, 16–18), washing away the stains of the holy head, both outward and inward.

Whenever rain-bearing clouds covered the sky with a misty darkness, threatening some harm to befall the unfortunate country people, he considered that harm his own sin: he had offended God so greatly that he had brought that evil not only upon himself but also upon the country in which he lived.

For this is what saints often do: they reckon such things to themselves; they take the faults of others upon themselves—not through a deceitful wish, but through the anxious fear of God—not the servile fear that love casts out, but the chaste fear that endures for ever and ever. They do this not because they fear the punishment which, after their conversion, they presume—with God’s promise—to have escaped, but lest, growing sluggish through security, they become unworthy to behold the glory of holiness without love.

[Note: In the manuscript, a point is marked after “glory,” followed by the words “holiness or love, vices, etc.,” without sense. The contextual sentence supports the conjectural emendation. Shortly afterward, *non dedocet* means the same as *docet*, “teaches.”]

They avoid vices not only because of the command of the Lord who orders them to do so, but also intensely abhor them out of hatred, as a certain exceedingly careful writer of verse among his people teaches:

> The good hate sin for love of virtue.  
> (*Horace, Epistles* 16.)

## 8.

Behold the school in which you were educated, most obedient and truly modest disciple of Christ; the arena in which you exercised yourself, athlete of that heavenly king; the fire in which you were burned as a most acceptable offering to Christ.

What did you think, most holy man? What did you say against the one who, nevertheless, envying your salvation, had driven you to this—to a torment that you were compelled to undertake as though it meant a thousand deaths?

Clearly, you turned back upon him the torments you were ordered to suffer, burning him with unspeakable envy because of the victory that was to come to you through God’s mercy.

[Note: Construe: “when you burned him with unspeakable envy because of the victory that was to come to you through God’s mercy.”]

And what of this? Bound in public with a chain like bears, lions, panthers, or Hyrcanian tigers, made a spectacle to angels and human beings, did you see or hear around you crowds laughing, rejoicing, constantly celebrating weddings and continually holding banquets, making frequent collections for their feasts,

[Note: *Symbola* is to be taken in the ablative case. It means a contribution of money collected from those who were going to dine or sup at common expense.]

indulging in the enticements of revelry, while their laughter and games, according to a custom utterly different from yours, were exceedingly offensive to you?

You perceived these things, I believe, with deaf ears, like that other man once perceived the song of the Sirens.

[Note: Construe: “You perceived these things, I believe, with deaf ears, as that other man once perceived the songs of the Sirens.”]

What understanding did you bring to all this? What emotion? What martyrdom was it?

Yet I know, I know—and without hesitation; let others know as well, for I am not afraid to declare what you were doing. Clearly, by prayers you summoned angels, by tears you stirred archangels to help you, by groans you called upon the apostles, and you entreated martyrs, confessors, and virgins to fight on your behalf against the most envious enemy.

What shall I say about that queen of them all? With modesty serving her, I think—modesty, which among the good possesses undeniable power of intercession—you prayed to her all the more effectively the more humbly and modestly you supplicated her.

For I think that no one polluted by carnal pleasure—such as our company—strikes upon her most inviolable hearing without shame, unless he is insane.

The mother of the man clothed with God through the unity of one person in two natures deserved to become his mother because God regarded her humility, incomparable to that of all others. Humility alone is capable of guarding the state of the good with the greatest perseverance. Thus she was able to remain a virgin before childbirth, in childbirth, and no less after childbirth.

It is morally appropriate for everyone to hate what is contrary to the thing he loves most. Therefore, because the holy Mother of God loved chastity above all things, I believe that she holds the opposing lust in greater hatred in all who follow Christ.

With what audacity, then, should lips polluted by seductive kisses and a tongue befouled by obscene speech dare to name the most chaste Virgin, especially since she is also the mother of the inward judge?

How should a heart polluted by wanton meditation presume even to recall her name, venerable to the angels themselves?

But what a guilty conscience refuses to undertake, the mercy of her most merciful Son makes possible, together with a faithful consideration of his incarnation. For I think that he mercifully prevents her from being indignant when even the most wicked servant represents to her the flesh that he mercifully assumed from her for the cleansing of sinners’ offenses.

[Note: Construe: “For I think that her Son mercifully prevents her from being indignant when even the most wicked servant represents to her the flesh that he mercifully assumed from her for the cleansing of sinners’ offenses.”]

And therefore, now that you are secure as a martyr, intercede humbly for us before that same Mother of God, using the same modesty on our behalf.

## 9.

But why do I, most unskilled, attempt this vainly?

> Eloquence failed me; I cannot raise you up.  
> If I possessed Ciceronian eloquence,  
> it could not recount the victorious force  
> of what my heart longs to tell about you.  
> Yet I shall try again, although the power of speech  
> does not follow the will that forbids me to be silent.

I say that every day you labored to sacrifice a victim to the Lord and slaughter a burnt offering—not from another’s flock, but from your own body.

You were the priest; you were the victim. You were the executioner; you were the martyr. You were the torturer; you were the one who endured the torture. You were the throat; you were the one who cut the throat. You were the avenger of the crime, the preserver of the disciple, the neglecter of the flesh, and the guardian of the mind.

I confess that you hated yourself greatly, such as you judged yourself to be, while you tortured yourself so fiercely. You longed to subject the flesh to reason; for that reason you afflicted it so cruelly. But in truth you loved it by hating it, while you reconciled it to the Lord in this way.

For true is the saying: “No one has ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it” (Ephesians V, 29). He speaks of the flesh so that we may not regard the vices of the flesh as things to be loved—a distinction you certainly understood.

[Note: That is: “so that we may not regard the vices of the flesh as things to be loved,” which was by no means unknown to you.]

You knew that the vices proceeded from evil, but that the flesh was made by the one who saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good (Genesis I, 31).

Therefore, martyr, you pursued the vices, not the flesh, when you tormented it in so many different ways—just as a physician attacks a disease with cautery while wishing to help a person by the remedy, despite the flesh’s discomfort.

With what severity, then, good physician, did you torment yourself with the cautery of beloved salvation by burning yourself? With what bitterness of potions did you daily fail to cease treating the interior parts of your soul?

How necessarily you sometimes nourished the flesh as well as the soul, which, having received immortality, would live forever—it would take too long to recount.

### 10

Yet I cannot see what your victory for a time, most troublesome enemy, achieved for you against Christ’s soldier [Note: Construe: “Yet I cannot see what that victory of yours for a time, most troublesome enemy, achieved for you against Christ’s soldier.”]. For we rejoice more triumphantly that you yourself were conquered by his very fall than if, in that hour, you had most foolishly continued your hand against him. Perhaps you had forgotten, most impious one, that the Savior most mercifully declared that there is joy in heaven over one sinner who repents, more than over ninety-nine righteous persons who have no need of repentance (Luke 15:7). For he, perhaps trusting too sluggishly in his own righteousness, had scarcely presumed, as many do, upon forgiveness of sins not especially grave but nevertheless innumerable. Hating that crime into which you had driven him, he did not hesitate to rise up most fiercely against you, exerting all his strength, seizing the sword of divine aid, covered by the shield of the Lord’s protection, wearing you out with Entelline cestuses, constantly shooting arrows and hurling missiles, wrestling with you without respite, naked—God’s grace stripping him naked, so that he might leave you nothing by which you could hold him—and, prudently, attacking you from afar with arrows sent from Jesus’ quiver, and surrounding himself without interruption with the rampart of God’s protection by continually seeking divine help, so that he might remain forever inaccessible [Note: Construe: “For he, perhaps trusting too sluggishly in his own righteousness, had scarcely presumed, as many presume, upon forgiveness of sins not especially grave but nevertheless innumerable; hating that crime into which you had driven him, he exerted all his strength, seized the sword of divine aid, covered by the shield of the Lord’s protection, and did not hesitate to rise up most fiercely against you. He wore you out with Entelline cestuses, shot arrows constantly, hurled missiles, and wrestled with you without respite, naked—God’s grace stripping him naked, so that it would leave you nothing by which you could hold him—and, prudently, etc.”].

Did you not know, or perhaps did you not remember, most wicked one, what that once most noble conqueror had asserted from your dung heap—or rather, what he had said to him who had handed that man over to you to be tested but not at all to be conquered—that God comes from the whirlwind? I mean, did you not remember that an opening had been made in your jaw by the bracelet enclosing us through divine mercy [Note: That is, “an opening had been made by the bracelet of divine mercy enclosing us”], through which all who produce worthy fruits of repentance could escape from the crushing of your jaws [subauditur: “can escape”] (Job 40:21)?

For from where, most wretched one, forgetful of what has passed—from where, I ask, did Peter escape, from where Paul after being made from Saul, from where did so many others escape your jaws, except through that opening? And see, wretched one, what has happened to you. For when you assaulted his heart with carnal wantonness, against your will you drove him more forcefully toward love of the Lord, most unhappy one. Hence, once the most merciful Judge had been appeased, his peace with repentance was stronger precisely where, most impious one, he undertook a harsher struggle against you.

Rightly, therefore, you are called *follis* in the rustic speech of Latium [Note: *Follis* is an old word, from which the Italian *folle* and the French *fol* or *fou* derive; it signifies “empty” and “foolish.” William, abbot of Metz, testifies that it was used by country people in Letter 3: “I pass over the fact that . . . you called me *follem* in a rustic word.” John the Deacon, in *Life of St. Gregory*, Book IV, chapter 96, says that it was customary in Gaul: “But he, rebuking the holy old man in the Gallic manner, called him *follem*.” When Ratherius, however, attributes a Latin rusticity to the same word in a work composed at Verona, he indicates that it was also current among our own country people as a designation for a demon; hence perhaps those evil spirits later came popularly to be called *folletti*. Ratherius’ text suggests a Latin origin from *follis*, which is filled only with air and is empty within.]—because you are empty of truth, although crammed with falsehood, and therefore you deceive yourself, most foolishly, so very often.

Thus you caused Abel to become the first martyr; thus you caused Shem and Japheth to be blessed; thus you caused Joseph to be glorified. And, so that our invective against you may not proceed endlessly, thus you alienated from yourself the sovereignty of the entire world of believers, when you persuaded the disciple to sell his Teacher, God and Lord, and persuaded the buyers to cry, “Crucify him, crucify him!” Yet you immediately regretted having done this, when, by troubling Pilate’s wife in a dream, you compelled her to send a message asking her husband to withdraw from the crime.

But the heavenly Disposer, who knew how to use your malice benevolently, worked condemnation for you and your accomplices on account of so great a crime, and redemption for all the saints—as it happily happened also to this blessed man. And, to bring forward something from more recent times with which to refute you, ancient serpent, I want you to consider what harm you did to Moses and Macarius, who were to become most famous hermits: persuading one of them to commit robbery and the other murder (Tripartite History, Book VIII, chapter 1).

Therefore, finally, be ashamed—be ashamed, I say, although uselessly I admonish you—so multiply conquered; and restrain your now-empty efforts against God’s elect, most wretched one. For the heavenly Physician knows—as a certain outstanding orator most elegantly says—how to accomplish many good things even through the wicked, when he turns to assistance what had been prepared for harm.

Nor should you believe, in your most cunning folly—as I may so call it—that the Lord had handed one of his own over to you to be overcome, if you had understood how that light had prevailed over you in the deepest darkness: the light which blinded you still further when, giving you everything that the man whom you had proposed to attack possessed [supply: “he possessed”], he commanded you to preserve his life (Job 2:6). For how would you preserve what, once preserved and destined to be preserved, you hasten instead to destroy? Yet by saying, “Preserve him; do not touch him,” he made it understood that you were to preserve him. Unless you touched his soul by suggestion, how, most deceived one, could you turn him by pleasure toward consenting to curse God—even in this at least?

Most truly, therefore—and the same could be believed of any of your accomplices—you may recognize as spoken about you: “Woe to him who deceives; will he not himself be deceived?” Indeed, you are often deceived; deceived, I say, most poisonous dragon, fashioned for mockery of you, as the Psalmist sings (Psalm 103:27). For there is also this distinction between malice and goodness: the souls whom God especially loves, you especially hate.

Why did you not consider that nothing you would regard as a great prize was being preserved for you, since you were permitted to afflict the body, which would eventually be corrupted even if this had not been granted to you, but were commanded not to harm the incorruptible soul? You who devour the river of paganism, do you not marvel and take confidence that the Jordan of Christianity flows into your mouth? (Job 40:1.) What else can this mean except baptismal water, by which souls are washed clean—souls whose descent into perdition you thirst for insatiably, in order to swallow them?

It is therefore astonishing that you did not understand that, by such a concession, you were being deceived—a particular deception of the deceived [Note: “A particular deception of the deceived” addresses the devil in the vocative case. The author says that it is astonishing that he did not understand that he himself was being deceived by the sort of concession by which he was permitted to rage against Job’s and other righteous persons’ bodies while their souls were nevertheless preserved.].

If you had merely demanded tribute from your own people for the dominion once invaded, there would not have been so much cause for complaint. Why do you intrude upon what belongs to another—and, what is even more astonishing, upon the right of one who has confirmed his own by the promise of his own mouth [Note: Construe: “Why do you intrude upon what belongs to another, and indeed upon the right of one greater—which is even more astonishing—of him who has so confirmed his own by the promise of his own mouth, etc.”]: “Father, those whom you have given me, I have not lost any of them” (John 18:9).

But because you regarded the past tense as implying that he did not care about the future, most foolish one, you do not cease to harass them without end. But hear, together with your detestable counsel: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28:20). Believe me, he will not expose any of his own to you as helpless, so that you may rejoice in a complete victory. Although he permits countless people to be harassed for a longer time by the malicious fraud of your assault, the Merciful One will raise them, as he raised this man, to the fullness of victory [Note: Construe: “Believe me, he will not expose any of his own to you as helpless, so that you may rejoice completely. The Merciful One will also raise to the fullness of victory those whom he permits to be harassed for a longer time by the malicious fraud of your assault, although they are countless—that is, although they are innumerable—as he raised this St. Metron.”].

The distinction between power and omnipotence is ultimately this: the former can do certain things, the latter everything. It is therefore clear from this distinction that power is powerless when omnipotence opposes it. Consequently, it is rightly concluded that God can draw to himself from your ranks whomever he wishes and in whatever manner he wishes, despite your opposition; but you should not even dare to attack any of his own unless he permits it—even a herd of swine you did not dare invade in any way unless permission had been given (Matthew 8:31), as you, wretched one, most clearly experienced.

His drawing is salvation; your drawing is perdition—from which he also habitually mercifully liberates countless people. For even though your whelps growl in order to snatch their prey, they nevertheless seek their food from God, as is read in the Psalm (Psalm 103:21), desiring that he withdraw his protection from those whom their malice might attack.

Although you are also said to have dragged, or to be dragging, or to be about to drag a large part of the stars from heaven down to earth by your tail (Revelation 12:4), I warn you not to be deceived. For this is not said of those who will shine like the sun in everlasting eternities (Matthew 13:43), and like the brightness of the firmament (Daniel 12:3), who instruct many; no, it is not said of those who truly cleave to the true light and truly shine. Rather, it is said of those who, imitating [supply: “you”], are not afraid hypocritically to transform themselves into angels of light (2 Corinthians 11:14), destined to fall with you into the abyss of hell—stars outwardly, darkness inwardly, if I may put it so.

For I cannot see how those who shine like the brightness of the firmament—namely, those who strive as far as they can to imitate the steadfastness of the holy angels, who have attained the grace of immutability when you fell—could ever be enveloped in your eternal darkness, since their names are written in heaven (Luke 10:20) [Note: Construe: “But those who, imitating you and destined to fall with you into the abyss of hell, are outwardly stars and inwardly darkness, if I may so speak, are not afraid hypocritically to transform themselves into angels of light. For I cannot see how those who shine like the brightness of the firmament—namely, those who strive as far as they can to imitate the steadfastness of those angels who attained the grace of immutability when you fell—could be enveloped in eternal darkness, since their names are written in heaven, etc.”].

Believe me, they will never be found in the diptych of your perdition, blackest Lemur—even if you desire to stain them with the disease of a thousand crimes—for they have surely been cast out through the opening in your jaw, as was this man of ours, from your throat (Job 40:21).

### 11

Nor can we sufficiently praise you, blessed martyr, who endured so much; nor can we sufficiently censure him who drove you to endure those things of necessity, as he deserves, and pursue him with hatred equal to his envy toward us. In the midst of all this, we are exceedingly wretched and unhappy: while we attempt to praise you with our words, our conduct is contrary; while we proclaim you in speech, our deeds are unlike yours.

You are glorified by the blessed palm of victory; we, on the contrary, are accused by an unhappy conscience. And lest it be said to any one of us, “Out of your own mouth I judge you, wicked servant” (Luke 19:22), whatever is suspect causes us altogether to fear.

For if you held such a treasure, why did you treat it with such contempt? Why did you allow so precious a pearl to be stolen from you [Note: Here *sublego* is understood as “steal,” as it can also be found in reputable authors]? Why did you not guard with the greatest care a coin of such brilliance? Since you rightly praise him for having done this with respect to one crime, why do you not strive to do the same with respect to innumerable crimes of no different kind of condemnation [Note: Construe: “Why do you not strive to act with respect to innumerable crimes in a manner no different from the condemnation—or malice—which you rightly say he displayed in the case of one crime?”]?

If by repentance he deserved to receive not only forgiveness, as you credibly assert, but also the palm of martyrdom, why do you, through impenitence, store up wrath for yourself (Romans 2:5), and an eternally unquenchable flame? But this is what our instability and weakness accomplish, most steadfast athlete—we do not deny it. May your constancy and firmness come to our aid, I ask.

### 12

Someone may wonder that I so often call you a martyr, most holy confessor, since you did not attain the end through the shedding of blood. But rather, I say, let him wonder that he does not remember what the Lord said to the sons of Zebedee: “You shall drink my cup” (Matthew 20:23), although only one of them passed from the world through the shedding of blood for Christ, while the other [Note: That is, one of them alone—St. James, not St. John—passed from the world through the shedding of blood for Christ, while the other, etc.], like you most happily, endured many torments for God, but, called to rest in peace, did not lack the glory of martyrdom. The testimony of Christ’s levite Vincent, who was not among the least even among the most eminent, shows that this happened to him before death, in death, and after death, and likewise to many others.

The tyrant’s sword did not drive his soul from his body. Rather, after he had cheerfully overcome for Christ the dreadful punishments of torments and had steadfastly completed the contest of his blessed struggle—as is most beautifully sung of him—he was at last released into precious death and, triumphing in heaven, gave back his spirit, like Agatha also, the blessed woman.

“The sword will pass through your own soul” (Luke 2:35), the just Simeon says to the blessed Mother of God, clearly prophesying that she would undergo the martyrdom of sorrow, not of death.

### 13

Rejoice, therefore, martyr; rejoice, I say, be glad and exult, and, we ask, always intercede with God for our undeserved misery.

For you imitate the gentleness of that man [that is, the ancient Joseph]—if you freely spare guilty servants—who once forgave his brothers, the men who had sold him, with such kindness, though he addressed them truthfully. Yet we have not so far been able to discover any seller of your holy body. To do this would have been the crime of Judas the betrayer; to imitate it would be the sacrilege of some wicked criminal or gravedigger [Note: Construe: “To do this would have been to imitate the crime of Judas the betrayer, or the sacrilege of some wicked criminal or gravedigger.” From this it is clear that it was uncertain whether the body of St. Metron had been sold for a price or secretly stolen.].

But, holy one, alas for the wickedness! We lament that you were neglected by us to such an extent that your venerable tomb could somehow be approached by theft. We do not deny that this deed too was abominable. For who, unless mad, would neglect such a patron, even if he possessed the neighboring presence of a thousand saints’ bodies?

Therefore, most merciful Father, considering us degenerate sons—or rather, most wicked servants—who now remember you absent with a devotion more fervent than that with which we once honored you present, since this often happens, we beg you not to repay us in kind for our evils. Do not abandon us in your protection, even though you may have abandoned us, though utterly unworthy, by your departure; but, being most present to us in Christ your Head, do not cease, we ask, to reconcile him to us through your merits—not only for this offense but also for guilt of every kind [Note: Construe: “Therefore, most merciful Father, considering us sons—or rather, most wicked servants—who remember you absent with a more devout affection than we, degenerate as we are, once honored you present, since this often happens, we beg you not to repay us in kind for our evils, not abandoning us, etc. The manuscript copy had *repende*, ‘repay,’ for *noli, te precamur, rependere*, ‘do not, we beg you, repay’; we introduced the emendation into the text because it is necessary for the sense.”].

Let this have happened to you through our fault and neglect—something we cannot rightly deny; but we cannot deny that it happened by the will and arrangement of him who governs earthly things together with heavenly things, whose ordinance no opposition has ever been able to resist.

For he wished to raise you from the earth, where you had been pressed beneath the mound of burial [Note: Hence, until Ratherius’ time, the body of St. Metron had remained lying in the ground where it had been buried and had not been raised from the earth, as was accustomed to be done elsewhere with holy bodies. This was evidently the ancient custom of the Church of Verona: to bury sacred bodies beneath the ground. Thus, in the eighth century, St. Bishop Anno brought the bodies of the martyrs Firmus and Rusticus and four other martyrs to Verona and placed them in a subterranean stone coffin—that is, in a coffin buried beneath the earth. Similarly, the body of our bishop St. Proculus was found in his confession, buried seven feet underground, in the year 1492, although an earlier translation of the same body had taken place, recorded in the ancient calendar of the Church of Verona on the Kalends of May.], and place you in a fitting position.

For people more devoutly honor the limbs of one whose soul is in heaven if the earth does not cover them, but the adornment of a mausoleum beautifies them.

If this was truly done as is believed, there is no doubt that this example, which we shortly before recalled concerning Joseph and his brothers, harmonizes with your case: “Do not be afraid,” he said to those who feared him; “can we resist the will of God? You thought evil against me, but God turned it to good, in order to exalt me” (Genesis 50:19–20).

Therefore, I ask, let your exaltation not become our condemnation; let your departure not become our destruction. But, we ask, may it instead benefit one of us, if, with a sincere heart, he has not opposed your being exalted in this way, although perhaps so darkened by the darkness of his own crimes that, compelled by sudden admonition, he did not remember the command addressed to him: “Let your eyelids go before your steps” (Proverbs 4:25), and forgot what had been foretold to him: “There are ways that seem right to human beings, but their end plunges down to the depth of hell” (Proverbs 16:25) [Note: Construe: “But, we ask, may your exaltation benefit one of us, if, with a sincere heart, he has not opposed your being exalted in this way, although perhaps he is so darkened by the darkness of his own crimes that, compelled by sudden admonition, he has not remembered the command addressed to him, ‘Let your eyelids go before your steps,’ and has forgotten what was foretold to him, ‘There are ways,’ etc.”].

But while the Lord revives such faintheartedness in this manner and says, “If your eye is single, your whole body will be full of light” (Matthew 6:22), may he enter, under your guidance, martyr, into whichever of the three cities of refuge he wishes, between hope of forgiveness and fear of hell (Joshua 20:7). There, if necessary, he may cry out intelligibly concerning this crime, as concerning countless others, in the Psalmist’s words:

“Evils without number have surrounded me; my iniquities have overtaken me, and I was unable to see; they are multiplied beyond the hairs of my head, and my heart has abandoned me. Be pleased, O Lord, to deliver me” (Psalm 40:12–13) [Note: That is, “May he, trusting in your guidance, martyr, enter whichever of the three cities of refuge he wishes, between hope of forgiveness and fear of hell, so that, if necessary, he may cry out intelligibly in the Psalmist’s words concerning this crime, just as concerning countless others: ‘Evils without number,’ etc.”].

Moreover, this visible sun of mortals, borne aloft with its flame-bearing horses, seeks the heights and produces better benefits for those born of earth. But the sun of your light is Christ himself, the infuser of light. Let him himself be the narrator of his own action:

“I am going,” he says, “to him who sent me, and none of you asks me, ‘Where are you going?’ But because I have spoken these things to you, sorrow has filled your heart. Yet I tell you the truth: it is better for you that I go away” (John 16:5–7). And again: “If I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself” (John 12:32).

Therefore, not without reason, that man rejoiced, though we know Christ according to the flesh, but now we no longer know him in that way (2 Corinthians 5:16).

It is therefore established, and cannot be doubted, that if faith suffers no loss in the saints through death, it suffers still less through absence. Consequently, we confidently believe that, if we follow your footsteps, your departure has benefited us; and it does not benefit us now to know that you are dead and have you dwelling among countless others in our vicinity [Note: In our vicinity means “in our same city,” which included the suburbs. Thus, in *Deliberative Conclusion*, no. 8, *vicinitas* means the same city; and in the *Apologeticus*, no. 5, *vicinus* means an inhabitant of the same city or place. Construe: “Nor does it now benefit us to know that we have you, dead, in our vicinity; rather, it benefits us to know that, as truly holy, you have by God’s favor been translated with the highest honor to that place where the martyrdom of your struggles is cultivated day and night with due veneration.”].

For us, whatever its value may be, what we believe is an easing of guilt: we have ceased, though late and very improperly, to treat you in that way; we have learned, at least from the example of others, to honor you as we ought with fitting honor; to mourn you as a lost father; by mourning, to love you more ardently; by loving, to remember you more frequently; and by remembering, to pray to you with greater reverence.

You have drawn us to yourself, martyr, if we may speak so, when you were exalted by God as you deserved; you have drawn us, and, by leaving us, you possess us all the more firmly, the more devoutly we remember you in holiness.

For every prudent and religious person now visits the relics of your ashes more diligently than, in former times, everyone honored the place where the guardian of your entire holy body, together with the others, was kept. Consequently, wherever our devotion toward you, martyr, increases, there it is necessary that your piety and, we must hope, your providential care toward us also increase.

As for those who dared profane the shrine of your relics, I warn them to approach the inner counselor and diligently ask him what impulse of intention they followed in such a great crime, and to release the act itself to his judgment. For if in this they followed the simple eye of their desire as their guide, they can, I admit, rejoice that they have attained what they desired [Note: *Adepto* seems to be the reading required: “that they have attained what was in their desire.” The text that follows is very corrupt, unless perhaps it should be construed as follows: “But if otherwise, we may, I think, greatly fear how the authority of him who says the following will strike them in this matter: ‘If anyone violates the temple of God, God will destroy him.’ I rejoice in the saying—and how elegantly!—‘Have charity, and do whatever you wish. For charity,’ etc.”].

But if otherwise, we may, I think, greatly fear how the authority of him who says, “If anyone violates the temple of God, God will destroy him” (1 Corinthians 3:17), will strike them. In this matter we may appeal to the saying: “Have charity, and do whatever you wish” (1 Corinthians 13:4). And how elegantly I rejoice in the words: “For charity,” as another says, “does not act wrongly.”

Is charity therefore idle? God forbid. Hear the most truthful confession: “The love of God is never idle; for, if it exists, it accomplishes great things; and if it refuses to act, it is not love.”

### 14

When these matters concerning the worship and veneration of your limbs, holy one, have thus been brought together—wherever it is said that they were carried—and of your ashes, wherever it is believed that they were left, one can determine with complete certainty what sort of reward from God anyone may hope to receive, whether from those who carried them away or from those who lost them [Note: Construe: “When these matters concerning the worship and veneration of your limbs have thus been brought together—wherever your holy limbs are said to have been carried—and of your ashes, wherever you are believed to have been left—that is, at Verona, where only your ashes are believed to have remained—one can determine with complete certainty what reward from God anyone may hope to receive, whether from those who carried you away—that is, those who stole your holy body—or from those who lost you—that is, those who lost that same body.”].

Yet we pray, most gracious and holy Father, that we may find in you, who pardon the excesses committed by both parties against you, an unfailing intercessor for us before the Lord Jesus Christ, the most merciful redeemer of the world, and the most just examiner not only of our deeds but also of our intentions. He lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## Fragment of the Same Work

Composed during Ratherius’ earliest labors and previously edited from a manuscript of the cathedral chapter of Verona.

### 1

As the most sacred and truthful chronicler of former times tells us, when God’s mercy had long intended mercifully to free his afflicted people from the hands of the Memphite tyrant—or rather, from the jaws of the monster of the Nile [Note: In the first hand of the Verona manuscript from which this fragment was first published, *Niliaei* was written. The alteration to *Memphitici* was inserted both in the printed Verona edition and, during his final revisions, in the Freising manuscript.], among the other measures appropriate to this work he commanded that, before departing, each individual member of that people should borrow from his friend vessels of silver and gold. Thus the people destined to be swallowed by the waves of the baleful sea [Note: Above *venefici*, Ratherius wrote *spumei*; the Freising manuscript has *punicei*.] would be stripped of possessions long held unjustly, and the God-worshipping offspring of Abraham would be enriched by a heavenly gift.

Yet, if the impenetrable obscurity of human wisdom—which God confounds—is considered, the cause of this event will prove almost analogous to the mystery of that most fraudulent deception which is rightly censured. Here, however, there presents itself the greatest wisdom and knowledge of God, whose depth (Romans 11:33) it is fitting for a sound-minded person to admire with the Apostle, spokesman for God, rather than investigate and condemn with the mad catalogue of heretics. This incomprehensibility of divine disposition has been displayed and shown to us through those who, as we read, were given authority to fill twelve baskets (Matthew 14:20).

When we attentively consider the many mysteries of this incomprehensibility, insofar as that most merciful distributor of graces deigns to add them to our sluggishness through the zeal of personal inquiry, it very often happens that we experience what the incomparable wise man was not ashamed to confess:

“I searched out wisdom,” he says, “and it was far from me” (Ecclesiastes 7:24).

And rightly so.
