For from the two fish, acquired only through laborious ingenuity from the waves of an uncertain abundance, and from the five loaves, again not without a mystery in their number, these fragments were filled into twelve baskets (Matthew 14:17). If one wishes to store them in the belly of memory, one will certainly experience the truth of the saying: “He who adds knowledge adds labor” (Ecclesiastes 1:18).

For they are not loaves of wheat, so that they could easily be stripped; they are barley loaves (John 6:9), to whose marrow even the most devoted labor can scarcely penetrate. Therefore, with the upper millstone turned in a circle and the lower one lying as though idle, this barley material, which we have undertaken to winnow before us, having necessarily been ground, tastes to us—once it has been brought near to the palate—as signifying Egypt, the world lying in wickedness; Pharaoh, the devil, prince of the world; the people oppressed by mud and bricks, the human race, whom the Lord descended when sent to liberate; the Red Sea, baptism dyed with the blood of Christ; those submerged, sins; and those liberated, people washed in baptism and redeemed from the death of the soul by our Savior’s blood.

With regard to the gold and silver vessels, stolen by the liberator’s advice through borrowing [Note: In the printed edition, *si* was missing, and shortly afterward *opes . . . et fallere* had been printed corruptly; that verb completely reverses the sense of the sentence. The manuscript itself supplies the correction.], a question arises: what are the wealth—or the ornaments—of secular books, which, as we see, were wholly taken from the pagans and, through Christ’s gift, passed long ago into the possession and adornment of the Church [Note: Thus Ratherius wrote in a second hand in the same Verona manuscript; in the first hand he had written *jamdiu*.]?

“What purpose do these things serve?” asks the inquisitive questioner. Surely this: that we may acknowledge that the Apostle did not cry out without reason: “Where is the wise person? Where is the scribe? Where is the inquirer of this age? Has not God made foolish the wisdom of the world?” (1 Corinthians 1:20).

By now, indeed:

> Another Joshua had destroyed Kiriath-sepher,  
> and had utterly cast down Jericho’s walls upon the earth;  
> all the crossroads of the world resound with rejoicing saints.

### 2

While our historians eagerly strove with no less zeal to describe the contests of martyrs, the merits of confessors, the celibacy and continence of virgins and widows [Note: We have corrected this from the manuscript. The printed edition incorrectly had *et constantiam*. The noun *celibatus* refers to virgins, and *continentia* to widows. Hence in the ancient litanies found in manuscript 33 of the Verona Chapter, after *holy virgins* comes *holy continent women*, that is, holy widows. We published *extollere* rather than *attollere* after several words, on the authority of the cited manuscript.], and the repentance of converts, those men celebrated throughout the whole world for the beauty of their eloquence—the inventors or propagators of the liberal arts, whom lying Greece produced above all, and whom poetic chatter, always puffed up with falsehood adorned with ornament, never ceased to exalt with praises as its heroes—

now, alas for shame, in our own times and those of our ancestors, so great a scarcity of writers has invaded the world that, if any distinction of merit has shone forth either in our times or in the times of those whom I have mentioned, the common people rather than any learned person has proclaimed it. This compels us to infer that the arrival of him concerning whom it was prophesied is not far away, before whose face poverty will go (Job 41:13).

Let them tell me, then, I demand, to what use the Egyptians lent those vessels which they possess, gold or silver, if they do not display any adornment from them in the tabernacle or temple of the Lord.

“Horma” to them, I fear—Horma, I say, on account of the stolen golden bar [Note: The printed edition had “Onna, I fear, Onam.” The manuscript has “Orna, I fear, Ornam.” It would have been better written *Horma*, meaning “devoted to destruction” or “anathema,” a word taken from Numbers 21:3. Since the theft of the golden bar in Joshua 7:21 is indicated, Ratherius, through a lapse of memory, wrote “Moses” instead of “Joshua.” He later corrected this in his final revisions, as is clear from the Freising manuscript.]—which was not shown to Moses.

The Lord Jesus was casting out a demon, and it was mute; and when he had cast out the demon, the mute man spoke (Luke 11:14). May God repeat this miracle, we pray, and may our mouth speak the praise of the Lord (Psalm 145:21).

### 3

[An extensive lacuna occurs here.] Now, therefore, I shall rightly be angry with the scholars of our own age and that of our uncles, and I shall recount the matter with mournful speech [Note: The printed edition had “me stud . . . depromam.” We corrected it with the aid of the Verona manuscript; in the Freising manuscript, during his final revisions, Ratherius wrote *moestiloquo*—“with mournful speech”—instead of *moesto*.].

The first occurrence, I confess, happened recently—that is, at the time when the most glorious, just, and pious Otto, emperor Augustus, celebrated throughout the whole world, had happily entered Italy to triumph—a very serious loss to the people of Verona, caused not only by the fault of the man who was then most unworthily in charge there, but also by the passage of sixty years, during which his predecessors had held office.

For the body of a certain saint, Metron—whether I should call him a confessor or a martyr I hesitate—had been carried away from the suburb of that same city, which contained the basilica of the blessed martyr Vitalis. The theft was praiseworthy, but the loss blameworthy.

Since the common crowd, moved by religious love, regularly visited the memory of this saint because of the innumerable miracles performed there through that blessed man, the place had nevertheless become so worthless—alas for the wickedness!—to the most wretched bishops alone and to those who, with most vain labor, devoted themselves to eating the husks of pigs rather than the loaves of wheat’s sweetness, by which the generous man returning to his father lamented that the multitude of hired servants abounded while he himself was perishing from hunger, that, once the revenue owing to that church had been bestowed on soldiers [Note: So the manuscript reads. The printed edition incorrectly had *ejusdem*, “of the same.”], there was not even a priest there who would care for the place containing so precious a treasure.

> Alas, sorrow! Weeping dwellers of the world, I beg you, weep.

Who, indeed, could sufficiently censure—or rather lament you (which is safer and more reasonable)—wretched Italy? You abuse the princes of the apostles most disgracefully; you trample upon martyrs; you crush the confessors beneath your feet; with your most filthy feet you grind down the venerated tombs of virgins; and, like a dog preventing others from reaching the hay, with envious barking you persecute by curses those whom, while present, you had refused to venerate, when they departed—or, more truthfully, when they fled from you and sought others. O most unhappy woman, ought you not rather to have rejoiced in the honor of those [that is, the saints] who had become cheap in your sight because of their multitude, and not begrudged the desire, devotion, and [lacuna] of those who, having none, when they were in need, deserved to receive a few from the Lord [Col. 0474B] [Note: The words “when they were in need,” which were absent from the common edition, have been supplied from the Verona manuscript.]? Why, at least in this matter, does it please you not to remember that apostolic saying: “If anyone has the world’s goods and sees his brother in need, yet closes his heart against him, how does the love of God abide in him?” (1 John 3:17). And: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matthew 19:19). Why do you grieve over what was lost, which, while you had it, you did not love very much? But in truth you do not grieve; you falsely pretend to grieve in order to wound certain people. For if you truly grieved over those who were lost, you would cultivate those who remained with more devoted worship.

### 4

Yet although you are able, as you strive to do, to criticize by railing against those placed over you, I urge you to consider that you have hardly deserved better men. For it is most truly written concerning God that “he makes the hypocrite reign because of the sins of the people” (Job 34:30). And he himself says: “I will give them kings in my wrath, and in my anger” (Hosea 13:11). If you loved your martyr so greatly, why did you guard him so badly? Your bishop may have consented, as you insist on accusing him, to a disposition arranged according to some higher and perhaps more suitable plan. But you, who abhorred so great a crime, I wish to know why you abhorred it.

“Because,” you say, “it is most evil that we should thus lose our saints.”

Most truly—but you would speak more appropriately if you admitted: “It is disgraceful that our saints thus flee from us” [Note: Ratherius first wrote *fatereris* (“you would admit”) instead of *diceres* (“you would say”).]. Since no saint is greedy for shameful profit, no saint is found to have fled from honorable profit. Honorable profit, however, is that which enriches heaven and strips hell.

But if it pleased some saint, fleeing from you, to go by whatever effort to that place where, in return for the reverence that he had by no means honorably received, love offered to him for Christ’s sake might fill the heavenly paradise with devout souls [Note: The manuscript has this wording. The common edition had, less appropriately, “the lower Tartarus would be emptied.” Shortly afterward, where it reads “had deserved from your people ... you may seem,” Ratherius’s first manuscript had “had deserved from your countrymen ... you may appear.”], and the infernal Tartarus might be emptied, when throughout so many years none of your people had deserved this for a similar devotion, beware lest you appear to envy heaven’s gains and rejoice in its losses. This too, which you display by your example, you neither desire to have honored among you nor allow the saints to have honor elsewhere.

### 5

But, great Verona, once a town like that other [Note: We have added *ut altera* (“like that other”) from the manuscript; from the same source we have written *pro* (“for”) where the common edition had *prae* (“before”).] Platonic Athens, or another city esteemed for its multitude of wise men, why did you not exalt your saint in high-sounding strains? Why did you not publish the wonders that God had worked through him, if not in meter, at least in a popular prose style [Note: The common edition reads *sale* (“with wit”), less correctly. The manuscript’s true reading is *stylo* (“in style”).]? Believe me, you would have read more honorably what the unlearned populace sang, and you would have adorned this tabernacle of God with Taphnite gold, offering also what the cultivator of the soil had borrowed, and furnishing it with silver [Col. 0475B].

For, to your disgrace, when someone who perhaps knew of so precious a deed had asked your bishop how holy his saint had been [Note: The common edition had mutilated the sentence, reading *qui ...*; we supplied the complete wording from the manuscript.], why did he not turn to the book of his deeds and learn from the stu— [lacuna] of those who, wishing with the Psalmist to sing the songs of that holy man, [lacuna] reported [Note: The common edition had *can ... ferentibus*. There is indeed a lacuna in the manuscript; but we have reproduced whatever it was possible to read.] that the saint, in his youth, had been entangled in such worldly activities as the divine book describes: “Those who desire to become rich in this world fall into a snare and a trap of the devil” (1 Timothy 6:9).

When, with God mercifully permitting it—as had often happened to many others—he was moved by consideration of his guilt, he did not delay to rise up against himself and abandon everything in this world, so that he might serve the Lord alone more freely and without encumbrance [Note: The manuscript has this reading. The common edition was erroneous: “When ... mercifully permitting ...”].

Like Zacchaeus, he climbed the sycamore of the cross in order to see Jesus and be liberated (Luke 19:4). And, so that he might not bear the same cross in compulsory service with Simon, but might bear that same cross, being put to death with his vices and desires—not merely for a time, but daily—he chose for himself such a punishment that, even if he wished to escape after being overcome by the wantonness of the flesh, he would be wholly unable to do so [Note: The common edition reads *cadere* (“to fall”). Certain letters, revealed by more careful examination of the manuscript, establish the true reading, which is especially confirmed by the Freising manuscript.].

Judging himself to be a publican and sinner beyond all others, he shut himself out from the thresholds of the church. Standing at a distance, he took care that he could cry out with that other man who was mercifully justified: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner” (Luke 18:13) [Col. 0476A].

### 6

But why do I bring forward something that is not appropriate—“standing”—as though we had ever heard of anyone before or after him inflicting upon himself a martyrdom of this kind?

I shall pass over those torments that concern the belly or stomach—for I leave their assessment to anyone who considers the rest—and, turning to outward things, I shall describe the punishment inflicted upon him, a punishment unheard of before.

As though he were saying to himself the words of a most impious and cruel torturer, “Because, when you were in honor, you did not understand; compared with foolish beasts, you became like them. Restrict yourself with the bridle of beasts, lest in your wantonness you should be able to wander any further” (Psalm 48:13), he placed a chain on his foot, fastened it with lead to the great stone that still lies before the door of the basilica, and secured the ring around his foot with a lock used for doors. He threw the key into the whirlpool of the nearby Athesis, a well-known river on whose bank the aforementioned basilica stands (I speak somewhat crudely, so that the meaning may be understood). Perhaps he asked God’s mercy that he might never see the key until the clemency of the Almighty had forgiven the sins that he had resolved to lament.

I have therefore used the adverb “perhaps” because, although I did not learn these things by report [Note: The common edition reads “reported miracles,” and shortly afterward *sacris* instead of *supernis*. The readings here expressed are those that could be established from the Verona manuscript; the Freising manuscript makes them more certain.], it has been discovered through a miracle that this happened to him, God granting it by the outcome.

Thus for seven years he remained chained beneath the open sky to the stone, until God, mercifully willing to bring an end to the things that accompanied such a punishment and to crown his martyr with heavenly honors, caused fishermen to bring a fish to the bishop. In its belly that holy key was found, and it announced that all his crimes had been forgiven.

When the key was recognized, and the chained fetter unlocked by the bishop; when that blessed man had been washed, clothed, restored to the Church, and refreshed by participation in the holy body and blood of the Lord, with *vestigio* [lacuna], the Lord’s most [lacuna] holy victim, at the departure of his spirit, was borne heavenward by the rowing of angels [lacuna].

---

# [THREE DOCUMENTS]

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING THREE DOCUMENTS

We present here together the following three documents, which ought, in chronological order, to be placed after the preceding *Invective*, because all of them concern clerics ordained by Milo, “the invader of the see of Verona,” as the author calls him. Ratherius doubted the legitimacy of their ordination and of their exercise of the orders they had received.

All were written in the year 963, as we have shown more fully in the *Life*, §14, after Ratherius had been restored to his see for the third time and had been confirmed in it both by a decree of the Roman pontiff and by the judgment of the synod of Pavia.

The first two are decrees. In the first, written on 8 February, he ordered the same clerics to abstain from office until the day of a legitimate ordination should arrive. In the second, issued on the following day because disturbances had been stirred up by those same men, he treated them as to be left to their own consciences, in effect revoking the first decree.

The third document, signed on the Kalends of August, has the appearance of a letter and was printed by Acherius among the letters. Properly speaking, however, it is not a letter but a booklet written by Ratherius in the name of the clergy of Verona and addressed in its title to the Roman Church. In it the same clerics are introduced as setting forth the canons and decrees brought against them by the bishop, as though they were submitting such a case for judgment by the Roman see. See what we have discussed more fully concerning this matter in the cited place of the *Life*.

# DECREES AND BOOKLET OF RATHERIUS

[Note: We recovered this previously unpublished decree from the Freising manuscript, where it follows the preceding *Invective*. We supplied the missing title.]

## Concerning clerics ordained by Milo, the invader of his see

### I. DECREE OF RATHERIUS CONCERNING CLERICS ORDAINED BY MILO, THE INVADER OF HIS SEE

We command that those ordained by the invader of this see, mitigating the canonical sanction imposed upon them [Note: This refers to the canons found in the third document, or booklet written in the name of the clergy of Verona, which were collected by Ratherius himself. They prescribe something stricter than what is decreed in the present document.], abstain, by the authority of God, of holy Mary, of the holy apostle Peter, prince of the apostles, and of all the saints, from the office into which he illegally instituted them, until the day of a legitimate ordination shall arrive.

Done on the Second Sunday of the month of February [Note: Since in the year 963, when we have established in the *Life*, §14, that this decree was issued, the solar cycle was XX and the Sunday letter was D, the Second Sunday of February fell on the eighth day of that month.].

### II. ANOTHER DECREE OF THE SAME MAN ON THE SAME MATTER

[Note: In the Freising manuscript this decree follows the preceding one; it was published from that manuscript by Father Bernhard Pez, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. VI, p. 93.]

RATHERIUS, BISHOP OF VERONA, TO ALL THE CLERICS OF HIS CHURCH

Although I may have learned from Tully that laws are silent amid wars, not from the teaching of Augustine, when I observed that you had not praised yesterday’s promulgation with unanimous agreement, it was easy to recognize that from it would arise rather the murmur of many than an announcement of rectitude or any fruit beneficial to the salvation of souls.

Therefore, lest I be judged a rash self-praiser and an avenger of an injury inflicted upon me rather than an executor of the laws; lest, not daring to call the invader of my office a bishop, I condemn myself by my own words; and lest, by judging those instituted by him not to be priests or deacons in any respect, I seem to have deposed my own clergy—I now leave to the judgment of God and to their own discretion, having somewhat lightened the canonical sanction that I imposed upon them yesterday, whether they will dare to exercise the offices imposed upon them by the invader. My force does not prevent them from doing so [Note: The adverbs *hodie quoque* (“today as well”) seem to indicate that Ratherius again insisted on 9 February that his clerics carry out the preceding decree, issued the day before, and that he thereby confirmed it once more. But since they continued to cause disturbances, he issued this second decree, by which, suspending the earlier decree, he left them to divine judgment and their own consciences.].

If they are afraid, my command does not compel them to be afraid [Note: This is the reading of the Freising manuscript, whose copy we received. P. Pez has *sed timent* (“but they fear”), less correctly.]. Let it be their concern whether they themselves decide to use or abuse the Lord’s command, while I am entirely free of blame in this matter.

As for the bishops whom he is alleged to have ordained to the presbyterate, my inactivity satisfies me in no other way than by answering that “each will bear his own burden” (Galatians 6:5) [Note: This passage clearly indicates that some Veronese whom the invader had ordained to the presbyterate had already been made bishops.]. Would that their transgression could at least serve as their defense.

Nevertheless, I declare that there will be no lack of someone who has seen a bishop made from a deacon without the order of presbyterate, the authors of the deed asserting who was a bishop and consequently that he was a presbyter, or certainly a priest [Note: This is noteworthy testimony concerning bishops ordained by promotion over an intermediate order.]. Let those who have obtained the episcopate by such an ordination see to it that they received the diaconate from a legitimate pontiff [Note: Our copy has “who was a presbyter, or if a priest,” where *if* is superfluous. The apparent sense is that the authors of the deed, in defending the ordination of bishops from deacons without presbyteral ordination, asserted that whoever was a bishop was consequently a presbyter or priest, since presbyterate is contained in the episcopate. Aeneas of Paris made the same argument when he replied to the Greeks, who objected to the Latins that certain men had been promoted from the diaconate to the episcopate without presbyteral ordination. See his *Book against the Greeks*, chapter 210; Acherius, *Spicilegium*, vol. I, p. 148. Compare P. Chardon, *History of the Sacraments*, vol. V, part I, chapter 5, p. 92. P. Pez thought the passage should be emended to “who was a presbyter, if a priest.”].

### III. BOOKLET INSCRIBED IN THE NAME OF THE CLERGY OF VERONA AND ADDRESSED TO THE ROMAN CHURCH

[Note: This booklet was produced from the Laon manuscript in Acherius’s edition. It has the appearance of a letter, but more correctly it is a booklet inscribed by Ratherius in the name of the Veronese clergy. For more on it, see §14 of the author’s *Life*.]

To the lord of the holy Roman see, whoever he may be, the apostolic one; to the entire senate; to all the legislators of holy and canonical law; and finally to the holy assembly of all who live under the Catholic faith: the entire clergy of the holy Church of Verona offers the service of due submission.

### 1

We know that the invasion formerly carried out here, most holy Fathers, at the instigation of the devil, is not unknown to your paternal authority [Note: He calls Milo’s invasion “formerly carried out,” since he had occupied the see of Verona at least from the year 951.]. In that invasion, since public illegality occurred, as is alleged, we who were many were assigned to various offices—not indeed promoted to them, but appointed to them. We therefore ask here, on bended knees, as we have done, that your holiness, to whom the unique authority of judging such matters is known to have been granted, mercifully provide us with the counsel that we ought to follow.

For our bishop recites that there are innumerable obstacles by which we are prevented from remaining in the office granted to us, asserting with the Apostle that “whatever was written was written for our instruction” (Romans 15:4) [Note: The obstacles are, of course, the canons set out below, which were recited by Bishop Ratherius and prevented those ordained by invaders from remaining in the office or order granted to them.].

From the Council of Antioch, chapter 13 (Antioch I, Dionysius’s version):

> “If anyone, without being asked, hastily and in disorderly fashion undertakes to settle certain ordinations or ecclesiastical affairs that do not belong to him, let what he does be invalid. Let him himself undergo punishment for his disorderly movement and unreasonable boldness, already condemned for this by the holy council.”

From the Council of Constantinople, chapter 3 (Constantinople I, the same version):

> “Concerning Maximus the Cynic and his disorderly appointment, which took place at Constantinople, it was decided that Maximus neither is nor was a bishop, nor are those clerics who were ordained by him in any grade; since everything carried out by him appears to have been annulled.”

From the letters of Pope Innocent, chapters 53 and 54 (Innocent I, Letter 22, chapter 3, in Dionysius’s collection, chapters 53 and 54):

> “We agree, and it is certainly true, because he could not give what he did not possess. He gave the condemnation that he possessed through a perverse laying on of hands; and we cannot discover how one who became a participant in the condemned man should receive honor. But it is said that the true, just, and legitimate blessing of a priest removes every fault that had been introduced by the faulty man. Therefore, if this is so, let sacrilegious men, adulterers, and those guilty of every crime be admitted to ordination, since through the blessing of ordination crimes or faults are thought to be removed. Let there be no place for repentance, because ordination can provide what long satisfaction has been accustomed to provide.”

From the letter of Pope Nicholas addressed to the see of Constantinople (Nicholas I, Letter 10):

> “Having utterly cut out the love of primacy, as a certain evil root of scandals *exordinandorum* [perhaps *exordiendorum*: ‘to be initiated’] in the Church [Note: The words enclosed by asterisks are not found in the printed editions.], and condemning by a just decree Photius, who rashly and treacherously and *in regularitatem* [perhaps *inregulariter*: ‘irregularly’], like a savage wolf, leapt into Christ’s fold and filled the world with a thousand tumults and disturbances, we proclaim that he was never previously, nor is he now, a bishop; nor can those whom he consecrated or promoted to any priestly rank remain in the rank to which they were advanced.
>
> “Moreover, we restrain from such protection those who received the customary prayers for promotion to a position of leadership from an outsider. We further decree that the churches which, as is thought, were dedicated either by Photius or by those whom he consecrated, or in which they set up moved altars, be dedicated again [Note: The text read *redicari*, but this is explained in Cangius’s additions as meaning “to be dedicated again.” Since *rursus* (“again”) precedes it, there is no doubt that *dedicari* is the correct reading.], enthroned, and established, with everything done in receiving or condemning a priestly rank declared invalid.”

From the same letter:

> “As for those whom Photius, a newly converted man and invader of the see of Constantinople, promoted to any ecclesiastical order, since it is manifest that they agreed in all the wickedness of their consecrator and joined him after his invasion, we deprive them of every clerical office; and by apostolic and canonical authority, as well as by synodal decree, we separate them.”

### 2

If it should please your lordship, our bishop says that he has found no other assistance than this.

From the Council of Pope Stephen III [Note: He says “Stephen III” instead of “Stephen IV.” Since Stephen II lived only three days and was immediately succeeded by another pontiff of the same name, the two were sometimes conflated and counted as one Stephen II; consequently, some—including Ratherius here—gave the name Stephen III to the man who was actually Stephen IV. Anastasius, cited in the preceding note, also attributed this decree to him.], act three:

[Note: Although a large part of this council, held in 769, was published from the manuscript of the Chapter of Verona by Cajetan Cennio and inserted by P. Dominico Mansi into his supplement to the councils, this fragment is absent from that collection and is preserved only in Ratherius’s booklet. Anastasius mentions the provisions made in this fragment in his *Life of Stephen IV*, and a summary of the same fragment, in exactly the same sense, is found in Sigebert’s *Chronicle* under the year 768. At the Roman Council of 964 under John XII, men ordained by Leo VIII, the invader of the Roman see, were likewise deposed according to the method of this decree and restored to their former rank.]

> “After these matters, the most holy bishops said:
>
> “Since, with God’s assent, all these matters that concern the salvation of all who have gone astray are known to have been discussed and decreed, it now remains that we declare before everyone what we have determined by common agreement concerning the ordination of bishops, presbyters, and deacons carried out by the aforementioned Constantine, the invader of the apostolic see.
>
> “First of all, we decree that the bishops whom he consecrated, if they had previously been presbyters or deacons, return to that former rank and afterward, once their election has been made according to customary procedure, come with the people and the decree to the apostolic see for consecration, and receive consecration from our apostolic lord as though they had never previously been ordained. Everything else that the same Constantine performed in the sacred offices, except baptism alone, shall likewise be repeated.
>
> “But those presbyters or deacons whom he ordained in this holy Roman Church shall return to their former order of subdeacon, or to whatever office they previously held, since it will afterward be in the power of your most holy graciousness either to ordain them or to dispose of them as you please.
>
> “As for those laymen whom he tonsured and consecrated, we decree and establish that they either be confined in a monastery or, remaining in their own homes, lead a spiritual and religious life.”

### 3

The aforesaid prelate of our Church also adds and admits that, since the Lord says, “A disciple is not above his master” (Matthew 10:24), he will regard as settled whatever you decree in this matter. He would wish, however, that your judgment, which he considers should be followed here, might in no respect differ from the authority of the canons.

Nevertheless, he leaves it to your own judgment, most holy Fathers, whether you wish to follow the judgment of your predecessors. If you deign to come to the aid of us who are in such great danger of our souls, you certainly do not need to be instructed concerning the rewarder whom you should expect for this.

Since we are many, we promise that there will be no lack of someone who will return to your holiness, giving glory to God through you and to your paternal authority, venerable Quirites whom we especially beseech here, a fitting reward.

Dated on the Kalends of August.

---

# LITTLE WORK OF RATHERIUS ON HIS OWN FALL

[Note: This little work now appears for the first time from the manuscript of the Chapter of Freising. Acherius mentions it in the list of the second volume as drawn from the Lobbes manuscript. Although in the preface to the works of Ratherius he promised to publish in the third volume those writings that had been sent to him from that same manuscript, he nevertheless did not publish it. In the cited Freising manuscript it is copied among the works that Ratherius composed after being restored for the third time to the see of Verona. It was written after Pentecost in 963 and before Lent in 964, as will be evident from the observations we shall make in the notes to the first sermon on Lent.]

### 1

“Blessed is the man who is always fearful” (Proverbs 28:14), as one of the ancient speakers said [Note: The author customarily calls the ancient holy Fathers, the writers of sacred Scripture, *prisciloqui*, or “ancient speakers,” as may be gathered from book six of the *Praeloquia*, where see the note.]. But the conscience of the guilty person is always in punishment, while one of the moderns, almost as though contradicting him, yet with a single breath, makes a double-sounding pipe resound: “Blessed” and “guilty.” I cannot in any way see how these can belong together.

Nevertheless, since the one is fearful and the other is always said to be in punishment, it is clearly shown that both lack blessedness. And indeed fear and punishment refer to that passion of the soul of which it is said: “They fear.” Those who fear are afraid; those who are afraid are not free from punishment.

How, then, is the fearful person blessed, when passion is far removed from blessedness, while blessedness feels no punishment at all?

It therefore seems to me that, if someone is fearful before guilt—that is, anxious lest he fall into guilt—he is blessed by that very fact, at least in hope if not in reality, because he takes care not to fall into guilt, lest, while standing, he suffer a fall, become guilty, take punishment upon himself, and fall into evil.

The contrary is certainly shown by what follows immediately: “But he who is hard of heart will fall into evil”—namely, that evil in which the guilty person, always fearful, is occupied in punishment.

But why do I say this? For this reason, I say: by these two sentences we learn that three classes of human beings are designated. One is the class listed under the saying, “He who is hard of heart will fall into evil.” Another is the class from which comes the person who is blessed because he is always fearful. The third is the class to which belongs the person of whom it is said: “The conscience of the guilty person is always in punishment.”

### 2

Would that I had recognized this class by report alone [lacuna], rather than perceived it through my own [lacuna] guilt! Since such a punishment does not cease—would that it were only temporary!—this punishment is not like that punishment in comparison with which this is indeed a punishment, but that other is eternal [Note: In our copy the reading was “this and that,” which made no sense. We have thought it should be emended slightly. The appropriate sense seems to be: this punishment, namely the temporary one, is not like that one, even though this too is punishment, since it is not eternal as the other is.].

For when he transgresses that fear which makes a person blessed, the one who possesses a hard heart falls into that evil in which, because of the enormity of his crimes, he considers himself so guilty that his conscience is occupied day and night—as ours is now, alas!—with continual fear, not indeed of God, but of those things that the Lord is able to inflict [lacuna: perhaps “is tormented”].

This usually happens to anyone of such a kind as happened to the man of whom it was said: “When the wicked comes into the depth of evils, he despises” (Proverbs 18:3). But what the apostle John says always happens: “He who fears is not perfected in love” (1 John 4:18).

Would that at least this psalm verse could have been applied to such a man: “Your eyes saw my imperfect state” (Psalm 138:16).

For when the same apostle says, “There is no fear in love” (1 John 4:18), he is proved entirely to lack love of God. Love never delights his conscience; rather, the punishment of Gehenna torments it without ceasing.

Therefore the man who, by his behavior, always feels God to be opposed to him never loves the Lord, although he fears him irrationally. He himself indicates this where he says that the word of God will be opposed to us and kindly exhorts us to obey it while we follow the way of life, lest we be sent forever into the prison of Gehenna [Note: He repeats a similar sentence in the second sermon on Lent, which he delivered shortly after the present work. There, in no. 40, we read: “For such a man is in no way proved to love God, although he fears him irrationally, because he feels him opposed to him in his behavior.” In both places the adverb *irrationally* should be understood as “not rightly,” or “not with right reason.” He fears God irrationally—that is, without right reason—when he fears punishment alone and does not fear in order to be recalled from sin. The same adverb is used in exactly this sense in sermon 10, no. 4.].

### 3

To touch upon only this one point from countless others: how, I ask, can that man love the Lord who knows that the Lord said of him, “Whatever an unclean person touches shall be unclean” (Numbers 19:22)?

How can he love him who hears him cry out concerning himself: “A man who is a priest, descended from Aaron, who has a blemish shall not offer the breads to the Lord” (Exodus 21:17); and who, despite these blemishes and those listed there, is compelled to offer sacrifice to the Lord while holding that very office unworthily?

What wonder, then, if he is restrained from offering, when he is not even permitted to taste what has been offered, the Lord prohibiting it entirely:

> “Whoever,” he says, “eats any of the flesh of the sacrifice that belongs to the Lord, while his uncleanness is upon him, that soul shall perish from his people” (Leviticus 7:20).

[Note: Saint Zeno of Verona quoted this Leviticus text in the same words in book I, tract 15, no. 6, except that he adds the word “salutary” after “sacrifice.”]

Finally, how is he proved to love the Lord when the Lord is known even to deny him the authority to speak about him: “Why do you recount my justices?” (Psalm 49:16).

Concerning this class of people, I confess that no other consolation now occurs to me except this alone: “Man does not know whether he is worthy of hatred or love, but all things are kept uncertain for the future” (Ecclesiastes 9:1).

For I think that the other statements concerning God’s incomprehensible mercy apply only to those for whom the saying is beneficial without qualification: “Love covers all offenses” (1 Peter 4:8).

### 4

For this reason it seems to me that we should grieve more because someone among us has endured offending so kind a Father, and lament it inwardly with the greatest wailing, than despair of his mercy—that is, fear irrecoverably the punishment of Gehenna—since God hates no sin more than this one, when he sees it to be unforgivable: the sin of apostasy alone [Note: Construe: “since God hates no sin more than despair of his mercy,” because he sees this sin of despair alone to be unforgivable, since it is also apostasy. We should be more ashamed that he yielded to the devil than afraid that he might be condemned with him: he did not abstain from carnal desires in accordance with the apostolic admonitions, but, most wretchedly, made those desires fight against him at the devil’s command and even allowed them to triumph over him.].

He should therefore be more ashamed that he yielded to the devil than afraid that he will be condemned with him: he did not abstain from carnal desires, as the apostolic admonitions commanded (1 Peter 2:11), but, most wretchedly, made them fight against himself at the devil’s command and granted them the further triumph of conquering him.

Let such a man grieve more that he offended so merciful a Redeemer than fear that he will see him as a terrible judge [Note: Construe: “than fear that he will see him as a terrible judge.”]; more that he unworthily received his body and blood than that he recognizes that he took them for judgment upon himself; more that he postponed celebrating the paschal Pentecost with spiritual joy because sorrow over the burden of his sins interrupted the joy of that feast [Note: That is, he postponed celebrating the paschal Pentecost with spiritual joy because sorrow over the burden of his sins interrupted the joy of Pentecost.]; more that he himself brought punishment upon himself for those same crimes; more that he did not persevere until the end, when at least the conclusion of the solemnity was already near; more that, when the solemnity had ended, he was unable to resist his habitual conduct and returned to his harmful wickedness as to vomit; more that, in the deepest sadness, he celebrated the feast of Pentecost, the most festive of all, although he certainly knew—and did not deny—that the joy of Pentecost ought to be more splendid than Easter [Note: The copy seems corrupt here, reading *cui* instead of *cujus*. The construction should be: “he certainly knew, and did not deny, that the joy of this feast of Pentecost ought to be more splendid than Easter itself.”];

more than all these things, that in the presence of God himself, who was most fully present and observing, he neither feared nor blushed to say or read something that was certainly an indication of unbelief or open rebellion [Note: Compare the word *turpe* (“shameful”), which he condemns in another little work, *On Idle Speech*, no. 5. See also the conjecture concerning *qualitatis*, no. 7.].

But since the Lord says, “Take away the evil of your thoughts from my eyes” (Psalm 1:16), how much do we think he offended him by shameful deeds performed in the presence of his majesty, when the same is said even of evil thoughts?

### 5.

And indeed it is less serious for anyone to be deceived by himself through ignorance than to become rebellious against the Lord through pride; an injury, however great, when unseen is more tolerably borne than a small one inflicted in one’s presence; nor are a transgression and contemptuous premeditation weighed alike, nor the necessity of a sudden occurrence and will. Would that the narrator of these things had taken precautions, so that the anguish of a hastened offense might not, as can be seen, remain as such a grave punishment in his conscience [Note: The construction is: “Would that the narrator of these things had taken precautions, so that the anguish of the offense hastened”—that is, “because of the hastened offense”—“might not remain as such a grave punishment in his conscience.” Perhaps one should read “of the offense committed.”].

This certainly would not have happened to him if that fear which makes a person blessed had possessed him before he fell: that fear, namely, which, when expelled by love, introduces that other fear which is known to remain forever, being pure. Nature itself truly teaches us that there is a great difference between the fear of an evil servant and the fear and love of a good son. The former’s love depends upon fear of the Lord; the latter’s love depends upon love of the Father. The Lord himself does not contradict this, saying: “Now I shall no longer call you servants, but my friends” (John 15:15). The Apostle likewise says: “You have not received the spirit of slavery in fear, but you have received the spirit of adoption as sons, in which we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Romans 8:15).

Therefore, whoever calls the Father “Lord” declares that he is free, not a servant. Let him consequently be more ashamed than afraid to offend the one whom he presumes to call Father. Nevertheless, let him not despair of reconciliation if he has offended him, even if he has offended him gravely. For he is a Father; he is merciful; he is good—not merely good, but also kind, which is greater still. And just as the Lord’s clemency is immeasurable, so it is omnipotent. May he deign to instill in us some portion of his love—something that must indeed be prayed for without interruption—which certainly was lacking in this man. That love will undoubtedly make us both abandon evils and replace their place with good things.

The Lord himself is powerful enough to grant that we should no longer need to fear Tartarus, but should confidently hope for heaven, so that with the Psalmist we may cry out:

“According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, your consolations have gladdened my soul” (Psalm 93:19);

and:

“Why are you sad, my soul, and why do you trouble me? Hope in God, for I shall still confess him, the salvation of my countenance and my God” (Psalm 42:5).

He indeed assumed our countenance—that is, our flesh—who is our teacher and Lord and protector, Jesus Christ. With God the Father and the Holy Spirit, the consoler of the faithful, he is one Lord, inseparably blessed forever. Amen.

---

[Column 485]

## TWO PARTS OF RATHER, BISHOP OF VERONA, ON CONTEMPT FOR THE CANONS. 337–338

[Note: Rather himself is the author of this title. This work, published from a manuscript of Laon, was brought out by d’Achery. Fulcuin calls it *The Plumb-Line* in *On the Deeds of the Abbots of Lobbes*, chapter 24. Rather himself also cites it in the *Discordia* under the name of a letter to Hubert, no. 5. Lucas d’Achery reports, in volume I of the *Spicilegium*, p. 401, from a letter of John Bona, later cardinal, that the title *The Plumb-Line* had also been prefixed to the work by a contemporary writer, Atto of Vercelli; the work teaches how to refute harmful things and establish honorable ones.

As for the date of Rather’s work, the words of the first part, no. 8, should be noted: “Once, when we were being compelled by an imperial command to besiege the fortress of Garda.” This fortress was captured in the year 963, as the continuator of Regino attests. Moreover, when Rather, addressing Hubert of Parma in no. 15, says, “Let that prudence of yours consider, lord, which, as is said, is worthy of being placed before the universal Church,” he indicates by these words that Hubert was considered worthy of the supreme pontificate at the Roman pseudo-synod that deposed John XII in that same year 963, and which Hubert attended.

He also alludes to that same John XII, after he had recovered the Roman see, in no. 19: “What sort of man is he, who, perhaps guilty of such things, does not fear to occupy the apostolic dignity—as has now happened, alas—an elevated position.” The words “as has now happened” are especially significant: that is, “he now occupies it,” after recovering the pontificate, or “has now happened to occupy it,” when he first obtained the pontificate.

Although Leo VIII, the antipope installed after John XII’s deposition, had more truly occupied the apostolic see, and after being expelled by John had later recovered that same see through the agency of Emperor Otto in June 964, Rather nevertheless, since he is speaking not against the intruder but against the legitimate pontiff, hints by the words “perhaps guilty of such things” at certain vices that are found charged not against Leo VIII but against John XII in the council mentioned above.

This John recovered the pontificate in February 964 and died not long afterward in the same year. Therefore, since John XII was still holding the pontificate in that year, Rather wrote this work during that year. Accordingly, he says that the imperial order concerning the siege of Garda had once been issued because it had been issued in the year 962, as will be established from the note.]

## THE VOLUME OF RATHER OF VERONA’S “PLUMB-LINES,” OR THE SIGHT OF A CERTAIN MAN HUNG WITH MANY OTHERS ON THE THIEF’S CROSS, ADDRESSED TO HUBERT, BISHOP OF PARMA

[Note: This Hubert, a close associate of Emperor Otto, possessed great authority. In addition to the episcopate, he held the county of Parma, and after the year 965 was elevated to the dignity of archchancellor of the Italian kingdom.]

## ON CONTEMPT FOR THE CANONS: PART ONE

[Column 485C] To the venerable lord in Christ, HUBERT, fellow bishop, RATHER, a sinner.

[Column 486C]

[Note: The construction is: “Although, I think, I agree with the opinion of that orator—whose urbanity, I believe, is not unknown to your Grace—that it is the height of folly to strive in vain and, by laboring at something else, to seek nothing but hatred; although, I say, I too agree with this, since I do not cease to do precisely that, when the madness of rebellious clerics once rose up against me and left me nothing of that office concerning which it was said to someone, ‘Feed my sheep,’ leaving me, I say, nothing except the making of chrism and the power to chrismate anything whatever, until my public expulsion—I have taken pains, as far as memory permits, to gather here from the holy canons the following few testimonies, though relevant to the matter, even if elsewhere lamented, perhaps rather culled.

When he says that nothing was left to him except the making of chrism and the power to chrismate anything whatever—whether in ordinations or in the consecration of churches, altars, and so forth—this is a formula indicating the power of orders, the exercise of which, since it harmed no one, was left to Rather. It was not so with the power of jurisdiction, especially legislative and coercive jurisdiction, which was necessary for correcting morals and restoring discipline but had been obstructed, as the following note will show; nor with distributive authority, from which he especially complains in this work that he was prohibited. He repeats the same formula in the same sense in the *Itinerary*, no. 4.]

I think that, according to the opinion of that orator whose urbanity is not unknown to your Grace, it is the height of folly to strive in vain and, by laboring at something else, to seek nothing but hatred—although I too, who do not cease to do this, agree that it is so—when the madness of rebellious clerics once rose up against me [Note: He refers to the rebellion of the clerics which he describes in this way before his second expulsion, in Letter 5 to John XII, no. 6: “With Count Milo himself supporting them against me, I did not dare to hold a synod, attend the clerical chapter, even mention something that needed correction, make any decision, or depose anyone.”], leaving me nothing of that office concerning which it was said to someone, “Feed my sheep” (John 21:17), until my public expulsion [Note: He calls it a public expulsion because he was driven from the see of Verona by order of King Lothair in the year 948.] except the making of chrism and the power to chrismate anything whatever.

As far as memory permits, I have taken pains to gather here from the holy canons the following few things relevant to the matter, although elsewhere lamented [perhaps “culled”] in vain [Note: It follows from this that the canons which are now set forth had once been collected by Rather to assist his memory during the earlier rebellion of his clerics, before he was expelled from Verona for the second time. They were now arranged and published as a coherent work, which gave rise to the dispute, as he indicates in the *Discordia*, no. 5.].

After you have seen these things, lord [Note: *Creveritis* comes from *cerno*, “I see”; Rather frequently uses it in this sense.], it will be appropriate for you likewise to recognize the purpose for which I undertook so great a labor and to judge how far it has been useful. The beginning of these such lamentations [Note: He calls them “lamentations” in the sense of those who held the sacred canons in contempt.] is as follows.

### In the Canons of the Apostles, chapter 39

“Let the bishop have charge of all ecclesiastical affairs, and let him administer them as though God were observing.”

Likewise, chapter 41:

“We command that the bishop have authority over the possessions of the Church. For if the souls of human beings have been entrusted to him as precious things, much more ought he to take care of money, so that everything may be distributed through presbyters and deacons to those in need, and administered with fear and every diligence. From these resources he himself may also receive what he needs for his own necessities and for the use of visiting brothers, so that he may in no way lack anything. For the law of God commands that those who serve at the altar should be fed from the altar (1 Corinthians 9:13), since a soldier does not take up arms against his enemies at his own expense.”

Likewise, chapter 40:

“Nothing is to be done without the bishop’s permission.”

### From a Letter of Pope Clement, letter 3, near the end

“All the faithful, and above all presbyters and deacons and the other clerics, must take care that they do nothing without the permission of their own bishop. No presbyter is to celebrate Mass in his parish without the bishop’s command; no one is to baptize or do anything whatever without his permission. Likewise, the rest of the people, both great and small, are to do whatever must be done by his permission; nor are they to leave their parish without his permission, nor dare to remain there when they arrive from elsewhere. Their souls have been entrusted to him; therefore they must do everything according to his counsel and do nothing without consulting him.”

### Likewise from the Council of Antioch, title 9

“For each bishop is to have authority over his own parish, so that he may govern it according to the reverence due to each person and exercise care over every possession that is under his authority.” 340

Likewise, chapter 24:

“Let the things that belong to the Church be preserved with every diligence, good conscience, and faith in God, who observes and judges all things.” [Note: Read this as it appears in Dionysius Exiguus, from whom these canons were taken: “and with a good conscience.”] “They are also to be administered according to the judgment and authority of the pontiff, to whom the people and the souls gathered within the Church have been entrusted.”

Likewise, chapter 25:

“Let the bishop have authority over ecclesiastical property, so that he may distribute it to all who are in need, with the utmost reverence and fear of God. He himself too may share in whatever he needs, if indeed he needs it, for the necessary use both of himself and of the brothers whom he receives, so that on no account and under no pretext may they be defrauded, according to the holy Apostle who says: ‘Having food and clothing, with these we are content’” (1 Timothy 6:8).

### Likewise from the Decrees of Pope Gelasius, title 27

“Just as it is the priest’s responsibility to provide the Church’s ministers with the full amount mentioned, so the clergy must know that they are to seek nothing beyond the sum assigned to them.”

### Likewise in the Canons of Gangra, chapter 7 or 8

[Column 489C]

“If anyone wishes to receive or give the offerings of the baptismal Church outside it, without the knowledge of the bishop or of the person to whom these duties have been entrusted, and without acting according to his counsel, let him be anathema.”

Likewise:

“If anyone gives the offerings of the Church to anyone other than the bishop or the person appointed by him to distribute them, let both the giver and the receiver be anathema.”

### Likewise in the Canons of Chalcedon, chapter 26

“Since certain persons, apart from the bishops’ stewards, handle ecclesiastical resources, those who do this are to be corrected by canonical penalties.”

Likewise, chapter 8, concerning clerics who are in poorhouses (*ptochia*), monasteries, and martyria under the authority of the bishops of each city:

“Clerics placed in charge of poorhouses (*ptochia*), or ordained in monasteries and basilicas of martyrs, are to remain under the authority of the bishops in each city, according to the traditions of the holy Fathers, and are not to separate themselves insolently from their bishop. Those who dare to overturn this arrangement in any way and do not submit to their own bishop—if they are clerics, they shall be subject to canonical correction; but if they are laymen or monks, they shall be deprived of communion.” 341

### Likewise from a Letter of Pope Urban, chapter 2

[Column 490A]

“Church property granted to the Church was anciently under the authority of bishops, who hold the place of the apostles in the Church; it remains so still and ought to remain so in future times.”

### Likewise concerning hospices and monasteries of both monks and nuns, from the decrees of the council of Pope Eugenius, chapter 24, and likewise in the same words from Pope Leo IV, chapter 23

“Through the care of the bishops, these institutions, which belong to their dioceses, are to be organized for the same purposes for which they were established, so that the appointed provisions and other things may be returned to those who ask for them, in such a way that those devoted to God may not be occupied by poverty or need but, with every care removed, may remain with pure minds in the service of God.”

### 3.

While I was rashly slandering these matters, as one who chattered uselessly, I began once again to quarrel with myself in this way. But why, following the practice of certain most foolish people, do I labor to establish this with a thousand testimonies, when one is enough? Ask anyone, then, where that custom arose by which the leaders of the Church are called shepherds. After that emblematic custom of the patriarchs—feeding flocks—and after the voice of the prophets who spiritually turn that image toward our own age, does not that supreme prince of shepherds appear and say, “I am the good shepherd” (John 10:11)?

And so that you may know that the one who is shepherd of the Lord’s flock is consequently also a bishop, hear him speak: “You were like wandering sheep, but now you have returned to the shepherd and bishop of your souls” (1 Peter 2:25). [Note: The latest editor of d’Achery’s *Spicilegium* added this note: “Here the reading was *eum quem*, certainly incorrectly. The copyist seems to have been misled because, in the manuscript from which he was copying, both words appeared, but one in its proper place and the other between the lines, so that either *eum* or *quem* could be read. The entire passage suffered from faulty punctuation in the earlier edition, which read *poscendi*; we have restored *pascendi*.”]

Saint Peter follows him in due order [that is, Saint Peter], whom, eagerly desiring to establish as bishop, so to speak, he carefully asks whether he loves him more than the others. The purpose is to show that the chief rule for feeding the rational flock is the power of love—namely, love of God and love of one’s neighbor, who has been entrusted to him by God (John 21:15).

When Peter, answering the one who questioned him three times, confessed three times, in the knowledge of that same Lord, that he loved him, the Lord also said to him three times, “Feed my sheep.” This amounted to saying: “Be the shepherd of intellectual sheep,” that is, “the bishop of believing peoples.”

Let no one expect to hear from me whether that feeding is uniform or manifold, bodily or of the soul (*animalis*), or both. Let him ask those eminent teachers who have faithfully published holy books on the Gospels. If they agree that some care of bodies belongs to those who hold in the Churches the place of the one to whom this was first said, let them show how anyone can feed bodily those entrusted to him if he is not even permitted to know from what he is to feed them.

And since the guardians of the Lord’s tabernacle—that is, the clerics of the Church—are to live from the offerings and tithes of the faithful, if the bishop does not know how many tithe-paying units (*decimani*), how many holdings (*mansi*), how many modii of wheat, and how many congii of wine are sufficient for such and such clerics’ food and clothing, is he not shown either not to be a shepherd or certainly to be a foolish shepherd, one who does not know where the pastures are or where he ought to lead the livestock entrusted to his provision? [Note: We have moved the conjunction *et*, which had been wrongly placed before *utique*, to this position, where it was required.]

### 4.

And, to return to our own affairs—that is, alas, to worldly matters—since you very rarely see anyone enter into alliance freely, but rather through fear or confederate love, from what will a person fear you if you are able to take nothing away from him? From what will he love you if you can confer nothing upon him?

If, then, nothing belongs to the bishop from the resources by which the clerics ought to live, either he ought not to provide them in due time with a measure of wheat, bodily as well as spiritual, or, as the *Acts of the Apostles* relates, the provisions are not divided among individuals by the bishop or by anyone else appointed by him for this duty according to each person’s need. Rather, the clerics themselves divide them among themselves according to how powerful each of them is (Acts 4:35).

And not according to the custom of other Churches, which grants what has been assigned to the Church to all the Church’s clerics, but according to their own will, what has been bestowed upon the Church of Verona is to pass only to deacons and presbyters, so that, having been enriched, they may have the means to rebel against their bishop, to dominate the others, and, through secular power, to compel them whenever they wish to come to their aid and to order them to swear an oath of loyalty to another bishop whom they themselves may have attracted; and, if they do not obey, to be able to expel them from the Church [Note: The construction is: “so that they may have the means to order an oath of loyalty to be sworn to another bishop whom they themselves have drawn to them.” The word *possint* should be noted: it signifies the possibility of commanding, not an action actually performed. The meaning is therefore that all the goods of the Church of Verona were to pass to the presbyters and deacons so that they could rebel against their bishop, and through secular power could compel their inferiors, whenever they wished, to aid them and to take an oath to another bishop, if they chose to draw one to themselves—as once happened when Rather was compelled by King Lothair’s command to yield his place to Bishop Manasses. See Letter 5, no. 7.]

They are also to have the means to acquire wives for their sons, husbands for their daughters, vineyards and fields, and finally the means to serve mammon of iniquity.

What are subdeacons, acolytes, and the others among the clerical orders to do? From what are they to live? For what reason are they to serve the Church, keep watch, and at least endure blows while learning letters, when no one has yet answered the Apostle’s question: “Who ever serves as a soldier at his own expense?” (1 Corinthians 9:7) by saying, “This man or that one”?

Although even those for whom I am arguing do not entirely approve of this quarrel of mine against the contemptors of the canons, they nevertheless act for two reasons: first, so that on this pretext they may withdraw themselves from the service of God; second, because each of them hopes to live long enough to inflict upon others what he now suffers from these men. Deceived by this hope, many of them have endured the greatest need in this world; and in the next, it is to be feared that they may perhaps suffer hell.

For the madness from which all their fraud and treachery takes its origin arises here: like those of whom it is said, “You abandon the commandments of God and hold to the traditions of men” (Mark 7:8), they utterly disregard canonical law and hold to the customs of their predecessors [Note: The kings meant are Berengar I, who was killed at Verona, and Louis, son of Boso, who was likewise blinded at Verona.], namely, kings who either killed or blinded bishops, or compelled them to live in disgrace—or, if they could not endure this, as this man of ours could not patiently endure their wickedness [Note: This is Rather himself.], used Iscariot-like law to make others suffer what they had inflicted upon him, while acting with the greatest deceit [Note: d’Achery says that *Scariotico jure* means “by that law by which someone is struck from the number of soldiers,” that is, discharged. The latest editor of d’Achery’s *Spicilegium* replies that although he recognizes this as the meaning of “Scariot-like law,” he denies that such an interpretation suits this passage. Rather calls it “Scariot-like law” when someone causes the evil he himself inflicted to appear to have been inflicted by another. Thus, to state the editor’s view: Rather writes that his clerics used the same treachery against him that Judas Iscariot used against Christ. Just as Judas betrayed his Lord and ours and then acted in such a way that he could appear not to have consented to the consequences of the betrayal, so they had, so to speak, slandered Rather before the emperor—more accurately, King Lothair, who ordered Rather to yield his place—and then testified that their bishop had been driven into exile not by them but by the emperor, or more accurately the king. If this interpretation is accepted, the reading should be *Iscariotico*. We have written *ipsi*, where the text had *quid ipsi*. Thus far the editor. We add only that the correction to *Iscariotico* is not necessary, since *Scarioth* was often written for *Iscariote* in earlier times, as we proved in note 34 on treatise 2 of Book I of Saint Zeno; moreover, Rather himself uses *Scarioth* elsewhere as well.].

Who would prefer their customs to the sacred laws, unless he is not frightened by the judgment pronounced against King Jehoshaphat: “You give help to the wicked and join yourself in friendship with those who hate God” (2 Chronicles 19:2), and so forth? There is also the Apostle’s saying: “Not only those who do these things, but also those who consent to them” (Romans 1:32).

Jerome likewise says: “Let the one defending the wicked be destroyed, and let the defended and the defender be condemned by the same punishment.”

Again: “Do not defend someone unjustly, lest you become justly bound and subjected to another’s penalty; for whoever strikes down the wicked because they are wicked is the minister of the Lord.”

Again: “To punish murderers and sacrilegious persons is not the shedding of blood but the ministry of the laws.”

Notice that he did not say “to kill,” but “to punish,” using vigilant and deliberate language. Thus another says: “Strike the sides of your son while he is an infant, but do not set your soul upon killing him” (Ecclesiasticus 30:12).

The Lord says to a certain man: “Leave the dead to bury their own dead” (Matthew 8:22). Wishing to explain this, the truthful expositor says:

“A dead man buries a dead man when a sinner defends a sinner and, so that he may not rise again to correction, buries him beneath a heap of falsehood.”

The Lord also says through the prophet: “Woe even to those who sew cushions beneath every elbow” (Ezekiel 13:18). Who are these, if not those of whom it is said elsewhere: “Woe to you who call evil good and good evil”? (Isaiah 5:20.)

### 5.

The objector, on the contrary, says: “As long as I am the apostle of the Gentiles,” says the excellent Teacher, “I will honor my ministry” (Romans 11:13). Consider, by contrast, how excellently you honor the ministry of this bishop of yours, when you insist that he ought to measure out wheat and wine, distribute money to the clerics, and perform the rest in the manner of that Sardanapalus who, although he was—or rather ought to have been—the king of that greatest and most famous empire, was found weighing things out and distributing them among serving women. [Note: “Your own bishop,” that is, Rather.]

To this I reply: If you had perceived with inward vision the things set forth above as the grounds of my argument [Note: The Acherian edition read *sunt*, which did not fit the preceding sentence. The latest editor of the *Spicilegium* thought it should be emended to *sunt causae isthic praemissae*. That is still unsatisfactory. Only the comma after *sunt* should be removed. The passage should be construed as follows: “If with inward vision you had perceived what has been set forth above”—that is, the preceding canons—“as the reason for establishing what had been proposed, you would certainly have been able to discern the manner of feeding the Lord’s flock, most properly depicted here in the complete condition of pontifical dignity.”], you would certainly have been able to discern, in the complete condition of pontifical dignity, the manner of feeding the Lord’s flock so excellently depicted here.

It has been shown that these things ought to be done by the bishop through presbyters and deacons, provided that faithful men can be found, not by the bishop himself [Note: See above, the Apostolic Canon 41 and the two canons of Gangra.]. Yet even if necessity compelled him to carry them out himself, pride [Note: d’Achery’s edition read *non perhiberet*. We have adopted the latest editor’s emendation. After a few words, the corrupt text read *cantatur donasse*.] would not prevent him; such conduct would in no way offend in practice the one who said: “Whoever wishes to become greater among you, let him be the servant of all” (Mark 10:44).

Let no one, however, disdain to reread the *Acts of the Apostles* and the letters of the Teacher of the Gentiles. There he will find most clearly who ought to command these things and who ought to perform them.

Let him also revisit the Passion of the blessed martyrs Sixtus and Lawrence. In it, one of them is introduced as saying to the other: “Take and distribute the resources of the Church.” After distributing them faithfully, the other is sung as having said: “Do not abandon me, holy father, for I have now spent your treasures.”

Understand and grasp, if you can, that one of them said “the resources of the Church,” while the other said “your treasures”: the former asserting that those treasures belonged to the Church, the latter that they belonged to the bishop. Thus, for example, what belongs to a wife belongs to her husband, and what belongs to a husband belongs to his wife [Note: The construction is: “what belongs to a husband belongs to a wife, and what belongs to a wife belongs to a husband.” Shortly afterward the common text had *praelatio*, where, as the sense requires, we have corrected it to *prolatio*. The latest editor of d’Achery’s *Spicilegium* noted the words “hear examples”: “We have removed no small error from this passage. The printed text had *audi exempla*. The copyist was misled by the abbreviation *exempla*, which caused the error.”].

If the utterance of such terms scandalizes you, hear something similar from a letter of Pope Evaristus:

“It is not lawful for the Church to dismiss its own bishop in order to receive another while he is alive, lest it incur the crime of fornication or adultery. For if it commits adultery—that is, if it joins itself to another bishop, or brings another bishop over itself, or causes or desires one to exist—then it must either be reconciled to its own bishop through the most severe penitence or remain unmarried.”

What, then, is a married woman except one joined to a husband? And what is an unmarried woman except one not given to a husband? From this word, therefore, of that most truthful pope, you can recognize that, according to the law of a spiritual, not carnal, marriage, the bishop is the husband and the Church assigned to him is the wife—even if you have not noticed the other points.

And that what belongs to the Church belongs to the bishop, and what belongs to the bishop belongs to the Church, you can recognize if you do not lack those ears of spiritual understanding [Note: That is, if you possess those spiritual ears which the Lord required, you can observe that, when the right of the bishop in question has been considered, the things belonging to this person—that is, to the Church—also belong to him, namely the bishop.] which the Lord required (Matthew 11:15), once you have carefully considered the relevant right (Mark 4:9).

The ancient laws promulgated by the world also seem, unless I am mistaken, to support this. For why would the settlement of immunities pertain to the bishop unless the thing against which an injustice had been committed—or, as it is read there, something evil had been done—were his own?

Repent, then. Let your mad loquacity, which strives against right and justice, cease at last; and, since you have found nothing just that you can say in reply, place your finger upon your sacrilegious mouth.

6. While I was thus disputing these matters like another Chremes, exceedingly angry and with swollen face (HORACE, *To the Pisones*, line 94), I began, in the secrecy of my heart, to try to discover, if I could, how it had come about that this general contempt for the divinely promulgated canons was so widespread—

[Note: [Col. 0494C] The Vulgate has *solibus*, incorrectly. He says *solis istis* for “these lands” or “these regions,” that is, the Italian ones; for in part II, no. 2, he complains that the Italians are especially contemptuous of the canons. The fact that he places all these people among the despisers of the canons must be taken hyperbolically, as referring to very many, not strictly to all, as though not a single person in Italy cared about those canons. For although in no century did such corruption rage as in the tenth century, especially in Italy, where the greatest upheaval of affairs disturbed everything, there were nevertheless at that time men there distinguished both for piety and for learning, to whom the canons were dear, as can be seen more fully in Mabillon, preface to the fifth century of the Benedictine order, § 1. The supreme pontiff whom Ratherius soon attacks without naming was Octavian, son of Alberic. After seizing Rome by tyranny when his father died, he entered the Roman see at scarcely eighteen years of age, changing the name Octavian to John XII. His crimes and scandals had become notorious, especially at the time when Ratherius was writing, since shortly before—at the end of 963, in fact—he had been deposed in a pseudo-synod on account of those same crimes and scandals. Ratherius nevertheless calls him the supreme pontiff, not only because that deposition was invalid, but also because he wrote this after the same pontiff had recovered the Roman see at the beginning of 964 and had deposed Leo VIII, the antipope elected in that pseudo-synod, in a Roman council.]

—so that I could not find anyone among them who was its guardian, from the very lowest member of the Church to the most eminent, from the most foolish to the one who strives to be called the wisest, from the layman even to the pontiff—shameful to say, the supreme pontiff. As I lamented these things with groans, and found absolutely no other cause, when I had considered everything [Col. 0495A] to the point of fainting, this came to mind [Note: [Col. 0495D] Where we have placed dots, the printed editions had *quae post*, entirely corruptly; or, if it is not an error, several words had been omitted through a leap. Since the isolated words disturb the sense, while without them the sense is sufficiently clear, we thought they should be deleted and that the dots should indicate some loss of words.] [lacuna] the evangelical commandments, threats, and works in which Christ himself is especially despised. Such, for example, is the saying I cited above, when I complained that I was opposed chiefly by clerics: “If you love me, feed my sheep” (John 21:17). For a pastor of souls who is shown not to love Christ is plainly not proved to be a pastor.

He is denied to love Christ who does not follow his commandments, since the same Christ is read to have said in the Gospel: “He who hears my words and does them is the one who loves me” (John 14:21). But if I attempt to recite all the threats of evils, I shall necessarily turn over the entire volume of the Gospels, especially the passage where he inveighs against the scribes, Pharisees, and hypocrites. While he censures their crimes, he contradicts all the false prelates of this age as well—unless they cease, I admit, from imitating them. His works, moreover, are those which he both displayed in the present by making a whip from cords (John 2:15), and signified when he is described as a king entering the wedding of his son (Matthew 22:2); and he testifies that the man whom he finds not clothed in a wedding garment, after rebuke, is to be sent with hands and feet bound into the outer darkness, that is, Gehenna.

He is shown to be about to condemn most severely the entire catalogue of false pontiffs—those, namely, who, without charity, that is, without love of God and of the people entrusted to them for governance, thought that “Feed my sheep” belonged to them, although it had been granted to that first man, Peter, because of the same charity [Note: [Col. 0495D] Construe: those who, without charity—that is, love of God and love of the people entrusted to them for governance—thought that this belonged to them: “Feed my sheep,” which was granted to that first man, Saint Peter, because of the same charity; since it had first been said there: “If you love me,” and so forth.]—although there it had first been said, “If you love me.” These men are plainly proved not to have done so, and therefore to have been not shepherds but rather wolves and hypocrites.

7. After these matters—so difficult, so opposed to the unwilling, and so impossible to do—when I had passed over the things contained in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms, which they read to no purpose, what is that passage: “Woe to those who devise useless things!” (Micah 2:1); and “Woe, woe” so many times to the shepherds of Israel (Ezekiel 34:2), and to those others and those others; and: “Cursed are those who turn aside from your commandments” (Matthew 23:13); and: “Cursed is he who performs the work of the Lord negligently” (Psalm 118:21)—and the many other passages which, all of them, impose impossibility upon those who offer themselves but are unwilling?

Then the Apostle appears, like another rigid Cato; and as though he were eager to remove every opportunity for presuming to seek the episcopate, he cries out: “It is necessary for a bishop to be without blame” (Titus 1:7); and, what is still more impossible, “to be irreproachable, the husband of one wife” (1 Timothy 3:2), and so forth. These words are read today by those same men with the deafest and most hardened ears.

They in no way took care to lighten that rule for choosing bishops, unspeakably austere as it is, who decreed more than once: “Let bigamists neither be chosen nor received into the clergy.” (See the decrees of Siricius, Innocent, Leo, and others.) But if they are not to be received into the clergy, how are they to be received into the priesthood?

Would that none of these had ever been born, seen, heard, or called a centigamist—shameful to say!—indeed, in the neighboring [lacuna] and this anyone. [Note: [Col. 0496D] *Centigamus*, that is, one who had known one hundred or more women. Later, in no. 14, he calls him a *multigamist*.]

The multitude of those Fathers—that is, the three hundred and eighteen gathered in that assembly—seems, by the very posture of its speech, to terrify the whole assembly of hearers; and, as history reports, with God himself present, it decreed (Council of Nicaea, canon 3):

> “The great synod absolutely forbids any bishop, presbyter, deacon, or anyone at all who belongs to the clergy to have a *subintroducta* woman, unless perhaps she be his mother, sister, aunt, or only such persons as escape suspicion.”

[Note: [Col. 0496D] The printed edition incorrectly has “deacon.”]

But the rigid Augustine says (Possidius, *Life*, chapter 26):

> “I do not want my sister to be with me,” he said, “because the woman who is with my sister is not my sister.”
