Since Scripture says, “For when the wicked has come into the depths of evils, he despises” (Proverbs 18:3), and he lies in the depths of such transgression, while hearing the Psalmist cry, “You commanded your commandments to be kept exceedingly” (Psalm 118:4), and yet feels himself keeping them not even a little—if he is hardened by despair, does it seem surprising to you? Especially if he does not know how to moderate the sentence of James, who says: “Whoever offends in one point will be guilty of all” (James 2:10).

8. Behold the cause, behold the pretext which lovers of the world, transgressors of the canons, put forward when they say that it is impossible for everything written in the canons to be observed. Indeed, many, driven mad by the demon of despair, have gone so far that I recently heard with these ears a certain man of episcopal rank, seeking to refute all the Scriptures that promise Gehenna, say of the Gospel itself:

> “Whatever is written on sheepskin is also read there,”

as though falsehood could be contained in the Gospel just as truth can. [Note: [Col. 0496D] That is: Whatever is written on sheepskin or parchment, whether true or false, is likewise read; as though, just as truth can be contained in the Gospel, so too falsehood could be contained in it.]

For I myself once, when by imperial command we were being compelled to besiege the fortress of Garda, and the bishops and clerics of that province, not out of love of religion but out of hatred of the labor, claimed that this did not at all belong to their order, answered them impudently, as I often did:

> “Just as the canons do not permit a cleric to fight, so neither do they permit him to commit fornication.”

For, says one who cannot lie:

> “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you tithe mint and dill and cumin, and have left the weightier matters of the law—judgment, mercy, and faith” (Matthew 23:23).

9. When I was also disputing with a certain man about my enthronement at Liège, while he tried to defend it against me by the authority of Pope Antherius, he kept opposing me with these two chapters of the Council of Sardica, the first [I] (letter, at the beginning) (from Dionysius Exiguus):

> “Bishop Hosius said: A bad custom no less than a pernicious abuse must be eradicated utterly. Therefore, let no bishop be permitted to pass from his own city to another city. For the reason why they attempt this is obvious, since no bishop has ever been found in this matter to pass from a greater city to a lesser one. Hence it is apparent that they are inflamed by the ardor of avarice, serve ambition, and seek power so that they may rule. If it pleases everyone, let this kind of wickedness be punished more severely and more strictly, so that such a man may not even have lay communion. All replied: It pleases us.”

> “II. Likewise concerning the same bishops: if they have changed their see through ambition, let them not even receive lay communion at the end of their life.”

> “Bishop Hosius said: Even if some such rash man should arise as to assert, perhaps offering the excuse, that he had received letters from the people, although it is manifest that a few people without sincere faith could have been corrupted by reward and payment to cry out in the church and make it appear that they themselves were asking for him as bishop, I consider that these frauds must be condemned altogether, so that such a man may not receive lay communion even at the end of his life. And if it pleases all of you, decree it. The synod replied: It pleases us.”

I anxiously maintained that I had been enthroned not for the sake of avarice or pride, but that, driven by necessity from my own see [that is, from Verona], I had then approached that most pious and now most glorious Caesar [Note: [Col. 0497C] He says “now” because, when he was elected bishop of Leodium in 953, Otto had not yet been proclaimed emperor, as he was when Ratherius wrote this work.] and consult the council of bishops about the matter; and that they had mercifully chosen me and, with the people’s assent joined to theirs, had fraternally enthroned me. I had also claimed that this had been done for their benefit [Note: [Col. 0497D] That is, also on the ground that this election of Ratherius was advantageous to them. This passage is wonderfully explained by contemporary writers: Rotger, *Life of Saint Bruno, Archbishop of Cologne*, chapter 34, and Fulcuin, *On the Abbots of Lobbes*, chapter 23. One copied nearly the same words from the other. They testify that Ratherius was promoted to the see of Leodium because he was thought likely to be highly beneficial not only to the church over which he presided but also to many others around it; and also because in those regions [lacuna] certain priests of the Lord, often relying more than was right upon earthly power, were scandalizing the ignorant people. Bruno, Archbishop of Cologne, mentioned above, believed that he could finally silence the hostile mouths of those who spoke if no occasion for scandal could be found in their bishop, judging—as was true—that Ratherius, previously expelled from Verona and neglected, could be brought by this great benefit into such an alliance of faith and truth that no one would be able to seduce him.]

And since I could not silence even such men, I learned from hearsay—although I did not know whether it was true—that he might nevertheless be uxorious. [Note: [Col. 0498C] Acherius has *similitudinem* here and, shortly afterward, *auditu quondam*. The correction of the latest editor was preferred.]

Inflated with power, though not in actual conduct [Note: [Col. 0498C] *Ampullatus*, that is, inflated or swollen, from *ampullor*, “I speak grandly,” a verb also used by Horace, Book I, *Epistle* 3, line 14: “He swells in his art.” To “return an anapaest” to someone means to turn the opponent’s argument back against him, from the Greek ἀνάπαιστος, a metrical foot opposed to the dactyl. Here Ratherius counters those who opposed him with canons by bringing forward other canons against them.], I returned this anapaest to him.

In the Apostolic Canons—unless you reject them as apocryphal—the seventeenth title is so headed; likewise in the Council of Laodicea, title 1; in the decrees of Pope Siricius, title 11; in the decrees of Pope Innocent, titles 11, 12, 13, and also 29 [Note: [Col. 0498D] The text had “and 38.” We corrected it, as it appears in the Dionysian-Hadriana collection, from which Ratherius extracted the canons and papal decrees with the titles given there. The decrees of Innocent do not deal with bigamists under title 38, but under 29.]; and also in the decrees of Pope Leo, title 2, it is prescribed that bigamists are not to be admitted into the clergy. And, miserable that I am, if not into the clergy, how into the priesthood? For priests ought not even to dine at the wedding of a bigamist, as the Council of Neocaesarea says in chapter 7:

> “It is not fitting for a presbyter to dine at the wedding of a bigamist, because, since a bigamist needs penance, what presbyter could, for the sake of a banquet, give consent to such a wedding?”

As for those who have married many times, inquire what is read in the same council, title 3. [Note: [Col. 0498D] The printed edition has “in the same canon,” incorrectly.]

10. While he babbled in a frenzied manner, eager to give one answer after another, and, as always, with his veins swollen from yesterday’s wine, played at dice as well (Virgil, *Eclogue* 6, line 15) [Note: [Col. 0498D] The text had *joco*. Rather, says the editor of Acherius’s *Spicilegium*, it means wine. Since the verse is taken from Virgil, *Eclogue* 6, line 15, it should be corrected to *Iaccho*, that is, Bacchus, and by metonymy “wine.”], I became angry once more:

“If you did not reject the Apostolic Canons together with the apostles themselves, I would tell you that in those same canons, titles 42 and 43, it is contained that a bishop, presbyter, or deacon must not be a gambler and drunkard such as you are; and that, if he has been such, he must either cease or be deposed.

“Also inquire in the Council of Sardica, title 15, whether it is permitted for you to be absent from your church for more than three weeks. [Note: [Col. 0498D] We have expanded the printed letters *qq.* as *quaere* (“inquire”), just as above, at the end of no. 9, the text was written and printed as *inquire, tit. 3*.]

“And see likewise whether it is permitted for you to keep dogs for hunting or hawks for fowling, as you certainly have in abundance, if I descend from greater matters to lesser ones. Also consider, both in the Apostle and in the canons, whether it is permitted for you to conduct secular affairs—that is, to handle certain cases which ought to be handled only by secular persons. And cease reproving the fraternal clemency of wiser men.”

These things, whether spoken by me or rather thought by me, are sufficient.

11. To relate what I heard: I myself discovered two men of the same order, one using a coat of mail and the other a mistress for the time, each reproaching the other. [Note: [Col. 0499D] This canon is not found among the Apostolic Canons. Something similar is found in the Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 45.]

To one of them an Apostolic Canon applied:

> “A bishop, presbyter, or deacon who has taken up arms in any sedition shall be deposed from the entire assembly of Christians.”

To the other, this canon applied:

> “A bishop, presbyter, or deacon who takes a wife shall be expelled” (Council of Neocaesarea, chapter 1).

I have known such a man who committed adultery before ordination and afterward lived as though continent; and another who took a wife after ordination. The latter reproached the former, and the former reproached the latter.

Yet to both of them the Doctor of the Gentiles cried out, as though to one alone—to the first because of his empty boasting of continence, and to the other because of his unlawful taking of a wife:

> “Do you not know that the patience of God is waiting for you for repentance? But you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and the revelation of the just judgment of God” (Romans 2:4–5).

To the first:

> “Do not be high-minded” (Romans 11:20),

because of your present continence, certainly, but fear because of your former incontinence, which has probably not been erased by any satisfaction, although it was omitted. [Note: [Col. 0499D] The latest editor of the *Spicilegium* noticed that the next five words had been omitted through a leap, but did not dare to insert them. Yet the sense compelled us to insert them. For the following words can be verified not concerning continence but concerning incontinence: “nor probably erased by any satisfaction.” The words “but fear” also belong to the preceding Pauline text.]

To the other:

> “Neither will adulterers possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 6:9).

Could it have happened that both men, brought up together and instructed alike, had in adolescence become wanton through mutual acquaintance, and that, having been promoted to the episcopate without examination, one had pursued womanizing and the other warfare? Neither of them is to be named. Perhaps habit had renounced the most shameful depravity.

To each, however, the canon assigns his own offense in a distinct chapter. To the first it says:

> “A presbyter who takes a wife after ordination shall be deposed” (Council of Neocaesarea, chapter 1).

To the other:

> “Moreover, he must be expelled if he has committed adultery” (ibid.).

It condemns both in a single chapter, namely chapter 9 of the Council of Nicaea, as follows:

> “If some have been promoted without examination, or, when they were being examined, have confessed their sins, and men, moved against the canons, have attempted to lay hands upon those who confessed, the rule does not admit such men; for the Catholic Church defends what is irreproachable.”

Likewise the Council of Neocaesarea, chapter 9:

> “If a presbyter confesses that before ordination he sinned by a bodily offense, let him not consecrate the offerings, while remaining in the other offices on account of his good zeal.”

The austerity of the law is extreme, I admit. For, miserable that I am, if he has lived continently after ordination, will he not be permitted, at least on account of his good zeal—namely, to please God—to consecrate the offerings?

12, 13. The second man, however, is convicted in two ways, since, in addition to what was said above, he knows himself to be condemned by this chapter:

> “A bishop, presbyter, or deacon who has taken up arms in any sedition shall be deposed from the entire assembly of Christians.”

This offense, which today is considered the lightest of all the lighter ones—such as gambling, drunkenness, fowling, and hunting—is treated as negligible, as though, for the sake of loyalty to his lord, a presbyter in armor would rather fight than be called a perjurer, although perjury is said to be expiated by the gravest penance, while this offense is expiated by none.

Perhaps the Lord seemed to have said to someone from this number of those mentioned above:

> “If you love me, feed my sheep” (John 21:17),

although he did not say it, since they are plainly not proved to love him. [Note: [Col. 0499D] The edition of Acherius has *quorum alicui*. The correction of the latest editor of Acherius is preferable. Construe and explain it as follows: Perhaps the Lord seemed to have said to someone among these—that is, from the number mentioned above—“If you love me, feed my sheep,” although he did not say this to any of them, since they are certainly not proved to love him.]

The Apostle appears rather to exclude such men from the priesthood than to choose them, when he says: “It is necessary for a bishop to be without blame” (Titus 1:7); or, more explicitly: “irreproachable, the husband of one wife” (1 Timothy 3:2). That cohort of Christ’s soldiers [Note: [Col. 0500D] The cohort of Christ’s soldiers who, following the Apostle, decreed that bigamists should not be admitted to the clergy are those Fathers and pontiffs whom he cited earlier.] follows him as its standard-bearer and commands that bigamists not be admitted to the clergy.

But if not bigamists, how can polygamists? If not into the clergy, how into the priesthood?

Suppose, however, that one of them had been a bigamist before entering the clergy, or had been wanton while in the clergy; afterward, following the priesthood, he had married many times, been warlike, perjured, and addicted to hunting, fowling, gambling, or drunkenness. Suppose that, on some pretext, he were sought for the apostolate of that Roman see, where, as a customary matter, the man about to be ordained is warned:

> “See that you have made no promise to your electors. Know that this is simoniacal and contrary to the canons” (above, no. 8).

If such a man, in open illegality—bravely resisting that Hosius mentioned above, together with all those who, from the same council, condemned him by their repeated “It pleases us”—were perhaps installed in the Apostolic See, God, who is long-suffering, could patiently permit this, as he permits many other things. [Note: [Col. 0500D] These words are found not only in the ancient ordines but also in the received Roman Pontifical, under the heading “Concerning the Evening Scrutiny,” which the ancients used before the man elected bishop was consecrated. In this scrutiny, among the other questions of the ordaining bishop, appears the question which Ratherius presents here. After “some things” the latest edition of the *Spicilegium* retains *permittere valet*; previously the text read *permitteret valet*.]

But if I were to approach him as one injured, going to a minister of justice so that justice might be rendered to him by the pontiff, and if that pontiff, attempting to avenge my injuries—or rather those of God who forbids such things, and of the holy Gospels, the apostles, apostolic men, canons, and decrees that forbid such things—were to send him a letter of Apostolic authority, would not the man who had injured me so sacrilegiously, though not so sacrilegiously as that pontiff had injured God and all divine and human law, if the pontiff, as I have said, ordered him something at least more severe on my account, immediately be able to write back to him the saying from the Gospel:

> “Why do you see the speck in your brother’s eye, but do not consider the beam that is in your own eye?” (Matthew 7:3).

[Note: [Col. 0501C] Construe and explain it as follows: If I were to approach him as one injured, going to a minister of justice so that justice might be rendered to him by the pontiff, and if the pontiff, attempting to avenge my injuries—or rather those of God, and of the holy Gospels, apostles, apostolic men, canons, and decrees that forbid such things—were to send him a letter of Apostolic authority, would not the man who had so sacrilegiously injured me, though not so sacrilegiously as this pontiff had injured God and all divine and human law, if the pontiff presumed to have been badly elected and, as I said, attempted to avenge my injuries, order him something at least more severe on my account? Would he not immediately be able to write back to him that Gospel saying? The latest editor of the *Spicilegium* thought that something was missing here. But after the punctuation was corrected and the parenthesis introduced, nothing appears to be lacking. The words “would not he” repeated after the parenthesis continue the sense. Thus the words that follow the parenthesis are to be explained.]

And what a certain pirate is said to have replied to Alexander the Great on the river Ganges. When the king, looking upon him with a threatening face, had addressed him in this way: “Most wicked thief, why do you not allow us to rest?” the pirate began to laugh loudly. The king, greatly astonished, said to those standing with him: “Are you laughing?” He replied: “Indeed, and justly.” The king again asked: “Why?” He answered:

> “Because you, being yourself a thief of thieves, the greatest plunderer, the most savage of all robbers, who from the Ocean to the eastern boundaries have ravaged every kingdom, the founder of all brigandage, call me a thief—me, who with a single little boat carried on my back and launched into the river steal very little from this shore, either someone’s cloak or merely a bridle.”

The king and all his companions nearly died of laughter and admitted that he had spoken most wisely (see Augustine, *City of God*, Book IV, chapter 4).

But he will not do this. [Note: [Col. 0502D] “He” is understood: the man whom he has hypothetically supposed to have been promoted to the pontifical see while a bigamist and entangled in other vices. Shortly afterward the text incorrectly read *exspectant*; we corrected it to *expetant*.] He will not send him a letter containing anything severe; he will not condemn or excommunicate anyone for such an act. For similarity of desires always produces equality of effects, and human friendship seeks equal minds and not dissimilar wills.

It is written of such men in the description of the members of the head of the devil, or of that vessel of Antichrist:

> “The members of his flesh cling to one another” (Job 41:14).

And under the image of scales, concerning his satellites:

> “One is joined to another, and no opening passes between them” (ibid., verse 7). [Note: [Col. 0502D] Acherius did not realize that this “one is joined to another” passage was taken from the Book of Job and wanted *Aetnae spiraculum* to be read here. So too did the latest editor of the *Spicilegium*.]

For the more closely the wickedness of all such men is joined together in mutual agreement, the more strongly it is armed against the justice of God.

> “For,” as blessed Gregory says, “just as it is very harmful when unity is absent from the good, so it is exceedingly dangerous when it is not absent from the wicked” (Gregory, *Moralia on Job*, Book 34, chapter 4).

This was proved in the case of the Apostle Paul. When both Pharisees and Sadducees had attacked him unanimously, he introduced division among them by saying, “Men, brothers, I am a Pharisee” (Acts 23:6). Thus he was assisted by the Pharisees and defended against the attack of the Sadducees; the crowd that had pressed upon him was divided, and Paul’s innocence emerged unharmed.

14. There is also another ground for my distrust in this matter, namely the Lord’s saying:

> “The thief comes only to steal, kill, and destroy” (John 10:10).

Who, then, is that thief except the one of whom he likewise says:

> “He who does not enter through the door into the sheepfold of the sheep, but climbs up by another way, is a thief and a robber” (ibid., verse 1)?

And what is the door except the one of whom the Psalmist sings:

> “For the lawgiver will give a blessing” (Psalm 83:8),

and who declares concerning himself:

> “I am the door” (John 10:9)?

He then grants the blessing only to the pontiff who is being ordained when the man is chosen according to the law laid down by him. That the sheepfold is the congregation of the faithful is indicated by the words spoken to Peter: “Feed my sheep” (John 21:17).

To climb up by another way means not to enter lawfully. The man who is said in the canons to have obtained a church by using secular powers is proved to have climbed up rather than entered:

> “If anyone, using secular powers, obtains a church through them, let him be deposed; and let those who communicate with him be separated from communion” (Apostolic Canon 31).

15. Let that prudence of yours, Lord, consider—for it is said to have been judged worthy of being preferred to the universal Church [Note: [Col. 0502D] He addresses Hubert, Bishop of Parma, to whom this work was dedicated. It is reported by Liutprand, or his continuator, Book 6, chapter 2, that Hubert was present at the pseudo-synod held in November 963, at which John XII was deposed and Leo VIII elected antipope, although “Hubert, Bishop of Parma” is corruptly written there as “Bubtus of Parma.” This passage of Ratherius seems to indicate that Hubert was considered by some of the fathers of that pseudo-synod worthy to become universal—that is, Roman—bishop.] Let it consider, I say, whether this is not an evident ascent, since he is said to have used secular powers; yet he is judged worthy of deposition by the judgment of the one who says in the Gospel:

> “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled” (Luke 14:11).

Notice, however, that it does not say, “Everyone who is exalted must be humbled,” but rather the one who has exalted himself—that is, lifted himself up or himself judged himself worthy.

To ascend by another way means either to rise by a simoniacal practice or by any other illegality. He is called a thief because of his cunning; a robber because of violence and plunder.

What each such man ought naturally to do by right is readily recognized again by anyone from the same authority. For he says:

> “The thief comes only to steal, kill, and destroy” (John 10:10).

What does he steal? First, the words of God’s law, by concealing them and not proclaiming them according to decree; then the property of another church, which belongs to it by right.

What does he kill? Souls, to be stored in the devil’s belly; whereas to the other man it is said:

> “Rise, Peter, kill and eat” (Acts 10:13),

that is, remove them from the life of paganism and store them in the belly of Christianity.

What does he destroy? Whom rather than himself first? And then his followers.

Therefore, I advise anyone who approaches such a man in order to be helped to beware lest he should instead be harmed by him [read: *noceatur*]. If perhaps such a person is of a milder disposition, and an invader of some church is accused before him—as though that church were a wife [Note: [Col. 0503C] Acherius has: “he is the accuser, invader, of some church or wife.” The latest editor of the *Spicilegium*, by conjecture, corrected it to: “he is the accused invader of some church, as of a wife.” We, taking less liberty, have retained *est* and changed only *aut* to *et* and *accusator* to *accusatus*.], and remembers that he himself has done the same, he fears hearing:

> “Let the one among you who is without sin be the first to throw a stone at her” (John 8:7).

Oh, how truly he is not without sin—the man struck with the leprosy of Gehazi, condemned along with Simon Magus, a polygamist, and polluted perhaps by the corruption of some woman, although all the women of his diocese are his spiritual daughters; the man rebuked in many ways by the holy canons and corrected in no way.

If such a man is afraid to correct even a minor criminal, do you think he ought to be reproved?

At last, our Flaccus sings most charmingly:

> “O greater one, spare the insane lesser one.”

16. What, then, is the position of one who, by his own admission, is not even permitted to call God himself “Lord,” since he says: “Why do you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and do not do what I say?” (Luke 6:46). Or even to call him God [understand: “to call him God”], since through the prophet he likewise complains: “If I am God, where is my fear?” (Malachi 1:6). Nor may he call him Father, as he continues: “If I am a father, where is my lover?” (ibid.). He is restrained even from announcing his commandments, as the Psalmist shows: “Why do you recount my statutes?” (Psalm 49:16).

Nor can he sanctify anything, as Scripture testifies: “Whatever an unclean person touches shall be unclean” (Numbers 19:22). Yet since the word *priest* (*sacerdos*) appears to be formed from *sacred* (*sacrum*) and *given* (*datum*), alas for me! how can that which is unclean be made—or at least be thought capable of being made—sacred, while that which an unclean person touches is made clean, contrary to the assertion of the one who is uniquely clean, and without whom no one is clean?

Here, nevertheless, the testimony that the Baptist gives about the Lord, divinely revealed to him, seems to offer assistance: “Upon whomever you see the Spirit descending and remaining upon him, he is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit” (John 1:33)—that is, he who bestows the Holy Spirit upon the baptized.[^c0052-1]

What, however, shall we do if this was said specifically of that one mystery? Let it nevertheless also be said of all [the sacraments]. [lacuna]—how it is permitted for anyone else to administer this to one who is not believed to taste of it. For you have the Apostle saying: “Whoever eats and drinks the body and blood of the Lord unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (1 Corinthians 11:29). The holy teachers define that person as receiving the Eucharist unworthily who presumes to communicate at the time when he ought to be doing penance; for he is thereby convicted of making light of what follows, hearing it with deaf ears: “If we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged” (ibid., 31). For while we spare ourselves excessively in the present, we bring it about that we will not be spared even a little in the future.

[^c0052-1]: The following testimony of John the Baptist offers assistance, or resolves the objection raised above, insofar as it asserts that the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit—that is, who bestows the Holy Spirit upon the baptized—is Christ himself. Whoever the minister who baptizes may be, whether clean or unclean, it makes no difference; for the holiness of baptism is to be attributed only to him of whom it is said: “This is the one who baptizes,” as Augustine explained at length in *Tractate 6 on John*. Ratherius followed him in the *Confession*, no. 13, where he wrote things implying that the same must be understood of all the sacraments. We shall quote the text in the following note.

[Note: The new editor of the *Spicilegium* appended this note. I firmly assert that no one can understand this passage as it has been printed, and that it is not for just anyone to emend it. For who would suspect that beneath these words there lies the word *sacramento* (“sacrament”), which the copyist may have written there in order to interpret the word *mysterio* (“mystery”)? I have no doubt that *mysterio* is the true reading. “Let this also be said of all,” and so forth. The meaning is: Someone might object that the words of John the Baptist pertain to only one sacrament of confirmation [read: baptism]; but in order to prove that the same can be said of all the sacraments, it will suffice to produce another example concerning the sacrament of the altar. Therefore, whoever restricts these words of John in this way, we shall ask whether one person can share with another in something of which he himself does not partake, and so forth. We do not, however, believe that this difficult passage will remain obscure if, after the lacuna marked by the dots, a few words are supplied mentioning the sacrament of the altar, to which what follows certainly refers. It will be enough, after the word “said,” to supply “as it is said concerning the sacrament of the altar,” passing over in a small leap the copyist’s words, omitted because of the occurrence of the similar expressions “said” and “is said.” Everything is then properly understood: “Let this also be said of all, as it is said concerning the sacrament of the altar: how anyone whatsoever is permitted to administer this to another who is not believed to taste of it,” that is, to receive its fruit, as sinners do. For you have the Apostle, and so forth. In the *Confession*, no. 13, Ratherius applies to all the sacraments what John the Baptist taught concerning baptism: “For the sacraments of God,” he says, “belong neither to this man nor to that”—that is, neither to the just nor to the sinner—“but to him of whom it is said: ‘Upon whomever you see the Spirit descending and remaining upon him, he is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.’” It is therefore clear that Ratherius recognizes that all the sacraments, even when administered by sinners, confer holiness, because the author of holiness is not the minister but Christ.]

17. Behold from where this general contempt for the canons of the present age—indeed, for the Gospels and all the Lord’s commandments—has arisen: namely, when someone supposes that observing lesser matters will benefit him nothing because he knows that he has despised greater ones.

For what difference does it make under this rule [Vulgate: “what benefit does it bring,” incorrectly] if someone has no dogs for hunting but abounds in prostitutes for fornication? If he does not take up arms for the defense of himself and others, but does not cease committing criminal acts for his own destruction and that of many others? If he does not strike delinquent faithful persons—something also forbidden by the canons—with his fist or a staff, yet kills them by the scourge of adulterous absolution, largesse, or at least blessing, or by the example of the worst actions?[^c0052-2]

And since Scripture everywhere censures the silence of those ordained for this office, while commanding and praising preaching to such an extent that even to everyone—that is, without excluding laypeople—it says through the prophet: “Let the one who hears say, ‘Come’” (Revelation 22:17), and through the Apostle James: “If anyone among you should stray from the truth and someone should convert him, let him know that whoever converts a sinner from the error of his way will save his soul from death and cover a multitude of sins” (James 5:19), where no one is excepted, but whoever does this is said to be enriched with such a reward[^c0052-3] that he has both worked for the salvation of his brother’s soul and is said to have attained salvation for his own.

[Note: If you construe this passage correctly, you will think that nothing needs to be emended or supplied, as the most recent editor of the *Spicilegium* believed that something else should be read in place of *asserto*. Construe it thus: “Since the silence of those ordained to that office”—namely, the episcopal office—“is everywhere censured by the assertion of Scripture, while preaching,” etc.]

Since other examples, one after another, prove that the Lord not only commands his words and statutes to be proclaimed, but also promises rewards to those who do so, while vehemently reproving those who do not, and threatening that he will require from them the blood—that is, the sins or souls—of those whom they failed to correct by warning them—let us consider what kind of guilt, or how great a guilt, belongs to one whom he counts as so unfit to proclaim his statutes that he must be restrained by rebuke.

So that we do not wander in uncertainty, let us examine what follows, and we shall immediately find the reason: “But you,” he says, “have hated discipline”—and it is not contrary to the meaning to understand this as the canonical law—and “you cast my words behind you” (Psalm 49:17); that is, you placed your own judgment, custom, or decision above my law. And how? “If you saw a thief,” he says, “you ran with him” (ibid., 18); that is, you did not observe what I had commanded through the Apostle: “Lay hands hastily on no one, and do not share in the sins of others” (1 Timothy 5:22). “And you made your portion with adulterers” (Psalm 49:18), clearly by defending them and providing them with a privilege—which would that I had never experienced it—so that they might remain firmly established in their adultery.[^c0052-4]

“Your mouth abounded in wickedness” (ibid., 19), as you heaped up utterly false authorities to prove that what was never permitted to anyone was nevertheless permitted to you. “And your tongue, in asserting this, contrived deceit.” “You sat and spoke against your brother” (ibid.), namely, against a lawfully instituted co-bishop, or against any Christian, the son of your mother—that is, of the Catholic Church—to whom no greater scandal can be imposed than to receive an adulterer as bishop and a wolf in place of a shepherd.

[^c0052-2]: Gerard, in his *Life of Saint Ulrich, Bishop of Augsburg*, chapter 11, no. 40, relates of a certain man who had taken something from a church: “Returning to Augsburg, he brought back what he had unjustly seized there and asked the bishop to impose lashes upon him with brooms in Christ’s name.” The custom of striking penitents is indicated; they could be struck with brooms, rods, or a cudgel, but not with fists or a staff. The distinction among absolution, largesse, and blessing is noteworthy. “Adulterous absolution” is called that which is more readily granted to a sinner without suitable penance.

[^c0052-3]: The reading in Acherius is *asserit* (“he asserts”). The new editor of the *Spicilegium* rightly emended it, as also below he correctly wrote *quod utinam nunquam* (“which would that never”), where the reading had been *quod utique nunquam*.

[^c0052-4]: “A privilege given to adulterers,” that is, invaders of another’s see, is reported as having been experienced by him as well. Does he call “privilege” the permission granted to Milo, invader of the see of Verona, which the supporters of his ordination boasted that they had obtained from the Apostolic See? See Letter 5 to John XII, note. Here, however, not merely permission to ordain but something more seems to be indicated—something by which the invader might remain firmly established in possession of the see. Since Ratherius was compelled to yield the bishopric of Liège to Baldwin, he likewise regarded Baldwin as an adulterer, or invader, as is clear from the *Deliberative Conclusion*. Moreover, he had to yield to him in such a way that all hope of his restoration was removed, as Rotger relates in the *Life of Saint Bruno*, chapter 34. Was some apostolic privilege obtained in this matter by which Baldwin might remain firmly established in the see of Liège, so that this passage should rather be referred to the see of Liège and to Baldwin than to the see of Verona and to Milo? In the absence of clearer documents, we dare not determine the matter. Interpret and construe it as follows: “Your mouth abounded in wickedness,” by piling up authorities utterly false for this purpose—that is, distorted by false interpretation—to prove that what had never been permitted to anyone was nevertheless permitted to you. When Ratherius was expelled from the see of Liège, we learn that authorities of the sacred canons opposed to Ratherius’s transfer from the see of Verona to Liège were brought forward in defense of Baldwin’s ordination. See the *Deliberative Conclusion*, no. 40.

[^c0052-5]: The new editor of the *Spicilegium* notes that this place is manifestly corrupt and cannot be completely restored except with the aid of a manuscript. Nevertheless, it can be understood from the passage of Leviticus cited above: the author ought here to have explained what mental “eye disease” was meant. Certainly the words “if he is bleary-eyed” are missing.

18. When people do these things, they do not proclaim God’s statutes for the benefit of their hearers, but for their destruction, corrupting the Lord’s words by sinister interpretation and bending Scripture, which resists them, toward themselves; and God is silent—that is, he permits no opponent to contradict them.

But let them hear what follows, and afterward, abandoning such people, let them honor God with the sacrifice of praise: proclaiming first by their examples and then by their words that the words of God’s law are to be embraced, feared, and followed. For there, that is, in the sacrifice of praise to God, is the road to the salvation of God (Psalm 49:23)—that is, the road by which we reach Jesus Christ our Lord.[^c0052-6] Indeed, in the praises of God contained in the pages of Scripture, we find what we must follow, what we must do, what we must avoid, and what we must hope for.

Therefore anyone, even a sinner, may safely proclaim God’s statutes, provided that he does not hate God’s discipline—which is certainly the promulgation of the canons; provided that he does not place his own constitution above God’s commandments; provided that, seeing a thief while God himself points him out,[^c0052-7] he does not run with him—that is, does not consent to or defend him; provided that he does not make his portion with those who adulterate God’s word and despise the decrees of the canons; provided that his mouth does not abound in wickedness by speaking against the law’s rectitude, nor his tongue contrive deceit in order to deceive anyone; and provided that, sitting in the judgment-seat, he does not speak against his brother or place any stumbling block before him on the Lord’s way.

For if anyone does such things, although the Lord remains silent toward him—that is, although he permits those who are ignorant, unable, or unwilling to contradict him to remain silent—let him not therefore suppose that the Lord is like him in will, or that the Lord approves his deeds.[^c0052-8] For he will one day be rebuked, and his works and intentions will be set before his face.

With these points established, or certainly ascertained, against one who is so wavering, besides the many other things that might be said here, we must know that no one is restrained from proclaiming God’s statutes so that they may be silenced, but so that they may be spoken sincerely and proclaimed by one who loves them and strives, insofar as he can, to keep them.

For since we hear every day, “Jesus said to his disciples,” that person is truly a disciple of Jesus, and Jesus speaks to that person, who loves Jesus’ discipline. For when he himself says of such people, “Whoever is of God hears the words of God” (John 8:47), he adds what he thinks of the rest: “For this reason you do not hear, because you are not of God” (ibid.).

[^c0052-6]: The Vulgate reads “that is, Jesus … but surely.” Since the conjunction *ac* is superfluous here, we have written *ad* and placed it before *Jesum*, where it was lacking. Construe it as follows: “that is, the road by which we reach Jesus Christ our Lord.”

[^c0052-7]: That is, “if, while God himself points out the thief, he does not run with him.” The reference is to John 10:1: “Whoever does not enter the sheepfold through the gate, but climbs in by another way, is a thief and a robber.”

[^c0052-8]: Construe it as follows: “although the Lord remains silent toward him,” that is, permits those who are ignorant, unable, or unwilling [the earlier printed text had “dared,” incorrectly] to contradict him to remain silent; he must not therefore suppose that the Lord is like him, that is, approves his deeds.

19. How far these things, drawn in advance here from the psalm, are from one who is supported by no authority, and how closely they apply to one who stands pre-eminent in the greatest authority, the prudent reader can perceive. Such, indeed—compare note 733—is the man who, perhaps guilty of such things, does not fear to seize apostolic dignity, as has now happened, alas, by occupying the elevated office.[^c0052-9]

For one to whom neither the legality of ordination nor the uprightness of conduct lends support, and who lacks that integrity of mind and body which suits him all the more, if the authority to preach is forbidden him, do not be surprised that the power to minister to the Lord is likewise forbidden him.

“For you shall speak,” the Lord says to Moses, “to Aaron your brother, and you shall say to him: Any man who is a priest of the seed of Aaron and has a blemish shall not offer loaves to the Lord his God, nor shall he approach his ministry” (Leviticus 21:17, 20). He then adds: “If he is blind, if lame, if he has a small, large, or crooked nose, if he has a broken foot or hand, if he is hunchbacked, bleary-eyed, has a white spot in his eye, a persistent scab, a skin disease, or is swollen” (ibid., 18).

Your most discerning courtesy should consider with what kind of stupefied insensibility or madness such a man’s heart is hardened when, understanding all these things morally through Gregory and spiritually expounded by him (*Pastoral Care*, book 1, final chapter, near the beginning), he is not pierced to the heart—especially if he sees any of these conditions present in his own soul.

If all these plagues dominate him, and he is not restrained from either seeking or retaining the priesthood, what does your lordship think of him? If anyone is blind in mind; if he limps through weakness of spirit and cannot walk the path of life with an even step, although he sees it; if he has a small nose—that is, little discernment—and equates good things with evil or perhaps prefers evil to them; if he has a large but crooked nose—that is, if he possesses discernment to such an extent[^c0052-10] that he is so fraudulent that he is commonly called a *bausiator*—[^c0052-11]

if he has a broken foot or hand and is unable to walk from virtue to virtue, like those who are to see the God of gods in Zion, or to accomplish any good work (Psalm 83:8); if, bent down by the hunchback of excessive earthly anxiety, he attends only to those things that are trodden underfoot, bending himself toward them;—to pass over the demons[^c0052-12]—whose wretched soul they do not cease to say is, in its mental vision, blind to the things that ought to be done; if he is blinded by the white film of pride, judging himself destined to be wise or just; if the scab of carnal wantonness continually dominates him; if a disease resembling avarice possesses him, because, although it monstrously disgraces his soul, once he obtains on earth what he desires, he feels no pain over what he has lost in heaven; if he is so ravaged by sexual lust that, even when he does not enact it, he never withdraws from the thought of it and, like one weighed down, never rests—how does he presume to offer loaves to the Lord, when he hears every day that he is forbidden by the one to whom they ought to be offered?

[^c0052-9]: The passage may be corrupt; the wording has been retained as far as possible.

[^c0052-10]: The reading was formerly *nullatenus* (“not at all”). The new editor of the *Spicilegium* detected the error. Since Ratherius said that the man with a small nose is one endowed with little discernment, it is clear from his meaning that the man with a large nose must be one endowed with great discernment, not one who possesses no subtlety of discrimination. The emendation proposed by that editor—“if he possesses very great discernment but is fraudulent”—changes the text too much. We have therefore made the lighter correction, writing *eatenus* (“to such an extent”) for *nullatenus*.

[^c0052-11]: Acherius says that by the word *bausiator* he thinks a double-minded man is meant. But Ratherius, in the *Conjecture of Quality*, no. 14, understood the verb *bausiare* to mean “to commit fraud”: “I have no trusted person to whom I can entrust this ministry; for I discovered that the man to whom I had entrusted one pound of silver for the purchase of beams last year had defrauded me monstrously.” Thus *bausiator*, a word used by the common people, means the same as “fraudulent” or “deceiver.” In the same sense, in Letter 12 to Ambrose, no. 2, he says: “He called me a felon, a deceiver, and a perjurer.”

[^c0052-12]: The editor of the *Spicilegium* notes that this passage is plainly corrupt and cannot be wholly purged except with the aid of a manuscript; nevertheless, it can to some extent be understood. From the passage of Leviticus cited above, it appears that the writer ought here to have explained what the mental disease of “bleariness” was. Certainly the words “if he is bleary-eyed” are missing.

20. Leaving aside the other matters, let us set down only three of these causes of rejection here, since doing so is not burdensome. If he has even the white film in his eye, if he has a persistent scab on his body, or if he is swollen, is he not sufficiently disqualified?

These three signify both spiritual pride—which God resists (James 4:6)—and bodily corruption, of which it is said that its fire has been kindled in the Lord’s anger (Deuteronomy 32:22). Who would not be disturbed by recognizing these things in himself? Who would not be terrified by hearing of them?

Of these two things the blessed Job says concerning the devil: “He sleeps under the shadow, in the secret place of reeds, and in damp places” (Job 40:16). God is said to resist the one, as we have stated; the fire of the other is said to have been kindled in his anger.

One of them made a devil out of an archangel; the other makes a son of the devil out of one who, existing as a son by grace, ought most readily to have called God his Father at his command, but is called the devil’s son because of the uncleanness of his life. Here I shall use the authority of the blessed Zeno, in the sermon which, following his customary eloquence, he composed on the patriarch Judah and his daughter-in-law Tamar, where he says: “The devil is the father of all who live corruptly” (book 2, treatise 14).[^c0052-13]

And yet one in whom the devil rests through these three vices, namely pride, hypocrisy, and lust, does not eat the venerable flesh of the Lord or drink his blood, although he appears to communicate with the faithful, when the Lord says: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him” (John 6:57)? This can also be resolved by reversing the formulation: “Whoever remains in me, and I in him, is the one who eats my flesh and drinks my blood.”

For I do not see how the devil could sleep in one in whom God remains and who himself remains in God. But he sleeps in one who, through hypocrisy or pride, is shadowy and empty, and through lust is dampened. What, then, does such a person eat when he communicates? If you answer, “Judgment” (1 Corinthians 11:20), you nod along with the Apostle and remind me to understand likewise that he will be judged—that is, condemned—because, being unworthy, he dared to eat Christ’s flesh and drink his blood. Thus what ought to have been salvation for him became condemnation.

Since my present question concerns the bodily substance that he receives, I shall now yield to myself as well and speak as follows: Since it is true flesh for the worthy recipient, although it appears as bread, which it formerly was, and true blood, although it appears as wine, what it is for the unworthy recipient—that is, for one who does not remain in God—I confess to myself to be not merely unspeakable but inconceivable.[^c0052-14] Let this saying also be applied here: “Do not seek what is too high for you, and do not search out what is deeper than you” (Sirach 3:22).

[^c0052-13]: Certain heterodox writers twist this passage—which belongs not to Saint Zeno but to Ratherius—as though Ratherius had believed that sinners do not receive the true flesh or true blood of Christ in the Eucharist. But if the Eucharist received by sinners contains neither the true blood nor the true flesh of Christ, they argue that the Eucharist received by the just must likewise be understood differently. How correctly Ratherius understood and transmitted the doctrine of the Eucharist is clear from the *Confession*, and especially from Letter 1 to Patricius. The sense in which he speaks here is made perfectly clear by the entire context. He does not deny that both the just and the wicked receive true flesh and true blood; he merely teaches that the latter do not receive the effect of the true flesh and blood as the former do. That the just plainly receive true flesh and true blood is certainly asserted by these words: “For it is true flesh to the worthy recipient, although what was formerly bread appears to be bread, and what was formerly wine appears to be blood.” Here he admits that after consecration the bread and wine that formerly existed no longer exist as such but only appear to do so, since in reality they are the flesh and blood of Christ. The entire difference concerning sinners therefore concerns the effect alone, as he explains most clearly below, especially in the words spoken after the testimonies of Saints John Chrysostom and Augustine: “In this sense, then, this sacrifice appears to me to be the same for the good person and the bad person, the same sacrifice—that is, the same flesh and blood—but it does not produce the same result: for the worthy it gives life, while for the unworthy it gives death; for the worthy it gives grace, while for the unworthy it gives wrath.” Do you see that the entire difference is placed in the difference of effects? Likewise, speaking in the *Synodical Letter*, no. 5, of sinners who eat the flesh of the Lamb and drink his blood, he says: “Woe to those for whom so great a good is turned into so great an evil, while eating the Lord’s flesh and drinking his blood unworthily, they eat and drink judgment upon themselves.”

[^c0052-14]: The numbering in the supplied text is 361.

21. But let us hear what someone—namely, John Chrysostom—says about this; perhaps from it we shall be able to infer something. “Let no one,” he says, “be a Judas at the table. This sacrifice is spiritual food. For just as bodily food, when it finds the stomach occupied by harmful humors, injures it more, does greater harm, and provides no help, so this spiritual food, if it finds someone polluted by wickedness, will destroy him more—not by its own nature but through the vice of the one who receives it. Let the mind, therefore, be pure in every respect, and the thought pure, because the sacrifice too is pure. Let us therefore prepare a holy soul for such a sacrifice.” (*Treatise 61 on John*).

Augustine likewise says: “What Judas received was good, but he received the good to his own harm. It is therefore no wonder if the bread of Christ was given to Judas, through which he might be handed over to the devil, when you see, conversely, that an angel of the devil was given to Paul, through whom he might advance in Christ” (*Treatise 62*, near the beginning).

In this sense, then, this sacrifice appears to me to be the same for the good person and the bad person, the same for the worthy and the unworthy; but it does not produce the same result. For it gives life to the worthy, but death to the unworthy; grace to the worthy, but wrath to the unworthy. Thus the Psalm also says: “While their food was still in their mouths, the wrath of God rose up against them” (Psalm 77:30), referring, of course, to the manna that they despised. There is no obstacle to understanding this also of the Lord’s sacrifice received unworthily, since Judas’s destruction demonstrates it; and something must be understood in the Lord’s saying: “Whoever eats my flesh worthily and drinks my blood worthily remains in me, and I in him” (John 6:57).

If this is so, we must consider to whom the following words are spoken: “Come to Bethel”—that is, to the house of God—“and commit impiety, and sacrifice praise from leaven” (Amos 4:4). I have no doubt that the sacrifice offered worthily is flesh. Nevertheless, when Christ’s Apostle had said of it, “Let us therefore feast,” he added: “not with the old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness” (1 Corinthians 5:8). In these words every malicious intention is driven out, both from those who are about to receive and from those who are about to distribute the body and blood of the Lord.

And since the offering is consecrated with that particular prayer when God is addressed: “Our Father, who are in heaven” (Matthew 6:9), I leave it to others to consider what the one who lives corruptly and is, as Saint Zeno asserts, the devil’s son, thinks and how greatly he should fear; I myself am not equal to the task.[^c0052-15]

It can easily be considered in the psalm how, in these two things—pride and lust—one depends upon the other, when the Psalmist pleads: “Let not the foot of pride come to me” (Psalm 35:12); that is, “Let not the demon of boasting trample my life on earth” (Psalm 7:6), persuading me to pursue only earthly things. Then follows: “And let not the hand of the sinner move me” (Psalm 35:12)—namely, the spirit of fornication, which, whenever the spirit of vainglory has occupied the heart of any religious person, immediately agitates his body with the movement of lust.

Why, then, does he, once moved, work iniquity? This is shown when it is added: “There the workers of iniquity have fallen” (ibid., 13). Where? First into pride, and then into the abyss of lust. And why? “Because they were cast out,” he says. From where? From the grace of God. And therefore they could not stand, having become utterly unworthy to taste the Eucharist, while the Lord declares: “Whoever eats of the flesh of the sacrifice that belongs to the Lord, while his uncleanness is upon him, that soul shall perish from his people” (Leviticus 7:20–21).

[^c0052-15]: Ratherius wrote this in the same sense in which Saint Gregory says in book 9, Letter 12 of the Maurist edition, to John of Syracuse: “We say the Lord’s Prayer immediately after the prayer [that is, after the canon], because it was the custom of the apostles to consecrate the sacrificial offering by that prayer alone. And it seemed to me wholly inappropriate to say over the offering a prayer composed by a scholar, while not saying over Christ’s body and blood the tradition composed by our Redeemer himself.” Since the holy pontiff affirms that the Lord’s Prayer is said immediately after the prayer or canon because it seemed inappropriate to recite any other prayers over Christ’s body and blood rather than this one handed down by Christ himself, he presupposes that Christ’s body and blood already existed in the offering before that prayer. Thus, when he says that the sacrificial offering is consecrated by this prayer, he does not understand “consecrated” in the sense ordinarily signifying the making of Christ’s body and blood; rather, he means that the already-confected sacrament is, in the canon, commended and offered to God by this prayer, the most excellent of all prayers. In the same sense Ratherius says here that the offering to be presented to the people is specially consecrated by the prayer in which God is addressed: “Our Father,” and so forth. On Saint Gregory’s statement that the apostles customarily consecrated the sacrificial offering by this prayer alone, see P. Le Brun, *Explanation of the Mass*, vol. 2, dissertation 2, article 2, nos. 7–8.

22. But since it is written that nothing on earth happens without a cause (Job 5:6), I confess that I seem often to be able to see how the cause itself may arise. Suppose that any noble boy is handed over to the schools—a practice which today appears to happen more through ambition for the episcopate than through eagerness to serve the Lord. Behold, one foot of pride: the arrogant will of his parents.

When he begins to grow older, whether because of that very nobility, or because of some sharpness of understanding, or perhaps because of bodily beauty, or because—as Jerome reports of a certain person—his voice may be sweeter than the song of a swan, he begins to grow insolent.

Thus, trampled down by these demonic feet of pride, he is weakened; and because of vainglory, just as the former was cast into the denser air, so the latter is cast into a more shameful wantonness. From that point, having become not merely a bigamist but a polygamist, he is advanced to the priesthood without examination,[^c0052-16] and this is plainly the occasion of all the evils that follow, even to the destruction of souls.

For when those among the laity who are not wholly without literary education hear, on the second day of Pentecost, that Jesus said to his disciples—both to those who were present then and to those who now hate his discipline, that is, his teaching, instruction, correction, and prohibitions—“Whoever does not enter the sheepfold through the gate, but climbs in by another way, is a thief and a robber” (John 10:1), they know that the Truth could not have lied. They also understand that one who is a thief cannot at the same time be a shepherd.

They understand the sheepfold to be the Church, which contains those sheep who will be placed on the right at the judgment, although within it there are also mingled those who will be placed on the left, for whom perpetual woe will never be lacking.

They see an unlawful shepherd,[^c0052-17] a thieving bishop, a false prelate. What concern do they have for the provision made by one whom they know the head of the household did not install, but who himself imposed himself by robbery? What concern do they have for the blessing of one whom they know to be accursed, since Gregory testifies that blessing is turned into a curse for the one who is promoted in order to become a heretic?

But what kind of sect’s heretic is he? That one, certainly—that one whose author, we read, Peter addressed: “Your money be with you unto perdition, because you thought that the gift of God could be obtained with money” (Acts 8:20).

And since one who communicates with a heretic is himself a heretic, what, I ask, should be done, thought, or judged concerning such people? How much can he fear their excommunication, when he knows from the canonical laws that they have been excommunicated not once but a thousand times? How much can he embrace consecration, when the Lord says: “Whatever an unclean person touches shall be unclean” (Numbers 19:22)? How greatly can he fear condemnation, when Christ urges: “Let the one among you who is without sin be the first to cast a stone at her”—that is, at the prostitute (John 8:7)? For these are especially the men who order little prostitutes to be tied to stakes so that their skins may be stripped.[^c0052-18]

[^c0052-16]: Read what our author said earlier, in no. 11, concerning those ordained without examination. It was through this negligence that men were promoted who ought to have been excluded by the sacred canons.

[^c0052-17]: Read “an unlawful shepherd.” The correction is required by the context.

[^c0052-18]: Note the rights and power of the bishops of this period.

[Col. 0513A] **23.** I remember that I once endured great fear on the two-horned Rhine, with heaps of waves boiling up like hills, so that I thought no strait—even the Euxine—could be greater. But when I saw the sailors joking confidently because of their skill in navigation, my fear vanished and I remember that I took up no small courage.

[Note: Construe: Thus it should be judged not inappropriate to use this example here, if secular people had seen us awaken at such thunderclaps of divine terror—which I depicted there, and which, as we read them, we cannot deny that we understand—so that they too would nevertheless have feared.]

Accordingly, it should not be judged inappropriate to use this example here: if secular people had seen us awaken at such thunderclaps of divine terror as I have depicted here—and which, as we read them, we cannot deny that we understand, however imperfectly—they too would at least have feared them. But when they often see us reading even these things while laughing, resisting such matters so obstinately and so boldly, and becoming hardened through open rebellion against God, can anyone be surprised if they do not care about such things?

[Col. 0513B] They do not know what is being said, much less understand it, or whether it is truly being said. Hence they make little of our excommunications together with our absolutions, because, as far as they can understand, they know both that we ourselves are excommunicated by the holy canons and that no one can bind or absolve anyone else according to his own arbitrary will.

When it comes to preaching, indeed, we arrive at it uselessly. Although the Lord is remembered to have said, “Do what they say, but do not do what they do” (Matt. 23:3), they do not believe that the Apostles lack words with which to intensify the charge. What do you preach—that one must not steal—while despoiling the poor in order to enrich yourself? You steal far worse (Rom. 2:21). You say that one must in no way commit adultery, yet by acting in a thousand ways you commit adultery still worse (ibid., 22), while you do not even fear becoming involved with many marriages.

But let no one demand to learn from me what results from this. Let him hear Gregory: “The cause of the people’s ruin is wicked priests.”

[Note: This text is from Hosea, chapter 5, verse 1, in the ancient version. Since Ratherius did not find it in the Vulgate text but had read it only in Saint Gregory’s Commentary on the First Book of Kings, book 2, chapter 23, where it is indeed attributed to Hosea, he cites Saint Gregory. We are not unaware that learned men dispute whether the author of that Commentary was Saint Gregory; but whatever the truth may be, Ratherius’s manuscript certainly bore Gregory’s name.]

For unless they despised the canons—or rather, unless they regarded prophetic, Gospel, and apostolic sayings as worthless—no secular person would, in such madness, make so little of these things; instead, all would recognize that what we so diligently venerate is altogether worthy of veneration. They would in some measure venerate them among us if they loved them. They would love them if those things had not been so sternly enjoined which are contrary to the accursed lust and debauchery whose detestation no educated person, even if he wished, is permitted to ignore. Yet all hate it and love its pleasure, although many avoid it through fear of Gehenna;

[Note: Is a word missing here which ought to govern all those infinitives, “to hate,” “to love,” “to avoid,” and so forth? Below we have printed *libros* where the text had *liberos*. Shortly afterward read *sciendum ex eo quod*, where Acherius had printed *sciendum vero quod*. Thus the most recent editor of the *Spicilegium*.]

[Col. 0513D] and consequently, as Christ testifies, the divine word exists for us as an adversary in the course of the present age.

[Col. 0514A] **24.** Whether we wish it or not, we shall have as judges the very books of God’s law, which we now hate and despise so obstinately; and we shall have as accusers those who ought to have been our defenders. For it is written: “The court sat, and the books were opened” (Dan. 7:10). Although this may also be understood of the consciences of individuals, it must be recognized that everyone will be judged according to what is contained in the books.

Another Prophet shows this, saying: “I turned and lifted up my eyes, and I saw, and behold, a flying scroll. And he said to me, ‘What do you see?’ And I said, ‘I see a flying scroll; its length is twenty cubits, and its width is ten cubits.’ And he said to me, ‘This is the curse that goes forth over the face of the whole earth; for every thief, as it is written there, shall be judged, and every one who swears shall likewise be judged from this.’ And I will bring it forth, says the Lord of hosts, and it shall come to the house of the thief and to the house of him who falsely swears by my name; it shall remain in the midst of his house and consume him, its timber and its stones” (Zech. 5:1, 4).

“Listen,” says another, “so that I may pass on to other matters; listen, priests, and attend, for judgment is yours, because you have become a snare to the watchtower” (Hos. 5:1). What could be understood more clearly, what could be more explicit? He indicates that the bishop ought to be a watchman who says: “I have appointed you as a watchman, says the Lord of hosts, over the house of Israel” (Ezek. 3:17). Hence *episcopus* is called in Greek, and in Latin means “overseer.”

If he either does not know how to do this, neglects it, or—what is more serious—presumes to do it without being commanded, he undoubtedly becomes a snare to the watchtower, that is, to the episcopal order, and a cause of destruction, especially if he acts not in ignorance but knowingly. For the foremost of the Apostles says of such people: “It would have been better for them not to have known the way of truth than, after knowing it, to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to them” (2 Pet. 2:21).

Supporting this, I cry out from my inmost being—with the one who expressed the same thought before me, leaving it to them what others may think about themselves: “Would that I had not been a man possessing the spirit, and that the word of the Lord had not been spoken to me!” (Mic. 2:11). For what is the word of the Lord to one who lives corruptly except a manifest indication of rebellion against him and an accumulation of my destruction?

[Note: The printed editions read *apte viventi*, “to one living suitably,” but this is erroneous; the word of the Lord to one living badly is a clear indication of rebellion against God and an accumulation of destruction. What should replace *apte* to signify “badly” is aptly suggested by Saint Zeno’s text, previously cited by Ratherius: *corrupte viventium*, “of those living corruptly.”]

For when he promises rewards to the good and pardon to those who turn away from evil, he deceives no one. He says to all: “The Son of Man will come in the glory of his Father with his angels, and then he will repay each according to his works” (Matt. 16:27). Following him, the Apostle says: “We shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may render an account of the things done in the body, whether good or evil” (Rom. 14:10).

Someone else, no less truthfully—although the Veronese *cleronomi* do not wish to sing his words—says:

“At his coming, all shall rise with their bodies and shall give an account of their deeds; those who have done good shall go into eternal life, but those who have done evil into eternal fire.”

[Note: *Cleronomia* means a college of clerics or monks who sing praises to God. The *Acta Sanctorum*, May, volume 6, page 753, says of Saint Caraunus: “For the apostolic man instituted both an abbot and a beautiful succession of the *cleronomia*.” Hence *cleronomi* are the same as canons and other clerics who sang in the choir. For *nomos* in musical terminology means a melody composed according to a fixed rule. See Salmasius on Suetonius, *Nero*, chapter 20: “Nor did he cease singing before he had completed the *nomos* he had begun.” The words quoted below, “At his coming,” are from the creed commonly called the *Quicumque*, attributed to Saint Athanasius. The Veronese cardinals, or canons of our cathedral church, did not wish to sing it publicly, as Ratherius records more explicitly in his *Itinerary*. Compare the note there.]

[Note: The sense is: We must ask that Christ then assist the man who may fear hearing there, that is, at the last judgment: “From your mouth and your writings I judge you, wicked servant” (Luke 19:22); and who may fear being reproached for having used a mole’s sight toward himself and the sharp sight of goats toward others. “Amen” means that in judging his own actions he was blind like a mole, whereas toward others he applied the keenest sight of goats.]

May Christ then assist him, however, one must pray, since he may fear hearing there: “From your mouth and your writings I judge you, wicked servant” (Luke 19:22), and being reproached for having used a mole’s sight toward himself and the sight of goats toward others. Amen.

**366. ON DESPISING THE CANONS, PART TWO**

[Col. 0515B] So that what follows may properly answer what came before, the reader’s careful consideration should note that, despite my amazement and most diligent inquiry, I have been unable to find any other cause for such widespread—alas!—contempt of the divine canons than the fault of false bishops. The matter itself has been stirred up by the hand of the sinner, that is, the devil, in vengeance for pride; I say, stirred up through the enervation of lust, which, kindled in the fire of God’s anger, burns today in the world and will burn to the very end of Hell, devouring the earth where the vineyard of the Lord of hosts has been planted, together with the growth of good works that it ought to have produced; or perhaps that of any wretch, while by burning it temporarily it makes for him a return [read: *reditum*], so that he does not cease to be burned eternally with his soul.

[Note: Construe this as follows: The reader should consider that I could discover no other cause, to my amazement and most diligent investigation, for such general contempt of the divine canons—alas!—than the guilt of the false bishops; and that the matter itself was stirred up by the hand of the sinner, that is, the devil, in vengeance for pride, through the weakness of lust, which, kindled in the fire of God’s wrath, burns today in the world and will burn until the final depths of Hell, devouring the earth where the vineyard of the Lord of hosts was planted, together with the growth of good works that it ought to have borne. In what follows something is corrupt or displaced, unless it is preferable to supplement and correct it in this way: or else, “with the growth” of any wretched person, while by burning it temporarily he makes for himself a return, so that he may not cease to be burned eternally with his soul; or else, “he devours the earth with its growth,” while, as another says, he leads to destruction everything good that he has done, and so forth.]

Or else it devours the earth with its growth, while, as another says, it so brings everything good that he has done to destruction that nothing benefits him if he has ever done anything good. Yet I think this was said of the persistence of that lust of which God himself, complaining through prophetic speech, acknowledges: “The beasts have rotted in their dung” (Joel 1:17).

And it burns the foundations of the mountains—that is, of the bishops (Deut. 32:22)—that is, the very beginnings of learning God’s law, through such deadly lust, to such a degree that, when the need arises, scarcely anyone can be found fit to choose, and no one who, though legally elected, would—horrible impiety!—lay hands upon one entirely worthy.

Since matters stand thus, and since these people especially embrace what the holy canons chiefly detest, while they refuse to avoid these things, they do not hesitate to regard the rest as worthless. [Col. 0516B] All the sons of the Church, observing this, also make little of everything contained in Scripture, relying solely on the examples of such men. Believing themselves to possess God’s mercy beyond what he has promised, they put his justice behind their backs; and therefore all of them without fear give themselves indiscriminately to their pleasures and deadly desires.

Why ecclesiastical law is held in such contempt, while secular law is so greatly feared, is easily answered: evidently, they fear losing money more than losing their souls; they fear temporal punishment more than eternal damnation.

**2.** Someone may also ask why, among the other peoples reborn through baptism, the Italians are especially contemptuous of canonical law and disdainful of clerics. I confess that the reason is the one given above. For their greater lustfulness, the more frequent use of drinks or foods that nourish lust, continual drinking of wine, and the more negligent discipline of teachers bring this about.

[Note: *Pigmentum* generally means a drink made from various ingredients. Hence *pigmentata potio*, “spiced drink,” occurs in Peter Damian, book 1, letter 11, and in Uldaric, book 2 of the *Customs of Cluny*. See Du Cange. In book 1, number 9 of the *Prefaces*, Ratherius calls beverages prescribed by physicians *pigmenta*. Here, however, *pigmenta* are drinks that nourish sexual desire, or even foods stuffed with spices and made hotter. The principal vice of the Italians of Ratherius’s age in food and drink is also lamented by a contemporary panegyrist in praise of Berengar I:

“O Italians, sacred cups are more dear to you,

and often to loosen the stomach with gleaming rich foods.”]

This custom and the examples of their ancestors have long driven them to such shamelessness that, apart from shaving the beard, leaving the crown of the head bare with a slight difference in clothing, and the considerable negligence with which they conduct themselves in church, you may see them differ from the layman only in this. Yet they strive more to please the world than God.

[Note: *Barbirasium* means the shaving of the beard, with the crown of the head bare—that is, the entire upper part of the head shaved—while the lower part was surrounded by a circle of hair, the clerical tonsure. Similar remarks occur in book 5, number 18 of the *Prefaces*: “Having abandoned our rite, our dress, and even our manner of clothing, following the customs and pursuits of the world, we use garments to such an extent that, so to speak, apart from the *barbirasium* and the tonsure, and whatever praises we seem to offer to the Lord—only with the mouth, and that very rarely—we appear in no respect different from secular people.”]

Therefore, I confess, those people despise them and rightly hold them accursed.

[Note: “Those people” means the Italian laymen whom he shortly before called despisers of clerics.]

For God promised this through the person of Eli, who detested the insolence of his sons: “Whoever honors me, I will honor; but those who despise me shall be held of no account” (1 Sam. 2:30).

Through Malachi also, after he had spoken of the upright—“The lips of the priest guard knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, for he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. 2:7)—we must see what he says about the reprobate: “But you have departed from the way and have caused many to stumble in the law. You have invalidated the covenant of Levi; therefore I have made you contemptible to all peoples” (ibid., 8).

And through another Prophet: “They provoked me with what was not God and angered me with their vanities. And I will provoke them with what is not a people, and with a foolish nation I will anger them” (Deut. 32:21).

He then adds that worst lot, mentioned here more than once, from which we have said all these evils arise: “Fire has been kindled in my wrath”—which is certainly understood to be the fire of lust—“and it will burn to the depths of Hell; it will devour the earth with its growth, and burn the foundations of the mountains” (ibid., 22), that is, the beginnings of Christianity, with apostasy following.

[Col. 0517B] For now such a withdrawal from God and from the faith received is evident, when someone, in God’s presence, is not afraid to commit against him things that he threatens to avenge by an unquenchable burning, to such an extent that nothing good he has done up to the baptism he received can benefit him—especially if he commits these things not unknowingly but with complete awareness.

**3.** For, alas, I learned from another relating the very matter that a certain man, at almost the very same hour at which that same wretch had sung, also recalled in the history of Job, “It is a fire devouring unto destruction” (Job 31:12), and was not ignorant of its exposition. Remembering, moreover, that the Apostle had said of God, “All things are naked and open to his eyes, to whom our speech is directed” (Heb. 4:13)—that is, even the things we think speak to him, let alone the things we commit—he was so inflamed by this very deadly fire that, scratching an itch beneath an alluring and most lustful touch, he made himself aroused to his own destruction, reciprocally enjoying the pleasure of obscene discharge to the very nail; less shamefully than others, indeed, if anything in such shamefulness can be called not utterly shameful.

[Note: The accusative *quemdam* must be joined with what follows after some intervening words: he had been so inflamed by this deadly fire, namely lust, that, and so forth.]

What was the point of his having attended those morning praises, I ask, except the public declaration of rebellion against God, with the service he had performed for the Lord plainly proving fruitless? It would have been incomparably better for him to have slept through the morning prayers than, after completing them, to have committed so great an evil.

For, as Gregory testifies (*Morals on Job*, book 1, chapters 3 and 7), evils displease God so greatly that no good mixed with evils pleases him.

[Col. 0518B] Still less should we most deludedly [read: *seductissime*] imagine that those good deeds please him when they have been offset by the succession of evils that follow them: “The garment mixed with blood shall be for burning, and shall be fuel for fire” (Isa. 9:5). Another says: “I will change their glory into disgrace” (Hos. 4:7). And, so that you may not doubt of whom he speaks, he adds: “They shall eat the sins of my people and shall lift up their souls to their iniquity. And it shall be: as the people, so the priest. I will visit his ways upon him and repay him for his thoughts. They shall eat and shall not be satisfied; they committed fornication and did not cease, because they abandoned the Lord by failing to keep him. For fornication, wine, and drunkenness take away the heart” (ibid., 8)—that is, they destroy reason.

Likewise: “They shall not pour wine offerings to the Lord, and they shall not please him. Their sacrifices shall be like the bread of mourners; all who eat it shall be defiled, because their bread is for their own souls” (Hos. 9:4). A most fearful sentence!

But if anyone insists that these words apply only to Jewish priests, let him hear the Apostle contradicting him: “Whatever was written was written for our instruction” (Rom. 15:4).
