And when the same Apostle says of such people, “How shall they preach unless they are sent?” (Rom. 10:15), if they had been sent rather than merely permitted—that is, if they had been lawfully assumed, elected, and ordained, and were doing what suited them—they would deserve an everlasting crown, not only for their own salvation but also for that of countless others. Conversely, as things now stand, they deserve everlasting disgrace, together with the unfailing interest of punishments to be mourned.

[Col. 0519A] “When you come to Babylon, there you shall be delivered, and there I shall redeem you” (Mic. 4:10), says the Lord, who speaks through another: “You have the forehead of a prostitute; you refused to be ashamed” (Jer. 3:3).

Would that these two passages admonished us, most wretched as we are, and that, like King Josiah, they moved each of us to say to the rest: “Go, consult the Lord for me, for the people, and for all Judah” (2 Kings 22:13). By “Judah” we may understand, through confession of God, the distinguished Catholic Church, concerning the words of these scrolls—namely, the canons and decrees contained in the archives of the churches.

“For great,” he says, “is the wrath of the Lord that has been kindled against us, because our fathers did not listen to the words of these books, to do everything written in them”; by “fathers” understand the bishops of the churches.

May he at least deign to reply to each of us: “Thus says the Lord God of Israel: Because you heard the words of the scroll, and your heart was terrified, and you humbled yourself before the Lord when you heard the words concerning this place and its inhabitants—that they would become a desolation and a curse—and you tore your garments and wept before me, I also have heard you, says the Lord. Therefore I will gather you to your fathers, and you shall be gathered to your tomb in peace, so that your eyes may not see all the evils that I will bring upon this place” (ibid., 18).

**4.** But why all this, if the envy of rivals eager to defame should ask? Certainly, so that what the preceding discussion could not make known might be shown near its conclusion—namely, so that anyone seeking to know the source of this present, universal contempt of the holy canons might understand it.

Our inquiry and investigation have reached this conclusion: it undoubtedly happened through the fault of those who, although they read and understand the canons, regard them as worthless. We have also investigated why they do this together: evidently because they gladly do what the canons most strictly forbid, while they absolutely refuse to carry out what they most earnestly command.

[Note: Baluzius warned that the text should be read in this way, as the most recent editor of the *Spicilegium* reports. The printed edition had *quae percipiunt*, “which they perceive.”]

What are those things? Two: the illicit, repeatedly forbidden sexual activity of the teachers of the Church, or the seductive and non-uniform pleasure that God detests even more; and the neglect of the chastity beloved by Christ.

[Note: Rather, there are two, as above. He notes only two kinds of lust: the first, in which sexual desire is poured out upon women; the second, as he himself says, “non-uniform,” namely that whose form he described above in number 3. He declares that what happened to that cleric was indeed utterly shameful, but in such a way that something else is still far more shameful. This is also the interpretation of the editor mentioned in the note.]

These three things cause, together with everything else contained in the divine books, all such things to be held wholly in contempt; God has rightly shown that the despisers themselves are rejected in return.

[Note: “By a reciprocal right”: just as they despise the canons and sacred Scriptures, so God in turn shows that they are despised and rejected by others, as was demonstrated earlier.]

And their rejection is followed by eternal punishment, not only for one sin but also for the evil example by which they ruin others.

**5.** Since I have set forth no remedy for this pestilence, I confess that I would have failed unless three things previously mentioned had come to mind. What are they? The Prophet says: “They committed fornication and did not cease” (Hos. 4:10).

When I compare this with the passage that says, “You have sinned; cease” (Ecclus. 21:1), and with the one that reads, “Let the one who stole steal no longer” (Eph. 4:28), it seems to me that something would have benefited fornicators if they made an effort to cease from fornication.

“The remains of thought shall keep a feast day for you” (Ps. 75:11), the Psalmist also says to God. He seems to indicate that, once wicked thought has been abandoned, we must strive lest the poison of deadly pleasure emerge in the form of a criminal action, like the worst scabies of the skin breaking out from within. That day will be solemn for us before God if a depraved deed does not follow our will.

[Note: Construe this as follows: Let us take care lest the poison of deadly pleasure, like the worst scabies of the skin, emerge from within into the accomplishment of a wicked act.]

When I read, “When you come to Babylon, there you shall be delivered” (Mic. 4:10), it seems to me that this is of great benefit to anyone who is ashamed of crimes previously committed.

I am also greatly delighted by the example of King Josiah when I compare it with what is read in the Pentateuch: “Whoever feared the word of the Lord among Pharaoh’s servants made his animals and cattle flee into the house, and hail did not fall upon them” (Exod. 9:20).

And also: “Blessed is the man who is always fearful; but whoever is hard of heart shall fall into evil” (Prov. 28:14).

The Lord says: “Have you seen how Ahab has humbled himself before me? Because he has humbled himself for my sake, I will not bring evil in his days” (1 Kings 21:29).

**6.** I do not deny that these things bring me some small relief, although they provide no security. For I am greatly terrified when I read elsewhere that, just as medicine administered to a wounded man does not help if the iron still remains in him, so repentance does not benefit one who does not abandon the sin he laments—as the remorse of Balaam and the distress of Esau reveal.

The Lord confirms the same when he says: “How vile you have become by repeating your ways” (Jer. 2:36).

When I read or hear Gregory (*Homily 37 on the Gospels*) say that one cannot reach great rewards except through great labors, and I consider my own conduct, if I am not terrified, I confess that I am insane. For if one does not reach great rewards, it follows that one certainly reaches the greatest punishments. What is there in heaven that is not a great reward? What is there in Hell that is not the greatest loss?

I cannot say how sweetly the Lord’s voice delights me when he says: “There is joy in heaven over one sinner” (Luke 15:7), and how immediately it terrifies me when he adds, “who repents.”

[Col. 0521A] When I consider what repentance is, either in the holy canons or in the examples of those who performed it worthily, and when I attend equally to my own laziness, I am compelled to cry out only, “Woe, woe, woe!”

For, once crimes have been abandoned, we hold as most true and pious the promise of him who says: “Turn to me, and I will return to you” (Zech. 1:3).

But concerning those things that cannot be abandoned, I remain uncertain what to think, much less what to say. For I know that it is written of God: “If he shuts a man in, who can say to him, ‘Why do you act thus?’” (Job 18:8).

And of anyone of this sort: “For he has cast his feet into a net, and he walks in its meshes.”

Whether he who is sung of as one “who opens and no one shuts, who shuts and no one opens” (Rev. 3:7) will deign to absolve such a person or not is not for human beings to judge in this world.

For it is written: “A man does not know whether he is worthy of hatred or love, but all things are kept uncertain for the future” (Eccl. 9:1).

Yet, just as this sentence removes despair from the sinner, so it adds concern to the righteous person, provided that he does not cease to do what is fitting. Thus no one in this life should be without care. Let the one who hopes in the Lord hope, but in such a way that he does not vainly hope for something other than what the Lord himself promised; and let the one who boasts, if he boasts, boast not in himself—that is, in his work and virtue—but in the Lord (2 Cor. 10:17).

[Col. 0522A] **7.** But let these matters now suffice, since the source of contempt for canonical sanction has been amply demonstrated. Scripture itself shows that it is characteristic of fools to pour out their entire mind (Prov. 29:11).

At the same time, I must take care lest I rightly be blamed for carrying wood into the forest and, foolishly, bringing water from a river to thirsty gardens.

[Note: Construe as follows: I must take care lest I rightly be blamed for carrying wood into a forest and, foolishly, bringing water from a river to thirsty gardens. Since your courtesy once deigned, if you remember, to ask about my laziness and how I should pray, I confess that my modest abilities found in the book of your friend and namesake, and companion in persecuting me, Hubert, what I should earnestly pray for. I therefore thought it worthwhile to place it here. The following prayers were excerpts made by Ratherius from the book of a certain Hubert, who had entered into an alliance with his adversaries. He calls him your namesake because he addresses Hubert of Parma, to whom he dedicated this work.]

**COLLECT**

O Lord, overthrow with the right hand of your power those who conspire against the strong foundation of your righteousness, so that iniquity may not rule over justice, but falsehood may always be subjected to truth. Through the Lord.

**SECRET**

O Lord, we ask you to be appeased by the gifts offered, and mercifully deliver us from our enemies. Through the Lord.

**POST-COMMUNION**

May this communion, O Lord, both free us from all sins and powerfully defend us from the snares of our enemies. Through the Lord.

[Col. 0521]

# RATHERIUS’S LITTLE WORK, INSCRIBED “A CONJECTURE OF SOMEONE’S CHARACTER”

[Note: This little work was edited by Acherius from a manuscript at Laon. Fulcuinus lists it among Ratherius’s writings in chapter 24 under the title “A Conjecture of His Life.” Nearly the whole work is devoted to explaining his character and manner of life through a certain sharp and ironic method, in which a malicious quibbler pretends, by perverse interpretation, to twist all his actions—even the better ones—into something blameworthy.

As for its date, most people thought that this work was written in the year 972, because number 13 says: “It is now almost forty years since I began to seek power,” that is, the bishopric, and because he presents himself as so old that he thinks scarcely a year of life remains to him.

But apart from the fact that “almost forty years” should not be reckoned from the beginning of his episcopate, or from the year 932, but from the time when he began to seek the bishopric, as we shall explain in note 62, it is certainly clear from many passages of the work itself that it was written while he held the bishopric of Verona and refused to surrender it to Milo. He did surrender it in the year 968. It therefore seems that the work should be assigned approximately to the beginning of the year 966.

At that time Ratherius’s enemies, having learned from his letters to Milo, written toward the end of 965, and from the final number that he added at the same time to the *Deliberative Conclusion*, that he did not wish to surrender the bishopric unless compelled by an imperial decree, tried to denounce his life and character before the emperor through various quibbles, in order to obtain such an imperial decree.

Ratherius, anticipating their quibbles, presented in this little work whatever might be alleged against him, whether true or false, so cleverly in their own words that it may appear at once a censure and a defense.

We assign it to the beginning of 966 because at that time the troubles concerning his surrender of the bishopric were boiling over most fiercely; they seem almost to have subsided during Lent of that same year, when, freed from such difficulties, he convened a synod and published a synodal letter. Compare the author’s *Life*, number 109.]

**373 1.** I am compelled to answer the quibbles of my haters concerning all my actions, words, and even intentions, as though I alone were someone who did not have to come to that supreme judgment where everything left uncorrected here must be examined, but instead had to render an account to human beings of everything in this world.

It is as though I alone were not permitted to speak except to someone previously designated—[understand: nor were I permitted] to pass from one room to another without giving an account—although, by God’s mercy and the alms of the one who bestowed these things upon me, I possess many things and am not forbidden the freedom to enjoy them.

If such people themselves barked at one another about such matters, it would not have been surprising. But it is hardly a small wonder if such men dared to weary imperial ears with matters of this kind.

[Note: Construe as follows: It would be no small wonder if such men dared to weary imperial ears with such matters. What need is there to report to one who must think about the entire monarchy of our region whether some poor little man moves from one bed to another, or whether someone turns from one side to the other? Thus there is material for the quibbler: I may serve up to him what he is intent on doing, joining false things to true, the probable to the certain, and piling up here, as far as I can, your little rumors, so that I may satisfy you all. Anticipating such a charge by this sort of preface—one similar to which, I believe, no one before me has made about himself—I try to bring forth an account of myself: what you say about me and with what meaning you are able to say it. We have restored the words, which were wrongly transmitted in the printed editions before *monarchia*, to a more appropriate place.]

For what concern is it of one who must think about the whole monarchy of our region whether some poor fellow moves from one bed to another, or whether anyone turns from one side to another? Thus there is material for the quibbler. In order to serve the purpose to which he is earnestly devoted, I shall join false things to true, the probable to the certain, piling up here, as far as I am able, your little rumors, so that I may satisfy you all.

Anticipating in this way what you say, and what you are able to say about me, and in what sense, I myself now attempt, by a sort of preface—similar to which, I believe, no one before me has made about himself—to produce an account concerning me.

Let whoever wishes read it and bring forward something worse about me, if he can.

## 2.

“They say that he never ceases to call servants whom he does not dare to flog bad servants. He says that, because he is spirited and extremely poor, he does not want to have a servant or chaplain whom he does not dare to call a *fillo* [Col. 0524A].

[Note: [Col. 0523D] Kero the monk: *verbera fillo*, “strike the *fillo*”; *verberum fillonum*, “the blows of *filloni*.” Hence *fillones*, *verberones*, “fellows deserving blows,” and *nebulones*, “good-for-nothings.” Since he used neither servants nor chaplains, he had to do everything himself. For that reason Ratherius seems to call himself spirited: while other bishops carried out many things through servants, he did not fear undertaking everything himself. Hence, below, no. 14: “I have no trustworthy servant to whom I can entrust this. I myself do what I can for myself.”]

He complains insistently that the soldiers do not help him, and that they allowed him to be captured and carried away.

[Note: [Col. 0524B] The soldiers of whom he speaks were noble vassals of the Church, who were obliged to serve in war for the Church and the bishop. Ratherius is reported to have complained that they did not help him and that they allowed him to be captured and carried away, when, namely, he was captured and carried away by Milo, his rival; see below, no. 833. Concerning what is added shortly about the clerics’ singing, two things may be noted. In the work *On Rebellious Clerics*, no. 1, after mentioning prophets, psalms, hymns, and songs, he says: “Things which you boast that you celebrate more frequently in the other churches of Italy.” Conversely, he reproaches them because they were unwilling to sing the Creed of Saint Athanasius. Compare *Itinerary*, no. 7, and *On Contempt for the Canons*, part I, no. 24.]

He criticizes the conduct, reading, and singing of the clerics. He calls an unlawful marriage adultery.

[Note: [Col. 0524C] In *Discord*, no. 1, he says: “For us, an adulterer is one who is married contrary to the canons.” And in the *Apology*, likewise attacking the marriages of clerics, he says, no. 7: “Do they regard as nothing those who, while it is public adultery to be monogamous, and while an unlawful marriage is certainly involved, are nevertheless trigamists and, shamefully, quadrigamists—and this among priests and deacons—when even bigamists from among the laity cannot at least become clerics?”]

He insists that the law [understand: rather than custom] must be observed. He forbids servile labor on the Lord’s Day.

[Note: [Col. 0524C] In Letter 12 to Ambrose, no. 3, he says: [Col. 0524D] “With excommunication I forbade them to cease from servile work on the Lord’s Day. Since I was in no way able to enforce this, I ordered the gates to be barred against the approaching wagons. They judge that this deed ought to be expiated either by my death or by my expulsion.”]

He orders those dedicated to God [that is, converted or consecrated to God] to serve in a manner not only unusual but unheard-of. He never stops proclaiming that no one can attain great rewards except through great labors (*Gregory, Homily 57 on the Gospels*). Where, then, are the kings? Where are all those abounding in riches, those who live by walking in pleasure? For by this saying he promises the kingdom of God only to the unfortunate.

His nose is always in a book, and from there he never ceases to chatter [Col. 0524B]. He rebukes absolutely everyone, being attached to no one whose conduct pleases him.

[Note: [Col. 0524D] “Attached,” that is, inclined in mind, close, or friendly; just as *contiguity* is used in Barthius’s Glossary, from Guibert’s *History of Palestine*, to mean kinship and friendship.]

But whom does he praise, when he always censures himself? Perhaps he was deceived by that most truthful saying of the Apostle, though he understood it badly: “If we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged” (1 Cor. 11:31)—as though it were enough for a sinner to confess himself to someone, if he does not abandon the sin he confesses; although, if someone else said this to him, he would bear it most bitterly.

What he says and writes, and what he desires to leave for posterity to read, so that they may disparage those living now, he records eagerly. He calls his *Chronography*—vainly Greekifying, though he is not even a Latin—the sort of writing appropriate to his own time, since it contains the life of his contemporaries. Gnawing at himself first, then in the middle, and finally at the end, he never ceases to sink his genuine tooth into all those who live in their own way, leaving no one untouched.

[Note: [Col. 0524D] Miraeus, in his notes to Sigebert’s book *On Illustrious Men*, where he discusses Ratherius, lists his *Chronography* among the manuscript codices of the library of Gembloux. Since that library was consumed by fire, this codex will now be sought in vain. Someone might perhaps suppose that the title *Chronography* denotes Ratherius’s *Confession*, which we published from a manuscript of Lobbes [Col. 0525C]. It contains, indeed, a description of this kind: he censures himself first, that is, at the beginning of the work; himself in the middle, that is, in its middle; and himself finally, that is, at the end of the same *Confession*; and on this occasion repeatedly stings others. Yet, since in the *Confession* he does not strike everyone so as to leave untouched no one whom he attacks, as he is reported to have done in the *Chronography*, we think that another, lost work bore the title *Chronography*. He mentions it again in the *Itinerary*, no. 8: “O Ratherius’s most wretched *Chronography*!” There he also seems to indicate that in it he attacked the conduct of his clerics, something you will not find in the book of the *Confession*. Compare the note there.]

[Col. 0525A] Hence, since his tongue is against everyone, the tongues of everyone are deservedly against him.

His insolence of tongue could somehow be endured; but someone would rightly break the rebellious fingers of the man who writes such things for future generations.

[Note: [Col. 0525D] Construe: “Someone would rightly break his rebellious fingers, which write such things for those to come.” The words imply that his conduct could be tolerated if he attacked only with his tongue; but that publishing the same things in writing and transmitting them to posterity cannot be tolerated.]

What more need be said? His life is unlike that of all who care about honor. He is not adorned with clothing [Col. 0525D], his footwear is disgraceful, he does not seek *scamnalia*, he needs table coverings, and he is content with ordinary bedding and the rest of his furniture; he does not pursue costly things.

[Note: [Col. 0525D] Earlier editions printed *non comiter* incorrectly, as the latest editor of the *Spicilegium* noted. Shortly afterward, where the text has *scamnalia*, Acherius thought *scamella* should be read. The editor just mentioned, however, rightly believed that nothing should be changed: for in his *Testament* Ratherius likewise names these three things—*scamnalia*, *mensalia*, that is, coverings for benches and tables, and bed coverings. In the *Confession* as well, no. 34, mention is made of *mensalia* and *scamnalium*.]

Nothing in him appears connected with glory, nothing with honor [Col. 0525B]. He washes only his hands and lips before taking food, and likewise after taking it; his face he washes rarely.

Perhaps because in his homeland he had been a *bacularis*, every sort of honor is so worthless to him.

[Note: [Col. 0525D] *Baculares* were attendants, so called because they carried a staff. Thus, in Letter 12 to Ambrose, no. 4, he calls the attendants of the Church *baculares*: “If a cleric or servant of his, summoned by the bishop, does not come at his own will, he sends his *baculares*, and by force they seize him and lead him to the bishop.” Ratherius, however, was said by some, in mockery, to have been a *bacularis*, or the son of a carpenter. Yet he himself, the mocker, asserts that the matter was commonly told quite differently among us—that is, among the Veronese. For he was a nobleman, as we have shown in the *Life*, § 1, and was also described as such by many people who came from Germany to Verona and knew his family. It is worth noting that “carpenter” can refer to one who also constructs things from stones. Elsewhere too we shall see Ratherius occupied with building and rebuilding churches.]

Although among us it has often been said quite differently—that he was the son of a carpenter—he is therefore so skilled and so willing to build or rebuild basilicas; he is always handling and rehandling stones, and he often joins them together himself.

## 3.

He does not disdain doing what belongs to servants [understand: the things belonging to servants]; yet he so neglects the practices of masters that, having set aside the pontifical curule seat, he more often lies on the ground.

[Note: [Col. 0526D] Acherius says that perhaps *pontifical dignity* should be read; but evidently he was thinking of something else. For *curule* here means a seat of the sort used by magistrates and by those possessing some public dignity. Thus the latest editor of the *Spicilegium*. Construe what follows as: “and, like another Epicurus, who thinks that the highest good lies in pleasure, he is content if the belly, the side, and the feet are well, and if he is sufficient for himself and his own.”]

Like another Epicurus, who thinks that the highest good lies in pleasure, he is content if the belly, the side, and the feet are well, and if he is sufficient for himself and his own. When he is eating, he does not care whether any company sits beside him [Col. 0525C]. His table is free of the rich; he does not reject the companionship, and not improperly that of the lowly, asserting that a poor table disdains wealthy guests.

Between noble and ignoble, so far as carrying out what is useful to him is concerned, he makes no distinction [Col. 0526A], asserting that many nobles have often done ignoble things and many ignoble people noble things, and that nobility depends more upon power and one’s own actions than upon another person’s status, as Sallust testifies.

By fleeing the person he pretends to be, he perhaps seeks to purchase honor in this way. As is evident, he seeks it only by display; he exchanges true glory for empty show.

We suppose that he became stained by such things and perhaps fell into those very actions which he almost always bewails in his discourses: moved by the hand of the sinner, trampled by the foot of pride, inflamed by the breath of Behemoth, expelled from the grace of God, unable to stand upright, and perhaps having done something unclean and consequently wicked.

[Note: [Col. 0526D] These words are taken in an opposite sense from Psalm 35:12: “Let not the foot of pride come against me, and let not the hand of the sinner move me.” The following words, “inflamed by the breath of Behemoth,” refer to Job 41:12: “His breath makes coals burn, and a flame comes forth from his mouth.”]

For when he visits his own appearance, he sins so often that, just as that man once said in the *Lamentations* concerning others, so this man can truthfully say of himself:

“My eye has plundered my soul” (*Lamentations* 3:51).

[Note: [Col. 0526D] This too is contrary to Job 5:24: “When you visit your appearance, you will not sin.”]

Indeed, unless this were unquestionably so, and unless he had recognized that he had either done or was doing such things as deserved to suffer infernal punishments, he would have dined, though extremely gluttonous, at the hour when the others dine [Col. 0526B].

[Note: [Col. 0526D] Thus Ratherius dined later than the others, and did not always eat meat, as the others did.]

He would have eaten meat sometimes, as the others always did; nor would he have cried out, “Woe is me, woe is me,” so many thousands of times, as he is said to have done while alone.

For there are those who very often hear him quarreling alone, as though with another person, and sometimes saying:

“What do you want again, devil? Have you not grown old in such things with me? My limbs are exhausted and powerless—why do you still tear my body apart? Have I not been surrendered to you enough? Have I not purchased hell sufficiently? What more price do you seek? Eternal life could have been bought for less.”

“If what is written in the book of my *Confession* is not enough, return, malicious one, to your own book. There, as I know, none of my evils has been omitted; those things were enough—though I confess they could have been enough—which Italy sings, France, and Noricum; which Burgundy does not ignore, Provence recalls, Septimania remembers, Saxony recounts, and Swabia bears in mind.

[Col. 0527A] It could rightly have been enough for you, malicious one, that I be known and called an old man of evil days.”

[Note: [Col. 0527C] The provinces listed are those in which Ratherius spent some time. Compare the note on the book of the *Confessions*.]

Yet I know, I know your cunning: you do not seek me, whom—alas!—you hold, but you strive to acquire others through me.

[Note: [Col. 0527D] The earlier edition of Acherius had *pro me acquirere*. We have adopted the emendation of the new editor.]

## 4.

When we hear these things, how highly can we esteem him? We recognize that he displeases God; how can we make him pleasing to us? Since these are words of despair, what can our judgment of him be, when he even censures his own conduct? And since, according to the Apostle, a bishop ought to be irreproachable (1 Tim. 3:2), who could endure the discovery of so many and such reprehensible things in one man?

Among all his qualities, however, his loquacity is especially astonishing, since no ability in eloquence supports him, nor the authority of teachers, nor an abundance of reading. If God is wondrous in his saints and in his works (Ps. 67:36), then, so to speak, he is even more wondrous in granting such things in such a manner to such people.

We may compare him to Balaam’s donkey (Num. 22:28), or to that same idolatrous sacrilegious man: prophesying and deceiving, blessing and cursing, repentant and hardened. We may also liken him to Elihu, although he is believed to be the same sort of person as Balaam—the man whom the Lord himself marvels to see wrapping his judgments in unskilled speech (Job 38:2), which this man never ceases to do.

We may fit him to a lamp that illuminates others while burning itself.

If some goodness is seen to exist in him, it should be regarded more as hypocrisy than as true goodness. For, they say, even if he rebuilds or constructs basilicas, he does so from the vice of vainglory.

Would that they were lying—or rather, mistaken! Yet this is precisely what the Apostle forbids when he says: “Do not judge before the time, until the Lord comes, who will both bring to light the hidden things of darkness and reveal the counsels of hearts” (1 Cor. 4:5). Nevertheless, I myself confess that in this matter I do not wholly disagree with them.

## 5.

“What use,” they say, “is such a man’s episcopate? He does not serve the emperor, not at all the duke [Col. 0527D], never goes into the army, and goes to court very rarely [Col. 0528A]; and if he does happen to go, he does not do so willingly.

[Note: [Col. 0527D] “The duke,” that is, Henry, the nephew of the emperor Otto through his brother. He was duke of Bavaria and margrave of Verona; or rather, Judith, the mother of that duke, who, while governing the duchy and the march for her young son, is praised three times by Ratherius under the title “duke”—twice in this work, nos. 9 and 14, where he calls her a renowned duke, and once in the *Itinerary*, no. 4, where he calls her a most distinguished duke. See further on this matter in the author’s *Life*, § 12, nos. 75 and 76. As for how unworthy Ratherius considered it for a bishop and clerics to enter military service, consult part I of *On Contempt for the Canons*, no. 4.]

If he does do so, he goes to the palace only after at least four days have passed; as soon as he can, he returns to his lodging and takes up his book again. He asks the emperor for nothing, seeks nothing from him, and pleads with his mercy for none of his own people. He acquires nothing for his Church and allows much to be lost.

He conducts no business of the kingdom with the leading men; he does not visit their lodgings, thinks little of their conversations, and invites none of them to his own lodging. He gives none of them anything and asks nothing from them; he always returns home empty-handed. He offers an oath to no one and requires one from no one.

He does not involve himself in any glory of this world by following the example of others.

[Note: [Col. 0527D] *Inframittere* means “to interpose” or “to involve oneself.” Likewise in the *Apology*, no. 7: “So that from now on any bishop who should involve himself in the affairs of clerics would be condemned by an anathema.” Construe: “He does not involve himself in any glory of this world, following the example of others.”]

He says that he detests glory for this reason: when he wanted it, he was unable to obtain it; now, since it will not be granted to him to enjoy it, it is the height of foolishness to pursue it.

If anyone wishes to kiss his foot [Col. 0528D], he drives him away with a great outcry.

[Note: [Col. 0528D] Note the custom of kissing the feet of bishops.]

If it were permitted, he would sit alone all day, turning and re-turning books. He hates crowds and loves solitude. He does not play at hoop, avoids dice, cares nothing about dogs, and nothing about hawks.

Sometimes he is extremely talkative, sometimes almost mute; at one moment dissolved in laughter, then exceedingly sad, and quickly ready to quarrel. Yet whether happy or angry, he is always ready to utter scurrilous or idle words and anything that provokes laughter.

[Note: [Col. 0528D] That is, he is “always ready to utter them,” whether he is happy or angry.]

Whether he gives or does not give, he will in no way wish to be asked [perhaps the reading is *vult* or *vellet*]. He is always impatient, often extremely patient; and even when he gives something to someone, he permits no one to promise anything.

He would be extremely deceitful, if he did not disdain to lie; he would be cunning, if he himself did not hate the cunning and did not believe that God hates them.

[Note: [Col. 0528D] Construe: “He would be cunning if he himself did not hate the cunning and believe that God hates the cunning.”]

He is ambiguous to everyone and therefore agreeable to no one.

From being once extremely generous—and, to speak more truthfully, prodigal—he has recently become so miserly [Col. 0528C] that he seems to have been changed into another man.

[Note: [Col. 0528D] This recent change, by which he passed from extreme generosity to miserliness and might have appeared ridiculous, seems to have arisen because he had recently decided to build or repair basilicas that had been destroyed or burned partly by age and partly by the incursions of enemies, especially the Hungarians. See the *Apology*, no. 5.]

From this his instability can clearly be inferred.

He says, “Eat”; if you do not wish to, he applies no compulsion. “At least drink,” he says; but he does not force the unwilling. He does not say, “Sit,” but he never fails to rebuke someone who does not sit.

[Note: [Col. 0528D] Does *excultare* here stand for *auscultare*, “to listen more attentively”? Or should *exculcare* be read, meaning “to place in a seat”? For *culcare*, in the sense of “to place,” is found in medieval authors. See Du Cange, under *Colloco*.]

If you ask him something too insistently, he becomes angry; if it is something necessary, he is silent, and then becomes more violently irritated; if it is cleverly put, he begins to rage.

If he wants you to do something, he says, “Do not do it”; if he does not want it done, he says, “Do it.”

He is deceitful, although he asserts that in reports he always tries to present himself as truthful, and that in promises he wishes to be truthful.

He has never begun any good undertaking that he has brought to completion.

## 6.

He continually removes the tail from the sacrifice offered to the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 0529D] The tail of sacrificial animals was to be offered. See Exod. 29:23; Lev. 3:9 and 7:3. Here the tail is understood as final perseverance in goodness.]

By doing so, the most wretched man deprives himself of salvation. For, according to the Lord’s testimony, “the one who perseveres in goodness to the end will be saved” (Matt. 24:13), whereas the one who perseveres in evil, as this man seems likely to do, will undoubtedly be lost.

And alas, miserable and unhappy man! Why does he not at least turn back at this point of life where he now stands?

But it seems to us that he is desperate because he has put his foot into such a net that, walking among its meshes, he cannot in any way free himself.

[Note: [Col. 0529B] In the *Confession*, no. 28, when explaining why he is prevented from returning to the monastic way of life, he uses a similar allegory taken from Job 18:8: “The snares in which I bound myself hold me, and the spots of the net into which, heedless, I thrust my foot.” He explains this net and these spots by saying that he accepted the episcopate not because he was ordered to do so, but voluntarily; yet even if he wishes to resign it, he may not do so voluntarily. Hence at the end of this section he says: “He would wish to, if it were permitted; he does not wish to, because it is not permitted.”]

For while he was a monk and is now a bishop, if he abandons his sheep and returns to the monastery, he fears hearing: “O shepherd and idol, abandoning the flock” (Zech. 11:17). But if he does not, he fears that the Apostle has said of him: “Having condemnation because they have made their first faith void” (1 Tim. 5:12). He also fears the Lord’s words: “No one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of heaven” (Luke 9:62).

Thus, when he had been captured [Col. 0529D], the most foolish man began to sing: “Behold, now I see what I desired.”

[Note: [Col. 0529D] That is, when he had been captured by Milo, his adversary, about whom more will be said below, no. 14. He rejoiced because in this way he would not resign the episcopate voluntarily but under compulsion, and thus, having left the episcopate without illegality, he could return to the monastery. He sang in his joy: “Behold, now I see what I desired” (better, “what I longed for”), as in the antiphon for the feast of Saint Agnes. He seems to have sung it for that reason, because he had been captured through Milo’s agency on that feast day in the year 965.]

For he admits that he thought he would then be completely expelled, and he rejoiced that he himself had not abandoned the episcopate, but that the episcopate had abandoned him. By this stratagem, he says, he wanted to return to the monastery, promising himself that the Lord himself had therefore said to him: “Turn to me, and I will return to you” (Zech. 1:3).

But since this did not happen at all, in the depth of his despair he thinks that this saying was spoken about him: “If God consults a man, who can say to him, ‘Why do you do this?’” (Job 9:12).

[Note: [Col. 0530D] Construe: “For he says that we do not allow him, much less to do penance for past deeds, even to exercise any abstinence at all from evils committed, although he could altogether fear eternal condemnation for our crimes, if he had none of his own; crimes which he certainly neither restrains by his words, nor corrects by his example, nor wipes away by his merits.”]

For he says that we do not allow him, much less to do penance for past deeds, even to practice any abstinence at all from evils committed, although he could altogether fear eternal condemnation for our crimes, if he had none of his own—crimes which he certainly neither restrains by his words, nor corrects by his example, nor wipes away by his merits.

Caught, namely, in this threefold misfortune, he was compelled in another of his works to cry out to God:

“If you permit my deadly attempts, Lord, to prosper, what confidence in escaping do you leave me? And if I do not cease from present evils, what forgiveness do I hope for past ones?”

[Note: [Col. 0530D] This work is the second sermon for Lent; there, no. 23, the words quoted here are found.]

He says that this, this indeed, is the conclusion into which anyone who falls will perish eternally, with God closing it and not opening it. He will perish justly. For justice cannot do anything unjustly, as this man declares, giving the Apostle’s example: “Who was made for us by God our righteousness” (Gal. 3:13).

Because of this sorrow of his, some of our people, deceived, think that he wishes to resign the episcopate, since he himself says as much and does not deny that he both wishes and does not wish to do so.

He would wish to, that is, if it were permitted; he does not wish to, because it is not permitted.

## 7.

He says that we invent so many things about him falsely, and that these alone make him abominable to everyone; and, although he is extremely spirited, they torment him most bitterly.

Yet he cares so little, for the most part, if anyone speaks ill of him [Col. 0530B], that quite recently he gave twelve coins to someone who reviled him all day, as a reward.

He says that he is so preoccupied by fear of hell that he has no need to fear anything further.

He also admits that he once uttered a single idle word—and, as he forces us to believe, a most shameful one—in such a place that, when he recalls it and hears himself called to account for it on the day of judgment, he regards all the shame of this world as nothing in comparison with it.

[Note: [Col. 0530D] See the work *On Idle Speech*, no. 5, from which the whole meaning of this passage may be understood.]

He insists that it is utterly impossible for anyone who must give an account on the day of judgment for such a word, uttered in such a place and on such an occasion, to hear the words “Come, blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom” (Matt. 25:34) spoken to him together with the assembly of the blessed.

For blessedness is wholly free from misery, whereas shame arising from such things belongs to the greatest misery. How, then, could anyone who had given an account of such speech before the sight of every rational creature—both angelic and human—ever be blessed?

## 8.

What more need be said? Anyone who wishes to know him should make a point of reading his entire book of the *Confession*. For if he is as he represents himself there, no one in the world is worse than he; but if he lies in claiming to be such a man, he is proved to be the greatest liar.

Moreover, there is no book, no speech, no history of his, and finally nothing that he has ever dictated for posterity to read, which, if properly understood, does not accuse him of wickedness.

He says that he sings the psalms not because he knows that they are heard, since he is always thinking about something else, but because, feeling that he sings them most unwillingly, he thinks that the very force which, by reciting them against his will, he imposes upon himself has some value against what he willingly does against God—whether to compel at least his lips themselves to serve God, even though his mind wanders and his other limbs rebel against God, since in none of them is he more inclined to provoke God than in the excesses of his tongue.

[Note: [Col. 0531B–C] Construe: He says that he sings the psalms not because he knows them to be heard, since he is always thinking about something else, but because, when he feels that he sings them most unwillingly, he thinks that the force he imposes upon himself by reciting them against his will contributes somehow to what he himself willingly does against God—namely, to force at least his lips to serve God, although his heart wanders and his other members rebel against God. For in none of these is he more prone to provoke God than in the excesses of his tongue.]

He says the same about fasting and everything else that he appears to do well. For among all evils he is so lazy that, unless he is always working, he falls asleep through torpor; yet even while sleeping he cannot remain still, although he does this more willingly either on a bench or on the ground.

He says that, by fasting until the ninth hour and then afterward being sated, he does penance for the sins of others; whereas in truth he does penance for his own sins, though most inadequately.

### 9.

Toward some people he is so benevolent at one time and so malevolent at another that everyone is astonished. Yet he dares to tell those who wonder why he does this. For he says that there is no one on earth who, in a matter concerning him [Col. 0532A], draws upon himself any authority to which he would not dare, or even wish, to resist.

Moreover, when he has a friend, he says that he will indeed do what an unavoidable authority commands; nevertheless, throughout all the days during which the person to whom he gave something in this manner retains it, he will always bear resentment against him.

[Col. 0531C note: That is, there was no one who, in a matter concerning him, drew upon himself some authority to which he would not dare, or even wish, to resist. Moreover, although he had a friend, he said that he would do what an unavoidable authority—that is, a secular authority—commanded; nevertheless, he would always bear resentment against anyone to whom he had given something, throughout all the days during which he retained what had been given to him in that manner. The examples that follow make the meaning of this passage sufficiently clear. There were evidently people who used secular authorities either to extort from Ratherius some of the Church’s property belonging to him, or to secure by some charter the estates he had granted, so that they could not be reclaimed for any reason. He maintains that, in matters of this kind concerning him, there was no authority to which he would not dare or wish to resist. But if, to oblige those who were his friends, he granted something which an unavoidable authority had ordered to be granted, or to be regarded as ratified and secure, then—even if he did not resist—he remained inwardly alienated from them for as long as they retained what had been granted or confirmed in this manner.]

This he said at the beginning to the illustrious duchess; he demonstrated it in the case of Sikerus and Lanzo.

[Col. 0531D note: It was mistakenly read *Deo, cui* (“to God, to whom”).]

[Col. 0531D note: The illustrious duke—or duchess—is Judith, daughter of Arnold, duke of Bavaria, wife of Henry I, likewise duke of the Bavarians, and mother of Henry II. After her son had obtained the aforementioned duchy and the march of Verona following his father’s death, she exercised supreme authority in that march while he was still young. Consequently, she was the person who above all others insisted that Ratherius be released from the prison into which Milo had cast him and restored to his see. See the *Itinerary*, no. 4. That she was in Verona is established especially by this passage and by other passages of this work to be mentioned later. No one should suppose, however, that under the name Judith one should understand Gisla, wife of Henry II. Since Henry II, born in 951, was still very young at this time, that is, in 966, we do not believe that he had married Gisla; thus Judith his mother, rather than Gisla, is indicated here.]

First, after the countless wrongs that the same Sikerus had inflicted upon him on three occasions, he became his very close friend and allowed him to retain such a castle for four years. Apart from another service, he could obtain from it six pounds of Venetian denarii every year. Moreover, he had stipulated that all the land belonging to the Church of Verona across the lake should be divided between Sikerus and his son-in-law—not for any other reason than that, on the day when Milo had thought he would prevail over him and obtain the bishopric, Sikerus, mentioned twice above, sent him in a brief memorandum everything that he himself had bestowed upon him as a friend, asserting that he had not given these things in payment of any composition, but for the acquisition of land.

[Col. 0532B note: Since the land that Sikerus had obtained from Ratherius lay across the lake, that is, across Lake Benacus, this castle too was probably situated in that part of the diocese of Verona. It was therefore one of the two castles of Lonate or Desenzano, which are listed among the older possessions of the bishopric of Verona in the privilege of Eugene III dated 1145, in Biancolini, vol. I of *The Churches of Verona*, p. 193. In a charter of 1154 to Theobald, bishop of Verona, Frederick I, in Ughelli, vol. V, col. 795, mentions a place called Disincianum with all its adjacent and appurtenant lands, including the castle. The four years during which Ratherius allowed Sikerus to retain this castle should be reckoned from the end of 961, when he was restored by Otto to the bishopric of Verona. Thus, after the four years during which he allowed Sikerus to retain the castle, one arrives at the year 965, when Milo hoped to prevail over him in the matter of the bishopric, as we explained more fully in the *Life*. It should also be noted that the word *servitium* (“service”) signifies any service owed by the inhabitants of the castle. The mention of Venetian denarii should likewise be noted, since it demonstrates both the use and the antiquity of this currency.]

[Col. 0532D note: Sikerus certainly possessed this land, as is clear from what follows. The words “he had stipulated,” and so forth, imply that Ratherius wished the land he had given him not to belong entirely to him, but to be divided between him and his son-in-law.]

[Col. 0532D note: Milo was the grandson of Milo, count of Verona, as Ratherius calls him in Epistle 5 to John XII, no. 7. After he had occupied the see of Verona following Ratherius’s second expulsion, when Ratherius returned to his Church for the third time, he first carried him off as a prisoner after stirring up a conspiracy; then, near the end of 965, after Ratherius had already been restored to liberty, he pressed him more forcefully to yield the bishopric to him. On the day when Milo most hoped by this second means to prevail and obtain the bishopric, Sikerus sent Ratherius, in the little memorandum—that is, in the schedule—all that he had bestowed on Ratherius, asserting that he had given it not as part of any composition, that is, as a payment of a fine or redemption of a penalty, but in order to acquire land. From this he argued that the land was his as though purchased, and that he could never be compelled to restore it to the Church. Perhaps by this device he wished to obtain some assurance from Ratherius that he would suffer no trouble concerning that land from Milo, whom he believed would soon become bishop.]

384

When the bishop, being—as he certainly is—*scardus* (“sparing,” or “stingy”), had replied that he would give him nothing more except from the archbishopric of Milan—for he possessed nothing from its property, and by this formula indicated that he would give nothing, since from the bishopric of Verona, which he held, he would not give even half a *mansus*, nor did he allow him to retain one—the castle that he himself had given would be sufficient for him.

[Col. 0533C note: *Scardus*, that is, “sparing,” one who gives sparingly; hence the Italian *scardo* and the French *eschars*. The following should be understood as follows. When the bishop, being—as he certainly is—sparing, had sent him a reply, that is, had answered him, that he would give him nothing more except from the archbishopric of Milan, since he possessed nothing from its property and therefore indicated by this formula that he would give nothing, because he affirmed that from the bishopric of Verona, which he held, he would not give even half a *mansus*—and neither did he allow him to retain one, that is, he neither permitted nor wished him to hold the *mansus*, or land, which he had granted him—the castle that he himself had given would be sufficient for him. He left him only this, and when Sikerus replied that he wished to retain the *mansus*, or land, by his own choice, in place of what he had bestowed upon Ratherius, as though it were the property of a felon, he refused to attribute the castle to Ratherius’s gift, because, as far as the castle was concerned, he would hold it by a gift from the emperor and empress—although in this he was lying, since he had truly received it from Ratherius. Angered by this last point, Ratherius took the land away from him. The word *gratus* should be understood as “by his choice,” as is clear from no. 13, where we read: “My parishioners, and even my bitterest enemies, hold that land without my *gratus*,” that is, without my consent.]

And when Sikerus had replied that he wished to retain that *mansus*, or land, by his own choice, in place of what he had bestowed upon Ratherius, as though it were the property of a felon—for property of felons, that is, rebels, is held as purchased by the treasury—and that he would retain the castle by a gift from the emperor and empress, although he was lying about this, that holy bishop, that preacher, that abstainer, but in truth that hypocrite, burst into such anger that he immediately took the land away from him.

[Col. 0533D note: This is how the edition of Acherius reads it. The latest editor of the *Spicilegium* thought that *tenere* should be corrected to *teneret*, but this is less correct: for it cannot be said that Ratherius “held even half a *mansus* of the bishopric of Verona.” We have explained the suitable sense of this passage in the preceding note.]

But Lanzo, when Arnostus and Bucco had managed, only with the greatest difficulty and by promises that they would acquire for him an exceptionally favorable position with the emperor, to persuade such a fierce adversary as Ratherius to bestow a very great military benefice upon his son, thereafter retained the entire great benefice for himself. Although he was a good soldier and very dear to the bishop, he allowed the son to retain nothing from it; instead, he compelled him, utterly poor and most disgracefully, to serve his lord—that is, the same bishop, whose soldier or vassal he was. For this tiny offense, that frenzied devil hated him so much that he could not even look at him with a straightforward gaze.

385

[Col. 0534B note: Lanzo, who gave the Veronese canons the estate called Quinto, situated in the county of Monselice, is mentioned in Otto II’s charter of 983, in Ughelli, vol. V, col. 746. Lampaldus, who is called Lanzo, is recorded with the title of viscount in the pseudo-charter of Patriarch Rodoaldus dated 968, which will be published in the appendix. In an authentic document of 969, among the oldest documents of the Chapter of Verona published by the canon Marquis Giovanni Jacopo Dionisi, no. 26, this same Lampaldus, who is called Lanzio, although he lacks the title of viscount, is nevertheless recognized as holding some rank, since he is said to have been sent from the public authority. Whether Lanzo was the same person as Ratherius’s Lanzo or a different one, we do not know. Bucco was at this time count of Verona, and will be mentioned again below. Arnostus, who is named before him, seems to have been of greater rank and authority. The passage should apparently be construed as follows: “But Lanzo, after Arnostus and Bucco had, with the greatest difficulty and promises, barely obtained from so fierce an adversary—Ratherius—that he grant his son a very great military benefice which they would acquire for him from the emperor, afterward retained the entire great benefice for himself. Although he was a good soldier and very dear to the bishop, he allowed the son to retain nothing from it, but compelled him, utterly poor and most disgracefully, to serve his lord, that is, the same bishop, whose soldier or vassal he was. For this tiny offense,” and so forth.]

When he had done the same to Grimaldus and Conrad, who wished to retain his land against him, and since he is hostile to everyone who tries, through someone else’s authority and without legal right, to retain anything belonging to his jurisdiction, it is astonishing that such a devil is even allowed to live. Who, then, could love such an adversary? Yet if he happens to please anyone, he pleases him more by his buffoonery than by any goodness of his; and by that very buffoonery he is proved agreeable even to his enemies.

### 10.

He does not greatly love gifts that demand a return. If a poor man brings him anything, he calls him a fool, since he ought either not to have kept it for himself or to have brought it to someone better. He prefers to be sufficiently provided for rather than rich; to be in need rather than be compelled to give something more abundantly [perhaps: “to affluent persons,” *abundantibus*]; to squander everything in this world rather than, after his death, have some wealthy person happen to rejoice in his possessions.

He never ceases urging everyone to remember the cuirass of Galivertus the physician, and the fraud and treachery of the testamentary executors, by which that cuirass perhaps came into the possession of others against Galivertus’s wishes.

[Col. 0534D note: *Rogatarii* are the same as *erogatarii*, that is, executors of wills. In the will of Engelbertus, executed at Erbeto in the diocese of Verona in 846, published by the aforementioned canon Dionisi, no. 4, they are called *rogatores*. Construe: “He never ceases urging everyone to remember the cuirass of Galivertus the physician, and the fraud and treachery of the *rogatarii*, by which that cuirass perhaps came to others contrary to Galivertus’s wishes.”]

He also urges them to remember the wealth of bishops, rightly converted into the property of kings. Let kings hear this, and consider what sort of thanks they return to such a man.

He says that he wishes to die so completely a beggar that his corpse may be covered by another person’s alms; for he calls his body vile on this account.

[Col. 0534D note: The Vulgate reads *prae utilitate* (“because of its usefulness”), but the correction *prae vilitate* (“because of its vileness”) was rightly made in the errata.]

Now greedy to acquire, and then lavish; continually enervated, and feebly self-restrained, he shows that he would suffer no voluntary good [perhaps: “rather,” *potius*] than embrace the Lord’s words that restrain people from sins.

By pursuing earthly glory he flees it in a wondrous manner, and by fleeing it he is sought after [perhaps: “he seeks,” *captat*]. Himself pompous, he never ceases attacking the empty pomp of this age; most wicked, he condemns wickedness.

He does not deny that by his own ingenuity many people could be deceived, if he did not know that they would exact from him an oath—which he greatly fears—or if he did not fear that the devil would say to him at the end: “You have acted deceitfully with a sharp razor” (Psalm 51:4).

[Col. 0535C note: Construe: “If he did not know that they would exact from him an oath, which he greatly fears, or if he did not fear that the devil would say to him at the end, ‘You have acted deceitfully with a sharp razor.’”]

386

### 11.

Although he is wicked toward everyone, he is worst toward the Jews—not because he scourges them, since he does not dare; not because he plunders their possessions, but because he never ceases reviling them.

He reproves all who exalt them above Christians, and those who permit them to blaspheme the Lord Jesus Christ and his holy Mother.

[Col. 0535D note: Agobard, bishop of Lyons, who flourished in the preceding ninth century, reproves Christians for similar behavior toward the Jews in his book *On the Insolence of the Jews*, and censures those who regarded them as better than Christians.]

He gives the example of kings, asking whether they wish to regard as faithful a man who patiently tolerates hearing someone say something evil or dishonorable about them. He reproves anyone who at least greets them or responds to their greetings, let alone gives them a kiss or eats with them.

[Col. 0535D note: Agobard, in his book *On Jewish Superstitions*, no. 2, likewise reports from the *Life of Saint Hilary* that Hilary so abhorred such enemies of the Church that he shared with them neither a meal nor even a greeting when he passed them; in the following sections he further establishes that no food should be taken with them.]

He cites the authority of the Apostle, who says: “If anyone does not love the Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 16:22), and that one should not even eat with such a person (1 Corinthians 5:11). He also says: “The one who says, ‘Hail,’ shares in his evil works” (2 John 1:11).

He reproves all who do business with them more willingly than with Christians. He bears witness from the curses pronounced against them in the Pentateuch, where their commerce is also said to be cursed.

He does not, however, object when they are defended by Christian kings and princes. In their person he says that Jeremiah [the source text reads “Isaiah”] told Christ: “Under your shadow we shall live among the nations” (Lamentations 4:20).

[Col. 0535D note: Read “Jeremiah.” Since Ratherius usually quoted his authorities from memory, he wrote “Isaiah” here by a lapse of memory.]

And the Psalmist: “He gave them into the mercies of all those who had taken them captive” (Psalm 105:46).

He reproves only the fact that they are allowed to revile the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, to assert that he is not God, and to say that his holy Mother was not a virgin before childbirth, a virgin in childbirth, and a virgin after childbirth, nor did she give birth to God.

“For who,” he says, “could patiently endure this, unless he were the devil himself?” For no one can endure hearing someone speak evil of his lord, except one who is proved to be the greatest felon.

The son of the devil says that the Lord Jesus Christ—who created me, redeemed me, sustains me, feeds me, protects me, and finally promises me eternal life—is not the Son of God. And shall I not be angry with him?

That most wicked felon says that his Mother did not bear from the Holy Spirit the Son to whom I never cease crying, “Lord, my helper and my redeemer” (Psalm 18:15). Shall I not be indignant—or rather, shall I not go mad?”

[Col. 0536C note: Construe: “The most wicked felon says that his [Jesus’s] Mother did not bear from the Holy Spirit the Son to whom I never cease crying, ‘Lord, my helper and my redeemer.’ Shall I not be indignant—or rather, shall I not go mad?”]

He says that the soul of Saint Peter is there where the soul of his father is; and shall I, who am the servant of Saint Peter, be his friend?

He says that I worship idols; and shall I disdain to offer him a kiss, even if I do not dare to strike him?

He who does not become angry at such a man is worse than the Jew and like the devil himself. He denies God who loves the Jew who denies God. He is not a Christian to whom the Jew who blasphemes Christ is pleasing. He is not a friend of God to whom God’s enemy is pleasing. He is not faithful to the king to whom the king’s infidel is not displeasing.

If kings judge in this way about themselves and their infidels, why do they not judge the same way concerning Christ and the enemies of Christ? Since he is the King of kings, and since he gave them the kingdom which they ought to possess and govern under him, why do they permit a race hostile to God to bark at him within the kingdom entrusted to them?

It would have been enough if they allowed them to live somehow; they should not permit them to blaspheme the Lord Jesus Christ so publicly. “For under your shadow we shall live,” the prophet says concerning them (Lamentations 4:20). “We shall live,” he says, “not delight in ourselves”; and “he gave them into mercies” (Psalm 105:46), not into exaltation, not into friendship, and not into any honor.

What sort of thing is it, then, that when a cleric contends for Christ and a Jew blasphemes Christ, and a fight breaks out, if the cleric strikes the Jew, the Jew strikes the cleric—or rather Christ in the cleric, for thus it was said to Saul (Acts 9:4)—our Erimbertus, a twister of words and distorter of laws, says that a triple composition, that is, a fine, should be paid to the king for striking a Jew, while no composition should be paid to anyone for striking a cleric?

[Col. 0536D note: The text formerly read *in coelo* (“in heaven”). The latest editor of the *Spicilegium* thought it should be corrected to *in clero* (“in the clergy”). *In clerico* (“in the cleric”) seems better. The passage should be construed as follows: “If the cleric strikes the Jew, and the Jew the cleric—or rather Christ in the cleric, for thus it was said to Saul—our Erimbertus, a twister of words and distorter of laws, says that a triple composition, that is, a fine, goes to the king for striking a Jew, but that no composition for striking a cleric goes to anyone.” This Erimbertus was a judge at Verona and subscribed the will of Milo, marquis, in 955, in vol. V of *Italia sacra*, col. 740: “I, Erimbertus, judge, having been requested, have subscribed with my own hand.” The same man, although his name is suppressed, is also attacked by Ratherius in the treatise *On a Certain Unlawful Marriage*, no. 3, where Ratherius records that in another work of ours—that is, in this one—he called him a twister of words and distorter of laws.]

O Saint Josaphat, a king otherwise excellent, if only you had been here! You would have said what the Lord once commanded you through his prophet: “You give help to the impious, and you join in friendship with those who hate the Lord” (2 Chronicles 19:2).

[Col. 0536D note: The same passage may be read in the aforementioned work of Agobard, *On Jewish Superstitions*, no. 22.]

What is this? For in these very words kings customarily speak of themselves and of those who are friends with their infidels. What, I ask, do they then think about Christ, about themselves, and about the Jews who are enemies of Christ the King?

Since they know with complete truth that the Jews always speak evil of the Lord, and yet do not even prevent them, what do they think of what the Apostle says? “Not only those who do these things, but also those who approve those who do them, are worthy of death” (Romans 1:32), we read that he said.

And this judgment concerning the Jews seems to him sound, just, and pleasing to God, although it is in fact empty chatter.

[Col. 0537C note: Construe: “This judgment concerning the Jews seems to him sound, just, and pleasing to God, although it is in fact empty chatter.”]

### 12.

388

To return once more to the faults of Ratherius himself, he says specifically that in this world he loves no one except the emperor and himself, while in general he hates no one. We cannot understand what this means.

He shows no concern for his relatives, either because he thinks that none of them is so needy that he should know only himself and his brother to be poor among them; or because he knows that canon law forbids him to give them anything; or because, being old, he thinks that he has no relatives, since those who exist are already, for him, in the sixth generation, and the line of brothers has been succeeded by a series of great-grandchildren. This is what he says—being, as he certainly is, a chatterbox—in a chattering and most mendacious fashion.

He does not return the greeting of one who greets him; rather, he becomes angry with him, saying that if he had encountered his enemy, he would have greeted him in the same way.

Though you often hear him wailing—or rather howling—you rarely see him weep. You can perceive that he is troubled alike by hardness of heart and by fear.

“A spirit broken with sorrow is a sacrifice to God” (Psalm 50:19); but when he often sings this, we suppose that he thinks sadness of heart accomplishes the same thing as weeping.

[Col. 0537C note: Construe: “But when he often sings, ‘A spirit broken with sorrow is a sacrifice to God,’ he thinks, we suppose, that sadness of heart produces the same effect as weeping.”]

When he recalls that Augustine also said that one should never pray without groaning, he believes, we think, that groaning is one thing and weeping another, and that groaning can occur without tears, whereas weeping cannot. For where it says, “And Peter went out and wept bitterly” (Matthew 26:75), he says: “Happy indeed were your tears, Peter.”

[Col. 0538A] **13.** If someone says to him, “Go to the emperor and ask that what was taken from the Church during your tenure be restored to you,” he replies: “What further need have I of it, when I am going to die within this three-year period? Shall I now, as an old man at the point of death, begin to raise an army for the preparations of war, carry out plundering expeditions, perform sentry duty for kings, heap up wealth for them to possess after I have been thrust into hell, acquire soldiers for the man who will come after me [that is, my successor], and prepare for him, as though for a son, what will succeed to him?

[Note: At this point I am pleased to inform the reader how many errors we have purged from the text. Although each was slight, all of them together prevented Ratherius from being understood. In the earlier edition it read: “*Stultissimus se* [lacuna] *non sinerem divites* [lacuna] *quod rogo conferret* [lacuna] *in infernum audire*” (“Most foolish … I would not allow the rich … what, I ask, would it contribute … to hear in hell”). There were also errors of punctuation, the common failing of the earlier edition. Thus the most recent editor of the *Spicilegium*.]

I would be the most foolish of men if I did such things. For one who lives within the bounds of sufficiency, what is lacking to me except integrity? I do not seek better clothing; my daily food, suited to my needs [or, perhaps, to my lowliness], does not fail me. Even if I had more, the rich would not allow themselves to give it to me for the sake of my soul [Note: “For the sake of my soul,” that is, for the sake of the remedy or redemption of the soul: this was a customary formula in donations of things granted to churches.]; they would rather force me to consume it in vanity.

Yet I do not deny that I eagerly wished to be exceedingly wealthy, if I had perceived that the time for enjoying it had arrived for me, or if I had been granted, as I wished, something that I could spend.

[Note: Since this little work was written at Verona in the year 966, nearly forty years must be reckoned—not from the beginning of Ratherius’s Veronese episcopate, which he entered upon in 932, but either from the time when he came into Italy around 926 in the company of Hilduin, or from the time when Hilduin obtained the bishopric of Verona in 928. For it was then promised to Ratherius that, when Hilduin had been transferred to another church, he himself would be placed over the Veronese Church. See Letter 5 to John XII, §3, and Fulcuin, chapter 19. Compare what we have observed more fully on this matter in the *Life of the Author*, §3, no. 13.]

It is now nearly forty years since I began to seek power; I have never been able to attain it, or, if I attained it, it could not remain with me for long. If it were granted to me now, when I am about to die, what, I ask, would it contribute, since I would not be allowed to enjoy it even for a year?

If it should especially happen that, merely because of this, I were to hear in hell: “Son, remember that you received good things during your lifetime” (Luke 16:25), and were to lose the rewards which, according to Gregory, no one can reach without great labor (*Homily 57 on the Gospels*)—since in this country one cannot obtain even the extravagant expenditure they require without very great sin, much less find the vast wealth consequently required [Note: That is, the extravagant expenditure alone that they require.]—would I not be utterly insane, he says, if I acquired wealth for others at the cost of my soul’s destruction?

[Note: Construe: “Especially if it should happen that I heard in hell merely because of this: ‘Son, remember …,’ or, with the Vulgate text, ‘because you received good things in your lifetime’; and that I lost the rewards to which, etc.”]

When I consider that the messenger of death, long since sent and summoning me to render an account of the long exercise of power wickedly administered, is at hand, shall I, a madman, not fear to increase the grounds on which I must render an account? [Note: The latest editor of the *Spicilegium* judged this passage certainly corrupt, not understanding what the word *missum* indicates. We believe that it can be understood as the *missus*, or messenger, of death, whom Ratherius, because of his decrepit age, had long felt to be summoning him to render his account to God and now near at hand. Construe: “When indeed,” he says, “I consider—for ‘I consider’—the messenger, long since sent and summoning me to render an account of the wickedly administered long exercise of power, shall I, a madman, not fear to increase for myself the grounds on which I must render an account?”] “You can no longer manage the estate” (Luke 16:2): I understand the very age itself to be crying this out. And should I myself desire that the administration of several estates be entrusted to me?

[Note: He means that his very age is crying out, “You can no longer manage the estate”: since he was decrepit, and, as he said above, if power were now granted to him at the point of death, what, he asked, would it contribute, when he would not be allowed to enjoy it even for a year.]

[Col. 0539A] I admit that this would be enough for me, while at the same time being most odious to all the rich, if only those things were restored to me which have unjustly been transferred from the right of the Church into the right of kings, so that I could no longer recover them unless they were now returned to the Church.

[Note: Construe: “At the same time, being exceedingly odious to all the rich, he admits that this would be enough for him, if only those things were restored to him which, etc.” The words “most odious to all the rich” can be explained from what is said in §9: “On every day during which he retains what he has thus given to the one to whom he gave it, he will always bear enmity toward him.” There he is speaking of those who had obtained something from the Church’s possessions through secular power. See note 856. The words “all the rich” therefore seem to refer to those who possessed Church property, which nearly all the rich enjoyed.]

I would also ask, he says, that what his predecessors [that is, the emperor’s predecessors] granted or confirmed to our church by their decrees, he might deign to defend for us against counts, viscounts, and *scoldasci*.

[Note: He in fact obtained from the emperor in the following year, 967, on 5 November, what he here says he would request, as will be clear from the diploma, corrected from the autograph, which we shall publish after the author’s *Itinerary*.]

[Note: Acherius conjectures that we ought to read *soldarios*. But the form *scoldascios*, or *sculdascios*, should especially be retained, as is confirmed by the cited diploma of Otto, issued in Ratherius’s favor. There a count, viscount, and *sculdasius* are twice mentioned in the sense required by this passage. On the word *sculdascius*, compare note 31 on Book I of the *Praeloquia*.]

If anything has been done, whether by those two usurpers [Note: That is, Manasses and Milo. In the privilege of Otto mentioned earlier, everything done to the prejudice of the Church of Verona from the time Ratherius was ordained bishop is rescinded—namely, everything done both under Ratherius and under those two usurpers.], or by me through necessity, or through the surreptitious acquisition of some fraud, or by way of exchange [Note: These three kinds of contracts harmful to churches are likewise distinguished by Otto in the cited privilege: *libellary* contracts, exchanges, and *precariae*. *Libellary* contracts were so called from the written petitions (*libelli*) formerly presented in order to obtain an immovable property under the title of emphyteusis. They are the same as emphyteutic contracts, by which some payment had to be made to the churches. See examples of such *libelli* in Muratori, vol. III of the *Antiquities of Italy*, p. 144. These *libellary* contracts worked to the prejudice of churches when they were made without any benefit or necessity for the churches, as when a payment disproportionately small in relation to the emphyteutic estate was imposed. Exchanges were made to the Church’s detriment when, in return for obtaining some larger estate from the Church, a smaller one was offered. When someone requested an estate and at the same time offered another to the bishops, but in such a way that both were granted under precarious tenure, this was more properly called a *precaria*. The prejudice to the Church in such an arrangement is obvious. Documents concerning this last type of contract may be found in Muratori at the place cited, pp. 175 and following.], or under the name of a *libellary* contract, or what they call a *precaria*, contrary to God and righteousness, he should order all of it (*omnem*; read *id omne*) to be rescinded by his authority.

Nor would I ask that these things be restored to me; rather, they should be granted in usufruct to whomever he wished, provided only that they were not alienated from the Church. I would demand nothing else for myself except that the authority of the most pious Caesar deign merely to answer my littleness: who ought to restore our destroyed diocesan churches [Note: The churches of the diocese in particular had been ruined by the frequent vicissitudes of war in the tenth century, especially by the incursions of the Hungarians, and required restoration. Since, according to the sacred canons, all ecclesiastical revenues were under the bishop’s administration, and it was his responsibility to provide for the clergy and the church buildings, while through the abuse mentioned in the preceding notes many Church possessions had been dispersed, the question arises who ought to restore or rebuild these churches, and from what resources. At this time the responsibility for repairing churches and the revenues assigned to their maintenance had not yet, as happened later, been transferred to anyone other than the bishop. See Ratherius’s *Synodica*, no. 14.] and from what source; what I ought to possess from which I might feed the flock entrusted to me by God and by him; who ought to administer what has been granted to holy Mary, the Mother of God, and where or how that person ought to distribute it [Note: Construe: “Which person ought to administer what has been granted to holy Mary, the Mother of God—that is, to the cathedral church of Verona, dedicated in honor of Mary, the Mother of God—and where or how he ought to distribute it.” Ratherius was deeply concerned with the proper distribution of the revenues of the cathedral church, about which he dealt at length in *On Contempt for the Canons*, Part I, and later discussed more fully in the *Judgment*, the *Discord*, and the *Apologetic*.].

As for me, I know that I ought to despise earthly things and love heavenly things. Would I not have enough for my living [Note: “For my living,” that is, for my food. Hence the expression *per il mio vivere* in the dialect of our region. A little later, “without my consent” means without my agreement and will; for here he is speaking of Church lands that had been occupied without his consent. From this passage it may further be inferred that most of the possessions of the Veronese Church which he said shortly before had been alienated under the names of exchanges, *libelli*, or *precariae* had passed not into the hands of the Veronese, whom he calls his parishioners, but into those of other powerful men. For he suggests that the lands which had come to his parishioners without his consent were so meager that, if he held them, he would have enough for his living.] if I held at least that land which my parishioners, and even my bitterest enemies, hold without my consent?”
