Yet he admits that he would not have said all these things unless the fidelity which he had solemnly sworn to him compelled him to care greatly about the emperor’s disposition. The madman never ceases to say that he has no hope of prospering during the emperor’s lifetime.

But if, through his own sin, it should happen to him to hear that the emperor had died—which God forbid—he does not despair that he himself would immediately have to be killed, nor does he nevertheless care [Note: We have retained Acherius’s correction *neque tam* (“nor nevertheless”), rather than the new editor’s emendation.]. For he has no friend useful to him in this world except the emperor himself, although the emperor himself does not cease to assist his enemies against him and to bestow upon them what has been taken from him.

Such, then, is the man—such a man, since he admits that he loves no one and is loved by no one. “What,” they ask, “does he want from the world?” “Nothing,” I reply; “nothing.”

**14.** For what if such people knew my inmost thoughts and understood why I am of this disposition? Yet I will not leave those same men suspected of having ascended this mountain and of having remained on it for a long time.

[Note: The Vulgate reads, erroneously, *linguam* (“tongue”). The new editor of the *Spicilegium* observed that the name of some field or mountain in the Veronese territory might lie hidden in the words *montis ne linguam*, but he more correctly noted among the errata that *linquam* (“I shall leave”) should replace *linguam*. The mountain is hinted at in an ancient plan of the city of Verona, recently published from a manuscript containing Ratherius’s work by Giovanni Battista Biancolini in a book entitled *The Bishops and Governors of Verona*. In it the following verse is found:

“From the summit of the mountain the fortress looks out over the city.”

The fortress was the name for the entire area beyond the Adige enclosed by walls, where the church of Saint Peter still stands. Hence, in a Ratherian document of the year 947, published in the *Collection of Diplomas* by Canon Marquis Dionisi, p. 111, it is said to be situated in the Veronese fortress. Ratherius had withdrawn here to a safer place after abandoning the episcopal buildings, in which he had been captured, as will become clear from what follows. Shortly before this, Louis III, son of Boso, likewise withdrew into the same church of Saint Peter as a place of safety; but Berengar I, having corrupted the guards, entered it at night, captured and blinded him, as Liutprand records in Book II of his *History*, chapter 11.

Construe the passage as follows: “But lest I leave those same men suspected of having climbed this mountain and of having remained there for a long time—for I have learned from an evidently true report that they are now being tormented even more because of it—let them be present, I ask, and I say,” etc. Ratherius was therefore staying on the mountain mentioned when he wrote this, and had already been living there for some time, having gone up there shortly after Easter of the preceding year, 965.]

From that place I have learned through an evidently truthful report that they are now suffering even more. Let them be present, I ask, and I say:

When this illustrious duchess [Note: “Duchess” means Judith, mother of Henry II, duke of the Bavarians and margrave of Verona. See above, note 858.] learned such conduct on my part, and consequently that I had many enemies and had been deprived of the protection of friends, being a foreigner among all of them [Note: Similarly, Emperor Otto I says of Ratherius in his diploma of 967: “Because he is needy and a stranger, and lacks every assistance save that of God and ourselves, he has already suffered many hardships,” etc.], she feared that something worse might happen to me than what had already occurred and entrusted me to the protection of a not-unknown count [Note: This count was called Bucco. Under him the conspiracy occurred about which Ratherius says in Letter 12 to Ambrose, §3: “In the presence of Bucco they made a conspiracy against him and me”—the same conspiracy that he indicates below. Whether this was the same Bucco who, while following the emperor’s retinue, is listed among the dead in the disastrous battle in Calabria under Otto II in 983 is unknown. See the *Royal Chronicle of Saint Pantaleon* in Eckhard, vol. I of the *Writers of the Middle Ages*, p. 896.].

What more? I accuse no one; I excuse no one; I blame no one, nor do I praise anyone either. I was captured [Note: The author of this deed, whom he does not name here, was Milo, Ratherius’s antagonist, as he relates shortly after the beginning of Letter 8 to the same man: “Indeed, you seized me, carried me off, despoiled me, and exiled me.” Compare also *Itinerary*, no. 4.], led away, and brought back. The count, who has just been mentioned, said that this had happened to me through my own lack of foresight: for he had ordered me to climb the fortified place [the text has *illum* (“him”); read *illud* (“it”)] called the Palace [Note: “Fortification” here means a fortified location to which the count had ordered Ratherius to withdraw for safety. It was called the Palace. This Palace, situated beyond the Adige, is shown on the aforementioned plan of the city of Verona. Although the plan does not clearly place the Palace on the mountain of Verona near the church of Saint Peter, its ancient draftsman was insufficiently skilled in representing distance and elevation by drawing. Thus he depicted the amphitheater, which is called the theater there, outside its actual location because he intended to show its form rather than its position; the same happened with the Palace. That it was built on the mountain is clear from the words “I climbed,” “I ascended the Palace,” and “I descended,” all of which suit a mountain. Hence he had shortly before written of climbing this mountain. The Palace is said to have been enormous. John, a mansionary of the Church of Verona who composed an imperial history at the beginning of the fourteenth century, now preserved among the cathedral chapter’s manuscripts, also calls it a huge palace and says of its location: “The remains of this palace are still visible beside the church of Saint Syrus, in the place called Castellus.” The church of Saint Syrus is located on the mountain mentioned. The contemporary name *castellus* corresponds especially well with the word *praesidium* used by Ratherius.], but that I had refused.

He warned me not to entrust myself any longer to the house [Note: The episcopal residence is meant. Before Ratherius was captured, Count Bucco had ordered him to go from the episcopal residence, which was less safe, to the Palace. Since he had refused to leave that house, he was captured there and suffered many other things, as is clear from Letter 12 to Ambrose, §4. Once he had been freed from prison, the count warned him not to trust himself again to that same house.] in which I had suffered other things, but to inhabit the High Court, which was more secure [Note: The High Court was a public and fortified building near the church of Saint Fermo, which is still called *Curte alta*. Some remains of the ancient building still survive; most recently, certain underground spaces belonging to it were discovered in the palace of the Counts Miniscalchi, whose plan Count Aloysius had made. Since the High Court was more strongly fortified than the episcopal residence, while not being far from the cathedral church, the count advised Ratherius that, if he did not wish to be far from the cathedral, he should inhabit the High Court rather than the episcopal residence.].

I trusted him, acted accordingly, and made the fortified place still more strongly fortified. He ordered me again to ascend to the Palace if I left that place, saying that it would be safer. I obeyed. It was enormous, and I quickly restored it [Note: *Recuperare* is used in the sense of “to restore.” See examples in Du Cange.].

When this was completed, he again ordered me to allow his wife and children to live there with me, while he remained in the Circus, as he had begun to do, for the city’s guard [Note: The arena, by which name we still call the amphitheater, was called the circus because it was circular, though somewhat more elongated in shape—that is, elliptical. Similarly, our theater, which forms a half-circle, is called the “middle circus” in a document of Berengar I from the year 895, edited by Panvinio. In the manuscripts and editions there had previously been read: “and he began to make the city,” which made no sense. The emendation introduced because of the sense will be approved by everyone. In the aforementioned plan, the amphitheater, where it is called the theater, is shown surrounded by walls. In the Middle Ages buildings of this kind were often converted for use as fortifications, as is clear from the amphitheaters at Capua and Nîmes. See Du Cange under *Arena*. Thus Count Bucco remained in the fortification of the Arena to guard the city, which was being shaken by great disturbances—especially since the disturbances had been raised not only against Ratherius but also against Count Bucco himself, who favored Ratherius, as we learn from Letter 12 to Ambrose, §3, whose testimony was given shortly above in note 899.], which is called the Arena.

It seemed utterly absurd, as everyone knew except any fool among them. Here again I neither accuse nor excuse anyone’s intelligence. Nevertheless, I descended and returned to the house, although it was frightening [Note: Since it seemed utterly absurd for Ratherius to live in the Palace with the count’s wife and children, he descended from the Palace, which, as we have seen, stood on the mountain, and returned to the episcopal residence, though he feared it. He calls it frightening because he had previously been captured there and, while living there, had been exposed to many dangers.].

Not daring to remain there long, I began to set out for Garda [Note: Garda was a very strongly fortified castle in the diocese of Verona, and Ratherius wished to go there so that he might be in a safer place.]. But I changed my plan out of reverence for the approaching Easter. I chose a corner of the city, sought his [that is, the count’s] consent, and he also gave assistance. I built a structure there; it was immediately burned down. No one, however, asked who had done it. I rebuilt it better, but I was forbidden by him to do so. Permission was again given to rebuild it—while he sang praises after reproaches with a more favorable lyre [Note: This passage is explained by Letter 11 to Count Nanno, who had succeeded Bucco. Referring to this matter, the author writes in §3: “For it would have been more tolerable to bear your domination if I feared and loved the same man, as I had begun to do with Bucco; and I made that Nasonean verse suit him:

‘The insults he had earlier spoken against the wife of Therapne,

soon he began to sing praises with a more favorable lyre.’

Bucco had first been hostile to Ratherius, but later began to favor him, after the illustrious duchess had entrusted Ratherius to the count’s protection. Hence he adds: ‘After I had said of him, “May he who freed Israel from the hand of Pharaoh free Ratherius from the hand of Bucco,” when he began to improve as he was about to depart, I too began to sing to him in this manner,’ namely by quoting Ovid’s verses.], singing praises after insults. Such things begin to make others suspect me.

My fear again considered fleeing to Garda. While I was considering this, Lord John the deacon came and began, in my presence, to lament the portico of Saint Peter [Note: That is, the church of Saint Peter on the mountain; hence he adds later, “I ascended.” The restoration of churches belonged to the bishop. Compare note 892. The surviving portico of this church is believed to be the one restored by Ratherius. We have corrected the text with the latest editor of the *Spicilegium* to read “I promised,” not “he promised,” and below “for restoring,” not “for being restored.”], which was plainly threatening to collapse unless help were quickly given it. I promised assistance and did not delay providing it. I ascended, inspected it, and prepared my shoulders to come to its aid.

As my desire to help grew stronger, I saw that many more repairs were necessary—more than I trust could be completed during my lifetime. I have no reliable servant to whom I can entrust this task, since I learned that the man to whom I had entrusted one pound of silver last year for buying beams had cheated me outrageously [Note: *Bausiasse* means “to deceive.” See note 65 on the first part of *On Contempt for the Canons*.].

I do for myself what I can. When I have finished it [Note: That is, when I have completed the restoration of the church of Saint Peter mentioned above, I shall return to the episcopal residence, to which the bitterest caviller was urging me to return. He had still not entered that episcopal residence in 968, when he wrote to Ambrose. The words “enter your furnace” may perhaps be explained by the rustic proverb quoted by the author himself in the *Discord*, no. 1 at the end: “He who has been in the furnace seeks his equals there.”], I shall return home, if you order me to, most bitter enemy, who are so concerned about it. You, if you wish and whenever you wish, may enter your furnace; I do not forbid you.

**15.** There is one reasonable reason among eight for remaining here for a while [Note: This one reason among eight was the restoration of the portico of Saint Peter, which Ratherius, trusting no one else, had to supervise himself. He suppresses the other reasons here. He indicates another in Letter 12 to Ambrose, §4: “What could a bishop do when one prince from among your people was leaving that house, another succeeding him, and another succeeding that one? Could the bishop live in one house with them?” See Sermon 6, *On the Octave of Easter*, §1. The stronger reason, however, was that he might remain in a safer place, as he indicates below.].

As for the purpose of your malice, I know very well that you preferred me to remain in such a place that I would be hateful to my enemies; you are not sorry that I left the house I feared, but that I settled in a safer place, and for this reason you cannot escape being a murderer of me, although God’s providence still preserves my life.

Nor should you think that you do not kill me yourself every day by your schemes, even though you unwillingly see me living, when you hear that God said of another’s sin: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew 5:28). Jerome likewise says: “Woe to us wretched people: as often as we desire, so often do we fornicate.”

So you too could say: “Woe to me, wretched man, who, as often as I lay snares to deceive this captive into dying, so often kill him.” You could accuse me of lying if the beloved disciple of Christ had not been read to say, concerning the lesser offense: “Everyone who hates his brother,” that is, any Christian, “is a murderer” (1 John 3:15).

But I shall be avenged—I shall be avenged; know this with absolute certainty, I say, I shall be avenged. “Vengeance is mine,” says the Lord—I may understand the unspoken continuation as “I reserve it for myself,” while I permit the guilty man (*reum*; read *eum*, “him”) to be scourged. “I myself will repay,” says the Lord (Romans 12:19).

For if the Psalm sings of us: “But if his sons forsake my law and do not walk in my judgments; if they profane my ordinances and do not keep my commandments, I shall visit their iniquities with a rod and their sins with blows. But I shall not remove my mercy from him, nor shall I deal falsely in my faithfulness” (Psalm 88:31–34)—

in this sense, with your permission, I should call those bishops exceedingly fortunate who have been driven from their bishoprics because of their crimes, compared with those of whom a certain truthful speaker says: “They spend their days in prosperity, and in a moment they descend to the underworld” (Job 21:13).

But what the Lord says through another prophet about those who scourge them, with your permission, whom I behold, I shall set forth [Note: Construe: “With your permission, I shall set forth what the Lord says through another prophet about those who scourge them.”]: “I was angry,” says the Lord, rebuking impious Babylon; “I was angry with my people, and I delivered them into your hand. You showed them no mercy, nor did you remember their end” (Isaiah 47:6–7). “Evils will come upon you, from which you will not be able to escape. Calamity will fall upon you, and you will not know its rising” (ibid., 11).

Thus I do not prevent you from saying that I am such as I have described, if you wish; if it pleases you, say that I am anything even worse, if you are able [Note: The Vulgate reads *sibi libet tibi male*. Construe: “I do not prevent you, then, from saying, if you wish, that I am such as I have described; say, if you please, that I am even anything worse—if, at least, you are able.”].

Yet I think I have left you nothing more blameworthy or more disgraceful that you could say about me. I do not fail to recognize, however, what you can now bring against me: “By your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned,” as Scripture says (Matthew 12:37). Your own confession proves you liable to condemnation [Note: Construe: “Your confession itself proves you liable to condemnation, since Scripture says, ‘By your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned.’” A little later: “But he who is reported to have mercifully said to certain people, while writing with his finger on the ground, ‘Let the one among you who is without sin be the first to throw a stone at her’—he, I say, does not cease to promise me that my condemner is far away, because no human being present in this world is without sin. But, alas for the sacrilege! Out of fear of this argument of the *anapaest*—that is, out of suspicion that this argument may be turned back against the opponent—many things are left uncorrected in this world. For those who ought to correct them are sinners, and they fear that Christ’s saying may be turned back against themselves.”].

“I neither confess nor deny it,” I say. But the one who, while writing with his finger on the ground, is said to have mercifully told certain people, “Let the one among you who is without sin be the first to throw a stone at her” (John 8:7), never ceases to promise me that my condemner is far away.

Yet, alas for the sacrilege, because of fear of this *anapaest* many things are left uncorrected in this world, reserved for everlasting fire, while each person, conscious of his own guilt, spares another.

What judgment can be formed even now concerning the substance of such a sacrifice remains, I confess, entirely unknown to me. We can, I confess, lament that we lack health from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head (Isaiah 1:6), and that even today there is no one, not a single person, who does good (Psalm 13:3).

16. Although it is readily understood that by “the one” we should understand God himself, the head of all good things together with some of his members, nevertheless, because so few of our countrymen belong to him, would that we were at least able to recognize here as specially indicated one individual—would that it were the most glorious emperor of the present age! For, among all who have governed the Roman Empire during this period of three hundred years, although the kingdoms have been divided, he alone abounds in an exceptional degree in nobility, power, energy, industry, virtue, prudence, wisdom, kindness, constancy, courage, clemency, equity, wealth, generosity, and every other resource needed for accomplishing this task. Would that almighty divine grace might uniquely grant him this: that he should strive first to turn himself, and then the empire entrusted to him, toward the good that has been altogether neglected.

[Note: Construe the passage as follows: since it is readily understood that “the one” means God himself, the head of all good things together with some of his members, and since so few of our countrymen belong to him, would that we might at least recognize here as specially indicated one individual—namely, the most glorious emperor of the present age! Among all who, although the kingdoms have been divided, have governed the Roman Empire during this period of three hundred years, he alone abounds in nobility, power [lacuna], and every resource needed for accomplishing this task. Would that almighty divine grace might uniquely grant him this: that he should strive first to turn himself, and then the empire entrusted to him, toward the good that has been altogether neglected.]

For, since all Christians, alas, and especially their rulers, have been corrupted by disgraceful and abominable deeds, divine worship has so completely perished in every respect that, I confess, we see nothing more at odds with one another than what the Lord commands and what the whole community, alas for the shame, does.

[Note: The Vulgate has *divinis*, incorrectly; the text should read *divinus*.]

Since, with God’s favor, we eagerly desire to welcome that one man—that is, the most devout emperor—we would, if we dared to advise him, strive by every means to have him add to the other qualities in which he excels that particular good which would make applicable to him the saying of the most holy Job:

[Note: He repeats this testimony here and elsewhere because he feared that, in the emperor’s absence, his opponents might spread slanders and that the emperor might lend them a readier ear and, without sufficiently examining the case, take some action against him. What he feared in fact happened. Thus, in Letter 13 to the empress Adelaide, he says: “How greatly it would benefit all who are placed in authority—and how often I have suggested this to Your Lordship—if they did not reach decisions so precipitately, but attended to that saying of blessed Job: ‘I investigated most diligently the case I did not know.’”]

“I investigated most diligently the case I did not know” (Job 29:16).

For Gregory says:

“What wonder if we are sometimes deceived, since we are human beings? Nothing harms those human beings who are placed over others more than the fraud and treachery of their advisers, especially if that prophetic saying is applied to them at last: ‘Woe to those who call evil good and good evil’” (Isaiah 5:20).

A certain wise man says that informers will never be lacking if someone is willing to believe them:

“Flee the questioner,” he says; “for the other is a chatterer as well.”

Since miserable Italy is filled above all other kingdoms with such people, and since the treachery of interpreters is excessively ready for carrying out these practices, vigilance must be exercised toward them with all the greater care, the more ingenious they are in doing such things and the more ready their malice.

To give one example out of countless cases: when Hubert of Parma was pressing me to yield to that rival of mine, after receiving payment for souls—

[Note: “Rival” means Milo, against whom he resisted rather than surrendering the bishopric. See Letter 8 to Milo and the deliberative conclusion at the end. Shortly afterward he approaches “our leader,” namely Judith, concerning whom see the note above, 858. We have likewise corrected the text below, where *totidem* stood; *itidem* is appropriate in the same sense and occurs shortly afterward.]

—one of my closest friends appeared, though not entirely without payment. Although he had promised me his assistance in this very important matter, he approached our leader and took pains to inform her that the most just emperor likewise wished—or, I do not know whether he added, had ordered—that I should yield.

A miracle, I say—a miracle! Such an emperor, so just, so much a lover and reverer of God, should testify that he wished to do what was so contrary to God!

[Note: The Vulgate has *hic*, less correctly. Construe the sentence: “Could it really have happened that so great a Caesar was deceived by someone’s lie, when that person said that I likewise wished to yield?” Shortly afterward he calls the alms of the emperor the favor by which he was restored to the see of Verona. Thus, in the sermon *On the Octaves of Easter*, no. 3, praising the emperor, he says: “who established me there in the bishopric as an act of almsgiving.” Referring to this, in the present work, no. 1, he says: “Since, by God’s mercy and the alms of that emperor who bestowed it upon me, I possess many things, and my permission to enjoy them has not been forbidden.” The author commonly uses the word “alms” for “mercy”; see note 14 on the second sermon for Lent. Indeed, what he calls the emperor’s alms here, he calls the mercy of the most devout Caesar in the *Itinerary*, no. 4. “Destruction” (*diffactio*) comes from the verb *diffacere*, elsewhere *disfacere*, Italian *disfare*. See Du Cange, under *Diffacere*. “The destruction of that act” means the destruction of the act by which Rather had been restored to the bishopric.]

It could certainly have happened that Caesar was so deceived by someone’s lie that the person told him I indeed likewise wished to yield. And while the seizure of me, my expulsion, stripping, abduction, imprisonment, plundering of the church, destruction of the episcopal residence, erasure of the emperor’s benefaction, destruction of the act by which I had been restored, assault upon the city, contempt for imperial authority, and many other matters connected with these still were—and still are—at issue,

[Note: Something seems to be missing here; or perhaps *perageretur* should be read as *peracta est*, “was carried out.” “Improvement” here means restoration or correction. Rather complains that, although so many crimes were involved, and although the correction or settlement of all of them had been left aside, the sole matter pursued was one act of perjury—namely, the violation of the oath sworn to the emperor during the conspiracy raised against him. In the *Itinerary*, no. 4, he explains the words “with the correction left aside” as follows: “Although all these things, which he listed as crimes, had been left unexamined, as though nothing could be found in them that could even lightly be censured by the laws.” He explains the charge of perjury in Letter 8 to Milo: “I am glad that you consider how you act against yourself, since you swore to the emperor, as I did, a very solemn oath of fidelity, while you seek to destroy his edict and compel those who swore the same oath to him to commit perjury.” In Letter 12 to Ambrose, no. 3, a fine of one hundred pounds of silver is reported to have been imposed under the heading of “correction” or “settlement,” on account of a conspiracy directed not so much against Bishop Rather as against Count Buccon. This fine demonstrates still more clearly the rebellion and the charge of perjury. Shortly afterward the conspiracy against the bishop is called a homicidal case. For this reason, earlier, in no. 15, he says that one of his adversaries cannot be excused from being a murderer of him, although God’s providence still preserves his life: “Nor should you believe that you do not kill me daily by your machinations,” and so forth.]

—the case alone was pursued as one of homicidal perjury, with the correction of everything else left aside [or: “the case was completed”].

One must especially beware of such people for this reason also: it is certainly found to be the custom of our countrymen that those who are guilty of any offense first appeal to whatever authority they can, before the person against whom they have inflicted the injury can do so. This is known to have happened most recently with a man who, being the chief contractor among all those who once captured me, and who was constantly contriving and inflicting countless evils upon me and mine, had moreover been advanced to the diaconate by the invader of my bishopric after thefts and sacrileges imputed to him by those who claim to know him. Although he had been advanced contrary to law and right, he held and plundered land belonging to us by force of authority; then, fleeing to the feet of the lord emperor without anyone pursuing him, he falsely claimed that I had taken away his benefice.

How many such things do people like this perpetrate? Who can avoid them except one who strives to investigate most diligently a case he does not know? And what king can otherwise be reconciled with the King of kings, unless he carefully strives to do this? What judge can render a just decision without it? May our most devout Lord, the King of kings himself, graciously grant that he may do so; and may he repay the one who does this with a fitting recompense, so that in this long-lasting age he may rule happily, and in the age to come reign eternally with Christ. Amen.

# RATHER’S DECREE

[Note: This work, which Rather calls a decretal in the text, was published by Acherius from a manuscript at Laon. Since its opening complains that he was at that time being fiercely persecuted by the malicious through their taunts and through testimony that was either true or false, just as he explains more fully at the beginning of the preceding work, we believe that this decree was composed at approximately the same time, that is, around the year 966. The little abbey afterward called a small monastery, known as Magonzianus—or, as other documents give it, in agreement also with the modern name, “de Maguzano”—lies near Desenzano and Lonato, on that bank of Lake Benacus within the diocese of Verona that extends toward the diocese of Brescia. This monastery, with its chapels, tithes, and appurtenances, is listed among the possessions and property of the bishopric of Verona in a privilege of Eugene III from 1145, in Biancolini, book 1, *Notizie delle Chiese di Verona*, p. 193, and afterward in subsequent privileges. After various changes, it has since the fifteenth century been annexed to the monastery of Saint Benedict at Polirone in the diocese of Mantua; several monks of that monastery reside there.]

From the little abbey of Magonzianus, after the monks had been sent away, clerics were substituted.

[Col. 0547]

[Col. 0547D] 399

## 1.

While, as Aurelius of most august memory confirms (*Sermon* 46, no. 27), everything is so full of rash judgments that even I, being at this time fiercely persecuted by the taunts of malicious people, have become so distrustful of myself that I am very often uncertain what I am doing and with what intention; while, that is, I compare their false or true testimony about me with what is known to me more fully than is necessary—I intend, by this decretal writing, to make clear what I recently decided concerning the little abbey called Magonzianus, and to send it to those living now and those who will come after, so that both may judge it.

This same place, however small it may be, came to our Church from a small estate by the arrangement of certain persons, under the following provision: whenever the abbot died or perpetrated something wrongly and incorrigibly, another from our diocese would be appointed there by the bishop, so that he would compel the monks serving there to live according to monastic law.

[Note: This special arrangement had been established by the founder at the foundation of the little monastery: after the abbot’s death, or if he became incorrigible, another was to be chosen and appointed not by the monks but by the bishop, from the diocese of Verona, to compel the monks to observe regular discipline.]

But since, as things turned out, this did not proceed as the founder had intended—for the little monastery was burned by the Hungarians—

[Note: The Hungarians repeatedly invaded Italy and devastated it by fires and plundering from the year 900 until the year 947. See Liutprand’s *History* and other tenth-century writers.]

—it had come to this miserable state: the man who alone wore the cowl under the false title of abbot could not in any way abstain even from a wife, much less could the others renounce their own wills, as the monastic rule commands.

[Note: At this time there was one abbot at the monastery of Magonzianus, without monks; he also had a wife and, as is related below, children by her. Hence shortly afterward Rather calls him “one false cowl.”]

Since, therefore, I had been unable by every possible effort to induce one of such men to do what ought at least to be done in accordance with the circumstances, and since, after fleeing three times, he was moreover trying through intermediaries to infect me with the leprosy of Gehazi—that is, he was attempting to induce me, in return for money received from him, to allow him to hand over to the devil, as he had done before, what had been offered to the Lord—

[Note: That is, to allow him to spend the revenues of the little abbey, as explained below, on his wife, his natural children, his brothers, and his nephews.]

—while I refused what he wanted and he requested what, out of regard for God, I avoided, and since the matter had broken down on both sides, my mind was left wondering what I could do.

For if I retained for myself, as though I were going to administer it better, the little possession given to the Mother of God, or gave it to one of my own people, I was somewhat afraid that one of my successors might, following my example, likewise destroy the alms represented by those goods.

If, on the other hand, because of one false cowl—called an abbot, that is, the falsest father but in reality the truest stepfather—I allowed it to be spent on his wife, his natural children, his brothers, and his nephews, I feared that I would incur no less the punishment of a foolish steward than of an unfaithful one.

For since the monastic profession is exceedingly arduous and wholly unsuitable for such people—just as nothing is holier than a monk, so nothing is more wicked than a hypocrite—I abandoned the impossible and devoted my efforts to what was possible.

## 2.

I therefore decreed that, if the resources prevented there being more, at least three priests who knew their duty should serve there at all times, so that no day would pass there without Mass; also one deacon, one subdeacon, and several minor clerics.

Each of the priests would receive annually ten modii of grain and rye—

[Note: Acherius perhaps understood this as wheat. The recent editor rightly believed that nothing should be changed; the Italian word *segala* derives from it. Other writers use *sigalum*, others *segalis*, as may be seen in Du Cange’s *Glossary*. Fortunatus uses *panis segalacius* in the *Life of Saint Radegund*, chapters 15 and 21.]

—ten modii of legumes and millet, ten modii of *suricum*—

[Note: *Suricum* is not Indian corn, which was introduced into Italy at a later time, but a kind of grain from which bread is still made in some places and which in Italian is called *sorgo*.]

—and twelve modii of wine.

[Note: The *modius* was a measure not only for dry goods but also for liquids, varying according to locality, as is shown more fully in the latest edition of Du Cange under *Modium* and *Modius*. Thus, when the author says in part 1 of *On Contempt for the Canons*, no. 3, “How many congii of wine,” rather than “how many modii,” the *congius* was a smaller measure than the *modius*, which consisted of several congii.]

The deacon was to receive five modii of all these things, and six modii of wine. The subdeacon was to receive three modii, and four modii of wine. For clothing, the priests were to receive five solidi, the deacon two solidi, and the subdeacon one solidus.

None of them was to wear a cowl. Nevertheless, in memory of the ancient custom, they were to sing hymns at Lauds, Matins, Prime, Terce, Sext, None, Vespers, and Compline, all of which I decreed were to be celebrated at the proper hour.

And because I despaired that this could be done without some form of supervision, I appointed there, in addition to those three, one honorable priest who was not inexperienced in his ministry. I decreed that, if he died or refused to carry out the decrees, another would be substituted for him by the bishop of Verona; and that this priest, after distributing all these things as set out above—not by vineyards and fields but by measures—would have whatever remained.

[Note: That is, a priest who, after distributing all these things by measures, not by vineyards and fields, would have what remained. Similarly, in the *Judicatum*, no. 2, he establishes that revenues are to be distributed by modii and sextarii, that is, by measures, not by fields and vineyards. This distinction between fields and vineyards is noteworthy; see note 11 on that same *Judicatum*.]

On the principal feast days he was to make those five eat with him, abundantly and as far as possible providing them with the same food and drink as himself.

On those days, however, we decree that they should have a reading at table and, after the meal, sing what the monks sing.

[Note: That is, they should sing the same things that the monks sing. Whether many words or only a few are missing at the end is unknown.]

But especially . . . [lacuna]

# [SYNODICAL LETTER]

[Col. 0551]

## INTRODUCTION TO THE FOLLOWING SYNODICAL LETTER

### I.

Rather’s *Synodical Letter* is not only one of the most outstanding and famous of his works, but also one of the most important documents relating to ecclesiastical discipline from the entire tenth century. Since the author intended by it to instruct the clergy of his diocese in the duties they were required to perform, he indicates with the greatest possible precision almost every principal matter of ecclesiastical discipline. From these instructions we learn what had been retained from the older discipline in that century, and what had been introduced, changed, or softened.

In the *Itinerary*, which, as we shall establish in its proper place, he wrote in December 966, the author mentions the *Synodical Letter* and gives the following as the occasion for composing it, in no. 6:

> “After inquiring into the faith of those who had come to the synod, especially from the diocese, I discovered that very many did not even know the Creed itself, which is believed to have belonged to the apostles. On this occasion I was compelled to write a *Synodical Letter* to all the priests, in which the following was first proposed: ‘I therefore admonish you paternally and command you pastorally,’” and so forth.

He recites the whole of the first chapter of the *Synodical Letter*.

He adds that the synod on whose occasion he issued this *Synodical Letter* was held “during,” that is, in the middle of, Lent. That it was written before Easter is also clear from the words at the end of the work: “Since the authority of the Easter festival also compels us, we admonish your charity,” and so forth.

It is therefore clear that the *Synodical Letter* itself must be assigned to Lent of the year 966. Moreover, in the same section of the *Synodical Letter*, he commands every rural priest to learn by heart the three Creeds—the Apostles’, the Nicene-Constantinopolitan, and that of Saint Athanasius—and afterward recite them for himself “when,” as he says, “he has next been summoned here by us.” The adverb “next” indicates that this was not to be postponed for long.

In the sixth section of the *Itinerary*, cited above, he explains the matter as follows:

> “After I had given them these three faiths, or three Creeds, during Lent, to be written out and committed to memory at the synod, and had seen that they were disobedient—that is, when they were next summoned; while I was considering what I could canonically do about it, such fear seized some of them that, after promising me assistance for undertaking the journey, they further promised that they would sing the writing of blessed Athanasius,” and so forth.

The journey he mentions is the Roman journey, on account of which he wrote the *Itinerary*. Thus, in Lent of the same year, 966, he issued the *Synodical Letter*. Several months later he summoned those who, instead of paying a fine for their disobedience, had promised assistance for the journey to Rome, in order to make them give an account. Finally, in December, he compiled the *Itinerary*. From this it may be gathered that the synod on the occasion of which he issued the *Synodical Letter* had recently taken place, as he relates in no. 5 of the same *Itinerary*.

### II.

Among the many noteworthy features of this *Synodical Letter*, several of which we shall touch upon in the notes, one must especially be explained here because it will help in understanding many passages.

Observe the words in no. 6: “as we found written elsewhere.” What Rather found “written elsewhere” is everything that he presents in that sixth section and in the following sections, through the whole of section twelve. We find that he transcribed these passages from a kind of solemn formula which, in manuscripts of better quality, is entitled *Admonition* or *Synodical Sermon* and was intended to be read or recited at a synod.

The copy prefixed to Burchard’s decree bears the title *Admonition*, with this heading:

> “An admonition to be read by the deacon at the synod after the Gospel has ended, while the bishop and the others are seated in due order.”

The same wording appears in a manuscript cited by Baluzius in his notes on Regino, p. 532:

> “When these things have been completed, while the bishop and the others are seated in due order, let this Admonition be read by the deacon.”

In Hittorp’s Roman Order, instead of “let it be read by the deacon,” the text says either “by the bishop himself” or “let this Admonition be read by the deacon as the bishop’s representative.”

The Roman Pontifical of Augustine Patricius likewise gives a similar heading. In the *Sacerdotale*, chapter 13, where only certain excerpts from the same admonition are reproduced, the following title is found:

> “What priests and clerics ought to observe, excerpted in summary from the Synodical Admonition.”

The heading *Synodical Sermon* appears in a manuscript from the diocese of Augsburg at Neresheim in these words:

> “Synodical Sermon to be proclaimed at synods to parish priests,”

as may be seen in Labbe, volume 2 of the *Councils*, Venetian edition, column 1075.

### III.

It is very important to distinguish two formulas that agree perfectly in their statements and almost equally in their wording, and that seem to have been composed by the same author.

One is the *Admonition*, or *Synodical Sermon*, just mentioned. The other is the work prefixed by Regino under the title *Inquiry* to his work *On Ecclesiastical Discipline*.

In that rough age, when rural priests in particular were generally immersed in the greatest ignorance, it was necessary to set before them a very brief summary of the canons embracing the principal points of ecclesiastical discipline. This summary is presented in the *Admonition*, or *Synodical Sermon*, which was to be read at the synod.

What had been proposed and prescribed at the synod then had to be investigated during visitations to determine whether it had been put into practice. Hence, at the same period and apparently by the same author, the *Inquiry* was composed for the use of bishops and their ministers when visiting parishes.

Regino, who has preserved it for us in full, gives it this title:

> “Here begins the Inquiry concerning the matters that the bishop or his ministers ought to investigate in their district or territory, throughout the villages, settlements, and parishes of their diocese.”

The same author prefixed the part of this *Inquiry* concerning ecclesiastical matters to his first book. There, treating of clerics, he confirms each of the chapters of the *Inquiry* by canons. He relegated the final part, concerning laypeople, to chapter 5 of the second book, where, treating of laypeople, he likewise establishes the remaining chapters of the *Inquiry* by canons.

### IV.

Velserus, who knew only the *Admonition*, or *Synodical Sermon*, from the Augsburg manuscript, conjectured that Saint Ulrich, bishop of Augsburg, was its author, because most of the matters that, according to Gerard in his *Life*, chapter 6, that saint usually investigated in the chapters concerning clerics correspond exactly to the instructions of the *Admonition*, or *Sermon*.

But this proves only that Saint Ulrich used that *Admonition*, or rather the *Inquiry*. Gerard is speaking of the matters that Ulrich investigated during his visitations.

Others believe that the *Admonition*, or *Synodical Sermon*, was composed by Leo IV. A Vatican manuscript containing the *Book of Censuses*, from which it was published in volume 9 of the Venetian edition of the *Councils*, column 1031, attributes it to him under this title:

> “Homily of Pope Leo IV on pastoral care and its office and duty, which he wished to be communicated through the bishops to all priests entrusted with the care of souls.”

The same pope may also be intended by the heading prefixed to the same *Synodical Sermon* in another Vatican manuscript, no. 1355, p. 370:

> “Sermon to be delivered at the synod, composed by Saint Leo the pope.”

Why, however, we believe that such a *Sermon*, or *Admonition*, cannot be attributed to any Roman pontiff, you will gather from note 29.

Since some of the disciplinary provisions prescribed there derive from the Gallican Church, we believe that the same *Admonition* was composed in Gaul. Stephen Baluzius, in his notes on Regino, p. 534, considers it older than Leo IV, composed in the time of Saint Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, or at least not long afterward.

The same should be thought of the *Inquiry*, which, because its statements and wording agree with those of the *Admonition*, recognizes the same parent. The only difference between the *Inquiry* and the *Admonition* is that the words presenting the form of a decree in the *Admonition* take the form of questions in the *Inquiry*.

The Gallican origin of the latter can certainly be confirmed by Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims. When he entitled his second capitulary “Concerning the matters that masters and deans ought to investigate in each church and report to the bishop,” he clearly had this *Inquiry* before his eyes; for the chapters that follow are the same as those found in the *Inquiry* mentioned above.

These matters seemed worth explaining at greater length beforehand, so that it might be clear from what source Rather inserted the seven chapters in question into his *Synodical Letter*.

### V.

Since this source is much older, it is especially important to observe that no one should attribute everything contained in the chapters transcribed from the *Admonition* to Rather’s age or to the people and clergy of Verona in his time.

For, when he transferred the complete chapters of the *Admonition* into his *Synodical Letter* in the same words, he did not wish to remove or alter anything. Some things will occur there that belong to other regions and to an earlier age; anyone who thought they had to be applied to the tenth century and to the people of Verona in that period would be seriously mistaken.

Thus, at the end of no. 11, the custody of the sacred chrism is prescribed under lock and seal on account of certain unbelievers. We should certainly not conclude that some unbelievers existed at Verona in the tenth century.

For the same reason, Baluzius, in his notes on the words in book 1 of Regino’s *Inquiry*, no. 18—“And let no one presume to hand over Communion to a layman or woman for carrying it to the sick”—wisely remarked on p. 536:

> “The celebrated Henry Valesius, since he did not notice that this Admonition was much older than the age of Rather, bishop of Verona, and of Ulrich, bishop of Augsburg, inferred from this passage that the practice of handing Communion to laymen and women for carrying it to the sick had continued in the Church until the tenth century. An erudite man who recently published a history of the Eucharist later adopted this conjecture. The argument is false. For if this method of reasoning were permissible, we would with equal necessity infer something that everyone knows to be completely false: namely, that the same practice of sending the Eucharist to the sick through laymen and women still continues in the Church, since the *Synodical Admonition*, which bishops read every year throughout all the Churches of the West at their diocesan synods, is written in the Roman Pontifical in these very words: ‘Let no one presume,’ and so forth.”

### VI.

Since Rather’s chapters were copied from the *Admonition*, editions of the *Admonition* produced from different manuscripts should be mentioned, both because they attest to its fame and because they will be useful to us.

Apart from the copies in which the *Admonition* is found in Hittorp’s *Roman Order*, in the *Pontifical*, and in the *Sacerdotale*, Gretser published it from the Augsburg manuscript in volume 6 of the latest edition of his works, p. 232.

It appears twice in Labbe’s *Councils*: first in volume 9 of the Venetian edition, p. 1031, and again in volume 2, column 1075. Hugo Mauthoud printed it in his observations on Robert Pullus, p. 403. Baluzius printed it three times in the appendix to Regino, pp. 602 and following. Later, Fathers Martene and Durandus printed it in volume 7 of the *Collection of Ancient Writers*, p. 1, under the special title:

> “Admonition of a certain bishop to priests.”

Finally, it appears in volume 3 of Dominicus Georgius’s appendix to the Roman liturgy.

Although the ancient copies generally agree, they differ in some minor matters. The copy used by Rather comes closer to the readings of the *Admonition* that appears in the *Councils* under the title *Homily of Pope Leo IV*, volume 9, column 1031, as will be clear from the notes, especially note 975.

When we cite certain readings from the *Inquiry*, we shall use the edition of Regino prepared at Paris in 1671 by Stephen Baluzius.

[Col. 0553]

# RATHER’S SYNODICAL LETTER

[Note: This *Synodical Letter*, cited by Fulcuin in chapter 24, was printed by Acherius from a manuscript at Laon and afterward reproduced by Labbe in volume 2 of the Venetian edition of the *Councils*, column 811. We have received it transcribed from the manuscript at Freising, whose readings have proved useful for supplementing or correcting the text in several places. In the title of that manuscript, the words *forinsecus, id est* are omitted.]

To the priests and the other orders established throughout the diocese.

[Col. 0553A] 409

Since I know that you are wondering—or rather, I do not fail to know that you are grumbling, which is worse—that I have now summoned you for the third time and have dealt with you as though I had done nothing with you, do not suppose that I did this in vain. I confess that I did it in order to test you, and I found you, alas, to be just as I had judged I would find you.

It immediately seemed to me, in my great misfortune, that the following passage from the Book of Wisdom applied:

“Do not rejoice in foolish children, if they multiply; do not delight in them if the fear of God is not with them” (Ecclesiasticus 16:1).

[Note: We supplied the word *nihil*, “nothing,” from the Freising manuscript. Shortly afterward we likewise corrected *Sapientiae*, “of Wisdom,” from the same manuscript, where the common text had *Sapientiae*. When he says, “I have now summoned you for the third time,” no one should suppose that three synods are being indicated. For it may be gathered from the *Itinerary*, no. 5, that after his third restoration he held no other synod before this one, because he did not know at all from where he ought to synodize. Rather is therefore to be understood as having summoned or assembled them three times for the purpose of this one synod, just as at the end of the first section he says that he will summon them again shortly. We explained this in the *Admonition*, no. 1.]

## 1.

I therefore admonish you paternally and command you pastorally to remember the Apostle’s statement that “without faith it is impossible to please God” (Hebrews 11:6)—that is, without the belief that has been handed down to us through the apostles and their successors—and that “the just person lives by faith,” that is, by his belief (Romans 1:17), and that “whatever is not from faith,” that is, belief in God, “is sin” (ibid. 14:23).

But faith—that is, belief in God—if it does not have good works, “is dead in itself” (James 2:17). Therefore, hasten to prepare this faith—that is, belief in God—in three forms for memorization [understand: “that faith”]; that is, according to the Creed, or the collection of the apostles, as it is found in corrected Psalters;

[Col. 0555A]

[Note: From this it may be suspected that in the Church of Verona the Apostles’ Creed had received some addition, as happened in certain places, especially in the metropolitan Church of Aquileia. Since Rather did not approve such additions, he referred readers to corrected Psalters, in which the same Creed was written.]

and according to the Creed that is sung at Mass; and according to that of Saint Athanasius, which begins:

“Whoever wishes to be saved” (*Quicumque vult salvus esse*).

Therefore, whoever wishes to be, to become, or to remain a priest in our diocese,

[Note: The common text reads *illa fratres*, “those things, brothers.” We have corrected it not only from the Freising manuscript but also from the *Itinerary*, no. 6, where this first chapter of the *Synodical Letter* is recited. Shortly afterward we likewise corrected the reading from the same *Itinerary*: the text had *proximo* instead of *proxime*.]

must recite those three [understand: “faith[s]”] to us from memory whenever he has next been summoned here by us.

## 2

I also admonish you concerning the Lord’s Day: think—or, if you do not know how to think, ask—why it is so called. For in everyday usage we call those things “lords’ possessions” which properly belong to their respective lords. In this sense, therefore, the day is called the Lord’s Day because it properly belongs to the Lord, that is, Jesus Christ. Yet since all days belong to him, as do all things that are in heaven, on earth, in the sea, and in all the depths (Psalm 134:6), we must ask why this day alone is said to be his. Clearly, because on it he rose again.

> **Note:** This is how the Frisingensis manuscript reads. The Vulgate has *in eo* (“on it”), incorrectly. Shortly afterward, *in quibus Kalendis* means “on which day of the month.” For *Kalendae* was used not only for the first day, but for any day of the month; thus, in *The Life of Saint Landricus, Bishop of Metz*, no. 11, it is said that for many years the *Kalenda*, that is, the day of Saint Landricus’s feast, lay covered by the rust of forgetfulness. Ratherius therefore declares that it is entirely immaterial on which day of the month the Lord’s Day on which Christ rose happened to fall.

But do not concern yourself with which day of the month [understand: on which he rose]; think only about the day. On Thursday, after evening, he was handed over; on Friday, he was crucified; on the seventh day, he rested in the tomb; on the eighth day, he rose from the dead; and, having completed three days—as he had promised—between part of two days, or the whole of two nights, he returned from the heart, that is, the inner parts of the earth (Matthew 12:40), to the Apostles.

> **Note:** The Vulgate reads: “and between part of two days, or the whole of three nights, or three days.” From the Frisingensis manuscript we have removed *trium* (“of three”) and *vel* (“or”) before *triduo* (“for three days”), although *vel* is placed before *noctium* (“of nights”). If *trium* were to be retained, we would prefer to read: “and between part of three days, or the whole of two nights, for three days,” and so forth. Shortly afterward, we have written *rediit* (“he returned”) and *eveniat* (“happens”) from the same Frisingensis manuscript, where the Vulgate had *redit* (“he returns”) and *evenerit* (“has happened”).

Hence this eighth day, or first day of the week, is called the Lord’s Day; and on whatever day of the month it happens to fall, it is always Easter—that is, the Lord’s passage from death to life—and it is to be observed in one and the same way, whatever you eat or drink.

> **Column reference:** 0555C.

But from what is it to be observed? From servile work. And what is servile work? Sin, for whoever sins serves the devil.

If, therefore, every Lord’s Day is Easter, we must ask what we ought to do on it. Let the Apostle speak: “Passover,” he says, “our Passover, Christ, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7).

Why is Christ the Passover? Because he was sacrificed.

> **Note:** Acherius has *pro nobis immolatus* (“sacrificed for us”). The words *pro nobis* are absent from the cited Frisingensis manuscript and should rightly be rejected; otherwise one would seek them in vain in what follows. Why was he sacrificed? The answer would be “for us,” but that would be pointless if *sacrificed for us* had already been stated.

Why was he sacrificed? So that he might die for us. Just as previously that victim was sacrificed whose blood purified the people so that they might be delivered from Egypt, so this one was sacrificed in order that he might die; for this reason he was slain, so that, freed by his blood from the destroying angel of the world, that is, the devil, we might be rescued from Egypt, that is, from hell; and, led through the Red Sea—that is, through baptism made red by the Lord’s blood—and through the desert of the present life, we might be able to reach the promised land, that is, eternal life.

You have Easter, that is, a good passage; you have the Lamb slain for you; you have crossed the Red Sea; you are walking through the desert. See where you are walking. Strive to arrive where it is beneficial for you to come.

> **Note:** We have added the particle *ut* (“so that”) with the help of the Frisingensis manuscript.

Work, with God’s help, lest you return to Egypt or perish in the desert, but reach the heavenly homeland. Understand that you are returning to Egypt if you presume to repeat the sin you abandoned. You perish in the desert if you do not persevere in labor and good works.

## 3

But let us return to the Apostle: “Passover,” he says, “our Passover, Christ, has been sacrificed.”

Afterward: “Therefore let us feast.” Do you think he means: “Let us devote ourselves to gluttony and drunkenness”? Certainly not. For he continues: “Not with the old leaven,” that is, with inflation of the belly; or with the swelling of former sin; or with a desire to return to past crimes or to commit others; “nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (1 Corinthians 5:8)—that is, so that in our conduct we may be upright, in our thoughts simple, and in our speech truthful.

When? At all times, but especially at the paschal solemnity, that is, on every Lord’s Day throughout the entire year. For if it is the Lord’s Day, it is certainly not our day. If it belongs to the Lord, the Lord’s honor must be honored.

But which lord? Truly, the one who made us when we did not exist; who restored us when we had been lost; who governs, feeds, nourishes, and protects us; who preserves our life here for as long as it pleases him; who, when he wills, will change it from this place and return it to us either better according to our merits or worse; and finally, who will judge us and either condemn us without end in hell or crown us eternally in heaven.

Since this day properly belongs to a Lord of such and so great a power, let it be honored as befits the dignity of so great a Lord. Yet it can in no way be honored except in an orderly manner. For unless Friday precedes Saturday, and Saturday the Lord’s Day, the day is in no sense the Lord’s Day.

## 4

What, then, is Friday, the day of preparation? Let the Apostle speak: “Let a person examine himself,” he says, “and so eat of that bread and drink from that cup” (1 Corinthians 11:28).

What bread? The bread of which he says: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John 6:41).

From what cup? “Your cup that intoxicates—how splendid it is!” (Psalm 22:5), that is, Christ, satisfying us with his blood; “how beautiful,” that is, “fair in form beyond the sons of men!” (Psalm 44:3).

Therefore the bread is the Lamb; the Lamb is Christ; Christ is the Passover; and the Passover is the one sacrificed for us.

He is the day which the Lord made—not by working, but by begetting him coeternally: “Let us exult and rejoice in it” (Psalm 117:24). He is, I say, the day; he is the Lord whose day this is.

What shall we do concerning his Sabbath? “Be still,” the Lord says through the Psalmist, “and know that I am God” (Psalm 45:11). Sabbath means cessation or rest: that is, that we should rest from evil works and devote ourselves to divine service.

Friday, however, is called preparation, meaning that we should prepare the dwelling places of our hearts for Christ, who is coming to us through the substance of his body and blood.

If, therefore, every eighth day is the Lord’s Day, and the Lord’s Day is so called because of the Lord’s resurrection—or, as someone is found to have said very elegantly, “The Lord made all the days by his command; he made the Lord’s Day by his blood and consecrated it by his price”—then every Lord’s Day needs a Friday of preparation or a Sabbath.

Preparation, that is, is nothing other than what we have stated: that a person should examine himself, that is, investigate what his disposition is—whether he stands, with God’s grace, in a will to improve, or in the hardness of deterioration.

> **Note:** The Vulgate adds *jus* (“rightly”), incorrectly. The first alternative is this: if he stands in his conscience in a will to improve, with God’s grace.

If he finds the first condition in his conscience, trusting in God’s mercy, let him eat the lamb with wild lettuce (Exodus 12:8), that is, with contrition of heart and groans of bitterness, his loins girded.

> **Note:** This is how the Frisingensis manuscript reads. The Vulgate has *et amaritudine gemitus* (“and with bitterness of groans”) and *accinctis renibus* (“with loins girded”).

If not, I do not dare advise him to do so. Let each person see to what he should do.

Every Lord’s Day, therefore, is paschal because it is adorned by the Lord’s resurrection; and our Passover is Christ because he was sacrificed for us.

## 5

Every Lord’s Day, therefore, the Apostle cries out to us: “Therefore let us feast,” that is, let us eat the Lord’s flesh and drink his blood.

Where, then, are those who celebrate Mass every day, make Easter every day—that is, eat the flesh of the Lamb and drink his blood—and, to say nothing of the rest, very often beget sons and daughters from adulterous intercourse?

> **Note:** We have supplied *saepissime* (“very often”) from the cited manuscript. He calls the intercourse of those priests who had contracted an illicit marriage “adulterous intercourse,” for, as stated in *The Conjecture of Quality*, no. 2: “He calls an illicit marriage adultery.”

Where are those who belch yesterday’s drunkenness or gluttony before the Lord’s altar, over the very flesh or blood of the Lamb? Those who are occupied with continual quarrels; who burn with greed; who waste away with envy or hatred; who never cease to spread snares of deceit for those whom they ought to love as themselves?

When has any such person observed the Friday of preparation or the Sabbath just mentioned? I fear for such people—and would that they were not like me—that while they think they are eating the Lamb, they may instead be eating the goat; and would that it were not that goat which was sent away into the desert—the one who is called in Latin *emissarius*, “the one sent away,” and in Hebrew *hazezel*, that is, “the cruel one of God.”

> **Note:** The words *qui Latine*, through *et vestibus omnibus*, are absent from the Frisingensis manuscript, which immediately continues: “but rather the kid sacrificed by the whole people on the fourteenth day toward evening.” Later, after *vertitur in malum* (“is turned into evil”), the Vulgate adds: “that is, the gentleness of God into cruelty.” These words appear to be a gloss, and we have deleted them on the authority of the same manuscript.

The one who sent him into the desert (Leviticus 16:22) is not worthy to enter the camp of God unless he has first washed his body and all his garments (ibid., 26). Rather, let them be eating the kid sacrificed by the whole people on the fourteenth day toward evening.

> **Column reference:** 0558B.

Woe to those for whom so great a good is turned into so great an evil, while they eat the Lord’s flesh and drink his blood unworthily, thereby eating and drinking judgment upon themselves.

> **Note:** The word *Domini* (“of the Lord”) has been added from the same manuscript.

Woe, I say, to us wretched people—yes, a thousandfold woe. For since we are called priests for no other reason than that we ought to prepare and give what is sacred to the people, while Holy Scripture says the opposite: “Whatever an unclean person touches shall be unclean” (Numbers 19:22), how can anything sacred even be said to have been handled by our most filthy hands?

And since our special teacher and provider, the blessed Zeno, says—in the sermon which he composed with such elegance concerning Judah, son of Jacob, and his daughter-in-law Tamar (*Book II, Tractate 14, no. 4, p. 180, Veronese edition*)—that the devil is the father of all who live corruptly, what does it accomplish that, in the sight of all who know us to live corruptly, that is, to serve lust, we cry out to God: “Our Father, who art in heaven” (Matthew 6:9), when he immediately answers us through the prophet: “If I am a father, where is my love?” (Malachi 1:6).

What are you doing for my love?

Because I grieve that you are entirely ignorant of these matters and similar ones—or rather, because I groan that you care nothing about such things—I command you pastorally to hasten to learn them. And because you are ignorant of instruction by word, I ask you to strive to instruct God’s people by good example.

## 6

We also admonish and beseech your fraternity, as we find written elsewhere, to think carefully about your common salvation, to listen more attentively to our admonition, to commit to memory what we suggest to you, and to strive to put it into practice.

> **Note:** He says “elsewhere” because everything through section 12 was copied by Ratherius from the *Admonition*, or synodal sermon, as we observed in the preceding admonition. The words “as we find written elsewhere,” which are absent from the synodal sermon and from other copies of the synodal admonition, are found in the published homily attributed to Leo IV.

First of all, we admonish you that your life and conduct be irreproachable: specifically, that your cell be beside the church and that you have no women in it.

Rise every night for nocturns; sing your office at fixed hours; perform the celebrations of Mass reverently; receive the body and blood of the Lord with fear and reverence; wash and dry the sacred vessels with your own hands.

Let no one sing Mass unless he is fasting; let no one sing who does not communicate; let no one sing without an amice, alb, stole, fanon, and chasuble. Let these vestments be clean and be used for no other purposes.

> **Note:** Rabanus explains the fanon in *Book I of On the Instruction of Clergy*, chapter 18, as follows: “The mappula, or cloth, is the priest’s garment, which is commonly called the fanon. We more often call it the maniple.” At first it was a linen sweat-cloth; hence Ivo of Chartres, in his sermon on the meaning of priestly vestments, says: “On the left hand is placed a certain cloth, which often wipes away the discharge from the eyes and removes the soreness of the eyes.” Robert Pullus likewise says in *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, book I, chapter 51: “Finally, the priest places the fanon on his left arm; they called it both the maniple and the sweat-cloth, by which sweat and the uncleanness of the nose were formerly wiped away.” Shortly afterward, the Frisingensis manuscript has *munda* (“clean”) instead of *nitida* (“bright” or “shining”).

Let no one presume to sing Mass in the alb which he uses for his ordinary purposes.

> **Note:** It may be inferred from this that priests formerly always wore an alb; a remnant of this survives among the Canons Regular, who wear a shorter alb, commonly called a rochet. For this reason it was forbidden that, in sacred ministry, priests should use the alb which they wore for their ordinary, that is, common, purposes. The same is read in the *Inquiry* preserved by Regino, no. 66: “If he presumes to sing Mass without an alb, or in that alb which he uses daily for his ordinary purposes.” In the capitulary of Riculphus, bishop of Soissons, chapter 7: “This, however, we forbid absolutely: that no one use in the sacred mysteries that alb which he wears in daily or external use.” Shortly after *praesumat missam cantare* (“presume to sing Mass”), Acherius adds: “Let no one do so with knives hanging outside; let no one do so with spurs.” We have deleted these words on the authority of the Frisingensis manuscript. From it we have inserted similar words in the following section. They are also absent from other copies of this synodal admonition. Later, the cited manuscript has *capsa et reliquiae* (“a reliquary and relics”). We have retained the Vulgate reading, since the same reading is supported by the other copies of the synodal admonition. In the homily attributed to Leo IV, the reading is *capsae cum reliquiis* (“a reliquary with relics”).

Let no woman approach the altar or touch the Lord’s chalice. Let the corporal be perfectly clean. Let the altar be covered with clean linens. Let nothing be placed on the altar except a reliquary and relics, or perhaps the four Gospels and a *buxida*—that is, a pyx—with the Lord’s body for the viaticum of the sick. Let everything else be stored in a clean place.

> **Note:** Acherius printed *buxida*, although he noted in the margin that perhaps *pyxis* should be read. The most recent editor of the *Spicilegium* inserted *pyxida* into the text. Some copies of the synodal sermon do indeed have *pyxis*. We have nevertheless retained Acherius’s reading *buxida*, confirmed by the Augsburg copy of the synodal sermon, although the Frisingensis manuscript differs slightly, reading *buxita*. *Buxis* and *buxida* mean the same as *pyxis*. Thus Saint Peter Damian, *Book VI, Letter 21*, writes: “When the Eucharist had been reserved in a *buxis*.”  
> In the *Inquiry* preserved by Regino, no. 10, the same words occur: “If he has a full Missal, a Lectionary, and an Antiphonary, for without these Mass cannot be celebrated perfectly.” The sacramentary contained the canon, prayers, and prefaces. The full Missal added the Gospels and Epistles. In the testament of Count Heccard of Autun, preserved by Perard, p. 26: “a full Missal with the Gospel and Epistles.” Leo of Ostia, book III, chapter 19: “For until that time both Epistles and Gospels were read in the full Missal.”

Let every church possess a full Missal, a Lectionary, and an Antiphonary.

> **Column reference:** 0560A.

Let a place in the sacristy or beside the altar be prepared where water can be poured when the sacred vessels are washed; and there let a clean vessel filled with water hang, and there let the priest wash his hands after communion.

## 7

Let no one sing Mass outside the church, in houses, or in unconsecrated places. Let no one sing Mass alone.

> **Note:** *Cantet* (“let him sing”) means “let him recite.” For someone who sings alone is understood not properly to sing but to recite. Remigius of Auxerre uses the word in this sense when explaining why the canon of the Mass is recited in a subdued voice: “For this reason the custom arose in the Church that the prayer and consecration themselves should be sung quietly, that is, in a lowered voice, by the priest, lest such sacred words should be cheapened.” Hence the expression “to sing a private Mass” occurs in the *Constitutions of Hirsau of Saint William*, book I, chapter 86. Compare what Mabillon noted in the preface to the second century of the Benedictine Order, no. 36.

Let no one sing Mass wearing spurs—what we call in rustic speech *sperones*—or with knives hanging outside, since that is indecent and contrary to ecclesiastical discipline.

> **Note:** We have added here, from the Frisingensis manuscript, the words “Let no one with spurs,” through “it is an ecclesiastical rule.” The version of the synodal sermon published from the Augsburg manuscript agrees; it has *quos sporones rustice vocamus* (“which we call *sporones* in rustic speech”) instead of *quos sperones rustice dicimus*. These words alone are absent from the homily attributed to Leo IV. In Acherius, the preceding sentence was mutilated, as may be seen in note 951. Shortly afterward, from the Frisingensis manuscript, we have supplied *et oblata* (“and the offering”), and then *ut plurimi vestri faciunt* (“as many of you do”), and later *recluso* (“enclosed”) instead of *incluso* (“included”).

Sign the chalice and the offering with a proper cross, that is, not in a circle and with the fingers spread apart, as many do, but with two fingers held straight and the thumb enclosed within them, by which the Trinity is signified. Strive to make this sign, +, correctly; for you cannot bless anything in any other way.

Visit the sick and reconcile them. According to the Apostle (James 5:14), anoint them with holy oil and give them communion with your own hand.

> **Note:** The Vulgate has *ungite* (“anoint”), but we have preferred the reading of the Frisingensis manuscript, which agrees with the other copies of the synodal sermon.

Let no one presume to give communion to a layman or woman to carry to the sick.

Let none of you demand a reward or gift for baptizing infants, reconciling the sick, or burying the dead.

See that through your negligence no infant ever dies without baptism.

> **Note:** This is how the same manuscript reads. In Acherius, *nullus* (“no one”) appears before *unquam* (“ever”). The reading *ullus* (“any”) in the homily attributed to Leo IV is better. Baluzius has *ut . . . nullus* (“so that . . . no one”).

## 8

Let none of you be a drunkard or quarrelsome, because “the servant of the Lord must not quarrel” (2 Timothy 2:24).

Let none of you carry weapons in an uprising, because our weapons ought to be spiritual.

Let no one devote himself to amusements involving dogs or birds.

Do not drink in taverns.

Care for the poor, orphans, and pilgrims, and invite them to your little meals.

Be hospitable, so that others may take a good example from you.

Every Lord’s Day before Mass, prepare holy water with which the people may be sprinkled, and keep a vessel for this purpose alone.

Do not give the sacred vessels or priestly vestments in pledge to a merchant or tavernkeeper.

> **Note:** The Vulgate incorrectly has *negociato* (“to a negotiator”); the reading here is “merchant.”

Let none of you bring an insufficiently worthy penitent to reconciliation for any reason [understand: to the bishop], or carry him a certificate of reconciliation.

Let none of you exact interest or become a tenant of his lord.

> **Note:** Here, instead of *sui senioris* (“of his lord”), the text had incorrectly read *fenoris* (“of interest”). The correction is certainly established by copies of the *Inquiry* and the *Admonition*. The reference is to the third canon of the Council of Chalcedon, which forbids clerics to become tenants of another person’s estates. *Senior* here means lay lords and wealthier men who possess estates. Shortly afterward we have written *et ad aliam* (“and to another”) from the Frisingensis manuscript, where the Vulgate had wrongly omitted the preposition *ad*.

Know that the property and resources which you acquire after the day of your ordination belong to the church.

## 9

Let no one acquire a church without our knowledge and consent.

Let no one obtain a church through secular power.

Let no one supplant another in a church through money.

Let no one abandon the church to which he has been appointed and move to another for the sake of gain.

Let no one sing Mass in another’s parish without the consent and request of the parish priest, if he is present.

Let no one receive a tithe belonging to another.

Let no one invite a penitent to eat meat or drink wine unless he has presently given alms on his behalf.

> **Note:** From this passage we learn that even at the time when this *Admonition* was written, public penance could be redeemed by almsgiving. This is explained in Regino, *Book I*, chapter 259, from *Book I of the Capitularies*, title 151: “Let no priest or layman invite a penitent to drink wine or eat meat unless he has immediately given one or two denarii on his behalf, according to the nature of the penance.”

## 10

Let no one presume to baptize except at the vigil of Easter and Pentecost, unless there is danger of death.

Let each person have a font; and if he cannot have a stone one, let him have another vessel prepared for this purpose, in which nothing else is done.

See that you teach all your parishioners the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer.

Impress upon your congregations that the fast of the Four Ember Days, the fast of the Rogation Days, and the major litany must be observed in every respect.

> **Note:** That the fast of the Rogation Days was instituted in Gaul is clear from the First Council of Orléans, chapter 27; from Avitus, in his sermon on the Rogations and in books I, letter 7, and VII, letter 14; and from Saint Gregory of Tours, *History*, book II, chapter 34. Muratorius conjectures that this fast was introduced into the Church of Milan only after the middle of the eleventh century, *Italian Antiquities*, vol. IV, p. 852, because in the *Life of Saint Arialdus*, written by Andrew, a monk of Vallombrosa, and published by Puricello, chapter 21, these words are found: “For he greatly detested that three-day fast which, contrary to the statements of the ancient holy men, had recently begun to be observed among the holy paschal days.” We, however, conclude that this fast was accepted not only at Milan but also in other cities, at least in our regions, even in the tenth century, not merely from this testimony of Ratherius but especially from the first sermon on the Ascension. Saint Arialdus, being most devoted to the rites of the Roman Church, saw this fast being practiced among his Milanese and, because it had not been received by that Church and was indeed foreign to the ancient discipline—which forbade fasting during the paschal days—he detested it and accused it of novelty. Since the Roman Church did not approve this fast, the often-mentioned homily attributed to Leo IV is certainly shown to be foreign to it, because that homily contains this passage.

On the Wednesday before Lent, invite the people to confession and impose penance upon them according to the nature of the offense—not according to your own judgment, but as it is written in the Penitential.
