> **Note:** The Vulgate incorrectly has *plenam* (“full”) instead of *plebem* (“the people”). Penance is not to be imposed from the heart—that is, from some impulse of the mind or personal discretion—but insofar as it has been prescribed in the Penitential.

Four times a year—that is, at the Nativity of the Lord, the Lord’s Supper, Easter, and Pentecost—admonish all the faithful to approach for communion of the Lord’s body and blood.

> **Note:** Both the Laudunensis and Frisingensis manuscripts agree with the Vulgate, as does the homily attributed to Leo IV and the Augsburg manuscript of the synodal sermon. But other copies of the *Admonition*, or synodal sermon, read: “Three times a year, that is, at the Nativity of the Lord, Easter, and Pentecost,” and the same occurs in Regino’s *Inquiry*, no. 58: “Three times in the year, that is, at the Nativity of the Lord, Easter, and Pentecost.” These three times alone are prescribed in the Council of Agde of 506, chapter 18, and in *Book II of the Capitularies*, chapter 45. When Jonas of Orléans, in *Book II of On Lay Instruction*, chapter 18, reports that most people receive communion on only three feasts, more from custom than devotion, he is referring to these same three times. Ratherius appears to have derived the mention of four times from some copy of the synodal sermon resembling the one from which the same mention passed into the homily attributed to Leo IV.

At appointed times exhort married people to abstain from their wives.

After Mass on feast days, distribute *eulogiae* to the people.

> **Note:** This passage is explained in Regino’s *Inquiry*, book I, no. 61: “If, from the offerings made by the people on the Lord’s Day and feast days, he distributes *eulogiae* to the people after Mass has been completed.” Hincmar of Reims explains it more clearly in *Chapters for the Priests of His Diocese*, chapter 7: “From the offerings made by the people, and left over after consecration, or from the loaves which the faithful bring to the church, or certainly from their own, let the priests have suitable portions in a clean and appropriate vessel, so that after the solemnities of Mass those who were not prepared to communicate may receive *eulogiae* from them every Lord’s Day and on feast days; and let him first bless in these words what he is going to distribute as *eulogiae*, and then distribute it to those who are to receive it.” The Council of Nantes, chapter 9, contains similar provisions.

## 11

Let no one travel without a stole.

> **Note:** The words “Let no one travel without a stole,” which were published from the Laudunensis manuscript, are absent not only from the Ratherian Frisingensis manuscript but also from the homily attributed to Leo IV. They are nevertheless found in other copies of the synodal sermon, as well as in the *Inquiry* transcribed by Regino; in these, only *vel orario* (“or an orarium”) is added, which is synonymous with *stola*. This was an indication of priestly dignity.

Let no one wear lay clothing.

Let no one presume to sell, exchange, or alienate by any means any object, possession, or slave belonging to the church.

Teach the people to celebrate the Lord’s Day and the other festivals without servile work, from evening to evening.

> **Note:** In ancient times feast days were observed from evening to evening. See the Capitularies of Aachen of 789, chapter 15; the Council of Friuli of 791, chapter 13; the Council of Frankfurt of 794, chapter 21; and many other provisions of the same kind. Shortly afterward, we have restored the words “songs,” and so forth, through “forbid,” which were absent from the Vulgate, with the help of the Frisingensis manuscript. This restoration is confirmed by the aforementioned homily, by the other copies of the synodal sermon, and by Regino’s *Inquiry*.

Forbid women’s songs and dances in the church courtyard.

Forbid the devilish songs which the common people customarily sing over the dead at night, and the loud laughter which they practice under invocation of almighty God.

Do not associate with excommunicated persons. Let no one presume to sing Mass for them; announce this also to the congregations entrusted to you.

Let none of you attend weddings.

> **Note:** Here *nuptiae* means wedding banquets. That clerics should not attend them was forbidden by the Council of Vannes, chapter 11, and the Council of Mainz, chapter 39.

Announce to everyone that no one may take a wife except after a public wedding has been celebrated.

Absolutely forbid abduction; forbid anyone to approach a close blood relative; and forbid anyone to take another man’s betrothed.

Make pig herders and other shepherds come to Mass, even on the Lord’s Day.

Let godfathers teach their godchildren the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer, or have them taught.

> **Note:** Acherius printed *patroni* (“patrons”) in the text from the Laudunensis manuscript, but noted *patrini* (“godfathers”) in the margin. The most recent editor of the *Spicilegium* accepted this correction. Although *patroni* is also read in the Frisingensis manuscript, since *filiis suis* (“their children”) refers not to patrons but to godfathers, we have retained the same correction, all the more readily because it is confirmed both by manuscript copies of the synodal sermon and by Regino’s *Inquiry*, book II, chapter 5, no. 74, in which *patrini* is read. Shortly afterward, we have written *sub sera* (“under lock”) in agreement with the Frisingensis manuscript and other copies of the *Admonition*, where the Vulgate had *sub cera* (“under wax”).

Let the chrism always be kept under lock or seal because of certain unbelievers.

> **Note:** These words indicate that the *Admonition* inserted here by Ratherius was originally composed in a place where some unbelievers, that is, pagans, still lived.

## 12

We also wish to know of every priest whether he was born of free parents or of servile condition; whether he was born in our parish or ordained there; and to what place he has been assigned.

If he was a slave, let him produce his charter of freedom.

> **Note:** We have added *suae* (“his”) from the Frisingensis manuscript, from which we have also shortly afterward corrected *scriptas* (“written”) to *scriptam* (“written”).

If he is from another parish, let him produce letters of commendation, which are called *formatae*.

We also take care to admonish you concerning the ministry entrusted to you: if possible, let each of you have written out for himself an exposition of the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer according to the tradition of the orthodox, and let him understand it fully. Then, if he knows it, let him diligently instruct the people entrusted to him by preaching; if he does not, let him at least retain it or believe it.

Let him understand well the prayers of the Mass and the canon.

> **Note:** This is how the same manuscript reads, and the copies of the *Admonition* and *Inquiry* agree with it. The Vulgate has *Missae* (“of the Mass”).

If he cannot, let him at least be able to recite them from memory and distinctly.

Let him be able to read the Epistle and Gospel well; and would that he could at least explain their meaning literally.

Let him know how to recite the words and divisions of the Psalms regularly from memory, together with the customary chants.

> **Note:** “From memory” means “by heart.” Similarly, the Council of Reims, preserved by Regino, book I, chapter 272, speaking of the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer, says: “When they come to confession during Lent, let the priest have each parishioner sing these by heart; and let him not give anyone holy communion before he knows how to recite them from memory.” What was said in the first clause as “by memory” is expressed in the second by the words “from the heart.”

Let him know by heart the sermon of Athanasius, bishop, on the faith of the Trinity, which begins: “Whoever wishes.”

Let him be able to recite clearly and distinctly the exorcisms and prayers for making a catechumen, for consecrating the font, and the other prayers over a male and a female, in both plural and singular forms. Likewise, let him know the order for baptizing in order to assist the sick.

> **Note:** For the order of baptizing in order to assist the sick, see *Book I of the Gelasian Sacramentary*, chapter 72 and following.

Let him also know the order for reconciling, according to the manner canonically reserved to him, and for anointing the sick; and let him at least know how to read well the prayers appropriate to that need.

Likewise, let him know the order and prayers for conducting the funeral rites of the dead.

Likewise, let him know by heart the exorcisms and blessings of salt and water.

Let him know the nocturnal and diurnal chant.

Let him understand, if possible, the lesser computus—that is, the epacts, concurrent cycles, regulars, the paschal term, and the rest.

> **Note:** *Concurrentes* and *regulares* are technical terms belonging to ecclesiastical computation; writers on that computation explain them more fully.

Let him have a Martyrology and a Penitential, and so forth.

> **Note:** Here ends what was excerpted by Ratherius from the synodal *Admonition*. It is surprising that he wrote “and so forth” and omitted the few words which are added in the same *Admonition* preserved by Baluzius, as also in the *Inquiry*: “so that, according to what is written there, he may question the person confessing, or impose on the person who has confessed the proper manner of penance.” These words, however, are likewise omitted in the Augsburg manuscript’s synodal sermon, which, after “Let him have a Penitential,” also adds, like Ratherius, “and so forth.”

## 13

Concerning those who are to be ordained, know for certain that they will in no way be promoted by us unless they have spent some time either in our city, or in a monastery, or with some learned man, and have acquired at least a little learning in letters, so that they may appear suitable for ecclesiastical dignity.

> **Note:** This passage indicates three kinds of schools in which clerics were instructed: one in the city, perhaps at the cathedral; another in monasteries; and a third under some learned man.

## 14.

Since ecclesiastical authority also contains the provision [Col. 0564C] that, from ecclesiastical revenues, four portions ought to be made—one for the bishop, another for the church building, a third for the clergy, and a fourth for the poor [Col. 0565A] and guests—if you have your full share, do not be envious of those portions that belong to the bishop, the building, or the poor, remembering that the Lord commanded: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s property” (Exod. 20:17); and: “Do not concern yourself with property that does not belong to you.” But concerning the portion that belongs to you, maintain trust among yourselves and divide it communally, whether it is large or small, knowing that the Apostle said: “Let no one defraud his brother in business,” that is, in the matter of the remaining portion, “because the Lord is the avenger of all these things,” as we foretold and testified to you (1 Thess. 4:6). Know also that it is better for every Christian to suffer fraud than to commit it (1 Cor. 6:7).

[Note: [Col. 0565B] The adverb *pleniter* is absent from the Freising manuscript; from that manuscript we subsequently added *non* before *pertinet*, since the discussion there concerns things that do not belong to you but to others. In what follows, however, the subject is what belongs to you. It should be noted that at this time the clergy belonged only to that portion of the church’s revenues which was theirs, and not to the other three portions belonging to the bishop, the building, or the poor, since these were at the bishop’s disposal.]

## 15.

Observe Lent equally, except on Sundays; for if you fast one day and gorge yourself the next, you have kept not Lent but a twentieth. [Col. 0565B]

[Note: [Col. 0565B] Compare the second sermon on Lent, no. 1, where the author attacks this abuse.]

During the Advent of the Lord, unless a feast intervenes, know that for four weeks abstinence must be made from meat and sexual intercourse.

[Note: [Col. 0565B] Abstinence, especially from meat during Advent except on feast days, was prescribed in our regions in the tenth century and deserves notice. This abstinence, together with fasting, is recorded as having been imposed during Advent upon all who were able to observe it, but especially upon clerics, in the Council of Aprincat in 1072, canon 11. Menard, note 540 on the Gregorian Sacramentary, p. 445, demonstrates that this discipline was older and varied in Gaul. Furthermore, when the author says that at certain times one must abstain from intercourse, and then that one must abstain entirely even from licit intercourse, he addresses priests and other clerics because above, no. 10, he had prescribed from the formula of the Synodal Admonition: “Exhort married men to abstain from their wives at certain times.” Here he teaches them which times these are. The common text soon after reads *liti[aniarum]*; the correction is supplied by the excellent Freising manuscript. The days called “litanies” are the days of the Greater Litany and of the Rogations.]

At the Nativity of the Lord, for twenty days and nights, one must abstain entirely even from licit intercourse; likewise during the octave of Easter and of Pentecost, on the days of the litanies, on the vigils of all feasts, and also on Fridays, but especially on all Sundays, by day and by night. Since the authority of the paschal feast compels us, we sincerely admonish your affection, whom we ought to love in Christ, brothers, to fast on Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday of Holy Week until the ninth hour,

[Note: [Col. 0565C] What Rather says here about fasting on the weekdays of Holy Week is taught in the same way concerning the entire Lenten period in the second sermon on Lent, nos. 3 and 6. This is the first testimony from a certain author to a mitigated rule requiring the Lenten fast to continue only until the ninth hour; according to the older discipline, the fast had to continue until evening. Two other testimonies occur among the sermons attributed to St. Ambrose and may appear older than Rather. One is read as sermon 26 in the Roman edition, the other as sermon 33, which in the Appendix to the latest Benedictine edition alone is numbered sermon 25.

The earlier sermon says concerning Lent: “During this appointed season, except on Sunday and Saturday, let no one presume to eat before the ninth hour.” The other says: “What sort of Christian is one who does not fast during such a season, even until the ninth hour?” And shortly afterward: “Let none of you, unless perhaps he is sick or an infant, eat or drink before the ninth hour until Easter, except on Sundays.”

The first sermon, however, numbered 26 among the Ambrosian sermons, is attributed in the appendix to volume 5 of St. Augustine to St. Caesarius of Arles; moreover, it lacks not only the words “and Saturday” but also “before the ninth hour.” Consequently, these words were inserted at the discretion of some copyist, as often happens in lectionaries, apparently at a later time, when the Lenten fast was customarily broken at the ninth hour. The words “and Saturday” were certainly also added in the place where Saturday was excluded from fasting during Lent.

The other sermon, no. 33 in the Roman edition, was rightly removed from St. Ambrose by the Benedictine Fathers, both because it mentions the ninth hour itself and because its author is uncertain. It belongs either to a later period or, if it is somewhat older than Rather, has suffered an interpolation in the word “ninth” at the discretion of some copyist who wished to express the practice of his own time and place.

The ancient discipline of fasting until evening during Lent remained in force in some places not only in Rather’s time, when the milder discipline began, but for a considerable period afterward. St. Udalric, bishop of Augsburg and a contemporary of Rather, ate during Lent only after evening, as Gerard relates in his Life, chapter 4, no. 18. Micrologus, a witness of the following, eleventh, century, says in *On Ecclesiastical Matters*, chapter 49: “Nor are we judged to fast in the Lenten manner according to the canons if we refresh ourselves before evening.” From the twelfth century there is likewise the notable testimony of St. Bernard, sermon 3 on Lent, no. 1: “Until now we alone—that is, the monks—have fasted until the ninth hour; now all alike will fast with us until evening: kings and princes, clergy and people, noble and common, rich and poor, together as one.”

The Council of Rouen in 1072 seems to have established something somewhat milder, permitting the fast to be broken after the ninth hour, at the beginning of evening, in canon 21, in these words: “Let no one eat during Lent before the ninth hour has been completed and evening has begun; for one who eats beforehand is not fasting.”]

except for infants, those worn out by advanced age, and the sick. On Thursday, come to the mother church at the ninth hour, all who are to be reconciled.

[Note: [Col. 0566D] “Mother church” means the cathedral church, to which all penitents had to come on Thursday of Holy Week to be reconciled by the bishop. Earlier, in no. 10, parish priests had been instructed to invite the people to confession on the Wednesday before Lent and to impose penance upon them according to the character of their offense. But the reconciliation of public penitents, which took place on Maundy Thursday, belonged exclusively to the bishop; priests were to bring to the bishop those who had suitably performed their penance and to provide testimony that the penance had been completed. In this sense he had earlier prescribed, no. 8: “Let none of you bring anyone who has done penance less worthily, for whatever reason, to reconciliation” [understand: to the bishop], “or provide him with testimony of reconciliation.”]

On Friday fast until the ninth hour, and longer if anyone wishes. On Saturday let no one presume to sing Mass before the tenth hour [Col. 0567A] or to celebrate a general baptism.

[Note: [Col. 0567A] A “general baptism” was so called because it was administered generally to everyone at the appointed time of the Easter or Pentecost vigil. Hence above, no. 10, it is prescribed: “Let no one presume to baptize except at the vigil of Easter or Pentecost, unless there is danger of death.” Baptism administered outside those times to persons in danger of death was called “particular baptism.” The same sense of “general baptism” occurs in the Council of Rouen of 1072: “Let no general baptism take place except on Easter Saturday and Pentecost Saturday, while this provision is observed: that infants, whenever and on whatever day they ask for it, must not be denied the bath of regeneration.” This exception for infants seems to have been introduced because their lives are easily endangered.]

If, because of illness, someone cannot fast, the fast observed by the universal Church should benefit him; for we are all one body in Christ. Only let no one, through his own obstinacy, compel the whole of our Church to offend against the Lord and to violate in any respect so glorious a feast. Know that you may impose penance for hidden sins; concerning public sins, recognize that they must be reported to us.

[Note: [Col. 0567B] Thus the Freising manuscript reads, better than the printed texts, *deferendum* rather than *referendum*.]

Let none of you make a cleric without our permission; let no one make a stammerer, or one who lisps beyond measure, or one who has a dull understanding of letters.

[Note: [Col. 0567B] “Let him make a cleric,” that is, let him enroll him among the clergy or clothe him in clerical dress. At this time the rural parish priests whom he addresses had already claimed this power for themselves. He censures them for it in the *Judicatum*, no. 5: “How little knowledge he has of the whole of canonical law is readily apparent who thinks that what another is permitted to do—to send a cleric to a church—is the same as making a cleric or expelling him from it, unless the person who can, whenever he wishes, make an acolyte from a cleric is also able to make a cleric.” He indicates that just as the ordination of clerics belongs to the bishop alone, so does their making.]

If a feast that is not a feast of holy Mary, the Mother of God, or of the apostles occurs during Lent or during the fasts of the four seasons, know that the fast must be observed rather than the feast celebrated—

[Note: [Col. 0568A] Here Rather is demanding that no feasts of the saints be celebrated during Lent or the Ember fasts, except the feasts of Blessed Mary, the apostles, and the patron saint of the church. This derives from ancient discipline; see the Council of Laodicea, canon 51. His reason—that on these days the fast must be observed rather than the feast celebrated—refers to the discipline by which fasting was not observed on feast days, nor on the Sundays of Lent, since they too were feast days. Hence the commonly attributed Alcuin, *On the Divine Offices*, says: “We celebrate solemnly and with great rejoicing the days of the saints on which they departed from this world, so much so that on those days, relaxing somewhat the severity of abstinence, we live a little more leniently.” For this reason the feasts of ancient saints whose death days fell during Lent were transferred to another time.]

unless perhaps it is the feast of a saint whose shrine lies in the same parish. For God takes pleasure in no solemnity more than in that fast by which one abstains from food and from vices: “Idleness is also an enemy of the soul” (St. Benedict, *Rule*, chapter 48). Consider whether, without knowledge of what we have set forth above, you can perform your ministry, lead the peoples entrusted to you to life, and present them to Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0568B] Thus the Freising manuscript reads; the printed texts incorrectly have *praesumimus* instead of *praemisimus*.]

[Col. 0567]

# RATHER’S LITTLE WORK

## On Someone’s Unlawful Marriage

[Note: [Col. 0567C] Acherius published this little work from the Laon manuscript. Since it condemns a marriage entered into during Lent, it was written shortly after Lent. Since no. 3 mentions another work, namely the *Conjecture of Quality*, composed around the beginning of 966, this work must have been written after Lent of that year or, at the latest, the following year. It does not seem possible to assign it to 968, since Rather gives no indication in it of the disturbances stirred up against him during and after Lent of that year, which led him to resign the episcopate. If he had written this work after Lent of 967, upon returning from the Council of Ravenna and insisting, with the authority of the council, the supreme pontiff, and the emperor behind him, that clerics must dismiss their wives, it is wholly incredible that he would have mentioned no such authority when, in this work, he urged that daughters not be given in marriage to clerics. We therefore believe that this work was composed earlier, after Lent of 966.]

“Upon my back sinners have built” (Ps. 128:3), the Psalmist cries out; and the Apostle likewise: “Not only those who do these things, but also those who consent to those who do them, are worthy of death” (Rom. 1:32). While my own burdens are exceedingly heavy, I am most wretchedly weighed down by burdens belonging to others beyond measure. Constrained, therefore, by this twofold anxiety, I grieve over John, a son of our Church,

[Note: [Col. 0568C] John was a son of our Church, that is, a cleric. Shortly afterward, Acherius’s edition reads *quanquam* where it should read *quamdam*.]

because, as is reported, he had a certain girl betrothed to his son during Lent and took her home on Sunday night—an illegality, namely, a double one, just as our Pedrevertus had done earlier.

[Note: [Col. 0568C] This double illegality can be understood and explained in two ways. First, since in no. 2 the author censures this marriage under two headings, writing that he “began it during the days of holy Lent and completed it on Sunday night,” one illegality seems to arise from violating the Lenten season and the other from violating Sunday. Yet the words in the present text, “had betrothed [her] in Lent,” which correspond to “began it during the days of holy Lent,” refer to the betrothal. How could this be said to violate Lent, if the sacred canons forbid weddings, not betrothals, during that season? Moreover, since the words “took her home on Sunday night,” which correspond to “completed it on Sunday night,” refer to the marriage, how can the marriage be said specifically to have violated Sunday, if on Sundays outside the prohibited seasons marriages were not forbidden, but only marital intercourse, as is clear from the Synodal Admonition, no. 15?

Could Rather, although in the note concerning Lent he mentions betrothal with the word *despondi*, have intended not to mark the betrothal but only the marriage with a double illegality—that is, because, having been entered into immediately after the betrothal, it violated the prohibited Lenten season, and because it was not only entered into but also consummated on Sunday, violated that day as well?

Another explanation may perhaps be more likely: one illegality refers to the cleric’s marriage, which the author immediately attacks at greater length below, while the other lies in the marriage itself, contracted and consummated by the same cleric after the betrothal during the prohibited season. Rather likewise reproaches Pedrevertus for this double illegality. You may prefer either explanation.]

When anyone brings his son into the clergy, it seems that, as he in fact does, he removes him from the world and gives him to the Lord. Thus, whereas previously he ought to live by the law by which the commonwealth lives, afterward he begins to live by canonical law; and just as at first he belonged to the official authority of the commonwealth, afterward he belongs to the prelate of the Church—that is, to the bishop lawfully instituted. Since this is so, when someone dedicates his son canonically to the Church, so that he may serve the Lord, and afterward acquires for him a secular marriage, it is plainly evident that with the same hand by which he had given him to God he takes him away from the Lord, and, having taken him away from the Church, returns him—oh, sacrilege!—to the secular court.

[Note: [Col. 0569C] This passage may suggest that clerics who married no longer remained in the clergy. Yet in the following section he says: “How good is that father . . . who, taking him [his son] away from God’s portion for the sake of three fields of vines, returns him to the power of this world!” Nor should the contrary be persuaded upon us by what he says in no. 4 concerning incontinent priests: “Since, alas, you are in no way able to be restrained from women, at least let the sons born from you remain laymen, and join your daughters to laymen.” In no. 5, addressing the woman who had given her brother’s daughter in marriage to John’s clerical son, he says: “Would that you had given his daughter, blessed with his possessions, to one good layman, not to a cleric.”

Thus, when clerics married, they did not fall from the clerical order and rank. For this reason he complains that adultery of this kind does not come to an end: clerics bound by this unlawful marriage begot sons and daughters; these in turn, likewise clerics, took wives, and the women were given to clerics, and so on without end, as he explains more fully in no. 4. As for the extent to which clerics were subject to the secular court on account of such marriages, they were subject not on their own account but on account of the women and children; see Atto, bishop, letter 9, to the clergy of Vercelli. In these practices the beginnings of that corruption are already apparent—not slight or obscure—which spread more broadly in the following century, when clerical marriages came to be thought permissible. We have discussed this at greater length in the *Life of the Author*, section 15.]

Let him who does this, therefore, not be angry, I suggest, if God takes away from him some of what He mercifully granted him, whether through the violence of a storm or through the oppressive action of some power, either in this world or in the next. Otherwise, speaking as I may, God would seem not to know how to act, and could learn from his example, as though He were saying: “You took away from Me what you had given; following your example, I take away from you what I had given.”

## 2.

O insatiable greed of the human race, how much you are not ashamed to commit against God—how unlawful, how shameful, how dishonorable!

[Note: [Col. 0570C] “Insatiable” modifies the greed of the human race: how many things you are not ashamed to commit against God, how unlawful, and so forth.]

Since every cleric is so called because he is “of the Lord’s portion,” that is, because he belongs to God’s share, what a good father he is, what a lover of his son, who for the sake of three fields of vines—

[Note: [Col. 0570C] These words indicate the dowry given to the son. Since this is the only passage in Rather’s works that prefers a vineyard consisting of fields, whereas elsewhere he always distinguishes fields from vineyards, one may suspect that here too we should read “for the sake of three vineyards and fields.”]

—takes him away from God’s portion and returns him to the power of this world, and consequently of the devil. For the devil is called by the Lord “the prince of this world” (John 16:11)—not of heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them, but of wicked people who, loving the world more than God, enjoy it temporarily, destined to lose what they ought eternally to possess in heaven, serving the devil rather than Christ.

Suppose, however, that both of them did this because, in comparison with a worse evil, they judged it better for him to be joined to one woman than to wander about more dangerously among many.

[Note: [Col. 0570C] John and Pedrevertus are meant. For John is said to have committed the same act—giving a wife to a clerical son—and to have done so at a prohibited time, as Pedrevertus had earlier done. Their common crime was therefore the same. John preceded Pedrevertus in one respect: Pedrevertus contrived to commit the act secretly, whereas John did it so openly that he did not allow anyone in the city to remain unaware of it.]

Yet this man, the subject of our mournful discourse, surpasses the other in crime because he began this during the days of holy Lent and completed it on Sunday night; whereas the other contrived to carry it out secretly, this man did it so openly, alas, that no one in the city could remain unaware of it.

[Note: [Col. 0570D] The discipline forbidding marriages during Lent was evidently so firmly established that those who violated it did so secretly. This man, however, who violated it so openly, is charged with a much greater crime, and the public scandal, it is thought, must not be left without public condemnation. Hence public penance is also prescribed for such offenders in no. 6.]

Therefore, this does not seem to us something that ought to be suppressed in silence. For if it is left without reproach, it will plainly appear to have been rightly done. No one will fail to take an example from it once he learns that no one has condemned it.

## 3.

Amazingly, someone else also did this—the man who in another work of ours is described under his proper name as a “twister of words” and a “distorter of laws”—

[Note: [Col. 0570D] “In another work of ours” means the *Conjecture of Quality*, no. 11, where he calls the person mentioned here Erimbertus. We judged that his proper name should replace the suppressed name found in the printed texts, unless one prefers to write “with the name suppressed,” which amounts to the same thing. The passage should be construed and explained as follows: “While he could often hear, together with the other lawmakers, the saying addressed to him: ‘Love justice, you who judge the earth,’ etc.” Erimbertus was evidently a judge. “And while no law, as we suppose, contains the provision that something once legally given to someone should be taken away from him without a legitimate complaint. Since reason indicates that the complaint itself must be either some fault or some necessity, after examining and reexamining everything, we find that it is God against whom this injury is seen to have been committed, in whom,” etc. It is therefore clear that Erimbertus too joined a son once dedicated to God—that is, a cleric—in marriage.]

while he could often hear himself addressed, together with all the other lawmakers, in the words: “Love justice, you who judge the earth” (Wis. 1:1); and while, as we suppose, no law contains the rule that a thing once legally given to someone ought to be taken away from him without a legitimate complaint. Since reason indicates that the complaint itself must be either some fault or some necessity, after examining and reexamining everything, we find that the one against whom this injury is seen to have been committed is God, in whom neither fault can be found nor necessity demonstrated.

For He feeds all things; still less can His specially assigned portion perish from hunger.

[Note: [Col. 0571D] “His specially assigned portion,” that is, the cleric specially assigned to God. He is called a cleric because he is “of the Lord’s portion,” as the author explained in the preceding section.]

He would certainly have acted better if, since as a father he owed his son this duty, he had contributed from his modest means some assistance for the son’s service to the Lord. Yet afterward, it is reported, he drove him away, unwilling to grant him the same allowance.

[Note: [Col. 0571D] This seems to indicate that Erimbertus induced his clerical son to marry and afterward drove him from the house because he was unwilling to grant him from his modest means the allowance which, as a father, he owed him. The son, on contracting the marriage, may be presumed to have acquired a sufficiently substantial dowry and therefore no longer needed his father’s support.]

## 4.

And alas, how grave a crime it is—one that cannot come to an end even when the criminal dies! For example, if someone unjustly invades another person’s field, as often happens, and leaves that field to his son with the same injustice, and his successor in turn leaves it to his own successor, and so on, until the end of the world, with all those descended by one succession or another from that first invader doing the same: when will the injustice of the man who first sowed that field come to an end, unless only when all creation comes to an end?

In the same way, since everyone knows that anyone who has intercourse with a woman other than his lawful wife commits fornication or adultery, and since a priest or deacon cannot have a lawful wife, if a priest makes a presbyter of a son begotten through fornication or, worse, adultery, that man makes another presbyter of a son similarly begotten; that one again makes his own, and his own successor another. As this proceeds little by little until the end of the world, whose adultery is it except that of the man who first sowed it?

[Note: [Col. 0571D] *Adultery* is used here in the broader sense of any illicit sexual union; see Du Cange. Here, as elsewhere, Rather calls the unlawful marriage of clerics adultery. It is called adultery in a somewhat more proper sense because it violates persons consecrated to God.]

Therefore, brothers, you must be admonished and entreated: since, alas, you are in no way able to be restrained from women, at least let the sons born from you remain laymen, and join your daughters to laymen, so that your adultery may at least come to an end with your death and never last until the end of the world.

[Note: [Col. 0572C] In the *Itinerary*, no. 5, he charges several clerics with the vice of womanizing; and in no. 10 he says that scarcely any are free from this crime. Hence we understand why it is written that “you are in no way able to be restrained from women.”]

## 5.

You will reply: “The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father” (Ezek. 18:20), and so forth. We reply in turn: “I am,” He says, “a strong God, jealous, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children” (Exod. 20:5), and so forth.

The blessed Gregory, treating these two sayings of the Lord as though they were contradictory—in one of which it is said, “The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, nor the father that of the son,” and in the other, “I am a strong and jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children to the fourth and fifth generation”—brings them into agreement through what follows, namely, “among those who hate me” (Moral. book 15, chapter 31). He asserts that if the evil will of the children does not agree with the evil will of their fathers, just as the will of the apostles did not agree with the will of their parents, the wickedness of evil fathers does no harm to the good will of good children. But if the children do the same things that their fathers, who hated God, did, they will be condemned not only for their own wickedness but also for that of their fathers. And their fathers, I think, are justly punished not only for their own sin but also for that of their children, who followed their fathers’ example and did not cease to practice the same things their fathers had done.

O that you, my lady,

[Note: [Col. 0572C] He calls “my lady” the paternal aunt of the girl whom she had given in marriage to the clerical son of the aforementioned John. The girl’s father, who was already dead and had left considerable property to his sister and daughter, had been a cleric, as the following words suggest: “you had put an end to his sin.” His sin is understood to be the marriage he had entered into as a cleric. That sin would already have come to an end in him if his daughter had married a layman rather than a cleric.]

to whom such a good brother left such great possessions, had thought of this beforehand and had given his daughter, blessed with his property,

[Note: [Col. 0572D] The printed texts read *benedicta*. The new editor of the *Spicilegium* suspected that something was missing here and proposed the following: “It would have been more advisable if her aunt had not allowed that cleric’s daughter to marry; but if she was to be given in marriage, she ought to have been married to another, namely, to one who was a layman and the son of a layman.” We think it sufficient to print the lighter correction *benedictam* instead of *benedicta*. He calls the daughter “blessed” because she received a considerable part of her father’s possessions.]

to one good layman, and had put an end to his sin. As long as it continues, that sin will scarcely be expiated by innumerable almsgivings, I hope you understand.

But when the Lord says to certain people: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you tithe mint and dill and cumin, and have left aside the weightier matters of the law—judgment, mercy, and faith” (Matt. 23:23)—

[Note: [Col. 0573B] Here we believe Rather is expressing the wish that the body of that cleric, who was the brother of the woman mentioned, might be buried in a public cemetery where rain would fall upon it day and night. At this time the custom of burying people in a church or in a special tomb had not prevailed, whether for clerics or priests. But since his sister was wealthy, she took care that her brother’s body would not be buried under the open sky; instead, she arranged for a tomb to be constructed either in the church or in the cemetery itself, which protected the body from the rain.]

would that rain fell day and night upon your brother’s body, which you took the greatest care to prevent; and would that this moisture, so harmful, so foul, so loathsome, did not so grievously afflict, soil, stain, and torment his soul.

## 6.

I therefore advise the persons prescribed above, and all who recognize that in such a crime they have violated either Lent, or some especially solemn fast, or Sunday night, or any distinguished feast, to do penance with me for forty days. I too have until now been consenting because I did not resist.

[Note: [Col. 0573B] Since this forty-day penance was imposed after Lent, it also includes the hours of eating that are not appropriate during Lent. Eating at the third hour was suitable on days when no prescribed fast was in force. On some fasting days outside Lent, no food could be taken before the sixth hour; on others, not before the ninth. During Lent, food was to be taken after evening, unless the milder discipline prevailed by which the fast could also be broken after the ninth hour during Lent, as is established from Rather’s Synodal Admonition. See the note there, no. 980, col. 565.]

Thus, if the other faithful take food at the third hour, we should take it at the sixth; if they at the sixth, we at the ninth; if they at the ninth, [Col. 0574A] we should fast until evening. Let us by no means cease from giving alms according to our ability; yet let us not even for that reason believe that we have thereby been justified. For this is not a crime that can easily be corrected.

Nevertheless, let us not despair of God’s mercy: “For a man does not know,” it says, “whether he is worthy of hatred or love, but all things remain uncertain for the future” (Eccles. 9:1). But if you reject this—as I suspect, indeed as I am certain you do—and do not wish to fast with me, then either I excommunicate you temporarily or God condemns you eternally. The matter will be your concern, and no fault of mine. Likewise, I invite you, whom I addressed somewhat earlier, to penance; for it is advantageous to you and perhaps will benefit your brother.

[Col. 0573]

# RATHER’S LITTLE WORK

## On Idle Speech

[Note: [Col. 0573C] We here publish for the first time this little work from the Freising manuscript. Acherius had received it from a copy made from the Lobbes manuscript and had raised hopes of publishing it; yet it never appeared anywhere. In the margin of the Freising manuscript, another, as it were, title is recorded: “Invective against any instructor, especially a spiritual one.” The “idle word” reproved here in no. 5 is ascribed to Rather himself by a scoffer in the *Conjecture of Quality*, no. 7: “He even admits that he uttered one idle word, and, as he compels us to believe, a most shameful one in such a place,” etc. Furthermore, it may be inferred from the cited Freising manuscript that this little work was written by the same author at Verona after his third restoration, since it contains no works of his except those of the same period. Since, moreover, in the same manuscript, which seems to follow chronological order—as we shall show more fully in the notes on the first sermon on Lent—this work is placed after the Synodal Admonition and the sermon on Mary and Martha, which were composed in 966, it too seems to be assigned to that year, having been written after the sermon on Mary and Martha, delivered after the feast of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary.]

[Col. 0573B] 431–432

### 1. A Statement

[Note: [Col. 0573D] Construe: “To demonstrate briefly that the statement of a certain passage of Scripture, already made familiar by fourfold mention because I said that I was restored from despair only by this, while I weighed the deeds of myself and of those like me; to demonstrate, I say, that the statement of a certain passage of Scripture has not yet satisfied me, I repeat it, as often, in the same words: ‘Man does not know …’” To this statement, if permitted, I shall append something for my own case. We find this statement, “Man does not know …,” reported in seven of Rather’s works: namely, in the *Confession*, no. 26; in Sermon 2 on Lent, no. 23; in another sermon on Pentecost, no. 2; at the end of Book II of *On Contempt for the Canons*; in *On His Own Fall*, no. 3; *On an Illicit Marriage*, no. 6; and in the *Itinerary*, no. 10. By “fourfold mention,” we believe, he indicates four of these works, which had previously been composed at Verona. The book of the *Confession* was written not at Verona but in a Belgian monastery. We think that the *Itinerary* was arranged somewhat later than this work. The Freising copy read *quod ait me* (“which says me”); the sense requires *quod hac me* (“which this [saying] caused me”).]

To demonstrate briefly that the statement of a certain passage of Scripture, already made familiar by fourfold mention because I said that I was restored from despair only by this, while I weighed solely the deeds of myself and of those like me, has not yet satisfied me, I repeat it, as often, in the same words:

“Man does not know whether he is worthy of hatred or of love; but all things are kept uncertain for the future” (Eccles. IX, 1).

To this, if permitted, I shall append something concerning myself. I do not deny that I myself do not know why or for what reason I have brought it forward so often. I know, I know that I am truly worthy of hatred if I do not cease from the things to which I am accustomed.

[Note: [Col. 0574D] The Frisian copy has *ab assertis* (“from things asserted”), and later *et efficio* (“and I accomplish”); both are erroneous.]

[Col. 0575A] But whether it is granted me to cease from them entirely before the appointed end of life, I confess that I do not know at all. For I try to become better, and I am defeated; I labor, and I fail; I rise, and I fall back again; I never remain in the condition of any good.

[Note: [Col. 0575D] Construe: “For, unhappy and wretched, frequently returning to the habit of the dog’s vomit and the pig’s wallowing”—an allusion to 2 Peter II, 22: “The dog has returned to its own vomit, and the washed sow to her wallowing in the mud”—“and restoring myself only by this statement, since I cannot find anything else, I despair while hoping,” and so forth.]

For, unhappy and wretched, I repeatedly return to the dog’s vomit and the pig’s wallowing (2 Peter II, 22); and, restoring myself only by this statement, since I am unable to find anything else, I despair while hoping, hope while despairing, trust while distrustful, and distrust while confident. For I am confident that he will grant everything that the Lord has promised; but I distrust that I can be found worthy for him to bestow the promises upon me. Yet he promises forgiveness to no one except the converted; and when I see myself incapable of conversion, I do not despair of his mercy, but I tremble at my own hardness.

And what more? I both know and confess that I am more worthy of hatred than of love, if I die as I now am. But whether it is destined for me to die in such a state, I do not know at all. If I die in such a state, I do not deny that everyone could be certain of my destruction.

### 2.

Since many are accustomed to postpone conversion until the end of life, while sudden death, snatching away countless people, makes them altogether insensible—not merely many of them—I hesitate about what I should think of those people; but, if this were to happen to me, I am almost in despair concerning myself.

Some people, while lying sick in bed, made many promises to God, which, once they recovered, they paid no attention to at all. What, then, when they fell again? If they had not made promises, they were rightly thought to have perished once more through despair; but if they had made promises and, after recovering again, proved false, what will such people do afterward?

What? May God’s mercy teach them. Yet this is what seems to me: even if this should happen to them a thousand times through the devil’s prompting, they should not therefore despair of the Lord’s mercy, although they can place no confidence in such unstable promises. For a person does not know whether he will be worthy of hatred or of love in the future (Eccles. IX, 1), although he knows that at present he is worthy of hatred, since Scripture says: “The Almighty hates sinners and has mercy on the just” (Ecclus. XII, 3).

For the just could not have been made from sinners in any other way except by being converted from evil to good after being preceded by God’s mercy; nor could the others have remained in their sins in any other way except by being permitted, through God’s justice, to be hardened. Hence there is also that fearful statement of the one who says:

“If the Lord has shut a man in”—that is, if he has permitted him to be shut in—“who can say to him, ‘Why do you do this?’” (Job IX, 12.)

### 3.

O then, O inscrutable judgments of God! O unsearchable ways of his! For who among those like me can avoid fearing that he will inevitably be shut in and thereby become worthy of hatred?

Is anyone not worthy of hatred—leaving the rest aside—about whom the Apostle seems to say:

“Know this and understand: no fornicator, or unclean person, or covetous person—which is the service of idols—has an inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God” (Ephesians V, 5)?

Since countless people converted from such practices and ceased to be fornicators, unclean persons, or covetous persons, it is plainly understood that this was said concerning those who remain in such crimes.

A person remains in crime when, as long as age or health supports him so that he can commit it, he does not cease committing it; or, if he ceases, does not strive to cleanse it away through repentance. When old age or illness prevents someone from carrying it out, it is not the crime that has ceased, but the crime that is proved to have abandoned him. Thus, even someone who ceases from fornication does not cease to be a fornicator if he does not stop fornicating for as long as he can, and does not strive to cleanse the fornication he has abandoned through fasts, almsgiving, and tearful groans.

Therefore, when we read or hear, “A person does not know whether he is worthy of hatred or of love,” unless we understand “in the future” as implied, so that the sense is that no one knows whether he will be granted conversion before death or whether he will remain in sins until the end of his health, I confess that I am completely ignorant of what the statement intends to establish.

### 4.

Although one should not despair that illness itself may cleanse anyone of his former sins, provided that it is received gratefully—though I think this can happen only through a prolonged illness, endured patiently, as I have said—even if someone who sings such a verse has understood it more lightly:

[Col. 0576C]

“And brief punishment here ends harmful crimes,

lest guilty people bear punishment without end.”

But Gregory says: “Temporal scourges free from eternal punishments only those whom they change.”

[Note: [Col. 0575D] Construe: “Therefore, while relying upon that statement which says, ‘Man does not know …,’ I await these two things: either a saving conversion or the support of God’s scourges. If I do not remain suspicious and fearful of the third—namely, certain destruction—I believe that I am truly insane, and I do not know where to turn my desire, what to wish for, or what to embrace.”]

Therefore, while relying upon that statement which says, “Man does not know whether he is worthy of hatred or of love,” I await these two things, namely either a saving conversion or the support of God’s scourges. If I do not remain suspicious and fearful of the third—namely, certain destruction—I truly believe that I am insane, and I do not know where to turn my desire, what to wish for, or what to embrace.

For, while I fear that sudden destruction threatens me, I confess that I desire a prolonged illness—if I deserve it—yet hear the Apostle, though I am deaf, immediately condemning me, saying:

“Do you not know that God’s patience is leading you to repentance? But you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of God’s just judgment” (Romans II, 4–5).

[Note: [Col. 0576D] It seems that *prolixam aegritudinem* (“a prolonged illness”) should be restored and supplied here: this agrees with what precedes, “which nevertheless, I think, can happen through a prolonged illness,” and so forth.]

Unhappy is such longevity, followed by so great a calamity: it accumulates a contemptible span of time, which this miserable reprieve has granted for piling up such a treasure, so as to enlarge the punishment of crimes. It would have been better, I confess, for the most wretched man to have received a just sentence at the first contempt of God than, after being awaited so long, to have accumulated so many offenses, each of which he must suffer eternal punishment for.

### 5.

In this state of affairs, a shorter life seems more fortunate to me than a longer one. For the prophet says:

“Woe to you who drag iniquity with cords of vanity!” (Isaiah V, 18.)

The Lord is indeed merciful and ineffably compassionate, but he is also truthful and indescribably just. He promises forgiveness and reckons guilt; he grants forgiveness to those who are perfectly converted, but reserves guilt for those who are hardened and turned away.

Is not the reckoning of guilt clearly shown by the statement:

“Amen I say to you, people will give an account on the day of judgment for every idle word that they have spoken” (Matthew XII, 36)?

Was anything ever said more terrifying? Let others see what they think about this; it seems to me that it would have been more bearable if he had said: “They will deserve a punishment of a thousand years for it.”

For nothing is less useful than shameful things. What if, in that same place—

[Note: [Col. 0577D] See *A Conjecture on Quality*, no. 7, and *On His Own Fall*, no. 4.]

—and perhaps in such a place that someone would disdain even to eat there—someone, while doing something shameful, said something exceedingly shameful? Afterwards he repented of the shameful deed he had committed; but what, I ask, will become of the shameful thing he said?

If, then, at the judgment he is reproached for having said such a thing in such a place and for such a reason, can it be thought that he will in any way be able to hear among the others, “Come, blessed of my Father” (Matthew XXV, 34)? After such great shame before the entire human race, can we suppose that he will possess any glory at all, much less heavenly glory?

Will not what he did also be revealed, when perhaps he did what he said and said what he did? A fitting punishment for a rebel: since he did not revere the Lord, nor the name “Christianity” that he derived from him, and, knowing that the Lord was present in such a place and remembering him, did not fear to dishonor him so shamefully, let him perish, dishonored in the sight of the whole creation.

But what will wretched people say about their very frequent perjuries, their constant slanders, their continual lies, their deceptive words, their mocking words, their most fraudulent promises, their frequent curses, if we are to undergo judgment for “Raca,” hell for “Fool,” and give an account for an idle word? (Matthew V, 22.)

[Col. 0577D] Understand with me, you who with me forget God, lest we be suddenly snatched away and rescued by no one (Psalm XLIX, 22).

### 6.

“I understand,” you say, “that, alas, I have forgotten God more often than was necessary and, indeed fearing, [corrupt passage], you intimate that you should act lest you be suddenly snatched away and rescued by no one.”

But when I compare with this the Apostle’s statement about the voluntary judgment inflicted upon us by ourselves—

[Note: [Col. 0577D] Construe: “But when I compare that apostolic statement about the voluntary judgment inflicted upon us by ourselves—when, I say, I compare it with what I remember hearing very recently, I confess that I am greatly encouraged.”]

—which I remember hearing very recently, I confess that I am greatly encouraged.

For the following was read:

“If you have rightly considered your sins, you have judged yourself; if you have cast them away, you have killed them.”

[Col. 0578A] To make this clearer—although many things could be supplied, it must be explained how that one divine statement which you uttered is sufficient for us—he says:

“People will give an account on the day of judgment for every idle word that they have spoken” (Matthew XII, 36).

What is an idle word? An unprofitable one. But, as you said, nothing is less useful than shameful things. To these we can add harmful, insulting, mocking, deceitful, perjured, fraudulent, cursing, lying, sacrilegious, heretical, apostate, blasphemous, false-witness-bearing, furious, and quarrelsome words.

From all these, by presenting one of them in his earlier argument, you concluded that no one could be believed destined for salvation if, on the last day of judgment, it were reproached before the entire human race that he had said such a thing in such a place and for such a reason.

But while you grant that we must hold most firmly that nothing can be done temporally against right and justice without temporal expiation, we are compelled to despair of the one who said that shameful thing, unless we provide him with help by which he may act before he comes to that reproach.

Let us therefore first say what will happen to those who will have to give an account on the day of judgment for every idle word that we have spoken—namely, to those to whom it will be said:

“Go, accursed, into eternal fire, because I was hungry and you did not give me food” (Matthew XXV, 41–42),

and:

“Amen I say to you, you will not go out from there until you have paid the last quadrans” (Matthew V, 26).

And why, you ask, will this be said to them? Because they did not listen to the one saying:

“Repent, and iniquity will not be your ruin” (Ezekiel XVIII, 30),

and:

“Turn back to me, and I shall return to you” (Zechariah I, 3).

Finally, because they stopped the ear of their heart while the Apostle cried:

“If we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged” (1 Corinthians XI, 31),

and while Augustine likewise continued:

“If you have rightly considered your sins, you have judged yourself; if you have cast them away, you have killed them.”

This must be understood in the same sense concerning the other crimes as concerning this shameful speech: namely, that you, who uttered it, should make the day of judgment for yourself concerning it here; condemn it according to its most equitable quality as a judge; punish what you have condemned; kill what you have punished—that is, by rejecting it, do not utter it again for all eternity—and, censuring the *turpigerum* (“shame-bearing thing”) as *turpiloquium* (“shameful speech”), and the *turpigerum* as *turpiloquium* [the transmitted wording is corrupt], strive with all your strength, with Christ’s help, to abstain from similar things as well.

For it seems to me that the matter stands thus: if the shameful deed you committed has been completely consumed through repentance, the shameful thing you said on its account will likewise have been slain, with the help of his mercy who came into this world to release us from our crimes, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0579]

## THE ITINERARY OF RATHER ON HIS JOURNEY TO ROME

[Note: [Col. 0579B] This *Itinerary* of Rather as he traveled to Rome, mentioned by Fulcuin in chapter 24, was published by Acherius from the Laon manuscript. The Freising copy assisted us. Three indications establish the date. The words at the beginning of no. 1, “What you have just heard from the Gospel concerning Peter and Andrew, urged in this way: ‘Come after me,’” indicate the Gospel read on the feast of Saint Andrew. The adverb “just now” shows that this was written on Saint Andrew’s day itself or at the beginning of December. Two facts make it certain that this belongs to December of the year 966: the mention of Pope John and the Roman council that was to be held in the presence of Otto I. When he mentions Pope John in no. 2, it is established that he is not speaking of John XII, as some have thought; for in no. 4 he indicates that John XII, by whose command he had been restored, was already dead, writing that he had been restored by the command of the Apostle who was then presiding over the Roman see. That Rather is speaking of John XIII will become more certain from what is said in note 1025. Moreover, Rather does not doubt that Emperor Otto, who had come to Italy, would attend the council being convened at Rome together with the bishops. “I plan,” he says in no. 1, “to attend the council of so many who, under the leadership of the most devout Caesar, are going to come there to the apostolic see.” And in no. 3: “For I know that the wisest men, both from this kingdom—that is, the Italian one—and from those Germans who came with our lord, ever Augustus, will be present there.” Otto came to Italy under Pope John XIII after August of 966; he proceeded to Rome toward the end of that year and celebrated the Christmas festivities there. Finally, it is clear that the council was held at Rome at the beginning of the following year, with the same emperor attending together with both Italian and German bishops, from a privilege of that emperor granted in favor of the monastery of Subiaco on the third Ides of January in the year 967. It was published by Muratori in volume V of *Italian Antiquities*, dissertation 65, and reprinted by Canon Garampi from the papers of Domenico Giorgi in the book entitled *On the Silver Coin of Benedict III*, p. 169. Therefore the *Itinerary*, which Rather composed at the beginning of December, under Pope John XIII, after Otto I’s arrival in Italy and before this council, must be assigned to the beginning of December 966.]

[Col. 0579A] 437

I know, brothers and sons, that you know that I desire presently to go to Rome, but that you are entirely ignorant for what reason [supply: “I desire to go”].

For I am not going there for the sake of prayer, since I read in the Gospel:

“Woman, believe me, the hour is coming when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem” (John IV, 21);

and it follows:

“God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and in truth” (John IV, 24).

This, of course, anyone can do at home.

I am not going there by imperial command, since I have not been commanded to go there; I have only been ordered by him to send my soldiers.

[Note: [Col. 0580C] The Vulgate reads *hoc sit*. The correction is supplied by the Freising manuscript. Since Otto I came to Italy in 966 to suppress the rebellion raised at Rome against John XIII, perhaps for this reason he ordered Rather to send the soldiers who were requested from the bishops themselves as vassals of the empire. Hence also, in the sermon on Mary and Martha delivered after the feast of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary in the same year, no. 4, he says: “When have I ever compelled my own soldiers to battle at the emperor’s command?”]

[Note: [Col. 0580C] Construe: “I am not going there in order to learn there what is good and pleasing to God.”]

Nor am I going there to learn what is good and pleasing to God, since I recognize that this is frequently sung at this time:

“I shall show you, man, what is good, or what the Lord requires of you: to do judgment and justice, and to walk carefully with your God” (Micah VI, 8);

not only when we go to Rome, but wherever we remain [variant: *existimus*, “we exist”].

[Col. 0579B] 438

For the one who never departs from his commandments in disagreement always walks with God. Everyone is urged to do this more attentively—that is, to serve him in fear and rejoice in him with trembling (Psalm II, 11). For, as Gregory says, hope and fear must remain continually in the breast of the sinner.

What, then, is it to do judgment except to observe what the law commands? What was it, indeed, that you have just heard urged from the Gospel concerning Peter and Andrew:

“Come after me” (Matthew IV, 19)?

For this is the law and the prophets: that at all times we must follow Christ in thought, speech, and action.

And what is the justice that we are urged to do except the state of right—that is, of the law? But whose law? Christ’s, of course. How do we fulfill it once it has been made? “Bear one another’s burdens,” says the one who knew, “and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Galatians VI, 2).

But what burden is heavier for anyone than when someone is weighed down by ignorance of those things which he ought especially to know?

[Col. 0580B] 439

Since we cannot fulfill this law except by beginning it, nor begin it except by recognizing it, and since we see that it is as though it disagreed in many respects because it is not understood, I plan to attend the council of so many who, under the leadership of the most devout Caesar, are going to come there to the apostolic see, so that I may first investigate those matters which have been put forward as though they were discordant, to what harmony they can be brought.

[Note: [Col. 0580C] The disagreement with his clerics is intended: they seemed to think that the law permitted many things because they did not understand it; they believed that certain things were lawful which Rather prohibited as unlawful. Shortly afterward, *fasce* (“bundle”) is used for “burden,” as in Virgil, *Eclogue* IX, verse 69:

“. . . . . . I shall relieve you of this bundle.”]

[Note: [Col. 0581C] So the Freising manuscript reads. In the printed editions, *disponere* was incorrectly printed for *dissona*. Construe: “First striving to investigate to what harmony those things that have been put forward as though discordant can be brought.”]

For example, when we read in the canons of the Apostles:

[Note: [Col. 0581C] This is the heading of a canon prefixed by Dionysius Exiguus to the feast of the Apostles. It correctly reads *caste* (“chastely”) in the Freising manuscript, not *castam* (“chaste”), as in Acherius.]

“Let a bishop or presbyter not abandon his wife, whom he ought to govern chastely,”

and when we see the following stated so strictly in the Council of Nicaea, chapter III:

“The great synod entirely forbids a bishop, a presbyter, a deacon, or anyone at all who belongs to the clergy to have a woman introduced into his household, unless perhaps she is his mother, sister, aunt, or only such persons as escape suspicion”;

and when the canons say that if someone communicates with excommunicated persons, he himself is likewise excommunicated (Council of Zaragoza, canon 5; Council of Carthage II, canon 7, and so forth), while Augustine instructed a certain excommunicated man, Classicianus, in something that seems contrary to this (Augustine, Letter 250, to Auxilius, and the fragment addressed to Classicianus);

and when I see that none of our people cares whether the excommunication of any one of us is just or unjust, although I am not entirely ignorant of what blessed Gregory says about this (Letter 26, Book III),

[Note: [Col. 0581C] Construe: “I gladly wish to discuss this matter with that holy council”—namely, the council which, as he had said, was to be convened at Rome. Augustine likewise says in the fragment of the letter to Classicianus appended to Letter 250, concerning the question under discussion: “And in our council,” he says, “I wish to deal with it, and, if necessary, to write to the apostolic see.” Here Rather indicates that he wishes to discuss at the council the clerics’ relations with women, on account of which he perhaps thought someone ought to be excommunicated. The matter of clerics’ relations with women was in fact discussed in the following year at the Synod of Ravenna, held after the Roman council, which Rather attended, as is reported in Letter 12 to Ambrose, no. 1.]

I gladly wish to discuss this matter with that holy council.

### 2.

I greatly desire to investigate what the sacred assembly itself thinks concerning the chapters appended here, which have been set aside almost everywhere, except for very few.

[Note: [Col. 0581D] Construe: “These chapters make me—indeed, make me, though some falsely proclaim me learned—entirely ignorant of what I can at least think about them, much less say, since everyone, because of the prohibition of the one who says, ‘Let the one who is without sin …,’ fears to correct in another what he recognizes in himself; while the canons, with such authority, command that these things not be left uncorrected. Atto of Vercelli, criticizing this abuse in Letter 9 to his clergy, says: ‘Although there are some who neither cast the beam from their own eye nor presume to remove the splinter from their brother’s, they fall silent in confusion when they recognize themselves as reprobate.’”]

For, since everyone, because of the prohibition of the one who says, “Let the one among you who is without sin cast the first stone at her” (John VIII, 7), and, “Hypocrite, first cast the beam out of your eye” (Luke VI, 42), fears to correct in another what he recognizes in himself, while the canons, with such authority, command that these things not be left uncorrected, they make me—though some falsely proclaim me learned—entirely ignorant of what I can at least think about them, much less say.

[Col. 0581C] 440

How could I be stripped of this ignorance better or more suitably than by being taught at Rome? For what is known anywhere concerning ecclesiastical doctrines that is unknown at Rome?

There are the supreme teachers of the whole world; there the outstanding leaders of the universal Church have shone forth. There are the papal decretals, the assembly of all, the examination of the canons, the approval of what is to be received, and the rejection of what is to be scorned. Finally, nowhere is anything ratified that there was seen to be invalid, nor is anything invalid that there was seen to be ratified.

Where, then, is my ignorance better cared for than where the fountain of wisdom is seen to be?

A further advantage is added to the sum of this benefit: the mercy of the Creator has granted us an exceedingly just, devout, and wise emperor—namely, our most glorious lord Caesar—who surpasses beyond measure all those under heaven in the qualities just mentioned, as well as in the other marks of royal prerogative, has appointed as pope of the city of Romulus the most holy pope, the lord Bishop John, who, according to the proper meaning of his name, was chosen by God’s grace for this very work;

[Note: [Col. 0581D] The verb *instituit* (“appointed”) is governed by the preceding relative pronoun *qui*, referring to Caesar Otto I. These words plainly show that the sermon is not about John XII, who was elected in 956, when Otto did not yet rule in Italy; they agree with John XIII. For after the Roman antipope Leo VIII died at Rome, and at about the same time Pope Benedict V died in exile at Hamburg, the Romans sent two legates to Otto I to appoint whomever he wished as Roman pontiff, as the Continuator of Regino says under the year 965. When Otto then sent two bishops to Rome, John, bishop of the Church of Narni, was elected by all the Roman people and enthroned as pontiff of the apostolic see under the name John XIII, as the same Continuator of Regino records.]

—and has granted him to the whole world as a most worthy Father and diligent provider. May God grant his holy Church a universal synod, which they will convene, as is expedient, for its benefit.

[Note: [Col. 0582C] The synod was indeed convened at Rome at the beginning of 967, as we observed in note 1016. Whether Rather attended it is unknown because of the lack of evidence. He certainly did attend another synod, which was subsequently held at Ravenna in April of the same year and may be regarded as an appendix to the Roman synod.]

### 3.

I shall therefore be present, if, with God’s approval, I am able, and, restraining my little tongue with my finger, I shall take care to listen to those who will be present there with humility proportionate to my greater awareness of my need.

[Note: [Col. 0582D] It is clear from the privilege mentioned in the first note that bishops both from the Italian kingdom and from Germany attended the synod at Rome, which was held at the beginning of 967. In that privilege, granted at Rome on the third Ides of January in the year 967 of the Lord’s incarnation and the fifth year of the reign of the most devout Caesar Otto, indiction 10, concerning George, abbot of Subiaco, the same emperor says: “He came into the bosom of the basilica of Saint Peter, prince of the Apostles, where, together with Lord John XIII, pope, we were attending the holy synod for the benefit of the same Church and of venerable places, while many bishops from the Roman territory and Italy, and from the transalpine kingdom—that is, Germans—sat around us with the archbishop of Ravenna.” They had come to Italy with the Caesar after August of 966; for the same Caesar held a great assembly in Germany in mid-August before undertaking his Italian journey.]

[Col. 0583C] 441

For I know that the wisest men, both from this kingdom and from those who came with our lord, ever Augustus, will be present there. I desire to be taught by their instruction concerning at least those matters which I have here gathered in chapters, for this reason: I trust that their fullness is contained in their books.

These are matters that all could observe if they wished to be obedient to God. They are not contrary to the times or unsuitable to the fatherland; I omit those things which seemed appropriate only to the ancients or to peoples overseas, not to us.

Since, then, bodily remedies have been collected in certain medical books, while these are remedies for souls gathered in the holy canons—so that, just as one who has learned what is read in medical books is freed from illness, while one who neglects it dies by his own fault—so I desire to learn how one who despises the remedies of souls can in any other way escape eternal death.

I remain ignorant, and therefore foolish.

The Apostle also says:

“If we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged” (1 Corinthians XI, 31).

We must be judged both by secular judgment according to worldly law and ecclesiastically by canonical sanction. Let anyone else say whether one who despises being judged temporally by these laws can in any way escape that judgment by which every condemned person will perish eternally; for I am completely silent about this.

How do we carry out judgment if we neglect the law prescribed for us by God through the most holy Fathers? What justice do we have if we do not observe the canonical law? How do we walk with God if we stray from those things which he commands us to follow?

Moreover, harmful is the concern which upright conduct in one’s deeds does not produce (2 Corinthians V, 10), since it is certainly evident that everyone will receive according to what he has done, whether good or evil.

Therefore, wandering outside the line of canonical uprightness, what confidence can I have concerning salvation, I ask, when it is written:

“You shall not measure the outer court, because it has been given to the nations” (Revelation XI, 2)?

And to what nations is it given, except those concerning which the Psalmist is understood to have said to the Lord:

“My deliverer from angry nations” (Psalm XVII, 48)?

For just as a wicked man is elsewhere called the devil, so here the legion of demons appropriately bears the name “nations.” Therefore he is handed over to demons who is found in the outer court; because one who conducts himself outside the norm of ecclesiastical uprightness, even though he is bodily placed within the Church [variant: *ecclesiae*, “of the Church”], is seen to be inside physically but is proved to stand carnally in the outer court.

Or certainly he is given to the nations who associates with pagans. Although he is called a Christian, one who is opposed to Christ is by no means a Christian; and whoever does not obey the holy canons rebels against Christ.

Unless he gathers himself back within the measure of the line, he will be given to the nations, since [*quoniam quidem*; variant *quandoquidem*, “since indeed”] he will not be able to join the fellowship of those whose law he did not wish to observe, whose discipline he did not wish to accept for correction, and whose customs he did not wish to imitate.

Woe to any one of us who is found outside the canonical measure when the people of the elect begin to be counted.

For no one is elect who is not canonical; and no one [supply: “is”] canonical who is not elect.

[Note: [Col. 0583C] We supplied the repetition of the word *canonicus* (“canonical”) from the Freising manuscript.]

### 4.

Let one of you say, surely: “What concern is it of yours to do such things to others—and indeed to those superior to you—who care nothing whatever about them?” It does concern me, I say; it concerns me in every way, and it is so beneficial that I could proclaim, “O all you who pass along the way, attend and see whether there is any sorrow like my sorrow” (Lam. I, 12), if I were not languishing in the stupor of insensibility.

I shall omit, then, [Note: [Col. 0583D] In Rather’s epitaph he is said to have been an exile three times: first under King Hugh, secondly under Lothair his son, and thirdly either when he was seized by the invader Milo, as is related below, and driven from his see, or rather when he was at last compelled to leave Verona. Yet here, when he declares that he had been exiled three times before being driven out by the invader Milo—an expulsion which he reports in what follows as later—he seems to have counted as the third exile his coming to Italy in 951 to recover his episcopal see. But, finding Milo, nephew of Count Milo, occupying that see, which he had obtained from Manasses, he had to yield and return to Germany. See Letter 5 to John XII. Indeed, in the work *On Rebellious Clerics*, written at the end of 967, he recalls four expulsions which may broadly be called exiles, saying in no. 2: “You have now driven me four times from that Church [of Verona]”: namely, first under Hugh, secondly under Lothair, thirdly in 951, and [Col. 0584C] fourthly in 964, when he was seized and expelled by Milo; thus, when he finally left Verona in 968, this may be counted as a fifth kind of exile. In the epitaph, however, he is called an exile three times because only the three greater [Col. 0584D] exiles were counted, in which he was driven from the see that he held. Hence there “three times bishop” and “three times exile” are contrasted, because he obtained the episcopate three times and lost it three times. Although in 951 he sought to recover the episcopate, he did not obtain it. The exile of 964, moreover, was ended shortly afterward. When he says that the bishopric was taken from him unlawfully, he means unlawfully, without canonical judgment.] that I was exiled three times against the canons, insulted a thousand times, deprived of my bishopric unlawfully, and that another was brought in over me as an adulterer and received.
