[Note: “Another,” that is, the aforementioned nephew of Milo, who was likewise called Milo; for this reason he later calls him an invader.] Then, through the mercy of the most pious Emperor [Otto I], at the command of the apostolic [John XII], who at that time presided over the Roman See, I was restored synodally by the judgment of the bishops [Note: Namely, at the synod held at Pavia in 962, which Rather mentions in his *Apologeticus*, no. 7]. Later, having been seized by that same invader—though you were not altogether so ignorant of these matters, nor so opposed to him, that there were not a thousand who believed that almost all of you had not merely consented but had contrived this against me [Note: That is, at the beginning of 965. On these matters compare the *Conjecture of Quality*, no. 16, and the note there]—I was driven out, insulted, stripped, and handed over to custody. Yet, leaving all these matters aside, although they were so entirely unexamined, as though nothing could be found in them that could even slightly be reproved by the laws, I was again, through the mercy of the Creator and the clemency of the most pious emperor [Note: The adjective “most pious” has been added from the manuscript of Freising. The most excellent duchess through whose assistance he is said to have been rescued and brought back was Judith, mother of Henry II, duke of Bavaria and margrave of Verona. See the note to the *Conjecture of Quality*, 1054. Shortly afterward we have written *conjectari* on the authority of the cited manuscript, where the printed editions had *conjecturari*], rescued and brought back with the assistance of the most excellent duchess, but received by you so inhumanely that it was not difficult to discern from your faces how unwillingly you saw my return. From that time you have not ceased to harass me with so many insults that you have not allowed me to retain any privilege of the episcopal order, either as before [Note: “As before,” that is, in the time of Count Milo. See Part I, *On Contempt of the Canons*, no. 1, where Rather says that, from the time of that count until his second expulsion, nothing was left to him by the rebellious clergy except the making of chrism and whatever authority to chrismate. We explained this formula in the note there. What is added here, “with subscriptions,” may indicate documents—for example, in consecrations, ordinations, and other uses of chrism—on which the bishop would subscribe], or afterward, so that you leave me nothing except the making of chrism and the authority to chrismate anyone, with subscriptions.

I am also so dishonored by you that, while all the other fellow bishops who come there have their clergy obey them in that place with honor, I shall have not one of you. Yet I am not so inhuman toward my little poverty that I should not have, through a military benefice [Note: A “military benefice” was an estate granted by usufructuary right; whoever received it was required to provide military service, or soldiers when necessary. Rather had given ten clerics of the cathedral church whom he is addressing several estates belonging to episcopal property in the form of military benefices. He says “from my little poverty” because many goods of the Veronese bishopric had already been alienated and seized, as he complained in the *Conjecture of Quality*, no. 13. He adds “freely” because such benefices were sometimes granted in return for a payment], and that freely, ten of you enriched.

### 5.

Nevertheless, as I said, I shall overlook all these matters for the sake of him who said, “Do not resist evil” (Matt. V, 39). What should we do about the synod recently held by us [Note: Construe: “What should be done by us concerning the synod recently held?” He held a synod during the Lent of this year, 966, from which he issued a synodical letter]?” (Nicene Council, canon 5; Apostolic canon 38.)

You know, indeed you know, that I have always postponed doing this because, although the same command requires it to be done twice a year, I used to say that I did not know at all what I ought to synodize about. For at synods, if anything has been done against the canons, it is usually corrected. But if I had attempted this, while you were turning over everything written in the canons, I would have seen that you cared about none of it in any way.

If I were to bring forward even some of these matters—if what I touched on above were read, namely, “To have a woman introduced into one’s household, unless she be one’s sister,” and the rest of what is noted there (Council of Nicaea, canon 3)—which of you could I have exempted from neglecting this precept? Again, if this were read in full: “If any presbyter takes a wife, let him be deposed; but he ought rather to be expelled if he has committed adultery” (Council of Neocaesarea, canon 1), which of you would have gone away without deposition? Again, if this were recited: “We command that bigamists not be admitted to the clergy” (Innocent I, Letter 4, chapter 2; Gelasius I, Letter 9, near the end), which of you could I suppose to have been lawfully advanced to the priesthood?

And, to come to lesser matters—and to pass over very many things concerning you—if it were read that those who despise the canons must be rebuked more severely (Second Council of Seville, canon 4), and if I were to synodically investigate conspiracies [variant: “plots”], conspirators, perjurers, drunkards, those who drink in taverns, and those who devote themselves to usury, which of you would I leave without punishment? If I myself were to prescribe the penance imposed by the laws for perjurers, which of you would I permit to celebrate Mass? If I expelled those who have married many wives from the clergy, whom would I leave in the Church except little boys? If I rejected bastards [Note: In his *Confession*, no. 5, Rather explains from Deuteronomy XXIII, 2: “*Manzeres*, that is, one born from a prostitute, or illegitimate”], which of those same boys would I permit to stand in the choir?

“I waited,” he says, “for you to do justice, and behold, iniquity; and for righteousness, and behold, a cry” (Isa. V, 7). What cry? The worst reputation, the evil example. “The cry,” he says, “of Sodom has come to me” (Gen. XVIII, 20).

I shall put it briefly [manuscript of Freising: “Very briefly”: the cause of the destruction of the entire people entrusted to me is the clergy who dwell among them [Note: “Those who dwell among them,” namely, the clerics who live together with the people, or laymen]. Whom among the laity would I have dared to summon before a synod for adultery [Note: Here he appears to call “synod” the assembly convened during visitations of churches, where an inquiry was made concerning the laity. See the note on Letter 5 to John XII, in which the word “synod” is used in this sense. It cannot mean the diocesan synod that Rather held during the Lent of this year and discusses in the following section, since laymen were not summoned to it and no inquiry concerning laymen was conducted there, as happened at synods convened on the occasion of visitations. Inquiries concerning clerics were conducted in the chapters of the visitations, discussed in the same note, and also in the diocesan synod, to which only clerics assembled, as the following section makes clear. In such synods, constitutions were sometimes issued for the governance of laymen, but the laymen themselves, even if guilty of some crime, were not summoned there], or for perjury, or for any crime whatsoever, when I was deprived of the judgment of the clerics? For who would there be to whom that man would not immediately say in his heart—although he might not dare say it with his lips—“Hypocrite,” that is, false cleric, “first remove the beam from your own eye, and then you will see how to remove the speck from my eye” (Matt. VII, 5)?

### 6.

Since, then, no inquiry whatsoever is made among us concerning such matters [Note: This may be explained from what follows. Since there ought to be no inquiry or investigation among us concerning such crimes and criminals, what purpose could a synod serve? He then gives an example from the diocesan synod that he held during the preceding Lent, where an inquiry was made only about psalms and other similarly minor matters by the person responsible for it, nothing further requiring correction having been found. They were unwilling to investigate the more serious matters, in which most of them were involved], for what purpose should a synod be held; where, where, I ask, should a council be held?

You remember—I know that you do—that I ordered [Note: [Col. 0587B] These matters refer to the diocesan synod held in the preceding Lent of 966. The rite by which such a synod was celebrated deserves notice. A similar rite was also observed in synods convened during visitations in the individual rural parishes. For Regino preserves the following canon of the Council of Rouen in Book II, *On Ecclesiastical Discipline*, chapter 1: “When [Col. 0587C] the bishop makes a circuit of his diocese, the archdeacon or archpriest must go before him one or two days through the parishes which he is to visit; and, having summoned the people, must announce the arrival of their own pastor and require all to attend his synod unfailingly on the appointed day. … Then, having taken with him the presbyters who ought to render service to the bishop in that place, he should strive to correct and amend whatever he can among the lesser and lighter cases, so that, when the pontiff comes, he may not be wearied by easier matters,” etc. Not dissimilarly, when a diocesan synod was to be convened, two days beforehand the archpriest and archdeacon, sitting together with the *ordinarii*, that is, the canons of the cathedral church, had to examine those summoned to the synod from the city’s titular churches and from the rural parishes, diligently investigating anything that required correction; on the third day, when the bishop presided over the synod, they were to report the matters needing correction. The canons of Verona cathedral were called *ordinarii*, just as the canons of Strasbourg cathedral were called by the same name, and the canons of Milan are still called *ordinarii* at this time. Regino’s continuator, under the year 925, attests this concerning the Strasbourg canons, reporting that Beno was appointed successor to Witger, bishop of Metz, from among the *ordinarii* of Strasbourg. Ancient documents in Puricelli and Ughelli likewise prove that the Milanese were called *ordinarii* even in ancient times. Lest anyone dismiss as insignificant examples sought from other churches, an outstanding document of our Veronese Church is at hand: it was recently published by Marquis Giovanni Giacomo de Dionysiis, a canon, in the *Collection of Diplomas*, no. 31, p. 148, and was written in 973. In it one reads in precisely the same manner: “The archpriest, the archdeacon, and the other *ordinarii*”; and likewise *ordinarii* occurs repeatedly in the same document, meaning canons. Hence, when Rather says in Letter 12 to Ambrose, no. 2, “I made a certain deacon … an *ordinarius* beyond expectation,” he indicates that he promoted him to a canonry of the cathedral. These canons, whom he here calls *ordinarii*, he shortly afterward calls *cardinales*: for the canons of Milan cathedral are found endowed with both titles in Landulf the Younger, *History of Milan*, chapter 22, vol. V of *Rerum Italicarum*, p. 492, where the address of their letter reads: “The *ordinarii cardinales* of the holy Church of Milan.” Beroldus too, in the order of the Church of Milan published in vol. IV of Muratori’s *Antiquitates Italicae*, pp. 861 ff., calls the same Milanese canons now *ordinarii*, now *cardinales*. It is likewise worth noting that the archpriest, who is placed before the archdeacon, held at this time the first dignity in our cathedral church; whereas at the beginning of the preceding century the archdeacons Pacificus and Audo held first place, as was generally also the case in other churches. Hence in the cited canon of Rouen the archdeacon is placed before the archpriest.] that, two days beforehand, the archpriest and archdeacon, while I was absent, should come with all the *ordinarii*, who were to sit together, and examine everything; and that on the third day they should read to me everything requiring correction. It was done.

While seated, I asked what had been done. The person responsible replied that you had inquired about psalms and matters of that kind and, thanks be to God, had found nothing especially wrong. What else, then, should I have had to say about so many holy men except “Thanks be to God”? If they knew the psalms reasonably well and were free from all other faults, where, I ask, should a synod be held?

Understanding, therefore, that this was a great deception of souls, I said one thing in my heart and uttered another with my lips. In my heart I complained to myself in this way: “Who are you here—or rather, who is here?” With my lips, however, I answered in these words: “If the inquiry in this council is to concern psalms and nothing else, bring me first to examination [variant: ‘lead me first to examination’]. For it can be proved that I do not know them as I ought. Since, then, nothing further requiring correction has been found, where is the synod to be held?”

Accordingly, when I inquired into their faith, I found that many did not even know the creed that is believed to have been that of the apostles. On this occasion I was compelled to write a synodical letter to all the presbyters, in which the following exhortation is given first:

> “I therefore admonish you paternally and command you pastorally to remember the Apostle’s words: ‘Without faith it is impossible to please God’ (Heb. XI, 6)—that is, without the belief which has been handed down to us through the apostles and their successors—and also: ‘The just person lives by faith,’ that is, by his belief (Rom. I, 17); and: ‘Whatever is without faith,’ that is, without belief in God, ‘is sin’ (cf. Jas. II, 17). Faith, moreover—that is, belief in God—if it does not have good works, is dead in itself.
>
> “Let it be your urgent care, therefore, to prepare this faith—that is, this belief in God—in three forms for memorization [Note: Thus the manuscript of Freising, in agreement with the text of the synodical letter itself. The printed editions read *praeparare*. *Parare memoriter* means what we say in Italian, *imparare a memoria*, ‘to learn by heart’]. That is, prepare it according to the Creed, the ‘collation’ of the apostles, as it is found in corrected psalters; prepare also the creed that is sung at Mass; and the creed of Saint Athanasius, which begins: ‘Whoever wishes to be saved.’
>
> “Whoever, therefore, wishes to be or become or remain a priest in our parish must recite these three creeds to us from memory when he has next been summoned here by us.”

### 7.

Although, in the middle of Lent, I had given these three creeds to them to be written out and committed to memory [Note: The printed edition has *Istud*, “this,” together with *mediantem Quadragesimam*, “during the middle of Lent,” for those things to be written and memorized. With the help of the manuscript of Freising we have corrected it to *istas*, “these,” namely, the three creeds mentioned above, and to *mediante Quadragesima*, “in the middle of Lent.” The “middle Sunday” was the fourth Sunday of Lent, which fell in the middle of Lent; the entire following week was therefore called “middle week.” It was at this time that Rather held the synod. The following words, “and had found them disobedient,” refer to the later time mentioned in the quoted fragment of the synodical letter: “when he has next been summoned here by us.” He seems to have summoned them not long before writing this *Itinerary*. Fearing a greater punishment, they promised him, in place of the assistance they had promised for his journey to Rome, that they would henceforth sing the Creed of Blessed Athanasius and do the other things written there [that is, in the synodical letter] according to their ability], and found them disobedient, such fear seized some of them that, after promising me assistance for undertaking my journey, they promised that thereafter they would sing the Creed of Blessed Athanasius and do the other things written there according to their ability.

When I had found all the *titularii* and those from the rural parishes ready, thanks be to God [Note: He distinguishes three classes of Veronese clerics. The *titularii* are the clerics of the churches in the city and suburbs, which are called *tituli* in the synod of Verona held in 995 and published by P. Bernardo de Rubeis in *Monumenta Ecclesiae Aquileiensis*, col. 484, and by Muratori, vol. V of *Antiquitates Italicae*, col. 1003. Those of the rural parishes are the clerics of rural churches, which are called *plebes*. Finally, the *cardinales* are the canons of the cathedral church; this term was likewise used for the canons of the cathedrals of Milan, Aquileia, Naples, Capua, Lucca, and many others. See Du Cange, under *Canonici cardinales*, and Muratori, cited above, Dissertation 61. In a document of 932 published by Giovanni Battista Biancolini, *Historical Notices of the Churches of Verona*, book II, p. 698, the cathedral of Verona is called the cardinal church; its canons are named: “The archpriest, archdeacon, and the other priests and deacons of the holy cardinal church of Verona”], I still see you, the cardinals, who, like the scribes and Pharisees of old, send all these men to destruction, remaining rebellious here to such a degree that you choose to be condemned eternally with Arius, the enemy of the same faith, rather than be salutarily defeated by singing, as the clerics of other churches do, this creed publicly [Note: Bishop Haito of Basel, in a capitulary written about the year 820 and published by Acherius, vol. I of the *Spicilegium*, p. 584, chapter 4, prescribed that priests should learn the faith of Saint Athanasius and recite it from the heart every Sunday at Prime. In an ancient catalogue of the abbots of Fleury, ending with Theodulf, later bishop of Orléans, who flourished under Louis the Pious, published in vol. I of Baluze’s *Miscellanea*, p. 492, we read: “He published an exposition of the Creed of Saint Athanasius, which the monks read daily at Prime after the three regular psalms.” In the *Thesaurus anecdotorum* of Martène and Durand, vol. I, p. 63, a statute of the chapter of Saint Martin of Tours from the year 922 prescribes that the faith of Saint Athanasius be sung at Prime both on feast days and on ordinary days. From these Gallic testimonies it is clear that this rite was first introduced in Gaul, gradually spread, and had been adopted by several churches in Rather’s time, as we learn from the present text. Since the rite was new, the Veronese canons were reluctant to accept it and refused to sing the same creed publicly, as is also related at the end of Part I, *On Contempt of the Canons*].

### 8.

When such necessity presses upon me, most wretched as I am, would I not have to go there, where I might find some counsel in this matter?

O worst of Rather’s *chronography* [Note: The printed edition has “O chronology.” We preferred the reading of the excellent manuscript of Freising, with which another work of Rather’s, the *Conjecture of Quality*, agrees. There, in no. 2, he calls a *chronography* a work that contains the life of his contemporaries, and it is said to attack not merely himself but everyone, leaving no one untouched. Perhaps in it he described the conduct and vices of his clerics, and for that reason he calls this *chronography*, which deals with vices, “the worst.” Compare the note to the same *Conjecture of Quality*. He further says, “O truth hateful to it,” because it was painful to him that the vices he had described in that *chronography* were true; hence he adds that he would have preferred to be the only liar rather than be able to speak truthfully about such things concerning almost all of you]! O truth hateful to it! I cannot even estimate how much more desirable it would have been for me alone to be a liar than to be able to speak truthfully about such things concerning almost all of you; nor can I, unhappy man, estimate how much I am compelled to utter such things.

Therefore we must cry out, cry out, and say without ceasing: “Turn us, O God our Savior, and turn away your anger from us” (Ps. LXXXIV, 5).

For a tendency of this kind, excessively mindful of itself, rightly distresses me [Council of Sardica, canon 1]: “An evil custom no less than a pernicious corruption must be eradicated from the roots,” as that most rigorous Hosius cried out in the Council of Sardica; and elsewhere another said: “Let custom yield to authority; let law and reason overcome corrupt usage.”

As I consider you clinging so obstinately to the custom of your predecessors—who were likewise rebels against God himself, who is known to have instituted these same canons—while utterly disregarding the authority of the canons [Note: Construe: “As I consider you, while utterly disregarding the authority of the canons, clinging so obstinately to the custom of your predecessors, who were likewise rebels against God himself, who is known to have instituted these canons, I find that you must cry out to God with me without ceasing, both for them and for yourselves: ‘We have sinned with our fathers, we have acted unjustly, we have committed iniquity’”], I find that you must cry out to God with me without ceasing, both for them and for yourselves: “We have sinned with our fathers, we have acted unjustly, we have committed iniquity” (Judith VII, 19).

With the most holy King Josiah we must also say to one another [that is, we must all cry out]: “Go, inquire of God for me, for my people, and for all Judah” (whom [as is likewise understood in Part II, *On Contempt of the Canons*] we may understand as the Catholic Church, distinguished by its confession of God) “concerning the words of these books”—namely, the canons and decrees contained in the archives of the churches. “For great,” he says, “is the wrath of the Lord that has been kindled against us, because our fathers did not listen to the words of these books, so as to do everything that is written in them” (2 Kings XXII, 13).

Understand “fathers” to mean not only the bishops of the churches but also their elders, so that at least one of them might deign to answer each of us:

“Thus says the Lord God of Israel: Because you heard the words of the book, and your heart was terrified, and you humbled yourself before the Lord when you heard the words against this place and its inhabitants—namely, that they would become a desolation and a curse—and because you tore your garments and wept before me, I also have heard you, says the Lord. Therefore I shall gather you to your fathers, and you shall be gathered to your grave in peace, so that your eyes may not see all the evil that I shall bring upon this place” (ibid., 18–20).

“Go around,” says the Lord elsewhere, “go around the streets of Jerusalem, look and consider, and seek in its squares whether you can find a man who does justice and seeks faithfulness; and I shall be gracious to them. But even if they say, ‘As the Lord lives,’ they will swear falsely. Lord, your eyes look for faithfulness; you struck them, but they did not grieve [Note: The printed edition has *indoluerunt*, “they did not feel pain.” The manuscript of Freising, agreeing with the reading of the Vulgate translator, is better]; you consumed them, but they refused to accept discipline; they hardened their faces more than stone and refused to return.

“I, however, said: ‘Perhaps they are poor and foolish, ignorant of the way of the Lord and of the judgment of their God. I shall go, therefore, to the great men and speak to them; for they know the way of the Lord and the judgment of their God.’ And behold, these together had broken the yoke even more and had torn the bonds. Therefore the lion from the forest struck them, and the wolf at evening laid them waste” (Jer. I, 1–6).

The roaring lion seeking someone to devour is the devil (1 Pet. V, 8); and the wolf is likewise the one who, because of the negligence of hireling shepherds—shepherds who possess the title not lawfully but usurp it unlawfully—carries off and scatters the sheep (John X, 12), not only by himself but also through members cooperating with him, laying waste to his own vineyard and that of the Lord of Hosts from its very beginning.

### 9.

And alas, how closely such things correspond to us in our misery! For we ourselves are, in estimation though not in reality, the great men: we, I say, whom the divine discourse addresses after leaving aside the poor and those utterly ignorant of God’s law.

We know the way of God by reading, yet we decline to follow it. We know the judgment of our God, but by despising it—and despising ourselves even more—we have, as it were, broken his easy yoke, easy for those who are willing, and his light burden, which those who do not disdain to bear [Note: The printed edition has *dignantibus*, “for those who deem it worthy,” whereas we have preferred the better reading of the manuscript of Freising, *dedignantibus*, “for those who do not disdain.” Construe: “We know the way of God by reading, yet decline to follow it; we know the judgment of our God, but by despising it, and despising ourselves even more, and despising his easy yoke, easy for those who are willing, and his light burden, yet not disdaining to bear it, we have broken it and torn the bonds,” and so forth]. We have torn the bonds of the canonical law by caring nothing for it.

Therefore we must fear that worse things may happen to us than to those about whom these words were then spoken in their own presence. For we despise not only those who were speaking then, but God himself, who now speaks to us not only through them and their followers but also through himself.

The lion that devours souls is much worse than the lion that tears apart animals; the wolf that spiritually destroys human beings is worse than the wolf that bodily devours sheep. This is especially so if it happens to us at evening—that is, when we bring our present life to an end.

Fear of this danger compels me to undertake this journey, in search of counsel from others, because I find none within myself.

### 10.

I confess that, as I seek this, these matters torment me greatly: whether, once these things have been disregarded, any other way of salvation remains—a possibility I do not even suspect. For if “what is canonical the Catholic Church defends,” I think that the person who presumptuously resists the holy canons falsely claims to be Catholic (Council of Nicaea, canon 9).

Moreover, as we sing, unless each person preserves the Catholic faith whole and inviolate, he will undoubtedly perish forever (Creed of Saint Athanasius).

O firm confession, then: that one is not Catholic who rejects the canonical law, and that no one can attain eternal life unless he is Catholic [Note: The most recent editor of the *Spicilegium* corrected this to *confessio*, “confession,” instead of *concessio*, the reading found in Acherius’s Laudun manuscript and in our manuscript of Freising].

Since this is established so firmly and certainly, what are we to think, what can we estimate, concerning that so public contempt for the canonical law which exists among us? What are we to think of the fact that not only those things concerning the cohabitation of women, so strictly forbidden to ministers of the Church and decreed in the Council of Nicaea (Council of Nicaea, canon 3), but also that which elsewhere is punished with such severity [Note: The printed edition, together with our manuscript, incorrectly has *fertur*. We have corrected it to *feritur*, “is struck,” that is, “is punished,” as the context requires and as is read at the end of this section, “are struck by the canonical sword”], as stated above; and the Council of Neocaesarea likewise contains a provision of no lesser severity:

“If a presbyter confesses that before ordination he sinned by bodily sin, he shall not consecrate the offerings, but shall remain in the other offices because of his good zeal” (canon 9).

When recognized in oneself, these matters could plunge anyone into the abyss of despair, unless it had been said beforehand: “A person does not know whether he is worthy of hatred or love, but everything remains uncertain for the future” (Eccles. IX, 1–2) [Note: Thus the manuscript of Freising. The printed editions have the faulty reading *emergere*, “to emerge.” The cited manuscript also reads *praedicatum*, “proclaimed,” instead of *praedictum*, “said beforehand”].

If someone who confesses that he sinned bodily before ordination is punished with such severity, what shall be said of someone known to have committed adultery a thousand times after ordination?

Although some may appear—very few indeed—to be free from these more serious vices, what are we to say or think about the supposedly lesser offenses so habitually practiced that they are no longer even regarded as sins? For example:

“Let a bishop, presbyter, or deacon who has taken up arms in any sedition be deposed from the entire assembly of Christians” (Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 45).

And:

“Let a bishop, presbyter, or deacon who devotes himself to gambling and drunkenness either desist or be deposed” (Apostolic canon 42).

There are countless other provisions of this kind, which are struck by the canonical sword no less severely than the cohabitation of women, fornication, or adultery, and even incestuous conduct, which is contrary to nature itself.

### 11

Having thus arrogantly disregarded these matters, I do not see how anyone can rightly be called, or even be considered, Catholic, since, as I stated above, it is recorded as having been said at the Council of Nicaea: “What is canonical, the Catholic Church defends.”

[Note: This sentence, “What is canonical, the Catholic Church defends,” is read somewhat differently in canon 9 of Nicaea, in these words: “What is irreproachable, the Catholic Church defends.” The author quoted this reading verbatim in Part I, *On Contempt for the Canons*, no. 11. Above, in this work, no. 10, he quoted the former reading.]

For although—when the Lord says, “Let the dead bury their own dead” (Matt. 8:22), speaking of those who are like the guilty in defending or concealing them—no one legally deposes those who ought to be deposed, and no one condemns those who ought to be condemned, they will not thereby be able to escape the condemnation inflicted upon them by the Holy Spirit; nor will those whom the Lord himself calls thieves and robbers be able to become shepherds of his sheep.

[Note: Construe it thus: Although the Lord says to those who are like the guilty in defending or concealing them, “Let the dead bury their own dead”; although, I say, no one legally deposes those who ought to be deposed, nor anyone condemns those who ought to be condemned, they will not thereby be able to escape the condemnation inflicted upon them by the Holy Spirit, nor will those whom the Lord himself calls thieves and robbers be able to become shepherds of the Lord’s sheep.]

For whoever perpetrates anything simoniacal will not be able to escape Simon’s condemnation, nor be free from the leprosy of Gehazi, if he himself does what Gehazi did. “That the blood of all the prophets which has been shed upon the earth may be required of this generation,” says the Lord—as though speaking of the Jews alone—“from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah, son of Barachiah, whom you killed between the temple and the altar” (Matt. 23:35).

Those to whom he said this had certainly killed neither Abel nor Zechariah, nor any prophet; but because they were like those who had done these things in wickedness, they therefore deserved to be punished by a similar vengeance (ibid., 30–31).

Again, the Lord says elsewhere—in words that must one day be spoken: “Gather the weeds first, and bind them into bundles to burn them” (Matt. 13:30); that is, join together in a similar condemnation those who are equal in crime.

If this is so, then just as Maximus Cynicus was condemned, so also are his associates in the same crime;

[Note: See the document of the Veronese clergy addressed to the Roman Church, in which the author recounts the very records by which Maximus Cynicus, Photius, and Constantine were condemned.]

 as Photius was condemned, so also are his imitators; as Constantine, the invader of the Roman See, was condemned, so also is every imitator of his. And just as their ordination was invalid, so also is the condemnation of these men no different.

[Note: On what Ratherius thought about ordinations of this kind, and why, see the prefatory *Admonition* to Ratherius’s decree, *On Clerics Ordained by an Usurper*, nos. 1 and 2.]

And alas, integrity of the Catholic faith, ancient holiness, and true Christianity—where have you gone?

[Col. 0593C] “Do you ask?” Let us make it answer as though it were present. For it is present, although it is hidden because of its extreme scarcity. The time has not yet passed which the Lord himself appointed for it when he spoke thus: “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 8:20).

### 12

Let it therefore be silent about itself and speak about that which is falsely called Christianity:

“Those who go on amid the cares and riches and pleasures of life,” says the Lord, “are choked, and they do not produce fruit” (Luke 8:14).

What fruit, indeed? Fruit by which they would certainly be nourished in the kingdom of heaven, while at the same time incurring the hatred of the Most High.

[Note: The common editions add *Christianitates* here. We have more rightly deleted it with the aid of the Freising manuscript, from which we also deleted *et* shortly afterward, before the word “Apostle.”]

For the Apostle testifies thus: “Whoever wishes to be a friend of this world is constituted an enemy of God” (Jas. 4:4).

Yet unless this is understood as having been expressed by that figure of speech in which what is contained is shown through that which contains it, it appears to imply a kind of ingratitude toward the things that God has bestowed upon us. For if we do not love the world that God made for our sake, we are, as it were, ungrateful toward its Creator and Giver:

“God saw,” says Scripture, “God saw everything that he had made, and it was very good” (Gen. 1:31).

If, therefore, something is very good in God’s own judgment, how ought it to appear hateful to us?

Let us understand, then, that we ought not to hate that world which is called the cosmos—that is, heaven, earth, the sea, and everything that is in them—or those revolutions of time on account of which this present life of ours is called “the world.” Rather, we ought to hate what is wrongly done in this world: first, the circuit of excess in those things which this world supplies for our use; then pleasure; and after that every kind of vice.

[Note: Construe it thus: We must understand that everyone ought to hate not that world which is called the cosmos—that is, heaven, earth, the sea, and everything that is in them—or those revolutions of time on account of which this present life is called “the world,” but what is wrongly done in this world; that is, first, the excess of those things which this world supplies for our use, then pleasure, and afterward every kind of vice.]

Whatever, therefore, appears good to God, let us love as useful; whatever is evil, let us hate as harmful, so that we may escape God’s enmity and in some way be counted among those who are truly Christians. Yet we can do this in no way unless we do what the holy canons command.

### 13

But, to return to myself and those like me—that is, to those who until now have rebelled against the holy canons—how can we do this, when remedies of penance after a fall have been granted generally to everyone, but the Lord himself says to us, the most wretched of men, that if the salt—which we ought to have been—has lost its savor, it is useful for nothing, not even for the manure heap (Luke 14:34)?

Elsewhere we have the following words, by which penance is represented:

“Lord, let her alone this year also, until I dig around her and put manure on her” (Luke 13:8);

that is, by recalling to her memory the stench of her crimes, I will compel her to do penance.

[Note: The edition of Acherius, together with our manuscript of Freising, has *quod ... figurari*. It should read either *vel quo* or *figurare*. We have retained the first expression, introduced by the new editor of the *Spicilegium*.]

And yet even this is denied to us, the most unhappy of men, since after penance no one is permitted by canonical law even to remain a cleric (Siricius, letter to Himerius, no. 18; Innocent, letter to Macedonius, no. 11, and letter to the Apulians).

What, then, shall we wretched men do, shut in on every side? We are ceaselessly told:

“Whoever eats of the flesh of the sacrifice belonging to the Lord, while his uncleanness is upon him, that person shall perish from his people” (Lev. 7:20).

And again:

“A man who is a priest, of the seed of Aaron, who has a blemish, shall not offer the bread of his God, nor approach his ministry” (Lev. 21:17–18).

[Note: Acherius reads *ad ministrum*. The correction of the new editor of the *Spicilegium* is supported by our Freising manuscript and by the Vulgate translator.]

How, then, how can we, the most wretched of men, be washed from that uncleanness, how can we be cleansed from these blemishes, when, after the penance that heals crimes, we are not permitted even to remain in the clerical order, much less to exercise the priesthood?

[Note: The Vulgate has *non permittamur*. The reading of the cited manuscript is better.]

Suppose that this alone were an immense obstacle to us wretched men: what should be thought of those entrusted to us?

[Note: Construe: What should be thought of those entrusted to us? That is, of those who have been committed to our care.]

What of those things which ought to have been washed, cleansed, and blessed by us, but which our touch—alas!—has consequently made unclean, since the Lord says: “Whatever an unclean person touches shall be unclean” (Num. 19:22)?

If we had been few—would that we had been!—perhaps men who could suffice, by God’s grace, for us unworthy and rejected men might have been found, and the danger would not have been so great.

[Note: The Freising manuscript has *digno*, perhaps *digne*, instead of *Dei gratia*, and this is perhaps better. Construe it thus: Would that we had been few—that is, perhaps men could have been found who, by God’s grace (or worthily), would have been able to suffice for us, who are unworthy and rejected. Acherius’s edition formerly had *num* instead of *nunc*, perhaps through a typographical error; the latest editor corrected it, and our manuscript confirms the correction.]

But now, alas for the impiety!—while the Lord cries out in complaint, saying, “Yet they all together broke the yoke; they shattered the bonds” (Jer. 5:5), what remedy has the deceived Church, which we ought to have governed, found, when the Lord’s voice complains that all of us together have broken the yoke and shattered the bonds?

For James says: “Confess your sins to one another, so that you may be saved” (Jas. 5:16).

[Note: With the aid of the same manuscript we deleted *est*, which was wrongly read in the common editions after the word *capitulo*. A little later Acherius read, “Who sings the table?” We have adopted the correction of the new edition, “Who celebrates Mass?”; the Freising manuscript also has *missam*.]

But since the canon written above of the Council of Neocaesarea states:

“If a presbyter confesses that he has committed a bodily sin before ordination, he shall not consecrate the offerings, while remaining in his other offices because of his good zeal” (canon 9),

who can celebrate Mass, when this sentence forbids almost everyone to consecrate the offerings?

[Note: It forbids it, namely, when it says: “He shall not consecrate the offerings.”]

And observe how much contradiction is contained here. You are not permitted to consecrate the offerings if you confess that you have sinned; yet you will not attain salvation unless you confess that you have sinned.

[Note: This is the reading of the Freising manuscript. In the common editions, since *nisi* was not read but *si* was, the passage was supplemented as follows: “If you do not confess that you have sinned.” Later we have twice printed *timeo, timeo* with the same manuscript, from which we also printed *oblata nisi contra vetitum* (“the offerings unless contrary to the prohibition”). Perhaps *non nisi* should be read here, as Mabillon rightly observed in Ratherius’s eulogy, no. 21, volume 7 of the *Acta Sanctorum* of the Benedictine Order, p. 481.]

What, then, shall I do with you, my brothers and fellow presbyters? If you do not confess your sins, I fear—indeed, I fear—that you will not be saved. If you confess them, you consecrate the offerings unless contrary to the prohibition; and if you consecrate them contrary to the prohibition, you kindle a strange fire [read: eternal fire].

Therefore we must fear that we may perish in the likeness of those whose example we follow.

### 14

I would therefore be compelled to despair of you together with myself, unless I recalled again and again what I had read:

“Man does not know whether he is worthy of hatred or of love” (Eccl. 9:1).

For who knows whether it has been granted to any one of us to be converted before dying?

Happy, therefore, are those who have been deposed under this law; happy those who have been expelled; happy those who have been stripped of their possessions and deprived of their episcopate—provided that something similar happens to them as we heard happened to two Scots.

A certain more powerful man attacked a weaker one, drove him from his own see, and took possession of it. There was there a certain poor man whose entire body was contracted. As the usurper was leaving, he addressed him thus:

“Father, to whom are you abandoning me?”

“To God,” he replied.

“Will you ever return?”

“Not unless you bring me back,” he said.

He then withdrew and approached the Lord’s tomb.

After some time had passed, such a plague invaded the whole province from which that holy man had been expelled that scarcely a tenth of the people survived. When the Lord was entreated by the persistence of fasts, litanies, and almsgiving, he answered in the manner that pleased him and showed, through the confession of the usurper, that that destruction of the people had occurred because of his crime.

[Note: This is the reading of the same Freising manuscript. The common editions have *suscitatus*. Construe it thus: When the Lord had been entreated by the persistence of fasts, litanies, and almsgiving, he answered in the manner that pleased him, and so forth.]

Moved, therefore, by consideration of his guilt, he abandoned the episcopate which he had usurped and withdrew to a certain island to do penance until the end of his life.

[Note: We have corrected *episcopio* in the common editions to *episcopatu* with the Freising manuscript, because of the relative pronoun *quem*. That manuscript, however, omits the words *relicto quem invaserat*. Immediately afterward, we have followed the same manuscript in reading *introivit*, whereas the printed editions have *introiit*.]

He had wished to remain alone, but the benevolence of his neighbors frequently visited him. Suddenly, however, when the inhabitants had perished, an immense famine invaded the region and compelled the generosity of those who fed that holy man to slacken somewhat.

A large ship had happened to stop at the shore. The boys whom he was educating entered it; compelled by hunger, they fell asleep after whatever game they had been playing. While they slept, they were brought by angelic rowing to another shore of a virtually unknown land.

[Note: The cited manuscript has *triremis*. Immediately afterward it reads: “while they slept, to another shore of an almost unknown land.”]

The king of that land, riding around the shore, waited in great amazement as he saw the ship approaching perfectly straight without any men aboard. He found only the boys sleeping in it. After they awoke, he asked them where they were from.

When he learned from them—insofar as children of that age were able to explain it—about the famine that afflicted the man of God, he first refreshed the boys with food, then ordered the boat to be loaded with grain.

[Note: The printed editions wrongly have *cubam*. We have correctly written *cumbam* from the Freising manuscript. *Cumba* is the same as *cymba*, or the vessel previously called a *triremis*. See Du Cange, s.v. *cumba*.]

The boys were sent back inside, and immediately, by God’s will, they were overcome by sleep. The boat was carried to the other bank without anyone rowing it [the boat being understood], and the servant of God, together with the entire island, was freed from the danger of starvation.

[Note: The following seven words, necessary to the story and absent from the common editions, have been inserted from the same manuscript.]

Moreover, the people, deprived of their shepherd, began to seek him, but no one knew where he had gone. As they were searching, someone offered this advice: he had heard the man say that he would never return unless that bedridden man brought him back.

[Note: *Clinicus* refers to that poor man who was previously described as contracted in all his limbs and later called paralyzed. *Clinicus* derives from the Greek κλίνη (*klínē*, “bed”); it denotes one who is confined to bed by some illness, for example paralysis or contraction of the limbs. See examples in Du Cange. The words following *eum* are absent from the Freising manuscript.]

They therefore took counsel among themselves, trusting in the mercy of their bishop, and ordered the man, in the name of the Lord, to rise and hurry after him as quickly as possible.

Wonderful to relate! He rose, set out, found him in Jerusalem, brought him back, was received, and was restored to his own see.

### 15

Let anyone who is able judge whose merits were greater, those of the expeller or those of the expelled.

The former, by his penance, compelled angels to come to his aid—or rather, to speak in that way, to serve him.

[Note: The common editions wrongly have *coegerunt* (“they compelled”). A little later Acherius and our manuscript read *sancto decreto interdicat clericatum canonico*; we have willingly adopted the correction of the new editor of Acherius’s *Spicilegium*, which is necessary to the context and sense. Construe it thus: It is astonishing that a canonical decree should forbid the clerical order to a holy man, perhaps because he had become such as this man became, when no one can seem more worthily to become a cleric than one who has happened to become holy through penance.]

The latter caused a paralytic to traverse half the world.

But since the perfection of penance has such power, it is astonishing that a canonical decree should forbid a holy man from the clerical order, perhaps because this is what he had become, when no one could appear more worthy of becoming a cleric than one who had become holy through penance.

[Note: The Freising manuscript has *sanctum*, whereas the common editions wrongly have *sanctam*. Immediately afterward, the same manuscript has *ad vindictam tantam pertinens sceleris*. By “so great a crime” he means the usurpation of the episcopate.]

If anything of this sort, or anything else contributing to the punishment of so great a crime, happened to such a man, or if he himself voluntarily became the avenger of his own crimes, I have no doubt about him after his end.

But if I consider that nothing unfortunate happened to another in this world, let someone else form whatever judgment he can about him. I, relying with profound fear upon that sentence which is spoken concerning such men—“They spend their days in prosperity, and in a moment they descend to the underworld” (Job 21:13)—fear that the following saying of the apostle John applies to him:

“There is a sin unto death”—that is, a sin continuing until death—“and I do not say that anyone should pray for it” (1 John 5:16).

Why? Because, as blessed Gregory explains:

“To have beasts rot in their own dung is for carnal people to end their lives in the stench of lust” (*Moralia*, book 24, chapter 16).

Nor is there any obstacle to understanding this of other crimes as well, because the Lord says that “the one who perseveres in the good will be saved” (Matt. 24:13); conversely, the one who perseveres in evil will undoubtedly be lost.

And woe to me! How can the one about whom the Apostle cries out fail to be lost?

“But understand this,” he says, “knowing that no fornicator, or unclean person, or covetous person—which is the service of idols—has any inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God” (Eph. 5:5).

Woe, then, woe to us wretched men! For who else are there in this multitude except—alas!—men of this sort?

[Note: Explain it thus: Who are those in this multitude of men except, alas, men of this kind—namely, fornicators, unclean persons, and covetous people? For he often warned that there are very few good men.]

It is clear that every illicit intercourse is either fornication or adultery. Yet no law grants marriage to ministers of the altar. These unclean or covetous fornicators, then, are none other than those who happen to die in these same crimes.

But the Lord mercifully promises:

“At whatever hour the sinner is converted and groans, he will be saved” (Ezek. 18:21).

Behold your counsel; behold your remedy.

Would that our remedy were equally easy to obtain!

For concerning us the Lord addresses the prophet Ezekiel as though asking him, saying:

“Son of man, what will happen to the wood of the vine?” (Ezek. 15:2), and so forth.

[Note: The Freising manuscript has *inde sentiat* instead of *indesinenter*, and afterward *videremus* instead of *fideremus*.]

No one who knows what Gregory continually means can judge anything more terrifying than these words.

What, then, shall we do?

### 16

I found in certain Psalters a little prayer which, if we were to pour it out daily before the Lord, and strive with all our strength to obtain through cooperation that we might deserve to be heard, we might trust would benefit us in some measure. It is as follows:

“Save us, almighty God, and through the merits and intercession of holy Mary, Mother of God, and of all the saints, be favorable and merciful to us. Having granted pardon for our past sins, give us henceforth the will, ability, and accomplishment to do what pleases you and is beneficial for us. Give us consolation in tribulation, aid in persecution, and strength in every temptation. Grant us pardon for the past, correction of our present evils, and deign to bestow protection upon us from future evils. Through …”

But what are we to do again, brothers? Behold, once more there is the greatest contradiction. For we are told:

“Whoever turns his ear away so as not to hear the law, his prayer will be accursed” (Prov. 28:9).

How great our turning away from the law is here becomes clear from this: once the Lord had said reproachfully, “And it shall be as with the people, so with the priest,” now, alas, our priests are far worse than the laity.

[Note: The common edition has *adversio* and immediately afterward *exprobrando*, but omits *dixerit*. We have accepted the correction and addition found in the Freising manuscript.]

[Note: “Popular” here means “lay.” *Populares* is contrasted here with priests and clerics; hence the expression “clergy and people” became established.]

### 17

Thus, obstructed by such great difficulty in finding counsel, and compelled to seek advisers—since I find no one anywhere—I am hastening, as I said, to Rome. May God’s mercy prosper my purpose in this matter.

I have learned, however, that many of you rejoice because of my departure, as though I ought never to return there. I consider it necessary to warn you that you should understand this common lot of mine and yours to be in every respect as follows: if it has been determined that I am to die there, I cannot die here at all; but if you must complete the time granted to you there, you can in no way reach the end of your lives here.

Whatever your disposition toward me may be, departing from here compelled by the love of learning, I commend you to the protection of divine mercy.

[Note: Construe it thus: “Departing from here, compelled by the love of learning, I commend you to the protection of divine mercy.”]

[Col. 0599]

## 457 — Privilege of Emperor Otto I Granted to Bishop Ratherius and the Church of Verona

[Note: Ughellius first published this privilege in volume 5 of *Italia sacra*, column 735. It is now presented in full and in a more correct form, according to the original, preserved in the archive of the chapter of the cathedral Church of Verona, of which Bartholomaeus Campagnola, formerly chancellor of that chapter and now archpriest of Saint Cecilia, supplied us with an exact transcript.]

[Col. 0599B] In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Otto, by the favor of divine clemency, august emperor.

[Note: This indicates the intervention of Otto’s son, who, on coming into Italy, had been received by his father at Verona a few days earlier.]

Let the diligence of all our faithful, both present and future, know that, at the intervention of our dearest son and namesake, we have granted to the Veronese Church, over which Bishop Ratherius is known to preside by our imperial clemency and through God’s appointment, for the love of God, of holy Mary, Mother of God, and of holy Zeno, whatever remains of that which our predecessors conferred upon his predecessors as pertaining to the two gates of the city: one, namely, called the gate of Saint Zeno, and the other called by the name of Saint Firmus, together with the toll on wagons and every revenue owed to us from them.

[Note: The words “whatever remains” indicate that certain other revenues arising from the two gates mentioned here, which had previously belonged to the Veronese Church, had been alienated from it, as Ratherius complains that many other things had been alienated in the *Conjecture of Quality*.]

[Note: This passage reveals the antiquity of the toll of the city gates granted to the bishopric, some remnants of which still accrue to that episcopate.]

We also grant—or rather, restore to him—the market on the feast of Saint Zeno or on Palm Sunday, as our predecessors are said to have granted it to that Church.

We also grant him two portions of the riverbank tax, and the riverbank tax in its entirety, in the castle called Portus.

[Note: *Ripaticum* is a tax collected from riverbanks. Note the ancient origin of this riverbank tax, which is still paid to the bishopric today.]

[Note: The Portus that now forms one town together with Leniacum. For what happened to the rights that the episcopate possessed at Portus, see the document of the year 1217 in Ughellius, volume 5, columns 822 and following.]

Whatever our predecessors have granted to that Church down to our own time and confirmed by charters, we grant in its entirety and confirm by this charter.

We also cut off and remove every public obligation from its castles—those now existing and those that will perpetually belong to the same Church—in such a way that neither count, viscount, nor *sculdascio* shall have any power to reside in them or to exercise coercion over anyone there.

[Note: From this passage it is clear that the episcopate had been granted complete jurisdiction, independent of the governors of the city of Verona, over all the castles—that is, the villages and settlements—belonging to it. From this we recognize the origin of similar jurisdiction over places now possessed by the same episcopate.]

Rather, all those dwelling in them shall remain under the authority either of this bishop or of whoever, through the succession of time, presides over the aforesaid Church, so that no power subject to us may anywhere have permission to coerce them.

But if anything wrong has been done by the *massarii*, or by the castellans, or by the *plectitii*, or by the *incensiti*, or by the *commodati*, or by his clerics or servants, let it be justly and legally corrected either by him himself or by his *ministerialis*.

[Note: *Massarii* were those who cultivated estates called *massaritiae*; in certain neighboring regions they are still commonly called *massari*. *Castellani* means inhabitants of castles. We shall discuss *plectitii* in a note on the *Judicatum*. *Incensiti* means peasants subject to a census, as Du Cange demonstrates. *Commodum* is taken here as a stipend or wage, as the same author shows. Thus *commodati* were men hired for wages.]

Furthermore, no one may presume to fish in his waters unless he has had permission from ancient times.

And because he is poor and an immigrant, deprived of every support except that of God and ourselves, and has already suffered many hardships, we wish to relieve him by this act of assistance, so that, in addition to being our bishop in the kingdom like the others, he may also be protected by our special prerogative of *mundeburdium*.

[Note: Ratherius himself indicates his poverty in the *Conjecture of Quality*, no. 13, and in no. 14 declares that, as an immigrant, he is deprived of the support of all his friends. In many places he testifies that after God he has confidence only in the emperor.]

Thus, if anyone should henceforth presume to trouble him as they have done until now, or should prove rebellious, or should contradict God by failing to render what belongs to his ministry:

[Note: On the back of the parchment on which this original privilege is written is a note in an ancient hand, which the aforementioned Archpriest Campagnola showed us as having been written either by Ratherius himself or at least at his dictation. Since it refers to the word “rebellious,” we append it here. The rebellious clerics are properly those who disdain to obey him and seek the patronage of anyone whatsoever without his permission. If any man should maintain that this is truly said without qualification, and maliciously mutilate or perhaps erase it from here—that is, from this privilege—may he be erased from the book of the living and not be written with the righteous.]

if he is a cleric, after everything he possesses has been placed under Ratherius’s authority, let him be expelled from the Church until he has made legitimate and appropriate satisfaction;

if he is a servant, let him suffer what belongs to servants and remain under Ratherius’s authority as a matter of obligation.

[Note: The author explains the word *mundeburdis* in book 4, preface, no. 12, of the *Prologues*. In common usage *mundeburde* denotes a certain kind of royal protection. Whoever possesses it is protected by royal authority through a special privilege, usually in such a way that no one may subject him to violence or legal proceedings—even if he is discovered to be at fault—before he has been heard in the presence of the same majesty. The present *mundeburdium* secured not only Ratherius’s person but also his rights.]

Let the faithful and friends have permission, without fear of any penalty, to act on his behalf in these matters and in everything beneficial to him, and to help him as far as they can.

[Note: When writing the *Conjecture of Quality*, the author indicated in no. 13 that he would ask the emperor for what he obtained here: “I would also ask,” he says, “that he deign to defend for us against counts, viscounts, and *sculdasci* what his predecessors conferred upon or confirmed for our Church by their charters.”]

If a count, viscount, *sculdascio*, or any secular authority does this, and interferes against his will in what properly belongs to him—that is, if he holds his land without any payment, or accepts one of his clerics or servants into his protection without his permission, or inflicts anything similar upon him—let him pay us one hundred pounds of gold; moreover, let him restore to him legally the damage that he has inflicted.

No one shall lure away any castellan of his from his castle and place him in his own, since this is most unjust. If anyone does so, let him be compelled to pay the injured party for the violation of immunity and to us the ban.

The same punishment shall legally be suffered by anyone who contradicts him concerning anything belonging to these Churches [read: belonging to the same Church] when he attempts to do what is proper to himself and pleasing to God, and by anyone who presumes to be the guardian, defender, or patron of any of them in so great a crime.

[Note: In the cited *Conjecture of Quality*, in the same section, he likewise says that he would ask this of the emperor: “If anything, whether by those two usurpers or by me, through necessity, by the fraudulent concealment of something, by exchange, under the name of a *libellarius*, or through what they call a precarious grant, has been done against God and justice, may he order it all to be rescinded by his authority.” It was not unusual to grant this to Churches. In the *placitum* of Lucca in the year 853, a privilege of Emperor Louis II from the year 852 is reported, by which he ordered all *libelli* prejudicial to the Church of Lucca to be declared void. See Muratori, volume 3 of *Italian Antiquities*, column 170. Likewise, in the year 998 Otto III issued a constitution rescinding *libelli* and emphyteutic grants contracted to the detriment of Churches, as is clear from the *Chronicle of Farfa*, volume 2 of Muratori’s *Italian Things*, part 2, column 496. We have explained in a note on the *Conjecture of Quality* what *libellariae*, exchanges, and precarious grants are.]

If any fraudulent *libellariae*, exchanges, or precarious grants have been made from the time the bishop was ordained, we wish and command that they be completely rescinded and corrected according to what is pleasing to God.

Thus, freed from all the disadvantages which, with Christ’s favor, we are able to remove from him, he may serve God securely, and you may all be able to pray to the end to divine clemency [supply: “divine”] for the safety of ourselves, our dearest wife, and our offspring.

[Col. 0602B]

## 461 — Sign of Otto, Most Serene Emperor

## 462

[Note: In the following year, 968, Ratherius sent letter 12 to this chancellor Ambrosius, and shortly before that he had sent him the work entitled *Discordia*. Hubertus, bishop and archchancellor, is Hubertus, bishop of Parma, to whom he sent the books *On Contempt for the Canons* in the year 964.]

I, Ambrosius, chancellor, acting in the place of Hubertus, bishop and archchancellor, have examined and subscribed this document.

Given on the Nones of November, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 967; in the sixth year of the reign of our lord Otto, most pious Caesar; indiction 11.

Done at Balsemade, happily. Amen.

[Note: Balsamede is mentioned in the privilege of Frederick I in the year 1154, in Ughellius, volume 5, column 795, as a place called Balsamede, not far from the river Mincio. Even now, in the territory and diocese of Verona belonging to Monzambano, there is a site that retains the same name in common usage and is called *la contrada di Balsemate*. There was formerly a village or settlement there which, after being destroyed by the changes of time, was replaced by the settlement of Monzambano, mentioned only in later documents. The *Saxon Annalist*, under the year 967, relates that Emperor Otto I, who had celebrated the feast of All Saints at Verona on the first day of November of that year, afterward proceeded to Mantua. Thus, while he was at Balsamede on this journey, he issued this privilege on the fifth day of November.]

## [THE JUDICATUM]

[Col. 0603]

## 463–464 — Admonition to the Following *Judicatum*
I. The following little work was first printed from the Freising manuscript by Father Bernard Pez in volume VI, part I, column 102, of the *Anecdota*, or *Diplomatic Code*. Since he found no title for it in the manuscript, he prefixed this one in his edition: “Ratherius’s foundation and endowment of the poorer clerics of the Church of Verona.” We have taken the title *Judicatum*, which we have placed above it, from Ratherius himself. For he twice cites this little work under that same title:

1. In the *Testament*, no. 2, where he says: “If there should be one pound, let it be given to those responsible for my funeral; the other, unless it should be lacking, to the clerics possessing the church of Saint Mary the Consoler, together with the others described in the same *Judicatum*.”

2. In the *Discordia*, no. 8: “Moreover, making a certain document for some people, which they call the *Judicatum*, that is, a decree, for the poorer clerics of the same Church—that is, for the priest-chaplains, the seven subdeacons of the sacristy, the seven singers, the seven sacristy acolytes, the five cantors, the six doorkeepers, and so forth”—as many, in fact, as are listed in the little work itself.

These considerations prove not so much the title as the work’s own authenticity. A *Judicatum* was a decree by which someone judged and disposed of property. Thus, in the will of the bishop of Tortona, in Ughelli, volume IV, we read: “The page, then, of their *Judicatum*, or of my disposition, in this manner,” and so forth. Likewise, the marquis Milo, in his testament written in 955 at the estate of Runci in the diocese of Verona, twice calls the document a *page of the Judicatum*, as we learned from old copies that agree with one another. For in Ughelli’s edition of the Veronese bishops, *pagina judicari* was mistakenly printed instead of *Judicati*.

II. Ratherius calls this *Judicatum* a “charter,” when he mentions in Letter 12 to Ambrose, no. 4, a charter confirmed not only by his own hand but also by that of the patriarch and metropolitan of Aquileia and of all the co-bishops of our province. Ratherius had been angered on seeing the revenues of the cathedral church distributed among its senior clerics in such a way that almost nothing was left for the others of lower rank. To provide appropriately for these men, he pressed the claims of the *Judicatum*. To make it valid and secure, he arranged for it to be confirmed by the signatures of the patriarch and of the bishops of the province. Nor was it unusual to seek the confirmation of the metropolitan and the bishops of the same province. Muratori, volume V of the *Italian Antiquities*, column 986, cites a synodal decree of the year 842, subscribed by Angilbert, archbishop of Milan, and seven other bishops of his province. By it the privilege of immunity granted by Bishop Rambert to the Brescian monastery of Saints Faustinus and Jovita was confirmed. That decree is distinct from Rambert’s foundation, which was written at a different place and time.

Ratherius’s foundation, however, is indicated as having been subscribed at the same place and time both by the founder and by the patriarch of Aquileia and the neighboring bishops, because they had all assembled at Verona. For the same reason, the original foundation of the table of the Veronese Chapter, made by Bishop Ratold in 813, had been signed by that bishop, by the patriarch of his time, and by the other bishops of the province, as may be seen in the appendix to the theological history of Marquis Scipione Maffei, p. 95, and in the more accurate copy printed by us in the work *Confirmation of the Falsity of Three Documents, etc.*, p. 123. The occasion on which the patriarch and the neighboring bishops were at Verona at the time when Ratherius issued the *Judicatum* must now be explained.

III. When Otto, son of King Otto I, the emperor, first came to Italy in 967, he found his father at Verona and celebrated there with him the feast of All Saints, as the Saxon Annalist records. There can be no doubt that the patriarch of Aquileia and the other bishops of that province assembled there in order, according to custom, to pay homage to such great princes. On this occasion, which Ratherius had foreseen, he obtained from them the subscriptions to the *Judicatum*.

That gathering of so many bishops appears to have been the synod which Ratherius mentions in two places, joining it with the emperor’s presence: “Trusting in the imperial presence and in the synod that was to be assembled,” he says in the *Discordia*, no. 5. Likewise, in his sermon on the octave of Easter, no. 4: “Trusting in the presence of the emperor, who decides nothing other than what is just, and in the synod that is to be convened.” Here he plainly indicates the hope he placed both in the emperor Otto and in the bishops who, for the reason stated, were expected to assemble at Verona. See note 10 on the *Discordia*.

From the emperor, when he departed from there, he obtained on 5 November the privilege already printed, by which he hoped to be protected from enemies and powerful men. The patriarch and the other bishops, apparently assembled in a kind of synod after the emperor’s departure, subscribed the *Judicatum*. Thus the *Judicatum*, prepared earlier, was furnished and published after the emperor’s departure—that is, after 5 November 967—with the subscriptions of so many bishops.

IV. Near the end, we must not omit the effort of a recent writer, who attempted to cast suspicion on this *Judicatum* as a forgery. He seems to have undertaken this not because he inwardly and with complete certainty believed it to be so in itself, but because he thought it useful to his own cause to introduce some doubt about it.

We had proved two privileges of the Veronese Chapter attributed to Bishop Ratold to be spurious, chiefly because several passages from Ratherius’s much later *Judicatum* had been copied into them by the forger. When that writer undertook to defend these privileges, he read Ratherius’s *Judicatum* in his first booklet of vindications as a genuine work of Ratherius, without hesitation, and proposed that Ratherius could have copied those passages from Ratold’s privileges.

But after we had demonstrated in several ways that this answer was wholly empty, he adopted another course in his second defense of the same privileges. He did not dare to declare Ratherius’s *Judicatum*, which most clearly exposed the forgery of those privileges, absolutely apocryphal; instead, he thought it sufficient to scatter certain doubts, as though we had not attacked those privileges with sufficiently firm reasoning on the basis of the *Judicatum* itself. The published letter bears more than sufficient witness to the weight of the arguments we directed against the privileges themselves.

Everyone of sound judgment will understand that it is useless to doubt a *Judicatum* which Ratherius himself, in the three places already cited, declared to be his own work. In addition, its style is so distinctively Ratherian that it suits no one but him.

V. Anyone who carefully considers the reasons for doubt advanced by an otherwise most learned and acute man will find them so slight and weak that they accomplish nothing against such evident arguments for authenticity. It will be sufficient here to present three or four of the principal ones.

He objects to the symbolic style and the appearance of dialogue, which, he says, are unsuitable for an act of foundation. But this was Ratherius’s particular character. When he wrote the *Judicatum*, he did not wish to follow the notaries’ customary practice; he used his own style and manner, as he did also in the *Decree concerning the Little Abbey of Magonziano*, which contains another foundation, and in the *Testament*. In these works the method of writing is found to be plainly similar to that of the *Judicatum*.

He insists on the absence of chronological notes, subscriptions, and other formulas that are usually found in such documents, as well as on the absence of the subscriptions of the patriarch of Aquileia and the other co-bishops, which Ratherius himself reported as having been attached to this foundation. But are chronological notes, subscriptions, and other formulas not likewise absent from the *Testament* and the *Decree concerning the Little Abbey of Magonziano*? Yet no one will for that reason call those works into question.

We would indeed miss none of these things if the original act, or an authentic copy, had come down to us. But in the old Freising manuscript this document, like the other works, was copied from Ratherius’s papers not as a public charter—which requires chronological notes, subscriptions, and fixed formulas—but as a little work of Ratherius, for which such things are unnecessary.

VI. A more serious objection would be the one which the critic thought he saw in the *Judicatum*: namely, that Ratherius wished, contrary to the principles for which he had fought so fiercely, to exempt the lower clerics in some manner from himself and from his successors.

But where does he establish this in the *Judicatum*? Is it because he there commands: “If any one of them should neglect anything concerning the service of God, or should not apply himself diligently to learning his ministry, nevertheless neither the bishop nor the clerics shall have the right to take anything whatever from these men”?

These words merely imply that Ratherius forbade any bishop to take something away from this foundation on account of the crime or negligence of any cleric, since he wanted the foundation to be perpetual. He did not, however, remove from the bishops any other jurisdiction over those clerics. Otherwise, since he forbids not only the bishops but also the clerics of the same college to do the very thing in question, he would have withdrawn such offenders from the jurisdiction and correction even of the provost and of the other clerics, to whom he explicitly granted the authority to correct them:

“The provost already mentioned, whom they shall place over themselves, shall together with all the others summon him; and if he refuses to amend, he shall distribute among the others what he has taken from him. Or let them themselves devise among themselves a penalty by which such negligent men and those unwilling to learn letters ought to be corrected.”

Here he does not name the bishop—not in order to exempt these men from the bishop, but because he established an easier and domestic method of correction. If in some case this correction were neglected or proved ineffective, where in the whole document will one find a prohibition against the bishops’ bringing a remedy, provided that nothing is taken away from the foundation?

Nor should the words which Ratherius uses when extending his foundation not merely to the clerics who now exist but also to their successors move us: “even though they too are ungrateful.” The learned critic interprets this as though Ratherius were calling all the present clerics and all their successors ungrateful and rebellious. But the words “even though they too are ungrateful” plainly refer to those whom he had previously described with the words “who now exist.” They alone are the ungrateful ones who, as he says, either deceived by the seduction of their elders, or terrified by threats, or infected by the poison of their conspiracy, opposed the bishop. These characteristics do not apply to successors and cannot be made to do so.

We pass over the other, less important objections.

VII. Perhaps someone may think that, although this little work is plainly Ratherian, it is not the foundation itself, because the words “I have assigned certain things, and I have also given” seem to indicate that the foundation had already been established by another document.

But the *Decree concerning the Little Abbey of Magonziano* was written in a similar manner, although within its own body it is called a “decretal writing,” by which, evidently, the property and the foundation itself were established. We have received a more carefully copied transcript from the Freising manuscript, from which we shall make several corrections.

[Col. 0605]

## Ratherius’s *Judicatum*, or Foundation and Endowment of the Poorer Clerics of the Cathedral Church of Verona

[Col. 0605A] 469

### 1

Ratherius, by the grace of God alone bishop of Verona, to all his successors.

Because I was utterly unable to prevail against the customs of the wicked, which were growing powerful against the commandments of God and the decrees of the saints, so that either, according to the judgment of the blessed Apostle, each person in our Church might receive his own reward according to his labor (1 Corinthians 3:8), or, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles, the things bestowed might be distributed among the clerics [Note: Pez has *ecclesiis*, “among the churches,” instead of *clericis*, “among the clerics,” incorrectly. We have preferred the reading of our copy, with which the book of the *Discordia*, no. 5, also agrees: when this same passage is quoted there, it reads *clericis*, not *ecclesiis*.] according to each one’s need (Acts 4:35); but because, through a wicked interpretation of that saying of the Lord which reads, “To everyone who has, more will be given, and he will abound; but from him who does not have, even what he has will be taken away” (Matthew 25:29), the most unjust decision-makers judged as though the one who had more ought to receive more from the goods assigned by the Church [Note: The manuscript read *minus*, “less”; we have corrected it to *magis*, “more,” on the basis of the sense. Alternatively, the copyist may have skipped over part of the sentence in an easy leap because of the repeated occurrence of *haberet*. What must be supplied would be: “that the one who had more should receive more, while the one who had less should receive less from the goods assigned by the Church.” The construction is: “the most unjustly deciding”—namely, those who were wickedly interpreting the Lord’s testimony—as though it were held that the one who had more should receive more, while the one who had less should receive less from the goods assigned by the Church.]—whereas he intended this to be understood rather as meaning that, for the one who possesses charity, the other virtues are added, while for the one who does not possess it, the remaining virtues are reckoned as nothing—lest the compassion by which I grieved that these men were both perishing through poverty and being drawn away from the service of God should prove entirely vain, it came into my mind to give them something from my own.

But when I say “my own,” I mean what was entrusted to my judgment for administration and which, if I wished, I might enjoy while I lived. [Note: Pez incorrectly has *reum*, “guilty,” instead of *meum*, “my own.”]

Another consideration also impelled me to undertake this and not hesitate to bring it forward [Note: The construction is: “So that I might not hesitate to bring forward another reason which impelled me to undertake this”; namely, that, alas, I had always been so idle in the service of God from childhood that, etc.]: because, alas, from childhood I have always been so idle in God’s service that, miserable man, I never deserved to occupy in the Church the place of a cedar, a myrtle, an olive tree, or any other such tree.
