I might at least thereafter be able to perform the office of an elm, supporting those who bore good fruit—that is, those devoted to the Church’s watch—so long as it is day, so that, as one collaborating with them in all their labor, I might have a share in it. And just as the one who receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward (Matthew 10:41), so I too, by helping these men and their successors in the service of God, might always receive the same reward as they, in a manner producing through their hands after my death what I, unhappy man, had neglected to do with my own hands while alive. So it was said of the man who was then called Saul and later, by God’s gift, Paul—then the persecutor of believers, later the outstanding teacher of the nations—that he stoned Stephen with the hands of all, because he guarded the clothing of those who stoned him (Augustine, Sermon 279, no. 1).

### 2

Considering, therefore, that there were men who endured greater labor in the Church and a harsher poverty, so that they continually complained and, because of want, even hastened unlawfully to enter the sacred orders in order to find some support from these things, though at the greatest danger to their souls—for their age did not admit them, their learning did not recommend them, and the uprightness of their conduct did not distinguish them—I assigned certain things [Note: The author explains this in the *Discordia*, no. 7: “When certain of them”—the senior clerics, or canons, of the cathedral church—“held benefices from me, I threatened them that, if they prevented me from obtaining what was due to me”—namely, a more equitable distribution of the revenues of that church, by which provision would be made for needy lower-ranking clerics—“I would take away what I had granted them.” They replied that they cared so little that, if he took away anything he had given to one of them, and so forth. Later, indicating that he had taken those benefices away from them because of their ingratitude, he adds in no. 8: “What I had brought forward as a threat, I did not delay to turn into an accomplished deed.” Then, relating what he did with the benefices recovered because of their ingratitude, he indicates that through the *Judicatum* he assigned part of them to the poorer clerics in precisely the order and number described here. The benefices recovered by Ratherius seem to be understood as those which, when the canons declared that they did not care if he took away what he had given them, he regarded their response as a kind of renunciation.] very recently recovered from the ungrateful, to certain priest-chaplains [Note: Priest-chaplains were not canons; hence even today they are called chaplains in our church.], subdeacons, acolytes, and doorkeepers of our mother Church—those now existing, and after them seven sacristy subdeacons, seven singers [Note: These seven singers, mentioned after the seven sacristy subdeacons and before the acolytes, were seven subdeacons who sang in the choir. Shortly before this passage Ratherius names only three orders, and shortly afterward likewise names subdeacons, acolytes, and doorkeepers; but he divides both the subdeacons and the acolytes into two classes, some being called “of the sacristy” and others “singers.” Three kinds of subdeacons are distinguished in the Roman Church by an old manuscript cited by Baronius under the year 1053, no. 22, and by John the Deacon, *On the Lateran Church*, in Mabillon, volume II of the *Museum Italicum*, p. 567: seven were regional subdeacons, who sang the Epistles and lessons at the station churches; seven were palatine subdeacons, who performed the same duty in the Lateran Church; and seven others, called the School of Singers, who sang only when the supreme pontiff celebrated. In the Church of Verona, however, there were only two classes of subdeacons. From Ratherius’s text, seven were “of the sacristy,” serving the celebrating bishop, and seven others were singers who sang in the choir. Likewise, there were seven sacristy acolytes who served in sacred functions, and five other acolytes who were singers.], seven sacristy acolytes, five singers, and six doorkeepers—although even they too were ungrateful [Note: That is, “even those whom he previously described as ‘those now existing.’” The benefices recovered from the ungrateful senior clerics, he says, were assigned to the lower clerics who now existed, although these men too were ungrateful, since they opposed Ratherius as well, either deceived by the seduction of their elders, terrified by threats, or infected by the poison of their conspiracy. See Admonition, no. 6.]—because they had either been deceived by the seduction of their elders, or terrified by threats, or infected by the poison of their conspiracy.

In addition to what had long ago been customarily assigned to them by the good, God-fearing, and charity-filled men, they shall receive the following: [Note: He now begins to enumerate what, by this disposition, he gave from his own resources to the clerics just mentioned. First he names the church, or the revenues of the church of Saint Mary, which, to distinguish it from other churches dedicated to the Virgin Mary and designated by their respective particular names, was called Consolatrix. This church is a short distance from the cathedral. Since everything he gave to these clerics was among goods subject to episcopal jurisdiction and disposition, this church too was of that kind; it later passed into the right of the Chapter. Although it had its own priest serving there, not all the revenues of the church belonged to him: only a certain portion was assigned to him, and, in this disposition of those revenues for the benefit of the clerics mentioned, that portion had to remain intact for the same priest.] the church of Saint Mary, which has acquired the surname “the Consoler,” together with everything that belongs or will belong to it, except for the portion of the priest serving there. It shall nevertheless be in the power of these men, if he should fail, to substitute another in his place, but they shall take away nothing of what he is justly entitled to possess.

If they should decide that the chaplains themselves should sing Mass in that church by turns, or that they should choose some of their number to sing it completely, they shall retain for their own use the amount which it was customary for the priests serving there to have, specifically so that they might sing there; but they shall divide the remainder equally with the subdeacons, acolytes, and the doorkeepers already mentioned. [Note: Here, as also in the *Decree concerning the Little Abbey of Magonziano*, no. 2, and in part II of *On Contempt of the Canons*, no. 4, Ratherius distinguishes vineyards from fields. “Fields” seem to mean lands in which grain or other crops were sown; “vineyards” those from which wine was obtained. In Sermon 2 on the Ascension, no. 4, he wrote *vineyards and fields*. A *modius* was a measure both of liquids and of dry goods; the *sextarius* was a portion of a *modius*, differing according to local custom, just as the *modius* itself did not everywhere contain the same quantity. Ratherius did not want particular fields assigned to individual clerics, from which the prebends were later gradually established—for by that arrangement almost everything had fallen to the senior and more powerful clerics, leaving the others in poverty. Instead, he wanted the revenues arising from the assigned estates brought into a common table, as it is called, so that they might be divided in equal portions among the poorer clerics listed here.] They shall not divide it, however, by fields and vineyards, but by *modii* and *sextarii*, so that no occasion for quarrel or envy may arise, but all may rejoice in the peace which the Lord has specially bestowed upon people of good will.

I also gave another church of the holy Mother of God, called “at the Star” [Note: It is now called *delle Stelle*. It is a church in the hills of the Paltinate valley, from which excellent oil is obtained in abundance.], so that the lamp-oil which comes from it may serve the church already mentioned and that of Saint John the Baptist [Note: This church is near the cathedral and is called Saint John at the Font, where the baptistery of that cathedral is located]. They shall divide the remainder among themselves. For it is unlawful that what is placed upon altars should serve privies [Note: He is speaking allegorically, setting privies against altars just as he sets the devil against God. A privy is a place into which the filth of the city is cast. He means that the revenues of the Church must not be converted to profane, especially base and wicked, uses.], or that what is offered to God should serve the devil.

I granted also from the estate of Saint Proculus in the Paltinate valley, at a place called Cuscianus [Note: Pez has *Tuscianus*. We preferred the reading of our copy, *Cuscianus*. It is a place in the Paltinate valley now called Cuzano.], one small estate. In the valley of Salla, at Saint Justus, I gave two *massaritiae* near the walls [Note: *Massaritiae* were estates cultivated by distinct tenant farmers, or, as they were called, *massarii*. See Muratori, *Estense Antiquities*, part I, p. 82, where he cites a document listing many *massaritiae* with their respective farmers. Compare the note on the *Discordia*.].

I also assigned the little estate called Paltiniacum, with its male and female servants and everything belonging to it; also the tithes from the castle of Hupedanum, and that which is called “of the Forentani” [Note: Pez has *de Forendarus*. We have followed our copy. From it we also added *aliam* before *pertinent*. It should further be noted that Tumba—now Tomba Susana—Roveclaria—now Roverchiara—and Cereda—now Cerea—were perhaps already parishes at this time.], that is, those tithes which belong neither to Tumba, nor to Roveclaria, nor to Cereda, nor to any other parish, together with the church of Saint Peter of Persiano and everything belonging to it.

### 3

I and they also wish and decree that they shall have no superior over them except one whom they themselves choose or appoint from among themselves. He shall collect all these things together with his junior [Note: Formerly we thought that *cum suo juniore*, “with his junior,” should be corrected to *cum suo jure*, “with his right,” a reading preferred by the ancient spurious document attributed to Ratold, whose fabricator copied this entire passage from Ratherius’s *Judicatum*, as we clearly demonstrated in the appendix to our dissertation *On the Privileges and Exemption of the Cathedral Chapter of Verona*, p. 65, and more fully in another Italian work entitled *Confirmation of the Falsity of Three Documents Published in Ughelli in Favor of the Chapter of Verona*, pp. 8 and 25. This spurious document appears in Ughelli, volume V, column 707d. We now think, however, on better judgment, that the reading of the genuine *Judicatum*, which Father Pez published from the Freising manuscript, should not be abandoned. Among medieval writers, *juniores* were those subordinate to senior men of special authority, while nevertheless holding some authority or office. See Du Cange. Thus, in monasteries, *juniores* were called those who assisted another in an office. In this sense, the *junior* in our little work seems to be the person who assisted the provost in collecting the revenues. This reading is confirmed by the plural *eis* below, which requires at least two persons to whom something may be given as *calceradigum*, provided it is not much: namely, both the man whom they have chosen as provost and his junior, or assistant. Otherwise, if one provost who collected everything “with his right” were intended, the text would have to read *ei*, “to him,” not *eis*, “to them.”], and, as we have said, divide them equally by measure and number.

If they wish to give him something as *calceradigum*, it shall be in their power, provided that it is not much. [Note: The same Freising manuscript adds the particle *non*. In Pez, *jure*—“by right”—is omitted, as is suggested by what follows, “provided it is not much,” namely, the thing which they are permitted to give him if they wish. *Calceradigum* signifies some compensation to be given to the provost and his junior for their office; thus *pro calceradigo* means “as compensation for the office,” or “for the office.”]

If, however—as is human misery—any one of them should neglect anything concerning the service of God, or should not apply himself diligently to learning his ministry, neither the bishop nor the clerics shall for that reason have the right to take anything whatever from these men. Rather, the aforementioned provost whom they have placed over themselves shall summon him together with all the others; and if he refuses to amend, he shall distribute among the others what he has taken from him. Or let them themselves devise among themselves a penalty by which such negligent men and those unwilling to learn letters ought to be corrected.

But if that minister should be dull, fraudulent, or useless, or if he should not dare to correct offenders, let him be removed by those same men, and let another from among the same presbyters or subdeacons be substituted for him.

### 4

Moreover, I granted whatever belonged to that exchange which I made with John, son of Bertana [Note: Our copy has *Berdanae*. From it we corrected *factae* to *facta* below. For the nature of the contract called a *precaria*, see the note on the conjecture concerning *Qualitas*.], concerning the dwelling near the forum, which was a *precaria* made for a certain Dominic the moneyer [Note: A moneyer, that is, one who struck coins. This testimony establishes the antiquity of the Veronese mint, which is also proved by later documents. Dominic the moneyer of the city of Verona is mentioned and is also read as a subscriber in the testament of Notherius, bishop of Verona, dated 15 November 927, not 928. It was published by Canon Marquis de Dionysius in his collection of charters, p. 105.].

I granted it in such a way that, in addition to the portion which they would receive with the others, Galivertus [also Galibertus] the priest and Martin the junior subdeacon should divide it between themselves during their lifetimes [Note: What he granted from that exchange is meant. He gave it during their lifetimes to Galivertus—also Galibertus—the priest, and to Martin the junior subdeacon, both of them belonging to the number of those clerics for whom this *Judicatum* provided an equal share. He gave it to them during their lifetimes in addition to the portion which, equally with the others, was due to them, so that after their deaths it would return to the community—that is, to the common table—being granted to no one thereafter as a special possession, but divided by *sextarii*.]

But because my poverty could in no way obtain even this—that these things should be divided among each of the designated men according to each one’s need—I endeavored to arrange that I might assign at least something from that little poverty of mine to some of them, so that each might receive his own reward according to his labor.

Therefore, in addition to what I assigned for common division among all, I assigned to the aforementioned priests, subdeacons, and sacristy acolytes: at Bodanigo [Note: Our copy has *Bodanico*. Yet *Bodanigo* is also read in a charter of 959 published in the collection of charters mentioned above, p. 125. In the privilege of Eugene III of 1145, granted in favor of the Church of Verona, it is called *Bonadiguus*; it is now Bonavigo.] one estate; at Porto three fields; at Cereta one garden; at Roveclaria one estate, with three *plecticii* [Note: That certain rural people were called *plecticii* is clear from the privilege of Otto I which we prefixed: “If anything should be wrongly done by the *massarii*, the castellans, the *plecticii*, the *incensiti*, or the *commodati*”—all of them rural men—and so forth. The three *plecticii* mentioned here were attached to the estate. Above, in section 2, one estate and two *massaritiae* are mentioned. A *massaritia* seems to have been a large estate, while an estate (*casale*) seems to indicate a few fields. The rural people who cultivated the *massaritiae* were called *massarii*; those who received an estate, or a few fields, to cultivate were called *plecticii*. Shortly afterward, for *Naudosiola*, the privilege of Frederick I granted to the Church of Verona in 1155 more accurately reads *Nauclesiola*, now Nichesola.];

at Naudosiola, from which nine solidi are paid as rent; at Caput Alponis one small estate [Note: The common text has *casariaclum*. *Casariculum* seems to be the same as *casaliculum* in a document of Farfa cited by Du Cange, that is, a very small estate. This *casariculum* at Caput Alponis, now Cavalpone, is said to have been situated there. Shortly afterward the common editions have *in Bogosis*. We have corrected it from our copy to *in Bogosio*, a reading also supported by the document of Frederick I mentioned above; the place is now called Begosso.]; at Bogosio one estate, so that they may possess these separately and not divide them with the others [Note: “The others” are not only the doorkeepers, but also the subdeacons and singer-acolytes whom he distinguished above from the sacristy subdeacons and acolytes.].

The steward of these possessions shall provide for the church of Saint John in the House [Note: “House” was the name given to the cathedral. The church of Saint John in the House is the Saint John the Baptist mentioned above, adjoining the cathedral and containing its baptistery.]. He shall also appoint there two doorkeepers from the same company, who shall guard the basilica and keep watch over the entrance of the treasury [Note: The *cimeliarchium* is the place where the church’s treasures—that is, its sacred vessels and valuable movable goods—are stored and guarded. See Gregory the Great, book III, letter 50.] throughout the night, either continuously or, if it should seem better, by turns. [Note: Our copy has *saepe*, “often,” instead of *semper*, “always.”]

For I considered that, since, in addition to the ministry they perform in the Church, these three orders [Note: Namely, the subdeacons, acolytes, and doorkeepers.] devote themselves more particularly than all the others to the bishop’s service, they ought to receive something special from the bishop for the special service rendered to him. I granted little to them for this reason: I was not so well supplied with things to give, since, while others were ruling, I could only sing in mourning, and I thought that I myself ought to avoid becoming a cause of envy against them.

But if—as we confidently trust will truly happen—while they faithfully serve the Lord, inspiration should be given to any of the faithful to add something to what they have, we wish it to be divided among them commonly, just as the other things are, so that neither contention nor hatred may prevail among them, but the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, may guard their hearts and their thoughts (Philippians 4:7).

But if, as often happens when the devil instigates it, one of them should be unlawfully expelled from this mother church because of envy and hatred [Note: “Mother church” means the cathedral church.], he shall not for that reason lose from this church of Holy Consolatrix what he had been accustomed to receive. He shall also receive what the others receive and devote himself there to the service of the Lord, if he wishes or if it is permitted [Note: Pez has *dedat*, “let him give himself,” as the text allows. We have corrected and supplemented it from our copy: *sese dedat*, “let him devote himself.”].

476. It is easy to recognize how wholly devoid he is of knowledge of canon law, when he holds that one person may send a cleric into a church or expel him from it, unless he is someone who can, whenever he wishes, make an acolyte out of a cleric.  
[Note: No one, of course, except a bishop may make an acolyte out of a cleric, nor can anyone make a cleric without the bishop’s permission. Hence the author states in *Synodica* no. 15: “Let none of you make a cleric without our permission.”]

But since malicious people are never without something they desire wickedly, even if they cannot accomplish it, I bind what I am doing with this safeguard: whether he is called a bishop (for he will not be one), or whether it is the presbyters and deacons of this same Church of ours who attempt either to destroy this arrangement or to diminish anything from what good predecessors of theirs have justly and lawfully been accustomed to provide from our Church—so that, for example, they might say: “You have your stipend; let that suffice,” or, “If you wish to divide what is ours with you, send into our common fund what has been given to you”—let such men have no share in the next life with any of the saints, but with Ham, Dathan, and Abiram, or with those whom either the Flood drowned or the earth swallowed up, and with Pilate, Annas, and Caiaphas, Judas the betrayer of Christ, and Simon the magician, and also Ananias and Sapphira, whom blessed Peter condemned for defrauding the Church of money; and let them be anathema, *maranatha*, and excluded from eternal life, unless they repent.

[Note: Pez reads *si efficere* (“if they can accomplish it”). We have written *etsi efficere* (“even if they cannot accomplish it”) in accordance with our copy, which agrees with the pseudo-document attributed to Ratoldus. In that document this period was partly transferred, together with several other passages of this *Judicatum*, by the compiler from other sources. See our dissertation *On the Privileges and Exemption of the Chapter of Verona*, p. 74, and Ughelli, vol. V, col. 709.]

[Note: Pez’s edition has *nobiscum vestra* (“your things with us”), incorrectly. Our copy has *nobiscum nostra* (“our things with us”). The sense suggested the correction *vobiscum* (“with you”).]

But if they say, as those do who “turn aside to words of wickedness to excuse their sins” (Ps. CXL, 4): “We cannot give them as much as our predecessors gave to their predecessors,” we answer them: “Do not be deceived; God is not mocked” (Gal. VI, 7). They gave what they could; you too give what you are able, if you wish to escape the curse pronounced above.

6. “You are causing a schism,” they say, “by turning them away from the discipline of their forefathers.” I am not turning them away from discipline; rather, if it were possible, I desire to rescue them from poverty and from the opportunity to neglect the service of the Lord. Nor do I forbid delinquents to be corrected; but I do not want them to lose, under the pretext of correction, what I provide. Therefore I decree that what I have granted them be withdrawn from their own minister.

[Note: “Let them be withdrawn from what I have granted them” means that they should be punished by having withdrawn from them what had been granted to them, as he had established in no. 3: “If he refuses to amend, let him distribute to others what he has taken away from him.”]

Their masters, however, should compel them by discipline, not by poverty, to do what must be done. I would cause a schism if I allowed what they have always possessed to be taken away from them because of what I add to it. Nor would that be an addition, but an exchange and a separation from your brotherhood. May the person who contrives this be separated from God and excluded from the fellowship of the saints.

I further beg whatever successors I may ever have that, when they read this written document, they carefully remember: “Son, if you are wise, you will be wise for yourself” (Prov. IX, 9), so that they may understand from a similar case that, if they are good, nothing will benefit anyone more than themselves.

[Note: In *Discordia* no. 8: “making,” he says, “a certain written document called the *Judicatum*, that is, the Decree.”]

For, as blessed Augustine says with complete truth, no one sins against another before first sinning against himself.

And if, because of my unworthiness, I should not obtain the reward I hope for from this matter, at least let the most pious emperor, in whose time this was done, receive from it the reward that is due to him—he who was also the Church’s most merciful supporter, establishing me in it precisely so that I might diligently carry out what had to be carried out and neglect what had to be neglected. Relying on his aid, I undertook this; and therefore it is more his work than mine. May he, I beg, grant him an everlasting recompense for it—he who caused that poorest household of clergy to be sustained in this manner, providing it with an annual allowance; who makes him reign powerfully in this world and glorifies him eternally in the next. Amen.

[Note: Our copy has this reading. Pez reads *conceditur adipisci* (“is permitted to attain”). Construe: “And if, because of my unworthiness, I should not happen to attain the reward hoped for from this matter, at least the most pious emperor, in whose time this was done, may obtain the reward due to him.” This emperor is Otto I, who was also the Church’s most merciful supporter, establishing me in it, and so forth.]

[Note: This is the imperial confidence in the emperor’s presence which Ratherius mentions both in *Discordia* no. 5 and in the sermon *On the Octave of Easter*, no. 4. Compare what we said about this in the preface, no. 3. From this it may be inferred that Ratherius, trusting in imperial assistance, contrived this arrangement and communicated it to the emperor who was present; since the emperor did not object, he hoped that Caesar would protect it by his authority and refuse to listen to those who protested. How greatly this hope deceived him will become clear from Letter 12 to Ambrosius.]

[Col. 0613]

# A LITTLE WORK OF RATHERIUS  
## ON CLERICS REBELLING AGAINST HIM

[Note: Acherius published this little work from the Laon manuscript. Its date can be recognized from three indications. At the beginning the author quotes a passage from Isaiah, chapter XXX, which he heard in the nocturnal reading. He therefore wrote this during Advent, when Isaiah was still read at the night office. Moreover, the words in section 2, “imperially sanctioned,” refer to the privilege of the Emperor Otto, granted on 5 November 967, as will be evident from note 1148. The complaints brought before the same emperor are also mentioned there; an envoy of the most pious Caesar was expected, who, after hearing both parties and conducting an inquiry, would report. Compare note 1152. This little work was therefore composed during Advent of the year 967, when the canons stirred up a rebellion; hence the title, *On Clerics Rebelling against Him*.]

479. While I was attending to the nocturnal reading, it happened that I heard words of the following kind—not unsuitable to us, and, would that it were only venially so:

> “It is a people provoking to anger, and lying sons, sons unwilling to hear the law of God, who say to those who see: ‘Do not see’; and to those who look: ‘Do not look for us upon what is right; speak to us things that please us; see for us errors. Take away from me the way; turn aside from me the path; let the Holy One of Israel cease from before us’” (Isa. XXX, 10).

[Note: The Vulgate reads, incorrectly: “When I had compared this with these things, which [are said] to others, and in the same [office].” For the sense to be clear, we moved *which* to follow *the other things*. Construe and explain it thus: “When I had compared this with these other prophets, psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, which I had also heard in the same—namely, the nocturnal office—which you boast of attending more than the other Churches of Italy.” Note the frequency of the choir even in the nocturnal office.]

When I compared this with the other things I had heard in the same office—prophets, psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, which you boast that you frequent more than the other Churches of Italy—and with the word of the Lord, which, in harmony with the prophet sent by him, speaks thus to your authorities:

> “This people honors me with its lips, but their heart is far from me. In vain do they worship me, teaching doctrines and commandments of men” (Matt. XV, 8).

And when the Apostle also says:

> “There will be a time when they will not endure sound doctrine, but according to their own desires they will heap up teachers for themselves, having itching ears; and they will indeed turn their hearing away from the truth, but will turn to fables” (II Tim. IV, 3),

I, most wretched man—alas for the sorrow!—was compelled to understand that we are the people provoking the Lord to anger, not unaware that the Apostle most truly testified: “Whatever things were written were written for our instruction” (Rom. XV, 4).

For who can more aptly be understood as the sons unwilling to hear the law of God—if I may say so with your pardon—than those who desire to be called canons and who continually complain about the stipend assigned to canons, yet refuse so utterly to be canons that, relying only on the customs of wicked men, they cannot endure even to read or perform anything that the holy canons decree, much less to hear it?

[Note: The stipend assigned to the canons properly means the revenues of the cathedral church that had been assigned to them. Since the more substantial revenues of that Church had been divided among the senior clergy—that is, the canons—while only a very small portion had been left to the lesser clergy, so that they were oppressed by poverty, Ratherius once arranged for something to be deducted from the revenues held by the canons in order to provide more fairly for the lesser clergy. When those same canons fiercely resisted this division, Ratherius, in order to provide for the lesser clergy by another means, took away from ten canons the benefices that he himself had granted them and decided that some lesser clerics should be supported from part of those benefices, in the *Judicatum* mentioned above. Although they had in a certain sense consented to the removal of those benefices, provided that the bishop spared the canons’ own revenues, once they saw themselves secure in those same revenues after the *Judicatum*, they treated the benefices once granted and then withdrawn from them as their own possessions and arranged for the *Judicatum* to be rescinded. For this reason they attacked the bishop with accusations before Caesar and requested that an envoy be sent by him to investigate the entire matter and report on it. Their efforts eventually led to the *Judicatum* being rescinded by a special command of the emperor. Thus the stipend assigned to the canons, about which the canons complained, should be understood not only as the cathedral revenues divided among them, but also—and in this passage chiefly—as the benefices which Ratherius, from his own very limited resources, had granted them and later taken away.]

They say to those who see, that is, to those who perceive the danger to their souls: “Do not see”; and to those who look upon their depravity: “Do not look for us upon what is right.” That is, do not speak what is true, but what seems right to us; tell us what pleases us, not God; “see for us errors”—that is, allow us to be deceived by our own inventions and by the wicked customs of our predecessors.

“Take away from me the way” (Isa. XXX, 10)—that is, the one who says: “I am the way” (John XIV, 6). “Turn aside from me the path” (Isa. XXX, 11), namely, the narrow and constricted way leading to life. “Let the Holy One of Israel cease from before us” (ibid.)—that is, let the Holy One cease troubling us by setting before us the holiness we must follow and showing us the vision of true and everlasting peace; let the Lord’s word, which you press upon us, cease.

2. What, then, sons—concerning whom we are divinely warned not to rejoice “when you are multiplied” (Ecclus. XVI, 1)—what, I ask, will happen if, after hearing the promise of the most merciful God, who says:

> “If you return and keep quiet, you will be saved. In silence and in hope shall your strength be” (Isa. XXX, 15),

and shortly afterward:

> “The Lord waits, that he may have mercy on you” (ibid., 18),

you disregard it, answering by your conduct, even if not by your words:

> “By no means; we will flee to the horses” (ibid., 16)?

[Note: The canons sought the patronage of powerful men in order to resist Ratherius. See *Discordia* no. 8. Construe as follows: “The horses” may reasonably be understood as any powerful men whose patronage you rely upon, and so you hold ecclesiastical discipline in such contempt. Even if it should happen that the Lord answers you literally, with the authority of Pope Gregory: “Therefore you shall flee,” and you reply, “We shall mount swift horses,” he will respond: “Therefore those who pursue you shall be swifter.” In Isaiah these words are spoken by the Jews: “We will flee to the horses.” The Lord answers: “Therefore you shall flee.” They continue: “We shall mount swift horses.” The Lord replies: “Therefore those who pursue you shall be swifter.” Then follow: “A thousand shall flee at the threat of one; at the threat of five you shall flee,” and so forth. Hence Ratherius’ text appears to require correction or explanation. He indicates that the patronage of powerful men will do nothing for rebellious clerics against the Lord, who can answer them just as he once answered the Hebrews, vindicating the enormity of their rebellion, and so forth.]

There is no obstacle to understanding it thus: “[Even if] it should happen that the Lord answers you literally, with the authority of Pope Gregory: ‘Therefore you shall flee. And we shall mount swift horses; therefore those who pursue you shall be swifter’” (ibid.), temporarily avenging the enormity of your rebellion, lest, as we do not cease to fear, he condemn you eternally.

What, I ask, is the evident greatness of the most merciful God, and what the supreme easing of just retribution?

For this reason, in accordance with the Apostle who says, “Be imitators of God, as beloved sons” (Eph. V, 1), I have not dared to pursue cruelly those whom, as I suppose, he mercifully awaits, perhaps promising myself your conversion in a vain hope. I had resolved to expel you as rebels—not merely against me, contemptible as I am, but against Caesar, whose power is incomparable, and indeed against God, whose omnipotence is fearful—from the Church, as both canonically and imperially sanctioned.

[Note: Construe as follows: “For this reason, in accordance with the Apostle who says, ‘Be imitators,’ and so forth, I, not daring cruelly to pursue those whom he mercifully awaits, as I suppose, promised myself your conversion, perhaps in a vain hope. I had resolved to expel you from the Church as rebels not merely against me, most contemptible as I am, but against Caesar, whose power is incomparable, and indeed against God, whose omnipotence is fearful; I mean to expel you from the Church, as both canonically and imperially sanctioned, from which you have already expelled me four times. But my mind spared you from clothing you in the cloak of shame.”]

[Note: “Canonically,” that is, according to the canonical laws. Thus in the *Itinerary*, no. 5, it is said that he was advanced to the priesthood canonically; and shortly afterward: “If I should act synodally according to the canons.” In both places *canonically* means “according to the canonical laws.” Nothing is more frequently prescribed in the canons than that clerics resisting their bishop should be expelled from the clergy or excommunicated. He says “imperially” because Otto’s privilege had previously decreed that if anyone should again presume to disturb Ratherius or rebel against him—as they had done until then—then, if he were a cleric, after everything had been placed in Ratherius’ power, he should be expelled from the Church until he had made legitimate and worthy satisfaction.]

from which you have already expelled me four times.

[Note: Compare note 1029, col. 583, in the *Itinerary*.]

My mind spared you from clothing you in the cloak of shame. I would certainly have done so if, by excommunicating you as you deserve, I had condemned you eternally, and if I had prepared something against you before the ears of the most formidable emperor. I neglected to do this, sending no envoy on my behalf; but if it should happen, you will readily see what I would have prepared for you.

[Note: In the commonly printed editions another reading and punctuation appeared: “and by excusing you before the ears of the most formidable emperor, which I neglected to do, sending no envoy on my behalf.” This would make it appear that Ratherius had sent an envoy to the emperor to excuse the canons. Apart from the fact that he was unsuited to such duties, as is stated in *Qualitatis conjectura*, no. 5, the whole context contradicts that interpretation. He says that he did not wish to cover them with shame; he would have done so if he had condemned them by excommunication, as they deserved, and if he had arranged something else against them before the emperor. What he would have arranged, if he had done so, would clearly have been something hostile to them and would have brought them shame. Hence we have corrected *excusing* to *accusing*. Just as he indicates that he did not excommunicate them, so he also says that he neglected to accuse them before the emperor, sending no envoy on his behalf; the punctuation therefore required correction as well.]

[Col. 0618A] 3. In the sense in which it was said, “Let the one who does harm continue to do harm” (Rev. XXII, 11), I entrust to God’s majesty whatever his providence may either wish to inflict upon you through me or permit to be inflicted by you, and I grant you permission to serve the Lord in whatever church of this diocese you prefer, until, with God’s consent, an envoy of the most pious Caesar comes, hears what I have ordered, compares it with what you have made known about me to his imperial ears, reports to him whatever he wishes, and he decides what I ought to do.

[Note: Since Ratherius has declared in the preceding passage that he refrained from excommunicating the canons, while here he gives them permission to serve the Lord in whichever church of the diocese they prefer, but refuses to see them in person or deal with them, he appears to have interdicted them from office in the cathedral church.]

[Note: Such contention had been stirred up by the canons against the bishop over the commands he had issued that they sought to accuse and incriminate him before the emperor, who had departed for Rome. For this reason an imperial envoy was expected, who, after hearing Ratherius’ commands or decrees and comparing them with what the canons had arranged to bring before the emperor concerning him, would report to Caesar whatever seemed appropriate, so that Caesar himself could decide what should be done. Thus the envoy was not to judge the case here, but only to investigate it and report. Although no envoy in the strict sense was sent directly to Verona for this purpose, two persons who dominated Verona and had been corrupted by money performed something similar during Easter Week of the following year, 968, as will be evident from the sermon *On the Octave of Easter*. The entire case against Ratherius was judged by Nanno under a special command of the same emperor on 30 June of that year, as is clear from Letters 11 and 12.]

I avoid doing this together with certain members of your group—not out of contempt for brotherhood, but because of the rustic proverb by which I have been warned: “What the eye does not see, the heart does not grieve over.” It seems that my sorrow will be greatly relieved if, by not seeing those who have inflicted such great evils upon me and do not cease to inflict them, I can for a little while be spared remembrance of their evils, while a little forgetfulness casts a shadow over their authors.

[Col. 0617]

# RATHERIUS’ LITTLE WORK ENTITLED  
## DISCORD  
### Between Ratherius himself and the clerics

[Note: Acherius printed this little work from the Laon manuscript. We received a mutilated copy, ending at no. 4, transcribed from a manuscript at Freising. It was addressed to Ambrosius, chancellor of the Emperor Otto I, as we shall show in note 1182. Its composition during Lent is proved by the statement in no. 7: “Throughout all the sermons that I delivered to the people during this Lent,” and so forth. Since in no. 6 he mentions the imperial will concerning the abandonment of keeping women, expressed at the synod held at Ravenna in April 967, as we shall prove in note 1169; and since in no. 8 he mentions the *Judicatum* issued in November of that year, it is clear that this work was written during Lent of 968. This was the Lent following the Ravenna synod and the first after the *Judicatum*, while it was also the final Lent of Ratherius’ episcopate.]

485. 1. They say that these days have produced the greatest discord between the bishop and the clerics of Verona. But who are they who say this? Surely those who are completely unaware of when it began to be produced. For example, they are like those who think that Judas first perished when, in his misery, he sold the Lord, although he had already perished long before, while he was bodily present with the apostles—when, intoxicated by the poison of greed, he did not cease thirsting for profit until he finally reached the noose in his misery.

[Note: Acherius reads *quam hinc jam*. The latest editor of the *Spicilegium*, although unwilling to alter the text, correctly noted that it should be read *qua me hinc jam*; we have adopted this reading on the authority of the Freising manuscript. When the author here counts three expulsions, or banishments, from the bishopric of Verona, the first is the expulsion under King Hugh, the second that under Lothair, and the third through the usurper Milo.]

“In these days,” they say. This is This is not entirely false, but it is truer in appearance than in action. Once discord has been shown for what it is, it will never be proved that concord existed between me and them, especially since tradition bears witness that they have already expelled me from here three times.

[Note: Construe as follows: “For if, according to the one who first said this, that friendship alone is firm in which people wish and refuse the same things; or if, according to another, human friendship so greatly seeks equal minds and undissimilar wills that a diversity of character can never attain firm concord, then our friendship, always desiring contrary things, has never been able to obtain stability either among them or among me, nor will it be able to do so. For they have always preferred the custom of their predecessors, who were continually rebellious toward their bishops, to the holy canons decreed by God; whereas I have thought that the holy canons decreed by God ought to be preferred to customs invented by the devil.”]

For if friendship is firm only when, according to the person who first said this, people will and refuse the same things—or if, according to another, human friendships so greatly desire equal minds and undissimilar wills that diversity of character can never arrive at firm concord—then our friendship, always desiring contrary things, has never been able to obtain stability either among them or among me, nor will it be able to do so.

They have always preferred the custom of their predecessors, who were continually rebellious toward their bishops, to the holy canons decreed by God; whereas I have thought that the holy canons decreed by God ought to be preferred to customs invented by the devil.

To keep women, forbidden by the Council of Nicaea, in such a customary and public manner, with such contempt for the reverence owed to God and men, and with the fear of hell itself so completely set aside that they think this not merely permitted but even required—so that anyone who avoids doing it appears to them incapable of avoiding that abominable crime which the Apostle mentions in his Epistle to the Romans (Rom. I, 27)—does this not seem to you to have been invented by the devil?

And, O holy and immaculate chastity of virgins, are you not everywhere disgraced if this is true?

[Note: The Vulgate has: “You, who are nowhere without infamy among the ruined, if this is true.” The reading of the Freising manuscript is better. Explain it thus: “How—and to what extent—you too are nowhere without infamy, if this is true,” namely, if it is true that no one who avoids women can be free from the worst crime, that is, the Sodomitic crime.]

How utterly ruined is the whole company of the tonsured, if no one among them is not either an adulterer or an *arsenoquita*!

[Note: *Arsenoquita* is Greek for “one who lies with males.” Immediately afterward, where the text has *nobis* (“for us”), the Freising copy reads *omnis est* (“everyone is”).]

For us, an adulterer is one who, contrary to the canons, is married. What, then, is a cleric? An adulterer is in no way a cleric; the other—that is, the *arsenoquita*—is even less so.

[Note: “The other,” that is, the *arsenoquita*, is even less a cleric.]

For if a cleric is called such because he belongs to the Lord’s portion, what fellowship, I ask, can anyone have with the Lord while remaining in any one of these crimes?

Woe, moreover, to the whole body of Christians if, according to their judgment, no one among them can be found who is not either a hypocrite with the Pharisees or a publican among the pagans.

A publican is one who is openly an adulterer; a hypocrite is one who, under the cloak of religion, is utterly irreligious; under the mantle of chastity, incestuous; under the pretext of justice, most unjust.

I attack him with the superlative degree of comparison for this reason: I remember having read more than once, “The hypocrites and the crafty provoke the anger of God” (Job XXXVI, 13).

Since this is so, and hypocrisy and incestuousness greatly surpass other crimes in wickedness, the other crimes are more serious insofar as they are more public. For the former kill only their perpetrators, whereas the latter kill both their perpetrators and harm those who observe them.

Because hidden sins do not come under judgment, everyone is permitted to speak about manifest sins, but no one about hidden ones. For if, as may already have happened, someone secretly lies with an animal in some corner, with God alone observing it, and you censure him merely on suspicion—as you could have done if you had seen it—what are you doing except arrogating to yourself what belongs to God alone?

Who cannot invent whatever he wishes about another? And why does anyone attempt to measure others by himself, thinking that others cannot exist in any other condition than his own? The rustic proverb, suitably enough, says: “The one who has been in the oven looks for his equals there!”

2. And is it not, in your view, an invention of the devil to do or say all these things by custom, to rebel against pastors by custom, and to divide what has been assigned generally to all clerics so unequally and by *massaritias*, so that some of them become extremely wealthy from it, some moderately so, and some receive almost nothing at all—according to the custom of those whom the abyss has held for a long time?

[Note: *Massaritia*, from *massa*, denotes a union of several fields; therefore to divide “by *massaritias*” means to divide by fields and vineyards. This easily produced inequality, since the more powerful claimed the greater number or better quality of fields. To remove this inequality, Ratherius decreed in the *Judicatum* that revenues should be distributed not by fields and vineyards but by bushels and measures. See notes 1163 and 1168 there.]

And is it not an invention of the devil to violate by custom all laws, both divine and human?

When what is found written in the Law of Moses, in the Prophets and Psalms, in the Gospel, the Acts, and the preaching of the apostles, in the decretals of bishops, and in the constitutions of the canons does not shine forth to you as inspired by God, while you cannot find anything in these writings that agrees with your already mentioned customs, by what law do you judge yourselves to live?

Between one who forbids such things—or, if he does not dare to forbid them, at least reproves and condemns them—and those who do such things, what concord can there be, especially since the Lord declares that he came to send precisely such discord under the name of the sword?

For he says—it is well known and clear:

> “Do not think that I have come to send peace upon the earth. I have not come to send peace, but a sword. For I have come to separate a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law” (Matt. X, 34–35);

and what he had already said through the prophet:

> “A man’s enemies are those of his own household” (Mic. V, 6).

The reason why a person’s enemies are chiefly those of his own household is evident: when certain people are enclosed within the same walls, yet have contrary and divergent dispositions, it often happens that the husband is sober while the wife is drunk; he is gentle while she is angry; he acts from fear of God, while she acts according to her own will; he is inspired by God, while she is stirred up by the devil.

What concord, peace, or friendship can exist between such people, when he does not want what she desires, since such quarrel has proceeded from God himself? He commanded gentleness, forbade anger, and through the Apostle permitted no one to give assent to another for evil, saying:

> “Not only those who do them, but also those who consent to those who do them, are worthy of death” (Rom. I, 32).

[Note: The Vulgate has *nulli alteri* (“to no other”), and shortly afterward *ita docendo* (“thus teaching”), rather than *ita dicentem* (“saying thus”). We have preferred the reading of the Freising copy.]

3. When you act against the law of God, ought I, who have been appointed by God to correct you, not at least bark?

When you prefer the custom of those whom hell undoubtedly holds to the statutes of those who dwell with God in heaven, should I not even dare to mutter?

What, then, shall I do, when, with you present, it may be said to me along with certain wretched men:

> “You have not gone up to confront them, nor opposed a wall on behalf of the house of Israel, to stand in battle on the day of the Lord; and I tested you at the waters of Contradiction” (Ezek. XIII, 5)?

Can your friendship there benefit me in any way—you who now persuade me to maintain peace with you, so that with others I may be able to say:

> “We have made a covenant with death, and with hell we have made an agreement” (Isa. XXVIII, 15)?

For, according to the saying of that most holy teacher, it is safer for a man to have earned the devil’s enmity than his peace, since through you iniquity does not cease to oppose justice, blindness to oppose light, and falsehood to resist truth.

When I see you rebelling against the Lord in such a way that you do not even deign to hear what he has commanded you, but, in Jewish fashion, abandon the commandments of God and cling so obstinately to human traditions and custom, can you persuade me to forget that it has been said of you:

> “The sin of Judah is written with an iron stylus” (Jer. XVII, 1);

or that I have ever heard:

> “If you do not announce his iniquity to the wicked man, I will require his blood at your hand” (Ezek. III, 18);

and:

> “Woe to those who call good evil and evil good” (Isa. V, 20);

and:

> “Let the dead bury their dead” (Matt. VIII, 22);

and:

> “You offer aid to the wicked and join friendship with those who hate God” (II Chron. XIX, 2);

along with the countless thunders of divine threats that follow from this?

I read in a book of blessed Columbanus that the priest has the same function in the Church as the stomach possesses in the human body. The stomach digests the food it receives and distributes it to all the limbs; each limb converts it into its own nature, so that what the liver receives becomes blood, what the gall receives becomes bile, and what descends into the lungs becomes phlegm.

If, then, following this example, it should happen that what I say benefits some of those who hear it unto life but provokes anger in many others—for example, as that man experienced who said:

> “As vinegar upon nitre, so is one who sings songs to a wicked heart” (Prov. XXV, 20),

should one of those people who might benefit from what is said have been neglected because of fear of the others?

And where would be the word that the Lord is said to have spoken to Ezekiel in this way:

> “Son of man, do not fear their words, and do not be afraid of their faces, for they are a rebellious house” (Ezek. II, 6)?

Where would be the saying:

> “Whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, of him the Son of Man will be ashamed when he comes in his glory, and in the glory of his Father and of the holy angels” (Luke IX, 26)?

4. If you object that the scandal of the Church ought to be avoided, I do not contradict you. Yet I set before you two passages from the Gospel.

The first is where the Lord is reported to have said to Peter: “Simon, from whom do the kings of the earth receive tribute—from their own sons or from strangers?” When he answered, “From strangers,” he said: “Then the sons are free. But lest we scandalize them, go to the sea, cast a hook, and take the first fish that comes up; when you open its mouth, you will find a stater. Take it and give it to them for me and for you.”

The second is where Peter, speaking with the others to the Lord, said: “Do you know that the Pharisees, when they heard this word, were scandalized?” (Matt. XV, 12). To show that such scandal should not be a concern, he said: “Leave them” (ibid., 14)—that is, leave them to be scandalized.

Why? He adds the reason:

> “They are blind and leaders of the blind. But if the blind lead the blind, both will fall into a pit” (ibid.).

It is as though he had said: “Because they themselves are blind and provide other blind people with leadership into the pit of destruction, their scandal is not to be a concern.”

For, according to a certain authority, it is better for scandal to arise than for truth to be abandoned (St. Gregory, *Homily* 6 on Ezekiel, book I). Even if the affirmation of truth is abandoned for their sake, they will not thereby be improved; rather, as they have begun, these miserable men will become worse, rushing into the pit of destruction destined for them from the beginning.

5. And although these matters may suffice, we must ask how this discord between us nevertheless arose. But if anyone considers what was said above about Judas, he will see not merely that this discord arose, but that from the time of my ordination there has never been concord between us. A thousand indications will prove this, if anyone is able to remember what sorts of things have already happened to me and how many.

> **Note:** [Col. 0623B] The Vulgate reads *acciderunt; quanta*, although this requires a different punctuation and the addition of the conjunction *et* in order to make sense.

> **Note:** [Col. 0623B–D] Ratherius also mentions confidence in the imperial presence and in the assembling of a synod in his sermon *On the Octave of Easter*, section 4. After revealing that discord had arisen from the day of his ordination, he adds: “It has now been brought into the open because of confidence in the presence of the emperor, who decides nothing but what is just, and in the assembling of a synod.” Here there is a gap, and what is undoubtedly missing is what he had done in reliance on that confidence and from which the discord at last broke out. From the present work one may infer what these things were. Since in both places he joins the assembling of a synod with the imperial presence, by “synod” he appears to mean the bishops who gathered at Verona from the whole province of Aquileia on the occasion of the emperor’s presence, when Ratherius met him there with his son arriving from Germany at the end of October 967 and celebrated with him the feast of All Saints on 1 November. It will become clear from what follows that the *Judicatum*, by which Ratherius later withdrew certain benefices formerly bestowed by him upon the canons in order to provide for poorer clerics, gave rise to open dissension. This *Judicatum* was made in reliance on the imperial presence and the assembling of a synod. Ratherius shows his confidence in the emperor at the end of the *Judicatum*, writing: “Relying also on his—the emperor’s—assistance, I have undertaken this.” The subscriptions of the patriarch of Aquileia and of the bishops of our province prove his confidence in the synod to be assembled; Ratherius testifies in letter 12 to Ambrose that these were appended to the same *Judicatum*. In this double confidence he issued the *Judicatum*. When the canons grieved that they had been deprived of certain benefices, the discord that had previously been creeping along came into public view and stirred up a very great rebellion against the bishop. From this we fear that something is also missing here. For it is not confidence that is now openly marked, but the discord produced by the *Judicatum*, which, although prepared in reliance on the imperial presence and the assembly of a synod, was promulgated only after imperial assent and synodal confirmation. It might be supplied thus: “Although now the discord on account of the *Judicatum*, which I resolved to make in reliance on the imperial presence and the assembling of a synod, has been openly marked”—that is, as he says in the sermon *On the Octave of Easter*, has now been brought into the open—“yet we have this occasion for quarrelling.” He then adds the more ancient origin of this quarrel.

Although the confidence placed now openly in the imperial presence and in the assembly of a synod may be identified as the occasion, the reason why we have quarrelled is nevertheless this: namely, that I have shown them certain matters suppressed here because they are contained in the letter addressed to Bishop Hubert—that is, the work *On Contempt for the Canons*. This letter did not compel them by force to follow those matters, but urged them by reason to weigh them carefully.

> **Note:** Construe: “Namely, that I have shown them certain things here omitted—or passed over—because they are contained in the letter addressed to Bishop Hubert” (the work *On Contempt for the Canons), “not compelling them by force to follow them, but urging them by reason to consider them carefully.” These matters concerned the authority over and distribution of ecclesiastical revenues, which the canons assign to bishops. From this authority Ratherius thought that a fairer distribution of the revenues of the cathedral church of Verona should be introduced, so that the senior clergy would not consume nearly everything while the rest were oppressed by poverty.

[Col. 0624A] 491 In the *Canons of the Apostles*, chapter 39:

> **Note:** [Col. 0624B] This is the first canon Ratherius adduced in the first part of the work *On Contempt for the Canons*, in order to show the authority assigned to bishops mentioned above.

> “Let the bishop have charge of all ecclesiastical affairs, and let him distribute them as though God were watching,” etc.

> **Note:** By “and so forth” he indicates the other authorities suppressed here, which will be found transcribed in the work mentioned above.

6. Let anyone who wishes, then, come and judge which of these alternatives would have been better or worse: whether, through fear of those provoking God, I should have endured them, as it were patiently, for nearly thirty-five years, or whether, even though so late, I should have brought these matters against them—

> **Note:** [Col. 0624C] Previously, when the author had shown that the canons grant the bishop authority over ecclesiastical revenues, he had sought to induce the canons to a fairer distribution by reason rather than force. But now—that is, most recently, after nearly thirty-five years—thinking that this plan should be put into effect, he began to press them more vigorously, as he explains shortly.

—especially since, as Gregory most truthfully teaches, I have learned that “to tolerate an enemy but hate him is not a virtue of love, but a covering for fury”; and since I am thoroughly convinced by Augustine when he says, “He refuses to be in Christ’s body who does not wish to endure the world’s hatred together with its head.”

> **Note:** Ratherius had patiently tolerated for nearly thirty-five years those who resisted the bishop’s authority and a fairer distribution of revenues, out of fear of provoking God. He entered the episcopate around August 932. Thus nearly thirty-five years bring us to 967, when, after returning to Verona from the synod of Ravenna, he began to deal with them more forcefully than before, in approximately June or July.

For besides the fact that I reproached them for doing these things contrary to the decrees of the holy canons—

> **Note:** Construe: “For besides reproaching them for doing these things contrary to the decrees of the holy canons,” and so forth. The “things” were their opposition to a fairer distribution of revenues and their denial of the bishop’s authority in this matter. How greatly these actions opposed the canons he proved more fully in the first part of the aforementioned work *On Contempt for the Canons*.

—even this circumstance recently moved me most deeply: when the august will of the emperor had thundered against them concerning the abandonment of their relations with women, almost all of them offered the excuse that this could in no way be done because of their poverty, but that it could somehow be done if they had received the stipend owed to them from the church’s property.

> **Note:** [Col. 0625B–C] This excuse is explained by the contemporary writer Atto, bishop of Vercelli, in his letter to his clergy against incontinent clerics, published by Acherius, *Spicilegium*, vol. I, p. 440: “There are those who seek to excuse themselves for cohabitation with women by setting forth what they call their necessity. For they say that, unless they were supported by those women’s hands, we would already perish from hunger or nakedness.”

> **Note:** This is explained in letter 12 to Ambrose, section 1. He says there: “After the universal synod had been celebrated at Ravenna in mid-April 967, I returned and summoned priests and deacons from all the parishes of our diocese, in order to report, by command of the most serene emperor, what had been established there. Everyone was to attend the council.” Among the matters he announced to those assembled, he mentions only one command: that they should abandon their relations with women. What he relates here on the same subject therefore belongs to the same diocesan council, held immediately after the universal synod at Ravenna, in approximately June or July 967.

It seemed to me that they could have done so if each of them received in the church his own payment according to his labour, as the Apostle says (1 Cor. 3:8), or if, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles, the resources assigned to the clergy were distributed according to each person’s need (Acts 4:35).

For this reason I wished to learn everything that had either been granted by my predecessors or had been bestowed upon them by men who feared God; and these resources would have been entirely sufficient if I had not wished providently to supplement them with the very things that I had once foolishly granted to certain ungrateful and hostile men.

> **Note:** The manuscript reading was *admodum timentibus* (“greatly fearing”), while the printed editions insert the preposition *ab* within brackets because of that phrase. The reading should be *a Deum timentibus* (“by men fearing God”); the same wording occurs in the *Judicatum*, section 2: “which was assigned by good men fearing God …” Immediately afterward, concerning *si non vellem* (“if I did not wish”), the new editor of the *Spicilegium* wondered whether *si modo vellem* (“if only I wished”) should be read. We, on the contrary, judge the printed reading entirely suitable. The sense is that the common revenues of the cathedral church would be sufficient if properly distributed, even if Ratherius did not wish to supplement them with the benefits that he had once granted to certain ungrateful and hostile men and later took away from them in order to provide for poorer clerics’ needs—a matter he explains below.

They refused this so resolutely that they declared they would rather die beforehand than see it done. And not without reason. For although their resources, thanks be to God, are by no means insignificant, they are so divided among farms and other such properties that some of them grow very wealthy from them, while the multitude languishes in poverty. And—shame upon it!—those who render the greater service to God in the church receive either nothing or very little, while those who scarcely ever perform any service for the Lord become rich from ecclesiastical property.

> **Note:** Here *causa* means “a matter” or “a thing”; Du Cange confirms this meaning with numerous examples. See *Causa* 2.

> **Note:** Compare note 1159 above.

If any one of them even tried to mutter against such arrangements, he was told: “Just as I awaited the death of my masters who preceded me, so await mine; and strive after my death to enjoy the goods that I presently enjoy.”

This is practically equivalent to saying: “Now that I have been placed where those are whom I am determined to imitate, try to follow me and fall into the same pit of the abyss into which I fell.” Thus it truly means that a blind man provides a blind man with guidance for falling.

7. “What, then,” you ask, “did you do about these matters?” I showed them canonical authority; they appealed against it to customary practice. I sent them some of their neighbours—

> **Note:** *Vicini* are people from the same village or parish, from which the term *vicinia* derives. The word has the same sense in the *Apologeticus*, section 5: “All the neighbours abandon me alone and utterly incapable either of raising up or restoring the basilicas of our diocese,” and so forth. Similarly, Bishop Atto of Vercelli, speaking in a letter to his clergy about incontinent clerics, says: “They also commonly incur, for such a crime, the hatred of their neighbours and fellow-neighbours.”

—and adjured them by the fidelity that they had sworn to me more than once not to conceal from me any authentic justification they might have for their conduct, lest, when we came to the synod, they should cause me embarrassment if they proved that I was demanding something unjust.

> **Note:** The matter of abandoning relations with women was dealt with at a diocesan synod, as shown above in note 1169. A different synod, soon to be convened, is indicated here. This is undoubtedly the synod that he joined to the imperial presence in section 5 and mentioned in his sermon *On the Octave of Easter*, section 4. Compare note 1162 above. Indeed, the words “lest, when we came to the synod, they should cause me embarrassment if they proved that I was demanding something unjust” are especially appropriate to a provincial synod. At that assembly he wished to have confirmed what he had established concerning a fairer distribution and provision for poor clerics; if the canons had proved there that he was demanding anything unjust, they would have caused him considerable embarrassment before the assembled bishops. To prevent this, he asked them not to conceal any documents or privileges they possessed that might prohibit the bishop from introducing a fairer distribution. This discussion with the canons, through which he sought to introduce a fairer distribution of revenues, took place after the diocesan synod and before the provincial synod.

And, to show that I could never have placed any confidence in their oaths, they declared—shame upon it!—that they knew perfectly well that they had sworn many oaths which they could in no way fulfil, adding that it was foolish for them to try to teach me.

I again instructed some of them that they would be guilty in both respects if they knowingly allowed either me to contend against them or themselves to contend against me.

The man most concerned replied that he would be acting most foolishly if he presumed to teach either me, who had been proclaimed throughout the whole world, or his own masters.

> **Note:** This makes clear the renown of Ratherius, who throughout the world—that is, everywhere—was celebrated as highly learned and literate. Compare *Phrenesis*, section 11. The words “my masters” indicate his predecessors, whose examples and traditions the senior clergy followed. One of them had said in the preceding section: “Just as I awaited the death of my masters who preceded me.”

Since this accomplished nothing, I tried in another way to compel them to peace—not indeed the peace of the world, but the peace of Christ. When certain of them held benefits from me, I threatened that, if they prohibited me from doing what was within my right, I would take away what I had granted them.

> **Note:** Perhaps *de meo* (“from my property”) should be read. In the following section he says: “if I took away what they held from my property.” In the *Itinerary*, section 4, he explains what they held as their own in these words: “Since, from my little property, I am not so inhuman toward you as to have ten of you enriched by a military benefice—and that without charge.” Since he converted what he took from them to a use appropriate to an ecclesiastical rather than a military benefice—some he gave to the cathedral church, some to St Stephen, and some to support poorer clerics, as will become clear in section 8—it may appear that he had granted them not only military but also ecclesiastical benefits. Yet if he had given them any benefits beyond the military ones, he would certainly not have omitted them from the *Itinerary*, where it was especially important for him to list and contrast accurately the benefits granted to them. It is also known that benefits that were ecclesiastical in origin assumed the character of military benefits when they were granted to someone for life according to the terms and form of military benefices. Thus, for example, the revenues of the church of St Vitalis, which were certainly an ecclesiastical benefice, passed into a military benefice when they were subsequently assigned to soldiers. See the *Invective on the Translation of St Metron*, section 3, and the note there, 641. Why should the same benefits not recover their former ecclesiastical character when they were assigned to churches or to a definite body of clerics? Thus Ratherius restored to their original nature the revenues of his bishopric that he had granted to those ten canons in the form of military benefices, when he took them away from the canons and assigned them to the two churches mentioned and to the college of poorer clerics.

They replied that they cared so little about this that, even if I took away something I had given to one of them, they would not therefore be any less faithful to me—provided only that I ceased to disturb them concerning these other matters.

> **Note:** “These matters” means the goods and revenues of the cathedral church that the canons enjoyed. They answered that they cared nothing if Ratherius took away the benefits he had granted them, so long as he abandoned all thought of distributing those revenues more fairly and allowed the canons to enjoy them peacefully.

And most truthfully so: they were never faithful to me because something had been given, nor less faithful because something had been taken away—for they could not be so. For they never ceased to be utterly unfaithful to me at any time—may the Lord forgive them.

But why? Let the Apostle answer. I admit that I am exceedingly weary of repeating this so often. “There will be a time,” he says, “when they will not endure sound doctrine, but, driven by their own desires, they will heap up teachers for themselves, having itching ears; and they will turn their hearing away from the truth and turn instead to fables” (2 Tim. 4:3).

> **Note:** Understand that he called the most flagrant violations of the canons “fables,” for a fictitious matter is properly called a fable.

Throughout all the sermons that I delivered to the people during this Lent—

> **Note:** Four sermons dealing with peace survive; they were delivered at Easter 968 and afterward: the second sermon on Easter, another on the octave of Easter, a third after Easter, and the second sermon on the Ascension. Of those delivered during Lent of the same year, none has so far come down to us.

—I never ceased urging everyone with me not to delay returning to peace, but to return to the peace of Christ, which—alas!—we had never possessed. Those who had injured others should remember the Lord’s command, which I was entirely prepared to fulfil: “If you are offering your gift at the altar …” (Matt. 5:23), and so forth; while those who had been injured should remember the command of the one who said: “When you stand to pray, forgive whatever you have against anyone” (Mark 11:25). I never ceased promising them that I was fully prepared to do this, if only they had deigned to ask—or, perhaps, to be asked—and wished to bring about true peace in this matter.

> **Note:** He never ceased urging everyone to return to peace—both those who had caused injury and those who had suffered it. The former, namely those who had injured others, should not delay returning to peace, remembering the Lord’s command, “If you are offering your gift …”; the injured should likewise not delay, remembering the Lord’s command, “When you stand …” Ratherius himself was prepared in every way to act according to these commands.

Yet this increased their pride still further and inflamed their malice even to the point of accusing me, so that they compelled me to believe worse things about myself than was the case, as I had most recently written to you, my dearest Ambrose, and would not even allow others to judge anything good about me.

> **Note:** Ambrose was the chancellor of Otto I, to whom Ratherius later sent letter 12. Ambrose had signed the imperial privilege granted to Ratherius on 5 November of the preceding year, 967. On that occasion Ratherius may perhaps have recently left him a written work, the *Qualitatis*, in which he set out the censures and accusations levelled against him by the cavillers. Here he indicates still worse accusations, concerning which he says in the *Apologeticus*, section 7: “After such great, such extraordinary, such foul, disgraceful, unbelievable things, even contrary to my age,” and so forth. It is therefore clear that the present work *On Discord* was addressed to the same Ambrose; on this same occasion Ratherius may perhaps also have sent him the *Judicatum*, which he shortly declares to have been the cause of the discord and which, in letter 12, section 4, he says he sent to him under the name of a document.

8. Since the treacherous always become worse through receiving benefits, and anyone who grants them something does nothing except supply them with strength to fight against him and labour to propagate their treachery, I did not delay turning the threat I had made into an action.

> **Note:** Earlier he had threatened to take away the benefits he had granted the canons from his own property.

Following the command that says, “Give to the good, and do not receive the sinner” (Ecclesiasticus 12:5), I took those things away from them and gave them—or rather returned them—to the blessed Mother of God and to Saint Stephen the protomartyr. In addition, concerning certain matters I produced a document called the *Judicatum*, that is, a decree, for the poorer clerics of that same church—for whose sake alone I had undertaken the labour—namely, for the priests serving as chaplains, seven subdeacons of the secretariat, seven singers, seven acolytes of the secretariat, five singers, and six doorkeepers. I did this not, indeed, so that they would become more faithful to me, but so that they might become more ready in the service of the Lord and, with poverty no longer providing an excuse, more diligent in serving the Lord by day and by night.

> **Note:** The “blessed Mother of God” means the cathedral church, dedicated under the name of the holy Mother of God. The church of St Stephen the protomartyr is the other principal church after the cathedral. These goods appear to have been assigned for the restoration or adornment of these churches, just as Ratherius says in letter 12, section 1, that he applied a certain fine imposed on some clerics to the restoration—or, more accurately, the decoration—of the church of the blessed Mother of God. His words “or rather I returned” seem to indicate that the benefits he had granted the canons in the form of military benefices, and afterward taken away from them, were goods that had previously belonged to those churches. It is otherwise clear from note 1177 that he had given the same benefits from his own property. Everything can be reconciled if one considers that the revenues of all the churches, except for the portion assigned to the clergy of each individual church, belonged to the bishop’s jurisdiction and disposal. Accordingly, Ratherius gave from his own property even when he gave goods that had been donated by the faithful to the blessed Mother of God or to St Stephen, because those goods had passed into the bishop’s jurisdiction.

> **Note:** This *Judicatum* was edited earlier; the points summarized here were explained there.

Thus this discord, now grown old over several years—not newly carried out, as they report, but, what is better, under a feigned peace—does not cease, as always, to direct the worst schemes of ambushes against me, though I am not unaware of them.

> **Note:** Acherius’s edition read *pace facta* (“peace having been made”). The emendation of the latest editor of Acherius’s *Spicilegium* is preferable. Construe: “Thus, this discord, having now grown old for several years—not, as they report, having been acted out now, but, what is better, with a feigned peace—does not cease to direct against me, as always, the worst schemes of ambushes, though I am not unaware of them.” The sentence continues with “and those who said …”

And those who said that they did not care if I took away what they held from me, and that they would not therefore be less faithful to me, so long as I ceased disturbing them concerning the matters over which I had challenged them—now secure because I have ceased from my efforts—strive, through the patronage of certain powerful men, to harass me on the grounds that I have recovered from them what was mine because of their ingratitude.

> **Note:** “Secure because I have ceased” refers to Ratherius’s abandonment of the plan to introduce a new distribution of the cathedral church’s revenues, from which he would have provided for poorer clerics.
