They were secure because Ratherius had appeared to abandon that plan when he preferred to take away the benefits he had granted them and provide for poorer clerics through the *Judicatum*, rather than trouble the canons with a new distribution. Those who were secure in this matter, however, were attempting, through the patronage of certain powerful men, to harass Ratherius before the emperor, destroy the *Judicatum*, and have the benefits taken from them restored. In the sermon *On the Octave of Easter*, section 1, he complains that two leading figures of the region had also allegedly been corrupted by money. See what we shall note there.

May the Lord mercifully regard me, prepared to undergo the scourges inflicted for my sins, and kindly defend me from their snares, granting them forgiveness and implanting true peace in their hearts, so that all of us together may deserve to be reconciled in peace with Christ.

But if, with little regard for what blessed Job once said—

> “I investigated most diligently the case that I did not know” (Job 29:16),

—it should happen to me, most wretched as I am, what happened to those wretches of whom it is written: even if they had pleaded their case before the Scythians, they would undoubtedly have been dismissed without blame.

> **Note:** The same passage from Job is repeated in this same matter both in letter 11 to Nanno and in letter 13 to the empress Adelaide. There he indicates that the case at issue was insufficiently known and that a decree contrary to him had been extorted, without his being heard, through mere underhandedness and deceit. Construe and explain as follows: “If it should happen to me, most wretched as I am, that what happened to those wretches should happen to me—of whom it is written that even if they had pleaded their case before the Scythians, they would undoubtedly have been dismissed without blame”—for if this should happen, it will be appropriate to me, who am prepared for scourges to the extent I have said, since my grief is always before my eyes: the grief by which I both mourn that I suffer such things for my sin and fear that I may suffer worse things in the future. If this, I say, should happen to me, it remains for me to do nothing other than …

For me, I say, nothing remains but to wish and pray to God without ceasing that the man to whom I remember having sworn fidelity—

> **Note:** Construe: “But may it never happen to him”—that is, the emperor Otto I, to whom Ratherius remembers having sworn fidelity—“to do anything by which he would irrecoverably lose God’s favour. Rather, may divine mercy grant him to do what will enable him to rule happily here for a longer time and to rejoice eternally with Christ in the future.”

—may never do anything by which he would irrecoverably lose his grace. Rather, may divine piety grant him to do what will enable him to rule happily here for a longer time and to rejoice eternally with Christ in the future. Amen.

[Col. 0629]

# RATHERIUS’S APOLOGETIC BOOK

> **Note:** This was edited by Acherius from the Laon manuscript. It was written toward the end of Lent in 968. The end of Lent is indicated by the words in section 7: “the solemn celebrations of the Mass are to be held even on the very imminent Easter.” Since section 2 mentions the emperor, who, as he was about to leave Verona, entrusted Ratherius with money for the completion—or rather restoration—of the church of St Zeno, and since the emperor left Verona at the beginning of November 967, this work must be assigned to the end of Lent of the following year, 968, the final year of Ratherius’s episcopate. The caviller to whom he responds is counted among the canons in section 4. See note 1203.

[Col. 0629D] 499 To a certain principal caviller, an indefatigable critic not only of his actions and speeches but also of his intentions, and a supporter and defender of his adversaries, Ratherius submits all these matters, touched slightly by fear of Jesus at the throat, yet ready to endure rather than yield.

Your great urbanity—that which you draw from Martianus and others of that kind—

> **Note:** He means Martianus Capella, whose satire, divided into nine books and composed partly in prose and partly in verse, was assigned to young people in the schools. Learned men have noted this from Gregory of Tours and other medieval writers. See Fabricius, *Bibliotheca Latina*, book 3, chapter 15. This first period is extremely long and, because of its length and syntax, very obscure. Its meaning may be stated briefly. The caviller’s conversations with Ratherius, which displayed foolish wit, and the little writings sent to Ratherius, which contained more aloe than honey, had so exhausted him that he thought he could apply to the caviller the words of David: “The wicked have told me fables,” and so forth.

> Construe as follows: “That great urbanity of yours, which you derive from Martianus and others of this sort, concerning whom I admit that I am all the more secure and free from desire as I fear that a certain characterization, already truthfully uttered long ago about some people, may to some degree apply to me as well—and which can also rightly be uttered about you: ‘always speaking and never coming to a knowledge of the truth’ (2 Tim. 3:7)—this same great, utterly foolish, indeed almost nonexistent urbanity of your vainglorious wit affects me so deeply that, while I am weighed down by distress and we converse, while you send me little darts—or little writings and trifles containing more aloe than honey, more certain poison than salutary antidote—I become so exhausted that I would gladly cry out with that famous Psalmist, speaking of many people but especially of you: ‘The wicked have told me fables,’ and so forth.”

> The utterly wicked servant whom he would have wished to be prevented from speaking with the cavillers, much less from demanding assistance from them, may have been Ratherius himself, since he complains that, in the distress weighing upon him, their conversations and writings burdened him rather than relieved him. The adjective “utterly wicked” should not cause surprise, for he repeatedly portrays himself as though he were the most criminal of men.

—which I admit leaves me so much the more secure and free from desire, insofar as I fear that a certain characterization already truthfully uttered long ago about some people may to some extent apply to me—“always speaking, and never coming to a knowledge of the truth” (2 Tim. 3:7), a characterization that can rightly be applied to you as well—this same utterly foolish, indeed almost nonexistent, vainglorious wit of yours affects me so greatly that, while we converse and I am weighed down by distress, and while you send me little darts or trifles containing more aloe than honey, more certain poison than salutary antidote—

so that I would now wish that some utterly wicked servant were forbidden even to speak with you, much less to demand any assistance from you—

—that I become so completely exhausted that I long to cry out with that most famous Psalmist, speaking of many people and especially of you:

> “The wicked have told me fables, but not according to your law, O Lord” (Psalm 118:85).

But, compelled by you, and wishing, in keeping with the appropriateness of the season—

> **Note:** That is, because Easter was already approaching.

—to be at least now somewhat at leisure, I undertake to dictate this little apology.

> **Note:** Supply: “I ought to dictate.”

## 2

When the most glorious Emperor Augustus (Otto I) had decided to depart from here, he entrusted a certain amount of silver to my fidelity, from which I was to complete the basilica of Saint Zeno, our particular patron, as is known, [Col. 0631D] after everything on which I had depended for my livelihood had been consumed—not to mention that anything would have remained from which, as you advise, I could make some alms, once this work entrusted to my care had been abandoned—by his presence, not, I say, by his power, nor do I allege by his violence, but certainly by his presence.

[Note: At this time the basilica of Saint Zeno had not yet been completed; indeed, its tower was begun only in the following century, in the year 1045. But since Panvinio reports that Saint Zeno’s church, which stood in the suburb, was among the churches burned and destroyed by the Hungarians (*Antiquities of Verona*, Book V, chapter 25), one may doubt whether *reficere*—“to repair”—should be read instead of *perficere*—“to complete.” In fact, he mentions only the rebuilding of churches afterward; and more clearly in section 3, when he says that, according to the cavillers, poor prelates were compelled to rebuild the basilica, he designates the basilica of Saint Zeno as the one that had to be rebuilt. The money contributed by the emperor for its reconstruction, they thought, ought rather to be distributed among the poor. [Col. 0632C]

The next passage should be construed as follows: “after, namely, his—the emperor’s—not, I say, power, nor do I allege violence, but certainly his presence—on account, of course, of the enormous expenses of hospitality—had consumed everything from which I had been accustomed to live, much less anything had remained from which I could make some alms, as you advise, after abandoning this work entrusted to my fidelity.” We have changed nothing in the text except that we wrote *aliquas*—“some”—where *quas*—“which”—was read. [Col. 0632D]]

And oh, how true is that statement of Aurelius (Augustine, *Sermon* 46, section 27), that all things are full of rash judgments! For since Saint Gregory, who is no less authoritative, asserts that one must never do evil for the sake of obedience, although one must sometimes interrupt a good work (*Moralia on Job*, Book XXXV, chapter 10), who could believe that the money entrusted by one to whom I had sworn so sacredly ought to have been spent elsewhere than where he had been pleased to command?

“Give it to the poor,” says the defamer, as did that former betrayer of Christ (Matthew 26:9). But I should like to know where these poor are. For I discover that there are no poor here—thanks be to God—so poor in resources that the rebuilding of churches ought to be abandoned for their sake, even if it were undertaken at my own expense, as it ought to have been. I say that there are no poor here except me and those whom I myself ought to support as members of my household—wonderful to say and incredible to hear. [Col. 0632A]

But I suppose that among you the poor are supported only by the bishop. Yet the liberality of all who inhabit this country loudly declares that this is not necessary here: all, I say, commonly observe the command, “Do not raise up the one whom you pity,” and compel them—the poor—even before the appointed hour, to excess and drunkenness, contrary to God’s command, although they themselves ought also to keep the solemn fast, that is, the Lenten fast, as the other faithful do. [Col. 0632B]

[Note: The passage should be construed as follows: “The liberality of all who inhabit this country loudly declares this: all, I say, commonly observe the command, ‘Do not raise up the one whom you pity,’ and compel them—the poor—even before the appointed hour, to excess and drunkenness, contrary to God’s command, although they themselves ought also to keep the solemn fast, that is, the Lenten fast, as the other faithful do.” [Col. 0632D]

Three things should be noted here. First, he calls the “solemn fast” the Lenten fast; we proved that this work was written during Lent in note 1191. Second, he states that the poor, like the other faithful, ought to observe the same fast; hence, in the *Synodical Letter*, section 15, he exempts from the law of fasting only young children, those weakened by advanced age, and the sick. [Col. 0633C] Third, by “before the hour” he understands before the ninth hour, until which, according to a milder discipline, he taught that the fast was to be observed during Lent, in the cited *Synodical Letter*, section 15, and in Sermon 2 on Lent, sections 3 and 5. Moreover, in the same sermon, section 1, he reproves certain people who, during the fasting period, were consuming solemn meals before the hour, even to excess and drunkenness. [Col. 0633D]]

## 3

Oh, if only those who know, approve, and love the methods of distributing alms prescribed by blessed Gregory—at least as well as I do—would do so! They would undoubtedly discover that divine almsgiving is entirely withheld from such people as you prefer to the necessity of rebuilding our Lord’s basilica. For, he says, “Give to the just man, and do not receive the sinner” (Ecclesiasticus 12:2).

[Note: Construe and explain the passage as follows: “By that command, those to whom you advise that the imperial revenue entrusted to me be given for the restoration of the basilica of Saint Zeno are rejected because of a particular fault; and blessed Zeno, whom you maintain is being defrauded of the payment granted to him, is himself assumed as the one who is to receive it on the basis of his own justice.” [Col. 0633D]]

By that command, therefore, those to whom you advise that the imperial revenue be given are rejected on account of a particular fault; and blessed Zeno, whom you contend is being defrauded of the payment granted to him, is himself assumed as the recipient on the basis of his own justice. [Col. 0633A]

It is more fitting to believe that he himself should be called a brother seated in the seat of majesty [Acherius printed *sedentis*, “of one sitting”] than any of those whom one must fear will hear: “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 23:41). For such a curse is seen to be directed not against brothers but rather against complete outsiders. [Col. 0633D]

Since, however, friends are to be made for us from the mammon of iniquity so that they may receive us into the eternal dwellings (Luke 16:9)—and the command does not say “let them send us,” but “let them receive us”—we must consider who would be more able to receive us there, if we were to give from our own resources: the holy man who, together with the Judge, will judge those who hear “Come,” or those to whom it will be said, “Depart”?

Therefore the poor in spirit are to be chosen on the authority of this passage; for theirs is the kingdom of heaven (Luke 5:3). If they wish to bestow it upon us—as their own, of course—we believe that they can. For who gives to another what he does not possess? Who is unable to bestow what is his own upon whomever he wishes?

Nor do we say this in order to advise that fellowship in nature should be neglected in any respect, whether the person be just or unjust. Rather, we say it so that we may crush with such a pestle the genuine tooth of yours that gnaws at us.

[Note: He calls the *genuini* the innermost teeth, as Cicero observed in Book II, chapter 54, of *On the Nature of the Gods*. The opposing teeth are sharp and divide food by biting, whereas the innermost ones grind it up; these are called *genuini*. Hence *genuino rodere* means “to detract from” or “to bite with one’s words.” In Persius, *Satire* 1, line 115, the phrase is *genuinum fregit*, “he broke his molar.” [Col. 0633D]]

For although we know that benevolence is to be shown to all on account of the likeness of nature, we nevertheless understand that it must be shown more particularly to the household of faith (Galatians 6:10), through whom it is extended also to the household of God. And for this reason I cannot believe anyone—not even an angel—if he advises that it would be more acceptable to God for our own substance to be distributed, with reasonable grounds, to those of whom it will be said, “Depart, you accursed, into the eternal fire” (Matthew 25:41), while those who are going to hear, “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom” (ibid., 44), are neglected. [Col. 0633C]

[Note: Construe the passage as follows: “For this reason I cannot believe anyone, even an angel himself, if he advises that it is more acceptable to God for our own substance reasonably to be given to those to whom it will be said, ‘Depart, you accursed, into the eternal fire,’ while those who will hear, ‘Come,’ and so forth, are neglected.” [Col. 0634C–D]]

How much less should what has been delegated to us by someone else and entrusted to us be taken away from them and given to those others, when the Book of Wisdom most plainly contains this statement concerning them: “Forbid giving bread to them” (Ecclesiasticus 12:6), and the Apostle declared concerning such people, who went around the houses although they were able to acquire some food by their own hands, “Let the one who does not work not eat” (2 Thessalonians 3:10). [Col. 0634A]

[Note: Construe and explain the passage as follows: “For the Book of Wisdom most plainly contains the statement concerning them, ‘Forbid giving bread to them’; and the Apostle declared concerning such people—namely, those who went around the houses although they were able to acquire some food by their own hands—‘Let the one who does not work not eat.’” [Col. 0634D]]

## 4

What more can be said? I see that a great battle is pressing upon me from every side. I confess that it is not while drowsing that one must cry out to God: “Give me, O Lord, a sign for good, so that those who hate me may see it and be put to shame; for you, O Lord, have helped me and comforted me” (Psalm 35:17). [Col. 0634B]

Some people hurl accusations at me, whether you think so or whether they have rather fabricated them for themselves. Others do not cease to darken whatever good I may appear to do with sinister interpretations. I judge those more tolerable who, although they are plainly evil, bring forward evil things—whether falsely invented or true in fact—in an evil manner than those who, while striving to appear good, maliciously report whatever good they perceive in me and stain what is white with black.

But tell me as a friend, I ask you: do you not think that the expenses contributed for building or rebuilding churches—not to mention adorning them—are being distributed to the poor? Whose interests do they serve? Do they not serve those who would otherwise stand under the open sky, be scorched by the sun, soaked by rain, and chilled by frost? And who make up the greater part of those entering the church, the rich or the needy? [Col. 0634C]

Thousands [*f.*, perhaps *millia*, “thousands”]—do you judge it better, then, to provide a house protecting thousands of people of both classes from these three hardships, or to grant someone a very cheap garment?

[Note: Construe the passage as follows: “Which, then, do you think is better: to provide a house protecting thousands of people of both classes from these three disadvantages—that is, a church protecting them from sun, rain, and frost—or to give someone the cheapest garment? Is it better to provide the community with roof tiles growing old with the age of the world, and stones that will endure as long as the world itself, than to provide someone with loaves that will immediately turn into dung?” [Col. 0634D]]

May lying lips be silenced, those that speak wickedness against the just (Psalm 30:19)—not so that you should think that “the just” has been applied here to me, but to the one who said, “Woe to those who call evil good” (Isaiah 5:20).

As for asking friendship for what belongs to it, I acknowledge that you have always shown me more effectively by giving than by offering advice something worth recognizing—for I do not doubt that you know very well what ought to be offered. Since whatever is contributed to the church is the Holy of Holies of the Lord and belongs to the right of priests, I profess that I understand the matter as follows: whatever is offered to the Lord is holy, and is assigned for the use not of just anyone, but of the holy—those, certainly, who either rest in our dwellings or are venerated there in a particular way. Their use, therefore, should be the use of those who serve them. [Col. 0635A]

[Note: Construe the passage as follows: “But in order to demand from friendship what belongs to it—which, I do not deny, you have always shown me better by giving than by advising, offering me something recognizable, since I do not doubt that you know very well what ought to be offered—since whatever is contributed to the church is the Holy of Holies of the Lord and belongs to the right of priests, I profess that I understand this by resolving it as follows: whatever is offered to the Lord is holy, and is delegated for the use not of just anyone, but of the holy, who certainly either rest in our dwellings or are especially venerated there,” and so forth. [Col. 0634D–0635C]]

And because priests are especially obliged to serve them, what has been contributed to their right ought appropriately to remain in their possession. Yet the holy canons prescribe that it be divided into four parts: one is assigned to the bishop’s sustenance; another to his provision—that is, to the arrangement of resources for building or restoring basilicas; a third is likewise entrusted to the uses of the poor; and the fourth is destined for the necessities of the clergy. To which of these, I ask you, do you think it was entrusted? [Col. 0635B]

But if, since you yourself are a canon, you do not disdain to heed the canonical rule, I do not doubt that you will have to reply that the bishop has the power to dispose of all ecclesiastical property.

[Note: The canon opposing Ratherius here, whom he calls in the title the principal supporter and defender of his adversaries, seems not to have been a canon of Verona but of another church, as appears from section 2: “But I suppose that among you the poor are supported only by the bishop. Yet the liberality of all who inhabit this country loudly declares that this is not necessary here.” In the former statement the poor are those among you who were thought to be supported by the bishop of that place; in the following statement, the adverb “here” distinguishes them from the Veronese poor, whom the liberality of all who inhabit this country proclaimed not to need the assistance of the bishop of Verona. [Col. 0635C–D]]

But when the matter comes to poorhouses, hospices, and other offices of this kind, I think that the statement of Eugenius in his decrees will be sufficiently clear to you: “Let all these things be distributed through priests and deacons under the bishop’s supervision” [This does not appear in the editions. [Col. 0636A]]

But let this be discussed elsewhere (see Part I, *On Contempt for the Canons*, section 5).

## 5

Since it is useful to return to the subject, I ask your advice concerning the two remaining portions, excluding the portion assigned to the clergy and the sustenance assigned to bishops.

For since the man to whom it was said, “If you love me, feed my sheep” (John 21:17), must feed the flock both spiritually and, if necessary, bodily, and since that third portion has been assigned for this purpose; and since, thanks be to God, famine does not oppress this country, and there are more people able to support others than there are people who need to be supported by alms; while all the churches of this country are everywhere either completely ruined or largely destroyed by the burning of the pagans or through the negligence of pseudo-bishops; and since, if necessity arose, the third and fourth portions ought to have been supported from the first and second, while the second is in the greatest need of relief, what, I ask you, do you decree should be done? [Col. 0636B]

[Note: Acherius’s edition mistakenly reads *alii*; we have adopted the new editor’s correction. The pagans here are the Hungarians, who in this age repeatedly invaded Italy and burned the churches, especially those of our diocese. See Panvinio, Book V of *Antiquities of Verona*, chapter 25. Ratherius himself explicitly names the Hungarians in the *Decree concerning the Little Abbey of Magonziano*: “When the little monastery had been burned by the Hungarians.” The pseudo-bishops are Manasses and Milo, who occupied the see of Verona during Ratherius’s lifetime. [Col. 0635D–0636A]]

For the third portion I have countless helpers; for the fourth, I have clergy who provide for themselves beyond what is proper and sufficient. [Col. 0636C]

[Note: “Second,” that is, the portion belonging to the churches, stood in greatest need of support or repair. Next, the printed texts read *inculcat*, where *inculcet* had to be corrected. He had countless helpers for the third portion—that is, for aiding the poor—because, as he said above in section 2, all the Veronese showed great generosity in this matter. As for the fourth portion, destined for the clergy’s necessities, he says that they provided for themselves beyond what was proper and sufficient because, as he complains elsewhere, the more powerful clerics devoured almost everything for themselves. [Col. 0635D–0636C]]

But for this second portion I can use the words of that Martha who said: “Lord, do you not care that all the neighbors leave me alone and utterly unable either to raise up or restore, and, if that is not granted, to adorn, the basilicas of our diocese?” [Col. 0636A]

[Note: The passage should be explained as follows: “For the second portion—that is, for building or rebuilding churches—I can use the words of that Martha who said: ‘Lord, do you not care that all the neighbors leave me alone and utterly unable to raise up or restore, and, if that is not granted, to adorn, the basilicas of our diocese?’” Here “neighbors” means the inhabitants of the same village, or, as we call them, the neighborhood. Thus also in *Discord*, section 7: “I sent them some of the neighbors.” He declares himself utterly unable to rebuild the churches because, since the revenues of most churches had been alienated through leases, exchanges, emphyteutic contracts, or military benefices, on account of the intolerable abuse of his age, as he complains in the *Conjecture of Quality*, and since the bishop was burdened by many expenses, especially those of hospitality, he himself had been reduced to poverty. [Col. 0636D]]

Moreover, if I do anything—namely, for rebuilding the churches—even those who strive to be thought my friends habitually reproach me and declare that it would have been better to squander it, that is, to dissipate it for an alien and unnecessary use. [Col. 0636D–0637A]

[Note: This amounts to saying, “It is useless to serve the Lord” (Malachi 3:14); it is to prefer uncertainty to certainty, since the need of the churches is certain, whereas he later declares the need of the poor, to whom they wished the portion owed to the churches to be handed over, to be uncertain. It is to place sinners—whom he earlier said were poor people indulging in excess and drunkenness—ahead of the most holy, to whom the churches have been dedicated; and to assert that God values their excess more highly than the glory of these holy places. This is what you are doing when you say that it would have been better for me to distribute what I possess as alms to those two groups—the needy and the clergy who do not need so much, since they are partly provided for by their own provision and partly by the generosity of others—and entirely to neglect this second portion, namely, the portion necessarily required for building or rebuilding churches. You not only think this, but say that it would have been better. What ear could endure such wickedness? Such an opinion, I confess, belongs not to a friend but to the bitterest enemy. [Col. 0637C]]

That is to say, to declare, “It is useless to serve the Lord”; to prefer uncertainty to certainty; to place sinners before the most holy; and to assert that God values their excess more highly than the glory of these holy places. [Col. 0637A]

This is what you are doing when you say that it would have been better for me to distribute what I possess as alms to those two groups—the needy and the clergy, who are not so much in need because they are partly provided for by their own resources and partly by the generosity of others—and entirely to neglect this second portion, that is, the portion necessarily required for building or rebuilding churches. You not only think this but say that it would have been better.

What ear could endure such wickedness? I confess that such an opinion belongs not to a friend but to the bitterest enemy. [Col. 0637B]

## 6

Although I may most truly call you, my very dear friend, the chief supporter of all my enemies, I am not so greatly angered by the fact that the clergy who tear me apart are none but rebels against the Lord himself. For I know beyond doubt that you do this not out of hatred for me but out of hatred for your own bishop.

Except for those who aspire to the height of the episcopate, nearly all the clergy agree that they would rather hear the Apostle saying, “Not as lording it over the clergy” (1 Peter 5:3), than, “Command and teach these things” (1 Timothy 4:11); or another apostolic injunction: “Speak these things and exhort with all authority; let no one despise you” (Titus 2:15); and, “Rebuke them sharply” (Titus 1:13). [Col. 0637C]

And if I bring forward other similar statements, I know that this can be thrown back at me: “The fool speaks out all his mind” (Proverbs 29:11). [Col. 0637D]

For today no one except a very powerful, very rich, very fierce man—and therefore, in their view, not a bishop but, as they mutter, some tyrant—is accorded by his clergy the privilege of episcopal honor. All the clergy seek to have bishops subject to themselves; yet they all listen harshly, whenever they think of bishops, to the Lord’s saying: “The disciple is not above his teacher” (Matthew 20:24). [Col. 0638A]

Nevertheless, it is very pleasing to all of them when they compel their subjects to render them honor, even honor that is not owed [perhaps *debetur*, “is owed,” or one should supply “which ought not to be rendered”], by this example: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do also to them” (Luke 6:31). At the end of the section, *quodcunque audierit* was read, where it had to be corrected to *quod quicunque audierit*.

Likewise, without drinking in what is offered to them, they listen affectionately when it is read: “Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger” (Ephesians 6:4); and they complain that we do not observe this when we demand from them what belongs to God or to us. They turn a deaf ear when they hear: “Children, obey your parents in everything” (Colossians 3:20). They hear “Entreat” more patiently than “Argue” or “Rebuke.”

They attach little importance when the curse of Ham, who disclosed his father’s shame, is directed against them (Genesis 9:25); but they consider it highly significant whenever some disgrace, true or false, is brought against us.

Oh—here, so that I may single myself out more particularly—oh, wretched me! “A word has become a reality in my days in Israel; whoever hears it, both his ears will tingle because of it” (4 Kings 21:12). [Col. 0638B]

## 7

After such great, such numerous, such foul, shameful, incredible things—things also contrary to my very age—which you have brought against me as this year’s balsams [*dihorno* is a very difficult expression. *Horno* means “this year.” Did he ironically call the accusations recently brought against him “this year’s balsams”? In any event, the meaning is: “After such great, such numerous, such foul, and so forth, things as you have brought against me.” Earlier, in section 4, he had said: “Some people hurl accusations at me, whether you think so or whether they have rather fabricated them for themselves.” [Col. 0637D]]—and I think you did not hear them with complete displeasure—it is horrifying to state to what madness the rashness of that Martianist of yours has recently proceeded. [Col. 0638C]

[Note: Above, in section 1, he referred to a certain manner of writing which, he said, you derive from Martianus and others of the same kind. We observed there that Martianus Capella is meant, since he was then used in the schools. The “Martianist” whom he attacks here was therefore perhaps some hostile cleric who took particular delight in the study and style of that same Martianus. [Col. 0638C]]

I fear that this pestilential company may be infected by your stench, which I have absolutely no doubt will happen.

For after all those things, when he had dared, with unheard-of recklessness, to go without my permission to the imperial court—although the canons decree that one who does so is to be deposed—and had approached that venal city, as Sallust calls it (*War with Jugurtha*), carrying letters as though apostolic, bought there for money, as everything has been from ancient times, he struck both me and all my successors without exception with the sword of an anathema, so that henceforth any bishop who involved himself in the clergy’s affairs would be condemned, as they say, by perpetual anathema. [Col. 0639A]

[Note: “The imperial court” signifies the emperor’s court, or the place where the emperor was residing. Concerning those who traveled to the imperial court, see the decrees of the Council of Sardica, canons 8–11 of the Dionysian collection, and canon 106 of the African Church. Pope Zosimus likewise complains in his *Memorandum* to the priests and deacons established at Ravenna about certain clerics of his own: “They wished to go against us to the imperial court, daring to do so, I do not know with what recklessness, contrary to the canons.” The penalty of deposition is decreed in canons 11 and 12 of the Council of Antioch.

Why, then, does he introduce the imperial court here, when the subject is a delegation to the Roman pontiff? It is clear from the work *On Rebellious Clerics* that the canons sent a delegation to the emperor toward the end of the year 967. Perhaps the same delegation of the canons that approached the emperor also visited the Roman pontiff; for this reason Ratherius joins the imperial court with the journey to Rome.

The pontiff’s rescript could not have been obtained until Lent of the year 968. News of it was brought to Verona very recently—that is, shortly before Easter—when Ratherius wrote the *Apologetic*. The sharper style in which the author describes this event should be forgiven in a man who was naturally severe in writing, who was irritated by the customs of the age and by the very novelty of the unexpected rescript, and who wrote in a kind of frenzy.

He did not wish to interfere in the revenues of the canons in order to claim either all or part of them for himself or to distribute them to others. He saw, and grieved, that what had been generally contributed to the cathedral church was divided so unequally that the greater men, appropriating nearly everything to themselves, lived in abundance, while the other clergy of the same church were consumed by poverty. See Part I, *On Contempt for the Canons*, sections 3 and 4. [Col. 0639C]

To remedy this evil, from which many other evils followed, he thought that, following the more equitable custom of other churches, a fairer distribution of their revenues should be established among all the clergy of the same church. But the canons had drawn even all the lower clergy into their own party, so as to defend the special custom they claimed and obtain a papal rescript. What they represented to Roman ears, while Ratherius was absent and unable to defend either his own cause or his own plan, is unknown. [Col. 0639D]]

Now, since a *res* (“thing”) is properly called an invisible substance—as was implied by the man who very briefly defined a noun as a part of speech signifying a body or a thing—what things belong more particularly to clerics than their souls? [Col. 0639B]

Nevertheless, I do not doubt that I shall not escape reproof on this account too: namely, because in this matter of religion I have introduced the testimony of a pagan author. Yet I rely on the authority of the Apostle, who uses that saying in his letter to Titus against idle talkers and deceivers, so that you may not go away unbitten.

[Note: The Roman rescript ruled only concerning material goods, that is, the ecclesiastical revenues assigned to the cathedral church’s table. Ratherius’s extension of this ruling to the souls of the clergy was an excessively forced interpretation, prompted by the pain of what we might call a recent wound. To the extent that the administration of church property contributes to the advancement of souls, he explained the matter more reasonably in Part I, *On Contempt for the Canons*, sections 3 and 4. [Col. 0639D]]

Yet since the clergy themselves are corporeal, while the clergy-state itself is incorporeal, I most confidently conclude that, if I abstain from all their possessions—both their bodies and the material resources assigned to their support—I must likewise abstain from their souls and, in addition, from the clergy-state itself, since these too are realities.

The realities themselves—that is, their persons—consist, as I have said, chiefly in their souls. Since these, more than their other possessions, have been forbidden to me by this anathema, I clearly understand that care for them, together with all their possessions, has been entirely taken away from me. [Col. 0640A]

If you can, then, give me some advice.

For if I make light of the anathema of the apostolic see, I pave a bridge for everyone toward an example of the worst kind, besides another matter that ought not to be treated lightly. If I do not, then at least I shall not celebrate Mass for them—for since they themselves are realities, and the chanting of the Mass belongs to the greatest possible involvement with their possessions, it pertains wholly to such involvement.

If I do not celebrate Mass for them, I plainly show that I am at least not their priest, much less their bishop.

But if I am truly bishop of the Veronese, as was once proclaimed at the synod of Pavia—for a bishop is said to mean one who supervises—over whom do I exercise supervision, I who see myself subjected to all? [Col. 0640B]

[Note: In the *Itinerary*, section 4, he states that he was restored synodally by the judgment of bishops. Here he indicates which synod this was, namely, the Synod of Pavia in 962, by which he was restored to the Church of Verona for the third time. [Col. 0640C]]

Is it these men, who, although it is public adultery for them to be monogamists—since this is certainly an illegal marriage—consider it nothing to be trigamists and, shamefully, quadrigamists? These are priests and deacons, even though laymen who have married twice cannot at least become clerics. [Col. 0640A]

[Note: Ratherius frequently uses *fore* for *esse*, “to be.” He is speaking of clerics among whom he calls monogamy an illegal marriage and therefore public adultery. Thus, in *Discord*, section 1, he says: “For us, an adulterer is one who, contrary to the canons, has a wife.” And in the *Conjecture of Quality*, section 2, his accusers declare concerning him: “He calls an illegal marriage adultery.” The passage should be construed as follows: “Although it is public adultery for them to be monogamists—since it is certainly an illegal marriage—they consider it nothing to be trigamists and, shamefully, quadrigamists,” and so forth. [Col. 0640C–D]]

Are these the men who, although they read that the practice of trade has been entirely forbidden to them, recklessly become usurers? Who have renounced faith to such an extent that they do not even deign to deny, many times over, that they are perjurers? Who appropriate to themselves what has been contributed generally to the church so completely and so particularly that, except for those who, in the manner of the scribes and Pharisees, hold preeminence over others, the rest, while I look on from below and am unable to render any assistance, suffer severely from the plague of starvation? [Col. 0640B]

Who, fighting among themselves in the bosom of the Church with fists, or rather with boxing gloves—so that this may be said in reference to Virgil’s Entelline fighters (*Aeneid* V)—do not fear violating the temple of the living God to such an extent that, unless it is reconciled in person, the laws prohibit the solemn celebration of Mass there, even on that most immediate Easter?

One of those deacons even had his own servant publicly and most arrogantly slap the priest Ordinary in his presence before the very doors of the church.

[Note: “Ordinary” means one of the canons. See note 1042 in the *Itinerary*. [Col. 0640D]]

In short, are these the men over whom I exercise supervision, when one who traveled to Rome without my permission acted so that, after an anathema had been hurled against me, all involvement with such matters was forbidden to me? [Col. 0640D]

[Note: This is how the most recent editor of the *Spicilegium* reads the passage; Acherius’s edition previously had *ejus ne*. The verb *superintendo*, “I exercise supervision,” is understood from the preceding context.]

[Col. 0640C] **8.** To leave such things and countless others, no less in need of correction, wholly uncorrected while the opportunity does not follow—is that, I ask, to exercise oversight? But to be wholly unable to exercise oversight—is that to be a bishop? And for one who is not a bishop to sit in the episcopal chair—is that, I ask, acceptable and lawful?

[Col. 0640D] To this, certainly, if I report something previously unheard as inspired, although I am sure that I shall not be regarded by you as blameless, nevertheless know that I shall do this without hesitation, unless God prevents it—even though it may seem to you, as to a carnal man who does not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God, to have been done most foolishly; yet it will not have been so, if God grants it. By “inspired” he understands something drawn from sacred authority. For in *Discordia*, no. 2, he says: “Whatever is found written in the Law of Moses, and in the Prophets, and in the Psalms, and whatever is found in the Gospel, the Acts, and the preaching of the Apostles, in papal decretals and canonical constitutions—does it not again shine forth to you as INSPIRED by God?” In our text, however, he seems to indicate that he intends to write a short work in which he would prove by sacred authorities that one who cannot exercise oversight, and leaves uncorrected what ought to be corrected, is not a bishop and cannot sit in the episcopal chair. In this passage, Acherius had *non praecipit* instead of *non percipit*.

Although you are able to rejoice that Ratherius has been defeated in this way, I advise you not to celebrate too greatly, thinking that Antonius can be defeated in such a manner; for if it could happen, it would undoubtedly already have happened, since it is not unknown to everyone what difference there is between a man and a little man.

[Construe: “Certainly, since you can rejoice that Ratherius has been so defeated, I advise you not to exult too much, thinking that Antonius can be defeated in such a way; for, if this could happen, it would undoubtedly already have happened, since it is not unknown to everyone what difference there is between a man and a little man.” By “a man” he means a powerful man, who could not be defeated as he himself had been by the canons. He calls the former Antonius; himself, having been defeated, a little man—that is, weak and feeble. We do not know who this Antonius was. Is some bishop more powerful than Ratherius meant? Liutprand, in book V, chapter 13 of his *History*, records that Antonius, bishop of Brescia in this period, attended the council of Ravenna with Ratherius in 967. Liutprand testifies in the cited passage that, after Joseph’s expulsion, Berengar II installed him in the see of Brescia without consultation and without any deliberation by bishops. We do not understand what business the Veronese canons could have had with him, or in what matter they vainly attempted to defeat him. But if he was a native of Verona, as Faynus reported in *Coelo aureo*, and especially if he was related by blood to Milo, count of Verona, as Rubeus affirms in his manuscript *History of Brescia* under the year 960, cited by Giovanni Maria Viemmi, vol. II, *History of Brescia*, p. 204, some controversy may perhaps have existed between him and the Veronese canons—for example, concerning some estate which they attempted, unsuccessfully, to claim for the capitular property. But to conjecture without documents is to divine.]

[Col. 0641B] But as for my invective against you, dearest friend, which you wish to be believed to be directed against you, lest it continue indefinitely, I wish to set a limit to it here. I am not unaware that I must make haste to avoid the use of many words, lest it happen that I incur, together with that loquacity, the sin of abusive speech—which is a much worse guilt [read: a worse guilt]. Especially if someone, overstepping the bounds of truth and neglecting, in a way impossible to discover, the law of charity, joins uncertainties to certainties, gathers false accusations from every side because he cannot produce true ones, and, even though the smallness of his intellect prevents him from fabricating them as supposedly plausible, changes white things into black and black things into white, and pursues them—something which, as the Psalm reveals, causes God himself to pronounce woe upon him (Ps. XV, 20) for such an exchange. In my misery I consider this and burn myself, as though with a fiery cautery, irreparably kindled by another’s prosperity. May the ineffable mercy of Christ turn this away from both of us—Christ, whose majesty with the Father and the Holy Spirit is one and the same, just as his power to act is one and the same, and his reign one and the same, throughout endless ages. Amen.

[Construe: “Moreover, may my invective against you, dearest friend, as you wish it to be believed, not strive to proceed without end; here I wish to set it a limit, not unaware that it is expedient for me to hasten as quickly as possible to avoid the practice of much speaking, lest I happen to incur, together with that loquacity, the sin of abusive speech, which is a much worse guilt [read: worse guilt]; especially if anyone, transgressing the bounds of truth, neglecting the law of charity in an undiscoverable manner, joining certainties to uncertainties, gathering false calumnies from every side when he cannot produce true ones, and, though the smallness of his intellect prevents him from inventing even seemingly plausible ones, changes white into black and black into white, pursues …,” etc. In these words something is either lacking or certainly corrupt. A Psalm appears to be cited in place of Isaiah.]

[Col. 0641]

[Col. 0641D] This Testament was printed by Father Bernard Pez from the Freising manuscript, and we received a useful copy of that same manuscript. Since it was transcribed from Ratherius’s papers as a work of Ratherius, it lacks the clauses, chronological notes, and subscriptions with which documents of this kind, written by notaries, are usually provided. The *Decree concerning the little monastery at Mainz* and the *Judgment* likewise were transcribed and published without the customary clauses, chronological notes, and subscriptions. Furthermore, the Testament and the Appendix to the Testament, added at its end, must be distinguished. Since the *Judgment* is praised in the Testament, and praised in such a way that it is presumed still to be valid and binding, we recognize that the Testament was written after the beginning of November 967, when the *Judgment* was issued, and before 30 June of the following year, when Nanno, acting as the emperor’s envoy, publicly annulled that *Judgment*. We infer that the Appendix attached at the end was added after the Testament itself. See note 1230.

**RATHERIUS’S TESTAMENT**

[Col. 0641D] **511** Ratherius, by the ineffable mercy of the Creator tolerated for a very long time, and still alive, although merely nominally a bishop [*Nuncupatively only* he calls himself a bishop because he very often complains that he was prevented from exercising episcopal authority], is certainly destined at the appointed time to become ashes.

[Col. 0642D] **1.** Since the instability of passing life [The Vulgate adds *meae*, “of my life”; we deleted it with our copy. *Recula* means a small thing, a small possession.] permits no person of sound mind to remain secure, I wish, while still alive, to arrange the little things that I seem to possess in such a way that after my death those to whom I have given them may possess them in undisturbed right—however little they may be, so that those who are found to grieve somewhat at my absence may nevertheless receive some consolation.

**2.** First of all, I wish that if I hold anything unjustly, it be restored entirely to the person to whom it belongs. Next, whatever is found among my household furnishings is to be distributed among my household members—that is, among the clerics who serve me, and, if there are not too few, among certain laymen also: dwelling furnishings, benches, bedding, little curtains [*Curtinulae* is a diminutive of *curtina*, elsewhere *cortina*, which among medieval writers means hangings or curtains], if there are any, clothing, and other things of this kind.

But if I have any money, I wish it to be divided as follows. If there is one pound, let it be given to those who arrange my funeral; another, if there is one, to the clerics who possess the church of Saint Mary of Consolation, together with the other things described in the same *Judgment*. Whatever remains—whether it is much, which I do not believe; or little, or certainly nothing, which I do not disbelieve—let Martin [Our copy reads *Maran*], who now keeps my little chests, or whoever holds that office at the time of my death, have it. Whoever takes anything whatever from him shall be accursed and suffer everlasting disgrace.

As for what pertains to food, I wish it to be granted to the churches which, alas, I began too late to restore [*Too late*, that is, after his third restoration to the see of Verona, when he showed himself concerned with restoring the churches. See *Conjecture concerning his Condition*, no. 2, and the *Apologeticus*]. May God repay each person accordingly for what he has done.

As for horses, or any other aids I may have for undertaking a journey, and perhaps weapons as well, let them be given to those who are with me at that time and need to transfer themselves elsewhere—especially if they are from my homeland and family.

Since these things and those connected with them will certainly not be of great value, may the Almighty, whose right hand crushes them, and the anathema of all the saints, prevent those who oppose them from seizing them. Amen.

**3.** These provisions are made in fear of a sudden event, whether it occurs or whether the promised withdrawal is granted, as is hoped [The same copy reads this way. Pez’s edition has *quisve contingat*, incorrectly. The sudden event he feared is death; the promised withdrawal he hoped for is the one indicated in his letter 13 to Empress Adelaide: “I desire rather to be healthfully withdrawn and to dwell in the solitude of my monastery.” This paragraph, which in the manuscript follows the Testament after a blank space of several lines, appears to have been added by Ratherius when the order to depart, which he had begun to seek, was promised to him].

I commend to your protection, exalted father [By the name “exalted father” he seems to mean his successor, whose brothers he calls the Veronese clerics. To him he commends this final will, and especially the decree of his grant, that is, the *Judgment],* all those listed in the decree of my grant, on this condition: that you defend them against all your brothers by asking your brothers to do so, and against the others with whatever strength you can muster.

In particular, I commend to the two clerics Martin and Gisempert the lease which I made: namely, the estate called **[lacuna]** [The lacuna left in the manuscript itself contained the proper name of the estate, which the copyist could not read], which is now inhabited by two men, Albo [The name of the other of the two who inhabited the estate is also missing: **[lacuna]**]. Since the deacon Benedict had fraudulently acquired it, I took it away from him and granted it to these men, but on the condition—for it could not be otherwise—that while I remained alive they should enjoy it together with me, and after my departure they should possess it for a period of twenty-nine years, as is customary for the others [This was evidently the arrangement in emphyteutic contracts: they were not to exceed twenty-nine years, in order to prevent the acquisition of a thirty-year prescriptive right. We published an older example of such a contract, from Pope Honorius I, dated 625, from a Vatican manuscript in the treatise *On Ancient Collections and Collectors of Canons*, part III, chapter 14, p. 306, vol. III of the latest edition of Saint Leo].

**THE SECOND PART OF THE WORKS OF RATHERIUS, BISHOP OF VERONA**

[Col. 0643]

# LETTERS (G)*

**521. LETTER I. TO PATRICUS**

[Col. 0643D] This letter was published separately by Acherius from the Lobbes manuscript, book XII. In the latest Spicilegium edition of Acherius, it was reprinted together with other works of Ratherius in volume I. We have adopted the readings of the same manuscript after a more careful collation. We believe that Ratherius wrote this letter in Belgium before his episcopate at Verona. He nowhere mentions either episcopal dignity or the reversals that he suffered as a bishop. Moreover, he testifies that he rarely, indeed extremely rarely, celebrates Mass—something suitable to a monk, but not to a bishop. Add that he calls Conrad “our lord,” although Conrad was not a bishop, as is clear from note 1238. If Ratherius had been a bishop, would he have bestowed such a title on someone inferior to himself? We infer that he gave this letter to Patricus in Belgium, where he had lived as a monk, because he is responding not in writing but in words to a question posed by Patricus when Conrad performed ecclesiastical offices in a place called Horna. Horna is a county in the diocese of Liège; hence even now the bishop of Liège is styled, among other titles, Count of Horna. We assign this letter the first place because all the others were composed by Ratherius after he had already become a bishop.

**Concerning the Body and Blood of the Lord**

[Col. 0643D]

**RATHERIUS TO PATRICUS, the most miserable to the miserable**

[Col. 0643D] [The printed editions add the sigla “V. S.,” which are absent from the manuscript.]

You recently asked someone, when our lord Conrad performed the ecclesiastical offices at the place called Horna [As *Ordines* are the booklets prescribing the rite and order of each ecclesiastical function, so the ecclesiastical functions performed according to the rule of those *Ordines* are sometimes themselves called *ordines*. We have no doubt that the words “when our lord Conrad performed the ecclesiastical offices” must be understood in this sense. The place called Horna—for we have corrected the printed editions, which incorrectly read *Hornon*—is situated in the diocese of Liège, as we observed in note 1236. Conrad, who performed ecclesiastical offices there, was certainly not the bishop of Liège, as is evident from the succession of those bishops transmitted to us by writers contemporary with Ratherius. Since the bishop of another place could not confer holy orders in a diocese not his own, this passage cannot be understood of the conferral of holy orders. Conrad, who, although he was not the bishop of Liège, is nevertheless acknowledged by both Ratherius and Patricus as superior to them by virtue of the title “our lord,” must therefore have performed at Horna some sacred and solemn function designated by the name *ordines*. Perhaps it was the solemn celebration of Mass, on the occasion of which Patricus appropriately asked someone whether Ratherius had sung Mass during that week. Ratherius seems to have written in a similar sense in Letter 5 to Pope John, no. 6: “One day, while I was performing the ecclesiastical offices.” Soon the pronoun *tu* refers back to *interrogasti*. To sing Mass is the same as to say or recite Mass. See note 954 in the *Synodica*].

—you asked pointedly [read: openly], but in your usual manner [“In your usual manner” is understood], that is, inquisitively rather than charitably, whether I had celebrated Mass during that week.

I answer for myself: Would that neither you nor I had done so on the Lord’s Nativity! For I do so rarely [The manuscript reading *raro*, “rarely,” has been adopted; the printed editions incorrectly had *ruor*], and in this, alas, most unworthily; you do so daily, and do so in a white garment [On the authority of the manuscript we have added *hoc*, “this”; shortly afterward we likewise added *et pariter* before *mihi*. The passage seems to be construed as follows: “This white garment God, as I think, values in no one’s body more highly than in yours—and, I fear somewhat, believe me, in your mind blacker than soot, as it is in mine”].

For I recognize that you serve that seventh vice with the greatest zeal—a vice that God detests [The Lobbes manuscript reads *ejus detestatur*; the printed editions, with different punctuation, read *suis detestatur anima, te*, and in neither case is there a suitable meaning. We believe we have restored the true reading by writing *Deus* for *ejus*. The seventh vice is sadness, or negligence and sluggishness in good works, a vice that God rebukes in many places in sacred Scripture. The ancient question is whether it is preferable to receive the Eucharist frequently or rarely. Patricus, celebrating daily, received it daily; Ratherius rarely. He presents himself as unworthy, but indicates that Patricus must greatly fear the vice of negligence or sluggishness to which he was devoted]. I recognize that your soul serves it most zealously—and would that I alone recognized this!

Therefore, let the Apostle judge which of us two, one receiving the Eucharist extremely rarely and the other daily, receives it more dangerously and unworthily (I Cor. XI, 27). If we were to read attentively the sermons of John Chrysostom on the same Epistle to the Hebrews, they would restrain both me from celebrating Mass altogether and you, I believe, from celebrating it daily [The manuscript reads *legeremus*, “we were to read”; Acherius had *legerimus*].

**2.** When I also hear that you were scandalized by my bathing on the vigil of the Lord’s Circumcision, I cannot sufficiently marvel at the very clean purity of your most chaste body [We have added the adjective *castissimi* from the manuscript. Construe as follows: “I cannot sufficiently marvel at the very clean purity of your most chaste body, when I hear that you were scandalized at my bathing”—that is, at the use of the bath—“on the vigil of the Lord’s Circumcision; you, I say, evidently inexperienced in what the flesh subdued by the law of sin may suffer even against the will of the mind, unless perhaps by your authority it is permissible to handle polluted holy things without the twofold cleansing of the bath.” On the use of bathing before Communion, especially on solemn days, see Mabillon, preface 2 to the fourth century of the Order of Saint Benedict, no. 187].

But it is said: “Cleanse yourselves, you who carry the vessels of the Lord” (Isa. LII, 11). And “Be sanctified” is often said whenever anything sacred is commanded to be done in the Old Testament, even in that symbolic one. Concerning David and the loaves of the Presence, which he took because of necessity, it says: “If the young men are clean” (I Sam. XXI, 4).

**3.** But perhaps you take the words superficially, or even think that you are speaking figuratively when you say to the communicant: “May the body of our Lord Jesus Christ be beneficial to you unto eternal life.”

If this is so, the blindness of your understanding ought to be grieved over and instructed rather than marveled at and mocked—namely, the blindness by which, unable to avoid the pit of presumption, you never cease frequently doing what you do not know the power of.

But believe, brother: just as at Cana of Galilee true wine, not figurative wine, was made from water by God’s command, so here, through God’s blessing, this wine becomes true, not figurative, blood, and the bread becomes flesh.

If the taste remains the same and the color seems to deny that this has occurred, I propose another example to you [The manuscript supplied the verb *propono*, “I propose,” which was absent from the printed editions]. Do you believe the authority of Scripture, which says that man was formed from the clay of the earth? I have no doubt that you will answer that you believe it.

Moreover, do you know the saying: “You are dust, and to dust you shall return” (Gen. III, 19)? “I know it, I think,” you say, “and I believe it to be so.” Therefore you are dust. The man whom you see before you is dust and ash.

“He is indeed,” you say, “because he was made from clay.” What, then, is this figure of clay? None: call it rather earth. Is it some kind of earth? Not some kind [The Vulgate reads: “Not some kind, and yet it is earth. What of the figure of clay?” We have adopted the manuscript’s reading].

And yet is man earth? He is.

What of the figure of clay? It has been transformed by the wisdom of the one who formed it.

Does the substance nevertheless remain? It remains.

So here too, while the color and taste remain, believe that what you perceive is true flesh and blood, through the operation of the same wisdom—just as, conversely, although the form of man was changed in creation [the printed editions have “the form of man having been changed, in the creation of man.” We have not ventured to alter the manuscript’s reading. We would more willingly emend it to “the form of clay having been changed, in the creation of man”], you do not deny that the substance of clay remained.

**4.** But you ask whose body this flesh is [We supplied the noun *caro*, “flesh,” from the manuscript; from the same source we corrected *delata* to *deleta*], perhaps improperly, as human curiosity’s vanity dictates: where it comes from, from whom it has been cut away, whether it itself has been removed and the bread perhaps invisibly taken away, or whether the bread itself has been changed into flesh.

These, I think, are the stones by which the beast—that is, the carnal heart—and the natural man, who does not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God (I Cor. II, 14), are struck if he presumes to touch the mountain of God’s mysteries (Heb. XII, 20).

Let us therefore question the Gospel. “Jesus took bread,” it says, “gave thanks, and gave it to them, saying: ‘Take and eat; this is my body.’ Likewise also the chalice, after he had supped, saying: ‘This is the chalice of my blood, of the new and eternal covenant, the mystery of faith, which will be poured out for you and for many for the remission of sins’” (Matt. XXVI, 26; I Cor. II, 24).

[Col. 0647C] You have the answer concerning whose body this flesh and blood are, all the more certainly because you have been instructed by the voice of that same Truth who speaks. As for the rest, I ask you not to be anxious, since you hear that it is a mystery—and a mystery of faith. For if it is a mystery, it cannot be comprehended; if it is of faith, it must be believed, not investigated.

**525. LETTER II**

[Col. 0647C] This letter, cited by Fulcuinus in chapter 20, was published by Fathers Martène and Durand from the Lobbes manuscript in volume IX of the *Collection of Ancient Writers*, p. 965; we have received a more accurate collation of the same manuscript. Wido was archbishop of Lyon, and Sobbo archbishop of Vienne in Gaul. Although the sees of the others are unknown, since they belonged to the council to which Ratherius also appears to have been invited, there is no doubt that they too were bishops subject to the metropolitan bishops of Lyon or Vienne—all of them, that is, in that part of Gaul which was then called the kingdom of Burgundy. This letter was written while Ratherius, released from the prison at Pavia, had been sent into exile. Hence he calls himself an exile in the heading. He remained in exile at Como for two years and somewhat more, as he himself reports in Letter 5 to Pope John XII, no. 5—namely, from August 937 until approximately the beginning of 940. From this period the date of the present letter can be inferred. At the same time he wrote another letter to the same men assembled in council, or rather an annotation in the form of a letter, which was inserted into the fifth book of the *Praeloquia*; see col. 302 and note 297.

**TO WIDO AND SOBBO, ARCHBISHOPS, AND GODESCALC AND AURELIUS, BISHOPS**

To the most holy and beloved fathers, the archbishops WIDO and SOBBO, and the bishops GODESCALC and AURELIUS, RATHERIUS, sinner and exile.

[Col. 0647D] Unless a little sheet were lacking—for misery most wretchedly brings my hardships to their greatest strait [The printed editions read “the distress of misery oppresses”; the correction is supplied by the Lobbes copy. Ratherius indicates that he was suffering such great hardships at Como, where he was in exile, that he even lacked a small sheet, or piece of paper, on which to write a longer letter]—I would produce an adequate excuse, not for deliberate disobedience but for ineffective disobedience, in a lengthy explanation [The printed editions read “I would produce an excuse for disobedience by a long continuation,” or, in other words, “badly.” The reading of our copy, which we have preferred, indicates that because of his lack of paper Ratherius could not produce, in a lengthy continuation—that is, in as many words as he would have wished, as was fitting for one writing to such distinguished bishops—an excuse for disobedience that was not deliberate but ineffective. The disobedience refers to an order by which the bishops had perhaps invited him to the council; for another letter, or annotation in letter form, addressed to the same bishops while they were sitting in council, is inserted in the fifth book of the *Praeloquia*. He calls this disobedience not deliberate but ineffective because, although he greatly wished to visit the bishops when invited, he could not, since as an exile at Como he was not his own master], as would be appropriate from the most unworthy and most unfortunate of all men to lords most worthy and most fortunate, bishops—and yet, by God’s mercy, to fellow bishop.

But what shall I do? What I could not convey in dignified speech, I shall strive to convey in brief speech. This above all, my lords, is the reason why I did not come before your lordships in accordance with your command: I am not my own master, and, finally, no one attempts to descend into himself.

As for thinking anything sinister of the Elder, much less saying it—for I speak to the prudent—I judge that an execrable crime. Nor is it necessary for me to present myself before the eyes of just anyone in order to have my condition examined [The printed editions read “to investigate,” and afterward “to be presented.” Construe as follows: “It is not necessary for me to present myself before the eyes of anyone whatever in order to have my condition”—that is, my manner of life, as also in Letter 3, “the character of my life”—“examined.” Hence the title of the work *Conjecture concerning his Condition*].

[Col. 0648B] For insofar as it concerns the worse, in accordance with that saying of Terence, the whole people takes care of it. But insofar as it concerns the better, by the grace of God I am whatever I am; yet I am in every respect a thousand times less than the person whom my friends’ praises proclaim me to be.

[Col. 0648C] The misery of my misfortune, lying between these two opposites [The misery of my misfortune, midway between these two different conditions—that is, between the worse and the better—is openly apparent to everyone], lies broadly open to all. I ask you, for God’s sake, to have compassion on it in two ways: by supporting me with prayer and helping me with your resources. I need both these things most of all; and I know that you are both under an obligation and, through God’s mercy, abundantly able to discharge that obligation.

For the rest, I send this little work of my labor to your judgment [The work is the six books of the *Praeloquia*. For this reason, in book V he inserted an annotation in the form of a letter, by which he urges these same bishops to reread and weigh especially those passages that might move them to pity him and provide assistance, since he was confident that they possessed great influence with their fellow-countryman, King Hugh]. Read it charitably, for God’s sake. Farewell in the Lord, remembering us everywhere.

**527. LETTER III. TO ROTBERT, ARCHBISHOP**

[Col. 0649C] This letter too, mentioned by Fulcuinus in chapter 20, was printed in volume IX, p. 965, of the *Collection of Ancient Writers* by Fathers Martène and Durand from the Lobbes manuscript; a copy of that manuscript sent to us supplied several corrections. Rotbert, to whom this letter was sent, was archbishop of Trier, son of Duke Theodoric of Saxony and brother of Saint Mathilda, who is celebrated under many titles as the mother of Otto, king of Germany and later emperor. He was elevated to the renowned see in 928 and died in 956.

The date of the letter must be deduced from several indications. Since Ratherius presents himself as ready to serve Rotbert, he shows that when he wrote this he was his own master; consequently, he had been released from his exile at Como, from which he was rescued after the beginning of 940. We should also note what he says in section 1: after leaving “that place”—that is, Belgic Gaul—he had devoted himself to no books by pagan writers. Previously, when he was a monk among the Belgians, he had occupied himself with the books of profane authors; but after becoming bishop in Italy, he had taken leave of them. The words “after I left that place” show that he was still away from Belgium. He first returned to Belgium in 944. The letter therefore appears to belong to the intervening period, between 940 and 944. Since, after his release from exile, he went to Provence, where he placed himself under the instruction of Roestagnus, while he wrote this letter in need of everything and bound to no one, seeking aid from Rotbert and offering himself in his service, it is quite credible that it was written before he undertook Roestagnus’s instruction, which provided sufficiently for him—that is, around 940.

To the most reverend lord ROTBERT, most noble of archbishops, RATHERIUS, most faithful servant.

**1.** I offer your lordship, most loving father, not adequate but abundant thanks for the promised distinctions of benefits bestowed upon my littleness by your magnificence [So the Lobbes manuscript reads. The printed editions arbitrarily have “to your lordship”]. I pray that he who inspired you to promise may likewise grant and bring it to completion, so that you may deserve to receive from my smallness the most ready return of service [The printed editions read *necessitudinem*, “relationship,” instead of *servitii vicissitudinem*, “return of service.” Our copy supplied the correction], and from him an eternal reward in return.

Moreover, in order to answer the questions of your lordship, I confess that, after leaving that place, I have studied no books [The verb *fateor*, “I confess,” has been supplied from the same copy. Construe as follows: “In order to answer the questions of your lordship, I confess that, after leaving that place, I have not studied any books”—that is, books by profane writers, to which he had previously devoted himself while he was there, namely in the kingdom of Lothair, where both Trier and the monastery of Lobbes were located. For below he states that after becoming bishop he applied his mind to sacred studies. We therefore learn that Rotbert’s questions concerned profane studies].

I grieve that I have forgotten far too much of what I had learned. Hence I profess that it is more fitting for me to be taught than to teach. Although, at the very beginning [At the very beginning—that is, when Ratherius first came to Italy in the company of Hilduin—certain Milanese put several questions to him. When he answered them, he says that he seemed to have answered some of the questions Rotbert had asked], when I was quite seriously pressed by the little questions of certain Milanese, I seemed to have touched briefly upon some of the matters which I do not doubt that you are seeking; once I had been invested with this burden which, by God’s mercy, I bear, I immediately ceased to pursue this activity, reflecting that, under the office imposed upon me, I ought rather to meditate day and night on the law of God [The printed editions insert *in*, “in”; we have deleted it from the Lobbes copy. What Ratherius says here about himself was likewise done by Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, as is clear from his Letter 33 to Damnoaldus: “You have sent us questions from secular literature to solve. But it is not fitting for an episcopal purpose to devote oneself to such studies. Once, indeed, we spent our youth on these things; but when we approached pastoral care, we resolved to renounce them.”]

## 2.

Thus, despising what lying Greece and poetic chatter always report about falsehood adorned with ornament, I devoted myself to learning what the purest sincerity of the Latin language and of apostolic men has proclaimed.

[Note: The printed editions read *authenticorum virorum* (“of authoritative men”). We have followed the Lobbes manuscript.] I set aside the Caballine spring and the two-peaked Parnassus; had I known the fountain of life, I believed it would lead not only to salvation but also to knowledge—namely, Jesus Christ, and him crucified (1 Cor. 2:2), placed as the cornerstone at the head of the Church (Matt. 21:42).

For although the ancient law does not forbid us to marry a foreign woman, nevertheless, unless she is lawfully taken after her head has first been shaved and her other superfluities have been cut away—not without mystery, as you know better—then we are compelled to fear the Syromast, Phinehas (Num. 25:7).

[Note: So the same manuscript reads. In the printed editions, *rescissis* (“cut off”) is found instead of *recisis*. Moreover, he calls Phinehas a *Syromastes*, that is, a “Syrian striker,” because he struck down a Syrian woman, or Midianite.]

Similarly, the golden or silver vessels were not commanded to the Jacobites [that is, to the Israelites, the sons of Jacob] to be stolen from Egypt so that they might remain in the same use among them, but so that, once the reprobate nation had been despoiled, the people of the Hebrews might be enriched by the same resources and afterward adorn the temple of the Lord.

[Note: The printed editions read *conderet* (“might build up”); the manuscript has the better reading, on whose authority we have soon inserted *ille* before *nequam*.]

That wicked servant in the Gospel was condemned to the sentence of eternal damnation because he preferred to bury the talent of understanding in the earth rather than devote it wholly to heaven (Matt. 25:28).

This comparison, as I think, teaches among other things that I, a sinner possessing only the very small talent of intelligence which I have obtained through God’s generosity, ought rather to sharpen it where Christ is seated at the right hand of God than entrust it to earthly vanity and thereafter gain nothing except empty wind, and that not without the greatest loss to my soul.

[Note: We would prefer to read *acuere* (“to sharpen”), so that the construction is: “I, a sinner, ought rather to sharpen—that is, to stir up—this small portion of intelligence … toward that place where Christ sits at the right hand of God, than to entrust it to earthly vanity,” etc.]

## 3.

But to whom am I saying these things, and for what purpose? Let idle loquacity at last be silent; let rusticity, at least excused, at last yield to refinement.

For this reason, difficulty prevented me from taking up any book except this one,

[Note: This book, which he sent to Rotbertus, is the *Agonisticus*, or the books of the *Praeloquia*, as we learn from Fulcuinus. See the *Admonition* prefixed to those books, no. 4.]

which I am sending to you, my lord, for your faithful reading and for your prompt return to me: for reading, so that you may correct whatever in it is inept; for returning, so that on my return I may have it as my companion.

Since I desire above all to place my confidence in your clemency, I beg you to notify me authoritatively concerning your service.

[Note: We have added *me* from our copy.]

For you should know that I am entirely ready, to the best of my ability, for everything you may wish to command.

But if you deign to grant to the destitution of my lowliness any prop of assistance, my Lord knows very well whom he ought therefore to hope will reward him.

[Note: The printed editions read *Destina*, and, shortly afterward, *prorogare*. The manuscript supplies the corrections. *Destina* is understood as a prop or support. He asks that any *destina* of assistance—that is, some support by which he might be sustained—be granted to the want of his lowliness, which was deprived of many resources and in need.] 

[Note: So the manuscript reads. The printed editions have *habere* (“to have”).]

We wish your splendor happiness and that you may graciously remember us to the very end; and we pray that he who is blessed throughout the ages may preserve your everlasting honor, for his own praise and glory. Amen.

[Note: We have added *Amen* from the manuscript.]

# LETTER IV. TO BRUNO

[Note: This letter was written by Ratherius to Bruno, son of Henry, king of Germany, and brother of Otto, likewise king and later emperor. Fulcuinus mentions it in chapter 20. Ratherius wrote it after he had again been driven from the see of Verona in 948 and, afflicted by complete poverty, sought to be summoned into Bruno’s service—or rather, he openly begged to be summoned by sending him the books of the *Praeloquia* together with this letter.

He was summoned by Bruno before Bruno was consecrated archbishop of Cologne—that is, before 953—as is clear from Rotgerus, *Life of the Archbishop*, no. 24, and from Fulcuinus, *Deeds of the Abbots of Lobbes*, chapter 22. Compare what we observed in the author’s *Life*, section 9, where we establish the date more fully.

This letter was first published by Jean Chapeauvillain in *Deeds of the Bishops of Tongeren*, vol. I, p. 186, from the Lobbes manuscript; Lucas Acherius later reprinted it from Chapeauvillain. We have received it after a more careful collation with the cited Lobbes manuscript, and from it we have supplied in the title the name Bruno, which was absent from the printed editions, as well as the word *probitate* in the first line of the letter.]

[Col. 0651C]

To his lord, a little servant; to the most worthy, the most unworthy; to Bruno: Ratherius sends service more faithful than that owed to the most faithful, together with continual prayers.

I am sending this little work to your lordship for examination, since I can find nothing more worthy in moral excellence, more distinguished in splendor, or sharper in intelligence—I mean, in sound understanding—among the men of our order.
