I am striving both to receive it back more correctly and, through it, to bring knowledge of myself to your nobility.

Thus, when you see in it, as it were, the outline of my character, you can judge very well what I, a barbarian,

[Note: *Barbarian* here means foreigner, or a person of another and unknown nation. Bruno was a Saxon by nationality, whereas Ratherius was a Belgian.]

may or may not be able to do in your service. If the work pleases you, then may its little servant, the executor of the work, also please you.

Nor should you disdain to inform me, after learning a little about me.

[Note: It seems that the following is understood: “if this little servant, the executor of the work, is worth anything.” He asks that Bruno learn and indicate whether he might be of some use in his service. Perhaps, among the thousands of more distinguished men who served Bruno—for he supported many learned men and teachers—this little servant, Ratherius, might also obtain a place. He did obtain the first place, as Fulcuinus reports in chapter 22: “Ratherius is summoned and is held first among the palace philosophers.”]

For perhaps, among the thousands of more distinguished men, he too will obtain his place.

You may also, if you wish, acquire him for your service. I have heard that avarice is very far removed from you, while you possess those worthy manners which divine providence has always rightly sought among the wealthy of this world.

Therefore, removing all difficulty, exercise your power,

[Note: Acherius corruptly has the final word.]

knowing that I eagerly desire this.

For my prescient mind seems almost to foresee that, through your splendor, my destitution will be relieved. Only may I be able to render a service worthy and appropriate to your lordship: faithful to your honor in all things as your little client, and in every respect your most trustworthy commendatory servant.

[Note: We have supplied from the Lobbes manuscript the words “faithful to your honor,” which the printed editions omitted, marking a lacuna. In the manuscript alone, *fidelitas* (“faithfulness”) was read instead of *fidelis ad* (“faithful to”). Shortly afterward, perhaps one should read *proprius commendatus* instead of *commendator*: that is, one who commends himself to someone’s protection and binds his service to him. See the note on Book One of the *Praeloquia*, where *commendatus* is used in the same sense.]

May it also come to pass, through his desire and our prayer, that he who granted your beautiful character the distinction of flourishing in royal lineage may deign to advance it so far that, both in the clergy of the present age, everything may be entirely beneath you, and in the future nothing may be found above you among them.

[Note: The manuscript supplies the conjunction *et* both here and before the words referring to the future.]

I have appended no verses here, as some customarily do; believe me, I am not a poet, although I am not wholly unaware of the rules of poetry. For I have always embraced a more expansive mode of expression, avoiding, out of hatred for obscurity, a more compressed style.

# 531–532. ADMONITION ON THE THREE FOLLOWING LETTERS

## I.

The three following letters will be presented here in the same order in which they occur in the Lobbes manuscript, the only manuscript that transmitted them to us. From it the fifth and seventh letters were first published by Jean Chapeauvillain [vol. I of *Deeds of the Bishops of Tongeren*], and afterward by Acherius [vol. I of the new edition of the *Spicilegium*]; the sixth was published by Fathers Martène and Durand [vol. IX of the *Collection of Ancient Writers*].

The fifth letter had also been inserted by Fulcuinus into the *Deeds of the Abbots of Lobbes*, chapter 19; but only its beginning was found in Fulcuinus’s Lobbes manuscript, as is also read in the printed *Deeds*.

All these letters were written at the same time and with the same purpose, as the similar statements contained in all of them suggest. Ratherius repeatedly presents himself as having been expelled from the bishopric of Verona, as another person having been intruded into his see, as abandoned in every respect, and as contemplating the solitude of a monastery.

Yet he indicates that he was diverted from this plan by the objections of certain people. Unless he answered them in a canonical judgment, he would be judged criminal or a fugitive.

Accordingly, abandoning his plan of returning to monastic solitude, he requests a canonical judgment: in the fifth letter, from the pope; in the seventh, from the bishops. He asks that it be decided whether he or his rival is the legitimate bishop of Verona. Since he saw that a Roman judgment would proceed more quickly, in the sixth letter he implores the assistance of all Christian faithful so that he may undertake the journey to Rome.

It may be inferred from note 1337 on Letter VI that he wrote these letters in Germany, to which he had withdrawn.

## II.

The time or year in which they were written presents a difficulty. Letter V to Pope John is said in the margin of Acherius’s edition to have been sent to John XIII. This cannot in any way be correct, since reliable documents make clear that Ratherius had already been restored to his church under John XII.

Indeed, in the *Itinerary* composed under Pope John XIII, no. 4, he himself says that he was restored to his see by the command of the apostolic ruler who was then presiding over the Roman see. By the adverb “then,” he indicates that the pope at whose command he had been restored had already died.

John XI cannot be intended, since the letter itself mentions matters belonging to the year 941, long after John XI’s death.

Thus there can be no doubt that the heading of the letter should read “to John XII.” Some think that the letter should be assigned to approximately the year 956, when he began his pontificate; others assign it to 961 or 962, shortly before Ratherius was restored to his see.

Those who assign it to 961 or 962 are forced to emend the text of the letter, no. 1, where the author says that he had suffered calamities for twenty years already; they think “thirty” should be read instead.

Unless something from another source compels us, we do not think that the manuscript reading “twenty,” which is also the reading of the printed editions, should be abandoned.

## III.

They object on the basis of the following words of the letter, no. 8:

“Afterward, when an interval of time had passed, and our most glorious and most pious king, celebrated throughout the whole world, had entered Italy, I was present with his illustrious son, attempting, if the opportunity were granted, to be restored to my own place.”

They think these words must be understood of Otto I’s second arrival in Italy in 961. They suppose that in the following year, 962, Ratherius came with his son Otto II and, taking advantage of this opportunity, wrote the letter to John XII. Through Otto’s intervention and the council later held at Pavia, he is thought to have obtained restoration.

They refer this also to another testimony of Ratherius in the *Itinerary*, no. 4, where he states that, through the mercy of the most pious Caesar and by the command of the apostolic ruler who then presided over the Roman see, he was restored synodally by the judgment of the bishops.

But we are entirely certain that the quoted passage of the letter must be understood not of Otto’s second entry into Italy but of his first, in 951; and that the son of Otto with whom Ratherius was present was not Otto II but Duke Liutulf.

For this purpose, we must consider what immediately follows in the same letter:

“But it prevented this that the king found another man instituted there, namely the little grandson of Milo . . . . . to whom Manasses had sold the see.”

Here the reference is to Milo, bishop and grandson of Count Milo, to whom Manasses had sold the bishopric. That this Milo held the see of Verona in 951 is clear from a document of the Church of St. Stephen, which John Baptist Perettus saw [*Catalogue of the Bishops of Verona*, p. 61].

In that year, 951, King Otto and his son Liutulf came to Italy. Otto II, however, did not come in 962, as they suppose, but only in 967, when Ratherius had already long since been restored to the bishopric of Verona.

Nor do documents from the year 962 establish Otto II’s arrival in Italy in that year. In them, the first year of Otto the emperor and of Otto his son, king in Italy, is recorded.

For when Otto the father undertook his second journey to Italy toward the autumn of 961, he did not take his young son Otto with him but entrusted him to the care of William, archbishop of Mainz, as the Continuator of Regino and the Saxon Annalist report.

Those documents prove only that when Otto the father ascended to the imperial dignity in 962, he arranged for his son Otto—whom he had secured as king-elect of Germany in the preceding year—to be proclaimed king of Italy as well, although absent.

If, therefore, that testimony in the letter is to be understood of Otto’s first arrival in Italy and of his son Liutulf, nothing here forces us to assign the letter to the year 962.

Indeed, in the same letter, in the same section 8, it is added that, although Ratherius had come to Italy on that occasion to recover his bishopric, he did not obtain restoration but rather had to yield to royal majesty. This does not fit Otto’s second arrival, during which Ratherius was actually restored.

## IV.

Since the year 951 does not accord with the letter’s heading to John XII, who was promoted to the Roman see only in 956—and since Liutulf, Otto’s son, came to Italy again in that year to expel Berengar II from the Italian kingdom—others interpret the quoted passage of the letter not of Liutulf’s first arrival but of this later one.

They therefore suppose that Ratherius, driven from the see of Liège, came to Italy with Otto’s son only in 956.

They think this journey to Italy after his expulsion from the bishopric of Liège can be proved from Fulcuinus, who says in chapter 24:

“After spending nearly two years in this abandonment of his” [that is, after that expulsion], “Ratherius returned to Italy . . . . .”

Since he found Milo bishop in the see of Verona, and Milo prevented Ratherius’s restoration through Liutulf’s assistance, they think that Ratherius appealed to the judgment of the newly elected John XII in this letter. For that reason, they suppose that he wrote it after twenty years of his calamities, counting from his captivity in 935.

## V.

We cannot agree with this opinion.

For in the quoted passage of the letter Ratherius does not say that he went to Italy only with Otto’s son. Rather, he says: “when our king had entered Italy, I was present with his son,” and so forth.

Nor does he assert that he was prevented from recovering the bishopric because of that son, but because the king himself found another person instituted there.

Therefore both the father, the king, and the son had come to Italy when Ratherius hastened there.

Thus the testimony of the letter, which we have seen must be understood of Liutulf, belongs to the arrival of 951, when both were in Italy.

We have demonstrated in section 13 of the author’s *Life* that Fulcuinus’s words contain some error and must be explained in another sense.

Nothing, therefore, supports assigning Ratherius’s journey to Italy to the year 956; on the contrary, his journey cannot be excluded from the year 951.

But can the letter to John XII also be assigned to that year, when he had not yet begun his pontificate?

## VI.

Before expressing our opinion on this matter, we must especially observe that the letter contains certain details which plainly require a date earlier than 956.

First, in section 5 Ratherius says:

“Berengar seized me at the instigation of Manasses, the most holy archbishop, and the man who lawfully holds the place of Ambrose.”

He says “holds,” not “held.” Clearly, therefore, he assumes that Manasses was still occupying the see of Milan when he wrote this.

But Manasses had left that see in 953.

Moreover, in section 7 he says that this same Manasses presided over several bishoprics but benefited no one. This cannot fit any year after 953, as will be shown in the note.

Second, in section 8, speaking of Milo, the bishop who was the grandson of Count Milo and who had already been ordained bishop of Verona in 951, he addresses the supreme pontiff as follows:

“But the supporters of this kind of ordination boast that they received permission from the apostolate of your lordship.”

Later he says that he yielded to the apostolic authority and attributed to the divine disposition what that same pontiff had done. He adds:

“I believe that your fatherhood neither wished nor dared to grant anyone permission to do anything against the canonical law.”

These words plainly appear to have been written to the pontiff who presided over the apostolic see when Milo was ordained, and whose permission for this ordination Milo’s supporters therefore claimed.

At that time—namely, around the time of Milo’s ordination in 951—not John XII but Agapetus II held the Roman see. He had been raised to it in 946 and died in 956.

Third, in section 9 he adds that he had respected this apostolic disposition, by which Milo appeared to have been established in the see of Verona, and had considered returning to his monastery. But, he says, taking care lest he be judged

“not indeed uncalled, but challenged, to wish to evade judgment by hiding away,”

he prostrates himself at the feet of the apostolate and says:

“I wish to hear which of us two is the bishop, since one church cannot admit two men sitting as bishops.”

From this point to the end of the letter, while imploring the judgment of that same pontiff, he proceeds in such a way as to appear to be seeking the judgment of the pontiff who was said to have granted permission for Milo’s ordination.

These circumstances fit the time when Ratherius came to Italy with Liutulf under Agapetus II and found Milo already ordained.

The same period—namely, the end of 951 or the beginning of 952—also fits more strictly the twenty years already begun during which he declares in section 1 that he had been wearied by every kind of calamity.

For in section 5 he says that from the beginning of his episcopate, that is, from 932, he had suffered many things from King Hugh; and similarly, in section 1, he says:

“From the very day of my ordination I was appointed to the destruction which I now lament.”

The whole context of the fifth letter therefore agrees most suitably with the year 951 or 952.

## VII.

The context and sequence of events in the other letters, VI and VII, which were written together, demand the same date even more strongly.

Nothing narrated in those letters is later than 951 or 952.

The last event they report is the following: after his second expulsion, which occurred in 948, Ratherius returned from Germany, where he had withdrawn, to Italy in 951 in order to recover his bishopric. Finding Milo in the episcopal see, he abandoned hope of recovering the bishopric.

At first he was thinking of returning to the solitude of a monastery, and with this plan he returned to Germany. But after hearing the objections of certain people, who claimed that he had been justly deprived of the bishopric, he decided that he must abandon his plan of going to the monastery and appeal to the Roman pontiff and to all the bishops. He also decided to ask the Christians for charitable assistance in undertaking the journey to Rome.

Are these events not known to have occurred immediately in the year 951, or at the beginning of 952, when he discovered that every hope of recovering the bishopric had been cut off?

Moreover, in Letter VI he says that, after finally leaving Italy, he found nowhere any rest or hospitality, nowhere any assistance except in places of mercy, and he indicates in Letter V, section 2, that these places were German bishoprics.

He also clearly implies that, having been diverted from his plan of returning to solitude, he did not go to a monastery and found no settled residence anywhere.

These circumstances are utterly incompatible with the year 956, and still more with 962. For before 956 he was received by Bruno and lived with him for some time; afterward he held the see of Liège for a year or more; and finally, after being expelled from it, he was placed in charge of a monastery so that he might have a means of livelihood.

If, however, the year 951 or 952 is assumed, both the context of all the letters and the sequence of events agree perfectly.

## VIII.

Only the heading of the fifth letter presents an obstacle, since it ought to be said to have been given not to Pope John but to Agapetus.

What, then, should be thought?

Since the strongest considerations arising from the context and history of the letters require the year 951 or 952 under Agapetus II, and since the heading of the fifth letter cannot be rejected even though it is supported by only one example, the Lobbes manuscript, which gives “John”—

[Note: In Fulcuinus’s manuscript, which preserves the beginning of this letter, the pope’s name is absent; it was likewise omitted in the printed editions.]

—it is permissible only to suspect and conjecture that this letter was indeed written together with the other two in 951, or at the beginning of 952, to Agapetus II. But when every hope of obtaining anything had vanished, it was suppressed at that time and later addressed to John XII in 956 or 957, when, at the beginning of his pontificate, after Liutulf had returned victorious to Italy, hope of recovering Ratherius’s see was raised; or at least in 961, when news had arrived of Otto’s return to the same Italy to defeat Berengar and be crowned emperor by John XII.

It is especially strange that Ratherius, although changing the heading, changed nothing in the text of the letter itself and added none of the events that happened to him after 952.

Hence it may be doubted whether this letter was actually sent to John XII; and regarding the other two, it is no less uncertain whether they were sent to the persons to whom they are addressed.

Compare the end of section 9 of the author’s *Life*. We have received a very careful and useful collation of these three letters with the Lobbes manuscript.

# 537. LETTER V. TO JOHN, SUPREME PONTIFF

To the supreme pontiff of the first—that is, Roman—see, the most reverend lord patriarch John: Ratherius, sinner and exile.

## 1.

Casting before the feet of your fatherhood this small condition of my lowliness, wearied for twenty years now by every kind of calamity,

[Note: Some think that “thirty” should be read. But that the manuscript reading should not be abandoned will be shown by the preceding *Admonition*, sections 2 and 6.]

and most unhappily rolled from the shores of childhood to the shores of old age through innumerable reefs of misery, I beg you, most reverend lord, archbishop of archbishops, and—if this may rightly be said of any mortal—one who should be called universal pope, for the love of the Almighty, to receive patiently and kindly the complaint of my miseries and, even if late, to assist me in the stead of him whose see you occupy for this reason: that you may not permit the gates of hell to prevail against the Church (Matt. 16:18), insofar as you are able to resist them with the help of God himself.

But if you ask about the person who complains, cries out, and screams under the pressure of anguish, I am he—I, my lord, am that most wretched man who, given to the Veronese as bishop, was, on the very day of my appointment, if I may speak neither improperly nor absurdly, destined for the destruction which I now lament.

In persecuting me, almost the whole world conspired in such a way that I, most wretched and deprived of the assistance even of all my relatives, have very often seemed to myself to find no one so just who was not most unjust toward me; no one so generous who was not most grasping; no one so pious who was not cruel;

[Note: The words “who was not cruel,” as well as “who was so submissive to others through humility,” were omitted in the printed editions and have been inserted from the Lobbes manuscript. After several words, we have likewise written *a summo* (“from the highest”) from the same manuscript, where the printed editions read *e summo*.]

no one so submissive to others through humility who did not seem to me another Tarquin; no one so truthful who deigned to speak to me even a single word of truth in his promise—from the highest rank of nobility down to the lowest condition of servitude.

## 2.

But if anyone can be excepted, let the Germans be excepted,

[Note: After his second expulsion from the see of Verona, Ratherius withdrew to Germany, where he obtained some assistance from the German bishops.]

and among them only the bishops—and that with the greatest difficulty, since iniquity abounded and charity grew cold (Matt. 24:12). For, as I think, if they conferred any benefit on me, they acted out of fear of that statement in the decretal letter of Pope Alexander (Letter II), where he says:

“Whoever from your college withdraws himself from the assistance of those bishops—namely, bishops who have been abandoned—shall be judged not a priest but a schismatic.”

## 3.

I am he, my lord, I, whom Greece can report to the East and Spain to the West to have seen pale with sadness or blush with shame; I am he whom it shames to be seen everywhere and called by everyone a wandering gyrovague.

Let someone wonder how what was a song to all could have remained concealed from your apostolate.

This also adds to the burden of my condemnation, deserved on account of my sins: I have never been able to find an intercessor either at your most sacred see or among any prince or powerful man.

But just as Paul once appealed to Caesar (Acts 25:11), so I appealed to the Roman see.

[Note: While writing the fourth book of the *Praeloquia* in the prison at Pavia, he sought especially the judgment of the Roman see, section 4. In the following letter also, he implored the assistance of the faithful for the journey to Rome which he was planning to undertake, so that he might be judged by the supreme pontiff.]

But, to clarify briefly what I have touched upon, and as concisely as I can:

At the request of Notger, bishop of blessed memory, who, as we think, was seeking better things, the episcopal see was given to my lord Hilduin by right of stipend, while the king’s promise remained in force—

[Note: He says “by right of stipend” because Hilduin, having been expelled from the bishopric of Liège, was substituted by King Hugh, his relative, for Notger, or Notherius, in the bishopric of Verona—not so that he might remain there permanently, but so that he might meanwhile receive the revenues of that bishopric until, as soon as a more worthy see became vacant, he could be promoted to it.]

—that when an opportunity arose to promote him to a higher position, I would be given as bishop to those who requested me.

When he had been enthroned at Milan,

[Note: Hilduin was advanced from the see of Verona to that of Milan through Hugh’s efforts in the year 931.]

then, as worldly instability often contains the instability of its own fickleness, the king decided far otherwise than he had promised. For, as rumor had it, he preferred to enthrone one of three men: either a certain Aquitanian, or a certain Garafridus, or Manasses, archbishop of Arles, contrary to the right of the canons.

[Note: So the Lobbes manuscript reads. The printed editions have “against the law.” These words, “contrary to the right of the canons,” refer to Manasses, archbishop of Arles; if he held the see of Verona together with the see of Arles, as later happened, this would be contrary to the decrees of the canons.]

## 4.

While these matters were in progress, I returned from the Roman see after completing my embassy, carrying the privilege issued for my aforesaid lord,

[Note: “Privilege” means the confirmation of the Roman see, which the archbishops of Milan in particular were required to obtain together with the pallium.]

together with the archiepiscopal pallium.

Letters from the lord pope John, a man of glorious character at that time, were also brought with these. They contained his prayers, and those of the whole Roman Church, that I should be given as bishop to the Veronese.

[Note: This was John XI, who ascended to the apostolic see in 931. Although he was already dead, Ratherius calls him a pope of glorious character. Some have wrongly designated him a pseudo-pope or intruder, contrary to the judgment of the Church, which counts him among the legitimate successors of Peter.]

The king was greatly displeased by this, since he was working toward the opposite; but the apostolic petition prevailed, with my aforesaid lord, together with the leading men of the kingdom, earnestly pressing the request.

I was lying almost half-dead, seriously ill. I think that people who were devoted to me persuaded the king that I would not survive.

Led on by this hope, he consented, eager to satisfy both the lord pope and the others whom it seemed improper to offend when they were making their request.

I recovered from the illness; I was ordained.

He became extremely angry and swore by God—and he did not lie—that throughout the days of his life I would not rejoice over that ordination.

Therefore he sent in a little document

[Note: These small sheets or brief booklets, on which something was written, were called *pitacia* or *pittacia*. In this little document Hugh declared the amount of the stipend that he granted Ratherius from the revenues of the church of Verona, and he required him to swear that he would demand nothing more so long as Hugh and his son Lothair, who had been raised to the kingship, lived. Since Ratherius did not agree to this, it became the source of the discord which he described in Book Four of the *Praeloquia*, section 20.]

a fixed amount of the stipend which I was to hold from the property of the church, demanding from me an oath that I would not seek anything more during his lifetime or that of his son.

Understanding what great absurdity would follow from this, I did not consent.

What more can I say? He brought in persecutors and adversaries from every side, who would either frighten me so that I fled, or provoke me so that I might commit an offence against him, and so that he might find an occasion to expel me.

He found one.

[Note: When Ratherius, together with Count Milo, received Arnold, duke of Bavaria, into Verona, Hugh seized this as an opportunity to expel him. After Arnold had been driven out and Verona recovered, Hugh ordered that the bishop, as a rebellious captive, be brought to the tower at Pavia, which shortly afterward is called Walbert’s little tower—perhaps after Walbert, a powerful judge of Pavia, who, after conspiring against Hugh, was captured and beheaded, as Liutprand reports in *History*, Book III, chapters 10 and 11.]

He seized me and shut me in custody in a certain little tower at Pavia. I do not say that this was without any fault of mine—for whoever does not offend even in speech amid such circumstances is a perfect man (Jas. 3:2)—but he acted against the law and without a hearing.

Let each person say what he wishes; for, according to Augustine (Sermon 46, no. 27), everything is full of rash judgments.

But I confess that from the time I first saw him until he cast off the human condition, I always wished for him the imperial good fortune of Theodosius, and even now the memory of him weighs heavily upon me with grief.

### 5

For two and a half years, unless my memory deceives me, I endured the earlier persecution [Note: He calls that the “earlier persecution” which Hugo, from the beginning of his episcopate, as he wrote above, directed everywhere through persecutors and adversaries, who either frightened me so that I would flee or provoked me so that I would overstep against him, thereby giving him an opportunity to expel me.], and for an equal length of time imprisonment as punishment; released from there, I entered an exile of equal duration [Note: Namely, the exile to which he was banished at Como.]. But when, by God’s mercy, I had been freed from it against his will, while he, by God’s justice, had been deprived of the honor of ruling, I resolved to approach him [Note: Ratherius, now freed from exile, wished to approach Hugo—not, while at Como, where he had been an exile, fleeing from there against Hugo’s will at the end of 939 or the beginning of 940, but when Hugo had been deprived of the honor of ruling in 945.] and to console his calamity by my service throughout all his days. For someone had not failed to inform me—late, indeed, as I fear, and I pray that God avert it from him—that, often repentant, he had wished that God would grant that I come to him, and that, if he had the power, he might obtain my restoration; or, if not, that he might give me enough money so that I would no longer be in want.

I was coming, when Berengar arrested me [Note: Since Ratherius was arrested by Berengar, margrave of Ivrea, who under King Lothair, Hugo’s son, exercised supreme authority in Italy, he must be said to have been captured in that region subject to Berengar’s power. He had undertaken his journey intending to approach Hugo, not in Provence, where Hugo had first withdrawn, but in Italy, to which Hugo returned in 946 in order, if possible, to recover the kingdom. He was arrested, moreover, at the instigation of Manasses, who occupied the church of Verona and feared that, once Manasses had been excluded, Ratherius might be restored to that church.] at the instigation of the most holy archbishop Manasses [Note: He ironically calls Manasses “the most holy archbishop,” and the one who rightfully holds the place of Ambrose, since, through Berengar’s influence, he obtained the see of Milan in 948 and still held it when Ratherius wrote this.], who rightfully occupies the place of Ambrose.

Held again in custody for three and a half months [Note: We have added the adverb “again” from the Lobbes manuscript and Chapeauvill’s edition. He is said to have been held in custody again because previously he had been imprisoned for two and a half years in the tower at Pavia.], then released, brought to Verona, and received there deceitfully by Milo [Note: Milo was count of Verona and initially supported Arnold against Hugo. Although he was later reconciled with Hugo and governed Verona, after subsequently supporting Berengar he feared that Manasses—who occupied the Veronese episcopate and, equally favorable to Berengar, had harmed Hugo—might, moved by repentance, help his uncle, the king. If Hugo recovered the kingdom in Italy through Manasses’ assistance, Milo would suffer loss.]—supposedly so that he might expel Manasses, lest, moved by repentance, Manasses should help the uncle whom, as is said, he had greatly harmed.

### 6

If I attempt to recount the martyrdom that I endured for two years through the schemes of that same Milo, you may think it a history. To sum it up as briefly as possible: with him himself defending all the clergy, nobles, tenants, and servants against me, I did not dare to hold a synod, attend the chapter of the clergy, or even mention anything that needed correction; I could nowhere establish anything whatsoever or remove anyone; I could say nothing that he might wish to know without his immediately knowing it, for I believe he had extorted an oath to that effect from everyone. [Note: Ratherius calls these people in Book III of the *Praeloquia*, no. 22, “free laborers and slaves” and “soldiers of the kingdom”; here he calls them “soldiers, tenants, and servants.” The soldiers are understood to be nobles. See the note at that passage. Tenants (*coloni*) were peasants attached to the cultivation of the land, but not properly slaves, as the servants were. His further statement—“I dared neither hold a synod nor attend the chapters of the clergy”—is to be understood of the synods and chapters held during visitations of the churches of the diocese, as we have shown more fully in the author’s *Life*, §8, no. 37. This also explains why on this occasion he mentions not only clergy but also soldiers, tenants, and servants.]

And when all his men slandered me before him, he alone acted as though he were on my side against them all, so that, provoked, they would report even greater accusations. You might therefore have thought him another Antipater, son of the wicked Herod; for it was not within my power or permission to do anything good or bad. [Note: The printed editions read *non enim boni aliquid malive agere* (“for it was not within my power to do anything good or bad”).]

Even what I did at his command [Note: The common text reads *aiebam* (“I was saying”), but *agebam* (“I was doing”) is preferable.]—for I did not dare oppose his orders—he turned into a fault, secretly fabricating an accusation against me among the clergy, while deceitfully promising me sufficient vengeance against them.

This went so far that one day, while I was performing the ecclesiastical offices [Note: This should not be understood as the conferral of sacred orders, but as some sacred and solemn function, as we have established in the author’s *Life*, §8, where this passage is explained.], the archdeacon went out with the entire clergy, leaving me alone in the church, and claimed another church for himself against me.

O times! O morals! O public conspiracy against canon law! O, if I may put it so, abomination of desolation! O word spoken in Israel, so that whoever hears it will rightly have both ears tingle! (Jer. 19:3.) The archbishop of Arles, laying snares for the bishop of Verona, consecrated a certain bishop of his own diocese to the title of the Church of Verona. Who would not marvel? Who would not be astonished? Where was what is lawful? Where was the law? Where was secular [understand: law] distributing to each province its fixed boundaries, immutably assigning them? Where was the regard of the One who sees all things? Where was: “You shall not move the ancient boundary which your fathers have set”? (Prov. 22:28.)

Those who do not know how far Verona lies from the land of Arles do not understand that this applies here. Where was what the law says (Callistus, Letter II, 24): “If any metropolitan should attempt to act in anything except what pertains solely to his own parish [Note: Thus the Lobbes manuscript reads, agreeing also with the wording of the pseudo-letter of Callistus. Acherius has *quodammodo* (“in some way”).], he shall be exposed to the danger of his rank”? And where should the archdeacon [probably: archbishop], not exceeding what the canons prescribe for him, hold his appointed place with humility?”

But these things concern those who are archbishops of a single see. As for one who is allowed to preside over five bishoprics, yet benefit none, what could he not be permitted to do? [Note: Manasses is being censured here. He had held five bishoprics—Arles, Verona, Mantua, Trent, and finally Milan—as can be gathered from Liutprand. Since the passage indicates that, when Ratherius wrote this, Manasses still presided over several bishoprics while benefiting none, it fits the year 952. In that year, although he had previously sold the bishopric of Verona to Milo, Manasses held four other bishoprics. It does not fit the later years, since in 953, whether voluntarily or unwillingly, he resigned the archbishopric of Milan, went to Gaul, and appears to have retained only the see of Arles until his death.]

Although Milo was the instigator and author of all these things, he nevertheless sought to be seen and called my advocate and protector. Thus he afflicted me with such cunning that scarcely anyone in the kingdom failed to think him entirely my friend. But I was wretched, so exhausted and anxious day and night that I was weary of my life; and I would rather have sat, as once before, in Walbert’s little tower [Note: He says that he would rather hunger under Hugo because, in Walbert’s tower—or the tower at Pavia—in which he had been detained for two years and more, he endured hunger among his many hardships.] than sit in the Veronese cathedral, hungry under Hugo, rather than feast with Milo.

### 7

After enduring this for two years—the most grievous prison of all the miseries I had suffered before and afterward—while I was going to celebrate the evening service, a messenger of our lord King Lothair appeared and ordered me to leave the city and make way for Manasses to invade my see. He added a sufficiently friendly [that is, amicable] piece of advice: it would be better for me to withdraw than to be dismembered or killed through Milo’s treachery, or—or what would be much lighter than these but would be most grievous to me—to be captured and taken wherever I least wished to go.

I refrain, although I could, from accusing some unfortunate man, lest I add to his wounds some pain which the prophet forbids one to add by lamenting over him (Ps. 68:27). [Note: Acherius reads: “Although I can, I refrain from accusing anyone, nor will I add anything.” We have preferred the reading of the Lobbes manuscript. The unfortunate man whose pains Ratherius avoids increasing may be the same Count Milo, a supporter of Berengar II, who at this time—perhaps in 951 or 952—may have suffered some grave setback at Otto’s hands, when Otto expelled Berengar from almost all Italy.]

What more is there? I did, because ordered, what earlier I would most gladly have done without being ordered, had the Lord not forbidden it when he spoke in the Gospel about the hireling (John 10:12). But I could not do it with impunity. Those wolves [Note: The wolves who attacked Ratherius seem to be Manasses, for whom he had been ordered to make way, and perhaps also the man whom Manasses consecrated bishop to the title of the Church of Verona.] were not seeking to attack the flock but the shepherd; and although pursued in one city, I could lawfully flee to another.

### 8

After some time had passed, when our most glorious and most devout king, celebrated throughout the whole world [Note: King Otto is meant. The word “had entered” refers to his first entry into Italy, which occurred in 951. Consequently, the son of Otto who was with Ratherius in Italy was not Otto II but Liudolf, as we established more fully in the preceding Admonition.], had entered Italy, I appeared with his illustrious son, trying to see whether an opportunity might be given for me to be restored to my position.

But this was prevented by the fact that the king found another man installed there, namely Milo’s young nephew [Note: This was the nephew of Count Milo, who in 951 held the bishopric of Verona, as we learn from documents cited by Giovanni Battista Peretto. The author calls him “a young nephew” because he was a youth of about eighteen years. He had been born after Ratherius had been consecrated bishop of Verona, as is clear from Letter VIII to that same Milo.], so that it is not difficult to conjecture for what reason he inflicted such evils upon me. Manasses had sold the see to him [Note: Liutprand also reports this in Book IV, chapter 3.]; but the supporters of this appointment boast that they received permission for it from the apostolic authority of your lordship [Note: In the preceding Admonition we have shown that this applies to Agapetus II, not John XII. The permission said to have been granted by the apostolic see may perhaps refer to a dispensation on account of Milo’s age, since as a youth he could not, according to the canons, be promoted to the episcopate.].

Therefore, believing that it would be safer to yield both to your apostolic authority and to his royal majesty than to criticize whatever you might decree, I had resolved—freed by God’s mercy from prisons and exiles and brought out into the breadth of free choice [Note: Acherius printed *et latitudinem* (“and breadth”), while the latest editor of the *Spicilegium* thought *adeptus* (“having attained”) should be read instead of *eductus*. But the correction to *in latitudinem*, inserted on the authority of the Lobbes manuscript, leaves no reason to alter *eductus*.]—to seek the solitude of a monastery and there await God, who would save me from faintness of spirit and the tempest of persecutors (Ps. 54:9); and, repenting, to exact from myself the causes of my expulsion, judging myself so that I would not be judged, and believing that what you had decreed had been decreed by God. For the supreme pontiff ought to be censured by no one, and the heart of a king is in the hand of God (Prov. 21:1).

These two things, I believe, admonish both men: the former—that is, the pontiff—not to do what deserves censure; the latter—that is, the king—not to remove his heart from the hand of God, that is, from God’s governance, in arranging the necessities of the kingdom, if he wishes rightly to be a king rather than merely to be called one.

I believe that your fatherhood neither wished nor dared to give anyone permission to do anything against canon law. I believe that he [the king] sought the Italian kingdom under no other compulsion than to compel, by imperial power, a kingdom distorted by many volumes of injustices—such as this and other disorders—back into conformity with Christian law. [Note: Beware of inferring from the phrase “by imperial power” that Otto I had already been raised to the imperial dignity when this was written, or when, on entering Italy, he found Milo bishop of Verona, and therefore that this letter was written much later than we believe. Ratherius never calls Otto “emperor” or “Caesar” in this letter, although in his other works written after Otto began his imperial rule he consistently does so; here he calls him only king. The adjective “imperial” can also be applied to a king, as is clear from Book III of the *Praeloquia*, no. 22, where the author, though addressing a king while there was then no emperor, says: “They are of your imperial jurisdiction.” Ratherius was right to write that Otto had sought the Italian kingdom under no other compulsion than to compel a kingdom distorted … back into conformity with Christian law by imperial power, because Otto obtained the kingdom of Italy in 951, before ceding it to Berengar under certain conditions at the Diet of Augsburg in 952. Hence documents survive from 951 and the beginning of 952 in which Otto’s first year as king in Italy is recorded. See the *Collectio diplomatum canonicorum de Dionysiis*, pp. 117, 118, and 120, and Muratori, *Annali d’Italia*, under the year 951, pp. 375 and 377.]

### 9

I had resolved, then, as I began to say, to seek the monastery in such a condition of release. But, thinking again about what rank I ought also to have there—whether that of bishop, priest, some other order, or no order at all—for perhaps one of those arrogant men who habitually speak in their hearts, as even this publican does, will say that I ought not to be admitted even with good laymen to the public station of the church [Note: Acherius reads: “who ought not be admitted even with good men.” The latest editor of the *Spicilegium* emended this to: “who ought not to be admitted even with good laymen.” We have preferred the reading of Chapeauvill, which the Lobbes manuscript also exhibits.]; while, conversely, another, more worthy by as much as he has been worn down by punishment, may say so—the mind, wavering among these possibilities, does not know to which it should give assent.

Afterward, receiving through a truthful and unexpected report that my rivals were bringing certain charges against me, on account of which they claimed that I should be deprived not by force but by right of the priestly ministry, I feared lest my surrender or patience should become the deposition of someone else, present or future, from his proper dignity. For the posterity of the old Adam is always inclined toward worse things, and since there is no one to stand as a wall for the house of Israel, standing for battle on the day of the Lord (Ezek. 13:5), it must be feared that, through this permission, the serpent may make a future wound far worse, like fire which, licking up a little straw, burns down great cities when it is not extinguished through negligence. [Note: We have added “it must be feared” from the Lobbes manuscript.]

I also took care not to seem, according to the statement of that man in the decretals, to confess myself guilty by fleeing from judgment: “It is manifest that he confesses himself guilty who, being canonically summoned, avoids judgment.” I judged that, although not summoned, I had been challenged, and that by hiding I might seem to wish to evade judgment. I cast myself at the feet of your apostolic authority and wish to hear which of us two is bishop, since one church does not admit two seated bishops.

If I am the bishop of Verona, then let it be so; if he is, my rejection ought not to be secret but public, lest the land of the church cry out against you, together with its furrows, because of a false report arousing the contrary suspicion, as Gregory says. [Note: The printed editions read “against us.” We corrected it from the same manuscript, and rightly so. He indicates that his removal from the episcopate ought to have been public, or established by public judgment; otherwise the Church would protest if the pontiff did not condemn a removal carried out without lawful judgment on the basis of private and false rumors.]

I also wish to learn from your fatherhood whether it can rightly appear to any Christian that a bishop may be deprived of his bishopric before the outcome of his case is known. For I, wretched and utterly inexperienced, have searched and reread many things on my own behalf, but nowhere have I been able to find this. If the fault is of such a kind, it seems more fitting that the man first be deprived of his office by degradation and afterward of his bishopric, lest the action appear to have been carried out not justly but out of hostility.

### 10

Therefore, lest I seem to be accused as a criminal or, when challenged, to be a fugitive, I ask for a hearing—I demand a hearing—and, together with the shepherd of all shepherds, boldly call the invader of my church a thief and robber (John 10:1), because he climbed in from elsewhere and did not enter through the door. For while the husband is alive, a woman is not permitted to marry another man [Note: We supplied the words “to marry another” from the Lobbes manuscript, which were absent from Acherius. The manuscript reads *non dimittitur* (“is not permitted”) rather than *non permittitur*.].

Before the apostolic authority of your see I challenge him to canonical contest, even on this condition, if it pleases your lordship: whether the law prevails for me or for him, grant the bishopric to whomever you deem fit, only in the Lord. For I no longer desire to preside if, as before, I am able to benefit no one.

### 11

I fear that my somewhat greater severity than was fitting, and my speech resembling an invective against my adversaries, may have offended the most sincere hearing of your fatherhood. But I ask that pardon be granted to my most afflicted weakness. For if you employ toward my misery a compassionate rather than disdainful disposition, the most prudent regard of your piety will be able to perceive that I have touched no other fault of theirs than the one that harms their service to me.

I call God to witness, most readily and solemnly, that I would rather have found in one the character of Probus, and in the other the character of Ambrose, than anything sinister to criticize, especially among the things I have endured. [Note: The comparison with the Emperor Probus suits King Hugo better than the simple count Milo. Since above, in no. 4, he touched Hugo more lightly and professed that, from the time he first saw him until he laid aside his human life, he had always wished for him the happiness of the Emperor Theodosius and still felt deep grief at his remembrance, while he brought much graver charges against Count Milo, these words in one case seem better understood of Milo, who was then still alive, rather than of Hugo, who had long been dead. There is no doubt that the words in the other case refer to Manasses, the successor of Saint Ambrose. Shortly afterward we corrected *caperem* (“I would take up”) to *carperem* (“I would criticize”) with the help of the Lobbes manuscript; the new edition of the *Spicilegium* had it incorrectly, although the same correction appears among its errata.]

But, to sum up briefly what I desire: either let me be proved to belong to the Veronese, or let me be no bishop at all. For it does not follow in any way that I am a universal bishop [Note: A universal bishop means one attached to no particular see, but a bishop indefinitely in the universal Church.], and I am weary of continuing either to err in this matter or to provide others with causes for error. I am even less able to remain unaware of how dangerous it is for a non-bishop to presume to perform episcopal functions, since every day I see that no layman at all presumes to celebrate Mass. [Note: Construe: “Since even the reasoning of infants, if they possess any, can sufficiently clearly grasp that one of us two is not a bishop …”]

That one of us two is not a bishop even the reasoning of infants, if they possess any, can sufficiently clearly grasp. But which of us it is, your pastoral care must determine; you cannot leave the matter unexamined without the greatest danger to yourselves, if I may dare to say so, since the controversy has arisen from this question.

## Letter VI. To All the Faithful

[Note: This title, “To All the Faithful,” is absent from the Lobbes manuscript, where only *Item* appears in place of a title; nevertheless it can be gathered sufficiently from the letter itself.]

I, the same wretched, most unfortunate, and most deceived man, abundantly sated with the figures and riddles of those who speak promises [Note: The common text reads *promissis loquiorum*. We have accepted the manuscript’s reading. Those who are *promissiloqui* are people who offer promises in words alone but lack deeds. Shortly afterward, where we have inserted *adhibere* (“to give credence”), the printed editions had *adhibens* (“giving credence”).], and now, far too late, forbidden by the instruction of experience to give them further credence, address all who wish to fulfill the law of Christ.

### 1

Deprived of the stewardship of the episcopate granted to me—that is, of the Veronese episcopate—and exposed to the pity of all good people, unable to dig, since I can no longer labor vainly as I have until now, lacking the denarius of recompense and deprived of every kind of income [Note: Construe: “Compelled to beg, which I have always been ashamed to do, whether because of the stigma of pride or because of confidence in recovery”—that is, recovery of the episcopate, since everything seemed bearable when compensated by the hope of enjoying it for at least one day, if that should be granted—“compelled, I say, to beg, finding no third course of action, that is, no middle way between the proceeds of labor and the attainment of the episcopate, I seek charity, if it exists anywhere, and so on.”], finding no third course of action, I have been compelled to seek charity, if it exists anywhere, and, repeating my cry, I beg that it look upon my calamity.

For nowhere is there any rest for me, even in lodging; nowhere any refuge, except among those places of mercy belonging to people in whose hearts the Gospel speaks: “When you give a dinner or a supper, invite the poor, and you will be blessed, because they have nothing with which to repay you; for you will be repaid at the resurrection of the just” (Luke 14:12).

The example of the rich miser must also be feared. He did not perceive why Lazarus had been permitted to lie before his door (Luke 16:20), and thus, though he could have obtained the greatest refreshment, he failed to prevent himself from kindling an unending fire. Because he did not give a compassionate hearing to the poor man’s cry, he experienced in himself the truth of the saying: “He who turns away his ear from the cry of the poor will himself cry out and not be heard” (Prov. 21:13).

And therefore, when the wretched man asked for a drop of water, he was not heard, because he had not given one; and in this the truthful advocate speaks thus: “He who turns away his ear so as not to hear the law—his prayer will be accursed” (Prov. 28:9).

Although the law belonged to the earlier age, it was given so that each person would do for another what he would wish another to do for himself; and the succeeding law, so that it might not suppress natural goodness in any respect, was given through the Decalogue: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind, and with all your strength, and your neighbor as yourself” (Matt. 22:37; Deut. 6:5; Lev. 19:18). [Note: The manuscript supplies the word “each.” The law given in the earlier age means the natural law. Shortly afterward the printed editions incorrectly read *catalogum*; the manuscript has *decalogum*, “Decalogue,” and we have also added “and with all your mind.”]

The third law, under grace, is this: “Bear one another’s burdens,” says he who was caught up even to the third heaven, “and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Gal. 6:2)—of Christ indeed, of Christ. For when someone asked him what the great commandment in the law was, after stating the first and greatest, he confirmed that the second was like it. And, in order also to separate his own from the others, he said: “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13:35).

### 2

“I love God,” says everyone when questioned, even the worst of all, even any tyrant. But, alas, brotherly hatred has today increased everywhere to such an extent that no class is more gloriously esteemed in the world than—alas for the wickedness!—that of murderers. [Note: The words “no class … in the world” are necessary to the sense and had fallen out of the printed editions.]

But, reclining upon the breast of the one who gave the commandment, he says: “If anyone says, ‘I love God,’ and hates his brother, he is a liar; for whoever does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?” (1 John 4:20). And: “Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3:15). And: “You know that every murderer has no share in the kingdom of Christ and of God” (Eph. 5:5).

“Everyone,” he says—everyone: that is, neither any of those whom I shortly before lamented as unhappily glorious [Note: The printed editions omit “unfortunate,” which is necessary here.], nor any hater of his brothers.

“I hate no Christian,” another says. Then you love everyone, for there is no third possibility. And this is the charity that the Apostle places even before martyrdom. Since I need it unspeakably [Note: The common text reads *incredibiliter* (“incredibly”); the manuscript has *indicibiliter* (“unspeakably”). Shortly afterward the printed editions incorrectly read *omnes* (“all”) instead of *omnesque* (“and all”).], nothing is sweeter to me than to hear that passage when it is read, and I would wish everyone to act accordingly: “Whoever has the substance of the world, and sees his brother in need, and closes his compassion against him—how does the charity of God remain in him?” (1 John 3:17). And elsewhere: “My little children, let us not love in word or tongue, but in deed and truth” (1 John 3:18).

And the psalmist says: “Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and the poor” (Ps. 40:2). After I read that blessed Gregory had described the modes of this understanding in the music of nine distinctions, I receive no less consolation when I find written in the works of blessed Aurelius Augustine, of revered memory: “Mercy is rightly owed to all the needy, but our compassionate feeling is especially stirred toward those who, from nobility and wealth, have fallen into the lowest condition.” Jerome agrees with this when he says that assistance should rather be given to those who are ashamed after receiving it.

But let the most sincere charity that I seek consider—moved by this thought, I myself beg—that the whole community of the pious should recognize how harsh and shameful it is for one who has undertaken the office of distributing aid to declare himself unworthy of assistance, and who, groaning no less inwardly than outwardly, can say in poverty: “All day long my shame is before me, and the confusion of my face has covered me” (Ps. 43:16); and likewise: “Have mercy on us, Lord, have mercy on us, for we are filled exceedingly with contempt; our soul is exceedingly filled with the scorn of those who abound and the contempt of the proud” (Ps. 123:3).

### 3

Since it is evident that no one can suffice for more people than those who possess more, while small resources suffice for fewer, I fear that someone’s prudence may wonder at the great necessity I have for begging, especially after my own earlier profession, when I had no house of my own. [Note: The printed text repeated *nullos* before *quam qui*; we deleted it on the manuscript’s authority. Construe and explain: “Since it is evident that those who have more are sufficient for feeding more people, while small resources suffice for fewer …”]

To answer this question satisfactorily, let it be known, I ask, that, after I had lost the episcopate and the hope of recovering it had deceived me, I wished to hurry somewhere where I could remain forever—that is, to a monastery. [Note: The printed editions lack *perdito* and then read *episcopii*. We have followed the manuscript. Construe: “Let it be known, I ask, that, after I had lost the episcopate, when the hope of recovering it had deceived me, I wished …” By saying that he wished to go somewhere where he might remain forever, he means a monastery, mentioned in the preceding letter, no. 8: “I had resolved to seek the solitude of a monastery.” The same matter is repeated at the beginning of the following letter.]

But my rivals, the contentious litigants, most shrewdly, as it seemed to them, accumulating causes of dispute for themselves [Note: We have added *sibi* on the authority of the manuscript. Construe: “But my rivals, contentious litigants, most shrewdly, as it seemed to them, accumulating causes of dispute for themselves, provoked me, while I had resolved to spare them by keeping silent, with certain oblique insinuations.” Similar passages may be seen in the preceding letter, no. 9, and shortly after the beginning of the following one.], provoked me, as I was intending to spare them by keeping silent, with certain insinuations—not openly, but indirectly.

Unless I answer them canonically, I am judged either a criminal or a fugitive; and, branded with the cautery of the worst suspicion, I burn with infamy in the very office I perform. But, since I lack the means to do so, especially because, being far away, I am compelled to go to the Roman Church for this purpose, if it is possible [Note: The printed editions read: “The Roman Church, for this reason, must be approached.” The manuscript’s reading is better: *cogatur* is construed with *videor*. The meaning is that he lacks the means to answer his rivals’ insinuations canonically, since for this purpose—that is, for canonical judgment—he must travel to Rome, while public conveyances, such as once existed through the generosity of emperors, are no longer available to transport bishops to councils. He therefore asks for charitable assistance from good people to complete this journey. He says that he is far away from Rome because he did not write this in Italy but in Germany, where, having abandoned all hope of recovering the episcopate, he had withdrawn to return to a monastery. He acknowledges that assistance was given to him by the German bishops in Letter V, no. 2.], and since the generosity of emperors long ago ceased to provide public conveyances for transporting bishops to councils, I do not wish to abandon this journey, which is so necessary, though I cannot complete it. Therefore I ask for the assistance of all good people, for the love of God, asking no one among the wicked to suffer any inconvenience; I ask only for the help of charity.

## Letter VII. To the Bishops of Italy, Gaul, and Germany

[Note: This letter was written at the same time as the two preceding ones. See the Admonition prefixed to Letter V.]

To the lords, fathers, and most reverend fellow bishops established in the Lord throughout Italy, Gaul, and Germany, RATHERIUS, sinner and exile.

1. Indeed, most holy Fathers, after being driven from my proper see, that is, Verona, I had resolved to yield to the malice of my persecutors—as we read that some of the most approved men did—and to seek the solitude of a monastery, there to await the Lord, who would save me from faintheartedness of spirit and storm (Psalm 54:9) amid the impious chatter of those speaking against right and justice. But when I learned through a truthful report that my adversaries were bringing certain charges against me, on account of which they asserted that I should be deprived of the episcopate not by force but by right, and when the Apostle says, “All things are lawful, but not all things are expedient” (1 Corinthians 6:12), I feared that this liberty of mine might result in harm or calumny to someone else, whether present or future. Or, in accordance with what Pope Julius says to the accusers of Athanasius—“For if,” he says, “you trusted in your true innocence, you would in no way withdraw yourselves from a canonical summons”—I judged that I ought not to seek leisure so eagerly that I would dare to be absent from a judicial proceeding. Although no one canonically summons me [or: calls me together], I most steadfastly appeal to your most sacred assembly.

[The Lobbes manuscript reads *ulli Christiano*, “to any Christian”; the vulgate editions mistakenly read *illi Christiano*, “to that Christian.”]

I implore counsel and aid for the love of the truth, which is Christ; but at present I ask for nothing other than a synodal assembly and the law promulgated by the holy Fathers. Whether it can rightly seem permissible to any Christian to deprive a bishop of his episcopate before the outcome of his case has become clear, I leave to your fatherhood to judge.

Whether, moreover, the crimes of conspiracies and the dissension of the people against their bishop should, with holy Pope Callistus and his very numerous predecessors among the bishops—to use his own words—be struck with the spiritual sword, or whether you will patiently allow them to grow and multiply to the prejudice of our entire order, will be for you to decide, not for my silence.

[The editor notes that the word *nemo*—“no one”—was supplied from the Lobbes manuscript because it is required by the sense. The Fourth Book of the *Praeloquia*, chapter 4, establishes that the judgment of universal councils or of the apostolic see should be sought in episcopal cases. Just as in the fifth letter he sought the judgment of the supreme pontiff, so now he appeals to the synodal judgment of the bishops, so that his case may be decided canonically. He wrote to both parties, so that assistance might be provided either by one authority or by both.]

2. Therefore, lest I seem either a criminal who has been accused or a fugitive who has been challenged, I appeal to a council; I demand a council. I summon the invader of my Church to canonical combat, calling him—with the shepherd’s own Shepherd—a thief and robber, because he has climbed in from elsewhere and has not entered through the door. And if he should evade the matter, I answer, “Amen”: let him be justly struck with perpetual anathema, together with the most sacred laws, as is clear to everyone of sound judgment, unless he comes to his senses through repentance.

[The words “I demand a council” were added from the Lobbes manuscript. Similarly, in the fifth letter: “I ask for a hearing, I demand a hearing.” At this point something appears to be missing, perhaps “let him be struck,” that is, with anathema.]

Nor do I omit, for your fatherhood’s admonition and on my own behalf, that chapter of Blessed Pope Alexander: “Whoever,” he says, “is from your college and withdraws himself from the assistance of those bishops” (that is, bishops unjustly deprived of assistance), “shall be judged not a priest but a schismatic.”

Nor do I omit the prophet’s reproach: “You have not gone up to confront the enemy, nor have you built a wall for the house of Israel, so that you might stand in battle on the day of the Lord” (Ezekiel 13:5); and: “Mute dogs, unable to bark” (Isaiah 56:10).

[Both the Lobbes manuscript and Isaiah’s text supply the word *mute*.]

Nor do I omit the Lord’s saying: “Whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, of him the Son of Man will be ashamed when he comes in his glory, and that of the Father and of the holy angels” (Luke 9:26).

This I most earnestly demand and desire, as I hope: may the God of peace swiftly crush Satan beneath your feet. May the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ always be with you.

## Letter VIII. To Milo, the Invader of the See of Verona

[This letter was extracted and published by the archpriest Bartholomew Campagnola from manuscript 17 of the cathedral chapter of Verona, at the end of the work entitled *The Book of the Civil Law of the City of Verona*, p. 243. The parchment leaves on which this letter, as well as the fragment of the following letter, were copied present the first draft of Rather’s own hand. Several words have been deleted, while others have been written above them between the lines; these alterations came from the author himself. The same happened with the *Invective on the Translation of the Body of Saint Metron*, whose fragment the aforementioned archpriest published from similar chapter parchments, as will be evident from the Admonition prefixed to that *Invective*. The marquis de Dionysius, a canon, communicated to us an exact collation of this letter.

Since the manuscript from which the letter was made public does not give the full name of the person to whom Rather wrote, but indicates it by the initial M, the aforementioned archpriest interpreted it as a letter addressed to Manasses, who occupied the see of Verona. But apart from the fact that Otto is called emperor in this letter, whereas Manasses died before Otto’s reign, the matters indicated here fit Milo, to whom Manasses had sold the episcopate, not Manasses. Among other things, consider the words in section 1: “You seized me, carried me away, drove me into exile”; compare the *Itinerary*, section 4, and the note there.

There is therefore no doubt that this letter was addressed to Milo. Rather wrote it after escaping from the prison into which Milo had thrown him, when various circumstances were driving him to surrender the episcopate to Milo. He escaped from prison at the beginning of the year 965, as we established in the *Life*. The question of surrendering the episcopate began to arise somewhat later. Since he composed this letter as the day of Christmas approached, on which he was required to celebrate the sacred rites, it must be assigned to the end of the year 965.]

To the most vehement assailant, M., the Vicentine: R., bishop of Verona, most vehemently assailed, compelled by his assailant.

[The designation “Vicentine” appears to refer to Milo not because he was bishop of Vicenza, as some may think—for no evidence suggests that Milo, who had invaded the episcopate of Verona while still very young, also obtained the episcopate of Vicenza—but because he was Vicentine by origin. Count Milo, whose little nephew he was, and his relatives possessed many estates in the Vicentine territory.

Rather calls him an “assailant” because Milo had attacked Rather—whose episcopate of Verona had been restored after Milo was excluded—and was still attacking him through many schemes, in order to make him surrender the episcopate.]

1. Since the necessity of the festival is pressing upon me—this festival, which must certainly be celebrated more carefully than the others that have recently passed, since its highest solemnity consists chiefly in the mystery of distributing and receiving the sacrifice through which the Lamb is asserted to have been born so that he might suffer for us—I am often troubled by the question whether he to whom God himself, who is also the Lamb, is known to have said to the disobedient, “If you offer your gift” (Matthew 5:23), and so forth, may safely presume to do this.

[The adverb *utique*, “certainly,” absent from the vulgate text, was supplied from the manuscript. The festival indicated is Christmas.]

Since I know that you have something against me, and since I am compelled to offer to God the gift of this same solemnity, I desire to investigate the very fault through which I might be reconciled. I can find no other fault than that I dared to admit myself for consecration to the episcopate of the Church of Verona before you yourself were able to be born.

[The first hand in the manuscript had originally written *compelled* instead of *I am compelled*.]

[From this we learn that Milo was born after Rather had been consecrated bishop of Verona. For this reason, in the fifth letter to Pope John, section 8, he calls him “the little nephew,” that is, the adolescent, of Count Milo. These circumstances, as well as others below, cannot at all fit Manasses, already an elderly archbishop of Arles. Other examples from this period show that certain adolescents were promoted to the episcopate; Atto of Vercelli condemns this abuse in his book *On Ecclesiastical Distresses*, volume I of Acher’s *Spicilegium*, p. 423.]

But what would I have feared even if I had been able to know that you would be born, when I did not know at all whether you would be a woman or a man? This, then, is my earlier fault against you, for which you seized me, carried me away, and drove me into exile—all of this, nevertheless, to the disgrace of the emperor and our dukes, although they conceal it—and against the command of the one who forbids all evil. But you must see to that.

[The sentence should be construed: “All this is to the disgrace of the emperor and our dukes, although they conceal it, and against the command of the one who forbids every evil. But you must see to that.” By “the one who forbids every evil,” God is meant. The disgrace of the emperor is involved because, after entering Verona and restoring Rather, and after all had pledged their loyalty to him, the emperor ordered that no further evil be attempted against that same bishop. Whatever Milo and his associates subsequently dared to do against Rather therefore brought disgrace upon the emperor and opposed not so much God’s command as the emperor’s. The same actions also brought disgrace upon the dukes, who, complying with the emperor’s favor toward Rather, so openly supported him that the illustrious duke commended him to the protection of the count then governing Verona. See the *Conjecture on Character*, section 14.

Rather calls “dukes,” in the plural, Henry II, nephew of Emperor Otto through his brother, and Judith, widow of Duke Henry I of Bavaria and mother of Henry II. Henry II held his father’s duchy together with the March of Verona. Judith, who possessed great influence at Verona, is expressly mentioned in note 39 to the *Conjecture on Character*. Hence below, in section 3, he again requires an explicit command of “our emperor and dukes.”]

2. My more recent—indeed, most immediate—fault [understand: fault] is that I neither die nor undertake, as you urge, flight. But who can die when God preserves his life? And how can one flee who knows very well that the same God says to him: “The hireling flees because he is a hireling” (John 10:13), seeing the wolf coming; and: “Whoever divorces his wife, except on account of fornication, makes her commit adultery” (Matthew 5:32)?

But whoever makes another commit adultery does he not consequently kill the soul, since it is written: “The soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezekiel 18:4)? The one who says, “Do not set your soul upon the killing of your son” (Proverbs 19:18), forbids me to do this. If one must not set one’s soul upon the killing of a single son, how much less upon the killing of so many sons of my lawful wife.

[The manuscript reads *ad filii*, whereas the vulgate editions mistakenly read *ad filium*. The meaning is: if one’s soul must not be set upon the killing of one son, much less upon the killing of so many. He calls the Church of Verona his lawful wife because, as a bishop canonically consecrated, he lawfully took her as his spouse; he calls the Veronese his sons.]

If you are not ashamed to be called a wolf here, as elsewhere a thief, beware lest you yourself be called a hireling.

[“Elsewhere,” that is, earlier, following the Gospel parable, he called Milo a thief because, like a thief, he ascended to the episcopate of Verona not through the door but from elsewhere. “Here,” that is, now, he calls him a wolf because Milo urged Rather to flee, while Rather refused to flee lest he be a hireling.] For I desire to be found among the shepherds, when each person rises in his own order (1 Corinthians 15:23). In that judgment, since even the goats, as the Gospel says, are to be condemned so severely (Matthew 25:33), consider what the wolves that devour the lambs will suffer.

And beware, I warn you, of this kind of designation. For when these two things are compared with one another, they show that every sheep, even if a sinner, is one who suffers unjustly at the hands of the person inflicting harm; whereas the wolf is the one who inflicts it.

[The vulgate text reads *ostenditur*, “is shown,” incorrectly; both context and sense require *ostendunt*, “they show.”]

Indeed, when you hear that “whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery” (Matthew 5:32), if you do not fear committing adultery, I fear that you should know that I am called a Nicolaitan. These, then, are the faults against you that I assert to be incapable of correction.

[The earlier statements should be recalled: Rather said that he could find no other interior fault in himself than that he had been consecrated bishop of Verona before Milo was born; his more recent fault was that he neither died nor fled to make room for Milo. Here he calls both faults incapable of correction: the first because it could not have happened otherwise than that he was consecrated before Milo and was the lawful bishop of Verona; the second because, with God preserving his life, he could not die, and because, as a true shepherd rather than a hireling, he could not flee.]

3. As for your own fault against me, I would rather have you examine it yourself than that I should offend you by admonishing you in this way: “Vengeance is mine”—understand, reserve it for me—“I will repay,” says the Lord (Romans 12:19).

[The vulgate reads *quam contra te*, “than against you”; the manuscript has *quanquam*, but the sense of the context requires *quamque*, “and how.”]

To prevent anything more harmful from befalling you in that repayment, I advise you to consider how you are acting against yourself, after swearing fidelity—as I did—to the most holy emperor, while you strive to destroy his edict and compel those who swore the same oath to him as you did to perjure themselves by drawing them into providing you assistance in this matter;

[The manuscript is disordered at this point; the vulgate consequently printed a lacuna before “his edict.” The missing words have been restored from the context. Perhaps the bishops who urged Rather to yield to Milo are meant: in the *Conjecture on Character*, section 14, Rather mentions Hubert of Parma, who pressed him to yield to his rival in exchange for “the price of souls.”] while you make bishops grievous transgressors of the canons by making them your supporters; while you compel a father to suspect his sons and sons to hate their father without cause; while you cause perjuries to be disregarded and compel anathema to be treated as nothing, so long as you do not refuse to promise a reward to someone who says, “What will you give me, and I will hand him over to you?” (Matthew 26:15).

Since you do these and similar things against me—or rather, against yourself—I leave it to you to weigh them. Just as I cannot die under that judgment, so I fear that I cannot safely withdraw [apparently: for your sake].

[The printed text reads “that he cannot”; the correction “that I cannot” is established by the adjective *secure*, “safely,” and especially by its agreement with the preceding statements, in which Rather explained from the Gospel parable that a shepherd cannot flee as a hireling flees.]

If you never intend to come to your senses, I suggest that you try to carry out by another route what you have begun. Try, I say, if you can, to obtain the command of the emperor and our dukes by which I may withdraw—and obtain it not through some implied indication, but plainly and openly, in terms that can be understood. Otherwise all your schemes are futile, unless perhaps God has permitted you to do what he permits the wolf to do to the lamb—and I believe this will harm you more than me.

[The passage should be construed: “I suggest that you try to carry out what you have begun by another route: try, I say, if you can, to obtain the command—that is, the order—of the emperor and our dukes by which I may withdraw; and obtain this command not through some implication,” and so forth. Similarly, at the end of the *Deliberative Conclusion*, Rather declares that he does not wish to surrender the episcopate to Milo except by the authority of the most pious Caesar.]

## Letter IX, or rather, Fragment of Another Letter to the Same Milo

[This fragment was printed by the aforementioned archpriest Campagnola from a parchment of manuscript 17 of the chapter of Verona, at the end of the *Book of the Civil Law of the City of Verona*, p. 241. It was written at approximately the same time and on the same occasion as the preceding letter, and perhaps somewhat earlier, in the year 965, while Rather was suffering one attack after another from Milo and his supporters, before he was pressured to surrender the episcopate.]

I am prepared for scourging—understand, for the scourging of my sins—not unaware of my faults. But what the just Judge thinks of you, who inflict scourging upon me, though I am innocent, you yourself must see.

[The reading had been: “who inflict scourging upon you, though innocent; you yourself seem so to me.” Since the parchment is worn and, as the editor noted, admits erasures, alterations, and additions, it was easy for something contrary to the genuine sense and proper position to intrude. Certainly *to you* does not fit: Milo was not inflicting scourging upon himself but upon Rather. We have therefore substituted *upon me* in its proper place for *upon you*; the sentence then makes excellent sense.]

But if you are deceived by ignorance of this, hear what the prophet says to Nebuchadnezzar in a similar case: “I was angry with my people, says the Lord, and I delivered them into your hand. You showed them no mercy, nor did you remember your end.
