Therefore evils shall come upon you, from which you will not be able to escape; calamity shall fall upon you, and you will not know its rising” (Isaiah 47:6–11).

[These are the Veronese whom he designates in the preceding letter, section 3, with the words: “Those who swore to the emperor the same oath as you did, you compel to perjure themselves by drawing them into providing you assistance.”]

Those who assist you in so great a crime should hear this: “You offer help to the wicked, and you join in friendship with those who hate God,” and so forth. Let them also hear the Psalmist: “For they persecuted the one whom you struck, and they added to the number of my wounds; add iniquity upon their iniquity” (Psalm 68:27–28), and the rest, which you do not fail to know.

But those who, though able, do not restrain you from such an attempt need no more obscure warning. Let them hear the Apostle saying most aptly: “Not only those who do such things, but also those who consent to the one doing them, are worthy of death” (Romans 1:32).

[These are the bishops whom he calls Milo’s supporters in the preceding letter, section 3.]

Those, however, who do not provide me assistance against you should not pretend that they have failed to hear Pope Alexander and martyr, since in his decrees he is recorded as saying: “Whoever from your college withdraws himself from their assistance shall be judged more a schismatic than a priest.”

Whether you, or those who consent to you, or those who do not bring me assistance, are acting not only against me but also against all who from the beginning of the world have suffered persecution for justice, hear the Gospel, if you do not know: “So that upon you may come all the righteous blood poured out upon the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah, son of Barachiah, whom you killed between the temple and the altar” (Matthew 23:35).

If I am refuted in this matter, I patiently endure being refuted with Jerome asserting the same thing—provided that you tell me how the scribes and Pharisees could have killed Zechariah, whom they never saw. “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Matthew 13:43), and let him justly raise whatever objection he wishes.

[This passage is explained by what Rather wrote in the *Itinerary*, section 11: “The Lord speaks as though he were referring only to the Jews, saying: ‘The blood of all the prophets that has been shed upon the earth shall come upon this generation, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah, son of Barachiah, whom you killed between the temple and the altar,’ although those to whom he spoke had killed neither Abel nor Zechariah nor any prophet. But because they were like those who had done these things, they deserved to be punished with a similar vengeance.”]

## Letter X. To Martin of Ferrara

[This letter was published by Acher from the Laudun manuscript, whose title identifies Martin’s episcopate with the words: “A letter addressed to Martin of Ferrara.” We compared it with the Frisingen manuscript, whose copy we received.

Martin, bishop of Ferrara, took part in the Roman council of 954, according to Rubeus, *History of Ravenna*, book 5. He subscribed to the synod of Ravenna in 967, and is said to have obtained diplomas from John XIII in 972, in *Italia sacra*, volume II, column 532. Although no other record of him is supplied there, it can nevertheless be inferred that he was a much older bishop, so that Rather could call him a *silicernius*, an extremely aged man, from the fact that the Ughellian succession could find no other bishop before Martin except Constantine, who, according to the records, was alive in 898.

Rather wrote this letter while presiding for the third time over the Church of Verona, since all his writings contained in both the Laudun and Frisingen manuscripts belong to the same period. Hence Rather calls himself an old man, which does not entirely fit the years of his second restoration. During the time of his third restoration, although he was more an extremely aged man than merely an old man—as he calls himself in the *Conjecture on Character*, section 13—he nevertheless names himself an old man in this letter only in relation to Martin, who was much older and whom he therefore calls an extremely aged man.

It will become clear from note 1371 that the letter was written on the first Sunday of Advent. Since the Frisingen manuscript, which we have observed follows chronological order, places it before the work entitled *Discord*, composed at the beginning of 968, we think this letter was written on the first Sunday of Advent in 967, the year in which Rather had come to know Martin at the synod of Ravenna.]

To the lord Martin, venerable fellow bishop, Rather, a sinner.

Although the Apostle commands that an elder be entreated and forbids that he be rebuked, the charity with which I love you compels me to reveal to you—for I count it murderous to conceal it—how the sons of your Church disparage you, especially concerning the illicit ordination of boys. They add that you also carry them out for a price, which is simoniacal and condemned by the holy canons with perpetual anathema.

Therefore, as a son I entreat a father, as a servant a lord, as an old man an extremely aged man: remembering what was read more especially for you and me today—that is, “Knowing that the hour has already come for us to rise from sleep” (Romans 13:11)—do not neglect to recall the apostolic command to Timothy: “Lay hands hastily on no one” (1 Timothy 5:22); nor Peter’s words to Simon: “May your money be with you for destruction” (Acts 8:20); nor the words of many who say, “Let both the giver and the receiver be anathema” (Second Council of Orléans, chapter 3; Third Council of Constantinople, chapter 22).

At last rise from the sleep of such public contempt for the canons, and, I beg you, cease from such ordinations.

[“Today” means the first Sunday of Advent, on which the following words from Paul’s Epistle are read. *Silicernius* means an extremely aged man.]

Perhaps the one who said, “You have sinned; be still,” and, “Turn to me, and I will turn to you” (Zechariah 1:3), will not despise this late return of yours, since he is gracious and merciful and does not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live (Ezekiel 33:11).

Know, moreover, that from now on no one will disparage you more than those whom you have ordained in this manner, or those at whose requests you have done the same.

[The printed text had “his own,” but the correction in the errata gives “you,” as also found in the Frisingen manuscript.]

## Letter XI. To Nanno, Count of Verona

[This letter was published by P. Bernard Pez from the Frisingen manuscript, whose copy we obtained. It was written after the council of Ravenna in 967, whose decree concerning clerics dismissing women is indicated in section 2, as may be gathered from note 1381.

In the same section, the letter is dated by reference to a feast day, or the octave of the feast of Saint John the Baptist, on which the verse of the third nocturn’s responsory was sung—and is still sung today: “For this is the prophet, and more than a prophet.” See the responsorial published by Cardinal Tomasius, volume IV of his works, p. 119.

Since the same section alludes to a sentence pronounced by Nanno as the emperor’s envoy against Rather on 30 June 968, as we shall infer in note 6, this letter must be assigned to 1 July 968, the octave of Saint John the Baptist.]

To the lord Nanno, an illustrious and most necessary prince bestowed upon us according to our deserts, Rather, a sinner and, whether he wishes it or not, the bearer of what he deserves.

[He calls Nanno a “prince” because he governed Verona as its count. But since Nanno offered protection to rebels against the bishop, Rather says in section 2 that he did not rule and govern but “more than commanded.”]

1. My little poverty has learned that your lordship’s excellence threatens to bring me the greatest shame before the majesty of the most pious emperor [Otto I]. In the folly of my self-confidence, I had thought that my conscience had endured no shame at all. But perhaps you have entered more deeply into it—as I deserve—and you know what things, spoken in bedrooms, will be proclaimed upon the rooftops, unless God spares me (Luke 12:3).

As for everything else, I trust that you are as ignorant of it as the whole community has already grown weary of listening to the lies of those who disparage me.

But what will you do, my lord? When words cease, deeds will speak. More than once I myself have urged the lady empress [Adelaide]; so I beg you, do not suppose that the most wise emperor has entirely forgotten the saying of blessed Job: “The case I did not know, I investigated most diligently” (Job 19:16). Nor suppose him so credulous toward you that he cannot remember the saying—not merely spoken long ago but made thoroughly familiar through frequent use—“The mouth of the enemy does not speak truth.”

[“Lies” means fabricated accusations, about which Rather complains both in the *Apologeticus*, section 7, and in the *Discord*, section 7; they are explained especially in the following letter to Ambrose.]

But, O cloths—the worthless gifts of the most worthless Rather—what can they possibly contribute to him except such things? O Venetia, whose cloths are so cheap even to those who receive them freely that not even favor itself—ineffective and conferring nothing—can be purchased by them! True is the saying, suited to this age: “It is arranged in this way: you overthrow former benefits unless you support them with later ones. For if you deny one thing to an unjust and ungrateful exactor, you destroy thousands of gifts.”

[“Cloth” means silk or a more costly material. Thus in Book 5 of the *Praeloquia*, section 10, Rather speaks of heresies “from the finest cloth,” that is, a cloak made of the finest fabric. Compare the note there.

He indicates that such cloths were woven in Venetia, where “Venetia” should be understood not as the city but as the province, which retained that ancient name and meaning in this period. Verona was also included in this province, where excellent cloths were produced.

Rather had given some of these cloths to Nanno, the new count, at the beginning of his administration, in order to win his favor. But they were useless to him because, as he hints below, he did not later show the same generosity toward the count. The words “except such things” refer to what Nanno had done against Rather.]

2. O those who are otherwise guilty of the greatest offense, to whom it is granted neither to ask successfully nor to obtain safely what the Psalmist says: “Cleanse me, Lord, from my hidden faults, and spare your servant from those belonging to others” (Psalm 18:13)!

I earnestly beg you to stop terrifying me continually with the sentence of the most pious Caesar [the emperor], since you cannot do so. For I fear you a thousand times more than I fear him. Since good things are usually loved, while evil things are correspondingly feared, I serve two masters in an impossible manner: I love him, but I fear you.

Let him to whom this pertains consider why; but I hope that the one to whom it belongs will consider it.

Meanwhile, as we sing—and since we cannot forget what has just been said concerning John, “For this is the prophet, and more than a prophet”—be careful lest this be more than commanding: while the most glorious emperor permits even the bodies of his parishioners to obey their bishops, you seize their very souls from them.

You forbid them to come to the synod, to hear the pope’s legation concerning dismissing their wives, and to obey their bishops in every respect. Instead, you receive the priests into your hands like soldiers, and you do not fail to offer them protection in all the abominations they commit against God. You make them disregard our prohibition altogether, as though it had been said to you: “Whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew 16:19).

[These matters concern the synod that the bishop convoked at Verona after the council of Ravenna. In the following letter, section 1, speaking of the same synod, he says: “When those who did not come had been summoned again and again, Giselpert was sent, and in the name of his master—that is, Count Nanno—he forbade them under penalty of the ban to come to our council under any circumstances.

The pope’s legation concerning dismissing wives refers to the decree of the council of Ravenna, presided over by Pope John XIII. In the following letter, section 1, the same command is attributed to the emperor, because imperial authority also prescribed the execution of that synodal decree. Rather says that after the council of Ravenna he summoned all the priests and deacons of his diocese to report, by order of the serene emperor, what had been established there; the principal statute concerned dismissing wives.

The words of Atto of Vercelli should not be omitted here. In a letter to his clergy against incontinent clerics, he writes: “There are men who, when they are reproved by their bishops for such a crime—that is, incontinence—reject paternal charity and disdain obedience. They do not fear to violate the fidelity they had promised under oath; instead, they attack their bishop with worldly power and entrust themselves and their entire household to his adversaries.” This is what the incontinent Veronese clerics did when they entrusted themselves to Count Nanno, Rather’s adversary.]

This indeed is commanding, and more than commanding; it is not, I say, ruling. For to rule rightly is to act rightly, or to govern what one possesses—that is, to administer it.

3. Therefore, if only I could wish that you, even as you possess me, had also governed me, and that, just as you love to command me, you had likewise loved to rule me! For it would have been more tolerable to bear your domination in such a way that I both feared and loved the one whom I feared, as I had begun to do—that is, the man concerning whom I adapted to myself that line of Naso:

> He who had earlier uttered reproaches against the husband of Therapne,  
> soon sang his praises with a more prosperous lyre.

For after I had said of him, “He who delivered Israel from the hand of Pharaoh” (Exod. 18:10), “may he deliver Ratherius from the hand of Bucco,” when he had begun to improve as he was about to depart, I too began to address him in this way:

> If God wishes to grant me someone better than Bucco, may he take you away; if someone worse, I beg him to preserve you for me.

Since I was unable to obtain this—that is, someone better than Bucco—because he gave me someone worse under the same grammatical ending, I demand that the corresponding harmony of the same prayer fall upon him: namely, “He who delivered Israel from the hand of Pharaoh, may he also deliver Ratherius from the hand of Nanno.” May God, not indeed by overthrowing but rather by converting, deliver from your hands at least the souls whom, out of hatred for me, you compel to rebel against the Lord, even if he has disdained me. Yet you should know that, on account of such things, I fear you a thousand times more than the emperor. For he does not neglect salvation so greatly as you appear to neglect the salvation of souls.

[Note: This is better in our copy than in Pez, which has “me” also.]

[Note: “That man” means Count Bucco, Nanno’s predecessor. Although he initially opposed Ratherius, Ratherius had often said of him: “He who delivered Israel from the hand ...,” as he reports in the sermon On the Octave of Easter, no. 1. Later, when Bucco was about to depart and had begun to be made better, Ratherius adds: “I too began to address him in this way,” and so forth. In the conjecture On Quality, no. 14, as we observed there in the note, he made the lines from Ovid, “The reproaches of the Therapnean wife ...,” fit Bucco himself.]

[Note: “If God wishes to grant me someone better than Bucco, may he take you away”: this passage, omitted by a leap in P. Pez’s edition, has been supplied from our copy. It was desired to substitute “someone better than Count Bucco.”]

[Note: Construe and explain as follows: “Since I was unable to obtain this”—that is, someone better than Bucco—“because he gave me someone worse under the ending of the same declension” (for he gave me Nanno, whose name is expressed with the same declensional ending as Bucco), “I demand that the corresponding harmony of the same prayer fall upon him”—namely, “He who delivered Israel from the hand of Pharaoh, may he also deliver Ratherius from the hand of Nanno”—so that God, not indeed by overthrowing but rather by converting, may deliver from your hands, even if he has disdained me, at least the souls whom you compel, out of hatred for me, to rebel against the Lord.]

[Col. 0678D] [Note: The passage is omitted here.]

[Col. 0678C] “He who had earlier uttered reproaches against the Therapnean wife,  
soon sang her praises with a more favorable lyre.”

[Col. 0679A]

[Col. 0679B] [Note: The words “If God wishes to grant me someone better than Bucco, may he take you away; if someone worse, I beg him to preserve you for me,” omitted by a leap in P. Pez’s edition, have been supplied from our copy. It was desired to substitute “someone better than Count Bucco.”]

561. LETTER XII. TO AMBROSIUS, CHANCELLOR OF EMPEROR OTTO I

[Note: This letter too was edited by P. Pez from the Frisingen manuscript, but has now been more carefully checked against the same codex. It was composed at approximately the same time as the preceding letter, namely immediately after Nanno’s hearing, held on 30 June 968, as will be shown in note 1403. Ambrosius, to whom this letter was sent, was Otto I’s chancellor. He is subscribed to the privilege granted by that emperor in Ratherius’s favor in the preceding year, 967, and in this same year, 968, our bishop addressed to him a short work entitled Discordia. The learned and cultivated Count Francesco Florius, primicerius of the cathedral of Udine, reasonably believed that this was the same man as the priest of the Milanese Church to whom Atto of Vercelli gave the letter printed in volume I of Acheri’s Spicilegium, p. 438 of the new edition. We add that he appears to be the same man who was later promoted to the see of Bergamo. He is indeed absent from Ughelli’s catalogue of the bishops of Bergamo, but that Ambrosius of this period must be added to that catalogue is clear from two contemporary witnesses: (1) the author of the work entitled The Discovery of the Saints Found by Lord Bishop Deoderic of Metz, published by Acheri in volume II of the Spicilegium, p. 134, records that the work was made by Ambrosius, bishop of Bergamo, in 972; (2) the same is confirmed by a document of 972, found in P. Bernard de Rubeis, Monuments of the Church of Aquileia, chap. 52, col. 474.]

RATHERIUS TO AMBROSIUS.

1. After returning from the universal synod celebrated at Ravenna in mid-April, I summoned priests and deacons from all the parishes of our diocese, to report what had been established there by command of the most serene emperor. All were summoned to the council.

[Note: This Ravenna synod, which Ratherius attended, established many measures for the benefit of the holy Church, as the Continuator of Regino reports under the year 967. Nothing survives from it except the sentence against Herold, archbishop of Salzburg, to which Ratherius is recorded as subscribing along with the others. The synod is said to have been celebrated in mid-April—that is, around the middle of April 967, after Easter, which that year fell on 31 March. The sentence of the same synod agrees with this date: it is dated 7 Kalends of May, as may be seen in volume II of Labbe’s Venetian edition of the Councils, col. 911.]

[Col. 0680C] [Note: The synod of Ravenna was presided over by Pope John XIII, and Emperor Otto I also attended it, as the Continuator of Regino testifies. Both authorities evidently joined forces to eradicate the unchastity of the clergy, which had infected many. Ratherius praised the pope’s commission, or command, in the preceding letter to Nanno, no. 2. Here he introduces the emperor’s command, as he also does in Discordia, no. 6: “When the imperial will thundered concerning the abandonment of unchastity.”]

[Col. 0680A] [Note: “The council” means the diocesan council, which he summoned after returning to Verona from the universal synod at Ravenna, in the same year, 967, in June or July. Concerning this council he later says: “Those who did not come were forbidden ever to come to our council.” Shortly afterward, our copy reads saepe, “often,” instead of semper, “always.”]

When, through the cunning of certain members of the senior clergy of our mother church—rebels against me and plotters against my life—some of them disdained to come, certain among those who had assembled, with the greatest arrogance, resolved that they would neither abandon their unchastity nor cease from office. I had them arrested and ordered them to be committed to custody until they made satisfaction.

[Note: “The senior clergy of our mother church,” that is, of the cathedral church, is Ratherius’s designation for the canons.]

[Note: From this it can be inferred that the decree of the Ravenna synod against incontinent clerics was of the following kind: they were to abandon the women, and if any refused, they were to cease from office. Similarly, in the following century, under St. Gregory VII, when the struggle against clerical incontinence was at its height, it was decreed that such clerics should either abandon the women or be deposed.]

The substance of their satisfaction I assigned to the restoration—or, more truly, the adornment—of the church of the blessed Mother of God, in the hope that, since they were utterly ineffective in doing penance, being exceedingly drunkards, the intercession of the Mother might at least obtain pardon for them from the Lord, since they would make no other amendment—that is, satisfaction—of their own accord.

[Note: That is, the cathedral church, which was dedicated under the name of the Blessed Virgin Mary.]

When I had repeatedly arranged to summon those who did not come, there appeared a messenger named Giselpert, who, acting on behalf of his master, forbade them under the ban to come in any way to our council.

[Note: In the preceding letter to Nanno, no. 2, Ratherius attributes this prohibition to Count Nanno himself: “You forbid the priests to come to the synod, to hear the pope’s commission concerning the dismissal of wives, and to obey the bishops in every respect.” Nanno must therefore be understood as acting in the name of his master, and Giselpert was his messenger. Not only those sent by the emperor but also those sent by counts, bishops, or anyone else on some business, to represent the sender’s person, were called “messengers of the count,” “of the bishop,” “of the monastery,” and so forth. Shortly afterward, our copy reads “prejudicial crimes,” where the printed edition has “various crimes.”]

2. Certain townsmen, accused of various crimes, had disdained to come to make satisfaction. I therefore sent men from my side, together with the church doorkeepers, and had them arrested, as is customary; and I applied the satisfaction that was made to the same work.

[Note: Unless the particle “together with” is considered superfluous, the words famuli or bacularii, “servants” or “staff-bearers,” are certainly missing here. For, as is related shortly afterward, the bishop sent these men to bring by force to the bishop someone who had been summoned but refused to come: “He sends his staff-bearers, and by force they seize him and lead him to the bishop.” The words “from my side” indicate that these men stood beside the bishop to be ready for his commands. Construe as follows: “I sent servants or staff-bearers from my side together with the church doorkeepers; I had certain townsmen, accused of various crimes, arrested, as is customary, because they had disdained to come to make satisfaction; and I had the satisfaction made applied to the same work,” that is, to the adornment of the cathedral church.]

A certain priest called me “mouth of the womb.” I likewise had him arrested, and when he had escaped by flight, I took from him what I could. I did not, however, give it to the church, because I scarcely dared to offer God vengeance for my injury; rather, I ought to have been its reliever than its avenger.

A certain deacon, whom in the preceding year I had made an ordinary canon, contrary even to expectation,

[Note: “Ordinary” means a canon of the cathedral church. See note 1036 in Itinerary.]

had, from me, one of the better parishes together with a curtis, while I had none. Since he called me a felon, a deceiver, and a perjurer, I took it away and retained it for myself because it was necessary.

[Note: The common edition reads curae haberet, “had care of,” incorrectly. Our copy has the better reading. In a privilege of 1145, Eugene III, listing the possessions and goods belonging from earlier documents to the bishops of Verona, mentions several parishes with chapels and tithes and sometimes adds “with a curtis” or “with half a curtis.” Curtis therefore denotes other goods or estates besides tithes, situated within the boundaries of the parish and generally granted to the bishopric with some jurisdiction. Thus the parish with a curtis which the deacon held from Ratherius designates a parish church—whatever church it may have been—with its tithes and, in addition, some estate situated in that parish. All these possessions had been handed over by the bishop to the same deacon. This parish, entrusted to the deacon and certainly involving the care of souls, recalls an original document dated 7 March 839, which records an exchange between Audibert, abbot of St. Mary in Organo, and Audon, a deacon and rector of St. Martin’s, situated—so the text reads—in the Paltenate valley. This church of St. Martin, situated in the Paltenate valley, is the one called in other ancient records the parish of Grezzana. Just as the deacon Audo, evidently a Veronese cathedral cleric, as we learn from other documents, presided over this parish under the title of rector, with a priest certainly administering the care of souls under him, so another deacon, who was an ordinary canon of the cathedral, was placed by Ratherius over a wealthier parish. Since Ratherius adds here that, after assigning such a parish to the deacon, he had no other parish, it must be said that at this time the other parishes, or the tithes of the parishes belonging to the bishop, had been alienated, as he indeed affirms in On Quality, no. 13, that many goods of the Veronese Church had been alienated and usurped, to such an extent that he himself was oppressed by poverty. As for the word bausiator, that is, “deceiver,” see the note in the first part of On Contempt for the Canons.]

3. It is now nearly four years since I placed one pound of silver upon the altar of blessed Lawrence. A certain priest received it on the condition that he return it. He did not do so, and he came to none of my synods.

[Note: That is, neither to the diocesan synod of 966 nor to the other of 967; these are the only two synods which we know Ratherius to have celebrated after his third restoration.]

He suffered no inconvenience on account of these matters. He went to the majesty of the emperor, as has been said; I do not know on what grounds he lodged a complaint; he brought back some written document, gladdened all my enemies, and stirred them up against me.

I had a meadow beside the river, in the midst of vineyards belonging both to me and to my servants. Those coming and going there never ceased to trample it down; they ravaged the adjoining vineyards and continually demanded an additional tax from me. When I therefore had it plowed, I ordered millet to be sown in it.

[Note: We have added “belonging to me” from the Frisingen copy. From the same copy we have written detundere, “to trample underfoot,” where the text had devertere. A little later, the same copy omits semper, “always,” perhaps correctly.]

Most foolishly, I spent forty pounds on repairing and enlarging the house, but the Bavarians and, above all, the neighboring clerics and servants destroyed it and blame me for it.

[Note: Later he attributes this damage to neighbors and outsiders. The neighbors here are explained as the clerics and servants living nearby. The outsiders were chiefly those here called Bavarians or Bavarii. Further below he identifies as outsiders those who went to the emperor or returned from him and were received as guests in the episcopal house. This agrees with the sermon On the Octave of Easter, where the matter is described more fully: “Those lodging there do not cease, by force and power, to destroy that house—the episcopal house—while I am unable to resist any one of them ... since it is clear that they were chiefly returning from the imperial army or going to it.” Those who caused the principal damage are known to have been Bavarians—not princes passing through, but those who went to the army in their company or returned from it.]

Day and night the canons and servants do not cease plotting my destruction; and they falsely accuse me of intending never to cease testing them.

When I prohibited them under excommunication from engaging in servile work on Sunday, and was in no way able to enforce this, I ordered the gates barred against the approaching wagons. They judge that this crime must be expiated either by my death or by my expulsion.

[Col. 0682B]

They formed a conspiracy against Bucco in his presence and against me.

[Note: Bucco was count of Verona. Although initially hostile to Ratherius, he later favored him at the recommendation of the duchess. See On Quality, no. 14, and note 899 there. Hence the conspiracy of Ratherius’s enemies attacked not only Ratherius but also Bucco, who favored him. The reference is to the conspiracy that occurred at the beginning of 965 and is described in the work cited, no. 14.]

[Col. 0683A]

When they were brought to settlement and compelled to pay one hundred pounds of silver, they came to me and borrowed nearly thirty pounds from the church treasury, under this condition: if they had not repaid it by the appointed time, they would pay double as a penalty.

[Note: He is speaking of the settlement imposed in 965, when those responsible for the conspiracy mentioned above were fined one hundred pounds. See note 920 in On Quality.]

Three years have now passed, and they have paid back absolutely nothing.

[Note: If three years had already passed by the beginning of July 968, when this letter was given, the thirty pounds had been lent in 965, after the conspiracy had been settled and judgment had been rendered against the rebels, with a fine of one hundred pounds.]

4. May your incomparable piety, I beg and demand, now see how forgetful and ungrateful they are for so great a benefit; and, unless help is provided, may it hasten to succor me, who am perishing, for God’s sake.

On the very solemnity of the blessed apostle Paul, nearly the whole city was present, and Nanno, seated in the tribunal, began to speak as follows:

[Note: Our copy has the excellent reading “on the solemnity of the blessed apostle Paul.” The printed editions incorrectly have “he himself from the blessed one.” We formerly believed that this referred to the feast of the conversion of St. Paul on 25 January 968. But we observed that Ratherius, in the sermon On the Octave of Easter, preached on the octave itself, 26 April of that year, clearly indicates that the opponents’ machinations against him had been conceived throughout Lent of that year and broke out after Easter, when they bribed two leading men of the city and led them around the entire episcopal house, trying to attribute its damage and ruin to the bishop. Although this accusation was utterly false, it was especially pressed upon the emperor’s ears, as can be gathered from the words of the following letter to Adelaide: “If you are doing this for the sake of the bishopric ...” It was also the principal material and cause of the hearing which Nanno held against Ratherius and which is described here. Therefore this hearing must be assigned not to the feast of St. Paul’s conversion on 25 January but to the feast commemorating the same apostle on 30 June 968, in which year Ratherius soon afterward abandoned the bishopric.]

“What do you townsmen think about this meadow, which you see plowed up?”

They all answered unanimously, “Very badly”—although they could have answered better and more justly: “What is that to us? The man who was able by right to gather hay from it was also able to plow it legally.”

[Note: There is a textual error in the word ausus. The meaning is nevertheless clear: the man who could lawfully gather hay from the meadow could also lawfully plow it.]

Again he asked: “What do you judge concerning this house, which you see destroyed in this way?”

“It is the bishop’s fault,” they all replied.

Yet they could have answered better: “Let it be investigated whether any of the neighbors did this, and let him be compelled to make lawful restitution.”

As for the outsiders, it was your responsibility to provide for them, since the duty of receiving and arranging for them appears to have been entrusted to you. For who among us could have prohibited them when they were either approaching the emperor or returning from him?

[Note: “Your responsibility” refers to Nanno, count of Verona, whose duty it was to provide lodging for those going to the emperor and returning from him.]

The bishop, as it is said, spent forty pounds on its restoration, enlargement, and adornment, merely restoring six doors, which had partly been taken away by theft—that is, secretly—and partly by force. He consumed no small amount of money, and it did him no good. What more could he have done?

[Note: Since the episcopal house was not safe for Ratherius, who had been captured there in 965, Bucco, then count of Verona, advised him not to entrust himself to that house again. See On Quality, note 902.]

It was most unsuitable for him to stay in it, lest he either be captured, as before, or, if he tried to defend himself, the neighboring basilicas might be burned with fire—for what does the Veronese populace not dare?—because of him.

[Note: The basilicas adjoining the episcopal house are three: the cathedral, St. John the Baptist’s, where the baptistery is located, and St. George’s, now commonly called St. Helena’s.]

But if neither of those things happened, what could he do, when, as one of your princes left it, another succeeded him, and another that one, and yet another the other?

[Note: Just as those going to the emperor and passing through Verona were Germans, especially Bavarians, and lodged in the episcopal house, as stated in note 1390, so these words “one of your princes” plainly indicate that Nanno belonged to the same nation. Both these words and the entire context are addressed to Nanno.]

Could the bishop live in one house with them? They said none of these things; rather, all spoke as badly as each of them could.

[Note: This agrees with our copy. Pez has “which of them,” less suitably. Construe as follows: “They said none of these things; rather, they all spoke worse, according to what each of them was able to say.”]

Then he said again: “What do you say about these clerics who have lost their benefices in this way?”

[Note: Pez printed dicitis, “you say,” instead of clericis. The reading clericis must certainly be retained, as in our copy. A verb seems to be understood from the preceding context, such as judicatis, “do you judge.” By “clerics” he chiefly means the ten canons from whom Ratherius had withdrawn the benefices he had once granted them, as he relates more fully in Discordia, no. 8. See note 1177 there.]

They all shouted, “Nothing could be worse.”

Yet if they had been good sons and had not proved ungrateful for their benefices, they could have answered, as above: “What is that to us?” Almost all human beings do this; God himself does it. He gave Saul a kingdom and took it away; he gave Judas the apostolate and did not leave it to him; finally, he first gave heaven to the devil and afterward hell. But although God did this justly, a human being ought not to do it unjustly.

Again he asked: “What do you say concerning this: if a cleric or his servant, of his own will, does not come to the bishop when summoned, he sends his staff-bearers, who seize him by force and lead him to the bishop?”

[Note: Pez printed episcopum, “the bishop,” although the man had not been summoned. We have drawn the correction from our copy. On the staff-bearers, see above, note 1934, and On Quality, note 832.]

Here, although they could all have answered with the greatest justice in the words of Terence, “Well done!” they all instead shrieked together with a pig-like squeal.

Then he said: “I have been sent to you on behalf of the emperor and my lady [Otto I and the empress Adelaide], so that if any one of them should henceforth dare to do this, everyone is to resist him with all his strength.”

[Note: Since Otto I’s privilege had confirmed Ratherius’s authority over his subjects in such a way that anyone who impeded him or resisted his ministers was forbidden under the gravest penalty, a special command was necessary if anyone was to resist the staff-bearers sent by him. Shortly afterward Ratherius calls this judgment of Nanno “an edict issued on behalf of the emperor for resisting me with all one’s strength.”]

When he had said this, he restored to all my adversaries everything I had taken from them and had granted to the poor clerics by a charter sent to you and confirmed by the hand of the patriarch, by my own hand, and by the hands of all the co-bishops of our province. He said that the emperor had sworn that he would never allow this arrangement to remain in force.

[Note: The charter is the Judgment, which we previously noted as having been sent to Ambrosius in note 1182 on Discordia. It was proved in note 1162 of the same work that the subscriptions of Ratherius, the patriarch, and the neighboring bishops were appended to this Judgment at a synod held in November 967. Nanno’s sentence therefore rendered this Judgment invalid.]

5. But if this is true, you acted badly in not telling me about it beforehand. You know very well what I deserve if I break the subscription of my own hand.

[Note: This can be explained from the solemn formula found in many ancient documents of donation or testament: “Nor may it ever be permitted to me to refuse what I have willed; rather, I promise inviolably to observe what has once been done or written by me.” See the testament of Notherius, bishop of Verona, of 927; another of Ingelbald the deacon, of 981; and the offering of Waldo the acolyte, of 982, in the collection of Veronese charters edited by Canon Marquis Dionysius, pp. 107, 164, and 167. See also the testament of Dagibert, deacon of Verona, of 931, in Biancolini, Notices of the Churches of Verona, book II, p. 699.]

What more? You see the conspiracy made against me; you can consider the edict issued on behalf of the emperor for resisting me with all your strength; you see the danger. If you are able to help me and do not do so, you yourselves are killing me. For true is the inference of the one who grants: he who does not remove death from a sick man when he could have done so inflicts it upon him.

But if matters are as Nanno never ceases to assure everyone, and the empress desires nothing more than my destruction, while the emperor cares for nothing less than my safety and welfare, then neither of them even regards me as baptized. Unless this belief is shown to be false, and this incitement, provocation, conspiracy, and audacity against me are quickly suppressed by an imperial letter, the matter is finished concerning my life.

568. LETTER XIII. TO ADELAIDE, THE EMPRESS

[Note: This letter too, published by P. Pez from the Frisingen codex, was written at the same time and for the same reason as the preceding letter.]

To the most serene Augusta, Lady Adelaide, whom no one disdains, Ratherius, a sinner, offers faithful service beyond what is owed and beyond his ability.

If what Nanno is trying to persuade all my adversaries of is true—that you desire nothing more than my destruction, while your husband cares for nothing less than the condition of my safety—

[Note: The common edition incorrectly reads desiderans, “desiring.” The correction desideratis, “you desire,” instead of desideras, “you desire,” is confirmed by the words of the preceding letter, no. 5, with which this passage entirely agrees: “The empress desires nothing more than my destruction, while the emperor cares for nothing less than my safety and welfare.” When writing to princes and others holding high office, the author customarily uses the plural rather than the singular.]

But if you are doing this for the sake of the bishopric, take care, by your power, to preserve my small life until I have completed the church of the blessed Mother of God.

[Note: Construe as follows: “For you should know—I call God to witness—that I shall be entirely ready to do whatever you thereafter command me, guided by reason.”]

Know, I call God to witness, that I shall be entirely ready to do what you thereafter command me, guided by reason. For I desire rather to withdraw safely and dwell in the solitude of my monastery, and there await the Lord, who will save me from faintness of spirit and storm (Ps. 54:9), than to continue any longer enduring such things uselessly and also to the detriment of my soul.

O how beneficial it would be to all who are placed in authority—as I have more than once suggested to your lordship—if they did not rush headlong into judgments, but attended to what blessed Job said: “I investigated most diligently the case that I did not know” (Job 9:16).

[Note: Pez published what follows as though it were another letter, prefacing it with the title “To the same.” The codex does indeed have something similar: “The same to the same.” But what follows is rather an appendix, or postscript, in which Ratherius, fearing that these words might anger the empress, attempts to excuse himself on the grounds that his spirit, filled with bitterness, cannot speak more sweetly, nor praise what deserves hatred. We have corrected the text from our copy. Pez had timens, “fearing,” instead of tumens, “swollen,” and gessit qui laudat, “he has carried out what he praises,” instead of gestit laudans, “he desires while praising.”]

“Like aloe, lady, a swollen stomach does not belch forth the sweetness of honey; and one who craftily desires to deceive praises what he hates.”

569. LETTER XIV. OF EVERACLUS, BISHOP OF LIÈGE, TO RATHERIUS, BISHOP OF VERONA

[Note: Fulcuin calls him Evracrus in Deeds of the Abbots of Lobbes, chapters 27 and 28. Anselm the canon, in Chapeauvill’s volume I of The Deeds of the Bishops of Tongeren, calls him Eraclius. But in the same work, in the fuller and more corrected version published by Fathers Martène and Durand, volume IV of Collection of Ancient Writers, p. 860, he is called Everaclus. He became bishop of Liège in 959 and died in 971. This letter was written while Ratherius, holding the bishopric of Verona for the third time, was considering leaving after suffering many hardships at Verona in 968. Chapeauvill, in the cited volume, p. 190, note 2, printed the letter from a Lobbes manuscript, from which we received a more accurate copy.]

[Col. 0687A]

To Lord and father, thrice-blessed bishop Ratherius, a man of distinguished reputation, great and most approved, Everaclus, servant of the servants of Christ, unworthy though he may be called his son, sends whatever is most prosperous in Christ Jesus.

1. Setting aside hyperbaton with its circumlocutions, I am pleased to describe in plain and open speech how great a part of my soul is yours—scholastically, if I cannot, then, I hope, at least rustically, but not falsely—for I draw forth in a pure voice what lies hidden, from an inner fiber that cannot be told; I desire to mark how firmly I have fixed you in my winding heart.

You know that comic saying (Terence, Andria 1.2): “I am Davus, not Oedipus, so that I might deceive my hearers with embellished words.” But enough of this.

2. When I had heard and attentively understood your sweet embassy, although I had not yet seen or received the balm which you sent out of pious love, and although your letter had not yet been read, the undiminished affection toward me of so great and distinguished a man, whom I came to know, brought no small joy to me, so insignificant a person. The precious liquid, of which I was almost destitute, greatly brightened my face when it was given.

When at last I heard the epithet that did not correspond to my name, which your affection had added to me without any commendation of my deeds, it gladdened my spirit beyond belief. From there, a hundred times bending my knees toward Verona, as though kissing your footprints, I return a thousand times a thousand thanks to you.

[Note: Chapeauvill has potuit, “was able,” and afterward omits “and never.”]

But if you wish to learn by experience what virtue may have appeared in me, although I possess no virtue that shines before me—nowhere and never will its likeness be absent from you.

I often place before my eyes the sweetness of former times, and gladly repeat it in frequent conversations: how you cherished me, so that, like nurses feeding infants who cannot yet eat, you transferred chewed food into my mouth. What should I recall before or after this great benefit? I am inexperienced and ignorant.

For who is superior to you in wisdom, integrity, devotion to the best arts, innocence, or any kind of praise? The Ciceronian voice resounds; the Ciceronian trumpet thunders (Pro Marcello): “No stream of talent is so great, no power or abundance of speaking or writing is so great that it could, I will not say adorn, but even recount the praises of your virtues.”

[Note: “The voices of the trumpet of Cicero resound,” a passage absent from Chapeauvill, has been inserted from our copy.]

If patience is mentioned—if it is permissible to say so without violating faith, lest I offend God—you are patience itself. You have not gulped down Mercurial saliva, and, as Persius says (Satires 5.112), you were able to step over a coin fixed in the mud.

Let us leave the satirists and return to the simple and holy. You not only did not seize what belonged to others, you did not even desire it; you gave away what was your own, grieving over the misery of others and not envying another’s happiness. You became all things to all people, that you might win all (1 Cor. 9:22).

Your native country stretches out suppliant hands to you and invites you to return. All who belong to either order, clerical or military—that is, noble—

[Note: The military order, or order of soldiers, means the nobility. See note 144 in book III of The Prologues.]

cry out in mind, will, zeal, gesture, and voice that you should come; they desire to see you. We set no limit, either in number or in manner, to the service we shall render you. Everything that is ours shall be in your hand, according to what has settled in your heart, beloved Ratherius. Foresee everything, arrange everything, establish everything, and act in all things as you please.

Under your skilled and practiced thumb, I shall not be ashamed to place my hand beneath the rod. Farewell, applaud yourself, and may the grace of our Lord continually protect you from every evil assault.

THE THIRD PART OF THE WORKS OF RATHERIUS, BISHOP OF VERONA

SERMONS

[Col. 0689]

### 571–577 SERMON I [or II]

**Note:** We obtained a copy of this sermon, which was edited by Acherius from the Laon manuscript, from the Freising manuscript. It was delivered after Ratherius’s third restoration to the see of Verona; all the works transcribed in these manuscripts belong to that period. The same must be said of the other sermons supplied by these codices. This sermon, which in the printed editions is placed second under *On Lent*, we place first because, according to the order of the Freising codex—in which Ratherius’s sermons and books appear to have been transcribed in chronological sequence—it not only precedes the sermon that stands first in the printed editions, but is separated from it by four other treatises inserted between them. This indicates that the compiler followed not the order of subject matter but chronology.

To make this clear, we present here the series of treatises contained in the aforementioned codex. First is read the *Invective on the Translation of the Body of Saint Metron*, which was said to have been stolen on 27 January 962. II. A decree issued against clerics ordained by the usurper, dated 8 February 963. III. Another decree on the same matter, dated 9 February of the same month and year. IV. The first sermon on Lent. V. The first sermon on Easter. VI. The first on the Ascension of the Lord. VII. Another on the feast of Pentecost. VIII. A short work on his own fall. IX. The following note occurs: “This is to be appended to the sermon which the same Ratherius made longer on Lent.” The sermon indicated is the second on Lent, to which the apology for that same sermon is said to be appended; this apology is transcribed in the same codex after the note. X. The synodical letter issued in Lent of 966. XI. The sermon on Mary and Martha, delivered around August of the same year. XII. The short work *On Idle Speech*.

Two sermons on Lent deserve particular attention. They are not joined together, as those who follow the order of subject matter do, for any other reason than that the compiler followed not the order of topics but that of time. For the same reason he did not join all the sermons together, but inserted various others between them, as the sequence of events required. Thus the first sermon on Lent, which in the codex follows two short works written in February 963, may suitably be assigned to Lent of that same year. Accordingly, the three sermons that follow—on Easter, the Ascension, and Pentecost—belong no less to that year than does the short work *On His Own Fall*, although the latter may fit the beginning of the following year, before Lent. All these therefore precede the longer second sermon on Lent, delivered, as we shall say in its proper place, in 964.

## ON LENT

[Col. 0689A]

### 1

I exhort and admonish you—and any among this congregation who are like me—to heed with the ear of the heart the prophetic counsel that says, “Return, transgressors, to the heart” (Isa. 48:6). Let each of us consider why he was created, why he was born, why he was reborn, at what price and for what reason he was redeemed. Let him ask whether he has rendered due thanks to his Creator, Maker, and Redeemer, and whether he has obeyed, as he ought, his most salutary commands.

And if, as I would wish, he does not find himself blameworthy in this, let him give thanks to his Maker, Redeemer, and Protector, not arrogantly attributing it to himself. Let him rejoice humbly, continually desire from him a good outcome in such matters, and unceasingly beg that he may never rightly be called a transgressor.

**Note:** The Freising copy reads *non inveniet* (“will not find”) rather than *non invenit* (“does not find”).

### 2

I admonish those who have acted otherwise not to despair, but, remembering God’s mercy toward sinners, attested by countless examples, let them hasten with the utmost speed to turn from their wickedness while they are sound and unharmed, lest, when they wish to do so, they be unable because they did not wish to do so while they could.

Yet if they do this, they will undoubtedly stir up against themselves that ancient adversary, who will immediately exert all his strength against them and try to entangle them in their former vices.

**Note:** The same copy reads *pejoribus* (“worse [vices]”).

“But everyone,” as the Apostle says, “who competes in the contest abstains from everything” (1 Cor. 9:25). Since these days have been assigned to us above all, generally and individually, for struggling against so savage, cruel, and crafty a tyrant—with God’s help—let us abstain from everything

**Note:** We have supplied *nos* (“ourselves”) from the same codex. that makes him stronger and us utterly weaker.

What these things are, let the Apostle say more clearly: “I beseech you,” he says, “as strangers and pilgrims, to abstain from carnal desires, which wage war against the soul” (1 Pet. 2:11). Behold what makes us weak and what makes him strong: carnal desires.

**Note:** The printed editions read *efficient* (“makes”). By failing to abstain from them, we make our souls vulnerable to attack.

For since no one serves as a soldier except for someone, and since it is not explicitly stated for whom carnal desires serve as soldiers, while they are said to wage war against the soul, they are plainly shown to serve the devil.

**Note:** The printed editions read *dicitur* (“is said”). Construe: “Since no one serves as a soldier except for someone, and since it is not stated more explicitly here for whom carnal desires serve as soldiers, when they are said to wage war against the soul, etc.” There is no other adversary of our souls except the one who immediately attacks them when God, in his just judgment, abandons them. God abandons them in just judgment if they themselves have first abandoned him—although he has by no means abandoned countless others who abandoned him; in that case he acts more from mercy than from justice.

### 3

Since carnal desires wage war against our souls on behalf of the devil, let us oppose abstinence to them, lest their commander triumph over us; and, with God’s help, we shall have the victory.

Let us therefore return to the Lord, brothers, with all our heart, in fasting, weeping, and mourning (Joel 2:12). But from whom to whom do you think we are being told to return? From the enemies of our souls—carnal desires—to the abstinence that is their friend; from the devil, on whose behalf they serve as soldiers, to the Lord, who, if we wish, fights against him for us day and night.

But if we wish to fight against him, let us strive to drive him far from us and cast him out of our hearts, rather than fostering him within ourselves. For, as the Lord says, he sleeps “under the shadow, in the secret place of the reed, and in moist places” (Job 40:16). The shadows are the crafty; the reed signifies hypocrites, outwardly pleasant but inwardly empty; the moist places are the limbs of the voluptuous and their lustful hearts.

Nevertheless, let us know, on the testimony of the Lord, that no one can cast out this kind of spirit either from himself or from another except by prayer and fasting (Mark 9:28). But how can he cast the devil out of himself by prayer, when it is said, “Whoever turns away his ear so as not to hear the law, his prayer shall be accursed”? (Prov. 28:9.) Would that our prayer, even if it were not heard, were at least not accursed!

And elsewhere: “Whoever turns away his ear from the cry of the poor, he himself shall cry out and not be heard” (Prov. 21:13). Here something still deeper is implied: unless you help the poor person who cries out to you, God will not hear you when you pray.

**Note:** The printed editions have *praeter quid*, incorrectly. We have preferred the Freising codex, in which *quid* is used in the sense of *aliquid* (“something”); and, relying on the same codex, have added *freti* (“relying [on his help]”).

But how do you fast? By abstaining from vices, surely, since the Lord says, “Do not fast as you have done until this day” (Isa. 58:4), followed by the rest of that passage.

Therefore, if we wish to drive the devil from our hearts, let us fast, pray, and give alms according to our ability; but let us also have the Lord as witness that we wished to go beyond our ability. Thus, relying on his help, we shall be able to overcome the carnal desires that wage war against our souls.

### 4

But someone says: “If we abstain from everything the flesh desires, how shall we live?”

**Note:** Thus the Laon and Freising codex; the printed editions read *vivimus* (“do we live”).

 Does not a hungry person desire to eat, and a thirsty person to drink, even if not excessively or expensively? Does not someone suffering from sleep—for these are merely examples from among countless things that are honorable and necessary—wish to sleep?”

The answer is that this commandment does not forbid what is necessary, but what is superfluous, harmful, disgraceful, and prohibited by God.

Hence the other Apostle says, “Make no provision for the flesh in its desires” (Rom. 13:14). Here we are certainly commanded to supply the body with what is necessary in such a way that we submit our mind to no pleasure. Otherwise, while reason ought to be the mistress and the flesh the servant, we would crush the mistress because of the servant, making the one who ought to obey command and the one who ought to command obey.

Our abstinence, moreover, is useless for perfection in every respect unless it is threefold: first, that we cease from wicked thought; second, from harmful speech; third, from evil action, out of fear or love of God. Thus, cleansed by God’s merciful gift from every defilement of flesh and spirit, we may at least during these holy days celebrate with joy and gladness the most holy Easter that is to follow them.

May he help us who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns as God, forever and ever. Amen.

---

### 581 SERMON II [or I]

## ON LENT

Inscribed by the author:

**Note:** Since this heading, presenting the title of the sermon, was prefixed by the author himself, we place it among the sermons with Acherius, although it is more a book or treatise than a sermon. Sigebert, in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 127, calls it a little book; Giles of Liège, in chapter 45, cited in Chapeauvillium’s first volume of the *Deeds of the Bishops of Tongeren*, page 176, follows him: “He wrote a book which he entitled *Ineffectual Chatter*, as it seemed to him.”

The same book, which refutes the Anthropomorphites at length in sections 29 and following, was also mentioned by Fulcuin in chapter 24, with the title *Ineffectual Chatter* suppressed, in these words: “There is also a little book by the same Ratherius against the Anthropomorphites, who depict God—that is, the invisible Godhead itself—through the outlines of bodily members.”

We believe this was the reason why Sigebert and others who followed him praised it as a work distinct from *Ineffectual Chatter*—although it is one and the same work—namely, because it attacks the Anthropomorphites. He wrote against the heresy of the Anthropomorphites, that is, against those who said that God had a bodily and human form. See what we have observed more fully in the general preface, § 2, at the end.

Sigebert assigns this tenth-century heresy of the Anthropomorphites—which, through ignorance, deceived some people only in these regions—to the year 939 in his *Chronicle*, and others later wrote the same thing on Sigebert’s authority. But when Sigebert did not know the precise date of events and had to assign them to some year in his *Chronicle*, he arbitrarily attached them to one year or another, as could be shown by many other examples. Consequently, no certain year can be extracted from his *Chronicle* in this matter either.

Ratherius himself refers to this sermon under the name of another work in *The Conjecture of Quality*, section 6, where he quotes several words from it. *The Conjecture of Quality* was written at the beginning of 966.

All Ratherius’s works collected in the Laon and Freising manuscripts belong to the period during which he presided over the see of Verona for the third time. This sermon was edited by Acherius from the Laon manuscript. Although it is missing from the Freising manuscript, its apology—written shortly after the sermon—is inserted there and will be appended to it. In the note given above, the sermon is indicated in these words: “This—that is, the apologetic work—is to be appended to the sermon which the same Ratherius made longer on Lent.”

This sermon was therefore composed by Ratherius after he had been restored to the see of Verona for the third time. In the Freising manuscript, where Ratherius’s short works appear to have been arranged chronologically, this sermon is listed after four sermons delivered in 963—on Lent, Easter, the Ascension, and Pentecost—and after the short work *On His Own Fall*, composed in that same year or at the beginning of the next, as we noted in note 1429 to the preceding sermon.

This sermon was therefore delivered either earlier, during Lent of 964, or later, during Lent of 965, before Ratherius wrote *The Conjecture of Quality* at the beginning of 966. Since during Lent of 965 he was driven about by great hardships and took refuge now here, now there, that period seems less suitable for composing so lengthy a sermon, or rather treatise. This sermon, or rather treatise, should therefore more probably be assigned to Lent of 964; and the error of the Anthropomorphites attacked in this sermon should be assigned to the same period.

*A very lengthy sermon on Lent by Ratherius of Verona, or, as he himself judged while alive, “Ineffectual Chatter.”*

### 1

Since no one instructed in divine doctrine is unaware that these forty days, which we have before us to cultivate in the manner of frugality, were instituted with this number because, besides having been prefigured by the Flood, they were also fulfilled by Moses and Elijah—the ministers of the Law and of prophecy—and continuously by the Lord himself, the inspirer of the prophets, the giver of the Law and its fulfiller, the giver of grace, and the founder of the Gospel—we cannot sufficiently marvel at the superstitious observance of those who, tasting nothing for twenty days, not forty, and spending the remaining twenty days at formal meals before the appointed hour, even to the point of gluttony and drunkenness, nevertheless do not hesitate to call Lent an observance of this sort of trifling. They ought rather to call it “Twentieth,” not “Fortieth.”

**Note:** This abuse is again restrained in the *Synodical Letter*, section 15. The text formerly read *licet omnino* (“although entirely”), which was less satisfactory. We corrected it to *nihil omnino* (“nothing at all”), in accordance with what is stated in section 2: “On one day they consume nothing,” and so forth.

Nor should you think, hearers, that by beginning a discourse of this kind we are trying to criticize the religious devotion of those who, in addition to what has been legally prescribed for all Christian people, impose upon themselves a stricter abstinence on two, three, or at least one day each week, remembering the saying, “Whoever has committed unlawful acts ought to abstain from lawful ones” (Gregory); and, “These things you ought to have done, without neglecting the others” (Matt. 23:23); and, “Whatever more you spend, when I return I will repay you” (Luke 10:35).

We do not criticize them, I say, but praise and approve them. Let them merely take care lest this also be said of them: “Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward” (Matt. 6:42).

### 2

Rather, the madness of those who on one day taste nothing, but on the next day—as we remember having seen more than once—indulge before the third hour in such excess that, alas, we have seen some staggering because of gluttony and drunkenness even at the third hour of the day on that most holy Saturday, when none of our people is permitted to celebrate Mass before the evening hour, is to be mourned.

**Note:** Construe as follows: “On the other day”—that is, the day on which they indulge in gluttony and drunkenness before the third hour—“so that, as we remember having seen more than once, we have even seen, alas, some staggering from gluttony and drunkenness at the third hour of the day on that most holy Saturday, when none of our people is permitted to celebrate Mass before the evening hour. For we cannot complete Lent according to the Western rite unless we extend the fast until the evening of that holy Saturday.” The reason Ratherius mentions the Western rite will be understood from section 5.

What else can one say that such people have done except that on Good Friday they fasted, as it were, for the Lord, while on Saturday they received from the devil, as compensation for their fast, that very gluttony? Unless perhaps someone is so foolish as to think that this Lent has earned the privilege that, contrary to the established order of other times, it should contain a day that does not begin in the morning and end in the evening.

### 3

The opportunity for sinning by those who violate Lent is plainly similar to that of those who violate the Lord’s Supper. For the sacred canons state: “If anyone says that the fast ought to be broken on the Thursday of Holy Week, let him be anathema.” And after the ninth hour of the day, the joy of those who rightly celebrate the greatest day of that solemnity is most properly expressed.

**Note:** The occasion for the transgression is similar in the case of those who violate Lent on the Lord’s Supper: they dine beforehand and do not wait for the evening, when the office of that day, begun at the ninth hour, ends.

The person who, having fasted until that same hour as on other days, comes to church, dines with the Lord—that is, receives on that very day the sacraments instituted under his body and blood—then eats modestly in great joy, washes the feet of the poor, sits down and drinks in God’s name without excess, gives thanks to God, blesses himself as he goes to bed, fortifies himself with the Lord’s sign, and departs, is defended as not having broken the fast.

Before the ninth hour, however, since the custom of no nation has ever called any meal “supper,” we cannot cease wondering how anyone dares to celebrate before that hour a Mass

**Note:** The printed editions read *saltem eamdem* (“at least that same [hour]”), incorrectly; the sense of the context supplies the correction. Those criticized dared to celebrate Mass on the Lord’s Supper before that ninth hour and then to break the fast.

 which contains nothing other than the Lord’s Supper, celebrated in the evening, just as the office of Saturday represents the Lord’s Resurrection.

**Note:** Construe and explain as follows: Both of these observances make empty the excuse that some people offer, namely, that two additional days have been added to the forty. There were people who tried to excuse the violation of the fast on these two days—the Lord’s Supper and Holy Saturday—by claiming that it was compensated for by two other fasting days added to Lent, namely the Wednesday and Thursday before the First Sunday, since formerly the beginning of the fast was counted from the First Sunday, not from Ash Wednesday, as later became customary.

These two observances, then, make empty the excuse that some people put forward on the basis of two days added to the forty.

### 4

We add further that, according to the exhortation of blessed Gregory (*Book I, Homily 16 on the Gospels*, section 5), we cannot give God a tenth of our days unless we take care to extend Lent until the evening of Holy Saturday.

### 5

It must certainly be understood that, although the Churches share one faith, their customs differ. The Eastern Christians make Lent both longer and stricter than we do; therefore they begin the paschal joy at the third hour of Holy Saturday, as is said—something that we are by no means permitted to do.

For they are said to celebrate Baptism, not on that day as we do, but only at Epiphany and Pentecost, contrary, indeed, to the regulations of our canons.

**Note:** Here Ratherius was misled by someone else’s report and thereby took occasion to err. The Easterners, or Greeks, did not fast during Lent on Saturdays, except Holy Saturday, on which alone they observed the fast. On the Saturdays when they did not fast, they celebrated Mass at the third hour. On those days of Lent when they observed the fast, they did not celebrate the Eucharist.

What belongs to the other Saturdays of Lent Ratherius mistakenly thought applied to Holy Saturday, on which they observed a solemn fast, so that neither was the sacred rite celebrated nor could paschal joy begin at the third hour.

### 6

We also condemn the excessively ridiculous folly of those who, contrary to the permission granted to everyone to take whatever they wish at the ninth hour of the day, choose to prolong the fast every day until night so that at night they may stuff their bellies as though with permission.

For since the sacred Gospel reading tells us of the Lord that, “When he had fasted forty days and forty nights” (Matt. 4:2), he afterward became hungry, but did not consent to the tempter who urged him to eat, the person who, hungry after fasting, does not overcome the appetite of the throat—as the Lord overcame the devil who tempted him—is not shown to fast according to the Lord’s example.

**Note:** Construe as follows: The person who, hungry after fasting, does not overcome the appetite of gluttony, as the Lord overcame the devil the tempter.

**Note:** The same expression occurs in the *Synodical Letter*. Those who extend their fast until evening are not criticized for fasting according to the ancient discipline, but because they choose this fast so that at night they may, as though licensed, gorge their bellies.

### 7

Those also fast badly who do not give to the poor what they take away from their bodies, but preserve it either for their own belly or, what is worse, for Mammon, that is, the demon of greed.

### 8

God does not approve the fast of those who, on days of abstinence, devote themselves to slander, quarrels, and criminal actions.

**Note:** Abstinence from wine in the Lenten fast is noteworthy in this period. The author of Sermon 443 in the appendix to Augustine uses similar reasoning: “What profit is it not to drink wine and to be drunk with the poison of anger? What profit is it to abstain from meats created for eating and to tear the limbs of one’s brothers with malicious slanders?” They abstain from wine, but are always drunk on the poison of envy; they do not eat meat, yet by gnawing at others they continually tear their reputations to pieces. The sweetness of drink is absent from them, but the more pernicious bitterness of wicked thoughts torments them throughout the night.

Against the madness of both the former and the latter, we approve instead what the most learned Jerome says: “It is better to take a little every day than enough only rarely.” Truly, truly: it is better, and safer against vainglory. For who, observing you eating little at the permitted hour of the day with others, can judge whether you do this from fear of God or, like many, because you are unable to eat?

As the same writer says, two-day or three-day fasts are often certainly performed not for God but for vainglory.

**Note:** Acherius reads *et justorum clementiam* (“and the clemency of the righteous”); we have adopted the correction introduced by the most recent editor of the *Spicilegium*.

### 9

But gluttons commonly offer this defense, though it is not entirely false: “It is better to abstain from vices than from food.”

But how, I ask, does the person who serves his appetite abstain from vices? Is not gluttony one of the eight principal vices, and threefold? When eating the forbidden fruit caused man to lose paradise, how will someone gain heaven by sometimes fasting but always sinning?

“What harm is there,” they say, “if I eat before the ninth hour, since I fast by eating only once a day?”

We reply: What did it profit Adam that he ate only once from the fruit of the forbidden tree and afterward abstained from that fruit? Did not that very disobedience to the divine command make him guilty forever? The one who forbade him to eat from that tree has commanded you to abstain until the ninth hour on days of fasting. If you dare to disregard this in disobedience, what kind of fast do you think you have performed?

### 10

Why is gluttony called threefold, unless because its first vice is eating before the appointed hour, and its second is eating a great deal at the appointed hour?

The third was omitted, evidently through the scribes’ error. It should be supplied as follows: “the third is eating more expensive and more delicious foods,” or something similar. This is clear from what follows, where either the abundance or at least the pleasantness of the foods compensates for the fast.

For, as someone says, God’s fast throughout the whole day is scorned when, in the evening or certainly on the following day, it is compensated for by the belly’s gluttony, either by a multitude of expensive foods or at least by their deliciousness.

“Give alms,” they say, “and eat what God permits.”

### 11

They would speak better if they said: “Give alms, fast, and pray.” Unless our fasts are carried upward by these two wings, they cannot ascend to heaven: namely, with the aid of prayer and almsgiving.

These three mutually support one another with such assistance that almsgiving and prayer carry fasting, prayer and fasting carry almsgiving, and almsgiving and fasting carry prayer to the rewarder of those who perform them—undoubtedly God—provided they are performed sincerely.

But unless they continually assist one another, any one of them, deprived of the other two, cannot, as we fear, appease the altogether just Judge who requires all three, God who loves perfect goodness.

### 12

Since this is so, and since we must not remain silent about prayers, which move our spirit, we likewise do not cease to rebuke those same people to whom the Apostle James says: “You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly” (James 4:3).

For the person who does not ask for what the Lord commands, but rather for what he forbids, asks wrongly. He commands us to desire and seek heavenly things; we, by contrast, desire and long for earthly things. He commands us to pray for those who persecute and slander us; we, on the contrary, pour out accursed prayers against those who persecute and slander us.

What is the character of those who spend the nights devoted to psalmody and prayers, but during the day occupy themselves with slander, wicked speech, idleness, and laziness, when night has rather been granted for rest and day for labor?

We believe that the one who said, “At midnight I rose to confess to you” (Ps. 118:62), and, “In the morning I will meditate on you” (Ps. 62:7), knew this very well. He consecrated only two hours to the night, yet said, “Seven times a day I have praised you” (Ps. 118:164).

We, brothers, must avoid with God’s help whatever is wrongly done, and must not forget the Apostle’s words: “Whether we are awake or asleep, let us live together with Christ” (1 Thess. 5:10). At night let us raise our hands—that is, our works—toward the holy place and bless the Lord (Ps. 133:2). After resting, let us rise and believe that, in accordance with the same Apostle, we ought to pray without ceasing even while remaining silent. Let us recall above all his words: “Whoever turns away his ear so as not to hear the law, his prayer shall be accursed” (Prov. 28:9).

But true worshipers, as the Lord’s voice tells us, “will worship the Father in spirit and truth” (John 4:23). Let us ask God not for what he forbids us to desire, but for what he commands us to desire, so that he may deem us worthy of the answer he gave Solomon when Solomon asked for wisdom (1 Kings 3:11).

The Gospel agrees with that answer: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things”—that is, the things necessary for the body—“will be added to you” (Luke 12:31).

### 13

What sort of prayers, and how heard, are those of people who, at the time of prayer, traverse everything, so to speak, while meditating upon theft, robbery, murder, adultery, the many kinds of fornication, and countless things like them, remembering in no way either the God whom they appear to be asking or the matter for which they are asking?

What, I ask, do they ask? Whom do they ask? For whom do they ask?

### 14

But since this is brought about by the plots of demons, who naturally begrudge the progress of prayer, and since worldly concerns, together with the things we so often see, say, and hear, greatly obstruct this undertaking, we must do what that blind man in the Gospel is recorded to have done.

**Note:** The words in brackets, absent from the text, have been supplied as required by the context, as the most recent editor of the *Spicilegium* rightly observed.

When passersby rebuked him to be silent, he cried out all the more loudly: “Son of God, have mercy on me!” (Mark 10:48).

Our mouth—for let us use the language of the most truthful truth in this matter—is heard so much less in prayer the more it is defiled by shameful speech.

### 15

Since we have now said enough about prayers for the present, let us turn to almsgiving. Although *eleemosyna* appears to derive its name from mercy (*misericordia*) [Note: The Vulgate has *a miseria*, “from misery.” We have corrected it from the meaning of the Greek word ἐλεημοσύνη, “mercy.” Shortly afterward, the most recent editor of the *Spicilegium* likewise correctly printed *misericordiae impendamus*, “let us expend mercy,” where the reading had been *miseriae impendamus*, “let us expend misery.”], nothing, as it seems to us, can more fittingly hold the first place in this order than the almsgiving of which the Wise Man admonishes us in these words:

> “My son, have mercy on your soul, pleasing God” (Ecclus. XXX, 24),

so that we may first of all extend this mercy to ourselves, by earnestly striving to do what pleases God. And because we are commanded to love our neighbor as ourselves, let us, with sound judgment, direct that same neighbor into the Lord’s way whenever it seems useful—whether by admonishing, entreating, or reproving him. If he lacks the necessities of the body, let us provide them for him from our lawful labors, according to what we are able.

For we hold it written:

> “He who offers sacrifice from the substance of a poor man is like one who sacrifices a son in the sight of his father” (Ecclus. XXXIV, 24).

When we do this, let us remember that Lord’s saying:

> “When you make a dinner or a supper, do not invite the rich, because they have the means to repay you; but invite the poor, and you will be repaid in the resurrection of the righteous” (Luke XIV, 12–14).

No one is rich in that matter in which he needs assistance. Accordingly, what we give him we do not give to a rich man but to one in need. Let us do this solely out of reverence for God and love of Christ, guided by the authority of that commandment:

> “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do likewise to them” (Matt. VII, 12).

When we are urged to make friends for ourselves from the mammon of iniquity (Luke XVI, 9), this is not said so that we may take from one person what we give to another. As Augustine says, it is better to give to no one than to take from someone. Rather, we are to recognize that although riches have been given communally to the whole world, no one can gather them in any way without the evil of greed. For, as Jerome says:
