> “Every rich man is either unjust or the heir of an unjust man.”

And since the Psalmist says:

> “Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and the poor” (Ps. XL, 2),

let us take care that the one who needs more receive more, and the one who needs less likewise receive less. Since we are also commanded to do this, let us give preference to the good over the wicked, if we are able to distinguish them. If we cannot, let us follow the one who says:

> “Do not choose whom you will have mercy on.”

Let us also beware of provoking anyone, even if he asks too insistently:

> “God loves a cheerful giver” (II Cor. IX, 7).

And because, as blessed Ambrose says, the bestowal of good things has often incurred offense through delay, let us carefully heed the one who says:

> “Do not say to your friend, ‘Go and come back, and tomorrow I will give you,’ when you are able to give immediately” (Prov. III, 28).

In all these matters let us take care that we perform the good we do not for empty glory, but in obedience to God’s command and out of consideration for our common nature. For the Lord commands:

> “When you give alms, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing” (Matt. VI, 3).

This saying may also seem to command that nothing be found in our almsgiving which has been acquired from a left-hand work—that is, from unjust labor. [Note: The same editor aptly observed: “If it were left to my judgment, I would read: *quod sequitur . . . innuit* [‘what follows . . . indicates’].”] The following words, however, seem rather to indicate that ostentation is what is being condemned. He continues:

> “Let your almsgiving be in secret, and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you” (ibid., 4).

The Apostle likewise says:

> “He who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly” (II Cor. IX, 6).

And because, just as water extinguishes fire, almsgiving extinguishes sin (Ecclus. III, 33), let us consider what a little water does when thrown upon a very great fire.

For this consideration the advice which Tobias, in a play on the same word, gave his son is very useful:

> “My son, if you have much, give abundantly; if you have little, strive to share even that gladly” (Tob. IV, 9).

Nothing is dearer to God than good will. Even a cup of cold water given with good will does not lack the reward of recompense, as the Lord himself says in the Gospel (Matt. X, 42). To him the devoted Psalmist sings:

> “In me are your vows, O God” (Ps. LV, 13),

that is, “the good will which, since you see all things, I offer to you.”

Therefore, if someone is so poor that he has absolutely nothing to give, let him believe that giving himself is sufficient. For it is said:

> “Give to everyone who asks you” (Luke VI, 30),

that is, “give yourself both to the one to whom you give something and to the one to whom you give nothing.” For example, someone asks you to give him bread, but you have no bread to give. Give yourself—that is, give your good will, by which you would most gladly give him bread if you had any. And because

> “A good word is better than the best gift” (Ecclus. XVIII, 17),

strive with all your strength so that, if food to extend is lacking in your hand, a good word to answer with may not be lacking from your tongue.

### 16

Since all these things, when offered without charity—wondrously, yet truly, to say it—will profit nothing, as the Apostle testifies:

> “If I distribute all my possessions to feed the poor, and if I hand over my body so that it may burn, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” (I Cor. XIII, 3),

in order that we may preserve the laws of that same charity unbroken, let us lend the ear of our heart to the one who says:

> “If you offer your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go first to be reconciled to your brother; then come and offer your gift” (Matt. V, 23–24).

If the person who, by injuring his brother, has grieved him in some way does not disdain to do what the Lord has urged, let the person who has something against his brother because he has been injured likewise not turn a deaf ear to this admonition:

> “When you stand to pray, forgive whatever you have against anyone, so that your heavenly Father may also forgive you your sins. But if you do not forgive, neither will he forgive you your sins” (Mark XI, 25–26).

[Note: The reading is corrupt, says the editor cited above; it may be restored as follows: *suasum … dedignetur*, “let him not disdain to do what has been urged,” referring to the preceding text: “let him not disdain to do what the Lord has already urged,” namely, “If you offer…” This is indeed the wording in Sermon II on Easter, no. 2. I would suggest that those who remember having injured someone should recall the saying, “If you offer…,” while those who have themselves been injured, and whose offender has sincerely sought forgiveness, should not forget the saying, “When you stand to pray…”]

### 17

There are, however, people like our own kind who are extremely ready to forgive what is committed against God, but, if they could, would pursue what is done against themselves with perpetual hatred. Yet charity would demand rather that they easily forgive offenses committed against themselves and exact the strictest vengeance for offenses committed against God—though without forgetting the saying:

> “Let the one among you who is without sin be the first to throw a stone at her” (John VIII, 7).

Moreover, let us not believe that any good should be done as compensation for evil: that you fast for this reason, give alms for this reason, weary the air with prayers for this reason, or forgive what has been done against you for this reason—namely, so that you may think yourself permitted to commit adultery, fornication, or anything similar with impunity. For forgiveness of sins is promised to no one unless, after turning back, he abandons them.

### 18

Since our fasts, prayers, and almsgiving are thus—alas!—often contemptible, we may fear that what Jeremiah lamented about us has come to pass:

> “The enemies saw her and mocked her Sabbaths” (Lam. I, 7),

and that the Lord has commanded us through another prophet:

> “Do not fast as you have done until this day” (Isa. LVIII, 4).

### 19

According to the Apostle, whatever is done without faith is sin (Rom. XIV, 23), while faith without works is idle or dead (Jas. II, 20). Therefore we must by no means pass over those deceivers of souls who, contrary to the confirmation of the Catholic faith—which contains the teaching that the Lord will come to judge the living and the dead (Athanasian Creed), and the world by fire, and that “those who have done good will go into eternal life, but those who have done evil into eternal fire” (John V, 29)—in their miserable wickedness promise impunity to all the baptized.

They say:

> “God is so pious and merciful that he permits no Christian to enter hell.”

They would be speaking truly if they were able to believe that only the one who does Christ’s will is a Christian. But when they hear the Apostle Peter saying:

> “It would have been better for them not to have known the way of truth than, after knowing it, to turn back” (II Pet. II, 21),

of whom, I ask, do they suppose this was said?

### 20

And since sacred authority maintains that four orders will be present at the final judgment—one, namely, which will judge with the Lord; another, which will be rewarded through judgment; a third, which will be condemned through judgment; and a fourth, which will neither be rewarded nor condemned through that judgment, since it is written in the Gospel:

> “He who does not believe has already been judged” (John III, 18),

and the Psalmist’s words are spoken:

> “Therefore the wicked do not rise in the judgment” (Ps. I, 5),

as though he were saying more plainly: “Even if they rise, they do not rise for the purpose of being judged, because they have already been judged; they rise so that, having received their bodies, they may go where they were destined before the ages”—

and by these wicked we must understand only unbelievers and those who were not baptized at all—what, then, does the third order of the condemned seem to you to be, except the order of believers, that is, of the baptized? Because they possessed faith but lacked the works of faith required there, they will justly be condemned to the eternal fire, which will unquestionably be hell, and will go there.

### 21

It is therefore most certainly established that the Lord warned someone:

> “Behold, you have been made well; go, and now do not sin, lest something worse happen to you” (John V, 14),

and said in another place:

> “The last state of that man becomes worse than the first” (Matt. XII, 45).

You are to understand that those redeemed by the immense humiliation of God descending from heaven to earth for human beings—through so many indignities and reproaches endured by him, through hunger, thirst, weariness, spitting, mock genuflections, false testimonies, vinegar, gall, a crown of thorns, and finally the cross, the piercing of his side, the pouring out of blood and water, the nailing of hands and feet, and the disgrace of an ignominious death; those washed in sacred baptism, enriched by the illumination of the Holy Spirit, endowed with knowledge of God’s will, tolerated for a very long time while doing evil, instructed by paternal scourges, drawn by the sweetest promises, invested with various secular and ecclesiastical honors, invited by the alluring promise of immeasurable benefits, and enriched by countless other privileges of grace—deserve greater punishments than those to whom no such things were granted.

For:

> “From everyone to whom much has been entrusted, more will be demanded,”

as a certain man not least among the Benedictines says (St. Benedict, Rule, ch. 2). And:

> “The servant who knows his master’s will and does not do it will deservedly be beaten with many blows” (Luke XII, 47).

### 22

But since God is omnipotent, and his mercy is nothing other than God himself, and his omnipotent mercy, like his justice, is likewise nothing other than God himself—we believe it apostasy even to doubt this—let us turn to that mercy while we live. When we are dead, we will do absolutely nothing; we will receive what we have done. And if someone does some good on our behalf, even if it does not benefit us, it will benefit him.

As for those purgatorial punishments after death, let no one flatter himself, I warn you, because they are not established for crimes but for lighter sins, which are signified by wood, hay, and straw (I Cor. III, 12).

But with these things established so certainly, what are we to say, or what counsel can we give, when we know that some are bound by evil habit, some by an oath, and some by magical practices or by certain other causes which, as they claim, cannot be avoided, so that they are in no way able to rise toward amendment? Whatever we say to them, they will undoubtedly answer—if not in words, then by the effect of their conduct—as did those invited to the supper in the Gospel (Luke XIV, 18, 20); and there is reason to fear that, similarly abandoned by the inviter, they may perish like Pharaoh in their hardening.

### 23

These are plainly the people who, although they could have been free, have voluntarily thrust their wretched feet into a net and walk among its meshes (Job XVIII, 8). While they extricate themselves from one danger, they fall into another, and there is reason to fear that they have been enclosed by the Lord in a way from which there is no escape.

But let us make an effort and say something. We urge them not to plunge themselves in any way into the abyss of despair, since they do not know what has been destined for them. For, as Scripture says:

> “A human being does not know whether he is worthy of hatred or love, but all things remain uncertain for the future” (Eccl. IX, 1).

Let them reflect on Lazarus, who was raised after four days. Let them cry out with that blind man even more insistently, persisting in fasting, prayer, and almsgiving—not so that they may thereby be permitted to sin, but so that by mercy they may be freed from sin. Let them cry aloud with the Canaanite woman, saying:

> “Have mercy on me, Son of David; my soul is grievously tormented by a demon” (Matt. XV, 22);

and:

> “Do not, Lord, do not let my evil overcome you, but overcome my evil with your good” (Rom. XII, 21);

and:

> “Rescue me, Lord, from the evil man; deliver me from the unjust man” (Ps. CXXXIX, 2),

that is, rescue me and restore me to you, my most merciful Maker and Redeemer. You certainly do this mercifully if you cause me, whether I wish it or not, to abandon whatever I contemplate against you. But if you permit my deadly efforts to prosper, what confidence in escape do you leave me? And if I do not cease from my present evils, what forgiveness can I hope for my past ones?

Let someone who groans under such burdens cry out insistently, as though complaining, until he deserves to be heard:

> “How long will my enemy be exalted? Look upon me and hear me, Lord my God” (Ps. XII, 3);

and:

> “Give me, Lord, a sign of good, so that those who hate me may see and be confounded, because you, Lord, have helped me and comforted me” (Ps. LXXXV, 17).

[Note: Construe the passage as follows: “By wearying the ears of the Lord, who most eagerly desires to hear, with these and similar cries, in heart, mouth, and deed, unless he ceases before the end of life, perhaps his mercy—who, when he wills, is powerful, and so forth—when knocked upon by the prayers of the saints, will answer him, who is thus wearying his ears, what he answered the woman who cried out insistently: ‘O woman…’”]

By wearying the ears of the Lord, who is most eager to hear, with these and similar cries, in heart, mouth, and hand, unless he ceases before the end of life, perhaps his mercy—who, when he wills, is powerful enough to raise up children for Abraham from stones (Matt. III, 9), and who “does not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn back and live” (Ezek. XXXIII, 11)—when knocked upon by the prayers of the saints, will answer him as he answered that woman who cried out insistently:

> “O woman”—that is, one who acts nowhere manfully but, with womanly softness, weakly succumbs to vices—“great is your faith,” that is, your perseverance in prayer; “let it be done for you as you wish” (Matt. XV, 28).

And his soul will be healed in that hour. May the mercy of our Redeemer grant this to all of us.

[Note: These words correspond to those in the Church’s secret prayer of the Mass on the Saturday before the Lord’s Passion: “Mercifully compel even our rebellious wills to turn to you.” Shortly afterward, Ratherius quotes the words “But if you permit my deadly efforts to prosper” in his *Qualitatis conjectura*, no. 6.]

### 24

There is also another clear proof of those who perish forever. Although we read in the Gospel that the Lord raised three dead people, we also read that he refused to raise a fourth who had been announced to him, and said instead:

> “Let the dead bury their dead” (Matt. VIII, 22).

These three dead people signify three kinds of dying souls: one hidden, another public, and a third habitual. The latter is said to stink, that is, to infect those nearby with the despair of recovery. Yet since nothing is impossible for God, and since all such people were in his sight from the beginning as he foresaw they would be at the end, he is shown to have loved them when their unexpected amendment is seen.

The fourth kind, however, is that death of which the Psalmist says:

> “For the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the unjust man is blessed” (Ps. X, 3),

and of whom the prophet says:

> “My people, those who call you blessed deceive you” (Isa. III, 12).

When someone both defends the evil he himself does and is further elated by the praises of flatterers, never returning to knowledge of himself, that most wretched man is buried beneath the false praise of flatterers just as a dead man is buried beneath a burial mound. One who never recognizes himself as dead never comes back to life; nor does one return to salvation who does not believe that he needs salvation.

Therefore, there is no doubt that the person who ends his life in such a condition has perished forever. With God’s help let us strive above all to avoid this kind of death. Let us not believe the flatterers’ lies about ourselves, but let us accuse our own sins and not become angry with those who accuse us.

Let no one therefore think it a trivial sin to raise up someone who is acting badly with false praises. When he hears the Lord’s words spoken about such a person:

> “The dead bury the dead,”

he should know that the flatterer irrecoverably kills one who might perhaps have risen to a life of amendment, had he not continually overwhelmed him with his flatteries.

### 25

Since, as blessed Augustine acknowledges (*On Lying*, ch. 14), there are eight kinds of lies, I confess that the lie of flatterers is the worst of all. They are especially the killers and buriers of souls—above all, of kings, leaders, counts, bishops, abbots, and the powerful of this age. They are not afraid of that terrible curse of the Lord spoken through the prophet:

> “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil” (Isa. V, 20),

and so forth.

Their deadly proclamations are symbolically cursed, as we read, first by Job and afterward by Jeremiah:

> “Let the day perish,” says Job, “on which I was born, and the night in which it was said, ‘A male child has been conceived’” (Job III, 3).

The other says:

> “Cursed be the man who brought news to my father, saying, ‘A male child has been born to you’” (Jer. XX, 15).

Against them the Psalmist invokes the Lord’s help:

> “Let those who say to me, ‘Well done, well done,’ be turned back at once in shame” (Ps. LXIX, 4).

### 26

We ought to abstain all the more from every lie because we can perceive with certainty that it proceeds from the devil, as the Lord testifies concerning him:

> “When he speaks a lie, he speaks from his own things, because he is a liar and its father” (John VIII, 44),

that is, the father of lying. The Psalmist says to the Lord:

> “You will destroy those who speak lies” (Ps. V, 7).

But if we understand this as applying to every lie, we shall judge no one free from destruction. For the same Psalmist says elsewhere:

> “Every human being is a liar” (Ps. CXV, 11).

“Then are you yourself, O prophet, a liar when you say this?” Far from it. In the first passage I referred to a particular lie which only the children of destruction speak; and I called every human being a liar in ecstasy—that is, in contemplation of God’s truth.

[Note: Thus in Psalm CXV, verse 2: “I said in my ecstasy: Every human being is a liar.”]

So too my Ecclesiastes (Eccl. III, 19), and after him the Apostle (Rom. VIII, 20), called humanity subject to vanity. Another writer further warns us how harmful every lie is:

> “The mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wis. I, 11);

and:

> “A false witness will not go unpunished” (Prov. XIX, 5).

### 27

How far a lie ought to be from the rulers of the Church can be recognized from a certain condemnatory saying, well worn by popular usage:

> “The words of a priest are either true or sacrilegious.”

Conversely, how greatly truth is loved by God is shown by God made man, when he speaks of himself and says:

> “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV, 6).

And through the prophet the Lord God says:

> “Love peace and truth” (Zech. VIII, 19).

The Apostle likewise urges us to celebrate Passover with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth (I Cor. V, 8).

After rejecting certain actions of his people, the Lord added:

> “These, then, are the things that you shall do: speak the truth, each one with his neighbor” (Zech. VIII, 16).

And repeating the command:

> “Judge truth and justice in your gates” (ibid.).

### 28

Behold, brothers and sons—may God grant that he has mercifully looked upon us—behold how many true evils, how many false goods, and how many evils mixed with goods we have recalled. What must we do in response to these things except, as we said earlier the Lord commanded, not fast in the same manner, not pray in the same manner, and not give alms in the same manner as we have fasted, prayed, and given alms until this day, lest we offer our enemies, namely the malignant spirits, further opportunity to mock us?

Rather, serving the Lord rationally in simplicity of heart, let us first take care that our goods are not false. Let us take care that afterward they are not nonexistent, later not few, and not disordered [understand: “that they be not”]. Let us never forget the advice which, although fruitlessly, we read was given to someone:

> “You have sinned; cease” (Ecclus. XXI, 1).

Let us also recall with it this most charming saying of one of our own writers, corresponding to it:

> “Do not be a doer of evil, and you will be a destroyer”—namely, a destroyer of evil deeds.

And let us not forget the other saying:

> “My son, do not add sin upon sin, saying, ‘The mercy of God is great’” (Ecclus. V, 5).

Reflecting on what follows, let us not be so contemptuous that, having composed prayers to appease him, and having undertaken fasts, prayers, almsgiving, and vigils contrary to reason—fasts, prayers, almsgiving, and vigils as perverse as those we have practiced until now—we believe that we can deceive the one who, invisible to all, penetrates everything with his gaze.

But if we wish to please him, let us strive to serve him as he commanded, so that we may deserve to receive forgiveness of sins and recover his grace, solely through his mercy—the mercy which we lost through the merit of our own free will.

### 29

When we thought that the end of our speaking had come here [Note: Thus with the most recent editor of the *Spicilegium*. Acherius had *cum hic non putavissemus*, “when here we had not thought.”], a reason arose for not being able to remain silent at all.

For a certain ancient heresy appeared here among us, although it was believed to have been exhausted everywhere—or rather, it appeared to have been dormant. The Latins have likewise become accustomed to calling it, borrowing the name from Greek, the heresy of the Anthropomorphites.

Only the day before yesterday, one of our countrymen reported to us that priests of the diocese of Vicenza, our neighbors, believe God to be corporeal. They were led to this belief by the fact that Scripture reads:

> “The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are toward their prayers” (Ps. XXXIII, 16);

and:

> “Your hands made me” (Job X, 8);

and:

> “Let us make humankind in our image and likeness” (Gen. I, 26).

Yet this likeness, or unlikeness, plainly pertains not to the body but only to the soul, which is indeed spirit—although a bounded and comprehensible spirit. Similar expressions are also found in Scripture [understand: “are to be read”]. These most foolish people do not understand that God is so inconceivable, inscrutable, ineffable, and incomprehensible that no human mode of speech can express anything proper concerning him.

[Note: Concerning this heresy among the ancients, see Theophilus of Alexandria’s Paschal Letter, Epiphanius, and especially Augustine, *On Heresies*, no. 50. Shortly afterward we wrote *quaedam*, “a certain,” where the text had *quosdam*, “certain people.” Construe the passage as follows: “A certain ancient heresy, which the Latin language has likewise become accustomed to calling the Anthropomorphites, borrowing the name from Greek, appeared here among us, although it was believed to have been exhausted everywhere; rather, it appeared to have been dormant.”]

### 30

For who would dare even to think—to mention only one example among many—that Christ, by nature, was a worm or a beetle? Yet by a certain likeness, speaking figuratively but truthfully about himself, he says:

> “But I am a worm and not a human being” (Ps. XXI, 7);

and through the prophet:

> “The beetle will cry out from the wood” (Hab. II, 11, from the Septuagint).

When this had disturbed us greatly [Note: Acherius’s edition had *promovisset*, “had advanced.” The most recent editor of the *Spicilegium* correctly emended it.], alas for the wickedness! we discovered that the same unbelief had so clung to the flock entrusted to us that, after we had spoken publicly about the danger and established by testimonies of Scripture that God is spirit, incorporeal, invisible, intangible, and immeasurable, some—alas, what grief!—even of our priests, murmuring, said:

> “What are we to do now? Until now we seemed to know something about God; now it seems to us that God is absolutely nothing if he has no head, no eyes, no ears, no hands, and no feet.”

To one of them we offer this reply:

> “Then, most foolishly, does your soul—or mine—seem to you to be nothing simply because you cannot see it? What sort of head does your soul have, what hands, what feet, or what other limbs? Show me, if you can, at least its color. If you cannot, I will show you its power.”

Set before me here two bodies, one with a soul and the other without a soul. Which of these two will see, hear, speak, and walk? The one that has a soul, or the one in which there is no soul?

You will answer, without doubt, that it is the one that has a soul. I, on the contrary, ask: Why not the one that does not have a soul? Plainly, because it lacks that very force, that very power, that immeasurably better and stronger principle which governed it so that it could do something, and without which it could do absolutely nothing.

For reason teaches that there is nothing visible which is not governed by the invisible.

### 31

Behold how much more powerful the invisible soul is than the visible body. What do you think of the life of the soul? Is it not itself much more invisible than the soul itself? And what would the soul be worth—or rather, what would the soul itself be—without life?

Absolutely nothing. For it is written:

> “The first Adam was made a living soul; the second, a life-giving spirit” (I Cor. XV, 45).

If, then, the soul—which is indeed spirit—is so much more powerful than the body that, without it, the body cannot even move itself, while the life of the soul—which is still more invisible—is so much more powerful than the soul that, without it, there cannot even be a life-giving spirit, which is God; and if the more invisible God is, the more inward he is to all things, so that, if one could properly speak in this way, he may be called the most invisible of all spirits and the most spiritual spirit of all spirits; and the more invisible he is to all spirits, the more inward he is to all; and the more inward he is, the more he must be believed to be the ruler, inspirer, mover, and giver of life to all spirits, just as the soul is to all bodies, or rather, just as life is to all living beings—and all the more excellently, the more ineffable and powerful he is.

### 32

For just as the soul would be nothing if life did not exist, so every creature, whether visible or invisible, corporeal or incorporeal, would be absolutely nothing if God did not exist—the God who, so to speak, gives life to all things, as the life-giving Spirit. The more inward he is to all things, the more invisible he is; just as the spirit in bodies is more inward in proportion as it is more invisible, and more invisible in proportion as it is inward even to ineffability.

Accordingly, he is so powerful even to omnipotence that whatever exists exists through him; whatever lives lives through him; whatever moves is moved through him—again, to ineffability.

We said “to ineffability” because we recall the movements of murderers, thieves, and adulterers. They would not have the very movement which they most wickedly abuse unless they received it from God, even though they possess in themselves the vice of evil motion.

### 33

Such is the force, such the power, such the immeasurable and impenetrable nature, such the inscrutable substance, such the incomprehensible divinity, such the immeasurable greatness, such the beauty radiating from itself upon all things, such the gaze penetrating everything with inward sight, such the invisible hand containing all things, such the brightness illuminating the universe, such the height surpassing everything, such the depth enclosing all things, such the activity accomplishing all things, such the immovable motion leaving nothing inaccessible to it, such the flavorful sweetness nourishing all things, such the breath capable of distinguishing everything, such the subtle hearing that recognizes from afar not only the voices but also the intentions of all things.

[Note: That is, hearing so subtle that it recognizes from afar not only voices but also the intentions of all things; it is said that Moses cried out to it in silence. Shortly afterward Acherius’s edition had *sermonem*, “speech,” where the most recent editor of the *Spicilegium* correctly printed *sermones*, “speeches.”]

And, so that we do not carry on to infinity about the one whom the words of all who have been, are, or will be have not been, are not, and will not be able to bring to an end, let us say this: he is ineffable, inconceivable, and everything to all; finally, he is uncircumscribed, wholly everywhere, nowhere less and nowhere greater. He contains the thrones of heaven and looks into the abysses; he weighs the mountains and encloses the earth in his palm. To him all heavenly, earthly, and infernal beings bend the knee.

He is the Spirit who is the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; one God, spirit individually, spirit indivisibly, who is above all, through all, and in all—God blessed forever.

Does he seem to you to be nothing because he does not have a body which you can see? Have you not taken the trouble, either by reading or by asking those who read, to learn who those eyes of the Lord are that are upon the righteous (Ps. XXXIII, 16), or what his ears are that attend to their prayers, or what his face is that is against those who do evil, to destroy their memory from the earth (ibid., 17), or what his hands and feet are?

Instead, foolishly turning all these things over in your craftsman’s imagination, you said—not merely in your heart but, with much greater madness, to me:

> “There is no God”; or, more shamefully, “God is nothing if he does not have feet and hands.”

Rather, precisely because you were created rational, you ought to infer from reason that the one who created you is all the more God the less you are able to see him.

As blessed Gregory says, to see him now is to perceive his reason by reasoning. We know something of him as though in part when we recognize that we cannot know him worthily; we see him as though in part when we do not fail to understand that he can be seen by no one.

### 34

> “We considered him, and there was no appearance; therefore we did not esteem him” (Isa. LIII, 3).

This is what those accomplices of yours are recorded to have said about God’s Wisdom incarnate for our sake. But you have spoken more madly about the whole Trinity, imitating those who, while Moses delayed on Mount Sinai, said to Aaron his brother:

> “Make gods for us to go before us; for we do not know what has happened to Moses” (Exod. XXXII, 1).

So too, when you grew weary of being led from Egypt—that is, from the darkness of ignorance—to the light of knowledge of the invisible God, you began, in one way or another, most foolishly to manufacture idols for yourself in your heart. Forgetting God’s immensity, you depicted some great king, as it were, sitting on a golden throne. You imagined the angelic host as winged men, such as you are accustomed to see painted on walls, clothed in white garments and standing beside him.

Yet those beings are spirits and, according to their nature, invisible. When they appear to human beings, they do not appear in their own nature but in a form which God chooses to give them—whether from this bodily air, however tenuous it may be, or from whatever source he wills—or, if it pleased him, as it did at the beginning of the whole creation, from nothing, so that they may be seen by bodily eyes. They also produce a voice from that same air, through their airy—so to speak—lips, mouths, and throats, in a manner incomprehensible to us but nevertheless perceptible to those to whom it has been divinely granted to see or hear such things.

35. “On Monday,” they say, “the archangel Michael celebrates Mass for God.” O blind madness! [Note: The same editor corrected this. In Acherius it reads *clementia* (“clemency”); below, *an adeo insanus* (“or are you so insane?”).] What, then, do you think makes the first or second feria for us? Is it not the rising and setting of the sun? And what other sun is there in heaven except the Sun of Justice, Christ, with the Father and the Holy Spirit? Or are you so insane as to think that there is night in heaven, whose illumination makes the following day? How, then, is the light there eternal if any darkness interrupts it?

In what temple does holy Michael sing Mass, when John says in the Apocalypse: “I saw no temple in it” (Rev. 21:22)? “The Lord,” it says, “is in his holy temple; the Lord is in heaven” (Ps. 10:15). Do you want me to answer you concerning that temple which now comes to mind? The Lord was in the womb of his virgin mother, without leaving the Father in heaven—at one and the same moment both in heaven and in the Virgin’s womb: in heaven timelessly, in his mother in time.

“You sit upon a throne,” says the Psalmist, “you who judge equity” (Ps. 9:6). We too have often sung: “You who sit upon the cherubim” (Ps. 79:2). We have understood *cherubim* to mean “fullness of knowledge,” and that this throne is called by the same name—namely, an angelic spirit, or rather, both throne and cherubim signify legions of angels. But upon whom among the angels does the Lord not sit, since Scripture also says of the soul of a righteous person that it is the seat of wisdom, while the Wisdom of God the Father is God the Son? And where does Wisdom sit without the one whose Wisdom it is?

36. But since it is characteristic of this heretic that he can be thoroughly refuted, yet not easily defeated, let us rejoice if, through this entire argument, we can persuade him not of what God is but of what God is not: namely, that he is neither corporeal, nor visible, nor measurable, being the Spirit of spirits, the most invisible of all spirits; and let us rejoice that the enemies of truth have been refuted.

But you, O sons, to whom we speak, we admonish to cast aside such trifles and falsehoods, remembering the one who warns: “Do not seek what is too high for you, and do not search out what is too deep for you” (Sir. 3:22). For there are many who, disdaining to become disciples of truth, become teachers of error, “understanding neither what they say nor the matters about which they make assertions” (1 Tim. 1:7). Turn instead to the Angel of Great Counsel, who says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6), and: “No one comes to the Father except through me” (ibid.). Consequently, neither does anyone come to the Holy Spirit except through him.

When Philip asked him to show them the Father, he answered: “Whoever has seen me”—that is, with those interior eyes by which God can in some manner be seen; for “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8)—“has seen the Father” (John 14:9). And he added: “Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?” (ibid., 10). This entire statement cannot stand unless you refer it to the invisible divinity of the Father and the Son. For whoever saw the Son in the flesh that he assumed for us did not thereby see the Father.

Otherwise, the Jews who persecuted him would also have seen him, though the Lord’s voice says to them: “You know neither me nor my Father. If you knew me, perhaps you would know my Father also” (John 8:19)—that is, if you had recognized my invisible and incorporeal divinity hidden within me, and had possessed a pure heart with which to contemplate it, then you would consequently have known my Father, who remains in me and in the Father.

He, therefore, who by this instruction made us understand that the Father himself, and the Son who said this, and the Holy Spirit are one God, said: “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19). He, I say, who with bodily lips moved by the God within him gave this command to the disciples—let him tell us what God is. “God is spirit,” he says (John 4:24); and after the resurrection he said to the doubting apostles: “Touch and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I have” (Luke 24:39).

37. If, then, a spirit does not have flesh and bones, how does it have a head, which certainly consists of flesh and bones? How does it have hands, arms, or, finally, lips, a tongue, a throat, lungs, arteries, the hollow of the palate, or four front teeth—by all of which, without question, voice is formed and speech produced? Yet Michael is said to sing Mass with these.

But you, who previously said, “Glory to God in the highest” (Luke 2:14), who sang it first? We answer: the angels. How? When it pleased God to grant them the ability to produce something that the shepherds could hear or understand, since they could in no way do this in their spiritual nature, they did so in the air, which, when struck, produces sound and is also called “heaven,” whence birds are called “birds of heaven.” They did not do so in the ether, nor in heaven, where no one needs to learn anything through the clamor of a voice—least of all God, who knows everything.

[Note: Construe: “Where no one needs to learn anything through the clamor of a voice, still less God,” and so forth.]

For the voice of the angels in heaven is nothing other than perpetual wonder at God’s splendor and ineffability, without movement of the tongue and without the clamor of a voice.

Even on earth God is more pleased by this, as we stated a little earlier, when he said: “God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth” (John 4:24).

And since, while Mass is being sung, the one who sings is refreshed by participation in the Lord’s body and blood, show me the bread and wine by which this is accomplished. “He gave them the bread of heaven,” you reply (Ps. 77:24). It is written: “Man ate the bread of angels” (ibid., 25). What other bread of heaven is there except the Lord Christ? From him heavenly beings receive spiritual food and enjoy it with immeasurable delight. Christ is rightly called the bread of angels, because they are truly nourished by his praise. For we must not believe that angels eat bodily bread.

What will you do concerning the wine? “I will not drink,” you reply, “from now on of the fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new with you in the kingdom of God” (Mark 14:25). This does not help your case at all. By “the kingdom of God” he means the Church, in which, as the Psalmist sings, he began to reign “from the wood” (Ps. 95:10 according to the Septuagint), and in which he began to give the inhabitants of that kingdom new wine—that is, his blood—together with the bread of his flesh. After his resurrection he appeared to the apostles for forty days, speaking about the kingdom of God and eating with them (Acts 1:3); consequently, there can be no doubt that he also drank with them.

Behold, wretched man: more foolish than the priests of Bel, you fed that corporeal god of yours for a year with half a lentil (Dan. 14:7). Turn your attention, at last, to our true God: invisible, incorporeal, intangible, immeasurable, uncircumscribed; creator of all things that were, that are, and that will be; ruler and disposer of all things. His eyes behold everything; his ears penetrate even the inner recesses of hearts; his arms contain all things; his hands accomplish all things; his feet move immovably through all things. All these things are God the Spirit—namely, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—whose unity consists in the Godhead and whose Trinity consists in the persons.

Our God, I say, must be recalled with great trembling and reverence and embraced with the greatest love. Turn your attention at last to such a God, who eternally nourishes his angels—even if you will not be convinced by us, at least be convinced by Augustine; and would that you might be converted. For concerning God’s speech to the angels and theirs to God, Gregory teaches you abundantly if you consult his *Moralia*.

[Col. 0711A]

38. Since, as can be seen, you are entirely unable to detach yourself from a carnal understanding, cling at least to that flesh which the Wisdom of God deigned to assume for us. That flesh undoubtedly sits in heaven at the right hand—that is, in equality with—the Father, who is everywhere “right-handed” and nowhere left-handed, since God is an uncircumscribed spirit. It sits with bones, which a spirit entirely lacks.

[Note: It is that flesh, with bones—which a spirit entirely lacks—that undoubtedly sits.]

Incorporeal spirits, namely the holy angels, stand incorporeally before his divinity; so too do the blessed souls, and, as some have thought, the bodies of the saints who rose with the Lord (Matt. 27:52), together with the souls of the righteous.

You are not of such merit that you can say with the Apostle: “Even though we once knew Christ according to the flesh, we know him now no longer” (2 Cor. 5:16). Yet if you desire in any way to investigate his divine substance, listen most attentively to that same one: “Philip,” he says, “whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9). That means: no one has seen either me in my divinity—which, if you perceived it, you could never say this—or him. “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). You see me in the flesh that I assumed for you; you do not see me in the divinity by which I am one with the Father. Therefore, if you wish to see the Father, cleanse that eye of the heart which can in some manner contemplate the invisible God. In looking upon me, you will see him—not by touching him with bodily light, but by contemplating him according to the measure of your spiritual capacity.

If you are concerned about his food, hear that same one: “My food is to do the will of him who sent me” (John 4:34); and: “Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Matt. 4:4); and: “I was hungry, and you gave me food” (Matt. 25:35)—speaking, of course, about the poor.

39. But since we have brought forward these complaints about our priests, by way of suggestion we admonish them along with ourselves to meditate day and night on the law of God and to search the Scriptures better than they have done until now. “For if the blind leads the blind, both will fall into a pit,” as the Lord says (Matt. 15:14).

Let them always consider the things God has commanded, keeping this commandment above all others before their eyes, since it is of the greatest importance and benefit. Necessity compels them to celebrate the Lord’s Passover not once a year but every day.

“You shall gird your loins” (Exod. 12:11)—that is, you shall strive to practice chastity. And: “Purify yourselves, you who carry the vessels of the Lord” (Isa. 52:11). “Everything touched by the unclean shall be unclean” (Num. 19:22), says the Lord, who does not lie.

“If they are clean,” someone said, “the young men, especially from women” (1 Sam. 21:4), speaking, of course, about the bread of the Presence, which prefigured our sacrifice.

Since this is so, how can we wretched men think about ourselves, or consider why we are called priests, when we bear such unclean hearts? Can what we offer be called holy when it has been handled by our most polluted hands? Is the blessing we pour forth, along with other things, from a mouth polluted even by a lustful kiss, truly a blessing?

Woe to us wretched men on account of such things—indeed, a thousand times woe! It had long ago been foretold: “As the people, so the priest” (Isa. 24:2). But would that at least any of the more honorable among God’s people were priests of this kind!

Furthermore, we urge them not to be so alienated from God that, first deceiving themselves and then fatally deceiving others, they should imagine that they can make the Holy Spirit lie through the mouth of the Apostle, who says: “Neither adulterers, nor fornicators, nor drunkards shall inherit the kingdom of God” (Gal. 5:21); and: “Know this, understanding it well: every fornicator, or unclean person, or adulterer, or covetous person—which is the service of idols—has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God” (Eph. 5:5).

But lest this entirely truthful speech drive them to despair, let them know that it is not spoken of those who were once adulterers, fornicators, and covetous, but of those who persist in such things to the end and neglect to turn back to God. If they were granted eternal life, they would not cease sinning eternally; therefore they justly deserve to suffer eternal punishments, since they are worthy of them.

For we have learned of a certain man of our own time—would that no human being had known him, if it was destined that he should die in such a condition—and we grieved to find him so insolubly entangled in these vices that, when wretched old age was almost upon him, the reproach of conscience prevented him from daring either to kiss the book of the Gospel or to kiss the priest who was about to give him Communion. Miserably considering that the priest would be polluted by his kiss, he called to mind the saying: “Everything touched by the unclean shall be unclean” (Num. 19:22). He judged himself unworthy, especially because his mouth, together with his hands and arms, was polluted by a lustful embrace, and he feared even to touch the vessel that had touched so great a sacrament. Yet there was no sign of repentance in his hardened heart.

[Note: Read *hisque vitiis* (“and in these vices”), or something similar. Construe: “For we have learned of a certain man of our own time (would that no human being had known him, if he was destined to end such a course—that is, to die in the condition in which he now was), and we grieved to find him so insolubly entangled in these vices that, when wretched old age was almost upon him, the reproach of conscience prevented him from daring either to kiss the book of the Gospel or the priest who was to give him Communion. In his misery he thought that the latter would be polluted by his kiss, recalling the saying: ‘Everything touched by the unclean shall be unclean.’ He judged himself unworthy, especially because his mouth, together with his hands and arms, was polluted by a lustful embrace, so that he feared even to touch the vessel that had touched so great a sacrament; and yet,” etc. We have retained the reading of the most recent editor of the *Spicilegium*. Previously it read *proximarit* (“should approach”), and afterward *formidarit* (“should fear”). Note the kiss customarily given to the priest administering Communion.]

For this reason, we found two occasions that must not be passed over: first, that we should strive to avoid his example; and second, that we should plead God’s mercy for him all the more earnestly, the more we recognize his need of it.

40. For such a man is proved unable to love God at all, although he fears him irrationally, since he perceives God to be so opposed to his conduct.

[Note: Nothing could have been more corrupt than what Acherius had published: “He cannot possibly love him irrationally, while he fears God”; below it read: “who evidently … because the commandments.” The most recent editor of the *Spicilegium* corrected both passages excellently. See also note 723 on the meaning of this passage in the short work *On His Own Fall*.]

41. Nor is that promise of the Lord contrary to this, in which it is said: “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved” (Mark 16:16). For although someone of this sort may believe in God, he does not believe God, since he does not keep his commandments or preserve by his life the sacrament he received through faith; rather, by his conduct he destroys the very faith that the word establishes.

With the other faithful, he says, by the Lord’s permission: “Our Father, who art in heaven” (Matt. 6:9). But the devil is the father of all who live corruptly. Blessed Zeno, on the contrary, says this (St. Zeno, *On Judas*, treatise 14, book II, no. 4).

[Note: Compare note 1550 on Sermon II on the Ascension, where we explain, from Rather’s thought, the distinction between believing in God and believing God.]

May the piety of the one who came into this world to save sinners turn this away from us—Jesus Christ our Lord, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God, for ever and ever. Amen.

## Apologetic Appendix against the Critics of the Same Sermon

[Note: This apology for the preceding sermon was published by Acherius from the Laon manuscript. It was also possible to compare it with the Freising manuscript, which prefixed the note that will be found transcribed in note 1438 on the preceding sermon. This same sermon was composed somewhat later.]

1. Ratherius, bishop of Verona, does not say that God the Son, our Lord Jesus Christ—that is, the Wisdom of God incarnate for us—does not have a head, eyes, hands, feet, and the other members of a human body, together with a rational soul, full of God; for he truly believes that Christ ascended into heaven with body and soul, while his divinity had never been absent from heaven, and that, as the angels taught, he will come to judge the living and the dead (Acts 1:11).

Ratherius the bishop says that God—that is, the substance of divinity—does not have a body and is not a body that can be touched and seen, because “God is spirit” (John 4:24), as the Lord Jesus Christ said; and: “A spirit does not have flesh and bones” (Luke 24:39), as Christ himself says in the Gospel.

[Note: The Vulgate reads *Deo, cum corpore plena* (“full of God, with a body”). We have removed the words *cum corpore* (“with a body”), which were wrongly inserted, on the authority of the Freising manuscript; shortly afterward we have added *credat* (“he believes”), and then *nec est corpus* (“and is not a body”).]

2. Ratherius the bishop does not say that a man does wrong when he goes to the church of Saint Michael or hears the Mass of Saint Michael.

[Note: The church of Saint Michael at the gate is indicated; it is now commonly called the Gate of the Bursarii. From this passage we learn that this church was frequented on Mondays in the tenth century. The Mass of Saint Michael celebrated on Monday was, as they say, a votive Mass. At the end of the Ottobonian codex containing the Gregorian Sacramentary, in a script dating from approximately the eleventh century, among several votive Masses one reads: “On Monday, a Mass for requesting the assistance of the holy angels.” See Muratori, *Roman Liturgy*, vol. II, p. 386.]

Ratherius the bishop says that the man who claims that it is more appropriate to go to the church of Saint Michael on Monday or to hear the Mass of Saint Michael than to do so on another day is lying. Bishop Rather says that the man who claims that Saint Michael sings Mass is lying, since no creature can sing Mass except a human being alone: because a human being is rational, he has flesh and bones, without which Mass cannot be sung.

But a spirit, as the Lord says, does not have flesh and bones, although the angelic spirit—that is, the spirit who is angelic and not apostate—possesses reason more powerfully than a human being. Michael is a spirit, and an angelic spirit, and he always stands in God’s presence without flesh and bones. He praises him unceasingly without the book with which Mass is customarily sung, and without the bread and wine from which the Lord’s body and blood are customarily made in the Mass.

3. But if you ask what Saint Michael sings, “Work,” says Bishop Rather, “with God’s help, so that after death you may ascend to heaven; there you will hear what he sings.”

And if you wish to go to the church of Saint Michael, understand, says Bishop Rather, that Saint Michael does not receive you more willingly on Monday than on another day.

If you wish to ask him for something, understand, says Ratherius the bishop, that Saint Michael does not hear you more mercifully on the second feria than on the first, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, or seventh feria.

Since this is what Bishop Rather thinks, says, and asserts, whoever wishes may, if he can and dares, refute him; he does not forbid him but rather requests it—for he himself asks to be refuted.

## SERMON III

[Note: We now publish this sermon for the first time from the Lobbes manuscript, whose title attributes it to our author in these words: “A sermon of Rather, bishop of Verona, to be delivered to the people on the Lord’s Supper.” Fulcuin praises it in chapter 24. The lacunae marked by dots are due to the parchment having been eaten away.]

### ON THE LORD’S SUPPER

1. No one among the faithful, brothers, can doubt that if you have turned to the Lord with your whole heart, and possess in your hearts the humility that you display in your clothing, there is greater joy today before the angels of God over one of you than over ninety-nine righteous persons who have no need of repentance (Luke 15:7; Matt. 18:13), as Truth itself and our Redeemer says.

But please pay attention to what I prefaced: “if you have turned with your whole heart.” For if we do not turn with our whole heart away from the things for which we ask the Lord’s forgiveness, we ask God in vain to remove from us what we ourselves refuse to relinquish. Indeed, we kindle the Lord’s anger against ourselves all the more severely because we not only remain in our sins but also falsely pretend before human beings, with a deceitful heart, that we have turned from them.

For the most holy Job says: “Hypocrites and the crafty provoke God’s anger” (Job 36:13). He says “provoke.” How greatly should we fear if he had said merely “deserve”? But since he says “provoke,” who would not tremble? Who would not, as it were, breathe out his spirit almost at the sound of this thunder?

One who has no hypocrisy rightly does not tremble. But how can one in whom hypocrisy is partial or complete stand before a voice of such magnitude?

Or is it because he lies there asleep not merely in slumber but in death? Let him awaken, I beg; let him rise, I urge—for perhaps I am speaking to myself. Let him hear the girl being called: “I say to you, arise” (Mark 5:41); or, certainly, because of the weight of his stony habit: “Lazarus, come out” (John 11:43).

The former reference signifies death lying in thought; the latter, the most wretched persistence of habit. Let him come out, even if bound; the merciful kindness of God will release him if he reveals himself through confession, and will disclose to his face the light of which he was deprived while he failed to see how gravely he was offending—indeed, provoking—the Lord.

2. And I ask you, brother, whoever you are who are such a person—and certainly like me—if you had an enemy most hostile to you, a wicked plotter against all your honor and even your life, and I were to take away your tunic and give it to him, would you not be more fiercely angry because I had given it to him than because it had been taken from you?

So, yes, so does the Almighty, believe me, bear more heavily the fact that what belongs to God is given to the devil than the fact that it is given neither to God nor to the devil.

Fasts, prayers, almsgiving, and other things of this kind belong to God alone; they must be performed solely out of love or fear of him. Whoever therefore performs them with a deceitful heart for human praise or the empty glory of this world—what else does he do but lavish God’s property upon the devil?

Therefore I beg you, repeating my warning again and again, to display in your hearts what you display in your clothing, so that you may obtain remission of your sins.

But hear what this remission is and how it comes to us: “If the wicked man turns away from his wickedness and does judgment and justice, he shall live with life and shall not die” (Ezek. 18:27). “He shall live with life,” it says. What life? Temporal life? No; the righteous die just as the unjust do. But the righteous die temporally, whereas the wicked die eternally.

[Note: Supply “they will die eternally.”]

The wicked do not die eternally in the flesh, for they will rise on the last day; but in the soul whoever dies in sin dies eternally, since in the present age he does not merit to rise through confession, repentance, and God’s mercy.

Have you therefore turned away from iniquity? Do judgment and justice, and you shall live with life and not die—that is, do not fall back into sin. What do I mean? “Turn away from evil and do good, and dwell for ever and ever” (Ps. 36:27).

For if you turn away from evil but do not do good, hear this: “Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matt. 3:10). And concerning the unclean spirit: “When it comes,” he says, “it finds the house empty, swept clean and decorated. Then it goes and takes with it seven other spirits more wicked than itself; they enter and dwell there, and the final condition of that person becomes worse than the first” (Matt. 12:44).

A recurrent fever is wont to kill more often than the first. But if you begin to do good and do not dwell in it by persevering forever and ever, beware lest you suddenly hear: “How have you fallen from heaven, Lucifer?” (Isa. 14:12). For since “whoever perseveres in good works to the end will be saved” (Matt. 24:13), without doubt whoever does not persevere will be lost.

3. Therefore, standing in God’s presence and asking for and awaiting mercy and remission of sins, I urge you carefully to consider two things: on the one hand, what you have done; on the other, what you must receive in return for your deeds unless Christ’s clemency comes to your aid.

Let each person question himself and see in how many things he can discover himself guilty. Since it is absolutely clear to every person of sound mind that everything pleasing to the devil displeases God, we must understand that we can never better determine what someone who serves a particular vice deserves than by considering whose companion he is in his actions.

For Truth says that at the end of the harvest the farmer will say to the reapers: “Gather the weeds first and bind them into bundles to burn” (Matt. 13:30). What else does this mean but: join together those who are alike in crime for a similar punishment?

Whoever, therefore, walks swollen with pride and despises others—what else does he seek, if he could, but to set himself, together with that chief pride, against him who rightly, as Lord and creator of all, surpasses everything?

Whoever wastes away with envy—does he not associate himself with that same one and with his members, namely the faithless Jews, as partners in his jealousy?

Whoever pants in the heat of avarice and greed—what else does he represent in his conduct, all the more strongly, than the one who greedily desired to be like the Most High (Isa. 14:14), and Judas, intoxicated with the poison of avarice by which the greedy man desires to become rich?

Whoever burns with the torches of lust—what else does he bring upon himself than the pyre of future and perpetual conflagration, together with those who fornicated most wantonly with the daughters of Moab and perished under the judgment of heavenly vengeance (Num. 25:1)?

Those who rage publicly in such conduct strive to harmonize with the cry of the Sodomites. But those who conceal their lust from human sight beneath the cloak of chastity attain the likeness of the Pharisees, of whom it is said: “Woe to you, for you are like whitewashed tombs, which on the inside are filled with the bones of the dead” (Matt. 23:27).

In whose mouth, alas, as in the case of very many people of the present age, falsehood is more abundant than truth, the devil’s falsehood is rightly made equal to them, for he has always been a liar and the father of lies (John 8:44).

Those who slander their brothers—do they not make themselves like the Pharisees, of whom it is said: “Their arrows are the wounds of children” (Ps. 63:8); and: “They bent their bow to shoot bitter things in secret” (Ps. 10:3)?

Those who persecute and afflict them gratuitously with hatred merely because they see them existing and doing good, and hinder them from good works as far as they can—what else do they resemble but those whose faithlessness is described: “When I spoke to them, they attacked me without cause” (Ps. 119:7)? For those to whom their very good action is intolerable are the same people who say in the Book of Wisdom: “He is grievous even for us to look upon” (Wis. 2:15).

Those who also contradict—who are they other than the persecutors of Christ? For whoever contradicts Christ, whether he is preaching or praising him, tries, as it were, to erase the name of Christ.

Whom shall I call thieves, if not the Philistines? Whom shall I call plunderers, if not the Babylonians? For although such a one is a scourge of God, nevertheless [lacuna] because it is broken when the son is chastised. But any murderer—what [lacuna]—is, of course, reckoned the worst executioner of his brother. For if it is true what has been said, that [lacuna] the killer of any Christian can excuse himself that he has not killed his brother, unless Christ [lacuna]. But if Christ is the head of the Church, and every Christian his member [lacuna], but whoever bodily or spiritually harms someone [lacuna].

4. From these few examples, dearest brothers, offered in compensation for the countless ways in which human mortality falls, you can clearly gather how greatly detestable vices must be rejected and how greatly God’s commandments must be embraced.

For just as by doing evil we acquire fellowship with the wicked, so by doing good we gain, conversely, the companionship of the saints. Indeed, the name “children of God” comes to us with the reality itself, for he says: “Be merciful, just as your heavenly Father is merciful” (Luke 6:36).

Since you have gathered here today to obtain release from your crimes, consider, I beg you, what you are seeking, and stand all the more attentively in prayer the more seriously you recognize that you have sinned.

Cry out with your voices; cry out with your hearts, saying: “To you, Lord, we have sinned.” Let no one excuse himself by claiming not to have sinned; let no one be deceived. For, as Job asserts, God permits nothing to go unpunished (Job 24:12).

Hear the Apostle; it is read today: “If we judged ourselves, we would not be judged” (1 Cor. 11:31). Let us therefore judge ourselves, brothers, here and now, and condemn ourselves, lest we be judged in the future. Let us be our own torturers, so that we may not feel the executioners of hell.

And what more shall I say? This day is called the Lord’s Supper. The word “supper” derives from the communion of those who eat together; but there is no communion where division through discord exists.

Therefore, whoever retains the poison of hatred in his heart should not approach this banquet of charity. Whoever has not washed away the defilement of lust through at least a little repentance should not receive this supper with an unclean stomach.

Passover is near—indeed, it begins today. Passover means “passing over.” Let us therefore display in our actions what we understand in the name. For if we have been buried with Christ through the putting to death of vices, we shall certainly rise with him through the manifestation of virtues. But if we bury no vice in ourselves through amendment, what Passover—what passage—are we carrying out?

And if there is no cleansing from the old leaven (1 Cor. 5:7), how can there be a new kneading in us?

Hear, I beg you, the one who commands. I believe that you will not despise me when I admonish—or, to speak more truthfully, when I remind you again—for what I seem to be suggesting to you I am certainly saying to myself.

He says: “Thus you shall eat it: you shall gird your loins, you shall have sandals on your feet, you shall hold staffs in your hands, and you shall eat in haste” (Exod. 12:11).

To gird one’s loins means to restrain lust. To have sandals on one’s feet [supply: “means”] to fortify oneself with the examples of the saints who have died to the flesh, so that neither the thorn of vices weakens the step of the mind nor the bite of poisonous deeds infects it.

For just as lust pricks a person’s heart and makes the desire for pious action limp, like a thorn makes the foot limp, so the soul that wastes away with envy grows pale from the livid poison that spreads through it.

To hold a staff in our hands means to restrain illicit desire with the strictness of heavenly discipline and, so that we do not suffer a harmful fall on the slippery road of the present life, to carry in the hand of action a certain support of the fear of God.

It also means to preside over ourselves in the pastoral office, setting God over the soul and the soul over the flesh.

5. If we carry this out diligently, we rightly celebrate the Lord’s Passover, hastening to reach the place where we know that Christ sits at the right hand—that is, in equality—with the Father; for this is called *phase*, that is, “the Lord’s passage.” And if we pass over from vices to virtues, from earthly things to heavenly things, in a most salutary conversion—and this ought to be done without ceasing—I urge that it be accomplished at this most sacred season with all the greater attentiveness, the more worthily the mystery is required to be celebrated. Most miserably, [lacuna] begins in the season of Lent. After Easter has passed, [lacuna] returns to vices, as though [lacuna] had departed not for God’s sake but only for that particular day, [lacuna] having merely been interrupted for a little while. What else is this to do but [lacuna]?

How long Christian Easter ought to extend, the Psalmist declares in the hundred and seventeenth psalm, which is entirely sung in praise of this day, saying: “Establish the day amid dense growths”—or, as another edition reads, “in assemblies”—“up to the horn of the altar” (Ps. 117:27). “Amid dense growths” means in the hidden places of the mind; “in assemblies,” however, means in practice, habit, or continuous observance. Our Passover, that is, Christ, must never depart from the heart; we must celebrate him through continual veneration up to the horn of the altar. But what is this altar? Christ, certainly, who exists at once as priest, altar, and victim. Until we see him, let us never cease seeking him.

What kind of observance is it to fast on the vigil of the solemnity and, on the solemnity itself, to be bloated with gluttony? On the Lord’s Supper to wash the feet of the poor, and during its octave to plot the death of a Christian? On Good Friday to give a single denarius, and after Good Friday to take away a hundred? To devote oneself to psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs during Lent, but at Easter to idleness—or, worse, to quarrelling or slander? [Note: Ratherius testifies here and elsewhere that abstinence from one’s wife during Lent was observed even in the tenth century.] To abstain then from one’s own wife, but at Easter to be defiled even by fornication? During Lent not to eat one’s own bread, but after Easter to seize another’s food? What is worse? What more contradictory could be devised?

## 607 — SERMON IV

[Note: We received this sermon, edited by Acherius from the Laon manuscript, checked against the Freising manuscript. It belongs to the period when Ratherius, restored for the third time to the see of Verona, presided there; it should probably be assigned to the year 963, as will be evident from what we observed in note 1429 on Sermon I, *On Lent*.]

## ON EASTER I

### 1

Today, dearest brothers, we are about to receive the Easter banquet and, as duty requires, to minister it to you—that is, the most holy nourishment of that Lamb whom the Forerunner, pointing to him with his finger, proclaimed: “Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29). [Note: Acherius reads *quam*; the Freising manuscript more correctly reads *quem*. After a few words this manuscript likewise—and equally appropriately—omits *individua*.] The lamb of the ancient type (Exod. 12:3) could merely prefigure this Lamb; it could not forgive sins, which this Lamb alone can uniquely accomplish in the divine nature that he possesses indivisibly with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

Since, then, today we are to handle more solemnly the body and blood of this Lamb and offer them to your devotion, we ask that none of you take it amiss if we interpose a small portion of wild lettuces [Note: Thus the Freising manuscript. Acherius has *aliquantulum interponimus*, “we interpose a little.”], since we do this also at the command of the Lord himself. Although it harms no one so greatly to be ignorant of the bodily appearance of these vegetables, it is no small impediment if someone cannot recognize and retain in his mind their spiritual meaning.

The nature of this vegetable, they say, causes the eyes of the person who eats it to stream with tears and cleanses the teeth. [Note: The latest edition of Acherius’s *Spicilegium* has *dente*, “tooth,” through what we believe to be a typographical error. Immediately afterward Acherius has *quid significat? Facit*, “What does it signify? It does.” We preferred the reading of the Freising manuscript. The passage is to be explained as follows: “But the nature of what this vegetable signifies causes,” and so forth.] But the nature of what it signifies causes the perception of body and heart to be stirred to salutary mourning.

Those who seem to treat of natural science also say that if an eagle should lose, for any reason, the sharpness of sight in which it is especially powerful, it recovers it by tasting this herb. A very fitting likeness, brothers, is offered by this example: whoever has contracted dimness of inner sight through the persistence of sins should strive to recover—or, alternatively, restore—it by tasting such lettuces.

### 2

But now let us adorn the table we promised. “This is the day which the Lord has made,” says the most holy Prophet; “let us exult and rejoice in it” (Ps. 117:24). Brothers, did the Lord not likewise make yesterday? Certainly—but he consecrated that day to fasting and this one to joy; that day brought mourning to the disciples, this one the greatest gladness.

What, then, should we do? As reason teaches, if yesterday we mourned with the apostles, let us rejoice today with them and with all the saints. Nor should we fear that we will be told, “Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall mourn and weep” (Luke 6:25), since, because of our former abstinence and sadness, we are refreshed by the consolation of the one who says—to the apostles before his Passion, and to us before the day of the Lord’s Resurrection:

“And you therefore now indeed have sorrow; but I will see you again, and your heart shall rejoice, and no one shall take your joy from you” (John 16:22).

This was said to the apostles; it is said also to us. [Note: Acherius reads *dicit*, “is said.” A little later our Freising copy has: “For what other reason?”] The apostles mourned because of Christ’s death—though that death was exceedingly necessary for them—and they rejoiced over his resurrection with immeasurable joy and immense thanksgiving. We imitated their mourning yesterday; let us imitate their joy today.

But if we wish to imitate them, let us take from them the rule of joy. Tell us, then, holy Apostle—called after all the others, but divinely carried up to the third heaven in a manner that you yourself know better—tell us, I say, and satisfy those who ask from what source we ought to rejoice. “Christ our Passover,” he says, “has been sacrificed” (1 Cor. 5:7).

Is that all? We had understood the sacrifice itself to be the same death which the apostles had mourned, and whose sorrow we imitated yesterday. We ask you, then: continue, and tell us what we should do today and how we should act. He adds:

“Therefore let us feast”—that is, let us eat the Lord’s flesh and drink his blood—“not in the old leaven, nor in the leaven of malice and wickedness, but in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (ibid. 8).

“And truth,” I say. Why is this so? Because the same Apostle says elsewhere:

“We have been buried with Christ through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too may walk in newness of life. For if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall also be planted together in the likeness of his resurrection” (Rom. 6:4–5).

Therefore, dearest brothers, if by our actions we preserve what we believe, then, reborn in Christ, having suffered in Christ, having died in Christ, we have also been raised from the dead in Christ; and for this reason we have the greatest grounds for joy. Therefore, brothers, since the Lord made this day not for himself alone but also for us, let us exult and rejoice in it.

### 3

Behold, these are the most fitting Easter delicacies that we promised you: now displayed to you, and shortly to be served. [Note: The vulgate text reads, “now displayed to you, shortly to be displayed.” The newest editor of the *Spicilegium* recognized the corrupt passage and thought it should read, “now displayed to you, shortly to be eaten.” The Freising manuscript supplied the true reading.] But what shall we do, children, about the promised wild lettuces? [Note: Construe: “But what shall we do, children, about the promised wild lettuces?”]

Let them come also. Let them cleanse the rheum of the teeth—that is, the impediments in our minds arising from a heap of crimes [Note: That is, “the impediments of the minds arising from a heap of crimes.”]—and compel streams of water to flow from the eyes of those who come to eat the Lamb.

“Not in the old leaven,” he says—that is, in the swelling of former sin, or in the desire to commit the same sin or another; in other words, so that today you may not be what you were yesterday. “Nor in the leaven of malice and wickedness”: as if he were saying, “Change former malice into goodness; abandon wickedness if you wish to eat the flesh of the Lamb of God [alternative: the divine Lamb] and drink his blood.”

It follows: “but in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.” Understand, brothers—indeed, understand [Note: The latest editor of the *Spicilegium* not improperly thought that the text should be restored to *imo intelligitis*, “indeed, you understand”; but he did not venture to alter the text. We altered it even less, since the Freising manuscript also prefers *imo intelligite*, “indeed, understand.”—if perhaps some of you here are like me: certainly malicious and full of wickedness.

If you wish to rejoice healthfully, rejoice in the Lord, not in excessive jokes, not in idle stories, not in harmful obscenities, not in seductive touches, not in gluttony and drunkenness, not in the vanity of songs. If you desire to exult, “serve the Lord in fear, and exult in him with trembling” (Ps. 2:11). If you desire to celebrate a legitimate Passover, celebrate it with unleavened bread.

But if you ask what this unleavened bread is, I answer: sincerity and truth. For the worst leaven is duplicity in pretence; harmful leaven is the will to falsify. Since leaven is named from *fervere*, “to boil” or “ferment,” we can understand malice itself, wickedness itself, and the entire practice of the old Adam under this name; yet we can imagine nothing more opposed to sincerity and truth than the deceit that teaches one to deceive one’s neighbor, by which the mind of the fraudulent seethes without end.

Since this will is chiefly intent on perpetrating some evil, we urge you, brothers, to abstain from it—that is, from deceit—all the more earnestly the more greatly divine majesty is offended by it and the honor of Easter defiled. For if this were not so, the Apostle would never have commended those same two inviolable virtues—sincerity and truth—so emphatically in the banquet of the Easter feast, both by prohibiting their opposites and by commanding them, repeating the same thought under different names and saying:

“Therefore let us feast, not in the old leaven, nor in the leaven of malice and wickedness, but in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (1 Cor. 5:7).

Indeed, the person who has an evil will in his heart celebrates no Easter festival at all; nor does anyone possess glory in the heights with God, or true peace on earth with human beings, unless he possesses a good will. [Note: The Freising manuscript agrees with ours in reading *nec*. Acherius has *cum nec … habeat*, “since he neither has …”; the intervening words are missing.]

### 4

This most biting truthfulness—and most truthful bitterness—I call wild lettuce. I earnestly ask that, received by the spiritual taste of our hearts and bodies, it change their condition: stirring the heart to sighs, the body to lamentation, and both to abandon the efforts of an evil will.

We undoubtedly believe that this will come about if we also strive to relate to the nature of these lettuces what the Lord, through the minister of the Decalogue [that is, Moses], commands us concerning the celebration of Passover:

“Thus shall you eat it: you shall gird your loins, you shall have sandals on your feet, holding staffs in your hands, and you shall eat in haste” (Exod. 12:11).

What could be said more sternly, brothers, what more sharply, to the person who understands these words and remembers that he did not celebrate the preceding Passover at all while observing these same requirements?

Whoever did not obey the Psalmist when he said, “Gird your sword upon your thigh, O most mighty one” (Ps. 44:4)—that is, “strongly”—but, surrendering himself feebly to lust, dared to approach to receive the body and blood of the Lamb of God [alternative: the divine Lamb]; whoever did not follow the examples of the holy fathers who have already died in Christ; whoever did not defend himself with the staff of governance against the roaring lion—that is, the devil seeking to devour him; whoever did not hasten through pious desire—that is, did not wish “to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1:23)—I do not see how such a person can presume today to receive the Lord’s body and blood without groaning and sighing, unless I believe him to be hardened by deadly despair or deceived by false hope.

But I urge him not to act so; I warn him not to despair; I beg him not to deceive himself any longer with false hope. Let him attend to what follows, sigh, and groan: “For it is *phase*, that is, the Lord’s passage.”

It is as though he had said: The person who passes from the devil to Christ is the one who restrains his loins from lust; who fortifies the steps of his works with the examples of the saints; who defends himself from the devil with the staff of governance; and who hastens, through desire, to reach the heavenly homeland.
