To this person alone, therefore, is granted the celebration of the Lord’s Passover—and yet not even to him without wild lettuces, that is, without remembrance of past crimes and the most beneficial shedding of tears.

### 5

But now we must return to the Apostle, forgetful of our inability. “Christ our Passover,” he says, “has been sacrificed.” [Note: The Freising manuscript omits *nunc*, “now.” Construe: “But now we must return to the Apostle, who can accomplish the task we have proposed, forgetful of our inability; the Apostle is indeed able to accomplish it: ‘Christ,’ he says,” and so forth.]

We may suppose that he meant to say: “Christ was sacrificed for us so that he himself might be our passage to himself, and he himself alone might be our joy.”

Therefore, each of us should ask as follows, I urge: “Let us exult and rejoice in him.” For he is our peace, he is light, he is guide, he is day, he is sun, he is salvation, he is life, he is resurrection, he is true joy, he is everlasting blessedness, he is eternal happiness, he is unfailing gladness. Finally, he is the day that the Lord made by begetting, not by working—and this in a truly ineffable manner. Let us exult and rejoice in him.

Let the joy of our table also extend to Christ’s poor; let our abundance supply their want. Let the poor themselves also help one another. Let one give what another lacks, if he has it; if he does not have it, let him at least desire to have given it, so that in every way and in all things the one sacrificed for us as our Passover, Christ, may rejoice in us.

And let this be the day that the Lord has made, so that we too may now and without end be able to exult and rejoice in it, and may receive his body and blood in such a way that it may come to us not for judgment—as, alas, happens to many—but for everlasting healing, as happens to the blessed. [Note: Construe: “so that this may come to us not for judgment, as—alas!—it happens to many, but for everlasting healing, as it happens to the blessed.”]

May he who gave his only Son to death for us assist this desire of ours and sanctify the act; he who, with the Son and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON V

[Note: This sermon, published by Acherius from the Laon manuscript, was delivered on Easter Day in the year 968. See note 1492.]

## ON EASTER II

### 1

Since the Prophet commands us all to exult and rejoice on this day (Ps. 117:24), I greatly fear the charge of reproach if, following my customary practice, I introduce some element of sadness into my sermon. But let the reprover be absent; for the inner Counsellor forbids me to be sad. Just as Tobias answered the angel, so I too can fittingly answer anyone who urges me to rejoice: “What joy,” he says, “shall I have, who sit in darkness and do not see the light of heaven?” (Tob. 5:12).

It is not inappropriate to call our festival itself the light of heaven, of which it is said, “Let the heavens rejoice, and let the earth exult” (Ps. 95:11)—not that earth of which it was said to the serpent, the persuader of evil, “You shall eat earth all the days of your life” (Gen. 3:14), but rather that earth of which it had previously been said, “Let the earth bring forth green herbs” (Gen. 1:11), and so forth—things that are sufficiently good according to the letter, but far better according to their mystical meaning.

With what presumption may I rightly declare that I enjoy the joy of this day, when I cannot see the light of heaven—that is, the one who illumines heaven itself—because I am surrounded by the cloud of sins? [Note: We supplied *lumen*, “light,” from the preceding text of Tobit, to which this passage refers.]

For when we know that those forty days were instituted for the purpose that, with our minds cleansed through penance during them, we might be able to see the holy day of new things and celebrate it with joy—and when we have not done this—what joy, what exultation, what gladness can we possess?

For the holy Apostle, as you heard read, says in praise of this same joy: “Therefore let us feast” (1 Cor. 5:7). What did he say? Let us receive with exultation the body and blood of Christ, who was sacrificed for us. Let us do so, then.

### 2

But what will happen if we cannot do so worthily and justly? [Note: In the first Acherian edition the text reads *Sibi jungit namque* and, below, *timore anterioris*; the newest editor rightly judged these to result from scribal or typographical carelessness, and we have adopted his corrections. With him we also retain, a little later, *possidet puritatem*, “possesses purity,” where the first edition incorrectly had *possidet veritatem*, “possesses truth.”] For he adds and says: “Not in the old leaven”—that is, in the swelling of former sin—“nor in the leaven of malice,” namely, the desire to inflict evil on some Christian; “nor in wickedness,” namely, the attempt to do this unjustly. But how, then? “In the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.”

Sincerity is purity—that is, something that contains nothing except what it displays. When Pilate asked what truth was (John 18:38), he did not wait to hear the answer; therefore he did not deserve to rejoice in it.

Thus one who possesses neither truth in his mouth nor purity in his heart must consider how he dares to eat Christ’s flesh, especially since the Apostle expressly forbids this, using no circumlocution, when he says: “Whoever eats the body of the Lord unworthily eats judgment upon himself” (1 Cor. 11:29).

And oh, how can such a person exult and rejoice today when, instead of salvation, he will receive judgment, and instead of life, destruction?

This—this, I say—is what throughout almost this entire Lent compelled me to cry out: that, “putting away all malice, all deceit, hypocrisy, and envy” (1 Pet. 2:1), we should all strive to turn toward Christ—that is, toward true peace. [Note: Similarly in *Discordia*, written during Lent of the year 968, no. 7. “Throughout all the sermons,” he says, “which I delivered to the people during this Lent, I never ceased urging everyone with me not to delay returning to peace,” and so forth. There he also introduces the same Gospel testimonies that follow here, one for those who have injured someone and another for those who have been injured. Hence it is clear that this sermon was delivered in the same year.]

Because many people do not know how to do this, I set before you a kind of rule and urged you as follows. Those who remember that they have injured someone should recall the saying:

“If you offer your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go first to be reconciled to your brother; then come and offer your gift” (Matt. 5:23–24).

Those, however, who have been injured by someone, if the offender has truly sought forgiveness, should not forget the saying:

“When you stand to pray, forgive whatever you have against anyone, so that your heavenly Father may also forgive you your sins. But if you do not forgive, neither will your heavenly Father forgive your sins” (Mark 11:2).

### 3

But, alas, I have seen some people so contemptuous of this counsel—and would that they were not especially those who ought to have offered a good example to others—that even while he himself [Note: This is Ratherius, whose enemies did not cease plotting his destruction on the very day of the Lord’s Supper, when he communicated them.] was sending the holy bread into their mouths, saying, “May the body of our Lord Jesus Christ benefit you unto everlasting life,” [Note: This is a notable and distinctive formula for administering the Eucharist, which Ratherius repeats in the following sermon, no. 2. It resembles the formula cited by Ratherius in Letter I to Patricus: “May the body of our Lord Jesus Christ be beneficial to you unto eternal life.” In the Council of Rouen of 650, canon 2; in the Council of Tours as reported by Regino, book I, chapter 199; and in a Mass published by Illyricus, which preserves the Romano-Gallican liturgy, the fuller formula reads: “May the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ benefit you for the remission of sins and unto eternal life.”] they did not cease to spread snares of destruction and, as though to Pilate on those same days, to cry out, “Crucify, crucify!” (John 19:6), in other words, not remembering the saying: “Woe to the wicked traitor; woe to his accomplices, even today in his Church.”

Today I commanded certain of them in the place of our Lord to stop doing this; and if they do it, let them do it to themselves. For the most learned and elegant Jerome says: “To have erred once may be an accident; why err deliberately, and repeatedly?”

For unless they take care, it is to be feared that what happened to those of whom it was said may happen to them: “While their food was still in their mouths, the anger of God rose against them” (Ps. 77:30). And likewise what was read yesterday concerning Judas, the Lord’s betrayer: “After the morsel, Satan entered into him” (John 13:27)—through the effect of an evil deed, which had already been present in him through the inclination of an evil will.

If they had believed the Apostle when he said, “Let a person examine himself, and so eat from that bread and drink from the cup” (1 Cor. 11:28)—that is, let him examine the disposition in which he stands: whether it is one of sinning or of amendment, of harming someone or helping, of hatred or brotherly love—if, I say, they had salutarily considered such matters, they would at least have avoided receiving the sacred sacrament from the hand of the person whom they hated, lest they become imitators of Judas in so public a manner.

But since conversion is neither difficult nor slow with God, I urge such a person, a member of the human race, not to despair. For the Passover of the Jews belongs to a fixed time, whereas that of Christians belongs to every time—and especially to the Lord’s Day, the day of communion and conversion from worse things to better.

Since Passover is interpreted as “passage,” at whatever time, on whatever day, at whatever hour, and finally at whatever moment a person passes from the devil to Christ, from vices to virtues, from darkness to light, he truly celebrates the Easter solemnity.

For when the Psalmist says to the Lord, “The remnants of thought shall keep a feast for you” (Ps. 75:11), anyone celebrates the Lord’s solemn Passover who, abandoning what he has thought wrongly, strives to do what God himself has commanded.

## 614 — SERMON VI

[Note: This sermon was printed by Acherius from the same Laon manuscript and was delivered in the same year, 968, as the preceding one.]

## ON THE OCTAVE OF EASTER

### 1

“Before I eat, I sigh” (Job 3:24), blessed Job is read to have said. He adds the reason: “For the fear which I feared has come upon me, and that which I dreaded has happened” (ibid. 25). To apply this to myself—though I am as far removed from him as the aerial heaven is from the ethereal—I confess that I grieve that what I uttered in fear on the Lord’s Day has happened to some among you. [Note: He indicated this fear quite plainly in the preceding sermon, §3, where, speaking of those plotting against him, he says: “It is to be feared that what happened to those of whom it was said may happen to them: ‘While their food was still in their mouths,’ etc.; and what was read yesterday concerning Judas, the Lord’s betrayer, … ‘After the morsel Satan entered into him’—through the inclination to an evil work, which was already effectual in him through the disposition of an evil will.” If, then, what he feared on Easter Day happened, what they had previously entertained in their minds and undertaken in intention came to effect after Easter and before the octave day.]

For I fear that something has happened to certain persons—alas!—such as the Psalmist once sang concerning the Jews: “While their food was still in their mouths, the anger of God rose against them” (Ps. 77:30). For, when after the morsel Satan had entered into them through evil action—though he had already long been in them through their utterly wicked purpose—as though they had heard from him who handed them that morsel, “What you are doing, do quickly” (John 13:27), from that point they did not cease to carry out as swiftly as possible what they had already been plotting, especially throughout this entire Lent: when, that is, they had been earnestly admonished by word and example to be reconciled to God and to injured brothers, and not to reject those who genuinely desired reconciliation. [Note: Construe: “When they had been earnestly admonished by word and example to be reconciled to God and injured brothers, and not to reject those who genuinely desired reconciliation; they did not deign even to imitate those who once said, ‘Not on the feast day,’ but publicly circulated through everyone they could all their schemes of ambush and all their utterly false fabrications against that same man—whom would that no one knew to be myself—fabricating of him things which no one could believe unless he had done many things the same or similar.”]

They did not deign even to imitate those who once said, “Not on the feast day” (Matt. 14:2), but circulated publicly, through everyone they could, every scheme of ambush and every utterly false fabrication against that same man—whom would that no one knew to be myself—fabricating of him things which no one could believe unless he had done many things the same or similar. They also, it is reported, bribed with money two persons who ruled the country. [Note: The two country-ruling persons said to have been bribed with money were Count Nanno and perhaps another, a viscount.]

Would that one of them had been the same in rank and name as the one of whom I have often already spoken, so that I might state more openly that I am the man who suffers such things: “May he who delivered Israel from the hand of Pharaoh” (Exod. 18:10), etc.—names sufficiently recognizable because their words fall under the same declensional ending. [Note: This one person is Nanno, count of Verona; Ratherius wishes that he were the man of whom he had already said, “May he who delivered Israel from the hand of Pharaoh deliver Ratherius from the hand of Buccon.” See Letter 2, where this entire text occurs. The names Nanno, Buccon, and Pharaoh take the same declensional ending. He wishes for Buccon rather than Nanno because Buccon, though hostile at first, later proved favorable, as he testifies in the same letter. The printed editions incorrectly read *Hierusalem* for *Israelem*.]

They led these persons through the entire house of the Church and, changing the force of the words, these miserable liars were not ashamed to make an active construction out of a passive one: they pretended, that is, that I was doing what I most sorrowfully suffer, as though it had therefore been necessary for them repeatedly to cry, albeit in other words, “Crucify, crucify” (John 19:6). [Note: This is what Ratherius’s enemies carried into effect after Easter Day. Having bribed two persons who ruled Verona, they led them around the entire episcopal residence to inspect its ruins and, by the grossest calumny, represented Ratherius—who had suffered these losses—as the author of all the damage. This was the principal accusation against him; afterward Nanno, acting as the emperor’s envoy, held a hearing against Ratherius. See Letter 12. Construe: “Leading them through the entire house of the Church, and miserably and most deceitfully changing the force of the words, not ashamed to make an active construction out of a passive one, they pretended that I was doing what I most sorrowfully suffer, as though for that reason they had repeatedly to cry, ‘Crucify, crucify.’”]

For although in these three years I have spent nearly forty pounds on restoring this same episcopal house, as those who served in this work report, after I had been driven from it by those same persons and it had remained without an inhabitant, those who bring this charge against me—as the coherence of the passage indicates—do not cease to destroy it by stealth; while those lodging in it do not cease to destroy it by force and power. I cannot resist any of them: the thieves, because I am far away; those lodging there, because I seem far too unequal to them in strength, particularly since they are known to be returning from the imperial army or going to it. Yet these consummate liars, having hired inspectors, accuse me of destroying it, as though it could be believed that I should either destroy, or willingly permit to be destroyed, what I built at such cost to myself. [Note: Construe and explain: “Since in these three years—that is, from 965 to 968—I spent nearly forty pounds in restoring this episcopal residence, as those who served in this work report; when the house had remained without an inhabitant after I had been driven from it by those same people—that is, after he had been captured and brought into it, and later, once freed, did not dare entrust himself to that house again—since those who bring this charge against me, as the syntax indicates, do not cease to destroy it by theft—that is, secretly—while those lodging there do not cease to destroy it by force and power, I being unable to resist any of them: the thieves, because I am remote from that house; those lodging there, because I seem far inferior in strength, especially since they are known to return from the imperial army or to go to it; these consummate liars, with hired inspectors—whom, as he said above, they led around to inspect the entire house—accuse me of destroying it.”]

[Note: The printed text read, “the same man who brings this charge against me”; but not only the following noun *furibus* (“thieves”) but also Letter 12 to Ambrose requires the plural. There, in §4, this same occurrence is explained thus: “The bishop spent, as they report, forty pounds in restoring, enlarging, and adorning that house, restoring six doors alone, which had been removed partly by theft—that is, secretly—and partly by force.” A little earlier he attributes this damage to several persons: “In restoring and enlarging the house I spent, most foolishly, forty pounds. Bavarians and the neighboring clerics and servants, especially, are destroying it.” Compare the fuller description there, which admirably illuminates this passage. We also corrected *cessent*, as required by the sense of the context, where the text read *cessant*.]

Indeed, those lodging in it destroy it with such authority that, if any servant whose duty it is comes there to inspect it, they immediately seize him and, after flogging him most severely with thongs, bind him fast.

[Col. 0728A] **2.** Since I endure all these things in deepest grief, while the nature of the words has, as I said, been reversed, these slanderers confess that I am doing what I am rather suffering—along with everything that any of the most mendacious people has ever been able to fabricate about anyone. But O the insane madness of the most faithless! O the utterly outrageous falsehood! O the devil’s cunning, which, through serpents [or: through the serpent], is no longer ignorant of how to speak!

For if the emperor were not my lord, and I were equal to him in power, I could in some fashion defend my house and its 616 work against his loyalists. [Note: That is, guests loyal to the emperor, who, as he had said shortly before, lodged in the episcopal house while travelling to the imperial army or returning from it.] Moreover, unless these men had driven me from that same house by their treachery, I could, being present, guard it day and night against their thefts. [Note: These are the aforesaid neighboring Veronese clerics and servants, mentioned in Letter 12, note 1393; he consequently adds below that he later gave them Holy Communion.] But now, since he is also my lord, and since to fight against my lord’s loyalists, even if I were able to do so, would be not only treacherous but, so to speak, apostasy—for whoever rebels against the earthly lord assigned to him by God withdraws from God; for it is said that whoever resists the authority placed over him by God resists God’s ordinance (Rom. XIII, 2)—these men, following the example of the devil, do not cease striving to accomplish something that harms and disturbs me, even without any advantage to themselves. What can I do against these two impossibilities?

[Note: The words “Since this is so,” which disrupted the entire sense, had been wrongly inserted here; we have removed them.]

O that, when I was offering such men the sacred morsel with the hand they wished to have cut off, saying, “May the Body of our Lord Jesus Christ profit you unto eternal life,” one of them had cried out to the others what that former stoning man cried to the stoners of the holy apostle James, who is called the Lord’s brother, as even today blood-relatives are called brothers: “Spare him,” he said, “what are you doing? This righteous man whom you are stoning prays for you.”

I was indeed righteous in relation to them, although God knew my offenses, unknown to them. I was meditating on returning good to them for evil, while they were meditating on returning evil to me for such and so many good deeds, often bestowed on them without any obligation.

[Note: Understand and explain as follows: If they had alleged, or complained, about some injury I had inflicted on them, this would not have been greatly surprising, although even for that reason they ought first to have approached me humbly according to the judgment of the canons, rather than attacking me by the evil arts previously mentioned and soon to be mentioned again.]

But if they were to say something about an injury I had inflicted on them, that would not be very surprising, although even on that account I ought first to have been approached humbly, according to the judgment of the canons.

**3.** But to bring accusations concerning matters that have nothing to do with them; to say such things about me as no one could believe before God without offending him; to cause everyone to disparage me; to corrupt whatever good there may be in me by giving it a bad interpretation; to investigate zealously whatever evils either are or have been in me, and to display them most zealously to others—what is this except to testify most openly that they are perjurers not only against me but also against the most pious emperor, who appointed me there [Note: Compare note 920 on the conjecture concerning “qualification.” “There,” that is, to the bishopric of Verona, where the emperor installed Ratherius when he arranged for him to be restored to that bishopric. Concerning this, in the *Itinerary*, no. 4, he says: “Again, by the mercy of the most pious Caesar, by the command of the apostolic [pope] who then presided over the Roman see, I was restored synodally by the judgment of the bishops.” Shortly afterward we wrote “the army of young men” where “the army of a young man” had wrongly stood; and later we corrected *locavimus* to *locant*.] by alms?

And, as someone says: “Alas, alas, the dreadful condition of fury! He who suffers violence is more tightly bound.” For the river of their evil activity flows from them toward me, and I am accused—after the example of the lamb in the fable—of muddying it (Phaedrus, Book I, Fable 1).

A certain king had an army of young men and a multitude of wise men. Since the young men could not do what was proper to young men, because the wise men restrained their folly, they took counsel to kill each man’s own father. This was carried out. But one of them, unable to endure the commission of so great a crime, said to his wife: “If I kill my father, lest we perish because our counsel has failed, I am very much afraid.”

His wife agreed, in order to preserve her father-in-law’s life, and secretly placed him in her storeroom and provided him with food. The father instructed his son that, whenever questioned by the king about any matter of counsel, he should not answer before referring the matter to him. Obeying him, the young man became so capable a counselor to the king that all his companions grew jealous of him.

They therefore went to the king and threatened that, unless he killed the young man, he would certainly destroy them all. The grieving king consented, but asked them on what pretext he could do this. “Above all,” they replied, “let him come tomorrow bringing with him only one servant, one friend, and one enemy.”

Terrified by this statement, the young man went to consult his father. His father said: “Do not be distressed, but prepare an excellent meal for us; you will receive very good counsel from me.” After dinner, his father secretly said to him: “You have an excellent donkey; load it with bread, wine, and meat and take it with you. You have a little dog, very ready to defend your possessions; keep it with you. Also bring your wife with you. Offer the donkey as your servant, the dog as your friend, and your wife as your enemy.”

He did so. He took the donkey, brought the dog along with him, and did not leave his wife behind. He approached the deeply troubled king and begged him to consider what he had brought. “This one,” he said, pointing to the loaded animal, “is my servant; that other one is my friend; this third one is my wife, and I hope I have no enemy more hostile than she.”

When she heard this, she said, inflamed with anger over the fire: “Do you declare that I am your enemy?” “Rightly so,” he replied, “for, against the king’s command, I preserved your father’s life, obeying you.”

The young man turned to the king: “Does Your Majesty think that this woman is my enemy?” “Very much so,” he replied; “but I wish to learn whether it is true.”

“It is true,” said the young man. The king, overjoyed, replied: “Thanks be to God.”

“Run, then, run,” he said, “and hasten to bring him back to me.” This was done. The excellent counselor was restored to the king, the young man was freed from the imminent danger of death, and his wife was shown not to love the young man, as she had seemed to do; she would certainly have been thought his greatest friend had she not been tested in this way.

If I had not moved these men somewhat by this example, I would not have been able to know them so convincingly, although I had always placed this confidence in them. Yet may God, I ask, deign to convert them, show them the way of true peace and charity, and grant that they walk in it, lest what God forbid should happen to us together because of such deeds—lest punishment suddenly seize us, as the kite is fabled to have carried off the frog together with the mouse.

[Col. 0730C]

**4.** Since this entire argument may appear not to be preaching but rather an attack against those lying in wait for my life and my possessions, I believe it should now be set aside, and that pastoral attention should henceforth be directed toward admonishing everyone together, friends as well as enemies.

First, although this has already been done more than once, it is appropriate to show where and from what cause the disagreement between us arose. To answer briefly at the end: it is certain that it did not merely arise recently but existed between us from the day of my ordination. It has now been brought into the open because confidence in the imperial presence, which decides nothing other than what is just, and the prospect of a synod being convened, [Note: We inserted the points, which indicate that something is missing here. Compare note 1162 on “discord,” where we explained this passage.] have shown on this occasion that we disagree frequently, not only in words but also in writing.

[Note: The work *On Rebellious Clerics* is intended, and especially the book *On Discord*, whose substance he briefly summarizes here.]

The substance of that disagreement, although there are many words, is shown to be this: I decide that God’s law must be followed, while they decide that human traditions and the custom of the wicked must be followed. Is he not truly wicked who distributes what has been given jointly to him and me in such a way that I become utterly poor from it, while he becomes extremely wealthy?

If I consent to this by keeping silent—or rather by praising it—I shall certainly be convicted of having denied God, abandoning the truth because of the friendship they would wish to have with me. [Note: The common text incorrectly has *nisi*; we have adopted *nae*, that is, “certainly,” as required by the sense.] Whoever advises me to fear this is proved to be an enemy of my soul; still less ought I myself to be one.

**5.** Having briefly demonstrated this, therefore, I admonish you with me, brothers, that each of us inquire of himself how he spent that holy Pascha—that is, these eight days—and whether he spent them in such a way that he could safely answer “Amen” when the priest said:

“Grant, we beg you, almighty God, that we who have celebrated the paschal festivals with reverence may, by your gift, preserve them in conduct and life.”

Let each person therefore ask himself whether the priest spoke truly about him: that is, whether he received the Lord’s body and blood in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth; whether in his heart he plotted no evil against anyone during Pascha; whether he said anything about another’s deeds knowingly except what was true; whether, while the food of Christ’s body was still in his mouth, he caused God’s anger to rise against himself through hatred, envy, greed, avarice, or lust; whether, after the morsel, he allowed Satan to enter his soul—that is, whether he hastened to carry out the evil he had previously conceived; finally, whether during the feast, that is, during these eight days and for as long as “This is the day which the Lord has made” was sung, he polluted himself by adultery or any impurity, or wickedly injured any of the brethren.

If he finds none of these things in himself, let him rejoice that he has celebrated the Lord’s Paschal festival with reverence, answer humbly “Amen,” and never cease asking with hand, tongue, and heart that God in his mercy grant him to preserve these things in conduct and life.

But if, as I fear, he finds otherwise in himself, let him grieve that he did not at least strive to imitate those who did not say such things on the feast day—that is, that just as they feared the tumult of the people if they should seize the Lord, so he, fearing the Lord’s anger if he violated the most holy festival, should have endeavored, with God’s help, to restrain himself from such temptation for at least those eight days and to hold himself back from injuring his brother.

[Note: Understand it as follows: Thus, fearing the Lord’s anger if he violated the most holy festival, this man should have attempted, with God’s help, to restrain himself from such temptation for at least those eight days and to restrain himself from injury toward his brother.]

Finally, let him grieve that, following the example of Judas the betrayer, he has incurred condemnation; but let him turn not, like Judas, to the noose in despair, but, like Peter, to tears in repentance. Let him abandon what he wickedly conceived and hasten, while there is time, to celebrate the feast for the Lord. Thus, with God’s help, he may recover the lost Pascha, which is indeed a passage toward good, and appease God’s anger—God who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, never ceases to reign as God for ages of ages.

**620 SERMON VII**  
[Note: Acherius published this sermon from the Laon manuscript. It was written in the same year, 968, as the two preceding sermons, since it bears their summary.]  

**AFTER PASCHA**

**1.** “I judge you from your own mouth” (Luke XIX, 22), the Lord will say at the final judgment to the wicked servant. But to whom? He makes this clear by adding: “You knew that I was an austere man,” and so forth.

[Note: Understand it as follows: By this sentence it is established—or made certain—that a greater judgment awaits the one who knows than the one who does not know. Therefore those who know good and do evil have very much to fear—very much indeed, especially if they also speak of those same good things.]

By this sentence, then, it is certain that a greater judgment awaits the one who knows than the one who does not know. Those who know good and do evil must therefore fear greatly—fear, I say, fear greatly, especially if they also speak of those same good things.

For some speak of good things while knowing neither what they say nor, still less, actually saying them. Such, for example, are the many who recite the Gospels and the Apostles in fulfillment of the office entrusted to them. When they perform in whatever fashion what has been imposed upon them, they fulfill not the ministry of a teacher but that of a listener.

They are judged from their own mouths because they do not know what they are saying, yet they are accused unless they act accordingly. Wretched teachers, therefore, given to the world on both sides—wretched, I say, and unhappy, if they either do not know how to teach or, while teaching what they do not practice, are judged solely from their own mouths.

[Note: The common text has *obeditoris* incorrectly. The correction is supported by the sense of the context: those are being criticized who recite the Gospels and the Apostles but do not know what they are saying, as happens to those who listen but, unless a teacher explains what they hear, do not understand it.]

For if they recognize the punishments of Gehenna but do not make them known to others, they will be guilty of all those whom they ought to have taught, if those people fall into them through ignorance. But if they make them known to others and do not themselves avoid them, what is more wretched, or, I ask, more foolish than they? And if, after showing others the fountain of life, they themselves perish through drought, who ought to grieve for them?

[Note: Understand and explain as follows: Recently, with the Apostle, we cried out—namely, with the words which he quotes shortly afterward and which had been read in the Epistle for Easter Day, “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed.” We cried out, and would that we had done so not rather to be judged from our own mouths, for that fault, namely, because we cried out wrongly, as for many other faults, than to be delivered, as the prophet once promised.]

Recently we cried out with the Apostle; we cried out—and would that we had not cried out, for this as for many other faults, more for the purpose of being judged from our own mouths than of being delivered, as the prophet once promised. We cried out for ourselves and for you, but may God’s mercy grant that our crying out was not useless for all of us.

Yet we cried out; we cried out with the Apostle, brothers; we cried out: “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (1 Cor. V, 7). But would that, as he was sacrificed for the one who returns him worthy thanks, so he might be sacrificed for us! For he was sacrificed for the person rendering him worthy thanks; but we must beware lest, God forbid, he be sacrificed by us, ungrateful for so great a benefit.

[Note: Understand it as follows: He was sacrificed so that we might return worthy thanks to him; but we must beware lest, God forbid, he be sacrificed by us ungrateful for so great a benefit. This is what the following words imply.]

For this is implied by the one who says: “Whoever eats the body of the Lord unworthily will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord” (1 Cor. XI, 27); that is, the guilt of shedding the blood of Jesus Christ will be attributed to him if he dares to drink unworthily the blood which the Jews shed. This means: if he proves in his conduct to be what they were in faith.

**2.** Finally we added and declared: “Therefore let us keep the feast, not with the old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (1 Cor. V, 8).

[Note: These matters are explained in detail in Sermon II *On Pascha*.]

We explained all these things so fully that we thought we had satisfied even little children. But would that we had ourselves done what we admonished others to do, and had cast away, through sincere reconciliation and fruitful repentance, the leaven of evil will or harmful action which we previously possessed.

We said ironically: “How very well may he rejoice and be glad today who is about to receive judgment instead of salvation, destruction instead of life.”

We applied to this the Psalmist’s testimony, spoken then of the Jews—but would that it were not now spoken of us: “While their food was still in their mouths, the anger of God rose up against them” (Ps. LXXVII, 30).

For when Satan entered Judas after the morsel, as the Gospel indeed says (John XIII, 27), he had already been present in him before the morsel through his evil action, since he had already been present in him by his most wicked will. We must fear lest something similar has happened to us.

[Note: These matters are explained more fully in Sermon VI *On the Octave of Pascha*.]

That is, lest, because of the holy sacrifice which we ought to receive at Pascha, we had postponed some crime and, after receiving the sacrifice, hastened to commit it before the eighth day, forgetting the cry, “Not on the feast day,” of those who were themselves attempting to seize the Lord.

O the impatience of the utterly weak, and the excessive insanity which is strong enough to endure neither the injuries of enemies nor the goads of vices! In whichever of these you caused us to fall, you compelled us, alas, to violate the Lord’s Pascha by your destructive influence.

But the witnesses of God, renewed against us, ought to have been considered: in both sexes they endured with the greatest fortitude the most severe punishments from adversaries and the longest temptations from their own flesh. God’s grace, anticipating us and not abandoning us, would have led us to follow them; but our own sluggishness prevented us, as did the temptation supplied too generously to the body, while the hand of the sinner, raised in pride, also stirred us up.

There we fell, committing such wickedness; expelled from God’s grace because of empty glory, we miserable people could not persevere in good. Thus we must also confess that we are judged by God from our own mouths.

Although we knew this with complete certainty, we nevertheless, as the most unhappy of men, disdained to avoid it, because our proud contempt outweighed the fear of God. Thus we have been handed over to destruction through our own merit, not because God neglected us; condemned by ourselves, we are destined to be condemned eternally unless God’s mercy quickly comes to our aid.

**3.** But what are we to do if this is so, brothers? It is so—alas, it is so. Give us, we beg you, the return of counsel, if you can; give it. Say at least what we have said; bring forth what we have brought forth; persuade us as we have persuaded you. We find nothing else that we can do: since we have proved like Judas in such matters, let us henceforth beware of his example—not hastening with him to the deadly noose of despair, but rather, with Peter, to the life-giving lamentation of conversion.

Let us ask the Lord’s mercy to enable us, aided by his merits, to do what he did and obtain what he obtained: namely, that the Lord may mercifully look upon us as he looked upon him, and that by weeping toward him we may be able to turn back to him. Then, somehow recovering his grace, we may at some time celebrate the Lord’s Pascha more truly than we have ever done, and, by his help, pass from the devil to him irrevocably thereafter.

May he deign to grant this to us, utterly unworthy as we are—he who deigned to be our Pascha in order to reconcile us to God the Father through his blood (Rom. V, 10), and to make those rescued from the power of darkness into a people acceptable to himself and zealous for good works. He lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, God, for ages of ages. Amen.

**SERMON VIII**  
[Note: We recognized this sermon, printed by Acherius from the Laon manuscript, by comparison with the Freising manuscript. It seems to belong to the year 963, as may be gathered from note 1429 on Sermon I *On Lent*. We therefore place this as the first sermon *On the Ascension*, although in the printed editions it is presented as the second; the other sermon *On the Ascension*, first in the common editions, was delivered in 968.]

**ON THE ASCENSION OF THE LORD** [another version: II]

**1.** We would very much wish, dearly beloved brothers, [Note: Thus the Freising manuscript; the common editions incorrectly have *laborare* (“to labor”).] that you remember that our labor at this time has reached such an end that, having gathered a supply of words drawn from the testimonies of orthodox Fathers, we might make known to your community what we ought to do, why, and how during the Lent preceding the Lord’s resurrection; how we ought to exult and rejoice at Pascha; and after Pascha—rather, during the fifty days of Pascha—that we ought to cease from fasting, sing “Alleluia” day and night;

[Note: Understand it as follows: We would explain to your community what we ought to do, why, and how during the Lent preceding the Lord’s resurrection; how we ought to exult and rejoice at Pascha, after Pascha, and so forth.]

but that we should not return to the vices exhausted by fasts, prayers, and almsgiving, with God’s grace assisting us, so that we should have no reason for despair.

[Note: Understand it as follows: We must by no means return, with God’s help, to the vices exhausted by fasts, prayers, and almsgiving, so that we should not in any way despair.]

Otherwise, after leaving Egypt, eating the lamb, crossing the Red Sea, and tasting the heavenly manna, we would be returning, through desire for the meat, melons, and onions of Taphnis, [Note: Thus the Freising manuscript; the common editions incorrectly have *desideria* (“desires”).] to the Egypt we had left; we would be deprived of the promised homeland flowing with milk and honey; and, together with those whose many thousands perished in the wilderness, we would undergo the condemnation of eternal destruction.

To persuade us of this, we have been able to find nothing more suitable than singing “Alleluia” day and night—that is, crying out to one another, “Praise the Lord,” and striving for all of us to do this without interruption. For in truth, what place is there for sin where there is no failure in praising God?

[Note: Since Saint Mamertus of Vienne preceded Saint Gregory by nearly a hundred years, “first to Blessed Mamertus, afterward to Blessed Gregory” should have been written. Saint Gregory instituted the litanies which we call the greater litanies without fasting; Saint Mamertus introduced the three-day litanies before the Lord’s Ascension, called the lesser litanies, with fasting. Ratherius, in the *Synodica*, no. 10, recommends that fasting be observed in both. See note 961 there. Here he seems to append an apology for this fasting, which was especially foreign to the rite of the Roman Church during the paschal fifty days.]

If, in a similar necessity, it seemed right first to Blessed Gregory and afterward to Blessed Mamertus, archbishop of Vienne, to institute certain litanies during this Fifty Days, what harm does this do to the Lord’s saying, “Can the children of the bridegroom mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them?” (Matt. IX, 15), since Latin usage judges litanies to signify rogations?

[Note: Understand it as follows: Since Latin usage considers litanies to mean petitions—for litanies, called so in Greek, are called *rogationes* in Latin, as stated in the third supplement to the Capitularies, chapter 120—what harm does this do to the Lord’s teaching? We wrote *innuere* from the Freising manuscript; the common editions have *innui*. If the passive infinitive were accepted, one would have to write *litaniis*.]

At what time is God entreated more solemnly than on feast days?

If one lives soberly, justly, and piously at Pascha, what harm does this do to what the Apostle advises, after saying that Christ himself is our Pascha and adding: “Therefore let us keep the feast”? When he condemns those who serve gluttony, drunkenness, and the other vices, he adds: “Not with the old leaven”—that is, with the swelling of an unrenounced offense and the will to repeat crimes already committed or to commit others—“nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.”

If, therefore, we abstain from gluttony and drunkenness; if, by mutual agreement, we abstain even from lawful intercourse during these three days, out of divine love; if we abstain from jokes and wantonness, from the vanity of songs and games; finally, if, ceasing from every servile work—that is, service of the devil—we take care to serve God during these three days, as we rightly did on the Sundays of Lent, what harm do we inflict on paschal joy? In these practices also we have not entirely neglected the observance of the Lord’s resurrection, provided that we have done what we ought.

Since, as we have often said, it is necessary to make some preparation on Good Friday—that is, to prepare in some way before being refreshed by the Lord’s body and blood, lest anyone receive so great a sacrament unworthily—and since we may suppose [Note: Thus the Freising manuscript; Acherius has *possumus* (“we can”).] that the solemn vigils preceding the feasts were instituted for this reason, what harm is there if, during so great a festival, we use these three days in place of vigils and wash away whatever we have committed amid these paschal joys, while never ceasing to sing “Alleluia” and always exulting and rejoicing in the Lord?

[Note: The Freising manuscript has *dilecto* for *dilectione*. The word is used for “love” in the same way in Sermon II *On Mary and Martha*, no. 1. It does not mean “out of love of justice,” but “out of love,” as opposed to hatred.]

For the apostle James says: “We all offend in many things” (James III, 2). Who would dare boast that, through so many days and nights, he has committed nothing requiring satisfaction and cleansing, so that he might worthily honor so great a festival?

**2.** Thus far, dearest brothers, our common concern for our common salvation has advanced, and our effort has proceeded.

[Note: Understand it as follows: Our effort, that is, our exertion or endeavor, dearest brothers, has progressed this far for the sake of our common salvation. During this fifty-day period there remains the day of singing “Alleluia” without interruption, of exulting and rejoicing; and the most glorious day of the Lord’s Ascension does not permit us to be silent. The word *enim* was added from the excellent Freising manuscript.]

During this fifty-day period there remains the singing of “Alleluia” without interruption, as well as exultation and rejoicing; and the day of the Lord’s most glorious Ascension does not permit us to be silent.

For how can we be silent as we remember all the miracles—if one considers only the more wondrous miracle than all miracles—that a human being, not carried by angelic flight as Elijah once was, nor by winged flight like that poetic figure, but by the bodily mass itself of a perfect human being, that is, one about thirty-three years old, as the Apostle promises will one day come to us—“until we all attain to a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ our Lord” (Eph. IV, 13)—was lifted up while speaking, in the sight of reliable witnesses, and received by a cloud, with angels affirming that he would return in this way to judge all the living and the dead left here from the beginning to the end of the age?

[Note: The same manuscript has “Icarus’s flight.” With its help we deleted “our flight” before “flight.” Understand the passage as follows: How can we be silent as we remember the miracle more wondrous than all miracles, if we consider only the human being: that this human being, Christ, was lifted up while speaking before trustworthy witnesses, not carried by angelic flight, as Elijah once was, nor by winged flight, like the poetic Icarus, but by the bodily mass itself of a perfect man—about thirty-three years old, as the Apostle promises that we shall one day become?]

Who can express this worthily in praise? Who can praise it sufficiently with words? We pass over the matter in wonder if we reflect that the God who remains within was carrying the human being whom he took from us for our sake.

If we could do so, we ought to offer worthy thanks solely for his mercy. The rest is ineffable, and we express it better by silence than by speech.

Let us turn our mouth’s service only toward the promise of his unutterable kindness which we have just heard from the Gospel: “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved” (Mark XVI, 16). Thanks be to God, the whole assembly cries out. For we believe, and we have been baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. We all say this; we all hope through this to be saved; we truly believe and confess that no one can be saved without it.

But concerning whom does the one who heard this—Peter—speak? Peter, I say, to whom, together with the others, it had been said more specifically: “Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark XVI, 15).

[Note: We supplied the following eight words from the Freising manuscript.]

Concerning whom, I ask, if this is so, does the Apostle say: “It would have been better for them not to have known the way of truth than, after knowing it, to turn back” (2 Pet. II, 21)? Clearly, as may most truly be inferred, he speaks of those whose faith the apostle James describes for us: “Faith, if it has no works, is dead in itself” (James II, 17). And again: “They profess that they know God, but by their deeds they deny him” (Titus I, 16).

These are those who destroy by their conduct the faith they affirm with words.

For it must be feared above all that the Lord may also say of such people: “When the unclean spirit has gone out from a person, it passes through waterless places, seeking rest and not finding it; then it says, ‘I will return to my house from which I came.’ And when it comes, it finds it swept and put in order. Then it goes and brings seven other spirits more evil than itself, and entering in they dwell there; and the last state of that person is worse than the first” (Luke XI, 24–26).

If these statements, so true, applied to none of those who profess to believe and are baptized, where would be the Lord’s saying: “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. XX, 16), and: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. VII, 21)?

Who are those called, except those who have entered the Church through baptism? Who are the few chosen, except those who have preserved by living the sacrament they received through faith? Who are those not chosen, except those who have not kept what they promised?

And what did they promise? Let each person recall in thought what he either promised himself or had promised in his place before he was baptized. It is little; it can readily be remembered. If he observes it, let him rejoice, secure in his salvation.

But if he has sinned, [Note: The common editions have “if he has not sinned”; we have adopted the reading of the Freising manuscript.] let him first be still—that is, let him cease sinning—and then let him do penance. “For the kingdom of heaven is at hand” (Matt. III, 2): that is, as all earthly things pass away, indeed flee away, heavenly things draw near—but only to those who, with God’s grace assisting them, have earned the heavenly things through diligent action.

**3.** Who these people are, the same most merciful Promiser demonstrates by adding the following. For after he had said, “Whoever does not believe will be condemned” (Mark XVI, 16), wishing to distinguish believers from unbelievers by various signs, he added:

“These signs will accompany those who believe: in my name they will cast out demons; they will speak in new tongues; they will pick up serpents; and if they drink anything deadly, it will not harm them; they will lay hands on the sick, and they will be well” (Mark XVI, 17–18).

What does this mean, brothers? Who today performs these signs bodily? No one, dearest ones, no one. Does no one therefore believe? God forbid. Thanks be to God, many believe, so that the Psalmist’s words apply to them: “I proclaimed and spoke; they were multiplied beyond number” (Ps. XXX, 6).

How, then, do they believe, when only those who perform these signs are said to believe, whereas these people do not perform them? They do perform them—indeed, some do—but they do not perform them bodily. They do so all the more usefully insofar as the spirit is distinguished from the body.

They cast out demons in Christ’s name when, by his power, they drive from their hearts the vices which demons inspire. They speak in new tongues when, abandoning evil speech, their tongue resounds with God’s praise and their speech brings forth what is useful. They pick up serpents when they do not do what that ancient serpent suggests; and when they feel the devil’s suggestion inwardly but do not do what he suggests, what they drink is indeed deadly, but it will not harm them.

“For we shall all stand,” says the Apostle, “before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may give an account of his own deeds in the body, according to what he has done, whether good or evil” (Rom. XIV, 10).

They lay hands on the sick so that they may be well when they hasten to compensate for the sins they have committed by devoting themselves to good works, so that they may advance toward better things.

Behold the proof; behold the inference; behold the sign of believers and unbelievers, brothers. Whoever recognizes in himself something of these signs should say that he believes. Whoever does not should prepare himself for belief rather than boast that he believes.

### 4.

Here too the Lord says to the blind man: “Do you believe in the Son of God?” (John 9:35), with the preposition, of course. And to the Samaritan woman: “Woman, believe me” (John 4:21), without the preposition.

**Note:** The manuscript cited does not have these words without the preposition.

Here, however, he says absolutely, “whoever has believed,” with neither “in God” nor “God” being added (Mark 16:16). It may therefore be inferred that two things are required: that we believe in God and that we believe God. He believes in God who believes catholicly; he believes God who obeys his exhortations. Whoever does both, and has been washed in orthodox baptism, brings us, thanks be to God, the greatest security.

**Note:** The same manuscript has *ita agit* (“acts thus”), a better reading than the printed texts’ *itaque agit* (“therefore acts”). Such a person will undoubtedly be saved—provided, of course, that he perseveres.

Would that no one in this congregation of ours were found who did not believe that what we hear in John’s Gospel is true, namely: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:3). For although they are unbelieving about everything else, by not believing this one thing they admit that a storm can be produced by a human being, even though the Psalmist cries out most clearly: “Fire and hail, snow and ice, stormy wind, which do his word” (Psalm 148:8)—that is, the Lord’s word.

And in another psalm, concerning God: “He gives snow like wool; he scatters mist like ashes. He casts his ice like morsels; before his cold who can stand?” (Psalm 147:16–17), and so forth.

**Note:** Compare Agobard, bishop of Lyon, who rejects at length in his book *On Hail and Thunder* this foolish opinion concerning those who send storms. See also our author’s *Prefaces*, book I, no. 10, and note 32 there.

How, then, does he believe in God who does not believe that God is the creator of all things? How does he believe God who turns a deaf ear to him as he cries out and says:

> “See, see that I alone am, and there is no other god besides me. I kill, and I make alive; I strike, and I heal; and there is no one who can rescue from my hand” (Deuteronomy 32:39).

Let your charity pay attention. Against those who say that an evil human being or the devil produces a storm, scatters hailstones, devastates vineyards and fields, sends lightning, and kills beasts, cattle, and human beings themselves, against them, I say, this statement is effective: “I kill, and I make alive.” Against those who say that by their incantations they themselves turn such storms aside, this statement is effective: “There is no one who can rescue from my hand” [Col. 0739C].

**Note:** The Vulgate has *quod etsi Elias* (“which, although Elias”), and this is read a little later. We follow the Frisingen manuscript.

If Elijah is read to have held off rain for three years by prayer, and to have restored it again by prayer when he wished; if he is read to have sent fire from heaven upon the impious ministers of an impious king; if Samuel is read to have caused thunder to roar at a time contrary to nature; and if many other saints, both in the Old and in the New Testament, are read to have displayed various signs from heaven, earth, and sea, they did not perform these things themselves, but God performed them through them. Faith itself did this, of which the Lord himself speaks to the apostles in this way:

> “If you had faith like a grain of mustard seed, you would say to this mountain, ‘Move from here and cast yourself into the sea,’ and it would obey you” (Matthew 17:19).

The devil cannot do this, nor can any malicious member of his. God does it through his servants whenever it pleases him, and, since he is supremely good, he does it kindly, as the good God.

### 5.

But let us return to the feast of the Lord’s Ascension. After he had said these things, says the distinguished narrator of so great an event, “while they watched, he was lifted up, and a cloud received him from their eyes. And while they were looking intently toward heaven as he went, behold, two men stood beside them in white garments, and they said: ‘Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven’” (Acts 1:9–11).

Here, listener, I ask you to pay attention for a little while. Christ is first seen rising in Galilee; Christ is shown ascending only to men of Galilee; to them he is promised as the one who will return.

Who, then, are or were the Galileans, or who will be, except those who inhabited Galilee, inhabit it, or will inhabit it in times to come?

**Note:** The Vulgate incorrectly has *id est* (“that is”) instead of *vel* (“or”).

Galilee, as we have received from our predecessors, is interpreted as “transmigration.” And how have we come to know this?

**Note:** The Frisingen manuscript has this twice. Since it was done three times, one must settle on the first instance. Let us speak briefly: “They migrated,” and so forth. The passage appears corrupt both in the Vulgate and in this manuscript. From the two, however, one may piece together the more suitable reading.

This happened twice—or rather, it happened three times—and we must pause over the first and then speak of the two joined to the third: the sons of Zebedee migrated from their father to Christ; Christ, rising from the tomb, came to them; and finally they migrated from Galilee to the mountain which he had appointed for them, and, while they looked on, he was lifted up from there into heaven [Col. 0740B].

Let the person who desires to follow him there migrate from the devil to him; let him consider him dead and buried for his sake; let him rejoice that through his resurrection he has been raised, and through his ascension into heaven has been carried upward—provided that he fixes his desire most firmly upon this.

Therefore, dearest ones, let each of us strive so that, just as Christ today ascended into heaven with our body, so each of us may ascend there in hope, migrate there in desire, and strive to reach it by his conduct, in whatever way he can.

Remarkable though it is to say, we can ascend into heaven even through our vices, if we make a point of trampling them down. For in a certain sense we make a ladder out of them for ourselves if we crush them by correction [Col. 0740C]. They lift us up if they are beneath us; they press us down if they are above us.

Our flesh ascended into heaven in Christ; let our soul follow it in desire. Christ’s soul desires to carry our souls there; let us cooperate with its desire. God is the one who bears it; omnipotent mercy and grace are active. Let us not despair of the possibility, provided that we do not fail in our will.

Let us carry virtues with us as the equivalent of our travelling expenses. Let us leave vices here, as deadly poverty and perpetual hunger, and likewise the adversary that obstructs our ascent throughout the night. While we linger here, let us never cease hastening toward there. For without a doubt we shall arrive where Christ is with our flesh, if we do not cease desiring him, with the help of his clemency, who with the Father, and so forth [Col. 0740D].

## SERMON IX. [Note: This sermon was printed by Acherius from a Laon manuscript; it must be assigned to the year 968, as will be clear from note 1548.]

### ON THE ASCENSION OF THE LORD II [alternatively, I]

#### 1.

Since in almost everything the quality of our life differs from the pursuits of the ancient Fathers as much as our doctrine does, I confess that we also differ from them considerably in this respect: when they first composed sermons from the Gospel’s teaching on solemnities such as this one, they initially stirred their hearers’ minds toward consideration of that solemnity. Then, at the end, they brought forward a brief exhortation, opened up as much as they were able, admonishing more earnestly those whom they had addressed to restrain themselves from evil and persist in what is pleasing to God.

For us, by contrast, it is fitting at the very beginning of our speaking to observe what the Psalmist urges:

> “Let us anticipate the face of the Lord in confession” (Psalm 95:2)

—with our sins understood—and what another says:

> “You speak first of your iniquities, that you may be justified” (Isaiah 43:26);

that is, “that you may be justified, not judged.”

“For if we judged ourselves,” says the Apostle, “we would certainly not be judged” (1 Corinthians 11:31)—that is, if we ourselves truly accused ourselves, we would not be condemned by the Lord.

A person truly accuses himself when he says nothing about himself other than what he remembers having done; when he is angry with no one else if that person says the same thing about him; when he detests the evil he confesses and strives with all his strength to amend it; when he fears voluntarily repeating it; and when he is healthfully ashamed of it.

Otherwise, the Lord’s voice says to such a soul:

> “How vile you have become by repeating your ways” (Jeremiah 3:36).

It is also forbidden to do this in the following words:

> “Do not repeat the word in your prayer” (Ecclesiasticus 19:17),

that is, do not repeat what you have confessed, so that it becomes necessary for you to confess that sin again.

For when we both recognize and confess that we have sinned grievously, we also report the punishments which we are bound to undergo on account of it. If even fear of those punishments does not restrain us from committing evil, we ourselves compel the words to be shouted indirectly at us:

> “Out of your own mouth I judge you, wicked servant” (Luke 19:22).

But if we do this especially in the case of a bodily offense, we forbid ourselves altogether to consecrate the offerings, unless we pretend not to know what is contained in canon 9 of the Council of Neocaesarea.

**Note:** In canon 9 of the Council of Neocaesarea the matter concerns a bodily sin committed before ordination: “If a presbyter who has been overtaken by a bodily sin is promoted, and he confesses that he sinned before ordination, let him not consecrate the offerings.” Ratherius thought that what applied to a sin committed before ordination applied much more strongly to one committed after ordination, and therefore elsewhere cited the same canon against clerics entangled in carnal guilt. See part I of *On Contempt for the Canons*, no. 11, and the *Itinerary*, no. 10 [Col. 0742D].

#### 2.

Since this is so, what can we say, or at least think, about ourselves? If, when we are about to speak to you, we anticipate the face of the Lord in confession (Psalm 95:2)—that is, if, before we come to his judgment, we truly accuse ourselves to you—by what right do we consecrate the bread to be offered to you? If we do not do this, what beginning do we make to our speaking—or rather, what do we ever say to you as our duty?

For concerning rejoicing we can say nothing else about ourselves than what we learn Tobias to have replied to the angel:

> “What kind of joy will there be for me,” he said, “who sit in darkness and do not see the light of heaven?” (Tobit 5:12.)

For we ourselves are witnesses that we sit in darkness [Col. 0742A], since, with the eyes of our mind obscured, we do not perceive that we are proceeding toward the fire as we ought.

**Note:** Construe: “Because, with the eyes of the mind obscured, we do not see ourselves proceeding toward the fire as we ought.”

The light of heaven is the brightness of Christ, by which the angels above and holy human beings below are illuminated: the former in order to possess it, the latter in order to desire it, and both in order eventually to enjoy it together.

Who, then, is not now illuminated so as to desire it—do you think he can then be illuminated so as to possess it? What joy of this kind can anyone have in any solemnity, unless it is altogether empty?

#### 3.

Yet today is a very great feast, brothers—indeed, a very great feast. But for those who are neither able nor willing to consider the light of heaven, it is nothing, nothing, I say, nothing.

**Note:** Construe: “Although today is truly the feast of the Lord’s Ascension, how can at least a little practiced chatter—especially episcopal chatter, even if eloquence is lacking—be allowed to remain silent?”

Since today truly is the feast of the Lord’s Ascension, how can at least a little practiced chatter, especially of the episcopal kind, be allowed to remain silent, even if eloquence is lacking?

But whose feast of the Lord is this, I ask? It is Christ’s, certainly, and Christ’s precisely because Christ deigned to become what he became for us.

> “You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity”—the Psalmist sings concerning him.  
> “Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Psalm 45:7).

What righteousness? Clearly, that by which he judged it right that the creature should serve the one who created it.

What iniquity? Clearly, that by which human beings served the devil, although they had been created to serve God.

Therefore God anointed him with the oil of gladness—that is, mercy itself clothed him with it, the mercy that would make the angels rejoice over the reconciliation of the human race, which had been excluded from their fellowship by the devil’s fraud.

And because, through that same mercy, some of the children of the devil were destined to become children of God by adoption, and thus to become companions of him who was the Son of God not by adoption but by nature, he is said to have been anointed “above his companions.” For the same grace of the Holy Spirit was given to the others according to measure, but in him “the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Colossians 2:9), that is, fully: God filled the very body which he assumed for us so completely that, just as his mind was filled with God, so also his flesh was filled with God. Thus, from two natures and in two natures, there is not two but one Lord Jesus Christ, true God in every respect, like the Father and the Spirit, and, with them, not three but one living God forever.

**Note:** Acherius’s edition reads *mente cujus* (“whose mind”), and below *cumque illi non tres* (“and with him not three”). We have adopted the corrections of the latest editors.

Therefore, unless God had mercifully clothed himself in our flesh, he would not have raised it into heaven; unless he had raised it into heaven, he would not have dedicated this day to us.

This, then, is Christ’s solemnity, brothers—but not without his companions. For, astonishingly, he carried them with him into heaven, even though they had not yet been born on earth.

#### 4.

Since all the progressions of the solemnities have been instituted as belonging to Christ and to his companions, whoever wishes to have a share in any one of them should strive to do what Christ himself did.

But alas, our sorrow! We have neglected to do so. Although we had exhorted you repeatedly in the days preceding these solemnities to be diligent in preserving the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace (Ephesians 4:3), and to forgive one another if anyone had a complaint against another (Colossians 3:13), so that, being about to eat the flesh of the Lamb, we might be shown to celebrate the Lord’s Passover not in the leaven of malice and wickedness but in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth (1 Corinthians 5:8), we who gave this warning did not act with the zeal with which we spoke.

**Note:** The days preceding these solemnities are chiefly the days of Lent in the year 968; during that period he plainly testifies in *Discord* no. 7 that he had striven to exhort everyone to peace. Compare note 1492 on sermon 2 *On Easter*. In what follows he presents a summary of what he had discussed in his exhortations, as he did in other words in sermon 7. There is therefore no doubt that this sermon also belongs to the year 968.

The most sacred day of the Lord’s Supper arrived. What the Apostle had said was read, and we urged observance of his warning, namely, that we should not receive the Lord’s body to our judgment.

There were, indeed, some who received the sacred morsel from the hand which they would have wished to be cut off—shame upon them! There was one who wished there had been no one for him to give it to.

And alas, with what deadly leaven both of them were swollen!

And when we had urged certain people, beginning with the very lawful season, to abstain from intercourse during this Lent, so that, purified, they might be worthy to receive the Lord’s sacrifice at Easter, woe to those who, after receiving the sacrifice, were unable to abstain from adultery even until the Lord’s octave.

For we are assured that what we have often sung in the psalm applies to them: namely, that after the morsel, as in the case of Judas, Satan entered them (John 13:27)—that is, an unclean spirit with seven heads (Luke 11:26), which alone was believed to have been expelled through fasting (Mark 9:28).

While their food was still in their mouths, the wrath of God rose against them (Psalm 78:30).

**Note:** Construe: “When the wretched people had been exposed as violators, not worshipers, of so great a solemnity.”

They were found to have been, in their misery, violators of so great a solemnity, not its worshipers.

Let them therefore choose what they will do. If, despairing of themselves, they harden their hearts, then, by repeating the same conduct, they strangle themselves with Judas’s noose. If they imitate Peter’s tears, they obtain forgiveness; if they obtain forgiveness, they follow Christ in heaven, now in affection and later in its actual fulfillment.

If they deserve neither of these two things, let them know that this solemnity belongs to God, the angels, and people of good will, as it was sung, while they themselves remain entirely excluded from it.

#### 5.

But lest they flatter themselves by quoting that statement of the Lord:

> “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved” (Mark 16:16),

let them know that, although it is entirely true, since it was spoken by the mouth of Truth, it is true only for those to whom it properly applies.

“For,” he says, “these signs will follow those who believe:

> ‘In my name they will cast out demons’” (ibid. 17),

and so forth.

If anyone recognizes these signs in himself when they are understood soberly, let him rejoice securely concerning his salvation. Whoever does not, I advise him to tremble; and unless he strives to believe not only in God but also God, let him know that believing will not suffice for him.

**Note:** Augustine’s well-known distinction between believing in God and believing God is at issue here. A person believes God when he believes the truths God has revealed. He believes in God when he not only believes the truths God has revealed but also loves God by believing and directs himself toward God with the faith that works through charity. See Augustine, *Tractate XIX on John*, and elsewhere. Hence it might seem that here one ought to correct the text to read “believe not only God but also in God.” But, as Ratherius explained himself in the preceding sermon, no. 4, he uses “believe in God” of one who believes catholicly, while he uses “believe God” of one who obeys God’s exhortations. This seems to have been taken from Ecclesiasticus 32:28: “He who believes God attends to the commandments.” Accordingly, in sermon 2 *On Lent*, no. 41, he similarly says: “Even if someone believes in God in such matters, he does not believe God if he does not keep his commandments, nor does he preserve by his life the sacrament which he received by faith,” and so forth.

> “Out of your own mouth I judge you, wicked servant” (Luke 19:22).

But, Christ, I beg you, do not hasten to pronounce it. Merciful one, I ask you, delay the blow; most compassionate one, suspend the vengeance. Say to the executioners of my life, I implore you, in your mercy:

> “Let her alone this year also, until I dig around her and put manure on her; perhaps she may eventually improve through your grace” (Luke 13:8).

**Note:** Construe: “I beg you, merciful one, say to those who would cut short my life: ‘Let her alone this year also, until I dig around her and put manure on her; perhaps I may eventually be able to improve through your grace.’”

For I still remain uncorrectable in deadly ingratitude. I do not moisten my eyes with tears of conversion; rather, I tighten the throat of my dying mind with the cords of deadly delay and of worsening each day.

I descend alive into hell—not unaware, as many are, but knowingly—and I do not even conceal it. Hence I fear that it may not be shouted at me without cause:

> “Out of your own mouth I judge you, wicked servant,”

along with those who say good things and do the worst.

I make known to others the severity of your punishment; I am fully aware that you are present everywhere; yet I do not shrink from saying or doing what dishonors your regard.

But what am I doing, Lord? I would flee if I had the power to flee anywhere. Since I cannot, at the urging of your truthful Augustine, I flee in fear to you—from you, that is, from your justice to your mercy.

Therefore, just as you consider what is unbecoming to you, so, Lord, I beg you to consider what is necessary for me, freeing me from the deadly impatience that compels me to transgress your commandments so terribly.

For unless I am quickly rescued from it, I await eternal destruction, though I am ignorant, Lord, of your plan concerning me. Your ways are not human ways; they belong solely to your power, you who do not condemn unjustly those whom you created kindly.

But you, brothers, fear for yourselves what you have heard from us about ourselves. Abandon as quickly as possible the evils you habitually commit. While there is still time, apply yourselves to unfamiliar good deeds. Beware of hell; ascend into heaven by desire. Strive to hasten there, relying on his help, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God.

Think carefully that the hour is pressing upon you in which you will either ascend there or fall below, and that here you will not remain much longer. Otherwise, God forbid, you may suddenly be seized and dragged there where no one will be able to help you.

May Jesus Christ our Lord, who came into this world to save sinners, deign to avert this from all of us. He lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON X. ON THE FEAST OF PENTECOST

**Note:** Among Ratherius’s sermons, Fulcuinus, chapter 24, mentions one “on the day of Pentecost.” Acherius, in the table of contents of volume II of the *Spicilegium*, counts two sermons on Pentecost among Ratherius’s unpublished works, and in his preface to Ratherius’s works states that he received their exemplar from the Lobbes manuscript. Although he promised that he would publish them elsewhere, he did not do so. We carefully examined the Lobbes manuscripts so that these sermons too, together with the other unpublished works, might be brought into public circulation. Yet despite every diligence, nothing of the sort could be found. Only one sermon was possible to find in the Frisingen manuscript, and this is the one we are now going to publish. It was delivered in the year 963. See note 1438 on sermon 1 *On Lent*.

### 1.

Come now, what am I to do, brothers? If I remain silent, I defraud reality of what ought to have been administered through me; I become guilty before you of that same fraud; and I conceal from myself also what this day is, and how great it is.

If I desire to speak, I fear that I may succumb to the greatness of the subject itself about which I wish to speak. Yet I shall do what I can, for I consider no one more indebted.

Today Pentecost is fulfilled, brothers. What did I say? Today the fiftieth day after Easter comes to an end. What follows from that? Let the one who knows say:

> “Better is the end of a prayer than its beginning” (Ecclesiastes 7:9).

Let the one who can pay attention do so:

> “Whoever perseveres to the end,” says the Lord, “will be saved” (Matthew 10:22).

Blessed are those who have kept these fifty days as they ought, never ceased from moral “Alleluia,” and did not abandon it even while sleeping.

Yet if such people wish to be saved, let them show today, I suggest, the devotion of their perseverance. Today is the fiftieth day from the Lord’s Resurrection, the tenth from his Ascension. A great mystery, and an indescribable gift!

Today is the fiftieth day since we rose in Christ; the tenth since we ascended into heaven with him. Of whom am I speaking? Clearly, of those to whom the Apostle boldly says:

> “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God,” that is, in equality with the Father; “set your minds on the things that are above, not on the things that are on earth. For you have died”—namely, you are free from sin—“and your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Colossians 3:1–4).

Blessed are those who are such; most wretched are those who perpetually fall away from their company. For the former will appear with Christ in glory, but the latter with the devil in everlasting condemnation.

### 2.
