Yet, presuming that we still belong to their company—for, as someone says, “A person does not know whether he is worthy of hatred or love, but all things are kept uncertain for the future” (Ecclesiastes 9:1)—let us speak without despairing of ourselves, since today is the fiftieth day since we rose in Christ, the tenth since we ascended into heaven with Christ.

What are we awaiting today? Gifts, certainly; divisions of graces; charisms of every blessedness. But what are those gifts? Let the Apostle bring them forth:

> “The love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Romans 5:5).

But for what purpose was he given? Without doubt, as a pledge. For just as we have here no enduring city, so also we do not yet possess secure blessedness.

How do we know that we have received the Holy Spirit as a pledge? The Apostle says:

> “He who gave us the pledge of the Spirit” (2 Corinthians 5:5).

Behold, we shall have the benefit of the pledge we have received.

How do we know that we received that gift today? Let the historian speak; let Luke the physician testify:

> “When the day of Pentecost was being fulfilled, all the disciples were together in one place” (Acts 2:1).

In what place? “And while they were looking into heaven as he went”—he had already brought this forward—“behold, two men stood beside them in white garments, and they said: ‘Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven.’

> “Then they returned to Jerusalem from the mountain called Olivet, which is near Jerusalem, a Sabbath day’s journey away; and when they had entered the upper room, they went up to the higher part, where Peter and John, James and Andrew, Philip and Thomas, Bartholomew and Matthew, James the son of Alphaeus and Simon the Zealot, and Judas the son of James were staying. All these were persevering with one accord in prayer, together with the women and Mary the mother of Jesus, and his brothers” (Acts 1:10–14).

When they were therefore in the same place, suddenly there came from heaven a sound like that of a mighty rushing spirit, and it filled the entire house where they were sitting. And divided tongues appeared to them as if of fire, and one rested upon each of them. They were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in various languages, as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance (Acts 2:2–4).

### 3.

O how this abyss of the Old Testament calls upon the abyss of the New! O how the earlier things harmonize with the later!

On the fiftieth day after the killing of the lamb and the crossing of the Red Sea, the Decalogue was given to Moses on Mount Sinai. On the fiftieth day after Christ’s Resurrection, the Holy Spirit was sent to the apostles.

The fiftieth year is the year of remission; our fiftieth day has been consecrated to grace. On that day God the Son descended upon the mountain; on this day—our day—God the Holy Spirit of the Father and the Son came, displayed in fiery tongues.

In both cases the Trinity fulfilled its purpose. There the Father sent the Son to Moses; here the Holy Spirit, sent and proceeding from the Father and the Son, poured himself into the apostles by his spontaneous power.

There were thunder and voices, and the mountain smoking; here, men aflame with various tongues—the apostles, of course—burning with the ardors of divine fire.

Finally, this is the fiftieth day of the Lord’s Resurrection. All the patriarchs and prophets, assigning all the other days from Easter to this one to due veneration, celebrated this day above all.

The clearest witness to this is Tobias, who was blind yet saw so clearly; so too the Apostle, carried up to the heights of the third heaven:

> “I was going,” he says, “to our festal day of Pentecost, which is holy from the weeks” (Acts 20:16).

**Note:** This reading presents the ancient version of the Book of Tobit from the Greek, which Father Sabatier published from the Royal and Saint-Germain manuscripts. Ratherius combined one text from two. He took the word “I was going” from chapter 1, verse 6, where it reads: “I alone used to go at times to Jerusalem on the feast days”; the rest comes from chapter 2, verse 1, where it reads: “On Pentecost, our feast, which is holy from the weeks.” These words are likewise quoted by Lucifer of Cagliari in his book *On Not Sparing Those Who Sin Against God*. See volume I, part II, page 713, of Father Sabatier’s *Sacred Bibles of the Ancient Latin Version* [Col. 0748D].

The blessed Paul is read to have hastened to celebrate this day in Jerusalem because he knew that it surpassed all others.

“Holy from the weeks,” he says. Do not count it carelessly, I insist: for from Easter to our most holy Pentecost you will find, unless I am mistaken, only seven weeks.

Read the prophet, and you will discover that the sevenfold Spirit rested upon the flower growing from the root of Jesse (Isaiah 11:1).

### 4.

Who is that Spirit, then, except the one who descended upon the Lord in the form of a dove and upon the apostles in fire?

Why did he appear upon the Lord in the form of a dove, but upon the apostles in fire? Surely because the Lord, coming in gentleness, wished to show himself to human beings through a gentle sign; but, since he was about to send the apostles to announce his judgment, he wished to show with what terror he would come to judge.

He came meekly so that he might not be judged, manifested by a more violent sound.

Why did he display fiery tongues? Surely to show that his servants ought both to be fervent in charity and most ready in speech. They were to proclaim with the truth which they had heard—and what is this, brothers?—what the Evangelist reports:

> “Jesus said to his disciples: ‘If anyone loves me, he will keep my word,’” and so forth (John 14:23).

Whoever possesses a fiery tongue would dare to obscure this by sophistical evasion? It is clear; let it be stated clearly. There is no middle position.

Either we love the Lord or we do not love him. If we love him, we do what he commands. If we do not love him, we do not keep what he orders.

If we love him, we are loved by him. If we do not, then, however irrationally we may fear him, we should not presumptuously suppose that we are loved.

Yet let us not despair that this can happen. For it is sung concerning him:

> “You have mercy on all, Lord, and you hate nothing that you have made” (Wisdom 11:24–25).

**Note:** This is sung in the Introit of the Wednesday after Ash Wednesday and is taken from the Book of Wisdom, chapter 11, verses 24–25.

Nothing is truer. The Lord does not hate what he made in you; he hates what you yourself do to your own detriment. Therefore he is so pious, so merciful, and so ready to forgive those who turn back that we may know that he does not hate the substance he created in us, but rather curses our wickedness.

If we desire to be changed by his help, let us also show that, when we are angry with one another, we do not therefore hate one another, but hate the evil which we recognize in one another.

Since our loves—and likewise our hatreds—are changeable, we love God so much more unchangeably and steadfastly when we recognize that his will is the same as he himself is [possibly: “the same as himself,” with “is” understood].

**Note:** The adverb *irrationabiliter* (“irrationally”) should be understood according to Ratherius’s intention; this was explained in note 723 on the work *On His Own Fall*.

Hence no measure is imposed upon us in our love of God; but in our love of our neighbor a condition is imposed: that we love our neighbors as ourselves—that is, among other things, that we desire them to be such as we ourselves ought to have been.

Let this brief treatment of the Gospel reading suffice.

### 5.

Let us turn to proclaiming today’s solemnity.

Just as, brothers, there is a *Song of Songs* and a King of kings, so this day is the solemnity of solemnities.

For Christ was born for this purpose: to suffer. He died for this purpose: to rise again. He rose for this purpose: to raise into heaven the flesh which he had taken from us and for us. He transferred it there for this purpose: to make it immortal and forever blessed.

But since this could not happen without the gift of the Holy Spirit—for unless we were regenerated through baptism and made new people, we could not possibly be saved while remaining in our old condition, and we could in no way be baptized except in the Holy Spirit and fire (Matthew 3:11)—today he sent the Holy Spirit to us in fiery tongues.

Thus, having been baptized, speaking about God, and fervent in love of him and of our neighbor, we might eventually be transferred to that place to which we could in no way be transferred without charity.

For, as the Apostle says:

> “If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him” (Romans 8:9).

But whoever does not belong to him consequently cannot be a participant in his kingdom.

Possession of the Spirit is itself evidence of charity, since the same Apostle says:

> “The love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Romans 5:5).

**Note:** Construe: “Since possession of charity itself is evidence of the Spirit”—that is, since possessing charity is a sign that someone has the Holy Spirit—the same Apostle says, and so forth.

We are therefore better able to recognize whether someone has the Holy Spirit the more fervent we see him to be in charity.

But the Apostle says:

> “If anyone has the world’s goods and sees his brother in need, yet closes his heart against him, how does the love of God abide in him?” (1 John 3:17).

Since this is so, the proof of charity is undoubtedly, as Gregory says, the exhibition of works; and the exhibition of works is the demonstrator of the Holy Spirit, whom we received today in the apostles.

As it is sung in the psalm:

> “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive” (Psalm 68:18),

that is, he led captive our flesh with its soul, which had once been held captive by the devil.

> “He gave gifts to human beings” (Ephesians 4:8),

that is, Christ, ascending on high, gave the apostles today the charisms of the Holy Spirit.

**Note:** That is, Christ, ascending on high, gave the apostles today the charisms of the Holy Spirit, he who with the Father and the same Spirit is blessed throughout the ages.

Amen.

# SERMON XI. ON MARY AND MARTHA

*[Note: Fulcuinus also praised this sermon under the title “On the Feast of Saint Mary,” in which he expounds the Gospel of the feast of the Assumption of the same Virgin. Acherius had obtained it from the Lobbes manuscript with the title “On Mary and Martha,” as it is also inscribed in the Freising codex, from which we now publish it for the first time. We conjectured in note 1017 of the *Itinerary* that this sermon was delivered in the year 966, after the feast of the Assumption of the Blessed Mary, when Otto I had already advanced to the imperial dignity—for he designates him by the name “Caesar” in section 4. Since at that time the disturbances that had broken out against Ratherius in the preceding year were still spreading, he says in section 1: “We considered that we were not greatly loved, and for that reason were despised”; and he introduces further indications belonging to that period. See note 1029. This is confirmed even more strongly by the order of the short works set out in chronological sequence in the Freising manuscript: there this sermon appears after the *Synodical Letter*, which was published during Lent in the year 966. See note 1429, on Sermon I concerning Lent.]*

## 1

Would that you might remember, brothers, that at the preceding solemnity of the holy Mother of God, Mary, you had rendered the service of your attendance to our assembly, when from the Gospel reading we demonstrated that what was said to the Blessed Mother of God—“Mary has chosen the better part, which shall not be taken away from her”—applies no less to her than to the one whose voice, the Lord’s own voice, uttered it.

When, from the same sequence of the Gospel reading, our poverty of eloquence had brought forth for your filial devotion whatever it could, I saw all of you, alas, unmoved, as though nothing severe had been said, judging from the faces of some among you. No tears were seen there; no sighs; no sound of a contrite heart was heard. Then it became most evidently true what we read Augustine to have said more than once: namely, “Unless the one who teaches burns, he is quite unable to set his hearer on fire.” And when we considered that we were not greatly loved, and for that reason were despised, we also recognized the truth of Gregory’s saying: “It is difficult for one who is not loved to be heard willingly, however correctly the teacher may preach”; and again: “When a man’s life is despised, it remains that his preaching too will be scorned.”

Nevertheless, we saw that this complaint of ours agreed—although in a manner far from corresponding to the prophet—with the words: “The house of Israel does not wish to hear you, because it does not wish to hear me” (Ezek. 3:7); and with the Lord’s words: “If they have kept my word, they will also keep yours” (John 15:20). “What are we?” says the one whose estimation we cannot approach. “What are we,” I say, “but your murmuring is not against us, but against the Lord” (Exod. 16:7–8).

Since, alas, we are blameworthy in countless matters, when none of you censures what deservedly ought to be reproved in us, but instead rightly censures what ought rightly to be praised, he proves that he does this not from love of justice [that is, with love], but from hatred of those things which he would in no way wish to hear.

O those among you who are such! Would that they applied themselves as eagerly to serious matters as they do to what we utter—not only useless but even harmful—and attended to the advancement of their own souls as much as they attend to the harm of those souls while we, with eyes certainly closed, speak to them!

## 2

But now we must say what was said by us there. As had often been stated before us, we said that these two matrons signify two ways of life. One, named from action, is called *praktikē* (πρακτική), that is, active; the other, named from vision or leisure, is called *theōrikē* (θεωρική), that is, contemplative—leisure, namely, by which one rests in contemplation.

For no one magnifies the things that are to be seen inwardly more than the one who withdraws more fully from activity.

*[Note: Construe as follows: “When, following the ancients, I had said that these two blessed sisters signified these two ways of life, their devotion indicated that this was most truly so, since one is said to have been busy—that is, to have devoted herself or labored—‘about much serving,’ meaning not that she had then begun it for the first time, but that by the frequency of her activity she had converted it into a habitual practice,” and so forth.]*

Having followed the ancients and said that these two blessed women signified these two ways of life, their devotion indicates that this is most truly so: one is said to have been busy—that is, to have applied herself or labored—“about much serving,” meaning not that she had then begun it for the first time, but that through repeated activity she had made it habitual; namely, that she might serve the Lord from her modest means, as she had done in many ways.

The other is said to have preferred to sit at the Lord’s feet—not with that idleness which is hostile to the soul, but with that of which the Lord himself cries out through the Psalmist: “Be still and see that I am God” (Ps. 45:11). Yet she too was diligent, just as the other was in serving, so she was diligent in listening to the things that proceeded from the Lord’s mouth.

And truly, no one in the Church does anything except these two things when he does what he ought to do. There is no place here for fornication; adultery is far away; drunkenness is distant; falsehood nowhere; and, lest our speech proceed to infinity, every fullness of wickedness is wholly absent from such people.

One of these ways belongs to secular persons, the other to spiritual persons. The first belongs to those who will hear: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25:34): “For I was hungry, thirsty, a stranger, sick, and in prison”—in my members, nevertheless—and endured many such things, and you relieved me.

The other belongs to those who have already heard, in the apostles themselves and together with them: “Amen, I say to you, that you who have left everything and followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man shall sit on the throne of his majesty, you also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19:28).

## 3

What now, brothers? When these things stand in such a way, is there no one within the enclosure of these four walls who ought rightly to beat his breast, sigh, and groan? Where, then, are my likenesses?

Here no other lot or condition is heard of concerning those who act in this way—unless our wickedness may suspect it—than: “Depart from me, you cursed, into everlasting fire, which is prepared not for human beings, but for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41). These are either those who fell from heaven with him, or those who attended upon him in this world. For an angel is called almost *aggelus*—*agchelus*, from the Greek ἄγχι, “near”—that is, one standing close by. These wretched people offered the devil the same service that those happy people just mentioned offered God: they ministered to him what he sought, namely, deeds of many kinds of wickedness; they continually attended upon him, eagerly embraced his suggestions, and carried them out in action.

No such person has imitated Mary or Martha; no one has taken Leah as wife—

*[Note: Augustine taught in book XXII of his work against Faustus, chapter 52, that Leah represented active life and Rachel contemplative life. Gregory joined together the figures of Mary and Martha, as well as those of Rachel and Leah, in book II of his *Homilies on Ezekiel*, homilies 2, sections 9 and 10. Ratherius, thoroughly versed in the reading of the Fathers, drew from these sources and inserted into this sermon on Mary and Martha a mention also of Leah and Rachel.]*

—none has taken Rachel as his wife. No such person has loved one of them and tolerated the other—that is, from love of seeing the Lord, he has done the good he could.

*[Note: Construe as follows: “Let whoever wishes speak, and, if he can, persuade me to hope for what the Lord has not promised: namely, that one who commits evil may receive good, and that those who neither serve God actively like Martha nor sit contemplatively at his feet like Mary should expect the reward promised only to those who have done one of these two things; whereas he cries out,” and so forth.]*

Let whoever wishes speak and, if he can, persuade me to hope for what the Lord has not promised: namely, that one who commits evil should receive good, and that those who neither serve God actively like Martha nor sit contemplatively at his feet like Mary should expect the reward promised only to those who have done one of these things. For he cries out in opposition: “Every tree that does not produce good fruit” (Matt. 7:19)—that is, one of those fruits which either Mary or Martha produced—“shall be cut down and cast into the fire.”

And concerning merely useless thought he himself promises us woe: “Woe to those who devise what is useless” (Micah 2:1).

*[Note: The manuscript had *quae nobis* (“which for us”). We have introduced the emendation from the passage in Micah to which the author alludes, where it reads: “Woe to those who devise what is useless.”]*

He has also said that we shall give an account on the day of judgment even for an idle word (Matt. 12:36).

*[Note: Construe as follows: “And when, after looking around at the great multitude within this enclosure—that is, this temple—I find no imitator here at all of those women, it is not greatly inappropriate that I too should have changed my manner of speaking here for the sake of propriety; since, as I said, I am unable to find any imitator of them here, and I see myself more than all the others deprived of their lot, who would encourage me to restrain myself from that fear which, though in a spirit of rivalry, torments me?”]*

And when, after looking around at the great multitude within this enclosure, I find no imitator here at all of those women, it is not greatly inappropriate that I too should have changed my manner of speaking here for the sake of propriety. Since, as I said, I can find no rival of those women here, and I see myself more than all the others deprived of their lot, who would encourage me to restrain myself from the fear that torments me, however competitively?

*[Note: Construe as follows: “For surely I do not trust that I shall become blessed through that fear, while abandoning no vice on account of this fear, although my conscience is always in punishment, as Scripture says that the conscience of one who has done wrong is always in punishment.”]*

For surely I do not trust that I shall become blessed through that fear, abandoning no vice on account of it, although my conscience is always in punishment (Wis. 17:10), as Scripture says that the conscience of one who has done wrong is to be in punishment.

## 4

And alas, how unlike that Sicilian tyrant am I in such a condition!

Since I know that, in the office which I grieve to bear unworthily—that is, which weighs upon me—I am debtor to both obligations, namely, that I must minister to the Lord in his members, that is, to the sons of the holy mother Church, and yet must never cease contemplating him, but meditate upon his law day and night (Ps. 1:2), and since I see myself doing neither of these things, but instead corrupting not only myself but also all those entrusted to me, especially those who are more necessary to me, provoking him day and night to anger—although no passion can befall him—what can I say or think about myself?

*[Note: Construe as follows: “What can I say—and, suppressing shameful matters, let me mention only honorable ones, although they are forbidden—what, I say, can I say or think about myself, if I do not meditate day and night upon the law of God, although I know that I am a debtor, when I read Catullus, previously never read; when I read Plautus, whom I had long ago not read; when, often asked, I explain music,” and so forth. He seems to have found at Verona a copy of Catullus which he had not previously read, and perhaps also a copy of Plautus.]*

What can I say or think about myself—and, suppressing shameful matters, let me mention only honorable ones, although they are forbidden—if I do not meditate day and night upon the law of God, although I know that I am a debtor: when I read Catullus, whom I had never read before; when I read Plautus, whom I had not read for a long time; when, often asked, I explain music, although I cannot even, with the first aid of arithmetic, [lacuna]; when I compel my soldiers to battle because of the emperor’s command; when I send them hunting?

*[Note: In the *Itinerary*, written toward the end of the year 966, section 1, he says that he was going to Rome, not by imperial command—for no such command had been given—but only because he had been ordered to send his own soldiers. See also note 1017 there.]*

Here there is no collusion, no rest is permitted. Rather, that man is absolutely declared blessed who meditates upon the law of the Lord day and night.

But alas, most wretched that I am, how I descend alive into hell amid such things, and even more detestable ones! That is, I do not fail to know that, if I am judged apart from mercy, I shall undoubtedly go into hell on account of such things.

And when I see neither my laypeople nor my clergy busy with the Lord’s frequent—that is, customary—service, since I plainly see the former not carrying out works of Christianity and the latter wholly turned away from the canonical law even to public marriage—

*[Note: That is, to public weddings. Elsewhere too he frequently condemns the clergy’s public marriage.]*
    
—and when I see that my monks likewise do not wish in any way to withdraw themselves from worldly activities for love of contemplating the Lord, to the extent that I even observe that this anchorite in whose presence we stand has not entirely renounced transitory things:

where, wretched man that I am, shall I find Martha, where her sister Mary, where Leah, where Rachel, when the Lord will demand an account from me, the most miserable of men, concerning all of you, as concerning sheep entrusted to me, on the day of judgment?

Where, finally, in these buildings is the one who defeats the devil, who, while desiring one of these two—that is, the contemplative life—obtains both, passing through temporal goods while ministering to Christ in such a way that he does not lose eternal goods?

## 5

These words might seem excessively severe and invented by us to our detractors—

*[Note: He refers to the detractors whose excessively captious and defamatory accusations against him he described in the *Conjecture on Quality*, composed shortly before this, namely at the beginning of the year 966.]*
    
—of whom there are far too many, unless I had drawn harsher words today from the sayings of Gregory.

Would that the hardness of our understanding had been able to grasp and usefully distinguish what both these words and those words are!

For when he marks out our company, saying that, when we suddenly attempted to teach what we had learned more by meditation than by practice, and wished to undertake this with another’s assistance, we came upon his Gospel homily in which, on seeing the city of Jerusalem, the Lord is reported to have wept and foretold its destruction, I am not reluctant to run through the whole passage, so that one fully able to weigh whether he ought to mourn may cease being angry with us.

Indeed, after considering the whole sequence of that sermon, while I contemplated it more as containing gall than honey, I began to consider whether some consolation might be found there that could refresh my spirit, which was wavering through a fear that, although useless, was nevertheless unchangeable.

For when I had reached that most dreadful passage, where it is written as follows (Gregory, *Homilies on the Gospels* II, homily 39, section 8):

> “Therefore we must take care, and think every day with great weeping, how severe, how free, how terrible the prince of this world will come at the time of our departure, demanding his works in us (John 14:30), if he came even to the Lord dying in the flesh and sought something of his own in him, in whom he could find nothing. What, then, shall we wretched people say? What shall we do, who have committed innumerable evils? What shall we say to the adversary when he demands and finds in us many of his works, except only what is for us a certain refuge and solid hope: that we have been made one with him in whom the prince of this world sought something of his own and could not find it? For he alone is free among the dead (Ps. 87:5). And we are released from the service of sin by true freedom, because we are united to the one who is truly free.
>
> “For it is established, and we cannot deny it, but must truthfully confess it: the prince of this world has many things of his own in us. Nevertheless, at the time of our death he can no longer seize us, because we have become members of the one in whom he has nothing.”

I had most foolishly thought that this saying of Paul’s would greatly assist me—

*[Note: This saying is Paul’s, namely in Rom. 12:4–5; 1 Cor. 12:13; and Eph. 4:16, where he taught that we are all members of Christ the Head.]*
    
—although he was speaking this more about himself and those like him. But when I read what followed—

*[Note: “What followed” means what Saint Gregory immediately adds after the passage quoted, and what the author quotes shortly afterward: “But what does it profit,” and so forth.]*
    
—the same thing happened to me that often happens.

For when I hear that there is joy in heaven over one sinner who repents, more than over ninety-nine righteous persons (Luke 15:7), if he said this absolutely, as it is placed here, I would think that something of it applied to me. But when he adds “who does penance,” I see that this concerns me as much as black concerns white: I am a wretch who never does penance and is always heaping up things for which penance is required.

So also here, when the most holy teacher makes the same point and says, “But what does it profit if we are joined to him by faith and separated from him in conduct?” (Gregory, cited above, section 9), he himself says:

> “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ shall enter into the kingdom of heaven, but he who does the will of my Father, who is in heaven, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 7:21).

I see that I have every right to be afraid.

*[Note: Construe as follows: “I see myself wholly foreign to not fearing rightly”; that is, I perceive that I rightly ought to be afraid.]*

## 6

But what is the will of the Father except what Martha or her sister Mary did?

For nothing else is commanded to us except that we either minister to Christ in his members or sit at Christ’s feet, contemplating his will. If we have neglected one of these, let us sigh, weep, beat our breasts, and do penance; let us either resume the Lord’s frequent service, or, devoting ourselves to prayers and heavenly desires, let us in no way be torn away from the feet of the merciful Jesus, until we reach that one thing which alone is necessary: the Lord himself, who alone is sufficient for us.

You reply in opposition—and this is the customary human saying: [lacuna]—“Although I do not do as much good as I ought, I do some; and believing perfectly in God, I hope for what the Lord commanded his faithful to hope for.”

Oh, would that I could be confident, brother [possibly “brothers”], that you possess these two things in reality! I would certainly be sure of your salvation: namely, that you believed perfectly in God and hoped only for those things which the Lord commanded to be hoped for.

The Psalmist says: “Hope in the Lord” (Ps. 36:3). You answer, “I hope.” “Do good,” he says (ibid.). Therefore, if you hope in the Lord, I urge you: do good, and I promise that you do not hope in vain.

For James says: “What does it profit, my brothers, if someone has faith but has no works? Can faith alone save him?” (Jas. 2:14.)

Only one answer can be heard to this. If you believe perfectly in God and hope for nothing other than what he commanded you to hope for—namely, if you have good works—then, provided you persevere in this way, you need not doubt the perpetual reward.

But what are good works except those that proceed from love? If you do not possess love alone, I tell you that you neither trust in faith nor hope for what the Lord promised his faithful.

“For faith, if it has no works, is dead in itself” (Jas. 2:17); and: “Hope does not disappoint, because the love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5).

Therefore, if you do not have love in your heart, you have hope uselessly. If you do not have the Holy Spirit, you do not belong to Christ, for it is said: “If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he is not his” (Rom. 8:9).

But what love toward the Lord does anyone possess, at least at the present time, when he is shown not even to fear him—not to mention loving him—since, while the Lord is present, he does not fear committing adultery, to mention only this one example among countless others?

For if he does not believe that the Lord is present, how does he believe in him—not to say perfectly, but even to some degree? But if he does believe this, does he not plainly exist as a rebel against the Lord, in whose sight the wretch and self-destroyer dares to commit so foul a deed?

What does anyone among us say to this? He perishes, I say; he perishes, unless he immediately takes refuge in the Lord’s mercy by truly doing penance.

Experience teaches that more recent wounds are cured more quickly than older ones. This is evidently indicated by the one who says: “Let not the sun go down upon your anger” (Eph. 4:26).

Perhaps someone might say that these words of mine are at issue. What Jacob and Paul say—are they mine, beloved?

## 7

But lest you perhaps say that I wish to drive you to despair, I confess that, if you wish and whenever you wish, with God’s help you can imitate not only Martha but also Mary, who chose the better part.

You know what she was before, if you recognize what is to be known. You can also acknowledge what she became after God’s mercy, if you are willing; nor should you in any way despair that the same may happen to you.

Therefore, I say, do what she did, and hope for what she deserved.

Oh, how I would think that no such person existed anywhere—

*[Note: Construe as follows: “But I, the most foolish of the nations, considering myself, would think that no such person existed anywhere, if I did not hold fast to the promise,” and so forth.]*
    
—I, the most despairing of the nations, considering myself, would think this if I did not hold fast to the promise: “Behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20)!

For with whom among us is he, except with those whom he possesses among his own? If he is not with me because of my wickedness, he is with me because of the goodness of the one who is with me.

For he promised this when he said: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Matt. 18:20).

Would that the devil also had not been able to say this concerning those of his own who live among us! For certainly none of us would then be proved to have heard the Lord say: “Therefore you do not hear, because you are not of God” (John 8:47).

Those to whom this was said were neither deaf nor absent; rather, they were absent in will and became deaf through hatred, because they did not wish to assent to what was being said.

And although God’s patience and long-suffering are marvelous, worthy of embrace, and worthy of glorification, they are nevertheless to be feared because of what the Apostle says about them. They must not be provoked or irritated, but must be entreated and implored with the greatest persistence.

For a person measures the Lord’s anger by himself: after he has gravely offended the Lord, he is afraid to approach him in order to praise him, since he would undoubtedly himself disdain being praised at that very hour by one who had dishonored him.

But the one who says, “If the spirit of one who has power rises up against you” (Eccl. 10:4), advises that this must not be done—

that is, the evil spirit of God [supply: “the evil spirit”], which tormented Saul (1 Sam. 18:10), when, through its most cunning suggestion, it prevails over you even to the point of a deadly consent—

“do not leave your place” (Eccl. 10:4): that is, do not abandon that condition of goodness in which you were when you fell into the crime which it suggested to you. He adds the reason: “For healing”—that is, repentance or God’s mercy—“will cause sins to cease” (ibid.).

Hence Augustine also says admirably, as Augustine: “Everything that is reasonably feared is avoided. God alone is to be feared in such a way that one flees from him to him.”

But the man who measures the Lord by the most childish standard thinks him so compassionate that he does not care how much he is injured by anyone, but that, without the satisfaction that is owed, he grants not only forgiveness but also rewards to the undeserving.

If that were so, a person could believe—although falsely—that the Lord loves evil. But it does not follow that the just man can love injustice.

## 8

But for this purpose we have a most useful counselor, who says:

> “Do not be without fear concerning a forgiven sin, and do not add sin upon sin by saying: ‘The mercy of God is great; he will have mercy on the multitude of my sins.’ For mercy and wrath quickly draw near from him, and his wrath looks upon sinners” (Ecclus. 5:5–7).

And again:

> “Show mercy to the just, and do not receive the sinner; for the Most High also hates sinners, and he has mercy on those who do penance, but he will repay sinners with vengeance, preserving them for the day of vengeance” (Ecclus. 12:3–4).

And again:

> “Do good to the humble, and do not give to the ungodly; prevent bread from being given to him, lest he become stronger than you through it. For you will find two evils in all good things, because the Most High also hates sinners and will repay the ungodly with vengeance” (ibid., 6–7).

Oh, then, if this is so, how ought the sinner to be without fear?

*[Note: Construe as follows: “If this is so, oh, how ought no sinner at all—not to mention anyone like us—to exist without fear even for a little while! But let us examine more particularly the Book of Wisdom, which itself sings this; whether there can be anything in it that ought not to be believed. For Wisdom itself is the one who says in the Gospel, ‘I am the truth.’ Since it is granted that nothing can exist in that book which ought not to be believed, let anyone say what could contradict so great a truth.”]*

If this is so, how can anyone be without fear even for a little while—let alone anyone like us?

But let us examine more particularly the Book of Wisdom, which itself sings this, to see whether there can be anything in it that ought not to be believed. For Wisdom itself is the one who says in the Gospel: “I am the truth” (John 14:6). Since it is granted that nothing can exist in it which ought not to be believed, let anyone say what could contradict so great a truth.

Let anyone say whether anything more marvelous can be expressed.

For although almost universal opposition from you now openly resounds against us—

*[Note: This contradiction against Ratherius is evident from the books *Conjecture on Quality* and the *Itinerary*, written at this same time.]*
    
—there are nevertheless some among you who say: “Why does the bishop consent to such things being done?”

We do not delay in giving an answer to this. The Apostle commands and says to us in the person of Timothy:

> “Reprove”—that is, censure;
>
> “Entreat”—that is, admonish and exhort in the love of God;
>
> “Rebuke” (2 Tim. 4:2)—that is, even with insults, excommunications, and blows, if appropriate, while nevertheless not neglecting charity, wear down those entrusted to you.

When a rightful rebuke of those who ought to be rebuked, made by our mouth, accomplishes nothing, and entreaty obtains nothing either out of regard for us or out of regard for God; when the matter has come to rebuke, we rightly confess that someone will regret—though too late—not having once heeded the advice of one who said:

> “Do not seek to become a judge, unless you are able by strength to break through iniquities, lest you fear the face of the powerful and bring scandal upon your justice” (Ecclus. 7:6).

*[Note: Construe as follows: “When the rebuke of those who ought rightly to be rebuked, delivered by our mouth, accomplishes nothing, and entreaty obtains nothing either out of regard for us or out of regard for God; if the matter comes to rebuke, we rightly confess that someone will regret, though too late, not having once heeded the most useful advice of one who said,” and so forth. By this he wished to indicate why he restrained sinners neither with insults—that is, harsher rebukes—nor with excommunications, as he says in the short work *On Rebellious Clerics*, section 2, nor struck servants with blows, as is reported in the *Conjecture on Quality*, section 2: namely, because he expected no result from the protection of the powerful who defended them.]*

## 9

But reserving these matters for another place, we must say what we have already said: this reading has been read today because what this Mary was doing at that time, when she sat at the Lord’s feet, the Lord’s homonymous Mother had begun to do from the day of her birth, choosing the better part—namely, what is best among existing things—earnestly desiring the Lord in her inmost being.

Because she loved him above all others, she deserved to enjoy him above all others, to such an extent that she first bore him in her mind and afterward bore him both in mind and in her womb.

This part was never taken away from her, nor will it ever be taken away from her, since she was a virgin before childbirth, a virgin in childbirth, and remained a virgin after childbirth.

May she, by her most devout prayers, deign to make her Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, propitious toward us. He lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

# APPENDIX TO THE WORKS OF RATHERIUS

## [DOCUMENTS]

### NOTICE CONCERNING THE TWO FOLLOWING DOCUMENTS

#### I

Two apocryphal documents concerning Ratherius are to be presented first in this Appendix.

One is the sentence—or rather, the record of the sentence—of Rodoaldus, patriarch of Aquileia, concerning the exemption of the property of the cathedral chapter of Verona from the authority of the bishop. We extracted it from the archive of the aforementioned chapter and published it at Verona in 1754 in a work entitled *Confirmation of the Falsity of Three Documents Published by Ughelli in Favor of the Chapter of Verona*, pages 101 and following.

The other is an abridgment of the same sentence, which had been published by Ughelli in volume V of *Sacred Italy*, in the section on the bishops of Verona, column 737.

Although we exposed the imposture of this latter document in the book *On the Privileges and Exemption of the Cathedral Chapter of Verona*, printed at Venice in 1753, and confirmed it more clearly in the fifth letter of the aforementioned Italian work entitled *Confirmation*; and although in the same fifth letter we demonstrated at length the falsity of the other document as well, nevertheless, since these documents cannot be omitted from an edition of Ratherius’s works and have an appropriate place in this Appendix, it will suffice to indicate here, as briefly as possible, the principal critical observations by which their falsity is chiefly revealed.

First, something must be said about the sentence itself, or the record of the sentence, of the patriarch Rodoaldus.

#### II

In this document the chronological indications contradict one another.

Only the eleventh indiction agrees with the year 968; all the others disagree with it. For in May of that year it was not the second but the third year of John XIII, the supreme pontiff; it was not the ninth but the seventh year of Otto I’s imperial rule; it was not the third year of the reign of Otto’s son but the first year of his empire; and the age of the moon on the day before the Ides of May was not twenty-three—as lunar age, which was not usually designated in similar documents, was given there—but twelve.

The time stated in the record itself conflicts even more strongly with the year. The event is said to have taken place immediately after the synod of Ravenna. But this synod was held in the middle of April of the year 967. Therefore, if Rodoaldus’s judgment had been delivered immediately afterward, in the month of May, it would have to be assigned to the year 967, not to 968.

Moreover, as Easter of the year 968 approached—the Easter on which Ratherius wrote the *Apologeticus*—apostolic letters had arrived which, under penalty of anathema, ordered that he, or any other successor of his, should in no way interfere with the property and goods of the canons of the cathedral church, as is reported in the same *Apologeticus*, section 7.

After the sentence of this supreme tribunal had been issued before Easter—which in the year 968 fell on April 19—there was no place in May of that same year for the sentence of the patriarch Rodoaldus, who was in any case an inferior judge, concerning the same matter.

#### III

Nor should anyone suppose that, through some error of a copyist, the year 968 was written in place of 967, to which the record itself teaches that Rodoaldus’s sentence should be assigned immediately after the synod of Ravenna.

For although the year 967 may appear to agree with the context of the same record, it is wholly inconsistent with the other chronological indications and with the history of Ratherius’s actions, which can be established with certainty from his works.

Indeed, in May of the year 967, the indiction does not agree: it should have been the tenth. Nor does the year of Otto I’s empire agree: it was the sixth. Nor does the year of his son Otto agree: in that month he had not yet been elevated to the imperial dignity, and was in the sixth year of his reign, not the third. Nor does the age of the moon agree: on the day before the Ides of May it was the first, not the twenty-third.

One or another error caused by a copyist’s carelessness is occasionally detected in certain genuine documents. Such a mass of errors, however, cannot be attributed to a scribe; it must be attributed to an impostor who, composing the document much later, was unable to calculate the years correctly or reconcile so many chronological indications distant from his own age—indications which every notary, even a less skilled one, knows well when recording an act of his own time.

### IV

But the history contained in the *Notitia* itself conflicts with Ratherius’s works much more clearly. For it states that, at the council of Ravenna, after hearing the delegation of the canons, the emperor ordered Bishop Ratherius [647–648] not to interfere in any way with their affairs and possessions; and that he instructed Patriarch Rodoaldus, when traveling from Ravenna to Verona, to investigate the case between the bishop and the canons immediately.

It adds that Rodoaldus, having at once summoned the bishop and the canons at Verona and examined the documents produced by the canons, delivered a judgment against Ratherius. The bishop is said to have assented to it in such a way that he subjected himself to anathema if he attempted anything contrary to it. “At this the bishop fell silent, remained silent thereafter, and said: ‘Let whoever acts otherwise be anathema.’”

In Ratherius’s works, however, no other imperial command issued at Ravenna is recorded except the command concerning the abolition of clerical marriage. In order to carry it out, Ratherius immediately after the council of Ravenna convened a diocesan synod at Verona, at which he publicly communicated the same order to the priests and deacons. “After the universal synod at Ravenna,” he says in Letter XII to Ambrose, no. 1, “had been celebrated in mid-April, I returned and summoned from all the parishes of our diocese the priests and deacons, in order to report, by command of the most serene emperor, what had been established there.”

That the emperor’s command concerned the execution of the decree requiring the abandonment of clerical marriage is shown not only by what he adds there, but also by *Discordia*, no. 6, where, speaking of the celebrated diocesan synod, he says:

> “What recently moved me most was this: when the Augustan will had thundered against them [the clergy] concerning the abandonment of clerical marriage, almost everyone offered the excuse that this could in no way be done because of poverty; yet it could have been done, at least to some extent, if they had possessed the stipend owed to them from the property of the church.”

Two points must be noted here:

1. The emperor’s command concerned not the affairs and possessions of the canons, but clerical marriage.
2. For this reason Ratherius celebrated a diocesan synod immediately after the council of Ravenna; it was not Patriarch Rodoaldus who summoned the bishop and the canons to investigate and judge the chapter’s affairs and property.

### V

Moreover, Ratherius understood that the reason given by several clerics for claiming that they could not abandon clerical marriage was poverty—the poverty from which they suffered because ecclesiastical property and revenues were distributed inequitably. He therefore sought to remove every excuse from them by instituting a fairer division of those revenues. “For this reason,” he adds in the passage cited from the same *Discordia*:

> “I wished to ascertain everything that had either been granted by my predecessors or bestowed upon them by men who feared God.”

We therefore recognize as false what is reported in the spurious *Notitia* of Rodoaldus’s judgment: namely, that at the council of Ravenna the emperor, and immediately afterward the patriarch himself, prohibited Ratherius from interfering in any way with the canons’ property; that the bishop consented to the patriarch’s judgment; and that he confirmed the same judgment by an oath of anathema.

Rather, at this time the same bishop, in order to advance the execution of the imperial command concerning the abolition of clerical marriage, sought to remove the obstacle of poverty that was being alleged. In the diocesan synod he therefore dealt with the canons in order to introduce a fairer distribution of that property.

### VI

The same canons, however, resisted this distribution with all their strength. “They refused it so resolutely,” Ratherius adds in the cited passage, “that they declared that they would rather die beforehand than see this done.”

What did the bishop say to this? “I showed them,” he says in the same work, no. 7, “the authority of the canons”—that is, the authority by which the administration of ecclesiastical property is subjected to the power and judgment of bishops. They, on the contrary, appealed to established custom.

If an imperial prohibition and a patriarchal judgment had preceded this, those matters above all ought to have been brought forward by the canons. Ratherius then says:

> “I commanded them, adjuring them by the fidelity which they had sworn to me more than once, that if they had any authentic justification for their position, they should not conceal it from me, lest, when we came together in synod, they should bring shame upon me by proving that I was demanding something unjustly.”

This is the synod that was to be convened, which Ratherius connects in two places with the emperor’s presence: it was to be convened when, on the occasion of the imperial presence at Verona, Patriarch Rodoaldus and the other bishops of the province were required to assemble there, as we have shown in the note on this passage of the *Discordia*.

At this synod Ratherius intended to bring forward the matter, and he trusted that the patriarch and the bishops would confirm the fairer distribution of the property that he believed ought to be instituted—unless the canons possessed some authentic justification, that is, legitimate documents or privileges, that would prevent it. He therefore asked them not to conceal such documents from him, lest they should bring shame upon him at the provincial synod by proving, through authentic documents and arguments, that he was demanding something unjustly.

But if, in the negotiations held with the canons somewhat after the council of Ravenna—that is, approximately in June or July of the year 967—Ratherius knew of no authentic justification opposed to introducing a fairer division of the chapter’s property, and hoped that, since nothing stood in the way, the same division would be confirmed at the provincial council by the patriarch and the neighboring bishops, how could he not certainly have been ignorant of the patriarch’s judgment and prohibition, which the *Notitia* claims was issued in May on the basis of several authentic documents?

If that judgment and prohibition had indeed preceded this, and if Ratherius had assented to it, how could he so quickly have forgotten it and believed that he ought to propose to the same patriarch and the other bishops precisely what the patriarch had forbidden, while hoping that they would confirm it?

All these points that we have observed thus far plainly show that the following *Notitia*, which presents Rodoaldus’s judgment as having been issued in May, agrees neither with the year 967 nor with the year 968, and that this judgment is therefore wholly fictitious. If desired, compare the letter mentioned at the beginning, in which we have assembled further evidence by which the same forgery is demonstrated even more clearly, and by which we seem to have uncovered the time when it was fabricated.

### VII

Furthermore, the abridgment of the same judgment, or *Notitia*, produced by Ughelli reveals the interpolation and falsity much more clearly. For, apart from containing nearly the same marks of forgery that we explained in the same *Notitia* [Col. 0761], it adds certain details that go beyond the evidence of the *Notitia* itself and expose one forgery added to another.

It states that Rodoaldus’s judgment was delivered at the command of Pope John, and that the canons produced almost innumerable privileges obtained from popes and emperors. Yet the *Notitia* mentions an imperial command, not a papal one, and praises a single imperial privilege, no papal privilege.

The more substantial forgery lies in the fact that the abridgment asserts not merely the exemption and immunity of the chapter’s property, which alone is at issue in the *Notitia*, but also the exemption and immunity of persons—as though the dispute between the bishop and the canons had been raised and settled no less concerning personal immunity than concerning property.

A comparison of the *Notitia* and its abridgment shows that the words “affairs and possessions,” which occur in the *Notitia*, were changed by the author of the abridgment into “property and persons.” This manifest fraud aggravates the forgery of the same abridgment.

See the many other observations we have made on this abridgment in *De privilegiis et exemptione capituli cathedralis Veronensis*, p. 77. These few indications, however, seem more than sufficient here.

[Col. 0761]

## NOTICE OF THE SPURIOUS JUDGMENT OF RODOALDUS, PATRIARCH OF AQUILEIA, AGAINST RATHERIUS ON BEHALF OF THE VERONESE CANONS

*(From an old copy in the archive of the chapter of Verona.)*

[Col. 0761A] In the year 968 from the incarnation of the Lord; likewise in the second year of the pontificate of Lord John, bishop of the holy Roman Church and universal pope; in the ninth year of the empire of Lord Otto, the most devout emperor Augustus; and in the third year of the reign of Lord Otto, his son; on the day before the Ides of May; on the twenty-third day of the moon; in the eleventh indiction.

Let the account of this document be believed to be true, and let no one doubt that Lord Ratherius, the most prudent bishop of the city of Verona, had brought forward a complaint in litigation against the canons of his church, saying that canonical authority entitled him to dispose of the revenues of estates assigned by the faithful and by men who feared God, just as he appeared entitled to dispose of and administer the property of his episcopate.

In reply, the aforesaid canons, having become united and unanimous, answered and said:

> “Already, good and pious shepherd, it seems fully to be two hundred years since none of your predecessors, down to the present day, ever interfered in this matter, as you appear to be doing. Whatever our predecessors held in peaceful possession through the favor of lords, kings, and emperors, we too wish to hold in the present time under all your predecessors who were bishops in this city, through the favor of this most serene emperor.”

While this dispute was being prolonged in this manner between the two parties, behold, a herald of the embassy sent by Lord the emperor and Lord Pope John throughout the entire kingdom proclaimed that all bishops should hasten to Ravenna to celebrate the holy synod, as had previously been announced to them.

When the aforesaid bishop therefore appeared to be hastening to Ravenna, the aforesaid canons immediately sent an embassy on their behalf to obtain the favor of Lord the emperor. Through intermediaries they humbly implored his clemency that, if the same bishop wished at the holy synod to dispute, among other matters, concerning their canonry, no assent should in any way be granted to him, but that the emperor should keep their affairs and possessions under the protection of his defence, just as all his predecessors had done.

Because their petition seemed to him just and reasonable, he ordered the same bishop not to interfere in any way with the affairs and possessions of the aforesaid canons, so that, living in peace, they might be permitted to entreat God and his saints on behalf of themselves and the stability of his kingdoms.

And so that no further dispute might ever be brought by him or by any other bishop of Verona concerning the frequently mentioned property—and, if one were brought, that it might be invalid, empty, and void—he ordered Lord Rodoaldus, the most reverend patriarch of the holy Church of Aquileia, when returning from Ravenna, to remain at Verona until he could carefully investigate what right the frequently mentioned bishop, or the repeatedly mentioned canons, possessed in the same affair and property.

When the patriarch had arrived and had taken his seat at the monastery called Saint Mary at the Organ, he immediately, as he had been commanded, summoned the same bishop and his canons and said:

> “You canons, if you possess any documents establishing your title, any testamentary records, or any royal commands concerning your affairs and possessions, which you say that you hold, display them before us, before your bishop, and before the others sitting here, so that we may determine the truth of the matter.”

Then Ambrose the archpriest, Peter the archdeacon, John and Peter the deacons, together with some of the senior [Col. 0762B] and junior canons, immediately rose from their seats and displayed the pages of their testamentary records and the royal commands. They said:

> “These, lord, are the pages of the testamentary records by which we defend the affairs and possessions granted to us.”

It was ordered that these should be read aloud in the hearing of those seated and standing around. During the reading, the document adjudicated in favor of Peter the cleric, of pious memory, was read first; thereafter that of Giselbert; and then those adjudicated in favor of the bishops Notker and Billongus.

These written documents testify with equal and manifest clarity that, if any bishop of Verona should ever attempt, by virtue of his authority over the ordination and provision of the archpriest, archdeacon, priests, and deacons, to remove their affairs and possessions, they would immediately pass into the power and administration of whichever of their relatives might be found, and that they would have God as their judge—and *anathema maranatha*.

The command of Lord Louis, the most devout emperor Augustus, was also read. It ordered that no bishop and no other person, great or small, should presume to interfere in the same affair and property without their counsel and consent.

The grant of Ratoldus concerning the frequently mentioned affair and property was also read. Other documents were then produced, which, if they were read, would require more than a day.

When the patriarch saw that, according to the contents of the documents, possession of the property granted to the canons in no way belonged to the bishop’s judgment, he ordered the same bishop Ratherius, on behalf of almighty God, no longer to interfere with the possessions granted to them by faithful men.

[Col. 0763A] At this the bishop fell silent and thereafter remained silent; and he said:

> “Let whoever acts otherwise be anathema.”

These are the names of the clerics and laymen who were present at this dispute, in whose hearing the pages of the documents were read: Penzo the archdeacon; Peter the priest; Rozo the subdeacon; Giso the cleric; Erizo, Peredeus, and Azo, together with the other comrades-in-arms; Garimbertus the abbot, with his clerics, the household of the place, and his other faithful men.

From Verona: Lampaldus, called Lanzo, the viscount; Ermarius, called Erizo, the vicedominus; Ermimberius, Landbertus, and Azo, judges; Pezo, Ernaldus, Ubertus, and Valderius, comrades-in-arms of Lord Ratherius the bishop; Azo; and many others.

I, Isembardus, notary, saw and read the authentic original of this copy. It contained the same text as this copy, except for a greater or lesser number of letters, and I wrote this copy.

[Col. 0764A]

## Abridgment of the same spurious judgment

In the year 968, on 14 May, at the monastery of Saint Mary at the Organ, at the command of Pope John, in the eleventh indiction, and in the seventh year of the emperor Otto, Rodoaldus, patriarch of Aquileia, after hearing Ambrose the archpriest, Peter the archdeacon, John and also Peter the deacons, together with many other Veronese, produce almost innumerable privileges and other rights obtained two hundred years earlier from popes and emperors—by which they attempted to show that their rights, their property, and their persons were wholly exempt and immune from Ratherius’s authority, while he vigorously maintained the contrary—finally enacted, declared, and pronounced in a judgment rendered after both parties had been heard that their property and persons should never be disturbed either by the said Ratherius or by his successors. Ratherius submitted to the judgment, consented to it, and praised it.

## SERMON FOR THE FEAST OF SAINTS FIRMUS AND RUSTICUS

[Col. 0763]

## Prefatory Notice to the Following Sermon

667–668. In the manuscript of Freising, which contains several works of Ratherius composed after his third restoration to the bishopric of Verona, a small page follows the works bearing only this title: “Preachings for Certain Feasts.” Eight sermons are appended, a copy of which we have received.

After examining them, we found them wholly unlike Ratherius. This difference is sufficiently indicated not only by their position, since they are separated from all the other sermons and brief works of Ratherius, but especially by their style, which differs greatly from Ratherian style.

We further discovered that the author assembled these sermons almost entirely from passages excerpted here and there from the Fathers, especially Saints Augustine and Gregory. We infer that the author himself was Veronese not only because sermons of this kind are found after the works of Ratherius, bishop of Verona, in a manuscript that we believe belonged to the church of Verona, but also because one of the sermons is about the holy martyrs Firmus and Rusticus, who received and preserved the glory of martyrdom at Verona and whose feast was always celebrated in that Veronese church.

For this reason the author calls those martyrs “our” martyrs and indicates that the sermon was delivered on the very day of their feast. We have wished to present this sermon among the others in this appendix because it concerns our martyrs; from it the character of the author and the method of the other sermons will be sufficiently apparent. In the notes we shall indicate the passages of Saint Gregory from which he joined together and arranged this sermon.

[Col. 0763]

## Sermon for the Feast of the Holy Martyrs Firmus and Rusticus

[Col. 0763B] 669. 1. “Come, children, listen to me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord” (Ps. 33:12). “Draw near to him and be enlightened, and your faces shall not be put to shame” (ibid., 6).

We wish you to know, brothers, that almighty God does not abandon his Church without worthy administration. For when he calls the strong to their reward, he strengthens the weak for the contests in their place; when he receives and rewards the former, he supplies the latter with the virtues of their labors, which he is to reward.

Strengthened by these virtues, Saint Firmus and Saint Rusticus together advance boldly into battle against the enemies of the faith, and by suffering they despise those who rise against them. [Note: [Col. 0763B] The following passages, down to the end of this section, were taken from Saint Gregory’s thirtieth book on Job, chapter 25, no. [Col. 0763C] 75; nevertheless, certain words have been inserted, a few prefixed, and others transposed, as will be explained by way of example in note 1579.] For our leader brought into the battle of preaching such men as these, who, having disregarded the safety of their bodies, would overthrow their enemies by dying and overcome their swords not with weapons or swords, but with endurance.

Our martyrs, brothers, came armed for battle under their leader in three ways: with trumpets, jars, and lamps. They sounded the trumpets when they preached; they broke the jars when they offered their bodies, which were to be dissolved in martyrdom, to their enemies; they shone as lamps when, after the dissolution of their bodies, they flashed forth [Note: “With miracles” should be supplied from Saint Gregory; rightly so, since shortly afterward they are seen to shine with miracles.]

Then their enemies were put to flight, because, when they saw the bodies of the dead martyrs flashing with miracles, they were broken by the light of truth and sang what they had attacked. [Note: [Col. 0763B] Saint Gregory, in the passage cited, [Col. 0764B] expresses this as follows: “Therefore they sounded the trumpets, that the jars might be broken; the jars were broken, that the lamps might appear; [Col. 0764C] the lamps appeared, that the enemies might be put to flight”—that is, the martyrs preached until their bodies were dissolved in death; their bodies were dissolved in death, that they might shine with miracles; they shone with miracles, that by divine light they might overthrow their enemies, so that, etc. Our author presented these same points [Col. 0765C] differently, appending the phrase “that is” to each of the first three statements together with its respective explanation.]

> “Our soldiers therefore sounded the trumpets, so that the jars might be broken”; that is, our martyrs preached until their bodies were dissolved in death. The jars were broken so that the lamps might appear; that is, their bodies were dissolved in death so that they might shine with miracles. The lamps appeared so that the enemies might be put to flight; that is, they flashed with miracles so that they might overthrow their enemies by the divine light, so that those enemies would no longer resist God in their arrogance but, subjected to him, would fear him.

[Col. 0765A] 2. “By the voice of the holy martyrs,” the Psalmist says to God: “You humbled us in the place of affliction, and the shadow of death covered us” (Ps. 43:20). [Note: [Col. 0765C] In Saint Gregory, book IV on Job, chapter 16, no. 30, the following three periods are arranged differently: “The shadow of death is understood as the death of the flesh, because just as true death is that by which the soul is separated from God, so the shadow of death is that by which the flesh is separated from the soul. Hence the prophet rightly says in the voice of the martyrs: ‘You humbled us in the place of affliction, and the shadow of death covered us.’ For since they plainly die not in spirit but only in the flesh, they say that they are covered not by true death but by the shadow of death.”] The shadow of death therefore means the death of the flesh, because just as true death occurs when the soul is separated from God, so the shadow of death occurs when the flesh is separated from the soul. Since it is clear that they die not in spirit but only in the flesh, they rightly say that they are covered not by true death but by the shadow of death.

The place of affliction is the present life [Note: See Saint Gregory, *On Job*, book XIX, chapter 27, no. 56]. Our martyrs were therefore humbled in this place of affliction, because in eternal life—that is, in the place of joy—they are exalted.

Indeed, they are exalted to such a height that it is entirely certain that they will come with God as judge, though now they are unjustly judged for his sake. [Note: [Col. 0766C] Saint Gregory, book X on Job, chapter 31, no. 52, writes this of the righteous; here, to the end of the section, the author applies it to the martyrs with a few changes, additions, or omissions. Shortly below, *venturos* (“about to come”) is preferable to *venire* (“to come”). We have also corrected *injuste* (“unjustly”) from the same Gregory, where *juste* (“justly”) had been wrongly read.] Their light then shines more broadly in proportion as the hands of their persecutors now constrain them more harshly. Then it will be revealed to the eyes of the wicked that those who voluntarily abandoned all earthly things were supported by heavenly power.

Finally, aroused here by the stimulus of divine love and fear, they abandoned what they possessed. For that reason they will unquestionably obtain the height of judicial power, so that they may then come as judges together with the Judge—those who now, in consideration of judgment, chastise themselves through voluntary poverty.

Of the Bridegroom of the holy Church it is said through Solomon: “Her husband is noble at the gates, when he sits with the senators of the land” (Prov. 31:23). Hence Isaiah says: “The Lord will come to judgment with the senators of his people” (Isa. 37:14). Hence Truth itself declares that these same senators are no longer servants but friends, saying: “I no longer call you servants, but my friends” (John 15:15). Behold: by abandoning temporal things, they have deserved the glory of eternal power.

3. What, then, is more foolish in this world than to abandon one’s possessions, and what is nobler in eternity than to come as judges with God? It is right that those who perfectly abandon the present age at the word of God should dispute with God concerning peoples in judgment. [Note: [Col. 0766C] These words, down to “they sought,” may be found in Saint Gregory, book XV on Job, chapter 31, no. 37.] For it is written:

> “He will call the heavens above and the earth, to distinguish his people” (Ps. 49:4).

He calls the heavens above when those who, abandoning all their possessions, have maintained the conduct of heavenly life are summoned to sit with him in judgment and come as judges with him. He calls the earth above when those who had been bound by earthly pursuits nevertheless sought heavenly things more than earthly things.

Those who, abandoning everything, gained more through ready devotion than they had heard commanded in general truly sought heavenly profit [Note: These words, up to “he did not wish to be supported,” are found in nearly the same form in Saint Gregory, *On Job*, book XXVI, chapter 27, no. 31].

By a special command directed to a few who were more perfect, and not generally to everyone, the rich young man heard: “Go, sell all that you have, give to the poor, and come, follow me” (Matt. 19:21). For if a general command bound everyone under this precept, it would certainly be a sin for us to possess anything in this world.

But one thing is commanded generally to all through Sacred Scripture, and another is ordered specially to a few who are more perfect. For just as those who, persuaded by unbelief, disdain to keep the law are judged and perish [Ps. 15], so those who, persuaded by piety, advance beyond the general precepts of divine law are not judged but reign.

Paul, the vessel of election, surpassed the special precepts and displayed by his deeds more than he had received by a permission of instruction. For although he had received permission to live from the Gospel while preaching the Gospel, and although he imparted the Gospel to those who lived by it, he nevertheless did not wish to be supported by the expenses of the Gospel [2 Thess. 2:7].

But because it has not been granted to us to surpass the general or special precepts of divine law, let us strive humbly to beseech these holy martyrs of God, whose feast we celebrate today, that through the merits of their intercession we may at least be able to fulfill what is commanded generally to all. Thus may we deserve to rejoice with them in eternal joy—those who, desiring nothing earthly and nothing carnal, deserved to attain this end and become martyrs of Christ—through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom are honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

## An Ancient Rhythmic Description of Verona

[Note: Above I published an ancient description of the city of Milan, composed rhythmically in the manner permitted by the rude and unlearned ages, and drawn from an excellent manuscript of the chapter of the canons of Verona.

I then conceived the idea of adding another description, already published by the most celebrated Benedictine scholar Jean Mabillon of the Congregation of Saint Maur in the *Ancient Analecta*, p. 409 of the latest edition. From it you learn what the city of Verona was like more than nine hundred years ago, what relics or bodies of saints were venerated there at that time, and who its first bishops were.

Around the year 760 Saint Hanno, bishop, flourished there, distinguished by many good works. The author of the poem especially praises him for transferring the sacred bodies of the martyrs Firmus and Rusticus from the city of Tergeste, or, as he says here, from the islands of the sea, and bringing them to Verona.

The author may perhaps have known Hanno personally, for he committed these things to writing while King Pippin was living at Verona. Pippin, the son of Charlemagne, was appointed king of Italy by his father in 781 and established his residence in Italy a few years later. We may therefore suppose that the poem was written around the year 790.

Since Bishop Ratherius copied this text from a Veronese manuscript around the year 970, we may now infer with greater confidence that the other poem published above—the description, namely, of the city of Milan—also appeared in the same eighth century, either by the same author or at least by a contemporary author.

What follows is what Mabillon noted concerning this fragment of antiquity.

**Muratori.**—Ratherius, bishop of Verona, brought this description of Verona, awkwardly constructed in rhythmic lines, from Italy during the reign of Pippin, son of Charlemagne, who ruled among the Lombards. He arranged for it to be appended in the Laubian original manuscript from which I extracted it, together with an iconographic depiction of the same city painted in minium.

From this description we learn what temples Verona had in antiquity and who its first bishops were. Ughelli, in volume V of *Sacred Italy*, composed a wholly different succession of them when listing the first Veronese bishops in this order: 1. Euprepius; 2. Cricinus; 3. Agapius; 4. N., that is, one of unknown name; 5. Saturninus; 6. Lucillus; 7. Diomidianus; 8. Zeno; 9. Proculus.

Here you see that Dimidrianus, whom Ughelli calls Diomidianus and places seventh, is second in this description; Proculus, who is fourth here, is ninth according to Ughelli; and Gricinus, who is seventh here, is Ughelli’s second bishop, called Criscinus. Finally, Ughelli numbers several others whose names do not appear in this list.

**Mabillon.**]

## Written around A.D. 790

*(In Muratori, *Italian Writers*, vol. II, part II, p. 1095.)*

[Col. 0765] 1094. This great and splendid city is powerful in Italy, in the region of Venetia, as Isidore teaches; it is called Verona, ancient from of old.

It is constructed in a square and strongly fortified with walls; forty-eight towers shine brightly all around it, of which eight are lofty and rise above all the rest.

It has a high, great labyrinth extending around it, from which one who does not know the way out cannot escape except by the light of a lamp or by the thread of a ball of wool.

There is a broad, beautiful forum paved with stones, where a great vaulted structure stands at four corners; the streets are wonderfully paved with cut stones.

Ancient temples were built in the names of the gods: Luna, Mars, Minerva, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, and the Sun, which shines above them all.

No tongue can describe the form of this city. Within it gleams; outside it shines, enclosed with plates, with gilded weights of common metal in bronze.

It has a great and lofty fortress, strong battlements, and stone bridges founded over the river Adige, whose ends reach in a circle toward the town.

Behold how well it was founded by wicked men who did not know the law of God and worshiped new and ancient images together, wooden and stone.

But after [lacuna] the fullness of time came, the Godhead was incarnate, being born from a Virgin; he emptied himself and ascended the gallows.

[Col. 0767B] Then, taken down, he was delivered to the exceedingly wicked people of the Jews and placed in a tomb. There he remained for three days; then, rising in triumph, he sat at the Father’s right hand.

When the Gentile world learned this, it hastened to believe, because the very God, creator of heaven and earth, appeared in the world through Mary’s womb.

From this stock proceeded martyrs, apostles, confessors, doctors, and most holy prophets, who brought the world into harmony with the Catholic faith.

Thus David’s saying was fulfilled: the heavens clearly proclaim the glory of the Most High, from the summit of the heavens to the ends of the earth.

Euprepius the bishop first preached at Verona; Dimidrianus was second; Simplicius third; Proculus the confessor, shepherd and excellent man, fourth.

Saturninus was fifth, and Lucillus sixth. Gricinus, teacher and bishop, was seventh; Zeno, a renowned martyr, shepherd and confessor, was eighth.

By preaching, he brought Verona back to baptism; he healed the daughter of Gallus from an evil spirit; and he brought back from the sea oxen together with [lacuna] turning [*vergentem*, uncertain].

He also freed many from the destructive enemy [lacuna]. I cannot tell of the many deeds of this holy man, which almighty God displayed through him as he came from Syria all the way to Italy.

[Col. 0768A] O happy Verona, enriched and renowned! How are you surrounded by most holy guardians who defend you and drive away the most wicked enemy.

From the east you have the first martyr Stephen, Florentius, Vindemialis, and Maurus the bishop, Mamma, Andronicus, and Probus, together with forty martyrs.

Then Peter and Paul, the apostle James, John the Forerunner and Baptist, and the martyr Nazarius, together with Celsus, Victor, and Ambrose.

The renowned martyrs of Christ Gervasius and Protasius, Faustinus and Jovita, Eupolus, Calocerus, Mary the Mother of the Lord, Vitalis, and Agricola.

In the southern regions are Firmus and Rusticus, who once received crowns of martyrdom in you, whose bodies were carried away to the islands of the sea.

When it pleased God, the invisible King, the restoration was accomplished in you through Hanno the bishop, in the time of the royal rulers Desiderius and Adelchis.

The saints had remained there for a long time and did not return; the bishop laid their bodies together with spices—galbanum, storax, *argoido* [uncertain], myrrh, balsam, cassia, and the brightest frankincense.
