A golden tomb, covered and surrounded by proclamations, encircles them; its rubbed color delights human senses, at one moment white, at another black, between two purple colors.

As far as he was able, the renowned bishop Hanno prepared this. Through his flame he shines by his good works, from the boundaries of *Austra* [uncertain] to the limits of our land.

From the west, Sixtus and Lawrence, Hippolytus, Apollinaris, the twelve apostles of the Lord, and the great and most holy confessor Martin guard you.

No longer need the city in Ausonia be praised before you: shining, powerful, and fragrant with the bodies of saints, rich among the hundred cities of Italy.

For Aquileia praises you, Mantua praises you, Brescia, Pavia, Rome, and Ravenna likewise; through you there is a harbor extending everywhere to the borders of Liguria.

The great king Pippin, most devout, dwells in [lacuna], not forgetful of piety or righteous judgment; acting well, he always makes all things prosper.

Let us sing glory to God, the invisible King, who adorned you with such mystical flowers, so that you shine like the rays of the sun.

## Around A.D. 972–974: Liutprand, Bishop of Cremona

[Col. 0769]

## Historical and Bibliographical Notice

*(Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, Writers, vol. III.)*
[Col. 0769A] Liudprand—or, with the name contracted, Liuzo or Liuso—was a Lombard, born, as some have thought, in his homeland at Ticinum [Note: [Col. 0769B] The passages adduced in support of this are insufficient; for in III.1 the word *patria* simply means “city,” and in III.2 he could have called Saint Syrus “our excellent father” because he himself was a deacon of Ticinum. It would be superfluous to discuss here his fictitious Spanish origin, built upon the corrupt reading in Book V, chapter 1, “Abderahaman, our king” (instead of “your king”), or the *Chronicle* and *Adversaria* falsely sold under his name, the disreputable offspring of the Spanish impostors Hieronymus Higuera and Laurentius Ramirez de Prado [ [Col. 0769C] See below, the Appendix to Liutprand. EDITORS OF THE *PATROLOGIA*.].], and was born of no lowly family; for his father and stepfather undertook embassies to the Constantinopolitan emperors on behalf of Kings Hugh and Berengar [Note: [Col. 0769C] III.22–23; V.14.].

His father, an upright and eloquent man, died about the year 927. Liudprand was then left a small child, as he himself relates, and was taken in by his stepfather, “a man adorned with dignity and full of wisdom” [Note: [Col. 0769C] III.25.], who taught him Latin and Greek literature. Evidence of the learning he began to acquire in childhood is found in the Roman authors praised in his writings—Terence, Cicero, Virgil, Horace, Juvenal, Vegetius, and Boethius—to whom he added knowledge of the Holy Scriptures and the Fathers.

In the year 931, the boy, gifted with a fortunate talent and commended to King Hugh because of the sweetness of his voice [Col. 0769B] [Note: [Col. 0769C] IV.1.], entered the court. Having gained the king’s favor, he was afterward enrolled among the clergy and appointed deacon in the Church of Ticinum [Note: [Col. 0769C] The *Legation* and the beginning of the *Antapodosis*.].

When Hugh was driven out in 945, his stepfather purchased for the young man, at great expense, a position at the court of Berengar, then margrave and soon afterward king. Thus Liudprand became privy to secrets and was appointed signer of the royal letters [Note: [Col. 0769C] V.30.].

In the years 948–950, at his stepfather’s expense, he was sent as Berengar’s envoy to Constantine Porphyrogenitus. What he did there on Berengar’s behalf he described in the sixth book of the *Antapodosis*. During this journey he observed the customs and institutions of the Greeks and acquired a considerable knowledge both of their language and of their authors. He displayed this knowledge in his writings by inserting complete Greek words and sentences [Col. 0770A] and by adopting the florid and verbose style customary among the Byzantines; he later found it useful in conducting the affairs of the Emperor Otto.

On returning to his homeland, he incurred, for reasons unknown, the intense hatred of Berengar and Willa. Though he had served them well, he was treated badly; he therefore left Italy and fled to King Otto I. Received by Otto, he spent several years in exile, although at times he bore its hardships only with the greatest difficulty [Note: [Col. 0769C] VI.1.]. He complained that nothing bad remained for him except death or the amputation of his limbs, while all good things had to be hoped for. He then learned the language of the Germans, which was extremely useful in conducting imperial affairs during the Italian expedition.

At Otto’s court, in the spring of 956, he became acquainted with [Col. 0770B] Recemund, bishop of Iliberis and envoy of King Abderahaman. Recemund, who had stayed at Frankfurt from the feast of the Epiphany until Palm Sunday [Note: [Col. 0770B] He came to Córdoba afterward, in June. At that time Abderahaman discussed with John of Gorze, Otto’s envoy, the revolt of Conrad, who, after seducing Liudolf, had led the Hungarians through the middle of the kingdom to devastate it. Since Recemund reported these events as now completed, one might therefore believe that he returned in 955 rather than 956, after Conrad’s death. But since Otto’s charters show that he stayed at Frankfurt and in its vicinity in the years 956 and 958, and Liudprand appears to have remained attached to the royal court, I have preferred those years.], succeeded, through his prayers, in persuading Liudprand to think about writing an account of the events of his own time [Note: [Col. 0770C] Henschenius had already suspected this, but because of the corrupt reading of the editors he could not establish the matter with “Raimund.” The whole *Antapodosis* is dedicated to Recemund, as the prefaces to the books and the address “excellent father” in IV.27 attest.].

Only two years later, therefore in the spring of 958, while our author was at Frankfurt [Note: [Col. 0770C] III.1.], he began writing his *Antapodosis*, or “Retribution”—by which he would repay his friends with good and Berengar and Willa with the evil they had inflicted upon him. He did not complete the work in a single effort. The first three books, in which he says that he reports what he had heard from highly reputable men, carry the history from the year 893 to the beginning of 931. He began the first of these at Frankfurt in 958 [Col. 0771A], the second and third [Note: [Col. 0771B] III.26.] likewise before the death of Constantine Porphyrogenitus in 959; and he began the third [Note: [Col. 0771B] III.1.] while travelling on the island of Paxos [Note: [Col. 0771B] The reason for the journey is unknown. Perhaps Otto had sent him to test the disposition of the Greeks toward making an alliance against Berengar, but he did not reach Constantinople.].

He wrote the fourth book while Berengar was still raging [Note: [Col. 0771B] IV.7.], and therefore before the year 961. He added the final chapter of the fifth book, together with the sixth book, during Otto’s reign [Note: [Col. 0771B] VI.4: “the envoy of our lord, then king, now emperor”; [Col. 0771C] the authentic manuscript shows that the final chapter of the fifth book was written at the same time.], after February 962, in Italy, where he was accompanying his patron. Yet he did not complete the sixth book. For although he had certainly planned to carry the work down to the period of his exile [Note: [Col. 0771C] II.73; III.20 at the end; IV.13; IV.15; V.30.], and although he indicated that more than fifty chapters of the sixth book remained to be written, leaving space for the insertion of so many headings, he stopped at the ninth chapter.

The cause appears to have been the increasing mass of business and the new order of events: once Berengar had been broken and his hatred satisfied, the *Antapodosis* was no longer needed [Col. 0771B]. In the following winter [Note: [Col. 0771C] This seems evident. Immediately after the coronation, as the preface to Book VI shows, the wheel of Fortune had not yet turned; and in the summer of 963 he calls himself bishop of Cremona. I therefore suppose that Otto, who in the autumn and winter of that year devoted himself at Pavia to arranging the affairs of Lombardy, then promoted him while he was still in exile.], the wheel of Fortune turned, and Liudprand received as the reward for his loyalty and services to Otto the bishopric of Cremona. Thereafter he was assigned to the most serious affairs of the Empire and took a leading part in Italian and Greek matters.

First, in the summer of 964, he was sent as envoy, together with Landohard, bishop of Minden, to Pope John XII [Col. 0772A]. After Rome had been restored to the emperor, he attended the council held against the pope [Note: [Col. 0771C] *History of Otto*, chapter 10: “we could have.”], and interpreted Otto’s speech for the Italians [Note: [Col. 0771C] *History of Otto*, chapter 11.]. He must also be regarded as having taken part in the election of Leo VIII and the deposition of Benedict.

He himself, present amid these events, composed their history from the year 960 to 23 June 964, or at the beginning of the following year while Leo VIII was still alive [Note: [Col. 0771C] *Ibid.*, chapter 6: “Leo, now in the same seat of blessed Peter, vicar of the apostles.” Leo was consecrated on 6 December 963 and died in March 965.]. In the account of the death of John XII, he says: “We repeatedly heard this from his relatives and household attendants who had been present” [Note: [Col. 0771C] *History of Otto* 18.]. This work, unlike the *Antapodosis*, was written with a more mature mind and in a weightier, more composed style, although it everywhere reflects Liudprand; its spirit is that of a spectator rather than an adversary [Note: [Col. 0771C] For this reason he speaks of himself in the third person.].

It is preserved in the same autograph manuscript that we hold in our hands, prefixed to the books of the *Antapodosis*, but it breaks off in the middle of a sentence [Col. 0772B], although space remained.

About the same time he appears to have transferred the body of Saint Hymerius, bishop of Amelia, to Cremona. Ughellius published a brief account of this event from an old manuscript [Note: [Col. 0771C]:

“There lived in the days of Otto the Great, the most renowned emperor, a certain Cremonese bishop of blessed memory, Liuzo, the king’s most intimate adviser, prudent in counsel and, finally, filled with divine love, so that he might become the fortunate discoverer and bearer of so great a Father, Hymerius.

“Frequently entering and leaving the royal presence, and faithfully carrying out imperial commands, he was in the Roman territories. There came to him the bishop of Amelia, whom malicious disturbance and envious accusation had excluded from the royal presence. He began to speak in a mournful voice:

“‘Most beloved father, whom the emperor has established at the second height of his kingdom, I beg you to help me, for having been condemned on some petty and unjust accusation and struck by a severe sentence, I have been deprived of imperial favor. Now help me, compassionating my complaint; I shall repay you with whatever gift you wish.’

“To him the other replied: ‘If, by placing some saint’s body in my possession, you make me fortunate, I shall restore you to the king’s former goodwill.’

“To this he answered: ‘I do not dare to satisfy your request in this matter. The bodies of the saints have been placed beneath sacred altars. But I have one in a wooden coffin, whom the inhabitants of that place venerate with the highest honor, named Hymerius. If I could somehow bring him to you and transfer him to your homeland, I know that you would rejoice in possessing so blessed a Father.’

“After these words had been exchanged, they immediately came to the town of Amelia and, with pious cunning, entered the church, as though they were going to celebrate the nocturnal rites [Col. 0772B]. Having prostrated themselves in prayer, they spent a long time in many vows and prayers, asking that the saints favor their petitions. Scarcely had they finished praying when the whole place where Saint Hymerius lay began to tremble.

“Although the bishops were terrified, they nevertheless drew nearer in trusting hope [edit. *tam*]. Meanwhile, while the guards slept in a deep sleep, the bishops approached the tomb of Saint Hymerius. When they began to break open the coffin and attempted to extract the blessed body, one of the guards awoke and began to shout:

“‘Rise, brothers, rise quickly! The body of blessed Hymerius is being stolen from us.’

“When the excellent bishop Liuzo heard this, he went to meet the guard, immediately gave him gifts, and asked him to keep silent. The guard, having received his gift and seen his bishop, remained silent and gave his assistance. Then, lifting the bishop’s body with solemnity, they worshipped it, rejoicing in so great a gift.

“Having placed the most holy remains in a very pure vessel, they left the town secretly. When the aforesaid bishop returned to Cremona, he brought with him the joy he had desired. Entering his own city, he summoned the people and displayed to everyone the body of the most blessed Hymerius. The people prostrated themselves in prayer and earnestly praised the Lord, who had given them such a patron.

“As they continued praising the holy Father, many resorted to the church and celebrated the sacred rites in his honor. Then the holy body was placed in a suitably decorated shrine behind the altar of the holy Mother of God, which at that time had been built in the southern part of that church. There it remained for a long time, not placed upon the altar because there was no place for its burial; nevertheless, it was honored as a saint every year.

“The aforesaid bishop, rejoicing in possessing so great a Father, carefully considered how he might establish the sacred relic. But this was not granted to him, because, compelled by imperial service, he was sent to Constantinople and never returned there again.”]

On 24 February [VI Kal. Martii] 965 he exchanged certain lands of the Church of Cremona for others [Note: [Col. 0772D] Muratori, *SS.* II, 420–421.].

In the same year, immediately after the death of Leo VIII, he was again sent to Rome as envoy, together with Otger, bishop of Speyer, to arrange the election of a pope [Col. 0773A] [Note: [Col. 0773C] Continuation of Regino, year 965.]. After discharging this very important office, we do not know whether he returned from there to Germany and then to Cremona, or whether he awaited the emperor’s arrival in Italy.

On 8 November 966 he exchanged certain property of the Church of Cremona with Count Wifred [Note: [Col. 0773D] Muratori, *ibid.*, 421.].

In 967 he took part in the synod of Ravenna, to which Emperor Otto had summoned Pope John and many nobles. There, for example, on 7 April, he was present at the judgment issued by Pope John and Otto I on behalf of Peter, archbishop of Ravenna [Note: [Col. 0773D] Fantuzzi, *Monumenta Ravennatensia* II, 28.]; on the 25th of the same month he subscribed the decree against Herold, archbishop of Salzburg [Note: [Col. 0773D] *Juvavia*, 183.]; and on the 29th he is mentioned in Otto’s decree on behalf of Rodald, patriarch of Aquileia [Note: [Col. 0773D] Ughelli, *Italia Sacra* V, 45.].

In the same year he certainly took part in the Roman synod and in the coronation of Otto II on Christmas Day [Col. 0773B], since a few days later, on 3 January 968, he subscribed the bull concerning the establishment of the bishopric of Meissen [Note: [Col. 0773D] Harzheim, *Concilia* II, 634–637.].

Soon afterward he went to Greece to obtain Theophanu as a wife for Otto II. On 4 June he entered the imperial city [Note: [Col. 0773D] *Booklet on the Embassy*. Liudprand’s subscription to the bull of the year 968 concerning the establishment of the archbishopric of Magdeburg must have been inserted by Harzheim after his return.]. But since the mission was far from successful, he departed from there on 2 October and, after travelling through Greece, set sail for Italy from the island of Corfu on 7 January 969.

After his return he reported the outcome of the mission to the emperors Otto and the empress Adelaide, and subscribed the bull concerning the establishment of the archbishopric of Magdeburg, having again been sent as envoy to Constantinople. In the same year, on 26 May, he agreed at Rome to a decree concerning the establishment of the archbishopric of Benevento [Note: [Col. 0773D] Ughelli VII, 63.].

On 22 March 970, at Ferrara, in Otto’s presence [Col. 0773C], he took part in deciding the dispute between Peter, archbishop of Ravenna, and the county of Ferrara [Note: [Col. 0773D] Hieronymus Rubeus, *History of Ravenna*, p. 262.].

In 971, if we believe the author of the *Translation of Saint Hymerius* [Note: [Col. 0773D] From what precedes it is clear that this can refer only to the embassy of that year. It is not implausible that Liudprand undertook a second embassy, previously assigned to him, together with Gerō, archbishop of Cologne. Hugo of Flavigny mentions that Gerō was sent with two bishops, dukes, and counts, in Labbe, *Bibliotheca manuscriptorum* I, 166.], he was again “compelled by imperial service and sent to Constantinople,” and never returned to Cremona.

He therefore appears to have died either in Greece or, after Theophanu had already been brought over, in Italy during the earlier months of 972. Certainly, in July of that year, a new agreement was made concerning the lands between the Adda and the Oglio which Liudprand had previously held, between the churches of Bergamo and Aquileia [Note: [Col. 0774C] On 20 July. Lupus, *Codex diplomaticus Bergomensis* II, 302.]. But since the document calls him *domnus Liuso*, not “the former Liuso, bishop of the Church of Cremona,” he could be considered to have survived this date [Col. 0774A], though not by much, since on 28 March 973 Otto I confirmed the privileges of that Church for his successor in the Church of Cremona, Bishop Olderbert.

He therefore died between his fiftieth and sixtieth years, a man seemingly born by talent, learning, eloquence, social position, and aptitude to write the history of his own age. One thing could have damaged his fidelity to truth: his intense partisanship and hatred of Berengar. Yet he was less subject to this bias than might have been expected, because he touched upon the reign of Berengar and Willa only at its beginning and end; and his general judgment of their cruelty and tyranny is confirmed by writers whose reliability is in no way suspect, Hrotsvit and Widukind.

Nor did he exceed the truth in his praises of his benefactor Otto I, of Otto’s father Henry, of Mathilda, of Duke Henry, of Bruno, or of Liudolf [Col. 0774B] [Note: [Col. 0774D] For example, IV.14–16, 25.]. The same may be said of his history of John XII, Leo VIII, and the antipope Benedict, unless one wishes to number him among those who, with Baronius, disdain truth when it is less agreeable.

His morals were not altogether chaste or orderly, as is shown by his sometimes unrestrained freedom of writing and by youthful jokes. His speech is sharp, abundant, varied—now brief, now verbose and inflated—witty and ironic [Note: [Col. 0774D] For example, IV.28, in the death of Giselbert; V.15, in the description of the defeat of the Russians.], although not rarely too convoluted and obscure. His later works, however—the *History of Otto* and the *Booklet on the Embassy to Constantinople*—deserve greater praise in this respect as well.

In the *Antapodosis*, especially in the earlier books, where he relies on the narratives of others and often neglects chronological order, he must be illuminated [Col. 0774C] and corrected from authentic documents [Note: [Col. 0774D] In the account of Arnulf’s expedition, from the *Annals of Fulda*. But even where he was mistaken—for example, attributing to Pope Sergius what belonged to Stephen VI—he consulted trustworthy witnesses: “For I often heard this from the most religious men of the city of Rome” (I.31.)]. In the remaining books he himself, as an excellent eyewitness, claims the primary place [Note: [Col. 0774D] Nevertheless, he was mistaken in IV.16 when he called Otgit the daughter of Adelstan’s brother.].

Since he wrote only what he had either seen himself during his travels and at the courts of Hugh, Lambert, Berengar, Otto, John XII, Leo VIII, and John XIII, and at those of Constantine Porphyrogenitus and Nicephorus, or heard from trustworthy men, his books must necessarily be counted among the principal sources for the tenth century [Note: [Col. 0774D] The distinguished Martini vigorously refuted Muratori’s and others’ unjust judgments concerning Liudprand’s truthfulness in his essay *On Liudprand the Historian*, in the *Memoirs of the Royal Academy of Sciences at Munich for the Years 1808 and 1809*, Munich, 1811.].

He wrote in language that was generally pure, but, in attempting to display his knowledge of Greek by mixing Greek words and sentences into the Latin text, he used Latin somewhat carelessly: specifically, he employed words with meanings not their own [Note: [Col. 0775D] *Leviter* for *faciliter*, II.50; and *singulosque pilos* for *singulaque pila*, II.49.], neglected spelling [Note: [Col. 0775D] *Foere* in III.29 for *fere*; *paroentes* in III.26 for *parentes* (from *parere*), with the *o* inserted by Liutprand’s own hand; *ex improvisu*, *fortuitu* in IV.25; *lurica*, *monisse* in VI, for *lorica* and *munivisse*; *infortunia* in VI.1; indeed *da Deum omnipotentem* in VII.13 for *de Deo omnipotenti*, which reveals him to be Italian.], used faulty verbal forms [Note: [Col. 0775D] *Phaleribus* in II.31 for *phaleris*; *cubiculos* for *cubicula* in V.22; deponent verbs used either with active form or passive meaning: *depopulabat* I.38, *depopulare* II.51; *confabularent* III.25; *vaticinare* IV.7; *execrare* IV.13; with passive meaning: *depopulari* II.24; III.24; V.9; *hortatur* II.21; *testaretur* II.29; *queritur* II.31; *sciscitatus* II.62; III.26; *ulcisci* V.6; *perscrutari* I.14; V.18; *econtra aestuari* for *aestuare* I.17.], and used syntax that was not fully correct [Note: [Col. 0776D] *Noceo aliquem* in IV.27; *da Deum omnipotentem* in VII.13. The pluperfect for the perfect: *responderant* I.11; *deguerat* IV.3. For the imperfect subjunctive: *cupierat*, *History of Otto* I. The imperfect for the perfect and pluperfect: *imponerent . . . suffocarent* III.43; *inescaret et caperet* (for the pluperfect) IV.3; *viderent* (for the pluperfect), *History of Otto* 10; *prorumperet*, 11. The perfect for the imperfect: *reppererint* IV.11 for *repperirent*. The present for the perfect: *velle* for *voluisse* III.14. The subjunctive for the indicative after *quod* IV.26. The indicative for the infinitive: *instabat*, *History of Otto* 6. The infinitive after *ut* II.55: *ut suos . . . reddidisse . . . tenuisse . . . liberasse*. A preposition omitted in II.39: *Tuscia rediens*.].

It is not entirely clear by what fate Liudprand’s books came to Germany. Browerus copied the *Booklet on the Embassy*, found in the cathedral library at Trier, and sent it to Welser, who communicated it to Canisius. We may therefore suppose that it was sent there either by the Ottos or by the Empress Adelaide, whose dowry included the Abbey of Saint Maximin in the suburb of Trier.

The *Antapodosis* and the *History of Otto*, written in a single manuscript, also reached Germany at once, though precisely how remains uncertain. For copies made from it in Germany in the tenth and eleventh centuries—the Spanheim and Gemblac manuscripts, and the twelfth-century Otterburg manuscript—might seem to suggest that the autograph was first kept in the diocese of Mainz or Trier and was then brought to Freising. In support of this view one might point out that Otto, bishop of Freising, used Regino very extensively in his *Chronicle*, but Liudprand hardly at all.

Yet perhaps Otto considered a writer excerpted by Ekkehard, and therefore to be disregarded because of his embarrassment to the Roman Church, and the inscription of the eleventh or twelfth century shows that in Otto’s time the manuscript was kept in the Freising library. I therefore do not oppose the opinion of those who think that the book was brought to the Freising library by Abraham, bishop of Freising, Liudprand’s contemporary and associate at the Roman council of 969 and elsewhere. His interest in good books is proved by books written at his command.

Together with the other Freising books, it was brought in our own age to the Royal Library at Munich. I examined it there in 1833 and now handle it with my own hands, with the agreement of His Serene Highness the King of Bavaria’s most excellent minister, L. B. von Giese, and through the agency of the illustrious Count Ludwig von Kielmansegg, the envoy of His Serene Highness the King of Hanover at the Munich court. I have marked it as number one.

**1) The Royal Munich Manuscript**

The Munich Royal Manuscript, properly counted among the richest treasures of the very wealthy library, II.2.d., formerly Freising no. 188, contains two books bound together in a single fifteenth-century binding: Regino from folio 86 to 198, and Liutprand from folio 1 to 85. Each begins with the inscription: “Book of Saint Mary and Saint Corbinian of Freising” [Note: [Col. 0776D] “Of Freising” appears in the Regino.].

Liudprand, who alone is under discussion here, is written in a smaller and somewhat broader folio, or large quarto, by a mid-tenth-century hand. It presents the *Antapodosis* in nine and a half quires (folios 8–85); seven leaves placed before them (folios 1–7) preserve the *History of Otto*.

The first page of the *Antapodosis* was left blank, except that it received the final 10¼ lines of the *History of Otto*, because no other space was available; the remaining 15¾ lines are still blank. The *Antapodosis* is written on Italian parchment, in blackish ink, by an Italian hand and therefore by one of Liudprand’s associates. Liudprand himself, however, corrected, completed, explained, and finally brought it to an end in innumerable places, using very dark brown ink.

There are generally twenty-seven lines per page, rarely twenty-five or twenty-eight, but thirty lines on the final page. Three books of the work—the first, fifth, and sixth, and perhaps the others as well—were arranged so that at the beginning space remained blank for receiving a list of chapters; only as the book progressed was this space filled, and it was not completed until the book itself was finished. This is proved both by the ink and script being different and by the blank space at the end of the summaries of the first and sixth books.

Almost all the Greek passages, together with their explanations—for which the scribe had left space—belong to Liudprand’s hand, as do many other additions that I have indicated in our *Annals*, vol. VII, p. 293. These include glosses written above words or in the margins, which have likewise been placed in the margin of our edition, as well as the final chapter of the fifth book and the whole of the sixth book.

Liudprand’s spelling in *Sarraceni*, *pulchritudo*, and other words consistently differs from the scribe’s *Saraceni*, *pulchritudo*, *set*. Hence the manuscript has a distinctive appearance, which I have taken care to reproduce in the accompanying plate, so that the blackish ink shows the scribe’s writing and the brown ink Liudprand’s hand.

Given the manuscript’s character, it will not be surprising that its text is also of the highest quality, with only a very small number of scribal errors, from which no author is entirely free. This is even more true of the *History of Otto*, since it was written entirely by the author’s own hand, and with greater care and diligence, so that the writing is generally somewhat more elegant and composed, though the same strokes of each letter and word are repeated [Note: [Col. 0776D] A comparison establishes beyond doubt that the restored reading *id vocum* occurs on folio 7, line 9, and *stituta* on folio 43, line 11.]. As noted above, two or three years intervened between the sixth book and the *History of Otto* [Col. 0777A].

Finally, all the other manuscripts descend from ours, so that even their obvious and distinctive errors and defects can be understood as having arisen from a faulty understanding of our manuscript. I have supplied many examples of this in the critical notes.

Having obtained such a manuscript, I decided to reproduce it literally. This was done with the greatest care, and only in a very few places, where it was clear that the author had written incorrectly through a slip of the pen [Note: [Col. 0777D] The Greek sentences are consistently written in the following order: first the Greek words, then the Latin pronunciation assigned to them, and finally the Latin interpretation. Since this order is occasionally neglected on the first pages, I nevertheless decided that it should also be established there in accordance with the author’s intention in the edition.], did I depart from it, while adding the manuscript’s reading.

Closest to the Munich manuscript is the following one.

**2) The Royal Brussels Manuscript**

The Royal Brussels manuscript, on parchment in quarto, was written in Germany at the end of the tenth century. In the fifteenth century it was inscribed “Codex of Saint Martin at Spanheim.” In 1826 I collated it in its entirety for our use and proved in our *Annals*, vol. VII, p. 396, that it was copied from the Munich manuscript. A specimen of its script is given in the accompanying plate.

So far as can be judged from passages compared, this manuscript appears to have been in the hands of Trithemius of Spanheim. Quires II and IV have now fallen out, containing almost the whole of II.1–13 and II.3–34, as well as the page containing the end of Book V, chapter 32, then chapter 33, and the summary of Book VI.

The former disturbance of the order of the Freising quires VI and VIII caused an entire passage—from the summary of chapter 31 of Book IV, “On Frederick,” to the words of chapter 24 of the same book, “Therefore of Constantine”—to be inserted in the middle of chapter V.9, before “alone endured the attack.”

Apart from these two manuscripts, only they preserve the final chapter of Book VI in full [Col. 0777C].

**3) British Museum Manuscript**

The British Museum manuscript among the Harleian manuscripts, no. 2688, is a folio parchment manuscript in a thirteenth-century Italian hand. It appears to have descended from a copy defective in individual quires, which itself would have been derived from the Freising manuscript.

It has a distinctive text in I.42. Passages in II.6 and II.26–40, II.45–66, III.26, IV.6, and IV.9–14 are almost entirely missing, though the lacunae are not indicated. It ends in V.18, at the words “he showed himself half-naked to the king.”

The following manuscripts, which I examined in Austria, belong to the same class, since they exhibit the same text in I.42 and the same lacunae in II.6 and II.45–66:

**3a) Manuscript of the Palatine Library at Vienna**

Among the *Historiae profanae*, no. 338, parchment, twelfth century. Some of its readings are cited in Muratori, *SS.* II.B, 1089 and following. It ends in III.37, at “the firstborn, to the Lord. Amen.”

**3b) Manuscript of Klosterneuburg**

A twelfth-century parchment manuscript. In III.37 it ends one line earlier, in the syllables of the word “Con—”.

**3c) Manuscript of Zwettl**

A twelfth-century parchment manuscript, likewise as [the preceding; the source breaks off].

**3c*) Palatine Vienna Manuscript**

Among the *Historiae profanae*, no. 178, a thirteenth-century parchment manuscript. Muratori cites a few of its readings [Col. 0778A] at *ibid.*, 1081. It ends in III.32, at the word *suscipito*.

**3d) A Manuscript Represented by Excerpts in the Farfa Chronicle**

A manuscript of the same class seems to have been the source of the excerpts that we read in the *Chronicle of Farfa* in Muratori, *SS.* II.B, pp. 415–417 and 455.

Since this author, who wrote in the early years of the twelfth century, offers only excerpts from chapters I.1, 3, 5, 27, 30, 31, 37; II.1, 9, 15, 17, 20, 32, 37, 41, 42, 44, 47, 48, 60; and III.13–17, and since, judging from the plan of the work, he would have excerpted the remaining material concerning Italy as well, had it been available to him—especially on pp. 475–476, where he already follows Abbot Hugh—it may be inferred that his manuscript, like all the Austrian manuscripts, stopped in the first part of Book III.

If this was so, the manuscript was copied from the surviving chapters II.26–40 and 45–66 [Col. 0778B]. In Book I, chapter 37, he rightly, though perhaps too strongly, calls Lambert “a very warlike king,” in agreement with manuscripts 1, 2, and 3.

It is therefore clear that the now-lost manuscript from which the Austrian and Italian manuscripts 3), 3a), 3b), 3c), 3c*), and 3d) descended was written in the tenth or eleventh century; it may perhaps be assigned to the middle of the tenth century, as will be suggested below under no. 5.

**4) Harleian Manuscript**

The British Museum manuscript among the Harleian manuscripts, no. 3685, a folio paper manuscript of the sixteenth century, formerly belonging to Peutinger, places the *History of Otto* before the books of the *Antapodosis*, just as manuscripts 1 and 2 do. The former is complete; the latter, whose ending is more difficult to read, ends at the beginning of chapter VI.10.

**5) Harleian Manuscript no. 3713**

A parchment quarto manuscript of the eleventh century, originating in Germany, as shown by a thirteenth-century note by Everwicus [Col. 0778C] of Stegrauen and by other sixteenth-century notes by Marie Wolters and Wicbolde. It too descended from a faulty understanding of the Freising manuscript.

A quire containing III.25–44 has fallen out. Book VI ends at the words “of the candidate spearmen.” The *History of Otto* was added as a seventh book, and ends: “We no longer send [him] to Rome, but into exile.”

The readings of this manuscript were once recorded by P. Scriverius, whose notes are preserved in the Heidelberg Library. I myself examined it in 1827. The following manuscript agrees extensively with it, though with additional errors.

**5a) Formerly Gemblacensis, Now in the Royal Brussels Library**

A parchment manuscript of the eleventh century. We infer, with reasonable probability, from readings taken from it that it was available to the author of the *Life of Saint Gerard, Abbot of Brogne* [Note: [Col. 0778D] In Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, fifth century, pp. 264–265, several sentences from IV.24, 14, and 29 are cited.], to Ekkehard of Aura, Sigebert of Gembloux, and Alberic, monk of Trois-Fontaines.

The same lacunae and readings show that it was copied from the Harleian manuscript before the relevant quire had been lost, or from another manuscript of the same class. The scribe nevertheless attempted in several places to remedy passages that had already been corrupted or that he had misunderstood, making slight conjectures and even attempting to assist the style. The first edition descended from it or from a copy of it.

**5*) First Edition of William Parvus**

The first edition, by William Parvus, published in 1514 in folio with Ascensian type [Col. 0779A], is marked throughout by all the lacunae and corrupt readings of the Gemblac manuscript. The editor sometimes helped these with his own conjectures, not unsuccessfully; more often, however—as might have been expected from Liudprand’s peculiar manner of writing—he attempted to correct them with unfavorable results.

**6) Royal Paris Manuscript**

The Royal Paris manuscript, no. 5922, is a parchment manuscript written in Germany in the twelfth century. In the fifteenth century it was inscribed “Book of Saint Mary the Virgin at Otterburg, in the diocese of Mainz.”

It contains the first three books and the beginning of the fourth book of Gregory of Tours’ *Ecclesiastical History*, followed by Regino’s *Chronicle* without its continuations. Added to these are *Antapodosis* I.5–11; VI.5, from “the trees are carried up”; VI.8–9; and chapter 15 of the *History of Otto*, from “After these things were said” through chapter 20, “for the sake of almsgiving.” These passages [Col. 0779B] likewise, as [the source breaks off].

**7) Brussels Manuscript**

A folio paper manuscript of the sixteenth century, formerly belonging to Antonius Caucius, archbishop of Corfu, and—

**8) Ambrosian Manuscript**

A paper manuscript of the sixteenth century, which ends in the same words as the editions. These manuscripts were so constituted that I realized we could dispense with them entirely in a new edition.

Liudprand’s history was adapted for their own purposes by historians of the eleventh and twelfth centuries: by the author of the *Life of Saint Gerard of Brogne*, Ekkehard of Aura, the Farfa chronicler, and Sigebert of Gembloux; in the thirteenth century by Alberic, monk of Trois-Fontaines; in the fourteenth by Henry of Hervorden; and in the fifteenth by Abbot Trithemius of Spanheim.

As stated above, the first edition, published in 1514, was reproduced by Hervagius in the Basel edition of 1532, though he used in a few places a manuscript of good quality, whose readings thereafter remained in the text.

All subsequent editors reproduced the Basel book: Justus Reuberus in the *Scriptores* of 1584 and 1619; Laurentius Ramirez de Prado in the Antwerp edition of Liudprand’s works of 1640; Chesnius in volume III of the *Scriptores Francici* of 1641; Joannes in the new edition of Reuber’s *Scriptores* of 1726; and Muratori in the *Scriptores rerum Italicarum* of 1723 and 1726, volume II. One might say that Muratori gave the work a third round of attention, since in volume II.B he introduced several readings from the Viennese manuscripts 3a and 3c* [Col. 0780A].

After three centuries, let the readers judge how much a new edition established according to the autograph differs from the others and how greatly it now benefits the history. I have cut away the very abundant harvest of readings that I had collected from the Brussels, London, and Austrian manuscripts before the autograph came into my hands, and have chosen to report only those [Col. 0780B] that make it possible to recognize the different classes of manuscripts. I followed the same principle with the most corrupt readings of the editions.

For, once the purest gold has been refined, it is pleasant to leave the dross behind.

The little book of the Embassy, first published by Canisius together with the chronicles of Victor of Tunnuna and John of Biclaro at Ingolstadt in 1600, in quarto, and thereafter reproduced by Baronius under the year 968, by Muratori in volume II of the *Scriptores*, and by my Niebuhr in volume XI of the *Byzantine Scriptores*, we judged it wrong to leave untouched, now that we had experienced the method of composition and corruption of the texts in the already published *Antapodosis* and *History of Otto* of Liutprand—even though the sole Trier manuscript had perished. Once the work had been undertaken, it happened beyond expectation that we were able to present it to readers restored in several passages of great importance [Col. 0780C]. Niebuhr praises the Embassy as “full of envy and hatred, yet even so exceedingly useful for the knowledge of events”; and students of these matters will judge that in it Liutprand’s spirit attained the summit of vigor and eloquence prepared for him.

[Col. 0781] Royal Munich manuscript, formerly Freising.

Royal Brussels manuscript, formerly Spanheim.

Royal Brussels manuscript, formerly Gembloux.

[Col. 0783]

## A SECOND BIBLIOGRAPHICAL NOTICE ON LIUTPRAND

*(In Fabricius, Bibliotheca of Middle and Low Latin, volume IV, p. 291.)*

[Col. 0783A] Luitprand—also called Liutprand, Litobrand, Eutrand, and so forth—according to Trithemius, chapter 362, was born in the city of Pavia; others, less probably, call him a Spaniard. He was certainly distinct from Luitprand of Toledo, if such a person existed, and, from being a deacon of Ticinum or Pavia, became bishop of Cremona. He carried out two embassies to Constantinople: one from Berengar II, margrave, to the emperor Constantine Porphyrogenitus in 946, and the other from the emperor Otto I and his son to Nicephorus Phocas in 968. Labbe, volume II, p. 33, *On Sacred Ecclesiastical History*; Cave, under the year 940; Francesco Arisi in *Cremona Litterata*, volume I, p. 58 ff.; and above all Nicolaus Antonius, VI.16 of the *Bibliotheca Veteris Hispana*, have treated him sufficiently carefully.

Sigebert, chapter 1260, says that he wrote the celebrated *History of the Deeds of the Kings and Emperors of His Age*, which he entitled *Antapodosis*, that is, “retribution” [Note: Properly, Luitprand entitled the third book *Antidosis*, attacking Berengar, by whom he had been offended, and his wife Willa, while in turn praising those who had treated him well.], in a polished and alternating style [Note: Partly in prose and partly in metrical composition], addressed to Regimund [also Roymund, also Tractemund], bishop of the Spanish church of Eliberis. Trithemius, when mentioning the same work, says that it consisted of seven books; yet only six books are visible in the printed editions, and the final six chapters of the sixth book were not written by Luitprand himself but were added later by another author, as Vossius, p. 345; Baronius under the year 963, no. 3; Miraeus, chapter 270 of the *Auctarium*; and others have observed. Perhaps Trithemius counted the history of the later embassy, discussed below, as the seventh book.

Those six books, written between the years 957 and 960 (Pagi, under the year 963, no. 3), and touching briefly upon the affairs of both empires from 891 to 946 [Col. 0783C], appeared among the writings of Justus Reuberus, p. 86; in volume III of André du Chesne, p. 562; among the works of Luitprand, Antwerp 1640, folio; and in Muratori’s *Thesaurus of the Writers of Italy*, volume II, p. [Col. 0784A] 417, where on p. 1078 one will also find variant readings from three manuscripts of the Imperial Library.

A description of the embassy undertaken to Nicephorus Phocas in 968, dedicated to the emperors Otto and his son, and to the empress Adelheid, first published by Heinrich Canisius together with the chronicles of Victor of Tunnuna and John of Biclaro and the Bavarian synod of 772 under Duke Tassilo, Ingolstadt 1600, quarto; also in Baronius under the year 968, no. 11 ff.; in the *Luitprand of Ramírez*, Antwerp 1640, folio; and in the second volume of Muratori’s *Thesaurus of the Writers of Italy*. In this description Luitprand recalls his earlier embassy, p. 115 of the first edition, in these words:

> “In the time of the blessed emperor Constantine I came here [to Constantinople], not as a bishop but as a deacon; nor sent by an emperor [Col. 0784B] or king, but by Berengar the margrave,” and so forth.

These two alone are the genuine and worthwhile little works of Luitprand. The rest are spurious: the *Chronicle*, from the year of Christ 606 to 960, and the *Adversaria* [Note: In these *Adversaria* he says that he was librarian at Fulda, pp. 473, 483, 484, and 490], in which, on p. 464, there is mention of a *Chronicle* addressed to Heronius, bishop of Braga, together with a letter addressed to the same man. These works, published and supplied with notes by Jerome de la Higuera, S.J., and Lorenzo Ramírez de Prado, Antwerp 1640, folio, together with the earlier works, are proved false by Labbe, Cave, and others, but especially by Nicolaus Antonius in volume I of the *Bibliotheca Veteris Hispana*, p. 585 ff.

The *Lives of the Roman Pontiffs*, from Saint Peter up to Pope Formosus, who died in 895, which John Busaeus published at Mainz in 1602, quarto, together with an excerpt from Anastasius made by Abbo of Fleury, have likewise been noted by Vossius and others to have another author—more probably a German than Luitprand—and to have themselves been excerpted from Anastasius.

[Col. 0785]

## PREFACE OF LUDOVICO ANTONIO MURATORI TO HIS EDITION OF LIUTPRAND’S WORKS

*(Italian Affairs, volume II.)*

[Col. 0785A] If any century was bleak in Italy because of its vices and barbarous customs, surely the tenth century after Christ surpassed all the others in such misery. At that time even the face of the Roman Church itself was utterly disfigured; dreadful wars raged throughout Italy, the laws were trampled underfoot, and, above all, the condition of humane letters had been cast down. Liutprand the historian must therefore be highly commended by us. In that iron age he rose so far above the ignorance of the others that, although he used a harsh style sufficiently reflecting the character of his uncivilized age, even in our own times he still attracts the reader most willingly to read his works. He possessed a lively and penetrating intellect, and set forth what he wrote with rare vitality and freedom.

Most recent scholars have become accustomed to call him Luitprand; but among the ancients his name was Liutprand or Liutbrand. Public inscriptions, archival documents, and ancient manuscript codices assure us of this. In them I have always noticed the name Liutprand written, never Luitprand [Col. 0785B]. For the fact that some call him Litobrand and even Eutrand undoubtedly arose from the careless error of scribes.

“An Italian by nation and born in the city of Pavia,” as Trithemius wrote, is how both ancient and modern authorities have judged him. Yet, as William Cave notes in his *Ecclesiastical Writers*, “Francisco Bivario, in the critical judgment prefixed to the works of Liutprand, argues, with conjectures not wholly contemptible, that he was Spanish by race, Cordoban by family, or at least Baetican, and that he fled with his parents from the Saracens and settled in Italy.” Such is Cave’s statement. He nevertheless understood very well that a certain *Chronicle* attributed to our Liutprand in Spain, and first published at Madrid by Tamayo, then by Ramírez and by Jerome de la Higuera at Antwerp with notes in 1640, is full of old-womanish tales and every kind of fraud. It was chiefly from this work that the peddlers of nonsense took their opportunity to insert the Italian Liutprand among the Spanish people.

[Col. 0785C] Yet Nicolaus Antonius, the Sevillian jurist, must not be deprived of his due praise. In the century just past he won a great name among the Spaniards by his learning no less than by his love of truth. In book VI, chapter 16 of the *Bibliotheca Vetus Hispana*, using refined critical judgment, he consigned that entire *Chronicle*, together with certain *Adversaria* attributed to the same Liutprand, to the realm of fable, and branded the falsifiers of his nation with his censures. He judges that the Italian nation must in no way be deprived of possession of Liutprand.

One point that seemed capable of introducing some legitimate doubt on this matter must not be concealed. In his genuine *Chronicle*, book V, chapter 1, Liutprand writes to Raymund, bishop of Eliberis in Spain, concerning a certain eclipse of the sun:

> “On that same day our king Abd al-Rahman was defeated in battle by Ramiro, the most Christian king of Galicia.”

But Nicolaus Antonius advises that the passage should be lightly corrected, namely, that it should read “your king.” And indeed it is impossible that Liutprand, who had lived in Italy for so many years and had been enrolled among the clergy of the Church of Ticinum, should have called a Saracen king “his own king,” since he had no further connection with him—indeed, had never had any.

It remains, therefore, since no arguments oppose it, that Liutprand was born in Italy and, as is probable, at Ticinum, which is also Pavia, and that he was of Lombard stock. His name itself seems sufficiently to suggest this, as does his office, for he calls himself a Levite, that is, a deacon, of Ticinum.

In book III, chapter 1, he describes the burning of Pavia in these verses:

> Unhappy Pavia, once beautiful, is burned;  
> And Vulcan, raising his limbs with blasts,  
> climbs upon the temples of God and over the whole fatherland.

By these words, unless I am mistaken, he plainly calls Pavia his native city. His father was sent as an envoy by Hugh, king of Italy, to the Roman emperor of the Greeks around the year 927 after Christ; from this too one may see that his parent lived in Italy. At that time Liutprand was a small child.

After several years, however, he was enrolled among the palace pages and won the favor of King Hugh by the sweetness of his voice, as he himself testifies in book IV, chapter 1. When Hugh and then Lothair, kings of Italy, had been overthrown, Berengar II seized the scepter and appointed Liutprand “privy to his secrets and signer of his letters.” Indeed, knowing his ability well, he sent him in 946 to Constantine Porphyrogenitus, the emperor of Constantinople.

Many vices disfigured Berengar and soon made him hated by good men. Consequently Liutprand himself, after a long period of service, finally incurred his hatred to such an extent that, stripped of his possessions and fearing worse for himself, he was forced to withdraw to Germany to King Otto. In that exile, around the year 958, he completed his *History*, comprising six books and begun at Frankfurt on the Main.

In 961 Otto the Great, king of Germany, invited once again by the Roman pontiff and by most of the nobles of Italy to oppose Berengar’s tyranny [Col. 0786C], gained possession of the Lombard kingdom; in the following year he was also made emperor of the Romans. In so fortunate a reversal of affairs Liutprand returned to Italy. Since he was among the few especially dear to Otto, through Otto’s favor he was advanced to the bishopric of Cremona.

Ughellus dates Liutprand’s accession to this new and illustrious dignity to 963. Certainly in that year he was already a bishop and was sent by the aforementioned Augustus to Rome, to Pope John, where he took part in the synod, or rather council, convened against that pontiff.

Then, in 968, he undertook a second embassy, sent by Otto the Great to Constantinople to ask Nicephorus, emperor of the Greeks, for Theophania, daughter of Romanus the Younger, as wife for Otto’s son, who had been associated with him in the Roman Empire.

In what year Liutprand departed this life is not known. Nevertheless, in Ughellus’s *Italia Sacra*, volume IV, under the bishops of Cremona, we find a description of the translation of the body of Saint Himerius, bishop, to the city of Cremona, carried out by Liutprand. There he is called [Col. 0786D] “Liuzo [or Liuzo], bishop of Cremona, of blessed memory, the intimate royal counselor, prudent in counsel and filled with love of divinity, whom the emperor, at the height of his second reign, appointed [I read ‘placed’], frequently entering and departing from the royal presence.”

From these words we understand that Liutprand also bore the name Liuzo. We may suspect, however, that among the common people of that age it sounded or was identical with Liutprand. At the same time, it becomes clearer how much authority the same Liutprand possessed and how highly he was honored and favored by Otto Augustus.

The same account adds:

> “The aforesaid praiseworthy pontiff observed how he might deposit the sacred relic of the saint”—

namely, the body brought to Cremona—

> “but this was not granted to him, because, compelled by imperial service, he was sent to Constantinople and did not return there again.”

These words suggest to the reader that Liutprand did not long survive the completion of his embassy. Indeed, that he was in Italy in 970 and took part in the synod convened in the city of Ferrara is testified by the Acts cited by Rubeus in book V of his *History of Ravenna*. There too he is listed as Liuzius, bishop of Cremona; likewise the Continuator of Regino and the Saxon Chronicler call him Liuzio under the year 965.

No surviving records after that year present Liutprand as alive. Only Julian of Toledo, an ancient historian—if heaven approves—claims that in 973 Liutprand came to Toledo and died and was buried there not long afterward. But, as is now clearer than daylight among scholars, the *Chronicle* of that Julian, and of Dexter, Haubert, and the other historians of that sort, are mere inventions fabricated by the most shameless men, published by the excessively credulous and well-meaning, and now rejected and despised even by the Spaniards of keener judgment. Consequently, the stories told by those impostors about the pilgrimage of our Liutprand to Spain and his death there must be counted among the fables.

[Col. 0787C] Liutprand was educated in letters beyond the measure of that most unhappy age. For he was proficient not only in Latin but also in Greek; indeed, he knew the Saxon, or German, language. He gave a striking demonstration of this knowledge at Rome in the synod where, when Otto the Great Augustus spoke in his native language, the bishop of Cremona translated his words into Latin for the fathers of the council.

Nor did he exercise his talent only in prose; he also practiced it in verse. Some accuse him of excessive freedom because he vividly depicts, and perhaps even exaggerates, the vices and disgraces of the men of his own time, including princes and both men and women of rank. It is not the place here to weigh such an accusation.

As for us, a *Chronicle of Spanish affairs* is attributed to our Liutprand, as are certain *Adversaria*, in praise of which Francisco Bivario collected much material. Lorenzo Ramírez and Jerome de la Higuera likewise illustrated them with notes, publishing them at Madrid and Antwerp. We have already said that these works belong among Roman fables, since they are entirely spurious and filled to satiety with lies.

At Mainz in 1602 there also appeared a book on the deeds of the Roman pontiffs, from Saint Peter to Pope Formosus, attributed to this same Liutprand. But learned men insist that this work too must be wholly denied to him, since it differs too greatly from his style and more probably came from some idle German, perhaps even from a later period.

We therefore now bring to light again the genuine writings of Liutprand. They are the six books of the *History of Affairs Transacted in Europe in His Own Time*, which was printed at Basel in 1532 and subsequently reproduced by Justus Reuberus in the volume of *Ancient Writers* published at Hanau in 1619.

The final six chapters of the sixth book, which concern the condemnation of Pope John XII, have been debated by Baronius, Vossius, Cave, Dupin, and others: whether they have Liutprand as their author, or some other continuator of the same history who nevertheless lived at that time or shortly afterward. The dispute remains undecided.

For my part, I think that Liutprand’s history has not come down to us complete. For we do not read in it of events closer to the time when he wrote, especially the deeds of Berengar II, which tormented him most sharply and drove him to write.

Liutprand’s other work is the *Embassy to Nicephorus, Emperor of Constantinople*, which he both carried out and described himself. Christopher Browerus of the Society of Jesus sent this little book, extracted from a Trier manuscript but mutilated, to Marcus Welser; Welser commended it to Heinrich Canisius, through whose care it was printed at Ingolstadt in 1600. Cardinal Baronius afterward incorporated it into his *Annals* under the year of Christ 968.

The reader will here have both works joined together, especially useful for Italian history.

[Col. 0787]

# THE HISTORY OF THE DEEDS OF KINGS AND EMPERORS, OR *ANTAPODOSIS*, BY LIUTPRAND, BISHOP OF CREMONA

*(In Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, Writers, volume III.)*

## [BOOK ONE]

### [CHAPTERS]

[Col. 0787D] In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, begins the book of *Antapodosis*, that is, of retribution [Note: Above, the word “of retribution” appears before *antapodoseos*, but I judged that it should be placed after the words “that is”; I have done the same in the following passages], concerning the kings and princes of part of Europe, published by Liudprand, deacon of the Church of Ticinum, ἐν τῇ ἐχμαλοσίᾳ αὐτοῦ (*en tē echmalosiā autou*), that is, “in his sojourn” [Note: “of him,” manuscript 1], addressed to Recemund, bishop of the Church of Eliberis in the Spanish province.

1. [Note: The argument is missing in manuscript 3.] Preface.

2. On the fortress of Fraxinetum [Note: *Fraxaneto* corrected consistently to *Fraxinetum* in manuscript 1] and its situation.

3. How the Saracens first obtained Fraxinetum.

4. How, through the envy of the Provincials and at their invitation, the Saracens devastated Provence.

5. Which emperor then ruled the Greeks; which kings ruled the Bulgarians, Bavarians, Franks, Saxons, Swabians, and Italians; and who was pope at Rome.

11. How the emperor Leo was captured at night by his own men, not recognized, handed over to the guards, and scourged; how the prison guard released him; how the emperor himself scourged those who had not scourged him [Note: The word is written twice in manuscript 1] and honored those who had scourged him.

12. On the excellent game played by that same emperor Leo, involving sleepers and gold coins.

[Col. 0789C] 13. Why King Arnulf broke the fortified barriers and allowed the Hungarians to come out [Note: *Hungarius* corrected to *Hungarios* in manuscript 1].

14. On Wido and Berengar, who confirmed their friendship by an oath but did not keep it, and on the fact that such a friendship cannot be preserved.

17. On Wido’s return to Italy.

18. On the battle between Wido and Berengar.

19. On another battle between them and Berengar’s flight.

[Col. 0790A] 21. How a Lombard killed a Bavarian in single combat.

24. On the people of Milan and Pavia who came to Arnulf.

42. How Lambert was killed at Marinco by Hugh, the son of Maginfred, in revenge for his father [Note: *Marico* in manuscript 1].
