44. Praise of King Lambert [Note: *Lantberti* is written consistently in manuscript 5a].

# BOOK ONE BEGINS

[Col. 0789]

[Col. 0789D] To the reverend and wholly holy lord Recemund [Note: *Regemund* in manuscripts 5 and 5a], bishop of the Church of Eliberis, Liudprand [Note: *Liuprandus* in manuscript 3. Hence it seems to be indicated that the reading in the very corrupt third chapter also flowed from manuscript 1, a codex not yet corrected in every respect], a Levite of the Church of Ticinum, though not by his own merits, sends greetings.

For two years, dearest father, because of the smallness of my talent I delayed your request, by which you compelled me to set down the deeds of all the emperors and kings of Europe, as one who was not uncertain from hearsay but assured by sight. These events, the scarcity of eloquence of which I am utterly destitute, and the envy of detractors have deterred my mind from beginning the task [Col. 0790D]. These men, swollen with arrogance, idle in reading, and, according to the judgment of the learned Boethius [Note: *On the Consolation of Philosophy*, book I], possessing a fragment of the philosophical garment while thinking that they possess the whole, will insult me by saying:

> “Our predecessors wrote so much that readers will fail much more than readings.”

They will also babble that comic line:

> “Nothing will be said that was not said before.”

To their barking I reply that philosophers, like those suffering from dropsy, grow thirstier the more they drink; so the more frequently they read, the more eagerly they seek out anything new.

If they are wearied by the intricate reading of witty Cicero, let them at least be refreshed by such trifles. For, unless I am mistaken, just as the eyes, unless some substance intervenes, are dulled when struck by the sun’s rays and cannot see it purely as it is, so the mind of the Academics, Peripatetics, and Stoics is weakened by continual meditation upon their doctrines unless it is restored either by the useful laughter of comedies or by the delightful history of heroes.

And if, following the custom of the ancient and accursed pagans, something not merely unprofitable but even rather harmful to hear is inscribed for remembrance in books, why should the wars of these emperors be silenced, when they ought to be compared with the praises of Julius, Pompey, Hannibal and his brother Hasdrubal, and Scipio Africanus, famous commanders [Note: Missing in the vacant space of manuscript 3]? Especially since in these matters there is the goodness of our Lord Jesus Christ to recount when they lived holy lives, and, when they committed offenses, the salutary correction administered by him.

Let no one be troubled if I insert into this little book the deeds of feeble kings and effeminate princes. There is one just power of almighty God—namely, of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—which justly restrains some of them for their crimes and raises others according to their merits.

This, I say, is the true promise of our Lord Jesus Christ to the saints:

> “Observe and hear my voice, and I will be an enemy to your enemies, and I will afflict those who afflict you, and my angel shall go before you” (Exodus XXIII).

Through Solomon too, Wisdom, who is Christ, cries out:

> “The world will fight on his behalf against the senseless” (Wisdom V).

That this happens every day, even the man who snores notices [Note: Missing in manuscript 5 and 5a].

To provide an evident example from countless others, the town called Fraxinetum will speak without my saying anything [Note: The reading is *loquitur* in manuscript 3], a town which plainly stands on the boundary between the Italians and the Provincials [Note: Fraxinet, not far from Fréjus].

2. So that its situation may be plainly evident to everyone—and I do not think it is hidden from you, indeed you know it better, as you can infer from those who are tributaries of your king, namely Abderrahman—it is bounded on one side by the sea and protected on the others by a very dense forest of thorn bushes [Col. 0792A]. If someone enters it, he is held fast by the curvature of the thorns [Note: *T.* and *a.* in manuscripts 5, 5a, and 5a*] and pierced by their exceedingly sharp points, so that he has no possibility of advancing or returning except with great labor.

3. *(Year 891.)* But secretly—and since it cannot be otherwise, by the just judgment of God—twenty Saracens set out from Spain in a tiny boat and, against their will, were carried there by the wind. These pirates disembarked by night, secretly entered the village, and slaughtered the Christians, alas! They claimed the place for themselves and prepared Mount Maurus, adjoining the little village, as a refuge against the neighboring peoples. In this way they made the thorny forest larger and denser for their protection, so that if anyone cut even a branch from it, a man would emerge at the stroke of a sword [uncertain reading] [Col. 0792B]. Thus it came about that every entrance except one exceedingly narrow path was blocked.

Confiding in the roughness of the place, they secretly reconnoitered the neighboring peoples all around. They summoned many messengers and sent them to Spain; they praised the place and promised that they themselves held the neighboring peoples in no account. Finally, they soon brought back with them only one hundred Saracens [Note: *Oppido* corrected to *mox* in manuscript 1; *oppido* in manuscripts 3], who would establish the truth of the matter.

4. Meanwhile the Provincials, who were the people nearest to them, began to disagree among themselves: one slaughtered another, seized his property, and did whatever evil could be devised. But because one faction could not satisfy the other, as envy and grief demanded, they called upon the Saracens mentioned above, no less cunning than treacherous, for aid; and together with them they crushed their nearest neighbors.

Their assistance did not merely help slaughter their neighbors; it also turned a fertile land into a desert. [Note: From *proximum* (“neighbor”) to *feliciter regnat* (“reigns happily,” in chapter 5) is in Liutprand’s second hand in manuscript 1; thus I have marked the chapters of the earlier editions.] But let us see what envy achieved according to a certain writer [Note: *justa*, that is, *juxta* (“according to”)], who describes it in this way:

> Nothing is more just than envy, which immediately  
> Gnaws at its author and tortures his heart.  
> While it tries to deceive, it is deceived;  
> While it seeks to extinguish, it is extinguished.

What follows? Since the Saracens could not accomplish this by their own strength, they defeated one faction with the aid of the other. As they continually increased their forces from Spain, they pursued in every possible way those whom at first they had seemed to defend. Thus they rage, they destroy, they leave nothing behind.

The other neighboring peoples now tremble, because, according to the prophet, “one of these pursued a thousand, and two put ten thousand to flight” (Deuteronomy XXXII). And why? “Because their God sold them, and the Lord shut them in.”

5. *(Years 886–912.)* At that time Leo Porphyrogenitus, son of the emperor Basil and father of the Constantine who still survives and reigns happily [Note: He died in 959], ruled the empire of the city of Constantinople.

Simeon, a powerful warrior, was in command of the Bulgarians—a Christian, but a bitter enemy of the neighboring Greeks (883–927). The nation of the Hungarians, whose savagery almost all peoples have experienced, but which, through the mercy of God and the power of the most holy and unconquered King Otto, as we shall state more fully, is so terrified that it dares not even mutter [Note: *Mutriee* in manuscript 1; *mittere* in manuscript 3; *muttire* in manuscript 5; *muttire*, corrected to *mutire*, in manuscript 5a], was at that time unknown to all of us [Note: *Hababatur*, corrected to *habebatur*, in manuscript 1].

For it had been separated from us by certain very difficult barriers, which the common people call *clusae* [Note: *Clusurae* in manuscript 1; but *clusas* below, chapter 13], so that it had no opportunity to go out either toward the southern or toward the western region.

*(During the same period, August 887–December 900.)* After the death of Charles, surnamed the Bald [Note: the Fat], the most powerful King Arnulf ruled over the Bavarians, Swabians, Teutonic Franks [Note: The words *f. t.* are joined together in manuscript 1 and should not be separated], Lotharingians, and the bold Saxons [Note: *Principatur* in manuscript 1].

Centebald, duke of the Moravians, resisted him bravely (892–893). The emperors Berengar and Wido were contending for the kingdom of Italy (888–894). Formosus, bishop of the city of Porto, was regarded as supreme and universal pope of the Roman See (September 19, 891–April 896).

But now let us explain as briefly as we can what took place under each of these men.

6. *(Years 886–912.)* Leo, therefore, the most devout emperor of the Greeks, whom we mentioned above, namely the father of this Constantine Porphyrogenitus, ruled the empire of the Greeks in holiness and justice, enjoying peace everywhere.

I call him Porphyrogenitus not because he was born in purple, but because he was born in the house called Porphyra. And since the matter has come before us, let us relate what we have heard about the origin of this Porphyrogenitus.

7. The emperor Constantine Augustus, from whose name the city of Constantinople received its name, ordered this house to be built—τὸν οἶκον τοῦτον (*ton oikon touton*), that is, “this house”—and gave it the name Porphyra. He wished that the offspring who would succeed to his nobility should come into the light there, so that those born from his line would be called by this splendid title, Porphyrogeniti.

Hence some say that this Constantine, son of the emperor Leo, derived his origin from that blood. But the truth of the matter is as follows.

8. The emperor Basil Augustus, this man’s grandfather, had sprung from a humble family in Macedonia. He descended to Constantinople under the yoke of poverty—τῆς πτωχείας (*tēs ptōcheias*), which means “of poverty”—in order to serve a certain hegumen, that is, an abbot.

The emperor Michael, who was emperor at that time, came to this monastery for the sake of prayer, where Basil was serving. He saw that Basil was distinguished above the others in appearance, summoned τὸν ἡγούμενον (*ton hēgoumenon*), that is, the abbot, and asked him to give him the boy. Receiving him into the palace, he appointed him to the office of chamberlain.

Not long afterward he became so powerful that he was called emperor by everyone as a second emperor.

9. But because almighty God visits his servants with just judgment of whatever kind, he had permitted this emperor Michael for a time not to be sound of mind, so that, the more severely he pressed him in the depths below, the more mercifully he might reward him in the heights above.

For, as the story goes, during the period of his madness he had even ordered members of his household to be condemned to death. Yet when he came to his senses he would inquire after them in this manner: unless those whom he had ordered to be slaughtered were brought back, the men who had carried out the order themselves would be condemned to the same sentence. Through this terror, those whom he had ordered to be condemned were kept safe.

But when he did this repeatedly, and again to Basil, Basil received the following counsel from his attendants—an abominable thing:

> “Lest the mad command of the king someday be deliberately carried out by men who do not care for you, or rather who hate you, you should kill him instead and take up the imperial scepters.”

Basil fulfilled this without delay, compelled by fear and deceived also by desire to rule. Once Michael had been killed, Basil became emperor.

10. *(Years 886–912.)* After a short time had passed, our Lord Jesus Christ appeared to him in a vision, holding the right hand of that emperor whose death Basil had caused, and addressing him as follows:

> ἵνα τί ἔσφαζες τὸν δεσπότην σου βασιλέα;  
> *Hina ti esphazes ton despotēn sou basilea?*  
> “Why did you kill your lord, the emperor?” [Note: In manuscripts 5 and 5a the words *hina ti esphazes ton des* are missing; *esphazes* is absent in manuscripts 3, 3a, and others.]

When he awoke, he recognized that he was guilty of so great a crime. Immediately returning to his senses, he considered what he should do about it.

Strengthened by this salutary and truly acceptable promise of our Lord through the prophet—“On whatever day the sinner groans, he shall be saved” (Ezekiel XXXIII.12)—he confessed with tears and groans that he was a sinner, that he was guilty, and that he had shed innocent blood.

Having received good counsel, he made friends for himself from the mammon of iniquity, so that those whom he consoled with temporal assistance might free him from the eternal fire of Gehenna through their prayers.

He built, with precious and marvelous workmanship, a church beside the palace, facing east, which they call Nea, that is, “New,” in honor of the supreme commander of the heavenly host, the archangel Michael, who in Greek is called ἀρχιστράτηγος (*archistratēgos*, “commander-in-chief”).

### 11

Now, let it not be burdensome to insert into this little book two events [Col. 0795A] performed by the son of that same Basil, the emperor Augustus Leo already mentioned—events worthy of both laughter and remembrance.

The city of Constantinople, formerly Byzantium and now called New Rome, is situated among exceedingly savage peoples. To the north it has the Hungarians, Pechenegs, Khazars, Rus’—whom we call by another name Northmen—and the Bulgarians, who are excessively close to it; to the east, Baghdad; between east and south, the inhabitants of Egypt and Babylon [Note: [Col. 0795] “babilioniaeque” in 1 and 55]; to the south, Africa and that much-too-near island of Crete, which is hostile to it. The other nations lying under the same climate—namely, the Armenians, Persians, Chaldeans, Abasgians—serve this city.

The inhabitants of this city surpass those peoples in wealth and likewise in wisdom. For it is their custom, lest they be oppressed by neighboring nations, to station armed soldiers throughout the city’s lanes, crossroads, and four-way intersections every night, to guard the city and keep watch over it. Thus, if after twilight the guards should encounter anyone walking about somewhere, he is immediately seized, beaten, bound in the prison in fetters under unremitting guard, and kept there to be brought before the authorities on the following day. In this way the city is preserved unharmed not only from enemies but also from robbers.

The emperor Augustus Leo, wishing to test the loyalty and steadfastness of the watchmen, descended alone from the palace after twilight and reached the first guard post. When the guards saw him fleeing and apparently avoiding them out of fear, they seized him and asked who he was and where he was going. He replied that he was one of many and was going to a brothel. Immediately they said to him: “We shall have you severely beaten, bound in fetters, and kept until tomorrow.”

He answered them: “Μὴ, ἀδελφοῖ, μὴ—mi, adelfi, mi,” that is, “No, brothers, no; take what I carry and let me go where I wish.” After accepting twelve gold pieces, they promptly released him.

Passing on from there, he came to the second guard post. There, just as at the first, he was seized and released after giving twenty gold pieces.

Then, when he reached the third post, he was seized. But he was not released, as at the first and second posts, after giving gold; instead, they took everything from him, bound him tightly in heavy fetters, beat him for a long time with fists and whips, and kept him under guard until the following day, when he was to be brought before the authorities.

After these guards had departed, the emperor summoned the prison guard to him and said: “Φίλε μου—file mu,” that is, “my friend: do you know the emperor Leo?”

The guard replied: “How could I know someone whom I do not remember ever having seen? Indeed, when he proceeds in public—although rarely—I seem to see from a distance, since I cannot approach him, something marvelous and not a human being. But it is more advantageous for you to attend to how you may leave here unharmed than to ask me such things. Fortune does not favor you equally: σὲ εἰς τὴν φιλάκην καὶ αὐτὸν εἰς τὸ χρυσοτρίκλινον—se is tin filakin ke auton is to chrisotriclinon—that is, ‘you in prison, and him in the golden banqueting hall.’ These bonds are too slight; let heavier ones be added, so that you have no opportunity to think about the emperor.”

The emperor answered him: “Stop, stop; for I myself am the emperor Augustus Leo, who came down from the dignity of the palace under an evil omen.”

The prison guard, hoping that what he had said was untrue, replied: “Am I to believe that an impure man, squandering his possessions with prostitutes, is an emperor? Since you have neglected yourself, I shall examine your horoscope for you. Mars is in trine, Saturn regards Venus, Jupiter is in square, Mercury is angry with you, the Sun is round, the Moon is in a leap; evil Fortune presses upon you.”

The emperor replied: “To prove that what I say is true, come with me to the palace when the morning signal has been given—for before then we have not dared to do so—under a better omen than that under which I descended. If you do not see me received there as emperor, kill me. For it will be no lesser crime to have said that I am emperor if I am not than to have killed someone. But if you fear suffering any harm on that account, may God bring such things upon me and add such things to them if you do not receive a reward rather than punishment for this.”

The prison guard therefore became convinced. When the morning signal was given, as the emperor had said, he accompanied him all the way to the palace. When he arrived there and was received with extraordinary honor by those who knew him, he left his companion utterly stunned by amazement. As he watched all the dignitaries come to meet the emperor, offer him praises, adore him, remove his slippers [Note: [Col. 0795] “ocurre” in 1.], and perform various services for him, he would then have thought it preferable to die and live.

The emperor said to him: “Now consider your astrology. If you truly foretold under what omen you would come here, you will prove that you possess genuine knowledge of augury. First, however, please tell me what illness it is that has made you so pale.”

He replied: “Of the Fates [Note: [Col. 0795] “parcar earum” in 1, across two lines.], excellent Clotho has now ceased spinning; Lachesis no longer wishes to labor at twisting; but the most savage of them, Atropos, already holds the joints of the shears in her bent hand [Note: [Col. 0795] That is, holding the joints of the shears already in her curved hand (κόνδυλος).] [Note: [Col. 0795] “articulis jam inconditum solam” in 5 and 5a.] and awaits only the sentence concerning your rule, so that, drawing the threads tight, she may break them. The cause of the pallor in my face is that my soul has descended from my head and, together with it, has drawn the blood into the lower part of my body.”

The emperor therefore smiled slightly and said: “Take back your soul, take it back, and with it accept four pounds of gold. Tell no one anything about me except that I have fled.”

When this had been done, the emperor ordered the guards who had released him after accepting payment and those who had beaten him and handed him over to custody to come before him. He said to them:

“While you are keeping watch and guarding the city, do you ever encounter thieves or adulterers?”

Those who had released him after taking payment answered that they had seen nothing [Note: [Col. 0797] “ita” in 1]; those who had beaten him and handed him over to custody answered as follows [Note: [Col. 0797] “ita” in 1]:

“Your holy dominion, δεσποτία σοῦ ἡ ἅγια—despotia sui agia—that is, ‘your holy lordship,’ commanded that if the guards should encounter anyone walking about somewhere after twilight, they were immediately to seize him, beat him, and hand him over to custody. In obedience, therefore, to your commands, most holy ruler [Note: [Col. 0797] “sanctisime” in 1], during the night preceding this present day we seized someone running through the brothels, flogged him, and placed him in prison, where, by your holy command, we kept him to be brought before the authorities.”

The emperor said to them: “My imperial authority commands again and again that he be brought immediately before me.”

Without delay they hurried off to bring him, bound as he was. When they heard that he had fled, they returned to the palace half dead. When they had reported this to the emperor, he immediately showed them that he had been stripped and severely beaten by them, and said:

“Δεῦτε—deute,” that is, “come! μὴ δειλιάσηται—mi diliasete,” that is, “do not be afraid. I myself am the one whom you flogged and whom you confidently suppose has now fled from prison. I know, and truly believe, that you intended to beat not the emperor but an enemy of the emperor. My authority not only wishes but commands that those who released me, not as emperor but as a robber and an assailant of my life, be beaten until death and expelled from the city, deprived of all their possessions. But to you I give not only my own wealth but also the riches of these wicked men.”

How wisely he acted in this matter, your Paternity will be able to observe from the fact that from then on the others guarded the city with the utmost care and feared him, even when absent, as though he were present. Thus it came about that the emperor no longer descended from the palace at night, while his guards faithfully watched over everything.

### 12

I judge it absurd to conceal in silence another jest that he himself performed.

The palace of Constantinople was guarded for the emperor’s safety by numerous troops of soldiers. A substantial daily allowance of food and pay was provided for the guards [Note: [Col. 0797] “C. v. v. c. c. n. p. i.” are absent in 5, 5a, and 5a*; present in the Hervagian edition.].

It happened that twelve of them, after refreshing their bodies, lay down to rest together in one house during the heat of the day. The emperor’s custom, however, was to creep through the entire palace while everyone was resting. One day, when he had reached the place where the twelve men had surrendered themselves to sleep [Note: [Col. 0797D] That is, to sleep], he used a small piece of wood—as a shrewd man—to lift the door-bolt and make himself an entrance.

While eleven were sleeping, the twelfth, in order that one art might deceive another, had begun to snore wide awake, as though sleeping; with his arms folded over his face, he watched very carefully everything the emperor did. The emperor entered, and when he saw that everyone was asleep, he placed a pound of gold coins on each man’s chest [Note: [Col. 0797] “adposuit” corrected to “apposuit” in 1]. Then he secretly went out again and closed the door as it had been before.

He did this so that, once awakened, they might rejoice over their profit and wonder considerably how it had happened. After the emperor had departed, the one who alone had remained awake rose, took the sleeping men’s gold coins for himself, and put them away; afterward he gave himself over to rest.

The emperor, therefore, concerned about this jest, ordered the men mentioned above to come before him after the ninth hour and addressed them as follows:

“If the vision of a dream has frightened or gladdened any one of you, my authority commands him to bring it into the open; and likewise, if anyone, upon waking, has seen anything unusual, I order him to disclose it.”

They replied that, since they had seen nothing, they had seen nothing [Note: [Col. 0797] “ita” in 1]. Even more astonished at this, they remained silent:

> They fell silent . . . and held their faces fixed in attention.  
> [Note: [Col. 0798D] Virgil, *Aeneid* II, 1.]

The emperor, supposing that they were keeping silent not through ignorance of the matter but through some cunning, grew angry [Note: [Col. 0797] “succensus” corrected to “suscensus” in 1.] and began threatening those who remained silent with various terrors. The man who was aware of everything heard this and addressed the emperor in a most humble and submissive voice:

“Φιλάνθρωπε βασιλεῦ—filanthrope vasileu,” that is, “most humane emperor, I do not know what these men saw; but I saw a delightful dream—would that it might happen to me very often.

“Today, while these eleven fellow servants of mine were sleeping, truly but inopportunely, I seemed to be keeping watch as though I were not asleep. Behold, the greatness of your empire, as if secretly opening the door, entered stealthily and placed a pound of gold upon the chest of each of us.

“When I saw your empire, as though turning back, and my companions sleeping in this vision, I immediately rose joyfully, took the eleven pounds of gold coins belonging to the sleepers, and placed them in my purse, in which there was already one pound, so that, in transgression of the Decalogue, there would not merely be eleven, but, with my one added in memory of the apostles, there would be twelve.

“This vision, Augustus, has not frightened me until now but has made me cheerful. Oh, would that another interpretation not please your empire! For it is plainly evident that I am a μάντις καὶ ὀνειροπόλος—mantin ke oniropolon—that is, a diviner and interpreter of dreams.”

When he heard this, the emperor was overcome by loud laughter. Yet he admired the man’s prudence and resourcefulness even more, and immediately said:

“Previously I had heard that you were neither σὲ οὔτε μάντην οὔτε ὀνειροπόλον—se [Note: [Col. 0797] Absent in 1] ute mantin ute oniropolon—that is, ‘neither a diviner nor an interpreter of dreams.’ But now you have explained this matter so openly that you used no circumlocution at all.

“Since, however, you could not possess the ability to keep watch or the skill of augury unless it had been given to you as a divine gift—whether what we hope, indeed believe, is true or false—καθὼς ὁ Λουκιανὸς—cathos o Lukianos—that is, as Lucian says of a certain man, that while asleep he discovered many things but found nothing after being awakened by a cock: nevertheless, whatever you see, whatever you perceive, and whatever you discover shall be yours.”

When they hear this, each person, taking upon himself the role of the others, will be able to perceive how greatly the rest were filled with confusion and how full this man was of joy.

### 13

Meanwhile Arnulfus (892), the most powerful king of the peoples beneath the Bear, since he was unable to conquer Centebald, the duke of the Moravians whom we mentioned above, who was vigorously resisting him, removed—alas!—those extremely well-fortified barriers which we said are commonly called *clusae*, and summoned the Hungarian people [Note: [Col. 0799] “huncgariorum” in 1.] to his aid: a people greedy, bold, ignorant of almighty God, not unfamiliar with every kind of crime, and desirous only of slaughter and plunder. Yet it may be questioned whether this could be called aid, since shortly afterward, when he died, it became a grave danger, indeed a destruction, both for his own people and for the other nations dwelling in the south and west.

What, then? Centebald is defeated, subjugated, and made tributary—but not alone.

O blind desire of King Arnulfus for ruling! O unhappy and bitter day! The overthrow of one little man becomes the ruin of all Europe. How many widows, bereaved fathers, corrupted virgins, the captivity of priests and peoples of God, the desolation of churches, and the solitude of inhabited lands your blind ambition prepares [Note: [Col. 0799] “solitududinem” in 1]!

Have you not read, I beg you, the words of Truth himself: “What does it profit a man if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul? Or what exchange will a man give for his soul?” (Matthew XVI; [Note: [Col. 0799] “detrimendum” in 1].)

And if the severity of the true Judge did not terrify you, at least the common bond of humanity should have tempered your fury. You were a man among men: though exalted in rank, you were not different in nature.

Mournful and pitiable is this condition: those species of beasts, serpents, and birds whose intolerable savagery and deadly venom cause them to be kept apart from human beings—such as basilisks, cockatrices [Note: [Col. 0799] This word begins in 2], rhinoceroses, or griffins, which by their very appearance seem harmful to everyone—nevertheless remain peaceful and harmless among themselves through the common bond of their origin and natural affinity. Yet man, formed in the image and likeness of God, conscious of God’s law and capable of reason, delights not merely in failing to love his neighbor but is exceedingly able to hate him.

Let us therefore see what John—not just anyone, but that excellent virgin, conscious of heavenly mysteries, to whom Christ on the cross entrusted his Virgin Mother to the virgin—said about such matters:

“Whoever hates his brother is a murderer; and you know that every murderer does not have eternal life abiding in him” (1 John III; [Note: [Col. 0799] “nentem” in 1]).

But let us return to the matter. After Centebald, duke of the Moravians, had been defeated [Note: [Col. 0799] “dulce” corrected to “duce” in 1], Arnulfus, having made peace, secured the kingdom. Meanwhile the Hungarians, watching for an opportunity and surveying the region, were plotting in their hearts the evil that afterward appeared openly [Note: [Col. 0799] That is, *apparuit*, “appeared.”] (893).

### 14

While these things were taking place, King Charles of Gaul, surnamed the Bald [Note: [Col. 0799D] “the Fat”], changed his life by dying in the present year, 888, on January 13.

While he lived, two powerful noble princes from Italy served him [Note: [Col. 0799] “praepositentes” corrected to “praepotentes” in 1]: one was called Wido, the other Berengarius. They were bound together by so strong a bond of friendship that they promised one another by oath that, if they survived King Charles, each would yield to the other’s arrangement: Wido would obtain what they call Roman France, while Berengarius would possess Italy.

But there are various uncertain and unstable kinds of friendship, by which the human race is joined in a fellowship of affection. Some are brought into friendship by an earlier recommendation; others by similarity in business, military service, craft, or study. These friendships, just as they are acquired through various associations—whether for profit, lust, or different necessities—are dissolved when any occasion for separation intervenes [Note: [Col. 0799] “uarium” in 1].

There is, however, this kind of friendship—indeed, this is the kind—which has most often been demonstrated by many trials: those who have entered into a bond of friendship through conspiracy have never been able to preserve unbroken harmony.

That most crafty enemy of the human race, wishing to make men transgressors of their oath, works more quickly and more shrewdly to break friendship. If we ask those who possess less sound judgment about the true kind of friendship, we shall answer that harmony and true friendship [Note: [Col. 0799] “amicititiam” in 1.] cannot stand except among men of reformed morals who share the same virtue and purpose [Note: [Col. 0799] “proposito” in 1].

### 15

It happened, then, that both Wido and Berengarius were absent from King Charles’s funeral. When Wido heard of his death, he set out for Rome and, without the consent of the Franks, received the imperial anointing over all France (late 887, early 888). The Franks therefore, since Wido was absent, made Odo king.

Berengarius, following Wido’s counsel as he had promised him by oath, assumed the rule of the Italian kingdom. Wido, however, set out for France (January 13, 888).

### 16

As he passed through the kingdoms of Burgundy and wished to enter the France called Roman, messengers from the Franks met him and announced that he should turn back. Exhausted by their long waiting, they had chosen Odo with the agreement of all the powerful men, since they could not remain without a king for long.

It is said that the Franks refused to accept Wido as king on this occasion. For when he was about to come to the city of Metz, which shines as the most powerful city in the kingdom of Lothair, he sent ahead his steward to prepare food for him in royal fashion.

When the bishop of Metz [Note: [Col. 0801D] At that time, Ruodbertus] supplied him with a large quantity of food according to Frankish custom, he received this reply from the steward:

“If you give me even a horse, I shall arrange for King Wido to be satisfied with a third part of this food [Note: [Col. 0801] “obsonat” in 1 and 2].”

When the bishop heard this, he said: “It is not fitting that such a king should rule over us—a king who prepares cheap food for himself at the price of ten drachmas.”

And so it happened that they abandoned Wido and chose Odo.

### 17

Wido, greatly disturbed by the embassies of the Franks, began to be troubled by many thoughts: both because he had promised the Italian kingdom to Berengarius by oath and especially because he knew that he could not obtain France.

Amid this conflict of anxiety, since he could not be king of the Franks, he resolved to break the oath he had made to Berengarius. Having gathered an army as best he could—for he had also drawn a certain line of kinship from the Franks—and entering Italy swiftly, he approached the Camerini and Spoletans confidently as relatives. He also won over those favoring Berengarius’s side, making them unfaithful through the lure of money. Thus he prepared for war against Berengarius.

### 18

After forces had been gathered on both sides, they prepared a civil war beside the river Trebia, which lies five miles from Piacenza. When many fell on both sides, Berengarius took flight, and Wido obtained the victory.

### 19

Not long afterward, after a few days had passed, Berengarius gathered a multitude and prepared for war against Wido in the broadest fields of Brescia. When a very great slaughter took place there, Berengarius saved himself by flight.

### 20

Now, since Berengarius was unable to resist Wido because of the smallness of his forces, he appealed for aid to the very powerful King Arnulfus whom we mentioned above [Note: [Col. 0801] “arnulfulfum” in 1, across two lines]. He promised that he and his people would serve Arnulfus’s power if, with the aid of his valor, he overcame Wido and claimed the Italian kingdom for himself.

Summoned by the attraction of so great a promise, King Arnulfus sent his son Centebald, whom he had fathered by a concubine, with a strong army to Berengarius’s aid. They came with all speed to Pavia.

Wido had fortified the little river that washes one side of Pavia, called the Vernavola [Note: [Col. 0801] “uernavolum” in 5a and 5a*], with both stakes and an army, so that, with the river running between them, neither side could attack the other.

### 21

Twenty-one days had already passed during which, as we said, neither side could harm the other. Every day one of the Bavarians taunted the Italian troops, loudly proclaiming them unwarlike and ignorant of horsemanship.

To increase their disgrace, he even charged among them, knocked a spear from the hand of one man, and returned joyfully to his own camp.

Hubaldus, father of Bonifatius, who in our own time later became margrave of Camerino and Spoleto, being eager to avenge so great a disgrace to his people, took up his shield and immediately advanced to meet the Bavarian.

The latter, remembering not only his former triumph but made bolder by it, as though already secure in victory, hurried toward him gladly. He began alternately to release his agile horse with a powerful charge and to draw it back by tightening the reins.

Hubaldus, however, advanced directly toward him. When they were about to strike each other with mutual wounds, the Bavarian, as was his custom, began running about on his nimble horse in various intricate and winding turns, so that by these maneuvers he might deceive Hubaldus.

But while he was turning his back by this stratagem so that he might soon return and strike Hubaldus from the front, the horse on which Hubaldus was mounted was driven hard with the spurs; before the Bavarian could turn back, it pierced him through the shoulders with a lance as far as the heart.

Hubaldus therefore seized the Bavarian’s horse by the bridle, stripped the man, and left him in the middle of the river’s channel. Thus, as avenger of the insult to his people, he returned to his own men more joyful in triumph.

This deed brought no small terror to the Bavarians and boldness to the Italians. After the Bavarians had taken counsel [Note: [Col. 0801] “quipe” in 1], Centebald, having received a considerable weight of silver from Wido, returned to his own country.

### 22

When Berengarius saw that circumstances were turning against him wherever he looked, he approached the power of King Arnulfus together with Centebald, praying and promising that, if Arnulfus helped him, he would subject himself and all Italy to his authority, as he had promised before.

Moved, as we have said, by the attraction of so great a promise, Arnulfus gathered a substantial army and entered Italy (894). To give proof of his promise, Berengarius brought him his shield as a pledge of his good faith.

### 23

Received by the people of Verona, he set out for the city of Bergamo. There, while the inhabitants, trusting—or rather deceived—by the exceptionally strong fortifications of the place refused to come out to meet him, he pitched camp and, by the strength of war, captured the city, slaughtering and massacring its people (January).

He also had the city’s count, Ambrosius by name, hanged before the gate with his sword, belt, armlets, and other most precious garments.

This deed [Note: [Col. 0801D] Compare the *Annales Fuldenses*, year 894.] caused no little terror among all the other cities and all the princes; whoever heard of it had both ears ringing.

### 24

The people of Milan and Pavia, terrified by this report [Note: [Col. 0802D] Compare the same annals, the *Annales Fuldenses*], did not endure awaiting his arrival. Instead, they sent an embassy in advance and promised to obey his command (894).

He sent Otto, the most powerful duke of the Saxons—the grandfather of that most glorious and unconquered King Otto who now survives and reigns happily [Note: [Col. 0803] “hujus” in 1] [Note: [Col. 0803] “ita” in 1 and 2]—to Milan for its defense; he himself proceeded directly toward Pavia.

### 25

Wido, unable to withstand his attack [Note: [Col. 0803] “fere” in 1], began to flee toward Camerino and Spoleto [Note: [Col. 0803] “fuge” in 1]. The king pursued him fiercely without delay, subduing by force every city and castle that resisted him.

Indeed, there was no fortress, even one fortified by nature itself, that attempted to resist his valor. And what wonder was this, when Rome itself, the queen of all cities, could not withstand his attack? (896.)

But when the Romans denied him confidence that he could enter the city, he summoned the soldiers to him and addressed them as follows (April):

### Verse

### 26

Magnanimous nobles, renowned in fortunate war,

whose zeal is to make weapons shine with tawny metal,

Romulids, accustomed to commit their deeds to vain writings,

now take courage; let your fury supply you with weapons!

Pompey is not here, nor that fortunate Julius,

who subdued our fierce ancestors with the sword;

for he led the greatest men of this stock down to Argos [Note: [Col. 0803D] Into Greece, Constantinople],

and the holy British mother brought him into the light [Note: [Col. 0803D] The emperor Constantine the Great, son of the holy British Helena].

Your zeal is to catch fat catfish with twisted

hemp, not to carry gleaming shields in your hands!

[Note: [Col. 0803] This verse is absent in 2.]

### 27

Their courage inflamed by these heroic words, they despise life in their eagerness for glory. Covered in ranks with shields and wickerwork defenses, they hasten to the walls. They had also prepared many instruments of war when, in the midst of the operation, while the people were watching, a little hare, terrified by the shouting, happened to flee toward the city.

When the army followed it with a violent charge, as is customary, the Romans thought that they were being attacked and threw themselves from the wall. Seeing this, the people cast down beside the wall the packsaddles and saddles on which they had been riding and climbed the wall over the heap.

Some of the people immediately took a beam fifty feet long, battered the gate, and captured by force the Rome they call Leonine, in which the precious body of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, rests. The rest of the people who were across the Tiber, compelled by this fear, submitted their necks to his rule.

### 28

At this time Pope Formosus, a most religious man, was being fiercely harassed by the Romans; at his urging, King Arnulfus had also come to Rome.

Upon entering, in order to avenge the pope’s injury, he ordered many Roman nobles who were hastening to meet him to be beheaded.

[Note: [Col. 0803D] What follows was copied in the account of Formosus by the compiler of the history of the Roman pontiffs, published under the false name of Liudprand.]

### 29

The cause of the quarrel between Pope Formosus and the Romans was as follows.

After Formosus’s predecessor had died, a certain Sergius, a deacon of the Roman Church, was present; one faction of the Romans had chosen him as pope. Another faction, not the lesser, eagerly desired to make Formosus, bishop of the city of Porto, pope because of his true religion and knowledge of divine teachings.

For when Sergius was about to be ordained vicar of the apostles, the faction favoring Formosus expelled Sergius from the altar amid considerable tumult and abuse, and made Formosus pope.

### 30

Sergius descended into Tuscany so that he might be aided by Adelbert, the most powerful margrave; and this indeed happened.

For after Formosus had died and Arnulfus had perished in his own country, the man who had been appointed after Formosus’s murder was expelled, and Sergius was made pope through Adelbert.

Once installed, Sergius, as an impious man ignorant of sacred teachings, ordered Formosus to be dragged from his tomb and placed in the Roman pontifical seat dressed in priestly vestments. He then said to him:

“When you were bishop of Porto, why did you usurp the universal Roman see through the spirit of ambition?”

When these proceedings were complete, he ordered him to be stripped of his sacred vestments, to have three fingers cut off, and to be thrown into the Tiber. He also reordained all those whom Formosus himself had ordained, after they had been deposed from their proper rank.

How wrongly he acted in this, most holy father, you will be able to observe from the fact that even those who had received an apostolic greeting or blessing from Judas, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ, before the betrayal were not deprived of it after the betrayal and the hanging of his own body—unless perhaps wicked crimes had defiled them.

For the blessing bestowed by Christ’s ministers is poured out not through the priest who is seen but through the one who is unseen. “Neither he who waters is anything, nor he who plants, but God who gives the growth” (1 Corinthians III, 7).

### 31

We can gather how great the authority and holiness of Pope Formosus were from the following event. When he was later found by fishermen and carried to the church of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, certain images of the saints reverently greeted him while he lay in the coffin.

I have often heard this from highly religious men of the city of Rome. But, leaving this aside, let us return to the order of the narrative.

### 32

King Arnulfus, having attained the fulfillment of his desire, did not cease pursuing Wido [Note: [Col. 0804D] Wido had died before the capture of Rome]. He set out for Camerino and besieged the fortress called Firmum, both by name and by nature, in which Wido’s wife was staying (May) [Note: [Col. 0804D] Today, Fermo].

Wido, meanwhile, hid in uncertain places.

The aforesaid fortress, Firmum by name and by nature, was surrounded by a rampart, and all the instruments of war by which it could be captured were prepared [Note: [Col. 0805] “paratur” in 1].

When Wido’s wife was being pressed by great difficulties on every side and all hope of escape had been denied her, she began, with viperine cunning, to seek means of bringing about the king’s death.

She summoned one of King Arnulfus’s closest associates and, offering him lavish gifts, begged him to help her. He declared that he could do so only if she surrendered the city of her lord to his authority. She repeatedly promised him weights of gold and even handed them over immediately, begging him to make his lord the king drink from a certain cup which she gave him—not to cause the danger of death, but to soothe the harshness of his mind.

To make her words credible, she first made one of her own servants drink this potion in her presence. He stood before her for an hour and then departed in good health.

But let us bring forward the truthful judgment of Maro [Note: [Col. 0805D] *Aeneid* III, 56–57]:

> Accursed hunger for gold, what do you not compel mortal hearts to do?

For he hastily offered the deadly cup to the king. When the king had received it, such a force of sleep immediately seized him that the noise of the entire army could not awaken him for three days.

It is said that, while his attendants disturbed him now with noise, now with touch, he opened his eyes but could neither feel anything nor speak distinctly. Yet, placed in an excess of mind [Note: [Col. 0805D] That is, an ecstasy], he seemed to utter a bellow rather than words.

This affair compelled everyone to turn back rather than fight.

### 33

I believe that King Arnulfus incurred this kind of affliction by the judgment of a strict Judge.

When prosperity made his rule highly esteemed everywhere, he attributed everything to his own valor and did not render due honor to almighty God. Priests of God were dragged away in chains; sacred virgins were violated by force; married women were assaulted. Nor could churches serve as asylums for those fleeing to them.

In these places they held communal banquets, obscene gestures, comic songs, and drunken revelries. Women, too—shameful to say—were publicly prostituted there.

### 34

At last, as King Arnulfus was returning slowly in serious ill health, King Wido pursued him. When Arnulfus climbed Mount Bardonis, he decided, on the advice of his men, to deprive Berengarius of his sight and thus secure Italy for himself.

One of Berengarius’s relatives, who was closely attached to King Arnulfus through a considerable bond of familiarity, learned of this plan and without delay disclosed it to Berengarius.

As soon as Berengarius understood what had happened, he handed the lamp he had been carrying before King Arnulfus to someone else, fled, and hurried to Verona.

### 35

From that time all the Italians began to despise Arnulfus and regard him as worthless. Thus, when he came to Pavia, a considerable sedition arose in the city; so great a slaughter of the army took place there that the city’s crypts, which are otherwise called sewers, were filled with their corpses.

When Arnulfus saw this, since he could not pass through Verona, he decided to return by Hannibal’s road, which they call the Bard [Note: [Col. 0805D] Where today you see the castle of Bard overlooking the road leading from Ivrea to Aosta. But it is clear that Liudprand wrongly assigns to another journey what the *Annales Fuldenses* relate concerning Arnulf’s first return from Italy.], and over Mount Jupiter.

When he reached Ivrea, the margrave Anscarius was there; at his urging the city was rebelling. Arnulfus had sworn, however, that he would never depart from that place until they presented Anscarius to him.

But Anscarius, being a very fearful man, was entirely like the one of whom Maro says [Note: [Col. 0806D] *Aeneid* XI, 638]:

[The supplied text ends here.]

Generous in resources, better in speech, but cold in war—

Dextera left the castle and hid beside the city wall in rocky caverns. He did this so that they could lawfully satisfy King Arnulf by asserting that Anscarius was not in the city. Thus the king accepted this oath and departed by the road he had taken.

### 36. (Year 899, December 8)

Having set out for his own country, he died in the most shameful illness. For he was severely afflicted by tiny worms, called *pedunculi*, and gave up his spirit. It is said that these worms swarmed to such an extent that no medical treatment could diminish them. Whether, for so immense a crime—namely, the unleashing of the Hungarians—he was, according to the prophet, crushed by a double affliction, or whether through this present punishment he obtained pardon in the future (Jer. 17:13), let us leave this to the knowledge of the One of whom the Apostle says:

> “Do not judge before the appointed time, until the Lord comes, who will both bring to light the hidden things of darkness and disclose the purposes of hearts; and then each person will receive praise from God” (1 Cor. 4:5).

### 37. (Year 896)

Thus the just God prepared for Wido’s wife, who had arranged this man’s death, the grief of widowhood. For, as we have said, while King Wido followed the returning Arnulf closely, he died beside the river Taro. When Berengarius heard of his death, he hastened to Pavia and took possession of the kingdom by force.

But Wido’s faithful supporters and partisans, fearing that Berengarius might avenge upon them the injury they had inflicted, and because the Italians always wish to have two lords, so that they may restrain one by fear of the other, made Wido’s deceased son, named Lambert, king. He was an elegant young man, still a youth and exceedingly warlike. At length the people began to approach him and abandon Berengarius.

When Berengarius was unable to oppose Lambert, who was advancing toward Pavia with a great army, because his own forces were too few, he went to Verona and lived there in safety. Not long afterward, however, when King Lambert had proved a stern man, he seemed burdensome to the nobles. Therefore they sent envoys to Verona, asking King Berengarius to come to them and Lambert to be expelled.

### 38

Moreover, Magimfred, an exceedingly wealthy count of the city of Milan, had remained in rebellion against him for five years. He had not merely defended the city in which he was rebellious—namely Milan—but had also devastated excessively the neighboring regions all around that were subject to Lambert.

The king did not allow this deed to go unpunished [Note: Witness 1 reads *multum*, “much,” at this clause.], often turning over in his mind that line of the psalmist [Note: Witness 1 reads *spalmographum*, a transposition for *psalmographum*, “psalmist.”]:

> “When I receive the appointed time, I will judge justly” (Ps. 74:3).

For shortly afterward he ordered him to be condemned by a sentence of death. This affair brought no small terror upon all the Italians.

### 39. (Year 898)

Finally, at this same time, Adelbert, the illustrious margrave of Tuscany, and Ildeprandus, a most powerful count, attempted to rebel against him. Adelbert possessed such great power that, among all the princes of Italy, he alone was called “the Rich” by surname.

He had a wife named Berta, the mother of Hugo, who later became king in our time; at her instigation he himself undertook such unspeakable crimes. For, having gathered an army, he hastened steadily toward Pavia with Count Ildeprandus.

### 40

Meanwhile King Lambert, unaware of these events, was occupied with hunting at Marinca, about forty miles distant from Pavia. When the aforesaid margrave and count crossed Mount Bardon with an immense but ineffective Tuscan army, the king, who was hunting in the middle of a forest, was informed of the situation.

He, being a man steadfast in spirit and powerful in strength, did not wait for his soldiers. Instead, gathering those whom he had with him—about one hundred soldiers—he hastened at full speed to meet them.

### 41

He had already reached Piacenza when it was announced that the others had pitched camp beside the river Sesterione, near the borough in which the body of the most holy and precious martyr of the Lord was honorably preserved and venerated [Note: “Borgo San-Donnino”; the river is today called the Stirone. *Sanctissimi* is repeated in one manuscript].

Not knowing what the coming night would bring, they became drunk and, after some useless tragic performances—that is, songs—gave themselves over to sleep and snoring. Others suffered nausea from excessive drinking.

The king, fierce in spirit and shrewd in intelligence, attacked them in the very silence of the night: he struck those who were sleeping and slaughtered those who were yawning. At last they reached those who were leaders of this army. Since the king himself, rather than anyone representing the multitude, was the bearer of news of this remarkable deed, terror deprived them not only of the ability to fight but even of the ability to flee.

Ildeprandus, however, escaped and abandoned Adelbert, who was hiding inside an animal stall. When Adelbert was discovered and brought before the king, the king immediately addressed him as follows:

> “We believe that your wife Berta prophesied with a Sibylline spirit when she promised that, by her knowledge, she would make you either a king or an ass. But since she did not wish—or, as is more credible, was unable—to make you a king, she made you an ass, so that she would not lie, when she compelled you to retreat with the livestock of Arcadia into a stall!”

In addition, several others were captured with him, bound, brought to Pavia, and handed over to custody.

### 42

After these events, King Lambert again occupied himself with hunting at the aforesaid place, Marinca (October–November), while the decision concerning what should be done with the captives was being deliberated by decree of all the princes.

But if only this hunting had captured wild beasts and not kings! It is commonly said that he fell and broke his neck while pursuing unbridled boars on horseback, as is customary [Note: *effreni*, that is, “unbridled”].

But I will not say that it is unreasonable to give credence to this account. For there is another account of his death, which seems more plausible to me and is related by all peoples.

[Note: Manuscripts 3, 3a, 3b, and the others transmit what follows, up to “he broke his neck,” in this form:]

> “But since, according to blessed Job’s judgment, his appointed end could not be passed over, he fulfilled the Lord’s saying, ‘A man’s enemies are those of his own household’ (Mic. 7:6). King Lambert had made a certain Magimfrid his privy counsellor: this was the son of that powerful Magimfrid, count of Milan, whom, as we said shortly above, royal command had caused to be executed for rebellion. The king endowed the son with fatherly benefits and admitted him to great intimacy, both because of his steadfast fidelity and because he had forgotten his father’s death. [Witness 3 reads *ad secretum*, ‘into secrecy/private counsel,’ for *a secretis*, ‘as a privy counsellor.’] The king ordered him to accompany him to the aforesaid place for hunting—if it can be called hunting when the king, rather than the boar, is captured. While the other hunters pursued the boar through the middle of the forest, it happened that the tracking of the beast’s winding course should have separated the king and his guard Magimfrid at the branching paths. [Witness 3 reads *undago* for *indago*, ‘tracking.’]

> “While the king, wearied by excessive waiting at this guard, entrusted the watch to Magimfrid’s sight and gave himself over to rest, Magimfrid—forgetful not of his father’s death but of all the benefits the king had conferred upon him—soon took a substantial piece of wood and, with an atrocious blow, broke the neck of the sleeping hero.”

Magimfred, count of the city of Milan, whom we mentioned shortly above, when he was condemned to death for the crime committed against the commonwealth and against the king, left behind his only heir, his son Hugo. When King Lambert saw that this young man was not only exceptionally handsome but surpassed many in courage, he sought to soothe his considerable grief over his father’s death by conferring many benefits upon him. Thus he granted him the privilege of intimacy above all others.

It happened that, while King Lambert was hunting at the aforementioned place, Marinca—for it is a grove of extraordinary size and beauty, especially suitable for hunting [Note: One manuscript reads *ueneraretur* (“he venerated”) instead of *venaretur* (“he hunted”)]—and while everyone was running here and there, as is customary, the king remained in the forest alone with Hugo.

As the king waited for a boar to pass and grew weary from the long delay, he gave himself over for a short time to rest, entrusting the watch to this faithless man as though he were faithful. With everyone else absent, Hugo’s mind—rather, the mind of a traitor and executioner—forgot the many benefits bestowed upon him and began to turn over his father’s death.

He did not consider that his father had suffered a just death. He did not fear violating the oath he had sworn to the king. He was not ashamed to be called a substitute for Judas, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ. And, what is more serious, he did not fear that he would suffer eternal punishment. Instead, with all his strength, he broke the sleeping hero’s neck with a substantial piece of wood.

He was afraid to strike him with a sword, lest the obvious evidence of the crime should prove him to be its author [Note: After “With a sword … let it come into public view,” the words are absent from the manuscripts]. His perverse mind therefore arranged matters so that, when those who found the body saw not the mark of a sword but the evident impact of wood, they would believe that the man had fallen from his horse and died from the breaking of his neck.

The affair remained hidden for many years. But as time passed, when King Berengarius ruled the kingdom manfully, with no one resisting him, Hugo himself, as the perpetrator of his own guilt, became its betrayer. He fulfilled what the king and prophet sings [Note: One manuscript reads *impletque* (“and he fulfills”) for *implevitque* (“and he fulfilled”)]: “For the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the one who acts wickedly is blessed” (Ps. 10:3).

Nor could he avoid fulfilling the other words of Truth:

> “Nothing is covered that will not be revealed, nor hidden that will not come to light” (Matt. 10:26).

### 43

After these events, King Berengarius was honored with greater royal dignity than before; Margrave Adelbert and the others were sent back to their own lands.

### 44

It is fitting, dearest father, both to write while mourning and to mourn while writing the death of so great a king. He possessed an honorable integrity of character, a holy and awe-inspiring severity; and while splendid youth adorned his body, a holy old age of mind dignified him.

In truth, he himself bestowed more distinction upon the commonwealth than the commonwealth bestowed upon him. If swift death had not carried him away, he would have been the man who, after the power of the Romans, would have bravely subjugated the whole world to himself.

**THE FIRST BOOK ENDS.**

[Column 0812D]

## THE SECOND BOOK BEGINS

[Column 0811]

### 1. (Year 900, January 21)

After the vital heat left the limbs of King Arnulf and rendered his body lifeless, his own son Hulodoicus was appointed king by all the people. The news of the fall of so great a man could not remain hidden from his neighboring Hungarians, any more than from those living throughout the world. Indeed, the day of his death was more joyful to them than any festival and more precious than all treasures. What, then—

### 2

In the first year of this man’s death and of his son’s accession, the Hungarians gathered a very large army and claimed for themselves the people of the Moravians, whom King Arnulf had subdued with the aid of their strength. They also occupied the borders of the Bavarians, destroyed fortresses, consumed churches by fire, slaughtered the people, and, in order to make themselves feared more and more, drank themselves full of the blood of those they had killed.

### 3. (Year 910)

King Hulodoicus, understanding the devastation of his people and this cruelty, inflamed the courage of all his men with such fear that, if anyone happened to be absent from that battle which he was about to wage against them, he would undoubtedly end his life by hanging.

That innumerable and most wicked multitude of that people hastened to meet his immense forces. You would not see a thirsty soul drink the water of a cool stream more eagerly than this cruel people desired the day of battle; for nothing pleased them except to fight.

As I learned from the book entitled *On the Origin of This People* [Note: Jordanes, chapter 24], as soon as their mothers gave birth to their children, they cut their faces with a very sharp iron [Note: One manuscript reads *accutissimo*], so that, before they received the nourishment of milk, they would be forced to undergo the endurance of wounds. The wounds inflicted upon the living bodies of their relatives because of grief for the dying bear witness to this claim.

They shed blood—*ἄθεοι καὶ ἀσεβοῖς ἄντι τῶν δακρείων*, *athei ke asevis anti ton dacrion*, that is, “godless and impious instead of tears” [Note: The manuscript’s lineation produces the reading *Sanguinem neque*: the scribe began *Sanguinem* on the preceding line but, lacking space, carried its final syllables into the next].

King Hulodoicus had now arrived at Augusta with his gathered host. This is a city on the frontier of the Suevi, Bavarians, or eastern Franks, when the unexpected—indeed, more unwelcome—proximity of this people was announced. On the following day the two armies met beside the fields of the river Lemannus [Note: That is, the Licus], which by their spaciousness were suitable for military action.

### 4

Before Dawn left the saffron bedchamber of Tithonus (Virgil, *Georgics* 1.447), the Hungarian people, thirsty for slaughter and eager for war, fell upon the Christians while they were still yawning [Note: In manuscript 1, the passage from *alios* (“others”) through *exitarunt* (“roused”) was first omitted at the foot of the page and then written after *remugit*, with a reference sign; disregarding that sign, manuscripts 5, 5a, and 5a* wrongly place it there]. Some, indeed, were struck by missiles before they awoke at the shouts; others, pierced in their beds, were roused by neither noise nor wounds—for their spirit departed sooner than their sleep. A grievous battle consequently arose on both sides; and, turning their backs as though in flight, the Turks shot their *boelae*, that is, arrows, fiercely and struck down very many.

**Verses**

> When venerable almighty Elohim begins  
> To hide the lights of golden-haired Phoebus in dark clouds,  
> And when heaven roars at its highest summit with a mighty clang,  
> Frequent fiery flashes fly, sent down from the Thunderer’s throne;  
> Then those who turn black things white tremble,  
> And their hearts, conscious of their crimes, fear to be furrowed,  
> Destined alike to fall beneath a wound from above:—

> No differently, shaken from empty quivers, the arrows fly;  
> By them the backs of strong corselets are split.  
> As proud hail itself, rushing down, batters the crops,  
> A din arises,  
> And a resounding clash echoes through the roofs.  
> Thus helmets struck by drawn swords ring out;  
> Thus bodies fall, pierced by arrows from both sides.

[Note: Manuscript 1 has *vulno* for *vulnero*; 3e* has *vulnero*; 5 and 5a* have a lacuna; 5a* reads *judicio* (“by judgment”); Hervagius reads *et*. Manuscript 3 has *quis terga*; 5 and 5a leave *quis terga* blank; 5a* reads *scolades galeaeque* (“… and helmets”); Hervagius has *queis tergo*.]

The sun, descending, had already occupied its seventh hour, and Mars still favored Hulodoicus’ side, when the Turks, being not without cunning, pretended to flee after placing an ambush opposite. While the king’s people, ignorant of the trick, pursued them with the greatest force, the ambushes emerged from every side, and the men who seemed defeated themselves killed the victors.

The king himself was amazed to find that he had been defeated after being victorious, and an unexpected and more grievous disaster befell him. You would have seen woods and fields strewn everywhere with corpses, and streams and rivers reddened by mingled blood. Then the neighing of horses and the blaring of trumpets terrified the fugitives again and again, while encouraging the pursuers more and more.

### 5

Moreover, once the Hungarians had obtained what they wanted [Note: Some manuscripts read “having obtained their wish”], they were not satisfied with their own wickedness by this immense slaughter of Christians. Rather, to satisfy the rage of their treachery, they passed through all the kingdoms of the Bavarians, Suevi, Franks, and Saxons, setting them ablaze.

There was no one who could withstand their arrival except in places fortified either by no small labor or by nature; and for several years certain peoples became tributary to this people.

### 6

At this time a certain Adelbert—not an ordinary man, but that great hero—was practicing considerable hostility against the commonwealth in a castle called Bavemberg (year 906). King Hulodoicus often gathered everyone and attacked him.

The aforesaid hero did not prepare for battle beside the castle, as most people usually do, but far from the fortification. Before the king’s soldiers had actually had the opportunity to marvel at his audacity, they planned, going ahead of the king as a preliminary to the battle, to lure him outside the castle and kill him.

Adelbert was not only aware of this preliminary maneuver but also intoxicated; he had advanced so far to meet them outside the castle that the soldiers did not recognize him as one of their opponents until his sword, eager for slaughter, raged upon their necks.

Thus, when Adelbert had practiced this rebellion for nearly seven years, Hulodoicus, knowing that he could overcome the hero’s strength and audacity only by some stratagem, consulted Hatto, archbishop of the see of Mainz, about what should be done.

Hatto, being skilled in cunning, said:

> “Stop worrying. I will free you from these anxieties. I will arrange for him to come to you; you take care that he does not return.”

Hatto, therefore, encouraged by the confidence of spirit with which he had turned certain misfortunes into successes, went to Bavemberg as though he intended to share Adelbert’s troubles. He said to him:

> “Even if you thought that you had no life beyond the present one, you would still be acting unjustly by rebelling against your lord, especially since you are doing what you do without cause. You do not understand how greatly you are loved by everyone, especially by the king, because of the fierceness of spirit by which you allow yourself to be overcome. Therefore accept the faith of one who gives you counsel. Accept an oath by which you may leave the castle and return without any hesitation of mind. If you do not trust the promises of my priesthood, at least do not distrust my oath: just as I shall lead you safely and unharmed out of this castle, so I shall arrange to bring you back.”

Adelbert, therefore, drenched—or rather deceived—by speeches sweeter than honey, accepted an oath from Hatto and immediately invited him to dine with him.

Hatto, mindful of the evasion he had soon begun to practice, absolutely refused to dine with him. Without delay, Hatto left the castle. Adelbert took him by the right hand and immediately followed him.

When Hatto saw him outside the castle, he said:

> “I regret, excellent hero, that, following your advice—especially since a very long journey lies ahead—I did not refresh your body with some food.”

Adelbert, unaware of how much harm and misfortune this statement contained, replied:

> “Let us return, my lord, and, lest the body waste away through the hardship of fasting, refresh it at least a little with food.”

Hatto, therefore, yielding to his requests, turned back by the route through which he had led him out [Note: Some manuscripts read “by the road”], and returned while holding his right hand.

Without delay food was taken, and on that same day they hastened together to the king. A cry arose in the camp, and considerable tumult followed, because it was announced that Adelbert had arrived before the king [Note: That is, “had come to the king”].

The king, greatly delighted at his arrival, ordered the nobles to come to him and sit in judgment. He said to them:

> “For nearly seven years we have learned in reality, rather than through rumor, what slaughter Adelbert has inflicted, what disturbances he has caused us, and how many disasters of robbery and burning he has brought upon us. Therefore we await your judgment concerning what compensation he should now receive for this most remarkable crime.”

By the decision of all, in accordance with the institutions of the ancient kings, he was adjudged guilty of treason and beheaded.

But while he was being dragged away in chains to his death, he looked at Hatto and said:

> “You will be guilty of perjury if you allow me to suffer death.”

Hatto replied:

> “I promised to lead you safely out of the castle and likewise to bring you back. I understood that I had fulfilled this promise when, after leading you out of the castle, I brought you back safe and unharmed—indeed, very quickly—into the castle.”

Then, grieving that he had come there and sighing because he had understood Hatto’s deceit too late, Adelbert followed the executioner so unwillingly that he would have lived gladly if he had been permitted to do so.

### 7

After a few years had passed, when no one resisted the Hungarians in the eastern or southern region—for they had made the Bulgarians and Greeks tributary to them—they strove to see the nations dwelling under the southern and western skies, so that nothing might remain untested by them.

Having gathered an immense and innumerable army, they came to wretched Italy. After pitching their little tents—or rather their blankets—beside the river Brenta, and sending scouts for three days to examine the character of the land and the size or smallness of the population, they received the following report when the messengers returned:

> “This plain is full of numerous inhabitants; on one side, as you see, it is bounded by exceedingly rugged and fertile mountains, and on the other by the Adriatic Sea. Its towns are numerous and very strongly fortified. Although the weakness or strength of the people is unknown, an immense multitude is nevertheless visible. We do not advise attacking it with so few forces.

> “Yet since there are several things compelling us to fight—our accustomed triumph, courage of spirit, knowledge of warfare, and especially the wealth whose possession we desire, of which there is as much here as we have neither seen nor hoped to see in the whole world—we advise that we return. The journey back is neither long nor difficult and can be completed in ten days or fewer. Then, when spring comes, we shall return after assembling all the bravest men of our people, so that these people may fear us both for our courage and for the size of our numbers.”

### 8

As soon as they heard this, they returned to their own country and spent the whole severity of winter making weapons, sharpening arrows, and teaching the young the knowledge of war.

### 9

The sun had not yet left Pisces and occupied Aries when they came to Italy with an immense and innumerable army (year 899). They passed through the extremely well-fortified cities of Aquileia and Verona and came to Ticinum, now distinguished by the more eminent name of Pavia, without anyone resisting them.

King Berengarius could not sufficiently marvel at this remarkable and unprecedented deed—for he had never before even heard the name of this people. He therefore ordered some Italians, Tuscans, Volscians, Camerinans, and Spoletans to come by written summons and others by messengers; all were nevertheless commanded to assemble as one. An army was formed three times as strong as the Hungarians’.

### 10

When King Berengarius saw that so many forces were present, inflated with the spirit of arrogance and attributing victory over the enemy’s multitude more to his own army than to God, he alone, with a few men, remained in a certain small town and devoted himself to pleasure.

What then? As soon as the Hungarians saw such a multitude, they were dismayed and could not decide what to do. They were utterly afraid to fight and entirely unable to flee. Yet amid this conflict of mind they preferred flight to battle; and, while the Christians pursued them, they crossed the river Adda by swimming, so that in their excessive haste many were drowned.

### 11

The Hungarians, having adopted no bad counsel, asked the Christians through intermediaries to allow them to return unharmed after restoring all the booty with its profit. The Christians utterly rejected this request and, alas, mocked them, seeking rather the chains in which the Hungarians would be bound than the weapons by which they would be killed.

When the pagans could not soften the Christians’ minds in this way, they sought to free themselves by flight, judging their former plan better, and thus, fleeing, reached the broad plains of Verona.

### 12

The foremost Christians now pursued the hindmost Hungarians, and a preliminary engagement took place in which the pagans prevailed. When the stronger army approached, however, they continued along the route they had begun, without forgetting their flight.

### 13

The worshipers of Christ and the idolaters came together beside the river Brenta; for their excessively exhausted horses denied the Hungarians the opportunity to flee [Notes: *fluium* (“river”) appears in one manuscript; *defetigati* (“exhausted”) is repeatedly written in that form; one manuscript has *necabant* (“were killing”) for *negabant* (“were denying”)].

The two armies therefore met, separated only by the bed of the river just mentioned. Compelled by extreme fear, the Hungarians promised to surrender all their equipment, the captives, all their arms, and their horses, retaining only one horse apiece on which they might return. They added this to lend weight to their request: if, after giving up everything, the Christians would permit them to return with life alone, they promised never again to enter Italy and offered their sons as hostages.

But alas! The Christians, deceived by the swelling of pride, pursued the pagans with threats as though they were already defeated, and immediately sent them this *ἀπολογείαν* (*apologeian*), that is, reply:

> “If we were to receive a gift from those who have opposed us—especially from those who have opposed us and are now dead dogs—and enter into some treaty with them—”

> “An insane Orestes would swear that the sane were mad!”

### 14

Thus, driven to desperation by this embassy, the Hungarians gathered their bravest men together and consoled one another with the following speech:

> “If, once the daylight now before our eyes has been lost, nothing worse can befall human beings, and since there is no place of refuge and every hope of flight has been taken away, while to submit our necks is to die, what have we to fear in rushing amid the weapons themselves and inflicting death by death? Is our misfortune not to be attributed to fortune rather than to weakness? To fall while fighting bravely is not to die but to live.

> “Let us leave to our heirs this great fame, this *κλιρονομείαν* (*clironomian*), that is, inheritance, which we received from our fathers. We ought to trust ourselves—at least trust ourselves who have been tested—for we have sometimes struck down very many despite the smallness of our forces.

> “Certainly a very large gathering of an ineffective populace is exposed only to slaughter. Moreover, Mars very often destroys the fleeing man but protects the one who fights bravely. Those who show no pity to us in our supplication do not know or understand that victory is indeed good, but overwhelming victory is exceedingly hateful.”

15. Thus, somewhat restored in spirit by this exhortation, they set ambushes in three divisions. Crossing the river directly, they rush into the midst of the enemy. For many of the Christians, exhausted by their long wait for the messengers, had gone down through the camp to refresh themselves with food; the Hungarians stabbed them with such speed that they pierced some in the throat while they were eating, while from others they took their horses and denied them the possibility of flight. They killed them all the more easily because they saw that they were without horses. Finally, to increase the Christians’ destruction, there was considerable discord among them. Some Hungarians not only offered no battle, but eagerly desired that those nearest to them should fall; and, perverse themselves, they had perversely acted for this purpose, so that, when those nearby had fallen, they alone might rule, as it were, more freely. Those who neglect to aid their neighbors in distress and delight in their death bring death upon themselves. Thus the Christians flee, and the pagans rage; and those who earlier could not, despite their supplications, obtain mercy through gifts, afterward did not know how to spare those who supplicated [Note: [Col. 0817] *pascere* (“to feed”) in witness 1.]. [Col. 0818D] After the Christians had been killed or put to flight, the Hungarians traversed every region of the kingdom, raging throughout it. There was no one who dared await their presence except perhaps in the most strongly fortified places. Their strength had indeed prevailed to such an extent that one division of them laid waste to Bavaria, Swabia, Francia, and Saxony, while another devastated Italy.

16. For their strength had not earned this result, but the true word of the Lord—more enduring than earth and heaven—could not be changed. Thus, through the prophet Jeremiah, he threatens all nations in the person of the house of Israel, saying:

> “Behold, I shall bring upon you a nation from afar, a strong nation, an ancient nation, a nation whose language you will not know, nor understand what it says. Its quiver is like an open tomb; all are mighty; and it shall eat your crops and devour your bread; it shall eat your sons and your daughters, it shall eat your flocks and your herds, your vineyard and your fig tree; and it shall crush with the sword your fortified cities in which you place your trust.
