Nevertheless, in those days, says the Lord God, I shall not make an end of you.” (Jer. V, 15–17)

[Col. 0819B] 17. In this same period King Louis died (A.D. 911, November 8). Conrad, of Frankish descent, an energetic man and trained through the practice of war [Note: [Col. 0819] *exersitio* in witness 1.], was appointed king by all the peoples.

18. Under him there were the most powerful princes: Arnold in Bavaria, Burchard in Swabia, the exceedingly powerful count Everard in Francia, and Duke Giselbert in Lotharingia. Among them Heinrich, the mighty duke of the Saxons and Thuringians, stood out.

19. In the second year, therefore, of his accession to this kingdom (913), the aforementioned princes, especially Heinrich, rebelled against him. King Conrad overcame them both by the force of his wisdom and by the strength of his courage, and brought them to loyalty. Arnold, however, compelled by excessive fear of him, fled with his wife and sons to the Hungarians (A.D. 917), and remained there as long as the vital breath of King Conrad governed his limbs.

20. Finally, in the seventh year of his reign, he recognized that the time of his calling to God had come (A.D. 918, December 23) [Note: [Col. 0819D] Cf. the continuation of Regino, s.a. 919, where several things are very similar, though not identical—for example, that he sent him the scepter, crown, and other ornaments of royal dignity [Col. 0820D].]. Having summoned the aforementioned princes to come to him, with Heinrich alone absent, he reached this agreement with them:

> “As you see, the time of my calling from corruption to incorruption and from mortality to immortality is at hand. Therefore I earnestly urge you to pursue peace and concord. When I, a man, depart, let no desire to rule, no ambition to preside, inflame you. Choose Heinrich, the most prudent duke of the Saxons and Thuringians, as king; appoint him as lord. For he is strong in knowledge and rich in the judgment of righteous severity.”

After these words had been spoken [Col. 0819D], he ordered his own crown—adorned, indeed weighed down, not with gold, by which princes of almost every rank are distinguished, but with the most precious gems—as well as his scepter and all the royal garments, to be brought forth. Then he uttered words such as these:

> “I appoint Heinrich heir and representative of royal dignity through these royal ornaments. I do not merely advise you to obey him; I beg you to do so.”

Death followed this command, and obedience soon followed death. For when he had died, the aforementioned princes presented the crown and all the royal garments to Duke Heinrich and, just as King Conrad had said, related everything in due order. Heinrich, who had first humbly declined the height of royal dignity, soon afterward accepted it without ambition. Yet if pale death—which strikes the huts of the poor and the towers of kings with an equal foot [Note: [Col. 0820D] Horace, *Odes* I, 4, 13.]—had not carried off King Conrad so swiftly, he would have been a man whose name ruled over many nations of the world.

21. At this same time Arnold, returning from Hungary with his wife and sons, was honorably received by the Bavarians and by the Eastern Franks. Nor was he merely received: they strongly urged him to become king. [Col. 0820B] When King Heinrich saw that all his subjects obeyed his commands, while Arnold alone resisted, he assembled a very powerful army and marched toward Bavaria. When Arnold heard this, he did not allow Heinrich to await his arrival in Bavaria; instead, gathering whatever forces he could, he hastened to meet him [Note: [Col. 0819] *ouiam* in witness 1.]. He himself had indeed desired to become king. When they were about to begin the war together, the wise and God-fearing King Heinrich, considering that irreparable harm could arise on both sides, sent word to Arnold [Note: [Col. 0819] *arnaldaldo* in witness 1.] that he wished to speak with him alone. Arnold therefore, thinking that Heinrich was summoning him to single combat, arrived alone at the appointed place at the appointed hour.

22. As he hurried to meet him, King Heinrich addressed him in these words:

> Why, with a mad mind, do you resist the Lord’s commands?  
>   
> You should know that the people desire me to be king,  
> By the power of Christ, through which the fabric of the world stands;  
> Tartarus fears him, Phlegethon has feared him;  
> He crushes shining kings, once long ago dreadful,  
> And, when he wills, the lofty, long-feared kings; here he raises the wretched,  
> So that through the ages they may render the Lord his deserved praises.  
>   
> Do you, proud man, guilty, treacherous, harsh, savage,  
> Touched by the goads of envy and savage desire,  
> Thirst greatly to destroy the bodies of Christ’s worshipers?  
> If the people desired to place you first as king,  
> I would at once be the one who desired this most [Note: [Col. 0819] *oc* in witness 1.].

By this fourfold manner of speaking—copious, brief, plain, and ornate—King Heinrich, wise in spirit as he was, soothed Arnold’s mind and returned to his own men.

23. When Arnold had reported all this to his followers, he heard from them the following *ἀπόκρισις*, *apocrisin*, that is, “response”:

> “Who can doubt the judgment of that wise man—or rather of true Wisdom—which says: ‘Through me kings reign, princes command, and the wise decree justice’ (Prov. VIII, 15), or that of the Apostle who says [Note: [Col. 0819] *dicentes* (“saying,” plural) in witness 1.] that every ordinance is from God, and that whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance (Rom. XIII)? For there could not be one mind in the election of the whole people unless he had first been chosen, before the foundation of the world, by the supreme Trinity, which is one God. If he is good, he must be loved and God praised in him; but if he is evil, he must be endured with equanimity. For the merits of subjects often require that they be oppressed, rather than governed, by their rulers. It seems fair and just to us that, without dissenting from the others, you should choose him as king, and that he should in turn choose you, so as by this arrangement to bless so fortunate and wealthy a man and soothe the fury of your spirit, granting you what your predecessors did not possess: namely, that all the bishops of Bavaria should then be subject to your authority and under your power, so that, when one has died, you may appoint another.”

Arnold, therefore, consenting to this excellent and good counsel of his men, became a soldier of King Heinrich; and, as has already been said, he was honored by him through the bishops of all Bavaria being granted to his authority.

24. At the same time, when the Hungarians heard of the death of King Conrad and Heinrich’s succession to the kingdom (A.D. 919), they addressed one another in these words [Note: [Col. 0821] *adgressci* in witness 1.]:

> “Perhaps the new king wishes to use new laws. Let us therefore assemble a considerable force, go up, and investigate whether King Heinrich wishes to pay the tribute that is owed. If, as we believe, he differs from the other kings in this, let his kingdom be devastated by slaughter and immense fires. Let us first occupy not the lands of the Bavarians but those of the Saxons, where the king himself is, so that, if he should wish—which we do not expect—to gather an army, he may not be able to meet us in time from Lotharingia, Francia, Swabia, or Bavaria. The land of the Saxons and Thuringians is also easily devastated, since it is protected neither by mountains nor by very strong towns.”

25. King Heinrich was confined by a very serious illness (A.D. 933), and the Hungarians’ arrival was announced to him as imminent. He had scarcely heard the messenger’s words to the end [Note: [Col. 0821] *nuntiatis* in witness 1.] when he sent messengers throughout Saxony and, after four days, ordered as many men as possible to come to him under penalty of death. Thus, after assembling a very powerful army within four days—this is a praiseworthy and imitable custom of the Saxons, so that no soldier may be absent from war after one year and twelve months—although weak in bodily strength, he was animated by vigor of mind, mounted his horse as best he could, gathered his forces together, and aroused them to the fury of battle with these words [Note: [Col. 0821D] i.e. *excitavit*, “he aroused.”]:

26. Noble Saxon people, like a growling lion,  
Once you were a nation in countless wars.  
You resisted Charles with bloodied sword,  
Who had laid the whole world low for himself [Note: [Col. 0821] the following words through *civitas est* are lacking in chapter 40 of three manuscripts; no lacuna is indicated.];  
Defeated, he fled—victor everywhere—  
When he returned and subjected us all to himself [Note: [Col. 0821] *Subdidit* in witness 1.].  
The mercy of the Lord accomplished this, because  
He wished us to share in salvation.  
Now the evil nation of the Turks, ignorant of Christ,  
Hostile to God,  
Rejoices to bring the sword against all the people of the Church.  
Alas, heroes! Ah, how greatly they now  
Desire to subject our necks to tribute!  
Now take courage in manly fashion!  
I beseech you to cut their limbs and strike with force!  
Let there be, ah, a burning fury, a holy desire;  
Let these gifts carry them back to the Stygian waters [Note: [Col. 0821] *stigia stigias* in five witnesses, with the notation “5 a 5 a.”],  
And let them count their warm coins in the fire!

[Col. 0822B] 27. When the king saw that the spirits of his men had been inflamed to battle by such exhortations, he ordered everyone to be silent and, touched once more by the gift of the divine breath, added the following:

> “The deeds of ancient kings and the writings of the holy Fathers indicate to us what we ought to do. For it is not difficult for God to strike down the many through the few, provided that the faith of those who wish to do this deserves it—faith, I say, not merely of profession but of action, not only of the mouth but also of the heart. Let us therefore make vows and, according to the Psalmist, fulfill our vows—I, I say, first, since I appear to be first in dignity and rank. Let the simoniacal heresy, hateful to God and condemned by the most blessed prince of the apostles, Peter, which our predecessors have rashly maintained until now, be expelled from our kingdom in every way. Let the love of unity bind together those whom the devil’s cunning has divided.”

28. The king wished to say some things similar to these when a swift messenger announced that the Hungarians were at Merseburg, a fortress on the borders of the Saxons, Thuringians [Note: [Col. 0821] *turingionum* in witness 1.], and Slavs. He also added that they had taken a considerable number of children and women as booty, while they had inflicted an immense slaughter upon the men; for they had agreed that from the age of ten onward they would leave no one alive, so that by this means they might inspire the Saxons with no small terror. The king, therefore, steadfast in spirit, was not frightened by such reports; rather, he encouraged them more and more to fight for their homeland and to fall honorably.

[Col. 0822D] 29. Meanwhile, the Hungarians ask whether they are to be attacked. When these men testified that it could not be otherwise, they selected scouts [Note: [Col. 0821] *ita* in witness 1, that is, either *dilectis* or *directis*] and sent them to discover whether this could be true. The scouts set out and saw King Heinrich with an immense army beside the aforementioned town of Merseburg. Finally, they could scarcely return to their own men to announce the army’s arrival; for there was no other messenger of war for them—the king himself was that messenger.

30. Without delay, the battle began. From the Christian side a holy and wondrous cry, *Κύριε ἐλέησον*, *kyrie eleison*, “Lord, have mercy,” was frequently heard; from the other side, the shameful and diabolical cry “Hui, hui.”

31. Before the battle began, King Heinrich had given his men this wise and salutary advice:

> “When you begin to hurry toward the prelude to Mars’ game [Note: [Col. 0823] *proludium* in five witnesses; “5 a, 5 a*.”], let no one attempt to pass ahead of his companion on a faster horse, however swift it may be. Rather, shielded on both sides by your shields, receive the first blows of their arrows upon your shields; then rush upon them at a rapid pace and with the greatest force, so that they cannot shoot a second volley at you before they feel the wounds inflicted by your weapons [Note: [Col. 0823] *impetuque* in witness 1.].”

The Saxons, therefore, not forgetful of this most salutary admonition, advanced in an evenly ordered line, and no one passed a slower rider on a faster horse. Rather, covered on both sides by their shields, as the king had commanded, they received the harmless blows of the arrows upon their shields. Then, as the most prudent man had said, they came upon the enemy at a headlong gallop, so that the life of the Hungarians fled first with groaning, before they could launch a second volley of missiles. By the mercy of the divine gift, it came about that they were more inclined to flee than to fight. Then the swift horse is complained of as slow [Note: [Col. 0823] That is, “is called”; the rider of the swift horse complains of it as though it were slow. The author uses *queritur* passively.]. The adornment of the trappings and the splendor of their arms were not a protection to the Hungarians but a burden. For, throwing away their bows, abandoning their javelins, and casting aside even their trappings so that their horses might run more freely, they devoted themselves solely to flight. But almighty God, who had taken away their courage to fight, entirely denied them the opportunity to flee. After the Hungarians had been killed and put to flight, an immense multitude of captives was dispersed, and the cry of groaning was changed into a song of joy. This triumph, worthy both of praise and remembrance, King Heinrich ordered to be recorded at Merseburg in the upper room of a house by means of a *ζωγραφεία*, *zographia*, that is, a painting, so that you might see the event as more true than merely probable.

32. While these things were happening, almost all the Italians sent messengers to invite a certain Louis, born of Burgundian blood, to come to them, take the kingdom from Berengar, and secure it for himself [Note: [Col. 0823] *adueniad*, corrected to *adueniat*, in witness 1.].

[Col. 0823D] 33. The author of this shameful crime was Adelbert, margrave of the city of Ivrea, to whom that same Berengar had joined his daughter, Gisla, in marriage [Note: [Col. 0823] *conjungio cupularat* in witness 1.]. By her he had fathered a son, to whom he had given his grandfather’s name. This, I say, is that Berengar whose immense tyranny now makes all Italy mourn, and through whose enticement it is destroyed, rather than aided, by whatever peoples attack it. But, to return to the matter, it is enough for now to have said this much.

34. Moreover, that same Adelbert, whose character should be a warning to all good men, was of the most wicked disposition [Note: [Col. 0823] In an erasure: “... he was of a similar disposition” in witness 2; “so that no one was similar in appearance” in witness 5; “he was of the most wicked envy” in witness 5a; “he was by no means like himself” in witness 5a*.]. For while, in the heat of his blood, he led a youthful life, he was a man of remarkable humanity and remarkable holiness [Note: [Col. 0823] *mireque* in witness 1.]. Indeed, if a poor man met him as he returned from hunting, and the poor man lacked something else that Adelbert could not provide, Adelbert would immediately give him the horn that hung from his neck by golden clasps, and afterward purchase it back from him for whatever it was valued at.

Later, however, he became a man of such terrible reputation that the following true song about him was sung by old and young alike. Since it sounds better, let us say it in Greek:

> **Αδελβέρτος κόμις κουρτὴς, μακροσπάθης, γουνδόπιστις**  
> “Adelbertos, short-haired, long-sworded, a man of little faith” [Note: [Col. 0823] *Αδεβερτος* in witness 1.].

This means and says that he used a long sword [Note: [Col. 0823] *eo* (“with it”) in witness 1.] and possessed very little fidelity.

35. At the urging, finally, of this man and several other Italians, the aforementioned Louis came into Italy. As soon as Berengar learned of it, he marched to meet him. When Louis saw that large forces were present with Berengar, who was coming against him, while his own forces were small, fear compelled him to promise Berengar under oath that, if he released him then, he would not come into Italy again, even if summoned by promises of various kinds. For through the presentation of many gifts Berengar had made Adelbert, the most powerful margrave of Tuscany, [Col. 0824C] very loyal to him; and for this reason Louis was expelled so easily.

36. After a short interval of time had passed, King Berengar found the aforementioned Adelbert burdensome. His wife Berta, the mother of King Hugh, who ruled in Italy in our own time, provided no small encouragement for this. It therefore happened that, after consulting the same Margrave Adelbert, the other Italian princes sent for that same Louis, inviting him to come. In his desire to rule, he forgot his oath and hastened into Italy.

37. When Berengar saw that Louis was being received by the princes both of Italy and of Tuscany, he set out for Verona. Louis, however, did not cease pursuing him with the Italians; he even expelled him from Verona [Col. 0824D] [Note: [Col. 0823] *veronam* corrected to *verona* in witness 1.] and bravely subjected the entire kingdom to himself.

38. When these events had taken place, Louis thought it a good idea that, just as he saw Italy all around, he should also see Tuscany [Note: [Col. 0823] Perhaps *viderat*, “he had seen.”]. Finally leaving Pavia, he set out for Lucca [Note: [Col. 0825A] *proficitur* in witness 1.], where Adelbert received him suitably and with marvelous display.

39. When Louis saw that an elegant force of so many soldiers was present in Adelbert’s house and observed such dignity and such great expenditure [Note: [Col. 0825] *inpenses* in witness 1.], touched by the zeal of envy he began to say secretly to his own men [Note: [Col. 0825D] That is, *clanculum*, “secretly”]:

> “This man could be called a king rather than a margrave; indeed, he is inferior to me in nothing except in name.”

This remark could not remain hidden from Adelbert. When Berta, being a woman of no little shrewdness, heard it, she not only removed her husband from Louis’s allegiance but also made the other princes of Italy disloyal to him. Thus it happened that, while returning from Tuscany and proceeding toward Verona (A.D. 905), he stayed there without hesitation and suspecting no evil, while Berengar, having paid a price, corrupted the city’s guards [Col. 0825B] and, gathering the strongest men, entered the city in the deepest silence of night (July).

40. The river Athesis runs through the middle of Verona, just as the Tiber runs through Rome. A great marble bridge of marvelous workmanship and extraordinary size has been built over it. On the left bank of the river, which lies toward the north, the city is fortified by a steep and difficult hill, so that even if the part of the city washed by the aforementioned river on the right were captured by the enemy, it could still be defended bravely. At the summit of this hill stands a church of precious workmanship, consecrated in honor of the most blessed Peter, prince of the apostles; because of the church’s pleasant setting and the strength of the place, Louis was staying there.

[Col. 0825C] 41. As we have said, Berengar entered the city at night and secretly crossed the bridge with his soldiers toward Louis; at the first twilight of dawn he reached him. Roused by the shouting and din of the soldiers, Louis asked what was happening and fled into the church. No one except one of Berengar’s soldiers knew where he was. Moved by compassion, this soldier did not wish to betray him but to conceal him. The same soldier, however, fearing that Louis might be discovered and betrayed by others and put to death, went to Berengar (A.D. 905) and addressed him as follows:

> “Since God has considered you worthy to place your enemy in your own hands, you too ought to value his admonitions, indeed his commands. For he says: ‘Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful. Do not judge, and you will not be judged; do not condemn, and you will not be condemned’ (Luke VI, 36).”

Berengar, being a man of no little shrewdness, understood that the soldier knew where Louis was hiding, and deceived him with this sophistical reply:

> “Do you suppose, fool, that I wish to kill the man—indeed, the king—whom the Lord has delivered into my hands? Could not holy David also have killed King Saul, whom God had delivered into his hands, but did not wish to?” [Note: [Col. 0825] *set*, corrected to *sed*, in witness 1; frequently.]

Persuaded by these words, the soldier showed him the place to which Louis had fled. After Louis had been captured and brought before Berengar, Berengar rebuked him in these words:

> “How long, Louis, will you abuse our patience? Can you deny that at that time you were surrounded by my defenses and my vigilance, and that you could not move against me? Did I not, moved by mercy—which you deserved in no way—release you? Did you not realize, I ask, that you were bound by the bands of perjury [Note: [Col. 0826D] That is, *fasciis*, “bands, bonds.”]? You solemnly promised me that you yourself would never enter Italy again. I grant you life, just as I had promised it to the man who betrayed you to me; but I not only order you to lose your eyes—I compel you to do so.” [Note: [Col. 0825] The following words are missing in witness 2 at the foot of the page.]

When these things had been completed, Louis was deprived of his sight, and Berengar gained possession of the kingdom.

42. Meanwhile, the fury of the Hungarians, since they could not prevail against the Saxons, Franks, Swabians, and Bavarians, spread throughout all Italy, where no one resisted them. But because Berengar could not securely retain loyal soldiers of his own, he had made the Hungarians his friends in no small number.

43. The Saracens, too, who, as I have said, inhabited Fraxinetum, after the weakening of Provence, were grievously ravaging many neighboring regions of Italy. They devastated many cities and came to Acqui [Note: [Col. 0826D] Acqui, situated on the river Bormida.], a city located approximately forty miles from Pavia [Note: [Col. 0825] *discans* in witness 1.]. It had also acquired this name because of the baths established there for washing, arranged in a marvelous quadrangular form. Such fear had seized everyone that there was no one who dared await the presence of these men except perhaps in the safest places.

44. At the same time, the Saracens, sailing from Africa, occupied Calabria, Apulia, Benevento, and nearly all the cities of the Romans so completely that in each city the Romans held one half and the Africans the other. On Mount Garigliano they had established a stronghold, in which they kept their wives, captive children, and all their property quite safely. No one from the west or from the north could travel to Rome for the sake of prayer, to the threshold of the most blessed apostles, without either being captured by them or being released after paying a considerable price. Although wretched Italy was oppressed by the disasters inflicted by the Hungarians and by the Saracens from Fraxinetum [Note: [Col. 0825] *fraxeto* in witness 1.], it was nevertheless harassed by no raids or pestilences as it was by the Africans.

45. It is said that they left Africa and came into Italy on the following occasion. When the emperors Leo and Alexander had died, Romanus, as we shall explain more fully, governed the Constantinopolitan Empire together with Constantine, who survives to this day, the son of the Emperor Leo. As usually happens, in the first year in which Romanus assumed the imperial power, certain peoples—especially the *ἀνατολικαί*, *anatolikai*, that is, the eastern peoples—attempted to rebel against him. While the emperor was sending an army to conquer them, Apulia and Calabria, two regions that at that time were subject to him, also rebelled. Since the emperor, having sent his largest forces toward the East, could not dispatch a multitude of troops there, he first asked them voluntarily to return to their former loyalty. When they refused and declared that they would by no means do this, the enraged emperor immediately sent to the African king, asking him by a payment to assist him and to subject Apulia and Calabria to him with the aid of his strength. Summoned by this embassy, the African king sent innumerable forces by ship into Calabria and Apulia and subjected both regions most powerfully to the emperor’s rule. But in the course of time, when they withdrew from these regions, they turned their army toward Rome, claimed Mount Garigliano as their chief defense, and captured many very well-fortified cities by force after defeating them.

[Col. 0827B] [Note: The following material through “the slaughter of the slain,” chapter 66, is absent from three manuscripts.]

46. But our Lord Jesus Christ, coeternal and consubstantial with the Father and the Holy Spirit, whose mercy fills the earth, who wishes no human being to perish but all to be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth, so that the human being whom God alone foresaw before the foundation of the world might not perish—the human being whom, after creating every other creature, he created as lord, using and ruling over the rest, and whom, at the end of time, by the shedding of his blood [Note: [Col. 0827] *effusione* in witness 1.], the true man and true God, not two but one, redeemed—invites some to love him and affection for their own homeland through benefits, and compels others through terrors. He does this not because he can receive any increase from our goodness, as the prophet testifies, saying, “You have no need of my goods” (Ps. XV, 2), nor suffer any loss from our wickedness [Note: [Col. 0827] *sumere* in witness 1.], but so that it may benefit us. Since we were unwilling to be corrected by benefits, it pleased him to chastise us for a time through terrors of this kind. But lest the Saracens continue to insult us and say, “Where is their God?”, God changed the hearts of the Christian people, so that they now had a greater desire to fight than previously to flee.

[Col. 0827D] 47. At that time John of Ravenna held the supreme pontificate of the venerable Roman see. By such a wicked crime, contrary to law and right, he obtained the height of the pontificate.

48. The shameless prostitute Theodora, grandmother of this Alberic who recently died, held the monarchy of the city of Rome with considerable force [Col. 0828A], a fact too disgraceful even to recount. She had two daughters, Marozia and Theodora, who were not merely her equals but even more ready to practice sexual vice [Note: [Col. 0827] *exorcitio* in witness 1.]. Marozia, through the pope Sergius, whom we mentioned above, gave birth in a wicked adultery to John, who after the death of John of Ravenna obtained the dignity of the Roman Church; through Margrave Alberic she bore Alberic, who in our own time usurped for himself the rule of that same city of Rome.

At the same time, Peter governed the pontificate of the see of Ravenna, which was regarded as second in rank after the Roman archbishopric. Since he repeatedly and again sent the aforementioned John, who at that time was regarded as the minister of his church and later became pope, to Rome in the service of the required submission, Theodora, as I have testified [Note: [Col. 0827] *testatur sua* in witness 5a; *testatur uita* in witness 5a*.], a most shameless prostitute, inflamed by the heat of lust, burned intensely with desire for the beauty of his appearance [Note: [Col. 0827] *exarscit* in witness 1.]. She not only wished to have intercourse with him, but afterward compelled him again and again to do so.

While these shameless acts were taking place, the bishop of the Church of Bologna died, and this John was chosen in his place. Shortly afterward, before the day of his consecration, the aforementioned archbishop of Ravenna died [Note: [Col. 0827D] Archbishop John appears in the Ravenna charters in A.D. 906, July 15, and 911, September 4, in Fantuzzi, vol. I.]. At Theodora’s instigation, this John, swollen with the spirit of ambition, abandoned the Bolognese church he had previously held and unlawfully usurped the position of the deceased man, contrary to the institutions of the holy Fathers. He came to Rome and was immediately ordained bishop of the Church of Ravenna.

After a short interval, by God’s calling, the pope who had unjustly ordained him died. But Theodora’s perverse mind, lest she should enjoy her lover (*glycerius*, “sweet love,” from Greek *γλυκύς*, “sweet,” and *ἔρως*, “love”) only rarely because Ravenna is separated from Rome by an interval of two hundred miles, compelled him to abandon the archbishopric of Ravenna and, shamefully, to usurp the Roman supreme pontificate. Once this representative of the holy apostles had been established in this manner, the Africans, as I have already said, were miserably ravaging Benevento and the Roman cities (A.D. 914, April) [Note: [Col. 0827] *miserere* in witness 1.].

49. Meanwhile, it happened [Note: [Col. 0827] *Acidit* in witness 1.] that a certain young African, provoked by injuries, abandoned the Africans and came to Pope John. Touched by divine inspiration, he addressed him as follows:

> “Great priest, if you were wise, you would not allow the Africans to ravage so grievously the people and land subject to you. Choose young men, swift as though endowed with excessive mobility, who will readily heed me as commander, instructor, and lord. I permit none of them to possess anything except a single shield, a single spear, a single sword, and plain clothing with a small amount of provisions.”

50. Finally, having found sixty men of this kind and entrusted himself to them, he hastened against the Africans and hid beside the narrow roads along which the Africans traveled. Whenever the Africans returned from ravaging the surrounding countryside, these men suddenly and unexpectedly leapt from ambush with a great shout and easily slaughtered them. A cry burst from their mouths at the same time as blows from their hands. The Africans could not know what was happening until the spears of these men were embedded in their bodies. At length, summoned by this reputation and this practice, some Romans were inspired [that is, provoked] and struck down the Africans in many places. Worn down by this clever African strategy, the Africans abandoned the cities, the treaty having been completely broken, and chose Mount Garigliano alone as their fortress.

51. After John had been established as pope, as we have said, a certain Landulf, an energetic man and trained through the practice of war, stood out as prince of all the people of Benevento and Capua. Since the Africans were seriously undermining the state, Pope John consulted this excellent prince about the matter and about what the Africans were doing. When the prince heard this, he addressed the pope through messengers as follows:

> “This matter, spiritual father, must be investigated through great deliberation. Send to the emperor of the Argives, whose land across the sea they likewise do not cease to ravage, just as they ravage ours. Invite also the Camerinans and Spoletans to our aid; with God as our protector, let us wage a fierce war against them. If we win, let victory be attributed not to the multitude but to God; but if the Africans win, let it be attributed to our sins and not to negligence.”

52. After hearing this, the pope immediately sent messengers to Constantinople, humbly requesting that the emperor provide him with aid. The emperor, a most holy and God-fearing man [Note: [Col. 0829] *sanctisimus* in witness 1.], sent troops transported by fleet without delay. As they sailed up the Garigliano River, Pope John was also present (A.D. 916), together with Landulf, the most powerful prince of the Beneventans, and with the Camerinans and Spoletans. A sufficiently dreadful battle then arose between them. When the Africans saw that the Christian side was prevailing, they fled to the summit of Mount Garigliano and attempted to defend only the narrow paths.

[Col. 0829D] 53. On the side where the ascent was more difficult [Note: [Col. 0829] *dificilior* in witness 1.] and the route more suitable for the Africans’ flight, the Greeks established a fortress that very day. Taking up their positions there, they watched the Africans so that they could not escape, and each day, attacking them, slaughtered no small number.

54. Thus, while the Greeks and Latins fought every day, God having mercy, not a single African survived who was not either slaughtered by the sword or immediately captured alive. The most holy apostles Peter and Paul [Note: [Col. 0829] *sanctisimi* in witness 1.] were seen by devout believers in that same battle; we believe that through their prayers the Christians deserved that the Africans should flee and that they themselves should gain the victory.

55. At this time Adelbert, the powerful marquis of Tuscany, died, and his son Wido was appointed marquis in his father’s place by King Berengar. His wife Berta, together with her son Wido, became after her husband’s death no less powerful than her husband had been. By her cunning [Note: [Col. 0829] *callidate* in witness 1.], her gifts, and also by the sweetness of her Hymenaean arts, she had made some men loyal to her. Hence it happened that, when shortly afterward she was captured by Berengar together with her son and held in custody at Mantua, her own men nevertheless did not surrender any of the cities or castles to King Berengar, but held them firmly; and afterward he released her from custody together with her son.

56. As rumor has it, she had borne three children by her husband: the Wido whom we mentioned above; Lambert, who survives to this day deprived of his sight; and Ermengard, her daughter, equal to her mother in Aphrodite’s sweetness, whom she had joined in marriage to Adelbert, marquis of the city of Ivrea, after Gisla, the daughter of King Berengar and mother of this King Berengar, had died. She bore him a son named Anscar, whose great virtue and great audacity the following book will make clear.

57. At this time that same Adelbert, the king’s son-in-law and marquis of the city of Ivrea, as well as Odelric, count of the palace, who traced his origin to the blood of the Suebi, and also Gislebert, a very wealthy and energetic count, together with Lambert, archbishop of Milan, and several other princes of Italy, were in rebellion against Berengar. The cause of their rebellion was this. When Lambert was to be ordained archbishop of Milan after the death of his predecessor, King Berengar demanded from him a considerable sum of money, contrary to the institutions of the holy Fathers. He ordered that, after the money had been paid to him, it should be written in the registers how much the chamberlains, how much the doorkeepers, how much the peacock-keepers, and even the keepers of the poultry, were to receive. You may therefore understand how painfully Lambert, strongly moved by his love for the archiepiscopal office, paid whatever the king had demanded from him, from what the following account will make clear.

58. Berengar was then holding Odelric, the count of the palace whom we mentioned above, in chains. When he appointed Lambert archbishop, he entrusted Odelric to him until he could deliberate and act concerning him. Lambert, however, mindful of the large sum of money that he had spent for the episcopate, began with his captive to investigate his infidelity.

59. After a few days had passed, King Berengar sent messengers and ordered Odelric to come to him. There is no doubt that Lambert met them with this ironic reply: “I should be completely unworthy of the priestly office if I handed anyone over into another’s hands to be slaughtered.” The messengers therefore understood that he had openly rebelled, since they knew that he had released, without the king’s permission, the man whom the king had entrusted to him [Note: [Col. 0831] *dimisse* in witness 1.]. They returned immediately to the king and gave him, as their answer, that line from Terence [Note: [Col. 0831D] *Adelphi* III.iii.19.]:

> “Entrust him to this man, if you want anything properly attended to.”

60. At that time the most arrogant King Rudolf ruled over the Burgundians. To increase his power, he had taken in marriage Berta, the daughter of the most powerful Suevian duke Burchard. The Italians therefore sent messengers asking him to come and expel Berengar.

61. While these things were in progress, it happened that the Hungarians arrived at Verona, unknown to the others (921). Their two kings, Dursac and Bugat, had been very close friends of Berengar. While the marquis Adelbert, Count Odelric of the palace, Count Gislebert, and many others were holding meetings in the mountains of the city of Brescia—which lies fifty miles from Verona [Note: [Col. 0831] *dictat*, evidently for *distat*, in the printed witness]—for the purpose of overthrowing Berengar, Berengar asked the Hungarians to attack his enemies if they loved him. Since they were eager for slaughter and desirous of war, they immediately accepted Berengar as their leader and came by unknown roads upon the men from behind. They stabbed them with such speed that the men had not even time to put on or take up their weapons. After many had been captured and killed, Odelric, count of the palace, who had not defended himself manfully [Note: [Col. 0831] See note, witnesses 5 and 5a.], was killed; but the marquis Adelbert and Gislebert were captured alive.

62. Adelbert, however, being a man not warlike but extremely shrewd [Note: [Col. 0831] *sagatitatis* in witness 1.] and cunning, when he saw the Hungarians rushing upon him from every side and realized that every hope of escape had been taken away, threw off his belt, his golden bracelets, and all his costly equipment. He put on the cheap clothing of one of his soldiers, so that the Hungarians would not recognize who he was. When he was captured and asked who he was, he replied that he was a soldier belonging to a certain soldier. He asked to be taken to a nearby castle called Calcinaria, claiming that he had relatives there who would ransom him. Since he was not recognized, he was therefore purchased for a very low price. His own soldier, named Leo, bought him.

63. Gislebert, however, because he was recognized, was flogged, bound, and led half-naked before King Berengar. When he was led before him without breeches, dressed in a shortened *endromis*, and fell quickly prostrate at the king’s feet, everyone nearly died laughing at the sight of his exposed private parts. But the king, being a lover of compassion, was moved to pity, although Gislebert deserved none; and he did not repay evil with evil, as the people desired. Instead, he immediately had him washed and dressed in the finest clothing, and promised that he might depart. He also said to him:

> “I demand no oath from you; I entrust you to your own faith, knowing that, if you act wrongly against me, you will have to give an account to God.”

64. As this man returned to his own country, the king’s son-in-law Adelbert and the others who had rebelled with him sent him to summon Rudolf, forgetful of the favor he had received. Gislebert set out and, before thirty days had passed, forced Rudolf to come to Italy. Received by everyone [Note: [Col. 0831] *supsceptus* in witness 1.], Rudolf left Berengar nothing from the whole kingdom except Verona, and he held the entire kingdom vigorously for three years (January 922–July 926).

65. If, within twelve hours, a person may please and displease himself, love one thing and immediately reject another [Note: [Col. 0831] The words designated “*i. m. a. q. f. p. ut o. s. ae. p.*” are absent in witness 2; *asperneretur* occurs in witness 1.], how can he always please everyone with equal composure? Thus, within those three years, King Rudolf seemed good to some and burdensome to others. As a result, half the people of the whole kingdom wanted Rudolf, while the other half wanted Berengar. They therefore prepared a considerable civil war; and because Wido, bishop of the city of Piacenza, favored Berengar’s side, they arranged a battle twelve miles from Piacenza, near Florentiola [Note: [Col. 0831] *parant* in five witnesses.].

Then a sufficiently dreadful battle

arose, civil and dark,

alas, four days before the Kalends

of August—four [Note: [Col. 0831] *quattuor* in five witnesses and 5a.]—while Phoebus himself

was causing his rays to emerge,

and Mars, when the high trumpet sounded,

was roaring.

The Father himself brings upon his son

everlasting destruction,

and the son destroys his father—what grief [Note: Witnesses 5 and 5a read *heu quantus*, ‘alas, how great [the grief]’],

alas, is this?

Behold, the great-grandfather prepares

a joyful thing for his grandson,

only to be struck down by him;

driven on by dark Furies,

one brother wounds another from afar.

Berengar himself rushes forward,

the king, swiftly through the midst

of his enemies,

hurrying [Note: [Col. 0831] *Properas* corrected to *Properans*; *Properans* in witness 1, *Properas* in witnesses 2 and 5, *Properat* in 5a.] like lightning from on high;

with his sickle [Note: [Col. 0831] *falfalce* in witness 1.] he cuts down

the new ears of grain beneath

the heavy constellation of Cancer.

Likewise, fierce and savage,

King Rudolf himself

strikes down the wretched common people

with his sword.

66. King Rudolf had given his sister Waldrada, an honorable matron both in beauty and in wisdom, who survives to this day, in marriage to Count Boniface, a most powerful man who, after our own time [Note: [Col. 0832D] In the year 946, according to the *Chronicle of Farfa*], became marquis of Camerino and Spoleto. Boniface had come with a multitude of men, together with Count Gariard, to Rudolf’s aid. Being as cunning as he was bold, he preferred to wait in ambush with his men for the outcome of the affair rather than withstand the first assault of the battle.

By now almost all of Rudolf’s soldiers had fled, while Berengar’s men, after the signal of victory had been given, were busily gathering the spoils. Then Boniface and Gariard, suddenly rushing out of their ambush, attacked them all the more easily because the assault was unexpected. Gariard spared some of them, striking them with his spear but not with his sword; Boniface, however, sparing no one, created an immense slaughter. Boniface therefore sounded the signal of victory, and those who had fled from Rudolf’s side gathered together. Pursuing Berengar’s men, they forced them to take flight. Berengar himself went to a familiar refuge at Verona. So great was the slaughter of those killed at that time that, even to this day, there is a very great scarcity of soldiers.

67. When these things had been accomplished, King Rudolf subjected the kingdom to himself with the greatest power. He came quickly to Pavia, and, when all had assembled, said:

> “Since, by the generosity of heavenly grace, it has fallen to me, after conquering my enemies, to obtain the throne of the kingdom, it is now my desire to entrust the Italian kingdom to your loyalty and to visit my old homeland, Burgundy.”

The Italians immediately replied: “If this seems good to you, we are ready.”

68. After King Rudolf’s departure, the Veronese, having adopted an evil plan, attempted to plot against Berengar’s life; this did not escape Berengar’s notice. A certain Flambert was the savage instigator and contriver of this crime. Since the king had received his son from the sacred font, he had made Flambert his godfather. On the day before he was to suffer, he ordered this same Flambert to come to him. He said to him:

69. “If there were not many and just reasons [Note: Witness 1 has the misspelling *case* for *causae*, ‘reasons/causes.’] for my loving you until now, then, however matters might stand, what is being said about you could be believed [Note: Witness 1 reads *que de te credi*, ‘what is said about you [could] be believed.’]. They say that you are plotting against my life; but I do not believe them. I want you to remember that, however much increase of fortune and dignity you may have received, you could have obtained it only through my favors. Therefore you ought to be disposed toward us in such a way that my dignity may rest upon your love and loyalty. Nor do I think that anyone’s safety and fortunes have ever been of as much concern to anyone as your honor has been to me. In this city I have fixed all my efforts, all my labor, care, diligence, and thought. Take this one thing as certain: if I learn that your loyalty toward me has been preserved, my own safety will not be as dear to me as the piety I shall find pleasing in returning your favor.”

70. When he had finished speaking, the king handed him a golden cup of considerable weight and added:

> “Drink what it contains for the sake of my love and safety; keep the vessel that contains it.” [Note: [Col. 0833] *libito* in witness 1, perhaps for *libato* or *bibito*.]

Truly and without ambiguity, after drinking, Satan entered into him, just as it is written concerning Judas, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ: “After the morsel, Satan then entered into him” (John 13:27).

71. Forgetful of the past and present favor, Flambert spent that sleepless night inciting the people to the king’s murder. That night the king, as was his custom, stayed near a church—not in a house that could be defended, but in a very pleasant little hut. He had not even set guards that night, suspecting no evil.

The cock, first shaking itself,

cries out when it awakens

mortals; as usual it sounds;

and the bronze instrument, now struck,

sings to God.

It invites them, teaching them well

to reject heavy sleep [Note: [Col. 0833D] That is, sleep.],

and to render praises in this way

to him who grants and gives life

and allows us rightly to seek

the holy homeland above.

Here the king seeks the church

and sings praises to the Lord.

Flambertus flies forward in haste,

with a large band accompanying him,

so that they may kill the good king.

The king, wakeful but unaware of these men,

hears the noise; fearing nothing,

he hastens quickly to see

what this may be. He sees

an armed band of soldiers.

From a distance he calls Flambertus:

“What is this crowd, good man?

What does the people now desire,

bringing armed hands?”

He replied: “Fear nothing.

This crowd does not rush upon you

to kill you; rather, it eagerly

wishes to fight with the party

that now seeks to take

your life.”

Deceived by trust,

the king hastens this way

into their midst. Then [Note: [Col. 0833] “*Tunc*,” that is, *tunc*, in witness 5a.] he is wickedly seized

and led away;

the impious man strikes him

from behind with a sword.

Alas, the pious man falls

and devoutly commends

his blessed spirit to God!

72. Since we remain silent about how innocent a blood they shed and how perversely the wicked acted, a stone placed before the door of a certain church bears witness to it, displaying his blood to all who pass by. For although it is smeared or sprinkled with no liquid, it does not disappear.

73. King Berengar had raised and generously maintained in his household a young man, indeed a certain hero, named Milo, worthy of great remembrance and praise. If the king had relied upon his counsel, he would not have found all his fortunes so opposed to him—unless perhaps this was the plan of divine foreknowledge, that things could not happen otherwise.

That very night on which King Berengar was deceived, Milo, having gathered forces around him, wished to provide the king with a nighttime guard. But the king, deceived by Flambert’s promises, not only refused to allow Milo to guard him, but repeatedly and vehemently forbade it. Milo, however, as a faithful and upright man, and mindful of the favor conferred upon him by the king, since he had been absent and unable to defend him, took care to avenge him sharply and quickly. On the third day after the king’s murder, he ordered Flambert and those who had connived with him in the wicked crime to be captured by force and to end their lives by hanging. This man possessed several complete virtues, which, with God’s favor, will not be concealed in silence in their proper places, while his life continues.

**THE SECOND BOOK OF THE ANTAPODOSIS ENDS.**

**[BOOK THREE.]**

**THE CHAPTERS OF THE THIRD BOOK BEGIN.**

1. On the title of this work, and why it is called *Antapodosis*.

2. That, after Berengar’s death and Rudolf’s departure from Italy, the Hungarians ravaged Italy.

3. A metrical description of the lamentable burning of Pavia.

4. That the sword of God did not utterly destroy Pavia [Note: Witness 1 reads the malformed *destuxerit* for *destruxerit*, ‘destroyed.’], but that his mercy wonderfully freed it from the Hungarians.

5. That it was freed through the merits of blessed Syrus, its patron.

6. That the same blessed Syrus, coming to Pavia, foretold in the spirit of prophecy its abundance and the fall of Aquileia.

7. Why Ermengard [Note: [Col. 0835] *ermenga* in witnesses 1 and 2.] became so powerful after the death of her husband Adelbert.

8. After King Rudolf returned from Burgundy, Ermengard shortly afterward rebelled against him and held Pavia with the Italians.

9. King Rudolf advances with his army toward Pavia [Note: [Col. 0835] *papaam* in witness 1.].

10. That Ermengard acted with such cunning that Rudolf abandoned his men by night and became a deserter to her side.

11. When the matter became known in the morning, Rudolf’s soldiers fled to Milan.

12. The Italians send for Hugh.

13. Rudolf therefore goes to Burgundy and brings his father-in-law Burchard to his aid [Note: [Col. 0835] *burchardum* in witness 2.].

14. On what occasion Burchard went to Milan, and why, after being honorably received there, his death was plotted.

15. Burchard, returning from Milan, comes to Novara, where he and all his men are killed by the Italians.

16. After Burchard’s death Rudolf flees to Burgundy, and Hugh comes to Italy across the Tyrrhenian Sea.

17. Some of the Italians meet him at Pisa, where messengers of Pope John also arrive; at their urging the king proceeds to Pavia and is made king.

18. Concerning Wido, King Hugh’s brother, who then held Tuscany and had Marozia, the Roman harlot, as his wife.

19. Concerning the many virtues of King Hugh, which luxury defiled.

20. That the same King Hugh then had two sons.

21. That King Hugh makes King Henry his friend.

22. Which messenger the king sent to Constantinople to the emperor Romanus.

23. Concerning the two dogs sent to the emperor, which wanted to tear him apart.

24. Why the messenger of King Hugh was received with extraordinary honor by the emperor.

25. Concerning the most savage lion that killed the Romans.

26. How Romanus was first made *droungarios* and afterward appointed father of the *basileus*.

27. The *domesticus* Phocas, fighting against Simeon, king of the Bulgarians, voluntarily fled when he heard that Romanus had become father of the *basileus*.

28. How Phocas, coming to Constantinople, was captured by Romanus and deprived of his sight.

29. Concerning Simeon, king of the Bulgarians, who was first a monk and afterward became an apostate [Note: [Col. 0835D] That is, guilty of apostasy, having returned to the secular world.].

30. Concerning Romanus, who gave his daughter Helena in marriage to the emperor Constantine.

31. Why emperors are called *porphyrogeniti*, “born in the purple.”

32. How Basil became emperor after killing his lord, the emperor Michael.

33. That our Lord Jesus Christ terrified Basil in a vision concerning Michael’s death [Note: [Col. 0835] “*visione*” in witness 1.].

34. Basil’s repentance and the church built with marvelous workmanship because of his guilt.

35. How Romanus addressed the princes and became emperor, having been made father of the *basileus*.

36. That Romanus was born of a humble family.

37. Romanus makes his son Christopher emperor and unjustly places him before his own lord Constantine.

38. How peace was established between the emperor Romanus and Simeon.

39. Concerning Walpert and Gezo of Pavia, who raised a revolt against King Hugh.

40. That they were deceived by the king’s humble embassy.

41. Shortly afterward Walpert was beheaded and Gezo was deprived of his sight.

42. Concerning Bishop Ildoin and the monk Rather, of whom Ildoin was made archbishop of Milan by King Hugh, and Rather bishop of Verona.

43. How Pope John was captured, handed over to custody, and died there; who was ordained after him; and that Wido died and Lambert was appointed marquis.

44. Concerning the fortification placed at the entrance to the city of Rome, in which King Hugh was received, and from which he was disgracefully expelled not long afterward by Alberic.

45. That this happened by divine disposition.

46. How and why King Hugh [Note: Witness 1 reads *Hogo* for *Hugo*.] captured his brother Lambert and, on the advice of his brother Boso, blinded him, also giving him a march.

47. King Hugh obtains an oath from King Rudolf and makes King Henry his friend by means of gifts.

48. Arnald, duke of the Bavarians, hastens into Italy at the urging of Count Milo and Bishop Rather; King Hugh quickly goes out to meet him.

49. Concerning the Bavarians killed by the soldiers of King Hugh.

50. Why Milo abandoned Arnald and went over to King Hugh.

51. Arnald, after storming the fortification at Verona, returns to Bavaria.

52. Concerning the restoration of Verona to King Hugh, and Bishop Rather’s capture and the book he composed with considerable wit.

**THE CHAPTERS END.**

**THE THIRD BOOK BEGINS. BOOK C.**

1. I do not doubt, most holy father, that you are sufficiently astonished at the title of this work. Perhaps you say: “Since it presents the deeds of illustrious men, why is the title *Antapodosis*—Ανταπόδοσης, ‘requital’ or ‘return of recompense’—inserted into it?”

To this I answer [Note: [Col. 0837] *respendeo* in witness 1.]: The purpose of this work is to describe, display, and proclaim the deeds of this Berengar, who now does not reign in Italy but tyrannizes, and of his wife Willa, who, because of the enormity of her tyranny, is called a second Jezebel, and because of her insatiable greed for plunder is called by the proper name “Lamia.” They have freely inflicted upon me, my household, my kin, and my family such a multitude of darts of lies, such losses through plunder, and such assaults of impiety that neither tongue can express nor pen is able to write them.

Therefore let this present page be their *antapodosis*, that is, their recompense, when, in exchange for my calamities, I have exposed their τὴν ἀσεβείαν, *tēn asebeian*, that is, “their impiety,” to mortals living now and to those yet to come. It will likewise be an *antapodosis* for the most holy and fortunate men who have bestowed favors upon me. Among those mentioned or to be mentioned, scarcely anyone—or no one—is found, except this one impious man Berengar [Note: Witness 1 reads *Berenga* for *Berengario*.], whose benefactions have not made us, whether parents or offspring, exceedingly grateful.

Finally, the fact that this little book is said to have been written ἐν τῇ εχμαλοσίᾳ, *en tē echmalosia*, that is, “in captivity” or “in exile,” is indicated by my present banishment. It was begun at Frankenenvurd, a place twenty miles from Mainz, on the island of Paxu [Note: [Col. 0837D] South of Corcyra, on the coast of Epirus.], more than nine hundred miles from Constantinople, and it is still being written to this day. But let us return to the matter.

2. After King Berengar’s death (12 March 924), and while Rudolf was absent, the fury of the Hungarians, led by Salard, spread throughout Italy. They even surrounded the walls of the city of Pavia with a rampart and, having fixed their tents all around it, prevented the citizens from going out. Since the citizens could not resist these forces on account of their meriting them through their sins, nor appease them with gifts—

**Verses**

3. The bright Phoebus [Note: Witness 1 reads *Poebus* for *Phoebus*.], departing from the star

into which he had been infused,

begins as usual to climb

the first constellation of the zodiac

and to dissolve the cold hoarfrost

upon the hills;

Aeolus too sends forth his two winds twice,

while the raging band of Hungarians rejoices

to pour flames into the city,

aided by the blasts of Aeolus. [Note: This verse and the preceding verse are absent from witness 3.]

A small fire is spread by powerful winds;

nor does it suffice the Hungarians

to burn these people with flames alone.

They gather from every side

and threaten to bring death;

they stab with weapons those

whom the hot fire has terrified.

Unhappy Pavia, once beautiful,

is burned!

And Vulcan, raising his limbs

with his blasts,

climbs together with the churches

over the whole homeland.

Mothers, boys, and unmarried girls

are extinguished [a hypermetrical verse];

the holy throng of catechumens

dies in great numbers [Note: [Col. 0838D] That is, the people.];

in his own city the holy bishop

and priest also dies,

whose proper name was John,

and who was called “the good.”

Behold, what had long been shut

within its chests lies exposed,

lest a foreign hand touch the gold;

and through immeasurable conduits

it is dissolved by fire.

Unhappy Pavia, once beautiful,

is burned!

Anyone who was present would see

streams of silver and shining cups;

the bodies of great men

burned everywhere.

The value of green jasper

and gleaming topaz is despised,

as are sapphire [Note: [Col. 0839] *carus* is inserted in witness 3; there is a lacuna in 5a; *ortyx* in 5a*; *onyx* in Hervagius.] and beautiful beryl.

Alas, no merchant then

turns his face toward the gold.

Unhappy Pavia, once beautiful,

is burned!

Nor does the bright Ticino draw

the countless ships out from its source;

the bilge-water too is poured out

with fire.

Unhappy Pavia, once beautiful,

was burned

in the year 924 of the Lord’s Incarnation,

on the fourth day before the Ides of March,

in the twelfth indiction,

on Friday, at the third hour.

I earnestly ask you and all who read this to commemorate with devoted remembrance those who were burned at that same time.

4. Yet the sword of the most merciful and almighty Lord, of whom the prophet sings mercy and judgment and whose mercy fills the earth, did not rage to the end. For although Pavia was burned because its sins deserved it, it was not handed over to the hands of its enemies. What the king and prophet sings was fulfilled:

> “Will God cast off forever?  
> Or will he never again be favorable?  
> Or will he cut off his mercy forever,  
> from generation to generation?  
> Or will God forget to be merciful?  
> Or will he restrain his mercies in his anger?”  
> (Psalm 76:8.)

Another prophet likewise says to him:

> “When you are angry, you will remember mercy”  
> (Habakkuk 3:2).

The survivors who remained [Note: [Col. 0839] *supererant* in witness 1.] therefore resisted the Hungarians with no lack of courage, so that they joyfully sang with the prophet:

> “This is the change of the right hand of the Most High”  
> (Psalm 76:11) [Note: [Col. 0839D] That is, “of the Most High.”].

5. To this was added, and great assistance was provided by, the glorious intercession of our most holy father [Note: Witness 1 reads *sanctisimi* for *sanctissimi*, ‘most holy.’] and outstanding teacher, blessed Syrus, whose relics rest in the city mentioned above [Note: [Col. 0839] *excubiae* in witnesses 1 and 2.]. And so that his prophecy would not prove false, the aforesaid city of Pavia was struck so that it might fall, yet it was mercifully rescued by the Lord. The most blessed father had been sent to Pavia for the sake of preaching by blessed Hermagoras, the disciple of the evangelist Mark; through the spirit of prophecy he honored the city with this kind of foretelling:

6. “Rejoice in gladness, city of Pavia, because rejoicing will come to you from foreign mountains. You will not be called small, but abundant among neighboring cities.”

And so that this prophecy of his might be believed more firmly, at that same hour he announced the fall of Aquileia, a well-known city, in these words:

> “Woe to you, Aquileia, because when you have fallen into the hands of the impious, you will be destroyed, and you will not rise again, rebuilt.”

That this was fulfilled is made clear by the evidence visible to the eyes. For Aquileia, once a very wealthy and immense city, was captured and utterly devastated by Attila, the most impious king of the Huns, and afterward was not raised again [Note: [Col. 0839] *ulte terius* in witness 1, over two lines.], as can be seen at the present time. Pavia, however, just as the most holy man had said, is both called and seen to be abundant. It surpasses not only neighboring cities in wealth but also cities situated far away.

Why should I mention other cities, when Rome itself, illustrious and known throughout the whole world, would be inferior to this city if it did not possess the precious bodies of the most blessed apostles? It is therefore clear that Pavia was rescued by the intercession of our most blessed patron Syrus, who honored it with such a true and precious prophecy.

After Pavia had been burned and considerable plunder had been made throughout all Italy, the Hungarians returned to their own land.

7. At this same time, after Adelbert, marquis of the city of Ivrea, had died, his wife Ermengard, daughter of Adelbert, the powerful marquis of Tuscany, and of Berta, held the rulership of all Italy. The reason for her power was this: something shameful even to say—that she engaged in sexual relations with everyone, not only with princes but also with men of low birth.

8. At that time [Note: [Col. 0839] *idem* corrected to *id* in witness 1.] King Rudolf, returning from Burgundy, came into Italy and, after Berengar’s death, gained the kingdom by force. After several days, however, all the Italians began to disagree among themselves. They were drawn by considerable jealousy, in accordance with the corruption of this flesh, because of Ermengard’s beauty: she granted sexual access to some and denied it to others. As a result, the wealthy archbishop of Milan and several others favored King Rudolf’s party; while on Ermengard’s side there were so many rebels together that they vigorously prevented the king from possessing Pavia, the capital of the kingdom.

9. It happened that King Rudolf, having gathered his forces, advanced toward Pavia. He pitched camp a mile from the city, at the place where the Ticino and that great river, the Po, meet—of which Maro sings these praises [Note: [Col. 0839D] Virgil, *Georgics* I.482.]:

> “The Eridanus, king of rivers.”

And likewise [Note: [Col. 0840D] Virgil, *Aeneid* VIII.77.]:

> “The horned river, ruler of the waters of Hesperia.”

10. Ermengard, being no fool, sent King Rudolf this message by night across the bed of the river mentioned above:

> “If I wished to destroy you, you would have been dead long ago. For all your men are striving to abandon you and come eagerly to me, if only I were willing. You are in places where you would already be captured and bound, if I had followed their counsels before now.”

The king, not only credulous but also frightened by such messages, sent messengers back to say that he would do whatever she advised. Without delay, on the following night King Rudolf secretly abandoned his guards and all his men, leaving behind even his properly arranged tent and bed. He boarded a small boat, deserted his men, and hurried as quickly as possible to Ermengard.

11. When morning came, the king’s soldiers quietly surrounded the tent. When the princes arrived, they were greatly astonished that the king was sleeping at such an unusual hour. They tried to wake him with a commotion, as the eunuchs once tried to awaken Holofernes, but he gave no answer at all, just as Holofernes himself had not. When they entered the tent and found nothing, some shouted that he had been carried away, others that he had been killed. No one, however, could in any way perceive that he had become a deserter.

While they were wavering in this astonishment, a messenger arrived saying that King Rudolf intended to attack them with their enemies. Immediately dismayed, they began to withdraw in such rapid flight that, if you had seen them, you would have said not that they were running but that they were flying through the air.

12. When they had reached Milan, a secure place, Archbishop Lambert, with the consent of all, sent word to Hugh, the most powerful and wisest count of Provence, that he should come to Italy, take the kingdom from Rudolf, and obtain it for himself by force. For a long time Hugh too had been testing, by various means, whether he might perhaps obtain the Italian kingdom. He had come to Italy with many men even during the time of the already-mentioned King Berengar; but because the time for his reign had not yet arrived, Berengar frightened him and drove him away.

13. Since Rudolf could not overcome the aforesaid adversaries because of the disloyalty of his own men, he departed for Burgundy (926) and announced to Burchard, duke of the Suebi, whose daughter he had married, that he should come to his aid. Burchard gathered his forces and immediately set out with Rudolf for Italy. When they had reached Ivrea, Burchard addressed Rudolf as follows:

14. “It seems reasonable that I myself should go to Milan under the pretext of an embassy. On this occasion I shall be able to inspect the city and learn their intentions.”

When he had set out and had reached Milan, before entering the city he turned aside to the church of the blessed and precious martyr Lawrence for the sake of prayer—but, as they say, not so much for the sake of prayer as for another purpose. They say that, since a church constructed with marvelous and costly workmanship stood near the city, he wished to establish a fortification there, by which he intended to restrain not only the Milanese but also many princes of Italy.

When he departed from there and was riding beside the city wall, he addressed his men in his own language, that is, German:

> “If I do not make all the Italians use only one spur and force their shapeless mares to gallop, I am not Burchard. I count the strength of this wall, or the height by which they trust they are protected, as nothing. With a cast of my spear I shall hurl my enemies down dead from the wall.”

He said this because he thought that none of his opponents there understood his language. But, as an evil omen, someone was present who, although ragged and despised, understood his speech and quickly became a messenger of all these matters to Archbishop Lambert.

Lambert, being shrewd by nature, did not despise Burchard. He received him with evil intent but honored him magnificently. Among other things, he granted him, as though it were a privilege of affection, permission to hunt a stag in his own park [Note: [Col. 0841] *veneraretur* in witness 1.]—a privilege he had never granted except to his dearest and greatest friends. Meanwhile Lambert invited all the people of Pavia and several princes of Italy to kill Burchard, and he detained him until he hoped that all those who were to kill him could be assembled.

15. It therefore happened that, when Burchard departed from Milan, he reached Novara on that same day. After spending the night there, he rose at dawn and set out toward Ivrea (April 29). Suddenly the Italian forces appeared and rushed upon him. He hurried to meet them as a warrior, but soon began to flee. Since, according to the statement of blessed Job, his appointed limit could not be passed (Job 14:5), and since “the horse is a false hope for salvation” (Psalm 33:17), his horse fell into the ditch surrounding the city walls and threw him off. The attacking Italians then pierced him with their spears, and he exchanged life for death.

When his men saw this, because they could do nothing else, they fled into the church of the most holy confessor of Christ, Gaudentius. The Italians, inflamed and angered to no small degree by Burchard’s threats, broke down the church doors and stabbed everyone they found inside, even beneath the altar itself.

[Col. 0842C] 16. When Rudolf heard this, he abandoned Italy and hurried to Burgundy. While these things were happening, Hugh, count of the Arelatenses or Provincials, had boarded a ship and was hastening to Italy across the Tyrrhenian Sea. God, who wished him to reign in Italy, therefore brought him swiftly by favorable winds to Alpheus—that is, Pisa, which is the capital of the province of Tuscany. Concerning this, Maro writes [Note: [Col. 0841D] *Aeneid* X.179.]:

> “Pisa, from the origin of Alpheus.”

### 17

When he had reached the same place, there was present a messenger of the Roman pope—namely, of John of Ravenna [Note: [Col. 0841] *nuntios* in witness 1.]. Messengers also arrived from nearly all the Italians, inviting him by every means to reign over them. Since he had long desired this, he hastened to Pavia and, with everyone agreeing [Col. 0842D], accepted the kingdom (July 9). Shortly afterward he went to Mantua, where Pope John also met him and struck a treaty with him.

### 18

At that time Berta, the mother of King Hugh himself, died. Wido, her son, whom she had borne from Adelbert, as we said earlier, held the march of Tuscany [Note: [Col. 0841] *tenebant* in witness 1.]; he had taken Marozia, the Roman prostitute, as his wife.

### 19

King Hugh was a man of no less learning than daring, and of no weaker courage than cunning [Col. 0843A]. He was also a worshiper of God and a lover of lovers of holy religion; attentive to the needs of the poor; very solicitous toward churches; and he not only loved religious and philosophical men but also honored them vigorously. Although he shone with so many virtues, he befouled them with the allurements of women.

### 20

From the Frankish people of the Teutons he had taken a wife named Alda, who bore him a son named Lothar. At that time he had also, from a certain most noble woman named Wandelmoda, a son named Hubert, who survives to this day and is regarded as the powerful prince of the province of Tuscany. With God’s favor, his deeds will be set forth in their proper places.

### 21

When King Hugh had been established, he began, like a most prudent man [Col. 0843B], to send his messengers everywhere throughout the world and to seek the friendship of many kings and princes, especially of the most famous King Henry, who, as we mentioned above, ruled over the Bavarians, Swabians, Lotharingians, Franks, and Saxons. He also subdued the innumerable people of the Slavs and made them tributary to himself. He was likewise the first to subdue the Danes and compel them to serve him, and thereby he made his name famous among many nations [Note: [Col. 0843] that is, *among many nations*.].

### 22

Thus, while King Hugh was acquiring kings and princes as friends all around him, he also took pains to make his name known far from us among the Achaeans—that is, the Greeks. At that time they were ruled by an emperor of the Romans worthy of considerable remembrance and praise: liberal, humane, prudent, and pious. Both because of his moral excellence and because of his refined speech, Hugh sent my father to him as a messenger.

### 23

When my father had reached him, among the other gifts that King Hugh had sent to the Roman emperor [Note: [Col. 0843] *munera* in witness 1.], he brought two dogs of a kind never before seen in that country. When they had been led before the emperor, they would immediately have torn him apart with their bites unless many arms had held them back. I think that, when they saw him covered in a Greek fashion with a *teristrum* [Note: [Col. 0843D] A covering, a woman’s cloak.] and dressed in unusual clothing, they thought him not a man but some kind of monster.

### 24

Finally, he was received by that emperor with great honor [Note: [Col. 0843] *suspeptus* in witness 1.]. Yet this was not so much because of the novelty of the matter or the magnitude of the gifts as because, when the aforementioned father had come to Thessalonica, certain Slavs who had rebelled against the Roman emperor and were ravaging his land attacked him. But by God’s providence it happened that two of their leaders were captured alive, while many others were killed. When my father presented them to the emperor, the latter was filled with immense joy, and my father, having received a great gift from him, returned happily to King Hugh, who had sent him there [Note: [Col. 0843] *tranmiserat* in witness 1.].

After his return, a few days later he was seized by illness, went to a monastery, and assumed the habit of holy religious life [Col. 0844A]. There, after fifteen days, he died and departed to the Lord, leaving me a little child.

But now, since mention has been made of the emperor Romanus—Ῥομανός, that is, “Romanus”—it does not seem inappropriate to insert here who he was and how he attained the summit of imperial power [Note: [Col. 0843] The following material through chapter 44, namely one quire, has perished in witness 5.].

### 25

During the reign of Leo, the father of this Constantine, this emperor Romanus, although πτωχός (*ptochos*), that is, “poor,” was nevertheless considered by everyone χρήσιμος (*chrisimos*), that is, “useful.” He was one of those of modest station who had received pay from the emperor for naval warfare. Since, time and again, εἰς τὴν μάχην (*eis tēn machēn*), that is, “in battle,” he performed many χρησιμώτατα (*chrisimotata*), that is, “most useful” services, he was so greatly ἐτιμήθη (*etimēthē*) by his superior [Note: [Col. 0843] *ἐτημιθη* in witness 1.] ὅπως πρωτοκαραβός (*hopōs protokarabos*)—“he was honored so that he deserved to become first among the ships,” that is, chief commander of the fleet.

One night, while he had gone out to reconnoiter the Saracens, and there was in that place a marsh and a considerable reed bed, it happened that a most savage lion leapt from the reeds, drove a multitude of deer into the marsh, and seized one of them, thus appeasing the ravenousness of its belly.

Ῥομάνος δὲ τὸν αὐτῶν ψόφον ἄκουων ἐδειλίασεν σφόδρα  
*Romanos de ton auton psofon acuon ediliasen sfodra*—“But Romanus, hearing their noise, was greatly afraid.” [Note: [Col. 0843] I have written *Romanus* thus; in the manuscript a proper name is read.]

For he thought that it was a multitude of Saracens who wished to kill him by some deception when they caught sight of him.

Ὄρθρου δὲ βαθέως  
*Orthru de vatheos*—“But, at deep dawn,” or “rising very early,” he examined everything most carefully. When he saw the tracks, εὐθέως (*eutheōs*), that is, “immediately,” he recognized what had happened [Col. 0844C].

Since the lion was staying in the reed bed, Romanus ordered Greek fire—which is extinguished by no liquid except vinegar—to be cast throughout the reeds. There was, however, a heap full of reeds within the reed bed; the lion fled into it and was saved there from the fire. For the wind, blowing from the opposite direction, drove the fire away so that it did not reach the heap.

After the fire had gone out, Romanus, with only one attendant, carrying merely a sword in his right hand and a cloak in his left, went around inspecting the whole place to see whether perhaps he might find a bone or some other sign of what had happened. When he was already about to withdraw, having found nothing, he decided to investigate what sort of marvel it was that the heap had been saved from the fire [Col. 0844D].

When the two of them were standing nearby [i.e. beside it] and conversing with one another about various matters, the lion heard them, although it could not see because its eyes were dimmed παρα τῷ καπνῷ (*para tō kapnō*), that is, “because of the smoke.” Wishing to vent upon them the fury of its spirit, which it had conceived against the fire, the lion sprang with a rapid leap between them, toward the place from which it had heard their voices.

But Romanus, standing not in the fearful state of his attendant but rather with such courage that, even if the world should shatter, the ruins would strike him unafraid [Note: [Col. 0845D] Horace, *Odes* III.3.7], thrust the cloak he was carrying between the lion’s forelegs. While the lion tore it apart, thinking it a man, Romanus struck it from behind with all his strength between the joints of its thighs with his sword [Note: [Col. 0845] That is, it seems that *junturas* should be read.]. Since its legs had been torn apart and divided [Note: [Col. 0845] So in witnesses 1 and 2, but *cruribus*—“legs”—should be read.], it could not remain standing and fell completely.

After killing the lion, Romanus saw his half-dead attendant lying on the ground some distance away. He began calling him loudly. But when he gave no answer at all, Romanus stood beside him and, striking him with his foot, said:

ἐγειρε, ειπεν, ἀθλιε καὶ ταλεπορε, μη φοβοῦ  
*Egire, ipen, athlie ke talepore, mē fobu*—“Rise,” he said, “wretched and miserable man; do not be afraid!” [Note: [Col. 0845] *μη φοβοῦ* is absent in witness 1.]

When the attendant rose, he had no breath left in him from astonishment as he looked upon the lion’s enormous body.

Εξεπλισσοντο δὲ πάντες πέρι τοῦ Ρομανοῦ τάυτα ἀκούσαντες  
*Exeplissonto de pantes peri tu Romanu tauta acusantes*—“But everyone was astonished when they heard these things about Romanus.”

Thus it happened that, both for his other achievements and for this splendid deed performed before their eyes, he was not long afterward honored by the emperor Leo with such distinction:

ὅπως πάντα τὰ πλοῖα  
*Hopōs panta plia*—“so that all the ships would be in his hands,” and would obey his commands.

### 26

Finally, Leo, the most pious emperor of the Greeks, whom we mentioned above, paid the debt of the human body and entered upon the way of all flesh (A.D. 912). He left as heir to his kingdom his full brother Alexander, and also his little son Constantine, who survives to this day and reigns successfully, and who, as the Greeks say, was ἄλαλον (*alalon*), that is, “unable to speak.” To guard the palace and protect the private property, as is customary there, he appointed a eunuch to the office of *parakoimomenos* [Note: [Col. 0845D] Παρακοιμώμενος, prefect of the sacred bedchamber.]. He made Phocas δομέστικος μέγας (*domestikos megas*), “great domesticus,” that is, commander of the land army. Romanus, however, not distinguished by the nobility of his birth but by the magnanimity of his heart, he appointed δελουγάρης τῆς πλόως (*delongarēs tēs ploōs*), that is, commander of the naval army [Note: [Col. 0845] I write it thus; in the manuscript the preceding words are in Latin.].
