Alexander soon died, leaving the empire to the boy Constantine alone (A.D. 913). At the time when the great emperor Leo departed to Christ, the aforementioned Phocas, the *domesticus* and commander of the land army, had led forces against Simeon, king of the Bulgarians, and had resisted him with no little courage when he wished to come to Constantinople [Col. 0845D].

But Romanus, being no fool, heard of the deaths of the emperors—Leo and Alexander—gathered a fleet not far from the city, and came to a small island near Constantinople, assembling his ships in such a way that the island could almost be seen from the palace (A.D. 919). He did not cross over to the palace, however, nor did he sing the customary praises to the Porphyrogenitus. This caused no small astonishment and fear to the eunuch *parakoimomenos* and to all the leaders of Constantinople.

Through intermediaries they asked what this strange thing meant: why he had not approached the emperor [Note: [Col. 0845] *audierit* in witness 1.] and had not paid the customary praises [Note: [Col. 0846] That is, “he inquired.”]. Romanus replied that, fearing for his life, he had avoided the palace. He added that, unless the *parakoimomenos* came to him together with the other leaders and swore to guarantee him life and honor, he would immediately go over to the king of the Cretan Saracens and, through the strength of his assistance, wage war against the kingdom of the Argives. How craftily he said this, the outcome will show.

Thus, as we said, the leaders, driven by terror and unaware that a snake lay hidden in the grass, all approached him confidently, eager to carry out what he had commanded. He, having accepted their proposal—not a good one—bound them all after throwing them into a sewer; then, secure, he hastened to the city with a great retinue. He cleared the palace of those whom he suspected and installed there those who obeyed his party [Note: [Col. 0845] *paroentes* in witness 1, written by a second hand.] [Note: [Col. 0846D] That is, “those who obeyed his party.”]. He made his own the rector, the magistrates, the patricians, the *logothete*, the *eparch*, the *kitonitai*, the chamberlains, the *protospatharii*, *spatharii*, *spatharocandidati*, and *parathalassitai*; the others, as we have said, he removed.

To establish more firmly what he had begun, he also joined himself in a marriage of delightful pleasure to Ζοη (*Zōē*), the mother of the Porphyrogenitus [Note: [Col. 0845] I write it *Zoi*; *Zoi* in the manuscript, *zoē* in witness 1; the letter *i* is in a place scraped by a second hand.] [Note: [Col. 0845] The following material through IV.6 is absent from witnesses 1; no lacuna is indicated in witness 3.]. Soon the whole city was crowned, and everyone called Romanus “father-emperor.”

### 27

While Phocas the *domesticus* was fighting the Bulgarians—and he too ardently desired to become “father-emperor”—he had already gained a victory over the enemy in the battle when news was brought to him of what Romanus had done. Immediately thrown into confusion and overcome by immense grief, he cast away the standard by which he had been pursuing the enemy, turned his back, and made his men begin to flee.

The Bulgarians therefore recovered their courage at Simeon’s urging and pursued those from whom they had earlier fled under adverse fortune, now under favorable fortune. So great a slaughter of the Achaeans then took place that, long afterward, the field could still be seen covered with bones.

### 28

The aforementioned Phocas the *domesticus* returned to Constantinople with all possible haste. He desired to enter the palace and strove by force, not by craft, to become “father-emperor” [Col. 0846D]. But since force, lacking counsel, collapses under its own weight, and, as Flaccus says [Note: [Col. 0846D] *Odes* III.4.63],

> The gods raise the measured man to greater things,

this *domesticus* was captured by Romanus and deprived of both eyes. The power of the Bulgarians increased greatly [Col. 0847A], and double retribution was paid to the Greeks for their ravaging.

### 29

They said that this Simeon was ἡμίἀργων (*emiargon*), that is, “half-Greek,” because from childhood at Byzantium he had learned the rhetoric of Demosthenes and the syllogisms of Aristotle. Afterward, however, abandoning his studies of the arts, he is said to have assumed the habit of holy religious life. But shortly afterward, deceived by his desire to reign, he passed from the peaceful quiet of the monastery into the storm of the world and chose instead the apostate Julian rather than follow the most blessed Peter, the key-bearer of the heavenly kingdom.

He had two sons: one named Bajan, and the other, who survives to this day and powerfully rules the Bulgarians, named Peter [Note: [Col. 0847D] A.D. 927–969.]. Bajan, however, had learned magic so thoroughly [Note: [Col. 0847] that is, “almost.”] that you might see him suddenly become a wolf from a man, or transform into any beast whatsoever.

### 30

In the same year in which Romanus was made “father-emperor” [Note: [Col. 0847] *constitus* in witness 1.], he gave his daughter Helena in marriage to the boy emperor, his lord, Constantine Porphyrogenitus. I call him “Porphyrogenitus” not because he was born in purple, but because he was born in the house called the Porphyra, as we wrote above.

And since the matter has come before us, let it not weary me to report again what we have heard about the birth of this Porphyrogenitus, just as you will find it written in the earlier book, in the same words, under chapters 6, 7, 8, 9, and 10 [Note: [Col. 0847] The words *iterum* and what follows were added by a second hand in witness 1.].

### 31

The emperor Augustus Constantine, from whose name the city Constantinople received its designation, ordered τὸν οἶκον τοῦτον (*ton oikon touton*), “this house,” to be built, and gave it the name Porphyra. He wished the offspring of his noble line who would succeed him to come into the light there, so that those born from his stock would be called by this splendid name, Porphyrogeniti.

For this reason some say that this Constantine, the son of the emperor Leo, derives his origin from his blood. But the truth of his birth is this:

Τῆς γενέσεως δὲ αὐτοῦ ἡ ἀλήθεια αὕτη ἐστίν  
*Tēs geneseōs de autou hē alētheia hautē estin*—“But the truth of his generation is this.”

### 32

The emperor Augustus Basil, his grandfather, had been born from a humble family in Macedonia. He came down to Constantinople under the yoke of poverty in order to serve a certain ἡγούμενος (*hēgoumenos*), that is, an abbot.

The emperor who was ruling at that time, named Michael, went to that monastery for the sake of prayer. When he saw that Basil was outstanding among the others in appearance, he summoned τὸν ἡγούμενον (*ton hēgoumenon*), “the abbot,” and asked him to give him the boy. Taking him into the palace, he assigned him to the office of chamberlain [Note: [Col. 0847] *cubillarii* in witness 1.].

Before long he became so powerful that everyone called him “second emperor.” But because almighty God justly visits his servants with whatever chastisement he wills [Note: [Col. 0847] *cessura* in witness 1.], he had allowed this emperor for a time not to possess a sound mind [Col. 0848A] [Note: [Col. 0847] *mentes* in witness 1.], so that the more severely he oppressed him in the depths, the more mercifully he might reward him in the heights.

For, as the story goes [Note: [Col. 0847] Thus above, in I.9; *nam infertur* in witness 1.], during the period of this madness he even ordered his attendants to undergo the sentence of death [Note: [Col. 0847] *etia* in witness 1.]. Yet, when he came to himself, he demanded them back in this manner: unless those whom he had ordered to be slaughtered were returned, the very men who had carried this out would be condemned to the same sentence. Through this terror, those whom he had ordered to be condemned were kept alive.

But when he did this repeatedly to Basil, the men serving him received the following wicked counsel:

> “Take care lest the insane command of the king someday be deliberately carried out by men who do not serve you faithfully, but rather hate you. You should kill him instead and take up the imperial scepters.” [Note: [Col. 0847] In this word the Codex bibliothecae Caesareae Vindobonensis, *Hist. prof.* no. 178, comes to an end.]

Basil fulfilled this without delay, compelled both by fear and deceived by his desire to reign [Col. 0848B]. Having killed him, he became emperor.

### 33

After a short time, our Lord Jesus Christ appeared to him in a vision, holding the right hand of this emperor, the author of whose death Basil had been [Note: [Col. 0847] *extirat* in witness 1.], and addressing him as follows:

> “Basil, why did you kill your lord, this emperor Michael?”

When he awoke, he recognized that he was guilty of so great a crime, and, coming to himself, began to consider what he should do about it.

### 34

Strengthened by the Lord’s salutary and truly acceptable promise through the prophet—that on whatever day a sinner should groan, he would be saved (Ezek. 33:12)—he confessed with tears and groans that he was a sinner and a shedder of innocent blood [Col. 0848C].

Having accepted good counsel, he made friends for himself from the wealth of iniquity, so that, by consoling them with temporal support, he might be freed through their prayers from the eternal fire of Gehenna.

He built beside the palace, toward the east, a church of precious and marvelous workmanship in honor of the supreme prince of the heavenly army and the archangel Michael [Note: [Col. 0847] *prinpis* in witness 1.], who in Greek is called ἀρχιστράτηγος (*archistratēgos*), that is, “commander of the army.”

Some call the church itself νεάν (*nean*), that is, “new”; others call it ἐννεάν (*ennean*), which in our language signifies “nine-yearly,” because there the mechanism of the ecclesiastical hours sounds after being struck nine times.

### 35

In the second year after Romanus had been made “father-emperor,” he summoned the leaders to himself [Col. 0848D] and addressed them as follows:

> “Princes of Roman dignity—*archontes*, that is, rulers—since, after your consultation, I have been made not only ‘father-emperor,’ but also joined in marriage to the fidelity of the most holy emperor through Helena, the *glaucopis*, that is, ‘green-eyed,’ I think it worthy that this should be shown on my body by some sign of imperial adornment, since the populace celebrates it according to the name of my dignity.”

The people therefore judged, and it was decreed by common agreement, that since he possessed such dignity and had joined his daughter Helena, the *feucolenon*, that is, “white-armed,” to imperial dignity, he should wear boots of red-dyed leather, as is customary among the emperors there.

But even this did not seem sufficient to him. Indeed, after one year’s *synaxis*, when his power had already grown greater, he addressed the same leaders in these words:

> “Since by your common judgment it has been determined that I should wear imperial boots, περιφανέστατοι ἥρωες (*periphanestatoi hērōes*), that is, ‘most illustrious heroes,’ the precious gifts—ἀγλαὰ ἄπινα (*aglaa apina*), that is, ‘splendid gifts’—which the goodwill of your authority has bestowed seem, when I consider them more carefully, to make me walk like an actor or mime. Such men, in order easily to provoke crowds to laughter, paint themselves in various colors. I make others laugh, and even laugh at myself, when I seem to imitate the emperor with my feet and the common people with my head. What comedy is this? What mime could be better? Therefore either provide a crown, or take away the imperial boots in which I appear ridiculous to the people.” [Note: [Col. 0849] *riculu* in witness 1.]

Having said this—and even more because of the authority of his power over everyone—he received the crown by universal judgment (A.D. 920), while losing none of the splendor of the boots.

Let no one marvel at his prudence, but let him offer praise from the innermost heart to God, who raises up the fallen and releases the bound (Ps. 145), in whose hand is a cup of unmixed wine, full of mixture, inclining from one side to the other (Ps. 74:9) [Note: [Col. 0849] *mitti*, corrected to *mixto*, in witness 1.].

### 36

He had been born from a humble family, namely from the people of the Armenians [Col. 0849C], and had not even conceived in his mind that he would one day be in a king’s court, much less hold the imperial scepters.

But what does the prophetess Anna say?

> “The Lord makes poor, enriches, humbles, and exalts; raising the needy from the earth and lifting the poor from the dungheap, so that he may seat him with princes and hold the throne of glory. For the hinges of the earth belong to the Lord” (1 Sam. 2:7).

To him, therefore, the immortal and invisible God alone, be honor and glory throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

### 37

After Romanus had been made emperor, he made Christoforus, whom he had had before attaining imperial dignity, emperor as well. After his own imperial elevation, his wife bore him a son named Stephen. When she conceived again, she bore him another son named Constantine [Col. 0849D] [Note: [Col. 0849] The words *vocabulo* and the final words of the Codex Claustroneoburgensis end on the following page, which has been cut away.].

Having made all of them emperors, he placed himself and Christoforus, his firstborn, ahead of his own lord, the emperor Constantine Porphyrogenitus, against both law and right [Note: [Col. 0849] The Codex Vindobonensis, *Hist. prof.* no. 338, ends with this word.]. So completely did he do this that, when they proceeded εἰς τὴν πρόλημψιν (*eis tēn prolempsin*), that is, “to the public ceremony”—namely, to Hagia Sophia, or to Blachernae, or to the Holy Apostles—Romanus, together with his firstborn Christoforus, went before them, while Constantine Porphyrogenitus and the other two followed.

How indignantly the just Judge endured this, the punishment that followed made clear. For shortly afterward Christoforus died.

Constantine Porphyrogenitus, devoting himself both to prayer and to readings, commended himself entirely to the Lord and sought his livelihood by the work of his hands. He practiced τὴν ζωγραφίαν (*tēn zōgraphian*), that is, “painting,” with exceptional skill.

### 38

At the same time Simeon the Bulgarian began severely to ravage the fields [Note: [Col. 0849] So in witness 1; perhaps *Argos* should be read instead of *agros*, “fields.”]. Romanus restrained him from the fury he had begun by giving his son Christoforus’s daughter in marriage to Peter, Simeon’s son, who survives to this day, and by joining himself to him in an agreed treaty.

For this reason the girl, having changed her name, was called Irini, that is, “peace,” because through her a very firm peace was established between the Bulgarians and the Greeks [Col. 0850B] [Note: [Col. 0849] *costituta* in witness 1.].

### 39

At this time Walpertus and Gezo, surnamed Heverardus, were the most powerful judges at Pavia. The reason for Walpertus’s power was that, at Cumae, a very wealthy place, he had made his son Peter a bishop, while he had joined his daughter Rosa in marriage to Gilbert, count of the palace [Note: [Col. 0849] So in witness 1; perhaps *Gislebertus* should be read.].

At that time, however, both of them had died. All the people of Ticinum—that is, Pavia—had therefore gathered around Walpertus and deliberated all their cases and disputes before him. Because the aforementioned Gezo, surnamed Heverardus, shared in this power and was related to him by a certain affinity, he too was regarded as immensely powerful.

He disgraced his nobility by his evil conduct. He was exceedingly ambitious, greedy, envious, seditious [Col. 0850C], a corrupter of justice, and forgetful of God’s commandments. God did not allow this to go unpunished. To avoid prolonging the account, he was altogether like Catiline: just as Catiline had tried to kill the consul and defender of the republic, Marcus Tullius Cicero, so Gezo plotted to deliver King Hugh to death.

One day, while King Hugh was staying at Pavia with a few companions and suspecting no evil, Gezo, having stirred up a sedition, wished to attack him. But Walpertus, who was not of so fierce a character, delayed him and held him back.

### 40

King Hugh restrained them no less from their attempted fury by means of his rhetorical speeches, sweeter than honey. When he learned that a sedition had arisen against him and gathered in Walpertus’s house [Note: [Col. 0849] *eogretam* in witness 1.], he addressed them all through intermediaries in these words [Col. 0850D]:

> “What is the reason, brave men, that you have been stirred up so violently and unexpectedly against your lord—indeed, your king? If something has been done that displeases you, let it be repaired. For a late correction is not usually condemned, especially if no negligence has been left unaddressed.”

When they heard this, they all calmed the fury of their hearts. Gezo alone remained in the insolence he had previously displayed and worked to make them all attack the king [Col. 0851A] and torment him with the most disgraceful death. But, by God’s arrangement, his evil intention could not achieve its effect.

The messengers therefore returned to the king and reported what they had seen and heard.

### 41

King Hugh, treating all these matters in his deceitful mind as though they were nothing, left Pavia and hurried toward a distant destination. Sending letters all around [Note: [Col. 0851] So in witness 1, as also in Book II.9.], he ordered his soldiers to come to him.

Among them came the powerful Count Samson, who was already the bitterest enemy of the aforesaid Gezo. When he saw the king, he addressed him as follows:

> “I see that you are troubled by the urban affairs that have been tumultuously and vexatiously conducted against you in these days. But if you listen to me and obey me, they will be caught in their own snares. It is not easy to find another who could give better counsel than I; certainly no one will give better counsel to you yourself. I ask only one thing: when they have been captured through my agency, let Gezo, together with his entire estate (*hypostasis*), be handed over to my control.”

When the king promised that he would be handed over, Samson continued:

> “Leo, bishop of the city of Ticinum, is not a friend of Walpertus and Gezo; they oppose him in every way and by every means. You know, moreover, that it is customary for the stronger citizens to meet the king outside the city when he approaches Pavia from elsewhere. Therefore secretly instruct the bishop that, when you come to Pavia at the appointed time and they themselves come out to meet us beyond the city, he should have all the city gates shut and keep the keys for himself. Then, when we have begun to capture them, they will be unable either to flee into the city or to await assistance from the city.”

And this was done. For when the king was approaching Pavia at the appointed time and the men mentioned came out to meet him, the bishop willingly did as he had been commanded.

The king therefore ordered them all to be captured, as Samson had advised. Immediately Gezo was handed over to Samson, deprived of both eyes, and the tongue that had spoken blasphemy against the king was cut out. O that this deed had been good if, just as he was blind, he had also remained mute for all time! But alas for the crime: although his tongue had been cut out, he did not lose the power of speech, and, according to the tales of the Greeks, he prolonged his life by the loss of his eyes—a life that has not ceased to be harmful to many even to the present day.

Let us insert here, according to the foolishness of the Greeks, the amusing tale explaining why blind men live so long. It is as follows:

Ζεὺς καὶ Ἥρα ἤρισαν περὶ ἀφροδισιῶν, τὴς πλειόνα ἔχει ἥδομας ἐν τῇ συννουσῖα· καὶ τότε Τιρεσίαν Ἑβρου υἱὸν ἐζήτησαν. Οὗτος γὰρ ἐν ταῖς ἀμφοτέραις φύσεσι μεταμορφώθη, ἐπειδὴ δράκοντα ἐπάτησεν. Οὗτος οὖν κατὰ τῆς Ἥρας ἀπεφήνατο, καὶ Ἥρα ὀργισθεῖσα ἐπήρωσεν αὐτόν, Ζεὺς δὲ ἐχαρίσατο αὐτῷ πολλοῖς ζῆσαι ἔτεσι, καὶ ὅσα ἔλεγεν μαντικὰ λέγειν.

*Zeus ke Hēra ērisan peri aphrodisiōn, tēs pleiona echei hēdomas en tē synnousia; kai tote Tiresian Hebrou huion ezētēsan. Houtos gar en tais amphoterais phy sesin metamorphōthē, epei drakonta epatēsen. Houtos oun kata tēs Hēras apephēnato, kai Hēra orgistheisa epērōsen auton, Zeus de echarisato autō pollois zēsai etesi, kai hosa elegen mantika legein.*

This is the interpretation:

> Jupiter and Juno contended over sexual matters—who had more pleasures in intercourse. Then they sought Tiresias, son of Euerus. For he had been transformed into both natures because he had trodden upon a serpent. He therefore gave judgment against Juno. Juno, angered, blinded him. But Jupiter granted him many years of life and granted that whatever he said he might speak prophetically.

But let us return to the matter. As we said, Gezo, his limbs having been disfigured, was stripped of his property. Many others were handed over to imprisonment. Walpertus was beheaded the following day, and his immense treasure was plundered. His wife Cristina was captured and torn by various instruments of torture so that she would hand over the hidden treasures.

From then on the king’s fear grew not only at Pavia but throughout all the borders of Italy. No one treated him lightly, as they did other kings; rather, they honored him in every way.

### 42

At the same time Ildoinus, bishop of the church of Liège [Note: [Col. 0851D] *Leodiensis*], having been expelled from his own see (A.D. 928), came to Italy to King Hugh, to whom he was connected by a family relationship.

Received honorably by him [Note: [Col. 0851] That is, *susceptus*.], Hugh granted him the bishopric of Verona for his support and maintenance. It happened afterward that Archbishop Lampertus died and Ildoinus was ordained bishop of Milan in his place.

A certain monk named Ratherius had come with the aforementioned Ilduinus. Because of his religious devotion and his knowledge of the seven liberal arts, he was made bishop of Verona, where Milo, whom we mentioned above, was regarded as count (A.D. 932) [Col. 0852C].

### 43

Meanwhile Wido, margrave of the province of Tuscany, began to discuss intensely with his wife Marozia the deposition of Pope John. They did this because of the hatred they bore toward Peter, the pope’s brother, since the pope honored him as his own brother.

While Peter was staying at Rome, it happened that Wido secretly assembled many soldiers. One day, while the pope was in the Lateran palace with his brother and a few others, Wido’s and Marozia’s soldiers attacked them and killed Peter, the pope’s brother, before his eyes. They seized the pope himself and handed him over to custody, where he died not long afterward [Note: [Col. 0851] That is, *defunctus*.]. For they say that they placed a pillow over his mouth and thus suffocated him most cruelly.

After his death [Note: [Col. 0851D] Also after the deaths of those who had succeeded him, Leo VI and Stephen VII.] (A.D. 928), they made Marozia’s son, named John, whom the prostitute herself had borne from Pope Sergius, pope [Note: [Col. 0852D] John XI, who obtained the supreme pontificate in March of A.D. 931.].

Wido died not long afterward, and his brother Lampertus was appointed as his successor.

### 44

Marozia, a sufficiently shameless prostitute, sent her messengers to King Hugh after the death of her husband Wido (A.D. 932), inviting him to come to her and take for himself the most noble city of Rome. She declared, however, that this could not be done unless King Hugh made her his wife.

### Verses

What drove you, Marozia, compelled by Venus’s savage torches?

Behold, you gaze upon the embraces of your husband’s brother,

Striving to marry two brothers, like Herodias,

And, blind, you seem forgetful of John’s command,

Who forbade a brother to violate his brother’s wife.

These verses of Moses the prophet do not provide this for you:

He commanded a brother to produce offspring

In his brother’s name, if the first could not beget a child for himself.

Our ages know that you have borne a child by your husband.

You reply, I know: “Drunken Venus cares nothing for this.”

The desired King Hugh arrived for you, as a bull led to the altar,

Moved rather by the Roman city [Col. 0853B].

What does it profit you, polluted woman, thus to destroy a holy man?

While you strive through so great a crime to appear a queen,

You lose Rome, great in the judgment of the Lord.

That this had been rightly done was noticed not only by rational but also by irrational creatures [Note: [Col. 0853] Codex 1 seems to indicate that another chapter begins here.]. At the entrance to the city of Rome stands a fortification of marvelous workmanship and extraordinary strength; before its gate a very fine bridge has been built over the Tiber, passable both for those entering Rome and for those leaving it; nor is there any other way of crossing except by it. Yet this cannot be done without the consent of those guarding the fortification. The fortification itself—leaving aside its other features—is of such height that the church visible upon its summit, built in honor of the supreme and heavenly army’s prince, the archangel Michael, is called “the church of the holy Angel reaching to the heavens.”

Finally, King Hugh, confident in the strength of the fortification, left his army far away and came to Rome with a few men. Received suitably by the Romans, he withdrew into the aforesaid fortification, to the bedchamber of the prostitute Marozia [Note: [Col. 0853] *miretricis* in codex 1.]. Once he had obtained her incestuous embrace, he began, as though already secure, to look down upon the Romans.

Marozia had indeed had a son named Alberic, whom she had borne to Alberic the margrave. When, at his mother’s urging, he poured water for King Hugh—his stepfather, that is—to wash his hands, Hugh [Note: [Col. 0853] Codex 5 continues here.] struck him in the face as a correction because he had poured the water neither moderately nor decorously [Note: [Col. 0853] “so” in codex 1.]. To avenge the injury inflicted upon him, Alberic assembled the Romans and addressed them in the following speech:

“The dignity of the city of Rome has been reduced to such folly that it obeys even the rule of prostitutes. For what is more shameful, what more disgraceful, than that the Roman state should perish through the incest of one woman? That Romans should at some point be ruled by their own slaves—Burgundians, that is? If he struck the face of his own stepson, especially when he is regarded as a new guest, what do you think he will do to you, who are already long-established? Or are you unaware of the greed and arrogance of the Burgundians?

“Consider at least the etymology of their name [Note: [Col. 0853] *etimoligiam* in codex 1.]. They are called Burgundians because, when the Romans had conquered the world and were leading many captives from this people, they ordered them to build houses for themselves outside the city. Shortly afterward they were expelled by the Romans because of their arrogance. Since they call a collection of houses not enclosed by a wall a *burgus* [Note: [Col. 0853D] Italian *borgo*.], the Romans called them Burgundians—that is, those expelled from the *burgus* [Note: [Col. 0854D] That is, “without a *burgus*” (*ohne* in German).]. In their natural name, however, they are called Gauls, or Allobroges.

“As for me, according to the *phronesis*—that is, wisdom—that has been handed down to me [Note: [Col. 0853] Codices 5a and 5a* omit *secundum mihi traditam*.], I call them, as it were, *gurguliones*—throat-men—either because they speak from the whole throat on account of their arrogance, or, what is more accurate, because they indulge excessively in gluttony [Col. 0854B], which is practiced through the throat [Note: [Col. 0853] *edaciti* in codex 1.].”

No sooner had they heard this than all abandoned King Hugh and chose that same Alberic as their lord. Before the king could even have time to bring in his soldiers, they immediately began to attack the fortification.

### 45 [Note: [Col. 0853] Chapter XLVI in codex 1.]

It is clear that this was a plan of divine providence: what King Hugh had begun so shamefully through crime, he was by no means to be able to obtain. For he was compelled by such terror that, lowering himself by a rope from the side where the fortification was joined to the city wall, he abandoned it and fled to his own men. Thus expelled, King Hugh, together with the aforementioned Marozia, left Alberic in control of the Roman city, while his brother John occupied the see of the supreme and universal bishopric [Col. 0854C].

### 46 [Note: [Col. 0853] Chapter XLVII in codex 1.]

Some say that Berta, the mother of King Hugh, bore no son to her husband, the margrave Adelbert, but secretly obtained sons from other women and, pretending to have given birth, substituted Wido and Lambert as her own, so that after Adelbert’s death Berta would not lack sons through whose assistance she might possess all her husband’s power. This falsehood seems to me to have been invented so that King Hugh might conceal his incest by this pretext and escape the disgrace—*hybris*, that is, shame—of it.

Nevertheless, what is now to be related seems to me a more plausible explanation of why this was said. Lambert, who after the death of his brother Wido held the march of Tuscany, was a warlike man and daring in every undertaking. King Hugh was extremely suspicious of him because of the Italian kingdom. He feared that the Italians might abandon him and make Lambert king.

Finally, Boso, the king’s brother by the same father, had prepared snares of conspiracy for him, since he himself was passionately eager to become margrave of Tuscany. At his advice, therefore, King Hugh solemnly ordered Lambert not to dare any longer to call himself his brother. But Lambert, being fierce and undisciplined in spirit, replied not moderately, as he should have done, but without restraint:

“So that the king cannot deny that I am his brother, and that we came forth into the light from one and the same body by the same passage, I wish to prove this before all by single combat” [Note: [Col. 0855] *copio* in codex 1.].

When the king heard this, he chose a certain young man named Teudinus, who engaged in single combat with Lambert for this purpose. But God, who is just and whose judgment is right (Psalm 118:137), in whom there is no iniquity, caused Teudinus to fall very quickly and Lambert to obtain the victory, in order to break the ambiguity and reveal the truth to everyone. For this reason King Hugh was greatly confounded.

After taking counsel, however, he seized Lambert himself and handed him over to custody. He had feared that, if he released him, Lambert would take the kingdom from him. Having captured him, therefore, he handed the Tuscan march over to his brother Boso; and not long afterward he deprived Lambert of his sight.

### 47

At this time the Italians sent to Burgundy for Rudolf, asking him to come. When King Hugh learned this, he sent messengers to Rudolf and gave him all the territory in Gaul that he had held before assuming the kingdom [Note: [Col. 0855] *suseptionem* in codex 1.]. From him he also obtained an oath that he would never come to Italy.

He had likewise made Henry, whom we mentioned above, the most powerful king, his friend by presenting him with many gifts. Henry’s name was then especially renowned among the Italians because he alone had defeated and made tributaries of the Danes, who had previously been subject to no one (A.D. 934). They are an untamed people dwelling beneath the north in the ocean, whose savagery has often caused the nobility of many peoples to mourn.

At one time they ascended the Rhine in fleets, following the violent river channel, and horribly tore everything apart with iron and fire. They also conquered by force and captured the most noble cities themselves—Agrippina, now called Cologne, and Trier, situated far from the Rhine—as well as several others in the kingdom of Lothar. After taking everything away, they burned whatever they could not carry off with them. They also burned the baths of the palace of Grannus, and the palaces [Note: [Col. 0855D] Compare the Annals of Vedastinus, whose wording—“the palaces of kings and the villas also were consumed by fire”—may perhaps have occasioned the plural *palatia* here instead of *palatium*.]. But, leaving this aside, let us return to the sequence of the narrative.

[Col. 0856A] ### 48

Arnald, duke of the Bavarians and Carantanians, whom we mentioned above, since he was not far from Italy, arrived with his forces in order to take the kingdom from Hugh (A.D. 935). Passing through the march of Trent, the first part of Italy on that side, he reached as far as Verona. There he was gladly received by Count Milo and Bishop Rather, since they had invited him. When King Hugh heard this, he gathered an army and advanced to meet him.

### 49

When he had reached the same place and was sending cavalry detachments—“horse-rides,” as they commonly say—around in every direction, a considerable part of the Bavarians, coming out from a fortress called Gauseningo, began to fight with the Italians. They were severely pierced by the Italians, and scarcely one escaped who could report what had happened to the others. As a result, Duke Arnald was filled with no small confusion.

### 50 [Note: [Col. 0855] I begin chapter 50 here, following the index.]

It therefore happened [Note: [Col. 0855] *factutu* in codex 1.] that, after taking counsel, he wished to seize Count Milo and take him with him into Bavaria, abandoning Italy, so that, after restoring his army, he could return with him again. Milo was not unaware of this.

### 51

Agitated by various thoughts, Milo was utterly uncertain what to do. He was afraid to approach King Hugh, plainly as he deserved; but to be taken with Arnald into Bavaria he regarded as nothing less than death and hell. In this uncertainty, since he knew that King Hugh was quickly inclined to mercy, he resolved to flee from Arnald and make his way to him.

Arnald, however, returned to Bavaria as quickly as he could. First attacking the fortification that stood in the same city, he took with him into Bavaria Milo’s brother and the soldiers who had tried to defend it.

### 52 [Note: [Col. 0855] In codex 1 this chapter begins already at the word *Munitionem*.]

When Arnald departed [Note: [Col. 0855] *discedente* appears as *discente* in codex 1.], the city was soon restored to King Hugh. Rather, the bishop of that same city, was captured by him and confined in exile at Pavia. There he began to compose, with quite entertaining wit, a book about the misery of his exile. Anyone who reads it will find there certain events polished through this occasion, which may please readers’ understanding no less than they benefit it.

[Col. 0855] **THE THIRD BOOK OF THE ANTAPODOSIS ENDS.**

# [BOOK FOUR]

## THE CHAPTERS OF THE FOURTH BOOK BEGIN

[Col. 0855D] 1. What he has heard and written up to now; what he is about to write [Note: [Col. 0855] *amodo* in codex 1; a second hand deleted the line with two transverse strokes, so that codex 2 may have read *ciamodo*.] he has seen.

2. King Hugh makes his son Lothar king and advances to Rome with an army.

3. King Hugh gives his daughter in marriage to Alberic in order to deceive him through her.

4. The Saracens come from Fraxinetum to the Baths, where they all perish in battle.

5. A fountain of blood flowed in the city of Genoa, which was captured by the African Saracens in that year.

6. How Manasses, bishop of Arles, says that he abandoned his own church and assumed another, and how it is proved by testimonies from Scripture, in an invective reply, that he did not act rightly.

7. Whom Berengar took as his wife, and concerning his brother Anscarius.

8. Concerning Tedbald the margrave, who fought against the Greeks and castrated those whom he captured.

9. By what great mockery a certain woman freed her husband from being castrated.

10. King Hugh seized his brother Boso, who had become treacherous to him at the counsel of his wife, and handed him over to custody.

11. How King Hugh expelled Willa, Boso’s wife, from Italy, and concerning a belt found in a shameful place.

12. Concerning the death of King Rudolf, whose wife King Hugh married, and how he gave Rudolf’s daughter to his own son.

13. Concerning King Hugh, who hated his wife because of his concubines.

14. Concerning the death of King Henry, where he was buried, and his sons.

15. Concerning the prudence of King Henry, who made his son Otto king.

16. Concerning the daughter of the brother of the king of the English, whom King Otto married before assuming the kingdom.

17. Concerning Henry, who, at the counsel of wicked men, rebels against his brother.

18. A metrical invective addressed to Henry, and against the devil, through whose work he desires to fight with his brother.

[Col. 0857C] 19. Concerning Heverard, who, at the beginning of his rebellion, captured Henry, still faithful to his king and brother, while he was living in a certain castle, and led him into Gaul.

20. By what means Heverard separated Gislebert from loyalty to the king.

[Col. 0858A] 21. Gislebert and Heverard release Henry from custody.

22. By what cunning Heverard attempted to deceive Henry and Gislebert while acquiring the kingdom.

23. Concerning the remarkable victory that King Otto obtained by prayer, and concerning Henry, who was wounded in the arm [Note: [Col. 0857] *brahio* in codex 1.].

24. How King Henry acquired the holy lance.

25. An argument from Holy Scripture that this victory, or war, occurred not by chance but by God’s arranging.

26. Concerning the many who abandoned the king while he was besieging the fortress of Brisach, at the counsel of Archbishop Frederick [Note: [Col. 0857] *briuicau* in codex 2.].

27. Concerning the remarkable steadfastness and reply of King Otto.

28. How, with God fighting for the king, Gislebert and Heverard were killed by Huto and Chuonrad at Andernach.

29. Concerning the messenger who announces their death to the king while he was going to church.

30. King Otto announces to Bertold, duke of the Bavarians, the death of these men and his willingness to give Bertold either his own sister or his sister’s daughter as wife.

31. Concerning Archbishop Frederick, who had long since abandoned the king and went to the city of Metz to gather an army, where he heard of their deaths [Note: [Col. 0857] The first letter of the word is scarcely distinguishable. *Exercitu* has been erased from the line in codex 1.].

[Col. 0858C] 32. Concerning the same archbishop, captured and handed over to custody.

33. Concerning Henry, who is prevented by his sister from entering fortifications against the king.

34. Concerning the same man, who afterward comes to the king’s mercy.

[Col. 0857] **THE CHAPTERS END.**

## THE FOURTH BOOK HAPPILY BEGINS

[Col. 0857D] ### 1

Up to this point, most holy priest, I have set forth what I heard from very weighty men who had seen these things [i.e. *viderant*]; but what is now to be narrated I shall explain as one who was present. At that time I was of such standing that I acquired King Hugh’s favor through the sweetness of my voice. For he valued euphony—[that is, greatly]—so highly that none of the boys of my own age could surpass me in it.

### 2

Accordingly, when King Hugh saw everything prospering for him, he established his son Lothar, whom he had begotten by his wife Alda, as king after himself, with everyone consenting (A.D. 931, May 15). Once this had been done, he considered how he might obtain Rome, from which he had been disgracefully expelled. Gathering a multitude, he set out for Rome. Although he brutally devastated its surrounding places and provinces and attacked the city itself daily, he could not achieve the result of entering it.

### 3

Finally, hoping that through his cunning he could deceive Alberic, he ordered him to take his daughter Alda—full sister of his son Lothar, the king—in marriage, so that, with peace established, his own son might remain secure. Alberic, therefore, like a foolish man, joined her to himself in marriage, but did not surrender Rome, for which he was burning with desire, and placed no trust in Hugh.

King Hugh would indeed have ensnared and captured Alberic by this means, **τούτῳ τῷ * ἀγκήστρῳ**, *toto to agkistro*, “by this hook,” if his own soldiers had not prevented it through their treachery, since they did not wish him ever to make peace with Alberic. Whenever the king wished to punish one of his men, that man immediately hastened to Alberic, by whom, out of fear of the king, he was gladly received and lived honorably at Rome.

### 4

While these things were happening, the Saracens inhabiting Fraxinetum, having gathered a multitude, had advanced as far as *Aquas* (the Baths), fifty miles distant from Pavia. Their *πρώβωλος*, *provolos*, that is, their leader, was the utterly wicked and impious Saracen Sagittus. Yet, with God propitious, when battle was joined, he himself, *ταλέπορος*, *taleporos*, that is, “wretched,” perished with all his men.

### 5

At about the same time, in the city of Genoa, which is in the Cottian Alps, eight hundred *stadia* distant from Pavia and situated above the African Sea, a fountain flowed very abundantly with blood, clearly announcing the ruin that was about to follow for everyone. For in that same year the Carthaginians arrived there with a multitude of ships and, while the citizens were unaware, entered the city. They slaughtered everyone except children [Note: [Col. 0859] *exeptis* in codex 1.] and women, loaded all the treasures of the city and of God’s churches onto their ships, and returned to Africa.

### 6

At this time Manasses, bishop of the city of Arles, having recognized the power of King Hugh, from whose family line he himself drew his blood through kinship [Note: [Col. 0859] *afinitatis* in codex 1.], abandoned the church entrusted to him and, driven by ambition, went to Italy to violate—or rather tear apart—many churches [Note: [Col. 0859] *ui uiolaturus* is marked by two lines in codex 1.].

King Hugh, hoping to possess the kingdom more securely if he granted offices of the realm to those related to him, against right and justice entrusted—or, more accurately, gave as bait—the churches of Verona, Trent, and Mantua. Not content even with these, he acquired the march of Trent, so that, under the devil’s prompting, he might begin to be a soldier and cease to be a bishop.

It is pleasing, holy father—*agie*, that is, “holy”—to linger briefly over this matter and, by God’s grace [Note: [Col. 0859] *largente* in codex 1.], to refute his own assertion by its own terms:

“Blessed Peter, after establishing the church at Antioch, later flew to the city of Rome, which then ruled all nations by the greatness of its power. There, when by God’s providence he had founded a holy church revered throughout the whole world, he entrusted the former church, that of Antioch, to his disciple, blessed Mark the Evangelist; yet he himself first established the church of Aquileia and then hastened to Alexandria. We know that no one who has read their deeds can fail to know that this happened so.”

But so that you, O Manasses, may recognize through our reply that you do not hold a true opinion about these matters, you will understand that your parents, observing the meaning of your name, gave a prophetic sign. For *Manasseh* is interpreted as “forgetful” or “forgetfulness of the Lord.” What could your parents [Note: [Col. 0859] Codex 3 continues here.]—that is, the prophets—have foretold more truly or clearly under this name? You are so forgetful of yourself, I say, that you do not even remember that you are a human being.

The devil knows the Scriptures; yet, being perverse, he interprets them perversely, and when he uses them, does so for destruction, not salvation. Do you know how, when he impiously attempted to wound our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ with the arrows of temptation, he misused these prophetic words?

“For he will command his angels concerning you, and they will lift you up in their hands, lest you ever strike your foot against a stone” (Luke 4).

No believer doubts that this is written and spoken about him. But you may observe how fraudulently that Leviathan uttered these true words from the response of the one who surpasses the understanding not only of mortals but also of angels: “You shall not tempt the Lord your God,” he said.

You too, therefore, see that you use true but fraudulent assertions, just as the apostate Julian is said to have replied to Christians whom he defrauded of their property through his greed for plunder: “Do not possess gold or silver,” says your master [Note: [Col. 0859] *possidete* in codex 1.]. And also: *Εὐκοπώτερον γάρ ἐστην κάμηλον διὰ τρυμαλίας ραφίδος εἰστελθεὶν ἢ πλουσιον εἰς τὴν βασιλεῖαν τοῦ Θεοῦ*, *eucopoteron gar estin camilon dia trimalias rafidos iselthin i plusion is tin basilian tu theu*, that is: “It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God” (Mark 10:25).

And likewise: “Whoever does not renounce all that he possesses [Note: [Col. 0859] *posidet* in codex 1.] cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:33).

Come then [*Cedo*], what could that man be thought to have said more perversely or more shamefully than you? For what Peter directs toward righteousness, you turn toward guilt. I am confident [Note: [Col. 0859] Codex 3 notes that he certainly did not say *τὴν πρᾶξιν τῶν ἀποστόλων*, “the deed of the apostles.”] that you did not understand the Acts of the Apostles—or, what is more believable, that you did not read them at all.

There you will plainly find written that the faithful sold their estates and laid the price at the apostles’ feet, that they held everything in common (Acts 2:35), and that no one claimed anything as his own; rather, it was distributed to each according to his need (Acts 4:45).

If, therefore, Peter refused to touch gold—the most precious thing in human wealth and dearer to you than your own soul—as though it were something deadly, by what reasoning do you claim that, after abandoning Antioch, he flew to the church at Rome? If you accuse him of having sought wealth—which is entirely false—I affirm that he sought the gain of souls and glorious martyrdom.

For his master—indeed, his creator and redeemer—had foretold this to him:

“When you were younger, you girded yourself and walked wherever you wished; but when you grow old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish to go.”

He said this to signify by what death he would glorify God (John 21:18). Finally, in another place, after the resurrection, when Peter asked the Lord where he was going, the Lord is read to have replied: “To Rome, to be crucified again.”

Peter therefore came, not puffed up by ambition but animated by martyrdom; not seeking gold but the gain of souls. O fortunate—or rather blessed—would you be if your conscience bore witness that you were such a man!

Nor, I say, can you deny that you did not sell the bishopric of Verona, something we have never learned happened to Peter—not to just anyone, but to that apostle [Note: [Col. 0861] That is, “to that one.”]. From this we have learned that you were deprived not only of spiritual but also of bodily honor, through the animation of wealth [Note: [Col. 0861] That is, because he was animated by wealth and was greedier for wealth.].

For now, let these remarks suffice as we return to the subject, until, God granting it, we come in its proper place to explain how you usurped the see of Milan.

### 7

At that time [Note: [Col. 0861] Codex 3 reads: *ουτος ὁ Υεριγγεριος ουτου τυρανρηδσω αλη η ιταλαω νω eporegie* (materially corrupt).] this Berengar, whose tyranny now causes all Italy to mourn, was considered margrave of Ivrea. King Hugh gave him his niece, named Willa, as wife. She was the daughter of Boso, margrave of the province of Tuscany and the king’s brother, whom he had begotten by his wife Willa.

Anscarius, Berengar’s brother, whom Hermengarda, the sister of King Hugh, had borne to Adelbert, was distinguished for courage, power, and boldness.

### 8

There was also a certain nobleman named Tedbald [Note: [Col. 0861] *Thiedbaldus* in codex 5.], closely related to King Hugh by near kinship. He was margrave of Camerino and Spoleto. He went to the aid of the prince of Benevento against the Greeks, who had grievously oppressed him. When he brought war against them, he gained the victory.

It happened that he captured many Greeks who had by then seized not fields but camps. While he was cutting off their manhood, he sent the following message to the commander in charge of them:

“Since I have learned that nothing is more precious to your holy emperor than eunuchs, I have taken care to send him these few, modestly enough; with God’s favor I shall send more as quickly as possible.”

### 9

Let us insert here the mockery—or rather wisdom—that a certain woman displayed at that time. One day, when the Greeks went out with the inhabitants of that land from a certain fortress to fight against the aforementioned Tedbald, some of them were captured by him.

While he was castrating them and sending them into the castle, a certain woman, burning with love for her husband and deeply anxious about his limbs [Note: [Col. 0861] *sollita* in codex 1.], rushed out of the castle in a frenzy, her hair disheveled. Tearing her face with bloody fingernails and weeping before Tedbald’s tent in loud cries, she was asked:

“Woman, what is the reason that you complain in such resounding tones?”

She replied—as it is the height of prudence to pretend stupidity when circumstances require it:

“This is a new and unheard-of crime, noble sir: that you wage war against women who are not fighting back. None of us traces her ancestry from the blood of the Amazons; devoted only to Minerva’s works, we are utterly ignorant of arms.”

When Tedbald said to her, “What sane-minded nobleman, except in the time of the Amazons, has ever waged war against women?” she replied:

“Tell me, what could be more cruelly done to women, or what more harmful thing could you take from them, than to fight their husbands in order to cut off their testicles [*orchidia*] [Col. 0862A]? In them lie the refreshment of our bodies and, most important of all, the hope of offspring yet to be born.

“When you castrate them, you take away not what belongs to them but what belongs to us. Was it the abundance of cattle or sheep that you took from me the day before yesterday that forced me to come to your camp? I commend the losses of animals that you inflicted upon me; but this loss, so great, so cruel, and so irreparable, I abhor, flee, and reject in every way. Holy men of God, all of you, avert such a plague from me!”

When they heard this, everyone was stirred to overwhelming laughter, and such favor for her arose among the people [Note: [Col. 0861] Codex 3 omits what follows through “into Saxony” in chapter 14, without indicating any lacuna.] that she was deemed worthy to recover not only her husband intact but also all the animals that had been taken from her.

When she was leaving with these things restored, Tedbald sent a boy after her and asked what she would have taken from her husband if he came out of the castle to fight against him again.

“His eyes,” she replied, “his nostrils, his hands, and his feet. If he does that, let him take away what belongs to him; let him leave what belongs to me, his little maidservant.”

But because she understood that, through her first speech, laughter and the gift of her husband had won her the people’s favor, she later sent back this reply through a direct messenger.

### 10

At about the same time, King Hugh’s brother Boso, urged on by his exceedingly greedy wife Willa [Note: [Col. 0861] *cupudissima* in codex 1.], undertook to do certain new and perverse things against the king. Hugh was not unaware of this. He was therefore seized and immediately handed over to custody.

The cause of his downfall was as follows. When Boso had obtained the Tuscan march after Lambert, whom we mentioned above, had been deprived of his sight, his wife Willa began to burn with a love of money, to such an extent that no noblewoman in the entire province of Tuscany, whatever her wealth, adorned herself with ornaments of such value.

Although she had no male offspring, she had four daughters: Berta, Willa, Richilda, and Gisla. Of these, Willa—truly the wife of the Berengar who still survives—accomplished this much: she ensured that her mother was not the worst of all women. To avoid setting down her deeds through lengthy circumlocutions, one extremely shameful example will allow you to perceive what sort and degree they were in the others.

### 11

Her husband Boso possessed a golden belt of remarkable length and breadth, which shone with the brilliance of many precious gems [Note: [Col. 0861] *spendebat* in codex 1.]. When Boso was captured, the king ordered that it be diligently sought above all his treasures. After taking the wealth, he ordered his wife, as a profane woman and the author of every crime, to be shamefully expelled from the Italian kingdom and led into Burgundy, from which she had originated.

But when the messengers, having carefully searched everything, did not find the belt, they returned to Hugh carrying the rest of the report. Then the king said:

“Return, overturn all the equipment of her saddle-cloths, and also the cushion that she presses while riding. If you cannot find the belt even there, strip all her clothing from her, so that it cannot be hidden anywhere upon her. I know how cunning and how greedy she is.”

When they returned and obeyed the king’s order, they found nothing in all their searching and stripped her of all her clothing. Since no respectable person could look upon such a shameful and unheard-of deed except with averted eyes, one of the servants, staring directly, saw a purple, spindle-shaped strap hanging beside her buttocks. Seizing it impudently and pulling it disgracefully, he drew the belt out from the innermost part of her body.

The same servant, not only shameless but made even more cheerful by that very disgraceful deed, said:

“Ha! Ha! He! What a skilled soldier in midwifery! A red-haired boy has been born to our mistress; I pray that he may survive [Note: [Col. 0863] Compare Terence.]. O fortunate me—indeed, happier than everyone—if only my wife would bear me at least two such sons! I would send them as messengers to Constantinople, since, as I have learned from merchants, the emperor gladly receives messengers of this kind.”

Confounded by such words, Willa burst into tears and revealed to everyone the grief hidden in her heart. But the servant, as is customary with people of his kind, was not softened by her humiliation; rather, he was emboldened, and added the following to deepen the wound of her sorrow:

**Verses**

“Willa, why do you rave? Why do you begin to hide gold

[Col. 0863C] In your blind members? O unheard-of desire!

Driven by Alecto’s furies, you conceal gems in your body [Note: [Col. 0863] *cordis* in codices 1 and 2.].

It is strange for mothers to produce such offspring;

No ten months of pregnancy had brought you such disgust.

Nurturing mother, do not cease to bear us such offspring,

Who, once born, may outlive you, their parent!”

As she hesitated, one energetic man struck her neck and condemned her with bitter words.

When these things had been done, the belt was brought to the king, and she was sent to Burgundy. Whether the woman who hid it or the man who ordered the search acted more shamefully, seems to me indeed ambiguous. It is clear, however, that both were driven by excessive greed for gold and gems.

### 12

Moreover, Rudolf, king of the Burgundians, died (A.D. 937, September). After Alda, the mother of his son King Lothar, had died, King Hugh joined Rudolf’s widow, named Berta, to himself in marriage. He also took as wife for his son, King Lothar, Rudolf’s daughter by Berta, named Adeleid, a woman both most distinguished in appearance and gracious in the uprightness of her character (December).

This seems improper to all Greeks: namely, that if the father takes the mother as wife, although the two are one, the son should be able to join the daughter to himself in marriage without guilt.

### 13

Finally, Hugh, deceived by the allurements of many concubines, not only ceased to love his aforementioned wife Berta with marital affection but began to hate her in every way. How justly God punished this, I shall not hesitate to set forth in its proper place.

Although he had several concubines, he burned with the most shameful love for three above the others: Pezola, born of the blood of the vilest servants [Note: [Col. 0863] *servorum* appears as *sueuorum* in codex 5a.], by whom he also fathered a son named Boso, whom the Church ordained bishop at Piacenza after Wido’s death [Note: [Col. 0863D] In A.D. 945, on March 11, Wido was still alive; in the following year, on February 14, we find Boso as bishop. Campi, *Hist. di Piacenza* [*History of Piacenza*] I, 488; I, 263.];

then Roza, daughter of the aforementioned Walpert, who had been beheaded, and who bore him a daughter of extraordinary beauty;

and third, Stephania, a Roman by birth, who also bore a son named Tedbald. He later made this son archdeacon in the church of Milan, intending that, when the archbishop died, Tedbald himself should be installed as his vicar.

What it was, however, that prevented God from allowing this to be accomplished, the order of events, with life as my companion, will reveal in writing.

The people also called these women by the names of goddesses because of their shameful immorality: Pezola Venus, Roza Juno, because of the rivalry and perpetual hatred between them—for Roza appeared more beautiful than Stephania according to the corruption of the flesh—and Stephania Semele. Since it was not the king alone who made use of them, their children trace their origin to uncertain fathers.

[Col. 0864C] ### 14

At that time King Henry, seized by a very serious illness in a castle on the border of Thuringia and Saxony called Himenleve [Note: [Col. 0864D] Memleben.], departed to the Lord (A.D. 936, July 2). His body was carried to Saxony [Note: [Col. 0863] Codex 3 continues at this word.] and, with immense veneration, placed inside the church of the most noble and religious monastery of women, plainly situated on the estate of that same king at a place called Quitelingburg [Note: [Col. 0864D] Quedlinburg.].

There his venerable wife and partner in the kingdom, Machtild, of the same people, continues to offer, beyond all the noblewomen I have seen or heard of, a celebrated funeral office for the expiation of sins and a living sacrifice to God [Note: [Col. 0863] *desinet* corrected to *desinit* in codex 1; *desinat* in codex 2; *desinit* in codices 5a and 5a*; Hervagius reads *desivit*.] [Note: [Col. 0864D] She died on March 14, A.D. 968.].

Before he assumed the kingdom, she bore her husband a son whom she named Otto—this Otto, I say, under whose rule the northern and western regions of the world are governed by power, pacified by wisdom, gladdened by religion, and terrified by the severity of just judgment.

After he had attained royal dignity, she bore two more: one whom she named after his father, Henry, endowed with considerable charm, prudent in counsel, and attractive in the brightness of his face, peaceful in the watchfulness of his eyes [Col. 0865A]. For his recent funeral [Note: [Col. 0865D] A.D. 955, November 1.] we still shed no insignificant tears.

Then the other, named Bruno [Note: [Col. 0865D] He died on October 11, A.D. 965.]. Because the Normans had utterly destroyed the church at Utrecht, his holy father wished him to serve in its recovery.

But so that we may explain the deeds of these men more fully in their proper places, let us return to the subject.

### 15. How great King Henry’s prudence and learning were

How great was King Henry’s prudence and learning can be proved from this: he made the most excellent and religious of his sons king. For, most prudent king, the downfall of the entire people was threatening at your death, if so great a successor had not assumed the royal dignity. Therefore, in praise of both, we compose these verses:

He himself who once was accustomed to overcome impious nations  
In bloody war—we now know, O king,  
How many ruins you gave the people  
By your own death.

The throng, striving with one another, widowed of its dear  
King, should now cease to weep, since  
Another, revered throughout the world, arises,  
A son like his father in shining renown:

King Otto, who with great authority  
Will crush the nations and bring blessed peace.

Whatever perished with Henry’s departure,  
This man restored to the peoples at his illustrious birth:  
Gentle, mild, and patient toward the holy,  
But destructive, harsh, and raging toward the cruel.  
[Note: *duris* (“the harsh”) in 5a.]

Many wars must be waged by you;  
From them, bearing your name to the stars,  
You will trample beneath your feet throughout the world  
All that slow-radiant Boötes presses down,  
And all to which the nourishing Hesperus gave its name:

That same star, again called Lucifer,  
Rises, hastening with radiant dawn.

[Note: “Rises,” that is, “with dawn”: *cum eoo* in 2; “rises,” but with *cum eoo* in 5a; the word *voce* is supplied, with *s.* understood as *scilicet* (“namely”), and *mare* understood.]  
[Note: The final syllable of this word has the superscript *sa* in witnesses 1 and 2.]

### 16.

Before assuming the kingship, that same King Otto had taken as his wife from the most noble English people the daughter of King Athelstan’s brother [Note: Athelstan’s sister], named Otgith; by her he fathered a son named Liutolf. Whenever we recall him because of his recent loss [Note: 6 September 957], we fill our bosoms with tears. Oh, if only he had never been born, or had not died so prematurely!

### 17. (A.D. 939)

At that time King Henry’s brother opposed him excessively, instigated by certain wicked men. He, who immediately after his creation had wished to make himself like his Creator in the most illustrious dignity, stirred Henry against his brother—indeed, against his king and lord [Note: Namely, against his fidelity]—through his agents with words such as these:

“Do you think that your father acted rightly, when, although you were born to royal dignity, he proposed another who was not born to the same dignity? Clearly, he did not weigh this with the judgment of discernment, but went astray through the magnitude of his passion. Therefore act—for you will not lack resources: overthrow your brother, seize the kingdom, and let the power of reigning belong to you, since, by God’s generosity, birth in that same dignity has fallen to your lot.”

### Verses

What such savage desire for kingship in you, young man,  
Best of the Saxon race? God forbids it—  
Not father Henry, for he gave the scepters;  
The good and merciful star-ruling God himself warned you,  
Without whom neither is a kingdom seized nor are times brought to a halt.

Whatever occurs in the world, God commands;  
Through him rulers see justice and kings triumph.

Now, now you wickedly desire to clash with your brother’s armies,  
Deceitful, cruel, unjust?

+ Impious Leviathan, Behemoth, you prepare  
To renew the ancient conflict by your fraud.

For this one crime you shall pay the penalty;  
Because, condemned by the number of the wicked,  
You have sinned in this age, you shall suffer punishment together.  
And all the fiery bonds owed to the wicked—  
You have earned them, miserable man; nor,  
Rightly plunged into the fire-belching waters of hell [Note: Thus it must be supplied in 5a; “to the shadows” in 3],  
Will you drag with you Christians who will burn with you forever—  
For if those washed in sacred baptism  
Have afterward incurred debts, the grace of God remains,  
Which has raised the fallen by freely given blood.

### 19.

Heverard the count proved to be the instigator of this great and disastrous crime. During the first rebellion (in the year 938), Henry had given his brother, his king and lord, the assistance he owed him, and with all his strength harassed his adversaries. But because negligence sometimes prepares a fall not only for those devoted to temporal affairs but also for those devoted to eternal matters and established in the very vision of inward contemplation—and, as Vegetius Renatus says in his book on military affairs [Note: Book III, chapter 22], “the security that is necessarily greater is accustomed to involve the graver danger”—the aforesaid Heverard besieged Henry, who was staying in a certain town and guarding himself carelessly, with a gathered multitude; before his brother the king could come to his aid, he stormed it and carried Henry himself, together with no small amount of treasure, into his own territory. The king, therefore, wishing to avenge so great a disgrace against his brother—or rather against himself—pursued the aforesaid Heverard and those who were allied with him with all his might.

### 20.

Heverard had indeed detached Gislebert, duke of the Lotharingians, from the king’s allegiance, and with his assistance resisted the king not a little. Although Gislebert had the king’s sister as his wife, he nevertheless, encouraged by hope of obtaining the kingdom, preferred to resist the king rather than assist him, as he ought, against his rivals. But when they saw that they could not resist the king even in this way, they adopted a plan that was not unskilful according to human judgment [Note: *incalide* (“not craftily”) in 1], but foolish according to God, and addressed Henry in these words.

[Note: From here, line 6 of folio 64 through the end of the first page of folio 65, Liudprand himself wrote.]

### 21.

“If you promise us by oath that you will obey our counsels, we will not only release you because you have been captured, but—what is more—if you nevertheless wish to become king, we will make you our lord.”

They did not say this because they intended to do it, but so that with his assistance they might more easily defeat the king.

### 22.

The king plainly had several very powerful forces: namely, Herimann, duke of the Swabians; his brother Huto; and Chuonrad, surnamed the Wise. Although they were connected to Heverard by ties of kinship, they nevertheless preferred, if necessity should arise [Note: The words *si … c. r. o. q. i.* are missing in witnesses 2 and 3], to fall justly with the just king rather than triumph unjustly with their kinsman.

Henry, therefore, deceived by the promise already made, soon gathered his own forces, began to assist them with all his strength, and attacked the king (in the year 939). But since it is written, “Iniquity has lied to itself” (Psalm 26:15), let us linger briefly and explain how iniquity then lied to itself.

Heverard could not separate Gislebert from the king’s loyalty until he promised to make him king. Gislebert, however, intended to deceive Henry by this scheme: while overcoming the king with Henry’s assistance, he would depose Henry himself and obtain the throne of the kingdom for himself. But Heverard had planned something quite different. If he could defeat the king, he wanted to deprive both men of the kingdom and usurp it for himself, as we may infer from words he spoke to his wife shortly before he died. While he held her close to his breast, he said:

“Rejoice in the count’s embrace; before long you will rejoice in the king’s arms.”

That this did not happen, and that iniquity lied to itself, the present catastrophe makes clear.

### 23.

Therefore, as we have said, encouraged—or rather deceived—by this promise, they gathered an army and prepared war against the king, Gislebert and Heverard together. The king hastened against them gladly, not frightened by their numbers but trusting in God’s mercy.

But so that you may know how easily God conquers the many through the few, and that no one will be saved by the abundance of his own strength (Psalm 33:17), hear of an ancient miracle renewed by the Lord.

The king’s soldiers had reached a place called Bierzuni above the Rhine [Col. 0867D; Note: Birthen; compare the continuation of Regino under the year 939], and had already begun to cross the bed of the Rhine, unaware that Henry and the aforementioned counts were already so close to them. At last, only a very few had disembarked from the ships and could scarcely mount their horses and put on their armor when the legions of the men named above were not reported as approaching but were seen with their own eyes to be present.

They then addressed one another in this way:

“As you see, the breadth of this river prevents our companions from coming to our aid and prevents us, even if we wished, from returning to them. Nor is it hidden from us how disgraceful it would be, especially for our peoples, for brave men to surrender themselves to their enemies and, by refusing to resist, flee death only to purchase eternal reproach.

“Although the despair of escape—which sometimes harms the enemy—and the perpetual shame of begging offer us confidence to fight, nevertheless the cause for which we fight, namely truth and justice, compels us to do so. For if, by resisting injustice, our earthly house is destroyed, we shall receive in the heavens an eternal house not made by human hands.”

Inflamed by these words, they rushed at the enemy in a swift charge.

The king, perceiving that such great steadfastness among his men could not exist without divine prompting [Note: *instinctu* in 1], could not come to their aid in bodily presence because the river intervened [Note: *fluio* in 1]. Remembering the people of the Lord, who had defeated the Amalekites opposing them through the prayers of Moses, God’s servant, he immediately dismounted from his horse and, shedding tears with all the people, devoted himself to prayer before the victory-bearing nails fastened to the hands of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ and set upon his own lance. How powerful at that time was the prayer of a righteous man [Note: *viri* (“man”) erased in 1], according to the statement of blessed James (James 5:16), the outcome plainly demonstrated.

While he was praying, none of his men fell, but all the enemies were put to flight. Some of them did not know at all why they were fleeing, since, on account of their small numbers, they could not see the enemies pursuing them.

After many had been killed, Henry was struck severely in the arm. Although the strength of a triple coat of mail did not allow the sword’s edge to reach the flesh, the force of the fierce blow nevertheless turned his arm so dark with bruising that no medical treatment could prevent him from suffering great pain when the following year returned. For this reason, long afterward, on the occasion of this deed, they themselves confessed that he had proved to be a man [Note: *homie* for *homine* in 1].

Since we have mentioned his lance, let us insert here how it came into his possession.

### 24.

Rudolf, king of the Burgundians, who ruled over parts of Italy for several years, received that lance as a gift from Count Samson. It was distinguished from other lances [Note: *exepta*, that is, *excepta* (“distinguished”), in 1] and fashioned in an unusual manner and shape [Note: *elaborata* in 1], having windows on both sides beside the middle of the shaft. These two beautiful edges, intended for the thumbs, extend down to the middle slope of the lance.

They affirm that it had belonged to Constantine the Great, son of Saint Helena, discoverer of the life-giving cross. In the middle of its spine, which I called above its shaft, it has crosses formed from the nails fastened into the hands and feet of our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ.

King Henry, therefore, being a man who feared God and loved every form of religion, heard that Rudolf possessed so priceless a heavenly gift. He sent messengers and tried to acquire it by various rewards, so that he might prepare for himself, against visible and invisible enemies, invincible weapons and perpetual triumph.

When King Rudolf declared in every way that he would never do this, King Henry, unable to soften him with gifts, took great care to terrify him with threats. For he promised that he would ravage his entire kingdom with slaughter and fires.

But because the gift he possessed was one through which God had joined the heavenly and earthly realms [Note: *conjunjunxerat* in 1]—namely, the cornerstone that made both one—it softened King Rudolf’s heart. He delivered it face to face to the just king, who was justly and rightly making a just request [Note: *petententi* in 1]. For where peace was present, there was no place for hostility. Indeed, when the one who was crucified on these objects was hastening from Pilate to Herod, they became friends on that day although previously they had been enemies of one another.

How greatly King Henry loved the aforesaid priceless gift became clear in many matters, and especially in this: he honored the giver not only with gifts of gold and silver, but also with a considerable portion of the province of Swabia.

God, however, who observes what each person undertakes in his heart, is not an inspector and rewarder of the gift’s quantity but of good will. By certain signs he also revealed in this age how great a reward he would grant the pious king in the eternal world for the matter just mentioned: whenever enemies rose against him, he terrified and drove them away, with this victorious sign going before him.

On this occasion—or rather, by God’s will—King Henry acquired the holy lance. When he died, he left it by hereditary right, together with the kingdom, to his son, about whom we are now speaking [Note: *suo unde* in 5, 5a, and 5a*; *Vita S. Gerardi Broniensis*, chapter 18].

How greatly his son honored this priceless gift will be shown not only by the present victory but also by the marvelous bestowal of divine gifts, as we shall relate. Thus, after the enemies had been terrified and put to flight, the king returned, greatly exalted by divine mercy.

### 25.

Let us linger briefly and relate that these events occurred not by chance but by God’s ordering. This will become clearer than daylight to us [Note: *con constabit* in 1, over two lines] if we bring forward the appearance of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, which took place after the Resurrection before the women and the disciples.

Thomas firmly knew of Peter’s faith and of John’s love, as he reclined upon the breast of the Master at supper. He had heard that they had run to the tomb and found nothing except the linen cloths. He also knew that visions of angels, who asserted that Christ was alive, had appeared to the women.

But let us grant it: perhaps, considering the weakness of women, he did not believe them. Come then, holy Thomas, if you do not believe the two disciples hurrying to the village of Emmaus, to whom he not only appeared but also opened the Scriptures that concerned him [Note: That is, *aperuit*, “opened”; *apperuit* is an orthographic form], and even, according to his customary practice, blessed, broke, and gave bread—if you do not believe them, how do you persist in refusing to believe all your fellow disciples, to whom he appeared when the doors were closed?

Do you remember, I ask, that your Lord and teacher, with whom you promised to die, foretold all these things before his Passion? For he said:

“Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and everything that has been written by the prophets concerning the Son of Man will be fulfilled. For he will be handed over to the Gentiles, mocked, scourged, and spat upon; and after they have scourged him, they will kill him, and on the third day he will rise again” (Luke 18:31).

Why, then, do you doubt that he has risen, when you see that he was handed over to the Gentiles, scourged, spat upon, and crucified, just as he had foretold?

It is not without reason that you insist on handling your God with your own hands. For our King himself, who worked salvation in the midst of the earth before the ages (Psalm 73:12), who knows all things before they happen, foresaw that many would perish through this error. Since he is merciful and compassionate, he said:

“Put your finger here, and place your hand in my side, and do not be unbelieving but believing” (John 20:27).

**Ἐξαύδα δὲ, Θομὰ ἅγιε** (*exauda de, Thoma agie*): “But speak out, holy Thomas”; that is, “Confess, holy Thomas,” and by your doubt exclude all ambiguity from our own faith.

“My Lord and my God.”

O ambiguity most worthy of all praise! O doubt to be proclaimed throughout all ages! If you had not doubted, I would not have believed so firmly.

If we were to recount to the heretics the faith of the believing women and of the fellow disciples, those who barked that our Lord Jesus Christ had not risen in a true body, they would oppose us with many arguments through diabolical cunning. But when they hear that doubting Thomas handled the body, touched the scars of the wounds, and immediately, once his doubt had been removed, cried out, “My God and my Lord,” those who had previously been so loud at once become silent as fish. They recognize both that it is true flesh, which could be handled, and that he is God, who entered through closed doors.

Thomas’s doubt, moreover, was not accidental but a divine dispensation. Thus, most pious king, thus was the unexpected victory, achieved despite the small number of soldiers, a design of divine providence: God wished to show mortals how dear to him was the man who, by praying, deserved to obtain so immense a triumph with very few men.

Perhaps—or rather, certainly—you too were previously unaware of how dear you were to God. He caused you to know it afterward, when he honored you with so great a victory. For holy men do not know what virtue they possess or how highly they stand in the sight of the divine tribunal unless they have been tested. We can gather this from the words of the angel to Abraham, who desired to sacrifice his son [Note: Read “desiring to sacrifice”; the construction is: “which we can gather from the words of the angel speaking to Abraham, who desired to sacrifice his son.”]. For he said:

“Do not stretch out your hand against the boy, nor do anything to him; now I know that you fear the Lord” (Genesis 22:12),

that is, “I have caused you yourself and your descendants to know it.”

The Lord already knew, before Abraham wished to sacrifice his son, how greatly the holy patriarch loved him. But the one who loved did not know how perfectly he loved until it became completely clear through the sacrifice of his beloved son.

We can also confirm this interpretation from the promise of blessed Peter. “Lord,” he said, “I am ready to go with you both to prison and to death.” The Lord replied: “I tell you, Peter, the cock will not crow this night until you have denied three times that you know me” (Luke 22:33).
