O holy Peter, the one who made you knew you better than you knew yourself. You profess true faith as you think it to be; but he who knows all things before they happen foretold that you would deny him three times.

Mindful of this statement, when he later asked you whether you loved him [Note: *diligires* in 1], believing him more than yourself, you declared your love in this measured reply:

“Lord, you know all things; you know that I love you” (John 21:15).

“My conscience indeed tells me that I love you more than myself, except that by loving you I love myself. But whether the truth is as I believe it to be, you yourself know better than I, for you made me to exist and kindled me with the most righteous love so that I might love you.”

Therefore, good king, this was done not for your sake but for the faith of the weak, who think that victory consists only in numbers and that human affairs come about only by chance. For we know that even if you had crossed over with twelve thousand legions [Note: *XII milibus* in 1, 2, 3, and 5; *XII* in 5a; *duodecim* in 5a*] and obtained victory, you would have attributed it not to yourself but to the Lord.

This is why he wished you to conquer through prayer with only a few: both to kindle more strongly those who hope in him to love him, and to reveal to those who did not know it how greatly he loved you.

But leaving these matters aside, let us return to the sequence of the narrative [Note: “Let us hasten to other matters” in 5, 5a, and 5a*].

### 26.

In the regions of Alsace there is a fortress called, in the native language, Brisicau [Note: Breisach]. The Rhine, encircling it like an island, and the natural ruggedness of the place protect it. In this fortress Heverard had stationed a multitude of soldiers. By their terror he not only claimed a large part of the aforesaid province for himself but also cruelly ravaged the king’s faithful subjects throughout the surrounding region.

The good king, considering not what belonged to himself but what belonged to his people, gathered an army and set out for Alsace to besiege the aforesaid fortress.

When he arrived there, at the urging of Frederick, archbishop of the see of Mainz, who was then present with him, very many bishops secretly abandoned the king. At night they struck their tents, departed, and secretly fled to their own cities, while Frederick treacherously remained with him.

When the king’s soldiers saw this, they addressed the king in these words:

“Look to your safety, O king, by abandoning this place and making for Saxony. You are not unaware that your brother Henry is attempting to wage war against you. If he perceives that your forces with you are so few, he will suddenly attack in such a way that there will not even be room for flight. It is therefore better to rebuild your army and return again than either to die miserably or to flee shamefully.”

The king, undaunted, replied to them as Judas, surnamed Maccabaeus, once replied to his own men:

“Do not, do not speak such things. Even if our time has come, let us die bravely and not bring a charge against our glory” (1 Maccabees 9:10).

For it is better to undergo death for true justice than to live shamefully by fleeing from it. Finally, if it pleases those who resist God’s ordinance, who hope for assistance only from numbers and not from God, to fight unjustly, die, and descend to the unforgivable punishments of hell, let it nevertheless please us—or rather, let it please us more ardently—to fight, since we can fight confidently for justice and, by fighting, die with greater confidence if the lot of all flesh should befall us. For those who intend to fight for justice to turn their backs before the test of battle because their forces are few is to distrust God.

Having said this, he not only recalled them from their intention to flee but also immediately encouraged them to fight with great vigor.

### 27.

I wish you to attend carefully to one matter—one matter, excellent father—for when you hear it, you will marvel that he overcame the passions of his soul more than his enemies.

With God’s permission, even sinners can sometimes conquer adversaries in this way. But to preserve unshaken strength of soul—to be neither elated by prosperity nor broken by adversity—is the characteristic only of the perfect.

Listen, then, to the ardor of faith with which he was founded upon the rock that is Christ amid this great and wavering storm.

A certain count, then exceedingly wealthy, was with him, and the multitude of his soldiers added splendor to the king’s army. Seeing many men from the king’s ranks becoming deserters and turncoats, he considered not the inner but the outer man and began silently to revolve these thoughts:

“Whatever I ask of the king, who is placed in this turmoil, I shall undoubtedly obtain, especially since fierce battle threatens us and he will fear that I may desert him.”

He therefore sent messengers and begged the king to grant him a certain abbey called Laresheim [Note: The words are absent in 3; *Lauresheim* in 2; *Lauresheim* or *Loresheim* in 5], extremely rich in estates, so that he might use its possessions to supply what he lacked and provide for his soldiers.

The king, stuffed not only with dove-like but, as he was, with viper-like cunning, was entirely unable to perceive what this implied [Note: *pordenderet* in 1]. He therefore gave the messengers this answer:

“I shall explain in person what I think about this matter, rather than through messengers.”

When the one who had sent them heard this, he was filled with immense joy, hoping that he had obtained what he had requested. Impatient of delay [Note: *more* in 1], he approached the king and asked him to pronounce his decision on the matter.

The king, with the people standing around, said to him:

“It is more necessary to obey God than human beings. For what sane and sensible person does not understand that you said this not with the humility of a petitioner but with the authority of a threat?

“It is written: ‘Do not give what is holy to dogs’ (Matthew 7:6). Although teachers proclaim that this should be understood spiritually, I nevertheless judge that I would truly be giving what is holy to dogs if I took away the estates of monasteries, which have been entrusted to religious men serving God, and gave them to men serving the world.

“To you, who ask so unjustly and brazenly, I testify before the whole people that you will never receive either this or anything else from me. If it is in your heart to fly away with the other faithless men, the sooner you do so, the better.”

When he heard this, because the face is the mirror of the heart, he exposed his shame by the redness of his face [Note: Witness 1 places points after *mentis* and *cordis]. He hurriedly fell at the king’s feet and confessed that he had sinned and grievously offended.

Consider, therefore, with what steadfastness this athlete of God crushed not only visible but also invisible enemies. The ancient enemy did not think that he had harmed the king when he persuaded so many powerful princes to rise against him and incited even his brother to take the kingdom from him, because he recognized that these were merely external losses.

For this reason he also incited the aforementioned count to seek the inheritance of the saints, so that the king might more quickly incur God’s displeasure by unjustly handing over the stipends of God’s servants to his own soldiers.

But because he was unable to do so, let us now bring forward how greatly the holy king increased, with God fighting on his behalf because of his steadfastness in this temptation.

### 28.

Holy David speaks from the person of the Lord:

“If my people had listened to me, if Israel had walked in my ways, perhaps I would have humbled their enemies for nothing and laid my hand upon those who afflicted them” (Psalm 80:14).

The reasoning I shall now present will show that this was fulfilled in the case of this king, who listened to the Lord and walked in his ways.

When Heverard and Gislebert heard that the king was in Alsace, fearing no one who might resist them, they gathered a very large army, crossed the bed of the Rhine at Andernach, and proceeded to destroy the king’s faithful subjects throughout the surrounding countryside.

Huto, brother of Herimann, duke of the Swabians, and Chuonrad, surnamed the Wise, whom we said above were faithful to the king, were in those regions. But because their forces were much smaller than those of the others, they were afraid to meet them [Note: *occurre* in 1].

Nevertheless, at God’s command—not by spoken instruction but by inspiration—they followed the others as they returned with much plunder.

After they had advanced a little, a priest met them, weeping and lamenting. When they asked him where he was going and why he was weeping, he replied:

“I am coming from those robbers, who have enlarged the misery of my poverty by taking away the one animal I possessed.”

When the aforesaid Huto and Chuonrad heard this [Note: *praefato* in 1], they carefully questioned him about whether he had seen Gislebert and Heverard. He answered:

“Because almost all of them have been sent across the Rhine with the booty, they alone, together with their chosen soldiers—may it not turn out well for them—are taking their meal.”

They rushed upon them with such speed that, if you had seen them, you would not have said that they were running [Note: *curre* in 1] but flying [Note: *tranuolare* in 1].

What more is there to say? Heverard was killed by the sword; Gislebert was submerged in the waters of the Rhine. Because he could not swallow them on account of the multitude [Note: *exorhere prae multitudine* in 5 and 5a; *Vita S. Gerardi Broniensis*, chapter 19], he perished as his soul departed. Of all the others, no one escaped who was not either bound alive or cut down by the sword.

You see, therefore, how the Lord laid his hand upon those who afflicted the king, whom he had recognized as walking in his ways.

### 29.

While these events were taking place, the king, unaware of them in Alsace, was prepared to die rather than flee from his adversaries.

It happened, then, that, as was his custom, he mounted his horse early in the morning [Note: *coscenderet* in 1], since the church was far away, and went forth fortified by prayers. As he looked attentively into the distance, he saw a man approaching him at great speed, and immediately understood that he was a messenger [Note: *intelexit* in 1; the passage from “And because he who had come was bringing good news” to “he displayed in advance” is missing in 5, 5a, and 5a*].

Since the newcomer was bringing good news, as soon as he saw the king he displayed in advance, by a certain prelude of cheerfulness, the joy that would follow.

From this sign those who were present understood that he was announcing favorable news and ran with pricked ears to hear him. His measured gait, the orderly arrangement of his hair and clothing, and his honorable greeting were his adornment.

The king saw the people panting and noticed that they were deeply annoyed by the messenger’s delay in speaking [Note: *momoram* in 1]. He said:

“Come, say what you were sent to say. Reverse the order and first set forth the matter [Note: *injuce* in 1]; remove the fear of those standing around and fill their hearts with joy. Then, through long introductions and the rhetorical prefaces of orators, soothe us with greetings. The present moment awaits not how you speak but what you say. We would rather rejoice in rustic simplicity than be endangered by Ciceronian elegance.”

When he heard this, the messenger immediately announced that Heverard and Gislebert had been stripped of human life. He wished to continue with an account of how this had happened, but the king restrained him with his hand. He then dismounted and, giving thanks to God with tears, devoted himself to prayer.

When the prayer was completed, he rose and proceeded toward the church, commending himself to God along the route on which he had begun his journey.

### 30.

At this time Bertald, duke of the Bavarians and brother of Duke Arnulf, a vigorous man, supported the king’s cause with all his strength.

The king therefore wished him to share in the present joy just as he had shared in the earlier tribulation. The following day he sent messengers and revealed to him how great were the benefits the Lord had bestowed upon him.

He also wished to increase his joy, since he was not at all bound by a marital tie [Note: *cojugali* in 1]. He instructed him and made him promise by oath that, if he could have the king’s sister—that is, Gislebert’s wife—he would unite her to Bertald in marriage. If this could not be arranged, he would give him in marriage Gislebert’s daughter by that same sister, whom he had with him and who was now nearly of marriageable age.

When Bertald heard this, he was filled with immense joy. He preferred to wait for the daughter, who was not yet marriageable, rather than take the mother, who was already married.

### 31.

At last Frederick, archbishop of the church of Mainz, on whose counsel certain bishops had abandoned the king so that the infidelity he had been harboring secretly might become evident to all, deserted the king almost ten days before the death of the aforesaid leaders and hurried to Mainz.

He did not remain there long but went to the city of Metz. For King Henry, the king’s brother, had planned to gather an army there with Frederick when Heverard and Gislebert returned, and thus to prepare a great war against the king, who was staying in Alsace.

When the named archbishop arrived there, messengers unexpectedly and inopportunely met him. They reported that the aforementioned princes were no longer alive, death having intervened. On hearing this, he was struck with terror and had no idea at all what to do.

### 32.

Meanwhile the king, leaving Alsace, occupied Francia [Note: *occubabat* in 1]. Because of fear of him, the citizens of Mainz did not receive the returning archbishop within the walls of the city.

As a result, not long afterward he was captured by the king’s faithful men, brought before the king, and handed over to custody in Saxony. After remaining there for some time, he was restored, through the king’s mercy, to his former dignity.

### 33.

At last Henry, terrified out of his mind by the king—his own brother—wanted to enter a fortress called Capraemons, fortified not only by human ingenuity but also by nature itself.

His sister, the widow of Gislebert, learned of this beforehand and not only prevented him from doing it but also addressed him in these words:

“Alas! Are you not wearied of my sufferings, which I endure after my husband’s death, unless you also, by shutting yourself up in my fortifications, pour the king’s anger over this region like water? I shall not bear it, I shall not endure it, I shall not permit it. I shall not possess such madness that you should obtain your advantages from my disadvantages.”

### 34.

When Henry heard this, and did not know what else to do, he took with him certain bishops whose support might aid him. One day, barefoot, he came without the king’s knowledge to the king’s feet. Humbly, he implored mercy.

The king said to him:

“Your unworthy deed does not deserve mercy. But because I see you humbled before me, I will not bring evil upon you.”

The king therefore ordered him to proceed to his palace in Francia, situated in a place called Ingelheim, and had him guarded with vigilant care until, once the sickness of anger had somewhat subsided, he could determine, with the counsel of wise men, what he should do concerning him.

[Col. 0875] **Here ends Book Four. Thanks be to God.**

## [Book Five]

### Contents of Book Five begin

[Col. 0875C]

1. How Herimann, duke of the Swabians, gave his daughter, named Ita, in marriage to Liutolf, the king’s son.

2. On an eclipse of the sun and the appearance of a comet.

3. How King Hugh oppressed Rome every year.

4. On Berengar and Anscar, brothers, of whom he made Anscar margrave of Camerino and Spoleto.

5. On Serlio, whom King Hugh sent against Anscar, and on Anscar’s words.  
[Note: Up to this point the index of manuscript 3; its text, however, ends only at chapter 18.]

6. On the good counsel of Wikbert, a good soldier, and the bad counsel of Arcodus, a bad soldier.  
[Note: Up to this point in the first hand; the remaining chapters of the index are in a second hand in manuscript 1.]

7. On the first battle between Sarlio and Anscar, in which Wikbert was killed and Arcodus fled.

[Col. 0875D]

8. On another battle, in which Anscar killed Count Hatto with a spear; afterward, when Anscar fell from his horse, he himself was killed by the enemy, and Sarlius gained the march.

9. On King Hugh, who sent messengers to Constantinople concerning ships and Greek fire.

10. On King Hugh, who wished to blind Berengar but could not because of Lothair, who informed Berengar of this; and on the flight of Berengar and his wife.

11. Invective against the mountains that allowed Berengarius and Willa to cross.

12. How Duke Herimannus received Berengarius and led him into the presence of the king.

13. How King Hugo sent his envoys to King Otto, promising money if he would not receive Berengarius—something he was wholly unable to obtain.

14. How Romanus, emperor of the Greeks, asked King Hugo to give his daughter in marriage to his own grandson, the son of Constantine.

[Col. 0876D] 15. Of the naval battle that Romanus fought with Inger, king of the Rus, whom he remarkably defeated.

16. How King Hugo, proceeding to Fraxinetum, sent the Greeks there with ships.

17. How King Hugo could have destroyed Fraxinetum but did not wish to.

[Col. 0877A] 18. Of Amedeus, Berengarius’s soldier, who came to Italy to reconnoiter.

19. How King Hugo made a pact with the Hungarians and sent them into Spain.

20. How King Hugo sent his daughter, whom he had had by a concubine, to Constantinople.

21. Of the strength and beauty of the Constantinopolitan palace, and how Stephanus and Constantinus expelled their father from the palace and made him a monk.

22. How these same men wished to overthrow Constantinus Porphyrogenitus; how they themselves were captured by him and sent to a monastery; and through whom their plot was revealed.

23. Of the father’s ironic reception and speech [Col. 0877B] when his sons came to the monastery.

24. The prayer of the emperor Romanus, which he offered for his sons, giving thanks to God.

25. How Constantinus and Stephanus were kept under guard.

[Col. 0878A] 26. Of the arrival in Italy of the long-desired Berengarius, and that Mannasses favors his cause.

27. Which princes first deserted Hugo, and why.

28. How King Hugo sent his son Lotharius to Milan, to the mercy of all the Italians.

29. Of Bishop Joseph, expelled from Brescia by Berengarius, and of Antonius, appointed in his place.

30. Why Berengarius dismissed the bishops of Piacenza and Pavia, and why Liudprandus’s parents commended the cleric Liudprandus to Berengarius.

31. Of King Hugo, who went into Provence with all his money, and of Raimundus, who became his soldier.

[Col. 0878B] 32. Of Berengarius’s wife, who was accused of incest, and how she was freed from it.

33. Of the money that Berengarius took from the poor and the churches of God on account of the Hungarians.

[Col. 0877] THE CHAPTERS END.

THE FIFTH BOOK BEGINS.

[Col. 0877C] 1. (Year 939.) It happened that, after the death of Heverardus and Gislebertus, and likewise after the imprisonment of Heinricus, the king’s brother, when nobles from every side were coming to the king to offer congratulations, there also came the very wealthy Herimannus, duke of the Suevians. After he had had his fill of congratulations, he addressed the king in these words:

“Since I am rich both in the extent of my estates and in the immensity of my wealth, it is not hidden from my lord that I am without children; nor is there anyone except one little daughter who, when I depart this life, may become heir to my possessions. Therefore, may it please my lord the king to adopt his little son LIUTOLF as my son, so that, joined to my only daughter in marital union, he may, when I depart, become the distinguished heir of my property.”

Since this counsel pleased the king, he fulfilled without delay what had been requested.

2. At this time (July 19), as you yourselves know well, the sun suffered a great and terrifying eclipse on a Friday, at the third hour of the day. On that same day Abderahamem [Note: [Col. 0877] “Abdaram” in witnesses 5 and 5a.]—your king—was defeated in battle by Radamirus, the most Christian king of Galicia [Note: [Col. 0877D] Compare the Greater Annals of Saint Gall, year 939.]. But in Italy also, for eight consecutive nights, a comet of remarkable size appeared, pouring forth fiery rays of excessive length from itself and foreshadowing a famine that followed not long afterward and that, by its magnitude, miserably devastated Italy.

3. At that time, with King Hugo shamefully expelled, Albericus, as we have said above, held the sovereignty of the Roman state. King Hugo oppressed him severely every year, consuming with sword and fire everything he could [Note: [Col. 0877] That is, “destroying.”], to such an extent that he took away all the cities except Rome, where Albericus himself had established his seat. He would undoubtedly have sought to take Rome as well, both by laying it waste and by corrupting its citizens with gifts, had not the hidden judgment of the just God prevented him [Note: [Col. 0877] “Judgment” is written “sentia” in one witness.].

4. During this period Berengarius and Anscarius were renowned in Italy. They had one father, Adelbertus, marquis of the city of Ivrea, but were born of different mothers. Berengarius, as we have said above, was born to Gisla, daughter of King Berengarius; Anscarius was born to Hermengarda, daughter of Adelbertus, marquis of the province of Tuscany, whom Adelbertus had fathered by Berta, King Hugo’s daughter. Berengarius was prudent in counsel and shrewd in intelligence; Anscarius, however, was ready for every crime. King Hugo was exceedingly suspicious of him, fearing that he might kill him and seize the kingdom for himself [Note: [Col. 0877] One witness reads “to kill.”]. Having therefore taken counsel, since Tedbaldus, the marquis, had died, he appointed Anscarius marquis of the Spoletans and Camerinans, so that he might live more securely the farther he knew him to be separated from himself. When Anscarius had gone there, since he was impatient in spirit, he continually revealed by the signs of his actions whatever evil his mind suggested to him as he brooded over the king. This did not escape Hugo.

5. (Year 940.) Therefore, considering what remedy he might apply to this sickness, Hugo summoned to himself Sarlio, descended from the Burgundian race [Note: [Col. 0877] “Burdionum” in one witness.]. He said to him:

“I am not unaware of the loyalty of the men of Camerinum and Spoleto. It is like a reed: if a man leans upon it, it will pierce his hand. Go, therefore, and, having received money from me, corrupt their minds, remove them from their affection for Anscarius, and attach them to yourself. No one can do this better or more conveniently than you. For you have the wife of that excellent marquis Tedbaldus, my deceased nephew; relying on her assistance, the entire people will come over to you.”

When he had set out, the people of Camerinum and Spoleto acted exactly as the king had predicted. Having gathered a multitude, Sarlio hastened toward the city in which Anscarius was staying [Note: [Col. 0879] One witness reads “hasten.”]. When Anscarius heard this, he addressed his standard-bearer, named Wikbertus, in these words:

[Col. 0879B] Verse.

“Sarlio, unwarlike, trusting in the arms of many,

Approaches to fight; the brave in heart and arms

Must meet him and bring on bloody war.

A chosen band of young men, exercised in many wars,

Is here, and, accompanying me as their lord,

Will come at once, adorned with gleaming metal.”

6. When Wikbertus heard this, being a man who relied not only on courage but also on knowledge, he said:

“Wait, and gather forces as best you can. It is extremely difficult for so few to confront an army so numerous. Moreover, if you observe with whom we are dealing, they are heroes, no less accustomed to war than we are.”

Anscarius had already resolved to follow Wikbertus’s sound advice and, having sent messengers in every direction, was eager to gather an army, when a certain Arcodus, born of Burgundian blood, rebuked Wikbertus with these bitter words:

“You resemble Chremes, who, out of fear of Thraso, advised Thais to shut the doors until he could lead those summoned to her from the forum. When Thais tried to stop him, he said [Note: [Col. 0879D] Terence, *Eunuchus* IV, 6, line 24.]: ‘When you can guard yourself safely, it is foolish to admit him. I would rather we look after ourselves than avenge an injury once received!’

“Very well, Wikbertus, you have recalled the soldier Thraso, who, after raging first with a savage mouth, when it came to the actual matter placed Syriscus on the right wing and Symalio on the left [Note: [Col. 0879D] Terence, *Eunuchus*, book VII, line 5.], chose a place for himself behind the front ranks [Note: [Col. 0879D] Terence, *Eunuchus*, line 11.]. Everyone who knows the Burgundians agrees that they are talkative, greedy, and unwarlike. And the scars on your body show both how bravely you have often acted and what wounds you have avoided by fleeing.”

7. Thus provoked by such words, Anscarius and Wikbertus, as soon as they heard that Sarlio was there with many men, hastened to go against him with a few. Sarlio had six battle lines, three of which he had directed against the one line of Anscarius, in which Anscarius himself was present. Sarlio himself, watching the outcome from across the intervening river, remained with three lines. He feared that even so great a multitude could not protect him if Anscarius were able to turn his gaze upon him.

Without delay, battle began. In it Arcodus was not seen, because he had fled; Wikbertus, however, was wounded to the point of death, since he considered it better to die than to flee. After Anscarius had defeated all these men, Sarlio again sent two battle lines against him, retaining only one with himself. When Anscarius wished to discover which of his men had fallen in the field, Wikbertus came before him, stained not only with the blood of others but also with his own. He said to him:

“Two beautifully armed battle lines are approaching us, and I repeatedly urge you to evade them rather than await them. You yourself know well how Arcodus, the instigator of this battle, has fled. As for me, I lie at the point of death; I no longer think about battle, but pray to the merciful God for my soul, that he not reckon against me the crimes I have incurred today out of love for you, by giving many bodies over to the slaughter of men.”

When he had finished speaking, he died.

8. Anscarius therefore gathered as many men as he could and, meeting the two phalanxes, furiously rushed between them and inflicted an innumerable slaughter. A certain count named Hatto commanded those two battle lines. He confronted Anscarius with confidence because, after his lance had already been broken, he had seen that Anscarius held only a spear in his hand.

When Anscarius saw him, he said:

“Are you the man who, despising the oath sworn by the cross and the saints, abandoned me, your lord, as a perjurer in the name of your God, and went over to the fox Sarlio as a deserter and renegade?

‘That there are spirits and subterranean realms

in which perjurers are punished,

and Cocytus also, and black frogs in the Stygian whirlpool’ [Note: [Col. 0880D] Juvenal, *Satires* 5, lines 149–150.]—

what you have until now dreamed, experience in reality at once!”

As he said this, he hurled the spear, which had no iron point, forcefully through Hatto’s mouth and drew it out through the back of his head, spattered with blood and brain. Then he drew his sword and began to fight vigorously, since many were rushing upon him. While he alone, without anyone supporting him, endured the attack of nearly all the enemy, running here and there, the horse on which he was mounted fell into a pit so completely that, with its neck beneath him and its feet raised upward, it lay upon Anscarius until he was killed by missiles directed at him by the attacking enemy.

When he was dead, Sarlio securely gained the marquisate, and King Hugo was filled with immense joy.

[Col. 0881A] 9. While these events were taking place, the Saracens inhabiting Fraxinetum were most cruelly devastating the mountainous region by which Italy is enclosed on its western or northern side [Note: [Col. 0881] “Devastated” is corrected to “devastates”; the passive form is used with active meaning.] (year 941). For this reason, after taking counsel, King Hugo sent envoys to Constantinople, asking the emperor Romanus to send him ships with Greek fire, which the Greeks call *chelandia* in their native language. He did this so that, while he himself traveled by land to destroy Fraxinetum [Note: [Col. 0881] “Fraxenetum” is corrected to “Fraxinetum.”], the Greeks might blockade by sea the side protected by the sea, burn the enemy ships, and take the greatest care that no provisions or military reinforcements should reach them from Spain.

10. Meanwhile Berengarius, the aforementioned brother of Anscarius and marquis of the city of Ivrea, secretly began to plot something against the king. When this became known to the king, he pretended goodwill and concealed his anger; when Berengarius came to him, he intended to deprive him of his sight. His son, named Lotharius, himself still a child and not yet aware of the necessities of life, had been present at these counsels. As a boy he could not conceal the matter; instead, he sent a messenger to Berengarius and revealed to him what his father intended to do.

When Berengarius heard this, he immediately left Italy and hastened over Mount Jovis into Swabia to Duke Herimannus. He ordered his wife Willa to come to the same province by another route. At the time of her departure, she was pregnant and close to giving birth. I cannot sufficiently marvel at how she could cross such rugged and impassable mountains on foot [Note: [Col. 0881] That is, “could have crossed”], unless it is because I know for certain that all circumstances were adverse to me.

But ah! Lotharius, ignorant of the future, could not see what a trap he was preparing for himself. By advising Berengarius, he prepared for himself the loss of both kingdom and life. Therefore I direct my curse not against Lotharius, who sinned through the lightness of childhood and afterward bitterly repented of it, but against those cruel mountains, which, contrary to the custom of all others, readily offered him a path. Thus I now wish to cry out against them:

11. Wicked Mount Avium, why

do you preserve such a pest?

You are accustomed also to be impassable

at the season when the reaper

[Col. 0881D] when Ceres

[Col. 0882A] is burning with Phoebus’s rays,

but now, most wickedly, are passable in an unheard-of way?

Would that you could be torn away

straightway into the abyss!

Behold, Mount Jovis preserves Berengarius—

no wonder—

and preserves wicked men, they say,

who delight in human blood.

What shall I say? Behold, I wish you,

ripped apart by the thunderbolt,

to be destroyed together with all things—

you who are not worthy of the name

by which you now can be destroyed—

when the fiery sun burns,

the curved sickle reaps [Note: [Col. 0881] One witness reads “crab.”];

the constellation of Cancer scorches [Note: [Col. 0881] One witness reads “the rigid one.”],

in the season of harsh winter.

Would that you went to other mountains,

and allowed my present wishes to prevail,

and, on a straight path,

helped destroy those accustomed

to destroy the holy,

alas, whom they call Moors,

[Col. 0882B] and helped those who live by plunder.

May you be burned by lightning,

and become so throughout all time.

[Note: [Col. 0881] Codex 3 has the following in the margin: “A dactylic Alemannian meter consisting of a catalectic trimeter, which is composed of a spondee, a dactyl, and a spondee; but in place of the first spondee there is, where we find the transmitted anapest, ‘the whole race of human beings on earth.’”]

12. Herimannus, duke of the Suevians, therefore kindly received Berengarius when he came to him and led him with great honor into the presence of the most pious King Otto. My pen doubts that it can write how devotedly the king received him, with how many gifts he endowed him, and how greatly he honored him. Yet, insofar as it can, it will indicate these things; and the prudent reader will easily perceive what holiness and humanity the king possessed, and also how great Berengarius’s wickedness was.

13. When King Hugo heard of Berengarius’s flight, he sent his envoys to King Otto (year 942), promising, according to his considered intention, that he would give him an abundance of gold and silver if he did not receive Berengarius or provide him with assistance. The king gave them this reply:

“Berengarius has approached our piety not because of the overthrow of your lord, but, if he is able, for the sake of reconciliation. If I can assist him in this matter with your lord, I not only refuse to accept the treasures he has promised me, but most willingly offer him my own. To command that assistance not be given to Berengarius—or to anyone imploring the clemency of our piety—is the height of folly. Consider, therefore, with what great affection the pious king loved him: he wished not only to refuse the promised money but also to give his own on his behalf.”

[Col. 0882D] 14. While these events were taking place [Note: [Col. 0881] A witness has “Romanus” in Greek letters.], the emperor of Constantinople likewise sent his own envoys with King Hugo’s envoys, declaring that he would give Hugo ships and everything he desired if Hugo would give his daughter in marriage to the emperor’s little namesake, Romanus, the son of Constantine.

By Constantine I mean the son of the emperor Leo [Note: [Col. 0881] “The son of the same Romanus” in Greek: *huion tou autou Romanou*], not the son of Romanus himself. For three men were reigning jointly with Romanus: his two sons, Stephanus and Constantinus, and also this Constantinus of whom we are now speaking, the son of the emperor Leo.

When King Hugo heard this embassy, he again sent envoys and informed Romanus that he had no daughter born of a legitimate marriage. But if Romanus wished to accept a daughter of one of his concubines, Hugo could offer him a girl of outstanding beauty. Since the Greeks, in determining nobility of birth, inquire not who the mother was but who the father was, the emperor Romanus immediately prepared ships with Greek fire, sent magnificent gifts, and ordered Hugo to unite the girl with his grandson.

But since my stepfather, a man adorned with dignity and filled with wisdom, had been King Hugo’s envoy, it will not be burdensome for me to insert here [Note: [Col. 0883] That is, “what he said about the wisdom and humanity of the emperor Romanus (*peri tou basileos Romanou sophias kai philanthropias*) and how he conquered the Rus.”] what I often heard him say about the emperor’s wisdom and humanity, and how he defeated the Rus.

15. There is a people settled in the northern region whom the Greeks call *Ρουσιος* (*Rusios*, “Rus”) because of their bodily appearance; we, however, call them Nordmanns from the position of their land. In the language of the Germans, *nord* means “north,” while *man* means “man” [Note: [Col. 0883] So also in witnesses 5 and 5a.]. Thus we may call them “northern men.”

The king of this people was named Inger. Gathering a thousand or more ships, he came to Constantinople. When the emperor Romanus heard this [Note: [Col. 0883] “Romanus” in Greek letters.], since he had sent his naval army against the Saracens and for the protection of the islands, he began to be troubled by anxious thoughts. While he spent many sleepless nights in no small concern, and Inger was plundering everything near the sea, Romanus was informed that he had fifteen half-broken *chelandia* [Note: [Col. 0883] Greek *χελανδια*.] left, which the people had retained only because of their age.

When he heard this, he ordered the *καλαφάται* (*tous kalaphatas*), that is, the shipwrights, to come to him, and said to them:

“Hurry without delay and prepare the *chelandia* that remain. Also place the device by which fire is thrown not only in the prow but also in the stern, and in addition on both sides.”

After the *chelandia* had been fitted out according to his command, he placed the wisest men in them and ordered them to meet King Inger. When they had set out and King Inger saw them on the open sea, he ordered his army to capture them alive and not kill them.

Then the merciful and compassionate Lord, who wished not only to protect those who serve, worship, and entreat him but also to honor them with victory, made the sea calm at that time. Otherwise the Greeks would have been hindered by the discharge of fire.

Placed among the Rus, they cast fire all around them. When the Rus saw this, they immediately threw themselves from their ships into the sea, choosing to be submerged by the waves rather than burned by fire. Some, weighed down by coats of mail and helmets, sank to the depths of the sea, never to see the light again; others, swimming amid the waves, were burned, and no one escaped that day except those who saved themselves by fleeing to land.

The ships of the Rus, because of their small size, pass wherever the water is shallow, which the Greek *chelandia* [Note: [Col. 0883] Greek *χελανδια*.] cannot do because of their depth. Inger [Note: [Col. 0883] The word appears to have been erased in one witness.] later returned to his own land in great confusion [Note: [Col. 0883] One witness reads “confusiose.”].

The Greeks, having won the victory and taking many survivors with them, returned joyfully to Constantinople. Romanus ordered all of these men to be beheaded in the presence of King Hugo’s envoy—my stepfather.

16. King Hugo therefore gathered an army and sent fleets through the Tyrrhenian Sea toward Fraxinetum; he himself proceeded there by land. When the Greeks arrived, they cast fire and immediately burned all the Saracens’ ships. King Hugo also entered Fraxinetum and forced all the Saracens to flee to Mount Maurus. He could have captured them by besieging them there, had not the matter I am about to relate prevented it.

17. King Hugo was especially afraid that Berengarius might gather forces from both France and Swabia, attack him, and take the kingdom from him. Therefore, following bad advice, he immediately sent the Greeks back to their own country. He himself made a treaty with the Saracens on these terms: they were to remain in the mountains dividing Swabia from Italy, so that, if Berengarius should wish to lead an army across, they would prevent him from crossing by every means.

While stationed there, how much Christian blood they shed from those traveling to the thresholds of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, only he knows who keeps their names written in the book of the living.

How unjustly you strive, King Hugo, to defend your kingdom! Herod killed many innocents so that he would not be deprived of an earthly kingdom; you, in order to retain yours, release the guilty and those deserving death—and would that those guilty men had then remained alive on that account, so that they might not afterward do harm [Note: [Col. 0883] That is, “those who would cause harm”; the editors read “innocent.”].

I think—but, more truly, I believe—that you have not read, indeed have not even heard, how King Ahab of Israel incurred the Lord’s anger when he released Ben-hadad, king of Syria, a man deserving death, after making a treaty with him. For one of the sons of the prophets said to Ahab:

“Thus says the Lord: Because you have released from your hand a man deserving death, your life shall be for his life, and your people for his people” (1 Kings 20:42).

And so it happened. But how much this matter harmed you, my pen will relate more appropriately in its proper place.

[Col. 0884D] 18. At the time when Berengarius fled from Italy (year 943), he took with him a certain soldier named Amedeus, exceedingly noble and, as later became clear, inferior to Ulysses neither in cunning nor in daring.

Since the most powerful King Otto, hindered by various affairs and also softened each year by immense gifts from King Hugo, was unable to provide forces for Berengarius, the aforementioned Amedeus addressed Berengarius as follows:

“It is not hidden from you, my lord, how hateful King Hugo has made himself to all the Italians through his harsh rule, especially since he has bestowed honors upon the sons of his concubines and upon Burgundians, and no Italian can be found who has not either been expelled or deprived of every dignity.

“The reason they do not plot something against the king is that they have no one whom they might establish as their prince. If, therefore, one of us were to go there in altered clothing, so that he would not be recognized, and inquire into their wishes, he would undoubtedly discover a good plan for us.”

Berengarius replied:

“No one can do this better, or more conveniently, than you.”

Amedeus therefore changed his clothing and, as though going to Rome with poor people who were traveling there for the sake of prayer, made his way to Italy. He visited the princes and asked what each held dear. He did not present himself to everyone in the same clothing: to one he appeared black, to another whitish, to another reddish, and to another spotted [Note: [Col. 0885] “To some black, to others whitish, to others reddish”; other witnesses vary.].

But Fame—than which nothing is swifter in motion [Note: [Col. 0885D] Virgil, *Aeneid* 4.174–175.]—made it known to the king that Amedeus was in Italy. When the king ordered that he be diligently sought, Amedeus smeared his long and very beautiful beard so thoroughly with pitch, changed his golden hair by blackening it, disfigured his face, and made himself appear lame. Thus, among the poor who were eating in the king’s presence, he displayed himself naked [Note: [Col. 0885] Codex 3 reads “half-naked”], received from the king clothing to wear, and listened to everything the king said about Berengarius and about himself.

After carefully investigating everything in this manner, he returned with the envoys in a guise different from that in which he had come. The king had ordered the guards of the passes not to allow anyone through unless they first carefully investigated who he was. When Amedeus heard this, he crossed by certain pathless and rugged places that were not guarded, and reached Berengarius with the message he had wished to hear.

19. At this time King Hugo, paying ten bushels of coins, made peace with the Hungarians. After taking hostages from Italy, he expelled them and sent them into Spain with a guide [Note: [Col. 0885] “Praeducere” is corrected to “praeduce”; perhaps one should read “praeduce ire,” “to go with a guide.”]. The reason they did not reach Spain, or the city itself in which your king dwells, Córdoba, was that they spent three days crossing a waterless region devastated by thirst [Note: [Col. 0885] “Thirst … thirst” is omitted in witnesses 5 and 5a.]. Thinking, therefore, that both their horses and themselves would perish from thirst, they beat their guide, granted to them by Hugo, almost to death, and turned back with a swiftness greater than that with which they had departed.

[Col. 0885D] 20. At this same time (year 944), King Hugo sent his daughter Berta, whom he had fathered by the prostitute Pezola, through Sigefredus, the venerable bishop of the church of Parma, to Constantinople, to be joined in marriage to the little Romanus, son of Constantinus Porphyrogenitus.

The elder Romanus held the supreme power of the empire, together with his two sons, Constantinus and Stephanus. After the younger Romanus, Constantinus, son of the emperor Leo, held precedence [Note: [Col. 0885] The syllables “fil,” “ex,” and “ma” are cut off in the margin.]. The latter’s little son, born of Helena, daughter of the elder emperor Romanus, had married the already mentioned Berta, whom the Greeks, after changing her name, called Eudokia [Note: [Col. 0885] The syllables “fil,” “ex,” and “ma” are cut off in the margin.].

While these four were ruling—the brothers Stephanus and Constantinus, without the knowledge of Constantinus, the son of the emperor Leo, were plotting certain *σφάλματα* (*sfalmata*), that is, schemes, against their father Romanus. They were weary of being unable to do whatever they wished because of the discipline imposed by their father’s severity. Therefore, after quickly accepting evil counsel, they considered how they might overthrow their father.

21. The palace of Constantinople surpasses in beauty and also in strength every fortification I have ever seen. It is likewise guarded by a very substantial continuous presence of soldiers.

It is customary for the palace to be open to everyone immediately after the morning twilight. After the third hour of the day, when everyone has been sent out, a signal is given—called *mîs*—and access is forbidden to all until the ninth hour.

Romanus, therefore, living in great power in the *chrysotriclinon*—that is, the golden triclinium, the most distinguished part—had assigned the other parts of the palace to his son-in-law Constantinus and to his sons Stephanus and Constantinus.

These two, as we have said, could not endure their father’s just severity. Having gathered many troops in their chambers, they appointed a day on which they could overthrow their father and reign alone.

When the desired day arrived, and everyone had left the palace according to custom, Stephanus and Constantinus attacked their father after making an assault upon him. Without the citizens’ knowledge, they deposed him from the palace and sent him to a nearby island, where a large community of coenobites pursued philosophical contemplation. There, after shaving his head as was customary, they sent him to practice philosophy—that is, to live as a monk.

Soon a rumor-filled uproar arose throughout Constantinople: some loudly proclaimed that Romanus had been expelled, while others said that his father-in-law Constantinus had been killed. There was no delay before the whole populace rushed to the palace.

Romanus was not sought as though he were an illegitimate emperor; rather, everyone asked whether Constantinus was still alive. When a considerable disturbance arose during the search for Constantinus, at the request of Stephanus and Constantinus, Constantinus, with his hair unbound, exposed his head through the lattice on the side where the size of the Zucanistrium was displayed. By showing himself, he immediately calmed the people’s tumult and compelled each person to return home.

This event caused the two brothers great distress. They said:

“What advantage was there in repudiating our father if we must endure as master another man who is not our father? It would be more tolerable and more proper for us to endure paternal rather than foreign rule. What is this, they say, that in support of this man not only our own nations but also foreign peoples have come? For Bishop Sigefredus, King Hugo’s envoy, bringing with him peoples of his own tongue—Amalfitans [Note: [Col. 0887] That is, “Amalfitans.”], Romans, and Gaetans—has been a support to him and a means of our destruction.”

22. After these words, they filled their chambers with armed men, just as they had done on their father’s behalf (year 945). Diavolinus was in command of them; he had been the instigator of all these events and shortly afterward became their betrayer.

He approached Constantinus, who was absorbed in his books, and said:

“Your religious devotion, which has long remained in you, does not know what misfortunes your brothers—or rather, your enemies—Stephanus and Constantinus are preparing for you. If you recognized the disasters being prepared for you, you would consider how you might remain alive.

“Your wife’s brothers, Stephanus and Constantinus, have gathered armed men and already enclosed them in their chambers. They are not merely planning to expel you from the palace as their father; they are planning to kill you here.

“The occasion of your death will be this: after three days they will invite you to dinner [Note: [Col. 0887] One witness reads “on the day after tomorrow.”]. When you attempt to take the place of honor in the middle of the seating, as is customary for your rank, they will strike a shield. At once those shut up in the chamber will leap out and end your life by shedding your blood.

“If you ask for proof of what I have reported, I confirm it immediately with these pieces of evidence: I show you through the cracks the persons who have been shut inside; and, what is more important for your safety, I hand you the keys to the doors.”

When Constantinus heard this, he said:

“Since you have revealed the treachery of the conspirators, express your advice, so that I may overcome it. My safety is not so dear to me as it will be pleasant to my devotion to return thanks.”

Diavolinus replied:

“It is not hidden from you that the Macedonians are both devoted to you and tough in war. Send for them, therefore, and, without Stephanus and Constantinus knowing, pack them into their chambers [Note: [Col. 0887] One witness reads “bedchambers.”].

When the appointed day of the banquet arrives and rivalry breaks out because of the arrogance of the seating, give the signal as I said—namely, strike the shield. Then, when the armed guard cannot be available to them, your men will suddenly leap out, seize them all the more easily because they are unsuspecting, and send them to the nearby monastery to which they had sent their father, your father-in-law. There, after their hair has been cut according to custom, they will be sent to practice philosophy.

“The rectitude of divine justice will indeed support your cause: by its recompense, it did not frighten them from sinning against their father, and it guarded you from offending him.”

That this happened by the just judgment of God is now sung not only throughout Europe but also throughout Asia and Africa. On the appointed day, while the brothers Stephanus and Constantinus, pretending peace, invited this Constantinus to dinner, and while a disturbance arose over the arrogance of the seating, the Macedonians suddenly burst forth when the shield was struck, as had been said. They immediately seized the two brothers, Stephanus and Constantinus, shaved their heads, and sent them to the nearby island where they had sent their father, to practice philosophy.

[Col. 0888A] **23.** When their father heard of the Romans’ arrival, he gave thanks to God and, meeting them outside the monastery gates with a cheerful face, said:

“An auspicious occasion, I think, has compelled your Imperial Highness to visit our humility. I suppose that the affection which drove me from the palace did not permit your Sonship to remain there long. Oh, how well it happened that you sent me ahead some time ago! For my fellow monks and companions-in-arms, occupied only with the philosophy above, would not know how to receive emperors, had they not already had me, long accustomed to imperial usages, among them. Cold water, now prepared—water from the Cottian Alps [Note: [Col. 0887] *parata*, ‘prepared,’ in witness 5a.] [Note: [Col. 0887] *occisis*, ‘slain,’ in 5a; *occiduis*, ‘setting,’ in 5a*] and boiled with frost [Col. 0888D; Juvenal, *Satires* V, 50]—is ready; sweet beans, fresh cabbage [that is, herbs], and leeks are here. Here it is not the delicacies of the sea that produce illnesses, but rather frequent fasts. Yet our modest establishment cannot receive this great and costly throng; it receives only your Imperial Highness, who has come lest he abandon his father’s old age.”

While the Romans were being addressed by these and similar words, Stephen and Constantine, their sons, looked at the ground with downcast eyes. There is no need to ask how unwillingly they were seeking the monastery; one must simply believe it. Thereafter, prostrate with outstretched hands on the threshold of the altar [Note: [Col. 0887] *alteris*, ‘on other things,’ for *altaris*, ‘of the altar,’ in witness 1], he poured forth to God the following prayer with tears:

**Verses**

**24.**

Christ God, with whom the Father and the Spirit are one,

Word of the Father by right, through whom the Father made known

All the secrets of heaven to the world, revealing its hidden mysteries,

Look upon the creature fashioned by your own goodness.

[Col. 0888C]

Do not, I beg, allow me to perish through the demon’s deceit [Note: [Col. 0887] *frade*, an OCR or scribal form of *fraude*, ‘deceit,’ in witness 1],

Whom, by your sacred blood, you willed to restore to life!

Grant, God, that I may now be able to trample the world’s proud attempts,

And that the corruptor of evil, whose labor is always to defile blessed souls,

May stand far away.

When I held the scepters of empire, I took delight in them; now I do not—so be it!

Let it be a grace to you that you have deigned to drive out the wicked [Note: [Col. 0887] The editor corrects the text thus: “Let it be a grace to you that you have deigned to drive out the wicked”; witness 1 reads *pollere*, “to be powerful,” instead of *pellere*, “to drive out.”],

Lest they unjustly possess the ancestral throne of empire.

**25.** After these events, Stephen and Constantine were kept under continuous guard, while their father endured with equanimity what had happened to him. For they say—and confirm it under oath—that when his brothers reproached him over lentils for a purgation, he replied that he ruled more splendidly by serving the humility of God’s servants than one who commanded the powerful sinners of the world.

**26.** Meanwhile, the long-awaited Berengar, coming from the regions of the Suebi with a few companions, sought Italy from Swabia through the Venosta Valley [Note: [Col. 0887D] *Vinstgau*]. He pitched his camp beside a fortress called Formicaria [Note: [Col. 0888D] Formigara, according to Muratori], which, as we have already said, had been entrusted by Manasses, archbishop of the see of Arles and at that time invader of the sees of Trent, Verona, and Mantua, to the guard of his cleric Adelard.

When Berengar saw that he could capture the fortress neither by any apparatus of siege nor by any assault of war, and recognized Manasses’ ambition and *kenodoxia*, that is, vainglory, he asked Adelard to come to him and said:

“If you hand this fortress over to my power and bring your lord Manasses over to assist me [Note: [Col. 0889] The text is uncertain. One reading says: “If you are able to bend him, I shall promote him to the archiepiscopal chair of Milan”; witness 5a has a related reading], I shall grant him the dignity of archbishop of Milan and you that of bishop of Como once I have obtained royal power. And so that you may trust my promise, I confirm by oath what I pledge in words.”

When these words were reported by Adelard to Manasses [Note: [Col. 0889] *mannase*, a variant spelling in witness 1], Manasses ordered not only that the fortress be handed over to Berengar, but also invited all the Italians to come to his aid.

[Col. 0889B] **27.** Thus Rumor, an evil swifter than any other in its mobility [Note: [Col. 0889D] Virgil, *Aeneid* IV, 174–175], quickly announced Berengar’s arrival to everyone. Soon some began to abandon Hugh and attach themselves to Berengar.

Milo, the extremely powerful count of the Veronese, was the first of these. Since Hugh suspected him and had him kept under guard by secretly stationed custodians, Milo pretended not to understand that he was being watched and prolonged dinner almost until midnight. When everyone, overcome both by sleep and by wine [Note: [Col. 0889D] *Lyaeo*, that is, Bacchus], surrendered his body to rest [Note: [Col. 0889] *tradererent*, an error for *traderent* in witness 1], he hurried to Verona accompanied only by the man who had carried his shield. He sent messengers and summoned Berengar, whom he received at Verona so that he might resist Hugh more firmly.

In truth, no infidelity separated him from Hugh; rather, it was certain injuries inflicted upon him by Hugh, which he could no longer endure. Wido, bishop of the church of Modena [Note: [Col. 0889] witness 1 has *mutiniensi*, “of Modena”], followed him—not because he had been unjustly provoked, but encouraged by that great abbey of Nonantola, which he had by then acquired. He not only abandoned Hugh himself, but also brought over a large multitude.

When Hugh heard this, he gathered his forces and came against Wido’s fortress at Vignola [Note: [Col. 0889] *neolam* in one manuscript; *vineolam* in another; the printed form is Vignola] [Note: [Col. 0889D] Vignola, near the Panaro, Muratori’s birthplace], and attacked it bravely but unsuccessfully. How far this is from falsehood the following statement will make clear. While Hugh remained there, Berengar, summoned by Archbishop Arderic, left Verona and hurried to Milan. When King Hugh heard this, he came sadly to Pavia.

Meanwhile all the leading men of Italy began, under an unfavorable omen, to abandon Hugh and attach themselves to the impoverished Berengar. I call him impoverished not because he possessed nothing [Col. 0889D] [Note: [Col. 0890D] The words that follow, through “most certain and genuine wealth,” are copied almost word for word from Cicero, *Paradoxa* VI, 3], but because a man for whom nothing is ever enough is impoverished.

For the wicked and greedy, who possess uncertain goods dependent upon chance and always desire more—indeed, no one among them has yet been found for whom what he possesses would be enough [Col. 0890A] [Note: [Col. 0889] *qsq*, an abbreviation for *quisquam*, “anyone,” in witness 1; witness 5a reads *adhuc sibi sufficiens inventus*, “one hitherto found sufficient to himself”]—must be judged not merely not rich and prosperous, but needy and poor. The only rich people are those who possess fruitful and everlasting things, who are content with their own property and believe that what exists is enough. Not to be covetous is true wealth; not to be acquisitive is revenue.

Let us therefore admit: who is richer, the one who lacks or the one who has more than enough? The one who needs or the one who abounds? The one whose possession, the greater it is, demands more to protect it, or the one who supports himself by his own strength? For to be content with one’s own possessions is the greatest and most certain wealth.

But let what has now been said about this suffice. Let the pen’s attention return to Berengar, at whose arrival everyone promised a golden age and proclaimed that happy times had raised up such a man.

[Col. 0890B] **28.** While he was staying at Milan and distributing the Italian dignities among those who adhered to him, King Hugh sent his son Lothair not merely to Berengar but into the presence of the whole people. He asked that, since they rejected him as one who would not conform to them, they should at least, for the love of God, receive his son, who had done them no wrong [Note: [Col. 0889] *deliquerat*, “had done wrong,” in witness 1], and make him conformable to their wishes.

When Lothair was traveling to Milan, King Hugh left Pavia with all his money and considered abandoning Italy and going to Burgundy [Note: [Col. 0889] *bregundiam* in witness 1]. But this affair detained him. For when they were moved by pity, raised Lothair, who had been prostrate before the cross in the church of the blessed confessors and martyrs Ambrose, Gervasius, and Protasius, and made him their king, they immediately sent a messenger after Hugh, promising that he would again reign over them.

This plan—or rather deception—was devised not by everyone but by Berengar, who was, as usual, stuffed with cunning. He did not intend these men to reign; rather, as later became clear, he wanted Hugh not to depart and summon against him the immense wealth he possessed and the peoples of Burgundy or other nations.

**29.** At this time a certain Joseph, old in character but young in years, was distinguished as bishop of the city of Brescia. Berengar, as he was God-fearing [Note: [Col. 0889] Witness 1 has *deitimens* and, in the margin, *yronicos*; witness 2 reads *dei tiyronicos mens*; witness 5a reads *dei tironicosus mens*; witness 5a* adds *tyrannus vehemens*, “a violent tyrant”], deprived him of the bishopric for his upright character and appointed in his place, without holding any council or obtaining the deliberation of the bishops, Antony, who still survives.

At Como also, instead of Adelard, as he had sworn, he ordained a certain bishop named Waldo, out of affection for the archbishop of Milan. How well he acted is recounted by the devastation of his subjects, the cutting out of vice, the stripping of trees of their bark, [Col. 0891A] the putting out of many eyes, and the most frequent renewal of strife, told both by signs and by groans. He appointed Adelard over the church of Reggio.

**30.** He also considered expelling Boson, the bastard of King Hugh, from the see of Piacenza, and Liutefred from the church of Pavia; but, after a payment had intervened, he pretended that he had spared them for the love of God.

What immense joy there was then among the Italians! They shouted that another David had come. In their blind minds they even preferred him to great Charles. Although the Italian nobles repeatedly received Hugh and Lothair as kings, they regarded Berengar, in name merely a margrave but in power a king, as their king, while they regarded those whom they called kings in name as not even counts in reality.

What more can I say? Moved by Berengar’s immense fame, kindness, and generosity, my parents summoned me and handed me over to him for service. After presenting him with immense gifts [Note: [Col. 0891] *oblati* for *oblatis* in witness 1], they made me his confidant in secret matters and entrusted me with the sealing of his letters.

When I had faithfully served him for a long time, he rewarded me with the payment that, alas, I shall relate in its proper place [Note: [Col. 0891] *prosecurus*, “shall pursue,” in witness 1]. This repayment would almost have driven me to despair if, in a similar matter, it had not produced many companions in misfortune.

Of this man we may aptly understand the saying: “The wings of the ostrich are like the wings of the hawk and the heron. When the time comes, he raises his wings high; he mocks the rider and his mount” (Job XXXIX, 13). While Hugh and Lothair survived, this great and voracious ostrich appeared not good, but like the good. But when they died and everyone advanced him to the heights of royal power, how greatly he raised his wings and how greatly he mocked us all, I relate not so much in words as with sighs and groans.

But leaving this aside, let us return to the sequence of the narrative.

**31.** Since King Hugh could neither avoid divine punishment nor prevail over Berengar, he left Lothair behind and, having handed him over to Berengar’s protection under a pretense of peace, hastened with all his money to Provence.

When Raymond, prince of Aquitaine, heard this, he approached him. For a thousand minas [Note: [Col. 0891] the wording following this phrase is missing in witnesses 5 and 5a] he engaged himself as a soldier and confirmed by oath that he would keep faith with him. He also promised that, after gathering his forces, he would enter Italy and defeat Berengar [Note: [Col. 0891] *debelaturum*, variant spelling in witness 1].

How much this made us all laugh is made clear by the baseness of his people [Col. 0891D]. Even if it could have provided assistance, it would not have brought the matter to completion, since, when called by the Lord, King Hugh soon entered the way of all flesh [Note: [Col. 0891] *ingresus*, variant spelling in witness 1] (April, 947), leaving money to his niece Berta, widow of Boso, count of Arles.

After only a short interval, the aforementioned Raymond, a prince of the most impure nation and himself more impure still [Note: [Col. 0891] *inpudissimae*, “most shameless,” corrected to *inpurissimae*, “most impure,” in witness 1], had made her his wife. Refined [Col. 0892A] observers of beauty repeatedly and emphatically affirm that he was unworthy not only of her embraces but even of her kiss.

[Col. 0892A] **32.** At this time his sister, namely Willa, Berengar’s wife, suffered the crime of incest. That this happened is proclaimed not only by courtiers and chamberlains, but also by huntsmen and kitchen servants.

She had a little priest as chaplain named Dominic: short in stature, dark-complexioned, rustic, bristly, unlearned, uncultivated, barbarous, harsh, hairy, long-tailed, insolent, mad, rebellious, and wicked. Under his instruction Willa had placed two daughters, namely Gisla and Girberga, so that he might make them drink deeply of the knowledge of letters.

On account of these girls, whom the shaggy, unwashed priest Dominic was teaching to make things, [Col. 0892B] their mother had propitiated him, giving him delicate food and precious clothing [Note: [Col. 0891] The words represented by *t. d. c. v. p. M. o. c. c.* are absent from witnesses 5 and 5a]. Everyone wondered why she was generous to this man when she was hateful, disagreeable, and grasping toward everyone else.

Yet the saying of Truth, “Nothing is hidden that will not be revealed, and nothing secret that will not come into the open” (Matthew X, 26), did not allow people to wonder for long. For one night, while Berengar was absent, when this same unkempt man wished, as usual, to approach his lord’s bed, a dog was there. It roused those nearby with terrible barking [Note: [Col. 0891] The words from *isthic* through *excitavit* are absent from witnesses 5 and 5a] and tore him with a violent bite.

Those who were in the house finally arose, seized him, and asked where he was going. Anticipating this explanation, the mistress gave the answer: “The wretch was going to our women!”

The little priest therefore hoped that things would go more gently for him if he agreed with his mistress’s statement: “It is so,” he said.

The mistress then began to plot his death and to promise a reward to anyone who would take his life. But because everyone feared God and his death was delayed, the report reached Berengar.

Willa began to seek out diviners and sorcerers, so that their incantations might aid her. Whether she was helped by their spells or by Berengar’s softness, her mind was so bent that

“Of her own will she offered her lips to the marital halter” [Note: [Col. 0891D] Juvenal, *Satires* VI, 43].

Since the little priest had neighed toward his mistress’s followers, he was released after his manly organs had been cut off; but Berengar loved the mistress all the more. Those who castrated him said that the mistress rightly loved the man who was known to carry Priapic weapons.

**33.** At that time Taxis, king of the Hungarians, came into Italy with a great army. Berengar gave him ten *modii* of coins, not from his own money but from collections taken from churches and the poor.

He did this not out of concern for the people, but to use the occasion to gather a large amount of money. And he succeeded. Every person of either sex, both the weaned and the nursing [Col. 0893A], contributed a coin for himself. By mixing bronze with these coins, he made ten *modii* from a small amount; the rest, and whatever he took from the churches, he kept for himself.

[Col. 0893] **THE FIFTH BOOK ENDS. THANKS BE TO GOD.**

# [BOOK SIX]

## THE CHAPTERS OF BOOK SIX BEGIN

[Col. 0893A]

**1*.** [Note: [Col. 0893] The number is missing.] Prologue.

**2.** How the emperor Constantine sent a messenger to Berengar.

**3.** With what cunning Berengar sent a messenger to Constantinople, to whom he gave nothing.

**4.** At what time that messenger left Pavia and at what time he arrived at Constantinople.

**5.** On the remarkable palace called Magnaura and the reception of the messenger.

[Col. 0893B]

**6.** On the gifts that Berengar’s messenger gave the emperor from his own possessions, on behalf of Berengar, who sent nothing.

**7.** How the emperor invited Berengar’s messenger to his table.

**8.** On the remarkable palace called Decanea and the three great golden vessels.

**9.** On the remarkable game performed at the table [Note: [Col. 0893] “The chapters end. Book Six begins,” in witness 5a].

**10.** [Note: [Col. 0893] The number and summary are missing; the author omitted them when bringing his writing to an end, and nearly two pages are blank in witness 1.]

**1.** The character of the present time compels me to seek a tragic poet rather than a historian, unless the Lord were preparing before my eyes a table in the presence of those who trouble me. For I cannot explain how many hardships shake me whenever I travel abroad [Note: [Col. 0893D] That is, outside my native land of Lombardy, perhaps to Rome], and it is more fitting for the outward man to mourn than to write.

The inner man, however, strengthened by apostolic teachings, glories in such tribulations, knowing that “tribulation produces endurance, endurance character, and character hope; and hope does not disappoint, because the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (Romans V, 3).

Let the outward man therefore obey the inner man and not only refuse to shrink from his misfortunes, but rather rest in them. While he applies himself to writing and says that Fortune’s wheel raises some and lowers others, he will feel his present hardship less; and, rejoicing in its instability, he will no longer fear worse things—which cannot occur unless death or bodily debility intervene—but will always await better fortune.

For if the present situation changes, it will bring the health that is lacking and drive away the misfortune that is present. Let him therefore write and add the following truths to what has gone before.

**2.** After King Hugh died in the regions of Provence [Col. 0894A] (An. 848, 849?), Berengar’s name became famous among certain nations, especially among the Greeks. He ruled over all the Italians by power, while King Lothair possessed only the name.

Constantine, who governed the empire of Constantinople after deposing Romanus and his sons, heard that Berengar surpassed Lothair in power. Through a certain Andrew, who was called *comis* by office [Note: [Col. 0893] One part of a gloss in witness 1 perhaps indicates that *comis* should be joined to the following word, since in the manuscript the words are written on two lines. Witness 2 has *comis* as one word and *curtis* as another] [Note: [Col. 0893D] Greek: **Κόμης τῆς κόρτης**, “count of the court,” that is, prefect of the praetorium], he sent Berengar a letter stating that he very much wished to see Berengar’s messenger, through whose return he would learn how greatly he loved him.

He also wrote a letter of recommendation for Lothair, asking Berengar to be a faithful administrator to him, since by God’s generosity he had become his governor. Constantine, in fact, had considerable concern for Lothair’s safety, religiously mindful out of love for his daughter-in-law, who had been Lothair’s sister.

**3.** Berengar, stuffed with the cunning he possessed, considered whom he should send—someone to whom he would provide no expense because of the journey’s great distance. He went to my stepfather, under whose care I then lived, and said:

“How valuable to me would it be if your stepson were not ignorant of Greek letters?”

When he replied, “I would distribute half my wealth for that advantage,” Berengar said:

“You do not need to do that, nor do you need to contribute even a hundredth part. The emperor of Constantinople has written asking me to send him a messenger. No one can do this better because of steadfastness of mind, or more suitably because of eloquence. What should I say? How easily will he absorb Greek learning, when at so childish an age he drank deeply of Latin learning!”

My stepfather, immediately encouraged by this hope, provided all the expenses and sent me to Constantinople with great gifts.

**4.** On the day of the Kalends of August I left Pavia and came in three days through the channel of the Eridanus to Venice. There I found Salemon, a Greek messenger, a *kitonitan*, a eunuch, returning from Spain and wishing to travel toward Constantinople. He was also taking with him a messenger of our lord—then king, now emperor—namely Liutefred, the richest merchant of Mainz [Col. 0894D].

On the eighth day before the Kalends of September we left Venice [Note: [Col. 0894D] Henschenius, *Acta Sanctorum*, February, vol. I, preface, p. XIX, incorrectly reads *die Veneris*, “on Friday,” for *Venetia*]; on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October [Note: [Col. 0893] *octobris* in the manuscript] we arrived at Constantinople [Col. 0895A]. It will not be tedious to write how we were received in an unheard-of and marvelous manner.

**5.** At Constantinople there is a palace adjoining the imperial palace, of remarkable size and beauty, which the Greeks call *Magnaura*, written with **v** in place of digamma, as though it meant “great aura.”

Constantine ordered it prepared in the following manner, both because of the Spanish messengers who had recently arrived there and because of me and Liutefred.

Before the emperor’s throne stood a bronze but gilded tree, whose branches were filled with gilded bronze birds of various kinds. These emitted the voices of different birds according to their species.

The emperor’s throne had been constructed by such an art that in an instant it appeared low, then higher, and immediately afterward elevated. Around it stood lions of immense size—whether bronze or wooden I do not know, but covered with gold—as though guarding it. They struck the ground with their tails and, with open mouths and moving tongues, emitted a roar [Note: [Col. 0895] The words “which struck the ground with their tails, with open mouths and moving tongues, emitted a roar” are absent from witnesses 2, 5, 5a, and 5].

Thus I was carried on the shoulders of two eunuchs and brought before the emperor. When the lions roared at my arrival and the birds shrieked according to their kinds, I was moved neither by fear nor by astonishment, since I had questioned those who knew all these things well.

After bowing prostrate three times in worship of the emperor, I raised my head. I had first seen him sitting only moderately elevated from the ground; immediately afterward I saw him sitting near the ceiling of the palace, dressed in different clothing. I could not imagine how this had happened, unless perhaps he had been raised by some *argalium* [Note: [Col. 0895D] Greek **τὸ ἐργαλεῖον**, “the instrument”], by which the beams of wine presses are raised.

He himself said nothing to me then, since even had he wished to do so, the great distance between us would have made it improper. Through the *logothete* he asked about Berengar’s life and health. After I had replied accordingly, I left at a signal from the interpreter and was immediately received into the lodging assigned to me.

**6.** Nor should I hesitate to record what I did for Berengar at that time, so that it may be understood how greatly I loved him and what sort of recompense I received from him for my good services.

The Spanish messengers and the aforementioned Liutefred, our lord King Otto’s messenger, had brought gifts to Emperor Constantine, most of them from their lords. I, however, had brought nothing on Berengar’s behalf except a letter—and that letter was full of lies.

My mind therefore burned with considerable shame, and I thought carefully about what he should do in this matter. While I was burning with anxiety and wavering greatly, my mind suggested that I should present, on Berengar’s behalf, the gifts that I had brought from myself to the emperor, and embellish the small gift as best I could with words.

I offered the emperor nine excellent coats of mail, seven excellent shields with gilded bosses, two gilded silver cups, swords, spears, javelins, and four slaves called *carzimasia*, gifts more precious than all those previously named.

The Greeks call a *carzimasium* a boy whose testicles and penis have been cut off, a eunuch. Merchants from Verdun [Note: [Col. 0896D] *Virdunenses*] customarily do this for immense profit and take such boys to Spain.

**7.** After these events the emperor ordered me, three days later, to be summoned to the palace. He spoke with me in person and invited me to a banquet; after the banquet he gave a great gift to me and to my attendants.

Since the opportunity for telling about it has arisen, I think it proper not to remain silent but to write about the nature of his table, especially on feast days, and the kinds of games performed at it.

**8.** Near the Hippodrome, toward the north, there is a house of remarkable height and beauty called *Decanneacubita*. It received this name not arbitrarily, but from visible reasons. For *deca* in Greek means ten in Latin, *ennea* means nine, and *cubita* may be understood as “inclined” or “curved from reclining.”

This is because ten and nine tables are set up in it opposite the Nativity according to the flesh of our Lord Jesus Christ. On these days the emperor and his guests feast not seated, as on other days, but reclining; and on those days they are served not in silver vessels but only in golden ones.

After the meal, fruit was brought in three golden vessels. Because of their immense weight, they were carried not by human hands but in vehicles covered with purple cloth.

Two of them are placed on the table in the following manner. Through openings in the ceiling, three ropes covered with gilded leather, fitted with golden rings, are lowered. They are attached to handles projecting from the trays and, with the assistance of four or more men below, are raised to the table by a revolving instrument above the ceiling; they are lowered in the same way [Note: [Col. 0895] That is, *deponuntur*, “are lowered”].

I shall omit the games I witnessed there, since it would take too long to write about them. But I shall not hesitate to insert one here because of its astonishing character.

**9.** A man came carrying on his forehead a wooden beam more than twenty-four feet long, without any support for his hands. One cubit below its upper end it had a transverse piece two cubits long [Note: [Col. 0895] *tranuersim*, a variant spelling of *transversim*, “transversely”].

Two naked boys were brought in, though wearing loincloths—that is, having brief coverings. They climbed onto the beam and played upon it; then, with their heads turned downward, they descended along it [Note: [Col. 0895] The words describing their climbing, playing, and descending are absent from witnesses 5, 5a, and 5a*]. They kept it motionless, as though it had been rooted firmly in the earth.
