After one had descended, the other, who had remained above and had played alone on the beam, left me even more astonished. As long as both boys had been playing, the feat seemed possible, since they guided the beam on which they had climbed, despite its marvelous nature and its considerable weight [Note: [Col. 0895] The relevant words are absent from witnesses 5, 5a, and 5a*].

But the one who remained at the top of the beam astonished me so greatly that the emperor himself could not fail to notice my amazement. He had balanced himself so evenly that he both played and descended safely.

The emperor therefore summoned an interpreter and asked what seemed more marvelous to me: the boy who had controlled himself so skillfully that the beam remained motionless, or the man who had held it on his forehead with such ingenuity that neither the boys’ weight nor their play bent it even slightly.

When I said that I did not know which of these seemed more *thaumastoteron*, that is, more marvelous, the emperor, bursting into loud laughter, replied that he likewise did not know.

**10.** Nor do I think I should pass over in silence another new and remarkable thing that I witnessed there.

In the week before *vaiophoron*—what we call palm branches—the emperor distributes gold coins to soldiers and to those appointed to various offices, according to what each person’s office deserves. Since he wished me to attend this distribution, he ordered me to come.

It was conducted as follows. A table ten cubits long and four cubits wide had been set up. It held coins tied into packets, according to what was owed to each person, with numbers written externally on the packets.

The recipients entered before the emperor not in confusion but in order, according to the voice of the caller, who recited the men’s names in accordance with the dignity of their office.

The first called was the master of the palace. The coins, together with four *scaramangia* [Note: [Col. 0897C] a *penula*, a kind of military cloak], were placed not in his hands but on his shoulders.

After him *o domesticos tis ascalonas* and *o delongaris tis ploos* were called. One of them commands the soldiers, the other those who sail.

Since their dignity was equal, they received an equal number of coins and *scaramangia*. Because of the quantity, however, they no longer carried them on their shoulders, but, with the help of others behind them, dragged them away with difficulty.

After them twenty-four magistrates were admitted. They were given pounds of gold coins, each receiving twenty-four according to the same number, together with two *scaramangia*.

Next came the order of the patricians, who were presented with twelve pounds of coins and one *scaramangium*. I do not know either the number of patricians or the number of pounds, except what was given to each individual.

After this an immense crowd was summoned: *protospatharii*, *spatharocandidati* [Note: [Col. 0897] The remainder of the chapter is missing in witnesses 5, 3a, and 5a*; at this point a leaf has been cut from witness 5a. The first printed edition adds: “and clients of that kind.”], *kitonitai*, *manglavitai*, and *protocaravoi*. One received seven, another six, another five, four, three, two, or one, according to the degree of dignity.

I do not want you to think that this was completed in a single day [Note: [Col. 0897] *patratum*, “completed,” rather than *paratum*, “prepared,” in witness 2]. It began on Thursday, from the first hour of the day until the fourth hour [Note: [Col. 0897] *die*, “day,” in witness 1; another reading has *diei*] and was completed by the emperor on Friday and Saturday [Note: [Col. 0897] One witness reads “the fourth hour of Friday and Saturday”; another has a more elaborate wording].

To those who received less than a pound, it was no longer the emperor but the *parakoimomenos* who distributed gifts throughout the entire week before Easter. While I stood there and observed the matter with astonishment, the emperor asked through the *logothete* what I thought of it [Note: [Col. 0897] *suscitatus*, “roused,” in witness 2].

I replied: “It would certainly please me if it were beneficial. In the same way, rest appeared beneficial to the rich man tormented by thirst when he saw Lazarus, if only it had come to him [Note: [Col. 0897] A word is missing in witness 2]. Since it did not happen to him, how, I ask, could it have pleased him?” [Note: [Col. 0897] The final word is obscure in witness 2.]

The emperor smiled, somewhat embarrassed, and beckoned me with his head to come to him. He gave me a large cloak together with a pound of gold coins; he gave it willingly, and I received it even more willingly.

[Col. 0897]

# LIUTPRAND, BISHOP OF CREMONA: BOOK ON THE DEEDS OF EMPEROR OTTO THE GREAT

[Note: [Col. 0897] The title “Here begins the book on Otto’s deeds” appears only in witnesses 5 and 5a. I have supplied the division into chapters, which is absent from the manuscripts.]

[Col. 0897D] **(An. 960.) 1.** [Note: [Col. 0897] Witness 2 begins with the words *Waldpertus sanctae*.] While Berengar and Adalbert were reigning—or rather raging—and, to speak more accurately, exercising tyranny in Italy, John, the supreme pontiff and universal pope, whose church had then experienced the savagery of the aforementioned Berengar and Adalbert, sent messengers of the holy Roman Church [Note: [Col. 0897] The final *e* is deleted in witness 1], namely John, cardinal deacon, and Azo, keeper of the archives, to the most serene and devout king—then king, now august emperor—Otto.

Through letters and signs of the situation, he humbly begged him, for the love of God and of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, whom he desired to be the remitters of his sins [Col. 0899A], to free him and the holy Roman Church entrusted to him from their jaws and restore it to its former safety and liberty.

While the Roman messengers were making these complaints, the venerable Walpert, archbishop of the holy church of Milan, having been freed half-alive from the fury of the aforementioned Berengar and Adalbert, approached the power of the aforesaid Otto, then king and now august emperor. He declared that he could neither endure nor tolerate the savagery of Berengar and Adalbert, and also of Willa, who had appointed Manasses, bishop of Arles, over the see of Milan contrary to justice and right.

He asserted that this was the calamity of his church: what ought to have been taken by him and his people was being intercepted.

Waldo, bishop of Como, followed Walpert. He loudly declared that he had suffered, from Berengar, *Adalperto* [i.e. Adalbert], and Willa, an injury no different from that suffered by Walpert.

Several men of another rank had also come from Italy. Among them was the distinguished margrave Otbert, who had accompanied the apostolic messengers and was seeking counsel and assistance from the most holy Otto, then king and now august emperor.

**(An. 961.) 2.** The most devout king, moved by their tearful complaints, thought not of what belonged to him but of what belonged to Jesus Christ. Contrary to custom, while still a boy, he made his son, who bore the same name as himself, king and left him in Saxony; then he gathered his forces and hurried into Italy.

He expelled Berengar and Adalbert from the kingdom all the more swiftly because he had the most holy fellow soldiers, Peter and Paul, the apostles. Thus the good king gathered what had been scattered and repaired what had been broken. After restoring to each person what belonged to him, he went on to Rome to do similar things there.

**(An. 962.) 3.** There he was received with marvelous ceremony and new magnificence and received the imperial anointing from that same supreme pontiff and universal pope, John. The pope not only restored what belonged to him, but also honored him with immense gifts of jewels, gold, and silver (February 2).

From Pope John he obtained an oath over the most precious body of Saint Peter, and from all the leading men of the city, that they would never assist Berengar or Adalbert. After this he returned as quickly as possible to Pavia [Note: [Col. 0899] *Papiam* or *patriam* in witness 2; *patriam* in witness 5a] [Note: [Col. 0899D] In 962, on April 2, 9, and 20, he issued diplomas there.]

4. Meanwhile, the aforementioned Pope John, forgetting the oath and promise which he had made to the holy emperor, sent word to Adalbert that he should come to him, assuring him by oath that he would aid him against the power of the most holy emperor. The holy emperor had so terrified that same Adalbert, the persecutor of God’s churches and of Pope John himself, that, abandoning all Italy, he went to Fraxinetum and entrusted himself to the faith of the Saracens. Finally, the just emperor could not sufficiently wonder why Pope John now loved Adalbert, whom he had previously pursued with vehement hatred. Summoning certain familiars to ask why, he sent them to Rome to inquire whether this was true. When the messengers arrived there, they received the following reply—not from just anyone or from a few, but from all the Roman citizens:

> “There seems to be no different reason why Pope John should hate the most holy emperor, his own liberator, namely, from the hands of Adalbert, and why the devil should hate the Creator. As we have learned by experience, the emperor tastes, practices, and loves the things of God: he protects ecclesiastical and secular affairs with arms, adorns them with his conduct, and purifies them by laws. Pope John opposes all these things.
>
> “What we confess is not hidden from the people. The widow of his own soldier Rainerius is a witness: seized by blind passion, he bestowed upon her many sacred golden crosses and chalices of blessed Peter from the aforesaid city. Stephana, his aunt, is a witness: in a miscarriage she expelled the newly formed human being whom she had conceived by him. Even if everything else were silent, the Lateran palace—once a lodging-place of saints, now a brothel of prostitutes—will not be silent concerning his aunt, his wife, and the sister of his other concubine Stephania.
>
> “Women of every nation except the Romans are witnesses by their absence. They fear visiting the thresholds of the holy apostles to pray, since a few days ago they heard that he had violently assaulted married women, widows, and virgins. The churches of the holy apostles are witnesses: they admit not drops of rain but rain through the entire roof inside, even above the very sacred altars. How greatly the timbers terrify us when we ask divine help from that place! Death reigns upon the roofs; it prevents us from wishing to pray at length and forces us soon to leave the house of the Lord.
>
> “Witnesses are not only the female servants of the reed-mat chambers, but also the women of public daily resort. For him, ‘the women who trample the black flint beneath their feet’ [Juvenal, *Satire* VI, 350] and those who are carried about with the assistance of great beasts are one and the same. This is the reason for his great discord with the holy emperor—‘as great as that which by lot has fallen to wolves and lambs’ [Horace, *Epodes* 5, 4, 1]. So that these things may be permitted him with impunity, he prepares Adalbert as his father, guardian, and defender.”

5. When the emperor heard this from the returning messengers, he said:

> “He is a boy; he will easily be changed by the example of good men. I shall hope that through honorable rebuke and generous persuasion he will easily emerge from those evils. We shall say with the prophet: ‘This is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High’ (Psalm 76:11).”

He added:

> “First, as the order of events demands, let us drive back Berengar, who is resisting on Mount Feretratus; then let us approach the lord pope by paternal *abdicatione* [perhaps *applicatione*, “appeal”]. If not by willingness, then at least through shame he will change into a mature man. Thus, perhaps, once overcome, he will be ashamed to learn good habits and abandon his bad ones.”

6. When these matters had been completed, he boarded a ship at Pavia and reached Ravenna by way of the channel of the Heridanus [perhaps *Heridari*]. Proceeding from there, he laid siege to Mount Feretratus, called Saint Leo, where Berengar and Willa were staying (May, June, July).

The aforementioned pope also sent to the holy emperor as messengers Leo—then a venerable *protoscriniarius* of the holy Roman Church, now vicar of the apostles in the same see of blessed Peter [he occupied the see from December 963 to March 965]—and Demetrius, the most distinguished of the Roman nobles. He instructed them to say that it was no wonder if, until then, overcome by the fire of youth, he had acted like a boy; the time had now come when he wished to live according to another’s way of life.

He also deceitfully alleged that he had received Bishop Leo and Cardinal Deacon John, his disloyal subjects, and that the holy emperor was violating his promise by binding on oath to himself, rather than to the pope, those who were staying in that place.

The emperor replied:

> “I give thanks for the correction and change of conduct which he promises. As for the change of promise of which he accuses me, consider for yourselves whether I have made it, if the charge is true. We promised to restore all the land of Saint Peter that should come under our power; and this is precisely why we are laboring to drive Berengar and his entire household from this stronghold. For how can we restore this land to him if we do not first seize it from the hands of violent usurpers and bring it under our authority?
>
> “We have neither seen nor received Bishop Leo and Cardinal Deacon John, his disloyal subjects, whom he accuses us of having received. When the lord pope sent them to Constantinople because of our injury, they were, as we have heard, captured at Capua.
>
> “With them, as we have also heard, were captured Saleccus, Bulgarian by birth but Hungarian by upbringing, a close associate of the lord pope; and Zacheus, a rejected man ignorant of divine and human letters, newly consecrated by the lord pope as bishop of Gezani near Velletri and sent to the Hungarians to preach, so that they might attack us. We would believe that the lord pope had done these things even if no one told us, if letters did not establish their truth—letters sealed with lead and displaying the characters of his name.”

7. After this, he sent to Rome Landohardus, a bishop from Saxony and of Minden, and Liudprand, a bishop from Italy and of Cremona, together with the aforementioned messengers, so that they might prove to the lord pope that he was without blame. The just emperor also imposed this duty upon their men: if the lord pope did not believe otherwise, they were to prove the truth by judicial combat.

Accordingly, the aforementioned bishops Landohardus and Liudprand came before the lord pope in Rome and were received with such honor that they could not fail to perceive how much the holy emperor was detested and resented. Nevertheless, when they recounted everything in order, just as they had been instructed, the pope refused to accept satisfaction either by oath or by combat, and remained in the same hardness of mind.

Yet, craftily, after eight days he sent Bishop John of Narni and Cardinal Deacon Benedict with them to the lord emperor, thinking that he could deceive him by his tricks; but it was exceedingly difficult to deceive him with words.

Before their return, Adalbert, having been invited by the pope, returned from Fraxinetum and arrived at Centumcellae. Then he proceeded to Rome, where he was received by the pope not, as he ought to have been, with rejection, but honorably.

8. While these events were taking place, the emperor was driven away from the Roman fortresses by the heavy, seething constellation of Cancer under Phoebus’s rays (July). But when the virginal constellation returned and brought agreeable moderation, he gathered his forces and, at the secret invitation of the Romans, came to Rome (September).

Why do I say “secretly,” when most of the Roman nobles had seized the fortress of Saint Paul and had invited the holy emperor, even giving hostages? Why delay with many words? When the emperor encamped near the city, the pope and Adalbert fled from Rome together.

The citizens, however, received the holy emperor and all his men into the city and renewed their oath of fidelity. They added this firmly sworn promise: they would never elect or ordain a pope except with the consent and election of the lord emperor Otto Caesar Augustus and his son, King Otto.

9. Three days later, at the request both of the Roman bishops and of the people, a great assembly was held in the church of Saint Peter. The archbishops and bishops who sat with the emperor were as follows:

From Italy, in place of Ingelfred, patriarch of Aquileia, whom a sudden illness—as commonly happens—had seized in that city: the deacon Rodalfus; Waldpertus of Milan; and Peter of Ravenna.

From Saxony: Adeltac, archbishop; and Landohardus, bishop of Minden.

From Francia: Otkerius, bishop of Speyer; and Hupertus of Parma.

From Italy: Liudprand of Cremona; and Hermenaldus of Reggio.

From Tuscany: Cuonradus of Lucca; Everardus of Arezzo; Pisanus of Siena [the manuscript does not distinguish whether this is a personal or a place-name]; Florentine of Pistoia; Peter of Camerino; and the bishop of Spoleto.

From the Romans: Gregory of Albano; Sico of Ostia; Benedict of Porto; Lucidus of Gabii; Theophylact of Palestrina; Wido of Silva Candida; Leo of Velletri; Sico of Blera; Stephanus of Cerveteri; John of Nepi; John of Tivoli; John of Forum Claudii [the place formerly stood near Calinum]; Romanus of Ferentino; John of Norma; John of Beruli; Marinus of Sutri; John of Narni; John of Sabina; John of Gallese; the bishop of Falerii [the towns are Gallese and Falerii]; the bishop of Alatri; the bishop of Orte; John of Anagni; the bishop of Trevi; Sabbatinus of Terracina; Cardinal Stephanus, archpriest of the title of Balbina; Dominicus of the title of Anastasia; Peter of the title of Damasus; Theophylact of the title of Chrysogonus; John of the title of Equitius; John of the title of Susanna; Peter of the title of Pammachius; Adrian of the title of Callixtus; John of the title of Cecilia; Adrian of the title of Lucina; Benedict of the title of Sixtus; [the priest] of the title of the Four Holy Crowned Martyrs; Stephanus of the title of Sabina; Cardinal Benedict, archdeacon; John, deacon; Bonofilius, cardinal deacon and *primicerius*; Georgius, *secundicerius*; Stephanus, *aminiculator*; Andreas, treasurer; Sergius, *primicerius* of the defenders; John, treasurer [the first manuscript reads *secellarius*]; Stephanus; Theophylact; Adrian; Stephanus; Benedict; Azo; Adrian the Roman; Leo; Benedict; Leo; another Leo; and Leo, notaries; Leo, *primicerius* of the choir school; Benedict, subdeacon and *oblationarius*; Azo; Benedict; Demetrius; John; Amicus; Sergius; Benedict; Urso; John; Benedict, subdeacon and *subpulmentarius*; and Stephanus, archacolyte, with all the acolytes and regionaries.

From the leading men of the Roman city: Stephanus, son of John the *superista* (overseer); Demetrius Meliosi; Crescentius of the Marble Horse; John, surnamed Mizina; Stephanus of Imiza; Theodorus of Rufina; John of the *Primicerius*; Leo of Cazunuli; Rihkardus; Peter of Canaparia; and Benedict with his son Bulgamino.

From the people, Peter, also called Imperiola, stood present with the entire Roman militia.

10. When all these men were seated and maintaining complete silence, the holy emperor began as follows:

> “How fitting it would be for the lord pope John, so distinguished and holy, to be present at this council. But why he has avoided this gathering so completely, we ask you, holy fathers, since you have shared life and common business with him.”

Then the Roman pontiffs and cardinal priests and deacons, together with all the people, said:

> “We marvel at your most holy prudence in asking us about something that is hidden neither from the Iberians, nor the Babylonians, nor the Indians. There is no longer any need here to speak of those who come in sheep’s clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves. He rages so openly and conducts his devilish affairs so publicly that he uses no circumlocution.”

The emperor replied:

> “It seems just to us that the accusations should be stated by name; afterward, let us deliberate by common counsel what must be done.”

Then Cardinal Priest Peter rose and testified that he had seen him celebrate Mass without communicating.

John, Bishop of Narni, and John, Cardinal Deacon, declared that they had seen him ordain a deacon in a horse’s stable and not at the appointed times.

Cardinal Deacon Benedict, together with the other cardinal deacons and priests, said that they knew he sold the ordination of bishops for money and that he had ordained a ten-year-old as bishop in the city of Todi.

Regarding sacrilege, they said there was no need to inquire, since we could know more by seeing than by hearing.

Regarding adultery, they said that they had not seen it with their eyes, but knew with complete certainty that he had abused Rainerius’s widow, Stephana, his father’s concubine, and Anna, a widow, together with her granddaughter, and that he had made the sacred palace a brothel and a house of prostitution.

They said that he had publicly practiced hunting; deprived his spiritual father Benedict of his sight, after which Benedict soon died; murdered Cardinal Subdeacon John after cutting off his genitals; and committed arson while girded with a sword and dressed in helmet and armor [that is, *lorica*, breastplate].

They all—clerics and laymen alike—shouted that he had drunk wine in the love of the devil.

They said that, during games of dice, he had sought the aid of Jupiter, Venus, and the other demons.

They declared that he had not celebrated matins or the canonical hours and had not fortified himself with the sign of the cross.

11. When the emperor heard this, because the Romans could not understand his own speech, namely Saxon, he ordered Liudprand, Bishop of Cremona, to express in Latin to all the Romans what follows. Rising, he began thus:

> “It often happens—and we believe it from our own experience—that men placed in positions of dignity are stained by the slander of the envious. A good man displeases the wicked, just as a wicked man displeases the good. For this reason we regard the accusation against the pope, which Cardinal Deacon Benedict has just read and brought before you, as ambiguous, uncertain whether it burst forth from zeal for justice or from the spiteful hatred of impiety.
>
> “Therefore, in accordance with the authority of the dignity granted to me, unworthy though I am, I appeal to all before God—whom no one can deceive, even if he wishes to—and before his undefiled holy mother, the virgin Mary, and before the most precious body of the prince of the apostles, in whose church these things are being recited: let no insults be hurled against the lord pope unless they concern acts committed by him and witnessed by thoroughly trustworthy men.”

Then the bishops, priests, deacons, the rest of the clergy, and the entire Roman people, as one man, said:

> “If Pope John did not commit the crimes read out by Deacon Benedict—and crimes still more shameful and more numerous—may the most blessed prince of the apostles, Peter, who by his word closes heaven to the unworthy and opens it to the just, not absolve us from the bonds of our sins. Rather, may we be bound by the bond of anathema and placed on the left hand at the last day, with those who said to the Lord God: ‘Depart from us; we do not desire the knowledge of your ways’ (Job 21:14).
>
> “But if you do not accept our testimony, you ought at least to believe the army of the lord emperor, which he [Pope John] confronted five days ago, girded with sword, shield, helmet, and armor. Only the Tiber, which flowed between them, prevented the army from capturing him in such attire.”

Immediately the holy emperor said:

> “There are as many witnesses to this matter as there are warriors in our army.”

The holy synod said:

> “If it pleases the holy emperor, let a letter be sent to the lord pope, so that he may come and clear himself of all these charges.”

Then the following letter was sent to him.

12. “To the supreme pontiff and universal pope, the lord John: Otto, emperor augustus by the favor of divine mercy, together with the archbishops and bishops of Liguria, Tuscany, Saxony, and Francia, sends greetings in the Lord.

“While coming to Rome in the service of God, we asked your sons—namely, the Roman bishops, cardinal priests and deacons, and also the entire people—about your absence and about the reason why you did not wish to see us, the defenders of your church and of yourself. They made such statements about you, and statements so obscene, that if they had been made about actors, they would have brought shame upon us.

“Lest all these things remain hidden from your greatness, we briefly set some of them down; for even if we wished to state everything by name, a single day would not suffice.

“Know, therefore, that you have been accused—not by a few, but by all, both of our order and of the other order—of murder, perjury, sacrilege, incest with your own relations, and incest with two sisters. They also report another thing horrible even to hear: that you drank wine in the love of the devil and, while playing dice, sought the aid of Jupiter, Venus, and the other demons.

“We therefore earnestly ask your fatherhood not to delay coming to Rome and clearing yourself of all these charges. If you fear the violence of the rash multitude, we assure you by oath that nothing will be done beyond the provisions of the holy canons.

“Given on the eighth day before the Ides of November.”

13. When he had read this letter, he wrote the following defense:

> “John, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to all the bishops.
>
> “We have heard it said that you wish to make another pope. If you do this, I excommunicate you before almighty God, so that you may not have permission to ordain anyone or celebrate Mass.” [*da* is an Italianism for *de*, “before.”]

15. When this letter was being read in the holy synod, the religious men who had previously been absent arrived: from Lotharingia, Heinrich, archbishop of Trier; from Emilia and Liguria, Wido of Modena, Gezo of Tortona, and Sigulfus of Piacenza. On their advice they sent the following reply to the lord pope (November 22):

> “To the supreme pontiff and universal pope, the lord John: Otto, emperor augustus by the favor of divine mercy, and the holy synod assembled at Rome for the service of God, send greetings in the Lord.
>
> “At the preceding synod, held on the eighth day before the Ides of November, we sent you a letter containing the words of your accusers and the grounds of the accusation. In that same letter we asked your greatness, as justice requires, to come to Rome and clear yourself of the charges brought against you.
>
> “We have received a letter from you—not one demanded by the gravity of the occasion, but one prompted by the vanity of ill-advised men. There ought to have been a reasonable excuse for not coming to the synod. Your representatives also ought to have been present, to explain either that illness or some definite difficulty had caused you to avoid the holy synod.
>
> “There is also something written in your letter which it would be fitting for a child’s folly, not for a bishop, to write. For you excommunicated all of us, declaring that, if we established another bishop for the Roman see, we should not have permission to celebrate Mass or perform ecclesiastical ordinations. For this is what was written: ‘You may not have permission to ordain anyone.’ Until now we have thought—indeed, we truly believed—that two negatives make an affirmative, unless your authority overturns the judgments of the ancient authors.
>
> “We shall answer your intention, not your words. If you do not delay coming to the synod and clearing yourself of the charges, without doubt we shall obey your authority. But if, which God forbid, you delay coming and clearing yourself of the capital crimes brought against you—especially since nothing prevents your coming, neither the crossing of the sea, nor bodily illness, nor the length of the journey—then we shall disregard your excommunication and rather turn it back upon you, since we can justly do so.
>
> “Judas, the betrayer—or rather the seller—of our Lord Jesus Christ, had earlier received from his master, together with the others, the power of binding and loosing in these words: ‘Amen I say to you, whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven’ (Matthew 18:18). For as long as he was good among his fellow disciples, he was able to bind and loose. But after he became a murderer through greed and sought to kill the life of all, whom could he afterward loose when bound or bind when loosed, except himself, whom he strangled with a most wretched noose?”

“Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of December and sent through Adrian, cardinal priest, and Benedict, cardinal deacon.”

14. When they reached the Tiber, they did not find him. For he had already gone, quiver-bearing, into the countryside, and there was no one who could tell them where he was. Since they could not find him, they returned with the same letter to the holy synod, which was then held for the third time.

Immediately the emperor said:

> “We awaited his arrival so that, with him present, we might bring our complaint against him. But since we now know with certainty that he will not be present, we earnestly ask you to recognize carefully how treacherously he has acted toward us.
>
> “Therefore we make known to you, archbishops, bishops, priests, deacons, and the rest of the clergy, as well as counts, judges, and the entire people, that this same Pope John, oppressed by Berengar and Adalbert, our rebels, sent messengers to us in Saxony, asking us, for the love of God, to come to Italy and free the church of Saint Peter and himself from their jaws. What we did with God’s help need not be explained, since you now see it.
>
> “After he had been rescued by my efforts from their hands and restored to the honor due to him, he forgot the oath and loyalty that he had promised me over the body of Saint Peter. He caused that same Adalbert to come to Rome and defended him against me; he fomented seditions and, in the sight of our soldiers, became a leader in war, dressed in breastplate and helmet. Let the holy synod declare what it decides concerning this.”

The Roman pontiffs, the rest of the clergy, and the entire people replied:

> “An unheard-of wound must be cauterized with an unheard-of remedy. If, through his corrupt morals, he harmed only himself and not everyone, he might in some way be tolerated. How many chaste people have become incestuous by imitating this man? How many upright people have become depraved by following his example of conduct?
>
> “We therefore ask your imperial greatness to expel from the holy Roman Church that monster, redeemed by no virtue from his vices, and to appoint another in his place who can preside over us and benefit us by the example of good conduct; who may live rightly for himself and offer us an example of good living.”

Then the emperor said:

> “What you say pleases me, and nothing would be more agreeable to us than to find such a man to place over this holy and universal see.”

16. After these words, all said with one voice:

> “We choose Leo, the venerable *protoscriniarius* of the holy Roman Church, an approved man worthy of the highest priesthood, as our shepherd, so that he may be the supreme and universal pope of the holy Roman Church, while John the apostate is rejected for his wicked conduct!”

When they had all said this for the third time, with the emperor’s approval they led the named Leo with acclamations to the Lateran palace, according to custom. At the appointed time, they raised him to the supreme priesthood by holy consecration in the church of Saint Peter and promised by oath to remain faithful to him (December 6).

17. (Year 964.) After these things had been accomplished, the most holy emperor, hoping that he could remain in Rome with only a few men so that the Roman people would not be consumed by the size of the army, gave many permission to return home.

When John, who was called pope, learned this, knowing how easily money could corrupt the minds of the Romans, he secretly sent messengers to Rome, promising the money of blessed Peter and of all the churches if they would attack the pious emperor and the lord Pope Leo and impiously slaughter them.

Why delay with many words? The Romans, trusting—or rather deceived—by the small number of the army and encouraged by the promise of money, rushed forward at the sound of the trumpet to attack the emperor and kill him.

The emperor met them above the Tiber bridge, which the Romans had obstructed with wagons. His brave soldiers, accustomed to war, fearless in breast and armor, sprang among them and terrified them like hawks scattering a flock of birds, with no one resisting.

Neither hiding places, baskets, hollow pieces of wood, nor caves used as filthy receptacles could serve as protection for the fugitives. They were killed, and, as commonly happens to brave men, were wounded in the back as they fled.

Who among the Romans would then have survived this slaughter if the holy emperor, moved by mercy—which they deserved not at all—had not restrained his men, who were still eager to kill them, and called them back?

18. After all had been defeated and hostages had been taken from those who remained, the venerable Pope Leo fell at the emperor’s feet and begged him to return the hostages to the Romans and entrust himself to their loyalty.

Finally, at the request of the venerable Pope Leo, the holy emperor returned the hostages to the Romans, not unaware of what those whose actions I shall recount were about to undertake. Thus he entrusted that same pope to the loyalty of the Romans, as one entrusts a lamb to wolves.

Then he left Rome and hurried toward Camerino and Spoleto, where he had heard that Adalbert was staying.

19. Meanwhile, the women with whom John, who was called pope, practiced the sport of his pleasure—women neither lowborn nor few—incited the Romans to destroy Leo, the supreme and universal pope elected by God and by themselves, and to receive John into the city.

When they had done this, the venerable Pope Leo was freed from their hands through God’s mercy. Accompanied by a few men, he set out for the mercy of the most pious Emperor Otto.

20. Finally, the holy emperor, deeply distressed by this great disgrace—both by the expulsion of the lord Pope Leo and by Cardinal Deacon John and the notary Azo, whom the deposed John had disfigured: the former by cutting off his right hand, the latter by cutting off his tongue, two fingers, and nose—decided to return to Rome after assembling his army.

Before the holy emperor’s forces had been gathered, however, the Lord wished to make known to all ages how justly Pope John had been rejected by his own bishops and the entire people, and how unjustly he was later received.

One night, outside Rome, while he was enjoying himself with the wife of a certain man, the devil struck him so violently in the temples (May 14) that he died of the wound within eight days.

But, at the instigation of the one who had struck him, he did not receive the Eucharist as viaticum. We heard this repeatedly under oath from his relatives and familiars who were present.

21. After his death, all the Romans, forgetting the oath they had sworn to the holy emperor, made Cardinal Deacon Benedict pope. They further promised by oath that they would never abandon him but would defend him against the emperor’s power.

When the emperor heard this, he surrounded the city and allowed no one to leave without being mutilated. He afflicted them with siege engines and famine until he recovered the city against the Romans’ will, restored the venerable Leo to his rightful see (June 23), and brought Benedict, usurper of the supreme see, before Leo.

22. While the lord Leo, supreme and universal pope, was seated in the Lateran church, together with the most holy emperor Otto, the Roman bishops, Italian bishops, and archbishops, bishops, priests, deacons from Lotharingia and Saxony, and the entire Roman people—whose names will be written below—Benedict, the usurper of the apostolic see, arrived, led in by the hands of those who had elected him and dressed in pontifical vestments.

Cardinal Archdeacon Benedict addressed him in these words:

> “By what authority or by what law, O usurper, have you arrogated to yourself these pontifical garments, while the venerable lord Pope Leo is present—the very man whom you elected with us to the height of the apostolate after John had been accused and rejected?
>
> “Can you deny that, in the presence of the lord emperor, you promised by oath that you would never elect or ordain yourself pope, together with the other Romans, without the consent of the emperor and of his son, King Otto?”

Benedict replied:

> “If I have sinned, have mercy on me.”

Then the emperor, shedding tears and showing how merciful he was, asked the synod not to prejudice Benedict’s case. If he wished and was able, let him answer the questions and defend his cause; but if he could not or would not, and made himself culpable, let him nevertheless find some mercy for the fear of God.

When he heard this, Benedict himself hastily fell at the feet of Pope Leo and of the emperor and loudly confessed that he had sinned and was an usurper of the holy Roman and apostolic see.

After this, he removed the pallium from himself and returned it to Pope Leo, together with the pontifical staff that he had been carrying. The same pope broke the staff and displayed the broken pieces to the people.

Then he ordered Benedict to sit on the ground. He also removed from him the *casula*, which is called the *planeta*, together with the stole.

Afterward he said to all the bishops:

> “We deprive Benedict, the usurper of the holy Roman and apostolic see, of every honor of the pontificate and priesthood. But by reason of the favour of the lord emperor Otto, through whose efforts we have been restored to our rightful see, we permit him to retain the order of deacon; and no longer in Rome, but into the exile to which he has been assig—”

[Manuscript 1 breaks off in the middle of a word, at the end of a page and the beginning of a line; manuscripts 2 and 4 break off in the same way. Manuscript 5 reads *sed in exilium destinamus*, “but we send [him] into exile”; 5a reads *sed in exilio destinamus*, “but we send [him] in exile”; the printed editions and Alberic read *sed in exilium destinamus*. The sense seems to require: *destinatus est abeat*, “let him depart to the exile to which he has been assigned.”]

# Liudprand, Bishop of Cremona: Report of the Embassy to Constantinople

Liudprand [the spelling is emended throughout; Canisius printed *Luitiprandus*], bishop of the holy church of Cremona, earnestly longs, desires, and wishes that the most invincible Roman emperors augustus, Otto and Otto, and the most glorious empress augusta Adelheid, may always be well, prosper, and triumph.

1. The following account will explain why you did not previously receive either my letters or my messenger. [Manuscript C reads *literas*; it likewise gives *qui etiam, millia, littus, opportunus, imo, tentare, solennis, quotidianus, quatenus, eleemosyna, Joannes,* and *nuncius*, spellings contrary to Liudprand’s usage, which have been corrected.]

We came to Constantinople on the day before the Nones of June and were shamefully received, to your insult, and treated gravely and shamefully. We were confined in a palace that was indeed sufficiently large and open, one that shut out neither the cold nor the heat. Armed soldiers were assigned as guards; they prevented all my men from leaving [C reads *exitium*, “destruction”] and everyone else from entering.

The house itself was accessible only to us who were confined within it, and it was so far removed from the palace that our breath was cut short if we went there not on horseback but on foot.

Our misfortune was increased by the fact that Greek wine was undrinkable for us because of its mixture with pitch, resin, and gypsum. The house itself had no water, and we could not even quench our thirst with water that we might purchase with money.

To this great “woe, woe” another was added: a man, *scili[lacuna]orum* keeper [the reading is *Sciliorum*, alternatively *Siciliorum*, in C; perhaps one should read: “a man, namely, keeper of our [houses?]”]. If you seek his equal, perhaps hell, not earth, will provide one. For whatever calamity, whatever robbery, whatever loss, whatever grief, whatever misery he could devise, he poured upon us like a flooding torrent.

Not one of the hundred and twenty days passed without bringing us at least sighs and grief.

Editorial notes and variants omitted above: §4: “[Col. 0899D: Liudprand?]”; the corrected Roman reading is “not from just anyone or a few, but from all”; manuscript 1 has *divina* for *divinam*; “not only female servants but also public prostitutes”; Juvenal, *Satires* VI.350; Horace, *Epodes* IV.1. §5: manuscript 1 has *pudebis*, “you will be ashamed,” for *pudebit*. §6: manuscript 1 reads *heridari*; its preceding line has *quia et* and the following one *quod*. §9: manuscript 1 has *Cuoradus*; it does not distinguish *Pisanus*; it reads *secellarius*; and it has *imperiola*. §10: manuscript 1 originally had *io* for *eo*; its reading of *vita* is indicated only by the stylus, though manuscript 2 reads *eo vita*; it has *exprimitur* and *cardinales*. §11: manuscript 1 has *sidonus* for *synodus*. §12: manuscript 1 has *adfirmus*. §13: manuscript 1 has *ullum*, but the following context shows that *nullum* must be read. §15: the clause asking John to come to Rome is absent in 5a and 5a*; manuscript 1 has *gatiua* for *negativa*; the words of Matthew 18:18 from *ligata erunt et in caelis* through *erunt soluta et in caelis* are absent in 5a and 5a*; *cupiditatis causa* is absent in 5a, while 5a* has *veneno*, “by poison.” §14: manuscripts 1 and 2 lack a word after *episcopis*. §17: manuscript 1 has *irruent*; 5a* has *sicientes* for the difficult *sciscientes*. §20: manuscript 1 has *percussera* and glosses *Roma* as “to Rome.” §21: manuscript 1 has *nra* for *nomina*. §22: manuscript 1 glosses *peccasse* as “he had sinned.”

2. On the day before the Nones of June, as we wrote above, we arrived at Constantinople before the Carea Gate [Note: [Col. 0911] Perhaps the Golden Gate.] and waited there with our horses until the eleventh hour, in no slight rain. At the eleventh hour, however, Nicephorus, judging us unworthy to ride in such splendid fashion under your mercy, ordered us to come on foot; and we were led as far as the aforesaid marble house, loathsome, without water, and open to the elements. On the eighth day before the Ides [Note: [Col. 0911] That is, “the eighth day before the Ides.”]—the first day of Pentecost—I was led before the presence of his brother Leo, the curopalates [Note: [Col. 0911] Always written *coroplati* in C.—Curopalates. Corippus, Book 2: “made immediately *cura palatii*”; and Book 1: “called *cura palatii*.”], and the logothete, where we were wearied by a long dispute concerning your imperial title.

For he called you not “emperor”—that is, *basileus* (βασιλεύς)—in his own language, but, out of indignation, *rhegas* (ῥῆγας), that is, “king.” When I told him that the thing signified was the same, although the signifying terms were different, he replied that I had come not for peace but for contention. Then, rising angrily, he received your letters, truly indignant, not himself but through an interpreter. The man was physically quite tall, falsely humble; if anyone leaned upon him, his hand would pierce him.

3. On the seventh day before the Ides [Note: [Col. 0911] That is, “the seventh day before the Ides.”]—namely, on the holy day of Pentecost, June 7—I was led into the house called *Stephana* (Στεφάνα) [Col. 0911C], that is, “the Crowned House,” before Nicephorus: a thoroughly monstrous man, a pygmy, fat-headed, mole-eyed because of the smallness of his eyes, disfigured by a short, broad, thick, half-gray beard, deformed by a neck no thicker than a finger, and, because of the length and thickness of his hair, sufficiently bristly [*hyopam*, “hirsute”] [Note: [Col. 0911D] Presenting a face like a pig (*hys*, ὗς) and a snout (*ops*, ὄψ).]. In complexion an Ethiopian, whom you would not wish to encounter halfway through the night; with an extended belly, dry buttocks, thighs short in proportion to his body yet excessively long, short legs, and heels and feet of equal length. He was dressed in a woolen [*byssino*, “linen”] garment, but one excessively old and, through its very age, foul-smelling and pale; he wore Sicilian shoes. In speech he was shameless, in character a fox [Note: *ingeniis* perhaps for *ingenio*, “in character”], and in perjury or lying an Ulysses.

I kept saying to myself: “How handsome my lords, the august emperors, have always seemed—how much more handsome than this man! How splendidly adorned—how much more splendidly adorned than he! How powerful—how much more powerful than he! How gentle—how much gentler than he! How full of virtues—how much fuller than he!”

Two small emperors sat on his left, not on the same level but far below [Col. 0912A] [Note: [Col. 0911D] Basil and Constantine, sons of the Roman emperor.], once his masters and now his subjects. This was the beginning of his speech:

4. “We ought, indeed we wished, to receive you graciously and magnificently; but the impiety of your lord does not permit it. He seized Rome for himself in so hostile an invasion; he deprived Berengar [Note: [Col. 0912D] He died in the year 966.] and Adalbert of life against all right and justice; he slew some Romans by the sword, others by hanging; he deprived some of their eyes and banished others into exile [Note: [Col. 0912D] At the beginning of the year 967. *Continuation of Regino*.]; and, in addition, he attempted to bring the cities of our empire under his control by murder or fire [Note: [Col. 0911] *Subducere* in Brower, *Annales Trevirenses*, p. 471, on the basis of a manuscript.]. Since his wicked purpose could not achieve its end, he has now sent you to us, under the appearance of peace, as the instigator and prompter of this wickedness, like a spy—*askopos* (ἄσκοπος) [Note: [Col. 0911] Perhaps *kataskopos* (κατάσκοπος), “spy.”].”

[Col. 0912B] 5. I replied to him: “My lord did not invade the city of Rome by force or tyrannically; rather, he freed it from the yoke of a tyrant—or rather, of tyrants. Were not effeminate men ruling it? And, what is more serious and shameful, were not prostitutes ruling it? At that time, I suppose, your power was asleep—indeed, the power of your predecessors, who are called Roman emperors in name alone, but not in reality. If they were powerful, if they were Roman emperors, why did they allow Rome to remain under the control of prostitutes?

“Were not some of the most holy popes banished, while others were afflicted by you, so that they could obtain neither their daily expenses nor alms? Did not Adalbert send insulting letters to the Roman and Constantinopolitan emperors, your predecessors? Did he not strip the churches of the holy apostles through plunder? Which of you emperors, moved by zeal for God, took care to avenge so shameful a crime and restore the holy Church to its proper condition?

“You neglected it; my lord did not neglect it. Rising from the ends of the earth and coming to Rome, he removed the wicked and restored all power and honor to the vicars of the holy apostles. Afterwards, those who rose up against him and against the apostolic lord—as violators of their oath, sacrilegious men, torturers and robbers of their apostolic lords—he struck down, slaughtered, hanged, and banished into exile, according to the decrees of the Roman emperors Justinian, Valentinian, Theodosius, and the others. If he had not done so, he would have been impious, unjust, cruel, and tyrannical.

“It is well known that Berengar and Adalbert, having become his soldiers, received the Italian kingdom from his hand under a golden scepter [Col. 0912D] [Note: [Col. 0912D] At Augsburg in the year 952.], and, in the presence of your servants who still survive and live in this city, promised him their allegiance by oath. Since, at the devil’s prompting, they treacherously violated that oath, he justly deprived them of the kingdom as deserters and rebels against him. You would do the same to those subject to you who later became rebels.”

6. “But,” he said, “Adalbert’s soldier does not admit this.”

I replied: “If he says otherwise, one of my soldiers, if you order it, will demonstrate tomorrow in single combat that this is how the matter stands.”

“Granted,” he said, “that he did these things, as you say, justly. Now explain why he has attacked the borders of our empire with war and fire. We were friends and were planning to establish an unbreakable alliance through a marriage.”

7. “The land which you claim belongs to your empire,” I replied, “is shown by its inhabitants and language to belong to the Italian kingdom. The Lombards held it in their power; and Louis, emperor of the Lombards—or of the Franks—freed it from the Saracens after overthrowing their multitude.

“Landulf, prince of Benevento and Capua, also subjected it to himself by force for seven years. It would not even now have escaped the yoke of his servitude, or that of his successors, if the Romans had not, after paying an immense sum of money, purchased the friendship of our king, the emperor Hugh [Note: [Col. 0913] Alternatively, ‘the best pledge.’]. This was the reason why he joined in marriage his nephew and namesake—the bastard son of our king, that same Hugh [Note: [Col. 0913D] See *Antapodosis* V.14.].

“And, as I understand it, you attribute to my lord not generosity but incapacity, because after acquiring Italy or Rome he left it to you for so many years. As for the alliance of friendship which you say you wished to establish through a family connection, we recognize fraud and deceit in it. You demand truces [*pausanas*, ‘pauses’], although reason compels neither you to demand them nor us to grant them.

“But so that deception may be carved away and truth not concealed: my lord sent me to you so that, if you are willing to give the daughter of the Roman emperor and the empress Theophano in marriage to my lord’s son, the august emperor Otto, you may affirm this to me by oath; and I, in return for this favor, shall affirm by oath that my lord will do and observe these and those things for you.

“Moreover, my lord has now bestowed upon your fraternity an excellent pledge of friendship, when, through my intervention—though you say that this evil was brought about by my suggestion [Note: [Col. 0913] *Romanus* in C.]—he placed all Apulia under your authority. There are as many witnesses to this as there are inhabitants of all Apulia.”

8. (June 7, 968.) “The second hour,” said Nicephorus, “has already passed. We must celebrate the *proeleusis* (προέλευσις), that is, the procession. Let us attend to what is now before us. We shall answer these matters when the opportunity is suitable.”

[Col. 0913D] 9. I should not hesitate to describe the procession itself [Note: [Col. 0913D] Compare Constantine Porphyrogenitus, *The Book of Ceremonies of the Byzantine Court*, Book I, chapter 9.] and let my lords hear of it.

A great multitude of merchants and obscure persons, gathered for that solemnity [Col. 0914A], occupied the edges of the road like walls from the palace to Hagia Sophia, for the reception and praise of Nicephorus. They were disgraced by very thin little shields and cheap spears. To increase this disgrace, the greater part of the common people themselves proceeded barefoot in his praise. I suppose they thought that in this way they would better adorn the holy procession.

His nobles too, who had crossed through that plebeian and barefoot multitude with him, were dressed in tunics cracked by great age and excessively worn. They would have proceeded much more decently dressed in their everyday clothing. There was no one whose great-grandfather possessed a new garment of that kind. No one there was adorned with gold, no one with gems, except Nicephorus alone, whom the imperial ornaments, borrowed and fitted from the persons of former emperors, had made even uglier.

“By your welfare, which is dearer to me than my own: one precious garment of one of your nobles is more valuable than a hundred or more of these!”

I was led to the procession itself and placed in a prominent position beside the singers, that is, the cantors.

10. As that monstrous creature proceeded, crawling along as it were, the flatterer-singers shouted:

“Behold, the morning star comes; the Dawn rises; he strikes back the rays of the sun with his gaze; the pale death of the Saracens, Nicephorus the *medon* (μέδων), that is, prince!”

And they sang:

“To the prince, Nicephorus, many years”—*medonti Nicephoro, polla etē* (μέδοντι Νικηφόρῳ, πολλά ἔτη) [Note: [Col. 0913D] Codinus Curopalates, *Book on the Offices of the Court of Constantinople*: “As soon as the emperor appears, the singers immediately sing the *polychrōnion*, ‘for many years.’” Curopalates calls the singing itself, or the act of praying for many years, *polychrōnisma*.].

“Peoples, worship him; honor him; submit your necks to him, so great is he!”

How much more truthfully they might then have sung:

“Come, extinguished coal, *melle*; old woman in gait; Silvanus in face; rustic, [Col. 0914C] wanderer through the woods; goat-footed; horned; two-natured; bristly; unteachable; savage; barbarian; harsh; hairy; rebellious Cappadocian!”

Thus puffed up by those lying dirges, he entered Hagia Sophia, while his imperial masters followed him from a distance and bowed down to the ground in the kiss of peace. His armor-bearer placed in the church a year-marker made from a reed, with an arrow inserted into it [Note: [Col. 0913] Alternatively, “an altar.”] [Note: [Col. 0914D] That is, the year of his reign.]. It records the time at which he began to reign, and in this way those who did not witness it understand the year.

11. On that same day he ordered me to dine with him. But, judging me unworthy to be seated before any of his nobles, I sat fifteenth from him without a coverlet. None of my companions—not merely did they fail to sit at the table, but none of them even saw the house in which I was dining.

At that dinner, which lasted a considerable time and was disgraceful, he asked me many questions about your power, your kingdoms, and your soldiers. The meal was steeped in oil, as is customary among drunkards, and sprinkled with some exceedingly foul fish-sauce.

When I answered him appropriately and truthfully, he said: “You are lying! Your lord’s soldiers are ignorant of riding and unskilled in fighting on foot. The size of their shields, the weight of their cuirasses, the length of their swords, and the heaviness of their helmets prevent them from fighting on either side.”

Then, smiling, he added: “They are also hindered by *gastrimargia*, that is, gluttony of the belly. Their god is their belly; their courage, drunkenness; their strength, intoxication; their fast, dissolution; their fear, sobriety.

“Nor does your lord possess a sufficient number of fleets at sea. The strength of seafarers belongs to me alone. I shall attack him with fleets, destroy his maritime cities by war, and reduce to ashes those situated near rivers. Who, tell me, could resist me on land even with a small number of troops?

“His son was not absent [Note: [Col. 0915] *Adfuit*, ‘was present,’ in C.], nor was his wife lacking; the Saxons, Suebi, Bavarians [Note: [Col. 0915] *Boarii* in C.], and all the Italians were present with him. Yet when they did not know—indeed, were unable—to capture a single little city that resisted them, how will they resist me when I come, followed by troops as numerous as the ears of corn at Gargara [Note: [Col. 0915D] Ovid, *The Art of Love* I.56], as the clusters of grapes at Methymna,

as the stars in the sky and the waves upon the sea!”

12. When I wished to answer him and vomit forth an apology worthy of such inflation [Note: [Col. 0915] *Emovere* in C.], he did not permit me. Instead, as though to add insult, he said: “You are not Romans, but Lombards!”

When I still wished to reply, and he signaled with his hand that I should be silent, I said, angered: “The chronicles have made known that Romulus, the fratricide from whom the Romans received their name, was *porniogenitus*, that is, born from adultery. He made for himself an asylum in which he received debtors who owed another man money, runaway slaves, murderers, and those deserving death for their crimes; he gathered a certain multitude of such men around himself and called them Romans.

“From that nobility those whom you call *kosmokratores*, that is, emperors, have themselves sprung. We—namely Lombards [Note: [Col. 0915] *Longobardi* in C.], Saxons, Franks, Lotharingians, Bavarians [Note: [Col. 0915] *Baoarii* in C.], Suebi, and Burgundians—despise them so greatly that, when provoked against our enemies, we use no other insult than ‘Roman!’ By that single name, the name of Romans, we comprehend whatever there is of ignobility, cowardice, avarice, lust, falsehood—indeed, whatever vices there are.

“But since you call us unwarlike and ignorant of riding, if the sins of Christians deserve that you continue in this severity, the coming wars will show what you are and how warlike we are.”

13. Provoked by such words, Nicephorus ordered silence with a gesture, had the long, narrow table carried away, and ordered me to return to the loathsome house—or, to speak more truthfully, the prison.

There, after two days, I was overcome by great weakness, both from his indignation and from heat and thirst. None of my attendants escaped without, after being intoxicated by the same cup, fearing that his final day was near. Why, I ask, should they not have fallen ill, when their drink, in place of the finest wine, was brine; when, in place of a mattress, they had not hay, not straw, not even earth, but hard marble; and when, in place of a pillow, they had a stone? Their open house warded off neither heat, rain, nor cold. Even health itself, if it wished, could not have saved them, surrounded as they were by these circumstances, as the common saying goes.

Thus weakened by anguish, both my own and that of my companions, I summoned my guardian—or rather, my persecutor—and by prayers, but also by payment, obtained that he should take to Nicephorus’s brother a letter containing the following:

14. “To Leo the curopalates and logothete of the *dromos* [Note: [Col. 0915D] The logothete of the *dromos* was John Tzimiskes, Nicephorus’s successor, of whom Zonaras says: ‘Having removed him [Nicephorus] from military command, he transfers him to civil office as logothete of the *dromos*.’]—Liudprand, bishop.

“If the most serene emperor intends to fulfill the petition for which I came, the sufferings which I endure here do not weary me. Let my lord be informed only by my letter and messenger that I am staying here for no irrelevant reason. But if the matter is otherwise, there is here a Venetian merchant ship [Note: [Col. 0915] *Et* in C.] [Note: [Col. 0915] *Onerariaque* in C.] preparing to depart. Let him permit me, though ill, to board it, so that, if the hour of my dissolution has arrived, at least my native soil may receive my corpse.”

15. When he had read this, he ordered me to come to him after four days. The wisest men, eloquent in Attic speech, sat with him to deliberate on your affairs according to their custom: Basil the *parakoimomenos* [Note: [Col. 0915] *Paracknoumenos* in C.], the *proto a secretis*, the *protovestiarius*, and two magistri. Their speech began as follows:

“Explain, brother, what is the reason that you have wearied yourself by coming here.”

When I told them that the occasion was the family connection, which would establish unending peace, they replied:

“It is an unheard-of thing for a purple-born woman (*porphyrogenita*), that is, a daughter born in the purple of a man born in the purple, to be joined to foreign peoples. But since you are asking for so exceptional a thing, if you give what is appropriate, you shall receive what you desire: Ravenna and Rome, together with all the territory extending from them to us.

“But if you desire friendship without a family connection, let your lord permit Rome to be free; and let him return the princes, namely the princes of Capua and Benevento, once servants of our holy empire and now rebels, to their former servitude.”

16. I replied: “You yourselves are not unaware that my lord has Slavs more powerful than Peter, king of the Bulgarians, who took the daughter of the emperor Christopher in marriage.”

“But Christopher,” they said, “was not born in the purple.”

17. “As for Rome,” I replied, “which you loudly insist you wish to be free, whose servant is it? To whom does it pay tribute? Was it not previously enslaved to prostitutes? And while you were asleep—or rather, unable—did not my lord, the august emperor, free it from so shameful a servitude?

“Constantine, the august emperor who founded this city after his own name, as *kosmokrator*, bestowed many gifts upon the holy apostolic Roman Church—not only in Italy but in nearly all the western kingdoms, and also in the eastern and southern regions, namely Greece, Judea, Persia, Mesopotamia, Babylonia, Egypt, and Libya, as the privileges in our possession testify.

“Indeed, whatever there is in Italy, and also in Saxony, Bavaria [Note: [Col. 0917] *Baoaria* in C.], and all the kingdoms of my lord that pertains to the church of the blessed apostles, he bestowed upon the most holy vicar of the apostles. And if it is true that my lord possesses from all this cities, villages, soldiers, or dependents, then I have denied God.

“Why, then, does your emperor not do likewise? Why does he not return to the church of the apostles what belongs to his kingdoms, and, through the labor and generosity of my lord, make that church rich and free—indeed, make it still richer and freer himself?”

18. “But he will do this,” said Basil the *parakoimomenos* [Note: [Col. 0917] *Parakimomenos* in C.], “when Rome and the Roman Church are governed at his command.”

Then I said: “A certain man, after suffering much injury from another, assailed God with these words: ‘Lord, avenge me against my adversary!’ The Lord replied: ‘I shall do so on the day when I repay each person according to his works.’ But the man said: ‘How slowly!’”

19. Then all of them, except the brother, burst into laughter, ended the discussion, and ordered me taken back to the loathsome house. They ordered me to be guarded with great care until the solemn feast of the holy apostles.

At that celebration he ordered me, though quite ill, and the Bulgarian envoys, who had arrived the day before [Col. 0917C], to meet him at the Church of the Holy Apostles (June 29). After the chatter of dirges and the celebration of the Mass, when we were invited to the table, he placed before me, at the nearer edge of the long table, which was narrow, a Bulgarian envoy tonsured in the Hungarian fashion, surrounded by a bronze chain and, as my mind suggests, a catechumen—plainly to the insult of you, my august lords.

“You were despised in me, rejected in me, cast aside in me. But I give thanks to the Lord Jesus Christ, whom you serve with all your spirit, that I have been deemed worthy to suffer insults for your name.

“Yet, my lords, because I considered not my own injury but yours, I left the table. As I wished to depart in indignation, Leo the curopalates, the emperor’s brother, and Simeon the *proto a secretis* followed behind me, barking these words:

“When Peter, the *vasileus* of the Bulgarians, took Christopher’s daughter as his wife, written agreements—that is, *symphona*, concordances—were confirmed by oath, so that among all the nations’ apostles, that is, envoys, the Bulgarian apostles among us should be placed first, honored, and loved.

“That Bulgarian apostle, although, as you say—and it is true—he is tonsured, unwashed, and encircled by a bronze chain, is nevertheless a patrician. We decree and judge it unlawful to place any bishop before him, especially a Frankish one.

“And since we know that you take this badly, we are not now allowing you to return, as you suppose, to your lodging; instead, we compel you to taste food with the emperor’s servants in some lodging-house.”

20. Because of the incomparable sorrow in my heart I replied nothing to them, but did what they had ordered. I judged it an indignity that at a table not I—that is, Liudprand the bishop—but the Bulgarian envoy should be placed before your envoy.

Yet the holy emperor relieved my pain with a great gift. He sent me one of his most delicate foods: a fat kid, from which he himself had eaten, lavishly stuffed with garlic, onion, and leeks, and steeped in fish-sauce. I wished that it were present at your table at that time, so that those of you who do not believe that the holy emperor’s delicacies are auspicious might believe it at least after seeing them.

21. After eight days had passed, when the Bulgarians had already departed, he compelled me, though still quite ill, to dine with him in the same place, believing that I would enhance his table. He was present with several bishops and the patriarch [Note: [Col. 0917D] The patriarch here was Polyeuctus.]. In their presence he posed many questions to me about the sacred Scriptures. By the inspiration of the Holy Spirit I explained them elegantly. Finally, wishing to make sport of you, he asked what councils we recognized.

When I named Nicaea, Chalcedon, Ephesus, Antioch, Carthage, Ancyra, and Constantinople, he said: “Ha! Ha! He! You have forgotten to mention the Saxon council. If you ask why our books do not contain it, I answer that the Saxons are still uncultivated and have not yet been able to reach us.”

[Col. 0918C] 22. I replied: “The member in which weakness reigns must be burned with the cautery. All the heresies flowed forth from you and flourished among you; among us—that is, among the westerners—they were strangled and killed.

“We do not count among these the Roman, or Papian, council, although there were often such councils. For the Roman cleric Gregory, later universal pope, whom you call ‘the Dialogist,’ freed Eutychius, patriarch of Constantinople, from this sort of heresy.

“That Eutychius not only said but taught, proclaimed, and wrote that at the resurrection we would assume not true flesh like that which we possess here, but a kind of fantastic flesh. Gregory orthodoxly burned the book of that error. But Evodius, bishop of Pavia, was sent here—that is, to Constantinople—by the Roman patriarch because of another heresy, which he suppressed and reformed into the Catholic and orthodox faith.

“The race of the Saxons, from the time when it received the holy washing and knowledge of God, has not been stained by any heresy, so that no council needed to be held there to correct an error when there was none.

“Since you say that the faith of the Saxons is uncultivated, I affirm the same thing myself. Among them the faith of Christ is always uncultivated and not old, where works follow faith. Here faith is not uncultivated but old, where works do not accompany faith and where, as though from excessive age, it is despised like a discarded garment.

“But I know with certainty that this council was held in Saxony: there it was discussed and confirmed that it is more fitting to fight with swords than with pens, and to meet death before turning one’s back to enemies. Your own army has experienced this! I said in my heart: ‘Let it also experience in reality how warlike they are!’”

23. Yet on that same day, after midday, he ordered me—so weak and transformed that the women who encountered me earlier, turned to astonishment of mind, cried out “Mother, mother!” [Note: [Col. 0919] That is, “mother, mother.”] and beat their breasts with their fists in pity for my misery—to meet him as he returned to the palace.

It was said: “Poor and wretched man!” (*tapeine kai talaipōre*, ταπεινὲ καὶ ταλαίπωρε!) [Col. 0919B].

As for what I wished for then, with my hands raised to heaven, against Nicephorus as he approached and in your absence, may it come to pass!

But I would have you believe me: it made me laugh considerably. For, sitting upon an impatient and unbridled horse—quite small upon a very large one—my mind pictured him as a doll, which your Slavs, tying to a horse-foal, let follow its mother as she goes before at a reckless pace.

24. When these matters were finished, I was taken back to my fellow citizens and cohabitants, the five lions, in the aforesaid loathsome house. There, after a period of three weeks, I was visited by no one except my own companions.

From this circumstance my mind pictured Nicephorus as never intending to release me. Excessive sadness so added illness to illness that I would have departed this life [Col. 0919C], unless the Mother of God had obtained this for me by her prayers from the Creator and her Son, as was shown to me in a vision—not a fantastic one but a true one.

25. During those three weeks Nicephorus had a *metastasis* outside Constantinople—that is, a station—in a place called *Eis pēgas* (Ἐις πήγας), that is, “At the springs.” He ordered me to come there as well.

I was so weak that not only did the station but even sitting itself seem a burdensome delay to me. Nevertheless, with my head uncovered—something extremely contrary to my poor health—he compelled me to stand before him, and said:

“The envoys of your lord, King Otto, who preceded you last year, promised me by oath—and the written oath is here at hand—that they would never in any matter offend our empire. What greater offense is there than that he calls himself emperor and appropriates the themes of our empire to himself? Neither thing can be tolerated; and if both are intolerable, this is the one that must not be endured, indeed not even heard: that he calls himself emperor.

“But if you confirm the same things that they did, the majesty of our empire will quickly send you away fortunate and rich.”

He did not say this because I could hope that you would be preserved if my folly did such a thing. Rather, he wanted to have in hand something that he could display in praise of himself and to our disgrace in future times.

26. I replied: “Recently my most holy lord, being as wise and filled with the Spirit of God as he is, foresaw these things which you assert. To prevent me from transgressing the limits he set for me, he wrote an *entolina* (ἐντόλινα), that is, a command, and sealed it with his own seal, so that I should not act otherwise.

“You know, my august lord, with what confidence I said this.

“Let this *entolina* be produced before us, and whatever it commands, let it be confirmed to you by my oath. But the earlier envoys promised, swore, and wrote these things beyond the command of my lord.

“Thus it is as Plato says: ‘The cause lies with the one who desires; God is beyond blame.’”

27. When these matters were finished, we came to the noble princes of Capua and Benevento, whom he himself calls servants and because of whom inward anguish torments him.

“Your lord,” he said, “takes my servants under his protection. If he does not release them and restore them to their former servitude, he will lose our friendship. They themselves beg to be received into our empire; but our empire refuses them, so that they may learn and experience how dangerous it is to turn away from one’s masters and escape servitude.

“It is more fitting for your lord to hand them over to me as a friend than to release them to me unwillingly. They shall certainly experience, with life as their companion, what it means to deceive a master and what it means to desert servitude. And, I think, they now feel what I am saying, through the actions of our soldiers who are beyond the sea.”

28. He did not permit me to answer them. Instead, when I wished to depart, he ordered me to return to his table. His father sat beside him, a man who, as it seemed to me, had been born one hundred and fifty years earlier. The Greeks praised him just as they praised his son—or rather, shouted their empty flatteries—and cried, “May God multiply his years!”

From this we can infer how foolish the Greeks are, how fond they are of this sort of glory, how flattering, and how eager for it. They alone wish not merely for years but for a very old man [Note: [Col. 0920D] An utterly decrepit old man.] to live longer, although they know for certain that nature itself does not allow it. And the decrepit old man rejoices that they wish for him things which he knows neither God can accomplish nor, even if accomplished, could benefit him rather than harm him [Note: [Col. 0919] *Tibi* in C.].

Why, I ask, should Nicephorus rejoice in the peace of [lacuna] they were crying out, calling him also the light-bearer [Note: [Col. 0919] Something is missing here in C.]. To call a powerless man virile, a foolish man wise, a short man great, a black man white, and a sinner holy is, believe me, not praise but insult.

And the man who rejoices more in having others acclaim him than in his own qualities is entirely like birds, whose sight the night illuminates and the day blinds.

29. But let us return to the matter. At this dinner [Note: [Col. 0919] *Caena* in C.], something he had not previously done, he ordered a homily of blessed John Chrysostom on the Acts of the Apostles to be read aloud, in a raised voice [Note: [Col. 0919] Alternatively, *voscelatus*; I correct to *voce elata*. C. has *voce* in the Latin text.].

After the reading was finished, when I asked permission to return to you, he indicated with his head that he would do so and ordered my persecutor to take me back to my fellow citizens and cohabitants, the five lions.

From that time I was not seen by him until the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August (July 20), but I was carefully guarded so that I could not enjoy conversation with anyone who might inform me of his actions.

Meanwhile, he ordered Grimizon, Adalbert’s envoy, to come to him, and then ordered him to return with his naval force. There were twenty-four *chelandia*, two Rus’ ships [Note: [Col. 0921] Thus corrected by me; *Russorum* in C.], and two Gallic ships. If he sent more, I do not know, since I did not see them.

The strength of your soldiers, my august lords, does not need the weakness of its adversaries to be roused; this has often been demonstrated among those peoples whose weakest men, even when compared with the others, have overthrown and made tributary the Greek strength.

Just as I would not frighten you if I proclaimed them mighty and like Alexander of Macedon, so I do not incite you when I describe their weakness, which is real. Believe me, I ask—and I know that you will believe me—that your entire army, if ditches or walls do not impede it, could kill that whole army with four hundred of your men [Note: [Col. 0921] That is, “of you.”].

And, as I suppose, to insult you, he placed at the head of that army a certain person—though I say “a certain person” because he has ceased to be a man but cannot become a woman.

Adalbert informed Nicephorus that he had eight thousand armored men, with whom, aided by the Argive army, he said he would rout or crush you. He asked his rival that money be sent to him, with which he might urge them more eagerly into battle.

[Col. 0921C] 30. But now, my lords,

“Receive the ambushes of the Danaans [Note: [Col. 0921D] Virgil, *Aeneid* II.65],
and learn from one crime the nature of them all.”

Nicephorus gave a sufficiently large sum of money to that slave to whom he had entrusted the collected and hired army, on the following terms: if Adalbert should approach him with seven thousand armored men or more, as he had reported, the slave was to distribute that gift among them; his brother Cona was to attack you together with him and the Argive army; and Adalbert was to be carefully guarded at Bari until his brother returned victorious.

But if Adalbert came without bringing so many thousands of men that he could be captured, bound, and handed over to you when you arrived, Nicephorus ordered that the money owed to him should also be placed in your hands.

O what a warrior! O what a faithful man! He wishes to betray the man for whom he prepares a defender; he prepares a defender whom he wishes to destroy. In neither matter is there faithfulness; in both there is treachery. He did what he had no need to do and needed what he had not done. But so be it; he acted as was fitting for Greeks! Let us return to our subject.

31. On the fourteenth day before the Kalends of August (July 19) [Col. 0922A], he dismissed that collected naval force while I watched from the loathsome house.

On the thirteenth day (July 20), the day on which foolish Greeks celebrate the prophet Elijah’s ascent into heaven with theatrical games, he ordered me to come to him and said:

“Our empire intends to lead its forces against the Assyrians, not against Christians, as your lord does. Last year I wished to do the same thing; but when we heard that your lord intended to invade the territory of our empire, we dismissed the Assyrians and turned the reins toward him.

“His envoy, Dominicus Venedicus, met us in Macedonia. With much labor and sweat he deceived us into turning back, affirming to us by oath that your lord would never even contemplate such a thing, much less carry it out.

“Return, then”—when I heard this, I silently said, “Thanks be to God!”—“and report these matters and those matters to your lord. If he makes me master of the situation, let him return himself.”

32. To him I said: “Let your most holy Imperial Majesty order me to fly quickly to Italy, on the firm understanding that my lord will fulfill whatever your Empire desires, so that I may return to you gladly.” [Note: [Col. 0921] C. has “Emperor.”] Alas, he was not unaware of the purpose with which I had said this. For, smiling slightly, he nodded and ordered me—after I had prostrated myself before him and was going out—to remain outside, and to come to dinner, which smelled strongly of garlic and onion and was filthy with oil and fish sauce. By earnest entreaties that day I succeeded in inducing him to accept my gift, which he had often scorned.

33. Accordingly, as we sat at a table long rather than broad, covered to the width of a *pallium* [Note: [Col. 0921] Alternatively, “of a cloak,” or “of a palm’s breadth,” C.] and half-bare along its length [Col. 0922C], he made sport of the Franks—for by that name he includes both Latins and Germans—and asked me to say in what place the city of my bishopric was situated and what name it bore.

I replied: “Cremona, quite near the river Eridanus, king of the rivers of Italy.
