And since your Empire is preparing to send *chelandia* there, may it benefit me to have seen you, may it benefit me to have known you! Grant peace to the place, so that through you at least he may be able to endure who cannot resist you!”

But that cunning man recognized that I had said these things ironically (*εἰρωνικῶς*, “ironically”), and, lowering his face, promised and swore to me that he would do so. He swore by the power of his holy Empire that I would suffer no harm, but would prosperously reach the port of Ancona quickly in his *chelandia*. He swore this to me also, striking his chest with his fingers.

[Col. 0922D] 34. But observe how impiously he perjured himself. These events and words took place on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August, a Monday [Note: [Col. 0921D] In fact, this year the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August fell on a Monday.], and from that day until the ninth day of the pay-periods I received nothing from him, although such famine prevailed at Constantinople that I could not restore twenty-five of my retainers and four Greek guards with three gold pieces at a single meal. On the Wednesday of that same week (July 22) [Col. 0923A], Nicephorus left Constantinople, setting out against the Assyrians.

35. On Thursday (July 23) his brother summoned me and addressed me as follows:

“Since the holy Emperor has gone ahead, I remained at home today for the sake of arranging the same matter. Now, if you desire to see the holy Emperor, and if you have anything that you have not yet disclosed, tell it.”

I replied: “I have no reason either to see the holy Emperor or to report some new matter. I ask only this: that, in accordance with the promise of the holy Empire, he escort me in his *chelandia* as far as the port of Ancona.”

When he heard this—for Greeks are always ready to swear by another’s head—he began to swear by the Emperor’s head, by his own life, and by his children, whom may God preserve, as he has said is true, that he would fulfill this [Col. 0923B]. When I asked him, “When?” he replied: “Immediately upon the Emperor’s departure. For when Delongaris, under whose command lies all authority over the ships, withdraws with the holy Emperor, he will take care of you.”

Deluded by this hope, I withdrew from him happily.

36. But on the following day, Saturday (July 25), Nicephorus ordered me summoned to Umbri, a place eighteen miles distant from Constantinople, and said to me [Col. 0923C]:

“I thought that you were a great and honorable man and had come here for the purpose of establishing perpetual friendship between me and your lord by fulfilling my will in every respect. Since, however, because of the hardness of your heart, you are unwilling to do this, at least accomplish one thing that you can justly do: namely, ensure that your lord will give no counsel to the princes of Capua and Benevento, my servants, whom I am preparing to attack. If he does not give them what belongs to him, let him at least leave what belongs to us. It is a well-known fact that their fathers and grandfathers paid tribute to our Empire; but our army will strive to make these men do so shortly.”

I replied: “These princes are exceedingly noble, and are my lords’ soldiers. If he learns that your army is attacking them, he will send them forces with which they will crush your troops and will prevail in taking from you those two *themata* that you possess beyond the sea.”

Then, swelling and becoming agitated like a toad, he said: “Depart. By myself and by the parents who made me such” [Note: [Col. 0923D] Virgil, *Aeneid* I, 606.], “I shall ensure that your lord thinks of something other than defending runaway slaves.”

37. As I was leaving, he ordered his interpreter to make me his dinner companion. After summoning the brother of those princes and Byzantios Barisianos, he ordered them to spew forth great insults against you and against the Latin and German peoples.

But as I myself was leaving the filthy dinner [Note: [Col. 0923] C. more often has *coeua*.], they secretly sent messages to me through intermediaries and swore [Col. 0924A] that they had said what they had barked out, not of their own will, but because the Emperor wished and threatened it.

The same Nicephorus also asked me at that dinner whether you possessed *perivolia*, that is, *briolia* [Note: [Col. 0923D] *Περιβόλαια*, groves for wild animals enclosed by walls or hedges [Col. 0924D.]], or whether you had wild asses or other animals in your *perivolia*. When I affirmed that you possessed *briolia* and animals in the *briolia*, except for wild asses, he said:

“I shall lead you into our *perivolium*, whose size and wild asses—that is, wild donkeys—you will be astonished to have seen.”

Accordingly, I was led into a sufficiently large, mountainous, fertile, but by no means pleasant [Note: [Col. 0923] C. has *amaenum*.] *perivolium*. As I rode wearing a hat, and the *coropalates* saw me from a distance, he quickly sent his son to tell me that, wherever the Emperor was, no one was permitted to wear a hat, but must walk wearing a *teristratum*.

I replied: “Our women wear tiaras and *teristrata*; our men ride wearing hats. Nor is it right for you to compel me here to change my ancestral custom, when we allow your people, on coming to us, to retain their ancestral custom. For among us they ride and walk about wearing sleeves, bandages, brooches, and long hair, dressed in ankle-length tunics; they sit at table and—and what seems exceedingly shameful to all our people—they alone kiss our Emperors with their heads covered.”

“May God never permit this to happen again!” I said silently.

“Then return!” he said.

38. As I was doing so, animals mixed with goats met me, which the Greeks themselves call wild asses. But, I ask you, what sort of wild asses? The same kind as the domestic ones at Cremona. The color is the same, the shape the same; they are likewise long-eared, and similarly begin to bray; their size is not different, their speed is the same, and they are equally sweet to wolves [Col. 0924C].

When I saw them, I said to a Greek riding beside me: “I have never seen such creatures in Saxony.”

“If your lord behaves obediently toward the holy Emperor,” he replied, “he will give him many such animals, and it will be no small glory for him when he possesses what none of the lords who preceded him ever saw.”

But believe me, my august lords: my confrater and co-bishop, my lord Antony [Note: [Col. 0924D] Bishop of Brescia.], can provide animals no inferior to these, as the commerce conducted at Cremona bears witness. His animals are not wild asses but domestic ones; they do not come empty but laden.

When the same man had reported the words written above to Nicephorus, Nicephorus sent me two goats and gave me permission to leave. On the following day he set out toward Syria.

[Col. 0924D] 39. But observe, I ask, why he has now led his army against the Assyrians [Note: [Col. 0923] C. omits “now.”]. The Greeks and Saracens possess books that they call Daniel’s *ὁράσεις*, or visions, but which I call Sibylline books. In them it is written how many years each Emperor will live; what sort of times will come during his reign; whether there will be peace or conflict; and whether the affairs of the Saracens will prosper or go badly.

It is therefore read [Col. 0925A] that in the time of this Nicephorus the Assyrians will be unable to resist the Greeks, and that he will live only seven years. After his death, however, an Emperor worse than this one—but I fear that such a person cannot be found—and more unwarlike is destined to arise. In his time the Assyrians will become so powerful that they will possess everything by force as far as Chalcedon, which is not far from Constantinople.

Both peoples, then, take the times into consideration. Encouraged by one and the same circumstance, the Greeks press on, while the despairing Saracens do not resist, awaiting the time when they too will press on and the Greeks meanwhile will not resist [Note: [Col. 0925] Alternatively, “again they do not resist”; C. supplied this in the margin.].

40. A certain Sicilian bishop, Hippolytus, also wrote the same things about your Empire and our people—by “our people” I now mean all the people subject to your Empire [Col. 0925B]—and would that what he wrote about the present times were true. Everything else that he wrote has been fulfilled up to this point, as I have heard from those who possess knowledge of these books. Let us bring forward one of his many statements. For he says that now the prophecy will be fulfilled which says, “The lion and the cub will together pursue the wild ass.”

That is how it is in Greek: *λέων καὶ σκίμνος ὁμοδιώξουσιν ὄναγρον*.

In Latin it is as follows: “The lion and the cub will together destroy the wild ass.”

According to the Greeks, its interpretation is this: the lion, that is, the Emperor of the Romans or Greeks, and the cub, namely the king of the Franks, will together, in the present times, destroy the wild ass, that is, the Saracen king of Africa.

This interpretation does not seem true to me, because the lion and the cub, although unequal in size, are nevertheless of one nature and species, or disposition [Col. 0925C]. And, as my own knowledge suggests, if the lion is the Emperor of the Greeks, it is inappropriate for the cub to be the king of the Franks. Although both are human beings, just as both the lion and the cub are animals, they differ in disposition—not merely as much as species differ from species, but as much as sensible beings differ from insensible ones.

The cub differs from the lion in nothing except age: the form is the same, the rage one, the roar identical. The king of the Greeks is long-haired, robed, sleeved, *teristrated*, deceitful, treacherous, without mercy, foxlike, proud, falsely humble, stingy, greedy, feeding on garlic, onions, and leeks, and drinking bathwater. The king of the Franks, by contrast, is handsomely shorn, dressed differently from women’s clothing, wears a hat, is truthful, has no deceit, merciful enough where it is fitting, severe where necessary, always genuinely humble, never stingy, and does not eat garlic, onions, or leeks, so that he may spare animals and, since they are not eaten but sold, gather money [Col. 0925D].

You have heard the difference. Do not accept this interpretation; either the future will prove it, or this interpretation is not true. For it is impossible that Nicephorus, as the Greeks themselves falsely claim, should be the lion, and Otto [Note: [Col. 0925] C. often has *Otho*.] the cub, who together will destroy [Note: [Col. 0925] C. has the singular *exterminet*.] anyone.

For sooner shall the exile, having ranged through the territories of both, either the Parthian drink the Arar or Germany the Tigris, than Nicephorus and Otto join in friendship and make a treaty. [Note: [Col. 0925D] Virgil, *Eclogue* I, 62–63.]

41. You have heard the interpretation of the Greeks; now hear the interpretation of Liudprand, bishop of Cremona. I say—and do not merely say, but affirm—that if this prophecy is to be fulfilled in the present times, the lion and the cub, father and son, Otto and Otto, equal in every respect and differing only in age, will together, in this present time, destroy the wild ass, that is, the wild ass Nicephorus [Col. 0926A].

He is not inappropriately compared with a wild ass on account of his empty and vain glory and his incestuous marriage with his mistress and godmother [Col. 0926B] [Note: [Col. 0925D] Theophano: Romanus, joined to her by affinity from baptism, finally carried her into his bedchamber, even against the will of the patriarch. Thus he became her fellow godparent; this too then constituted an impediment to marriage. *Canon*. [Col. 0926D]].

If this wild ass is not now destroyed by our lion and cub, Otto and Otto—namely, the father and son, august Emperors of the Romans—then what Hippolytus wrote will not be true; for the Greeks’ earlier interpretation must be rejected.

But, good Jesus, eternal God, Word of the Father, who speak to us unworthy men not with a voice but through inspiration, may you wish no other interpretation of this sentence than mine. Command that these lion and cub destroy and humble this wild ass bodily, so that, returning to his right mind and submitting to his lords, the Emperors Basil and Constantine, his spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord.

42. Astronomers also make the same prediction about you and Nicephorus. It is a marvelous matter, I say [Col. 0926C]. I spoke with a certain astronomer who truly described the appearance and character of you, my august lords, and of your august namesake, exactly as they are; and he described all my past as though it were present.

No friend or enemy whom my mind prompted me to ask about was omitted: he described the appearance, bearing, and character of each. Whatever misfortune befell me on this journey, he foretold would happen.

Let everything he said be false [Note: [Col. 0925] C. has *omen*, “omen.”]; let only this one thing, I ask, be true: what he foretold that you would do to Nicephorus. May it happen—would that it happen, would that it happen!—and then I shall understand that I have suffered no harm.

43. The aforementioned Hippolytus also writes that the Greeks are not destined to crush the Saracens, but the Franks. Encouraged by this reading, three years ago the Saracens prepared for war against Manuel the patrician, Nicephorus’ nephew, near Scylla and Charybdis in the Sicilian Sea [Col. 0926D]. After they had overthrown his immense forces, they captured him, cut off his head, and hung up his headless body [Note: [Col. 0925] Perhaps *truncated*, BAR.].

When they captured his companion and fellow soldier, who was of neither sex [Note: [Col. 0926D] That is, he was a eunuch. He was Nicetas, eunuch and *drungarios* of the fleet (*τοῦ στόλου δρουγγάριος*). *Canon*.], they did not deign to kill him. Instead, after binding him and tormenting him in prolonged captivity, they sold him for a price so high that no sane person would have paid so much for any such mortal [Col. 0927A].

Not long afterward, strengthened by the same reading, they confronted the *magister* Exaconta. When they put him to flight, they utterly crushed his forces.

44. There is yet another reason that has now compelled Nicephorus to lead his forces against the Assyrians. For, as the appointed time approached, famine, by God’s command, so devastated the whole region of Argos that not even two Papienses *sextarii* of wheat could be bought for a gold piece, and this in a place where abundance supposedly reigns.

With the help of mice he spread this plague so widely that at harvest time he collected whatever grain existed anywhere in the world, paying the owners the smallest possible price while they lamented. When he did this near Mesopotamia, where, in the absence of mice, the abundance of crops had increased, he made the quantity of grain equal to the multitude of sand upon the sea [Col. 0927B].

Thus, while famine raged shamefully everywhere through this cheap commerce, he gathered eighty thousand men under the pretext of military service. For a full month he sold them for two gold pieces what he had bought for one.

These, my lord, are the circumstances that have now compelled Nicephorus to lead his forces against the Assyrians. But what sort of forces, I ask? Truly, I say, they are not men but men’s likenesses; their tongue alone is bold, but their “right hand is cold in war” [Note: [Col. 0927D] Virgil, *Aeneid* XI, 338.]. Nicephorus does not consider their quality, but only their quantity. How dangerous this will be for him, he will regret too late, when the many unwarlike men, encouraged by their multitude, are crushed by our very few who know—indeed, who thirst for—war.

[Col. 0927C] 45. When you were besieging Bares, only three hundred Hungarians, near Thessalonica, captured five hundred Greeks and led them into Hungary. Because this succeeded, two hundred Hungarians were compelled to do the same thing in Macedonia, not far from Constantinople. Of these, while they were imprudently returning along a narrow road, forty were captured.

Nicephorus has now brought these men out of custody, clothed them in the most expensive garments, and made them his patrons and defenders, leading them with him against the Assyrians. But from this you can infer what his army is like, since the men who excel among the rest are Venetians and Amalfitans [Note: [Col. 0927] C. has *amalphitiani*.].

46. Now, leaving these matters aside, observe what happened to me. On the sixth day before the Kalends of August (July 27), outside Constantinople at Umbri, I received permission from Nicephorus to return to you [Col. 0927D].

When I came to Constantinople, the eunuch patrician Christophorus, who was acting there in Nicephorus’ place, sent me word that I could not then depart, because the Saracens had occupied the sea and the Hungarians the land; I would have to wait until they themselves had withdrawn.

But, alas, both statements were lies. Guards were then placed to prevent me and my men from leaving my house [Col. 0928A]. They seized and beat poor Latin-speakers who came to me for alms, and handed them over to custody. They did not permit my *Graecolonus*—that is, the man who knew the Greek language—to go out, even to buy provisions, but allowed only the cook, who knew no Greek, to do so. The buyer and seller communicated not by signs but by movements of the fingers or nods of the head; and the cook bought with four coins what the *Graecolonus* bought as provisions with one.

When one of my friends sent spices, bread, wine, and fruit, they poured everything onto the ground and dismissed the messengers after loading them with slaps. And unless divine compassion had prepared a table before my eyes against those who afflicted me [Note: [Col. 0927D] Compare *Antapodosis* VI, 1.], I would have accepted death as the only fate prepared for me.

But he who allowed me to be tested mercifully then granted me endurance [Col. 0928B]. This danger tormented me at Constantinople from the second day before the Nones of June until the sixth day before the Nones of October—that is, for one hundred and twenty days.

47. Yet, to increase my calamities, on the Assumption of the holy Mother and Virgin of God Mary (August 15), the messengers of the apostolic and universal Pope John arrived—under an evil omen for me [Note: [Col. 0927] C. has *domini*.]—with letters asking Nicephorus, Emperor of the Greeks, to establish kinship and firm friendship with his beloved spiritual son, Otto, august Emperor of the Romans.

What voice, what inscription—according to the Greeks, sinful and reckless—could fail to kill its bearer? Why did it not crush him before he was harmed? In other matters I often seem to be a chatterer and loud-voiced; in this matter I seem mute as a fish [Col. 0928C].

The Greeks cursed the sea and called down imprecations upon the waters, marveling beyond measure that it could have carried that sin, and asking why the strait, opening wide, had not swallowed the ship.

“They were not ashamed,” they said, “to style Nicephorus, universal, august, great, and sole Emperor of the Romans, merely Emperor of the Greeks, and some barbarous, poor man Emperor of the Romans [Note: [Col. 0928D] That is, Otto]! O heaven! O earth! O sea!

“But what,” they said, “shall we do with these wicked, criminal men? They are poor, and if we kill them, we stain our hands with worthless blood. They are ragged, slaves, peasants; if we flog them, we disgrace not them but ourselves, since they are not worthy even of a gilded Roman whip or of such crosses.

“O that one were a bishop and the other a margrave! For after being sewn into sacks, after bitter blows from rods, after their beards or hair had been pulled out, they would be sunk into the sea.

“But let them be kept,” they said, “and, until the most holy Emperor of the Romans, Nicephorus, learns of these crimes, let them be tormented in strict custody.”

48. When I learned of these things, I judged them fortunate because they were poor, and myself unfortunate because I was rich. When I was at home, my own will excused me for being poor; but once placed at Constantinople, fear itself declared that I possessed the wealth of Croesus [Note: [Col. 0929] C. has *Craesi*.].

Poverty had always seemed burdensome to me; then it seemed light, welcome, and worthy of embrace—indeed, worthy of embrace because it does not permit its own people to be killed or those subject to them to be flogged. And because this poverty alone at Constantinople so protects its own people, it should be loved for that reason alone.

49. After the apostolic messengers had been handed over to prison, that publican-like letter was sent to Nicephorus in Mesopotamia. Its messenger did not return from there until the second day before the Ides of September [Note: [Col. 0929] I have corrected the reading thus; C. has “the fifth.” But the manuscript read II, not V, as the word “two days” below proves.], bringing a message of defense.

When he returned, though I remained unaware of it, two days later [Note: [Col. 0929] C. has *bidivum*.]—namely, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October [Col. 0929A]—I succeeded, through prayers and gifts, in being allowed to worship the life-giving and saving wood. There, amid a great tumult of the people and secretly from the guards, certain men approached me and made my sorrowful mind cheerful with furtive conversations.

50. On the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October, balanced between death and life, I was summoned to the palace. When I came into the presence of the eunuch patrician Christophorus, he received me kindly and rose with three others.

Their speech began as follows:

“The pallor settled upon your face, the emaciation throughout your body, your long-haired head, and your beard, grown long contrary to custom, show that immense grief fills your heart because the time for returning to your lord has been delayed.

“But we beg you not to be angry either with the holy Emperor or with us. We shall explain the reason for your delay. The Roman Pope—if indeed he should be called pope, since he shared communion and served together with the son of Alberic [Note: [Col. 0929] C. has *albericii*.], an apostate, adulterer, and sacrilegious man [Note: [Col. 0929D] Pope John XII.]—sent letters to our most holy Emperor, worthy of himself and unworthy of him, calling him Emperor of the Greeks and not of the Romans. That this was done on your lord’s advice is not disputed (*ἀμφίσβητον*, “not open to dispute”).”

51. “What word am I hearing?” I said to myself. “I am lost! There is no doubt that I shall go straight to the praetorium.”

“But listen,” they said. “You wish to say that the pope is more foolish than all men; we know it and admit it.”

“I do not say that,” I replied.

“Then listen. The foolish, witless pope does not know that the holy Constantine transported the imperial scepters here, together with the entire Senate and the whole Roman army, while at Rome he left only worthless slaves—fishermen, sellers of delicacies, bird-catchers, bastards, commoners, and slaves [Col. 0929D]. He would never have written this except at the prompting of your king; and how dangerous this will be for both of them, unless they come to their senses, the near future will reveal!”

“But,” I said, “the pope, distinguished by his simplicity, thought that he was writing this to praise the Emperor, not to insult him. We know for certain that Constantine, Roman Emperor, came here with the Roman army and founded this city in his own name [Col. 0930A]. But because you have changed your language, customs, and clothing, the most holy pope thought that the name ‘Roman’ displeased you as much as Roman clothing does.

“This will be shown, with life as witness, in future letters, whose superscription will read: ‘John, Roman Pope, to Nicephorus, Constantine, and Basil, great Roman Emperors and august rulers!’”

Now listen, I ask, to why I said this.

52. Nicephorus attained the summit of kingship through perjury and adultery. Since the salvation of all Christians belongs to the concern of the Roman pope, let the lord pope send Nicephorus a letter altogether like the tombs that are white on the outside but inside are full of the bones of the dead. Let him reproach him inwardly for the manner in which, through perjury and adultery, he seized sole rule over his lords [Col. 0930B]. Let him invite him to a synod, and, if he does not come, strike him with an anathema.

If its superscription is not of this kind, it will not be carried to him at all.

53. Now let us return to the subject. When the princes I have mentioned heard the promise contained in the superscription above, and thought that it held no deceit, they said [Col. 0930C]:

“We give you thanks, bishop. It is fitting for your wisdom to intercede as mediator in such important affairs. You alone among the Franks are one whom we now love. But when, at your urging, they have corrected what has been corrupted, they too will be loved; and when you come to us again, you will not depart without receiving a gift!”

“When I return here again,” I said silently, “Nicephorus will give me a golden crown and scepter!” [Note: [Col. 0929] C. has *donabis*, “you will give.”]

“But tell us,” they said, “does your most holy lord wish to establish friendship with the Emperor by a marriage alliance?”

“When I came here, he did,” I replied. “But because he received no letters while I was detained here so long, he thinks that the fault (*σφάλμα*, “fault”) lies with you, and that I have been captured and bound. His whole spirit is raging like a lioness whose cubs have been snatched away, until she exacts a justly bitter vengeance; he rejects marriage and pours out his anger upon you.”

“If he makes the attempt,” they said, “we do not speak of Italy—but not even Italy itself will contain him, nor the poor and *gunnata* (that is, fur-clad) Saxony in which he was born. We shall use the money at our disposal to summon every nation against him, and, like a clay vessel (*κεραμοῦ*), which cannot be remade once broken, we shall shatter him.

“And since we think that you have bought certain cloaks for your adornment, to be brought out publicly, we declare that those which are suitable for you shall be marked with a lead seal and left to you; but those which are *κωλυόμενα*, that is, forbidden to all nations, especially before us Romans, shall be taken away after the price has been returned.”

54. When this was done, they took from me five extremely costly purple garments, judging it unworthy for you and for all Italians, Saxons, Franks, Bavarians [Note: [Col. 0931] Alternatively, *Baoarians*, C.], and Swabians [Col. 0931A]—indeed, for all nations—to go about adorned in such clothing.

How disgraceful and insulting it is for soft, effeminate, sleeved, tiara-wearing, *teristrated*, lying, sexless [Note: [Col. 0931D] That is, eunuch-like, C.], sluggish men dressed in purple to walk about, while heroes—that is, strong men, skilled in war, full of faith and charity, subject to God, and full of virtues—may not! What is this, if not an insult?

“But where,” I asked, “is the imperial word? Where is the imperial promise? When I took leave of him, I asked that, for the honor of the Church, he allow me to buy cloaks at any price. He replied: ‘Whatever kind and quantity you wish’—*ποιότητα καὶ ποσότητα*, that is, quality and quantity—clearly making no distinction by saying, ‘except these and those.’

“His brother Leo the *coropalates* is a witness; so too is the interpreter Euodisius Johannes, a Roman. I myself am a witness, since I understood what the Emperor said even if the interpreter had been absent [Col. 0931B].”

“But these are *κωλυόμενα*, that is, forbidden,” they replied. “And when the Emperor said what you claim he said, he could not have been thinking of such things, not even in a dream. For just as we ought to surpass the other nations in wealth and wisdom, so too we ought to surpass them in clothing, so that those who possess exceptional grace in virtue may also possess exceptional beauty in dress.”

55. “This clothing cannot possibly be exceptional,” I replied, “since among us women who earn an obol and old monks [Note: [Col. 0932D] Elderly monks.] wear such things.”

“From where do you obtain them?” they asked.

“From Venetian and Amalfitan merchants,” I replied, “who sustain their own lives by bringing these things to us in exchange for our provisions [Col. 0931C].”

“But they will do this no longer,” they said. “They will conduct a thorough search, and if anything of this sort is found, the offender will be beaten, have his hair cut, and suffer punishment.”

“In the time of the blessed Emperor Constantine I came here—not as a bishop but as a deacon, and sent not by an Emperor or king but by the margrave Berengar—and I bought many more and much more costly cloaks. They were neither searched nor seen by the Greeks, nor marked with lead.

“Now, by God’s mercy, I am a bishop and have been sent by the magnificent Emperors Otto and Otto, father and son, yet I am dishonored so greatly that my cloaks are marked in the manner of Venetian goods, and those that appear to be of any value are taken away, although they are intended for the use of the church entrusted to me [Col. 0931D].

“Are you not weary of my insults—or rather, of those of my lords, in whom I am despised? I have been handed over to custody, tortured by hunger and thirst, and detained here so that I could not return to them; was it also necessary, to complete their disgrace, that I be stripped of my own possessions? At least take away what was purchased; leave what was given to me as gifts by friends.”

“Constantine the Emperor,” they replied, “a gentle man who remained perpetually in the palace, had made the nations his friends by such gifts. Nicephorus, however, the *basileus*, is a *ταχύχειρ*, that is, devoted to military affairs; he detests the palace as though it were a plague. We call him almost a lover of conflict and a contriver of plots: he does not make peoples his friends with money, but subjects them to himself through terror and the sword.

“And so that you may understand how highly we regard your lord kings, whatever was given to you of this kind and whatever was purchased shall return to us by the same route [Col. 0932A].”

56. After these words had been spoken and carried out, they gave me a *chrysobullion* (*χρυσοβούλλιον*), that is, a letter written and sealed in gold, to deliver to you—but, as my mind believes, not worthy of you [Col. 0932B].

They also brought out other letters sealed in silver and said:

“We judge it unworthy that your pope should receive imperial letters. The *coropalates*, the Emperor’s brother, is sending him a letter sufficiently worthy of him—not through his own poor messengers but through you—so that, unless he comes to his senses, he may learn that he has utterly perished.”

57. When I had received this letter, they said farewell to me and dismissed me, offering eyes sufficiently cheerful and sufficiently friendly. But as I was departing, they assigned me an escort worthy not of me but of themselves: they gave horses only to me and my men, but none for the baggage.

Thus, disturbed beyond measure, as the circumstances required, I gave goods worth fifty gold pieces to my guide, the *diasostes*. Since I had nothing at that time with which to repay Nicephorus for his misdeeds, I wrote the following verses on the wall of my hateful house and on a wooden table:

**Verses** [Note: [Col. 0931] I have supplied the word.]

> Argolic faith is unsafe; keep far away, O Latin,  
>   
> Remember neither to trust nor to apply your mind to words!  
>   
> While it can conquer, how piously Argos has perjured itself!  
>   
> This lofty, waterless house, open with great windows of varied marble,  
>   
> Open to the sun, though I am confined,  
>   
> Receiving the cold and not warding off the fierce heat,  
>   
> Liudprand, bishop from Ausonia, in the city of Cremona,  
>   
> Having set out for Constantinople from love of peace,  
>   
> Has been confined here for four summer months.  
>   
> For Emperor Otto had climbed the Bares,  
>   
> Attempting to subdue the places by slaughter and flames together,  
>   
> But, victorious through prayers, he returns to the Roman cities,  
>   
> Thence to my own people. Lying Greece promised a bride;  
>   
> She would neither have been born nor grieved that I had come,  
>   
> Nor would I be able to reckon your rage, Nicephorus—  
>   
> You who forbid a stepdaughter to be joined to her lord’s son.  
>   
> Behold, the day approaches; driven on by bitter Furies,  
>   
> Unless God turns it away, Mars will rage throughout the whole world,  
>   
> And peace, desired by all, will be silenced because of your crime!

58. Having written these verses, on the sixth day before the Nones of October (October 2), at the tenth hour, I departed from that once extremely wealthy and flourishing city—now famine-stricken, perjured, lying, deceitful, rapacious, greedy, avaricious, and vainglorious—with my *diasostes* in a small boat [Col. 0933A].

After forty-nine days—riding donkeys, walking, riding horses, fasting, thirsting, sighing, weeping, and groaning—I reached Naupactus (November 20), the city of Nicopolis. There my *diasostes*, abandoning me, placed me aboard two small ships and entrusted me to two agents, who were to convey me by sea to Otranto.

But since they did not possess an *entolina*, that is, an order, from the Greek princes granting them the right of capture, they were despised everywhere; and it was no longer we who were fed by them, but they by us.

How often I angrily repeated to myself that line from Terence [Note: [Col. 0933D] *Eunuchus* IV, 6, 32.]:

> You need a guardian for those whom you prepare as defenders.

59. Accordingly, on the ninth day before the Kalends of December (November 23), I departed from Naupactus and reached the river Offidar after two days [Note: [Col. 0933] Alternatively, Ophidarus, C.], while my companions did not sit in the little boats, which could not contain them, but proceeded along the shore.

Thus stationed on the river Offidar [Col. 0933B], we saw Patras, on another shore of the sea, eighteen miles distant. Because we had visited and worshiped this place of the apostolic Passion while ascending to Constantinople, we now delayed visiting and worshiping it—confessing my sin!

This was caused, my august lords, by my unspeakable desire to return to you and to see you; and if this alone had not existed, I think I would have perished forever.

60. The South Wind fought against me, disturbing the sea with gusts from its deepest foundations (968, November 30). And when it continued doing this for successive days and nights, on the day before the Kalends of December, that is, on the very day of the Passion [Note: [Col. 0933D] The day of St. Andrew.], I understood that this had happened to me because of my own fault. Affliction alone gave understanding to the hearing. For hunger was grievously oppressing us. The inhabitants of the land were planning to kill us in order to take away our possessions; the sea, boiling with waves so that we could not escape, was preventing our flight. Then, turning toward the church that I could see, weeping and wailing, I said:

“Holy Apostle Andrew, I am the servant of your fellow fisherman, brother, and fellow apostle Simon Peter. I did not shrink from the place of your Passion, nor did I avoid it out of pride; the august command to return home [Note: [Col. 0933] It seemed that *visio* should be corrected in this way; *jussio* in C.] burns me, and so does the august love. If my sin has moved you to indignation, may the merit of my august lords draw you toward mercy. You have nothing to bestow upon your brother; bestow something upon the august men who love your brother, by clinging to him who knows all things. You know with what labor and sweat, and with how many vigils and expenses, they have enriched, honored, exalted, and restored to its proper condition the Roman church of your brother, the apostle Peter, after rescuing it from the hands of the impious. If my deeds are bringing me to ruin, let their merits at least deliver me—those whom your aforesaid brother in faith and blood, the prince of the apostles, the Apostle Peter, wishes to rejoice and prosper in other matters, and not to be saddened in this matter, namely, in me, whom they themselves had sent!”

61. I speak truly, my august lords and emperors: this is not flattery, nor am I now sewing cushions beneath the elbow of my hand; the matter, I say, is true. (December.) Two days later, through your merits, the strait was calmed with such tranquility that, although the sailors fled from us, we ourselves sailed as far as Leucas—that is, one hundred and forty miles—suffering no danger or sadness except for a little at the mouth of the Achelous, where its swiftly running waves beat back the sea’s water.

62. What, therefore, most powerful august lords, will you repay the Lord for all that he has repaid to you in me? I will tell you what. This is what God wishes; this is what he asks. Although he can accomplish it without you, he nevertheless wishes you to be the *hypurgos*, that is, the ministers, of this matter. For he himself gives what is to be offered to him and preserves what he is to demand, so that he may crown what he provides.

Pay attention, then, I beg you. Nicephorus, although he is an impious man toward all the churches, in the envy with which he abounds against you, ordered the patriarch of Constantinople to extend the Hydruntine church to the dignity of an archbishopric, and not to allow the divine mysteries to be celebrated any longer in Latin throughout Apulia or Calabria, but in Greek. He says that the former popes were merchants and sold the Holy Spirit, by whom all things are given life and governed, who fills the world, who possesses knowledge of speech, who is coeternal and consubstantial with God the Father and his Son Jesus Christ, without beginning and without end, remaining true, and who is not valued at a price, but is purchased by the pure in heart at whatever worth they assign him.

Accordingly, Polyeuctus, patriarch of Constantinople, wrote a privilege to the bishop of Hydruntum, granting him authority to consecrate bishops in Acerenza, Tursi, Gravina, Matera, and Tricarico [Note: [Col. 0934D] Acerenza, Tursi, Gravina, Matera, Tricarico.], which seem to belong to the consecration of the apostolic lord.

But why should I mention this, when the church of Constantinople itself is rightly subject to our holy Catholic and Apostolic Roman Church? We know—or rather, we see—that the bishop of Constantinople does not use the pallium except with the permission of our holy father. But when the most impious Alberic, whom not a trickle but a torrent of greed had filled, usurped the city of Rome and kept the apostolic lord in a chamber as his own slave, the Roman emperor appointed his son, the eunuch Theophylact, patriarch. Since Alberic’s greed was not unknown to him, the emperor sent him sufficiently large gifts and brought it about that letters were sent in the pope’s name to the patriarch Theophylact, by whose authority both he himself and his successors might use the pallia without the permission of the popes. From this shameful commerce there arose the reprehensible custom that not only patriarchs but also the bishops of the whole of Greece should use the pallia. No censor is needed to show how absurd this is.

My advice, therefore, is that a holy synod be held and that Polyeuctus be summoned to it. If he refuses to come and to correct canonically his *σφάλματα*, that is, his faults mentioned above, then let what the most holy canons have decreed be done. Meanwhile, most powerful august lords, work as you have begun. Ensure that if Nicephorus, whom we intend to accuse canonically, does not wish to obey us [Note: [Col. 0935] I have corrected this to *nobis*; C has *vobis*.], he will listen to you, whose forces he, corpse-like as he is, does not dare to confront.

This, I say, is what our apostles [Note: [Col. 0935D] Peter and Paul.], our lords and fellow soldiers, wish to accomplish. The Roman place must not be held in contempt by the Greeks because the emperor Constantine departed from it; rather, it must be honored, venerated, and adored all the more, because the holy apostles and teachers Peter and Paul came there. Let it suffice that I have written enough about these matters until, by God’s generosity and through the prayers of the most holy apostles, rescued from the hands of the Greeks, I may come to you. Then let it not weary you to say what here I have not been reluctant to write. Now let us return to our subject.

63. On the eighth day before the Ides of December (December 6) we came to Leucas, where we were received and treated most inhumanely by the eunuch bishop of that place, as everywhere by the others. Throughout Greece, I speak the truth and do not lie, I found no hospitable bishops. They are rich; they are poor: rich in gold, with which their full chest is played; poor in servants or utensils. They alone sit at bare tables, placing before themselves *paximacium* [Note: [Col. 0935D] That is, sailors’ bread. BAR.] and not drinking *balaneum* [Note: [Col. 0935D] Or wine mixed with a great deal of water?] from a small glass, but merely sipping it.

They themselves sell, they themselves buy; they themselves close the doors, they themselves open them; they are themselves stewards, themselves grooms, themselves *capones*—but, ah! I meant to write *caupones*. Yet the fact itself, which is true, compelled me, against my will, to write the truth. For we say that they are *capones*, that is, eunuchs, which is not canonical; and they are *caupones*, that is, tavern keepers, which is contrary to the canons. Of them:

> And lettuce closes the persistent dinner,  
> which lettuce used to close the dinners of our ancestors!  
> [Note: [Col. 0935D] Martial, *Epigrams* XIII, 14.]

I would judge them happy if this poverty imitated Christ’s poverty! [Note: [Col. 0936D] I would judge them happy if, etc., they were poor.] Harsh money and the accursed hunger for gold do this. [Note: [Col. 0936D] Cf. Persius, *Satires* III, 69; Virgil, *Aeneid* III, 57.] But may God spare them! I think they do this because their churches are tributary.

The bishop of Leucas swore to me that every year his church had to pay Nicephorus one hundred gold pieces, and the other churches likewise, more or less according to their means. How unjust this is is demonstrated by the deeds of our most holy father Joseph: when, during the time of famine, he made all Egypt tributary to Pharaoh, he nevertheless allowed the land of the priests to remain free from tribute.

64. Accordingly, on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of January (December 14) [Note: [Col. 0935] I have corrected this in this way, since above he said that he had arrived at Leucas on the eighth day before the Ides of December; C has “of December.”] we departed from Leucas. Since the sailors had fled, as we wrote above, we ourselves continued sailing and arrived on the fifteenth day (December 18) at Coriphus [Note: [Col. 0936D] The island of Corfu.]. Before we left the ship, a certain *strategos* met us, named Michael Chersionites, from the place called Cherson. He was gray-haired, cheerful in face, pleasant in speech, and always charming in laughter; but, as later became evident, a devil in mind. God also showed this to me by clear signs, if only my mind at that time had been able to understand it.

As soon as he gave me with a kiss the peace that he did not carry in his heart, all Coriphus—that is, the great island—trembled; and it trembled not once but three times on that same day. Four days later, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of January (December 22) [Note: [Col. 0935] I have corrected Canisius’s reading in this way: “But after three days, namely on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of December.” That reading is both senseless—for three days after the fifteenth day before the Kalends cannot again be the fifteenth day before the Kalends—and contrary to nature, since the eclipse occurred on December 22, as Curopalates, the Annals of Cavenses above, p. 188, and the astronomical tables show. The copyist of the manuscript read XI where XV stood.], while I was sitting at table eating bread, he who was lifting up his heel against me did so as the sun, ashamed of so disgraceful a deed, concealed the rays of its light and suffered an eclipse. It terrified that Michael, but did not change him.

65. I shall therefore say what I did for him as a token of friendship, and what I received from him in return. When I was going up to Constantinople, I gave his son that most precious shield of yours, gilded and fashioned with marvelous workmanship, which you, my august lords, had given me, along with the other gifts, to present to my Greek friends.

Now, on my return from Constantinople, I gave his father a most precious pallium. For all these gifts he distributed the following thanks: Nicephorus wrote that, at whatever hour I came to him, he should immediately place me on a *chelandion* and send me to Leo the *kitonites*. He did not do this. Instead, he detained me for twenty days and supported me at his own—not his official—expense, until a messenger came from the aforesaid Leo the *kitonites*, who rebuked him for delaying me (969, January 7).

But when he could no longer endure my rebukes, complaints, and sighs, he departed and entrusted me to a man so unjust and wicked that he would not even permit me to purchase my expenses, until he had received from me a curtain worth a pound of silver. When, after twenty days, I was leaving that place, the very messenger to whom I had given the curtain ordered the shipmaster to let me, once placed beyond the *acroteria*, that is, a certain promontory, perish from hunger.

He did this because, to make sure that I had no purple garments hidden away, he searched through my cloaks; when he wanted to take one of them, he did not take it. O Michael, Michael, where have I found so many such men together! My Constantinopolitan guardian entrusted me to his rival Michael: a bad man to the worst, the worst to the unjust.

My *diasostes* was also called Michael, a simple man indeed, whose holy simplicity nearly harmed me as much as the perversity of those others. But from these little Michaels I stumbled upon you, great Michael, half-hermit and half-monk. I speak the truth, and I speak it truly: your bath, in which you continually drink yourself in love of blessed John the Forerunner, will not benefit you. For those who seek God hypocritically never deserve to find him. . . . . .

Here it is clear that some material has fallen out.

# APPENDIX TO LIUTPRAND

[Col. 0937]

## A Dissertation by D. Antonius of Seville on the Books Falsely Fabricated under the Name of Liutprand

(*Bibliotheca Hispana vetus*, volume I)

### CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0937B]

Liutprand, deacon of the Church of Pavia and bishop of Cremona, an Italian, made subdeacon of the Church of Toledo at great expense by Higuera of Toledo, and the writer of our affairs. Certain details of his life are demonstrated by comparison with what the *Chronicon* and *Adversaria*, falsely attributed to him, contain. These matters are treated at length in the following chapters.

1. Liutprand, deacon of the Church of Pavia and later bishop of Cremona in Italy, is one of those whose authority and reputation the many-formed Proteus of Toledo used as a disguise when he conceived the plan of fabricating a false history of our people to occupy the place of a genuine and truthful one.

Yet, since according to the divine saying a net is cast uselessly before the eyes of winged creatures, although he once imposed his deceitful bird-catching—by no means without some loss to Spanish dignity—upon certain people of good faith, lovers of their country, and attracted by the allure of his materials, now that the light of a purified judgment has been kindled, he has begun to fall from his purpose and hope. The more prudent, warned of the stretched nets of ambush, turn elsewhere; bound, so to speak, to the mast of truth, they pass them by with deaf ears.

2. Liutprand was indeed a not insignificant writer of histories in this age. But the very books attributed to him necessarily prove that he was someone other than the man whom they present to us as the author of a certain *Chronicon*, or of the continuation of the *Chronicle of Dextrus and Maximus*: a Toledan subdeacon who died at Toledo.

To begin, then, our defense of the truth by distinguishing the genuine Liutprand from the spurious one, let us see what the writer of the *Chronicon* related about himself, and what Julian then related about him.

3. In Liutprand one reads that in the year 937 John Servus Dei succeeded Bonitus III as bishop of Toledo, and that in the year 944, as though continuing what he had prefaced as having occurred seven years earlier, he says:

> “I, a subdeacon at Toledo, knew him and experienced him at Toledo as a holy man burning with the Spirit of God.”

Likewise Julian, in his *Chronicon*, no. 503, speaking under the year 946 about John Servus Dei, says:

> “Bonitus III had been elected before him [John], but had not entered upon the pontifical dignity. Under him [John] was the subdeacon Eutrandus, or Liutprandus, archdeacon of Pavia, a by no means obscure writer of histories and likewise an excellent poet.”

It will be highly worthwhile to compare this testimony of Julian with the same passage in his published *Chronicon*, just as Hieronymus Higuera presented it in the preface to Liutprand’s *Chronicon*. It runs as follows:

> “In the year 946 Bonitus, bishop of Toledo, for two years. Under him flourished Eutrandus, or Liutprandus, deacon of Pavia and subdeacon of Toledo, and Tractemundus, priest and later bishop of Iliberis, sent by the same Bonitus.”

Do you see how the one witness gives evidence perversely, and how Higuera has one version in the edition and another in his own mouth? But let us pass on to other matters.

4. Liutprand likewise says in *Adversaria* 48 that in the year 960 he passed through the city of Tarragona and composed a poem in praise of Saint Thecla, virgin and martyr, part of whose body is preserved there. In that poem he says of himself:

> Behold Liutprand, no longer a new inhabitant of the Spanish land,  
> gladly approaches foreign soil in song.

Julian likewise says that the archdeacon Liutprand returned to Toledo after his pilgrimage and died there (no. 113):

> “In the same year [973] Eutrandus the subdeacon came to Toledo; he had formerly been there, a noble historian, and not long afterward died. He was honorably buried by Felix [the bishop] in the church of Saint Justa.”

We have already dealt more distinctly with Liutprand and Tractemundus in the two letters prefixed to the spurious *Chronicon*. The letters themselves are no less spurious, as we shall see in their proper place when we pass judgment on the *Chronicon*. The first is said to be from Tractemundus, bishop of Iliberis, to Liutprand; elsewhere he is called Regimundus. The second is Liutprand’s reply to Tractemundus, from the monastery of Fulda in Germany.

Tractemundus consoles Liutprand in the distress of his German pilgrimage and urges him to endure it patiently. Having fled the cruelty of Berengar, king of Italy, he had come there from Italy. There, Tractemundus says that he was living in the town of Granada, near the city of Iliberis, among faithful Mozarabs, strengthening them and refreshing them with the nourishment of instruction.

5. He adds that he had received his book—that is, his history of events in Europe—and also the *Antapodosis* (as though these were separate works), “woven in verse and prose, as the wise Boethius once did in the book *On the Consolation of Philosophy.” He continues:

> “I remember that we two carefully read through that book of Boethius Severinus at Toledo, when I was a priest and you were a subdeacon of that holy Church of Toledo, which has always truly been the firstborn daughter of the holy Roman Church and, after the Roman Church, deserves to be compared with the patriarchal churches; its pastor is the primate and patriarch of all Spain.”

Such importunate and foul flattery exposes the impostor.

6. Finally, Liutprand is entreated to send him certain books, namely:

> “The Life of Saint James of Spain, who died a holy death in Picenum on November 1,”

a saint whom all Martyrologies have left unpraised.

Also requested is:

> “The book of Metasthenes the Persian, *On Monarchies*.”

For a long time learned men have observed that this writer was called Megasthenes, not “Metasthenes,” and that this is an abortive product of Johannes Annius—or of another, an egg laid by him—who was published together with Berossus and others.

The letter continues:

> “In which book he places among the Persians [supply: in their order, or among their kings; the text is defective] Darius, Cyrus, Cambyses, Artaxerxes, and afterward Darius Longimanus.”

And also:

> “If they are hiding anywhere in the libraries of Germany, the parchment Chronicles of Dextrus and Marcus Maximus—why not paper as well?—which he had never been able to find in Spain.”

He asks that copies, transcribed by Liutprand, be sent to him as soon as possible and that Liutprand add to his own work “from the year 612, where Maximus ended, to his own times, that is, to the year 960.” How did he know this, when he had not seen Maximus’s work?

The genuine author would have said “to our times,” or “to this year,” speaking of the present matter. The foolish mention of the year reveals the spurious and recent author. This is the substance of Tractemundus’s letter. But the letter that follows from Liutprand destroys not only Tractemundus’s credibility but its own as well, as will become clear in due course.

7. As far as the present matter is concerned, Liutprand expresses sorrow that Tractemundus was being harshly treated by the Moors at Granada:

> “For we were not treated so harshly,”

he adds,

> “but somewhat better, when we once lived together at Toledo. On the one side, the singular authority of the Toledan bishops softened the fierce minds of the barbarians; on the other, their remarkable goodness and patience,”

and so forth.

Further on he says:

> “As for the *Chronicon* that you request, I found it copied on ancient parchment in this library and added, as you instructed, the sequence of years down to the present time, that is, to the year 960. I congratulate myself that, when I set out for Italy from Toledo, where I was a subdeacon under the most holy bishop of Toledo, Bonitus, I carried several history books with me. In them was collected, in order, a series concerning many bishops of Spain, whom I also found in this library. I believe they had been brought from Spain at the command of Saint Charles the Great, emperor; they say that the most holy Elipandus, bishop of Toledo, had offered them to him after he seriously and truly repented of his error concerning the adoption of Christ.”

8. These are the claims concerning Liutprand’s residence at Toledo and his service as subdeacon in that Church under Bonitus III and his successor, the archbishops John Servus Dei.

Following the authority of these testimonies, Franciscus Bivarius, a Cistercian, in the *Censura of Liutprand’s Works* addressed to Laurentius Ramirezius and prefixed to the Plantin edition, after being confronted with nearly all the evidence that we shall shortly produce in support of Liutprand’s Italian origin, birth, and life spent almost entirely in his homeland, nevertheless argues that Liutprand was Spanish by origin—that is, the son of a Spaniard who, weary of captivity, had gone to Italy. He maintains, however, that Liutprand, drawn by longing for his homeland, came to Toledo, where he became acquainted with Tractemundus.

He also judges his Spanish origin to be supported by the fact that Liutprand somewhere calls Abderrahman, the Saracen ruler in Spain, that is, the king of Córdoba, “our king,” meaning his own and Tractemundus’s. Hear his words in *Deeds Accomplished in Europe in His Own Time*, book V, chapter 1:

> “At this time, as you yourself, father, know well, the sun suffered a great eclipse, terrifying to all, on Friday, at the third hour of the day. On that same day Abdaram [for Abderrahman], our king, was defeated in battle by Radamirus, the most Christian king of Galicia.”

9. This is at least something drawn from his well-known historical work. The rest is empty and built upon sand without any mortar. Yet even this collapses with the easiest effort if we read “your king” instead of “our king,” as a similar passage at the beginning of the history shows (book I, chapter 1):

> “As you can infer from those who are tributaries of your king Abderrahman.”

For it would have been foolish, indeed impious, for Liutprand to call a Saracen king “his own king” merely because that king was ruler of the Toledans, among whom Liutprand had once lived. Indeed, elsewhere Liutprand calls Otto his lord (book VI, chapter 2).

10. Nor does the sequence of events that he himself recounts, no mean distributor of its materials, seem to allow either a Spanish pilgrimage or Spanish ancestry. In the year 924 a fire occurred in the city of Pavia, where we believe he was born; he deplores it in book III, chapters 1 and 2.

In the year 924 Hugh, count of Provence or of Arles, assumed the kingdom of Italy. Not long after his entry into Italy, as appears from what follows, Hugh approached Romanus Lecapenus, emperor of the Greeks, by an embassy, among the other princes whom he carefully sought to reconcile to himself. Liutprand’s father was his envoy, although, when speaking of the matter, the son did not call him by name. He adds in book III, chapter 5:

> “After his return, however, with only a few suns having intervened, he was seized by illness, sought a monastery, and assumed the habit of holy religious life. There, after fifteen days, he died and departed to the Lord, leaving me a little child.”

After her husband’s death, Liutprand’s mother married a second husband. Liutprand relates that this man, also named Hugh, went several years later as a messenger to the same Lecapenus:

> “Since my stepfather, a man adorned with dignity and full of wisdom, had been King Hugh’s messenger, it will not be burdensome for me to insert what I often heard him say about the emperor’s wisdom and humanity, and about how he defeated the Rus.”

Baronius notes that this occurred in the year 941, citing John Curopalates (under that year, no. 3).

11. In the year 945 Hugh relinquished the kingdom of Italy, leaving his son Lothar in his place in name, but in reality handing the kingdom over to Berengar. Liutprand lived in great favor with this Hugh because of his skill in singing, by which he surpassed other boys his equals; he was always present at Hugh’s court and in his retinue.

He indicates this sufficiently when, at the beginning of book IV, he says:

> “Thus far, most holy priest, I have set out what has been said, as I heard it from the most serious men who had witnessed it. But what must now be narrated I shall explain as one who was present. For at that time I was of such an age that I won the favor of King Hugh through the sweetness of my voice. He greatly loved musical harmony, and none of the boys my age could surpass me in it.”

This association at court, from which he could have obtained the firsthand knowledge of events that he says he will subsequently narrate, certainly began in the year 932 or the following year, in the sixth or seventh year of Hugh’s reign. For in the former year, as is clear from Sigebert [“under this year” in the *Chronicon*], Arnold, duke of Bavaria, invited by Ratherius, bishop of Verona, attacked King Hugh in Italy. Hugh not only put Arnold to flight but also captured Ratherius. Since Liutprand brought this war to an end at the conclusion of book III, he says that from that point he will explain what follows as one who was present at those events.

12. On this foundation—that Liutprand was present at all the events he subsequently narrates from this year up to 946, when he himself undertook an embassy to the emperor Constantine in Berengar’s name—we may rightly conclude that throughout this period he was nowhere but at Hugh’s court, or at least at Pavia or in Italy. His genuine historical narrative ends with this embassy, namely in book VI, chapter 5, as the most learned men have noted [Note: [Col. 0941D] Baronius under the year 963, no. 3; Bellarmine, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*; Vossius, *On Historical Latin Literature*, book II, chapter 40.].

Liutprand himself no less clearly implies in book VI, chapter 1, that he remained at home under the care of his stepfather until this expedition to Constantinople. It consequently follows that it is wholly untrue that he served as subdeacon in the Church of Toledo under Servus Dei, bishop of Toledo, who held the episcopate from 937 to 947—if we believe Liutprand himself [under the year 937]—or that, as the spurious Liutprand explicitly says, he knew the praised bishop at Toledo in the year 944.

13. To continue the genuine Liutprand’s history from the beginning: in the year 945 of this century, his parents placed this Liutprand in Berengar’s service. He became acquainted with Berengar’s secrets and served as the keeper of his correspondence seals until, after a long period of service, he was treated by him most ungratefully and inhumanely, like many others, as he himself relates in book V, chapter 14.

This also confirms Liutprand’s presence in Italy and at Berengar’s court during the years following 946. In the year 941, however, Emperor Otto the Great came into Italy against Berengar (Baronius, under that year, no. 1). In the following year he again handed the kingdom of Italy over to Berengar to administer under his allegiance (Baronius, no. 2). Berengar retained it for several more years, until the Italians, unable to bear his tyranny, summoned Otto again in the year 961. Otto easily stripped Berengar of the kingdom (Baronius, under that year, no. 1), and in the following year was solemnly crowned emperor at Rome by Pope John XII.

14. Shortly afterward, however, when John deserted the emperor’s party, Otto came to Rome again. John refused to appear, so Otto compelled a council of all the bishops of Italy to convene and expelled him from the Roman See by judgment.

At this council, held in the year 963 (Baronius, under that year), among the others, Liutprand, by then bishop of Cremona, is recorded as having signed. The acts were preserved by an anonymous writer who continued the thread of his narrative with Liutprand’s own history and openly reveals himself, as we noted above, to be a different person from Liutprand. Baronius transferred these acts from him into his *Annals* [Note: [Col. 0941D] Read “Liutprand of Cremona’s memory” under the cited year, no. 12.].

This Liutprand, after Berengar and his household, family, and relatives had been cruelly and impiously harassed—as he himself relates in the prologue to book III—retreated to Germany to Otto and stood in great favor with him. Indeed, later made bishop of Cremona, he went as Otto’s envoy to Nicephorus Phocas, emperor of the Greeks, in the year 968. He described this embassy in a separate little book, published by Henricus Canisius in his *Antiquae Lectiones* and afterward at Antwerp together with his other works.

15. Nothing should be regarded as lying more securely beyond the realm of conjecture than the claim that the deacon Liutprand of Pavia and Liutprand, bishop of Cremona, were one and the same person [Note: [Col. 0941D] Thus teach Vossius, *On Historical Latin Literature*, book II, chapter 40; Miraeus, *Supplement to On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 290; Baronius under the year 973, no. 3; Bellarmine, *On Writers*, under the year 946.].

The style of the *History*, which he wrote as a deacon, and of the *Embassy*, which he wrote as a bishop, is the same: the same love of inserting certain Greek words awkwardly into Latin so that he might appear Greek-like, and of inserting poems into prose outside the rules of historical writing.

Moreover, the author of the *Embassy* identifies himself when he says that he addressed these words to Nicephorus:

> “In the time, I say, of the blessed Emperor Constantine, I had come here, not as a bishop but as a deacon; and I had been sent not by an emperor or king but by Berengar the marquis”—

thus contemptuously calling the tyrant of Italy—

> “and I bought many more and more precious pallia,”

and so forth.

16. Since these things are so—namely, since Liutprand had been made bishop of Cremona before the year 963—how can we fail to hiss at the pseudo-Julian, who dared to write that in that same year, 963, Liutprand, or Eutrandus, the subdeacon, came to Toledo, a noble historian who had formerly been there, and died and was buried there shortly afterward?

Even without this, who would believe that an Italian, compelled by no force and attracted by no desire, left his homeland to live in a city of Saracens; and not just once, but returned again after so many years, supposedly drawn by love to undertake a yoke that citizens forced by necessity could scarcely endure?

17. The very name Eutrandus is also discordant. Only Trithemius—and the Toledan innovator who follows Trithemius in authority—assigns this name to the man who is truly called Liutprand, or Luitprand, and occasionally Litobrandus, by his Germanic or Lombard name [Note: [Col. 0942D] Vossius, *On Historical Latin Literature*, book II, chapter 40; Tamayo, notes to Liutprand, p. 1.], in all the manuscripts and printed books, both of his works and of Sigebert’s little book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*.

The sole exception is a manuscript of the monastery of Green Valley, which Suffridus Petrus praises in the Cologne edition of Sigebert and other writers on similar subjects (in a note to Sigebert’s chapter 127). For Eutrandus sounds like a certain Greek name, whereas Liutprandus or Luitprandus is Lombardic.

Thus we have abundantly demonstrated that the lives of the two Liutprands, the genuine and the spurious, are in no way mutually compatible.

18. The genuine offspring of this man is the *History of Events Accomplished by the Emperors and Kings of Europe*, of which the *Antidosis* is a part—unless we apply this name to the entire work, a matter discussed below—and likewise the *Embassy to Nicephorus, Emperor of Constantinople*, undertaken on behalf of the august Ottos and Adelhaida, their wife and mother. And, if God wills, also the book *On the Lives of the Roman Pontiffs*, though many do not believe this to be his.

We readily believe that the claim that this Italian came to Spain, lived familiarly at Toledo with the aforementioned bishop of Iliberis, and—what would be the greater achievement—wrote certain remarkable records of Spanish affairs, before which gold and jewels would be worthless, was deliberately attributed to him by those whose purpose was to stage, under the persona of ancient men, a drama of pseudo-history in the modern theater. These are the *Chronicon*, said to be a continuation of another chronicle by Maximus, bishop of Zaragoza, and the *Adversaria*.

19. D. Thomas Tamayo de Vargas, royal historiographer, first published both works at Madrid, adding learned notes at least to the *Chronicon*. Later, through the care and industry of D. Laurentius Ramirezius de Prado, Liutprand in his entirety, assembled from old and new materials, was issued from the Plantin press and circulated throughout Europe.

It has long been firmly established among both our own and foreign scholars who have once reflected upon the fraud that the *Chronicon* and *Adversaria* are works by a recent hand, invented by the same man who, in one and the same abortive birth, produced the twin Pseudo-Dextrus and Pseudo-Maximus.

To establish this by arguments drawn both from elsewhere and from the very fabric of these works will be the subject of the following chapter and those attached to it. Meanwhile, as though glimpsed through a lattice, let us indicate that the friendship of Liutprand and Tractemundus—who is truly Recemundus, by his Gothic name—was formed when the latter was sent as an envoy from Abderrahman, king of Córdoba, to Otto. This has been learnedly demonstrated from a genuine writer, John, abbot of Saint Arnulf, by D. Gaspar Ibáñez de Segovia, marquis of Mondéjar and Acropolitan, in the second volume of his *Ecclesiastical Dissertations*; he seems born to tear down and eradicate fables.

### CHAPTER TWO

The two preliminary letters to the *Chronicon* of Pseudo-Liutprand are attacked on two grounds: first, because of the errors, affectations, and improbabilities contained in them. The first kind occurs in the prior letter from Tractemundus to Liutprand: the name of Tractemundus, bishop of Iliberis, to whom the letter is said to be addressed, instead of Regimundus; the title *Antapodosis*, the name of one of Liutprand’s books, instead of *Antidosis*; and the false distinction between this work and the history. On this occasion a difficult passage in Liutprand’s history is explained.

There is also a chronological error concerning the time of Pope Hadrian I; the spurious mention of Saint James of Picenum; and several affectations, signs of novelty. Among the absurdities is the request that a foreigner living far away should supply a continuation of the history of Spanish affairs.

Higuera does not mention this first letter in his *History of Toledo*, but he does mention the second, Liutprand’s letter to Tractemundus. This published letter is compared with the one that we read in the same *History of Toledo* and in one of our unpublished manuscripts; from their variation we infer fraud.

This second letter of Liutprand’s reply is likewise full of faults similar to those of the first. It falsely assigns a commission to the care of the Toledan bishops Servus Dei and Heronius of Braga, most conspicuously outside their proper period. The letter is burdened by other absurdities and affectations.

### 20

We now investigate the *Chronicle* that he calls his own, and especially the letters prefixed to it. One of these, as we recently stated, is from Tractemundus, bishop of Illiberis, to Eutrandus or Liutprandus; the other is Liutprandus’s reply to Tractemundus. Both are written in the same recent style. We shall shake and overthrow them by a twofold assault. The first will be supplied by the very matters they contain; the second by investigating, examining, and comparing with one another those passages [Col. 0943C] from which, not long ago, these ill-omened productions burst forth.

Indeed, the facts themselves cry out that these matters cannot properly or suitably be said to belong to the period they claim or to the author they profess to present. They must instead be charged either with an error committed, with the affected insertion of certain matters that someone wished to fasten upon genuine history as falsehoods, or with improbability and absurdity.

### 21

I speak first of the error—at present we are discussing Tractemundus’s letter to Liutprandus. That bishop of Illiberis is recorded as Regimundus, certainly not Tractemundus, by Sigebert (*On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chap. 127), Trithemius (*On Ecclesiastical Writers*), and the others who remember this designation. Reuberus published the name Raimundus—which is the same name—in his *German Histories through Their Authors*, among whom this history of Liutprandus appears. Hence Ramirezius preserved that name in his edition.

I also possess it in my manuscript of fragments of Dex­ter, Maximus, and this Liutprandus, from the library of the Marquis Estepano. We have stated more than once elsewhere that what has survived from these chronicles may be judged to have reached us in a pure form, or at least in one very close to the purest [Col. 0943D].

### 22

Only one catalogue of the bishops of Illiberis is said to have Tratemundus—or Tractemundus—in it. The bishops of Granada succeeded them, and the catalogue remains among the Granadans. When the Toledan inventor of these novelties came upon it, he thought that he would thereby prove himself a great defender of antiquity if he asserted the corrupted name of the bishop, as is probable, on the authority of his own writers, while condemning the common reading, Tractemundus, found in all the others, relying on a single witness.

Why should this catalogue have so much authority that everything belonging to the ancient monuments must yield to it? No manuscript of venerable antiquity is even paraded before us as the keeper and preserver of this catalogue. And if we believe the fictions—which nevertheless are Apollonian oracles—to which those whom we are attacking appeal, then, since Tractemundus is placed in that catalogue as the fortieth bishop from Saint Caecilius, the first bishop, how can it be that in another catalogue of Hauberti of Seville no fewer than fifty-three bishops are counted from that same Saint Caecilius to Samuel II—that is, down to the year 910 and several years before Tractemundus’s episcopate? And how can Tractemundus be counted as the seventy-first from the martyr Caecilius in the most recent *Martyrology* of our John Tamayus (vol. IV, 17 August, p. 494)?

Go on, then: believe catalogues whose author and date are unknown. Certainly, we shall be committing a grave error if we follow Hauberti and Tamayus as guides in denying authority to the Granadan catalogue [Note: [Col. 0943D] In the catalogue of the bishops of Illiberis in the Aemilianensis manuscript, fol. 360, p. 2, the name is given as Tretemundus, and he is forty-first in order from Saint Caecilius. In the chronological series of engraved bronze-table images of the bishops of Granada, which we have at hand, the name is likewise Tretemundus; but he is forty-fourth from Caecilius [Col. 0944D], and is said to have begun his episcopate in the year 704 of Christ. Bermudezius Pedraza, *History of Granada*, part II, chap. 25, counts him as fiftieth from Caecilius and asserts that he presided over the see of Granada before the destruction of Spain. We set out the series of these catalogues [Col. 0943].]

### 23

Second, if Liutprandus intended by the name *Antidosis* to designate either the complete history of events in Europe or a portion of it, then this letter contains a grave and twofold error: not only does it pronounce *Antapodosis* instead of *Antidosis*, but it also distinguishes this work from the history.

Regarding the name proposed by the author, we ought to believe him rather than anyone else. In the prologue to the third book of the history he says:

> “I do not doubt, most holy Father, that you are sufficiently surprised by the title of this work. For you say: ‘When the deeds of illustrious men are being presented, why is *Antidosis* inserted as its title?’ To this I reply: the purpose of this work is directed toward designating, displaying, and proclaiming the deeds of this Berengar, who now does not rule in Italy but tyrannizes, and of his wife …” [Col. 0944C]

And lest we should at some point suspect that an error had arisen from contraction in the Greek word, he adds:

> “Let this page, therefore, be *Antidosis* for them—that is, requital—since, in place of my misfortunes, I shall expose their τὴν ἀσέβειαν, that is, their impiety, to mortals present and future. It will also be *antidosis* for the most holy and fortunate men, in return for the benefits they have bestowed upon me.”

The editions of Sigebertus lie in error here, and John Trithemius repeated the error, substituting *Antapodosis*, a meaningless word in relation to the author’s intention. Thomas Tamayus himself admits this in his notes on this letter (p. 15), and the very explanation of the word given by Sigebertus proves it. Francis Bivarius may offer an excuse, arguing that the terms *Antidosis* and *Antipodosis* amount to the same thing. For *antipodosis* is a rhetorical figure produced when the middle corresponds to the first and last parts, and it signifies correspondence. Yet we are not now asking what he might have called the work, but what he did call it [Col. 0944D].

### 24

Moreover, it is clear from the following words that the author of the letter distinguished this *Antidosis* from the history:

> “I gratefully received your book—that is, your history of events accomplished in Europe—and, in addition, your *Antapodosis*, composed in verse and prose …” [Col. 0945A]

Sigebertus explicitly says that the works were not distinct: namely, that Liutprandus wrote a history *On the Deeds of the Kings and Emperors of His Time*, which he entitled *Antapodosis*, that is, requital. Trithemius says the same.

This is also clear from the aforementioned prologue to Book III, although, unless I am mistaken, copyists foolishly attached it to this book when they ought to have attached it to Book V. The reason is obvious. Neither the third nor the fourth book of the history contains anything about Berengar’s affairs for which Berengar could be said to have been repaid or retaliated against by the author for his crimes. The surviving chapters of Books V and VI, up to the fifth chapter, speak entirely of Berengar.

It is therefore absolutely certain that the history remained acephalous, as is sufficiently clear from its beginning, or at least reached us mutilated—deprived, namely, of its ending. That ending must have contained the section now missing: all Berengar’s crimes, up to his final expulsion from Italy and Otto’s coronation.

### 25

But what is said in the prologue to the *Antidosis* about the place where he wrote this history is certainly a cross to me, and I see no Liutprandus who described events here. He says:

> “Finally, since this little book is said to have been written in captivity or exile, the present exile itself shows the truth of the matter. For it was begun at Franconovord—Frankfort, today a city of Franconia—which is a place twenty miles distant from Mainz, and is continued to this day on the island of Paxu, nine hundred and more miles from Constantinople.”

This island of Paxu—or the Paxae Islands—lies near Corcyra in the Ionian Sea. They are called Greater Paxu and Lesser Antipaxu. A ship could have reached that place if its admiral had conveyed Liutprandus to Constantinople.

### 26

But to which of the two embassies sent there can the time devoted to writing be assigned? This is the work, this is the difficulty. It fits neither.

During the first embassy Liutprandus enjoyed Berengar’s favor, since it was in Berengar’s name that he approached Constantine [Col. 0945C]. It is therefore far from plausible that at that time he could dishonor Berengar—as he does in the prologue to the *Antidosis*—by calling the honor of this mission an exile, or by addressing as a tyrant a lord who was still beneficent toward him.

The later embassy was undertaken to Nicephorus Phocas, after Liutprandus had already been made bishop of Cremona. He went in Otto’s name, after Berengar had been driven from the kingdom and perhaps had died childless, in the year 968. Yet in this prologue there is not the slightest trace of that office.
