This period fits even less well the lamentation of the same prologue against Berengar as though he were present and still possessed of power as a tyrant.

Therefore, if we do not reject this prologue and the places within it where the history is said both to have been begun and continued, we must admit a journey by Liutprandus between the two embassies mentioned above—at least as far as the western regions of Greece and the Ionian Sea—at a time when he was fleeing Berengar. This would have been around the fifty-fourth year of the century, for in that year Alberic, the tyrant-marquis of Rome, was killed [Col. 0945D], and the author mentions his recent death in Book III, chapter 13.

### 27

Third, Tractemundus says that he has read among the afflicted Mozarabic Christians of Granada a letter of the holy pope Adrian, which Adrian had once sent on this subject to Egilo, bishop of Illiberis. When was this? Liutprandus himself will answer: in the year 748. For he expressly states in the *Chronicle* that this occurred in that year (year 748, no. 224).

But you will send this trifler away when you notice that Pope Adrian I, the first of that name, was not made pope until after the year 772. We criticize this anachronism here, although it does not belong to the letter, because the author of the letter is one and the same as the author of the *Chronicle*, even if they appear to be two persons, and although they travel in the same vessel.

### 28

Fourth, I count among the errors the fact that Tractemundus wishes Liutprandus to send him the life of Saint James, the Spanish confessor who died a holy death in Picenum on the first day of November. For this Saint James the confessor is mentioned in none of the catalogues of the saints, whether ancient or recent [Col. 0946A].

### 29

The affectation of inculcating matters without any adequate reason proclaims the novelty of the letter and its author’s impotent desire to assert and establish certain points of history that he wished the general public to believe above all. Such matters include the distinction made between the municipality of Illiberis and the town of Granada; the mention of Caecilius as its first bishop; the intrusive assertion of the primatial and patriarchal dignity of the bishop of Toledo; and the claim that he read the books of Boethius’s *Consolation* together with Liutprandus, while one was serving as a presbyter and the other as a subdeacon at Toledo.

### 30

And is not the following another such mark? It was foolishly added to the *Chronicle* bearing the common name of Liutprandus in order to support that name. Tractemundus asks Liutprandus to copy out and send him as soon as possible from Germany the chronicles of Dexter and M. Maximus, which he could never have found in Spain:

> “And from your own work,” he says, “add the period from the year 612, where Maximus ended, up to your own times—that is, to the year 960.” [Col. 0946B]

Could the pseudo-chronicle, continued up to this year by a fig-tree craftsman, have been indicated more explicitly—or with more offensive affectation? The real Tractemundus would have said only “up to our times” or “up to your times,” as we noted above.

### 31

What absurdity is not contained in the request that Liutprandus, a foreigner living so far from Spain, should be asked by Tractemundus, a Spaniard and inhabitant of Spain, to complete so quickly a chronicle of Spain covering more than three hundred years—that is, a continuation of Maximus?

This is especially absurd since, with the help of his old friends among the citizens of Toledo, Tractemundus could have examined even at Granada that exceedingly rich treasure, the library of the church of Saint Justa, which Julian is so accustomed to praise and boast about. He could have obliged and satisfied himself and others more readily than any foreigner, who could not have equipped himself from that Toledan storehouse of fig-tree manufacture.

### 32

Nor should we pass without censure the fact that Tractemundus addresses the letter to Liutprandus as a Ticinian deacon and Toledan subdeacon, as though the order of subdeacon were being added to the order of deacon as a new and noteworthy dignity.

Likewise, the subscription “the sinful bishop of the Church of Illiberis” is foolish and does not appear to have been customary. The usual form among many was rather expressed with reference to the person, not the dignity: “Tractemundus, sinful man, bishop of the Church of Illiberis,” or “unworthy bishop,” as is frequently read in the councils.

### 33

I add to these points that Hieronymus Romanus de la Higuera, whom we contend was the architect of this elaborate and multifaceted construction, made no mention of this first letter in his still unpublished *History of the City and Kingdom of Toledo*. Yet he not only remembered Liutprandus’s later reply to Tractemundus, but also inserted it, translated into the vernacular, in chapter … of his book.

Nor does my Estepano manuscript contain that first letter, although it contains this later one in the form that we shall immediately display [Col. 0946D].

### 34

For when we come to Liutprandus’s reply, it reveals itself through signs even more evident as false—or, to put it as moderately as possible, as enlarged and adulterated for the greater part. If anything genuine, and German—that is, sent from Germany—remains in it, Hieronymus Romanus, whom we have just mentioned, rendered all of it into Spanish and wished to make it part of his *History of Toledo*.

The text of my Estepano manuscript corresponds throughout to the Spanish words of that translation. From this a very strong argument arises that this was the first version conceived, whether by Liutprandus himself or, more probably, by the man who, pretending to be Liutprandus, dared under that mask to present himself to posterity.

Since displaying this to everyone’s eyes carries great prejudice against the work, we shall place here, in three parallel columns: first, Higuera’s Spanish translation; second, the plain Latin of the Estepano manuscript; and third, the adulterated and expanded text of the common editions of Liutprandus. To make the difference and the deception immediately visible even to those who will not compare the texts carefully, whatever in the third-place vernacular text does not depart from the other two has been printed in the same type, while whatever does depart has been printed in a different type.

### 35. From the *History of Toledo*, Book XV, chapter 11: Spanish translation of the letter

[Col. 0947A]

To the holy Father and lord Agismundus [thus the name is read], bishop of Illiberis, every blessing.

I was pleased, most blessed Father and lord worthy of the greatest reverence, that our *Antipodosis* has come into your hands, in which I sometimes use verse and sometimes prose [Col. 0947B]. Nor was I less pleased by what you now command me: that in the library of the monastery of Fulda, where I remain in exile, I should seek the *Chronicle* of Dexter, which Maximus, archbishop of Zaragoza, continued at the request of Bishop Agebad, and, if it seemed appropriate, should continue it up to our own times.

For you tell me that you are in great want of certain books and that, living among barbarous and inhuman Saracens, you can scarcely obtain what is necessary to sustain life [Col. 0947C]. I grieved over your condition, that you should pass your life in such hardship. Yet, placed amid such distress and constraint, you have one consolation: that, as a good shepherd, you are ready to comfort and help your sheep, and that every day you hazard your life for their sake.

The *Chronicle* that you requested I found in this library of Fulda, written in an ancient parchment book [Col. 0947D]. I added to it, as you command, the events that occurred in our own times—that is, up to the year 960.

I am also glad that, when I departed from Toledo for Italy, where I served as subdeacon in the time of the holy archbishop of Toledo, Bonitus, I brought with me certain history books in which the succession of many bishops of Spain was set out in order. I found these books here as well. I believe that they were brought here from Spain at the command of the holy emperor Charlemagne [Col. 0949A], to whom the holy archbishop of Toledo, Elipandus, offered them after he had truly and effectively repented of the error he had held concerning the adoption of Christ made man.

Commend this exiled servant of yours to God.

*End of the letter.*

### Latin letter of the *Chronicles of Dexter, Maximus, and Liutprandus* in the Estepano manuscript

[Col. 0947A]

Eutrandus, Ticinian deacon and Toledan subdeacon, to the holy Father Regimundus, bishop of Illiberis:

Eutrandus, an unworthy servant, to Saint … .

I was pleased, most blessed Father and lord, that our *Antapodosis*, in which we now play with verse and now with prose, at last came into your hands [Col. 0947B]. Nor is it less pleasing that you now order me to search for you in the library of the monastery of Fulda, where I am presently living in exile, for the *Chronicle* of Dexter, which Maximus, bishop of Zaragoza, continued at the request of Bishop Argebad *(the word “continued” is missing)*, and, if I had leisure, to bring it down to our own times.

For you say that you suffer from the greatest scarcity of certain books. Among barbarous and inhuman Saracens there is no abundance even of things necessary for life [Col. 0947C], much less an abundance of good books. I certainly grieved over your situation, that you should lead your life in such hardship. But what consoles you, placed amid such great difficulties, is that, as a good shepherd, you are a comfort and help to your sheep, for whose sake you daily undergo death.

The *Chronicle* that you request I found in this library, written on ancient parchment. As I was ordered, I added a sequence of years down to the present time—that is [Col. 0947D], down to the Spanish era 960.

I congratulate myself that, when I departed from Toledo for Italy, where I served as a subdeacon under the most holy bishop Bonitus of Toledo, I carried with me several books of history. In them was collected in order a succession of many bishops of Spain. I also found these books in this library. As I believe, they were brought from Spain at the command of Saint Charles the Great, emperor, and had been offered to him, as they say, by the most holy Elipandus, archbishop of Toledo, after he seriously repented of his error [Col. 0949A] concerning the adoption of Christ.

I have done what you commanded, most blessed Father. Whether the attempt has answered your wishes, you will judge, since you gave the command. Farewell, and commend this exiled servant to God in exile.

*End of the letter.*

### The common Latin letter of Liutprandus’s *Chronicle*

[Col. 0948A]

To the most reverend and wholly holy Tractemundus, bishop of Illiberis in Spain, Liutprandus, by no merits of his own a levite of the Church of Ticinum, sends greetings and every expression of respect.

I was pleased, most blessed pope and greatly revered lord, that our *Antapodosis*, in which I now play with verse and now with prose, at last came into your hands [Col. 0948B]. It is no less pleasing to my mind that you have read my history of events in Europe, which is beginning in some way to please me, since I see that it is in some way approved by you, a righteous and learned man.

I would follow your judgment in this matter if I did not know that love sometimes grows blind. Yet the integrity of your life and your love of truth—which has always clung to your inmost thoughts since adolescence—free you from such blind judgment.

Finally, I was no less pleased that you now order me to seek for you in the library of the monastery of Fulda, where I remain in exile as librarian, the *Chronicle* of Dexter, which Marcus Maximus, a Benedictine monk and later bishop of Zaragoza, continued. In addition, you earnestly ask me to bring its sequence of years down to our own times.

For you say that you suffer from a great scarcity of certain books. Indeed, among barbarous and inhuman Saracens there is no abundance of things necessary for passing life, much less a supply of good books [Col. 0948C].

I certainly grieved over your situation, most reverend Father, that you should lead your life so harshly in this city of Baetica, which is by no means insignificant. We did not live so harshly, but somewhat better, when once we lived together at Toledo.

On the one hand, the singular authority of the Toledan bishops softened the ferocity of the barbarians; on the other, so did their remarkable goodness and patience. Their authority rested partly upon the remaining brilliance of their ancient greatness and partly upon the favor of the Catholic kings of Oviedo, who frequently commended the affairs, authority, and good treatment of Toledo, both of all the faithful and especially of the Toledan bishops.

This was, as you know well, something like a bridle, preventing them from thinking that everything they wished was entirely permitted to them. The same did not happen to the bishops established in Baetica, over all of whom the most powerful emperor presides.

But let it console you, excellent Father, placed amid such great difficulties, that you, as a good shepherd, are both comfort and help to your sheep, for whose sake you willingly undergo death every day.

I beg you to send to the most holy pontiff, Servusdei in reality and in name, those books of councils and decretal letters, together with the names of the holy martyrs of Spain [Col. 0948D].

As for the *Chronicle* that you request, I found it written on ancient parchment in this library. As you ordered, I added a sequence of years down to the present time—that is, to the year 960.

I congratulate myself that, when I departed from Toledo for Italy, where I served as a subdeacon under the most holy bishop Bonitus of Toledo, I carried with me several books of history. In them was collected in order a succession of many bishops of Spain. I found these books here as well, brought from Spain, as I believe, at the command of the emperor Charlemagne. They had been offered to him, as they say, by the most holy Elipandus, bishop of Toledo, after he seriously and truly repented of his error concerning the adoption of Christ.

To make this manifest, he gathered a council of the suffragan bishops and abbots and, having publicly abjured his error, confessed before them all the faith of the Holy Roman Church, as you know better than anyone [Col. 0950A].

Therefore I have done what you commanded, most blessed Father. Whether the attempt has answered your wish, you will judge, since you gave the command. Commend this exiled servant to God in your prayer. Farewell.

Nevertheless, I shall begin with the year 606, Spanish era 644, and follow in writing the order followed by Maximus: on one side according to the eras of the Spaniards, on the other according to the years of Christ. I shall include nothing about the consuls or the Hegiras of the Moors, and I shall bring this *Chronicle* of ours down to the year 960.

*End of the letter.*

### 36

Thus far there are three versions of Liutprandus’s letter: Higuera’s Spanish translation from the Latin, and the Latin versions both of our Estepano manuscript and of the common editions.

You can now see, reader who loves truth, that the Spanish translation consistently follows not the common editions but the Estepano Latin text, with very few exceptions. It is therefore necessary to conclude that the letter was originally formed in the more recent conception or invention preserved by Higuera. Yet the Latin text of the same letter, repeated in the two editions, differs enormously from these versions. It is manifestly the product of the author’s second efforts, or of a revised composition—truly a second offspring, distinct from its first edition [Col. 0949B].

No conjecture is needed here, but only an examination by the eyes, for those willing to consult this Toledan history preserved in manuscript in the Toledan Jesuit college, or to consult copies of it. Several such copies were recently in Madrid in the library of the most excellent Count Villumbrosani, now deceased, former president of the great senate of Castile; another was once in the possession of the Count of Mora.

### 37

We confirm this especially well from the fact that the Franciscan Didacus Murillo, author of the *History of the Virgin of the Pillar*, who published his work before Liutprandus’s *Chronicle* appeared, shortly after news of the invention had been spread among us and after Hieronymus Romanus, its inventor, had communicated portions of it to certain intimate friends—including the aforementioned Murillo, who published them—did not use this later, looser, and longer version of the letter.

Instead, when speaking of Liutprandus and this work of his, Murillo incorporated into his apologetic prologue the shorter and more concise version that we have produced from our Estepano manuscript [Col. 0949C]. Rodericus Carus transferred this version into his notes on Dexter’s *Chronicle* (in the prologue), as did Franciscus Bivarius in his commentary on the same *Chronicle*.

They were genuinely following that version, not deceived; nor did they present it as mutilated as though it were complete, as Thomas Tamayus claims [p. 25].

### 38

Now that the difference of this letter from itself has been exposed, and with it the resulting suspicion—or rather proof—of forgery, we shall not hesitate to apply the censor’s rod to its wording. It is plainly burdened with the same faults of falsehood, affectation, and absurdity as the other letter.

First, the name *Antipodosis* is false, as is the distinction from the history, as we have already said.

It is false that Tractemundus is asked to send “those books of councils and decretal letters, and the names of the holy martyrs of Spain, to the most holy pontiff, Servusdei in reality and in name.” For if Servusdei ceased to live in the year 947—as Liutprandus himself testifies in the passage quoted above [namely, under the year 947]—while Liutprandus was writing this in exile in Germany, after composing the history and undertaking his first embassy to Constantinople, and after Berengar’s anger against him had arisen, then all of which, as anyone can establish from the preceding account of his life and affairs, occurred at least before the year 954.

If we admit these two points as entirely true, we must affirm one of two things: either the letter is spurious and false, or Liutprandus intended these books to be sent to Servusdei for so long after Servusdei’s death.

No one can suitably evade this by saying that Liutprandus did not know that Servusdei had died after such a long interval. For in the *Chronicle*, to which this letter serves as a preface, he records Servusdei’s death in the stated year and the substitution of Visitani in his place [Col. 0950A]. These facts are clearer than daylight.

### 39

It is also false and contradictory that he says at the end:

> “After this I sent these things to Heronius—or Heromo [Note: [Col. 0949] This is how it was printed at Antwerp; in the Madrid edition this clause is absent.]—bishop of Braga.”

I understand this to mean the addition to Maximus’s *Chronicle* down to the year 960. What else could it mean?

Liutprandus himself confirms this statement in *Adversary* 32:

> “I also sent my *Chronicle*, which I had sent to Tractemundus, and also a part of it to Heronius, the most holy and aged bishop of Braga, and I wrote him the following letter.”

Yet in the very wording of the letter addressed to Heronius, which he appends, he plainly shows himself to be false and forgetful—indeed, he proclaims the blindness and thoughtlessness of the impostor.

The ending of the letter states that it was given at Toledo in Spanish era 981. This is the forty-third year of the present century, when John Servusdei was alive as bishop of Toledo; Liutprandus sends greetings to Heronius in his name.

Yet this year preceded by so many years Liutprandus’s exile in Germany, his discovery of the chronicles of Dexter and Maximus in the Fulda library [Col. 0950C], and his continuation of the history from the point where Maximus ended, that only a careless and insane man could have subscribed this year to the letter in which he both sends that continuation to Heronius and mentions that the same work had already been sent back to Tractemundus.

Wretched is the man who knows neither how to tell the truth nor how to deceive!

### 40

It is absurd and incredible that, in this reply to Tractemundus’s letter, Liutprandus should have sent him a *Chronicle* of three hundred years—not a brief and meager work dealing with one nation, but an extensive work rich in the succession of foreign events as well. Such a work could not have been completed without constant study and diligence over many months.

It is absurd that he should have imagined that the kings were still called kings of Oviedo, since they had generally been called kings of Galicia or León nearly a century earlier, as is clear from the letter of Pope John to Alfonso the Great in Sampirus, and from what Ambrosius Morales repeatedly noted, together with others (*Book XV*, chapters 37 and 42).

It is absurd and rashly stated that the Christians of Granada were harassed by the Moors because, when Liutprandus wrote this, the most powerful emperor presided over all the bishops established in Baetica—as though Abderrahman Almanzor, whom he has in mind, did not hold under his rule all the cities of Spain that obeyed the Moors in Baetica and in what is now the kingdom of Castile [Col. 0950D].

It is absurd that he says he sent Tractemundus, along with the other materials, “the names of the holy martyrs of Spain,” as though this would be something separate or of any value after sending Dexter’s *Chronicle*, which is entirely blank concerning Spanish martyrs.

Nor will I be insulting if I add another absurdity to those already mentioned: he says that in his continuation he will follow the years of Christ and the eras of the Spaniards, adding “nothing about the consuls” or the Hegiras of the Moors—as though the reckoning of consuls and the computation of time by consuls were still in use at the period when he takes up Maximus’s thread, namely, in the year of the Lord 606 [Col. 0951A].

### 41

The affectations are intolerable and reveal the author’s lack of talent, as though he were striving to display himself in his assumed persona. Everything that has been attached to the old thread, as we have seen, proves this.

Thus, where Maximus, bishop of Zaragoza, was formerly praised as the author of the *Chronicle*, the forename Marcus and the status of a Benedictine monk were added. This accords with the Toledan forger’s fixed and perpetual purpose of combining Marcus the Benedictine with Maximus, bishop of Zaragoza, as we have already noted in its proper place.

Likewise, there is the intrusive mention of the former authority and splendor of the Toledan bishops, which somehow softened the ferocity even of the ruling Moors.

No less affected is the claim that a volume of councils and decretal letters was sent to Tractemundus along with the other materials. This alludes to what was long circulated under the collection of Isidore Mercator as an ancient and genuine work, although today scarcely any learned person applauds it as a legitimate monument of antiquity [Col. 0951B].

Finally, the repentance of Elipandus and the council he convened at Toledo are most offensively thrust forward. Liutprandus himself acknowledges that Tractemundus was not ignorant of these matters in that foolish parenthesis, repeated so often throughout the letter: “as you know better than anyone.”

But let us now turn our attention to the *Chronicle* itself.

## CHAPTER III

The *Chronicle* itself, as it exists in one of our manuscript fragments, is compared with the published and common version for only twenty-three years. From this comparison the additions and interpolations subsequently made are proved false and are marked as removed or altered.

When he wrote this, the author of the *History of Toledo*, Higuera, used our fragment, not the complete common *Chronicle*.

### 42

Above all, it must be observed that in my Estepano manuscript—which, in our judgment, represents the genuine or nearly genuine chronicles of Dexter, or of another author, and of Maximus [Col. 0951C]—there is a sufficiently brief fragment of a continuation of Maximus’s *Chronicle*, attributed to Liutprandus.

This is the same manuscript that Hieronymus Higuera alone possessed and used when he was occupied with composing his *History of Toledo*, as we repeatedly emphasize.

It begins with the year 606 as follows:

| ERA OF CAESAR | YEAR OF CHRIST |
|---|---|
| 644 | 606 |

> “Ildephonsus is born at Toledo to distinguished parents; he later became bishop of Toledo.”

> “A synod is convened at Toledo.”

| ERA OF CAESAR | YEAR OF CHRIST |
|---|---|
| 645 | 607 |

> “Muhammad comes to Spain to pour in the poison of his error. He begins to sow it at Córdoba, Seville, and Toledo. He is driven from Toledo by Aurasio.”

> “Victericus persecutes the Catholics,” etc., up to the year 629 and the clause that we place below.

| ERA OF CAESAR | YEAR OF CHRIST |
|---|---|
| 667 | 629 |

[Col. 0951D]

> “Svinthila, driven from the kingdom, dies. After Helladius has been removed, and Sisenandus is now king, Justus the archdeacon succeeds him, as does Braulius of Zaragoza succeed John.”

### 43

With these words the fragment appended to Maximus, comprising only twenty-three years, comes to an end.

For the greater part it differs from the corresponding years of the common edition. In it one finds individual chapters interpolated by the removal, addition, and alteration of several passages, as well as other material inserted wholesale between them.

This will easily be detected by anyone who wishes to consult, at the end of this section of the library, the appendices of several ancient monuments and, among them, this text together with the Estepano examples of the chronicles of Dexter and Maximus.

### 44

For the reader’s convenience, we shall present here one or two examples. Let the first be the very first chapter of the interpolated material in the fragment.

[Note: [Col. 0952A] The following fragments are printed in parallel in Migne.]

#### In the Estepano manuscript

[Col. 0952A]

> “Ildephonsus is born at Toledo to distinguished parents; he later became bishop of Toledo.”

#### But in the common editions

> “Saint Ildephonsus is born at Toledo to the most illustrious parents, Stephen and Lucia, on 18 December, in the house that is now that of the noble Mozarabs of Toledo. He later became bishop of Toledo.”

Who does not see that these details were added to the simpler account for the purpose of supporting the credibility of Julian’s epigram, which attributes Stephen and Lucia as the parents of Saint Ildephonsus [Note: [Col. 0951D] In the collection of poems at the end of the works]; and also of confirming, through this testimony of Liutprandus, the tradition concerning the origin of the Mendoza counts of Orgaz as descendants of the line of Ildephonsus [Note: [Col. 0952D] Tamayus, in his notes on this passage]?

[Note: [Col. 0952A] The following fragments are printed in parallel in Migne.]

#### In the Estepano manuscript

Spanish era 652, year 614.

> “After the death of Aurasio, Helladius is unwillingly appointed to the see [Col. 0952B] of Toledo.”

#### In the common editions

[Col. 0952A]

Spanish era 651, year 613.

> “After the death of Aurasio, Saint Helladius, a most holy and learned pontiff, succeeds him in the see of Toledo: an outstanding and pious man, a Benedictine monk. Already advanced in age, he is summoned to the heavenly realms.”

Do you see how the eagerness to vindicate the Benedictine monastic profession of Helladius and of all the other eminent men, which is constant and conspicuous throughout the whole Chronicle and in the Chronicles of Liutprand and his fellow-companions, has left its unmistakable imprint upon this passage?

[Note: [Col. 0952B] The following fragments are printed in parallel in Migne.] In Estepano.

Era 660, in the year 622.

“Maximus, formerly a monk, is regarded as a distinguished bishop of Zaragoza.”

In the vulgar editions.

Era 660, in the year 622.

“Marcus Maximus, previously a Benedictine monk and afterward bishop of Zaragoza, is held in renown after his death.”

Previously it was unknown that Maximus had borne the first name Marcus, that he had been a monk of the Benedictine order, and that he was still alive in this year; for he died in the year 624, as is reported below under that year. All these claims later hands abandoned—would that they had been wiser!

[Note: [Col. 0952C] The following fragments are printed in parallel in Migne.] 45. In Estepano.

Era 662, in the year 624.

“After returning from Seville, Ildephonsus. Helladius wanted to make him a deacon. But he, renouncing the world, led his life in the monastery of Agali, which, as you know, is in the suburb of Toledo, toward the north, not far from the river Tagus, and about 300 paces from the Praetorian church of Saint Leocadia, which I frequently visited while I was in Toledo.”

In the vulgar editions.

[Col. 0952C]

In the same era and year.

“When Ildephonsus had returned from Seville to Toledo, Helladius wanted to make him his archdeacon. But he withdrew and diligently lived in the monastery of Agali, which is in the suburb of Toledo toward the north, not far from the river Tagus, and outside the walls, on the plain, near the Praetorian church of Saint Leocadia; I frequently visited it while I was in Toledo. There is also another monastery, almost a colony of this Agalian one, at a village called Benalgovia by the Moors, three miles from Toledo. But Saint Ildephonsus lived in the former monastery, which was not far from the hermitage of Saint Susanna, near the Tagus. As I said, I visited it when I was a subdeacon at Toledo under Bonitus, the first archbishop of Toledo of that name, formerly abbot of Agali.”

[Col. 0953A] 46. You see, reader, a notable addition made to the shorter account of Ildephonsus and his monastery. Previously it read, “he wanted to make him a deacon,” that is, to initiate him into the sacred orders. Later it was preferred to read, “he wanted to make him an archdeacon,” that is, to adorn him with that dignity in the Church of Toledo. Previously it read, “renouncing the world,” as though saying that Ildephonsus had first devoted himself to the religious life after returning to Toledo. Later they preferred to change these words to “he withdrew and diligently,” perhaps so that we might understand that, while still a boy in Seville and being kept with Saint Isidore, he had long before professed himself a monk. The same is true of what follows concerning the monastery of Agali and another supposed colony of it: both additions, introduced by Tractemundus, who was familiar with the matter, are foul and absurd! Clearly they were inserted so that the recent fabricator of these trifles might, under the brand of the name Liutprand, sell his own opinion about the ancient site of this monastery.

[Col. 0953B] 47. Many more commands of the old text were also ordered to give way and to appear nowhere; for example:

From era 645, in the year 607:

“Witteric persecutes the Catholics.”

Era 647, in the year 609:

“The Synod of Lugo in Spain. Aurasius presided over it.”

Era 662, in the year 624:

“Tonantius, bishop of Palencia, dies.”

Era 664, in the year 626:

“On the Kalends of January, Fulgentius, bishop of Écija, dies.”

Era 667, in the year 629:

“Swinthila, expelled from the kingdom, dies; and, after Helladius had been removed, when Sisenand was already king, Justus the archdeacon succeeds him, as does Braulio succeed John of Zaragoza.”

And many other similar entries, unworthy of being passed over.

48. You will also observe that certain passages were reshaped into almost the opposite meaning from what they formerly had.

[Note: [Col. 0953C] The following fragments are printed in parallel in Migne.] Era 652, in the year 614.

[Col. 0953C]

“The holy man Vincent, bishop of Carthage, dies at Rome.”

Era 656, in the year 618.

“The city of Assota is deprived of its bishops.” And afterward, under era 661: “The see of Assota is transferred to Bigastrum.”

In the vulgar editions:

[Col. 0953C]

“Vincent, bishop of Carthage Spartaria, dies.”

In the vulgar editions:

“The city of Assota, in Contestania and on the border of Bastetania, which was once an episcopal see, is destroyed.” And immediately afterward: “The Assotan see is transferred to Bigastrum, which is Murcia” (in Tamayo’s edition, “which is Mentua”). But enough of this.

49. The Chronicle is also battered by another ram no less massive and powerful, and one wielded with the strength and shoulders of that same Liutprand. I mean Liutprand, who first came from Germany into the hands of Jerome Romanus [Col. 0953D] and whom the latter used to embellish the events of his history of Toledo. In chapter 1 of book II of that history, these words are plainly read concerning the Chronicle of Maximus and the continuation by Liutprand, which we translate from the vernacular into Latin:

“And with these words Maximus of Zaragoza brought his Chronicle to an end. We, however, shall use, as far as it extends, the continuation which Eutrandus, a Toledan subdeacon and deacon of the venerable Church of Ticinum, a man of great learning and literary culture, composed; although it is very defective and abridged in comparison with what he left behind.”

No fragment of our codex could have been identified more openly, nor could the commonly circulated Chronicle have been more clearly rejected—complete in every respect, had it established its own reliability. We have already often observed that, when Higuera wrote these words, he had in his bosom and arms the entire collection of the Chronicles and Adversaria of four authors—Dexter, Maximus, Liutprand, and Julian—sent to him from Germany and perhaps elsewhere, and that he drew their testimonies throughout this entire history. We shall also collect those passages of the same history in which either what appears in the vulgar editions but is entirely absent from our codex is passed over in silence, or what is reported from Liutprand is given not according to the vulgar editions but according to the wording of our codex.

50. In book II, chapter 2, he mentions a council held at Toledo in the time of Witteric, king of the Goths, “which,” he says, “Eutrandus, or Liutprand, mentions, without adding anything further.” Hear his words as my codex presents them:

“A synod is convened at Toledo, namely in era 644, or the year 606.”

There is no trace whatsoever of this event in the vulgar editions.

51. A little later in the same chapter 2, when discussing Gundemar’s election as king of the Goths and successor to Witteric, he says:

“We have spoken of his election because Saint Isidore and Liutprand speak so simply about this succession that they would certainly not have failed to note it had he entered by force or tyranny. I also regard it as certain that he was crowned in the church at Toledo by Bishop Aurasius, as his two predecessors had been.”

Here are Liutprand’s words under era 648:

“After Witteric died at Toledo, Gundemar was installed in his place.”

Nothing could have been stated more simply. But what Higuera infers concerning the coronation merely from the custom of earlier kings is already expressed in the commonly circulated Liutprand:

“After Wicteric died, Gundemar succeeded him. He was anointed by Aurasius of Toledo, as once the Greek emperors were by the patriarchs of Constantinople, in the church of Saints Peter and Paul at Toledo.”

52. Beyond the aforesaid era 667, or the year 629, the author of this history makes no mention of Liutprand, since the fragment of Liutprand that he possessed evidently extended only to that year. Nowhere, however, does the history mention those events relating to the city of Toledo which are now present in the vulgar editions but absent from the fragment of our codex. Namely:

Under era 644, the mention of Saint Adelphius, archbishop of Toledo and Metz.

Under era 649, Adeodata, a Benedictine nun of Toledo, to whom Saint Gregory wrote.

Under era 660, the dedication by Saint Leander of Seville, in the city of Toledo, of a church to the martyr Saint Thyrsus.

Up to this point, then, we have drawn from the celebrated history, and from the fragment of Liutprand that was available to that historian, arguments against the common form of this Chronicle—arguments directed, as the logicians say, ad hominem.

## CHAPTER IV

Certain topical passages reveal the character and purpose of the Pseudo-Liutprandine Chronicle. First, by abusing the ambiguity of names—whether of persons or places—it assigns foreign men and councils to Spain. Examples include Saints Magnus, Columbanus, and Gallus, and Saint Fara, a nun of Gaul; also the Council of Augsburg. Sometimes it does so without even the pretext of an ambiguity. Examples include the bishops Veranus and Ostanus, and Adeodata, the virgin known from the letters of Saint Gregory the pope.

53. We shall now offer, as it were, a specimen of the entire Chronicle, and display its inventor’s purpose as in a mirror, gathering together certain headings, or topical passages, by which he sought to impose upon credulous readers—passages which he especially wanted to make persuasive and to leave, in his own judgment, patched and protected against every modern attack, as though fastened with a great beam-nail.

54. You have often heard, when our present study was concerned with Dexter and Maximus, about the chief purpose of Jerome Romanus de la Higuera. I mean his plan to magnify everything connected with Toledo, especially its ecclesiastical affairs; to vindicate and assert, by assembling arguments from every quarter, the perpetual primatial and patriarchal dignity of that most extensive Church, self-sufficient in its own resources; to enrich and glorify Spain with honors and illustrious men, however obtained or extracted from elsewhere; and to exalt the Benedictine order above all praise, whether justly or unjustly, by extraordinary means.

For he could not more conveniently or effectively promote belief in the inventions he fabricated about Toledan affairs than by scattering and casting this ancient and precious treasure of the most eminent men and of deeds once performed piously or magnificently into, so to speak, the bosom of every province, city, place, and religious community. Intent upon this purpose, he tried in many ways to fortify this route for himself. We have already shown the passages to which all his inventions and imaginings can easily be reduced.

55. I. By abusing ambiguities of names or places, he established in Spain men illustrious for holiness whose birthplaces lay elsewhere, along with their deeds. He does the same by assigning foreign councils to Spain.

II. Even without ambiguities or the pretext of places or names, he assigns to Spain the homeland or death of men illustrious for holiness and celebrated in ecclesiastical calendars.

III. When summoned neither by necessity nor invitation, he intrudes himself as judge to resolve and determine matters in our history that are controversial and ambiguous, displaying everywhere an affected novelty.

IV. He eagerly seeks to shed light and explanation upon matters insufficiently expressed in ancient records, so that he may confer honor and splendor upon the places and persons he names, and win credibility for himself from those who are beholden to him.

V. Where only some obscure memory of events survives in ancient inscriptions found among us, he attempts to cast upon them the brighter torch of pseudo-history.

VI. To support his fictions, he recommends poems composed by himself but inscribed and attributed to ancient authors, so that he may deceive more securely.

56. I intend to set out examples of each of these places or headings—not all of them, but the more conspicuous ones. I say that he plays upon ambiguities of names, persons, or places, so that he may transfer to our people men of other nations who were celebrated for holiness and praised in martyrologies.

57. Let the first example be Saint Magnus, disciple of Saint Gall. A place was assigned to him in the calendars of the Church on September 6: in the ancient calendars, that of Bede; among the more recent, those of Maurolycus, Galesinus, and Ferrari. Galesinus added: “At Fauces, Saint Magnus the confessor,” and so forth.

Fauces, today Fuescen, is a town in Swabia, not obscure, according to Philip Ferrari, a most accomplished geographer, in his notes for this day in his Martyrology: “built beside the river Lech, at the narrow passes of the mountains, between Kempten, from which it is five German miles distant, and Laude, meeting the town of the county of Tyrol, where stands the celebrated monastery of Fuescen in the diocese of Constance.”

Hence in his own eulogy he writes: “At Fauces in Swabia, Saint Magnus, first abbot of Fuescen.” John Trithemius also writes (On Illustrious Men of the Benedictine Order, book III, chapter 107): “Abbot, as is said, at Fauces,” and so on.

But why do we still need witnesses two centuries old, when there exists a Life of Saint Magnus written by his companion Theodore and corrected and arranged by the monk Hermenricus of Ellwangen [Note: [Col. 0955] Rerum Alemannicarum, volume I, p. 190, and in Benedictus Gononus, Appendix of the Lives of the Fathers of the West, p. 456]? In it the historian expressly relates, in book II, chapter 7, that Blessed Magnus, when asked by Wichpert, bishop of the city of Augsburg, where he wished to remain, replied:

“With the Lord’s help, I have been directed to the place called Fauces, where the sources of the Julian Alps are nearby,” and so forth.

58. It is clear from what follows that he built a monastery there and presided over it. For chapter 12 of the same book II begins:

“While blessed Magnus was living in the monastery that he had prepared for himself at Fauces, he performed great miracles there for twenty-five years.”

Nor did he depart from there during the whole of his life, as chapter 13 plainly shows. Theodore the disciple placed the Life he had written, together with Magnus’s body, in the tomb. Hermenricus, a monk of Ellwangen, added an appendix to it at the command of Lantus, bishop of Augsburg; in his own time Lantus found the body of Blessed Magnus, venerated because of its many miracles, together with the book of his life, and transferred it to a more elevated place.

This is the truth handed down to posterity by a contemporary writer. The monk Ekkehard of Saint Gall confirms it in his book On the Misfortunes of the Monastery of Saint Gall, in these words:

“Into which church the arm of Saint Magnus, given and conveyed by Bishop Adalbero, was taken from Fauces,” and so forth.

Consult Melchior Haiminsfeld’s note on this passage. Liutprand tried in vain to attack this truth, composing the following under era 659, in the year 621:

“At Fauces of Spain, in Lusitania, commonly Garganta-la-Olla, Magnus, surnamed John, flourishes as abbot.”

59. Nor was the author satisfied with this. He also wished to transform Lantus, the sixteenth bishop of the most distinguished city of Augsburg in Swabia, into a bishop of Zaragoza or Mérida-Augusta, using these words of Julian, the author who is Liutprand’s twin:

“Bento [rather Lanto], bishop of Zaragoza, or Augsburg, by the authority of Pope Adrian” (there is no mention of this in his Life, nor was this ceremony practiced at that time), “enrolls Saint Magnus among the saints in a town of Lusitania called Fauces.”

Yet it is clear from Higuera’s note on the earlier Liutprand that this testimony is now corrupt. For, after citing it, he says that this Lantus was bishop of Mérida-Augusta during the time of the captivity.

Nevertheless, men otherwise most learned, Thomas Tamayo and Lorenzo Ramírez, who have devoted themselves to embellishing these trifles, accept these claims and dare not utter a word against them. John Tamayo also, who collected everything carefully and suspected no deception, believes every written word as though it were a Sibyl’s leaf, and strives to display his ingenuity by reconciling sheer fables with the truth. He says that Magnus traveled through the territories of both towns—the Swabian and the Spanish—called Fauces, fitting his acts together to this effect.

60. It is equally false that Saints Columbanus and Gall, whom Saint Magnus followed as teachers, came to Spain and landed at the port of Brigantium in Galicia, which at that time was ruled by Duke Gunzo; or that they visited a church in the fortress of Arbona and that Saint Gall rejected the bishopric of Lugo, which was then the city called Martia Constantia by the emperor Constantius; or that the mountains of the Asturians were the Rhaetian Alps, as reported from Julian’s playful Adversaria, numbers 268–271.

The author extracted all these details from the Acts of Saint Magnus in order to serve his fable. In book I, chapter 4, mention is made of the river and town once called Brigantium, later of Lake Brigantinus, and of the place Arbona:

“They therefore proceeded to Lake Brigantium, on whose shore they found an ancient ruined place called Arbona,” says the author of the Life, and so forth.

And in chapter 8:

“After not much time, blessed Gall, recovering through divine mercy, after freeing Duke Gunzo’s son from a demon, humbly refused the bishopric of the Church of Constance, which the same prince offered him,” and so forth.

All these things are read no less clearly in the Life of Saint Gall the abbot, written by Walafrid Strabo.

61. We are saying things known to children learning their alphabet, but they need to be emphasized. Brigantinus, or Lake Acronius, is now Lake Constance, and the celebrated city itself is Constance; likewise Brigantium, today Bregenz, and Arona, now Aron, are towns on its shore. These are the very places mentioned in the Acts of Saint Magnus. There is no need to resort to our port of Brigantium, now La Coruña or Betanzos, or to an invented Spanish Arona, and lend an ear to the fable.

They transform Lucus-Augusta, a city of Galicia, into Martia Constantia, and the mountains of the Asturians into the Rhaetian Alps [Note: [Col. 0957D] Among our authors, the name Alps is commonly applied to all lofty mountains. Sampirus, in Sandoval’s History, in its penultimate column, says: “The Normans plundered all Galicia until they reached the ALPS, the mountains of El Cebrero”—the district that Spaniards today call El Cebrero. Lucas of Tuy, Illustrious Spain, volume IV, p. 90: “When he himself, King Sancho, surnamed Abarca, was in the Pyrenean mountains beyond the ROSY ALPS OF THE VALLEY”—today Roncesvalles. And on p. 86: “To the ALPS of Mount Cebrero.” Not only later writers, but also Prudentius, in the Peristephanon, in the hymn to Saint Lawrence:

“Us, the Basque Iberus, divides,

separated by TWO ALPS,

beyond the ridges of the COTTIAN MOUNTAINS,

and beyond the snowy PYRENEES.”

The Alps may be spoken of any mountains and of the Pyrenees; Lipsius also noted this in his commentary on Trajan’s Panegyric; likewise Scaliger, book II of his Ausonian Readings, chapter 16; and Joseph Maria Suárez, in On the Synonymy of Various Places and Rivers, p. 44. But what has this to do with the Rhaetian Alps?]

Only those familiar with Julian’s geography know how to refute this transformation; for everyone else, it is superfluous.

62. Fara, otherwise Burgundofara, a Gallic nun, is famous in all the records of that people. Sigebert writes under the year 620 in his Chronicle:

“The virgin of Christ Fara shines in France; her brother Faro, imitating her holiness, a count turned cleric and then bishop of Meaux, also shines.”

For this reason the martyrologists frequently assign Fara to Gaul and to the territory of Meaux: Usuard (December 7), Vincent of Beauvais (Historical Mirror, book XXIII, chapter 15), Equilinus (Catalogue, book I, chapter 39), Trithemius (On Illustrious Men of the Benedictine Order, book III, chapter 55), Andreas Saussay (Gallican Martyrology, December 7), and especially the Roman Martyrology on December 7:

“In the territory of Meaux, Saint Phara, virgin.”

All of them saw her Acts and those of her brother Faro, bishop of Meaux; the latter are found in Surius under October 28. The same is true of the Life of Saint Eustasius, abbot of the monastery of Luxeuil, written by Jonas, a monk of Bobbio and his contemporary, as we shall soon explain.

63. From all these records it becomes clear that Fara, otherwise Burgundofara—as she calls herself in her testament—was the daughter of the most noble parents Agneric the Burgundian and Leodegunda. According to the Acts of Saint Faro, she had as brothers Faro himself, Walbert, and Chagnoald; according to Fara’s testament, which the brothers of Saint-Martin published from the archives of the monastery of Fare, commonly Faremonstier or Farmontier (Gallia Christiana, volume IV, letter F, under “Fare-monastery”), she had Faro, Chagnulf (the same as Chagnoald), Burgundus (perhaps the same as Walbert), and Agnetrud.

Fara chose God as her spouse and, although her father Agneric resisted, devoted herself to the religious life, with the counsel and assistance of Eustasius, or Eustace, abbot of Luxeuil, a disciple of Saint Columbanus and a man of great learning and holiness. She built for herself and her companions, whom she gathered in large numbers from every direction, the monastery of Eboriacum in the district of Brie. Hence Bede calls it the monastery of Brie in book III, chapter 8, of his Ecclesiastical History of the English. It still exists today as a Benedictine abbey in the diocese of Meaux, in the province of Brie. All this is established by the Acts.

64. The aforesaid brothers of Saint-Martin describe the monastery as follows in the place just cited, as does Augustine Lubin in his historical notes on the Roman Martyrology, table 3 of Gaul, under “In the territory of Meaux,” p. 74.

The city of Meaux, called Meldi by Pliny and also Melda beside the Matrona, or Marne, today Meaulx or Meaux, gave its name to the territory, or district, of Meaux. This is not found only in Usuard, so that you may not suppose that he diverged from the truth, but also in the testament of the holy virgin Fara already mentioned, where the city is called Meldicensis.

Her own brothers Walbert and, after him, Faro were bishops there. The same city is called the city of the Melodori by Jonas in the Life of Saint Eustasius of Luxeuil.

[Col. 0957D] Jonas was a Segusian by birth and a monk of the monastery of Bobbio, founded by Saint Columbanus. He lived there under Attala, Columbanus’s successor, and under other abbots. Bollandus—or the Antwerp Jesuits, those energetic defenders of the saints—has more to say about him in the Life of Saint Attala on March 10 and the Life of Saint Eustasius on March 29. He wrote the Acts of Saints Columbanus, Eustasius, Attala, and Bertulf, the abbots, as well as of our holy Burgundofara, which are wrongly attributed to Bede and published in volume III of his works. Those Fathers published all these works on their respective feast days.

John Mabillon published a more accurate Life of Burgundofara than the editions of Bede and Surius, among the Acts of the Saints of the Benedictine Order (eleventh century, p. 438). It is rather a book On the Virtues and Miraculous Events Performed in the Monastery at Eboriacum Founded by Fara. This indicates that Jonas wrote it while she was still alive. In the Life of Saint Eustasius it is reported that he built Fara’s monastery on her paternal land between the rivers Mogra and Alba, about which Mabillon comments in his notes. Charles Le Cointe mentions all these brothers in the Ecclesiastical Annals of the Franks (volume III, under the year 672, no. 12 onward).

65. Yet against Burgundofara, or Fara, the virgin born in Gaul, founder in Gaul of the monastery of Eboriacum under Eustasius, abbot of Luxeuil, not far from the city of Meaux, and finally called to heaven in Gaul—a history supported by the records of contemporaries and certain to every later historian—someone dared to oppose the assumed names of Liutprand and Julian.

Listen, reader, to the man’s invention. Liutprand writes under era 677, in the year 639:

“Saint Fara, a Benedictine virgin, fleeing her father, came to Tuy. A monastery is built by Anastasius, bishop of Tuy. She dies in the year 650.”

And Julian, in the Chronicle, number 326:

“In the Galician town of Meladense, or Melducense, Saint Fara, a Benedictine virgin and nun, lived under the emperor Heraclius.”

And elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0958D] Thomas Tamayo cites this in his notes on Liutprand, p. 56, but it does not appear in the published Chronicle of Julian]:

“The monastery of Saint Fara near Tuy, at Aquas Calidas, is destroyed by the Moors in the year 670.”

Here we see the city of Meaux in Gaul transformed into the Galician town of Meladense or Melducense, and Eustasius of Luxeuil into Anastasius, bishop of Tuy, sought for this purpose among the subscriptions to the councils of Toledo of this period—as though by a stroke of Circe’s wand.

[Col. 0958C] 66. To strengthen this manifold error, Higuera and John Tamayo each contributed his own share. The former appealed to the very ancient martyrology of the Church of Plasencia, and from it quoted these words:

“At Tuy, in the district of Meladense, Saint Fara, virgin.”

Sandoval in his History of Tuy, folio 34, John Tamayo in his Martyrology, volume VI, December 7, p. 566, and in the Life of Saint Epitacius, chapter 2, no. 24, folio 137, as well as Thomas Tamayo in his notes on Liutprand, refer to this codex.

No one, however, saw it; and it may be established that the Plasencian martyrology was praised by Higuera alone, from what the same Sandoval notes elsewhere (History of Tuy, folio 18). There he drank these waters at Higuera’s own sources while Higuera was still alive. It was Higuera’s custom to commend his assertions by confirming them with such manuscripts of the Spanish churches. If only he alone had done so!

For John Tamayo too, from his own book of poems by Aulus Hali—which fills all the pages of the Spanish Martyrology (how shameful for us!), and which was accustomed to provide him with everything he wanted—produced an epigram in which a poet of the same flour as our historians tried to establish that Fara was Galician by race, a nun at Tuy, that Anastasius, bishop of Tuy, built her a monastery, and that she died gloriously there.

Consult, if you care to, the passages of Sandoval and Tamayo and the names they sought in Galicia. So that the credibility of their assertions might not collapse altogether, they argued that these details corresponded to the Liutprandine and Julianic accounts. We are truly weary of lingering here any longer.

67. Nor does Liutprand’s practice of deceiving and making fools of his readers with a single phantom name yet come to an end. Under era 989 we read:

“A council was held in Spain, in the city of Zaragoza, commonly called the Augustan Council, of twenty-five bishops.”

This is utterly insane, not merely falsely and ridiculously invented. Since Tamayo, committed to that side, did not dare to say more, he gave this judgment:

“Concerning this, I pronounce the ancient judicial formula in due and solemn form: N. L. (non liquet, ‘it is not clear’).”

Let us nevertheless hear Higuera’s note. It will lead us where we are going:

“Onuphrius mentions the Council of Zaragoza, which Liutprand records here, in the year of Our Lord 951; and so it was held under John, bishop of Toledo.”

Onuphrius himself, without intending to do so, plainly mocked him in these words in his Ecclesiastical Chronicle. He understood the Augustan Council to mean one convened at Augsburg, a city of Germany. Hermannus Contractus records it under the same year, 951:

“A synod of twenty-five bishops is assembled at Augsburg in the presence of King Otto.”

The year 952 is preferable, as it appears in the so-called Austrian Chronicle of Matthew Marschalk von Bappenheim, canon of Augsburg, published by Freher (among other German authors of history, p. 311):

“A synod of twenty-five bishops is assembled under King Otto.”

The same synod appears in editions of the councils (in the latest Paris edition, volume IX, column 635), with a preface listing the names of those who attended: bishops of Italy, Gaul, and Germany living under Otto’s authority.

Yet to this incautious man it seemed permissible to turn Augsburg into Zaragoza, as though a single testimony of Panvinio could so quickly establish the reliability of the account and the place where the council was held.

[Col. 0959C] 68. The same stamp appears in his praise of Saint Veranus, bishop of Tarragona, whom he makes an exile in the district of Carpetania and the territory of Orléans under era 782, in the year 744. Julian agrees in his Chronicle, number 381.

The commentators understand the territory of Orléans to mean the territory of the town of Oreja in the kingdom of Toledo. They say that Veranus, seeking to avoid the oppression of the Moors, went from Tarragona to the city of Toledo as to a refuge. More may be seen in John Tamayo, volume V, March, October 19, together with the solemn poem of his Aulus Hali.

The opportunity for this fable arose because on October 19 the Roman Martyrology reads:

“In the territory of Orléans, the deposition of Saint Veranus, bishop.”

Baronius did not dare identify which of several men of this name was intended in his notes for that day. But what connection has the name of the territory of Orléans with the town of Oreja, when no geographer mentions an Aurelia in Spain and no trace of it exists in ancient records?

[Col. 0959D] 69. Likewise Saint Ostanus is fabricated as a bishop of Auch in Spain, as having attended the Council of Oviedo, and as having died in the territory of Bivar on July 30. Liutprand gives this under era 933, in the year 895. His glossator Julian added that Bivar should be understood as the town that was the birthplace of Diego Rodríguez, surnamed the Campeador.

You ask where this came from. It came, naturally, from the fact that on this day Usuard, from whom the Roman Martyrology derived its entry, records the commemoration “in the territory of Viviers, of Ostanus, priest and confessor.” Galesinus and Molanus discuss him in their notes on Usuard, where Molanus says that his Acts exist.

Equilinus, however, by calling him not a priest but a bishop at the end of his catalogue (book XI, chapter 130, no. 183), where he deals in a mass with men of whom he knew nothing beyond their names and certainly nothing of their deeds, provided the occasion for fabricating among us a bishop of Auch who never existed: the very man whom Usuard, an author of the eighth century, commended to posterity as known only by the title of priest.

Nor did any bishop Ostanus of Auch attend the Council of Oviedo, held under King Alfonso III in the year 901. Sampirus of Astorga names all who came there, including, among others, John of Oca, who beyond doubt was bishop of Oca (Aucensis).

70. This same perverse ambition—to make foreigners who had died outside Spain into Spanish citizens—drove him to the books of Saint Gregory’s letters. There, having found certain names ready and suitable for this purpose, he proceeded according to his custom and inserted into our nation Adeodata and Dulcidius, to whom the most holy pontiff had written, although they belonged elsewhere, namely to Italy.

Adeodata was a woman devoted to God. Books VII, letter 55, and VIII, letter 62, are addressed to her, as is also Gregory’s letter of recommendation on her behalf to Venantius, bishop of Luna, book VII, letter 28. In this last letter Gregory urges Venantius to act on Adeodata’s behalf before her mother Fidentia, so that—as is implied—she might provide her with food, support, or other assistance enabling her to appear in religious dress. If Fidentia was unwilling to do this voluntarily, Gregory asks Venantius to defend Adeodata in court and to treat her as commended to him in every respect.

71. Luna, a city on the border of Tuscia and Liguria beside the river Magra, is now destroyed, and Sarzana has taken its place; accordingly, the bishop of Sarzana has already succeeded to the title of bishop of Luna. One of these bishops was Venantius, recognized as such by Ughelli in his Sacred Italy, volume I, column 894. To him Pope Gregory, perhaps as the proper bishop of Fidentia and possibly also of her daughter Adeodata, sent the aforesaid letters urging him to fulfill his duty.

But it is also certain that Adeodata founded a monastery in Sicily, specifically in the city of Lilybaeum. Lilybaeum was formerly an episcopal city at the promontory of that name and is now Marsala. She served as abbess there. This is established by two other letters of Gregory, numbers 63 and 64: the first is addressed to Decius, bishop of Lilybaeum, and the second to Hilary the notary.

Moreover, Gregory says to Adeodata (letter 55, book VII) that he has entrusted the case of Bishop Decius—who else could he be but the same bishop of Lilybaeum?—to Bishop John and the glorious Leontius. To me, John is the bishop of Syracuse, or perhaps another bishop of Palermo, while Leontius was an ex-consul exercising judicial authority in Sicily at that time; the letters of the most holy pope to them are frequent.

Go now and lend your ears to Liutprand’s nonsense:

“Adeodata, a most holy virgin of Toledo,” he says under the year 614, or era 652, “a Benedictine nun, flourishes; Saint Gregory wrote to her today.”

We believe the same sort of thing is meant by what he says about Dulcidius a little later, under era 652, or the year 614:

“Dulcidius, a deacon of Zaragoza, flourishes; Saint Gregory commends him wonderfully in his letters.”

There is no letter of Gregory to Dulcidius; nor is there time here to investigate whether there is any letter concerning Dulcidius.

## CHAPTER V

Liutprand claims as our countrymen those who flourished elsewhere in the reputation of holiness. First example: Saint Babylas the martyr. Higuera’s and John Tamayo’s codices are highly suspect. Second: Raymond of Medellín, a shepherd who was truly the founder of the Order of Calatrava and a Cistercian monk. Third: Anacirardus, a monk of Agaune. Fourth: Cornelius Proculus and Cornelius Bassus, known only from inscribed stones. Fifth: Genesius the martyr. Everything in our country bearing this name appears to have been dedicated to Genesius of Arles, not to some Spaniard who never existed.

72. We shall now further expose this man’s eagerness to enroll among the saints of Spain those who truly are not Spaniards. For whenever the ancient Spaniards dedicated some sacred place to a person, he immediately asserts that person to have been a citizen of Spain.

Babylas was bishop of Antioch and a martyr, celebrated on January 24 in the records of all the Greek Fathers and not infrequently in those of the Latins as well. Some, however, distinguish him from another Babylas, a schoolteacher. For these matters, so that I do not repeat what has already been done, Baronius and Bollandus may be consulted for this day, January 24.

Certainly our Saint Eulogius praises Bishop Babylas in his Memorial of the Saints, book I, among those who voluntarily offered themselves to martyrdom, as did Saints Sebastian, Thyrsus, Adrian, Eulalia, and others. Baronius maintains that this Babylas, and no other, existed.

### 73

But when he learned that near the town of Odón in the district of Madrid there existed a little hermitage called San Babilès, he thought he would gratify the inhabitants of that town if, taking advantage of their anxiety to discover the deeds of Babylas of Antioch and perhaps of another schoolmaster, he vindicated this latter—whom Baronius had reckoned an illegitimate martyr—and asserted that he was attached to this place, time, and manner of martyrdom. With these words he imposed upon people ready to believe whatever might be told them (*Chronicon*, under the year 715):

> “At this time Saint Babylas, bishop of Virinensis and Pamplonensis—for he preached in both places—came to Toledo with the intention of seeing the captives and wretched Mozarabs, and from there to the town of Odón; and nearby, in a little hermitage—do you hear this?—he taught boys their first letters. He came with two brothers, who became hermits, and afterward all suffered martyrdom.”

*Virinensis* was badly printed in place of *Iruniensis*. That a bishop of Pamplona was at some time called by this name, from *Iruna*, the vernacular name meaning “good city,” is certain.

[Note: Oihenart, *Notitia Vasconiae*, book II, chapter 2, p. 77; Garibay, book XXIII of the *Compendium of Spanish History*, chapter 9.]

Julianus, playing the same game (*Chronicon*, no. 413), writes:

> “Saint Babylas, bishop of Pamplona, after Pamplona was captured, came into Carpetania and, near the town of Odón, taught boys; and with eighty of them he suffered martyrdom at the hands of the Saracens on 20 October.”

### 74

Those who delight in carrying these masked authors about as much as the followers of Pythagoras carry their master would like this to have happened, and they employ a twofold argument on behalf of this Spanish Babylas.

The first is that our Saint Eulogius, in book I of the *Memorial of the Saints*, praised him among those who voluntarily offered themselves for martyrdom.

[Note: John Tamayo uses this argument, *Martyrologium Hispanicum*, vol. I, January, p. 277.]

But this is a leaden weapon: for Sebastian, Adrian, and Thyrsus, foreign martyrs, are praised there together with him.

The second is that Babylas was formerly honored in Spain with what they call a proper office, as is read in the Isidorian Breviary. But we too twist this argument in the opposite direction, since the hymn of that office is addressed to Babylas, bishop of Antioch, as John observed against Thomas Tamayo in the same place, p. 275. For it says:

> Babylas the bishop supplies the model, etc.

And afterward:

> This man, fortified by the virtue of faith,  
> Had ruled the citadel of Antioch;  
> He despised the profane Numerianus  
> In the sacred courts.

Hence it is easy to believe that the hermitage we have mentioned, which the calendars of our Church deemed worthy of this martyr’s special commemoration, was once dedicated to him; and that we search in vain for another fellow citizen of ours whom antiquity knew nothing of. Nor, if he had been Antiochene—that is, foreign—would antiquity have placed him second.

To him also we readily assign the church of San Babil, near the town of Sangüesa in the kingdom of Navarre, which Garibay mentions in book XXI of his *History of Spain*, chapter 6.

### 75

Nevertheless, as usual, John Tamayo, out of partisan zeal, insists that there was among us a third Babylas, distinct both from the Antiochene bishop who was killed with three and from the schoolmaster of that same city who was killed with eighty-four boys—both of whom the Greek *Menologion* commemorates on 4 September—yet himself put to martyrdom with eighty boys.

He produces here also his manuscript, and from it a hymn which vouches for all the falsehoods of Liutprandus and Julianus, in verses whose peculiar rasping betrays their true author.

Liutprandus is also wrong in distinguishing Pamplona from Iruna as though they had been different places, if Garibay, who was thoroughly versed in the history of Cantabria and Navarre, writes correctly in book XXII, chapter 16, and elsewhere.

I therefore hope that those who have once perceived this man’s purpose will place no confidence in these trifles: he took advantage of the opportunity offered by the obscure or ambiguous dedication of some sacred building, so as—if I may put it so—to abuse it in order to insinuate his pious impiety, swollen with his fables.

### 76

Relying on the same ambiguity of names, he considered it sport to make two saints into one and the same person.

The Church of Beauvais celebrates its so-called apostle and first bishop, Saint Lucian, who came to Gaul with Saint Dionysius and suffered martyrdom on 8 January.

[Note: Bede, Usuard, Ado, the Roman Martyrology, and others cited by Baronius on 8 January, and Bollandus on the same day; Saussay, *Gallican Martyrology*; Vincent of Beauvais, *Historical Mirror*, book X, chapters 25 and 26.]

We are not now asking which Dionysius announced the Christian Gospel to the Gauls, or at what time. Whatever the case may be, the acts of the martyr Lucian, said to have been written by Odo I, bishop of Beauvais, under Charles the Bald, leave no room for doubt either about his contest or about his companions in the contest, namely Maximian—also called Messian—and Julian. Bollandus discusses them carefully in his notes for 8 January; he also observes, from ancient manuscript martyrologies, that a translation of the bodies of these three companions took place on 15 September and 16 October.

### 77

Entirely different from this Lucian of Beauvais is Lucian, martyr of Vicus, a city of Catalonia, who triumphed together with his companion Marcian during the persecution of Decius.

Their acts likewise seem genuine and of sincere antiquity, committed to writing in the solemn style then customary for recording such religious matters. They were preserved in the breviary of that same Church of Vicus and in a very ancient book of saints written in the old language of the region, which is also used by the Provençal Gauls. He also had at hand another very ancient account preserved in the archive of that Church, which the equally learned and devout Antonius Vincentius Dominicus, of the Order of Preachers, reproduced in his *History of the Saints of Catalonia* (fol. 99); and from him Hieronymus Pujades drew material for book IV, chapter 55, of his *Chronicle of that principality*.

### 78

Yet this Pseudo-Liutprandus did not hesitate, as though we were all shadows, to utter these words under the Spanish era 940, A.D. 902:

> “The bones of Saint Lucian, bishop and martyr, companion of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite, were transferred from Beauvais to the city of Vicus.”

He was animated by the same genius for deception as his twin, Pseudo-Dexter, when the latter left this written under the year 308:

> “The relics of Saint Lucian, bishop, are transferred to Vicus.”

[Note: Neither the name of Vicus nor that of the city of Vicus is found while Decius was persecuting the Christians; it is known nowhere before the time of Louis the Pious. He restored, to some extent, the city of Ausona, or Ausa, which had been destroyed by the Moors; and because its small and sparse population was unequal to sustaining the title “city,” he called it Vicus Ausensis, or Ausonensis, as we have said elsewhere. Today the inhabitants call it Vich d’Osona, commonly Vique.]

This was nevertheless more than six hundred years before the translation mentioned by Liutprandus.

These are the marks by which liars are detected. For wickedness often lies to itself, as sacred Scripture warns us.

### 79

Nor was he content to abuse this veil of similar names. He also makes heavenly citizens of our nation out of heavenly citizens of foreign nations, or praises as known those who are known nowhere.

He speaks, for example, of Paul, bishop of Jaca:

> “The memory of Saint Paul, bishop of Jaca, who, while visiting Rome, suffered martyrdom with two others under Decius on the sixth day before the Ides of February.”

[Col. 0963A]

He had his eyes on 8 February in the Roman Martyrology, where Baronius restored at Rome the commemoration of Saints Paul, Lucius, and Cyriacus from a manuscript of the monastery of Saint Cyriacus. Galesinus added that this Paul had been a bishop.

In the ancient Martyrology of Florentinus one reads at Rome: “The burial of Saint Paul, bishop.” See Florentinus there, and Bollandus in his great work *The Acts of the Saints*. All of them complain that the place of his bishopric is nowhere indicated.

Through this open door our author rushed in and, as though from behind a curtain, pronounced him bishop of Jaca—a city now called Jaca in the Pyrenees and in the kingdom of Aragon.

### 80

Baronius and Galesinus praise Celestine, companion of Saints Saturninus and Neapolus, Roman martyrs, on 3 May. Elsewhere his place is not stated, namely in the Martyrology of Florentinus, about which more will be said here in the Notes.

Pseudo-Liutprandus invents that this man was a *consularis* in Spain and that his memory flourished among us.

### 81

He says under the Spanish era 888, A.D. 850:

> “Anacirardus, a hermit, came from Germany into Lusitania and lived a holy life on the bank of the Tagus near the city of Scalabis. Returning to Italy, he was overcome by wounds not far from Lake Zurich and was martyred on 4 February.”

Here Higuera pretends not to know the matter and identifies Anacirardus with Lietphardus, whom Molanus commemorates on 4 February; or at least the note attached to this passage belongs to someone other than Higuera.

For Liutprandus’s twin, Julianus, calls him Hancarardus, with little alteration of the name, and relates the same things about him in *Chronicon*, no. 436, adding these particular details:

> “Some traces of the arrival of this holy abbot in Lusitania remain in the towns of that province, Atouguia and Meinardo.”

If we seek the interpretation of this observation, John Tamayo comes to our aid. He says that Atouguia, a town near Scalabis, or Santarém, lies beside the Tagus. In this he detected a trace of the name of Augia Major, or Reichenau—an important monastery whose German name means “rich island”—which the false chronicler had hinted at. He also says that near the same town there is a valley called Bollardo, adding that this word scarcely differs from Meinardo and that the latter was in fact the truer and more usual name of the holy hermit.

### 82

But I gladly leave this conjecture of Tamayo, colder than Alpine snows, for sane readers to judge.

The acts of this holy Swiss hermit and martyr Meinrad, or Meginrad, survive. He had first been a monk in the monastery of Augia-Dives, then lived for twenty-six years in the hermitage of the Black Forest, and was finally killed by two robbers. Bollandus reasonably judged the anonymous author of these acts to have been Bennon, a subsequent inhabitant of that hermitage.

Surius published these acts with some alterations; Christoph Hartmann published them in his annals of the monastery of Einsiedeln, Saint Meinrad’s monastery, later erected at the same place as his martyrdom; and, finally, the Bollandus just mentioned published them in the *Acts of the Saints* for 21 January.

There we are expressly told that our hermit lived for seven years in a place of solitude near Lake Zurich, chosen by himself, and then withdrew four miles farther inland into another valley of the wilderness, where he lived alone until his death.

These are the words from chapter 2 of the *Life*, or *Acts*:

> “When he had served the army of the heavenly King there for seven years, unable to bear the multitude of people coming to him, he changed his place. Four miles distant from the shore of the aforesaid lake, he found a level site among mountains, extremely difficult of access. There, with the help of religious men, and especially of a certain abbess named Heiluviga, he built the dwelling necessary for his purpose and remained in that place for the rest of his life.”

Prudent readers may judge how much more plausible this is than the Liutprandian and Julianian migration of Meinrad to Lusitania. At that time the Christian kings of Galicia, or Oviedo—Alfonso the Chaste, Ramiro I, and Ordoño I—who lived at the same time as Meinrad, were waging war against the Saracens; among them a Christian man seeking a quiet and solitary life could scarcely have hoped to find such an opportunity.

### 83

With the same recklessness, which should be restrained at the cost of every danger to reputation, the Toledan fabulist raises Christian and apostolic men and martyrs out of ancient pagan inscriptions of Roman rite and period.

Are we not to understand this of his statement that Cornelius Proculus and Cornelius Bassus, converted by disciples of Saint James and made bishops and martyrs, are celebrated at Antiquaria in Baetica, as is read in Liutprandus under the Spanish era 724, A.D. 686?

He had in mind two inscriptions, one of which Marcus Cornelius Proculus dedicated to Livia Augusta, and the other Cornelius Bassus dedicated to Gaius Caesar—each calling himself a priest of the Caesars. Even now the twin stones bear these inscriptions at the city of Antiquaria.

[Tamayo in the notes to this passage.]

[Note: I saw and copied all the stones of Antiquaria that survive today three years ago; nowhere did I find the surnames Proculus or Bassus among the Cornelii. On the outermost part of the old principal temple, and on the wall of its cemetery toward the river, there is a reference to M. CORN.]

### 84

And to whom else are Saints Mary, Joseph, Victor, and Theodore known, martyrs of Castro Octavianus in Catalonia, whom Liutprandus mentions under the year 785, or Spanish era 823? Or Genesius, who suffered at Córdoba under Nero and whom Liutprandus mentions under the year 668, or Spanish era 706?

Certainly Higuera very earnestly insists that this latter was a Spanish citizen and martyr, because the martyr Genesius is frequently invoked in certain Spanish churches, although the memory of either Genesius of Arles or the Roman Genesius has not rightly been abolished.

Julianus also repeatedly enters the contest—*Chronicon*, no. 376, and *Adversaria*, nos. 149, 389, and 481—citing a Toledan church dedicated to Genesius, martyr of Córdoba. From him we learn that Genesius was a Spaniard and a legionary soldier in the castle of Nunetum—Nuez, near Toledo, at the foot of the mountain called Altamira—that his feast was celebrated on the 20th, or, as it should be read, on 25 August, and that his body was transferred from Córdoba to Alarcurrim and from there to Toledo.

### 85

All this appears in the *Adversaria*, nos. 149 and 481. In those passages he clearly distinguishes this Genesius from another Genesius, the companion of Anastasius, a martyr on 11 October in Rutenia of Spain; Dexter says that he was killed at Mantua Carpetanorum under the year 353. Julianus mentions him in the *Adversaria*, no. 326.

For this reason the distinguished D. Laurentius Ramirez de Prado ought not, in writing to Franciscus Bivarius about the Genesii, to have taken all these testimonies of Julianus as referring to the same Genesius and wished to correct the difference in the day of his martyrdom. Bivarius warned him of this in his reply, attributing Julianus’s variation to the character of the *Adversaria*, which have the form of hurried observations.

Whatever he may say, then, about four Genesii—first, the Genesius of Arles; second, the Roman Genesius; third, the one born at Barcelona and killed at Mantua Carpetanorum, whose acts he produces; and fourth, the Genesius of Córdoba, of whom we are now speaking—it must be regarded as absolutely certain that the Spanish cult publicly offered in the dedication of churches belonged to no one other than the first, Genesius of Arles, the notary or shorthand writer.
