This must be admitted especially of the sacred buildings in the city and territory of Toledo, which includes Mantua Carpetana, or the district of Madrid, and which were dedicated to Genesius the martyr. For no one will deny that whatever was collected in the Gothic books of ecclesiastical rites, commonly called “Isidorian” after Isidore of Seville, whether by Isidore himself or by other Toledan bishops, chiefly concerns the affairs and usage of Toledo. From this material, therefore, the intention of the ancients in performing these sacred offices must be determined.

### 86

Yet it is of no one other than Genesius of Arles that the Gothic Breviary and Missal speak on 25 August. There stands the proper office of this martyr, with a hymn from which we have transcribed the following relevant verses:

> Thus that young Genesius,  
> An eminent citizen of the town of Arles,  
> In the first flower of his youth,  
> Obeys the order imposed upon him.  
>   
> Thus, while the notary was beginning to shine,  
> And was writing the public commands on tablets,  
> Suddenly inspired by a heavenly gift,  
> By which he completed his pious vows,  
>   
> At once he rejected the impious office,  
> And refused to impress his hand upon the wax,  
> Desiring to become a citizen of the heavenly life,  
> In life, vows, and conduct, etc.

And do you suppose that a solemn office of worship was once directed toward another, while sacred temples were dedicated to a different Genesius—not only at Madrid, Toledo, or Córdoba, but also at Seville, Salamanca, and perhaps elsewhere?

Let Bivarius, Ramirez, Tamayo—who adduces a certain poem of his counterfeit Cyprian of Córdoba—and Argaizus believe this, as they superstitiously exalt these false divinities of history. Let others not believe it, those who have already been so often warned to avoid these reefs against which we have almost wrecked the authority of all our antiquities.

## Prologue of Father Hieronymus de la Higuera to the *Chronicle of Liutprandus*

*(In Reuber, *Collectanea of Ancient Writers*, Antwerp, 1640.)*

From a Gothic book removed from the library of Fulda and brought to Worms, the *Chronicle of Eutrandi*, or Luitprandus, formerly subdeacon of Toledo and later deacon of Pavia, was extracted.

I shall first say what authors report about him. Onuphrius Panvinius mentions him at the beginning of his *Ecclesiastical Chronicle*, and in the Chronicle itself, under the year 959, in these words: “Witichindus, monk of Corvey, and Luitprandus of Pavia, historians.” He is also mentioned by Don Diego Hurtado de Mendoza in his *Memorial*, by Father John Mariana, by Cardinal Robert Bellarmine, by Caesar Baronius in his *Ecclesiastical Annals*, and by Trithemius in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, as follows:

> “Eutrandus, or Luitprandus, deacon of the Church of Pavia, born in the city of Pavia, formerly scribe and secretary of Berengar, king of Italy, a man sufficiently learned in secular letters and not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, sharp and vigorous in intellect, skilled in Greek and Latin speech, and no less excellent in poetry than in prose, is said to have written several distinguished little works by which he made his name known. Driven from Italy by King Berengar, he came to Germany. Settled near Frankfurt, he wrote a notable work, a history of his own time containing an account of Berengar’s tyranny. As though in retaliation for the injuries he had received from him, he entitled it *Antapodosis*, that is, ‘Retaliation,’ in seven books. While others were reigning—or rather raging—I saw nothing. He wrote this volume to Regimundus, bishop of the Church of Illiberis in Spain, sometimes employing verse and sometimes the Greek language, and inserting much concerning the deeds of the Germans. He flourished under the Emperor Otto in the year of the Lord 950.”

It should be read “Tractemundus” instead of “Regimundus.” The same error occurs in the *History*: “Raimundus” instead of “Tractemundus.”

Julianus, the Toledan subdeacon, also mentions him in his book *On the Order of the Archbishops*, as follows:

> “In the year 946, while Bonitus was bishop of Toledo, Eutrandus, or Luitprandus, deacon of Pavia and Toledan subdeacon, flourished under him for two years; and Tractemundus, a priest and afterward bishop of Illiberis, was sent by the same Bonitus.”

He was a learned man, whose testimony grave authors gladly use. Among them is Gabriel Vázquez, in his book *On the Adoration of Images*, which he published about ten years ago with such learning as to arouse the admiration of the most learned men and to earn great praise from the distinguished University of Louvain.

But why delay in listing authorities? No one expresses himself better in his own colors than he himself does. Thus, at the beginning of his *History*, in the letter, he writes:

> “To the reverend and most holy lord Raimundus—read Tractemundus, bishop of the Church of Illiberis—Luitprandus of the Church of Pavia, levite by no merit of his own: greetings.
>
> “For two years, dearest Father, I delayed your request because of the smallness of my intellect: you compelled me to set down the deeds of the emperors and kings of all Europe, as one who was not uncertain through hearsay but certain through sight. These matters indeed deterred my mind from beginning—or perhaps undertaking—the task, because I possess no abundance of expression and because of the envy of detractors. Swollen with pride, lazy in reading, and possessing—as the learned Boethius says—only a fragment of philosophy’s garment while thinking they possess it all, they will insult me in these words: ‘Our ancestors wrote so much that readers are far fewer than books’; and they will chatter the comic saying: ‘Nothing is said that has not been said before.’
>
> “To their barking I reply that philosophers, like dropsical men—who grow thirstier the more they drink—the more often they read, the more eagerly they seek whatever is new. If they are wearied by the intricate reading of eloquent Cicero, let them at least be encouraged by plain trifles. For, unless I am mistaken, just as the sight of the eyes is dulled unless it is reflected by some intervening substance against the rays of the sun, so the mind of academics, Peripatetics, and Stoics is weakened by continual meditation upon their doctrines unless it is refreshed either by the useful laughter of comedies or by the delightful history of heroes.
>
> “But if the accursed customs of the ancient pagans are not merely unprofitable—as I say—but also considerably harmful even to hear, and are inscribed as something memorable under the title *Thronus*—or *Tonus*—why should the deeds of these emperors, Julius, Pompey, Hannibal, his brother Hasdrubal, and Scipio Africanus, equal in fame to the praises of distinguished commanders, be kept silent? Especially since, when they lived honorably, the goodness of our Lord Jesus Christ is present in them for recitation; and when they committed some fault, the salutary correction of that same Lord is to be remembered.
>
> “Nor should anyone be disturbed if I insert in this little book the deeds of weakened kings or effeminate princes. There is one just power of almighty God—namely, of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—which justly crushes some for their crimes and raises others up for their deserving merits. This, I say, is the true promise made by our Lord Jesus Christ to the saints: ‘Observe and hear my voice, and I will be an enemy to your enemies; I will afflict those who afflict you, and my angel will go before you’ (Exodus 23:21–23). Wisdom also, which is Christ, cries through the mouth of Solomon: ‘The world will fight for him against the senseless’ (Wisdom 5:21). Everyone notices this daily, even the man who snores.”

Later, in the first chapter of this work, the same author speaks as though he were not ignorant of Spanish affairs:

> “As I think your prudence is by no means unaware—or rather, knows better—as you can infer from those who are tributaries of King Abderahamen.”

He tells there that twenty Saracens came from Spain in a small boat and attacked a certain small fortified place, perhaps called Fraxinetum, on the borders of Provence and Italy; and that when one hundred Moors came from Spain, they remained there with their assistance.

In book V, chapter 3, he likewise says:

> “At this time King Hugh, having given ten measures of money, made peace with the Hungarians. He expelled them from Italy after receiving hostages and sent them toward Spain with a guide. The reason they did not reach Spain, and the city itself in which the king resided, Córdoba, was this: after they had been led for three days through a waterless and rugged region, and feared that they would perish of thirst, their guide, granted to them by Hugh, was mortally wounded, and they returned by a more rapid route.”

Cardinal Nicholas of Cusa, in the work he wrote on *Catholic Concordance* for the Council of Basel, cites Luitprandus as a serious and especially truthful author.

But this may suffice as a kind of preface. Now to the matter itself.

## Chronicle of Liutprandus, Deacon of Pavia but Toledan Subdeacon, Addressed to Tractemundus [also Regimundus], Bishop of Illiberis

[Note: Enough has been said about Eutrandus, or Luitprandus, Toledan subdeacon but deacon of Pavia, who was secretary to Berengar the younger emperor. He later came to Germany and in the year 970 wrote the *Chronicle*, which we are attempting to illuminate with notes. In the year 973 he came to Toledo from the monastery of Fulda; worn out by old age and illness, he surrendered to fate. He was buried in the same basilica, as Julianus, archpriest of Saint Justa, reports. He was a man endowed with exceptional intelligence and naturally well suited to poetry. I followed this order in illuminating Dexter and Marcus Maximus, and I shall follow it here as well. Father Higuera.]

### Preface

#### Letter of Tractemundus [also Regimundus], bishop of Illiberis in Spain, to Luitprandus, deacon of Pavia and Toledan subdeacon

To the holy and beloved son Luitprandus, formerly subdeacon of the Church of Toledo and levite of Pavia, Tractemundus, sinful bishop of the Church of Illiberis: greetings in our Lord Jesus Christ.

Having read your letter, dearest son, I was filled with great consolation, knowing that you are well and that, in your long pilgrimage through Germany, you are making great progress in the very useful exercise of patience.

For our life is a military campaign—

[Note: “For our life is a military campaign.” He adds the text of Job 7:1 and supplies a genuine explanation of that passage. He acknowledges the dangers of life and that we may not speak of departing from it on our own initiative unless the Lord commands it. The Septuagint interprets “military campaign” as *peiratērion*, an exercise or trial; for what else are the dangers of military service but trials and exercises? It should also be observed that, just as the period of military service is not long and the opportunity for battle brief, so it is with life; and just as an engagement lasts two or three months and afterward the retreat is sounded, so we live for a time and labor until the appointed time. Then the commander grants discharge, and the soldier leaves the garrison. Cicero expresses this most aptly in *On Old Age*: “Pythagoras forbids us, without the command of the commander—that is, God—to depart from the garrison and station of life.”
>
> “I shall add a new ancient testimony, which, lest it perish, eaten away by bookworms and moths, I publish and bring to light; it will illuminate the whole matter. It is by Don Alfonso de Santa María, archbishop of Burgos, who, at the command of John II, king of Castile, published and illustrated with notes several works of Seneca translated into Spanish. I possess all these works written in very ancient characters; Ferdinand del Pulgar mentions them under *Illustrious Men*, no. 22. He says, in chapter 15, fol. 35:
>
> “‘It seems that in all these words Seneca wishes to conclude that it is lawful for a man to flee from life. This is not so; rather, it is a thing greatly condemned, not only according to Catholic truth but also according to the pagans. Thus Cicero, in the *Dream of Scipio*, says that the soul should not leave the body except by the command of him who placed it there, namely God. Otherwise it would appear to flee from the duty and charge that God gave it. For just as no one should depart from the army without the command of the prince, so from this life—which, as Job says, is like military service upon the earth—no one should depart except when God calls him.’”
>
> He develops this at greater length, but I omit it to preserve brevity. He therefore teaches that the soul must be kept in the custody of the body and that we must not depart from this life without the command of him who gave us life.
>
> For this reason the Hebrews called dying “[Hebrew term omitted in source],” and the Greeks called it ἀπολύεσθαι, that is, “to be released,” as is found at the end of Numbers 20. The common Greek expression is rendered by Themistius in *On the Soul*: Ἀπολύεσθαι τὸν ἀποθνήσκοντα, καὶ τὴν τελευτὴν ἀπόλυσιν καλοῦσιν—that is, “they say that the one who dies is released, and they call death a release.” Plutarch, in the *Consolation*, writes: Ἕως ἂν ὁ Θεὸς αὐτὸς ἀπολύσῃ ἡμᾶς—“until God himself releases us.” See Saint Augustine, *City of God*, book I, chapter 19 and following chapters, whose words are cited in chapter *Si non licet*, distinction 23, question 5. Among our jurists, Don Balthasar Gómez de Amescua, a Toledan, has gathered much material in his special treatise *On Power over Oneself*; Grotius, *On the Law of War*, book II, chapter 19, no. 5, draws from foreign authorities. D. L.]

—which has long been burdensome and difficult and exposed to innumerable dangers and inconceivable hardships, until the Lord grants us to reach the shore of our most desired homeland.

As for what you wish to know about me, understand that we are staying in that town of Granada, near our city of Illiberis,

[Note: “We are staying in that town of Granada, near our city of Illiberis.” See what I noted on *Chronicle*, no. 202. D. L.]

among the faithful Mozarabs, who, struggling as best we can against the wicked Saracens, die daily. But thanks be to God the Father and to our Lord Jesus Christ, his Son, who grants us the ability to endure and to confess the Catholic faith manfully amid so many adversities.

Every day I pray frequently for all my sheep. On Sundays I exhort them to patience and steadfastness. Sometimes I have them read the letter of Saint Pope Adrian, which he sent on this subject to my predecessor, the bishop Egilo of blessed memory. It is reverently preserved in the archives of our Church, together with the writings of other Roman pontiffs, the sacred diptych, and the list of the bishops of this Church.

Its first pastor was Caecilius, the inseparable companion of Saint James when he came from Jerusalem to Spain. There is also the perpetual memory of the holy martyrs who steadfastly suffered for the Catholic faith during the persecutions of the Church; nor are there lacking those whom the Saracens slaughter and send daily to heaven, killed by the sword.

Pray for me, dearest son.

I received your book with gratitude—that is, your *History of Events in Europe*—and, in addition, your *Antapodosis*, composed in verse and prose, as the wise Boethius once wrote his *Book of the Consolation of Philosophy*. This book of Boethius Severinus, I remember, the two of us carefully read through at Toledo, when I was a priest and you a subdeacon of that holy Church of Toledo, which was always the true firstborn daughter of the holy Roman Church and deservedly comparable, after the Roman Church, with the patriarchal churches; its pastor is primate and patriarch of all Spain.

The books you sent plainly bear the marks of a frequently replenished lamp and exude your fortunate talent. Alas! Know that we are deprived of every comfort necessary for life. We scarcely sustain life in this mournful and harsh captivity, much less are we able to import from elsewhere a large supply of books.

Therefore, dearest son, I beg you, and earnestly implore you by our old friendship, to send me as soon as possible a copy of the *Life of Saint James of Spain*, who died a holy death in Picenum on 1 November; the book of Metasthenes the Persian, *On Monarchies*, in which he places Darius, Cyrus, Cambyses, and Artaxerxes among the Persians, followed by the second Darius Longimanus; and, if the manuscripts of Dexter and Marcus Maximus lie hidden in the libraries of Germany, copies of their chronicles, which I have been unable to find anywhere in Spain.

Add a work of your own from the year 612, where Maximus ended, to your own time—that is, to the year 960.

Perhaps I burden you heavily, but this task will be very easy for you and certainly delightful for me, not to say almost owed to my love for you.

Farewell, dearest son, and pray to God at greater length for this old man.

### Luitprandus’s Reply

[Note: “Luitprandus’s reply.” Julianus mentions this letter and the person to whom Luitprandus replied in the *Chronicle*, no. 505:

> “At that time Trasemundus—read Tractemundus—a priest at Toledo and afterward bishop of Illiberis, a holy man, was also flourishing. To him Eutrandus wrote, a Toledan subdeacon and afterward a deacon of Pavia; and he too writes.”

D. L.]

To the most reverend and most holy Tractemundus [also Regimundus], bishop of Illiberis in Spain, Luitprandus, levite of the Church of Pavia by no merit of his own: greetings and every expression of respect.

I was pleased, most blessed pope and greatly revered lord, that our *Antapodosis*, in which I now play in verse and now in prose, has finally reached your hands; and it pleased me no less [Note: “It pleased me.” Used in the obvious sense of “to please.” Virgil, *Aeneid* II: “And this sits well with my mind”; the expression is not unknown to jurists. Ulpian attests it in the law *Si fidejussor*, paragraph π, concerning those who are required to give security: “If this should sit well with the judge.” D. L.] that you have read through my History of the Deeds Accomplished in Europe [Col. 0970C]. My works are beginning, in a certain way, to please me, when I see that they are, in a certain way, approved by you, a righteous and learned man; and I would follow your judgment in this matter, if I did not know that love sometimes grows blind. Yet, to free you from the charge of so blind a judgment, there are the integrity of your life and your love of truth, which from your youth has always clung to your inmost senses.

Finally, it pleased me no less that you now command me to search for you in the library of the monastery of Fulda—where I, an exiled librarian, now reside—the Chronicle of Dexter, which the monk Marcus Maximus of the Benedictine order, later bishop of Zaragoza, continued. Moreover, you earnestly ask me to carry the sequence of years down to our own times, for you say that you are suffering from the greatest shortage of certain books. Indeed, among the barbarous and inhuman Saracens there is not an adequate supply even of the necessities of life, much less a well-stocked library.

I certainly grieved for your situation, most reverend Father, that you should be forced to pass your life so harshly in this city, none of the least among the cities of Baetica; for we did not live so harshly, but somewhat more gently [al.: better], when once we lived together at Toledo. For the ferocity of the barbarians’ spirits was softened, on the one hand, by the singular authority of the bishops of Toledo and, on the other, by their remarkable goodness and patience. Their authority, as you well know, rested partly on the still-surviving splendor of their ancient greatness, and partly on the fact that it was supported by the favor and protection of the Catholic kings of Oviedo, who in frequent letters commended to the kings the affairs, authority, and good treatment of Toledo, both of all the faithful and especially of the bishops of Toledo. This was, as you well know, like a kind of bridle, so that they would not suppose that everything they wished was entirely permissible.

The same did not happen to the bishops established in Baetica, over all of whom the most powerful emperor presides. Yet you, excellent Father, are accustomed, when placed in such great straits, to be comfort and aid to your sheep as a good shepherd [Col. 0972A], since every day you willingly face death on their behalf.

Please arrange for these books—the books of the councils and of the decretal letters, together with the names of the holy martyrs of Spain—to be sent to the most holy pontiff, truly a servant of God in deed and in name. As for the chronicle you requested, I found it written on ancient parchment in this library; and, as you ordered, I added the sequence of years down to the present time, that is, to the year 960.

I congratulate myself that, when I departed from Toledo—where I had been a subdeacon under the most holy bishop of Toledo, Bonitus [Note: “Under the bishop of Toledo Bonitus.” See Julian in his *Chronicle*, where he discusses Bonitus at no. 440, in the year 859: “When this became known, a synod was again compelled to meet in April, and without any difficulty Saint Bonitus was elected bishop of Toledo, a Gaul by nationality and a citizen of Auvergne”; and nos. 441, 442, and 444. D. L.]—for Italy, I carried away with me several historical books in which a succession of many Spanish bishops had been collected in order. I found these books also in this library. I believe they had been brought from Spain by order of the holy emperor Charles the Great [Col. 0972B], and, as they say, had been presented to him by the most holy archbishop of Toledo, Elipandus, after he had seriously and truly repented of his error concerning Christ’s adoption [Note: “The most holy archbishop of Toledo, Elipandus, after he had seriously and truly repented of his error concerning Christ’s adoption.” Concerning the abbot Genesius, whom Charlemagne sent as legate to Spain to turn Elipandus and his other followers away from this error, see Julian in the *Adversaria* and what we said at nos. 103 and 265. His words are: “Not long afterward Genesius went to Spain, sent by Charlemagne to Felix, bishop of Urgel, and Elipandus of Toledo, concerning the question of Christ’s adoption; and he went to Rome to Pope Hadrian and brought his letter to Charles and the bishops. He took part in the councils of Frankfurt and Italy. He brought Charles’s letter to Elipandus, with whom he debated, and Elipandus came to his senses through his arguments and prayers, while Felix the bishop remained in his error.”

Father James Sirmond has recently published the letter of Pope Hadrian and Charlemagne, the Council of Frankfurt, the booklet sent by the Italian bishops according to the council’s decree—of these Julian speaks in his *Chronicle*, no. 402—and the synodal letter sent by the bishops of Gaul and Germany to the bishops of Spain, in volume II of the *Gallican Councils*, folios 161, 167, 175, 186, and 193. He also includes the first canon of the council, in which the heresy of Elipandus and Felix is condemned; Felix is declared bishop of the see of Urgel, not of Toledo, as we shall discuss fully elsewhere.

Concerning Elipandus, who erred over the adoption which he attributed to our Lord Jesus Christ, the same Julian writes in his *Chronicle*, no. 402. He came to his senses through the admonitions of Pope Hadrian and the emperor Charlemagne, as stated in no. 402; see further nos. 404, 406, 409, 410, and 411. He gives thanks to Charles in no. 414 and dies a holy death in no. 415.

Now I produce as an irrefutable and wholly candid witness Jonas, bishop of the Church of Orléans, who wrote three books *On the Worship of Images* for Charles the Bald against the heresy of Claudius, bishop of Turin, more than 770 years ago. Although, as the most eminent Cardinal Baronius says in volume IX, under the year of Christ 825, Jonas fashioned the beast in such a way that he was by no means judged worthy of reward by the Catholic Church—and Father Jerome de la Higuera notes this at no. 292—Jonas says at the beginning of his work:

“Therefore, to pass over the others, from that same Spain there arose, in the time of the blessed and most pious and invincible Augustus Charles, a certain Felix by name, unhappy in conduct, bishop of the city of Urgel. He dared, after joining Elipandus [read: Elipandus], bishop of the city of Toledo, to his most wicked error, to preach that according to his humanity Christ was not the proper Son of God but an adoptive son.”

Julian supports this in the cited no. 265 of the *Adversaria* and in *Chronicle* no. 401: “Elipandus, the disciple of Felix, pontiff of Urgel,” and so forth. Jonas adds nothing concerning Elipandus’s repentance; concerning this Luitprand again writes in *Chronicle* no. 259, and Julian mentions it as far as nos. 402, 411, and 415. See also Aimoin, book IV of *On Frankish Affairs*, no. 83; Regino in his *Chronicle*; Ado of Vienne, book II; among more recent authors, Morales, *History of Spain*, book XIII, chapter 26; Schott the jurist, *Bibliotheca Hispana*; and John de Mariana, book VII of his *History*, chapter 8.

Many acknowledge that Beatus and Etherius wrote against Elipandus. Julian left this on record in his *Chronicle*, no. 401: “Etherius wrote against him [Elipandus], with Beatus assisting him; and this book is in our library.” John Eusebius Nieremberg, a learned Jesuit priest, treated these matters eruditely, as is his custom, in a letter which he wrote to me and which I arranged to have printed among the notes to the letters of the bishops, lest I deprive you of so much learning. Father Jerome de la Higuera wrote briefly on these matters at no. 260 of our Luitprand’s *Chronicle*. D. L.]

To make this clear, he assembled a council of the suffragan bishops and abbots; and, publicly abjuring his error before them all, he confessed the faith of the holy Roman Church, as you know better.

Thus I have done what you ordered, most blessed Father. Whether the effort has answered your wish, you will judge, since you gave the order; and commend this exiled servant to God in your prayers. Farewell.

Nevertheless, I shall begin with the year 606, Spanish Era 644, and in writing I shall follow the order followed by M. Maximus: on the one side by the eras, according to Spanish custom, and on the other by the years of Christ—without mentioning consuls or the *hegira* of the Moors [Col. 0974A]—and I shall carry this Chronicle of ours down to the year 960. Later I also sent this to Heromo, bishop of Braga.

# CHRONICLE OF LUITPRAND

[Col. 0973]

## ERA 644. YEAR OF CHRIST 606

### 1.

[Note: Concerning the most fortunate birth of this most holy pontiff, no one before this author says anything; afterward Julian gives a still more detailed account. P. H.]

Saint Ildefonsus is born at Toledo to very distinguished parents, in the house of Stephen and Lucia, on December 18, in the house which now belongs to the noble Mozarabs of Toledo. He later became archbishop of Toledo.

### 2.

Saint Rufus flourishes at Metz. He was the uncle of Saint Adelphus, formerly abbot of Agali and archbishop of Toledo, later bishop of Metz; Saint Adelphus succeeded his holy uncle Rufus.

## 645. 607

### 3.

[Note: Concerning Muhammad’s arrival in Spain and his attempt to spread his deeply corrupt sect at Seville, Córdoba, and Toledo, many testify. M. Maximus, under the year 606, writes: “Muhammad, an impious and wicked man, ravages Spain.” Here the most learned Father Francis Bivar—alas, once my own friend!—writes with a full and scholarly hand. If only premature death had not forestalled the editor and the edition! Unable to endure envy, death was nevertheless able to remove him from our midst and snatch him away from us.

Lucas of Tuy, in his *Chronicle*, book II, Era 653, says: “At that time Muhammad, shamefully driven from Spain, preached the wickedness of his profane law to foolish peoples in Africa.” And in book III: “Nevertheless, as it is said, the devil, transformed into an angel of light, foretold certain future things to him. Hence, at the beginning of his deceitful preaching, he went to Spain and taught his sect of perdition at Córdoba.”

And, what is more, our king Alfonso, surnamed the Wise—or the compilers who wrote the general Chronicle at his command—in part II, chapter 40, says: “He [Muhammad] came to Spain and went to Córdoba, and there preached that evil sect of his.”

Alfonso de Espina, an ancient author of no small authority, writes in *The Fortress of the Faith*, book III, in the fourth expulsion: “In his time [he is speaking of Sisebutus], the impious Muhammad was driven from Spain into Africa.” He admits that he took this from the archives of Brother Gil of Zamora, a son of Saint Francis and historiographer of King Saint Ferdinand III.

Werner Rolevinck, in the *Fasciculus temporum*, year 31; John Vasaeus, under the year 605: “This year, they report that the pseudo-prophet Muhammad attempted to spread the poison of his heresy among the Spaniards at Córdoba.”

Ludovicus Mayerne Turquet, in his *General History of Spain*, book V, p. 182, relates that in 605 Muhammad went to Spain to preach his doctrine in the city of Córdoba; but when he secretly realized that he would be captured after his wickedness had been discovered, he fled. They also write that he was driven out by Saint Isidore, bishop of Seville. King Alfonso likewise says there, in these words:

“And when the good Father Saint Isidore learned that he was then returning from the Roman court, he sent his men to Córdoba to capture him and bring him to him. And the devil appeared to Muhammad and told him to leave that place. Then he left Córdoba and fled, and crossed the sea, and preached in Arabia.”

Vasaeus agrees above: “When this became known to Saint Isidore, who at that time was returning from Rome, whither he had been summoned by the supreme pontiff for a council, and he had sent men to capture him, Muhammad—whether warned by a demon or by someone else—saved himself by flight and returned to Africa. From the *Fortress* and the Breviary of Évora.”

An ancient manuscript book, preserved with great care and reverence in the archive of the church of Saint Mark at León and graciously lent to me for transcription, confirms this. Its words, at the end of the second part, are:

“And as Saint Isidore was thus going on his way to the city of Seville, he was told that a wicked man named Muhammad, with a viper’s mouth, was preaching and teaching many errors and heresies never before seen or heard, by which he deceived and poisoned many souls. And as soon as Saint Isidore heard this, he sent to arrest Muhammad. But the demon, who learned of it, transformed into an angel of light and told him, as though he were God’s messenger, to go immediately to other lands, lest Saint Isidore, who was powerful in that country, have him arrested.”

And shortly afterward:

“When Saint Isidore reached a place near Córdoba called Santa Olalla, he was told that at that time a dreadful dragon was roaming in that country, near that place. It had appeared there from the time Muhammad had come to Spain and was doing great harm in the land. Saint Isidore immediately went there and wonderfully cast out that dragon.”

Don Rodrigo, archbishop of Toledo, gives nearly the same account in his *History of Spain*, written in the Spanish language, which is expanded in its third part beyond the Latin version, chapter 102. I arranged to have it copied from an ancient autograph preserved at the monastery of the Carthusian Saint Jerome in Seville, presented to the religious there through the generosity of the Marquis of Tarifa.

Alfonso Morgado, in his *History of Seville*, book I, chapter 1, writes:

“Coming [Saint Isidore] to Spain, our Lord worked great miracles through his intercession. Muhammad did not dare await him at Seville, nor anywhere in Spain where, during Isidore’s absence, he had intervened, so that the false prophet might practice in those regions the accursed sect and errors which he later practiced in Barbary and in which his followers still persist.”

Ambrosius Morales, book I of the *History of Spain*, chapter 21, denies this. He says that no defense is needed for one who denies that Muhammad came to Spain. Padilla supports him, seventh century of *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 21. Father John de Mariana, book VI of *On the Affairs of Spain*, chapter 3, calls it an old wives’ tale and says that a correct reckoning of the dates clearly proves it so. Against him Father Diego Bleda, in his *History of the Moors*, at the beginning, where he discusses Muhammad, chapter 15, vigorously and learnedly defends the chronological position.

Antonius de Quintana Dueñas treats the matter briefly but clearly in his book *Lives of the Saints of Seville*, under Saint Isidore, § 4, p. 161. I rightly decline to transcribe these authors, since the reader can consult them, and since those cited above affirm that the story is true; nor are there lacking other writers who recognize the astonishing virtue of Saint Isidore in his deeds.

Let the reader examine the matter again and judge it; and in place of *ab Aurasio* let him read *ab Isidoro*. Although Ruderic Caro admits that it was impossible at the place where M. Maximus records it, he does not dare contradict the ancient writers. Nevertheless, he chooses a middle course, believing at least that some disciples of that pseudo-prophet came, in order by their deceptions and tricks to drive the Spaniards into such madness. What Maximus and others affirm, he denies; and what he himself maintains, I have seen no one else write. D. L.]

Muhammad, spreading the poison of his error throughout Spain, began to sow it at Córdoba, Seville, and Toledo. He is driven from Toledo by Aurasio, archbishop of Toledo; and Catholic teachers pursue the detestable error in word and writing.

## 646. 608

### 4.

[Note: Gregory of Tours asserts this in his *History of the Franks*. Morales discusses it in his *History of Spain* under the Visigothic king Witteric. P. H.]

Theodoric, king of Metz, returns his betrothed Hermemberga, still untouched, to her father, Witteric, king of the Visigoths, together with gifts; her father takes this badly.

## 647. 609

### 5.

[Note: Concerning Flavius Claudius Paulus of Mérida, Saint Gregory the pope. P. H.]

Flavius Claudius, nephew [read: grandson] through the sister of Saint Masona, bishop of Mérida, and son of Claudius of Mérida, a man of the highest distinction, flourishes.

### 6.

[Note: Concerning this victory, Saint Isidore, Morales, and other authors. P. H.]

At Segontia, a city of the Celtiberians, the commanders of King Witteric engage the Romans and utterly rout them in battle.

## 648. 610

### 7.

[Note: Concerning Saint Isidore’s arrival at Rome in the time of Gregory, Lucas of Tuy and Father Ribadeneira in the *Life of Saint Isidore*. The same.]

In the time of Pope Gregory the Great, Isidore goes to Rome; received honorably by the Roman pontiff, he returns home in high esteem.

### 8.

[Note: That the Gothic kings were crowned and anointed, they did in imitation of the emperors of Constantinople, whose actions, both civil and ecclesiastical, they imitated in every respect. Just as the emperors called Constantinople the royal city, so the Visigothic kings likewise called Toledo a royal city. The emperors struck coin bearing the sign of the cross, and so did the Goths. The emperors rode in an ivory chariot, and so did the Gothic kings. The emperors were crowned and anointed at Constantinople; the Goths at Toledo. The emperors were crowned by the patriarch of Constantinople, as primate of their whole empire; likewise the Goths by the bishop of Toledo, as patriarch of the Gothic empire. I say nothing here about laws, punishments, and statutes, all of which were collected from the laws of the emperors of Constantinople; nor do I discuss the officials of the palace and the offices of the royal household, since these matters belong to a larger leisure and another place.

That the Gothic kings were anointed is clear first from the Chronicle of Saint Julian, which says:

“Now the glorious lord Wamba assumed the government of the kingdom on the very day on which Recesvinth died, namely the eighteenth day before the Kalends of September, in the aforesaid year; the solemnity of the anointing was postponed until the thirteenth day before the Kalends of October, on the twenty-second day of the moon, in Era 710.”

And concerning King Ervig:

“On the following day, Monday, the glorious lord Ervig immediately assumed the scepter of the kingdom. This was the third day before the Ides of October, Era 718; the solemnity of the anointing was postponed until the following Sunday.”

And concerning King Egica:

“Our lord Egica was anointed as king in the church of Saints Peter and Paul at the Praetorium, on the eighth day before the Kalends of December, a Sunday, Era 725.”

And concerning Witiza:

“Witiza was anointed as king on the day that was the eighteenth day before the Kalends of December, Era 729.”

The twelfth Council of Toledo likewise says in canon 1:

“For in what manner and by what order the most serene prince Ervig ascended to the height of royal power and received authority to reign through holy anointing…”

And below:

“Another instruction was also given to the aforesaid man in the name of our honorable and most holy brother, the bishop of the see of Toledo, who likewise charged him that, according to every order of due care, our aforesaid lord Ervig should be anointed as king, and that the celebration of that anointing should be performed with every diligence.”

From this it is gathered that the Gothic kings were accustomed to be anointed in the royal city of Toledo and by the archbishop of Toledo, as primate of all Spain. Thus they could not be, and were not, kings or possessors of power in the Gothic kingdom except through anointing, as the holy twelfth Synod of Toledo teaches.

For this reason some misunderstand the statement concerning King Wamba that he was to be anointed in the land of the Campos, as though he could be anointed anywhere other than Toledo. Because of this he postponed his coronation and anointing until he came to Toledo.

Here I shall add the words of Father John de Mariana, volume I, book VI, chapter 12, in the vernacular:

“Wamba yielded to these threats, but accepted the election in such a way that, contrary to custom, he did not wish to allow himself to be anointed before going to Toledo. He intended to reserve that for that city; and during the intervening time he expected either that the minds of those who had elected him would change or that he would win the favor of all the others, so that no disturbance would arise from the diversity of opinions. With this he set out for Toledo, where on September 29—Wednesday, the day of Saint Michael the Archangel—he was anointed and crowned in the church of Saints Peter and Paul, which stands near the royal palace. Before all else, he swore expressly to preserve the laws of the kingdom and to watch over the common good. Quiricus, archbishop of Toledo and successor of Saint Ildefonsus, performed the ceremony of anointing.”

Thus Mariana.

That the emperors of Constantinople were crowned after being anointed by the patriarch of the royal city is taught at length by Zonaras and Cedrenus, and is plainly gathered from the letter of John, patriarch of Constantinople, to Pope Hormisdas, in these words: “Since he adorned such a head with such a crown.” Hence Baronius and the author of the *Epitome* conclude that it was customary for the elected emperors of the Eastern Empire to be crowned by the bishop of Constantinople.

Others have written much on this subject. Father H. [P. H.]—There is much written by many authors on the anointing of Gothic kings. Our Julian speaks of it frequently; Father John Benedict Guardiola, in the final chapter of *The Nobility of Spain*, gives further material; our Garsias de Loaysa, in his remarks on the Councils of Toledo, in the exhortation to the prince which he published from the Codex Albeldensis, p. 34; among jurists, Camillus Borrellus, *On the Preeminence of the Catholic King*, chapter 49, no. 83, p. 50.

Luitprand, no. 87, says:

“He [Recesvinth] was crowned and anointed at Toledo by Eugenius, bishop of Toledo, in the church of Saint Mary, which in the Arabic vernacular is called Alficensis, or Lower.”

The literary glory of our Spain, Don Gregorio López Madera, knight of the Order of Santiago and counselor of the royal senate, most recently treats the matter in chapter 12, § 6, of *On the Preeminence of the Spanish Monarchy*, drawing on councils, chronicles, and many testimonies gathered from various places. He writes similarly in his *Gallic Mars*, or *On the Justice of the Wars and Treaties of the King of France*, chapter 10. Alexander, patrician of Armagh, whose true name was Dr. Cornelius Jansenius, bishop of Ypres.

Many authors report that the Greek emperors were accustomed to be anointed by the patriarchs of Constantinople. One author may stand for all: Codinus Curopalates, *On the Offices of Constantinople*, chapter 27, *On the Coronation of the Emperor*, no. 18, according to the recent translation:

“After this,” he says, “the new emperor removes the covering from his head, whatever it may be. Immediately all who are in the church stand there with uncovered heads. Then the patriarch anoints the emperor’s head with holy oil in the form of a cross, accompanying it in a loud voice with the word: ‘Holy.’”

Here Father James Gretser, a Jesuit priest, cites our Luitprand, book VI of *The Deeds of Princes throughout Europe*:

“Received by that same supreme pontiff with wondrous adornment and wondrous ceremony, he also received the anointing of the empire.”

The annotator of the *History of Paul the Deacon of Forum Julii* cites this at p. 276–277, referring to p. 92. Julius Caesar Bulenger, *On the Emperor*, book II, chapter 3, p. 89. D. L.]

After Witteric’s death, Gundemar succeeds him; he is anointed by Aurasio of Toledo—just as formerly the Greek emperors were anointed by the patriarchs of Constantinople—in the church of Saints Peter and Paul at Toledo.

### 27.

[Note: Assota is a city in the Bastetani, two leagues from Caravaca, where Las Cuevas now stands. The remains of a huge city can be seen there. From that place a stone was brought to Caravaca bearing the name of the Republic of the Assotani; it now stands as the façade of the very ancient church of the place. We discuss it in our *Geography of Spain*. Ptolemy calls this city Asso, with the name shortened, instead of Assota. It was once an episcopal city, but in these times it was destroyed. P. H.

Assota is a city in the Contestani. Brother John Gil of Zamora mentions this city in these words:

“The city of Lacedaemon is founded near Caravaca or Theodomirus by the Greeks; it is called Assota by Africans who came from a city called Assota, now said to be destroyed near Melilla.”

Our Julian speaks more clearly in the *Adversaria*, no. 70:

“Saint Indaletius is held in the highest renown along the coast of Carthagena. He is said to have preached at Assota and Lacedaemon, neighboring cities separated by the intervening river Ripar; they lie on two mountains, Assota to the east and Lacedaemon to the west.”

In place of *Ripare*, however, one should read, according to Aegidius, *Quipare*. To make this clear, I shall transcribe his words:

“The Capipa River, commonly called Quipar, near Carabum or Theodomirus, is so named because, from the fragrance of roses and flowers in early spring, it gives off an almost divine scent. The name came from those arriving from the city of Capipa in Africa, on the bank of the River Magrada.”

The archpriest Julian again discusses these same cities in the same work, nos. 83, 84, 85, and 475. It should be noted in passing that Saints Crispulus and Restitutus suffered not far from them, in the town of Caravaca, as Julian testifies at the cited no. 84. Bede and the Roman Martyrology state that they won the crown of martyrdom in Spain on June 10.

Friar Don Prudentius de Sandoval, bishop of Pamplona, collects much learned material in his notes on Tuy, p. 17; and Licentiate John de Robles, in his booklet *On the Cross of Caravaca*, book I, chapter 2, folio 5, published the following ancient inscription, found eighty-five years ago among the ruins of Assota, long buried beneath the earth and brought out from the rubble:

“Lucius Aemilius Rectus, son of Marcus, grandson of Marcus, of the Quirina tribe, born at Rome, who was also Carthaginian, Silicitanian, Assotanian, Lacedaemonian, Bastetanian, and Argive; secretary to the quaestor, secretary to the aedile; granted a public horse by the emperor Caesar Trajan Hadrian Augustus; aedile of the colony of Carthage; patron of the Republic of the Assotani. He ordered this to be made, with an annual banquet added.”

Ptolemy lists this city, though with the abbreviated name Asso—unless, with Julian in the *Adversaria*, no. 100, you prefer to hold that “Asson” and “Assota” were different cities, founded by citizens of Assos, a city in Asia Minor mentioned by Saint Luke in Acts 20:13–14 and 27:13.

It was an episcopal see, according to Luitprand, no. 27: “which was once an episcopal see”; and no. 38: “the see of Assota, Bigastrum, which is Murcia, is transferred.”

There exists a remarkable stone, an irrefutable testimony to this matter, found in the countryside of Orihuela. It bears an ancient inscription of a Catholic bishop, adorned with the letters Alpha and Omega:

“Alpha. Leander, servant of God, bishop of the holy Church of Illici or Belsa near the River Segura, and bishop of Assota, died in peace. Omega. Era 723.”

That is, in the year of the Lord 685.

Twelve years earlier he subscribes at the eleventh Council of Toledo; and at the twelfth, four years before his death, in sixth place. Two years before his death he attended and subscribed at the thirteenth Council of Toledo, and at the fourteenth Council of Toledo he subscribes after Julian, pontiff and primate of Toledo.

At the fifteenth Council of Toledo, Bishop Emila of Elici [read: Illici] and Dotana subscribes in twenty-fifth place, for the two sees, just as Leander did.

This Leander succeeded Ubinabi the Illicitanean, who confirms—or whose vicar Agricius confirms in his place—at the tenth Council of Toledo, Era 694, that is, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 656.

At the Toledan synod under Gundemar, Era 648, in the year of Christ 610, Sanabilis, bishop of the holy Church of Elota, confirms; and at the seventh Council of Toledo, Era 684, “Winibal” confirms in these words:

“Winibal [others read Vinibal], by the mercy of God bishop of the Church of Illici, also bishop of Elota, having defined these statutes, have subscribed.”

A learned man believes that in both places one should correct the text to *Assota* instead of *Elota* and *Elothana*. I would believe—if conjecture is permitted—that the bishop of Eliocroca, or of Lorca, migrated to become bishop of Assota. For mention is made at the Council of Elvira, convened 1,300 years ago in Era 362, of Successus, bishop of Eliocroca.

And at Gundemar’s synod, three hundred years later, mention begins to be made of the bishopric of Assota, never again of Elota or Eliocroca. This gives room for the conjecture that the Assotan see first began at that time, after the earlier see of Eliocroca had been abolished.

Nevertheless, Julian in the *Adversaria*, no. 81, says that Saint Indaletius established bishops at Bigastrum, Assota, and Eliocroca:

“Saint Indaletius preached at Carthagena, Illici, Assota, Lacedaemon, and Eliocroca, where he established bishops.”

Concerning Saint Indaletius, who preached at Eliocroca, see Flavius Lucius Dexter, under the year of Christ 54, no. 1. There the great man of incomparable learning, the glory and ornament of Spain, Father Francis de Bivar, learnedly cites Lucas of Tuy, where he discusses King Wamba, and Ambrosius Morales, book X of the *History of Spain*, chapter 32.

Concerning the transfer of the see of Assota to Bigastrum, see what is noted at no. 38. D. L.]

Assota, a city of the Contestani and on the border of Bastetania, once an episcopal see, is destroyed.

[Note: Ad Fauces. In Lusitania there is today a town called Gargantalaolla: the Latins call these places Fauces, the Spaniards Gargantas. There are references to the ancient Fauces, and ruins lie between Gargantum and the town of Quacum. St. Magnus, a disciple of St. Gall, preached here. He also commissioned Emeritus, a highly learned monk of the monastery of Elefantia, to compose the Life of Magnus and commend it to posterity.”

This Lantho was bishop of Augusta Emerita (Mérida) at the time of the captivity; Julian, archdeacon of St. Justa, mentions him under the year 870. He was a Benedictine monk, a learned and exceptionally holy man. P. H.

In the archetypal manuscript of Julianus belonging to P. Hieronymus Higuera, the reading is as I published it:

“Bento, bishop of Caesaraugusta, or Augsburg, by the authority of Pope Adrian, enrolled St. Magnus among the saints at the Lusitanian town called Ad Fauces. This man of God wrote in an elegant style against the heretics called Iconoclasts.”

But, on the basis of the note of Molanus cited above, Lantho should be read instead of Bento. D. L.]

### 38.

[Note: Concerning this translation of the see, Maximus of Caesaraugusta also writes. Murcia was also called Acarta, according to a Gothic manuscript of the monastery of Parraces, which reads:

“Acarta, Bigastrum. Here lies Restis, bishop of Vergara.”

Therefore Murcia was called Acarta and Bigastrum; and thus the bishops of Bigastrum belong to Carthage Spartaria. The see of Assota was therefore transferred here; and I believe that the see of Carthage in Spain was transferred here after it was destroyed in the time of Leovigild, or shortly before. P. H.]

The see of Assota is transferred to Bigastrum, which is Murcia.

I spoke at no. 27 about the city and episcopal see of Assota; now I shall discuss Bigastrum and Murcia, which are the same place, as appears here in our Luitprandus, in the Adversaria, no. 87, and in Julianus, Adversaria, no. 450.

The see of Bigastrum takes its name from the town of Bigastrum. Bigastrum is said to derive from the Greek expression ἀπὸ τῆς βίας καὶ γαστρός, that is, “from strength and belly,” because in that city there was vigorous provision for cultivating and caring for the belly. Luitprandus derives the name differently in the cited passage of the Adversaria, no. 87, where he writes that Bigastrum was so called as though it meant “double fortress.” Both explanations are not unreasonable, since the city is pleasant and produces noble and vigorous men distinguished in peace and war.

This is the city of Murcia, named from the word *myrtus*, “myrtle.” Pliny, Natural History, book XV, chapter 29, discussing the goddess Murcia, writes:

“There was also an ancient altar”—these are his words—“of Venus Myrtea, whom they now call Murcia.”

He mentions altars of Murcia at Veii in the Tusculan Disputations, book II, chapter 96. Festus likewise calls her Murcia and reports that she had a shrine beneath the Aventine. Yet his text must be corrected from Pliny. Festus now reads:

“There was a shrine of the goddess Murcia beneath the Aventine, which was formerly called Murcus.”

Correct this to: “which was formerly called Myrtea.” Or understand the common reading as retaining the name of the Aventine hill, formerly called Murcus; but I do not approve this interpretation.

Murcia, however, derived her name from the fact that she made men *murcidos*, that is, sluggish, through her delights. St. Augustine, City of God, book IV, chapter 16, writes of “the goddess Murcia, who would not move a person beyond measure and would make him,” as Pomponius says, “*murcidus* [or *murcus*], that is, excessively idle and inactive.”

Tertullian, On the Spectacles, chapter 8, lists the goddess Murcia, whom he says was a goddess of marble—perhaps because the idle people over whom she presided were like marble—or *marmoris* should be corrected to *amoris*, “of love,” since that name seems more appropriate to Venus. Thus Pamelius, whose view Cerda follows, rejects Turnebus, who in Adversaria, book XXII, chapter 13, thinks *marcoris* should be read.

Murcia, or Myrtea, promoted love among the ancients. Among them it is certain that the myrtle signified the mutual love of man and woman in marriage. Therefore Pliny, Natural History, book XV, chapter 29, writes that the Romans and Sabines, after the Sabine women had been carried off for marriage, made a friendly pact with verbena and myrtle. Of the three kinds of myrtle, the sacred one—called ἁγία, “holy,” by the Greeks—was dedicated to marriages.

Hence Catullus’ reading should be confirmed in the epithalamium of Julia and Manlius. Having received a good omen from the marriage, he gives them branches of sacred myrtle:

> Shining with flowering branches,  
> Like the myrtle *hagia*,  
> Which the goddess Hamadryads  
> Nurture as their plaything  
> With dewy moisture.

The learned F. Fortunatus Scacchus, of the Order of the Hermits of St. Augustine, writes in *Sacred Oil-Perfumes*, *Myrothecium* I, chapter 51, p. 495:

“Among the Romans, I say, *Murci* were those who, to avoid war and the clash of battle, cut off their own thumbs.”

Ammianus confirms that this custom became widespread in Italy. Speaking of the Gauls in book XV, near the end, he writes:

“Every age is exceedingly fit for military service; the old man and the grown youth alike are led to the field with equal strength of chest, their joints hardened by frost and constant labor, and ready to despise many things that others fear. Nor did any one of them ever, as in Italy, fearing the military service of Mars, cut off his own thumb; such men are jokingly called *murci*.”

There is an example in Suetonius, Augustus, chapter 24:

“He subjected to public auction the Roman knight who, on account of two adolescent sons and in order to evade the military oath, had cut off his thumbs, together with his property.”

Laevinus Torrentius comments on this passage. Quintilian also mentions it, Institutes of Oratory, book VIII, chapter 5. He speaks of a gladiator whose sister cut off his thumb so that he would not fight, in these words:

“As for the man whom his sister had often bought out of the arena, when he was acting against her in a retaliation because she had cut off his thumb while he slept: ‘You deserved to have your hand intact. Thus indeed he is heard, as though you were fighting to the death.’”

For a long time, since I was almost a boy, I read in Martial, *On the Spectacles*, the line:

“Thus you would fight to the finger.”

A little farther on, however, the poet writes concerning the same sister of the gladiator whom I have just mentioned:

“But I fought with a finger.”

This should be restored to:

“I fought to the finger.”

And, if I may pursue the matter, those who cut off their own thumbs were guilty of injuring the state. Fortunatianus, *Rhetorical Books*, book II, concerning Achronius, writes:

“Ten soldiers cut off their own thumbs in wartime; they are guilty of injury to the state.”

Our Luitprandus in *History of the Popes*, under Innocent, did not consign the word *murci* to oblivion. Speaking of the need for clerics, he says:

“When someone complained about the poverty of clerics and said that he had some *murci*—I read *murcii*—and some *digami*, he replied that a man who had willingly cut off part of his finger could not, according to the canons, be admitted to the clergy.”

This is the fourth letter of Innocent to Felix of Nuceria, as Franciscus Lindenbrogius reports in his notes on Ammianus, book XV, p. 45.

Arius Menander, the jurist, seems to have referred to this cutting-off of the thumb in the law beginning “Qui cum uno,” section 4, “eum, qui filium,” section 12, under the title *De re militari*. It reads:

“He who had disabled his son, when the levy had been proclaimed for war, so that he would be unfit for military service, was ordered by the decree of the divine Trajan to be deported.”

Dionysius Gothofredus explains the letter O in this passage in explicit terms.

The emperor Constantine, in book I of the Theodosian Code, title *De filiis militarium*, book VII, subjected to the municipal councils those who had voluntarily made themselves unfit for war by cutting off their fingers. The words are:

“We order that, if they are judged unfit for military service because their fingers have been cut off, they are without any ambiguity to be assigned to the duties and services of the municipal councils.”

Other emperors prohibited the practice in book IV of the same Theodosian Code, title *De tyronibus*:

“Let your sincerity not allow those who flee the camps by cutting off their fingers to protect themselves by deforming their hands, since those who have mutilated themselves voluntarily could be useful in some other part of the state, in accordance with the decree of the divine Constantine.”

Cujacius should be consulted, book XV, final observation, and chapters 21, 22, and 23 of the Apostolic Canons should be added.

As the empire and the Latin language declined, these same *Murcii* were called *Murcinarii*. Isidore writes in his Glossary: “*Murcinarius*, mutilated.” The Italians called such men *poltrones*, as though “truncated in the thumb”; hence the Italo-Latin word *pultrones*. St. Francis, volume I of the *Opuscula*, in *On True and Perfect Joy*, p. 94, says: “Go away from here, cowards.” Meursius discusses the matter extensively in *Critical Exercises*, part II, chapter 2, p. 67; Savaro in his notes on Sidonius Apollinaris, book I, letter 2, p. 12.

Thus the *Murcii* were pleasure-loving men, and their goddess was Murcia. Pleasures indeed suit her well, for the mildness of the air, the great abundance of water, fertility, wealth, an abundance of riches, gardens, groves, and springs make her the most indulgent of all the cities in the whole world. Her inhabitants, moreover, being strong and fit for the practice of arms, make her exceptionally well fortified.

García de Loaysa implies that Bigastrum succeeded Carthage. In his notes on the councils of Toledo, while explaining certain ancient names, he writes:

“Acarta, Bigastrum—that is, from Carthage to Bigastrum.”

He places it between Illici and Carthage. Thus Murcia, or Bigastrum, lies between Carthage and Orihuela, which is Illici. Loaysa should be consulted in his notes on the council held at Lucus by the prince Theodemir, p. 151, under the word *illicis*.

Bigastrum also shared boundaries with Urci and Illici. This is found in the division of boundaries made by King Wamba:

“Let Urci hold from Gesta to Carthage, and from Pugilla to Losola; let Illici hold from Pugilla to Losola.”

Losola is today La Losilla, which gives its name to the rural inn for travelers going from Murcia to Toledo, commonly called *la venta de la Losilla*. It is therefore clear that the boundaries of the bishopric of Bigastrum were enclosed between Carthage and Illici.

It is also helpful that the gate of the city of Illici leading to Murcia is now called the Puerta de Magastre, that is, the gate by which one goes to Bigastrum.

The most distinguished among the great investigators of antiquities, P. Juan de Mariana, writes in his *History of Spain*, book VI, chapter 15:

“Bagastra. No trace of this city survives; it is thought to have been situated toward Orihuela, both from the order of the places and from the name of the Migastri Gate”—he wrote in Spanish, *de Magastro*—“which is in that city.”

The learned Franciscus Martínez discusses the same gate in his treatise *The Antiquity of Orihuela*, chapter 3, p. 154.

There is also the testimony of the Saracen historian Rasis, who in the year 900 lists the bishopric of Murcia among those subject to Toledo.

Therefore the see of Bigastrum is the see of Murcia; the city of Murgis, and Bigastrum, are one and the same. And so that readers may have no remaining doubt, let us hear Julianus in his work *On Hermitages*, no. 14:

“The hermitage of St. Mary of Arraxaca”—thus it should be read there—“at Murcia, which in Gothic times was called Bigastrum, to which the bishopric of Carthage Spartaria was transferred. In that hermitage St. Leander and his sister Theodosia were baptized. Theodosia was the first wife of the Visigothic king Leovigild and the mother of the most holy kings Hermenegild the martyr and Reccared, the most devout and religious king. They were baptized by Dominicus”—read *Domitianus*—“the first bishop of that name of Carthage. After the captivity, during the time of the Moors, there was a church of the Mozarabs at Murcia.”

This bishop confirmed the sixth place at the Second Council of Toledo and was the predecessor of Licinianus. King Alfonso the Wise adds his name to the catalogue of bishops in his *General History*, part II, chapter 51.

[Col. 0985A]

That Murcia is an ancient city is shown by its situation and by the convenience of its river. Because of the great advantages it brings to the inhabitants, the Greeks call it Theodorus, that is, “gift of God.” Luitprandus discusses this in the *Adversaria*, no. 296, and says that Leander and Theodosia were born there.

This clearly indicates that, in the age of the Goths, it was a principal city. It should not be attributed to chance that Theodora gave birth there twice; rather, she had her residence there. Most importantly, the author M. Maximus, who wrote a thousand years ago, calls the city Murcia in the year of Christ 534:

“Murcia, which the Goths called Bigastrum.”

A Greek commentator, discussing the works of Pomponius, reads *Murci* and *Murgis*, or *Murcis*, instead of *Urci*.

Once again—and I must often call the council held at Lucus to witness—I seem to be whitening two walls with one brush. On p. 138 it reads:

“Let Urgi hold these boundaries: from Egesta to Carthage; from Gastri to Munda.”

I would read it as follows:

“Let Urci hold these boundaries: from Egelesta to Carthage; from Bigastrum to Munda.”

The same correction should be made in Julianus, *Adversaria*, no. 346:

“There was a little town called Egesta”—read *Egelesta*—“not far from the town of Portilla.”

And again, no. 484:

“And Egesta”—write *Egelesta*—“the town of Cuevas, near Portilla, was made from the ruins of Egelesta.”

Again, no. 364: the name of the town Portilla, or Portillia, is found in a diploma of King Sancho, dated in the era 1077, that is, in the year of the Lord 1039. Ambrosius Morales reports it in book II of the *Memorial of St. Eulogius*, chapter 7, no. 8, p. 59, and also Julianus himself in the *Adversaria*, no. 484:

“In the division of the bishoprics,” he says, “made by King Wamba, among the bishoprics of Aelita and Secura, the name Montania occurs. It is Montania Ningida and Egelasta. The little town of Cuevas, near Portilla, was made from the ruins of Egelasta.”

From these passages Julianus’ text in the *Adversaria*, no. 30, should be corrected. If Urci and Almería are not the same place—which is the view to which I am more inclined—they must at least have been situated close to one another:

“Urci, in the province of Tarraconensis, which is now called Almería, was an episcopal see on the shore of the Mediterranean, not far from Carthage. There St. Indaletius, a bishop and disciple of St. James, preached. It shares boundaries with the bishopric of Bastetania through Egelesta”—now called Vélez-Blanco—“with Bigastrum, namely Murcia, and with the river and town of Munda.”

Luitprandus had earlier said in the *Adversaria*, no. 291:

“Julianus himself acknowledges this in his account of the capture of Almería, which he described in verse.”

The learned P. Franciscus Bivarius pointed this out to me, pointing with his finger to the printed work issued by Don Fr. Prudencio de Sandoval in his *History of the Emperor Alfonso VII*. I had previously sought it in Julianus’ edition, having been alerted by Julianus himself in the *Adversaria*, no. 482, and by P. Portocarrero of the Society of Jesus in his excellent little work *On the Death of the Blessed Virgin Mary*, fol. 91, as I stated in my dedicatory letter. I have now not only seen the printed work, as I said, but possess a manuscript copy together with the *History of the Emperor Alfonso VII*, composed by our Julianus. If time permits, I shall publish it.

Julianus, I say, acknowledges this when, discussing the attack on Almería—during which the courage of Count Pontius shone out like the moon among the lesser stars—he says:

> He himself prepares the food, offers his own wines  
> To the weary soldiers, while the dreadful helmet is raised.  
> To the Moors he is a plague; afterward Urci—read *Urci*—bore witness.  
> This fortress is taken, and Urci itself is also laid low.

Hence our archpresbyter must again be illuminated in the *Adversaria*, no. 363:

“And because it has been said that the passage concerning St. Indaletius speaks of Urci, where he was bishop, and his body was found at Almería, certain ancient writers, deceived by this, called Almería Urci.”

He does not admit that Urci and Almería are the same; but he necessarily recognizes that they were not far apart. First, from the passage in the *Adversaria*, no. 363; more clearly, in no. 482:

“Here”—that is, from this point—“after the city was destroyed”—namely Urci—“the Christians changed their see and carried with them to Almería the body of the holy pontiff and martyr, who suffered in the city of Urcitania in the third year of Nero. He is celebrated on 15 May.”

The verses and notes published by Archbishop García de Loaysa in the council held at Lucus, p. 264, confirm this. He says that, in the monastery of Parraces, where the life of regular canons had formerly flourished in holiness and where the observance of St. Jerome was then practiced, while our Catholic king Philip II was staying there, he came upon a parchment manuscript in which he read:

“Urci, which is now called Almería; hence the verse:

> Indaletius, devoted to his work, came to Urci,  
> Which, later changed, was called Almería.”

D. Ferdinand de Mendoza, a highly learned man, following this opinion in his *Council of Iliberis*, book I, chapter 11, fol. 97, writes:

“16 January: Urci. Otherwise Virgi, commonly Almería.”

The holy abbot Juan Briz also gathers much material, and does so learnedly, concerning St. Indaletius, Urci, and Almería, in his *History of St. John of the Peña*, book III, chapter 28, through the end of the book.

Finally, to put an end to so long an excursus, it should be known that, when Spain came under the power of the Saracens, this place bore the name Murcia, as Morales reports from Rasis in book XII, chapter 22, and as Francisco Cascales states at length in chapter 1 of his *Description of Murcia*.

Julianus discusses Bigastrum and Murcia again in the *Adversaria*, no. 86, in connection with Saints Rusticus and Crispulus. On them write Juan de Robles in his little work *On the Cross of Caravaca*, book I, chapter 2, fol. 5, and D. Fr. Prudencio de Sandoval, bishop of Pamplona, in *The Antiquity of the Church and City of Tui*, fol. 17, columns 1 and 2.

Julianus asserts in the *Adversaria*, no. 4, that St. Crispulus was a friend of M. Valerius Martial. Nor does chronology oppose this, since several writers teach that Martial lived even under Nero—the emperor under whom Crispulus suffered—including Matthaeus Raderus, a priest of the Society of Jesus, in his commentary on Martial, *third revision*, in the poet’s Life, p. 3.

By way of a corollary, Julianus writes in the *Adversaria*, no. 365:

“The boundary of this bishopric of Urcitania is the river Munda, where it flows into the Tader, or Segura; Carthage and Murcia, formerly called Bigastrum; and the fortress of Dotana, now Totana.”

See also no. 66. D. L.]

The see of Assota is transferred to Bigastrum, which is Murcia.

DCLXII. DCXXIV.

[Col. 0985]

### 39.

[Note: This is not the emperor Heraclius Augustus mentioned at no. 44. He did not die either in this year or in battle, but, as Luitprandus observes below at no. 72, in the year 642. There he deliberately, not inadvertently, says that Heraclius, who restored the Cross, had died, as though distinguishing him from this Heraclius, the Roman commander, whom the writers of the Life of the emperor Maurice mention. Among these writers shines, like the moon among the lesser stars, our Petrus Mexia, a noble Spaniard, in his *Caesars*, in the Life of Maurice. D. L.]

Heraclius, the Roman emperor, dies in battle.

### 40.

[Note: The return of St. Ildefonsus from Hispalis to the royal city of Toledo is frequently mentioned in the Life of Ildefonsus, written by Cixila and Julianus, bishop of Toledo. We have explained more fully where the Agalian monastery was in our *Ecclesiastical History of the City of Toledo*, and therefore there is no need to discuss its location further here, especially since Luitprandus describes it sufficiently vividly and shows that, under Bonitus, bishop of Toledo, he was then in that city and had extensive dealings with the abbot of Agali. P. H.]

Ildefonsus returned from Hispalis to Toledo; Helladius wished to make him his archdeacon. But, withdrawing from the world, he lived in the Agalian monastery, which is in the suburb of Toledo—as you know—toward the north, not far from the Tagus River and from the Praetorian church of St. Leocadia outside the walls, on the plain. While I was at Toledo I frequently visited it.

I also visited another colony of this Agalian monastery, at the village called by the Moors Buralgania—read *Benalfavia*—more than three miles distant from Toledo. But Ildefonsus lived in the former monastery, which was not far from the hermitage of St. Susanna near the Tagus.

As I said, I visited it frequently when I was a subdeacon at Toledo under Bonitus I, archbishop of Toledo of that name, formerly abbot of Agali.

### 41.

[Note: St. Ildefonsus writes about Tonantius. He was an exceptionally devout and learned man and presided over the Church of Palentia. He died in the year of the Lord 624. P. H.]

Tonantius, bishop of Palentia, a holy man, dies.

DCLXIII. DCXXV.

### 42.

[Note: The fame of the holiness of the most blessed bishop Helladius spread far and wide throughout every part of Spain, especially his extraordinary generosity toward the poor. Thus St. Ildefonsus writes of him in magnificent language:

“His acts of compassion and abundance of almsgiving,” he says, “are shown to have been bestowed upon the needy so generously that you might have thought poverty descended from his stomach into his limbs and warmed his inner organs.”

P. H.]

St. Helladius, bishop of Toledo, is held in renown for the holiness of his life and his merciful almsgiving to the poor.

DCLXIV. DCXXVI.

### 43.

Primogenius, patriarch of Grado, flourishes greatly.

DCLXVII. DCXXIX.

### 44.

The emperor Heraclius, having recovered the Cross, enters the holy city of Jerusalem in triumph from Persia.

DCLXIX. DCXXXI.

### 45.

[Note: Concerning Ambracia in Lusitania, now Placentia, see what has already often been said elsewhere. Regarding the bishop Protasius, however, I have found nothing elsewhere. P. H.

Protasius, bishop of Ambracia. Ambracia is a town called *municipium* by way of emphasis. Thus Julianus, in his treatise *On Hermitages*, no. 16:

“The town of Ambracia was emphatically called a *municipium*. In the Council of Iliberis the archpresbyter Eucharius confirms this by saying ‘from the *municipium*.’ He is said to have been bishop at the time when the church was founded, and was an exceptionally holy and learned man.”

He is speaking of the same Eucherius, who held the thirteenth place among the priests at the Council of Iliberis.

D. Ferdinand de Mendoza thinks the *municipium* was Calahorra, book I, chapter 11, fol. 97. D. Gregorius López Madera, in *The Sacred Mountain*, chapter 23, fol. 92, p. 2, asserts that it was the Florentine *municipium* of Iliberis. P. Franciscus de Bivar, in his notes on Dexter, year of Christ 300, commentary 1, no. 5, explains it as the *municipium* of Alba, now called Arjona.

Julianus has brought light and dispelled the darkness cast over antiquity. Concerning the city of Ambracia, the same most learned P. Franciscus de Bivar writes in his notes on Dexter, year 268, no. 4, p. 294, where he says that Greeks founded this city. Our Julianus teaches the same in the cited passage, no. 16, in these words:

“From the time of Constantine, after peace had been granted to the churches, the hermitage of St. Mary of the Fountain of the Ladies was built at the expense of the most holy queen Helena from the temple of Berecynthia, the Mother of the Gods, near the city of Ambracia.”

It should incidentally be noted that Julianus says two things: that the hermitage was built from the time of the emperor Constantine, and that Benedictine nuns afterward lived there. D. L.]

Protasius, bishop of Ambracia in Lusitania, near Laconimurgum, flourishes through wondrous virtues.

DCLXX. DCXXXII.

### 46.

[Note: Hieronymus Romanus discusses Arthuagus, an Augustinian monk, at length in the history he wrote brilliantly concerning his order. P. H.]

#### Arthuagus

Julianus, *Chronicle*, no. 325, under the year of Christ 659:

“At this time Arthuagus, an Augustinian monk, a man exceptionally fervent in zeal for God, dies at Toledo in January.”

M. Maximus, under the year of Christ 584:

“Arthuagus the Goth, a monk of the Order of St. Augustine, flourishes in holiness at Scisla in Toledo.”

Ambrosius de Morales, book XII, chapter 18; Rodericus Carus, beloved of the Muses, in his notes on Maximus, under the year 584, p. 202; and B. Gabriel Pennotus in *The Tripartite History of Clerical Canons*, book I, chapter 56, nos. 1 and 2, where he cites our author.

P. M. Joannes Márquez, book *On the Order of St. Augustine*, chapter 11, section 2, likewise does not spare our Luitprandus and attacks his own antagonist. The chronology differs among the authors. D. L.

#### Scisla of Toledo

Concerning Scisla, or Sisla, or Cisla, a monastery at Toledo, see below, no. 293: Juan Beuter and Escolano in their *History of Valencia*; Joseph of Sigüenza in the *History of the Order of St. Jerome*; Alcocer and Pisa in their *History of Toledo*; and among the ancient writers, Julianus in his *Treatise on Hermitages*, no. 9:

“The monastery of St. Mary of Cisla was possessed in Gothic times by Augustinian monks; the Pantoja family claims descent from King Athanagild, and therefore they are patrons of this hermitage.”

Marcus Maximus, under the year of Christ 362:

“The monastery of Scisla of St. Augustine was built at Toledo by Athanagild, king of the Visigoths.”

P. M. Joannes Márquez proves this extensively and learnedly in *On the Origin of the Order of St. Augustine*, chapter 11, sections 2 and 3. Pennotus disputes him in book I of *The History of Regular Clerics*, chapter 57, section 6, and removes Flavius Lucius Dexter, M. Maximus, and Luitprandus from the text, although I do not find in Bivarius’ text the testimony of Flavius Lucius Dexter cited by Márquez. ID.]

On the first day of May, Arthuagus, an Augustinian monk of Scisla in Toledo, dies at Toledo in holiness and disciplined conduct.

### 47.

[Note: I have dealt elsewhere at length with Orosius, bishop of Elbora in Carpetania, and with the bishopric of Elbora or Talabrica. Its bishopric now survives in the archdeaconry of Talabrica, which shows that an episcopal see once existed there. In antiquity it was called Talabrica, or Elbora, an Aquatic City, because of the abundance of good waters visible throughout its villages. P. II.

At this time Orosius, bishop of Elbora, flourishes in Carpetania, a deacon. Julianus, cited passage, no. 325:

“At that time Orosius, bishop of Elboracum, a holy man distinguished by the praise of his learning, flourishes.”

D. L.]

At this time Orosius, bishop of Elbora, flourishes in Carpetania.

### 48.

[Note: [Col. 0988C]

48. Here he places two Justuses in the Church of Toledo, but both as bishops: one was a Toledan, a holy, learned, and highly religious man; the other, however, was the deacon of Saint Helladius, not his successor. Apart from what Luitprand says here, and in nos. 51 and [Col. 0989A] 52, this is clearly gathered from Ildefonsus himself, whose carefully considered words distinguish between the two Justuses:

“Again, when Justus the deacon insulted Helladius, bishop of that see, with the arrogance of pride, after the death of his pontiff he indeed lived as a bishop, but he himself wasted away; and, having turned to a depraved understanding because of the intemperance of his conduct, he died strangled in his sleep by a noose by the ministers of his altar.”

Indeed, if this Justus had been archbishop of Toledo, he would not merely have said, “after the death of his pontiff he lived as a bishop,” but would have added, “his successor”; just as, when speaking of Justus of Toledo, he says: “Likewise, with Justus the bishop, his successor,” and so forth. For, since he was abbot or rector of Agali, he was summoned to the see of Toledo immediately after Helladius. How, then, could he have been a deacon at Toledo and at the same time abbot of Agali? These offices are so demanding that the same person could in no way perform one together with the other.

Thus, when Saint Ildefonsus was made rector in the monastery of Agali, third after Saint Helladius, “he served as rector for three years.” But you may say: He was made a deacon at Toledo from a monk and afterward became abbot of Agali. You are telling me of something unusual for those times, as may be seen in the case of Eugenius the monk, who was summoned to the Church of Toledo with Helladius and, by that same Helladius, never returned to the monastery; for that reason he was not abbot of Agali. The same thing happened to Maximus, the Benedictine monk of Zaragoza, who, after becoming archdeacon of the Church of Zaragoza and of Saint Mary of the Pillar, never returned to the monastery.

But it is better to set down the words of the holy doctor Ildefonsus exactly as they stand:

“This Eugenius, namely, Helladius took with him from the monastery when drawn to the pontificate; and, having been instructed by him in the clerical orders, he became the third rector of his see after him.”

Add that Justus was not ordained by Helladius except as a lector. Thus Saint Ildefonsus says: “Eugenius, Helladius’s disciple, associate and companion of Justus.” [Col. 0989C] Therefore he was made lector at the same time as Eugenius.

Fourth, how could Saint Ildefonsus contradict himself, when in the preface he had said of that Justus:

“When Justus the deacon insulted Helladius, bishop of that see, after the death of his pontiff he indeed lived as a bishop; and he himself wasted away, but, having turned to a depraved understanding because of the intemperance of his conduct, he died strangled in his sleep by a noose by the ministers of his altar”?

This seems to indicate that this intemperate, proud, and thieving Justus died in mortal sin. How, then, if he is the same man who was archbishop of Toledo, does he say of him in the Life of Saint Eugenius:
