“And the good merit of the old man, who deserved to leave to two disciples and holy sons the inheritance of the Church of God to be governed”?

How, then, if he died intemperate in conduct and utterly wicked, does he call him Helladius’s holy son?

Let there therefore be two Justuses, differing in status, conduct, and manner of life: one a layman, the other a monk; one intemperate, the other trained from childhood in holy ways. Both, nevertheless, became bishops after Helladius: one Toledan and his successor in the primatial see. He was a secular cleric; some believe him to have been bishop of the Church of Acci. He confirmed at the Church of Toledo the acts of the Sixth Council of Toledo, no. 44, in the year 638, seven years after the death of the most holy pontiff Helladius. Clarentius and Serpentinus were present. He may have belonged to another church; but the name and the proximity in time make it very likely that he was this man.

Yet truly, if Justus had been such a man, Saint Ildefonsus would not have kept silent about it in his Life, where he says:

“Justus, after Helladius, his disciple and successor, a man distinguished and refined in bodily appearance and intellectual merit; a monk from infancy, abundantly trained and instructed by Helladius in the virtue of monastic discipline, was made rector in the monastery of Agali, third after him. He served as rector for three years. He died in the time of Sisenandus; that king departed this life on the nineteenth day after him.”

Moreover, since the monasteries were governed by the counsel and direction of the bishops of Spain, it is not credible that the most holy and innocent Helladius would have consented to the appointment of a wicked, proud, insolent man of evil conduct to govern a monastery where monastic discipline and the vigor of holiness flourished so greatly, and where the Benedictine order preserved them for so long. Reason, prudence, and love for his own religious order could in no way have permitted this.

From these considerations it follows that those writers badly went astray who, reading Saint Ildefonsus so carelessly, made one unjust man out of two Justuses and cast so conspicuous a stain and reproach upon the Holy Church of Toledo and the most holy Benedictine order—not deliberately, certainly, but through negligence. It would therefore be worthwhile for good authors to proceed not asleep but awake and extremely attentive, comparing passages with passages.

I too would have fallen into the same error, had not Luitprand, a careful author and a man of keen judgment, now tugged my ear. He wrote certain things to Achilanus, abbot of Agali. P. H.]

Justus, the secular deacon of Saint Helladius, bishop of Toledo and primate of the Spains (as the others had been, [Col. 0989] namely by Saint Elpidius, Julian, Saturninus, and Maximus Marcellus Eugenius), troublesome to that holy pontiff through mockeries, insults, and an evil tongue, ended an evil life by a most wretched kind of death, as a Gallic bishop.

49. [Note: [Col. 0990B]

49. The death of Saint Helladius occurred at the beginning of the reign of Sisenandus, that is, in the year 631. His feast is celebrated in the Martyrology recently published at Rome, on 18 February; concerning him see Saint Ildefonsus, On Illustrious Men, and Rodericus, book II, chapter 7. Thus the Church venerates the venerable Helladius, metropolitan bishop of the see of Toledo, resplendent with the renown of holiness, while the supreme pontiff, by his authority, presents the Martyrology to the whole Church, so that only those are regarded as saints who are written there—and this is what it means to canonize saints. For what is canonization except to present someone as a saint to the entire Church of God, to be regarded, honored, and named as a saint? This is done insofar as Saint Helladius is presented to the universal Church. Therefore he has already been canonized, although no office was celebrated for him in Spain, as certain learned men complain.

Saint Helladius died on 18 February in the year 632, the first year of Sisenandus, whose reign began on 8 September. Six months had already elapsed. He governed for three years and six months, from approximately the beginning of March until two or three days of September. Thus, according to Ildefonsus, he had been administrator of the patrimony for three years; and, according to Luitprand, Toledan pontiff for six months. We owe much to the latter. P. H.]

In this year, on the eighteenth day of February, the most holy pontiff Helladius of Toledo, a very old man, dies a holy death.

50. The faith of Christ, preached by the disciples of Saint James during the first century, is growing in the Canary Islands. Saint Avitus suffers in the Canary Islands, and it still endures in the islands.

51. Saint Justus, a Benedictine monk from the monastery of Agali and administrator of the patrimony, is chosen as Toledan bishop; he is entirely different from the secular man. This holy and pious man, innocent and trained in the finest conduct, presides over his monks for three years.

52. [Note: [Col. 0990D]

52. This council is cited by the illustrious García de Loaysa from Gothic manuscript books; there Justus is confirmed as [Col. 0991A] bishop of Toledo. It was held in the year 633, on 9 December, the feast of Saint Leocadia, and in her church, namely in the basilica. This was the third year of King Sisenandus. The first had begun on 8 September; the second had ended on 8 September 633. From that day the third year of Sisenandus had begun; three months and one day of that year had elapsed. So that the feast of Saint Leocadia might be more splendid on that day, a synod of sixty-two bishops was held in the basilica of that holy martyr—probably in her parish church. P. H.]

Under this bishop Justus, and under the Visigothic king Sisenandus, the Fourth Council of Toledo was convened, consisting of sixty-two bishops distinguished by dignity, learning, and conduct; Saint Isidore presided.

DCLXXII. DCXXXIV.

[Col. 0991]

53. Pope Honorius died on the third day before the Ides of October; he occupied Peter’s see for one year, seven months, and eighteen days.

DCLXXIII. DCXXXV.

54. Alexandria and Egypt were harshly captured by the Saracens [or, by the leader of the Saracens].

55. [Note: [Col. 0991A]

55. Justus died in the year of the Lord 635, on 3 September, that is, several years and some months after the blessed departure of Saint Isidore, bishop of Seville. I believe that he was buried in the monastery of Agali, unless you prefer the praetorian church of Saint Leocadia, where Saint Helladius was buried. Marieta and Prudentius de Sandoval regard him as a saint.

Not yet sufficiently known on earth, most renowned in heaven,

Alas! Justus, you die, glory of your people.

From childhood you were a monk, following Benedict’s camp,

A disciple dearer than others to holy Helladius.

Iria gave you birth; Toledo nourished you amid

The strict observances of the order and called you to the chair.

Before this you were in the Agalian school of piety;

From there you were called, exalted, to distinguished sheep.

Learned, loving what is right, chaste, moderate, honorable,

Sober, you excelled in intellect and religion.

As you had been a diligent abbot, so you were yourself a provident

Bishop, and thus worthy in both offices.

Alphonsus calls you holy—and he himself most holy;

You are worthy, and the equal of Bishop Helladius.

The third day of September brought your merit to the stars;

A tomb was prepared for you in Leocadia’s church.

Those who believe that you lived as the deacon

Of blessed Helladius, I think they are greatly mistaken.

This man was Helladius’s lector; while Helladius ruled,

He was abbot of Agali.

From there he ascended as bishop to the city of Toledo,

In conduct and wisdom no less than Helladius.

Pray for us, most righteous bishop Justus,

Known to God, known to learned men, known to pious men. P. H.]

Justus, archbishop of Toledo, a Benedictine monk and a man of great religious devotion, dies a holy death on 3 September.

56. [Note: [Col. 0991C]

56. Saint Ildefonsus writes in the Life of Justus about Sisenandus’s death, nine days after the death of the holy bishop Justus. P. H.]

Sisenandus, the Catholic Visigothic king, dies at Toledo on 22 September; he is buried in the praetorian church of Saint Leocadia.

57. [Note: [Col. 0991C]

57. Isidore, Ildefonsus, and Rodericus, in the chapter cited above, discuss the election of Cintila; as for the date, no one does so except Luitprand. P. H.]

Cintila is chosen in Sisenandus’s place toward the end of September; he was a vigorous man, energetic in the practice of arms.

58. [Note: [Col. 0991C]

58. Concerning Eugenius, see also the Third Council of Toledo; and the illustrious Ildefonsus writes of Eugenius I as follows:

“Eugenius, Helladius’s disciple, associate and companion of Justus, became pontiff after Justus. A monk from infancy, he was instructed by Helladius together with Justus in the sacred disciplines of the monastery. Helladius took him with him from the monastery when drawn to the pontificate; and, having been instructed by him in the clerical orders, he became the third rector of his see after him. Thus the old man earned the good distinction of having left the inheritance of the Church of God to be governed by two disciples and holy sons.

That same Eugenius was grave in conduct and bearing. For he knew the numbers, phases, increases and decreases, courses and recourses of the moon with such expertise that the considerations of his discussions turned his listener to astonishment and led him into profound learning. He lived in the priesthood for nearly eleven years, under the kings Cintila, Tulga, and Chindasuintus.”

So far Ildefonsus. Eugenius took part in the Fifth, Sixth, and Seventh Councils of Toledo. Saint Ildefonsus calls him holy, just as he had called Justus holy, speaking of the two as disciples and holy sons. He occupied the primatial see for nearly eleven years. In his honor it is fitting to add this epitaph:

Eugenius, bishop most worthy of the Olympic laurel,

To whose intellect the whole structure of things is subject:

It is uncertain whether you should be called greater in piety

Or in learning, since you shine in both.

You are a diligent shepherd, an excellent Father to all alike;

By religion you surpass the loftiest houses.

Having triumphed over death, you climb victorious above the heavens,

And a sacred laurel wreath encircles your brow.

Among the apostles you shine as an apostolic man,

No less than Eugenius, no less than Helladius.

Pour forth prayers for us, most holy bishop,

And outstanding monk, distinguished bishop.

May you rule your homeland and your people most gently,

The people themselves imploring you with anxious prayer.

Garibay, Mariana, Marieta, Master Prudentius de Sandoval, and other more recent writers also remember him. P. H.]

Eugenius is chosen in place of Justus, archbishop of Toledo.

59. [Note: [Col. 0992B]

59. In the Gothic manner Eugenius consecrated, anointed, and crowned Chintila on 25 October, a Sunday, in the praetorian church of Saint Leocadia [Col. 0992C] where his body lay. To the people of Toledo this sacred basilica is called Santa Leocadia de Afuera. P. H.]

On 25 October, Eugenius consecrates, anoints, and crowns King Cintila [or Chintila, according to the manuscript] in the presence of many bishops and courtiers, in the urban church of Saint Leocadia.

DCLXXIV. DCXXXVI.

60. [Note: [Col. 0992C]

60. Concerning the council held under King Cintila in the first fortunate year of his reign—which is fifth in sequence—where Saint Eugenius was present, as the illustrious archbishop Loaysa says. This synod is found in many manuscript codices. Rodericus writes of it as follows in book II, chapter 19, of his History:

“After the death of Sisenandus, Quintilla was placed over the Goths, in the era 697, and, with one year and some months counted, reigned for four years. He arranged the Fifth Council of Toledo, consisting of twenty-four bishops, under Eugenius, primate of the royal city. There not only many things concerning worldly affairs, but also many things concerning divine matters, were poured from the light of grace into ignorant minds.

The fifth gathering of holy bishops, with their deputies assisting and with the elders of the palace who were deemed worthy to take part in the council, was assembled in the church of Saint Leocadia the virgin, as the Book of Canons gloriously declares. In this synod Braulio, bishop of Zaragoza, shone forth more illustriously than the rest and fittingly infused pious teaching into Christian minds; his little works the Church still venerates to this day. Rome, mother and mistress of cities, admired his eloquence through an exchange of letters. In this council Selva of Tarragona also subscribed, together with some of his suffragans and the deputies of absent bishops.”

So writes Rodericus, who seems to have possessed copies very different from those we now have. For although the Fifth Council of Toledo, both the printed edition and the manuscript copy presently before me, contains twenty-four bishops, including Braulio, bishop of Zaragoza, neither Selva confirms there, nor does any deputy or courtier.

Nor do I think it should be passed over in silence that not all the princes of the palace took part in the councils. Rather, as our Rodericus correctly observes, those were admitted who were judged worthy by their conduct, purity of life, and gravity of counsel to be present among so many pontiffs. Since the number of courtiers was very large, if all had been present they would plainly have outnumbered the bishops who gathered from every direction for the councils. Whether this selection was made by the courtiers themselves, by the king, or by the bishop, I have nowhere read, so far as I know. It is more likely that, when councils dealt also with secular matters, they were selected either by the people or by the king; but where the worthy are distinguished from the less worthy, there was a selection. P. H.]

On the Kalends of December, the Fifth Council of Toledo was held in the basilica of Saint Leocadia the confessor, in the first year of the most serene king of the Visigoths, Flavius Cintila.

[Col. 0993] 61. [Note: [Col. 0993B]

61. Verecundus flourished at Toledo as archpresbyter. He is the man whom Eugenius II, newly elected, sent to Isidore, as Isidore himself testifies in his letter to Eugenius; when near death, Isidore sent him back to the aforementioned Eugenius, in these words: “Receiving the letters of your holiness through the messenger Verecundus.” More will be said about him later in what follows. ID.]

Verecundus, archpresbyter at Toledo, flourished; Saint Isidore mentions him. He later became bishop of Utica in Africa.

62. [Note: [Col. 0993C]

62. I do not wish to conceal the prodigies that occurred at the actual beheading of our most blessed apostle, which until now have lain hidden among moths and cockroaches, to the great detriment of the memory of so great a patron. I extracted them from the History of Saint James, which, attributed to Calixtus II, Roman pontiff, exists in a manuscript codex of the library of the monastery of Sandoval. My Bivarius, who had recently been presented with the Cross of the Order of Saint James, willingly gave me a copy of it, and makes it publicly available in his commentaries on Maximus in the Chronicle under the year of Christ 583, no. 2.

The beginning of the History is: “After the Lord’s Ascension”; at the end, however, these most worthy words are found:

“The executioner drew his sword, raised it high, struck him twice on the neck, and cut off his most holy head. Immediately precious blood flowed; and his head did not fall to the ground, but the blessed apostle, full of the power of God, received it in his arms, which he had raised toward heaven. Thus he remained kneeling, holding his head in his arms, until night came, when his disciples would take his body.

Meanwhile, certain men who had been sent by Herod attempted to seize his head, but they could not; for their hands stiffened upon the most precious body of blessed James. Immediately the executioner beheaded Josiah, the martyr of Christ and disciple of blessed James.

Then a great earthquake occurred, the heavens opened, the sea was shaken, an intolerable thunderclap sounded, and the earth opened and swallowed the greater part of the wicked. A great light shone forth in that region, and an angelic host was heard by many in the air, carrying their souls to the heavenly dwellings, where they rejoice without end.

When the day had passed, his disciples came to him on the following night and found him as we have said, kneeling and holding his head in his arms. They placed his body and head, with precious spices, in a deerskin bag and carried it from Jerusalem to Galicia, an angel of the Lord accompanying them across the sea. There they buried it, where it is venerated to this very day.” [Col. 0994B]

Thus far the Acts, to which our Julian agrees in the Chronicle, no. 24, thereby greatly strengthening their authority. His words are:

“This too I heard blessed Calixtus II say when he was preaching in Rome on the feast of Saint James, 25 July: When the apostle’s head was cut off, it did not fall to the ground, but the most holy apostle caught it between his hands and held it for a long time. Nor could the executioners take it from him; for when they tried, their hands and arms withered. Then Josiah was beheaded, and a wondrous light appeared; earthquakes and flashes of lightning followed, and the earth swallowed many of the executioners. The faithful, who had raised a great lamentation over the apostle’s body, were wonderfully delighted by these prodigies and tended it with the greatest honor.”

Nor will I allow you to remain unaware that Luitprand calls Saint James “our” James in the Adversaria, no. 33, where he appends a letter that he wrote to Heronius, bishop of Braga, and says:

“When I visited the sacred threshold of Saint James, son of Zebedee, our teacher and apostle, in fulfillment of my vow,” and so forth.

This makes it still clearer that the Ticinensian deacon was Spanish, at least by origin, as my most learned Father Franciscus Bivarius vigorously defends with exceptionally strong conjectures and arguments near the end of his Censure of the Works. P. H.]

The feast of Saint James, son of Zebedee, is celebrated throughout Spain this year more solemnly than it has been for many centuries.

63. [Note: [Col. 0994C]

63. Bonifacius, bishop of Coria, took part in the Sixth Council of Toledo in eleventh place. The synod was held on the fifth day before the Ides of January. Afterward he died and was honorably buried by Eugenius II in the church of Saint Justa, which at that time was a church of Toledo. He is said to have been a pious man, as those holy Fathers were. P. H.]

Blessed Bonifacius, bishop of Coria, dies at Toledo. He is honorably buried by Blessed Eugenius in the church of Saint Justa.

DCLXXVI. DCXXXVIII.

64. [Note: [Col. 0994C]

64. Concerning Eugenius and the council held under him, see Rodericus of Toledo, book II, chapter 19:

“The Sixth Council, concerning the observance of the Catholic faith and other ecclesiastical disciplines, was held in the time of the same prince Cintila, under Eugenius, metropolitan primate of the royal city, with Selva of Narbonne, Julian of Braga, Honoratus of Seville, Protasius of Tarragona, and their suffragans and deputies subscribing.” P. H.]

In this year, under the same pontiff, in the second year of King Cintila, on the fifth day before the Ides of January, the king assembled a gathering of his courtiers in the praetorian church of Saint Leocadia.

65. [Note: [Col. 0994D]

65. We discussed the day and year of Saint Isidore’s death above, in the section on Maximus. ID.]

Saint Isidore, who had already died on 4 April in the year of the Lord 635, shines forth with many miracles and with glory.

DCLXXVII. DCXXXIX.

[Col. 0995]

66. Severinus succeeds Honorius as Roman pontiff; John IV succeeds Severinus, and dies this year, on the Ides of October.

67. The see is vacant for one year, thirteen months, and seven days.

68. Saint Fara, a Benedictine virgin, fleeing from her father, comes to Tude. A monastery is built by Anastasius, bishop of Tui. She dies in the year 650 [or 657].

DCLXXVIII. DCXL.

69. [Note: [Col. 0995A]

69. Isidore and Rodericus, in the chapter cited above, discuss the death of King Cintila, except that Rodericus places his death in the era 683, that is, in the year of the Lord 645, whereas it really occurred in the era 778, that is, in 640. He died this year on Saint John’s day, and also on a Monday. P. H.]

This year, on 26 June, King Cintila dies.

70. [Note: [Col. 0995A]

70. Tulga is chosen in place of Cintila. He was consecrated on the feast of Saint James, patron of Spain, by Eugenius II, in the presence of bishops and courtiers, in the church of Saint Mary Major. He reigned for two years and two months. Rodericus writes of him in the same chapter:

“After Cintila’s death, Tulga, of good character and descended from the Gothic stock, assumed the kingdom in the era 678 and reigned for two years. He was found to be gentle and Catholic in all things. He peacefully extended the realms subject to him. In judgment he was a righteous judge; he was distinguished by generosity and was greatly marked by gentleness. The Gothic people grieved that they had so quickly lost such a character, with all mourning, because the flower of so fine a disposition did not grow into fruit. He died a natural death at Toledo.”

Joannes Mariana writes of Tulga in book VI, chapter 8:

“In place of Cintila, by the vote of the great men of the kingdom, Tulga was appointed—a youth in age, but old in virtues. In particular he distinguished himself in justice, zeal for religion, prudence, government, and skill in matters of war. He was very generous toward the needy, a virtue especially proper to kings, who ought to consider that their abundance and riches should not serve their private advantage and pleasures, but to help the weak and provide relief for the entire people.

He was advancing from these beginnings and seemed destined to rise to the summit of every virtue and valor, when death arrested his steps. It came upon him through illness in the city of Toledo in the year of our salvation 641, and he held the kingdom for only two years and four months.

Sigebert of Gembloux says that King Tulga was a frivolous youth and that, through his freedom and looseness, he gave his people an opportunity to rise against him and drive him from the kingdom. Reason demands that in this matter greater weight be given to what Saint Ildefonsus reports as an eyewitness than to what a foreigner wrote, whether out of hatred for our nation or, more probably, through error caused by the distance of the place and the time in which and at which he wrote; for circumstances of this kind easily lead to the alteration of facts.” P. H.]

It is credible that he was buried in the praetorian basilica of [Col. 0996A] Saint Leocadia; for this reason the Saracen historian Rasis calls Saint Leocadia “of the kings,” because the Gothic kings were accustomed to be buried there. In honor of this king I have also added an epitaph:

Alas! You die, Tulga, in the first flower of youth,

Though you deserved to live for many years.

With splendid character, like Titus, you rise into the world;

In mid-course the Fates cut short your thread.

In you religion shone, and piety and faith:

Generous to the poor, steadfast in justice.

One who counts your years would call you young;

One who counts your virtues would call you old.

Boys weep for you, and young men and old;

The city of Toledo calls you its father.

As king you are summoned to kingdoms better than your own,

Where peace is unbroken and the day without a cloud.

By the lot of burial, the virgin Leocadia, Tulga,

Has been joined to you, forever your friendly companion,

A companion on earth and a faithful companion above the heavens;

Everywhere she rejoices in your goodness, noble king.

You are taken from the earth, prince, so that you may tread the stars:

Your virtues opened the way for you.

The glorious King Tulga died at Toledo on 25 October, in the era 680. P. H.]

Flavius Tulga succeeds to the kingdom of the Goths; he reigns for two years and four months. He is chosen on the feast of Saint James, patron of Spain, and on that same day he is consecrated, anointed, and crowned by Eugenius of Toledo in the church of Saint Mary of Toledo.

71. [Note: [Col. 0996B]

71. Besides the testimonies already given, this is a strong and compelling argument for distinguishing between two Justuses: the man who was strangled was not bishop of Toledo, but a deacon who later became a bishop. He died more than six years after the Toledan Justus.]

This year Justus, Helladius’s deacon, because of the insolence of his tongue and the lack of restraint in his conduct, is strangled in bed with a noose by his own clerics, having been made bishop of some city—I do not know which. Some suspect that this bishop was from the city of Acci and that he took part in the Council of Toledo. Others think that he was entirely different from this man and very unlike him. All agree that he was not the Toledan pontiff.

DCLXXX. DCXLII.

72. [Note: [Col. 0996B]

72. Ecclesiastical historians have written much about the discovery of the Cross, which the emperor Heraclius brought back from Persia to Jerusalem. P. H.]

This year the emperor Heraclius, who restored the Lord’s Cross after it had been taken from the hands of the Persians, dies in May.

73. Theodorus, son of Theodorus, a Jerusalemite and Greek by nation, occupies Peter’s see after John IV; he sits for six years and five months.

74. [Note: [Col. 0996B]

74. On 16 October, the Gothic king Cindasuintus succeeds the Gothic king Tulga. Julian writes of him in the Chronicle:

“Cindasuintus reigned alone for six years, eight months, and twenty days; then together with his son, Lord King Recesuintus, for three years, seven months, and eleven days”—that is, ten years and four months in all.

Rodericus writes of him in book II, chapter 20:

“After Tulga, Chindasuintus seized the Gothic kingdom by tyranny and began to rule Iberia triumphantly in the era 685; he reigned for ten years.”

Alphonsus’s General Chronicle gives the era 689, that is, the year of Christ 651. But it is clear from the Seventh Council of Toledo that this king was in his fifth year in 646. Therefore it is necessary that on 16 October 646 Chindasuintus had completed his fourth year, and that his fifth year began on the seventeenth. Thus, by 15 October—namely, on 18 October, which was a Wednesday—only two days of that year had elapsed. The Lord Eugenius II consecrated, anointed, and crowned this king in the praetorian church of Saints Peter and Paul with great pomp and ceremony, in the manner of the Greek emperors of Constantinople. P. H.]

This year, on 14 October, King Tulga dies. Cindasuintus is chosen as king of the Goths and, on the feast of the Two Hundred Holy Martyrs, is crowned by Eugenius in the praetorian church of Saint Peter, in the presence of bishops and courtiers. In the Gothic kingdom he reigns alone for six years and seven months [or nine], and afterward together with several sons.

75. [Note: [Col. 0997A]

75. Concerning Eufridius and Gerontius, deacons, read the illustrious Ildefonsus, archbishop of Toledo, in the prologue to his book On Illustrious Men. ID.]

Fridenandus [or Eufridius the deacon], relying on the favor of King Cindasuintus, invades the dignity of the presbyterate and seizes as his own certain estates assigned to the Holy Church of Toledo. He was divinely punished, just as the presbyter Gerontius had mistreated Justus, bishop of Toledo—Justus being not the monk but the secular deacon of Toledo who had treated Saint Helladius in an unworthy manner.

DCLXXXI. DCXLIII.

76. In the see of Constantinople, Paul the heretic is installed.

DCLXXXII. DCXLIV.

77. A Roman synod is convened against Paul, the heretical patriarch of Constantinople, and three African synods are assembled against the heretics, the Monothelites.

DCLXXXIV. DCXLVI.

78. [Note: [Col. 0997A]

78. Rodericus writes as follows about the Seventh Council of Toledo in book II, chapter 20, when discussing Chindasuintus:

“In the city of Toledo, in the fifth year of his reign, he laudably ordered the synodal decree of thirty bishops to be celebrated, together with all the clergy and the deputies of those bishops whom illness or poverty had kept away, and with the body of courtiers who deserved to take part in councils. Only the notaries needed for the reading of the proceedings were present. This was the Seventh Council of Toledo, under Eugenius, metropolitan and primate of the royal city.” [Col. 0997B]

Observe two things here. First, bishops could sometimes be unable to attend a council because of illness or poverty, since they could not meet the expenses demanded by episcopal dignity in comparison with the meagerness of their annual revenues. Second, not all courtiers were customarily admitted, but only those who deserved it. P. H.]

At the beginning of the fifth year of King Cindasuintus, on 27 March, Saint Braulio, bishop of Zaragoza, a man of exceptional learning and holiness and descended from the most illustrious Gothic stock, dies. On the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November, the Seventh Council is convened at Toledo; thirty-nine bishops and deputies assemble.

DCLXXXV. DCXLVII.

79. [Note: [Col. 0997B]

79. Saint Eugenius II died fewer than many years—indeed, not even a full year, but nine months—after the council, on the first day of July. He lies in the praetorian church of Saint Leocadia, virgin and martyr. P. H.]

On the first of July Saint Eugenius II, a holy man, dies at Toledo; he is buried in the church of Saint Leocadia the martyr.

80. [Note: [Col. 0997B]

80. Verecundus, bishop of Utica, formerly archpresbyter of Toledo, died in the year 647. Felix speaks of him in his Addition to the Chronicle of Saint Ildefonsus, bishop of Toledo, On Illustrious Men.

He was first archpresbyter of Toledo and afterward bishop of Utica; he was a poet, not a bad one for those times. Felix writes of him:

“Verecundus, an African bishop, eloquent in the study of the liberal arts, published in dactylic verse two modest and brief little books. The first he published On the Resurrection and Judgment; the other, On Penance, in which he laments his own sins from infancy in verse.”

I possess the latter with notes by Juan Ruiz de Azagra, secretary to the princes of Bohemia, a truly learned man, written from an ancient Gothic manuscript on parchment. It begins:

“Who will give me a sorrowful face with tearful showers?”

Ruiz considers this to have been the man whom Victor of Utica mentions in the Chronicle. But he is mistaken: Utica is in Italy, not Africa. Felix calls him an African bishop. Clearly he is that Utican whom Saint Eugenius sent with letters to Isidore, as is clear from Isidore’s letter to Eugenius; he dedicates this work to his teacher Eugenius of Toledo.

There is also Verecundus, the holy bishop of Verona, whose annual feast is celebrated on 22 October and whom both Galesinus and the Roman Martyrology remember. In Gothic fashion he calls him Vergundus: for the Goths changed *c* into *g*, as in *locus*, *lugar*; *Graecus*, *Griego*; likewise *Verecundus*, by syncope, *Vergundus*.

Regarding the seventh synod of Toledo, Roderic mentions it in Book II, chapter 2. Saint Braulio did not attend it, perhaps because he was detained by illness. That he was still alive at the time is clear because M. Maximus died in 616; John, according to Ildefonsus, succeeded him and held the see for twelve years, until 628—beginning toward the end of 616 and continuing until 628, perhaps 629, when Suinthila also ended his life. Saint Braulio began his episcopate under King Sisenand, namely in 629 or 630, and continued for several years into the reign of Chindaswinth, almost until 648 or 649. For he held the see for approximately twenty years, as is clear from Saint Ildefonsus’s words:

> “He held the priesthood for nearly twenty years. When these had been completed, he closed the day of his present life. He continued in government during the reigns of Sisenand, Chintila, Tulga, and Chindaswinth.”

Therefore, if the Seventh Synod was held in 646, in the fifth year of King Chindaswinth, two conclusions follow from the foregoing: Saint Braulio was then alive, and Tajo of Zaragoza was not yet bishop, because, if he had been, he would have signed the council; in fact, he does not sign it. Moreover, at the Eighth Synod of Toledo he signs first among fifty-two bishops. From this it appears that he was made bishop of Zaragoza either in that year or shortly beforehand. But if he had already been a bishop when he went to Rome, seven years would already have passed, and he would not have occupied so lowly a place. I therefore believe that he went to Rome at that time as archdeacon, deacon, or presbyter, to seek out Saint Gregory’s *Moralia*. Afterwards, having returned when Saint Braulio was already dead—perhaps in 650 or 651—he became bishop of Zaragoza, and thus signed at the Eighth Council of Toledo among the last of the bishops.

When Tajo came to Rome, Saint Martin of Todi, later a martyr, was bishop of Rome. His history is also narrated by Roderic of Toledo and appears in a manuscript codex written in Gothic letters on very old parchment. I believe that King Chindaswinth, at the request of the Eighth Council of Toledo, sent letters to the holy pontiff Martin so that the portion of the *Moralia* which Saint Gregory had completed after Leander’s death, and which had been brought to Spain but could not be found, might be returned by him. These letters have entirely disappeared. What survives is only the reply to a letter from Marcus Amandus, bishop of Castellón near Gaul, a man by nationality a Gaul. Saint Martin replies to him and at the same time sends the encyclical letter of the council, after Tajo’s arrival, together with the books of Saint Gregory’s *Moralia* which Saint Leander had brought from Constantinople. He asks him to notify all the metropolitans and the king of France, since he was a neighbor and a Gaul by nationality; and this he did. [P. H.]

Verecundus, a Benedictine monk and deacon of Saint Eugenius, dies.

## 81

[Note: 81. Bishops were accustomed to use the mitre, with which they used the *petalum*, etc. It should be read: “with which they used the *petasus*.” The *petasus* is a broad-brimmed hat, which the Italians call a *capello*: a kind of wide hat by which travelers protect themselves against the sun’s heat, such as poets represent Mercury wearing. Plautus writes in the *Amphitryon*:

> “I have feathers as far as my *petasus*.”

Suetonius explains the word in *Augustus*, chapter 82:

> “In summer, with the doors of his bedroom open, and often in the colonnade, with water spraying and even someone providing ventilation, he slept. He could not endure the sun, not even in winter; during the day he walked about at home wearing a *petasus*.”

The word is Greek, πέτασος, from the verb πετάννυμι, “I spread out.” For the *petasus*, being spread out, covered and protected the head and shaded the face. Hesychius calls πέτασον ῥιπίδα ἐκ χοίνων “a fan made of reeds,” a broad-brimmed hat of wickerwork, which perhaps served as a parasol.

George Cedrenus, in the *Historical Compendium*, page 139, line 59, in the edition of John Oporinus, writes:

> Ἕϛι δὲ καὶ ἕτερα κατασκευὴ σπυρίδος, ἀντὶ πίλου τῇ κεφαλῇ τιθεμένη· καλεῖται δὲ παρ` Ἰταλοῖς κάμελα, ἐξ οὗ καὶ καμελαύκια.

“There is also another kind of basket, placed on the head instead of a felt cap; among the Italians it is called *camela*, from which comes *camelaucia*.” Xylander translates it in this way.

The *petasus*, therefore, is a broad-brimmed hat and, together with the mitre, an insignia of bishops or pontiffs. Among the Romans, the *apex*, *tutulus*, and *galerus* were among the pontiff’s ornaments. On these see Jacobus Gutherius, Book I of *On the Ancient Pontifical Law*, chapter 29. The *galerus* was called σκουφία; concerning it see George Codinus the *curopalates*, *On the Offices and Officials of the Great Church and the Imperial Court of Constantinople*, chapter 15, no. 52, page 36; and Jacobus Gretserus, Book II of the *Commentaries*, chapter 6, no. 25, page 212.

Hence we Spaniards use *scofia* to mean the nighttime covering for the head of those who sleep. Alcuin, *On the Divine Offices*, writes that the Greeks call caps *cuphias*. Hugh of Saint Victor, Book I of *On the Sacraments*, chapter 55, likewise takes *mitra*, *tiara*, *infula*, and *pileus* as equivalent. Papias does the same: “*Cidaris*, mitre, tiara, priestly cap, *cuphia*.” See what Meursius noted in his *Greek-Barbarous Glossary*, under the word Σκουφία, and Caesar Bulengerus, *On the Worship and Dress of the Pontiffs, Bishops, and Priests of Christ*, Book I, chapter 6, toward the end. D. L.]

Bishops used a mitre, with which they used a *petasus* [read: *petaso*], as did all the Apostles.

## 82

Verecundus, bishop of Utica in Africa, a man of great talent and author of pious books, dies.

**DCLXXXVI. DCXLVIII.**

## 83

Martin, son of Fabricius, of Todi, later a martyr, occupies the see for six years, four months, and seven days. Theodore succeeds him.

**DCLXXXVII. DCXLIX.**

## 84

Saint Eugenius III flourishes at Toledo in learning and holiness; later he ruled the patriarchal see of Toledo.

## 85

[Note: 85. On the synod held in Spain against the Monothelites, Onuphrius makes mention in his *Chronicle*, as does Magnus, archpresbyter of Saint Justa, in his own *Chronicle*, under the year 652—approximately the last year of Chindaswinth and the fourth of Recceswinth, who were ruling Spain together. Since this matter is quite notable, it must be examined somewhat more carefully. I find mention of it, though obscurely, in the *History* of Roderic, prelate of Toledo, Book II, chapter 22:

> “While Eugenius, metropolitan of the royal city, was shining forth,” he says, “a council of forty-six bishops was convened at Toledo, together with an innumerable clergy, deputies of the absent, and officials—highly distinguished members of the palace—in the praetorian basilica of the holy apostles Peter and Paul. There he undertook to instruct minds ignorant not only concerning worldly affairs but also concerning the mystery of the Holy Trinity.”

This was not one of the three synods celebrated at Toledo by that king; it was not, I say, the Eighth, Ninth, or Tenth. It was a separate council. For the Eighth had fifty-two bishops, as he himself reports shortly afterward; the Ninth had fifty-six bishops; and the Tenth had twenty bishops and five deputies. Therefore that other council, which had forty-six bishops, was none of these but a distinct one.

Add that divine matters are treated here—namely, the confirmation and acceptance of the Lateran Council against the Monothelites. That council was held at Rome in 652, and in the same year, under the aforesaid kings, this council of forty-six bishops was held at Toledo, toward the end of Chindaswinth’s reign, against the Monothelites, as Onuphrius teaches in his *Ecclesiastical Chronicle*, and Julian of Toledo in his own.

For a better understanding of this, one must observe that Saint Martin, Pope Martin I, in a letter to Marcus Amandus, bishop of Castellón—Castellón de la Plana, as it is commonly called—in the kingdom of Catalonia, indicates the discovery of the books requested by Tajo, but says that he had not waited for the *Moralia* to be copied. The holy pontiff writes:

> “As for the relics of the saints, about which the bearer of this letter reminded us, we ordered that they be given. For the books have already been examined by our library, and we had no way at all to give them to him; moreover, he could not copy them, because he hurried to return quickly from this city.”

The book was later copied and sent from Rome to Spain.

Regarding the subject of this council, Saint Martin writes to the said bishop:

> “We believe that it has reached you how, in the disturbance of the true faith and the trampling down of the Church, a detestable and abominable heresy arose a little more or less twenty-four years ago through Sergius, the false bishop of Constantinople, with the emperor Heraclius assisting him. It renewed the error of the Apollinarists and Manichaeans. His successor Pyrrhus, who was also a bishop and who seized the see of Constantinople through the arrogance of ambition, increased it for the worse.

> “For this reason the Apostolic See repeatedly admonished them through exhortations, protests, and many rebukes, so that they might withdraw from such error and return to the light of piety from which they had fallen. They not only refused entirely to do this, but now his successor Paul, the Constantinopolitan bishop and violator of the faith, has devised another and more wicked attempt against the Catholic faith. He seemed to be destroying what his predecessors had explained heretically, yet by sacrilegious audacity he persuaded our most merciful pontiff to issue an imperial *Type* full of every kind of perfidy, in which it was promulgated that all Christian peoples ought to believe.

> “Therefore we judged it necessary, lest through some negligence and to the detriment of the souls entrusted to us we be bound by the guilt of wrongdoing, to assemble in this Roman city a general gathering of our brothers and bishops. In their presence the criminal writings of the aforesaid heretics were examined and exposed; with one voice and one spirit we condemned them by the apostolic sword and by the definitions of the Fathers, so that all who recognized the error contained in them might not be defiled in any way by their pollution.

> “Accordingly, we have decided to send you the volumes of the synodal proceedings together with our encyclical letter, from whose sequence you can learn everything in detail and extinguish their darkness with us, as children of light. Therefore let your fraternity make these matters known to everyone, so that they may execrate with us so abominable a heresy and may learn the sacraments of their salvation. When the synodal assembly of all our brothers and bishops in those regions has been held according to the tenor of the encyclical sent by us, let them celebrate with us by sending back the written acts together with your signatures, confirming and consenting to what has recently been established for the orthodox faith and the destruction of the madness of the heretics.”

Marcus Amandus, having received the letters from Saint Martin the pope, was sent to the kings, who ordered Eugenius to assemble a synod at Toledo. This was the council against the Monothelites. Thus we may see how great was the Spanish kings’ observance toward the Holy Roman See and the bishops’ obedience: after holding the synod at Toledo, where the Lateran Council was honorably received, and after renouncing and detesting the Monothelite heresy, they sent this synod to Rome together with the bishops Tajo and Marcus Amandus.

It is astonishing that this synod has disappeared, although we find its traces clearly expressed in Onuphrius, Roderic, and Julian of Toledo. Roderic therefore rightly praises the piety and holiness of King Chindaswinth and King Recceswinth, who issued so many councils. Eugenius II did not attend this council; Eugenius III did. P. H.]

Synod of Seville against the Monothelites.

## 86

After Saint Eugenius II, pontiff of Toledo, died at Toledo in March of the year 649, Eugenius III of that name, a holy and learned man, succeeded him in the see of Toledo.

**DCXCI. DCLIII.**

## 87

[Note: 87. In this year, in the month of October, Chindaswinth died at Toledo. He died on the first day of October, a Tuesday, and was buried in the praetorian church of Saint Leocadia. Recceswinth was consecrated anew by Eugenius III in the church of Saint Mary of Alficen, as it is called, on the twentieth day of October. In the same year he summoned a council, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of January—that is, on the sixteenth day of December—on the eighth day of Saint Leocadia’s moon; it was held on a Sunday with a procession.

That the death of Recceswinth’s father was recent—namely, only two and a half months earlier—is shown by Recceswinth himself at the beginning of the council in these words:

> “Although the supreme Author of all things raised me from the times of my divinely remembered lord and father to the throne of the kingdom and made me a participant in his glory, now, however, since he has attained the eternal rest of the dwelling places, the divine power has entirely subjected to me the rights of the whole government which he left transferred to me.”

When he says “now,” he means this year. For according to Julian, his father died on the Kalends of October in the era 691—that is, in the year 653, as I have said. From this council it is also plainly evident that, while his father was still alive, Recceswinth already shared with him in the government of the entire kingdom. P. H.]

Recceswinth, the son, is named, crowned, and anointed. We have discussed the sacred anointing of kings at no. 8; now add Book XIII, title 4, part I, especially the passage:

> “For this reason they anoint kings at this time with sacred oil on the shoulder of the back of the right arm,”

where Gregorius Lopez comments, gloss 1, under the words “to the kings.” See also below, no. 123.

**Alficensis**, or “Lower.” The very ancient church of Saint Mary of Alficen was so called because it was assigned to Arabs coming from Africa Sitifensis—of which Isidore speaks in Book IV of the *Etymologies*, chapter 5, and frequently in the Theodosian Code. Thus Julian writes in his *Adversaria*, no. 516:

> “From Africa Sitifensis, now Fez, at the time of Chindaswinth there came to Toledo noble Christian Arabs, who taught the Goths the Arabic language; this later proved of great assistance to them for their future captivity. The church of Saint Mary was given to them, and by the Sitifensians it was commonly called Alficen, an Arabic word in their native language.”

He also asserts in the *Adversaria*, no. 214, that the little town of Getafe was named by them:

> “While I was writing this, the town of Getafe, which is near Madrid, was restored. The Saracens who conquered Spain wished to name it after the old African town of Satafi—read Sitifi, according to Saint Isidore, in the passage cited above—using a corrupted form and their native language.”

Hence the fortress of Alficen was likewise so called, not far from the city of Granada, where it is easy to believe that these same Arabs established a colony.

Licentiate Rades de Andrade writes similarly in the *Chronicle of the Order of Calatrava*, in the life of Master Don Rui Pérez Ponce, under the year 1292, page 47, column 2:

> “In that same year,” he says, “the master, with a famous army of the knights of this order and of its vassals—for they were many and very rich—entered the land of the Moors through the regions of the bishopric of Jaén, until he reached the kingdom of Granada. His expedition prospered at the beginning, because he seized a strong castle called Alficen, caused it to be destroyed, and found in it great quantities of gold, silver, clothing, and other things which the Moorish villagers had gathered there to keep them safer.”

Again, concerning the church of Saint Mary called Alficen in Arabic, see nos. 222, 225, and 376 of the *Chronicle*.

Luitprand calls this church “the Lower,” and Julian, in the *Chronicle*, no. 464, does likewise, because it was counted as the third—that is, the last and lower—among the three most ancient churches of Toledo. Julian explains this interpretation in the *Chronicle*, no. 74, in these words:

> “Paulatus—elsewhere Privatus—bishop of Toledo, in the year 280, lies with his predecessors at the church of Saint Mary. It is now commonly called Alficen; it was the third church of Toledo. The second was the praetorian church of Saint Leocadia, virgin and martyr; the first was Saint Mary, still consecrated to the living after the church of Zaragoza.”

Accordingly, the following passage of the same author in *On the Hermitages*, no. 15, should be corrected:

> “A hermitage at Toledo, in the suburb of Saint Mary of Alficen, from the most ancient times [there were] three churches of Toledo”—

read: “the third church of Toledo.”

> “At the time of the captivity this was the church of King Alfonso VI, where the archpresbyter of the Holy Church of Toledo almost always sat, under the patronage of the Toledo family of the Eculneos Portocarreros.”

Because these most holy churches had been erected in ancient times, the images of the Blessed Mary placed in them were also called “Ancient.” At Valladolid it is now called *Nuestra Señora de la Antigua*—“Our Lady of the Ancient.” At Ávila:

> “where, among very ancient ruins, such an old monument and tomb was unearthed a few days ago—a distinguished monument which I thought it not inappropriate to have engraved on bronze. Here it is.”

[Col. 1003] It is evident from the aforesaid no. 15 that Saint Mary of Alficen was the church of Alfonso VI and the archiepiscopal see after he captured the city. Pisa writes thus in *The History of Toledo*, Book II, chapter 21, page 15, column 4:

> “At that time the archiepiscopal see was, as it were, temporarily established in the church of Saint Mary of Alficen, in which divine worship and the Christian religion had continued uninterrupted throughout the entire period of the captivity.”

Alfonso himself asserts this in the royal donation by which he most generously favored the monks of Saints Servandus and Germanus:

> “And for the increase of monastic life, and for the reception of its servants and guests, I testify that there is there an ancient church called Saint Mary of Alficen, which never lost the title of Christianity, even in the time of the pagans, nor did it cease to be inhabited and venerated by Christians, although under the yoke of a faithless people.”

You can also establish this clearly from Julian, whose testimonies we render into a mosaic in the *Chronicle*, no. 554, under the year of Christ 1085:

> “At that time the most glorious emperor Alfonso, ever a magnificent victor, was besieging the royal city. I, however, was keeping watch as vicar for the archbishop in the vacant see, and I heard that King Alfonso was consulting the apostolic lord about appointing his kinsman Sancho as bishop of Toledo. Sancho knew little of letters, and Alfonso wished to make his cathedral—or rather the archbishopric—at Alficen. But the Holy Roman Church did not admit him, nor did the apostolic lord wish it, because he did not know letters, unless King Alfonso should designate a learned and holy man.”

Don Fray Prudentius de Sandoval mentions this passage in the *Life of King Alfonso VI*, folio 68, column 1.

The decretal letter of Pope Gregory VII, in which he replied to King Alfonso, is found in Volume III of the *General Councils*, part II, Book IX of the letters of Pope Gregory VII, letter 2, page 368, column 1; and in Volume III of the *Decretal Letters of the Supreme Pontiffs*, printed at Rome in 1591, from Book IX of Gregory VII’s Register, letter 2, page 852.

I received it through the kindness of the most learned Don Vincent Turtureti, a man who, through truly learned and deeply recondite scholarship, nourished and illuminated both his own homeland and our Spain while residing there in the public service of learning.

Since the words of his letter are highly relevant, I thought it worthwhile to set them down, so that everyone may see and recognize how great is the authority and truthfulness of Julian’s *Chronicle*. In them one may also admire the prudence and religious moderation of the supreme pontiff, who, so that Sancho’s rejection would not bring him disgrace when he reported it to the emperor, spared his name. The supreme pontiff says:

> “Regarding the person who was to be chosen as archbishop, we say that although he appears sufficiently prudent and generous, nevertheless—as is known to us and as your letter does not deny—he lacks the foundation of learning, namely, knowledge of letters. You yourself understand how necessary this virtue is not only to bishops but also to priests, since without it no one can either teach others or defend himself.

> “Therefore it is fitting that Your Serenity should strive, with the advice of our aforesaid legate Richard, abbot of Marseille, and of other religious men, to select from there, if one can be found, or otherwise to seek elsewhere, a person whose religion and learning may bring honor and salvation to your Church and kingdom.

> “Nor should you be troubled or ashamed to appoint to the government of your Church—whose proper desire is for good men—perhaps an outsider or a man of humble birth, provided that he is suitable. For the Roman commonwealth, both in pagan times and under the title of Christianity, grew chiefly, with God’s favor, because it judged not the nobility of family or homeland but the virtues of mind and body to be worthy of consideration.”

The illustrious Cardinal Baronius cites this letter in Volume XI of the *Annals*, under the year of Christ 1080, as though the supreme pontiff had written it at that time. He says that those who assign the capture of Toledo by Alfonso to the year 1085 should be corrected, since he himself is persuaded that Gregory VII wrote the letter in 1080. Yet in Gregory’s letter I find neither day nor year; indeed, I recognize it as having been placed in Volume III of the *Decretal Letters* after the council convened in 1081.

Or, if someone moved by this difficulty should prefer to think that Gregory was speaking of another archbishop rather than the archbishop of Toledo, Baronius wholeheartedly adopts that opinion. Julian resists this later conjecture, while nearly all Spanish chroniclers and historians resist the former, including Pisa, Book III of the *History of Toledo*, chapter 17, page 151, column 1; and the matter is mentioned below at no. 210.

I think it preferable to understand that, even during the captivity, Alfonso consulted Pope Gregory about the appointment of this archbishop Sancho. For the church of Alficen existed during the captivity, and there the archpresbyter of the Holy Church of Toledo sat, as Julian writes in *On the Hermitages*, no. 15; Alfonso was arranging matters for the future so that Sancho might be confirmed as archbishop.

This seems to be indicated by Julian’s words in the *Chronicle*:

> “Alfonso was consulting the apostolic lord concerning Sancho, his kinsman, for the bishopric of Toledo.”

The royal diplomas also agree with this. They are found written in the year 1083, in which the king calls himself “at Toledo”—not because Toledo had then been captured, as Pisa says, but because Alfonso, with God’s help and guidance, constantly held this intention in his mind and was already planning it in advance.

Then, when the see became vacant after the death of Peter, archbishop of Toledo, and the bishops could not meet to elect someone because of the siege, he consulted the Holy Roman Church. Thus our Julian writes in the *Chronicle*, no. 552:

> “In the year 1081 the bishop of Saint Justa, worn out by age and troubles, died at Toledo toward the end of the year, and the see became vacant because the metropolitan bishops whose duty it was to elect could not come to Toledo on account of the close siege.”

Therefore, in the year 1085, at the aforesaid no. 554, Julian says of himself:

> “At that time I was also keeping watch as vicar for the archbishop in the vacant see.”

D. L.]

In the same year, on the sixteenth day of October, Chindaswinth, king of the Visigoths, dies. His son Recceswinth succeeds him; he is crowned and anointed by Eugenius, bishop of Toledo, at Toledo in the church of Saint Mary, which is commonly called by the Arabic name Alficen, or “the Lower.”

[Col. 1003]

When the monks of Our Lady of the Ancient in the city of Ávila were opening the foundations in the year 1630 for a chapel that they were building in their church on the Gospel side, at the place where they say another chapel dedicated to Saint Andrew had formerly stood, several very ancient tombs were found. In one of them was a body with a lead tablet, of the form and bearing the letters engraved here.

It is held certain that this was a church from the time of Saint Secundus, the first bishop of Ávila and a disciple of Saint James. Reckoning the years, in the era 716—which is the year 678—it was called Saint Mary of the Ancient. Afterwards it was given to the Benedictine monks, who possess it in the year 1630 and maintain there a priory subject to Our Lady of Valvanera. Before the loss of Spain it had been an abbey, and in Ávila it had four other monasteries of its order.

In other tombs spurs, buckles, and pieces of armor were found, like those carved here. From this it is clear that those buried there were nobles, as is also stated on the tablet. A coin was found, but its lines and letters could scarcely be distinguished; what could be recognized on it was extracted.

Flavius Heraclius, descended from Constantine [read: “born of Constantine,” or “Pogonatus,” which I approve; and write *Constantinus* instead of *Constantino*], is named co-ruler of the empire by his father the emperor on the Kalends of March.

**DCXCIII. DCLV.**

## 93

Fortis, the thirty-ninth archbishop of Milan.

## 94

[Note: 94. The Ninth Synod of Toledo was convened in the seventh year of King Recceswinth. As in the Eighth, it dealt extensively with the reform of bishops and clergy and with the immoderate and disgraceful custom of women conducting burials, as Martin teaches from the letters of Amandus. He writes:

> “For it has been reported to us that priests, deacons, and others in priestly office, after their ordination, become defiled by falling into sin; and for this reason your fraternity is bound by excessive sorrow and wishes to lay down the pastoral office or service on account of their disobedience.”

On the occasion of this letter, and because the necessity of the matter required it, after they had already completed what concerned the confirmation of the Lateran Council, the Fathers assembled in the Eighth Synod of Toledo decreed many things concerning polluted bishops, priests, and deacons—not less holily than sharply and severely—as can be seen in canons 4, 5, 6, and 7, where the matter is strictly and distinctly prohibited. P. H.]

This year, the seventh of Recceswinth, king of the Visigoths, the Ninth Synod of Toledo was assembled under Eugenius III of that name.

**DCXCIV. DCLVI.**

## 95

[Note: 95. At the Tenth Synod of Toledo, in the eighth year of King Recceswinth—that is, in the year 658—the feast of the Incarnation was established for December 18. Some say that it was restored by Saint Ildefonsus, but they are mistaken, because Ildefonsus did not preside over the Tenth Council of Toledo and was not then bishop of Toledo. In reality, as Julian of Toledo, the archpresbyter, teaches, he was the first to propose it at this council; and at his request, and because of his singular devotion to the Holy Virgin, the holy Fathers instituted it.

It is certainly true that the first archbishop of Toledo to put this council’s canon into execution was Saint Ildefonsus, who held the see in the following year, as the same Julian excellently notes, as can be seen in his *Chronicle*. P. II.]

This year, the eighth of Recceswinth, king of the Visigoths, the Tenth Synod was convened at Toledo.

**DCXCV. DCLVII.**

## 96

[Note: 96. This year, on November 13, which was a Monday, Eugenius, who had already been regarded as a saint since the time of Luitprand and had been received among the blessed, died. The much earlier Usuard attests to this on that day, as does Gelasius, although he confuses him with a much more recent martyr.

Ildefonsus writes of him in *On Illustrious Men*:

> “Eugenius the Second was appointed pontiff after Eugenius. While he was an outstanding cleric of the royal Church, he delighted in the life of a monk. Fleeing secretly, he made his way to the city of Zaragoza, where he clung to the tombs of the martyrs and there properly cultivated the study of wisdom and the monastic vocation.

> “Brought back by royal force and elevated to the pontificate, he lived a life marked more by the merits of his virtues than by bodily strength. His body was frail and his physical strength small, but his spirit burned greatly with the power of virtue. Pursuing the force of good studies, he corrected chants corrupted by careless voices through his knowledge of melody and distinguished the omitted orders and care of the offices.

> “He wrote a little book on the Holy Trinity, polished in expression and clear in the truth of its subject. It could have been sent quickly to the regions of Libya and the East, had storms and tossing seas not delayed the uncertain journey of frightened travelers.

> “He also wrote two little books, one in various poetic meters and the other in prose on various subjects, composed so as to commend his holy memory firmly to the diligence of many. [On Dracontius, see Julian in the *Adversaria*, no. 498, and what I noted there; now add Isidore, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 37. D. L.] He also revised the books of Dracontius on the creation of the world, which antiquity had transmitted in corrupted form. By removing, altering, or improving whatever careless transmission had introduced, he brought them into such a beautiful form that they seem to have proceeded more beautifully from the correcting craftsman than from the author’s hand.

> “Since Dracontius, by completely passing over the seventh day, seemed to have left his work incomplete, Eugenius also marked out a recapitulation of the six days in individual verses and added, concerning the seventh day, whatever seemed to him elegantly expressed.

> “He was renowned in the time of the kings Chindaswinth and Recceswinth, holding both the dignity and the glory of the priesthood for nearly twelve years. Thus, after the setting of worldly light, he occupies the dwelling of his tomb in the basilica of Saint Leocadia.”

That is what Ildefonsus says. He also adorned Eugenius’s death with a funerary poem:

> Here lies the venerable body of Bishop Eugenius,  
> Whom the sacred temples of Leocadia hold.  
> Here he became a monk, fleeing mortal shadows,  
> And later an aged bishop in the city of Toledo.  
> The disciple gives his beloved master final verses,  
> Mindful enough of his merited service.  
> Ildefonsus, a monk, for the holy [one] [lacuna],  
> And for learned Eugenius does this out of devotion.

Saint Julian often mentions this Eugenius, in Book III, chapter 17:

> “For, to say nothing of the others, I shall briefly repeat these words of our outstanding teacher Eugenius of the see of Toledo: ‘We most truly confess the resurrection of the flesh—not as some explain it, as though we should rise in an aerial or any other flesh, but in this flesh in which we now exist and in which each person will deserve to receive a crown for rightly conducted deeds or punishment for wrongly conducted deeds.’”

And in the same book, chapter 24:

> “There will be, as our holy teacher Eugenius teaches, such and so great a beauty of the body that it will delight the sight and in no way bend the heart toward vice.”

And in the same place:

> “In accordance with the clear statement of our teacher, this is asserted: in that future glory of the resurrection, where there will be no deformity in holy bodies and no adversity of pain or labor, there will also be no need for clothing, since Christ will be all things in all.”

There exist books of Dracontius, many epigrams, and letters. Father Mariana doubts whether Eugenius should be numbered among the saints, because the records of the Church of Toledo do not list him as a saint. But since the old and the new Roman Martyrologies do list him, it is of no consequence that he is not listed by the Church of Toledo, which alone cannot make saints, nor can it refuse veneration to those whom the Roman Church venerates as saints. This is especially so because, according to the brief of Gregory XIII, all who are in the Martyrology are proposed as saints to be regarded as such by the whole Church. For he wishes that throughout the entire Church only this Martyrology be received and that such saints be recited every year. This is, in a certain sense, a tacit method of canonization.

The book of this holy teacher on the Trinity has entirely disappeared, unless it lies hidden in some basilica, just as certain works of Saint Ildefonsus lay hidden until the works of the learned Father Francis Feuardentius of the Franciscan order brought them to light. P. H.]

This year, on November 13, Saint Eugenius III dies at Toledo. He is renowned throughout Spain and celebrated as famous for miracles. He lies at Saint Leocadia outside the city; others maintain that he was buried in the house of Saint Leocadia.

## 97

[Note: 97. Concerning the election of Saint Ildefonsus to the see of Toledo in the year 657, see Cixila and Julian. The see of Toledo was vacant for seventeen days. When these had elapsed, during the nine-day office for the deceased pontiff and in consultation with the king, on the first day of December, which was a Sunday, sacred to the martyrs Saints Chrysanthus, Daria, and Maurus, Saint Ildefonsus, abbot of Agali, was placed in the see of Toledo, being fifty-three years old.

He was truly a holy, pious, learned man, wonderfully burning with the zeal of charity. He was consecrated by the suffragan bishops amid the greatest joy of the clergy and people of Toledo. Throughout the whole course of his life he was a pontiff complete in every respect, such as the collapse of ecclesiastical discipline and the corruption of morals required. He corrected the faults of his subjects more by the example of a holier life than by severity or excessive reproach. He was never burdensome to anyone and was always loved by all. ID.]

Saint Ildefonsus, abbot of Saints Cosmas and Damian.

In the year 657 the blessed Ildefonsus was elected abbot, if Luitprand is to be trusted. Accordingly, in Julian’s *Chronicle*, no. 330, it should be read as follows:

> “At this time the blessed Ildefonsus governed the Church of Toledo in holiness and piety. In the year 656”—formerly it read 636—“he was elected abbot of the holy martyrs Cosmas and Damian in the suburb of Toledo.”

By the vote of Recceswinth, king of the Visigoths, and of the clergy and people of Toledo, he was appointed as successor to the deceased. This was the ancient form of electing a bishop. For, according to the changing circumstances of the times, different methods of episcopal election were designated by the supreme pontiff, and it was not permissible to go beyond them; likewise, in accordance with various circumstances and contingencies arising from the times, the right of electing a bishop was granted or permitted by the same pontiff to different persons.

At first elections were conducted with the authority of the entire clergy and people, as is gathered from *Nosce*, *Cleri*, and *Vota*, in Distinction 63, and from Luitprand here, [Col. 1009A] as well as from Julian in the *Chronicle*, no. 542:

> “Afterward, having returned to his homeland, he [Sigefridus, abbot of Fulda] was created bishop of Mainz by the clergy and people.”

At times it was granted to secular princes that an election made by the clergy would not be valid unless their consent were added, as in *Quia igitur*, Distinction 63, chapter 9:

> “By the united consent of the whole council and the will of the most serene prince, he declares that the man should be summoned.”

Among the Spaniards there is an outstanding monument to this matter in *Cum longe*, Distinction 63, dictum 25, in these words:

> “Therefore it pleased all the bishops of Spain and Gaul that, without prejudice to the privilege of each province, it should henceforth be lawful for the bishop of Toledo to appoint as prelates in any provinces and in the sees of their predecessors whomever the royal power had chosen and the aforesaid bishops of Toledo had judged worthy,” etc.

From those distinguished times when the kings of Spain rescued the country from the jaws of the Moors—the gloss near the end of *Adrianus*, Distinction 63—the right of patronage in churches belongs to them, subject to the expected confirmation of the supreme pontiff. A celebrated text appears in Law *Antigua*, 17, title 5, Partida I:

> “And this superiority and honor belong to the kings of Spain for three reasons: first, because they conquered the land of the Moors, made the mosques into churches, expelled from it the name of Muhammad, and introduced there the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

Gregorius Lopez explains this learnedly; Gabriel Pereira cites him, together with several others, in *Manu Regia*, vol. II, chapter 22, no. 14. Rodrigo, archbishop of Toledo, agrees in book III of his *History of Spain*, chapter 12; and in our new *Recopilation* the law cited above, Law 14, title 3, book I, supports it:

> “The kings of Castile and León, with fervent devotion, Catholic and courageous hearts, and by shedding their own blood and that of their subjects and natural-born people, conquered and liberated this land from the infidel Moors, enemies of our holy Catholic faith; they placed it under the obedience of the holy Catholic faith; and the land, which for so many ages had been defiled by the Muslim sect, was recovered and cleansed by them. The churches, which for so long had been houses of blasphemy, were not only recovered by them for the praise of God and the exaltation of our holy faith, but were also abundantly endowed.”

And a little farther on:

> “And the saints Fathers have always provided the greater prelacies and dignities at the supplication of the king who was reigning at the time.”

I placed an example among the matters I noted above from our Julian in the *Chronicle*, no. 554, and in the law cited above I marked the adverb *siempre* (“always”) in red ink, so that we may trace the right of patronage of the kings of Spain back many years. I found a similar example of the election of bishops in Blasius Ortiz’s *Description of the Church of Toledo*, chapter 36; and, so that I might not deprive you of the charm of this antiquity, I did not hesitate to transcribe it:

> “Here lies Don Martín Martínez of Calahorra, archdeacon of Calatrava and canon of Calahorra. He was unanimously elected to be bishop of the church of Calahorra and La Calzada, but he did not wish to accept it, out of honor for the church of Saint Mary of Toledo. He died on the ninth day of April in the year 1368.”

The entire matter is confirmed by the inauguration of Dominic, bishop of Burgos. It was commonly reported that, during the reign of Don Pedro, king of Castile, after the death of his predecessor Ferdinand, when the clergy had divided into two opinions, Dominic had been chosen as arbiter by the will of both sides in the dispute, and that, setting aside his rivals, he had named himself bishop. The assent of those present approved this remarkable boldness; the pontifical insignia were brought to him, and the confirmation of Gregory XI, Supreme Pontiff, followed. Ferdinand Pérez de Guzmán recounts the matter in his booklet entitled *Valerio de las historias*, book VIII, title 11, chapter 4. Father Juan de Mariana follows the same line in his *General History*, written in Spanish, book XVII, chapter 8.

A similar example and the same outcome in the election of another Dominic, bishop of Civitas, during the reign of Alfonso, surnamed the Wise, was written by Antonio Sánchez Cabañas in his history of that city, which I possess in manuscript, part II, book III, chapter 6. There he adduces two diplomas of King Alfonso, one from the year 1264 and the other from 1270, in which he confirms Dominic Martin, bishop, the second of that name. On these matters see what Doctor Augustine Barbosa gathers in *De officio episcopi*, title 1, chapter 3, throughout.

Most recently, the most illustrious lord Rodrigo de Acuña, archbishop of Braga, whose innate nobility, made illustrious and conspicuous by the splendor of his learning, is revered and acknowledged by all, treats the matter in numbers 1–4 of his commentaries on Gratian’s *Decree*, on *Cum longe*, Distinction 63, chapter 25. There he reviews many authors with great learning and industry.

As an additional appendix I add the bishop of Pamplona, Don Fray Prudencio de Sandoval, in his *Chronicle of the Emperor Alfonso VII*, chapter 8. He inserts a letter of Peter, abbot of Cluny, to Innocent III, Supreme Pontiff, in which he discusses the election of a bishop by clergy and people. I also add the jurist Diego Pérez, in Book II, title 6, book I of the *Ordinances*, column 251, at the entry: “Likewise, the kings of Spain.” [D. L.]

Saint Ildefonsus, a monk of Agali, a man noble and religious, renowned for his reputation for varied learning, abbot of Saints Cosmas and Damian—the monastery distinct from Agali and dedicated to Saint Julian the martyr—was appointed in place of the deceased bishop (namely Eugenius, his kinsman), by the vote of Recceswinth, king of the Visigoths, and of the clergy and people of Toledo.

**DCXCVIII. DCLX.**

**98.** [Note: [Col. 1010B]]

**98.** Cixilla touches somewhat on the character of the king in the *Life of Saint Ildefonsus*:

> “But the former prince Recceswinth, who was reigning at that time, having laid aside earthly glory and ferocity, and though he had looked upon him with a proud eye when reproved for his iniquities, offered him with tears a small knife that he kept in its sheath. With bowed neck and suppliant hands extended from his throne, he earnestly begged that it be brought to him, asking that he not judge unworthy the man who offered it with tears.” [P. H.]

Saint Ildefonsus reproved the corrupt morals of court officials, and even the king himself, with Christian freedom; for this reason he seemed harsh both to them and to the king.

**99.** He baptized several Jews who had been converted to the faith.

**100.** [Note: [Col. 1010C]]

**100. Taio, bishop of Zaragoza.** Julian agrees with Luitprand. In the year 698 of the era, that is, in the year 660, no. 331, he says:

> “At that time the memory of Saint Taio, bishop of Zaragoza, a learned and devout man, was flourishing. He died in peace on the fourth day before the Kalends of February, in the year 698 of the era.”

In the Eighth Council of Toledo, which was celebrated in the year 691 of the era, that is, in the year 693, I find that he signed in the fiftieth place, as follows: “Taio, bishop of Zaragoza.” Yet Valderedus’s poem on Heleca, bishop of Zaragoza, in the fragments published from the poems of Maximus, differs by one year, since it establishes from him that Taio died in the year 697 of the era, that is, in the year 659. I shall not hesitate to transcribe the verses, which are highly relevant:

> I, Valderedus, myself the servant of Taio,  
> Unworthy bishop in the city of Caesaraugusta,  
> Set forth funeral verses for my beloved holy Father,  
> Clearly bearing witness to my heart in this matter.  
>   
> Taio, while life remained, was rich in virtues,  
> Noble in understanding, though weighty in speech.  
> To Spain we owe from him the volume of Gregory the Great’s *Moralia*;  
> He brought whatever that author had given.  
>   
> For this reason he sought Rome; but, divinely warned,  
> He miraculously discovered Gregory’s work.  
> Thence he returned with greater renown, unchanged in virtue,  
> And labored greatly over Gregory’s immense work.  
>   
> Now, weighed down by age, he had become filled with rich gifts;  
> In life his hand was generous and his conduct upright.  
> Dead, he is buried in the ancient church of the Column,  
> And the bishop’s good mind flies to the heavens.

> “The most holy bishop, God’s servant Taio, died in peace at Zaragoza, in the year 697 of the era, on the fourth day before the Kalends of February.”

Taio is held in great renown and glory among the Spaniards. For, as you have now clearly seen written, he brought to Spain from Rome the books of the *Moralia* of Saint Gregory the Great, the pontiff; and he was sent for this purpose with the approval of the Third Holy Council of Toledo. Rodrigo relates the matter in book II of his *History*, chapter 20:

> “At this council” [he is speaking of the Seventh], “there was great disturbance because the book of the *Moralia*, which Blessed Gregory had composed at the request of Blessed Leander, had been lost through negligence and was not available in Spain. Therefore the same prince, with the approval of the holy council, sent Taio, bishop of Zaragoza, who signed the Eighth Synod, outstanding in religion and learning and devoted to the Scriptures, by ship to the Roman pontiff with his request for the books of the *Moralia*.”

On this matter, and on the miraculous appearance of the books of the *Moralia*, consult what the most eminent García de Loaysa published from a very ancient manuscript in his *Seventh Council of Toledo*, page 414. But Archbishop Rodrigo narrates the matter much more fully; our Luitprand refers to him below, no. 365, where, at the end of the *Chronicle*, he gathers several things worthy of remembrance.

An outstanding memorial of Taio survives in a poem which he composed with tears for Honoratus, bishop of Seville, as follows:

> “Taio, archdeacon of Zaragoza, dedicates this sepulchral poem to the most holy bishop Honoratus, his brother from Zaragoza and archbishop of Seville:
>
> > Bishop Honoratus had succeeded Isidore here;  
> > Seville holds his blessed bones.  
> > Now, while life remained and he rejoiced through nine lustrums,  
> > His spirit holds the stars, while his body lies in the urn.  
> > His life was better than his speech, but his speech was restrained.  
> > Now he rejoices and fears no hostile threats.”

> “The same bishop died on the day before the Ides of November, in the year 678 of the era. He held office for five years and six months.”

The most learned Rodrigo Caro illuminates this inscription in his additions to the *Chronicle of Maximus*, page 232, as does Don Francisco Fernández Beltrán, abbot of Olivares, in his treatise on the subject. Most recently, the distinguished Paulus de Espinosa de los Monteros has done so in his *History of Seville*, book II, chapter 23.

Father Diego Murillo had previously discussed Taio more clearly and fully in his *History of Zaragoza*, treatise 1, chapter 29, page 242, and the books of the *Moralia* that Taio himself brought to Zaragoza in the same work, chapter 1, page 2, column 1, and chapter 3, page 16, column 2. Murillo asserts that they were deposited in the library of the Holy Church of Saint Mary of the Pillar, in a certain cabinet bearing this inscription:

> “In this chest are contained the *Moralia* of blessed Gregory, miraculously found at Rome by Taio, bishop of Zaragoza.”

The Reverend Don Coccinus, dean of the Roman Rota, mentions these books and adds other matters worthy of remembrance in his decision in the case concerning the cathedral church of Zaragoza, page 9, at the beginning.
