Perhaps Taio also composed some writings, concerning which Julian speaks in the *Chronicle*, no. 414. [D. L.]

Taio, bishop of Zaragoza, is held in glory.

**DCXCIX. DCLXI.**

[Col. 1011]

**101.** [Note: [Col. 1012A]]

**101.** Julian says in the *Life of Saint Ildefonsus* that there were three heretics. It is commonly accepted that these three heretics attacked the virginity of Saint Mary, Mother of God, and that Ildefonsus published a book to overcome them beginning, “My Lady and sovereign Lady,” etc. But that book contains much about the heretics, though more about the praises of the Blessed Virgin. Thus Rodrigo, book II, chapter 22:

> “In his time, when Elvidius and Pelagius, coming from Gaul, had infected many parts of Spain by defaming the virginity of Blessed Mary, Blessed Ildefonsus confronted them with testimonies from the sacred Scriptures, with honeyed speech, and with grace poured upon his lips. He refuted their doctrine and drove them, confounded, from Spain.”

Neither Julian nor Cixilla recounts the history of this wicked doctrine in the way it is told here. Julian merely indicates, when discussing Saint Ildefonsus’s books, that in the book he published *On the Childbearing of the Blessed Virgin Mary*, Ildefonsus wrote against certain people who then said that the Blessed Virgin had remained a virgin both before childbirth and after childbirth, while maliciously asserting that she had given birth in the natural manner, as other women give birth, through the dilation of the birth passages. Hence, says the holy doctor, they wished in reality, although not in clear and explicit words, to teach the contrary: namely, that she had not remained a virgin, just as other women do not remain virgins when they give birth according to the customary law of nature.

The holy doctor, warning King Recceswinth of the danger to the faith, requested that, in view of the gravity of so great a matter and the manifest danger to the people, he order a national council to be convened at Toledo, so that the heretics, convicted there, might renounce their heresy, or that the obstinate might be sent into exile. When the synod had been held, the heretics who remained in their perfidy were expelled from all Spain with disgrace and dishonor, as Julian, archpriest of Saint Justa, reports. And, lest the dangerous heresy spread—as cancer customarily does—Ildefonsus composed a book and dedicated it to the Toledan nuns of Saint Benedict.

This book had lain hidden for many years. It was discovered in Gaul by Doctor Fray Francisco Feuardent, a Franciscan, and printed in volume IX of the *Library of the Ancient Fathers*, published at Paris. There it is called *The Book on the Childbearing of the Blessed Virgin Mary*:

> “Although the virginity of the blessed and glorious Mother of God Mary is the adornment, honor, and model of virtue for all the Churches, it is especially so for religious women and virgins, whose chastity is particularly illuminated by her virtues, formed by her examples, and strengthened by her merits. Therefore, to venerate and contemplate her most sacred childbirth with the deepest devotion of mind and heart is a grace of divine favor.
>
> “To fight and conquer on her behalf against heretical depravity, however, is the work of the Holy Spirit and the power of the Most High, who overshadowed her, so that without intercourse with a man and without any corruption she might give birth to God and man, and might always remain a virgin. On her behalf, we read that Blessed Jerome once wrote against the heretic Helvidius and his associates; he so thoroughly defeated and conquered them that from then until the present no renewed error against her has arisen.
>
> “But because the shameless boldness of certain brothers is again troubling itself with questions, I have decided to write to you, women of Christ, about those matters which they attempt to explain with greater curiosity than reverence against her modesty. By examining her childbirth and the womb of her chastity, they introduce, as though they were highly skilled philologists, with a sufficiently cunning argument, a defilement of vices in which very many dangers of error converge.
>
> “For they say that the blessed Virgin Mary could not, and ought not, have given birth in any other way than according to the common law of nature and in the manner customary among all women, so that Christ’s birth might be called a true birth. Others say: ‘If he was not born as other infants are born, it is not a true birth.’ And therefore, lest he be thought a phantom, or lest he be believed to have been born through the Virgin’s womb as water passes through a channel, without the ordinary process of birth, they consider it pious to believe that he was born according to the law of nature, as other infants are born, and that she gave birth as other women give birth.
>
> “O blind piety, which thinks so impiously about the Virgin Mary, and blind presumption, which speaks so impiously about Christ! I do not say that they claim she lost her virginity—she who, without knowing a man, conceived as a virgin, gave birth as a virgin, and remained a virgin—but they deny the very thing they confess when they say that she brought forth her son as a woman in childbirth according to the common law of nature.
>
> “But if it is as they maintain and assert—God forbid—then Mary is no longer a virgin; Christ was born under a curse, a son of wrath, from sinful flesh; and she who is proclaimed blessed by the angel, still remaining under a curse, gave birth under a curse.
>
> “Otherwise, why do they seek the law of nature in Mary, where everything that was in her was possessed by the Holy Spirit? For the power of the Most High overshadowed her.”

From this it is easily gathered that the error of those Gauls who descended from the province of Narbonne did not consist in verbally denying that the Holy Virgin had remained a virgin while denying it in reality. For, although she conceived as a virgin, if, during that dilation and in the manner customary to women giving birth according to the law of nature, the virginal barriers were opened—as they asserted—she would not have remained a virgin.

When Saint Ildefonsus learned of this, he warned the king that a council of the entire nation, as Julian says, ought to be convened at Toledo, where this error was to be debated. The heretics were indeed convicted at the council by Saint Ildefonsus’s most powerful arguments; but, since they refused to repent, they were condemned to exile, which the king ordered to be carried out.

Otherwise, it seemed strange to me that, in so great a danger to the Spanish people, a council was not assembled, and that during the nine years in which Saint Ildefonsus presided no council was held at Toledo, especially since his predecessors had held many. Afterward, not content with the council’s decision, and wishing to satisfy his own piety and oppose the persuasion of the people, he wrote the book *On Virginity* that I have cited, which he decided to dedicate to the Toledan nuns of his order.

From this one may understand how great was the devotion of the Spanish people toward the Blessed Virgin. Saint Ildefonsus defended her honor and virginal dignity by assembling a synod and publishing books. And where was this pernicious heresy, born in Gaul, to be destroyed except in Spain, which the most holy Virgin chose before all the nations of the world? While still alive she had favored Spain and, by her bodily presence, had most clearly enriched it.

Spain, therefore, is the sword of heresies and the place where all errors are put to death. By divine providence, heresies that arise elsewhere are finally driven there to be pierced and slaughtered by the sword, and this by a particular privilege of the Virgin. No heresy has thus far arisen in Spain; those that erupted and were born elsewhere were suffocated there. So it was with the Arian, Priscillianist, and Vigilantian heresies.

And if the diligence, zeal, piety, and vigilance of the most holy Office of the Inquisition have always been sufficiently active, now especially—all things belonging to pure faith and religion having, as all acknowledge, been entrusted to it by God through the intercession of the Blessed Virgin and Saint James, with voices raised in proclamation, since Spain plainly possesses a great deal of these things, more than the other regions of the world—and deservedly so.

But let us return to our Luitprand. He had certainly read the books of Saint Ildefonsus and, as the matter actually stands, understood the error of those who had descended from Gaul, when he says that they held that “by the virginal barriers being dilated and loosened in the manner of other women, our Lord Jesus Christ had been born.”

He also remembers the council, saying:

> “Saint Ildefonsus refuted them by the council, by his speeches, and by the books he published, and caused the king Recceswinth to exterminate them from all Spain.”

But that this book was not the same as the other book, the one he published under the title *Synonyms*, is made clear by the same author, who says:

> “Before these times he had composed the book *Synonyms*, in which he speaks tenderly and devoutly with the holy Virgin in the manner of a soliloquy. It begins as follows: ‘My Lady, my sovereign Lady,’ etc.”

But you may ask: When was this synod held? I answer that it was held on the first day of December and, according to Julian, extended until the end of the month. [P. H.]

Heretics coming from Narbonne, Goths by nationality—theudius and Helladius—wandering *tominae* through Spain. Read *temere* (“rashly”). On these heretics see below, no. 3; Julian in the *Chronicle*, no. 338, where I cite Father Gabriel Vázquez, part III, disputation 121, chapter 21; the man of exceptional learning Father Alfonso Vázquez, in his *Ildefonsus*, book IV, chapter 3, folio 275; and Father Francisco Portocarrero, in the golden little book *On the Descent of the Virgin Mary, Mother of God*, folio 34B. See again Julian in the *Chronicle*, nos. 342 and 344. Add the notable passage of Pelagius, bishop of Oviedo, cited by me below, no. 197, concerning Helvidius and Jovinian; on them see Father Theodorus Petreius, in the *Catalogue of Heretics*, under “Helvidians,” page 83, and “Jovinianists,” page 203; Bishop Guido of Perpignan, in the *Summa on Heresies*, chapters 60 and 61, and under heresy 47. [D. L.]

Heretics coming from Narbonne, Goths by nationality—Theudius and Helladius—wandering through Spain in a most wicked manner [correction: “most wickedly,” evidently for the corrupt reading *tominae*], and rashly holding opinions concerning the virginity of the Blessed Virgin Mary, namely, that she had given birth to Christ the Lord, true God and man and her son, with the virginal barriers dilated in the manner of other women: Ildefonsus vigorously refuted them in fourteen speeches and in published books, distinct from the *Soliloquies* beginning “My Lady.” Having chastised them by order of King Recceswinth, the Catholic and most severe [or, alternatively, “most serene”] prince, he compelled them to go into exile throughout Spain.

**[Col. 1013] 102.** [Note: [Col. 1014B]]

**102.** On the ninth day of December, when the bishops were going in procession to the church of Saint Leocadia, the miracle of the apparition of the holy virgin took place. Besides what Julian of Toledo says, Cixilla teaches the same thing in the *Life of Saint Ildefonsus*, in these words:

> “And the most beautiful Virgin, answering his gaze, came before him, while the bishops, princes, and priests were crying out…”

For no bishops other than those who had assembled for the council could have been present there. For this reason Saint Leocadia said: “By the life of Ildefonsus my Lady lives,” because he had labored greatly to convene the synod and had convicted the heretics in the public light and before the eyes of the entire council through debate. The Son most graciously wished to repay this service rendered to the Virgin with a similar sign of favor.

The council was therefore held in the year 661, and in that year the remarkable apparition of Saint Leocadia, virgin and martyr, took place. Six years after the first miracle, a second occurred, concerning the apparition of the Blessed Virgin, namely, in the year 667; for in that year the Dominical letter was C, and the nineteenth day of December was a Saturday.

Concerning the loss of the memory of Saint Leocadia’s body, see Cixilla in the *Life of Saint Ildefonsus*; concerning the ivory chair, the same source; and the *Breviary* or *Tables* of the Holy Church of Toledo, collected by the Sacred Congregation of Rites and approved by Father Ribadeneira in the *Life of Saint Ildefonsus*. [P. H.]

**102.** In this year she appeared on the nineteenth day of December. Our Julian discusses this apparition in the *Chronicle*, no. 345, as do Cixilla in the *Life of Saint Ildefonsus* and many others.

Many have been uncertain about the name by which the church was known where Saint Leocadia appeared to Blessed Ildefonsus. It should be known that three churches had been dedicated to Saint Leocadia, virgin and martyr: two collegiate churches and a third parish church.

They were: the church in which the virgin was born and brought up; the church near the royal citadel, which held the martyr in prison; and the church situated on the river Tagus in the suburb of Toledo, which guarded her burial place.

Blasius Ortiz, canon of Toledo, gives a vivid account in chapter 12 of his description of the great church of Toledo, folio 36:

> “Three churches have been dedicated in this city to the divine martyr Leocadia. Two of them are collegiate; the third is parochial and, as I have received from our ancestors, was built in her own house. Of the collegiate churches, one stands at the prison adjoining the royal capitol on its southern side, where she gave back her spirit to the Most High. There, in a certain cave in which she was held bound, she impressed the sign of the cross upon the stone with her own fingers; this is still venerated with great devotion. The other stands outside the walls of this city, where her body was committed to burial.”

The most eminent Cardinal Caesar Baronius briefly embraces the whole matter in the *Roman Martyrology* on 19 December:

> “Three basilicas erected in her memory still remain there: the first where she was born, the second where she suffered, and the third where she was buried.”

The most illustrious Archbishop García de Loaysa explains it more fully in his notes on the Fourth Council of Toledo, page 364. Francisco de Pisa relates the same in his *History of Toledo*, book II, chapter 17, folio 85, column 2. The sixth reading in the proper office of this unconquered martyr sings in nearly the same manner. In these churches various councils were held at various times:

> “Such honor was bestowed upon them that many councils of Toledo, and those held very frequently, took place especially in them.”

This is manifest from the Fourth Council, which was celebrated in the basilica of Saint Leocadia, and from the Fifth, which was assembled in the same place. In both cases the matter is expressly written.

The Fourth says:

> “For when the entire assembly of all of us was already present together in the basilica of the most blessed and holy confessor Leocadia…”

The Fifth says:

> “At the city of Toledo, priests of the Lord from different provinces of Spain, we who were seated together in one college of Peace, in the basilica of Saint Leocadia the confessor…”

Likewise the Sixth Council, whose wording is as follows:

> “And having taken our proper seats in the Toledan praetorium, in the church of Saint Leocadia the virgin…”

Finally, the Seventeenth says:

> “While in the church of the glorious virgin and confessor of Christ, Saint Leocadia, which is in the suburb of Toledo, where her holy body rests…”

You see that the assemblies of the councils did not meet in one and the same church, but in churches of Saint Leocadia. Yet it is useful and necessary to examine the matter precisely, while preserving the number and order of the councils.

The Basilica of Saint Leocadia mentioned in the Fourth and Fifth Councils was understood to be the church where the most holy virgin was born and brought up. Its name and form make this clear.

Its name does so because it is distinct from the praetorian church and from the other one in the suburb. Thus it was a basilica that was parochial, situated in the virgin’s own house and erected in the city of Toledo, which King Sisebut built.

Saint Eulogius, although he does not use the word *basilica*, demonstrates the point through a periphrasis and elegant description, calling it a royal hall in his *Apologeticus of the Martyrs*, folio 80B:

> “At Toledo also”—these are his words—“the hall of Blessed Leocadia, by order of the aforesaid prince [Sisebut], stretches upward with a lofty roof, built with marvelous workmanship.”

What else can *basilica* signify but a royal structure built with marvelous workmanship and a lofty, hanging roof, truly the building described by Eulogius? Let us, if you please, borrow a proper explanation of *basilica* from the most eminent Caesar Baronius, under 5 August, at the words: “At Rome, on the Esquiline, the dedication of Saint Mary Major.” He says:

> “Although this word seems to have been received from the pagans, it is nevertheless not foreign to the diction of divine Scripture. For the greater court of Solomon’s temple is called a basilica in 3 Chronicles, chapters 4 and 6, although in Greek it is read as *aulēn* (αὐλήν)—observe that *basilica* and *aula* have the same meaning—which others translate as ‘court.’ Among us, however, usage has prevailed so that not every church is called a basilica, but only those whose size is more august. As to why churches of this kind came to be called basilicas, Isidore says in book V of the *Etymologies*: ‘Basilicas were formerly called the dwellings of kings; hence they also have their name.’”

After a brief interruption he takes up the thread again:

> “As for their structure, several porticoes were joined together lengthwise, supported by columns set at equal intervals and joined above by architraves, as though woven together with one another.”

Ovid, in book II of the *Metamorphoses*, elegantly describes a basilica in Roman style and language:

> The palace of the Sun stood high on lofty columns,  
> Bright with shimmering gold and with pyrope imitating flames.

Perhaps Sisebutus joined several houses into one, among which he included the dwelling of the holy virgin. Archbishop Rodrigo of Toledo supports this view in book II of his *History*, chapter 17, where he says of Sisebut:

> “He built the church of Saint Leocadia at Toledo with marvelous workmanship.”

He did not say that it was the praetorian church, nor that it was in the suburb of Toledo, but simply “at Toledo,” that is, in the center of Toledo. This excludes the interpretation of Ambrosius de Morales in his *Apologeticus of Saint Eulogius*, where he asserts that Sisebut’s temple was the very one that still survives outside the city today, not far from the river Tagus.

Julian himself removes the matter from doubt and explains it in his *Adversaria*, nos. 287–288:

> “The parish church that Sisebut built for Saint Leocadia is called a basilica. According to the tradition received from our ancestors, there stood beside the house where Saint Leocadia, the Toledan virgin and martyr, was born and brought up, a huge temple or basilica dedicated to Minerva Carpetana, where the Gothic kings once lived. Sisebut made this, together with the holy woman’s house, into a church consecrated to the same divine martyr. It contained many porticoes and spacious walks, and was commonly called the basilica of Saint Leocadia.”

Which church was called the praetorian church? The question is difficult and uncertain.

Here lies the task, here the labor … But to bring the dispute to an end, it is certainly necessary to state beforehand that among the Romans the imperial residence was called a *praetorium* because the ancients called any military commander a *praetor*, and called their tents *praetoria*. Hence the prefects of the praetorium received their name.

There is an important testimony to this in the final law of the *Code*, *On the Office of the Governor of a Province*, where the emperor Anastasius—not Leo, as in the commonly printed texts—wrote to the prefect of the praetorium in these words:

> “No judge who governs provinces may, in cities where sacred palaces or praetoria exist, abandon them and claim the houses of private persons for his own habitation as though they were praetoria.”

In these buildings, therefore, praetors or governors customarily lived or administered justice. Dionysius Gothofredus gathers further evidence under the cited final law, as does Guido Pancirolus in *Thesaurus of Various Readings*, book II, chapter 191, pages 283–284.

Hence it is clear from Saint John, chapter 18, verse 28, that the Jews did not enter the praetorium:

> Καὶ αὐτοὶ οὐκ εἰσῆλθον εἰς τὸ πραιτώριον  
> “And they themselves did not enter the praetorium,”

so that they would not be defiled, but might eat the Passover.

*Praetorium* is a Greek-barbarous word, as is demonstrated by various passages of authors cited in the *Greek-Barbarous Glossary* of John Meursius, under the word Πραιτώριον.

Saint Eulogius gives a particularly apt account of the meaning of *praetorium* in *Memorial of the Saints*, book I, near the beginning, page 17B, where he speaks of the steadfast and powerful ardor of the martyrs:

> “And thus, he says, they stood undaunted against the public enemy, raising the banner of truth openly, as though before the doors of the praetorium and at the very entrance of the palace, bearing witness, the charge of perdition, confusion, and disgrace.”

Tertullian must be understood as referring to such a praetorium in *To Scapula*, chapter 3:

> “Claudius Herminianus in Cappadocia, indignant that his wife had joined this sect, treated the Christians cruelly. He alone was ravaged by disease in his praetorium, and while still alive boiled with worms.”

Saint Jerome merrily calls the jar of Diogenes a *praetorium* in book II *Against Jovinian*. [D. L.]

A *praetorium* was also a more spaciously built part of a country estate, set aside for the master of the household’s dwelling. The jurist Ulpian, in Law *Plenum*, 12, title *On Use and Habitation*, says:

> “He must have full use if both the villa and the praetorium have been left to him.”

Neratius likewise says in Law 2, title *On Rural Servitudes of Estates*:

> “The servitudes of rural estates include the right to raise a building higher and to obstruct the neighboring praetorium.”

The same Ulpian closes the series in Law *Urban Estates*, 198, title *On the Meaning of Words*. There John Gaeddeus, no. 5, and Dionysius Gothofredus, under the letter M, discuss the matter; and under Law *To Titius* 34, section 3, title *On Legacies*, book II, they lead the procession. Among the poets our Martial brings up the rear, book X, epigram 79:

> Torquatus has his praetorium at the fourth milestone;  
> At the fourth milestone Otacilius bought a small country estate.

From this I illuminate the matter with the words of the Sixth Council of Toledo, at its very beginning. They are these:

> “And, in the praetorium of Toledo, in the church of Saint Leocadia the virgin, after the proper seats had been arranged.”

Hence it is clear that the council was convened in the church adjoining the praetorium, which was the august residence of the Gothic kings; therefore we read “in the praetorium of Toledo,” that is, in the royal citadel. Ambrosius de Morales interprets it in this way, *History*, part II, book XII, chapter 23:

> “The Sixth Council of Toledo was celebrated in the church of Saint Leocadia, and it seems that this was the one in the Alcázar, because it is specifically stated to have been in the Praetorium of Toledo; and nothing else can be understood here by ‘Praetorium’ except the Alcázar or Royal House. The Goths, a warlike people, may be believed to have called it by the same name by which the Romans, whom they imitated, named the general’s tent in war. In peace they used the name in some fashion, as is seen in sacred evangelical history and elsewhere; and it seems that, to distinguish it from another church of this saint, this title was added to it.”

The most learned Father Juan de Mariana expressed the same view in his *History of Spain*, written in Latin, book VI, chapter 6, where he discusses the Sixth Council of Toledo:

> “The assembly was held before the church of Saint Leocadia, near the praetorium (now joined to the royal citadel, preserving traces of its former elegance and grandeur), on 9 January, in the year of salvation 637.”

The words of the council—“in the praetorium of Toledo”—clearly demonstrate this, I say, as though establishing a distinction between the praetorian church adjoining the citadel and the praetorian church situated in the suburb. The latter (and this is the third church of Saint Leocadia) is mentioned in the Seventeenth Council of Toledo:

> “While many bishops of Spain and Gaul had assembled in the church of the glorious virgin and confessor of Christ, Saint Leocadia, which is in the suburb of Toledo, where her holy body rests…”

Concerning the suburban praetorian church, our Julian says in his *Chronicle*, no. 343:

> “In this year [667], Saint Leocadia, virgin and martyr, appeared on the ninth day of December to Saint Ildefonsus, archbishop of Toledo, in her suburban praetorian church, adjoining the river Tagus.”

And Luitprand, although he marked the church in which he says that the blessed virgin appeared to King Sisebut merely with the designation *praetoriensis*, sufficiently indicates—as if pointing with an extended finger toward the source—that it was suburban, by the apparition itself as he relates it. The same Luitprand says plainly below, no. 282:

> “When Muhammad was king of Toledo, a marvelous bridge was built over the Tagus at the column of Saint Leocadia the praetorian.”

He said that the praetorian church of Saint Leocadia was near the Tagus.

Thus I reconcile those whom Father Juan de Mariana reports as disagreeing with one another in the aforementioned chapter 6 of book VI of his *History of Spain*, published in our vernacular:

> “The council, which was the sixth among those of Toledo, was celebrated in Saint Leocadia the praetorian. Some understand this to have been the church of the saint situated beside the Alcázar, which is called *praetorium* in Latin and, in its old age, shows traces of its former refinement and grandeur. Others maintain that the praetorian church of Saint Leocadia was the one outside the city, because country houses too are called *praetoria*.”

These are the additions Mariana made in the final edition, composed in Spanish in the year 1617.

Rasis calls this church royal, perhaps because it preserved buried the bodies of several Gothic kings:

> “And in his time [that of Theodosius] they built in Spain the church of Toledo, which they call that of the Kings, and which the Christians call Saint Leocadia.”

In another Latin translation of the historian, it is read as follows:

> “In the time of Diocletian, the Christians who were in Toledo in Spain began to build a church, which afterward was called the Church of the Kings. The Christians call it Saint Leocadia.”

From our Julian’s *Adversaria*, no. 289, it is evident that the apparition of Saint Leocadia took place in the suburban praetorian church, as he himself reported in the aforementioned *Chronicle*, no. 343, and that the church was called royal. Hear Julian:

> “I also learned from my elders that, in the royal chapel of Saint Leocadia, the body was buried in the greater chapel of the palace; and that near the Virgin’s tomb, a throne had been placed against the wall for King Receswinth, covered with purple and gold according to Gothic custom. He sat so near the tomb that the king himself, on his own authority, gave the little sword to Saint Ildefonsus, which is preserved with the veil in the greater church.”

Whether this was in the royal chapel of the church itself is examined and debated by the most learned V. D. Vincent Turturetus in his book *On the Royal Chapel*, chapter 2, page 29.

Julian, so that we may leave no stone unturned, writes that the apparition of Saint Leocadia occurred in the same year in which the most holy Virgin Mary appeared to Saint Ildefonsus; Luitprand places it six years earlier, as the most learned Father Hieronymus de la Higuera observes. D. L.]

In this year, on the ninth day of December, Saint Leocadia, virgin and martyr (whose body was unknown as to where it lay), appeared to the holy pontiff in the Praetorian church. From that time Ildefonsus became an object of admiration and wondrous reverence to the Catholic king.

[Col. 1017] 103. [Note: [Col. 1018B]

103. He is also called Abelardus. Others read *Adhelardus*; *Adalardus* is better. See Surius, volume I, on the second day of January. Concerning this Saint Genesius, abbot of Corbie, see Julian in the *Adversaria*, nos. 246, 253, 254, 255, 256, and 266. In Usuard, on the second day of January, you will find Adalardus: “At Corbie, the deposition of Saint Adalardus, abbot.” His life, John Molanus says, was written by Saint Ratbertus, abbot and sixth successor of Saint Adalardus in French Corbie. Our Julian, however, in the *Adversaria*, no. 253, asserts that in Usuard there is found the feast of Genesius Adelardus, though on 21 May, not 2 January, as in Usuard and Surius. His words are:

> “Usuard mentions the translation of Saint Genesius, surnamed Abelardus [read: Adelardus], from Corbie into Spain in the Martyrology on 21 May, together with that of the same saint and others celebrated on that day.”

Concerning his translation, in the *Chronicle*, no. 420:

> “From there [from the monastery of Corbie], after a hundred years, he was transferred to a hermitage on the seacoast near Carthage Spartaria, where he had lived while alive; there he is visited by a great multitude of Mozarabs from the surrounding towns.”

And no. 461:

> “The body of Saint Abelardus [Adelardus], or Genesius, was brought by certain Gallic monks to the coast of Carthage, from ancient Corbie, his former home and the abbey of the holy man.”

That Odo succeeded Saint Genesius in the abbacy of Corbie is attested by the same Julian in the *Adversaria*, no. 255, as is his participation in the Council of Soissons.

Concerning Adelardus, sent to Rome by the Emperor Charles to Pope Leo, there is testimony in the Council of Aachen in the year of Christ 809, most recently published among the Gallican councils by the most learned Father Jacobus Sirmondus, priest of the Society of Jesus. I was permitted to enjoy the gentleness of his character, his innate mildness, his universal learning, and his profound religious devotion when I was staying in Paris, having been sent by our most powerful and Catholic king Philip IV to Louis XIII, the Most Christian King of France. He published it, I say, in volume II of the *Councils*, folio 256. The words are:

> “For the purpose of settling this question [concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit], Bernarius, bishop of Worms, and Adalardus, abbot of the monastery of Corbie, were sent to Pope Leo in Rome.”

From this it follows that the year of his death assigned by me in Julian must be corrected. For he was performing the office of legate in the said year 809, whereas in the printed Julian he seems to have died in the year 800, as is clear from the margin at the aforementioned no. 420. This conjecture—or rather, I should say, this evident correction—is especially confirmed by the fact that at the Council of Noyon, held in the year 814, we know that Adelardus was assembled with the other abbots, as is clear in volume II of the Gallican Councils, folio 327; and again at the Council of Attigny, in the year 822, folios 448 and 450. This correction is also suggested by the fact that in Julian’s margin no intercalary number of years is appended from the year 800 through the year 828. Hence it may easily be believed that the number of years was omitted in the aforementioned no. 420, and that the true number, corresponding to the chronology, ought to be written.

After I had set these matters down, I obtained Julian’s *Chronicle*, written in the very hand of Father Hieronymus de la Higuera. In it, the events concerning Saint Adelardus at no. 420 are assigned in the margin to the year of Christ 820, while those that follow at no. 421 are recorded as having occurred in the year 826. Thus a suitable place is also provided for Adelardus’s embassy and for the subscriptions, which do not extend beyond the year 822, while the events that Julian relates at the aforementioned no. 420 could, according to the notation of the years, have occurred as late as 826.

Unless you prefer, so that I may leave no stone unturned, to say that Julian, in the history of the year in which Adelardus had not yet died, spoke by anticipation of his death. Many things in the *Chronicle* must be understood in this way, as he himself testifies concerning the Acts of the Apostles in the *Adversaria*, no. 485, and as the most learned Father Franciscus de Bivar notes in his commentary on Flavius Dexter at the year of Christ 308, commentary 2, no. 2. D. L.]

The holy pontiff had composed, for his private devotion, a certain book of *Soliloquies with the Blessed Virgin*, called *Synonyma*. Afterward he wrote, in elegant style, books and sermons against these heretics. This is established by the letter of Genesius, the second of that name, of Lyons—also called Abelardus [or Adelardus]—formerly abbot of Corbie and afterward bishop of Urcia.

DCCI. DCLXIII.

[Col. 1019]

104. Reparatus, the thirty-sixth bishop. The Ravennate flourishes.

105. Theodore, a native of Tarsus, archbishop of Canterbury, flourishes with a reputation for rare wisdom and prudence.

DCCII. DCLXIV.

106. A British synod is held concerning the controversy over Easter between the English and the Irish, or Scots.

DCCIII. DCLXV.

107. Flavius Gundebertus [or Gondebertus] and Flavius Protharisus [or Portharisus, or Bertarisus], sons of King Arebettus [or Ariperth], reign in Italy for one year.

DCCIV. DCLXVI.

108. Gundebertus [or Gondebertus] is killed; Protharisus [or Bertarisus] is driven into exile.

109. Flavius Grimoaldus, after defeating the sons of Ariperth, eventually becomes king of the Lombards.

DCCV. DCLXVII.

110. [Note: [Col. 1019B]

110. And the stone is preserved. A marble stone, held in the highest honor and reverence by the people, is preserved today in the chapel of the Descent of the Blessed Virgin Mary in the church of Toledo. P. H.

He gives a cape wrought in heaven. Concerning the word *cappa*, see Julian in the *Chronicle*, nos. 343 and 347, and in *On the Hermitages of Spain*, no. 30; and Nicolaus Rigaltius, a most learned man with whom I recently entered into a literary friendship in Paris, in his *Greek-Barbarous Glossary*, under the word Κάππα, “kappa”; Cerda in the *Sacred Adversaria*—whom I rightly and willingly name, with admiration, as my teacher, although he sometimes suppresses my name in his works—under the word *Cappa*; Convarruvias in the *Thesaurus of the Spanish Language*, under *Cappa*; Father Franciscus Portocarrero in his booklet *On the Descent of the Virgin Mary*; and also the others whom I have seen and praised in the aforementioned no. 343 of Julian’s *Chronicle*. Most recently I add V. C. D. Vincent Turturetus in *The Royal Chapel, or On the Chapels and Chaplains of Kings*, chapter 1, nos. 2 and following. D. L.]

On Thursday, the eve of the Expectation of the Blessed Virgin Mary—which was celebrated on the following day—the feast of the Incarnation is celebrated in Spain, that is, on 18 December; and from this time the stone is preserved on which the Blessed Virgin placed her feet. Saint Ildefonsus, archbishop of Toledo, saw—after the apparition of Saint Leocadia, excluding the nine intervening days—the Blessed Virgin accompanied by many hosts of angels and heavenly beings, seated on an ivory chair, on which he himself used to sit while addressing the people [alternatively: preaching, or believing], in the chief church dedicated to that Virgin. The chair is now preserved in great honor in the church of Saint Justa. The Virgin spoke sweetly to him and gave him a cape wrought in heaven.

DCCVI. DCLXVIII.

111. [Note: [Col. 1020A]

111. Concerning the men of Elbora, also Luitprand and Julian of Toledo. P. H.—Elbora in the Carpetanian region. Read what I noted above at no. 101. D. L.]

The men of Elbora in the Carpetanian region, Theudius and Helladius, troublesome heretics who had returned to Spain and were reclaiming Elbora, boldly and madly raging, scourge them disgracefully and drive them shamefully from their seats.

112. [Note: [Col. 1020A]

112. D. Laurentius to his Bivarius, greetings.

In Córdoba, Toledo, and other places in Spain, the memory of Saint Genesius, a Spanish martyr, is most celebrated. Concerning Saint Genesius the soldier, a Spanish martyr who suffered at Córdoba, Julian frequently mentions him in the *Chronicle*, no. 376, in these words:

> “The sacred churches of Saint Genesius, a Spanish soldier who suffered at Córdoba, have been destroyed.”

In the *Adversaria*, no. 139:

> “At Toledo, Saint Genesius, a martyr of Córdoba, who suffered under Nero, is held in honor.”

The author himself seems to recognize this at no. 326, when he says that, in the first persecutions of the Church—that is, those under Nero—Saint Genesius suffered with his companions on 11 October. The Roman Martyrology assigns the same day to him, although it does not explain under which emperor he obtained martyrdom. Its words are:

> “Likewise, the passion of Saints Anastasius the presbyter, Placidus, Genesius, and their companions.”

There the most illustrious Cardinal Baronius cites only ancient manuscripts.

Saint Eulogius frequently mentions Saint Genesius in book II of the *Memorial of the Saints*, chapter 10, no. 13; in the *Apology for the Martyrs*, no. 19; and in the *Life of Saint Pelagius*, page 114. Julian also testifies to this in the *Adversaria*, no. 289:

> “There is frequent remembrance in Saint Eulogius the martyr of Saint Genesius, a Spanish soldier and martyr who, as they report, suffered near Córdoba.”

Ambrosius de Morales, in his *Apology for Eulogius*, no. 19, writes that the monastery of Saint Genesius was situated near the village of Tertios, following the authority of Alvarus in the *Life of Saint Eulogius*. But since Morales had not yet recognized Genesius as a Spanish soldier and martyr of Córdoba, he summons two martyrs named Genesius—one Roman, the other Arelatensis—celebrated and entered in the Martyrology on 25 August: the former an *exceptor* [short-hand writer], the latter a mime; and he confuses them with the Spaniard. Hence churches in Spain were consecrated to Genesius, their own soldier and martyr. Many of them have stood or been rebuilt for many years.

Julian gives the following account in the aforementioned no. 289 of the *Adversaria*:

> “The body of this Genesius was brought by the Christians of Córdoba from Córdoba to Alarcurrim; and when the Lord revealed it to King Alfonso, who won Toledo, he restored at Toledo the old parish of Saint Genesius for this reason. It is celebrated on 20 August [read: 25].”

These words—if conjecture is permitted—entered the text from the margin, written by someone ignorant of this hidden antiquity. For the martyrdom of Saint Genesius the Spaniard is commemorated on 11 October, as we have said.

But the injury of time, which often buries the truth through the circumstances of its setting, and the confusion of identical names, caused Saint Genesius to be celebrated on 26 August by those who knew only the Roman and Arelatensian martyrs, whose feast day is in the Roman Martyrology. Hence the people of Madrid seized upon 25 August as a day to be dedicated to Saint Genesius.

For it is neither credible nor likely that the Spaniards in ancient times marked their churches with the name of Saint Genesius of Arles or Rome, when they possessed a martyr who was the glory and ornament of their homeland, one who could rightly, not wrongly, be counted among their protectors.

Learned men hold this opinion, as Hieronymus de Quintana judiciously notes in his *History of Madrid*, book I, chapter 43, folio 63, column 3, and he calls others to share his view. This equivocation arising from the same names is not unusual among writers. We have seen Genesius of Arles confused with Genesius of Rome by Mombricius and Petrus in the *Catalogue*, as Baronius testifies in the Roman Martyrology on 25 August, letter E.

And, what is even more significant and highly relevant here, I find that the same thing happened in the feast of Saint Columba, at which the readings of the *Life of Saint Columba of Gaul* were read before the memory of the Cordoban saint came to light. The most learned Father Martinus de Roa, a master of both Latin and Spanish eloquence, noted this in prose and verse in the *Flower of the Holy Martyrs of Córdoba* on 18 September, page 149. I consider it worthwhile to transcribe his words:

> “The reading at Matins of the history of the holy woman of France had no other cause than that the history of this other woman of Córdoba was unknown, and that people had been deceived by the similarity of the name, because the writings of Saint Eulogius, which did not appear until the year 1572 in the archives of the Church of Oviedo, were lacking.”

He adds that when the readings of the Gallican Saint Columba were being read, the Supreme Pontiff Clement VIII assigned proper readings to the Spanish Columba.

The most learned Father Franciscus de Soria, a pupil of the household of Saint Basil the Great, said these things with elegant eloquence and singular learning in his sermon on Saint Genesius, folio 4, page 2.

Flavius L. Dexter supports this conjecture. He restored to the church of Palencia its true patron, the Spanish martyr Antoninus, who suffered under the fury of the pagans, whereas until then, from the restoration of that city, the people of Palencia had recognized only the Gallic martyr Antoninus, whose fame was then more widespread. Hence they adopted the emblems of the Gallic crown—that is, the three golden lilies—and, as a royal veil, hung and affixed them throughout our legal jurisdiction to all the churches and to their doors, by which the church claimed them for itself in place of distinguished titles.

This same name of the two martyrs Antoninus misled the citizens; Flavius led them by the hand toward the truth. The same course is followed in the account of Saint Antoninus of Palencia given by Vincent of Beauvais in the *Historical Mirror*, book XIII, chapter 35, where *Carrion*, not *Avarion*, should be read as the name of the river; beside it Antoninus received martyrdom and was cast into its waters.

Saint Antoninus also presents the account in part I of his *History*, chapter 1, title 8, § 42; Esquilinus does not depart from it in book III of his *Catalogue*, chapter 24. I noted it in my French *Itinerary* when I came to the city of Palencia, and most recently Father F. Bivar in his supplicatory booklet. He had already said the same in the year of Christ 308, commentary II, no. 11; and Dom Franciscus de Sandoval, abbot of Saint Savior and canon of Palencia, followed the same trail in his *Apology for Saint Antoninus the Spaniard*, § 3, from page 11.

Flavius Lucius Dexter presents Genesius the Spaniard to us in the year 353, no. 3, and, as many interpret it, the Genesius of Mantua in Carpetania, not the Cordoban; he says that he suffered there and under the Emperor Julian. His words are:

> “At Mantua of the Carpetanians, Anastasius the presbyter, Placidus, Genesius, and their companions are held in honor, because afterward, under Julian, they suffered an illustrious martyrdom together there for the faith of Christ.”

Let a threefold wedge come to the aid of a threefold knot. Since Luitprand and Julian deny the matter, I consult Oedipus concerning this sphinx; and, as they say, from the tripod I seek an oracle from that mitred initiate, Father Franciscus de Bivar, who happily unlocks the innermost shrines of more expert learning through doctrine, erudition, and knowledge of languages. O that he might give an answer! To depart from him would be impious and sacrilegious. I hope he will do so, for the good and learned man knows how to reconcile things.

The passage requires a physician’s hands—or, I should say, a butcher’s. I shall add, as an appendix, whatever he may call his lot; and beyond the lot there will be an addition and an excursion in which, since I have wandered widely, a legitimate excuse may be found: my household gods and ancestral spirits stand across from the church of Saint Genesius, whose divine power they devoutly regard and venerate.

Bivarius to D. Laurentius.

> “Whatever grace and affection absent friends can bestow upon one another, I think I ought to owe you, and you ought to owe me, not only because we share a purpose, but also by reason of the obligation of our mutual fellowship” (*Bernard, Letter 75).

Bernard could not have spoken these words more truly to his own abbot of Pultaria than I can speak them to you, my most learned Laurentius. But now, as the proverb has it, I do not doubt that you come from the Academy: so learnedly, subtly, and elegantly do you write about Genesius.

Yet why do you seek an oracle from the tripod when you yourself speak from the tripod? “But I am speaking with a friend,” you say. Yet a friend extends only to the altars; now you seek a friend upon the very altars. To deny anything at the altars is impious and sacrilegious. Accept what I am going to say about Genesius, then, as though I were offering ivy after the *anthesteria*—that is, as something needing the support of your floral wreaths.

I recognize four martyr Genesiuses—leaving aside Genesius Adelardus, whom Luitprand also mentions: the Roman, an archmime; the Arelatensian, an *exceptor*; whose names the Church annually repeats with praise on 25 August; and two Spaniards, the Cordoban and the Mantu(an). For there are many things that prove that the latter two differ from one another no less than from the others.

First, a third Genesius must be admitted, neither a mime nor an *exceptor*, but a companion of Anastasius the presbyter. The Roman Martyrology itself proclaims this on 11 October; Dexter asserts that he was a Spaniard, and Julian and Luitprand likewise affirm that Genesius was a Spanish martyr.

Moreover, Dexter makes no mention of the Cordoban, nor Luitprand of the Mantu(an). That there were actually two men is clearer than daylight from the time, homeland, and tombs of each. The Cordoban Genesius suffered under Nero, according to Luitprand and with Julian’s support; you, my lord, cite his words. The Mantu(an), however, the companion of Anastasius and Placidus, suffered under Julian the Apostate, three hundred years after the death of the Cordoban.

For the persecution of Nero raged in the year of Christ 60—indeed, witnesses are the martyrs of Ilipula, or Granada, who were killed for Christ in Spain as early as the year 57, that is, in the eleventh year of Nero, according to the lead tablets agreeing with Dexter. Julian began his reign in the year of Our Lord 361 and spent two years in it. Will a gap of three hundred years, then, fail to distinguish these martyrs?

As for the difference of homeland, the Neronian martyr served as a legionary soldier at Rutenium in Celtiberia and gave his neck to Christ at Córdoba. The Julianic martyr lived as a citizen of Lisbon, as Dexter also testifies in the year of Christ 308—not because he had already been born in that year, but because, in speaking there of Vincent and the sisters of Lisbon, fellow citizens of Genesius, Dexter found the occasion to discuss Genesius and his companions—and he died at Mantua.

I take this from the same Dexter at the year of Christ 353, together with what Julian says in the *Adversaria*, no. 149.

Again, Genesius the Cordoban, or Rutenian, received a tomb at Córdoba and was afterward transferred from there to Alarcurrim. The Mantu(an), or Lisbonian, is believed by his presence to protect Mantua; for nowhere is it written that he was transferred from there.

A further distinction, not to be despised, is drawn from the companions: the Cordoban was crowned with martyrdom without any companion, whereas the Mantu(an) suffered with two companions known by name, Anastasius and Placidus, and with nearly twenty others who remain anonymous.

[Col. 1023B]

Here, then, Dexter, Luitprand, and Julian are reconciled. Julian alone differs from himself for a time, when in the *Adversaria*, no. 149, he says:

> “Saint Genesius, a martyr of Córdoba, who suffered under Nero, is celebrated on 20 August [or rather, as you correct it, 25]. He is said to have been a Spaniard and a legionary soldier in the fortress of Rutenia.”

And rightly so. But later, at no. 326, he seems to confuse the two, saying:

> “At Rutenia in Spain, in Celtiberia, on 11 October, the feast of the holy martyrs Anastasius the presbyter, Genesius the soldier, and their companions, who suffered in the first persecutions of the Church.”

But he wrote this in the *Adversaria*, which were being drafted hastily, before the codex had reached its mature form, lest the memory of events should fade; from these notes proper and lasting tables were later to be made.

> “If the *Adversaria* have the same force, diligence, and authority as the tables”—

as Cicero once said concerning Quintus Roscius—

> “what need is there to establish a codex?”

He says that Anastasius and Genesius, whose feast is celebrated on 11 October, were killed in the first persecutions of the Church. But this is beside the point, since they suffered in the final persecution; it is useless to associate them with the fortress of Rutenia, which they share only with the Cordoban. We must therefore stand by the earlier writing at no. 149 and reject the later one.

We must stand by the same Julian, and by Luitprand also, who establish the worship of the Cordoban Genesius by the temples erected to him at Toledo and Córdoba, provided that we say that the church in Madrid was dedicated to its own Genesius—even though, as time passed and the memory of so great a martyr was obliterated, it yielded to the veneration of the Arelatensian.

I shall add, as a crowning ornament, a pearl with which your household gods may joyfully meet their own Genesius and adorn the church before its doors. From my papers, to which I attach great weight, I shall produce for you the Acts of our martyrs Anastasius, Genesius, Placidus, and their companions. These will provide an outstanding support for what has been said and will be most pleasing to my Mantuans in accordance with their desire.

Would that they might burn more fervently in veneration of their patrons, visit the church dedicated to Genesius more frequently in memory of them, and henceforth celebrate 11 October as the proper feast day of their saints, a day worthy of veneration under many titles. The account reads as follows:

**The Martyrdom of Saints Anastasius, Placidus, and Genesius, and Their Companions.**

> “After Constantine and his sons had died, Julian took up the reins of the Empire. Having apostatized from the faith of Christ, which he had professed in baptism, he took care to restore idolatry and reestablish it throughout the Roman Empire. Taking this as his opportunity, he put many Christians to death as martyrs. Among these were Anastasius, Placidus, and Genesius, and their companions, who were killed for Christ in the region of the Spaniards. We have judged it worthwhile to relate how this occurred, for the devotion of those who come after us and for the glorification of the saints.

> “These three athletes of Christ were born in Lisbon, a city of Lusitania, but in such a way that only Placidus had parents who were citizens of Lisbon. Anastasius’s parents were citizens of Mantua, a city of the Carpetanians, while Genesius’s were from Barcelona. Nevertheless, they were all related to one another by blood.

> “While they were staying in Lisbon on business, it happened that Anastasius and Genesius were *aucti fuerint* [“were increased”; the printed reading and its syntax are uncertain]. Together with Placidus, a boy of similar age, they were educated in the whole sacred law of God and in the study of the sciences, in which they became highly accomplished. Still more, they began to flourish in holy conduct and deeds, so that their virtue and learning became widely known.

> “As time passed, Anastasius was admitted to the order of presbyters and devoted himself more freely to evangelical preaching. Genesius and Placidus were his most faithful assistants in it. They preached against the error of the Arians, which caused many Christians to stray from the purity of the faith, and against the worship of idols, which Julian was striving to introduce through his ministers.

> “After they had remained for a long time in Lisbon, devoting themselves to many works of charity, Anastasius decided to return to his homeland, Mantua, where by hereditary right he had received considerable property from the death of his mother. Placidus and Genesius, his most faithful friends, accompanied him.

> “They lived in one house and went about together, devoting themselves to preaching and works of charity. They gave alms to the poor and consolation to the afflicted, and especially visited and encouraged Christians detained in prison.

> “When the reputation of the saints reached the ears of the governor of the city—who was most devoted to the worship of idols and for that reason held twenty professors and defenders of our religion bound in chains—he ordered the holy martyrs to be brought before him. Having ascertained their faith, he tried to make them renounce it, now by promises, now by threats and the severity of the punishments he would inflict.

> “But when he saw that his effort was fruitless and could not soften the hearts of the saints, he ordered them, bound with harsh chains, to be led into a dark prison, where they were tortured most severely for several days. Even there, however, they did not cease preaching. By this means they made some of those who were wavering in the faith because of the severity of the torments firm and constant in spirit.

> “Finally, on the eleventh day of October, they were led to a field outside the city, beheaded for the Lord, and received the palms of martyrdom. Their relatives gathered their bodies and buried them within Anastasius’s own house. Eight days later, those twenty men were led to the same place of execution and likewise, beheaded for their confession of Christ, flew up to heaven. The Christians buried their bodies at night in the same place in the field, through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ,” and so forth.

Thus far what Father Franciscus de Bivar wrote back to me. The deed fulfilled the wish, and the outcome answered the prophecy. I give the token of a friend as a token of ecclesiastical antiquity and an everlasting memorial, and I write the name beneath Bivar’s token. I do not refuse to append a little sketch, or *hypomnema*, written with my light hand, if I may put it so: it preceded—not, however, so that the priest might recite it with me leading the way—the bringing of the Acts of Saint Genesius to light and the illumination of his memory. D. L.]

In Córdoba, Toledo, and other places in Spain, the memory of Saint Genesius, a Spanish martyr who suffered at Córdoba in the most savage persecution of the Emperor Nero, is most celebrated.

[Col. 1023] 113. [Note: [Col. 1024D]

113. Concerning the sword that was preserved with the veil, and is still preserved in the treasury of the Holy Church of Toledo, see Doctor Blasius Ortizius and others. Today it is enclosed in a silver pyx by order of the most illustrious Cardinal Gaspar de Quiroga. P. H.

But I learned that a considerable part of this chair had been transferred elsewhere. The words of Aegidius Zamorensis cast light for Luitprand and very clearly disclose the place where the chair is kept. They are these:

> “I heard that, at the arrival of the Saracens, the Christians of Toledo carried into a forest twelve thousand paces distant from Trogillo and there hid the chair, a piece of the Cross, and a certain image; and that from ancient times lights have appeared in the air.”

This tract is today called by the inhabitants Santa Cruz de la Sierra, and, as is fitting, its name is derived from this holy piece of wood. A most brilliant cross likewise hangs at night in the empty air, seen by many; it bears witness to the hidden wood and also gives and imposes its name upon the town.

It was an ancient Roman colony, afterward occupied for a long time by the Arabs, and finally captured, after Córdoba had already been taken, by the holy king Ferdinand III and brought under his rule.

Now it remains ennobled by the dominion and protection of Don Juan de Chaves y Mendoza, Count of la Calzada, a most deserving counselor of our Catholic king Philip IV the Great of Spain in the Supreme Council and Royal Chamber, and likewise president in the assembly of the military orders, who adorns our Spain with the splendor of nobility and the ornament of letters.

Concerning the antiquity of this town and the appearance of the lights, see the marvelous though true little narrative in Father Franciscus Portocarrero’s golden booklet *On the Descent of the Blessed Virgin Mary to the Church of Toledo*, chapter 24. D. L.]

In this same year, a little sword was placed in the treasury of the Holy Church of Toledo. King Receswinth of the Goths had given it to Saint Ildefonsus for cutting the veil of Saint Leocadia, who had appeared by divine power.

It is now in the treasury of the cathedral of Saint Justa, together with a marble stone of the purest white color. When the most holy Virgin Mary descended from heaven, she placed her feet upon this stone; it served as a footstool for the archbishops of Toledo. The Blessed Virgin wished to adorn it and add authority to the chair which, from Saint James onward, had always been the first-born daughter of the Roman Church and the teacher of truth. But I learned that a considerable part of this chair had been transferred elsewhere.

[Col. 1025] 114. [Note: [Col. 1025B]

### 114.

Julian and Gudila have often been mentioned above, in the nineteenth year of King Reccesuinth and the eighth year of Ildefonsus’s pontificate. He died at Toledo on 23 January, as appears from the Toledan tables, the Roman Martyrology, and Julian, who writes:

> “On the following day, the tenth day before the Kalends of February, he was released from the dwelling of the flesh and buried in the church of Blessed Leocadia, laid at the feet of his predecessor, with whom he is believed to enjoy the eternal dwelling of glory.”

He died on a Tuesday, in that leap year, with the Dominical Letters B and A. Saint Julian, his disciple, composed this funerary poem for him. He was a distinguished and outstanding teacher of Spain, called the Chrysostom, the torch of the divine Spirit, the anchor of faith, and the hammer that most powerfully crushed the boldness of exultant heretics.

Of the holy doctor’s works Julian writes:

> “He certainly wrote very many books, powerful in a most polished style, which he judged should be divided into so many parts: namely, a book of prosopopoeia concerning his own weakness; a book *On the Virginity of Saint Mary* against three unbelievers; a short work *On the Properties of the Persons of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit*; a short work of *Annotations on Divine Action*; a short work of *Annotations on the Sacraments*; one book *On the Administration of Baptism*, and another *On the Progress of the Spiritual Desert*, which he wished to be joined as a whole to the volume of the first part. The book of the second part is also a book of *Letters*, in which he treats various Scriptures in enigmatic forms; he also introduced persons into titles, and in it obtained from certain people more polished answers to his writings. He said that the third part consisted of Masses and hymns. Finally, there is a book of a further part, the fourth, composed in verse and prose, in which many epitaphs and certain epigrams are recorded. He also wrote many other things which, hindered by various occupations and troubles, he left partly begun and partly incomplete.”

There is, however, the greatest doubt as to how Saint Julian does not mention the book *On Illustrious Men*, nor the *History of the Goths*, which we know with certainty to be by Saint Ildefonsus; nor likewise the book *Synonyms*, since the book *On Virginity* is the one I mentioned. It is first established that the book *Synonyms* is Saint Ildefonsus’s from the testimony of Liutprand, and because I myself saw a manuscript, written in Gothic letters on parchment 540 years ago, preserved in the monastery of the Holy Trinity at Toledo. This gives me reason to think that Saint Ildefonsus left it not entirely finished and completed, as also happened with *On Illustrious Men*: had he lived, he would have wished to add more men to it.

Nor do I find the solution of Graialis, or of the teacher Grialis, satisfactory, since it is like an appendix to the books of Saint Isidore. Concerning the *Chronicle*, there seems to me to be no doubt, for the author Julian of Toledo mentioned it more than five hundred years ago; Lucas of Tuy, Morales, Don García de Loaysa, and especially Don Rodrigo of Toledo also mention it, Book II, chapter 22, in these words:

> “And when Blessed Isidore wrote the origin of the Goths down to the fifth year of Suinthila, Saint Ildefonsus faithfully continued the history of the Goths, Alans, Vandals, and Suevi from the fifth year of Suinthila down to the eighteenth year of Reccesuinth.”

The general *History of Spain*, Cardinal Baronius, and Morales cite this book. Since it was not wholly complete in every respect, perhaps the holy doctor did not intend to publish the book, but to suppress it. I possess this *Chronicle*, illuminated with annotations.

Julian, who later became archbishop of the royal city of Toledo, flourished in reputation for wisdom and holiness together with the other deacons of the Toledan church, Gudila and Felix.

### 115.

On the twenty-third day of January, Saint Ildefonsus, most renowned for wisdom, holiness of life, and miracles, departed to heaven. He was buried in the church of Saint Leocadia, which had been his home, at the feet of his predecessor Saint Eugenius. His disciple and archdeacon Julian composed the following funerary verses for him and had them placed there:

> This venerable body of Alfonso lies beneath this stone,  
> Than whom the land of Toledo bore nothing better;  
> Born to Lucia and Stephen, of illustrious Gothic stock,  
> He shines, made nobler still by virtue.
>
> As a young man he found a harbor and, abandoning the world,  
> Loved the cells of the Agalian monastery.  
> From there he was carried away as bishop to the city of Toledo,  
> For it had been his desire to dwell in his own see.

### 116.

Saint Torquatus was among the companions of the archbishop of Acci.

### 117.

[Note: Recesuinthus, abbot of the Order of Saint Benedict and a citizen of Braga, is also mentioned by Julian. According to Julian, he was an excellent poet and a most learned theologian.]

Recesuinthus, a Benedictine abbot of Braga, flourished.

### 118.

[Note: Much is said in his Life about Quiricus, citizen and bishop of Barcelona, who founded the monastery of Saint Eulalia in the bishopric of Barcelona. He confirmed the Tenth Council of Toledo in tenth place under the name “Quiricus, bishop of Barcelona.” In the Eleventh Council he is bishop of Toledo; that council was held in 675, while the Tenth was held in 656. The Eleventh Council of Toledo was held nearly twenty years after the Tenth. He died immediately after the fatal potion had been administered to Wamba.

This Quiricus was a monk and abbot of the Agalian monastery, of the Order of Saint Benedict, an outstanding and exceptionally learned man. Thus Julian:]

> Quiricus, who piously bears the name received from the Lord,  
> Monk and bishop of Barcelona, hail.  
> You were once the most holy abbot of Agali,  
> And Barcelona rejoices greatly in you as bishop.  
> Piety appointed you over the Toledan flock:  
> As a loving bishop, you behold the divided sees.  
> Nothing was better than you, nor more holy than you alone;  
> And you die grieving when the king has fallen into madness.  
> Leocadia receives you as a companion in joyful arms,  
> A man in body, placing your rejoicing mind in the heights.  
> Rejoice in your lot, venerable bishop Quiricus;  
> Thus you are lord on earth and lord in heaven.

In the same year Quiricus, previously bishop of Barcelona, governed the Toledan Church not long afterward; he had become bishop of Barcelona after being abbot of Agali.

This year, on the Kalends of September, the emperor Flavius Reccesuinth died at Toledo. He was buried in the church of Saint Leocadia, where the blessed virgin and martyr is said to have been confined [read: slain].

### 123.

[Note: Julian says much about the election of King Wamba in his book, as do Morales and Mariana, and Julian of Toledo. It is established that the coronation was performed by Quiricus of Toledo in the church of Saint Mary Major with great solemnity. — P. H.]

The anointing was delayed. Concerning the anointing of kings, see what I noted under numbers 8 and 87. — D. L.

“On the Sunday mentioned above, sacred Januarius and his companions.” Perhaps because 19 September of that year was a Sunday; or, in place of *supradicto*, one should read *dicato*, and in place of *sacro*, *sancto*. — I. D.

“The first Toledan church.” See what I said under number 87 concerning the words “Alficensis, or lower.” There I cite Julian in the *Chronicle*, number 74. — I. D.

In the same year, but on the Tuesday of that month, Flavius Wamba, a palace official of the noblest Gothic lineage, was elected king of the Visigoths. His anointing was delayed until the nineteenth day of the same month, so that it might take place in the presence of the bishops and palace officials, on the Sunday mentioned above, dedicated to Saint Januarius and his companions, in the principal church, consecrated to the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary—the first church of Toledo, established by the holy Fathers. He was crowned, consecrated, and anointed king by Quiricus, archbishop of Toledo, with the other bishops assisting.

### 126.

[Note: The Eleventh Council of Toledo, held under King Wamba, is mentioned in the Toledan Councils themselves, both manuscript and printed. It was convened in the fourth year of Wamba’s reign, in the era 713, on the seventh day before the Ides of November. Wamba began his reign in 672, on the first day of September; the year was completed on 1 September of this year 675; the fourth year began on the first day of September, from the year 661 or 662.

For thirteen years no synod had been convened at Toledo, as the same Eleventh Council observes in noting the length of this interval. Rodrigo writes of it in Book III, chapter 11:

> “This Wamba, in the fourth year of his reign, prepared a council of salvation in the city of Toledo, in the atrium and sanctuary of Blessed Mary ever-virgin, after eighteen years had passed amid disturbances and various disasters; and this was the Eleventh Council of Toledo under Quiricus, primate of the royal city. Sixteen bishops and many representatives of absent bishops attended this council, and with them they lamented the years passing without a council. Thus speaks the holy synod: ‘For we had remained unstable here amid the pollution of the declining age, because the long succession of years, with the light of councils withdrawn, had increased not so much vices as it was introducing the wickedness of all those ruling into idle minds [variant: ignorance, the mother of all errors],’ etc.”

And below:

> “So that, after the passage of eighteen, namely, waning years, we might at last deserve to be gathered together in one assembly concerning the matters mentioned above.”

He is not speaking of councils held elsewhere, but of those held in the royal city; for it is clearly established that councils had been convened in Zaragoza nineteen years earlier and in Mérida nine years earlier.

Sixteen bishops were assembled, besides Quiricus, together with many representatives. In the printed editions two are listed, “the bishop of Arcavica and the bishop of Segovia,” along with seven abbots. From this it may be inferred that Don Rodrigo read the bishops and representatives of this holy council differently from the way we now read them in our copies. — P. H.]

The Eleventh Synod of Toledo was convened at Toledo by seventeen bishops, under the presidency of Quiricus, bishop of Toledo, on the seventh day before the Ides of November, in the fourth year of King Wamba, in the basilica of Saint Mary.

### 127.

Gratindus, abbot of Saints Cosmas and Damian, flourished.

**DCCXIV. DCLXXVI.**

### 128.

[Note: In the year 676, after the wars had been quieted, King Wamba adorned Toledo with public buildings, walls, fortifications, and bridges. Rodrigo writes of these matters in his *History*, Book III, chapter 11:

> “After the king had been restored in triumph to the royal seat, meditating upon the scepters of his kingdom, he elegantly renewed the city of Toledo with a wall and elaborate workmanship. Praising it also in verse, he had the following inscription written in letters cut with an iron stylus on polished, gleaming marble above the gates:
>
> Wamba, illustrious king, raised this city,  
> Extending the renowned honor of his people, with God’s favor.
>
> On the memorials of the martyrs, which he inscribed upon the same towers of the gates, he likewise wrote:
>
> Holy lords, whose presence shines here,  
> Preserve this city and its people with your customary favor.”

The general *Chronicle*, under King Ildefonsus X, says where these inscriptions of the holy martyrs were placed:

> “He likewise had these verses written on separate marbles and placed them on the towers of the city gates, at those belonging especially to the holy martyrs whose dedications they were.”

Thus, at the Cambrón Gate, Saint Leocadia; to the south, Saints Felix and Peter; in the tower opposite Saints Peter and Paul, the Praetorian apostles; opposite Saint Julian, Saints Cosmas and Damian; Saint Torquatus; Saints Justa and Rufina; Saint Mark; Saint Sebastian; Saint Luke; Saint Eulalia; and Saints Servandus and Germanus.

On this subject the scholar Juan de Mariana writes in Book IV, chapter 14:

> “The King”—namely Wamba—“took care to beautify his kingdom in every way, and especially enlarged the royal city of Toledo. For its fortification he raised a new wall with towers, battlements, and parapets, extending through the suburb of San Isidro from one bridge to the other. Toledo is enclosed on more than three of its four sides by the Tagus, which channels itself between very high cliffs and runs through great rocks and narrow passes. The fourth side has a very steep and difficult approach, where it is enclosed by a Roman-built wall narrower than the one King Wamba constructed; traces of it can be seen at the Zocodover square and at the Iron Gate. Wamba, intending to bring the suburbs within the city and to strengthen it further, added the other wall lower down. Stones were brought from every direction for the work, apparently from a Roman structure shaped like a cart, which stands nearby and bears figures carved upon it, resembling a rose or wheel. The common people imagine these to be Wamba’s arms. The stones themselves show otherwise, for they are without order or design: the workmen set them just as they brought them.”

This is Mariana’s account. Those roses or little wheels are the *masopae* of buildings, brought from the circus itself; Vitruvius mentions them more than once, as Juan Bautista Montenegro, an excellent Toledan architect, informed me. — P. H.]

To Saint Thyrsus, a citizen of Toledo and a martyr who suffered abroad. [Col. 1029D] The most learned Father Francisco Bivar discusses Saint Thyrsus fully and learnedly in his commentary on Dexter, under the year of Christ 286, number 2, after the commentary, folio 303.

Liutprand says that he “suffered abroad,” because he won the palm of martyrdom at Apollonia in Greece. Below, under number 233, he writes:

> “At Toledo a church was built for Saint Thyrsus, Christ’s native servant, a citizen of Toledo, who suffered at Apollonia in Greece.”

He called him *vernula*, meaning native or natural—just as we speak of a vernacular language and a native flavor. Saint Leocadia is commemorated illustriously and in explicit terms in an ancient hymn, as is also attested by testimony; these are discussed below, under number 75 of the Toledan Council, at the end, among Liutprand’s *Adversaria*. Of Saint James likewise:

> O truly worthy and holier apostle,  
> Illustrious head, shining over Spain,  
> Our protector and native patron.

My most learned Bivar teaches and proves this in his commentary on Dexter, under the year of Christ 286, number 2. Julian also agrees and supports it in his *Chronicle*, number 73:

> “In the city of Apollonia in Greece he gave an illustrious testimony to the faith under Decius”;

and number 397:

> “Cixilanus founded at Toledo a church of Saint Thyrsus, a citizen of Toledo who suffered at Apollonia in Greece.”

In both places I have shaken out certain sparks. — D. L.

The Iron Bridge Gate was dedicated to Saints Damasus and Melchiades, citizens of Mantua Carpetana. Many people have written much about these two shining lights of Madrid. Concerning Saint Damasus, the most learned Father Francisco Bivar wrote learnedly in his commentary on Dexter, under the years of Christ 366, number 3, and 388, number 8, drawing on Baronius, Volume IV of the *Annals*, and others. Most recently and fully, Jerome de Quintana treats him in his *Madrid*, Book II, chapter 4, where he answers those who defend his Lusitanian origin. Among them I add Augustine Barbosa, in *Remissions of Learned Men concerning Words*, entry 131, number 5, page 62, column 2, and in *On the Office of a Bishop*, Part III, allegation 60, number 11.

Although Quintana does not remove from the manuscript of Dexter the words that gave rise to disputes and disagreements—namely, “a support and prop”—as our Father Francisco Bivar does, branding them as spurious and corrupted, he nevertheless thinks it preferable to attempt a response to those who oppose him. Father Andreas Schott, a priest of the Society of Jesus, a man of exceptional industry and great judgment, reviews both opinions in his *Spanish Library*, Volume II, class 1, “Ancient Authors,” page 183. Most recently, Antonius de Sousa e Mazedo asserts the Lusitanian position at length in his book entitled *Flowers of Spain, Excellencies of Portugal*, chapter 9, page 93.

The same Father Bivar discusses Melchiades in his commentary on Dexter, in the favorable and illuminating sections for the years of Christ 248 and 299, number 3, and 308, Commentary 2, number 15. Quintana should be consulted in his *Madrid*, Book II, chapter 1, especially folio 104, column 4. There he cites our Julian in the *Chronicle*, number 72:

> “Melchiades, who later became pope, was born in Spain, namely to African parents, near the city of Mantua Carpetana.”

Don Gregorio López Madera, counselor to our great king Philip IV—whom I must often mention—discusses both stars most splendidly of all in his book *On the Excellence of the Spanish Monarchy*, chapter 6, § 2, page 45, columns 2 and 3, where he calms and reconciles the disagreements. — D. L.

And especially to Saint Michael, guardian saint of this city, from the foundations of its churches, and guardian angel of the city. Saint Michael is acknowledged as its guardian saint and guardian angel. Concerning the hermitage of Saint Michael before the gate consecrated to him, see Julian, *On Hermitages*, number 5, in these words:

> “The hermitage of Saint Michael on the eastern side of Toledo—contemporary with the Sevillian hermitage, where the image of Blessed Mary [lacuna]—four miles from the royal city, not far from the River Tagus, founded by Athanagild; it is now held by right of patronage by the Columbans, a noble family of Mozarabs.”

It was the custom of the ancients to dedicate hermitages before the entrances of cities to angels, so that they might guard and defend them, as is the office of angels who protect cities; and, by their commands, each city has its appointed angel.

Among all devotions, devotion to Saint Michael shines forth. He is known to preside over the protection of the Christian Church, as is evident from his various apparitions, by which he has been made conspicuous through many miracles, partly in the Western Church and partly in the Eastern Church. Formerly he presided over the Jews, as is clear from Daniel, chapter 10, verse 13, where Michael, the fourth of the angels, is appointed prince of God’s people. Martin Becanus, a priest of the Society of Jesus, draws this from the words:

> “I have no helper in all these matters except Michael, our prince.”

See his *Scholastic Theology*, Volume I, Part I, Treatise 3, *On Angels*, chapter 6, folio 388. He recounts Michael’s deeds from that chapter, from chapter 12, from the canonical Epistle of Jude, and from Revelation, chapter 12. Hence the many basilicas erected to Saint Michael, concerning which Christoph Besoldus writes in his discourse *On the Angels, or Genii, of Empires*, pages 2–3.

I said that angels are appointed for their protection. Clement of Alexandria agrees in Book II of the *Recognitions*. I know, however, what Bellarmine and others judged concerning the books of the *Recognitions*—Bellarmine in *On Free Will*, Book V, chapter 25, and in his treatise *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under the year of the Lord 300—but I am not concerned with these matters at present. See Saint Dionysius the Areopagite, *On the Celestial Hierarchy*, chapter 9.

Among the pagans the same idea is found everywhere: Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Book VIII; Crinitus, *On Honorable Learning*, Book IX, chapter 3; Servius on the First *Georgic*; Gebhard Elmenhorst in his *Observations on Arnobius*, folio 14; and the ancient inscription:

> TO JUPITER, BEST AND GREATEST,  
> AND TO THE GENIUS OF THE PLACE.

Guido Pancirolus supplies another in his *Treasury of Various Readings*, Book II, chapter 128:

> To Quintus Volusius Saturninus and Publius Cornelius, consuls, Augustales, who held games for Nero Claudius Caesar Augustus and Agrippina Augusta, to Jupiter Best and Greatest and to the Genius of the colony, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of March.

For he says:

> “A fate or a genius is assigned to every people or city,  
> According to our custom of souls,  
> Which enter new bodies under unequal destinies.”

Prudentius, *Against Symmachus*, Book II.

From sacred writers, Saint Jerome writes on Ezekiel, chapter 28:

> “The provinces have been entrusted to angels for governing, as to judges by an emperor.”
