For God, in the most beautiful order, scattered throughout the body of the universe those who guard the parts of the earth and preside over peoples and places—*φυλάττοντας μέρη τῆς γῆς, καὶ ἔθνων καὶ τόπων προϊσταμένους*: “guarding the several parts of the earth and placed over peoples and places.”

Our Liutprand, who knew all these matters thoroughly and outwardly, added that the guardian angel stood against the demons of midday. He was expressing exactly the passage of Psalm 90, verse 6, where the holy king speaks of the angels, describes their powers, promises that the man protected by them will be safe, and likewise declares him free from the danger that walks in darkness and from the attack and demon of midday—that is, from dangers threatening secretly and openly, by night and at midday, especially from demons; sometimes through the mere terror of apparitions, sometimes through a pestilential demon and its poisonous breath.

Father Juan de Mariana interprets it thus:

> “From the plague that rages openly, not from hidden causes.”

Genebrard had previously said the same:

> “You will not fear the plague, whether it rages by night or by day.”

Juan Bochius, as is his custom, states briefly that this is the opinion of the Hebrews:

> “Although the Hebrews read ‘the midday plague or destruction,’ nevertheless some think that by the midday demon one should understand a certain scare-spirit, which they call an *empusa*.”

In his *Heroic Parodies* on the same Psalm 90, he follows the former interpretation:

> You will run with an untroubled mind,  
> You will dread no dangers of the night, nor will you be permitted  
> To fear the arrows sent with twanging bow;  
> You will not fear the plague hidden in blind darkness,  
> Nor the destruction that rages openly at midday.

Another sang in almost the same strains:

> Through the blind silences of black night  
> You will not fear unseen dangers;  
> You will not fear destruction raging in the daylight,  
> Nor open wars.

Lorinus, Janssenius, and many others understand *the midday demon* as the plague. Nor do those who, as Bochius says in the passage cited above, explain the midday demon as an *empusa* depart from them. For the scholiast on Aristophanes’ *Frogs* confuses the *empusa* with the midday demon; they say that the *empusa* is an apparition that used to appear to the wretched and unfortunate. Consult the *Etymologicum* under the word Ἔμπουσα concerning the force of that name.

John Bourdelotius collects much material in his commentary on Petronius, page 114, on the satirist’s words “by no other kind of fury, by night and by day,” page 1, line 1; and the compiler of proverbs under *empusa*. Julius Caesar Bulengerus, Book II, *Against the Magi*, chapter 59; Gyraldus, *Syntagma* 12 on the gods, page 349; Raderus on Quintus Curtius, Book VI, chapter 7, page 348, who cites several others; and among them the most learned Don Antonio Ponce de Santa Cruz, in his *Lectures at Valladolid* on Hippocrates’ *On the Sacred Disease*, text 17, pages 23–24. He was a true Spanish Aesculapius, that is, a physician and defender of health, bringing useful remedies to light from the innermost chambers of philosophy and medical science.

Fortunius Licetus gathers still more with learned skill in his *Encyclopedia*, under the Lemnian altar of Dosiades, that most ancient and obscure poet, on the words ἐμπούσας κόρος, page 124.

This interpretation also suits an approaching pestilence, for many teach that such terrors and similar apparitions wander about before the pestilence rages. Our Martin Delrio—alas, once my friend, the most brilliant light of divine and human letters—observes this from Procopius, Book I, *Persian War*, in Book II of his *Magical Investigations*, question 27, section 2, number 8.

When Procopius describes that immense and astonishing plague which devastated the whole world in the time of Justinian, he says that demons were reported to have appeared in human form, striking those whom they encountered with a poisonous and burning breath. The Hebrews called them *meririm* and *ressaphim*. This happened to some who were awake in broad daylight—notice the midday demon—and to others in dreams at night—notice the nocturnal demon.

I add Dio’s account under Titus, where he writes that people of gigantic size walked through the cities when Mount Vesuvius vomited flames. Dionysius of Halicarnassus also bears witness, Book VIII:

> “New forms of apparitions appeared before the eyes of the Romans, and these were often presented to human eyes and ears.”

I judge that these are called demons in Holy Scripture, Isaiah, chapter 34, verse 14:

> “And demons shall meet with goat-deer, and the hairy one shall call to the other.”

Hence among us Spaniards such a scare-apparition is called *Estantigua*, because the devil appears under that form and is called by sacred writers and the holy Fathers “the ancient enemy.” Thus Saint Gregory, Book II, Letter 23, to the prefect Justin, cited in the chapter *Habet*, 2, question 5:

> “It is characteristic of the envy of the ancient enemy that, when, with God opposing him, he cannot overthrow people by the perpetration of evil deeds, he tears apart their reputation by presently piling falsehoods upon them.”

So too Jonah, bishop of Orléans, in Book I of *On the Worship of Images*, at the beginning:

> “Since they themselves were not apostles of Christ but heralds of the ancient enemy.”

John Montholonius collects further material in his *Dictionary*, under “Devil,” page 156.

There is a famous mention of the *Estantigua* in the *History of the Granada War*, written in our vernacular by Don Diego de Mendoza, page 124, in these words. He is discussing the war between Caesar and Sextus Pompey in Baetica near Munda:

> “Where even today, as I have said, one sees impressions of the spoils of arms and horses; and the inhabitants see squadrons encountering one another through the air, and hear voices like those of people attacking. The Spanish common people call such appearances or phantoms *Estantiguas*, which the vapor of the earth forms in the lower air when the sun rises or sets, just as clouds formed into various figures and likenesses are seen in the higher air.”

The pagans likewise use a similar expression, though in another form, for what the royal poet had declared. Ovid, *Fasti* IV, addressed to Pales:

> You, goddess, appease for us the springs and the powers of fountains;  
> You, the gods scattered throughout every grove.  
> May we see neither the Dryads nor Diana’s pools,  
> Nor Faunus when he presses the fields at midday.

Here he joins the time of day to the place: the time is daylight, that is, midday; the place through which Faunus moved is the fields. Poets drew much from sacred writings, as I showed in my *Pentecontarchus*, chapter 26, being learned in the reading of the Bible.

Ovid was not among the least knowledgeable in this matter, nor should he be ranked among the lowest by those who have read the books of the *Metamorphoses*. They will readily find them filled with distorted elements of sacred history and polluted by his own false teaching.

Perhaps he had read in the Old Testament that “midday” and “desert” are often used for the same thing. Hence, among learned writers, the midday demon and the demon of the desert are identical. Procopius and Cyril on Isaiah teach that this demon delights in forests and inhabits deserts. For that reason Ovid wrote that Faunus pressed the fields at midday, as though raging and running wild.

According to the opinion of the ancient pagans, Pan—one of the midday demons, as Delrio reports—was then believed to be especially angry and fearsome. Theocritus attests this in *Idyll* I, when the day was burning; Psellus gives the reason in his book *On the Nature of Demons*:

> “This kind is solar, and therefore has the nature of a lion.”

Then, “just as in the darkness of night”—these are the words of Origen on Job, chapter 1, verse 19, if Origen is indeed the author of that work—“so likewise in the middle of midday more temptations of demons show themselves than at other times.”

From these things, to return to the point from which we digressed, it is now clear that the midday demon signifies disease and plague, against which the guardian angel rises in defense of his city.

Let there be an incontrovertible witness: the basilica erected at Rome in the Mausoleum of Hadrian by Boniface, Roman pontiff, and dedicated to Saint Michael, for this very reason—that Michael appeared there sheathing a sword that had previously been drawn, as a sign that the plague was ending.

Gregory of Tours supports this. In Book IV of his *History of the Franks*, chapter 5, he says that another plague was driven away when Saint Gall prayed and the angel of God himself ministered. The most learned and devout Father Martin de Roa, richly adorned with varied learning, cites him in his *Florets of the Cordoban Saints*, on the feast of the guardian angel, page 10.

Liutprand said that the gate was dedicated to the guardian angel against the midday demons. This had always been King Wamba’s intention, and he dedicated the gates to various divine saints. He likewise saw to it that the following verses were inscribed on the buildings he erected:

> Holy lords, whose presence shines here,  
> Preserve this city and its people with your customary favor.

Doctor Francisco de Pisa reports this in his *Description of Toledo*, Book I, chapter 9, as does our most learned Father Jerome de la Higuera in his elucidation of this memorial; earlier, Mariana, Book VI of his *History*, chapter 14, page 285, column 2.

The Mozarabs also prayed to Saint Leocadia, patroness of the city of Toledo, to free them from contagion:

> You, our illustrious citizen,  
> You are our native patroness;  
> From the boundary of this city  
> Drive far away the affliction.

The imperial emblems of Toledo allude to this. At their summit appears a guardian and protecting angel, drawing his sword to defend his city. Above the gate in Madrid formerly called the Guadalajara Gate—whose name is still remembered—there likewise stood a guardian angel in a similar form, as Don Gregorio López Madera told me: a knight of the Order of Saint James, counselor to Philip IV, Catholic king of Spain, a man of eminent learning, an antiquary most knowledgeable about Spanish affairs, and a most prudent and learned jurist.

[Col. 1034A] Concerning the midday and nocturnal demon, see Father Martin Delrio in the passage cited above, where he teaches that Blessed Basil and Theodoret handed down that the Psalmist spoke of the midday demon in this sense. But I bring to light a more expert witness from the obscure Chaldean Paraphrase on Song of Songs, chapter 4, verse 6. The words are:

> “He held in his hands the art of his righteous fathers; harmful spirits of darkness, and demons of morning and midday, fled from among them, because the majesty of the glory of the Lord dwelt in the sanctuary-house built on Mount Moriah, and all demons and harmful spirits fled from the scent of the fragrant incense.” — D. L.

King Wamba, after defeating Paul and routing all his enemies, enjoys glorious repose. He enlarges Toledo, the royal city, and surrounds it with walls. He dedicates the gate facing north to Saint Thyrsus, a citizen of Toledo and a martyr who suffered abroad; likewise to Saint Leocadia, virgin and martyr; and the gate facing east to Blessed Marciana, a citizen, virgin, and most holy martyr. Above the bridge, he dedicates the gate to Saint Julian, martyr of Toledo; the Iron Bridge Gate to Saints Damasus and Melchiades, citizens of Mantua Carpetana; and especially to Saint Michael, guardian saint of this city, from the foundations of its churches, and guardian angel of the city against the midday demons.

### 129.

Around this time Pipin I flourished in Austria [variants: in Neustria; or Austrasia; or Aquitaine], surnamed Ubertinus, mayor of the palace of Austrasia, father of Charles Martel, called “the Great,” father of Milo, surnamed of Angers, of Bernard, and of King Pipin II, and father of Charlemagne, as well as of others.

### 130.

[Editorial note begins at Col. 1034A; the supplied source ends incompletely here.]

### 130. [Note: [Col. 1034A]

Here Luitprand, an author of 640 years ago, mentions the division of episcopal sees carried out by King Wamba; so does Julian, an author of 450 years ago; also the older author of the book entitled *Idatius*; and the general *History of King Alfonso*, of 350 years ago. There, in a most ancient Toledo manuscript, the following is found at the end of the divisions:

“These things were enacted at Toledo in a general council, with everyone saying aloud: ‘It pleases us, it pleases us’;” in the presence of and with the subscriptions of the unconquered and most serene King Wamba, and Quiricus, archbishop of Toledo and primate of the Spains; and of the other archbishops, together with their suffragans of the aforesaid dioceses; in the church of Saint Leocadia, in the era 710, by the hand of Peter.”

This King Wamba, however, lived for more than five years thereafter and died. I believe I read *X*, as I have already written, although by this notation the number fifteen is indicated. Thus this synod was held in the year 677, and the elapsed years up to the beginning of the year 681 amount to five years. Those are therefore mistaken who think that this was done at the Eleventh Council of Toledo. For, besides the fact that no mention of such a division of sees occurs in that council, this one was held in a general and national council of all Spain, whereas the eleventh, under Quiricus, bishop of Toledo, was merely provincial. Nevertheless, in accordance with the chronology, it must be inserted between the Eleventh and Twelfth Councils of Toledo; these three councils were assembled consecutively over the course of three years.

I think the reason why no record or memory of such a synod has survived is that no canons were decreed there concerning the reform of morals, but rather concerning the sees that the bishops of Spain could use for the reform of their subjects. Therefore those portions of the councils that pertain solely to secular matters were entirely torn away, the Fathers calling “canons” only those matters that could assist either faith or moral discipline.

The histories of the ancient kings and the ancient divisions of the sees were read before the king. As Julian of Toledo adds, three palatine officials were assigned to each metropolitan see, so that they might serve as eyewitnesses in the division of the individual sees and in counting out and assigning their boundaries according to the ancient rule and allocation.

In this King Wamba imitated the Romans. When they ordered the regions of the world to be measured, they appointed to each task serious and highly experienced men, as the Greek historian Atticus teaches; according to the opinion of some, he lived in the time of Augustus.

All the more recent authors mention these divisions: Garivay, Vasaeus, Mariana, Morales, and others, such as Peter Alcoçer in his *History of Toledo* and Doctor Beuter in his *Valencian History*. Julian, archpriest of Toledo, discusses this matter at greater length. P. H.

The true calculation of the years of King Wamba’s life compelled our Jerome de la Higuera to take this mark, which he found in a manuscript, as fifteen; yet it undoubtedly signifies forty, as the Bishop of Pamplona, D. F. Prudentius de Sandoval, clearly established by collating many Gothic manuscripts in his *Observations on the History of Saint James*, by Don Mauro de Castello Ferrer, when the opportunity arose to elucidate the epitaph of Queen Urraca, wife of King Ramiro, p. 233.

I would prefer to suppose that it was written in that manuscript exactly as it appears, but was corruptly transcribed by an ignorant copyist—namely, as *Xv*. For when *X* precedes and is joined to *L*, that is, *XL*, it signifies forty; but if *X* precedes *V*, as I suspect it did in the autograph, it denotes fifteen. Thus, according to the various ways in which the signs are placed and joined, it conveys and demonstrates different numbers, and provides an opening for errors in calculation when it is not properly and precisely examined.

Ambrosius de Morales held the same view in the third part of his *Spanish Chronicles*, in the excursus he appended to the end of the prologue, where he discusses the examination of charters learnedly:

“ There is also another great difficulty in very ancient privileges written in Gothic script, in reading their numbers. It is this: the tens represented by *XX* very often have such entanglements among themselves that, unless one has considerable practice in knowing that script and has seen much written in it—and, in addition, unless one observes the numbers with great vigilance and care—it is very easy to make a mistake in a ten.”

Thus far he. Nor am I unaware that among the Romans, according to Peter the Deacon in *On the Notes of Letters*, this was customarily used to signify ten times; yet without a stroke it represented ten. Aldus Manutius agrees in his *Commentary on the Explanation of Ancient Notae*. But these matters are either very well known to the sons of notaries or to the children of scribes. ]

The Twelfth Council of Toledo is recorded as having been held at Toledo in November, in the sixth year of the most glorious King Wamba of the Visigoths [Col. 1035A], I say, where all the bishops of Spain and Narbonese Gaul assembled, under the presidency of Quiricus, metropolitan of Toledo, as patriarch of all Spain and Narbonese Gaul. All the sees of Spain were divided, together with their boundaries and limits—just as Constantine the Great had once divided them when, by the authority of Sylvester, he convened at Toledo a council of the bishops of all Spain and is said to have presided over that council. Thus, under King Wamba, the ancient boundaries were assigned anew to the individual sees. The violence of the persecutions that had arisen, the fury of so many wars, and the iniquity of the times had for the most part obliterated them; he restored them completely through his diligence and industry.

In the fifth year of King Wamba, this great synod was convened at Toledo. In it the sees were divided by him, in the presence of the metropolitans and the other bishops, abbots, and palatine officials of Spain. He had instructed them to divide the dioceses as seemed appropriate, in the presence of the representatives: for Toledo and its suffragans, Sullo, Athanegon, and Reccared; for Seville and its suffragans, Adilogo, Ela, and Witiza; for Braga, Wimar, Vitula, and Hicadile; for Mérida, Idigno, Theodulph, and Ostulph; for Narbonne, Salaminus, Egisibarinus, and Theudegild. The representatives of Toledo divided the territory on one side with Complutum and on the other with Elbora.

This formula of the divisions was drawn up and committed to writing by Peter, deacon of Saint Leocadia. The council was held in the presence of Quiricus, archbishop of the royal city and primate of all Spain, both Citerior and Ulterior.

Judges were appointed: for Toledo, Quiricus the archbishop; for Seville, Julian; for Braga, Liuba; for the province of Mérida, Stephen; for Narbonne, Crescentius. All appealed to the primate of Toledo, and, in the case of the people of Toledo, to the abbot Suasilius, by common consent. Through Quiricus’s prudence, many disputes that had arisen were suppressed. The council lasted until the end of the month.

### 131. [Note: [Col. 1036A]

Concerning the designation of new bishoprics in Wamba’s time, mention is made in the Twelfth Council and in the first council held under Ervigius at Toledo. For, in order to please the king, the bishops assented, contrary to the decrees of the Fathers, when the king requested that a bishop be installed at Toledo in the praetorian see of Saints Peter and Paul, and in a small village near Elbora or Talavera, in the monastery of Saint Pimenus [read: Pigmenius], as well as in other more obscure places. This was attributed to the king’s frivolity and, in the bishops, to flattery. D. L. ]

Outside the city, near the road to Talabrica or Elbora, about 1,500 paces away, King Wamba newly endowed the praetorian see of Saints Peter and Paul with an episcopal chair subject to the patriarch of Toledo, despite the objection of Quiricus of Toledo and the chapter of Toledo. In the town of Aquae—now Talavera—which was formerly called Elbora and had an episcopal see subject to Mérida, he established an episcopal see in the small village of Aquae—now Cazalegas—with the consent of the metropolitan of Mérida, in honor of Saint Pimenus [or Saint Pigmenius; concerning him, see Baronius under 24 March in the *Martyrologium*], the most ancient martyr resting there. This arrangement continued for a long time.

### 132. [Note: [Col. 1036A]

And it was consecrated to the immaculate conception of the same Virgin, which all the apostles preached. Entire volumes on the Immaculate Conception already exist. See Julian in the *Chronicle*, no. 607:

“He [Saint Bernard] was most devoted to the Blessed Virgin. He had the feast of that Lady celebrated with great devotion, and he had her feast of the Immaculate Conception celebrated with even greater devotion—this feast having been preached in Spain by Saint James and having begun with the apostles, who decreed it in this council.”

In the *Adversaria*, no. 395:

“The tradition”—these are his words—“was that, when the apostles had assembled in council, the blessed Virgin Mary had been untouched by original sin.”

See also what Aegidius the Lusitanian noted in his book *On the Immaculate Conception*, book III, question 3, single article, section 1, no. 3, fol. 160, col. 2. An ancient marginal gloss exists on chapter 1, at the word *Nativitas*, *De consecratione*, distinction 3; it ought to be examined and brought under proper critical judgment, yet, so far as I have seen, no one has cited it for this purpose. ]

The most blessed shrine of the Pillar in the city of Zaragoza, built at the Virgin’s command by Saint James when he preached in Spain in the year 37 from the Lord’s birth, and consecrated to her Immaculate Conception—which all the apostles preached everywhere—is at this time visited by a very large company of pilgrims.

DCCXVIII. DCLXXX.

### 133. [Note: [Col. 1037A]

Concerning the confession and penance of King Wamba, Alfonso—or rather Sebastian of Salamanca—writes in the *Chronicle addressed to Ervigius*:

“ Plotting against the king, he mixed into his drink a herb called *spartus*, and immediately the king lost his memory. When the bishop of the city, or the leading men of the palace who were loyal to the king—men entirely unaware of the cause of the potion—saw the king lying without memory, they were moved by compassion and, lest the king should depart this life without proper order, immediately administered to him the rite of confession and penance. When the king recovered from the potion and understood the order imposed upon him, he sought a monastery and remained there in religious life for as long as he lived. He reigned eight years and one month, and lived in the monastery for seven years and three months.”

Julian asserts that in his youth he had been a deacon of the bishop of Segovia, whom he represented in confirming the acts of the Sixth Council of Toledo. Once his prudence, courage, and excellence of character, joined with the highest piety, became known, he was held in the first rank among the palatine officials. After Reccesuinth’s death, when he was already nearly sixty, he was elected, willingly or unwillingly. He was an exceptionally holy man, and God greatly favored him. He never had a wife and fathered no son. After receiving penance, since he had been devoted to ecclesiastical affairs, he voluntarily sought a monastery. He died on 20 September, in the year 88, at the age of seventy-five, on a Sunday, the day before the feast of Saint Matthew the apostle and evangelist. At his tomb Saint Julian added this poem:

Wamba, once you were Peter, minister of the Mass;  
By your religion you shine, king of the Gothic people.

You did not seek the royal summit of your own desire,  
But, compelled, you undertook the great burden of empire.

Relying upon the virtue of the Almighty,  
You stand forth having accomplished unheard-of deeds.

Nothing is ever more pleasing to such a man than this repose:  
After the sacred scepters, you gladly seek the monastery.

There, as a monk, you happily pass seven enduring years;  
Then, blessed by the death granted you, you go to heaven.

Happy Wamba, you are judged to have been fortunate in your lot:  
He who so well treads upon scepters will fly among the stars.

For seven years you governed the scepters of your people,  
Which you relinquished—not under the burden of illness, but willingly yourself.

And after receiving the habit of a Benedictine monk, he is said to have gone with Count Albert to Pampliega and elsewhere. A privilege, or charter, of King Peter of Castile, dated 15 October in the era 1389, relates that Wamba took the monastic habit in the monastery of Saint Vincent of Pampliega. Francis de Pisa reproduces it in full in his *History of Toledo*, book I, chapter 24.

The writer of the perpetual gloss on the books of John de Mena, the first among the greatest Spanish poets, relates the same thing in poem 272, in these words:

“Afterward this holy king”—he is speaking of Wamba—“became a monk in the monastery of Pampliega, and remained in the religious life for seven years; and he died there most holily.”

The Archbishop Rodrigo calls the place Pannisplica in book III, chapter 11 of his *History*. See also what Father Antonio de Yepes wrote learnedly and fully in the *Benedictine History*, volume II, century 3, in the year of Christ 681, fol. 333. Add our Julian in the *Chronicle*, no. 362.

Where Wamba was finally buried is variously reported by the authors. See Morales, book XII of his *History*, chapter 52; Mariana, book VI, chapter 14; Count Don Peter in the *Nobiliary*, title 3, where he writes about the Gothic kings; and Yepes, cited above, p. 335, col. 1, under the words *Lo segundo se muestra* [“The second point is shown”], where he adduces mutually contrary opinions and their foundations. D. L. ]

On the fourteenth day of October of this year, penance was administered to King Wamba—for it was a Sunday—at the first hour of the night. The king, having recovered his senses, was tonsured and, after receiving the habit of a Benedictine monk, is said to have gladly gone with Count Albert to Pampliega, the principal monastery of that order [or, but incorrectly: “he went and is said to have done so”].

### 134. [Note: [Col. 1038A]

Concerning the election and coronation of Ervigius, Julian in his *History*, and Julian in his brief *Chronicle*, write as follows:

“Then, immediately on the following day, Monday, the glorious lord Ervigius received the scepters of the kingdom. This took place on the Ides of October, in the era 718. The solemnity of the anointing was postponed until the Sunday that followed, the thirteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the same era 718. The same glorious King Ervigius reigned for seven years and twenty-five days.”

Thus far he. He understands the beginning of the reign to be reckoned from the day of the coronation. P. H.

When Wamba sought the monastery, what happened to Quiricus is variously reported by the authors. Some say that he died from grief over the injury inflicted upon King Wamba; others that he resigned the episcopate; this author adds that he went with the king to the monastery of Pampliega. The writers on Spanish affairs say nothing about this, nor do those who write about the Benedictines. P. H.—Father Jerome de la Higuera says here that he did not find Quiricus to have been a monk in the Benedictine annals; Father Antonio de Yepes asserts it in the *Benedictine History*, volume II, century 3, fol. 335, col. 4. See him. D. L. ]

On the following day, Monday, 15 October, by the votes of all the palatine officials, Ervigius—who is said to have driven the king insane by administering the potion—was elected king. His coronation and anointing were postponed until the following Sunday, which, as some maintain, was performed by the archpriest or archdeacon Julian—for Quiricus, the archbishop of Toledo, had fallen ill. Quiricus, whether overtaken by death, as is commonly said, or ill, or departing from the archbishopric of Toledo [or, having been cast out], because of Ervigius’s crime and imposture, went with Wamba to the monastery, where he laudably completed the remainder of his life with the king.

### 135. [Note: [Col. 1038B]

Gudila, archdeacon of Toledo, is mentioned in the council assembled in the year 675:

“I, Gudila, archdeacon of the church of Saint Mary of the royal see, have subscribed these synodal acts determined by the council.”

Felix, archbishop of Toledo, writes in the *Life of Saint Julian*:

“Finally, when he had reached the age of boyhood, he was joined to his colleague Gudila the deacon by such a bond of companionship and united to him by such an inviolable charity and undivided union that inviolable love showed both of them to be one, and the unity established in them revealed that there were not two souls in them but one. So great was the communion of the unanimity they had attained that, according to the history of the Acts of the Apostles, they were reckoned as only one in two bodies, and as one soul.

They stood prudent in counsel, of one mind in judgment, and harmonious in praiseworthy action. For, with the divine Spirit breathing upon them, they desired to enjoy the good of the pleasure of contemplation—that is, of contemplative repose—and to be bound by the restraint of monastic discipline. But since the judgment of the supreme God ordained otherwise, their devotion was nevertheless frustrated. Although they had not completed the course of the journey they desired, they did not cease from the pursuit of pious devotion. While they had wished to benefit only themselves in retreat, they later began, with growing aspirations, to strive for the salvation of their neighbors.

Indeed, in teaching their subjects they displayed laborious virtue; they were desirable in promoting their progress and fervent in the service of God; zealous in their longing for the beauty of the Lord’s house; ready in obedience to their elders; and they attained, as far as possible, the benefit of every virtue to which they devoted themselves with fervent spirits.

Therefore, by the dispensation of divine judgments, Gudila the deacon, of holy memory, on the sixth day before the Kalends of September, in the eighth year of the reign of Wamba, under a worthy confession of God, closed the final course of his grievous life. His little body rests honorably buried, through the sacred offices of his most beloved companion, in the monastery of Saint Felix, dedicated in the estate of Canne.”

In the manuscript *Martyrology of the Holy Church of Piacenza*, written more than 200 years ago, it is found as follows:

“27 August. At Toledo, Saint Gudila, archdeacon, confessor and doctor, companion of Saint Julian, archbishop of Toledo.”

It is remarkable that he was not included in the recently revised Roman Martyrology, especially on the testimony of the most holy man Felix, archbishop of Toledo.

A part of my soul and half of myself. The ancients use similar expressions. Ausonius:

I go, but without myself, because without you; and only with you  
Shall I be wholly myself, though I am but the other part of you, Galla.

[Col. 1039C] “Neither violets nor tender roses, etc.” He refers to the ancient custom of crowning tombs with roses and flowers. Laevinus Torrentius discusses this in his commentary on Suetonius, *Augustus*, chapter 18:

“And he honored it after scattering flowers. When asked whether he wished to look upon Ptolemy, the king, he replied that he had wished to see kings alive, not dead.”

See also Joannes Kirchmannus, *On Roman Funerals*, book IV, chapter 3; Jacob Gutherus, *On the Law of the Spirits of the Dead*, book II, chapter 10, pp. 220–221; Petrus Morestellus, *On the Funeral Procession*, books VIII, chapters 14 and 15; Joannes Meursius on Lycophron’s *Alexandra*, p. 208; Godescalcus Stewechius on Apuleius’s *Golden Ass*, pp. 388–389; and most recently Antonius Santorellus, *Medical Post-Practice, or On Treating the Dead*, chapter 45. This was often ordered by testament.

For various inscriptions, see Justus Lipsius and Janus Gruterus, pp. 237, no. 5; 744, no. 1; 804, no. 5; and elsewhere. The most ancient Christians, however, abhorred this custom, as Minucius Felix testifies in the *Octavius*, where he reports that Caecilius brought it against them among their crimes in these words:

“Thus you fear the gods whom you deny: you do not crown your heads with flowers, nor adorn your bodies with perfumes; you reserve unguents for funerals and even deny garlands to tombs, pale, trembling, and deserving of pity.”

Geberhard Elmenhorstius gathers further material there on p. 20; Joannes a Woveren briefly touches upon it on p. 130; and see Clement of Alexandria, *The Instructor*, book II, chapter 8, and Carolus Paschalius, book IV, *On Garlands*, chapter 5.

Later Christians, however, embraced the practice. Let Saint Jerome testify twice. In letter 3, chapter 1, written to Heliodorus, he says:

“Whenever I strive to break forth into words and scatter flowers upon his tomb, so often my eyes are filled with tears.”

And to Pammachius, on the death of his wife Paulina, volume I, letter 26, chapter 2:

“Other husbands scatter violets, roses, lilies, and purple flowers over the tombs of their wives, and console the sorrow of their hearts by these acts.”

Prudentius, hymn 10, *On the Funeral Rites of the Dead*:

[Col. 1040A] We shall cherish the covered bones  
[Col. 1040B] With violets and abundant foliage.

There Joannes Weitzius cites Desiderius Heraldus, book I of the *Adversaria*, chapter 6; Jacobus Pontanus, volume III of the *Progymnasmata*, part 2, fol. 879 and following; Franciscus Bencius, *Oration* 26, *On Roman Burial*; and I add Thomasius Porcacchius, *On the Ancient Funeral Procession*, written in Italian, in the third funerary tablet, fol. II; Petrus Bacherus, *Apologeticus for the Dead*, chapter 13, p. 222; and most recently Julius Lavorius, *On Ancient and Recent Funeral Customs*, title 2, chapter 1, beginning at no. 115.

Let our own vigorous literary soldier, Don Luis de Góngora, close the procession. He varied his writings with various star-like signs, full of ancient splendor, and deservedly may be compared with the ancients:

Some heavenly courtiers preserve their garments, though torn.  
Adorn them with flowers, stranger.

Finally, it seemed not irrelevant to observe that the Romans were accustomed to plant trees and flowers on the tombs of those who had deserved well of them. Theophrastus, book VI of the *History of Plants*, chapter 7:

“Likewise, the plant called *pothos* [πόθος, ‘yearning’] has two kinds: one whose flower resembles the hyacinth, and another, pale and white, which it is customary to use on tombs; the latter is also the more long-lasting.”

Pliny likewise, book XXI of the *Natural History*, chapter 11:

“But the most remarkable is *pothos*. There are two kinds of it: one whose flower is that of the hyacinth, and another, whiter, which generally grows on tombs because it lasts longer.”

From Theophrastus, Athenaeus, book XV of the *Deipnosophists*, in the latest edition of Isaac Casaubon, fol. 679. Jacobus Dalechampius, in later annotations together with Isaac Caupani’s recently published commentaries, says that some maintain *pothos* to be jasmine—*jazmín* among the Spaniards.

Persius alluded to this in satire 1, verse 53:

Will violets not now arise from the tomb  
And from the fortunate ashes? …

On this passage, Theodore Marcilius.

Α. Ω. These signs, or letters, were placed on tombs in antiquity to indicate that they belonged to Catholics, not Arians. For they were the device of the labarum of Constantine the Great, as is commonly known. Christ our Lord, who is the beginning and the end, showed by these letters—the first and final letters of the Greek alphabet—that his divinity is equal to the Father’s divinity: “I am Alpha and Omega” (Revelation 1), “the beginning and the end.” The Arians denied this.

Ambrosius de Morales, book XI of his *History*, chapter 41, p. 48, bears witness to this interpretation and to this very common Spanish custom during the Gothic period. So too Don Francisco de Padilla, *Ecclesiastical History*, century 4, chapter 49, fol. 249, part 2. Most recently and at length, with useful observations concerning Spanish matters, González Argote de Molina, book I *On Nobility*, chapter 47, p. 39, and Quintana in his *Madrid*, book I, chapter 48, have discussed it.

They were prompted to bring this antiquity to light by the celebrated verses inscribed above one of the gates of the church of Saint John in Madrid, which I thought worth transcribing:

For a thousand years I have stood, consecrated for three hundred;  
On the standard, Arius denies Α and denies Ω.

Quintus bears the grave burden; Paulus holds the city and the world;  
Here the third Philip, the Iberian, holds the scepters.

I observed in my *Itinerary*, on the day I reached Carrión while serving as royal envoy and making my way to Paris, that these signs were also carved on the tombs of great men. For on the sarcophagus of the Counts of Carrión, on the very shield of the coat of arms, I found this sacred sign engraved. I likewise observed it in royal charters; Argote notes it in the place cited above.

To make this clear, I had the sign and the wheel of confirmation engraved. Here it is:

[Col. 1041B]

[Col. 1041D] This sign of the standard and the wheel of confirmation can be seen in a certain privilege—commonly called *rodado* because of the same wheel—of Saint Ferdinand III, King of Castile, drawn up at Guadalajara on 20 September, in the era 1264—that is, in the year 1226. In it the king confirms the donation of houses and vineyards that Don Giles, priest of Saint Giles of Guadalajara, gave to the Great Virgin and the other virgins of the monastery of Saint Dominic of Madrid; and he provided and granted that they should have and possess them perpetually by hereditary right.

[Col. 1042A] And, more remarkably still, the same appears on the collars of runaway slaves, in Laurentius Pignorius’s little book *On Slaves*, p. 21, where he says that he saw it at Rome among antiquities observed by Laelius Paschalinus:

HOLD ME, FOR I HAVE FLED, AND RETURN ME TO MY MASTER BONIFACE LINARIUS. Α Ω Χ.

Since among Catholics the disfigurement of slaves’ faces was prohibited, lest the image formed in the likeness of heavenly beauty should be defaced, as the emperor decreed in the law *Si quis*, title *De poenis*, and as Petrus Ostermannus learnedly observes in his juridical commentary on the law *Stigmata*, title *De Fabricensibus*, section 4, p. 9, Catholics guarded against this by a kind of abbreviated method. They achieved the same result as if they had disfigured them with a brand, while obeying the law; and, to give a token of the faith, they decorated their collars with these signs.

Lamps also intended for sacred use were marked with this character of Christ our Lord. Just as the ancient Romans manifested the worship of idols by lamps that they kept burning, of which Pliny speaks in book XXXIV, chapter 3, so Christians also used lamps in their oratories, gradually redirecting and purifying rites of idolatry wherever they did not conflict with the faith. I discussed this long ago in my *Pentecontarchus*, chapters 26 and 49. I present an image of a lamp from Fortunatus Scacchi’s *Sacred Oil-Chrism Treasury*, book I, chapter 7, volume I, where you may find more extensive and learned material.

[Col. 1042D] On their rings as well, soldiers used to carry not scarabs or military emblems, but the image of a fish, in memory of Christ, who was the mystical fish—ἰχθύς—of the Sibyls; or that of a fisherman, in reverence for the Apostle; or a dove, in remembrance of the Holy Spirit; or a ship, as an image of the Church.

Thus Clement of Alexandria advises in book III of *The Instructor*:

“Let our seals be a dove, or a fish, or a ship running before the wind, or a musical lyre; and if someone is a fisherman, he will remember the Apostle.”

That is: “These signs shall be ours: a dove, or a fish, or a swift ship, or a harmonious lyre; and if someone is a fisherman, he will remember the Apostle.”

Carrying images on rings, as a sign of obedience or love, was always customary among ancient peoples. An example of obedience is found in Suetonius, *Life of Tiberius*, chapter 38:

“Little by little this form of accusation advanced to such a point that it became a capital offense even for a slave to fall near an image of Augustus, or to carry an image stamped on a coin or ring into a latrine or brothel.”

See also Valerius Maximus, book III, chapter 5, speaking of the son of Africanus:

“Moreover, they pulled the ring from his hand on which the head of Africanus had been engraved.”

Thus Lentulus possessed an image of his grandfather, as Cicero writes in the third *Catilinarian*:

“Then I showed Lentulus the tablets and asked whether he recognized the seal. He nodded. ‘It is,’ I said, ‘a familiar seal indeed: the image of your grandfather, a most illustrious man, who loved his country and fellow citizens above all. This image, even though mute, ought to have recalled you from so great a crime.’”

You will find an example of a token of love in Ovid, book I of the *Tristia*, elegy 6:

Though you dissemble, you nevertheless perceive that everything is said,  
You who bear and turn me upon your finger.

Embracing my likeness in yellow gold,  
You behold, as best you can, the dear features of the exile.

They therefore carried on their rings not merely a token of obedience, but also branded the body itself with such signs. Saint Chrysostom recognized this in homily 3 on Saint Paul’s Second Epistle to the Corinthians, when he calls the image and name of the emperor, branded into the skin of Roman soldiers with a red-hot iron so that they might be reminded of their loyalty and courage, “the seal of soldiers”:

“For just as there is a seal for soldiers, so also the Spirit is imposed upon the faithful; and if you desert the ranks, you become conspicuous to everyone.”

Prudentius uses the same word and recalls the same custom in *On the Crowns*, hymn 1:

What happens when he receives the little seals,  
When he is to be consecrated?

They bring fine needles from the furnaces;  
With these they proceed to burn the limbs. When they have heated them,  
Whatever part of the body the glowing mark  
Has branded, they declare that part consecrated.

George Fabricius comments:

“Σφραγίς means a sign or mark impressed, either for the sake of remembrance, as with a ring, or for religious purposes, as with a heated iron.”

Concerning the ring, Saint Jerome writes in his commentary on Isaiah, chapter III, at the words “The Lord will take away the rings”:

“Rings, by which we are marked for the military service of God.”

Saint Augustine speaks clearly of the branded name of the emperor in letter 50 to Boniface, quoted in *Quemadmodum*, section 1, question 23, canon 7:

“Why, then,” he says, “do you not baptize me, so that you may wash me from my sins?” I reply: “Because I do not insult the emperor’s mark when I correct a deserter’s error.”

In the same letter he again calls this sign or mark the royal character:

“Thus the sheep’s error must be corrected without corrupting in it the seal of the Redeemer. For if someone is marked with the royal character as a deserter who has been marked, and receives pardon, and the former returns to military service while the latter begins to serve in the army in which he had not previously served, is that character erased in either of them? Or rather, is it recognized in both and approved with the honor due to it, because it is royal?”

Saint Ambrose agrees in a full-voiced passage in his oration *On the Death of the Emperor Valentinian*:

“Servants are inscribed with the Lord’s character, and soldiers are marked with the emperor’s name.”

From this, those ancient Fathers, in the earliest times of the Church, clearly manifested their piety in this matter, carrying in their flesh, by means of a Christian brand, the venerable name of Jesus or the sign of the cross.

Procopius of Gaza observed this in Isaiah 44:5, at the words “This one will say, ‘I am God’s’”: “The phrase ‘by the hand’ is used because perhaps many used to tattoo upon their wrists or arms either the sign of the cross or the name of Christ.”

Saint Paul may perhaps have referred to this in Galatians, chapter 6, verse 17—alongside other interpretations, both accepted and admitted according to taste, which Claudius Dausquius learnedly approves and lists in his book entitled *The Holiness of Saint Paul*, book II, chapter 13—when he says:

“I bear in my body the stigmata of the Lord Jesus.”

As though he were saying: “I bear on my body not only those stigmata of Jesus Christ, as his servant, but also his name branded upon me, so that all may recognize me as such.”

For a royal name imposed upon something clearly demonstrated that it was devoted to the ruler. Thus the emperors Honorius and Theodosius state in book I, title *That No Private Person May Use Titles*, and there:

“Therefore let everyone understand that whatever bears the Lord’s name must be assigned to public ownership.”

I discussed this not without interest in *A Token of the Laws, or Afternoon Summer Leisure*, on the law *Super creandis*, title 9, *On the Law of the Treasury*, book X, p. 11 and following.

After writing this, I saw that Aloysius Novarianus had alluded to the same matter in book III of the *Sacred Selections*, chapter 14, no. 467, writing as follows:

“Let no one brand himself except with the mark of the heavenly emperor; let no one seal his body except with the characters of Christ, so that he may say with Paul: ‘For I bear in my body the stigmata of the Lord Jesus’—not of Caesar, nor of any other earthly emperor.”

Here he says that he has erased the suspicion of the great Justus Lipsius, who candidly admits in book I of *Roman Military Affairs*, dialogue 9, that he does not know what was written by a military brand, although he acknowledges that he suspects it was something.

Our Accursius—who was not, as some boast and mockingly proclaim, ignorant of antiquarian matters—grasped these venerable and most ancient monuments. In his marginal gloss on the law *Stigmata*, title 5, *On the Fabricenses*, book II, he says:

“Stigmata were instruments by which their arms were marked with the fortunate name of our piety impressed upon them, just as happens with recruits, as he adds here.”

Lucas de Penna, at the end of his commentaries on the same passage, writes:

“In the first gloss there, after ‘they were marked,’ add: ‘And this stigma is called the emperor’s character.’”

Concerning the brands of slaves, I played fully, though at that time still of tender age, in my notes on Martial, book II, epigram 29, no. 5.

I shall not omit here something that is by no means irrelevant to the subject: it reveals that the letter A was originally represented under a triangular figure, in this form, Δ, when God first delivered the alphabet to mortal men from the time of Adam. John Martin Siliceus, archbishop of Toledo, attests this in his book *On the Divine Name Jesus*, chapter 3, p. 22, from which he explains with a great mystery the passage of Saint John’s Apocalypse, chapter 1, cited above:

“In polygonal figures—that is, figures with several angles—the first figure is the letter Δ, namely an equilateral triangle; the last, though not polygonal, is the letter Ο, which is the most capacious of all figures. No Christian will be received within the circumference of the letter Ο unless he has first paused at the letter Δ, which is the beginning and foundation of the Christian religion: in that beginning there is one essence and three persons.

“Whoever therefore wishes to approach God, infinite and all-encompassing, signified by the letter Ο, must first believe that he is one and triune: one in essence and three in persons, which we have said is signified by the letter Δ.”

Thus far the archbishop. ]

In this year, or the preceding one, Julian buried the most holy Gudila, archdeacon of Toledo and his fellow student, in the monastery of Saint Peter and Felix, situated beside the river Tagus. For him he composed the following sepulchral poem, placed on the tomb:

[Col. 1039A]

Buried beneath this monument lies Toledo’s glory,  
Gudila, a part of my soul and half of myself.

From tender youth he preserved the ways of the aged,  
And, though a young man, he did nothing here that was childish.

The Spirit of Christ dwelt in his holy breast;  
In conduct, speech, and hand he expressed him wholly.

He was food for the poor, comfort for widows,  
Grateful healing for the sick; for all the wretched he was their sole support.

By many merits you purchase heaven, good Gudila;  
Our longing for you continues to torment us.

We mournfully call him whom the ether has taken away,

and accompany his funeral with pious little tears.

[Col. 1040A] We do not scatter violets, delicate roses, or pale lilies

over the tomb, but your good [vows?; the printed reading is *vola*], Gudila.

Therefore, look down upon us, radiant one, from your heavenly citadel;

and may love and concern for me move you, Gudila.

Drive illness away from the native walls, and hunger,

and hostile threats, false doctrines, and deceit.

Do not despise Toledo’s prayers [alternative: “and hear Toledo’s prayers”], nor the requests of your companion,

who gives you this poem—Julian, loving you:

and he lays your sacred bones in the church of Felix,

whose mind is joined to the heavenly choirs. Α Ω [Col. 1039] “The servant of God, the lord Gudila, archdeacon of the holy Church of Toledo, died in peace on the sixth day before the Kalends of September, in the era 718, that is, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 680.

DCCXIX. DCLXXXI.

[Col. 1043]

136. [Note: [Col. 1044D]

136. Julianus was consecrated in the church of Saint Mary on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, on that very holy day of the Nativity of the Lord, in the year 680, which that year fell on a Monday, although it had a Dominical Letter. A. P. H.]

In this year, on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, in the church of Saint Mary Major of Toledo, the holy man Julian, already made a priest, was consecrated in the presence of all nineteen bishops of his metropolis [alternative: “his nineteen metropolitan bishops”], the palatine officials, and King Flavius Ervig.

DCCXXI. DCLXXXIII.

137. [Note: [Col. 1045A]

137. The Twelfth Council of Toledo was convened at Toledo in the second year of King Ervig, on the fifth day before the Ides of January. Rodericus says that it was convened on the fifth day before the Ides of May. Thus he writes in Book III, chapter 12: “He”—that is, Ervig—“in the second year of his reign arranged for the Twelfth Council of Toledo to be held on the fifth day before the Ides of May. Thirty-five bishops were present, together with an immeasurable number of clergy and a gathering of Christian laymen. This council was held under Julian, primate of the royal city; and Julian of Seville, Liuba of Braga, Stephen of Mérida, their suffragans, and the representatives of absent prelates signed.” Nothing is said here about abbots or palatine men. Felix, in the Life of Julian, writes: “Julian obtained the primacy of the aforementioned city.” The phrase “the primacy of the aforementioned city” is emphatic, as though the primacy of all Spain resided in that city. ID.—Concerning Liuba of Braga, see the illustrious D. Rodericus de Acuña, *Catalogue of the Archbishops of Braga*, chapter 97, p. 404. D. L.]

In the eleventh year of King Ervig, on the fifth day before the Ides of January, a council of Toledo was held in the royal city, in the basilica of the holy apostles Peter and Paul. It was presided over by Julian, metropolitan of the royal city and primate of the Spains, together with Julian, bishop of the see of Seville; Liuba of Braga; Stephen of Mérida; and Argebadus, bishop of the city of Illiberis—men of the greatest learning and holiness. It admitted thirty other bishops, three representatives, four abbots, and fifteen palatine officials.

138. Isidore of Xàtiva, who attended the Sixteenth Council of Toledo, composed the order of the council and the collection of Councils called that of Isidore the Fisherman or Merchant, in the *Chronicle*. Isidore was called by this surname in addition to the name Isidore.

139. [Note: [Col. 1045B]

139. Concerning the Thirteenth Council of Toledo, from Rodericus in the passage cited above: it was held in the fourth year of King Ervig. There were forty-eight bishops. P. H.]

On the day before the Nones of November, in the fourth year of that king, the Thirteenth Council of Toledo was held under the same Julian. It consisted of twenty-eight bishops, eight abbots, twenty-six palatine officials, and twenty-seven representatives of absent bishops; among them were the priest Gratianus [alternative: Gratinus], representative of Argebadus of Illiberis.

DCCXXII. DCLXXXIV.

140. [Note: [Col. 1046A]

140. It was held in the fifth year of King Ervig, after the fourth year had been completed and six days had passed into the fifth—that is, on 20 November. As D. Rodericus notes, it was held on the twelfth day before the Kalends of December, on a Sunday. Neither the day nor the fact that it was a Sunday appears in the manuscript.]

In the fifth year of King Ervig, in the suburban Praetorian church of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, under the same president, the Fourteenth Council of Toledo was held.

DCCXXIII. DCLXXXV.

141. [Leo I, pope, is missing. D. L. … wrote to the bishops of Spain, to King Ervig, and to the bishop of Toledo and count Simplicius, concerning the acceptance of the Sixth Council of Constantinople.

DCCXXIV. DCLXXXVI.

142. Pope Benedict, while still only elected, writes to Peter the regional notary [the words “concerning the acceptance of that same Sixth Ecumenical Council” are missing].

143. [Note: [Col. 1046A]

143. The fathers of the Thirteenth Council of Toledo, and so forth. See numbers 144 and 149, and Julian in the *Chronicle*, no. 361. “Saint Julian,” he says, “sends an *Apologeticus* with explanations to Pope Sergius, and poems to the emperor Heraclius Justinian in his praise. They reply to him with an elegant letter.” It should be read according to our Liutprand, cited at no. 149, where he says: “And he received letters from both.”]

The fathers of the Fourteenth Council of Toledo write that the *Apologeticus* was composed by Saint Julian, the pontiff; and in that council they approve what Saint Julian the pontiff had thought and written.

144. When the envoys of the Fourteenth Council of Toledo, carrying the *Apologeticus*, came with it to Rome, Pope Benedict was there. The names of the envoys were these: Benedict the priest, Innocent the deacon, Constantine the subdeacon [in other accounts, Benedict later became bishop of Pax Augusta], afterward bishop of Pax Augusta; Vincent [alternative: Innocent], bishop of Dumium; Constantine of Egabria [alternative: Constantius of Egitania]. …

145. [John V is missing; for he succeeded Benedict. D. L.] … The pope placed the canons of the Fourteenth Council of Toledo before Saint Peter.

146. The body of Saint Asodus or Asodanus, who suffered martyrdom at Gaza, was transferred to Rome; and in Antiquaria in Baetica the memory remained of Cornelius Proculus and Cornelius Bassus, slain pontiffs who had been converted by the disciples of Saint James at the end.

DCCXXV. DCLXXXVII.

147. [Note: [Col. 1046A]

147. Concerning Ervig’s abdication of the kingdom and the placing upon the royal throne of the Goths of Egica, the husband of his daughter and therefore his son-in-law, Saint Julian writes as follows in his short *Chronicle*: “On that day, placed in the extremity of illness, he chose for himself as successor to the kingdom our glorious lord Egica. On the following day, which was the seventeenth day before the Kalends of December, a Friday, the same lord Ervig received penance and absolved all the senior officials, so that they might approach the glorious prince, the lord Egica, at his royal seat in Toledo.” Saint Julian writes this concerning the anointing of King Egica: “Our lord Egica was anointed into the kingdom in the church of the holy Peter and Paul at the Praetorium, on the eighth day before the Kalends of December, on a Sunday, on the fifteenth day of the moon, in the era 725.” Thus he writes. P. H.]

In this year, King Ervig, placed in Toledo in the extremity of illness, set his most glorious son—or son-in-law—Egica upon the royal throne, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of December, a Thursday. On the following day, Friday—that is, the sixteenth day before the Kalends of December—he received penance and released all the senior officials from the oath of loyalty and obedience that they had sworn to him, so that those officials might approach to receive the said prince Egica as lord and king, and might accept him and swear allegiance to him. The royal oath, or the oath on behalf of the king, was received by the lord Julian, primate of Toledo. Egica was then anointed under the same patriarch in the church of Saints Peter and Paul within the city, on the eighth day before the Kalends of December, and was crowned in the era 725, in the presence of many bishops, abbots, and palatine officials.

DCCXXVI. DCLXXXVIII.

148. [Note: [Col. 1047A]

148. Concerning the Fifteenth Council of Toledo, held under Egica, king of the Goths, Rodericus writes in Book III, chapter 14, in these words: “In his time”—that is, Egica’s—“the necessity of the groin-plague became prevalent in the province of Narbonne. On account of this, the bishops belonging to the see of Narbonne were excused by the Council of Toledo, but on the condition that the regulations of that sacred council should be announced and accepted in each cathedral church; and if any bishop failed to do this, he would be struck with anathema and fined a fifth part of his goods. In the first year of his reign, the Fifteenth Council was celebrated in the Praetorian Church of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, with all the bishops of Spain and Gaul assembled, the blessed Julian of holy memory presiding, with nearly sixty bishops and a numerous gathering of Christians assisting all around. In it, on various grounds, and for the absolution of the oath which he had injuriously sworn to the aforesaid prince Ervig, he petitioned the synod to release him from the oath. In his time, the book concerning the three substances, which the most holy primate Julian had previously sent to Rome and which Pope Benedict of Rome, treating the matter less cautiously, had ordered to be rejected because it said that will generated will, Saint Julian confirmed as true in this council by truthful testimonies, at the demand of the aforesaid prince, through the declarations that he had sent to Rome. He composed an *Apologeticus* and sent it to Rome by his envoys—a priest, a deacon, and a subdeacon—most learned men, servants of God in all things, and trained in the divine Scriptures. He sent with them acclamatory verses, just as he had formerly sent verses in praise of the Roman emperor. Rome, receiving it piously and worthily, ordered it to be read publicly by all; and the emperor, acclaiming, ‘Praise of you, O God, reaches to the ends of the earth,’ often made it known by having it read. He also sent back, through the envoys mentioned above, a reply to the lord Julian, with thanks and honor, and declared that everything he had written was just and pious. This was the Fifteenth Council of Toledo, celebrated in the first year of King Egica, on the fifth day before the Ides of May, under Julian, primate of the royal city. Senfredus of Narbonne, Floresintius of Seville, Faustinus of Braga, and Maximus of Mérida, metropolitans, signed, together with Sisuldus, representative of Cyprian of Tarragona, and the other representatives of bishops who had not come because lawfully prevented. Apart from the representatives, there were sixty-one.”

But let us see what Julian, archpriest of Saint Justa in the church of Toledo, also says about this. Thus, in his *Chronicle* under the year 689—a passage that will shed much light on this history and will show the piety and obedience of the Spaniards—he writes: “Pope Leo II sent the Sixth Council of Constantinople to the bishops of Spain in the year 633 with Peter the regional notary, asking them to confirm it for him. The bishops sent an *Apologeticus* with the envoys whom we shall name below, composed by Saint Julian, in which he said: ‘Will generated will’; and that Christ consisted of three natures or substances.

“Pope Leo had already died, and Benedict succeeded him. Before his consecration he wrote to Peter the regional notary as follows:

“‘Benedict the priest, and by the grace of God the elect of the holy apostolic see, to Peter, notary and regional representative: In accordance with what your apostolic diligence has remembered, the lord Pope Leo intended to go to the province of Spain, to the most excellent and Christian king, to the most holy archbishops and all the prelates of the Churches established there, and likewise to the glorious count, in order to make known the definition of the venerable Sixth Synod, together with the acclamation called the *prosphoneticum* of the most reverend bishops who assembled in that council gathered by God, addressed to the most merciful prince, and sent everywhere generally by the edict of that most pious prince. Carry out the ministry entrusted to you with the utmost devotion, for the firmness of our apostolic faith; and take care, with the greatest diligence and vigilance, to append the subscriptions of the most reverend bishops after that synod and definition. In this way the most reverend bishops, and through them the whole devout province, may prove themselves participants with us in the Catholic and apostolic tradition and faith; and the commendation and reception of that faith before God, to whose glory the praise and stability of the Christian faith are directed, may result in the salvation of souls.

“‘Adorn the office of piety that you have undertaken with vigilance and diligence, and hasten to complete it; for you are storing up for yourself the fruit of a good work, and you are providing for those who receive it the opportunity to attain the blessedness of the heavenly kingdom through the confession of the true and apostolic faith.’”

He also sent another letter to Quiricus, who by that time had already departed for the monastery.

Pope Benedict received the letters and the *Apologeticus* of Saint Julian. The new Pope Benedict had been offended by the novelty of the expressions—namely, “that will generated will” and “that Christ consisted of three natures,” or essences. He wrote to Julian courteously and instructed the bearer orally to admonish him concerning those propositions. When the holy teacher saw that some people had been scandalized by the novelty of these expressions, he sent the pope himself a little book of replies with Peter the regional notary, and together with it certain poems [Col. 1048C] in praise of the empire. I have excerpted them from the works of Saint Julian; they are as follows:

The majesty of the empire extends farther and passes beyond the world;

if piety is present, it flies beyond the stars.

For the sword of Caesar ought to defend the see

of Peter, over which God himself presides.

From him you received your strength and the summit of your title;

should you not, Caesar, be willing to offer him aid?

The glory of the Roman empire brings yokes upon kings;

it moves peoples, it is present among nations.

Justiniane, may every barbarian, every sluggish and treacherous man,

be broken by the strength of your right hand.

With you as Caesar, may the new Rome bear celebrated triumphs;

may ancient Rome envy its noble name.

With you as Caesar, may the Church bear green laurels,

and carry glory away from heretical bondage.

And may the impious Monothelites submit their necks to you,

O pope, holy shepherd, and to Peter the key-bearer.

May he conquer, and may the sacred see enjoy eternal peace;

with you as Caesar, Justinian, may he hold the earth.

Live long, Caesar; adore the commands

that Benedict gives. Thus, too, you will be a fortunate Caesar.

He wrote back to Julian, and he still pressed the matter; and he ordered Julian, after consulting with King Egica, to convene at Toledo a council of the bishops of the Gothic people and of his own realm, a national and universal council, in the first year of King Egica. There, after the letters had been read, Julian explained his position and composed another *Apologeticus*, with a poem in praise of Saint Pope Sergius, who had succeeded Benedict after the others in the year 687. He also sent three most wise and holy men from the clergy of the holy Church of Toledo, as so great a matter required: Felix, archpriest; Ubisandus, archdeacon; and Musairus, chief clerk or subdeacon, with letters, the book of the *Apologeticus*, and the poem.

After the letters and book had been read, Saint Pope Sergius approved it and made it available for all to read. Having given thanks for the labor and devotion, he sent the envoys back with relics and his blessing, together with a reply in writing. These poems are taken from the epigrams of Saint Julian, which are in the manuscript book of Saint Justa:

To you I gladly send this book, most holy Sergius,

you who rule and govern countless sheep.

The famous report of your praises has reached us:

that you are good and merciful, a lover of piety.

In heart, voice, and the manner of your life you represent Christ,

whose office on earth you also discharge.

Live long for us and for the world, radiant Sergius;

Julian, rejoicing, gives kisses to your feet.

Receive with a merciful countenance, most holy Sergius,

my writings; correct, O pope, my vigils.

Read through whatever our letter teaches,

and run with gliding spirit over its brief notes.

Whatever you yourself say is God’s judgment;

what you declare, God in heaven will regard as approved.

The highest power has been granted by the Lord Christ;

you are able to close the heavens and to open them again.

Therefore, Father Sergius, bless your little brother,

so that abundant grace may flow upon our head.

Remember King Egica and his faithful people;

then bless the peoples of your bishops.

By your dew the Spanish field will flourish abundantly,

and for all time it will cultivate the Catholic faith.

No savage storm, however great, with the whirlpool of Phlegethon,

will carry it away from pious tongues and hearts.

Alas for me! How I fear that evil error may ensnare us,

and that we may be given over as a reproach to unspeakable peoples!

Africa, full of warlike men, threatens with arms,

and day by day the victorious Agarene people rage.

So that this fear of mine may not prove true, through Christ our avenger,

pray for your peoples, best of popes;

that God may turn the axe away from our neck,

and, as you weep, the merciful one may grant pardon to the guilty.

Felix, archbishop of Toledo, recalls both *Apologetici* in the Life of Saint Julian, in these words: [Col. 1050A] “The *Apologeticus* of the faith, which was sent to Benedict, pope of the city of Rome. Likewise, another *Apologeticus* concerning the three chapters, about which the bishop of the city of Rome appeared, though without cause, to have doubted.”

I do not think that the history of these events can be gathered more effectively from anywhere else than from the Fourteenth and Fifteenth Councils of Toledo, where everything is explained sufficiently and abundantly. For in the Fourteenth Council, canon 4, we read:

“It was therefore decided that, at that time, by the answers of our apologetic defense, we should satisfy the Roman pontiff, confirm the acts themselves, and set forth the meaning of our faith by the purest clarification of words. And because there they indicate copiously and clearly what is true concerning this double will and operation of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, these matters have already been sent to the Roman region through the envoys of Spain.”

And in the Fifteenth Council:

“After the confession of faith, we immediately turned to examine those chapters, for the defense of which, two years earlier, Benedict, the Roman pope of blessed memory, had warned us by the indication of his letters. Yet he did not take care to record them in his own writings, but instructed our man to report them orally. To this he was sufficiently and appropriately answered that same year. Nevertheless, when we now reread more carefully that report by our man, we found that, in the book of the reply to our faith which we had sent through Peter, the regional representative of the Roman Church, the first chapter had appeared to the aforesaid pope to have been placed there by us incautiously. There we had said, with reference to the divine essence: ‘Will generated will, just as wisdom generated wisdom.’ But that man, passing over these words in a careless skim of his reading, thought that these very names …”

These words are from Saint Julian himself. From them it may be inferred that Peter, the regional notary, had gone to Rome somewhat less than two years earlier and had brought Saint Julian’s *Apologeticus*, which Pope Sergius carefully read and approved. The Master of the Sentences cites some portions of it.

In the year 690, on the day before the Nones of March—which fell on a Sunday—Saint Julian, archbishop of Toledo [Col. 1050C] and an eminent teacher, died. He was buried in the basilica of Saint Leocadia, as his predecessor had been.]

At the beginning of the first year of King Egica, on the fifth day before the Ides of May, the Fifteenth Council was held at Toledo in the Praetorian Church—that is, the suburban church—of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, toward the north. The same Julian, primate of Toledo, was present, together with Suniefredus of Narbonne, Floresindus of Seville, Faustinus of Braga, Maximus of Mérida, John of the see of Illiberis, and fifty-five other bishops, eleven abbots, five representatives of bishops, and seventeen palatine men.

DCCXXVII. DCLXXXIX.

[Col. 1049]

149. [Note: [Col. 1050C]

149. In this year the lord Julian sent the letter. We spoke above, at no. 143. D. L.]

In this year the lord Julian, archbishop of Toledo and primate of the Spains, sent the council’s decrees [the printed *creta* may represent *decreta*] and poems to Pope Sergius and to the emperor, and received letters from both.

150. In this year the holy and universal Council of Nicaea, consisting of 350 bishops, was held against the heretics who opposed images.

DCCXXVIII. DCXC.

151. [Note: [Col. 1050C]

151. In this same year, namely 690, Sisebertus was consecrated in the see of Saint Mary—as some maintain, he had been a Benedictine abbot—as archbishop of Toledo, in place of Saint Julian, pontiff of Toledo, on a Friday, the eighth day after the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ. P. H.]

In this year, on the day after the Nones of March, the holy and most wise pontiff Julian died at Toledo. Among other works, he wrote a *Chronicle of the Visigothic Kings*, from the era 450 to the time of King Egica. The rest was added by Felix and Guntericus, archbishops of Toledo. The holy pontiff Julian was buried in the church of Saint Leocadia, which had been his residence. Felix, bishop of Toledo, placed this funeral poem for him:

You succeed the holy Quiricus in the see, Julian,

the best in life and renowned in eloquence.

A blameless life, a generous hand, faithful care,

and zeal for God [alternative: “a gathering”], and the radiance of judgment,

made you greatly beloved by the Spanish people,

by every rank, by the common people, and by men.

Behold, you leave the earthly seat [alternative: “alas, the throne”], but God has brought you to the stars;

your life is worthy to be blessed in so great a place.

You dwell among the apostolic ranks, Julian;

you complete and adorn the apostolic strength.

Remember your own Felix, gracious Father, the Levite,

so that your servant may be worthy of honor through your prayer.

And we place your limbs in the tomb; Leocadia, a citizen,

is guardian of your body; here was her cradle. Α Ω [Col. 1049] 152. “The most holy pontiff Julian died in peace at Toledo on the day before [alternative: the day after] the Nones of March. He sat upon the patriarchal throne for ten years, eleven months, and nine days, and died in the fifth year of the glorious King Egica, in the era 728. Felix the Levite, who succeeded him in the same see.”

153. [Note: [Col. 1050C]

153. At that time there were ten languages in Spain, [Col. 1051A] and so forth. He cites a passage from Strabo to confirm what he reports—namely, that the inhabitants of Spain spoke various languages—and that the same situation existed in the time of Augustus and Tiberius Caesar, under whom Strabo flourished. According to the edition of Isaac Casaubon, the passage is as follows, Book III:

“These people”—the Turdetani—“are judged the most learned of all the Spaniards. They use grammar, possess records of ancient history written down, and poems, and laws composed in meter, said to be six thousand years old. The other Spaniards also use grammar, though not all of one kind; indeed, they do not even use the same language.”

It is better translated by those who render it “language.” In Greek it reads:

Καὶ οἱ ἄλλοι δ᾽ Ἴβηρες χρῶνται γραμματικῇ, οὐ μιᾷ ἰδίᾳ, οὐδὲ γὰρ γλώττῃ ἰδίᾳ.

“And the other Iberians also use writing, not one single distinctive form; nor, indeed, do they possess one single distinctive language.”

The writer Father Juan de Mariana cites this passage in *On the Affairs of Spain*, Book I, chapter 5, to establish the same point.

That is why the most learned D. Alfonso de Madrigal, bishop of Ávila, said in *Paralipomena*, Part I, chapter 1, question 5:

“Because Tubal had one language, he named one people, although it is said of all these peoples in Genesis 10:5 that they were all in their own languages—that is, each had one language distinct from another. Yet there were, and still are, many languages in Spain from the beginning. Therefore Tubal alone did not inhabit this land, but other peoples came with him.”

From this I draw two conclusions: first, that the principal language of the people of Tubal was also the common native language of the Spaniards; second, that he brought with him other peoples of another language, who also spoke in different tongues. Hence there were several languages in Spain.

I further confirm the first point by the authority of the same bishop of Ávila, an authority whom I esteem highly and rightly so. In his commentary on the second part, chapter 25, written in our own language concerning the *Chronicle of Eusebius*, he says:

“It should be considered that, as reliable authors say, Spain was populated by Tubal, the fifth son of Japheth. At the dispersal of the peoples, when the languages were divided, he came with many people of his own language, which is now ours, although it has been greatly refined and altered from that first condition.”

What commotion the testimony of Maximus caused in the year of Christ 514! His words are these:

“Besides the Latin, Cimbrian, and Gothic languages, there was in Spain the Cantabrian language, and the more polished native Spanish language, which differed from Cantabrian in abundance of vocabulary, elegance, and grandeur.”

In learned and painstaking writings, the distinguished gentleman D. Gregorius López Madera taught us this in the second edition of *The Spanish Monarchy*, chapter 13. The very learned Bernard Joseph de Aldrete had also spoken of these matters in *On the Origin of the Spanish Language*, Book II, chapter 15. He again intends to show himself a great champion in that same vast and admirable spectacle of learning, although he will not enter the same arena; and most recently he gathers and arranges everything, writing with subtle intelligence and great judgment in his commentaries on Maximus, so that nothing further can be desired or discovered.

I shall add another passage from Julian’s *Chronicle*, no. 376, which is no less similar to milk than milk is to milk:

“The Mozarabs spoke the customary Spanish language and Gothic; especially the people of Toledo, who were more polished than the rest, preserved the native refinement of the vernacular language among the Moors. [Col. 1051D] This had its beginning from Tubal. In contracts and ordinary speech with the Saracens they spoke Arabic; among themselves they spoke [alternative: used] the Gothic or ancient Spanish language.”

He said that the Toledans were more polished than the others—a distinction long observed and continuing to our own times. King Alfonso, also called the Wise, ordered in the courts assembled at Toledo that, if doubt arose concerning the meaning of any ancient Spanish word, the interpretation assigned by the Toledans should be followed. D. Francisco de Pisa reports this in Part I of his description of Toledo, Book I, chapter 35, folio 56, column 3, previously in Alcoçer’s *History of Toledo*. I do not remember having read the law concerning this matter in the *Seven Parts*, although it is commonly asserted that it is found there. D. L.]

At that time there were ten languages in Spain, as under Augustus and Tiberius:

I. Old Spanish;  
II. Cantabrian;  
III. Greek;  
IV. Latin;  
V. Arabic;  
VI. Chaldean;  
VII. Hebrew;  
VIII. Celtiberian;  
IX. Valencian;  
X. Catalan.

Strabo discusses these in Book III, where he teaches that there were several forms of writing and several languages in the Spains.

154. In this year, on the Kalends of April, Sisebertus was consecrated bishop of Toledo in the church of Saint Mary, in the presence of the suffragan bishops. As some maintain, he had been an abbot; he was sharp-witted, moderately learned, but related by royal kinship and connected with King Wamba. He was extremely arrogant and eager for innovations, although he was steadfast in the Catholic faith and a vigorous defender of it. For that reason he was later removed from his dignity.

DCCXXIX. DCXCI.

155. [Note: [Col. 1052A]

155. The Council of Zaragoza is mentioned in the councils of D. García de Loaysa as having been held on the Kalends of November, a Sunday, in the era 729—that is, in the year of Christ 691, the fourteenth year of King Egica. P. H.]

On the Kalends of November in this year, the fourth year of King Egica, a council was held in the city of Zaragoza.

DCCXXX. DCXCII.

156. [Note: [Col. 1052A]

156. Sisebertus wished to put on the garment that the Blessed Virgin had given to Saint Ildefonsus. Father Mariana, Book VI, chapter 18, and Garivay, Book VIII, chapter 44, say that he put on a cape; but Cixila says that he did not put on this garment, but sat upon the ivory chair on which the most holy Virgin had presided. I shall append the words of Cixila, bishop of Toledo, which are these:
