“He found the Lady herself seated in the chair where he himself was accustomed to sit and greet the people. Afterward no bishop dared approach that chair except the lord Sisebertus, who immediately lost it and was sent into exile.”

From this point he began to fall into the abyss of evils.

On Friday, 11 May, in the sixth year of King Egica, the year of Christ 693, Sisebertus was deprived of his see and possessions and driven into exile, to the prison-house of his order. Concerning him, the sixteenth Council of Toledo says in chapter 9, as follows:

“Therefore Sisebertus, bishop of the see of Toledo, was found to have been marked by such schemes: because he had determined not merely to deprive our most serene lord, King Egica, of the kingdom, but also to kill him together with Flogellus, Theodemirus, Liubilanus, Liubigitho, Thecla, and the others, and had planned to bring disturbance and destruction upon his people and country. By the decision of our decree he already stands deprived of place and honor.

“Therefore our whole college jointly decrees by this canonical sanction that this decree of our unity, which we have also decided to attach to these synodal definitions, shall remain supported by its full authority and shall possess perpetual, unshakable force.

“As for Sisebertus himself, because of his violation of his oath and his such great criminal conspiracy, according to the institution of the ancient canons—which prescribe that whoever is found to have done such things, and while the prince is alive to have turned his attention to another in hope of a future kingdom, is to be excluded from the assembly of Catholics by a sentence of excommunication, deprived at once of honor and position, and stripped of all possessions, which are to be placed under the authority of the aforesaid prince—and is to remain confined in perpetual exile, receiving communion only at the end of his life, unless royal mercy should beforehand judge him worthy of absolution.

“Likewise, all others among the religious, whatever their order or rank, who from this time forward are found to have done or planned such things against the prince are to be punished by censure.”

And in chapter 12:

“Therefore, because Sisebertus, bishop of the see of Toledo, did not at all prefer to submit humbly to the salutary admonitions of those men, so that he might govern the Church of God in due order, instruct it in humility, and summon it by salutary examples to the heavenly kingdoms, but struck himself with a two-edged sword—namely, pride and perjury—and wished not only to deprive our glorious lord King Egica of the kingdom but also to destroy him by inflicting death, it is not fitting for us to begin the council before he has first been punished by canonical and legal censure and another has been substituted in his place to occupy the see of Toledo.

“Therefore, when we had all been gathered together, the same bishop Sisebertus was presented to our assembly, and with open speech he confessed the conspiracy of his disloyalty. Accordingly, by the formula of this decree, we depose the aforementioned Sisebertus from the episcopal order and honor, according to the ancient edict of synodal sanction and the decree of the law promulgated concerning such matters. We declare him excommunicated from the reception of the body and blood of Christ and sentenced to remain in perpetual exile, receiving communion only at the end of his life, unless royal mercy, together with priestly connivance, should choose to absolve him.” ID.]

Sisebertus wished to put on the garment that blessed Ildefonsus had received from heaven, despite the opposition of the Toledo clergy; and, driven mad, he pursued revolutionary measures against the king.

DCCXXXI. DCXCIII.

[Col. 1053]

157. In the sixth year of the glorious King Egica, on the sixth day before the Nones of May, the Sixteenth Council of Toledo was held, consisting of fifty-nine bishops, in the basilica of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, on a Friday, the feast of Saint Athanasius, pontiff and confessor. In it—by authority, we believe, of the Roman pontiff, who had been consulted concerning the matter—Sisebertus, bishop of Toledo, was deposed because he was pursuing revolutionary measures against the king and the royal offspring, namely Flogellus, Theodemirus, Liubilanus [alternative: Labilanus], Vugiosana [corrected to: Liubigitho], Thecla, and the other sons of King Egica, whom he had attempted to kill. Stripped of all his possessions, struck with anathema, and deprived until death of participation in the Holy Eucharist and association with Catholics, he was thrust into perpetual exile in the monastery of Saint Peter Caradinensis, without support or position, with all his goods confiscated.

158. [Note: [Col. 1053B]

158. Concerning the election of Felix, who had been the disciple of the most holy Julian and archpriest in the Toledo church, and from there had advanced to the Church of Seville, and who was substituted for Sisebertus of Toledo, as the apostle Matthias was substituted for the traitor Judas, the same holy synod says in chapter 12:

“Therefore, since, with the Lord’s favor, the council must be begun as quickly as possible in accordance with the prior choice and authority of our aforesaid lord, by which he previously ordered our venerable brother Felix, bishop of the see of Seville, to undertake due care of the aforesaid Toledo see, reserving him to be formally appointed afterward by the same decree, for this reason we, with the consent of the clergy and people belonging to the aforesaid see of Toledo, canonically transfer our aforementioned venerable brother Felix from the see of Seville, which he has governed until now, to the see of Toledo. In that same see of Seville we likewise substitute our brother Faustinus, bishop of the see of Braga; and we also substitute Felix, bishop of the Church of Portus, as bishop in the aforesaid see of Braga.”

From these words, and from the edict of Egica, which adds, “with another bishop established there by royal choice,” it may be inferred, first, that the Gothic kings possessed the right to nominate bishops in their kingdom. Second, that a bishop could lawfully pass from the city of Seville to Toledo, as to the primatial see of all Spain. Third, that the see of Braga was not primary, since one did not ascend from it to Seville, but rather descended, as actually happened: the bishop of Braga moved to Seville. Concerning Felix, Rodericus writes in Book III, chapter 13: “He was distinguished by an extraordinary excellence of gravity and prudence.” The same is said in the *General History* and in Loaysa’s account of Gundemar. Although he held the younger see, at least in relation to Seville, he nevertheless presided as the acknowledged primate of all Spain.]

Felix, Julian’s disciple, already made bishop of Seville, a man distinguished by the praise of gravity and exceptional prudence, was appointed to the see of Toledo at the king’s request and that of the metropolitans, with the assent likewise of the entire council. He somewhat enlarged the *Chronicle* of his teacher, Saint Julian, archbishop of Toledo.

DCCXXXII. DCXCIV.

159. [Note: [Col. 1054B]

159. Concerning the seventeenth Synod of Toledo, which was held in the church of Saint Leocadia in the year 697, Rodrigo says in book III, chapter 13:

> “In the seventh year of King Flavius Egica, on the fifth day before the Ides of November, the seventeenth Council of Toledo was celebrated in the church of Saint Leocadia, where her holy body rests, in the suburb of Toledo, under Felix, primate of the royal city, who was endowed with an extraordinary excellence of gravity and prudence. Faustinus of Hispalis, Maximus of Emerita, Vera of Tarragona, and Felix of Braga, the metropolitans, signed, apart from those absent, who sent representatives in their place. In this council the same king was personally present; prostrating himself on the ground before everyone, he commended himself to their prayers. Offering the tome that he held in his hand to the primate and the council, he requested that they satisfy him concerning the matters contained in it. All these things are explained most fully in the book of the canons.”

At this point it must not be passed over that the most learned Rodrigo, bishop of Toledo, not only believed that the primacy of Toledo began with Bernard, but with the martyr Eugenius, and consequently that under the Gothic kings the bishops of Toledo had been primates. P. H.]

In this year, on the fifth day before the Ides of November, in the seventh year of King Egica, the seventeenth Council of Toledo was held under Felix, bishop of Toledo, in the church of Saint Leocadia.

DCCXXXIV. DCXCVI.

160. In this year, Justinian was deposed as emperor and Leo succeeded him.

DCCXXXVI. DCXCVIII.

161. [Note: [Col. 1054C]

161. It is established from the histories of the Goths and others that the kingdom of Galicia existed. P. H.]

In this year Flavius Witiza lived in Galicia with royal authority, his father, King Egica, having so arranged it.

162. [Note: [Col. 1054C]

162. Julian Lucas, who collected and arranged much material about both Berosi. We spoke of Julian in the *Adversaria*, no. 36. Concerning Valerius Hispanus, who collected the fragments of Berosus, see Flavius Dexter, year 300, no. 13. Many writers have written many things about Berosus. See most recently Father Alfonso Maldonado, *Universal Chronicle*, treatise 15, p. 92. D. L.]

Julian Lucas flourished at Toledo; he collected and arranged much material concerning both Berosi [another reading: continued it].

[Col. 1055A] 163. [Note: [Col. 1055A]

163. Corduba flourished. There is still disagreement among authors: some say, others deny, that Corduba was founded by the Persians. Ambrosius de Morales, in volume II of his *History*, where he treats Corduba separately, tractate 4, folio 113, and in volume IV of *Hispania Illustrata*, rejects and condemns as futile the arguments advanced by those who assert this. Stephen of Garivay stands opposed in book V of his *Compendium of History*, p. 129, no. 25; he cites Pliny, book III, chapter 1 of the *Natural History*, in support of his view, since Pliny reports, on the authority of Marcus Varro’s tradition, that the Persians reached the whole of Spain. He would now defend this more vigorously if he had been able to see our Luitprand, who so confidently relates that Corduba was founded by the Persians. It is also plausible that, after the fashion of the cities that existed in Persia, they founded others in Spain bearing the same names—just as those first Spanish settlers of the New World did among the Indians in the western regions.

In Persia, near the river Tigris, there lies a province called Corduena; with a slight alteration, our city may have been called Corduba from it. Concerning Corduena, Ammianus Marcellinus writes in book XXV:

> “During that interval, before these men were sent, if the misled emperor had gradually withdrawn from hostile lands, he would certainly have reached the defenses of Corduena, a fertile region belonging to us, separated by one hundred miles from the place where these events were taking place.”

He says the same elsewhere several times.

Nor will it be unreasonable to conjecture that the name Corduba was formed from *Corduena* and *Duba*, a Persian region and word. For *Duba* seems to signify “summit”; and both in Corduba and in Salduba—which is now Zaragoza—it denotes a summit. In Corduba, whoever gave the city that name may have intended, under a favorable omen, to foretell that it would become the summit, or highest point, of an unending number of days. In Salduba, the intention may have been that it should be recognized as the summit of peace. What else does *sal* signify than peace? In 1 Esdras, chapter 4, verse 14: “We remember the salt.” Bernardinus Gomez discusses salt at length in *Commentary* 4, beginning with no. 9. Joachim Zechner, an author requiring expurgation, writes in the third century of the *Sacred Adages*, adage 54, no. 3: “A word, I say, familiar to the Persians, or at least not unknown to them.” Thus Barreirus believes that the name came from the numerous saltworks in that region; for it is well known that mountains rich in salt lie not far from this city. Ludovicus Nonius reports and follows him in his *Hispania*, chapter 82, p. 252. Again Bernardinus Gomez, *On Salt*, book I, § 38, p. 39.

Others derive the etymology of Corduba from elsewhere: John, bishop of Gerunda, book I of the *Paralipomena*; Gerardus Mercator, in the *Greater Atlas*, in his description of Baetica; Georgius Merula, in his *Cosmography*, part II, book II, chapter 24, p. 366. They derive it from *cor* and *Baetica*, as though it meant “the heart of Baetica.” Much of this was pointed out to me by the most learned Father Francis de Bivar, which I gladly and candidly acknowledge. [Col. 1055D]

Finally, from this disagreement among authors arises a matter requiring greater examination: the determination of Avicenna’s homeland. Many recognize him as Corduban, from Hispania; not a few recognize him as Corduenian, from Persia. To reduce these views to calculation and report them is neither worth the leisure nor the labor. I pass over those who assign him to Hispalis, and those whose authority Paschasius Gallus followed in the *Medical Library*: Conrad Gesner, Conrad Lycosthenes, and Josias Simler of Zurich; also Gaspar Bauhin of Basel.

What shall I say about our Rodrigo González de Clavijo, in his *Itinerary of the Embassy to the Great Tamerlane*? He says that Avicenna was born on the island called by the ancients Ebusus, or Ebosus, now Ibiza; and that there still stood there, in his own time, a certain tower bearing the name of Avicenna. Yet from an Arabic history translated into Spanish by Marcus Obelus, the royal interpreter, it is clear that he was a native Persian. Although I am usually most eager to claim what is mine, I am not accustomed to arrogate to myself what may belong to another.

The same doubts and conjectures must be examined and clarified concerning a work commonly attributed to Avicenna, as though it had come from the same vessel and had the same author. For in an ancient manuscript preserved in the church of the city of León, dedicated to Saint Isidore—I possess a copy of it—the work is asserted to be Isidore’s and falsely attributed to Avicenna. With the assistance of Theodiscus, archbishop of Hispalis, Avicenna is represented as a plagiarist who published it under his own language and name. As testimony, Lucas of Tuy, deacon, is cited in book III of his *Chronicle*, near the beginning:

> “Theodiscus succeeded the most blessed doctor Isidore. He was Greek by nation, learned in a variety of languages, outwardly polished in speech, but inwardly, as his end showed, a most ravenous wolf beneath a sheep’s skin. For certain books on the nature of things and the art of medicine, as well as *The Art of Notory*, which Father Isidore had composed in an eloquent style but which had not yet been made public, he corrupted out of hatred for the faith, cutting out what was true and inserting what was false; and through a certain Arab named Avicenna he translated them from Latin into Arabic.” [Col. 1056B]

The most eminent Cardinal Caesar Baronius, in volume VIII of the *Annals*, under the year of Christ 636, no. 9, cites the very passage of Lucas of Tuy and adds at the end:

> “These are the words of Lucas of Tuy; Francis Pegna, auditor of the Rota and most devoted to me, supplied us with a copy transcribed from the original.”

I do not, however, refuse to transcribe the words of the Spanish manuscript. They breathe antiquity and are wonderfully useful for illuminating the matter:

> “And Don Lucas of Tuy also says that Saint Isidore made a very excellent book of medicine, which remained in his chamber when he departed from this world. Before the said book came into the hands of anyone who knew it, a wicked bishop came from the regions of Africa to succeed to the archiepiscopal see of Seville. He was infected with the Arian heresy; his name was Theodiscus, and he was Greek by nature. He took many books that Saint Isidore had left in his study, and among them he found that book on medicine. Because he needed to understand certain Arabic names, he sent for a learned Moor to explain them to him. The Moor was a physician and was called Avicenna. As payment for his work, he gave him the book that Saint Isidore had written, so that the Moor might give it his own title and present it as though he himself had composed it. Thus the memory of Saint Isidore was lost.

> “As for the said book, many affirm that it is the very book which physicians now regard as their principal work and which is called Avicenna. They say that when the book was then translated from Latin into the vernacular so that the Moor could understand it, he composed it in his Arabic language, and afterward it was translated back into Latin, as it now exists. They say that in those translations, because the words were not properly understood, many errors arose, which are found in the book even today. Physicians have often discussed correcting these errors of Avicenna, because they say that they are very harmful, especially to inexperienced and untested physicians. May God grant that this be done soon and well, so that the harms arising from them to the bodily health of countless persons may cease. Many believe that, considering the abundance of knowledge and understanding that Saint Isidore possessed concerning all natural things, if that book of his on medicine had not been corrupted and its true original had been found as he wrote it, that one book alone would have sufficed to cure all illnesses insofar as human nature permitted, and there would have been no need for another book of medicine.” [Col. 1057B]

Thus far the manuscript.

Father John de Mariana of the Society of Jesus, in his *History of Spain* written in Latin, book VI, chapter 7, takes the opposite position under the year 639 and derives his argument from the chronological situation, which he says is wholly contradictory:

> “After Isidore’s death, Theodiscus, a Greek by nation, was appointed his successor in the Church of Hispalis after some interval. Some assert that he gave Isidore’s books, corrupted in many places, to the Arab Avicenna, so that, once translated into Arabic, he might publish them under his own name. This is false concerning Avicenna: for the testimony of Sorsanus, his contemporary, in the life of Avicenna himself, establishes that Avicenna lived more than three hundred years later, did not come to Spain, and prolonged his entire life in the royal court of the Persians.”

This agrees with the Arabic history related above in its description of Avicenna’s urban and courtly life, though it differs in the calculation of the years—which is the principal and only foundation of Mariana’s opinion. That history places Avicenna’s birth around the year 428, unless, as I think more correctly, the reckoning is made according to Arabic custom, namely from the flight of Muhammad; in that case it would favor Mariana rather than oppose him.

Ambrosius de Morales preceded Mariana in volume II of his *History of Spain*, book XII, in the life of King Chintila, folio 127, letter E. He reports in almost the same words the same account concerning Avicenna’s books as Mariana:

> “The rest of what is written about his life in a book printed many years ago at Salamanca I do not regard as equally authentic, in many of the matters there written about his life and death; although the other book concerning the translation and miracles of this saint, which is joined to it, has considerable authority, both because it was written by Bishop Don Lucas of Tuy and because many of the things related there are by their nature well known and are attested by other good authors.

> “Concerning the other matters of his life, because they are commonly believed without foundation, it will be necessary to show that they lack one. It is said there that the great work of medicine commonly called Avicenna’s is Saint Isidore’s, because Theodiscus, who was archbishop of Seville shortly after Saint Isidore, a bad Christian and a wicked man, needing the services of a Moor learned in his law and in other matters, called Avicenna, for certain of his wicked deeds, gave him that work of Saint Isidore as payment for what he had done at his command, so that, by translating it into his Arabic language, he might publish it as his own. Avicenna did so and gained much fame and wealth from the saint’s work.

> “They add there that Saint Ildephonsus exposed this falsehood, and many other falsifications by which that wicked Theodiscus also attempted to corrupt the other works of his master. On the saint’s side there are many things that contradict this, and likewise on Theodiscus’s side. But, leaving all that aside, the matter concerning Avicenna cannot possibly be true, because Sorsanus, Avicenna’s disciple and lifelong companion, wrote his life, which is printed with his works. From it we learn that he lived more than three hundred years after the time of Saint Isidore.

> “Avicenna was also raised and favored by the kings of Persia, and always traveled with them, as Sorsanus himself, who accompanied him, affirms; thus he never came to Spain. What concerns the wicked archbishop Theodiscus will soon be seen in its proper place.” [Col. 1058B]

Thus far Morales.

Accordingly, in so doubtful a matter, with interpreters and writers contending on both sides, I have been permitted to collect evidence, not to assert a conclusion. Let the reader be free—and through me it will be permitted—to argue and decide. D. L.]

Corduba flourished; the Persians founded it as though it were the summit of months, and Salduba as though it were *Salemduba*, the summit of peace.

DCCXXXVIII. DCC.

[Col. 1057A]

164. Decentius, bishop of Segovia, flourished. Under him Segovia was destroyed by the Moors, and many Benedictine monks were killed by the Moors; among them Saint Fructuosus suffered.

165. [Note: [Col. 1058C]

165. Much is said here about Felix. He died in the year 700, on Wednesday, June 2, the feast of Saint Marcellinus. He wrote the *Life of Julian*, archbishop of Toledo, his teacher. He lies in the suburban church of Saint Leocadia. Truly happy and fortunate was the man whom God removed, so that he could not survive in the flesh to witness so great a disaster as the captivity of Spain. I would suppose that the verses that follow were composed by Gunderic, his successor, a learned and holy man indeed. P. H.]

In this year Felix died a holy death at Toledo. He had written the *Life of Saint Julian*, archbishop of Toledo, his teacher. He died on the fourth day before the Nones of June and was buried, according to ancestral custom, in the basilica of Saint Leocadia, where the virgin is said to have been born and raised. Gunderic, his archdeacon, composed this poem for him:

> You, holy Father Felix, are held in body  
> By the virgin Leocadia, but your spirit, flying, holds the stars.  
> No Spaniard bore anything more heavily, nor did the world more justly, than you;  
> Felix, you were a shepherd while life was yours.  
> Iria, Toledo, and Hispalis themselves first saw you as father,  
> And were sufficiently refreshed by your conversation.  
> Gunderic gives you these final verses, loving you,  
> As testimony to his grief.  
> If I could purchase with tears and the metal of gold,  
> I would purchase, Felix, that you might not die so soon.  
> You are taken from your homeland, weighed down by age and troubles:  
> You alone were a great benefit to the peoples. [Col. 1058A]  
> Yet from your station above you will be able to lift them,  
> Though lesser than Alfonso and Helladius in merit.  
> The Gothic cause, unless I am mistaken, has threatened ruin,  
> And the work struggles beneath its immense weight.  
> Give strength, and favor your people and your homeland.  
> Hold Isidore’s mournful song and threats [another reading: “and fear, flashing”].

Α Ω 166. Felix, the pontiff of holy memory, archbishop of Toledo, primate and patriarch of the Spains, died in the final year of the glorious King Egica, on the fourth day before the Nones of July, in the current year 738 of the era. He was an outstanding poet, a great preacher, a most zealous defender of the faith, and a servant of the Blessed Virgin Mary.

167. [Note: [Col. 1058C]

167. In this same year Gunderic succeeded Felix; he was from Saguntum and had been confirmed in the sixteenth Council of Toledo, in the fourteenth place. I believe that he had previously been a cleric of the Church of Toledo; on account of the excellence of his character and the greatness of his learning, King Egica placed him over the Church of Toledo. He was Gothic by nation, as his name indicates.

Rodrigo says of him in book III, chapter 14:

> “At this time Gunderic, primate of the see of Toledo, was renowned for the gift of holiness and was celebrated as even more distinguished in many miracles.”

The most illustrious prelate García de Loaysa, speaking of Eugenius I and the others—Paternus or Patruinus, Montanus, Julian I, Euphemius, Helladius, both Eugenius II and Eugenius III, Felix, Ildephonsus, Julian XXI, and Gunderic—says:

> “Their upright and most holy character, and their outstanding and singular virtues, separated them from every mortal custom, so that both alive and dead they performed miracles before the eyes of men.”

The *General History* says:

> “In that time Genderic was archbishop of Toledo. He was a chaste man and of great holiness, and through him our Lord God performed many virtues and many miracles; for divine service he had made him so.”

Garivayus says the same in book VIII, chapter 46.

M. Alvarus Gomezius writes in his life of him:

> “The death of Felix brought great harm to the commonwealth; for immediately Witiza, having lost his guardian and ruler, began to give signs and proofs of his very evil nature. Gunderic, however, succeeding Felix, was also a man distinguished for the uprightness of his character—as authors of his time say, he was numbered among the saints because of his notable virtues and the miracles associated with him. He restrained the man’s erupting insolence. Although Witiza was being swept by the wantonness of youth into every kind of license, nevertheless, because he was still young and had not yet broken through the restraints of modesty, he showed reverence to Gunderic and, moved by his admonitions and persuasion, performed some good examples.

> “For at that time certain writers reported that he had built a monastery in the suburb of Toledo, two thousand paces west of the city, on the road leading to Talabrica. Arched structures made in the form of vaults had been built there to carry water into the monastery. The place is now called Algondorinum, an Arabic name; it contains estates and olive groves, along with other trees planted together with vines.

> “He dedicated the monastery to Saint Peter and ordered women to live there who, according to the rule of Benedict, covered their heads with dark veils. Since women of more mature age, already wearied by worldly affairs, were admitted there, the monastery retained the name ‘the convent of matrons,’ whom that age called ladies.

> “But as the offspring of a wicked father degenerated into a vicious nature—or as the king himself afterward gave himself over to every crime, violating them or offering license in solitude—when they were forbidden to live incontinent lives, they were later transferred, through the care of the bishop of Toledo, to the Gate of Aguila. The authors say that this was the place now called Galliana and the Virgin’s Conception.

> “Aguila, however, king of the Goths, reigned in Spain in the year of the Lord 542. The authors do not transmit in what year the transfer of the matrons into the city took place, nor whether Gunderic or his successor Sinderedus was responsible for it. I would not believe that, during the short time Gunderic lived, they so quickly abandoned that holy discipline which usually burns fervently at the beginnings of religious institutions; rather, I think it happened after Gunderic’s pontificate, when Witiza, having forgotten religion and modesty, loosened the reins on every vice.

> “A few paces farther on, where the gardens of Dacian now are, I suppose that our ancestors built, among the remains of this monastery, a small chapel in memory of that same saint, at the far end of the plain lying below the city. It now bears the name of Green Peter. It lies, if I am not mistaken, among the gardens near the Tagus; for, whatever the season of the year, the entire place seems to remain in spring.

> “Gunderic lived among the living for a year or a little more; for he too, beloved of God, flew from these regions to heaven before the impending evils broke upon them, in the year of the Lord 704. Who he was, and where he was born, is unknown because of the scarcity of ancient records. That he was of Gothic blood is shown by his name.

> “Gunderic, bishop of Segontia, signed the sixteenth Council of Toledo; his bishopric belonged to the province of Carthaginensis. He could easily have advanced from a provincial church to a provincial rank. Taking this abbreviation as their basis, some later called him Gutericus, others Goter, and from that Godel [commonly Gudiel]. He gave his name to the family of the Godels, an old family of our city, from which several archbishops came. Yet, as the long passage of time consumes nearly everything, the name survives among very few citizens.”

Our Luitprand says that he began his pontificate on June 24, the feast of Saint John the Baptist, which in that year was Thursday, namely in 700. First, I think, he was a disciple, deacon, and archpriest together with Felix—for both were disciples of Saint Julian—and was therefore nurtured in the holy Church of Toledo. He passed through all the grades up to the episcopate of the Church of Saguntum. From there he was transferred to Toledo on account of his merits. ID.]

Gunderic, formerly bishop of Segontia, was elected to the see of Toledo; he had been Felix’s companion and fellow disciple when he was archdeacon and archpriest of Toledo. On Saint John the Baptist’s day, June 24, he was placed in the see of Toledo by the suffragans and court officials.

[Col. 1059A] 168. The Goths destroyed Lacobriga near Bursada [another reading: Bursanda; another: Ursanda, P. H.], that is, Molina, where Sertorius defeated Metellus, the Roman commander.

DCCXXXIX. DCCI.

169. [Note: [Col. 1060B]

169. Authors differ concerning the year in which King Egica died. Godericus says that he died in the year 740 of the era, that is, in the year of Christ 702; but Don García de Loaysa and others say 701, followed by Garivayus, Father John Mariana, and other writers. P. H.]

In this year Egica, king of the Goths, died at Toledo on the fifth day before the Ides of November. He was buried in the church of Saint Leocadia outside the walls, near the Tagus, with his ancestors.

170. [Note: [Col. 1060B]

170. In the same year Witiza alone assumed the royal crown, although he had reigned jointly with his father for several years. He was crowned and anointed—not in the church of Saint Peter outside the city—on Monday, November 14, on the eve of the feast of Saint Eugenius, archbishop and martyr of Toledo. The consecration took place in the church of Saint Mary the Minor at Toledo, as is most reasonably believed, with the greatest rejoicing. Garivayus asserts that Witiza was then nineteen years old.

It is established from a seal found there that in this year Gunderic consecrated the church of Saint Torquatus the martyr, as I explain more fully in my *Ecclesiastical History of the City of Toledo*. ID.—We discussed the coronation and anointing above, under nos. 8 and 87; concerning the church of Saint Mary of Alficén, under no. 87. D. L.]

Flavius Witiza, his son, succeeded him in the kingdom of the Visigoths. He was consecrated, anointed, and crowned—as the emperors of Constantinople customarily were, by the hand of the patriarch of that city—on Monday, the seventeenth day before the Kalends of September, by Gunderic, bishop of Toledo, in the presence of the metropolitan and court bishops, in the church of Saint Mary, now called that of Alficén.

171. Gunderic, archbishop of Toledo, together with his suffragans, consecrated the church of Saint Torquatus, a disciple of Saint James, whom, together with eleven others, he made disciples in Ireland from among the nobles, as though they were apostles. This was one of the seven churches that remained in Toledo under the agreements made with the Moors, and it still remains.

DCCXLII. DCCIV.

172. [Note: [Col. 1060C]

172. Concerning the council summoned at Toledo, which was the eighteenth, Rodrigo says in book X, chapter 14:

> “At this time he held a council in the church of Saint Peter, which is outside Toledo, with the bishops and nobles, concerning the ordering of the kingdom; but it is not found in the body of the canons.”

I believe that “the body of the canons” means the diptych or table of the councils of Toledo. According to the testimony of our Luitprand, it was held on the eighth day before the Kalends of November, concerning the formation of character and the preservation of the faith, which was gradually declining through the corruption of morals. Faustinus, archbishop of Hispalis, presided, and other most wise and holy bishops assembled—men who supported Spain’s collapsing affairs by their prayers before God and defended them with distinction. P. H.]

With Gunderic, bishop of Toledo and patriarch of the Goths of Spain and Gaul, presiding; with Faustinus of Hispalis and four other metropolitans, together with many bishops and court officials, the Council of Toledo was celebrated in the urban Praetorian basilica of Saints Peter and Paul, in the fourth year of King Flavius Witiza, on the eighth day before the Kalends of November. [Col. 1061] It concerned the preservation of the faith and the reform of morals, through those most holy bishops who shone throughout Spain with zeal, faith, and the wondrous light of holiness.

173. [Note: [Col. 1061A]

173. The one man who opposed the unrestrained efforts of the young Witiza with the greater force of character was the holy bishop Gunderic. He surpassed the others in the greatness of his zeal just as in holiness; moreover, because he saw affairs more closely and was involved with the king’s corruption, he could not help being intensely distressed and afflicted by so many evils rushing upon them one after another, as they multiplied daily, amid the present calamity. ID.]

Gunderic, bishop of Toledo, distinguished for wisdom and prudence and, as some maintain, for the glory of miracles, strongly resisted the lust and wantonness of the most wicked King Witiza.

DCCXLIV. DCCVI.

174. [Note: [Col. 1061A]

174. Concerning the detestable wicked law that Witiza enacted permitting the keeping of several wives, Rodrigo of Toledo writes:

> “Although previously he had acted wantonly in secret, he now openly made public the luxury of his indecency. Once the reins had been loosened, he withdrew from no vice; and would that he alone had perished in his filth, and had not infected the nobility of the Goths, clergy and people alike, with his impurities! For he reached such a summit of destruction and dissolution that he kept several wives and concubines simultaneously, to satisfy his lust. By a similar example he led the distinguished and leading men of the Goths into similar crimes; and through their example similar sins overflowed among the lower classes of the people.”

And in chapter 15:

> “Witiza, a criminal, fearing that they might oppose his crimes and recall the people from obedience to him, granted permission—indeed, he issued an order—to all clerics to have wives and concubines, one or several, according to the pleasure of their desire.”

These are the words of Rodrigo of Toledo.]

King Witiza, plunging headlong into every kind of outrage, enacted a most wicked law, so that, following the custom of the Saracens, any layman or cleric might keep at home, with impunity, as many wives and concubines as he was able to support.

DCCXLV. DCCVII.

175. [Note: [Col. 1062A]

175. Amid these things the consecrated bishop Gunderic did not remain silent. Rather, in accordance with the rules of prudence and charity, he first attempted to bring the king back by gentle exhortations and admonitions. But when this failed, he immediately pressed him publicly, with threats of anathema and harsh reproofs. P. H.]

At first Gunderic gently resisted the king’s corrupted laws; soon afterward he opposed them openly in public addresses and frightened him with the threat of imposing anathema.

DCCXLVI. DCCVIII.

176. [Note: [Col. 1062A]

176. In this year, on January 20, 708, he died—or rather, the holy bishop Gunderic was transferred from mortal life to blessed life. He was buried amid the many tears of all the poor and good, in the basilica outside the city, that is, in the suburb of Saint Leocadia.]

In this year, on the fourth day before the Kalends of January, the holy bishop Gunderic, worn out by age, evils, and suffering, rested peacefully and holily in the Lord. He was buried in the native home of Saint Leocadia, virgin and martyr. He was carried out amid the mourning of widows, the needy, and orphans, who grieved for him as a father and as the light they had lost. Synderedus, his archdeacon, a poet of no little grace, placed this epitaph upon him:

> Father Gunderic, a support to widows, a light to the needy:  
> Every orphan now rejoices in this bishop.  
> You encountered, O father, the times of a rocky life;  
> Alas, that doing good has harmed you so greatly!  
> Freed yourself from every evil, you rejoice in heaven,  
> And there receive the worthy rewards of your zeal.  
> Your disciple, as custom requires, gives this poem to his master,  
> Synderedus, who loves you; receive it, I ask, gladly.  
> Remember us; remember me, a member of the Gothic people.  
> May King Witiza reign long and ascend to the stars.

Α Ω [Col. 1061] The most holy bishop Gunderic died in peace, worn out by age, eighty-five years old, on the fourth day before the Kalends of January, in the year 746 of the era.

DCCXLVII. DCCIX.

177. [Note: [Col. 1062A]

177. Concerning Synderedus, Rodrigo says in book III, chapter 53:

> “Synderedus, bishop and primate of the royal city, distinguished for his devotion to holiness, succeeded Gunderic and remained renowned until the time of Rodrigo; under him the city of Toledo was lost.”

Alvarus Gomezius says much about him. He stained his holiness and purity of mind in this one matter: according to Rodrigo, “out of zeal for holiness, though not according to knowledge, he began to persecute severely the aged and honorable men whom he had found in the Church of Toledo after the death of Saint Felix and Gunderic, his predecessors; and he did this at the instigation of Witiza, who, because of his own wickedness, feared their righteousness.”

Thus far the archbishop of Toledo. P. H.]

Saint Synderedus, a Roman by birth, succeeded him in the royal see. He had been raised through all the grades and orders, even to the priesthood, in the Church of Saint Mary Major at Toledo. On the very day of the Lord’s Circumcision, in the principal church of Saint Mary, in the presence of King Witiza himself, the metropolitans, the bishops, and the court officials, he was consecrated and received with joy.

178. This bishop confirmed what Gunderic had done while alive. He transferred the nuns of Saint Benedict, who lived far from the city in solitude near the road leading to Elbora, or Talavera, to the Praetorian church of Saints Peter and Paul.

179. Since this transfer had been made by Gunderic, Synderedus favored it, honoring the memory of his teacher and predecessor.

180. [Note: [Col. 1062B]

180. This account of the cities is taken from Lucas of Tuy, concerning whom Rodrigo says nothing, because it is later collected from the best authorities that the Saracens demolished the walls while conquering the cities. ID.]

In this year Witiza ordered that the walled cities be stripped of their walls and that their weapons be thrown down, except for Toledo, León, and Astorga, because he persuaded himself that they would remain loyal to him in every circumstance.

181. [Note: [Col. 1062B]

181. At that time Constantine was pope, and his second year was running. He sent an envoy to Witiza to recall the impious and sacrilegious law that had been enacted contrary to every rule of decency and piety. King Witiza received this embassy bitterly and impatiently. Resenting the reproof, he replied that he would soon go to Rome and, after the fashion of his predecessor King Alaric, destroy Rome. I have been unable to find this in any other author whom I remember. ID.]

Pope Constantine warned Witiza to abolish the law concerning priests taking wives; otherwise, Witiza would be deprived of his kingdom. But Witiza, impatient in his anger and in no way reformed, threatened the most holy pope that he would soon march to Rome with his armies and, after capturing it, strip it of its sacred ornaments, as his ancestors had once done, or else lay it waste and desolate.

182. Concordius, a deacon of Toledo, composed a homily in praise of Saint Turibius, a Benedictine monk who became bishop of Palencia. It begins: “Into our…”

183. Synderedus, bishop of Toledo, at the command of King Witiza, mistreated the priests of the holy Church of Toledo, who were bravely opposing the king’s criminal efforts [another reading: “because he was bravely opposing the king’s criminal efforts”].

184. [Note: [Col. 1063A]

184. Concerning Oppa’s invasion—whether he was Witiza’s son or brother—Rodrigo of Toledo writes in book IV, chapter 16:

> “Witiza, however, an enemy of the sacred canons, handed the Church of Toledo over to his brother Oppa, archbishop of Hispalis, while Bishop Synderedus refused, so that, just as he had defiled himself carnally, his brother might defile himself through spiritual adultery.”

Here he calls Oppa the king’s brother. ID.]

At the counsel and instigation of Witiza, Synderedus of Toledo allowed Oppa [archbishop of Hispalis], Witiza’s brother—according to others, his son—whose morals were no better than Witiza’s, to invade and violate the most chaste, holy, and immaculate see of Toledo. Until then it had lived most holily and happily, joined to one lawful spouse; now, unhappily, it suffered Oppa as its violator.

DCCXLIX. DCCXI.

185. [Note: [Col. 1063A]

### 185.

Three questions must be investigated here. First, whether Roderic entered the kingdom of the Goths through tyranny and force, or by election. Second, where Witiza died. Third, in what year he began his reign.

Sebastian of Salamanca says that it was by election; Roderic of Toledo, however, says that it was through tyranny. He writes:

> “Accordingly, Roderic, son of Theudefred, whom Witiza had had deprived of his eyes, as he had deprived his father, resolved openly to rebel against Witiza with the support of the Roman senate, which loved him because of its gratitude toward Reccesuinth. Being superior in strength, he captured Witiza and did to him what he had done to his father; and, having expelled him from the kingdom, he claimed the kingdom for himself by election of the Goths and with the support of the senate.”

Here he answers two of the questions. Roderic says that Witiza died at Córdoba, and Garivay says the same. Roderic writes:

> “Thus Witiza, full of abominations, deprived of the kingdom, bereft of his eyes, died at Córdoba—the place to which he had exiled Theudefred—an exile and an ex-king, by his own death, in the era 751.”

Sebastian of Salamanca and Liutprand say that he died at Toledo and was buried there; our author, however, says that he was buried in the church of St Leocadia at the Praetorium, because, as Garivay rightly explains, this was the royal burial place of the Goths.

Sampiro is mistaken, since he places Witiza’s death in the year 709, implying that he understands Roderic to have rebelled in that year. But he says nothing about a rebellion; rather, he states that Roderic was elected after Witiza’s death, on 29 November. Witiza died, therefore, on Friday, 22 November. Roderic was consecrated and anointed in the church of St Leocadia at the Praetorium, in the royal city, by Synderedus, the legitimate bishop of Toledo, in the presence of Oppas, the intruder; Roderic refused to be consecrated by Oppas. A great number of bishops and palatines attended the royal coronation. P. H.]

Roderic, a palatine of royal Gothic blood, with the support of certain members of his nation and lineage, seizes the government in opposition to Witiza. Witiza, whether from illness or by slaughter, dies at Toledo in the tenth year of his reign, on the twentieth day of December: a tyrant hated by God and humanity. He is buried without tears in the church of St Leocadia at the Praetorium in the city.

### 186.

When Synderedus had gone to Rome, unwilling to endure the violence and tyrannical oppression of the intruding Oppas, and fearing the invading Saracens, he abandoned the see of Toledo and set out for Rome.

### 187.

After Synderedus had gone to Rome, as we have said, Suincredus succeeds him in the see of Toledo. He was archbishop of Toledo on the twenty-second day of the same month, which was a Sunday, in the presence of Oppas, King Roderic, the bishops, and the palatines.

### 188.

[Note: Concerning this law, Alvarus Gomezius says in his *Life of Synderedus*:

> “Nevertheless, I saw in the church of Toledo an ancient codex of Gothic law. In its third book, title 9, law 18, there is a very severe law against the impurity of priests, issued under the name of King Roderic, by which wives are forbidden under the gravest penalties.”

More recent codices read “Reccesuinth” instead of “Roderic”; but this is an error, as the sequence of events demonstrates. Before Witiza, that disgrace had not infected Spain. Whoever looks for the law, however, will find it in an old manuscript codex of mine under the name of King Reccared:

> “Since sacred authority commands bodily purity with such force, and since the cry of all its ministers urges them to seek it, we are rightly compelled to put an end to unlawful attempts, because we also endeavor most devotedly to please the divine will.  
> 
> “Therefore, whenever it has become completely evident that any presbyter, deacon, or subdeacon has entered into marriage or adultery with a devout widow or penitent woman, or with any virgin, woman of low station, or secular woman, as soon as a bishop or judge discovers it, he shall not delay in dissolving such a union. The offender shall be placed under the authority of his bishop, and, amid the lamentations of penance, shall be deposed by him according to the sacred canons.  
> 
> “But if negligence should fail to carry out the severity of this discipline, that bishop shall pay two pounds of gold to the treasury and shall not delay in avenging the offense. If he is unable to correct it, let him either appeal to a council or report the matter to the king’s court.  
> 
> “Women who have been involved in such impurities shall be beaten by the judge with one hundred lashes, and all access to intercourse with them shall be entirely denied. The bishops shall observe, concerning this offense in both sexes, the judgment of the Fathers, which is recognized as established by the decrees of the canons.  
> 
> “Nevertheless, in punishing such crimes, we do not grant everyone indiscriminate permission to accuse or punish, unless the crime has become evident through manifest offenses or the same evil has been lawfully accused and proven. This is so that we may not appear, under any pretext or by any arrangement, to transgress the commands of the holy Fathers or oppose the sacred laws of the ancients.  
> 
> “Flavius Roderic, king.”

This is what the law contains. P. H.]

Roderic issued a law against Witiza’s law, and so forth. Many have written much about the promulgation of Witiza’s law, nearly all our historians among them. Stephanus de Garibay discusses it in book VIII, chapter 47, of his *Compendium of History*. Father Juan de Mariana writes in book VI, chapter 19, of his *History of Spain*:

> “He kept a great number of concubines in the place and with the status of lawful wives, and issued a law allowing this for everyone—both the common people and the nobles, and also consecrated men.”

Earlier, Roderic, archbishop of Toledo, had written in book III, chapter 15, of *On the Affairs of Spain*:

> “Although previously he [Witiza] had behaved wantonly in secret, now he makes the luxury of his immorality public [better, as in other copies: ‘the luxury of immorality is made public’] and, with the reins loosened, held himself back from no vice. Would that he alone had perished in his filth, so that he might not have infected the Gothic nobility, clergy, and people with his impurities! For he reached such a height of ruin and dissolution that he kept several wives and concubines simultaneously, in order to satisfy his lust; and by a similar example he led the distinguished and more prominent men of the Goths into similar crimes.”

Lucas of Tuy, in his *Chronicle of the World*, when treating the era 733, writes of Witiza:

> “And lest the holy Church rise up against him, the lascivious king ordered bishops, presbyters, deacons, and the other ministers of the Church of Christ to have carnal wives. And lest they obey the Roman pontiff, he forbade it under threat of death.”

Alfonso de Spina uses nearly the same words in the *Fortress of the Faith*. [Father Juan de Mariana affirms this in book XXII, chapter 13, of *On the Affairs of Spain*; the manuscript *History of Enrique III, Catholic King of Spain*, supports it at its end, in the account of his death.] The work is wrongly attributed by Possevinus in book IX, chapter 3, of his *Bibliotheca* to a certain William; likewise by Thomas Bozius in book I, sign 16, chapter 11, example 11, page 385, of *On the Signs of the Church*, and in book VII, chapter 4, page 638, of *On the Ruins of Nations against Impious Politicians*.

Lucas of Tuy, in the passage cited above, recognizes this law as the cause of the devastation of Spain:

> “This indeed was the cause of Spain’s destruction, as it is written: ‘Iniquity increased, and the charity of many grew cold.’”

Alfonso de Spina says almost the same thing in the passage cited earlier:

> “This,” he says, “was indeed the cause of Spain’s destruction. For the entire Gothic nobility, immersed in feasts, lusts, and vices, provoked the Most High to anger.”

There is also a notable testimony in a decretal taken from the letter of the martyr Boniface to Ethelbald, king of the Angles, quoted in chapter *Si gens Anglorum*, distinction 56. Since its words encompass the entire matter, I shall not hesitate to transcribe them here:

> “If the people of the Angles—as has been spread throughout these provinces, and is reproached to us in France and Italy, and is a reproach even among the pagans—despising lawful marriages, have led a shameful life through adultery and lust, after the manner of the Sodomite people, then from such intercourse with prostitutes one must expect degenerate and ignoble peoples, raging with lust, to be born; and finally the whole people will turn toward what is worse and more ignoble, and at last will become neither strong in secular war nor steadfast in faith, neither honorable among men nor beloved by God. The same happened to other peoples of Spain, Provence, and Burgundy: after turning away from God, they committed fornication until the almighty Judge—or Avenger—permitted the avenging punishments for such crimes to come upon them and rage against them through those ignorant of the law of God, that is, through the Saracens.”

Bishop Ivo of Chartres gives the same passage in part VIII, chapter 224, of his *Decretum*, where the most illustrious and learned Lord Roderic de Acuña, archbishop of Braga, gathers further evidence. Juan Filesacus reports the same matter, though not in the same words, in book I, chapter 9, pages 139–140, of his *Selecta*.

These events had been foretold by St Methodius and by other men truly great in holiness and learning, as Master Diego de Valera testifies in part IV, chapter 125, folio 114, column 3, of his *History*, and Stephanus de Garibay in his *Compendium of Spanish History*, chapter 49, under the year 714, page 376.

Concerning St Methodius, Alfonso de Spina discusses the matter in book IV, chapter 8, of the work called the *Fortress of the Faith*, beginning *Primus passus*, folio 344, column 2. The Spanish teacher and wonder of the world, Alfonso Tostatus, bishop of Ávila, most richly furnished in every discipline, speaks fully on the subject near the end of his commentary on Genesis 16. Listen, for he speaks most appropriately while explaining the words, “He called his name Ishmael”:

> “Abraham gave this name to his son either because he learned by revelation what had taken place between Hagar and the angel, or because Hagar herself revealed to Abraham what has been described, as it happened.  
> 
> “Of this Ishmael the martyr Methodius speaks, he who described the millennia of the ages in certain mysteries: From the race of Ishmael four princes were to arise, who are called ‘sons of the vineyard’—perhaps he called them this because of their madness, as though they were drunkards—namely Zeb, Zebee, Oreb, and Salmana. They went out from the wilderness against the sons of Israel, but, defeated by Gideon, they were driven back into the wilderness from which they had come.  
> 
> “He also says that the sons of Ishmael will one day go forth and possess the world for eight weeks of years, that is, for fifty-four years, and that their way will be called the way of distress. In the holy places they will kill priests and sleep with women there; they will tie their beasts to the tombs of the saints. This will happen because of the wickedness of the Christians.  
> 
> “Concerning this the Lord says through Ezekiel: ‘Son of man, call the beasts of the field and exhort them, saying: Gather together and come, because I am preparing a great sacrifice for you; eat the flesh of the mighty and drink the blood of the exalted.’  
> 
> “All these things, foretold literally by this holy man, came upon us in miserable Spain when, in the time of King Roderic, the Arabs devastated the whole country and held the land for a long time. These matters are clear from the widely circulated chronicles of the Spaniards.”

Thus far Tostatus, who occasionally inserts the words of St Methodius. Friar Alfonso de Spina transcribed the same and other material from St Methodius, including this noteworthy passage:

> “Greece will be in captivity; Africa will be in slaughter. Likewise the eastern Egyptians and Asia will be under a heavy tribute in gold and silver. Spain will perish by the sword, and its inhabitants will be led away captive.”

These words are found in nearly the same form in the *Bibliotheca of the Ancient Fathers*, from the edition of Michael Sonnius, Paris, 1585, volume II, column 522, under the title *The Revelations of St Methodius, Bishop and Martyr of Patara, Concerning Events That Happened from the Beginning of the World and Those That Must Happen Hereafter*, translated by an unknown author through paraphrase.

Various writers have translated the words of St Methodius in different ways, although their meaning appears to be the same. The work was written in Greek by its author; only a very old Latin manuscript survives in the library of Saint Victor in Paris. From it I took a copy while serving in a royal embassy. The same thing has happened with other works of the Greek Fathers.

A testimony of St Cyril is also relevant: the *Hypomnema*—“Commentary” or “Memorandum”—on St John, concerning which Heinsius writes in his *Sacred Aristarchus*, or *Sacred Exercises on Nonnus*, chapter 11. Salianus, however, in volume I of the *Annals*, under the year of the world 1756, mentions a Greek-Latin edition printed in the *Orthodoxographi* edited by Grynaeus at Basel. Yet, following Pererius, he believes that certain portions of these Revelations are not writings of St Methodius but rabbinic commentaries.

Torniellus, taking a middle position, considers them so doubtful and uncertain that he affirms that they can neither be wholly approved nor wholly rejected. Jacobus Bolduc agrees with him in book I, page 67, of *On the Church before the Law*. The most eminent Cardinal Bellarmine says in *On Ecclesiastical Writers* that this little book of the Revelations is to be regarded as spurious. Gerardus Joannes Vossius numbers it among the doubtful and uncertain Greek histories in book II, chapter 16, page 199.

I shall cite only one testimony, leaving others aside, based on my own conjecture, in defense of the Revelations of St Methodius circulated under his name. In their text one finds the following passage, where it discusses the Saracens invading Spain and Gaul:

> “And they will be like locusts in multitude, gathered together by the wind; and pestilence and famine will be among them. The heart of the destroyers will be exalted, and they will be lifted up in pride; they will speak lofty things until the time appointed for them.”

He foretold the multitude of the Moors under the figure of locusts. [Father Juan de Mariana, book VI, chapter 3, volume I, of his *History of Spain*, under the year 733; Scipio Dupleix, volume I of his *History of Gaul*, under AD 726, page 262, from Paul the Deacon and Rodrigo Ximénez, archbishop of Toledo, and passim in descriptions and itineraries of Gaul; likewise Paulus Merula, *Cosmography*, part II, book III, page 494.] They traversed a large part of Gaul, burst into Aquitaine with victorious arms, crossed the Garonne, and, after destroying the churches, devastated Bordeaux. They also consumed the peoples of Angoulême, Périgueux, Saintes, and Poitiers in the same fire of war, until Charles Martel advanced against the enemy near Tours, having crossed the Loire so that it might serve as a defense behind him.

There, with the arrival of the barbarians, battle was joined on both sides with all their strength, and through the valor of the Christians innumerable enemies were defeated: 375,000 of their army were slain. For this reason the nobles of Tours introduced locusts into their coats of arms, signifying the trophy of the victory won from the Moors.

The multitude of a people is signified by comparison with locusts in Judges 6:5 and 7:12. This is sufficiently well known. Here, however, the comparison concerns devastation, just as bees were used as a sign of building, since the ancients regarded a swarm of bees departing to establish colonies and found cities as a favorable omen.

For example, Athens, acting on the responses of the Delphic Apollo, led thirteen colonies into Asia at one time under the command of Ion, son of Xuthus and Creusa. Vitruvius wrote this in book IV, chapter 1, and Velleius Paterculus supports him in book I of his *History*. The leaders of the fleet were the Muses, appearing in the form of bees, as Philostratus testifies in his *Melete*.

The chief of those colonies was Ephesus, famous for the earliest Christian assembly, as is recorded in Acts 20. It was also renowned for the sojourn and death of St John the Evangelist, and was recognized and honored as the commercial center of all Asia. It was necessary for a proconsul traveling there to touch it, as Ulpian, the jurist, states in book IV of *On the Office of the Proconsul and Legate*.

For this reason the Ephesians marked their coins with the image of a bee and with the symbols of Diana. See, in this symbol and token of faith, this monument of venerable antiquity. Pliny also records in book XI, chapter 17, of his *Natural History*, that a swarm of bees had sometimes been favorable even according to the vanity of the haruspices.

Finally, there were marks indicating the colonies that had been sent out. Thus Varro writes:

> “When a swarm is about to depart—which usually happens when many young bees have been born successfully and the elders wish to send out offspring as a colony, as the Sabines once frequently did because of the multitude of their children—the two signs that ordinarily go before it make the event known.”

Virgil wonderfully applies this matter in book IV of the *Georgics*, where, among many other things, he describes the nature of bees:

> “First they lay the foundations of the honeycombs; then  
> they hang the tenacious wax. Others raise  
> the grown offspring, the hope of the race; others pack  
> the purest honey and fill the cells with liquid nectar.”

Seneca quotes and illustrates this passage in Letter 84:

> “We ought, as they say, to imitate the bees, which wander about and gather flowers suitable for making honey; then they arrange and distribute through the honeycombs whatever they have brought back.”

You will find more on this subject in Laurentius Pignorius, *Epistolary Book of Emblems*, letter 48, page 205.

Concerning St Isidore, let me now bring this very long digression to an end and take up the thread again: Lucas of Tuy discusses him at the beginning of book III of his *Chronicle*. From him, Cardinal Baronius drew material in volume VIII of the *Annals*, under the year of Christ 636, page 340, letter D; so did Constantine the Abbot Cajetanus in his work on St Isidore of Seville, Father Juan de Mariana in book VI, chapter 7, volume I, of his *History of Spain*, and Father Jacobus Bleda in book II, chapter 1, of his *Chronicle of the Moors*.

Master Agidius Gonzales d’Avila, royal historian—born for the public good of letters—communicated to me St Isidore’s prophetic words, written in very ancient characters on ancient parchment. They are these:

> **WOE TO YOU, SPAIN, TWICE LOST, TO BE LOST A THIRD TIME BECAUSE OF BAD MARRIAGES.**

Master Diego de Valera translated this from Latin into our language in part IV, chapter 125, of his *History*, in a letter to King John II of Spain, entitled *Give Peace, Lord*, page 116, column 3:

> “Therefore, my lord, you alone, to whom by God’s will the care of these kingdoms has been entrusted, should grant peace in our days, and should not wish that in your time the saying of Isidore be fulfilled, which said: ‘O wretched Spain, twice you have been destroyed, and a third time you will be destroyed by unlawful marriages.’”

Although this seems to imply that the prophetic threat had not yet been fulfilled, Father Jacobus de Bleda likewise discusses it at the beginning of book II, chapter 1, of his *Chronicle of the Moors of Spain*.

This prophecy was completely fulfilled in the time of Roderic, king of the Goths, who resembled his predecessor Witiza—even though he abolished the law allowing clerics to marry and to take several wives. It was Spain’s third devastation. [Stephanus de Garibay, *Compendium of History*, book VIII, chapter 48, year 750, page 372; Thomas Bozius, *On the Signs of the Church*, volume I, book V, sign 16, chapter 11, example 11, page 385, and *On the Ruins of Nations*, book VII, chapter 4, page 638.]

The words of St Isidore clearly confirm this, since he says that Spain had already been destroyed twice and would be devastated a third time. All those who say that St Isidore was speaking of Witiza’s most wicked marriages, supported by legal authority, agree with this; at the very least, they thereby acknowledge that two destructions of Spain had preceded the time of St Isidore.

As he is accustomed to do, the most illustrious archbishop of Braga, Lord Roderic de Acuña, explains everything learnedly in part I, chapter 11, folio 119, of his catalogue of the bishops of Portugal. Finally, a good reckoner will make the totals agree, if he knows by touch and ear how to distinguish truth from falsehood and to assess with sound judgment the arguments in which he will find the three devastations and destructions of Spain.

I am not counting those that occurred before the Christian faith had been accepted throughout all the kingdoms of Spain, but only those that completely overturned the country after the Christian religion had everywhere flourished there. For a state truly flourishes where the true God is worshiped, feared, and loved; and its ruin is certain when it departs from the path of the true God and divine worship.

#### 1.

Spain embraced this faith with all its strength in the time of Tertullian, during the reign of Septimius Severus, under whom Tertullian lived. His words are found in book I, chapter 7, *Against the Jews*:

> “In whom else have all the nations believed, except in Christ, who has already come? For in whom else have other nations believed?”

A little later, after enumerating many nations, he speaks of Spain:

> “All the boundaries of the Spains.”

The emperor Diocletian, in the year of Christ 303, intensified with more cruel edicts the savage persecution he had begun eight years earlier. According to St Augustine, it was ordered that the temples of the Christians be overthrown, the sacred books burned, Christian people branded as infamous, and excluded from public offices. It was later added that the leaders of the churches should be killed.

In the consulship of Diocletian for the eighth time and Maximian for the seventh, he attempted through fires, proscriptions, and killings to eradicate the worship of Christ from the earth, so that no persecution had been longer-lasting or more monstrous.

Thomas Bozius, in volume II, book XVII, sign 76, chapter 3, page 392, of *On the Signs of the Church*, still attests that an inscription could be read in Spain, engraved by Diocletian:

> “From the Spains the name of Christ was completely abolished and erased.”

I regard this as having been placed there more for flattery than for truth, in order to praise Diocletian. For the name of Christ was not entirely driven from the boundaries of Spain, although the persecution was monstrous.

The eminent Cardinal Caesar Baronius mentions this stone in volume II of the *Annals*, under the year of Christ 304, page 787, and affirms that it stood at Clunia, which we call Coruña del Conde. Our learned Bernard Joseph de Aldrete cites it for this purpose in book II, chapter 22, page 310, of his *Various Antiquities of Spain*.

The inscription is as follows:

> **DIOCLETIAN JOVIUS AND MAXIMIAN HERCULIUS, CAESARS AUGUSTI, HAVING EXTENDED THE ROMAN EMPIRE THROUGH THE EAST AND WEST AND THE NAME OF THE CHRISTIANS HAVING BEEN ERASED, WHO WERE OVERTURNING THE STATE.**

And another is as follows:

> **TO DIOCLETIAN CAESAR AUGUSTUS, WITH GALERIUS ADOPTED IN THE EAST, THE SUPERSTITION OF CHRIST HAVING BEEN EVERYWHERE DESTROYED AND THE WORSHIP OF THE GODS HAVING BEEN EXTENDED.**

Justus Lipsius includes these inscriptions among those he caused to be published, page 280, numbers 3 and 4, from the notes of Schottus and others. Adolphus Occo also gives them in his *Ancient Inscriptions of Spain*, page 24, numbers 2 and 3. He reports that they were taken from Ambrosius de Morales, who first published them in volume I, book X, chapter 26, of his *Chronicle of Spain*, in the section on Diocletian and Maximian.

The religion of Christ flourished in Spain under the emperor Theodosius the Great, who issued a public law ordering that the decisions of Damasus, the Roman pontiff, and Peter, bishop of Alexandria, concerning religion—which was being divided by the opinions of sects—should be regarded as authoritative. Thus Father Juan de Mariana writes at the beginning of book IV, chapter 20, volume I, of his *History of Spain*. Thomas Bozius says the same in *On the Ruins of Nations*, book VII, chapter 4, drawing on Sozomen and Theodoret.

Then, through the execrable sect of the Priscillianists, the Christian cause suffered a great new loss, and Spain was devastated by the Visigoths. Salvianus, who lived in the year 460, mentions this loss in book VI, page 224, and book VII, page 255, of *On the Government of God*, in the edition of Rithershusius; Cardinal Bellarmine also mentions it in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, page 122.

Others mention it as well: St Isidore, archbishop of Seville, in the treatise *On Birth and Death*, volume II, page 165, column 1, of the Madrid edition; Hydatius in his *Chronicle*, edited by Bishop Don Fray Prudencio de Sandoval, page 29, number 16; and Thomas Bozius in volume I, book V, sign 16, chapter 11, examples 9 and 10, and volume II, book XXIV, sign 99, chapter 1, of *On the Signs of the Church*.

After the truth of the Christian religion had been restored by the emperor Reccared, King Witiza and Roderic departed from it. Under Roderic Spain was destroyed for the third time, when the Saracens occupied it, to the greatest disgrace and damage of the Christian law. Thus the prophetic predictions of St Isidore were fulfilled.

Cabam Florindam, the daughter of Count Julian.

There is an uncertain and disputed question among authors concerning the name of Count Julian’s daughter. Many call her Florinda, among them Abū al-Qāsim Ṭāriq, if we believe Michael de Luna in book I, chapter 8, of his *History of King Roderic*; Bleda in book II, chapter 4, folio 127, column 1, of his *Chronicle of the Moors of Spain*; and Abbot Dom Martin Carillo in his *Annals*, under the year of Christ 711.

Others call her Caba: Stephanus de Garibay in book VIII, chapter 48, of his *Compendium of History*, and Father Juan de Mariana in book I, chapter 21, volume I, of his *History of Spain*, following the ancient historical records of King Roderic.

Our Liutprand marked her with both names, as though indicating that her proper name was Florinda and that Caba was an additional name. Among the Arabs, *Caba* denotes a dishonorable woman; the word is derived from the Hebrew verb “to curse,” as though meaning “cursed woman,” one who, with loose morals and devoted to lust, offers herself to everyone. Hence the word *brothel*.

Sebastian de Covarrubias collects and arranges much about this in an erudite fashion in his *Treasury of the Castilian Language*, under the word *Cava*. Nearly all who have written about the destruction of Spain agree. One or another learned and highly educated man disagrees, denying that she was called Caba in his first Milanese edition of his *Annotations on Father Mariana’s History*, page 98, although he omitted this in the latest Madrid edition. Whether by chance or deliberately, I do not know; let the reader see and judge. D. L.]

Roderic, at the beginning of his reign, issued a law abolishing Witiza’s law allowing clerics to marry and at the same time to support several wives [alternatively, “to have several wives with them”]. He expelled Oppas from the Church of Toledo and violated Caba Florinda, daughter of Julian, count of the African frontier. The Arabs came to Spain.

**750. 712.**

### 189.

After Suincredus died, the elders of the Church of Toledo appointed Julian, surnamed Urbanus, to the see of Toledo. He was advanced in age and a disciple of St Ildefonsus of Toledo.

### 190.

A synod was convened at London in England in defense of the sacred images, as had been the case with the First Synod of Constantinople.

**751. 713.**

### 191.

The First Roman Synod was held in defense of the sacred images.

**752. 714.**

### 192.

[Note: Some place the first arrival of the Arabs in Spain in the year 709; others in 710. I believe that different writers may be referring to different eras and calendars.

According to Roderic, book III, chapter 18, the first crossing took place in the era 750, when one hundred horsemen and four hundred infantry crossed near Algeciras with Count Julian and Ṭāriq. They crossed in four ships. This was the Arab year 91 of the Hijra, in fact the year 709 of Christ, in the month called Ramadan.

This is called the first Saracen incursion into Spain, but the month is mistaken. These five hundred Moors—one hundred, as stated, cavalry and four hundred infantry—first plundered Algeciras. Then they scattered along the coast of Lusitania and Baetica, through the county of Niebla, the marquisate of Gibraleón, and the Algarve. After killing many and stripping others of their possessions, they returned home laden with captives and precious spoils.

Roderic says that all these things occurred during the first Saracen entry, while Witiza was still alive. Immediately afterward he relates that Synderedus, archbishop of Toledo, left Toledo for Rome. But how could the city of Toledo have been lost under him if he had fled? The city was lost in the year 709, as will later be established, first from the histories and secondly from the privilege of King Alfonso VI.

Roderic also shows that Synderedus fled during that first entry. After recounting the first Saracen entry, he adds:

> “In those days Synderedus, of whom we have spoken, bishop and primate of the royal city, terrified by the arrival of the Arabs and driven away by Witiza’s insolence, gave himself over to the Roman land, abandoning his sheep like a hireling and not like a shepherd. They entered again…”

Third, this is clear from chapter 19 of Roderic’s book III.

The authors do not entirely agree about the day and month on which Roderic was defeated. Roderic says that it was on Sunday, the fifth day before the Ides of the Arab month Xabel, in Hijra year 93—he should say 96—and in the year 714. Garivay says 4 September; but in fact it was Sunday, 11 November, the feast of St Martin, bishop and confessor, in the Arab Hijra year 96, which was the year 714.

Xabel began that year on 3 November. The dominical letter was G, and therefore Sunday fell on 11 November. P. H.]

On 11 November, a Sunday, Roderic, the last king of the Goths, was carried in an ivory chariot drawn by six very white horses, adorned [alternatively, clothed] with silk and gold. After eight days and various uncertain reverses of war, he was defeated in battle by the Saracens. From that time Spain gradually came into the hands of the Arabs, who exulted in victory and ravaged the country.

### 193.

At Betonia, a town of Sarandula, near a certain mountain where, from the earliest beginnings of the Christian religion, a very famous church of St Saviour had been built, many bishops fled from various regions. They instructed the peoples who took refuge there and nourished them with the food of the sacraments.

When the Moors besieged them while they were engaged in sacred rites, the bishops preserved the most holy Eucharist in a deep well, but all were killed. Among them were the bishops of Coria, Elvira, Ciudad Rodrigo, Salamanca, Viseu, and Lamego, together with not a few most holy priests and deacons.

**753. 715.**

### 194.

In this year the Byzantine emperor Anastasius was compelled to abdicate the empire on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of September.

### 195.

[Note: Around this time lived St Babylas. Julian likewise reports the event in his *Chronicle*, number 413, although he differs concerning the date.

There still exists a little hermitage called “of San Babyles,” three leagues from Madrid and half a mile from the town of Odone; St Babylas may have given it its name. His memory is commemorated at Odone on 24 January, and some assert that his body is preserved and venerated there. D. L.]

Around this time St Babylas, bishop of Virinus and of Pamplona—for he preached in both places—came to Toledo, wishing to see the captive and wretched Mozarabs. From there he went to the town of Odone. Nearby, in a little hermitage, he taught children their first letters. He came with two brothers, who became hermits; afterward all of them suffered martyrdom.

**754. 716.**

### 196.

In this year Gregory, the second pope of that name, succeeded Pope Constantine in the most holy see of Peter, prince of the apostles.

### 197.

In the same year a Roman synod was held under Pope Gregory II.

**755. 717.**

### 198.

[Note: Some think that Urban was called Julian and that Julian carried the relics of the holy chest from Toledo with Pelagius. Our author thinks that the man was not Julian but Urban, because Julian the holy teacher, the fourth archbishop of Toledo, lived before Synderedus.

This is indeed correct; but our Liutprand says that Urban had two names. He is therefore not the same person as St Julian, archbishop of Toledo, but a much later and entirely different man. He is also distinct from Julian, the deacon of Toledo, who wrote the life of King St Pelagius.

There is more concerning St Serranus in the work of Maximus of Zaragoza. P. H.]

They carry the ark from Toledo into Asturias, etc. For the transfer of these relics, see Rodrigo, archbishop of Toledo, *History*, book IV, chapter 3 [Col. 1071C]; Isidore of Beja, under the year 719; Sebastián, bishop of Salamanca, in the *History* published by Don Fray Prudencio de Sandoval, bishop of Pamplona, p. 45, columns 1–2, and p. 50, column 2; our Julian, in the *Chronicle*, no. 377, p. 87 [Col. 1072A], where he describes everything vividly, and had written earlier in nos. 369 and 371.

I shall cite a celebrated testimony from a very ancient manuscript codex on parchment, written in Gothic letters, which was communicated to me by the illustrious and most learned Don Francisco de Eraso, count of Humanes. He combined nobility with knowledge of the sciences and an outstanding gentleness of character; he was councillor to our most powerful Catholic king Philip IV of Spain in the supreme Council of the Indies during peace and war, chamberlain to the most serene Cardinal Ferdinand the Infante, and first commander of the knights. The manuscript reads:

> “Then Pelagius, son of Fafila, who was of the Gothic race, having received the ark with the relics of the saints, by which Oviedo now glories, entered Asturias with Julian, archbishop of Toledo, and with many Christians; Asturias was enclosed by mountains and uninhabitable.” [Col. 1072B]

Sebastián had said almost the same thing in the passage cited above:

> “By the presence of this ark the lofty See of Oviedo now glories.”

See Baronius, under the year 791, volume VIII, p. 414; earlier, Don Luis, bishop of Tuy, in the *Chronicle of Spain*; Ildefonsus of Cartagena, bishop of Burgos, in the *Anacephalaeosis of Spain*; Vasaeus in the *Chronicles*, under the year 791; Lucius Marineus Siculus, book I of the *History of Spain*, chapter “On Sacred Buildings,” and book V, chapter [where] he lists the relics of the sacred church of St. Saviour of Oviedo, which were indeed taken from this ark; Ambrosius de Morales, book XIII of the *History of Spain*, in the life of Ildefonsus the Chaste, as he is called, chapter 38; Aldefonsus Venero in the *Chronicle of the Ages*, folio 44; and the Dominican Jacobus Bleda in the *Book of Miracles of the Cross*, miracle 61, where he speaks of the cross made by angels around the year 826, and of Ildefonsus, miracle 35.

Add the clear account of Father Francisco Portocarrero, in his book *On the Descent of the Blessed Virgin Mary into the Church of Toledo*, chapters 29 and 30, where he appends a catalogue of the relics, though not a complete one. It is included in the testimony given, as a votive offering, to pilgrims travelling to Oviedo to visit them [Col. 1072C]. The words are:
