> “To all and each of Christ’s faithful who shall inspect these present letters, we make known that God, by his wondrous power, transferred a certain ark made of incorruptible wood, fashioned by the disciples of the apostles and filled with images of God, from the city of Jerusalem, at the time when it was devastated by Chosroes, king of the Persians, to Africa; from Africa to Carthage; from Carthage to Seville; from Seville to Toledo; from Toledo into Asturias, to a mountain called the Sacred Mountain; and from there to this holy church of St. Saviour, which is called Oviedo.
>
> “This ark was opened there. When they opened it, they found many little chests of gold, silver, and ivory. Opening these with the utmost reverence, they saw certain writings attached to each of the relics stored there. All these writings made the contents perfectly clear. They found a large part of the Lord’s shroud, in which he lay wrapped in the tomb, and his precious sudarium, marked with his most holy blood, with which his most beautiful face, together with his most sacred head, had been covered and wrapped. This is displayed three times each year, with the reverence that is fitting: namely, on the solemn feast of the said holy relics, which falls on 13 March; on Good Friday; and on the feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, on 14 September. [Col. 1073A]
>
> “A considerable portion of the true cross of the Lord; eight thorns from the Lord’s crown; pieces of the cloth in which he lay wrapped in the manger; bread from the Lord’s Supper; manna which the Lord rained down upon the children of Israel; a large fragment of the knife of Blessed Bartholomew, with which he was flayed; and the cloak which the Queen of Heaven gave to Ildefonsus, archbishop of Toledo,” and so forth. [Col. 1073B]

After many other relics have been listed, the following words occur:

> “In confirmation and testimony of these things, we, the dean and chapter of the venerable church of Oviedo, have caused these present letters to be drawn up.”

Thus far the material found in Portocarrero. A fuller version is found in Pelagius of Oviedo, whose inclusion of it is acknowledged and defended by Don Prudentius de Sandoval, in his *History of Sebastián, Bishop of Salamanca*, p. 50, column 2, and p. 51, column 2. Here it is:

> “Having set out these matters, we have written beneath them which most glorious relics of the saints the ark contains, making them known to the faithful people. It contains a crystal flask with the blood of the Lord that was shed—namely, from the side of that image which a certain Christian brought with him into the city. For, through the treachery of certain Jews, who sought to suppress the truth of Christ, the wooden likeness of Christ on a wooden cross was pierced in the side; from it blood and water came forth, to convict those Jews of treachery and strengthen the faith of the holy Church. [Col. 1073C]
>
> “A piece of the Lord’s wood; a piece of the Lord’s tomb; part of the crown of thorns; part of the Lord’s shroud; part of the Lord’s tunic; pieces of the cloth in which he lay wrapped in the manger; bread with which the Lord satisfied five thousand men; bread from the Lord’s Supper; manna which the Lord rained down upon the children of Israel; earth from the Mount of Olives, where the Lord placed his feet when he was about to ascend; earth where the Lord placed his feet when he raised Lazarus; and a piece of Lazarus’s tomb.
>
> “What deserves the highest veneration is that the church of St. Saviour possesses one of the six water-jars in which the Lord changed water into wine at the wedding, as the complete truth of the Gospel demonstrates. [Col. 1073D]
>
> “Milk of the Lord’s Mother; part of her clothing; the very cloak which the Queen of Heaven gave to Ildefonsus, archbishop of the See of Toledo, in return for the praises he had celebrated in honour of her holy virginity—where that holy and glorious bishop had spoken against the heresiarchs Helvidius and Jovinian”—[Against them he wrote the *Book of Synonyms*. See what Jerome de la Higuera noted on this matter, no. 101, and what I briefly touched upon there.]—“saying to him, while numerous choirs of angels and saints stood around, encompassed by indescribable light: [Col. 1074A]
>
> “ ‘Receive this gift, which I have brought you from the treasury of my Son.’
>
> “The hands of St. Stephen; the right sandal of the apostle St. Peter; the forehead of John the Baptist; hair and finger joints of the Innocents; bones of the three boys, Ananias, Azariah, and Misael; hair with which Mary wiped the Lord’s feet; a piece of the rock of Mount Sinai; part of Elijah’s cloak; a piece of roasted fish and part of a honeycomb.
>
> “There is also a small key containing iron from the chains of blessed Peter the apostle, and a cross containing wood from the Lord’s cross, together with hairs of blessed John the Baptist. Pope Gregory sent these to blessed Leander, archbishop of the Church of Seville.
>
> “Many further bones of holy prophets, and many different relics of other holy confessors and sacred virgins, are kept there in golden and silver boxes. Their very number prevents us from writing them all down. A cross made by angelic workmanship is displayed there in a remarkable form.
>
> “Now let us return to the preceding history from which we began.”

Finally, in order to serve the commonwealth of letters, I shall not hesitate to transcribe an ancient account of this ark, preserved among the archives of the Church of Oviedo and communicated to me by the learned Don Luis Tribaldos of Toledo, a glory of our Spain [Col. 1074B]. It runs as follows:

> “During the reign of Sisebut in Spain, in the time of Heraclius, when Chosroes destroyed Jerusalem, the priest Philip took an ark which was in the Holy House and had been made by the hands of the disciples of the Apostles from incorruptible setín wood. He gathered inside it the principal relics that were in the Holy House and embarked with them toward the West, so that they would not fall into the hands of unbelievers.
>
> “He landed at Tunis, where it remained until the era 658, which was the year of Our Lord 620. From there Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe, carried the ark to Cartagena in Spain, and from there to Seville, and from there to Toledo, where it remained until the destruction of Spain, in the era 763, which is the year 725, when Spain was then being lost. [Col. 1074C]
>
> “Prince Don Pelayo and Don Urban, archbishop of Toledo, carried it, together with the chasuble of St. Ildefonsus and other books and relics, into Asturias. Placed on the Sacred Mountain, it remained there until the time of Don Alfonso the Chaste, in his third year, which was the era 830, that is, the year 792, when this king brought it with reverence to the holy church of Oviedo.
>
> “After some time Bishop Ponce wished to visit it, and such a great brightness came forth that many of those present were blinded. Later, in the era 1513, which was the year 1075, King Don Alfonso the Sixth went there from Zamora on pilgrimage with great devotion, summoning the bishops of Astorga, Palencia, and Oviedo. After many processions, prayers, fasts, and sacrifices, God allowed so great a treasure to be opened and revealed to all. Its catalogue is long and marvellous.”

The chronological matters contained in this account are carefully examined by Father Francisco Portocarrero in his book *On the Descent of the Blessed Virgin Mary*, chapter 28, where the history of Pelagius, bishop of Oviedo, provides him with the opportunity [Col. 1074D]. As a conclusion, I add Marieta, book XXII, *On the City of Oviedo and the Ark*. D. L.]

### 198

In this year Julian, surnamed Urbanus, together with Prince Pelagius and other palatine commanders, carried from Toledo into Asturias the ark of the holy relics and the bodies of Saints Julian and Asturius of Complutum, surnamed Serrano, once most holy bishops of Toledo, fearing that, if the city were captured—or, in the variant reading, subjected to captivity—by the Saracens, they would treat them irreverently and impiously.

**DCCLVI. DCCXVIII.**

[Col. 1073]

### 199

[Note: [Col. 1074D–1075A] In the year 718, shortly before the capture of the royal city of Toledo, certain relatives of St. Ildefonsus carried his body from Toledo to Zamora, and the bearers remained there. Thus, four years after the death of Roderic, the body of the most holy doctor and citizen of Toledo, Ildefonsus, was carried from Toledo. P. H.] [Col. 1074D]

In the same year, on 4 July, certain men of St. Ildefonsus’s family, among the first and noblest of the palatine class, who had once believed that Toledo could be defended and had therefore delayed transferring him to Asturias, now despairing of its defence, dug up the body of their most holy kinsman, citizen, and patron of Toledo, and carried it to the city of Zamora. There they remained with the heavenly treasure, and when they died, the memory of the body faded from their minds.

**DCCLVII. DCCXIX.**

### 200

[Note: [Col. 1075A] There is great disagreement among authors about the year in which the city of Toledo was captured. Rodrigo thinks it happened shortly after the Saracens entered and established their rule. But our present author, Julian, and others think it occurred in the year 719. Assuming as a true foundation that the city was captured and restored to the Christians on Sunday, 25 May, the feast of St. Urban, astronomical calculation makes it necessary that this occurred in the year 1085, as the *Toledan Annals* attest. This is also shown by a donation made at Cella Nova on 10 August, in the era 1123—that is, in the year 1085—“at the time of the most serene Prince Alfonso, in the year when he pressed Toledo from the Saracens.” Taking this as a firm foundation, a privilege of King Alfonso called “The Dowry of the Holy Church of Toledo,” dated 18 December in the era 1124, in the year and approximately seven months after the capture of the city, says: “This city, by the hidden judgment of God, was possessed by the Moors for 366 years.” [Col. 1075B]

“Counting backward from 1085, when it was recovered, to 719, exactly 366 years are obtained: no year is added, left over, or missing. Therefore it was recovered on the same day on which it had been captured, namely 25 May; it was captured on a Friday and recovered on a Sunday, the feast of St. Urban, pope and martyr. P. H.]

On the twenty-fourth day of May, the feast of St. Urban, pope and martyr, on a Friday, the Arabs occupied the city of Toledo under the agreement that seven churches should remain for the Christian Mozarabs living there, though subject also to a heavy tribute.

**DCCLX. DCCXXII.**

### 201

[Note: Synderedus attended a Roman synod and afterward died and was buried in the church of St. Peter, prince of the apostles. For the synod, see the fuller discussions in the councils, Garibay, Morales, and others. P. H.] [Col. 1075B]

Synderedus, formerly archbishop of Toledo, attended and confirmed a certain Roman council under Pope Gregory II. Not long afterward, he died in Rome at an advanced age, overcome by grief at the misfortunes of Spain, and was buried in the basilica of St. Peter.

### 202

[Note: The city of Granada, also called Florentia Illiberis, was flourishing. From the inscriptions it should be read *Illiberris*, and it was called *Florentina*. Thus it is found engraved on a stone preserved at Granada in great honour, dedicated to Furia Sabina:

> “To Furia Sabina Tranquillina Augusta, wife of the Emperor Caesar Marcus Antonius Gordianus Pius Felix Augustus, the council of the municipality of Florentia Illiberritana, devoted to the divine power and majesty, set this up at public expense by decree.”

And on another likewise: I suppose that mention is made of this Valerius Seneca, since it identifies him as a Spanish orator. [Col. 1076A]

The Licentiate Francisco Bermúdez de Pedraza mentions these stones in his book entitled *The Antiquity and Excellences of Granada*, book II, chapter 7, pp. 35–36, where he explains them learnedly. I add Julian in the *Adversaria*, no. 175:

> “Illiberis, or the Florentine municipality Illiberritanum, is the same place; and the Illiberritani, or Florentines. In some corrupt manuscripts *Liberini* is read instead. From this municipality certain men proceeded before the birth of Christ and founded the city of Florence in Italy.”

He had said in the *Chronicle*, no. 22:

> “Basil, a citizen of the Florentine municipality, or rather of Illiberris, etc.”

And in the *Adversaria*, no. 171:

> “Basil—that is, Basileus—a citizen of the Florentine Illiberritan municipality.”

The learned doctor Gregorio López Madera, councillor to Philip, Catholic king of Spain, fills out, arranges, and decides this matter with a full, learned, and polished hand in chapter 23 of his *Sacred Mountain of Granada*, where he cites Don Diego de Mendoza in his history of the Granada War and Hieronymus de Zurita in the *Annals*, book XX, chapter 42. I refer you to that learned man as one points with a finger to the source: it will be worth your while to consult him, as well as Don Fernando de Mendoza, *On the Council of Illiberis*, book I, chapter 1, pp. 4–6, where he lists these and other stones. [Col. 1077B]

Different authors say different things about Natta. Don Gregorio López Madera writes much on the subject in the same book, chapter 17, and Covarrubias in his *Treasury of the Spanish Language*, under the word “Granada.” Whatever is missing cannot be read in the autograph; let the reader conjecture and supply it. D. L.]

The city of Granada, also called Florentia Illiberis, was flourishing. Its first mistress was called Natta, because [lacuna].

**DCCLXII. DCCXXIV.**

### 203

Bede, an Anglo-Saxon Benedictine monk, flourished.

### 204

John Mansur of Damascus, a learned and pious man.

**DCCLXIII. DCCXXV.**

### 205

A synod of Eastern bishops was convened at Tyre in defence of the sacred images, through the efforts of John of Damascus.

**DCCLXIV. DCCXXVI.**

In this year the holy ecumenical Roman synod was held against the heretics who opposed images.

**DCCLXV. DCCXXVII.**

Flavius Eutychius the patrician succeeded Paul as exarch of Ravenna. He was an excellent and outstanding man. At Toledo the memory of the holy Justus and Abundius, who suffered under Numerian in Baetica, was celebrated from the time of St. Isidore the doctor, who honoured them with an elegant hymn.

**DCCLXVII. DCCXXIX.**

### 207

The Constantinopolitan synod against images.

**DCCLXVIII. DCCXXX.**

### 208

Gregory II died at Rome on 11 February.

**DCCLXIX. DCCXXXI.**

### 209

Gregory III succeeded Gregory II in the See of Peter.

**DCCLXX. DCCXXXII.**

### 210

A synod was convened at Augsburg in Germany by St. Boniface.

**DCCLXXII. DCCXXXIV.**

### 211

Theodore, the forty-fourth bishop of Milan, and St. Boniface, the first archbishop of Mainz, flourished.

Urbicarius, the first archbishop of Vienne, is commemorated.

**DCCLXXVIII. DCCXL.**

### 213

Gregory III died on 28 November.

The emperor Leo died at Constantinople on 19 June.

**DCCLXXIX. DCCXLI.**

### 215

Zacharias, a monk, was made pope from the rank of cardinal priest on 1 December and consecrated on 3 December.

### 216

[Note: Our Liutprand tells us the day of St. Urban’s death: “On 4 October, in the year 741, the twenty-second year after the capture of Toledo, he died a holy death, on a Friday.” It is often questioned, however, whether he should be counted among the bishops of Toledo. [Col. 1077B]

First, he is found in none of the ancient catalogues of Toledo’s bishops—not in that of St. Aemilianus, nor in the Toledan treasury, written from the time of King Alfonso VI onward.

Second, Pelagius, bishop of Oviedo, twice calls him the old Melodius of the royal city of Toledo. His words are:

> “At that time Frodoarius, bishop of the See of Acci, [and] Urbanus, the veteran Melodius of the cathedral royal city of the Toledan See…” [Col. 1077C]

And shortly afterward:

> “At that time, he says, the learned men Urbanus and Evantius, most distinguished for their devotion to holiness, went joyfully to the Lord and rest in peace.”

Third, one and the same see cannot have two living bishops. Synderedus was still living in Rome when Urbanus was elected; therefore he does not seem to have been bishop of Toledo.

Nevertheless, Don Rodrigo, archbishop of Toledo, repeatedly calls him archbishop of Toledo, as do the *General History of Spain*, Lucas of Tuy, and Don García de Loaysa, archbishop of Toledo—twice, once in his catalogue and again in his discussion of the primacy of the Church of Toledo, which will be considered later. Before these writers, Liutprand, an author from nearly seven hundred years earlier, and Julian the archpriest do so, as do Garibay, Morales, Mariana, and I in the *History of Toledo*, together with Doctor Blasius Ortiz, a canon of Toledo, Alcozer, book II, chapter 3, Er. Juan Marieta, and others.

The objections may be answered as follows. [Col. 1077D]

To the first, it may be replied that the catalogues of Toledo’s bishops have been extraordinarily abridged.

To the second, Pelagius’s authority should not be regarded as so great that it overrides the testimony of so many authors who consulted Pelagius’s writings repeatedly. This is the view followed by Master Álvaro Gómez in his life of Urbanus, the pontiff. [Col. 1078A]

To the third, we must believe that, given the holiness of Synderedus, he did not flee but went to Rome, driven by the injuries he was receiving from Oppas. If he intended not to return to Toledo, he freely resigned; and therefore the Toledan priests, after consulting King Roderic, elected the holy pontiff Urbanus.

Nothing else can be thought or said—either about the prudence of the Toledan priests and the archdeacon Evantius, as though they could appoint Urbanus in place of Synderedus while the latter was still alive contrary to law and right, or about Urbanus’s holiness and moderation, as though he could accept an election made contrary to justice. He was therefore canonically elected and undertook the pontificate not from a desire to rule but from the will to serve God and his homeland.

Besides the praises of Pelagius, bishop of Oviedo, in book III, chapter 18, we have this:

> “The long-lived men of whom we have spoken chose Urbanus, a man of holiness, as bishop.”

Thus García de Loaysa, folio 278, in the Toledan councils:

> “Urbanus, the bishop, because Synderedus had departed, assumed the honour of the primacy. Being a holy man, he endured with steadfast, courageous, and unconquered spirit that notable calamity. Evantius, archdeacon of Toledo, gave him great assistance in bearing the burden of miserable servitude. Both had been excellently instructed in learning and formed in that ecclesiastical knowledge with which the most holy Ildefonsus had educated the Church of Toledo. [Col. 1078B]
>
> “Thus Urbanus, amid so great a change of circumstances, did not cease to provide what he could. He carefully gathered many books and the sacred relics and bodies of the saints, collected with devotion and care, enclosed them with the greatest reverence in an ark, and arranged for them to be diligently carried into the mountains of Asturias.
>
> “This blessed chest was afterward venerated with great devotion in the church of Oviedo, together with many other relics gathered there in holiness, and it is still preserved there. It was given the name ‘the Holy Chamber.’
>
> “During Urbanus’s pitiable times, divine worship and the use of the sacraments began to change and diminish greatly at Toledo. For the former extent and supreme authority of the Toledan bishop were reduced to only six parishes and a small number of faithful, confined within very narrow boundaries. [Col. 1078C]
>
> “Nor was it enough that they had been reduced in number. Those faithful who survived, having frequent dealings and associations with the Moors and being deterred by the most savage persecution, began shamefully to waver in religion and in Christian institutions. Urbanus, Evantius, and the other pious men devoted the greatest care and effort to making them firm in the faith and rousing them to face danger.”

Álvaro Gómez thinks that Urbanus died at Oviedo and, because of grief, despondency, and the natural impediment of advancing age, did not return. But in my judgment the following carries greater weight: he knew that he was bishop of Toledo, and in such a disruption of affairs and danger to his sheep he could not excuse himself for leaving them in the hands of wolves.

Without doubt he came to Toledo and died there in the year 741. He was buried, as I believe, in the church of St. Justa, which was then the seat and cathedral of the Toledan bishops. He was a man worthy of the immortality which he enjoys, and worthy to be entered in the catalogue of the saints, as was also Gunderic, his third successor. It is nevertheless enough that he and many other most holy Toledan bishops have been written in the eternal book of life, which I piously believe they attained. D. L.] [Col. 1078D]

On 4 October the holy man Julian, surnamed Urbanus, died at Toledo. He was a pious and learned man of outstanding spirit. Not long afterward, St. Evantius, the archdeacon, also died.

**DCCLXXXII. DCCXLIV.**

### 217

[Note: Julian reports the same in the *Adversaria*, no. 550:

> “In certain places in Spain the sound of bells is frequently heard beneath the earth. Monasteries of sacred virgins are believed to have stood there; to prevent themselves from falling into the hands of lustful Moors, they asked to be swallowed by the earth. This happened on the peaks of the Carpetanian Mountains near Margeliza, in Carpetania, at the church of St. Quiteria, and elsewhere.” D. L.] [Col. 1079A]

In the territory of Carpetania, many Benedictine nuns, fearing violation by the Moors, obtained from God that they should be swallowed by the earth. A small bell, by which they had been summoned to prayers, is heard at fixed hours of the day.

### 218

[Note: Liutprand makes Suineredus the successor of Urbanus. The catalogue of the Church of Toledo calls him Sugifredus; Loaysa calls him Sumeredus; Julian the archpriest and others call him Sunideredus. Garibay, Morales, Mariana, and Loaysa mention him in the catalogue which he constructed above the Toledan council under King Flavius Gundemar. Some substitute Cixilanus for Urbanus.

Liutprand assigns him eleven years; Julian of Toledo, six; Loaysa’s manuscript, twenty. I do not doubt that he was a most holy man, as those truly calamitous and unhappy times urgently required. We must not think otherwise about divine providence: when circumstances are afflicted and almost desperate, it presents such shepherds, who lead by the example of their lives and continually refresh the sheep entrusted to them with the nourishment of saving doctrine. [Col. 1079B]

His name indicates that this bishop was Gothic. It seems highly probable to me that he was brought up in the Church of Toledo, died there, and was buried in the Toledan church of St. Justa. P. H.]

At this point some place Suineredus and say that the holy Church of Toledo was governed by him for eleven years, amid a most miserable succession of troubled times and circumstances.

### 219

[Note: Aurelia is a town in Carpetania, not far from Ocaña. Liutprand says that St. Veranus was exiled there, supposedly sent there by the Moors; or, as I am more inclined to believe, that he went there from Tarragona, just as Frodoarius, bishop of Acci, went to Toledo.

He was a holy man. No such bishop appears in the records of Aurelia; he is said to have been from Tarragona. His feast is celebrated on 19 October, and the more recent Roman Martyrology says on that day: “In the territory of Aurelia, St. Veranus, bishop.” [Col. 1079C]

Baronius thinks this was the bishop of Chalon because Gregory of Tours speaks of him in book IX, chapter 4, in these words:

> “For at that time this bishop himself was endowed with great virtues, so that often, when he placed the sign of power upon the sick, he immediately restored them to health, with the Lord’s approval.”

He flourished in the year 580.

But this is another man, as anyone who observes the see, time, and place can easily recognize. There was another Veranus, bishop of Lyon, to whom Pope St. Hilary wrote. Peter de Natalibus, book X, chapter 50, places Veranus, bishop of Gévaudan, in the time of the emperor Valens.

I would believe that this most holy bishop Veranus lived for many years in Toledo and was supported by Urbanus’s resources, until he died happily in the district of Aurelia, or Aurelian territory, in Carpetania. And, as is reasonable to believe, his most holy body was brought to Toledo.

For bishops fled to this royal city, although it was held by the Moors, as to a dwelling-place of piety and the safest harbour for shipwrecked men: Odoarius, Clemens, Veranus, and others did so. This greatly increases the esteem for the pious care which this royal city has always been accustomed to show toward afflicted and wretched bishops. [Col. 1080A]

In this, certainly, canon 21 of the Council of Sardica is observed. Under the presidency of Hosius of Córdoba, it commands that bishops driven from their sees be received kindly and humanely in other cities, as the men mentioned above were received. D. L.]

In Carpetania and the district of Aurelia, St. Veranus, bishop of Tarragona, lived in exile. His feast is celebrated on 19 October.

### 220

After Pelagius had been freed by divine intervention in a cave, his son Froila succeeded him; Froila’s son-in-law Alfonso the Catholic succeeded Froila.

**DCCLXXXIV. DCCXLVI.**

### 221

[Note: There is astonishing disagreement among the authors concerning Peter Pulcher, for no ancient diptych of the Toledan bishops includes him. Vasaeus testifies that he read of him in Pelagius of Oviedo; but the manuscript in my possession does not mention him. Don García de Loaysa, Master Álvaro Gómez, Liutprand, and Julian, archdeacon of St. Justa, follow Vasaeus, but they disagree about how and where to place him.

Vasaeus places him after Cixilanus; the Worms catalogue places him after Concordius and before Cixilanus; Liutprand places him in the year 746, after Suineredus and Concordius; Julian does the same. I have chosen to follow them.

García de Loaysa says of him, in his account of Gundemar:

> “Although Toledo was under the dominion of the Moors, it exercised the primacy by right and authority. For Peter, who was surnamed Pulcher because of the elegance of his bodily form, was appointed in place of the deceased Cixila. He was exceedingly learned in letters and so aflame with observance of religion and piety that he not only devoted himself diligently to the care of his own city and provided carefully for all its dangers, but also thought it necessary to attend to the needs of the other bishops of Spain.
>
> “When word reached him that the computation of Easter was not being observed properly and canonically at Seville, he wrote to the bishop and clergy of Seville concerning what should be held on that matter. As for the computation of Easter, the decrees of the councils permitted no one except the primate bishops to decide what was settled and firm. This was established in the Third Council of Carthage, canons 1 and 12; Toledo IV, canon 4; Braga II, canon 9; and the First Council of Arles, canon 4.” [Col. 1080B]

Master Álvaro Gómez, distinguished for the praise deserved by his intelligence and judgment, teaches in his life of Peter that Peter was so devoted to and protective of chastity that he contended with King Froila for the enactment of a law abolishing the most shameful and incestuous marriages of priests and clerics, which had survived in Spain through the permission of the rash Witiza. After five years in the priesthood, worn out by age and grief, he died.

He could not see without the deepest sorrow the injuries which Toledo suffered from the Moors. He was buried, like his predecessors, in the church of St. Justa. I suspect that he sent the book to Heera, archbishop of Seville, who presided over that Church at this time. I believe that this Peter was included in the Gothic canon.

Concordius succeeded him. He is mentioned by three diptychs of the Toledan archbishops—the Worms diptych, those of Julian, Liutprand, Ortiz, Morales, Garibay, Peter of Toledo, Zamalloa, and Don García de Loaysa.

Álvaro Gómez places him in the age of King Silo, but he is mistaken, because he precedes Cixilanus and Elipandus; Elipandus lived during Silo’s reign, wrote to him, and received letters from him. In Don Loaysa’s catalogue, Concordius is placed under the year 760, Cixilanus under 775, and Elipandus under 784. [Col. 1081A]

He therefore could not in any way have lived in Silo’s time. Silo’s reign lasted nine years, and Concordius belongs to the period of Cixilanus, as is plainly shown by the letters just mentioned.

Concordius died in the year 775, after fifteen years in the pontificate and many labours undertaken to protect his flock and defend the religion of Christ. I am convinced that, just as these labours abounded in hardships, so they were divinely repaid by the greatest consolations and flourished greatly in the praise of holiness. P. H.]

Peter, surnamed Pulcher, governed the Church of Toledo after Concordius, and previously for another five years. He was a distinguished writer and a most vigorous defender of the faith.

[Col. 1081]

### 222

[Note: Besides Florianus Ocampo, Garibay and Liutprand testify that Julian Lucas, a Thessalonian by birth, flourished at Toledo at this time and committed the events of those times to the memory of posterity. See what I said about Julian Lucas in the *Adversaria*, no. 36. D. L.] [Col. 1081A]

At this time Julian Lucas, a deacon who was already advanced in age, also wrote at Toledo. He published books on the affairs of Spain.

**DCCLXXXVI. DCCXLVIII.**

### 223

[Note: Concerning Odoarius, bishop of Acci, see Pelagius of Oviedo, Rodrigo, the *General History*, and others. Concerning John of Seville, Rodrigo says in book IV, chapter 3:

> “At Seville there was a glorious and most holy bishop named John, whom the Arabs called Caut Almatram. He shone with great knowledge of the Arabic language and was illustrious through many miraculous works. He also explained the sacred Scriptures in Catholic commentaries, which he left composed in Arabic for the instruction of posterity.” [Col. 1081B]

Álvaro Gómez and others think that he was archbishop of Toledo. D. L.]

The most holy man Odoarius [variant: Frodoarius], bishop of Acci, was also flourishing at Toledo, as was John, bishop of Seville, who translated the sacred Scriptures from Latin into Arabic, which was by then the common language in Spain; the Latin language was in little use.

### 224

Pope St. Hadrian wrote to Egila, bishop of Illiberis, formerly abbot of the Agalian monastery of Toledo.

### 225

St. Urbicius transferred the bodies of the holy martyrs Justus and Pastor into the city of Complutum—that is, Guadalfaxaram—from the Campo Laudable, where they had previously been buried and discovered by divine revelation by Asturius Serrano. They were first transferred to Gaul and afterward to a place near the city of Huesca.

### 226

[Note: Tader is the name of a river called the Segura, which passes by the city of Murcia and empties into the sea not far from there. The city is called Securis, near which the Tader rises. P. H.]

Tadere, or Secura, was his birthplace. Julian likewise reports this in the *Chronicle*, no. 388: “Egila, born in the city of Tadere, which is now Secura, abbot of Agalia, flourished at Toledo in holiness and learning.” Frequent mention is made of the city of Tadere under the name Secura. Thus, in the division of diocesan territories made by King Wamba, when assigning the boundaries of the bishopric of Mentesa, he says: “Mentesa: let it hold from Ecija as far as Secura, and from Lila as far as Puxilena.” And concerning the see of Acci: “Acci: let it hold from Secura as far as Montanea, and from Arcatel as far as Carachuel.”

Our most learned and devout friend Father Francisco de Bivar, as is his custom, explains this very well, in his notes on Flavius Dexter, year 308, commentary II, no. 3: the name Secura was not new under Wamba, as is clear from Hydatius, year 925. Within the town there is a street commonly called the Street of the Phoenicians, which is believed to have been made by the Phoenicians, for they once lived there. It is constructed with vaults and arches of extremely ancient workmanship. Nor can anyone reading history doubt this, since it is plainly evident that the Romans and Carthaginians either settled there or frequented and visited the place. Festus Rufus Avienus, writing about the sources of the River Theodorus and its vicinity, says:

> “The Phoenicians formerly inhabited these places.”

Yet the authors do not state by what name Secura was called in Roman times. Molezius, in his *Observations on Ptolemy*, maintains that it was Seguisa. Its location is not inconsistent with this: Ptolemy assigns it eleven and a half degrees of longitude and thirty-eight and a half of latitude; and just as there are eight leagues from Secura to the sources of the Baetis, so there are from Seguisa to those same sources. The case is further supported by the fact that the name *Segura* appears to have been corrupted from *Seguisa*. Antonio de Nebrija, who deserved exceptionally well of the whole of Spain, reached the same conclusion.

Others say that the city took its name from the river; for it is not unusual for cities and rivers to share the same name. Julian confirms this in the *Chronicle*, no. 178, which must be corrected from Higuera’s manuscript as follows:

> “Of Secura, which is also called Tadere because of its proximity to the river flowing through its territory, in the name of Saint Briana, most holy virgin.”

Concerning this river, and others of the same kind, Bernard Joseph de Aldrete writes learnedly in *On the Origin of the Castilian Language*, book I, chapter 15, p. 102.

It was once called Altamira, as though “high watchtower,” because from it there was an extensive view in every direction; indeed, from Secura many regions could be surveyed. Hence it was corruptly called Copea, as though *Scopeum*, and Dianium was called Meroscopeum, as though “daytime watchtowers.” In the time of the Saracens it was called Toman or Odonam, that is, “Security,” because the place was inaccessible and safe.

If one may venture an assertion, it would not be unreasonable to conjecture that the goddess Security (*Securitas*) was worshiped there by the Romans. She was represented seated on a kind of royal chair, with one hand raised to her cheek and holding a staff in the other. I possess a bronze coin bearing this inscription:

> **NERO CLAVDIVS CAESAR AVG. GERMAN. PONT. MAX. TRIB. POTES.**

On the other side:

> **SECVRITAS AVGVSTI**

with the image of that goddess.

There is another coin of Marcus Julius Philippus, bearing on its obverse:

> **IMP. M. AVRELII SECVRITAS PERPET.**

and on the reverse:

> **SECVRITAS ORBIS.**

The goddess Security holds a cornucopia in one hand. On other coins one finds the inscription **SECVRITATI PERPETVAE**. On a coin of Antoninus Pius, the goddess Security appears crowned with laurel, with the inscription:

> **SECVRITAS PVBLICA.**

This goddess was therefore worshiped in that town because the town was called Secura. Accordingly, we may reasonably affirm that the city was at different times called Tadere, sometimes Seguisa and Altamira, and finally Secura.

Concerning Secura and its river, I possess, through the kindness of that most learned and erudite man—“equal to all,” as I might say with Tacitus—Don Bernard Joseph de Aldrete, a manuscript in the Spanish language by the Saracen historian Rasis:

> “The territory of Lérida borders that of Tarragona; Lérida lies north of Tarragona, toward the rising sun from Córdoba, and lies on the River Segre [read: Segura]; this river rises in the Sierra Segura. When they founded this town, this river took its course through the territory of Pilares, and this river enters the Ebro below a castle called Menaça or Viçueça. This river produces fine gold, which other rivers do not; another river, called Vocaira, enters it; and this river and the others flow into the River of the Olives, which they call Cleridas.”

It must not be passed over that the River Tadere runs through the town of Cieza, which I think is Viçueça, and that this was called Menaces—though some have also attributed it to Malaca. Thus Festus Rufus Avienus, in book *On the Coasts of Spain*, according to the Lyon edition of Jacob Chouet, 1596, says:

> “And the River of Malaca, with the city of the same name,  
> Which in the earlier age was called Menace.”

Strabo censures this in book III, in these words, from the translation of Guilielmus Xylander and the recension of Isaac Casaubon:

> “On this coast the first city is Malaca, at a distance from Calpe equal to that from Malaca to Gades. It has a marketplace used by those who live on the opposite shore, and much salted fish is prepared there. Some think that this is the same place as Maenaca, which we are told was the last city of the Phocaeans toward the west. But they are mistaken: the ruins of Maenaca, which lies farther from Calpe and has been destroyed, preserve the traces of a Greek city, whereas Malaca is more Punic in appearance.”

From this, as if through a lattice, we should note that Maenaca and Malaca were not the same city but were very far apart. Maenaca was therefore far from Gades and Calpe; Malaca was the westernmost city of our sea, while Maenaca lay considerably farther east. Malaca was Punic in form, whereas Maenaca was Greek. For this reason I think that Maenaca is the place of which the historian Rasis spoke; he finally calls Secura Tademir, in these words:

> “The territory of Jaén borders that of Todemir; Todemir lies toward the rising sun from Córdoba. Todemir is a highly esteemed place, with very fine groves, and its entire land is watered by two rivers, as happens in the Promised Land, which has good and naturally fertile soil. Here there are veins from which good silver is extracted. Todemir possesses together all the advantages of sea and land. From Todemir to Córdoba is a journey of four days for a mounted man.”

Licentiate Juan de Robles, in *History of the Apparition of the Holy Cross of Caravaca*, chapter 1, p. 3, takes Theodomira to be Caravaca; and our most learned man, Ludovicus Tribaldus of Toledo, professor of the liberal arts, follows him in his *Iberian Epaenesis*, p. 31:

> “Theodomira shines with the splendor of the Christ-bearing cross.”

But, what is more remarkable, in the year 1519 the name Todomir was still in use for this town. I found it written in a little book entitled *Question of Love*, at the very beginning:

> “A knight named Vasquiran, of Spanish nationality, a native of the city of Todomir.”

It was formerly the seat of a kingdom, as appears from a privilege of Emperor Alfonso, son of Count Raymond, which he granted to Peter and to the Church of Orense—as I hear it is preserved in the register of that see—in the year 1195 of the Spanish era. There, among others, the king of Secura confirms the document, for he was subject to that emperor.

Our Luitprand of Tadere discusses this in his *Adversaria*, no. 291, where he speaks of the river and city of Munda, as we shall say there. Julian likewise discusses it in his *Adversaria*, nos. 365 and 366.

The emblems of Secura were an axe and a pine tree. The pine was an emblem of Cybele, the mother of the gods, among the Romans. We may reasonably suspect that they regarded her as the tutelary deity of the very ancient city of Secura. The axe, in that vain discipline of the Romans, signified Jupiter, the god of the balance, because in the Lydian language *libra* means “axe,” as Pierius testifies in book XLII of his *Hieroglyphics*, under the word “axe.” The axe also signified security in the infliction of punishments. Hence the kings of Lydia, and the consuls and magistrates, were preceded by lictors carrying axes. Demosthenes called Phocion an axe because he cut through everything one by one. In the same way, the people of Secura were so powerful in sharpness of intellect that they dissected, examined, and understood everything. [D. L.]

The memory of Egila, abbot of Agalia and later bishop of Illiberis, is celebrated at Toledo. He was born in the city of Tadere, or Secura.

### 227. [Note: [Col. 1084A]]

Egila was abbot of Agalia and showed remarkable devotion toward afflicted Christians. I think that he later became bishop of Illiberis, to whom Pope Adrian wrote, as well as to John, his archpresbyter. At that time many errors were current in Spain, partly through ignorance of good literature and partly through the reappearance of former abuses concerning the celebration of Easter, fasting on Friday and Saturday, and clerical chastity. Concerning these and other matters, Baronius writes in volume IX, under the year of the Lord 795, no. 12:

> “He wrote to others as well, including Egila, bishop in Spain, and exhorted him to preserve orthodox faith concerning the Friday and Saturday fast. Adrian also wrote to Egila, or to the presbyter John, urging that chastity be preached and preserved in the regions of Spain, and concerning the celebration of Easter, so that it might be celebrated at the time when the Roman Church celebrates it. He likewise warned him about the predestination of human beings, whether to good or to evil; about the pollution of those people both in food and drink; about various errors; and about their false priests, who, while their husbands were living, took wives. He also warned him concerning free will and many other matters that had arisen in those regions against the Catholic faith. Finally, he urged them all to be united and to observe the canons, so that all who disobeyed salutary commands might be excommunicated.”

Meanwhile, it should be noted that this abbot Egila obtained from Pope Adrian permission to be consecrated by Wilichar, the thirty-eighth archbishop of Sens in Gaul. After he had been consecrated, he sent the deacon Serrano and the cleric Victorian to Rome with letters and asked the pope’s advice on many questions. The pontiff willingly supplied it, provided that Egila submit himself to the Roman see, accept the papal formularies (*characteres pontificios*), and oppose those who rejected the Friday and Saturday fast, as is evident from the letter addressed to Egila himself, the bishop. [P. H.]

Under Egila, Venantius, a monk at Toledo, flourished. He composed a homily on Saint Adelphus, bishop of Toledo, which is falsely attributed to Peter, bishop of Ravenna.

### 228. [Note: [Col. 1084C]]

The martyrdom of Saint Nicholas of Ledesma, suffered this year on the day before the Kalends of November, is described in an elegantly written *Life* by Doctor Friar Juan Aegidius, a Franciscan monk. It is preserved both at his tomb and in the books of the library of Saint Francis of Zamora. He was an illustrious martyr and is held in great veneration there. [ID.]

We have spoken of Juan Aegidius and his works in the dedicatory letter to Julian. [D. L.]

Saint Nicholas suffered at Ledesma, which in Latin is called Bletissa. He was an eleven-year-old boy, called by his native name Halli when he was a Saracen, the son of Alcaman, a Saracen prince, and the brother of Galafre, king of Toledo. He was the paternal uncle [alternative reading: paternal uncle] of Galliana, Charlemagne’s wife; and, together with him, two Christian Mozarab priests, Nicholas and Leonard, suffered on the day before the Kalends of November.

**790. 752.**

### 229. [Note: [Col. 1084D]]

Cixila is mentioned in all the diptychs of the bishops of Toledo. He wrote the life of Saint Ildefonsus and a letter to Silo, and received Silo’s reply; this correspondence, written in Lombard letters, was formerly preserved in the church of Toledo. Concerning him, the illustrious Loaysa writes in his account of Gundemar:

> “Cixila likewise performed the same service with no less diligence. For he was distinguished in piety and in the discipline of the Holy Spirit.”

That is what he says. According to Luitprand himself, Cixila was the archdeacon of Peter the Fair. [P. H.]

Cixila, archdeacon of Peter the Fair, becomes bishop of Toledo. He presides for twenty-one years under Juceph [or Juphed] and Abderahman, kings of Toledo.

**794. 756.**

### 230. [Note: [Col. 1085A]]

In the year 756, the body of Saint Leocadia was transferred from Toledo to Oviedo. The reason for transferring the body was that Abderahman, king of Córdoba, or Miramolin of the Saracens, prompted, as it were, by demons, began throughout Spain to destroy the magnificent basilicas of the saints and burn the bodies of holy martyrs. To prevent this supreme impiety from being committed against the precious relics of Saint Leocadia, citizen, patroness, and martyr of Toledo, Argericus, abbot of Agalia; Peter, abbot of Saint Leocadia; and Andreas the Mozarab, son of Abenlupus Ficulneus, a leading man of Toledo, carried them away with the greatest care and secrecy. At Oviedo there remains an altar large enough to contain the holy relics, bearing the name of the holy virgin; it is now empty, but it is an evident memorial of their sacred resting place. [P. H.]

This year the body of Saint Leocadia, virgin and martyr, citizen and patroness of Toledo, was transferred from Toledo to Oviedo by Argericus, abbot of Agalia; Peter, abbot of Saint Leocadia; Andreas the Mozarab, son of Abenlupus Ficulneus; and other leading men of Toledo.

**809. 781.**

### 231. [Note: [Col. 1085B]]

The arrival of Charlemagne in Spain is attested by the annals of the Spaniards, especially the *General Chronicle*, Onuphrius, and others who drew from Onuphrius’s *Caesars* and *General Chronicle*, as well as from Nicolaus Clemens Traelaeus. Thus he writes under Charles:

> “Charlemagne had many wives. Galliana, daughter of the king of Toledo, bore Charles, Pepin, and Louis, namely Louis the Pious, his successor in the empire.”

His secretary makes no mention of this wife. Traelaeus had noticed this, and nevertheless makes Galliana his first wife and Louis the Pious her son. This is no small glory for the people of Toledo, from whom came a woman whose fertility in childbirth provided rulers for the Roman Empire. At Toledo there is a certain shortcut called Galliana’s Path; Toledo also has royal gardens called Galliana’s; and a fortress near Saint Faith was once called Galliana’s Fortress. In Gaul there is a palace that to this day is called Galliana’s. King Galafre is mentioned by Rasis the Moorish historian and clearly by the historians of Toledo. [P. H.]

In the manuscript history of Archbishop Rodrigo, translated into Spanish by Rodrigo himself, of which more below, there is the following account of this king—or viceroy:

> “And Count Don Morante went to the city of Toledo, where at that time Galafre was king on behalf of Abderahman.”

[D. L.]

At this time Charlemagne came to Toledo, and so forth. Our most learned Father Francisco de Bivar—“O delight and sweet glory of the Muses and of me!”—writes learnedly about these matters in a letter sent to me, *On the Author and His Writings*, section 2, where he discusses the *Chronicle*.

Historians call Galliana the daughter of Galafre. Among them is Don Rodrigo, archbishop of Toledo, not in his Latin history but in the history composed in Spanish, which I possess in a manuscript translated by the archbishop himself and enlarged and supplemented by an unknown author. This historiographer’s passage occurs in the *Life of Don Fruela*, chapter 34, whose heading is:

> “Of the events that took place in the ninth year, and how Charles came to Toledo.”

He differs from Luitprand regarding the year, for he says that Charles came to Toledo in 761:

> “After nine years of King Don Fruela had passed, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 761, Charles, whom they called Maynete, having a great disagreement with his father, King Pepin, over things that he did which did not seem right, took with him a count named Don Morante, because he already knew those lands of the Moors and was well known there, and went to the city of Toledo.”

A little later, in chapter 35, he reports that Charles married Galliana and that Don Morante carried her to Gaul. His words are:

> “Then Don Morante went with Galliana through those mountains, fearing that the Moors might attack them. He traveled for seven days without ever entering a settled place, because the whole land was full of Moors. After a few days they reached Paris. When Charles learned that they were coming, he went out to receive them with a great company of knights and led Galliana to his palace. He immediately had her baptized and made her a Christian, and married her, just as he had promised her. Charles then received the crown of the kingdom, and from that time onward they called him Charles the Great.”

He also differs from Luitprand in saying that Galliana was baptized at Paris, whereas Luitprand says that she was baptized at Toledo.

Concerning Galliana, see above, no. 248. The Gallic historians support the account, most recently the author of the *Epitome of the Kings of France*, who wrote an account of this emperor in his own language. Doctor Pedro de Salazar y Mendoza, penitentiary canon of the Church of Toledo, a most learned man and well versed in Spanish history, likewise discusses the matter in his prologue to the reader in the *Chronicle* he wrote about the great and illustrious Cardinal Mendoza. There he both reports and denies the story. I thought it worthwhile to reproduce his exact words:

> “In his time the Emperor Charlemagne, king of France, came to Toledo and left King Galafre as his very close friend. The rest—that he took away his daughter Galliana and married her, and built her a palace in Bordeaux; the story of the Moor Bradamante, and the battles he fought in Valsamonial, between Olías and Cabañas—I neither tell nor believe.”

He asserts the last point again in the same *History*, book II, chapter 56, p. 388, column 1. Our Julian likewise records, in no. 395, the same account as Luitprand here, and adds that Galliana was an exceptionally honorable and beautiful virgin. [D. L.]

At this time Charlemagne came to Toledo under King Galafre and married his daughter Galliana, who had been made a Christian by Cixila, bishop of Toledo. On her account he entered into single combat with Bradamant, prince of Complutum, or Guadalfaxara, a giant of enormous stature and grim appearance. He defeated and killed him in battle.

### 232. [Note: [Col. 1086C]]

Saint Urbicius carried away the bodies of the holy martyrs Justus and Pastor on nearly the same occasion on which the people of Toledo carried away Saint Leocadia’s body, and he brought them to Gaul. On his return he lived near Huesca, in the Valley of Nocita, under the discipline of Saint Lifard, a Benedictine abbot. The holy man died on the day before the Kalends of November in the year 771. Famous for miracles, he is venerated at Huesca and was honorably buried in a tomb. Much is said about him in the book *The Translation of the Holy Martyrs Justus and Pastor*, which Ambrosius Morales, royal historian, composed devoutly. [P. H.]

Saint Urbicius, disciple of Saint Bafardus [read: Bassacius], a Benedictine abbot, flourishes in Valle-Nocita [read: Valle-Nocita; see Friar Diego, *Antiquities of Huesca*, book II, chapter 33, folio 275, column 2. D. L.]. He is venerated on the Kalends of November.

### 233. [Note: [Col. 1087A]]

Concerning the church at Toledo dedicated to Saint Thyrsus, there exists a letter from King Silo to Cixila, bishop of Toledo, written in Gothic letters and now printed together with the *Apology*. The letter testifies that Cixila built the church, as does a hymn composed by Cixila himself in praise of the holy martyr, in which he says, among other things:

> “Cixila built this for you, Lord.”

We spoke of Saint Thyrsus under no. 128. [D. L.]

A church was built at Toledo for Saint Thyrsus, Christ’s native servant, a citizen of Toledo, who suffered martyrdom at Apollonia in Greece. It stood near the Great Mosque and was consecrated by Don Cixila, archbishop of Toledo, at great personal risk.

### 234.

Abdalla, the first king of Secura, flourishes remarkably in wealth and reputation.

### 235.

Peter, abbot of Agalia, is held in esteem at Toledo.

### 236. [Note: [Col. 1087A]]

A council was convened at Toledo by Cixila, bishop of Toledo, against Egila, or Egilan, bishop of Illiberis. Besides the testimony of this author, the council can be inferred from Pope Adrian’s letter to all the bishops of Spain. For when Pope Adrian lovingly urged Egila not only to observe the Friday and Saturday fast himself but also to persuade those who opposed it, Egila replied somewhat uncivilly and immodestly that he disagreed with Adrian. The holy pontiff took this badly and wrote to the bishops of Spain. Before them he accused Egila of embracing the errors of his teacher Vincentius and of attempting to teach outside Catholic discipline, and he warned them to beware of Egila’s errors and to strive to bring him back to the right path.

They could not have done this more suitably than by bringing him before a national synod, which was held at Toledo under the presidency of Cixila, as primate of the Spains. There, I believe, after abandoning his errors, the man came to his senses. A sufficiently strong argument for this is that Egila was not removed from the diptychs of the bishops of Illiberis; otherwise he would certainly have been removed if he had persisted in his position. This, I believe, should be attributed to the prayers of Mary, Mother of God, and to the present patronage of Saint James and the martyr Caecilius, the first apostle of the people of Illiberis.

This clearly reveals the remarkable reverence and obedience of the Spanish bishops toward the Holy Roman See. Even amid the harshest captivity, they did not hesitate, as they had been ordered, to assemble a synod of many bishops at Toledo and there examine the case of Egila, the bishop. [P. H.]

Against Egila, bishop of Illiberis, who was unwilling to abstain from meat on Saturday. Gregory VII, Supreme Pontiff, issued a decree concerning abstinence from meat on Saturday in a synod held at Rome. Gratian reports it in *On Consecration*, distinction 5, chapter *Because the Day*, in these words:

> “Because Saturday has been observed among our holy Fathers as a distinguished day of abstinence, we, following their authority, salutarily admonish that whoever wishes to be considered a participant in the Christian religion should abstain from eating meat on that day, unless a greater feast occurs or illness prevents it.”

This is an admonition, not a command. Pope Innocent I, however, established fasting on Saturday; Gratian mentions him in his *Decrees*, *On Consecration*, distinction 3, chapter 13, from letter 1, chapter 4.

In Spain, either Innocent’s decree was not then fully received, as it was not in the Eastern Churches, or it was later abolished by a contrary custom during the prolonged and extremely burdensome wars against the Arab Muslims, who had occupied nearly the entire province. These wars continued for seven hundred years and more, and the decree was abolished amid the most severe scarcity of food, as Father Alfonso Chacón says in these exact words in his treatise *On Fasts and Their Various Observances among the Ancients*.

I also find that the Spaniards sometimes abstained, as our Luitprand reports, and sometimes did not; hence a variable custom arose from time to time. See the notable testimony from the time of King Alfonso VIII, who, after achieving the victory called that of Las Navas de Tolosa, devoutly vowed in thanksgiving to abstain from eating meat on Saturdays. Father Juan de Mariana, the light of letters and ornament of Spain, reports this in book X of his *Histories*, chapter 24:

> “It does not rest on much greater evidence, however, that I find some people asserting, on the testimony of a certain historian, that from this time the practice was adopted in Spain of abstaining from meat on Saturdays and eating only the entrails and extremities of animals, this being a softened form of the ancient custom which the Goths brought from Greece, where they first received the sacred rites.”

He took this from Fernando Pérez de Guzmán’s book entitled *Valerio de las Historias*, book I, title 4, chapter 7, where he says in our Spanish language:

> “A vow was made in Spain not to eat meat on Saturday.”

Cixila was held in the highest renown in Spain because in the year 776 he convened a council at Toledo, by command and through letters of Pope Adrian, against Egila, bishop of Illiberis, who refused to abstain from meat on Saturday. Bishops came to the council from all parts of Spain.

**820. 782.**

### 237 and 238. [Note: [Col. 1088B]]

Morales, Mariana, Gómez, and Loaysa discuss Elipandus; together with Baronius, they accuse him of heresy. Yet the man should in no way be branded in this fashion, since he did not adhere to his error maliciously or obstinately, but, after being warned by Pope Adrian, collected himself and came to repentance, as Gabriel Vázquez, professor of theology at the College of Complutum, teaches well in his book *On the Adoption of Christ*. Our Luitprand teaches the same in explicit words under no. 239. [P. H.]

Elipandus, archdeacon of Cixila, bishop of Toledo, succeeds his teacher Cixila in the patriarchal see of Toledo. He presides until the year 810.

### 239.

Through the bad persuasion of his teacher, Felix, bishop of Urgel, he falls into the shameful error concerning the Adoption of Christ. But through the letters of Pope Adrian and of Charlemagne, son of Pepin, king of the Franks, he returns to the mind and true sense of the Church.

### 240.

John the presbyter, learned and holy, flourished at Toledo. Pope Adrian of Rome sent letters to him.

### 241. [Note: [Col. 1088C]]

Concerning the persecution suffered by the Mozarabs of Toledo at the hands of the Saracens, no greater proofs are needed than the ferocious and uncivilized character of the Moors, their stubborn hatred of Christians, and the wretched condition of captives. Saint Eulogius, an outstanding martyr and elected bishop of Toledo, gives a fuller account of the similar sufferings endured by the Christians of Córdoba sixty years later. [P. H.]

At this time the Mozarabs of Toledo were severely oppressed by the Moors, who imposed new taxes.

### 242. [Col. 1089]

This year I was at Lyon, and from my intercourse with the men and archivists of its Church I learned that there had been two Genesii. One was the elder, who died about two hundred years earlier [more probably read: “who died not many years earlier”], or at least 140 [or 150] years earlier; the other, who had died somewhat earlier, was called Abhelardus. He was a kinsman of Charlemagne and, as a Benedictine monk, preferred quiet to public affairs.

### 243.

This same man attended the Council of Frankfurt and did not assent to the error of the Gauls and Germans, who asserted that sacred images should be possessed but not venerated. All the teachers of Spain held the contrary opinion.

### 244. [Note: [Col. 1089A]]

Magic was called the “Toledan Science” because it was taught at Toledo in a cave called that of Hercules, a place well suited to such enchantments and demonic illusions. Let the *Life of Saint Giles the Dominican* be read. It says that when he was traveling to Paris to study medicine, he was invited on the road by a demon to spend several years in this cave, where he learned magic from that same demon as his teacher.

Magic was taught at Toledo by demons. Julian discusses Toledan magic in his *Adversaria*, no. 198, in these words:

> “Magic has continued at Toledo from the earliest Phoenician times, in a certain cavern dedicated to Hercules; it is still practiced and is called the Toledan Science.”

He referred to the same matter in his *Chronicle*, no. 624:

> “The slippery practices of magic have been made at Toledo.”

Garivayus, book V of the *Compendium of History*, chapter 4, p. 131, writes as follows:

> “In time the inhabitants of Toledo, as very learned men, came to teach the people various sciences, especially astrology. They did not stop there, but did the same with magic, which for this reason was called the Toledan Art and has preserved that name to this day, being so called in some places.”

The Spanish historians say much about the cave of Hercules. Don Francisco de Pisa, in book I, chapter 5 of his *History of Toledo*, distinguishes this cave from the prophetic cave of King Roderic, but does not add a word about the necromancy taught there.

Father Martin Anthony Delrío—alas, once my teacher—mentions this cave in the prologue to his books on magic:

> “We read that after the Saracen flood throughout Spain, magic became so powerful that, when there was an extreme scarcity and ignorance of all good literature, almost only demonic arts were publicly taught at Toledo, Seville, and Salamanca.”

Again, in book II, question 27, section 2, p. 132, column 2A:

> “Was Satan, then, the tormentor of Job of this kind? I think so, and likewise those who, within the memory of our grandfathers, taught magical and curious arts in a cave at Salamanca and Toledo.”

Concerning the history of Saint Giles, which Father Jerome de la Higuera refers to in his notes on this number, see Abraham Bzovius, *Ecclesiastical Annals*, year 1230, no. 9; Maximilian Sandaeus of the Society of Jesus, *Profane Grammar*, commentary VII, section 25, p. 225; and the Reverend Father Ferdinand del Castillo, an illustrious light of the Order of Preachers, who writes at length in the *General History of Saint Dominic*, part I, book II, chapter 72. There he recounts the demonic agreements that the students entered into and swore to before entering the cave.

First, they were to depart entirely from the Catholic faith and the law of God and submit themselves to the power and will of the devil, their teacher of magic. Second, they were to blaspheme the faith and baptism and renounce them. Third, in recognition of the devil’s supreme dominion, they were to rubricate and write out a document strengthened by the contracting parties’ own blood, as a detestable guarantee and homage to such madness; for demons rejoice in blood and are said to love it. Therefore, whenever necromancy was performed, blood was mixed with water, and the demons were easily attracted by its color.

There is a chapter, *Nor Is It Surprising*, question 26, distinction 5, section *Necromancers*, from which Father Ferdinand extracted this account. It is reported by Paulus Grillandus in chapter 2 of his treatise *On Sorcery*, and by Don Manuel de Valle de Moura in *On Enchantments, or Healing Charms*, little work 1, section 1, chapter 2, no. 14.

And, to illustrate the yawns and gaping openings of the Toledan cave, read without yawning the amusing little story of Count Lucanor, chapter 13, about a certain dean named Don Illán who lived at Toledo. There you will find not ruins or rough remains, but some clearly drawn outlines of the cave.

Concerning Salamanca, I cannot refrain from adding verses composed in our old meter and language in a little book entitled *The Triumph of Raymond*, in which its author, Pedro González de Trasmiera, sang the genealogical descriptions and pedigrees of that city:

> “The Necromancers’ School,  
> Of the Cyprian cave,  
> Where it is Castilian opinion  
> That seven remain and one is captive.”

Although Don Francisco Torreblanca Villalpando mocks certain traces of this cave in book II of *On Divinatory Magic*, chapter 11, no. 4, in these words:

> “Besides what the common people jokingly say about the cave of Spain called Peña Clemensi, that demons were accustomed to give answers there—for it was once the underground church of Saint Cyprian in the city of Salamanca, where Clement Potosí, its sacristan, after professors of magic had been expelled from Spain, gave rise to the story by secretly teaching there, as I learned from my teacher Gabriel Henríquez, principal doctor of civil law at Salamanca and now royal councillor.”

Thus far Torreblanca.

Nevertheless, the most learned Delrío says in the prologue mentioned above that he saw that crypt:

> “I too saw a vestige of that infamous school, which Queen Isabella, that woman of manly spirit, wife of Ferdinand the Catholic, had ordered to be blocked with mortar and stones scarcely one hundred and thirty years earlier.”

[D. L.]

Magic was taught at Toledo by demons in a cave which the common people say Hercules built. From there it began to spread throughout Spain and is called the Toledan Science.

### 252. [Note: [Col. 1091A]]

The seventh general Council of Nicaea was convened in the year 788, with three hundred and fifty bishops, according to Onuphrius in his *Ecclesiastical Chronicle*. Nicephorus, archpresbyter of Saint Mary of the Column of the church of Zaragoza, founded by Saint James, and Agapius, abbot of Saint Thyrsus of Toledo and vicar of Elipandus, archbishop of Toledo, were sent there. This shows the diligence of the Spanish bishops, who were never absent when necessary matters were at stake, but assisted the Christian cause by going in person or through their representatives to cities, however distant, wherever councils were convened concerning important and necessary matters. [ID.]

Badae. In Flavius Dexter, year 353, no. 2, *Bagae* is read. I would read *Badae* in both places, for it is the place now called Baza. See our Father Francisco de Bivar. [D. L.]

“Now so called.” In the manuscript it reads, “now called, or nearly so,” because it may formerly have been called Baga. [ID.]

Pantaleon, bishop of Valencia in Spain, and Theodore, presbyter of Bada near Carthage Spartaria (now so called, or nearby), formerly called Thyar, were present. Also present were Nicephorus, presbyter of the church of Saint Mary of the Column at Zaragoza, and Agapius, abbot of the monastery of Saint Thyrsus at Toledo, representing Elipandus, bishop of Toledo, and acting as his vicar.

**259. [Note: [Col. 1091B]]**

Concerning the council that Elipandus convened at Toledo, at the urging of King Charlemagne and through the instigation of Gumesindus, archdeacon of Toledo, and Lupus the Mozarab, Julian also makes mention in this same year. It was held on the very day of Saint Hermenegild, king and martyr, 13 April, which that year fell on a Monday. Elipandus, archbishop of Toledo, convened a synod at Toledo this year at the request of the holy King Charlemagne and at the urging of Gumesindus, archdeacon of Toledo and his disciple, and of Lupus, a Mozarab and leading citizen of Toledo, on 13 April, a Sunday, on the feast of Saint Hermenegild, king and martyr, at the secretariat of Saint Justa. Many bishops and abbots assembled for it. In their presence Elipandus declared that he adhered to the decision of the holy Roman Church concerning the matter of Christ’s adoption—a matter in which he had been deceived—and he said this with tears, as did the others.

There is frequent and extensive mention in Julian of the thanks given by Bishop Elipandus to Charlemagne. Of any thanks given to Adrian, there is no mention elsewhere, except that I believe that on this occasion Pope Adrian ordered Elipandus, as primate of the Spains, to proclaim throughout Spain litanies on 23, 26, and 28 June for the safety of King Charlemagne. Adrian explains this to Charlemagne himself and asks him to order that the same be done on those days in his own kingdoms, just as it was done in Spain. This shows how highly Charlemagne was esteemed in Spain [Col. 1092B]. See also what I noted concerning the letter sent by Tractemundus to Luitprand, no. 6. D. L.]
