**270.** Gumesindus, his successor and disciple, placed over him, according to Gothic custom, a funerary poem.

**271. [Note: [Col. 1093A]]**

Many people from Spain, especially from among the Mozarabs of Toledo [Col. 1093B], migrated to Gaul because of the continual oppression of the Moors. Charlemagne first received them kindly, and Louis later granted them lands. The following diploma of Louis concerns this matter, and in it his piety, charity, and love for his native Toledo shine forth splendidly.

Baronius speaks of the matter as follows in volume IX of his *Annals*, under the year 815:

> “At that same time in the West, while the peoples of Spain were being crushed under the harshest yoke of the Saracens, many people, unable to endure severe slavery and preferring to serve Christians rather than the Mohammedans, enemies of Christ, migrated from there to Gaul, leaving behind their possessions. But the most pious emperor Louis was so far from wishing to receive them as slaves that he wanted them all to be free on the same terms as the Franks, granting them fields as well, which they could cultivate and from which they could live. What is more, he wished them to be exempt from the payment of taxes.”

Two letters on this subject exist, preserved by Pithaeus from the archives of the metropolitan Church of Narbonne, which formerly belonged to the Goths. I believe that at that time, among the families that migrated from Toledo to Gaul, the ancient family of the Figueras also made the journey [Col. 1094A]. Some of their descendants still exist today, men distinguished by nobility and sufficiently commendable for the glory of their achievements, named John and Peter Figuera; they have their residence not far from the town of Saint-Flour.

But let us return to the earlier letter, which reads as follows:

> “This is the ordinance of remission, or concession, which the Emperor Louis made for the Spaniards who had taken refuge with him:
>
> “In the name of God and of our Savior Jesus Christ. Louis, by divine ordinance and providence, emperor Augustus, to all the faithful of the holy Church of God and to our subjects, present and future, residing in the regions of Aquitaine, the province of Septimania, and Spain, specifically in those places which, as we have said, had been taken from the Saracens by the Franks.
>
> “Since we think that it has escaped no one’s knowledge how certain men, because of the unjust oppression and most cruel yoke which the people most hostile to Christianity, the Saracens, imposed upon their necks, left their own dwellings and possessions, which belonged to them by hereditary right, and fled to us from the regions of Spain; and how they settled in Septimania and in that part of Spain which had been reduced to desolation by our margraves, taking up residence there; and how, withdrawing themselves from the power of the Saracens, they submitted themselves freely and willingly to our dominion—we wish it to come to the knowledge of all that we have resolved to preserve these same men, received under our protection and defense, in freedom.
>
> “They shall, namely, proceed to the army with their count in the same manner as other free men, and in our march, according to the reasonable arrangement and admonition of our count, they shall not neglect to perform reconnaissance and watches, which in the customary language are called *vastas*. They shall prepare provisions for our envoys, or for those of our son whom we may send to those regions as circumstances require, when those envoys have been sent to us from the regions of Spain, and they shall provide them with horses for transport. No other census shall be exacted from them, either by the count or by his subordinates and officials [Col. 1095A].
>
> “For major cases—such as homicides, abductions, arson, plunder, mutilation of limbs, thefts, robberies, invasions of another’s property, and any matter in which he has been accused by his neighbor, criminally or civilly, and summoned to court—he must in every way appear before the court of his count. In lesser cases, however, they shall not be prevented from settling matters among themselves by mutual agreement, as they are known to have done until now.
>
> “If any of them brings other men from elsewhere into the portion of land which he has occupied for habitation and causes them to live with him in the share which he has brought them to divide, he may use their service without anyone’s contradiction or hindrance; and they may appoint among themselves those who are to administer such justice as they can settle among themselves. Other criminal judgments and legal actions shall be reserved for the count’s examination.
>
> “If any of those men who has been brought in by one of them and settled in his portion should leave the place, nevertheless the place that has been abandoned shall not pass from the lord of the man who previously held them [Col. 1095B].
>
> “If, because of the leniency and gentleness of their count, they should offer that count something from their possessions as a mark of honor and service, he shall not count it as any kind of tribute or tax; nor shall that count or his successors presume to establish it as a custom, nor compel them to furnish lodging for himself or his men, to provide transport, or to render any tax, tribute, or service beyond what has been specified above.
>
> “It shall be permitted both to those Spaniards who now reside in the places mentioned and to those who may yet flee from the power of the wicked and gather under our protection, who, with the permission of us or of our count, have confidently built structures in deserted and uncultivated places and cultivated fields, to remain in freedom under our protection and defense according to the manner stated above, and to provide us, together with their count and his envoys, promptly and faithfully, as circumstances require, with the services described above [Col. 1095C].
>
> “The same Spaniards should nevertheless know that permission has been granted to them that, if they should enter into vassalage with our counts in the customary manner, and if any one of them should receive a benefice from the person to whom he has commended himself, he must render to his lord such service from it as our native subjects customarily render to their lords from a similar benefice.
>
> “Therefore we have resolved to issue these letters of our authority to them, by which we decree and order that this constitution of our liberality and gentleness toward them be inviolably preserved forever by all the faithful of the holy Church of God and by our subjects.
>
> “We wish there to be three copies of this constitution in each city where the aforesaid Spaniards are known to have been accustomed to live: one to be held by the bishop of that city, another by the count, and a third by the Spaniards themselves who reside in that place. We judge that a copy of these letters should be placed in the archives of our palace [Col. 1095D], so that, by consulting it, a dispute may be settled whenever—as commonly happens—they themselves bring a complaint, or the count or anyone else has a case against them.
>
> “We have also subscribed this constitution with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring, so that it may be believed for a long time by the faithful of the holy Church and by our subjects, and preserved more faithfully.
>
> “+ Sign of the most serene lord emperor, Lord Louis.
>
> “D. Uzadus the deacon, acting in place of Helisachar, reviewed this document.
>
> “Given on the Kalends of January, in the third year, with Christ propitious, of Louis, most pious emperor Augustus, in the eighth indiction. Issued at Aachen in the royal palace, in the name of God. Amen.”

But those who were placed over these Christians treated them unjustly and harshly [Col. 1096A]. They were themselves among those who had come from Spain, and the Christians complained about them to the emperor. He replied as follows:

> “In the name of the Lord. Amen. Let it be known to all the faithful of the holy Church and to our subjects, present and future, and also to our successors:
>
> “After the Spaniards who had withdrawn from the power of the Saracens and come over to our faith or to that of our father had done so, we ordered an ordinance of our authority to be written and given to them, setting out how they ought to conduct themselves in our kingdom with their counts and perform our service. Some of our Spanish subjects brought to our ears a complaint consisting of two points.
>
> “The first is that when these Spaniards came into our kingdom and, by the ordinance of our lord and father and by our own, acquired for themselves and their successors a deserted place which they had occupied for habitation, those among them who were greater and more powerful came to the palace [Col. 1096B] and received these royal ordinances. Having received them, they attempted, by their own ordinance and authority, either to drive away altogether those among them who were lesser and weaker and seemed to have cultivated their lands well, or to subject them to themselves for service.
>
> “The second is that, in a similar manner, people coming from Spain commended themselves to our counts or vassals, or even to the vassals of counts, and received deserted places for habitation and cultivation; but when these places had been cultivated by them, their superiors wished, on various pretexts, to drive them from the land, retain them for their own use, or give them to others as a reward.
>
> “Neither of these things appears to us just or reasonable,” and so forth.

He prohibits such conduct from occurring again. He also ordered seven copies of this constitution to be written: one to be kept at Narbonne, another at Carcassonne, a third at Roussillon, a fourth at Empúries, a fifth at Barcelona, a sixth at Girona, and a seventh at Béziers. He ordered copies of them to be placed in the archives of our palace, so that the aforesaid Spaniards might receive and possess copies from those seven exemplars [Col. 1096C].

Given on the fourth day before the Ides of February, in the year—with Christ propitious—of the reign of Lord Louis, most pious emperor and most pious Augustus, [the year is defective], in the ninth indiction. Issued at Aachen in the royal palace, happily, in the name of God. Amen. Arnaldus, acting in place of Helisachar, reviewed this document.

Later Septimania was given to Bernard, duke or count of Barcelona, whom the emperor had summoned from Spain and placed over his chamber; thus he wished colonists brought there from Spain to be governed by a man from Spain. This Bernard was called duke of Septimania in Narbonensian Gaul.

It was not then, but later, that Alvarus and Isidore, brothers of Saint Eulogius, the teacher of Córdoba and elected bishop of Toledo, went into exile from the city of Córdoba. Concerning this matter, in a letter of Eulogius himself to Vilesindus, bishop of Pamplona:

> “Formerly, most blessed father, when the dreadful fortune of the world—which tore my brothers Alvarus and Isidore from their native soil—nearly forced them into exile with King Louis of Bavaria in the farther regions of Toga-wearing Gaul; and when it also compelled me, because of them, to undergo various regions and unknown and arduous journeys, and so forth.” P. H.]

Many people from Spain, especially from Toledo and from among the Mozarabs, oppressed by the Saracen yoke, sought opportunities and secretly fled to Gaul as best they could.

**[Col. 1095] 272. [Note: [Col. 1096D]]**

In the year of the Lord 834 the body of Saint Leocadia was brought from Oviedo to Soissons by a certain count of Anjou, who came to assist Ordoño, son of Ramiro, against Musa, king of Toledo. Since he was especially devoted to the holy virgin and martyr Leocadia, whose body was kept at Oviedo, he requested the sacred body from the king and brought it to Angers. It was finally placed there in the year 839, as Baronius relates in volume IX of the *Annals*, under the year 841, no. 7.

Thus the historian Nithardus, grandson of Saint Charlemagne through his daughter Berta, says:

> “When Charles was making for the city of Soissons, the monks of Saint Medard went out to meet him, begging him to transfer the bodies of Saint Medard, Saint Sebastian, Tiburtius, Peter and Marcellinus, Marius, Martha, Audifax, Abacum, Onesimus, Meresina, Leocadia, and Remigius, archbishop of Rouen, into the basilica where they now rest, which even then had been built for the most part. He agreed to their request and remained there; and, as they had asked, he carried the bodies of the blessed saints on his own shoulders with every mark of reverence. In addition, he added to the property of that church a village called Bernacha.”

So much for him.

From this monastery the body of this glorious martyr was later transferred to Flanders. Hence it is rightly said in her very ancient life, sent to the fathers of Toledo, that her sacred relics were first brought from Spain to Gaul. From there the holy virgin was in fact transferred to the monastery of Saint Gislenus on Mount Hainaut; from there she returned to Toledo 340 years after the translation to Soissons.

Another celebrated translation of the body of Saint Leocadia, together with her veil, from one place to another for greater honor is reported to have been made by the archbishop of Cambrai. Nor was that the first translation made from the monastery of Anjou in Gaul to the Belgian monastery of Saint Gislenus on Mount Hainaut, since nothing concerning the first translation is found among those monks. P. H.]

This year the Count of Soissons obtained the body of Saint Leocadia from Alfonso and carried it from Oviedo to Soissons.

**854. 816.**

**[Col. 1097]**

**273.** This year a synod was convened in Germany at Trier [elsewhere: Aachen].

**274.** In this same year a synod was convened at the estate of Theodon.

**855. 817.**

**275. [Note: [Col. 1097B]]**

Saint Genesius of La Xara is held in the highest esteem in the territory of Carthage Spartaria. His body is said to rest there, although nothing certain is known about his life. It is further reported that his feast falls on the feast of Genesius of Arles in August; on that day, a very large crowd of people from the Carthaginian countryside gathers there for religious purposes.

He is said to have been a relative of Charlemagne, his sister’s son, and the brother of Roland, the most courageous leader of the Gauls, according to Julian of Toledo and Luitprand. This saint had two names: in Gaul he was also called Adelard, while in Spain he is frequently called Genesius.

Thus, in an old Spanish song:

> “Saint Genesius did not weep, for he was a holy person,  
> but he prayed to the God of heaven that, when it pleased Him, He might help him.”

And in the same song, speaking with the Blessed Virgin:

> “The other time when you delivered me,  
> I made you a crown of silver;  
> but if now you deliver us,  
> I shall make it entirely of gold.”

I believe that when he departed from Gaul for the island of Eruson, or Ebusus, and was tossed about by a very severe storm, he founded monasteries on that island. He was the father of many monasteries, and his body was brought to a certain shore of Carthage, where while alive he had also led a heavenly life for several years. But he died at Corbie, and there his sacred tomb bears a funerary poem.

His anniversary is celebrated on 2 January. Galesinus writes of him in his martyrology:

> “At Corbie, the burial of Saint Abelard, abbot. Born of royal stock and a cousin of Charlemagne, he despised and rejected the affairs of this world and became a monk in the twentieth year of his life. In this way of life, among his other virtues, he had this distinction: every day, at least twice, morning and evening, he lamented his own and other people’s sins with an abundant flood of tears. When he was made abbot, he flourished in every virtue, so that some called him by the name of the most holy abbot Anthony. Thus, after a life spent in religious devotion and distinguished by the greatness and abundance of his merits, he gave his soul back to God.”

On this same day Molanus writes:

> “At Corbie, the burial of Saint Adalard, abbot.”

His scholia state:

> “Saint Ratbertus the abbot wrote the life of Adelard. He was the sixth successor of Saint Adalard in Corbie in Gaul, and is more commonly called Paschasius.”

Just as Ratbertus was also called Paschasius, so that he had two names, Saint Adelard was likewise also surnamed Genesius. In that region of Carthage several men named Genesius are mentioned. Such is the devotion of the people to that most holy abbot.

These remarks are offered for the benefit of the people of Murcia and Carthage. Elsewhere, in the *Ecclesiastical History of Spain*, the matter is treated at greater length. ID.

A little book on Saint Genesius of La Xara exists in our own language, written by Father Melchior de Huclamo, a Franciscan. Francisco Cascales treats the subject fully in his *History of Murcia*, final discourse, chapter 7, pp. 451 and following. See below, nos. 291 and 307, and Julian in the *Adversaria*, nos. 435, 436, 437, 438, 439, and 450. D. L.]

At Carthage Spartaria the memory of the holy abbot and bishop Abelard, surnamed Genesius, is held in high honor. He was of the family of the Emperor Charlemagne and later lived there.

**276. [Note: [Col. 1098B]]**

Nicander, a Spanish poet, flourished at Toledo in the year 815 under Gumesindus. He wrote in verse the *Martyrdom of Saint Cyriacus*, bishop of Ancona, as Galesinus reports in his annotations to the fourth day before the Nones of May, fol. 102, p. 2. I have seen nothing concerning this work. Julian also mentions him in this year [in the *Chronicle*, no. 421] and makes him a citizen of Toledo. This adds to the glory of the Toledans: in so barbarous an age Toledo produced such gems and, in the middle of winter, such roses. P. H.]

I suppose the following verses belong to this poet. They are placed at the beginning of Silius Italicus’ work in the edition of Gislenus Jansenius, Antwerp, 1101. The verses and their inscription are:

**“Ambrosius Nicander of Toledo’s *Catalepses* on the individual books of Silius Italicus.”**

**[Col. 1098C] Catalepsis of the First Book**

1. Here are the causes of the wars, and Saguntum besieged by the Carthaginian;  
under his leadership she sends ambassadors to the Latin shores.

2. Hannibal prevents the Roman ship from reaching the harbor;  
to him the shield is given, and lofty Saguntum falls.

3. The Carthaginian goes to Gades; Bostar seeks omens at sea;  
the leader crosses the Alps, where he who sits in the fields of the Taurini dwells.

4. The disaster of Ticinum and the ruin of the Trebia are sung;  
here the Carthaginian crosses the Apennines with his army.

5. The Tyrian commander lays an ambush; then Trasimene  
mourns the Roman slaughter, and the Italian land trembles.

6. Everyone makes for Rome; Serranus hears of the first Punic wars,  
as Maro relates, and the Carthaginian moves his armies.

7. Fabius comes to meet Hannibal; he rescued his fallen  
colleague from death, and pays him honors.

**[Col. 1099A]**

8. The cohorts assemble under Varro’s leadership for savage warfare,  
and the ill-fated signs of Italy’s disaster arise.

9. Against his colleague’s advice, Varro begins the battle at Cannae.  
He enters foolishly; the omens forbid it, and he flees covered in blood.

10. Paulus falls at Cannae, and the Carthaginian honors him;  
Fabius renews Italy’s hopes after Varro’s recovery.

11. The allies defect to the Tyrians; Teutras sings with the lyre of the deeds of heroes,  
and Mago fights at Carthage.

12. The Carthaginian commander approaches Parthenope and halts at Nola;  
he advances toward Capua and stretches toward the walls of terrified Rome.

13. The Carthaginian returns from the city to Capua; in Iberian land  
the Scipios fall, and the son descends to Avernus.

14. By skill, on land and sea, Marcellus captures Syracuse;  
a plague defiles everything far and wide.

15. **[Col. 1099B]** Scipio, then a young man, sails to the Spanish shores,  
and Marcellus falls, while Hasdrubal falls by Nero’s sword.

16. The commander Scipio defeated the Spaniards; he goes straight to Syphax  
as a guest and celebrates games at his father’s funeral.

17. Cybele is brought to Rome; then Scipio  
casts down Hasdrubal and triumphs over his prostrate enemy.]

Throughout Spain, the Catholic Epistle of Saint James, son of Zebedee, is held in the highest honor. It was written to the twelve tribes dispersed throughout Spain, as later generations received it from the disciples of the apostle James; from them Saint Melantius preserved it down to the present time, and from this source Dexter, Maximus, and Isidore collected it.

It is also found in the Mass of Saint James, from the Our Father onward—a Mass begun by the disciples of Saint James and expanded by Melantius [elsewhere: begun by his disciples, by Mantius, and expanded by others]. In it testimonies from this Epistle are cited as belonging to James the son of Zebedee. This Mass was common to all Spain and Narbonensian Gaul. Eusebius of Caesarea could not have seen it, and therefore attributed it to James of Jerusalem, as the better-known figure.

**277.** At this time Nicander, the Spanish poet, flourished at Toledo.

**[Col. 1099] 278. [Note: [Col. 1099B]]**

Concerning Artinodus, see Julian in the *Chronicle*, no. 422, and Father John Márquez in book 1 of *On the Order of Saint Augustine*, chapter 2, § 3. We spoke above about Scisla, no. 46. D. L.]

Artinodus [elsewhere: Erthinodus], a Gothic Augustinian monk in the Toledan monastery of Scisla belonging to this order, is held in honor as a martyr.

**283. [Note: [Col. 1099B]]**

After Gumesindus’ death, Wistremirus, a citizen of Toledo, was elected by the metropolitan bishops. He belonged to the family of the Ficulnei and was archpresbyter of Saint Justa. He was a most holy man, as Saint Eulogius, martyr and elected bishop of Toledo, testifies in his letter to Wiliesindus, bishop of Pamplona:

> “Five days later I returned to Toledo, where I found our most holy old man Wistremirus still flourishing—the torch of the Holy Spirit and the lamp of all Spain [Col. 1099C]. The holiness of his life illuminates the whole world, and to this day he nourishes the Catholic flock by the uprightness of his conduct and the loftiness of his merits. We spent many days with him and remained in the companionship of his angelic life.”

This letter was written in the year of the Lord 841. At that time this Church was governed by a man illustrious for the holiness of his life, the integrity of his conduct, his learning, and his wisdom, whom one may rightly compare with Ambrose and Augustine. Eulogius calls him above all “the torch of the Holy Spirit, the lamp of all Spain, whose holiness was so great that his radiance flooded the whole world.” He calls the people of the Mozarab Church of Toledo Catholic.

Happy the flock governed by such a shepherd [Col. 1100A].

Morales speaks beautifully about him in this passage:

> “It was certainly a source of immense glory for the Christian Mozarabs of Toledo to have had such a great man as their bishop at this time. But from this there also derives an exceptionally honorable distinction for my people of Córdoba: namely, that at this very time they possessed the blessed Eulogius, who, through the suffrage of many bishops and the holy devotion of the people of Toledo, was deemed worthy to succeed Wistremirus—what sort of bishop, good God! This was done with prudent judgment and mature deliberation, since, during his residence among them, the Mozarab Church of Toledo had learned through distinguished experience what kind of man it should seek with fitting devotion and by the will of the people.
>
> “The holy Church of Toledo owes a great debt to Saint Eulogius for preserving the memory of so holy a bishop, and likewise to Alvarus of Córdoba, who transmitted to our own age knowledge of the elected bishop who would finally deserve to become a martyr.”

But when Eulogius says “to this day,” it may be understood that Wistremirus the archbishop was still alive in that very year in which the letter was written [Col. 1100B]. Alvarus, however, calls him Wistremirus, the holy bishop of blessed memory.

He is recorded in three ancient episcopal diptychs of Toledo, in Luitprand, Julian, the catalogue of García de Loaysa, Morales, and Ortiz. But one of these corruptly calls him Henistrentius instead of Wistremirus. Gomezius also mentions him, as do I in my *History of Toledo*, Pedro de Alcocer in his *History of Toledo*, Mariana, and many others.

Wistremirus was a man worthy of being numbered among the most holy bishops in the Martyrology; but I suppose that its revisers were entirely unaware of the date of the death of this most holy man. I shall discuss this elsewhere. I believe that the approval of this most holy old man played no small part in persuading the people of Toledo to approve the election by the metropolitan bishops of Saint Eulogius to the summit of the Toledan episcopate. P. H.]

Wistremirus, archpresbyter of Toledo, a holy and pious man exceptionally generous toward the poor, succeeded Gumesindus, archbishop of Toledo, in the see. He occupied it for twenty-eight years under Ambrosius, governor of the city of Toledo.

**284. [Note: [Col. 1100B]]**

I am not surprised that an academy was established at Toledo in which philosophy, astrology, and medicine flourished [Col. 1100C], since this royal city had always been the nurse and foster-mother of every art. ID.

At Toledo an academy of philosophy, medicine, astrology, and so forth is established. Spain has an ancient tradition of academies and academic degrees. Alvarus, in the *Life of Saint Eulogius*: “But when he had already reached the years of youth” (these are his words), “he undertook the ministry of the diaconate, and thus, having deservedly advanced in a short time to a higher rank, he was elevated to the priesthood; then, after teachers had been admitted in due order—that is, according to the practice of an examination—and after his conduct of life had been considered, he was enrolled among them.”

Our Julian, in the *Chronicle*, no. 521, where he speaks of the monastery of Agali, says: “Thus that house came to an end—that house which had been a workshop of holiness and religion, and which for more than 450 years had given so many archbishops to the patriarchal see, had contributed bishops to so many sees, and had supplied so many teachers to all Spain and to former Narbonese Gaul. From it, as from the Trojan horse, so many most holy and most learned men came forth eagerly, one after another.” On this subject there is further mention elsewhere in Julian and in Luitprand, no. 244, where see what we have said; and in Paulus Jovius, book XXXIII, whose words are these:

“Finally, as the sect of Muhammad gained strength, the Saracens, drawn from Syria, Egypt, and Arabia and impelled by religious motives, invaded Africa with such force that, after driving out the Christians and introducing and widely propagating superstition, they advanced victoriously as far as Spain. And when the Africans, Numidians, Moors, and finally all the Punic peoples had readily accepted the new rites, the seat of the Moors was established at Illiberis, the royal city of Baetica which our people call Granada, and at Córdoba a school was founded together with a celebrated library. There, professors of Arabic letters flourished with remarkable glory by teaching the young and taking up the disciplines of the best sciences and arts that were dying out among the Greeks.”

Theodorus Zwinger reports this in the *Theatrum vitae humanae*, vol. 26, single book, fol. 4063, col. 2. On academies and their antiquity, Jacobus Middendorpius published a special commentary, learned indeed and laborious; and on the usefulness, necessity, and antiquity of schools, Johannes Althusius wrote a panegyrical *Admonition*, an author prohibited until it should be expurgated.

From the time of Ogyges onward, academies in Spain were famous and distinguished, especially in the Baetican and Turdetanian region, whose inhabitants were regarded as the most literate. That region was called Baetica from its river, and Turdetania by its inhabitants. Thus Strabo says at the very beginning of book III:

“These people”—he is speaking of the Turdetanians, according to the recension of Isaac Casaubon—“are judged the most learned of all the Spaniards. They use grammar and possess written records of antiquity, as well as poems and laws enclosed in verse, dating, as they say, from six thousand years. The other Spaniards also use grammar, though not all in one and the same form, since they do not even speak the same language.”

Asclepiades of Myrlea taught grammar in Turdetania, as the same geographer records in the same book. From him Alfonso García Matamoros likewise draws his account in the *Apologetic Narrative concerning the Academies and Learned Men of Spain*. His words are these:

“In those times Palamedes had not yet brought letters into Greece, and Baetica flourished in many poets and in philosophy. After that famous Phoenician marketplace of letters—which Xenophon reports to have been the first founded in the world—it is said to have possessed a distinguished academy, in which Strabo records that Asclepiades of Myrlea taught letters.”

Morales gives a second account in his *Córdoba II*, volume of the *History*, p. 107:

“Thus Córdoba remained in this region of the Turduli, of whom this same author [Strabo] says that they were commonly regarded in Spain as the wisest of all its peoples. They possessed letters and studies of them, and books of distinguished antiquity; they practiced poetry, and had their laws written in verse in an ancient age, which they said reached six thousand years.”

Jacobus de Valdés also mentions Strabo in his book *On the Dignity of the Kings and Kingdoms of Spain*, chapter V, no. 8, and Brother Juan de la Puente, book III of *The Compatibility of the Two Monarchies*, chapter 21, § 2, although Valdés is reproved by letter G.

More recently, P. Roa has written learnedly, as is his custom, on the academy of Córdoba and on the other illustrious academies of Spain, in book 6 of *The Principality of Córdoba*, p. 25, B. Oldradus de Ponte says in *Consilium* 84, beginning “Whether it is expedient to possess many books,” that the Spaniards have an innate love of seeking out books and learning the arts. He also writes the following amusing little story:

“And the Spaniards were accustomed to be curious about this matter. Thus John relates that the Spaniards, wishing to have an abundance of books, invited him and gave him red wine mixed with white wine, so that, when he was drunk, he would lend them his books; and he himself notes this in the Code under *On Deceit*, law *Dolum*.”

So far Oldradus.

In those ancient academies, just as in our more recent ones, teachers were honored by a rank or title of dignity. We have already shown this from Saint Eulogius and from our Julian. I shall now add that they were customarily called grammarians, philosophers, and doctors.

Suetonius Tranquillus reports that at certain times there were more than twenty celebrated schools of grammar in the city. Grammarians, as Cicero says, are interpreters of poets; they concern themselves not only with language but also range over histories and poems. In Latin they are called *litterati*—men of letters.

Among the Greeks they indulged themselves excessively in debating useless questions: How many rowers had Ulysses? Was the *Iliad* written before the *Odyssey*? And other questions of that kind. Seneca attacks them in *On the Shortness of Life*: “Those who occupy themselves with the study of useless literature,” he says, “are laboriously doing nothing; and even among the Romans there is now a great crowd of them.” Quintilian, book I, and Aulus Gellius, the last book, ridicule this excessively anxious and futile concern of the men of letters.

Again Seneca, letter 88:

“Let us therefore learn those things which made Homer wise. To ask whether Homer was older than Hesiod is no more relevant than to know whether Hecuba was older than Helen, and why she bore old age so badly.”

Tiberius tested them with such tricks—or rather kept them entangled in them—as Suetonius reports in his *Life*, chapter 70:

“Who was the mother of Hecuba? What name had Achilles among the maidens? What songs were the Sirens accustomed to sing?”

But good grammarians, and not mere grammar-teachers, avoid that foolish labor of trivialities. They shun and flee from it more than a dog or a snake, deserving well of the republic of letters and caring for the public good.

They are mentioned by L. C. in the law *Si duas*, § “Grammarians,” in the *Digest*, *On the Excuses of Tutors*. Immunity from public duties was granted to them, but denied to those who taught only the first elements of letters, in book II, final paragraph, of the *Digest*, *On Exemption from Public Duties*, and in the law *Ne gradatim*, final paragraph, of the *Digest*, *On Public Duties and Honors*. Cujacius discusses this learnedly in his *Readings on the Pandects*, under the cited law *Si duas*, § “Grammarians.”

Those who professed the liberal arts and faithfully learned and taught them were called Doctors. Suetonius says this repeatedly, for example in *Julius*, chapter 42:

“Julius Caesar”—these are his words—“granted citizenship to all who practiced medicine at Rome and to the teachers of the liberal arts.”

Of Hadrian, Spartianus says in his *Life*:

“He dismissed from their profession teachers who seemed incapable of it through old age or illness, after enriching and honoring them.”

Lampridius, concerning Alexander Severus, says:

“He established salaries for grammarians and founded lecture halls; and he ordered that students, together with grain allowances, be assigned the sons of the poor, provided that they were freeborn.”

Here one sees that salaries were established.

Let Suetonius, often summoned, now descend into the arena. In the *Life of Vespasian*, chapter 18, he says:

“Vespasian was the first to establish from the treasury annual payments of one hundred thousand sesterces for Latin and Greek rhetoricians.”

Capitolinus, in *Antoninus Pius*, says:

“He established honors and salaries for rhetoricians and philosophers throughout all the provinces.”

Eusebius, in his *Chronicle*, reports that Quintilian was the first to receive a public school at Rome and a salary from the treasury. The great Lipsius attempts to reconcile him with Suetonius in his *Louvain*, book III, chapter 7; there, with a full and learned hand, he collects and properly arranges much material on this subject, as he does in his *Treatise on Libraries*, chapter 11.

A second authority in this inquiry, and by no means a secondary one, is Samuel Petit, book IV of the *Miscellanies*, chapter 1, on the number, heresy, and salaries of grammarians, rhetoricians, and philosophers, drawing testimonies from every direction. There is no need to transcribe them here; indeed, doing so would be an unprofitable task.

In the New World also there were schools, teachers, and salaries. Lipsius transcribed from Gomara in chapter 6 of his *Louvain*, where he says that he had read that the Mexicans had schools in their temples, to which they were accustomed to send their sons, especially the rich and noble, from the age of five. There they were taught and disciplined by their teachers; they were not permitted to leave; and for the use of the young men of that land they were given fields and farmland, from which they gathered produce and grain.

In the East, the Brahmans and Gymnosophists had their own communities for teaching and learning. Even today the name of the Brahmans persists, and in Japan that of the Bonzes, who maintain large communities of students in the principal towns.

[D. L.]

An academy of philosophy, medicine, and astrology is established [another reading: chosen] at Toledo, the most learned men of Spain gathering there.

DCCCLXXIV. DCCCXXXVI.

[Col. 1103]

### 285. [Note]

In the year 836, in the territory of Zamora, at the town of Albuga, commonly called Albugela—Latin *Albucella* in Antoninus and *Albocella* in Ptolemy, among the Vaccaei—Saint Saeculina, a virgin and, I believe, abbess of the Benedictine order, flourished. Her memory is preserved in the *Hispanic Martyrology* and in the parchment breviary of the holy Church of Ávila; on July 23 a simple feast is celebrated there in her honor. It reads as follows:

“Saint Saeculina, born of illustrious parents in the town of Albuga, persuaded the noble man to whom she had been joined in marriage, with God granting her request, to embrace continence. After he had been taken from this life, she chose the monastic life and entered the monastery which her father had built. There, together with many women, devoting herself to fasts and prayers, she humbly served God. After many signs, she gathered her sisters, gave them the kiss of peace, and departed to Christ.”

Nowhere have I found any mention of her, either in the *Martyrology* or elsewhere, except here in Luitprand and in the tables of the Church of Ávila.

[P. H.]

In the territory of Zamora, at the town of Albuga, the Benedictine virgin Saeculina flourishes, renowned for an extraordinary sanctity.

DCCCLXXVI. DCCCXXXVIII.

### 286.

Alvarus and Isidore, brothers of Saint Eulogius, who was later elected archbishop of Toledo, go into exile in Bavaria.

DCCCLXXVIII. DCCCXL.

### 287. [Note]

Theodemirus, a Benedictine monk and later bishop of Calahorra, a man exceptionally pious and learned, wrote an elegant book in defense of images against Claudius, the Spanish bishop of Turin and an iconoclast. Claudius was a deceitful man who, having been made bishop of Turin from being Louis’s chaplain, often fought against the Moors, as is clear from the history of the Augustan city of Turin. Against him, as has been said, Theodemirus wrote, as did Jonas, bishop of Orléans, and the holy old man Wistremirus, bishop of Toledo, stirred by the Spirit of God, a torch of the Holy Spirit.

Concerning Claudius, Walafrid Strabo says in *On Ecclesiastical Matters*:

“Claudius indeed was bishop of Turin, but, wavering on the road of truth—as though in accordance with the similarity of his name—among the other absurdities of his vanities, wishing to renew the heresy concerning images, perished before he could be struck by the weapons of various writers against him, having been condemned by his own judgment. Perhaps the man who despised the emperor’s image as though it were on a coin paid before his tribunal the penalties of his insolence and likewise of his ingratitude or restlessness. For the powerful of this world do not consider an injury done to them a light matter if they discover that their image or name on any coin has been despised and trampled upon by their subjects.”

Walafrid Strabo was living at that time; therefore credence ought to be given to a witness who was present and alive. Claudius was a disciple of the heretic Felix of Urgel; the son was altogether like his father.

[P. H.]

The Benedictine monk Theodemirus, later bishop of Calahorra, succeeds Claudius, bishop of Turin.

DCCCLXXXII. DCCCXLIV.

### 288.

In this year Gunderic, a pious and just man who greatly feared God, becomes judge of the Mozarabs at Toledo.

DCCCLXXXIV. DCCCXLVI.

### 289.

Martinus II, famed as Roman pope [another reading: brother], flourishes in Galicia.

### 290. [Note]

Alvarus of Córdoba, the companion of Saint Eulogius, is mentioned frequently by him. He was born of a very illustrious family, as one whom the holy and most modest Saint Eulogius calls “most serene”—a title which we see applied only to kings or to those born of royal blood.

He wrote the life of Saint Eulogius, his death, and an office of prayers; he composed a hymn in his praise in Asclepiad verse; and he wrote a book called *The Spark*, compiled from testimonies of the holy Fathers. That work was extremely necessary at that time, when there was such a scarcity of all books. The *Luminous Little Index* is not his, as we shall soon see.

I do not believe that he married, but that he lived a celibate life. Approximately twelve years after the death of Saint Eulogius, he died most holily at Córdoba, on May 4: the light and splendor of the Mozarabs of Córdoba, a holy man worthy, as is said, of being entered in the catalogue of the saints.

He was, in accordance with what those times allowed, a thoroughly learned man. In his praise I wish to append this poem:

> Alvarus, glory of the Mozarabs, whom Córdoba proclaims  
> > Distinguished, bind your head with the sacred wreath.  
> > Piety, ancient faith, and the pursuit of knowledge  
> > Joined you to Eulogius in a bond of friendship.  
> > It is enough to have said this, for the rest time has carried away;  
> > Envious posterity will sing of him in wonder.

What P. Higuera wrote is confirmed by Julian’s testimony in the *Chronicle*, no. 433, under this same year:

“Alvarus, of the royal stock of the Goths, the friend and fellow student of Saint Eulogius, flourishes at Córdoba in letters and in the reputation of holiness.”

The same Julian also mentions him in no. 430. I now possess the works of his that survive in manuscript in the archive of the holy Church of Córdoba, and I shall bring them to light if time permits.

[D. L.]

Saint Alvarus, companion of Saint Eulogius, flourishes remarkably at Córdoba.

### 291.

The memory of Saint Fructuosus is held in renown among the Ligurians.

### 292. [Note]

Many wrote against Claudius the Iconoclast, including Walafrid and Jonas of Orléans [“For Jonas, see note 6 on the letter of Tractemundus.” D. L.]; but they did so weakly, and not altogether in accordance with the doctrine of the Catholic Church, the teacher and rule of all the churches.

The Church teaches two things concerning sacred images: that they are in no way to be broken or cast away, but are to be venerated with the honor due to them. Those Fathers who assembled at the Council of Frankfurt, at the insistence of the legates of the holy Roman Church, judged that images should be received and retained, so that they might be, as it were, alphabets for the unlearned and ignorant, but in no way venerated.

On this subject Baronius says, volume IX, under the year of Our Lord 825, no. 74, p. 761:

“But,” he says, speaking of Jonas of Orléans, who wrote against Claudius the Iconoclast, “Jonas so subdued the beast that he was nevertheless judged by the Catholic Church to be altogether unworthy of reward. For although he fought against the Iconoclasts, he did not fight from the camp of the orthodox Church, from which he partly dissented through an earlier error. He proclaimed that images should not be broken, but nevertheless asserted that they should not be venerated; he was one of that party which held that images in churches should exist only for ornament and for instructing the faithful in historical events, and not for veneration. Together with the other members of that sect we refuted him above.”

So Baronius.

Lupus, abbot of Ferrières, wrote to Jonas in letter 27:

“To the most excellent bishop Jonas, Lupus sends eternal greetings in the Lord. We have read through your book, as you requested, but, to put it as briefly as possible, we wished to alter nothing in it, so that you yourselves might be the correctors of your work, whose authors you are. We had to take account of our own tenderness and weakness, and to consider your age and rank. Nor ought we to have imitated the ease and a certain pleasure in fault-finding which we are accustomed to notice in some people.”

So he writes.

Baronius adds:

“The learned and pious man ought to have reproved the bishop for the error against the Church insinuated here.”

Besides the Benedictine monk Theodemirus, Dungalus, a by no means obscure writer of the same period, and Wistremirus, archbishop of Toledo—a most learned and holy man, since he wrote against the Iconoclasts and the errors concerning images—and Lupus himself wrote on the adoration of the cross and of images.

This is clear from a letter of Lupus himself to Einhard, the writer of the deeds of Charles. It is letter 4, written on the occasion of rebuking Claudius, bishop of Turin, who denied that sacred images should be venerated.

The matter came to the ears of the Greek emperor Michael, who sent his legates to the emperor Louis. Louis was in error on this point, saying that images certainly ought to be retained, but in no way adored. He also sent his envoys to Pope Eugenius, asking the pope that learned Gauls should debate the matter.

The holy pontiff rebuked the envoys—namely, Bishop Freculphus and Adegarius—for their rashness, because they wished, with a kind of reckless audacity, to call into question a matter observed by the Church for so many centuries and established as certain and fixed. Finally, when they persisted, he granted the permission they had requested.

A collection was made near Paris in the year of Our Lord 825; it was not a synod duly convened. Posterity is sufficiently ashamed of what was decreed in that collection. The acts of Frankfurt were published without the name of the author or of the library from which the manuscript had been taken; the most learned and devout Cardinal Baronius clearly thought that this had been done tyrannically.

At that time the seventh general synod was rejected. On this subject Baronius says under the year 794:

“The oldest chronicle of all, written in this period under the emperor Louis, the son of Charles, says that the synod which a few years earlier had been assembled under Irene and her son Constantine, and which they themselves had called not only the seventh but also general, was rejected by everyone as altogether superfluous, so that it was neither held nor called the seventh or universal.”

The same words are found copied in Aimon. A chronicle likewise written at that time, recently published by Pithaeus, says in the same year and in the same words:

“The false synod of the Greeks, held by bishops in favor of the adoration of images, is condemned, namely in that Council of Frankfurt.”

Ado of Vienne, who wrote under the grandson of this Charles the Great, says the same thing in the same words. Regino does likewise, as do many other authors of far greater renown.

But, concerning the original authors themselves who took part in that Council of Frankfurt, it must first be investigated how, from the writings of their opponents—namely, from that capitulary book—they were induced to condemn the Council of Nicaea.

It is astonishing how those learned men were blinded: without examining the true acts, and despite the protests of Hadrian’s legates and the contrary evidence that deceived them, they preferred to believe otherwise. The explanation may be that the synod had been convened by Constantine and Irene, who refused to receive the daughter of Charlemagne as the wife of their son.

Jonas of Orléans also held the opinion of this error, as follows:

“You wrote, in order to fortify the error of the worshipers of images, that you had responded in this way, saying: ‘We do not believe that there is anything divine in the image which we adore; rather, we adore it with veneration for the honor of the one whose likeness it is.’ But we reproach and detest those who, although they have not evaded knowledge of this matter, say that there is nothing divine in images and therefore deserve even greater condemnation because they have bestowed upon a weak and needy image the honor due to divinity.

“It is unnecessary for me to explain individually how far the followers and defenders of this error have strayed from true religion. Some Orientals are likewise enslaved to the same most wicked error. But to those who rebuke them they customarily reply: ‘May the Lord, in his gracious mercy, grant that at last both these and those may be stripped of the same superstition and, wholesomely instructed in the apostolic disciplines, be restored to ecclesiastical tradition.’”

And below:

“Those who, through an excessive and indiscriminate love, beseech images in honor of the saints—I do not know whether they are rashly idolaters or should appear to be called such—ought rather to be recalled from this superstition by the exercise of reason than named idolaters, since they certainly truly believe and proclaim the faith of the Holy Trinity.”

Walafrid Strabo seems to have held the same bad opinion in *On Ecclesiastical Matters*, chapter 8:

“Now something must be said concerning images and paintings, by which the beauty of churches is increased, because their variety also is not to be honored with some immoderate worship, as certain foolish people think.”

And below:

“For if, because we know that icons are not to be adored or worshiped, paintings are therefore to be trampled underfoot and destroyed—”

So he writes.

Amalarius, Altigarius, or Elisagarus, Trevolphus, and Adegarius belonged to the same party. Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, must also be numbered among them, in his work against Bishop John, chapter 20:

“The seventh synod, called universal by the Greeks, a false synod concerning images—which some said should be broken and others adored, although neither side defined the matter with sound understanding or with the authority of the apostolic see—was held at Nicaea not long before our own times by very many bishops and sent to Rome; and the Roman pope forwarded it to Gaul.

“Therefore, in the time of the emperor Charlemagne, by order of the apostolic see, a general synod was celebrated in Gaul, namely at Frankfurt, after the aforesaid emperor had summoned it. Following the course of Scripture and the tradition of the ancestors, that false synod of the Greeks was destroyed and entirely rejected. Concerning its destruction, the same emperor sent a fairly substantial volume through a certain bishop, which, when I was a young man at the palace, I read.”

And below:

“By the authority of this synod—that is, of Frankfurt—the veneration of images was somewhat restrained. Nevertheless, Hadrian and the other pontiffs persisted in their opinion; and after Charles’s death they promoted the worship of their puppets with greater force, so that Louis, the son of Charles, attacked the worship of images in a much larger book than Charles had done.”

So Hincmar writes.

In that passage he speaks with sufficient irreverence both concerning the worship of sacred images and concerning the irrefragable judgment of the Roman pontiffs. Nor could those Fathers have been unaware that the holy Roman see is the infallible rule of truth.

But Anastasius the librarian, in the preface which he prefixed to the seventh synod, says:

“What this present synod teaches concerning the adoration of venerable images—namely, the Council of Nicaea—your apostolic see also, as certain writings have recorded, held from ancient times; and the universal Church has always venerated these things, and to this day venerates them, with the exception of certain Gauls, to whom their usefulness has not yet been revealed.

“For they say that no work of human hands should be adored, as though the book of the Gospels were not a work of human hands, which they adore daily while kissing it. They will surely not deny that a dog, which is not a work of human hands, is more venerable; likewise the form of the holy cross, which all Christians everywhere admit that they adore.”

From Anastasius draw two conclusions: only certain Gallic pontiffs, not all of them, rejected the adoration of images; and apart from these, no bishops of other nations did so. Thus, although Gaul is near Spain, this pernicious heresy did not reach its members there and did not infect them.

Indeed, when Claudius, a Spaniard and bishop of Turin, had written that images should not be adored but broken, and when that book, as the work of a Spanish writer, was being handled by Spaniards, Wistremirus, the pontiff of Toledo and primate of the Spains, burning with zeal for God like a torch of the Holy Spirit, lest that book should harm anyone or the opinion of the Gallic Fathers deceive them, wrote a brilliant book against the Iconoclasts and against those who do not reverently adore the most sacred images of the saints.

I believe this was done after the metropolitan bishops and men distinguished for the splendor of their learning and the holiness of their lives had been summoned to the Council of Toledo.

This redounds to the greatest praise both of the Spanish nation and, above all, to the glory of the holy see of Toledo, which, by divine favor, as the mother of Spain, has always obtained such pastors and pontiffs—men no less learned than holy, burning with zeal for the Catholic faith and distinguished for the fame of their reputation.

Would that this work, so pious and excellent, still existed! In it the diligent reader might behold, as in a perfectly clear mirror, the distinct image of the character and learning with which the most holy man and pontiff Wistremirus illumined all Spain, as with brilliant rays. May God grant that, if so great a treasure lies hidden anywhere, it may at last come to light, for his glory and the benefit of many, and so that all may understand how highly the Toledan pontiffs have always valued the judgment of the most holy Roman pontiffs: that they never departed from their views and decrees by so much as “the breadth of a fingernail,” but readily and willingly, as was proper, lent an attentive ear to their statutes.

Against Claudius, bishop of Turin and an Iconoclast, Saint Wistremirus, archbishop of Toledo, writes.

DCCCLXXXVI. DCCCXLVIII.

[Col. 1107]

### 293. [Note]

The memory of Saint Blasius, a Spanish martyr who suffered under Decius, is celebrated among the Spaniards. His sacred skull is preserved at Toledo in the monastery of the Holy Trinity. There survives a charter of donation by John and Manuel, dating from approximately three hundred years ago, concerning the monastery of Saint Blasius of Centumfontes; it says that the donation was made out of reverence for Saint Blasius the martyr, who was buried there.

[P. H.]

Concerning Saint Blasius, Julian says in the *Chronicle*, no. 434:

“Saint Blasius suffered martyrdom in Spain, near the town called Centumfontes, in Celtiberia, during the persecution of Nero.”

It did not seem irrelevant to me to append the words of Brother Thomas of Truxillo, who says the following in volume II of the *Treasury of Preachers*, fol. 637, col. 2, under the title “On Blessed Blasius the Spaniard”:

“In the town of Cifuentes, at the extremity of the kingdom of Toledo, in a certain monastery of nuns of Blessed Dominic, there is a remarkable tomb of alabaster stone, where the body of Blessed Blasius the Spaniard is said to lie. Some, however, say that he is the same Blasius whom the Catholic Church celebrates on February 3.

“That this saint was called Blasius is certainly true, for everyone there affirms it. But that he is the Blasius of whom we spoke above is a matter of great difficulty, although they point out, near the river Tagus, the ruins of a city which they say was called Sebaste. They also show a cave in which the holy man lived, and where the governor Agricola ordered him to be arrested after he had been betrayed by hunting dogs.

“They further indicate and assign there the name of the province of Cappadocia, and they show many other things which seem to suit that other holy bishop Blasius. Nevertheless, the whole Church has now received the Blasius mentioned above as a bishop and martyr at Sebaste in Cappadocia, in that Asia Minor, and not in the Alcarria. Therefore this Blasius must be another man; yet he has the same name and was also a saint.”

So far Brother Truxillo.

Morales, Marieta, and Dadilla say the same.

[D. L.]

Saint Blasius, bishop and martyr, who suffered in Spain at Centumfontes, a town of Celtiberia, during the persecution of Nero, in the year 67, shines forth, celebrated for miracles [another reading: numerous miracles].

DCCCLXXXVIII. DCCCL.

### 294. [Note]

Molanus mentions Anacirardus on February 4, but calls him Lietphardus. Consult Surius on this day.

[P. H.]

Saint Anacirardus, a hermit, came from Germany to Lusitania and lived holily on the bank of the Tagus, near the city of Santarém. Returning to Italy, not far from Lake Zurich, he was martyred on February 4, overcome by wounds.

DCCCXCV. DCCCLVII.

### 295. [Note]

See P. João de Rea, S.J., *Life of the Martyrs of Córdoba*, p. 41, B.

[P. H.]

Rodericus and Salomon, Lusitanians by origin, suffer martyrdom at Córdoba, near the city in Baetica called Old Tucci, and by some Fossina.

### 296.

In this year Wistremirus, primate of Toledo, orders Samuel, bishop of Illiberis, to be deposed on account of his unspeakable life. David, archbishop of Seville, carries this out; he supplies Gervasius in his place.

### 297. [Note]

Urci, now Portella. We spoke under no. 38 of the little town Portella, or Portiella or Portellia—here it should be read Portellia, Portella, or Portiella—where I praised the charter of King Sancho. I do not hesitate now to append the words relevant to the matter:

“I give you, then, in the valley of Ostella, near the village called Portiella, the monastery called Saint John, with its boundaries; and in Pamplona the parish of Saint Cecilia; and in the valley of Garonio, the monastery called Zeyazahassa.”

[D. L.]

In this year, after the bishop of Urci—Urci, now Portella—had died, Genesius, otherwise called Bishop Abhelardus, is appointed in his place by Wistremirus of Toledo. He had been bishop of Lyon in Gaul, a holy man, son of Milo surnamed Bernard and brother of Roland, the Palatine duke.

### 298. [Note]

Luitprand, who lived almost a hundred years after this period, can inform us about the blessed death and day of death of the most holy Wistremirus, bishop of Toledo. Much has been said about him above.

[P. H.]

Wistremirus, a holy man—Saint Eulogius called him “the Torch of the Holy Spirit”—brother of Lupus Ficulnus, a native of Toledo and born among Toledo’s own Mozarabs, dies worn out by old age. He is buried in the church of Saint Justa. Bonitus succeeds him and placed this funerary inscription:

> Α. Saint Wistremirus died in peace, 31 December Ω.

DCCCXCVI. DCCCLVIII.

### 299. [Note]

Concerning the election of Saint Eulogius as bishop of Toledo, in place of the most holy pontiff Wistremirus, Alvarus says this in the *Life of Saint Eulogius*:

“Nor do I think that this should be omitted in this work: after Wistremirus, bishop of the see of Toledo, of blessed memory, [a portion is missing] he was elected to the same see by all the bishops of the province and neighboring regions, was deemed worthy, and was approved according to everyone’s report.”

He has already been entered after Wistremirus in the sacristy or secretariat of the holy Church of Toledo. Moreover, D. García Loaysa, in the *Diptychs of the Toledan Pontiffs*, places him under the year of Our Lord 859 with this epitaph: “Saint Eulogius, elected, martyr.”

[P. H.]

Saint Eulogius is elected at a council of bishops at Toledo.

DCCCXCVII. DCCCLIX.

### 300. [Note]

Bonitus, archdeacon of Saint Wistremirus, whose *Luminous Little Index* is derived from Julian and is commonly circulated under the name of Alvarus, succeeds Saint Eulogius by election of the provincial bishops.

[P. H.]

I shall speak below, under no. 309, about the *Luminous Little Index*.

[D. L.]

But when Bonitus was at Toledo, he wrote to Samson of Córdoba and himself absolved him. Samson lived at Córdoba during the time of Saint Eulogius and later became abbot of Saint Zoilus. He was a learned man of subtle intellect, versed in the study of philosophy and sacred letters, as Ambrosius de Morales says.

At the Council of Córdoba, Hostegesis, bishop of Málaga, branded this Samson with the mark of reproach and called him a heretic. Samson therefore took the occasion to write an *Apology* against him, divided into three books, of which he makes extensive mention in the preface to the work.

Our Julian summarizes everything in the *Chronicle*, no. 440:

“Bonitus did not wish to attend the Council of Córdoba, at which a grave error was committed against Samson the abbot; and Samson was a most learned and holy man. He composed an *Apology*, which is preserved in the library of Saint Justa at Toledo.”

Perhaps Julian said “a grave error was committed” with reference to the insult of Hostegesis. Bonitus absolved Samson, as Luitprand says. Not content with this, Julian, Bonitus’s successor, convened a synod in defense of Samson. Our archpriest testifies to this in the *Chronicle*, no. 444, in these words:

“He [Julian] compelled a synod, together with the council, in defense of Samson.”

A certain inscription concerning Samson was found on a bronze cymbal, not very far from the town called Trasierra. We owe its publication in print to Ambrosius de Morales, who deserved well of the republic of letters. In his notes on book I of Saint Eulogius’s *Memorial*, no. 9, the inscription reads:

> SAMSON THE ABBOT OFFERS THIS GIFT IN THE HOUSE OF SAINT SEBASTIAN, MARTYR OF CHRIST. ERA 913.

See also the epigram composed by Cyprian, archpriest of Córdoba, whose heading is “Epitaph,” which he likewise published on the tomb of Lord Samson, in heroic meter:

> Who or how great was Samson, the most illustrious abbot,  
> > Whose sacred limbs remain in this tomb beneath this roof?  
> > Hesperia resounds, sustained by his renown [reading uncertain].  
> > Bend God by your prayers—now, reader, I beseech you, bend him—  
> > So that he may be able to ascend the heavens with his sins cleansed.  
> > He departed, widely known and full of days;  
> > For on the twenty-first day of the month of Sextilis [August],
The twenty-first day of the month of Sextilis [August].

Era 928.

That Cyprian was a poet is apparent from the Epitaph and [Col. 1110B] from other verses collected by the same Ambrosius de Morales in the same place, no. 6. Our Julianus supports this in his Chronicle, no. 519: “Cyprian, his disciple, composed a poem for him [Blasius].” And in his Adversaria, no. 284: “On this subject there exists a hymn that begins as follows: ‘Rejoice, Toledo’; Cyprian, archdeacon of Córdoba, composed it at the request of Count Adulfus, Abbot Anathagildus, and the priest Valentinianus, natives of Toledo.” Elsewhere Julianus writes about Samson’s Apologeticus: “When the holy man Cyprian came from Córdoba to Toledo, he brought with him the book of the Apologeticus of Lord Samson, which was placed in the library of Saint Justa as a great treasure.” D. L.]

Bonitus, archdeacon of the holy Church of Toledo, is elected bishop of Toledo. It is said that he went to his homeland, Clermont in Auvergne, and there was endowed by the blessed Virgin Mary with a heavenly garment; but while in Toledo, writing a letter to Samson of Córdoba, he himself absolved him.

301. Leander, the thirty-sixth abbot of Agali, flourishes.

DCCCC. DCCCLXII.

302. [Note: [Col. 1110B]

302. Julianus the archdeacon succeeds Bonitus, bishop of Toledo; he had previously been a monk of Agali. P. H.]

Julianus succeeds the holy man Bonitus in the see of Toledo. He was learned, as those times permitted. He convened a synod.

DCCCCIII. DCCCLXV.

303. [Note: [Col. 1110B]

303. Petrus, a learned man, succeeds Julianus in the see of Toledo; he too held a synod at Toledo concerning matters necessary for religion. ID.

[Col. 1110C] See Julianus in his Chronicle, no. 448, in these words: “When Julianus the holy bishop of Toledo died, Petrus, his archdeacon, succeeded him in the see of Toledo. He fittingly composed Julianus for Saint Justa, the metropolitan church of Toledo, as the times permitted, and added that man’s memory among the saints together with a poem.” Thus it is found in the manuscript of Father Hieronymus de la Higuera. D. L.]

Petrus, a pious man, succeeds Julianus. He convened a synod.

DCCCCIV. DCCCLXVI.

304. Another Petrus succeeds Petrus in the see of Toledo, a good man.

305. The memory of Saint Crescentius flourishes at Caesarone and at Vienne, where he was bishop.

306. Saint John Guarinus the hermit flourishes on Mount Serrato.

DCCCCVII. DCCCLXIX.

[Col. 1111]

307. [Note: [Col. 1111A]

307. Dulcidius, a priest of Toledo, is famously mentioned in the histories of Spain. Since he knew the Spanish and Arabic languages thoroughly, he was accustomed to be sent as an ambassador by the kings of Oviedo to the kings of Córdoba. I believe that he was different from the man who, seventy-five years later, was bishop of Salamanca. P. H.]

About this time Dulcidius, a priest of Toledo, born from Berta, the sister of Osorius Gundericus, was ambassador of the king of León to the emir of Córdoba.

308. In this year the relics of Saint Obdulia are transferred from Palma to Toledo.

309. [Note: [Col. 1111A]

309. The Little Book, which Bonitus composed at Córdoba while staying there on business, is brought from Córdoba to Toledo after Bonitus’s death. ID.]

There are various and conflicting opinions about the author of the luminous Little Book. Almost everyone acknowledges that it was Alvarus. Thus the bishop of Placentia, whom Ambrosius de Morales cites at the end of his Life of Saint Eulogius, although he does not follow him with complete certainty—for at first he attributes the work to Alvarus, but shortly afterward expresses doubt in these words: “There is one thing that entirely persuades me not to believe that work to be Alvarus’s: namely, that no mention at all is made there of Saint Eulogius. Nor do I think that Alvarus could have restrained himself amid such affection from remembering him when writing the same work.” [Col. 1111B] Nevertheless, as he says, being led by better reasoning, he recanted this view in part 3 of his General History, book IV, chapter 3, folio 95, relying on this support: namely, that in his Life of Saint Eulogius Alvarus states that he had composed a work of this kind.

Julianus attributes it to Wistremirus in his Chronicle, no. 438, and Father Hieronymus de la Higuera supports this in the notes above at no. 300. Although we might say that he merely reports what he admits he found in Julianus, rather than expressing his own opinion on the matter. Finally, either Luitprandus here praises another author—namely Bonitus—or, if the meaning permits, he affirms only that Bonitus wrote the Little Book, not that he composed it. Julianus too, unlike himself, follows Luitprandus’s footsteps in the prosphonetical letter written to Albert of Fulda, in these words: “The luminous Little Book of Bonitus, bishop of Toledo.” Therefore he must be corrected in one place or the other. Yet among the works of Alvarus preserved in the holy Church of Córdoba, the Little Book is found, and its own wording seems to call the same Alvarus “father”; I therefore incline more readily to that view. D. L.]

The luminous Little Book, which Saint Bonitus wrote at Córdoba, is brought to Toledo.

310. The holy and distinguished Alvarus died at Córdoba on the fourth day of the month of May.

DCCCCXX. DCCCLXXXII.

311. [Note: [Col. 1112A]

311. Julianus of Toledo provides further information about Marinus the Spaniard. (See below, no. 320.)]

Marinus, son of Columbus, from Galicia, with a Spanish mother and a father named Fabricius, is consecrated pope from the rank of cardinal deacon (see below, no. 320).

DCCCCXXI. DCCCLXXXIII.

312. Theophylactus, archbishop of the Bulgarians, flourishes.

313. [Note: [Col. 1112A]

313. “And he went directly to him.” It should be read from the better manuscript: “And he rightly assisted him.” This is confirmed by Julianus’s Adversaria, no. 450, where we read: “And he rightly assisted King Alfonso, called the Chaste.” D. L.

After Julianus, bishop of Toledo, died, John succeeds him. After John, Saint Bonitus II succeeds him in the primatial see. P. H.]

Count Milo [another reading: Count Rolandus, whose father was Milo] of Angleris, surnamed Bernardus, the brother-in-law of Charlemagne, was regarded in Spain as a martyr. This Milo came to Spain with his son Abhelardus, surnamed Genesius, and went directly to Alfonso the Chaste, the Catholic king of León and Oviedo. He brought the body of Saint Leocadia from Soissons [another reading: from the people of Soissons], as Nithardus, Charlemagne’s nephew, reports.

314. Selva, abbot of Agali, flourishes splendidly at Toledo.

DCCCCXXVIII. DCCCXC.

315. John, bishop of Toledo, occupied the see for nine months.

316. [Note: [Col. 1112A]

316. In the town of Prunis or Prusae, which is five miles from Oceania, there was a holy shepherd named Raymundus, so full of faith and burning with works of charity that he became renowned both during his life and after his death, and was distinguished by many miracles. He is said to have been from Medellín in Lusitania, where his memory remains alive even now; for the hill overlooking the river Ana is called Raymundus Hill. Perhaps, while driving his flock there in the depths of winter, he used to pasture it in that place. The townspeople’s devotion to this holy man is remarkable: every year many people from the surrounding towns gather for a public procession in his honor. ID.

In the town of Prunis or Prusae. See below, no. 331. Julianus, in his Chronicle, no. 453, writes: “In the town of Prunis, Prusae, or Clusae, in Carpetania, now Cirvelos, Raymundus the shepherd, by birth from Medellín, and at Puteoli likewise a holy patron, because he was bishop of Puteoli in Spain. Raymundus was, as I said, from Medellín, at the time when Saint Brother John Guarinus, a Lusitanian, flourished in Catalonia. He was regarded as renowned for holiness and illustrious signs; at that time the citizens of Prunis erected an oratory for him near the Tagus. His day has been celebrated from ancient times on the third day of the Lord’s Easter.” Thus I found it, after Julianus had been printed, in the autograph manuscript of Father Hieronymus [Col. 1112C] de la Higuera. D. L.]

In the town of Prunis or Prusae, in Carpetania, Raymundus of Medellín, a Lusitanian shepherd, flourishes as a saint, remarkable for his generosity toward the poor.

DCCCCXXX. DCCCXCII.

317. Bonitus the Second, a man of outstanding character, very attentive to the poor and to his own people, succeeds John of Toledo in the see.

DCCCCXXXIII. DCCCXCV.

318. [Note: [Col. 1112C]

318. Bivarium: today Bivar, near Burgos, the celebrated homeland of the commander Roderic Díaz, who has never been praised sufficiently according to his dignity, [Col. 1113A] and from which the district of Bivar derives its name. He died on July 30: “Ostanus, bishop and confessor, fell asleep in the Lord in the territory of Bivar on the same day.” He was bishop of Oca; this is confirmed by a charter of the year 890, where he says: “By the grace of God, Ostanus the bishop confirms.” P. H.]

Saint Ostanus [another reading: Ostianus], bishop of Oca in Spain, attended the Council of Oviedo; he died in the district of Bivar on July 30. He is listed among the saints in the catalogue.

[Col. 1113] 319. The Christian Mozarabs of Córdoba build a church within the city. It is uncertain whether it was dedicated to the martyr Genesius, who suffered there during the persecution of the emperor Nero, or to Abhelardus, surnamed Genesius, a kinsman of Charlemagne and a glorious bishop and abbot.

DCCCCXXXIV. DCCCXCVI.

320. [Note: [Col. 1113A]

320. Some read Martinus, others Marinus, as I noted. Our Julianus mentions Marinus in his Chronicle (as Father Higuera says), no. 458: “Marinus and Romanus, Galicians by nation, are sent to Spain to King Adefonsus of León by Pope John of Rome. On arriving at León, they are received courteously by the king.” Julianus likewise recognized him as a deacon in his Chronicle, no. 501: “Marinus the deacon was sent by John to the king of Oviedo,” and so forth; Luitprandus says that he was made supreme pontiff from the rank of deacon. D. L.]

Martinus [others read Marinus, following Julianus. See what we said above at no. 311. D. L.] and Romanus, Galicians by nation, are sent by Pope John to Alfonso, king of León and Oviedo.

DCCCCXXXVIII. DCCCC.

321. [Note: [Col. 1113A]

321. In the year 900, the holy man Raymundus died in the town of Prunis. Although poor, I believe that he was exceedingly rich in merits, and that many angels were not lacking to accompany him, together with miracles that would make his death more glorious. P. H.]

In Prunis [see above, no. 316. D. L.], in Carpetania, the holy Raymundus the Shepherd dies: a pious, simple, gentle man, and most generous toward the poor.

DCCCCXL. DCCCCII.

322. [Note: [Col. 1114A]

322. The archdeacon Servus Dei succeeds Bonitus in the see of Toledo. He was a distinguished writer; for he wrote a book proving that Christ saw the Father, against certain people who wrongly denied this. It is astonishing how richly endowed this holy Church of Toledo was with very holy and learned bishops: from it, as from the Trojan horse, the most distinguished writers emerged eagerly one after another, and, by their lives as well as by their published books, wonderfully illuminated the holy Church of God. P. H.]

After Bonitus was taken from the living, his archdeacon, Servus Dei—“Servant of God,” not merely in name but also in deed—succeeds him in the patriarchal see of Toledo. He wrote a book asserting that Christ, the Son of God, sees the face of the Father in heaven. He occupies the see for seven years.

323. The bones of Saint Lucianus, bishop and martyr, companion of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite, are transferred from Beauvais to the city of Vich. Others believe that the body of Leucianus, a prince of the Carpetani who suffered with Quiteria, was brought there together with the body of Saint Marcus [another reading: Martianus; another: Martia].

324. There was an opinion that Saint James preached the Gospel in Spain—the Gospel not yet written by Brother John, as Chrysostom teaches—and proclaimed to the world the mysteries of the clear divinity.

325. The body of Saint Vincent, a Levite of Agen [another reading: Nonnagen], was brought to Valencia by certain persons; it is now preserved in the Algarve.

DCCCCXLIII. DCCCCV.

326. Two synods of Rheims were assembled concerning various matters.

DCCCCXLVIII. DCCCCX.

327. [Note: [Col. 1114A]

327. The distinguished man Orontius succeeds Servus Dei in the governance of the Church of Toledo. He was precisely the kind of man demanded by those difficult and most calamitous times: a man who surpassed others in pastoral stature and holiness of spirit, capable of undertaking every great danger, of which the faithful were then especially confronted. P. H.]

Orontius, bishop of Toledo, governs Toledo for nineteen years while Abd al-Rahman and al-Mansur rule there.

DCCCCLII. DCCCCXIV.

328. [Note: [Col. 1114A]

328. This holy bishop, mindful of his episcopal office, gathers a council amid the dangers posed by the Saracens. P. H.]

Orontius convenes a council of bishops at Toledo.

DCCCCLIV. DCCCCXVI.

329. Regino, abbot of Prüm, the Benedictine historian.

DCCCCLVI. DCCCCXVIII.

330. Aegidius, bishop of Tusculum and apostolic legate of Pope John, converts the Poles to the Christian faith.

331. The holy man Rudesindus died on the eve of November; he was buried at Dumium.

DCCCCLX. DCCCCXXII.

332. Rodulfus the Burgundian is made emperor against Berengar, the emperor of Italy; he remains in power for four years.

DCCCCLXII. DCCCCXXIV.

333. At that time the Christian Mozarabs are treated by the Saracens in miserable ways; their hatred makes this clear.

334. Saint Eugenia, virgin and martyr, flourishes. She suffered in the territory of Córdoba, in the city of Utica (now Marmolejos), in the year 923, and was beheaded before the Christian citizens of Córdoba. The Christian Mozarabs, in memory of her martyrdom, erected a cenotaph with acrostic verses.

DCCCCLXVIII. DCCCCXXX.

335. The Benedictine virgin Thecla flourishes in holiness at Concha of the Campos.

DCCCCLXIX. DCCCCXXXI.

[Col. 1115]

336. [Note: [Col. 1115A]

336. I believe that this body of Cyriacus is that of the holy martyr of Ancona, who, on May 4, suffered the gravest kinds of torture for Christ at Jerusalem together with his mother Anna. P. H.]

The body of Saint Cyriacus. Julianus mentions Saint Cyriacus in his Chronicle, no. 468, where the autograph manuscript of the learned Father Hieronymus de la Higuera, which I fortunately acquired after the Paris edition, reads as follows: “The body of Saint Cyriacus was transferred to the Gauls from Spain; it was found at Hivernis by a ploughman in the year 930.” Perhaps *ad Gallias* should be read instead of *ad Gallaecias*; and *by a herdsman* (*a bubulco*) instead of *by Vebulcus* (*ab Vebulco*), if Julianus is compared with Luitprandus. See what I noted in the margin. D. L.]

In this year the body of Saint Cyriacus [perhaps it should be read as Cyricus, the boy and son of Saint Julitta. D. L.] was found by a certain oxherd; it had previously been brought from Spain to Gaul.

DCCCCLXX. DCCCCXXXII.

337. [Note: [Col. 1115A]

337. Bishop Basilius is regarded as distinguished. Seeing Christians becoming remarkably corrupt through frequent association and conversation with the Saracens, he convened a council of the neighboring bishops in order to apply a salutary remedy to this deeply rooted evil. P. H.]

Basilius occupies the see of Toledo for twenty-three years, an upright man.

338. In this year the king greatly enlarges the Great Mosque of Toledo.

339. Basilius writes to the priests Silvanactus and Florecindus.

340. [Note: [Col. 1115B]

340. Marinus the deacon, and so forth. Julianus mentions the visitation made by Marinus in his Chronicle, no. 501. I shall append his words, since they also clarify Luitprandus in the following entry: “Marinus the deacon was sent by John to the king of Oviedo; examining [perhaps, ‘inspecting’] the excellent Gothic books, he found them Catholic.” *Visitanis* should be read *Visitanus* and joined with the following word *clarus*, so that it reads: “Visitanus is renowned for learning and holiness of life. He convened a council at Toledo to find a remedy so that the Mozarabs of Toledo, indeed of all Spain, who were associated with the Saracens, would not participate in their ceremonies.” D. L.]

Marinus, a Spanish deacon coming from Gaul, is sent by Pope John to the bishop of Toledo. Examining the Gothic liturgical books—the Missals, breviaries, sacramentaries, and prayer books—he found them Catholic.

DCCCCLXXIV. DCCCCXXXVI.

341. Basilius convenes the Council of Toledo, by which provision is made to prevent Christians from suffering harm through association with the Saracens.

342. [Note: [Col. 1115B]

342. Bonitus III of this name succeeds Basilius. Under him our Luitprandus was subdeacon at Toledo, and afterward deacon of Pavia. P. H.]

Bonitus the Third succeeds Basilius; he occupies the see of Toledo for two years.

DCCCCLXXV. DCCCCXXXVII.

343. [Note: [Col. 1115B]

343. Authors speak variously about the dates of John Servus Dei. García de Loaysa thinks that he died [Col. 1115C] in the year 926, but in the manuscript of Saint Aemilianus it reads: “John, era 964.” Morales and Loaysa read era 964; but in reality it is 994, because according to Garibay, book IX, chapter 4, X equals forty; thus he died in the year of the Lord 926.
