Brother Bernardo Brito of Braga, a remarkably learned and skilled man, expresses the same opinion in a letter that he sent me.

Here it must not be omitted that Alvarus Gómez, followed by Morales and Loaysa, believed this man to have been the last of the bishops of Toledo. I shall quote Loaysa’s words under Gundemar, which read as follows: “John, Servant of God, distinguished in life and miracles”—he is mistaken in what follows—“who,” he says, “in nearly the same times in which Eulogius suffered martyrdom, held the first see of Toledo with the consent of clergy and people; amid such a transformation of affairs and such evident danger, he performed his duty vigorously and courageously. He resisted the untamed fury and the savagery of the enemy by his most holy conduct, and opposed their uncontrolled tyranny through the established principles of his life. Therefore, when John had been deprived of life, they did not allow Maurus to be designated as his successor. John was thus almost the last of the bishops who governed Toledo under Moorish domination. Hence it lacked a shepherd for one hundred and fifty years, until the city was attacked by King Alfonso VI. Although the Christian Mozarabs lacked a public and primary shepherd, in spiritual matters they appointed the parish priest of Saint Justa in the manner of a bishop; when elected, they looked up to and venerated him with the greatest respect.”

García de Loaysa obtained this from the papers of the learned Gómez; but it rests on a rather weak foundation. Since they did not find the bishops of Toledo readily at hand, they assumed that this first bishopric of Spain had entirely ceased, and that no other reason for its cessation could be given than the prohibition of the Moors. These claims, made merely for appearance’s sake, lack all probability and [Col. 1116B] evidentiary force. For if the bishops of Toledo ceased entirely because they opposed the designs of the Moors, I would ask: in what matters? And if the bishops of Toledo were hateful to the Saracens, why would the bishops of Córdoba, Seville, and the other sees not have been hateful to them as well? Yet we see that after the death of this John, Servant of God, there were bishops at Córdoba, Seville, and elsewhere. Why, then, should there not have been one in the royal city of Toledo?

At the end of a manuscript book containing the New and Old Testament written in Gothic letters, preserved in the library of the holy Church of Toledo, the following is found: “In the name of the Lord our Savior Jesus Christ. The author of this book, in which the entire New and Old Testament is preserved, was Servandus, of blessed memory. Born and educated in the blessed see of Seville, he afterward deserved to occupy the chair of Basti. This illustrious man granted this codex to John, his close companion and intimate friend. After John had been transferred to this more distinguished see of Seville by his uncle, Stephen of blessed memory, the most wise and eloquent bishop of the see of Seville, he had been nurtured by Felix, likewise bishop of the first see of Toledo, dedicated to the priestly order, and sent as bishop to the see of Carthage; and, transferred again from there, he was elected bishop of Córdoba, that great and royal see. From that see, sound in body and mind and distinguished in every respect, he resolved to offer this completed codex to the Lord God in the aforementioned see of Seville, before the memory of holy and ever-virgin Mary, on the tenth day before the Kalends of January, in the era 1026, on the condition that no cleric should dare remove or alter this codex from the aforementioned see. And if anyone should do so—which God forbid—let him be condemned by God, his angels, and all the saints.”

From this passage it is clear that in the year 988—that is, thirty-eight years after the death of John Servus Dei—there were bishops: Stephen of Seville, Servandus of Basti, afterward John, first bishop of Carthage and soon afterward bishop of Córdoba, and Felix, bishop of the see of Toledo. To these I may add that twenty-five years before Toledo was conquered by Alfonso, emperor of the Toledoans, there was Paschal of the see of Toledo, whom Lord Loaysa cites in his Councils. He is also depicted among the bishops of Toledo in a book entitled *On the Blessed Virgin Mary*, written in Gothic letters. The book belonged to Brother Master John de Vega, once a celebrated preacher, and is now preserved in the monastery of the Most Holy Trinity at Toledo. At the end it reads:

“Blessed are you, Lord, who have helped me and comforted me. I, wretched Solomon, archpriest, an unworthy servant of God and a sinner, wrote this little book *On the Virginity of Saint Mary, the Virgin and Mother of God the Lord*, and completed it in the city of Toledo, in the church of Saint Mary the Virgin, under the metropolitan lord Paschal, archbishop of the see, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the era 1105, recorded on Friday, at the third hour, on the day of Saint Cyprian the bishop.”

That year was 1067, with Sunday Letter G; therefore the feast of Saint Cyprian is celebrated on September 14. The memory of Saint Mary the Virgin of Alficen in the city of Toledo should be noted.

From these facts it appears that there were bishops at Toledo even after John, and that the bishops of Saint Justa were bishops of Toledo. They were called by this name because they gathered in that church as though it were the principal church of the Toledo Mozarabs, and because the bishops of Toledo possessed their episcopal see and jurisdiction there. P. H.]

John, Servant of God, succeeds to the see; he occupies it for ten years.

[Col. 1117] 344. [Note: [Col. 1117B]

344. That there was a great persecution of Christians under John Servus Dei, and that many suffered martyrdom, is taught by his letter to all the Christian Mozarabs of Spain. It is now preserved in the archive of the church of Saint Clement at Toledo, belonging either to the Benedictine nuns or to the Cistercian nuns. Luitprandus acknowledges in this Chronicle, under the year 944, that this bishop was known to him, and he weaves remarkable praises of him. P. H.]

Under him and in this year many martyrs suffered in Spain, while some fell away from the faith. On this matter there exists a most elegant letter, full of zeal and fervor for the faith, written by Saint John Servus Dei, primate of Toledo, to all the Mozarabs of Spain. As primate and patriarch of all Spain, he wrote to all the Churches of Spain.

DCCCCLXXXII. DCCCCXLIV.

345. I knew him at Toledo when I was a subdeacon and found him to be a holy man, fervent in the Spirit of God, at Toledo. His letter begins: “According to the report of many.” He also wrote to Marinus before Marinus became bishop of Toledo; and Pope Marinus replied to him, sending letters full of love and goodwill as well.

346. The memory of Saint Agathangelus, who suffered with Saint Clement, bishop of Ancyra, is celebrated in Spain. Agathangelus was born in Spain, at Elche, to a Roman father.

347. At Bletisa the bodies of three holy shepherds flourished.

DCCCCLXXXV. DCCCCXLVII.

348. [Note: [Col. 1117C]

348. Here he discusses the death of Saint John, bishop of Toledo, saying that he died at Toledo in the year of the Lord 860 and lies buried at Saint Justa. P. H.]

The holy bishop of Toledo, John, surnamed Servus Dei, died and was buried in the church of Saint Luke the Evangelist.

349. Vissitanus, a man of great counsel and unusual piety toward all the afflicted Mozarabs, succeeds him in the patriarchal see.

DCCCCLXXXVI. DCCCCXLVIII.

350. The Synod of Ingelheim in Germany, consisting of thirty-four [another reading: thirty-one] bishops.

DCCCCLXXXVIII. DCCCCL.

351. Berengar, the younger king of Italy, is made king in this year.

DCCCCLXXXIX. DCCCCLI.

352. [Note: [Col. 1117B]

352. Nunilo and Alodia in this year, and so forth. This year, too, sufficiently confirms the authority of our Chronicle. For only a contemporary writer of Nunilo and Alodia could lead all historians of Spanish affairs, wandering in Cimmerian darkness, back to the light and the path of truth.

As for the chronology and geography of the acts of these virgins, the reader will easily discover from what follows that many errors have been admitted; from these errors we are unexpectedly freed by Luitprandus’s present account. Regarding the chronology, the variation among authors is remarkable. Saint Eulogius, book II of the *Memorial of the Saints*, chapter 7, himself a contemporary of the virgins, states that they were crowned with martyrdom in the year of Christ 851, or era 889. His view is followed by Marinus Siculus, book V of *On Spanish Affairs*, chapter 28; Tarapha, in his book *On the Kings of Spain*, under García; and Baronius, volume X, under the same year. Many breviaries of the Churches of Spain likewise assign this year in the nocturnal lessons for the office of these virgins.

The same year is assigned in many manuscript books called sanctorals, especially in the venerably ancient and substantial Toledo manuscript of the monastery of Saint Bernard. There, no. 70, on five large parchment leaves, their history is found under the title: *The Passion of the Virgins of Christ Nunilo and Alodia in the City of Osca, under the governor Zamael*. It begins: “The holy virgins of God”; somewhat farther on it has these words verbatim: “It happened, therefore, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 851,” and so forth. John Maldonatus and Zacharias Lippeloo, volume IV of *Lives of the Saints*, October 22, subscribe to this view.

Ambrosius Morales, however, disagrees with them, both in his scholia on the seventh chapter of Saint Eulogius and in volume III of his *History of Spain*, book XIII, chapter 44, maintaining that they suffered in the year of Christ 840. He relies on the argument that in the preceding year, 839, Saint Eulogius revisited the monastery of Leyre, as he himself admits in his letter to Willesindus, bishop of Pamplona, and in his *Apologeticus* to Alvarus. At that time, he heard absolutely nothing about the martyrdom of the holy women; yet, as a most learned man and an especially devoted student of the martyrs of his own age, he certainly would have heard of it if it had occurred—particularly since the virgins are believed to have surrendered their necks for Christ not far from the monastery of Leyre.

We therefore know with certainty [Col. 1118C] that they did not suffer before the year 840. That they were killed before 842 he infers from the privilege of the king of Navarre, Enneco Eximenius (Iñigo Ximénez), surnamed Arista. The original document is preserved in the monastery itself, while a copy is found in Stephen Garibay’s *Compendium of the Kings of Navarre*, book XXII, chapter 1.

It contains the donation of the villages of Esana and Banasa to God the Savior and to the holy martyrs Nunilo and Alodia, whose bodies had from that time been resting in the same monastery of Saint Savior at Leyre. At the end it reads: “This charter was made in era 880”—that is, in the year of the Lord 842—“on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of July, placed upon the altar of Saint Savior, and entrusted to Fortunius the abbot and his monks, in the presence of the people celebrating in that place the feast of the reception of the saints’ bodies.”

Therefore, if the bodies of the holy virgins were transferred to the monastery of Leyre on that same day and in that same year—for the people of Navarre celebrated their reception—they undoubtedly received the palm of martyrdom before the year 842. Otherwise, since it is established that they were killed on October 21 or 22, as all the martyrologies and breviaries state, they could not have been transferred in July and then died in the following October of the same year; they must necessarily have died before the aforementioned year 842.

Nor can this privilege be accused of falsification, since it is supported by many other privileges of subsequent kings, which Garibay likewise produces in book XXII, chapters 3, 6, 10, 14, and 16. The first, issued by García, the son of the aforementioned Enneco, is dated era 914, or the year of Christ 876. The second, issued by Fortunius, García’s son, is from era 939. The third, issued by Sancho, Fortunius’s brother, is from era 957. The fourth, issued by García, the offspring of that same Sancho, is from era 982. The fifth, issued by Sancho, García’s son, is from era 1019.

In all these documents the kings donate certain towns and villages under their authority to the aforementioned monastery of Leyre out of reverence for the holy martyrs of Christ, who are said to have been buried and lying there at the time. An ancient charter or tablet of the monastery agrees with this, listing the bodies of the kings buried there. For when it speaks of Enneco Arista and his wife Oneca, it says: “In their time the martyrs were transferred from Osca to the monastery of Leyre.” On this subject Yepes should be consulted, decade 4, under the year of Christ 840. Garibay agrees with Morales in the aforementioned chapter 1 of book XXII.

Despite all this, many others maintain that the virgins were killed in the year of Christ 950, which is what we now hear from Luitprandus. Some of the older breviaries of the Churches of Spain agree with him, especially the breviary of Salamanca, a copy of which I obtained in the library of the monastery of Valparaíso, and John Vasaeus in his Chronicle under that year. Vasaeus reports that the Seville Breviary says that they died in the following year, that is, 951; and Garibay, suppressing the name, cites certain authors in support of this opinion. Thus these opinions differ from one another by a hundred years or even more.

Nor are the geographical obscurities concerning these virgins any less serious. All the martyrologies say that they suffered in the city of Osca, or Hosca: the Roman Martyrology, that of Ado, that of Usuard, those of Galesinius and Maurolycus, and any others that exist. They are supported by Esquilinus, book IX, *Catholicus*, chapter 96; by the previously cited Marinus Siculus and Tarapha; and by the manuscript of Saint Bernard of Toledo.

Others place them in the city of Bosca, near the town of Barbetanus [another reading: Barbitunum]. Thus Saint Eulogius is printed and explained by Morales, and so Vasaeus has it in the cited passage. Both maintain that Bosca stood near the city of Nájera.

Finally, Luitprandus now asserts—as you see—that the event took place in the castle of Bergetum [another reading: Vergetum], in the Castra Vinaria, in Bastetania. Hence many, confusing the two towns, say that the virgins ended their lives “in the territory of Barbitanum, near the town and very ancient castle called Castro Bergeti, in the village of Osca.” These words occur in many breviaries, especially those of Palencia and Seville, and in the Burgos breviary explained by Maldonatus. Zacharias Lippeloo follows him in volume IV of *The Lives of the Saints*, under October 22.

A certain Legend printed at Seville in the year of Christ 1503 has *Abosca* instead of Osca or Bosca. Morales, rejecting Osca and not finding Bosca, makes a small alteration and reads Oca, formerly Auca, from which the forest of Auca derives its name, *los montes de Oca*. Yet, still uncertain and excessively preoccupied with the problem, he adds: “All of this is conjecture, because nothing more can be done. The difficulty nevertheless remains: it appears from the history that they suffered and were buried at Oca, where Governor Zamael was; and I cannot say anything that satisfies me, because I do not satisfy myself with anything.” His only assertion beyond doubt is that they were killed in the Old Castle near Nájera, on the testimony of the townspeople, who continue to venerate there both the place of their martyrdom and their former burial place. He also says that the names themselves—Urbebetanum and Castrum-Virgetum—sufficiently indicate that they derive from *castro viejo*, commonly called “the Old Castle.”

But Luitprandus wonderfully dispels so great a darkness when he asserts: “While I was alive, they suffered in this year,” and so forth—that is, in 950. If this testimony is compared with the other testimony of Lord Eulogius, it will become entirely clear that two pairs of sisters, bearing the same names and likewise virgins and martyrs, were killed for Christ the Lord in Spain.

But how could this be? Simply because one pair was separated from the other by an interval of one hundred years, although each author was, as it were, an eyewitness of the holy women’s passion. Eulogius recognized that they had been killed while he was writing, in the year of Christ 851; Luitprandus, however, who was living in Spain in the year 950, asserts that they were crowned with martyrdom during his lifetime. Yet it is impossible that the virgins who triumphed in the year 950 were the same as those who had already received their crowns a hundred years earlier.

Therefore both authors must be believed according to their integrity, and it must be said that entirely different sisters, bearing the same names, are being referred to.

And the names of the towns or cities that they ennobled with their blood strongly reinforce this conclusion. The earlier pair suffered at Osca in the kingdom of Aragon, while the later pair offered their throats at Castro Vergetum. Thus the purest reading of the martyrologies says that, when speaking of the earlier pair, they suffered at Osca. Usuard’s words, to which Ado agrees, under 22 October, are:

> “At Osca, the holy virgins Nunilo and Alodia, who, having been worn down by prolonged imprisonment for their confession of Christ and condemned to death, completed their martyrdom.”

[Col. 1120C] The Roman Martyrology has:

> “At Osca in Spain, the holy virgins Nunilo and Alodia, sisters, who, condemned to death by the Saracens for confessing the faith, completed their martyrdom.”

The earlier manuscripts of their acts likewise read this way; and, what deserves still greater weight, Saint Eulogius wrote precisely this. For the city called Bosca in printed manuscripts was called Osca in the original, as Morales himself plainly admits, although he corrupted the text while believing that he was restoring it. In his notes on chapter 7 of book II of the *Memorial of the Saints*, no. 4, he says:

> “In the old exemplar it was Osca, not Bosca. I restored the more familiar name”—

familiar, however, in corrupted Sanctorals—

> “for I do not believe that the holy virgins were brought to Osca, a city very far away in Aragon.”

Therefore, when we read in Eulogius’s text, “We learned that in the city of Bosca, near the town of Barbitanum, there were two virgin sisters,” and so forth, that phrase, “near the town of Barbitanum,” was inserted into the text by some ignorant person, [Col. 1120D] many years after Eulogius’s death and after the later virgins—plainly after confusion regarding the acts of the holy sisters had once become established through the passage of time. This is demonstrated by the authors of the aforementioned martyrologies, who took their information about the holy Nunilo and Alodia from Eulogius: none of them mentions the town of Barbitanum, but only Osca.

Eulogius’s own context again cries out that the phrase is foreign to the text. If they suffered at the city of Osca, how could they also be said to have suffered near the town of Barbitanum? And what town is that near Osca? Moreover, the name itself is incorrectly given, for it ought to be called Bergitanum, or, with the letter V, Vergitanum.

Yet this is undoubtedly the town in which, or near which, the later virgins were put to death. For Ptolemy makes it clear that the Bergitani were situated farther away from the people of Osca in Aragon and from the people of Naxara. He assigns Birgetum, or Bigertum, to the Bastetani, while Luitprand and Pliny, book III, chapter 1, place among the same people the *Castra vinaria* near Osca, which perhaps are called Vineolae by Antoninus, on the route from Carthage to Castulo. You may therefore wonder at Luitprand’s extremely precise geography concerning the places connected with the acts of the later virgins, and at the fact that Birgetum lies very far from Castro Vetus near Nájera, almost the entire breadth of Spain intervening.

To this may be added that Zumael, the tyrant under whom they are said to have suffered, was, according to Julianus (in the *Adversaria*, no. 450), king of Caravaca. That town is certainly situated near Osca in Baetica. The very ancient Granadan Breviary, formerly used at Osca, likewise repeatedly asserts this in explicit terms; and, on the basis of a tradition handed down from their ancestors, claims the martyrs as its own. Even today Osca fervently venerates and praises them as its patronesses and acknowledges that, through their intercession, it experiences God’s great benevolence toward it from day to day.

A correction of equal importance is required concerning Morales’s contention, contrary to Saint Eulogius’s testimony, that the martyrdom of the earlier virgins occurred in the year of Christ 840, [Col. 1121B] not in 851, as Eulogius writes. The sole reason for his dissent from so great a writer, who recorded the events of his own time, was a copy of a privilege of the monastery of Leire, in which they are said to have been transferred there in the Spanish era 880—that is, in the year of the Lord 842.

But I have no doubt that this resulted from a copyist’s error, as so often elsewhere. The testimony of Eulogius himself establishes this, and I value it far more highly than a thousand transcriptions by others, especially since the oldest acts of the holy virgins agree with it and affirm that they were killed in the year of the Lord 851. That privilege of Enneco, called Eximenius Arista, cannot be supported by the privileges that follow, since those are much later than the year of their death mentioned above and merely confirm the existence of the holy virgins at that place in subsequent years—something no one denies.

From this one must judge that very ancient document which Blancas produces in his *Commentary on Aragonese Affairs*, taken from the archive of the monastery of San Juan de la Peña, under the title *The Canonical Church of Saint Peter of Taberna*. If it possesses any authority, it must certainly be regarded as important, since its author is said to have witnessed with his own eyes, under King Roderic, the disaster and most savage devastation of Spain.

The writer’s imposture, however, seems to be exposed by his assertion that at that time Bishop Beutius of Zaragoza fled with many relics of the saints to the monastery of Taberna. Among the others, he lists the head of Saint Nunilo and the shoulder blade of Saint Alodia, which he says Beutius placed beneath the altar of Saint Stephen. If this were true, since the devastation of Spain occurred in the year of Christ 714, the relics of these sacred virgins would have been venerated 170 years, or more, before their martyrdom—which we have shown took place in the year of Christ 851.

Nevertheless, I think that the entire document is not necessarily forged. In the course of time the relics of these holy virgins could have been brought to the same monastery and placed with the others beneath the older altar of Saint Stephen; their names could then have been inserted into the document itself, just as we have shown that something was later added to the text of Saint Eulogius.

Or, if that document is to be judged equally ancient throughout, I do not hesitate to concede three pairs of virgins and martyrs, crowned at different times but bearing the same names, Nunilo and Alodia: the first pair before the year of Christ 714, that is, before the devastation of Spain; another pair after them, in the year 851, according to Eulogius’s testimony; and the last pair around the year 950, which Luitprand almost witnessed himself.

This is supported especially by Julianus’s authority. He expressly asserts it in the *Adversaria*, nos. 292 and following. I would maintain that the earlier pair were killed under Diocletian at Osca in Aragon and that their remains were carried to Bologna during the disaster of Spain; that the second pair suffered near Nájera, or Tricio, and became the ornament of the monastery of Leire; and that the third pair were claimed by Osca in Baetica. Hence Julianus says:

> “Osca in Baetica has some as patronesses, Tricio has some, and Osca in Aragon has some.”

The differing burial places also help to establish the distinction between the holy women: some are said to have been buried at Bologna, others in the monastery of Leire.

Nor does the similarity of their names, kinship, and martyrdom stand in the way. We often find the same thing occurring, and Dextrus contains many examples of it. For example, at Blanda in Catalonia two holy martyrs, Bonus and Maximianus, died; others bearing the same names died at Urgavo in Baetica. Under the names Felix and Fortunatus we know of three pairs of martyrs, namely those killed at Valencia, Ebura, and Carthage. We have also recognized two Eulalias, of nearly the same age and possessing similar crowns; and among the apostles there were two Simons, two Jameses, and two Judases. I say nothing of the fact that the later Nunilo and Alodia undoubtedly received their names in honor of the venerable memory of the earlier pair; there is no contradiction in that.

This, given the shortness of time, should suffice as what I have said in favor of Luitprand concerning the holy girls.

In literary matters I have always thought—and it will remain my judgment—that one should seek, indeed demand, the judgment of great men, and openly and honestly acknowledge those through whom one has advanced. When a person judges himself unequal to carrying a burden, it is a sign of a sound mind to desire mutual assistance.

What the most learned Father Francisco de Bivar wrote to me about Nunilo and Alodia, I now write out again. I consider myself to have served liberal studies well by enabling the reader to enjoy this treasure of learning. I add a small contribution—though a slight one—from three passages in Luitprand, who is entirely consistent with himself in the *Adversaria*, no. 212. His words are:

> “In the wine-making camps, in Bastetania, Saint Nunilo and Alodia, in the year 951.”

Likewise, in our Julianus, *Adversaria*, no. 540, which agrees with the title of the manuscript, or Sanctoral, of the monastery of Saint Bernard in Toledo cited at the beginning of this excursus, the title reads:

> “The Passion of the Virgins of Christ, [Col. 1122C] Nunilo and Alodia, in the city of Osca, under the governor Zumail.”

Julianus’s words are:

> “Nunilo and Alodia suffered under Zumaila, king of Caravaca.”

Truth answers to truth.

Again, in Julianus, *Adversaria*, nos. 292, 293, and 294, no. 292 agrees with those who affirm that they suffered in the year 851, and in no. 293 one should read:

> “At the town of Osca, near the town of Bergetanum—or Vergetanum—now called Berbetanum, near Antoninus’s Barbariana, the most holy virgin sisters Nunilo and Alodia suffered in the year 950.”

The rest should be deleted, since it was inserted incorrectly by copyists.

That town is now called Castro Vegeto and lies only three leagues from the city of Osca, Huesca, in Bastetania. Julianus attests that in his time the town of Bergetanum was called Berbetanum. I suppose that both names derive from the river flowing near the little hermitage, now called Barbata, lying two stone-throws away from it.

I derive another testimony from our indefatigable reader, Father Jerome de la Higuera, who asserts that there was a pair of martyr sisters bearing the same names, although, following Father Francisco Bivarius, I acknowledge three pairs. He left handwritten notes, which I preserve, so that, adorned with the name of their own parent, they may see the light, if time permits.

Francisco Diego de Aynsa y de Iriarte writes at length about Nunilo and Alodia and collects much material, with great learning, in his *Antiquities of Osca*, book II, chapters 24 and 25.

It is also worthwhile to cite the wording of the lessons from the Breviaries, especially from the manuscript Sanctorals, in which mention is made of the garment in which Alodia was dressed when she suffered martyrdom. Morales cites it in his notes on Saint Eulogius, book II of the *Memorial of the Saints*, chapter 7, no. 6, folio 58:

> “O marvelous power of the Most High! The girl who could not avoid a sword flashing not far away did not fear when it descended upon her own neck; instead, she grasped the sindon, tied it around her leg, and wiped her face with her hair.”

The *sindon* was a garment common to men and women, although they used it in different ways. It was linen and white, though sometimes Tyrian and silk; it was worn by Hebrew women and by Arab women.

Among many authors one finds much material. I shall select and bring forward only a little of it, both to clarify the name and to illuminate certain very ancient monuments of Spain.

There is a notable testimony concerning the Hebrews in Isaiah, chapter III, where, speaking of women’s adornment, he says:

> “And changes of garments, and little cloaks, and linens, and needles, and mirrors, *sethinim*, sindons, and ribbons.”

Saint Thomas, under the word *sindones*, writes:

> “Fine coverings with which the shoulders are covered, as is done in Campania by women.”

In Proverbs, the last chapter:

> “She made a sindon and sold it, and delivered a girdle to the Canaanite.”

Earlier he had said that she made, first, ornaments for covering the shoulders.

Bishop Jerome Osorius, in his *Paraphrase*, interprets it as “linen garments and coverings”; Saint Jerome translates it as *amictoria*, coverings.

Blessed Isidore gives an especially apt explanation in book XIX, chapter 25, of the *Etymologies*, “On women’s cloaks”:

> “An *anaboladium* is a woman’s linen covering, by which the shoulders are covered; the Greeks and Latins call it a *sindon*.”

The ἀναβόλαιον, or ἀναβολάδιον, was among the ancients a garment by which women’s breasts and shoulders were protected. The most learned and, in the knowledge of humane letters, unrivaled V. C. Puteanus explains this word learnedly in the second collection of his *Epistolary Trifles*, letter II.

It is therefore worth observing that the mark properly branded upon Nero was his disgraceful adornment with women’s clothing. Dio is the authority, saying that he wore linen around his neck. In Greek, σινδόνα. Suetonius, in his *Life of Nero*, chapter 51, calls it a *sudarium*, a sweat-cloth. In describing Sardanapalus’s obscene lust, Xiphilinus uses the same word:

> “He shook the sindon fastened with golden rings, so that by his soft and effeminate voice he might attract passers-by.”

This is translated by William Blanco.

Seneca criticizes Maecenas, whose head was wrapped in a cloak, in letter 114:

> “This is the man who appeared in the tribunal, on the speaker’s platform, and in every public assembly with his head covered by a cloak, his ears excluded on both sides.”

Plutarch likewise, criticizing the arrogance of the freedman Demetrius, a partisan of Pompey, writes that he wore a garment on his head reaching to his ears.

Such effeminate men took pleasure not only in the common dress of men and women but also in feminine gestures and in wearing clothing in a feminine manner. Hence Ulpian, in the law *Vestis*, 23, section 2, concerning gold and silver bequeathed, lists cloaks among women’s garments. Scaevola the jurist, in the law *Titia*, 38, section 1, of the same title, adds:

> “Women’s garments are those intended for the materfamilias, which a man cannot easily use without disgrace, such as stolae and cloaks.”

To resume our thread and return to the point from which we digressed, Rabbi Jonathan Benzahir explains the whole matter, as I learned from the most learned Father Master Bernardo Brito, the Portuguese historiographer. His words, on Isaiah III, are:

> “Sindons are very soft and extremely fine garments, with which the noblest women in Judea customarily covered both their bodies and their very heads decently and gracefully.”

Levi Benzemerah gives a graphic description of their form in chapter 31 of Proverbs:

> “It was a common garment in Palestine, Arabia, and Egypt, with this one difference: when worn by men, it was fastened at the left shoulder and hung down almost to the ankles; when worn by women, it was attractively wrapped around them and, passing over the arms, was fitted to the crown of the head. Thus for married women it was an ornament and veil, while for virgins it was both ornament and covering.”

A little later, discussing the material, he writes:

> “Sindons were woven chiefly from linen in Galilee, but silk sindons in Phoenicia and in the city of Sidon, from which they derived both their praise and their name.”

Tertullian is to be understood as speaking of this kind of clothing in book *On the Veiling of Virgins*, chapter 17:

> “The pagan women of Arabia will judge you, for they cover not only their heads but their entire faces, and, with one eye balanced, are content to enjoy half the light rather than expose their whole face.”

Tacitus mentions this device—or rather this hooked form of seduction—when he writes of Sabina Poppaea in book XIII of the *Annals*:

> “She rarely went out in public, and then with part of her face veiled, either so that she might not satisfy the gaze or because this was considered becoming.”

This veil was well known and customary among Jewish women, so that they could be recognized by it.

Tertullian again asserts in book *On the Crown of the Soldier*, chapter 4, that it was a kind of garment, not merely a veil. He draws this from Genesis XXIV, verse 65, concerning Rebecca, whom Isaac was approaching:

> “But she took up her cloak and covered herself.”

Xantes Pagninus translates it as “covering,” and it must have been large, since it wrapped around the head and the entire body, like the *palla* among the Latins. Ruth was commanded to spread such a garment for Boaz, so that she might receive six measures of barley in it, Ruth III, verse 5. In Greek one reads περίζωμα, that is, a covering garment.

There are indeed garments used as coverings, especially in Spain, where they were commonly worn. Accursius understood the jurist Aristo, quoted by Ulpian in the law *Argumento*, 27, Digest, concerning gold and silver bequeathed, to have been speaking of these when he explains the word *coactilia*:

> “They are garments that constrict because of their tightness, as in Spain.”

Lazarus Bailius, in *On the Art of Clothing*, chapter 21, adopts another view. He says that *coactilia* means garments more tightly compacted from thick wool, rejecting John Baptist Egnatius’s interpretation in his notes on *Pertinax* in Aelius Spartianus, namely that they were garments such as *thoracomachi*, worn over cuirasses.

Pliny provides support for this in book VIII, chapter 48, where he writes:

> “They make garments from wool that has been compacted by itself.”

The ἀφέλετρα also belong to this class, namely protective coverings for horses. Nicetas Choniates mentions them, as does Leo in constitution 6, section 8, concerning military horses. They were called *feltra*, as our people call them *fieltros*, felts.

Thus the ancient laws of the Bavarians say:

> “If anyone in the army steals anything—a shepherd’s crook, a halter, a bridle, a felt, or violates anything whatever …”

Pliny says that such materials, when treated with vinegar, resist iron. Hence, in an ancient inscription, a craftsman of felts is called a *coactor*:

> **To the departed spirits. To Lucius Cornelius Januarius, who lived seventeen years, a wool-worker and felt-maker.**

And in the Glossary:

> Πιλωτόν: compacted felt; Πιλωτοποιός: maker of compacted felt.

See Jacobus Cujacius, *Observations*, book V, chapter 2, and Nicolaus Rigaltius in his *Greek-Barbarous Glossary*, under the word Ἀφέλετρα. A person who makes or sells compacted garments is also called a wool-worker and felt-maker. Thus on a very ancient stone:

> **M. L. Lariscus, wool-worker and felt-maker.**

Enough concerning covering garments.

Saint Eulogius himself likewise used “linen garments” for the *sindon* when speaking of Saint Columba in book III, chapter 10, folio 69, of the *Memorial of the Saints*:

> “Without delay, since the corpse was dressed in linen”—that is, in a sindon—“the rulers ordered it to be put into a basket and thrown into the riverbed.”

At first those Arab women who came to Spain with their husbands or lovers in disguised clothing wore the masculine sindon, that is, the garment common to men and women, but in the manner in which men customarily wore it. King Miramolin therefore forbade them to bring such women with him.

Our Julianus says in the *Chronicle*, no. 620:

> “The Saracens use the same garments which they brought with them from Africa; they had come here with their men in disguised clothing. For Miramolin had forbidden women to cross over into Spain. Saracen lovers brought some girls in male dress, of the kind now worn by the women of Baetica and formerly also by Christian women living among the Moors. They call them *mantos* and *almalafas*.”

Concerning the women of Toledo, in the *Adversaria*, no. 416:

> “The women wear *cyclades*, slippers, and little turbans on their heads. They wear cloaks variegated with different colors over the turbans; these hang down to their ankles. They use silk bodices, curl their hair in the Gothic fashion, and arrange it with curling irons.”

Concerning linen and silk sindons, Brother Alphonsus de Spina writes in book III, “On the Jewish War,” of the *Fortress of Faith*, folio 222:

> “When that year and appointed day came, they rose very early and went to their synagogues to worship God, dressed in white linen or silk sindons, as is customary on the Day of Atonement, namely, on the tenth day of the seventh month.”

Similar to sindons were *theristra*, coverings or cloaks “which, hanging down from the head over the shoulders, served as veils.” In Genesis XXIV, verse 63, concerning Rebecca, the Vulgate reads:

> “But she quickly took up her cloak and covered herself.”

The Septuagint translates:

> Ἡ δὲ λαβοῦσα τὸ θέριστρον περιεβάλετο.

> “But she took the *theristrum* and wrapped herself in it.”

The Vulgate retains the word *theristrum* in Genesis XXXVIII, verse 14, speaking of Tamar:

> “She removed the garments of her widowhood, took a *theristrum*, changed her clothing, and sat at the crossroads.”

Saint Cyprian, book III *To Quirinus*, question 36, renders the passage:

> “Tamar covered herself with a cloak and adorned herself.”

Saint Jerome explains it in the Hebrew traditions:

> “A *theristrum* is called a cloak; it is also a type of Arabian garment with which the women of that province are still veiled.”

In his letter to Laeta, *On the Education of a Daughter*, he appears to take *theristrum* for *calyptra*, a covering of the head:

> “Let them not take away,” he says, “the *theristrum* of modesty.”

He explains it more fully in his commentary on Isaiah III:

> “*Theristra*, which we may call little cloaks, are the coverings in which Rebecca was wrapped in Genesis XXIV, and in which the women of Arabia and Mesopotamia are still covered. In Hebrew they are called *redidim*, in Greek θέριστρα, from the fact that in summer—that is, in the heat—they protect women’s bodies. The same word occurs in Hebrew in both places, chapter XXIV, verse 65, and chapter XXXVIII, verse 14. Saint Jerome translates it as *pallium*, cloak, and Saint Pagninus, following him, translates it as *theristrum* in his *Thesaurus*.”

Saint Basil gives an especially appropriate explanation in his commentary on Isaiah III, from the latest Paris edition of 1618:

> “A *theristrum* is an outer garment which women wrapped around themselves during the summer so that they would not be oppressed by excessive heat. Thus in Genesis we learn that Rebecca wore a *theristrum* when she went to meet Isaac.”

Our Luitprand mentions the *theristrum* in book III, chapter 5, of *Deeds Performed throughout Europe*:

> “For I think that, when they saw him covered in the Greek fashion with a *cheristrum*—read *theristrum*—and dressed in unusual clothing, they believed him to be not a man but a monster.”

He mentions it more than once in his *Embassy*.

Jacob Gretser of the Society of Jesus, with his customary learning, lists further examples in book I, chapter 7, page 76, of his posthumous *Various Matters*. It was an extremely fine and translucent garment, like the sindon. Perhaps the following Greek verse, published among the ancient Oracles together with the Sibylline Oracles, page 61, under the care and labor of John Opsopaeus, encompasses both:

> Σινδόνας ἀμπέταβον, νεφέλην λῦσόν τε δοχεῖα  
> *Sindonas laxato, nebulam solve, et acceptabulum.*

> “Loosen the sindons, release the cloud, and the receptacle.”

Petronius Arbiter called a linen cloud and woven wind, speaking in the person of the mime-poet P.:

> “It is fitting to clothe the bride in woven wind;”

> “To expose her naked in a linen cloud.”

Such garments were devised by feminine luxury. Tertullian says in *On the Apparel of Women*:

> “In these garments there is, I do not say, no help for the body, but no protection for modesty. When she has put them on, a woman will scarcely swear that she is not naked.”

Seneca mocks this in book VII of *On Benefits*, chapter 9:

> “Our matrons display no more of themselves in the bedroom to adulterers than in public.”

The illustrious Cardinal Cajetan mentions this passage in his commentary on the *Second Part of the Second Part* of Saint Thomas, question 169, article 2, response to objections 1–5, concerning adornment.

The Philosopher attacks matrons who were covered with garments like prostitutes. Although the latter were covered by such garments, they walked about almost naked. Hence Horace, in book I, satire 2, advises in satirical fashion that one should avoid matrons, since from them one derives more harm through labor than profit from the thing itself:

> “Cease to pursue matrons: from that pursuit one draws  
> More painful toil than one plucks profit from the thing.  
> Nor, amid snowy-white and greenish jewels, even if this is yours, Choerillus,  
> is the thigh or leg more tender, straighter, or more shapely  
> than is very often that of a toga-clad woman.  
> Add to this that she displays her merchandise without cosmetics;  
> she openly shows what she has for sale.”

And shortly afterward:

> “The other has no obstacle: in Coan silk  
> You can almost see her naked; let her not have  
> An ugly leg or an unsightly foot,  
> So that the side can be measured by the eye.”

They exposed to view not merely the breast but the entire body through that fine covering. Cajetan solves the question from this custom.

Ezekiel also sheds light on the matter, chapter XVI, verse 7:

> “Your breasts have swelled, your hair has grown, and you were naked and full of shame.”

He says “naked,” that is, dressed in transparent garments of the sort prostitutes used.

Martial, as is his custom, wittily praises while reproving this in book VIII, epigram 68:

> “Thus a woman’s body shines through silk.”

Against this garment, though thin, yet a sharp stimulus to lust, Saint Jerome instructed the modest girl in his letter to Laeta:

> “Let her prepare such garments,” he says, “as repel the cold, not such as strip naked the bodies they clothe.”

The Septuagint translators called garments of this kind τὰ διαφανῆ, λακωνικά in Isaiah III, verse 21—that is, “transparent Laconian garments.” Suidas likewise explains διαφανῆ χιτώνια, “transparent tunics,” as τὰ ἴχνη δ’ ὧν διαφαίνεται τὰ σώματα τῶν γυναικῶν, “thin garments through which women’s bodies shine.”

They were called Laconian from the name of the Lacedaemonians, because the lasciviousness and indecency of the Lacedaemonians in exposing women’s bodies by every means was notably—and deservedly—detestable beyond that of other peoples. Kimchi, in his Lexicon, says that undergarments or tunics were called this because they were thin and delicate, and because the body showed through them on account of their excessive fineness.

Jacob Gretser collects further material in the place cited above. So does John Filesacus in *The Proper Wife*, chapter 4.

These *theristra* were used in two ways: either for wearing or for spreading over beds. Julius Pollux, book VII, chapter 13, speaking of the *peplos*, says:

> “The use of the *peplos* is twofold: namely, for putting on and for spreading over something.”

The Septuagint reading in the aforementioned passage of Isaiah III, verse 21, clearly suggests both uses:

> Καὶ θέριστρα κατάκλιτα.

> “And reclining *theristra*.”

Saint Basil explains:

> Ἅ δὲ νῦν διαβάλλει ὁ λόγος, θέριστρα λέγεται, τὰ ἐν τῶν κατακλίνεσθαι δι’ ὑπερβολὴν τρυφῆς ταῖς κλίναις ἐπιβαλλόμενα.

> “Those things which Scripture now censures are called *theristra*: the coverings spread over beds so that people might recline more softly because of their excessive luxury.”

Martial speaks of the sindon in book II, epigram 16:

> “Zoilus is sick; the blankets produce this fever.  
> If he becomes well, what will scarlet garments do?  
> What does a couch from the Nile matter? What does a couch dyed  
> With fragrant sindon matter?  
> What does sickness reveal except that wealth is foolish?”

Finally, with a *theristrum*, just as with a sindon and a *palla*, the entire body was wrapped. D. L.

Nunilo and Alodia are suffering this year, while I am alive, at the fortress of Wergetum, that is, Castellón; in the wine-making camps in Bastetania.

[Col. 1125] **353.** A council was held in Spain, in the city of Zaragoza, commonly called the Augustan Council, consisting of twenty-five bishops.

DCCCCXCI. DCCCCLIII.

**354.** Adelagus—read Adelgarius—archbishop of Bremen, legate of the Apostolic See, flourished greatly in virtue, learning, and religion.

DCCCCXCIII. DCCCCLV.

**355.** Bruno, brother of the emperor Otto the Great, archbishop of Cologne, was regarded as a man distinguished in every respect.

[Col. 1127] **356.** John XII succeeded Pope Agapetus in the See of Saint Peter.

DCCCCXCV. DCCCCLVII.

**357.** A council was convened this year in the city of Ravenna.

DCCCCXCVI. DCCCLVIII.

**358.** The Council of Ingelheim, consisting of sixteen bishops.

DCCCCXCVIII. DCCCCLX.

**359. [Note: [Col. 1127A]**

The Council of Zaragoza, which Luitprand also mentions here, is mentioned by Onuphrius under the year of the Lord 951, and was held under John, bishop of Toledo. P. H.]

Smaragdus and Serlofridegodus—read Ceolfridus—English Benedictine monks, men outstanding in character and distinguished theologians.

**360. [Note: [Col. 1127A]**

He admits that the lives circulated without an author’s name at the end of the *Chronicle of Saint Ildefonsus* were added by Saint Felix, bishop of Toledo. He says that Verecundus, bishop of Utica in Africa, had been a bishop and archpriest of Toledo. P. H.]

The lives appended to Ildefonsus’s *Chronicle of Illustrious Men* were composed by Felix, archbishop of Toledo. They begin: “Although above very many …”

He wrote twelve lives: of Xystus, Roman pontiff; Macrobius the deacon; Philastrius, bishop of Brescia; Theodore, bishop of Mopsuestia; Tyrannius; Rufinus; Verecundus—also called Vergundus—bishop of Utica in Africa and formerly archpriest of Toledo; Victorinus, bishop of León; Idacius, bishop of Lamego; Eusebius, bishop of Dor; Cerealis of Castulo; Ferrandus, deacon of Carthage in Africa; Peter, bishop of Lleida; and Marcellinus, a schismatic presbyter.

**361. [Note: [Col. 1127A]**

He teaches that Saint Julian, bishop of Toledo, wrote the life of Saint Ildefonsus, the most deserving bishop of that same city. The *Chronicle* circulated under the name of Vulsa is also Julian’s, except that the material concerning Witiza was added by Gunteric, although he leaves this last point as uncertain. I. D.]

Saint Julian wrote the life of Saint Ildefonsus. Felix additionally wrote the life of Saint Julian, bishop of Toledo, and also appended it to the *Chronicle*, which begins:

> “In the name of the Lord: here begins the Chronicle which Saint Julian composed.”

The passage, “Witiza was born,” or “was obtained”—the variant is *nactus*—is attributed by some to Gunteric. No certain evidence of an addition has so far been found.

**362.** Velascus, bishop of Alavend, or, alternatively, of Albige, wrote the life of Salla, abbot of Alavend, alternatively Salvius, abbot and bishop of Albige, his disciple, who lies at his feet.

**363.** Saints Godina and Gervasius died in Lusitania this year, on the first day of October.

**364. [Note: [Col. 1127B]**

I myself wrote this. I did not find this work of Luitprand, although I searched for it carefully. “Bishop” should be read in place of “archbishop,” for in the period when Saint Peter flourished the See of Compostela had not yet been raised to an archbishopric; this occurred only in 1096, through the efforts of Dalmatius.

Thus in Baronius’s martyrology, under 10 September:

> “At Compostela, Saint Peter the bishop, who shone with many virtues and miracles.”

Earlier, in Usuardus, the reading was faulty, though it was removed by Molanus’s corrections:

> “On the same day, 10 September, Saint Peter the archbishop, who shone with many virtues and miracles.”

Our Julianus states the matter clearly in the *Chronicle*, no. 510:

> “Hymn: *Salve, Regina, mater misericordiae*, composed in Greek by the apostles and translated from Greek into Latin by the most holy man Peter, bishop of Compostela.”

And no. 517:

> “The memory of Saint Peter, Benedictine monk and bishop of Compostela, numbered among the saints, flourishes. He is celebrated on 10 September.”

Some assert that he was the author of the hymn *Salve, Regina*. Claudius de Rota says in chapter 137:

> “Hermannus Contractus the German composed the antiphon *Alma Redemptoris Mater*; and Simon Bar-Jona; but Peter, bishop of Compostela, composed *Salve, Regina*.”

Antonius Demochares gives the same testimony in book IV of *On the Institution of the Christian Religion*:

> “Hermannus Contractus the German, inventor of the astrolabe, also composed those sequences: *Rex omnipotens*, *Sanctus Spiritus*, *Ave Maria*, *Alma Redemptoris*, and *Simon Bar-Jona*. Peter, bishop of Compostela, composed the following: *Salve, Regina, mater misericordiae, vita, dulcedo et spes nostra, salve*.”

Durandus, in the *Rationale of the Divine Offices*, supports this.

Our Julianus, however, recognizes him as translator, not author, and says that the apostles composed this holy hymn. He supports this with no slight foundation from the words of Saint Bernard—or, better, if one reads it so, of Dom Bernard, archbishop of Toledo—taken from the first of his five sermons on *Salve, Regina*. Gillotius published these sermons separately from Saint Bernard’s other works in the Paris edition, volume II, folio 367, where he believes that the author was not Saint Bernard but Dom Bernard.

The words are:

> “We have taken up, brothers, this sweet song and most noble melody, which our order sings with the greatest devotion four times a year in honor of holy Mary, to stir up our devotion, because it is filled with a special sweetness and we repeat it through continual meditation. For that song came forth from the highest lips. It has a foundation: ‘Its foundation is in the holy mountains.’ Its foundation is the sweetness of inward delight. And where is this found, if not in the holy mountains? That is, in our minds”—read “mountains,” as above, for “minds” does not fit the sense—“composed by the saints, instituted by the saints, and therefore rightly to be repeated by the saints.”

Thus far Dom Bernard.

From this and other evidence it is clear that the hymn was composed by the holy mountains. These are none other than the twelve most holy apostles. This divine song is rightly said to come from them and to have been poured forth from the highest lips.

The apostles were called mountains, as nearly all the Fathers interpret the words of Psalm 86, “Its foundations are in the holy mountains.” Arnobius says:

> “According to the foundation of the apostles.”

Haymo states the matter more explicitly and gives the reason:

> “The mountains are the apostles, because our faith is founded upon them.”

Cassiodorus explains it differently:

> “They are mountains because of the firmness of their faith and the excellence of their life.”

Ludolfus likewise says:

> “For there the faith of the Church was first established. They are mountains because of the sublimity of their faith; holy because of the purity of their life. Through their faith, teaching, and example the Church was founded.”

Saint Augustine treats the matter more fully in the same place and says that Saint Paul understood it in the same way in Ephesians II, verse 20:

> “Built upon the foundation of the apostles.”

Saint Ambrose gives the same testimony in his sermon 22 on Psalm 118, in his commentary on Saint Luke XVII, and in his book *On Noah*, chapter 32. Saint Augustine again does so in his first tractate on Saint John and in his commentary on Psalm 35; Saint Jerome in his commentary on Psalm 45 and on Isaiah XIV; and Saint Gregory in book XII of the *Moralia*, chapter 11.

The most learned men were also called giants. This occurs frequently in Sacred Scripture, where the term does not refer to men endowed with enormous bodily size but to those who excelled in holiness, wisdom, and admirable dignity.

Jacobus Boulduc collects further material in *On the Church before the Law*, chapters 8 and 9. He interprets Deuteronomy II, verses 10 and 12, and cites the Vulgate, which translates the names *Nephilim*, *Zuzim*, and *Rephaim* as “giants” in this sense.

Most recently, Louis Cresollius of the Society of Jesus has assembled much learned material in his *Mystagogue*, or *On the Discipline of Sacred Persons*, book I, chapter 13, section 1 and following. There he asserts that ecclesiastical persons are prefigured by mountains in Sacred Scripture and draws the truth from a varied store of authorities.

Neither would St Bernard (to take up the thread again, if conjecture is permissible) have said that the hymn was composed by saints unless he attributed to it greater authority than to Hermannus Contractus’s hymn. Moreover, the phrase itself indicates this; for it is Greek and Hebrew: in their dialect they used the genitive in place of an adjective. I said in my *Pentacontarchus*, chapter 9: “men of blood,” in place of “bloodthirsty men”; “God of peace and mercy,” in place of “merciful God.” St Paul, in his Epistle to the Romans, chapter 7, verse 6, called it “the law of death,” meaning “deadly.” And in Ecclesiasticus, chapter 44, verse 27, one finds “men of mercy,” meaning “merciful men.” Thus, in the divine hymn, “Queen of mercy” (as St Bernard, St Bonaventure, Martinus de Magistris, and the ancient breviaries read it) means “merciful Queen.” Canisius was therefore not without reason, in book 5 of *On the Blessed Virgin*, chapter 13, after affirming that Hermannus Contractus composed the hymn and this most sweet melody, to show himself wavering and almost to appear to retract when he writes that, even if Hermannus did not compose it, he nevertheless published it—as though withdrawing from his initial opinion. His words are:

> “Although it can plainly be perceived from other and more ancient ecclesiastical writers that Mary had long before been saluted and publicly honored with praises similar to, and even more excellent than, those contained in this very hymn, whoever first composed or published this hymn within the last six hundred years adds nothing new. Note the disjunctive wording: ‘composed or published.’”

Where one reads *Mansonii*, or *Monsorii*, it should be written *Monsoncii*. Thus in the manuscript *Compostellan History*:

> “In his honor, therefore—namely, Pelagius’s—Peter of Monsoncio, that is, the abbot of Antealtaria, was appointed by divine providence.”

For he was called Peter Martinez of Monsoncio; Martin was his father, and he devoted himself to the religious life in the monastery of Saint Mary of Monsonço. Stephanus de Garibay gives a different account in his *Historical Compendium*, book 9, chapter 36, folio 473, where he calls him Peter of Monsorio. P. Joannes Mariana, *History of Spain*, book 8, chapter 8, folio 388, column 2, calls him Pedro Mansorio. Master Antonius de Yepes, a member of the Benedictine order, gathers nearly all these matters fully and learnedly in his *General History*, century or volume 5, for the year 986 after Christ was born, folio 216, page 2; he should be consulted without fail. Nevertheless, in support of his opinion—though generally and under a veil of words—he cites Petrus Bergomensis, book 12 of the *Supplement to the Chronicles*. Bergomensis, however, adopts the contrary view in the year of Christ 1049, folio 318; for he admits that Hermannus Contractus was the author of the hymn *Salve, Regina*.

I nevertheless considered two points worthy of notice. First, Peter Monsoncio was bishop of Compostela—not, as Fr. Alfonsus de Yepes records, in the year of Christ 986. Pelagius, his predecessor, having been removed from the see after the advice of the nobles had been taken, Peter himself was elected while Beremund II was reigning; and, according to the almost unanimous reckoning of all, Beremund did not live beyond the year 983. Nor was Peter exercising episcopal authority in the year 981, as P. Joannes Mariana writes in book 8 of his *History of Spain*, chapter 8, folio 388, column 2. For, as Stephanus de Garibay and Zamalloa report in the place cited above, with the manuscript *Compostellan History* leading and preceding them, he obtained the dignity in the year 963 or 964. Our Luitprandus supports this, for he traced Peter Monsoncio’s life and brought his own account to an end around the year 973. Our friend P. Franciscus de Bivar proves the point learnedly in *Censure of Works*, section 7. Therefore Peter could by no means have been appointed in Pelagius’s place in 986, as Fr. Alfonsus de Yepes supposes. Ambrosius de Morales does not contradict me; indeed, he supports me in book 17 of his *History*, chapter 20, where he records that in the year 999 Pelagius, son of Count Roderic Velasquez, was removed from the see and that Peter Monsoncio had already become his successor, although he does not assign a year.

Second, it should be noted in blue rubrication that the author wrote certain matters at the end of the *Chronicle* as appendices or supplementary pieces, as was customary among writers of that age—not arranged chronographically by years or aligned with exact chronological sequence, especially since the account was intended to enumerate his own works rather than to compose a history. Thus Julianus, at the end of his *Chronicle*, lists everything he had written. Hence even the most fastidious reader will not object to the conclusion that Luitprandus’s *Chronicle* ends in the year 960, while P. Monsoncio was still alive in 963, although thirteen years intervene between the year 960 and Luitprandus’s death. During those years Luitprandus could have brought Monsoncio’s life to an end and written of his miraculous deeds.

Girardus, the author of the second and third parts of the manuscript *Compostellan History*, which I value highly, again gives us this same election of Monsoncio in these words:

> “That Beremund, having taken the advice of great men, expelled the aforementioned Pelagius from the see and ordered Peter, son of a certain Martin, a wise monk of the monastery of Monsoncio and venerable abbot of the arch-presbytery before the altar, to be elected by all the elders as the tenth bishop and to be consecrated.”

These words strongly prepare the way for correcting Luitprandus’s text, which was badly disfigured by ignorant copyists. For when they found written *F. Marti.*, taking the *F* for an initial letter and reading *martyris* (“of the martyr”) instead of *Martini* (“of Martin”), the Italians falsely wrote *martyris*. He was a Spaniard from the province of Galicia, and he died at Compostela not as a martyr but as a confessor, as the ecclesiastical records themselves proclaim. [D. L.]

I wrote the life of St Peter, archbishop of Compostela, surnamed Mansonius, an Italian martyr [read: son of Martin].

[Col. 1129] 365. [Note: [Col. 1130D]

365. What happened concerning the books of the *Moralia*: St Gregory had sent part of them to Leander, while the rest had entirely disappeared. P. II.]

The portion of the books of the *Moralia* that Leander himself had brought was carried from Constantinople to Spain. Taio [elsewhere Tico; D. L.: Above, no. 100, we spoke of this Taio, bishop of Zaragoza] was sent for the remaining books; and this portion, as Rodericus seems to think, was lost. Only this part was then at Rome; afterward the remaining books were brought over, and St Isidore mentions them in his account of Leander.

366. [Note: [Col. 1130D]

366. Concerning the diptychs of the churches of Spain, Luitprandus presents many matters beautifully. In particular, there are two diptychs beginning in the year 309, for certain bishops distinguished by holiness are listed here, both outside Spain and within Spain. Outside Spain: Hilary, bishop of Poitiers; Athanasius of Alexandria; Martin of Tours; Ambrose, bishop of Milan; and Augustine, bishop of Hippo in Africa. These are outside Spain. Within Spain: Leander, Isidore, David, Julianus of Seville, Julianus of Toledo the doctor, Peter of Ilerda, and Peter the Fair of Toledo. This follows the practice of the Greeks, who at the beginning of their diptychs placed certain catholic pontiffs with whom they were accustomed to communicate according to catholic custom. P. H.]

“For the spirits of those who rest.” First concerning the word, then concerning the custom. The Latin word is *pausa*, which the ancients used. Lucilius, book 1 of the *Satires*:

> “When this had been said, he makes a pause in speaking.”

Plautus, in the *Poenulus*, act 6:

> “When he was unwilling to be content with what was enough,  
> I made a pause.”

Lucretius, book 3:

> “When once the cold pause of life has followed him.”

The word is derived, with only slight alteration, from the Greek source *παύω* (*pauō*), meaning “to rest,” whose future is *παύσω* (*pausō*). Hence the Latin verb *pauso*. Plautus again uses the verb in the *Trinummus*, act 4: “By pausing, you have defeated your chastiser.” In the Greek-Latin *Glosses*: “He pauses,” *ἀναπαύεται*, “and he gives rest,” *ἀναπαύει*. Obertus Gifanius, in his notes on Lucretius under the word *pausa*, admits that the Romans took it from the Greeks, but says that the Greeks called it *παῦλα*.

Thus “for the spirits of those who rest” means the same as “for the spirits of those who are at rest,” that is, the dead. The word was commonly used in the Gothic period. St Eugenius writes in his *Epigram*:

> “Now a pause from evils,”

meaning “for the spirits of those who rest,” that is, those who have obtained rest and have now ceased from their labors. “Henceforth,” says the Spirit in the *Apocalypse*, “let them rest from their labors; for their works follow them.”

The custom, moreover, was to pray for the living and the dead; hence the two diptychs, about which elsewhere. I shall nevertheless add that a diptych exists in the Isidorian tablets, which P. Hieronymus de la Higuera saw printed one hundred and twenty years ago. In it these same words occurred:

> “For the spirits of those who rest.”

Immediately there followed a prayer composed by the priest:

> “Receive, good Jesus, on this feast of the birth of your apostle James, the vows of those who offer them, and grant refreshment to the spirits of the departed, so that, through his intercession with you, your grace may bestow forgiveness upon the dead.”

The ancient Church did not borrow this memorial from the Salii’s hymn—as Casaubonus falsely maintained in his notes on Athenaeus, book 6, chapter 14—in which the Romans placed in song the names of those whom they wished to honor exceptionally, but from the Old Testament, as the most learned Father Heribertus Rosweydus asserts, following St Dionysius, in the *Onomasticon* published at the end of the *Lives of the Fathers*, under the word *Diptych*, page 776, column 2. Those pagans appropriated and distorted our sacred practices from the divine books, as we have often said in various places and in the *Pentocontarchus*, chapter 26. I now add to the testimonies cited there Tertullian, in the *Apologeticus against the Nations*, chapter 47:

> “Which poet, which sophist, has not drunk entirely from the fountain of the prophets?”

He develops this at greater length and says at the end of the chapter:

> “Whence, I ask you, do philosophers or poets derive such close likenesses? Only from our mysteries.”

Concerning the diptychs, see Wilhelm Lindanus, bishop of Ghent, in his *Annotations on the Liturgy of St Peter the Apostle*. There he says that he saw the diptychs of the Church of St George, situated on the shore of the Ocean Sea, or of Biscay, at Portugalete. See also the recently published Facundus, bishop of Hermianum in the African province, *For the Defense of the Three Chapters of the Council of Chalcedon*, book 4, chapter 1, and P. Jacobus Sirmondus of the Society of Jesus, page 142. An earlier, truly learned excursus was made by P. Christophorus Browerus of the same Society of Jesus in his notes on Venantius Honorius Clementianus Fortunatus, book 10, letter 7, page 229. Among jurists, see Guido Panciroli, *Treasury of Various Readings*, book 1, chapter 28, page 30. E.; consult also what concerns Julianus in the collection of various poems, page 158, and the short essay that I arranged to have published as a colophon. [D. L.]

The churches of the Spaniards possess many diptychs known to them. The Toletan diptych, from the time of the captivity, has the same opening that all the others have from the year 360:

> “For the spirits of the resting saints: bishops Hilary, Athanasius, Martin, Ambrose, Augustine, Fulgentius, Leander, Isidore, David, Julianus, likewise Julianus, Peter, likewise Peter.”

From Felix through Julianus, after Bonitus III, bishops are listed who greatly aided the affairs of Spain: namely, Hilary, bishop of Poitiers; Athanasius of Alexandria; Martin of Tours; Ambrose of Milan; Augustine of Hippo; Fulgentius, from Carthage in Hispania Spartaria, bishop of Écija; Leander; Isidore; David; Julianus of Seville; Julianus of Toledo the doctor; Peter of Ilerda; and Peter the Fair. This follows the custom of the Greeks, who at the beginning of episcopal diptychs placed bishops of other churches, distinguished men with whom the bishops of their own churches had at some time communicated. The Ethiopian bishops did the same.

367. [Note: [Col. 1132B]

367. It is said that formerly only the primate of Spain, namely the bishop of Toledo, possessed the right of the pallium, just as the Carthaginian primate in Africa and the Thessalonian primate in Macedonia enjoyed the same right. P. H.]

The right of the pallium in Spain. The pallium, in which resides the fullness of pontifical office—as Innocent III says in chapter *Nisi*, concerning the authority and use of the pallium—is an archiepiscopal insignia. For this reason Luitprandus recognizes it as the distinctive vestment and jurisdictional emblem of the Toletan primates. Many writers have said much about it. In his customary learned and comprehensive manner, Augustinus Barbosa gathers the material in his *Collections on the Decretals*, under the title “On the Authority and Use of the Pallium.” He had earlier discussed it in his *Pastoral*, or *On the Office and Power of a Bishop*, part 1, title 3, chapter 1, number 20, page 215, column 1, and reference 50, section 3. Nicolaus Alemannus brings many further points from ecclesiastical antiquity to light in his *Historical Dissertation on the Lateran Walls*, chapter 10, numbers 72, 73, 79, and 81.

The supreme pontiff was accustomed to give the pallium after the council had been celebrated at which this matter had been discussed. Julianus, in his *Chronicle*, number 612:

> “Urban honored St Bernard, archbishop of Toledo, exceedingly. In the council of Piacenza he consecrated him, together with certain patriarchs, and in the presence of the entire council gave him the pallium.”

St Bernard confirms this in the *Life of St Malachy*, under Pope Innocent II, where he teaches that the holy man went to Rome after the year 1130. When Malachy had received the office of apostolic legate, he requested the pallium, and the supreme pontiff replied. His words are:

> “After this,” says St Bernard, “Malachy asks that the establishment of the new metropolitan see be confirmed and that the pallia of both sees be given to him. He immediately received the privilege of confirmation. But concerning the pallia, the supreme pontiff said, ‘The matter must be handled with greater solemnity. When bishops, clergy, and the leading men of the land have been summoned, you shall celebrate a general council; and then, with the consent and common vote of all, you shall request the pallium through suitable persons, and it shall be given to you.’ Then, removing the mitre from his own head, he placed it on Malachy’s head; he also gave him the stole and maniple, which he himself used when offering the sacrifice.” [D. L.]

The bishop of Toledo alone, as primate of Spain, formerly possessed the right of the pallium in Spain.

[Col. 1133] 368. [Note: [Col. 1134]

368. Even in the midst of the captivity, obedience and reverence were always shown to the Toletan bishops as primates of Spain. P. H.]

Even in the midst of the captivity, the Spanish bishops always maintained obedience and reverence toward the Toletan bishop as patriarch and, from the beginning of the Church, as primate of all Spain.

[Col. 1133]

# LUITPRANDUS’S ADVERSARIA

[Col. 1133A] 1. There are two places called Legio. One is called Seventh, Twin, Pious, and Fortunate; among the Goths it is the flower of cities. It was a royal and episcopal seat, subject to none of the Spanish bishops except the Roman pope. The other is bathed by the river Urbicus and is called Benavento. It obeyed the bishop of Astorga and now obeys the bishop of Oviedo. This is called Urban Legio.

2. Legio Gemina, an episcopal see, was subject to Braga until the time of Pope St Lucius. He is believed to have exempted the bishop of León from the bishop of Braga because the former had worked marvelously with words, writings, and deeds against his neighboring bishop Basilides of Astorga, who had fallen away.

3. [Note: [Col. 1133C] 3. Aquae Quintianae, etc. See Ortelius under the word *Aquae Quintiae*, whose words are: “Aquae Quintiae, or Quintianae, *ὕδατα κουΐντινα* [Quintian waters] in Ptolemy, a town of the Seurri in Tarraconian Spain. Molezio calls it Aquecaldes.”]

Aquae Quintianae, in the Lucensian part of Galicia—whose peoples Ptolemy mentions when listing them—are a certain spring on Mount Tebiceius which ebbs and flows and has waves like the Ocean, near the river Loria, commonly called Lor. When the praetor Quintus Metellus saw it, he marveled at it before the birth of Christ, in the year 140, and gave it and the neighboring town the name Aquae Quintianae. The river Loria is seen flowing nearby into the river Simlia [elsewhere Silum].

4. In the Spanish era 868, in the 830th year from the Lord’s birth, the most holy virgin Lumbrosa lived in the town of Cea. She attended the parish in the ruined monastery of the holy martyrs Facundus and Primitivus together with Mozarabic Christians, in great holiness of life. She remained in that parish until King Alfonso restored the monastery; she was then transferred there. She died not long before its restoration. Her relics are visited with the greatest popular veneration. She is honored on 1 November and lies in a tomb above two columns.

5. In Carthage Spartaria, St Constantine the Confessor, a most distinguished man renowned for the glory of many virtues, died as a confessor under Valerian on 11 March. On the same day, the Passion of the holy martyrs Heraclius and Zosimus, who suffered there for the faith of Christ, is commemorated.

6. As I was crossing the Pyrenees along the borders of Spain, I discovered that St Felix is honored in the city of Spalato, or Ispalo. Sent there by the Spanish bishops, he preached the Gospel and completed his martyrdom under Diocletian on the twelfth day before the Kalends of June. Some think that this is the same city as Spartulacum; they are mistaken, for in the town of Anzanego [elsewhere Onzanego] a holy bishop and martyr is honored. This Felix is believed to have been the man who, together with thirteen other bishop-confessors, attended the national Council of Elvira and presided as bishop of Guadix. He was sent by the Spanish bishops to strengthen the Spanish peoples in the faith because of his fervent charity, prudence, knowledge, and charm. He went to the Celtiberians, the Vascones, and those dwelling near the Pyrenees.

7. St Patrick, celebrated on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of April, was not bishop of Auvergne. He is believed to have been a man from Málaga who attended the Council of Elvira; later, while going elsewhere, he came to Auvergne and died there.

[Col. 1134B] 8. At Heraclea in Spain, a city called Calpe, the triumph of the martyrdom of St Januarius, bishop of Sarabria [elsewhere Salaria or Salerno], together with his companions, is commemorated on 7 January. Dexter mentions him and says that he suffered under Diocletian. He was a bishop who attended the Council of Elvira.

9. The Latins called Murcia; the Goths called it Bigastrum; the Moors called it Acatha, probably in the year 900. The bishop Thyestes of Bergara came there, died, and lies there [elsewhere: “and was martyred there”].

10. Melantius, or Melanius, born in Greater Britain, came to Rome and was sent by St Stephen to Rouen, where he exercised the episcopal office for some time. Later, for some unknown reason, he went to Athens; with Pope Sixtus he came to Toledo, where he succeeded Palmatius, or Paulatus, in the episcopal see. He attended the Council of Elvira. After the year 305 he returned to Rouen and died there most holily in 310; he was buried there on the eleventh day before the Kalends of November.

11. At the village of Cassina, which the Moors called Villa Castin, on the borders of Carpetania, St Nicasius, first bishop of Rouen, suffered together with his companions on 11 October under Domitian while preaching there. Fescenninus, by Domitian’s order [elsewhere: “Fescenninus was sent by Domitian, by order …”], sent men to kill them in Spain.

12. In the year of the Lord 302, when Constantius Chlorus and Galerius Maximianus were Caesars and consuls for the fourth time, on 3 April, Good Friday, or the day of the Lord’s Passion, persecution was proclaimed throughout the whole world. In the sixteenth year of Melantius, bishop of Toledo, under the same consuls, in the same month and on the same day, the Toletan church of the Blessed Virgin Mary of the Assumption was demolished. It had been erected by St Elpidius and enlarged in its dimensions by Blessed Martyr Marcellus. It was leveled to the ground by [the reading appears to be *Teucris*, but I would willingly read *Duumviris*], at the order of Diocletian, under P. . . . Dacianus, governor of Spain, who is said to have presided over the demolition.

From that time it is believed that the sacred assembly came to be held throughout the world in caves: at Rome in the cemeteries; at Augustobriga, called Cobisa by the Moors, at the edge of Carpetania, in a cavern; at Toledo in the cave commonly called Hercules’ Cave, built in Roman fashion; at Libana in Celtiberia, in caves called, because of their hollowness, “pierced caves”; and likewise in other caverns.

[Col. 1135B] 13. It cannot be said how great a collapse this demolition and burning of the books brought upon the spirits of the Christians. The holy man Melantius placed the Toletan books in a safe place and encouraged the Christians to endure suffering. The demolition lasted sixteen years, until, in the year 318, Constantine issued a law ordering that property, estates, and building sites be restored to the holy churches.

At that time the church of St Mary of the Column, the mother church of the world, was restored. Christians, assisted by Bishop Valerius and the archdeacon Vincentius, had hidden its image and column. At Toledo, the church dedicated to the Assumption of the holy Mother of God was restored; and another church, dedicated anew [elsewhere: “again”] to St Leocadia, the recently martyred citizen and patroness, was restored.

14. It should not be omitted, in these same *Adversaria* of mine, that Camerinus, or Marinus, or Tamerinus, bishop of Toledo, was taken to Sardinia with others and suffered martyrdom there on 21 August while Diocletian’s persecution was still continuing.

15. St M. Pomponius Januarius was bishop of Salaria [elsewhere Sarabria or Salanensis], a man of consular rank. As has been said, he attended the Council of Elvira; while preaching in the city of Heraclea on the Herculean Gulf, he triumphed with his companions through dreadful tortures for the faith of Christ.

16. [Note: [Col. 1135D] 16. St Vitalis, whom St Sebastian lifted from the baptismal font, etc. Concerning St Vitalis, father of St Natalis and of the holy martyrs Justus and Pastor of Complutum, see the Roman Martyrology, 2 July. Flavius Dexter supports this with all the indications agreeing among themselves, in the year 290, number 1, in these words: “In Campania of Italy, St Vitalis, a Spaniard from the town of Thermeda in Carpetania, father of the holy martyrs Justus and Pastor, who suffered at Complutum, converted to the faith by the exhortations of St Sebastian, suffers together with others.” Here our Bivarius cites the epigram of Valderedus, bishop of Zaragoza, “For St Vitalis.” Luitprandus gives the matter again, more clearly and fully, below in numbers 154 and 155; in number 154 he recognizes St Natalis as the son of St Vitalis the martyr, and likewise in number 155 as the grandson of St Natalis the Roman confessor. Hence Julianus’s text under the year 290, number 125, must be corrected. There, through an easy alteration in the formation of the letters and through the fault of an ignorant copyist, one reads “son of Natalis the martyr,” whereas it should read “of Vitalis the martyr,” whose son was St Natalis and whose grandson was St Natalis the confessor.]

St Vitalis, whom St Sebastian lifted from the baptismal font, went from Thermeda in Carpetania to Rome as a soldier. Leaving behind his little sons Justus and Pastor of Complutum, he suffered martyrdom near Padua [elsewhere Capua] on 3 July [read: 2 July, from the Roman Martyrology, 2 July], in the year 290.

17. In Nicomedia, during Diocletian’s persecution, the holy Flavius of Antioch, a man of consular rank and bishop of Elvira [elsewhere Illiturgis], suffered martyrdom. He had attended the Council of Elvira, held in the year 299 or thereabouts. Brought to Nicomedia on account of serious affairs, he suffered martyrdom with his brothers Augustus and Augustinus on 7 May.

18.
