In the year 313, when Constantine and Licinius were Augusti and consuls for the third time, under Pope Miltiades, a universal council of all Spain was convened at Toledo, with Camerinus, or Tamerinus, or Marinus of Toledo presiding. Leontius of Braga, Benedictus of Tarragona [elsewhere Tabelona], Sabinus of Seville, Marcus of Mérida, and many other holy bishops attended. They sent a conciliar letter to Miltiades, to which he replied.

19. Turibius, notary of St Leo and archdeacon of Tui, succeeded Ceponius as bishop of Tui. He died on the sixth day before the Kalends of November, having been translated in the year [elsewhere: era] 528. Earlier he had been of Tui [elsewhere Iria], when he wrote to Iditus.

20. The First Council of Braga [elsewhere: Mérida] was held at Braga, before that part of Galicia which lies from Compostela onward had come under the power of the Suevi. It was held in the third year of Richila and the second year of the Suevic king, on the Ides of March, in the year 481 of the era. Pancratius, worn out by hardships, died in the year 444; Balconius, a devout man full of zeal for God, succeeded him in the see of Braga.

21. Through the preaching of the holy bishop Balconius and the other bishops, while the errors of Priscillian were spreading and ravaging Galicia, Rechiarius became a Christian from paganism. He wonderfully fostered the churches and the Catholics, among whom the catholic faith was publicly preached, and he granted permission to convene a council at the old Aquae Celenes, as has been said.

22. The waters of the river Tenedus, especially near the town of Guarda, where the river flows into the Ocean, are called Celenes because they are muddy and obstructed by slimy shallows, as though they were darkened. Following the custom of the Spaniards, they gave their name to the town, just as Sucro, Vaccaea, and Eminius did elsewhere.

23. Varada is an ancient municipality of Carpetania on the road from Toledo to Complutum, as follows: from Toledo to Illescas, 24 Roman miles; to Titultia, 15 Roman miles; to Varada, 8 Roman miles; to Complutum, 30 Roman miles. M. Fulvius Nobilior, proconsul, had the road made from Varada to Segovia. At Varada the memory of Nereus, Saturninus, and 365 martyrs is commemorated. They were staying in summer quarters in this municipality during Diocletian’s persecution and suffered martyrdom on 16 October. I would believe that they suffered at Clunia and that some of their relics were brought from there to this place, and that they lived together there for several years in winter quarters [elsewhere: Titultia or Tullianus].

24. [Note: [Col. 1137C] 24. Concerning the Tamarici peoples. Pliny discusses the Springs of the Tamarici in book 30, chapter 2, and the most learned Ludovicus Nonnius in his *Hispania*, chapter 44, to the glory of our Spain.]

At Muris, a town in Galicia among the Tamarici peoples, where the sea and an overflowing river formed a peninsula, mentioned by Pliny in book 4, chapter 20, St Theodore the monk was honored. He was renowned for his life and miracles, on 2 April.

25. During the time of the Moors, an ark was brought from Toledo to Oviedo—which lies near Lucus Asturum, the royal city, and under the Suevi includes Lucus Augusti; at Lucus Asturum, under Theodomir, king of the Suevi, a national council of the Suevi was held—together with many relics and the cloak with which the Blessed Virgin honored St Ildefonsus [written: Elephonsus], the Toletan bishop. The cloak was of dazzling white, and the ark also contained the bodies of the saints Asturius, surnamed Serranius, and Julianus, bishops of Toledo.

26. In the Galician city of Lucus Augusti, the memory of the holy martyrs Proclus and Hilarion, who suffered under Trajan, is preserved; their relics and Acts are said to have been transferred elsewhere.

27. At Lucus Augusti the memory of the holiness of the holy bishop Odorius [elsewhere Odornis] flourishes. He restored this city and its church and restored its see in the year 744, twenty-seven years after the devastation of the city. He died afterward in great holiness.

28. A bishop remained at Acharte or Murcia, together with a temple and church [elsewhere Arcisa], during the time of the Moors.

[Col. 1137C] 29. Before the devastation of Spain by the Moors, the Eucharist was always kept exposed in the cathedral churches. The ancient churches maintained this custom, including those of Toledo, Braga, and Lugo, and others that were not captured by the Moors but were either abandoned or admitted [text incomplete]. In some churches where Saracens lived in great numbers and the churches were weak, this was sometimes done, but rarely.

[Col. 1138A] 30. The route of Antoninus from Mérida Augusta to Zaragoza is as follows: Castra Julia, or Trogilium—the Moors retain the latter name—17 Roman miles; Lacippea, 40 Roman miles; now Madrigalejo [elsewhere Mudragae]; Lauciana [elsewhere Leucipa], 24 Roman miles; Villare Pedrosi to the Moors; Augustobriga, 22 Roman miles; Calera; Toledo, 55 Roman miles [elsewhere 57].

31. The itinerary circulated under the name of Antoninus Augustus is remarkably corrupt, with quite a few stations added and subtracted. It was first begun under Gaius Caesar and extended under Augustus, with only the names of places given and no number of miles. Later the miles were added by Antoninus, and for that reason the work was attributed to him, although in fact it belonged to several authors. Names were added, such as Constantinople, Maximianopolis, and Diocletianopolis, which shows that the finishing hand was subsequently applied to the work.

32. [Note: [Col. 1137C] 32. When I crossed Lusitania under the public safe-conduct of the Saracens, I saw not far from Aeminium, in the Osensis plain, an ancient and miraculous pool. M. Maximus agrees with Luitprandus as an eyewitness in his *Chronicle* under the year 550: “Near Osset, a town of Lusitania in the diocese of Pax Augusta, the baptismal springs dry up on the vigil of Easter.” I read “are stirred up.” St Gregory of Tours supports this in book 6 of the *History of the Franks*, chapter 43: “After deliberation, therefore, he chose three hundred armed men from many thousands of men and shut them within the fortress of Osset, in whose church the springs are divinely filled” [namely, Hermenegild]. From the siege of St Hermenegild it is clearly proved that Osset, the town in which those miraculous baptismal waters were found, belonged to Lusitania, if we attend more closely to the words of M. Maximus under the year 581: “Leuvigild again besieges his son Hermenegild at the town of Osset in Lusitania, captures him, and leads him to Toledo.” Turonensis likewise speaks of these springs in book 5 of his *History*, chapter 7; Baronius, under the year of Christ 548, page 589; and Morales, book 2 of his *History*, chapter 54.

An ancient inscription illuminates the entire matter. I found it in Emmanuel de Faria y Sousa, *Epitome of Lusitanian History*, part 2, chapter 1, page 165, where Aeminium and Osset are mentioned, both of which Luitprandus discusses.]

> **IMPER. CAES. D. AVG. INTER. DIV. REL. COHORT. PRAESID. VACE. OSCEL. LANCO. CALEN. AEM. LEG. X. FRETENS. EJVS. NVM. SPECTACVLA. ET. LVD. GLADIAT. E. V. VRBES. LVSITA. L. A. EXP. ET. HECATOMB. D. D.**

“Imperial Caesar D. Augustus … [concerning] the cohorts or garrisons of Vace, Oscel, Lanco, Calen[a], and Aem[inium], the Tenth Fretensian Legion; spectacles and gladiatorial games … the cities of Lusitania … and a hecatomb, gave/dedicated.” [The expansion of this highly abbreviated inscription is materially uncertain.]

[Col. 1138D] Hence perhaps not *Osset* but *Oscel* should be read in Maximus, Luitprandus, and Turonensis. The inscription demonstrates that the Aeminian and Oscelian cohort gave spectacles and gladiatorial games under the emperor Augustus. Pliny discusses the river Aeminius in book 4 of his *Natural History*, chapter 22. P. Franciscus Bivar will shortly publish an excursus on this matter, learned and laborious indeed, in his highly erudite *Commentaries on M. Maximus*. I do not, however, deny that a town called Osset is found in Baetica. It is established from M. Maximus under the years 506 and 556 that these divine waters sprang up there. Whoever reads the exceptionally valuable little work of the most learned and devout man D. Joseph de Santa Maria of the Carthusian order may perhaps accept this view; he adduces so many and such great conjectures and testimonies in support of his judgment—which is indeed a supreme one.

When I crossed Lusitania under the public safe-conduct of the Saracens, I saw not far from Aeminium, in the Osensis plain, an ancient and miraculous pool that had performed so many miracles, as well as a standing church. In the year 942, amid the ruins of Braga [elsewhere Conchera], I met the holy old man Heronius, bishop of Braga, serving as a pastor among his flock in the office of a holy shepherd. At Aeminium I also met the holy man Gundisalvus, whom I heard, several years later, had succeeded Heronius.

33. [Note: [Col. 1138D]

33. Concerning the title “Most Eminent,” see note 1 on the letters.

[Col. 1139B] Whether his encyclical letter has reached your hands. [Col. 1139C] For a general discussion of encyclical letters, which are frequently mentioned by ecclesiastical authors, see the Most Eminent Cardinal Caesar Baronius, volume 2 of the *Annals*, under the year of Christ 142, page 105, letter C; and, most recently, Franciscus Bernardinus Ferrarius, *On the Ancient Form of Ecclesiastical Letters*, book 1, chapter 2; and what I wrote in the *Tessera of Laws* under *l. Certa forma. C, On the Law of the Treasury*, book 10, folios 52 and 53. They are so called because they were sent to all the faithful of Christ, as though in a circle, whether by a synod or by the supreme pontiff, or when issued by others on other occasions. Our Julianus discusses these encyclicals in his *Chronicle*, numbers 146 and 173.]

I also sent to Heronius, the venerable and most holy bishop of Braga, part of my *Chronicle*, which I had sent to Regimundus [elsewhere Tractemundus], and I wrote him the following letter:

[Col. 1138C]

> “To the most holy Father and most eminent pope Heronius, most deserving archbishop of Braga, Luitprandus, Toletan subdeacon, offers due obedience and prays for health and eternal happiness.

“By frequent, almost reproachful insistence you demanded from me, your servant—most holy Father and most eminent pope—what, on account of your eminence over me, you could more justly have commanded, and what, on account of my most deserving devotion toward you, I ought to have obeyed at once: that, when I visited the sacred shrine of Saint James, son of Zebedee, our teacher and apostle, according to my vow, as well as most of the more celebrated places of Lusitania and Galicia, and especially the sacred church and admirable relics of the most holy teacher, martyr, and apostle Peter, the first disciple of that same apostle and the first martyr of the Spaniards, I was received at Bracara Augusta with great kindness under your roof and that of your ministers.

“Then, when I was speaking of my little works, and among them of the continuation of my chronicle, carried down to the year 960, and of the Chronicle of L. F. Dexter and M. Maximus, Benedictine monk, most wise poet and most holy bishop of Caesaraugusta, you became eager to see my writings—for you had seen Dexter and M. Maximus, and by studying the sacred Scriptures and reading the histories of our people you alleviated the labors of your long and unpleasant captivity among the Moors.

“I immediately promised to send you my offspring, or rather my abortive fetus; and I preferred to send you something—whatever its quality—for correction, rather than send nothing, judging it better courteously to obey one who commanded than courteously to resist one who earnestly requested. Whether this little service of mine will please you, I utterly do not know. If it proves unwelcome, you must answer for it, since you ordered it; but if it pleases you, I shall send you the remaining years that I had added.

“Farewell, most holy pope, and greet your holy, though very poor, senate of the faithful, and especially your ministers and clergy, who live among wolves like gentle sheep and are exposed hour by hour to the slaughter of barbarians, enduring continual injuries and curses from the Saracens, whose sword hangs over their necks.

“Saint John, the holy old man and servant of God, bishop of Toledo, bids me give you many greetings; and he instructed me to ask you about yourself, whether his encyclical letter has reached your hands.

“Again and a third time, farewell.

“At Toledo, on the fourth day before the Ides of October, in the era 981 [A.D. 943].”

**34.** The river Sucro divided the more western Oretani from the more eastern Bastetani [another reading: the eastern from the more western]. In Antoninus, the peoples of Saltiga and Putealia are Bastetani peoples on this road.

**35.** The road is set out as follows in the more carefully corrected manuscripts: Saltiga, 16 miles; Putealia, 32 miles, near Paracuellos; Long Valley, 40 miles; Branchales, now called an oppidum, from which its beginning is taken; Urbiaca, 26 miles [another reading: Terbitium, 25 miles] (the Moors call it Arbeca); Allaborcium, 25 miles; Argiria, 6 miles (commonly Carinena [another reading: Cartena]); Carenas, or Callete, 20 miles; Carinena, called Longares in the language of the Moors, 7 miles; Caesaraugusta, 26 miles, which they call Zaragoza.

**36. [Note: [Col. 1139C]**

**36. Julianus Lucas, a Greek author, etc.** Florianus de Ocampo mentions this author in the preface to the first five books of his history, p. 5. Since he describes his homeland and writings with exactness, it will not be a waste of time to transcribe his account, nor likewise to read it. It is as follows:

“After the aforementioned Julian, another Julian, also a deacon and likewise a Toledan, who lived in that city, though apparently Greek by nationality—as he declares at the beginning of his Chronicle—continued the account of Spanish affairs much better than all the others. In it, before treating the events of his own times, he briefly recapitulates many Spanish antiquities, showing himself well read and highly practiced in the literature and learning of his Greek people. After this he proceeds to recount most of the hardships and victories of the holy king Don Pelayo; in whose age, he says, there occurred the invasion of those Arabs and African Moors whom we mentioned above.”

Garibay took this from Floriano, book IX, chapter 3 of his history, and reports it in these words:

“In those times, when arms resounded more loudly in Spain than letters flourished, there lived in the city of Toledo a most learned man, Greek by nationality, called Julian the Deacon, as Florian asserts, residing in that city. He is said to have written learnedly about the antiquities of Spain, being educated in the Greek and Latin languages; and he is said to have continued his history to the events of his own time, including most of the hardships and victories of this king Don Pelayo. In particular, he took up his history from the time of King Wamba.”

Our Julian had already said earlier in his Chronicle, no. 234:

“From this point Julian Lucas of Thessalonica, most celebrated archdeacon in the holy Church of Toledo, begins his history; he lived in the age of the most holy king and restorer of Spain, Pelayo.”

Again, no. 385:

“Julian Lucas of Thessalonica, Greek by nationality, a deacon at Toledo, is esteemed a distinguished writer; for he wrote a history of the Goths, especially of King Saint Pelayo.”

Therefore, do not confuse him with our Julian, as D. Paulus de Espinosa de los Monteros testifies that some have done, in the first part of his History of Seville, book II, chapter 1, fol. 30. Although P. Mariana, whom he cites, speaks of Julian Lucas at the end of book VII, chapter 3 of his History of Spain, not of Julian, archpriest of Saint Justa:

“‘A certain Julian,’ says Mariana, ‘a deacon, Greek by nationality, not unequal in knowledge of both languages, was illuminating the antiquities of Spain and the deeds of Pelayo in these times at Toledo by his writings. Someone is the authority for this.’”

There are also those who, led by no less weighty arguments, suppose that this Julian was the one whom Isidore of Pax attributes as the successor of Sindered and as having remained at King Pelayo’s side during the transport of the reliquary chest. See our Luitprand in the Chronicle, nos. 222 and 162; and see Ambrosius de Morales, who ridicules those who assert and defend that Julian Lucas emerged from the darkness of obscurity.

**Puteolos, or Putealia.** Concerning this town, destroyed by the Moors and restored in the time of King Alfonso VI, and concerning another town founded in Italy, Julian writes in his Adversaria, no. 296:

“Iscadia is a city in Carpetania, on the road from Toledo to Complutum, 32,000 paces from Toledo, where there is a very deep conduit divided by a hundred openings, as though by a hundred wells; and there is Iscadia. After Puteoli, Centum—said to have been founded by the Puteolans of Italy—is being restored in my lifetime; it had been destroyed by the Saracens.”

Julianus Lucas, a Greek author and Toledan deacon, reports that when the Greeks came to the Spains, they founded in Bastetania a town called Dicaearchia, or Puteoli, or Putealia, which the Moors destroyed. Later they came to Campania [another reading: Carpetania] and founded another town of this name.

**37. [Note: [Col. 1141D]** Saint Potamioena, etc. Saint Potamioena, virgin and martyr, is mentioned in the Roman Martyrology on 28 June.]

Saint Potamioena, a citizen of Putealia in Bastetania, was the daughter of M. Aurelius Decimus, prefect of the Seventh Legion, Gemina, Pia, Felix, and of Saint Quintia Marcella; she was the sister of Cecilia Quintia, who married Drusus Valerius Caelianus Valentinianus. These two were the parents of M. Aurelius Valentinianus, governor of the province of Hispania Citerior. This is established by inscriptions.

**38.** Paracuellos is so called, as it were, *παρὰ κόλεν* [Greek; the precise phrase is uncertain]. The Moors call Cole Almodovar.

**39.** The Cilicians, coming to Spain from the region of Cetide, founded Albacete, a town of the Bastetani. The Moors call this place Albacete, in corrupted form.

**40.** At Arbucara in Celtiberia is Saint Papius the martyr. Tortured by various kinds of torment, he finally died after offering his neck, on the fourth day before the Kalends of July, in the year 503, under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian and P. Dacianus, governor of Spain. His memory is celebrated there.

**41.** In the time of my parents, on 26 March in the year of the Lord 923, the most holy virgin Eugenia, daughter of Christian Mozarabs in the district of Utica, which in the Corduban region they called Marmolejos, suffered martyrdom by order of the king and of Miramolin Abderramen, a most savage tyrant, for the sake of the Christian faith. After imprisonment and tortures, she became a martyr by offering her neck. Under Blasius, bishop of Toledo, she was honorably buried at Corduba by N., with acrostic verses engraved in marble. She was venerated with extraordinary devotion and was present in Oviedo; she was honored at Toledo and in Galicia.

**42.** The relics of this most holy Spanish virgin and martyr were carried to various parts of Spain, where churches were built for her.

**43.** In the archive of Saint Justa I found this poem, composed by Lord Blasius, bishop of Toledo, the most distinguished poet of his age:

> Eugenia lies here in this tomb, a most renowned Virgin,  
> who testified to the faith of Christ with her blood.  
> Sacred purple adorns her with shining color,  
> and a doubled laurel wreath crowns her head.  
>   
> She endured much, but brings back greater trophies from the enemy;  
> heaven itself sings her victorious laurels.  
> The world, in wonder, shall sing of her through the ages to come,  
> so long as the earth stands supported by its own weight.  
>   
> Toledo, powerful goddess, and fortunate Corduba,  
> your fatherland, shall extend lasting honor to you forever.  
> The whole Church now proclaims the praises of your parents  
> and especially shall Iberia pay tribute to her own daughter.  
>   
> By death you prepare life; through burial you also enter heaven,  
> and your wounds have opened a way to the heights.  
> Reveal yourself graciously to those who beseech you, and be a haven of salvation;  
> goddess, teach the wretched; goddess, protect the guilty.  
>   
> May the grievous yoke that we endure become the cause of a crown:  
> Blasius, the bishop, celebrates you in this poem.  
> Remember your Toledo and the offspring of your ancient ancestors;  
> now protect your realms.  
>   
> You follow Eugenia, O Pelagius, most courageous martyr;  
> you are alike in character and equal in the fire.  
> The savage Abderramen Almanzor believed that he could destroy you both;  
> yet by death he prepares each of you for the stars [read: snatches each of you beneath the stars].  
>   
> Perhaps the same prison burdens you, bound in chains,  
> equal both in fetters and in devotion.  
> What conversations do you hold there about enduring death,  
> once for devotion and at the same time for chastity?  
>   
> Eugenia, O Pelagius, let this be a new cause of your crown;  
> enduring death, she teaches you to be a man.  
> Following whose footsteps, steadfastly bear witness to the faith;  
> she places more than one garland upon your head.  
>   
> You two rejoice above the stars, having overcome death;  
> you would wish to have endured still more for the name of God.  
> Roses and shining lilies adorn you as witnesses:  
> from one side redness, from the other whiteness covers your temples.  
>   
> Your earthly fatherlands are not alike; yet one royal fatherland  
> is common to both of you: the lofty kingdom of God.  
> Rejoice, O champions, and remember your dependents,  
> whom uncertain combat exercises and fear weighs down.  
>   
> Therefore be present to the peoples who are fighting:  
> if you look upon us, we conquer and rejoice.  
> If we conquer, the greatest part of the palm will be yours;  
> our glory will at the same time become your glory.

**44.** The most holy virgin and martyr Eugenia died on the seventh day before the Kalends of April, on the Wednesday of the week called Passion Week. Two years later she was followed, as is believed, by the most holy youth Pelagius, a Galician by nationality, who had Saint Eugenia as his leader and teacher unto martyrdom. This occurred in the era 961, in the twelfth year of Abderramen, the fourth of that name, called Almanzor; in the Hijra, 312. This emperor was exceedingly savage, inflicted many massacres upon Christians, and was an extremely fierce enemy of the Christian faith. Some believe that at that time Mary, the servant of God, was killed at Toledo.

**45.** Saint Pope Innocent I complains, in his letter to the bishops of Spain assembled at Toledo for a council, that bishops were being made from jurists and advocates—for example, a certain Flavius Rufinus, consul with Flavius Eusebius [another reading: Cuselio] in 347, became bishop in Spain in 360, and Gregory, formerly prefect of the praetorium of Gaul, became bishop of Illiberis. Although both were holy men of most praiseworthy lives, the pope forbids their becoming bishops.

**46.** Some say that Saint Thecla was born at Iconium, was Paul’s first female disciple, and was converted by his preaching; they say that her father was a Spanish Celtiberian, while her mother was an extremely hardened pagan woman from Iconium.

**47.** In the third year of Sisenand, under Audax, bishop of Tarragona, a chest was carried across the Mediterranean Sea, under the guidance of an angel, to Tarragona, containing part of the body of Saint Thecla, virgin and martyr, Saint Paul’s disciple. Inside was found an inscription signifying the following: in the year 633 it was received with immense joy by the bishop and citizens. The account, sent by letter from Bishop Audax to King Sisenand, brought extraordinary joy to Spain. During the captivity of the Moors, in the year 960, when I passed through that place, it was carefully guarded in the midst of captivity by Catholic Mozarabs, with the permission of the Saracens.

**48. [Note: [Col. 1142D]** “He happily approaches the foreign woman in verse.” He calls her foreign, although earlier he had said that she originated in Celtiberia; yet at that time, having been brought from Asia to Spain, she seemed foreign to a Spanish author. On the question of Luitprand’s homeland, consult Bivarius’s criticism at the end, and what we said in the notes to the Chronicle, no. 62.]

And at their request I composed this little poem, which I also presented to them:

> Powerful goddess, to be numbered among the heavenly companies,  
> first and richly endowed martyr of the female choir,  
> after so many passing years she returns to her fatherland  
> and preserves the Laietanian land.  
>   
> She crosses the sea with a heavenly minister going before her;  
> wind and wave alike obey her command.  
> Her father came forth from a Celtiberian city;  
> and Thecla cherishes those whom his daughter loves.  
>   
> Behold, Luitprand, no longer a new inhabitant of Spanish soil,  
> joyfully approaches the foreign woman in song.  
> Receive the verses that I, a suppliant, consecrate to you, O virgin;  
> in place of a temple, my heart shelters you as well, goddess.  
>   
> Your arrival is fortunate and joyful for the Iberians;  
> Tarragona has nothing further to desire.  
> With your coming, salvation comes, and the most holy woman with you  
> places a further limit upon her vows.  

In the time of the Mozarabs, the Church of Tarragona possessed an ancient church of Saint Thecla.

**49.** The river Sucro rises in Spain on a mountain called Megarutula, which the Saracens corruptly call Mogarruta, not far from the Turia, also called the Lesser Ebro, and by the Moors Guadalimar [another reading: Guadalaviar], as though one were to say “river of harsher [another reading: whiter] water.” It passes through the city bearing the same name, called Concha by the Moors, from the Celtiberian city Malacha, called Malca by the Saracens, and from the mountains that overhang Saguntum. The Carthaginians demolished this city and, rebuilding it, called it Carthage of the Edetani. Thus this river Sucro runs out into the Mediterranean Sea [another reading: overflows]; it is not far from that Carthage and from the Lesser Ebro.

**50.** There are two places called Segueda. One is the head-city of the Bellitani in Celtiberia, called Borgia by the Moors; the other is among the Arevaci, called Baleranica by the Saracens. The Saracens called the people of Titios Thaust, just as they called the Bisgorgitani Gobia, on the bank of the Ebro where Caesaraugusta stands. At Dertosa there are more than thirty Roman peoples.

**51.** The Saracens call the city Axenia, among the peoples of the Aristani [another reading: Anstani], Xixena.

**52.** The Moors called the city Colenda Maluenda; it was that colony’s exempt settlement.

**53.** Belsa is said to be named after Oriola.

**54.** Ocile, where the market of the Spanish Arevaci was held, the Moors call Ciria, shortening and corrupting the name (formerly from Ocili, Cilia), and, in an even more corrupt form, Cinar.

**55.** Confluentia, the boundary of the Arovaci, is Villanova, at the confluence of the rivers Arlanza and Arlanzón, which join there.

**56.** The Moors called these cities, situated among the Arevaci and in Celtiberia, as follows: Pallantia, Berlanga; Calagurris, Calervega; Sigeda, Caias; Laurona, Varzones.

**57.** Ausa, or Ausona, lies among the Ausetani and in the time of the Moors was called Manresa, as were Egara, Beseda, or Bosque de Malatesta [another reading: Malatosca; see no. 68].

**58.** In the councils of Toledo there was one bishop of Castulo and another of Castellum. Among the Castellani, Castellum was the chief city; the Moors call it Seselu. In the Third Council of Toledo, Bishop Froiselus, the Castellan, confirms the acts; he is distinct from the bishop of Castulo, who also confirms there.

**59.** Saint Maginus, also called Maximus, suffered martyrdom eight miles from Tarragona, on Mount Palfurius, on 25 August, under Diocletian, with Dacianus as governor of the Spains, in the year 302. He was a citizen of Tarragona and led the life of a hermit.

**60.** Palfurius Sura, a senator and friend of Martial, is believed in his old age to have been praetor of Tarragona under Claudius, and to have founded near Tarragona a town named Palfuria after himself, later called by the Moors, with the word corrupted, Bufagraña.

**61.** The body of Saint Sigismund, king of the Burgundians and martyr, is believed to have been taken from the city of Sedunum and carried to the district of Barcelona, where it was deposited on Mount Tesbiades. The Moors, shortening the word, call this mountain Monseve.

**62.** Saint Salvius, bishop of Amiens and martyr, is believed to have been brought near Barcelona, like Saint Valentinus, bishop and martyr—whom some make bishop of Interamnium Flavium in Spain, while others make him an Italian who suffered at Rome under the emperor Trajan—to a certain monastery near the city of Rubricata, now called Manresa. Others think that the confessor-bishop of Interamnium was from this city.

**63.** The relics of Saint Baudelius, deacon and martyr of Nemausus [another reading: Mamausus], who suffered for the faith under Julian, were carried to Roda, a maritime city near the Indigetes, and to Toledo; afterward they were carried in a sacred chest to Oviedo.

**64.** Saint Regina, virgin and martyr, suffered on 7 September near the city of Alesia, on the borders of Lusitania and Carpetania, under Olybrius, governor of the Spains, during the reign of Diocletian. Her relics were carried under the Saracens to the territory of Augustodunum. The Moors called the city of Alesia Alixa.

**65.** The Moors are believed to have devastated the city of Egara, formerly an episcopal see and, in the time of the Goths, a very extensive city. Its ruins are seen at the edge of Laietania, near the city of Basi, and near the source and springs of the river Clodianus, so called after the distinguished Roman Clodius. Its boundaries include Bordel, called Burdus; Palada, now Paladera; Montesam, “the great mountain”; Tespiades; and Povella, as it is now named.

**66. [Note: [Col. 1143D]** The passage is corrupt in the original.]

[The corrupt text reads:] “Bentas Sualdi pro Emilianae Montesano facta est ante 1, Toletum.”

**67.** At Lugodinum in Lusitania, which the Moors called Vitigodinum, were Saint Justus, believed to have been bishop of Egara and a signatory of the council convened at Egara, and Bishop Amicus.

**68.** The city which the Goths corruptly called Egara, the Latins called Baseda among the Castellani; Ptolemy mentions it (see no. 57).

**69.** In the Caesarean Era 759, John of Egara barely escaped after his city had been destroyed; old and worn out with age, he went abroad to another place.

**70.** The episcopate of Baseda is extremely ancient. Saint Fructuosus, bishop of Tarragona and martyr, is believed first to have been a citizen and bishop of Baseda, and from there to have been transferred to Tarragona, where he suffered a most illustrious martyrdom.

**71.** Froiselus, bishop of the Castellani, attended the Third Council of Toledo; he had been transferred there from the see of Dertosa by order of the most glorious king Reccared.

**72.** At Castellum Milledunum among the Castellani, corruptly called Milloz by the Moors, the miracles of Saint Leo, bishop and confessor, believed to have been bishop of Egara, are celebrated.

**73.** Some believe that this bishop was brought by the Venetians to Venice and given to Leo, bishop of the Mitamanenses in the Castellani, by the Mediterranean Sea. When the coastal town was submerged by the waves, he is said to have been carried to Milledunum and buried in the monastery of Saint Servulus the martyr. His body, or relics, is said to have been transferred there, to the town of Milledunum, which, as we said, the Moors now call Milloz in their manner.

**74.** In Spain, at the city of Octogesa, which the Goths corruptly and in shortened form called Ictosa, the martyrs Juvenalis, Bonosus, and Maximianus are honored; they suffered under Trajan. Saint Vildefrius, bishop and confessor of that same city, renowned for miracles, also lived before the time of Constantine. This see is ancient in Spain; it is subject to Tarragona, and its bishop can be compelled by no one other than the pope. Frontinianus of Ictosa attended the Council of Gerunda under John, bishop of Tarragona.

**75.** In the Asturians, at the Spanish city of Britonia, the holy martyrs Gorgonius, Firmus, Antonius, and Agapis the virgin are honored. Born at Nicaea in Bithynia and accidentally brought to Spain, they finally obtained the palm of martyrdom on 10 March through various terrible tortures during the persecution of the most cruel Decius.

**76.** Lucius, or Lucas, bishop of Britonia in Spain, while seeking Caesarea in Cappadocia—for the reason is unknown—suffered martyrdom with his companions during the persecution of Nero. His memory is honored both at Britonia, as in his own see, and at Caesarea in Cappadocia.

**77.** In the Asturians, near Balobriga on the Ocean Sea, ships of the Northmen were stationed. At the prayers of Saint Gundisalvus, bishop of Mondoñedo, or of Balobriga, they were sunk in the year 846. He himself died in the year 850 and is honored on 1 November.

**78.** Saint Martin came from the regions of the East to Galicia and converted the Suevi to the Catholic faith. He first became bishop of Britonia, or Mondoñedo; afterward, from Britonia, bishop of Dumium; and finally, from Dumium, archbishop of Bracara.

**79.** There are two sees of Dumium: one among the Asturians, which is Britonia; the other in Galicia, and this latter was the monastery founded by Saint Martin.

**80.** There are two places called Castulo, one called Castulum [another reading: Castellum or Cetulii]; both were episcopal sees.

**81.** In the division of the bishoprics under King Theodemir of the Suevian Magnetes, the episcopate of Portus, a town which the Saracens called Mauhnoca [another reading: Maulhoce], was made a see. It lasted only a short time.

**82.** Vectica, a see subject to Bracara, was also called Besea or Betaonia; among the Portuenses it was called Barbola by the Moors. Some say it was also called Betonica, founded by the neighboring Betoni.

**83.** Saint Thyphenes is believed to have suffered at Vectica under the judge Flavius Caesarius, who had formerly been prefect of Rome and later, under Julian, judge of Spain. Finally, in the year 397, under Honorius, already worn out by age, he was consul with Atticus.

**84.** In the fifteenth year of King Theudis of the Goths, and in the Caesarean Era 584, the Fathers of the province of Tarragona celebrated the Council of Vallis in the town of Valle, in the valley of Faventia. One must not read “Valentinum,” except through error, but “Vallense,” or, as other manuscripts have it, “Valletanum” or “Valetense.” There Saint Amatus, priest and abbot of Tamira, is honored on 12 September. Amatus was born at Valle to Theodorus Vallensis, a Spaniard who had taken a wife at Grenoble in Gaul. He was born in 635 and died in 695; afterward he was transferred to the city of Vallis in 712, and during the time of the Saracens was transferred elsewhere.

**85.** When I was librarian at Fulda, I came upon a parchment codex of the councils of Toledo, written in Gothic letters, which the most holy Elipandus, archbishop of Toledo, had sent to Charles Augustus the Great. In it is found a mutilated Council of Toledo under Julian, archbishop of Toledo, in the Caesarean Era 578, in the ninth year of the most glorious King Theudis. It appears to have been a national council, as follows:

**86.** In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ begins the Council of Toledo under Julian, metropolitan of Toledo, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of December, in the Caesarean Era 578, in the ninth year of the most glorious King Theudis.

“When, with the consent of our lord, the most glorious King Theudis, all the metropolitans of Spain and the other bishops had assembled at Toledo, the royal city, in the sacristy of the Basilica of Saint Mary the Virgin, which is called Jerusalem, and due mention had been made of the institutions of the most holy Fathers and the decrees of the canons, it pleased us, all gathered together, to discuss the reform of morals; and, if any decrees of earlier councils had been erased by the abuse of time, to restore them anew; and first of all to profess, in writing, in our minds, and with our voices, the faith of the holy Council of Nicaea.

“Here begins the faith promulgated by the holy Council of Nicaea: We believe in one God, the Father almighty, etc., as far as ‘the life of the world to come.’ Amen.”

Several leaves were missing from the synod itself, and therefore several chapters; the first four chapters were missing. Chapter five follows.

**Chapter V. On fictitious clerics.**—“Clerics who pretend, by their habit and name, to be monks . . .”

**Chapter VI. Whether a contumacious priest is to be excommunicated.**—“If a priest has been degraded by his bishop, or suspended from office for specific crimes, and he, through contempt and pride, has exercised any part of the ministries . . .”

**Chapter VII. On a priest after ordination.**—“Furthermore, if a priest acquires anything after ordination, the rule established in the canons concerning those who have obtained [another reading: consecrated] office while possessing nothing is to be observed.”

**Chapter VIII. On widows and religious girls.**—“Concerning widows and girls who have changed into the religious habit in their own homes, whether by the decision of their parents or on their own, if afterward contrary to the rule . . .”

**Chapter IX. On the complaint of the congregations.**—“A complaint of the congregations was brought before the holy synod: that there are certain bishops unwilling for a year to preach to, or confirm, their own [people] . . .”

**Chapter X. On the care of bishops.**—“We decree that all bishops must undertake the care of the laity, so that those whom they find faithful in the faith of Christ they may love with the utmost affection.”

**Chapter XI. That there should not be several baptismal churches.**—“There must not be several baptismal churches within one district.”

**Chapter XII. How abbots are to be chosen.**—“The community must choose an abbot for itself after the death of its abbot.”

**Chapter XIII. Kidnappers of other men’s betrothed women are to be punished.**—“It has been decreed by the sacred assembly that if anyone abducts another man’s betrothed, he shall be punished with public penance.”

**Chapter XIV. On the office of the archdeacon.**—“The office of the archdeacon is, whenever he wishes, to read the Gospel or to order another of the deacons to do so.”

**Chapter XV. On the office of the archpriest.**—“The archpriest must know that he is subject to the archdeacon and must obey his commands as those of his own bishop.”

**Chapter XVI. On the office of the sacristan.**—“The sacristan must know that he is subject to the archdeacon and that the custody of the sacred vessels and ecclesiastical vestments belongs to his care.”

**Chapter XVII. On a certain superstitious woman.**—“Concerning those matters about which you also asked, namely, the woman who mixed her menstrual blood into food or drink and gave it to her husband,” etc.

The conclusion of this canon was added from a council of Toledo during the time of the Moors.

**Chapter XVIII. On the custodian of the church.**—“The custodian must be diligent concerning the common ornamentation of the church and its lamps.”

**Chapter XIX. On the property of freedmen.**—“Concerning the property, or personal possessions, of those who are granted freedom by their own masters,” etc. . . .

**Chapter XX. How a charter of free status is to be made.**—“The aforesaid charters of free status must contain not only the name of the person who requests that they be made, but also the names of the priests . . .”

**Chapter XXI. On the instruction of the laity.**—“Moreover, the laity are to be instructed that they can in no way manumit elsewhere their own slaves whom they have decided to attach to the Lord’s camps,” etc.

**Chapter XXII. On another safeguard.**—“Not only those who are to be advanced in the Church to the order of the clergy,” etc.

**Chapter XXIII. On the reward of one who grants freedom.**—“One who suitably releases the bond and service owed to him,” etc.

**Chapter XXIV. On the ordination of slaves.**—“Concerning the ordination of slaves, by which they are indiscriminately advanced to ecclesiastical orders,” etc.

**Chapter XXV. On what is offered to parish churches.**—“Concerning what is offered to parish churches,” etc.

**Chapter XXVI. On fugitive slaves of the Church.**—“Fugitive ecclesiastical slaves who abandon their homes or families,” etc.

**Chapter XXVII. On one who enters a monastery unknown.**—“If anyone who is unknown wishes to enter a monastery,” etc.

**Chapter XXVIII. On one who eats meat during Lent.**—“Whoever during the days of Lent presumes to attempt the eating of meat,” etc.

**Chapter XXIX. On ordained men.**—“Concerning ordained men whose sins are hidden or manifest,” etc.

**Chapter XXX. On the frequent repetition of sins.**—“Those things that are repeated through frequent transgression are likewise to be condemned by frequent judgment.”

**Chapter XXXI. On the custodian of the church.**—“The custodian of the church is to guard those things that belong to the church,” etc.

Two canons are also missing.

**Chapter XXXIV. On the slaves of churches.**—“Concerning the slaves of churches, it has been decreed by common judgment,” etc.

Two more are still missing [perhaps one should read “up to chapter LXXXII”] concerning the ordination of slaves.

“Concerning the ordination of slaves, who are indiscriminately advanced to ecclesiastical orders, etc. Now, having observed those matters [another reading: sanctioned] that have come before us for discussion and establishment, we give thanks to almighty God; then to our lord, the most glorious prince Theudis, praying for divine clemency that he may spend the happiest years in his kingdom and that he may grant us permission freely to carry out whatever pertains to the worship of the faith. And I announce that you, most holy Fathers, are to assemble in the following year, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of October, at this same royal seat, unless you prefer to assemble in the city of Valentia, a suffragan of this metropolitan see. Go in happiness, most holy Fathers.”

Julian, metropolitan of Toledo; Eleutherius of Bracara; Celsinus of Tarragona; Emila of Emerita; with 64 other bishops of all the provinces, many abbots, and Palatine officials, signed.

**Council of Valentia, A.D. 541.**

**87.** The holy synod was convened in the Caesarean Era 579, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of October, in the happily completed tenth year of our most glorious Lord and King Theudis, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. A fragment of the canons remains: 4, 5, 16, 50, and 101. This is Valentia in Spain.

“When we, the bishops of all Spain, had assembled in the seat of the splendid city of Valentia on the appointed day, the twelfth day before the Kalends of October, in the happily completed tenth year of our most glorious Lord and King Theudis, who in his clemency graciously granted us broad authority for this purpose, so that, while defending the rule of the Catholic faith, we might also discuss morals. [The same Julian, metropolitan of Toledo, presided, together with the others who had attended the preceding council and confirmed it.]”

Here was inserted, as above, the rule of faith from the Council of Nicaea, followed by more than 120 canons.

When we were seated in the city of Valentia in Spain, it pleased us to determine certain matters for the strengthening of faith and morals.

**Chapter IV. On those who offer offerings.**—“Clerics, or even laypeople, who persist in retaining offerings left by parents or in wills, or who think that what they themselves have given to churches or monasteries may be taken away, shall, as the holy synod has decreed, be excluded from the churches as murderers of the poor until they make restitution.”

**Chapter V. On the offerings of the dead.**—“Those who either deny the offerings of the dead to the churches or return them only with difficulty shall be excommunicated as murderers of the needy.”

**Chapter XVI. Those who are not to be prohibited.**—“The bishop must prohibit no one from entering the church and hearing the word of God, whether gentile, heretic, or Jew, up to the Mass of the catechumens.”

**Chapter L. On an invalid donation by bishops.**—“A donation, sale, or transfer by bishops shall be invalid without their commendation and under seizure.”

**Chapter CI. On the blessing of betrothed couples.**—“The bridegroom and bride are to be blessed by the priest; they are to be presented to the priest in the church by their parents and attendants; and when they have received the blessing, they are to remain in virginity that same night out of reverence for the blessing itself.”

“When these matters had been completed, we give thanks to almighty God, who has brought us safely to this place and joined us together in the bond of charity and concord; then to our lord, his most glorious son, our king and lord Theudis, who in his clemency granted us broad permission to assemble in this place and freely determine matters of faith and morals. Go in peace, most holy bishops, and know that in the following year, on the tenth day before the Kalends of December, you are to assemble at Toledo.”

“I, Julian, metropolitan of the holy Church of Toledo, have signed these constitutions that the holy universal synod determined.”

“I, Benagius, acting for the bishop of Bracara and exercising his office, have signed.”

“I, Leontinus, acting in place of my lord Danila of Emerita, confirm.”

So did the remaining 64 bishops.

**88.** When the Goths and Suevi possessed Spain, after New Carthage, a most distinguished city and an episcopal see, had been destroyed, the see was transferred to Murcia. (Concerning Bigastrum and Murcia, see what I noted in the Chronicle at no. 38.) The Goths called it Bigastrum, as though “double fortress,” and the bishop of Carthage was called the bishop of Bigastrum. Under the Moors it was called Murcia and Oriola; finally, when Carthage was restored, the see and its name were restored to it, and it was called the Carthaginian see.

**89.** Florius was the last bishop of New Carthage, because after Carthage was destroyed that see was transferred to Bigastrum, that is, Murcia.

**90.** At Rome there is a very celebrated memorial of Saint Victoria, virgin and martyr, a Roman by birth. Fleeing from her fiancé Eugenius into Spain, to the region of the Marsi, she suffered martyrdom in the Bastetani city of Turbula, which the Saracens, corrupting the name, called Tovarra. There she founded a famous monastery of sacred virgins, and there she suffered martyrdom.

91. Saint Anatolia, sister of Saint Victoria, followed Saint Victoria to Spain; and, after the martyr had been left at Turbula on 23 December, returned to Italy and suffered martyrdom with Audax in the city of Thora on 9 July of the following year.

92. In former times both sisters were venerated at Turbula; but the memory of the holy virgins and martyrs died out with the arrival of the Moors.

93. Titus Aurelius and Gaius Lucius Eugenius, Spaniards, citizens of Turbula—or Tribula, as it is called in either form—possessed estates in that city and its territory, toward Hellanas, a Greek town where they had been born. Setting out for Rome, one married Victoria and the other Anatolia.

94. Some think that the Christians of Turbula transported the body of the holy virgin and martyr Victoria to Catalonia; others that it was left there, but hidden through fear of the Saracens.

95. Some think that the city of Victoria was first built by the Gothic king Suintila amid the ruins of ancient Velica, and that it was thus named by the Gothic king in honor of Saint Victoria, who suffered at Turbula. This Catholic king was exceedingly devoted to her, as he was to the other saints.

96. Saint Secundus was the first bishop of Abula in Bastetania, which is now ruined by the Moors and called Villa Gurda, where there are enormous ruins; it is about 26 Roman miles, more or less, from Turbula, or Tovarra. From there the same saint traveled through Spain preaching in Lusitania, at the city of Abila, where Saint Vincent and his sisters suffered martyrdom; there he himself endured martyrdom, and his body is preserved by the remarkable care of the Mozarabs amid the city’s ruins.

97. When I was at Carthage Spartaria, I read an inscription in honor of Saint Victoria, in which, on account of her outstanding holiness, she was called Most August, as follows:

> TO THE MOST AUGUST VICTORIA.  
> GAIUS VALERIUS FELIX, IN FULFILLMENT OF A VOW,  
> DEDICATED THIS,  
> UNDER THE CARE OF MAXIMIANUS,  
> PATRON OF THE CITY OF TURBULA.

98. After Paul had been left bound at Jerusalem, Saint Secundus, bishop of Abula, returned to Spain at Paul’s command and visited both Abulas.

99. The seven holy bishops first preached through the southern regions of Spain, namely at Acci, Basti, Málaga, Illiberis, Urci, Vergilia, Abula, and Illiturgi. Most of these places are in Bastetania: Urci, Acci, Illiberis, Vergilia, Illiturgi, and Abula; in Bastulia there was Carteia, near Calpe, a city of Baetica. Thus sings the sacred hymn by the holy bishop of Toledo:

> “Through these men,” it says, “the all-powerful grace of faith,  
> implanted, shone forth through the regions of Hesperia.”

By “the regions of Hesperia” it means the more southerly parts of Spain. Later they preached through the northern and eastern regions. Saint Secundus, bishop and martyr, died at Abula on the first day of May, in the year 65, after he had preached at Toledo following the death of Saint Elpidius, the first bishop of the Toledans, and had traveled throughout all Carpetania.

100. Abila was the city of the Lusitanians, while Abula or Abyla was the city of the Bastetani. Priscillianus was bishop there; because of the abhorrence in which he was held, after the arrival of the Goths it ceased to be a see, and the see was transferred elsewhere, namely to Obela or Abela among the Vettones, at the edge of Carpetania. After the arrival of the Moors and the recovery of Abila, through confusion arising from the name, it became an episcopal see. Abula, however, was destroyed by the Moors and has not yet been rebuilt from its ruins.

101. There is no lack of grounds for thinking that Saint Secundus the bishop—although he is not included in certain manuscripts—who suffered with others on the day before the Kalends of August, was the bishop of Abila who suffered at the town of Fumada, near Abila, in the year 65.

102. In the division of the sees subject to Mérida, when it is said that a village is the boundary between Corberia and Abila, or Obila, this village is understood to be Alcántara. The Moors called it this because of the fame of its bridge, just as the Goths called that town by the same name, *villa*.

103. It is believed that, at the command of the Catholic king Wamba, Quiricus of Toledo established a see, subject to Mérida, in a small village near Aquae, a town of Carpetania, which the Moors called Talavera, in honor of Saint Pimenus, bishop and martyr of that land. Afterward the Saracens called that little village Cazalegas.

104. Saint Pimenus is commemorated on 1 November. He is believed to have suffered under Hadrian shortly after the death of Saint M. Marcellus of Eugenius, in Hadrian’s sixteenth year, A.D. 135, when Hiberus and Silanus were consuls, in the first year—or, according to another reading, the fourth—of Saint Sixtus. This occurred under Saint Hermolaus, bishop of Toledo and later martyr. He is believed to have endured extremely severe tortures in his monastery at Cazalegas, under Quintus Matidius Gratillianus, governor of the nearer province.

105. A holy memorial of Saint Januarius, first bishop of Fibularia and afterward martyr of Benevento. See no. 226.

106. The monastery of Agali, situated north of the suburb of Toledo and founded by Athanagild, king of the Goths—apart from Karadinense—may be called the father of all the monasteries of Spain and of Narbonese Gaul in letters, religion, renown, its library, the number of its monks, and its distinguished men. There was a celebrated academy of letters there, and the nobility of the whole kingdom was instructed in wisdom and good morals. From there, as from the Trojan horse, abbots emerged for other monasteries, as well as most illustrious bishops for many churches of Spain.

107. Saint Ildefonsus, abbot of Saints Cosmas and Damian and later superior of the monastery of Agali, became bishop of Toledo. He wrote the books of the *Synonyms* and sermons against the heretics, which the provincial council approved. Under him a national council was convened at Toledo.

108. When Saint Ildefonsus went to Matins on the feast of the Incarnation, he took with him the book of the *Synonyms*, in which he converses with the Blessed Virgin, and the book of the fourteen *Sermons*, which he dedicated to the Deibiensian virgins, against three heretics.

109. Saint Walderedus, bishop of Zaragoza, in the era 739, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of December, was present at Toledo for the consecration and coronation of King Witiza. He died on 20 April, in the first year of King Roderic, in the era 748, after having governed his church for twenty-three years, or slightly more, and twenty-four years. He was buried in the most holy church of the Blessed Virgin of the Pillar, built by Saint James.

110. At that time a national council was held by Witiza, in his presence; the bishops of all Spain and of Narbonese Gaul assembled there.

111. In the era 688, on the Kalends of May, a national synod was held at Toledo against the Monothelites. Saint Ildefonsus, abbot of Saints Cosmas and Damian, showed himself remarkable there. Orontius, metropolitan of Mérida, Antonius of Seville, Eugenius, metropolitan of the royal city, and Potamius of Braga presided.

112. The reputation of Saint Ildefonsus’s chastity and learning reached the ears of the most holy bishop Martin the martyr, who wrote to Ildefonsus; and he replied.

113. More than two Roman miles north of Toledo, on a hill, there was a monastery of the holy martyrs Cosmas and Damian, a dependency of Agali. There is a spring there, supplied with running water, in honor of Saint Julian of Toledo, to whom Agali was consecrated. They think that the place was called Benhalgavia in Arabic.

114. The Arab Muza left Mahomat Ben-Ahuma as governor of Toledo and gave him part of the land near the monastery of Saints Cosmas and Damian, which was destroyed after some years.

115. The property, inheritance, and cultivated land extended as far as the valley of Menhalgavia—Benalabia or Benalgabia—which had the monastery of Agali and furnished meadows to its dependent foundation, namely the monastery of Saints Cosmas and Damian. Among the common people it was also called Lesser Agali.

116. Calocerus and Parthenius prepared the wife of Caesar Decius for the faith through their preaching.

117. Some think—and I also believe this—that Saint Leucadia was a nun of the Carmelite order, which the Carmelite monks, converted to the faith of Christ, had brought into Spain. Among these was Saint Elpidius, the first bishop of Toledo appointed by Saint James.

118. Saint Elpidius, whom Saint James appointed the first bishop of Toledo, was a Carmelite monk. He was converted to the faith during Peter’s first sermon and came to Spain with many companions. At Toledo he founded a monastery of virgins and monks; Agali was later situated there, and it had been consecrated to the Blessed Virgin, the mother of these nuns.

119. In the superiorship, or priorate, of the monastery of Agali, Saint Helladius was succeeded by Aemilianus, Aemilianus by Euphrasius, Euphrasius by Bacauda—also read Bacinda or Bacindae—and Bacauda by Justus, archbishop of Toledo, who held this office for three years. In the abbacy, Helladius was succeeded by Richila, who was abbot when his prior was elected archbishop of Toledo. Justus was a man of keen judgment, elegant bodily bearing, and knowledge of letters, and of the greatest religious devotion—another Justus, apart from the layman.

120. Avila, or Davila or Abula, abbot of Saint Julian, was bishop of Coria and confirmed acts in several Toledan councils.

121. In the year 870, in Catalonia, the holy hermit Brother John Guarinus, a Spaniard from Valencia, flourished. Near Mount Serrat he lived in a cave in which the Christian people of Barcelona had hidden an image of the Blessed Virgin Mary during the destruction of Spain. Deceived by a demon, he violated and killed Maria, the daughter of Count Gotfred Villoso. Moved to penitence, he went to Pope Stephen VI in the third year of that pope’s pontificate. Stephen ordered him to crawl like the beasts for seven years, until an infant said to him: “Rise, John; God has accepted your penance.” And this happened.

He died in the year 905, on the day before the Ides of June, and was buried in the cave. A monastery of holy Benedictine virgins was founded there. Maria, the count’s daughter, restored to life through the aid of the Blessed Mary, governed them and died in the year 909.

122. The image of the Blessed Mary of Mount Serrat dates from before the time of Saint Severus, bishop of Barcelona, under the Goths. That admirable bishop had extraordinary devotion to it, as, according to tradition, did Saint Eulalia of Barcelona.

123. Several images consecrated to the Blessed Mary are famous throughout Spain, such as those of Jéscar and Iznatoraf, and others. After the image of the Blessed Mary of the Pillar in the city of Zaragoza, there is the image of Madrid, which the companions of Saint Peter brought from Antioch to Madrid when the holy apostle came to Spain. About the year 718 or 720, the Mozarab Lord García of Madrid built a small hermitage for it; there the lady restored his son to life.

124. The stone image of the Blessed Mary that is kept in a chest of red stone, near the river Anas, was made before the Goths. The Mozarabs of that region placed it in a safe location.

125. The city of Lacurris was founded by the Carthaginians near Carcesa, called Cazorla by the Moors; by a corrupted form of the name the Moors call it Lariola. It has a certain strong fortress.

126. A high castle was called by the Christian Mozarabs the Rock of Saint Peter; likewise the town of Saltiga—also read Salega—on the Valazotus River, a city through which the river flows, is called by a corrupted form Tasola.

127. The town of Hippo in Carpetania was corruptly called Yepes and was destroyed not long after the devastation of Spain.

128. Theogenes and his companions from Carpetania, from Hippo or Yepes, suffered martyrdom at Laodicea; nor are there lacking those who say that they suffered at Hippo.

129. Saint Ildefonsus placed an image of the Blessed Mary by Saint Luke in the church of Toledo.

130. Saint Percellius, who suffered martyrdom at Rome, was a citizen of Hippo in Carpetania, concerning which see above.

131. [Note: [Col. 1153B]]

**Fonsa, Count of the Scantiae**

The office of Count of the Scantiae was a very well-known office of the imperial household. He was in charge of the cups; among us he would be called the chief cupbearer. Our Julian interprets it this way in the collection of various poems, p. 145, where he discusses Evantius, Count of the Scantiae under King Chindaswinth, in these words:

> “Evantius, brother of Lucia and Evantia, and Eugenius are prominently mentioned in a donation of Chindaswinth to the Benedictine monastery of Complutum in Asturias, issued in the era 684, which was the year 646 [this should be read from the autograph of the privilege itself]. There Evantius confirms as Count of the Scantiae, that is, as cupbearer.”

The most illustrious Archbishop García de Loaysa confirms this, though not with complete certainty, in his discussion of the Eighth Council of Toledo, p. 459, as does Father Pantinus in *On the Offices of the Goths*, in these words:

> “Some maintain that this Count of the Scantiae was in charge of the cups; others, that he was in charge of all the king’s banquets.”

Indeed, authors who are by no means obscure call him the superintendent of the household, as Doctor Salazar de Mendoza reports in book 3, chapter 5, p. 95, column 3, of *On the Offices and Dignities of Spain*.

Among the Gauls, however, a cupbearer, or pourer of drinks, is called *pincerna*, *pocillator*, or *échanson*. Different people derive the word in different ways. Some insist that it derives from *congius*, with the letter *i* easily changed into *k*, and maintain that instead of *congiare* one should say *canciare*. The Spaniards use the same word, somewhat altered and refashioned as *escanciar*, when wine is transferred from one larger cup into another and drunk freely; otherwise we call it *iarrear*.

Nor is this unfamiliar to the Greeks. The word κεράω means “to mix,” because drinking vessels were made from horns or fashioned in the shape of a horn; and a drinking vessel is called κέρας. Athenaeus uses this expression in book 4 of the *Deipnosophists*, where he calls cups κέρατα. Plutarch, in the *Symposiacs*, book 8, question 6, derives the Latin verb *misceo* from the Greek κεράω:

> Καὶ τὸ κεράσαι Μισκῆραι κατὰ Ὅμηρον.  
> “And *kerasai* (‘to mix’) is *miskērai*, according to Homer.”

Others derive it from the island of Scantia, which lies near the Arctic Pole. Because of the cold winter and the frequent, dense snows, its inhabitants are said not to use wine moderately. Quite a few, attracted by Pliny’s authority, derive it from the wine of the grapes of Scantia, mentioned by him in book 14, chapter 4, and book 15, chapter 14.

Many leap across to Arabia and derive it from a small Arab vessel called *cancia*, claiming that *escanciar* originally meant “to drink.” Others leap to Tuscany, where they find *schenth*, a Tuscan vessel. Sebastian de Covarrubias gathers all these explanations in his *Thesaurus of the Spanish Language*, under the word *Escanciar*.

Father John de Mariana writes that the word is Gothic, in book 5, chapter 1, p. 196, column 2, of his *History of Spain*; Duarte Nuñez, in his short work *On the Origin of the Portuguese Language*, attests that it was also used by the Portuguese. Claudius Duret, in his *Etymology of Languages*, and Caesar Oudin, in his *French Dictionary*, trace it to Hebrew sources, from *schaka*, that is, “to offer a drink.”

However this may be, the Count of the Scantiae is frequently mentioned by authors of the declining age. Julian, in no. 100 of his *Chronicle*, reports that Julian, Count of the Scantiae, built a magnificent church at Évora. These counts frequently confirm documents in the councils and in royal charters. See the Eighth Council of Toledo, in which Adulfus, Count of the Scantiae and duke, confirms in third place.

The most illustrious García de Loaysa, archbishop of Toledo, carefully notes this on p. 459 and examines the royal charter of Complutum, which Father Antonius de Tespes, a writer of painstaking diligence, published in volume 2 of his *Benedictine History*, A.D. 646, folio 174, column 3, and in the appendix, charter 13, p. 10. Ambrosius de Morales also mentions the office and the privilege in book 12, chapter 13, volume 2, p. 143.

I wrote a brief note on this, though with an unskilled hand, to Julian in the collection of various poems, pp. 146 and 148, near the end of the work. I also think that, taking this opportunity, I should point out that whenever one finds “Blaesilla” there, it should be corrected to “Blitissa,” on the basis of Father Jerome de la Higuera’s archetype:

> “Nicolaus married Blaesilla [read: Blitissa], daughter or sister of Chindaswinth.”

Finally, Andreas Burcus the Swede, in his *Republic*, p. 67, concerning the dominions and resources of the Swedish kings, attempts to prove that the Goths who established their empire in Spain came from Scandia. As the strongest evidence for this, he alleges that they had Counts of the Scantiae, as though, having entered into relations with the inhabitants of that province, they had members of that family serving as counts in the imperial household and subscribing the councils of Toledo. This is false, and Wolfgang Lazius is likewise mistaken in book 10 of *On the Migration of Peoples*, p. 572, from whom Burcus took it. The Licentiate Antonius de León, a relator in our Royal Council of the Indies, refutes them with considerable learning in his *Northern Peninsula*, a short work shortly to appear for the public benefit of letters.

Nicolaus, count, married Blitissa, sister or daughter of King Chindaswinth. By her he fathered Count Evantius and Duke Eugenius, who later became archbishop of Toledo, as well as Lucia and Evantia. The latter married Stephen; the former married Ophilo the Palatine. They were sons of King Athanagild and brothers of the queens Brunhild and Galswintha.

By Ophilo she bore Ophilo, Count and Duke of the Chamberlains, from whom came the house of Toledo; Stephen, however, fathered Ildefonsus, the most holy archbishop of Toledo. Stephen and Ophilo had—or, as seems to be read, “had as a brother”—Fonsa, Count of the Scantiae, father-in-law of King Reccared and father of Queen Bada; these three confirmed the Third Council of Toledo.

Ophilo, the son of Ophilo, confirmed the Eighth Council of Toledo in second place among the Palatines; Nicolaus also confirmed it as Count of the Scantiae.

132. When I was at Fulda, I found in the library a very old manuscript of Antoninus Pius. In the account of the extremely difficult journey from the mouth of the river Anas to Mérida, I found Antoninus discussing in the margin the small river Anas, which flows into the Baetis not far from Beatia. He calls its entrance a “mouth” because there it is closed off and concealed, just as someone who enters a house through a doorway goes inside and hides himself.

Two manuscripts read as follows:

> Praesidium, 30 Roman miles;  
> to Rubras, 27;  
> Onova, 28;  
> Illipa, 44;  
> Italica, 18;  
> Mount Marielo—also read Mariorum—12 Roman miles;  
> Curica, 36;  
> Contributa, 20;  
> Bercetana—also read Porcajana—23;  
> Mérida, 24.

133. Some identify the Mozarab Lord García Ramírez of Madrid, a kinsman of Lord Contericus, archbishop of Toledo, as the man who restored the church of Saint Torquatus, martyr of Toledo. Others identify him as the personal steward of King Roderic, a pious man and most devoted to the Blessed Virgin of Antioch.

134. The image of the Blessed Mary of Praesidium, which is and was in the church of Saint Justa—where the archbishops of Toledo lived—dates from the time of the Goths.

135. Euphemius restored the church of Saint Justa at Toledo, which Santina, wife of Theodoric, king of the Ostrogoths, had ordered to be founded.

136. Anatorgis is a city that the Saracens called Veas and which a stream flows past. Gnaeus Pompey fled there during a disturbance; the place to which he withdrew is called Iznatoraf, or “the earthen mountain.”

137. Saint Latro, as I read in the Gothic books of the Fulda library, in the collections of Saint Melantius, and in the book on the passion of Saint Serranus, archbishop of Toledo, as well as in the book of Saint John Damascene, was called Dimas, an Egyptian gentile. When our Lady and Joseph were entering Egypt, he encountered them intending to rob them; but when he saw the Virgin’s modesty and the child’s extraordinary beauty, he changed his mind, served them, and showed them the way.

138. Visitanus, bishop of Toledo, was from Biscay and the brother of Lord Zuria, prince of that people; he was a magnanimous man and ready for good works.

139. On the island of Scombrina, near Carthage, in the time of Athanagild and the succeeding Gothic kings, there was a monastery of Saint Martin of the Order of Saint Benedict, whose abbot possessed outstanding holiness.

140. Evantius, archdeacon of Toledo, was the uncle of Saint Ildefonsus; having abandoned secular military service, he wisely vowed to serve God.

141. Saint Eugenius, uncle of Saint Ildefonsus, was a monk. From my own time he was regarded and called a saint and venerated by all the Spaniards.

142. Saint Helladius, bishop of Toledo, has always been regarded and venerated as a saint; but the Gothic bishops, like others, were not accustomed to celebrate confessors. This holy bishop was born at Toledo to Helladius the Palatine, a kinsman of Liwa—also read Lucia—and of Leovigild, a Catholic man, as his son was.

143. Saint Ildefonsus composed a funerary poem for Justus. He lies at Saint Leucadia.

144. King Chindaswinth transferred the primacy of the Spaniards from Toledo to Seville, not long before, because of the heresy and Mohammedanism of Theodiscus, in the fourth year of Pope Theodore, who approved the transfer. The author is Ildefonsus, in his additions to the general *Chronicle* of Saint Isidore.

145. During the time of captivity, the bishop-patriarch of Toledo lived in the church of Saint Mary of Alficen, at Saint Justa. He performed the pontifical offices and administered the sacraments, and the canonical hours were recited.

146. Saint Parthemius—also read Pathenius—was the reason that the wife of Caesar Decius was converted to the faith through his preaching. He endured extremely severe tortures under the same emperor, in the year 260.

147. The municipality of Burginatum, which the Moors called Buxexar, lay twenty Roman miles from Osca—also read Orca—a town of Baetica. It was founded long ago by Germans who were citizens of Trajan’s colony, but the Moors destroyed it. In pagan times it was a celebrated meeting place for fairs. Two saints, believed to have been martyrs, Vincent and Julian, suffered there with their companions on 21 August, during the first persecutions of the Church.

It is believed to have been destroyed by the Saracens when the people of Burginatum resisted. The soil and climate are excellent; the land is fertile in crops if rain is not lacking. Here Oretania ends and the region of Bastetania begins.

148. The book of fables circulated under the name of Aesop the Phrygian is said to have been published under his name by the philosopher Socrates.

149. In the year 949, a certain Saracen king named Mahomat Zaquetus, lord of Tritium—Tritium, today Nájera—near Logroño, had a daughter who, associating with Christians, was baptized and wished to be called Columba. She was a virgin of extraordinary beauty and holiness.

When her father learned this, he took it badly and attempted by every means available to turn her away from the Christian religion and lead her to Mohammedanism. When he could not do so, he cut off her head. She lifted it up in her hands and carried it as far as the town of Saint Colonia, where she began to be venerated with extraordinary devotion by the surrounding towns. She died on 28 May.

150. Her father was Mahomat Zaquetus, duke of the king of Córdoba. He ordered his daughter Columba—who, as is believed, had been instructed by Saint Victor Cerasensis the priest—to be killed, and he also ordered the priest Victor to be killed on 16 August, A.D. 950, when I was at Toledo.

151. Natalis, bishop of Toledo, was present at the Roman council at which thanks were offered for Constantine’s baptism. In the year 324 he was also present at and subscribed the Council of Nicaea. After being honored with gifts by Constantine, he returned with Hosius to Rome and from there to Toledo, where he ensured that the statutes of the general council were observed.

152. The same Constantine, by the authority of Saint Silvester the supreme pontiff, ordered the primate—whose primacy had been confirmed at the Council of Nicaea—to commission, together with Hosius of Córdoba, an inquiry into the ancient boundaries of the Spanish bishoprics and their renewal. This was carried out over seven or nine whole years, with bishops delegated from each metropolitan church, who arranged for the matter to be determined through people knowledgeable about the localities.

153. Natalis of Toledo, returning from exile, was staying at Milan when the most holy Dionysius was driven into exile. He was elected bishop of Milan by the Catholics. Although he conducted himself as Dionysius’s vicar, he flourished through deeds so distinguished that he is said to have been numbered among the saints. He died in May of the year 354, a holy and learned man.

154. Saint Natalis, bishop of Toledo and later of Milan, was the son of Vitalis the Spaniard and the grandson of Saint Natalis the Roman confessor. He succeeded Saint Melantius the confessor. He was present at the First Council of Arles, the Roman council under Silvester, and the Council of Nicaea. After being sent into exile for the sake of the faith, he returned and was elected bishop of Milan. He died a saint.

155. Vitalis, his father, was born in Spain. Coming to Italy, he fathered Saint Natalis. After the death of his first wife at Thermeda in Carpetania, he married a Spanish woman, by whom he fathered the holy brothers Justus and Pastor, martyrs of Complutum. Thus these martyrs and Natalis of Toledo were brothers on their father’s side.

156. Saint Isidore of Seville wrote a book of the Prophets, which I saw written in Latin, Gothic, the common Spanish language, and Arabic.

157. Marinus, or Camerinus, bishop of Tucci, who attended the Council of Illiberis in the year 300 during the persecution, was the fellow bishop of Melantius the confessor and of Natalis, his successor. Some say that he attended councils and that the holy bishop Melchiades wrote to him, but Dexter does not mention him.

158. Some say that Natalis was also called Marinus or Camerinus, but incorrectly.

159. Patruinus, Paternus, or Paternianus, succeeded to the see of Toledo. After twenty-nine years as bishop, he withdrew to Palestine. There he became a monk and father of monks; soon afterward he became a bishop and died more than one hundred years old.

160. Maurentius, either his brother or his archdeacon, followed him.

161. Marinus, or Camerinus, became bishop of Arles.

162. At the First Council of Arles, Hosius and two priests sent by Silvester presided. Natalis of Toledo delivered an address and wrote the synodal letter; he served as secretary of the council together with another man.

163. The primacy of Toledo was declared at the Council of Nicaea with the assistance of Hosius.

164. Athanasius came to Córdoba twice, holding two councils there: once in the year 350 and again in 356.

165. The earlier account of Sardica, based on Theophanes, confirms the Council of Sardica, which Natalis of Toledo attended, and says that it absolved Athanasius and Paul.

166. From apostolic times there existed the greatest intimacy and a kind of fraternal fellowship between the Church of Toledo and the Church of Milan.

167. Athenodorus, bishop of Platea in Celtiberia, or of Turiaso, accompanied Saint Vitalis. After Vitalis’s death he returned to his own see and attended the Council of Sardica. He was a pious and Catholic man.

168. Severinus, surnamed Euphradas, a holy and Catholic man and one of the legates of the Council of Sardica, was substituted for Euphradas the first of that name, bishop of Agrippina, after the latter had been deposed as a heretic.

169. Saint Gerontius, the tenth bishop of Traiectum, is said, by a special privilege, to have lived for nearly four hundred years. Many authors say this.

170. Saint Hosius, bishop of Córdoba, died holily and in the Catholic faith at Córdoba on 3 May, the day on which the Finding of the Holy Cross is celebrated—a celebration which he himself had asked Silvester and Constantine to establish—in the year 360, when he was 110 years old. Many bishops and religious men were present.

He had been given poison to drink, ordered by Constantius out of hatred for the Catholic faith, because he had refused to follow the impious sect of the Arians, as many writers testify. In his own testament he declared that he was dying in the faith of the Council of Nicaea and detested the impious doctrine of the Arians and those who followed them. Although violence had been inflicted upon him through tortures so that he would communicate at Sirmium with Valens and Ursacius, he had never thought or preached otherwise.

171. After returning from the city of Sirmium, Hosius wrote a letter to Constantius beginning: “I have fulfilled the duty of confession.”

172. Peter, surnamed the Beautiful, both because of the elegance of his speech and, much more, because of the holiness of his conduct, was archbishop of Toledo. While traveling through the holy places, he was captured by the Saracens at Damascus, subjected to horrible tortures, and crucified. He completed his noble martyrdom in the year of the Lord 752.

173. There were two archbishops of Toledo named Olympius. One, formerly bishop of Thrace, was a holy man who succeeded Natalis and is mentioned by Saint Augustine; the other, formerly bishop of Osma, attended a council of Toledo. Both, nevertheless, were distinguished writers.

174. Peter the Beautiful, as primate, wrote to Clement, the first bishop of Seville, and to the clergy, concerning their having celebrated holy Easter on 29 March in the year 747, when it ought to have been celebrated on 2 April. Clement and the clergy replied with thanks.

175. Quintus Serenus, son of Quintus Serenus, to whom Saint Bacchius Justin, philosopher and martyr, wrote a long letter in the year 156—having written to Pope Anicetus in the year 154—was a Spaniard by nationality, from the Galician town of Samon, now commonly called Samos; hence he was called Samonicus.

According to some, he was the tutor of the younger Gordian, who lived thirty-five years. Not long afterward Caracalla ordered him to be killed in a bath. He is believed, like his father, to have been a Christian, and this may have been the reason for his execution. He was a very famous physician and wrote much on medicine, in which he excelled greatly.

Saint Serenus the martyr and Saint Serena, wife of the Emperor Diocletian, were descended from his family. Saint Susanna, virgin and martyr, daughter of Saint Gabinus the martyr, was the niece of Serena.

176. Zenas and Quintus Serenus of Samon in Galicia met Justin at Rome. Although they were married, after returning to Spain they served as catechists, as is clear from the philosopher Justin.

177. Quintus Serenus of Samon in Galicia died with a reputation for holiness in the year 165, leaving a young son who was an outstanding physician and deeply devoted to virtue and religion.
