The elder Quintus Serenus’s feast day is said to have been 16 February of that year. The two physicians, Quintus and Marcus Serenus, suffered martyrdom under Severus at Alexandria.

178. Likewise, Zenas and Quintus Serenus suffered with others in Africa under Diocletian.

179. Their sons were Lucius Serenus, a monk who was a familiar associate of Diocletian, and Publius Serenus, a martyr. The latter suffered in Africa, while the former suffered in Spain at Sexti Firmi in Baetica under Diocletian in the year 290. Saint Serena, wife of Diocletian, was their kinswoman.

180. Serena, wife of the Emperor Philip, was the mother of Serena, wife of Diocletian.

181. The holy Queen Geleswintha, wife of King Chilperic and daughter of King Athanagild, died by strangulation at her husband’s command on 14 May in the year 566. God glorified her death with great miracles, as Fortunatus and Saint Gregory of Tours report.

182. In the year 565, when Reccared was born to Leovigild and Leander became a Benedictine monk, Saint Severinus died at Seville on 22 March.

183. At the valley that the Moors call Menalhavia—also read Benalgavia—there was a monastery of Saints Cosmas and Damian, where Saint Ildefonsus was abbot while still a deacon. From there he was ordained priest and transferred as rector to Agali.

184. Valderedus of Toledo, a Benedictine monk and abbot of Saint Leucadia Praetoriensis of Toledo, became bishop of Zaragoza. He was a holy and learned man.

185. In the Order of Saint Benedict, *pater* and abbot mean the same thing; beneath him, immediately, or under the prior, came the rector and the superior. Thus at Agali Saint Ildefonsus was superior, or rector, of the patrimony, having previously been abbot of Saints Cosmas and Damian.

186. When Saint Ildefonsus became superior of the monastery of Agali, he increased its resources, restored the discipline that was collapsing, and preserved the monks’ way of life from the Palatines.

187. Saint James handed over to the bishops of Spain the Mass that he had established in the presence of the other apostles and that Peter and the others had approved. Saint Clement later committed it to writing, and for that reason it is commonly called the Mass of Saint Clement.

The Spaniards used it before the other regions of the West. Later Saint Torquatus and the other six disciples of Saint James also brought it into written form and promulgated it through southern Baetica—[the text is missing *praedicantes*, “preaching,” *promulgant*, “proclaiming,” or something similar]—where he had left no bishop, as Julian and Felix, bishops of Toledo, testify in books they published on this subject in confirmation of the Mass of Saint Isidore.

I read these books and sometimes examined them when I was a librarian in the Fulda library, begun by Charlemagne and very richly supplied with books.

188. Gregory, to whom Eusebius of Vercelli wrote, reproved Hosius for having agreed with the Council of Rimini. He was not bishop of Illiberis but bishop of Toledo.

189. There were two factions in Spain. One, together with the Luciferians, refused to receive not only the Arians—also read “Saracens”—but also those who had repented. Gregory of Toledo followed this faction, together with Vincent, his archdeacon and later archpriest, and Aurelius the deacon.

The other faction, aligned with the Gauls, Italians, and Damasus, rejected the heretics but received penitents, such as Hyginus of Córdoba, who had been touched by the Priscillianist heresy and was sent into exile at Trier, and Liriosus, a Spanish bishop of Tortosa.

There were astonishing devastations, battles, and killings among them. In the time of Theodosius, the faction that received penitents prevailed. Gregory of Toledo was wrong in this matter, and Damasus and his successors did not approve of the excessive rigor of these men.

190. Ruffus—also read Rufinus or Stasius—a Spaniard, bishop of Oretania and contemporary of Gregory of Baetica, was elected together with him, having previously been a judge. Innocent I ordered both men and others to be deposed; they would have been deposed had they not already died.

Saint Innocent was not speaking of Gregory of Toledo, because Gregory had already died, and the pope was not unaware that Gregory was dead.

191. Those who judge more accurately affirm that Gregory of Baetica lived until the year 424, already feeble with old age and near death.

192. Elpidius, a Spaniard of Toledo and a kinsman of Theodosius, was a man of great reputation for virtue and skilled in military affairs. Theodosius wished to marry him to Olympias, a widow and most holy woman, and the consul Symmachus wrote to him.

193. Some say that the body of Saint Elpidius, the first bishop of Toledo—called a confessor in the Gothic manner, although he was in fact a martyr—was transferred from the Chersonesus of Spain to Marsia in Italy. From there, at that time, it was transferred to Metz by Theodoric, bishop of Metz, together with other holy bodies, in the year 969.

194. A great part of those who, dispersed during the persecution of Saint Stephen, crossed into various regions—and very many of whom came to Spain—were monks of Mount Carmel [Col. 1161A], converted to the faith through the preaching of Christ and the apostles. Among them were Elpidius and his companions, bishops created by Saint James and afterward made martyrs.

195. Gregory, later bishop of Illiberis, was born at Complutum in Spain in the year 342. Throughout all his life he flourished in literature and good morals and applied himself to administration. Gratian made him prefect of the praetorium of Gaul.

196. After being removed by Maximus, he later returned to the Spains and became bishop of Illiberis. He succeeded Augustalis in 389. In 420 he wrote a book to Galla Placidia Augusta. He died in 424, when he was nearly eighty years old. He was enrolled among the saints; concerning him Innocent I complains that, although he had been a judge, he was immediately made a bishop. Some say that he had first been bishop of Málaga and was transferred from there.

197. Among other works he first composed a book On the Faith, even when he had only just begun to undertake the episcopate. At the request of Galla Placidia Augusta, in 420 he composed another, On the Trinity—which I believe Saint Jerome did not see—when she had already married Constantius Augustus, who began his reign in 419.

198. Hosius was a native of Córdoba, born to a father named Hosius, of Greek descent. Father and son were truly Catholic. He was educated in that church under the teaching of its bishop, N., a most holy man; he advanced through all the grades to the priesthood and succeeded him in the episcopate. He was born about the year 280, after the persecution of Decius. In childhood he lived with sufficient propriety to provide an indication of what he would become. [Col. 1161C] He possessed a keen intellect, was exceedingly wise in learning, and during the persecution of Diocletian in 295, under the governor Dacianus, he was most steadfast and courageous, together with many bishops of Spain, as a confessor of the faith of Christ.

199. Some believe—and not a few serious authorities testify—that the holy old man Hosius was killed by ministers sent by the emperor Constantius, out of hatred for the Catholic faith [Col. 1162A], and that he was therefore a martyr.

200. I remember having read in the Fulda library, in a book of Trogus Pompeius, that Augustus issued an edict for making a census of the world at Tarragona. The same edict was said in that book to have been “given at Tarragona”; nevertheless, its execution was long delayed because of the multitude of business.

201. In the year 38 before the birth of Christ, while he was at Rome, Augustus Caesar conceived the plan of taking a census of the whole world, Spain then having been pacified after the wars of the Pompeys. But fourteen years later [another reading: ten], when he was in Spain, he issued the edict at Tarragona and sent twenty men of approved character, who were to begin in the West, register all the peoples, and afterward [Col. 1162B] proceed toward the East. That edict was published at Jerusalem shortly before Christ was born, and those twenty men registered Palestine and the whole East. This census was carried out under Quirinius, because a second census was conducted afterward.

202. The virgin Irene brought from Spain to Thessalonica a great multitude of sacred books—for she is believed to have been from Illiberis—and concealed them at Thessalonica in the year 304. She suffered martyrdom on 5 April.

203. In a very ancient history concerning the affairs of Constantine I found that Constantius, the father of Constantine, to whom the government of Spain had fallen, ordered his son to favor the Spaniards, summon Hosius, bishop of Córdoba, a most holy and prudent man, never allow him to depart from his side [Col. 1162C], and follow his counsels. Constantine observed this instruction throughout his life.

204. [Note: [Col. 1161C]

204. “The very learned man Flavianus,” etc. Luitprand compresses much into a few words. First, that Flavianus was a learned man, that Symmachus wrote to him, and that he flourished under Theodosius; second, that the pagan Symmachus sent this pagan a panegyric composed in praise of Theodosius and delivered in the senate; third, that Festus Rufus Avienus dedicated his little book On the Stars to the same Flavianus.

1. In Ecclesiastical History, book II, chapter 33, Rufinus calls Flavianus a prefect and acknowledges his great superiority in wisdom and his prudence in political affairs. Sozomen agrees with Rufinus, reporting nearly the same things in book VII of his Ecclesiastical History, chapter 22. That he was prefect of the praetorium is indicated by Symmachus, book II, letters 27 and 75; and that he was prefect of the praetorium of Illyricum and Italy under Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius is shown by the inscription of law 6, On Contracts of Sale, and law 26, On Punishments, in the Theodosian Code. Franciscus Juretus accumulates further evidence for this in his notes on Symmachus, in the letter of Saint Ambrose sent to the emperor Eugenius, p. 333. The entire second book of Symmachus’s Letters to Flavianus is extant, as are other letters in the Appendix, including many to Theodosius; from these it is clear that Symmachus, Flavianus, and Avienus lived at the same time under Theodosius.

2. Symmachus presented the panegyric to Theodosius—to use the words of Prosper of Aquitaine—when he called for the restoration of the altar. Thus he says in book III of On the Promises of God: “Who among us is permitted to be unaware that, by the command of Theodosius, a religious prince, all the temples stripped of their possessions and their empty images were [Col. 1162C] destroyed by the counts Jovius and Gaudentius? To him that Symmachus, endowed with marvelous eloquence and learning, yet a pagan”—Luitprand says, “a pagan panegyric”—“in a proclamation of praise recited before the imperial council”—Luitprand says, “delivered in the senate”—subtly represented, by the art at which he excelled, that the Altar of Victory should be restored in the senate, and conveyed this message to the Christian prince, as he knew him to be. The prince immediately expelled him from his presence and ordered him, placed in an unbedded carriage, to remain there that day at the hundredth milestone.” Symmachus composed a defense of this panegyric, as he testifies in letter 31 of book II: “I do not think,” he says, “that in good times the condition of my case will be what it was under a tyrant; by whose letters, issued at Marcellinus’s suggestion, you know that my men were fined. I did not keep silent about this in the defense of my panegyric.”

3. Finally, Avienus’s dedication of a book On the Stars to Flavianus was neither inappropriate nor alien to Flavianus’s interests. For Flavianus was believed to observe the stars and to predict the future. Sozomenus bears witness in book VII of his Ecclesiastical History, chapter 22: “For Eugenius believed that he would attain what he was attempting without hindrance, persuaded by the words of certain men who promised that they could foretell the future from the sacrifice of victims, the inspection of entrails, and the observation of the stars. At that time, many other men of rank among the Romans were also devoted to these practices; among them was Flavianus, then prefect, an excellent man regarded as prudent in political affairs, who moreover was believed to foresee the future accurately through his knowledge of every kind of divination.” I can state with certainty that the book On the Stars mentioned by Luitprand and dedicated by Avienus to Flavianus is the Phenomena of Aratus, translated from Greek into Latin by Avienus. Aristotle and others often call the stars *phainomena* (“phenomena”). Cinna alludes to these labors of Aratus in his splendid epigram:

> These verses, long watched over by Aratean lamps,  
> Through which we learn the fires of the heavens,  
> Written on a smooth little book of dry mallow,  
> A Persian vessel has carried as a gift to you.

Cicero says clearly in book I of On the Orator, chapter 16: “It is agreed among learned men that Aratus, ignorant of astrology, wrote of the heavens and stars in the most polished and excellent verses.”]

The very learned man Flavianus, to whom Symmachus wrote and to whom Festus Rufus Avienus dedicated a book on the stars, flourished under Theodosius. Symmachus, a pagan, sent him a panegyric composed in praise of Theodosius the Younger and delivered in the senate.

205. [Note: [Col. 1163B]

205. “Rufus Festus Avienus died,” etc. Who Avienus was, and where he came from, has been investigated by many and remains doubtful to many. Some have regarded him as a Spaniard, as Crinitus reports in On Latin Poets, book V, chapter 80, and Gyraldus in the same history, dialogue 4. Avienus himself seems to suggest this in his little book On the Seacoasts, when he calls the sea that washes the Spanish coast “our sea,” in verse 83:

> … When this gulf of our sea  
> Opens out far, it is the Atlantic bay;  
> Here is Gadir, formerly called Tartessus;  
> Here stand the unyielding pillars of Hercules.

And in verse 180:

> … If anyone should make his way  
> To our sea and the harbor of Málaga.

M. Maximus asserts this more clearly in his Chronicle under the year 460 of Christ [Col. 1163C]; he is followed by Vasaeus in his Chronicle under the year 315, Morales in book X, chapter 34, and, according to the view of others, in the scholia to the Life of Saint Eulogius, no. 19. Damianus a Goes in his Spain addressed to Peter Nonius, Matamoros in his book On Academies, Mariana in book IV of his History of Spain, chapter 15—all of whom are cited by Father R. Francis Bivarius in his learned and laborious commentaries on M. Maximus, which I wish would appear in print as soon as possible.

He flourished in the age of the emperor Theodosius, as can easily be gathered from Saint Jerome. In his commentary on the Letter to Titus, chapter I, while explaining the words of Aratus used by Saint Paul, Jerome says: “A half-verse is read in the *Phenomena* of Aratus, which Cicero translated into Latin, as did Caesar Germanicus, and recently Avienus.” Gyraldus and Joannes Vossius, On Latin Historians, book II, chapter 9, assert that this establishes the point. It may also be supported by Macrobius, who likewise lived in the time of Theodosius and introduces Avienus as one of the speakers in book I and the following chapters of his *Saturnalia*. Moreover, a little book of Avienus’s own *Fables*, dedicated to that same emperor, is extant. Although Crinitus believed that he had arguments sufficient to place Avienus in the reign of Diocletian, M. Maximus deserves to be heard above all others, since he identifies the place and time in which Avienus flourished, saying: “In the Oppidana region and in Oretania [Carus reads it thus] of Spain there formerly flourished, under Castinus, bishop of Toledo, Rufus Magnus Festus Avienus, who wrote about the coasts of Spain and the arrangement of the world in various kinds of verse.” “Castinus” is read incorrectly. For he did not ascend the chair until the year 450 of Christ, as Maximus himself attests. The same author confirms by the words “formerly flourished” that Avienus belonged to an earlier period, since he mentions him under the year 460. Certainly, this manner of speaking does not signify merely an interval of ten years between 450 and 460. I would therefore have thought that “Majorinus” should be restored, were it not that the year recorded in Julian’s Chronicle, no. 216, objects: there it says that in 436 Majorianus, or Majorinus, succeeded Hesychius in the see of Toledo. Thus I think that Audentius or Gregory, bishops of Toledo who were contemporaries of Theodosius the Great, should be substituted for Castinus.

But we no longer need precarious evidence. Our Luitprand makes everything plain here: first, he recognizes Avienus as a Spaniard; second, he indicates his native land; third, he identifies his religion; fourth, he assigns his burial place; and finally, he states under which bishop he died, although I am uncertain and hesitate over the bishop’s name. For “Majorinus,” I think “Hesychius” should be written, on the authority of the same Julian, no. 216, in the Chronicle. Avienus flourished under Audentius or Gregory, bishops of Toledo; he died under Hesychius. Since it is established that Saint Augustine lived until the year 420 of the Lord, a year mentioned by Augustine himself in his letter to Hesychius, and since it also appears from the Chronicle of Saint Prosper that Avienus died in the year 433 of salvation, during the reign of Honorius, what we have observed concerning Avienus’s dates seems sufficiently confirmed: namely, that he lived in the age of Theodosius, in which Saint Jerome also lived, as Jerome testifies concerning himself at the end of his book On Illustrious Men. Luitprand, consistent with himself, makes this truth clear in the preceding number by listing Avienus and Flavianus as contemporaries. Vossius discusses at length the various forms of Avienus’s name, recording that he was called Avienus, Avianus, or Abidnus, as does Morales in the scholia to the Life of Saint Eulogius, no. 19. Whatever the case, he was an educated and elegant poet, to use Crinitus’s words, endowed with great learning and varied knowledge.

[Col. 1164C] We have spoken above about his writings, in the preceding number. I shall add further details. Servius, in his commentary on Virgil’s *Aeneid*, book I, verse 388, says: “Avienus rendered the whole of Livy in iambics.” He translated the work of Aratus from Greek into Latin with the greatest elegance and exactness; in this he was not inferior even to Cicero, as is shown by the learned Dionysius Petavius, S.J., in his various dissertations on the system of the sphere, and by Joseph Scaliger in his notes on the astronomical books of Manilius. He composed a book On the Situation of the Earth in hexameter verse, imitating the Greek poet Dionysius, as Crinitus teaches; not, as Gyraldus says—who is sometimes overly sparing of praise belonging to others—that he rendered Dionysius’s verses from Greek into Latin. His most recent editor and translator follows the same tracks, though without sound reasoning. This will certainly be evident to anyone who examines the work of both poets, as it was to our Bernardo Aldrete. In his elegant and learned treatise On Various Antiquities of Spain, book I, chapter 23, when he described Phoenicia, he first cited the view of Dionysius and then added that of Avienus, acknowledging that the latter was similar by imitation. He does the same in book III, chapter 18, and very often elsewhere; there it requires very little labor to recognize the difference between the two poets and their poems. Andreas Papius of Ghent, in his edition of Dionysius, although he admits that he had never seen Avienus, warns the reader of this truth in these words: “Nor do I promise an interpretation by Avienus, although I have never seen him, but rather a paraphrase; for it is likely that he reproduced the description of the earth from Dionysius in the same manner as he reproduced the description of the heavens from Aratus.” Anyone who considers the matter can easily judge this.

He also composed a second little book, On the Seacoasts, in iambic verse—a task untouched by Latin talents, according to Crinitus, and of such difficulty that he had to labor over it long and intensely before completing it.

He additionally composed Aesopic fables in elegiac verse and, like others, also rendered Virgilian fables in iambics. Alvarus of Córdoba lists either one of these works or both in the Life of Saint Eulogius, with Ambrosius de Morales’s approval, no. 19, where Alvarus discusses Eulogius’s journey in these words: “He also brought back the metrical fables of Avienus, the radiant poems of Catholic hymns, and many very brief treatments of sacred questions, gathered through the ingenuity of many men—not privately for himself, but collectively for the most diligent investigators.”

It is also known that he wrote other epigrams, which are found printed in *Ancient Poets*, book IV. In one of them he elegantly develops an allegory of the Sirens; in another he describes pomegranates and asks that they be sent to him by Flavianus; and in the last he gives his friends advice about rural life. This poem is commonly printed among Martial’s epigrams, book IV, no. 90; but Scriverius orders it to be cast away as spurious and unworthy of so great a poet. Other learned men have denied this. Whatever the case [Col. 1166D], no one doubts that it should be attributed to the noble and ingenious man Avienus.

Some believe that Avienus wrote the epitome of Roman affairs, widely handled by many hands, which was presented to the emperor Valentinian. Volaterranus supports this view in book XIX of his *Anthropology*, under the letter R, criticizing those who incorrectly write “Sextus” instead of “Festus” in the title. Nevertheless, I do not think that author was the same as Avienus. Avienus had a different mind, spirit, and genius from the other Rufus. If Philander is to be believed, that other Rufus is also said to have drawn up the description of the city of Rome that has until now circulated under the name of Publius Victor; Carlo Sigonio likewise supports this in his judgment concerning Latin historians. These are almost all the points drawn from the *Prosphonetica* letter of the most learned Don Pedro Melian, addressed to the works of Festus Rufus Avienus, which he is planning to publish shortly.]

Rufus Festus Avienus died, a Catholic man and a Spaniard, a citizen of Évora in the Carpetanian region of Spain [Col. 1164A], in the same year and on the same day on which Saint Augustine ascended to heaven in his own city. He was buried in the presence of Majorian [perhaps Hesychius should be restored, on the authority of Julian’s Chronicle, no. 216], archbishop of Toledo, in the church of Saint Leocadia.

[Col. 1165A] 206. That the holy old man Hosius departed in peace and in communion with the Church is taught, besides the testimony of the surviving Athanasius, by the words of his testament, in which he declares that he wished to die in the faith of the Council of Nicaea and exhorts everyone to live in it and altogether to desire to die in it.

207. He died at the age of one hundred and fourteen, already decrepit, as though childish in understanding and exhausted by weakness of strength. The force of pain and the severity of his sufferings may have been so great at that age that they left him no free control.

208. In a trustworthy codex I found that Saint Felix, surnamed Modica, was born at Seville to very noble parents. After being orphaned, she was brought to Rome by her uncle, an archdeacon of the Roman Church, in the time of Saint Urban [Col. 1165B]. When she refused to accept a most illustrious bridegroom, in order to preserve the faith and her virginity, she offered her throat with marvelous steadfastness in the year 246, at the age of twenty-six, under the judge Diocletius and the emperor Philip. Many were strengthened in the faith by her example and underwent martyrdom.

209. Carterius, who attended the Council of Zaragoza and was a cousin of Saint Gregory, came to Spain and became bishop of Uxama. He was a pious and learned man.

210. Gregory, having returned to Nazianzus, wrote to Audentius, bishop of Toledo, commending to him his cousin who was coming to the Spains.

211. The first heresy that came to be condemned in Spain was that of the Priscillianists. It broke out here from outside and was condemned in the sacristy of Saint Mary of the Pillar [Col. 1165C] at Zaragoza, which Saint James built; nor was it fitting that it should be condemned anywhere else.

212. At the Vinaria Camps, in Bastetania: Saints Nunilo and Alodia, in the year 931.

213. Chisax, one of the sons of Ursacius, was condemned to exile in the Carpetanian town of Évora, or at Aquis. By a rescript of Gratian he appealed to Audentius, primate and metropolitan, so that he might be restored to his episcopate. A council was convened at Toledo, and he was condemned in the year 382.

214. The most holy man Audentius, bishop of Toledo, elegantly wrote books against the Bonosians in defense of the inviolate virginity of Mary.

215. The confession of Dictinius and the others was made in the year 394 at the Council of Toledo [another reading: “Nicene”].

216. The holy man Audentius of Toledo died at Toledo on 3 December [Col. 1166A], more than ninety years old, full of days and of most holy works. He was buried in the suburban church of Saint Leocadia—where his body lay—which had been built at Helena’s command, on 3 December, amid the great grief of the needy, because he had been their father.

217. In the year 702, the second year of King Wittiza, at the queen’s request—she was related by blood to Sisebertus—he was recalled from exile. After being absolved from excommunication, he was appointed to a bishopric in Spain. He departed truly penitent and died on 1 June 715. The see of Toledo was offered to him, but he refused it out of humility.

218. When I was a subdeacon at Toledo, I saw the following matter disputed: whether the Blessed Virgin had brought Saint Ildefonsus an alb, a chasuble, or a pontifical vestment. A few said the last, while many said it was an alb. I believe that she brought the entire pontifical vestment; but because, when she clothed him, she touched the pallium with her hands, it was more sacred.

219. He celebrated Mass on Saturday, as he was accustomed to do, in the presence of the Blessed Virgin and the heavenly choir, which assisted at it with its songs, on Saturday in the year 665. For this reason he is called the Virgin’s chaplain. And for this reason, when the miracle had been spread throughout the world, King Recceswinth and Pope Vitalian, in their own names and in the names of their successors, vowed that they would see on the day of her Nativity the church which Saint Ildefonsus, because of the Virgin’s arrival, calls “terrible” in his book On Writers, in the addition to Isidore’s book.

220. Genesius, the first bishop of Auvergne, warned Ildefonsus and his contemporaries by letters about the heresy of Jovinian, stirred up by certain men at Auvergne. They said that the Blessed Virgin had remained corrupted in childbirth, and these men were making their way into Carpetania, intending by their utterly false arguments to weaken and wholly destroy the faith flourishing in the Blessed Virgin.

221. Peter, who afterward became bishop of Aquileia, was sent by Vitalian to Toledo to discover whether the miracle concerning the heavenly garment given to Saint Ildefonsus was true. He also became a companion of that same Church.

222. In the monastery of Magnilucum, which Genesius founded, he ordered that his answering letter, sent by Saint Ildefonsus, be preserved. In it Ildefonsus vigorously attacks that heresy of the men of Auvergne.

223. [Note: [Col. 1166D]

223. Concerning the monastery of Dubium, or Dibium, and the town of Illescas, see what I noted concerning Julian in the Chronicle, no. 330, where, in the words “who was elected abbot in the year 636,” read, from Luitprand, no. 97, “who was elected in the year 656,” or “who was elected in the year 657.”

“In his own oratory.” Oratories were also the name given to small sacred buildings at home, whereas public buildings stood outside. In the times of the primitive Church, imposing temples were scarcely built. “There were not,” says the most eminent Cardinal Baronius, volume I, under the year 211, fol. 298, “huge and enormous masses of buildings, nor the vast, spacious structures of public edifices, but small chapels, or oratories.” Concerning these little chapels our Julian says in the Chronicle, no. 477, p. 88: “Before the martyrdom of Saint Leocadia there was there a sacred chapel.” Doctor Augustine de Morlanes, in his petition on behalf of the church of Saint Mary Major at Zaragoza, nos. 45, 46, and following, collects many further examples with a full and learned hand. Julius Caesar Bulengerus, book III of On Temples, chapter 32. I add the authentic text of the law beginning “If anyone,” in the Code, under the Julian Law on Adultery, in these words: “If, nevertheless, they should be found conversing in a sacred oratory, after the three denunciations, as stated, the husband may hand both persons over to the defender of the Church or to other clerics, so that they may be kept separately at their peril.”]

In the monastery of Dubium, at the estate of Illescas, Saint Ildefonsus placed an image of the Blessed Virgin Mary, which he had in his own oratory [Col. 1167A]. The people of Évora, or of Talavera, venerated this image during the time of the Moors.

224. Hosius, bishop of Córdoba, invited the Eastern bishops to Córdoba for a council to examine the case of Saint Athanasius. All the Spaniards assembled at a national council. Athanasius himself was present and presented his confession to the synod, as he had done at Rome under Julius; it begins, “Whoever wishes to be saved.” The Fathers are said to have added from it at that council, in the article concerning the Holy Spirit in the Nicene Creed: “who proceeds from the Father and the Son.” Saint Damasus later confirmed this, and it was likewise included in the First Council of Toledo forty-six years afterward. From this council the clause is found that was first added in Spain to the Nicene Creed and was later accepted by the Roman Church. Hosius mentions this council in his letter to Constantius Augustus.

225. Calpurnius, the governor under whom Saint Eulalia of Mérida suffered—namely, in the year 270 of Christ—is believed to have been prefect of Rome under the emperor Claudius.

226. In the gorge of the Fibularian pass lies Fibularia, which the Moors called Xergal; it was an episcopal see. Thus, in the fourteenth canon of the Council of Illiberis, the place is confirmed by Januarius, bishop of Fibularia, according to certain codices.

227. Cornutus Tertullus, a young orator, accused Saint Paul at Jerusalem. Later, as an old man, he was Pliny the Younger’s colleague in the consulship; Pliny mentions him in book V of his Letters [Col. 1167C].

228. It is very probable that the Lord inspired Saint Gregory to pray for Trajan so that he might be saved, because Trajan ordered the edict against Christians to be moderated at the urging of Pliny the Younger, proconsul in Bithynia.

229. Some believe that Amaon, or Ammon, the son of Rufus and one of the seventy-two disciples, to whom Christ appeared with Cleopas while the two were going to the village of Emmaus, came to Spain. After preaching the Gospel there, he went on to Solia, a city of Cyprus; having preached the Gospel abundantly there, he suffered martyrdom on 9 February.

230. Eubulus, whom Paul mentions at the end of his Letter to the Romans, is believed to have been a Galilean from the city of Nain, the son of the widow whom the Lord raised. After following Christ and becoming his disciple, he later came to Rome [Col. 1167D] with Peter. He was a distinguished man and devoted to virtue from childhood. Saint Paul sent him as bishop of Pamphylia. Theodulus, who preached at Caesarea in Palestine, suffered martyrdom with others under the governor Firmilianus on 16 February.

231. It is credible that the seven holy disciples of James, having been forewarned by him, came to Baetica.

232. Some believe that Saint Rufus, one of the seventy-two disciples of the Lord, who was first bishop of Thebes and afterward of Tortosa, was left there as bishop by Saint Paul when he came to Spain. Saint Paul mentions him in the Letter to the Romans, and Saint Polycarp the martyr also mentions him. He suffered martyrdom with others in Armenia on 19 April. But I think it better to agree with those who believe that he suffered on 18 December with Zosimus, and that he was bishop of Thebes and Tortosa.

233. One thousand and ten soldiers were crucified near Alexandria, situated on the Tigris and Eulaeus rivers, upon a mountain that is a branch of the Candaean range. This place was first called Caucasus, or Candaeus, or Ararat. They were crucified near the aforesaid, fortunate rivers [Col. 1168B].

234. Others say that they were crucified at Mount Ararat, which in Latin is called Equinus, part of the Gordian mountains. At its summit, according to Josephus, Noah’s ark came to rest. The Tigris waters it as part of the Gordian range and soon passes into the plain of the region of the Gordians—which is also barbarously called Ararat—not far from the city of Charax, called Alexandria by Alexander. From its right side the river enters the Persian Gulf through many mouths, spreading widely.

235. In Roman times it was permitted to no one to bury or burn the bodies of the dead within the city. They were buried outside [Col. 1168C]. Thus Christians buried Saint Leocadia in the cemetery or suburb, which at that time lay farther from the old wall. The bodies of the saints and bishops were buried separately from those of Christians. That place was called the burial place of the saints.

236. Macer [another reading: Sacer] Hierotheus, a Spaniard from Emporiae, was formerly governor of Tarragona under the emperor Tiberius. From there he proceeded to Cyprus in the year 45. After hearing Paul, he was converted to the faith and followed him.

237. Tertius Fabius Terentius, Paul’s secretary and one of the seventy-two disciples, was first bishop of Media. He later suffered martyrdom at Iconium on 21 June in the year 88.

238. The town of Nervium, near Illiturgis in Bastetania, was founded by Nerva and is called Noepron by the Saracens [another reading: Negron].

239. Saint Sixtus—who afterward became Supreme Pontiff—attended the Council of Toledo as the pope’s legate [Col. 1169A]. Later he came to Huesca, from which he took with him Laurence, the son of Saints Orentius and Patientia. Returning through Spain to Rome, he became Supreme Pontiff. Foreseeing the martyrdom of Saint Laurence, he ordered the deacons to warn Orentius, his father, to build a church dedicated to Saint Laurence. Orentius did so, and afterward suffered martyrdom with his wife, who preceded him in martyrdom, on 1 May under Claudius.

240. Saint Fulgentius was twice bishop of Carthage. From there he was transferred to Écija and finally back to Carthage, where he lived only a few years—namely, two—in that episcopate.

241. In the more accurate codices the Fifth Council of Toledo is dated to the Spanish Era 676, the first year of Suinthila.

[Col. 1169B] 242. Paula, of the most distinguished Gothic lineage, was the mother of Theodora, or Theodosia Cervella, the wife of Severianus and the parent of Leander, Theodora, Florentina, Fulgentius, and Isidore, who were born in that order.

243. Severianus married Theodora Cervella when she was fourteen years old. Leander was born the following year, namely in 542; the following year Theodora, or Theodosia, was born. She was the wife of Leovigild and the mother of Hermenegild the martyr and Reccared. In the Spanish Era 588, Florentina was born on the feast of Saint Florentius the martyr. She died a holy death in 610 at the age of sixty.

244. Theodoric, king of the Ostrogoths, came to Spain and governed it for many years on behalf of his nephew Amalaric. He married at Toledo Santina, of the noblest Gothic family, by whom he had Severianus, lord of Carthage [Col. 1169C].

245. Karadigna, the first Benedictine monastery in Spain, where Santina, the wife of King Theodoric, lies buried and which has two hundred monk-martyrs, was called Karadimas in the time of the Goths and Romans.

246. Saint Charlemagne, although in his youth he was weak—as that age is said to have been—became, once he reached manhood, a most holy man. In Gaul, Germany, and Flanders he is venerated in memory as a holy confessor. He died at Aachen [another reading: Germaniis], more than seventy years old, on 28 January in the year 814.

247. Saint Charlemagne is believed to have been venerated by the people of Toledo after his death.

248. Saint Torquatus, a disciple of Saint James, crossed a deep river after the bridge had broken, and his feast is celebrated on 15 May [Col. 1169D].

249. Saint Montanus is believed, when he was archdeacon of Toledo, to have contributed greatly to the arrival and reception of Theodoric, king of the Ostrogoths, so that he might be received peacefully as guardian of his nephew, King Amalaric.

250. When Theodoric, king of the Ostrogoths, came to Spain, he had lost Andefleda, the daughter of King Clovis, by whom he had Amalasuintha.

251. The Spaniards of Córdoba, Seville, Illiberis, Mentesa, Toledo, and Complutum, weighed down by servitude under the Moors and having crossed the Pyrenees, were received with the greatest clemency by the emperor Louis the Pious.

252. Severianus is believed to have been sent into exile during the time of Agila [Col. 1170A], on account of the faith because he was a Catholic, together with his children Leander, Theodosia, and Florentina, and his wife Theodora Cervella. Fulgentius and Isidore were born at Seville.

253. Flavius Marcus Cervella, a Gothic duke of the most illustrious lineage, married Paula, a woman of the highest distinction. Their daughter was Flavia Theodora Cervella, the wife of Duke Severianus, a most Christian woman. She died on 6 May.

254. Severianus resisted Agila and, after being besieged in the city of Carthage Spartaria—which the Goths completely destroyed—was sent into exile at Seville in the third year of Agila, with his wife and children. He died there.

255. Leander wrote to his sister Florentina, a Benedictine nun, a book On Virginity, or On the Formation of Virgins and Contempt for the World, when she was nineteen years old, in the first year of his episcopate.

256. The houses of Severianus and his substantial property still remained at Carthage.

257. Leander obtained from Athanagild the recall of his mother, brothers, and sisters from exile. The mother, Theodora, had been strengthened in faith and virtues by the hardships of exile and did not wish to return to Carthage.

258. Saint Montanus wrote to Thuribius in the last year of Theodoric, while he was still in Spain and Erga was governor at Toledo.

259. The Serrated Bridge stood at Toledo opposite Saint Mary of Alfizén, at its side.

[Col. 1170C] 260. The virgin Santina of Toledo, later the wife of Theodoric, was born at Toledo in the year 480.

261. By Santina, or Sanctia, the wife of Theodoric, he had two sons: Theodoric, who died young and lies buried with his mother, Queen Sanctia, at Saint Peter of Karadigna; and Elverianus [another reading: Severianus], who was married.

262. Santina died on 8 May, the day on which the feast of Saint Michael and of the Council of Toledo is celebrated.

263. Saint Elpidius Julianus, martyr and disciple of Saint James, was the first bishop of Toledo.

264. Mamas the confessor, from the region of Tui, is believed to have been carried to Cyprus. He flourished in the time of the Goths, around the year 500. He died on 26 August and is a confessor. During the time of the Moors, Christians carried him to Cyprus, leaving his relics in Asturias and throughout Spain [Col. 1170D].

265. In the archives of the Holy Church of Mérida I found a codex written in Gothic letters, in which it was stated that Complutum was called Guadalfaxara by the Moors and was also called Eplacea.

266. In the same codex I also found the following universal Council of Toledo:

> “In the name of the Lord, here begin the synodal acts of the general Council of Toledo, held in the royal city, in the praetorian church of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, in the third year of the reign of the most glorious prince Wamba, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of December, in the Spanish Era 713, concerning the restoration of the boundaries of the churches and dioceses of Spain.
>
> [Col. 1171A] “The most glorious king attended the general council. After customarily greeting each of the bishops, he said:
>
> “ ‘Most holy Fathers, I see that you are engaged in very serious disputes over the boundaries of your dioceses, and that from this the gravest lawsuits and contentions arise among you. I have also learned that some of you invade the parishes of others and secretly attack another’s boundaries under one pretext or another. Therefore I have judged it worthy of the majesty of our high office to recall you to concord. Does this please you, most holy bishops?’ They all replied: ‘It pleases us; it pleases us all. May the serene and most glorious king and our lord, Flavius Wamba, live for many years.’ Then he ordered the chronicles and histories of the earlier kings first to be read carefully before him, so that he might more easily and fairly divide the parish boundaries [another reading: of the parishes], as antiquity indicated and the judgment of law required, and so that each Church might possess its own rights, as our judgment below sets out.
>
> [Col. 1171B] “ ‘First, we grant and confirm that, just as the Vandal kings Gunderic, Genseric, Huneric, Guntamund, Isoris, and Gumiel endowed the city of Lugo in Asturias near the sea, it shall peacefully and quietly retain the boundaries that will immediately be assigned to it:’ ”

“Entire Asturias: by the Pyrenees Mountains and by the great river Ove, and along the whole shore of the Ocean Sea as far as Biscay, by the summit of Rostrum and the summit of Cabrium, through the gates of Saint Agatha, by Pozal, by the Limbum of the sons, together with the field of Edolius [or Erbolius], by Gordon, as far as that tree of Quadros, by the streams of Humana, Luna, and Vandulia, as far as the Pyrenees Mountains; the town of Cojanca, Quexida, by Conjaquela, Montosa, as far as the river Urbetus in Galicia; Suerna, Long Valley, Vera, Flumosa, all of Sania, Panamum, as far as the river Minho; all of Lemos, Urnyso, Verasmo, and Semmamorum, and Troia, as far as the river Sil; all of Lumia with the churches of [Col. 1171C] Petrayo, which have been or are built between the river Arnoya and the Sil, from the boundary of Mount Buron, and by the water of Zore [or Zoze], as far as the source of the Arnoya, and along that division, or course, as far as the river Minho; Lueza as far as the Portela of Veneti; and the churches of Sallaz between the Arnoya and the Sil, together with the churches of Baroso, Castella with Sanea, Barnates and Avion, Azman, Caraba, Amanca, just as the Vandal kings endowed the said Church of Lugo.” And the bishops replied: “It pleases us; it pleases us all.”

“León, which the Roman legions founded, which in ancient times was called the Flower, and which enjoys perpetual liberty through the Roman pope—namely, Sylvester—and has been exempted from the other episcopal sees, and remains a royal see, and has never been subject or subordinated to any metropolitan see, shall retain its ancient boundaries, just as Hermeric, Rechila, Rechiar, Maldra, Frumarius, Remismund, [Col. 1171D] Theodomund, kings of the Suebi, and Theodomir endowed it.” And all the pontiffs replied unanimously: “It pleases us; it pleases us.”

“León shall extend by the Pyrenees Mountains and by the Red Rock, together with half of Levaca, Cervera, Black Rocks, and Annion, as far as the river Carrión by the town of Serna and the Dry Stream; as far as the town of Ardega by the Cervini, as far as the fortress of Pepi; by the town of Mana, as far as the tree of Quadros, on the borders of the Galician Sierra: the three fortresses of Turtures, Datineus, and Castelletum, and Navia.

“León, a priestly and royal city, and Lugo, which the Vandals rebuilt in Asturias, shall retain their ancient boundaries, just as King Theodomir assigned them; these shall be subject to no archbishop or primate.” All replied: “It pleases us; it pleases us all.”

“The see of Portugal likewise remains within its division, [Col. 1172A] as King Theodomir assigned it, together with those territories which we have added.

“Braga, the metropolitan see, shall hold the Hundred Cells of the Gentile people, Millia, Layneto, Gilioles, Adonyste, Aportis, Aylo, Centen, Donis, Iambis, Cilisto, Letania, Ceresis, Petroneyo, Equisis, as far as Saltum; likewise the districts of Panoleta, Bregantia, Astiatigo, Tarego, Aunego, Metrobio, Betise, Palam, Tusico, Celo, and Senequiemo: under one see, thirty.

“To the see of Dumium belongs the royal household [in Theodomir’s division: ‘To Dumium, the household of servants’; here, by calling it royal, he means monks who serve God, for to serve him is to reign].

“The see of Egitani shall hold all Egitani, Menecapio, and Foraneus.

“The see of Portugal shall hold, in the New Fortress, the nearby churches, namely Villanova, Betaonia, Vesea, Menturio, Torebra, Bramoste, Pengoaste, Lumbo, Nestis, Neapoli, Curmano, Magneto, Leporeto, [Col. 1172B] Melga, Tangobira, Villagomedi, and Tanerater; likewise the districts of Lambiencio, Alcobreo, Valericia, Turlango, Ceris, Mendiolis, and Palencia: under one see, twenty-five.

“Lamecum shall hold Lamego itself, Luencia, Aranor, and Crasubriana [lacuna], under one see, six.

“The see of Coimbra shall hold Coimbra itself, Eminium, Selium, Brine, Insula, Astrucio, and the Old Fortress of Portugal: under one, two.

“Veseus shall hold Veseo itself, Rodomirus, Submontia, Suberbenus, Osanca, Obelion, Tutela, Goleia, and Cabrabria, which later became a see among the Goths; under one, seven sees are assigned.

“Urci shall hold Uria itself and Deisum, as far as Cussancarus; and from the Baths of Rego as far as the shore of the Ocean Sea.

“Lugo shall hold the city itself with its neighboring territories, together with Cantoquia, Somos, Carabarcos, Montenegro, Parraga, Latra, Azumara, Sigros, Triavada, Pagento, Salvaterra, Monterroso, Doira [Col. 1172C] or Coyra, Deza, and Colea: under one see, sixteen.

“Auria shall hold Vesugium, Ruvale, Teporus, Sedisus, Prucia, Cisavium, Verenganus, Sanabria, and Greater Calabazas: under one, ten.

“Astorga shall hold Astorga itself, León, Superurbicum, Beriso, Petrasperanti, Autoribis, Caldelas, Upper and Lower Morillos, Sonure, Trogelos, and Pericos: under one, eleven sees.

“Britonia shall hold the nearby churches of Torelo and Torebera among the Britons, together with the monastery of Maximus, as far as the river Ove.

“Tuy shall hold Tuy itself, together with the nearby churches of Torelo, Torobera, Ludo Patre, Agnove, Sagria, Erbilio, Orunia, and Cartasse: under one see, fifteen sees are counted.

“To the metropolitan see of Toledo shall be subject the following sees in their entirety. Oretum: this shall hold from Galla as far as Euga, or Cecila, and from Petra as far as Campania. Mentesa: this shall hold from Euga, or Cecila, as far as Secura, [Col. 1172D] and from Delila as far as Polixena. Acci: this shall hold from Secura as far as Montanea, and from Architel as far as Caraval. Basti: this shall hold from Egesta as far as Montanea, and from Rauci as far as Susita. Urgi: this shall hold from Egesta as far as Carthage, and from Bigastrum as far as Munda. Bigastrum: this shall hold from Pugilla as far as Nisdomia, and from Serta as far as Lisbon. Illici: this shall hold the boundaries of Bigastrum, Setuli, and Denia. Setalis: this shall hold from Custo as far as Moleta, and from Togola as far as Nitria. Denia: this shall hold from Sosa as far as Tura de Silva, as far as Gil. Valencia: this shall hold from Silva as far as Musuetum, and from the sea as far as Alpout. Valena: this shall hold from Alpout as far as Tarrabila, and from Stazerola as far as Nenar. Secobriga: this shall hold from Alcout as far as Obia, and from Mora as far as Lustriania. Complutum: this shall hold from Alcout as far as Coste, and from Gusia as far as Costea. Segontia: this shall hold from Coste as far as Fusca, and from Godol as far as Pina. Oxoma: this shall hold from Fusca as far as the Arlanza, [Col. 1173A] as the road of Saint Peter runs, which goes to Saint James; its boundaries shall extend from Garise as far as Ermitas. Segovia: this shall hold from Almet as far as Mimbillum, and from Martel as far as the place called Vaso. Palencia: this shall hold from Mimbillum as far as Calta, and from Lulbonar as far as Tortosa.

“To the metropolitan see of Tarragona shall be subject these sees:

“Barcelona: this shall hold from Mina as far as Pugella, and from Usa as far as Bordel. Egara: this shall hold from Bordel as far as Paladera, and from Montosa as far as Portella. Gerunda: this shall hold from Pilida as far as Juxtamare, and from Alosa as far as Pinas. Eupiria: these shall hold from Juxtamare as far as Berga, and from Mentosa as far as Silva. Arisona: this shall hold from Berga as far as Aurita, and from Pursa as far as Mentia. Urgell: this shall hold from Aurita as far as Naiona, and from Murela as far as Vala. Lérida: this shall hold from Naiona as far as the fountain of Salla, and from Lora as far as Mata. Ictosa: this shall hold from the Fountain of Salla as far as Porsella, and from Morale [Col. 1173B] as far as Tormela. Tortosa: this shall hold from Porsella as far as Denia, and from Tormoga as far as Catena. Zaragoza: this shall hold from Moovia, or Denia, as far as Splana; and from Mount Olibia as far as Gordoto shall be the boundary of the Zaragozan see. Huesca: this shall hold from Splana as far as Cobello, and from Speslem as far as Ribera. Pamplona: this shall hold from Cobello as far as Mustella, and from Sparga as far as Ostural. Calahorra: this shall hold from Nampia as far as Sparga, and from Mustella as far as Loeal. San-Tirasona: this shall hold from Sparga as far as Plitena, and from Alto Monte as far as Mille. Areca: this shall hold from Planta as far as Amasa, and from the Infernal Foot as far as the Moorish Foot. The Balearic Islands: Majorca, Minorca, Formentera, and Usetica.

“To the metropolitan see of Seville shall be subject these sees:

“Italica: this shall hold from Ulea as far as Busa, and from Asa as far as Lancola. Asidonia: this shall hold from Busa as far as Sena, and from Lotesa as far as the Broad Way. Elipla: this shall hold from Sena as far as Data, and from Alisa as far as Cortesa. Málaga: this shall hold from Data as far as [Col. 1173C] Malexca, and from Temia as far as the Seats of the Field. Eliberis: this shall hold from Málaga as far as Sotella, and from Almica as far as the Seats. Astigi: this shall hold from Sotella as far as the Wall, and from Luca as far as Rauca. Córdoba: this shall hold from the Wall as far as Ubeda, and from Galla as far as Rana. Egabrum: this shall hold from Ubeda as far as Malamsaya, and from Gasta as far as Fuente. Tucci: this shall hold from Malasaya as far as Balijar, and from Guegara as far as Celonus. I believe ‘Azlona’ should be read in place of ‘Castulo.’

“To the metropolitan see of Braga shall be subject these sees:

“Dumium: this shall hold from Duma as far as Albra, and from Reantear as far as Aclasa. Pertucale: this shall hold from Elbora as far as Losola, and from Olmos as far as Sola. Portugal: this shall hold from Losola as far as Bigonia, and from White Mountain as far as Fetonsa. Auria: this shall hold from Cusanca as far as Silva, and from Vereginus as far as Celebacismum. Iria: this shall hold from Iso as far as Cusaca, and from the King’s Bath as far as the Shore. Lugo: this shall hold from Laguna as far as Bussa, and from Mount Soto as far as Quintana. Britonia: from Bassa as far as the Torrents, from Oetoba as far as Totella, and as far as the Ove. Astorga: this shall extend along the shore of the Valley of Corcer and by the rivers—or, namely, seas—Orbigo, Berrio, and Tavara.

“To the metropolitan see of Mérida shall be subject these sees:

“Pare: this shall hold from Baligur as far as Croca, and from the Mountain of Olla as far as Miratal. Lisbon: this shall hold from Darca as far as Ambra, and from Olla as far as Mara. Elbora: this shall hold from Sotobra as far as Petra, from Rucella as far as the Tower of Egitani, from Sabra as far as Nava, and from Sena as far as Muriela. Exoniba: this shall hold from Ambra as far as Sala, and from [or: from that] Rosa as far as the Tower. Coimbra: this shall hold from Nava as far as Berga, and from Torrente as far as Lora. Veseus: this shall hold from Berga as far as Sorta, and from Boncla as far as Ventosa. Biglimicum: this shall hold from Sorta as far as Petra, and from Sara as far as Ortosa. [Col. 1174A] Cabrabria: this shall hold from Sorta as far as Albenia, and from Soto as far as Fara. Salamanca: this shall hold from Allenia as far as Sotobra, and from Rusa as far as Siberus. Numantia: this shall hold from Penagodisse as far as the Tormes, above those baths; from the Valley of the King as far as the Douro; from Villa Valle as far as Otero; from Fumus, beside the Dry Stream, as far as Borito; and from Tavara as far as the Douro. Ávila: this shall hold from Petra as far as Vialla, and from Uriosto as far as Torrero. Cauria: this shall hold from Villa as far as the Tagus, otherwise the Douro.

“To the metropolitan see of Narbonne shall be subject these sees:

“Isetenis: this shall hold from Stalus as far as Barunona, and from Macu as far as Rib. Fora. Agatha: this shall hold from Nusa as far as Ribera, and from Galia as far as Mirla. Magalona: this shall hold from Nusa as far as Ribogar, and from the Castle of Millia as far as Angora. Nemausus: this shall hold from Gusa as far as Angora, and from the Castle as far as Samura. Luteba: this shall hold from Samba as far as Rebubal, and from Anges as far as Mount Rufus. Carcassonne: [Col. 1174B] this shall hold from Mount Rufus as far as Anger, and from Angosta as far as Mons. Elna: this shall hold from Strage as far as Rofilon, and from Literosa as far as Lanusa.

“These are the sees of the two Spains, eighty in number, under Gothic rule, both archiepiscopal and episcopal, through which the word of God is ministered to all the Spaniards; and from the Roman pontiff they receive—and always receive in these provinces—the communion of Catholic truth, so that, according to the tradition and teaching of the holy Fathers, we may govern the souls entrusted to us.”

The king adds: “Therefore let this ordinance of ours, made with the assent of all the archbishops and bishops of the said sees, by God’s authority, remain firm forever; and I command that it be read.” It was read by Peter, archdeacon of Toledo, in the presence of Quiricus, archbishop of Toledo, steadfast in the dignity of primate and in the Catholic faith, and of the other archbishops, who immediately subscribed, together with the bishops. Let all say: “It pleases us; it pleases us. Life and eternal glory to the Catholic, [Col. 1174C] most pious and most glorious prince, our lord Flavius Wamba.”

### Canon I

“Furthermore, it pleases us, gathered together as one, that all clerics henceforth live according to the rule of our most holy Father Isidore, bishop of Seville, as it is contained in his book *On the Honesty of Clerics*.”

### Canon II

“And whoever—whether an archbishop, bishop, cloistered abbot, or secular abbot—shall thereafter give the king more than a mina on account of rank, office, or any ecclesiastical benefice, or give it to any other person, let him be bound by the excommunication of perpetual anathema.”

“When these matters had been completed, we first offered immortal thanks to God, the author of all things and all good; then we prayed for a very long life for our glorious king, and after this age, eternal blessedness in the heavenly kingdom: for by such zeal for piety he has settled our disputes and joined us in an eternal [Col. 1174D] indissoluble bond.

“We appoint the council here for the following year.”

### Subscription of the Fathers

“Four vicars of the remaining four bishops, twelve abbots, and twenty palatines were present at this general council of all Spain and Narbonese Gaul: the vicars of Lugo, Egitani, Castulo, and Cursicania. These acts were conducted here at Toledo in the general council, with all seventy-five bishops present, together with four vicars of bishops, twelve abbots, and twenty palatines, all saying with one voice: ‘It pleases us; it pleases us.’ The invincible and most serene King Wamba was present and subscribed, together with Quiricus, archbishop of Toledo and primate of the Spains, and the other five archbishops with their suffragans from the aforesaid dioceses. The synod was begun partly in the praetorian church of Saints Peter and Paul and completed in the church of Saint Leocadia, virgin and martyr, citizen of Toledo and native patroness, in her praetorian temple, in the year 713 of the Spanish Era. The synod was written by the hand of Peter, archdeacon of the said collegiate church of Saint Leocadia.”

267. The aforesaid King Wamba lived for five years, up to the year 718 of the Era, and died after spending several years most devoutly as a monk of the order of the most holy Father Benedict, to whom he had withdrawn. [Col. 1177A] From there everything, or much of it, was transferred into the Ovetense codex of Itatius.

268. This synod deserves the highest esteem, since there was an enormous gathering of archbishops, bishops, abbots, and palatines, with King Wamba present. It necessarily continued for a long time, while each Church displayed the boundaries of its pontificate and the king himself heard the causes of their complaints. For that reason the synod was held in two churches and suburban temples: begun in one and completed in the other.

269. Sixty-eight bishops attended the Third Council of Toledo; sixty-nine attended the Fourth. Seven more bishops and four vicars attended this council, in which the sees were repaired and restored. Nor could matters have been handled otherwise than by having the king appoint certain judges for each of the metropolitan sees, who would refer to him the matters settled by them. [Col. 1177B] Thus the king’s judgment could be openly pronounced with the consent of all and approved by everyone, as is clear from the frequent repetition of the individuals acclaiming and repeatedly saying joyfully: “It pleases us; it pleases us.”

270. In this division the boundaries of the metropolitan Churches are not set out, for the reason that metropolitan jurisdiction extended not only through its own diocese but over all those subject to it, just as the warmth of the heart is common to all the limbs.

271. I remember reading in Germany, in an ancient codex written in Gothic letters, in the *Life of Blessed Ildefonsus*, also a bishop of Toledo, written by Cixila, archbishop of Toledo: “Leocadia said: ‘Ildefonsus, through you my lady lives.’” This reading is more pleasing than the other, which has: “Ildefonsus said: ‘Through the life of Ildefonsus my lady lives.’”

272. They say that royal eagles flew from pole to pole, and for this reason the apostles are called eagles, because they traversed the whole world, according to the saying in Ecclesiastes: “The way of an eagle in the heavens.” They also say that Jupiter sent two eagles, one from the east and the other from the west; and that at last they met at Delphi, a city of Greece, which is called the world’s ὀμφαλός (*omphalos*), that is, “navel.”

273. Illiturgi is a city in the Bastetani, five days’ journey from Carthage Spartaria. Livy mentions it, and Scipio destroyed it. Saint Euphrasius is believed to have preached there and to have been bishop of Illiturgi.

[Col. 1177D] 274. On a high crag stands a fortress called Tavia, in Greek Ancyra, named after a certain city so called, which Antoninus Pius mentions three times in the *Itinerary*.

275. Saint Ildefonsus was ordained lector, doorkeeper, exorcist, subdeacon, and levite by Saint Helladius in the praetorian church [read: in the *Bracarense Breviary*] of Saint Leocadia, after he had visited the monastery of Agali; from there he brought Saint Ildefonsus with him. By Justus, at the end of his life, namely in the year 636—as at the end of the life of Saint Helladius, levite, in the year 633 [perhaps one should read: “By Justus, at the end of his life, namely in the year 633, as subdeacon; and, at the end of the life of Saint Helladius, levite, in the year 636”]—he was consecrated a Benedictine abbot by Saint Eugenius.

276. In the third year of Aurasio, archbishop of Toledo, namely [Col. 1178A] in the year 644 of the Era, Saint Ildefonsus, later bishop of Toledo, was born in his paternal home.

277. In several corrected Livian manuscripts, in the third decade, book 8, *Iliturgis* is read with a single *l*, as it should be read to distinguish it from the other Baetican city, which is written with a double *l*. In Eulogius it is likewise written with a single one.

278. Those who think that Flaviobriga was the city which the Moors called Ordunia, the capital of the Amanian peoples, who are part of the Autrigonian peoples, have a probable view.

279. Uxama, Segisamunclum, Virbesca, Antecuia, Deobriga, Vindelia, Salionca, Tritium (different from Tricio Metello), and Vindelegra were subject to the colony of Flaviobriga, which was their capital; and they went there for the administration of justice.

[Col. 1178B] 280. The Romans fought at Belgida, or Vellia, or Velligia, or Vellica, among the Cantabri, as L. Florus reports. This is now called Spinosa by the Moors, like Araquellos, or Racim, or Arandillos, not far from the sources of the Ebro. Segisamona, however, is a people of the Turmodigi [or Curmodigi]—the Saracens call it Osorno—not far from the Segisamona of those same Turmodigi [or Curmodigi], whom Florus calls Curgonii.

[Col. 1178C] 281. In my time the body of Saint Laura the martyr was discovered at Córdoba, after she had been killed by the Saracens more than ninety years earlier. She belonged to the most noble family of the Mozarabs of Córdoba and was joined by a special bond of kinship to Saint Aurea, abbess of Cuteclara. Given by her parents in marriage to a noble man, she had two daughters. After being widowed of him six years later, she withdrew to the monastery of Saint Aurea. But Aurea soon afterward—namely, in the year 856, crowned with the blood of martyrdom—was succeeded by Laura, who governed the monastery for nine years. During that time she made marvelous progress in every virtue, always devoted to prayer and bodily discipline. At length, when rumor brought her before the Saracen judge, she remained steadfast in confessing the faith. She was cruelly beaten, cast naked into a bath of boiling pitch, and, by divine favor, completed three hours in divine praise; then she flew to heaven on 19 October in the year of the Lord 864. Saint Eulogius does not mention her, since he himself had been crowned with martyrdom in the year 859. The relics of Blessed Laura began to be distributed among many churches of Spain [Col. 1178D], and she herself came to be held in great honor.

282. The Port of the Juliobrigenses, consecrated to victory, was so called because the Cantabrian Juliobrigenses were defeated there when they attempted to repel the Roman fleet in the time of the emperor Augustus. Others more correctly think it was so called because the Juliobrigenses won a victory; for the victory is not said to have been “of the Juliobrigenses” as those defeated, but “of the Juliobrigenses” as those who won it.

283. Sarcimum is a village among the Cantabri in Spain, near the sources of the Ebro. Saint Eucherius, bishop of Orléans, was exiled there by order of Charles Martel. In his *Life* the reading *Hesbania* is corrupt. There was a monastery of Saint Trudo, a Benedictine, in Cantabria, as there was in Germany. In Spain Charles Martel had many friends, among the Cantabri; and what is now called Sarcimum among the Cantabri, or Sacernulum among the Astures, is called Barcena or Salcedo, certain insignificant little towns.

284. The most holy man Vera, archbishop of Tarragona, who attended the Sixteenth Council of Toledo, a pious, humble, and holy man, died on 20 October; he is celebrated in the territory of Orléans among the Carpetani.

285. There is an author who believes that Saint Exubius [or Exibius], a disciple of Saint Mark, preached the Gospel after his death in Caucasolia [or Centumcellae] in Lusitania, and afterward returned alone to Cyprus, where he was appointed archbishop. He is said to have performed the greatest miracles because of his works.

[Col. 1179B] 286. It seems to me highly probable—and I have read it in histories—that Elpidius and the other bishops whom Saint James appointed [or brought] to Spain, having been baptized by James himself, belonged to the number of the religious Carmelites who had introduced monastic life in Spain and in other regions. Eusebius calls them, in book II, chapter 3, “of the prophetic order.”

287. A large part of those who crossed from Judaea into Spain in the time of Nebuchadnezzar were disciples of the holy men Elisha, Elijah, and Enoch, and their successors.

[Col. 1179C] 288. I was able to see the *Life of Saint Syncletica*, an Egyptian virgin and abbess (whose feast day is 5 January). Saint Athanasius, the holy pontiff, wrote it so that, just as monks have a mirror in Antony, sacred virgins might regard her as a mirror. She is said to have been the mother of many virgins belonging to the prophetic and Carmelite profession.

289. C. Caninius [or Herminius] Rufus, praetor of Gades, set out for Rome in the year 84, the fourth year of the 215th Olympiad. He crossed into Spain [or remained in Spain] until the year 86, and, while attempting to travel from Gades to Tarragona, died on the road at the town of Villa Aenea, otherwise Alona or Delo, now corruptly called Villena by the Moors; he lies buried there.

290. [Note: [Col. 1179D] 290. Abula of the Bastetani. On Abula of the Bastetani, see Julianus in the *Adversaria*, no. 513: “Ptolemy places Abula among the Bastetani and Obila among the Vettones.”] Ten Roman miles westward from the town of Turbula or Tritubi [or Tibula or Tribula] stood the town of Abula of the Bastetani, now ruined.

291. Urci was the springs [or: see] of Saint Indaletius. [Col. 1179D] This is said to be Portella, and it divided its boundaries with the sees in the following manner: “It shall hold from Egesta [read: Egelesta; see what I noted at no. 38 in the *Chronicle* and at no. 242] as far as Carthage, and from Bigastrum or Murcia as far as Munda.” This city lies beside the river Munda, eight Roman miles before the Munda flows into the Tader; it either gave its name to the river or received its name from it.

[Col. 1180A] 292. Pliny the Younger, of venerable memory, wrote to Trajan in defense of the Christians. Some believe that, on his return from Asia, he was converted to the faith in Crete, and afterward, during the persecution of Antoninus Pius, suffered at Novocomum with others on 7 August; for so distinguished a work of defense ought not to have been deprived of its just reward.

293. In the fifteenth year of Trajan, in the year of the Lord 114 (at which time he was called Sarmaticus Arabicus), Pliny returned from Asia to Crete. He had a famous temple built to Jupiter in honor of Trajan; Titus destroyed it, and it was restored in the name of Jesus Christ. Pliny Secundus, together with his son [the words “together with his son” are absent in some copies], believed in Christ and was baptized by Saint Titus, bishop of the Cretans, as Zenas relates in his *Life*. Thus, [Col. 1180B] having returned to Rome as a Christian, he lived many years in holiness and piety. He was called Gaius Plinius by Trajan and Secundus by others; nor was there another man of consular rank named Secundus at that time.

294. Pompeia Celerina, the mother-in-law of Pliny the Younger, was the sister of Saint Celerina, who received the body of Saint Torpes the martyr when it miraculously came from Tuscany to the port of Sinus.

295. Some think that Pope Dionysius was African by birth and the author of the book *On the Situation of the World*, who endured martyrdom.

296. Theodorus, the river—that is, “gift of God”—is called the Tader and Staberus, because of the exceptional water it possesses through its union with the Munda, which enters the Mediterranean [Col. 1180C] near the city of Longuntica.

297. Saint Benedicta, who died victorious at Rome in the time of Nero, was born to pagan parents from Zaragoza in Spain. When she attained the palm which she had long and greatly desired, she was struck three or four times with whips and carried through the city with her body naked; but, by God’s favor, she appeared not naked at all. On 2 July, offering her neck, she flew to the Bridegroom. She was one of the earlier virgins of Christ killed at Rome for the faith.

298. In corrected manuscripts of Pliny, instead of *Alga minor*, which is found in the less-correct manuscripts, *Alba minor* is read.

299. Suel, between Alater and Siex [or Aodetera or Abdeera, and Exi], was called Sudal [or Siuel], and later, because of its strength, began to be called the Iron Castle.

300. The *Itinerary of Antoninus Pius Augustus* was compiled at his command, as you will read in the codices of Theodosius.

301. [Note: 301. The ten legates, etc. Concerning these legates, see Flavius Dexter in the *Chronicle*, under the year of Christ 35, no. 1, where the most learned Bivarius conducts himself learnedly. Julianus nevertheless differs in number in the *Chronicle*, no. 9: “Those Jews of Toledo sent Euphrasius and Indaletius, asking Peter and the other apostles to send James immediately; and when they came to Jerusalem, they gave their letters to Peter.”] Ten legates came from Spain to Jerusalem, five Gentiles and five Jews, to the apostles.

## In the Year of the Lord 975, Folquinus of Saint-Bertin, a monk.

[Col. 1181]

## Historical Notice

(Guérard, *Cartulary of Saint-Bertin*.)

Le cartulaire de Saint-Bertin was begun around the middle of the tenth century by a religious of that abbey named Folquin, who styles himself a monk and a levite. Folquin was born in Lorraine, into one of the noblest families of the region. His mother was named Thiédale, and his father Folquin. The latter was the son of Odwin, whose father—also named Odwin—was the brother of Saint Folquin, bishop of Thérouanne, and the son of Jerome and Ermentrude. The humble monk, who himself gives us this genealogy [Note: [Col. 1181] Guérard edition, p. 141], fails to mention that his great-great-grandfather Jerome was the uncle of Saint Adalard, abbot of Corbie, and the son of Charles Martel [Note: [Col. 1181] *Histoire littéraire*, vol. VI, p. 384; Mabillon, *Saec. Bened.*, IV, part I, p. 625, no. 6].

In the year 948, Folquin’s father and mother themselves brought him to Saint-Omer, where, at the beginning of November, they dedicated him to God in the abbey of Saint-Bertin [Note: [Col. 1181] Guérard edition, p. 146].

It is mistakenly that a sixteenth-century writer seems to give him the title of abbot [Note: [Col. 1181] Guérard edition, p. 372], and that certain scholars confused him with a monk of the same name who became abbot of Lobbes in 965 [Note: [Col. 1181] *Bibliothèque historique de la France*, vol. I, no. 12361]. Folquin does not appear ever to have left his abbey, where he died around the year 975 [Note: [Col. 1181] *Histoire littéraire*, vol. VI, p. 384. See Mabillon, cited work, and *Annales*, XLVI, 50]. He was still only a deacon, *levita*, when he began his cartulary, and nothing indicates that he ever advanced further in holy orders or was promoted to any position of distinction in his monastery. The subscription *Folquinus levita et monachus subscripsit*, placed at the foot of a charter whose summary he gives, proves only that he was employed in drafting the abbey’s documents. Perhaps he even had charge of the archives of Saint-Bertin; the speed with which he composed the collection bearing his name proves at least that he already possessed all its materials.

Folquin took up his pen at the order of Abbot Adalolph, elected on 4 April 961, and the last event he reports in his chronicle is the voluntary resignation of that same abbot, which occurred no later than the beginning of the following year. The first part of our cartulary was therefore written in 961.

It begins with a pompous eulogy of Saint Bertin. Folquin compares him to the sun, which he calls Titan. The poetic formulas with which he adorns his panegyric prove that he was not unfamiliar with secular literature. He then recounts, in a few words, Saint Bertin’s arrival at Sithiu and the construction there of a church in stone and brick. His narrative contains no allusion even to an old legend that embellishes the abbey’s second foundation with miraculous circumstances [Note: [Col. 1181] See the three anonymous Lives of Saint Bertin published in the Bollandists’ collection, under 5 September]. Although he is not entirely free from the pious credulity characteristic of his century, Folquin generally appears more judicious than his continuators: he is sparing in marvelous tales; he mocks those who attributed a direct influence over human events to the moon; and he seems, finally, to have possessed a judgment and critical sense uncommon for the period in which he lived.

In writing his work, Folquin intended to make known, in chronological order, the acts, *gesta*, of the abbots of Saint-Bertin and the donations of real property that had successively increased the abbey’s estate. As for the less important charters, he had formed a separate collection, whose divisions each corresponded to one of the monastery’s administrative offices, so that each official could, when necessary, find in a single chapter all the documents relating to his department.

When presenting his work to Abbot Adalolph, Folquin declares that he has written nothing except what he was able to learn from trustworthy witnesses or gather from ancient diplomas that had escaped the ravages of time and fire. These old documents are generally dated by the years of the kings’ reigns and the popes’ pontificates. To make research easier, Folquin added to these dates the years of the Incarnation, while taking care never to insert them into the text of the charters, so that he could not be accused of altering them. He deserves all the more credit for this precaution because, as Mabillon observed, his chronological concordance is often faulty; had he attached it to the acts themselves, most of those he reported would inevitably have been rejected as suspect.

Folquin’s collection is contained in a small parchment folio volume, apparently written at the beginning of the twelfth century, which now belongs to the library of Boulogne [Note: [Col. 1181] A copy of this manuscript, executed with great care by M. E. Miller, an employee of the Imperial Library, is preserved in that library among the cartularies, under no. 158]. [Col. 1183] It is divided into two books, preceded by a list of the abbots of Saint-Bertin. The first book consists of sixty-one chapters and the second of eighty-one; following these are eleven charters, transcribed or analyzed, recording donations or acquisitions of immovable property assigned to the monastery’s almonry. This brings the total for the second book to ninety-one chapters. It can even be seen from the table of chapters written at the beginning of the Boulogne manuscript that Folquin’s second book originally consisted, in that manuscript, of ninety-three chapters; but since the last leaf of the volume was torn out, chapter 93 is now entirely missing, as is the end of chapter 92, which, as will easily be noticed, is incomplete in our edition [Note: [Col. 1183] See p. 168 of Guérard’s edition. In the table of chapters of the Boulogne manuscript, this chapter 92 bears the number 93, while the chapter missing from the manuscript bears the number 94].

[Col. 1183]

# FOLQUIN’S CARTULARY

*(In D. Guérard’s, Cartulaire de Saint-Bertin.)*

## HERE BEGINS BOOK ONE

[Col. 1183A] In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Since in this codex we desire to draw out the deeds of the abbots of the Sithiu monastery, and to describe the transfers of possessions that the faithful, during the tenure of each one of them, granted to this sacred place together with the written charter recording them, let us begin this work with Christ, from its first builder, Lord Bertin, the abbot.

## I. Prologue of Folquin, levite and monk

That almighty God has often given his faithful two rewards in return—one during the pilgrimage of this present life, the other in the perpetual tranquility of the heavenly realms—the sacred little page, wisely furrowed by the knife of the goose-quill, has sufficiently revealed to those who examine it. For here it makes manifest among men, so long as they live, many whom it causes to glitter through the life-giving miracles of their virtues [Col. 1183B]; afterward, for the sweat of their labor, it grants them perpetual rest in eternal repose. Hence it also comes about that, by praising their memory, it continually magnifies on earth those whose names of everlastingness are written in white letters in heaven.

Among these, one patron above all others stands dear to us before God and the present age. When, as our mind’s vision rises to lofty heavenly contemplation, he appears glorious to us like golden Titan when, with the new morning, leaving his saffron sevenfold chambers, he sends forth his shafts of brilliant light throughout the sloping, revolving circle of the world, scattering the darkness. For in his likeness, through the gifts of the Holy Spirit, the hearts of the elect are often sufficiently kindled to the love of God.

Therefore, first of all, the Latin language earnestly asks permission to bring forth the etymology of his name, which all the people habitually utter in the simple vernacular form “Bertin,” since, although its meaning is profound, no one now knows how better to name it. The first letter of the name is B, because from infancy he had always been good. The syllable E-R follows in the same way, and this is understood to signify the whole meaning of inheritance; with *ti* changed into *na*, one syllable still remains, from the fact that he was born—so that the whole may be joined together and understood as: “the good heir born for us,” given forever by the Lord God, since his merits rightly demanded it, and therefore he stands daily as our principal intercessor for our crimes.
