Now it is neither necessary nor within our power to attempt, in the compressed brevity of this little work, to touch even slightly upon the many miracles of so great a patron, which the Lord deigned to perform through him while he was still living in the body. For everything that occurred while he was leading a blessed life in this world, or during the novelty of his passing, a highly skilled writer’s hand has clearly set forth for readers in his Life [Note: [Col. 1183] The Life of Saint Bertin was published by Mabillon, *Saec. Bened.*, III, part I, pp. 108 ff., and by the Bollandists, September, vol. II, pp. 586 ff., 590 ff.].

Meanwhile, if he himself also deigns to be present, we wish to turn your attention to his many labors, for which he toiled with unceasing exertion in raising up this place. For when, in accordance with the Lord’s command, he had left his homeland and come to Sithiu with two companions, he found everything at that time desolate because of the excessive corruption of the many marshes and the density of the woods; there was nothing useful for human purposes, except what even today is not lacking to the inhabitants for catching scaly creatures [i.e. fish]. In that place the holy man labored so greatly in the name of God that first he raised on high a noble temple composed of stones and red bricks intermixed. Near it were columns whose capitals, each bearing a vaulted structure, firmly support both walls; and no less inside the oratory he decorously adorned the pavement with a joining of multicolored stones, which in many places inlay golden plates. Anyone who wishes may examine before his eyes the structure of this temple.

We have gathered only this codex, made from parchment leaves, into the body of a single book, so that, if anyone should be eager to investigate the possessions of this place, he might turn to it. There he will be able to find, as quickly as possible, the number and names suitably joined under the headings of the years of the Lord’s Nativity or of whatever king was reigning at the time, insofar as our ability allowed [Note: [Col. 1185D] On this point, as Mabillon notes, Folquin frequently departed from the correct calculation]. But not everything, since much was neglected by our predecessors, partly through the burning of books and partly through the destruction caused by age.

## II. How Adroald transferred the village of Sithiu to Saint Bertin

At the beginning of the work, therefore, with Christ as our guide, we place first the transfer made by Adroald, at that time a most illustrious man, who, as is read in the deeds of our revered father Bertin [Note: [Col. 1185D] See Mabillon, *Saec. Bened.*, III, part I, p. 109, and the Bollandists, September, vol. II, p. 587A], since he had no hereditary possession of his property, began after the passing of human frailty to consider earnestly how he might entrust earthly things to Christ in order to purchase heavenly ones.

Accordingly, when Lord Bertin came into the territory of Carvanne at the urging of the blessed bishop Audomar, the aforementioned Adroald transferred to the revered Bertin a village belonging to his own right, called Sithiu, in the year of the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 640 [Note: [Col. 1185D] More correctly, in the year 648 or the following year, which agrees with the eleventh year of Chlothar’s reign], which was the eleventh year of King Chlothar, son of Dagobert, so that he might build there a monastery in honor of the prince of the apostles and inspire many to the monastic way of life by the example of his own conduct. We have taken care to place here before the eyes of those who wish to know it a copy of this transfer.

## III. Copy of Adroald’s transfer

[Note: [Col. 1185D] Published by Miraeus, *Opera diplomatica*, vol. I, p. 7.]

“ To the holy lords and fathers Bertin, Mummolin, and Ebertrannus.

“I, Adroald, in the name of God, being of sound mind and sound judgment, with complete deliberation, insofar as the Lord may deign to cleanse my worldly sins from their enticements, give to you all the property of my hereditary portion in the district of Taroanne, which we had wished to give to Lord Father Audomar, an apostolic man, for the construction of his *senodichium* [uncertain technical term]; but he gave us sounder and better counsel, namely, that I should transfer the property itself to you, so that you may build there a monastery in honor of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, where monks may live, and where the blessed poor in spirit and the members of the household of faith may be gathered together—those whose voices are known to resound daily in the ears of the Lord, whose petitions the Lord hears and fulfills.

“Therefore, to you, fathers in Christ, by this deed of donation, I give, in the district of Taroanne, a village belonging to my own property, called Sithiu, above the river Aa, with all its appurtenances, dependencies, and belongings. These are: the villages of Magnigeleca, Wiciaco, Tatinga, Ammeio, Masto, Fabricinio, Losantanas, and at Fundenis or Malros, Alciaco, the village of Laudardiaca, and Franciliaco, with all their appurtenances; with houses, buildings, cultivated and uncultivated lands; dwellings with woods, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, mills, slaves, and *acculabae* [an uncertain term]; flocks with shepherds; movable and immovable property; and every kind of benefit.

“All these things I transfer and confirm to you in full, so that you may have, hold, and possess them, and leave them to whomever you wish to possess them. If anyone—which I do not believe will happen—whether I, or any of my heirs, or any opposing person, should at any time attempt to act against this donation, may he immediately incur the anger of God and the offense of Saint Peter; moreover, compelled by the fisc, may he be forced to pay fifteen pounds of gold and thirty pounds of silver, and may he be unable to reclaim what he demands.

“And so that this donation may remain most firm for all time, we have strengthened it with our hand and have asked those who should mark or subscribe it to do so at present. This donation was made on the eighth day before the Ides of September, in the eleventh year of the reign of our lord King Chlothar [Note: [Col. 1186D] On the construction of the monastery and the other matters carried out after Adroald’s donation by Bertin, Mummolin, and Ebertrannus, see Mabillon, *Annales*, XIII, 49, vol. I, pp. 400 ff.].

“Executed publicly at Ascio, a royal estate, before the strong and distinguished persons whose names, with their subscriptions or marks, are inserted below.

“I, Adroald, have subscribed this donation made by me. In the name of Christ, I, Audomar, a sinner, a bishop in name but not in merit, have subscribed as witness. I, Agolfus, although unworthy, a priest, have subscribed. I, Ingobertus, although unworthy, a priest, have subscribed.

“+ The mark of Chunebertus, count. + The mark of Landebertus. The mark of Maurilio. The mark of Babo. The mark of [the] Sacebaro [Note: [Col. 1186D] Here “Sign.” appears to have to be deleted, so that the reading may be: “The mark of Babo, *sacebaro*”]. The mark of Adalbaldus. Abbot Leudolenus subscribed. [The mark of Waldegisilus. In the name of Christ, I, Ragnulfus, at the command of Lord Audomar, bishop, and at the request of Adroald, an illustrious man, wrote and subscribed this donation.]

“Witnesses to this transfer:

“The mark of Babbano. The mark of Seoguino. + The mark of Crodmarus. + The mark of Ermembertus. + The mark of Maurinus. + The mark of Adalcharius. + The mark of Rigobertus. + The mark of Chrodobaldus. + The mark of Vumegerus. + Danoaldus, priest, A. The mark of Ormarus. + The mark of Ineufus. + The mark of Bertolandus. The mark of [Col. 1186D] Tadobaldus. + The mark of Astronvaldus. + The mark of Gaibertus. + Bainus, A. The mark of Madalgisus. + The mark of Burgastus. + The mark of Madalaulfus. + The mark of Aldebertus. The mark of Traswaldus. + The mark of Macrinus. + Gislebertus, A. The mark of Badonus. + The mark of Radbaldus, priest. + The mark of Vualdmarus. + The mark of Anchaldus, priest, in the name of Christ, as above, A. The mark of Charricus. + The mark of Isbertus, priest. + The mark of Amalgarius.” 

## IV. Copy of the exchange of the estate between Saint Bertin and Bishop Mummolin

[Note: [Col. 1187D] Published by Mabillon, *De re diplomatica*, p. 625.]

[Col. 1187A]

Under the Frankish prince Chlothar, son of the aforesaid King Clovis, in the sixth year of his reign and in the year 660 of the Incarnate Word, the venerable man Mummolin, bishop of Noyon, and Lord Bertin, abbot of the Sithiu monastery, agreed to exchange certain small estates among themselves. The venerable Bishop Mummolin gave Lord Bertin, the abbot, a village called Vallis, which he had given from his share to the most reverend man Ebertrannus, abbot of the monastery of Saint-Quentin, in exchange for another village called Tunninio, together with Imbrago and Inglindono, and also Selerciaco. These five small estates he granted to Lord Bertin. Conversely, the revered Bertin gave Bishop Mummolin his portion of a village called Vausune, in the district of Coutances, and, in full, another place called the village of Lauvardiaca. They asked that this exchange be confirmed by royal authority, and this was done. It seemed appropriate to set forth a copy of the royal confirmation.

## V. Copy of the same

[Note: [Col. 1187D] In this precept of Chlothar, Folquin lacks the initial formula, which we have supplied within brackets. The subscriptions of the king and Queen Balthechildis are also missing, although both confirmed it with the mark of their hands, in the same manner as in the subsequent letters of Clovis III, in which Chrodechildis subscribes with her son Clovis under the formula: “The mark of the glorious King Clovis,” and “The mark of our exalted mother Queen Chrodechildis.” This formula is also preserved in the diplomas of the younger Clovis, and is entirely consonant with the Carolingian formula. A corruption seems to have entered the text of this diploma at the words “to Lord Mummolin, abbot or bishop,” since elsewhere he is simply called bishop, with no mention of an abbatial dignity, which some attribute to him before his episcopate. Moreover, Clovis III cites this precept, and also cites in this matter the diplomas of his uncle Childeric and of his father Theodoric. We do not possess Childeric’s letters; Folquin presents Theodoric’s precept as follows.]

[“Chlothar, illustrious king of the Franks.”]

Since the Lord has made us sit upon the throne of our parents, it is fitting that we should act beneficially and carefully consider what, in the name of God, we ought to undertake, so that whatever concerns the advancement of churches or the preservation of the property of the saints may be willingly granted by us, so that it may remain inviolate in the name of God, may count toward our reward with the eternal Requiter, and so that the congregation, singing to God, may strive to pray for the Lord’s mercy on our behalf.

Accordingly, the apostolic man Mummolin, bishop of the city of Noyon, and likewise the venerable man Bertin, abbot of the monastery of Sithiu, situated in the district of Thérouanne—both of whose works were seen to have built the monastery, constructed in honor of holy Mary, mother of our Lord Jesus Christ, and of Saints Peter and Paul the apostles, as well as the other holy lords—came into our presence and brought before the clemency of our reign a statement that they ought to exchange among themselves certain suitable and convenient small estates, both in the district of Coutances and in that of Noyon, Cambrai, or Vermandois, wherever they might identify a suitable place.

Therefore, the aforementioned Lord Mummolin, bishop, and the venerable man Bertin, abbot, unanimously asked us to grant them permission to exchange, both on the part of Lord Mummolin, bishop, and of the city of Noyon under his episcopate, and on the part of Bertin, abbot, and his monastery of Sithiu, whenever they should agree and find a place, so that they might have our permission to carry it out.

They found among themselves certain small estates with the following names: Vallis, which Mummolin the bishop gave to the aforementioned Bertin the abbot, having received it from the venerable man Ebertrannus, abbot of the basilica of Saint-Quentin, in exchange for another village called Tumninio, together with Imbrago and Inglindono, and also Selerciaco—five places in all. Similarly, Bertin the abbot gave the aforementioned Lord Mummolin, abbot or bishop, his portion of the village called Vausune, in the district of Coutances, in full, which he had received in exchange from the illustrious Agolfus for another village, Tranciliaco, and another small estate called the village of Laudardiaca, [Col. 1188B] in the district of . . . . ., in full.

All these places named above, out of reverence for that holy place, for Bertin, and for his monastery of Sithiu, we ought to confirm by the full force of our authority to those same Mummolin, bishop, and Bertin, abbot, just as we have said above. Know, therefore, that we have granted their request and confirmed everything.

We command that, just as is established concerning the things mentioned above—whatever has been said regarding those places, with everything belonging to them and in every respect, wholly and in full, namely, with lands, houses, slaves, mills, vineyards, and whatever else they have exchanged among themselves, cultivated and uncultivated, and whatever they appear to possess or control at the present time—so also henceforth, by our precept, everything is fully confirmed. The aforementioned Lord Mummolin, bishop, and Bertin, abbot, shall have, hold, and possess the aforesaid properties that have been transferred or confirmed by our hand, as we declare by this same document; and they may leave them to their successors with the grace of God and of us. Whatever they decide to do with them, they shall have full power in every respect.

No dispute or quarrel between them shall remain in future, nor shall any claim or counterclaim be made by Lord Mummolin, bishop, or by his successors in the city of Noyon; nor shall any be made on the part of Bertin, abbot, or of the monastery of Sithiu or its successors. Nor shall our successors, or anyone else, dare to enter the above-mentioned estate-courts with judicial authority. Rather, without judicial entry, for the sake of our reward, the aforesaid abbot or his successors residing there shall be able to possess them for the monastery, so that the holy congregation may be pleased, under God’s guidance, continually to pray for the Lord’s mercy on our behalf.

And so that this precept may be held more firmly and preserved in every respect by you and your successors through the ages, we and the exalted lady, our mother, Queen Balthechildis, are known to have confirmed it with the mark of our hands.

Done on the Kalends of February, in the sixth year of our reign, at the palace of Crisciacum.

## VI. Concerning the privilege of Saint Audomar, which he granted to Saint Bertin for the basilica of Saint Mary

*(662.)*

In that same year, under the same prince Lothar, the blessed Audomar, bishop of the Church of Thérouanne, made a privilege for Lord Bertin concerning his church, which he had built in the village of Sithiu in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God, for the burial of the bodies of the brothers [Note: [Col. 1189D] Concerning this church, which was later converted into a monastery and finally into the cathedral church of Saint-Omer, see Mabillon, *Annales*, XIII, 49, vol. I, p. 401]. He decreed that this basilica should, under the protection of the patronage of the aforesaid Abbot Bertin and his successors, be governed through succeeding ages until the end. The charter of this privilege bears witness to this, and we have also taken care to write it here as we received it, made at that time.

## VII. Copy of the same privilege

*(14 April 662.)*

“To the holy and venerable lords in Christ who are joined to me, both abbots and priests, deacons, and all the clergy of the Church of Thérouanne, as well as illustrious men, nobles, eminent persons, and very many others: Audomar, by the grace of Christ bishop of the Church of Thérouanne.

“Although it is fitting that we preserve with beneficial observance the constitutions established by the ancient rule, nevertheless, under divine inspiration and after useful deliberation, we have decreed that whatever does not derogate from sacred decisions shall be preserved through fearless observance.

“Since it pleased us, in accordance with fraternal consent and the affection of heartfelt piety, and since this so softened our heart inwardly, we have built, together with those monks, for their consolation and assistance, a basilica on the island of Sithiu, where previously a monastery appears to have been built in the name of God and where monks living according to the rule were established in freedom. We built it by common labor for the repose of their bodies and of ours, in honor of holy Mary, Mother of our Lord Jesus Christ.

“Thus, in the aforesaid basilica, in accordance with the fullest charity of those brothers, my little body, after my death, when it has been deposited and buried there, is to rest among the little bodies of those monks who, in religious habit, gathered at the word of almighty God from differing peoples and from the foulness of the world, and were united in the one bosom of holy Church, strengthened by the love of Christ. They have sought to shake the yoke of the world from their necks and minds, to abandon everything, lay down the burdens of earthly care, and open more broadly the bosom of their minds to heavenly desire. They have sought a withdrawn life in expectation of heavenly recompense, so that, devoted to holy prayers in it, they might separate the oldness of their hearts from the society and tumult of secular life, fuse it in the fire of the Lord’s love, and renew themselves for the contemplation of heavenly joy.

“Therefore, moved by what confidence I possess, I humbly ask my intercessors before the most merciful and almighty Lord to deign to provide me assistance through their prayers. I likewise make this request to that congregation: wherever it may happen that the Lord commands me to depart from this light, in joined charity, as we have made known to your ears, our will has decreed that I should have permission, with those pilgrims, to rest in that basilica which we built for their assistance, according to the will of those monks and with God’s help. The brothers themselves shall bring my body from whatever place to the aforesaid island and bury it there.

“Therefore I decree, and, with the consent of the clerical brothers of the Church of Thérouanne and of illustrious men, I forbid that this basilica, under the protection of the patronage of Abbot Bertin, who now appears to preside over the aforesaid monastery, or of his successors, be governed under the same administration with divine worship, the most devout affection, and the love that is fitting. Let them hold it, with the entire and undiminished integrity of the island of Sithiu monastery, by their own right, authority, and discretion, together with the properties belonging to it.

“Neither I nor any of my episcopal successors, whether by privilege or on the pretext of a gift, shall presume to make a claim concerning its assistance or concerning the preservation of the full liberty of the servants of God or of the monks themselves. And just as monasteries, both ancient and more recently founded, have obtained their own privileges, so this privilege too shall be preserved by our successors.

“Whatever is offered in that basilica or its monastery, the abbot and the monks serving there shall freely possess, with God’s help, without opposition or claim from any bishop. And, in accordance with what has been decreed, whatever the monks of the aforesaid basilica, living regularly under evangelical liberty, receive as a royal gift or from any Christians—lands, slaves, gold and silver, sacred books, or any other objects known to belong to the adornment of divine worship or to the work of those monks—or whatever other property has been given or may henceforth be given, during the present life and in the time of us or of my successors, neither I nor any bishop [Col. 1190D] or anyone from the order of the clergy ordained in the Church of Thérouanne shall presume to appropriate or diminish it for personal use, or carry any part of it to the city in any form.

“And whatever is offered to that altar in the name of God or sent there by anyone under divine inspiration, no bishop, archdeacon, or any ordained official of the Church of Thérouanne shall dare to claim anything from it for himself, out of reverence for holy Mary, in whose honor that basilica, as well as the relics of the other saints, appears to have been constructed.

“Nor, if I or our successor bishops or the archdeacon should be invited to prepare banquets in the fields belonging to it, shall we do so by force of will; rather, after the divine mystery has been completed, each should strive to return to his own place without causing any inconvenience.

“Nor shall any other authority be exercised in that monastery, as we have said, or over its property, its sacred rites, or its ornaments, nor over the persons serving that monastery, by giving or exchanging them, out of reverence for holy Mary or for the apostles Peter and Paul, or so that the monks who serve that monastery may live in quiet under the holy rule. Thus, under God’s guidance, the congregation may rejoice through the ages in perfect peace, following an unharmed path, and may happily reach the harbor of eternal rest.

“And just as many monasteries living in freedom are able to pray more fully in their place or at the relics of their saints for the condition of the Church, the safety of the king, the stability of the kingdom, and the tranquility of the homeland, so may these monks, with God’s help, persevere in accordance with the decrees of the ancient fathers.

“Accordingly, this letter, together with the privilege granted and bestowed under the liberty we have described, shall remain most firmly established, just as in many monasteries, so that the monks residing there may remain forever. Nothing is to be taken away from the aforesaid monastery or its cells that is granted to the members of the household of faith for the tranquility of peace or the reverence of the saints, since nothing is being removed from Catholic authority.

“It also pleased us to add that, without the entry of a bishop, the monks themselves, living under religious observance and the rule as we have said above, shall remain there, with Christ protecting them. May he assist those who preserve this letter and destroy those who presume to violate it.

“To ensure that this definition of our constitution may be valid in our own and future times, we have strengthened it with the subscription of our hand, and I have asked our brothers and the illustrious men also to confirm it.

“Done in the basilica itself, on 18 May, in the sixth year of the reign of our lord King Chlothar [Note: [Col. 1191D] A.D. 662. ‘Done in the year 660 of the Incarnate Word.’ Audomar Codex].”

“In the name of Christ, although a sinner, I, Audomar, a bishop in name but without merit, voluntarily dictated this letter and heard it read over; and I asked those who were to write below to do so. I made these words with my own eyes [i.e. personally dictated them], and another, holding my hand, wrote and subscribed them.

“In the name of Christ, I, Mummolin, although a sinner, bishop, having been asked, have subscribed as the memorandum of Lord Audomar. In the name of Christ, I, Andebertus, unworthy, have subscribed. In the name of Christ, I, Drancio, an unworthy bishop, have subscribed. In the name of Christ, I, Granvangerus, an unworthy bishop, have subscribed. I, Bertefridus the sinner, have subscribed this letter. In the name of Christ, I, Audobertus, bishop, have subscribed. I, Amlacharius, in the name of Christ, a sinner and bishop, have subscribed. I, Raginus, although a sinner, bishop, have subscribed. In the name of Christ, I, Abel, although unworthy, abbot, have subscribed. I, Ramnibertus the sinner, have subscribed this letter. I, Landebertus, although unworthy, a monk, wrote and subscribed this privilege at the request [of the parties] [Note: [Col. 1191D] Here the Audomar Codex reads: ‘With this sign the book of the old Folquin ends.’]”

Thus, when Lord Audomar, the bishop, died in a village called Worantis, situated nearly four miles from the Sithiu monastery, he was carried from there by Lord Bertin, in accordance with the request made by the blessed man himself in this privilege, and was buried in the aforesaid basilica before the altar [Col. 1192B] of the Mother of God. From then on, the basilica was subject to Lord Bertin [Note: [Col. 1191D] In the Audomar Codex, this note appears to have been written by the first hand: “From the papyrus book in which this letter is inserted, it is established both that this matter, which I unjustly erased, and the words ‘done in the year …’ are found there; likewise in the original, which I myself read by touching it today, 9 December 1512, God is my witness.”]

## VII*. How the blessed Walbert transferred the village of Arkas to the blessed father Bertin
After blessed Bertinus had foretold the grievous accident and fracture of the leg of Walbert [Note: [Col. 1191D] Walbertus, called by John of Ypres the count of Ponthieu, Tournai, and Arques, had, according to that same John, as his father Haugericus, mayor of the palace of Theoderic [Col. 1192D], king of the Burgundians, and as his mother Leodegunda. After transferring a large part of his inheritance to the monastery of Sithiu, he renounced the world and became a monk under Saint Bertinus, the abbot. Concerning this Walbert and another Walbert, who was abbot of Luxeuil, see Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, vol. III, part I, p. 113, and part II, p. 453; John of Ypres, *Chronicle*, book 1, part X; Bollandus, May, vol. I, p. 274.], a man of outstanding integrity, and had filled his wine-cellar, empty of wine, with the most fragrant pure wine through his sincere faith, moreover, when the same Count Walbert had once tasted the multiplied wine, he had recovered complete health, every pain having been removed. In return for this heavenly benefit, in the year 668 from the Virgin’s giving birth, Walbert permanently assigned the estate of Arques and many other properties to his blessed compatriot Bertinus and for the use of the brothers.

[Col. 1192C] May the county of Arques, grateful to you, be pleasing, I beg.

## VIII. King Theoderic’s Privilege Concerning What Lord Bertinus Purchased in the Estate of Attigny

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 676, indiction 4, while the glorious Frankish king Theoderic was reigning—the brother of the aforementioned King Chlothar—in the tenth year [Note: [Col. 1192D] According to Mabillon, Theoderic’s reign began at the start of September 673; it is therefore quite clear that the tenth year of that reign corresponds to A.D. 682.], the same King Theoderic issued a deed of security to Lord Bertinus concerning what he had purchased in the estate of Attigny. Its text is as follows.

## IX. Copy [Note: [Col. 1192D] Published by Mabillon, *De re diplomatica*, p. 625.]

[Theoderic, king of the Franks, illustrious man.] If we grant anything to the places of the saints for the assistance of God’s servants, we trust that this belongs to our praise and to eternal recompense. Therefore let your greatness, and all concerned, know that we have granted this benefit to the venerable man Bertinus, abbot of the monastery of Sithiu: whatever he had purchased from our fisc within Attigny, or might thereafter find available for purchase, except those manses from which cart-service is rendered, he shall hold as granted; and you must not demand or exact from them any land-rent or any public dues on this account.

Therefore, by this deed we especially decree and order—which we wish to remain in force forever—that neither you, nor your juniors or successors, nor anyone attached to judicial authority, shall at any time demand or exact from the lands within Attigny, in our fisc, which the aforesaid abbot has purchased, or which he himself, his successors, or the monastery’s community may thereafter purchase, except those manses from which carts are supplied, any land-rents or public dues. Rather, whatever the abbot himself, or the community of his monastery of Sithiu, or his successors may receive from those lands, or whatever our fisc might receive, shall be held as granted and bestowed by our generosity. And so that this decree may be held more firmly and better preserved through the ages, we have ordered it strengthened by the subscriptions of our hand.

Sign of the glorious King Theoderic.

Given on 23 October, in the tenth year of our reign, at the palace of Compiègne, happily, in God’s name [Note: [Col. 1193D] Theoderic’s customary manner of subscription was: “In Christ’s name, I, Theoderic the king, have subscribed,” as is evident from the formulas transmitted under his name. It may therefore be asserted that Folquinus has not correctly reproduced Theoderic’s own subscription here, since in this and in the preceding diploma of Chlothar he gives the initial formula; moreover, he omitted the subscriptions of the king, Queen Balthild, and the chancellor.]

## X. Concerning the Estate of Hunulfus

In the year from the Lord’s incarnation 677, indiction [Note: [Col. 1193D] Indiction 6 agrees not with A.D. 677 but with A.D. 678; neither of these years, however, agrees with the twelfth year of Theoderic III, which falls in A.D. 685.] 6, a certain distinguished man named Amalfridus gave Lord Bertinus the monastery which he himself had built on his own property, called Hunulfus’s Estate, in the county of Cambrai, on the River Scheldt [Col. 1193C]. There also, his daughter, the illustrious woman Auriana by name, appears to have been abbess and ruler of the nuns. The arrangement was that he himself, as long as he lived, should hold it by a precarious tenure, and after his death, and after the death of his daughter Auriana, the aforesaid Abbot Bertinus or his successors should have, hold, and possess it; and they should have the right to appoint there anyone whom they wished as provost. A copy of that conveyance, preserved by us to the present day, testifies to this in the following manner.

## XI. Amalfridus’s Conveyance of the Same Estate [Note: [Col. 1193D] Published by Mabillon, *De re diplomatica*, p. 607.]

I, Amalfridus, an illustrious man, in God’s name, have granted and assigned to the monastery of Sithiu, where the venerable man Bertinus appears to preside as abbot, with the consent and agreement of my daughter Auriana [Col. 1193D], who appears to be its ruler, namely our monastery called Hunulfus’s Estate, in the county of Cambrai, on the River Scheldt, which I built on my property in honor of Saint Mary, Saint Peter, Saint Martin, and Saint Pollina, where that precious jewel rests bodily [lacuna].

And we ask the brothers and rulers of the monastery to take care of that monastery with regard to the Mass, the liturgical office, and lights, and to show charity toward guests and pilgrims, so that they may receive a reward and record our name in the Book of Life.

Executed at Vermand, on 8 February, in the twelfth year of the reign of our lord, the most glorious King Theoderic [Note: [Col. 1193D] Folquinus closes Amalfridus’s document in this way, as does Ypres in the *Bertinian Chronicle*. Ypres reports the initial words of the instrument, which serve as a preface, as follows: “As far as human understanding and perception …” Folquinus seems to have cut away these words because they contributed nothing to the historical knowledge supplied by the diploma; but he ought not to have omitted the subscriptions, which read as follows: “Amalfridus: I have reread and subscribed this testament made by me. I, Auriana, abbess, consenting, have subscribed. Sign of Adalfridus; Vulfoaldus; Nivario; Angabertus; Hildramnus; Erchamfridus; Signius; Vuaraulfus the deacon; Ulitmarus; Crasmarus; Dudonus; Bruno; Ermenfridus; Constantinus; Gislefridus; Centenasius; Gerfridus; Balstrantus. Bladardus, asked to do so, wrote and subscribed this testament.”]

After this conveyance had been completed and confirmed by the subscriptions of distinguished men, so that it might remain unshaken through succeeding ages, less than two years after the aforesaid conveyance had been completed—in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 679 and the fourteenth year of the aforesaid King Theoderic [Note: [Col. 1194D] The fourteenth year of Theoderic III’s reign corresponds, in April, with A.D. 687]—Lord Bertinus the abbot and Amalfridus, the distinguished man who had made this conveyance, went together to the royal palace at Crisciacum and asked that the charter of the aforesaid donation be confirmed by royal authority. The king then graciously embraced their request and, with the subscription of the royal seal preserved by us, bears witness to it to this day, saying as follows.

## XII. King Theoderic’s Confirmation Concerning the Same Estate [Note: [Col. 1194D] Mabillon published this confirmation, but incompletely, in *De re diplomatica*, p. 607.]

The venerable man Bertinus, abbot of the monastery of Sithiu, which is built in the county of Terwaan [Col. 1194C] in honor of Saint Peter and the other saints, came into our presence at the royal palace in the estate of Cariciacum, with the consent and agreement of the illustrious man Amalfridus, his wife Childebertana, and their daughter Auriana, the abbess. They represented to our royal clemency that Amalfridus and his wife Childebertana had built, in honor of Saint Mary, mother of our Lord Jesus Christ, and Saint Pollina, at a place called Hunulfus’s Estate on the River Scheldt, and so forth.

Given on the Kalends of April, in the fourteenth year of our reign, at the palace of Cariciacum.

## On the Foundation and Dedication of the Monastery of Saint Berta at Blangiacum

[Col. 1194D] In the twelfth year of the aforesaid King Theoderic (685), son of Clovis and Queen Balthild, founder [Note: [Col. 1195D] Supply: “of the monastery”] of the monastery of the holy bishop Vedast of Arras, the most blessed Berta began to build a monastery [Note: [Col. 1195D] On the monastery of Blangiacum, see *Gallia Christiana*, vol. X, col. 1188 and following] at Blangiacum, in the county of the Morini, on her own property, around the eighty-second year of the Lord’s nativity [Note: [Col. 1195D] Correct to 685], as is clear from the written records of the aforesaid monastery.

When everything had finally been arranged for the adornment of the monastery, the most devout Berta summoned the venerable bishops together to dedicate the aforesaid monastery: namely Saint Ausbert, bishop of Rouen; Saint Walaric; Saint Germanus of the city of Paris; Saint Silvinus, a foreigner who had come from Toulouse; Saint Faro of Meaux, the brother of the Walbert mentioned above; the venerable Ravengerus, bishop of Terwaan, in whose diocese the monastery mentioned above was situated; and many other men of distinguished life.

There they all flourished at one time within the holy Church like the strongest pillars, and they assembled around the aforementioned Berta, eagerly desiring to support her devotion. Ravengerus, bishop of the Morini, in whose parish the ceremony was performed, asked whether everything necessary for the dedication was present. Berta immediately replied that everything was present. Then he said: “Bring hyssop, so that it may be prepared for the necessary use.” And she said: “Until now, Father, we did not know whether there was any need for it in this work.” Then, through divine fear, an angel in the form of a young man miraculously brought hyssop, through the merits of those standing there. This dedication took place on the ninth day of February.

## XIII. On the Death of Theoderic, the Succession of His Son Clovis, and Other Matters

[Col. 1195C]

Meanwhile, when the aforesaid glorious Frankish king Theoderic died, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 682, which was the year of his reign [Note: [Col. 1196D] Theoderic III died in A.D. 691, when, according to the preceding material, he was in the eighteenth year of his reign], his son Clovis, still a boy, was gloriously raised to the Frankish throne.

By royal authority he issued a privilege to Lord Bertinus concerning his monastery of Sithiu, in which he confirmed by royal privilege whatever had previously been granted to that place by his predecessors. He ordered, namely, that the place should remain under immunity through succeeding ages, without judicial authority, and that no public official should presume, under any constraint of coercion, to distrain the free men or dependants of that place. It has pleased us to insert that privilege here. It was executed [Col. 1195D] in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 672, which was the first year of the aforesaid king, as follows.

## XIV. King Clovis’s Privilege [Note: [Col. 1196D] Published by Mabillon, *De re diplomatica*, p. 607.]

Clovis, king of the Franks [illustrious man].

If we confirm by our decrees the benefits which our parents granted or conceded to the places of the saints, we both exercise the royal custom and trust that this pertains, in God’s name, to our praise and to the stability of our kingdom.

Therefore, the venerable man Bertinus, abbot of the monastery of Sithiu, which is built in the county of Terwaan in honor of Saint Mary, mother of our Lord Jesus Christ, and also of the apostles Saint Peter and Saint Paul and the other holy lords, came into our presence and represented to our royal clemency that our grandfather, the former King Clovis, had granted to his predecessor Mummolinus and to the aforesaid monastery, with complete immunity, all the small estates and villages of that monastery—whatever they possessed at that time, or might thereafter acquire from royal gifts, from grants of the people, by purchase, or through any other acquisition, in whatever counties and territories such property had been added or granted—so that no public judge should ever enter there to hear cases, demand fines, take sureties, make lodgings or provisions, distrain the people of the monastery, whether free or dependants living upon its lands, or demand or exact any payments; rather, under the name of immunity, the monastery’s community should possess all the granted fines forever.

He also showed us, for our inspection, the decrees of the princes and the confirmations of our uncles Chlothar and Childeric, as well as of our father, the former King Theoderic, by which they confirmed these and other estates that Abbot Bertinus subsequently received for the monastery through exchanges or written instruments [lacuna]. He asserted that these granted benefits had been preserved from that time until now, but the aforesaid abbot asked our Highness, for the sake of firmness, to confirm more fully by our authority what concerned that place.

Know, therefore, that in response to his petition, for the increase of our reward and out of reverence for that holy place, we have granted and confirmed everything in every respect. We command that whatever our grandfather, the former King Clovis, is known to have justly and reasonably granted or confirmed to the aforesaid Mummolinus concerning that immunity, as stated above, and whatever our uncles Chlothar and Childeric, and our father, the former King Theoderic, later granted or confirmed, and whatever has been preserved in a straight course from that time until now, shall likewise hereafter, by our decree, be more fully confirmed in God’s name.

Having examined the decrees of the aforementioned princes, as their contents make clear, may the benefits granted to Abbot Bertinus and his successors, or to the monastery of Sithiu, remain fully preserved in every respect forever; and may they never have to fear any opposition or impediment from public judges. For this reason, let that community continually beseech the Lord’s mercy for the stability of our kingdom and the safety of the country.

And so that this authority may be held more firmly and preserved in every respect, we have ordered it confirmed below by the marks of our hand and that of our exalted mother, Queen Chrodechildis.

Sign of the glorious King Clovis.

Sign of our exalted mother, Queen Chrodechildis [Note: [Col. 1197D] Folquinus omitted the place where the privilege was issued.]

Executed on 1 June, in the first year of our reign.

## XV. On the Death of Clovis, the Succession of Hildebert, and His Privilege

(698.) In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 684, when the aforesaid King Clovis died, in the second year of his reign [Note: [Col. 1197D] Clovis III began to reign in A.D. 691 after the death of his father, Theoderic III; he died in A.D. 695, in March, that is, in the fourth or at the beginning of the fifth year of his reign], his brother Hildebert gloriously assumed the rule of the Franks. In the third year of his reign, that same king issued a privilege of royal authority to Lord Bertinus, following the tenor of the document made by his predecessor, King Clovis, which we have already written above. We omit that privilege here [Col. 1197B], so that we may not appear to repeat what has already been written. Let us meanwhile hasten to what follows.

## XVI. That He Acquired Many Other Things During His Lifetime, and Concerning the Estate Called Woromhold and Saint Winnoc

While he was still alive, he enlarged his monastery with these and very many other possessions, through immense labor. Many additional things, partly destroyed through the negligence of those who came before us and partly through long antiquity, remain unknown to us to this day.

It is certain, however, that throughout his life he labored in preparing the place entrusted to him by the Lord. He did not cease until he had made it equal, in royal authority, royal privileges, and abundance of lands, to the ancient monasteries founded by kings.

Indeed, while he was still alive he also built other monasteries of monks. One of them is called Woromhold [Col. 1197C], and a certain wealthy man named Heremarus gave it to that man of God. Saint Bertinus, wishing to multiply the dwellings of God’s servants, entrusted this monastery to four men who had come to him from the regions of Britain, so that they might build and govern it: namely Quadonocus, Ingenocus, Madocus, and Saint Winnoc. He instructed them to establish there a reception house for the poor and to care generously for guests and pilgrims by providing what was necessary.

After the deaths of the three men mentioned above—Quadonocus, Ingenocus, and Madocus—Saint Bertinus permitted blessed Winnoc to preside over the community of brothers living there, because he had no doubts about his life and character. He had raised him from infancy with himself in the monastic school of the Lord. Anyone who wishes to investigate his life and virtues carefully can find an account written by a particularly excellent author among us [Col. 1197D]. Meanwhile, let us continue with what we have begun.

## XVII. That Blessed Bertinus, While Still Alive, Appointed Rigobert Abbot [Note: [Col. 1198D] See John of Ypres, *Chronicle*, col. 474.]

As blessed Bertinus was already advancing into old age, he entrusted the governance of his monastery to the venerable man Rigobert, so that, having set aside worldly entanglements, he might devote himself more freely to God.

During his administration, under the appointment and command of Lord Bertinus, Rigobert built a monastery in honor of Saint Martin. It now exists as the principal house of the place and the chief seat of the entire abbey. This occurred in the sixth year of Hildebert’s reign, which was the year of the Lord’s incarnation 689 [Note: [Col. 1198D] The sixth year of Childebert’s reign falls in A.D. 700 and 701], under Ravengerus, bishop of the Church of Terwaan.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 693, while the glorious King Hildebert was reigning in the tenth year of his reign, Rigobert also purchased from a certain man named Eodbert an estate called Rumliacum for 1,500 solidi. The charter of this purchase was drawn up as follows.

## XVIII. Abbot Rigobert’s Purchase at Nuntiacum [Note: [Col. 1198D] Published by Bréq, *Diplomata*, p. 267.]

To the holy lord and venerable man in Christ, Rigobert, abbot of the monastery of Sithiu: Eodebert, seller.

It is established that I have sold and, by a fully deliberate act of will, have handed over to you, and have now handed over, all my share of property at the place called Rumliacum, in the county of Terwaan. This came to me from the share of my son Chardebert, formerly, through a mournful inheritance—that is, together with lands, houses, buildings, dependants, woods, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, movable and immovable property, mills, flocks with shepherds, and all property, investigated or not, in its entirety: whatever my wife held there and left when she died, or whatever came from her share to our son named above and thus reached him.

The abbot himself or the community of his monastery shall, from the present day, receive and possess all this in its entirety, in their right and dominion. In return, we have received from you, at the agreed price, which pleased and suited us, 1,500 solidi in gold and silver only. From this day forward, therefore, the abbot himself or the community of his monastery shall have completely free and firm power in every respect to possess, hold, give, sell, exchange, or do whatever they wish with it.

If anyone—which we do not believe will happen—whether we ourselves, any of our heirs or descendants, or any opposing person, should presume to act against this sale, which I requested to be made and written out by my fullest will, and if it is not defended by me or my heirs, then we or our heirs shall pay as a penalty twice the amount we received from you, or twice the value that the property may have acquired through improvement by that time. The penalty shall be paid under the established condition, and the claimant shall not be able to recover what he seeks; rather, this present sale shall remain firm and inviolate forever, supported by formal stipulation.

Executed at the monastery of Sithiu, on 16 May, in the tenth year of the reign of our lord, the glorious King Childebert.

Sign of Eodbert, who requested that this sale be made.

Sign of Fladebert. Sign of Madalchar. Sign of Erlebert. Sign of Childolf. Sign of Mauriana. Sign of Sigebert.

Erchembodus, lector, wrote and subscribed this sale.

## XIX. That He Entrusted His Monastery to Erlefrid after Rigobert

Meanwhile, as the number of monks increased, blessed Father Bertinus, granting the aforesaid Rigobert relief from the labor of his office [Note: [Col. 1199D] See John of Ypres, chap. 2, col. 477], entrusted the governance of his monastery to the venerable man Erlefrid [Note: [Col. 1199D] See chap. 3, in the same work], whom he had himself raised. Bertinus, following the paths of a stricter life and withdrawn from worldly disturbance, devoted his whole mind to divine philosophy.

Among the other things that the most reverend Erlefrid accomplished, he purchased from a certain man named Darmundus the man’s share of property at the place called Saroald’s Lock, on the River Sumna, in the county of Vermand, and at Appiliacum, on the River Oise, in the county of Noyon, as well as at Diva and Corbunacum, for 1,500 solidi. The charter of this sale is inserted here.

## XX. Abbot Erlefrid’s Purchase of the Properties Written Below [Note: [Col. 1199D] Published by Bréq, *Diplomata*, p. 380.]

To the lord and venerable man Erlefrid, abbot of the monastery of Sithiu: Darmundus, seller.

It is established that I have sold to you, not by an imaginary right but by the fullest exercise of my will, and have thus sold, two parts of my share of property at the place called Saroald’s Lock, on the River Sumna, in the county of Vermand; likewise, at Appiliacum on the River Oise, two parts situated [Col. 1199C] in the county of Noyon; and also at Diva and Corbunacum, two parts in their entirety.

That is, in lands, houses, buildings, dependants, vineyards, fields, woods, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, mills, livestock, cultivated and uncultivated land: these aforesaid portions I now deliver to you and ask to transfer to you for perpetual possession. In return, I have received the price agreed between us, namely 1,500 solidi in gold and silver only, so that from the present day you may have, with Christ’s favor, completely free and firm power in every respect over these portions—to possess, hold, give, sell, exchange, or do whatever you wish with them.

If anyone—which I do not believe will happen—whether I myself, any of my heirs, or any opposing or foreign person, should act against this sale, we shall pay you twice the amount we received from you; and, under compulsion by the associated fisc, the offender shall pay twice the money, and shall not be able to recover what he claims. Rather, this sale shall remain firm forever, supported by formal stipulation.

Executed at the monastery of Sithiu, on 2 May, in the fourteenth year of the reign of our lord, the glorious King Hildebert.

I, Darmundus, the seller, requested that this sale be made [Col. 1200A].

Ravengerus, although unworthy, bishop, subscribed.

+ Fulbert. + Madalhar. + Humbert, deputy. Chrodbertus wrote and subscribed this sale.

## XXI. On the Passing of Lord Bertinus

During the administration of the aforesaid Erlefrid, blessed Father Bertinus, full of days and holiness, after a long period of service in the Lord, left his bodily prison and migrated to Christ, to receive from him the prize of eternal recompense. This occurred in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 698, the fifteenth year of the aforesaid King Hildebert [Note: [Col. 1199D] The fifteenth year of King Childebert corresponds to A.D. 709. See Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, vol. III, part I, p. 117; *Annales*, book XIX, no. 45, vol. II, p. 23; Martène, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. III, col. 475, note], indiction 11.

He was buried in the basilica of Saint Martin, where many miracles were performed by the Lord through his merits. The text of his Life has revealed this most elegantly.

At that same time [Note: [Col. 1200D] A.D. 711], the venerable King Hildebert also departed to the Lord, after reigning for sixteen years. His son Dagobert, still a boy, reigned in his place for five years [Note: [Col. 1200D] Correct to four]. During his reign, the aforesaid Abbot Erlefrid began to rebuild the basilica of Saint Martin above the tomb of the holy Father Bertinus on a larger scale.

## XXII. On Erkenbodus, Abbot and Successor of Erlefrid

After the many labors of the aforesaid Abbot Erlefrid—which he undertook with the most eager spirit after surviving his master—he migrated to the Lord and left Erchembodus as his successor, equal to him in wisdom and goodness.

During the reign of King Chilperic, successor to the aforesaid King Dagobert, he requested from that king a privilege constructed by royal authority. It was drawn up as follows.

## XXIII. King Chilperic’s Privilege during the Time of the Aforesaid Abbot [Note: [Col. 1200D] Edited by Mabillon, *De re diplomatica*, p. 608.]

[Col. 1200C]

Chilperic, king of the Franks [illustrious man].

If we confirm by our decrees the deeds of our parents, whatever they granted or conceded to the places of the saints, we exercise the royal custom and trust that this pertains, in God’s name, to our praise and to the stability of our kingdom.

Therefore the venerable man Erchembodus, abbot of the monastery of Sithiu, which is built in the county of Terwaan in honor of Saint Mary, mother of our Lord Jesus Christ, and also of the apostles Saint Peter and Saint Paul and the other holy lords, came into our presence and represented to our royal clemency that our grandfather, the former King Clovis, had granted with complete immunity to his predecessor, Lord Bertinus, formerly abbot of that monastery, and to the aforesaid monastery, all the estates and villages of that monastery—whatever they possessed at that time, or might thereafter acquire from royal gifts, grants of the people, purchases, or any other acquisition, in whatever counties and territories such property had been added or granted—so that no public judge should ever enter there to hear cases, exact fines, take sureties, make lodgings or provisions, or distrain the people of the monastery, whether free or dependants living upon its lands; nor should judicial authority ever enter there to demand or exact any payments, except that, under the name of immunity, the monastery’s community should possess forever all granted fines.

He further asserts that he has in his hands the decrees of that prince—our grandfather, Clovis—and the confirmations of our exalted uncles Chlodachar and Theoderic, as well as of our father Childeric, and also of our cousins, the former kings Clovis and Childebert. He states that the benefits granted by them have remained preserved from that time until now [Col. 1201B]. But the aforesaid abbot asked our Highness, for complete firmness, to confirm more fully by our authority what concerned that place.

Know, therefore, that in response to his petition, for the increase of our reward and out of reverence for that place, we have granted and confirmed everything in every respect. We command that whatever our aforesaid grandfather, the former King Clovis, is known to have justly and reasonably granted or confirmed concerning that immunity to the aforesaid Bertinus, as stated above, and whatever our uncles Chlodachar and Theoderic, our father Childeric, and our cousins, the former kings Clovis and Childebert, subsequently granted and confirmed, and whatever has been preserved in a straight course from that time until now, we likewise confirm more fully hereafter in God’s name by our decree.

Having examined the decrees of the aforementioned princes, as their contents make clear, may the benefits granted to Abbot Erchembodus and his successors, and to the monastery of Sithiu, remain preserved in every respect forever; and may they never have to endure any opposition or impediment from public judges. For this reason, let that community continually beseech the Lord’s mercy for the stability of our kingdom and the safety of the country.

And so that this authority may be held more firmly and preserved in every respect, we have ordered it strengthened below by the subscriptions of our hand.

Given in the third year of our reign [Col. 1201D] [Note: [Col. 1201D] Here Folquinus omitted the subscription of the king and the chancellor, as well as the place where the privilege was issued. In addition, the seal produced here is very different from the authentic seals of the first dynasty of kings and reflects the character and style of the tenth century [Col. 1202D].]

## XXIV. On Charles’s Battle at Vincy

(717.) During the reign of the aforesaid King Chilperic, Duke Charles, son of Pippin, came from Austrasia, raised an army, and engaged in battle against the aforementioned King Chilperic and his duke Ragemfrid. But after his army had first been slaughtered, he turned his back and fled.

Afterward, having renewed the attack, he advanced against Chilperic, his enemy, on a Sunday during Lent. Charles first asked that peace be made. When they refused, he entered battle on 21 March [Col. 1202A], and, with God’s help, defeated Chilperic and Ragemfrid and won the victory.

At this time blessed Silvinus, bishop of Terwaan, flourished, full of virtues and holiness. His body now rests, honorably buried, at Sithiu.

After the battle mentioned above had been completed, King Chilperic and Ragemfrid again sought the assistance of Duke Eudo and prepared to march against Charles. Charles met them fearlessly, defeated the enemy once more, and gained a triumph.

Later Charles made peace with Duke Eudo and was reconciled with King Chilperic, restoring him to his kingdom. But Chilperic did not remain long in this life; he died after reigning for five and a half years.

The Franks then set Theoderic, the son of the aforementioned young King Dagobert, over themselves as king. He granted a privilege to the aforesaid Abbot Erchembodus, confirming by royal authority what had been granted by his predecessors to this holy place. This too is inserted here before our eyes in the following form.

## XXV. Copy of the Privilege [Note: [Col. 1202D] Published by Miraeus, *Opera diplomatica*, vol. I, p. 128; and by Mabillon, *De re diplomatica*, pp. 608–609.]

(3 March 721.) “Theoderic, king of the Franks, to the illustrious men, the counts, and all their agents or subordinates, both present and future, in whatever affairs the monastery of Sithiu is seen to hold or possess.

“If we confirm by our decrees the acts of our forefathers which they bestowed or granted to holy places, we exercise the royal custom and trust that these things pertain to us. Therefore the venerable man Erchenbodus, abbot of the monastery [Col. 1202C] of Sithiu, situated in the county of Terouanne and built in honor of holy Mary, mother of our Lord Jesus Christ, and likewise of the holy apostles Peter and Paul and the other holy lords, came into our presence and reported to the clemency of our kingdom that our great-grandfather Clovis, formerly king, had granted to his predecessor Bertinus and to the aforesaid monastery of Sithiu, with full immunity, all the estates or villages of that monastery, whatever they then possessed or thereafter acquired from royal gifts, from grants made by the people, from purchases, from future purchases, or from anything else acquired, in whatever counties and territories it had been added or granted there. He had granted this so that no public judge might presume to enter there to hear legal cases, exact payments [Col. 1202D], take sureties, impose lodging or requisition services, distrain the men of the monastery, whether free or servile, who lived upon its lands, or demand or exact any dues; rather, under the name of immunity, with all the payments that had been granted, the monastery’s portion should possess these things perpetually for all time.

“Accordingly, he asserts that he has in his hands the charter of that prince, our great-grandfather Clovis, as well as the confirmations of our predecessors and uncles Clothar and Childeric, of our grandfathers Theoderic and Childebert, and of our cousin Chilperic, formerly king; and he declares that the benefits granted by them from that time until now appear to have been preserved. But for the sake of complete security, the aforesaid abbot Erchembodus requested our Highness to confirm these matters more fully, concerning that place, by our authority in the name of God. Know, therefore, that for the increase of our reward and out of reverence for that holy place, we have granted his petition in this way and confirmed everything.

“For we command and order that whatever our great-grandfather Clovis, formerly king, is known to have granted concerning that immunity, as described above, to the aforesaid Bertinus, his predecessor, or afterward his uncles, or our grandfather Clothar, and Theoderic, Childebert and Childeric [Note: [Col. 1203D] On Cointius’s authority, the order of the words should be restored from the preceding passage as follows: ‘His uncles Clothar and Childeric, or our grandfathers Theoderic and Childebert.’], and whatever the confirmations of our cousin Chilperic, formerly king, justly and reasonably granted or confirmed, and which has been preserved by a straight course from that time until now, we likewise confirm more fully hereafter in the name of God by our decree. Having examined the charters of the princes mentioned above, as their contents declare, let the benefits granted in every respect concerning the abbot Erchembodus, his successors, or that place, Sithiu, remain preserved for all time; and let them not fear that at any time they will suffer any opposition or impediment from public judges on this account [Col. 1203C]. Therefore that community must continually beseech the mercy of the Lord for the stability of our kingdom and the safety of the country. And so that this authority may be held more firmly and preserved in every respect, we have decreed that it be confirmed below by the subscriptions of our hand.

“Sign of the glorious king Theoderic.

“Given on the third day of March, in the first year of our reign, at the city of Soissons, happily in the name of God.”

### XXVI. Concerning another privilege of the same king Theoderic

In the same year, in the month of November, the same king Theoderic issued another document to the aforesaid abbot Erchembodus concerning the lands which Lord Bertinus, while still alive, had purchased from the fiscal property of the preceding kings in various places, and concerning all the property included therein. It read as follows.

### XXVII. Copy of the same privilege

[Note: [Col. 1204D] Published by Mabillon, *De re diplomatica*, p. 609.]

Theoderic, king of the Franks [illustrious man].

Whomever divine mercy raises to the kingship, it is fitting that he preserve the deeds of his forebears, especially those which royal clemency is proved to have granted, for eternal recompense, to the advantage of churches or holy places; these ought to be preserved forever.

Therefore let your Greatness and Excellency know that the venerable man Erkembodus [Col. 1204A], abbot of the monastery of Sithiu, through his messengers brought the following matter to the attention of the clemency of our kingdom: our great-great-great-great-grandfather Theoderic, formerly king, had granted by a charter subscribed with his own hand to his predecessor, Bertinus, formerly abbot, or to the aforesaid monastery of Sithiu, this benefit—that whatever he had purchased from our fisc, wherever it might be, in any counties or territories, or whatever he might afterward find available for purchase, and whatever good men fearing God had given or might thereafter give to the aforesaid monastery for the sake of their souls, should be granted to it. He had also granted that whatever had been acquired from our fisc, or might thereafter be acquired, except that land from which carpentry materials were obtained, should be exempt, so that no judicial authority should be able to demand, exact, or require from it any land revenues or public dues on this account [Col. 1204B].

Accordingly he affirmed that he had in his hands the charter of our aforesaid great-great-great-great-grandfather, and he displayed it to us in person for reading; he also asserted that the benefits granted had been preserved from that time until now. But for the sake of firm security he requested our Highness to confirm this concerning that holy place by our decrees. Know that, for the sake of the Lord’s name and out of reverence for that holy place, we have gladly granted this request and confirmed everything.

For we command that whatever our aforesaid great-great-grandfather Theoderic, formerly king, is known to have granted concerning that benefit, as described above, to the aforesaid Bertinus or to the aforesaid holy place for the increase of his reward, and whatever has been preserved by a straight course from that time until now, shall likewise hereafter, after examination of the charter of the aforesaid prince, be confirmed more fully in the name of God by our decree, as its contents declare. Under these terms, concerning the abbot Erkembodus or his monastery of Sithiu, may the benefits granted remain for all time, and may they be preserved in every respect; and may they not fear at any time to suffer opposition or impediment from public judges on this account. Therefore may that community gladly beseech the mercy of the Lord continually for the stability of our kingdom and the safety of the country. And so that this authority may be held more firmly and preserved forever in every respect, we have decreed that it be confirmed below by the subscriptions of our hand.

Sign of the glorious lord Theoderic.

Given on the tenth day of November, in the first year of our reign, at the fortress of Condé.

I, Conrad, having been ordered to do so, examined and subscribed.

### XXVIII. Concerning the bishopric of the same abbot

In the year of the same king Theoderic which was the year 710 of the Lord’s incarnation, the aforesaid abbot Erchembodus [Col. 1205A] [Note: [Col. 1205D] Erchembodus, or Erchembodo, abbot of Sithiu, was appointed to replace Raveinger, bishop of Terouanne, in the third year of the reign of Theoderic IV, that is, in the year of Christ 723. See John of Ypres, *Chronicle*, part II, chapter 4; *Gallia Christiana*, vol. III, col. 487.] had received the episcopate of the Church of Terouanne. This same Erchembodus, bishop and abbot, while retaining the abbacy together with the bishopric, in the third year of the aforesaid king Theoderic bought from a certain man named Rigobert his proprietary possessions at a place called Sethiaco, on the river Agniona, with the adjacent lands of Kelmias and Strato; and at Mempiscus, the estates of Leodredingas, or at Belrinio, situated on the river Canche in the county of Terouanne, together with their dependencies, including what lay in the county of Ponthieu, at a place called Monte, on the river Authie, for fifteen hundred solidi in gold and silver. The charter of this sale was drawn up in the following terms.

### XXIX. Purchase by the same bishop of the properties written below

[Col. 1205B]

“To the lord and apostolic father Erkenbodus, bishop and purchaser, and to his community residing there: I, Rigobert, have sold and presently delivered, namely, all my villas called Sethiaco, on the river Agniona, with their dependencies, Kelmias and Strato, and at Mempiscus, the estates of Leodedringas, or at Bebrinio, situated on the river Canche in the county of Terouanne, with their dependencies, which are in the county of Ponthieu, at a place called Mentek, on the river Authie.

“Done publicly at the monastery of Sithiu, on the fourth day before the Kalends of September, in the third year of our lord Theoderic, glorious king. I, Rigobert, have reread and subscribed this sale made by me. Sign of Dodo. Sign of Leudegesil. Sign of Chimbald, centenarius. Sign of Cherebald. Sign of Ellemberth. Sign of Ingomar. Winidmar, deacon, wrote and subscribed this sale.” [Col. 1205C]

### XXX. Concerning the death of Erchembodus, the succession of Waimar, and the privilege of Childeric

Meanwhile, as the aforesaid king Theoderic was dying, Childeric of the Franks assumed the government in the year 642 from the Lord’s incarnation [Note: [Col. 1205D] After Theoderic’s death in the year 737, Francia remained without a king until 742, when Childeric III, son of Chilperic II, was made king.]. At the same time the aforesaid Erchembodus, bishop and abbot, departed from this world [Note: [Col. 1206D] It is uncertain in which year Archembodus died—whether 734, 737, 740, or 742.] and was buried by the people in the monastery of Saint Omer, before the altar of the holy Mother of God [which is called “at the Bells”] [where his stone tomb can still be seen today]. Adalger succeeded him in the bishopric. Waimar undertook the governance of the abbacy. In the time of the aforesaid king Childeric, he obtained a privilege of royal authority according to the enactments of the preceding kings, who had granted these things to the monastery of Sithiu; it is established that the king confirmed it in the following manner, in the first year of that king’s reign.

### XXXI. Copy of the privilege of King Childeric

[Note: [Col. 1206D] Published by Mabillon, *De re diplomatica*, p. 610.]

Childeric, king of the Franks, to the illustrious men, the counts, and all their agents or subordinates, both present and future, in whatever affairs the monastery of Sithiu is seen to possess property.

Whomever divine mercy raises to the kingship, it is fitting that he preserve the deeds of his forebears, especially those which royal clemency is proved to have granted, for eternal recompense, to the advantage of churches or holy places; these ought to be preserved forever.

Therefore let your Greatness and Excellency know that the venerable man Waimar, abbot of the monastery of Sithiu, reported to the clemency of our kingdom that our kinsman Theoderic, formerly king, by his charter confirmed with his own hand, had granted to his predecessor Erkembodus, abbot, or to his aforesaid monastery of Sithiu, this benefit: whatever had been acquired within our fisc, wherever it might be, in any counties or territories, or whatever might thereafter be found available for purchase, and whatever good men fearing God had given or might thereafter give to the aforesaid [Col. 1206B] monastery for the sake of their souls, should be granted to it. Whatever had been acquired from our fisc, or might thereafter be acquired, except that land from which cartwrights’ work was produced, should likewise be granted, and no judicial authority should therefore demand, exact, or require from it any land revenues or public dues.

Accordingly he affirms that he has in his hands the charter of our aforesaid kinsman Theoderic, formerly king, and has now shown it to us for rereading; he asserts that the benefits granted have been preserved from that time until now. But for the sake of firm security he requested our Highness to confirm this concerning that holy place by our decrees. Know that, for the sake of the Lord’s name and out of reverence for that holy place, we have granted this request and confirmed everything.

For we command and order that whatever our aforesaid kinsman Theoderic, formerly king, is known to have granted concerning that benefit, as described above, to the aforesaid abbot Erkembodus or to the aforesaid holy place for the increase of his reward, and whatever has been preserved by a straight course from that time until now, shall likewise hereafter, after examination of the charters of the aforesaid prince, be confirmed more fully in the name of God by our decree, as their contents declare. Under these terms, concerning the abbot Waimar or his monastery of Sithiu, may the benefits granted remain confirmed in every respect for all time [Col. 1206D], and may they not fear to suffer at any time opposition or impediment from public judges on this account. Therefore may that community continually beseech the mercy of the Lord for the stability of our kingdom and the safety of the country. And so that this authority may be held more firmly and preserved in every respect through the ages, we have decreed that it be confirmed below by the subscriptions of our hand.

[Col. 1207A] Sign of the glorious king Childeric.

Given on the twenty-third day of April, in the first year of our reign, happily in the name of God, at the palace of Crisciacum. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 1207C]

It should be noted in this charter that Childeric, the last of the Merovingian kings, calls Theoderic of Châlons, his predecessor, his “kinsman,” and designates him as a prince without indicating a paternal relationship. From this a certain argument is drawn that Childeric was not descended from Theoderic of Châlons, contrary to the opinion of many more recent writers. For it is clear from all the instruments of the Merovingian kings published above that it was their established practice in writing to designate the father’s father and relatives by the term “kinsmen.” Thus Childeric had Chilperic as his father. Chilperic, unaware of his fate, granted immunity to that place, which he himself was shortly afterward to enter.

In the third year of the same King Childeric, a certain presbyter named Felix transferred to Abbot Nantharius a cell belonging to him by right, called Hrocasamo, or the place of Thevoaldus, in the county of Flanders. “I,” he says, “built it through my work in honor of Michael the Archangel, or of Saint John the Baptist, or of holy Mary, mother of our Lord Jesus Christ” [Col. 1208C], “and of the other saints. And we ask that the priests [Col. 1208D] who dwell in that monastery may deem it fitting to have my name in the book of life. Done publicly at the monastery of Sithiu, on the eighth day before the Kalends of August, in the third year of the reign of our lord Childeric, most glorious king. Sign of Chrodgarius, illustrious man. … I, Vioradus, deacon, wrote this at the request of others.”

From these letters we learn at what time Bertinus was given the title “Saint,” since this is the first charter in which the monastery of Sithiu is mentioned in this form: “to the monastery of Sithiu, which is in honor of the holy apostles Peter and Paul and of Saint Martin, or of Saint Bertinus the confessor, where that lord rests bodily,” and so forth. Moreover, the name Sitdiu, which is frequently found in these records instead of Sithiu, is also found in the *Annals of Bertin.]

### XXXII. Concerning Abbot Nantharius and the death of Waimar; and concerning Rokashem, which a certain Felix gave to us

After the death of the aforesaid abbot Waimar, Nantharius was elevated to the dignity of governing the entire abbacy. In the third year of the aforesaid king Childeric, a certain presbyter named Felix transferred to him, for the use of his monastery of Sithiu, a cell belonging to him by right, called Hrokashamo or the place of Therealdus, as the charter of that transfer testifies. We reproduce it here, to confirm its authenticity, in the wording of its ancient composition.

### XXXIII. Felix’s transfer of Rokashamo

[Note: [Col. 1208D] Published by Warnkönig in his *History of Flanders*, vol. I, documents, pp. 9 ff., from an ancient copy.]

[Col. 1207B]

(25 July 745.) “As the Lord says in the Gospel: ‘He who gives little acquires a kingdom for himself, and he who bestows a little money receives a measure without end.’ Therefore I, Felix, presbyter, in the name of God, inspired by divine clemency and for the remedy of my soul, have assigned, granted, and transferred by this deed of donation to the monastery of Sithiu, which is in honor of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and of Saint Martin, or of Saint Bertinus the confessor, where that lord rests bodily, and where the venerable man Nanthuarius appears to preside as abbot, namely my cell at a place called Rochashem or Therealdo’s place [Note: [Col. 1208D] Hrochashem or Hervaldolugo. Warnkönig.] in the county of Flanders, which I built through my work in honor of Michael the Archangel, or of Saint John the Baptist, or of holy Mary, mother of our Lord Jesus Christ, or of the other saints, and which I purchased from outsiders at a given price.

“I have done this as pleased me, on the condition that we should transfer to the monastery of Sithiu, for the work of Saint Peter, the aforesaid cell with all its entirety and solidity, and with everything belonging or pertaining to it. We have indeed done so in full, to be possessed perpetually, so that it must always remain subject and attached there, together with lands, manses, houses, buildings, slaves, dependents, both free and servile, fields, woods, meadows [Col. 1208A], pastures, waters and watercourses, mills, livestock, resources, movable and immovable property—in every respect and altogether, the whole property, whatever can be said or named. All this I give, deliver, and transfer to you, or for the use of the monastery of Sithiu, from the present day, to be possessed perpetually.

“After my death, may he who then exercises the governance of the abbacy, or the brothers of the aforesaid monastery of Sithiu residing there, have full power in every respect to appoint to that cell whatever provost they may wish.

“And we ask the brothers and rulers of that monastery of Sithiu, for God’s sake and for the sake of gaining our reward, to take care of that cell which we have transferred there, with respect to masses, the office—that is, the psalms [Note: [Col. 1208D] The words ‘that is, the psalms’ are written above ‘of the course’ in the manner of a gloss.]—and of the lights [Col. 1208B], and thereby to perform charity toward guests and pilgrims and gain merit.

“Only on this condition: as long as I live in this world, by Christ’s favor, I may use and possess that cell for the benefit of the monastery; but I shall have no power to give elsewhere, sell, exchange, alienate, or squander either that cell, which I have transferred to the monastery, or the property belonging to that place.

“And we ask that the priests who dwell in that monastery may deem it fitting to have my name in the book of life. After my death and departure from this light, the aforesaid cell, with all the property improved and added to it, shall, from the present day and without awaiting any hearing or formal transfer, be received in full into the right and dominion of the aforesaid monastery of Sithiu or its rulers, to be possessed; and they shall do with it whatever useful thing they choose.

“If anyone—and I do not believe this will happen—whether I myself, or any of my heirs or successors, or any outsider, should attempt to act against this donation or try to violate it, may he incur the wrath, judgment, and displeasure of almighty God’s supreme majesty; and before the tribunal of Christ may he render an account of this to the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and to Saint Martin and Saint Bertinus, to whom we have transferred this cell. May he be excommunicated and made an outsider from their churches [Col. 1209A], so that he may no longer appear there; and, compelled by the fisc, may he pay to the party of that monastery as much again as the cell, improved as it then is, shall be worth, or as much as I shall leave when I die in this world; let him make amends by a fine of double the money, equal to the then improved value of the cell with all the property belonging to it; and may he be unable to vindicate what he claims.

“But let this donation, so that this reward of mine may remain firm for all time, stand secured by stipulation.”

“Done publicly at the monastery of Sithiu, on the eighth day before the Kalends of August, in the third year of the reign of our lord Hilderic, glorious king.

“I, Felix, have reread and subscribed this testament made by me.

[Col. 1209B] “Sign of Chrodgarius, illustrious. Sign of Bimbert. Sign of Odbert. Sign of Godobert. Sign of Gumwin. Sign of Waning. Sign of Guntbert. Sign of Chramn. Sign of Erlarius [Note: [Col. 1209D] Sign of Dramni. Sign of Erlulf; Warnkönig.]. Sign of Clodbald. Sign of Clidebald [Note: [Col. 1209D] Childebald. Sign of Gumbarius, the scabinus. Same source.]. Sign of Gunthar, priest. Sign of Cherewin. Sign of Austroald, centenarius. Sign of Theodb­ert [Note: [Col. 1209D] Warnkönig reads Berdbert and adds: Sign of Gumard. [Col. 1210D] Sign of Vordbert. Sign of Widegrin.].”

“I, Viodarus, deacon, wrote and subscribed this at the request of others.”

### XXXIV. Concerning the death of Hilderic, the anointing of Pippin, and other matters
