Not long afterward the aforesaid King Hilderic, closing the final boundary of his life, was buried in the church of the blessed Bertinus at the monastery of Sithiu. After the death of the aforesaid abbot Nautkarius, Dadbert succeeded him in the governance of the said monastery.

In those times Stephen, Roman pontiff, came into Francia to Lord Pippin because of the oppression of the holy Church by the most savage and blasphemous king—whose name should not even be spoken—Hatstulf. There he fell ill until death and remained for some time in the county of Paris, in the venerable monastery of Saint Dionysius, martyr of Christ. When the physicians had already despaired of him, he was suddenly cured through the intervention of that blessed martyr, by means of a revelation, as the letter of that blessed pontiff testifies; this letter is also preserved among us, inserted into the Passion of Saint Dionysius.

In that revelation the martyr of Christ admonished him to dedicate the principal altar in honor of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, who, together with the aforesaid martyr, had appeared to him in the vision just mentioned. He immediately arose healthy, reported this to the aforesaid king Pippin and his nobles, and fulfilled everything he had been commanded.

Strengthened by the power of Christ, during the celebration of the consecration of the aforesaid altar and the offering of the most sacred sacrifice, he anointed the aforesaid flourishing king Pippin as king of the Franks, together with his two sons, Charles and Carloman. He also, in the name of God, consecrated his wife, the illustrious prince Pippin’s wife Bertrada, distinguished by royal robes, with the grace of the sevenfold Spirit of the Holy Spirit, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 754.

Having sanctified the Frankish nobles by apostolic blessing, he bound them by the authority of blessed Peter, entrusted to him by the Lord God Jesus Christ, and adjured them never, throughout the succession of future ages, to presume to establish over themselves a king from another lineage, but only from the offspring of those whom divine Providence had deigned to choose to protect the most holy apostolic see and whom, through that vicar of Saint Peter—or rather of our Lord Jesus Christ—it had deigned to raise to royal power and consecrate with the most sacred anointing.

After this the same pontiff returned to Rome, while Pippin, together with his sons, thereafter obtained the monarchy of all Francia.

### XXXV. Concerning Abbot Dadbert

As we have said, the aforesaid abbot Dadbert was elevated to the abbacy [Col. 1210B] after Nantharius. Nothing concerning his time is related in the deeds of this monastery, either concerning the acquisition of royal privileges, the making of other charters, or any benefit to this monastery. I do not know whether the brevity of his life prevented this, or whether perhaps the documents acquired by him concerning our predecessors were neglected through carelessness.

### XXXVI. Concerning Dadbert’s successor, Abbot Hardrad [and concerning Pippin’s successor, his son Charles, and the privilege he granted to this place]

When the aforesaid Dadbert had departed from this world, Hardrad succeeded him in the abbacy, an outstanding man in elevating the dignity of his monastery. His labor and industry shine forth in the charters preserved among us to this day under his name.

For when the aforesaid King Pippin died and his son Charles succeeded him most gloriously in the kingdom, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 768, the aforesaid abbot approached King Charles and asked him, by royal authority, to confirm the things which his predecessors appeared to have granted to this holy place through royal privileges. The same most excellent king received this request with great kindness and faithfully fulfilled it, so that the royal confirmation itself, bearing the impression of his seal, has remained manifest to us in the following form.

### XXXVII. Copy of the same privilege

[Note: [Col. 1210D] Published by Mabillon, *De re diplomatica*, p. 610.]

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks, illustrious man.

If we confirm by our decrees the acts of our royal predecessors which they bestowed or granted to holy places, we exercise the royal custom and trust that this pertains, in the name of God, to the praise of us and the stability of our kingdom.

Therefore the venerable man Hardrad, abbot of the monastery of Sithiu, situated in the county of Terouanne and built in honor of holy Mary, mother of our Lord Jesus Christ, and likewise of the holy apostles Peter and Paul and the other holy lords, came into our presence and reported to the clemency of our kingdom that the kings who were our predecessors had granted, with full immunity, to his predecessors or to the monastery of Sithiu all the estates or villages of that monastery, whatever they then possessed or thereafter acquired from royal gifts [Col. 1211A], from grants made by the people, from purchases, or from anything else acquired in whatever counties and territories it had been added or granted there.

They had done so so that no public judge might ever presume to enter there to hear legal cases, exact payments, take sureties, impose lodging or requisition services, distrain the men of the monastery, whether free or servile, who lived upon its lands, or demand or exact any dues. Rather, under the benefit of immunity, with all the payments and bans that had been granted, the monastery’s portion should possess these things perpetually for all time.

Accordingly he affirms that he has in his hands the charters of our predecessors and that the benefits granted have been preserved from that time until now. But for the sake of complete security the aforesaid abbot requested our Highness to confirm this more fully concerning that place by our authority. Know that, for the increase of our reward and out of reverence for that holy place, we have granted his petition in this way and confirmed everything.

For we command that whatever our predecessors are known to have justly and reasonably granted or confirmed concerning that immunity, as described above, and whatever has been preserved by a straight course from that time until now, shall likewise hereafter be preserved more fully in the name of God by our decree. Having examined the charters of the princes mentioned above, as their contents declare, may the benefits granted concerning the abbot Hardrad or his successors and the monastery of Sithiu remain preserved in every respect for all time; and may they not fear at any time to suffer opposition or impediment from public judges on this account. Therefore may that community continually beseech the mercy of the Lord for the stability of our kingdom and the safety of the country. And so that this authority may be held more firmly and preserved in every respect, we have decreed that it be strengthened by the subscriptions of our hand.

Sign of Charles, most glorious king.

Given in the month of July, in the first year of our reign. Done at Andiacum [Col. 1211D] [Note: [Col. 1211D] Andiacum, a palace in the county of Angoulême. But I fear that Charles the Great was not staying in this place in the first year of his reign. I would believe that he was residing at the palace of Audriacum on the Authie, not far from the monastery of Sithiu. For [Col. 1212D] in that very year he was staying at the villa of Audriacum, where he granted a privilege to Hado, or Chado, abbot of Corbie.]

### XXXVIII. Purchase of Rokashomo by the same abbot

(770.) In the second year of the same king, which was the year 774 of the Lord’s birth, the same abbot Hardrad purchased, for the use of the church called Therealdo’s Grove—which a certain presbyter named Felix had transferred to his predecessor, Abbot Nantharius—from a certain man named Sigerard his proprietary possessions at the place already mentioned, Hrokashem, whatever possession he appeared to have there, as the charter of sale testifies in the following manner.

### XXXIX. Copy of the same purchase

[Col. 1212A]

(770.) “To the lord, venerable father in Christ, Hardrad, abbot of the monastery of Sithiu, and purchaser. I, Sigerard, the seller, by this deed of sale declare that I have sold, not by fictitious right but by the free exercise of my own will, to you or to your church of Saint Michael, the holy basilica built at Heraldo’s Grove, where the presbyter Fugislus appears to serve, namely, all the property of my portion at a place called Hrokashem, in the county of Flanders—that is, lands and a mansus, together with all the buildings erected upon it, meadows, fields, slaves, common lands, ways, watercourses, livestock, resources, movable and immovable property; everything in every respect, both from my parents’ inheritance and from purchases or anything else acquired.

“I sell, deliver, and permanently transfer all this to you or to your church of Saint Michael, in full, to be possessed perpetually. In return I have received from you, from the property of your church, for the aforesaid property, the price assessed and paid, with which I was well satisfied: namely, two hundred solidi in gold and silver. Thus, from this day forward, you or your successors shall have, hold, and possess the property named above, and shall have free power in every respect to do with it whatever you wish.

“If anyone—and I do not believe this will happen—whether I myself, or any of my heirs or principal heirs, or any other opposing person, should wish to act against this sale or attempt to violate it [Col. 1212C], let him be compelled by the fisc to pay to you or your successors twice as much as we received from you, or twice as much as that portion, improved as it then is, shall be worth; and, in addition, let him be compelled to pay double the money, and may he be unable to vindicate what he claims. But let this sale remain firm for all time, secured by stipulation.

“Done at Therealdo’s Grove.

“Given in the month of January, in the second year of the reign of our lord Charles, most glorious king.

“Sign of Sigerard, who requested that this sale be made.

“Sign of Wiorad. Sign of Folchard. Sign of Thedulf. [Col. 1212D] Sign of Odelrad. Sign of Engelrad.

“I, Fulgislus, presbyter, wrote and subscribed this.”

### XL. Concerning Abbot Hardrad’s purchase at Loningahem

(776.) In the eighth year of the aforesaid King Charles, the same abbot Hardrad purchased from a certain man named Waldbert, for two hundred solidi, all his property at a place called Loningaheim, in the county of Boulogne—whatever hereditary possession he appeared to have there. His charter also testifies to this, saying as follows.

### XLI. Copy of the same purchase

[Col. 1213A]

(July 776.) “To the venerable man in Christ, Hardrad, abbot of the monastery of Sithiu and purchaser. I, Waldbert, the seller, declare by this deed of sale that, not by fictitious right but by my own voluntary decision, I have sold to you or to your monastery of Sithiu—and so I have sold and presently delivered—namely, all my possession, two parts in the place called Loningaheim, in the county of Boulogne [Col. 1213B]: lands, manses, enclosures, and one slave named Blidinarus, with all his *etnika* and personal property; meadows, woods, pastures, commons, access-ways and *wadriscapi*; everything in its entirety, the whole and undivided property, I sell, deliver, and permanently transfer to you or to your monastery of Sithiu from the present day, for possession.

For this I have received from you, from the property of your monastery, as the price assessed and paid for the aforesaid property, a sum with which I am well satisfied—namely, two hundred solidi in gold and silver. Thus, from this day, you or your successors shall have, hold, and possess the property named above, and shall have full power to do with it whatever you wish.

If anyone—which I do not believe will happen—whether I myself, or any of my heirs or heirs-to-be, or any other opposing person, should wish to act against this sale or attempt to invalidate it, and if it is not defended by me or by my heirs, then, under compulsion of the fisc, we shall pay you twice the amount that we received from you, or twice the value that the said portion may then have acquired [Col. 1213C]; and, in addition, the offender shall be compelled to pay double the sum and shall be unable to vindicate the claim he brings. Nevertheless, this sale shall remain firm for all time, supported by stipulation.

“Executed publicly at the monastery of Sithiu.

Given in the month of July, in the eighth year of the reign of our lord Charles, the most glorious king.

The sign of Waldbert, who requested that this sale be made.

The sign of Trudmar. The sign of Buginus. The sign of Randger. The sign of Udmar. The sign of Ermnulf. The sign of Winidger.

I, Henry the deacon, wrote and subscribed.”

### XLII. That he also purchased Fresingehem

He also purchased another piece of land, for one hundred solidi, called Fresingehem [Col. 1213D], from a certain woman named Sigeberta, according to the following charter.

### XLIII. Copy

(10 June 788.) “To the venerable lord in Christ, Father Hardrad, abbot of the monastery of Sithiu and purchaser. I, Sigeberta, the seller, declare by this deed of sale that, not by fictitious right but by my own free will, I have sold to you or to the aforesaid monastery of Sithiu—and so I have sold and delivered—namely, all my share of property in the place called Fresingehem, situated in the county of Haruan, on the river Agniona, except for one *jornale* [Col. 1214A], which I reserved from it for another property, in its entirety: that is, lands, manses, enclosures, buildings, fields, woods, meadows, pastures, commons, access-ways and *wadriscapi*. Everything in its entirety, the whole and undivided property, I sell, deliver, and permanently transfer to you or to the aforesaid monastery from the present day, for possession.

For this I received from you, from the property of your monastery, as the price assessed and paid for the aforesaid property, a sum with which I am well satisfied—namely, one hundred solidi in gold and silver. Thus, from this day, you shall have, hold, and possess it, and shall have power to do with it whatever you wish.

If anyone—which I do not at all believe will happen—whether I myself, or any of my heirs or heirs-to-be, or any other person who wishes to act against this sale or presumes to invalidate it, should do so, then, under compulsion of the fisc, we shall pay you or your successors twice the amount we received from you, or twice the value that the said portion may then have acquired [Col. 1214B]; and, in addition, the offender shall be compelled to pay double the sum and shall be unable to vindicate the claim he brings. Nevertheless, this sale shall remain firm, supported by stipulation.

“Executed publicly at the monastery of Sithiu.

Given in the month of June, on the tenth day, in the twentieth year of the reign of our lord Charles, the glorious king.

The sign of Sigeberta, who requested that this sale be made.

The sign of Hildebert. The sign of Snelger. The sign of Hildulf. The sign of Regenhar. The sign of Hildmar. The sign of Madalle. The sign of Bain. The sign of Guntbert [Col. 1214C].

I, Gerbald the deacon, wrote and subscribed.”

### XLIV. On Abbot Odland and Charles’s privilege

The labor of the aforementioned Abbot Hardrad brought these properties to the monastery of Sithiu. When Hardrad was departing from this life, he left as his successor in the governance of the monastery Odland, his equal in goodness and wisdom [Note: [Col. 1213D] A.D. 795, in John of Ypres, col. 498; cf. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, col. 487.]. This occurred in the year of the Lord 798, and the memory of his praise will remain among us forever.

Among his other achievements, Odland approached the aforesaid King Charles and begged the royal majesty to grant permission to the abbots of the monastery of Sithiu and to their people to hunt throughout all the abbey’s woods. The most excellent king granted this request and confirmed it by a royal privilege, ordering that no one should at any time presume to be hostile toward them on this account [Col. 1214D], but that, for the use of the monastery of Sithiu—to cover books or to make sleeves and belts—they should have permission to hunt in their own woods. This privilege, confirmed by royal authority, bears witness to that very grant and has hitherto been preserved among us with the royal seal.

### XLV. Copy of King Charles’s privilege concerning hunting in the woods [Note: Cointius, *Annales Ecclesiastici Francorum*, vol. V, maintains that this diploma is spurious.]

(See *Patrologia*, volume XCVII, among the works of Charlemagne.)

### XLVI. The transfer by Deodatus of the properties named below

(800.) In the year of the Lord’s Nativity 794, which was the thirty-second year of the reign of the aforesaid King Charles and the third year of the rule of the said abbot [Col. 1215A], a certain cleric named Deodatus sold, for a price received, to the same abbot, for the use of his monastery of Sithiu, his possessions in the following places: in Sanctum, in Ascio on the river Widolacus, in Fresinnium on the river Capriunus, in Hildwaldcurt, and in Lonastum on the river Abbunfontana, in the county of Tervan.

He sold all these properties for the use of the brothers and permanently transferred them by a deed of sale. The aforesaid Abbot Odland immediately assigned them for the brothers’ clothing, on the condition that Deodatus himself should hold them during his lifetime by a precarious tenure, and that after his death all improvements should revert to the aforesaid monastery.

### XLVII. Copy of this transfer

[Col. 1215B]

(3 August 800.) “To the venerable father in Christ, Odland, abbot of the monastery of Sithiu, and to all the congregation of your brothers residing there, I, Deodatus the cleric, a sinner. Since it is not unknown to everyone how my possessions lie in the places called Sanctum and Ascio, on the river Widolacus, and in Fresinnium, on the river Capriunus, and in Hildwaldcurt and Lonastum, on the river Abbunfontana, in the county of Tervan—that is, in the aforesaid places, lands, manses, enclosures, buildings, and the church of Saint Martin, which was built in honor of the aforesaid lord and Saint Martin in the said place, together with the saints or other churches, and whatever appears to belong or be subject to the aforesaid place of Sanctum or to the other places [Col. 1215C]; slaves with all their *etbuike* and personal property; fields, woods, meadows, pastures, access-ways and *wadriscapi*; waters and the courses of waters; mills; appurtenances; dependencies; cultivated and uncultivated land; everything in its entirety, whatever can be said or named; all that my possession or dominion was, however extensive, in the aforesaid places, whether from the inheritance of my parents, from purchase or exchange, or from anything acquired, and which is legally known to have come to me; church furnishings of gold and silver, embroidered cloths of diverse form or kind, various books, and whatever appears to belong to all the places written above—I permanently transfer all of it in its entirety to you, by title of sale and for a price received, for your church, from the present day [Col. 1215D].

The condition is that all the property described above shall be used to purchase clothing for the monks living in the aforesaid monastery of Sithiu, namely, cloth for shirts, called in the vernacular *berniscrist*, according to your wishes.

Afterward, however, you, with the consent of your brothers, in accordance with my request, promised to make the properties written above available to me for my ordinary use, by your gracious benefaction, so that I might cultivate and improve them. As we agreed, each year, on the feast of Saint Martin, we must give or pay to you or your successors a rent of two silver solidi. I shall have no right elsewhere to give, sell, exchange, or alienate the property, nor to dispose of it by any device; and my possession shall not be able to generate any claim from this, except that, as stated, for as long as I live I shall possess it as your benefice. After my death and departure from this life, you or your successors shall cause all the properties written above to be received in their entirety, without opposition from anyone, for perpetual possession [Col. 1216A].

And this precarious tenure shall remain firm for all time, supported by stipulation.

“Executed publicly at Sanclis.

Given in the month of August, on the third day, in the thirty-second year of the reign of our lord Charles, the most glorious king.

[Col. 1216B] The sign of Deodatus, who requested that this precarious tenure be made.

The sign of David, his consenting son.

The sign of Guntard. The sign of Herrad. The sign of Wigmar. The sign of Erembert. The sign of another Erembert. The sign of Egelulf. The sign of Rigfrid.

I, Guntbert, an unworthy deacon in the name of God, wrote and subscribed.”

### XLVIII. The work of the same Abbot Odland concerning the estate of Arecas

The labor and industry of this Abbot Odland shine forth especially in the estate called Arecas, which was one of the principal members of the abbey [Col. 1216C]. He established it as his own residence and adorned it with every distinction.

There he built a basilica in honor of Saint Martin; today only the foundations of that church present themselves to the eyes of those who look upon them. He also established—as those testify whose parents and grandparents had been tenants in the aforesaid estate—that each week five monks from the monastery of Saint Bertin and an equal number from that of Saint Audomar should be assigned there to serve the Lord.

There too, something remarkable still shown in our own times, he caused a mill to turn by waters running uphill against the mountain, and decreed that no one should presume to construct a mill outside the place just mentioned. This was preserved for a time for the benefit of the monastery of Sithiu [Col. 1216D].

This abbot is said to have possessed such an extraordinary ability that he could hear with his ears where water was flowing through unknown and hidden channels of the earth. There are also very many other praises of him that circulate on the lips of secular people; we omit them here so that they may not seem superfluous to the negligent.

[After Abbot Odland had lived for nearly nine years in the administration of his office, he cast off the fragile burden of the flesh, ready to render to the Creator an account of his talents. In the monastic succession, Nantharius, the second of that name, succeeded him.]

### XLIX. On the younger Nantharius, the anointing of Charles as emperor, and the same abbot’s purchase of Flitrinium

The younger Nantharius also became Odland’s successor in the governance of the monastery, in the year of the Incarnate Word 805 and the thirty-ninth year of the reign of the aforesaid Charles [Note: [Col. 1217D] Perhaps correct: 804, the thirty-fifth year of King Charles.]. The glorious King Charles, in the thirty-third year of his reign, went to Rome and was elected emperor by the entire people; on the day of the Lord’s Nativity, in the church of Saint Peter, he was consecrated by Pope Leo.

Abbot Nantharius, in the thirty-ninth year of the aforesaid King Charles and the fifth year of his empire, purchased from a certain man named Erlharius his property in the place called Flitrinium: namely, one mansus and, between arable land, meadow, and woodland, ten *bunnaria*. He also requested that these be granted to him by the abbot under precarious tenure, and the abbot did so.

### L. The purchase by Nautharius, abbot, of Flitrinium

(October 806.) “To the venerable father in Christ, Nautharius, abbot of the monastery of Sithiu, or of the cell called Hebrona, where Ebroinus appears to be provost [Col. 1217B]. I, Herlharius, the seller, declare by this deed of sale that, not by fictitious right but with complete free will, I have sold to you or to your monastery—and so I have sold and delivered, and presently delivered—namely, one mansus in the place called Fletrinium, in the county of Isseret, and, between arable land, meadow, and woodland, somewhat more or less than ten *bunnaria*.

By this deed of gift, as we have handed it over and declared, I give, deliver, and permanently transfer it for possession, on the condition that you shall have, hold, and possess it, and, with Christ’s favor, shall have full and firm power to do with it whatever you wish.

Because of this, your benevolence and piety granted a benefice both to me and to my children, whose names are Erkenrad, Baldrad, Errictrude, and Waldetrude [Col. 1217C]. Whichever of us outlives his or her companion, you promised to provide it to us for ordinary use, so that we might cultivate and improve it. As we agreed, each year we must give or pay to you or your successors, for that use, ten measures of salt as rent.

We shall have no right elsewhere to give, sell, exchange, alienate, or in any way dispose of your property, nor shall our possession be able to create any prejudice or claim against your monastery. We shall possess it only as stated, as your benefice, for as long as, with Christ’s favor, I remain in this world. After the death and departure from this life of all of us, you shall cause the properties described above to be received in their entirety, without opposition or judicial challenge from anyone, for perpetual possession [Col. 1217D].

If anyone—which I do not believe will happen—whether I myself, or any of my heirs or heirs-to-be, or any other opposing or foreign person, should wish to act against this sale or invalidate it, then, after investigation by the fisc, he shall be compelled to pay three ounces of gold and five pounds of silver, and shall be unable to vindicate the claim he brings. Nevertheless, this gift shall remain firm for all time, supported by stipulation.

“Executed at Beborna, in the month of October, in the thirty-ninth year while our lord Charles, the most glorious king, was reigning, and in the sixth year of his empire [Col. 1218A].

“The sign of Erlharius, who requested that this sale be made.

The sign of Erkenrad, his consenting son.

The sign of Folquin. The sign of another Erkenrad. The sign of Gerard. The sign of Elpharius. The sign of Herrad. The sign of Hardmann. The sign of Rantvuin. The sign of Guntfrid. The sign of Helinger. The sign of Heodrad. The sign of Engelger. The sign of Sicbald. The sign of Grimard. The sign of Godobert.

I, Guntbert, wrote and subscribed.”

### LI. The transfer by Lebdrudis of Gisna

In the following year [Note: [Col. 1218D] That is, 807.], in the month of October, a certain widow named Lebdrudis transferred to the aforesaid abbot [Col. 1218B], for his monastery of Sithiu, all her property in the place called Gisna or Totingelum, in the county of Boulogne. In return, she requested from the aforesaid abbot, as a benefice, property belonging to his monastery in the same county, namely two *bunnaria* in the place called Etloum, in the following words.

### LII. Copy

(October 807.) “To the magnificent lord in Christ, Father Nantharius, abbot of the monastery of Sithiu, which is built in the county of Tervan on the river Agniona, in honor of the blessed apostles Peter, Paul, and Andrew, and of Saint Martin and Saint Bertin, and of many holy martyrs and confessors, and also to the congregation of that holy place.

I, Lebtrudis, a widow, reflecting upon heavenly love and the cleansing of my crimes [Col. 1218C], decided that I ought to offer the Lord some small gifts from my poverty, and so I have done.

Therefore I give all my property in the place called Gisna or Totingetun, in the county of Boulogne, on the river Wuasconinga Wala: namely, manses with houses or enclosures, buildings, meadows, pastures, lands, access-ways and *wadriscapi*, and whatever appears to belong or be subject to that place, and whatever was my lawful possession or dominion, together with the whole and undivided property.

All the things described above I give, deliver, and permanently transfer by this deed of transfer to the aforesaid monastery, for possession.

In return for this gift and your piety, I requested from you some land belonging to your monastery [Col. 1218D], in the place called Ecloum, in the same county of Boulogne, namely two *bunnaria*, on the condition that I and my three children—Hildeberta, Nidlebus, and Erpsuvid—shall possess those lands for their fruits as your benefice for as long as we live.

For this use, each year, on the feast of Saint Audomar, on the Kalends of November, we shall pay two weights of cheese. We shall have no right to alienate those properties; we shall cultivate them only as your benefice for the use of their fruits. After the death of all of us, the administrators of your monastery shall immediately possess both properties as a perpetual holding [Col. 1219A].

If anyone—which I do not at all believe will happen—whether I myself, or any of my heirs, or any other opposing person, should wish to act against this gift or presume to invalidate it, may he incur the anger of God and of the aforesaid saints and appear excommunicated from the universal faith. In addition, under the constraint of the fisc, may he pay six ounces of gold and many weights of silver, and may he be unable to vindicate the claim he brings. Nevertheless, this present deed shall remain firm for all time, supported by stipulation.

Executed publicly at the estate of Gisna, when the month of October had reached its eleventh day, in the fortieth year of the reign and the eighth year of the empire of our lord Charles, the most pious emperor Augustus.

The sign of Lebdrudis, the widow who requested that this gift be made [Col. 1219B].

The sign of Madalger. The sign of Odilo. The sign of Engelbert. The sign of Bertland. The sign of Wendelger, centenarius.

I, Guntbert the priest, wrote and subscribed.”

### LIII. The transfer by Folbert of Campanias

(811.) A certain man named Folbert, in the forty-third year of the reign of the aforesaid King Charles and the tenth year of his empire, transferred to the same Abbot Nautharius, for the salvation of his deceased mother’s soul, his property at Campanias in the county of Tervan, in the following manner.

### LIV. Copy

(April 811.) “To the venerable father in Christ, Nautharius, abbot of the monastery of Sithiu, where the two saints, namely Audomar and blessed Bertin, rest bodily [Col. 1219C].

I, Folbert, declare by this deed of transfer that, for the remedy of the soul of my deceased mother Ebertana, I give, deliver, and permanently transfer to you or to your aforesaid monastery of Sithiu a certain part of my inheritance: namely, somewhat more or less than five *bunnaria*, and one meadow called Brattingadala, together with whatever appears to belong to that meadow, in the place called Campanias, in the county of Tervan, with its lawful access-way and *wadriscapus*. All this, in accordance with what has been set out above, I give, deliver, and permanently transfer to you or your successors for possession.

Therefore I implored your piety to allow me to use and improve this property. Afterward, you, with the consent of your brothers, in accordance with my request, promised that I might manage the property for as long as I live, so that I might cultivate and improve it. As we agreed, each year, on the feast of Saint Bertin, which is on the Nones of September, I must give or pay to you, for this use, a rent of four denarii [Col. 1219D].

If anyone—which I do not believe will happen—whether I myself or any of my heirs, should wish to act against this gift or attempt to invalidate it, let him be compelled, under the constraint of the fisc, to pay you four ounces of gold and five weights of silver, and let him be unable to vindicate the claim he brings. Nevertheless, this transfer shall remain firm for all time, supported by stipulation [Col. 1220A].

“Executed at Bagingatun, in the month of April, in the forty-fourth year while Charles the glorious king was reigning, and in the tenth year of his empire.

[Note: [Col. 1219D] The forty-fourth year of Charlemagne’s reign corresponds to A.D. 812, while the tenth year of his empire corresponds to A.D. 811. Greater credence therefore seems due to the chronological notices in chapter LIII [Col. 1220D], which agree with one another in indicating A.D. 811.]

The sign of Folbert, who requested that this gift be made.

The sign of Folchar. The sign of Abbo. The sign of Ingobert. The sign of Wendelgar, centenarius.

I, Guntbert the priest, wrote and subscribed.”

### LV. On the transfer of the estate of Calmont

The aforementioned Charles, desiring to increase his fame throughout the world—as is plainly evident from the reading of the many volumes that mention him—among other acts transferred the estate of Calmont [Col. 1220B] to God and holy Bertin. The charter of this transfer is held by the bishop of Noyon.

### LVI. On Charles’s death and Louis’s succession

After the renowned praises of the glorious deeds of the aforesaid King Charles, and after the conquest of the nations of many peoples—conquests that circulate even now on the lips of the living and will remain so forever—he paid the penalty of the first parent, returned his soul to his Creator, and, surrendering his body, so glorious yet soon to become earth, to the debt of nature, left it to be covered by the earth. This occurred in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 814, in the forty-eighth year of his reign and the fifteenth year of his empire [Note: [Col. 1220D] Correct to “the forty-sixth year of his reign and the fourteenth year of his empire.”].

I remember reading in a certain book entitled *The Visions of Wettin* that the same Wettin, while being led by an angel in ecstasy, saw among the other things shown to him the same King Charles standing with his whole body healthy and most beautiful [Col. 1220C]. He saw only a certain animal set against him, tearing at the genitals of the standing man. The angel told him that he suffered this because in the world he had been excessively uncontrolled in lust, but that, because of his other works of virtue, he would soon be rescued from this danger.

His son Louis therefore succeeded him in the kingdom, in every respect like him in glorious deeds. In his time a certain light of the Church arose, named Folquin. To prevent it from remaining hidden under a bushel, the king himself placed it upon the Church’s lampstand and appointed it to the episcopate of the city of Tervan, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 817 and the fourth year of the aforesaid king [Col. 1220D].

There was much that we could say about his life and virtues, and I would wish to touch briefly upon what he accomplished in this world. But, considering my own foolishness, I shrink even from touching what the most learned might fear to approach. His deeds surpass philosophical argument concerning worldly wisdom, even if someone, according to poetic fictions, should boast that he had fully drained the Hippocrene spring.

These few words alone I have brought forth in foolish chatter in his memory. I leave the rest of his works to be investigated by a man of keener intellect; and I myself, if it should be useful, shall later be ready, to the best of my ability, to recount what I remember [Col. 1221A].

### LVII. On Abbot Fridegisus

Meanwhile Abbot Nantharius, the younger, departing from this world in the eighteenth year of his administration, left as his successor the first destroyer of the regular life, namely Fridegisus, an abbot not even worthy of that name.

For although until then the sacred rule of the monks had, by God’s mercy, been preserved in this monastery, as its wealth increased the organization of the monastery was withdrawn from the monks and, by royal benefaction, bestowed upon outsiders. Thus it happened that the aforementioned Fridegisus, an Englishman by birth and abbot of Saint Martin at Tours, in the year of the Incarnate Word 820 and the seventh year of the reign of the aforesaid King Louis, received the abbacy [Col. 1221B] of the monastery of Sithiu to govern by royal grant.

At the beginning of his tyranny, when he saw that the whole abbey had been assigned to the uses of so many monks—namely, one hundred and thirty monks living between the two monasteries, Saint Bertin’s and Saint Audomar’s—and that nothing had been set aside for his own pleasures, he was pierced by the dart of avarice and shamelessly attempted to destroy the monks’ way of life, so that he might more easily subject to his own luxury the properties that the faithful had entrusted for their use.

What had been conceived in his mind through diabolical suggestion he completed by a wicked act. In the place of the apostolic leader, his holy Bertin, where eighty-three monks served the Lord, he retained sixty, more for human praise than for love of God [Col. 1221C]. The remaining men of stricter life, whom he judged unwilling to consent to his perversity, he expelled from the monastery and allowed to depart.

In the monastery of Saint Audomar as well, where forty monks were living according to the rule, he appointed thirty canons there to serve in the monastery of Christ.

After this, he went around the estates of the entire abbey. Since the number of monks was twice that of the canons, he granted the monks a double portion of the estates. To the canons, because they were fewer in number, he gave only a single portion, in contrast to the monks. He reserved for his own use whatever especially pleased him; and because he was a canon, he lived a secular life with the canons in the monastery of Saint Audomar.

What more should I say about this abbot’s cunning, when I could truthfully call him the first calamity of this place? In accordance with the truthful word of Truth, although others had labored, he entered into their labors; and he not only entered them, but also destroyed by reckless presumption what they had accomplished [Col. 1221D].

He was also the destroyer of fraternal charity between the two monasteries. The monks rightly claimed for themselves the honor of reverence handed down by the ancient Fathers and genuinely defended the subjection of the canons to themselves, while the canons, through the false assertion of that canonical abbot, claimed that authority over the monasteries belonged to them.

For all these things and the remaining acts of his tyranny, he is to this day cursed by everyone [Col. 1222A], and there is no doubt that he will also be cursed by those who come after.

### LVIII. On Louis the King’s privilege concerning hunting in the woods of the monastery of Sithiu

(820.) In the first year of his administration, this same abbot approached the aforementioned King Louis and requested permission from him to hunt in the woods of his monastery of Sithiu, under the pretext of obtaining books to be read or sleeves to be made for the brothers’ use—but, more credibly, in order to indulge his own empty amusement.

The king granted this without delay and ordered a privilege to be made by royal authority for this purpose. He himself also confirmed it by the impression of his seal, in the following words.

### LIX. Copy of the same privilege

[Col. 1222B]

(See among the privileges of Louis the Pious, in volume CIV of the *Patrologia*.)

### LX. The same king’s privilege concerning the monastery of Sithiu in the time of Abbot Fridegisus

The aforesaid Abbot Fridegisus also petitioned the same king a second time, asking that by his authority, through a royal privilege, he defend his monastery of Sithiu from every judicial power. Just as his royal predecessors were known to have granted this to the same place, so the glorious king himself might deign to confirm it by his authority.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 830, the king confirmed this by royal authority in the following manner.

### LXI. Copy of the same privilege [Note: [Col. 1221] Mabillon published it but omitted the chronological notices and the name of the place where the diploma was issued. See *De re diplomatica*, p. 612.]

(See above.)

### LXII. On the monk Guntbert

[Col. 1222C]

In the time of this abbot there arose a certain young man, soon to become a monk of this church. His praise and wisdom have continued to circulate in the mouths of all our people, as though he were still held alive in the body and in merit.

Because he was a skilled scribe, he renewed by his own industry the library of this monastery, whose books had almost all been destroyed by age. He also increased it with other volumes. Among these are two antiphonaries, which he wrote with his own hand: one he gave to Saint Audomar and the other to Saint Winnoc.

He wrote a third as well and illuminated it with more brilliant workmanship. He splendidly adorned its opening and the hymn for the major solemnities with golden letters. Because he judged it the more elegant, he gave it to Saint Bertin.

He also copied a computus, which he allowed us to possess, as well as other works which, if written here, would seem superfluous.

In his earliest youth, his father took him to Rome, where he presented him to Saint Peter, and Pope Eugenius made him a cleric. His father then brought him home and offered him as a monk in this monastery of Sithiu to Saint Peter and Saint Bertin; he also nobly endowed this place with his inheritance [Col. 1222D].

For he granted to the aforesaid monastery of Sithiu a monastery that he had built on his own property, named Steneland, and permanently assigned all his inheritance to the Lord Savior, in whose name he had built that monastery [Col. 1223A].

These are the names of the estates that the aforesaid Goibertus, father of the aforementioned Guntbert, transferred as alms to the basilica of the Lord Savior at Steneland: at Ricolvingeem; Hisdenne, with slaves; at Okkaningahem; at Hostede; at Lampanesse; at Simpaco; at Bortheem; at Reka; at Strate; at Hemmanwil; at Kiltiaco; at Hedenesberg; in the monastery, a mansus and garden; likewise at Ariaco; at Tervan, a mansus; likewise at Quentovic.

The following were likewise granted by others to the same basilica: at Kessiacum and Squerda; at Wesarinum; at Vostringe; at Tingriacum; at Wilere; Mestrugasele; at Loclesse; at Lonastingahem; at Gruonomberg; at Dagmaringahem [Col. 1224A].

All these properties the aforesaid Goibertus and his son Guntbert, partly from their own inheritance and partly through the gifts of others, though acquired by Guntbert himself, transferred by the firmest gift to the basilica of the Lord Savior at Steneland. They also granted the basilica and the gate of the monastery of Sithiu [Note: “At the gate,” according to the Codex Audomaropolitanus] with the readiest goodwill, so that alms might be distributed to the poor and pilgrims.

When we begin to speak of almsgiving in its proper places, we shall, God willing, describe all these things together with their charters.

[Col. 1223]

*The first book ends.*

## BOOK TWO

### I. On Abbot Hugh

[Col. 1223B]

When Abbot Fridegisus departed from this world [in the fourteenth year of his administration], Hugh the venerable, son of the great King Charles and brother of the Emperor Louis, succeeded him in the abbacy, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 834 and the twenty-first year of the reign of the aforesaid King Louis.

In the second year of his administration, he approached the aforesaid king and asked him to confirm by royal authority the grants that his predecessors, the kings of the Franks, appeared to have confirmed for the aforesaid monastery of Sithiu by royal privileges.

The most excellent king fulfilled this request as readily as Hugh had made it, loving him more than his predecessors, as a brother with fraternal affection from the heart.

### II. King Louis’s privilege in the time of Abbot Hugh [Note: [Col. 1223D] In Mabillon, *De re diplomatica*, p. 613.]

[Col. 1223C]

(See among the privileges of Louis the Pious, in volume CIV of the *Patrologia*.)

### III

At the same time, the aforesaid Abbot Hugh, grieving over the most wretched division and sundering of the venerable monastery of Sithiu caused by the wicked Fridegisus, inspired the venerable Bishop Folquin of the Morini, then in office, to restore the unity of the monasteries according to their former custom.

He also caused this to be confirmed by a privilege. The following is a copy of that privilege.

### IV. Copy [Note: [Col. 1223D] Mabillon published that privilege in *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, vol. III, part I, p. 122.]

[Col. 1224D]

I, Folquinus, by the grace of God bishop of the Morini, to all the faithful, present and future. Whatever, out of love for God, we may leave recorded for the knowledge of future generations, setting forth the truth of the matter, we hope will greatly benefit our souls, since we both make the truth known and condemn what has been falsified. For it is better to reveal the truth itself to the praise of God than to conceal it for the sake of profit or earthly business, lest a sinful man thereby appear to incur the offense of God and his saints. [Col. 1223D]

Therefore I, Folquinus the bishop, at the urging of Hugo, abbot of the Sithiu monastery, which was built on the island of Sithiu in honor of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, where blessed Bertinus rests in body, considering the grievous injustice which Fridegisus, predecessor of the aforesaid abbot, had inflicted upon that holy place, began with all earnestness to devise how I might restore that place to its former honor. [Col. 1224B]

It is certainly known to all the faithful that the holy confessors of Christ, Audomarus and Bertinus, while still in the body, jointly established a cemetery in the village of Sithiu, in an elevated place, for the burial of their own bodies and those of the monks. In its midst they had built a basilica in honor of Saint Mary. Blessed Audomarus also bestowed it upon Saint Bertinus and his successors, confirming it by a certain episcopal privilege, and in the same privilege requesting that his own little body be buried among them. [Col. 1224C]

The aforesaid abbot Fridegisus not only took it away from Saint Bertinus, but also—horrible to say—expelled with great disgrace his monks, who were serving God honorably there, and established canons in their place, although from the days of the saints Audomarus and Bertinus the monastic religious life serving there had flourished with the greatest devotion.

Moved by compassion for their tearful injustice and unceasing complaint, and yielding to the petition of the venerable abbot Hugo, I judged and decreed that the administration, or guardianship, of that basilica should be restored to Saint Peter and Saint Bertinus, and that a monk should be appointed there as its custodian. I also established that the solemn Masses should be celebrated four times each year, namely on the Tuesday of Rogation Days, on the feast of blessed John the Baptist, on the deposition of Saint Audomarus, and on the feast of All Saints. [Col. 1224D]

Whatever came to that altar, the monks of Saint Bertinus were to have, hold, and possess in perpetuity by everlasting right, without any contradiction, according to the ancient custom and in accordance with the decree of blessed Audomarus, which he wrote and prohibited in a privilege concerning the handing over of that place to the monks. [Col. 1225A] Neither the bishop nor his archdeacon, nor any of the clergy, nor any judge of secular matters, was to claim anything from it for himself.

Indeed, certain men had already arisen, deceived by reckless audacity, saying that the primacy of the places ought to belong to them. Resisting their presumptuous pride, I subjected them to this place by a capitular record, in the presence of certain leading men of the royal palace and of this region, and I destroyed their attempt. I judged that this writing too should be left to posterity, so that by means of it the evil will of enemies and the unjust attempt of those wishing to violate this arrangement might at some time be resisted.

Whoever in future times should presume either to destroy or to violate this arrangement—God forbid—let him be anathema by the authority of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, unless he should turn back through worthy repentance. [Col. 1225B]

Enacted in the year 839 of the Lord’s incarnation, in the second indiction, in the twenty-sixth year of the reign of King Louis, and in the twenty-third year of our episcopate, in the church of Saint Mary, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July, in the presence of the universal synod. [Col. 1225D]

[Note: From this one may infer that Folquinus was installed in the see of the Morini in 817. John of Ypres agrees, placing Folquinus’s inauguration in the fourth year of the Emperor Louis.]

I, Folquinus, with the consent and command of the lord Emperor Louis, have willingly confirmed these things and subscribed them with episcopal prohibition.

I, Maximus the archdeacon, subscribed.

I, Hugo the abbot, subscribed.

Sign of Adalard, monk.

Sign of Amalbert, monk.

Sign of Morus, monk.

[Note: John of Ypres’s words in chapter 12 concern this matter: “Hugo, abbot of the basilica of Saint Mary, appointed as its custodian a monk named Morus. This Morus later stole the body of Saint Audomarus, and he is listed among the witnesses in the privilege of blessed Folquinus.”]

Sign of Henry [another reading: Unricus], count. [Col. 1225C]

Sign of Odginus, advocate.

Sign of Everwinus, soldier.

Sign of Berarius, soldier.

I, Guntbertus, deacon and monk, at the command of the lord Folquinus the bishop, wrote and subscribed this charter.

[Note: John of Ypres praises this Guntbertus in chapter 2 with these words: “Under Abbot Fridegisus, this noble boy Guntbertus was received as a monk, born of a distinguished lineage, his father being Goibertus and his mother Ebertrudis. This Guntbertus, while still young, was taken by his father to Rome, where he was offered to Saint Peter and received the clerical order from Pope Eugenius. His father then returned home and offered him here in the monastery of Sithiu, to Saint Peter and Saint Bertinus, as a monk.”] [Col. 1226D]

### V. Copy

Whatever … [Note: This charter consists of the same words as the preceding one, with only several names, the date, and the final formula changed.]

### VI. On the Death of King Louis and the Division of the Kingdom among His Sons

The glorious king, Louis the Emperor Augustus, died from this world in the year 840 of the Lord’s incarnation, after he had reigned for twenty-seven years. Before his death, something marvelous and unheard-of occurred in the district of Thérouanne. For in that same year, after mid-January, at midday, fiery bosses fell from the sky with a great sound and presented a wondrous spectacle to all the people. [Col. 1225D]

After the aforesaid Emperor Louis had died, his son Lothar, who before his father’s death had been anointed emperor, came from Italy and desired to hold sole rule. But his brothers Louis and Charles, seeking a division of the kingdom, fought one another in a tremendous battle one year later in the district of Auxerre, at a place called Fontenay. [Col. 1226A]

There the Franks, together with all the nations subject to them, struck one another down in mutual slaughter. At last Louis and Charles, having put Lothar to flight, gained the victory. After the bloodiest battle, peace was made between them, and they divided the Frankish empire among themselves.

Lothar received the kingdom of the Romans and all Italy, the whole eastern part of Francia, and all Provence. Louis, apart from Noricum, which he already possessed, held the kingdoms his father had given him, namely Alamannia, Thuringia, Austrasia, Saxony, and the kingdom of the Avars, that is, of the Huns. Charles received the western half of Francia, all Neustria, Brittany, and most of Burgundy, as well as Gothia, Vasconia, and Aquitaine, Pippin, the son of Pippin, having been removed from there and tonsured in the monastery of Saint Medard. [Col. 1226B]

This extremely dangerous discord occupied five years without respite.

### VII. On the Translation of Saint Audomarus from the Village of Ligesburch

During this period we find it recorded in the nineteen-year cycles of the years of the Lord’s Nativity that in the year 843, in the sixth indiction, the body of Saint Audomarus was brought from the village of Liegesburch to the place of Sithiu. [Col. 1226C]

The solemnity of that translation is devoutly celebrated by the people of Thérouanne in the month of June. But most of the common people are ignorant of the reason for which it was originally established. I therefore consider it fitting, and beneficial to the Church, to arrange in this book, however unpolished it may be, an account of the causes of that solemnity, especially since the angel admonishes Tobias, saying: “It is honorable to recount and confess the works of the Lord.”

There is indeed in this event an occasion to praise the majesty of the Lord, if it is related, and an occasion to magnify the reverence due to that saint. I shall therefore begin to speak—not of what I presume to invent myself, but of what I know was reported to me by the elders.

### VIII.

The aforesaid abbot Hugo, otherwise a man worthy of praise in every respect, after he had commendably stabilized this place by his own ordinance—by which he had justly subjected the canons of Saint Audomarus to the monks of Saint Bertinus, also by a capitular record, and had appointed a monk from the lower monastery to guard Saint Audomarus—was struck by a diabolical arrow and began to devise how he might carry the body of Saint Audomarus as quickly as possible to the monastery of Saint Quentin at Vermand, which he also governed. By the aid and help of Audomarus, together with his companion Bertinus, the people of Thérouanne are governed. [Col. 1226D–1227A]

Nevertheless, fearing the hostility of the common people, he gathered a multitude of men from Vermand and attempted to carry it away by force, in case the people should try to prevent him. He then approached and, taking the sacred body of Saint Audomarus, our bishop and patron, while a certain monk named Morus was serving as custodian, carried it with his gathered multitude as far as a village called Liegesburch.

By God’s providence, they remained for three days in the aforesaid village with the sacred body.

Meanwhile it happened that the illustrious bishop of the city of Thérouanne, Folquinus, was making his episcopal visitation of the parishes of his bishopric, so that, as a diligent shepherd, he might learn whether anything was being done contrary to the decrees of the holy canons. With this pious diligence he reached a cell called Worumhold. [Col. 1227B]

When they had arrived there for the meal, at which most sumptuous provisions were being prepared, as befitted so great a bishop, the brother of that blessed prelate rushed in, announcing a grave and irreparable disaster for the region if it were completed: Saint Audomarus had been removed from his monastery and, unless help came quickly, was to be carried as far as Saint Quentin at Vermand.

When the holy priest of the Lord heard this, he was deeply disturbed within and said: “Go to my brother, and more carefully gather the whole people of my bishopric, and on the third day be present within the walls of the city of Thérouanne with everyone. I shall also be present with those whom, with Christ’s help, I shall bring with me from these regions. Then, if the saint himself gives help, I shall be entirely prepared to dislodge him.” [Col. 1227C]

When these instructions had been properly carried out according to the blessed bishop’s word, an innumerable multitude, almost never before seen, was present in the city of Thérouanne on the third day.

Then the priest of the Lord, with this entire multitude, pursued the aforesaid abbot and his companions with all speed, as far as the village named above. But when they eagerly tried to lift up the holy body and take flight, they could not lift it from the ground at all, despite the whole multitude.

When they tried to lift it two or three times, adding an even larger number of people, it nevertheless remained immovable, as though fixed to the ground by certain roots.

Then, without any further useful delay, they hastened their flight, abandoning the saint’s body.

Blessed Folquinus allowed them to flee, took up the treasure more precious than all gold, and, retracing the road with the entire multitude of the people, carried it back to the place from which it had been taken. [Col. 1227D]

When they reached Thérouanne, at the river called the Leia, the entire multitude mentioned above crossed the river on foot without any hesitation. After they had passed through the stream, not even a drop of moisture appeared on their clothing.

As they proceeded through the grain-bearing crops of the fields—for such a numerous crowd could not avoid them—the ears bent down to the ground as though shorn by threshing instruments. Once the multitude had passed, they so filled out the furrows that one could plainly recognize that the fields too rejoiced at the arrival of their protector.

The clerics of both monasteries stood anxiously awaiting the outcome. But when they were granted sight, though from afar, of the approaching multitude, they pulled the bell ropes and all raised the voice of praise on high. [Col. 1228A]

The aforesaid custodian of the church, Morus, had then sat down to dine. Hearing the sound of the bells, he asked what was the reason for which the people were rejoicing with such great happiness.

Those recounting the event told him that Saint Audomarus had been brought back by Bishop Folquinus, and that all the people were rejoicing so greatly for this reason.

When he heard this, he became extremely disturbed and immediately invoked the anger of God upon those who had brought him back.

Before the unlawful words had fallen from his mouth, he suddenly fell face-first to the ground. His whole body became rigid, the tendons of his limbs stretched out, and he withered away, half alive. [Col. 1228B]

Thus utterly stupefied, he was carried to Saint Bertinus, where he repented through a long illness of what he had committed by word. For although he recovered his sight and hearing, he was deprived of understanding to such an extent that he could never discern in what direction the monastery of Saint Audomarus appeared to be situated.

Bishop Folquinus buried the body of blessed Audomarus in the earth, lest it be carried away again by those who came afterward in a similar manner.

After this, Abbot Hugo was sent by King Charles [his nephew] to Aquitaine on account of that king’s loyalty, and was killed through Pippin’s treachery on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of June, in the year 844 of the Lord’s incarnation [in the tenth year of his rule over this place]. [Col. 1228C]

This was the same Pippin whom I mentioned above as having been tonsured in the monastery of Saint Medard. Having escaped from there by flight, he returned to Aquitaine and hid there for many days while fleeing from place to place. Later he was deceived by a certain Ramnulfus through a false pledge of loyalty, was captured, and brought before King Charles. He was assigned to perpetual exile at Senlis.

### IX. On Abbot Adalard

After the aforementioned Abbot Hugo [the twelfth], Adalard became abbot in this monastery of Sithiu. He had been offered to Saint Peter and Saint Bertinus by his father Hunrocus, but afterward became a canon [under Fridegisus].

He received the abbacy in the aforesaid year, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of August.

In the third year of his rule, which was the year 816 of the incarnate Word, the body of Saint Bertinus was, as is reported, transferred and buried by Saint Folquinus the bishop on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of August. [Col. 1228D]

During that year [and in its course] there was an exceedingly severe winter. Then, after five years, an intolerable famine arose. At that time Guntbertus, mentioned above, while still in the order of the diaconate, was elevated to the dignity of provost.

In the year 853 of the Lord’s Nativity, the basilica of Saint Peter’s asylum (*asili*) was covered; in the following year the church of Saint Bertinus was roofed with lead. In that same year, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of January, Guntbertus was ordained to the priesthood.

### X. Adalard’s Lease to Odgrimus the Advocate

In the year 854 of the Lord, the fourteenth year of the rule of the aforementioned Charles, the thirty-ninth year of the episcopate of blessed Folquinus, and the eleventh year of the rule of the aforementioned Abbot Adalard, [Col. 1229A]

[Note: The charter itself, reported below, was issued on the Nones of September, in the fourteenth year of the reign of Lord Charles—that is, on 5 September 853. The other dates recorded here by Folquinus do not fit this document and were wrongly assigned.]

that same abbot granted by lease to a certain man named Odwinus the land which the same man had held as a benefice at Cafitmere, namely thirty bunaria, together with a small parcel which the same Odwinus had given to the monastery of Sithiu in the district of Boulogne, at a place called Mighem, namely three bunaria.

The arrangement was that every year, on the feast of Saint Bertinus, on the Nones of September, he should pay five solidi worth of wax, so that a lamp might always be supplied specifically for the altar before which the father of the aforesaid abbot, Hunrocus, is known to have been buried.

### XI. Copy

(5 September 853.) [Col. 1229B]

“Whoever rightly and properly grants the requests of the faithful in devotion to God’s churches should not doubt that by doing so he is obeying the will of God.

Therefore, to our beloved son in the Lord, Odwinus, I, Adalardus, in the name of God abbot of the monastery of Sithiu, with the consent of our brothers, grant this lease.

It is known to many that recently you assigned to us and to the aforesaid monastery your small parcel in the district of Boulogne, at a place called Mighem, namely three bunaria, worth four pounds, requesting that we confirm you, together with your wife and children, in your benefice at Cafitmere—namely thirty bunaria and twelve dependents, whose names are: Ostarbaldus, Gernhardus, Heribaldus, Radburg, Sigberta, Thiobertus, Strilleburg, Wifhen, Lolithan, Liotburga, Winetberta, and Adalberta—for the custody of Saint Peter and Saint Bertinus, and specifically for the altar before which the body of our father Hunrocus rests, on the condition that you annually render our alms and his in the form of a lamp payment. [Col. 1229C]

Accordingly, in keeping with your request, we grant both properties to you, to your wife, and to your sons, to possess under this condition: that on the feast of Saint Bertinus, on the Nones of September, you pay five and a half solidi worth of wax, both for the aforesaid properties and for your persons, that is, for two days of mundborda service, and that no other service be imposed upon you.

If anyone should do so, or should attempt to remove you from the aforesaid holy place, let him incur the anger of almighty God and of Saint Peter and Saint Bertinus, unless he abandons his impious attempt.

And let this lease, confirmed by our hand and those of our brothers, remain firm, strengthened by a stipulation.” [Col. 1229D]

“Enacted at the monastery of Sithiu, in the basilica of Saint Bertinus, on the Nones of September, on his feast, in the fourteenth year of the reign of Lord Charles, son of Emperor Louis.

I, Adalardus, abbot, have confirmed this with my own hand.

I, Guntbertus, sinner and provost, subscribed.

Sign of Amalbertus, dean. Sign of Bavo, monk and priest.

Guntbertus wrote and subscribed.” [Col. 1230A]

### XII. On the Successor Appointed for Blessed Folquinus

Since I remember having mentioned blessed Folquinus, I would like to insert here one further deed of his, which I recall having learned from Bishop Wicfridus’s account.

He said: “When that same blessed bishop Folquinus, worn out by advanced old age—for he was then approaching his fortieth year in the episcopate—could no longer celebrate the solemn Masses publicly, the king, having learned this while he was still alive, appointed another bishop as his successor, contrary to the canons.

When the holy prelate heard this, he prepared himself, according to episcopal custom, for the celebration of Mass and completed the entire mystery with great vigor while the usurping successor stood present. [Col. 1230B]

When the time came to give the blessing, as is the custom of bishops, he reversed the order and pronounced a curse upon them.

They were terrified and wished to return to their homes after mounting their horses. But in the middle of the road the usurping bishop fell from his horse, broke his neck, and breathed out his life. All who had come with him died within a year through various disasters, and thus, together with those associated with him, he paid the penalty for his wickedness.”

### XIII. On the Death of the Same Blessed Bishop

When the time of his calling arrived, that same blessed bishop, although weighed down by prolonged old age, resolved to visit the parishes of his bishopric. He believed this to be the proper completion of his virtues: if the sons of the Church had strayed somewhere from the bosom of their mother, he would correct them according to the decrees of the canons and bring them back to her by his exhortations. [Col. 1230C]

With this purpose and devotion he came in pious concern to the church situated in Mempiscus, called Hicclesbecke.

After staying there only a short time, when he was already considering returning, he suddenly began to be deprived of bodily strength and afflicted by physical illness.

Then, having summoned his disciples and commended them to the almighty Lord, he gave back his soul to heaven, to be joined to the company of the saints.

He passed away in the village written above, in the year 855 of the Lord’s incarnation, in the third indiction, on a Tuesday, toward evening. It was the fifteenth year of the aforesaid King Charles.

[Note: In December 855 the sixteenth year of Charles the Bald was already running.]

It was the fortieth year of his episcopate.

[Note: Emend, apparently, to thirty-ninth. For from the preceding passages (I, 55, and II, 4) it is established that he was elevated to the see of the Morini in 817.] [Col. 1230D]

This occurred on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of January.

The same bishop had requested that, wherever his death should occur, his body should be carried to the monastery of Sithiu and buried in the basilica of Saint Bertinus.

After he had died, when his clerics were wondering how they could carry him to the aforesaid place, during that very night, while a south wind was blowing, the whole immeasurable depth of water surrounding the island of Sithiu froze so completely that, when they carried the holy body to the funeral rites in the morning, the frozen water provided a very firm footing across it for those bearing the holy body. This is something which the cold of winter can scarcely accomplish in seven days. [Col. 1231A]

They carried the body of the blessed man to the monastery of Sithiu, where it was buried on the right side of Saint Bertinus.

### XIV. Another Chapter

It is reported that this man of God had a certain horse which, whenever he wished to set out on a journey, bent its knees in the service of the man of God, so that he might mount its back without any exertion.

They say that this horse went ahead of the brothers who were carrying his bier, but afterward refused to carry any human being and did not allow itself to serve the pleasures of anyone after bearing the body of so great a bishop.

Not long afterward it died. When its flesh was placed as food for dogs, none of them touched it.

And rightly the dogs could not tear apart its corpse, since hymnic songs had so often been sung to Christ over it.

When the citizens saw this, they buried it in human fashion, for neither beasts nor birds had dared to touch it. [Col. 1231B]

### XV. A Brief Account of the Monks’ Villages and Provisions

But since, in recounting the deeds of blessed Folquinus, we have digressed for a short time from the deeds of the abbots, I now wish to turn my pen back to recounting them.

Accordingly, Abbot Adalardus ordered the villages belonging to the use of the brothers, or whatever income appeared to arise from them under any kind of service, to be described in the following brief form, apart from what had been distributed among other monasteries or granted as benefices to soldiers and cavalrymen.

[Note: The Audomarus manuscript adds here: “This we now omit, since it is of little importance.”] [Col. 1231C]

### XVI. Kelmis

At Kelmis the monks have one church, twelve bunaria, six dependents, and four lamp-payments. Each person pays one denarius’ worth of wax.

There is a demesne mansus with a house and other appurtenances: thirty-nine bunaria of meadow, one hundred eighty bunaria of arable land, thirty bunaria of large woodland, and fifteen bunaria of small woodland.

There are fifteen mansi of twelve bunaria each, and one half-mansus of six bunaria, with ten male servants, who perform three days’ work each week; six female servants perform six ladmones. Each of the other free women performs half a ladmon.

Each person prepares ten modii of malt and six of flour; three chickens and twenty eggs. For the vineyards, each household supplies two cartloads every year.

There are sixteen lunarii and seven prebendaries. Ded has six bunaria and plows two bunaria.

### XVII. Fresingahem

At Fresingahem, Ererwinus has five bunaria; he plows three jurnales and pays six denarii. [Col. 1231D]

In the same village Heleca has half a bunarium and plows one jurnal.

### XVIII. Lomisgahem and Elciacum

At Lomisgahem, Beregen has nine bunaria and plows four bunaria.

At Elciacum, Amalger has fourteen bunaria and three dependents; he plows four bunaria and pays two solidi.

### XIX. Morningehem

At Morningehem, Guntbertus has eight bunaria and plows four bunaria.

Gerbald has three bunaria and plows one bunarium.

Stracfret has six bunaria and plows one and a half bunaria.

Thegen the elder has a demesne house with other appurtenances: five bunaria of meadow, twenty bunaria of arable land, and five bunaria of small woodland; twelve dependents.

Berharius the cavalryman has a mansus with twenty bunaria of arable land, five bunaria of meadow, and six bunaria of small woodland. There are two mansi of twelve bunaria each. He performs as above. There are eight dependents.

Benemar has a house with other appurtenances: ten bunaria of meadow, thirty bunaria of arable land, and twenty-three bunaria of pasture and small woodland. There are three mansi of twelve bunaria each. He performs as above. There are twenty-four dependents.

Ostoradus has a mansus with appurtenances: twelve bunaria of meadow, twenty bunaria of arable land, and six bunaria of small woodland. There are three mansi of twelve bunaria each. He performs as above. There are twenty-four dependents.

Bavo has a house with other appurtenances: eleven bunaria of meadow, thirty bunaria of arable land, and four bunaria of small woodland. One house consists of eight bunaria. He performs as above. There are sixteen dependents.

Wendelardus has a house with other appurtenances: eleven bunaria of meadow, thirty bunaria of arable land, and three bunaria of small woodland. There is one mansus of twelve bunaria. He performs as above. There are fourteen dependents. [Col. 1232A]

Megenfridus has a house with other appurtenances: eleven bunaria of meadow, forty-five bunaria of arable land, and sixteen bunaria of small woodland and pasture. There are two mansi of twelve bunaria each. He performs as above. There are four dependents.

Balduinus has a house with other appurtenances: six bunaria of meadow, twenty bunaria of arable land, and twenty bunaria of small woodland and pasture. There is one mansus of twelve bunaria. He performs as above. There are nine dependents. [Col. 1232B]

### XX. Bermingahem

At Bermingahem he has mansi, with a stable, consisting of twenty-three bunaria of arable land and three bunaria of small woodland.

At Edenenas there are ten bunaria of land and ten dependents.

All, except Irembertus, plow four bunaria for the village itself, gather two, and bring them to the monastery; they also enclose fifteen bundles of rods. At the monastery all likewise enclose four bundles of rods. Each person performs twenty-four days’ work in summer each year.

Irembertus plows two bunaria and gathers one.

There are eleven lamp-payments. Together they pay seven solidi and eight denarii.

There are twenty men who perform three days’ work each year. [Col. 1232C]

### XXI. Attona

At Attona there is a church to which seven men each pay two denarii’ worth of wax for the lamps.

There is a demesne house with other appurtenances: eleven bunaria of meadow, two hundred bunaria of arable land, one bunarium of small woodland, and fifty bunaria of uncultivated pasture.

There are twenty-four and a half mansi, all of twelve bunaria, while the half-mansus consists of six bunaria, with eleven male servants who perform three days’ work each week.

Twelve female servants perform twelve ladmones. The other free men perform two days each week, and thirteen of the free women provide six and a half ladmones.

For the vineyards, six cartloads. Each person prepares ten modii of malt and six of flour; three chickens and twenty eggs.

There are fifteen lunarii and six prebendaries.

Wilbertus has twelve bunaria; he pays two solidi and oversees the woodland.

There are seventy-four men who perform two days’ work each week.

Iremharius the elder has a demesne house with other appurtenances: ten bunaria of meadow, twenty-two bunaria of arable land, and fifteen bunaria of pasture and small woodland. There are two mansi of twelve bunaria each. He performs as above. There are twenty-three dependents.

Hillefridus has a mansus: six bunaria of meadow and one jurnal, thirty-five bunaria of arable land, and six bunaria of small woodland. There are eight dependents. [Col. 1232D]

Bavo has a mansus with a house and other appurtenances: five and a half bunaria of meadow, forty-six and a half bunaria of arable land, and eight bunaria of small woodland. There are fourteen dependents.

These people perform two days each week. If they do not ride out on horseback, they enclose five bundles of rods; at the monastery they enclose four bundles among them all.

Lodberta has at Selem, which belongs to Attona, one precaria, from which she pays one solidus. [Col. 1233A]

### XXII. Botniggahem

At Botniggahem, Bertrada has another holding from which she owes plowing.

### XXIII. Berningahem

At Berningahem there are, between woodland and arable land, more than forty bunaria.

### XXIV. Beingahem

At Beingahem the village has a church, a demesne mansus with appurtenances: fifteen bunaria of meadow, one hundred twenty bunaria of arable land, forty bunaria of large woodland for fattening twenty pigs, and one hundred bunaria of small woodland.

There are eighteen and a half mansi of twelve bunaria each, while the half-mansus consists of six bunaria, with eleven male servants who perform three days’ work each week; nine female servants perform nine ladmones.

The other free men perform two days each week, and ten of the free women provide five ladmones.

For the vineyards, four and a half cartloads. Each person prepares ten modii of malt and six of flour; three chickens and twenty eggs.

There are twenty-one lunarii, six prebendaries, and ninety lamp-payments. Together they pay one pound and five solidi.

Brunger has six bunaria and plows half a bunarium.

Megel has one and a half bunaria and plows half.

Megenger has two bunaria and plows half.

Bavo has four bunaria and pays eight denarii.

Gundebertus has three bunaria and plows two bunaria.

Omes the dean has three bunaria and plows two bunaria.

Lanfredh has thirty-one and a half bunaria of land and three bunaria of small woodland; thirteen dependents. He plows two bunaria and pays two solidi.

Engelger the elder has forty-three and a half bunaria of land and ten bunaria of small woodland; twenty dependents.

Another Engelger has a house with appurtenances: forty-two bunaria of arable land and ten bunaria of small woodland; seven dependents.

These men each plow four bunaria and enclose fifteen bundles of rods. [Col. 1233B]

Gundelbertus has forty bunaria; from them he pays six solidi. Each week he performs two days’ work, and he has three dependents.

There are three mills. From one come one hundred modii; from each of the other two, sixty modii. The first supplies twenty chickens and two hundred eggs; each of the others supplies fifteen chickens and one hundred eggs.

Badager formerly held one precaria from it, namely one mansus, consisting of forty-four bunaria of land and two dependents.

These men each plow four bunaria and enclose fifteen bundles of rods; in summer each performs sixteen days’ work, gathers one and a half bunaria, and brings them to the monastery. At the monastery they enclose three bundles of rods among them all. They give two chickens and ten eggs. [Col. 1233C–D]

### XXV. Coiacum

At Coiacum there is a church with eighteen bunaria and two dependents. For the lamps, three solidi.

There is a demesne house with other appurtenances: forty bunaria of meadow, one hundred sixty bunaria of arable land, and thirty-five bunaria of small woodland.

There are twenty-one mansi of ten bunaria each. Among them are fifteen male servants, who perform three days’ work each week. Seven female servants perform seven ladmones.

The other free men perform two days each week, and each of the free women performs half a ladmon.

For the host, half a cartload. For the vineyards, three cartloads.

Each person prepares ten modii of malt and six modii of flour; three chickens and ten eggs.

There are twenty-four lunarii and forty-two lamp-payments. Together they pay twelve solidi.

There are six prebendaries.

There is one sedilia, from which one solidus is paid.

Walager has two bunaria and plows fifty bunaria.

There is one mill, which pays thirty modii.

One camba, which pays four solidi.

Megenhardus has three and a half bunaria and pays one and a half solidi.

There are thirty-seven men who perform two days each year.

The elder has a house with appurtenances: twenty-two bunaria of land, seven bunaria of small woodland, and four dependents. [Col. 1234A]

### XXVI. Bumingahem

At Bumingahem there is a mansus with appurtenances: fifteen bunaria of land and ten bunaria of small woodland. [Col. 1234B]

There are two and a half mansi of twelve bunaria each, while the half-mansus consists of six bunaria.

Three male servants reside in them; each performs three days’ work each week, and they serve all those mansi completely.

For the vineyards, half a cartload.

They prepare ten modii of malt; two chickens and twenty eggs.

There are thirteen lunar payments and ten lamp-payments. Together they pay two solidi and two denarii.

There are four men who perform two days each year.

There are fourteen bunaria. From them come ten weights of cheese as an incense payment.
