Likewise, from seven bunaria come seven weights of cheese.

### XXVII. Pupurmisga

At Pupurmisga the village has a church with eighteen bunaria and one demesne mansus; one hundred fifty-eight bunaria of arable land, four hundred bunaria of mixed large woodland, brushland, and small woodland, for fattening six hundred pigs. [Col. 1234C]

There are forty-seven and a half mansi: ten of them consist of twenty-four bunaria each; another ten of twenty bunaria each; another ten of fifteen bunaria each; all the others of thirteen bunaria each; and the half-mansus of eight bunaria.

Four male servants reside in them and perform three days’ work each week. Four female servants make four shirts (*camsiles*).

The other free men perform two days each week, and each of the free women pays four denarii.

There are no lunarii, but one hundred seventy-four lamp-payments. From them come two pounds and eighteen solidi.

There are one hundred nine heirs of [uncertain reading: *haeres carii*]. Fourteen solidi and seven denarii come from them.

From the censal land, one hundred eighteen bunaria, cultivated and uncultivated, come twenty-one weights of cheese as an incense payment, and twenty-five geese.

For the host, two cartloads; for the vineyards, two cartloads.

The four female servants prepare ten modii of malt.

Each person supplies two chickens and ten eggs.

Every third year, one pig worth four denarii.

The elder has four dependents.

From ten bunaria come three sextarii of honey. [Col. 1234D]

Godobert the cavalryman has a demesne house with other appurtenances: eighty-six bunaria of land and four bunaria of small woodland; six dependents.

Mortbert the cavalryman has a demesne house with other appurtenances: twenty bunaria of land and twelve and a half bunaria of small woodland; ten dependents.

There are four mansi of twelve bunaria each. Free men reside in them who perform nothing else throughout the entire year except two days each week.

Each of them gives one chicken and five eggs.

Each of them plows one bunarium, gathers one, and performs cavalry service.

From twelve bunaria of censal land come two sextarii of honey.

One swineherd has three bunaria for clothing. [Col. 1235A]

Likewise, from three bunaria they pay twelve flasks and one hundred bowls.

Engeten has four bunaria, plows half a bunarium, and works one day each week.

Radeken has three bunaria, plows half a bunarium, and performs two days’ work each week.

Aldbert has four bunaria and does likewise.

Abbo has five bunaria and plows half.

### XXVIII. Pascandala

At Pascandala he has three parts of one church and three mansi of twenty bunaria each.

Only an incense payment of two boards.

XXIX. At Weserinia he has a demesne church, a mansus with its appurtenances; sixteen bunaria of meadow, 159 bunaria of arable land, eighteen bunaria of woodland for fattening twenty pigs, 51 bunaria of small woodland, and sufficient common pasture. There are eighteen mansi: ten of them comprise twelve bunaria each; five comprise ten bunaria each; three, eight bunaria each; with twelve male serfs and eight female serfs. They perform three days’ labor each week, and eight ladmones. The other free tenants perform two days’ labor each week, and from the ten free women come five ladmones. For the host-service, half a wagon; for the vineyards, one and a half wagons. Each person prepares ten modii of malt-grain and six of flour, and gives two chickens and twenty eggs. There are five prebendaries, 36 monthly tenants (*lunarii*), and sixty tenants owing light dues (*luminarii*). Together they pay one pound. There are 21 men who perform two days’ labor per year. He has ten tenant holdings (*sedilia*) there: they yield eight and a half solidi of silver as incense-payment.

Tunel has fourteen bunaria; he plows two bunaria and guards the woodland. There are three mills; each pays thirty large modii. In one year he fattens two pigs, in another one; and he owes twenty chickens and two hundred eggs. There is also one mill, which pays five solidi. Winetmar the mayor has three bunaria of meadow, 32 bunaria of arable land, and five bunaria of small woodland. Two mansi. He performs as those above. Seventeen monthly tenants. Hlodoger the horseman has a demesne mansus: seven bunaria of meadow, 43 bunaria of arable land, and eight bunaria of small woodland. Twenty-one monthly tenants. Gerwinus the horseman has a demesne house with its appurtenances, fifteen bunaria of land, and two dependents (*mancipia*).

XXX. At Aldomhem he has a demesne house with its appurtenances; fifteen bunaria of meadow, 98 bunaria of arable land, fifty bunaria of woodland for fattening thirty pigs, and 53 bunaria of small woodland. Fifteen mansi of twelve bunaria each, with seven male serfs. They perform three days’ labor each week. Two female serfs perform two ladmones. The other free tenants perform two days’ labor each week, and from the free women come five ladmones. For the host-service, half a wagon; for the vineyards, one and a half wagons. Each person prepares ten modii of malt-grain and six of flour, and owes four chickens and twenty eggs. There are six prebendaries, eighteen monthly tenants, and 24 tenants owing light dues. Together they pay eight and a half solidi. There are two mills: one yields thirty large modii, and the other twenty. In one year he fattens two pigs, in another one; twenty chickens and two hundred eggs.

Otbert has this mill; he also has fourteen bunaria and five dependents, and guards the woodland. The dean has four and a half bunaria for the prebend. There are eighteen men who perform two days’ labor per year.

Saluca the mayor has a demesne house with its appurtenances; thirty bunaria of arable land and three bunaria of small woodland; twelve dependents. Suithger the horseman has a demesne house with its appurtenances; seven bunaria of meadow, 46 bunaria of arable land, and ten bunaria of small woodland. Three mansi of twelve bunaria each, with two male serfs; and he performs three days’ labor each week. Three free women each perform half a ladmo. They perform service as in the estate itself. He also has seven monthly tenants; and he has half a church with eight bunaria and two dependents, and fifteen tenants owing light dues. Together they pay four solidi and eight denarii.

XXXI. At Scala he has a demesne house with its appurtenances; seven bunaria of meadow, 82 bunaria of arable land, and sufficient common pasture. Sixteen mansi, all of twelve bunaria each, with five male serfs, who perform two days’ labor each week; two female serfs, who perform two ladmones; and other free women, each of whom performs half a ladmo. Each person prepares ten modii of malt-grain and the same of flour; three chickens and ten eggs. There are six prebendaries. Adalandus has twenty bunaria and plows three bunaria. The mayor has 24 bunaria; one dependent.

XXXII. At Gisna he has a church with twelve bunaria; three dependents. He has there a demesne house with its appurtenances; eighty bunaria of meadow, 148 bunaria of arable land, thirty bunaria of woodland for fattening twenty pigs, forty bunaria of small woodland, sufficient common pasture, and sixteen mansi. Of these, seven comprise seven bunaria each; three comprise eleven bunaria each; and three comprise nine bunaria each. Nine male serfs reside in them and perform three days’ labor each week; three female serfs perform three ladmones; the other free tenants perform two days’ labor each week; and the other free women each perform half a ladmo. For the host-service, half a wagon; for the vineyards, two wagons. Each person prepares ten modii of malt-grain and six of flour; three chickens and twenty eggs. Eighteen monthly tenants and 93 tenants owing light dues: together they pay one pound, one solidus, and eight denarii. There are forty men who perform two days’ labor per year. From censual land, twelve monthly payments yield nine solidi.

Megentio has twelve bunaria; he is a barber and looks after the woodland. There are also four prebendaries. The dean has five bunaria for the prebend. Harduinus, a *ferbicarius* (shepherd), has eight bunaria for the prebend. Theodratus, the horseman, has eleven bunaria. Stitwinus has twelve bunaria; he plows two *binaria* and provides wagons to Wadnam [Note: This word seems to us to refer to the name of a certain place and should not be taken in its ordinary sense, as Ducange conjectured, where it was thought to mean “a pond”], and to the monastery. From the eleven bunaria and two dependents come six sextarii of honey. Also, from six bunaria come as many fish as can be obtained. From censual land in the colony, and from the *frecarii*, come sixty cheese-weights. The mayor has a demesne mansus: 45 bunaria of arable land, one *jornale* of small woodland, and five dependents.

Roolf has a demesne house and is a horseman. Thirteen bunaria; two dependents. Godobert the horseman has a demesne house. Twenty-one bunaria of land; four dependents; four bunaria of small woodland. Adda has forty bunaria; fifteen dependents; he performs one ladmo, plows two bunaria, and gathers the harvest.

XXXIII. At Terwana he has a demesne house with its appurtenances; 53 bunaria of arable land, six bunaria of woodland for four pigs, four bunaria of small woodland, and ten mansi of twelve bunaria each. All are held by free tenants. They perform two days’ labor each week; for the vineyards, one wagon. Each owes four denarii, two chickens, and twenty eggs; they prepare ten modii of malt-grain and six of flour; no ladmones; nothing for the host-service.

Ango has two bunaria and plows one *jornale*. Megenlano has three *jornales* and plows half a bunarium. Hildeburg has two bunaria. Litlot has three bunaria and plows two bunaria. There are eight monthly tenants, and 155 *luminarii* and *herescarii* (tenants owing light and herescar dues). They yield two pounds, fourteen solidi, and eight denarii. He has 33 tenant holdings; from them come fifteen and a half solidi and two pounds. The mayor has eight bunaria. Berenger has one and a half bunaria and plows half a bunarium. Frumger has one and a half bunaria and plows one *jornale*. He has one mill there, which pays one hundred modii, thirty chickens, and three hundred eggs; he fattens one pig.

XXXIV. At Thorbodessem he has a church with eight bunaria and one *jornale*; one dependent, held in demesne: fifteen bunaria of meadow, 147 bunaria of arable land, nine bunaria of small woodland, and sufficient common pasture. Eighteen mansi: one of them comprises twelve bunaria, ten comprise ten bunaria each, and seven comprise nine bunaria each. There are twelve male serfs among them, who perform three days’ labor each week. Nine female serfs perform nine ladmones. The other free tenants perform two days’ labor each week, and the seven free women each perform half a ladmo. For the host-service, four solidi; for the vineyards, three wagons. They prepare ten modii of malt-grain and the same of flour; two chickens and ten eggs. Six monthly tenants and fifteen tenants owing light dues: together they pay two solidi and eight denarii. One mill; from it twelve modii come as a census-payment. Nine bunaria of censual land. He plows four bunaria and gives one wether.

Regenger has one bunarium and one *jornale*; he plows one bunarium. Alavius has two bunaria and plows one bunarium. Hisegeger the mayor has eighteen bunaria and eight dependents; one mill, which pays eleven modii. There are 29 men who perform two days’ labor per year. Saxger has twenty bunaria and three dependents; he pays three solidi. Amalwaldus has six bunaria, three dependents, and performs horse-service. Alfunard the Saxon has nine bunaria.

XXXV. Within the monastery, in the various workshops, he has 95 prebendaries; from the gardens come twenty pounds, if provisions, clothing, and utensils are supplied to them. He has at Videngonam a mansus with its appurtenances; twenty bunaria of land. Each day one serves the brothers in the kitchen by preparing the seasoning of the food. He also has thirty bunaria between Mighem and Huolingaam. Each day one serves at the *pithrinum* and the brewery by bringing wood. He also has four mansi at Boningoham, of twelve bunaria each. They do nothing else throughout the year except repair the roofs of the monastery. There is woodland between Vampingaham and Hilsferod from which fifty pigs can be fattened. He also has at the gate one mansus of fourteen bunaria. Each day one serves at the gate. One mill for their use.

XXXVI. How the abbey was taken from Adalard and given to Hugo; and concerning the pagan incursion

After these events, in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 858 and the twentieth year of the aforementioned King Charles, the aforementioned Abbot Adalard, accused before that same king in the sixteenth year of his rule, had the abbey taken from him and given to the younger Hugo on the ninth day before the Kalends of April. He was a canon, the son of Conrad, and the uncle of the aforementioned King Charles. We know nothing of his deeds, since he governed the aforementioned monastery for only two years.

In the second year of his rule, when the savage plague of pagans was ravaging not only the surrounding borders but also remote kingdoms, consuming everything with sword and fire, greedy for money through treacherous friendship and famished for plunder, they rowed with all their strength across the open sea, vigorously cleaving the foaming waves, and at last reached the territory of the Menapians, at the inlet called the harbor of Isere. Leaping ashore there, and sparing no place from fires and devastation, they hastened eagerly toward the renowned place where the bodies of Christ’s confessors Audomarus and Bertinus rested, hoping to seize its treasures.

On the Saturday of Pentecost week, at the second hour, they reached the place toward which they had been heading; but, through the providence of the protecting God, they found none of the brothers there. Obeying the Lord’s command, which says, “If they persecute you in one city, flee to another,” they had withdrawn for a time, preserving themselves for better and more favorable circumstances, except for four men who, if it had pleased God, had chosen to die there rather than survive the desolation of their place. Their names were Vuoradus and Winetbaldus, priests, and Gerwaldus and Regenhardus, deacons.

Of these, Vuoradus, already old, was struck in the monastery itself with dreadful blows of fists, and, after three days of nakedness and exposure to wild seaweed, was beaten nearly to death. Winetbaldus was weakened by severe beatings and, after his nostrils had been stretched by liquid poured into them, was left half alive. Gerwaldus, although subjected to various and much more grievous torments and mocked with their derisive insults, was nevertheless preserved by the Lord and, though not restored to his former health, was at least granted life.

The fourth, and the younger one, named Regenardus, broken by various tortures, resisted with whatever strength he had when they departed and tried to take him with them. He preferred, in confessing the name of Christ, if this could in any way be extorted from his enemies, to commend his soul to God in martyrdom there, to have his body burned in his fathers’ cemeteries, and to have his name entered in the brothers’ diptychs, rather than be polluted by the most accursed filth of their mockery.

Nevertheless, bound as he was with dreadful chains, he was dragged to the village of his birth, three miles from the monastery of Sithiu, toward the north, called Munninio. Surrounded by a crowd, when he noticed at twilight that they were passing through that place, he suddenly threw himself to the ground. When the enemies driving him with opposing weapons forced him by cutting at him to rise, and he declared that he absolutely did not wish to do so but preferred to die there for Christ, he was pierced by repeated thrusts of spears and, breathing out his soul amid the shedding of blood, offered it to Christ.

XXXVII. The restoration of the monastery and the unharmed fall of a carpenter

After the aforesaid danger had been overcome, the brothers of that monastery assembled and jointly resolved to repair completely the roofs of the churches and of the other workshops. Just as this work had been begun with the utmost devotion, so, with God’s help, it was completed more quickly than expected and with great beauty. The church of Saint Bertin was swiftly roofed with lead by marvelous workmanship, and they also undertook to build its tower, remarkable in size and extraordinary in construction.

Its length, standing on the ground, equaled the height of the roof of the church upon which it was to be placed—and no wonder: its *tristega*—that is, its three-chambered structure—had been made in three tiers, apart from the upper *elaxendix*. Thus, when the triumphant sign of the holy cross was being raised above the church’s superstructure, one of the craftsmen, named Bertus, standing above, seized a hammer and, as though rejoicing at the almost completed conclusion of so remarkable a work, carelessly struck a blow too far away, as if boastfully. But, alas, when the wheel rebounded and shook, he staggered, his feet slipped, and from such a height he fell headlong to the ground.

Yet, astonishing to relate and still more astonishing to witness, he suffered no injury. Indeed, when those who came to him offered him water for refreshment, he gave them a response both laughable and pleasing, saying that he would always prefer to quench his thirst with wine rather than water and that he had no need then of the offered liquid. The craftsmen, for this reason, not merely encouraged but strengthened, completed the work they had begun, steadfast and joyful. There was no doubt that he had been borne aloft by the wings of the intercessions of the blessed father Bertin, whom he served.

XXXVIII. The death of Abbot Adalard

After these events had been completed, in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 861, the abbey was taken from the aforementioned Hugo and again returned to Adalard on the eighth day before the Kalends of August, in the twenty-first year of the reign of the aforementioned King Charles [Note: Perhaps more correctly the twenty-second]. But he governed it for only three years thereafter.

In the fourth year, while he was ill at the monastery of Saint-Amand, he departed this life on the third day before the Nones of February, which was the year of the Lord’s Nativity 864. He was buried in that same monastery in the crypt, on the left as one enters.

Among the other gifts that he granted to this holy place of Sithiu, he gave a certain chasuble of purple color, magnificently adorned with gold and pearls [Note: After *insignitam*, the following is read in the Codex Aud.: “It was preserved until the time of Lord Antoninus of Bergues, abbot of this place, so that afterward mention might be made of it more clearly, Christ willing, under whom the writer of this page, Alardus the sinner, in the course of the present year, 1509 from the incarnation of the Savior, assumed the monastic habit and profession, serving him as chaplain.”].

His father Hunrocus—something omitted from the earlier account—laid aside the hair of his head at the monastery of Sithiu and assumed the monastic habit, submitting himself to the yoke of Christ. Since he was a very wealthy count, he gave the greater part of his inheritance to the aforementioned monastery. Among these possessions was a villa called Hunela, which he transferred on the condition that the custodian of the church to whom he entrusted it should, every year after his death, prepare from it a service for the brothers on the anniversary of his death.

He later died there and was buried before the altar of Saint Lawrence, on the left side as one enters, on the Ides of November. On that same day, when the feast of the translation of Saint Folquin and the deposition of Saint Briccius is also celebrated, a very sumptuous meal, as far as the custodian is able, has until now been provided for the brothers. At the same time, Zoppo, the vicar, was tonsured in the same monastery in a similar manner and received the monastic habit.

XXXIX. Concerning Bishop and Abbot Humfridus

After the death of the aforementioned Abbot Adalard, in that same year [Note: The year 864], Humfridus, bishop of Tarwan and a monk of the monastery of Prüm, by the unanimous choice of the clergy and people, undertook the governance of the abbey on the Ides of March, solely out of love and fear of God.

This Humfridus was the man who had succeeded the blessed Folquin in the episcopate, a man filled with every goodness and holiness. He governed this abbey for only two years. Under him, a certain Megenfridus, offered by his father Ruodwaldus, became a monk; and with him he gave a small portion of his property in the county of Boulogne, at a place called Diorwaldingatun, namely twelve bunaria, so that his aforementioned son might have there the provisions and clothing due to a monk.

XL. The transfer of Rodwaldus of Diorwaldingatum

(864 or 865.) “In Christ, to the lord and venerable father Humfridus, bishop and abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter, called Sithiu, and of the holy confessors Audomarus and Bertinus. I, Roudwaldus, transferor, in the name of God, by this deed of transfer, transfer to the aforementioned monastery of Saint Peter a small portion of my property in the county of Boulogne, at a place called Diorwaldingatum, beside the little river … [Note: The place for the name is blank], twelve bunaria and four dependents, on the condition that my son Megenfridus, for as long as he lives, may fully receive in that monastery the monastic provisions and clothing due to him.

“My request is that, for as long as I live, I may hold that land as a censual usufruct, paying on the Kalends of November two solidi of silver to the monks of the aforementioned monastery; and that after my death they may receive the same land for their own use, without any opposition.

“But if anyone—which I do not believe will happen—whether I myself (God forbid), or any of my heirs or successors, or any outsider, should bring a claim against this transfer, let him be fined, under the compulsion of the fisc, a payment of thirty pounds; let him not prevail in what he claims, and let this transfer remain firm for all time, supported by formal stipulation.

“Enacted at the monastery of Sithiu, in the church of the blessed apostle Peter, in the twenty-sixth year of the reign of Lord King Charles.

“Sign of Roudwaldus, who made and confirmed this transfer.

“Sign of Trudbertus. Sign of Hucbertus, advocate. Sign of Adalgisus. Sign of Guntardus. Sign of Hildmarus. Sign of Regemarus. Sign of Folradus. Sign of Folmarus. Sign of Vuillebaldis.

“I, Holdbertus, deacon and monk, wrote and subscribed.”

XLI. Concerning Abbot Hilduinus

(866.) After these events, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 866, King Charles took the abbey from Humfridus in disgrace and gave it to Hilduinus, a canon who had recently come over to him from Lothair’s lordship, in exchange for thirty pounds of gold, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July.

As I believe, given by the Lord to this place, which had almost fallen into ruin, Hilduinus—apart from Lord Bertin, the first founder of this place—so nullified the deeds of all his predecessors by the compensation of his own achievements that his name deservedly remains among us in blessing, without any forgetfulness, forever. Unless I am mistaken, the charters made in his time and acquired through his labor also testify to this; they must now be inserted here.

XLII. The transfer of Heribertus of Campania and Quertliacum

In the second year of his administration, on the third day before the Kalends of September [Note: The charter itself, which follows, reads “the fourth day before the Kalends of December”], a certain man named Heribertus and his wife Megesinda, together with their sons Ellembertus and Egilbertus, transferred to the aforementioned Lord Hilduinus, for the use of his monastery of Sithiu, their property at a place called Campania in the county of Tarwan, and at another place called Quertliacum, or Broma, or Minthiacum. They requested in precarious tenure certain property of the aforementioned abbot’s monastery at a place called Uphem in the county of Boulogne, and at Vuilera in the same county, on the condition that they should hold both the transferred and the precarious properties, for as long as they lived, under the census written below.

XLIII. A copy of the same

[Col. 1241D]

(28 November 867.) “To the venerable father in the Lord, Hilduinus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter, called Sithiu, where the bodies of the confessors of Christ the Lord, Audomarus and Bertinus, rest: we, Heribertus and my wife Megesinda, and also our sons Ellembertus and Egilbertus, all transferors and grantors in precarious tenure, in the name of God.

“We therefore transfer to the aforesaid monastery of Saint Peter, lawfully possessed, the property belonging to us in the county of Tarwan, at a place called Campania: a mansus with a house and other appurtenances and orchards, and, between that mansus and other arable land and meadow, 32 and a half bunaria; and seven and a half bunaria of beech woodland. Also, at another place called Quertliacum, or Broma, or Minthiacum, twenty bunaria in the county of Boulogne, beside the river Elna; and nineteen dependents, by these names: Thiodo, Hathalec, Regenfeth, Waldburg, Edeborg, Guodlia, Sigeberth, Rudborg, Hirmelind, Irmengard, Hildegard, Engelgard, Liodgard, Tanewara, Vodolberta, Betto, Thiodfred, Ruotholf [Note: Only eighteen dependents are named].

“All these things we lawfully transfer and reconfirm to the aforesaid monastery, to possess perpetually. Therefore we request from you, as precarious tenure, property belonging to your church: at a place called Uphem in the county of Boulogne, beside the river Helicbruma, a mansus with a house and other appurtenances, and, between that mansus and arable land and meadow, 102 bunaria; and at another place called Wileria in the same county, beside the aforementioned stream, eighteen bunaria, together with the lawful access-ways and watercourses of those places; and 38 dependents, by these names: Asbertus, Hildewara, Grimbertus, Egelwara, Ostoibertus, Radlia, Geldwara, Liodrada, Ereprad, Stillewara, Harduinus, Hildborg, Immo, Thegenrad, Megelind, Alfrec, Folclind, Adalind, also Megelind, Regenlind, Metendrodh, Eumbertus, Hincmar, Rotsind, Megenguara, Thiodsind, Irmelind, Lodwinus, Ehgelhild, Irmenhild, Erkenbrog, Megensind, Markwara, Frunger, Idwinus, Folcwara, Trasborg, Regenlind.

“To us—both to me and to my wife Megensinda, and to our aforementioned sons, and, if God should still give children to the two of us together—you shall grant both the aforesaid properties, those which we have given as well as those which we request, to all of us named above, for as long as we live, as precarious tenure, for use and improvement.

“The condition is that every year, on the feast of Saint Bertin, which is on the Nones of September, we shall pay three solidi as a census to the monks serving God in that monastery; and after the death of the two of us, our sons shall pay five solidi on the same feast. They shall presume to damage these properties in no way; but after the death of all of us, the monks of the aforesaid monastery shall receive both the properties we transfer and those we have received, with every improvement.

“But if anyone—which I do not believe will happen—whether we ourselves or any outsider, should attempt to break this transfer, let him be compelled to pay to the aforementioned brothers twenty ounces of gold and thirty weights of silver; let him not prevail in any claim he renews, and let this transfer remain firm, supported by formal stipulation.

“Enacted at the monastery of Saint Peter, called Sithiu, on the fourth day before the Kalends of December, in the twenty-eighth year of King Charles, son of Louis.

“Sign of Heribertus, Megesinda, Ellembertus, and Egelbertus, who made this transfer with the precarious grant.

“Sign of Vulframnus. Sign of Eigelramnus. Sign of Fridebertus. Sign of Rodfridus. Sign of Hucbertus, advocate. Sign of Ricuardus. Sign of Foldbertus. Sign of Baro, dean.

“I, Grimbaldus, deacon and monk, wrote and subscribed.”

XLIV. The transfer of Liodricus of Mekerias and Heingasele

On that same day, a certain man named Liodricus transferred to the aforementioned Abbot Hilduinus property belonging to him at a place called Mekerias and at another place called Heingasele. He requested these same properties as precarious tenure, together with other land of the monastery of Sithiu called Vualdringahem, in the following manner.

XLV. A copy

(28 November 867.) “To the venerable Lord Hilduinus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter and of the holy confessors of Christ, Audomarus and Bertinus, called Sithiu: I, Liodricus, in the name of God, transferor and grantor in precarious tenure.

“I therefore give, and desire that it be given perpetually and lawfully, by staff and hand-clasp, my property at a place called Mekerias, in the county of Terwan, within Mempiscus: a mansus with a house and, between that mansus and arable land, one bunarium and one *jornale*. At another place called Heingasele, in the aforesaid county, five bunaria of land beside the river Isere, together with the lawful access-ways and watercourses of those places.

“And therefore I have requested from you property belonging to your church, namely, at a place called Vualdringahem in the county of Tarwan, beside the river Dilgia, a mansus with a house and, between that mansus and arable land or meadow, twelve and a half bunaria, together with the lawful access-ways and watercourses. This property, for me and my wife Aldgudana, and for our children Liudricus, Grimbertus, Rocbodonus, Odgudana, Hiltruda, and Bertruda [Note: Supply *ut*], we shall hold for as long as we live, to cultivate, use, and improve.

“And every year, on the feast of Saint Bertin, which is on the Nones of September, my wife and I shall, in return for your benefaction, pay six denarii to the aforementioned monastery, to the monks serving God there. After us, our sons shall pay one solidus. We shall have no power either to give away or sell the properties, whether those we have given or those we have requested, or to damage them in any way. But after the death of all of us, both properties shall be received by the monks to be possessed perpetually, together with every improvement.

“Therefore let this transfer, together with the precarious grant, remain perpetually firm, supported by formal stipulation.

“Enacted at the monastery of Sithiu, in the church of Saint Peter, on the third day before the Kalends of December, in the twenty-eighth year of the glorious King Charles.

“Sign of Liodricus, who made this transfer.

“Sign of Suitgerus. Sign of Ermarus. Sign of Liodbertus.

“Megenharius, monk and priest, wrote and subscribed.”

XLVI. The death of Bishop Humfridus and the multitude of locusts

(870.) In the thirtieth year of the glorious King Charles, which was the year of the Lord’s incarnation 869, the glorious bishop of the city of Tarwan, Humfridus, departed to the Lord on the eighth day before the Ides of March, in the fifteenth year of his episcopate. Accardus succeeded him in the episcopal see and was ordained on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of October.

In the following year a great drought occurred in the month of June and lasted until the middle of August; afterward an innumerable multitude of locusts came, consuming the green grass and the grain. The Northmen also reached Angers in that same year and punished many people; but, when besieged by the Franks, they surrendered after giving hostages.

XLVII. The exchange of Lord Abbot Hilduinus and Rodfridus

(875.) After these events, in the thirty-fifth year of the aforementioned King Charles, the aforesaid Abbot Hilduinus and a certain man named Hrodfridus agreed to exchange their properties with one another; and they did so in the following manner.

XLVIII. (16 March 875.)

“In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. It pleased and was agreed between the venerable man Hilduinus, abbot of the monastery of Sithiu of Saint Peter, where the bodies of Saints Audomarus and Bertinus rest, and the whole congregation of that monastery, and a certain man named Hrotfridus, that they should conveniently exchange certain properties with one another; and they did so.

“The aforesaid venerable abbot therefore gave, on behalf of his monastery, to the aforementioned Hrotfridus, at a place called Stratsele beside the river Wiopa, in the county of Tarwan within Mempiscus, a curtilage with its appurtenances; and, between that curtilage and meadow and arable land, forty bunaria; and ten bunaria of woodland, together with the common rights, lawful access-ways, and watercourses of those places.

“In return, as compensation for these properties, the aforementioned Hrotfridus gave from his own property to the aforesaid venerable abbot, at a place called Crumbeke in the county of Tarwan within Mempiscus, beside the river Fleterna, two curtilages with their appurtenances; and, between those curtilages and meadow and arable land, 48 bunaria; and seven bunaria of woodland and one and a half *jornales*, together with the common rights, lawful access-ways, and watercourses of those places.

“So that this exchange might remain firm, they decreed that two documents written in the same form should be made, so that they might firmly retain what they had legally and suitably transferred to one another; and after the death of the aforesaid Hrotfridus and his sons, both properties should return to the aforementioned monastery.

“They added this also to its security: if they themselves, or their successors, or any outsider, should presume to oppose this exchange and precarious grant, whoever brings a lawsuit against his counterpart shall be compelled to pay ten ounces of gold, and his claim shall be null.

“Let this charter remain firm, supported by formal stipulation.

“Enacted publicly at the monastery of Sithiu, in the month of March, on the sixteenth day, in the thirty-fifth year of King Charles.

“Sign of Hrotfridus, who made and confirmed this exchange with the precarious grant.

“Sign of Theidstornus. Sign of Berengarius. Sign of Enoch. Sign of Vulfradus. Sign of Adolbaldus. Sign of Albuinus. Sign of Vuilharius. Sign of Odbertus, advocate. Sign of Godobertus.

“I, Megenharius, priest and monk, wrote and subscribed.”

XLIX. Famine and pestilence among human beings

(874.) In that year, 874, there was a great famine and a deadly mortality among human beings through a very severe pestilence. Wine, however, was abundant. In the following year, a very large ball of fire fell from the sky at dawn; likewise, a comet appeared on the sixth day before the Ides of June.

XLIX*. The transfer of Rodwaldus of Flitmum

Meanwhile, while the aforementioned venerable Abbot Hilduinus was residing in the monastery of Sithiu, in the church of Saint Bertin, in the third year, with the glorious King Charles reigning in his twenty-eighth year [Note: The fourth year of Abbot Hilduinus, which falls in A.D. 869 or 870, agrees poorly with the twenty-eighth year of King Charles, which is A.D. 867 or 868], a certain distinguished man named Rodwaldus, brother of Megenfridus, whom I mentioned above under Abbot Humfridus, began to consider dividing his inheritance among his children; and he did so.

Among the others, he gave to Saints Bertin and, on behalf of his son Megenfridus, whom he had previously made a monk there, at Flitmum, one mansus with one male servant, his wife, and his children, in the presence of many witnesses.

Grimbaldus, deacon and monk, wrote and subscribed.

L. The privilege of King Charles concerning the security of the monastery of Sithiu and the toll, in the time of Abbot Hilduinus

(874.) In the thirty-fourth year of the reign of the glorious King Charles, which was the year of the Lord’s Nativity 873, while that same king was residing at the monastery of Saint-Quentin, the aforementioned Abbot Hilduinus approached the aforementioned king and requested that, just as he himself or his royal predecessors had previously granted security to the monastery of Sithiu through royal privileges, so he too would renew it in his own time.

The king assented to his request and carefully fulfilled it, adding also what he had granted to no one else: namely, the market toll, as the same privilege, bearing the impression of the royal ring, testifies in the following manner.

### LI. (12 February 874)

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Charles, by the grace of God king. If, with the generosity of our customary benevolence, we grant that the petitions of our faithful, who devoutly serve us, attain their desired result, we undoubtedly exercise the royal and ancestral custom of our forefathers. Therefore let the diligence of all the faithful of holy God’s Church and of our own, both present and future, know that the venerable Abbot Hilduin, our most faithful servant and our ministerial notary—namely, abbot of the monastery of Sithiu, situated in the district of Thérouanne and built in honor of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, where the bodies of the holy confessors Audomar and Bertin are known to lie buried—has made known to our majesty how, some time ago, in the time of his predecessor, the venerable Abbot Hugh, our uncle, we had issued our charter for that same monastery, placing it, with everything belonging to it, under our protection, mundeburdium, and the guardianship of immunity. We had likewise decreed that none of its cells, estates, or other possessions situated in any districts or territories within the jurisdiction of our kingdom should be divided by us or by our predecessors, or converted to other uses, and that the household of the same monastery should provide fodder to no one. He has requested that we order this same charter of ours to be renewed in his own name.

“Accordingly, for love of God and reverence for those same saints, we have judged that our charter concerning the same place should be renewed, and by this present charter we confirm what had been decreed there. Therefore we have ordered these royal letters to be made, by which we admonish our successors that, just as we have granted the aforesaid monastery this privilege, so they should permit it to remain valid and secure: they must neither make nor permit anyone to make any division of the monastery or of its other possessions, nor divert them to other uses.

“By these royal letters we also sanction and decree that no public judge or anyone exercising judicial authority may ever dare to enter the churches, places, fields, or other possessions of the aforesaid monastery which it now lawfully and legally possesses, or which divine piety may henceforth wish to increase in the right and dominion of that holy place, in order to hear cases according to judicial custom, exact fines or banns, demand lodgings or provisions, exact fodder, take sureties, distrain the men of the monastery, whether free or enslaved, or seek any restitutions or unlawful pretexts; nor may he presume in any way to exact the things mentioned above. Rather, let the aforesaid abbot and his successors be permitted to possess the property of the aforesaid monastery in peace under the protection of our immunity, together with all fines or banns granted to it, as is contained in the charter which we granted to our uncle Hugh.

“We have also granted the aforesaid holy place a market for all time, on Friday, so that whatever can be acquired from that market, whether through its toll or its bann, may go toward the lights of those saints, Audomar [Col. 1246D] and Bertin; and once a year the churchwarden shall provide the brothers of that holy place with a meal from its proceeds. Thus may it please those servants of God who serve him there continually to implore the Lord’s mercy for us, for the queen and our offspring, and for the stability of our entire kingdom, granted and preserved for us by God.

“And so that this charter may remain unshaken in our own and future times, with the Lord’s protection, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be authenticated by the impression of our ring.

“Sign of Charles, the most glorious king.

“Gammo, notary, acting in the place of Goizen, examined and subscribed.

“Given on 12 February, in the sixth indiction [Note: Perhaps read ‘the seventh indiction,’ which agrees with the year 874], in the thirty-fourth year of our reign and the fourth year of the succession of King Lothair.

“Done at Saint-Quentin.”

### LII. The anointing of Emperor Charles

(875.) After this, Charles, king of Western Francia, came to Rome in the year 877 of the incarnate Word, with many gifts; on the very day of the Nativity of the Lord he was elected emperor and consecrated by Pope John, and undertook the government of Italy. After he had returned to Francia, his brother Louis, king of Eastern Francia, died. Then Emperor Charles proceeded to the palace at Aachen and reached the Rhine with his army. But his nephew Louis, having gathered the Eastern Franks and Saxons, came to meet his uncle and reached the Rhine with his army. After crossing it, he engaged in battle at the villa of Andernach; the Easterners were victorious, and the Westerners were put to flight. This took place on 6 April.

### LIII. The charter of Emperor Charles concerning Turringahem

After these events, at the request of the aforesaid venerable Abbot Hilduin, that same King Charles granted to the monastery of Sithiu, for the monks’ use, at the villa of Turringahem, a demesne mansus with the appurtenances named in the royal charter. The aforesaid emperor ordered this charter to be made for the same reason, containing the following terms.

### LIV. Copy

(27 June 877.) “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Charles, by the mercy of that same almighty God, Augustus emperor.

“If we provide the benefit of imperial majesty to places dedicated to divine worship, we confidently believe that this will help us both to pass through the present life more easily and to attain the future life more happily. Let the diligence, therefore, of all the faithful of holy God’s Church and of our own, both present and future, know that, at the petition of the venerable Abbot Hilduin, we grant to Saint Bertin and to the brothers serving the Lord there, for their use, in the district of Thérouanne, at the villa of Turringahem, a demesne mansus, together with fifty-four bunaria between woodland and arable land, thirteen dependants, and four servile mansi amounting to eight bunaria; at Monolvingahem, thirty bunaria belonging to the aforesaid mansus; at Belrimo, fifteen bunaria; at Menteka, eight bunaria; and at Vertuno, thirty bunaria.

“Therefore we have ordered this precept of our high authority to be made and given to the aforesaid brothers of Saint Bertin. By it we command and order that, from this day forward, they take the aforesaid property for their own use and have the power to administer and dispose of it eternally, just as they have hitherto possessed other property for their own use; so that they may more freely implore God for our safety, that of our wife and offspring, and for the stability of the whole empire entrusted to us by God, and so that, for the remission of the aforesaid Abbot Hilduin, they may strive to pray to the Lord without ceasing.

“And so that this may be preserved inviolate for all time, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be marked with our ring.

“Sign of Charles, the most glorious Augustus emperor.

“Audacher, notary, acting in the place of Gauzlin, examined and subscribed.

“Given on 27 June, in the tenth indiction, in the thirty-eighth year of the reign of Lord Emperor Charles in Francia and the second year of his empire.

“Done at the palace of Ponthion.”

### LV. The death of Abbot Hilduin, and his funeral and burial

[Col. 1248B]

Having related the transfers acquired under the most beloved Abbot Hilduin, it is now time to recount what end he had in this present life. Before I begin to set down my pen, I shrink from touching it with a trembling hand, for after him no cleric comparable in any goodness succeeded him; indeed, at the very end of his life he showed what love he had consecrated to the aforesaid place.

Finally, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 877, which was, according to the text, the thirty-seventh year of the aforesaid King Charles [Note: It seems that the text should read ‘the twenty-eighth’], and the second of his empire, that same glorious Abbot Hilduin departed from this world in the royal palace at Quierzy, in the twelfth year of his rule [Note: Perhaps ‘the eleventh’ should be read: Hilduin had in fact assumed the governance of the monastery of Sithiu on 19 June 866. [Col. 1248D] See above, chapter 41], on 7 June.

His body, as he himself had requested while still alive, was transferred to Saint Bertin. On arriving at Arras, it spent one night at the monastery of Saint Vedast, where a very precious pallium was given there for him. At last, when Sithiu was reached, the funeral was celebrated amid deeply mournful wails, and he was buried in the church of Saint Bertin opposite the chief altar of Saint Martin.

Among other gifts, he granted this sacred place a very precious pallium, a white-colored cope interwoven with red figures of birds, and a curtain of exceptionally rare and valuable pallium-cloth.

The glorious Emperor Charles, remembering the faithfulness and service of that abbot, granted the holy place a charter in which, as Hilduin had requested while alive, he arranged by royal authority for the government of the monastery after his death, in the following manner.

### LVI. The charter of Emperor Charles concerning the arrangement of this place

[Note: Published in *Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. III, documents, col. 110, and in *Scriptores rerum Francicarum*, vol. VIII, p. 664.]

(20 June 877.) “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Charles, by the mercy of that same almighty God, Augustus emperor. [Note: ‘If’ appears to be omitted.]

“We provide due care and defense for ancient places and for those serving God in them for the stability of the whole holy Church; we do not doubt that this will benefit us in passing happily through the present life and, with God’s help, the future one in every way. Let all the faithful of holy God’s Church and of our own, present and future, know that the venerable man Hilduin, abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter called Sithiu, where the blessed bodies of Christ’s confessors Audomar and Bertin enjoy peaceful rest, repeatedly represented to our majesty that the same holy place was in great danger because of the excessive diminution of its property. He recalled that the venerable Abbot Hugh had formerly wished and begun, with the greatest devotion, to arrange an appropriate government for that holy place, but, overtaken by death, had not completed it; while he himself, heir to his predecessor’s goodwill, humbly and devoutly begged that it should be completed.

“Therefore, recalling the supplicating devotion, sincere faith, and manifold service toward us of our dear Hilduin, recently deceased, and granting his petition concerning the matters mentioned, we decree by imperial authority that those serving God in the monastery of Saint Peter, where blessed Bertin rests, shall henceforth hold the following properties for the status of this holy place, without anyone’s molestation or diminution:

“For the monastery’s demesne mansus: the cow-pastures, with the adjacent woods, at Widingaham, Wolingaham, Vumpingaham with Limchold, Hilsferod with Lardbruca and Grevia, Hirnethold, Dakingahem, and Gruononberg, together with the other appurtenances and territories of the five carpenters lying there; and these villas: Vuesarinium, Tarnenna, Coiacus, Hiskinium, Aldomhem, Gisna, Scala, Thorbodashem, Pupurningahem, and, in the Marsh, Buoningahem; Recca, with its seats, its furnaces, and the land beside Merkisa; and Loom at Sentinas.

“At the villa of Calmontes, except for the properties that had been granted as benefices, half the mansi and dependants, two-thirds of the vineyards, and a demesne mansus with ten bunaria.

“These villas are assigned to the monastery’s one hundred and twelve servants: Kelmis, Atquinium, Beingahem with its territory, Bummingahem, Sinningahem, and Okkaningahem; and at the old monastery, the fishery, as before.

“To these properties we add, for the brothers’ food, the villa called Liegesborth, with all its full extent as it formerly was, except for three horse-breeding establishments.

“For the brothers’ treasury and wardrobe we add Krokashem with Westkerca and its appurtenances; and at Gelwaldastorp, a church, vineyards, and twelve mansi with their inhabitants; likewise at Kasello, beyond the Rhine, twelve mansi; at Frekena, ten mansi with the mother church and the tithe established there, together with its inhabitants; at the port of Daventre, seven mansi; and at the gate, before the church doors, a cow-pasture with a small garden; and at Loconesse, seven mansi with their appurtenances and dependants.

“We confirm also the territory and vineyards which the aforesaid Abbot Hilduin, from his own property, in the district of Vermandois, at the place called Hebbencurt, transferred to the same monastery for the salvation of his soul, for the lights of that church where he lies buried.

“We decree also that whatever, from the time of our exalted father, has been confirmed for the same holy place by the charters of transfer granted by the devout for the celebration of their commemoration shall remain established according to their grants and ecclesiastical sanction, as shall whatever the clemency of the Lord Savior may subsequently add in the same manner.

“We also establish that in the same monastery the number of fifty monks, according to the constitution of our lord father, shall perpetually be maintained; and that the provost and the other officers shall in no case be appointed except from among those brothers, through their election and the abbot’s consent.

“Let them therefore hold all the prescribed properties, strengthened by imperial authority, so that it may please these servants of God to implore the Lord’s mercy more abundantly for us, for our wife and offspring, and for the condition of our empire.

“And so that this charter may be preserved inviolate for all time, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be marked with the impression of our ring.

“Sign of Charles, the most glorious Augustus emperor.

“Audather, notary, acting in the place of Goslen, examined and subscribed.

“Given on 20 June, in the thirty-seventh year [Note: Here, it seems, Charles the Bald’s reign should be reckoned from the year 840], while Lord Charles was reigning, and in the second year of his empire.

“Done in the imperial palace at Compiègne, on the fourteenth day after the death of the aforesaid abbot.”

### LVII. The death of Emperor Charles

(877.) After this, in the same year, Emperor Charles, wishing to hasten to Rome, set out from Francia after mid-July. On arriving in Italy, he met Pope John at Pavia. Carloman, Charles’s nephew, came with many thousands of warriors from Bavaria and the other eastern German peoples, opposing him concerning the kingdom of Italy.

Since King Charles had no means of resisting the pope, he entrusted gifts to Saint Peter and turned back. He fell ill and died within the Alps on 5 October. His soldiers carried his body, embalmed with spices, for fifteen days; but, being distressed by the stench caused by the heat, they placed it in a wine cask for another fifteen days. At last, overcome by the excessive stench—for they had wished to transfer him to Saint-Denis—they buried him in the Burgundian monastery of Nantua, which is called Saint Marcellus.

His son Louis was established as king at the palace of Compiègne.

### LVIII. Concerning Abbot Folco

(878.) Meanwhile Folco, a canon, succeeded Hilduin in the abbacy on 9 February, the first Sunday in Lent, and governed it for four years. During his tenure, the circuit of the castle around the monastery of Saint Bertin was measured out and assigned among the various ministries; but, because several matters stood in the way, it was not completed.

In his first year, the monastery of Saint Peter and Saint Bertin was burned by the Northmen for the second time, on 28 July; and a solar eclipse occurred on 1 November [Note: Correct to ‘the fourth day before the Kalends of November,’ that is, 29 October], Wednesday, at the ninth hour. There was also a great mortality among humans and livestock.

Louis, son of Emperor Charles, died at the palace of Compiègne, before completing the second year of his reign, on 9 April, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 879. Then his sons Louis and Carloman divided his kingdom between themselves.

That same King Louis waged war against the Northmen in the district of Vimeu and gained a triumph; not long afterward he died, on 3 August, in the year of the Lord 881. He had reigned two years and three months.

After him, the King of the Swabians, son of Louis, king of Noricum, who was the son of Louis, son of Charles the Great, son of Pippin, assumed the monarchy of the entire Frankish and Roman empire in the year of the incarnate Word 885.

In the first year of the aforesaid King Carloman, Hincmar, archbishop of the Church of Reims, died; the aforesaid Folco succeeded him in office.

(During Folco’s time, that is, in the year eighty-five less than a century [Note: That is, 875. Baldwin’s death, however, seems to belong to the year 879], Baldwin, the first count of Flanders, paid the debt of death, after having lived for some time in the monastery of Saint Bertin under the monastic habit. His fleshly remains were buried in that monastery; but his heart and intestines are in the monastery of Saint Peter at Blandinium in Ghent.)

### LIX. Concerning Abbot Rodulf

After Folco had been elevated to the archbishopric, Rodulf assumed the abbacy in the same year. In the first year of Charles, king of the Swabians [Note: Namely, 883], a certain man named Rodin transferred to him, for the use of his monastery at Sithiu, his property, fully set out in the charter of his transfer, which was drawn up in the following terms.

### LX. The transfer of Rodin. Copy

(8 September 883.) “To the holy and venerable lord Rodulf, abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter and of the holy confessors of Christ, Audomar and Bertin, I, Rodin, a transferor and petitioner in the name of God.

“I therefore transfer my property to the aforesaid monastery, in the district of Ponthieu, on the river Authie, at the villa called Remmia: one church and one demesne mansus with its outbuildings, and, between that mansus and the arable land, meadow, or woodland, eleven mansi; likewise at Cathrin, in the same district of Amiens, in Sana Terra, at the place called Rosierias, one mansus with its outbuildings, together with the common rights, lawful roads, and watercourses of those places; and twenty dependants, namely: Anastasius with his wife and their six children; Adalrada with her two children, Gerland, Haldolf, Folcombert, Theodrad, Rodbert, Restald, Civireda, Rainilda, and Anstruda.

“All this, as stated above, I lawfully transfer and convey to the aforesaid monastery to be possessed forever, on the condition that I, together with my wife Ava, our sons and daughters, receive in precarium from your church, for your benefit, both the property I transfer and that which I request, namely:

“In the district of Amiens, in Sana Terra, called Rusticavilla, and at Roserias, a demesne mansus and, between that mansus and the arable land or meadow, twelve mansi; at Contla, one mansus; at Hunduncurth, a demesne mansus and ten mansi; likewise, in the district of Cambrai, at Finis, four mansi; and these dependants: Adoher; Folcard with his wife Oderna and their children; Gerbert Abbonessus; Rudoric; Siger; Rikard; and Bakaler with three others.

“For this usufruct, each year, on 5 September, I and my wife shall pay five solidi; after our death, our sons shall pay six solidi. But after the death of all of us, both properties named above, with all improvements and additions, shall be received without anyone’s opposition for the use of the brothers serving the Lord in the same monastery, to whom the rent shall be paid [Note: Perhaps read ‘shall be paid’].

“If anyone, as we attest for the future—whether we ourselves, or any of our heirs or pro-heirs, or any outsider—should attempt to oppose or infringe this transfer of ours, let him be compelled to pay twelve pounds of gold and thirty weights of silver, and let him not prevail in what he claims; but let this transfer, with its precarium, remain firm, supported by stipulation.

“Done in the monastery of Sithiu, in the church of Saint Peter, in the first year of Emperor Charles the Great, on 8 September.

“Sign of Rodin, who confirmed this transfer, together with its precarium.

“Sign of Albric. Sign of Vuadhar. Sign of Anselm. Sign of Guntard. Sign of Odgrin, advocate. Sign of Theodrad, scabinus. Sign of Adalwin.

“I, Grimbald, priest and monk, wrote and subscribed.”

### LXI. The transfer of Odgrin, with a precarium concerning Hamma

(877.) Likewise, in the third year of the aforesaid King Charles, Odgrin, advocate of the aforesaid monastery of Sithiu, transferred his inheritance to the same place, at the place called Hamma, on the river Marsbeke, in the district of Mempiscus. He therefore requested from the same abbot, by precarium, property of his monastery in the little villa called Sithiu; he obtained it without delay, according to this charter.

### LXII. Copy

(11 April 887.) “To Odgrin, a beloved son in Christ of the Church, Rodulf, by the grace of God abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter, called Sithiu, where the bodies of Christ’s confessors Audomar and Bertin rest, together with the entire community of monks living there.

“It is reported by the mouths of many and is known to many people how, in these days, you lawfully transferred your property to our monastery: namely, at the place called Hamma, on the river Marsbeke, in the district of Mempiscus, thirty-three bunaria, together with lawful roads and watercourses.

“Therefore you requested from us property of our church, namely fifty bunaria lying in the little villa called Sithiu, on the river Aa. We likewise, in accordance with your petition, grant to you and your wife Bertliana, and to your sons, both properties, those which you gave and those which you requested from us, for cultivation and improvement.

“And, as agreed, you shall endeavor each year, on 5 September, the feast of Saint Bertin, to pay us one solidus; and you shall have no power to give, sell, exchange, or alienate these properties elsewhere. Rather, as stated, for as long as you live, you shall possess them as our benefice. After the death of all of you, the aforesaid properties, with all improvements, shall be received in their entirety by us or our successors, to be possessed forever.

“Therefore let this grant remain firm, supported by stipulation.

“Done publicly at the monastery of Sithiu, in the basilica of Saint Peter the apostle, on 11 April, in the third year while Lord Emperor Charles was reigning in Francia, the grandson of Charles [Note: The authors of the *Nouvelle Gallia Christiana* believe that this charter was drawn up two years after Rodin’s charter reported above, namely in 885, because they reckon the beginning of Charles the Fat’s reign from the time when he had obtained authority in Lotharingia. This is correct with regard to Rodin’s charter; here, however, if one attends to the actual words of the instrument, there can be no doubt that it concerns the same Charles’s reign in Francia, whose third year must be assigned to 887].

“I, Rodulf, abbot, confirmed this with my own hand.”

### LXIII. The death of King Charles and the succession of Odo

(888.) After this, King Charles died in the fourth year of his empire; a certain Odo, who was not of royal stock, succeeded him in the kingdom. For, when the emperors had died, only Charles, the son of Carloman, remained as a child in his cradle. Since the Franks had lost hope in him, they set the aforesaid Odo over them as king, in the year of the Lord 888 [Note: Read 887].

In his second year, the monastery of Saint Bertin was thrown down by a storm, on 17 January.

### LXIV. The precarium of the monk Hucbald concerning Hildincurt

In the same year, that same Abbot Rodulf granted by precarium to Hucbald, a monk of the monastery of Saint Amandus, a villa of his monastery at Sithiu, in the district of Vermandois, called Hildini Curt, together with the little villas belonging to it. The charter of this precarium is as follows.

### LXV. Copy

[Note: Some clauses of this same instrument are reported by Mabillon, *Annales Benedictini*, vol. III, p. 280.]

“We wish it to be known how our beloved confrater Hugbald, sent from the monastery of the blessed bishop and confessor Amandus to instruct Lord Abbot Rodulf, our elder, with the permission and command of Gauzlin, abbot of that place, and with the consent of all the brothers of that holy congregation, requested from the aforesaid Lord Rodulf that certain properties, granted to him by Rodulf for the support of temporal necessity while he remained at his side, should be specially assigned and transferred for our use; on this condition, however, that each year, on the feast of Saint Amandus, which is 26 October, he should prepare a meal for us from those properties.”

### LXVI. The solar eclipse and the arrival of the Northmen

[Col. 1254A]

Three years after these events, a solar eclipse occurred on 15 August at the second hour. There was also a great drought in May, June, and July, and a comet appeared.

In the same year, that is, in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 891, on a Sunday after the ninth hour, 310 pagans were killed at Widingaham, at the little castle of the aforesaid saints, through the merits of Saints Audomar, Bertin, and Folquin.

On the following Sunday, at midday, the remaining pagan army, in greater numbers, came to the castle of the aforesaid saints. They fought from midday until evening, on 2 May, but achieved nothing. Some of them, however, entered the church of Saint Bertin; there twelve men were struck blind, and their standards were changed into another form. The booklet of the miracles of Saint Bertin bears most explicit witness to this.

### LXVII. How Abbot Rodulf died while ill at Arras

(892.) Then, two years after these events, Abbot Rodulf was at Arras during the days of the Lord’s octave. While he was having blood let on 4 January, around midnight his arm began to swell and grow inflamed. As the pain gradually advanced toward his vital organs, he died at daybreak, in the year of the Lord 892.

I have not said this to assert that Christians ought to observe the number and course of the lunar sphere according to the superfluous learning of worldly wise men—as though, which it is impious and dreadful even to say, Christ held power under the second, third, and fourth moons but lost it under the first, fifth, and eighth—but I say truthfully that God, who foreknows all things, wished to bring his predestined term of life to an end on this occasion.

That same abbot was buried in the monastery of Saint Vedast.

### LXVIII. How this place was thereafter reduced to lay control, and concerning the death of Archbishop Folco

After the death of Abbot Rodulf, the illustrious Marquis Baldwin [Note: Baldwin II, surnamed the Bald], count of Flanders, Boulogne, and Thérouanne, eager to hold the abbacy, approached the king of Francia to ask whether, in some way, the abbacy of the monastery of Sithiu could be granted to him.

When the monks of the aforesaid holy place heard this, they sent to the king a certain Grimbald, one of their own monks, who had been clothed under the aforementioned venerable Abbot Hugh, the twelfth abbot, and who was worthy of grace and honor, so that he might use every means and all his strength to thwart this plan if possible.

As Grimbald advanced, he met the same count, who asked where he was going. When Grimbald replied that he wished to seek the king, Baldwin told him that he could obtain the abbacy by royal grant if the monks’ will did not appear to oppose it, and earnestly asked him not to obstruct him in this matter. They parted with these words.

Grimbald continued along the road he had begun and reached the king. There he found the venerable Folco, formerly abbot of the monastery of Sithiu and then glorious archbishop of Reims. When Grimbald told him, on behalf of the monks, that they all unanimously preferred to abandon the place rather than see the holy place reduced to lay control, Grimbald asked him, in the name of almighty God, to entreat the king not to permit this to happen during his reign, since it appeared never to have been done by their predecessors.

When Archbishop Folco heard this, he sympathized with Grimbald’s petition and, remembering his former affection for that place, went with Grimbald to the king. He conveyed the monks’ words and earnestly begged that no layman be placed over the monks.

The king granted his request and finally entrusted the abbacy to Folco to govern through the brothers’ election [who governed it energetically for four years, restoring the monastery, which had been consumed by the storm under Abbot Rodulf. During his time, Cluny was founded].

This therefore became the seed of hatred between Folco, the bishop and abbot, and the illustrious Marquis Baldwin. Their hostility occupied almost eight years, until the aforesaid Count Baldwin vomited forth the crime he had conceived in his heart: he sent a certain soldier of his, named Winemar, to the boy King Charles, who was then reigning, for this same matter, so that he might appease the bishop’s mind and incline him to consent, if he could in any way do so.

When the bishop persisted in the position he had adopted and swore that he would in no way consent to a layman ruling the aforesaid abbacy contrary to the statutes of the holy canons, Winemar returned in anger. Since these events had taken place at the palace of Compiègne, he lay in wait for the bishop as he returned to Reims.

The bishop, unaware of this plot, arrived there with only a few companions. Then the aforesaid Winemar, the minister of evil, attacked him with great ferocity. Fearing neither justice nor God’s anger—and a deed horrible even to hear of—he killed the bishop by stabbing him with lances, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 900, on 17 June, Tuesday, at the sixth hour.

Behold how, in defense of the Church of Sithiu, the cultivator of the Lord’s vineyard fell, offering to the Savior his soul, to be joined with the choirs of the saints in everlasting joy.

They took up his venerable body and honorably buried it at Reims, in the church of the blessed Bishop Remigius. This unheard-of crime was immediately spread throughout the regions of every province and could not remain hidden from Rome, mistress of all cities.

Therefore the pope of that holy Roman Church bound the aforesaid Winemar with an apostolic sentence of anathema, writing to the bishops of all the provinces so that they too might condemn the perpetrator of so great a murder in the same manner; and it is established that this was done.

That same Winemar, the agent of the crime, persisting in the hardness of his heart, began to excuse himself entirely from guilt. For he asserted that he had committed this deed out of loyalty to his lord; therefore he remained under the anathema to the very end.

After this, Baldwin obtained the abbacy by royal grant.

### LXIX. The anointing of King Charles and his election as king of Francia

(893.) In the year of the Lord’s birth 893, Charles the boy, son of King Carloman [Note: Charles, surnamed the Simple, was Carloman’s brother, not his son], was established as king in the city of Reims on the feast of the Purification of Saint Mary, 5 February, and was consecrated by the aforesaid Folco, archbishop, while Odo, the aforementioned king, was still alive.

In his second year, the castle of Saint Audomar was consumed by fire. When King Odo heard that some of the Franks had anointed Charles as king, he pursued him with his mother Ermentrude throughout all the territories of the Franks.

At last the Franks who had set him over themselves as king attempted to extinguish King Odo’s life with poison, and they succeeded. After Odo’s death, King Charles assumed the rule of the Franks without any opposition.

Once established in the kingdom, he exalted a certain Haganus, whose lineage and nobility were unknown to the Franks, by showing him exceptional favor, and took him into his counsel more familiarly than the others.

When the Franks saw this, they did not tolerate lightly the friendship of an unknown man. Angered against the king on this account, they laid an ambush for him at Laon, a royal city. When King Charles learned of it, he escaped from there by flight and succeeded to the kingdom formerly belonging to Lothair.

The Franks, persisting in their decision, set up as king over themselves a certain Robert [Col. 1256C], brother of the aforementioned King Odo. He was the father of Hugh, later duke of the Franks, and reigned for almost two years.

### LXX. Charles’s battle against Robert
After this, King Charles, having assembled an army from the kingdom of Lothair and from the other eastern Franks, advanced to fight against the same Robert. At dawn on a certain Sunday, he crossed the ford of the river Isère with his army. The aforesaid Robert met him with a multitude of western Franks in the county of Soissons, at a place called [Note: The name of the place is lacking in the manuscript.] [lacuna]. There a very great mutual slaughter of Franks took place.

A certain Folbert, standard-bearer of King Charles, was seeking Robert especially intently in the battle. It happened that he encountered him with his beard exposed, which, though long, his coat of mail, fastened over it, had covered; immediately, without delay, the two pierced one another with their spears, and both fell to the ground, breathing out their lifeblood and their lives together. When the westerners heard that their king had fallen, they turned to flight, and victory fell to Charles and the easterners.

After the most bloody battle, Charles saw that he was still positioned amid the enemy: on one side, Hugh, son of the aforementioned King Robert; on the other, Heribert, his son-in-law [Note: Heribert II, count of Vermandois, concerning whom there will be discussion in the following chapter. Robert also had another son-in-law, Rudolf, who succeeded his deceased father-in-law.]. Fearing that they might fall upon him with a multitude of enemies, he returned with his men to the place from which he had come, into the kingdom of Lothair.

### LXXI. The Confinement of King Charles

After these events, the aforementioned Heribert, full of every kind of deceit, sent messengers to King Charles with peaceful words but treacherous intent. He said that he repented in every way of having attempted to act against him; therefore, if Charles would return, he promised to bring the kingdom of the Franks entirely under his authority.

When Charles heard this, he was delighted and returned as far as the fortress of Saint-Quentin in Vermandois. Heribert met him there, brought him into the same fortress, and prepared for him a very splendid banquet. When night had come and everyone was resting, buried in wine, Heribert ordered his men to leave and remove all their weapons, so that they would have no means of resisting what he was planning to do.

At sunrise, therefore, he seized the king and handed him over to custody. When the soldiers, taking refuge in their weapons, found that they were gone, they returned sorrowfully to their own homes. Heribert took Charles and led him to the fortress called Parona of the Scots; there he remained shut up under guard until the day of his death.

His wife, Queen Odgiva, who was of overseas origin and who herself had endured many persecutions during this period, sent her young son Louis to the English for protection, for they were also seeking to have him killed.

The Franks then set over themselves as king a certain Rudolf, son of Richard and of Auvergnat stock. During his reign, Stephen, bishop of the Church of Thérouanne, departed from this world. Wicfridus, provost of this monastery of Sithiu, succeeded him in the episcopate in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 925, and was consecrated by Archbishop Artaldus on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July.

In those days the Northmen, having gathered a multitude of ships at Rouen, were devastating the shores of the surrounding sea. When King Rudolf heard this, he assembled an army of Franks and advanced to fight them in the county of Thérouanne. On learning of this, the Northmen slaughtered the captives whom they had taken from various places. King Rudolf pursued them to the mountain called Falcoberg and engaged them in battle. After putting them to flight, he gained the victory, although at the greatest cost to his own men.

### LXXII. The Arrival of King Louis

**(929.)** In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 929, after these events, King Charles died in the fortress of Parona, in the custody to which he had been delivered, on the sixth day before the Kalends of October, and was buried in the monastery of Saint Fursey.

After this King Rudolf also died [Note: Rudolf died in the year 936, in the month of January]. When he had died, the Franks sent overseas for Louis, so that they might raise him to the kingdom of the Franks on his father’s throne. The nobles, bishops, and counts of the Franks went to meet him as far as the city of Boulogne, intending to receive the king with the greatest honor. Among them were Hugh, the renowned duke of the Franks; Heribert, the most deceitful of fraudsters; and Adalolf, the margrave.

They received the king in the city of Laon and escorted him with the greatest honor. There they raised him up as king and anointed him. Once established in the kingdom, he punished Heribert, the betrayer and tormentor of his father, who also desired to deceive him in a similar way, with the following vengeance, God rendering him a fitting recompense for his deeds.

Heribert had noted the day on which King Louis was to go hunting. He devised a plan by which, when he himself was engaged with the king in the sport of hunting, he would lure the king away from the hunters with his stories and then bind him and carry out his act of cruelty.

But, by God’s mercy, this plan could not remain hidden; it was reported to the king by one of those who appeared to be involved in it. When the appointed day arrived and they had gone out to hunt, the king placed some of his soldiers secretly in ambush and gave them a signal of recognition, so that, when they heard it, they might hasten forward immediately.

As the two proceeded while talking—the king and his would-be ambusher—the king seized Heribert, as though wishing to embrace him, and pulled away the twisted cord that was fastened to his saddle for the purpose of binding him. Immediately, when the signal was given, the ambush rose from its hiding place.

After Heribert had been captured, the king asked him what he intended with the cord he was carrying fastened to his saddle. He immediately confessed what he had plotted against the king with his wicked heart. The king then gave orders; they seized him and hung him from a nearby tree, bound beneath the armpit.

While he was still twitching as he hung from the tree, the king ordered that the rope by which he hung be cut and that he be entrusted to God’s power, if God wished to preserve his life in such a situation. But when God rendered him a just recompense for his deeds, after he had been released from the tree, he burst apart in the middle, for he was of immense girth. In such a death he brought his present life to an end.

### LXXIII. The Death of Abbot Baldwin

**(918.)** Baldwin (the Bald), count and abbot of the monastery of Sithiu, built the circuit of a fortress around the monastery of Saint Bertin and arranged it through various offices. After this [to summarize his deeds more briefly, he took more from the Church than he gave; and the monks, present and future, continue to experience the damage he inflicted], after having presided in name alone for seventeen years, he fell ill and died in the year of the incarnation of the Word 918, on the fourth day before the Ides of September.

When some of the soldiers wished to bury his body in the monastery of Sithiu beside his father [Baldwin Iron], his wife, named Elftrudis, desiring to be cremated together with him in a single cemetery, had him buried at Ghent, in the monastery of Blandinium.

For it was not yet permitted for any woman to enter the monastery of Saint Bertin, and it was considered a sacrilege if even some woman secretly entered its courtyard [Note: After this, the Audomarus manuscript adds the following:

> For by the celebrated law  
> concerning the female sex,  
> although she lived long,  
> it says, with a boundary fixed:  
> “Woman, fix your seat.  
>   
> This rule denies you  
> a holy house within these bounds;  
> thus the rule of the monks  
> commands.  
>   
> This place now observes  
> the rite established by the Father.”].

His sons divided his march among themselves. Arnulf, who was the elder, received Flanders; Adalolf received the city of Boulogne and the region of Thérouanne, and likewise assumed the abbacy of Saint Bertin. Those who still survive and knew him to the end testify to the love he had for that place.

### LXXIV. The Elevation of Saint Folquin, Bishop

**(928.)** In the year 928 after this, in the most blessed incarnation of Jesus Christ our Lord, during the time of the confined Charles and in the first indiction, my father, Folquin by name, father of me who write this very account, came here from the kingdom of Lothair with his brother, using such preparations as they could, wishing to raise the body of Saint Folquin, which until that time had been covered by the earth.

Both were close relatives of that blessed man by blood relationship. After permission had also been requested from the aforesaid count and abbot Adalolf, they came to the saint’s tomb with candles, censers, and a choir of singers, and raised the body on the Ides of November, on Thursday, at daybreak. The aforementioned men prepared refreshments for the brothers as best they could, for they had brought wine and everything necessary for food with them.

When these things had been done, they returned joyfully to their own homes. These men were Folquin and Regenwala, his brother, sons of Odwin, son of another Odwin, who was the brother of the blessed bishop Folquin. The father of that holy bishop was called Jerome, and his mother was named Hermentrude.

### LXXV. The Death of Abbot Adalolf

**(933.)** After this, Adalolf, count and abbot—a pious man who had presided over this monastery for fifteen years—fell ill in this monastery of Sithiu and died in the year of the Lord’s nativity 933, on the Ides of November.
