He was buried in the basilica of Saint Bertin, at the left altar of the principal altar of Saint Bertin.

Among his other gifts, he gave that place a golden cup for his own drinking and a belt, to be made into a chalice for the consecration of the Lord’s blood. He granted his bracelets to Saint Audomar for the making of a paten. Earlier he had also given the same Saint Audomar a pallium splendidly woven with gold and pearls. In contrast, Arnulf—the renowned margrave and abbot of this community, and brother of the now-deceased Adalolf—gave another pallium to Saint Bertin, outstanding in workmanship of the same kind.

After his sorrowful death, Arnulf, his brother, received the abbacy together with the rest of his county. Thus this Church, deprived of a religious shepherd, was possessed by married laymen as though by right of inheritance.

### LXXVI. The Entry of Women into This Monastery

**(938.)** The most noble wife of this abbot and count Arnulf, Adata, when she was very often burdened by serious illnesses, began to desire permission from the monks to enter this monastery, so that she might be allowed to prostrate herself before the altar of Saint Bertin and pray for her salvation.

For this reason she summoned the venerable bishops Wicfridus, bishop of the Church of Thérouanne, and Folbertus of Cambrai, and disclosed her desire to them. After permission had also been obtained from the monks, in the year of the Lord’s nativity 938, the fifth year [Note: Read “the second year” with Mabillon, *Annales*, volume III, page 441] of King Louis, on Easter Monday, the aforesaid bishops introduced her into the same monastery, not without the greatest trembling, since she was the first woman to presume to do what previously none of the queens had desired or even dared to do.

As she entered, she brought many ornaments to this place, and for as long as she lived she never ceased to make gifts.

At the very time of her entry, the renowned margrave Arnulf, at the request of that dearly beloved wife of his, handed over to the same place, for the use of the brothers, the estate of Merki with all its appurtenances: its church, dependents, buildings, cultivated and uncultivated lands, meadows, pastures, fisheries, and animals already obtained or to be obtained. The arrangement was that, for as long as he himself, his aforementioned wife Adata, and their son Baldwin lived, they would possess it under their own jurisdiction and pay the brothers one hundred solidi each year for the same estate; after their departure from this life, the entire possession would lie under the authority of the monastery.

He asked that this grant be recorded as a *precaria*, confirmed it with his own hand, and ordered the other nobles of his palace to record it. These are the witnesses: Unicfridus, bishop; Folbertus, bishop; Damasus, bishop; Hemfridus, priest; Engelandus, monk; Vuinetmarus, dean; Grimbaldus; Odarius, monk; Everardus, advocate; Vuinetmarus, layman; Rodulfus; Hericus, layman; Vuinetmarus, deacon and monk, subscribed.

Before this time, Adalolf—then a little boy, but now of mature age and also worthy to be honored with the priesthood—had been offered in this monastery to Saint Peter and Saint Bertin by his father Evehard, a man of the highest nobility, and his mother Ricsinda.

Rodulfus, the urban governor of the fortress itself, also carried his son, named Walter, in his own arms to the altar of Saint Bertin when the boy, suffering from the illness that physicians call smallpox, appeared to be near death. He vowed that he would make him a monk if the boy should be helped through the saint’s pious intercession. When the boy was immediately restored to health, he offered him to almighty God and to Saint Bertin as a monk, to remain permanently.

### LXXVII. The Conversion of the Monks to the Regular Way of Life

The aforementioned abbot and count Arnulf, grieving that the monastic religion which had earlier been established there by Saint Bertin and had flourished was at that time abolished, began to consider how he might restore the former religious observance and ennoble the place with its ancient sanctity.

But the will of the Most High God—who, although he sometimes permits his bride, the Church, to be tossed about, never permits her to perish—willed to wear down that same margrave with continual attacks of the stone, which obstructs urination and is commonly called a calculus.

For the purpose of curing him, many surgeons hastened to him, hoping to receive no small reward from a man who overflowed with wealth. They sought to exalt their knowledge of their art in his eyes, and by exalting it to display it. Under his observation, they took in eighteen men afflicted by the same illness; they cured all of them except one, who soon died.

Because this showed him that the cutting operation was to be avoided, he could no longer afterward bear to listen to those suggesting anything of the kind. Finally, turned toward himself by divine grace, he rejected the remedies of this world and ran in his mind to him who restores all things by a single word. He sought the presence of the venerable Gerard through a swift messenger.

When the man of God arrived, Arnulf disclosed his grievous condition and asked him to implore the clemency of the Almighty for the recovery of his bodily health.

After prayer had been poured out and the holy man had struck the margrave’s mind with his counsel—that he should give to the needy from the abundance of his possessions—the margrave obeyed God’s will. Masses were celebrated with sighs and tears, and a three-day fast was imposed upon him.

When this count had devoutly participated in the mysteries of the sacraments, the margrave was suddenly compelled by the urge to urinate. Having sought a suitable place of retreat, he discharged the burning stone without difficulty.

When he had been miraculously restored to his former health, it is beyond our ability to comprehend how great the rejoicing that filled his breast was, or how great the fitting reverence with which he honored the man of God.

The count, therefore, as a most generous repayer of the benefit bestowed, greatly desired to reward the man of God with many gifts. But Gerard is said to have rejected everything and replied to the count: “If we have abandoned our own things, how shall we accept what belongs to another?”

Bound, however, by terrible oaths, the count finally compelled him to accept a tenth of his possessions. He had first humbly declined this as well, but shortly afterward accepted it without greed and distributed it with prudent consideration.

Likewise, since the aforementioned count had a number of abbeys under his authority, it seemed useful to him to entrust their administration to Gerard.

**(44.)** For this reason he summoned a certain venerable abbot Gerard to himself, so that he might restore that monastery of Saint Bertin, deprived of regular observance, to the former honor of the holy Rule, and eradicate completely the perverse custom by which secular men thereafter usurped the office of abbot. He began to discuss the matter with the monks themselves, to see whether he might perhaps incline their minds toward agreement with this good counsel.

Since they remained hardened in mind and were moved neither by threats nor by blandishments, he ordered them to leave the monastery in the year of the most salutary nativity of Jesus Christ our Lord 964, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May. He handed the same monastery over to Abbot Gerard, who was almost alone and the first in the western regions in those final times to observe the norm of regular life, together with monks collected from various places, to be governed according to the Rule.

A considerable crowd of people had gathered for this spectacle. It was a sight to behold: at the departure of the monks there was immense grief for all and tears in the eyes of many, while the servants of that place and the rest of the common people wished to rise up against the regular monks and the count himself.

The count sent after them and asked them to return, promising to give them everything necessary, provided only that, on returning to their place, they professed that they would observe the monastic order. But they persisted in their decision and, departing with a great multitude of the people who followed them, remained for some time at a village belonging to the same monastery called Loconessa.

After a short while, most of them boarded a ship on the ocean and were carried to an overseas region. King Adalstenus [Note: Alternatively Aldestanus, son of Edward I and king of England] received them kindly and immediately granted them the monastery called “At the Baths.” This was chiefly because the brother of that renowned king, King Etwinus, had been buried in the monastery of Saint Bertin.

For in the year of the incarnation of the Word 932, that same King Edwinus, compelled by some disturbance in his kingdom, had boarded a ship in this part of the sea and wished to travel onward. A storm arose, the ship was shattered, and he was swallowed up amid the waves.

When his body had been carried to the shore, Count Adalolf, who was related to him by blood, took it with honor and brought it to the monastery of Saint Bertin for burial. After his death, his brother King Adalstenus sent many gifts to this place as alms for him and, for this reason, received the monks of that monastery affectionately when they came to him.

The rest of the monks, whose hearts God had enlightened by the grace of his visitation, embraced the monastic Rule and returned to their own monastery: namely, Engelandus, formerly provost of this place; Grimbaldus with Drothwinus, venerable in the white hair of their old age; and after them Adalolfus and Galandus, Siguvimus, Suavimus, Vulfricus, Sigebaldus, and Adalgerus.

Since Abbot Gerard held the monastery situated at Ghent, called Blandinium, and could not govern both this monastery and that one in person, the regular administration was entrusted—by order of the count and with the consent of Abbot Gerard—to a certain Agilo, a monk of Saint Aper of the city of Toul, together with Womar, a monk of the monastery of Blandinium, though not under the title of abbot.

Soon afterward Agilo died. At the request of Abbot Gerard and with the assent of Count Arnulf, Wido, Gerard’s nephew, was consecrated abbot in this monastery in the year of the Lord’s nativity 947. During his time, a certain little boy named Unago, offered here as a monk by his father Odo of the city of Montreuil, became a monk.

Later, that same Abbot Wido, because he pursued too ardently the pleasures of a vain youth, was accused before the count, deprived of the abbacy, and appointed abbot of the monastery of Saint Bavo. Womar, however, governed the monastic community under regular discipline.

At that time I myself, Folquin, who am writing these things, was brought here from the kingdom called Lothair by my father Folquin, mentioned above, and my mother Thiedala. In the year of the most blessed incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 948, on the feast of the Elevation of Saint Bertin, which follows the feast of All Saints, I was offered to Saint Bertin and made a monk—alas, only outwardly.

### LXXVIII. Abbot Hildebrand

The glorious margrave Arnulf mentioned above, a short time after the aforementioned Abbot Wido, handed over the same monastery to his nephew Hildebrand to govern. During his time, the religious life of holiness grew so greatly in this monastery that it became a model and example for all the monasteries established around it.

The monks rejoiced that they had been placed under so great a father, because by his exhortation he supplied nourishment for their inner minds and sufficiently provided what their bodies required externally. Among the other precepts of the holy Rule, he especially strove to obey this command: that the abbot should endeavor to be loved more than feared, lest, while excessively scraping away rust, he should break the vessel of human frailty.

He adopted such discretion in all his actions that his commands contained both what the strong desired and what the weak would not reject.

He was appointed in the year from the incarnation of the Lord 950, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April, by Wicfridus, bishop of the Church of Thérouanne.

Count Arnulf, the uncle of that abbot, restored for the use of the brothers living under him the village called Arcas. As I remember saying much farther below, it was one of the principal members of the abbey and had been assigned to the service of the abbot; in it, from ancient times, the abbot’s seat was frequented by the people who came to seek him. The count himself, since he had received the abbacy by paternal succession, had kept it appropriated to his own use.

He restored it to the use of the brothers on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July, in the year of the Lord’s nativity 951.

Afterward, he also directed Saint Walaric to this monastery, having had him brought there in the same way from his fortress and monastery, and on the sixth day after this—that is, on the fourth day before the Kalends of September—he ordered him to be brought there in the same manner for preservation, in the year from the Lord’s nativity 952.

The aforesaid abbot also received into the monastery a certain canon of Saxon origin, named Odoldus, who had fled to the monastic habit. He entrusted him with the school for instructing boys, for he was extremely skilled in literary learning. He also entrusted him with the care of the deanery, which, by God’s mercy, he still governs today.

### LXXIX. The Conversion of the Monks at Arras, and Abbot Regenold

While this place was flourishing under the aforesaid abbot with the religious observance described above, the glorious Count Arnulf conceived the idea of ennobling the monastery of Saint Vedast with an equal religious observance.

Accordingly, after summoning Lord Abbot Hildebrand, he sent him to that monastery—after he had presided over the community of the monks of Sithiu for four years—so that, by the example of his works and by his exhortation, he might kindle them to observe the monastic Rule.

When he had arrived there and was striving in every way to fulfill the purpose for which he had come, the aforementioned glorious count finally ordered those who refused to obey to leave the monastery. He ordered the same abbot to govern the monastery with those who remained.

While Hildebrand was diligently fulfilling this task for a time as far as his strength allowed, this place was neglected by him because of the labor and exhortation that had necessarily to be expended upon those men, who were still inexperienced.

The same abbot begged the renowned margrave Arnulf to entrust this monastery of Sithiu to one of the brothers for governance, lest, while attending to the concerns of one monastery, he neglect the other.

The count consented and, with Hildebrand’s counsel, raised a certain monk of that monastery, named Regenold, to the honor of abbot, despite the opposition of only the brothers’ will. He was appointed in the year from the incarnation of the Lord 954, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, by Wicfridus, bishop of the Church of Thérouanne.

Abbot Hildebrand, amid our weeping, entrusted the care of the souls to the same Lord Abbot Regenold and returned to Arras.

Abbot Regenold was very watchful and concerned about the governance of the souls entrusted to him; within a short time he became beloved and devoted to all.

Once established in the place, with the assistance of the renowned margrave Arnulf, he purchased from a certain very distinguished man named Hugh a church built in honor of Saint Michael, called Wacquinville, situated in the county of Boulogne, for five pounds of denarii.

During his administration, with the consent—indeed, at the urging—of the glorious Count Arnulf, he also transported the relics of Saint Audomar with the greatest honor and with the manifold and devoted service of the monks and canons to the royal palace of Nijmegen, so that he might acquire for this holy place lands situated beyond the Rhine, once granted to it by the faithful. At that time the glorious Otto, king of eastern Gaul, had arrived there.

When they came to the port of Thiale, the custodian of the church, blaspheming and insulting the holy relics, refused to open the church.

A short while later, someone hurried up and announced that the same custodian, having returned from the baths, had been seized by a sudden illness and, unless the monks came to his aid by their intercession, would soon die.

When the brothers heard this, one hastened to bring the Eucharist and another the consecrated relics. Then another messenger appeared and told them not to be troubled, because the priest had already ended his present life—the holy Audomar having rendered him a punishment worthy of his blasphemy.

When this became known, people came running from every direction to the church and honored the holy relics as best they could.

After acquiring, in part, the things for which they had come, and receiving the church at Frekenis by royal gift, they returned home with the saint’s relics.

During the first year of the aforesaid abbot’s rule, the most glorious King Louis of the western Franks departed from this world and was buried at Reims, in the monastery of Saint Remigius, on the ninth day before the Ides of September.

His son Lothair, still a boy, succeeded him in the kingdom and was consecrated king by Archbishop Artaldus of the Church of Reims on the third day before the Ides of November.

Under him, Count Arnulf, who was also, in temporal matters, administrator of the Church of Sithiu, obtained a privilege confirming the immunity and the goods granted by him and those to be granted thereafter, as well as the justice we ought to possess in all our places, according to the form inserted here word for word.

#### Copy of the Privilege Obtained

**(7 January 962.)**

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Lothair, by the ordering of divine Providence, king of the Franks.

“When we provide suitable assistance to places devoted to divine worship out of love for divine service, we clearly fulfill the imperial custom in a fitting manner, and we firmly believe that this will benefit us in attaining the rewards of eternal recompense.

“Therefore we wish it to be known to all the faithful, both those present and those to come, that the venerable Arnulf, margrave and abbot of the monastery of the community of Sithiu, situated in the county of Thérouanne and built in honor of holy Mary, ever Virgin and Mother of God, and of the apostles Peter and Paul, in which the bodies of the blessed confessors Audomar and Bertin rest, and where at the present time the aforesaid abbot appears, by God’s authority, to preside—we wish it known that he has informed our majesty how, long ago, in the time of our predecessors and relatives, namely the kings of the Franks, they had granted the same monastery such authority by royal privileges that it, with all that belonged to it, would remain under the perpetual security of their protection.

“But as a sign of firmness, they asked that we not only follow the custom of our royal predecessors and order such a decree of our authority to be made concerning that monastery for the sake of its protection, but also ensure that no one divide or convert to other uses any cells, villages, or other possessions of the aforesaid monastery that exist in any counties and territories within the jurisdiction of our empire; that the household of the same monastery give no fodrum (provisioning-duty) to any persons; and that we confirm by our authority the things recently granted by the faithful.

“We have willingly assented to their petitions. Accordingly, by this decree we grant and confirm everything: namely, the estate of Morke with all its appurtenances, which the renowned margrave Arnulf, our most faithful servant, had given to the same holy place, with the consent—or rather at the request—of Athala, his most noble wife, at the time when she, the first among women, attempted to enter the holy threshold of that monastery; also the village called Arcas, which the same man likewise enlarged for the sustenance of the brothers, and in which there was also the allod of the illustrious Everard, advocate of that place, which after his death he gave to the brothers to receive; also the monastery of Saint Michael called Wacquinville, with its appurtenances; and the church of Petresse, given by the aforementioned margrave’s grant. We confirm all these things to the same holy place by royal authority.

“Therefore we have ordered these royal letters to be made, by which we admonish our successors that, just as we have granted these things to the aforesaid monastery, so they should permit them to remain ratified and stable; that they neither make nor permit any division in monasteries, cells, villages, or other possessions, nor divert them to other uses.

“We also enact and decree that no public judge, nor anyone exercising judicial authority, should ever dare to enter the churches or other possessions of the aforesaid monastery, those which it now possesses or which divine power may hereafter cause to increase, in order to hear cases according to judicial custom, exact fines or ban-dues, make lodgings or provisions, exact lodging-duty, take sureties, distrain the men of the monastery, or seek any payments or unlawful pretexts; nor should anyone presume to exact any of the things mentioned.

“Rather, let the aforementioned abbot Arnulf and his successors possess the property of the aforesaid monastery in quiet order, with all fines and ban-dues granted under our protection, so that the servants of God may delight in continually imploring God’s mercy for us and for the stability of our entire kingdom, which God has granted to us.

“And so that this authority may remain unshaken in our own and future times, with God’s protection, we have confirmed it with our own hand and ordered it to be authenticated by the impression of our ring.

“Given on the seventh day before the Ides of January, in the reign of Lord Lothair, in the eighth year, in the sixth indiction.

“Given at Laon, happily.”

Thus signed below:

“Sign of Lothair, most glorious king of the Franks.

“Otto the chancellor recognized this.”

In the fifth year after this, a sign of the cross suddenly appeared marked on human garments, for some reason that I do not know. The garment had a color as though from some greasy liquid, and in places it appeared to have been stained in the form of a cross; but it was not known from what cause this had happened.

Therefore the people of this region, fearing that some scourge might be impending over them because of the anger of God, hastened more frequently to the work of prayer and visited the churches of the resting places of the greatest patrons, Audomar and Bertin, with whatever gifts they could provide.

Wicfridus, bishop of the city of Thérouanne, also ordered the people of his entire diocese during this crisis to come to the monastery of Sithiu and implore the Lord with the greatest earnestness.

Accordingly, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of February, after a fast had been appointed, the streets were filled with an innumerable crowd. The bishop himself was also present, and they raised the body of the most holy Father Audomar and carried it to the lower monastery amid a weeping multitude of people.

After prayer had been offered there, they lifted the body of the same saint and of Saint Bertin, the most merciful protector of his people in their necessities, and, together with Saints Richarius and Walaric, carried them back to the upper monastery by the road they had taken.

When they had reached a certain space between the two monasteries, while the bishop was addressing the people, Rodulfus, whom I mentioned above, gave to Saint Bertin for possession a certain piece of his hereditary property called [Note: The name of the place is lacking in the manuscript.] [lacuna], with the consent of his wife and sons.

His wife, for her part, willingly granted the same saint two golden crescent-shaped pendants.

After this, the bodies of the saints were carried to the monastery of Saint Audomar. At the entrance to the church, they were raised on beams above the height of a man, and beneath them crowds of people entered the church.

Since night was now approaching, Abbot Regenold, seeing that there would no longer be a return, spent that night there with the bodies of the saints.

The next day, with both monastic communities attending, they returned to their respective places of rest.

After this, a certain Rikelinus, then a little boy, was offered here as a monk. Together with him, his father, named Wualdo, gave this holy place a church belonging to his hereditary property in a village called Granai; he received it back by a *precaria* for the improvement of his own life and that of another son.

### LXXX. How This Place Began to Be Scourged by the Lord
In those times, I do not know whether because sins demanded it, or according to what is written: “The Lord chastises the one whom he loves; but he scourges every son whom he receives,” this place began, lamentably, to be scourged by God with elephantiasis—that is, leprosy. By this disease, a grievous thing to relate, lord abbot Regenoldus too was stricken; nevertheless, for almost a whole year afterward he governed the administration of this place as best he could, living privately in a cell, separated from the community of the brothers. At last, when Count Arnulfus avoided this place because of that disease, having withdrawn his visitation, Regenoldus was compelled to leave the monastery and retire to the place I mentioned above, called Vuachimvillare.

Before relinquishing the administration of the souls entrusted to him, however, at the command of the count, and with the brothers gathered together for this very purpose, he entrusted it, with their consent, to Adalolphus, already named above and a monk of the same monastery, on the solemn day of the Most Holy Supper, in the year 941 of the Lord’s nativity—that day having then fallen on the seventh day before the Ides of April, with Easter’s solemnity approaching on the second day before those same Ides.

Before this, something omitted above from memory: Wicfridus, bishop of the city of Thérouanne, departed from this world in the year of the Lord 959, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of November. David, a monk of Corbie, succeeded him in the episcopate.

Adalolphus was sufficiently solicitous for the congregation entrusted to him, although he was not consecrated in the abbacy. For the count was ingeniously arranging matters—as later became clear in the work that follows—in order that he might more easily bestow this place again upon his nephew Hildebrandus.

At that time the same count sent lord Adalolphus across the sea to the king of the English, with gifts. Once he had crossed the sea, Odoldus, mentioned above, our dean, returned from the regions on this side of the Rhine, where he had been sent to harvest grapes, with the wine of seven vessels.

At this time Count and Abbot Arnulfus had also come to this very monastery of Sithiu, together with his son Balduinus, most distinguished in the flower of his youth, and his recently married wife, Mathilda by name, equally conspicuous in the nobility of Saxon lineage. On her first entry into this monastery, she presented this place with a curtain of extraordinary size and exceptional workmanship, adorned with panels of various colors [which this church still uses as its Lenten veil].

Count Arnulfus sent instructions that the wine mentioned above should be received and reserved for his own use. In compensation, however, so that he might not appear to have incurred the stigma of a robber, he gave the brothers of the same monastery a church called Tetresse, which he transferred on the second day before the Kalends of December, the feast day of Saint Andrew.

These are the witnesses: Balduinus, his son, consenting; Odoldus the dean; Hemfridus the provost; Engelandus, Drothwinus, and Grimbaldus, monks; Arnulfus, the count’s nephew; Rodulfus, the urban prefect; Evehardus, the advocate; and Egelbodo, guarantors of the good faith. Folquinus, levite and monk, subscribed.

After this, when the day of Christ’s nativity arrived, the aforementioned Count Balduinus began to fall ill with the disease which physicians call smallpox, and by his illness made the feast sad for us. On the day of the Kalends of January, when the octave of the Lord’s nativity is celebrated—grievous even to relate—he ended the course of his present life. It was possible to see throughout the whole people, of both sexes and of every age, an intolerable grief, almost previously unseen.

He was buried in this very monastery, in the middle of the church of the resting place of the blessed father Bertinus, in the year of Christ’s nativity 961, in the fourth indiction, while King Lotharius was reigning in his eighth year.

When lord Adalolphus returned from the regions to which he had been sent, inquiry and election concerning the future abbot once again began to be discussed. Count Arnulfus sent for the aforementioned abbot Hildebrandus, his nephew, and once more entrusted this place to him; by God’s mercy he has governed it up to the present, which is the aforementioned year 961 of the Lord’s nativity.

This was easily done because he was greatly loved by the monks of this monastery for the uprightness of his life. Thus it is clear that Adalolphus, the monk of the aforementioned monastery, yielded to the will of the often-mentioned count, after administering it for scarcely a single year. Later, in the third year of the resumption of the government by our abbot Hildebrandus, his uncle Arnulfus, formerly count of Flanders and abbot, as has been shown above, completed the office of his life and was buried at Blandinium.

## LXXXI. I have now completed, with the Lord’s help, what you had commanded, most holy and beloved lord and father, Adalolphus

I have brought together in a single book the donations of the faithful with their charters, as well as the deeds of the abbots, from the first founder of this place, lord Bertinus the abbot, down to the last, who now presides in our own time.

As for myself, your brother in the truth, I testify that I have written nothing here other than what I was able to find in the exemplars of the ancients or to learn from the reports of able men. If some should wish to tear me apart out of envy, I beg that they be restrained by his paternal favor.

I have taken care to record separately the remaining charters assigned to the various offices, so that whoever makes inquiry may investigate more easily what was allotted to each office. I have also subscribed, in order, the names of our brothers whom I remember—when I was a young man and almost the last among them—to have lived a regular life in this monastery.

Lord abbot Hildebrandus; Odoldus the dean; Ingelandus; Vuinetmarus; Grimbaldus; lord abbot Regenoldus; Grunwaldus; Benedictus; Rikelmus; Drotwinus; Hemfridus; Adalolphus; Rodvinus; Signinus; Galandus; Liodricus; Odarius; Erembaldus; Suavinus; Adalgisus; Vuluricus; Sigebaldus; Engelandus; Sigelmus; Aldgerus; Vuago; Folquinus; Idelbaldus; Adalsigae; Adalardus; Matfridus; Amarlandus; Heremarus; Grimbaldus; Heimericus; Everardus; Liuzo; Everoldus; Legenfridus; Tiozo; Vulfandus; Reingerus; Nidgrimus; Humfridus; Folcarus; Regenerus.

## LXXXII. Hereafter follow the charters witnessing the alms-villages

Here too I shall undertake to write, without sparing my labor but looking to the advantage of the monastery, the small estates handed over by the faithful for the administration of alms, together with their charters. For I remember that I promised to do this when I mentioned Guntbertus under Abbot Fridogisus.

Almost everything that must be written here was handed over through the generosity of Guntbertus himself and of his father Goibertus. The same Goibertus had built, on his own property, as I said far above, a small cell in honor of the Lord Savior at a place called Stenetland. He had assigned to it a very large part of his inheritance, and granted this same cell to Saint Bertinus, on behalf of his son Guntbertus, whom he had made a monk in the same monastery, with perpetual security.

The first of the charters concerning the estates that he handed over with us to that same cell is the charter of Curmontium, which will be first in the order of those that follow.

## LXXXIII. Goibertus’s donation of Curmontium, in the time of Abbot Fridogisus

*(August 831.)*

“To the venerable lord in Christ, Father Fridogisus, abbot of the monastery of Sithiu, where two holy men, namely Audomarus together with the blessed Bertinus, confessors of the Lord Christ, rest bodily.

“I, Goibertus, in the name of God, together with my son Guntbertus, both donors, by this letter of donation give to you of our own free will whatever we appear to possess or control at the place called Curmontium, in the county of Boulogne, on the river Edivinia: namely, one mansus and the principal house built upon it, with the other structures and buildings belonging there, greater and smaller; together with arable lands, meadows, pastures, coppices, commons, lawful passageways, and wadriscapi; everything in every respect, the entire property, wholly and completely.

“In addition, ten slaves, by name: Ellefridus; Odbertus; Gerwaldus; Vuerembaldus with his two children; and Hildewif with her two children.

“All these things named above we lawfully hand over before witnesses to the tomb of Saint Bertinus, on this condition: that after us, those serving the Lord in the same place may have them for their particular consolation beyond their due.

“But if any of the rulers of the aforesaid monastery should wish, out of ill will, to take this away from them or to use it to make up their due, then it must by all means, without any objection, revert to our lawful heirs; and I, Guntbertus, on account of this gift, for as long as, with the Lord’s consent, I live, shall have my fullest due among those monks.

“If it should happen, as often happens, that on account of the envy or avarice of the provosts I depart from the aforementioned monastery, then, without any objection, I shall again receive my inheritance. And we wish this small inheritance to serve the church of the Lord Savior at Steneland.

“But if anyone—which we do not believe will happen—whether one of our heirs or further heirs, should this security remain firm, or any other or foreign person, should presume to act against this most devout donation of ours or attempt to violate it, let him incur the anger of that Lord Savior, almighty God, and of his saints. Moreover, under the compulsion of the treasury, let him be forced to pay ten ounces of gold and twenty weights of silver; and let him be unable to establish the claim he brings, but let this present donation remain entirely firm for all time, supported by formal stipulation.

“Done at the monastery of Sithiu, in the month of August, in the eighteenth year of the empire of Louis, the most pious Augustus.

“I, Goibertus, acknowledge this donation made by me.

“Sign of Guntbertus, his son, who likewise made and confirmed this donation.

“Sign of Gabriel; sign of Riquio; sign of Egedbodo.

“I, Vuinebertus, priest and monk, wrote and subscribed.”

## LXXXIV. They also gave the church at Steneland in honor of the Lord Savior

They gave the church at Steneland in honor of the Lord Savior, together with what appears to have endowed that church, and another part of the inheritance—manses, structures, movable and immovable property—entirely and completely, except for the slaves whom they wish to set free as alms for the sake of their father Thiodbertus, their mother Bertruda, and their son Guntbertus, so that from it an annual commemoration may be celebrated in alms for the brothers and the poor.

And let this church be maintained according to its course [Note: Above the word *curso* is written: “that is, with psalms”], with clerics and lamps, just as an account must be rendered before the Lord Savior on the day of judgment before Christ’s tribunal.

And that small property at Steneland itself and at Ricolvengahem, whatever I and Hlotildis and Heremarus assigned, up to sixty *bunaria*, belongs wholly and entirely to, and serves, the church of the Lord Savior.

## LXXXV. In the year of the Lord’s nativity 826, Goibertus made this memorandum

He made it when he took his mother Bertruda and his son Guntbertus to Rome, and there offered him to Saint Peter; Pope Eugenius made him a cleric there and confirmed him.

*(826.)*

“We have placed all our property in the hands of good men, both lands and slaves, personal possessions, securities, movable and immovable goods—everything and from everything, wholly and completely—on this condition: if my end should come to me on the journey which I am preparing to undertake to the region of Rome for the sake of prayer, they are to act as I have instructed them, for my alms and those of my father, mother, and son.

“First, that inheritance at Embriacum, to Saint Audomarus. And that at Curmontis and at Humbaldingahem: the boy Guntbertus, as his inheritance, and twenty slaves, if he returns to his homeland. If he does not come, then that property at Curmontis is to go to Saint Bertinus, for the use of the brothers, as my alms, so that they may have consolation beyond their due; and no abbot shall have power to take it away from them, so that they may offer for me, my son, my father, and my mother, and celebrate Masses or psalms.

“And Everwinus and Lothwinus are to administer those things, whatever they are able to work, for the use of the brothers; after their death, the person whom the dean shall appoint.

“And ten cows, fifty sheep, fifteen pigs, and four oxen.

“And that property at Humbaldingahem is given to Jedona, my kinsman. If the boy returns, then let him have that inheritance at Hethenesberg, which he acquired there; let Jejodo have it all. Otherwise, let them be sold to my kinsmen, and let the price be given to priests so that they may sing Masses for us and for the servants and handmaids of God, so that they may offer for us.

“And at Tathingahem, that marsh; and at Ganape, to my nephew Heremarus; and at Muldelhem, to Saint Audomarus, in place of that boy, and six slaves; and that allod at Aganesberga; and at Selis, that meadow; and at Vostringe, that *bunarium*: let all these be sold, and let the price be given as our alms.

“Let all the remainder be handed over to Saint Bertinus as our alms.”

## LXXXVI. Goibertus’s charter concerning the endowment of the church of the Lord Savior at Steneland

*(8 November 828.)*

“If we contribute anything of our property to holy places or to the substance of the poor, we trust beyond doubt that this will be repaid to us in eternal blessedness.

“For this reason, in the name of God, I, Goibertus, give to the church constructed at the place called Saint Savior, or Steneland, in honor of the Lord our God and Savior Jesus Christ, and also of holy Mary, the Mother of God, and of the holy apostle Peter, as well as of many other saints; and I wish what has been given to remain so forever.

“At the place called above Ennena, Araca: one mansus and two *bunaria*; and between Henrikingahem and Lonastingahem, thirteen *bunaria* and three and a half *jornalia*; and at another place whose name is Hiddigareta, and at Marisca, fourteen *bunaria*.

“There are altogether thirty *bunaria*, with passageways and wadriscapi, and six slaves, by name: Erkembaldus, Morellus, Evonus, Ostorbertus, Foleboldus, and Winebardus, together with their personal property.

“All these things, as stated above, I now give to the aforementioned holy place, so that the custodians of the same church may have, hold, and possess them, or freely do whatever they wish with them in every respect, while Christ governs it, and may enjoy the Church’s disposition.

“But if anyone—which I scarcely believe could happen—whether I myself, or any of my heirs or further heirs, should presume to raise any complaint against this letter of donation, let him first incur the anger of almighty God; moreover, under the compulsion of the treasury, let him be forced to pay one hundred pounds of gold and three hundred weights of silver; and let him be unable to reclaim anything that he seeks to recover. Rather, let this donation remain firm, supported by formal stipulation.

“Done in the same church, before the altar.

“Given on the sixth day before the Ides of November, in the fifteenth year of lord Emperor Louis.

“Sign of Goibertus, who requested that this donation be made.

“Sign of Guntbertus, his consenting son. Sign of Heremarus, his consenting nephew. Sign of Vurascolfus. Sign of Witolfus.

“Ratlandus, priest, wrote and subscribed.”

## LXXXVII. Concerning the death of Guibertus

*(838.)*

In the year of the Lord 838, the year of the Lord’s incarnation, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May, a Wednesday, in the second week of Easter, when Goibertus fell ill at the monastery of Saint Audomarus on the mountain, at the urging of his son Guntbertus he set free fifteen slaves for the church of the Lord Savior at Steneland, under the provision for lights, at four denarii each.

In the same year afterward, in the month of November, when, having fallen ill, he sensed that the day of his death was approaching, he himself wrote out, on wax tablets that were externally covered with the scales of a large fish and gilded beneath, how his property should be disposed of by the hand of a third party, on the fourth day before the Nones of November, a Monday, in this manner:

“At Humbaldingahem and Embreka and Hettesnamont, for the use of my son Guntbertus.

“At Ostringa, one *bunarium* to Guntbertus himself.

“At Ganape, to Trudlinda.

“At Winingahem, to Bertruda, except for the mansus which I gave to the church at Steneland.

“At Middelhem, to Saint Audomarus.

“At Anineshem, to Folbaldus, and that meadow which I had at Selem.

“At Fraxerias, at Frandris, the whole inheritance to my nephew.

“To Saint Savior, that stone quarry which I had near Scammis. I also wish to set free fifteen slaves for the same church, at four denarii each.”

He also ordered the memorandum to be read aloud before him and his friends on the second day before the Nones of November.

On the day before his death, he also set free four slaves at Steneland. On the following day, before he died, he handed and entrusted the keys of that church and of all the other workshops to his son Guntbertus, saying:

“Son, I confirm you as survivor over all these things, so that, while you live, you may guard with fitting care this house of God, and the alms of mine, of my predecessors, and also your own.”

After these words, his soul and body rested in the Lord, and he died on the Nones of November, on Wednesday at evening.

On the following day, they carried the body of Guibertus to the monastery of Sithiu and buried him in the basilica of Saint Bertinus, before the altar of the Lord Savior and of the Crucified One.

## LXXXVIII. Privilege of Abbot Adalardus concerning the cell of the Lord Savior at Steneland

*(27 March 857.)*

“Whatever rulers of the Churches grant in response to the requests of those who fear and love God, they do not doubt that in this they fulfill God’s will.

“Therefore I, Adalardus, in the name of God, abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter, called Sithiu, where the saints of the Lord Audomarus and Bertinus rest, wish it to be known to the worshipers of God in the holy Church, present and future, that Guntbertus, faithful to God, to that holy place, and to us, petitioned our smallness that we might confirm by our own testament his father Goibertus’s and his own donation concerning the cell of the Lord Savior at Steneland, or Saint Savior.

“Readily assenting to his will and petition, because of the devotion and great usefulness which he and his aforesaid father showed toward the aforementioned holy monastery, we establish in the place of God and his saints that, as the testament of the said donation declares, the properties themselves shall remain perpetually for the performance of the alms of their predecessors and themselves, without opposition from anyone.

“And Guntbertus himself, for as long as, with Christ’s consent, he lives, shall have their administration and control for the use of the monastery of Sithiu. If he should end his life earlier, he shall accept into the administration the person whom he approves or chooses.

“And so that, according to the charters, the donation may remain unshaken, we specify the properties by name: at Steneland itself; at Ricolvingahem; at Hisdonne, with the slaves; at Henrikingahem or Milhem; and at another Henrikingahem, with Trudbaldus and the lamps under his administration; at Ebresingahem; at Winingahem; at Curmontium; at Siningahem; and at Istem; at Hokingahem; at Hostede; at Lampanesse; at Simpiacum; at Burthem; at Reka; at Strate; at Hemmawic, the land of Frawivus; at Kilciacum, with Odlando the smith; at Etesnasberg; in the monastery, a mansus and garden; likewise at Ariacum; at Tarwana, a mansus; likewise at Quentwicum—whether acquired by any means or increased through our assistance, and whatever God’s mercy may add thereafter.

“Likewise at Kessiacum, Sperdia, Vuesarmium, Vostringe, Tingiacum, Vuilere, Mellingasele, Loclesse, Loninstagahem; the precarious holdings of Landbertus, Adalgerus, and Hildbertus; at Gruonoberg, a forest with land; at Dagmaringahem, both while Guntbertus himself lives and after his death, let these remain unshaken, just as they are known to belong there today.

“I also warn and charge, by the Lord Savior himself, all the present and future rulers of this monastery not to attempt by any kind of wickedness to violate this testament of our authority. But if anyone does so, I invoke against him almighty God and all his avenging saints, together with the souls devoted to God who bestowed these properties upon him.

“And so that the firmness of this testament might be fully strengthened, we have subscribed with our own hand and have asked our most reverend bishop Humfridus to reinforce it with his subscription.

“Done at the monastery of Aria, on the sixth day before the Kalends of April, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 856, in the first leap-year cycle, in the fifth indiction, and with the intercalary month, on the Saturday before mid-Lent, in the seventeenth year of the reign of lord Charles, together with his brother Louis and his nephew Lotharius.

“I, Adalardus, abbot, have confirmed this with my own hand.

“I, Humeridus, bishop, have confirmed this testament with my own hand.

“I myself, Guntbertus, a sinner, in the name of God, at the command of lord abbot Adalardus and with his assent to my petitions, together with the venerable bishop Humfridus, have subscribed.”

## LXXXIX. Privilege of King Charles concerning the cell of the Lord Savior at Steneland

*(25 July 866.)*

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity.

“Charles, by the grace of God king.

“We know that our royal excellence is obligated to provide both firmness and protection for the devout institutions of God’s servants; and we do not doubt that this will benefit us in the present life and in future blessedness.

“Therefore let all the faithful of God’s holy Church, present and future, know that the venerable man Humfridus, bishop and abbot, petitioned our loftiness concerning certain cells in his diocese, namely at the place called Saint Savior, or Steneland. The venerable matron Bertruda established this place in honor of the Lord God and Savior Jesus Christ, together with her son Goibertus, as part of her dower, when she went to Rome and there ended her life; and they wished it to be assigned for preservation and enlargement in the service of God to her nephew Guntbertus, the son of Goibertus, who still survives.

“And also concerning another place, on the island above the Agniona, near the monastery of Saint Bertinus, which the aforementioned Guntbertus, through the arrangement and assistance of the aforesaid venerable bishop, and through the support of other relatives and friends, has sought to devote to the service of that Lord Savior, though it is still almost entirely lacking all necessities: he asked that we strengthen these holy places, together with the small properties attached to them, by royal decree and protection.

“Therefore, in the place of God, we decree and confirm, and for future times we bind them also by divine oath, that these holy places remain inseparably joined under one administration in honor of our Lord Savior Jesus Christ, and that those serving God the Savior in them may enjoy the desired peace, suffering no opposition either from ecclesiastical prelates or from secular power.

“And let the properties dedicated to God the Savior by the aforesaid Bertruda, Goibertus, and Guntbertus, or increased from whatever source, and those which by God’s grace are yet to be increased, pay nothing whatsoever, now or in the future, to any person or dignity on any pretext, however necessary it may be judged, except for the food and clothing of those serving God there; the lamps of wax and oil before the holy relics; the necessities of restoration; care, according to their means, of the poor and guests; and, with all the resources of the aforesaid persons, an annual commemoration in alms for the servants of God and the poor.

“And, with complete integrity and with the appurtenances of their lands, both in land and slaves and in unassessed goods, just as they are now possessed, without any subtraction or diminution, the aforementioned faithful of God and of us, Guntbertus, a cleric tonsured by Pope Eugenius for the apostle Saint Peter, shall remain throughout his life as custodian of these holy places, in complete peace and without disturbance from anyone’s ill will. After him, the person whom he has raised in the service of the Lord Savior and found worthy and excellent; and thereafter, forever, let this be preserved for the holy community.

“We ask our successors and charge them by the Lord Savior himself not to allow this decree of ours to be overturned in any way by any contrivance, but rather to confirm it most firmly themselves.

“And so that this confirmation of our excellence may retain perpetual force in the name of God, we ordered it to be sealed beneath with our ring.

“Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of August, in the twenty-seventh year of King Charles.

“Andater, notary, at the direction of Gauzlinus, reviewed and subscribed.”

## XC. Memorandum concerning the property, revenue, and provisions of the Lord Savior, when Abbot Hilduinus unjustly took everything from Guntbertus on the Kalends of September, in the year of the Lord 868

### Concerning the ecclesiastical furnishings of the Lord Savior

There are four chests there, furnished with gold and silver; three crosses; one chalice with a silver paten; one bronze censer. Three hanging chalices; four bands on bell-ropes, fashioned with gold and silver.

### Concerning vestments

Four pallia; one linen pallium; two corporals; three girdles; one alb; two chasubles; one stole; one sub-cinctorium furnished with gold; one deaconal dalmatic.

### Concerning books

One missal; one lectionary; one antiphonary; three homiliaries; one book of Kings; one baptismal book; the Homilies of Gregory; the Epistles of Paul; Genesis; the Prophets.

At the church of the Lord Savior, by the gate, there are sixty-five *bunaria* of arable land; twenty *bunaria* of meadow; twenty *bunaria* of fattening and beech forest; and fifteen *bunaria* of small woodland. There are nineteen servants, men and women, who among them all possess no more than seven manses comprising twelve *bunaria*. There are fourteen slaves: the cowherd has four *bunaria*; the shepherd has three *bunaria*.

At Curmontium, between cultivated and uncultivated land, fifty *bunaria*; eight slaves.

For lights, construction, roofing, repair of the church, and incense, between Steneland and Winingahem there are twenty *bunaria* of land and forest.

At Triacum and the land of Trudbaldus; at Henrikingahem and Reka; in the marsh which Goibertus himself gave to the altar, twenty-six *bunaria*.

At Kilciacum, which was given as alms by Edeberga, twelve poor people are fed from it each year in her annual commemoration.

Likewise at Sethliacum and Campanias, eighteen *bunaria*, given as alms by Trudlinda, for whom one hundred poor people are fed in her annual commemoration.

At Quintuicum, one mansus.

Likewise, for the lights of Goibertus, Guntbertus, Trudlinda, and Riquio, from which one pound and five solidi must come between revenue and lamp-fund, for the making of alms and the needs of the clergy.

In the marsh at Hammavinc, one mansus given by Abbot Adalardus, from which ten solidi come.

At Simpiacum, twelve *bunaria*, which Zoppo gave for five pounds of silver, from which three solidi ought to come.

At Sedneversingahem, which Liodricus gave, eighteen *bunaria*, from which three payments are due.

Likewise, the forest at Gruonoberg, with the land at Dagmaringahem, which Abbot Adalardus granted, from which two solidi come.

From the lamps, from the administration of Trudbaldus, eight solidi come.

From the garden on the island, fifteen solidi.

Total: two pounds.

From precarious holdings come two solidi and six denarii; ten small measures of salt.

Likewise, what was expended annually from these properties for lights, wax, oil, fat, and all necessities in God’s sanctuary:

Eight clerics were fed and clothed on the Nones of November.

At Goibertus’s annual commemoration, five measures of fine flour for the brothers; two measures of flour for the provision of servants and the poor; three measures of beer; one payment of cheese; five solidi for fish; an unspecified number of sextarii of fat; one large sextarius of honey; one ounce of [Note: The name of the item does not appear]; one ounce of cumin; one ounce between cinnamon, galangal, and clove; seven or eight measures of wine; one measure for the Mount; three pounds of wax.

On the sixth day before the Ides of November, at the dedication of the church, for the use of the brothers and guests: five measures of fine flour; fifteen measures of beer; for guests and the poor, two and a half payments of cheese; four *frinsingae*; for 365 poor people, as much coarse flour as necessary; five solidi for fish; seven measures of wine; fifteen chickens.

On the sixth day before the Kalends of January, one measure of wine for the brothers; likewise on the Ides of January; likewise on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March, and one hundred poor people; two measures of coarse flour; one measure of beer with *compasse*.

On the Nones of March, one measure for the poor, as above.

On the octave of Easter, or on Easter in the following year, one measure for the poor, as above.

On the fourth day before the Nones of May, one measure for the poor, as above.

On the sixth day before the Ides of May, one measure for the poor, as above.

On the Ides of July, one measure for the poor, as above.

On the eighth day before the Ides of August, one measure for the poor, as above.

On the Ides of September, one measure for the poor, as above.

On the fourth day before the Nones of October, two chalices for the poor, as above.

At the beginning of the must, one measure.

Odlandus the smith has at Kessiacum as much of the poor land as Abbot Adalardus granted: fifty *bunaria*, no slaves.

Bernardus, the advocate, has at Vostringe the land which Goibertus gave: fifty *bunaria*, no slaves.

### Concerning the cowherds

Ratwinus has, among younger and older cattle, seven cows; two nursing cows with calves; three barren cows; three three-year-old heifers. He owes payments. Altogether there are twenty head.

### Concerning the sheep

Vodel has fifty nursing ewes; twenty-three barren sheep; thirteen wethers; fifty lambs. Altogether there are 136 head.

[Note: Perhaps read “or concerning the shepherds,” or “the shepherd.”]

At Curmontium, Huobbes has thirteen wethers; eight yearlings; thirty-six nursing ewes; fourteen barren sheep; thirty-six lambs. Altogether there are 106 head; he owes thirty payments.

At Steneland there are thirty pigs, large and small; two oxen for slaughter; twelve chickens; three ducks.

There are there, of spelt above the seed requirement, fifteen *bennae*; thirty wagonloads of *baliarchus* [an uncertain grain]; fifteen wagonloads of oats; two wagonloads of barley; thirty-five wagonloads of hay.

Altogether, among oxen, cows, sheep, and pigs, there are 300 head.

After this, I, Guntbertus, in the month of June of the following year, offered to the Lord Savior two tablets of purple marble worth four pounds; a subdeaconal dalmatic; a bracelet for a bell containing five silver solidi; and various quires of the Old Testament.

I also gave eight denarii at Boulogne for the material of the altar.

## XCI. *(27 July 868.)*

“In the year of the Lord 868 and in the twenty-eighth year of the reign of King Charles [Note: More correctly, it seems, the twenty-ninth], on the sixth day before the Kalends of August, while Guntbertus was preparing to go to Rome, at Vuaebrante, an episcopal estate, in the upper chamber, before lord Bishop Humfridus, Count Unigmarus, Meio, and Odbertus, Berhardus and Erkembaldus, acting as third parties on behalf of their father Asbaldus, gave, at Humbaldingahem and Embrica, in the county of Thérouanne, whatever Goibertus had there and had ordered to be given to his son Guntbertus; and after them Heremarus returned it to Folkramnus and Asbaldus, so that, if Guntbertus returned, they should act as he had ordered; but if he did not return, they should act as his messenger instructed, as third parties, in his own alms and those of his father, as those who would render an account before God.

“Done in the thirteenth year of the episcopate of Bishop Humfridus, while he too was preparing to go to Rome.

“Sign of Fardulfus, the advocate. Sign of Grimbaldus, the senior. Sign of Bertlandus. Sign of Brunstenius.

“In the name of God, I, Guntbertus, a sinner and priest, going to Rome, to my lord Saint Peter, to whom I was entrusted from infancy and where I was made a cleric, asking and charging by the Lord that these things be carried out in this manner, wrote this with my own hand, being very ill in head and eyes, and subscribed.”

## XCII. Concerning the land of Humbertusin, in the county of Beauvais, given to Saint Bertinus

“Let it be known to all the faithful that in the time of King Hugh, father of King Robert, and in the time of Abbot Unalterus of the monastery of Saint Bertinus, Saint Bertinus possessed a certain land in the county of Beauvais called Humbertusin, on the little river Tera. Over it there was placed a certain monk named Milo, indeed of Saint Bertinus, archdeacon of the Church of Thérouanne.

“But because he served worldly pomp too greatly, and on account of this neglected his fidelity to God, he gave that land to Rainardus of Baledin in exchange for money, on the condition that every year, for its rent, he would pay 200 solidi in Beauvais currency for as long as he lived. He transmitted this payment, for as long as he lived, through a certain John, an inhabitant of that land of ours, on the ninth day of September, on the feast of Saint Bertinus.”

The rest is missing from the manuscript.

# In the Year of the Lord 967. Gunzo the Grammarian, Deacon of Novara

[Col. 1279]

# Historical Notice Concerning Gunzo

*(Histoire littéraire de la France, vol. VI, p. 386.)*

## I.

Gunzon was a fairly common name in France and the neighboring countries in the tenth century. We have already seen a Gunzon, deacon of the church of Novara, from whom there is a letter to Atto, bishop of Vercelli. Orderic Vitalis (book III, p. 498) makes known to us another Gunzon, a priest in Lorraine, upon whom a striking miracle was performed through the intercession of Saint Josse after the discovery of his body, in 977.

We also find a third Gunzon (MAB. *An.* book L, no. 3), abbot of Sainte-Colombe at Sens under the reign of Hugh Capet. Finally, a work from the same century on grammatical subjects (MART. *Amp. Coll.* I, pp. 294–295) presents us with a fourth Gunzon, who is its author, and whom for this reason we have thought we could call the Grammarian.

There appear, then, at first sight, to be four Gunzons, each different from the others. But if one examines the matter more closely and investigates their history in greater depth, it may perhaps emerge that these four figures, apparently distinguished by their external characteristics, are in reality reduced to two.

It is beyond dispute that differences of status and variety of residence are not by themselves sufficient reasons for dividing or multiplying the persons in whom they occur. We have an irrefutable proof of this in the person of Saint Jerome and in that of Didier, a priest of Aquitaine.

On this basis, it may readily be the case that Gunzon, deacon of the church of Novara, was the same person as Gunzon, priest in Lorraine; that this priest was the author of the work mentioned above; and consequently that he was the same as Gunzon the Grammarian. What remains is to produce evidence showing that these various characteristics could be united in one and the same person.

First, there can be no doubt on the grounds of chronological agreement. It was around the middle of [Col. 1279C] this century that Gunzon exercised the diaconate in the church of Novara. The work in question was composed a few years later, and the priest Gunzon was still living in 977, doubtless at an advanced age.

Just as the different periods indicated above suit one and the same person, so too does the variety of his places of residence. Gunzon the Grammarian himself tells us that King Otto I summoned him from Italy to his territories, of which Lorraine then formed part. What he says about the usefulness of this migration, and the books that he brought with him, reveals the true reason for his change of residence. We need only recall here the careful attention paid by Brunon, Otto’s brother, to attracting to his court, from distant countries as well as from nearer ones, all the learned men of whom he heard. [Col. 1280A] There can reasonably be no doubt that Gunzon was among them. From this fact, once established, another follows: this Gunzon, summoned from Italy to Otto’s court, was probably the same as the deacon of Novara, who was already reputed to possess such learning that the learned Atton, bishop of Vercelli, sought his advice.

This probability gains new force from what our grammarian says about the means employed to bring him out of Italy. King Otto, he says, repeatedly had the reigning princes urged to let me come to his territories. But since I was not so subject to them, nor of so lowly a condition, that they could compel me, he decided to ask me himself; and I promised him that I would come. Thus, he adds, I left Italy with him, and in fact came here. All these circumstances suit a cleric perfectly, and [Col. 1280B] even imply that Gunzon was merely a subject in relation to Italy. This point deserves attention for our purpose, as will become clear below.

History does not inform us of all the events of Gunzon’s life after he had gone to Otto’s court. Probability must make up for this deficiency. There is every reason to believe that Brunon, having obtained from this learned deacon the literary assistance he had sought, raised him to the priesthood and gave him some benefice in Lorraine, of which he was duke while also being archbishop of Cologne. The undertaking by which this prince sought to organize and civilize the Lorrainers required him to place among them persons capable of helping him carry out his plan. Gunzon, who possessed learning and a library rich for his time, was particularly well suited to succeed in this. According to this plan, which is entirely natural and based on what was taking place then, it should not seem extraordinary that the same person who held the diaconate in Italy was raised to the priesthood in Lorraine. Such a thing happens commonly—or, rather, happens every day.

Having proved that Gunzon the Grammarian was the same as the deacon and priest of that name and period, it is impossible to show the same thing with regard to Gunzon, or Guncion, abbot of Sainte-Colombe at Sens. The learned M. l’abbé Le Beuf (vol. II, pp. 25, 116), to whom the contrary opinion seemed probable, failed to take account of two nearly conclusive reasons, which by themselves suffice to overturn it, or rather make it impossible to establish. On the one hand, it is certain that Gunzon the Grammarian was never a monk of the kind that the abbot of Sainte-Colombe was. This is evident not only from the events of his life just related, but also from various passages in [Col. 1281A] his own work, in which, wishing to express the contempt he felt for the monk of Saint-Gall against whom he is writing, he designates him by this humiliating name: “this hooded fellow,” *cucullatus*, equivalent to “this rough monk.” This certainly is not the language of a writer who had himself been a monk. Moreover, the dates do not agree. The dispute of our grammarian took place, and his work was consequently written, before 960; whereas the abbot of Sainte-Colombe first became known under the reign of Hugh Capet, around 988, and was still living under the reign of Henry I, his grandson, at least around 1027, when Gunzon the Grammarian had long since left this world. There can be no doubt of this, since at the time of his dispute he was already approaching old age.

There is some evidence that this grammarian was French by nationality and born in France. We saw above that he represents himself as a subject in relation to Italy. He may have gone there either in the retinue of King Hugh or of his son Lothair, or with one of those other Frenchmen who were then established there as bishops. It was also very common at that time for Frenchmen to settle beyond the Alps, especially in Lombardy. This feature of Gunzon’s history, together with what he says about the nature of his mother tongue, which had a close affinity with Latin—*quae latinitati vicina est*, “which is close to Latin”—shows that it was French. Indeed, at that time there was no language to which this description applied better. It is even known that French was formerly called Roman, partly because it had developed from the language spoken in our provinces by the Gauls who followed Roman law; and the language of our ancient Gauls was none other than Latin. It is under this latter designation that Ademar of Chabanais (LAB., *Bib. nov.*, vol. II, p. 166) presents the French language when he says that the Normans converted to the faith abandoned the language of [Col. 1281C] their country and became accustomed to speaking that of Neustria, where they settled in this century. There is no indication that the Italian language of that time differed from Latin; nor has there ever been any great affinity between Latin and the Teutonic or German language. Thus Gunzon’s expression can refer only to the French language.

It is true that Gunzon later seems to say in his work that he was Italian rather than French. This occurs where, comparing the temerity of his adversary with that of Dares, who dared to challenge Entellus of Sicily, he adds that an impudent monk also dared to attack Gunzon the Italian. But it is likely that he bore this designation because of the long residence he had made in Italy. There are a thousand examples of such a practice, especially in the centuries of the Middle Ages and later. Ademar (LAB., ibid., p. 205), whom we have just cited, provides a well-known example when he calls Saint Brunon, founder of the Carthusian order, who was from Cologne, “Brunon of Reims,” because of the long residence he had made at Reims.

When Gunzon left Italy, he departed in the retinue of King Otto. But he did not continue along the same route: he made his way by the abbey of Saint-Gall. In a conversation there with Ekkehard, the schoolmaster of the house, in the presence of the students, he happened to make a grammatical error. Pedantic minds are found in every age and every country. Ekkehard pointed out this error in a manner so impolite, not to say so coarse, that Gunzon was deeply offended and from that moment conceived the plan of taking revenge. He postponed carrying it out, and did not execute it until the work that we are about to discuss. Insult was added to his ill manners. Not only was he told that such an error deserved the punishment of a schoolboy, although the person who had committed it was already advanced in age; they also meant him to understand that a man capable of making such errors was wholly unfit for the purpose intended for him, and that he was therefore advised to return to the place from which he had come.

The advice was too humiliating and misplaced for Gunzon to follow it. He continued on his way and went to Otto’s territories. He brought with him about a hundred volumes, among them works of Plato, Aristotle, Cicero, and Martianus Capella on the liberal arts. This occurred in or around 957, on Otto’s return from his second expedition into Italy against King Berengar and his son Adalbert. What Gunzon says about the deposition of an abbot of Saint-Gall and the violent death of the man placed in his stead—events of which he speaks as still recent—leads one to this conclusion. Clearly he alludes to the fate of Abbot Cralon, deposed in 953, and to that of Annon, his brother and successor, put to death in 954. It is certain [Col. 1282B] moreover that this was before Otto attained the imperial dignity, and therefore before the end of 960.

We do not know where in France or Italy Gunzon studied; but what remains of his writings shows that he had received as good an education as could be obtained in his time, and that he possessed especially extensive knowledge of literature. He doubtless continued to cultivate it privately, and perhaps even publicly by teaching others, until his death, the year of which is unknown, although we know that he lived at least until 977, when the miracle mentioned above took place upon him.

## II.

On the supposition, already established and proved, that our grammarian was the same as Gunzon, deacon of Novara, we must count among the productions of his pen the letter that he wrote in that capacity to Atton, bishop of Vercelli. It has been preserved for us [Col. 1282C] together with several letters of that prelate. Atton, who paid particular attention to having the canons observed in every respect, consulted Gunzon about spiritual affinity in relation to marriage, specifically between a godson and the daughter of his godfather. Gunzon confined himself almost entirely to transcribing for him Pope Zachary’s rescript to Theodore, bishop of Pavia, on the same subject. This rescript, together with a brief exordium and a few lines of Gunzon’s own at its end, constitutes his reply to Atton.

The principal work of Gunzon known to us is a very long letter to the monks of Reichenau, which, because of its prolixity and the variety of subjects discussed in it, would better deserve the name of treatise or short book. It was written on the occasion and as a consequence of the grammatical error into which the author fell while passing through Saint-Gall, and of the coarse criticism that Ekkehard made of it. It followed that unfortunate event closely, and it appears that Gunzon began it as soon as he had arrived [Col. 1282D] in Otto’s territories. We therefore have its true date: between the years 954 and 960, before this prince, who is always called king, was recognized as emperor.

Gunzon is entirely occupied in it with avenging the intemperate criticism directed against his error and the offensive insult he received on that occasion. To form a proper idea of his work, one must view it both as one of the liveliest and most stinging satires and as a rich piece of learning, considering the century that produced it. Strictly speaking, it is a tissue of insults—but insults, although often coarse, always accompanied by some display of learning. In general there is wit, but not that refined, delicate, playful wit which gives such pieces their full value. The passion is too evident, and almost everything is said with as much arrogance and presumption as contempt and coarseness. [Col. 1283A] There is even something childish in it. Such is the malicious comparison he draws between Ekkehard, his critic, and Achan, who is mentioned in Joshua—a comparison on which he nevertheless dwells with a certain satisfaction. Gunzon, knowing as much as he did, could have taken revenge more effectively by taking revenge more nobly.

Gunzon’s error consisted in using an accusative where an ablative was required. He therefore undertakes to show that, because he made this error in familiar speech, he was no less well instructed in grammar and literature. After proving, by a great display of learning drawn from ancient orators, poets, and historians, that the best authors of Latin have sometimes used one case for another, in both prose and verse, he shows that in speech one should pay less attention to the letter than to the meaning. He then goes on to discuss almost all the [Col. 1283B] sciences then in use, especially the liberal arts. Although he does so with excessive ostentation, always accompanied by insults and sovereign contempt for his critic, it must be admitted that he treats the subject as a man who, for his time, possesses it thoroughly. He speaks not only as a grammarian but also as a physicist and astronomer. On the subject of astronomy, he rightly blames Ekkehard for objecting to its being studied. In treating this matter, he raises a highly relevant question: when Joshua halted [Col. 1284A] the course of the sun, did the other stars and planets stop as well? He does not forget music, of which he gives a very fine eulogy in a few words. One clear sign that he possessed some taste and discernment is the low opinion he had of the poetry of his age. He seriously doubted whether anyone then existed who was capable of composing a poem that truly deserved the name.

Finally, after uttering many insults, he comes to the precept of praying for one’s enemies. This he himself does in a prayer to God consisting of thirty-two hexameter verses, which show that he had applied himself to versification with more success than almost all the poets of his time. This is how he ends his work, which would be genuinely estimable if it were freed from the insults, contemptuous remarks, and displays of vanity, presumption, and affected self-satisfaction with which it is swollen. Otherwise, learning is scattered through it with a lavish hand. It contains citations of more than [Col. 1284B] twenty authors: Homer, Plato, Aristotle, Terence, Cicero, Sallust, Statius, Horace, Virgil, Cinna, Ovid, Persius, Juvenal, Lucan, Servius, Porphyry, Priscian, Donatus, Boethius, Fabius Planciades, and Fulgentius. Among the Fathers of the Church, only Saint Jerome and Saint Gregory the Great are cited.

This work had remained buried in obscurity until 1724. At that time Dom Martène and Dom Durand published it from a manuscript of the abbey of Saint-Amand, perhaps the only one in which it is now found.

[Col. 1283]

### Letter of Gunzo to Atton, Bishop of Vercelli

(See among Atton’s letters above, vol. CXXXIV, col. 111.)

[Col. 1283]

### Another Letter of the Same Gunzo to the Brothers of Reichenau

He attacks a monk of Saint-Gall who had held him in contempt because he had made a grammatical error in a certain case, and he shows that he was learned both in grammar and in the other liberal studies.

(Martenne, *Amplissima Collectio*, vol. I, col. 293.)

[Col. 1283C]

To the sacred congregation established at Reichenau, Gunzo offers the service of pure devotion.

I believe that an injury inflicted by human perversity on anyone should not be entrusted to popular judgment, but to those whom the matter concerns, so that not only the weight of the offense may be considered, but also its conformity with the rule. For the same thing is not good in every case, even though it is permitted equally to all. Thus marriage is permitted to laymen but denied to those in holy orders. In the sphere of vices also, certain things are permitted to some and not at all to others. For those who bear swords are permitted to strike down the enemies of the state without guilt. For, as the Apostle says, “they do not bear swords without reason”; yet the clerical order appears to stand far removed from this permission. Therefore something may be permitted to a layman that is not permitted to a cleric, especially a monk, whose [Col. 1284C] rule is stricter and whose transgression is consequently more blameworthy. Hence it is read concerning holy orders: “The higher the rank, the graver the fall”; and Juvenal’s couplet likewise accords with this judgment:

> Every fault of the mind bears a more conspicuous  
> guilt in proportion as the sinner is held in greater esteem.

But lest the understanding of your reverences be held back by the delay of a preface, in accordance with the rules of the art I ask you to be favorable, attentive, and teachable in hearing my complaint concerning an injury inflicted on me by a certain hooded fellow in the monastery of Saint-Gall. I call him “hooded” because I cannot properly describe a man absolutely corrupted by the deceptions of a fox, concerning whom Persius says:

> You preserve a cunning fox beneath your fetid breast.

Who would call him a monk in whom nothing worthy of that name is found? For a hood does not justify [Col. 1285A] the man whom fraternal hatred stains. O dreadful fate, by which human nature, abandoning the dignity of reason, conforms itself to a beast’s life, as it is written: “Man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared with senseless beasts and became like them.” Hence in the Gospel the Lord calls Herod a fox: “Go and tell that fox.” And the Psalmist says: “They shall be portions of foxes.” We also find wicked men called dogs and swine in the divine books: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor throw your pearls before swine.” They are called bulls and calves: “Many calves surrounded me; fat bulls besieged me.” In the sacred books we find wicked men called such names that they are compared not only with animals but even with insensible things. For it is written: [Col. 1285B] “Behold, the nations are as a drop from a bucket, and are counted as a speck on the scales.” Again: “All nations are as nothing before him; they are counted by him as nothing and vanity.” From this it is clearly inferred that those are counted among the nations who glory in being distinguished by the Christian name without works. Thus, abusing the free will granted to them, they are either compared with irrational animals or reduced to nothing; their end is the same. Do not suppose that I wish to speak here in a strictly doctrinal manner; nevertheless, I wish to rouse your minds, so that you may recognize both the wantonness of the hooded fellow and the fact that I am not what he thought me. The order of the narrative must therefore begin at this point.
