What I confess has perhaps reached your ears.

The venerable King Otto had frequently made efforts with certain princes of Italy [Col. 1285C] so that I might be summoned to these kingdoms. But since I was not so subject to anyone, nor considered so low in fortune, that I could be compelled, he turned to me with signs of entreaty and received from me a promise, as a pledge that I would come. Thus it happened that, when he returned from Italy, I came with him, undertaking, to speak truthfully, a task beyond my own strength. What does not drive us on through charity? What does not call us forward through brotherly delight? God, who searches hearts, knows that I did not come in order to harm anyone, but to benefit many. Nor did I advance like a Briton bristling with darts of criticism, but with the gift of charity. Those who have learned that literary duties are not wholly foreign to me know that I speak the truth. By “literary duties” I mean not lying in wait through deceit, but wishing through affection to be of service. Thus, across rugged mountains and precipitous valleys, we finally reached the monastery of Saint-Gall. I was so exhausted that I had almost lost the use of my hands, scorched by the mountain cold, so that I could neither mount nor dismount from my horse unless I were carried by other hands. Yet, as I arrived, I had the confident hope of peaceful rest in a place of monastic habitation. I saw frequent bowing of heads, hoods neatly arranged between the shoulder blades, gentle walking, and few words. I suspected nothing evil, except that Juvenal’s saying secretly [Col. 1286A] bit me, by which he condemns false philosophers in these words:

> Their speech is rare, but their desire to be silent is great.

Who would believe that this was said of a monk? How could a pagan know of hooded perversity? Unaware of the life there, I was delighted and waited to see whether, amid the rare whispers, some spark of philosophical study might shine. Nothing of the kind: schemes of deceit were being prepared. There was, in fact, a little fellow who lived among the leaders; his master, some sort of teacher, frequently looked at him with eyes turned toward the goats, and, as I believe, snarled while observing that his favorite clung to the powerful, considering no difference between the chastity of a turtledove and the obscenity of a partridge. Whenever he went out and came in, he entrusted to the disciple the deceptions he was preparing.

It was night, and sleep was pressing down cares with sluggishness,

> and Liber was demanding his rights in the well-filled belly.

When, as fortune would have it, I offended them in trivial conversation through a change of one case—namely, by putting an accusative for an ablative—then it was finally made clear that the master of dubious learning had spent the whole day teaching his pupil the praises of obedience. The boy whom I mentioned above was present; he condemned so grave a crime as the alteration of a single case, declared that I, an old man, deserved schoolboys’ rods, and expressed this in wanton verses, as though in this matter the hooded fellow considered himself wise. Yet who is unaware of the verses of a wanton monk? Having leisure, he opens his mouth and emits a poem, ignorant of the structure of verse. He does not know how to insert one or two purple patches that might shine brightly, how to make characters and ages resound, or how to observe dignity in poetry. He merely thrusts out his lips and ejects a poem; and Persius says that such poetry does not enter the mind but the loins:

> … when songs  
> enter the loins and are scratched within by trembling verse.

Again, speaking of those who delight in soft pronunciation, he says:

> What then? Is it to be read tenderly, with the neck relaxed?  
> They filled their grim horns with Mimallonian blasts,  
> and the Bassarid, having seized the head of a proud calf,  
> is about to carry it away.

Horace says of Lucilius:

> For he was often faulty in this respect: he dictated two hundred verses in an hour,  
> standing on one foot as though it were a great achievement.

I confess that as a young man I was touched by this fault. I am ashamed of it, but I was not, like a certain monk, covered in a sheep’s fleece without manners. Do not suppose that I say this because I wish to bring the study of poetry into contempt. I find even ecclesiastical men using poetry; but I wonder whether in our time a writer of true poetry can be found. For Cinna [Note: [Col. 1285] Cinna was a highly learned poet, a contemporary of Virgil, who mentions him in Eclogue 9:

> For neither do I yet seem to vary, nor to utter things worthy of Cinna,  
> but to honk like a goose among melodious swans.]

polished his book *Smyrna* for ten years, and Horace prescribed that poems should be brought forth only after nine years, without public display. Hence Juvenal says of the author of a poem:

> It is the work of a great mind, not something to be produced on a blanket.

[Col. 1287A] Persius likewise says:

> I shall not fear praise if something more fitting should happen to emerge,  
> since such a bird is rare.

Statius also, addressing his book, says:

> O Thebaid, watched over through twice six years,  
> live, I pray you; but do not attempt the divine Aeneid.

Yet the same *Aeneid* that Statius praises, when the poet was at the end of his life, he wished to consign uncorrected to Vulcan. They did not, I think, consider the labor devoted to verse a small matter. But now who belches forth and boasts of the finest poems, although a buffoon may produce them at every street corner, in Persius’ words:

> He neither beats his reading-desk nor knows the taste of bitten nails.  
> He wants to set in the middle of the earth and at the end the dung  
> that his wanton Muse, destined to live only briefly, has loosened for him.

Consider, I beg you, what that prudent man of whom we are speaking gained from criticizing one case, or what great thing he displayed about himself. Moreover, the *solecism* arising from changes of case is found frequently not only among writers of verse but also among those writing without meter. Virgil astonishingly used an accusative for a genitive or ablative:

> But with a rock and a huge fragment of mountain  
> he seizes Latagus by the mouth and opposing face …

instead of “he seizes Latagus by the mouth” or “Latagus’ face.” This figure is exceedingly rare among Latins but frequent in Homer, as in the expression *Ecrousen Achille ton poda*, that is, “he struck Achilles on the foot.”

Something must therefore be said about the alteration of cases, lest the foolish monk seem to excuse himself. In Terence, a genitive is used for a nominative: “this little matter I shall sleep off,” instead of “this little matter.” In Virgil: “whatever this kingdom,” instead of “whatever this realm.” A dative is used for a genitive: “the harsh Achilles,” instead of “of harsh Achilles.” An ablative is used for an accusative: “the cry goes to heaven,” instead of “into heaven.” A dative is used for an ablative in Juvenal:

> You weave Penelope better and more lightly than Arachne [does].

Persius used a vocative for a nominative:

> Do you greet your critic, you of the striped robe?

instead of “you in the striped robe.” Again, to find a nominative used for a vocative, I consider inquiry unnecessary, since the divine books are full of examples. Virgil nevertheless says:

> Horn-bearing river, ruler of the waters of the Hesperides,

instead of “O river.” If anyone wishes to know this matter fully, let him read Priscian’s books on construction.

Observe, I beg you, the madness of the wretched little man, who spent almost an entire day on so trivial a matter. Did he at least have a single little question to propose? Let him hear again an accusative for a dative in the Psalms: “I pleased [him] as a neighbor and as our brother,” instead of “as a neighbor and as a brother.” Perhaps he wishes to read *complangebam*, “I lamented.” So be it. In prose, Sallust uses an ablative for a genitive: “the side hesitated in battle,” instead of “of the battle line.” Likewise, a dative for a genitive: “concerning the Macedonian war of Perseus” (*ad bellum Persi Macedonicum*), instead of “of Perseus” (*Persis*).

In the Gospel, too, according to the grammarians, we find an accusative for a nominative: “Jesus whom you seek is not here,” instead of “Jesus.” And: “The word which you heard is not mine,” instead of “the word.” And in the Psalms: “The stone which the builders rejected,” instead of “the stone.” Such expressions, and a thousand similar ones, are attributed by the writers of the arts to error, as in Donatus: “The city which I am founding is yours.” But who is so brainless as to think that the words of sacred eloquence are bound by the rules of Donatus or Priscian?

It is read in sacred history: “We do not know what happened to this Moses, who brought us out of the land of Egypt.” Who speaks in such a way now? “We do not know what happened to this Moses to him”? And in the Psalms: “He sent Moses his servant, Aaron whom he chose, him.” Although some, for their own convenience, may wish to make this redundant, Virgil used the same construction when he said:

> Then the father of men and gods, smiling,  
> tasted kisses from his daughter.

But because this seemed harsh to Servius, he wanted *olli* to be an adverb of time, meaning “then.” “No one,” he says, “says, ‘he tasted kisses from that daughter.’” For a pronoun should be placed not with a pronoun but in the place of a noun.

Since the sequence of the divine Scriptures is thus constituted, who is so lost as to dare either criticize or alter such expressions? The monk of Saint-Gall falsely thought that I was removed from knowledge of the grammatical art, although I am sometimes hindered by the usage of our common language, which is close to Latin. We also sometimes go beyond the rule through negligence or human imperfection, of which Priscian says: “I believe that nothing in human inventions can be found perfect in every respect.” We sin through negligence, as Horace says of Homer:

> At times good Homer nods,

that is, he writes carelessly. We can also mark this in Virgil, where he says: “The ox stretched out on the ground.” It is a very poor verse, having a monosyllabic noun at the end, unless perhaps it concerns small animals, as in Horace:

> The mountains are in labor; a ridiculous mouse will be born.

Moreover, Servius says that our predecessors wished errors to lie not in expression but in meaning, as in Sallust: “The worse each person has acted, the safer he is.” It is stated in the art of grammar that *tam*, *magis*, *maxime*, *minus*, and *minime* are joined only with the positive degree. Therefore Sallust’s sentence agrees with sense and meaning, not with wording.

Aristotle agrees with this point in his book *Peri Hermeneias*, in these words: “Those things that are in the voice are signs of the affections that are in the soul. Every sign is the sign of something. The thing therefore exists before the sign. The thing must therefore be weighed before the sign.” Moreover, different things are accustomed to be signified by one and the same sign: for example, the lion signifies Christ and the devil. What madman would say that the devil is indicated where it is written, “The lion from the tribe of Judah has conquered,” or that Christ is indicated where it says, “Deliver me from the lion’s mouth”? It is plainly evident that not words alone must be examined, but meaning as well.

This is also confirmed in Moses, who, imbued with all the wisdom of the Egyptians, who are known to have been the discoverers of the liberal arts, is said to have spoken as follows when the Lord sent him to Pharaoh: “I beg you, Lord, I am not eloquent, neither yesterday nor the day before, nor since you began to speak to your servant; I am slow and heavy of tongue.” He was certainly admitting that he was slow in speech; yet no one can properly call him unlearned in philosophy, as the protomartyr Stephen testifies, speaking of him in the Acts of the Apostles: “Moses was learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians.”

Therefore, if you wish to hear more about the force of words and meanings, you must also consider calmly what follows. Listen to what Boethius, a most learned man, says in the second edition of his book *Peri Hermeneias*: “One should support obscure meanings with patience and agreement, insofar as this concerns the intention of the speaker, even if the structure of the expressions is not so constituted.”

This is enough to refute the brother’s stupidity. Or do you require more? Unless I am mistaken, the words formed from corruptions or contractions also prove that I speak the truth: in a brief utterance they convey much, as in the name *Verna*, which they say is composed from three corrupted words: *bonus*, “good”; *haereditarius*, “hereditary”; and *natus*, “born.” From the first part, therefore, nothing remains except a letter substituted for another—*v* for *b*—and for that reason some, preserving the proper letter, say *Berna*.

Likewise, a single word, even when uncompounded, can contain several elements, as in Lucan:

> We may overturn all the tombs of our ancestors.

They say that three parts of speech must be understood in this word: a conjunction, a noun, and the substantive verb, so that it means “it will be permitted,” provided that the conjunction is affirmative rather than doubtful.

Furthermore, if discourse consists only in wording and not in meaning, then in the invention of fables nothing is received except bare falsehood; everything that wise men transmit from them for the understanding of truth will be considered superfluous. Fulgentius’ book of mythologies [Note: [Col. 1289D] This Fulgentius was not that famous bishop of Ruspe, a vigorous defender of the Catholic faith against the Arians, but Fabius Planciades Fulgentius, who, besides the book of *Mythologies*, wrote for Chalcidius a book on ancient speech, published by Junius and Mercerus, and a *Moral Exposition of Virgil’s Aeneid*, published by Commelin.] will be regarded as worthless. The mystical meanings of the divine Scriptures will be despised as superfluous. What, then, will distinguish a Jew from a Christian once allegory has been removed? Subunderstandings in both divine and human writings will likewise be considered superfluous.

Terence will appear deranged when he says:

> “I?” “Her?” “What has she to do with him?” “What has she to do with me?”

An incomplete poet will also appear deranged when he says:

> Now you dare, without my divine will, to mingle  
> heaven and earth with the winds and raise such vast masses?

Whom I— . . . [Col. 1289D] Even in the Gospel the sentence will appear mutilated where we read: “Because if you also had known.” It is therefore plainly shown that wisdom consists not so much in words as in meaning, as the Apostle testifies when he says of himself: “Even if unskilled in speech, yet not unskilled in knowledge.” The most celebrated orator likewise admits that eloquence without wisdom is harmful, whereas wisdom without eloquence is beneficial and never harmful.

I could add many examples from divine and secular books, but I do not wish to burden the length of the letter with an abundance of examples. Nevertheless, since the outcome of every matter has its own cause—for, as we read in the Book of Job, nothing happens on earth without a cause—I want you to notice what I believe to be the cause of the unjust criticism directed at the monk of Saint Gall.

I imagine that he once entered the garden of a prudent man, where he tasted a radish grown in dog dung, which is the cause of a foul belch—that is, of malicious criticism. Therefore provide your orchards with barriers, locks, and guards, lest your sweet-smelling vegetables be spoiled by a disgraceful belch. “Bad company,” as the Apostle says, “corrupts good morals.” [Col. 1290B] Yet it should not seem surprising if someone does not fear becoming entangled in lesser vices when he is considered subject to greater vices.

Is not this man of whom we speak one of those who recently drove out their own abbot and brought about the ruin of the man appointed in his place? [Note: [Col. 1289D] Here he clearly indicates the deposition of Abbot Cralo by Lindulf, son of Otto the Great, which took place in the year [Col. 1290D] 953 because of his stricter discipline, which the brothers detested. Anno, his own brother, was substituted for him—“certainly most worthy of the mitre,” says Mabillon, “if he had been lawfully elected.” Shortly afterward they plunged him into ruin; that is, as I interpret it, they handed him over to death. Mabillon indeed reports that he died prematurely the following year, but did not know that he had been killed.] This is said because, unless the man who succeeded him had yielded to the exhortations of the perverse, he might perhaps still be alive.

It is well known that life is sometimes prolonged by good works and shortened by evil ones, as a certain wise man says: “Do not be excessively righteous, lest you die before your time.” In Job, too, we read of the wicked man: “Before his days are fulfilled, he will perish.” And the Psalmist says: “Men of blood and deceit will not halve their days.” In the divine Law also we frequently find: “If anyone does this or that, let him die.” Therefore, by not doing it, let him live.

Consequently, the person who deliberately gives deadly counsel and the person who accepts it are held bound in the same way. Do not, therefore, be surprised if one who kills his father beats his brother. I rejoice that I hear nothing of this sort about you.

“From the wicked,” as it is written, “wickedness proceeds”; for Pallas—that is, wisdom—is continually armed and fortified everywhere. Nevertheless, if you pay careful attention, our guest sinned from necessity. Throughout the day he searched for what he could bring to his hosts in the retreats of his hood, and in it he found nothing except the frauds he had hidden away. “The evil man brings forth evil things from his evil treasury.” Therefore he distributed what he had. Do not be surprised that I speak of a hood: I mean a hood of religion, a hood of disgrace.

Hence Juvenal, speaking of a prostitute:

> She orders the young man to hurry after putting on his hood.

I consider it entirely proper that the qualities of the other attributes be judged according to the character of the person. For it is written: “All things are clean to the clean.” If this is accepted, it follows conversely that all things are unclean to the unclean. Hence the divine Law decreed that whatever had touched unclean things should become unclean.

Nevertheless, because I had apparently suffered an insult from an ecclesiastical man, I bore it heavily. If an enemy had cursed me, I would certainly have endured it; and if one who hated me had spoken great things against me, I might perhaps have hidden myself from him. I was therefore indignant and, moved by human weakness, sought revenge. Yet I knew that the man of whom I am speaking was horned in his private chamber, so that no place for my defense would be available to me. I was a novice, and no one would have believed me even if I had wished to argue my case.

I was also held back by the command of the Wise Man, which says: “Do not answer a fool according to his folly, lest you become like him.” But since there is “a time to speak and a time to be silent,” I now answer, admonished by the same Wise Man: “Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he appear wise to himself.”

As I anxiously and attentively investigated these matters with myself, I examined the attributes of the person that might correspond to fraud. At last I detected in his face the color of base metal, by which precious things are commonly corrupted. Persius says:

> Lest something defective should ring beneath the bronze-gilded gold.

His hair was curled with tongs; his hood was more polished than propriety required; and the feet of his shoes clung to his feet [Note: [Col. 1291D] “Skins” (*pellibus*) should apparently be read here; the following passage from Jerome sufficiently suggests this, where he says, “lest the foot should puff through loose skin.”], so that they could not puff outward. By these signs blessed Jerome teaches that a bridegroom is indicated, saying:

> There are certain clerics of my order who concern themselves with their garments—whether they smell good, whether their fingernails shine, whether their hair pleases by its polished arrangement, whether their foot puffs out through loose skin. When you see such men, consider them bridegrooms rather than clerics.

Hence he himself gives a general judgment, saying: “Neither affected squalor nor elaborate cleanliness suits a Christian.”

Having observed these things, I began carefully to investigate whether the mark of his own name also corresponded to his deeds. Why should it not? [Note: [Col. 1291D] He clearly indicates the elder Ekkehard, [Col. 1292D] who at some time held the position of teacher in the schools of Saint Gall and later became dean. He also refused the dignity of abbot when it was offered to him—certainly not worthy, says Mabillon, of so biting and indecorous a criticism.]

For he was called Achar, as though he had received his name from the omen of a thief. It is well known that, when the city of Jericho was destroyed, Achar stole a golden rule, shekels of a fixed weight, and a scarlet cloak.

Since, then, the names correspond, it is clear that we must investigate how the deeds of the two correspond. The first Achar, whose name is interpreted as “anathema,” stole the golden rule; this second Achar despised the rule of good living. A rule is used so that uprightness may be preserved. Whoever despises the rule of good living steals away the golden standard by theft.

In sacred Scripture, gold generally refers to the splendor of wisdom. Hence blessed Gregory says: “We offer gold to God if we shine before him with the light of wisdom.” Anyone who turns the talent received from God to the use of wicked action is convicted of stealing it.

That same Achar is also said to have stolen two hundred shekels, by which the twofold virtue of charity is not improperly signified. For one hundred is a perfect number, not merely because it is made complete by ten, but because it is found consecrated in the divine books, as in the Gospel where we read: “Another seed fell on good soil and produced fruit a hundredfold.”

The shekel is a kind of weight, and everything is weighed by charity, as it is written: “On these two commandments hang all the Law and the Prophets.” These shekels are said to have been good silver. Silver in the divine books refers to the clarity of speech, as the Psalmist testifies: “The sayings of the Lord are pure sayings, silver tested by fire.”

Yet because the rejected despise charity both in mind and in speech, Achar is rightly said to have committed theft in speech, as though in silver, and in mind, as though in gold: in gold, as it is written, “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer”; in silver, as in the saying, “Whoever says to his brother, ‘Fool,’ will be liable to the fire of Gehenna.”

Moreover, because there are some who not only refuse to share themselves with their brothers but also deny them external goods, Achar is therefore remembered as having stolen, together with the golden rule and the two hundred shekels of silver, a scarlet cloak as well.

Scarlet is fiery in color, and charity is said to burn, as we read in the Gospel: “Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke to us on the road and opened the Scriptures to us?”

What, then, do you decide? Do you not see that in all the things for which the circumcised Achar sinned, the hooded Achar is found guilty? He stole the golden rule when he conceived hostility toward his brother in his mind; he took away the two hundred shekels of silver when he revealed by signs in his speech the hostility conceived in his mind; and he secretly seized the scarlet cloak when he turned the rights of hospitality to the use of wicked accusation.

If anyone foolishly wished to accept the palingenesis, or transmigration of souls, of Pythagoras, he would have no doubt that the soul of the circumcised Achar had entered the body of this man. The former curtailed the commonwealth by theft; this man wished to curtail the commonwealth still more when, having undertaken the journey, he attempted to remove me. Perhaps he himself will realize how much harm he wished to inflict on the commonwealth when, after I have arrived, he learns what useful work I have done.

Amalek met me on the road and wished to block the journey I had begun. The Lord threatened that he would erase Amalek’s memory from the earth. Amalek is interpreted as “a licking people.” Those who lick the surface of letters but do not reach the sweetness of their taste are rightly compared with them. No faithful person doubts that such people are to be compared with hypocrites: while they seek God falsely, they do not deserve to find him. Writers of worldly literature assign such people to servile status, as in Juvenal’s line:

> We strike the face of the slave who licks the pastry.

It is nevertheless astonishing why this most wretched man envied others the good that he did not wish to benefit from himself. Alas! [Col. 1293A] He imitated the devil, who envied humanity the good he had lost.

Such men are shown to have human faces but beastly minds; the Lord speaks of them in the Gospel: “They come in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravenous wolves.”

Would that the man of whom I speak wished to converse with me in your presence, whose prudence I hear has long been tested! I know Achar’s thefts; I know the fraud of the false monk. I am not ignorant on what poor anvil his shafts are forged, nor—having experienced it—how feebly they are hurled by his hand.

Let Horace know that he threatens for me:

> Against the wicked I raise my harshest horns,  
> like a Sygambrian rejected by a faithless son-in-law,  
> or a fierce enemy of Bupalus.  
> Or if someone attacks me with a black tooth,  
> shall I weep unavenged like a child?

A wanton monk, Gunzo the Italian, challenged Dares’ Sicilian Entellus:

> Let Entellus know, from his rash fellow’s fall,  
> with what force he struck down the prostrate Dares.

You have heard the cause of my complaint. You must also hear what the enemy—or, I do not know, the guest—did against the pursuit of literary study.

When I arrived, I was carrying almost a hundred volumes of books, the weapons, so to speak, of peace. An envious enemy turned them toward the pursuit of madness. Among them was Martianus’ compressed account of the seven liberal disciplines. Those who delight only in the pleasures of fable consider it unworthy of attention, although it cannot be fully grasped if the nature of truth is unknown.

There was also the scarcely understood profundity of Plato in the *Timaeus*; Aristotle’s obscurity in the book *On Interpretation* (*Peri Hermenias*), which has scarcely been attempted—or perhaps not understood at all—even in our own times; and the considerable worth of the *Topics* of Cicero and Aristotle.

While I thought that I should be questioned about these and other matters, I was not troubled by the agitation of trivial things but by the weight of an impulse sent from above. Who would have thought that someone should be criticized because of a change in a single grammatical case, when God had granted him many other gifts?

I did not believe that the thief Achar was alive, nor that, according to Pythagoras, souls passed into different bodies. If I accepted these notions, I would begrudge the body of that monk the soul of a human being. Someone defiled with filth joined a pig, rejoicing in frauds; rightly, therefore, the soul of a fox gives him life.

Do not think that I speak out of hatred. Far be it from me to hate what displays a living human being in human form. Although I hate the wickedness that has befallen the man, I nevertheless love his substance, even though that same wickedness, against the will of its possessor, has benefited me. For it has exposed the frauds of many, as Maro testifies:

> Now learn the ambushes of the Greeks,  
> and from one crime learn them all.

It has also stripped away the ignorance of many, and has shown with the clearest evidence that he was raised among the unlearned: he thought that the conceptions of the mind could be detected from the pronunciation of a single grammatical case.

We have often heard the most worthless things expressed in ornate language, and conversely things worthy of utterance marked by humble speech—as if someone were to write the name of the devil in letters of gold and the name of God in ink.

Furthermore, what should be said about people who live without learning? Are not some preferred to certain learned men by the sharpness of their intellect? Ulysses surpassed in intellectual vigor all those who attacked Ilium, so much so that he alone was found worthy of Achilles’ armor.

We also read of Adam’s prudence, by which he assigned names to all creatures—not, however, because he knew grammar, unless perhaps the monk of Saint Gall wishes the first man to have been created knowing all the arts, which he then lost by sinning.

If this is so, then all human beings naturally possess knowledge of every art. Yet we read that free choice was corrupted in the first man, not that knowledge of the arts was shut off. Let whoever can judge this. We, however, lest we become embroiled in controversy over a doubtful matter, shall leave the controversy over trivial things to the obstinate hooded man.

I had thought that he wished to demand from me the foundations of the whole discourse:

1. How are matters arranged so that vowels, semivowels, and mutes are not bounded by fixed intervals, but seem to be confused, so that they appear to have been placed according to the accident of a fool rather than according to reason?

2. Why, after the Latin letters have been received, is the digamma placed not after *v*, like *x*, but after *c*?

3. Are the liberal disciplines to be understood according to their proper force, or according to the capacity of those who apprehend them? For some doubt whether they ought to be taught as they are.

4. Did Donatus or Priscian arrange the parts of speech?

5. Which of them assigned definitions to those parts and their attributes with greater appropriateness? The ancients certainly expended great labor in arranging and defining things.

## On Grammar

Perhaps the swollen monk thinks that grammar, like some worthless object, is contained within his hood. Yet this is not so. He saw her back only once, and, hurrying to see her face, fell because his foot struck against something; he scarcely reached the region of her seat, and from this he becomes arrogant.

This woman yields differently to grammarians and to Aristotle. She teaches Aristotle that nouns cannot be named through oblique cases, while she teaches the grammarians that they can indeed be named in the oblique cases. At times she recalls figurative expressions in such a way as to show to which gender they ought to be assigned. She preserves many other things in which the rashness of fools goes astray.

Let those who have been fortunate enough at least to see Minerva in their dreams possess her, provided that they presume nothing about what follows. For she resists and flees, and even denies that some have seen her back. Yet to those to whom she does present herself to be seen, she does not appear with one identical face. She is shown with one face to this person and another to that.

## On Dialectic

This is shown by the fact that dialectic denied to Aristotle that genus, species, difference, property, and accident subsist, whereas she persuaded Plato that they do subsist. Do you think Aristotle or Plato should be believed more? The authority of both is great, so that scarcely anyone would dare to prefer one to the other in dignity.

This discipline is sometimes so obscured by ambiguity that it is difficult to discover what thing should be placed under what genus. For example, if someone proposes the following: Since everything that exists is regarded either as substance or as accident, what are we to say about difference, which can be called neither substance nor accident?

It cannot be called substance, because it is not predicated in answer to the question “what is it?” It cannot therefore be called an accident, because it informs substance. For whatever constitutes substance is predicated in substance.

This woman is so subtle in wisdom that she believes nearly the whole of logical philosophy can be enclosed within the conclusions of the ten and nine modes. She is thought to be so obedient to Aristotle that she is believed to be his nurse. She knows how to deceive fools by sophistical quibbling, yet she shows how quibbling itself can be avoided.

When she wishes, she stuffs falsehoods together with truths so that they seem properly to coincide at one and the same time and in one and the same place. By a mysterious method she pretends that being and not-being can occur together. She claims that the square of her propositions is arranged so that the return of the oblique sides sometimes comes back without compulsion and sometimes covers itself through compulsion.

For her it is not enough to say that what exists is evil; it must also be said that it is not good. She thinks that words, considered in themselves, are nouns. For the person who speaks produces hearing, while the person who hears rests; and she judges that these things can be said only in an instant of time.

Everywhere she turns toward individuals, like someone playing with the poisons of biting speech—poisons which, when displayed upon the skin, do not cut off life.

How good God is, who has deprived the envious hooded man of such things, by which he might have proved more powerful in frauds! It is well. He lacks the curse of which a certain wise man says: “Whoever speaks sophistically is hateful to God,” and so forth. I therefore congratulate him that he lacks this stain, although not by his own choice.

Perhaps the wretched man would wish to be more miserable than he is, but he is restrained by God’s goodness, and does not understand it. Sitting in the monastery’s private chamber, he thinks himself horned, according to Aristotle’s proverb:

> A snail in its own chamber seems horned to itself,  
> and thinks that in speed it can rival timid fallow deer,

although he can scarcely spend a little coin so as to share a dinner with a companion.

Do not attribute it as a fault that I often repeat the same thing. I follow the example of Juvenal, who says of Crispinus:

> Behold Crispinus again, whom I must often summon  
> to the scene . . .

Cicero likewise often repeats Verres in his *Verrine Orations*.

Nevertheless, since many things worthy of inquiry are found in the liberal disciplines, after briefly tasting a little from grammar and dialectic, I shall attempt to bring forth briefly the power of rhetoric:

> Through speech she promises to release whatever minds  
> she wishes, so that she may turn sad things into joys  
> for the sorrowful, and heal by the speech  
> of a learned tongue.

## On Rhetoric

Its subject matter, divided into three kinds, shapes the constitution of a case. Many things worthy of inquiry are found here, either because they are no longer in use or because they are found to vary in different ways among authors.

For some wished there to be only one kind of this art; others, as I have said, wished there to be three. Some wished the constitutions to number three, together with the parts of quality. A few said that there were four. Many wished the whole art to be divided into five parts.

Nevertheless, Cicero treats invention in only two books. Some affirm that the parts of cases number four, whereas Cicero adds two, namely confirmation and refutation. In probable narration, where others introduce seven points in which the truth of the matter is customarily found, Cicero varies the number. In all these matters the great necessity of inquiry is plainly displayed.

This woman, with prudent transgression, passes from genus to genus and from constitution to constitution. For when Virgil spoke about Turnus, she allowed a movement from quality toward a transitive conclusion. At the beginning she strives to show herself with one appearance, in the middle with another, and at the end with a third. In her progress and conclusion she reveals her changes more craftily.

When she speaks, she never walks without a clamor, unless perhaps at some time she appears to speak while silent. No one would doubt that she is Cicero’s foster child. Sheltered by her protection, he detected the conspirators against the commonwealth. Did anything else come to his aid when he expelled Catiline from the Senate through the gravity of his speech and arguments, by which free Rome called Cicero the father of his country?

With a single stroke she paints diverse colors and returns to her own chamber by fivefold paths, so that she gathers the turns of her roads by a brief return and seeks a presumption around the epilogue.

She is succeeded by one whom they call the sister of the wisest king, distinguished by subtlety of appearance and dignity of wisdom. The Hebrews say that Solomon was formed with delicate bodily features. This may also be gathered from the words of his son, who says: “My little finger is thicker than my father’s back.”

From this another point may be inferred: since Solomon’s slender body contained abundant wisdom, it is understood that subtle wisdom can scarcely be found in a corpulent body. Hence Persius:

> You are trifling, bald one, while a fat, water-jug belly  
> projects before you by a full foot and a half.

Statius too, enumerating the virtues of the body, says of Tydeus:

> Greater virtue ruled in a small body.

As though by a digression, I shall return to the matter at hand. I mentioned this slender-bodied virago because, separated from bodily things, she is not thickened by any corporeality in her nature.

She therefore claims for herself a fellowship with divinity—not wishing to be regarded as an accident in God, but as substance. For in the Trinity, the substance of the persons—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—is one. Therefore the Trinity in unity, and unity in the Trinity, is substance.

Among created things, too, according to the philosophers, number may in some way be seen as substance, unless someone should deny that number exists. Wise men say that “one” and “being” are the same, so that something exists for as long as it is one; and when it ceases to be one, it no longer exists. “Being” displays substance and is therefore called substantive by the wise.

Thus “one,” which possesses the same property as “being,” may not irrationally be assigned to substance, although all number is assigned to the genus of quantity.

This woman of whom I speak so forms herself in lesser numbers that in greater numbers she wishes to be regarded as male. Hence one might rightly believe her to be Caeneus or Tiresias—that is, capable of either sex.

Moreover, she sometimes produces a marvelous illusion when, without judging words, she reveals the secrets of certain minds. From this the fool is also convicted, for he thinks that he can detect sound-minded wisdom in a brief speech.

> Behold Crispinus again, whom I must often summon  
> to the scene.

This virago thinks that everything is contained within her to such an extent that, when she departs, she leaves nothing behind. Therefore, although she possesses such great dignity, she is burdened by the presumption of certain people who presume more about themselves than they ought. For it is difficult for the infinite to be confined by the finite. Anyone who attempts this is rightly considered insane.

Indeed, she contains many things whose changeable power is difficult to detect. At times she so surpasses the form of her own magnitude that she is judged comparable to a giant’s size. At times she falls so far below herself that she may not improperly be likened to a dwarfish maiden. Sometimes she can unite herself with such moderation that nothing greater and nothing lesser can be found in her.

Furthermore, whenever she comes to crossroads pierced through with openings, she demands to be regarded as mistress: teacher of the countryside, regulator of the stars, and dispenser of sounds. She thinks that she is sparing her own mastery.

For if Plato’s *Timaeus* is believed, the soul of the world is formed through this marvelous composition. Virgil says of it:

> In the beginning, spirit within nourishes heaven and earth  
> and the watery fields, the shining globe of the moon,  
> and the Titanian stars; infused through all their limbs,  
> mind moves the whole mass and mingles with the great body.

Here, too, as in the other disciplines, many matters require inquiry, though fools despise them as useless and unnecessary. At least the order should have been investigated: why Boethius placed this discipline first among the four liberal disciplines, while Martianus placed it second.

Perhaps no one investigates this because he thinks it happened by chance, or because he believes that Martianus contributed nothing worthwhile to the arts. In my judgment, however, the assessment of either division belongs either to a madman or to an illiterate.

This discipline is followed by the rustic woman whom I mentioned above, of such manly and tireless strength that she is thought not unknown even to heaven. She establishes her dwelling in the middle of worldly things in such a way that she possesses both the middle and the extremities. The following verse of Virgil rightly suits her:

> She enters the earth and hides her head among the clouds.

She measures the earth and divides the heavens by fixed lines. Without corporeality she assumes a body for herself; she constructs length without breadth as belonging to her—something not found even in a spider’s thread.

By a mysterious power she removes height from length and breadth joined together, which seems inappropriate to bodily things. Yet she admits that these theorems are properly owed to her. She joins together combinations of lines so that at times they meet at right angles, at times at obtuse angles, and at times at mixed angles. Thus it happens that things unequal to one another are joined together, not always remaining equal but possessing differing quantities.

Sometimes perpendiculars are joined to standing lines, and this not in a simple manner. Yet some things can be found that cannot be joined to others by any association. They rightly call them *aloga* (“irrational” or “incommensurable”), since they consist in quality, quantity, division, and position.

She encompasses within her own lines the circles of the planets, the revolutions of the zones, and the connected circles of the zodiac and the Milky Way. Whatever is accomplished by the drawing of lines she assigns to her own jurisdiction.

It is therefore plainly shown that no bodily dimension can be displayed without her lineaments, since she endeavors, by the incorporeal power of her intellect, to reveal how a body is bounded.

Someone might rightly call her the apostolic woman: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth.”

Next comes the woman called Astrea, of such great sharpness that she is never darkened by the interruption of night, never experiences gloom, and never grows black through the gathering of clouds. When she raises holy souls, released from their bodies, to heaven, she reminds them how densely they were covered by darkness while they remained attached to their bodies.

One might rightly call her Elijah’s companion, for she prepared a chariot for him from the innocent and transparent element of the ether. He is said to have been raised in a wooden chariot; yet one kind of fire consumes, while another merely shines.

The higher she is above the earth, the less known she is to mortals. She possesses her dwelling in the earth and, by a marvelous constriction, drives certain planets—at times leading them before her, at times forcing them to move backward, and at times joining them to a stationary position.

According to Plato, she taught that the circle of her own dwelling was second from the moon, Mercury’s third, and Venus’s fourth. Cicero and others, however, thought that the order of their distances should be understood quite differently, so that Mercury’s circle would be second from the moon, Venus’s third, the sun’s fourth, Mars’s fifth, Jupiter’s sixth, and Saturn’s seventh.

What, then? Do we criticize Plato? Certainly not. Cicero and the others, then? Far be it from us.

This woman moves the heavenly sphere with such speed that the courses of the planets revolve with it, while their encounters, by a certain marvelous law of nature, retard its speed. She admits that a lunar month is constituted one way when measured by the moon’s illumination and another way when measured by its journey through the zodiac—so that twelve months of lunar illumination equal thirteen months of zodiacal travel.

Through her it is discovered why the sun takes fewer days to ascend from Capricorn to Cancer than to descend from Cancer to Capricorn.

A great question also arises among philosophers concerning the heavenly bodies: whether they are animate or inanimate. Plato indeed considers them not only animate but rational and immortal. Aristotle considers them inanimate and immortal.

From this, according to Plato’s opinion, something contrary to Porphyry’s definition is produced. Porphyry affirms that differences are substantial and divisive for genera and constitutive for species. But according to Plato, the differences “irrational” and “immortal” constitute no species.

Although Aristotle’s opinion does not disagree with Porphyry’s definition, Solomon nevertheless seems to favor Plato when he says:

> The sun rises and sets and returns to its place;  
> it circles through the south and bends toward the north.  
> The spirit, surveying all things, travels around in a circuit  
> and returns to its circles.

This statement can be explained as follows: the sun is called spirit because all things that are born are brought to life and grow through its heat.

Hence certain pagans thought that nature should be defined in this way: “Nature is an artisan fire proceeding by a certain way toward the generation of sensible things.” But since this is not especially persuasive, we must consider the Apostle’s statement, with which the teachers of the Church agree in a single interpretation: “We know that the whole creation has been groaning and laboring in childbirth until now.” And shortly afterward: “Because creation itself will also be freed from slavery to corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God.”

Would it not be more fitting for a monk to occupy himself with matters pertaining to the instruction of the Christian religion than to devote himself to frauds? He considers it worthless to linger over liberal studies. He thinks nothing of investigating the apsides of the planets, their positions, their courses through the zodiac, and the revolutions of the circles among themselves.

At least he ought to consider the matters found in the divine books that derive from these arts. For example, in the sacred history, when Joshua commanded the sun and moon to stand still, did the remaining five planets and the innermost orbit of the world also remain stationary, or did they preserve their own courses?

If they did, then that heavenly harmony suffered dissonance, with two strings mutilated—especially since these are the points at which the first tetrachord ends and the second begins. But if the outermost sphere remained stationary together with the planets, the sweetness of the higher music fell silent.

Perhaps this is why we read in Job: “Who makes the harmony of heaven rest?” In this question so many problems arise that the Lernaean serpent seems to have been restored with the strength of Hercules.

## On Music

Nevertheless, since I have mentioned music, I shall say a little about its investigation. It possesses such great dignity that it is rightly believed to stand in attendance upon God. Examples of this present themselves so frequently that at times it may seem superfluous even to mention them.

Since music possesses such majesty that it serves the divine presence, it claims a monarchy for itself among the heavenly bodies. It continually constructs harmony in them and does not lose the dignity of Pythagorean silence. Thus it both resounds and preserves the measure of silence.

In the variety of the circles it regulates itself so that, contrary to the law of human melody, it may, according to the opinion of some, assign high sounds to the wider revolutions and lower sounds to the shorter ones.

A perplexing question also arises from the fact that the five planets are sometimes driven by the sun’s ray and at other times assigned to a stationary position. A stationary position lacks movement, but sound cannot exist without movement. Therefore, when some planets stand still, the uninterrupted harmony of the concord is not complete.

It must consequently be investigated, insofar as human knowledge permits, how the heavenly movements of the planets continually preserve the law of sonority imposed upon them, while never exceeding the stationary condition at times assigned to them. Among these questions, it is also asked whether the sphere of the world is driven by sound or moved in silence.

They say that everything in motion changes place, and that every corporeal thing, by changing place, produces sound. But the heavenly orbit does not change place, since it revolves within itself. Therefore it produces no sound by its rotation, and yet it is said to be moved with an immense clamor, just as I mentioned earlier, using the example from Job, the harmony of heaven.

Perhaps, however, that statement can be understood to refer only to the planets. Let whoever it is consider how much divine grace has been granted to him. For my part, let me be permitted to linger somewhat over the knowledge of earthly sonority, since many things are found in it that deserve frequent investigation.

In this discipline one must generally investigate its parts, which Virgil shows to be seven, saying:

> Number declares seven distinctions of voices.

In the brevity of this line the weight of the whole harmony is contained.

One must also ask what limits the infinity of voices; what movement belongs to hearing; how many symphonies there are and which may be called the first; in what way Plato thinks consonance should be defined; which voices are stationary and which mobile; whether consonances can be found in partitive numbers; whether sharpness and gravity, from which voices consist, are better said to belong to quality or to quantity; whether continuous or separated voices better suit harmony; whether every judgment of sounds should be entrusted to the ears or to reason; how much the ratio of meters contributes to music; how the diversity of the semitone is constituted; and how the variety of fifteen modes is formed from the matters mentioned above.

I have recalled these matters briefly, not in order to rank music as the first of the arts, but to criticize the stupidity of the unlearned monk. Since he lacked knowledge of the liberal arts, he preferred to appear a little grammarian through fraud rather than acquire even an external knowledge of the arts.

For there is an art within and an art without. Unfortunate man! Since perhaps he could not acquire the arts inwardly, why did he not at least acquire them outwardly?

Granted that he thought himself wise: should he not finally have investigated what others thought? For people hold different opinions about different matters. Hence Terence’s saying: “As many men, so many opinions.” Persius says of this also:

> A thousand kinds of men and varied use of things.

Perhaps he thinks he knows everything—a belief which no one fails to recognize as the height of madness.

He does not know what Cicero says on this matter: “One thing scarcely a few can do; both, no one.” And Maro:
. . . Not all of us can do everything. Let him who despises the testimony of pagan writers at least recall the Apostle’s statement, which says: “One judges in this way, another in that; one distinguishes one day from another, another regards every day alike.” Likewise: “Let each person abound in his own understanding.” Ought he not, then, to have carefully inquired whether I possessed at least a little understanding of the Scriptures? He was carried away by excessive boasting, so that he might appear wise among his own people, just as the poetic Cinero [reading uncertain] wished to appear more than human among his own. A frog in the mud does not hesitate to compare itself with the size of a cow; in the same way this monk, by a single accident, wishes to be considered learned. [Col. 1301A] But while he wished to appear wise, he showed himself a fool, according to Horace’s saying:

> While fools avoid their vices, they run into the opposite ones.

Perhaps the man of whom I speak is merely a grammarian; but it is well known that no one can fully acquire the knowledge of any one liberal art unless he has undertaken to give at least some small attention to them all. For the arts are called “cyclical,” and they so return into one another that they are sometimes found joined in groups of three sounds. For that Achar [possibly Achan], placed under the Law, whose soul, according to Ovid’s teaching, is revived by this Achar, did not stand at the foot of the mountain, nor hear the voice of the speaking Lord. Born in the wilderness, he grew up amid murmuring, and his soul still preserves the savage character by which that man fell away from Moses in the wilderness, and did not adhere properly to Joshua. He did not wish to persist in the active life, and never reached the contemplative life; therefore he failed on the journey and stopped short in tepidity. Perhaps now the rival of the human race has branded him with his cautery. Would that he were either hot or cold, for, according to the Apostle, it would have been better for him not to recognize the way of truth than, after recognizing it, to turn backward! I would urge you to provide him the help of medicine, but I fear that the disease has become chronic:

> Hellebore is useless when the diseased skin has already swollen,
>
> and you may see people asking that the advancing illness be met.

—Persius

I thought these matters ought to be communicated to you, so that you may come to know both the vanity of the foolish monk and the fact that I am not in every respect what he supposed. For there are certain fools who wish to measure others by their own standard, like this most wretched man, who, when he was praised by little boys in comparison with himself, thought nothing of anyone else. Let him therefore fail even in his own estimation and waste away under the judgment of the prudent, unless he openly demonstrates what sort of man he wished to show himself in the monastery’s chapter house.

Nevertheless, we, to whom it is commanded that we pray for our enemies, must see to it that we obey the divine commandments. I therefore thought it fitting to conclude this letter with prayers.

> Almighty Creator of all things, who governs everything,
>
> and who binds what has been loosed and brings what is scattered back into harmony,
>
> nor ever permits what has been placed on solid ground to be dissolved,
>
> for you there is nothing that can perish, nothing that can fail through an end.
>
> All things live for you; all things labor to serve you.
>
> Nothing beneath you dies, since you preserve the thresholds of life.
>
> Whatever ought to be present is there; nothing that should be absent remains.
>
> Grant, almighty Father, forgiveness; grant, I ask, a return.
>
> May those who have fallen, overwhelmed by their own crime, arise
>
> reborn beneath the tender name of the font.
>
> May the final day not send them to Avernus.
>
> [Col. 1302B] May that ferryman Charon not carry them across his muddy water.
>
> May fate withdraw far away, and may the urn of Minos cease.
>
> May those to whom Christ has granted the healing pledge in the water
>
> feel Ixion’s blow of the accustomed whirling.
>
> Let others roll rocks; let the liver here grow rich
>
> for the vulture’s frenzy; let the entrails be dissolved by thirst
>
> beside the waters of Eridanus, which may not be reached.
>
> Let him await great foods with empty jaws,
>
> whom a stolen evil prevents from touching the tables.
>
> Let the rest of the heathen multitude be confined by punishments,
>
> which lust, in the manner of beasts, snatches through various places,
>
> so long as those who confess themselves subject to Christ
>
> escape the snares and hostile arrows of the dragon,
>
> protected by a shield and by an armor that does not fail.
>
> Among them, if anyone happens to seek to gnaw at my life,
>
> once the stains and guilt of envy have been removed,
>
> may he fly upward, seeking the heights, and reject entanglements,
>
> and, joyfully joining himself to God at the final judgment,
>
> may he seek the right hand, where, already blessed by splendid praise,
>
> he may receive the joys of the money gained from the coin.
>
> May he likewise exclaim, “Well done,” and bear the Lord blessed without end.

**In the year of the Lord 979. Richard, abbot of Fleury.**

[Col. 1301]

## Historical Notice on Richard

*(Gallia Christiana, vol. VII, p. 1546.)*

[Col. 1301D] Richard, previously provost of the cell of Patriziacum, succeeded, according to Mabillon, the agreeable bishop Vulfard. In 964 he obtained from the matron Guntrude the estate of Percipiacum for the benefit of Letaldus. King Lothair gave him three charters: the first two in the thirteenth year of his reign, in the tenth indiction; the last in the twenty-first year, A.D. 974, perhaps after the second burning of Fleury. [Col. 1302D] “For,” says Aimoinus, “the monastery was consumed twice by devouring flames; in the second year, 974, it burned in a conflagration. But through the efforts of the venerable worshiper of God Richard, within the space of three years it was restored to its former state.”

In that same twenty-first year of King Lothair, on the sixth day before the Ides of September, with the third indiction reckoned from the beginning of the month, Adelelmus, a most noble knight, gave Saint Benedict a remarkable silver cross, engraved with the likeness of our Savior, as he was hung upon it in the impiety of the Jews for our offenses. “Moreover,” he says, “for the illumination of that same life-giving and venerable cross, I give a certain estate belonging to me, situated in the county of Sens and called Villaris, together with a church dedicated in honor of blessed Mary, etc., for the remedy of my soul and of my lord, the illustrious Hugh, duke of the Franks, and also of my father Robert and my mother Berta by name, and of Burchard and my other relatives. Done at Paris in a public assembly of nobles.”

Hugh, duke of the Franks; Odo, count; Adela, countess; Milocomes, her son; and others subscribed with Adelelmus. This charter is of no small importance for identifying the families of the princes of that age.

Richard attended [Col. 1304A] the funeral of Anno, abbot of Micy, in 972, according to Letaldus. In 978, William, son of Sancho, count of Bordeaux and duke of all Gascony, having heard of the religious life of the monks of Fleury, restored to them for governance the monastery of Squire, or De Regula, situated on the Garonne, together with his brother Gumbald, bishop of Bazas. Richard admonished Herbert, lord of Soliacum, who had invaded the monastery’s estates, of the divine vengeance, but in vain. Herbert soon experienced it and was buried at Fleury.

Aimoinus writes these and other things about Richard; Tortarius, in his history of the translation of Saint Maurus the martyr to Fleury, echoes him, calling Richard “great,” “the glory of abbots,” and “the most brilliant lamp of the Fathers.” He departed this life in the year 979, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of March.

[Col. 1303]

## Customs and Rights of the Church of De Regula, by Richard, Abbot

*(In Labbe, Bibliotheca nova manuscriptorum, vol. II, p. 744.)*

[Col. 1303B] It has been established that none of the provosts or priors, within the town or outside it, may dare to give houses, lands, vineyards, or any possessions without a fixed rent. If anyone should presume to do this, the transaction is not to be upheld, since it was prohibited under anathema for both giver and recipient.

It has also been established that if anyone wishes to sell possessions which he holds in fief from the Church, he may do so with the consent of the prior or provost. The prior himself may buy them if he wishes; otherwise he may sell them to whomever he wishes, saving the Church’s right—namely, one coin from every solidus.

It has again been established that from every house, within the town and outside it, the Church is to receive two men or women with hoes each year to weed the crops. Each person shall be given one pound of servant’s bread in Lent; at another time, in the morning, one round loaf from the oven and wine, and at night one pound. On the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul, they must bring the prior one bundle of grass from every house, and at the feast of the Chains of Saint Peter one loaf from every house, of a size sufficient for a man at table. One man from every house must also be provided for gathering the grapes.

It has also been established that all men who dwell in the town or in the prior’s domain, inside or outside it, owe justice to the prior and the key-bearer.

It has been established that whoever brings grain to the mills, or wine to be sold, is under the prior’s protection, so that no townsman may dare disturb them from the time they leave their houses until they return to their own. If anyone presumes to do this, he shall pay a fine; likewise, the mills are under the prior’s hand in the same manner.

It has similarly been established that if any townsman buys wine and later sells it, he shall give the lord one obol for every *saumata*. Moreover, the prior has the salt ban in the town for one month, and no townsman may dare sell or buy except with the prior’s consent. Whoever violates these provisions shall make compensation by paying sixty-six solidi.

It has been established that all shoemakers shall each year, on the feast of Saint Martin, render their best shoes. Likewise, all furriers must give the prior a good fur each year on Palm Sunday, on the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul, and on the feast of the Chains of Blessed Peter. Neither knight nor townsman nor any other person shall be exempt on these three days; they must pay the prior and the monks the dues on what they have sold or bought.

It has been established for all time that there is a market in the town of Regula on Saturday. The lord of Gironde holds jurisdiction over this market as a fief from the prior. No one should buy anything beyond the streams on any other Saturday. If this is done, jurisdiction belongs to the lord of Gironde; on Saturday that lord himself shall arrest or detain the offender for up to eight days. If he does not then pay, jurisdiction belongs to the prior or the key-bearer. The prior or key-bearer may likewise arrest or detain him.

The aforesaid lord of Gironde shall provide safe conduct for those coming to the market, both on their way there and on their return. Butchers are likewise protected from the hour at which they receive a pig, cow, or anything else pertaining to their trade, so that they may not be distrained without the advice of the prior or key-bearer.

[Col. 1304D] Those who come to the mills enjoy the same protection. Whoever violates either of these provisions shall pay six solidi. Our miller, however, may take one *couca* from each mill each day, if he wishes, for grinding. No miller may seek grain through the town; if this is done, he shall pay six solidi. Every Friday the millers shall pay the key-bearer, under oath, one quarter of the grain they have earned.

It has been established that the key-bearer shall receive an obol from every pig, and from a pig worth more than twenty denarii he shall have the loins; from a cow he shall receive two denarii, and the same from a bacon side. Meat may be sold only in the customary places, and the same applies to fish. On Sundays, Tuesdays, and Thursdays the key-bearer shall arrest or detain meat: a pig’s or boar’s loin for four denarii; a cow’s haunch for three denarii; a quarter of a ram for one denarius. Whoever sells meat shall observe the same custom.

If a stranger brings a sturgeon, the key-bearer shall receive one denarius. If the sturgeon is cut up there, the key-bearer shall have the cartilage and intestine, and shall receive the denarius as well.

[Col. 1305B] If two or three partners share ownership of a pig, cow, or ram, the key-bearer shall exact from each what has been stated above, even if one person sells on behalf of all. Likewise, if a stranger brings a salmon, he shall give an obol. If a stranger brings twelve lampreys, he shall give one denarius; if six, an obol. If he brings twelve *colagi* by water, he shall give one denarius; if six, an obol. If he brings them with a donkey, he shall give three denarii; with a horse or mare, mule or female mule, four denarii; if he carries twelve *colagi* or lampreys around his neck, he shall give one denarius.

Of the first sturgeon and salmon caught at the Beta, the fishermen shall give half. The two fishermen shall then receive two loaves of servant’s bread and two measures of wine. Thereafter, of all fish caught there, they shall give a tenth under oath.

If a whale is carried by sea, the key-bearer shall receive a portion. If it is carried overland, or if any other fish is carried, the procedure shall be as written above concerning *colagi* or lampreys.

Concerning things sold in the market: from a pig sold for more than twenty denarii, the key-bearer shall receive one denarius; if for less, an obol. The same applies to a goat and a cow; from an ox, one denarius. From a sheep, as from a pig; from a donkey, as from an ox; from a horse and a mule, four denarii. For *cifi* and salt-baskets, from a beast’s cart four *cifi* and the same number of salt-baskets; from a loaded pack, two. On Saturday no one may sell anything within or outside the town without paying the customary revenues to the key-bearer.

[Col. 1305D] It has also been established that if anyone buys a pig outside the town and sells it within eight days, he shall give one denarius. From *nomeria*, knives, digging tools, hoes, sickles, pruning knives, vessels, and other iron tools sold in the market, the key-bearer shall take one item from each seller once a year. From *retumba* vessels and glass cups, onions, and other goods, every Saturday and Sunday he shall take one cord, except from those of Papeyran; and from the *scaloria*, one sheaf.

Those living on the land of Papeyran are free from all dues on whatever grows in that land. If they acquire anything outside that land, they are not free.

The key-bearer also receives from those selling salt in the market on Saturday one palmful from each person, and likewise on Sunday. To conclude briefly: in whatever manner or on whatever day strangers bring something, or pass through with any thing, the key-bearer shall receive his right—whether salt, horses, pigs, sheep, oxen, grain, or anything else. In the market the key-bearer shall arrest or detain whatever he wishes for eight days.

The key-bearer shall also receive from all who sell salted meat, every fifteenth Saturday, one obolate. On the feast of blessed Peter, the key-bearer receives one strap from every hired laborer.

Passapont received in our name, at the market, from a bundle of flax one *paladuir*, and a full handful of wool, according to what was there. From hired laborers, on the fifteenth day, an obol; from those who bring glass vessels, one lamp; from a bundle of cups, one.

For these things Passapont and his successors are obliged to provide lighting in the dormitory and in the prior’s chamber whenever he is present. From mats the key-bearer shall receive one each year, and likewise from the other goods that are sold.

It has been established that the man whom the prior summons before the court must immediately appear before him with sureties, unless he has already washed his hands in preparation for eating or has already prepared himself to wash his head. If the prior summons him after vespers, he shall appear before him on the following day with sureties. Whoever fails to appear before the prior on the appointed day by the sixth hour shall be judged as convicted. If the prior is not present, he shall appear before the key-bearer.

From every *saumata* of firewood, one log shall be given to our house at all the gates by those who are outsiders.

It has also been established that during the grape harvest the prior shall send his messengers to all the town gates. In their presence the tenth of the wine and the fourth shall be faithfully rendered, as their written instructions shall specify. Those whose vineyards they are must carry the produce to the prior’s press without his assistance.

From all the *obliarii* who cultivate beans, one cook or another servant, laden with beans, shall be given to the community. In its season the kitchen servants shall gather unripe grapes from the vineyards; likewise vegetables from Christmas until Lent, and in Lent leeks in the same way.

It has further been established that all bailiffs are appointed for this purpose: to ensure that the dues of the bailiwicks are rendered to us without difficulty, namely grain, oats, and money. If on the feast of Saint Martin they have not compelled their subjects to pay the aforesaid dues, the bailiffs must distrain them; but jurisdiction belongs to the prior.

It is further established that the key-bearer may take donkeys throughout the town for carrying his grain.

When the count receives his provision, the key-bearer shall arrest or detain pigs throughout the town and take chickens from the houses.

It should further be known that throughout all our bailiwicks we receive from every peasant one chicken, two bundles of straw, one loaf, and a team of oxen on Christmas Eve.

All our bailiffs, inside and outside, must provide a provision for the prior once a year, except the men of Pins.

All the peasants of our bailiwicks must provide a provision for the prior once a year.

Boneta of Bordes and his successors must provide a provision for the prior at Bordeaux, together with all those whom he has with him. He must likewise provide horses, once a year.

The knights of Bordes shall pay the prior and his companions a full provision, together with all whom he brings with him; newcomers shall provide likewise. They must lend the prior one horse when he sends sturgeons [Col. 1307B] to Saint Benedict. If the horse dies on the way, the prior shall reimburse them its value.

It is the right of the prior and of the Church of Regula to settle disputes, disagreements, cases, and judgments through whatever judges he wishes, and from wherever he wishes, within or outside the territory. If any newcomer or native dies without a legitimate heir, his property belongs to the prior if he was unmarried; if married, half belongs to the prior.

William the Weaver, Peter Ogau, William Garcia, and Vitalis Julian of Lavizon must carry the prior and his companions by sea wherever he wishes, and bring them back in the same manner. They must likewise transport grain by sea wherever our house has property. On the night of their return, these carriers shall receive bread and wine from the storeroom.

The provost of Lobanaeg must provide a provision for the prior and his companions once a year. All those belonging to that provostship must provide another such provision for the prior and his companions once a year. The provost of Saint Aureliana, with his associates, must provide a provision for the prior once a year; and, upon each change of prior, fourteen Bordeaux solidi as a *sportula*. Aiquilinus of Fonte shall give six denarii as a *sportula*.

Amaneus of Lobengs and his men must render homage to the prior for his *mota*, for the fief of Regula, for the jurisdiction of the market, and for everything he holds from him within and outside the town. Moreover, for all these things they shall make a solemn payment to the entire community of Regula on Easter Day.

Arnaldus Bernard of Taurignac renders homage to the prior for the remission of Mary of Gironde’s toll, and moreover, for the community of the *casatus* with his associates, he shall pay annually, on the feast of the Chains of Blessed Peter, five Bordeaux solidi.

Helias of Barela must pay the community of Regula annually, on Palm Sunday, twenty-four loaves, twelve lampreys, and one *saumata* of wine.

The lord of Culed Maviron must render homage to the prior for the fief he holds in the town of Regula. The lord of Landerro and of Saint Basilica must render homage to the prior for what he holds in the market of Regula and in Salargiae, for the fiefs of the houses in that town, and for everything he holds from the stream called Merdanus as far as Regula.

Donatus Garcia, or Berned, and his successors must assist the prior in judgments for the fief he holds within Regula.

The men of Taurignac, the men of Saint Michael, and those of Guarzac must, if the prior has a war of his own, come to his aid for the fiefs they hold within the town.

If the prior has a war of his own for the disinheritance of his land, the townsmen shall pay half the expenses and the prior the other half. For such a war, the lord of Gironde, the lord [Col. 1308B] of Taurignac, and the lord of Berned are obliged to present themselves.

If any knight holding a fief from the prior should, God forbid, do wrong against the prior, the prior shall summon him before the court through his messenger and shall enforce in the prior’s hand whatever is just concerning the complaints. If he refuses to obey the law in the prior’s hand, the prior shall seize his fief.

It has further been established that if a Jew passes through the town, he shall pay the key-bearer four denarii. For a Spanish horse, four denarii; for a *traca*—perhaps, as later, a “load”—of ox, sheep, or goat hides, four denarii. For one hide, one denarius; for a load of tin or metal, four denarii. Whoever sells a horse in the market shall pay four denarii; a stranger, wherever he sells, shall pay likewise.

It has further been established and confirmed by oath [Col. 1308C] that neither the prior nor the key-bearer may overtake or arrest anyone, male or female, so long as that person can provide a surety acceptable to the prior.

No one may draw a knife, sword, lance, spear, axe, *besogium*, or any other sword in a quarrel. If anyone draws one, does not strike, and is convicted of having drawn it, he shall immediately give six solidi to the prior. If he strikes and sheds blood, he shall likewise give the prior sixty-six solidi and fully compensate the person struck for the damage. If he cannot do all this, one of his limbs shall be cut off. If the person struck dies, the striker shall be disinherited, and the whole inheritance and possession shall belong to the prior.

No one may presume to seize anyone, inside or outside the town, without the consent of the lord prior or the key-bearer. If it should happen by chance, he must present himself with the person seized before the prior or key-bearer, provided that the time is suitable. If he neglects to do this, he shall give six solidi to the prior. If anyone should strike another before the lord’s presence, he shall unquestionably restore the damage and satisfy the prior.

Concerning measures of every kind—such as bowls, rods, cubits, the *cani* by which cloth is sold, pounds, and scrapers with which salt and grain are measured—it was firmly established that all must be equal and just. If any false measure of these kinds is found in anyone’s possession, he shall pay six solidi [Col. 1309A] to the prior. If anyone makes a complaint and proves that he has been deceived by such measures, the deceiver shall restore the damage and pay six solidi to the prior.

Likewise, concerning the gardens established in the town and its surroundings, and concerning the vineyards, it has been established and confirmed by oath that no one may dare enter another’s garden or vineyard, or steal anything—whether vegetables, leeks, or fruit—if such things belong to another.

Likewise, from vineyards no one may take unripe grapes, grape clusters, stakes, or anything belonging to them. If anyone does so and is convicted of the act, he shall restore the damage and pay six solidi to the prior; if he cannot pay, he shall lose an ear.

It has also been established that no one may go on campaign without the prior’s consent, nor, persuaded by anyone’s entreaty or payment, enter a castle to defend it or go outside to attack. If he does so and inflicts a wound, he shall give sixty-six solidi to the prior and restore the damage to the person struck. If he kills a man, everything shall be confiscated to the prior.

But if anyone, inflamed by the torches of pride, carelessly leaves the town as a fugitive on the grounds that he says the townsmen or the prior himself has inflicted injuries upon him, and refuses to pursue those injuries through the town’s judicial process, then, after the prior has admonished him once and twice, either personally or through his men, such a man shall thereafter depart as an exile and fugitive for all the days of his life, never to return, and all his inheritance shall devolve upon the prior.

Finally, it has been established that whoever kills anyone, male or female, within or outside the town, shall incur the lord’s penalty without mercy.

For minor complaints—such as striking or shedding blood, insults inflicted, tearing out hair, and other matters of this kind—the customary and established rule shall be observed.

If anyone forcibly violates a virgin: if the woman is of lower rank than he, he shall, on the advice of his friends, give her a husband or take her as his wife. If the woman is of higher rank, he shall satisfy her according to the judgment of the prior and the woman’s friends, and shall pay sixty-six solidi to the prior.

If anyone violates any other woman, he shall give six solidi to the prior and satisfy the woman. If anyone abducts a married woman and flees with her, the town’s settlement concerning homicide shall be observed.

**In the year of the Lord 979. Adalbert, scholasticus of Metz.**

[Col. 1309]

## Historical Notice on Adalbert

*(Fabricius, Bibliotheca medii et infimi Latini.)*

[Col. 1309] Adalbert, a levite—or monk and priest—wrote *Flowers from the Moralia of Blessed Pope Gregory on Job*, and dedicated them to the priest Herimann. Edmund Martene published the prologue to Herimann in volume I of the *Anecdota*; he reports that it was taken from a manuscript dating from approximately six hundred years earlier.

[Col. 1309]

## Here Begins the Prologue of Adalbert the Levite to Herimann the Priest
