In it he promises to append to him a little work excerpted “like gleaming lilies from the *Moralia*, which blessed Gregory, inspired by the Holy Spirit, expounded in a most lucid discourse [Note: [Col. 1309C]

This little work exists in a manuscript of the monastery of Saint Illidius at Clermont, whose script represents approximately six hundred years. Mabillon testifies that he likewise found it in a Premonstratensian manuscript, volume I of the *Analecta*, p. 317. We too found it in the manuscripts of Saint Peter of Selincourt, of the Premonstratensian order in the diocese of Amiens; in that of Charroux, of the Cistercian order; and in that of Grandmont near Limoges. But in the Grandmont manuscript the following is read at the end:

“I, Adalbert, although an unworthy monk and priest, who have endeavored to gather flowers from the *Moralia on Job* published by blessed Pope Gregory, humbly and submissively beg, entreat, exhort, and advise all readers, through the ineffable Trinity, and earnestly implore them from the depths of my heart, to pour forth prayers from their inmost being to almighty God, who created all things from nothing, who made everything whatever he willed in heaven and on earth, who is judge of the living and the dead, for the burden of my sins, so that in his mercy he may forgive our errors and grant us, through his gratuitous and boundless clemency, to enjoy eternally his most glorious vision in the heavenly kingdom with all the saints. Amen.”

In another Grandmont manuscript there are other excerpts from the works of Saint Gregory, divided into sixteen books. They are preceded by an index of chapters with this title: “These chapters are in the Book of Distinctions and are not in Garnerius’s Gregorian collection.”]

.” 

*(In Martene, Anecdota, vol. I, p. 84.) (G)*

[Col. 1309C] To his most beloved in Christ and venerable father, the priest HARIMAN, ADALBERT, the humblest of levites, wishes everlasting happiness in the Lord.

[Col. 1310C] I frequently recall, reverend Father, the very numerous benefits of your kindness and charity bestowed upon me, as well as the sweet and exceedingly delightful conversations of your exhortations. Among the other consolations of your fatherhood, those things have remained especially fixed in my mind which, in turn, we discussed concerning the books of the most blessed Pope Gregory, with admiration, shared rejoicing, and equal fear.

Among those books, as we repeatedly turned over the *Moralia on Blessed Job*, attracted by the sweetness of their expressions, I excerpted certain passages for you at first, at your command and in your presence. Thus, prompted by your zeal and supported by your counsel, I have attempted to complete in the following manner what had previously lain hidden in the secret recesses of my heart: namely, to pass carefully through the thirty-five books of the memorable Pope Gregory, insofar as I could, and to gather together in a single volume whatever I found in those books that was most necessary concerning various matters, collecting it all and marking each saying with a chapter heading.

I carried out this work not as I ought, but as I was able. I did not undertake it, as it seems to me, with rash audacity, but rather with the greater diligence so that both I and those like me—who have little leisure to read, or, even if they have leisure, are prevented by laziness from reading through much, or, if they possess the desire to study, perhaps lack books, as often happens in many places—might, if they wished, pass through this little work of excerpts in brief and might in no way suffer the tedium of its length.

I also wish readers to know that, apart from the chapter headings and, in certain places, the suitability of the beginnings at the opening of the sentences, I inserted nothing of my own, except that I took care, insofar as I could, to correct those passages which I found badly corrupted through the fault of scribes [or: *sategi*, “I strove”; the printed form is uncertain]. Meanwhile, for the reader’s respite, I decided to divide this little work into four books. And because human life is distinguished there by manifold variety, I wished to call it by the name *Mirror*.

Finally, the shorter sayings, whose abundance in meaning and resonance, whether in sense or in words, delighted me everywhere—sayings extending over two or three lines, or a little more, but not so long as to require chapter headings—I collected separately in another volume. I thought it pleasing that only their headings, for the sake of distinction, should be begun in red.

Behold, I have run through most lovely meadows, green with the variety of their flowers and filled with every delight. I was so eagerly attracted by them, since everything was fragrant and everything redolent, that I desired them all completely. But because, endowed with only slight skill, I could not carry away with me everything I desired, I resolved to gather those flowers which I saw had the more beautiful colors and which I foresaw possessed the greatest number of medicines, so that every learned person and imitator of the divine will might be attracted by the beauty of the flowers and also driven or kindled toward their love by the salutary remedy.

But if anyone is stained by the poison of envy, which crawls within his inmost heart, and prefers with a malevolent tooth to disparage and ridicule this little work of ours, whatever its quality, rather than to rejoice with it or correct it, he must beware lest he be wounded together with the ancient enemy by that sentence—which God forbid: “Through the envy of the devil death entered the world.” Those who belong to his party imitate him.

Here I offer, amid the great and precious gifts of the rich, this little gift of my smallness; and I humbly plead that, if I cannot obtain favor among the powerful, I may at least deserve to have a place with that poor woman who, as we read, once brought two small coins into the treasury with a willing heart.

## A

What an abbot is, and his qualities, 165, 166. Who the false abbots are, 166. Abbots ought to obey the Rule, and sin if they arrange or command anything contrary to what the Rule has established, 183. The abbey of Maguzano, in the diocese of Verona, subject to the bishop’s administration, 399. Its monastery burned by the Hungarians, 399. Its incorrigible abbot expelled by Ratherius, 400. How prone adolescence is to falls, 63. Admonitions for adolescents, 62 ff., 67.

How harmful flattery is in crimes, 591. Flatterers, the worst kind, and how dangerous they are to princes and powerful men, 592. The evil effects of flatterers, 591.

The evils of adultery, 55. Adultery also used for every unlawful marriage, 375 note. Adultery committed by a married man, even if he violates no one else’s marriage bed, since he violates God’s temple in himself, 51.

During Advent, except on feast days, one should abstain from meat and from one’s wife, 420.

Saint Aldegundis, to whom Saint Ursmarus commended his niece in the monastery of Malbodium, 201.

The decree of Pope Alexander, 231, 538, 550, 556.

The monastery of Alne, originally attached to the abbey of Lobbes, but afterward belonging to the jurisdiction of the bishopric of Liège, and why, LXXXIX. Ratherius placed in charge of this monastery, ibid.

The altar should be covered with clean linens, and nothing should be placed upon it except boxes and relics, or the four Gospels, and a pyx containing the Lord’s body, 414. No woman should approach the altar, ibid. Christ is at once priest, altar, and victim, 606.

Saint Ambrose praised, 62, 70, 587. Two sermons attributed to Saint Ambrose: one by a much later author and interpolated with a certain expression; the other containing two expressions inserted later, 421 note.

Ambrose, chancellor of Otto I, to whom Ratherius’s letter was addressed, 561. He subscribed the privilege granted by that emperor on behalf of Ratherius and the Church of Verona, 462. Several observations concerning this Ambrose, 561 note.

True friendship cannot exist without harmony of wills, 485. The law of friendship is that we should ask nothing of a friend except what is honorable, 36.

The love of God must be requested without interruption, 336. No measure is imposed on us in the love of God; in our love of ourselves or of our neighbor, however, this condition is imposed: that we love our neighbors as ourselves—that is, besides other things, that we desire them to be what we ought to have been, 635. *Anapaestum*: so called when an argument is turned back against the person making it, 396 note.

[Col. 1314] The faith or creed of Saint Anastasius. See Faith.

The calumny detected against Athanasius, 98.

The decree of Pope Antherus cited, 231, 348.

The canons of Antioch cited, 329, 339.

The canons of the Apostles cited, 349, 439. Doubt expressed whether they are apocryphal, 349, 439, 491.

Water should be blessed every Sunday before Mass, 416. The exorcisms and blessings of salt and water should be memorized, 419.

The March of Aquileia, XCIV.

The palace at Aachen, 218.

Arator cited, 30.

The Arena, the amphitheater of Verona, 393. It was a fortified place for the defense of the city, ibid.

*Baculares*: attendants, 129, 376 note.

The duchy of Bavaria included Carinthia, CI. When these duchies were separated, CII. When they were reunited, CIII. When they were separated again, CIII. The March of Verona was not always subject to the duke of Bavaria, CII. Bavarians lodged in the episcopal house while going to or returning from the emperor, 564 note. How much damage they inflicted on that house, ibid.

Baldric, bishop of Utrecht, attended Ratherius’s election to the bishopric of Liège, 218 note. Uncle of another Baldric, bishop of Liège, 219. This Baldric was called “the elder,” 224. “General baptism,” as it was called, 421 note. Its proper time was the vigils of Easter and Pentecost, 410, 421 note. Bavaria. See Bavaria.

Bromius, 129, 143.

Saint Bruno, brother of Otto I, to whom Ratherius sent the books of the *Praeloquia*, 529. Ratherius sought his service, 530. He maintained learned men in his palace, including Ratherius, LXXV. *Cacabatus*: black like a cooking pot, 291 note.

*Centigamus*, 347.

What a candle-bearer from the minor orders was like, 164.

The canon of Chalcedon cited, 340.

Charity, without which one cannot have confidence either in faith or in hope, 642. Good works are not to be rewarded with an everlasting prize and recompense unless they proceed from charity, ibid. Whoever possesses charity will receive the other virtues; for one who does not possess it, the others count for nothing, 469. See Love.

The prerogative and necessity of charity, 171. All sins are extinguished by charity, 272.

[Col. 1316] The preparation of chrism and the authority to administer chrism belong to the bishop, 339, 443. If chrism consecrated by the bishop is lacking, the baptismal font is not blessed, 122. Chrism must be kept under seal, 418.

How much more severely Christians who are condemned will be punished, 590. Someone is not a Christian, though called one, if he is opposed to Christ, 442. Which Christians are called by Christ, and which are chosen, 625.

Christ the Son of God, not by adoption but by nature, 630. Christ God, having assumed humanity, is one person in two natures, 311. From two natures and in two natures there is not more than one Lord Jesus Christ, true God in all things like the Father and the Spirit; and with them not three gods but one living God throughout the ages, 630.

The Son alone was eternally born from the Father without a mother, and temporally from a mother without a father, 102. When he willed, by his own and his Father’s will, he came forth from the Father and came into the world without leaving either the Father or heaven, ibid. Through the body which the whole Trinity together formed in the womb of the virgin mother from the substance of that same ever-virgin mother, he became visible to human beings, ibid. When the Word became flesh, God was not changed into man; rather, while the substance of the unchangeable deity remained, the Word united humanity to himself so that, just as from body and rational soul there is one human being, so from man and God there is one Jesus Christ—not compounded, but ineffably existing and born, ibid.

Why Christ was sacrificed, 411. When Christ is said to have suffered, died, been buried, and on the third day risen and ascended into heaven, neither division nor passibility is attributed to Christ. Rather, just as a human being, who is in fact flesh and soul, is said to have been killed by someone although the rational soul does not undergo death, so God, in the man whom he assumed, endured all these things without suffering, 103.

Christ was handed over after evening on Thursday, crucified on Friday, rested in the tomb on Saturday, rose on the eighth day, and after a period of three days—formed from the portion, or fullness, of the two nights—returned from the heart, that is, the inner regions, of the earth to the apostles, 410.

His ascension into heaven, 624.

*Chronographia*, a lost work of Ratherius, XIV, no. 20. In it he described the life of his contemporaries, 376, 447.

Cicero praised, 30, 36, 112.

*Cineratus*, 290 note.

The circus, also called the Arena, meaning the amphitheater, 393.

Pope Clement cited, 124, 339.

Clerics should seek nothing besides God, 164. The orders of clerics, ibid. The various grades of clerics, 471. Three classes of clerics are distinguished: some called cardinals, others titular clerics, and others clergy of the plebs, or clerics of rural churches, 447 note. Some subdeacons and acolytes were called those of the secretary’s office, others singers, 471 note.

Whoever enters the clerical state renounces the world and consecrates himself to God, 424. He must live according to canon law and be subject to the bishop, ibid. A cleric is so called because he belongs to the Lord’s portion, that is, to God’s share, 425.

What is forbidden to clerics, 416 ff.: receiving interest and acting as contractors, ibid.; wearing secular clothing, 417; also forbidden are hunting, bird-catching, gambling, and so forth, 349, 311, 415; conducting business and secular lawsuits, 349; carrying weapons, ibid., 350, 351; attending wedding banquets, 418 note.

Clerics differ from laymen in ritual only by the shaving of the beard and the bare crown, together with a slight difference in clothing, and by the things they perform in ecclesiastical offices, 367. Why they were despised by laymen, ibid. Good clerics were so rare that, after all the unworthy had been rejected, scarcely could men be found who were suitable for them, 453. Some were much worse than ordinary people, or laymen, 456. What sort of bishops the corrupt clerics of that period desired and which they avoided, 506.

The incontinence of clerics condemned, 347, 427. How widely it extended, CXXIII, nos. 96, 97, 444, 450. It had become so openly prevalent and so deeply established by custom that people not only believed that it was permissible to have women, despite the prohibition of Nicaea, but that it ought to be done; and some believed that no one who refrained from this could be free from the worst crime, 486. Some even entered into marriages, which are condemned, 424 ff. And some entered them publicly, or by public wedding, 639.

A cleric who had taken a wife after sacred ordination, 350. No law grants marriage to ministers of the altar, 455. The marriages of two clerics, arranged by their fathers, who were likewise clerics, condemned on the ground of a double illegality, 423, 424 note. One marriage was contracted publicly, the other secretly, 426. The excuse of the parents who arranged these marriages is rejected: they claimed that, in comparison with the evil, it was better for their sons to be joined to one woman than to wander among several, 425. Daughters should not be given by their parents in marriage to clerics, but to laymen, 428. On the marriages of those born of clerics, 427.

A quarrel between two clerics, one wearing a coat of mail and the other having a mistress, 349.

The Veronese clerics attached to the choir did not wish to sing the Creed of Saint Athanasius, 365 note, 447.

The Veronese clerics swore fidelity to Bishop Ratherius several times, 493. Ratherius did not promote them unless they had been educated either in the city, in a monastery, or with some learned man, and unless they were suitable for ecclesiastical dignity, 419.

*Cleronomi*: those devoted to singing God’s praises, 365 note.

*Climax Syrmatis*, a little work by Ratherius, 203.

*Clinicus*: a man with contracted limbs and paralysis, 454.

At the Lord’s Supper, the washing of the feet of the poor, 606. The reconciliation of public penitents. See Penitents. Concerning Communion on the day of the Lord’s Supper. See Eucharist.

The synod of Cologne of bishops during Ratherius’s transfer to the see of Liège, 218 note. At it, the question was examined whether this transfer was contrary to the sacred canons, ibid. note. The judgment of the prelates, that is, the sentence issued in Ratherius’s favor, 207.

The book of Saint Columbanus, from which a certain comparison was excerpted, 489.

Clerics forbidden to visit the county court without the bishop’s permission, 507 note.

The counts of Verona. See Bucco, Milo, Nanno.

The fortress of Commaclae, called *Commachio* in Italian, 95.

Who were called *commendati*, 32 note, 34 note, 35.

The Communion of the Lord’s body and blood to be received four or three times a year. See Eucharist.

The communion of saints, through which, among other things, fasting benefits those who cannot fast because of illness, since the universal Church fasts, 421.

The regular community violated under the pretext of poverty, and the vice of private ownership introduced for that reason, 266 note.

*Componere*: to pay or expiate an offense by a monetary penalty or settlement, 35 note.

*Compositio*: payment of a fine or redemption of a penalty, 387 note.

The lesser ecclesiastical computation: what it included, 419. Clerics should learn it, if possible, ibid.

A *concentor*, more commonly called a compiler: one who constructs a work from the texts of others, 188.

A general council to be convened at Rome from among the bishops who were to travel with Otto I to the apostolic see was hoped for by Ratherius, 439, 440. He wished to go there to resolve a certain question, ibid. It was convened in the year 967, note 440.

The omission of councils, 150.

The necessity of confession: “You will not attain salvation unless you confess that you have sinned,” 453. Dead sinners rise again through confession, penance, and God’s mercy, 603. After sin, confession and penance should be undertaken with the greatest speed, 258. What benefit is confession if abandonment of the things confessed does not follow? 255. One must not return to crimes, 628.

The formula of confession, 251. The conditions of confession, 628. Confession of sins, 603. Also at the point of death, 73. Confession during Lent and in danger of death, 255. The people should be invited to confession on the Wednesday before Lent, 417.

A *congius*, a measure of wine smaller than a *modius*, 342.

A good marriage, 51. What marriage is blameless, ibid. What is venial, 52. Concerning those who take a wife for the sake of her dowry, 54. To what extent husband and wife are two in one flesh, 55, 56.

Marital intercourse undertaken with the intention of procreating is blameless, 52. When it is honorable, when venial or mortal, 53. Because of mere pleasure it is not free from fault, but on account of marriage it is venial. Married people should be admonished to abstain from their wives at certain times, 427. On which days, 420. With their wives’ consent, 55. By equal consent, 623.

Marriage is indissoluble, 51, 55, 56. While her husband lives, a woman is not permitted to marry another, 544.

Conrad, duke who acted against King Otto, 219. Also called Conon, brother of Warnerius, 251. Made duke of Lorraine by Otto and afterward deposed on account of rebellion, LXXVI. When he was reconciled with Otto, in whose cause he also died fighting, LXXIV.

Conrad, who exercised ecclesiastical offices at Horne, 521.

Who counselors ought to be, 35. Whom to choose, 36. Whom to avoid, ibid. Nothing harms those in authority more than the fraud and treachery of counselors, 397.

The canon of the Council of Constantinople cited, 329.

Constantine, usurper of the apostolic see, condemned, 331, 451.

The custom of predecessors contrary to the canons rejected, 343, 447, 481, 487, 488. Law rather than custom must be upheld, 375. Sins are so routinely practiced by custom that they are not even charged as guilt, 450. Even if the corruption of canonical discipline reaches the point that no one legally deposes those who ought to be deposed, and no one condemns those who ought to be condemned, nevertheless no guilty person will be able to escape condemnation, 450, 451.

Three contracts—exchange, *libellarius*, and *precaria*—by which property was improperly alienated by churches, 390 note. They were cut short by the emperor Otto, 460. And by other emperors, ibid., note. *Libellarius* contracts should not exceed twenty-nine years, and why, 514 note.

*Conversi*: penitents, 304.

Conversion comes from God, and whence hardening comes, 433. Conversion is neither difficult nor slow with God, who is pleased by the very beginning of righteousness, 76. Conversion must not be postponed, 178. Experience teaches why more recent wounds are healed sooner than older ones, 642. While they are healthy, sinners should hasten to convert with the utmost speed, lest, when they are able, they be unwilling, and when they become willing, they be unable, 578, 579. The elderly are urged to conversion, 72 ff. Conversion at the point of death, 73. Whenever someone converts and passes from the devil to Christ, he truly celebrates the paschal solemnity, 613. Various impediments to conversion cast in the way by the devil, 261. It is not enough for the convert to abandon evil; he must also do good, 603. A person who ceases from the sin of fornication because of illness or old age does not cease to be a fornicator if, for as long as he can, he does not cease to fornicate, and does not strive to cleanse the fornication he has abandoned through fasts, almsgiving, and tearful groans, 433. Concerning those who relapse after conversion, 431.

What the heart signifies, 132.

*Recitare ex corde*: to recite from memory, 419 note.

How great a crime it is, especially for prelates and superiors, to neglect correction. See Negligence.

What difference there is between believing God and believing in God. See Faith.

*Credulitas* used for faith, 469.

*Creperum*: doubtful, 196, c. 269.

How the cross is to be made over the offerings in the sacrifice of the Mass, 415.

*Cumba*: a boat, 354.

*Cuphia*: a type of small cap, 310 note.

*Curatura*: what Italians called a tax collected from public markets, 26 note.

*Cursus*: used for the canonical hours, 414.

Saint Cyprian praised, 58.

## D

By their nature demons can perform many extraordinary things if God permits them, 20. Why God permits this, ibid. The illusions of demons deceiving certain people, 20. A demon attacks souls immediately when God abandons them by a just judgment, 579. One must fight bravely against the demon, ibid.

The precepts of the Decalogue, 169, 170 ff.

Tithes of churches and parishes assigned to others, 563 note. Sometimes given to deacons and sometimes taken away for a reason, ibid.

*Decimani*, 342.

*Depretio*: to value more cheaply, to depress, 44.

Despair must be driven away, 159, 262, 335, 431, 578, 590, 622. Even at the point of death, 73. The remedy against despair is prayer, 262. Sorrow for sins, 335. One should despair of oneself, but not of God’s mercy, 264, 432. Why Ratherius, wishing to prove that one must not despair of anyone while he lives, often used the passage: “A man does not know whether he is worthy of love or hatred,” and so forth, 431 ff., 453.

God is better proclaimed by wonder and faith than by thought, reasoning, or speech, 81. Nothing proper can be said about God by human beings, 593. God’s ineffable power and nature, which the words of all who have been, are, or will be have neither been able, are able, nor will be able to bound, 595. It can be explained not what God is, but what he is not, 597. The immutable God contains mutable things in himself, 116. God’s power, 82. For God, being able and willing are the same, 96. God cannot do only what he does not wish to be able to do, 159. Every creature, whether visible or invisible, corporeal or incorporeal, would be absolutely nothing if God did not exist, God who gives life to all things, 594. Whatever moves is moved through him, so that murderers, thieves, and adulterers have from God the movement that they abuse most wickedly, while they have from themselves the fault of the evil movement, 595.

God knows all things before they happen, 175. God’s foreknowledge, 591. In his foreknowledge—or more safely, in his knowledge—what will undoubtedly happen already exists, 256.

God is unbounded, wholly everywhere, nowhere less and nowhere greater, 595. God’s presence must be contemplated, 642. God’s perfections indicated and some listed, 498. The error of those who attributed a body to God is refuted, 593.

God permits certain things although he does not will them, 119. To what extent all things are from God, 134. Sins are not from God, 135. Evil displeases God so greatly that no good mixed with subsequent evils pleases him, 368. We must not suppose that God is pleased by goods whose value has been offset by a succession of evils, ibid. God knows how to do many good things even through the wicked, when he turns into aid what had been prepared to harm, 314. He compels even things he does not love to serve him for whatever uses he wills, 135. In what sense certain passages are to be understood in which God is said to harden the heart, hand over to a depraved mind, and so forth, ibid.

God abandons souls by a just judgment if they have first abandoned him, 579. Although he by no means abandons the countless people who abandon him, this proceeds more from mercy than from justice, ibid.

Why God is called jealous, 57.

What deacons ought to be like, and the celibacy they must observe, 164.

How the day of the Lord’s Supper was celebrated, 583.

Why Sunday is so called, 410. If Sunday is the Lord’s day, it is certainly not our day, and as the Lord’s day it must be honored with reverence, 411. Every Sunday is paschal because it is adorned by the Lord’s resurrection, 412. The Lord made the other days by his command; he made Sunday by his blood and dedicated it by his price, ibid.

The man who celebrated a wedding on Sunday night is censured, 426.

On feast days one must abstain from servile work and from sins, 411. How they are to be observed, 411. In former times servile works were forbidden on these days from evening to evening, 417 note. Ratherius imposed under threat of excommunication that servile work cease on Sunday; and when he could not obtain this, he ordered the city gates to be barred against incoming wagons, 564. Swineherds and other shepherds should also come to Mass on Sunday, 418.

Dihorno, 506 note.

The various canons of discipline, since not everything suits all places and times, 441. The diverse customs of churches, 81.

How disciples ought to conduct themselves, 38. The diversity of disciples’ dispositions and abilities, ibid.

The rich should consider the changes of earthly goods, 40. They should not devote themselves to idleness, 41. The anxieties and torments of the rich, 42, 46. Two kinds of rich people, bad and good, 43. Who are good, ibid., 46. Who are bad, 43. Three kinds of bad rich people, 46. Ratherius preferred to be sufficient rather than rich, 385. Rich people whose humility surpasses the gentleness of many poor people, 48. What the proper distribution of riches is, 41. See Almsgiving.

How detestable it is to act deceitfully and hypocritically, 78.

How masters should conduct themselves toward slaves, 36. What discretion they should use, ibid. How they should correct them, ibid.

The dowry of three vineyard-fields, 425.

Druogo, bishop of Osnabrück, attended Ratherius’s election to the bishopric of Liège, 218 note.

The dukes of Friuli under the Lombards did not extend their authority beyond Friuli, XCV.

Who were called “our dukes” by Ratherius, 553 note, 554.

## E
The Catholic Church is one, 81. In it the wicked are mingled with the good, and those to be saved with those to be condemned, 363. Although there are many wicked in the Church, nevertheless that time has not passed which the Lord himself imposed upon it when he said: “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age,” 451. Kings are advocates of the Church, 137. The revenues of the Church belong by right to priests, that is, to bishops, 105, 503, 504. How the statement “Whatever is contributed to the Church is holy, the holy possession of the Lord” is to be understood, ibid. The revenues of the Church are to be divided into four parts according to the sacred canons, 145, 419, 504. Through abuse, they were given as benefices to soldiers, or to noblemen, 305 note. The equitable distribution of these same revenues was entrusted by the canons to the bishops’ discretion, 339, 491, CXXVIII, no. 101. This episcopal duty is extensively demonstrated, 342 and following. When and to what extent bishops ought not to perform this office, 344. The principal rule of distribution is to be drawn from charity, 341. A less equitable distribution noted by Ratherius in the revenues of the church of Verona, 492. For they almost exclusively went to priests and deacons, 342. But according to the custom of other churches they were divided among individuals according to each person’s need, ibid. How many evils the less equitable distribution produced, CXXVII. A more equitable distribution is to be made by modii and sextarii, not by vineyards and fields, 470, CLI, no. 122. From division by fields arose prebends belonging to particular priests and deacons, CXXVI. How useful contributions made to the Church’s worship of God are to those who make them, 470. To take away the Church’s property is sacrilege, 92. The Church’s goods are not to be alienated or exchanged, 417. Some seized them by force of authority, 385, 390, 398. By what contracts they were wrongly transferred. See Contractus. Whatever a priest or cleric acquired from the Church’s goods belongs to that same Church, 267, 416. What the cleric possessed beforehand he may dispose of at will, 266. Canon law forbids giving anything from the Church’s goods to relatives, 388. The church at Verona called Saint Mary Consolatrix, 471, 511. Elsewhere it is called, without Mary’s name, “Saint Consolatrix,” [Col. 1320] 475. The churches of Verona, whether through the fire of the pagans, the negligence of pseudo-bishops, or complete ruin, were everywhere destroyed or largely damaged, 504. The archives of the churches contained canons and decrees, 369. The customs of the churches are diverse, 81. Ecclesiastical authority, 81, 82. Egesippus cited, 138.

Almsgiving is to be distributed, 41, 42. It is not to be made from another’s property, 14, 126, 587. Nor from what someone gave for another purpose, even a pious one, 501 and following. The rich are to give alms while they live, 41. To what extent the poor too can give alms, 48, 588, 610. To whom alms should be given, 126. Especially to the saints and to the poor in spirit, 502. They should rather be given to those who are ashamed when they receive them, 548. Above all, they should be given to the rich and noble who have fallen into poverty, 131, 548. How almsgiving is to be practiced, 129. Let the one who is in greater need receive more, 587. Let us rather give to the good than to the wicked, if they can be distinguished; if not, let us follow the saying: “Do not choose whom you should pity,” ibid. What is to be said about those able to acquire their livelihood by the work of their hands, 503. Vain glory is to be avoided, 587. For almsgiving done for vain glory is vicious, 130. The merit of alms given for sins, 130. Yet it is not sufficient to cleanse more serious sins, 128. One form of almsgiving is to direct one’s neighbor into the Lord’s way by sound counsel—whether by admonishing, entreating, or reproving, 587.

Bishops were instituted by God as kings, but are much greater than kings, and why, 104. Woe to bishops who have not been sent by God, 105. How greatly bishops are to be venerated, 80, 82. Even when negligent, 86. Or wicked, 87. Why even wicked bishops are to be venerated, 262, 263. They are not to be insulted, 82, 84. The custom of kissing bishops’ feet, 379. They are called gods and angels, 80. How great their spiritual authority is, 81. How great their dignity is, 84, 110. The Holy Spirit is often present even with a sinful bishop, 87. Bishops are called salt, and why, 88. What bishops owe to kings, 105. The duties of kings toward bishops, ibid. To what extent bishops are to be judged, 106, 113. A Greek word for bishop, *episkopos*, means “overseer” in Latin, 364.

What a bishop should be like, 139 and following. The burden and weight of the episcopate, 141. Its duties, 109. Concerning those who neglect the duty of shepherding, 143. Let them not abandon the flock in times of common storm and need, 110, 151. Abuse directed against a bishop must be endured, 158. A bishop’s zeal when opposition is greatest, 151. A bishop must not be afraid in tribulations, ibid., 152. Three kinds of bishops: those who flee in storms, those who fall, and those who win victory, 151. A bishop must live both the active and the contemplative life, 639. The vices of certain bishops, 143 and following, 366. How much the bad life of bishops harms their office, 364. Contempt for the canons arose from their fault, 366. Because corruption had spread more widely, scarcely anyone suitable was found to be elected, ibid. A bishop mocked while playing at tables, 155. A bishop taken from among monks should retain the monastic habit, 156. Ratherius still wore this habit while bishop, 221. How a bishop taken from among monks should live, 156. If a bishop expelled from his see cannot recover it, he is canonically permitted to obtain another vacant bishopric, 206. To what extent such translations were approved, LXXI, 212, 218 note, 231, 348. Ancient examples of translations, 311. How a bishop was elected, 207, 218. With the king’s permission, 207. With the consent of the clergy, which the laws required, ibid. With the people’s combined assent, 348. A profession made by the ordained person that he would always obey canonical precepts, 208. The rite of instituting a bishop by presenting the pastoral staff before the altar, 209 note. A sermon delivered on the same day, 210. The election subscribed by the archbishop and co-bishops, 210 note. Acclamations and the ringing of bells, etc., ibid. Documents of orders conferred, consecrations, and other acts in which chrism was used appear to have been subscribed by the bishop, 443 note.

Bishops elected through abuse, not for the merit of their virtues but on account of earthly noble birth, 159. Or through votes and secular offices, ibid. Noblemen seemed to be sent to the schools more from ambition to become bishops than from desire to serve the Lord, 362. Some of them were promoted to the priesthood without examination, 350, 362. Concerning those who became bishops without suitable endowments, 142. Erimbertus, a twister of words and distorter of laws, 387, 426 note. Erminus (Saint), 202.

The Eucharist, in which the Redeemer’s flesh is present, 87. It is called the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, 252. Concerning the presence of Christ’s body in the Eucharist, 257 note, 258 note, 360. The transubstantiation of wine into true blood and of bread into Christ’s flesh explained, 523. Christ’s body and blood are made present in the Mass, 602. The body and blood of the divine Lamb are offered to those who are to receive Communion, 607, 609, 610. How the Eucharist is to be received, [Col. 1321] 257, 258. Before receiving it, the dwelling of the heart is to be cleansed; after receiving it, it is to be guarded, 259. Every malicious intention must be excluded, 361. The distinction between those who receive worthily and unworthily, 361. Concerning those who communicate unworthily, 413. The holy teachers define that person to receive the Eucharist unworthily who presumes to communicate at a time when he ought to be doing penance, 355. What should have been salvation for one who communicates unworthily becomes condemnation, 360. This happens not by the Eucharist’s nature but through the fault of the recipient, 361. The formula for administering the Eucharist, 612 note, 616. The Eucharist kept in a small box or pyx for the sick, 414. No one is to hand it to a layman or woman for carrying to a sick person, 415. It is to be received four times a year: at the Nativity of the Lord, the Lord’s Supper, Easter, and Pentecost, 417. Elsewhere it was said to be received only three times a year, omitting the day of the Lord’s Supper, ibid., note. On the day of the Lord’s Supper, the fast being kept until the ninth hour as on other days, the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood was received, 583. Concerning the question whether it is better to receive the Eucharist more frequently or rarely, 527 note. The kiss given to the priest administering Communion, 600.

A decree of Pope Eugenius is praised, 341, 504. Eulogiae are to be distributed after Mass on feast days, 417. What is meant by the name *eulogiae*, ibid. note. A decree of Pope Evaristus, 345. A letter of Everaclius of Liège to Ratherius, 569. He praises him and invites him to return to his homeland, 570. What kind of excommunication was imposed by a bishop upon an archbishop, 235 note. Those whose excommunication was usually despised, 363. One must not communicate with excommunicated persons, 417. Whoever communicates with an excommunicated person is excommunicated, 439. Examples of wicked people are of no use for defense or excuse, 89. Exorcists, 164.

## F

Those recently made rich are called *factitii*, 61. A magical production used for sorcery, 170. *Fanum*, used for a bundle or napkin in the celebration of Mass, 414 note. *Fello*, meaning “treacherous,” 292, 386. How women should conduct themselves, 51. Holy women martyrs, ibid. No woman is to approach the altar or touch the chalice, 414. A profession of faith made by Ratherius, 101. The mysteries of faith cannot be comprehended; they are to be believed, not scrutinized, 524. Let us believe what we do not yet understand about God, so that by believing we may be able to see and understand, 65. Faith and belief in God used interchangeably, 409. What difference there is between believing God and believing in God, 600, 626, 631 note. Three faiths, or three creeds, are to be memorized: the Apostles’ Creed, the one sung at Mass, and Saint Athanasius’s Creed, 409, 410, 419. The faith called Saint Athanasius’s, 103. Otherwise called the “description of blessed Athanasius,” 447.

The duties of children, 60. How disgraceful it is for a rich son to allow his father to beg, 61. How culpable it is to expose newborn children, 53. Who are called *fillones*, 375 note. Folbertus, bishop of Cambrai, attended Ratherius’s election to the bishopric of Liège, 218 note. *Follis*: the devil, as he was called in rustic Latin, and why, 313 note. The march of Friuli. See Marchia. What jurisdiction the dukes of Friuli possessed under the Franks, XCV. What fortitude is, 79. Frankish speech, 15. A passage of Fulcuinus discussed concerning Ratherius, CV. Another passage in which nothing needs correction, LXXIX. It is explained in LXXX, LXXXII and following.

## G

A Hungarian *galerus*, 147. A canon of Gangra is praised, 340. Garda, a strongly fortified castle in the diocese of Verona, 393 note. By an order of Emperor Otto, bishops and clerics were summoned to its siege; the extent to which they excused themselves, 348. When this occurred, CXIV. What was commonly called a *gastaldus*, 36 note. Gauseningi, a castle in the diocese of Verona, XLII. A decree of Pope Gelasius I is praised, 340. Giselpertus, envoy of Count Nanno, 562 note. The study of Greek was cultivated even in the tenth century, XXXI.

How much the grace of God can accomplish, 159, 262, 315, 642. The Lord’s grace drew the sinful woman inward through mercy, 65. God’s prevenient grace, 433. God’s anticipating grace, 621. [Col. 1322] God’s cooperating grace, 622. Grace cooperates with those who work, 625. God’s gratuitous grace, which in its mercy inspires what is to be accomplished and in its mercy helps bring it to completion, 171. Converted with the help of the grace of Saint Metro, 313. The necessity of divine grace, 59, 161, 178. The possibility of good comes from God, 59, 107. Let us not despair of possibility, provided that we do not fail in will, 628. The beginning and perfection of good works come from God, 167. God grants progress in goodness, 62. Let no one arrogantly attribute the good to himself, 578. Salvation comes from grace, 72, 136. We must ask God for the will, ability, and fulfillment of what pleases him and benefits us, 456. “I am what I am by the grace of God,” 526. God justly abandons souls if they have first abandoned him, 579. Yet he has not abandoned countless others who abandoned him; this proceeds from his mercy, ibid. Thanksgiving is to be offered to God, 578.

Saint Gregory the Great is cited, 28, 36, 38, 39, 59, 62, 74, 108, 127, 162, 169, 183, 184, 185, 232, 284, 287, 289, 293, 353, 358, 363, 370, 389, 397, 427, 483, 438, 455, 456, 482, 490, 491, 501, 544, 548, 583, 595, 598, 636, 637, 640. He instituted the major litanies, 623 note. Saint Gregory’s action concerning Bishop Maximus, 261. Archbishop William of Mainz. See Willelmus. Various sins of gluttony, 266. The threefold vice of gluttony on fast days, 584 note. What *gutta cadiva* is, 31 note. *Gutteria*, a disease of the throat, 201. *Gyrovagus*, 538.

## H

A *haeresium*, a garment made of the finest cloth, 147. It is characteristic of heretics that they may be thoroughly refuted, but are not easily defeated, 596. *Hauritorium*, an instrument for drawing water, 45. Henry I, duke of Bavaria and first margrave of Verona, C. Henry II, son of Henry I, was given the same Veronese march after his father’s death by Otto I, CI. Ratherius calls him and his mother Judith “our dukes,” ibid. Henry the Younger, son of Berthold or Bertolf, formerly duke of Bavaria, duke of Carinthia and margrave of Verona, CII, CIII. Herigerus, abbot of Lobbes, is believed to be the author of a work edited by Cellot, dealing with the Lord’s body and blood, XVIII. Herodias was set before certain people as a queen, indeed as a goddess, 20. This is explained, ibid. note.

Saint Jerome is cited, 28, 45, 59, 126, 166, 169, 260, 270, 343, 362, 395, 548, 556, 584, 587, 613. Hilduin, a cleric of Liège, was consecrated bishop of that same church, XXXIV. Because of this promotion, the case was brought into question and he lost it, ibid. He went to Italy to King Hugh; after Notger, bishop of Verona, died, the same king gave him Verona as his successor by stipendary right, 538 note. He was transferred to the see of Milan, ibid. Ratherius brought him the privilege, or apostolic confirmation, of the Holy See together with the archiepiscopal pallium, 538. The year of Hilduin’s translation to the see of Milan, XXXVIII, no. 16. Ratherius, whom Hilduin had brought with him, seems to have been hostile toward him after Hugh’s victory over Arnold, XLVI, XLVII. Hilduin, a trans-Rhenish bishop, attended Ratherius’s election to the bishopric of Liège, 218 note. The *Historia Tripartita* is cited, 99. Human beings are equal by nature, and whence inequality arises, 28, 29.

Honestus, bishop of Ravenna. See Peter of Ravenna. Whether one or two bishops named Honestus governed the church of Ravenna in the tenth century, CIX and following. The canonical hours are listed and are to be sung at the appointed hour, 401, 414. The reading of the night office, 479. Horace, Flaccus, is to be preferred to all satirical poets, 225. He is cited, 242, 293. He was extremely diligent in versification, 311, 354. Horna, a county in the diocese of Liège, 522 note. *Horno*, that is, “this year,” 166.

Hubertus, bishop and count of Parma, to whom Ratherius addressed the book *On Contempt for the Canons*, 337 note. It was written in the form of a letter, 490. He seemed worthy to be placed over the universal Church, 353. Ratherius consulted him about how he should pray, 372. He arranged for Milo to surrender the bishopric of Verona, 397. King Hugh of Italy gave Hilduin the bishopric of Verona by stipendary right, 538. When Hilduin was transferred to the see of Milan, Hugh replaced Ratherius in that same bishopric, 538, 539. The revolt of the Veronese against Hugh, XLI. He recovered Verona after Arnold had occupied it, XLII. The date of this victory, XLIV. He shut the captive Ratherius in the tower at Pavia, XLIII, 539. After a revolt arose in Italy under Berengar’s leadership, Hugh sent his son to Milan, and the terms on which the matter was settled, LVII, LVIII. He left Italy, and in what year, LIX. He died in Provence, where he had withdrawn, LX. The chronological notices concerning him and his son, which create difficulties, reconciled or emended, LX, LXI, LXII. The case of Hugh, bishop of Reims, decided in the synod of Pavia in 962, CXI.

Humility, the mother of virtues, 62. How pleasing it is to God, 61. Without humility, virtues are not virtues but vices, 62. The hymn sung and still sung on the feast of All Saints, attributed to a certain person, is vindicated, 116.

## I

Imperial authority was said of a king who was not yet emperor, 543 note. Hell, in which punishment is unceasing, 40. Eternal destruction, 72. Eternal punishments, 265. Everlasting punishments, 261. Eternal condemnation, 622, 633. Perpetual burning, 604. Unspeakable torments, 284. Everyone condemned will perish eternally, 441. There is nothing in hell that is not the greatest possible loss, 370. Those who are condemned are to be punished eternally for each sin, 434. A person who, insofar as he can, wishes that God had not created torments so that he might sin with impunity is opposed to God, 294. The error of certain people who denied that Christians would be condemned to eternal fire in hell is refuted, 589 and following. Christians who sin deserve greater punishments, 590.

The works of unbelievers. See Pagani. Enemies are to be forgiven, 173. The decrees of Innocent I are praised, 330, 349. The intention with which someone does something must be discerned, 78. Saint Isidore is cited, 26, 43, 48, 57. Italy is enriched by the bodies of many saints, 305. It abounds in malicious informers, 397. The division of Cispadane Italy between Waltfred and Mangifred into two parts under Arnulf, king of Germany, XCV.

## J

One must fast by abstaining from vices, 580. Those fast badly who do not give to the poor what they take away from their stomach, but reserve it either for their stomach or for Mammon, 584. Those who do not abstain from sins on days of abstinence are reproved, ibid. God delights in no solemnity more than in that fast by which one abstains from food and from vices, 422 note. The fast of the Four Ember Seasons, of the Rogations, and of the Litany, 416 note. The fast is to be prolonged until the ninth hour, 420, 583, 584. This is the first testimony to a mitigated discipline in the Lenten fast: previously it had to continue until evening, 420 note. Two testimonies believed to be earlier are answered; they mention prolonging the fast until the ninth hour, ibid. See Quadragesima. The different hours for breaking the fast according to the different days on which one must fast, 428 note. Without guilt, the fast is not to be broken before the appointed hour, 501. Three forms of gluttony are noted on fast days, 585 note. Abstinence from meat, wine, and beverages during the time of fasting, 584 note. Prayer and almsgiving are to be joined to fasting, 585. Against those who served gluttony while excusing themselves by saying that it was better to abstain from vices than from food, 585. The solemn fast called Lent, and how it was violated, 501.

Pope John XI was called a man of glorious character, 538 note. His letters, in which he petitioned with the whole Roman Church that Ratherius be given to the Veronese as bishop, ibid., 539. Ratherius’s fifth letter, addressed to John XII, was, as is believed, first written under Agapetus II, 535, no. 8. John XIII was instituted pope by Otto I, and why, 440 note. Saint John Chrysostom, called the “golden mouth,” is praised, 45, 48, 182, 523. Judas, into whom Satan entered after the morsel through an evil action, though he had previously been in him through a most wicked will, 621.

The Jews at Verona in the tenth century, 386. Ratherius attacks those who favored the Jews, ibid. And those who preferred doing business with Jews rather than with Christians, ibid. The Jews’ errors concerning Christ and the Blessed Virgin, ibid. And concerning Saint Peter, ibid. Against those who offered more protection to Jews than to Christian clerics, 387. A judge is so called as if “speaking the law,” 25. How judges should conduct themselves, 24. The necessity of judges, ibid. What must be guarded against in them, ibid. Greed does not distinguish what is just; indeed, it blinds the hearts of judges, 25. Judges must not show partiality to anyone, ibid. They must judge according to laws and rights, ibid. They must accept nothing in exchange for a just judgment, 26. With how much care cases are to be investigated, 397.

*Judicatum* is the name given to the charter of foundation or endowment made by Ratherius for certain clerics of Verona, 463, no. 1. It was subscribed by the patriarch of Aquileia and neighboring bishops, 567. The same practice was sometimes followed in other similar fourth-parts, 463, no. 2. The date of the same *Judicatum*, ibid., no. 3. Several doubts cast upon its authenticity are dispelled, 466, no. 5. Discord between Ratherius and his clerics arose chiefly from the *Judicatum*, 490 note.

How trials concerning accused persons are to be instituted, 106. The accused must not be left unexamined without danger, 545. What ecclesiastical judgments are, 106, 113. How harmful their omission is, 150. Concerning secular judgments, ibid. Just as judgment is rendered secularly by worldly law, so it is rendered ecclesiastically by canonical sanction, 441. The Last Judgment and the four orders that will exist in it, 114, 589. Concerning the universal judgment, 241. How great the shame of the condemned will be in it, 434. In this world we must conduct judgment upon our sins, so that we may not be judged by God at the final judgment, 436.

Which Judith, the illustrious duchess mentioned by Ratherius, was, 382 note. She commended Ratherius to the count of Verona, 392. Through her aid he was rescued from custody, 443. The opinion of Pope Julius is praised, 549. What justice is, 79.

## K

The name *Kalendae* was used not only for the first day but for any day of the month, 410 note.

## L

Some laborers were slaves, others free, 92, 105. Lanza’s action concerning Ratherius, 384. A canon of Laodicea is praised, 349. The thief on the cross, illumined by divine grace, soon obtained through his confession the clear vision of the Son of God; faith became a reward, punishment forgiveness, lamentation everlasting joy, while the confessor on the cross became the possessor of paradise after the cross, 299. The passion of Saint Laurence is praised, 344. Testimonies of the Fathers inserted into the text are called “readings,” 192 note. What a clerical lector should be like, 164. The name *legatio* was given to prayer. See Oratio.

Pope Leo I is praised, 28, 36, 157, 349. A decree of Leo IV is cited, 341. When the church of Liège was vacant after the death of Stephen, a great dispute over the succession arose between Hilduin and Richarius, and the see was adjudicated to the latter, XXXIV. After the death of Farabert, bishop of that church, Ratherius was promoted and expelled after nearly two years. See Ratherius. Baldricus was later installed by public force. See Baldricus of Liège.

The law of the preceding age, or natural law, commands that one do for another what one would wish another to do for oneself, 546. The whole law must be fulfilled, 169. The law, rather than custom, must be observed, 375. Whoever never departs from God’s law and commandments and never conflicts with them always walks with God, 438. Why ecclesiastical law is despised while worldly law is feared, 367. See Canones. Leah represented the active life, Rachel the contemplative life, 638 note. Free will, 161, 593. Lust causes hardness of mind, 60. The litanies are called rogations. See Rogationes. They were instituted by Saint Mamertus, 623 note.

Letters of commendation, called *formatae*, required from those to be ordained if they came from another parish, 418. The monastery of Lobbes belonged for some time to the right of the bishop of Liège, so that whoever was bishop of Liège was at the same time abbot of Lobbes, XXXIV. Several monasteries were subject to that monastery, LXXXIX. Ratherius presided over one of them, ibid. Who was called a *locotheta*, 24 note. Lay Lombards living according to Italian law, 271. Lothair, son of King Hugh, was sent by his father to Milan to suppress the rebellion; he was then made king, LVII. *Lumbare*, meaning undergarments or longer breeches, 147. *Lunis dies*, Monday, 31.

## M

How masters should conduct themselves, 37, 38. They should prefer being loved to being feared, 38. The method of teaching, 38. The variety of teachers, 39. Who was called *maior* by the Franks, 26. *Malampnum*, 15 note. Saint Mamertus, archbishop of Vienne, instituted the lesser litanies, 623 note. Manasses, archbishop of Arles, who also obtained the church of Milan, insisted that Berengar arrest Ratherius, 540. Lying in wait for Ratherius, he consecrated a certain man of his diocese to the title of the church of Verona, 541. He presided over five bishoprics, 542 note. Called the margrave of Trent, XCIV. He favored Berengar against Hugh, king of Italy, LVII. By Lothair’s order Ratherius was compelled to yield his place to Manasses, 542, LXVII. This Manasses sold the see of Verona to Milo, the count’s nephew, 543 note. In what year, LXXII.

A *mansus*, a particular quantity of fields, 342. By joining hands to hands, dependents and hired laborers entered into an obligation, 34. Whence *marchia* derives its name, XCIV. *Marchia* and *comitatus* were sometimes used interchangeably, XCVII. The march of Aquileia, XCIV. The march of Friuli must be distinguished from that of Verona, XCIV and following. The march of Treviso is not to be confused with that of Verona; when it began to be so called, and why, CIV. The march of Trent, XCIV. When it began to be called that, XCVIII. The first mention of the march of Verona, and when it was instituted, XCIV. The opinion that its institution was earlier, and that at first under the Franks it was called the march of Friuli, later being called the march of Verona, ibid. This opinion is refuted, XCV and following. The extent of the Veronese march, ibid. The margraves held precedence over all the counts of the cities of the march by a special right, XCV. They were attached to no fixed see, XCIX. The Veronese margraves who were at the same time dukes either of Bavaria or of Carinthia, listed, C and following.

Saint Mary, chosen as the Mother of God because of her humility, a virgin before childbirth, in childbirth, and after childbirth, 311, 644. She loved chastity above all, 311. She endured the martyrdom of grief, not of death, 317. Against the Jews who denied her virginity, 386. Praises of the Virgin Mary, 61, 311. How useful and effective her intercession is, 311, 644. Whether Mary Magdalene, Martha’s sister, was the same as that sinful woman, 65 note. Concerning her conversion, ibid. An explanation of the Gospel concerning Mary and Martha, 66, 637 and following. The Marsi, snake-charmers in Italy, 15 note. The work of Martianus Capella was accepted in the schools, 409 note. Those devoted to Martianus Capella were called *Martianistae*, 507, 509. Saint Martin, 158. Martin, bishop of Ferrara, was corrected for unlawful ordinations of boys and for simony, 557. Martyrs from among young boys, 62. Clerics should possess a martyrology, 419. Those who cultivated estates were called *massarii*, 458. Estates assigned to stewards were called *massaritiae*, 473 note, 487 note. A *massutior* was one who possessed several fields, 144. *Mastruga*, a cloak, 147. The kinds of mathematicians in Africa, 15. The sacrament of marriage is an indissoluble bond. See Conjugium. The duties of mothers, 60. Saint Maximus is cited, 14. Maximus the Cynic condemned, 329, 451. *Mediastino*, meaning “in the middle,” 376.

The duties of physicians, 14. The distinction between medicines and poisons, 15. Physicians must not use superstitious remedies, 21. Before his episcopate, the Milanese proposed to Ratherius questions to be solved from pagan authors, 527. The monastery of Malmedy, about twelve miles distant from Laubach, 199. Lying is to be avoided, 592. Especially by ecclesiastical prelates, ibid. In most people of the present age, falsehood is more abundant than truth, 604. Liars are made equal to the devil, ibid. How serious a crime it is not to pay hired laborers, or to delay payment, 28. The duties of hired laborers, 34. The merit of good works with grace cooperating, 625.

The unheard-of penance of Saint Metro, 307, 309, 312. No acts concerning him were written, 309. Rather, accounts received by tradition are reported, 307 and following. He was indiscriminately called both confessor and martyr, 304, 308 note. The title of martyr is vindicated, 316. His body was secretly stolen, and Ratherius wrote a short work about this, 301 and following, CXII. Whether and when such a theft occurred, 299. His body was buried in the church of Saint Vitalis situated in the suburb of Verona, 304. Miracles performed at his tomb, 305, 306.

It was erroneously said by some that Saint Michael celebrated Mass to God on Monday; they are refuted, 596, 601. The church of Saint Michael at the gate of Verona, and the crowd that went to it on Monday, 601 note. Those who went to such a church on Monday are not reproved, but those who thought it better to go there on Monday than on another day, ibid., 602. A *miles* was a nobleman living on his own patrimony, and why, 30 note, 31. The nobles were called the soldiers of the kingdom, 92, 105. They were distinguished from commoners, 114. Vassals of the Church and of bishops were called soldiers, 375. The emperor had ordered these to be sent, 437. The duties of soldiers, and what they must beware of, 13. A military benefice. See Beneficium. The military order, 570.

Milo, a Frank by birth, renowned under Berengar I and endowed with supreme power at Verona, XLI. The same Milo received Arnold, duke of Bavaria, at Verona against King Hugh, ibid. After Hugh recovered Verona, what Milo did, XLII. He favored Berengar II against the same Hugh, LVII. Through his agency Ratherius was restored to his Veronese see so that Manasses might be expelled, LVIII. Soon afterward he supported the clerics against Ratherius, LXIII. How many evils he inflicted on him, 540. He was also called margrave, and the march of Trent seems to have been given to him by Berengar II, XCVIII.

Milo, the little nephew of Count Milo, 542. A Veronese bishop born after Ratherius had been consecrated bishop of that church, 552 note. Why he was called Vicentine, 551 note. What he did against Ratherius, 552. When and why he hoped to prevail over Ratherius for the bishopric, 383 note. Manasses had sold the bishopric to him. See Manasses. In what year, LXXII. He was ordained with the permission of the Apostolic See, and why, ibid.

How a minister of the state should conduct himself, and what he must avoid, 26. Who was called a *ministerialis*, 459 note. The miracles and signs read about the saints were not performed by them but by God through them, 627. *Mirmicoleo*, 43 note. As generously as mercy is extended in the present, so severe a judgment is threatened against the ungrateful in the future, 76.

The Mass of Saint Michael. See Michael. The sacrifice of the Mass celebrated for the sins of the faithful, both living and dead, 299. Christ’s body and blood are made present in the Mass, 602. In what sense the author wrote that the offering in the Mass is consecrated most especially by the Lord’s Prayer, “Our Father,” 362 note. Some celebrated Mass daily, others rarely, 522, 523. Those who celebrate Mass daily make Easter daily—that is, they eat the Lamb’s flesh and drink his blood, 412. Prayers before Mass, 299. The vestments used for Mass are listed, 414. They must be clean and must not be used for other purposes, ibid. They must not be pawned, 416. Which books were used for singing Mass, 414 note. The kiss customarily exchanged during the solemn celebration of Mass, 148. No one is to sing Mass on the seventh day of Holy Week before the tenth hour, 421. No one is to sing Mass in another parish without the parish priest’s permission, 416. No one is to sing Mass unless fasting, nor may one sing who does not receive Communion, 414. Nor may anyone sing outside a church, in houses, or in unconsecrated places, 415. Nor may anyone sing alone, ibid. “To sing Mass” means to say Mass privately, 415 note. How crosses are to be made over the offerings, ibid. On every Sunday water is to be blessed before Mass, 416. Eulogiae are to be distributed after Mass on feast days, 417. Care must be taken that Mass is heard by pastors at least on Sunday, 418. What a *missale plenarium* contained, 414 note.

Modern examples of learned men are called testimonies of the Fathers, 188. The holy Fathers were called “moderns,” and the ancient writers of sacred literature *prisciloqui*, 333 note. A *modius* was a measure of liquids rather than of dry goods, varying according to place, 401 note. What a monk is, 165. What he should be like, and what he should avoid and pursue, 164. Monastic vows must be fulfilled, 259. Property is especially to be avoided, 165. A monk does not have his own will in his power, 267. In respect of poverty, he must possess nothing as his own, 267. How serious the crime is if he reserves anything for himself, ibid. The frightening examples of two people who offended in this matter, 266.

Whoever has left a monastery must return without fail, 271, 272, 273. What is to be done if return is impossible, 273. How a monk promoted to the episcopate should conduct himself, 156 and following. One constant in his vow does not abandon the monastery, 221. How greatly he should fear if he left it in order to become a bishop, 255, 260. Especially if he had sought the bishopric, 262.

The monastery. The rite for offering children to a monastery and the formula of profession, XXIX, C, 254. This offering, made by parents or others acting in the parents’ place, was later confirmed by the children when they reached a suitable age, 254 note, XXIX. The moneyer and coinage at Verona, 474 note. The death of the good is not death but birth; that of the wicked, however, is immortal death, calamity without end, 71. *Multigamus*, 351, 362. *Multinubus*, 351, 444. What *mundeburdium* is, 13. It was granted to Ratherius by a privilege of Otto I, 459. Ratherius often explained music when asked, 639.

## N
Nanno, count of Verona, called “prince,” 558 note. A letter of Ratherius to him, ibid. He harassed the bishop and supported his enemies, 559. He was said to have been corrupted by money, and what Ratherius did against him, 614 note. Giselpertus, his envoy, 562. Nanno’s legal proceeding against Ratherius, [Col. 1327] 564. He acted as envoy on behalf of the emperor and empress, 566.

The Nativity of the Lord, and abstinence from meat prescribed for the four weeks preceding Christmas, 420. Abstinence from wives prescribed both during Advent and for the twenty days after Christmas, ibid.

Negligence to be avoided, 261. The negligence of prelates in correcting their subjects censured, 265, 268, 269, 270. Correction must not be omitted out of fear or any other human consideration, 269. If some crime, especially a public one, is left uncorrected, it will certainly be regarded as legally permitted: for no one fails to take as an example what he has discovered that no one has censured, 426. Prelates are answerable not so much for their own crimes as for those which they neglect to prevent among their subjects, 267, 268, 269, 270.

Commerce, how dangerous to the soul, 22. How merchants ought to conduct themselves, 22. They were called *cupedinarii* (“dealers in delicacies”), ibid. note.

The canons of Neocaesarea praised, 349, 350, 450, 629.

Nero’s saying: “Now I have neither friend nor enemy,” 226.

The canons of Nicaea praised, 347, 350, 439, 450, 486.

A fragment of Pope Nicholas I from a letter addressed to the See of Constantinople, absent from the commonly circulated editions, 330.

How nobles ought to conduct themselves, 28. They were called “soldiers of the kingdom,” 92. Distinguished from commoners, 114. Many nobles have often performed ignoble deeds, and many ignoble people noble deeds, 277. The many distinct ranks of nobles, 30 note. Where true nobility is to be placed, 32. How bad pride in nobility is, 29. Nobility depends more upon one’s own conduct than upon that of another, 377. Nobility, or free birth, on account of the antiquity of one’s lineage, 221.

Notgerus, otherwise Notherius, bishop of Verona “of holy memory,” whom Hilduinus succeeded, 538. In what year his death occurred, XXXV, no. 12.

The marriage of two persons censured on account of a double illegality: because it was begun during the days of Lent and consummated on a Sunday night, 426. No one should take a wife except after a public celebration of the marriage, 418. No one should marry another man’s betrothed, ibid. Nuptial property, 54. See *Conjugium*.

## O

Obedience, on account of which one must never do evil, though one must sometimes refrain from doing good, 501.

Oderaldus, a monk censured for having purchased a prelacy for eighty pounds, 281.

*Olympionices*: one who won in an Olympic contest, 194.

The distinction between omnipotence and power is that the latter can do certain things, whereas the former can do all things, 315. Power is of no avail when omnipotence opposes it, ibid.

Works of mercy, 172. A work accepted for its usefulness, 275 note.

Prayer for the living is mutually beneficial, 299. Prayer called an embassy of petitions to God, 261, 273, 274. For whom prayer should be made, and what it ought to be like, 585, 586. One must pray without ceasing, 578, and perseveringly until we are heard, 591. One must pray with confidence in God, 262. One must never pray without groaning, 388. How harmful wandering of mind is in prayer, 586. “Unless you help the poor man who cries out to you, God will not hear you when you pray,” 580. A remedy against despair in prayer, 262. Prayer for the dead, 240. Prayer for obtaining conversion, 622. Prayer for the Sunday *in albis*, 618. How useful a prayer found in certain psalters is, if it is said daily and, through cooperation, obtained, so that we may deserve to be heard, 456. Anyone at home can worship God in spirit and truth, 437.

*Ordinarii*: the canons of the cathedral of Verona, 509, 563. They were also so called elsewhere, 445 note.

Those ordained by an invader are suspended, 327. This sentence is mitigated, 328. Certain priests ordained by him were promoted to the episcopate, ibid. Concerning a deacon promoted directly to the episcopate, ibid. To what extent such ordinations were defended by the authorities, ibid. note.

In what particular sense “to exercise the ecclesiastical orders” is understood, 521 note. Requirements for receiving orders, 418. Those arranging ordination without the necessary conditions, namely that they should have the means of living, are censured, 470. The illicit ordinations of boys, and ordinations performed for a price, are castigated, 577.

The rite for baptizing those in danger of death, 419. The rite for reconciliation according to the manner canonically reserved to oneself, ibid. Canons cited on this matter, 229 and following. The rite for anointing the sick, 419. The rite and prayers at the funerals of the dead, ibid.

The military order, 570.

*Orma* used for *anathema*, 322.

What a doorkeeper ought to be like, 164. Doorkeepers attended the bishop so that they might be ready for his commands; hence they are also called “sent from his side,” 562 note.

Idleness must be avoided even by the rich, 41. A person must work, ibid. Idleness must be avoided in the spiritual life, 26.

Emperor Otto I entered Italy twice in triumph, 299, no. 3, 531. The first entrance, with his son Liutulf, occurred in what year, LXIX. He attempted to restore Ratherius to the See of Verona, 217, 542. Why he was prevented, 542. His eulogy, 396, 440. The privilege granted by him to Ratherius and the Church of Verona, 457 and following. When he was about to leave Verona, he gave Ratherius money to complete the basilica of Saint Zeno, 500. His second entrance into Italy is assigned to the year 961, CV. In that year Ratherius was restored, CVI and following. His edict in favor of Ratherius is explained, CXII.

## P

Pagans are to be rewarded in the present life for whatever good they have done, but tormented eternally, 71.

Palaestrita, emperor, 10, 187.

The synod of Pavia of the year 962, and the three cases decided there, CVIII, no. 83 and following.

The glory of Paradise, in which holy souls dwell, 102. It is argued against someone’s error that being there and rejoicing with God is the same as reigning, 116.

Good Friday (*Parasceve*) explained morally, 412.

The child martyrs, 62. Admonitions concerning children, ibid.

Easter, that is, the Lord’s passage from death to life, 411. Christ is Easter, because he was sacrificed, ibid., 412. How and with what joy the Easter feast should be celebrated, 608. The body and blood of Christ the Lamb must be received during it, 607, 609, 610, 612.

The work of Paschasius Ratbertus, *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, praised, 286. It was wrongly attributed to Ratherius, XVII, no. 25.

Patricus, to whom Ratherius sent a letter, 521, 522.

The duties of fathers, 60.

To what extent the poor can give alms, 48. Against idle poor people, 49. They should obtain their livelihood by work, 47. What they should do if they cannot work, 49. The pride of certain poor people exceeds the arrogance of the rich, 48.

Regular poverty. See *Proprietas*, *Monachus*.

Public sins reserved to the bishop, 421.

Original sin, 62. Original and actual sin, 160. Daily and lesser sins, 127. How they are to be cleansed, ibid. Criminal and lesser sins must be distinguished, 590. The distinction between venial and mortal sin in marital intercourse, which is blameless when undertaken solely with the intention of procreation, 52, 53. The gravity of sin because God’s presence has been offended, 335, 642. In hell, whatever good things a sinner has done are of no benefit to him, 368. For those who relapse into sin and are never permanently converted, it would have been better to have received a just sentence for their first contempt of God than to have been spared so long and to have accumulated so many offenses, each to be punished eternally, 434. How grave is the crime that cannot come to an end even when the criminal is dying, 427. Whoever has fallen should not delay rising again, 178. Experience teaches that more recent wounds are healed more quickly than older ones, 642.

The *pedale*, a pontifical staff, 114.

Danger. What is dangerous for one person ought not indiscriminately to be sought by many, 25. How great the evil of perjury is, 26. How persecutions are to be endured, 85. How necessary perseverance is, 185, 603.

Persius cited, 39.

The case of Peter, bishop of Ravenna, decided at the synod of Pavia against Honestus, CVIII, no. 84.

Photius condemned, 330, 451.

*Pigmentum*: a drink made from various ingredients, 15. Its frequent use among Italians, 367.

*Pitaciolum*: a small sheet or short booklet in which something was written, 539 note.

Plato praised in the *Timaeus*, 183.

Plautus, 639.

Parish priests were forbidden to make someone a cleric—that is, to enroll anyone among the clergy or clothe anyone in clerical dress—without the bishop’s permission, 421. They could impose penance for hidden sins; but for public sins they had to refer the matter to the bishop, ibid. See *Poenitentia*.

What “the people with the estate” (*plebs cum curte*) signifies, 563 note.

Pliny the Younger cited, 242.

Penitents beaten with brooms or rods, 355 note. Penitents distinguished from others by their clothing, 602 note. A change of clothing is of no benefit to them unless there is a conversion of heart, ibid. Indeed, it provokes God’s anger when they not only remain in their sins but also, with a feigned heart, counterfeit conversion through their clothing, ibid. What is demonstrated by clothing should rather be exhibited in the heart, 603.

Concerning penitents, 172. There is a place of penance for every criminal, 452. Whoever has committed illicit acts should also cautiously restrain himself from lawful ones, 174. Penance is of no benefit to those who do not abandon the sin over which they grieve, 370. Those who do penance less worthily should not be brought to reconciliation, 416. After penance, namely public penance, no one is permitted by canon law to remain a cleric, 452. Penance is to be imposed according to the *Penitential*, 417. Parish priests imposed penance according to the character of the offense on the Wednesday before Lent, ibid. But only the bishop had authority to reconcile public penitents; this was done on Thursday of the Lord’s Supper, 42 note. Parish priests could impose penance for hidden sins, but public sins had to be referred to the bishop, 421. The example of a certain Scot, who had invaded the episcopate, and by what penance he was purified and how he was restored to the episcopate, 453. The redemption of public penance by almsgiving introduced, 416 note. Priests should possess a *Penitential*, 419.

Pollution of those sleeping or awake, 60.

Portus, a fortress in the diocese of Verona whose river dues were granted to the bishopric, 458.

The Lord’s commandments: some generally appropriate to everyone, others specifically appropriate to certain people, 12.

How displeasing plunder is to God, 13.

Preaching useful to some must not be omitted even if it provokes anger in others, 489.

Entire books were called by the name *Prefaces*, 188, 192.

Regular prelates must obey the rule, 284. The negligence of prelates in correcting their subjects. See *Negligentia*.

The powerful censured, 45.

How greatly God’s presence aggravates sins, 335, 336.

Priests were always dressed in a white garment, which they were not to use when celebrating the sacrifice of the Mass, 414 note. They should not travel without a stole, 417. A priest should have a cell beside the church, and no women should live in it, 414. He owes to his church whatever he acquired after the day of his ordination, 267, 416. Chaplain-priests distinguished from canons, 471 note.

The word *privatus* used to mean a familiar or intimate associate, 94.

The privilege granted by Otto I to Ratherius and the Church of Verona, 457 and following.

An agent who conducts another person’s affairs, 26.

How carefully regulars must avoid private property, 165. How empty the excuse based on the community’s poverty is, 266. Regular discipline was corrupted under this pretext, ibid. and note. Against those regulars who gather or reserve something for themselves, 267.

Saint Prosper praised, 59, 60.

Provincials supplying grain to soldiers, 68.

What prudence is, 79. Without simplicity it is cunning, 181.

Corrected psalters praised, 410.

The Psylli, snake-charmers in Africa, 15 note.

What bodily chastity is, 58.

The punishments of purgatory after death are assigned not to grave sins but to lesser sins, which are signified by wood, hay, and straw, 590. Prayer for the souls of the dead, that they may reach heaven, 210.

*Puta* used for “prostitute,” 292 note.

The letter Y of Pythagoras, signifying the two-branched path of life, 63 note.

## Q

During Lent one must fast every day except Sundays, 420. Why the forty days of fasting were instituted, 581, 611. Those are censured who, tasting nothing one day and indulging in gluttony the next, fasted for only twenty days, ibid. and 58. The abuse of those who prolonged the fast until nightfall so that at night they could, as if with permission, stuff their bellies, is censured, 584. The practice of extending the Lenten fast until the ninth hour, introduced by later discipline, of which Ratherius is the first witness, 420 note, 484. Previously it had to be extended until evening, and this was observed by many even somewhat after the eleventh century, 420 note. Whoever fasts must eat only once, 585. Who are exempt from the law of fasting, 420, 421. See *Jejunium*.

Marriages entered into during Lent censured, 423, 426. Even if they had been entered into secretly by someone, 426 note. Abstinence from one’s wife during Lent, 606, 630.

## R

Ratbertus, author of the work *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*. See Paschasius.

Ratherius’s homeland was Liège, XXVI, c. 206. His nobility, commended by its antiquity, XXVII. He was related to the foremost families of the Burgundian people, 99. His birth year is conjectured, XXVIII, no. 5.

As a little boy he was offered to God in the monastery of Lobbes with bread and wine, 254. His profession and the formula of his profession, ibid. He made great progress in his studies, 199. Yet he learned more by himself than from teachers, 220. He appears to have been instructed in Greek, XXXI. How great his ability was in reading books, 375, 379. His expertise in even profane authors, CXI. Questions were proposed to him for resolution by the Milanese and afterward by Robert, archbishop of Trier, 527. How excellent his memory was, IV.

Ratherius, the monk of Lobbes, clung inseparably to Bishop Hilduinus when the latter set out for Italy and was subsequently promoted to the Church of Verona, XXXIV. When Hilduinus was later transferred to the See of Milan, Ratherius was appointed in his place to the Veronese cathedral, XXXVII, no. 15. The year and month of the beginning of his Veronese episcopate are established, XXXIX, no. 17.

King Hugh of Italy, who had promoted him, became hostile and angry toward him, 539. Why, 122 note. He sought an opportunity to expel him, 539. During the rebellion of the Veronese against Hugh, Ratherius was captured and taken to the prison at Pavia, ibid., XLII. Whether the rebellion occurred through any fault of his, XLIII. How many evils the bishop suffered in the prison at Pavia, XLVIII and following. He endured persecution for the sake of justice, 50. Deprived of books in that prison, he wrote the six books of the *Praeloquia*, LI. He was afterward relegated to Como, LIII.
