There he corrected and more clearly described the Life of Saint Ursmar, ibid. He was invited by the Gallic bishops to a synod, ibid. Released from his exile at Como, he went to Gaul, LIV. In Provence he instructed Roestang in letters and composed a book *On the Art of Grammar*, LV, LVI. There the episcopate was offered to him, ibid. From there he moved to Laubies, having been received by Richarius, bishop of Liège and abbot of Lobbes, ibid. He left Laubies to meet Hugh, and on the journey was arrested by Berengarius, 540, LVIII. He was restored to the See of Verona, ibid.

After his restoration, how many harassments he suffered from the clergy, and why, 540, LXIII. He was compelled by order of Lothair to yield the place of Manasius, 542. He wandered through Germany, LXVIII. He came into Italy with Otto and his son Liutulf in the year 951 to recover his see, LXXI. Finding Bishop Milo in that see, the nephew of Count Milo, he returned to Germany, LXXII. He thought he should have recourse to the apostolic See, and what he wrote for this purpose, LXXIII. In Germany Ratherius was received by Bruno, Otto’s brother, among his household, LXXV. He became bishop of Liège, ibid. This was arranged by Bruno, who in the matter was guided not by human considerations but by the good of the Church, LXXVI. How this election of Ratherius was carried out, LXXVII. The date of the election recorded, 218 note 3. The two elections must be distinguished, ibid.

He was later driven from that see, LXXIX, no. 57. Why, LXXX, no. 58. Two short works were written on this occasion: one at Liège before he departed from there, LXXXIV, no. 60; the other at Mainz, where he withdrew and was most graciously received by Archbishop William, LXXXV, no. 61. Certain other short works written on this subject, now lost, are indicated, LXXXVI.

After his expulsion from the See of Liège, Ratherius was placed in charge of a certain abbey belonging to the monastery of Laubies, LXXXVII, no. 63. There he wrote an *Excerpt from a Dialogue of Confession*, XC, no. 65. In the year 961 he returned to Italy with Otto I, CV, no. 80, and was restored to his see, ibid. This restoration was confirmed by the apostolic See and by the synod of Pavia, 442, CVII, no. 82.

After returning to his church, he doubted whether those ordained by the invader had been validly ordained, and issued a decree on this matter, 327. Mitigation of the same decree, ibid. He sought to introduce a more appropriate distribution of revenues among the clergy of the cathedral, CXXVII, no. 100. By collected canons he proved that such distribution belonged to the bishop, CXXVIII, no. 101.

While Milo was acting as invader, Ratherius was captured, 552. He was rescued through the aid of the emperor and Duke Judith, 443. How he avoided rebellion and plots, CXXIX and following. A trial was instituted against the rebels, in which, however, only perjury was dealt with, 398. What that perjury was, CXXXII, no. 105. Ratherius was offered the proposal that he yield the episcopate to Milo, CXXXIII. He did not consent and sent two letters to Milo, 551 and following.

He wrote the *Conjecture of Quality*, 373. It contains censures of quibblers which ultimately redound to his praise, CXXXVII. Why he delayed holding synods, 443. At last he held a synod, and by what procedure, 445, CXXXIX, no. 111. He published the *Synodica*, an important document of the tenth century, 409 and following, CLX, no. 112.

Before setting out for Rome, he wrote an *Itinerary*, 437. He hoped that a council would be convened there at which judgment would be rendered in his case against the clergy and a remedy applied to abuses, CXLIV, no. 116. He took part in the Council of Ravenna of the year 967, no. 118. Soon afterward he convened another diocesan synod to promulgate the decrees of that council, 561. The proceedings of this synod, CXLVI, no. 118. Why he took away from ten clerics certain revenues that he had previously granted from his own income, and to what use he converted them, CL, no. 121.

He issued a judgment to provide for the poorer clerics, 469. It was subscribed by the patriarch of Aquileia and the neighboring bishops, 567. He obtained an imperial diploma, 457.

While the rebellion continued, he published a booklet *On the Clerics Rebelling against Him*, 479, CLV, no. 125. These men acted against the bishop before the emperor, sending a messenger to him, 482. He delivered sermons on peace, 494. He wrote a booklet entitled *Discord*, 485. In it he lists four causes of discord, ibid.

His enemies went to the pope, from whom they brought back letters forbidding the bishop to interfere in the property of the clerics, 507. He wrote an *Apology* against those who wanted the money given by the emperor for the restoration of the church of Saint Zeno to be distributed to the poor, 500, CLIX, no. 129. An investigation against Ratherius was conducted by two persons corrupted by money, 615, CLXI, no. 131. He wrote a testament, 512.

Nanno, count of Verona, held a legal proceeding against Ratherius, 565, 566, CLXIII, no. 133. He complained about this proceeding in two letters: one to Nanno himself, 557; the other to Ambrosius the chancellor, 561. He wrote to the empress Adelaide, 568.

As he was about to resign the episcopate, he sent to Fulcuinus, abbot of Laubies, a booklet entitled *The Conflict of Two*, now lost, CLXVI, no. 138. He also wrote to Everaclus, bishop of Liège, who praised him highly and urged him to return to his homeland, 569. Received by Everaclus and by Abbot Fulcuinus, he was placed in charge of several abbeys, CLXVIII. He was cleared of the purchase of the abbey of Saint-Amand by simony, CLXIX and following. He was placed in charge of the Abbey of Laubies, CLXVI, no. 142. Concerning his death, CLXXIII, no. 143.

With what spirit Ratherius bore misfortunes, 99, 100. His humble confession, 175, 190. He censured his own character and himself, 375. He censured not only others but also himself, 376. He diminished his own reputation and glory, 223. He did not care if anyone spoke ill of him, 381. How greatly he exaggerated certain crimes charged against him, 252 note, 281 note. What should be thought about the offenses listed in the booklet of his Confession, 245, nos. 3 and 4. He gave a few coins to someone who had insulted him, 381. His patience praised, 570.

He generously gave away his own possessions, grieving over the misery of others and becoming all things to all people so that he might win them all, 570. Because he was extremely poor, he did not wish to have a servant or chaplain, 375. He preferred to have enough rather than be rich, 385. He wished to die as a beggar, so that he might be buried from alms, ibid. He prepared a frugal table and invited the poor to it, 377. He used modest furnishings, 376. He often abstained from meat, 377, and almost always from wine; for this reason he was called *Abstemius*, 384. He more often slept on the ground, 377.

How great his care was in building and rebuilding churches, 376, 378, 390. How greatly he feared because he had abandoned the monastery for the sake of the episcopate, 255 note. He considered himself like a fugitive slave who needed to return to his master, ibid., 260. The obstacles raised to prevent his return, 260, 261, 380 note, XCI, no. 66. The provinces through which he wandered after being expelled from Verona, 250 note, 378 note. Ratherius, deprived of the support of friends at Verona because he was an outsider, 392. How many exiles he endured, 442 note.

In a certain doubt, following Augustine’s example, he wished to go to a council to be convened at Rome, 439, 456. Ratherius called a preacher, 384. He prayed with such fervor that he wailed, 388. Even when resisting, he was witty, 278, 379.

The synod of Ravenna of the year 967, which Ratherius also attended, was held in mid-April, 561. The decree issued there concerning the dismissal of clerical women, 491, 559, CXLVI, no. 118.

The Ravennate bishops Peter and Honestus. See *Petri Ravennatis*, *Honestus*.

How harmful relapse is, 605.

*Redimiculum*: a head ornament worn by women, 143.

Which queens women should imitate, 138.

Reginerus, count of Hainaut, a powerful man, 219 note.

The Rule of Saint Benedict praised under the name of Scripture, 226 note.

*Regulus*: the basilisk, 186.

The duties of kings, 77 and following. Their virtues, ibid., 80, 126, 137. Kings are stewards of what God has bestowed upon them, 126. They should give alms more than others, ibid. They must observe their own laws, 137. They must bear the people, not oppress them, 126. How they ought to conduct themselves toward churches and ecclesiastical property, 137. They should fortify ecclesiastical discipline, ibid. Why authority was granted to them in relation to the Church, ibid. The heart of kings is in God’s hand in three ways, 132. What ministers they should choose, 138. What they must avoid, ibid. The king is blessed who knows how to govern himself well, 136.

A passage from the synod of Reims of the year 992 explained, CXVIII, no. 83 and following.

Public sins reserved to the bishop, 420 note.

In what respects the true resurrection of the elect and of the reprobate differs, 103.

Richarius, abbot of Prüm, consecrated bishop of Liège by John XI, XXXIV. In what year he died, LVI.

Robert, archbishop of Trier, the most noble of the prelates, 527 note. He proposed questions to Ratherius for solution, and what Ratherius replied, ibid. Ratherius sought his assistance, 529. He sent him the books of the *Praeloquia*, [Col. 1332] 529. Robert delivered a sermon from the pulpit at the election of Ratherius to the See of Liège, 210 note. In it he praised Ratherius, 218, 229. He ordained Saint Bruno archbishop of Cologne, 208 note. He afterward arranged for Ratherius to be excluded from the See of Liège, 218. A false rumor had announced him dead, 222, 239.

The judgment of Rodoaldus, patriarch of Aquileia, in Ratherius’s case, 663. It is proved to be spurious, 658 and following. He subscribed, with the neighboring bishops, the Judgment of Ratherius, 567.

Executors of wills, 385.

Fasting on the days of the Rogations was introduced even in our regions in the tenth century, 416 note, 623 note. The Rogations were called by the name of litanies, 623 note. How they are to be observed, ibid.

The Roman See is universal, principal, and chief, because it is distinguished as the head of the Church, its nurse, mother, judge, and teacher of all, 106. Its doctrine surpasses that of the other churches, 440. Its eulogy, ibid. In it the canons are examined, those to be received approved, and those to be rejected condemned, ibid. Nowhere is what is invalid there valid, and nowhere is what is judged valid there invalid, ibid. Ratherius appeals to the apostolic Roman See against the invader, prepared to accept whatever sentence may be given, 545.

The Roman Council held by John XIII in the presence of Otto I in the year 967, CXLV, no. 117.

The Roman pontiff of the first See, supreme pontiff and patriarch, 537. He should be called the archbishop of archbishops, the universal pope, ibid. He holds the See of Peter so that he may not allow the gates of hell to prevail against the Church, insofar as he is able to resist with God’s help, ibid. The supreme pontiff ought to be censured by no one, 543.

Ruodvoltus, a powerful count, maternal uncle of Baldric, bishop of Liège, 219 note. He acted on behalf of King Otto against Duke Conrad, LXXXIII.

## S

The Sabbath is called release, or rest, so that we may rest from evil works and devote ourselves to divine service, 412.

Why *sacerdos* (“priest”) is so called, 354.

The rights of the priesthood were bestowed by God himself through the Holy Spirit, 93. The priesthood was bestowed by God alone and is superior to kingship, 92. The priesthood of the Church is royal, 97.

Whose work the sacraments are, 256, 354.

The shadowy sacrifice of the Old Law is distinguished from the true sacrifice of the New Testament, 87.

The pattern of the world, 9. Its cares darken the mirror of the mind, 10.

*Sagmio*: one who drives a packhorse, 30 note.

Sallust praised, 377, 507.

The merits of the saints assist us, 622. We should do what they did, ibid. Their invocation for aid and protection, 91, 311, 312, 456. Their intercession, 292. The souls of the saints and the righteous are in heaven with Christ, 598. The error of one who says that the saints rejoice in heaven but do not reign is refuted, 116. Many bodies of saints are in the cities of Italy. Some were stolen and carried elsewhere, 305.

Things offered to the Lord are called sanctuaries, 13.

The canons of Sardica praised, 348, 349, 447.

The space of sand designated for wrestlers is called a *scamma*, 177.

Pharisaic scandal is not to be heeded, 490. Preaching useful to some must not be omitted if it irritates others, 489.

*Scardus*: sparing, giving sparingly, 384.

There were three schools in which the Veronese clergy were instructed: one in the city, perhaps near the cathedral; another in the monasteries; and another under some learned man, 419.

Who was called a *Scoldascius*, *Sculsdacius*, or *Sculdais*, 30 note.

Holy Scripture is to be interpreted from tradition, 189.

The Acts of the Passion of Saint Sebastian praised, 16.

*Segalum* used for *siligine* (“rye”), 401 note.

Seneca praised, 34, 35, 43, 174.

The elderly should not be ashamed to learn what they do not know and ought to know, 69. They should not despair if they are wicked, but persist in penance, 72. Admonitions to the same, 68, 73.

Who is an aged *silicernius*, 72 note.

*Senio*: a type of game, 143.

*Senior* used for “Lord,” 26 note, 28 note, 34; for “prince,” 144, 152; for “king,” 325 note.

Burial, for which nothing should be demanded, 415.

What slaves should do and what they must avoid, 57.

Sigebertus attributes two works to Ratherius that are actually by Ratramnus, XVI, no. 24. He divided one work of Ratherius into two, XX, no. 29. The passages of the same work are noted, LXXVI–LXXXII.

Signs used for the sound of bells, 210 note, 239.

A person who is very old is called *silicernius*, 72 note.

If someone commits a simoniacal act, he will not be able to escape Simon’s condemnation, 451. Examples of simony in those who purchased the ranks of prelates for a price, 266 note, 281. With what zeal and how many labors these offices were acquired, and why, 283, 284. No one should demand anything for baptizing infants, reconciling the sick, or burying the dead, 215. Simoniacal ordinations noted, 557. A heretic is called a simoniac, 363.

The decree of Pope Siricius praised, 349.

The passion of Saint Sixtus, pope and martyr, 344.

Sobbo, archbishop of Vienne in Gaul, to whom Ratherius sent the six books of the *Praeloquia*, 526. A certain annotation inserted in the form of a letter to him in the fifth book of the *Praeloquia*, 150 note.

*Sperones*, a rustic term for spurs. See *Calcaria*.

Hope should be placed in God; as for oneself, one should despair, 264.

The Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, 82, 102. The consubstantial love of both was never absent from them, and it proceeds from the one to the other and from the other to the one—without place, without change, eternally, and therefore ineffably, ibid. Sent by the Father and the Son to inspire the minds of the elect, he comes from himself temporally, ibid.

Statius cited, 111.

Pope Stephen IV praised under the name of Stephen III, and why, 331 note. A fragment from a council of that same Stephen absent from the commonly circulated editions, ibid.

The stole is a sign of priestly dignity and must also be worn by priests while traveling, 417.

Strudo-Came, *ontis*, 205.

A bishop should devote himself to the study of sacred, not profane, books, 527, 528. To what extent profane studies should be converted to sacred use, 303, 528.

What a subdeacon ought to be like, 164. There were two classes of subdeacons in the cathedral of Verona: some called “of the secretariat,” others singers, 471 note.

*Summates*: noblemen, 30 note.

Pride, through which the righteous fall, 59, 60.

A superior will give an account for the offenses of his subjects which he did not prevent or neglected to correct. See *Negligentia*.

*Suricum*: a type of grain, 401.

A decree of suspension for a fixed period, 327. Revoked or mitigated by another decree, and why, ibid.

The Creed and the Lord’s Prayer are to be taught to parishioners, 416. Godparents must also teach them to their children, 418. The Creed, that is, the contribution of the Apostles, as it is found in corrected psalters, 410. In some places it contained certain additions not approved by Ratherius, ibid. note.

The Creed, or faith, called that of Saint Athanasius. See *Fides*. A fragment of it cited, 450, 589. The cathedral cardinals of Verona did not wish to sing it as the clergy of other churches sang it, 447.

The synodal sermon, or *Admonition*, containing a brief summary of the canons: to whom it should be attributed and to whom it is to be attributed, 405, nos. 3 and 4. What Ratherius inserted from it into his *Synodica*, 414 note.

Ratherius’s *Synodica*, 409 and following. Why he published it, 446. A diocesan synod is to be held twice a year, 443. Why Ratherius delayed it, ibid. In these synods, anything done contrary to the canons is usually corrected, ibid. A synod held by Ratherius in the year 966 during Lent, 443 note. What was done in it, 445. The noteworthy rite by which such synods were held, ibid. note.

Another synod held by him after the Council of Ravenna, 561. The synod of the bishops of the province of Aquileia held at Verona in the year 967, CLIII. The synod of Pavia, which restored Ratherius to his see after his second expulsion, 508 note. Concerning the acts of this synod, CVIII, no. 83 and following. The synod of the prelates of the province of Cologne concerning Ratherius’s election to the See of Liège, and its judgment, LXXVIII, 218. The synod celebrated at Ravenna in mid-April of the year 967, CXLVI, no. 118, 561. Its decree against the sexual misconduct of clerics, 562 note. The Roman synod of the year 967, CXLV. “To hold a synod” was said of a bishop when he was visiting rural parishes, LIV.

*Syrma*, 203.

## T
Taphus, a tomb, 72 note. Tasphorus, a back, 44. Pope Telesphorus cited, 232. Toll collector, 26. The toll duty of the two gates of the city of Verona granted to the episcopate, 457. What *temperentia* is, 79. Those who send storms, and the error censured concerning this matter, 21 note, 626 note. Temptations: what should be done in them, 178. [Col. 1334] The lukewarm rebuked, 168. The signs and effects of lukewarmness, 261. Terence cited, 77, 229, 566. What witnesses must beware of, 26. Theodosius, emperor “of most merciful memory,” 129. What servile fear is, 57. What chaste fear is, ibid. The distinction between the two kinds, 310, 336. Fear of hell is useful, 60, 274. It is from God, 274. God should be feared rather than hell, ibid. Which fear makes one blessed, 333. Which fear torments the conscience, ibid., 334. Whoever has sinned ought to fear, 643. How greatly those who relapse ought to fear, but they should not despair absolutely, 431, 432. Everything that is feared is rationally avoided, 643. Titular clergy: clerics so called from the churches of the city and suburbs of Verona, 447 note. Those assigned to a titular church were forbidden to abandon it and move to another church for the sake of profit, 416. The tradition of the Fathers, and how much Ratherius attributed to it, 189. Sacred Scripture is to be explained from tradition, ibid. From it Ratherius compiled six books of *Praeloquia*, 191. The transfer of bishops forbidden by the Council of Sardica, 348. When permitted by the canons. See *Bishop expelled from his see*. How tribulations are to be endured, especially by a sinner, 161, 433. Works of repentance must be joined to tribulations, ibid. Those who are changed in tribulation are freed from sins, 162. Temporal scourges free from eternal ones only those whom they change, 433. The March of Trent. See *March*. Presbyters married to a third or fourth wife censured, 509. The God of the Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—the unity of whom consists in the divinity and the Trinity in the persons, 598. The eternally equal, coessential, or consubstantial unity of the Trinity, and the Trinity of unity—that is, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, creator and governor of all things—so that the one and same substance remains, distinguished by the personal properties, 112. The Father is he who created all things; the Son, through whom all things were created; the Holy Spirit, by whom all things were created, ibid. The Father is the authority of the Son; the Son, the wisdom of the Father; the Holy Spirit, declaring the communion of the Father and the Son, ibid. The Father is from himself, not from another; the Son is from the Father alone; the Spirit is from the Father and the Son, ibid. Sadness is sometimes better than joy, 182.

U

King Hugh of Italy. See *Hugh*. A decree of Pope Urban praised, 341. The life of Saint Ursmar, abbot of Lobbes, 195 ff. The duties of wives toward their husbands, 57. What they should be within themselves, 58.

V

Varro cited, 30. Sacred vessels are to be washed by presbyters, 414. The water with which they have been washed is to be poured into a prepared place in the sacristy or beside the altar, 415. Sacred vessels and priestly vestments must not be given in pledge, 416. The province of Venetia, where costly cloaks were made, 558 note. Venetian denarii, 383. Verona was once esteemed, because of its multitude of wise men, as that Platonic Athens, 306. It seems to have been customary at Verona to insert monuments expressed in verse into the walls, 309 note. The fortress of Verona, or fortified castle on the mountain called the Palatium, 392 note, 393. The *Curtis Alta*, a public and very strongly fortified building at Verona, 393. The circus called the Arena, ibid. The clergy of the cathedral of Verona: some were the greater clergy, called ordinary or cardinal canons. See *ordinary cardinals*. Others were inferior and were called chaplain-presbyters; others, subdeacons of the sacristy; others, singing subdeacons; others, acolytes of the sacristy; others, singing acolytes; and others, doorkeepers, 47 note. The privilege granted by Otto I to the Veronese church under Ratherius, 457. Places across Lake Benacus subject to the Church of Verona, 383 note. The abbey of Maguzano belonging to the disposition of the bishop of Verona. See *Abbey*. Two diocesan synods of Verona under Ratherius. See *Synod*. The March of Verona. See *March*. Pontifical vestments, 114. *Vicinitas* used for the same city, 205. *Vicinium* in the same sense, 319 note. *Vicinus* for an inhabitant of the same city, 565. How a widow ought to conduct herself, 61. From where *vir* (“man”) is derived, 50. Who proves himself a man, ibid. Virgil cited, 509. How virgins should conduct themselves and what they should do, 61. [Col. 1335] Visits to rural parishes, in which sense a synod was said to be held and chapters of the clergy to take place, LXIV, LXV. The two lives, active and contemplative, explained through Martha and Mary, 637 ff. The church of Saint Vitalis in the suburb of Verona, where the body of Saint Metronus lies, 304 note. Its revenues formerly given as benefices to soldiers, 305 note. Nor was there a presbyter there to guard the sacred body, ibid. Capital vices, 170. Vices often pretend to be virtues, 78. Vices must not be cloaked, 79. *Vivere meum* used for *meus victus* (“my livelihood”), 391.

W

Count Waltfred of Verona in the year 880, XCVI. He must be distinguished from Margrave Valfred of Friuli, ibid. [Col. 1336] Warnerius, brother of Duke Cono or Conrad, 25. Archbishop Wido of Lyons, to whom Ratherius sent a letter and the books of the *Praeloquia*, 525. Ratherius’s annotation to the same man in the form of a letter, 150 note. What *wiffa* is, 114. William, archbishop of Mainz and son of Otto I, generously received Ratherius after he had been expelled from the see of Liège, 219.

Z

Saint Zeno, bishop of Verona, praised, 158, 360, 362, 502. Our special doctor and protector—or that of the Veronese—, 413. Our patron, 500. Money contributed by Otto I for completing his basilica, ibid.

[Col. 1335]

INDEX TO THE AUTHENTIC WORKS OF LIUTPRAND. The reader is referred to the columns of our edition. [Note: This index refers only to the authentic works of Luitprand between columns 0787 and 0938. It does not include the works of Pseudo-Luitprand.]

A

Count Adelbert of Baverburg rebels against King Louis and harasses him for seven years, 814. Entrapped by the words of Hatto, archbishop of Mainz, and brought to Louis, he is beheaded, 815. Margrave Adelbert of Ivrea, surnamed “the Rich,” marches his forces against Lanthbert, 807. But he is captured and mocked by him, 808. He is faithless toward his father-in-law, 823. In his youth he was good, but afterward degenerates from goodness, ibid. He is captured by the Hungarians on Mount Brixia but escapes by a trick, 831. When Emperor Otto came into Italy, he withdrew from Italy and commended himself to the Saracens, 897. On his return, he fled with Pope John, 896, 899.

Adelhard, a cleric of King Berengarius, draws Manasses, bishop of Verona, over to Berengarius’s party by the king’s promises, 889. But Berengarius did not keep faith with him, 891.

On what occasion the Africans invaded Italy in the time of the Roman emperor of Constantinople, 826.

Alberic, son of the harlot Marozia, beaten by his stepfather King Hugh, incites the Romans to drive him out, 853. He marries Alda, Hugh’s daughter, but nevertheless does not hand Rome over to him, 838. He is besieged at Rome by Hugh, 878.

Amedeus, a soldier of the margrave Berengarius, was a clever man, 884. In the guise of a poor man he enters Italy from Germany and often changes his appearance, 885. After stirring the minds of the Italians, he returns by unknown routes to Berengarius, ibid.

The friendship of conspirators is weak, 885.

There are two kinds of friends, 800.

The fear of Margrave Anscarius, 806.

Ansgarius, son of Adelbert and Ermengarda, King Hugh’s sister: a bold and powerful man, 861. He becomes margrave of Spoleto, 878. He was suspected by King Hugh, ibid. His valor and death, ibid.

Aquileia, destroyed by the Huns, never rose again, 839.

Archodus gives bad advice to Anscarius, who wished to repel the force of Sarlio, 879. He flees from the battle, 880.

Arnold, duke of Bavaria, flees to Hungary, 819. He returns with his men from Hungary, 820. He aspires to imperial power, but Emperor Henry wins him over and he submits to him, 821. He comes into Italy to take the kingdom from King Hugh, but Hugh defeats and routs him, 856.

King Arnulf disastrously calls the Hungarians against Zwentebald, 799. His rashness, ibid. and following pages. He sends aid to Berengarius, king of Italy, and on what terms, against Wido, 801. His metrical speech to his men, 802. He captures Rome with his men, ibid. He protects Pope Formosus, ibid. Besieged at Fermo by the wife of King Wido, he is given a drugged drink and put to sleep, 805. His insolence, ibid. He attempts to blind Berengarius so that he might obtain the kingdom of Italy, 805. He is despised by his own men, ibid. His dreadful end, 806.

The avaricious are truly poor, 890.

[Col. 1336] B

Baianus, son of Simeon, king of the Bulgarians, used magic to turn men into wolves, 847.

How Basil the Macedonian attained the imperial power of Constantinople; his lineage, 793. He kills the emperor Michael, 794. The Lord Christ appears to him and reproaches him for this murder, ibid. He does penance, ibid. He builds a church to Saint Michael, ibid.

The insolence of a certain Bavarian knight in provoking an Italian enemy, 801.

The right to appoint bishops within his territory is granted to the duke of Bavaria, 822.

Antipope Benedict strips himself of his pontifical vestments before the Roman council, 908. His repentance, ibid. He is punished with exile, 909.

Berengarius becomes king of Italy, 800. Wido makes war against him, ibid. He is twice driven to flight, 801. He seeks the aid of King Arnulf, ibid. He gradually occupies the cities that opposed him, 801. When King Arnulf wishes to blind him, he flees to Verona, 805. He reigns after Wido’s death, 806. But fearing Wido’s son Lanthbert, he withdraws to Verona, 807. He reigns again, 810. Why he did not march against the Hungarians who had entered Italy, 816. He discovers that his son-in-law, Margrave Adelbert of Ivrea, is faithless, 825. He is forced to leave Verona, ibid. Soon afterward he returns, having corrupted the guards with gold, ibid. He obtains the kingdom of Italy peacefully, 826. Various princes rebel against him, 830. He is defeated by Rodulf of Burgundy, 833. He suffers a danger to his life from Flambert, ibid. He gives him a golden cup as a sign of friendship, ibid. Nevertheless Flambert cuts his throat, ibid.

Margrave Berengarius of Ivrea, from Swabia, seeks Italy and through the agency of the cleric Adelhard draws Manasses, bishop of Verona, over to his side, 888. And many others, 889. He is restored to the kingdom, ibid. His cunning in receiving Hugh’s son, 890. He deposes and appoints bishops at will, 890 ff. His ingratitude toward his promoters and the change in his conduct in the kingdom, 891. He exacts an immense tribute from churches and the poor, 892. He sends Luitprand to Constantinople at his stepfather’s expense, 894. His insolence toward bishops, 897, 898.

Bertha, wife of Margrave Adelbert of Tuscany, was a wicked woman, 807, 823, 824, 830. Her offspring, ibid. Whether those accounts are true, 854.

Bertha, King Hugh’s daughter by a harlot, marries the grandson of the Roman emperor of Constantinople through his daughter Helena and is called Eudoxia by the Greeks, 886.

Bertha, widow of Boso, count of Arles, and niece of King Hugh, becomes heir to all his money, 892.

Margrave Boniface of Camerino defeats and routs the Berengarians, 833.

Boso, King Hugh’s brother, plots against Lambert, margrave of Tuscany, 854. Hugh appoints him margrave of Tuscany, ibid. He has a daughter, Willa, whom Hugh joins in marriage to Berengarius, margrave of Ivrea, 861. At Willa’s instigation he undertakes a new conspiracy against his brother, King Hugh, and is captured, 862.

The Bulgarians defeat the Greeks through the negligence of the general Phocas, 846.

Burchard, duke of Swabia, comes into Italy with his son-in-law Rodulf, 841. Entering Milan under the pretext of an embassy, he discovers that the citizens’ feelings have been alienated by certain rash statements of his and is killed on the road, 842.

From where the Burgundians are named, 853.

C

Large dogs sent by King Hugh to Constantinople nearly tore the emperor to pieces because he was dressed in furs, 843.

King Charles the Bald of Gaul dies, 801.

*Carsamatium* is what the Greeks call a castrated eunuch, 895.

The Greeks call ships *chelandria*, 881.

Among conspirators, firm friendship is rare, 800.

Conrad, son of Louis, becomes emperor after his father’s death and subdues the rebellious princes, 819. As he is dying, he summons the princes and urges them to make Henry, duke of Saxony, emperor, ibid.

The names, location, and neighbors of Constantinople, 795.

The emperor Constantine the Great ordered a house called the Porphyra to be built at Constantinople, and for what purpose, 793.

Constantine, son of the emperor Leo, was the son-in-law of Romanus. After Romanus had been driven from power by his own sons, Constantine is proclaimed emperor and is aided by King Hugh, 887. He writes to Berengarius on behalf of Lotharius, 894.

The religious devotion and discipline of Constantine Porphyrogenitus, 850.

He who is content with his own possessions is truly rich, 889.

Why blind people are generally long-lived, 832.

D

The Danes are subdued by Emperor Henry and made tributary; their savagery throughout Germany, 854.

The *Decaennea* was a house at Constantinople measuring nineteen cubits, and why it was so called, 895.

God chastises the sins of his own people with disasters, 827.

Diabolinus betrays his masters, Stephen and Constantine, sons of Romanus, and adheres to Constantine, son of Leo, 887. He gives him good advice, ibid.

Who should be called rich, 889.

Dominic, chaplain of Willa, wife of King Berengarius, had a deformed appearance, 892. A dog exposes his intercourse with her, ibid. He is castrated, ibid.

E

A solar eclipse occurred before King Radamir of Galicia’s victory over Abd al-Rahman, king of the Moors, 877.

Ermengarda, second wife of Adelbert, margrave of Ivrea, and daughter of Adelbert, margrave of Tuscany, 830. She gives birth to Anscarius, ibid., 878. Her power and wantonness, 840. By a stratagem she terrifies Rodulf of Burgundy, 840.

Everhard, son of Emperor Henry, captures Henry and carries him off to France; he incites Gilbert, duke of Lorraine, against Emperor Otto and compels him to defect from Otto, ibid. His crafty counsel, 867. He devastates Alsace, 871. He is killed, 873.

The guards of Constantinople, 795. Leo the emperor tests their loyalty, 796. He rewards the good with gifts and punishes the sluggish, 797.

F

Flambert lays an ambush for the life of King Berengarius, 833. In fact he strikes him down, 834. He ends his life by hanging, ibid.

Pope Formosus is persecuted by the Roman citizens: what was the cause of their mutual hostility, 803. Though already dead, he suffers outrages from Sergius, the antipope, 804.

The location of the town of Fraxinetum is described, 791. It is captured by the Saracens, ibid. After abandoning it, they came to Aquae, but all perished, 859.

When Archbishop Frederick of Mainz hears of the defeat of the conspirators, he is terrified, 875. He is captured and taken to Saxony, but at length, through Otto’s mercy, is restored to his former dignity, 876.

G

The vices of Gezo, judge of Pavia, 850. He conspires against King Hugh, 851. But through the counsel of Count Samson he falls into the king’s hands and is deprived of his tongue and eyes, ibid.

Count Gilbert rebels against Berengarius, 830. Captured by the Hungarians, he is brought before Berengarius, 831. But after being released by him, he breaks faith, ibid.

Gilla, daughter of Berengarius, was the mother of Berengarius, margrave of Ivrea, 878.

The later Greeks were unwarlike and unfit for war, 927. [Col. 1338] Their arrogance in refusing to acknowledge the Western emperors, 928. In marriages they did not inquire into the nobility of the mother but of the father, 882. They called themselves Romans, but the remaining Romans “Latins,” 915. They foolishly flattered their own princes, 920. What the Greek *περιβόλαιον* (*peribolaion*, “cloak” or “covering”) means, 924. What Greek fire is and of what nature, 844.

Guido. See *Wido*.

H

Most heresies were devised by the Greeks, 918.

Hatto, archbishop of Mainz, leads Count Adelbert of Baverburg, ensnared by his words, to King Louis; the king condemns him to death, 814.

Count Hatto is killed in battle by Anscarius with a wooden spear, 880.

Helena, or Irene, daughter of the Roman emperor of Constantinople, marries Constantine Porphyrogenitus, 847.

Henry, duke of Saxony, becomes emperor at the urging of the deceased Emperor Conrad, 820. He gathers forces against the advancing Hungarians, 821. He exhorts his men to battle and renders God favorable to him, 822. He engages them and routs them, wisely warning his men beforehand, 823. He subdues the Slavs and Danes, 842. He dies in Saxony, where he is buried, 864. His prudence, ibid. He acquires the Holy Lance, 869.

Henry, son of Emperor Henry, rebels against his brother Otto, 864. Our Luitprand inveighs against him, ibid. He is captured by Everhard but released so that, when he raised forces against his brother, he might make Everhard emperor, 867. Falling and being struck in battle, he dies the following year from the discoloration caused by the contusion, 868. Presenting himself as a suppliant to his brother, he is confined under guard, 875.

Herman of Swabia seeks a marriage for his daughter with Liutholf, son of Emperor Otto, 877. He commends to Otto Margrave Berengarius of Ivrea, who had fled to him, 882.

Hilduin, expelled from the bishopric of Laon, comes to King Hugh, his kinsman, and becomes bishop of Verona and afterward of Milan, 852.

Hippolytus, Sicilian bishop. What he foretold concerning future times and what authority his statements should have, 925, 926.

The valor of Hubald, margrave of Camerino, against an insolent Bavarian soldier, 801.

Hugh, count of Milan and son of Maginfred, defects from Lanthbert but, although favored by him with benefices, kills him while he sleeps, 807.

Hugh, count of Provence, covets the kingdom of Italy, 841, 842. He cultivated friendship with neighboring princes, ibid. Also with the emperor of Constantinople, to whom he sent Luitprand’s father, 843. An ambush is prepared for him, 851. He seeks Rome, but his folly as he travels there, 853. He is harsher toward his stepson and is driven from Rome by him, ibid. His incest, 852, 854. He does not wish Lambert to call him brother, ibid. He orders Lambert to be deprived of his sight, ibid. He cedes to Rodulf of Burgundy all the land he had possessed in Gaul before becoming king, 855. He associates his son Lotharius with him in the kingdom, 878. He attempts to enter Rome but in vain, ibid. He promises his daughter Alda to Alberic, intending to deceive him, ibid. He marries Bertha, widow of the deceased Rodulf of Burgundy, but soon came to hate her, 863. He had various concubines, but loved three above all, and had children by them, ibid. He besieges Alberic at Rome, 878. He sends Sarlio to Camerino to turn the citizens’ minds away from Anscarius, ibid. He sends envoys to Constantinople for ships and Greek fire against the Saracens, 881. He lays an ambush for Berengarius, margrave of Ivrea, but Berengarius flees, ibid. He sends ambassadors to Otto so that Otto will not receive the fugitive Berengarius, 882. He seeks the daughter of the emperor of Constantinople as wife for his own grandson, ibid. With Greek assistance he drives the Saracens from Fraxinetum, but soon makes a treaty with them because of the margrave Berengarius, whom he feared, 884. Luitprand blames him for this, ibid. He sends the Hungarians off to Spain, ibid. His daughter by a concubine marries Romanus the Younger, the Greek emperor. He is abandoned by the Italians, 888, 889. He humbly begs the Milanese, 890. He goes to Provence, leaving his son Lotharius in Italy, 891. His death, ibid.

Zwentebald is defeated by King Arnulf, 800. The savagery of the Hungarians against the Moravians and Bavarians, 813. They are warlike and fearless, ibid. They overthrow King Louis’s forces, 814. They devastate Swabia and France, 815. They decide to attack Italy, but after learning more about the region through scouts, they return home, 816. In the following year they return to Italy, ibid. Fleeing, they ask the Italians for peace, but in vain, 817. Thus driven to desperation, they rout the Italians, 819. They decide to invade Saxony, 821. They rage at Merseburg, 822. They occupy Verona, 831. They ravage the rest of Italy, 826. King Hugh sends them to Spain, but they do not reach Córdoba, 885. Under King Taxis they come into Italy, 892.

[Col. 1339] I

The emperor of Constantinople distributes gifts to his retainers and officials before Palm Sunday, 896.

Inger, king of the Normans, harasses Constantinople, 883.

The envious man kills himself, 792.

The Italians are unexpectedly slaughtered by the Hungarians because of their sins, 818.

Why they wish to have two kings, 806.

J

Pope John XI is thrust into prison by Wido, margrave of Tuscany, at the instigation of his wife Marozia; there he is believed to have been suffocated, 852.

John XII asks Emperor Otto to free the Roman Church from the tyranny of King Berengarius and Adelbert, 897. But after defecting from Otto, he favors Adelbert, ibid. His sacrileges and fornications, 898. His fraudulent messages to the emperor, ibid. His obstinacy, 899. The crimes charged against him by the Romans, 903, 904. He is summoned to come and clear himself, 904. He answers the charges, 905. He excommunicates those who are to deliberate about electing a new pope, 906. He is deposed by the council, 907. He attempts to incite the Romans with money to murder the emperor and Leo, the elected pope, 908. Restored to Rome with the aid of harlots, he rages against those obedient to Leo, ibid. He is killed by the devil, 909.

Another John, son of Marozia by the antipope Sergius, becomes pope, 852.

John, a presbyter of Ravenna, wickedly occupies the Roman see, 828.

The quip of Julian the Apostate against Christians, 859.

L

Lambert becomes margrave of Tuscany after the death of his brother Wido, 854. He challenges King Hugh to a duel to prove that he is Hugh’s brother; Hugh blinds him, ibid.

How the Holy Lance came to Emperor Otto, 863. Its description, ibid. His father Henry obtained it from Rodulf, king of Burgundy, 864.

Landulf, prince of Benevento, gives Pope John good advice, 830.

Lanthbert, son of Wido, becomes king of Italy, 807. But he was hated by his own men; he punishes Count Maginfred, ibid. He defeats and routs Adelbert’s forces, 808. His death is reported in different ways, ibid. Lamentation for his death, 809, 810.

Lanthbert, archbishop of Milan, cleverly admits Burchard into the city and treats him kindly, 842.

Emperor Leo Porphyrogenitus ruled the empire of Constantinople peacefully, 792. He tests the loyalty of his guards, 793. He also cleverly tests the vigilance of his personal bodyguards and rewards the diligence of one guard, 797. His successor was his young son Constantine, for whom he appointed various guardians, 845, 846.

Leo, chief secretary of the Roman Church, is elected pope after John is removed, 907. Through the counsel of harlots he is expelled and John is received again, 908.

“Leo and the cub will together destroy the wild ass”—an ancient writing; whether it should be understood of the king of the Franks and the Roman emperor, or of the emperor of Constantinople, 925.

Why Book III of Luitprand’s *History* is called *Antapodosis*, 837.

What books the Greeks call Daniel’s Visions, 924.

The remarkable Greek practice of carrying wood on the forehead, 897.

Liutprand writes the third book of his *History* in exile, 837. Where he began and finished it, ibid. His father is sent by King Hugh with gifts to the emperor at Constantinople, 844, 883. He writes in Book IV what he saw; he was dear to King Hugh, 857. He becomes secretary to King Berengarius, 891. At his stepfather’s expense he is sent by Berengarius as ambassador to Constantinople, 894. His journey is narrated, ibid. He is presented to the emperor Nicephorus Phocas of Constantinople, 895. What gifts he gave him, though at his own expense, and whether he presented them in the name of Berengarius, who sent him, 896. He writes the history of this embassy and of his entire journey, 909. In what house he was received there, ibid. What guardian he had, ibid. What he answered when taken for a spy, 910. He defends the deeds and name of Emperor Otto, ibid. and following pages, 920, 922. How indecently he was received at a banquet, 925. He defends the Westerners against the Greeks, ibid. and following pages, 928, 929. How disgracefully the Greeks treated him and his companions, 927, 928, 930. He wishes to be dismissed after receiving the answer concerning the matter for which he had been sent, 916. His discussion with the Greeks, who were making unjust demands, ibid. He is taken back to his house and kept under close guard, 917. Asked something different by the patriarch, he answers appropriately, 918. For three weeks he is visited by no Greek, 919. He falls ill, ibid. He wishes to be sent back to Italy, 923. He maintains his ancestral custom among the Greeks, 924. He is prevented from leaving Constantinople by a false lie, 927. He is forbidden to buy clothing, 929. He is released from Constantinople; but at his departure he writes certain verses on the wall of the house in which he had been detained [Col. 1340], to the contempt of the Greeks, 932. He suffers a storm, 933. He experienced all the Michaels as adversaries and unjust men, 936.

Lotharius, son of King Hugh, is associated with him in the kingdom of Italy, 857. He marries Adelheid, daughter of Rodulf, king of Burgundy, 864. He betrays his father’s plans to Berengarius, 881. He is king in name only, 891, 894.

Louis, son of Emperor Arnulf, is acclaimed emperor, 813. He hastens with his forces to meet the Hungarians, ibid. But he is defeated and destroyed by them, ibid. He dies, 819.

Louis of Burgundy, invited by the Italians, invades Italy, 823. But he soon withdraws, promising not to return there again, ibid. Breaking his promise, he invades it again, 824. Coming into Tuscany, he envies Adelbert’s power, ibid. While hiding at Verona he is betrayed and deprived of his eyes, 829.

M

Maginfred, count of Milan, defects from King Lanthbert and pays the penalty, 807. His son Hugh avenges his father’s death, 818.

The Magnaura, the palace of the emperor of Constantinople, is described, 895.

What Manasses signifies, 859.

Manasses, abandoning the bishopric of Arles, hastens to Italy to King Hugh in order to receive a larger one from him, 858. He defends himself by a bad example drawn from Saint Peter the Apostle, 859. After abandoning Hugh, he adheres to Berengarius, 889.

The harlot Marozia bore John by the antipope Sergius, and he afterward became pope, 828. After her husband Wido’s death, she invites Hugh, king of Italy, to seize Rome, arranging her marriage with him, 852. She has a son, Alberic, by Margrave Alberic, 853.

Matilda, wife of Emperor Henry, celebrated splendid funeral rites for the soul of her husband, 864.

The Moors invade Calabria and Apulia. Why they came from Africa into Italy, 826. They occupy Mount Garigliano, ibid. Defeated at various times, they retain only this place, abandoning the other cities, 828. They plunder Genoa and slaughter the citizens, ibid. See *Arabians; Saracens*, 859.

The Milanese rebel against King Berengarius, 830.

The emperor Michael, having lost his mind, condemns his attendants to death, 793. He is killed by Basil the Macedonian, 794.

Liutprand encountered various adversaries named Michael at Constantinople, 936.

Milo, a vigorous soldier, avenges the death of King Berengarius, forcing the murderers to end their lives by hanging, 835. After King Hugh’s abandonment, he adheres to Berengarius, margrave of Ivrea, 892.

Count Milo calls Arnold, duke of Bavaria, into Italy; but after defecting from him, he adheres to King Hugh, 856.

The Mole of Saint Angelo, or of Hadrian, is the fortification of the city of Rome, 853.

The dreadful death of King Arnulf, 806.

A certain woman, through a festive jest, prevented her husband from being castrated, 861 ff.

The emperor of Constantinople distributes gifts to his officials and retainers before Palm Sunday, 897.

N

How Nicephorus Phocas received Luitprand, who had been sent to him, 909 ff. His appearance, bearing, and conduct, 910, 914, 920, 925. His insolent self-boasting and humiliation of Westerners, 915, 921, 923. His dealings with Liutprand the ambassador and his various replies, 921. Why he led an army against the Assyrians, 924, 926.

The Normans are Russians, 795, 883. Their defeat by Greek fire at sea, ibid.

O

What the wild asses of Constantinople are like, 924.

Otto becomes emperor after his father Henry’s death, 864. His wife was the daughter of the king of England, 865. He finds his brother Henry opposed to him, ibid. His victory over him and his accomplices, 868. He values the Lance of the Lord, 869. His victory over the rebels was granted by God, 869. His noble reply to his soldiers advising flight, 872. He refused to grant abbey revenues to secular persons, 873. Through his dukes he crushes his adversaries Everhard and Gilbert, 874. On hearing of their deaths, he goes to a church to give thanks to God, 875. He offers Berthold, duke of Bavaria, marriage with his sister or daughter, ibid. He orders his brother Henry to rise as a suppliant and has him kept under close guard, 875. He joins his son Liutholf in marriage to the daughter of the duke of Swabia, 876. Though gold is offered, he refuses to surrender Margrave Berengarius of Ivrea, whom he had received kindly, 882. Coming into Italy, he drives out the tyrants Berengarius and Adelbert, 898, 899. He receives an anointing of the empire from Pope John, ibid. His reply to the Romans’ complaints about Pope John, 899. He besieges Mount Feretratus, with Berengarius and Willa inside it, ibid. [Col. 1341] Having received from the pope messages promising improvement, he does not believe them, 900. He returns to Rome, ibid. He proceeds moderately against Pope John, 901, 902. In the name of the Roman council he summons John to clear himself of the charges, 905, 906. He complains of John’s treachery, 907. He strikes down the rebellious Romans, 908. After returning from Rome, he goes back there again and forces the Romans, oppressed by hunger, to receive Leo, the elected pope, 909. Liutprand defends Leo and his deeds before Nicephorus Phocas, emperor of Constantinople, 913. He asks for the daughter of the Roman emperor as wife for his son Otto, 913. Otto the Younger becomes king of the Romans, 898.

P

The magnificence of the palace of Constantinople, 885.

The city of Pavia burns, 838. And when this happened, 939. Besieged by the Hungarians, it was not destroyed, owing to the merits of Blessed Syrus, its patron, ibid. His prophecy concerning it was fulfilled, ibid.

The Fates distribute the destinies of human life, 796.

Luitprand’s father is sent by King Hugh as ambassador to the emperor at Constantinople; on returning from there, he enters a monastery, in which he dies shortly afterward, 843.

Phocas the chamberlain, hearing that Romanus had been raised to imperial power, voluntarily yielded victory to the Bulgarians and fled amid great slaughter of his men; therefore Romanus captures him and deprives him of his eyes, 846.

A painting of the victory of Henry the Saxon emperor over the Hungarians is seen at Merseburg, 822.

Huge apples seen by Liutprand at Constantinople, 885.

The Porphyra, a house at Constantinople in which those born were called Porphyrogeniti, 793, 846.

Liutprand’s departure for Constantinople, 894.

R

Raimund, prince of Aquitaine, promises to restore King Hugh, an exile from Italy, to the kingdom, but in vain, 891. He marries Hugh’s niece Bertha, ibid.

Ratherius becomes bishop of Verona because of his learning, 852. He is captured and sent off to Pavia by King Hugh, 856.

The see of Ravenna is the first in Italy after Rome, 827.

Rodulf, king of Burgundy, is summoned to the kingdom of Italy, 831, 832. He reigns there, 833. He returns to Italy from Burgundy, where he had gone, 840. He besieges Pavia, but after being cleverly deceived by Ermengarda, wife of Margrave Adelbert, he secretly enters the city to reach her; thus the siege is lifted, 841. Returning again to Burgundy, he comes back to Italy with Burchard, duke of Swabia and his father-in-law, ibid. On hearing of the death of his father-in-law, he returns once more to Burgundy, 842.

Rome is captured by King Arnulf, 803. The terror of the Romans besieged by Arnulf, 803. Their complaints against Pope John, 899, 903, 904. Corrupted by the gold of Pope John, they conspire against Emperor Otto, 908. But Otto strikes and routs them, ibid. And again, 908.

Romanus, emperor of Constantinople, seeks the aid of the Africans against the rebellious Calabrians and Apulians, 826. He attains imperial power through various deeds, 844. He kills Leo with a sword, ibid. His crafty threats, 846. He becomes emperor, ibid. He joins his daughter in marriage to Constantine Porphyrogenitus, 847. Why he called the church he built “New” or “Nine-Year,” ibid. and following pages. He gives a speech to the princes of Constantinople, 848. His humble origin, ibid. He preferred his son Christopher to Constantine, the emperor’s son; but Christopher dies not long afterward, 851. He is driven from the throne by his sons Stephen and Constantine and confined in a monastery, 886. From the monastery he insults his sons and gives thanks to God that they are paying the penalty for their impiety, 888. His pious saying, 889.

The Roman Church is the head of the Church of Constantinople, 934.

The Russians are the same as the Normans, 883.

S

The Saracen commander Sagitus is defeated with his men, 859.

Count Samson gives King Hugh salutary advice, 851.

Events show how greatly the saints are cared for by God, 871.

The blood of the slain King Berengarius is displayed on a certain stone [Col. 1342] before the door of a church, 834.

The portent of blood flowing from a spring foretold a future defeat, 859.

The Saracens seize the town of Fraxinetum, 792. They fortify Mount Maurus, ibid. They summon allies from Spain, ibid. They harass various towns of Italy, 826. They ravage the region around Fraxinetum, 881. Their ships are burned by Greek fire, 884. King Hugh makes peace with them, and with what intention, ibid.

Sarlio is sent by King Hugh to Camerino and Spoleto to turn the citizens’ minds away from Anscarius, 878. He leads six battle lines against Anscarius, 879. After Anscarius is killed in this battle, Sarlio becomes margrave of Camerino, ibid.

The Ticinian revolt and slaughter in the time of King Arnulf, 806.

The deacon Sergius becomes antipope against Formosus, the true pontiff, 803. After Formosus’s death, Sergius becomes pope by force, 804. His savagery toward the deceased Formosus, ibid.

Simeon, formerly a monk, becomes king of the Bulgarians. He fathers two sons, 846. One son marries the granddaughter of the Roman emperor of Constantinople, 847.

The marvelous throne of the emperor of Constantinople, 895.

Stephen and Constantine, sons of Romanus, the Roman emperor of Constantinople, undertake a new conspiracy against their father and depose him from the empire, 885. But when they attempt to expel Constantine, their brother-in-law, Constantine captures them, 886. They are thrust into a monastery near their father, 887.

A synod is convened at Rome in the presence of Emperor Otto, and which bishops attended it, 903. What was done in it against Pope John, 904.

The relics of Saint Syrus rest at Pavia, 838. His prophecy concerning Pavia, and likewise concerning the fall of Aquileia, ibid.

T
## T

Theobald, margrave of Camerino, defeats the Greeks near Benevento and castrates those captured, 861. His death, 878. Theodora the prostitute’s uncontrolled domination at Rome, 827. He caused John, bishop of Bologna, to become bishop of Ravenna, 828.

## V

Description of Verona; the river Athesis flows through it, 825.

## W

The wickedness of Waldon, bishop of Capua, 890. Walpert, judge of Pavia, was extraordinarily powerful, and how this came about, 850. He is ordered by King Hugh to be executed by beheading, 852. Walpert, bishop of Milan, meets the emperor Otto, 899. Wibert gives good advice to Anscarius when the latter seeks war from King Hugh, 880. He is wounded in the battle against Sarlius, 881. He dies, ibid. Guido, bishop of Modena, having abandoned King Hugh, supports Berengar’s party, 891. Guido, margrave of Tuscany, marries Marozia, the Roman prostitute, 842. They hand Pope John over to custody through soldiers, 852. Guido dies, ibid. King Guido, also called Hugh, and Berengar enter into an alliance with one another, and what its terms were, 800. He is anointed king of France at Rome, but the Franks reject him, 800. Why, ibid. He wages war against Berengar contrary to the treaty, ibid. He drives him into flight, 801. But soon afterward he is himself put to flight by Berengar, supported by the forces of King Arnulf, 801. The stratagems of his wife, besieged by Arnulf at Firmum, 805. Guido himself dies at the river Taro, 806. Willa, his wife, and another daughter of Boso, margrave of Tuscany, 861. The former incites her husband to revolutionary undertakings, 863. Her greed: after her husband is captured by King Hugh, she hides his precious belt, ibid. She is expelled into Burgundy, 864. Willa, the niece of King Hugh, marries Berengar, margrave of Ivrea, 861, 863. Nevertheless, while pregnant, she reaches Germany through trackless mountains, 881. She is accused of incest, 892. Her cunning is detected, ibid.

## Z

Zwendebald is stripped of his dominion by King Arnulf through the Hungarians, 799.

# TABLE OF CONTENTS OF THIS VOLUME

## RATHERIUS, BISHOP OF VERONA

### Prolegomena

9. Dedicatory letter.

9. Preface to the edition of Ratherius’s works.

11. § I. On the author’s renown and on the usefulness and excellence of his works.

14. § II. On Ratherius’s works previously published and on the editions in which they are found scattered. On the unpublished works to be added in this edition. On the works still missing, as well as on other works attributed to Ratherius.

25. § III. What has been accomplished in this collection and edition.

## LIFE OF RATHERIUS

27. § I. His homeland and nobility. His year of birth is conjectured.

28. § II. He embraces the monastic life. On his studies. He writes a letter to Patricus. The opinion of some that the abbacy of Saint Amand, offered to Ratherius before his episcopate, is eliminated.

30. § III. Ratherius followed the party of Hilduin, bishop of Liège; after Hilduin was expelled from the see of Liège, Ratherius subsequently adhered to the bishop of Verona. He replies to questions that certain Milanese had proposed to Hilduin. Having been elected to the see of Milan, Hilduin travels to Rome; returning from there, Ratherius succeeds the bishop of Verona in that see. The year of Hilduin’s election and of Ratherius’s consecration is established.

34. § IV. How disastrous the beginnings of Ratherius’s episcopate were. Supporting Count Milo, he received Arnold, duke of Bavaria, into Verona against King Hugh. Captured by Hugh’s soldiers, he is thrown into the prison at Pavia.

39. § V. How much he suffered in the Pavia prison. He writes to Urso, a cleric of the Church of Verona. After the bishop was taken away, several infants died at Verona without baptism. During the leisure of his imprisonment he writes six books of the *Praeloquia*.

45. § VI. After the prison at Pavia, Como. He corrects and rewrites in a clearer style the life of Saint Ursmar, which he found there. Released from his exile at Como, he travels to Gaul. He writes to Rotbert, archbishop of Trier. In Provence he instructs Roestang in letters and writes a book on the art of grammar. He refuses the episcopate there and returns to Laubias, to his monastery.

48. § VII. Ratherius returns to Italy to confront King Hugh. He is captured by Berengar. Count Milo recalls him to the episcopate of Verona. King Hugh abandoned Italy in the year 947, not in 946; but he died in the province in the year 948, not in 947.

51. § VIII. How many hardships Ratherius suffered from the clergy after his restoration to his see, with Count Milo acting as their patron. What it means to hold a synod, to attend the chapter of the clergy, and to perform ecclesiastical orders. Manasses, archbishop of Arles, ordains one of the bishops of his own diocese to the title of the Church of Verona. After two years Ratherius is again expelled from the see of Verona, so that he may yield his place to Manasses.

53. § IX. Ratherius travels to Germany. He writes to Bruno, the brother of Otto I, concerning the beginning of Otto’s reign in Italy. Several chronological annotations of documents are corrected. Ratherius with Otto and his son Liutulf, in the year 951. He returns to Italy in the hope of recovering his episcopate. He finds the nephew of Count Milo established as bishop, to whom Manasses had sold the episcopate. He appeals to the supreme pontiff and to a synod of bishops. He writes three letters on this matter.

59. § X. Having returned to Germany, Ratherius is received among the household dependents by Bruno, the brother of King Otto. Through Bruno’s efforts he becomes bishop of Liège. The solemn rites of this promotion. He is subsequently expelled even from the see of Liège. For this reason he writes two short works. Which of his episcopal revenues were assigned to him for his support.

64. § XI. After his expulsion from the see of Liège, Ratherius is placed in charge of a monastery. Which monastery it was. He writes a book of confession. To what extent, while living there [Col. 1344] with the monks, he did not return to the monastic way of life, and why. He entitles a letter written under Agapetus II and suppressed, “To John XII.”

75. § XII. King Otto, leaving the Italian kingdom to Berengar, retained the march of Verona for himself. This march and its dukes are discussed at greater length, as is the march of Friuli; many matters previously obscure are explained, including several testimonies of Ratherius that mention dukes and a duchess. Some additions are made concerning the march of Treviso.

79. § XIII. Ratherius returns to Italy with Otto I in the year 961. A difficult passage in Fulcuin is examined. Through Otto’s action he is restored to the see of Verona. The decree of the supreme pontiff and of the council of Pavia is added. The proceedings of the synod of Pavia and its date. Peter, bishop of Ravenna, having been expelled from his see, obtains at the same synod a decree favorable to him, just as Ratherius did. Otto’s edict on behalf of Ratherius. The theft of the body of Saint Metronis and of Ratherius; a short work on the same matter, rewritten in the year 962. The emperor urges the bishop to send soldiers for the siege of Garda.

88. § XIV. Two decrees of Ratherius from the year 963 concerning clerics ordained by the usurper Milo. On the same matter he writes, in the name of his clergy, a short book to the Roman Church. Sermons of the same year, and a short work on his own lapse. During Lent in the year 964 he refutes the heresy of the Anthropomorphites, which had revived in these regions, in an extensive sermon; in it he also touches upon the error of certain people concerning Saint Michael. An apology for the same sermon, in which several passages that had been misunderstood are explained.

97. § XV. Ratherius’s book *On Contempt for the Canons*. The reasons for writing it. The vices and abuses that were rampant among the clergy. On the unlawful marriages of clerics. On the inequitable distribution of ecclesiastical revenues and the evils arising from it. Ratherius’s effort to establish a more equitable distribution and to vindicate the authority of bishops asserted by the canons. How greatly the clerics opposed him, and why.

102. § XVI. At the beginning of the year 965 Ratherius is captured through the agency of the usurper Milo. He is restored shortly afterward through the intervention of Duchess Judith. Judgment and settlement against the rebels. How great a danger he still faced, and with what care he protected himself. Pressed to grant the episcopate to Milo, he refuses. Two letters written to Milo during the Christmas season. He reproduces, with an addition, the conclusion of the deliberative argument. A very obscure passage concerning *sikerus* is explained.

107. § XVII. The acts of Ratherius in the year 966. He writes the *Conjecture of Qualitas*. At the abbey of Maguzano, after the badly behaved abbot had been removed, he installs clerics. During Lent he celebrates a synod and issues a synodical letter. His short work *On an Unlawful Marriage*. He plans a journey to Rome, and why. He publishes an itinerary.

113. § XVIII. The events of the year 967. On the Roman and Ravenna councils. A decree against the licentiousness of clerics. Having returned from the council of Ravenna to Verona, Ratherius convenes a diocesan synod. The proceedings of this synod. He makes provision for poorer clerics through a judgment signed by the patriarch of Aquileia and the neighboring bishops assembled in synod. The emperor’s privilege granted to Ratherius. The tumult of the Veronese clergy, and Ratherius’s short work on rebellious clerics. His letter to Martin, bishop of Ferrara.

120. § XIX. The events of the year 968. During Lent Ratherius delivers sermons on peace. He writes a short book entitled *Discord*. The canons send a messenger to Rome, who brings back a rescript in their favor. The bishop publishes an *Apology*. An investigation against him. Other sermons of Ratherius. His testament. Nanno, sent as the emperor’s representative, holds a hearing against him; Ratherius complains about this hearing in three letters. Everaclus, bishop of Liège, invites him. At last he resigns the episcopate and returns to Belgium.

129. § XX. Received by Everaclus, bishop of Liège, and Fulcuin, abbot of Lobbes, he is placed in charge of several small abbeys. He is cleared of the purchase of the abbacy of Saint Amand by simony. A passage of the *Praeloquia* in which the true facts concerning this abbey are set forth is transferred here. He is placed over the abbey of Lobbes by Everaclus. After Fulcuin is removed, he is restored by Notker, the successor of Everaclus. Ratherius’s death and the year of his death.

## APPENDIX

937. An inquiry by Don Antonio of Seville concerning the following books falsely fabricated under Liutprand’s name.

937. CHAPTER ONE.—That Liutprand, a deacon of the Church of Pavia and bishop of Cremona, an Italian, was made subdeacon of the Church of Toledo at great expense by Higuera, and was a writer of our affairs. Certain details of his life are demonstrated by comparison with the contents of the *Chronicle* and *Adversaria* falsely fabricated in his name. These matters are treated at length in the following chapters.

943. CHAPTER II.—The two preliminary letters to the *Chronicle of Pseudo-Liutprand* are attacked in two ways: both on account of the errors, contrivances, and improbabilities contained in them. Of the first kind are, in the earlier letter from Tractemund to Liutprand, the name Tractemund—although the person to whom the letter is said to be addressed is the bishop of Eliberis—in place of Regimund; the title *Antapodosis* for a certain book of Liutprand in place of *Antidosis*; and the false distinction between this work and history. On this occasion a difficult passage in this history of Liutprand is explained. There is an error concerning the time of Pope Hadrian I. The supposed mention of Saint James of Picenum. Several contrivances are noted as indications of novelty. Among the absurdities is the request that a continuation of the history of Spanish affairs should be sought from a foreigner living far away. Higuera does not mention the first of these letters in his *History of Toledo*; he does mention Liutprand’s later letter to Tractemund. This published letter is compared with one that we have read, unpublished, in the same *History of Toledo* and in one of our manuscripts; from the variation we infer the fraud. Like the first, this later reply of Liutprand is rife with defects. The false attribution of the matter to the care of Servideus of Toledo and of Heronius, bishops of Braga, is especially conspicuous because it places them outside their proper time. The letter is burdened with other absurdities and contrivances.

951. CHAPTER III.—The *Chronicle* itself, as it appears in one of our manuscript fragments, is compared with the published and commonly circulated version: it is only twenty-three years long. From this comparison the additions and interpolations subsequently made are proved false, and the passages that have been removed or altered are noted. When writing his *History of Toledo*, Higuera used our fragment, not the complete published *Chronicle*.

954. CHAPTER IV.—In certain characteristic passages the spirit and purpose of the Pseudo-Liutprand of the *Chronicle* are revealed. First, through an abuse of identical names, whether of persons or places, he assigns foreign people and councils to Spain. Examples are found in Saints Magnus, Columbanus, and Gallus; in Saint Fara, a nun of Gaul; and in the Council of Augsburg. Sometimes this occurs even without the pretext of an ambiguous name. Examples are found in the bishops Veranus and Osianus, and in Adeodata, the virgin known from the letters of Pope Gregory.

959. CHAPTER V.—Liutprand passes off as our own those whose reputation for sanctity arose elsewhere. The first example is Saint Babylas the martyr. The codices of Higuera and Juan Tamayo are highly suspect. The second is Raymond, pastor of Medellín, who truly was the founder of the Order of Calatrava and a Cistercian monk. The third is Anacirardus, a monk of Agaunum. The fourth is Cornelius Proculus and Cornelius Bassus, who are known only from inscribed stones. The fifth is Genesius, martyr of Arles, to whom all the churches of this name among us appear to be dedicated—not to some nonexistent Spaniard.
